pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 10–11 — round decimals to any place using place-value understanding; round any whole number to a required degree of accuracy.
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y6 'round any whole number to a required degree of accuracy'; Y5 round decimals with two places to the nearest whole number and to one decimal place.
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): 5.NBT.A.4 'Use place value understanding to round decimals to any place' and 4.NBT.A.3 round multi-digit whole numbers to any place.
• Operational details: Round via NEARNESS on a number line — locate the number between the two candidate rounding points, find the midpoint, and decide which it is nearer. Derive the 'look at the next digit' rule FROM the midpoint (5-and-above is at/past halfway) rather than teaching it as an unexplained rule. Cover rounding both decimals (to dp) and large whole numbers (to nearest 10^k), and rounding for estimation (4.83×2.17 ≈ 5×2).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): 'Round 3.46 to 1 dp.' Tier B: 'Round 7,654,321 to the nearest 100,000 and justify with the midpoint.' Tier C: 'Round 3.4567 to 2 dp and explain which digit decides it.'
bestPractices: Round as a nearness decision on a number line: mark the two candidate values, mark the midpoint, place the number, decide which it is closer to
Derive the next-digit rule from the midpoint (≥5 means at or past halfway → round up), rather than asserting it
Practise rounding decimals to a stated dp AND whole numbers to a stated place with the same nearness logic
Address the boundary/round-up cascade explicitly (rounding 3.798 to 2 dp → 3.80, and 9.96 → 10.0)
Connect rounding to estimation — round each factor to check a calculation — so rounding has a purpose beyond the drill
keyRepresentations: Number line with the two rounding candidates and a marked midpoint
Place-value chart to isolate the rounding place and the deciding next digit
'Rounding hill/valley' visual (nearer candidate is downhill) for the midpoint decision
Estimation strips pairing rounded factors with the exact calculation
commonMisconceptions: Rounding digit-by-digit / double rounding (3.4567 → 3.457 → 3.46 → 3.5) instead of one decision at the target place
'Always round 5 down' or inconsistent treatment of the exact-midpoint case
Truncating (chopping) rather than rounding (3.48 → 3.4 to 1 dp)
Forgetting the round-up cascade across a 9 (3.798 to 2 dp → 3.80, not 3.79 or 3.710)
Dropping the trailing zero that records the rounded place (writing 3.8 for 3.80 to 2 dp when the place must be shown)

learn.summary: For ages 10–11: round decimals to any place and whole numbers to a required degree of accuracy by treating rounding as a nearness decision on a number line. Learners locate the number between its two candidate rounding points, find the midpoint, and decide which it is nearer — deriving the 'look at the next digit' rule from the midpoint rather than memorising it. Work covers decimals to a stated number of places, large whole numbers to a stated place, carry/round-up cascades over a 9, placeholder zeros, the risk of double rounding, and rounding for estimation.

activities.title: Rounding as a nearness decision on a number line
feedback: If the learner chops instead of rounding (e.g. 3.4567 to 2 dp written as 3.45), have them look at the digit just past the cut: 6 ≥ 5 means 3.4567 is past the midpoint 3.455 and so is nearer 3.46. Place it between 3.45 and 3.46 to see which is closer. (To 1 dp, chopping would give 3.4, but the correct answer is 3.5.)

If they round digit-by-digit (double rounding), use 3.4547 to 2 dp to show why it fails: rounding to 3 dp first gives 3.455, which then rounds up to 3.46, but a single decision at the hundredths place (decider thousandths 4 < 5) gives 3.45. Double rounding changed the answer — compare the full number to the single midpoint for the target place.
When a carry crosses a 9 (3.798 → 3.80), confirm the trailing zero stays because '2 decimal places' means two digits after the point.
If they are unsure about the exact-midpoint case, reinforce that at the midpoint and beyond the number rounds up to the higher candidate.
activities.rationale: Deriving the next-digit rule from the midpoint gives the procedure a reason, directly targeting double-rounding and 'always round 5 down' errors; the 3.4547 contrast makes the double-rounding hazard observable because the two routes disagree. An interactive number line that auto-brackets candidates, marks the midpoint, lets the learner place the number, lights the nearer segment, and highlights the deciding digit can make the nearness judgement concrete; these interaction examples are optional ways to realise the mechanism, not requirements.
learnerActions: Pick a target precision (e.g. 1 decimal place) and draw a number line showing the two candidate values the number sits between — for 3.4567 to 1 dp, that is 3.4 and 3.5.
Mark the midpoint of the segment (3.45) clearly.
Place the number on the line (3.4567 lands just past the midpoint) and state which candidate it is nearer to.
State the rounded result (3.5) and point to the digit that decided it (the hundredths digit, 5, sits at/past halfway).
Repeat in whole-number mode: bracket 7,654,321 between 7,600,000 and 7,700,000, mark the midpoint 7,650,000, place the number, and round to the nearest 100,000 (7,700,000).
Try a round-up cascade: place 3.798 to round to 2 dp between 3.79 and 3.80, see it is nearer 3.80, and write the trailing zero.

Compare two routes for rounding 3.4547 to 2 dp: round straight to 2 dp (decider is the thousandths 4, so 3.45) and also round to 3 dp first (3.455) then to 2 dp (3.46). Notice the answers differ — so make one decision at the target place, not a chain of roundings.
activities.intendedInsight: The midpoint IS the '5-and-above' rule: a number at or past halfway rounds up to the higher candidate. Rounding is one decision made at the target place by comparing nearness, not a digit-by-digit chop — and chopping or double rounding can give a different, wrong answer.

activities.title: Isolating the deciding digit with a place-value chart
feedback: If the learner gives 3.5 when 2 dp is asked, have them count decimal digits: 2 dp needs two, so the answer is 3.46.
If the wrong place is read for a large number, re-anchor on the chart: find the hundred-thousands column, then look one column to its right (the ten-thousands digit decides).
Keep the focus on the single decider digit, not on re-rounding digits further along.
activities.rationale: A place-value chart separates the target place from its decider, addressing wrong-precision errors and misreading places in large numbers. A static chart illustrates a case clearly; it is a scaffold that does not by itself let learners test arbitrary numbers or feel the boundary cascade.
sourceClaims: 5.NBT.A.4: use place value understanding to round decimals to any place; 4.NBT.A.3 round multi-digit whole numbers to any place.
learnerActions: Write the number in a place-value chart spanning the decimal point.
Circle the place you must round to and underline the single digit immediately beyond it — the decider.
Round 3.4567 to 2 dp (3.46) and say which digit decided it (the 6 in the thousandths).
Round 7,654,321 to the nearest 100,000 (7,700,000) and name the deciding digit (the ten-thousands digit, 5).
Count the digits after the point aloud to confirm you gave the asked-for precision (e.g. 2 dp means exactly two decimal digits).
activities.intendedInsight: Only the digit one place beyond the required accuracy decides the rounding; naming the target place prevents rounding to the wrong precision.

activities.title: Keeping placeholder zeros after a carry
feedback: If the learner writes 2.4 for 2.397 to 2 dp, point out it now shows only one decimal place; the correct answer is 2.40.
Distinguish this from a rounding mistake — the rounding was right, only the recorded precision is missing the zero.
For 9.96 → 10.0, confirm the whole-number carry still leaves a tenths place that must read 0.
activities.rationale: Carries that produce placeholder zeros are a distinct performance slip from the rounding decision itself, so they need their own targeted practice.
learnerActions: Round 2.397 to 2 dp. The hundredths carry gives 2.40 — write the final 0.
Explain why 2.4 would be wrong for '2 decimal places' even though the value looks the same.
Round 9.96 to 1 dp (10.0) and keep the tenths zero.
Check each answer by counting that it shows exactly the required number of decimal places.
activities.intendedInsight: A rounded answer must display the required place even when a carry produces a zero there; the trailing zero records the precision, so dropping it changes what the answer claims.

activities.title: Rounding to estimate a calculation
feedback: If the estimate is far from the exact answer, check whether each factor was rounded to a sensible place.
Encourage stating the chosen rounding place so the estimate's accuracy can be judged.
activities.rationale: Connecting rounding to estimation gives the skill a real use and reinforces the nearness idea across operations.
learnerActions: Round each factor of 4.83 × 2.17 to a convenient value (5 × 2) and compute the estimate (10).
Compare your estimate to the exact product once calculated (≈ 10.48) and say whether the estimate is reasonable.
Try estimating another product or sum by rounding each number first, and state which place you rounded to and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding has a purpose beyond drill: it gives quick, sensible estimates to check whether an exact calculation is plausible.

constraints: Multiple-choice, slider, and fill-in response formats can consolidate and check rounding outcomes (e.g. a truncation distractor of 3.4 for 3.48), but recognising a correct rounded value does not by itself show the learner is reasoning from the midpoint; pair outcome checks with working that reveals the method.
A static annotated number line illustrates a single rounding case but does not let the learner test arbitrary numbers or experience a boundary cascade; use it as a scaffold, not the whole lesson.

Dialogue prompts (e.g. 'you rounded 3.4567 to 3.46 — walk me through why, not digit by digit') can surface double-rounding and truncation errors; the nearness decision can also be made where the number is placed and compared spatially.
Round in one decision at the target place; do not round digit-by-digit (double rounding) and do not truncate.
Treat the exact midpoint and above as rounding up to the higher candidate; avoid 'always round 5 down'.
Preserve trailing/placeholder zeros that record the required place (2.40, not 2.4; 10.0, not 10).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source marks the Common Core claim as verified:false and the DfE claim as verified:true; confidence of the original row was 'high'. No new verification has been performed here.

Self-audit: 3.4567 to 2 dp = 3.46 (decider 6 ≥ 5); to 1 dp = 3.5 (candidates 3.4/3.5, midpoint 3.45). 3.4547 to 2 dp = 3.45 directly, but 3.455 then 3.46 by double rounding (illustrates the hazard). 2.397 to 2 dp = 2.40 (carry keeps placeholder zero). 7,654,321 to nearest 100,000: midpoint 7,650,000, value above it, rounds to 7,700,000 (decider ten-thousands digit 5). 3.798 to 2 dp = 3.80. 9.96 to 1 dp = 10.0. 4.83×2.17 ≈ 5×2 = 10 (exact ≈ 10.48). All consistent and checked.

The original row and recommendation wrote the 1-dp candidates as '3.40 and 3.50', displaying two decimal places for a one-decimal-place rounding; corrected in the learner action to '3.4 and 3.5' (midpoint 3.45) to avoid reinforcing a precision confusion.

Activity 1's sourceClaims were set to [] because its rationale is a number-line/midpoint-derivation teaching principle that neither curriculum claim directly supports (the claims establish the topic/standard, not that pedagogy). The place-value-chart activity retains the CCSS 'use place value understanding' claim, which does support its principle.
The original diagnostic listed '2.40 (keeping the final zero)' for rounding 2.397 to 2 dp, which is correct; retained as the placeholder-zero teaching point.
The non-preferred 3D option was dropped because the source itself only noted it adds nothing for a one-dimensional number-line task; no universal claim about 3D is asserted.

probeDeeper: Round 2.397 to 2 dp — why must you keep the 0 on the end?
Round 3.4547 to 3 dp first, then to 2 dp. Now round 3.4547 straight to 2 dp — same answer? (double-rounding)
Round 7,654,321 to the nearest 100,000 — which digit decides?
assess.correctAnswer: 3.46; 2.40 (keeping the final zero); 7,700,000 — deciding by the digit one place beyond the required accuracy.

errorPatterns.pattern: Truncates instead of rounding: chops 3.4567 to 3.45 rather than 3.46
errorPatterns.nextMove: Look at the digit just past the cut (6 ≥ 5 → round up). Place 3.4567 between 3.45 and 3.46 on a number line to see which is nearer.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The kept digits are correct but never rounded up when the next digit is 5 or more.

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops the placeholder zero after a carry: writes 2.4 for 2.397 to 2 dp, so it no longer shows 2 decimal places
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach rounding — note that '2 dp' means two digits after the point, so the carried result is 2.40; the 0 must stay.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer to 2 dp has only one decimal digit.

errorPatterns.pattern: Rounds to the wrong precision — gives 1 dp when 2 dp is asked, or reads the wrong place for large numbers
errorPatterns.nextMove: Mark the required place, then its decider digit; count decimal places explicitly. Reground with a place-value chart spanning the decimal point.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 3.4567 comes back as 3.5, or the whole number is rounded to the wrong place.

responseLevels.gap: Truncates instead of rounding, or rounds to the wrong precision.
responseLevels.full: Rounds decimals to any number of places and whole numbers to any place, handling carries and placeholder zeros, and avoids double-rounding.
responseLevels.partial: Rounds simple cases but drops carried placeholder zeros or slips on the required number of places.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set the task and watch the working: 'Round 3.4567 to 2 decimal places. Round 2.397 to 2 decimal places. Round 7,654,321 to the nearest 100,000.' Watch whether they round or chop, and what they do at the carry.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 3.4567 distinguishes rounding from truncating (3.46 vs 3.45); 2.397 forces a carry that produces a placeholder zero the child must keep to show 2 dp (2.40, not 2.4); the whole-number item checks the same rule transfers to large places. Watching reveals which mechanism is running.

sources.claim: Y6 pupils round any whole number to a required degree of accuracy; Y5 round decimals to the nearest whole and to one decimal place.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (KS1–2)

sources.claim: 5.NBT.A.4: use place value understanding to round decimals to any place; 4.NBT.A.3 round multi-digit whole numbers to any place.
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Number & Operations in Base Ten Grades 4–5

pedagogy.summary: At 8-9, using structure becomes a deliberate calculating tool: breaking 7×13 into 7×10 + 7×3 with the distributive property, using place value to explain why ×10 shifts every digit one place left (not 'add a zero'), and using the quadrilateral hierarchy (a square is a special rectangle) to carry properties down from category to subcategory. The teaching aim is that the child looks for a known structure before grinding a procedure. The area model is the workhorse: it makes the distributive split visible as two sub-rectangles, and CCSS MP7 names exactly this partitioning as the heart of the practice.
bestPractices: Model 7×13 on a partitioned area rectangle (7×10 and 7×3) so the split is seen, then connect it to the numeric decomposition
Teach ×10 as a place-value shift using a place-value chart (digits move one column left; a zero fills the emptied ones place) rather than the 'add a zero' rule, which breaks for decimals
Use overlapping property sets / a shape family tree so squares sit inside rectangles inside parallelograms, and reason 'a square must have… because it is a rectangle'
Prompt 'is there a number fact or shape fact you already know that this is like?' before any standard algorithm
keyRepresentations: Partitioned area model / grid for the distributive split
Place-value chart showing digits shifting left on ×10/×100
Shape hierarchy diagram (quadrilateral → parallelogram → rectangle → square)
Arrays and factor trees linking multiplication structure
commonMisconceptions: Uses 'multiplying by 10 adds a zero', which fails for decimals (2.5×10 read as 2.50)
Splits distributively but forgets to multiply the second part (7×13 = 7×10 + 3)
Refuses that a square is a rectangle because the names/looks differ, so properties don't transfer down the hierarchy
Treats each multiplication as needing the column algorithm, not looking for a decomposition that makes it easy

learn.summary: For ages 8-9, this topic develops the habit of looking for known mathematical structure before grinding a procedure: splitting a multiplication like 7×13 into 7×10 + 7×3 (distributive property), explaining ×10 as a place-value shift (digits move one column left) rather than 'add a zero', and using the quadrilateral hierarchy (a square is a special rectangle) to inherit properties from category to subcategory. The partitioned area model is the central representation, making the distributive split visible as two sub-rectangles. Activities centre on learners partitioning, justifying and generalising the structural move, not just reaching a correct answer.

activities.title: Split the rectangle: 7×13 from two easy facts
feedback: If a learner writes 7×10 + 3 = 73, point back to the rectangle: the second part is also 7 tall, so it is 7×3 = 21, not 3. Have them shade the missing 7×3 block.
If a learner reaches 91 only by the column algorithm, ask them to show the two sub-rectangles and name the two easy facts, so the structure is made explicit.
When a learner tries a second valid split (e.g. 11 and 2) and still gets 91, confirm that any split works because the ×7 is shared over the parts — the choice is just about which parts are easiest.
activities.rationale: The area model makes the distributive partition literally visible as two sub-rectangles and ties the picture to the numeric decomposition. CCSS MP7 gives this kind of distributive split (e.g. 7 × 8 = 7 × 5 + 7 × 3) as one example of 'using structure', alongside other examples. An interactive version where the learner drags the divider and watches the parts recompute and slide together is one proposed way to make the mechanism operate under the learner's hand, and a drawn, cut or folded paper rectangle may serve the same purpose; the relative effectiveness of either medium is not established by the cited sources. An array alongside the area model (the original row's arrays/factor-trees representation) could optionally reinforce the same structure.
sourceClaims: Using structure includes partitioning a product distributively (e.g. 7×8 = 7×5 + 7×3) as the basis of the distributive property
Teaching should help pupils recognise and use mathematical structure and relationships, choosing representations (e.g. area models, place-value charts) that expose structure and are gradually removed
learnerActions: Face 7×13 drawn as a rectangle 7 tall and 13 wide; mark where to cut the width to make a friendly 10 and 3
Cut the rectangle into a 7×10 part and a 7×3 part and work out each: 70 and 21
Combine the two parts (70 + 21 = 91) and state the matching number sentence: 7×13 = 7×10 + 7×3
Explain in your own words why BOTH parts have to be multiplied by 7 (both sub-rectangles are 7 tall)
Try a different cut of 13 (for example 11 and 2, giving 7×11 = 77 and 7×2 = 14) and check you still reach 91; say which cut was easiest and why
activities.intendedInsight: A multiplication that feels hard can be assembled from two multiplications you already know; the distributive property shares the ×7 across every part of the 13, which is why both parts must be multiplied.

activities.title: Why ×10 shifts digits, not 'adds a zero'
feedback: If a learner writes 2.5×10 = 2.50, show the chart: 2.50 is the same value as 2.5, so nothing has changed — ×10 must make it ten times bigger, which means shifting to 25.
Reinforce that for 36×10 = 360 the zero appears because the ones column is emptied, not because we 'add a zero' as a rule.
activities.rationale: A place-value chart exposes the structural reason behind the ×10 pattern and provides a built-in counterexample (the decimal case) to the shortcut. A live chart where digits slide one column on ×10/×100 can make the shift concrete, and a paper chart with movable digit cards can serve the same purpose; the relative effectiveness of the media is not established by the cited sources.
sourceClaims: Teaching should help pupils recognise and use mathematical structure and relationships, choosing representations (e.g. area models, place-value charts) that expose structure and are gradually removed
learnerActions: Place a number such as 36 in a place-value chart (tens and ones), then multiply by 10 and move each digit one column to the left, writing a 0 in the emptied ones place to read 360
Now push 2.5 through ×10 in the same chart: move each digit one column left to get 25, and notice that appending a zero would wrongly give 2.50 (the same value as 2.5)
State a rule in your own words: ×10 moves every digit one place left; 'add a zero' only looks right for whole numbers because a zero happens to fill the empty ones place
Repeat for ×100 (two columns left) with one whole number and one decimal
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying by 10 (or 100) is a place-value shift of every digit; 'add a zero' is only a lucky special case for whole numbers and breaks for decimals.

activities.title: Nested shape families: a square is a special rectangle
feedback: If a learner denies that a square is a rectangle, use the nested sets: the square sits inside the rectangle set, so it must satisfy every rectangle property (four right angles).
If a learner claims every rectangle is a square, show a long thin rectangle as a counterexample — inheritance runs from the wider category to the narrower one, not back up.
activities.rationale: A shape family tree / nested property sets make the hierarchy visible and are intended to support reasoning by inheritance, which is the structural move for quadrilateral classification. Tappable property labels on a hierarchy diagram can serve as a reference; a sort by itself checks or teaches classification but does not itself elicit the learner's explanation, so pair the active sorting with a request to justify. The attached EEF claim supports using representations to expose structure in general and does not specifically evidence the nested-set method.
sourceClaims: Teaching should help pupils recognise and use mathematical structure and relationships, choosing representations (e.g. area models, place-value charts) that expose structure and are gradually removed
learnerActions: Sort a set of quadrilaterals into nested property sets so squares sit inside rectangles, which sit inside parallelograms
For a given square, list what must be true of it just because it is a rectangle (e.g. it has four right angles) — without measuring
Complete sentences of the form 'A square must have … because it is a rectangle' and 'A square must have … because it is a parallelogram'
Decide and justify: is every rectangle a square? Explain why the inheritance runs one way down the hierarchy
activities.intendedInsight: Subcategories inherit the properties of the categories that contain them, so knowing 'a square is a rectangle' lets you carry rectangle properties down without re-checking; but the reverse is not guaranteed.

activities.title: 'What do I already know that this is like?' — probing and generalising
feedback: Listen for a structurally justified decomposition such as '7×13 is 7×10 plus 7×3, that's 70 and 21, so 91 — I can split the 13 because multiplying is shared out over the parts.' The justification, not the answer 91, is the target.
If the learner reaches 91 only by running the column algorithm in their head, that does not yet show structural insight — ask them to name the parts and why the split is valid.
If the learner cannot say why the split works, return to the area model activity before pushing generalisation.
activities.rationale: The answer 91 is reachable by the column algorithm with no structural insight; what discriminates is whether the learner decomposes and can justify the split, and whether they transfer the move to related products. Open probes are intended to elicit the justification that a scored answer would hide.
sourceClaims: Using structure includes partitioning a product distributively (e.g. 7×8 = 7×5 + 7×3) as the basis of the distributive property
learnerActions: Work out 7×13 mentally using a fact you already know instead of the written column method, then talk through how you split it and why that split is allowed
Answer: could you have split 13 a different way and still got 91? Which split was easiest and why?
Generalise: how is splitting 7×13 like splitting 6×13 or 7×23? Describe the structural move you reused
Before any standard algorithm on a new product, pause and ask 'is there a number fact or shape fact I already know that this is like?'
activities.intendedInsight: Using structure is a deliberate, transferable habit: decompose into known parts and justify the decomposition, rather than defaulting to a procedure.

constraints: The teaching aim is that the learner looks for a known structure before applying a standard procedure; reaching the correct numerical answer by the column algorithm does not demonstrate this objective.
Target the justification, not just the result: a distributive split must be explained as sharing the ×7 over both parts, and ×10 must be explained as a place-value shift.

Tap-to-reveal annotations on a pre-split area model or a shape hierarchy are useful as reference scaffolds, but they do not let the learner choose the split point or watch the parts recombine; use them to support, not replace, active partitioning.

Recognition or matching checks (e.g. 'which split makes 7×13 easy?') can confirm the structural move, but a correct selection can hide the reasoning; pair any such check with a request to explain why.
Avoid teaching 'multiply by 10 adds a zero' as a rule; use it only as a named special case for whole numbers alongside the place-value explanation.
Inheritance in the quadrilateral hierarchy runs from broader to narrower categories (a square inherits rectangle properties), not the reverse; make this directionality explicit.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and medium/interaction choices are presented with proposed/may wording.

The legacy row rated dialogue ('conversation') and 3D as 'poor' with claims such as 'dialogue without the area model gives nothing to partition' and '3D adds load, not insight'. These comparative/necessity claims are not established by the cited sources and have been reframed as narrow scaffold limits rather than universal laws; the open probes retained here use discussion productively once a visual model is available.

The original keyRepresentation 'arrays and factor trees linking multiplication structure' was not carried into any activity as a standalone task; it is noted as an optional reinforcement in activity 1 and could be reinstated to enrich the distributive-split work. Flagged as a substantive representation gap rather than silently dropped.

The EEF source claim is a general representation/structure statement; attaching it to the shape-hierarchy activity supports the 'use a representation to expose structure' principle but does not specifically evidence the nested-property-set approach — treated as topical support, not validation.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 7×13 = 7×10 + 7×3 = 70 + 21 = 91 (correct); alternative split 7×11 + 7×2 = 77 + 14 = 91 (correct). The common error 7×10 + 3 = 73 is retained only as an explicitly labelled misconception with a correction, never as a valid answer. 2.5×10 = 25 (correct); 2.50 is flagged as the wrong 'add a zero' outcome. 36×10 = 360, 6×13 = 78 and 7×23 = 161 by the same method (used only as generalisation prompts, not as stated answers).

probeDeeper: Ask 'you split 13 into 10 and 3 — could you have split it a different way and still got 91? which split was easiest and why?' to test flexible, purposeful structure use
Counterexample tuned to this topic: 'does "add a zero" give the right answer for 2.5×10? why or why not?' to check the place-value structure beneath the rule
Ask 'a square is a rectangle — so what does that let you say about its angles without measuring?' to probe property inheritance in the hierarchy
Ask 'how is splitting 7×13 like splitting 6×13 or 7×23?' to see whether the distributive structure generalises
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for a distributive decomposition justified structurally: '7×13 is 7×10 plus 7×3, that's 70 and 21, so 91 — I can split the 13 because multiplying is sharing out over the parts.' The justification, not the 91, is the target.

errorPatterns.pattern: Splits distributively but multiplies only the first part, giving 7×10 + 3 = 73, because the split is treated as chopping the number rather than sharing the ×7 over both parts
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the area model: both sub-rectangles are 7 tall, so the 3 must also be multiplied by 7; see the missing 7×3 block
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says '70 plus 3' or otherwise leaves the second part un-multiplied

errorPatterns.pattern: Relies on 'multiplying by 10 just adds a zero', which misfires on decimals and hides the place-value shift
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a place-value chart to shift every digit one column left; contrast the whole-number case where a zero happens to fill the ones place
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked to explain ×10 or to do 2.5×10, the child appends a zero (2.50) instead of shifting digits

errorPatterns.pattern: Refuses that a square is a special rectangle, so shared properties don't transfer down the hierarchy
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort quadrilaterals into nested property sets so the square sits inside the rectangle set; reason that a square inherits rectangle properties
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked 'is a square a rectangle? so must it have four right angles?' the child denies the category link

responseLevels.gap: Reaches for the column algorithm or splits incorrectly (7×10+3), appends a zero for ×10, and won't accept the square-rectangle link
responseLevels.full: Chooses a distributive decomposition unprompted and justifies it via the area model, explains ×10 as a place-value shift, and reasons about inherited quadrilateral properties — applying 'what do I already know that this is like?' to new products and shapes
responseLevels.partial: Can carry out a distributive split or state a hierarchy fact when prompted, but cannot justify why the split is valid or transfers 'add a zero' unsafely to decimals

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work out 7 × 13 in your head, using a fact you already know instead of the written column method. Talk me through how you split it up and why that's allowed.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The answer 91 can be reached by the column algorithm with no structural insight. What discriminates is whether the child DECOMPOSES and can say why the split is valid. A child using structure partitions and justifies; a child without it either runs the algorithm mentally or splits wrongly (7×10+3).

sources.claim: Using structure includes partitioning a product distributively (e.g. 7×8 = 7×5 + 7×3) as the basis of the distributive property
sources.source: CCSS Standards for Mathematical Practice, MP7 'Look for and make use of structure'

sources.claim: Teaching should help pupils recognise and use mathematical structure and relationships, choosing representations (e.g. area models, place-value charts) that expose structure and are gradually removed
sources.source: EEF, 'Improving Mathematics in Key Stages 2 and 3' guidance report (Recommendations 2 and 4)

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 8-9 (META). Solve number and practical problems involving place value with increasingly large numbers — rounding, comparing, ordering, and interpreting real figures (populations, distances, prices) — choosing and justifying a place-value strategy. Applying, not learning, the four-digit toolkit.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 4): 'solve number and practical problems that involve all of the above [place value to 10,000] and with increasingly large positive numbers'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.NBT / 4.OA problem-solving with multi-digit numbers, rounding to assess reasonableness, and multi-step contexts.
• Operational details — Pose rich, often multi-step and real-context problems that reward rounding for estimation, comparing/ordering, and flexible partitioning. Model with number lines, bar models and place-value charts; require an explanation of WHY the chosen strategy fits. Emphasise using rounding to check reasonableness and choosing the right degree of accuracy.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8, emerging): solves a one-step problem (round/compare) with a model. Tier B (age 8-9, secure): solves multi-step place-value problems in context and explains the strategy. Tier C (age 9, extending): selects appropriate accuracy, uses rounding to justify reasonableness, and reasons flexibly with large numbers.
bestPractices: Pose rich, real-context, often multi-step problems (populations, distances, money) that genuinely reward place-value strategies.
Model with number lines, bar models and place-value charts; require justification of the chosen strategy.
Use rounding to estimate and to check the reasonableness of answers.
Teach choosing an appropriate degree of accuracy for the context.
Externalise reasoning (think-aloud, then child-explains) so strategy selection becomes deliberate.
keyRepresentations: Number line (comparison, rounding, estimation)
Bar model for multi-step problem structure
Place-value chart / counters
Real data sets (populations, distances) as problem material
Estimation/benchmark reasoning
commonMisconceptions: Reaching for a memorised procedure without checking it fits the problem.
Rounding at the wrong stage or to an unhelpful accuracy.
Comparing/ordering errors carried into problem contexts (multi-zero, mixed length).
Not sense-checking an answer against an estimate.
Losing place-value meaning when numbers get large or contextual.

learn.summary: Ages 8-9 applied place-value problem-solving: children choose and justify a place-value strategy (rounding, comparing, ordering, flexible partitioning) to solve rich, multi-step, real-context problems with increasingly large numbers (populations, distances, prices). This is a META topic — the learning target is deliberate strategy selection and using rounding to check reasonableness, not first-time acquisition of the four-digit toolkit.

activities.title: The large-number problem studio
feedback: Name the strategy the child used ('you ordered first, then rounded to estimate') so the choice becomes explicit and reusable.
After the exact answer, show it next to the child's estimate and ask whether the estimate was close enough for the purpose — reinforcing estimation as a reasonableness check.
If the child reached for a procedure that didn't fit, prompt: 'What is the problem actually asking you to find — a comparison, an order, or an estimate?'
activities.rationale: A META problem-solving objective is served by giving children the full toolkit and making them select among tools, so strategy choice and justification are rehearsed rather than a single procedure drilled. Modelling with number lines, bar models and charts and requiring justification reflects recommended place-value pedagogy.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'solve number and practical problems that involve all of the above and with increasingly large positive numbers'.
Strategy selection and using estimation to check reasonableness are central to place-value problem solving.
Solve multi-step problems with multi-digit numbers and use rounding to assess reasonableness (4.NBT / 4.OA.3).
learnerActions: Read a real-context problem such as: four cities have populations 53,847, 48,206, 51,330 and 49,975 — order them from largest to smallest and estimate the total.

Choose which place-value tool fits the task before computing: a number line (for rounding/estimating), an ordering rail (for comparing/ordering), a bar model (for multi-step structure) or a place-value chart (for partitioning).
Act with the chosen tool — e.g. place each population on the ordering rail, then round each to the nearest thousand on the number line and add the rounded values to estimate the total.
State aloud or in writing WHY that tool fit this problem, referencing place value.
Compute the exact answer and compare it against your rounded estimate to check reasonableness.
activities.intendedInsight: The right place-value move depends on what the problem asks; rounding gives a fast estimate that you can use to sense-check an exact answer.

activities.title: Mixed problem set with strategy matching
feedback: For a wrong 'best estimate' choice, place the candidate estimates and the exact figure on a number line to show which is nearer.
For comparison/ordering slips, draw attention to digit place (especially multi-zero numbers and numbers of mixed length).
Confirm when an estimate correctly predicted the size of the exact answer.
activities.rationale: Assessment-style items give varied practice and surface strategy-selection and comparison errors, though a fixed item set scaffolds strategy choice less richly than an open toolkit bench — so it works best as practice alongside the studio.
sourceClaims: Strategy selection and using estimation to check reasonableness are central to place-value problem solving.
Solve multi-step problems with multi-digit numbers and use rounding to assess reasonableness (4.NBT / 4.OA.3).
learnerActions: Work through varied items: multi-step word problems, 'which is larger / best estimate' choices, estimate-then-check tasks, and fill-in-the-blank computations.
For each item, match the problem to the place-value strategy that fits it (round, compare, order, partition) before solving.
Estimate first using rounding, then compute and confirm the estimate was reasonable.
activities.intendedInsight: Different problem shapes call for different place-value moves; recognising the shape is the first step to solving it.

activities.title: 'How did you decide?' strategy dialogue
feedback: Probe with: 'How did you decide what amount to round to for this puzzle?'
Probe with: 'When would you actually need the exact figure rather than a rounded estimate?'
Probe with: 'Would "about 30" be a fair way to describe a class of 27 children? When might that be fine, and when would you need the exact 27 — for example, when handing out one book each?'
activities.rationale: Socratic questioning externalises reasoning and elicits justification, which suits a META topic focused on metacognitive strategy choice; it supplements rather than replaces varied practice.
sourceClaims: Strategy selection and using estimation to check reasonableness are central to place-value problem solving.
learnerActions: Respond to a real-figure puzzle posed by a partner or teacher (e.g. 'about how many people live in these two towns together?').
Explain which place-value move you chose and why — did you round, compare, or order, and to what accuracy?
Answer probing follow-ups about your choice of accuracy.
activities.intendedInsight: Justifying a strategy out loud makes strategy selection deliberate and reveals whether the degree of rounding fits the purpose.

activities.title: Diagnostic: is 'about 54,000' fair?
feedback: If the child rejects 'about 54,000' only because it isn't 53,847: discuss why headlines round — the estimate carries the useful information; contrast a bill (exactness matters) with a crowd (it doesn't).

If the child treats all roundings as equally good: compare the candidates against 53,847 on a number line so the child can see that the nearest-thousand estimate (54,000) is much closer than the nearest-ten-thousand estimate (50,000). Then discuss that both are correct roundings, and which is more useful depends on the purpose.
This probe surfaces reasoning — use it to understand the child's stance on approximation rather than to grade a single calculation.
activities.rationale: The key judgement underlying large-number problem-solving is whether only exact figures count or whether a sensibly-rounded number is valid and purpose-fit; this open probe surfaces that stance and the common myth that rounding is 'cheating'.
sourceClaims: Strategy selection and using estimation to check reasonableness are central to place-value problem solving.
learnerActions: Consider: a news report says a football crowd was 'about 54,000'; the exact number counted was 53,847.
Decide whether 'about 54,000' is a fair thing to report or wrong because it isn't exact, and explain how you'd decide when a rounded number is good enough.
Compare candidate estimates against 53,847 — is 'about 54,000' closer than 'about 50,000'? Which would be more useful for a news report, and why?
activities.intendedInsight: A sensibly rounded number is a valid, purpose-fit answer; how much to round depends on the purpose of the number, and closeness can be judged on a number line.

constraints: This is applying the four-digit place-value toolkit, not first teaching it; learners should already round, compare, order and partition four-digit numbers before this work.

Choice/estimate items and fill-in-the-blank practice assess and rehearse strategy recognition but do not by themselves require the child to select a strategy from an open field — pair recognition tasks with open problems where the child must choose the tool.
The diagnostic probe is not scored; it is meant to surface the child's reasoning about approximation, not produce a mark.
Degree of rounding must be tied to purpose: an estimate fit for a crowd figure is not fit for a bill or a small exact count.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the worked example: 53,847→54,000, 48,206→48,000, 51,330→51,000, 49,975→50,000 to the nearest thousand; rounded sum ≈ 203,000; exact sum = 203,358 — consistent, so the estimate is a reasonable check. Ordering 53,847 > 51,330 > 49,975 > 48,206 is correct. (Example figures beyond the original crowd number were added to make the studio task concrete; flag if a different data set is preferred.)

The original 'about 54,000' is the nearest-thousand rounding of 53,847, which is correct; the contrast 'about 50,000' is deliberately a less-close candidate used diagnostically, not an error, and is never presented to the child as a valid answer.

Editor fix (second pass): Activity 3's third probe still cited 'about 54,000', a figure belonging to the Activity 4 crowd diagnostic and absent from the figure-free two-towns dialogue; it was rewritten to ask generically about rounding a small exact count (27 children) so the scenario stays coherent. A previous pass had fixed the parallel exact-figure probe but missed this one.

Source claims for CCSS-M and NCETM were marked unverified in the original row; do not treat them as confirmed. The DfE Year 4 claim was marked verified in the legacy row but has not been re-checked here.

Legacy artefact rankings and the 'no spatial payoff' dismissal of 3D were removed as catalog ranking rather than established pedagogy; the underlying pedagogical ideas (toolkit bench, varied quiz practice, Socratic dialogue, worked-example reference) are preserved as distinct activities, with medium limitations stated as scoped rather than universal.

probeDeeper: Is 'about 54,000' closer to the real crowd than 'about 50,000'? Which is fairer?
When would you actually NEED the exact 53,847?
How did you decide the nearest thousand was the right amount to round to?
Would 'about 54,000' be a fair way to describe a class of 27 children? Why not?
assess.correctAnswer: Not scored. A rich response accepts that rounding is legitimate and useful, that 'about 54,000' fairly stands for 53,847 (nearest thousand), and that HOW MUCH to round depends on the purpose of the number.

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes only the exact number is ever correct — rounding is 'wrong' or 'cheating'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Discuss why headlines round: the estimate carries the useful information. Contrast contexts where exactness matters (a bill) with where it doesn't (a crowd).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child rejects 'about 54,000' purely because it isn't 53,847.

errorPatterns.pattern: Accepts any rounding without judging closeness — 'about 50,000' seems just as fine as 'about 54,000'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare the candidates against 53,847 on a number line; the nearest-thousand estimate is the fair one. Tie the degree of rounding to the purpose.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child treats all roundings as equally good, ignoring which is nearer.

responseLevels.gap: Treats only the exact figure as correct, or accepts any rounding without judging closeness.
responseLevels.full: Judges a rounded number as fair or not by its closeness and by the purpose, and explains the choice using place value.
responseLevels.partial: Accepts rounding as valid but cannot yet justify how much to round for a given purpose.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'A news report says a football crowd was “about 54,000”. The exact number counted was 53,847. Is “about 54,000” a fair thing to report, or is it wrong because it isn't the exact number? How would you decide when a rounded number is good enough?' Surface the reasoning — don't grade it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The probe surfaces the child's stance on approximation: whether only exact figures count as 'right', or whether a sensibly-rounded number is a valid, purpose-fit answer. That judgement — not a single calculation — is what place-value problem-solving with large numbers rests on.

sources.claim: Year 4 pupils should 'solve number and practical problems that involve all of the above and with increasingly large positive numbers'.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (Year 4 Number & place value)

sources.claim: Solve multi-step problems with multi-digit numbers and use rounding to assess reasonableness (4.NBT / 4.OA.3).
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 4

sources.claim: Strategy selection and using estimation to check reasonableness are central to place-value problem solving.
sources.source: NCETM Primary Mastery PD: Place Value (Spine 1)

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 7-8 (Y2/Y3). Fluently add and subtract within 20 using mental strategies; KNOW FROM MEMORY all sums of two one-digit numbers. The automaticity endpoint of KS1 additive facts (centrality 0.15) — secure recall here is the platform for all multi-digit mental and written calculation.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y2): 'recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently, and derive and use related facts up to 100'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.OA.2 'fluently add and subtract within 20 using mental strategies; by end of Grade 2, know from memory all sums of two one-digit numbers'.
• Operational details — The goal is genuine automaticity: instant, accurate recall of single-digit sums and their subtraction partners, with a strategy to fall back on if a fact slips. Reach it by consolidating the within-20 strategies (making ten, doubles/near-doubles, bonds) into recalled facts through distributed, interleaved retrieval practice. Include all subtraction facts as members of fact families. Keep practice low-stakes to protect against anxiety while still valuing efficiency.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 7): recall most single-digit sums quickly, reconstructing the few uncertain ones via strategy. Tier B (age 7-8): recall all sums of two one-digit numbers from memory and the related subtractions. Tier C (age 8): apply recalled facts instantly to derive related facts to 100 (e.g. 8+5 → 80+50, 18+5).
bestPractices: Consolidate strategy-based within-20 work into recalled facts — automaticity should be the fluent endpoint of understanding, not rote learning bypassing it.
Use distributed, interleaved, low-stakes retrieval practice (little and often, mixed facts) which cognitive science shows builds durable recall better than massed drill.
Keep a reconstructable strategy available for slips (near-double, make-ten) so a momentarily forgotten fact isn't a dead end.
Practise subtraction facts as fact families with their additions, and stretch to derived facts to 100 to show the payoff of knowing them.
Avoid high-pressure timed testing as the main vehicle; monitor which specific facts remain non-automatic and target those.
keyRepresentations: Addition fact grid (sums of two one-digit numbers) for tracking coverage
Fact-family triangles linking each sum to its two subtractions
Doubles/near-doubles and make-ten visuals as fallback strategies
Quick-image/flash retrieval cards, interleaved
Derived-fact chains (8+5=13 → 18+5, 80+50) showing the payoff
commonMisconceptions: Still counting on/back for facts that should be recalled, indicating incomplete automaticity.
Knowing sums but not the related subtractions (fact family incomplete).
Speed-without-accuracy under timed pressure, or anxiety suppressing recall.
Treating memorised facts as disconnected from strategies, so a forgotten fact can't be reconstructed.
Failing to use known facts to derive related facts to 100 (recomputing 18+5 from scratch).

learn.summary: Ages 7-8 (Y2/Y3): build genuine automaticity with single-digit sums and their related subtractions within 20, with a reconstructable strategy (make-ten, near-doubles) as a fallback for slips. Practice should be distributed, interleaved and low-stakes, treat subtraction as members of fact families, and stretch to deriving related facts to 100. A workable progression is: recall most sums while reconstructing a few by strategy; then recall all sums and the related subtractions (aiming for recall within about 3 seconds); then apply recalled facts instantly to derive facts to 100. The original row recommended an adaptive fluency game; strong alternatives (speeded retrieval practice, oral quick-fire, and a static fact-grid/strategy reference) are preserved here with their distinct purposes and limits.

activities.title: Personal fact grid: track recall vs counting, little and often
feedback: If the child counts on by ones for 8+7 (9…10…11…12…13…14…15), rehearse make-ten as a bridge: 8+2=10, then 5 more is 15.
If a fact is reconstructed correctly but slowly, acknowledge it is right and re-serve it later to move it toward instant (around-3-second) recall.
If within-10 facts are secure but crossing-ten facts (8+7, 6+9) are shaky, focus practice on the crossing-ten set, mixing in only an occasional secure within-10 fact rather than re-drilling them.
Keep it low-stakes: value accuracy and strategy, not only speed, to protect against anxiety suppressing recall.
activities.rationale: Distributed, interleaved, low-stakes retrieval practice supports durable recall better than massed drill, and consolidating strategies into recalled facts keeps a fallback available. A live heatmap of mastered vs shaky facts (cells glowing green when recalled, amber when counted) and a one-tap strategy hint on hesitation are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete; the same can be done on paper.
sourceClaims: Automaticity is best reached as the endpoint of strategy understanding, via distributed interleaved retrieval, with a reconstructable strategy fallback.
learnerActions: Keep a grid of single-digit sums where each cell is a fact the child is practising (e.g. the row/column for crossing-ten sums like 8+7, 6+9).
Mark a fact as secure once it is recalled instantly (roughly within 3 seconds, no counting), and as 'still counting' when the child has to count on or pause.
Return frequently and briefly to the 'still counting' facts, mixed in with secure ones, rather than drilling one fact many times in a row.

When a fact slips, rebuild it aloud with a strategy — near-double (6+9 → 'double 6 is 12, plus 3 more is 15') or make-ten (8+7 → '8+2 is 10, then 5 more is 15') — then try it again cold a little later.
activities.intendedInsight: Automaticity is the fluent endpoint of understanding: instant recall for most facts, with a strategy to reconstruct any that momentarily slip, so recall stays connected to reasoning rather than brittle.

activities.title: Fact families: pull each subtraction from its addition
feedback: If additions are fluent but subtractions are slow or counted, make the fact family explicit and prompt 'think of the addition' for each subtraction.
If the child re-counts 15-8 from scratch rather than linking it to 8+7=15, point back to the triangle and the known addition.
activities.rationale: A common gap is knowing sums but not the related subtractions. Practising them together as fact families closes this. Fact-family triangles make the link between one sum and its two subtractions visible. The cited standards establish that subtraction facts within 20 should be recalled fluently, but the fact-family method itself is a research-informed scaffold not asserted by the sources, so no source claim is attached here.
learnerActions: For each secure sum, state the whole fact family: from 8+7=15, give 7+8=15, 15-8=7 and 15-7=8.
Practise subtraction prompts by first thinking of the matching addition: for 15-8, think 'what plus 8 makes 15?'
Use a fact-family triangle (15 at top, 8 and 7 below) to see all four facts come from the same three numbers.
activities.intendedInsight: Knowing a sum should give the related subtractions for free; subtraction within 20 does not need recounting from scratch.

activities.title: Derive to 100: show why knowing these by heart pays off
feedback: If the child recomputes 18+5 from scratch, prompt them to reuse 8+5=13 and add the ten back (18+5 = 13+10 = 23).
If the place-value jump to 30+50 is unclear, re-express it as 'how many tens' (3 tens and 5 tens make 8 tens) before converting to 80.
activities.rationale: Deriving related facts to 100 demonstrates the usefulness of automatic recall and meets the Y2 'derive and use related facts up to 100' standard. A derived-fact bonus round can motivate this.
sourceClaims: Y2 pupils recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently, and derive and use related facts up to 100.
learnerActions: Start from a recalled fact and derive related ones within 100: 8+5=13 → 18+5=23 and 38+5=43; 3+5=8 → 30+50=80.
Explain the link out loud: '3 ones plus 5 ones is 8, so 3 tens plus 5 tens is 8 tens, which is 80.'
Try a short chain of derivations from one known fact to feel the payoff of instant recall.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure recall of single-digit facts is the platform for fast mental calculation with larger numbers (the Tier C aim of applying recalled facts to derive facts to 100).

activities.title: Speeded retrieval practice (strong alternative): short, frequent, interleaved
feedback: Report which facts remain non-automatic and feed those back into the fact-grid practice.
Avoid making high-pressure timed testing the main vehicle; use it to diagnose, not to pressure.
activities.rationale: Speeded, interleaved retrieval is a genuinely appropriate practice/assessment vehicle for 'know from memory', though a fixed set of items is less adaptive and diagnostic than interleaved practice that targets each child's shaky facts, and should stay low-stakes to avoid anxiety.
sourceClaims: Automaticity is best reached as the endpoint of strategy understanding, via distributed interleaved retrieval, with a reconstructable strategy fallback.
learnerActions: Work through short, mixed sets of single-digit sums and differences, aiming for near-instant answers (roughly within 3 seconds per fact).
Note which specific facts were not automatic so they can be targeted next time.
Keep sessions brief and frequent rather than one long high-pressure test.
activities.intendedInsight: Speeded retrieval is close to the target behaviour of 'knowing from memory' and is a useful practice and monitoring tool when kept low-stakes.

activities.title: Oral quick-fire warm-up (alternative): fast spoken recall
feedback: Use probe questions to surface method: 'How did you work out 8+7 — did you make a ten?', 'You said 8+7=15; so what is 15-8?', 'Is 6+9 easier if you think of it as 9+6? Why?'
Notice which were recalled versus built, and follow up on the built ones later.
activities.rationale: Oral quick-fire builds recall and reveals reasoning, though on its own it can't deliver as many adaptive, spaced reps or track fact-level mastery as systematic written practice.
learnerActions: Run a short quick-fire round of spoken sums and differences as a warm-up.
Mix additions with their related subtractions so fact families surface in conversation.
Ask the occasional follow-up: 'did you just know that, or did you build it?'
activities.intendedInsight: Spoken rapid recall builds fluency and lets a teacher hear strategy use directly.

activities.title: Static fact grid and strategy reference (scaffold)
feedback: If the child relies on the grid to look up answers rather than recall them, move the grid out of sight for retrieval attempts and bring it back only for reconstruction.
activities.rationale: A static reference supports strategy fallback but cannot itself generate the retrieval practice that automaticity requires; it is a support used alongside active recall.
learnerActions: Keep a fact grid and a make-ten / near-doubles strategy card visible as a reference during practice.
Glance at it only to rebuild a slipped fact, not as the primary source of answers.
activities.intendedInsight: A reference anchor supports reconstruction but is a scaffold, not a driver of recall.

constraints: Automaticity should be the fluent endpoint of strategy understanding, not rote memorisation that bypasses reasoning; keep a reconstructable strategy (make-ten, near-doubles) available for slips.
Keep practice low-stakes; avoid high-pressure timed testing as the main vehicle, which can suppress recall through anxiety.
Include all subtraction facts as members of fact families, not just additions.
A static fact grid or strategy card is a reference scaffold and does not by itself drive the retrieval practice needed for recall.

A speeded quiz is close to the target behaviour but is less adaptive and diagnostic than interleaved practice that targets each child's shaky facts; use it to monitor which specific facts are non-automatic and target those.

Optional interface features (live green/amber heatmap, one-tap strategy hints, subtraction rounds, derive-to-100 bonus) make the mechanism concrete but are not required; the same practice works on paper or orally.

Focus practice on the facts that are still shaky (often crossing-ten sums); secure within-10 facts do not need repeated drilling, though they can be mixed in occasionally to keep practice interleaved and maintain them.
Treat the ~3-second recall benchmark as a guide to automaticity, not a pressure threshold to be enforced under anxiety.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original 'recommendation' and 'ideal' fit asserted that a coded 2D game does adaptive interleaving and strategy fallback in ways 'a fixed medium cannot', and that recall 'is not spatial' so 3D 'adds nothing'. These comparative-necessity claims are not established by the sources; they have been softened to narrowly scoped proposals with stated affordances, and the game's distinctive features retained as optional examples.
Two of three sources are marked verified:false in the row (CCSS-M 2.OA.2 and the Baroody/cognitive-science/NCETM claim); confidence was legacy 'high'. Treat these as unverified here.

The assessment's correctAnswer lists '15, 7, 15, 7' for the prompts 8+7, 15-8, 6+9, 13-6; checked: 8+7=15, 15-8=7, 6+9=15, 13-6=7, so the sequence is arithmetically consistent. No error corrected, noted for transparency.

The fact-family and speeded-retrieval methods are scaffolds supported by the fluency objective but not stated verbatim in the cited claims; the fact-family activity's sourceClaims were scoped to [] because the claim backs only the topic/objective, not the method, and efficacy of these methods remains untested.

probeDeeper: How did you work out 8 + 7 — did you make a ten?
You said 8 + 7 = 15; so what is 15 − 8?
Which of these did you just know, and which did you build?
Is 6 + 9 easier if you think of it as 9 + 6? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: 15, 7, 15, 7 — answered from memory or near-instant derivation (make-ten / near-doubles), with subtraction pulled from the related addition fact.

errorPatterns.pattern: No make-ten or derivation for crossing-ten sums — counts on by ones (8 + 7 → 9…10…15).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rehearse make-ten and near-doubles as bridges so crossing-ten facts become fast derived facts.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Slow finger-counting on the teen sums.

errorPatterns.pattern: Subtraction across ten re-counted from scratch, not taken from the addition fact (15 − 8 not linked to 8 + 7 = 15).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make fact families explicit and prompt 'think of the addition' for each subtraction.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Additions fluent, subtractions slow / counted.

errorPatterns.pattern: Within-10 secure but the specific crossing-ten facts (8 + 7, 6 + 9) shaky.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Target just the crossing-ten set; do not re-drill secure within-10 facts.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Hesitation isolated to the bridging facts.

responseLevels.gap: Counts on by ones for crossing-ten facts; subtraction re-computed.
responseLevels.full: Recalls all single-digit sums and the related subtraction facts within 20 rapidly, without counting.
responseLevels.partial: Derives sums via make-ten but not yet instant, or subtraction still counted.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Quick recall, no counting: 8 + 7? … 15 − 8? … 6 + 9? … 13 − 6?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: These all cross ten, so watch for recall or a fast make-ten derivation versus counting on by ones. Pairing 15 − 8 with 8 + 7 reveals whether the child uses the fact family or re-computes the subtraction.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 6-7 (Y1/Y2). Fluently add and subtract within 10 — quick, accurate, flexible recall of all facts to 10. A high-centrality fluency hub (0.17); automaticity here frees working memory for the making-ten strategy and all larger calculation.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1/Y2): number bonds and related subtraction facts within 20 (facts within 10 the core subset); Y2 'recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.OA.6 'add and subtract within 20… demonstrating fluency for addition and subtraction within 10'.
• Operational details — Extend within-5 fluency using derived-fact strategies: bonds to 10, doubles and near-doubles, +/−0 and +/−1. Push from counting toward recall via the ten-frame image and known-fact reasoning, then consolidate with short frequent retrieval practice. Include all subtraction facts and link them to their addition partners (fact families). Fluency = efficient + accurate + flexible, not speed alone.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 6): answer within-10 additions using a fast strategy (bonds, doubles) rather than counting all. Tier B (age 6-7): recall any within-10 fact quickly and give its related subtraction. Tier C (age 7): use within-10 facts fluently to reason about larger calculations (e.g. 6+7 via 6+6+1).
bestPractices: Anchor fluency in derived-fact strategies (bonds to 10, doubles/near-doubles, +0/+1) so facts are recalled meaningfully and reconstructable if forgotten.
Use the ten-frame image and rekenrek to move children from counting to 'seeing' facts, then fade the support.
Teach addition and subtraction as fact families (6+4=10, 10−4=6) so subtraction facts come from known additions.
Consolidate with short, frequent, low-stakes retrieval rather than long timed tests; interleave facts so children discriminate rather than pattern-guess.
Model choosing an efficient strategy for each fact (flexibility), not one method for all.
keyRepresentations: Ten-frame(s) for facts and complements within 10
Rekenrek (two rows of 5) for doubles and bridging
Doubles/near-doubles visual (two equal rows, one extra)
Fact-family triangle linking a bond's + and − facts
Quick-image flash cards for retrieval practice
commonMisconceptions: Persisting with count-all/count-on for every fact instead of using derived facts or recall.
Mastering additions but not the related subtractions within 10.
Treating fluency as pure speed, leading to errors under pressure or anxiety.
Not recognising doubles/near-doubles as a shortcut (computing 6+7 from scratch).
Confusing similar facts (7+2 vs 7+3) when practice isn't interleaved.

learn.summary: For ages 6-7, build fluent (efficient, accurate, flexible) addition and subtraction within 10, moving children from counting toward recall and derived-fact reasoning (bonds to 10, doubles and near-doubles, +/−0 and +/−1). Anchor facts in strategies so a forgotten fact can be reconstructed, link each addition to its subtraction partner as fact families, and consolidate with short, frequent, interleaved retrieval. The primary proposal is adaptive strategy-anchored retrieval practice with fading visual support; a fixed quiz, a static strategy anchor, and oral quick-fire are preserved as complementary tools with different purposes.

activities.title: Adaptive fluency practice with fading ten-frame support
feedback: If the child counts on each item, do not drill for speed under pressure or penalise counting; model count-on-from-the-larger-number and point to the known bond or double behind the fact — with continued short, frequent practice, automaticity typically develops.
If the child counts up from the smaller addend (e.g. 2 + 7 counted 3,4,5,6,7,8,9), prompt 'start from the bigger number' — this is an efficiency habit (commutativity), not a missing fact.
If complements to ten are slow (10 − 6 counted), pause and re-secure number bonds to 10 to automaticity; the rest of within-10 may already be fine.
When a fact is answered instantly, let the supporting image fade further so the child notices they now 'just know' it.
activities.rationale: Brief, low-pressure, strategy-anchored retrieval with fading support and interleaving is a key route to building meaningful automaticity; adaptivity lets support fade as recall strengthens and surfaces strategy hints when a child stalls.
sourceClaims: Fluency within 10 should be built from derived-fact strategies (doubles, bonds, near-doubles) and consolidated with frequent low-stakes retrieval and interleaving.
1.OA.6: add and subtract within 20, demonstrating fluency within 10, using strategies such as making ten, decomposing, and relationships between + and −.
learnerActions: Answer within-10 facts presented one after another (e.g. 6 + 4, 7 + 2, 9 − 4, 10 − 6), aiming to say the answer without counting.
Start with a faint ten-frame (or rekenrek image) behind each fact; as the child answers quickly, let the visual fade so they move from 'seeing' to recalling.
When a child stalls on a harder fact like 4 + 5, surface a strategy hint that shows the near-double (4 + 4 and one more) so they reconstruct rather than freeze.
Use a fact-family mode that surfaces the related subtraction for each bond (6 + 4 = 10 alongside 10 − 4 = 6, 10 − 6 = 4).
Interleave fact types (doubles, bonds, near-doubles, +/−1) so the child discriminates between similar facts (7 + 2 vs 7 + 3) rather than pattern-guesses.
activities.intendedInsight: A hard fact becomes easy when the child sees the double or bond inside it; isolated answers become a connected, flexible web of facts, including the subtraction partners — real fluency, not brittle speed.

activities.title: Interleaved fact quiz as a periodic check
feedback: Use results to spot which specific facts are still being counted and revisit the strategy behind them.
Favour short frequent sets over long timed tests, which can trigger errors or anxiety; fluency means efficient, accurate and flexible, not speed alone.
activities.rationale: Speeded retrieval practice drives automaticity, so fact quizzes are a legitimate practice and assessment tool; a fixed quiz is less adaptive than guided practice and is best used as a periodic check rather than the main teaching driver.
sourceClaims: Fluency within 10 should be built from derived-fact strategies (doubles, bonds, near-doubles) and consolidated with frequent low-stakes retrieval and interleaving.
learnerActions: Work short sets of within-10 fact items (multiple-choice or fill-in-the-blank), kept low-stakes and quick.
Include related-subtraction pairs alongside additions (e.g. 6 + 4 and 10 − 6) so both are practised.
Interleave fact types within a set rather than grouping all doubles or all bonds together.
activities.intendedInsight: Quick retrieval across mixed facts shows which facts are recalled versus still counted, and keeps subtraction facts practised alongside their addition partners.

activities.title: Oral quick-fire warm-up
feedback: Watch for recall versus counting on; the 10 − 6 item checks whether ten-facts are automatic (or whether the child counts back or counts up from 6), and the 7 + 2 item shows whether the child counts on from the larger addend.
Treat an exposed gap (e.g. ten-bonds not automatic) as the next thing to re-secure, not a reason to drill under time pressure.
activities.rationale: Oral quick-fire builds recall and makes reasoning audible; on its own it cannot deliver the volume of varied, adaptive repetition that written/adaptive practice provides, so it works best as a short warm-up.
learnerActions: Run a brief spoken quick-fire round of within-10 facts as a warm-up, e.g. '6 + 3? … 9 − 4? … 7 + 2? … 10 − 6?'

After an answer, ask follow-up questions: 'For 2 + 7, could you start from the 7 instead? Is it quicker?', 'How does knowing 6 + 4 = 10 help with 10 − 6?', 'Which did you just know without working out?', 'What's 9 − 4 — and how did you get it?'
activities.intendedInsight: Speaking facts aloud and explaining the strategy makes the child's recall-versus-counting visible and reinforces commutativity and fact-family links.

activities.title: Strategy reference anchor for derived facts
feedback: Use the anchor to prompt reconstruction, then return to retrieval so the child practises recalling without it.
Recognising a strategy on a wall is a scaffold; it does not by itself build the repeated retrieval that automaticity needs.
activities.rationale: A static strategy anchor aids recognition and reconstruction of facts but cannot drive repeated retrieval, so it supports rather than replaces active practice.
sourceClaims: Fluency within 10 should be built from derived-fact strategies (doubles, bonds, near-doubles) and consolidated with frequent low-stakes retrieval and interleaving.
learnerActions: Keep a visible reference wall or card of key derived facts and strategies: doubles (two equal rows), near-doubles (one extra), bonds to 10 on a ten-frame, and fact-family triangles linking a bond's + and − facts.
Point to the matching strategy when a fact is forgotten so the child reconstructs it (e.g. find 4 + 5 via 4 + 4 and one more).
activities.intendedInsight: Having the underlying strategies visible helps children recognise and reconstruct facts meaningfully instead of guessing.

constraints: Fluency means efficient + accurate + flexible, not speed alone; avoid long timed tests that cause errors or anxiety and use short, frequent, low-stakes retrieval instead.
Do not penalise counting under time pressure; model count-on-from-the-larger-number and derived-fact reasoning so automaticity develops naturally.
Include all subtraction facts within 10 and link them to their addition partners (fact families); mastering additions alone is incomplete.
Interleave fact types so children discriminate between similar facts rather than pattern-guess.
A static strategy anchor and an oral quick-fire are recognition/warm-up scaffolds; they do not by themselves deliver the repeated varied retrieval needed for automaticity.
Visual supports (ten-frame, rekenrek) should be faded as recall strengthens, not relied on permanently.
Number bonds to 10 are a prerequisite thread; if complements to ten are not automatic, re-secure number bonds to 10 rather than drilling all facts.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row framed non-adaptive and static media as 'impossible' or unable to drive fluency; these have been softened to scoped affordances/limits (a quiz and a reference anchor can support learning but are less adaptive and cannot alone supply repeated retrieval). Catalog fit rankings do not establish comparative efficacy or necessity.
Source CCSS-M (1.OA.6) and the NCETM/retrieval-practice claim are marked verified:false in the legacy row; do not treat them as independently confirmed.

CCSS 1.OA.6 supports only the strategy/relationships element of activity 1; the speeded-retrieval, fading-support and interleaving mechanism rests on the NCETM claim, not on the CCSS standard statement.
Checkpoint answers in the source ('9, 5, 9, 4' for 6+3, 9−4, 7+2, 10−6) are correct: 6+3=9, 9−4=5, 7+2=9, 10−6=4.

The legacy claim that small-fact fluency 'is not spatial' (used to skip 3D) is a design preference, not an established pedagogical law; it is retained only as a reason to prioritise other media, not as a universal rule.

The DfE 'recall and use fluently' claim supports the objective/standard but not the specific retrieval-mechanism rationale, so it was removed from activity 1's sourceClaims and is represented at summary/objective level instead.
The raw prerequisite micro-topic identifier was stripped from learner-facing constraints; the number-bonds-to-10 prerequisite relationship is retained conceptually.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts on from the first addend or from one, rather than recalling within-10 facts.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill for speed under pressure or penalise counting — model count-on-from-larger and use known bonds; automaticity follows naturally.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Nodding / finger counting on each item.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts on from the SMALLER addend — does not use commutativity, so 2 + 7 is counted 3,4,5,6,7,8,9.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Teach 'start from the bigger number' (commutativity) — this is an efficiency habit, not a missing fact.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child starts the count from the smaller number.

errorPatterns.pattern: Bonds to 10 not automatic, dragging down 10 − facts — 10 − 6 is counted.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-secure number bonds to 10 to automaticity; the rest of within-10 is fine.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Struggles specifically on complements to ten.

responseLevels.gap: Counts on/all by ones for most facts; ten-bonds not automatic.
responseLevels.full: Recalls within-10 facts, including complements to ten, quickly and accurately, using commutativity to be efficient.
responseLevels.partial: Recalls or derives most facts but still counts some, or starts counts from the smaller addend.

assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watch recall versus counting on. Within-10 fluency should not need finger-counting; the 10 − 6 item checks whether ten-facts are automatic, and whether the child counts on from the larger number rather than re-counting.
