pedagogy.summary: Children learn to order events in time and to USE relational time language — first/next/last, before/after, the deictic terms today/yesterday/tomorrow, and morning/afternoon/evening. The hard part is the deictic terms, whose referent shifts with 'now' (tomorrow becomes today the next day), and the relational before/after. It is learned by talking through the daily routine and retelling sequences, not by definitions.
bestPractices: Anchor in the child's own daily routine and shared class events, with a visual timeline of the day
Use the words in live narration ('first we…, next we…, after lunch we…') and in story retelling
Tie yesterday/today/tomorrow to concrete markers — what we DID and what we WILL do
Teach by modelling and eliciting USE, never by asking children to define the words
Revisit the terms daily so the shifting deictic meaning is rehearsed in context
keyRepresentations: A visual daily-timeline / sequence strip of routine events
Story-sequencing picture cards
A yesterday–today–tomorrow three-day strip with a moveable 'today' marker
commonMisconceptions: Swaps yesterday and tomorrow (both used loosely for 'a day that isn't today')
Reverses before/after, or uses 'next' for the last thing
Ties morning/afternoon to particular activities rather than the time of day
Sequences by salience (the most exciting event first) rather than chronology

learn.summary: For children aged 4-6, learning to order events in time and USE relational time language — first/next/last, before/after, the deictic terms today/yesterday/tomorrow, and morning/afternoon/evening. The hardest parts are the deictic terms (whose referent shifts as 'now' moves — tomorrow becomes today the next day) and the relational before/after. These are learned by talking through the daily routine, retelling sequences and stories, and anchoring words to concrete remembered and anticipated events — not by asking children to define words. Research describes deictic time words as acquired slowly and partially, so early slips are best treated as developmental rather than errors to drill.

activities.title: Order the day and slide the 'today' marker
feedback: If events are ordered by interest rather than time (e.g. the exciting event first), re-walk the actual order along the picture sequence, asking 'what happened right before this? what happened right after this?' — ground it in the concrete routine or story rather than labelling it wrong.

If the child swaps yesterday and tomorrow, anchor each word to a concrete event ('yesterday we had PE; tomorrow we go to the park') rather than correcting with a rule; these slips are expected at this age and resolve with exposure.
When the child narrates correctly, echo their words back to confirm: 'Yes — first wake up, next breakfast, last bed.'
After sliding the marker, prompt: 'Now that today has moved, what is yesterday? What is tomorrow?' so the shifting reference is rehearsed.
activities.rationale: A moveable 'today' marker makes the shifting deictic reference visible: sliding it and watching 'yesterday'/'tomorrow' re-label is a concrete way to rehearse the system that children otherwise learn implicitly from discourse. Drag-to-order supports sequencing as a natural action, whether for the daily routine or for retelling a story. The curriculum lists this vocabulary for Year 1, and the deictic shift is the documented difficulty.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils should 'sequence events in chronological order using language [for example, before and after, next, first, today, yesterday, tomorrow, morning, afternoon and evening]'; the bracketed vocabulary is illustrative (non-statutory), the statutory core being to sequence events chronologically using language.

Deictic time words are acquired slowly and partially: 3-year-olds perform at chance on deictic status, treating 'yesterday' and 'tomorrow' as merely 'non-present' before distinguishing past from future (so the two are readily interchanged); adult-like deictic status and sequential order emerge together and reach majority mastery before age 6 (status ~5;4, order ~5;8), while temporal remoteness develops independently and later, after age 7 (~7;3). Children PRODUCE these words around age 3 but do not comprehend them adult-like for several years, and they learn status/order from natural-language cues (tense, discourse) rather than explicit teaching — supporting treating early slips as developmental, not as errors to drill.
learnerActions: Put pictures of the day's events — wake up, breakfast, school, bed — into chronological order.
Narrate the ordered sequence aloud using 'first… next… last' (e.g. 'first we wake up, next we have breakfast, last we go to bed').
The same drag-to-order can be used with story-sequencing picture cards: retell a familiar story in order, not only the daily routine, narrating it with first/next/last.

On a scrolling strip of consecutive days with a moveable 'today' marker (e.g. Tuesday–Wednesday–Thursday), start with 'today' on the MIDDLE day so both neighbours are visible, and say what happened yesterday (the day before) and what will happen tomorrow (the day after).

Slide the view forward one day, keeping 'today' on the middle slot: the day that was 'tomorrow' is now 'today', the day that was 'today' is now 'yesterday', the oldest day slides off and a new day comes into view ahead, so all three relative labels stay represented and keep re-pointing.
activities.intendedInsight: Yesterday and tomorrow are not interchangeable words for 'a day that isn't today' — they name a definite place relative to where 'now' sits, and they re-point as 'today' moves. Sequencing follows real chronology, not how exciting an event is.

activities.title: Talk through your day with a character
feedback: Keep exchanges short and concrete for a 4-6 year old; follow the child's lead rather than quizzing.

If the child ties 'morning' or 'afternoon' to a particular activity rather than the time of day, gently re-anchor to the time of day itself — afternoon is the part of the day after the middle of the day (midday) until evening — and point out that several different activities can happen in the afternoon, so the label tracks the time, not one event.
Model correct use in the reply rather than correcting: if the child says 'yesterday' meaning tomorrow, respond with the concrete anchor ('oh, the park is tomorrow — the day that is coming!').
activities.rationale: Because the objective is USING the vocabulary in context, an in-role conversational partner is a proposed way to elicit authentic spoken production, which recognition or scoring alone does not capture. Research suggests children learn much about these terms from cues in everyday conversation, so modelling them in natural talk is a sensible approach.
sourceClaims: Deictic time words are acquired slowly and partially: 3-year-olds perform at chance on deictic status, treating 'yesterday' and 'tomorrow' as merely 'non-present' before distinguishing past from future (so the two are readily interchanged); adult-like deictic status and sequential order emerge together and reach majority mastery before age 6 (status ~5;4, order ~5;8), while temporal remoteness develops independently and later, after age 7 (~7;3). Children PRODUCE these words around age 3 but do not comprehend them adult-like for several years, and they learn status/order from natural-language cues (tense, discourse) rather than explicit teaching — supporting treating early slips as developmental, not as errors to drill.
learnerActions: Listen to a friendly character recount their own day in simple, concrete terms.
Tell the character what you did first and next in your own day.
Answer what you did yesterday and what you will do tomorrow, tied to real events you remember or expect.
Use 'morning' and 'afternoon' to say when something happened.
activities.intendedInsight: Time words are tools for talking about real, remembered and anticipated events — using them in authentic exchange is the goal, not reciting definitions.

activities.title: Name the parts of the day (naming scaffold)
feedback: If a child fixes 'afternoon' to a single activity, show the same part of the day with different activities so the label tracks the time, not the event.
Use this as a naming warm-up, then move to ordering and live narration where the child must actually use the words.
activities.rationale: A static tap-to-reveal timeline names the parts of the day usefully, but it does not let the child sequence events or experience the deictic shift, so it serves as a vocabulary scaffold rather than the full objective.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils should 'sequence events in chronological order using language [for example, before and after, next, first, today, yesterday, tomorrow, morning, afternoon and evening]'; the bracketed vocabulary is illustrative (non-statutory), the statutory core being to sequence events chronologically using language.
learnerActions: Tap parts of a daily-timeline picture to reveal labels — morning, afternoon, evening.
Match everyday activities to the time of day they usually happen.
Say when each shown activity happens using 'morning', 'afternoon' or 'evening'.
activities.intendedInsight: The day has named parts tied to the time of day, not to which single activity happens.

activities.title: Order a novel set of events
feedback: The shuffled-pictures item reveals a child who sequences by interest rather than time: re-walk the real order along the timeline.
The fresh-anchor deictic item separates a child who holds the system (answers shift correctly around 'today') from one who uses yesterday/tomorrow interchangeably for 'not-today'.
Probe gently if needed: 'You said tomorrow — is that the day that is coming, or the day that has finished?'; 'What do you do BEFORE you come to school, and what do you do AFTER?'
activities.rationale: Ordering and matching can be scored, but a fixed task cannot assess spontaneous USE in live context, which is the crux — so keep listening for correct use in the flow of talk. Using a novel set and a fresh anchor is intended to test transfer rather than a rehearsed routine.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils should 'sequence events in chronological order using language [for example, before and after, next, first, today, yesterday, tomorrow, morning, afternoon and evening]'; the bracketed vocabulary is illustrative (non-statutory), the statutory core being to sequence events chronologically using language.
learnerActions: Order a set of shuffled routine pictures (e.g. wake up, school, bed) into chronological order.
Narrate them with 'first', 'next', 'last' in true time order.
Match given activities to morning/afternoon/evening.

Answer a fresh-anchor deictic question, e.g. 'If today is Friday, is tomorrow a school day or the weekend?' (use this only where Saturday is a non-school weekend day for the child; otherwise choose days that match the child's own school week).
activities.intendedInsight: Demonstrate that sequencing and deictic reasoning transfer to a new, unrehearsed set of events and a fresh 'today' anchor.

constraints: Teach by modelling and eliciting USE; never ask a 4-6 year old to define a time word.
Anchor in the child's own daily routine, shared class events and familiar stories, and revisit the terms daily so the shifting deictic meaning is rehearsed in context.
Tie yesterday/today/tomorrow to concrete markers — what we DID and what we WILL do.
Anchor morning/afternoon/evening to the time of day, not to a single activity: afternoon is the time after midday until evening, and many different activities can happen then.

Treat early slips (swapping yesterday/tomorrow, reversing before/after, sequencing by salience) as developmental, expected and self-correcting with age and exposure — not as errors to drill or confront with a rule.
The static part-of-day timeline is a naming scaffold only: it does not let the child sequence or experience the deictic shift, so do not rely on it for the full objective.
Scored ordering/matching tasks cannot assess spontaneous spoken use in live context; combine them with listening for correct use in conversation.
Keep conversational exchanges short, concrete and child-led for this age range.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row. Sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified; the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Story-sequencing picture cards / story retelling, present in the original keyRepresentations and bestPractices, was missing from the prior candidate and has been restored as a drag-to-order alternative in the first activity.

The original rated a 3D artefact 'poor' with the claim '3D adds nothing'; this universal claim has been dropped — ordering events in time is not inherently spatial, but the source does not establish that 3D can never help, so no comparative-efficacy claim is asserted either way.

The original framed the conversational artefact as 'strong' and the 2D interactive as the single ideal; this rewrite preserves both as distinct activities with different purposes (deictic-shift visualisation vs authentic spoken use) rather than ranking them.

One source (Harner 1975) is marked verified:false in the row and is cited via later reviews; its specific finding (children confuse yesterday with tomorrow but not with today) is not used as an exact sourceClaim and is noted as supporting background only.

The mastery ages cited (status ~5;4, order ~5;8, remoteness ~7;3) sit partly inside and above this 4-6 band; teachers should expect many children in range to be mid-acquisition, consistent with the 'treat slips as developmental' guidance.

The prior candidate's morning/afternoon re-anchor example tied 'afternoon' to lunch and conflated midday with afternoon; it is corrected to anchor on the time of day with varied activities. The consecutive-day strip keeps 'today' on the middle slot and scrolls so yesterday and tomorrow stay represented before and after sliding.

probeDeeper: 'You said tomorrow — is that the day that is coming, or the day that has finished?'
'If today is Friday, is tomorrow a school day or the weekend?' (deictic reasoning on a fresh anchor)
'What do you do BEFORE you come to school — and what do you do AFTER?'
assess.correctAnswer: Uses 'morning' and 'after' correctly while narrating; correctly names yesterday as the day before and tomorrow as the day after today; orders the three events and narrates them with first/next/last in true chronological order.

errorPatterns.pattern: Swaps yesterday and tomorrow, using either loosely for 'a day that isn't today'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach or correct this with a rule — deictic time words (yesterday/today/tomorrow) resolve with age and exposure, so treat slips as expected, not as an error. Instead, anchor each word to a concrete event ('yesterday we had PE; tomorrow we go to the park') and use them daily in routine talk.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 'yesterday' when meaning tomorrow (or the reverse), or uses them at random

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses before/after, or uses 'next' to mean the last thing
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not confront this as an error or drill a rule — sequence ordering firms up with maturation. Instead, narrate the real sequence while pointing along a timeline strip ('this comes BEFORE this') and rehearse it in context.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 'we brush teeth after we go to bed', or picks the wrong relatum when ordering

errorPatterns.pattern: Sequences by salience or interest rather than chronology (puts the exciting event first)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not treat this as a misunderstanding to correct — it self-corrects with exposure. Instead, re-walk the actual order against the daily timeline, asking 'what happened right before / right after this?', grounding it in the concrete routine.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the shuffled pictures orders them by preference, then narrates out of true order

responseLevels.gap: Uses time words at random or interchangeably (yesterday = tomorrow); orders events by interest rather than time.
responseLevels.full: Uses the full set (first/next/last, before/after, yesterday/today/tomorrow, morning/afternoon/evening) correctly in narration, shifts yesterday/tomorrow appropriately as 'today' changes, and sequences a novel set of events chronologically.
responseLevels.partial: Uses first/next/last and before/after correctly for a concrete, rehearsed routine, but slips on yesterday/tomorrow or on a novel sequence.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In the flow of talk about the day and week, listen for correct USE (never ask the child to define a word): (1) 'Tell me what you do in the morning, and what you do after that.' (2) Pointing at a day-strip: 'Today is Wednesday. What did we do yesterday? What will we do tomorrow?' (3) Show three shuffled routine pictures (wake up, school, bed): 'Put these in order and tell me what happens first, next and last.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The yesterday/tomorrow item separates a child who holds the deictic system (whose answers shift correctly around 'today') from one who uses the words interchangeably for 'not-today'; the shuffled-pictures item catches a child who sequences by interest rather than by time.

sources.claim: Year 1 pupils should 'sequence events in chronological order using language [for example, before and after, next, first, today, yesterday, tomorrow, morning, afternoon and evening]'; the bracketed vocabulary is illustrative (non-statutory), the statutory core being to sequence events chronologically using language.
sources.source: National Curriculum in England: Mathematics, Year 1 Measurement (statutory), gov.uk

sources.claim: Deictic time words are acquired slowly and partially: 3-year-olds perform at chance on deictic status, treating 'yesterday' and 'tomorrow' as merely 'non-present' before distinguishing past from future (so the two are readily interchanged); adult-like deictic status and sequential order emerge together and reach majority mastery before age 6 (status ~5;4, order ~5;8), while temporal remoteness develops independently and later, after age 7 (~7;3). Children PRODUCE these words around age 3 but do not comprehend them adult-like for several years, and they learn status/order from natural-language cues (tense, discourse) rather than explicit teaching — supporting treating early slips as developmental, not as errors to drill.
sources.source: Tillman, Marghetis, Barner & Srinivasan (2017), 'Today is tomorrow's yesterday: Children's acquisition of deictic time words', Cognitive Psychology 92, 87-100

sources.claim: In a toy-hiding comprehension study, 3-year-olds understood 'yesterday' and 'tomorrow' as referring to non-present times and made errors confusing yesterday with tomorrow, but not with today — the classic demonstration that children first grasp 'not now' before differentiating past from future.
sources.source: Harner, L. (1975), 'Yesterday and tomorrow: development of early understanding of the terms', Developmental Psychology 11, 864-865 (classic primary source; cited via later reviews)

pedagogy.summary: This is the iteration idea: a/b is built by counting copies of the unit fraction 1/b — 3/5 is 'three one-fifths', 7/4 is 'seven one-quarters'. It reframes a fraction from a static shaded region into a COUNT of equal units, exactly parallel to how a whole number is a count of ones. The pivotal move is that the count can pass the whole: iterating 1/4 past the fourth copy (4/4 = 1) gives 5/4, 6/4, 7/4 — improper fractions that are perfectly ordinary numbers with a home on the number line. This unit-fraction-as-building-block view is the seed of adding fractions with like denominators (join the counts), of multiplication (a/b = a × 1/b), and of mixed numbers.
bestPractices: Teach 1/b as the unit you iterate, then build a/b by repeated addition of that unit — '1/5, 2/5, 3/5' spoken as 'one fifth, two fifths, three fifths' so the count is audible.
Use the number line as the primary model: start at 0 and make equal jumps of 1/b, landing on a/b; this makes iteration a physical count and naturally continues past 1 into improper fractions.
Deliberately cross the whole: iterate 1/4 to 4/4 = 1 and keep going to 5/4, 6/4, 7/4, so improper fractions arise as the natural continuation of counting units, not as a strange new object.

Link the count to notation: the numerator IS the number of unit-fraction copies, the denominator names the unit — so 7/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + ... (seven times), and adding like fractions just adds the counts.
Contrast unit-counting with the wrong move of adding denominators (1/4 + 1/4 = 2/8): on the line, two quarter-jumps land at 2/4, not at a smaller point, refuting it visually.
keyRepresentations: Number line with equal 1/b jumps from 0, continuing past 1 (0, 1/4, 2/4, 3/4, 4/4=1, 5/4, 6/4, 7/4)
Fraction strips / identical unit tiles laid end to end (seven 1/4-tiles making 7/4)
Repeated-addition equation 7/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4
Bar model spanning more than one whole to show 7/4 as one whole plus three more quarters (1 3/4)
Skip-counting sequence in unit-fraction language ('one-fifth, two-fifths, three-fifths...')
commonMisconceptions: Believing a fraction must be less than 1, so an improper fraction like 7/4 'isn't a real/proper number' or must be an error.
Adding denominators when joining unit fractions: 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/8 rather than 2/4.
Whole-number bias in placing improper fractions: reading 7/4 as near 7 (or treating the 7 as the dominant number) rather than as seven quarters just past 1 3/4.
Losing the unit: writing 3/5 = 1/5 + 1/5 + 1/5 but unable to say the denominator stays 5 because each part is the same size 1/5.
Thinking the number line 'stops' at 1 for fractions, so not continuing the jumps past the whole.

learn.summary: Teach a/b as a COUNT of unit fractions 1/b: 3/5 is 'three one-fifths', 7/4 is 'seven one-quarters'. The pivotal move is letting the count pass the whole — iterating 1/4 past 4/4 = 1 to 5/4, 6/4, 7/4, landing exactly on 1 3/4 — so improper fractions appear as the ordinary continuation of counting equal units on the number line, not a strange new object. This unit-as-building-block view seeds like-denominator addition (join the counts), multiplication (a/b = a × 1/b), and mixed numbers.

activities.title: Stamp the unit-fraction jumps and cross the whole
feedback: If a learner expects to stop at 1: iterate 1/4 aloud past 4/4 — 5/4, 6/4, 7/4 — each is one more quarter landing on a definite point; a/b counts copies of 1/b, so the count can exceed the denominator.

If two quarter-jumps are placed at a smaller point (2/8 thinking): on the line, two equal 1/4-jumps land at 2/4, not somewhere smaller; each jump is the SAME unit, so joining counts adds numerators while the unit (denominator) stays 4.
If 7/4 is placed far right near 7: count the seven small quarter-jumps together — they reach only 1 3/4, not near 7; the denominator sets the size of each counted unit.
Reinforce: at the fourth jump the point is 4/4 = 1 whole, and counting does not have to stop there.
activities.rationale: Letting the learner iterate the unit themselves and watch both count and position update makes iteration a physical, audible act and makes the crossing of the whole visible — the point where improper fractions stop being strange. A live count/value tally and growing equation make the numerator=number-of-copies link concrete. Live manipulation is proposed as a way to let the learner build the count by their own action; a pre-built illustration (below) conveys the same decomposition but without the learner's own iteration.
sourceClaims: Students should understand a fraction a/b as the quantity formed by a parts of size 1/b — i.e. a/b is built by iterating the unit fraction 1/b — and this includes fractions greater than 1; the number line is the recommended representation for building fractions by iterating unit fractions and for showing that fractions extend past 1.
Pupils should understand a fraction a/b as a sum of unit fractions 1/b (e.g. 3/5 = 1/5 + 1/5 + 1/5) and connect this to multiplication of a unit fraction by a whole number.
learnerActions: Work on a number line marked 0 to 2 with whole-number anchors at 1 and 2.
Add one 1/4 jump at a time starting from 0, saying each landing aloud: 'one quarter, two quarters, three quarters'.
Keep a running record that shows BOTH the count (number of copies) and the value n/4, alongside a growing equation 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 ...
On the fourth jump, notice the marker lands exactly on 1 and the tally reads 4/4; then deliberately keep going — tap again to step to 5/4, past the whole, still a definite point on the line.
Continue to the seventh jump, landing exactly on 1 3/4, with the equation showing seven 1/4's and the side note 7/4 = 1/4 × 7.

Switch the unit to 1/3 and repeat while keeping the whole-number anchors 1 and 2 fixed, counting up to six jumps (6/3 = 2) on this 0–2 line. To continue to seven jumps (7/3 = 2 1/3), extend the line past 2 first. Each jump is now larger: three third-jumps reach the same point 1 that four quarter-jumps reached.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction a/b is just a count of equal units 1/b; nothing forces the count to stop at the whole, so improper fractions like 7/4 are ordinary points on the line. The denominator names the size of the unit you are counting.

activities.title: Walk through a pre-built iteration and read the decomposition
feedback: If the learner thinks the count must stop at 1: point to the flap at 4/4 and the jumps beyond it — the sequence continues to 5/4, 6/4, 7/4.
If the learner loses the unit: have them restate that every tile and every jump is 1/4, so the denominator stays 4 the whole way.
activities.rationale: A pre-built reveal communicates the decomposition and crossing-the-whole clearly and is useful when a live iterator is unavailable; its limit is that the count is pre-baked rather than built by the learner's own action, so pair it with construction when possible.
sourceClaims: Students should understand a fraction a/b as the quantity formed by a parts of size 1/b — i.e. a/b is built by iterating the unit fraction 1/b — and this includes fractions greater than 1; the number line is the recommended representation for building fractions by iterating unit fractions and for showing that fractions extend past 1.
learnerActions: Study a 0–2 number line showing seven quarter-jumps, revealing the running total jump by jump (1/4, 2/4, ... 7/4).
At the 4/4 mark, read the flap '= 1 whole, keep going' and continue tracing to 7/4.
Read the side card showing 7/4 = 1/4 × 7 and 7/4 = 1 3/4.
Lay out seven identical quarter-tiles end to end and match them to the seven jumps, then state in words that each part is the same size 1/4.
activities.intendedInsight: Seven copies of 1/4 decompose 7/4, the count continues naturally past 1, and 7/4 equals exactly 1 3/4 — the same unit-count read from a worked layout.

activities.title: Predict-then-check: where do seven quarter-jumps land?
feedback: Full understanding looks like: seven equal 1/4-jumps passing 4/4 = 1 without pause to land exactly on 1 3/4, 7/4 written as seven 1/4's, and 7/4 justified as a real number because it is seven copies of the unit 1/4 — a definite point — with the same reasoning transferred to 7/3 on request.
Partial understanding: iterates and writes the sum correctly but hesitates to cross the whole, or places 7/4 correctly yet cannot explain WHY in terms of counting units.

If the learner says 7/4 'isn't a real fraction' or 'isn't a number', or stops at 1: iterate aloud past 4/4 — 5/4, 6/4, 7/4 — each one more quarter on a definite point. (7/4 is indeed an improper fraction, but it is still a real number.)
If the learner writes 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/8 or growing denominators: show two 1/4-jumps landing at 2/4 and re-establish that joining equal units adds numerators while the unit stays 4.
activities.rationale: The reason behind the prediction is the diagnostic part: a learner expecting the jumps to stop at or before 1 reveals the fraction-must-be-less-than-1 belief. The second-tier 'how do you know it's a number' separates lucky placement from understanding. This surfaces outcomes and misconceptions rather than teaching the iteration, so it complements, not replaces, the construction activity.
sourceClaims: Students should understand a fraction a/b as the quantity formed by a parts of size 1/b — i.e. a/b is built by iterating the unit fraction 1/b — and this includes fractions greater than 1; the number line is the recommended representation for building fractions by iterating unit fractions and for showing that fractions extend past 1.
learnerActions: Before making any jumps, PREDICT where seven jumps of 1/4 from 0 will land — before 1, exactly on 1, or past 1 — and state WHY.
Iterate the seven quarter-jumps, crossing 4/4 = 1 and landing exactly on 1 3/4.
Explain any mismatch between the prediction and the result.

Answer probing questions: Why doesn't 7/4 land near 7 when there's a 7 in it? If it were 7/3 instead of 7/4, would the jumps be bigger or smaller, and would you land further from or closer to 0, and why? When you write 7/4 as seven 1/4's, why does the bottom number stay 4 and not grow? At the fourth jump you reached exactly 1 — what is that point as a fraction, and why doesn't counting have to stop there?
Write 7/4 as a sum of unit fractions and answer: is 7/4 a real number, and how do you know?
activities.intendedInsight: Stating a reason, not just a landing spot, reveals whether the learner holds the fraction-must-be-less-than-1 belief or the add-denominators error, and distinguishes a lucky correct placement from genuine understanding that 7/4 is a count of seven units.

activities.title: Spot and refute the add-denominators move
feedback: Correct: two 1/4-jumps land at 2/4 — adding denominators would wrongly shrink the result; each jump is the same 1/4.
If jumps shrink across the sum: re-establish that every term is the identical unit 1/4, so the size does not change as you add more.

In ordering 3/4, 5/4, 7/4, 9/4: 7/4 sits between 5/4 and 9/4 and lands at exactly 1 3/4 on the line, while 9/4 lands at 2 1/4 (just past 2) — compare by the count of quarters, not the numerator against unrelated wholes.
activities.rationale: Contrasting unit-counting with the common add-denominators error and refuting it visually on the line targets a specific, documented misconception directly; the number line makes the equal-size units concrete.
sourceClaims: Students should understand a fraction a/b as the quantity formed by a parts of size 1/b — i.e. a/b is built by iterating the unit fraction 1/b — and this includes fractions greater than 1; the number line is the recommended representation for building fractions by iterating unit fractions and for showing that fractions extend past 1.
learnerActions: Consider the claim 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/8 and test it on the number line by making two equal quarter-jumps from 0.
Mark where the two jumps actually land and compare it with where 2/8 would sit.
State in your own words why joining two copies of the same unit gives 2/4, not 2/8.

Answer a quick check: 5/8 = 1/8 + 1/8 + __ (fill the remaining 1/8 terms to make five eighths — three more are needed); then order 3/4, 5/4, 7/4, 9/4 on a line long enough to reach 9/4 (use a 0–3 line, since 9/4 = 2 1/4 lies past 2).
activities.intendedInsight: Joining unit fractions keeps the unit (denominator) fixed and adds the counts (numerators); the jumps stay the same size.

constraints: Use the number line as the primary model with equal 1/b jumps from 0, extending past 1 so improper fractions arise as the natural continuation of counting; this representation is recommended by the cited guide.
Speak the count aloud ('one fifth, two fifths, three fifths') so the iteration is audible and the numerator is heard as the number of copies.
Deliberately cross the whole (4/4 = 1, then 5/4, 6/4, 7/4) rather than stopping at 1.

Keep the denominator fixed while counting copies of a unit. If the denominator changes, keep the whole-number anchors fixed and change the jump size: thirds reach1 in three jumps, quarters in four jumps.
When a task uses values beyond a whole (e.g. ordering up to 9/4 = 2 1/4), draw the line long enough to contain them rather than clipping to 0–2.
A pre-built reveal or worked illustration conveys the decomposition but does not have the learner iterate themselves; pair it with learner construction when possible.
Unit tiles and fraction strips are physical approximations of the ideal equal jumps; keep each tile the same size to represent equal units.

A quiz or fill-in check can verify the outcome (expressing a/b as a sum, placing an improper fraction), but recognition or selection alone may not elicit the learner's own construction of the sum or placement; use such checks alongside tasks where the learner builds and justifies, not as the sole learning surface.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One listed source (DfE National Curriculum) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its claim as unconfirmed.

The original row rated in-role dialogue and 3D rendering as 'poor' fit; these were catalog fit judgements, not pedagogical laws. They are reframed as narrowly scoped observations (iterating a unit along a line is inherently 1D/planar; a narrating character adds little over learner-built iteration) rather than universal claims that such media cannot teach.

Arithmetic checked: 7/4 = 1 3/4 EXACTLY (one whole plus three quarters), so seven 1/4-jumps land ON 1 3/4, not 'just past' it; seven 1/4's sum to 7/4; two 1/4's sum to 2/4; after two 1/8 terms, three further 1/8 terms are needed to total 5/8; 9/4 = 2 1/4. The ordering feedback references the set's actual neighbours (5/4 and 9/4) and now uses a 0–3 line so 9/4 fits.
The original row's probeDeeper and correctAnswer described 7/4 as a point 'just past 1 3/4'; this is an original error (7/4 = 1 3/4 exactly) and has been corrected in all learner-facing text here.
The add-denominators distractor (1/4 + 1/4 = 2/8, or 7/4 = 7/28) is intentionally presented only as a wrong move to refute, never as a valid answer.
Recognition/selection checks are scoped as not themselves eliciting independent construction (an observable affordance limit), not as a categorical 'quiz only assesses' claim.

assess.poeTask: Before making any jumps, ask the child to PREDICT where seven jumps of 1/4 from 0 will land: before 1, exactly on 1, or past 1 — and to say WHY. The stated reason is the diagnostic part: a child expecting it to stop at or before 1 reveals the fraction-must-be-less-than-1 belief. Then iterate the seven quarter-jumps together, crossing 4/4 = 1 and landing at 1 3/4, and have the child explain the mismatch with their prediction.
probeDeeper: You made seven jumps and landed just past 1 3/4. Why doesn't 7/4 land near 7, when there's a 7 in it?
What if the fraction had been 7/3 instead of 7/4 — would your jumps be bigger or smaller, and would you land further from or closer to 0? Why?
When you write 7/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + ... seven times, why does the bottom number stay 4 the whole way and not grow?
At the fourth jump you reached exactly 1. What is that point as a fraction, and why does the counting not have to stop there?
assess.correctAnswer: Seven equal jumps of 1/4 from 0, landing at 1 3/4; 7/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4. Yes, 7/4 is a real number — it is seven quarters, a definite point just past 1 3/4 on the line.

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes a fraction must be less than 1, so 7/4 'isn't a proper number' or must be a mistake — stops the jumps at 1.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Iterate 1/4 aloud past 4/4 on the line: 5/4, 6/4, 7/4 — each is just one more quarter and lands on a definite point. Reteach that a/b counts copies of 1/b, so the count can exceed the denominator.
errorPatterns.distractor: 7/4 isn't a proper number — the top can't be bigger than the bottom, so it must be written a different way.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Refuses to place 7/4 beyond 1, or says it should be written only as a mixed number because '7/4 isn't allowed'; answers the second tier with 'it's not a real fraction'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds denominators when summing unit fractions: 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/8, so the sum can never build to 7/4.
errorPatterns.nextMove: On the line, two 1/4-jumps land at 2/4, not at a smaller 2/8 point. Re-establish that each jump is the SAME unit 1/4, so joining counts adds numerators while the denominator (the unit) stays 4.
errorPatterns.distractor: 7/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + ... = 7/28, because you add the bottoms too.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 7/4 as a sum whose terms have growing denominators, or claims 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/8; the jumps get smaller instead of staying equal.

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number bias: places 7/4 near 7 (or treats the 7 as dominant) rather than as seven quarters just past 1 3/4.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the quarters together onto the line so 7/4 is felt as seven small jumps reaching only 1 3/4. Contrast with 7 whole-ones. Reteach that the denominator sets the size of each counted unit.
errorPatterns.distractor: 7/4 is close to 7 on the number line.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Marks 7/4 far to the right near 7, or orders it as if larger than 6/4-and-under by the numerator alone without regard to the unit.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot build a/b by iterating 1/b; stops at 1, denies 7/4 is a number, or adds denominators so the sum never reaches 7/4. Reads the numerator as a whole-number magnitude.
responseLevels.full: Makes seven equal 1/4-jumps, passes 4/4 = 1 without pause to land at 1 3/4, writes 7/4 as the sum of seven 1/4's, and justifies 7/4 as a real number because it is seven copies of the unit 1/4 — a definite point on the line. Explains the denominator names the unit being counted and transfers the reasoning to a different unit (e.g. 7/3) on request.
responseLevels.partial: Iterates 1/b correctly and writes 7/4 as seven 1/4's, but hesitates at or cannot justify crossing the whole, or places 7/4 correctly yet cannot explain WHY it is a legitimate number in terms of counting units — lists the copies without the relational 'count of a unit' reason.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show 7/4 on a number line from 0 to 2 by making equal jumps, and write 7/4 as a sum of unit fractions. Then tell me: is 7/4 a real number, and how do you know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands iteration counts seven equal 1/4-units, passes 4/4 = 1 without stopping, and defends 7/4 as an ordinary number. A child who believes fractions must be less than 1 balks at the improper form, stops at 1, or declares 7/4 'not proper'. A child who adds denominators writes 1/4+1/4=2/8 and cannot make the sum reach 7/4. The second tier — 'how do you know it's a number' — separates a lucky correct placement from genuine understanding of the unit-count.

sources.claim: Students should understand a fraction a/b as the quantity formed by a parts of size 1/b — i.e. a/b is built by iterating the unit fraction 1/b — and this includes fractions greater than 1; the number line is the recommended representation for building fractions by iterating unit fractions and for showing that fractions extend past 1.
sources.source: IES/WWC Practice Guide: Developing Effective Fractions Instruction for Kindergarten Through 8th Grade (Siegler et al., 2010; NCEE 2010-4039), Recommendation 2 and Recommendation 1

sources.claim: Pupils should understand a fraction a/b as a sum of unit fractions 1/b (e.g. 3/5 = 1/5 + 1/5 + 1/5) and connect this to multiplication of a unit fraction by a whole number.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics Programmes of Study, Year 4–5 Fractions

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 6–7 (UK Y2, US Grade 2). Recognising odd and even numbers — a first structural property of number, tied to the 2s table and divisibility by 2.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2 'recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 2, 5 and 10 multiplication tables, including recognising odd and even numbers'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.OA.3 'determine whether a group of objects (up to 20) has an odd or even number of members, e.g. by pairing objects or counting them by 2s; write an equation to express an even number as a sum of two equal addends'.
• Operational details: define even/odd by the PAIRING test — even = can be split into pairs with none left over (= 2×something); odd = exactly one left unpaired. Connect to the 2s table (even numbers ARE the multiples of 2) and to the ones-digit rule (ends in 0,2,4,6,8 = even). Note 0 is even.
• Checkpoint: classify by structure. Tier A (6): pair up counters and say odd or even for numbers to 10. Tier B (6–7): classify numbers to 20 and state the ones-digit rule. Tier C (7): explain even as 'two equal groups / 2×n' and why 0 is even.
bestPractices: Define odd/even by pairing objects (or making two equal rows), not by memorised endings first — even means everything pairs up with none left over; odd leaves exactly one.
Connect even numbers to the 2s multiplication table and to '2 × something' / two equal addends, so odd/even is understood as a multiplicative/divisibility property, not an arbitrary label.
Derive the ones-digit rule (ends in 0,2,4,6,8) from the pairing pattern rather than teaching it as a bare fact, and apply it to larger numbers.
Explicitly address that 0 is even (zero objects pair perfectly — none left over) and that odd/even has nothing to do with how big a number is.
Use the hundred square to see even/odd as alternating columns, reinforcing the pattern visually (links to the 2s skip-count pattern).
keyRepresentations: Pairing counters into twos (leftover = odd)
Two equal rows / the 2s array (even = two equal groups)
Ten-frame (full pairs vs one lonely counter)
Hundred square with even numbers shaded (alternating columns)
commonMisconceptions: Thinking odd/even is about a number's SIZE rather than divisibility by 2.
Forgetting that 0 is even.
Judging by the first (leading) digit instead of the ones digit.
Believing a number could be both odd and even, or neither.
Not connecting even numbers to the 2s table / '2×n' — treating the ending rule as unrelated to multiplication.

learn.summary: For ages 6–7 (UK Y2 / US Grade 2), teach odd and even as a structural property of number: even means a count can be split fully into pairs (or two equal groups) with none left over (= 2×something); odd leaves exactly one unpaired. Build the meaning by pairing physical or on-screen counters, connect it to the 2s table and the ones-digit pattern (ends in 0,2,4,6,8), and make clear that 0 is even and that odd/even has nothing to do with a number's size.

activities.title: Pairing machine: pair the counters and spot the leftover
feedback: When a number pairs cleanly, name it: 'Every counter has a partner — that's EVEN, two equal groups of the same size.'
When one is left over, point to it: 'That single counter with no partner is exactly what ODD means.'
On a ten-frame: 'See the filled pairs — if one cell sits alone with no partner, the number is odd.'
After several tests, highlight the shaded hundred square: 'See how even numbers fall in the same columns and all end in 0, 2, 4, 6, 8? That pattern comes from the pairing.'
For 0: 'No counters, so nothing is left over — zero pairs perfectly, so 0 is even.'
If a learner splits 7 into 3 and 4 and calls it even, line the two piles up one-to-one: 'The groups have to match exactly. One counter has no partner, so 7 is odd.'
activities.rationale: Odd/even is defined by the action of pairing, so letting children run the test themselves lets the leftover (the meaning of odd) be seen directly, and lets the digit rule be discovered from the pattern rather than memorised. A ten-frame, an on-screen pairing control with live hundred-square shading, and a two-equal-rows toggle are optional ways to make the pairing mechanism and its link to the 2s table concrete; equivalent work with real counters achieves the same.
sourceClaims: 2.OA.3 determine whether a group (up to 20) is odd or even by pairing or counting by 2s; write an even number as a sum of two equal addends.
learnerActions: Choose a quantity of counters (start with numbers to 10, then extend to 20).
Pair the counters up into twos — physically with real counters, or by tapping a 'pair up' control if using a screen model.
Optionally lay the counters on a ten-frame to see full pairs versus one lonely counter.
Decide: if every counter has a partner, the number is EVEN; if exactly one counter is left on its own, the number is ODD.
Test number after number and watch the result build on a hundred square (even numbers shaded) so the alternating-column / ends-in-0,2,4,6,8 pattern appears.
Use a '2×n' / two-equal-rows view to see each even number as two equal groups, linking it to the 2s table.
Test 0: zero counters, zero left over — so 0 is even.
activities.intendedInsight: Even means everything pairs up with none left over (two equal groups / 2×n); odd means exactly one is left unpaired. The ones-digit rule and the 2s table both come from this pairing structure, not from an arbitrary ending.

activities.title: Introduce with a paired vs leftover picture
feedback: Point to the leftover object: 'This one has no partner — that is what makes the set odd.'
On the hundred square: 'The shaded numbers all end in 0, 2, 4, 6, 8.'
activities.rationale: A fixed image can introduce the paired-vs-leftover contrast and the hundred-square pattern clearly. It cannot be re-run across many different numbers by the learner, so it works best as a first introduction or support alongside hands-on pairing where children test numbers themselves.
learnerActions: Look at a picture that contrasts a set whose objects all pair up (even) with a set that has one object left over (odd).
Tap or point to an even set to reveal its neat pairs; tap an odd set to reveal the single leftover.
Look at a hundred square with even numbers shaded to see the alternating pattern.
activities.intendedInsight: A set that pairs up completely is even; a set with one left over is odd — and even numbers fall in a regular pattern.

activities.title: Sort numbers and check the edge cases
feedback: For 0: 'Zero counters leave nothing over, so 0 is even.'

If a learner uses the first digit (e.g. calls 23 even because of the 2), redirect: 'Look at the ones digit — the tens always pair up, so the ones decide whether one counter is left over. 23 ends in 3, so it is odd.'
For two-digit numbers: 'Tens always pair up, so just check the ones digit.'
activities.rationale: Deliberate edge cases (0, large numbers, a leading-digit distractor) target the common errors that odd/even depends on size or the first digit. A sort can check and practise classification, but it can be answered by the digit rhyme alone without the pairing meaning, so it works best after that meaning is secure and alongside a show-or-explain step.
learnerActions: Sort a mix of numbers (including 0 and two-digit numbers to 20) into 'odd' and 'even' boxes.
Answer: is 0 odd or even? Explain why.
Find the number that breaks a stated rule, and resist a distractor that judges by the leading (first) digit instead of the ones digit.
activities.intendedInsight: The classification holds for every whole number, including0. In base ten, each ten can be paired fully, so the ones digit determines whether a counter remains unpaired; a number’s size or leading digit does not decide its parity.

activities.title: Predict before you pair: does adding one change it?
feedback: Strong reasoning sounds like: 'It will be odd, because the new one has no partner.'
If a learner cannot predict and only reports after counting, revisit pairing: 'Each pair needs two. One extra counter has nobody to pair with, so the total becomes odd.'
Confirm by pairing: '6 made 3 pairs; the 7th counter is left over, so 7 is odd.'
activities.rationale: Asking for the reason before observing distinguishes genuine pairing understanding from reciting the last-digit rule, which is the key diagnostic distinction for this topic.
learnerActions: Start with 6 counters (even). Before touching them, predict whether adding ONE more will keep it even or make it odd — and say why.
Add the counter and pair them up to check your prediction.
Explain the result using pairing: the new counter either finds a partner or is left alone.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding one counter to an even number leaves one unpaired, making it odd; the reason stated before checking shows whether a learner understands pairing or is only reading off a label afterwards.

constraints: Define odd/even by pairing (or making two equal rows) first; introduce the ones-digit rule as something derived from the pairing pattern, not as a bare fact to memorise.
Insist that the two groups be EQUAL and match one-to-one: splitting 7 into 3 and 4 does not make it even. Line the piles up so the unpaired counter is visible.
Explicitly address that 0 is even (zero counters, none left over) and that odd/even is independent of a number's size.
A paired-vs-leftover picture is an introduction/support: it cannot be run across many numbers by the learner, so pair it with hands-on testing.

A sorting/choice check can teach and check classification but may be answered by the digit rhyme alone; use it after the pairing meaning is secure, and include a show-or-explain step to confirm understanding.
Do not accept the last-digit rule as proof of understanding — ask the learner to show the pairing and explain why one is left over.
Recognition or labelling tasks do not by themselves show that a learner can construct and justify the pairing; include predict-and-explain or show-with-counters tasks.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original source asserted that a dialogue 'offers little a talking partner uniquely adds' and that '3D adds nothing' for this planar property; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the available sources and have been dropped rather than propagated. Spoken explanation (e.g. the predict-and-explain task) is in fact used here during teaching.

The original marked an on-screen pairing tool as the uniquely 'ideal' format; this has been softened to an optional way to make the mechanism concrete, since the sources do not establish comparative efficacy of one medium over hands-on counters.

The Y2 DfE curriculum statement ('recognising odd and even numbers' within the 2, 5 and 10 tables) is topic/coverage context only; it has been removed from activity sourceClaims because it asserts no teaching method, and is retained here solely as curriculum context. The 2s-table link remains as design rationale.
One source (CCSS 2.OA.3) is marked verified:false in the row; it is cited because it directly describes the pairing/counting-by-2s method, but its verification is unconfirmed.

Self-audit: pairing arithmetic checked — 8 = 4 pairs (even), 7 = 3 pairs + 1 leftover (odd), 6 = 3 pairs (even), adding 1 to 6 gives 7 (odd), 23 ends in 3 so is odd. The '3 and 4' split of 7 is correctly identified as unequal and therefore NOT evidence of evenness. The leading-digit distractor (e.g. 23 judged by the '2') is corrected to the ones-digit rule in the activity.

assess.poeTask: Give the child 6 counters (even) and ask them to predict, before touching them, whether adding ONE more counter will keep it even or make it odd — and to say why. Then add the counter and pair them up to check. The value is the reason stated before observing: a child who understands pairing predicts 'odd, because the new one has no partner'; a child on the digit-rule alone often cannot predict and only reads off afterwards.
probeDeeper: You paired them up. What does having one left over tell you about 7?
Is 10 odd or even? Can you tell without laying out ten counters?
If I add one more counter to an even pile, does it stay even? Why?
Someone split 7 into 3 and 4 and said it's even. What would you tell them?
assess.correctAnswer: 7 is odd, 8 is even. A child reasoning correctly pairs the counters up (or splits into two equal groups): 8 makes 4 pairs with none left over, so it is even; 7 makes 3 pairs with one left over, so it is odd — even means it can be shared into two equal groups (or all paired) with nothing left, odd leaves one.

errorPatterns.pattern: decides odd/even by counting-to-say only — knows the last-digit rule but cannot connect it to pairing; thinks 'even' just means 'a number you say when counting by twos'
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT accept the digit rule as proof — have the child pair the counters physically and name 'even = everyone has a partner, odd = one left alone'; connect it back to why the digits work only after the pairing meaning is secure.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child gives the right label but, asked to show it, cannot make the pairs relevant or says 'because it just is / because it ends in 8'

errorPatterns.pattern: thinks a number is even if it can be split into two groups AT ALL, ignoring that the groups must be EQUAL (splits 7 into 3 and 4 and calls it even)
errorPatterns.nextMove: insist the two groups match one-to-one; line the piles up side by side so the leftover in 7 is visibly unpaired.
errorPatterns.distractor: 7 is even (I can make two groups: 3 and 4)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child divides 7 into two unequal piles and declares it even 'because there are two groups'

errorPatterns.pattern: believes larger numbers are 'more even' or that odd/even alternates unreliably for big numbers — unsure whether e.g. 10 is even because 'it's a big number'
errorPatterns.nextMove: show that only the pairing of the LAST counter matters; group in tens (always even) and check the ones, so the rule scales.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child hesitates or guesses on two-digit numbers, treating the property as tied to size not structure

responseLevels.gap: labels by rote or guesses; cannot demonstrate with counters; or calls unequal-split numbers even.
responseLevels.full: shows even = full pairing / two equal groups and odd = one left over, explains the leftover as the defining feature, and extends the reasoning to larger numbers via the last digit.
responseLevels.partial: correctly pairs the counters and identifies odd/even for the presented numbers but relies on the last-digit rule for others with no link to pairing — cannot explain why the rule works.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are 7 counters. Is 7 odd or even? Now here are 8 counters — is 8 odd or even? For each one, show me with the counters how you can tell.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Many children label numbers odd/even purely by the last digit rhyme without any idea of WHY. Demanding they SHOW it with counters separates a memorised digit-rule from the pair/equal-share meaning. The child who only knows 'ends in 0,2,4,6,8' cannot demonstrate the leftover, and stumbles on the reason tier.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–10y; solve ×÷ problems USING knowledge of factors, multiples, squares and cubes (e.g. is 156 a multiple of 6? which two squares sum to 100? simplify 24×25 via factor pairs).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5 'solve problems involving multiplication and division including using their knowledge of factors and multiples, squares and cubes'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.OA.4 / 6.NS.4 (factors, multiples), 5.NBT.5–6 and 6.EE.1 (using structure/exponents) — applied within multiplicative problem solving.
• Operational details — this is the APPLICATION topic: number facts become STRATEGIC TOOLS. Three moves recur: (1) use divisibility/multiples to reason about membership ('156 a multiple of 6?' → divisible by 2 and 3); (2) use factor pairs to re-factor a hard product into an easy one (24×25 = 6×(4×25) = 6×100 = 600 — associativity + a friendly factor); (3) recall/search squares and cubes to solve puzzles (two squares summing to 100 → 36+64). The habit is to look for STRUCTURE before grinding an algorithm. Divisibility rules and the factor-rainbow support the reasoning; encourage justification.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): use a divisibility rule to test membership of a multiple. Tier B (age 9–10): simplify a product using factor pairs (16×25, 24×25) and find squares summing to a target. Tier C (age 10): choose the most efficient structural route for a calculation and justify it.
bestPractices: Frame number facts as strategic tools — re-factor a product into a friendly form (×25→×100÷4) using associativity, rather than computing directly.
Use divisibility rules (2,3,4,5,6,9,10) to reason about multiples and justify membership ('156 = even and digit-sum 12 divisible by 3, so ÷6').
Draw on the factor rainbow and known squares/cubes as a search space for puzzle-type problems.
Prompt 'is there a smarter route?' before any long calculation, building the look-for-structure habit.
Require justification and checking, not just an answer, so reasoning is explicit.
keyRepresentations: Factor rainbow / factor pairs — the re-factoring toolkit
Divisibility-rule checklist — reasoning about multiples
Array/area re-partition — showing 24×25 as 6×(4×25)
Squares/cubes list — search space for sum/target puzzles
commonMisconceptions: Grinding the standard algorithm instead of spotting a factor-pair shortcut.
Misapplying divisibility rules (e.g. thinking any even number is a multiple of 6).
Re-factoring incorrectly (breaking associativity: 24×25 ≠ 24×4×25).
Confusing factors, multiples, squares and cubes when selecting a tool.
Not justifying membership/answers, so errors go unchecked.

learn.summary: For ages 9–10: solve multiplication and division problems by USING knowledge of factors, multiples, squares and cubes as strategic tools, rather than grinding a written algorithm. Three recurring moves: (1) use divisibility rules to reason about whether a number is a multiple (e.g. is 156 a multiple of 6?); (2) re-factor a hard product into a friendly one using associativity (24×25 = 6×(4×25) = 6×100 = 600); (3) recall or search squares and cubes to solve puzzles (two squares summing to 100 → 36+64). The central habit is to scan for exploitable structure before reaching for a procedure, and to justify answers rather than just state them.

activities.title: Re-factoring: turn an ugly product into a friendly one
feedback: If a learner sets up long multiplication, prompt: 'Which two factors here make a round number?' then let them pull that factor out and re-pair it.
If a learner writes 24×25 = 24×4×25, flag that this changes the value: 24 must be split (24 = 6×4) before the 4 is moved, so it is 6×4×25, not 24×4×25.

When the re-group is correct, ask them to name the rule they used (associativity) and to sanity-check the answer against a rough estimate — e.g. round 24 up to 25, so 24×25 is a little under 25×25 = 625, which makes 600 a sensible result, confirming 6×100 = 600.
activities.rationale: Re-factoring products using associativity and a friendly factor is an efficient strategy worth teaching explicitly; manipulating the factors can make the structural insight concrete, and in an interactive setup the total can be shown to stay constant as the grouping changes.
sourceClaims: Re-factoring products using associativity and a friendly factor, and divisibility-rule reasoning, are efficient strategies to teach explicitly.
learnerActions: Face a product such as 24×25 and, before calculating, ask: which factors could pair up to make a round number?
Split one factor and re-group: pull a 4 out of 24 (so 24 = 6×4) and pair it with 25 to make 4×25 = 100, leaving 6×100 = 600.
Confirm the total is unchanged by the rearrangement — only the grouping changed, not the value (associativity).
Try the same move on 16×25 (= 4×(4×25) = 4×100 = 400) and other products with a friendly hidden factor.
State in words why the shortcut works and when it does NOT help (if no factor pairs to a round number).
activities.intendedInsight: A fearsome-looking product often never needs a written algorithm: spotting a friendly factor pair (like 4×25 = 100) and using associativity collapses it to a one-step mental calculation. Rearranging factors leaves the total unchanged.

activities.title: Divisibility detective: is it a multiple of 6?
feedback: If a learner says 156 is a multiple of 6 just because it is even, give the counterexample 8 (even, not a multiple of 6) and establish both conditions are needed.
If a learner relies only on the digit-sum (÷3) test, give the counterexample 9 (passes ÷3, not a multiple of 6).
If the strategy is right but the digit sum is miscalculated, do not reteach the method — ask them to re-add the digits and re-check.
activities.rationale: Using divisibility rules (2, 3, 6) to justify multiple-membership makes reasoning explicit and targets the common error of testing only one condition; a counterexample directly addresses the 'even means multiple of 6' slip.
sourceClaims: Factors/multiples (4.OA.4, 6.NS.4) and structural strategies underpin efficient multiplicative problem solving.
Re-factoring products using associativity and a friendly factor, and divisibility-rule reasoning, are efficient strategies to teach explicitly.
learnerActions: Test whether 156 is a multiple of 6 WITHOUT long division, by checking the rule for 2 (even?) and the rule for 3 (digit sum a multiple of 3?).
For 156: it is even (passes ÷2) and its digits sum to 1+5+6 = 12, a multiple of 3 (passes ÷3), so it passes BOTH and IS a multiple of 6 (check: 6×26 = 156).
Explain why passing only one test is not enough, using a counterexample: 9 is divisible by 3 but is NOT a multiple of 6; 8 is even but NOT a multiple of 6.
Repeat with 96 (even; digit sum 9+6 = 15 → multiple of 3; so yes, a multiple of 6) and a non-example such as 100 (even but digit sum 1, not a multiple of 3 → not a multiple of 6).
Justify each verdict out loud or in writing, naming both conditions.
activities.intendedInsight: Because 6 = 2×3, a number is a multiple of 6 only if it is divisible by BOTH 2 and 3. Divisibility rules let you reason about membership and justify it without dividing.

activities.title: Squares and cubes as a search space
feedback: If a learner guesses randomly, prompt the systematic method: 'Pick a square, subtract it from 100, is what's left also a square?'

Confirm 36 + 64 = 100 and ask whether any OTHER pair of nonzero squares also works (none does; 64 + 36 is the same pair in the other order, and the only other split, 0 + 100, uses 0, which the question excludes), reinforcing the exhaustive search.
If a learner confuses a square with a cube, re-anchor: a square is n×n, a cube is n×n×n.
activities.rationale: Drawing on known squares and cubes as a deliberate search space supports puzzle-type multiplicative problems and the habit of organised reasoning.
sourceClaims: Y5 pupils solve ×÷ problems using knowledge of factors and multiples, squares and cubes.
learnerActions: List the square numbers up to 100 (1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100) as a search space.
Find two square numbers that add to 100 by scanning the list: 36 + 64 = 100.
Describe the search strategy used (e.g. pick a square, subtract from 100, check if the remainder is also a square) rather than guessing randomly.
Extend to a cubes puzzle, e.g. list the cubes 1, 8, 27, 64 and find a cube greater than 1 that is also a square (64 = 8² = 4³; note that 1 = 1² = 1³ is also both, as a trivial case).
activities.intendedInsight: Knowing squares and cubes turns puzzle problems into an organised search: you can systematically test candidates instead of guessing, and some numbers belong to more than one family.

activities.title: Factor or multiple? Choosing the right tool
feedback: If a learner checks whether 6 divides into small numbers when the question asks whether 156 is a multiple of 6, re-anchor: a multiple of 6 appears when counting UP in sixes.
Reward naming the chosen route and giving a reason, not just the answer.
If a learner brute-forces every problem, ask them to find one problem in the set where a factor pair or divisibility rule saves work.
activities.rationale: Confusing factors and multiples drives wrong tool selection; explicitly distinguishing the vocabulary and prompting 'is there a smarter route?' builds the look-for-structure habit the standard targets.
sourceClaims: Factors/multiples (4.OA.4, 6.NS.4) and structural strategies underpin efficient multiplicative problem solving.
Re-factoring products using associativity and a friendly factor, and divisibility-rule reasoning, are efficient strategies to teach explicitly.
learnerActions: For each problem, decide first whether it is asking about FACTORS (numbers that divide into it) or MULTIPLES (numbers you land on counting up).
Re-anchor the vocabulary with a check: multiples of 6 are what you reach counting up in sixes (6, 12, 18, ...); factors of 6 are numbers that divide into it (1, 2, 3, 6).
Classify a mixed set of tasks: 'Is 156 in the six-times sequence?' (multiple), 'What divides exactly into 24?' (factor).
After choosing a strategy for a calculation, pause on the question 'Is there a smarter route than the algorithm?' and justify the chosen route.
activities.intendedInsight: Selecting the correct tool depends on distinguishing factors from multiples; the strategic habit is to look for structure and justify the route before computing.

constraints: Multiple-choice or fill-in tasks (e.g. 'is 156 a multiple of 6?' with justification options, 'the smartest way to compute 16×25', 'two squares summing to 100') are useful for checking divisibility judgements and strategy choice, especially with distractors built from the mis-applied-rule and wrong-re-factor errors; but recognition-only responses check rather than elicit the learner's own re-grouping, so pair them with tasks where the learner constructs the re-grouping themselves.

A worked gallery of shortcut exemplars (e.g. revealing the 6×(4×25) re-group) and a divisibility-rule reference card are helpful references, but the skill requires applying structure to NEW problems, which fixed exemplars alone do not demand.

A Socratic 'is there a cleverer way than the algorithm?' dialogue can build the strategic habit and prompt justification; the re-factoring step may be clearer when learners can physically rearrange the factors themselves, though this comparative benefit is untested here.
When re-grouping a product, a factor must be split before it is moved: 24×25 = (6×4)×25 = 6×(4×25). Writing 24×4×25 changes the value and is wrong.
Require justification and checking, not just an answer, so errors (such as a miscalculated digit sum) are caught; distinguish a strategy error from an arithmetic slip and respond accordingly.

Interactive re-grouping (e.g. dragging a factor to form a round number, or a panel showing instant pass/fail against each divisibility rule) is offered as an optional way to make the mechanism concrete, not a required mechanism.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Self-audit (arithmetic): verified 24×25 = 600 via 6×100; 16×25 = 400 via 4×100; 6×26 = 156; 6×16 = 96; digit sums 1+5+6=12 and 9+6=15 (both multiples of 3); 36+64=100; 64 = 8² = 4³. All check out.

Self-audit (divisibility): divisibility by 6 requires BOTH 2 and 3. The source counterexample '9 passes ÷3 but is not a multiple of 6' is correct and retained; an even-only counterexample (8) was added so both single-condition errors are directly refuted in the activity rather than merely cautioned.

The squares-summing-to-100 search confirms 36+64 is the only nonzero pair (0+100 is degenerate); the cubes puzzle names 64 as the non-trivial cube that is also a square and flags 1 = 1² = 1³ as a trivial qualifier.
The associativity pitfall (24×25 ≠ 24×4×25) is stated in both the activity-1 feedback and a constraint: split 24 = 6×4 before moving the 4.

Categorical medium-superiority claims from the row (3D 'adds cost without insight'; static formats 'test rather than build'; manipulation is where insight is 'felt') were not propagated as laws; they are reframed as scoped, untested trade-offs with may/can wording.

Standards citations (DfE Y5; CCSS 4.OA.4, 6.NS.4, 5.NBT.5–6, 6.EE.1) came from the row's pedagogy; two of three sources are marked verified:false, so no efficacy or verification claims are asserted here.

probeDeeper: Why isn't 'it's even' enough to show 156 is a multiple of 6?
Which two factors did you pair up to make 24 × 25 easy, and why those?
Find two square numbers that add to 100 — how did you search?
Is 96 a multiple of 6? Test it using divisibility, not division.
assess.correctAnswer: 156 IS a multiple of 6 (it is even AND its digits sum to 12, a multiple of 3, so divisible by both 2 and 3, hence by 6; or 6×26 = 156). 24 × 25 = 600 via 6 × (4 × 25) = 6 × 100. The teacher watches for use of divisibility tests / factor rearrangement (associativity) rather than a written algorithm.

errorPatterns.pattern: tests divisibility by 6 by checking only ONE of 2 or 3 (thinks even ⇒ multiple of 6, or digit-sum-of-3 ⇒ multiple of 6)
errorPatterns.nextMove: establish 6 = 2×3, so a multiple of 6 must pass BOTH the ÷2 and ÷3 tests; counterexample: 9 passes ÷3 but is not a multiple of 6.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child declares a number a multiple of 6 on the strength of just being even, or just divisible by 3

errorPatterns.pattern: does not rearrange factors — computes 24×25 by the column method, missing the 4×25 = 100 shortcut
errorPatterns.nextMove: prompt 'which factors make a round number?' — pull 4 out of 24 to pair with 25; name this as using associativity.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child sets up long multiplication rather than regrouping factors

errorPatterns.pattern: confuses factor and multiple — looks for factors when the problem asks about multiples, or vice versa
errorPatterns.nextMove: re-anchor the vocabulary: multiples are what you land on counting UP in sixes; factors divide INTO a number.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child checks whether 6 divides into small numbers instead of whether 156 is in the 6-times sequence

errorPatterns.pattern: right strategy, arithmetic slip (digit sum miscalculated, or 6×26 wrong)
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach strategy; have the child recompute the digit sum or the product.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: correct method, wrong number

responseLevels.gap: tests only one condition for divisibility by 6, or brute-forces every problem; confuses factor with multiple.
responseLevels.full: applies compound divisibility reasoning (both 2 and 3 for 6), rearranges factors to simplify products, and deploys square-number knowledge to solve problems efficiently.
responseLevels.partial: uses a divisibility test OR a factor rearrangement but not reliably, or needs prompting to see the structural shortcut.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child problems that require choosing a factor/multiple/square strategy, watching their approach: 'Is 156 a multiple of 6? Show how you know without long division.' and 'Work out 24 × 25 cleverly using factors, not the column method.' Watch whether they reach for divisibility reasoning and factor rearrangement rather than brute calculation.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: These problems can be brute-forced, but the objective is USING factor/multiple structure to simplify. Watching whether the child applies a divisibility test for 6 (needs BOTH 2 and 3) and rearranges factors to make 4×25 = 100 separates structural fluency from mechanical computation — a child lacking the structure still gets answers, slowly, missing the point.
