pedagogy.summary: Children read o'clock and half-past times on an analogue clock and draw the hands to show them. The representational crux is that the two hands mean different things and move together: at half past, the minute hand points to 6 and the hour hand sits HALFWAY between two numbers, and the time is 'half past the last number the hour hand has passed'. Taught by reading and drawing on a geared clock so hour and minute hands move in proportion.
bestPractices: Use a geared teaching clock so children see the hour hand creep between numbers as the minute hand goes round
Establish o'clock first (minute hand on 12, hour hand exactly on a number), then half past (minute hand on 6, hour hand between)
Teach that half past is 'the last number the hour hand has passed', not the number it is nearest
Always pair reading with drawing — given a time, draw both hands; given a clock, say the time
Link 'half past' to halves from fractions: the minute hand has travelled half way round
keyRepresentations: A geared analogue clock
Blank clock faces for drawing hands
A clock with the two hands colour-coded (short = hour, long = minute)
A half-circle sweep showing the minute hand's half turn
commonMisconceptions: Puts or expects the hour hand exactly on a number at half past, instead of halfway between
Confuses the minute and hour hands (reads or draws the wrong one)
Reads half past by the number the hour hand is nearest rather than the one it has passed (half past 3 read as half past 4)
Reads the clock as a bare number, matching a hand to a numeral, ignoring what each hand measures

learn.summary: Children aged 5–6 read and draw o'clock and half-past times on an analogue clock. The crux is that the two hands measure different things and move together: at half past, the minute hand points to the 6 and the hour hand sits HALFWAY between two numbers. The time is read as 'half past the last number the hour hand has passed' — not the number it is nearest. Establish o'clock first, then half past, pairing reading with drawing in both directions.

activities.title: Wind the clock and watch the hour hand slide
feedback: If the hour hand looks like it should be on a number at half past, wind the clock slowly and watch: the hour hand never jumps — it is only halfway between the numbers when the minute hand is on the 6.
If you say 'half past 8' when the hour hand is between 7 and 8, trace back to the number the hour hand LEFT: it has passed the 7 but not yet reached the 8, so it is half past 7.
A geared or linked clock where moving one hand moves the other makes the proportional link visible; a clock whose hands move independently will not show this and can reinforce the error.
activities.rationale: The hour-hand-halfway position is the representational heart of half past and the most common error point. Watching the hands move together is intended to address the misconception that the hour hand points straight at a number at half past; the approach is a research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: White Rose Year 2 Time (Step 1) teaches half past with the hour hand 'halfway between two numbers' and 'half past the last number the hour hand has moved past', and lists as 'things to look out for': children keep the hour hand pointing directly at a number for half past instead of halfway between, and children confuse the minute and hour hands; a reasoning task rebuts 'It is half past 11, so the hour hand should point to 11.'

In interviews with Grades 2 and 4, the hour hand was significantly more challenging to position accurately than the minute hand, and a common approach was 'Number Matching' — matching a digit to a numeral on the clock — which was accurate only about half the time; students also treated hour and minute units separately (e.g. reading 7:00 as 'six o'clock').
learnerActions: On a geared teaching clock (one where turning the minute hand drives the hour hand in proportion), start at 7 o'clock with the minute hand on 12 and the hour hand exactly on the 7.
Slowly turn the minute hand clockwise (the way clock hands normally go: 12, 1, 2, 3…) round the face to the 6, and watch the hour hand crawl away from the 7 toward the 8.
Stop when the minute hand reaches the 6 — half a turn round — and check where the hour hand is: it sits exactly halfway between 7 and 8.
Say the time aloud as 'half past 7', naming which hand told you it was a HALF (the minute hand, half way round) and which told you the hour (the hour hand, past the 7).
Repeat starting from several other o'clock positions (3, 9, 11) so you see the same halfway pattern each time.
activities.intendedInsight: At half past, the hour hand is dragged halfway between two numbers by the minute hand's half turn; 'half past 7' means 'half way past 7', not 'hour hand on 7 or 8'.

activities.title: Name each hand before you read
feedback: If you read half past 3 as roughly '6 o'clock', you are reading the long (minute) hand as if it gave the hour — check the short hand for the hour instead.
Colour-coding and naming each hand's job first is intended to help guard against swapping their meanings.
Matching a hand to the nearest numeral ('number matching') is unreliable: in the cited interviews it gave the right answer only about half the time.
activities.rationale: Aims to target the hand-confusion and bare-number-matching errors by prompting interpretation of each hand's measured quantity before any reading; this is a proposal informed by the documented error patterns, not a tested intervention.
sourceClaims: In interviews with Grades 2 and 4, the hour hand was significantly more challenging to position accurately than the minute hand, and a common approach was 'Number Matching' — matching a digit to a numeral on the clock — which was accurate only about half the time; students also treated hour and minute units separately (e.g. reading 7:00 as 'six o'clock').
learnerActions: Look at a clock where the short hand (hour) and long hand (minute) are colour-coded differently.
Before saying any time, point to each hand and say its job: 'short hand = the hour', 'long hand = the minutes'.
Read several clocks (e.g. 3 o'clock, half past 9) always naming the hand first, then the time.
Deliberately spot a swapped reading: if someone treated the long (minute) hand as if it gave the hour, explain why that reading would be wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: The two hands measure different quantities; reading a clock means interpreting what each hand tells you, not matching a hand to the nearest numeral.

activities.title: Draw the hands to show a time
feedback: If you draw the hour hand straight at the 7 for half past 7, compare with the geared clock: at half past the hour hand is always midway to the next number.
If you draw a long hour hand or short minute hand, recall that the short hand always shows the hour.
For 'half past 11', the hour hand goes halfway between 11 and 12, not on the 11 — this is the exact case where learners often go wrong.
activities.rationale: Drawing is a production task that requires constructing both hands. Unlike selecting among ready-made clocks (a recognition task), it can reveal whether a child places the hour hand between numbers — recognition alone does not elicit production. The curriculum explicitly requires drawing the hands.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils should 'tell the time to the hour and half past the hour and draw the hands on a clock face to show these times' (statutory), with non-statutory guidance to tell the time throughout the day 'first using o'clock and then half past'.

White Rose Year 2 Time (Step 1) teaches half past with the hour hand 'halfway between two numbers' and 'half past the last number the hour hand has moved past', and lists as 'things to look out for': children keep the hour hand pointing directly at a number for half past instead of halfway between, and children confuse the minute and hour hands; a reasoning task rebuts 'It is half past 11, so the hour hand should point to 11.'
learnerActions: On a blank clock face, draw both hands for a given o'clock time (e.g. 3 o'clock): long minute hand on 12, short hour hand exactly on the 3.
On a fresh blank face, draw half past 7: minute hand on 6, and the hour hand drawn HALFWAY between the 7 and the 8.
Check your own drawing by asking: has the hour hand passed the 7 but not reached the 8? Is the minute hand on the 6?
Explain in words why the hour hand is between the numbers and not on one.
Try several more (half past 9, half past 11) and each time place the hour hand between the two numbers.
activities.intendedInsight: Showing a time requires constructing both hands correctly — especially placing the hour hand between numbers for half past — which asks more of the child than recognising a correct clock.

activities.title: Which hour has it passed? (reasoning the half-past hour)
feedback: If you pick the number ahead (saying half past 4 when the hand is between 3 and 4), check which number the hand has gone past — it left the 3, so it is half past 3.
Connecting the minute hand's half turn to the idea of 'half' reinforces why the time is 'half past' rather than a whole hour.
The claim that the hour hand points to 11 at half past 11 is a classic error: it actually sits halfway between 11 and 12.
activities.rationale: Aims to address the 'nearest number' error and the number-matching habit by asking the learner to reason explicitly about which hour the hand has passed; a proposal informed by the documented misconception, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: White Rose Year 2 Time (Step 1) teaches half past with the hour hand 'halfway between two numbers' and 'half past the last number the hour hand has moved past', and lists as 'things to look out for': children keep the hour hand pointing directly at a number for half past instead of halfway between, and children confuse the minute and hour hands; a reasoning task rebuts 'It is half past 11, so the hour hand should point to 11.'
learnerActions: Look at a clock with the minute hand on 6 and the hour hand between two numbers (e.g. between 3 and 4).
Decide whether it is half past 3 or half past 4, and state the rule you used.
Trace which number the hour hand has already LEFT and which it is heading toward.
Respond to the claim 'It is half past 11, so the hour hand should point to 11' — explain why that is wrong and where the hour hand really goes.
Link to halves: the minute hand has travelled half way round the face, which is why we say 'half' past.
activities.intendedInsight: At half past you name the hour by the last number the hour hand has passed, not the number it is nearest or heading toward.

constraints: Use a geared or linked clock so the hour hand moves in proportion as the minute hand turns; a clock whose hands can be set independently will not show the proportional relationship and may reinforce the hour-hand-on-a-number error.
Establish o'clock (minute hand on 12, hour hand exactly on a number) before introducing half past (minute hand on 6, hour hand between numbers).
Always pair reading with drawing: given a time, draw both hands; given a clock, say the time.

Matching clocks to times by selecting among ready-made options is recognition, not construction; it does not reveal whether a child can place the hour hand correctly between numbers and should be followed by actual drawing.

A static labelled clock (e.g. tap-to-reveal names of the hands) can introduce which hand is which, but cannot show the two hands moving together or catch a mis-drawn hour hand; treat it as an introductory scaffold, not the main activity.
Colour-code the hands (short = hour, long = minute) and name each hand's job to help prevent swapping their meanings.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source claims support general teaching principles (curriculum requirement, half-past structure, documented error patterns) but do not establish the efficacy of any specific activity proposed here; efficacy wording is kept qualified (intended/aims to).

Activity 1's winding step was corrected: a half turn of the minute hand (to the 6) places the hour hand halfway between the numbers; the earlier 'full turn' wording conflicted with stopping at the 6 and was adjusted for coherence.

The original research rated a planar/3D comparison and an in-role dialogue as poor fits; these catalog fit rankings were dropped as product-ranking boilerplate. A clock face is a 2D representation, but this does not establish a universal claim that no spoken or three-dimensional treatment could ever contribute.

No conceptual errors were found in the source's time content; the half-past structure (minute hand on 6, hour hand halfway, named by the last hour passed) is consistent with the cited curriculum and scheme of learning.

probeDeeper: 'The hour hand is between the 7 and the 8. Is it half past 7 or half past 8 — how do you decide?'
'If I move the hour hand to point exactly at the 7, is it still half past 7? What time is it now?'
'Which hand did you look at first to know it was HALF past — and what told you it was a half?'
assess.correctAnswer: Reads 'half past 3', explaining the minute hand on 6 means half way round (half past) and the hour hand between 3 and 4 means it is past 3 (the last number passed). Draws half past 7 with the minute hand on 6 and the hour hand HALFWAY between 7 and 8.

errorPatterns.pattern: At half past, expects or draws the hour hand pointing straight at a number instead of halfway between two — 'it is half past 11, so the hour hand should point to 11'
errorPatterns.nextMove: On a geared clock, wind from 7 o'clock to half past and watch the hour hand travel to the midpoint; state and show 'half past = hour hand halfway between the numbers'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws half past 7 with the hour hand on the 7 (or 8); agrees with 'half past 11 → hour hand on 11'

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses the minute and hour hands — reads or draws their roles swapped
errorPatterns.nextMove: Colour-code and name each hand's job (short = hour, long = minutes) and read several times naming the hand first.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reads half past 3 as roughly '6 o'clock' (reading the minute hand as the hour), or draws a long hour hand / short minute hand

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads half past by the number the hour hand is CLOSEST to rather than the one it has passed (half past 3 read as half past 4)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Teach 'half past the LAST number the hour hand has gone past' and trace, on a geared clock, which number it left.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For a between-position, names the number ahead rather than the one behind

responseLevels.gap: Reads or draws by matching a hand to a numeral; puts the hour hand on a number for half past; confuses the two hands.
responseLevels.full: Reads and draws o'clock and half-past times with the hour hand correctly between numbers, explains what each hand means, and names the hour as the last one passed — transferring to an unfamiliar time.
responseLevels.partial: Reads o'clock correctly and half past on a clear clock, but draws the hour hand on the number, or hesitates over which hour a between-position shows.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Interpret, then translate. (Interpret) Show a clock reading half past 3 — minute hand on 6, hour hand halfway between 3 and 4: 'What time is this? How do you know — what is each hand telling you?' (Translate) Give a blank clock face: 'Now draw the hands to show half past 7.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Asking what each hand tells you catches a child who reads clocks purely by number-matching; the draw-half-past-7 task exposes the classic error of putting the hour hand exactly on the 7 — a child who understands places it between 7 and 8.

sources.claim: In interviews with Grades 2 and 4, the hour hand was significantly more challenging to position accurately than the minute hand, and a common approach was 'Number Matching' — matching a digit to a numeral on the clock — which was accurate only about half the time; students also treated hour and minute units separately (e.g. reading 7:00 as 'six o'clock').
sources.source: Earnest, Gonzales & Plant (2018), 'Time as a Measure: Elementary Students Positioning the Hands of an Analog Clock', Journal of Numerical Cognition 4(1)

pedagogy.summary: The general case: adding and subtracting fractions with UNLIKE denominators where neither is a multiple of the other (2/3 + 5/4), and mixed numbers (3 1/4 − 1 3/5). Both fractions must now be renamed to a shared unit — a common multiple of the denominators (twelfths for thirds and quarters) — scaling BOTH numerators, then combining like parts. Mixed numbers add a further demand: in subtraction the fraction part of the minuend can end up smaller than that of the subtrahend, forcing a regroup across the whole (borrowing a whole, or converting to improper fractions). It is the culmination of the whole add/subtract strand: the same 'make the units the same, then count' idea, now with no shortcuts.
bestPractices: Reinforce that BOTH fractions must be renamed to a common unit; a common multiple of the denominators (often the product, sometimes the LCM) gives it.
Insist both numerators scale with their denominators (2/3 → 8/12, 5/4 → 15/12) — the multi-conversion is where partial-scaling slips appear.
For mixed numbers, teach two secure routes and let pupils choose: regroup/borrow a whole, OR convert to improper fractions first (often cleaner when a borrow is needed).
Use estimation and benchmarks to gate the answer (2/3 + 5/4 is more than 2, so 7/7 = 1 is impossible).
Verify with a visual model or number line, per the topic's own evidence; simplify and write mixed-number answers.
Keep units constant in representations; avoid manipulatives that encourage adding without a common denominator.
keyRepresentations: Two strips/number lines re-gridded to a common denominator (thirds and quarters → twelfths)
Area/fraction-circle model showing both fractions recut to the shared unit
Mixed-number bars showing a whole tile broken into the common unit to enable borrowing (1 whole → 20/20)
Improper-fraction conversion as an alternative route (3 1/4 = 13/4) laid beside the mixed form
commonMisconceptions: Adds across the unlike denominators: 2/3 + 5/4 = 7/7, combining numerators and denominators.
Finds a common denominator but scales only one (or neither) numerator, or uses a wrong common denominator (2/3 = 2/12).

In mixed-number subtraction, subtracts the smaller fraction from the larger in each column regardless of position (does 12/20 − 5/20), never regrouping across the whole when the minuend's fraction part is smaller.

learn.summary: General case of adding and subtracting fractions with unlike denominators where neither denominator is a multiple of the other (e.g. 2/3 + 5/4), extended to mixed numbers (e.g. 3 1/4 − 1 3/5). Both fractions must be renamed to a shared unit — a common multiple of the denominators (twelfths for thirds and quarters) — which scales BOTH numerators, then like parts are combined. Mixed-number subtraction adds a further demand: the fraction part of the minuend can end up smaller than that of the subtrahend, forcing a regroup across the whole (borrow a whole) or a conversion to improper fractions. The unifying idea remains 'make the units the same, then count', now with no shortcuts.

activities.title: Shared-grid combiner: rename both fractions, then combine
feedback: If a learner writes 7/7 (adding tops and adding bottoms), re-partition both fractions on the strips and estimate first: 5/4 alone exceeds 1, so 2/3 + 5/4 must exceed 1, and 7/7 = 1 cannot be right.

If a learner finds the common denominator but leaves a numerator unscaled (e.g. writes 2/12 for 2/3), rebuild the equivalence on the model — one third cut into twelfths becomes FOUR twelfths, so 2/3 = 8/12 — and have them check both conversions before combining.
If the sum is left as 23/12, prompt converting to a mixed number and simplifying: 23/12 = 1 11/12.
Confirm with the estimate: 23/12 is more than 1 and a little less than 2, matching 'more than one (5/4) plus two-thirds'.
activities.rationale: Adding or subtracting unlike fractions requires rewriting both as equivalent fractions over a common unit; the add-across error and the 'use the larger denominator' error both come from not grasping this, and a chosen pair where neither denominator is a multiple of the other forces both numerators to scale, exposing partial-scaling slips. Estimation and benchmarks let learners judge reasonableness. A dynamic re-gridding model (strips that only align once a shared grid is chosen, with both numerators re-scaling as the grid is set) may make the re-unitising visible, but a fully worked static picture of 2/3 and 5/4 both shown as twelfths can also anchor the equivalence.
sourceClaims: Adding/subtracting unlike fractions requires rewriting both as equivalent fractions with a common denominator (a common unit fraction); the add-across error and the 'insert the larger denominator' error both stem from not grasping this. Teach with representations that cue the need for common denominators and use estimation to judge reasonableness.
The add-across error on different-denominator items is made mostly by lower- and middle-achieving pupils and remains common; visual work and staged conversion help.

Add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators including mixed numbers by using equivalent fractions to produce a common denominator; using common multiples to express fractions in the same denomination is a Year 6 expectation.
learnerActions: Set up 2/3 + 5/4 on two strips or two number lines, one gridded in thirds and one in quarters, and notice they will not combine while the units differ.
Choose a shared unit (a common multiple of 3 and 4) and re-grid both strips into twelfths, re-tiling each fraction: 2/3 becomes 8/12 and 5/4 becomes 15/12.

State explicitly that cutting each third into four pieces turns 2/3 into 8/12 — the top is multiplied by the same factor as the bottom — and check the same for 5/4 (each quarter cut into three, so 5/4 = 15/12) before combining.
Combine the re-tiled pieces to get 23/12 and regroup into the mixed number 1 11/12.

Before computing, estimate: 5/4 is already more than 1, so adding a positive 2/3 makes the sum more than 1 (indeed more than 1.5). That already rules out answers like 7/7 = 1; the true sum lands just below 2 (23/12, just under 24/12).
activities.intendedInsight: Unlike fractions can only be combined once BOTH are rewritten over the same unit; each numerator scales by the same factor as its own denominator, and estimation gates whether a result is even possible.

activities.title: Mixed-number subtraction with a regroup across the whole
feedback: If a learner subtracts the smaller fraction from the larger regardless of position (e.g. does 12/20 − 5/20 and writes 7/20), model breaking one whole of the 3 into 20/20 so 3 5/20 becomes 2 25/20, then subtract; or convert both to improper fractions (65/20 − 32/20) to avoid the borrow.
If a learner is stuck because '5/20 minus 12/20 can't be done', show that the whole provides the extra twentieths: 2 25/20 − 1 12/20 = 1 13/20.
Check that the final answer is written as a simplified mixed number where appropriate.
Verify with the improper-fraction route: 65/20 − 32/20 = 33/20 = 1 13/20, matching the regroup route.
activities.rationale: Mixed-number subtraction where the fraction part becomes smaller after conversion forces a regroup across the whole; offering two secure routes — borrowing a whole, or converting to improper fractions — lets learners choose and builds understanding of why the borrow is needed. A bar model in which a whole tile breaks into the common unit can make the borrow concrete; the improper-fraction conversion laid beside the mixed form shows an equivalent clean alternative. This targets the common error of subtracting smaller-from-larger in each column without regrouping.
sourceClaims: Adding/subtracting unlike fractions requires rewriting both as equivalent fractions with a common denominator (a common unit fraction); the add-across error and the 'insert the larger denominator' error both stem from not grasping this. Teach with representations that cue the need for common denominators and use estimation to judge reasonableness.

Add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators including mixed numbers by using equivalent fractions to produce a common denominator; using common multiples to express fractions in the same denomination is a Year 6 expectation.
learnerActions: Set up 3 1/4 − 1 3/5 and rename both fractions to a common denominator of twentieths: 3 5/20 − 1 12/20.
Notice that 5/20 is smaller than 12/20, so the fraction part cannot be taken directly — a regroup across the whole is needed.
Regroup one whole from the 3 into twentieths: break a whole tile into 20/20 so 3 5/20 becomes 2 25/20, then subtract to get 1 13/20.
As an alternative route, convert both mixed numbers to improper fractions first (3 1/4 = 13/4 = 65/20 and 1 3/5 = 8/5 = 32/20), subtract to 33/20, and convert back to 1 13/20.
Compare the two routes and decide which you find cleaner when a borrow is needed.
activities.intendedInsight: When the minuend's fraction part becomes smaller than the subtrahend's after finding a common denominator, you must regroup a whole into the common unit (or work with improper fractions) rather than subtracting the smaller fraction from the larger in each column.

activities.title: Explain and check with a model
feedback: Full understanding: renames both fractions to a real common denominator (scaling both numerators), combines, handles the mixed-number regroup, simplifies to a mixed-number answer, verifies with a model, and transfers to a new unlike-denominator pair including mixed numbers.

Partial understanding: finds a correct common denominator and adds unlike proper fractions reliably (23/12), but the mixed-number subtraction breaks down when a regroup is needed, or answers aren't simplified/converted — the procedure holds for the easy case but not the borrow.
Gap: adds across (7/7) or scales only one/neither numerator; in the mixed subtraction subtracts smaller-from-larger in each column and never regroups.
activities.rationale: A performance task in which neither denominator is a multiple of the other, and the mixed subtraction is built so the minuend's fraction part becomes smaller after conversion, discriminates whether equivalence, common-multiple choice, and regrouping are all in place. Asking learners to explain their choice of denominator and to test an absurd result against an estimate surfaces reasoning, not just answers.
sourceClaims: Adding/subtracting unlike fractions requires rewriting both as equivalent fractions with a common denominator (a common unit fraction); the add-across error and the 'insert the larger denominator' error both stem from not grasping this. Teach with representations that cue the need for common denominators and use estimation to judge reasonableness.

Add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators including mixed numbers by using equivalent fractions to produce a common denominator; using common multiples to express fractions in the same denomination is a Year 6 expectation.
learnerActions: Work out 2/3 + 5/4 and 3 1/4 − 1 3/5, showing every step and giving each answer in simplest form as a mixed number where appropriate.
Explain how you chose the common denominator and why BOTH numerators changed when you did.
Answer the challenge: a friend says 2/3 + 5/4 = 7/7 = 1 — but 5/4 on its own is more than 1, so can the total be exactly 1? Explain what went wrong.
For the subtraction, after reaching 3 5/20 − 1 12/20, explain what you do because you can't take 12/20 from 5/20 as it stands.
Verify 23/12 against the benchmark: confirm it is more than 1 (since 5/4 alone exceeds 1) and a little less than 2 — does that match adding 2/3 and 5/4?
activities.intendedInsight: A learner secure in this strand can rename both fractions to a genuine common denominator, handle a mixed-number regroup by either route, simplify, and verify a result against a benchmark estimate — not just execute steps.

constraints: Target age approximately 10–11 (Year 6); learners should already be able to generate equivalent fractions and convert between mixed and improper forms, since these are the enabling moves for the regroup.
A common multiple of the denominators gives the shared unit; the product always works and the least common multiple is sometimes tidier — do not teach that one specific denominator is required.
Both numerators must scale with their own denominators; the multi-conversion is where partial-scaling errors appear, so check both equivalences before combining.
Keep the unit constant within any representation and avoid manipulatives that let learners combine pieces without first establishing a common denominator.

Multiple-choice or fill-in-blank items (e.g. 2/3 + 5/4 with 7/7 as a distractor, or a mixed subtraction with the no-borrow answer as a distractor) can diagnose add-across, partial-scaling, and no-borrow errors, but recognising a correct option does not demonstrate independent construction of the renaming and regrouping; use alongside tasks where the learner carries out the full procedure.
A fully worked static picture can anchor one conversion or borrow but does not let the learner perform the re-gridding themselves; use it as a reference rather than the main activity.
Teach both the borrow-a-whole and convert-to-improper routes and let learners choose; the improper route is often cleaner precisely when a borrow would be needed.
Estimation benchmarks must be stated correctly: 2/3 + 5/4 is more than 1 (5/4 alone exceeds 1) and lands just below 2 (23/12); do not state it exceeds 2.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One source (DfE National Curriculum for England, Year 6) is marked unverified in the original row; the other two are marked verified. No new verification was performed here.

Corrected an arithmetic error inherited from the original row's bestPractices: it stated '2/3 + 5/4 is more than 2', but 23/12 ≈ 1.92 is less than 2. The valid benchmark that rules out 7/7 = 1 is that the sum exceeds 1 (because 5/4 alone exceeds 1). All learner-facing text now uses the 'more than 1, just below 2' benchmark.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 2/3 = 8/12 and 5/4 = 15/12, sum 23/12 = 1 11/12 (correct). 3 1/4 = 13/4 = 65/20, 1 3/5 = 8/5 = 32/20, 65/20 − 32/20 = 33/20 = 1 13/20; via regroup 3 5/20 → 2 25/20, minus 1 12/20 = 1 13/20 (consistent). The erroneous no-borrow answer 7/20 (from 12/20 − 5/20) is retained only as an error to diagnose, never as a valid answer.

Each of the two fractions must be renamed independently to the shared unit, and both numerators rescale by their own factor; this is a separate equivalence check per fraction, not a single rule applied once, and no 'denominator flip' reasoning is used.

probeDeeper: How did you decide what common denominator to use for 2/3 and 5/4 — and why did BOTH tops change?
A friend says 2/3 + 5/4 = 7/7 = 1. But 5/4 on its own is more than 1 — can the total be exactly 1? What went wrong?
In 3 1/4 − 1 3/5 you reached 3 5/20 − 1 12/20. You can't take 12/20 from 5/20 as it stands — what do you do?
Check 23/12: is that more than 2 or less than 2? Does that match adding 2/3 and 5/4?

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds across the unlike denominators: '2 and 5 is 7 on top, 3 and 4 is 7 on the bottom, so 7/7 = 1'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-partition both fractions to a shared unit on strips; estimate first — 5/4 is already more than 1, so 2/3 + 5/4 must exceed 1, and 7/7 = 1 can't be right.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 7/7 (or similar) for the sum; denominators combined.

errorPatterns.pattern: Finds a common denominator but scales only one numerator (or none): '2/3 + 5/4, common denominator 12, so 2/12 + 15/12' — leaves 2 on top of the renamed 2/3.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild each equivalence on the model — thirds cut into twelfths turn ONE third into FOUR twelfths, so 2/3 = 8/12; the top scales by the same factor as the bottom. Check both conversions before combining.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct common denominator but a numerator left unscaled (2/12 for 2/3); the equivalence is incomplete.

errorPatterns.pattern: In the mixed-number subtraction, subtracts the smaller fraction from the larger regardless of position: does 12/20 − 5/20 in the fraction column and never regroups across the whole.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model regrouping a whole: break one whole of 3 1/4 into 20/20 so 3 5/20 becomes 2 25/20, then subtract; or convert both to improper fractions (65/20 − 32/20) to avoid the borrow. Reteach mixed↔improper conversion as the enabling move.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Fraction part of the answer is 7/20 (took 5 from 12 the wrong way) or the child is stuck because '5/20 minus 12/20 can't be done'.

responseLevels.gap: Adds across (7/7) or scales only one/neither numerator; in the mixed subtraction subtracts smaller-from-larger in each column and never regroups.
responseLevels.full: Renames both fractions to a genuine common denominator (scaling both numerators), combines, handles the mixed-number regroup (by borrowing or converting to improper fractions), simplifies to a mixed-number answer, and can verify with a model; transfers to a new unlike-denominator pair including mixed numbers.
responseLevels.partial: Finds a correct common denominator and adds unlike PROPER fractions reliably (23/12), but the mixed-number subtraction breaks down when a regroup across the whole is needed, or answers aren't simplified/converted — the procedure holds for the easy case but not the borrow.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these out, showing your steps: 2/3 + 5/4, and 3 1/4 − 1 3/5. Give each answer in simplest form, as a mixed number where appropriate.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Neither denominator is a multiple of the other (3 and 4; 4 and 5), so the child can't convert only one fraction — both numerators must scale, exposing partial-scaling errors. The mixed-number subtraction is built so the minuend's fraction part becomes SMALLER after the common denominator (5/20 vs 12/20), forcing a regroup across the whole; a child who subtracts smaller-from-larger in each column reveals the borrowing gap. Add-across yields 7/7 = 1, absurd since 5/4 alone exceeds 1. Watching the steps shows whether equivalence, common-multiple choice, and regrouping are all in place.

pedagogy.summary: At age 12-14 students learn that a triangle can be pinned down by just three of its six measurements — but only in the right combinations: SSS, SAS, ASA (and their consequences AAS, and RHS for right triangles). The deep idea is DETERMINATION: which sets of data force a unique triangle, which allow more than one, and which allow none. The two hardest points are (a) SSA — two sides and a NON-included angle — is ambiguous (the 'swinging side' can meet the base in two places, giving zero, one or two triangles), and students wrongly assimilate it to SAS because both are 'two sides and an angle'; and (b) AAA fixes only the SHAPE (similarity), not the size, so equiangular triangles need not be congruent. Alongside this sits the correspondence convention: △ABC ≅ △DEF means A↔D, B↔E, C↔F, so the order of letters encodes which parts are equal. Teaching is most effective when students physically construct triangles from given conditions and discover for themselves when the data over- or under-determine the figure.
bestPractices: Have students CONSTRUCT triangles from given conditions (ruler, protractor, compass or dynamic geometry) so they discover empirically when data force a unique triangle and when a second triangle appears
Make the included-vs-non-included distinction explicit: for 'two sides and an angle', always check whether the angle is BETWEEN the two sides (SAS, unique) or opposite one of them (SSA, ambiguous)
Demonstrate the 'swinging side' for SSA with a compass arc so the two intersection points — two valid triangles — are seen, and analyse the zero/one/two outcomes
Separate congruence (same shape AND size) from similarity (same shape, possibly scaled): show that AAA equal angles give similar but not necessarily congruent triangles
Drill correspondence notation — the order of letters in △ABC ≅ △DEF names the matching vertices, sides and angles — and derive AAS from ASA (a second angle forces the third)
keyRepresentations: Dynamic triangle constructor / compass-and-ruler construction from given conditions
The 'swinging side' compass arc showing SSA's two intersection points
Side-by-side SAS (angle between) vs SSA (angle opposite) diagrams
Correspondence map △ABC ≅ △DEF with matched tick-marks and angle arcs
A one/none/many outcome table for given measurement sets
commonMisconceptions: Treating SSA as a valid criterion by conflating it with SAS — not checking whether the angle is included between the two sides
Believing AAA (equal angles) proves congruence, confusing congruence with similarity
Assuming any three given measurements determine a unique triangle
Mismatching corresponding parts — ignoring that the letter order in △ABC ≅ △DEF encodes the correspondence
Not realising AAS works (because the third angle is forced) while SSA does not

learn.summary: Students aged 12-14 learn which combinations of a triangle's six measurements (three sides, three angles) force a UNIQUE triangle: SSS, SAS, ASA, plus the derived AAS, and RHS for right triangles. The core idea is DETERMINATION — which data over-determine, under-determine, or exactly fix a figure. Two hard points: (a) SSA (two sides and a NON-included angle) is ambiguous — the free 'swinging' side can meet the other arm of the angle in two places, giving zero, one or two triangles — yet students wrongly treat it like SAS because both are 'two sides and an angle'; (b) AAA fixes only SHAPE (similarity), not size, so equiangular triangles need not be congruent. Alongside sits the correspondence convention: △ABC ≅ △DEF means A↔D, B↔E, C↔F, so letter order encodes matching parts. The strongest learning comes from physically constructing triangles from given conditions and discovering for oneself when data over- or under-determine the figure.

activities.title: Swing the non-included side: SSA's two triangles
feedback: If you predicted exactly one triangle and found two, that is the key surprise — the identical SSA data gave two genuinely different triangles. This is why SSA is called the ambiguous case.

If the compass arc crossed the 40° angle's other ray at two points, each crossing completes a valid but different triangle; if it just touches that ray at a single point there is one triangle (the tangent / right-angle case); if it crosses the ray at only one point because the other crossing falls behind the corner (this happens when the swinging side is at least as long as the base), there is also one triangle; if the arc never reaches that ray there is none.

When you fixed the angle BETWEEN the two sides (SAS), the third vertex was forced to a single location — the swing collapsed to one locked triangle. Notice you changed only where the angle sits, not the lengths.

If you justified 'one triangle' by naming SAS or 'two sides and an angle are given', check whether the angle is actually between the two named sides. Here it was opposite the 6 cm side, so SAS does not apply.
activities.rationale: Determination is a manipulable idea: fixing two sides and an angle and swinging the free side directly shows how many crossings occur (two for the 9 cm/6 cm/40° data; changing the swinging length can also show the one-triangle and no-triangle outcomes), and toggling the angle between included and non-included shows why SAS locks but SSA does not. Prediction-then-test makes the ambiguity felt rather than told.
sourceClaims: SSA (two sides and a non-included angle) does not determine a triangle up to congruence — the 'swinging side' yields two non-congruent triangles from the same data; AAA is also insufficient (it determines a triangle only up to similarity); AAS IS sufficient because two equal angle-pairs force the third; SSS, SAS, ASA each require three pieces of information.

KS3 statutory: pupils 'understand and use the relationship between parallel lines and alternate and corresponding angles' and work with congruence and standard triangle labelling as part of geometry and measures; drawing/measuring and constructing figures from given conditions underpins congruence reasoning.
learnerActions: Set up a fixed 9 cm base line. At one end, mark a 40° angle, drawing the second arm of that angle as a long ray rising from the corner. Pin a 6 cm 'arm' at the FAR end of the base (so the 40° angle sits OPPOSITE the 6 cm side, not between the two sides).
BEFORE moving anything, predict in writing: how many triangles can you complete, and WHY?

Swing the 6 cm arm (physically, or draw a compass arc of radius 6 cm centred at the far end of the base) and mark every point where the arc crosses the OTHER arm of the 40° angle (the ray rising from the angled corner) — each crossing is a possible third vertex.
Count the crossing points and draw each complete triangle you find.

Reconfigure with the40-degree angle between the6cm and9cm sides. Fix both sides on the two rays and join their free endpoints; compare this lockedSAS construction with the freeSSA arc. Rotated or reflected copies are still congruent, not different-sized solutions.
State in your own words why moving the angle from 'opposite' to 'between' changes the number of triangles.
activities.intendedInsight: Two sides and a non-included angle (SSA) do NOT determine a unique triangle — the free side can swing to meet the other arm of the angle in up to two places. When the angle is INCLUDED between the two sides (SAS), the triangle is locked. 'Included' is the word that matters.

activities.title: Construct from conditions: when do data fix a triangle?
feedback: For AAA you should have been able to build two triangles with identical angles but different sizes — equal angles fix the shape, not the size, so they are similar, not necessarily congruent.
For AAS, once two angles are known the third is forced (angles sum to 180°), so AAS carries the same information as ASA and fixes a unique triangle.

If every attempt 'worked' as a single triangle, revisit SSA and AAA carefully — valid AAA data always allow different sizes, and SSA data may give zero, one or two triangles depending on the measurements, so check whether a second triangle was possible.
Compare your outcome table with the construction you actually drew; a mismatch usually means a measurement was placed in the wrong position (e.g. the angle not truly between the two sides).
activities.rationale: Constructing triangles from given conditions lets students discover empirically which data over- or under-determine a figure, and separates congruence (same shape and size) from similarity (same shape, scaled) through a concrete size-changed counter-example rather than assertion.
sourceClaims: HSG.CO.B.8: 'Explain how the criteria for triangle congruence (ASA, SAS, and SSS) follow from the definition of congruence in terms of rigid motions.' The standard lists exactly and only ASA, SAS and SSS as the triangle congruence criteria.

SSA (two sides and a non-included angle) does not determine a triangle up to congruence — the 'swinging side' yields two non-congruent triangles from the same data; AAA is also insufficient (it determines a triangle only up to similarity); AAS IS sufficient because two equal angle-pairs force the third; SSS, SAS, ASA each require three pieces of information.

KS3 statutory: pupils 'understand and use the relationship between parallel lines and alternate and corresponding angles' and work with congruence and standard triangle labelling as part of geometry and measures; drawing/measuring and constructing figures from given conditions underpins congruence reasoning.
learnerActions: Using ruler, protractor and compass (or a dynamic geometry tool), attempt to construct a triangle from each data set: SSS (three given sides), SAS (two sides with the angle between them), ASA (two angles with the side between them), SSA (two sides with an angle opposite one), and AAA (three given angles).
For each, record whether you got exactly one triangle, more than one, or none.
For AAA, construct a second triangle with the same three angles but longer sides; compare it to the first.
Fill in a one/none/many outcome table listing each data set and its result.
Explain for AAS why giving two angles and one side forces a unique triangle even though you were not told the third angle directly.
activities.intendedInsight: CompatibleSSS,SAS,ASA,AAS orRHS data determine a triangle up to congruence. Invalid measurements may determine none;SSA can allow zero,one or two, and validAAA data allow different sizes with the same shape. Reflected or rotated copies count as congruent, not new non-congruent triangles.

activities.title: Correspondence notation: △ABC ≅ △DEF
feedback: If you wrote the vertices in an order that pairs a long side with a short one, the statement is wrong even if the triangles are congruent — reorder so matching parts line up.
Mark corresponding parts (ticks and arcs) before writing letters; this prevents reading off the wrong equal pairs.
A correct statement lets you list all three equal side pairs and all three equal angle pairs purely from the letters, with no diagram.
activities.rationale: Correspondence notation is a convention that must be practised: matching letter position means matching part, so a correct statement lets learners read off all equal sides and angles. A static labelled reference of the criteria (SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, RHS), with SSA shown as a non-criterion, and correspondence notation serves as a vocabulary anchor alongside this practice.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory: pupils 'understand and use the relationship between parallel lines and alternate and corresponding angles' and work with congruence and standard triangle labelling as part of geometry and measures; drawing/measuring and constructing figures from given conditions underpins congruence reasoning.

SSA (two sides and a non-included angle) does not determine a triangle up to congruence — the 'swinging side' yields two non-congruent triangles from the same data; AAA is also insufficient (it determines a triangle only up to similarity); AAS IS sufficient because two equal angle-pairs force the third; SSS, SAS, ASA each require three pieces of information.
learnerActions: Given a pair of triangles with matched tick-marks on equal sides and arcs on equal angles, identify which vertex matches which.
Write the congruence statement in the form △ABC ≅ △___ so that the letter order pairs matching vertices.
From your statement, read off which sides are equal and which angles are equal, without looking back at the diagram.
Check: does the position of each letter in the two names point to a genuinely matching part? Mark the corresponding parts first, then write the statement.
Given a WRONG statement whose letters pair non-matching parts, correct it and explain what went wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: The order of letters in a congruence statement encodes the correspondence: matching positions name matching vertices, sides and angles. The statement is only correct when every paired position is a genuinely equal part.

activities.title: Classify and reason: one, none or many?
feedback: For validSAS data, the included angle fixes a unique triangle up to congruence. ForSSA, inspect the actual measurements: there can be zero,one or two triangles, so a single solution is possible. The9cm/6cm/40-degree example has two; do not generalise that count to everySSA case. RHS is a valid special right-triangle criterion.
'Same angles so congruent' is a similarity-vs-congruence error: equal angles fix shape only, so the triangles may be different sizes.
Reasoning that merely names a criterion without saying why the data force (or fail to force) a unique triangle is incomplete — the justification is the point.
activities.rationale: Identifying the applicable criterion, judging one/none/many, and matching corresponding parts are assessable with selected-response and matching formats, and incorrect answer options can embody SSA-as-SAS and AAA-as-congruent errors. This format can check reasoning efficiently but does not itself elicit independent construction or the hands-on swinging experience, so it should follow the construction work rather than replace it.
sourceClaims: SSA (two sides and a non-included angle) does not determine a triangle up to congruence — the 'swinging side' yields two non-congruent triangles from the same data; AAA is also insufficient (it determines a triangle only up to similarity); AAS IS sufficient because two equal angle-pairs force the third; SSS, SAS, ASA each require three pieces of information.

HSG.CO.B.8: 'Explain how the criteria for triangle congruence (ASA, SAS, and SSS) follow from the definition of congruence in terms of rigid motions.' The standard lists exactly and only ASA, SAS and SSS as the triangle congruence criteria.
learnerActions: For each given data set, answer: which criterion applies (SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, RHS) — or none — and does it produce one triangle, none, or more than one?
When shown 'two sides and an angle', state explicitly whether the angle is between the two sides (SAS) or opposite one of them (SSA) before deciding.
When shown three equal angles, decide whether the triangles must be congruent, and justify.
Match corresponding parts in a △ABC ≅ △DEF item.
For each answer, write one sentence of reasoning that names WHY the data do or do not fix a unique triangle.
activities.intendedInsight: Deciding which criterion applies and whether a data set fixes a unique triangle requires checking the included/non-included distinction and separating congruence from similarity — not pattern-matching 'two sides and an angle = SAS'.

activities.title: Construct a right triangle from hypotenuse and one side
feedback: The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle; check that the5cm length isBC, not a second leg.
Only one intersection lies on the chosen ray. A mirror image acrossAB is congruent, so it is not a second non-congruent solution.
activities.rationale: Restores the statedRHS objective with a concrete compass construction, complementing the preservedSSA/SAS contrast. This activity is a proposed design, not a validated intervention.
learnerActions: DrawAB=3cm and a perpendicular ray fromA; the angle atA is90degrees.
Draw a circle centred atB with radius5cm. Its intersection with the chosen perpendicular ray locatesC, soBC is the5cm hypotenuse andAB is the3cm side.
Compare two constructions with the same data and explain why they are congruent, including reflected or rotated copies.
activities.intendedInsight: A right angle, the hypotenuse and one other side determine a right triangle up to congruence: this isRHS, not arbitrarySSA.

constraints: A static labelled panel of the cases and correspondence notation is a useful reference and vocabulary anchor, but a fixed image cannot let the learner swing the non-included side and see a second triangle appear; use it alongside, not instead of, construction.

Selected-response/matching items can check which criterion applies, the one/none/many judgement, and correspondence matching, and can use incorrect options that embody SSA-as-SAS and AAA-as-congruent errors — but recognition items do not elicit independent construction or the hands-on swinging experience, so pair them with hands-on construction.
For the SSA swinging-side task, require a stated REASON with the prediction; the reasoning (appealing to the non-included angle / swinging side) is the diagnostic part, not the bare count.
When demonstrating SSA, note that the swing can give zero, one, or two triangles depending on the measurements; the 6 cm/9 cm/40° setup is one specific case (two triangles), not a universal count.
In the swinging-side construction, the free arm meets the OTHER arm of the given angle (the ray from the angled vertex), not the base line itself; describe the crossing on that ray.

Distinguish congruence (same shape AND size) from similarity (same shape, possibly scaled) explicitly; AAA equal angles give similarity, which is a legitimate and useful relation, not merely a 'failed congruence'.
Paper/card strips and compass arcs are approximations of the ideal plane figure (real card has slight thickness); treat the drawn or physical triangle as a representation of the abstract triangle.

An optional interactive constructor can provide hinged rods, an angle setting, an arc/crossing counter and a correspondence readout. Ruler/protractor/compass work also permits constructing and comparing the triangles; no comparative learning-effectiveness claim is established here.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Correction applied: the original poeTask/recommendation described the swinging 6 cm side as meeting 'the base', which is inconsistent with the stated geometry (9 cm base, 40° angle at one end, arm pinned at the far end). The arm's arc crosses the OTHER arm of the 40° angle; actions, feedback and the audit were corrected accordingly.
Self-audit: AAS is correctly derived from the angle sum (two angles force the third = 180° total), consistent with the sources; retained as stated.

Self-audit on the specific SSA triplet (9 cm base, 6 cm arm, 40° opposite the 6 cm side): an editor arithmetic check gives perpendicular distance from the pinned end to the 40° ray ≈ 9·sin40° ≈ 5.79 cm; since 5.79 < 6 < 9 two solutions are expected, matching the source's 'two triangles'. This was computed by the editor, not re-verified against fresh sources; the general SSA outcome remains zero/one/two, and activities frame the count as learner-discovered.
RHS is listed as a criterion but is not developed in any activity; if RHS production is assessed, add an explicit right-angle–hypotenuse–side construction/example.

The source row's 3d and conversation entries claimed a third dimension 'adds nothing' and the concept 'cannot' be taught by an in-role exchange. These universal-necessity claims are not established by the sources and have been dropped rather than propagated; construction/manipulation is proposed as effective without asserting other media are useless.
Reteach-prerequisite links and the assessment diagnostic structure live in the source assess field and were not altered here; internal identifiers are omitted from this guidance.

assess.poeTask: Set up a fixed base line with a 40° angle at one end and a 6 cm 'swinging' side pinned at the far end (a card strip or compass arc). Ask the child to PREDICT how many triangles can be completed, and to say WHY, BEFORE they swing the side. Then let them swing (or compass) it and observe the two points where it meets the base — two different triangles from the same SSA data. The stated reason for the prediction is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: If the 40° angle were BETWEEN the 6 cm and 9 cm sides instead, how many triangles then — and why does moving the angle change everything?
Someone says 'these two triangles have all three angles equal, so they must be congruent' — do you agree? What could be different about them?
Write the congruence statement △ABC ≅ △___ for these two triangles — which vertex matches which, and how do you know?
What is the smallest set of measurements you would need to be SURE there is only one triangle?
assess.correctAnswer: More than one (here, two). This is SSA — two sides and a non-included angle, the ambiguous case: the 6 cm side can swing to meet the base ray in two different positions, so the measurements do NOT determine a unique triangle. Only SSS, SAS, ASA (and AAS, and RHS for right triangles) force a unique triangle; SSA in general does not. The reasoning must appeal to the angle being non-included / the side being able to swing.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats SSA as a congruence criterion by conflating it with SAS — 'two sides and an angle always fix a triangle' — without checking whether the angle is included
errorPatterns.nextMove: Run the swinging-side compass demo so two triangles appear from the same data; train the habit of checking whether the angle lies BETWEEN the two sides; have them construct both triangles themselves
errorPatterns.distractor: Exactly one — two sides and an angle always fix a triangle (SAS).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'exactly one triangle' and justifies it by naming SAS or 'two sides and an angle are given'

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes equal angles (AAA) prove congruence — confuses congruence with similarity
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast congruence (same shape AND size) with similarity (same shape, scaled); show AAA fixes shape only, enlarging one triangle to break congruence while angles stay equal
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a follow-up, claims two triangles with all three angles equal must be congruent

errorPatterns.pattern: Mismatches corresponding parts — ignores that the letter order in △ABC ≅ △DEF encodes which vertices, sides and angles correspond
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reground the convention: matching position in the two names means matching part; mark corresponding parts before writing the statement
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes a congruence statement whose letter order pairs non-matching sides/angles, or reads off the wrong equal parts

responseLevels.gap: Applies the criteria as memorised letters without meaning — treats any 'two sides and an angle' as fixing a triangle and confuses congruence with similarity.
responseLevels.full: Determines whether given measurements yield one, none or many triangles by reasoning about the included angle and the swinging side, distinguishes congruence from similarity, uses correct correspondence notation, and transfers the reasoning to a new configuration.
responseLevels.partial: Names SSS/SAS/ASA correctly and can match corresponding parts, but cannot explain why SSA is ambiguous or why AAA gives only similarity — lists the valid criteria without reasoning about what determines a unique triangle.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I give you two sides of a triangle — 6 cm and 9 cm — and an angle of 40° that is NOT between them (it sits opposite the 6 cm side). Is there exactly one such triangle, more than one, or none? Explain your reasoning.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A student who understands determination recognises SSA as ambiguous and reasons via the swinging side / non-included angle; a student who pattern-matches 'two sides and an angle = SAS' answers 'exactly one'. The non-included angle is the hinge — the correct answer requires the included/non-included distinction and cannot be reached by reciting 'two sides and an angle fix a triangle'.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 8–9y; multiply 2- and 3-digit numbers by a 1-digit number using formal written (short) multiplication, including carrying, and check with estimation.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y4 'multiply two-digit and three-digit numbers by a one-digit number using formal written layout' (short multiplication), building on Y3 mental→written 2-digit×1-digit.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.NBT.5 — 'Multiply a whole number of up to four digits by a one-digit whole number … using strategies based on place value and the properties of operations; illustrate and explain … using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models.' (CCSS emphasises area/place-value strategies before the compact algorithm.)
• Operational details — the formal algorithm must be built ON the area/partitioning model, not taught as disconnected digit-manipulation. Progression: partition (47×6 = 40×6 + 7×6), lay out as an area model / grid method, then compress to the columnar short-multiplication layout where carrying records the regrouped tens/hundreds. Insist children can explain what the 'carried' digit means (it's regrouped place value). Estimation first (47×6 ≈ 50×6 = 300) frames a reasonable answer and catches place-value errors.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8): 2-digit × 1-digit with the grid/area method (43×3). Tier B (age 8–9): 3-digit × 1-digit short multiplication with carrying (234×5) and an estimate. Tier C (age 9): explain each carried digit as regrouped place value and connect the compact layout back to the area model.
bestPractices: Build the algorithm from the area/grid method: 47×6 as 40×6 + 7×6 laid out as two sub-rectangles, THEN compress to the columnar form so 'carrying' is understood as regrouping, not a rule.
Require an estimate before calculating (rounding a factor) to set an expected magnitude and catch place-value slips.
Make the meaning of the carried digit explicit — it is regrouped tens/hundreds, written and then added in — not a mysterious little number.
Use place-value counters/columns alongside the written digits during the transition so each written step maps to a concrete regrouping.
Practise with numbers that force carrying in different columns, and check answers against the estimate and via the inverse.
keyRepresentations: Area/grid model (partition each factor by place value) — the conceptual home of short multiplication
Place-value columns with counters — makes carrying = regrouping visible
The compact columnar layout with the carry digit recorded
Estimation on a number line / rounding — to bound the answer
commonMisconceptions: Treating carrying as a meaningless ritual and misplacing or forgetting the carried digit.
Multiplying only the ones and 'adding' the tens digit rather than multiplying it (place-value error): 47×6 giving 42+... wrong.
Aligning digits incorrectly or dropping a place, producing answers off by a factor of 10.
Not connecting the compact method to the area model, so errors can't be self-diagnosed.
Skipping estimation, so a wildly wrong magnitude goes unnoticed.

learn.summary: For ages 8–9, build formal short (columnar) multiplication of 2- and 3-digit numbers by a 1-digit number ON TOP of the area/grid model so that 'carrying' is understood as regrouping place value, not a ritual. Estimate first to bound the answer, work partial products in columns with the carry recorded, then connect the compact answer back to the sum of the area sub-products. Core examples: 47×6=282 and 234×5=1170.

activities.title: Method bridge: area model beside the columns
feedback: If the tens digit comes out far too large, check whether you added the carry before multiplying: multiply the digit first (5×3=15), THEN add the carried number (+2=17).
If the answer is off by a factor of ten, check column alignment — only one digit belongs in each column and the extra ten/hundred must travel one place left.
When the area sub-products (1000+150+20) sum to exactly the column answer (1170), you have connected the two methods correctly.
If a single-digit product is wrong (e.g. 5×4 recorded as 25 instead of 20), pause and shore up that specific table fact before continuing.
activities.rationale: The UK Y4 standard requires using the formal written (short multiplication) layout; US 4.NBT.5 and NCETM guidance place that procedure on place-value and area/array strategies, and estimating first helps catch place-value slips. Showing the area model and columns updating together is a proposed way to make 'carry = regroup' concrete and self-checkable; it has not been separately validated here.
sourceClaims: Y4 pupils multiply two- and three-digit numbers by a one-digit number using formal written layout (short multiplication).
4.NBT.5 requires multiplying up to four-digit by one-digit using place-value/property strategies, illustrated with arrays and area models before/with the algorithm.
The formal written algorithm should be built from the area/grid model and place-value regrouping, with estimation used to check magnitude.
learnerActions: Estimate first by rounding a factor, e.g. for 234×5 use ≈200×5=1000 (or ≈50×6=300 for 47×6), and write the estimate down before calculating.
Draw an area/grid model splitting a factor by place value: for 234×5 make three sub-rectangles 200×5, 30×5 and 4×5; for 47×6 make 40×6 and 7×6.
Set out the same calculation in a short-multiplication column layout right next to the area model.

Work each partial product in the columns in lockstep with the matching sub-rectangle. For 234×5: 5×4=20 → write 0 in the ones and regroup 2 tens; 5×3=15, +2=17 → write 7 in the tens, regroup 1 hundred; 5×2=10, +1=11 → write 1 in the hundreds and 1 in the thousands, giving 1170.
Say aloud what each carried digit means, e.g. 'the little 2 is 2 regrouped tens'.
Add the area sub-products (1000+150+20=1170) and check they equal the columnar answer exactly.
Compare the finished answer against your estimate; if it is off by a factor of ten, look for a misaligned column.
activities.intendedInsight: The carried digits are the area model regrouped and folded into columns — multiply the digit first, THEN add the carry, keeping one digit per column.

activities.title: Make the carry visible with place-value counters
feedback: If you wrote a two-digit partial product all in one column, remember each column holds only one digit — the extra ten must move left as a counter.
If you forgot to carry, check whether any counters are left stranded in a column that should hold at most nine.
activities.rationale: Place-value counters alongside the written digits let each written step map to a concrete regrouping, a proposed way to target the 'carrying is a meaningless ritual' misconception.
sourceClaims: The formal written algorithm should be built from the area/grid model and place-value regrouping, with estimation used to check magnitude.
learnerActions: Under the column headings, lay out the first factor with place-value counters as many times as the one-digit multiplier says (e.g. 6 groups of 47 for 47×6), so the counters show the whole product.
As you compute each partial product, physically move a regrouped ten (or hundred) one column to the left to represent the carried digit.
Match each counter move to the little digit you write above the next column.
Narrate: 'ten ones regroup into one ten, so the ten moves left.'
activities.intendedInsight: Carrying is the physical act of regrouping ten of one unit into one of the next place; the written carry records that move.

activities.title: Annotated worked example as a reference anchor
feedback: Use this as a model to copy the layout and language, then work a fresh calculation yourself — a worked example shows the structure but does not test whether you can carry correctly on your own.
activities.rationale: A static annotated worked example is a strong reference anchor for the area-to-column link; its limit is that it does not give feedback on a learner's own fresh calculation.
sourceClaims: The formal written algorithm should be built from the area/grid model and place-value regrouping, with estimation used to check magnitude.
learnerActions: Study a worked 234×5 with the area model above and the matching short-multiplication below.

For each column, read (or reveal) the explanation of the partial product and what its carry stands for, e.g. 'this is 2 regrouped tens' (from 5×4=20) and 'this is 1 regrouped hundred' (from 5×3=15, +2=17).
Match each area sub-rectangle to the column it feeds into.
activities.intendedInsight: Every column in the compact method has a home in the area model, and every carry names a specific regrouped place value.

activities.title: Consolidation and error-spotting checks
feedback: Correct for 47×6: 6×7=42, write 2 carry 4; 6×4=24, +4=28, so 282. The carry is added AFTER multiplying.
For 234×5 the estimate ≈200×5=1000 tells you 1170 is reasonable; an answer like 117 or 11700 signals a misaligned column off by a factor of ten.
These items consolidate and assess the procedure; pair them with the area-model work so errors can be self-diagnosed, not just marked wrong.
activities.rationale: Short multiplication is procedurally checkable, so targeted fill-in, estimate-choice and spot-the-error items can consolidate it; the limit is that they test the procedure rather than building the area-model link, so they complement rather than replace it. No original source claim directly supports this consolidation principle.
learnerActions: Fill in the missing carry digit in a partly-worked 47×6.
Choose the best estimate for 234×5 from given options and justify the rounding.
Spot the error in a worked calculation where a carry was forgotten, and correct it.
Spot the error where someone added the carry before multiplying (e.g. did (4+4)×6=48 for 47×6) and explain the fix.
activities.intendedInsight: Short multiplication fails in specific, visible ways — a wrong magnitude, a missing carry, or a carry added before multiplying — and these can be diagnosed and corrected.

constraints: Build the algorithm from the area/grid model (47×6 = 40×6 + 7×6) before compressing to columns; do not teach column carrying as disconnected digit-manipulation.
Always require an estimate before calculating (round a factor) to set expected magnitude and help catch place-value slips.
Multiply the digit first, THEN add the carried number; do not add the carry before multiplying.
Only one digit per column; the regrouped ten/hundred travels one place left.
The written method assumes automatic recall of the relevant table facts; if single-digit products are slow or wrong, shore those up separately.
Recognition and fill-in items consolidate and assess but do not, on their own, elicit a learner independently setting out and carrying a full calculation — pair them with full worked practice.
Worked examples and annotated references anchor the structure but do not give feedback on the learner's own fresh calculation.
Practise with numbers that force carrying in different columns, and verify against the estimate and, where possible, the inverse operation.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Source row marks the CCSS (4.NBT.5) and NCETM/IES claims as verified:false in the original data; treat their support as unconfirmed.

A linked split-screen area/column tool with sliding place-value counters and a live estimate bar is offered as one concrete way to make 'carry = regroup' visible; it is an optional interaction example, not a required mechanism. Static media, counters, or paper can serve the same objective.

Original row asserted that dialogue 'can't' teach this and that a third dimension 'adds nothing'; these are not established by the available sources and have been softened — conversation and 3D are simply less suited to a planar, column-aligned procedure here, not universally incapable.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 47×6=282 (42, carry 4; 24+4=28) and 234×5=1170 (20→0 carry 2; 15+2=17→7 carry 1; 10+1=11) both check; area sub-products 1000+150+20=1170 are consistent. The 'add carry before multiplying' error (e.g. (4+4)×6=48) is retained only as an error to spot/correct, never as a valid method.

The UK Y4 source claim establishes the formal-layout requirement but not the area-model basis; the area-to-column pedagogy is supported only by the (unverified) US 4.NBT.5 and NCETM claims. Activity 1's rationale was adjusted to reflect this attribution.
Activity 4 (consolidation/error-spotting) sourceClaims set to [] because no original sources[].claim directly supports its teaching principle about procedural checkability and consolidation.

probeDeeper: When you wrote the little 4, what does it stand for — and when do you add it in?
You estimated 1000 for 234 × 5. Is 1170 close enough to be right?
Why does each column only hold one digit?
Show me where the carried ten goes and why it moves left.
assess.correctAnswer: 47 × 6 = 282 (6×7 = 42, write 2 carry 4; 6×4 = 24, +4 = 28). 234 × 5 = 1170 (5×4 = 20 write 0 carry 2; 5×3 = 15 +2 = 17 write 7 carry 1; 5×2 = 10 +1 = 11). Estimate 200×5 = 1000, so 1170 is reasonable. The teacher watches for correct carrying, adding the carry AFTER multiplying, and aligned columns.

errorPatterns.pattern: adds the carry BEFORE multiplying the next digit — e.g. for 47×6 does (4+4)×6 = 48 instead of 4×6 then +4
errorPatterns.nextMove: slow the step: multiply the digit first, say the product, THEN add the little carried number; expanded/grid method briefly to show the carry is a separate addition.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: tens digit is far too large; child incorporates the carry into the multiplication rather than after it

errorPatterns.pattern: forgets to carry, or writes the two-digit partial product fully in one column
errorPatterns.nextMove: reinforce 'only one digit per column; the extra ten travels'; use place-value columns/counters to show the ten must move left.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: e.g. writes 42 under the ones column, misaligning everything, or drops the carried ten

errorPatterns.pattern: does not know a needed table fact fluently, so the whole procedure stalls or errs
errorPatterns.nextMove: shore up the specific table facts; the written method assumes automatic recall.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: long pauses or wrong single-digit products (5×4 = 25)

errorPatterns.pattern: method correct but a single carry-addition slip; caught by estimation
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach; have the child compare to their estimate and re-do the flagged column.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: one column wrong; child's own estimate flags the answer as off

responseLevels.gap: adds carries before multiplying, forgets carries, or misaligns columns; no magnitude check.
responseLevels.full: sets out and completes short multiplication with correct carrying and alignment for two- and three-digit numbers, and verifies the result against a sensible estimate.
responseLevels.partial: executes the method correctly on the two-digit case but slips on carrying in the three-digit case, or does not use estimation to check.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to set out and solve 47 × 6 and then 234 × 5 using the formal short-multiplication column method, watching how they record and carry. Then ask them to estimate 234 × 5 to check. Watch the carry handling and column alignment, not an explanation.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Short multiplication fails in specific, visible ways: adding the carry before multiplying, forgetting to carry, or misaligning. Watching the procedure catches these; a correct final answer alone doesn't reveal whether the method is secure or was luck. The estimate step shows whether the child sanity-checks magnitude.

sources.claim: Y4 pupils multiply two- and three-digit numbers by a one-digit number using formal written layout (short multiplication).
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (KS1–2), Year 4 Number — multiplication and division

sources.claim: 4.NBT.5 requires multiplying up to four-digit by one-digit using place-value/property strategies, illustrated with arrays and area models before/with the algorithm.
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 4, Number & Operations in Base Ten (4.NBT.B.5)

sources.claim: The formal written algorithm should be built from the area/grid model and place-value regrouping, with estimation used to check magnitude.
