pedagogy.summary: Representing sums and differences on a number line is about mapping calculation onto MAGNITUDE: numbers are positions/lengths, and an addition is a forward jump of the added amount while a subtraction is a backward jump. The representational demands are that intervals (not tick marks) carry the quantity, spacing is proportional, and a jump's LENGTH is the amount added or subtracted (not its endpoint). Partitioning the jump (38 + 27 as +20 then +7) links the model to place-value strategy. The empty number line is the target tool.
bestPractices: Emphasise intervals over points: the amount is the SPACE jumped, not the marks counted — the classic off-by-one trap
Insist on proportional spacing so distance represents magnitude (a jump of 20 looks far longer than a jump of 7)
Model addition as forward jumps and subtraction as backward jumps, labelling each jump with its size
Partition jumps to mirror the mental strategy (bridge to the next ten, then the rest)
Move from pre-marked lines to the empty number line, and have children both READ a given diagram and DRAW their own
keyRepresentations: Empty number line (jumps labelled with amounts)
Pre-marked number line (equally spaced points)
Bead string / ruler (length model of number)
Partitioned jump (+20 then +7)
Backward-arrow subtraction diagram
commonMisconceptions: Counting tick marks (points) instead of intervals/jumps — off-by-one errors
Unequal or non-proportional spacing so distance doesn't represent magnitude
Reading a jump as its endpoint rather than as the amount added/subtracted
Drawing subtraction as a forward jump, or starting an addition jump from 0 rather than from the first number

learn.summary: Help 7-8 year-olds represent sums and differences within 100 on a number line by mapping calculation onto MAGNITUDE: numbers are positions/lengths, a jump's LENGTH is the amount added or subtracted (not its endpoint), addition is a forward jump and subtraction a backward jump. The key representational demands are that intervals (not tick marks) carry the quantity, spacing is proportional, and jumps can be partitioned to mirror place-value strategy (38 + 27 as +20 then +7). The target tool is the empty number line, and children should both READ a given diagram and DRAW their own.

activities.title: Build the jump: make each arrow's length equal the amount
feedback: If a jump of 20 is drawn the same length as a jump of 7, compare the two side by side against a ruler or scaled line so magnitude maps to length.
If the arrow is read as its endpoint ('+20' read as '58'), ask: does this arrow show the number 58, or does it show 'add 20'? What is the difference?
If subtraction is drawn going right, re-establish that subtraction moves left (gets smaller) and that a jump STARTS from the current number.
If the first addition jump is anchored at 0 instead of at 38, point out that the jump starts from the number you already have.
activities.rationale: A number line is a spatial-magnitude representation; letting a child size and place jumps so that length equals amount is intended to address the count-the-marks and equal-jumps errors as the child acts. An interactive version where arrow length is proportional (a +20 is longer than a +7) and that distinguishes forward-add from backward-subtract may make the mechanism concrete; this is an optional way to deliver the task, not the only way. Optionally, preserve the learner’s attempted arrow, compare it with the scaled target, then animate a corrected proportional jump and explain why its length changed; this feedback is a proposed scaffold, not evidence of superior effectiveness.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils represent and use number lines among the representations for numbers, sums and differences; number lines support addition as forward and subtraction as backward movement.

Children commonly misread number lines by counting tick marks rather than intervals and by ignoring proportional spacing; the empty number line is an effective model for representing addition and subtraction as jumps.
learnerActions: Start at 38 on a number line and add a forward jump of 20, then a forward jump of 7, landing on 58 then 65 (showing 38 + 27 = 65).
Notice and state that the +20 jump is drawn visibly longer than the +7 jump because the LENGTH of the jump is the amount.
Build 52 − 24 yourself using backward (leftward) jumps, e.g. −20 then −4, or −22 then −2 bridging 30, landing on 28.
Label each jump with its size and label the start and end points.
Both interpret a diagram you are given and construct one for a new calculation.
activities.intendedInsight: Distance on the line equals the amount: a jump represents 'add/subtract this much', not the point it lands on. Addition moves forward and subtraction moves backward, and partitioning a jump mirrors the mental place-value strategy.

activities.title: Label the spaces, not the marks
feedback: If the first mark is counted as 'one' of the jump, re-run it counting the gaps between marks instead.
If endpoints come out one off, re-step the jump labelling each space as you cross it.
activities.rationale: Explicitly counting intervals rather than points targets a common number-line error: counting tick marks instead of gaps, which gives off-by-one answers. Pre-marked lines and physical stepping aim to make the intervals tangible before moving to the empty number line.
sourceClaims: Children commonly misread number lines by counting tick marks rather than intervals and by ignoring proportional spacing; the empty number line is an effective model for representing addition and subtraction as jumps.
learnerActions: On a pre-marked, equally spaced number line, label the SPACES (intervals) between the marks rather than the marks themselves.
Physically step out a jump, counting the gaps crossed, not the ticks touched.
Check an endpoint: for a jump of 20 from 38, confirm it lands on 58 and not one mark off.
activities.intendedInsight: The amount is the number of intervals jumped, not the number of tick marks counted — this is the classic off-by-one trap.

activities.title: Interpret a given diagram, then draw your own
feedback: Reading correctly but drawing flawed lines (unequal spacing, starting from 0, or confusing amount with endpoint) shows partial command — practise producing lines from a blank start.
If spacing in a drawing doesn't match magnitude, compare against a ruler or scaled line.
Note: a hand-drawn or illustrated line is evocative, not exact, so proportional spacing can only be checked roughly; use a ruler or scale to tighten it.
activities.rationale: Interpretation exposes whether the child reads jumps as amounts and knows forward = add; translation exposes production errors invisible in reading (unequal spacing, counting marks, wrong direction, starting from 0). Requiring both read and draw gives a fuller picture of understanding; recognition or matching alone does not elicit the independent proportional drawing.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils represent and use number lines among the representations for numbers, sums and differences; number lines support addition as forward and subtraction as backward movement.
learnerActions: Interpret: shown a number line starting at 38 with an arrow landing on 58 labelled '+20' and then an arrow landing on 65 labelled '+7', state what calculation it shows (38 + 27 = 65) and what each jump means.
Explain that 27 has been partitioned into 20 and 7, each a forward jump of that amount.
Translate: on a blank line, draw a number line to show 52 − 24, using backward jumps totalling 24, landing on 28, with start, end, and each jump labelled and spaced proportionally.
Match number-line diagrams to the equations they represent.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a diagram and faithfully producing one are different skills; full command means you can do both, reading jumps as amounts and drawing proportional, correctly-directed lines.

constraints: Place whole numbers on a number line with equally spaced points; show addition as a forward jump and subtraction as a backward jump (within 100).
Intervals, not tick marks, carry the quantity; spacing must be proportional so a jump of 20 looks far longer than a jump of 7.
A jump's length is the amount added or subtracted, not the point it lands on.
Move from pre-marked lines to the empty number line as the target tool; have children both read and draw.

Matching diagrams to equations and drawing on a marked line can check interpretation and rough production, but recognition/matching alone does not elicit the independent, proportional drawing that shows full command.
Hand-drawn or illustrated number lines are approximations; proportional spacing cannot be rigorously assessed from an evocative illustration without a scale or ruler.
If points-versus-intervals is shaky, reteach the underlying number-line representation before proceeding.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources have not been re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

One source (empty number line / misconception research) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its claims, including that the empty number line is an 'effective model', as indicative, not confirmed.

The original row asserted '3D adds nothing' and 'talk cannot exercise the drawing-and-reading of a spatial representation.' These are catalog-fit opinions, not established pedagogical laws, and have been softened/omitted: a number line is primarily a 1-D/2-D spatial task that benefits from drawing, while spoken explanation can still support reasoning about it.

The original row framed an interactive tool that auto-stretches jumps as the moment the line 'stops being decoration'; this is a design claim, not evidence of efficacy, and has been presented as an optional delivery, not a requirement.

Efficacy wording in the activity rationales was kept to intended/may form because no cited source establishes that these specific activities outperform alternatives, and no source speaks directly to the read-versus-draw distinction beyond the forward=add convention.

probeDeeper: The arrow goes from 38 to 58 — does it show the number '58', or does it show 'add 20'? What's the difference?
Why should a jump of 20 be drawn longer than a jump of 7 — what would be wrong with the picture if they were equal?
Which way do the arrows point for a subtraction, and why?
If I drew the +7 jump LONGER than the +20 jump, what would be wrong even if the numbers were right?
assess.correctAnswer: Interpretation: it shows 38 + 27 = 65, with 27 partitioned into 20 and 7, each arrow a forward jump of that amount (a jump = an addition of its length). Translation: a number line from 52 with backward jump(s) totalling 24 (e.g. −20 then −4, or −22 then −2 bridging 30) landing on 28, start and end labelled, jumps sized and labelled, points spaced proportionally.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts the tick marks (points) instead of the intervals — a jump of 20 read/drawn as passing 21 marks, landing one off
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have the child label the SPACES between marks, not the marks; physically step the jumps counting gaps. Reteach number-line representation if points-vs-intervals is shaky.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Off-by-one endpoints; the child counts the first mark as 'one' of the jump

errorPatterns.pattern: Non-proportional spacing — draws a jump of 20 the same length as a jump of 7 (or ticks at irregular intervals)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare their jumps against a ruler/scaled line so magnitude maps to length; contrast a +20 and a +7 side by side.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In the drawn line, distance doesn't match magnitude; big and small jumps look alike

errorPatterns.pattern: Direction or anchor error — draws the subtraction as a forward jump, or starts the addition jump from 0 instead of from 38, or reads a jump as its endpoint (the +20 arrow read as '58')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-establish that subtraction moves left (gets smaller) and that a jump STARTS from the current number and its length is the amount, not where it lands.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Subtraction shown going right, the first jump anchored at 0, or the amount and the landing point confused

responseLevels.gap: Counts tick marks, spaces jumps unequally, or points them the wrong way; the diagram doesn't map to the calculation.
responseLevels.full: Reads jumps as the amounts added/subtracted (not endpoints), knows forward = add and backward = subtract, and draws a proportional, correctly-directed number line for a new calculation with jumps and endpoints labelled.
responseLevels.partial: Interprets a given number-line calculation correctly but draws one with flaws (unequal spacing, starts from 0, or endpoint/amount confusion) — can read but not yet faithfully produce (or vice versa).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: First, interpretation: show the child a number line starting at 38 with two arrows drawn — a jump landing on 58 labelled '+20', then a jump landing on 65 labelled '+7'. Ask: 'What calculation does this picture show, and what does each jump mean?' Then, translation: hand them a blank line and say 'Now draw a number line to show 52 − 24.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The interpret move exposes whether the child reads jumps as amounts (not endpoints) and knows forward = add. The translate move exposes production errors invisible in reading: unequal spacing, counting marks, wrong direction, or starting from 0. A child who can both read AND faithfully draw understands the representation; one who can read a given diagram but draws a flawed one has only partial command.

sources.claim: Year 2 pupils represent and use number lines among the representations for numbers, sums and differences; number lines support addition as forward and subtraction as backward movement.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (KS1)

sources.claim: Children commonly misread number lines by counting tick marks rather than intervals and by ignoring proportional spacing; the empty number line is an effective model for representing addition and subtraction as jumps.

pedagogy.summary: A scale diagram or map represents real distances by a fixed multiplicative scale, written as a ratio like 1:25000 (1 unit on the map = 25000 of the same units in real life). Fluency means (1) reading the scale as a pure multiplier, (2) going the right way — MULTIPLY a map measurement to get the real distance, DIVIDE a real distance to get the map measurement — and (3) converting units so the answer is sensible (1:25000 gives cm → cm, then convert to m or km). The two recurring hazards are direction (multiplying vs dividing) and the unit conversion buried in the scale; both are procedural and best caught by a magnitude sense-check ('should the real distance be far bigger?').
bestPractices: Read the scale ratio aloud as 'one centimetre on the map is 25000 centimetres in real life' so the shared unit and the multiplier are explicit before any arithmetic.
Establish the direction rule with a sense-check: real life is bigger, so map→real MULTIPLY, real→map DIVIDE; estimate the size of the answer first.
Do the unit conversion as a deliberate final step (cm → m ÷100 → km ÷1000), tracking units, rather than leaving an answer in centimetres.
Have pupils both READ a map (find a real distance) and CREATE a scale diagram (draw a room to a chosen scale), so the divide-direction is practised, not just the multiply-direction.
Use a double number line pairing map-cm with real-distance to keep the proportional relationship visible.
keyRepresentations: Scale ratio 1:n read as 'one unit = n units'
Double number line / ratio table (map distance | real distance)
Scale bar on the map for direct measure-and-read
Unit-conversion chain cm → m → km as an explicit final step
commonMisconceptions: Forgetting the unit conversion — leaving the real distance in centimetres (200000 cm) instead of converting to metres/kilometres, or converting with the wrong factor.
Going the wrong direction — dividing a map measurement instead of multiplying (or vice versa), producing a real distance smaller than the map one.
Misreading the ratio — treating 1:25000 additively, or reading it as '1 cm = 25000 km' (unit slip).
Applying the scale to only part of the problem, or mixing map units and real units without a common basis.

learn.summary: Learners work with scale on maps and diagrams, reading a ratio such as 1:25000 as a same-unit multiplier (1 cm on the map = 25000 cm in real life). The two recurring hazards are direction (multiply map→real, divide real→map) and the unit conversion buried in the scale (cm → m → km). Both are best caught with a magnitude sense-check and are practised in BOTH directions — reading a real distance off a map AND creating a scale diagram of a room.

activities.title: Measure, scale and convert on a map
feedback: If the working stops at 200000 and cm: 'That's the real distance in centimetres — now convert. How many centimetres are in a metre? In a kilometre? Walk the cm → m → km chain.'
If the real distance comes out tiny (e.g. 0.00032): 'Which is bigger, the map or real life? If the map is smaller, map→real should MULTIPLY, not divide. Re-estimate the size first.'

If the ratio was read as '1 cm = 25000 km': 'The 25000 is in the same unit as the 1, so both are centimetres. Keep the units the same while you scale, then convert carefully, for example by multiplying first and then converting cm to m to km.'

If arithmetic slips (e.g. 20000 or 2000000, or ÷10 instead of ÷100): 'Your method is right — estimate the order of magnitude first (hundreds of thousands of cm, a couple of km) and check your answer against it.'
activities.rationale: Direction and unit conversion are procedural hazards; reading the ratio aloud, estimating magnitude, and tracking units through an explicit conversion chain target both directly. A double number line or ratio table pairing map-cm with real distance can keep the proportional relationship visible.
sourceClaims: Pupils should use scale factors, scale diagrams and maps (e.g. a scale such as 1:25000), interpreting and creating scale drawings and solving problems involving proportional reasoning and metric units.
Students apply inappropriate additive strategies to multiplicative scaling situations, so scaling must be taught as a consistent multiplier applied in the correct direction.
learnerActions: Read the scale ratio aloud before calculating, e.g. 'one centimetre on the map is 25000 centimetres in real life' — emphasise that both sides share the SAME unit.

Measure the map distance between two points (e.g. two villages 8 cm apart on a 1:25000 map). Optionally, drag a ruler on a map and use a live panel that unfolds measured map-cm, multiplication by25000, then the cm-to-m-to-km conversion, with the scale bar alongside for checking.
Before calculating, estimate: real life is bigger than the map, so map→real MUST multiply — predict roughly how big the real distance should be.
Do the unit conversion as a deliberate final step, tracking units: 200000 cm ÷ 100 = 2000 m, then ÷ 1000 = 2 km.
Apply the scale to the whole measurement, keeping both quantities in a common unit — do not scale only part of the problem.
Cross-check against the scale bar on the map and against your estimate: is 2 km between villages sensible?
activities.intendedInsight: Scale is a consistent multiplier: going from a map measurement to the real distance means multiplying by the scale denominator for this reduced map; the reverse means dividing. Track the units at each step and express the answer in the units requested, here kilometres.

activities.title: Draw a room to scale (the divide direction)
feedback: If the drawn room balloons far larger than the reference doorway: 'A scale drawing is smaller than reality — you multiplied where you should divide. Real→map means DIVIDE by the scale factor.'
If the learner forgets to convert m to cm before dividing: 'Get both lengths into the same unit first (4 m = 400 cm), then divide by 100.'
If correct: 'Your 4 cm line represents a 4 m wall — explain how you'd go the other way, from the drawing back to the real wall.'
activities.rationale: Practising the divide-direction, not just the multiply-direction, prevents a one-directional, insecure procedure. Laying out against a known reference provides an immediate, concrete magnitude check.
sourceClaims: Interpreting and using scale drawings is a proportional-reasoning task requiring metric-unit work; a formative lesson is built around planning a layout to scale.

Pupils should use scale factors, scale diagrams and maps (e.g. a scale such as 1:25000), interpreting and creating scale drawings and solving problems involving proportional reasoning and metric units.
learnerActions: Choose a scale (e.g. 1:100) for drawing your own bedroom.
For each real wall length, work out the line to draw: divide the real length by the scale factor (e.g. a 4 m wall at 1:100 → 4 m = 400 cm, 400 ÷ 100 = 4 cm on the diagram).
Draw the walls at the computed lengths and compare the result against a reference object of known size (e.g. a doorway) to sanity-check.
Say aloud why this is a divide: 'the diagram is smaller than real life, so real→map DIVIDES.'

Check: if the drawn room looks absurdly large, you probably multiplied instead of dividing, so revisit the direction rule. If it shrinks to a dot, check your units. For example, dividing 4 m by 100 without first converting to centimetres gives 0.04, which is far too small to draw.
activities.intendedInsight: Going from real distances to a scale drawing requires dividing by the scale factor; seeing the room come out the wrong SIZE against a familiar reference makes the direction error concrete.

activities.title: Direction and conversion practice with sharp distractors
feedback: If 200000 is chosen: 'That is the real distance in centimetres — the question asked for kilometres. Convert cm → m → km.'
If 0.00032 is chosen: 'You divided; real life is bigger than the map, so map→real multiplies.'
If the wrong direction is picked for drawing: 'A drawing is smaller than reality, so real→map divides.'
activities.rationale: Items with error-patterned options can surface whether learners spot direction and conversion mistakes; this is a check that reinforces the correct-direction multiplier. It does not by itself elicit the independent construction of a scale drawing, which requires learners to compute and draw the lines themselves in the tasks above.
sourceClaims: Students apply inappropriate additive strategies to multiplicative scaling situations, so scaling must be taught as a consistent multiplier applied in the correct direction.
learnerActions: Answer targeted items such as: '8 cm on a 1:25000 map → ___ km' (correct: 2 km).
Identify and reject the error value 200000 (the real distance left unconverted, in cm).
Identify and reject the error value ≈0.00032 (the result of dividing instead of multiplying).
Decide which operation (multiply or divide) applies when drawing a room to scale versus reading a real distance.
Choose a sensible scale for a given object and justify it.
activities.intendedInsight: The common errors — leaving the answer in cm, and dividing instead of multiplying — produce predictably wrong magnitudes that a sense-check would have caught.

activities.title: Annotated map reference card
feedback: Prompt the learner to restate: 'Does 1:25000 mean 1 cm = 25000 cm = 250 m? Why not 25000 km?'
activities.rationale: A static annotated map consolidates reading and the conversion chain, but it does not let the learner measure a distance of their own choosing or draw to scale — so it supports, rather than replaces, the measuring and drawing tasks.
learnerActions: Reveal the scale meaning on a worked map, e.g. 'one cm here = 250 m out there' (for a 1:25000 map, 25000 cm = 250 m).
Follow a worked real-distance calculation between two named towns, with each conversion step shown.
Use the scale bar directly to cross-check a distance.
activities.intendedInsight: The reading of a scale and its worked conversion can be consolidated as a reference, reinforcing the same-unit meaning of the ratio.

constraints: Practise BOTH directions: reading a real distance from a map (multiply) AND creating a scale diagram (divide). A procedure learned in only one direction is not yet secure.

For real-distance questions requesting kilometres, show the explicit conversion chain with units (cm to m: divide by100; m to km: divide by1000). Do not stop at an unconverted centimetre value for those questions. Scale-drawing lengths may appropriately be given in centimetres.
Read the ratio as a same-unit multiplier — both sides of 1:25000 are the same unit — to block additive readings and unit slips like '1 cm = 25000 km'.
Apply the scale consistently to the whole measurement, keeping map and real quantities on a common-unit basis; do not scale only part of a problem.

The annotated/reference map is a scaffold for reading and consolidation; it cannot provide practice in measuring a self-chosen distance or in drawing to scale, so it should not be the primary teaching activity.

Recognition/multiple-choice items check whether errors are spotted; they do not elicit the independent construction of a scale drawing, which requires the learner to compute and draw the lines themselves.

A live-computing map tool and interactive layout are optional means to make the measure-scale-convert and divide-direction feedback immediate; the same learning can be reached with a paper map, ruler, scale bar and squared paper.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic checked: 8 × 25000 = 200000 cm; ÷100 = 2000 m; ÷1000 = 2 km. The dividing value 8 ÷ 25000 ≈ 0.00032 and the unconverted 200000 cm are consistent with the stated error patterns. A 4 m wall at 1:100 → 400 cm ÷ 100 = 4 cm line, matching the probe counterexample. For 1:25000, 25000 cm = 250 m, so 'one cm here = 250 m out there' is correct.

The original misconception 'applying the scale to only part of the problem, or mixing map units and real units without a common basis' is represented via the same-unit reading plus a whole-measurement constraint and learner action, rather than a dedicated activity.

The recognition-item rationale's point that such items are a 'check, not a substitute' is an unvalidated design observation about the affordance of recognition items, not a source-backed finding; the attached source supports only the correct-direction multiplier principle the distractors probe.

The original marked 'conversation' and '3D' as poor fit with reasoning that they 'add nothing'; this is a catalog ranking, not an established pedagogical law, so it was not propagated as a universal claim. The planar nature of maps is retained only as a neutral observation about this specific task.

probeDeeper: Which is bigger — the distance on the map or the real distance? So should you multiply or divide? Does your answer fit that?
What does the '25000' in 1:25000 actually mean — 25000 of what?
Now go the other way: your bedroom wall is 4 m long and you want to draw it at 1:100 — how long is the line on your diagram? (counterexample forcing the divide-direction: 4 cm.)
Your answer is in centimetres — talk me through turning it into kilometres. How many centimetres are in a kilometre?
assess.correctAnswer: 2 km. Real distance = 8 × 25000 = 200000 cm; convert: 200000 ÷ 100 = 2000 m, then ÷ 1000 = 2 km.

errorPatterns.pattern: Forgets the unit conversion — leaves the answer as 200000 (cm) or fails to reach km, or converts with the wrong factor
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do the conversion as an explicit final step with units tracked: cm ÷100 → m ÷1000 → km. Sense-check: 2 km between villages is reasonable; 200000 km is not. Reteach unit conversion.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 8 × 25000 = 200000 and stops, or gives '200000 km' / '2000 km' having muddled the cm→m→km chain

errorPatterns.pattern: Goes the wrong direction — divides the map measurement by 25000 instead of multiplying (treats the map as bigger than reality)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor the sense-check first: real life is far bigger than the map, so map→real MUST multiply. Estimate the answer's size before calculating. Reteach the scale-factor direction from similar shapes.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 8 ÷ 25000 (≈ 0.00032) and reports a tiny real distance, or on a draw-to-scale task multiplies when they should divide

errorPatterns.pattern: Misreads the ratio 1:25000 — reads it additively, or as '1 cm = 25000 km', or ignores that both sides share a unit
errorPatterns.nextMove: Read the ratio aloud: '1 cm on the map = 25000 cm in real life' — SAME unit both sides. Only after multiplying do you convert. Reteach the precise meaning of scale factor / ratio notation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Adds 25000, or converts 8 cm to 200000 km directly, treating the 25000 as already in kilometres

errorPatterns.pattern: Correct method but a place-value / arithmetic slip in the ×25000 or the conversion
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach: have them estimate the order of magnitude first (≈ hundreds of thousands of cm ≈ a couple of km) and check the answer against it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Sets up 8 × 25000 correctly but writes 20000 or 2000000, or divides by 10 instead of 100 in the cm→m step

responseLevels.gap: Divides the wrong way, or leaves the answer in centimetres, or misreads the ratio; cannot produce a sensible real distance in km.
responseLevels.full: Multiplies 8 × 25000 and converts cleanly to 2 km, explains that real life is bigger so map→real multiplies (and real→map divides), reads the ratio as a same-unit multiplier, and transfers to drawing a scale diagram of a room.
responseLevels.partial: Multiplies correctly to 200000 cm but stumbles on the unit conversion (wrong factor or stops at cm), or can do map→real but not the reverse (real→map) — the procedure is one-directional and not yet secure on units.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: On a map with scale 1:25000, two villages are 8 cm apart. Work out the real distance between them, and give your answer in kilometres. Show your working.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A pupil who understands both the direction (map→real multiplies) and the unit conversion reaches 2 km — a value only that full chain produces. Watching the working exposes exactly where a pupil stops: at 200000 (no conversion), at a tiny number (divided the wrong way), or at a wrong magnitude (bad conversion factor). Because the answer is demanded in km, the unit step cannot be skipped unnoticed.

sources.claim: Pupils should use scale factors, scale diagrams and maps (e.g. a scale such as 1:25000), interpreting and creating scale drawings and solving problems involving proportional reasoning and metric units.
sources.source: UK National Curriculum, Mathematics programmes of study (KS3 ratio, proportion and rates of change)

sources.claim: Interpreting and using scale drawings is a proportional-reasoning task requiring metric-unit work; a formative lesson is built around planning a layout to scale.
sources.source: Shell Centre / Mathematics Assessment Project (MAP), 'Drawing to Scale: A Garden' (Grade 7)

sources.claim: Students apply inappropriate additive strategies to multiplicative scaling situations, so scaling must be taught as a consistent multiplier applied in the correct direction.
sources.source: Shell Centre / Mathematics Assessment Project (MAP), 'Proportion and Non-Proportion Situations' (Grade 7)

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 9-10. Interpret negative numbers in real contexts (temperature, sea level, bank balance) and count forwards and backwards through zero with positive and negative whole numbers; place negatives on a number line and begin to find simple intervals (−4°C rises 7° → 3°C). Extends 'count back through zero' into using and reasoning with negatives.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 5): 'interpret negative numbers in context, count forwards and backwards with positive and negative whole numbers, including through zero'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): integers and their contexts are formalised in Grade 6 (6.NS.5-7); this is the pre-formal contextual foundation.
• Operational details — Ground negatives in multiple contexts (thermometer, sea level, money) and use the number line to count and to find intervals by 'counting the gap' through zero rather than by rules. Reinforce ordering (−4 < −1) and the meaning of the gap between a negative and a positive (the interval spans zero). Keep it count/interval based; defer formal signed arithmetic.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9, emerging): places negatives on a line and reads a sub-zero temperature. Tier B (age 9-10, secure): counts through zero and finds a simple rise/fall interval across zero. Tier C (age 10, extending): reasons about intervals spanning zero in context and orders mixed positive/negative sets confidently.
bestPractices: Use several contexts (temperature, sea level, money) so 'negative' is meaningful, not abstract.
Find intervals by counting the gap along the number line THROUGH zero, not by memorised sign rules.
Reinforce ordering across zero (−4 < −1 < 0 < 2) with the line.
Make the zero crossing explicit: the interval from −4 to 3 is 4 up to zero, then 3 more.
Keep to counting/intervals in context; defer formal negative arithmetic to later years.
keyRepresentations: Horizontal number line spanning negatives and positives
Vertical thermometer / sea-level scale
Number line 'gap counting' for intervals across zero
Real contexts: temperature change, floors/lifts, bank balance
Ordering strip mixing negatives and positives
commonMisconceptions: Ordering negatives by magnitude (−4 > −1).
Counting the interval across zero wrongly (forgetting the zero step or double-counting it).
Treating a negative as just its digit (ignoring sign).
Believing you 'can't go below zero'.
Applying whole-number intuitions (bigger digit = bigger) to negatives.

learn.summary: For ages 9-10: interpret negative whole numbers in real contexts (temperature, sea level, bank balance), place them on a number line, order mixed positive/negative sets, count forwards and backwards through zero, and find simple intervals that cross zero by counting the gap through zero (e.g. −4°C rising 7° reaches 3°C). Keep the work count- and interval-based in context; defer formal signed arithmetic to later years. Core misconceptions to confront: ordering negatives by magnitude (believing −4 > −1) and miscounting when crossing zero.

activities.title: Count the gap through zero on a thermometer/number line
feedback: If the learner lands on 11, pause: starting at −4 is to the LEFT of (below) zero, so counting 7 steps right/up only reaches 3. Contrast with starting at +4, where 7 steps reach 11.

If the learner lands on 2, check whether they counted the starting value −4 as a jump or counted zero twice; if they land on 4, check whether they skipped zero (jumping straight from −1 to 1). Count the jumps aloud together: −4→−3→−2→−1→0 is exactly four jumps, then 0→1→2→3 is three more; reaching zero takes one jump of its own, so zero is counted once, never skipped and never repeated.
When counting backwards from 3, check that after 0 comes −1, then −2 — the count continues below zero rather than stopping at 0.
When the learner splits the count as '4 up to zero, then 3 more = 7 steps total, landing on 3', confirm they have read the interval positionally rather than by a rule.
For −4°C rising 7°, the interval is 7 degrees (4 up to zero, then 3 more) and the landing value is 3°C.
activities.rationale: Grounding negatives in multiple real contexts and finding cross-zero intervals by counting the gap on the number line (before formal signed arithmetic) makes the zero crossing concrete and directly targets the magnitude-ordering and double-counting errors; counting both forwards and backwards through zero matches the stated standard.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils should 'interpret negative numbers in context, count forwards and backwards with positive and negative whole numbers, including through zero'.
Intervals across zero should be found by counting the gap on the number line through zero, in multiple contexts, before formal signed arithmetic.
learnerActions: Set a starting value in a real context, e.g. the temperature is −4°C, marked on a vertical thermometer or horizontal number line.
Apply a change, e.g. 'it rises by 7 degrees', and move a marker one step at a time, saying each value aloud: −4 → −3 → −2 → −1 → 0, then 1 → 2 → 3.
Deliberately split the count into two parts: how many steps up to reach zero (4), then how many steps beyond zero (3), and record the landing value (3°C).
Count backwards through zero as well: start at 3 and step down in ones — 3, 2, 1, 0, −1, −2 — saying what comes after 0, so you can move both forwards and backwards across zero.

Switch the SAME line into a different context — sea-level depth or a bank balance — keep the start and change equivalent, and notice the number behaves identically even though it means something different.
State in words where you crossed zero and why the total rise is 7 even though you land on 3.
activities.intendedInsight: An interval that spans zero is found by counting the gap along the line through zero — so many steps up to zero, then so many more beyond — not by a sign rule; you can count both forwards and backwards across zero, and negatives in different contexts behave the same positionally.

activities.title: Order and place mixed negatives and positives
feedback: If the learner places −4 as larger than (to the right of) −1, show both on the line: −4 sits further left/lower, so it is the smaller (colder) value; −7°C is colder than −3°C for the same reason.
Tie the feedback to the context: colder, lower, or more in debt all correspond to being further left on the line and therefore a smaller number.
Correct order smallest to largest: −4, −1, 0, 2, 5.
activities.rationale: Reinforcing ordering across zero with a concrete left-is-less experience confronts the seductive −4 > −1 magnitude error that the research flags as a common misconception.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils should 'interpret negative numbers in context, count forwards and backwards with positive and negative whole numbers, including through zero'.
learnerActions: Arrange a mixed set such as −4, −1, 0, 2, 5 from smallest to largest on a number line.
Place a single value such as −3 at its correct spot on a labelled line.
Decide which of two values is colder/lower/more in debt, e.g. 'Which is colder, −7°C or −3°C?', and justify using position on the line.
Explain why −4 is smaller than −1 even though 4 is a bigger digit than 1, referencing left-is-less on the line.
activities.intendedInsight: On the number line, further left (colder / lower / deeper in debt) means smaller, so −4 < −1 < 0 < 2 < 5 — the size of the digit does not decide the order for negatives.

activities.title: Explain the context (optional spoken/role-play extension)
feedback: Prompt the learner to justify answers by referring to the number line or scale, not just a figure, especially when a change crosses zero.
If a change does not actually cross zero (e.g. −30 m rising to −18 m), confirm that too — not every rise or fall passes through zero.
Keep answers interval/count based; avoid introducing formal signed-arithmetic rules at this stage.
activities.rationale: A character or role-play can motivate multiple real contexts and generate interval questions; the interval reasoning itself is still best grounded on the number line, so this is offered as a contextual extension rather than the primary mechanism.
learnerActions: Take on a role such as a submarine pilot describing depths below sea level, or a weather presenter describing temperature changes.

Pose and answer questions like 'We were at −30 m and rose 12 m — where are we now?' (−18 m, still below the surface) and 'It was −3°C and rose 8° — how warm now?' (+5°C, passing up through zero), and explain the crossing of zero where it happens.
Reason aloud about which depth/temperature is higher or lower and how you know.
activities.intendedInsight: Negatives describe real quantities (depth, temperature, balance); talking through changes rehearses counting through zero in meaningful situations, while noting that not every change actually crosses zero.

constraints: Use several contexts (temperature, sea level, money) so 'negative' is meaningful rather than abstract.
Find intervals by counting the gap through zero on the line, not by memorised sign rules; make the zero crossing explicit (e.g. −4 to 3 is 4 up to zero, then 3 more).
Support counting both forwards and backwards through zero, including stepping down below zero into the negatives.
Keep to counting and intervals in context; defer formal signed arithmetic to later years (US formalises integers in Grade 6; this is the pre-formal contextual foundation).

Ordering and placing tasks (ordering a set, placing on a line, fill-in-the-blank, multiple choice) can assess placement, ordering and simple cross-zero intervals, including the magnitude trap, but selection/recognition responses do not by themselves show the learner can count through zero and construct the reasoning aloud — pair them with the learner explaining their method.

A static thermometer or context poster is a useful reference and can introduce negative readings, but it cannot let the learner step through a changing value; use it as a scaffold alongside an activity where the learner actually counts the gap.
The 1D number line/scale is the natural representation for this topic; a 3D model is not needed here (this is a representation preference for this content, not a general claim that 3D adds nothing).
The role-play/spoken extension is optional and supplementary; do not treat it as a replacement for working on the number line.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source assessment lists distractor 'It is 2°C' while revealedBy says 'Answer is 2 or 4 (an off-by-one at the zero crossing)'. Both off-by-one outcomes (2 and 4) are plausible miscounts; feedback here addresses landing on 2 or 4 rather than asserting a single wrong value.

The original source labelled the 3D representation 'poor' with 'negatives live on a 1D line/scale; 3D adds nothing'. The comparative/necessity 'adds nothing' assertion is not established by the cited sources, so it has been reframed as a representation preference for this topic rather than a universal law.

Arithmetic checked: −4°C rising 7° = 3°C (four steps to zero, three beyond). Sign-stripping error gives 11 (4+7). Off-by-one at zero gives 2 or 4. Counting backwards from 3 through zero gives 3,2,1,0,−1,−2. Role-play examples: −30 m +12 m = −18 m (no crossing); −3°C +8° = +5°C (crosses zero). These are internally consistent and retained for diagnostic feedback.
The CCSS Grade 6 claim and the NCETM guidance claim were marked verified:false in the source; treat their status as unverified in any downstream use.

probeDeeper: Show −4 rising by 7 on a number line — where do you cross zero?
Which is colder, −7°C or −3°C? How does the line show it?
Count backwards from 3 in ones — what comes after 0?
assess.correctAnswer: 3°C. Count up 7 from −4: four steps reach 0, then three more reach 3 — you pass through zero.

errorPatterns.pattern: Ignores the sign and treats −4 as 4: −4 + 7 = 11
errorPatterns.nextMove: Put −4 on a number line to the LEFT of zero; count 7 steps right and see you only reach 3. Contrast with starting at +4.
errorPatterns.distractor: It is 11°C.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer is 11°C.

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscounts across zero — stops at 0, or counts 0 twice
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the jumps aloud on the line: −4→−3→−2→−1→0 is four jumps, not five; zero is a point you pass, not a step you repeat.
errorPatterns.distractor: It is 2°C.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer is 2 or 4 (an off-by-one at the zero crossing).

responseLevels.gap: Strips the sign (−4 + 7 = 11) or cannot count through zero.
responseLevels.full: Interprets negatives in context and counts through zero accurately (−4 + 7 = 3), reasoning from number-line position.
responseLevels.partial: Places negatives correctly and orders them, but miscounts by one when crossing zero.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask: 'The temperature is −4°C and it rises by 7 degrees. What is it now, and how did you work it out?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who reads negatives positionally counts up through zero and lands on 3; a child who strips the sign computes 4 + 7 = 11, and one who mishandles zero stalls at 0 or double-counts it. The reason tier reveals how they treat the crossing of zero.

sources.claim: Year 5 pupils should 'interpret negative numbers in context, count forwards and backwards with positive and negative whole numbers, including through zero'.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (Year 5 Number & place value)

sources.claim: Integers, their ordering and real-world contexts are formalised in Grade 6 (6.NS.5-7).
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, The Number System, Grade 6

sources.claim: Intervals across zero should be found by counting the gap on the number line through zero, in multiple contexts, before formal signed arithmetic.
sources.source: NCETM Primary Mastery PD: Number / negative numbers guidance

pedagogy.summary: Dividing a whole number by a unit fraction is the MEASUREMENT (quotitive) meaning of division: 4 ÷ 1/5 asks 'how many one-fifths fit inside 4 wholes?' — each whole holds 5, so 4 hold 20. The whole pedagogical battle is that the answer is BIGGER than the number you started with, which collides head-on with the whole-number intuition that 'dividing makes smaller'. Teach it by physically fitting unit-fraction pieces along a number line or ribbon, reason with estimation ('5 ÷ 5/6 is a bit more than 5 because 5/6 is nearly 1'), and cement it with the inverse check 20 × 1/5 = 4 — never as a rote rule.
bestPractices: Lead with the 'how many fit' question on a length model — lay 1/5 ribbons or number-line jumps across 4 wholes and count them to 20 — so the quotient is something the child physically counts, not computes
Confront 'division makes smaller' head-on: predict the count first, then fit the pieces and see it exceed the dividend; discuss WHY (small divisor → many copies)
Use estimation to police reasonableness (IES: 5 ÷ 5/6 ≈ just over 5) so an answer of 0.8 for 4 ÷ 1/5 is caught as absurd
Always tie back to the inverse: 4 ÷ 1/5 = 20 because 20 × 1/5 = 4 — the multiplication just learned justifies the division
Have children invent a story context ('how many 1/4-cup scoops in 6 cups?') so the measurement structure is owned, not memorised
keyRepresentations: Number line partitioned into fifths with jumps counted across 0–4
Ribbon/tape model: unit-fraction lengths laid end-to-end inside the whole (IES Fig 8 style)
Array of unit-fraction pieces filling the dividend
The inverse equation 20 × 1/5 = 4 written beside the count
commonMisconceptions: Quotient must be smaller than the dividend, so 4 ÷ 1/5 'can't' be 20 (whole-number over-generalisation that division shrinks)
Divides by the denominator instead: 4 ÷ 1/5 read as 4 ÷ 5 = 0.8 (treats the unit fraction as its denominator)
Confuses with multiplication: computes 4 × 1/5 = 4/5 (imports the more-familiar operation)
Treats numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers rather than 1/5 as one quantity

learn.summary: Dividing a whole number by a unit fraction is the measurement (quotitive) meaning of division: 4 ÷ 1/5 asks 'how many one-fifths fit inside 4 wholes?' Each whole holds 5 fifths, so 4 wholes hold 20. The central challenge is that the quotient is BIGGER than the dividend, which collides with the whole-number intuition that 'dividing makes smaller'. Teach it by physically fitting unit-fraction pieces along a length model, using prediction then counting, estimation to police reasonableness, and the inverse check 20 × 1/5 = 4 — never as a rote rule.

activities.title: How many fit? Predict then count on a length bar
feedback: If a learner predicts 'fewer than 4 because dividing shrinks', treat it as the teachable moment: lay the tiles and count to 20 together, then name the principle — a small divisor means many copies fit.
If a learner reads 4 ÷ 1/5 as 4 ÷ 5 = 0.8, rebuild what 1/5 IS (one part of a whole split five ways) and re-ask 'how many of THOSE fit in 4?'
If a learner computes 4 × 1/5 = 4/5, separate the two questions explicitly: '4 × 1/5 means four fifths; 4 ÷ 1/5 means how many fifths in four', and model both on the same bar.
activities.rationale: The measurement/quotitive meaning is made concrete by fitting unit-fraction pieces into the dividend and counting them, with a length/ribbon or number-line model. Prediction-first surfaces the 'division shrinks' misconception so it can be confronted directly.
sourceClaims: Division of a whole/number by a fraction is the measurement/quotitive question 'how many of the divisor fit in the dividend' (e.g. 1/2 ÷ 1/4 = how many 1/4s in 1/2), modelled with ribbons or a number line; dividing by a fraction can yield a quotient LARGER than the dividend, a key gap for students and teachers; estimation (5 ÷ 5/6 is a little more than 5) polices reasonableness

The misconception that operations shrink/grow numbers predictably (e.g. that multiplying/dividing must make numbers larger/smaller) and treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers interfere with computational understanding and must be confronted directly
learnerActions: Take a 4-unit strip/bar and a stack of 1/5 tiles (ribbon lengths or number-line jumps work equally well).
BEFORE placing any tile, write down a prediction of how many 1/5 tiles will fit, and a one-sentence reason.
Lay the 1/5 tiles end-to-end across the bar, counting as you go: 5 fill the first whole, 10 the second, and so on until you reach 20.
Compare the count (20) with your prediction, and discuss why the answer is bigger than 4.
Repeat with a different piece size (e.g. 1/2 gives 8, 1/10 gives 40) and describe how the size of the piece drives the count.
activities.intendedInsight: When the piece is small, many copies fit, so dividing a positive whole number by a fraction between 0 and 1 produces a count larger than the dividend. The quotient is something you can physically count, not a trick.

activities.title: Estimate first to catch absurd answers
feedback: If a learner cannot say whether the answer grows or shrinks, return to the 'how many fit' question with a concrete piece.
Praise reasoning that ties the estimate to the piece size relative to 1 whole (e.g. 'the piece is nearly a whole, so a bit more than 5').
activities.rationale: IES recommends estimation to police the reasonableness of fraction computations, which directly guards against the counterintuitive-result errors.
sourceClaims: Division of a whole/number by a fraction is the measurement/quotitive question 'how many of the divisor fit in the dividend' (e.g. 1/2 ÷ 1/4 = how many 1/4s in 1/2), modelled with ribbons or a number line; dividing by a fraction can yield a quotient LARGER than the dividend, a key gap for students and teachers; estimation (5 ÷ 5/6 is a little more than 5) polices reasonableness
learnerActions: Before computing, estimate whether the answer should be bigger or smaller than the dividend, and roughly how big.
Work an example like 5 ÷ 5/6: reason that because 5/6 is nearly 1 whole, the answer is a little more than 5.
Check a worked answer for reasonableness: decide whether 0.8 could possibly be the answer to 4 ÷ 1/5, and explain why not.
State a rule of thumb: dividing by a piece smaller than 1 gives more copies than the number of wholes.
activities.intendedInsight: Estimation acts as a reasonableness check: an answer of 0.8 for 4 ÷ 1/5 is immediately caught as absurd because many small fifths must fit in 4 wholes.

activities.title: Prove it with the inverse multiplication
feedback: If a learner cannot form the inverse, prompt: 'If 20 fifths make up 4, what multiplication says that?'
If the inverse product does not rebuild the dividend, revisit the count rather than accepting the quotient.
activities.rationale: Using the multiplication–division relationship to explain and verify the quotient is a core standard-aligned goal and avoids rote rule use.
sourceClaims: Interpret and compute quotients of whole numbers by unit fractions (e.g. 4 ÷ 1/5 = 20) using visual models and the relationship between multiplication and division; explain why the quotient is larger
learnerActions: After counting 20 fifths in 4 wholes, write the matching multiplication: 20 × 1/5 = 4.
Explain in words how the multiplication just learned justifies the division answer.
Gather or redraw the 20 fifths into 4 wholes to show the multiplication rebuilding the original dividend.
Apply the same check to a fresh case, e.g. verify 6 ÷ 1/4 = 24 by showing 24 × 1/4 = 6.
activities.intendedInsight: Division by a unit fraction and the related multiplication are inverse statements about the same quantity, so the multiplication check confirms the division.

activities.title: Invent and solve a measurement story
feedback: If a learner's story does not match a 'how many small pieces fit in a whole amount' structure, help reshape it before solving.
Draw out the prediction step: a learner who expects fewer scoops has surfaced the shrink misconception, which the count then resolves.
activities.rationale: Creating and solving a story context cements the quotitive 'how many fit' measurement meaning; a measuring/cooking persona can pose the prediction challenge, though the counting itself benefits from a visual or physical surface.
sourceClaims: Division of a whole/number by a fraction is the measurement/quotitive question 'how many of the divisor fit in the dividend' (e.g. 1/2 ÷ 1/4 = how many 1/4s in 1/2), modelled with ribbons or a number line; dividing by a fraction can yield a quotient LARGER than the dividend, a key gap for students and teachers; estimation (5 ÷ 5/6 is a little more than 5) polices reasonableness
learnerActions: Invent a real context for a whole ÷ unit-fraction, e.g. 'how many 1/4-cup scoops are in 6 cups?' or 'how many 1/3-cup scoops in this jug?'
Before counting, predict out loud whether there will be more or fewer scoops than the number of whole cups, and say why.
Solve the story by counting the pieces and state the answer with its meaning.
Match several division expressions (e.g. 6 ÷ 1/4, 4 ÷ 1/5) to the correct 'how many … in …' story.
activities.intendedInsight: Owning the measurement structure through a self-made context makes the 'how many fit' meaning transferable rather than memorised.

activities.title: Check your understanding (prediction, count, and reasoning)
feedback: If a learner picks an answer smaller than the dividend, return to fitting pieces and the piece-size-drives-count principle.
If a learner picks a denominator-division distractor (e.g. treating 6 ÷ 1/4 as 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5), rebuild what the unit fraction is.
If the number is right but the reason is missing or rote, treat it as partial and probe the 'why bigger than the dividend' explanation.
activities.rationale: Recognition and ordering items can test the counterintuitive 'bigger answer' and the divisor-vs-denominator error; requiring the reason guards against rote recall passing as understanding. Selecting answers checks the misconception but does not by itself elicit the independent construction and explanation developed in the earlier activities.
sourceClaims: The misconception that operations shrink/grow numbers predictably (e.g. that multiplying/dividing must make numbers larger/smaller) and treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers interfere with computational understanding and must be confronted directly
learnerActions: Answer 'how many 1/5 fit in 4?' using a number-line count or slider, giving 20.

Answer a multiple-choice item for 6 ÷ 1/4 = 24, ruling out derivable distractors such as 1.5 (from the denominator-division error 6 ÷ 4) and a value smaller than the dividend (from the 'division shrinks' misconception).
Order several whole ÷ unit-fraction quotients by size to expose the 'answer must be smaller' misconception.
For any answer, add a sentence saying WHY it is bigger than the dividend; a correct number without a correct reason is incomplete.
activities.intendedInsight: A genuine grasp of the measurement meaning produces both the right quotient AND a 'how many fit' justification; recalling a number alone is not sufficient.

constraints: Lead with the 'how many fit' measurement question on a length model; the quotient should be something the child physically counts, not a rule they apply.
Confront 'division makes smaller' directly: predict first, then fit pieces and see the count exceed the dividend, then discuss why (small divisor → many copies).
Always tie back to the inverse check (20 × 1/5 = 4); do not teach an invert-and-multiply rule without this meaning.

A static number-line image showing 4 wholes cut into fifths with 20 countable segments supports the meaning well, but does not let the learner vary the divisor to test the pattern; use it as a scaffold, not the whole lesson.

Recognition/multiple-choice items can check the misconception but do not by themselves elicit the independent construction and explanation; pair them with activities that require counting and justifying.

Optional interactive supports (e.g. dragging 1/5 tiles into a bar with a running counter, a divisor dial that swaps 1/4, 1/3, 1/10 and shows the count change, an inverse panel animating 20 fifths fusing into 4 wholes, a contrast switch to the partition case 1/3 ÷ 4) make the mechanism concrete; they are helpful examples, not required.
Keep the model one-dimensional ('how many lengths fit'); adding 3D depth risks implying volume and is not needed for this concept, though this is a design judgement, not a proven limitation.
Distinguish 4 ÷ 1/5 (how many fifths in four) from both 4 ÷ 5 (dividing by the denominator) and 4 × 1/5 (four fifths); model the contrasts explicitly.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and efficacy relative to other media is untested.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 4 ÷ 1/5 = 20 (each of 4 wholes holds 5 fifths; 4 × 5 = 20) and 20 × 1/5 = 4 — consistent. 6 ÷ 1/4 = 24 and 24 × 1/4 = 6 — consistent. 4 ÷ 1/2 = 8 and 4 ÷ 1/10 = 40 — consistent. 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 is the denominator-division error.

The original assessment text lists example distractors '0.24 and 1.5' for 6 ÷ 1/4: 1.5 corresponds to the plausible error 6 ÷ 4, while '0.24' has no clean derivation. The quiz activity names only derivable distractors and excludes the undefined 0.24 from learner-facing text; reviewers should confirm intended distractor values before authoring.
The Common Core 5.NF.7b source is marked verified:false in the row; the two IES claims are marked verified:true. The standards citation's status is carried as-is; no new verification was performed.
Softened the legacy '3D adds nothing' framing to a scoped design judgement about avoiding a volume implication, rather than a universal claim.

assess.poeTask: Give the child a 4-unit strip and 1/5 tiles. Ask them to PREDICT, and write down WHY, how many 1/5 tiles will fit before placing any. The reason is the diagnostic: a child expecting 'fewer than 4, because dividing shrinks' has surfaced the misconception. Then they lay the tiles and count to 20, and must reconcile the observation with their prediction — the gap between 'dividing makes smaller' and 20 tiles is the teachable moment.
probeDeeper: What about 3 ÷ 1/4 — more or fewer than 3, and why?
How could you PROVE 4 ÷ 1/5 = 20 is right using multiplication?
If it were 4 ÷ 5 instead of 4 ÷ 1/5, would the answer be bigger or smaller — how does the little line change everything?
How many halves are in 4? Is that the same kind of question as this one?
assess.correctAnswer: 20. Because 4 ÷ 1/5 asks 'how many one-fifths fit in 4 wholes?' — each whole contains 5 fifths, and 4 wholes contain 4 × 5 = 20. It is BIGGER than 4 because the pieces are small, so many of them fit; check: 20 × 1/5 = 4.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Dividing always makes it smaller, so the answer has to be less than 4' — rejects 20 or writes something under 4 because the result 'feels too big for a division'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do the measurement act physically — lay 1/5 pieces into 4 wholes and count 20 together — then name the principle: a small divisor means many copies fit, so dividing by a number below 1 grows the count; contrast with 4 ÷ 5
errorPatterns.distractor: Less than 4 — dividing always makes the number smaller
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: insists the answer must be smaller than 4, or changes a correct 20 when challenged; cannot explain the bigger result

errorPatterns.pattern: Divides by the denominator: reads 4 ÷ 1/5 as 4 ÷ 5 = 0.8, treating the unit fraction as the whole number 5
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild what 1/5 IS (one part of a whole split five ways) and re-ask 'how many of THOSE fit in 4?'; anchor fraction-as-a-single-quantity before recomputing
errorPatterns.distractor: 0.8 (four divided by five)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer 0.8 (or 4/5 framed as 'four divided by five'); the 1/5 is handled as '5'

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses division with multiplication: computes 4 × 1/5 = 4/5 because the multiplication is the more familiar recent operation
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the two questions explicitly — '4 × 1/5 means four fifths; 4 ÷ 1/5 means how many fifths in four' — model both on the same bar so the contrast is visible
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer 4/5; working shows a multiplication, not a 'how many fit' count

responseLevels.gap: Insists the answer must be smaller than 4, or computes 4 ÷ 5 = 0.8 or 4 × 1/5 = 4/5; no 'how many fit' meaning available.
responseLevels.full: Answers 20 and explains it as 'how many fifths fit in 4', accepts and justifies that the quotient exceeds the dividend, verifies with 20 × 1/5 = 4, and transfers the reasoning (with an estimate of reasonableness) to a fresh whole ÷ unit-fraction case.
responseLevels.partial: Produces 20, possibly by a remembered rule, but cannot explain why it is bigger than 4 — treats the large answer as a quirk rather than the natural result of counting small pieces, and cannot reliably transfer to 6 ÷ 1/4.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work out 4 ÷ 1/5. Then tell me why the answer comes out that way — is it bigger or smaller than 4, and how would you explain that to someone who thinks dividing always makes a number smaller?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who genuinely holds the measurement meaning answers 20 AND justifies it with 'how many fifths fit', comfortable that the answer exceeds the dividend. A child running on the whole-number rule 'division makes smaller' either refuses 20, or computes 4 ÷ 5 = 0.8, or slips to 4 × 1/5 = 4/5 — and crucially the SECOND tier exposes them even if they recalled 20 by rote: they cannot say why it is bigger. Right answer + right reason is hard to fake; the reason is where the understanding lives.

sources.claim: Division of a whole/number by a fraction is the measurement/quotitive question 'how many of the divisor fit in the dividend' (e.g. 1/2 ÷ 1/4 = how many 1/4s in 1/2), modelled with ribbons or a number line; dividing by a fraction can yield a quotient LARGER than the dividend, a key gap for students and teachers; estimation (5 ÷ 5/6 is a little more than 5) polices reasonableness
sources.source: IES / What Works Clearinghouse — Developing Effective Fractions Instruction K–8 (Siegler et al. 2010), Recommendation 3

sources.claim: The misconception that operations shrink/grow numbers predictably (e.g. that multiplying/dividing must make numbers larger/smaller) and treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers interfere with computational understanding and must be confronted directly
sources.source: IES / WWC Fractions Practice Guide — misconception step, Recommendation 3

sources.claim: Interpret and compute quotients of whole numbers by unit fractions (e.g. 4 ÷ 1/5 = 20) using visual models and the relationship between multiplication and division; explain why the quotient is larger
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics — 5.NF.7b

pedagogy.summary: At 6-8, interpreting categorical data means USING an organised display to answer questions: read how many in each category, total across all categories, and — the harder step — compare two categories with 'how many more/fewer'. This is Curcio's move from 'reading the data' (lift a value straight off) to 'reading between the data' (combine or compare values). The classic hurdle is that 'how many more' is a DIFFERENCE, not the larger value. Teaching should pose real questions about the child's own chart, model matching/subtracting for comparisons, and keep totals reconciling with the whole group.
bestPractices: Pose a ladder of questions on the child's own display: single-category ('how many chose…'), total ('how many altogether'), then comparison ('how many more… than…')
Model 'how many more' as finding the difference — match the two categories one-to-one and count the gap, or subtract — not reading the taller one
Check the total reconciles with the number of people/objects surveyed as a self-check
Use precise comparison language ('more', 'fewer', 'the difference is') and require the child to say how they got a comparison
keyRepresentations: Frequency table and the child's own pictogram/block diagram as the data source
Two category rows lined up one-to-one to expose the difference
Bar model / number line for the 'how many more' subtraction
A running total check against the full group
commonMisconceptions: Answers 'how many more' with the larger category's value instead of the difference
Finds the total by counting the number of categories rather than summing the frequencies
Reads the wrong value by misaligning a row/column or miscounting
Treats each question in isolation, never checking the total against the whole group

learn.summary: Children aged 6-8 learn to interpret categorical data by using an organised display (their own pictogram, block diagram, or frequency table) to answer a ladder of questions: how many in one category, how many altogether across all categories, and the harder 'how many more/fewer' comparison. The central hurdle is that 'how many more' asks for a DIFFERENCE, not the larger category's value. Activities pose real questions about the child's own survey, model matching/subtracting for comparisons, and keep the running total reconciling with the whole group.

activities.title: Question ladder on your own pets chart
feedback: If a child answers 'how many altogether' with the number of categories (e.g. 4 kinds of pet), return to the data and add the category counts, then check the sum equals the number of children surveyed.

If a child reads a neighbouring category's count or is off by one, steady the reading: track the row across to its count with a finger or ruler. This is a reading lapse to steady, not a concept to reteach.
Prompt 'how did you work out how many more?' to check a difference was computed rather than a value read.
activities.rationale: Curriculum and framework guidance describe interpretation at this age as asking and answering questions about counts, totals and comparisons using an organised display, moving from reading values straight off to combining and comparing them.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils ask and answer questions by counting objects in each category and about totalling and comparing categorical data; Year 3 pupils solve one- and two-step 'how many more/fewer' questions using scaled bar charts, pictograms and tables
At Level A the first stage is for students to read and interpret what the data show at a simple level, using the display to answer statistical questions about their group
learnerActions: Collect a small survey (e.g. favourite pet) from your class or family and build it into a pictogram or block diagram.
Answer single-category questions first: 'How many children chose rabbits?' by reading the one row/column.
Answer a total question: 'How many children are there altogether?' by summing ALL the category frequencies, not counting how many kinds of pet there are.
Check your total against the number of people actually surveyed as a self-check.
Answer a comparison question: 'How many more chose dogs than cats?' by finding the difference.
Each time you give a comparison answer, say out loud how you got it.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a single value, totalling all values, and comparing two values are three different moves; the total must reconcile with the whole group, and a comparison asks for a gap between two values.

activities.title: Line them up to see the difference
feedback: If a child gives the taller category's count (8) as the comparison answer, line the two categories up one-to-one, count the unmatched part, and name that 'how many more' means the gap/difference, then re-ask.
To test the comparison on a small gap, ask 'which two categories are closest — how many more does one have than the other?'
A bar model or number line can make the subtraction visible for the 'how many more' step.
activities.rationale: The classic error at this age is answering 'how many more' with the larger value instead of the difference; matching one-to-one and subtracting both make the difference concrete.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils ask and answer questions by counting objects in each category and about totalling and comparing categorical data; Year 3 pupils solve one- and two-step 'how many more/fewer' questions using scaled bar charts, pictograms and tables
learnerActions: Pick two categories to compare, e.g. dogs and cats.
Line the two rows up one-to-one so matching items sit directly beside each other.
Count the unmatched part that sticks out on the taller row — that is 'how many more'.
Confirm the same answer by subtracting: taller count minus shorter count (e.g. 8 dogs − 5 cats = 3).
Say the result in comparison words: 'There are 3 more dogs than cats' and 'there are 3 fewer cats than dogs.'
activities.intendedInsight: 'How many more' is the gap between the two categories — the unmatched part — not the height or count of the bigger one.

activities.title: Interactive chart with a comparison tool (optional scaffold)
feedback: If the child relies on the shading to answer, cover it and ask them to find the difference by matching or subtracting themselves.
Use a 'how many more' prompt whose tempting wrong answer is the larger category's raw value, to surface the difference misconception.
activities.rationale: A live display that recolours the gap between two categories may make the comparison concrete and targets the exact place children go wrong; such interactive highlighting is offered here as one supportive scaffold rather than the only route, and its comparative efficacy over a hand-drawn or manipulated display is not established by the cited sources.
learnerActions: Open or build an interactive chart with a question panel under your survey data.
Tap one category and watch its bar light up to answer a single-value question.
Tap two categories (e.g. 'cats' and 'dogs') so the bars glide side by side and the extra squares on the taller bar are shaded as the answer to 'how many more'.
Press a total button that sums the categories and checks the sum equals the number of children surveyed.
After using the tool, redo one comparison and one total by hand to show you can do it without the highlighting.
activities.intendedInsight: Sliding two bars together and shading only the extra squares shows that 'how many more' is the highlighted gap, not the height of the bigger bar; a total button can reconcile the sum with the group size.

activities.title: Combine and reconcile checks
feedback: If the combined total or grand total doesn't match the group, return to the organised data, re-add the category counts, and locate the misread or miscount.
Ask the child to state, in their own words, why the category totals must add up to the whole group.
activities.rationale: Reconciling the running total with the full group is a self-check recommended for this skill and guards against counting categories instead of summing frequencies.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils ask and answer questions by counting objects in each category and about totalling and comparing categorical data; Year 3 pupils solve one- and two-step 'how many more/fewer' questions using scaled bar charts, pictograms and tables
learnerActions: Answer 'if the rabbit and cat groups joined, how many would that be?' by adding the two category counts.
Answer 'does your total match how many people you actually surveyed?' and, if not, recount.
Explain why, when each person surveyed gave exactly one answer, the total of all categories should equal the number of people surveyed.
activities.intendedInsight: Categories can be combined by adding their counts, and the sum of all categories should reconcile with the whole surveyed group — a built-in check on your reading.

constraints: Use the child's OWN survey data as the display so the questions are real and the group size is known for the reconcile check.
Use precise comparison language — 'more', 'fewer', 'the difference is' — and require the child to say HOW they reached a comparison; confident numbers alone do not reveal method.
A tap-to-reveal or static chart can surface each category's count for reference but does not require the child to compute a comparison or total; pair it with tasks that demand the computation.

Recognition-only or multiple-choice items can test and give feedback on reading and comparing (including a distractor equal to the larger category's value), but do not by themselves elicit the child independently constructing the difference or total; include construction tasks.
Interactive highlighting of the gap is a scaffold: fade it so the child can match one-to-one or subtract unaided before you treat the skill as secure.
'How many altogether' means summing the frequencies, never counting how many categories there are.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research, re-audited independently without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated conversation and 3D as 'poor' and claimed 3D 'adds nothing' and dialogue 'supplies no data'; these comparative/universal claims are not established by the cited sources and have been dropped. Discussion can still support reasoning about a displayed dataset, and a physical/manipulable layout of the data is a legitimate alternative route.

The interactive comparison tool's sourceClaims are [] because the GAISE 'read and interpret' claim supports interpreting a display but not the efficacy of interactive highlighting; that efficacy remains untested.
Worked example 8 dogs − 5 cats = 3 and the rabbit+cat combine example were checked arithmetically and are correct.

probeDeeper: Ask 'how did you work out how many MORE?' to check a difference was computed, not a value read
Counterexample tuned to this topic: 'which two categories are closest — how many between them?' to test the comparison on a small gap
Ask 'does your total match how many children are in our class?' to surface the reconcile check
Ask 'if the rabbit and cat groups joined, how many would that be?' to probe combining categories
assess.correctAnswer: A correct performance: reads each category value correctly off the display, totals by summing ALL the frequencies (matching the number of children), and answers 'how many more' by finding the difference between the two categories (e.g. 8 dogs − 5 cats = 3), using comparison language.

errorPatterns.pattern: Answers 'how many more chose dogs than cats' with the dogs value (8) instead of the difference (3)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Line the two categories up one-to-one and count the unmatched part; name that 'how many more' means the gap/difference, then re-ask
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives the taller category's count as the comparison answer with no subtraction

errorPatterns.pattern: Finds the total by counting the number of categories rather than summing the frequencies
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the organised data: add the category counts and check the sum equals the number of children surveyed
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child answers 'how many altogether' with the count of category types (e.g. 4) instead of the sum

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the wrong value by misaligning a row/column or miscounting symbols
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold with a finger/ruler to track the row across to its count; a reading lapse to steady, not a concept to reteach
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child reads a neighbouring category's count or is off by one

responseLevels.gap: Reads single values only; gives the larger value for 'how many more' and counts categories for the total
responseLevels.full: Reads all category values, totals by summing frequencies (reconciling with the group), and computes 'how many more/fewer' as a difference, using comparison language independently
responseLevels.partial: Reads values and totals with support, but the comparison is unreliable or done without finding the difference

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is our finished pets chart. Answer these for me: how many children chose rabbits? How many children are there altogether? And how many more chose dogs than cats? (Set the questions and WATCH how each answer is reached.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching HOW each answer is produced is the assessment. A child who understands finds the difference for 'how many more' and sums frequencies for the total; a child who doesn't reports the taller category as 'how many more' and counts categories (getting 'how many kinds') for the total. Both may state numbers confidently — the method is what reveals understanding.

sources.source: National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study — Statistics (KS1 and lower KS2)

sources.claim: At Level A the first stage is for students to read and interpret what the data show at a simple level, using the display to answer statistical questions about their group
