pedagogy.summary: Sets & Venn diagrams is the procedural skill of organising and counting outcomes systematically — placing elements into the regions of a Venn diagram (or the cells of a two-way table), and reading off unions (A ∪ B), intersections (A ∩ B) and complements (A′). The crux is handling the OVERLAP correctly: elements in both sets belong only in the intersection, each element is counted once, and elements in neither set still live inside the universal set. Getting the region counts right is the foundation for all combined-event probability.
bestPractices: Fill the intersection FIRST, then subtract it from each set total so the circle-only regions are correct
Count the union by adding the distinct regions once — never |A| + |B|, which double-counts the overlap
Always account for the 'neither' region inside the universal-set rectangle; the regions must total the whole population
Use two-way tables as an alternative organiser for combined events, cross-checking against the Venn diagram
Practise shading A ∪ B, A ∩ B and A′ and stating in words what each region means
keyRepresentations: Two- and three-circle Venn diagrams with a universal-set rectangle
Two-way / contingency tables for combined events
Shaded regions for union, intersection, complement
Region-count totals reconciled against the population size
commonMisconceptions: Double-counting the intersection when finding the union (writing |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B|)
Writing each set's full total inside its circle without subtracting the overlap, so the diagram over-counts
Placing elements in the intersection that belong to only one set
Forgetting the 'neither' region, so the regions don't total the whole population

learn.summary: Learners organise and count outcomes systematically with Venn diagrams (and two-way tables), reading off unions (A ∪ B), intersections (A ∩ B) and complements (A′). The crux is handling the overlap: elements in both sets belong only in the intersection and are counted once, while elements in neither set still live inside the universal-set rectangle and must be accounted for so all regions total the whole population.

activities.title: Build the Venn and expose the double-count
feedback: If your two counts summed to 32 (18 in football + 14 in cricket with no overlap used), the 6 who like both were counted twice — subtract one copy: 12 + 6 + 8 = 26.
If your union came out 32, highlight the 6 sitting in both circles: adding 18 + 14 counts them twice.
If the placed region counts add only to 26, locate the 4 students who like neither inside the rectangle: 30 − (12 + 6 + 8) = 4, so the regions total 30.
A ∩ B = 6; A′ (not football) = cricket-only + neither = 8 + 4 = 12.
activities.rationale: Direct manipulation with a visible running count is intended to make double-counting and the missing 'neither' region observable and self-checking; sorting the actual items turns the subtract-the-overlap step into something the learner works through rather than recalls.
sourceClaims: In a Venn diagram, elements in both sets go only in the intersection; when counting the union each element is counted once (do not add duplicated intersection values twice), items in only one set go in that set's own region, and elements in neither set go inside the universal-set rectangle.
Organising the full sample space / set of outcomes is central to probability and frequently neglected; failing to represent all outcomes systematically underlies many probability errors.
learnerActions: Use 30 student tokens (physical or on-screen) and a two-circle Venn (A = football, B = cricket) inside a universal rectangle, with the facts: 18 like football, 14 like cricket, 6 like both.

Try the instinctive approach first: allocate 18 to the football circle and 14 to the cricket circle without using the overlap. Those two counts sum to 32 (18 + 14), yet only 30 students exist — on screen a counter reads 32, while with physical tokens you run out before finishing the cricket circle. Either outcome shows that some students are being counted twice — here, the 6 'both' students. Note that the excess of 2 (32 − 30) is not the size of the overlap, because 4 students like neither sport.
Move the 6 'both' students into the overlap region, then adjust so each circle's own-only region reads 12 (18 − 6) and 8 (14 − 6).
Place the 4 left-over students in the 'neither' region inside the rectangle, and check the regions total 30.
State the union count by adding the distinct regions once: 12 + 6 + 8 = 26.
Shade and state in words what each region means for A ∪ B, A ∩ B and A′.
activities.intendedInsight: Elements in both sets are counted twice if you compute |A| + |B|; filling the intersection first and subtracting it from each total gives the correct circle-only regions, and the 'neither' region must be included so everything totals the population.

activities.title: Classify, count, and cross-check with a two-way table
feedback: If you chose 32 as the union, that adds both set totals and counts the 6 shared students twice; the union is 26.
If the table and the diagram disagree, re-check which cell the 'both' and the 'neither' groups belong in — the two totals must match.
The row and column totals of the two-way table should reconcile to the whole population of 30.
activities.rationale: Classification exercises the enumeration and the double-counting trap, and the two-way table gives a second representation that can catch miscounts the diagram alone might hide; it checks and drills classification but does not itself elicit free shading or diagram construction.
sourceClaims: In a Venn diagram, elements in both sets go only in the intersection; when counting the union each element is counted once (do not add duplicated intersection values twice), items in only one set go in that set's own region, and elements in neither set go inside the universal-set rectangle.
Organising the full sample space / set of outcomes is central to probability and frequently neglected; failing to represent all outcomes systematically underlies many probability errors.
learnerActions: Sort each element into its correct Venn region (football-only, cricket-only, both, or neither).
Decide which count is the union of A and B, distinguishing the correct 26 from the double-counted 32.
Give the 'neither' count by reconciling against the total of 30.
Re-represent the same combined events in a two-way / contingency table and check the cell totals match the Venn region counts.
activities.intendedInsight: A two-way table is an alternative organiser for combined events; cross-checking it against the Venn diagram confirms every outcome is counted exactly once.

activities.title: Read the regions: tap-to-reveal reference
feedback: Confirm that A′ means everything not in A — which here includes both cricket-only and the 'neither' region.
Check that A ∩ B is the overlap only, not either whole circle.
activities.rationale: A static tap-to-reveal reference can teach the layout and notation; it is a scaffold because it does not let the learner build a diagram or test a miscount, so pair it with the construction activity.
sourceClaims: In a Venn diagram, elements in both sets go only in the intersection; when counting the union each element is counted once (do not add duplicated intersection values twice), items in only one set go in that set's own region, and elements in neither set go inside the universal-set rectangle.
learnerActions: Study a labelled Venn diagram and tap each region or shaded set to reveal its set notation (for example A ∩ B, or A ∪ B and A′, which are each made of more than one region), its plain-language meaning, and its count.
Match each shaded picture to its correct name and verbal description before building your own diagram.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency with the layout and the meaning of each shaded region supports accurate building and counting.

activities.title: Socratic overlap check
feedback: If the learner says 18 + 14, prompt them to find the 6 counted in both and subtract one copy to get 26.
If they omit the 'neither' group, ask what 30 − (12 + 6 + 8) tells them.
activities.rationale: Targeted questioning can surface the subtract-the-overlap and 'neither' errors; learners should still carry out the placement and counting themselves, so use dialogue alongside construction rather than instead of it.
learnerActions: Work through prompts such as 'Does the 18 include the 6 who like both, or not?' and explain your reasoning.
Answer 'How many like football OR cricket, and why isn't it simply 18 + 14?' in your own words.
Explain where the students who like neither go and how many there are.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating why the overlap must be subtracted once, and why the 'neither' group still sits inside the universal set, consolidates the enumeration logic.

constraints: Fill the intersection first, then subtract it from each set total so the circle-only regions are correct.
Count the union as |A unionB|=|A|+|B|-|A intersectionB|. Subtract the overlap once; if it is zero, direct addition is valid. In this example the union is18+14-6=26.
Always account for the 'neither' region inside the universal-set rectangle; the regions must total the whole population (30 here).
Tap-to-reveal and read-only diagrams teach layout and notation but do not let the learner build a diagram or test a miscount; use them as scaffolds alongside hands-on construction.
Choice/classification steps drill enumeration and the double-count trap but do not elicit free shading or independent diagram construction; pair them with a build/shade task.
Socratic dialogue can surface overlap and 'neither' errors, but learners should still do the placement and counting themselves.
The '32' (18 + 14) and '38' (football-only 18 + overlap 6 + cricket-only 14) figures are learner error patterns only and must never be offered as valid counts; the correct union is 26.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic checked: 18 − 6 = 12, 14 − 6 = 8, union 12 + 6 + 8 = 26, neither 30 − (12 + 6 + 8) = 4, and A′ = 8 + 4 = 12. The '32' figure (18 + 14) is retained only as the double-counted error to be corrected; the '38' figure (18 + 6 + 14 when full totals are placed plus a separate overlap) is likewise an error pattern only, not restated as a learner-facing count.

With 30 literal physical tokens a learner cannot place 32; the '32' is reframed as the arithmetic sum of the two attempted counts (on screen a counter reads 32; with physical tokens you run out), so the scenario stays coherent across both modalities.

The original row claimed '3D adds nothing' for this 2D organising task; this has not been propagated as a universal law. A 3D interaction is simply not proposed because the task is a 2D sorting/counting task, not because 3D is incapable of teaching.

Live counters, draggable tokens, and a shading tool are retained as concrete, optional interaction examples that may make the counting mechanism visible, not as mandatory mechanisms; physical tokens on paper can serve the same purpose.
Efficacy phrasing ('self-checking', 'visible', 'observable') reflects design intent inherited from the original rationale and is not independently validated.

probeDeeper: You wrote 18 in the football circle — does that include the 6 who like both, or not?
How many like football OR cricket? Why isn't it simply 18 + 14?
Where do the students who like neither sport go, and how many are there?
Shade 'likes cricket but not football' — which region is that, and what's the count?
assess.correctAnswer: A correct performance: 6 in the intersection, 12 in football-only (18 − 6), 8 in cricket-only (14 − 6), and 30 − (12 + 6 + 8) = 4 outside both circles. A ∪ B = 12 + 6 + 8 = 26 (not 18 + 14 = 32). A ∩ B = 6. A′ (not football) = cricket-only + neither = 8 + 4 = 12. Regions are filled by subtracting the overlap, the union is counted once, and the 'neither' region is included.

errorPatterns.pattern: Double-counts the intersection when finding the union (|A ∪ B| = 18 + 14 = 32)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Highlight the 6 who sit in both circles; adding 18 and 14 counts them twice, so subtract one copy — 12 + 6 + 8 = 26
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives the union as 32 by adding the two set totals without removing the shared 6

errorPatterns.pattern: Writes each set's full total inside its circle without subtracting the overlap, so the diagram over-counts
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fill the intersection first, then subtract it from each total to get the circle-only regions (12 and 8) before anything else
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Puts 18 and 14 in the whole circles and 6 in the overlap, giving more tokens than the 30 students

errorPatterns.pattern: Forgets the 'neither' region so the regions don't total the population
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reconcile against the total: 30 − (region counts) = the 'neither' region inside the universal rectangle; a quick lapse to scaffold, not a conceptual gap
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The placed counts add to 26, and the 4 students who like neither are never located

responseLevels.gap: Cannot place the numbers correctly; writes set totals in whole circles with no overlap handling and no 'neither' region
responseLevels.full: Fills each region by subtracting the overlap, counts the union once (26), includes the 'neither' region (4), and shades A ∪ B, A ∩ B and A′ correctly with their counts
responseLevels.partial: Places the intersection but then double-counts it in the union, or omits the 'neither' region; can shade single regions but confuses union with intersection

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child this and paper: 'In a class of 30, 18 students like football, 14 like cricket, and 6 like both. Draw a two-circle Venn diagram and fill in the numbers. Then shade and give the count for: likes football OR cricket (A ∪ B); likes both (A ∩ B); and does NOT like football (A′).' (Set the task and WATCH — watch whether they subtract the 6 from each circle, whether the union double-counts the overlap, and whether they place the students who like neither.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching shows whether they subtract the 6 (or over-fill the circles to a total of 38), whether the union comes out 26 or a double-counted 32, and whether the 4 'neither' students are placed — errors a single final answer would hide.

sources.claim: Organising the full sample space / set of outcomes is central to probability and frequently neglected; failing to represent all outcomes systematically underlies many probability errors.
sources.source: Bryant & Nunes, Children's Understanding of Probability: A Literature Review (Nuffield Foundation, 2012)

pedagogy.summary: At 9-10 arguments become genuinely multi-step and start reaching toward proof: a child proves 3/4 > 2/3 not by drawing two bars and eyeballing them but by converting to a common denominator (9/12 vs 8/12) and stating why that settles it, and critiques a peer's long multiplication by finding a misaligned partial product and explaining the place-value consequence. The practice now spans three arenas at once — fractions, angles, calculation — and the SMP3 demand sharpens: an argument must be a connected logical progression, and a critique must name the flawed step AND offer why the correct method works. This is the empirical-to-deductive transition Hoyles & Küchemann document as slow and fragile: children will still offer 'I tried it and it worked' as proof, and the teaching job is to make them feel the gap between a convincing example and a watertight general reason.
bestPractices: Demand a general reason, not a confirming example: after a child checks 3/4 > 2/3 with a picture, ask 'would that convince someone who couldn't see your drawing?' and push toward the common-denominator argument
Use deliberately flawed peer work across all three arenas (a misaligned partial product, a mis-added angle, a wrong common denominator) and require 'which step and why', per SMP3's explain-the-flaw
Teach the tear-and-arrange angle demonstration as an argument, not a fact to memorise — the arrangement into a straight line IS the reasoning that the three angles sum to 180°
Introduce the counter-example as a tool: one case that breaks a claim disproves it, whereas any number of confirming cases does not prove it (the asymmetry Hoyles & Küchemann flag)
Insist on because/therefore connectives linking each step to the next so a list of true facts becomes a valid chain
keyRepresentations: Common-denominator conversion (3/4=9/12, 2/3=8/12) as the engine of a size argument
Column/grid long-multiplication layout for locating a misaligned partial product
Tear-and-rearrange triangle (three corners meeting on a straight line) as a visual proof of the 180° angle sum
A because/therefore chain frame connecting givens to conclusion
commonMisconceptions: Treating a confirming example (or a careful drawing) as a proof of the general claim
Comparing fractions by whichever has the bigger numerator or bigger denominator rather than by a common referent
Critiquing by answer-agreement — 'the total's wrong' — without locating the misaligned step or explaining the place-value error
Believing the tear-and-arrange result is a lucky fact of that one triangle rather than a general property

learn.summary: For children aged 9-10, this guidance supports the empirical-to-deductive transition in mathematical reasoning (SMP3): constructing multi-step arguments and critiquing others' reasoning across fractions, angles, and calculation. The core teaching objective is to make learners feel the gap between a convincing example (or careful drawing) and a watertight general reason, and to critique flawed work by naming the specific broken step AND explaining why the correct method works - not merely noticing the answer is wrong. Dialogue with a skeptic is proposed as a strong vehicle because the defining moves are dialogic, while constructed-argument workspaces, annotated correct-vs-flawed comparisons, and limited recognition warm-ups each have a distinct, more limited role noted below.

activities.title: Convince the skeptic without a picture
feedback: If the learner offers more examples or a neater drawing, ask: 'How many would it take before you were CERTAIN? Is there any number that would make it a proof?'
If the learner converts to twelfths, revoice their chain back: 'so 3/4 is 9/12, 2/3 is 8/12, 9 is more than 8 - and that holds whatever you drew.'
Name success as locating a reason that covers every case at once, not as getting the right verdict.

If the learner senses the drawing isn't enough but stalls, scaffold: 'you're right it's not settled - what could you turn both fractions into so they're easy to compare?' and let them complete the chain.
activities.rationale: Empirical/example-based reasoning predominates at this age and the shift to deductive reasoning is slow; a skeptic who accepts only a because-chain targets the empirical-proof habit and exercises argument construction (one half of SMP3). A dialogic format may respond to the child's over-reliance on examples in real time.
sourceClaims: SMP3: construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others; make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements; if there is a flaw in an argument, explain what it is; distinguish correct logic from flawed.

Empirical/example-based reasoning predominates and the empirical→deductive transition is slow and fragile; a general counter-example gives insight into WHY a statement is false, whereas confirming examples cannot establish a general truth.

The describe→explain→convince→justify→prove ladder: convincing may be confident but incomplete, whereas justifying is a correct, complete because/therefore chain; recognising that specific examples do not constitute watertight proof is a key developmental step.
learnerActions: State a claim, e.g. 3/4 > 2/3, and offer your first justification however you like (a drawing is fine to start).

When challenged ('your drawing looks close - how do I know you didn't just draw it that way? Convince me without the picture'), reach for a general reason: convert to a common denominator - 3/4 = 9/12, 2/3 = 8/12, and 9/12 > 8/12.
State explicitly why this reason settles it for ANY representation, not just your drawing.
Respond to repeated pressing ('but ALWAYS?') and refuse to let 'I tried it and it worked' count as proof.
Try the same argument on a fresh pair, e.g. 5/8 versus 2/3, to test whether your method generalises (work out the common-denominator comparison rather than guessing).
activities.intendedInsight: A confirming example or a careful drawing can persuade, but a reason that holds independent of any picture is what actually settles a general claim.

activities.title: Find the broken step in a long multiplication
feedback: If the learner only says 'the total's wrong', redirect: 'which step caused it, and what did the misalignment do to the place value of that partial product?'
Confirm success when the learner links the misaligned column to the partial product sitting in the wrong place value.

A column/grid layout makes the misaligned partial product easier to locate; nudging a partial product in and out of column alignment can make the place-value cost felt (optional illustration, not required).
activities.rationale: Critiquing multi-step work by locating the flawed step and explaining why the correct method works is the critique half of SMP3. Using deliberately flawed work targets this directly rather than rewarding mere answer-agreement.
sourceClaims: SMP3: construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others; make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements; if there is a flaw in an argument, explain what it is; distinguish correct logic from flawed.
learnerActions: Examine a worked long multiplication in which one partial product has been shoved one column to the right of where it belongs (misaligned).
Identify WHICH step is wrong, not just that the final total is off.

Explain the place-value consequence: the partial product for the next higher-place digit should sit one column further LEFT than the previous partial product (or, equivalently, end in a placeholder zero). Shoved one column to the right, it lands in a place value that is too low, so it is added into the wrong columns and contributes only one tenth of its true value.
State what the correct alignment should be and why that fixes the value.
activities.intendedInsight: A valid critique names the flawed step and explains the underlying place-value error, which is deeper than noticing answer-disagreement.

activities.title: Tear and rearrange: from evidence to a reason why ALL triangles have angles summing to 180 degrees
feedback: If the learner treats the result as specific to their triangle, prompt: 'would this happen for a long thin triangle too? Try one and watch what the corners do.'

Name success as telling apart what the demonstration shows (strong evidence of about 180 degrees for the triangles tried) and a general reason that covers every triangle, not just reporting the 180 degree sum.

A draggable triangle that keeps re-forming the straight line as you deform it can make the pattern vivid (optional), but it is still a series of examples. Note the approximation: tearing and placing corners is imprecise, so a paper demonstration can only look close to a straight line. The exact 180 degree result is about the idealised mathematical triangle and is established by a general argument.
activities.rationale: Teaching the demonstration as evidence that motivates a general argument, rather than as a fact to memorise or as a proof in itself, connects a visual action to a general geometric claim. It also counters the belief that the result is coincidental for one triangle, and stays consistent with the point that confirming examples alone do not prove a general claim.
sourceClaims: SMP3: construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others; make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements; if there is a flaw in an argument, explain what it is; distinguish correct logic from flawed.
learnerActions: Tear the three corners off a paper triangle and arrange them so their vertices meet at a point along a straight edge.
Observe that the three angles together appear to form a straight line (about 180 degrees, within the precision of the tearing).

Treat the arrangement as evidence, not yet a proof: the corners appearing to meet on a straight line suggests that the three angles sum to 180 degrees. A torn paper triangle is only one approximate example, so ask what general reason would make this happen for every triangle.

Repeat with a differently shaped triangle (or deform a draggable on-screen triangle) and see that the corners again appear to form a straight line. Note that each successful case makes the claim more convincing, but more cases on their own still do not prove it for every triangle.

State the general claim that the angles of ANY triangle sum to 180 degrees, and explain the general reason (with teacher support): draw a line through one corner parallel to the opposite side. The other two angles reappear at that corner as equal (alternate) angles, so the three angles together fill a straight line, which is 180 degrees. This reason does not depend on the triangle's shape.
activities.intendedInsight: Tearing and rearranging corners convincingly suggests that a triangle's angles sum to 180 degrees, and repeating it builds confidence. But only a general reason (such as the parallel-line argument) shows that it holds for ALL triangles; examples alone are not a proof.

activities.title: Counter-examples and the asymmetry of proof
feedback: If the learner holds 'bigger denominator wins', have them test it on 1/4 versus 1/3 (equal numerators, larger denominator) and watch it fail; if they hold 'bigger numerator wins', have them test it on 3/8 versus 1/2 (differing numerators) and watch that fail - match the test case to the rule they actually hold.
Reinforce the connectives: ask the learner to join their true statements with 'because' and 'therefore' so the argument reads as a chain, not a list.

Distinguish an incorrect comparison rule (a false belief about fraction size) from a reasoning gap; if the learner misranks fractions, revisit comparison via a common denominator or a benchmark before judging their reasoning.
activities.rationale: Introducing the counter-example as a tool teaches the logical asymmetry between refutation and confirmation, a developmental step flagged as key; insisting on because/therefore connectives turns true facts into a valid chain. The 1/4 vs 1/3 case holds the numerator fixed to break the bigger-denominator rule, while the 3/8 vs 1/2 case has both parts differing and is used to break the bigger-numerator rule (3 > 1, yet 3/8 < 4/8 = 1/2). These vary different quantities to refute different single-component rules; this is not a denominator rule 'flipping'. Fractions remain comparable as numbers throughout.
sourceClaims: Empirical/example-based reasoning predominates and the empirical→deductive transition is slow and fragile; a general counter-example gives insight into WHY a statement is false, whereas confirming examples cannot establish a general truth.

The describe→explain→convince→justify→prove ladder: convincing may be confident but incomplete, whereas justifying is a correct, complete because/therefore chain; recognising that specific examples do not constitute watertight proof is a key developmental step.
learnerActions: Consider a claim such as 'the fraction with the bigger denominator is always bigger' or 'the fraction with the bigger numerator is always bigger'.
Test the bigger-denominator claim where the numerator is held fixed: compare 1/4 and 1/3 - the denominator 4 is larger, yet 1/4 is smaller than 1/3, so that claim fails.

Test the bigger-numerator claim on a case where the numerators actually differ: compare 3/8 and 1/2 - the numerator 3 is larger than 1, yet 3/8 is smaller than 1/2 (since 1/2 = 4/8), so that claim fails too.
State each breaking case as a counter-example that disproves the rule.
Articulate the asymmetry: one counter-example disproves a general claim, but any number of confirming examples does not prove it.
Build a because/therefore chain linking the givens to the conclusion so a list of true facts becomes a connected argument.
activities.intendedInsight: One counter-example is enough to refute a general claim, whereas confirming examples alone never establish one - and each step of an argument should be linked by because/therefore.

constraints: Do not accept a correct verdict (e.g. agreeing 3/4 > 2/3) as evidence of reasoning; a child can be right for the wrong reason via a single-component comparison rule. The discriminating act is explaining WHY examples don't settle it and producing the general reason.

Fixed-answer or 'spot the misaligned step' recognition tasks can serve as a warm-up but do not elicit a constructed general justification or a flaw explained in the child's own words; a score on such a task is not evidence of the reasoning practice, and recognition formats can inadvertently reward the confirming-example habit. Recognition alone does not elicit production.

Annotated correct-vs-flawed comparisons with tap-to-reveal explanations can seed critique talk but do not themselves respond to a child's over-reliance on examples or capture a constructed chain; use them to launch discussion, not as the assessment.

A single confirming example or drawing is a starting point for talk, not a proof; always push toward a reason that holds independent of the representation. Fractions remain comparable as numbers; the common-whole caveat applies only to comparing represented portions within a drawing.
Separate two distinct causes of wrong fraction comparisons: a faulty comparison rule (reteach comparison) versus a reasoning-articulation gap (scaffold and scribe); treat them differently.

Paper-corner tear-and-arrange uses physical cutouts as an imprecise, concrete approximation of idealised angles; a draggable on-screen triangle is a model of the same relationship. Both offer repeated examples that make the pattern vivid, but neither proves the general claim by itself, and neither is universally required.

Optional interaction examples (draggable triangle re-forming the straight line, nudging partial products in/out of column alignment, linked fraction/angle/multiplication tools) are illustrative mechanisms, not mandatory features. Comparative claims that one medium uniquely teaches, or that another 'cannot', are not established by the sources.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research, re-reviewed independently without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The original row's confidence was 'high' and its sources were marked verified; this review does not re-verify them and does not upgrade or downgrade that status.

Arithmetic confirmed: 3/4 = 9/12, 2/3 = 8/12, 9 > 8, so 3/4 > 2/3; 1/4 < 1/3; 3/8 < 1/2 (= 4/8); 5/8 = 15/24 and 2/3 = 16/24, so 5/8 < 2/3 (the 5/8 vs 2/3 pair is used only as a generalisation test, with no answer asserted in the activity).

Long-multiplication critique: a partial product belonging to a higher-place digit should be shifted one column to the LEFT; if instead shoved one column to the right it lands in a place value that is too low, so that partial product contributes too little. The source gives no concrete numeric example and describes this only as the 'wrong place value', so the net total direction is not asserted (an earlier candidate claim that the misalignment 'inflates the total' was incorrect - rightward columns are lower place values - and has been removed).

The original framed a 'doubting Thomas'/skeptic persona and claimed dialogue uniquely targets both halves of SMP3 and 'directly attacks' the empirical-proof habit; comparative necessity claims, or that other formats 'cannot' teach, are not established by the source citations and have been softened to scoped proposals with stated affordances and limits.

Counter-example wording was tightened: 1/4 vs 1/3 holds the numerator fixed to break the bigger-denominator rule, while 3/8 vs 1/2 is a case where both numerator and denominator differ (used to break the bigger-numerator rule, since any numerator-rule counter-example must vary both parts). This is a fair test of single-component rules, not a denominator rule 'flipping'.

probeDeeper: 'How many examples would it take before you were CERTAIN? Is there any number that would make it a proof?'
'Turn both fractions into twelfths for me — now what does that let you say, for sure?'
'A classmate says 3/4 > 2/3 because 4 is bigger than 3. Is that a good reason? Test it on 1/4 and 1/3.'
'Would your common-denominator argument still work for 5/8 versus 2/3? Show me.'
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child recognising that confirming examples/drawings do not constitute a general proof, and offering (or reaching for) a common-denominator argument (3/4 = 9/12, 2/3 = 8/12, 9/12 > 8/12) as the reason that settles it independently of any picture.

errorPatterns.pattern: Empirical proof scheme: treats confirming examples or a careful drawing as proof — 'I tried it and it worked, so it's true.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront the asymmetry: 'How many pizzas would you have to try to be SURE? Could there ever be one where it's different?' Then co-build the common-denominator reason and name it as the kind of argument that covers every case at once.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child endorses the classmate ('yes, that settles it') and, asked to show it themselves, offers another example or a neater drawing rather than a general reason.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares fractions by a single component — bigger numerator or bigger denominator wins — so any 'reason' given rests on a faulty comparison rule.
errorPatterns.nextMove: This is a false belief about fraction size, not an argument-skill gap — reteach comparison via a common denominator or a benchmark using bars. Do not accept the correct verdict as evidence of reasoning.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child justifies 3/4 > 2/3 with '4 is bigger than 3' or '3 is bigger than 2' rather than by a common referent; may get the right verdict for the wrong reason.

errorPatterns.pattern: Senses that 'drawings can be misleading' matters and rejects the example-proof, but cannot yet articulate the common-denominator reason — reasoning outruns the ability to state it.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT read as not-knowing. Scribe/revoice: 'you're right it's not settled — what could you turn both fractions into so they're easy to compare?' Let the child complete the chain; the discriminating instinct is already there.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 'no, that's not really a proof' or 'you need a proper reason' but stalls when asked to give one; may gesture toward twelfths without completing the chain.

responseLevels.gap: Accepts the examples/drawing as settling it and offers only more examples when asked to show it themselves.
responseLevels.full: Recognises confirming examples don't prove the claim AND produces a common-denominator (or benchmark) argument that settles it independent of any picture, explaining why that reason covers every case — and spontaneously applies the same 'examples aren't proof' stance to a new comparison.
responseLevels.partial: Is uneasy with the example-proof or gives the correct verdict, but justifies by a single-component rule or an unexplained drawing; can describe a comparison but not a reason that generalises.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A classmate says: 'I checked and 3/4 is bigger than 2/3 — I drew them and the 3/4 bar looked longer, and I tried it with a pizza too, so it's definitely true.' Do you think that settles it? How would YOU show whether 3/4 is bigger than 2/3, and would your way convince someone who says drawings can be misleading?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has crossed toward deductive reasoning is uneasy with 'I drew it and tried a pizza' and reaches for a reason that holds regardless of the drawing; a child still in the empirical-proof scheme is fully satisfied by the examples and sees nothing to add. The prompt separates them because it explicitly offers the empirical justification as 'settled' — a correct reasoner pushes past it, an empirical reasoner endorses it. Reasoning right for the wrong reason is hard here: agreeing 3/4 > 2/3 is easy, but explaining WHY the examples don't settle it and producing the common-denominator reason is the discriminating act.

pedagogy.summary: At 7-8, repeated reasoning matures into working the multiplication tables as a web of derivable facts and checkable patterns: noticing all multiples of 4 are even and using that to CHECK an answer, deriving 8×7 from 8×5 + 8×2, and describing the rule of a growing sequence ('add 50 each time') to predict onward. The MP8 emphasis on 'maintaining oversight… evaluating the reasonableness of intermediate results' becomes concrete here: a pattern (multiples of 4 are even) is not just noticed but used as a reasonableness check. Teaching should build tables from known facts and pattern, not rote alone, and always ask 'does that answer look sensible given the pattern?'
bestPractices: Derive harder table facts from anchor facts (×5 and ×2 to reach ×7) using an array split, so the table is a network not a list to memorise
Explicitly use pattern as a check: 'a multiple of 4 must be even — is your answer even?' to build reasonableness monitoring
Have children describe the rule of a growing sequence and predict several terms ahead, then verify
Surface and test near-generalisations ('all multiples of 4 are even — are all even numbers multiples of 4?') to sharpen what the rule does and doesn't claim
keyRepresentations: Arrays / area model split for deriving ×7 from ×5 + ×2
Multiplication grid highlighting column/row patterns (evens, digit patterns)
Number line with equal repeated steps for growing sequences (+50)
Hundred square shading multiples to reveal their pattern
commonMisconceptions: Skip-counts or guesses harder facts instead of deriving them from known ones (8×5 + 8×2)
Splits the derivation wrongly (8×5 + 2, forgetting to multiply the 2 by 8)
Accepts an unreasonable answer because the pattern check (multiples of 4 are even) isn't applied
Over-generalises a pattern from a few cases without testing, or reverses it wrongly (thinks every even number is a multiple of 4)

learn.summary: For ages 7-8, turn multiplication tables from a memorised list into a web of derivable facts and checkable patterns. Children derive a harder fact (8×7) from anchor facts they own (8×5 + 8×2 = 40 + 16 = 56) using an array split, use a pattern as a reasonableness check (multiples of 4 and 8 are even — is my answer even?), and describe/test the rule of a growing sequence ('add 50 each time') to predict onward terms. The core habit is deriving AND self-checking, plus probing what a pattern does and does not claim.

activities.title: Split an array to derive a hard fact
feedback: If a child skip-counts 8, 16, 24… or recalls insecurely: show the array split into 8×5 and 8×2 so the two anchor facts are visible to combine.
If a child computes 8×5 + 2 = 42 (forgetting to multiply the 2 by 8): return to the array — the second block is also 8 tall, so it is 8×2 = 16, not 2. This is a scaffolding nudge, not a full reteach.
Correct target: 8×7 = 8×5 + 8×2 = 40 + 16 = 56 (and equivalently 8×8 − 8 = 56).
activities.rationale: Deriving facts from known facts and using arrays that reveal structure supports reasoning over rote recall; a splittable/foldable array makes the decomposition something the child acts on.
sourceClaims: MP8: students notice repeated calculations, look for general methods and shortcuts (e.g. deriving facts), and maintain oversight by continually evaluating the reasonableness of intermediate results
Pupils should derive facts from known facts and recognise/use mathematical structure; teaching should use representations (arrays, grids) that reveal the pattern and support reasoning
learnerActions: Face 8×7 shown as an array 8 rows tall and 7 wide.
Cut the 7 into 5 and 2 (drag a divider, fold a paper array, or draw a line) so the array cleaves into an 8×5 block and an 8×2 block.
Read off 8×5 = 40 and 8×2 = 16, then combine the two blocks to get 56.

Try a different way to reach the same answer: 8×8 − 8 = 64 − 8 = 56 (take one group of 8 away from eight 8s). Compare which way you prefer and why — this uses one fewer group of 8, which is a different idea from cutting the 7 into 5 and 2.
activities.intendedInsight: A 'hard' table fact can be assembled from facts you already own; the array makes the decomposition (distributive idea) visible rather than relying on recall or skip-counting, and the 8×8 − 8 route is a distinct alternative strategy (adjusting from a near fact), not another split of the 7.

activities.title: Use a table pattern as a reasonableness check
feedback: If a child has no test when asked to check: practise 'multiples of 4/8 are even; is yours?' and connect it back to the shaded grid.

If a child accepts an odd number as a multiple of 4: point to the shaded multiples of 4 (a single column or row on a multiplication grid, a staggered pattern on a 10-wide hundred square) — no odd number is shaded.
A product that is odd cannot be a multiple of 4 or 8; a product well outside the 40–64 range for 8×7 should prompt a recheck — then confirm the exact value by the derivation.
activities.rationale: Maintaining oversight by evaluating the reasonableness of intermediate results is central to MP8; a shadeable grid makes the pattern visible so it can be used as a live check.
sourceClaims: MP8: students notice repeated calculations, look for general methods and shortcuts (e.g. deriving facts), and maintain oversight by continually evaluating the reasonableness of intermediate results
Pupils should derive facts from known facts and recognise/use mathematical structure; teaching should use representations (arrays, grids) that reveal the pattern and support reasoning
learnerActions: Shade the multiples of 4 (and of 8) on a multiplication grid or hundred square and observe that every one is even.
State the pattern as a check: 'a multiple of 4 must be even — is my answer even?'
Apply the check to a proposed product: given a candidate like an odd 'multiple of 4', decide whether it can be right and say why.
Estimate before computing: 'roughly how big should 8×7 be — between which two facts I know?' (between 8×5=40 and 8×8=64).
activities.intendedInsight: A noticed pattern is not just an observation — it becomes a tool you use to catch your own errors and judge whether an answer looks plausible (this check shows an answer is plausible, e.g. even and within range, not that it is exactly right).

activities.title: Describe and test a sequence rule
feedback: If a child only continues one step: ask them to state the rule explicitly first, then jump ahead using it.
Check predictions against equal repeated steps on the number line; a term that breaks the constant step signals an arithmetic slip.
activities.rationale: Describing the regularity in repeated reasoning and using it to predict, then checking, is the sequence form of MP8.
sourceClaims: MP8: students notice repeated calculations, look for general methods and shortcuts (e.g. deriving facts), and maintain oversight by continually evaluating the reasonableness of intermediate results
learnerActions: Given a growing sequence (e.g. steps of +50 along a number line), describe the rule in words: 'add 50 each time'.
Predict several terms ahead — e.g. the term after 350 (400), and the one after that (450) — then verify by stepping along the number line.
Say how sure you are and how you could check a predicted term.
activities.intendedInsight: A clearly stated rule lets you predict beyond what you can see and then verify, which is the predict-and-check habit in a sequence context.

activities.title: Test the limits of a pattern (don't over-reverse it)
feedback: If a child says 18 (or 6) is a multiple of 4 because it is even: offer the counterexample and ask them to list actual multiples of 4 (4, 8, 12, 16…) to see 6 and 18 are absent.
Correct distinction: 'multiple of 4 ⇒ even' holds, but 'even ⇒ multiple of 4' is false.
activities.rationale: Surfacing and testing near-generalisations guards against over-generalising a pattern from a few cases or reversing it wrongly; this is recognising precisely what the mathematical structure does and does not entail.
sourceClaims: Pupils should derive facts from known facts and recognise/use mathematical structure; teaching should use representations (arrays, grids) that reveal the pattern and support reasoning
learnerActions: Consider the claim 'all multiples of 4 are even' and agree it is true.
Now test the reverse: 'is every even number a multiple of 4?' Try 6 — it is even but not a multiple of 4.
State precisely what the rule claims and what it does not (every multiple of 4 is even, but not every even number is a multiple of 4).
activities.intendedInsight: A true pattern often does not reverse; testing a near-generalisation with a counterexample sharpens exactly what a rule does and doesn't claim.

activities.title: Check understanding with targeted questions
feedback: Include an '8×5 + 2' distractor for the split: the correct combination is 8×5 + 8×2, so the second term is 16, not 2 (giving 56, not 42).
For the sorting task, an even number that is not a multiple of 4 (like 6) tests whether the child over-reverses the pattern.
Pair each selection with a 'why' so recognition is backed by reasoning, not guessing.
activities.rationale: At this age, well-designed questions can probe the derivation and reasonableness-checking content when paired with a justification step; note this checks recognition and stated reasoning, not independent construction, so pair it with open construction tasks.
sourceClaims: MP8: students notice repeated calculations, look for general methods and shortcuts (e.g. deriving facts), and maintain oversight by continually evaluating the reasonableness of intermediate results
learnerActions: Answer 'which known facts can you combine to make 8×7?' and explain why your choice works.
Sort a set of numbers into multiples of 4 and not-multiples-of-4, including an even non-multiple to catch over-generalising.
Spot the unreasonable answer: given candidate products, identify one that breaks a pattern (e.g. an odd 'multiple of 8') and say which pattern it breaks.
activities.intendedInsight: Questions can check both the derivation route and the pattern-as-check habit, including whether a child is fooled by a plausible wrong split; this checks recognition and stated reasoning, not whether the child can construct the derivation unprompted.

constraints: Build tables from known facts and visible pattern, not rote memorisation alone; always ask 'does that answer look sensible given the pattern?'

Arrays and grids should be things the child acts on (cut, fold, shade) so the derivation and pattern are visible; a pre-split array or fixed shaded grid with tap-to-reveal annotations can illustrate and reference the method but does not let the child choose the split or test their own candidate answer against the pattern — treat it as a scaffold.

Recognition/selection questions check whether a child can identify a correct split or sort numbers, but do not by themselves require the child to construct a derivation unprompted; pair with a spoken or written 'why' and with open construction tasks.
Open discussion alone supplies nothing to split or shade; pair talk with an array, grid, or number line (a practical pairing, not a claim that talk cannot support reasoning).
These are flat number-and-pattern ideas; a 3D presentation is not needed and may add load — this is a practical note for this topic, not a universal claim about 3D.
Pattern-as-check establishes that an answer is plausible (e.g. even, within a range), not that it is exactly correct; keep both the derivation and the check.
Keep the 8×5 + 8×2 array split distinct from the 8×8 − 8 near-fact route; both reach 56 but they are different strategies (decomposition vs. adjusting from a known neighbour).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit (arithmetic): 8×5=40, 8×2=16, 40+16=56; alternative 8×8−8 = 64−8 = 56; both confirmed. Estimation bound 'between 8×5=40 and 8×8=64' is correct for 8×7=56. Sequence +50 from 350 gives 400 then 450.

Self-audit (pattern logic): 'all multiples of 4 are even' is true; its reverse is false (6 and 18 are even but not multiples of 4); 18 is not a multiple of 4. The '8×5 + 2 = 42' error is a genuine common slip and is used only as a diagnosed misconception, never offered as a correct option.

The original claims that 'open talk supplies nothing' and '3D adds load, not insight' were softened to scoped practical notes; catalog fit rankings are not evidence of comparative efficacy or necessity.

sourceClaims are exact copies of this row's two sources; neither establishes that any specific activity here was empirically tested, nor that questioning is a superior assessment method. Source 2 is retained for the near-generalisation activity only as structure-level support, not as direct evidence for converse-testing.

Editor correction: activity 1's alternative route (8×8 − 8) was reworded into child-friendly language and kept clearly distinct from the 5+2 array decomposition (a near-fact adjustment, not a split of the 7).

probeDeeper: Ask 'could you also get 8×7 from 8×8 minus 8? which route do you prefer and why?' to test flexible reuse of anchor facts
Counterexample tuned to this topic: 'all multiples of 4 are even — so is every even number a multiple of 4? what about 6?' to check the child does not over-reverse the pattern
Ask 'your sequence adds 50 each time — what will the term after 350 be, and the one after that? how sure are you?' to probe rule-based prediction
Ask 'without working it out exactly, roughly how big should 8×7 be — between which two facts you know?' to surface reasonableness monitoring
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for deriving 8×7 = 8×5 + 8×2 = 56, AND a reasonableness check such as '56 is even, and multiples of 8 (or 4) are even, so it looks right', or noticing it lies between 8×5 and 8×8. The derivation plus the self-check is the target.

errorPatterns.pattern: Skip-counts or guesses 8×7 rather than deriving it from the known 8×5 and 8×2
errorPatterns.nextMove: Split an array into 8×5 and 8×2 so the derivation is visible; connect it to the distributive idea they can see
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child counts 8, 16, 24… or recalls insecurely rather than combining the two anchor facts

errorPatterns.pattern: Splits the derivation wrongly — computes 8×5 + 2 (forgets to multiply the 2 by 8)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the array: the second block is 8 tall too, so it is 8×2=16, not 2; a scaffold not a reteach
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives 42, having added 2 rather than 8×2

errorPatterns.pattern: Does not apply a pattern as a reasonableness check, accepting an odd or wildly-off product; or over-generalises (thinks every even number is a multiple of 4)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Practise pattern-as-check ('multiples of 4/8 are even; is yours?') and test the reverse claim with counterexamples (6 is even but not a multiple of 4) so the rule's limits are clear
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked to check, the child has no test, or claims 18 is a multiple of 4 because it is even

responseLevels.gap: Skip-counts or guesses harder facts, mis-splits derivations, and applies no reasonableness check; patterns noticed but not used
responseLevels.full: Derives 8×7 from known facts, checks it against a pattern (even/between anchors), and states and tests a sequence rule — maintaining oversight of reasonableness and transferring the derive-and-check habit unprompted
responseLevels.partial: Derives a fact from anchors or states a pattern when prompted, but does not spontaneously check reasonableness or test/limit a generalisation

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You're sure that 8 × 5 = 40 and 8 × 2 = 16. Use those to work out 8 × 7 without counting up in eights. Then — how could you quickly check your answer looks sensible?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Reaching 56 by skip-counting shows no repeated-reasoning insight; deriving it from anchor facts AND checking it against a pattern does. A child with the habit both decomposes and monitors reasonableness; a child without either counts up or accepts an answer with no check.

sources.claim: MP8: students notice repeated calculations, look for general methods and shortcuts (e.g. deriving facts), and maintain oversight by continually evaluating the reasonableness of intermediate results
sources.source: CCSS Standards for Mathematical Practice, MP8 'Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning'

sources.claim: Pupils should derive facts from known facts and recognise/use mathematical structure; teaching should use representations (arrays, grids) that reveal the pattern and support reasoning
sources.source: EEF, 'Improving Mathematics in Key Stages 2 and 3' guidance report (Recommendations 2 and 4)

pedagogy.summary: Two shapes are SIMILAR when one is a scaled copy of the other: corresponding angles are equal and every pair of corresponding sides is in the SAME ratio (the scale factor). Solving similar-shape problems means (1) finding the scale factor from a known pair of corresponding sides, then (2) multiplying (to enlarge) or dividing (to reduce) the other sides by it. The pedagogical crux is that enlargement is MULTIPLICATIVE, not additive: every side is multiplied by the SAME factor, so the shape keeps its proportions. Children must resist adding a constant to each side (which distorts the shape) and, when area comes in, must learn that a length scale factor k multiplies AREA by k².
bestPractices: Establish 'same shape, sides in the same ratio, equal angles' as the definition of similar before any calculation; contrast a genuine enlargement with a stretched (distorted) copy.
Find the scale factor first from a matched pair of corresponding sides (new ÷ old), then apply it to every other side — make 'multiply by the SAME number' explicit.

Confront the additive error directly: show that adding the same amount to each side changes the shape (a 2×5 rectangle + 4 to each side is 6×9, no longer similar), whereas multiplying keeps it similar.
When perimeter/area appear, build the k² result from a diagram: doubling the sides of a rectangle makes FOUR copies fit inside, so area ×4 not ×2 (MAP Enlargements).
Use a ratio table / double number line pairing corresponding sides so the constant multiplier is visible across all pairs.
keyRepresentations: Ratio table pairing corresponding sides (old side | new side), scale factor as the column multiplier
Overlaid/nested shapes on a grid showing the enlargement from a centre
Area grid showing k² tiling (double sides → four sub-rectangles)
The scale-factor arrow (×k) applied to every corresponding side
commonMisconceptions: Additive enlargement — adding the same amount to each side instead of multiplying by the scale factor (distorts the shape; the classic Hart/CSMS rectangle error).
Treating 'similar' as 'roughly the same shape' or as 'congruent/identical', not checking that all sides share one ratio.
Believing that doubling the lengths doubles the area (area actually scales by k²; MAP Enlargements documents this as a persistent error).
Applying the scale factor to only one side, or using new÷old for one pair and old÷new for another (inconsistent direction).

learn.summary: Similar shapes are scaled copies: corresponding angles are equal and every pair of corresponding sides shares one ratio (the scale factor). Learners find the scale factor from a known matched pair (new ÷ old), then multiply the other sides by that same factor (a factor greater than 1 enlarges; a factor less than 1, such as 1/3, reduces — equivalently, when reducing you can divide by the enlargement factor). The pedagogical crux is that enlargement is MULTIPLICATIVE, not additive — adding a constant to each side generally distorts the shape (e.g. any non-square rectangle; a square or equilateral triangle is an exception) — and that a length scale factor k scales area by k² (and volume by k³ for solids).

activities.title: Enlargement studio: grab, scale, and compare with additive mode
feedback: If you scaled only one side: ask whether the new shape is still the same shape — overlay it and check that EVERY corresponding side grew by the same multiplier.

If additive mode looked 'about right', overlay it on the original's diagonal: a true enlargement stays on the diagonal; the additive copy of a non-square rectangle slides off it, showing distorted proportions.
When you predicted area, compare your guess with the tiled count: doubling sides gives four tiles (×4), tripling gives nine (×9) — area follows k².
activities.rationale: Live manipulation with a locked aspect ratio plus a contrasting additive mode may make the multiplicative nature of enlargement observable, so the documented additive error becomes visible rather than merely asserted. The tiling overlay builds the k² area result from a concrete diagram. The additive mode, ratio table, diagonal check and tiling overlay are optional illustrative mechanisms, not the only way to teach this.
sourceClaims: Students apply inappropriate ADDITIVE strategies to multiplicative scaling situations (adding a constant rather than multiplying by a scale factor) — a documented error in proportional-reasoning classroom trials.

Doubling the length and width of a rectangle multiplies its area by 4, not 2; for similar shapes the area scale factor is the square of the scale factor (k²) and the volume scale factor is k³ — documented as a persistent student misconception (treating price/area as scaling linearly).
learnerActions: Work on a grid with a non-square rectangle or triangle whose aspect ratio is locked. Drag a corner to enlarge it and watch a live scale-factor readout while every side multiplies by the same factor and the angles stay unchanged; for a rectangle enlarged from a fixed corner, notice the dragged opposite corner moves along the original's diagonal, showing it is the same shape.
Fill a ratio table alongside (old side | new side for each pair) and check that the same column multiplier appears for every pair of corresponding sides.

Flip to an 'additive mode' that instead ADDS your chosen number to each side of the non-square rectangle; observe it stretch lopsided and fall off the original's diagonal — it is no longer similar. Compare directly with the multiplicative result.
Turn on a grid-tiling overlay: with a scale factor of 2, see FOUR copies of the original tile the new shape; with a factor of 3, nine copies fit — connect this to area × k².
If a scaling touches only one side, use the flag that highlights the unchanged side and correct it so every corresponding side is scaled.
activities.intendedInsight: Enlargement multiplies every corresponding side by the SAME factor, preserving shape and angles; adding the same amount to each side of a non-square rectangle distorts it. Because the shape grows in two dimensions, area scales by k², not by k.

activities.title: Confront the additive error on paper
feedback: Compare the two ratios as numbers: 6/9 (= 2/3) does not equal 2/5, so the additive version is not a true enlargement.
If unsure, draw both shapes to scale and overlay a corner — the similar one nests exactly along the diagonal.
activities.rationale: Explicitly performing and comparing the additive versus multiplicative transformation targets the classic Hart/CSMS rectangle error. Worked on paper this needs no device and makes the ratio check the decider.
sourceClaims: Students apply inappropriate ADDITIVE strategies to multiplicative scaling situations (adding a constant rather than multiplying by a scale factor) — a documented error in proportional-reasoning classroom trials.
learnerActions: Take a 2×5 rectangle. Add 4 to each side to get a 6×9 rectangle, and draw both. Check whether the side ratios match: 2:5 versus 6:9 — they do not, so the shapes are not similar.
Now enlarge the same 2×5 rectangle by a scale factor, multiplying each side by 3 to get 6×15, and confirm 2:5 and 6:15 are the same ratio.
State in your own words why 'add the same to each side' changes the shape while 'multiply each side by the same number' keeps it.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding a constant to every side changed the proportions of the 2×5 rectangle (as it does for any non-square rectangle); multiplying every side by a common factor always keeps corresponding sides in a single ratio and preserves the shape.

activities.title: Solve and judge similar-shape problems
feedback: If you wrote 21, you added the 12 difference; instead find the factor (×3) and apply it — the correct missing side is 27 cm.
If you said the area is 3× bigger, tile it: a factor of 3 fits nine copies, so area is ×9 (54 → 486 cm²).

On a reduction, sense-check direction: the answer should be SMALLER than the side you began with, so divide by the enlargement factor (e.g. ÷3) or, equivalently, multiply by the new ÷ old factor (e.g. ×1/3).
Keep new ÷ old consistent — do not use new ÷ old for one pair and old ÷ new for another.
activities.rationale: These items make the scale factor, the additive distractor, the direction-of-application slip and the area-scaling error separately assessable. Watching the working (e.g. 27 via ×3 versus 21 via +12) reveals which strategy a learner used; recognition items alone would not elicit this production. Pair it with the manipulation activities so the rule is understood, not just recognised.
sourceClaims: Pupils should solve problems involving similar shapes where the scale factor is known or can be found (Year 6 ratio and proportion).

Doubling the length and width of a rectangle multiplies its area by 4, not 2; for similar shapes the area scale factor is the square of the scale factor (k²) and the volume scale factor is k³ — documented as a persistent student misconception (treating price/area as scaling linearly).
learnerActions: Given a rectangle 6×9 enlarged so 6→18, find the scale factor (18 ÷ 6 = 3) and the missing side (9 × 3 = 27 cm). Beware of adding the difference 12 to get 21 — that is the additive error, not a valid answer.
Find the scale factor between two similar triangles from a matched pair of side lengths, keeping new ÷ old consistent for the comparison.

Judge whether two given shapes are similar by testing EVERY pair of corresponding sides for the same ratio, not by appearance, and by checking that corresponding angles are equal (for triangles, matching side ratios are enough; for other polygons they are not, e.g. a square and a non-square rhombus). One mismatched ratio means not similar.

For a REDUCTION (e.g. 18 back to 6), decide first whether the answer should be bigger or smaller than the side you start from; then divide by the enlargement factor (÷3), which is the same as multiplying by the new ÷ old factor (6 ÷ 18 = 1/3).
On an area follow-up for the 6×9→18×27 rectangle, reason that area scales by k² = 3² = 9 (54 cm² → 486 cm²), not by 3.
activities.intendedInsight: Problem solving means finding the scale factor from a known pair, applying it in the correct direction to every side, checking similarity by shared ratio, and using k² for area.

activities.title: Optional extension: scaling a solid to feel k² and k³
feedback: If you expected volume to double when edges double, count the unit cubes: eight small cubes fit, so volume is ×8 (2³).
Keep the core objective in view — this 3D view is an extension beyond the 2D similar-shapes task.
activities.rationale: A solid-scaling sandbox may give a concrete feel for how area and volume grow with dimension, complementing the 2D work. This is explicitly optional and exceeds the stated 2D objective; it should not replace the primary 2D activities.
sourceClaims: Doubling the length and width of a rectangle multiplies its area by 4, not 2; for similar shapes the area scale factor is the square of the scale factor (k²) and the volume scale factor is k³ — documented as a persistent student misconception (treating price/area as scaling linearly).
learnerActions: Enlarge a cube or cuboid with a slider and watch surface area grow by k² and volume by k³.
Fill the enlarged solid with unit cubes to count that doubling every edge of a cube gives 2³ = 8 times the volume, and relate the growing faces to k² area.
Return to a flat similar-shapes problem and restate: length ×k, area ×k², and for solids volume ×k³.
activities.intendedInsight: Scaling length by k scales area by k² and, for solids, volume by k³ — the same multiplicative idea extended by dimension.

constraints: Establish the definition — same shape, equal angles, ALL corresponding sides in one ratio — and contrast a true enlargement with a stretched copy BEFORE any calculation.
Find the scale factor first from a matched pair (new ÷ old), then apply the SAME factor to every other side; make 'multiply by the same number' explicit.

A static nested-shapes diagram with tap-to-reveal '×k per side' and 'area ×k²' can consolidate the rule as a reference card, but does not let the learner manipulate and watch the additive distortion occur; use it after, not instead of, hands-on work.

Multiple-choice/recognition items (e.g. choosing which pair is similar) assess discrimination but do not by themselves elicit the independent construction of finding and applying a scale factor; include fill-in and show-your-working tasks for production.
Keep the direction of division consistent (new ÷ old) within a comparison, and sense-check whether the answer should be larger or smaller before computing.
The 3D solid-scaling activity is an optional extension that goes beyond the 2D similar-shapes objective and must not be the main teaching artefact.

Illustrative interface features (locked aspect ratio, live scale-factor readout, additive-mode toggle, diagonal check, tiling overlay, ratio table, single-side flag) are examples of the learning mechanism, not mandatory requirements.

The additive-mode distortion demonstration should use a non-square rectangle, since a square keeps its shape under equal additions; present the additive result (e.g. 21) only as a flagged error, never as a valid answer option.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support the underlying principle, not the specific activity designs.

Self-audit (arithmetic/logic): 18 ÷ 6 = 3 and 9 × 3 = 27 are correct; the additive distractor 21 comes from 9 + 12 where 12 = 18 − 6. For a scale factor of 3, nine copies tile the area (3² = 9) and area 6×9 = 54 cm² becomes 486 cm² (18×27=486=54×9). Volume for a doubled edge is 2³ = 8, correct. In Activity 2, 2+4=6 and 5+4=9 (additive, not similar: 2/5≠2/3); 2×3=6 and 5×3=15 (multiplicative, similar: 2/5=6/15).

The original design used a scale-factor-2 tiling example showing FOUR copies (2²=4), while the worked problem uses factor 3 giving nine copies (3²=9); both are internally consistent and kept distinct to avoid conflating the example with the problem.

Activity 1 keeps the enlargement studio's aspect ratio locked; otherwise a free corner-drag would change width and height independently and distort the shape, contradicting the same-factor/angle-preserving behaviour.

The additive-mode 'falls off the diagonal' behaviour holds for non-square rectangles; a square would remain similar under equal additions, so the demonstration is scoped to non-square cases and treated as an illustrative affordance, not an invariant law.

The original artefact framing asserted a conversation 'cannot exercise' the skill and that 3D 'overshoots'; these are softened to scoped limits (in-role dialogue is a poor fit for this spatial-procedural practice; 3D is an optional extension) rather than universal pedagogical laws.

The double-number-line representation from the original was folded into the ratio-table scaffold rather than dropped; centre-of-enlargement detail was not emphasised as it exceeds the stated scale-factor objective.

probeDeeper: Is your enlarged rectangle the SAME shape as the original — how could you check that all the sides grew in the same way?
What is the scale factor here, and what does it mean to say the sides are 'in the same ratio'?
Now think about AREA: the original is 6×9 = 54 cm². What is the area of the enlarged one — is it 3 times bigger? (counterexample forcing the k² idea: it is 9 times bigger.)
If instead I SHRANK the rectangle so the 18 went back to 6, what would you do to the other side — multiply or divide, and by what?
assess.correctAnswer: 27 cm. The scale factor is 18 ÷ 6 = 3, so every side is multiplied by 3: the 9 cm side becomes 9 × 3 = 27 cm.

errorPatterns.pattern: Additive enlargement — adds the constant difference (here +12) to each side instead of multiplying by the scale factor
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'is the new rectangle the SAME shape as the old one?' Draw both and overlay — the additive version is distorted. Rebuild on a ratio table: every side ×3. Reteach multiplicative missing-value ratio.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 9 + 12 = 21, having taken the 18−6 = 12 increase from the known side and added it to the other; no scale factor computed

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats 'similar' as 'roughly the same shape' or 'congruent', not checking that all sides share one ratio
errorPatterns.nextMove: Restate the definition: same shape, equal angles, ALL sides in the same ratio. Test each side pair — one mismatched ratio means not similar. Reteach the vocabulary of ratio/proportion/scale.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When judging whether two given shapes are similar, decides on appearance ('they both look like rectangles') without comparing side ratios, or assumes similar means identical

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes doubling the lengths doubles the area (ignores that area scales by the square of the scale factor)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Tile the enlarged rectangle with copies of the original on a grid — a scale factor of 3 fits 9 copies. Establish length ×k → area ×k². Reteach area of rectangles.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On an area follow-up, says the enlarged rectangle's area is 3× (or 2×) the original instead of 3² = 9×; treats area like a length

errorPatterns.pattern: Finds the scale factor correctly but applies it in the wrong direction (multiplies when reducing, or divides when enlarging)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach: ask 'is the answer meant to be bigger or smaller than the side you started from?' before computing, as a sense-check on the direction.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Computes the factor as 3 but on a REDUCTION problem multiplies anyway, giving a bigger shape when it should be smaller

responseLevels.gap: Adds the constant difference to the other side (21), or judges similarity by appearance; does not find or apply a scale factor.
responseLevels.full: Finds the scale factor (×3), applies it to give 27, explains that all corresponding sides share that ratio so the shape is preserved, correctly reasons that area scales by k² (×9), and handles a reduction by dividing — transferring the method to an unfamiliar shape.
responseLevels.partial: Finds the scale factor and the missing side correctly for lengths, but slips on area (says ×3 not ×9) or cannot reliably judge whether two new shapes are similar — the multiplicative rule is not yet secure across cases.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a rectangle 6 cm by 9 cm. I enlarge it so the 6 cm side becomes 18 cm, and the new rectangle is similar to the old one. Work out the length of the other side. Show your working.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child reasoning multiplicatively finds the scale factor (×3) and applies it to the other side, giving 27 — a value only that method produces. A child using the additive strategy sees the 6→18 side grew by 12 and adds 12 to the other side, giving 21. The two children produce different numbers by different routes, and watching the working (not asking them to state a rule) shows immediately which they used.
