pedagogy.summary: Year 6 (age 10–11) pupils convert between standard units using DECIMAL notation to up to three decimal places, moving in both directions (smaller↔larger), and can explain the mm–cm–m–km (and g–kg, ml–l) relationships as powers of 10. This is the decimal extension of Year 5 conversion: the same 'reason from unit size, move the digits' method, now with the decimal point in play. The load-bearing hazard is decimal place value — the 'add/remove a zero' shortcut fails (3250 g ÷ 1000 is 3.25 kg, not 325), and children who think 'the point is the decimal' misplace digits.
bestPractices: Convert by moving the DIGITS across a fixed decimal point (×/÷ by 10/100/1000), explicitly rejecting 'add a zero' and 'move the point' — use true/false error-spotting (0.45÷10 = .45?) to confront the shortcut (NCETM Spine 2.29).
Keep the unit-size reasoning from Year 5 ('larger unit → fewer → divide') so direction is reasoned, not guessed.
Make the powers-of-10 STRUCTURE explicit: 10 mm = 1 cm, 100 cm = 1 m, 1000 m = 1 km — so a conversion is one multiplication/division by a power of ten, and mixed chains compose.
Use a place-value chart extended to thousandths so pupils can state the value of each digit before and after, and place holder zeros correctly.
Include a reasonableness check (should the number get bigger or smaller?) to catch direction and decimal-placement errors.
keyRepresentations: Place-value chart extended to thousandths (digits slide, point fixed)
Powers-of-10 ladder mm×10→cm×100→m×1000→km
Double number line for the two units
Gattegno chart for ×/÷ by powers of 10
commonMisconceptions: 'Add/remove a zero' with decimals: 3250 g → '325 kg', or 0.45 km → '45 m' / '4.5 m'.
Reverses the multiply/divide direction, giving an answer orders of magnitude out (0.45 km → 0.00045 m).
'The point is the decimal' — mis-values digits after the point or treats 0.45 as the whole number 45.
Cannot articulate the powers-of-10 relationship, so treats each conversion as an isolated fact.

learn.summary: Year 6 pupils (age 10–11) convert between standard measurement units using decimal notation to up to three decimal places, moving in both directions (smaller↔larger), and explain the mm–cm–m–km (and g–kg, ml–l) relationships as powers of ten. This extends Year 5 conversion with the decimal point now in play: the method stays 'reason from unit size, then move the DIGITS across a fixed decimal point', using ×/÷ by 10/100/1000. The load-bearing hazard is decimal place value — the 'add/remove a zero' shortcut fails (3250 g ÷ 1000 = 3.25 kg, not 325), and children who think 'the point is the decimal fraction' misplace digit values.

activities.title: Move the digits, keep the point still (place-value conversion)
feedback: If a learner answers 325 kg for 3250 g, they removed zeros instead of moving digits three places. Rebuild it on the chart: 3250 ÷ 1000 moves each digit three places right, giving 3.25 — count the places, do not delete symbols.

If a learner answers 4.5 m or 45 m for 0.45 km, name the error precisely: 4.5 m is a one-place shift (as if ×10), and 45 m is a two-place shift (as if ×100). Both are wrong; 0.45 × 1000 moves digits three places left to 450 m. Have them name the value of the 4 (four tenths) and the 5 (five hundredths) first, then shift three places.
If an answer is wildly out (e.g. 0.00045 m or 3 250 000 kg), the multiply/divide direction was reversed. Re-reason from unit size before trusting the result.
If a learner treats 0.45 as the whole number 45, rebuild decimal place value: each column to the right is ten times smaller, so 0.45 is four tenths and five hundredths.
activities.rationale: Converting by moving digits across a fixed point directly confronts the 'add/remove a zero' shortcut, which fails for decimals; pairing it with explicit unit-size reasoning keeps direction reasoned rather than guessed, and the equal-value check (3.250 = 3.25) addresses holder-zero confusion. The 5 cm→0.05 m case instances the same method on a shorter chain.
sourceClaims: Convert measures by moving the DIGITS across a fixed decimal point via ×/÷ by 10/100/1000; the guide embeds 'add/remove a zero' as FALSE statements for decimals (0.45÷10 = .45; 25.34×10 = 25.340) to expose the misconception.
Grade 5 pupils convert among different-sized standard measurement units within a given system, with the parenthetical example 'convert 5 cm to 0.05 m', using decimal notation.
UK DfE Year 6 pupils solve problems involving conversion of units using decimal notation up to three decimal places, converting length/mass/volume/time from a smaller unit to a larger and vice versa.
learnerActions: Set up a place-value chart extended to thousandths. Write 3250 g in it, then convert to kilograms by sliding every digit three places to the RIGHT (dividing by 1000) while the decimal point stays fixed, landing on 3.25 kg; note that a holder zero is inserted only where place value demands it.
Before moving, state the unit-size reason aloud: 'Kilograms are the bigger unit, so there will be FEWER of them — I divide.' Then check the direction of the digit shift matches.
Convert the reverse case 0.45 km to metres (×1000), sliding digits three places LEFT to get 450 m; state that metres are smaller, so there are MORE.

Convert 5 cm to 0.05 m (÷100), sliding each digit two places to the right — a shorter example of the same digit-movement method with decimal notation; say why metres are the larger unit so there are fewer.
Confirm that 3.250 kg and 3.25 kg name the same quantity — the trailing zero after the last significant digit does not change the value.
Do a reasonableness check each time: 'Should this number get bigger or smaller?' and reject any answer that is orders of magnitude out.
activities.intendedInsight: A conversion moves the SAME digits across a FIXED decimal point; the point does not move. Converting to a larger unit gives fewer of them (divide, digits move right); converting to a smaller unit gives more (multiply, digits move left). 3250 g and 3.25 kg are one quantity; 3.250 equals 3.25.

activities.title: Spot the false shortcut (error-spotting with decimals)
feedback: If a learner accepts 0.45 ÷ 10 = .45, show on the chart that dividing by ten moves each digit one place right: 0.45 → 0.045. Nothing was divided in '.45'.
If a learner accepts 25.34 × 10 = 25.340, point out that 25.340 equals 25.34 (same value). Multiplying by ten gives 253.4 — digits move one place left.
activities.rationale: True/false error-spotting on carefully chosen decimal cases makes the failure of the zero shortcut explicit and forces articulation of digit movement and place value.
sourceClaims: Convert measures by moving the DIGITS across a fixed decimal point via ×/÷ by 10/100/1000; the guide embeds 'add/remove a zero' as FALSE statements for decimals (0.45÷10 = .45; 25.34×10 = 25.340) to expose the misconception.
A common decimal misconception is thinking 'the point is the decimal fraction'; place value must extend so each column to the right is ten times smaller, and holder zeros are understood.
learnerActions: Judge true or false and explain: 'Is 0.45 ÷ 10 = .45?' Correct it to 0.045 by moving each digit one place right.
Judge true or false: 'Is 25.34 × 10 = 25.340?' Explain that appending a zero after the last decimal does NOT multiply by ten; the correct answer is 253.4, with digits moving one place left.
For each false statement, state the correct conversion and justify it with the value of each digit and the direction of movement.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding or removing a zero is not the same as multiplying or dividing by a power of ten once decimals are involved. ×/÷ by 10, 100, 1000 moves the digits by one, two, or three places; the zero trick coincidentally works for some whole numbers but misvalues decimals.

activities.title: Climb the powers-of-ten ladder (composing conversions)
feedback: If a learner cannot say why 1 km = 1000 m, walk the ladder rung by rung (m → ×10 → tens of metres → ×10 → hundreds → ×10 → 1000 m) so the ×1000 is seen as 10×10×10.
If a learner treats g–kg differently from m–km, point out both are ÷1000 (or ×1000) — the same power-of-ten structure applies.
activities.rationale: Making the powers-of-ten structure explicit lets conversions be reasoned and composed rather than memorised, which supports transfer across length, mass and volume.
sourceClaims: UK DfE Year 6 pupils solve problems involving conversion of units using decimal notation up to three decimal places, converting length/mass/volume/time from a smaller unit to a larger and vice versa.
A common decimal misconception is thinking 'the point is the decimal fraction'; place value must extend so each column to the right is ten times smaller, and holder zeros are understood.
learnerActions: Build a ladder stating each relationship: 10 mm = 1 cm, 100 cm = 1 m, 1000 m = 1 km. For each rung, say whether you multiply or divide and by what power of ten.
Hop along the ladder to compose a chain, e.g. mm → cm (÷10) → m (÷100) → km (÷1000), and recognise that any single conversion is one multiplication or division by a power of ten.
Optionally use a Gattegno chart (rows for powers of ten) to see each conversion as a single ×/÷ by a power of ten — moving along a row, or jumping rows for the larger steps.
Explain in words why 1 km is a thousand metres and not a hundred, using the powers-of-ten structure rather than reciting it as an isolated fact.

Transfer the same structure to mass (g–kg) and volume (ml–l) to show the method is general across metric units, not tied to length. Then contrast with time (e.g. 2.5 h = 150 min, not 250 min) to see that time units use factors of 60 and 24, not powers of ten.
activities.intendedInsight: The metric system is built on powers of ten, so every metric conversion is a single ×/÷ by a power of ten and mixed chains compose; knowing the structure removes the need to memorise each conversion separately. Time units are not decimal (60 s = 1 min, 60 min = 1 h, 24 h = 1 day), so time conversions use those factors instead of powers of ten.

constraints: Reject 'add/remove a zero' and 'move the decimal point' as methods; teach movement of the DIGITS across a point that stays fixed.
Keep unit-size reasoning ('larger unit → fewer → divide; smaller unit → more → multiply') so direction is reasoned, not guessed, and pair it with a reasonableness check.

A fixed reference ladder of powers of ten can show the relationships but does not let a learner move digits or check direction themselves; use it alongside an activity where the learner performs the transformation (chart, writing, or spoken step-by-step), not as the only medium.

Matching, fill-in-the-blank and multiple-choice items (including true/false decimal cases) can probe direction and the add-a-zero error precisely, but recognition responses do not by themselves elicit independent construction of the conversion; include tasks where the learner produces the converted value and justifies it.
Ensure a holder zero is inserted only where place value requires it (e.g. 0.045), and that trailing zeros after the last significant decimal (3.250 vs 3.25) are recognised as equal value.

An extended place-value chart to thousandths, a double number line between the two units, and a Gattegno chart for ×/÷ by powers of ten are useful supports but are scaffolds; learners should also reason and state values without them to show secure understanding.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 3250 g ÷ 1000 = 3.25 kg (digits move three places right); 0.45 km × 1000 = 450 m (three places left); 5 cm ÷ 100 = 0.05 m (two places right); 0.45 ÷ 10 = 0.045 (one place right); 25.34 × 10 = 253.4 (one place left, NOT 25.340). All checked and consistent with the source's intended corrections. The misconception answers (325 kg, 45 m, 4.5 m, 25.340, 0.00045 m, 3 250 000 kg) appear only as errors to correct, never as valid answers.

The original source frames an interactive place-value slider as 'ideal' and a static image/3D/dialogue as 'poor' for this topic. These are catalog fit rankings, not established comparative efficacy; this rewrite retains the digit-movement mechanism as a concrete support while softening claims that other media 'cannot teach' the concept. A static ladder, Gattegno chart, and spoken/written reasoning can also support the objective.
The Gattegno chart from the original keyRepresentations is retained as an optional scaffold in the powers-of-ten activity and the scaffold constraint.
One listed source (DfE National Curriculum) carries verified:false in the row; treat its claim with appropriate caution pending verification.

probeDeeper: 'Kilograms are bigger than grams — so should the number of kg be bigger or smaller than 3250? Does 3.25 fit?'
'Is 3.250 kg the same as 3.25 kg? How do you know?'
'You wrote 0.45 km = ___ m. What is the 4 worth, and the 5? Now move them.'
'Explain to me why 1 km is a thousand metres and not a hundred — using powers of ten.'
assess.correctAnswer: 3250 g = 3.25 kg (÷1000, 'kg bigger → fewer'); 0.45 km = 450 m (×1000); explains 10 mm = 1 cm, 100 cm = 1 m, 1000 m = 1 km, each step a ×/÷ by a power of ten, digits moving across a fixed point.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Add/remove a zero' with decimals — divides 3250 by 1000 by deleting zeros ('325 kg'), or multiplies 0.45 by 1000 by appending/one-step zeros ('45 m' or '4.5 m').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Move digits three places on a place-value chart with the point fixed; use true/false items (0.45÷10 = .45? 25.34×10 = 25.340?) to show the zero shortcut fails for decimals.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The answer has the wrong number of decimal places; zeros were added/removed rather than digits moved three places.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses the multiply/divide direction — gives an answer orders of magnitude out (0.45 km → 0.00045 m, or 3250 g → 3 250 000 kg).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reason from unit size first ('metres smaller → more → multiply') and add a reasonableness check before trusting the answer.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The result is far bigger/smaller than sensible; no unit-size reasoning offered.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The point is the decimal' — mis-values digits after the point, treating 0.45 as the whole number 45 or misreading thousandths.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild decimal place value: each column right is ten times smaller; state the value of each digit in 0.45 (four tenths, five hundredths) before converting.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Digit values after the point are wrong; 0.45 handled as 45; three-decimal-place answers misplaced.

responseLevels.gap: Adds/removes zeros, reverses direction, or mis-values decimal digits; answers orders of magnitude out.
responseLevels.full: Converts both directions with correct decimal placement (digits move, point fixed), handles up to 3 dp, and explains the ×/÷ powers-of-10 structure linking mm–cm–m–km — transferring across length, mass, volume and time.
responseLevels.partial: Converts a friendly case correctly but slips on three decimal places or on the reverse direction, or converts but cannot explain the powers-of-10 relationship.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to think aloud through three tasks: (1) 'Convert 3250 g to kilograms.' (2) 'Convert 0.45 km to metres.' (3) 'Explain how mm, cm, m and km are related using powers of 10.' Watch the direction choice, where the decimal point ends up, and whether the powers-of-10 structure is understood — not just the final numbers.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A pupil with secure decimal place value moves the digits the right number of places in the right direction (3.25 kg; 450 m) and explains the ×10 chain; a pupil relying on 'add/remove a zero' produces 325 kg or 45 m, and one who thinks 'the point is the decimal' mis-values 0.45. Digit-movement understanding versus zero-shortcut diverge precisely on these decimal cases.

sources.claim: Grade 5 pupils convert among different-sized standard measurement units within a given system, with the parenthetical example 'convert 5 cm to 0.05 m', using decimal notation.

pedagogy.summary: Children learn the key time-unit facts — 60 minutes in an hour, 24 hours in a day — and use them in simple problems. Recall of the facts is usually secure; the conceptual work is grasping the non-decimal 60-grouping (time is NOT base-10) and that a whole day is two 12-hour sweeps of the clock (24, not 12). Taught by counting minutes in 60s on a clock/number line and tracking the hour hand's double sweep across day and night.
bestPractices: Count minutes in fives around the clock so 60 minutes visibly closes into one hour (the 60-grouping)
Track the hour hand round the clock twice — morning then night — to build 12 + 12 = 24, linking to am/pm and the 24-hour clock
Contrast time with money/base-10 explicitly: 60 minutes make an hour, not 100
Use simple duration problems (a 90-minute film) so children APPLY the facts, not just recite them
keyRepresentations: Analogue clock face
A number line marked in minutes and hours
A day-strip showing two 12-hour halves (day and night)
A 24-hour clock shown alongside the 12-hour clock
commonMisconceptions: Thinks a day is 12 hours because the clock face 'stops at 12'
Over-applies base-10 — treats 1 hour as 100 minutes, 90 minutes as 9 hours, or half an hour as 50 minutes
Fails to regroup at 60 when adding times (3:40 + 30 minutes = 3:70)
Muddles which unit is larger (minute vs hour)

learn.summary: Year 2 learners (ages 6-7) learn the key time-unit facts — 60 minutes in an hour, 24 hours in a day — and apply them in simple duration problems. Recall of the facts is usually secure; the real conceptual work is grasping the non-decimal 60-grouping (time is not base-10) and that a whole day is two 12-hour sweeps of the clock (24, not 12). The core approach is to count minutes in fives so a full 60 closes into one hour, and to track the hour hand's double sweep across day and night.

activities.title: The hour hand's double lap: why a day is 24 hours
feedback: If a learner says a day is 12 hours because 'the clock stops at 12', have them watch/track the second lap explicitly, naming the pm hours on the first lap (midday to midnight) and then the am hours on the second lap (midnight to midday), so they see the 12 numbers reused.
If they reach 24 but can't explain it, ask them to point to where the first 12 hours end and the second 12 begin on the day-strip.
Reinforce by matching times across the 12-hour and 24-hour clocks (1pm = 13:00) so the double sweep is anchored to a familiar format.
activities.rationale: The 12-hour vs 24-hour structure is a documented conceptual challenge, not a recall gap; children must grasp that the clock counts midnight-to-midday and again midday-to-midnight (one lap = 12 hours, two laps = 24 hours). Watching the hour hand complete a second lap is intended to make the reuse of the 12 numbers concrete. A live day-strip that fills as the hand moves, and a side-by-side 24-hour clock, are optional ways to make the double sweep visible; a labelled static clock with tap-to-reveal, or a character/dialogue that states and quizzes the facts, can serve as lighter-weight alternatives, but neither lets the learner watch the sweep unfold.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils should 'know the number of minutes in an hour and the number of hours in a day' (statutory Measurement content).

The 12-hour vs 24-hour structure is a genuine conceptual challenge: in a Years 3-4 interview study, an item asking how long the hour hand takes to go once round scored 12 h as fully correct and 24 h as the partial/incorrect response, and the authors stress children must grasp that a 12-hour clock counts from midnight to midday and again from midday to midnight; meanwhile basic unit facts (seconds/minute, minutes/hour, months) were largely a strength (>90%), with the difficulties lying in the deeper relational/duration concepts.
learnerActions: Move the hour hand slowly round an analogue clock from midday, naming the hours aloud as it passes the numbers.
When the hand returns to 12, pause and count: that first lap covered 12 hours (midday through to midnight).
Send the hand round a second time, now naming the night and morning hours, and track a day-strip that fills behind the clock — one half for the first lap, the second half for the second lap.
Write down the total: 12 + 12 = 24 hours in a whole day and night.
Line a 12-hour clock up beside a 24-hour clock so that, for example, 1pm matches 13:00, confirming the numbers 1-12 get used twice.
activities.intendedInsight: A whole day is 24 hours because the hour hand goes round the 12-number clock face twice — once from midday to midnight and once from midnight to midday — so 12 + 12 = 24, not 12. One lap alone is 12 hours; it takes two laps to make a day.

activities.title: Closing the hour at 60: the non-decimal grouping
feedback: If a learner says 90 minutes is 9 hours (or 0.9 of an hour), count minutes in fives to 60 on the number line so a full 60 closes into one hour before applying it to 90.
If they add times like 3:40 + 30 = 3:70, show that past 60 the minutes roll over into the next hour (3:40 + 30 = 4:10).
If they say half an hour is 50 minutes, count in fives to the halfway point and confirm it is 30, because half of 60 is 30, not half of 100.
Praise correct regrouping by asking them to explain WHY it is 60 and not 100.
activities.rationale: Children apply discrete whole-number / base-10 reasoning to time and struggle to coordinate the non-standard grouping of 60, so the hour-minute relationship — not fact recall — is the crux. Counting minutes in fives is intended to make the 60-grouping concrete before it is applied to durations. An optional container that only closes at exactly 60 and overflows at 90 is intended to make the regrouping visible; a slider or fill-in item can then check that the learner regroups rather than reciting the bare fact.
sourceClaims: Children apply discrete whole-number reasoning to time and struggle to coordinate the non-standard groupings of 12 and 60 (Kamii & Russell's 'inability to coordinate hierarchical units'), so the multiplicative hour-minute relationship, not fact recall, is the crux of difficulty.
Year 2 pupils should 'know the number of minutes in an hour and the number of hours in a day' (statutory Measurement content).
learnerActions: Count minutes in fives around a clock face or along a number line marked in minutes, saying 5, 10, 15 … up to 60.
Notice that it takes exactly 60 minutes for the minute hand to complete one full lap (twelve jumps of 5), so 60 minutes close into 1 hour.
Contrast this with money/base-10 out loud: an hour is 60 minutes, NOT 100 — time does not group in tens and hundreds.
Fill an 'hour container' that only closes at 60: pour in 90 minutes and watch it overflow into one full hour (60) with 30 left over.
Record the result: 90 minutes = 1 hour 30 minutes, because 90 = 60 + 30.
activities.intendedInsight: Minutes regroup into hours at 60, not at 100: a full 60 minutes makes one hour, so 90 minutes is 1 hour 30 minutes — the grouping is felt by counting and overflowing, not just recited.

activities.title: Apply the facts: simple duration problems
feedback: Correct answer, no reason: ask them to show where the 60 or the double sweep is doing the work.
For the day item, a 12-hour answer signals the double-sweep misconception — return to tracking the hour hand round twice.
For the 90-minute item, a 9-hour or 0.9 answer signals missing 60-regrouping — return to counting minutes in fives to 60.
Mark as secure only when the learner states the fact AND explains it AND applies it to a new duration.
activities.rationale: Simple duration problems require learners to apply the facts rather than recite them; a learner can correctly state '60 minutes in an hour' yet still not USE the 60-grouping, and asking for the reason separates memorisation from understanding. Fact-recall and duration items (fill-in, multiple choice offering a 12-hour wrong option, a '90 minutes = [ ] hour [ ] minutes' item) are a valid quick check of application but should be paired with a 'why' prompt.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils should 'know the number of minutes in an hour and the number of hours in a day' (statutory Measurement content).
learnerActions: Solve a duration problem such as: 'A cartoon lasts 90 minutes. How many hours and minutes is that, and how do you know?' and state the answer as 1 hour 30 minutes.
Answer a day question with reasoning: 'How many hours are in one whole day and night, and why — when the clock only shows 1 to 12?'
Decide which unit is larger, a minute or an hour, and justify it.
Explain each answer in words, not just give the number, so the reasoning is visible.
activities.intendedInsight: The time-unit facts are tools to be used: a learner who understands them can convert 90 minutes to 1 hour 30 and explain 24 hours as two 12-hour sweeps, transferring the reasoning to fresh problems.

constraints: Target the fact and its use, not the astronomy: the Earth-rotation cause of a 24-hour day is a different topic and is not the learning objective here.
Keep one-lap=12 hours and two-laps=24 hours distinct in all learner-facing wording; never state or imply that the hour hand goes 'once round' in 24 hours.

Recognition-only checks (multiple choice, fill-in) confirm recall and can catch some regrouping errors, but they do not by themselves show the learner can explain the double sweep or regroup a fresh duration — pair them with a 'why' prompt that elicits the reasoning.

A static labelled clock or day-strip, or a character/dialogue, can state the facts but does not let the learner watch the double sweep or the 60-grouping happen; treat these as lighter scaffolds, not replacements for counting/tracking the motion.
Explicitly contrast time with base-10 (60 not 100) rather than assuming learners will transfer money reasoning correctly; the base-10 over-application is the main error to pre-empt.
Half an hour is 30 minutes because half of 60 is 30; do not let '50 minutes' (half of 100) stand as an acceptable answer.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and scaffold efficacy wording is kept as 'intended'.

The cited Years 3-4 interview study reports that 24h was scored as the partial/incorrect response to 'how long the hour hand takes to go once round' — because one lap of the hour hand is in fact 12 hours, while a whole day (two laps) is 24 hours. The activities here keep this distinction explicit (one lap = 12h, two laps = 24h); reviewers should confirm learner-facing wording never conflates 'once round = 24h'.
Source claims are drawn from an age 6-7 context but one cited study is Years 3-4; the conceptual difficulty is relevant but the exact age transfer is a migration assumption worth noting.
The original reteach/prerequisite pointers and two-tier assessment structure were not reproduced as learner actions; reviewers should confirm diagnostic prompts align with local assessment practice.

probeDeeper: 'It is 12 o'clock in the middle of the day. When the hour hand gets back to 12 again, what time is it — and how many hours have gone by?'
'My clock says 2 o'clock. Could that be the middle of the night as well as the afternoon? How would we tell them apart?'
'Half an hour is how many minutes — and why isn't it 50?'
assess.correctAnswer: (A) 24 hours, because the hour hand goes round the clock twice — 12 hours through the morning and 12 more through the afternoon and night, so 12 + 12 = 24. (B) 1 hour 30 minutes, because 60 minutes make one hour and 90 = 60 + 30.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks a whole day is 12 hours because the clock face 'stops at 12' — doesn't realise the hour hand goes round twice
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront it directly: track the hour hand through a full day, naming am then pm as two 12-hour sweeps, and line the 12-hour clock up against a 24-hour clock so 13:00 = 1pm.
errorPatterns.distractor: 12 hours
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 12 to the whole-day question, reasoning that the clock only goes up to 12

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats hours and minutes as if they don't group at 60 — applies discrete whole-number/base-10 reasoning, so 90 minutes is read as 9 hours (or 0.9 of an hour) rather than regrouped into 1 hour 30
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count minutes in 60s on a number line or clock so a full 60 closes into one hour; make the non-standard grouping concrete before applying it to durations.
errorPatterns.distractor: 9 hours
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the 90-minute item gives 9 hours, 0.9, or otherwise fails to regroup 60 minutes into an hour

responseLevels.gap: Cannot reliably state 60 and 24, or insists a day is 12 hours; treats durations in base-10 (90 minutes = 9 hours).
responseLevels.full: States both facts AND explains 24 as two 12-hour sweeps and converts 90 minutes ↔ 1 hour 30 using the 60-grouping, transferring the reasoning to a fresh duration.
responseLevels.partial: States 60 minutes = 1 hour and 24 hours = 1 day, but recites them as bare facts — cannot explain the 12→24 double sweep or regroup 90 minutes into 1 hour 30.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the fact, then the reason. (A) 'How many hours are there in one whole day and night? ... The clock face only shows the numbers 1 to 12 — so how can a day have that many hours? Tell me why.' (B) 'A cartoon lasts 90 minutes. How many hours and minutes is that, and how do you know?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The 12-to-24 reason separates a child who has merely memorised '24' from one who understands the double sweep; the 90-minute item catches base-10/no-60-regrouping — a child can correctly state '60 minutes in an hour' yet still not USE the 60-grouping.

sources.claim: Children apply discrete whole-number reasoning to time and struggle to coordinate the non-standard groupings of 12 and 60 (Kamii & Russell's 'inability to coordinate hierarchical units'), so the multiplicative hour-minute relationship, not fact recall, is the crux of difficulty.

pedagogy.summary: Children convert between units of time — hours to/from minutes, minutes to/from seconds, years to/from months, weeks to/from days — including mixed quantities (3 hours 25 minutes = 3x60 + 25 = 205 minutes). The method is MULTIPLICATIVE (x60, x7, x12), using known number facts, and must resist the base-10 pull that assumes 100 seconds in a minute. The documented errors are additive rather than multiplicative reasoning, base-10 assumptions, and irregular groupings (months vary in length; a month is not exactly 4 weeks).
bestPractices: Use multiplicative reasoning with known facts (x60, x7, x12), not repeated addition
Convert mixed quantities in two parts: whole units x rate, then add the remainder (3x60 + 25)
Confront the base-10 pull explicitly: 60 seconds in a minute, not 100
Handle the reverse (150 s -> 2 min 30 s) by dividing and expressing the remainder
Flag irregular units — months vary; about 4 weeks in a month is approximate, not exact
keyRepresentations: Conversion tables (Days-Weeks, Years-Months, Minutes-Seconds)
The x60 / x7 / x12 rate as a known-fact chain (36 ÷ 6 = 6, so 360 s = 6 min)
A number track for counting leap years / weeks
A bar model splitting a mixed quantity into whole units + remainder
commonMisconceptions: Uses additive reasoning instead of multiplicative for conversions
Assumes base-10 (100 seconds in a minute, 100 minutes in an hour)
Thinks every month is exactly 4 weeks / all months are the same length
Converts a mixed quantity by ignoring the remainder or the second unit

learn.summary: Children convert between units of time — hours↔minutes, minutes↔seconds, years↔months, weeks↔days — including mixed quantities (e.g. 3 hours 25 minutes = 3×60 + 25 = 205 minutes). The core idea is MULTIPLICATIVE conversion (×60, ×7, ×12) using known number facts, and resisting the base-10 pull that wrongly assumes 100 seconds in a minute or 100 minutes in an hour. Reverse conversions require dividing and expressing the remainder (150 s → 2 min 30 s). Documented errors are additive rather than multiplicative reasoning, base-10 assumptions, mishandling the remainder/second unit in mixed quantities, and treating every month as exactly 4 weeks.

activities.title: Multiply-then-combine with a conversion machine
feedback: If a learner gives 180 minutes for 3 h 25 min, ask where the 25 minutes went; have them add the remainder back: 180 + 25 = 205. A bar model separating the whole units (3 × 60 = 180) from the remainder (25) can make the two-part split visible when the leftover is dropped.
If a learner reads 150 seconds as '1.5 minutes', group the seconds into sixties: two complete sixties and 30 left, so 2 minutes 30 seconds — 150 ÷ 60 = 2 remainder 30.
If a learner answers '2 minutes' for 150 seconds, point to the 30 seconds still unaccounted for and ask what happens to them.
If a learner uses ×100 for hours→minutes, contrast their answer with grouping into sixties so the 60-grouping is visibly correct.
activities.rationale: A visible multiply-then-add computation with a reverse divide-with-remainder makes the multiplicative structure and base-60 grouping concrete, directly confronting the additive and base-10 errors documented for this topic; the bar model scaffolds the whole-units-plus-remainder split.
sourceClaims: White Rose Y4 Time (Steps 1-2) documents that when converting units of time children may rely on additive rather than multiplicative reasoning, may assume base-10 (100 seconds in a minute / 100 minutes in an hour), and may think there are always exactly 4 weeks in a month; the method uses multiplicative reasoning and known number facts (e.g. 360 s = 6 min via the 6 times-table).

Children apply discrete whole-number, base-10 reasoning to time and cannot easily coordinate its non-standard groupings of 60, 12, 7, which underlies base-10 conversion errors and difficulty coordinating mixed units.
learnerActions: Take a mixed quantity such as 3 hours 25 minutes and convert it: multiply the whole units by the rate (3 × 60 = 180 minutes), then add the remaining 25 to get 205 minutes.
State out loud whether you counted up or multiplied, and why multiplying is faster.
Work a reverse conversion: take 150 seconds, group it into sixties — two full groups of 60 make 2 minutes, with 30 seconds left over, giving '2 minutes 30 seconds'.
Test the tempting '100 to a minute' idea against grouping real seconds into sixties, and describe what goes wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: Converting units of time is multiply (by the fixed rate) then combine the remainder — not counting up — and for seconds, minutes and hours the grouping is 60, not 100.

activities.title: Known-facts conversion with a base-10 trap item
feedback: For '1.5 minutes', re-ground on 60: 1.5 of 60 would be 90 seconds, not 150; 150 seconds is 2 minutes 30 seconds.
For '2 minutes', ask about the leftover 30 seconds.
For 8 weeks 3 days, confirm 8 × 7 = 56 then add the 3 loose days for 59.
activities.rationale: Targeted items with carefully chosen wrong-answer options can help surface which error a learner is making (base-10 vs dropping the remainder vs additive). Such items check and may provoke reasoning; use them alongside worked construction, since choosing an answer does not by itself show the learner can carry out the method independently.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils should 'solve problems involving converting between units of time'; the guidance adds pupils use all four operations in such problems, expressing answers appropriately (for example, days to weeks as weeks and days). Year 4 pupils 'solve problems involving converting from hours to minutes; minutes to seconds; years to months; weeks to days'.

Children apply discrete whole-number, base-10 reasoning to time and cannot easily coordinate its non-standard groupings of 60, 12, 7, which underlies base-10 conversion errors and difficulty coordinating mixed units.
learnerActions: Fill in conversions such as '3 h 25 min = ___ min' and show the multiply-then-add working.
Match a seconds amount (e.g. 150 s) to its minutes-and-seconds form.
Choose the correct reading of 150 seconds and explain why '1.5 minutes' (base-10 thinking) and '2 minutes' (dropped remainder) are both wrong.
Convert 8 weeks 3 days to days using 8 × 7 = 56, then + 3 = 59 days.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure conversions rest on known multiplication facts and on keeping the remainder; the common wrong answers to the 150-seconds item — '1.5 minutes' and '2 minutes' — correspond to base-10 thinking and to dropping the remainder.

activities.title: Irregular units: months, weeks and the calendar
feedback: If a learner converts months to days as ×28 or calls a month exactly 4 weeks, use the calendar to show months of 28, 30 and 31 days and distinguish the approximate month fact from the exact week-to-day fact.
activities.rationale: Addressing month-length variability with a concrete calendar directly targets the documented 'every month is exactly 4 weeks' misconception while keeping exact rates distinct from approximate ones.
sourceClaims: White Rose Y4 Time (Steps 1-2) documents that when converting units of time children may rely on additive rather than multiplicative reasoning, may assume base-10 (100 seconds in a minute / 100 minutes in an hour), and may think there are always exactly 4 weeks in a month; the method uses multiplicative reasoning and known number facts (e.g. 360 s = 6 min via the 6 times-table).

Year 5 pupils should 'solve problems involving converting between units of time'; the guidance adds pupils use all four operations in such problems, expressing answers appropriately (for example, days to weeks as weeks and days). Year 4 pupils 'solve problems involving converting from hours to minutes; minutes to seconds; years to months; weeks to days'.
learnerActions: Use a real calendar to count the days in several different months, including February, and record what you find: months have 28, 29 (February in a leap year), 30 or 31 days.
State why 'about 4 weeks in a month' is an approximation, not an exact conversion.
Contrast the exact fact (1 week = 7 days) with the approximate month fact, and explain how you would convert months to days versus weeks to days.
activities.intendedInsight: Some time units convert by exact fixed rates (7 days per week, 60 seconds per minute, 12 months per year) while month LENGTHS are irregular, so 'a month ≈ 4 weeks' cannot be used as an exact conversion to days.

activities.title: Pose-and-solve conversion word problems
feedback: Ask the learner to justify their chosen rate; if they add rather than multiply, prompt them to build the ×rate from a known fact.
Probe the remainder: 'Did you keep the leftover part, and where did it go in your answer?'
activities.rationale: Spoken or written word problems let a learner verbalise the method, which may expose additive-vs-multiplicative reasoning. On its own a spoken dialogue does not record whether the learner multiplied or added, so pair it with written working.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils should 'solve problems involving converting between units of time'; the guidance adds pupils use all four operations in such problems, expressing answers appropriately (for example, days to weeks as weeks and days). Year 4 pupils 'solve problems involving converting from hours to minutes; minutes to seconds; years to months; weeks to days'.
learnerActions: Read or hear a word problem (e.g. 'A film lasts 150 seconds — how long is that in minutes and seconds?') and solve it, saying each step aloud.
Explain for each problem which rate you used (×60, ×7, ×12) and how you handled any remainder or second unit.
activities.intendedInsight: Conversions apply in context; choosing the right rate and correctly expressing mixed/remainder answers is part of solving the problem.

constraints: Use multiplicative reasoning with known facts (×60, ×7, ×12), not repeated addition; for mixed quantities convert whole units × rate, then add or keep the remainder.
Confront the base-10 pull explicitly: 60 seconds in a minute and 60 minutes in an hour, not 100; the 100-to-a-minute idea should be shown wrong against real grouping, not merely stated wrong.
Handle reverse conversions by dividing and expressing the remainder (150 s → 2 min 30 s), not rounding or dropping the leftover.
Keep exact rates (1 week = 7 days, 1 year = 12 months) distinct from the approximate month-to-weeks relationship; month lengths vary from 28 to 31 days.

Choosing a correct option in a matching or selection item checks reasoning but does not by itself demonstrate independent construction of the method; include tasks where the learner carries out and shows the conversion.
A fixed conversion poster or table can display the rates but does not let the learner compute and see the remainder form; treat it as a reference scaffold rather than the main activity.
A bar model (whole units + remainder) and a number track for counting weeks/leap years are optional representations that can scaffold the split and the counting, not required mechanisms.
Illustrative interactions (feeding units into a ×rate step, grouping seconds into sixties, a toggle offering the base-10 reading) are ways to make the mechanism visible, not required mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic in the source was checked and is correct: 3 × 60 + 25 = 205 minutes; 150 ÷ 60 = 2 remainder 30 → 2 minutes 30 seconds; 8 × 7 + 3 = 59 days; 1.5 minutes = 90 seconds (so reading 150 s as '1.5 minutes' is genuinely wrong, as intended).

The source probe 'Is 90 minutes the same as 1.9 hours?' is a base-10 trap counterexample; the correct answer is that 90 minutes = 1.5 hours (since 60 minutes = 1 hour), not 1.9 hours. Retained only as a discussion prompt note, never as a learner answer option; any feedback must state 1.5 hours.

The original keyRepresentation 'number track for counting leap years / weeks' is retained as an optional scaffold in constraints and may be built into a dedicated activity where counting weeks or leap years is practised.

The source's assertions that '3D adds nothing' and that a static image or dialogue 'can't' teach the computation are catalog fit judgements, not established facts; they have been softened to scoped affordances/limits. Comparative efficacy or necessity of any single format is not established by the sources provided.

The sourceClaims on Activities 2 and 4 support the conversion content, the 'express answers appropriately' convention, and the documented errors, but do not validate the efficacy of selection/distractor items or spoken word problems; efficacy wording is kept conditional.

probeDeeper: 'You changed 150 seconds — is that 1.5 minutes or 2 minutes 30 seconds? Why?' (base-60)
'How did you turn 3 hours into minutes — did you count or multiply?'
'Is every month exactly 4 weeks? How many days are in this month?' (irregular units)
'Is 90 minutes the same as 1.9 hours? What is it really?' (base-10 trap counterexample)
assess.correctAnswer: 3 x 60 = 180, + 25 = 205 minutes; 150 ÷ 60 = 2 remainder 30 -> 2 minutes 30 seconds; 8 x 7 = 56, + 3 = 59 days — using multiplicative reasoning and correctly combining the mixed parts.

errorPatterns.pattern: Assumes base-10 grouping — 100 seconds in a minute or 100 minutes in an hour
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-ground on 60 by grouping actual seconds/minutes into sixties; contrast the base-10 answer with the real grouping so 60 sticks.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Converts 150 s as '1.5 minutes' or '1 min 50 s'; converts hours using x100

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses additive reasoning instead of multiplicative for conversions
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model x rate with known facts (3 x 60) built from a conversion table; show that multiplication is repeated addition made efficient.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Converts 3 hours by slowly counting up in 60s, or adds where they should multiply, and struggles with larger conversions

errorPatterns.pattern: Mishandles the mixed quantity — ignores the remainder or the second unit (3 h 25 min -> just 180; 150 s -> '2 minutes' dropping the 30)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the two-part split — convert the whole units, then add or keep the remainder; use a bar model separating whole units from the remainder.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives 180 minutes for 3 h 25 min, or '2 minutes' for 150 seconds

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks every month is exactly 4 weeks / all months are the same length
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a calendar to show months vary (28-31 days) and that about 4 weeks is approximate; keep the exact week-to-day fact distinct from the month facts.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Converts months to days as x28, or states a month is exactly 4 weeks

responseLevels.gap: Converts by adding or by base-10 (100 to a minute); drops remainders; treats all months as 4 weeks.
responseLevels.full: Converts all four unit pairs multiplicatively, handles mixed quantities (whole units + remainder) and reverse conversions (division with remainder) correctly, resists base-10, and treats irregular units (months) correctly.
responseLevels.partial: Converts simple whole-unit cases multiplicatively, but slips on the base-60 grouping in reverse conversions or drops the remainder in mixed quantities.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set conversion problems and WATCH the method: (1) 'Change 3 hours 25 minutes into minutes — show me how.' (2) 'A programme lasts 150 seconds — write that in minutes and seconds.' (3) 'How many days are in 8 weeks and 3 days?' Watch whether they multiply by the right rate (x60, x7) and handle the remainder, or add up, assume base-10 (100 to a minute), or drop the mixed part.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The 150-seconds item is the discriminator: a base-10 child answers '1.5 minutes', a drop-the-remainder child answers '2 minutes', a child using the 60-grouping answers 2 minutes 30 seconds. The mixed 3 h 25 min item catches additive reasoning and dropping the remainder.

pedagogy.summary: This topic has two linked strands: automatic recall of addition and subtraction facts to 20 (so 7+8 and 15−8 come without calculating) and derivation of related facts to 100 by scaling and using known bonds (6+4=10 → 60+40=100; 5+5=10 → 35+5=40). Recall is built from secure make-ten strategy plus spaced retrieval, not speed drills; derivation is built by treating tens as units, so a known bond reappears at a larger scale.
bestPractices: Build automaticity from strategy, then retrieval: secure make-ten within 20 first, then space low-stakes recall practice so facts move to memory (DfE: emphasis on practice aids fluency)
Teach fact families so + and − are learned together (7+8=15, 15−8=7, 15−7=8) and the inverse is available
Derive decade facts by scaling a known bond: 6+4=10 becomes 60+40=100 because six tens plus four tens is ten tens
Use the same visual at two scales (ten-frame counters vs ten-rods) to show 6+4 and 60+40 are one picture
Avoid timed pressure that induces anxiety; keep finger/strategy use welcome while retrieval matures
keyRepresentations: Ten-frame / double ten-frame (make-ten)
Fact-family triangle (shows the three related facts)
Bead string / Rekenrek
Base-ten ten-rods (scaling a bond to tens)
Number bonds part-whole diagram
commonMisconceptions: Recall not automatic — still counting on fingers every time for 7+8
Failing to scale the bond: knowing 6+4=10 but giving 60+40=10 or 70 or 700
Treating addition and subtraction as unrelated, so 15−8 is re-counted despite knowing 7+8=15
Applying a derived pattern blindly (e.g. 35+5=40 but then 35+50=40)

learn.summary: Two linked goals for ages 6–7: automatic recall of addition and subtraction facts to 20 (so 7+8 and 15−8 come without calculating) and derivation of related facts to 100 by scaling and using known bonds — 6+4=10 → 60+40=100 by scaling the bond to tens, and 5+5=10 → 35+5=40 by using the ones bond inside a larger number. Recall is built from a secure make-ten strategy plus spaced, untimed retrieval rather than speed drills; derivation is built by treating tens as units so a known bond reappears at a larger scale.

activities.title: Same bond, bigger units: scaling 6+4 to 60+40
feedback: If a child gives 60+40=10, 70 or 700, show 6+4 and 60+40 with the same picture at two scales (counters then ten-rods) and name that six tens plus four tens is ten tens = 100.
If a child says 35+50=40, slow down and count the tens being added: adding five tens to 35 gives 85, while adding five ones gives 40. Keep both comparisons visible side by side.
When a child derives correctly, ask 'how did you know that?' so the scaling or ones-bond reasoning is spoken, not just the answer.
activities.rationale: Using the same visual at two scales makes 'derive' concrete: a known within-ten bond is reused at the scale of tens by unitising. A manipulable or scalable model lets the learner see the identical make-ten action produce 10 and then 100; a fixed two-scale picture can also show this relationship.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently and derive and use related facts up to 100 (e.g. 3+7=10 → 30+70=100); an emphasis on practice at this stage aids fluency, and knowing number bonds establishes addition and subtraction as related operations.
Recall of pairs that make ten supports calculation, and known facts are extended by unitising tens so a within-ten bond is reused at the scale of tens.
learnerActions: Complete 6+4 on a ten-frame by sliding four counters in to fill all ten; confirm this is a known, secure bond making 10.
Switch the counters to tens: let each counter become a ten-rod (or restate each counter as 'one ten') so the same full frame now reads 100.
Say aloud what changed: 'six tens plus four tens is ten tens, which is 100' — the gesture and picture are identical, only the unit changed.
Repeat the tens-scaling with another known bond: 5+5=10 → 50+50=100 (five tens plus five tens is ten tens).
Separately, derive 35+5 by using the ones bond 5+5=10: 30 + (5+5) = 40, so here the 5 is added as five ones, not scaled to tens.
Deliberately contrast 35+5=40 with 35+50=85: in 35+50 you are adding five tens, not five ones, so the answers differ.
activities.intendedInsight: Deriving a decade fact like 60+40 is scaling a known bond, not memorising a new fact: six tens plus four tens is ten tens = 100. A different move is using a bond inside a larger number — 35+5 uses the ones bond 5+5=10 to give 40. Which unit you add (ones vs tens) decides the result, so 35+5=40 and 35+50=85 are different.

activities.title: Fact-family triangle: one trio, both operations
feedback: If a child re-counts 15−8 straight after giving 7+8=15, lay out the fact family 7, 8, 15 and show the same three numbers make both facts.
Prompt: 'If 7+8=15, what subtraction facts do you already know without working them out?'
A tap-to-reveal triangle is good reference for the inverse link but does not by itself build recall speed; pair it with retrieval practice.
activities.rationale: Teaching fact families makes the inverse explicit so + and − are learned together and the inverse is immediately available. This supports the misconception where subtraction is treated as a separate unknown fact.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently and derive and use related facts up to 100 (e.g. 3+7=10 → 30+70=100); an emphasis on practice at this stage aids fluency, and knowing number bonds establishes addition and subtraction as related operations.
learnerActions: Lay out the three numbers 7, 8 and 15 on a fact-family triangle (part–part–whole).
Cover one corner and read off the fact it reveals: cover 15 to get 7+8=15 and 8+7=15; cover 7 to get 15−8=7; cover 8 to get 15−7=8.
State explicitly: because 7+8=15, you already know 15−8 and 15−7 without re-counting.
Build a second family (e.g. 6, 9, 15, giving 6+9=15, 9+6=15, 15−6=9, 15−9=6) and name all its related facts the same way.
activities.intendedInsight: Addition and subtraction are the same relationship between three numbers; knowing one fact hands you the inverse, so 15−8 need not be re-counted once 7+8=15 is known.

activities.title: Spaced, untimed retrieval to build automatic recall
feedback: If a child counts on fingers for 7+8 every time with no drop in effort on a second asking, do NOT impose timed drills or penalise finger use — keep practising the make-ten strategy and spaced recall without the clock.
For a derive prompt like '6+4=10, so 60+40=?', if a wrong value such as 10, 70 or 700 is chosen, return to the two-scale picture and re-establish six tens plus four tens = 100.
Ask 'which of those did you just know, and which did you have to work out?' to make the recall/calculation distinction visible to the learner.
activities.rationale: Recall is built from a secure make-ten strategy then moved to memory by spaced low-stakes practice; timed pressure can induce anxiety and is avoided. A self-paced fill-in or choice format can exercise retrieval and check the derive insight, but repeated spaced practice, not a single check, is what builds automaticity.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently and derive and use related facts up to 100 (e.g. 3+7=10 → 30+70=100); an emphasis on practice at this stage aids fluency, and knowing number bonds establishes addition and subtraction as related operations.
Recall of pairs that make ten supports calculation, and known facts are extended by unitising tens so a within-ten bond is reused at the scale of tens.
learnerActions: Practise recalling facts to 20 in short, low-stakes sessions spread over days (e.g. 7+8, 15−8, 6+4, 9+4), rather than one long timed drill.
Mix in derive-a-fact prompts such as '6+4=10, so 60+40=?' and '5+5=10, so 35+5=?', choosing or writing the answer.
After each prompt, say which ones you just knew and which you had to work out.
Keep finger and make-ten strategy use welcome; the aim is that repeated facts need less effort each time, not beating a clock.
activities.intendedInsight: Automaticity grows from secure strategy plus spaced, untimed retrieval; a fact becomes 'known' when recalling it needs noticeably less effort on later encounters.

activities.title: Playful recall talk: 'how did you know that?'
feedback: Spoken back-and-forth gives retrieval practice but does not by itself build the make-ten strategy or the scaling insight; pair it with the ten-frame and two-scale work.
If a child cannot explain how they knew a fact, return to the relevant model (ten-frame or fact-family triangle) before more recall practice.
activities.rationale: A conversational recall routine offers extra retrieval opportunities and surfaces thinking, complementing the manipulative and the fact-family work without replacing the strategy-building they provide.
learnerActions: Trade quick spoken recall prompts back and forth with a partner or adult (flashcard-style), e.g. one asks 7+8, then 15−8, then 6+4.
For each answer, the asker follows up with 'how did you know that?' — did you just know it, make ten, or use the inverse?
Keep it low-stakes and untimed; celebrate strategy explanations as much as correct answers.
activities.intendedInsight: Verbalising recall and the reasoning behind it reinforces both the facts and the strategies (make-ten, inverse, scaling) that generate them.

constraints: Do not use timed drills or penalise finger/strategy use; automaticity is to grow from a secure make-ten strategy plus spaced, untimed retrieval.

A tap-to-reveal fact-family triangle is a reference scaffold for the inverse relationship; it does not exercise retrieval speed or the scaling derivation, so pair it with practice and the two-scale model.
A fill-in or choice retrieval format can check the derive insight and give recall practice, but a single check does not build automaticity; genuine fluency needs repeated spaced practice over time.
Recognition/choice responses alone do not elicit independent construction of a derived fact; include prompts where the child states or writes the answer and explains the scaling.
A conversational recall routine is a supplementary retrieval vehicle; it does not directly build the make-ten strategy or the scaling insight.

Keep the ones-vs-tens distinction explicit (35+5=40 by adding five ones vs 35+50=85 by adding five tens) so the derived pattern is not applied blindly, and keep scaling to tens (60+40) distinct from using a ones bond inside a number (35+5).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched, and activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit arithmetic check: 6+4=10 and 60+40=100 (six tens + four tens = ten tens) are correct; 5+5=10, 50+50=100, 35+5=40 are correct; 35+50=85 is correct. The original source field left 35+50 only as a 'why not same answer?' probe without stating the value; the correct value 85 has been added so the contrast is taught, not left ambiguous.

Scaling (60+40, 50+50) and using a ones bond inside a larger number (35+5) are kept as two distinct derivation types; the summary and intendedInsight were adjusted so 35+5 is not mislabelled as a scaling case.

The legacy claim that '3D adds nothing' and that number facts 'are not spatial' is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law; it has been dropped rather than asserted. Ten-frames and base-ten rods are themselves spatial supports for these facts.

The legacy framing that a scalable tool 'turns derive into it's the same fact' overstates necessity; a fixed two-scale picture can also show the relationship, so the activity keeps the model affordance without claiming one medium is uniquely required.
The original bead string / Rekenrek representation was not carried into these activities; it remains a valid make-ten manipulative if an implementer wishes to add it.

probeDeeper: You knew 6 + 4 = 10 — how does that help you with 60 + 40?
If 7 + 8 = 15, what subtraction facts do you already know without working them out?
You said 35 + 5 = 40. What about 35 + 50 — same answer? Why not?
Which of those did you just know, and which did you have to work out?
assess.correctAnswer: 15, 7, 10, 100, 40. Fluent: 7+8 and 15−8 recalled (or via make-ten) without counting; 60+40 derived by scaling 6+4 (six tens + four tens = ten tens = 100); 35+5 derived from 5+5=10 → 40.

errorPatterns.pattern: Recall not yet automatic — counts on fingers for 7+8 and 15−8 every time, no faster on a second asking
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT impose timed drills or penalise finger use — automaticity grows from spaced, low-stakes retrieval built on a secure make-ten strategy, not speed pressure. Keep practising strategy and recall without the clock.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct answers but visible counting each time; no drop in effort when the same fact recurs

errorPatterns.pattern: Fails to scale the bond — 'six and four is ten, so sixty and forty is ten' (or 70, or 700)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show 6+4 and 60+40 with the same picture at two scales (counters then ten-rods); name that six tens plus four tens is ten tens, which is 100.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 60+40 the answer ignores that each number is a group of tens; the bond isn't reused at the ten-scale

errorPatterns.pattern: Inverse not linked — answers 7+8=15 instantly but re-counts 15−8 as if it were a separate, unknown fact
errorPatterns.nextMove: Lay out the fact family 7, 8, 15 and show the same three numbers make both facts, so knowing one hands you the other.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: No drop in effort on 15−8 despite having just given 7+8=15

responseLevels.gap: Counts out every fact including 7+8; gives 60+40 as 10 or 70; treats + and − as unrelated.
responseLevels.full: Instant recall of facts to 20 and their inverses, derives 60+40=100 and 35+5=40 by scaling and using known bonds, and explains the link.
responseLevels.partial: Recalls within-20 facts but cannot yet derive the scaled facts, or derives 60+40 only with prompting; the inverse link is emerging.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Rapid-fire, watching for hesitation and finger-counting: ask 7 + 8, then 15 − 8, then 6 + 4; then 'use 6 + 4 to tell me 60 + 40', then 'what's 35 + 5?'. Note which come instantly and which are counted out.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Speed and effort on 7+8 and 15−8 separate recall from calculation. 60+40 separates a child who scales the known bond from one who says 10 or 700. 15−8 separates a child who uses the inverse of 7+8 from one who re-counts despite just answering 7+8.

sources.claim: Year 2 pupils recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently and derive and use related facts up to 100 (e.g. 3+7=10 → 30+70=100); an emphasis on practice at this stage aids fluency, and knowing number bonds establishes addition and subtraction as related operations.
