pedagogy.summary: Probabilities sum to one captures a structural truth: when you list ALL the possible outcomes of a trial, their probabilities must total 1. This lets a child find a missing probability, or the probability of an event NOT happening, by subtracting from 1 (P(not A) = 1 − P(A)) rather than counting every unfavourable outcome. The concept rests on the outcomes being both mutually exclusive and exhaustive — covering the whole of what can happen, with no overlap.
bestPractices: Model the whole of possibility as a bar of length 1 partitioned among the outcomes, so 'the rest of the bar' IS the complement
Establish that the list must be exhaustive (covers everything) and mutually exclusive (no overlaps) before the sum-to-1 argument applies
Teach P(not A) = 1 − P(A) as a shortcut, contrasting it with the slower count-all-the-others method on the same problem
Use spot-the-error tables whose probabilities don't total 1, and ask what must be wrong
Link back to calculating simple probabilities so children see favourable + unfavourable together exhaust the outcomes
keyRepresentations: Unit bar (length 1) partitioned into outcome segments
Complete outcome table with probabilities totalling 1
P(not A) shown as the remaining part of the whole
Spinner whose sectors fill the entire disc
commonMisconceptions: Ignoring the sum-to-1 constraint and assigning a missing outcome an arbitrary or 'equal' value by analogy to another
Treating 'not A' as a single other outcome rather than everything except A, or thinking P(not A) equals P(A)
Adding probabilities of overlapping or non-exhaustive events and still expecting them to total 1
Adding fractions without a common denominator when totalling probabilities

learn.summary: Teach that when you list ALL the possible outcomes of a trial — with no overlaps and nothing left out — their probabilities must total exactly 1. This lets a learner find a missing probability, or the probability of an event NOT happening, by subtracting from 1 (P(not A) = 1 − P(A)) instead of counting every unfavourable outcome. The reasoning only holds when the outcomes are mutually exclusive (no overlap) and exhaustive (cover everything).

activities.title: Fill the unit bar: the leftover IS the missing probability
feedback: If the learner says green = 1/6 'like blue': add the given segments (1/2 + 1/6 = 2/3) and point to the strip still unfilled — the missing value is whatever completes the whole to 1, not a copy of another outcome.
If segments overshoot the bar or leave a gap: these probabilities don't total 1, so the list is impossible — check it covers everything with no overlap.
If 'not red' is named as just blue or just green: highlight the whole rest of the bar — 'not red' means every outcome except red (blue AND green together).
activities.rationale: Partitioning a unit whole makes both sum-to-1 and the complement concrete: the remaining segment is literally the missing or complementary value, and an over- or under-filled bar flags an impossible set. This directly targets the misconception of assigning an 'equal' value by analogy.
sourceClaims: When outcomes are exhaustive (they cover all possibilities) and mutually exclusive, their probabilities total 1; a missing or complementary probability is found by subtracting the others from 1 (e.g. 0.2 + 0.45 + P = 1 gives P = 0.35).
Many probability misconceptions stem from a hazy grasp of the sample space — not representing the full set of outcomes — and from the equiprobability bias of assuming outcomes are equally likely.
learnerActions: Take a bar exactly one unit long that stands for everything that can happen when you draw a counter from a bag of red, blue and green counters.
Set red to one-half of the bar and blue to one-sixth, marking those segments.
Before being told, work out what must fill the remaining strip and state it: green = 1 − (1/2 + 1/6) = 1 − 2/3 = 1/3.
Mark 'P(not red)' by highlighting the entire rest of the bar (blue and green together) and give its value as 1 − P(red) = 1/2.
State in words why green could NOT be a free choice and why 'green must be 1/6 like blue' is wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: The whole of possibility has length 1; once some outcomes are placed, the leftover segment IS the missing probability, and 'not red' is the whole rest of the bar — everything except red — not a single other colour.

activities.title: Spinner that fills the whole disc
feedback: If the prediction ignores the total (e.g. guesses arbitrarily or copies a colour): add the known sectors and show how much of the disc is still empty — that gap is the missing probability.
If the fraction sum is slipped: rewrite with a common denominator (1/2 = 3/6, 1/3 = 2/6, so together 5/6; the rest is 1/6) before subtracting from 1.
activities.rationale: A full disc reinforces exhaustiveness visually and gives a second representation of the same structural truth, supporting learners who grasp area more readily than a linear bar; representing the full set of outcomes directly addresses the sample-space misconception.
sourceClaims: Many probability misconceptions stem from a hazy grasp of the sample space — not representing the full set of outcomes — and from the equiprobability bias of assuming outcomes are equally likely.
learnerActions: Look at (or draw) a spinner whose coloured sectors must fill the entire disc with no gap and no overlap.
Given red = one-half and blue = one-third, predict the remaining sector's probability (yellow) before it is revealed: 1 − (1/2 + 1/3) = 1/6.
Check the revealed sector really is a sixth of the disc.
Tap or mark each sector in turn and track the running total as it reaches exactly 1.
activities.intendedInsight: A spinner's sectors are another model of the whole-equals-1 idea: because the sectors must fill the disc, the last sector's size (and probability) is forced by the others.

activities.title: Complement shortcut versus counting the others
feedback: If the learner thinks P(not A) equals P(A): contrast the two methods — 'not 3' on a die is five outcomes out of six (5/6), clearly not the same as P(3) = 1/6.
If 'not A' is treated as a single other outcome: list what 'not A' actually contains and show it is every outcome except A.
If the learner struggles with the compound case: note that 'red or blue' already covers two of the three exhaustive colours, so green is simply whatever is left of the whole — 1 − 3/4 = 1/4.
activities.rationale: Running the slow count-all-the-others method alongside the subtraction shortcut on the same problem makes the equivalence explicit and justifies why the shortcut works, rather than presenting it as a rule to memorise.
sourceClaims: When outcomes are exhaustive (they cover all possibilities) and mutually exclusive, their probabilities total 1; a missing or complementary probability is found by subtracting the others from 1 (e.g. 0.2 + 0.45 + P = 1 gives P = 0.35).
learnerActions: Calculate P(not rolling a 3) on a fair six-sided die two ways: first by subtracting, 1 − 1/6 = 5/6; then by counting all the other outcomes (1,2,4,5,6) and adding their probabilities (five sixths).
Compare the two methods, note they give the same answer, and that subtracting from 1 is faster when there are many unfavourable outcomes.
For the counter bag, find P(not red) as 1 − P(red) = 1/2 and confirm it matches blue + green (1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2).

Extend to a compound complement: a different bag of red, blue and green counters has P(red or blue) = 3/4; find P(green) = 1 − 3/4 = 1/4, since each counter is exactly one of the three colours and the three colours exhaust the bag.
activities.intendedInsight: P(not A) = 1 − P(A) is a shortcut for 'everything except A', and it equals the sum of all the other outcomes because together they fill the whole; the same subtraction works when the known part is a compound event like 'red or blue'.

activities.title: Spot the impossible table
feedback: If a learner accepts 1/2 + 1/6 + 1/6: show the sum is 5/6, not 1, so one value must change — there is no rule forcing green to match blue.
If the learner cannot add the fractions: use a common denominator (1/2 = 3/6) before totalling, giving 3/6 + 1/6 + 1/6 = 5/6.
activities.rationale: Error-spotting forces the learner to apply the constraint actively rather than restate it, and directly confronts the equiprobability-by-analogy misconception.
sourceClaims: When outcomes are exhaustive (they cover all possibilities) and mutually exclusive, their probabilities total 1; a missing or complementary probability is found by subtracting the others from 1 (e.g. 0.2 + 0.45 + P = 1 gives P = 0.35).
learnerActions: Examine probability tables and decide which are impossible because the values do not total 1 (e.g. a table listing 1/2, 1/6 and 1/6 for three colours).
Add the values, compare the total with 1, and explain exactly what is wrong.
Correct one impossible table by finding the value that would make it total 1.
activities.intendedInsight: A complete list of outcomes that does not total 1 cannot be right. Checking the sum is a necessary test, but it is not enough on its own: a valid probability distribution also needs every value to be between 0 and 1, and the outcomes must be mutually exclusive and exhaustive.

activities.title: When the sum-to-1 argument does NOT apply: overlapping events
feedback: If a learner adds overlapping events' probabilities and is satisfied the total is 1: show that P(even or prime) is really 5/6, because outcome 2 was counted in both 'even' and 'prime' — reaching 1 here is a coincidence, not a valid use of sum-to-1.
If a learner thinks the rule never applies to dice: clarify it does apply to a complete list of distinct single outcomes (1–6), just not to overlapping compound events.
activities.rationale: Making the conditions explicit prevents over-generalising the rule. 'Even' and 'prime' sharing 2 on a die is a documented student error, so naming the overlap condition — and showing that its naive sum equals 1 by coincidence while the true union is 5/6 — guards against it.
sourceClaims: The addition/sum-to-1 argument only holds for mutually exclusive events; applying it to overlapping events (e.g. 'even' and 'prime' on a die, which share 2) is a documented student error.
Many probability misconceptions stem from a hazy grasp of the sample space — not representing the full set of outcomes — and from the equiprobability bias of assuming outcomes are equally likely.
learnerActions: Consider rolling a fair die and the events 'even' and 'prime'. List the outcomes for each: even = {2,4,6}, prime = {2,3,5}.
Notice that 2 belongs to both, so the events overlap and are NOT mutually exclusive.

Add P(even) = 3/6 and P(prime) = 3/6 and notice the total comes to 1 — then find the true chance of 'even or prime': the combined outcomes are {2,3,4,5,6}, which is 5/6, not 1. The naive sum reached 1 only by counting outcome 2 twice.
Explain why adding probabilities of overlapping events double-counts the shared outcome, so the total does not give P(even or prime), even when the arithmetic happens to land on 1.
Contrast with the counter-bag colours, which are mutually exclusive (a counter is exactly one colour) and exhaustive, so there the probabilities genuinely total 1.
activities.intendedInsight: Sum-to-1 and the complement shortcut only hold when the listed events are mutually exclusive and exhaustive; with overlapping events, adding probabilities double-counts shared outcomes, and the total — even if it coincidentally equals 1 — does not represent the combined event.

activities.title: Socratic challenge: do your outcomes cover everything?
feedback: If the learner cannot justify the total: return to the bar or disc model where the whole visibly equals 1.
If the learner asserts equal likelihood by habit: ask what evidence fixes each value — the total constraint, not similarity to another colour.
activities.rationale: Prompting for the conditions and the justification surfaces whether the learner is actually using the constraint and targets the equiprobability bias of assuming outcomes are equally likely; this works best alongside a filled-whole representation rather than in isolation.
sourceClaims: Many probability misconceptions stem from a hazy grasp of the sample space — not representing the full set of outcomes — and from the equiprobability bias of assuming outcomes are equally likely.
learnerActions: Respond to prompts such as 'Do your outcomes cover everything, with no overlap?' and 'What do they add up to?'
Defend or revise a claim like 'so green must be 1/6 too' by appealing to the sum-to-1 constraint.
Explain in your own words why all the outcomes must add to exactly 1 — not more and not less.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the exhaustive-and-mutually-exclusive conditions and the total-equals-1 constraint strengthens reasoning beyond pattern-matching.

constraints: The sum-to-1 argument and P(not A) = 1 − P(A) require the listed outcomes to be mutually exclusive (no overlap) AND exhaustive (cover everything); establish both conditions before applying the rule.
Do not present 'each outcome is equally likely' as a default; the sum-to-1 constraint, not sameness between outcomes, fixes a missing value.

Adding probabilities of overlapping events (e.g. 'even' and 'prime' on a die) double-counts shared outcomes; the resulting total does not represent the combined event even when it coincidentally equals 1 (here P(even)+P(prime)=1 but the true P(even or prime)=5/6). This is a condition failure, not a sum-to-1 counterexample.
Totalling probabilities given as fractions requires a common denominator; a wrong total here is an arithmetic lapse, not a probability misconception, and should be scaffolded separately.

A static tap-to-reveal partitioned bar or disc can show a complete set totalling 1 but does not let the learner test an incomplete or overlapping list; use it as a display scaffold, then move to a task where the learner constructs or corrects a list.

Choosing the impossible table from options can check whether a learner applies the constraint but does not by itself show the learner can independently construct a valid distribution; pair it with a construction task.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Independent re-audit: every fraction sum and outcome set was re-derived — green = 1 − 2/3 = 1/3; spinner yellow = 1 − 5/6 = 1/6; P(not 3) = 5/6 (matches counting 1,2,4,5,6); impossible table 1/2 + 1/6 + 1/6 = 5/6 ≠ 1; compound complement P(green) = 1 − 3/4 = 1/4; overlap P(even)+P(prime) = 3/6 + 3/6 = 1 while the true union {2,3,4,5,6} = 5/6. All consistent, and the overlap activity makes the coincidence explicit rather than claiming the sum fails to reach 1.

The legacy entry rated a 3D interactive 'poor' on the basis that '3D adds nothing'; this ranking is not an established pedagogical law and has been dropped rather than restated as a universal claim. Sum-to-1 is well modelled in 1D/2D, but no claim is made that a 3D medium could add nothing.

The legacy 'possible' static-image and conversation formats are preserved as the tap-to-reveal scaffold and the Socratic activity respectively, with their narrow observable limits placed in constraints rather than asserted as 'cannot teach' claims.
The tempting wrong answer '1/6 — green is one colour, the same as blue' is retained only as a misconception to confront in feedback, never offered as a correct option.

assess.poeTask: Show a spinner divided into unequal sectors you have pre-measured: red is one-half, blue is one-third, yellow is one-sixth. Cover the yellow sector. Say: 'The red part is a half and the blue is a third. Before I uncover the last colour, predict the probability of yellow — and explain how you got it.' A child ignoring sum-to-1 guesses arbitrarily or says 'a third, like blue'; the sum-to-1 reasoner predicts 1 − (1/2 + 1/3) = 1/6. Uncover the sector and check it really is a sixth of the disc. The reason given BEFORE uncovering is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: What is P(not red) for this bag? How did you get it — by adding colours or by taking red from the whole?
If I told you the three probabilities were 1/2, 1/6 and 1/6, what would be wrong with that?
Why do all the outcomes have to add up to exactly 1, and not more or less?
Suppose a bag had red, blue and green but you were told P(red or blue) = 3/4 — what is P(green)?
assess.correctAnswer: P(green) = 1/3. All the outcomes must total 1, so P(green) = 1 − (1/2 + 1/6) = 1 − 2/3 = 1/3. The classmate is wrong: there is no rule that each colour is equally likely — the sum-to-1 constraint, not sameness with blue, fixes the missing value.

errorPatterns.pattern: Ignores the sum-to-1 constraint and assigns the missing outcome an arbitrary or 'equal' value by analogy ('green is 1/6, the same as blue')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Add the given probabilities and show they don't yet reach 1; the missing value is whatever completes the whole, so subtract from 1 rather than copy another outcome
errorPatterns.distractor: 1/6 — green is one colour, the same as blue.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives P(green) = 1/6 or reasons that the colours must be equally likely, without checking the total

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats 'not A' as a single other outcome, or thinks P(not A) equals P(A), rather than everything except A
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show P(not red) as the whole rest of the bar (blue and green together) = 1 − P(red); 'not red' is every outcome except red, not a single one
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a follow-up 'what is P(not red)?' names just one colour, or gives 1/2 as if 'not red' mirrors red

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds the fractions without a common denominator when totalling
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the common-denominator step (1/2 = 3/6, so 3/6 + 1/6 = 4/6); this is an arithmetic lapse, not a probability misconception
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Computes 1/2 + 1/6 as 2/8 or similar, then subtracts wrongly

responseLevels.gap: Assigns the missing probability with no regard to the total; cannot find P(not A) except by trying to list every other outcome, often wrongly
responseLevels.full: Uses sum-to-1 to find the missing probability (1/3) and P(not A) = 1 − P(A), justifies by the outcomes being exhaustive and mutually exclusive, and spots tables that cannot be right because they don't total 1
responseLevels.partial: Knows outcomes should total 1 and can find a missing value in the simplest cases, but copies another outcome's value, mishandles 'not A', or slips on the fraction arithmetic — states the rule without applying it reliably

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A bag holds red, blue and green counters. P(red) = 1/2 and P(blue) = 1/6. A classmate says P(green) must be 1/6 as well, 'because green is just one colour, the same as blue'. Ask the child: is the classmate right? What is P(green), and why? Take the answer, then ask them to explain the reasoning fully (Tier 2).
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The sum-to-1 reasoner subtracts the known probabilities from 1; the surface reasoner copies blue's value or assumes the colours are equal; a complement-confused child mishandles what 'the rest' means. The Tier-2 explanation reveals whether the total-equals-1 constraint was actually used.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Determine the unknown whole number in an addition or subtraction equation relating three whole numbers, with the unknown in any position (8 + ? = 11; 5 = □ − 3; 6 + 6 = □). Ages 6–7, a procedural target resting on the meaning of '=' and the inverse relationship.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y1 'solve one-step problems... including missing number problems such as 7 = □ − 9' and Y2 'solve problems with addition and subtraction... and missing number problems'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.OA.8 'Determine the unknown whole number in an addition or subtraction equation relating three whole numbers. For example, determine the unknown number that makes the equation true in each of 8 + ? = 11, 5 = □ − 3, 6 + 6 = □.'
• Operational details: vary the unknown's POSITION deliberately (result unknown, change unknown, start unknown, answer-on-left) so the child cannot rely on 'add the two numbers I see'. Solve by choosing the inverse move and reading '=' as balance, not by keyword. Bar/part-whole models externalise which quantity is missing.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (age 6) — solves 6 + 6 = □ and 8 + ? = 11. Tier B (age 7) — solves answer-left and subtraction-position forms (5 = □ − 3) correctly. Tier C (age 7+) — chooses the inverse operation for the unknown position and checks the answer by substituting back.
bestPractices: Systematically vary the unknown position (a+b=□, a+□=c, □+b=c, and answer-left forms) so pupils build a flexible method, not a keyword habit.
Represent each equation on a bar / part-whole model first to see which quantity is unknown before calculating.
Teach solving-by-inverse explicitly: convert □ + 9 = 14 into 14 − 9.
Insist on substituting the answer back to check the equation balances.
Use non-standard forms (5 = □ − 3) early to defeat the left-to-right 'answer-comes-next' reading.
keyRepresentations: Bar model / part-whole diagram with the unknown segment shaded
Pan balance with an unknown mass on one side
Empty number line for count-on / inverse jumps
Fact-family triangle to pick the needed operation
Equation cards with the box in varied positions
commonMisconceptions: Adding the two visible numbers regardless of the box's position (8 + ? = 11 → 19).
Reading answer-left forms as backwards (5 = □ − 3 → writes 2, i.e. 5 − 3).
Always subtracting or always adding by keyword rather than by the unknown's role.
Not checking the solution by putting it back into the equation.
Treating '=' as 'work out the total' so a box before '=' is confusing.

learn.summary: Help 6–7 year olds find the unknown whole number in addition/subtraction equations where the unknown appears in any position (8 + ? = 11; 5 = □ − 3; 6 + 6 = □). The target is a flexible method built on reading '=' as 'both sides balance' and choosing the inverse move, not an 'add the two numbers I can see' habit. Vary the unknown's position deliberately (result, change, start, answer-on-left) and insist on checking by substituting the answer back.

activities.title: Balance the unknown with counters
feedback: If the child writes 2 for 5 = □ − 3: show that □ − 3 must equal 5, so starting from 5 we add back the 3 that was taken away, giving □ = 8 (5 + 3 = 8). Try more answer-left forms.
If the child adds the two visible numbers (8 + ? = 11 → 19): point to the bar — 11 is the whole, 8 is one part, the box is the missing part, found by 11 − 8 = 3.
Live true/false balance feedback as counters are added lets the child self-correct before stating an answer.
Praise explicitly when the child checks by substituting back, e.g. 'you put 3 back and 8 + 3 does make 11'.
activities.rationale: A missing-number target is procedural and benefits from repeated practice with immediate feedback across varied positions. A balance or part-whole representation externalises which quantity is missing and makes '=' mean balance rather than 'compute the total', which is intended to address the answer-left misread. Note that a physical two-pan balance shows addition most naturally; the subtraction form 5 = □ − 3 is modelled by filling the box and removing 3, an approximation of the equation. Optional interactions such as a slider, draggable counters, or a live beam that tips make the balancing mechanism concrete; they are helpful examples, not required.
sourceClaims: Varying the position of the unknown (result/change/start unknown) changes problem difficulty, and children commonly add the two visible numbers regardless of position.
1.OA.8 requires determining the unknown whole number in an addition or subtraction equation, with the examples 8 + ? = 11, 5 = □ − 3, 6 + 6 = □.
learnerActions: Set out an equation with a box, e.g. 5 = □ − 3, on a two-pan balance or bar model where one side already shows 5.
Add or remove counters in the box until both sides match: too few and the box side is too light, too many and it tips down.
State the value that makes both sides balance (for 5 = □ − 3 the box must hold 8, because □ − 3 has to equal 5).
Repeat with the unknown in every position: 8 + ? = 11, □ + 6 = 12, 6 + 6 = □.
Check each solved equation by putting the found number back in and confirming both sides match.
activities.intendedInsight: The box holds whatever value makes the two sides equal; '=' means balance, so an answer-on-left form like 5 = □ − 3 is not 'backwards' — it is the same balancing task. One balancing method works for every position.

activities.title: Solve by the inverse, then check
feedback: If the child only guesses and checks repeatedly: prompt the inverse move via the fact family — 'the whole is 11, one part is 8, so the missing part is 11 − 8' — to build efficiency. The concept need not be re-taught here.
If the wrong operation is chosen, return to a bar model to re-identify which quantity is unknown before computing.
Reinforce that the check (substituting back) is part of the method, not an optional extra.
activities.rationale: Choosing the inverse for the unknown's position is the efficient method the standard targets; a fact-family representation helps pupils map position to operation. Trial-and-error can give correct answers but does not build the intended fluency, so prompting the inverse addresses a genuine performance gap.
sourceClaims: 1.OA.8 requires determining the unknown whole number in an addition or subtraction equation, with the examples 8 + ? = 11, 5 = □ − 3, 6 + 6 = □.
Y1–Y2 pupils solve missing-number problems such as 7 = □ − 9 and problems with addition and subtraction.
learnerActions: Given □ + 9 = 14, convert it to the inverse: 14 − 9, and compute □ = 5.
Given 8 + ? = 11, use 11 − 8 = 3 rather than guessing and testing values.
Use a fact-family triangle (whole 14; parts 9 and 5) to pick the operation needed for the unknown's position.
Substitute the answer back and confirm the sentence is true.
Practise a mixed set covering result-unknown, change-unknown, start-unknown and answer-left forms.
activities.intendedInsight: Once you know which quantity is the whole and which is a part, you can go straight to the answer with the inverse operation instead of slow trial-and-error.

activities.title: Explain your move (strategy talk)
feedback: If the child says they 'added the two numbers', probe where the box sits and what '=' requires, then re-model on a bar.
Note that for 5 = □ − 3 and □ − 3 = 5 the answer is the same (□ = 8), because both say the box minus 3 equals 5; discuss why.
Accept any correct reasoning the child can justify; press for the inverse when they rely only on guessing.
activities.rationale: Discussion is a supporting diagnostic that reveals strategy, not just answers; it may complement rather than replace hands-on practice with feedback. It is especially useful for catching the left-to-right 'answer-comes-next' reading, though talk alone does not provide the repeated solving practice a procedural target needs.
sourceClaims: Varying the position of the unknown (result/change/start unknown) changes problem difficulty, and children commonly add the two visible numbers regardless of position.
learnerActions: Solve a varied-position equation aloud, e.g. 5 = □ − 3, then explain how you decided what to do.
Answer probes: 'Which of these could you check with an addition, and how?' and 'What if it were □ − 3 = 5 instead of 5 = □ − 3 — would the answer change?'
Show how you'd check that your answer to 8 + ? = 11 makes the sentence true.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the reasoning surfaces whether a child is using a keyword/positional habit or genuinely reasoning from which quantity is missing.

activities.title: Anchor each position to an operation (worked bar models)
feedback: Use the diagram to correct an added-the-two-numbers error by showing the box is a part, not the whole.
A fixed worked example can anchor the mapping, but pupils still need to then solve fresh items themselves to build fluency.
activities.rationale: A static annotated bar model is a useful anchor for connecting position to operation. On its own it does not provide practice with feedback, so pair it with solving fresh items; it is a scaffold toward the balancing/inverse practice rather than a substitute for it.
learnerActions: Study a worked part-whole/bar diagram for each unknown position (result, change, start, answer-left) with the missing segment highlighted.
Reveal, for each, which operation finds the missing part and why (whole − part = part; part + part = whole).
Then solve matching fresh equations and verify by substitution.
activities.intendedInsight: Each position maps to a specific inverse move once you identify the whole and the parts; the diagram makes that mapping visible.

constraints: Systematically vary the unknown's position (a+b=□, a+□=c, □+b=c, and answer-left forms) so pupils build a flexible method, not a keyword habit.
Introduce non-standard forms (5 = □ − 3) early to counter the left-to-right 'answer-comes-next' reading.
Read '=' as 'both sides balance', not 'work out the total'; a box before '=' is legitimate.
Insist on checking by substituting the found value back into the equation.

Fill-in-the-blank and multiple-choice practice (e.g. choosing the inverse calculation that solves □ + 9 = 14, with '2' as a wrong option for 5 = □ − 3) is useful for spaced retrieval and checking fluency, but recognition/selection does not itself require the child to construct and reason through the balancing move, so pair it with constructed solving.
Worked static diagrams anchor the position→operation mapping but do not themselves provide practice with feedback; follow them with fresh items to solve.
Trial-and-error can produce correct answers but does not build the intended inverse-method fluency; prompt the inverse once accuracy is secure.
Keep the wrong-answer value '2' (from 5 − 3) only as an incorrect option; the correct answer to 5 = □ − 3 is 8.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labels a numeric/non-spatial '3D adds nothing' claim; this comparative-necessity claim is not established by the cited sources and has been dropped rather than asserted. A 2D balance/bar is proposed on its affordances (making balance and the missing part visible), not as the uniquely necessary medium.

Self-audit of arithmetic and logic: 8 + ? = 11 → 3; 5 = □ − 3 → 8 (box minus 3 equals 5, so box = 5 + 3 = 8); 6 + 6 = □ → 12; □ + 9 = 14 → 5; □ + 6 = 12 → 6. The answer-left value '2' (from 5 − 3) is the misconception value and must only appear as a wrong option, never as a correct answer.

Representational caveat: a two-pan balance models addition most directly; the subtraction form 5 = □ − 3 is handled by filling the box and removing 3, which approximates the equation rather than weighing it literally. This is stated in Activity 1 so the scaffold's limit is visible to the teacher.
Noted and preserved the clarification that 5 = □ − 3 and □ − 3 = 5 have the same solution (□ = 8); the source probe asks pupils to consider this.

The standards claims (DfE; CCSS 1.OA.8) attached to Activities 1–2 ground the objective (determining the unknown across positions); they do not empirically establish that the inverse method or the balance representation is more effective than alternatives. Efficacy wording is kept as intended/proposed.

Source 'verified' flags are mixed (DfE true; CCSS and Cognitively Guided Instruction false in the row); confidence was legacy 'high'. No fresh verification performed, so no confidence upgrade is claimed.

probeDeeper: How did you decide what to do for 5 = □ − 3?
Which of these three could you check using an addition, and how?
What if it were □ − 3 = 5 instead of 5 = □ − 3 — would the answer change?
Show me how you'd check that your answer to 8 + ? = 11 makes the sentence true.
assess.correctAnswer: ? = 3; □ = 8; □ = 12. Watch for the child using the inverse (11 − 8 = 3; 5 + 3 = 8) on the first two and adding directly on the last, and for correct handling of the answer-left/subtraction-position form.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds the two visible numbers regardless of the box's position — 8 + ? = 11 becomes 8 + 11 = 19 in the box.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model on a bar: 11 is the whole, 8 a part; the box is the missing part, found by 11 − 8. Re-establish what '=' constrains.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 19 (or otherwise combines the two shown numbers) for a change-unknown item.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the answer-left form as backwards — 5 = □ − 3 solved as 5 − 3 = 2.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Balance model: □ − 3 must weigh the same as 5, so □ = 8; practise more answer-left forms.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 2 in the box for 5 = □ − 3.

errorPatterns.pattern: Solves only by slow trial-and-error / counting, never using the inverse to go straight to the answer.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the concept — prompt the inverse move via the fact-family triangle; build efficiency.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Guesses values and checks repeatedly rather than computing 11 − 8 directly.

responseLevels.gap: Combines the two given numbers regardless of the box's position (e.g. 19, 2); standard result-unknown may be right by habit only.
responseLevels.full: Solves all three fluently, selecting the inverse operation for the unknown's position and verifying by substituting the answer back into the equation.
responseLevels.partial: Solves result-unknown and change-unknown forms but stumbles on the answer-left/subtraction-position item, or solves all only by slow trial-and-error without using the inverse.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Solve these three and write the missing number in each box, working at the table while I watch: 8 + ? = 11; 5 = □ − 3; 6 + 6 = □.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The three items place the unknown differently — change-unknown, start-of-a-subtraction with the answer on the left, and result-unknown. A child running an 'add the two numbers I can see' habit produces tell-tale wrong values (19 for the first, 2 for the second) while getting the standard third right. Watching HOW they solve, not just the answers, separates a flexible inverse method from a keyword habit.

pedagogy.summary: Rearranging a formula ('changing the subject') isolates a chosen variable by applying inverse operations to BOTH sides — the same technique as solving a linear equation, except the 'answer' is an expression in the other letters. The key discipline is doing each inverse operation to the WHOLE side (every term), in the reverse order of the original operations, keeping the formula balanced. It is best taught by first solving the numeric equation, then generalising to letters, using a 'same to both sides' layout, and verifying by substituting numbers back.
bestPractices: Bridge from solving equations: solve 3x + 1 = 10 numerically, then rearrange y = 3x + 1 for x with identical steps — the letters just replace the number.
Apply each inverse operation to the WHOLE side, not one term, and undo operations in reverse order.
Use a balanced 'do the same to both sides' layout so no term is left behind.
Verify a rearrangement by substituting numbers into both the original and the rearranged form.
Handle harder cases explicitly: subject in a denominator, under a root, or appearing twice (multiply up, or collect and factor the subject out).
keyRepresentations: 'Same to both sides' balance layout
Function-machine / inverse-operation chain run backwards
Original vs rearranged formula checked by substitution
y = mx + c rearranged to x = (y − c) / m
commonMisconceptions: Applies the inverse to only part of the side: y = mx + c → x = y − c/m (divides only c by m, not the whole (y − c)).
'Swap side, swap sign' over-generalised to multiplication/division (y = mx → x = y − m).
Sign error when moving a term across (subtracts where it should add or vice versa).
Mishandles the subject when it is in a denominator, under a root, or appears twice.

learn.summary: Rearranging a formula ('changing the subject') isolates a chosen variable by applying inverse operations to BOTH sides — the same technique as solving a linear equation, except the 'answer' is an expression in the other letters. The core discipline is doing each inverse operation to the WHOLE side (every term), undoing operations in the reverse order from how they were built up, and keeping the formula balanced. It can be taught by first solving the numeric equation, then generalising to letters with a 'same to both sides' layout, and checking by substituting numbers into both forms (a check for errors, not a proof of equivalence), while noting any values that cannot be divided by, such as zero.

activities.title: From number to letter: rearrange with identical steps
feedback: If you reach x = (y − 1)/3, check it against the numeric case: the step that undid '+1' becomes '−1' and the step that undid '×3' becomes '÷3' — the structure is identical.

Subtractingc and then dividing bym is a convenient route. Another route can also work if each operation is applied correctly to both complete sides; for example dividing first givesy/m=x+c/m, then subtractingc/m isolatesx, providedm is nonzero.
activities.rationale: Bridging from a solved numeric equation to the lettered formula lets learners reuse an already-secure procedure and see that the 'answer' is now an expression. Both-sides and inverse-operation errors are documented difficulties in solving linear equations, the identical technique underlying changing the subject.
sourceClaims: Errors in applying inverse operations and in failing to do the same operation to the whole of both sides are documented difficulties in solving linear equations — the identical technique that underlies rearranging a formula to change the subject.
learnerActions: Solve the numeric equation 3x + 1 = 10 step by step, writing each inverse operation you apply to both sides (subtract 1, then divide by 3) to reach x = 3.
Now take y = 3x + 1 and rearrange it to make x the subject using the SAME two steps: subtract 1 from both sides, then divide the whole side by 3, reaching x = (y − 1)/3.
Write out, side by side, how each line of the numeric solution matches each line of the algebraic rearrangement.
Finally rearrange the general form y = mx + c for x, undoing +c first, then ×m, to get x = (y − c)/m, provided m ≠ 0.
activities.intendedInsight: Changing the subject is exactly the same balancing technique as solving an equation; the letters simply stand in for the numbers, so the inverse operations and their reverse order are unchanged.

activities.title: Divide the WHOLE side, not one term
feedback: If the shortcut x = y − c/m returned a wrong x (11 − 3/2 = 9.5) while x = (y − c)/m returned 4, that mismatch is the evidence: dividing only the last term leaves the rest of the side untouched.
If both versions seemed to 'work', recompute y first from the original formula, then substitute — the check only discriminates when you start from the original.
activities.rationale: Dividing only one term of a side rather than the whole side is a common change-the-subject error. A contrast between a flawed and a correct rearrangement, confirmed by substitution, makes the whole-side rule concrete. A manipulable layout where a chosen operation is applied to both sides simultaneously, paired with a substitution checker, may make the balance discipline visible, though a worked example on paper can also show it.
sourceClaims: Dividing only one term of a side (rather than the whole side) when changing the subject, and failing to isolate a subject that appears twice or in a denominator, are common rearrangement errors.

Errors in applying inverse operations and in failing to do the same operation to the whole of both sides are documented difficulties in solving linear equations — the identical technique that underlies rearranging a formula to change the subject.
learnerActions: Attempt to make x the subject of y = mx + c. First try the tempting shortcut x = y − c/m and notice it divides only the c-term by m.
Test this shortcut with numbers: let m = 2, c = 3, x = 4. Compute y from the original (y = 2×4 + 3 = 11), then put y = 11 into your shortcut and see what x you get back.
Now bracket the whole side before dividing: x = (y − c)/m. Substitute again (y = 11): x = (11 − 3)/2 = 8/2 = 4, recovering the starting value.
State in your own words why the division has to act on every term of the side at once.
activities.intendedInsight: An inverse operation must be applied to the entire side (every term), not a single term; the numeric check exposes the flawed version because the y-term was left undivided.

activities.title: Undo multiplication by dividing, not by sign-swapping
feedback: If x = y − m appeared, the numeric check (6 instead of 4) flags it: subtraction is the inverse of addition, division is the inverse of multiplication.
If a sign flipped the wrong way moving c, undo +c with −c on both sides and recheck the numbers.
activities.rationale: Over-generalising 'swap side, swap sign' to multiplication/division and making sign errors when moving terms are documented misconceptions. Naming the operation and applying its true inverse, confirmed numerically, targets both directly.
sourceClaims: Errors in applying inverse operations and in failing to do the same operation to the whole of both sides are documented difficulties in solving linear equations — the identical technique that underlies rearranging a formula to change the subject.
learnerActions: Take y = mx and make x the subject. Name the operation attaching m to x — it is multiplication.
Undo multiplication with its true inverse, division, to get x = y/m (provided m ≠ 0). Do NOT write x = y − m.
Check numerically: if m = 2 and x = 4, then y = 8, and y/m = 8/2 = 4 ✓, whereas y − m = 8 − 2 = 6 ✗.
Also practise a sign move: rearrange y = mx + c and confirm you subtract c (not add it) when moving it across, verifying with the same substitution.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Swap side, swap sign' applies only to addition/subtraction; a multiplied factor is undone by dividing, not by changing its sign. Keeping sign direction correct for added terms is a separate discipline.

activities.title: Harder structures: denominators, roots and the subject appearing twice
feedback: If you could not isolate a subject appearing twice, check you collected its terms together first; you cannot divide until it appears only once, as a common factor.

State which denominators must be nonzero before clearing fractions or dividing. When squaring or taking roots, keep the original domain and check for extra or missing solutions in the original formula.
activities.rationale: Failing to multiply up to clear a fraction, or to collect and factor out a subject that appears twice, are documented rearrangement errors. Scaffolding these harder structures distinguishes secure transfer from mechanical single-step undoing.
sourceClaims: Dividing only one term of a side (rather than the whole side) when changing the subject, and failing to isolate a subject that appears twice or in a denominator, are common rearrangement errors.
learnerActions: Warm up with a one-step case: make r the subject of C = 2πr by dividing the whole side by 2π to get r = C/(2π).

Now take a formula where the subject is in the denominator, for example make r the subject of t = k/r. Multiply both sides by r to clear the fraction (tr = k), then divide both sides by t to reach r = k/t.
For a formula where the subject appears twice, collect all terms containing the subject on one side, then factor the subject out before dividing.

Use an explicit example: fory=sqrt(x), withx>=0 andy>=0, square both sides to obtainx=y^2. Forx^2=y, the real solutions arex=plus-or-minus sqrt(y) wheny>=0, unless a stated context restrictsx to one sign. Check the original equation and domain rather than treating roots and powers as unrestricted inverses.
activities.intendedInsight: When the subject is in a denominator, under a root, or appears more than once, extra structural moves — multiplying up, factoring out, or applying root/power inverses — are needed before the ordinary balancing finishes the job.

activities.title: Spot the flawed step, transfer, and verify by substitution
feedback: If your identified error line and the numeric check disagree, recheck both: substitute the same consistent values (worked out from the original formula) into each line in turn. The first line that becomes false shows where an invalid step happened, but lines that agree at a few values are not proven valid.
Completing x = (y − c)/m (not y − c/m) shows you kept the whole numerator together over m.
When making m the subject, note you divide by x this time, not by m — the subject you isolate changes which letter you divide the whole side by.
activities.rationale: Identifying a flawed step and completing a correct form rehearse the procedure and the whole-side rule, while transfer tasks and substitution teach independent verification across formulae. These response formats test the procedure, though error-spotting and fill-in check recognition and completion rather than fully open construction from scratch.
sourceClaims: Errors in applying inverse operations and in failing to do the same operation to the whole of both sides are documented difficulties in solving linear equations — the identical technique that underlies rearranging a formula to change the subject.
learnerActions: Given a fully worked but flawed rearrangement, identify which single line first goes wrong and state the correct inverse operation that should have been used there.
Reconstruct the correct rearrangement from that point, writing each line in order.
Complete a partially written rearranged form such as x = (y − __)/__ for y = mx + c.

Transfer to new formulae: make t the subject of v = u + at (subtract u from both sides, then divide the whole side by a, giving t = (v − u)/a, provided a ≠ 0), and make m the subject of y = mx + c (subtract c, then divide the whole side by x, giving m = (y − c)/x, provided x ≠ 0).

Check every rearrangement you produce: choose several suitable values (avoiding any divisor of zero), compute the output from the original formula first, substitute it into the rearranged formula and confirm you recover the starting value. Remember this check can expose an error but does not prove the two forms are equivalent.
activities.intendedInsight: Substitution is a useful error check: a counterexample shows two forms are not equivalent, while agreement for a few chosen values is not a general proof. Justify the rearrangement through valid balanced operations and the stated domain.

constraints: Learners must actually construct the rearranged formula and carry out the inverse steps themselves; recognising a correct answer or reading a worked example does not demonstrate independent rearrangement.
A fixed worked inverse-operation chain can show the method but does not let the learner perform the balanced steps or catch a left-behind term; use it as a reference, not as the main practice.
Error-spotting and fill-in-the-blank tasks check recognition and completion; pair them with at least one rearrangement built from scratch to evidence full competence.

Use substitution with several suitable values to look for errors, but justify equivalence by valid algebraic operations. Agreement at one value does not prove a formula identity, and division or root operations require domain conditions.

When the subject is in a denominator, under a root, or appears twice, require the extra structural step (multiply up, apply root/power inverse, or collect and factor) rather than treating these as routine single inverse steps.
The substitution check only discriminates if the learner computes the known output from the original formula first, then substitutes it into the rearranged form.

State each harder-case formula and its restrictions. Forx=(y-c)/m requirem!=0; forr=k/t obtained fromt=k/r require the originalr!=0 andt!=0 for this rearranged form; for t=(v-u)/a requirea!=0; form=(y-c)/x requirex!=0. Handle excluded zero cases separately. Root/power examples must state domains and any sign choices.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified this session. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and no claim of empirical testing of these specific tasks is made.
One source claim (dividing only one term; subject appearing twice/in a denominator) is marked verified:false in the row ('not fetched this session'); treat its citation as legacy and unconfirmed.

Self-audit arithmetic checks pass: for m=2, c=3, x=4, original y = 2×4+3 = 11, and (11−3)/2 = 4 ✓; r = C/(2π) from C = 2πr ✓; t = k/r gives r = k/t ✓; v = u + at gives t = (v − u)/a ✓; y = mx gives x = y/m ✓. The flawed shortcut x = y − c/m with y=11 gives 11 − 3/2 = 9.5 ≠ 4, correctly exposing the error.

Softened the row's framing that an open dialogue 'cannot rehearse' the manipulation and that symbolic work 'has no spatial dimension': these are narrow affordance observations, not established universal limits; dialogue can still support reasoning about the steps even if it is less suited to rehearsing full written manipulation.
The transfer examples v = u + at and 'make m the subject of y = mx + c' were drawn from the row's assessment probes and reinstated to preserve concrete examples.

The KS3 curriculum claim was removed from the sourceClaims of the bridging and harder-structures activities because it supports only the topic/objective, not those activities' specific teaching principles; the objective remains represented in the summary and learnerActions.

probeDeeper: Substitute m = 2, c = 3, x = 4 into the original to get y, then into your rearranged formula — do you get x = 4 back?
In y = mx + c, why can't we just write x = y − c/m? What is m attached to?
Now make m the subject of the same formula — is it harder or easier, and why?
If the formula were v = u + at, how would you make t the subject?
assess.correctAnswer: (a) x = (y − c)/m — subtract c from BOTH sides, then divide the WHOLE side by m. (b) r = C/(2π). Check: y = 2×4 + 3 = 11; x = (11 − 3)/2 = 8/2 = 4 ✓.

errorPatterns.pattern: Applies the inverse to only part of the side — writes x = y − c/m, dividing only the last term by m instead of the whole (y − c)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Bracket the whole side before dividing: (y − c) ÷ m; the numeric check fails on the flawed version, forcing the correction.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The rearranged form has m under only the c-term; the numeric check returns the wrong x.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Swap side, swap sign' over-generalised — moves a MULTIPLIED term by changing its sign (y = mx → x = y − m) instead of dividing
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name the operation attaching m to x (multiplication) and undo it with its true inverse (division), not a sign change.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A factor is subtracted rather than divided when moved across.

errorPatterns.pattern: Sign error moving a term — y = mx + c → x = (y + c)/m, adding c instead of subtracting it
errorPatterns.nextMove: Undo +c with −c on both sides and confirm with the substitution check.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The constant's sign is wrong in the rearranged form; the numeric check is off by 2c/m.

errorPatterns.pattern: Mishandles the subject when it is in a denominator or appears twice — fails to multiply up to clear the fraction or to factor the subject out
errorPatterns.nextMove: Multiply through to clear the denominator, or collect the subject's terms and factor it out; scaffold the harder structure.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Given a formula with the subject in a denominator or on both sides, the child cannot isolate it and abandons or mis-cancels.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot isolate the variable; moves terms by changing signs indiscriminately or leaves terms undivided.
responseLevels.full: Makes the subject by undoing operations in reverse order applied to the whole side, verifies by substitution, and handles a harder case (subject in a denominator or appearing twice) — transferring the balanced-inverse method to a new formula.
responseLevels.partial: Rearranges one-step formulae (C = 2πr) correctly, but on a two-step formula divides only part of the side or slips a sign — executes single inverse steps without keeping the whole side balanced.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are two formulae. (a) Make x the subject of y = mx + c. (b) Make r the subject of C = 2πr. Then check your answer to (a) with numbers: let m = 2, c = 3 and x = 4 — work out y, then put it into your rearranged formula and see whether you get x = 4 back.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Part (a) exposes whether the child divides the WHOLE side by m or only the c-term (the y = mx + c → x = y − c/m error); part (b) tests one clean inverse pair; the substitution check reveals whether they can self-verify. Watching the steps, not asking about the method, is what shows the procedure.

pedagogy.summary: At 10-11, the capstone, precision covers the vocabulary of ratio, proportion, algebra, volume, coordinate geometry and circle parts, plus algebraic notation and order of operations. Two distinctions are load-bearing: the parts of a circle (radius is centre-to-circumference, diameter is all the way across = twice the radius, circumference is the distance around), and the difference between an expression, an equation and a formula (an expression has no equals sign; an equation asserts two things are equal; a formula is a general rule relating quantities). Following EEF, pupils should read expressions as descriptions of relationships, not just instructions to calculate, and use precise terms that reflect structure.
bestPractices: Sort algebraic objects into expression / equation / formula by their defining feature — the presence and role of '=' — and read expressions as relationships, not just 'work it out' (EEF; CCSS)
Label a circle so radius, diameter and circumference attach to features, and establish diameter = 2 × radius
Match volume units to the quantity (cm³ fills space) and keep them distinct from area (cm²)
Rephrase informal responses into precise mathematical language, choosing the formal register (EEF; the cross-curricular formal-vocabulary link)
Test definitions with non-examples — 'is 3x + 5 an equation?' — to sharpen the boundaries (EEF)
keyRepresentations: A labelled circle (radius, diameter, circumference) with diameter = 2r shown
Sorting cards: expression (3x+5) vs equation (3x+5=11) vs formula (V=l×w×h)
Unit-cube model for volume (cm³)
Ratio/proportion notation (a : b) with a bar or double number line
Order-of-operations worked expressions read as relationships
commonMisconceptions: Conflates expression, equation and formula — calls 3x + 5 an equation, or uses the terms interchangeably
Confuses circle parts — says the diameter is centre-to-edge (that is the radius), or calls the circumference the 'edge'/'side'
Omits the volume unit or uses the wrong dimension — '60' or '60 cm²' instead of '60 cm³'
Reads an algebraic expression only as an instruction to calculate rather than a relationship, mishandling order of operations

learn.summary: For ages 10-11, this capstone strand builds precise mathematical vocabulary and notation: distinguishing an expression (no equals sign; it can be evaluated or simplified but not solved) from an equation (asserts two things are equal; an equation such as 3x + 5 = 11 can be solved) from a formula (a special kind of equation that states a general rule relating quantities); naming circle parts correctly (radius = centre to circumference, diameter = all the way across through the centre = 2 × radius, circumference = the distance around); and attaching the right units to a quantity (volume in cm³, distinct from area in cm²). Following EEF, learners should read expressions as descriptions of relationships, not just instructions to calculate, and use terms that reflect mathematical structure.

activities.title: Sort algebra cards by the role of '='
feedback: If a learner labels '3x + 5' an equation, ask them to point to the equals sign — there is none, so it is an expression you can evaluate (for a given x) or simplify, but not solve.
If a learner cannot separate equation from formula, contrast '3x + 5 = 11' (a claim true for one value of x, which you solve) with 'V = l × w × h' (a general rule true for any box, which you use).
Praise a learner who names the defining feature spontaneously rather than guessing from the look of the symbols.
If a learner reads '3x + 5' only as 'multiply x by 3 and add 5', prompt them to also describe it as a relationship: '5 more than three times a number'.
activities.rationale: Sorting and justifying by a single defining feature sharpens the boundary between easily-confused terms, and reading expressions as relationships rather than instructions follows EEF guidance. An optional interactive sorting tool can highlight or colour the '=' in the last two cards as the learner sorts, making the defining feature visible, but the sorting and verbal justification carry the learning.
sourceClaims: Teachers should rephrase vague responses into language reflecting mathematical structure and encourage pupils to read numerical and algebraic expressions as descriptions of relationships rather than merely instructions to calculate
Proficient students communicate precisely with clear definitions, state the meaning of the symbols they use, and specify units of measure
learnerActions: Sort three cards — '3x + 5', '3x + 5 = 11', 'V = l × w × h' — into three bins labelled expression, equation and formula.

For each card, say out loud what makes it belong there: Does it have an equals sign? If it does, is it a statement of equality that is true only for particular values of an unknown (one you solve), or a general rule relating quantities that holds for any values (a formula, which is a special kind of equation)?

Explain the consequence: an expression can be evaluated (worked out once you know the value of the letter) or simplified, but not solved, while an equation like 3x + 5 = 11 can be solved (find the unknown that makes it true).
Test the boundary with a non-example question such as 'Is 3x + 5 an equation? Why not?' and 'What single change would turn 3x + 5 into an equation?'
activities.intendedInsight: The presence and role of '=' is the defining feature: an expression has none, an equation like 3x + 5 = 11 asserts equality for a particular unknown value (and can be solved), and a formula is a special kind of equation that states a general rule relating quantities for any values. The precise term changes what you are allowed to do with the object.

activities.title: Build the radius–diameter–circumference relationship on a circle
feedback: If a learner says the diameter is centre-to-edge, name that as the radius and have them re-mark the diameter all the way across through the centre.
If a learner calls the circumference the 'edge' or 'side', supply the precise term and tie it to 'the distance all the way around'.
Reinforce when a learner states diameter = 2 × radius and can explain why confusing the two matters.
activities.rationale: Attaching precise terms to features of a manipulated or drawn circle makes the relationship felt rather than memorised. An optional live diagram where dragging the radius auto-draws the diameter at twice its length and traces the circumference makes the 2× relationship dynamic; a drawn or physical circle achieves the same with manual marking.
sourceClaims: Proficient students communicate precisely with clear definitions, state the meaning of the symbols they use, and specify units of measure
learnerActions: On a labelled circle, point to and name the radius, the diameter and the circumference in your own words.
State how the radius and diameter are related and justify it: the diameter goes all the way across through the centre and is exactly twice the radius.
Using a drawn or physical circle, mark a radius, then mark the diameter as two radii end-to-end through the centre, then trace the full distance around for the circumference.

Catch a deliberate error: respond to 'the diameter is the distance from the centre to the edge' by correcting it (that is the radius) and explaining what difference the correction makes to any calculation.
activities.intendedInsight: Radius, diameter and circumference name distinct features that stand in a fixed relationship (diameter = 2 × radius), so the words are not interchangeable; swapping radius and diameter gives a wrong answer. For a length such as the circumference it halves or doubles the answer, and for an area it multiplies or divides the answer by 4.

activities.title: Attach the right unit to volume
feedback: If a learner writes just '60', ask '60 what?' and have them add the unit.
If a learner writes '60 cm²' for a volume, point out that cm² measures area (a surface); filling space needs cm³.
Confirm when a learner both gives the correct cubic unit and can say why space-filling means cubic.
activities.rationale: Grounding 'cubed' in a unit-cube model connects the exponent to physically filling space, and insisting on the unit follows the precision standard. The spatial unit-cube model is the one genuinely three-dimensional strand here.
sourceClaims: Proficient students communicate precisely with clear definitions, state the meaning of the symbols they use, and specify units of measure
learnerActions: Work out the volume of a box (e.g. with a unit-cube model, counting how many 1 cm cubes fill it) and write the answer with its unit.
State why the unit is cm³ and not cm² or a bare number: volume fills space in three dimensions, so it is counted in cubic units.
Contrast a volume (cm³) with an area (cm²) for the same figure, saying what each measures.
activities.intendedInsight: A quantity is incomplete without its unit, and the unit must match the dimension: volume fills space so it is measured in cubic units (cm³), distinct from area's square units (cm²).

activities.title: Expert dialogue: justify the precise term
feedback: When a learner slips (expression called an equation, radius called diameter), the questioner asks them to justify, prompting self-correction rather than supplying the answer.
Rephrase a learner's informal response ('the line across') into the formal register ('the diameter') and ask them to reuse it.
activities.rationale: Dialogue that demands justification surfaces the reasoning behind the vocabulary, which sorting alone may not elicit. Rephrasing informal talk into the formal register follows EEF guidance. This complements, rather than replaces, hands-on sorting and manipulation.
sourceClaims: Teachers should rephrase vague responses into language reflecting mathematical structure and encourage pupils to read numerical and algebraic expressions as descriptions of relationships rather than merely instructions to calculate
learnerActions: Respond to an in-role questioner who insists on the exact term: 'Is that an expression or an equation? What makes it one?'
When you use loose language, restate it in precise mathematical terms when asked.
Defend your classification or your circle-part naming with the defining feature, not just the answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to name the defining reason — the role of the equals sign, centre-to-edge versus all-the-way-across — is what distinguishes precise understanding from loose usage.

constraints: A sort-and-label task can check whether a learner picks the right category or label efficiently, but on its own it does not surface the reasoning that defines the terms; pair it with a task or dialogue that asks 'what makes it one?'.
A static labelled diagram or definition list is a useful reference, but it does not let the learner sort, manipulate or justify, so it cannot by itself build the distinctions.
Recognition-only responses (choosing the right label) do not elicit independent construction of a definition; include tasks where the learner states the defining feature in their own words.

A physical unit-cube model or paper circle has real thickness and can be handled; treat it as an approximation to the idealised mathematical figure (which has exact faces/edges or zero thickness) when discussing area versus volume.

Optional interactive features (auto-drawing the diameter at 2× the radius, highlighting the '=', tracing the circumference) make the mechanism concrete but are not mandatory; a drawn or physical circle and card sorting work equally well.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit: diameter = 2 × radius, centre-to-circumference radius, circumference as distance around, and volume in cm³ versus area in cm² are all internally consistent and correct as stated in the source. No arithmetic or conceptual errors were found to correct.

The original source asserted that a static image 'cannot' teach and that a quiz 'cannot surface the reasoning'; these have been softened to narrowly scoped limits (reference-only vs. construction-eliciting) rather than universal claims about media.

The source's '60 cm³' volume task does not specify the box dimensions; the rewritten activity frames it generically (count unit cubes) and uses 60 only to illustrate bare-number versus unit, so no unverified arithmetic is asserted.

Residual catalog/product vocabulary ('bench', 'screener') is absent from the final learner-facing guidance; a fresh scan confirms no artefactType labels, fit rankings, 'recommended' or quiz-step terms remain.

probeDeeper: Is 3x + 5 an expression, an equation or a formula? What would make it an equation?
Point to the radius, the diameter and the circumference — how are the radius and diameter related?
Is V = l × w × h an expression, equation or formula? Why?
You wrote the volume as 60 — 60 what? Why cm³ and not cm²?
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for '3x + 5 is an EXPRESSION' (it has no equals sign; an equation asserts equality like 3x+5=11, and a formula is a general rule like V=l×w×h) and 'the distance from the centre to the edge is the RADIUS; the diameter goes all the way across through the centre and is twice the radius'; and for why it matters (you can solve an equation but only evaluate an expression; confusing radius and diameter halves or doubles the answer). Surfaced for discussion, not scored.

errorPatterns.pattern: Conflates expression, equation and formula — calls 3x + 5 an equation, or uses the terms interchangeably
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort examples by the presence and role of '=' and read expressions as relationships not instructions; an equation asserts equality, a formula is a general rule. Reteach expressing problems algebraically.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels an expression an equation, or cannot say what distinguishes the three

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses circle parts — says the diameter is centre-to-edge (the radius), or calls the circumference the 'edge/side'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Label a circle: radius = centre to circumference, diameter = across through the centre = 2×radius, circumference = the distance around. Reteach naming parts of a circle.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Defines the diameter as the radius, or lacks the term circumference

errorPatterns.pattern: Omits the volume unit or uses the wrong dimension — '60' or '60 cm²' for a volume
errorPatterns.nextMove: Volume fills space, so it is measured in cubic units (cm³); contrast with area's cm². Reteach in place.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives a volume with no unit or a square unit

responseLevels.gap: Conflates expression/equation/formula, swaps circle parts, and drops or wrong-dimensions the volume unit.
responseLevels.full: Unprompted, distinguishes expression, equation and formula and the circle parts with defining reasons, uses cm³ correctly, and explains why the precise term changes what you can do or compute.
responseLevels.partial: When prompted, gives a distinguishing feature (the equals sign; centre-to-edge) but not reliably, or defines one pair while muddling the other.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A child said '3x + 5 is an equation', and 'the diameter is the distance from the centre to the edge of a circle.' Are these right? Fix them, and explain the difference each correction makes.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A precise child fixes both and names the defining feature — the equals sign, and centre-to-edge versus all-the-way-across; a loose child accepts them. The slips are invisible to numerical work elsewhere, so only attention to the vocabulary and its meaning separates the children.
