pedagogy.summary: Here the informal angle — a corner, a turn, an opening — is formalised as a geometric object: two rays (arms) sharing a common endpoint, the vertex, with size given by the amount of rotation between the arms. The central challenge (CCSS Progressions; Mitchelmore & White) is that children hold SEPARATE angle concepts for different physical situations — the turn of a door, the corner of a shape, the opening of scissors, the slope of a ramp, a bend in a road — and must abstract the common structure (two rays and a vertex) across all of them, including cases where one arm is only implicit (the horizontal in a slope).
bestPractices: Collect angles from many situations — open door, clock hands, scissors, a ramp, a bent straw, shape corners — and draw out what they share: two arms meeting at a point (varied situations → abstraction).
Name the parts explicitly and consistently: the vertex (the meeting point) and the arms/rays, marking the angle with an arc at the vertex.
Make the arms genuine rays — stress they can be extended without changing the angle — to pre-empt the arm-length trap.
Surface implicit arms: in a slope, or a 'how high is the tree' sighting, one ray is the horizontal — draw it in.
Contrast a static corner with the turn that opens it, so both the figure and rotation conceptions attach to the same object.
keyRepresentations: Two rays hinged at a vertex, with vertex and arms labelled and an arc marking the angle
A gallery of real situations (door, clock, scissors, ramp, road bend) each reduced to vertex + two arms
The clock face — hands as two rays from the centre — as a canonical everyday angle
A dynamic hinge showing the arms as extendable rays
commonMisconceptions: Holds separate, unconnected angle ideas for different contexts — a 'turn' and a 'corner' are treated as different things, with no single general concept
Judges or defines angle size by arm length or the distance between the arm-ends rather than the opening (persists even for doors and hinges)
Thinks the arms must be a fixed length, or that lengthening a ray changes the angle (arms are unbounded rays)
Only recognises an angle when both arms are drawn in a standard upright orientation — misses angles that are rotated or have an implicit arm (a slope)

learn.summary: Learners formalise the everyday idea of an angle (a corner, a turn, an opening) as a geometric object: two rays (arms) sharing a common endpoint (the vertex), with size given by the amount of rotation or opening between the arms. The central challenge is that children hold SEPARATE angle ideas for different physical situations — the turn of a door, the corner of a shape, the opening of scissors, the slope of a ramp, a bend in a road — and must abstract the shared structure (two rays and a vertex) across all of them, including cases where one arm is only implicit (the horizontal in a slope or a sighting line). Suitable for roughly ages 9–10.

activities.title: From many situations to one skeleton
feedback: If a learner says 'that's a corner, not an angle' or 'a door opening isn't an angle', lay the different situations side by side and strip each to a vertex and two arms, naming the shared structure they all have.
If a learner only accepts an angle drawn upright, rotate the examples off the upright and confirm the vertex and arms are still there.
If a learner cannot find the ramp's angle, point out that only the slope line is drawn and draw in the horizontal arm with them so both arms are visible.
Praise locating the vertex correctly and reducing a real object to the two-ray diagram, not just naming the object.
activities.rationale: Exposure to varied situations (turns, slopes, bends, corners, openings), including implicit-arm cases, is the recommended route to help children abstract 'angle' as two rays and a vertex rather than hold separate context-bound ideas. A tap-to-reveal interactive scene where each object highlights its vertex and arms and then drills down to the identical two-ray-and-arc diagram can make the abstraction moment concrete, but the same work can be done with physical objects and drawn diagrams.
sourceClaims: Recognize angles as geometric shapes formed wherever two rays share a common endpoint; the size of an angle is the amount of rotation between the two rays that form it.

Students in the early and elementary grades often form separate concepts of angles as figures and as turns, and hold separate notions for different turn contexts (e.g. a fan vs a hinge) and various bends; the remedy is exposure to varied situations (turns, slopes, bends, corners, openings), including cases where an arm is implicit (the horizontal in a slope or sighting), so they abstract angles as two rays and a vertex. Many students wrongly judge angle size by arm length, distance between endpoints, or area, and some think a right angle must 'point to the right' or be in a standard orientation.
learnerActions: Gather or look at pictures of angles in many different situations: an open door, clock hands, open scissors, a propped ramp, a bent straw, a bend in a road, and the corner of a shape.
For each one, mark where the two arms are and put a dot on the vertex (the meeting point), drawing an arc at the vertex to show the angle.
Strip each situation down to the SAME bare diagram — two rays meeting at a point with an arc — and lay these stripped diagrams side by side.
Say in your own words what the door, the clock and the scissors all share.
For the ramp, draw in the implicit second arm (the horizontal ground line) so the angle has both arms.
activities.intendedInsight: A door, a clock and a pair of scissors are all the same underlying thing — two arms meeting at a point — so an angle is that shared skeleton, not any one particular picture. Some situations (slopes, sightings) have one arm that must be drawn in.

activities.title: The arms are rays: lengthening does not change the angle
feedback: If a learner predicts 'it gets bigger' when arms are lengthened, show the extended arms lying along the same two lines — it is the same angle — and return to the opening as the measure of size. The reason stated first is the diagnostic part.
If a learner cites arm length or the distance between arm-ends when comparing, extend a ray to show the angle is unchanged, and redirect attention to the opening/turn.
Affirm reasoning that refers to the opening or turn between the arms rather than to arm length.
activities.rationale: Children commonly judge identical angles as unequal when the arms differ in length and think lengthening a ray changes the angle. A predict–then–test task targets this directly, and a live hinge with extendable arms and a fixed arc can make the ray-invariance visible. The prediction and the reason given first are the diagnostic parts; the hands-on resolution follows.
sourceClaims: An angle has two conceptions — static (a corner / two adjoining lines) and dynamic (an amount of turn) — which must be brought together; children judge identical angles as unequal when the arms differ in length.

Students in the early and elementary grades often form separate concepts of angles as figures and as turns, and hold separate notions for different turn contexts (e.g. a fan vs a hinge) and various bends; the remedy is exposure to varied situations (turns, slopes, bends, corners, openings), including cases where an arm is implicit (the horizontal in a slope or sighting), so they abstract angles as two rays and a vertex. Many students wrongly judge angle size by arm length, distance between endpoints, or area, and some think a right angle must 'point to the right' or be in a standard orientation.
learnerActions: Draw an angle, then predict (before doing anything) what will happen to the angle if you extend both arms to twice their length, and say why.
Now extend both arms — or slide an identical angle with longer arms on top, with the vertices aligned — and compare.
Describe what you notice: the longer arms lie along the same two lines, so the opening is unchanged.
Compare two angles that have the same opening but different arm lengths and decide whether they are equal, giving your reason.
activities.intendedInsight: The arms of an angle are rays that can be extended without changing the angle; the size is the opening (the turn) between the arms, not how long the arms are or how far apart the arm-ends sit.

activities.title: Connecting the corner and the turn
feedback: If a learner treats the corner and the turn as unrelated, slow down the opening of the hinge so they can see the same two arms both at rest and sweeping.
If a learner struggles to find the vertex on the clock, point to the centre where both hands begin and confirm the hands are the two arms.
Encourage describing the clock angle as the turn between the hands, linking it back to the corner view.
activities.rationale: Both the figure (static) and rotation (dynamic) conceptions need to attach to the same object; contrasting a static corner with the turn that opens it supports this. The clock face is a canonical everyday angle with the vertex at the centre and hands as rays. A live hinge can show both views on one object, but physical objects such as doors and scissors also serve.
sourceClaims: An angle has two conceptions — static (a corner / two adjoining lines) and dynamic (an amount of turn) — which must be brought together; children judge identical angles as unequal when the arms differ in length.
Recognize angles as geometric shapes formed wherever two rays share a common endpoint; the size of an angle is the amount of rotation between the two rays that form it.
learnerActions: Take one object, such as an open door or a pair of scissors, and look at it as a static corner: two lines meeting at a point.
Now open and close it, watching the arms sweep through a turn, and notice the amount of turn is the size of the angle.
Explain how the still corner and the turning action describe the same angle on the same object.
Use a clock face: point to the vertex (the centre) and name the two hands as the two arms, then describe the angle as the turn between them.
activities.intendedInsight: An angle has two connected conceptions — a static corner (two arms at a vertex) and a dynamic turn (an amount of rotation) — and these describe the same geometric object.

activities.title: Is it an angle? Including rotated and implicit-arm cases
feedback: If a learner misses the rotated angle, rotate it back to upright, confirm it is an angle, then rotate it again so they see the angle is unchanged by orientation.
If a learner denies the ramp has an angle because only one line is drawn, draw in the horizontal arm with them.
If a learner claims the parallel lines make an angle, trace both lines and show they never meet, so there is no vertex.
Confirm a full explanation that names two rays, a shared vertex, and the opening/turn between them.
activities.rationale: Including a rotated angle, a ramp with an implicit arm, and a non-angle separates a child who has abstracted the general two-ray concept from one who only recognises a prototypical drawn angle. Surfacing implicit arms and rejecting non-angles are key to the full understanding. This task also doubles as a diagnostic: the reason given reveals whether 'angle' means the structure or just a familiar picture.
sourceClaims: Students in the early and elementary grades often form separate concepts of angles as figures and as turns, and hold separate notions for different turn contexts (e.g. a fan vs a hinge) and various bends; the remedy is exposure to varied situations (turns, slopes, bends, corners, openings), including cases where an arm is implicit (the horizontal in a slope or sighting), so they abstract angles as two rays and a vertex. Many students wrongly judge angle size by arm length, distance between endpoints, or area, and some think a right angle must 'point to the right' or be in a standard orientation.
Recognize angles as geometric shapes formed wherever two rays share a common endpoint; the size of an angle is the amount of rotation between the two rays that form it.
learnerActions: Look at a set of pictures: a clearly drawn angle, an angle rotated off the upright, a ramp with only its slope line drawn, and two parallel lines that never meet.
For each picture, decide whether there is an angle and, if so, mark the vertex.
For the ramp, draw in the implicit horizontal arm and decide whether there is an angle there.
Say why the parallel lines do NOT form an angle (they never meet, so there is no vertex).
Explain in your own words what makes something an angle.
activities.intendedInsight: An angle is two rays meeting at a vertex, recognisable even when rotated or when one arm is implicit; two lines that never meet do not form an angle because there is no shared vertex.

constraints: Name the parts explicitly and consistently: the vertex (the meeting point) and the arms/rays, marking the angle with an arc at the vertex.
Stress that the arms are genuine rays that can be extended without changing the angle, to pre-empt the arm-length trap.
Always surface implicit arms: in a slope or a sighting ('how high is the tree'), one ray is the horizontal — draw it in.
Use at least one rotated angle and at least one non-angle (two lines that never meet) so recognition is not limited to the prototypical upright drawing.

Matching or multiple-choice tasks (e.g. identifying the vertex, matching situations to angle diagrams) can check recognition, but a recognition-only response does not by itself elicit the cross-context abstraction or the learner's spoken/written reason; include at least one task where the learner states why.
Paper cut-outs or physical hinges have slight thickness and are approximations; treat them as models of the ideal two-ray figure and keep attention on the vertex and opening rather than the material.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row, without fresh source verification; the sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and the cited claims support the underlying teaching principles, not the specific tasks.

The original row rated a 3D interactive scene 'possible' with the remark that '3D adds realism without conceptual depth'; this comparative claim is not established by the sources and has been omitted rather than asserted. A spatial scene could still help learners spot angles in their environment.

The original rated in-role dialogue 'poor', asserting it 'cannot deliver the see-the-shared-skeleton moment'. This universal claim is not established by the sources; it is reframed here as the narrower observable point that the core work is visual/constructive and that talk alone does not by itself require the learner to mark vertices and arms.

The predict-then-test prediction 'it gets bigger' is the expected misconception, not a correct answer; it is used as a diagnostic to be confronted, and the feedback corrects it. No arithmetic, fraction, or force/motion claims were present to audit.

Activity 2 re-uses the varied-situations abstraction claim; it is retained only because that claim explicitly names the arm-length/endpoint-distance misconception the activity targets, not for its abstraction content.

assess.poeTask: Draw an angle, then ask the child to predict what happens to the angle if you extend both arms to twice their length, and why, before doing it. Then extend them (or slide an identical angle with longer arms on top, vertex aligned). A child who predicts 'it gets bigger' confronts the arms lying along the same two lines — the same angle. The reason stated first is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: This ramp only has the slope drawn. Where is the other arm of the angle — is there still an angle here?
If I make the arms of this angle twice as long, is it still the same angle? Why?
Here are two lines that never meet. Is there an angle? Why not?
The clock hands make an angle — point to the vertex. What are the two arms?
assess.correctAnswer: Identifies angles including the rotated one and the ramp (recognising the implicit horizontal as the second arm), marks the vertex where the two rays meet, rejects the parallel-lines non-angle, and justifies that an angle is two rays/arms meeting at a point (a vertex) with its size the turn or opening between them.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats a turn, a corner and an opening as different things rather than one general angle ('that's a corner, not an angle', or 'a door opening isn't an angle')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Lay the different situations side by side and strip each to a vertex and two arms, naming the shared structure they all have.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Accepts the plainly drawn angle but denies the ramp or the door/turn is 'an angle'

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges the angle by arm length or the distance between the arm-ends, or thinks extending a ray changes the angle ('the longer one is more of an angle')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Extend a ray and show the angle is unchanged — the arms are rays (unbounded); return to opening/turn as the size.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When comparing or describing, cites arm length; claims a longer-armed angle is bigger, or that lengthening an arm changes it

errorPatterns.pattern: Only recognises an angle when both arms are drawn in a standard upright orientation — misses rotated angles or those with an implicit arm (a slope)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rotate examples off the upright and draw in the implicit horizontal arm on slopes and sightings.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Misses the rotated angle or denies the ramp has an angle because only one line is drawn

responseLevels.gap: Recognises only a prototypical drawn angle; treats turns, corners and openings as different things; cannot locate the vertex reliably, and misses rotated or implicit-arm cases.
responseLevels.full: Defines an angle as two rays sharing a vertex with size given by the rotation between them, and recognises that structure across new situations — including where an arm is implicit or the figure is rotated — while rejecting non-angles (relational).
responseLevels.partial: Identifies the vertex and arms in standard drawn angles and names several real examples, but as separate cases — does not articulate the common two-rays-at-a-vertex structure, and stumbles on the ramp (implicit arm) or a rotated figure (multistructural).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Lay out several pictures: a clearly drawn angle, a rotated angle, a ramp with only its slope line drawn, and a non-angle (two parallel lines that never meet). Say: 'Point to the angle in each picture and mark its vertex — and for the ramp, tell me if there's an angle there at all.' Then: 'Explain what makes something an angle.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Including a rotated angle, a ramp with an implicit arm, and a non-angle separates a child who has abstracted the general two-ray concept from one who only recognises a prototypical drawn angle. The tier-2 reason reveals whether 'angle' means the two-rays-at-a-vertex structure or just a familiar picture.

pedagogy.summary: Children convert between miles and kilometres using the approximate relationship 5 miles ≈ 8 km (equivalently ≈ ×1.6). The heart of the topic is proportional (multiplicative) reasoning: converting is scaling the ratio 5:8 up or down, not adding a constant. Key facts to establish are that one mile is a GREATER distance than one kilometre (so a distance is a bigger number in km than in miles), that ≈ means 'approximately equal to', and that the relationship is a direct proportion whose conversion graph is a straight line through the origin. The double number line, ratio table and conversion graph are three views of the same multiplicative structure, and comparing UK distances (miles) with European ones (km) gives authentic context.
bestPractices: Establish the ratio 5 miles ≈ 8 km and read it both ways; teach ≈ explicitly and expect 'about' answers.
Represent with a double number line and ratio table so children SCALE the ratio (5:8 → 15:24) multiplicatively, and explicitly contrast this with the wrong additive strategy.
Use a 'spot the mistake' task where a character adds or subtracts the same amount to both quantities, and have children explain why it is wrong.
Make the 'which unit is larger' point concrete: a mile is longer, so any distance is a bigger number of km than of miles; use this to sense-check the direction of a conversion.
Connect the conversion to its straight-line graph through the origin as preparation for proportional graphs, and to real comparisons (a 10 km race vs a 6-mile run).
keyRepresentations: Double number line (miles and km aligned from 0)
Ratio / conversion table
Conversion graph (straight line through the origin, gradient ≈ 1.6)
'Spot the mistake' worked example exposing additive error
commonMisconceptions: Additive rather than multiplicative reasoning ('two more miles means two more km'; from 10 miles ≈ 16 km, adds 5 to both to convert 15 miles).
Thinks a kilometre is longer than a mile because the same distance is a bigger number in km, so converts in the wrong direction.
Treats 5 miles = 8 km as exact rather than approximate, ignoring ≈.

learn.summary: Children convert between miles and kilometres using the approximate relationship 5 miles ≈ 8 km (equivalently ×1.6), treating conversion as proportional (multiplicative) scaling of the ratio 5:8 rather than adding a constant. Key facts: a mile is a greater distance than a kilometre (so any distance is a bigger number in km than in miles), ≈ means 'approximately equal to', and the relationship is a direct proportion whose conversion graph is a straight line through the origin. Double number lines, ratio tables and conversion graphs are three views of the same multiplicative structure; comparing UK distances (miles) with European ones (km) gives authentic context.

activities.title: Slide and scale: the conversion stays on one straight line
feedback: If a learner adds a constant (e.g. gives ~18 km for 15 miles by adding ~1 km per mile), show that 15 miles = 3 × 5 miles, so the km must also triple (8 → 24); plot the additive point to see it leave the origin line.

If a learner divides or gives fewer km than miles (~9 km), remind them a mile is the longer unit: 5 miles needs 8 km to cover the same distance, so any distance is a bigger number of km than of miles.
Reinforce that each answer is 'about': ≈ means approximately, so 24 km is a sensible estimate (true value ~24.14 km), not exact.
activities.rationale: Aligning a double number line, ratio table and conversion graph makes the multiplicative structure one coherent picture and prepares children for proportional graphs; an optional live/draggable version lets children watch scaled points stay on the origin ray while additive points drift further away from it (repeatedly adding the same amount to both gives points on a different straight line, with gradient 1, that does not pass through the origin). A 'spot the mistake' contrast targets the documented additive error.
sourceClaims: Year 6 statutory: 'convert between miles and kilometres.' Non-statutory notes: pupils 'know approximate conversions and are able to tell if an answer is sensible' and connect conversion (km to miles) to a graphical representation as preparation for linear/proportional graphs.

'Children need to know that one mile is a greater distance than one kilometre… 5 miles is approximately equal to 8 km.' Misconceptions verbatim: children may think a kilometre is longer than a mile since the same distance is a greater number in km (15 miles ≈ 24 km); and may use additive rather than multiplicative reasoning (10 miles ≈ 16 km, so add 5 to both for 15 miles).

'If five miles is equivalent to eight kilometres, how many kilometres is seven miles? Students may respond that two more miles means two more kilometres.' Students should see multiplication as scaling, not repeated addition; a proportional relationship y = kx plots as a straight line through the origin; scalar (along the line) vs functional (between the lines, ×1.6) multipliers.
learnerActions: Work with a double number line AND a matching ratio table, both with miles and km aligned from 0, showing the pairs 5↔8, 10↔16, 15↔24.

Scale the ratio up and down multiplicatively: state that 15 miles is 3 lots of 5 miles, so it is 3 lots of 8 km = 24 km; extend to 40 miles ≈ 64 km (×8), and confirm the ×1.6 'between the lines' multiplier.

Connect the pairs to a conversion graph: plot the pairs and confirm they lie on one straight line through the origin (with miles on the horizontal axis and km on the vertical axis, the gradient is about 1.6).

Then try a character's 'add 5 to both' shortcut (5 miles, 8 km → 10 miles, 13 km) and plot that point; notice it falls OFF the origin line (the true pair is 10 miles ↔ 16 km) and explain why the shortcut is wrong.
Use a compare task: place a 10 km race and a 6-mile run (≈ 9.6 km) on the same line and decide which reaches further (the 10 km race).
activities.intendedInsight: Converting means scaling the ratio 5:8 (multiplying), which keeps every point on the same straight line through zero; adding a constant to both quantities knocks points off that line and is wrong.

activities.title: Spot the mistake: additive versus multiplicative conversion
feedback: For the '23 km' example: adding 15 to both does not preserve the 5:8 ratio; scale instead — 20 miles is 4 lots of 5 miles, so 4 lots of 8 km = 32 km.
If ~18 km is chosen: this comes from starting at 5 mi ≈ 8 km and adding ~1 km per extra mile; triple the whole ratio instead (8 → 24 km for 15 miles).
If ~9 km is chosen: this divides and treats a km as the larger unit; a mile is longer, so the km figure must be larger than the mile figure (about 24 km).
activities.rationale: A dedicated 'spot the mistake' task where a character adds or subtracts the same amount to both quantities, with children explaining why it is wrong, is a recommended way to expose the additive misconception. Conversion and comparison items with documented distractors can check whether reasoning is multiplicative, though a selection item alone does not build graph intuition and should be paired with building pairs on a number line, ratio table or graph.
sourceClaims: 'Children need to know that one mile is a greater distance than one kilometre… 5 miles is approximately equal to 8 km.' Misconceptions verbatim: children may think a kilometre is longer than a mile since the same distance is a greater number in km (15 miles ≈ 24 km); and may use additive rather than multiplicative reasoning (10 miles ≈ 16 km, so add 5 to both for 15 miles).

'If five miles is equivalent to eight kilometres, how many kilometres is seven miles? Students may respond that two more miles means two more kilometres.' Students should see multiplication as scaling, not repeated addition; a proportional relationship y = kx plots as a straight line through the origin; scalar (along the line) vs functional (between the lines, ×1.6) multipliers.
learnerActions: Read a character's converted answer and decide if it is right, e.g. '5 miles ≈ 8 km, so 20 miles ≈ 8 + 15 = 23 km'.
Identify the wrong strategy (adding a constant to both quantities) and compute the correct answer multiplicatively (20 miles = 4 × 5 miles = 4 × 8 km = 32 km).
Convert 15 miles and choose among sensible and faulty options, explaining why the additive (~18 km) and wrong-direction (~9 km) options are wrong.
Explain the error in words: why does adding the same amount to both quantities break the proportion?
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising and articulating the additive error consolidates that conversion scales the ratio; the characteristic wrong answers (~18 km additive, ~9 km wrong-direction) typically come from misreading the proportional structure or the direction of conversion rather than from arithmetic slips.

constraints: Treat the relationship as approximate throughout: teach ≈ explicitly and expect 'about' answers; 5 miles ≈ 8 km (true value for 15 miles is ~24.14 km), never exact.

A static aligned double number line with tap-to-reveal pairs conveys the fact pairs but cannot show the additive error in motion; it can still display a plotted additive point statically. Use it as a scaffold and make the multiplicative/additive contrast explicit.

A single selection-based spot-the-mistake item can assess whether reasoning is multiplicative but does not by itself build graph intuition; pair it with construction of pairs on a number line, ratio table or graph.
Keep the direction check concrete: a mile is longer, so the km figure for a given distance is always the bigger number — use this to sense-check every conversion.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source/assessment example '20 miles = 8 + 15 = 23 km' is an additive error; the multiplicative answer is 32 km (4 × 8). It appears only as a 'spot the mistake' prompt, with the correct method supplied in actions and feedback.

Non-preferred alternatives from the original record (a 3D environment and a persona dialogue judged to add little here) were medium-ranking judgements, not established pedagogical laws; they are not asserted as universal and are retained only as removed ranking context.
The ratio table was added to activity 1 so all three named key representations are actually used, matching the preservation audit.

probeDeeper: Which is longer, one mile or one kilometre? How does 5 miles ≈ 8 km tell you?
A friend converts by adding: 5 miles = 8 km, so 20 miles = 8 + 15 = 23 km. What is wrong with that?
Is 5 miles EXACTLY 8 km, or about 8 km? What does the symbol ≈ mean?
A 10 km race or a 6-mile run — which is further, and how do you know?
assess.correctAnswer: About 24 km, reasoning multiplicatively: 15 miles is 3 lots of 5 miles, so it is 3 lots of 8 km = 24 km (equivalently ×1.6); and noting a mile is longer than a km, so there are more km than miles.

errorPatterns.pattern: Additive rather than multiplicative reasoning — 'two more miles means two more km', or adds a constant to both quantities instead of scaling the ratio.
errorPatterns.nextMove: On a double number line show that 15 miles = 3 × 5 miles, so the km must also triple (8 → 24); run a spot-the-mistake where adding a constant is shown to break the pattern. Reteach multiplication as scaling, not repeated addition.
errorPatterns.distractor: About 18 km (8 km for 5 miles, then add 1 km for each extra mile)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers about 18 km, e.g. starts from 5 mi ≈ 8 km and adds ~1 km per extra mile, or from 10 mi ≈ 16 km subtracts/adds 5 to both; explains by adding, not multiplying.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks a kilometre is longer than a mile (because a distance is a bigger number in km), so converts the wrong way and divides.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish that a mile is the longer unit: 5 miles needs 8 km to cover the same distance, so a given distance is always a bigger number of km than of miles. Use the double number line to show km outrunning miles.
errorPatterns.distractor: About 9 km (divides, treating a km as the bigger unit)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers about 9 km (≈ 15 ÷ 1.6), giving FEWER km than miles, and justifies it by treating a km as the larger unit.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats 5 miles = 8 km as exact rather than approximate, ignoring ≈.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reinforce that ≈ means 'about' and that the point of the fact is a sensible estimate; do not reteach the conversion — the method is sound.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives 24 km but insists it is exact, or is thrown when told the true value is ~24.14 km; knows the fact but drops the approximation.

responseLevels.gap: Adds a constant or divides the wrong way; shows no sense that a km is the smaller unit or that conversion scales the ratio.
responseLevels.full: Scales ×3 (or ×1.6) to 24 km, justifies it multiplicatively, states that a mile is longer so there are more km than miles, and transfers the relationship to compare a 10 km race with a 6-mile run.
responseLevels.partial: Recalls 5 miles ≈ 8 km and handles the 5→8 case, but reverts to additive reasoning for 15 miles, or reaches 24 by a method they cannot justify as scaling; lists the fact without multiplicative reasoning.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You know 5 miles is about 8 km. A road sign says the next town is 15 miles away. About how many kilometres is that — and explain exactly how you worked it out.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Correct multiplicative reasoning scales 5:8 up by three to 24 km (more km than miles). An additive reasoner adds a constant instead of scaling and lands near 18 km. A child who thinks a km is longer than a mile divides and lands near 9 km. Three distinct answers make the underlying reasoning legible at a glance, and the request to 'explain how' separates recall of 5≈8 from genuine scaling.

sources.claim: Year 6 statutory: 'convert between miles and kilometres.' Non-statutory notes: pupils 'know approximate conversions and are able to tell if an answer is sensible' and connect conversion (km to miles) to a graphical representation as preparation for linear/proportional graphs.
sources.source: DfE, National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study, Year 6 Measurement

sources.claim: 'Children need to know that one mile is a greater distance than one kilometre… 5 miles is approximately equal to 8 km.' Misconceptions verbatim: children may think a kilometre is longer than a mile since the same distance is a greater number in km (15 miles ≈ 24 km); and may use additive rather than multiplicative reasoning (10 miles ≈ 16 km, so add 5 to both for 15 miles).
sources.source: White Rose Education, Year 6 Autumn Block 5 'Converting units' — Step 4 Miles and kilometres

sources.claim: 'If five miles is equivalent to eight kilometres, how many kilometres is seven miles? Students may respond that two more miles means two more kilometres.' Students should see multiplication as scaling, not repeated addition; a proportional relationship y = kx plots as a straight line through the origin; scalar (along the line) vs functional (between the lines, ×1.6) multipliers.
sources.source: NCETM, KS3 Mastery PD 3.1 'Understanding multiplicative relationships'

pedagogy.summary: Children solve word problems about collections of US coins and bills — finding the total value, making change, and writing amounts with the $ and ¢ symbols appropriately. The deep difficulty is that a coin's value is ABSTRACT and matches neither its physical size nor the number of coins: a dime is smaller than a nickel yet worth more, and three dimes beat five pennies. Money is best taught as a MEASURE of value (like length or weight), using proportional manipulatives that make each coin's worth visible, introducing coins two denominations at a time to limit switches of counting pattern, and first building the skip-counting and place-value number sense that totalling coins depends on.
bestPractices: Treat money as measuring value — begin with barter and non-standard units so children feel why standard values are needed (Fanelli & Tracy)
Use PROPORTIONAL manipulatives (a dime shown as ten unit-squares) rather than realistic play coins, because a coin is not a concrete representation of its own value
Introduce coins two denominations at a time to reduce cognitive load and limit how often the counting pattern must switch
Build the underlying number sense first — skip-counting by 5s, 10s, 25s and place value — since totalling mixed coins is a skip-count-and-switch task
Teach 'counting on' from the largest coin; model correct $ and ¢ notation and when each is used (100¢ = $1)
keyRepresentations: Proportional value strips / 'proportional dollar' (a coin laid over its worth in unit-squares)
A number line or hundred-square for skip-counting coin values
A coin-value reference (penny 1¢, nickel 5¢, dime 10¢, quarter 25¢, dollar 100¢)
A part-whole bar for making change (cost and amount paid)
commonMisconceptions: Value = size: a bigger coin is worth more (nickel > dime; five pennies > three dimes)
Value = count: each coin counts as one, or all coins are counted by ones regardless of denomination (unitary thinking)
Cannot switch counting patterns — counts 25, 50, 75 then cannot shift to +10 for a dime or +1 for a penny
Notation errors — mixing $ and ¢ ($0.50¢, or $5 for a nickel), or writing 5¢ as $5
Overusing one denomination (all dimes) because counting by tens is easiest, rather than realistic combinations

learn.summary: Children solve word problems with US coins and bills — totalling value, making change, and writing amounts with $ and ¢ correctly. The core difficulty is that a coin's value is abstract and matches neither its physical size nor the number of coins (a dime is smaller than a nickel yet worth more; three dimes beat five pennies). Money is best taught as a measure of value using proportional representations that make each coin's worth visible, introducing denominations a couple at a time, and first building the skip-counting and place-value number sense that totalling mixed coins depends on.

activities.title: Proportional-coin workbench: build value and make change
feedback: When a learner picks the bigger or more-numerous set as worth more, lay each coin over its unit-squares so the 10 squares of the dime stand beside the 5 of the nickel — let the squares, not the coin size, settle it.
If a learner counts every coin by ones (2 dimes + 3 pennies = '5'), highlight that one dime is already 10 squares; start from a single denomination before mixing.
When a learner stalls switching from 25s to 10s to 1s (counts 25, 50, 75 then says '76' for a dime), model counting on from the largest coin and track the running total on a number line.
For a correct total reached by counting on, ask them to remake the same amount with different coins to confirm value, not a fixed coin set, is what matters.
activities.rationale: Fanelli & Tracy report that children equate value with size and that coins are not concrete representations of their own value, recommending proportional manipulatives over realistic play coins and teaching money as a measure of value. A running total that accumulates by value supports 'counting on' and switching counting patterns, which Chandler & Kamii link to the difficulty of coordinating tens and ones when making change (that source is marked unverified in the row). The side-by-side square comparison is a proposed way to target the size/number heuristics through what the learner sees and does.
sourceClaims: Children often equate value with size — believing nickels are worth more than dimes and that five pennies are more valuable than three dimes — because relative coin sizes do not correlate with relative values; coins are therefore NOT concrete representations of their value, so proportional manipulatives are recommended over realistic play coins, money should be taught as a measure of value, and these size-based misconceptions lessen around ages 7-8, making second grade the appropriate time for formal money instruction.

Giving change when payment is made with a dime is difficult for young children because of the difficulty of coordinating tens and ones — underlying the trouble children have switching counting patterns across denominations.

Grade 2 standard: solve word problems involving dollar bills, quarters, dimes, nickels, and pennies, using $ and ¢ symbols appropriately (e.g. if you have 2 dimes and 3 pennies, how many cents do you have?).
learnerActions: Place coins onto a mat; as each coin is placed, it opens into its worth shown as unit-squares (dime = 10 squares, nickel = 5, penny = 1, quarter = 25) while a running total counts on by value.
Set the small dime beside the fatter nickel and compare the stacks of squares: the dime's 10 squares visibly outstretch the nickel's 5.
Build a target amount such as 30¢ in more than one way (e.g. three dimes; or a quarter and a nickel) and compare the coins used.
Switch to a make-change task: an item costs 40¢; pay with coins totalling 46¢ and count up the 6¢ change.
Count a mixed handful (2 dimes and 3 pennies) by counting on from the largest coin: 10, 20, then 21, 22, 23.
activities.intendedInsight: A coin's worth is a number of cents you count on, separate from the coin's size or how many coins there are; proportional value makes 'smaller but worth more' visible and concrete.

activities.title: Coin denomination reference with the size/worth contradiction
feedback: If a learner guesses worth from size, draw attention to the stated value and the dime-vs-nickel fact.
Reinforce 100¢ = $1 so a nickel is written 5¢, never $5.
activities.rationale: Securing denomination values and surfacing the size/worth contradiction gives a foundation for totalling. This is exposition that establishes facts; on its own it does not provide totalling or make-change practice, so it is best used before or alongside the workbench rather than instead of it.
sourceClaims: Children often equate value with size — believing nickels are worth more than dimes and that five pennies are more valuable than three dimes — because relative coin sizes do not correlate with relative values; coins are therefore NOT concrete representations of their value, so proportional manipulatives are recommended over realistic play coins, money should be taught as a measure of value, and these size-based misconceptions lessen around ages 7-8, making second grade the appropriate time for formal money instruction.
learnerActions: Reveal each coin's value and a short fact (e.g. the dime is 'smaller than a nickel, but worth more').
Name each coin and state its cents value: penny 1¢, nickel 5¢, dime 10¢, quarter 25¢; then name the dollar bill (100¢) and state that 100¢ = $1.
Point out at least one pair where the smaller coin is worth more.
activities.intendedInsight: Each coin has a fixed cents value that must be learned, and a coin's size does not tell you its worth.

activities.title: Comparison and totalling checks with diagnostic distractors
feedback: When a learner picks the five pennies or says 'the same', treat it as the size/count heuristic and route back to laying coins over their proportional value; three dimes (30¢) is worth more than five pennies (5¢).
If notation is mixed (e.g. $0.50¢ or $5 for a nickel), show that $ and ¢ are not used together and that 5¢ means five cents.
A correct number with weak reasoning should be followed by 'show me why' using the coins.
activities.rationale: Comparison and totalling items with the count/size answer as the diagnostic distractor surface whether the size/number heuristic is still operating and check notation. A selected-response or slider item can reward a correct number without revealing the underlying reasoning, so pair these checks with the workbench or a 'show me why' follow-up rather than relying on them to fix the misconception.
sourceClaims: Grade 2 standard: solve word problems involving dollar bills, quarters, dimes, nickels, and pennies, using $ and ¢ symbols appropriately (e.g. if you have 2 dimes and 3 pennies, how many cents do you have?).
learnerActions: Answer 'Which is worth more: three dimes or five pennies?' and explain the choice.
Total a mixed set such as '2 dimes and 3 pennies — how many cents?' and show the count.
Write the answer using ¢ (or $ with a decimal) without mixing the two symbols.
activities.intendedInsight: Judging worth by value — not by coin size or number of coins — and recording amounts in correct notation.

activities.title: Build the prerequisite number sense: skip-counting and place value
feedback: If the learner restarts counting at each new coin, reinforce counting on from the running total.
When switching from 25s to 10s to 1s breaks down, slow it on the number line and name the jump size each time.
activities.rationale: Chandler & Kamii attribute change-making difficulty to coordinating tens and ones (this source is marked unverified in the row), and the pedagogy recommends building skip-counting and place value before totalling mixed coins. This activity targets that prerequisite so the workbench and comparison tasks rest on secure counting.
sourceClaims: Giving change when payment is made with a dime is difficult for young children because of the difficulty of coordinating tens and ones — underlying the trouble children have switching counting patterns across denominations.
learnerActions: Skip-count aloud by 5s, 10s, and 25s on a number line or hundred-square.
Practise switching patterns mid-count: 25, 50, 75, then +10, then +1 (as if adding a dime then a penny).
Count on from a starting number rather than restarting at one.
activities.intendedInsight: Totalling mixed coins is a skip-count-and-switch task that depends on fluent skip-counting and place value.

constraints: When making a coin's worth visible, use a proportional representation (each coin shown as its worth in unit-squares) rather than relying on a realistic play coin, since a coin is not a concrete representation of its own value; real/realistic coins remain useful for diagnosis and handling.
Introduce denominations a couple at a time to limit how often the counting pattern must switch.
Build skip-counting (5s, 10s, 25s) and place value before totalling mixed collections.
Model 'counting on' from the largest coin and correct $/¢ notation, including 100¢ = $1.
A static denomination reference establishes facts but does not provide totalling or make-change practice; use it to support, not replace, hands-on value building.

Selected-response or slider checks can reward a correct number without revealing the size/count reasoning behind it; pair them with a 'show me why' step or hands-on value work. A check of this kind can assess totalling and comparison but does not itself elicit the proportional-value reasoning.
Real or realistic coins are useful for diagnosis and handling, but when teaching the size/worth contradiction, add a proportional value representation so worth is seen apart from size.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The Chandler & Kamii (2009) source is marked verified:false in the row; its claim about tens/ones coordination is carried forward with that caveat and should be re-checked before relying on it.

The legacy row rated role-play/dialogue and 3D as poor with absolute claims ('a 3D environment adds nothing', an 'in-role dialogue cannot show' the contradiction). These are catalog preferences, not established facts, and have not been reproduced as universal laws. A shopkeeper role-play can still provide authentic make-change practice if paired with a proportional-value representation; it is omitted here only as a lower-priority format, not as pedagogically impossible.

Arithmetic checked: 2 dimes + 3 pennies = 23¢ (counted 10, 20, 21, 22, 23); three dimes = 30¢ vs five pennies = 5¢; 30¢ built as three dimes or a quarter and a nickel; paying 46¢ for a 40¢ item gives 6¢ change — all consistent with the source and retained.
The source's make-change scenario pays 46¢ for a 40¢ item (change 6¢); this is logically consistent but oddly chosen, so the activity states item cost and payment explicitly to avoid ambiguity.

The row's parentTitle labels this 'Halves and quarters (age 7+)', which does not match the money objective; the original field is left unchanged and the guidance follows the money description and evidence statements.

probeDeeper: Three dimes or five pennies — which would you rather have, and why?
This dime is smaller than the nickel — how can it be worth more?
Show me 30¢ a different way, using different coins.
If I gave you one more dime, how much would you have now?
assess.correctAnswer: Totals 2 dimes + 3 pennies as 23¢ by counting 10, 20, then 21, 22, 23; states three dimes (30¢) is worth more than five pennies (5¢) and justifies by value, not size or number of coins; assembles 46¢ and gives 6¢ change; writes amounts using ¢ (or $ with a decimal) correctly without mixing the two.

errorPatterns.pattern: Value = size: a physically bigger coin is worth more — nickel beats dime, or five pennies beat three dimes because the coins are bigger or more numerous
errorPatterns.nextMove: Lay each coin over its proportional value (dime = 10 unit-squares) so worth is seen apart from size; confront this preoperational value-equals-size heuristic directly
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Chooses the bigger or more-numerous set as 'worth more'; on a total, treats the nickel as greater than the dime

errorPatterns.pattern: Value = count (unitary thinking): counts each coin as one, or counts all coins by ones regardless of denomination
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach that a coin's value is a number of cents you count on, using proportional manipulatives; start from one denomination before mixing
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 2 dimes + 3 pennies is '5', or counts 1,2,3,4,5 touching each coin rather than counting on by value

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot switch counting patterns across denominations — skip-counts one coin but stalls moving from 25s to 10s to 1s when coins are mixed
errorPatterns.nextMove: Practise counting on from the largest coin, scaffolding the switch with a number line; reteach place-value-based counting
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Counts 25, 50, 75 then adds a dime as '76' or restarts the count; overrelies on dimes to avoid switching

responseLevels.gap: Reasons by size or number — picks the bigger or more-numerous set as worth more and counts coins by ones; cannot total a mixed handful.
responseLevels.full: Counts mixed coins by value with 'counting on', judges worth by value not size or number (three dimes > five pennies, with justification), makes simple change, and writes amounts with $ or ¢ correctly — transferring to a new collection.
responseLevels.partial: Knows individual coin values and can total a single denomination, but stalls switching counting patterns for mixed coins or slips back to size/count on a comparison; totals only with prompting.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put out real or realistic coins. Ask three things and WATCH how the child counts: (1) 'Here are 2 dimes and 3 pennies — how many cents altogether?' (2) 'Which is worth more: three dimes or five pennies? Show me.' (3) 'This costs 46¢ — pay with these coins; now suppose it cost 40¢, give me the right change.' Watch whether they count by VALUE (skip-counting and switching patterns) or by size/number, and whether they write the amount with $ or ¢ correctly.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Pitting three dimes against five pennies — fewer, smaller coins that are worth MORE — forces a choice between value-reasoning and the size/count heuristics: a child using size or number picks the pennies or says 'the same', while a value-reasoner picks the dimes and can show why. Watching the count on the 2-dimes-3-pennies task reveals whether they switch counting patterns or count every coin by ones.
