pedagogy.summary: At 8-9 the web of representations grows to include decimals and the area/distributive model, and the demand is fluency in ALL directions: represent a sharing problem as both a fraction diagram and a division equation, show how a bar model for 4×23 connects to the area model and the written method, and translate a decimal on a number line into a fraction and explain the equivalence (CCSS MP2). Two load-bearing ideas from the IES fractions guide anchor the level: a decimal and its fraction (0.3 and 3/10) are the SAME number — the same point/magnitude on a line, not two different kinds of thing — and area/strip models must be read as a single quantity, not a count of parts. The recurring failure is treating each representation as an unconnected procedure (the area model 'for pictures', the written method 'for answers') rather than as different views of one structure; good teaching keeps asking 'what's the same across these, and where is each number in the other?'
bestPractices: Put fractions and their decimal equivalents on the SAME number line (0.3 and 3/10 at one point) so equivalence is seen as sameness of magnitude, not a conversion trick (IES Rec 2)

Lay the area model, the bar model, and the written method for 4×23 side by side and map each partial product to a region, so the representations are one structure viewed three ways (MP2 coherent representation; NCETM structure)
Use unmarked number lines and 'what single quantity is this?' questioning to stop counting-parts-without-meaning (IES caution)
Translate both ways — diagram→equation AND equation→diagram — and require the child to say what each number represents
Watch decimals for whole-number thinking (0.35 vs 0.5) and route back through the number line's magnitudes
keyRepresentations: Number line carrying fractions and decimals at shared points (equivalence as one position)
Area model / array for multiplication linked to the written method
Bar model for sharing/division and for multiplication structure
Hundredths grid linking a decimal to its fraction
commonMisconceptions: Treats a decimal and its fraction as different kinds of number that can't share a point (0.3 ≠ 3/10 'because one's a decimal')
Applies whole-number thinking to decimals (0.35 > 0.5 'because 35 > 5'; reads 0.3 as 'three')
Reads the area/bar model as a separate procedure from the written method, unable to say how they show the same calculation
Counts parts of a diagram without seeing that numerator and denominator name a single quantity

learn.summary: For ages 8-9, build fluency in moving BETWEEN representations of multiplication, fractions, and decimals: a sharing story, a fraction diagram, a number line, an area/bar model, and a written equation are different views of ONE structure, not separate procedures. Two anchoring ideas: a decimal and its fraction (0.3 and 3/10) name the SAME number — one point/magnitude on a line, not two kinds of thing — and an area or strip model must be read as quantities (each part has a value relative to the whole, and the parts' values combine into the total), not as a bare count of pieces. The recurring failure is treating each representation as its own routine (the area model 'for pictures', the written method 'for answers'); good teaching keeps asking 'what's the same across these, and where does each number live in the other?'

activities.title: Same point on the line: 0.3 and 3/10
feedback: If the child places 0.3 and 3/10 in different spots or calls them 'different numbers because one's a decimal', put both on one number line and on a tenths grid until the shared point is undeniable, and revisit tenths/hundredths equivalence as the same quantity.

If the child reads 0.3 as 'three' or judges 0.35 > 0.5 'because 35 > 5', route placement through magnitude on the line and the tenths/hundredths grid so the value, not the digit string, drives position; revisit decimal place value. (0.35 lies between 0.3 and 0.4, so it is less than 0.5.)

When the child places both at one point, justifies with 'three tenths' reasoning, and carries the same reasoning to the fresh pair, treat that as secure magnitude understanding; transferring such reasoning spontaneously to new pairs is a further sign of security.
activities.rationale: Number lines show the relations among fractions and decimals as the same magnitude at one point, and whole-number thinking misapplied to decimals is a known hazard remedied by magnitude reasoning on a line and grid.
sourceClaims: Number lines show the relations among fractions, decimals and percents (the same magnitude at one point); students misapply whole-number knowledge to fractions/decimals, and area/strip models risk counting parts without seeing a single quantity — remedied by number-line magnitude reasoning.
learnerActions: Mark where 0.3 goes on a number line from 0 to 1, then mark where 3/10 goes, and say whether they land on the same point.
Explain in your own words why both are 'three tenths of the way from 0 to 1' — the same magnitude shown two ways.
Place 0.35 and 0.5 on the line and explain which is bigger and why (0.35 is less than 0.5), checking against a tenths/hundredths grid.
Apply the same reasoning to a fresh pair, e.g. 0.27 and 27/100: place both on the line and explain the equivalence.
activities.intendedInsight: A decimal and its equivalent fraction are the same number — the same position/magnitude on the line — so notation (decimal vs fraction) is not identity; magnitude is.

activities.title: Where do 80 and 12 live? Linking the area model and the written method for 4×23
feedback: If the child can do each separately but cannot say how one shows the other, overlay the area model and the written method and map each partial product to its region, asking 'what's the same, what's different?'

If the child treats the picture as decoration and the algorithm as the 'real' method and cannot point to where 80 and 12 live, go region by region, naming the multiplication each region represents (4×20=80, then 4×3=12) before summing to 92.
Confirm understanding when the child can trace 80 to the 20-strip, 12 to the 3-strip, and explain 92 as their sum in both the picture and the written form.
activities.rationale: Representations reveal a shared mathematical structure; the same structure underlies a bar/area model and the written method, so they should be connected rather than taught as separate procedures.
sourceClaims: Representations reveal a shared mathematical structure; the same structure underlies a bar/area model and the written method, so they should be connected rather than taught as separate procedures.
MP2: create a coherent representation; attend to the meaning of quantities and their referents; move between a situation and its symbolic representation.
learnerActions: Split 23 into 20 and 3 and draw an area model (rectangle) for 4×23, showing the two regions.
Point to the region that is 4×20 and the region that is 4×3, and state their values (80 and 12).
Write out the written method for 4×23 beside the rectangle and match each partial product to its region; check the two regions sum to 92.
Say out loud what is the same and what is different between the picture and the algorithm.
activities.intendedInsight: The area model and the written method are one structure viewed two ways: each partial product (4×20=80 and 4×3=12) is a region of the rectangle, and 80+12=92 is the total.

activities.title: One sharing story, three ways
feedback: If the child can only go one direction (diagram→equation but not equation→diagram, or vice versa), practise the missing direction explicitly, asking what each number stands for each time.
Prompt 'what does this number mean in the story?' whenever the child manipulates symbols without connecting them to the quantity.
Confirm when the child moves fluently between story, diagram, and equation and can name each number's referent in all three.
activities.rationale: Translating between a situation and its symbolic representation, attending to the meaning of quantities and their referents, is the core of coherent representation.
sourceClaims: MP2: create a coherent representation; attend to the meaning of quantities and their referents; move between a situation and its symbolic representation.
learnerActions: Tell a sharing story that 6÷4 (or another division) could represent.
Draw a fraction diagram for it and write the matching division equation.
Say what each number in the equation represents in both the story and the diagram.
Translate the other way too: given a diagram, write the equation; given an equation, draw the diagram.
activities.intendedInsight: A real-world situation, its diagram, and its symbolic equation are different views of the same quantity; fluency means moving in BOTH directions and naming what each number refers to.

activities.title: Convince a doubter: dialogue and discussion
feedback: This discussion is for reasoning, not scoring: focus on whether the child justifies with magnitude ('both are three tenths') and can locate numbers across representations.
If the child only asserts 'they're the same' without showing where each goes, press 'show me where each one lands' — the shared placement plus tenths reasoning is the point.
Encourage the child to address the doubter's specific claim rather than restate a remembered rule.
activities.rationale: Being asked to defend equivalence and shared structure is one way to prompt articulation of why representations coincide; an in-role partner asserting the misconception may elicit the child's reasoning. This is a proposed, untested complement to construction tasks, not a substitute for building and placing representations.
learnerActions: Respond to a partner (classmate, adult, or in-role character) who insists '0.3 and 3/10 must be different — one's a decimal!' and argue, with the number line and a tenths grid, that they share one point.
Have the partner point at an area model for 4×23 and ask 'which bit is the 80, which is the 12?' — answer by tracing each to its region and to the written method.
Explain your reasoning aloud rather than just stating an answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Being asked to defend equivalence and shared structure can push the child to articulate WHY representations coincide, not just that they do.

constraints: Require construction and explanation, not just recognition: the child should build diagrams, place values on lines, write equations, and say what each number means. A matching-type warm-up ('which decimal equals 3/10?') can activate prior knowledge but does not show the child can construct a translation or explain shared structure.

A static side-by-side of story, diagram, area model, and equation with tap-to-reveal links can illustrate connections and serve as a worked example, but it does not let the child build or vary the representations themselves; use it as a scaffold, then move to child-generated work.
Evocative illustrations cannot be trusted for exact decimal/fraction positions — placements on a number line need accurate, marked or verifiable scales.

Optional interactive supports (if available) can make the 'same structure, different view' idea concrete: linked panels where dropping 0.3 on a line snaps 3/10 to the same tick, or an area-model↔written-method splitter where dragging the 20+3 split recolours both the rectangle regions and the partial products together. These are helpful examples, not required mechanisms; the same goals can be met with paper, a drawn number line, and spoken explanation.
When comparing decimals, hold the comparison honest: 0.35 vs 0.5 is about magnitude (0.35 < 0.5), not about which digit string looks bigger — route placement through the value.
4×23 = 92: the partial products are 4×20=80 and 4×3=12, summing to 92. Keep these exact values in any example; '60' is not a valid partial product here.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The legacy source labelled all sources 'verified':true and confidence 'high'; this status was not re-checked here and should not be read as fresh validation.

The source recommendation narrative mentioned '60 glowing over the 20-strip' while elsewhere correctly giving 80 and 12 as the partial products for 4×23. The correct value is 4×20=80 (not 60); activities use 80. Any '60' should be treated as an error, not a valid alternative.

Legacy entries asserted that a 3D scene 'adds nothing' and that quizzes can only assess recognition. These are narrowed here to scoped observations (a number line and area model are planar and adequate for this magnitude/structure content; recognition-only items do not elicit construction) rather than universal laws.
The dialogue activity's efficacy relative to other media is untested; it is presented with hedged wording and no source cited for the dialogic mechanism, since no source[].claim supports it.

The fresh-pair transfer (e.g. 0.27 and 27/100) is now issued as an explicit learner task; because it is prompted, feedback credits the child for carrying the reasoning across when prompted and notes spontaneous/unprompted transfer only as an additional sign of security, not as the pass condition.

Reteach prerequisite links (e.g. decimal place-value and area/distributive prerequisites) were referenced in the source; the underlying reteach moves are preserved in feedback but specific internal prerequisite IDs are omitted as non-portable.

probeDeeper: 'Put 0.3 and 3/10 on the line — are they the same point or different? How can you be sure?'
'Where does 0.35 go compared with 0.5? Show me why.'
'In the rectangle for 4×23, point to the part that is the 80 and the part that is the 12. Where are they in the written method?'
'Tell me a sharing story that 6 ÷ 4 could be, and show it as a diagram AND an equation.'
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child placing 0.3 and 3/10 at the SAME point and explaining they are the same number/magnitude shown two ways (three tenths of the way from 0 to 1), rather than treating decimal and fraction as different kinds of thing living in different places.

errorPatterns.pattern: Decimal and fraction seen as different kinds of number that can't share a point: 0.3 ≠ 3/10 'because one's a decimal'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Put both on one number line and on a tenths grid until the shared point is undeniable; reteach decimal–fraction equivalence of tenths/hundredths as the same quantity.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child places them in different spots, or agrees they're 'different numbers', treating notation as identity rather than magnitude.

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number thinking applied to decimals: reads 0.3 as 'three', or judges 0.35 > 0.5 'because 35 > 5', misplacing the decimal on the line.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Route through the number line's magnitudes and the tenths/hundredths grid so the value, not the digit string, drives placement; reteach decimal place value.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Places 0.35 beyond 0.5, or lines decimals up by digit count rather than magnitude.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the area/bar model as a separate procedure from the written method — for 4×23 can do each but cannot say how one shows the other.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay the area model and the written method and map each partial product to a region ('what's the same, what's different?'); reteach the area/distributive model as the structure behind the algorithm.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats the picture as decoration and the algorithm as the 'real' method; cannot point to where 80 and 12 live in the rectangle.

responseLevels.gap: Places 0.3 and 3/10 apart or calls them different numbers; treats each representation as its own procedure.
responseLevels.full: Places 0.3 and 3/10 at one point and explains both are three tenths; maps numbers across diagram, area model, number line and equation (locating 80 and 12 in the rectangle and the algorithm) — and transfers the 'same quantity, different view' reasoning to a new pair (e.g. 0.27 and 27/100) unprompted.
responseLevels.partial: Says 0.3 = 3/10 or places them together, but justifies weakly (a remembered rule) or still misplaces 0.35 vs 0.5, or can map one pair of representations but not link the area model to the written method.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A classmate says: '0.3 and 3/10 are different numbers — 0.3 is a decimal and 3/10 is a fraction, so they'd go in different places on a number line.' Do you agree? Show me where each one goes on a line from 0 to 1, and explain what you find. Then tell me how you'd convince the classmate.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with a magnitude view puts both at one point and can justify it (both are three tenths); a child treating notations as separate 'things' places them apart or can't say they coincide. The prompt is hard to answer right for the wrong reason because merely saying 'they're the same' doesn't survive 'show me where each goes' — the shared placement plus the tenths reasoning is the discriminating act; a notation-bound child cannot produce it.

sources.claim: MP2: create a coherent representation; attend to the meaning of quantities and their referents; move between a situation and its symbolic representation.
sources.source: CCSS Standards for Mathematical Practice, MP2

sources.claim: Number lines show the relations among fractions, decimals and percents (the same magnitude at one point); students misapply whole-number knowledge to fractions/decimals, and area/strip models risk counting parts without seeing a single quantity — remedied by number-line magnitude reasoning.
sources.source: IES/WWC Practice Guide, Developing Effective Fractions Instruction for K–8 (Rec 2)

sources.claim: Representations reveal a shared mathematical structure; the same structure underlies a bar/area model and the written method, so they should be connected rather than taught as separate procedures.
sources.source: NCETM, 'The Bar Model'

pedagogy.summary: Finding a non-unit fraction of a quantity is a two-step operator procedure: divide the whole by the denominator to find one equal part (the unit fraction), then multiply that part by the numerator. The teaching goal at age 8-9 is fluency and reliable structure — children already know unit fractions of sets, so the new work is coordinating the divide-then-multiply sequence and interpreting worded problems ("3/8 of 24 sweets") into that structure. Best taught by making the two steps explicit and visible before compressing them, and by grounding the procedure in the meaning of the denominator (how many equal shares) and numerator (how many shares we take).
bestPractices: Make the two steps explicit: ring-fence 'divide by the denominator to get one part' as step 1, then 'multiply by the numerator' as step 2, before letting children compress it — many errors are a collapsed or reversed sequence, not arithmetic slips.

Anchor the procedure in the fraction-as-operator meaning: the denominator says how many equal groups to split into, the numerator says how many of those groups to take. This lets children self-check which number divides and which multiplies.

Use bar models / arrays: draw the whole as a bar, partition into 'denominator' equal parts, shade 'numerator' of them, and read off the total — the model makes the divide-then-multiply visible and catches the 'divide by numerator' error.
Sequence from unit to non-unit: confirm 1/8 of 24 = 3 first, then 3/8 = 3 x 3 = 9, so the new step (multiply by numerator) is isolated against secure ground.
Include a plausibility check: a proper fraction of a quantity must be smaller than the whole (9 red sweets out of 24), which catches multiply-the-whole errors.
Vary the worded contexts (sweets, money, measures, sets of people) so children practise translating language into the divide-then-multiply structure rather than pattern-matching one phrasing.
keyRepresentations: Bar model partitioned into denominator equal parts with numerator shaded (whole labelled, one part labelled)
Array / equal groups (24 counters in 8 groups of 3; take 3 groups)
Double number line: 0 ... whole on top, 0 ... fraction on bottom, marking one part then stepping along
Written two-step record: 24 ÷ 8 = 3, then 3 × 3 = 9
commonMisconceptions: Divides by the numerator instead of the denominator (3/8 of 24 read as 24 ÷ 3)
Stops after one step — finds the unit fraction (24 ÷ 8 = 3) and gives that as the answer without multiplying by the numerator
Multiplies the whole by the numerator (24 × 3) giving an answer larger than the whole
Multiplies numerator and denominator into the whole in the wrong order or muddles which is which under worded-problem load

learn.summary: Finding a non-unit fraction of a quantity (e.g. 3/8 of 24) is a two-step operator procedure for 8-9 year olds: divide the whole by the denominator to find one equal part, then multiply that part by the numerator. Children already know unit fractions of sets, so the new work is coordinating the divide-then-multiply sequence, grounding it in the meaning of numerator and denominator, and translating worded problems into that structure. Make the two steps explicit and visible before compressing them.

activities.title: The fraction-of machine: divide to build parts, then take them
feedback: If a learner takes 3 single sweets rather than 3 groups, pause: '3/8 means 8 equal shares - how many shares do you take, and how big is each share?' This shows the learner is treating the numerator as a number of single items and ignoring the denominator. Note that the answer (3) matches the size of one share here, so watch the action, not just the answer.

If a learner tries to make 3 groups instead of 8, use a meaning-based prompt (24 does divide evenly by 3, so the partition alone will not flag the error): 'Does the bottom number tell how many groups, or the top? /8 means 8 equal groups.'
If a learner stops after making 8 groups of 3 and reports '3', prompt: 'That is 1/8. The question asks for 3/8 - how many of those groups do we take?'

If a learner produces a number bigger than 24, ask the plausibility check: 'Can 3/8 of 24 be more than 24? A proper fraction of an amount is smaller than the whole.' Then rebuild the divide-first step.
When correct, confirm: dividing built the parts (24 ÷ 8 = 3) and selecting took 3 of them (3 × 3 = 9).
activities.rationale: Letting the child perform and see both steps, with a bar model shown alongside tying the actions to the written record, isolates the load-bearing skill (the sequence) and surfaces the two canonical errors in the action itself. Live partitioning, selecting groups, and a running total are optional interaction examples that make the divide-then-multiply mechanism concrete.
sourceClaims: Fraction-as-operator (a/b of a quantity = divide by b, multiply by a) is a core interpretation, and instruction should build it on the meaning of numerator and denominator rather than a rote rule; bar models and number lines support the structure.
Finding fractions of quantities is taught as divide-then-multiply, developing from unit-fraction-of-a-set to non-unit fractions; children should solve worded problems in varied contexts.
learnerActions: Set up the problem '3/8 of 24 sweets': start with 24 sweets to share.
Split the 24 sweets into equal groups, where the number of groups is fixed by the denominator (8 groups of 3).
Now take the numerator's worth of those groups: take 3 of the 8 groups and count the total (9).
Record the two steps in writing alongside the action: 24 ÷ 8 = 3, then 3 × 3 = 9.
Repeat with new fractions and new contexts (e.g. 3/5 of 20 pounds, 2/3 of 18 people) so the structure, not one phrasing, is practised.
activities.intendedInsight: The procedure is two distinct actions with two distinct results: dividing by the denominator builds the equal parts, and multiplying by the numerator (selecting that many groups) takes them. Children can self-check which number divides (how many equal shares) and which multiplies (how many shares to take).

activities.title: Isolate the new step: from unit fraction to non-unit fraction
feedback: If the learner re-divides when the numerator changes, point out the groups of 3 already exist - only the number of groups taken changes.
If the learner can do 3/8 but stalls on 5/8, they may be pattern-matching the last answer rather than using the structure; walk back to 'how big is one group?'
Praise explanations that reference meaning ('8 says make 8 equal shares, 3 says take 3 of them') over recited rules.
activities.rationale: Sequencing from unit to non-unit isolates the new multiply step against secure ground and builds the fraction-as-operator meaning rather than a rote rule.
sourceClaims: Fraction-as-operator (a/b of a quantity = divide by b, multiply by a) is a core interpretation, and instruction should build it on the meaning of numerator and denominator rather than a rote rule; bar models and number lines support the structure.
Finding fractions of quantities is taught as divide-then-multiply, developing from unit-fraction-of-a-set to non-unit fractions; children should solve worded problems in varied contexts.
learnerActions: First confirm the unit fraction on secure ground: find 1/8 of 24 (= 3).
Then isolate the new step: 'That is one group. For 3/8, how many groups do we take?' Take 3 groups to get 9.
Try the same whole with a different numerator: 5/8 of 24 re-uses the groups of 3 and takes 5 (= 15); notice you do NOT re-divide.
Explain in your own words why the denominator divides and the numerator multiplies.
activities.intendedInsight: The division step is shared across all eighths of 24; only the numerator (how many groups to take) changes. This separates the secure prior skill from the genuinely new multiply-by-numerator step.

activities.title: Bar models and arrays: making divide-then-multiply visible
feedback: If a learner partitions into the numerator's parts, compare: 'Which number tells how many equal parts to cut? The bottom (denominator).'
If a learner shades all parts or more than the whole, revisit: the shaded amount is part of the bar, so it cannot exceed 24.

A tap-to-reveal worked example (reveal the partition, then reveal which parts are taken and the total) can serve as a pre-teach, but it shows one case and does not let the child perform the procedure across varied quantities, which fluency requires.
activities.rationale: Bar models, arrays and number lines represent the operator structure concretely and catch the characteristic errors; a single revealed worked example is a useful scaffold but limited to one case.
sourceClaims: Fraction-as-operator (a/b of a quantity = divide by b, multiply by a) is a core interpretation, and instruction should build it on the meaning of numerator and denominator rather than a rote rule; bar models and number lines support the structure.
learnerActions: Draw the whole as a bar labelled 24; partition it into the denominator's number of equal parts (8 parts), label one part (3).
Shade the numerator's number of parts (3 parts) and read off the shaded total (9).
Build the same with counters: arrange 24 counters as 8 groups of 3, then ring 3 groups.
Use a double number line: amount (0 to 24) on top and fraction (0 to 1, marked in eighths) on the bottom, so 1/8 lines up with 3 and 8/8 lines up with 24. Mark one part, then step along to 3/8 (9).
activities.intendedInsight: The model makes the divide-then-multiply structure visible: partitioning is the division, shading/selecting is the multiplication. Reading the total off the model catches the divide-by-numerator error (wrong number of parts) and the multiply-the-whole error (answer must fit inside the bar).

activities.title: Varied worded problems and plausibility checking
feedback: If a learner computes 24 x 3 = 72, ask 'Can part of 24 be bigger than 24?' before rebuilding the divide-first step.
If a learner solves sweets but stalls on money, highlight that the structure is identical: divide the amount by the denominator, multiply by the numerator.

Scored practice can check fluency and capture the two-step structure: on a 0-24 slider an answer of 3 (stopping after one step) is a selectable error, while a free-entry answer can additionally surface an answer of 72 (multiplying the whole), and a fill-in-the-blanks format (24 ÷ ☐ = ☐, ☐ × ☐ = ☐) shows which step goes wrong. Recognising a correct option, however, does not show the child can independently construct the steps - pair it with doing.
activities.rationale: Worded problems in varied contexts are curriculum expectations; a plausibility check catches the multiply-the-whole error; talking a problem through may support translating worded language into the structure and should accompany, not replace, the independent practice a procedural skill requires.
sourceClaims: Finding fractions of quantities is taught as divide-then-multiply, developing from unit-fraction-of-a-set to non-unit fractions; children should solve worded problems in varied contexts.
learnerActions: Solve worded problems across contexts: sweets (A bag has 24 sweets, 3/8 are red - how many red?), money (3/5 of 20 pounds), measures (cm), and sets of people (2/3 of 18).
For each, write the two lines of working and name which number divides and which multiplies.
Before accepting an answer, run the plausibility check: a proper fraction of an amount must be smaller than the whole (9 red sweets out of 24 is reasonable; 72 is not).
Optionally talk a problem through aloud with a partner or in-role 'shopkeeper' who poses 'fraction of my stock' problems, explaining each step.
activities.intendedInsight: Translating varied language into the same divide-then-multiply structure prevents pattern-matching one phrasing, and the plausibility check guards against multiply-the-whole errors.

constraints: Keep the two steps explicit and ring-fenced before compressing them: many errors are a collapsed or reversed sequence, not arithmetic slips.
Anchor the procedure in meaning - denominator = how many equal groups, numerator = how many groups taken - so children can self-check which number divides and which multiplies.
A revealed/worked static example shows one case and cannot let the child perform the procedure across varied quantities; use it as a pre-teach, not the main practice.

Recognition-only response formats (selecting a correct option) can assess fluency and surface specific errors but do not elicit independent construction of the two steps; include tasks where the child builds or writes the procedure.
Talking a problem through supports translating worded language into the structure but should accompany, not replace, repeated independent doing for a procedural skill.

Do NOT rely on a visible remainder to flag the divide-by-numerator error in '3/8 of 24': 24 divides evenly by 3, so making 3 groups gives 8-per-group with no remainder. Use a meaning-of-denominator prompt instead.

Watch out for the diagnostic coincidence in '3/8 of 24': the group size (3) equals the numerator (3), so an answer of 3 could mean the child took 3 single counters (treating the numerator as a count of items and ignoring the denominator) or stopped after finding one group (1/8). Neither is divide-by-numerator confusion, which shows up as making 3 groups of 8. Watch what the child actually does, and also use a problem where group size and numerator differ (e.g. 3/4 of 24, group size 6) so these errors can be told apart.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One source (National Curriculum in England programmes of study) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its claim as unconfirmed.

The source row's own diagnostic note is self-contradictory: it states the design avoids numerator equal to group size, then states 24 deliberately gives group size 3 and numerator 3. The latter is correct for '3/8 of 24'.

The original 'fraction-of machine' design-note feedback claiming the division visibly stalls (trays won't divide evenly) when a child divides by the numerator does not hold whenever the numerator also divides the whole (as with 3 and 24); it was corrected to a meaning-based prompt in the activity feedback, not relying on a visible remainder.

Claims that a 2D interactive is uniquely 'ideal' or that 3D 'adds nothing', or that doing is inherently superior to talking, are catalog/efficacy judgements not established by the sources; reframed as affordances and qualified limits without asserting necessity or comparative superiority.

probeDeeper: Once they answer, ask 'how did you know to make 8 groups and not 3?' — listen for the denominator meaning, not a recited rule.
'Show me 1/8 of the 24 first — now how do you get to 3/8?' isolates whether the second step is understood or lucky.
Counterexample: 'What if I'd asked for 5/8 of 24 instead?' — a child with the structure re-uses the groups of 3 and takes 5 (=15); a child who pattern-matched the last answer stalls.
'Could your answer be bigger than 24? Why not?' surfaces whether the plausibility check is available.
assess.correctAnswer: 9. The child splits the 24 into 8 equal groups (24 ÷ 8 = 3 in each), then takes 3 of those groups (3 × 3 = 9).

errorPatterns.pattern: Divides by the numerator: reads '3/8 of 24' as 24 ÷ 3 and makes 3 groups (or takes just 3 counters), giving 8 or 3
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the meaning of the denominator: it says how many equal shares. Rebuild with 'how many equal groups does /8 mean?' before touching the numerator.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child makes 3 groups instead of 8, or grabs 3 counters straight away — using the top number as the divisor

errorPatterns.pattern: Stops after one step: finds the unit fraction (24 ÷ 8 = 3) and offers 3 as the answer, not multiplying by the numerator
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach division of sets — scaffold the second step only: 'that's 1/8; the question asks for 3/8 — how many of those groups?' Point back at the numerator's job.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child correctly makes 8 groups of 3 then reports '3' — the division is right but the second step is dropped

errorPatterns.pattern: Multiplies the whole by the numerator: computes 24 × 3 = 72, giving an answer larger than the starting quantity
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trigger the plausibility check first ('can 3/8 of 24 be more than 24?'), then rebuild the divide-first step with the bar model.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child produces a number bigger than 24 with no partitioning, or multiplies before dividing

responseLevels.gap: Cannot coordinate the two steps: divides by the numerator, or multiplies the whole, or produces the unit-fraction-only answer and cannot get further even with the numerator pointed out.
responseLevels.full: Reliably divides by the denominator then multiplies by the numerator, explains each step by the meaning of the fraction, transfers to a new fraction and a new context (money, measures), and checks the answer is smaller than the whole.
responseLevels.partial: Executes both steps for the practised case (makes 8 groups, takes 3, gets 9) but treats them as a memorised recipe — cannot explain why the denominator divides, or stalls when the fraction changes to 5/8 or the context changes to money.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are 24 counters. Find 3/8 of them. Do it however you like, and I'll watch — you don't need to tell me the rule.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Because the teacher WATCHES the procedure rather than asking about it, the two canonical breakdowns show themselves in the child's actions: a child who divides by the numerator makes 3 groups; a child who stops after one step makes 8 groups but reports 3; only a child who has the divide-then-multiply structure makes 8 groups AND takes 3 of them. 24 is chosen so 3/8 divides evenly (no remainder to mask the error) and the numerator (3) differs from the group size (also 3) is avoided — deliberately 24 gives group size 3 and numerator 3, so watch that they take 3 GROUPS not 3 counters: taking 3 counters instead of 3 groups is the exact tell for divide-by-numerator confusion.

sources.claim: Fraction-as-operator (a/b of a quantity = divide by b, multiply by a) is a core interpretation, and instruction should build it on the meaning of numerator and denominator rather than a rote rule; bar models and number lines support the structure.
sources.source: IES/WWC Practice Guide: Developing Effective Fractions Instruction for Kindergarten Through 8th Grade

sources.claim: Finding fractions of quantities is taught as divide-then-multiply, developing from unit-fraction-of-a-set to non-unit fractions; children should solve worded problems in varied contexts.
sources.source: National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (Year 3-4 fractions)

pedagogy.summary: This extends line plots to eighth-inch precision and, crucially, USES the plotted data for computation — finding the difference between the longest and shortest specimen, or totalling all the measurements — which requires adding and subtracting fractions with like and related denominators. Two skills are fused: build an accurate 1/8 scale, and operate on the fractions read from it. It is best taught by generating data, plotting to the nearest 1/8, then posing genuine questions answerable only from the plot (difference, total, redistribution), with the eighth scale showing equivalence (2/8 = ¼, 4/8 = ½) so common denominators are visible on the axis itself.
bestPractices: Measure to the nearest 1/8 inch with a subdivided ruler and scale the axis into equal eighths
Make equivalence visible on the scale — mark that 2/8 = ¼ and 4/8 = ½ — so common denominators for later arithmetic are seen, not just computed
Pose real difference and total problems that can only be answered by reading positions and adding fractions
Stress that a stack of Xs contributes its value once per X (three Xs at 3/8 add 3/8 three times) — multiplicity matters when totalling
Keep the one-X-per-case rule and connect eighths back to quarters and halves
keyRepresentations: A ruler subdivided to eighths
A number line in eighths showing equivalence (2/8 = ¼, 4/8 = ½)
Fraction bars for adding and subtracting like denominators
The plot itself used as a data source for computation
commonMisconceptions: When asked for a total length, adding or counting the Xs (frequency) instead of summing the measured values
Adding fractions by adding numerators AND denominators (3/8 + 3/8 = 6/16)
Spacing eighths unequally or not seeing 2/8 = ¼ and 4/8 = ½, so scales don't line up and common denominators are missed
Counting a value only once when several Xs are stacked on it while totalling

learn.summary: Grade 4 measurement line plots at eighth-inch precision, fused with using the plotted data for fraction arithmetic. Learners measure specimens to the nearest 1/8 inch, build an equal-interval eighth scale, plot one X per object, then answer genuine questions that require adding and subtracting fractions with like/related denominators: the difference between longest and shortest, and the total length of everything. The key insight comes when totalling over stacks: three Xs at 3/8 contribute 3/8 + 3/8 + 3/8, so frequency (how many Xs) and value (how much length) diverge. Marking 2/8 = 1/4 and 4/8 = 1/2 on the axis makes common denominators visible, so 1/2 − 3/8 becomes 4/8 − 3/8 right on the scale.

activities.title: Build-then-compute an eighth-inch line plot
feedback: If the learner gives the number of objects as the 'total', point to a stack of three at 3/8 and ask 'how much length is here?', holding 'how many objects' apart from 'how much length'.
If the learner adds each distinct axis value only once while ignoring stack height, show that each X on the stack contributes its value again (three Xs at 3/8 give 3/8 + 3/8 + 3/8 = 9/8).
If the learner writes 3/8 + 3/8 = 6/16, reteach fraction addition as joining same-size parts: the denominator (the size of the part) stays the same, so 3/8 + 3/8 = 6/8.
If ticks are mis-spaced or 1/2 − 3/8 is attempted without a common denominator, overlay quarter and half ticks on the eighth scale and use a fraction strip to find the common denominator (1/2 = 4/8).
activities.rationale: The standard asks learners both to make a line plot in fractions of a unit and to solve addition/subtraction problems using that plot, so building and computing should be fused rather than separated. Posing a total over stacked Xs directly targets the documented frequency-vs-value confusion.
sourceClaims: Grade 4 standard: make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8); solve problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions by using information presented in line plots.

Students transfer the bar-graph habit of reading bar height as a data value, confusing frequency (count / stack height) with the value of the variable; the confusion persists after instruction and appears in dot plots. This underlies totalling a plot by counting Xs rather than summing values.
learnerActions: Measure several real objects (e.g. seedlings or paper strips) to the nearest 1/8 inch using a ruler subdivided into eighths; include some objects that share a length.
Draw a number line marked in equally spaced intervals that each represent 1/8 inch, and plot one X per object at its measured value.
Mark where 2/8 lines up with 1/4 and where 4/8 lines up with 1/2 directly on the axis.
Find longest − shortest by subtracting the two fractional positions, converting to a common denominator on the scale (e.g. 1/2 − 3/8 = 4/8 − 3/8 = 1/8).
Find the total length of all objects by adding each object's value with multiplicity — a stack of three Xs at 3/8 contributes 3/8 + 3/8 + 3/8 = 9/8, not '3'.
Predict how the total changes if one more object at 1/2 is added, then check (the total rises by 1/2 = 4/8).
activities.intendedInsight: An accurate eighth scale makes equivalences (2/8 = 1/4, 4/8 = 1/2) and common denominators visible, and totalling over a plot means summing measured values with multiplicity — which is different from counting Xs.

activities.title: Compute from a given plot: difference and total
feedback: If the answer equals the count of Xs, revisit the distinction between how many Xs and how much length.
If a non-standard sum appears (e.g. denominators added, giving 6/16), reteach that same-size parts are joined with the denominator unchanged, so 3/8 + 3/8 = 6/8.
Confirm correct work by checking the common-denominator conversion against the axis ticks (e.g. 1/2 reads as 4/8).
activities.rationale: When the plot is given, the operate-on-data half of the skill — solving addition and subtraction of fraction problems from line-plot data — can be exercised in a focused, checkable way. This is a scaffold that isolates computation; it does not exercise constructing the scale or measuring to the nearest 1/8.
sourceClaims: Grade 4 standard: make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8); solve problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions by using information presented in line plots.

Students transfer the bar-graph habit of reading bar height as a data value, confusing frequency (count / stack height) with the value of the variable; the confusion persists after instruction and appears in dot plots. This underlies totalling a plot by counting Xs rather than summing values.
learnerActions: From a pre-drawn eighth-scale plot, state the longest and shortest values and compute longest − shortest over a common denominator.
Compute the total length, taking care that a stack of several Xs at one value contributes that value once per X.
Choose which of several candidate totals is correct, and explain why the count of Xs is NOT the total length.
activities.intendedInsight: Given an accurate plot, the difference and total are determined by reading positions and adding/subtracting fractions correctly, keeping multiplicity in mind.

activities.title: Reveal equivalence on the eighth scale (reference scaffold)
feedback: Confirm when the learner names an equivalence correctly; prompt 'what else is this the same as?' to surface 2/8 = 1/4.
If a stack's total is read as the number of Xs, reveal the repeated-value sum to contrast count with length.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal reference can make equivalence and stack contribution concrete and label positions, supporting the fuller build-and-compute work. As a reference it does not exercise measuring to the nearest 1/8 or performing the computations independently, so it supports rather than replaces the main activity.
learnerActions: Tap or point to a position on an eighth-scale line and read off its equivalent (2/8 = 1/4, 4/8 = 1/2).
Tap a stack of Xs to reveal its combined contribution to the total (e.g. three Xs at 3/8 reveal 3/8 + 3/8 + 3/8 = 9/8).
Name where 1/4 and 1/2 sit and what else each is the same as.
activities.intendedInsight: Equivalent fractions occupy the same point on an eighth scale, and a stack's contribution is its value repeated once per X.

constraints: Learners must construct the scale themselves and measure to the nearest 1/8 inch; a given-plot or tap-to-reveal task isolates computation or shows equivalence but does not exercise building an accurate eighth scale or measuring.
Scale-building should be assessed through actual construction; recognition-only responses do not elicit independent construction of an equal-interval scale.
Keep the one-X-per-case convention, and ensure eighth intervals are drawn equally spaced so quarter/half ticks line up.
The total must be computed by summing measured values with multiplicity, not by counting Xs; keep frequency and value explicitly distinct.

Adding fractions that have the same denominator keeps the denominator unchanged (3/8 + 3/8 = 6/8); adding denominators (giving 6/16) is an error. When denominators are related but different (e.g. 1/2 and 3/8), first rewrite them with a common denominator (1/2 = 4/8) before adding or subtracting.

An interactive panel showing live arithmetic (e.g. selecting a stack to lay out 3/8 + 3/8 + 3/8) or overlaying quarter/half ticks is an optional way to make the mechanism concrete, not a required tool; the same reasoning can be done with a ruler, drawn number line and fraction strips.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row asserted that a static image and a scale-blind quiz 'cannot' build the fusion of multiplicity and fraction addition, and that a spatial dimension or dialogue 'adds nothing'. These are catalogue-fit judgements, not established necessity claims; here they are softened to scoped affordances/limits (given-plot tasks isolate computation; tap-to-reveal is a reference).

The cited standard (4.MD.B.4) supports making the plot and solving add/subtract problems from it, but does not establish the comparative efficacy of any particular interactive or reference format; no efficacy claim is made, which is why the reference activity carries no sourceClaims.

The Kaplan et al. source documents persistent frequency-vs-value confusion in histograms/dot plots; its transfer to line-plot totalling is plausible and used to justify the total-over-stacks probe, but the source does not test this specific activity.
'Redistribution' appears in the source pedagogy as a third question type but is not separately operationalised here; difference and total are the operationalised computations.

Fresh independent review: fraction arithmetic (1/2 − 3/8 = 1/8; three at 3/8 = 9/8; +1/2 = +4/8; 3/8 + 3/8 = 6/8) verified; no categorical medium-superiority claims remain in summary, insights, actions, feedback or constraints.

probeDeeper: You have three Xs at 3/8 — how much length is that altogether, and why isn't it just 3?
To find longest minus shortest you need ½ take away 3/8 — how do you make those two comparable?
Where is ¼ on your eighth scale? What else is it the same as?
If I added one more object at ½, how would the total change?
assess.correctAnswer: Builds an equal-interval eighth-inch scale, plots one X per object, finds longest − shortest by subtracting the two fractional positions over a common denominator, and totals by adding each object's value WITH multiplicity (a stack of three at 3/8 contributes 3/8 three times), recognising 2/8 = ¼ and 4/8 = ½.

errorPatterns.pattern: When asked for total length, adds or counts the Xs (frequency) instead of summing the measured values
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point to a stack of three at 3/8 and ask 'how much length is here?'; hold apart 'how many objects' from 'how much length'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives the number of objects as the 'total', or adds each distinct axis value once while ignoring stack height

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds fractions by adding numerators and denominators (3/8 + 3/8 = 6/16)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach fraction addition as joining same-size parts using fraction bars, denominator unchanged
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Non-standard sums when totalling or differencing the measurements

errorPatterns.pattern: Spaces eighths unequally or doesn't see 2/8 = ¼ and 4/8 = ½, so scales don't line up and common denominators are missed
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay quarter and half ticks on the eighth scale to show equivalence; use a fraction strip to find the common denominator
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Mis-spaced ticks, or subtracting ½ − 3/8 without converting to a common denominator

responseLevels.gap: Cannot build an accurate eighth scale or cannot operate on the fractions; totals by counting Xs or adds denominators.
responseLevels.full: Builds an equal-interval eighth scale showing equivalence, plots one X per case, and computes both difference and total correctly — summing values with multiplicity and using common denominators — transferring to an added data point.
responseLevels.partial: Builds and reads the plot and can do one operation (e.g. the difference) but mishandles multiplicity in totals or needs prompting to find a common denominator; lists values without combining them correctly.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a ruler marked in eighths and several objects, some sharing a length. Say: 'Measure each to the nearest eighth inch, plot them, then tell me the difference between the longest and shortest, and the total length of all of them.' Watch the scale-building, and especially watch how they handle stacks of more than one X when totalling, and how they subtract the two fractional positions.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Asking for a TOTAL over stacks forces the child to separate frequency (count of Xs) from value (length) AND to add fractions correctly. A child running the bar-graph habit totals by counting Xs; a child adding numerators and denominators produces a specific wrong sum. Each error shows a different, diagnosable signature in both the plot and the arithmetic — which asking about the procedure would not reveal.

sources.claim: Grade 4 standard: make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8); solve problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions by using information presented in line plots.
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, 4.MD.B.4

sources.claim: Students transfer the bar-graph habit of reading bar height as a data value, confusing frequency (count / stack height) with the value of the variable; the confusion persists after instruction and appears in dot plots. This underlies totalling a plot by counting Xs rather than summing values.
sources.source: Kaplan, Gabrosek, Curtiss & Malone (2014), 'Investigating Student Understanding of Histograms', Journal of Statistics Education 22(2)

pedagogy.summary: Children calculate how long an event lasts from its start and end times. The reliable method is counting ON from the start to the end on a number line — jumping to the next o'clock (a number bond to 60), then whole hours, then the remaining minutes — NOT column subtraction, which fails when the hour is crossed because time is base-60, not base-10. Comparing two durations then follows from calculating each.
bestPractices: Count on from start to end via a number line: bridge to the next o'clock, add whole hours, add the remaining minutes
Make explicit WHY column subtraction fails when hours are crossed (60, not 100)
Use number bonds to 60 for the 'to the next hour' jump
Anchor in real start/end times (lessons, TV programmes)
Calculate both durations before comparing which is longer
keyRepresentations: Blank number line with jumps (to next o'clock, whole hours, remaining minutes)
Analogue / digital clocks showing start and end
Number bond to 60 for the bridging jump
commonMisconceptions: Uses column subtraction of end minus start, which breaks across the hour boundary
Thinks a later end time automatically means a longer duration
Works in 100s not 60s (treats the minutes as base-10)
Counts in the wrong direction or forgets the bridging jump to the o'clock

learn.summary: Children calculate how long an event lasts from its start and end times by counting ON from start to end on a number line: first bridge to the next o'clock (a number bond to 60), then add whole hours, then add the remaining minutes. Make explicit WHY column subtraction breaks when the end minutes are smaller than the start minutes, so you have to borrow across the hour (e.g. 4:10 − 2:50). Time is base-60 (60 minutes in an hour), not base-10. Comparing two durations follows from calculating each; a later end time does not by itself mean a longer duration.

activities.title: Build the jumps on a number line
feedback: General bridging slip (applies to any start time): if the learner makes the jump to the next o'clock too large — e.g. treating 10:15 → 11:00 as +85, or jumping 2:50 → 3:00 by more than +10 — remind them the minutes only run to 60. For 2:50 the jump to 3:00 is +10 (50 + 10 = 60); for 10:15 the jump to 11:00 is +45 (15 + 45 = 60).

If they skip the o'clock jump and land on the wrong minute, rebuild the three-part jump for the activity's own example: next o'clock first (2:50 → 3:00), then whole hours (3:00 → 4:00), then leftover minutes (4:00 → 4:10).

Column slip (a misconception, not a valid method): if, on the activity's 4:10 − 2:50 line-up or any hour-crossing subtraction, they 'borrow' as in base-10 (producing results like 0:85 for 11:00 − 10:15), show that base-10 borrowing assumes 100 minutes in an hour. An hour is 60 minutes, so counting on across the o'clock is the safe method.
activities.rationale: Seeing the jumps assemble the total, and seeing how column subtraction misleads at the minutes column, makes the base-60 structure visible as the child acts. Where a build-your-own number line is available, dragging each jump from the start time with an auto-shown bond to 60 and a running total, plus a 'try column subtraction' option that lines up end minus start, may make the mechanism concrete; a static annotated number line can show one worked example but cannot let the child build the jumps.
sourceClaims: White Rose Y3 Time (Steps 8-9) documents that children may think an event ending at a later time must have a longer duration, and may attempt to calculate duration using column subtraction (end minus start), which leads to problems when hours are crossed; the recommended model is a number line with jumps and number bonds to the next hour.

Children apply discrete whole-number, base-10 reasoning to time and cannot easily coordinate its base-60 groupings, which explains column-subtraction errors and base-10 slips when crossing the hour boundary.
learnerActions: Start at the first time (e.g. 2:50) on a blank number line.
Make the first jump to the next o'clock (2:50 → 3:00, a +10 jump) and say the number bond to 60 that produced it (50 + 10 = 60).
Make whole-hour hops next (3:00 → 4:00, +1 hour).
Add the remaining minutes (4:00 → 4:10, +10).
Keep a running total of the jumps to assemble the duration (1 hour 20 minutes).

Compare this count-on method with column subtraction: line up 4:10 − 2:50 and notice the minutes column needs borrowing, and that borrowing as if there were 100 minutes in an hour goes wrong, because the minutes are base-60, not base-10.
activities.intendedInsight: Counting on from start to end — bridging the o'clock, adding whole hours, then the remaining minutes — gives the duration reliably, and column subtraction misleads across the hour unless you remember an hour holds 60 minutes, not 100.

activities.title: Calculate then compare two durations
feedback: If the learner picks the activity that ends later without calculating, have them count on for BOTH events first, then compare the two lengths.
Use a short activity that ends late against a long one that ends early (e.g. the 8:55–9:00 versus 8:00–8:50 pair) to decouple end-time from duration.
On the crossing-the-hour item (2:50 → 4:10), a base-10 or nonsense answer signals column subtraction — return to counting on and the o'clock bridge.
activities.rationale: Anchoring problems in real start/end times (lessons, films, TV programmes) and requiring both durations to be calculated before comparing targets the 'later end = longer' misconception directly. Crossing-the-hour and decoupled end-time items are natural discriminators. These can be posed as questions, fill-in-the-blank sums, or spoken word problems; a character can pose start/end problems but cannot observe the counting-on method, so pair posed problems with the learner showing their jumps.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils should 'compare durations of events [for example, to calculate the time taken by particular events or tasks]'.

White Rose Y3 Time (Steps 8-9) documents that children may think an event ending at a later time must have a longer duration, and may attempt to calculate duration using column subtraction (end minus start), which leads to problems when hours are crossed; the recommended model is a number line with jumps and number bonds to the next hour.
learnerActions: Read a problem such as 'A lesson starts at 10:15 and ends at 11:00 — how long is it?' and count on to find 45 minutes.
Work a crossing-the-hour problem: 'A film starts at 2:50 and ends at 4:10 — how long is it?' bridging to 3:00, adding 1 hour, then +10 to reach 1 hour 20 minutes.
Compare two events, e.g. an activity from 2:20 to 3:00 versus one from 6:15 to 6:50, by calculating each duration (40 minutes vs 35 minutes) and only then deciding which is longer.
Test a tricky comparison: a 5-minute activity ending at 9:00 (so 8:55–9:00) versus one running 8:00 to 8:50 (50 minutes) — which is longer, and which ends later?
activities.intendedInsight: To compare durations you must calculate each one and compare the lengths; the event that ends later is not automatically the longer one.

constraints: Use number bonds to 60 (not 100) for the jump to the next o'clock; the minutes column does not carry in base-10.

Analogue/digital clocks showing start and end, and a blank number line with labelled jumps, support the method; a static worked number line can only annotate one example and cannot let the child build the jumps.

Recognition or multiple-choice items can assess duration and comparison but do not by themselves elicit the independent construction of the three-part jump — have the learner show or build the jumps at least once.
Scaffold the bond-to-60 jump and rehearse the three-part method rather than reteaching clock reading from scratch when the slip is in bridging, not in reading the clock.
Comparing durations depends on first calculating each duration; do not judge 'longer' by the later end time.
Keep every feedback example consistent with its activity's stated setup, or state explicitly that a slip is general to any start/end time.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched and the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Independent re-audit confirmed all worked examples are internally consistent and all feedback is anchored to its activity's figures or explicitly flagged as a general slip.

The legacy row claimed '3D adds nothing' for this task; that comparative media judgement is not established by the cited sources and has been dropped — duration work is not spatial, but no universal necessity/efficacy claim about any medium is asserted here.

Worked examples checked: 10:15→11:00 = 45 min (15+45=60); 2:50→4:10 = 10 min to 3:00, +1 hour to 4:00, +10 to 4:10 = 1 hour 20 min; 2:20→3:00 = 40 min and 6:15→6:50 = 35 min; 8:55→9:00 = 5 min versus 8:00→8:50 = 50 min. All consistent as stated.

The 0:85-style column result (from 11:00 − 10:15) is retained only as a learner misconception to be corrected, never as a valid method or answer option. Note that for 4:10 − 2:50 correct base-60 borrowing can reach 1:20, so feedback stresses the base-10 vs base-60 borrowing distinction rather than claiming column subtraction always yields a nonsense answer.

probeDeeper: 'Show me the jumps you made — where did you land first?' (o'clock bridge)
'Why doesn't 11:00 take away 10:15 give the answer if you do it in columns?' (base-60)
'This activity ends later — but is it really longer? How long is each one?'
'A 5-minute activity ends at 9:00; another runs 8:00 to 8:50 — which is longer? Which ends later?' (decouples end-time from duration)
assess.correctAnswer: Counts on 10:15 to 11:00 = 45 minutes; for 2:50 to 4:10 bridges to 3:00 (+10), +1 hour to 4:00, +10 = 1 hour 20 minutes; compares the two by their calculated lengths (40 minutes vs 35 minutes), not by which ended later.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses column subtraction (end minus start), which breaks when hours are crossed
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model counting on via a number line, bridging to the next o'clock; show explicitly that the minutes are base-60, so borrowing 10 doesn't work.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 4:10 minus 2:50 in columns and borrows base-10, or 11:00 minus 10:15 = 0:85

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks a later end time automatically means a longer duration
errorPatterns.nextMove: Calculate BOTH durations first (count on for each), then compare the lengths; show a short activity that ends late versus a long one that ends early.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the comparison item picks the activity that ends later without calculating each duration

errorPatterns.pattern: Works in 100s not 60s, or forgets the bridging jump — miscounts the step to the next o'clock
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the bond to 60 for the jump to the next o'clock (15 + 45 = 60); rehearse the three-part jump, don't reteach clock reading from scratch.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Bridges 10:15 to the next hour as +85 (base-10), or skips the o'clock jump and lands wrong

responseLevels.gap: Attempts column subtraction; judges 'longer' by the later end; can't cross the hour.
responseLevels.full: Calculates durations by counting on (bridging the o'clock, base-60), crosses the hour reliably, and compares two events by their calculated durations, not their end times.
responseLevels.partial: Counts on correctly within an hour, but slips when the hour is crossed or reverts to column subtraction, or compares by end time.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set duration problems and WATCH the method: (1) 'A lesson starts at 10:15 and ends at 11:00 — how long is it? Show me how you work it out.' (2) A problem that crosses the hour: 'A film starts at 2:50 and ends at 4:10 — how long is it?' (3) 'Which lasted longer — an activity from 2:20 to 3:00, or one from 6:15 to 6:50?' Watch whether they count on (bridging the o'clock) or attempt column subtraction, and whether the comparison rests on calculated durations or on the later end time.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The hour-crossing item (2:50 to 4:10) is the discriminator: a child using column subtraction produces a nonsense or base-10 answer, a child counting on bridges the o'clock correctly. The comparison item catches 'later end = longer'.
