pedagogy.summary: By age 10-11 children must fuse three ideas they have met separately: that a fraction IS a division (a/b = a ÷ b), that dividing gives a decimal, and that fractions, decimals and percentages are three interchangeable names for one quantity. The pedagogical work is not teaching a new procedure but building fluent, flexible movement between the three forms so a child can pick whichever form makes a comparison easiest — e.g. converting 30%, 1/3 and 0.35 to a common form to order them. The load-bearing insight is that the fraction bar means 'divide the top by the bottom', which lets 3/8 be evaluated as 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375.
bestPractices: Establish the fraction-as-division meaning explicitly: 3/8 means 3 shared into 8, and 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375 — connect the bar notation to a division the child can carry out.
Teach a small set of recall equivalents as landmarks (1/2, 1/4, 3/4, 1/5, 1/10, 1/3≈0.33) so children convert by memory for common cases and by division for the rest.
Make ordering across forms the core task: give mixed sets (30%, 1/3, 0.35) and require conversion to ONE common form before comparing — this is where the equivalence pays off.
Use the fact that percentages and decimals are hundredths and tenths to move fluidly (0.35 = 35% = 35/100), reserving division for fractions that aren't already tenths/hundredths.
Confront non-terminating cases honestly: 1/3 = 0.333... is NOT 0.3; round only when told to, and show why the division never stops.
keyRepresentations: Long/short division laid out for 3 ÷ 8 (with the decimal point and trailing zeros) to show a fraction becoming a decimal
A triple-labelled bar or hundred-grid showing the same shaded quantity named as fraction, decimal and percentage at once
A number line from 0 to 1 with fractions, decimals and percentages all plotted, so order is visible spatially
A double number line / equivalence table of the landmark fractions and their decimal & percentage partners
commonMisconceptions: Reverses the division: reads 3/8 as 8 ÷ 3 (divides the larger by the smaller out of habit), giving 2.67 instead of 0.375.
Compares mixed forms by surface digits — thinks 1/3 is largest of {30%, 1/3, 0.35} because '3 is a big number' or because the numbers look bigger, without converting to a common form.
Treats 1/3 as exactly 0.3 (or 0.33) and terminating, not recognising the recurring decimal.
Believes every fraction gives a neat terminating decimal, so is thrown when a division doesn't stop.

learn.summary: For ages 10-11, the goal is fluent, flexible movement between fractions, decimals and percentages as three names for one quantity. The load-bearing insight is that the fraction bar means 'divide the top by the bottom', so 3/8 = 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375. Learners should pick whichever form makes a comparison easiest, converting a mixed set to one common form before ordering (e.g. 30%, 1/3, 0.35 → 0.30, 0.333..., 0.35, so the order is 30% < 1/3 < 0.35). Note that 1/3 landing between 30% and 0.35 is counter-intuitive and is where the surface-digit misconception is confronted.

activities.title: Watch a fraction become a decimal: 3 ÷ 8
feedback: If you got 2.67, you divided 8 by 3 instead of 3 by 8. Re-read 3/8 as '3 shared among 8', which must be less than one whole — so it is 3 ÷ 8.
Model it concretely: 3 pizzas shared among 8 people gives each person less than half a pizza, so the answer must be below 1.
If you wrote 1/3 = 0.3, keep dividing 1 ÷ 3: the 3s never stop, so 1/3 is a little bigger than 0.3 and bigger than 30%.
If a division doesn't stop, that's expected for fractions like 1/3 — not every fraction gives a neat terminating decimal.
activities.rationale: Connecting bar notation to a division the learner actually carries out builds the fraction-as-division meaning, and watching a recurring case confronts the belief that every fraction terminates. Predicting before dividing surfaces the reversed-division habit at a teachable moment.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils 'associate a fraction with division and calculate decimal fraction equivalents [for example, 0.375] for a simple fraction [for example, 3/8]'; for simple fractions with recurring decimal equivalents pupils learn about rounding to three decimal places (statutory wording + notes).
Fraction-decimal-percentage equivalence and ordering across forms is a key Year 6 structural connection; the fraction bar (vinculum) is understood as a division.

Children commonly reverse fraction-as-division, computing a/b as b/a (dividing the larger by the smaller), rooted in the primitive 'divisor must be smaller than dividend / division makes smaller' model.
learnerActions: Before dividing, predict: will 3/8 be more than 1 or less than 1, and roughly what? Say why (3 shared among 8 people is less than one whole).
Carry out the division 3.000 ÷ 8 step by step, keeping the decimal point and trailing zeros, to reach 0.375.
Compare the result against your prediction. If you predicted more than 1, check whether you divided 3 by 8 or 8 by 3.
Try a case that never stops: carry out 1 ÷ 3 far enough to see 0.333... keep repeating, and note it does NOT equal 0.3.
Round only when told to (e.g. 1/3 ≈ 0.333 to three decimal places), and explain why the division never terminates.
activities.intendedInsight: The fraction bar means 'divide the numerator by the denominator'; 3/8 is 3 ÷ 8, and some divisions (like 1 ÷ 3) produce recurring, non-terminating decimals.

activities.title: Order a mixed set by converting to a common form
feedback: If you ranked 1/3 largest 'because 3 is a big number', convert first: 1/3 = 0.333..., which lands between 0.30 and 0.35.
Comparing by how big the written digits look is unreliable; the number line places each value by its converted size, so the order falls out of position.
To turn 30% into a comparable form, use that per cent means 'out of 100': 30% = 0.30 = 30/100.
If you treated 1/3 as exactly 0.3, place 1/3 and 0.3 as separate points — 1/3 is slightly to the right (0.333... > 0.30), so 1/3 > 30%.
activities.rationale: Ordering across forms is where cross-form equivalence pays off; requiring conversion to a common form before comparing directly targets the documented surface-digit error, and the counter-intuitive placement of 1/3 makes the need to convert felt.
sourceClaims: Comparing and ordering fractions, decimals and percentages requires converting to a common representation; comparing by surface digits (which look bigger) is a persistent, documented error.
Fraction-decimal-percentage equivalence and ordering across forms is a key Year 6 structural connection; the fraction bar (vinculum) is understood as a division.
learnerActions: Take the set 30%, 1/3 and 0.35. First predict the order smallest→largest by eye, and say why.
Convert all three to ONE common form (decimals: 0.30, 0.333..., 0.35), using that percentages are hundredths and division for 1/3.
Plot each converted value on a 0-1 number line and read off the order from position, not appearance.
Compare your conversion-based order (30% < 1/3 < 0.35) with your by-eye prediction and note where they differed — especially whether you expected 1/3 to be biggest.
Transfer the method to a new set, e.g. 30%, 2/5, 0.35: convert each (0.30, 0.40, 0.35) and say where 2/5 goes, and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Different forms cannot be reliably compared by surface digits; converting every item to one common form (then plotting on a line) makes the true order visible — and 1/3 sits between 30% and 0.35.

activities.title: Build a landmark equivalence set
feedback: If you wrote 1/3 = 0.33 exactly, flag it as approximate: the decimal recurs (0.333...), so 1/3 is a touch above 0.33 and above 30%.
Use the hundredths/tenths link to move fluidly: 0.35 = 35% = 35/100 without any new division.
A triple-labelled bar is for consolidating recall; pair it with the division and ordering tasks to practise flexible conversion, not just memory.
activities.rationale: A small set of recalled equivalents reduces load for common conversions so effort can go to the ordering work, and a shared representation reinforces that one quantity has three interchangeable names; noting which landmarks recur keeps rounding honest.
sourceClaims: Fraction-decimal-percentage equivalence and ordering across forms is a key Year 6 structural connection; the fraction bar (vinculum) is understood as a division.

Year 6 pupils 'associate a fraction with division and calculate decimal fraction equivalents [for example, 0.375] for a simple fraction [for example, 3/8]'; for simple fractions with recurring decimal equivalents pupils learn about rounding to three decimal places (statutory wording + notes).
learnerActions: For each landmark, show all three names on one shared bar or hundred-grid so the same shaded quantity is seen as fraction, decimal and percentage at once.

Match a form to its partners from memory (e.g. given 1/5, recall 0.2 and 20%); for fractions that are not landmarks, rewrite them as tenths or hundredths where easy (e.g. 3/20 = 15/100), and otherwise use division.
Note which landmarks are exact and which (like 1/3) are recurring, so you don't record 1/3 as a terminating 0.33.
activities.intendedInsight: Memorised landmark equivalents let you convert common cases instantly, reserving division for less familiar fractions, while a shared visual shows the three forms name one quantity.

constraints: A tap-to-reveal triple-labelled bar of landmark equivalents consolidates recall but does not let the learner choose and carry out a division or order an arbitrary mixed set, so it builds memory rather than the flexible conversion at the heart of this topic — pair it with active division and ordering work.

Recognition and matching checks (e.g. pairing 1/5↔0.2↔20%, or ordering a given set) can confirm the target skill but do not by themselves require the learner to independently construct a conversion; include tasks where the learner carries out 3 ÷ 8 and explains their ordering.
1/3 does not equal 0.3 or exactly 0.33: it is the recurring 0.333..., so it is slightly larger than 30%. Round only when instructed, and treat 33.3% as a rounded value too.
Read 3/8 as 3 ÷ 8 (numerator ÷ denominator), not 8 ÷ 3; the reversed division giving 2.67 is a misconception to correct, never a valid answer.

Interactive panels (a digit-by-digit division display, a draggable 0-1 ordering line, a convert-to-common-form toggle) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete; they are helpful illustrations, not required equipment, and the same tasks can be done on paper.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375 (confirmed). The reversed 8 ÷ 3 ≈ 2.666... ≈ 2.67 (confirmed as the misconception distractor, kept only in feedback/diagnosis, never as a valid answer). 1 ÷ 3 = 0.333... recurring (confirmed). Order 0.30 < 0.333... < 0.35, i.e. 30% < 1/3 < 0.35 (confirmed). Transfer set 2/5 = 0.40, so 30% < 0.35 < 2/5 (confirmed).

The source claim about reversing fraction-as-division (Fischbein et al.; Tirosh & Graeber) is marked verified:false in the source row; treat the cited mechanism as informative background, not established fact, in activity 1.
The original stated 1/3 ≈ 0.33 as a landmark; retained but flagged as approximate/recurring (0.333... ≈ 33.3%) to avoid teaching it as terminating or as an exact percentage.

Activity 3's sourceClaims: the NCETM structural-connection claim is the direct support for the three-interchangeable-names/recall principle; the statutory claim is retained only because action 4 covers the recurring/rounding sub-action, and gives partial (sub-action) support, not full principle support. No new source verification was performed.

assess.poeTask: Before dividing: 'I'm going to work out 3/8 as a decimal. First predict — will it be more than 1 or less than 1, and roughly what? Say why.' A child holding fraction-as-division predicts less than 1 (3 shared among 8) near a third-ish; a child reversing the division predicts more than 1 (8÷3). Then carry out 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375 and compare against the prediction — the mismatch is the teachable moment for the reversed-division child.
probeDeeper: You said 3/8 = 0.375 — is that bigger or smaller than 1? How do you know from the fraction itself?
How did you turn 30% into something you could compare with 1/3?
What if I'd asked you to order 30%, 2/5 and 0.35 instead — where would 2/5 go, and why?
Someone says 1/3 must be the biggest because 3 is the biggest number in the list. What would you say to them?
assess.correctAnswer: 3/8 = 0.375, found by dividing 3 ÷ 8. Order: 30% < 1/3 < 0.35 (i.e. 0.30 < 0.333... < 0.35), compared by converting all three to the same form — decimals: 0.30, 0.333..., 0.35.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses the fraction-as-division: 'I divide the big number by the small one, so 3/8 is 8 ÷ 3 = 2.67' — divides larger by smaller out of whole-number habit.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the meaning of the bar: 3/8 is 3 things shared among 8, which must be less than one, so it is 3 ÷ 8. Model with 3 pizzas shared by 8 people before re-doing the division.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 3/8 = 2.6 or 2.67, or says 'it's more than 1', and the shown method divides 8 by 3.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares mixed forms by surface digits: 'the biggest is 1/3 because 3, and 0.35 is smallest because it's tiny decimals' — ranks by how big the visible digits look rather than converting to a common form.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist on converting all three to one form first; use a 0-1 number line and plot each after converting, so the child sees the ordering fall out of position, not appearance.
errorPatterns.distractor: 1/3 < 0.35 < 30% (ordered by how small the written numbers look)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Orders without converting, e.g. places 1/3 largest or 0.35 smallest; explanation cites the size of the digits, not a common form.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats 1/3 as exactly 0.3 and terminating: 'one third is 0.3, so it's less than 0.35 and equal to 30%' — collapses the recurring decimal to one tenth.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Carry out 1 ÷ 3 far enough to see 0.333... never stop; place 1/3 and 0.3 as distinct points on the line and show 1/3 is a little bigger than 0.3, hence bigger than 30%.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 1/3 = 0.3 and consequently rates 1/3 = 30%, or cannot decide between 1/3 and 30%.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot convert 3/8 (or reverses to 8÷3), and orders the mixed set by appearance of digits with no conversion; cannot say how the three forms relate.
responseLevels.full: Divides 3÷8 = 0.375 the right way round, converts all of 30%, 1/3, 0.35 to a common form, orders them 30% < 1/3 < 0.35, and explains that comparison requires a shared form — transferring the method to a new item (e.g. 2/5) without prompting.
responseLevels.partial: Converts 3/8 correctly and knows the landmark equivalents, and can name each form, but when ordering the mixed set either doesn't convert to a common form or converts only some, so the ordering is unreliable and the comparison isn't explained.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Convert 3/8 to a decimal and show how you got it. Then take 30%, 1/3 and 0.35, put them in order from smallest to largest, and tell me how you compared them.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who genuinely holds fraction-as-division and cross-form equivalence divides 3÷8 the right way round AND converts the mixed set to a common form before ordering. A child operating on surface features reveals it two ways that a correct reasoner never would: dividing 8÷3 (bigger-by-smaller habit) and ranking 1/3 as largest 'because 3'. The reason-tier ('how you compared them') is what separates a lucky ordering from real equivalence reasoning — 1/3 sitting between 30% and 0.35 is counter-intuitive, so getting it right for a stated reason is hard to fake.

sources.claim: Year 6 pupils 'associate a fraction with division and calculate decimal fraction equivalents [for example, 0.375] for a simple fraction [for example, 3/8]'; for simple fractions with recurring decimal equivalents pupils learn about rounding to three decimal places (statutory wording + notes).
sources.source: DfE, National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study, Year 6

sources.claim: Fraction-decimal-percentage equivalence and ordering across forms is a key Year 6 structural connection; the fraction bar (vinculum) is understood as a division.
sources.source: NCETM Primary Mastery PD, Spine 3 (Fractions) Segment 3.10

sources.claim: Comparing and ordering fractions, decimals and percentages requires converting to a common representation; comparing by surface digits (which look bigger) is a persistent, documented error.
sources.source: SMART / Victorian Mathematics Developmental Continuum, 'Comparing Decimal Numbers' (Steinle & Stacey)

sources.claim: Children commonly reverse fraction-as-division, computing a/b as b/a (dividing the larger by the smaller), rooted in the primitive 'divisor must be smaller than dividend / division makes smaller' model.
sources.source: Fischbein et al., primitive models of division; Tirosh & Graeber on division misconceptions

pedagogy.summary: A fraction a/b means a ÷ b — the fraction bar IS a division sign. 3/4 is what each person gets when 3 wholes are shared equally among 4, and that is exactly 3 ÷ 4. This unifies fractions and division: every division has an exact answer even when the dividend is smaller than the divisor (3 ÷ 4 = 3/4), and any whole-number division with a remainder can be written as a mixed number (50 ÷ 9 = 5 5/9, the leftover 5 shared among 9). The inverse check 3/4 × 4 = 3 confirms the meaning.
bestPractices: Derive it from equal-sharing of SEVERAL wholes: share 3 bars among 4 by cutting each bar into quarters — each person collects 3 quarters, so 3 ÷ 4 = 3/4
Make the bar-as-division-sign explicit and verify every result with the inverse multiplication (3/4 × 4 = 3)
Connect remainders to fractional parts: 50 ÷ 9 gives 5 each with 5 left, and the 5 shared among 9 is 5/9, so 5 5/9
Contrast a ÷ b with b ÷ a (3 ÷ 4 vs 4 ÷ 3) so the direction of division carries meaning, heading off the 'always divide the bigger by the smaller' habit
Use the sharing model to show that a ÷ b is defined and exact even when a < b
keyRepresentations: Equal-sharing / partition diagram (3 bars each cut into 4, one quarter to each person)
Number line locating 3/4 and 3 ÷ 4 at the same point
The ÷ ↔ fraction-bar equivalence written side by side
Long division producing a fractional (not just whole + remainder) answer
commonMisconceptions: 'You can't divide a smaller number by a larger one', so 3 ÷ 4 is declared impossible or flipped to 4 ÷ 3
Reverses to bigger ÷ smaller (computes 3/8 as 8 ÷ 3)
Stops at a whole-number remainder ('5 remainder 5') instead of expressing it as 5 5/9
Treats 3/4 as only '3 out of 4 parts', unconnected to the division 3 ÷ 4

learn.summary: Teach a/b as a ÷ b — the fraction bar means divide — by having learners share several wholes equally among more people than there are wholes. Sharing 3 bars among 4 children gives each 3/4, making 3 ÷ 4 = 3/4 a result learners produce and see, not a rule to memorise. Verify with the inverse (3/4 × 4 = 3) and extend to division with remainders expressed as mixed numbers (50 ÷ 9 = 5 5/9, the leftover 5 shared among 9). Directly contrasting a÷b with b÷a keeps the direction of division meaningful.

activities.title: Share the bars: discover 3 ÷ 4 = 3/4
feedback: If a learner predicts it is impossible, don't correct the prediction — proceed to cut and deal, then revisit: everyone got 3 quarters, so 3 ÷ 4 is defined and equals 3/4.
If a learner flips to 4 ÷ 3, share 4 bars among 3 separately and place the two results side by side so the different answers show the direction of division carries meaning.
Confirm the inverse check out loud: four lots of 3/4 reassemble the original 3 bars, so 3/4 must be the right share.
activities.rationale: Equal-partitioning/sharing is a well-documented foundation for understanding a fraction as a quotient. Performing the share is intended to help resolve the 'you can't divide a smaller number by a larger' belief through a concrete action, and predicting before cutting is meant to surface that belief so the observed 3/4 can confront it. Contrasting a÷b with b÷a is aimed at heading off the 'always divide the bigger by the smaller' habit. These are research-informed proposals, not tested interventions.
sourceClaims: CCSS 5.NF.B.3: interpret a fraction as division of the numerator by the denominator (a/b = a ÷ b). It gives the exact examples this record uses: interpret 3/4 as 3 ÷ 4, noting 3/4 × 4 = 3 and that sharing 3 wholes among 4 people gives each 3/4; and 'if 9 people share a 50-pound sack of rice equally by weight, how many pounds each?' (50 ÷ 9 = 5 5/9, between 5 and 6). Answers to whole-number division can be fractions or mixed numbers.
Fractions arise from equal partitioning/sharing and are numbers in their own right; the equal-sharing interpretation underpins understanding a fraction as a quotient.

Üzel (2018), a peer-reviewed study of 84 eighth-graders, lists among documented division-of-fractions misconceptions 'Dividend must be bigger than divisor', 'Result must be bigger than 1' and 'Results must be integer number', tracing them to over-generalising whole-number reasoning ('multiplication enlarges; division reduces'); students over-apply memorised rules rather than reasoning about the quantities.
learnerActions: Set up the problem: 3 identical chocolate bars to share equally among 4 children.
BEFORE cutting, predict and give a reason: can everyone get the same, and if so how much each? Sit with the 'there aren't enough bars' feeling if it arises.
Cut each bar into 4 equal quarters.
Deal one quarter from every bar to each child, then count what ends up on each plate (3 quarters).
Write the result as a division: 3 ÷ 4 = 3/4.
Check in reverse: show that 3/4 × 4 rebuilds the 3 whole bars.
Compare directions: share 4 bars among 3 children and work out 4 ÷ 3 = 1 1/3; note that 3 ÷ 4 and 4 ÷ 3 give different answers.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction a/b is exactly the quotient a ÷ b; you can divide a smaller number by a larger one and the answer is a fraction. The order of division matters, so 3 ÷ 4 ≠ 4 ÷ 3.

activities.title: Remainders are divisions too: 50 ÷ 9 = 5 5/9
feedback: If a learner writes '5 r5' (leaving the remainder unshared) or '5.5' (mis-reading remainder 5 as a half — note 50 ÷ 9 ≈ 5.56, not 5.5), both are incomplete or incorrect: return to the sack and share the 5 leftover pounds among the same 9 people, giving 5/9 each, so 5 5/9.

Reinforce that in this rice problem '5 remainder 5' is an unfinished answer: rice can be split, so the leftover 5 pounds can be divided further by the same divisor, 9. (With things that can't be split, like people or cars, a whole-number answer with a remainder can be the right answer.)
activities.rationale: Connecting remainders to fractional parts extends the fraction-as-division idea to a new case and is intended to counter the 'results must be an integer' / stop-at-remainder error. Transferring to a different context (rice, not bars) is intended to probe genuine understanding rather than a memorised bar routine. Proposed activity, not an evaluated one.
sourceClaims: CCSS 5.NF.B.3: interpret a fraction as division of the numerator by the denominator (a/b = a ÷ b). It gives the exact examples this record uses: interpret 3/4 as 3 ÷ 4, noting 3/4 × 4 = 3 and that sharing 3 wholes among 4 people gives each 3/4; and 'if 9 people share a 50-pound sack of rice equally by weight, how many pounds each?' (50 ÷ 9 = 5 5/9, between 5 and 6). Answers to whole-number division can be fractions or mixed numbers.

Üzel (2018), a peer-reviewed study of 84 eighth-graders, lists among documented division-of-fractions misconceptions 'Dividend must be bigger than divisor', 'Result must be bigger than 1' and 'Results must be integer number', tracing them to over-generalising whole-number reasoning ('multiplication enlarges; division reduces'); students over-apply memorised rules rather than reasoning about the quantities.
learnerActions: Pose: 9 people share a 50-pound sack of rice equally by weight — how many pounds each?
Give out whole pounds first: 5 each uses 45 pounds, leaving 5 pounds.
Decide what to do with the leftover 5 pounds: share those 5 among the 9 people too.
Express that leftover share as a fraction: 5 ÷ 9 = 5/9.
Combine to the mixed number: 5 5/9 pounds each.
Sanity-check the size: the answer lies between 5 and 6.
activities.intendedInsight: A whole-number division with a remainder has an exact answer as a mixed number; the remainder is itself a division (the leftover shared among the same group).

activities.title: Check and discriminate: name the division and verify
feedback: If a learner answers 3/4 but calls it only 'three shaded of four' with no link to division, show the share and the division produce the SAME 3/4, then verify 3/4 × 4 = 3 to connect the two views.
If a learner flips to 4 ÷ 3, deal 4 bars among 3 to show 4 ÷ 3 is a different question with a different answer.
Treat a correct 'how much each' answer given with only a part-of-whole reason as partial: prompt for the division name and the inverse check before counting it as full understanding.
activities.rationale: Checkable items with carefully chosen wrong-answer options are intended to surface the reversal (computing 3/8 as 8 ÷ 3), the 'impossible' belief, and the stop-at-remainder error. Requiring both the answer and its division name with an inverse check is intended to distinguish rote part-of-whole reading from quotient understanding. Recognition and fill-in items can assess and rehearse the link but do not by themselves require the learner to perform and feel the share, so pair them with the sharing activity.
sourceClaims: CCSS 5.NF.B.3: interpret a fraction as division of the numerator by the denominator (a/b = a ÷ b). It gives the exact examples this record uses: interpret 3/4 as 3 ÷ 4, noting 3/4 × 4 = 3 and that sharing 3 wholes among 4 people gives each 3/4; and 'if 9 people share a 50-pound sack of rice equally by weight, how many pounds each?' (50 ÷ 9 = 5 5/9, between 5 and 6). Answers to whole-number division can be fractions or mixed numbers.

Üzel (2018), a peer-reviewed study of 84 eighth-graders, lists among documented division-of-fractions misconceptions 'Dividend must be bigger than divisor', 'Result must be bigger than 1' and 'Results must be integer number', tracing them to over-generalising whole-number reasoning ('multiplication enlarges; division reduces'); students over-apply memorised rules rather than reasoning about the quantities.
learnerActions: Given a sharing situation (e.g. 3 bars among 4 children), state how much each gets AND which division it represents.
Explain how to check the answer using inverse multiplication (3/4 × 4 = 3).

Answer a short set of linked items: 3 ÷ 4 = ? (compare against the tempting wrong answers 1 1/3 (which comes from working out 4 ÷ 3 instead) and 'impossible', both labelled as incorrect answers to 3 ÷ 4); fill in 50 ÷ 9 = 5 __/9; match each division to its fraction or mixed-number result.
Say in your own words why a share of 3 bars among 4 is less than one whole each.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to name 3/4 as 3 ÷ 4 and verify it with ×4 — not just read it as 'three out of four parts' — is what shows the division meaning has been grasped.

constraints: Target age 10–11; conceptual objective: interpret a/b as a ÷ b and solve whole-number division problems with fractional/mixed-number answers.
Derive the result from equal-sharing of SEVERAL wholes (not one whole cut up), so the smaller-divided-by-larger case is genuinely enacted.
Let the learner attempt to share before cutting so the 'not enough bars' impasse is felt before it is resolved; keep the prediction uncorrected until the share is performed.
Always close the loop with the inverse check (3/4 × 4 = 3) — naming the division alone is not sufficient evidence of understanding.

A static picture of finished shares (e.g. tap a plate to reveal '3 quarters = 3 ÷ 4') can illustrate the result and serve as a reference, but does not let the learner perform the share or experience the initial impasse; use it as a scaffold or companion, not as the main activity.

Checkable fill-in/matching items rehearse and assess the link and surface the reversal and stop-at-remainder errors, but recognition-only responses do not require independent construction of the share; pair them with hands-on sharing.

Represent the quotient in more than one way where possible (sharing diagram, number line placing 3/4 and 3 ÷ 4 at the same point, long division yielding a fractional answer) rather than relying on a single model.

Present reversal (giving 1 1/3, the value of 4 ÷ 3, as the answer to 3 ÷ 4; computing 3/8 as 8 ÷ 3) and 'impossible' only as labelled wrong-answer options to confront, never as valid methods. 4 ÷ 3 = 1 1/3 is itself true and may be worked out as a separate comparison question.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic self-audit (all confirmed): 3 ÷ 4 = 3/4; 3/4 × 4 = 3; 4 ÷ 3 = 1 1/3; 50 ÷ 9: 9×5 = 45, remainder 5, 5/9 each, so 5 5/9, which lies between 5 and 6 (decimal ≈ 5.56). No errors found; the reversal, 'impossible', '5 r5' and '5.5' are presented only as labelled wrong answers, never as valid answers.

The source listed two distinct 'bigger ÷ smaller' examples — the reversal of 3 ÷ 4 to 4 ÷ 3 = 1 1/3, and computing 3/8 as 8 ÷ 3. Both are preserved as misconception/wrong-answer patterns, not as correct methods.

The Üzel (2018) study concerns division OF fractions among eighth-graders; it documents the relevant 'dividend must be bigger', 'result must be >1', 'result must be integer' misconceptions but is not direct evidence about teaching a/b = a ÷ b to 10–11 year-olds. Treat its citation as support for the existence of the misconceptions, not for the efficacy of these activities.

Non-preferred artefact judgements from the source ('3D depth adds nothing', 'dialogue cannot teach this', static image 'cannot let the child perform the sharing') are catalog-fit opinions, not established pedagogical laws; recast as narrow scaffold limits in constraints without asserting universal necessity of any medium.
Source confidence was labelled 'high' and claims 'verified:true'; this rewrite does not independently upgrade or re-verify those ratings.

assess.poeTask: Before any cutting, ask: 'Can we share these 3 bars equally among 4 children so everyone gets the same, and if so how much each?' Have the child PREDICT and give a reason. Many predict it is impossible, or that each gets 'less than one but I can't say how much'. Then share for real — cut each bar into quarters and deal them out — and each child holds 3/4. The pre-cut reason is the diagnostic: a child expecting 'impossible' reveals the 'can't divide smaller by larger' belief, which the observed 3/4 directly refutes.
probeDeeper: 9 people share a 50-pound sack equally — how many pounds each? What do you do with the 5 pounds left after everyone has 5?
How could you check that 3/4 is the right share — what is 3/4 × 4?
Is 3 ÷ 4 the same as 4 ÷ 3? Share 4 bars among 3 children and compare the two answers.
If each bar is one whole, why is each child's share less than a whole here?
assess.correctAnswer: Each child gets 3/4 of a bar. This represents 3 ÷ 4 (the fraction bar means divide), and it checks because 3/4 × 4 = 3 — the three original bars.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'You can't share 3 among 4 — there aren't enough bars', so declares it impossible or flips it to 4 ÷ 3 = 1⅓
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the sharing engine: cut each of the 3 bars into 4 and deal them out; everyone gets 3 quarters, so 3 ÷ 4 is defined and equals 3/4. Contrast with 4 ÷ 3 to show direction matters.
errorPatterns.distractor: 3 ÷ 4 can't be done because 3 is smaller than 4
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 3 ÷ 4 can't be done, or gives 1⅓ by dividing the larger by the smaller

errorPatterns.pattern: Gives 3/4 but cannot connect it to division — 'it just means 3 parts out of 4', with no link to 3 ÷ 4 and no way to check
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the sharing produces the SAME 3/4 as the division; verify 3/4 × 4 = 3 to link the two views.
errorPatterns.distractor: 3/4 just means 3 parts out of 4 — it has nothing to do with dividing
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct tier-1 answer, but tier-2 reason is 'three shaded of four' and the child cannot say it is 3 ÷ 4 or verify with × 4

errorPatterns.pattern: Stops at a whole-number remainder for the sack problem — '5 remainder 5' — and cannot express the leftover as 5/9
errorPatterns.nextMove: Share the leftover 5 pounds among the 9 people: that is 5/9 each, so 5 5/9. The remainder is itself a division.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the 50 ÷ 9 probe, writes '5 r5' or '5.5' and treats the remainder as un-shareable

responseLevels.gap: Declares 3 ÷ 4 impossible or reverses it to 4 ÷ 3; stops at '5 remainder 5'; treats 3/4 as parts with no division meaning.
responseLevels.full: States each gets 3/4 = 3 ÷ 4, justifies by sharing, verifies 3/4 × 4 = 3, and solves 50 ÷ 9 = 5 5/9 by sharing the remainder — transferring the bar-as-division idea to a new case.
responseLevels.partial: Gets 3/4 each and can say it is 3 ÷ 4 in the sharing case, but cannot verify with the inverse (× 4) or extend to 50 ÷ 9 = 5 5/9.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are 3 identical chocolate bars to share equally among 4 children. How much does each child get? Then tell me: what division does this sharing represent, and how could you check your answer is right?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The first tier (how much each gets) can be answered '3/4' from part-of-whole habit. The second tier — naming it as 3 ÷ 4 AND checking with the inverse × 4 — is where understanding shows. A child who holds 'you can't divide a smaller number by a larger' declares the share impossible or flips to 4 ÷ 3; a child who sees 3/4 only as 'three out of four' cannot connect it to a division or verify it. Reasoning correctly and reasoning wrongly produce visibly different tier-2 answers.

pedagogy.summary: Children quantify capacity: how many cupfuls fill a container (non-standard units), then litres (standard), recorded as a number + unit. It uses repeated filling and pouring with IDENTICAL units and rests on the same unit-size principle as length and mass — a bigger cup means fewer cupfuls fill the same container. Reading a marked measuring vessel means valuing its intervals.
bestPractices: Fill with identical cups and count the cupfuls, recording number + unit ('4 cups', '2 litres')
Keep the unit consistent — mixing cup sizes breaks the count
Fill each cup to the same level (brim or a mark) so cupfuls are equal
Introduce the litre and a marked measuring jug; read the level against the intervals
Estimate first, then check by filling
keyRepresentations: Filling a container cupful-by-cupful with identical cups
A marked measuring jug / litre jug
The count record ('4 cups', '2 litres')
Identical unit-cups (equal measures)
commonMisconceptions: Uses different-sized cups yet counts 'more cupfuls = holds more' (unit-size ignorance)
Fills cups inconsistently (part-full) but counts them as equal
Reads a measuring jug by marks rather than intervals; misjudges a level between graduations
Loses count or spills, then reports the count anyway

learn.summary: Young children (around 5-6) quantify capacity by repeated filling and pouring with IDENTICAL units: counting how many cupfuls fill a container (non-standard units), then meeting the litre and a marked measuring jug (standard units), recording each result as a number + unit ('4 cups', '2 litres'). The core insight — shared with length and mass — is the inverse relationship: a bigger cup means FEWER cupfuls fill the same container. Reading a marked vessel means valuing its intervals, not just counting marks. Real water play is the natural companion to any screen model.

activities.title: Fill, count, record — then swap the cup
feedback: If the learner says a bigger cup needs MORE cupfuls, fill the same jug with both a big and a small cup and count both side by side: bigger cup, fewer cupfuls. Connect to 'larger unit → fewer units', as with length and mass.
If cups are poured part-full or overfilled but counted as equal, prompt: fill every cup to the same mark or brim before pouring, then re-count. This is a procedural fix, not a concept reteach.
If the learner loses count or spills and reports the count anyway, restart the count and agree to pour carefully so the tally stays accurate.
activities.rationale: Capacity is quantified by repeated equal-unit iteration, and holding the container fixed while only the cup size changes makes the inverse relationship observable rather than told. Insisting on identical, equally-filled units targets the common unit-size-ignorance misconception.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils 'measure and begin to record' capacity and volume; Year 2 pupils choose and use appropriate standard units to estimate and measure capacity (litres/ml) to the nearest appropriate unit using measuring vessels.

NCETM Year 1 introduces capacity units through equivalence and a unit greater than the item — 'comparing the capacity of a cup and a carton by filling each and pouring into matching bottles' — and frames measurement as comparison/equivalence as a practical activity.

The larger the unit, the fewer units in a given measurement (inverse relationship between unit size and count); counting discrete items can wrongly convince children that unit size doesn't matter, when in measurement it is critical.
learnerActions: Fill a container cupful by cupful using identical cups, filling each cup to the same mark or brim, and keep a running count (e.g. pour until the count climbs to 8).
Record the result as a number and unit, e.g. 'the jug = 8 cups'.
Now fill the SAME container again using a bigger cup, filling each to the brim, and count again (e.g. this time only 4).
Say out loud what changed: the container didn't change, so why did the count change? Record 'the jug = 4 big cups'.
Estimate first, then check by filling, for a new container.
activities.intendedInsight: The same container needs fewer cupfuls when the cup is bigger — a larger unit gives a smaller count (inverse relationship) — and a capacity measurement is only meaningful when the units are identical and consistently filled.

activities.title: Read the measuring jug by its intervals
feedback: If the learner counts the marks to get the number, pause and ask what one interval is worth first, then read the level to the nearest graduation.
If the learner can't read a level that falls between marks, discuss which graduation it is nearest to and why.

If the learner can't explain how they knew a line means half a litre, work out the interval value together: find two whole-litre marks, count how many equal spaces lie between them, and share accordingly.
Confirm correct readings by restating the interval value and the level together (e.g. 'each space is half a litre, and the water is at the second line above 0, so 1 litre').
activities.rationale: Standard-unit measurement at this stage requires reading graduated vessels, and distinguishing interval value from mark-counting addresses a specific reading error.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils 'measure and begin to record' capacity and volume; Year 2 pupils choose and use appropriate standard units to estimate and measure capacity (litres/ml) to the nearest appropriate unit using measuring vessels.
learnerActions: Work out what one interval on the jug is worth: find two labelled whole-litre marks, count the equal spaces between them, and share the litre between them (e.g. if one unlabelled line sits halfway between the 0 and 1 litre marks, there are two equal spaces, so each space is worth half a litre and that line marks half a litre).
Read the water level to the nearest interval and say how much water is in the jug.
Practise with a level that falls between two graduations and judge the nearest mark.
Explain how you knew a particular line means half a litre — justify it from the spacing you counted, don't just count lines.
Introduce the litre as a standard unit and record readings with number + unit.
activities.intendedInsight: A measuring vessel is read by valuing the spaces (intervals) between marks against the level, not by simply counting lines — the same skill as reading a ruler or dial.

activities.title: Practice and check: cupful counts, jug reading, and ordering
feedback: For the bigger-cup item, if 'more' is chosen, return to filling the same jug with both cups and counting; the bigger-cup-more-cupfuls confusion is the natural one to resolve by doing.

For the '4 big cups but 8 small cups — how can it be both?' probe: the container never changed, so both counts are correct. The big cup holds more, so fewer of them fill the jug; the small cup holds less, so more are needed — that is the inverse relationship, not a contradiction.
For a wrong jug reading, re-establish the interval value before re-reading.
Treat the egg-cup probe as a fresh case: a tinier cup holds less, so MORE cupfuls are needed — the inverse relationship again.
activities.rationale: Scored and discussion items check whether the inverse relationship and interval-reading transfer beyond the original activity; the bigger-cup confusion makes a genuine discriminating distractor because children often assume a bigger unit gives a bigger count. Recognition items confirm but do not by themselves elicit the independent filling, pouring and reading performance.
sourceClaims: The larger the unit, the fewer units in a given measurement (inverse relationship between unit size and count); counting discrete items can wrongly convince children that unit size doesn't matter, when in measurement it is critical.
learnerActions: Complete fill-in items such as 'the jug = ___ cupfuls' after a filling activity.
Answer 'read the measuring jug' items where you identify the level to the nearest interval.
Decide whether a bigger cup needs MORE or FEWER cupfuls to fill the same container, and explain why.
Sequence several containers by capacity.
Answer the probe: 'You needed 4 big cups but 8 small cups for the same jug — how can it be both?' and 'If you filled the jug with a tiny egg-cup instead of a mug, would you need more or fewer? Why?'
activities.intendedInsight: Secure that identical units and the inverse relationship govern capacity counts, and that jug readings depend on interval value — able to apply these to fresh cases.

constraints: Use identical cups filled to the same level (brim or mark) for any count; mixing cup sizes or part-full cups breaks the comparison and should be corrected before counting.
Keep the container fixed when demonstrating the unit-size effect, so only the cup changes.
A static tap-to-reveal jug ('this line is half a litre') can teach interval-reading but does not provide the filling/unit-swap experience; pair it with actual filling.
Recognition or multiple-choice items confirm understanding but do not elicit the independent pouring, counting and reading that the objective requires; keep hands-on filling central.
Real water play is the intended companion to any on-screen pouring model; a screen counter and a water tray teach via different experiences and neither is claimed as universally necessary.
Record every measurement as a number plus its unit so the unit is never dropped.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row asserted a 2D pouring simulation is 'ideal', that dialogue 'cannot supply' pouring/reading practice, and that 3D 'adds nothing' beyond realism. These are catalog preferences, not established efficacy claims; they have been softened to affordance/limit statements. Hands-on water play and an optional on-screen counter/cup-swap toggle are presented as concrete mechanisms, not mandatory ones.

Optional interaction examples preserved from the source: tap-to-pour cupfuls with a live counter, a cup-size toggle that re-fills the same jug, and tap-to-reveal interval labels. These make the mechanism concrete but are not required implementations.

The inherited age range (5-6, Year 1) is retained; reading graduated litre vessels to the nearest interval maps more to Year 2 in the cited curriculum. Not altered here, flagged for a teacher to pitch appropriately.

Activity 2's interval-value step was reworded so the child derives the value by counting equal spaces between labelled whole-litre marks rather than being told it, so the later 'how did you know?' justification is coherent.

probeDeeper: 'You needed 4 big cups but 8 small cups for the same jug — how can it be both?'
'If you filled the jug with a tiny egg-cup instead of a mug, would you need more or fewer? Why?' (inverse relationship, fresh case)
'On the jug, how did you know this line means half a litre?'
assess.correctAnswer: (1) Fills with consistently-full identical cups and reports 'N cupfuls', recording the unit. (2) FEWER cupfuls, because a bigger cup holds more so fewer of them fill the same jug (inverse relationship). (3) Reads the jug by valuing the intervals to the water level.

errorPatterns.pattern: Unit-size ignorance — 'a bigger cup means MORE cupfuls', or compares containers by cupful-count using different cups
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fill the jug with a big cup and a small cup and count both — bigger cup, fewer cupfuls; insist on identical units and connect to 'larger unit → fewer units'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task 2 says Priya needs more cupfuls with a bigger cup; or judges 'holds more' by a count taken with different-sized cups

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads a measuring jug by counting marks rather than valuing intervals, or misjudges a level between graduations
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish what one interval is worth first, then read the level to the nearest graduation — as with a ruler or dial.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task 3 counts the lines to get the number, or can't read a level that falls between marks

errorPatterns.pattern: Inconsistent filling — pours part-full or overfilled cups but counts them as equal
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fill every cup to the same mark or brim before pouring, and re-count — a procedural prompt, not a concept reteach.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Fills cups to different levels, or spills, and reports the count anyway

responseLevels.gap: Counts cupfuls with inconsistent or non-identical units; thinks a bigger cup gives more cupfuls; reads a jug by its marks.
responseLevels.full: Quantifies capacity with identical units, explains that a larger unit gives fewer units for the same container, and reads a measuring vessel by valuing its intervals.
responseLevels.partial: Fills consistently and counts with identical units, but is thrown when the unit size changes (can't explain the different count) or when reading a level between graduations.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a jug to fill, a set of identical small cups, a larger cup, and a measuring jug marked in intervals. Watch how they work: (1) 'Use this cup to find how many cupfuls fill this jug.' (2) 'Priya used a bigger cup to fill the same jug — will she need more cupfuls or fewer? Why?' (3) 'Read this measuring jug — how much water is in it?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Item 2 is the unit-size discriminator — the child who thinks more cupfuls always means more capacity predicts 'more' with a bigger cup; item 1 catches consistent filling; item 3 catches the marks-vs-intervals reading error.

sources.claim: Year 1 pupils 'measure and begin to record' capacity and volume; Year 2 pupils choose and use appropriate standard units to estimate and measure capacity (litres/ml) to the nearest appropriate unit using measuring vessels.
sources.source: National Curriculum in England: Mathematics, Years 1 & 2 Measurement (statutory), gov.uk

sources.claim: NCETM Year 1 introduces capacity units through equivalence and a unit greater than the item — 'comparing the capacity of a cup and a carton by filling each and pouring into matching bottles' — and frames measurement as comparison/equivalence as a practical activity.
sources.source: NCETM Primary Mastery Assessment Materials, Year 1 (Measurement Big Ideas)

sources.claim: The larger the unit, the fewer units in a given measurement (inverse relationship between unit size and count); counting discrete items can wrongly convince children that unit size doesn't matter, when in measurement it is critical.
sources.source: CCSS K–5 Geometric Measurement Progression (2012), Grade 2 2.MD.2 — ISBE mirror

pedagogy.summary: Children extend telling time to reading the nearest FIVE minutes on an analogue clock, writing it in 12-hour digital notation, and labelling it a.m. or p.m. The procedure rests on counting the clock's 12 intervals in fives (each interval = 5 minutes, via the 5 times-table), deciding whether a time is 'past' (right of the 12-6 line) or 'to' (left) the hour, and — for digital — using a colon, not a decimal point. a.m./p.m. requires grasping that the same clock time occurs twice a day, split at noon and midnight.
bestPractices: Count round the clock in 5s, tying each numeral to its minute value (numeral 4 -> 20 minutes, not 4)
Partition the clock vertically 12 to 6 to decide past (right) vs to (left) the hour
Match each analogue time to its 12-hour digital form and back, saying it aloud both ways
Anchor a.m./p.m. to real daily events (breakfast a.m., bedtime p.m.) and stress that each clock time happens twice a day
Record digital times with a colon, never a decimal point
keyRepresentations: Analogue clock with moveable hands
Counting the 12 intervals in fives (5 times-table)
Vertical 12-to-6 partition for past/to
12-hour digital display (h:mm)
A daily timeline split at noon and midnight for a.m./p.m.
commonMisconceptions: Reads the numeral the minute hand points to as the minutes (points to 4 -> '4 minutes past')
Confuses times past and times to the hour
Insecure 5 times-table blocks fluent counting of minutes
Writes a decimal point instead of a colon (3.25)
Thinks there are 100 minutes in an hour, so 50 past 3 = 50 to 4
Confuses a.m. and p.m. (1 a.m. 'should be' 1 p.m. because it feels late); doesn't know noon/midnight or that each time occurs twice a day

learn.summary: Children extend telling time to reading analogue clocks to the nearest five minutes, writing that time in 12-hour digital notation (h:mm with a colon), labelling it a.m. or p.m., and rewriting it in 24-hour notation (hh:mm). The core procedure: count the clock's 12 intervals in fives so each numeral maps to its minute value (numeral 4 -> 20 minutes, not 4); use a vertical 12-to-6 partition to decide 'past' (right) versus 'to' (left) the hour, with 'to' times named against the NEXT hour; anchor a.m./p.m. to real daily events, understanding that each clock time occurs twice a day, split at noon and midnight; and convert to 24-hour time (from 1 p.m. onwards add 12 to the hour, so 3:40 p.m. = 15:40; a.m. hours stay the same, written with two digits, e.g. 8:05 a.m. = 08:05; the 12 o'clock hour after midnight becomes 00, e.g. 12:15 a.m. = 00:15, and the noon hour stays 12, e.g. 12:15 p.m. = 12:15). Activities below include a manipulable clock (preferred), practice/discrimination tasks, a static labelling scaffold, and an elicitation conversation, each with its own pedagogical purpose.

activities.title: Drag the minute hand and watch the count-in-fives and digital readout
feedback: If the child reads the numeral literally (4 -> '4 minutes past'), re-run the count-in-fives tape aloud pairing each numeral with x5 until the 4 -> 20 link is fluent.
If the child keeps counting past the half hour ('40 past 3' for 3:40), point to the 12-6 partition: right is past, left is to, and 'to' times belong to the NEXT hour, so 3:40 is 'twenty to four'.

If the child treats the time as a decimal (e.g. thinks 3.50 means half past three, or that minutes run up to 99), model the colon convention and count the real 60 minutes on the dial to show the hour is 60, not 100.
If the child assigns a.m./p.m. by how late it feels, slide the day-strip marker so the same hand position lands once in the morning and once after noon, 12 hours apart.
activities.rationale: Reading to five minutes, the past/to decision, the analogue-to-digital rewrite and the twice-a-day idea are live-state relationships; letting the child move the hand and see the tape, readout, partition and day-strip respond is intended to make the numeral-to-minutes rule and the twice-a-day split visible rather than merely stated. The tape, 12-6 highlighter and day-strip marker are concrete feedback examples, not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils should 'tell and write the time from an analogue clock ... and 12-hour and 24-hour clocks' and 'estimate and read time with increasing accuracy to the nearest minute ... use vocabulary such as o'clock, am/pm, morning, afternoon, noon and midnight'.

White Rose Y3 Time documents the exact pupil errors: reading the numeral the minute hand points to as the minutes ('minute hand on 4 -> 4 minutes past'); confusing times past and to; writing a decimal point instead of a colon; thinking there are 100 minutes in an hour (50 past 3 = 50 to 4); confusing am/pm ('1 am should be 1 pm because it is late'); and not knowing noon/midnight or that times occur twice a day. Models: count the 12 intervals in fives (5x table), vertical 12-6 partition for past/to.

Children apply discrete whole-number reasoning to clock reading and struggle to coordinate the non-standard groupings of 12 and 60; the hour hand is significantly harder to read than the minute hand, and hour and minute are often read separately.
learnerActions: Drag the minute hand around a moveable-hands clock and watch a 'count in 5s' tape (5, 10, 15, 20...) unroll around the rim as a digital readout ticks alongside.
Pause when the minute hand reaches the numeral 4 and confirm the tape and readout say 20 minutes, not 4 — then do the same for numeral 8 (40 minutes).
Watch a vertical 12-to-6 line shade one colour on the right (past) and another on the left (to), and read 3:40 aloud as 'twenty TO four'.

Flip an a.m./p.m. toggle that slides a marker along a day-strip so the SAME hand position recurs 12 hours later — once in the morning (e.g. 8 o'clock breakfast, a.m.) and again 12 hours on in the evening (p.m.).
Write the shown time as h:mm using a colon with its a.m./p.m. label (e.g. 3:25 p.m.), then rewrite it in 24-hour notation (e.g. 15:25; 8:05 a.m. = 08:05).
activities.intendedInsight: Each clock numeral stands for its five-times value, 'to' times are named against the next hour, and every clock position recurs 12 hours later, so each clock time happens twice in one day, split at noon and midnight.

activities.title: Read, convert and sort: discrimination practice
feedback: '3:40' is 'twenty to four', not 'forty past three' — the minute hand is left of the 12-6 line, so name it against the next hour.
When a child treats the minutes as a decimal (e.g. 3.50 read as half past three), re-show the colon convention and count the 60 minutes on the dial so the hour is 60, not 100.
If a.m./p.m. sorting goes by 'how late it feels', revisit the noon/midnight split and that each clock time occurs twice a day.
activities.rationale: Matching, forced-choice and sorting items score cleanly and make natural discriminating items that help distinguish a child who runs the procedure from one who reads the numeral or display literally. Recognition and selection practice checks and rehearses the rule but does not by itself require the child to physically work the hands or construct the reading from scratch.
sourceClaims: White Rose Y3 Time documents the exact pupil errors: reading the numeral the minute hand points to as the minutes ('minute hand on 4 -> 4 minutes past'); confusing times past and to; writing a decimal point instead of a colon; thinking there are 100 minutes in an hour (50 past 3 = 50 to 4); confusing am/pm ('1 am should be 1 pm because it is late'); and not knowing noon/midnight or that times occur twice a day. Models: count the 12 intervals in fives (5x table), vertical 12-6 partition for past/to.
learnerActions: Match analogue clock faces (with a.m./p.m. given) to their 12-hour and 24-hour digital times (and back), e.g. twenty to four in the afternoon = 3:40 p.m. = 15:40.
Answer discriminating questions such as 'Is 3:40 forty past three or twenty to four?'
Sort daily activities (breakfast, school, bedtime) into a.m. and p.m.
Write a shown clock as h:mm, using a colon.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure practice separates past from to, maps analogue to digital, and connects a.m./p.m. to everyday events, while surfacing residual errors.

activities.title: Label the fives on a fixed clock face (scaffold)
feedback: If a numeral is read as its face value, re-reveal and count the fives aloud from the 12.
Confirm that numerals right of the 12-6 line are 'past' and those left are 'to'.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal static face can label the fives and rehearse the numeral-to-minutes mapping, which is a useful early step. Because the hands do not move, it cannot let the child convert a chosen time to digital or experience the twice-a-day split, so it serves as a scaffold toward the manipulable activity rather than a replacement for it.
sourceClaims: White Rose Y3 Time documents the exact pupil errors: reading the numeral the minute hand points to as the minutes ('minute hand on 4 -> 4 minutes past'); confusing times past and to; writing a decimal point instead of a colon; thinking there are 100 minutes in an hour (50 past 3 = 50 to 4); confusing am/pm ('1 am should be 1 pm because it is late'); and not knowing noon/midnight or that times occur twice a day. Models: count the 12 intervals in fives (5x table), vertical 12-6 partition for past/to.
learnerActions: On a static clock, tap each numeral to reveal its minute value (1 -> 5, 2 -> 10, ... 8 -> 40, ... 11 -> 55).
Read the revealed values aloud in order round the rim to rehearse the five-times link.
Point to the 12-6 line and say which numerals sit on the 'past' side (1–5) and which on the 'to' side (7–11), noting that 12 (o'clock) and 6 (half past) sit on the line itself.
activities.intendedInsight: Each numeral labels a five-minute step, and the rim splits into a past side and a to side.

activities.title: Talk about your day: eliciting a.m./p.m.
feedback: If a child says 1 a.m. 'should be' 1 p.m. because it feels late, place both on the day-timeline — 1 a.m. just after midnight and 1 p.m. just after noon — to show they are different moments.
If a child cannot place noon or midnight, mark them as the two split points on the timeline where a.m. and p.m. change over.
If a child thinks an unlabelled 3:40 is a single moment, show it occurs twice a day, once in the a.m. and once in the p.m.
activities.rationale: A short spoken exchange can prompt the child to use a.m./p.m. vocabulary in meaningful daily contexts and expose how they reason about morning/afternoon and about noon/midnight. Conversation elicits and consolidates the labelling but does not let an adult watch the hand-reading procedure, so pair it with the reading tasks.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils should 'tell and write the time from an analogue clock ... and 12-hour and 24-hour clocks' and 'estimate and read time with increasing accuracy to the nearest minute ... use vocabulary such as o'clock, am/pm, morning, afternoon, noon and midnight'.
learnerActions: Answer questions like 'What time do you have breakfast? Is that a.m. or p.m.?' and 'What about when you go to bed?'
Place named daily events on a day-timeline split at noon and midnight.
Identify which 12 o'clock is noon and which is midnight, and say where on the timeline a.m. changes to p.m. and back.
Explain, for a given event, whether the clock time is in the morning or after noon.
Given a digital time with no label (e.g. 3:40), say how many different moments in one day it could be and why.
activities.intendedInsight: a.m./p.m. labels connect to real daily events and to the noon/midnight split, so the same clock time can occur twice a day — once before noon and once after.

constraints: Secure recall of the 5 times-table underpins fluent counting of minutes; weak recall blocks fluent counting of the minutes, so rehearse it alongside clock reading. (It does not by itself block the past/to or a.m./p.m. reasoning.)

Write digital times with a colon (the convention used here; some styles write 3.25 with a full stop, but the separator is never a decimal point); the hour has 60 minutes, not 100, so '50 past 3' is 'ten to 4', not '50 to 4' via base-10 reasoning.
'To' times must be named against the NEXT hour (3:40 = 'twenty to four'), decided by whether the minute hand is left of the 12-6 line.
a.m./p.m. must be grounded in the noon/midnight split and the fact that each clock time occurs twice a day, not in how 'late' a time feels.

The static tap-to-reveal face and the conversation are scaffolds: the first cannot move hands or convert to digital; the second cannot show the reading method. Use them to support, not replace, work with moveable hands.
Recognition, matching and sorting tasks check and rehearse the rule but do not by themselves require the child to construct a reading from scratch or physically set the hands.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original source row claimed 'Reading a clock face is not a spatial task; 3D adds nothing.' This comparative/necessity claim is a catalog fit judgement not established by the cited sources, so it has been dropped rather than asserted as a pedagogical law; the original wording is flagged in the audit for reviewers.

The legacy fit rankings and product-format/quiz-step vocabulary and internal IDs were removed; the underlying pedagogical ideas (static labelling, dialogue elicitation) were retained as scaffold activities with stated limits.

Cited sources support the curriculum expectations and the catalogue of pupil errors and models; they do not establish comparative efficacy of the manipulable format over others. No efficacy claim is made here; efficacy wording is kept to 'intended/proposed'.

The 12 o'clock noon/midnight assessment probe and the twice-a-day counterexample from the original were reinstated in the conversation activity. The conventional 12 a.m./12 p.m. labelling is itself contested, so the guidance focuses on noon and midnight as the split points rather than drilling a fixed 12 a.m./12 p.m. answer.
The 'same hand position' examples were made 12 hours apart (e.g. 8 a.m. and 8 p.m.) rather than loosely paired (breakfast/teatime), since an identical analogue reading recurs only every 12 hours.

probeDeeper: 'The minute hand is on the 4 — how many minutes past is that? Show me how you worked it out.' (x5 vs numeral)
'You said forty past three — could we say that a different way using the next hour?' (past to to)
'Is 12 o'clock in the middle of the day a.m. or p.m.? What about 12 at night?' (noon/midnight)
'If a clock just shows 3:40 with no a.m. or p.m., how many different moments in one day could that be?' (twice-a-day counterexample)
assess.correctAnswer: Counts the intervals in fives (numeral 8 -> 40) rather than reading the numeral as minutes; reads 3:40 as 'twenty to four'; writes '4:25' with a colon; states breakfast 8 o'clock = a.m. and bedtime 8 o'clock = p.m., showing each time occurs twice a day.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the numeral the minute hand points to as the number of minutes (minute hand on 4 -> '4 minutes past')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Recount the rim in fives aloud, pairing each numeral with x5 on a moveable-hands clock so the numeral-to-minutes link (4 -> 20) is rehearsed until fluent.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says/writes 3:04 when the minute hand points to the 4 rather than 3:20

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses times 'past' and 'to' — keeps counting past the half hour ('40 past 3' for 3:40) instead of switching to '20 to 4'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the vertical 12-6 partition (right=past, left=to) and a number line showing 40 past = 20 to; stress that 'to' times relate to the NEXT hour.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reads 3:40 as 'forty past three'; never flips to naming it against the next hour

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the hour as base-10 — writes a decimal point instead of a colon and/or thinks there are 100 minutes in an hour (so 50 past 3 = 50 to 4)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model the colon convention and count the real 60 minutes on the clock face so the child sees the hour is 60, not 100 — ground it on the dial, not on the base-10 number system or 100-pence-in-a-pound.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes '3.25'; says 50 past 3 is 50 to 4

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses a.m. and p.m. — assigns p.m. by how late it 'feels' and doesn't grasp that each clock time occurs twice a day, split at noon/midnight
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor a.m./p.m. to concrete daily events on a day-timeline split at noon and midnight, showing the same clock time appears once in the morning and once after noon.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls 1 a.m. '1 p.m. because it's late'; can't place noon or midnight

responseLevels.gap: Reads the numeral as the minutes, or reads a digital time literally with no past/to sense; assigns a.m./p.m. by feel; writes times with a decimal point.
responseLevels.full: Reads any 5-minute analogue time by counting in fives, converts fluently between analogue and 12-hour digital (colon, correct past/to), and labels a.m./p.m. correctly, knowing each time occurs twice a day and what noon and midnight mean.
responseLevels.partial: Reads and writes 5-minute times correctly for 'past' times and simple cases, but is caught switching to 'to' times, or muddles a.m./p.m. and noon/midnight.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set reading and writing tasks and WATCH how the child works, never asking them to define terms: (1) Hand the child a moveable-hands analogue clock set to 3:40, then to 4:25: 'Read each one to me and write it as it would look on a digital clock.' (2) Show a 12-hour digital display 3:40: 'Say this time in words — is it past or to the hour?' (3) 'It's 8 o'clock and I'm eating breakfast — is that a.m. or p.m.? Now it's 8 o'clock and I'm going to bed — a.m. or p.m.?' Watch whether they count round in fives and land on past/to correctly, write with a colon, and separate a.m. from p.m.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the METHOD (does hand-to-minutes go via x5? does 3:40 flip to 'to'?) separates a child who has the procedure from one who names the numeral or reads the display literally; the two-events-at-8-o'clock item catches a.m./p.m. assigned by feeling rather than by the noon split.
