pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 9-10. Round any whole number up to 1,000,000 to the nearest 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000 or 100,000, using the same number-line nearness / midpoint reasoning applied to a chosen larger place — e.g. 456,782 to the nearest 10,000 is 460,000. Extends rounding to higher places and to boundary/cascade cases (950,500 to nearest 100,000).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 5): 'round any number up to 1,000,000 to the nearest 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000 and 100,000'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.NBT.3 'use place-value understanding to round multi-digit whole numbers to any place'.
• Operational details — Keep the number-line/midpoint meaning central but scale it to large bounding multiples; identify the rounding place and the single decider digit to its right (ignore the rest). Rehearse the target place selecting the bounding multiples, the halfway convention, and cascade cases where rounding up rolls a 9 over. Link explicitly to estimating large calculations.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9, emerging): rounds a six-digit number to the nearest 10,000 using a landmarked line. Tier B (age 9-10, secure): rounds to any specified place and explains via the decider digit / nearer multiple. Tier C (age 10, extending): handles cascade/boundary cases (950,500→1,000,000) and uses rounding to estimate sums.
bestPractices: Scale the number-line/midpoint model to large bounding multiples; keep 'nearer multiple' as the meaning.
Identify the rounding place and the SINGLE decider digit to its right; the rest are irrelevant.
Make explicit that the requested place chooses the bounding multiples (nearest 10,000 → bound by ten-thousands).
Rehearse the halfway convention and cascade cases (950,500 to nearest 100,000).
Link to estimating large sums/differences and checking reasonableness.
keyRepresentations: Number line with large bounding multiples and midpoint
Place-value chart marking the rounding digit and decider digit
0-1,000,000 line rescaled per target place
Estimation contexts (populations, budgets)
'Rounding hill' midpoint image scaled up
commonMisconceptions: Looking at the wrong decider digit or rounding to the wrong place.
Successive/chained rounding across places instead of one decision.
Truncating (always down) or always up.
Cascade errors (950,500 to nearest 100,000 mishandled).
Losing place value in the unchanged trailing digits (they become zeros).

learn.summary: For ages 9-10: round any whole number up to 1,000,000 to the nearest 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000 or 100,000. Keep the number-line 'nearer multiple' meaning central but scale it to large bounding multiples: identify the rounding place, read the single decider digit immediately to its right, zero everything after the rounding place, and handle halfway and cascade/boundary cases (e.g. 950,500 → 1,000,000). Link to estimating large sums and checking reasonableness.

activities.title: Scaled rounding bench: drag across the midpoint
feedback: If a learner reads a column other than the one immediately to the right of the rounding place: mark the target place and its single decider digit on a labelled six-digit place-value chart and look only at that digit.

If the rounded answer keeps later digits (e.g. 456,782 → 456,000 or keeps the 782): on the number line point out the answer must be a multiple of the target place, so everything after it becomes zero.
If a learner rounds step-by-step across several places instead of making one decision: return to the single decider digit for the chosen place only.
Reinforce correct work by having them say 'nearer to ___ than to ___, so it rounds to ___.'
activities.rationale: A draggable marker between large bounding multiples with a visible midpoint makes the nearness decision concrete and lets the decider-digit rule be derived rather than memorised; dragging across the midpoint and watching the result flip, plus watching trailing digits collapse to zero, ties the procedure to meaning. A place selector that rescales the line shows how the requested place chooses the bounds.
sourceClaims: Large-number rounding uses the same number-line/midpoint meaning scaled up; cascade cases and single-decider-digit reasoning are key.
Use place-value understanding to round multi-digit whole numbers to any place (4.NBT.3).
Year 5 pupils should 'round any number up to 1,000,000 to the nearest 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000 and 100,000'.
learnerActions: Round 456,782 to the nearest 10,000: place it on a number line between the bounding multiples 450,000 and 460,000, with the midpoint 455,000 flagged.
Decide which multiple it is nearer and state the rounded value (460,000); check it against the midpoint.
Change the target place to nearest 100,000 so the line rescales to the bounding multiples 400,000 and 500,000 (midpoint 450,000), and round 456,782 again (it is past the midpoint, so 500,000).
After each decision, write out the rounded number and confirm every digit after the rounding place is now zero.
Explain which single digit you used to decide (the one immediately to the right of the rounding place) and why the rest are irrelevant.
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding a large number is the same nearness decision scaled up: the requested place chooses the two bounding multiples and the midpoint, the one decider digit settles the decision, and all trailing digits become zeros.

activities.title: Cascade and boundary cases
feedback: If the boundary case is not carried (950,500 → 900,000): walk only the single carry rather than reteaching the whole rule — 9 hundred-thousands rounding up becomes 1,000,000. Rehearse near the boundary on a number line.
If a learner is unsure at the exact midpoint: state and apply the agreed halfway convention (conventionally round up) and name it aloud.
activities.rationale: Cascade cases are the common failure point and need targeted rehearsal at the boundary; animating or tracing the roll from 9 to the next place makes the carry visible.
sourceClaims: Large-number rounding uses the same number-line/midpoint meaning scaled up; cascade cases and single-decider-digit reasoning are key.
learnerActions: Round 950,500 to the nearest 100,000, placing it between 900,000 and 1,000,000 with the midpoint 950,000 flagged.
Decide whether it rounds up (it is just past the midpoint) and work the carry explicitly: 9 hundred-thousands rounding up = 10 hundred-thousands = 1,000,000.
Try a case that sits exactly on a midpoint (e.g. 950,000 to the nearest 100,000), state the convention you are using (round half up), and give the result (1,000,000).
Explain in your own words what happens when rounding up rolls a 9 over into the next place.
activities.intendedInsight: When rounding up at a 9, the carry rolls into the next higher place; the rounded value can gain a digit (950,500 → 1,000,000), and this is still a single rounding decision, not chained rounding.

activities.title: Round to estimate a large sum
feedback: If a learner computes the exact sum instead of estimating: ask them to round each number first, then add the rounded values.
If estimates are far off: discuss whether the chosen place was appropriate for the numbers involved.
Confirm a correct estimate such as 400,000 + 200,000 = 600,000 and relate it back to the rounding decisions made.
activities.rationale: Linking rounding to estimation of large, meaningful quantities gives the procedure a purpose and reinforces place-value reasoning; this is an explicit curriculum aim in the original pedagogy, though no source claim speaks directly to estimation.
learnerActions: Estimate 387,412 + 214,560 by rounding each addend to a sensible place before adding — for example, treat the numbers as two town populations you want a quick combined total for.
Round each number (e.g. to the nearest 100,000: 400,000 and 200,000) and add to get about 600,000.
State why the estimate is reasonable and how it could be used to check a full calculation (e.g. a budget total or population count).
Try estimating to a different place and discuss how the choice of place affects how close the estimate is.
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding supports quick, sensible estimates of large real quantities (populations, budgets) and a reasonableness check on exact answers; the chosen rounding place trades precision for simplicity.

activities.title: Consolidation: round to any specified place
feedback: If a rounded value is not a multiple of the target place, it is wrong — re-check that trailing digits are zeroed.

If a learner always rounds down (truncates) or always rounds up regardless of the digits: compare the number to the midpoint and read the decider digit — rounding up and rounding down each happen depending on that digit, not by habit.
For cascade traps, confirm the carry rolled into the next place correctly.
Use the decider-digit explanation as the mark of secure understanding rather than a correct answer alone.
activities.rationale: Practice with varied place targets, halfway and cascade cases consolidates the rule and surfaces the common misconceptions for feedback. This activity emphasises applied practice; items that only require selecting an answer check recognition and should be paired with learners stating their reasoning to elicit the procedure.
sourceClaims: Use place-value understanding to round multi-digit whole numbers to any place (4.NBT.3).
learnerActions: Given a six-digit number and a target place, state the two bounding multiples, the midpoint, the decider digit, and the rounded value.
Work a mixed set that includes a cascade trap (e.g. 950,500) and a halfway case.
Match several numbers to their rounded values for a stated place, and spot any that are not clean multiples of the target place.
Choose the place, then round — justify the bounding multiples the place implies.
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding to any place up to 100,000 becomes fluent and self-checked: the answer is always a clean multiple of the target place.

constraints: Keep 'nearer multiple' as the meaning; the requested place chooses the two bounding multiples (nearest 10,000 → bound by ten-thousands).
Use only the single decider digit immediately to the right of the rounding place; the remaining digits are irrelevant to the decision and become zeros.
Make one rounding decision per task; do not round step-by-step across successive places (chained rounding is an error).
State and apply a halfway convention explicitly (conventionally round up) and name it when at an exact midpoint.
Rounding direction depends on the decider digit relative to the midpoint; do not always round down (truncate) or always round up.

A static scaled 'rounding hill' or poster is a useful reference but does not itself require the learner to act on the decision; pair it with a task where the learner makes and justifies the rounding decision.
Selected-response items (multiple choice, matching) check recognition; to elicit the procedure, also require the learner to construct or explain the rounding decision.

Number-line nearness is a one-dimensional model, so a flat line with bounding multiples and a midpoint is sufficient and no 3D representation is needed for this objective; this is a scoped sufficiency note, not a claim that other media cannot teach it.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of worked values: 456,782 → 460,000 (nearest 10,000; decider digit 6 → up; bounds 450,000/460,000, mid 455,000) and → 500,000 (nearest 100,000; decider digit 5 → up; bounds 400,000/500,000, mid 450,000); 950,500 → 1,000,000 (nearest 100,000; decider digit 5 → up, carry rolls 9→10 hundred-thousands); estimate 387,412 + 214,560 ≈ 400,000 + 200,000 = 600,000. All consistent.

The original recommendation's '400,000–500,000' for nearest 100,000 are the correct bounding multiples for 456,782, and the rounded value is 500,000 (decider digit 5). There is no original error here.

The original fit judgements ('open dialogue adds little'; conversation/3D as poor fit) are catalog verdicts, not established pedagogy; retained only as narrowly scoped affordance notes (planar model suffices here; selected-response checks recognition), not as universal superiority claims.
Halfway convention (round-half-up) is a stated convention; alternative conventions exist and the choice should be made explicit to learners.
CCSS 4.NBT.3 and the NCETM source are marked verified:false in the row; claims are retained as cited without fresh verification.

probeDeeper: Round 950,500 to the nearest 100,000 — what happens when rounding up passes 900,000?
Is 456,782 nearer 450,000 or 460,000? Show it on a number line.
How did rounding each number help you estimate 387,412 + 214,560 quickly?
assess.correctAnswer: 460,000; 1,000,000; and about 400,000 + 200,000 = 600,000 — deciding by the digit one place to the right of the rounding place, zeroing everything after it.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses the wrong column to decide — not the digit immediately to the right of the target place
errorPatterns.nextMove: Mark the target place and its 'decider' (one to the right); look only at that. Reground with a labelled place-value chart for six-digit numbers.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rounding to the nearest 10,000, the child inspects the units or the ten-thousands digit itself rather than the thousands digit.

errorPatterns.pattern: Fails the carry when rounding up rolls into a higher place: 950,500 → 900,000 instead of 1,000,000
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the whole rule — walk the single carry: 9 hundred-thousands rounding up = 10 hundred-thousands = 1,000,000. Rehearse near the boundary on a number line.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The boundary case is not carried up to the next place.

errorPatterns.pattern: Rounds the target digit but leaves later digits unchanged (456,782 → 456,000 or keeps the 782)
errorPatterns.nextMove: On a number line show the answer must be a multiple of 10,000, so everything after the ten-thousands becomes zero.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rounded value is not a clean multiple of the target place.

responseLevels.gap: Uses the wrong decider column or leaves trailing digits; rounded value isn't a clean multiple.
responseLevels.full: Rounds to any place up to 100,000 accurately including boundary carries, zeroes trailing digits, and rounds sensibly to estimate sums.
responseLevels.partial: Rounds clear cases but mishandles the carry into a new place or which column to read for higher places.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set the task and watch the working: 'Round 456,782 to the nearest 10,000. Now round 950,500 to the nearest 100,000. Then estimate 387,412 + 214,560 by rounding first.' Watch which column they use to decide and what happens at the boundary.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 456,782 checks the child finds the correct decider column among many digits and zeros the rest; 950,500 forces a carry that rolls up into a new place (900,000 → 1,000,000); the estimate checks they round each addend to a sensible place before adding. Watching the columns used exposes the mechanism.

sources.claim: Year 5 pupils should 'round any number up to 1,000,000 to the nearest 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000 and 100,000'.

pedagogy.summary: Children recognise volume as ADDITIVE: a composite solid made of non-overlapping right rectangular prisms has a total volume equal to the sum of the parts' volumes. The skill is to DECOMPOSE an L-shaped or step-shaped solid into cuboids, find each volume with V = l × w × h, and add — correctly deducing any hidden dimension from the whole. The main hazards are choosing overlapping pieces (double-counting the shared region), mis-reading a missing dimension, and adding the volumes wrongly.
bestPractices: Decompose the composite into non-overlapping cuboids, and show that different valid splits give the same total.
Deduce missing dimensions from the overall measurements before calculating each part.
Find each cuboid's volume with V = l×w×h, then add; keep cm³ throughout.
Check that the parts do not overlap (no cube counted twice) and that none is left out.
keyRepresentations: L-shaped / step solid split into cuboids
Exploded decomposition diagram
Missing-dimension deduction from the whole
Sum of the part-volumes
commonMisconceptions: Chooses overlapping pieces and double-counts the shared region.
Mis-deduces a hidden dimension (uses an overall length for a part, or forgets to subtract).
Adds the part-volumes incorrectly, or omits one of the parts.

learn.summary: Learners recognise that volume is additive: a composite solid made of non-overlapping right rectangular prisms has a total volume equal to the sum of its parts. The core skill is to decompose an L-shaped or step-shaped solid into cuboids, deduce any hidden dimension from the overall measurements, find each part's volume with V = l × w × h, and add — keeping consistent cubic units (typically cm³) throughout, matching the labelled measurements. Chief hazards are choosing overlapping pieces (double-counting the shared region), mis-reading or mis-deducing a missing dimension, and adding the parts wrongly or omitting one. A key insight is that any valid non-overlapping split of the same solid yields the same total.

activities.title: Pull the step-solid apart (exploded decomposition)
feedback: If two pieces share a block, that region is being counted twice and the total will be too large — shade the two parts and assign the shared region to exactly one piece, then recount.
If an unlabelled edge was taken as a whole-figure measurement, mark the full length and subtract the known part to find the missing piece before calculating any volume.
If each part's volume is right but the sum is wrong or a piece is dropped, list every part-volume in a column and add carefully — the decomposition method itself is sound.
If a re-split gives a different total, revisit it: non-overlapping splits of the same solid must agree, so there is an overlap, omission or arithmetic slip to find.
activities.rationale: Decomposition is a spatial act — separating a composite solid into non-overlapping cuboids and seeing the pieces makes the non-overlap concrete, and a re-split demonstration makes additivity visible. A dynamic exploded view with overlap flagging, revealed deduced dimensions, per-part volume readouts and a re-split control makes the mechanism concrete; the same reasoning can also be carried out with physical interlocking cubes. Which medium is most effective is not established by the cited standards.
sourceClaims: 5.MD.C.5.c: 'Recognize volume as additive. Find volumes of solid figures composed of two non-overlapping right rectangular prisms by adding the volumes of the non-overlapping parts, applying this technique to solve real world problems.'

Year 6 statutory: 'calculate, estimate and compare volume of cubes and cuboids using standard units, including cubic centimetres (cm³) and cubic metres (m³)' — the standard-unit basis for summing decomposed cuboid volumes.
learnerActions: Meet a step-shaped or L-shaped block with most edge lengths labelled and one or two left to deduce.
Draw a cut line to split the solid into two (or more) cuboids, then separate the pieces into an exploded view so you can see each one whole.
Check that your pieces do not overlap — no cube belongs to two pieces and none of the solid is left out.

Find any missing edge from the labelled measurements (for example, subtract the known part from the overall length, add parts to get an overall length, or use a matching parallel edge), then write down each cuboid's l, w and h.
Compute each cuboid's volume with V = l × w × h, keeping consistent cubic units (cm³ here), and add them for the total.
Re-split the same block a different valid way and confirm you get the same total.
activities.intendedInsight: Volume is additive: a composite solid can be decomposed into non-overlapping cuboids, each cuboid's volume found by l × w × h, and the parts summed — and any valid non-overlapping split rebuilds the same total.

activities.title: Decompose on a diagram with dimension deduction
feedback: If pieces overlap on your diagram, you will double-count the shared region — redraw the splits so each region belongs to exactly one piece.
If a volume looks too small or too large, check whether an unlabelled edge was mistaken for a whole-figure length.
Confirm no region of the shape is left uncovered by your pieces.
activities.rationale: Working on a diagram assesses and exercises the decomposition and dimension-deduction ideas; it is a strong format, though the non-overlap is less vivid than when physical or on-screen pieces visibly separate.
sourceClaims: 5.MD.C.5.c: 'Recognize volume as additive. Find volumes of solid figures composed of two non-overlapping right rectangular prisms by adding the volumes of the non-overlapping parts, applying this technique to solve real world problems.'
learnerActions: On a labelled L-shape diagram, draw split lines to divide it into non-overlapping cuboids.
Deduce each unlabelled dimension from the labelled ones (for example, by subtracting a known part from the overall measurement, adding parts, or matching an equal parallel edge), and write it in.
Compute each part's volume with l × w × h and add for the total, keeping consistent cubic units (cm³).
Try a second valid set of split lines and check the total is unchanged.
activities.intendedInsight: A composite solid's volume can be computed by splitting its diagram into non-overlapping rectangular prisms, deducing missing dimensions from the whole, and summing the parts.

activities.title: Real-world composite volume problem
feedback: Check your split against the real object — do the pieces account for the whole structure without overlapping?
If the answer seems implausible, re-examine the missing-dimension deduction, the unit consistency and the final sum.
activities.rationale: Applying the technique to a real-world problem is required by the standard and shows learners the method is a tool, not just an exercise.
sourceClaims: 5.MD.C.5.c: 'Recognize volume as additive. Find volumes of solid figures composed of two non-overlapping right rectangular prisms by adding the volumes of the non-overlapping parts, applying this technique to solve real world problems.'
learnerActions: Read a real-world situation (e.g. a step-shaped concrete structure or an L-shaped container) with a labelled solid.
Decide how to split it into non-overlapping cuboids and deduce any missing dimension.
Calculate each part's volume and add for the total, giving the answer in consistent cubic units matching the labelled measurements (e.g. cm³ or m³).
State whether the total makes sense, and which part contributes the largest volume.
activities.intendedInsight: The additive-volume method applies to practical problems where a real object is modelled as a composite of rectangular prisms.

activities.title: Spot the overlap and the missing dimension (practice items)
feedback: A total that is too large usually signals a double-counted overlap region.
A single wrong part-volume usually signals an edge taken as a whole-figure measurement instead of being deduced.
Recognising the right answer checks and reinforces the idea, but it does not by itself require building a decomposition; carry out at least one full split-and-sum yourself.
activities.rationale: Targeted items with overlap and missing-dimension answer choices can sharpen discrimination of the common errors. This is recognition-style practice: it checks and reinforces but does not on its own elicit independent construction of a decomposition, so it is paired with a constructed split-and-sum.
learnerActions: Work through short items that ask you to split an L-solid, find a missing length, and compute the total.
For each item, examine the answer choices and identify which come from double-counting an overlap and which from leaving a dimension un-deduced.
Explain, in one sentence, why your chosen split avoids counting any cube twice.
Construct at least one full split-and-sum yourself so you produce the method rather than only selecting an answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising the specific error patterns — double-counting a shared region and mis-deducing a hidden dimension — supports more reliable use of the method; selecting a correct answer is not the same as producing a decomposition.

constraints: Pieces of the decomposition must be non-overlapping right rectangular prisms: each cube of the solid belongs to exactly one piece and none is omitted.

Missing dimensions must be deduced from the overall measurements (e.g. subtract a known part from the full length) before any volume is calculated — never take an unlabelled edge as a whole-figure measurement.
Keep consistent cubic units throughout and in the final total; cm³ is the usual unit here, with m³ appropriate for larger real-world objects — match the labelled measurements.

A static exploded diagram with tap-to-reveal part volumes and sum can show the method but allows no manipulation or re-splitting; treat it as a scaffold that demonstrates rather than one that elicits the learner's own decomposition.

Multiple-choice or fill-in items can assess the idea with overlap and missing-dimension answer choices, but recognition-only responses do not require the learner to independently construct a decomposition; pair them with at least one constructed split-and-sum.

This learning centres on spatial decomposition and calculation; a dialogue-only format does not by itself elicit the learner's spatial decomposition or the construction of the calculation, though explaining one's reasoning remains valuable alongside doing the method.

Physical interlocking or unit cubes are a standard concrete model for building and decomposing composite solids, and on-screen 3D models represent the same solid; neither medium is established by the cited standards as uniquely necessary or more effective.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The two cited sources support the additive-volume standard and the cubic-unit basis; they do not establish the comparative efficacy or necessity of any particular artefact (3D interactive, diagram, item set or static image). Format preferences from the original row are presented as proposals with stated affordances/limits, not as universal pedagogical laws.

Self-audit: the l × w × h method, the subtract-known-from-whole dimension deduction, the non-overlap / no-omission condition, and the invariance of the total across valid non-overlapping splits were checked for internal consistency and found sound; no specific arithmetic examples were asserted beyond the method itself.

The original row references reteach prerequisite IDs (e.g. mt_nTL-owFJTF, mt_JH_6RpNWjr) and other internal identifiers (microTopicId, taxonomyVersion) which are internal catalog data and were omitted from learner-facing guidance.

The physical-cube / on-screen-model comparison is an agent addition, not content from the original row; interlocking/unit cubes are the clearer concrete analogue for internal volume decomposition, while 'paper nets' (modelling faces/surfaces) are a weaker, unvalidated suggestion. The earlier draft's 'thickness/approximation of an idealised solid' framing was removed as a misapplication of flat-figure guidance to a 3D volume topic.

probeDeeper: Show me your two pieces — do they overlap anywhere? How do you know no cube is counted twice?
How did you work out the dimension that was not labelled?
Could you split this a different way and still get the same total?
Which part's volume is largest — does your total make sense?
assess.correctAnswer: Splits the solid into non-overlapping cuboids, deduces each missing dimension from the whole, computes each volume with l×w×h, and adds to the correct total in cm³ (splitting a different valid way gives the same answer).

errorPatterns.pattern: Chooses overlapping pieces and double-counts the shared region.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Shade the two parts to show they must not overlap; assign the shared region to exactly one piece and recount.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The two cuboids share a block that is counted twice, giving a total that is too large.

errorPatterns.pattern: Mis-deduces a hidden dimension — uses an overall length for a sub-part or forgets to subtract.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Mark the full length and subtract the known part to find the missing piece before calculating any volume.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: One cuboid's volume is wrong because an unlabelled edge was taken as a whole-figure measurement.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds the part-volumes incorrectly or omits a part (a lapse, not a misunderstanding of the method).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the addition — list each part-volume, then sum; the decomposition method itself is sound.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Each part's volume is correct but the sum is wrong or a piece is dropped.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot decompose; treats it as one prism, or overlaps/omits pieces; no missing-dimension reasoning.
responseLevels.full: Decomposes into non-overlapping cuboids, deduces missing dimensions, finds and correctly sums the part volumes in cm³, and recognises that a different valid split gives the same total.
responseLevels.partial: Splits into cuboids and finds part volumes but double-counts an overlap, mis-deduces a hidden dimension, or slips in the addition; the additive idea is present but not reliable.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give a labelled L-shaped (or step-shaped) solid with most dimensions shown and one or two to be deduced. Say: 'Find its total volume, and show how you split it up.' Then WATCH whether they split into non-overlapping cuboids, how they find the missing dimension, whether they multiply each part correctly and add, and whether they double-count the overlap.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the decomposition — the non-overlapping split and the missing-dimension deduction — separates a child who grasps volume as additive from one who mangles the pieces; double-counting the overlap and dimension errors show up directly in the split they draw.

pedagogy.summary: Year 3 (age 7–8) extends money problems to pounds AND pence together: totalling two or three priced items and giving change from a whole amount such as £5 or £10, and recording with £ and p notation (e.g. £3.47). The efficient route to change from a note is the counting-on / finding-the-difference strategy, not written column subtraction across zeros. The central hazard is that £.p looks like two separate whole numbers: pupils must exchange 100p for £1 and treat the amount as one quantity. (Note: the statutory Y3 guidance records £ and p separately and defers formal decimal notation to Y4; this topic's evidence uses the £3.47 form, so teach the notation carefully alongside the pence-and-pounds meaning.)
bestPractices: Find change from £5/£10 by counting UP from the total spent to the note (e.g. spent £4.45 → +5p to £4.50 → +50p to £5.00; change 55p), shown on an empty number line — avoids error-prone column subtraction across zeros.
Establish 100p = £1 concretely and insist that £ and p are one quantity, not two whole numbers; exchange 100 pennies for a £1 coin so the equivalence is enacted.
Use the part–whole structure for multi-item change: total the items first (the parts), then the note is the whole and change is the missing part.
Model and contrast correct vs incorrect notation explicitly (£3.47, not £347, 3.47p or £3.47p); have pupils see, say and record amounts in more than one way.
Encourage estimation before calculating (≈£4.50 spent, so change is small) so unreasonable answers are caught, and read amounts in a place-value-honest way rather than as two separate numbers.
keyRepresentations: Empty number line for counting-on change from a note
Real coins/notes with 100p→£1 exchange
Part–whole (bar) model: note = total cost + change
Place-value columns (£ | tenths/10p | hundredths/1p) shown aligned by the decimal point
commonMisconceptions: 'String-length thinking' — treats £ and p as two separate whole numbers (adds the pence column past 100 without exchanging, or writes £3.7 for £3 and 70p).
Notation errors — omits the decimal point, mixes units (£3.47p), or writes pence as if pounds.
Attempts change from £10 by column subtraction and makes 'take smaller from larger' / subtract-across-zeros errors instead of counting up.
'Most coins = most money' persists, and reading '£2.47' as 'two point forty-seven' reinforces the two-separate-numbers error.

learn.summary: Year 3 learners (age 7–8) total two or three items priced in pounds and pence, give change from a £5 or £10 note, and record amounts correctly (e.g. £3.47). The reliable route to change from a note is counting UP from the total spent to the note (finding the difference), not column subtraction across zeros. The central hazard is treating £.p as two separate whole numbers ('string-length thinking'); learners must exchange 100p for £1 and treat each amount as one quantity. Note: the National Curriculum's non-statutory notes and guidance for Year 3 say pupils record £ and p separately, and formal decimal recording of money is introduced in Year 4, so teach the £3.47 form carefully alongside its pence-and-pounds meaning.

activities.title: Shop till: total, pay, and count change up
feedback: If pence are added past 100 without exchanging (e.g. £2.60 + £1.85 written as £3.145 or £3.45), stop and build the pence physically, exchange 100p for a £1 coin, then re-read the total as a single quantity (the correct total is £4.45).

If change is reached by column subtraction from £5.00/£10.00 and digits are taken the wrong way across the zeros (e.g. 00 − 47 giving £1.47 or £2.53), redirect to counting UP from the total to the note on a number line.
Check any change by counting it back onto the total: does it rebuild £5.00? If not, the jumps were wrong.

OPTIONAL interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete: a total bar that sums items as they are added; a number line that draws each counting-on jump; a coin tray whose 100p visibly animates into one £1 coin. These are illustrative, not required — coins, a paper number line and spoken rehearsal achieve the same purposes.
activities.rationale: Counting up / finding the difference from the total to the note is an efficient change strategy that avoids subtract-across-zeros errors, and enacting 100p = £1 confronts the 'two separate whole numbers' misconception by making the exchange visible.
sourceClaims: Change is efficiently found by counting up / finding the difference from the total to the note (shopkeeper's method), avoiding column subtraction across zeros; many children count up more easily than they count back.

Children commonly treat pounds and pence (whole-number and decimal places) as two separate whole numbers rather than one decimal quantity ('string-length thinking'), partly because of whole-number language such as 'three pounds and seventy-six pence'; standard decimal vocal reading ('two point five four pounds') is recommended to counter this.

Year 3 pupils should add and subtract amounts of money to give change, using both £ and p in practical contexts; non-statutory guidance says they record pounds and pence separately and that decimal recording of money is introduced formally in Year 4.
learnerActions: Choose two or three priced items (e.g. a £2.60 car and a £1.85 book) and total them, building the total step by step (£2.60 + £1.85 = £4.45).
Pay with a £5 note and work out the change by counting UP from the total to the note, drawing each jump on an empty number line: £4.45 → +5p → £4.50 → +50p → £5.00, so change is 55p.
Collect the change as actual coins into a tray; when the pennies/pence in the tray reach 100p, physically exchange them for a single £1 coin and re-read the amount as one quantity.
Repeat for a single £3.47 item paid with a £5 note: count up £3.47 → £3.50 → £4.00 → £5.00 = £1.53.

Record the change in £ and p notation (e.g. £0.55, 55p), then say the amount in a place-value-honest way suitable for Year 3 (e.g. 'fifty-five pence'); avoid reading the pence as a compound whole number joined to the pounds (e.g. 'three point forty-seven' for £3.47). Reading the digits separately ('nought point five five') is also acceptable and is the decimal reading the cited research recommends.
activities.intendedInsight: Change from a note is a short counting-on jump from the total to the note, and an amount in pounds and pence is ONE quantity because 100p exchanges for £1.

activities.title: Record it right: correct versus incorrect money notation
feedback: If a learner writes £347 for £3.47, ask how many whole pounds that would be and compare with the coins in the tray.
If a learner writes £0.55p (£ and p together) or 55p inside pounds as £55, show the correct form next to it and ask which matches the coins.

Reinforce place-value-honest readings ('fifty-five pence', 'three pounds forty-seven pence') and reject only the compound-whole reading of the pence, such as 'three point forty-seven', which treats the pence like a separate whole number. Reading the digits separately ('three point four seven') is not an error and is the reading the cited research recommends.
activities.rationale: Notation and place-value errors (omitted decimal point, mixed units) are specific and nameable, and contrasting correct with incorrect forms at the moment of writing targets them directly.
sourceClaims: £ and p should not be written together (e.g. not £1.00p); pupils commonly record money incorrectly by omitting the decimal point or mixing units.

Children commonly treat pounds and pence (whole-number and decimal places) as two separate whole numbers rather than one decimal quantity ('string-length thinking'), partly because of whole-number language such as 'three pounds and seventy-six pence'; standard decimal vocal reading ('two point five four pounds') is recommended to counter this.
learnerActions: For a given amount of coins in a tray, write the amount in £ and p and check it against the coins.
Compare correct and incorrect recordings side by side (e.g. £0.55 vs £0.55p vs £55) and decide which one matches the coins, explaining how you know.
Record the same amount in more than one correct way where sensible (e.g. 55p and £0.55) and explain they are equal.
Practise see–say–record: see the coins, say the amount place-value-honestly, then write it without ever joining £ and p (never £3.47p).
activities.intendedInsight: Money notation carries meaning: the decimal point separates pounds from pence, £ and p are never written together, and the written amount must match the value of the coins.

activities.title: Estimate first, then check for sense
feedback: If an answer is wildly off (e.g. a change of £4.53 from £5 after spending £4.45, when only about 55p is expected), prompt the estimate check: does this match 'the change should be small'?
If the counting-back check does not rebuild the note, the jumps or columns were wrong — redo by counting up.
activities.rationale: Pupils rarely estimate first and so lack a sense of a sensible answer; building in estimation and a counting-back check gives a self-correction routine.
sourceClaims: Pupils make take-smaller-from-larger and subtract-across-zeros errors (e.g. in £10.00 − amount) reflecting weak exchange/place value, and rarely estimate first so lack a sense of a sensible answer.

Change is efficiently found by counting up / finding the difference from the total to the note (shopkeeper's method), avoiding column subtraction across zeros; many children count up more easily than they count back.
learnerActions: Before calculating change, estimate: 'I spent about £4.50, so the change should be small.'
After finding change, compare it with the estimate and say whether the answer is reasonable.
Verify change by counting it back onto the total to rebuild the note.
When paying with a £10 note instead of £5, predict how the change will differ and decide whether counting up or column subtraction would be easier.
activities.intendedInsight: Estimating before calculating catches unreasonable answers, and change from a note can always be checked by rebuilding the note.

activities.title: Quick checks on notation and reasonableness
feedback: For a wrong choice, point back to the coins or value the amount represents and ask which written form matches it.
Note: selecting a correct form checks notation and reasonableness but does not show the learner can carry out the counting-on process — pair it with the hands-on till activity.
activities.rationale: Short recognition checks are well suited to the crisply testable notation misconception and to reasonableness, as a companion to hands-on calculation rather than a replacement; recognition alone does not elicit the production of the counting-on method.
sourceClaims: £ and p should not be written together (e.g. not £1.00p); pupils commonly record money incorrectly by omitting the decimal point or mixing units.
learnerActions: Fill in the blank to record a shown amount in correct £ and p notation.
Choose which of several written forms correctly records a given amount (e.g. £3.47 among £347 and £3.47p, with the incorrect forms clearly present only as non-examples to be rejected).
Choose or state the correct change for a simple purchase from a note.
Put a set of money amounts in order from least to most to practise treating each as one quantity.
activities.intendedInsight: Correct notation and reasonable amounts can be recognised and chosen reliably once the single-quantity meaning is understood.

activities.title: Shopkeeper role-play to narrate the method (optional support)
feedback: Use this to rehearse and explain reasoning; it narrates the method but does not by itself give calculation practice with feedback, so follow it with actual totalling, change-finding and recording.
activities.rationale: Talking through the shopkeeper's counting-on method may support articulation of the strategy, but giving change is procedural and needs practice with feedback, which narration alone does not supply; the articulation benefit is a proposed, untested affordance.
learnerActions: Take the role of shopkeeper and, out loud, talk a 'customer' through giving change: name the total, then count up from the total to the note coin by coin.
Explain aloud why 100p becomes £1 while handing over the change.
activities.intendedInsight: Verbalising the counting-on method and the 100p→£1 exchange may help a learner articulate and consolidate the procedure.

constraints: Treat each money amount as ONE quantity: insist on exchanging 100p for £1, never carrying pence past 99 without exchanging and never writing three digits after the point.

Teach change from a £5/£10 note primarily by counting UP (finding the difference) on a number line; reserve column subtraction for cases without the across-zeros trap and only when done correctly with exchange.
Never present an incorrect money form (£347, £3.47p, £0.55p, pence written as pounds) as a correct option in a learner task; use such forms only as clearly labelled non-examples to be rejected.

Read amounts place-value-honestly for Year 3 ('three pounds and forty-seven pence', 'fifty-five pence'); the pitfall to avoid is reading the pence as a compound whole number joined to the pounds ('three point forty-seven'). Digit-by-digit decimal reading ('three point four seven') is acceptable and is the reading the cited research recommends.
Recognition/selection checks confirm notation and reasonableness but do not elicit the independent counting-on calculation; pair them with hands-on totalling, change-finding and recording.

The National Curriculum's non-statutory Year 3 notes and guidance say pupils record pounds and pence separately, with formal decimal recording of money introduced in Year 4; introduce the £3.47 form deliberately alongside its meaning, and expect some learners to still record pounds and pence separately.

Illustrative interactions (total bar, number-line jumps, 100p→£1 animation, coin tray) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete and must not be treated as the only valid medium; coins, paper number lines and spoken rehearsal achieve the same purposes.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source worked example £5.00 − £3.47 = £1.53 is arithmetically correct (count up: £3.47→£3.50 is 3p, →£4.00 is 50p, →£5.00 is £1, total £1.53); retained as stated. £2.60 + £1.85 = £4.45 is also correct.
The misconception examples '£3.145/£3.45', '£2.53' and '£1.47' are deliberately WRONG forms shown only as error patterns, never as correct answers.

Reading guidance: the original candidate banned 'point five five', but the Cambridge source actually recommends digit-by-digit decimal reading ('two point five four pounds') to counter string-length thinking; only reading the pence as a compound whole number ('three point forty-seven') reinforces the two-separate-numbers error. The Year-3-appropriate reading remains 'fifty-five pence'/'three pounds and forty-seven pence', with digit-by-digit decimal reading flagged as acceptable rather than wrong. The Cambridge source also flags compound whole-number language as partly causing the misconception, so the exact convention is a teacher judgement.

The shopkeeper role-play activity had its sourceClaims set to [] because the attached counting-up claim supports only the method content, not the untested principle that verbalisation/role-play aids consolidation; the benefit is stated as proposed/may.

One cited source (NCETM, 'Misconceptions with the Key Objectives') is marked verified:false in the row; its claim about take-smaller-from-larger, subtract-across-zeros and lack of estimation is used to inform feedback but should be treated with that lower confidence.

The row notes a genuine tension: evidence materials use the £3.47 decimal form while statutory Y3 guidance records pounds and pence separately and defers decimals to Y4; teachers should resolve this against their curriculum sequence.

probeDeeper: 'Read that amount to me — is £3.47 one number or two? What does the 4 mean, and the 7?'
'Check your change by counting it back onto £4.45 — does it rebuild £5?'
'You have £0.55 and £55 written down — which one matches the coins, and how do you know?'
'What if you'd paid with a £10 note instead of £5 — how would the change change, and would column subtraction or counting up be easier?'
assess.correctAnswer: Totals £2.60 + £1.85 = £4.45; finds change by counting up £4.45 → £4.50 → £5.00 = 55p (or column subtraction done correctly with exchange), and records it as £0.55 / 55p in consistent notation. For the game: £5.00 − £3.47 = £1.53, again best reached by counting on. Treats each amount as one quantity, exchanging 100p for £1 where needed.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'String-length thinking' — treats £ and p as two separate whole numbers: adds the pence beyond 100 without exchanging (£2.60 + £1.85 → £3.145 or £3.45), or subtracts pounds and pence columns independently.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Enact 100p = £1 with coins: build up the pence, physically exchange ten 10p (or 100 pennies) for a £1 coin, and re-read the amount as one quantity. Say amounts place-value-honestly, not as two separate numbers.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Column work where the pence exceed 99 without carrying a pound, or a total/answer with three digits after the point, or pence treated as their own number.

errorPatterns.pattern: Notation error — omits the decimal point or mixes units: records the change as £347, £55, 55p written inside pounds, or £0.55p (£ and p together).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show correct and incorrect side by side (£0.55 vs £0.55p vs £55) and ask which matches the coins in the tray; rehearse see–say–record and never writing £ and p together.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The written amount doesn't match its value, or combines £ and p symbols, or drops/misplaces the decimal point.

errorPatterns.pattern: Column-subtracts change from a whole note and makes take-smaller-from-larger / subtract-across-zeros errors (£5.00 − £3.47 treated as 00 − 47 = 47, giving £1.47 or £2.53) instead of counting up.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Redirect to the efficient strategy: find change from a note by counting UP from the total to the note on a number line, and reserve column methods for cases without the zeros trap.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A written vertical subtraction from £5.00/£10.00 with digits taken the wrong way across the zeros; an answer that doesn't survive a counting-back check.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot total £.p or exchange 100p→£1; treats pounds and pence as separate whole numbers and records inconsistent notation.
responseLevels.full: Totals two or three £.p items, finds change from £5/£10 by counting up, records £-notation correctly and consistently, treats each amount as a single quantity (exchanging 100p→£1), and transfers to a new price or note.
responseLevels.partial: Totals and gives change for a friendly case, but stumbles on change from a whole £5/£10 (column-across-zeros error) or records £.p inconsistently; can list the amounts but not treat them as one quantity throughout.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a small shop of priced items and real/realistic coins and notes. Say: 'Buy the £2.60 car and the £1.85 book. Pay with this £5 note, work out the change, and write down the change using £ and p.' Then: 'Now buy just the £3.47 game and pay with a £5 note — what's the change?' Watch the method and the notation, not only the final number.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with a single-quantity understanding of £.p counts up (or exchanges cleanly) and records £0.55 correctly; a child holding 'two separate whole numbers' adds/subtracts the pounds and pence columns independently (yielding e.g. £3.150, or £2.53 by taking 47 from 00), or writes £347/£0.55p. The counting-on change and the notation each expose a different, nameable error.

sources.claim: Year 3 pupils should add and subtract amounts of money to give change, using both £ and p in practical contexts; non-statutory guidance says they record pounds and pence separately and that decimal recording of money is introduced formally in Year 4.
sources.source: DfE, National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (Year 3 Measurement)

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–10y; solve WORD PROBLEMS involving multiplicative comparison, using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y4–Y5 scaling problems ('n times as tall/long/heavy') and multiplicative reasoning problem-solving.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.OA.2 — 'multiply or divide to solve word problems involving multiplicative comparison, e.g. by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number, distinguishing multiplicative comparison from additive comparison.'
• Operational details — this applies the multiplicative-comparison CONCEPT to problems and, crucially, requires solving for the unknown in any position: the compared quantity (blue is 3× the 7 cm red → 21), the referent (36 is 4 times a number → 36÷4), or the scale factor (24 is how many times 6?). Division appears when the unknown is the referent or the factor. The 4.OA.2 headline is DISTINGUISHING multiplicative from additive comparison in context ('5 more' vs '5 times as many'). Comparison bar models with a symbol for the unknown are the core tool; label which quantity is the referent.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): find the compared quantity ('3 times as long as 7 cm'). Tier B (age 9–10): find the referent or scale factor by dividing ('36 is 4 times what?'), writing an equation with a symbol. Tier C (age 10): sort mixed comparison problems into multiplicative vs additive and solve each correctly.
bestPractices: Use comparison bar models with a symbol for the unknown, labelling the referent bar and the n-times bar so the unknown's position dictates × or ÷.
Solve for the unknown in ALL positions — compared quantity (×), referent and scale factor (÷) — not just the forward case.
Explicitly sort and contrast multiplicative vs additive comparison problems (4.OA.2's central demand), using matched-number pairs to expose the difference.
Require an equation with a symbol for the unknown, tying the drawing to notation and the inverse.
Check answers against the bar model and the inverse (does the scale factor really map referent to compared?).
keyRepresentations: Comparison bar model with a symbol for the unknown (referent vs n-times bar)
Double number line — the scaling relationship, unknown at either end
Scale-factor arrow (×n / ÷n) linking the two quantities
Equation with a symbol for the unknown (b = 3 × 7; 36 = 4 × n)
commonMisconceptions: Adding/subtracting when the problem is multiplicative ('3 times as many' answered as +3).
Multiplying when the unknown is the referent or factor, instead of dividing (36 is 4 times what → wrongly 36×4).
Confusing which quantity is the referent, inverting the relationship.
Not distinguishing 'times as many' from 'more than' in the problem's language.
Writing an equation that doesn't match the comparison structure.

learn.summary: For 9–10 year olds solving multiplicative-comparison word problems (CCSS-M 4.OA.2; UK Y4–Y5 scaling and multiplicative reasoning). Learners draw comparison bar models (or an equivalent double number line / scale-factor arrow) with a symbol for the unknown, solve for the unknown in every position (compared quantity, referent, and scale factor), and — the heart of the standard — distinguish multiplicative ('3 times as many') from additive ('3 more than') comparison. Division appears when the unknown is the referent or the scale factor. Learners tie each drawing to an equation with a symbol for the unknown.

activities.title: Build the bar, place the unknown, decide × or ÷
feedback: If a learner multiplied 36 × 4 = 144: ask them to shade 36 as the big bar split into 4 equal parts; one part is the unknown number, so it must be smaller than 36, forcing division.
If the drawing shows the referent as larger than the n-times total, prompt: 'Which quantity is made of several copies of the other? That is the bigger one.'
When correct, ask them to state in words why they divided: 'The total of 4 copies is known, so I split it into 4 to find one copy.'
activities.rationale: Comparison bar models with a labelled referent and n-times bar — or an equivalent double number line / scale-factor arrow — let the unknown's position dictate the operation, covering forward (×), referent (÷) and scale-factor (÷) cases rather than only the forward case. An optional manipulable version — dragging a '?' marker and watching the implied operation update — may make the position-to-operation link more concrete, but drawn bars on paper achieve the same reasoning.
sourceClaims: 4.OA.2 requires solving multiplicative-comparison word problems with drawings and equations using a symbol for the unknown, distinguishing multiplicative from additive comparison.
Comparison bar models support solving for the unknown in any position; multiplicative vs additive comparison must be distinguished in context.
learnerActions: Read a comparison story, e.g. '36 is 4 times a number — what is the number?'

Draw a referent bar (the quantity being compared to) and an 'n-times' bar made of that many equal copies; a double number line or a ×n/÷n scale-factor arrow represents the same scaling relationship if you prefer.
Place a '?' marker on whichever bar is unknown.

Decide the operation from the position of the '?': if the whole n-times bar is unknown, multiply; if the referent or the number of copies is unknown, divide. For '36 is 4 times a number', the referent is unknown, so 36 ÷ 4 = 9.
Write the matching equation with a symbol for the unknown, e.g. 36 = 4 × n, then n = 36 ÷ 4 = 9.
Check: does your scale factor really map the referent to the compared quantity? (4 × 9 = 36.)
activities.intendedInsight: The position of the unknown in the comparison — not the presence of the word 'times' — decides whether you multiply or divide. A bar model (or number line) makes that position visible.

activities.title: Matched pair: 'more than' versus 'times as many'
feedback: If both stories get the same answer (e.g. 8 for both), have the learner build both with cubes or bars side by side; the two towers come out visibly different (8 vs 15), exposing that the operations must differ.

If the reverse ribbon problem gives 36 (12 × 3), point out that red would then be LONGER than blue, yet blue being 3 times as long as red means red must be the shorter one; the bar of 3 equal parts forces division.
When correct, ask them to generate their own matched pair — producing one that genuinely differs confirms they parse the structure.
activities.rationale: Matched-number pairs isolate the single differing word, so the operation a learner chooses reveals whether they parse the comparison structure or keyword-match. Pairing a reverse (÷) case with the forward (×) case guards against the reflex of multiplying whenever 'times' appears and shows the operation direction depends on the unknown's position. Side-by-side concrete building makes the additive/multiplicative difference something the learner sees rather than a rule to recall.
sourceClaims: 4.OA.2 requires solving multiplicative-comparison word problems with drawings and equations using a symbol for the unknown, distinguishing multiplicative from additive comparison.
Comparison bar models support solving for the unknown in any position; multiplicative vs additive comparison must be distinguished in context.
learnerActions: Solve two near-identical stories built on the same numbers: (a) 'Maya has 3 stickers. Tom has 5 MORE than Maya — how many does Tom have?' and (b) 'Maya has 3 stickers. Tom has 5 TIMES as many as Maya — how many does Tom have?'
Build or draw both: for (a), Maya's bar plus 5 more; for (b), 5 copies of Maya's bar.
Compute both and compare: (a) 3 + 5 = 8; (b) 3 × 5 = 15.
State in your own words why the two differ, then make up your own matched 'more'/'times' pair and solve both.
Try a reverse problem: 'A blue ribbon is 12 cm. That is 3 times as long as the red ribbon. How long is the red ribbon?' Build blue as 3 equal parts; one part is red, so 12 ÷ 3 = 4 cm.

Then try the forward direction: 'A blue ribbon is 3 times as long as a red ribbon of 4 cm — how long is blue?' Here the whole n-times bar is unknown, so 3 × 4 = 12 cm. Notice the operation ran the opposite way from the reverse problem.
activities.intendedInsight: 'More than' means add a fixed amount; 'times as many' means repeat the quantity. The same numbers give different answers, so you must read the comparison structure, not just spot a keyword — and which quantity is unknown decides whether you multiply or divide.

activities.title: Sort, match, and solve mixed problems
feedback: If a learner selects 144 for '36 is 4 times a number', return them to a bar of 36 split into 4 equal parts to see one part is 9.
If they classify a 'times as many' story as additive, re-read aloud and ask whether Tom's amount is Maya's amount repeated or Maya's amount plus a fixed number.
activities.rationale: Classifying and matching to equations verifies the distinguish-and-solve demand of 4.OA.2 with targeted distractors (e.g. 144 for the 36÷4 case). A sort/match task can teach and check classification but does not itself elicit the drawing or physical building, so use it alongside, not instead of, drawing and building.
sourceClaims: 4.OA.2 requires solving multiplicative-comparison word problems with drawings and equations using a symbol for the unknown, distinguishing multiplicative from additive comparison.
learnerActions: Given a mixed set of comparison stories, sort each into 'multiplicative' or 'additive' before solving.
Match each story to an equation written with a symbol for the unknown.
Solve for the unknown wherever it sits — compared quantity, referent, or scale factor.
Check targeted traps: for '36 is 4 times a number, the number is…', confirm the answer is smaller than 36 (9), not larger (144).
activities.intendedInsight: Deciding the comparison type and the unknown's position up front determines the operation; this is checkable and should be practised across varied contexts.

activities.title: Talk it through: which quantity do we know?
feedback: If a learner jumps to an operation, ask them first to say which bar would be unknown in a drawing.
Prompt 'so do we multiply or divide to find the missing one?' and have them tie the answer back to the referent.
activities.rationale: Spoken, probing dialogue may strengthen problem-parsing and can introduce varied contexts (efficacy untested), but it does not itself produce the drawn or manipulated bars; pair it with drawing so the reasoning is also made visible.
learnerActions: With a partner or guide, work a comparison story aloud, answering: 'Is this times as many or more than? Which quantity do we already know — the single amount or the repeated total?'
Decide together whether to multiply or divide, and justify the choice before computing.
Pose fresh contexts (heights, collections, lengths) and parse each one aloud.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the comparison type and which quantity is known is the parsing step that controls the operation.

constraints: Always require an equation with a symbol for the unknown alongside the drawing, so notation and model stay linked.
Cover all unknown positions: compared quantity (×), referent (÷), and scale factor (÷) — not just the forward case.

Sorting/matching and multiple-choice tasks verify classification and answers but do not by themselves elicit bar-model drawing or independent problem-parsing; use them after or alongside drawing and building.
Worked exemplars with reveal-the-answer are a reference scaffold; the skill requires learners to parse NEW problems and choose the operation themselves, so limit reliance on pre-solved examples.

Distinguish the execution slip (right set-up, wrong arithmetic) from the conceptual error: for a pure arithmetic slip, point back to the learner's own correct equation and have them recompute rather than reteaching comparison.

An optional manipulable bar tool (dragging a '?' marker, live operation hint) may make the position-to-operation link more concrete, but it is one way to reach the goal, not a requirement; drawn bars suffice.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Source legacy 'verified' flags were mixed (DfE Y4–Y5 claim marked verified; CCSS 4.OA.2 and NCETM claims marked unverified); no fresh verification was performed here.

Self-audit of worked examples: '3 times 7 cm = 21', '36 ÷ 4 = 9', '3 + 5 = 8' vs '3 × 5 = 15', reverse '12 ÷ 3 = 4 cm' and forward '3 × 4 = 12 cm' all check out. The 144 and 12×3=36-cm values are intentionally retained only as distractors/error patterns, never as correct answers.
Legacy guidance asserted '3D adds no value' for this planar topic; retained only as an observation that bars/number lines are two-dimensional, not as a universal claim about 3D representations.
Double number line (unknown at either end) and scale-factor arrow (×n/÷n) are preserved from the original as alternative representations of the same scaling relationship.

Activity 4's sourceClaims were set to [] because no source directly supports the efficacy of spoken dialogue; its benefit is stated as an untested proposal with only the narrow limitation that it does not produce drawn bars.

Independent re-review found the arithmetic, directional logic (forward × vs reverse ÷), and medium claims sound; no critical learner-facing errors were identified, and no new source verification was performed.

probeDeeper: Problems (a) and (b) start the same. Why did you add for one and multiply for the other?
In the ribbon problem, is red longer or shorter than blue? So should your answer be bigger or smaller than 12?
Make up your own 'times as many' problem for me and solve it.
What if the blue ribbon were 3 times as long as a red ribbon of 4 cm — how long is blue now? Which way did the operation go this time?
assess.correctAnswer: (a) 8 (additive: 3 + 5). (b) 15 (multiplicative: 3 × 5). Reverse: 4 cm (12 ÷ 3, because blue is 3 copies of red, so red = blue divided by 3). The teacher watches for the child selecting × for 'times as many', + for 'more than', and ÷ to find the smaller quantity in the reverse case.

errorPatterns.pattern: keyword-matches: multiplies whenever 'times' appears and adds whenever 'more' appears, without modelling the situation — so multiplies on the reverse problem too (12 × 3 = 36)
errorPatterns.nextMove: draw a bar model: blue as three equal parts, red as one of those parts; the picture forces division, breaking the 'times → multiply' reflex.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: on the reverse ribbon problem the child computes 36, making red LONGER than blue though the text says red is the smaller one

errorPatterns.pattern: collapses multiplicative into additive — treats 'times as many' like 'more than', solving (b) as 3 + 5 = 8
errorPatterns.nextMove: put (a) and (b) side by side and ask the child to build both with cubes; the two towers come out visibly different, exposing that the operations must differ.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child gives the SAME answer (8) to both (a) and (b), not noticing the word change

errorPatterns.pattern: sets up the right operation but slips in execution (miscounts groups, or writes 3×5 then computes 8) — the structure is understood, the arithmetic lapses
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach comparison; point back to the child's own correct set-up and have them recompute, or check with a known fact.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: correct expression written but wrong product, or self-corrects when asked to recount

responseLevels.gap: gives the same answer to the 'more' and 'times' problems, or multiplies on the reverse problem making the smaller quantity larger — keyword-driven, not structure-driven.
responseLevels.full: chooses × for 'times as many', + for 'more than', and ÷ to find the smaller quantity in a reverse problem — all from modelling the situation, and can generate a correct comparison problem of their own.
responseLevels.partial: solves the straightforward 'times as many' problem correctly but falters on the reverse (unknown referent) case, or needs prompting to notice the more/times distinction.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a mixed set of comparison word problems to solve on paper, watching how they set each one up (not asking them to explain the type). Include a matched pair that differs by one word: (a) 'Maya has 3 stickers. Tom has 5 MORE than Maya. How many does Tom have?' and (b) 'Maya has 3 stickers. Tom has 5 TIMES as many as Maya. How many does Tom have?' Add a reverse problem: 'A blue ribbon is 12 cm. That is 3 times as long as the red ribbon. How long is the red ribbon?' Watch which operation they choose for each.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The matched a/b pair is identical except 'more' vs 'times as many', so the operation chosen reveals whether the child parses the comparison structure or keyword-matches. The reverse problem catches children who always multiply when they see 'times'. Watching the setup (not an explanation) is the point: procedural competence shows in the operation selected, not in talk about it.

sources.claim: Y4–Y5 pupils solve scaling ('n times as many') word problems as part of multiplicative reasoning.

sources.claim: 4.OA.2 requires solving multiplicative-comparison word problems with drawings and equations using a symbol for the unknown, distinguishing multiplicative from additive comparison.
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 4, Operations & Algebraic Thinking (4.OA.A.2)
