pedagogy.summary: Year 2 (age 6–7) money problems stay within a single unit (pence): totalling the cost of items, and — the demanding part — finding change and answering 'how much more do I need?'. The pedagogical key is that change is a DIFFERENCE, and young children find it far easier to reach a difference by COUNTING UP (the 'shopkeeper's method') with real coins than by counting back or by written take-away. Teaching should make change a practical, coin-in-hand act before it becomes an abstract subtraction.
bestPractices: Build change by counting UP from the price to the amount paid, using real or realistic coins so the coins themselves record each step (e.g. 35p → +5p = 40p → +10p = 50p; change 15p) — the DfE mental-calculation guidance calls this the shopkeeper's method and notes many children find counting up easier than counting back.
Model the same jumps on an empty number line so the change is seen as the TOTAL DISTANCE travelled (the sum of the jumps), not a point on the line.
Connect 'how much more do I need?' to the identical counting-up structure — it is the same gap read the other way — so children see missing-addend and change as one idea.
Keep amounts to manageable, 'friendly' values first (bridging one multiple of ten), then extend; use role-play shops so the procedure is rehearsed in a real context.
Press children to CHECK reasonableness — count the change back onto the price to confirm it rebuilds the amount paid.
keyRepresentations: Real/realistic coins counted into the hand (coins as a record of the steps)
Empty number line showing change as jumps from price up to amount paid
Part–whole (bar) model: amount paid = cost + change
A shop/role-play till context
commonMisconceptions: 'More coins = more money' — thinks a fistful of small coins is worth more, so gives too many or judges having-enough by count not value.
Adds the two numbers (price + amount paid) instead of finding the difference, because early teaching over-emphasises 'take away' and difference is not recognised as subtraction.
Loses the running total or miscounts when bridging through a multiple of ten while counting up.
Counts single pennies one-by-one inaccurately instead of using coin values.

learn.summary: Year 2 (age 6–7) money problems stay within a single unit (pence): totalling the cost of items, and the more demanding work of finding change and answering 'how much more do I need?'. The core idea is that change is a DIFFERENCE, most easily reached by COUNTING UP from the price to the amount paid (the 'shopkeeper's method') with real coins, rather than by counting back or written take-away. Change should be a practical, coin-in-hand act before it becomes an abstract subtraction.

activities.title: Give change at a role-play market stall (count up with coins)
feedback: When your counting-on reaches the amount paid, confirm success: 'You've counted on to 50p — the 15p of change you built (10p + 5p), added to the 35p price, rebuilds the amount paid.' (Note the change coins total 15p; it is the running total counted on from the price that reaches 50p.)
If one coin too many goes in, show the running total overshooting the amount paid (past 50p) and invite the child to remove a coin and recount up.
If the running total is still short, point to the remaining gap: 'Counting on from 35p you've reached 40p — how much more to reach 50p?'

Optional live supports that make the mechanism visible: a running-total bar that starts at the price (35p) and rises with each coin to the amount paid (50p), and an empty number line on which each jump (+5, +10) draws itself from 35 up to 50.
activities.rationale: Counting up from the smaller to the larger value ('shopkeeper's method') is an easier route to a difference for many young children than counting back, and coins give a concrete record of each step. Physically building the change makes 'change as difference' felt before it is written.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils should solve simple problems in a practical context involving addition and subtraction of money of the same unit, including giving change.

Change/difference is best found by counting UP from the smaller to the larger number ('shopkeeper's method'); many children find it easier to subtract by counting up than counting back, and coins provide a record of how the change was given (worked example: 27p, change from 50p = 3p + 20p = 23p).
learnerActions: Set up a shop: a toy priced 35p, a 50p coin to pay with, and a pot of mixed coins.
Count UP aloud from the price to the amount paid, placing a coin into a change tray at each step: '35… (put in a 5p) 40… (put in a 10p) 50'.
State the change as the coins you built: 'The change is 15p — a 10p and a 5p.'
Check by counting the change back onto the price to confirm it rebuilds the amount paid (35p + 15p = 50p).
Repeat with other friendly prices (e.g. 45p paid with 50p gives 5p), then extend to the source worked example 27p paid with 50p, counting 27→30→50 to give 3p + 20p = 23p.
activities.intendedInsight: Change is the DISTANCE travelled from the price up to the amount paid — it is the total of the jumps you make when counting up (here 5p + 10p = 15p), not a take-away you have to work out on paper. The coins themselves record how the change was reached.

activities.title: 'How much more do I need?' — the same gap read the other way
feedback: Confirm when the count-up reaches the price exactly: '15 up to 20 is one jump of 5p — you need 5p more.'
If the child adds 15 + 20, re-anchor: 'You already have 15p; count on from there up to 20p to see what's missing.'
activities.rationale: Presenting change and missing-addend through the identical counting-up structure helps children treat the two situations as one move rather than as unrelated, and supports recognising difference (not only 'take away') as subtraction.
sourceClaims: Change/difference is best found by counting UP from the smaller to the larger number ('shopkeeper's method'); many children find it easier to subtract by counting up than counting back, and coins provide a record of how the change was given (worked example: 27p, change from 50p = 3p + 20p = 23p).
learnerActions: Set a toy priced 20p and give the child 15p.
Ask: 'How much MORE do you need to buy this?'
Count UP from what you have to the price: '15… (add a 5p) 20' and name the shortfall as 5p.
Line this up against a change task: notice that finding the shortfall and finding change are the same counting-up move, just started from a different amount.
activities.intendedInsight: Finding change and finding 'how much more I need' (missing addend) are one idea: closing the gap by counting up between two amounts.

activities.title: Value, not number of coins
feedback: When the child checks totals: 'A fistful of pennies can be worth less than one coin — it's the value that counts, not the number.'
Praise finding several coin combinations that make the same value.
activities.rationale: Directly addresses the common 'more coins = more money' misconception by making children compare totals by value and build equal values from different combinations.
sourceClaims: A common money misconception to address explicitly is 'if I have the most coins I will always have the most money'; children may confuse one pence and one pound, and value should not be judged by coin count or size.
learnerActions: Lay the child's handful of small coins beside a single 10p and 5p.
Count the total VALUE of each set and compare, e.g. show that ten 1p coins are worth less than one 20p.
Make the SAME value (e.g. 15p) with different coin combinations (10p + 5p; 5p + 5p + 5p; 10p + 2p + 2p + 1p).
activities.intendedInsight: Money is judged by total value, not by how many coins there are; many small coins can be worth less than one larger coin.

activities.title: Short written check on change and coin combinations
feedback: Mark correct amounts and valid combinations; for a wrong amount, send the child back to count up from the price with coins.
Note: a right answer here does not show the counting-up method — observe the hands-on building to assess the process.
activities.rationale: A brief recognition/short-answer check can confirm the answer, but it does not elicit the counting-up construction that is the heart of the objective, so it supplements rather than replaces hands-on work.
learnerActions: Given a price and an amount paid, state the change and the coins that make it.
Pick, from a set of options, coins that make a given change, and set a value (e.g. with a slider) to match the change for a given purchase.
activities.intendedInsight: A quick check confirms whether the child can land the correct change amount and a valid coin combination.

constraints: Keep amounts to friendly values that bridge a single multiple of ten first (e.g. 35p→50p), then extend once secure.
A tap-to-reveal picture of coins can serve as a reference to coin values; it does not let the child carry out or get feedback on the counting-up procedure, so it is a scaffold, not the main activity.
Recognition/short-answer checks assess the answer, not the method; they do not elicit the independent counting-up construction that is the objective.
Running-total bars (anchored at the price), number-line jumps, and a change tray are optional supports to make the gap visible — offer them to illustrate the mechanism, not as mandatory steps.

Keep the value of the change coins distinct from the running total: the change coins total the difference (e.g. 15p), while the running total counted on from the price reaches the amount paid (e.g. 50p).
Always have the child check reasonableness by counting the change back onto the price to rebuild the amount paid.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic checked: change 15p = 10p + 5p and 35p + 15p = 50p; worked example 27p→50p = 3p + 20p = 23p; 45p→50p = 5p; missing-addend 15p→20p = 5p; ten 1p = 10p < one 20p; 15p = 10p+5p = 5p+5p+5p = 10p+2p+2p+1p. All consistent.
The 27p→50p worked example crosses more than one ten boundary, so it is presented as an extension of the friendly single-ten cases rather than as itself a single-ten bridge.

Value/running-total distinction maintained in the first activity: change coins total 15p, whereas the running total counted on from the 35p price reaches 50p; no wording states the change coins 'add up to 50p'.

The source labelled a 3D shop rendering as adding 'handling friction' and a role-play conversation as unsuited; these are catalog-fit judgements, not established facts, and have been dropped rather than restated as universal limits. A spoken shopkeeper exchange could in fact narrate the counting-up steps.

One cited source (NCETM 'Misconceptions with the Key Objectives / Subtraction as difference') is marked verified:false in the row; the principle it supports (difference under-recognised because 'take away' is over-emphasised) is retained only as rationale framing, not cited as established evidence.

The original 'adds price + amount paid (35 + 50)' and 'counts single pennies inaccurately' misconceptions are addressed indirectly rather than as standalone correctives; a future revision could add an explicit change-activity prompt contrasting adding with finding the gap.

probeDeeper: 'Show me how you know that's the right change — can you count it back onto the 35p to make 50p again?'
'You gave me these coins; is there a way to make the same change with fewer coins?'
'What if the toy cost 32p instead of 35p — would the change be more or less? Why?'
'How is finding my change like working out how much MORE you need to buy the 20p toy?'
assess.correctAnswer: For change: counts up from 35p (e.g. +5p to 40p, +10p to 50p) and hands back 15p in coins, or otherwise establishes the 15p gap and gives it by value. For the second: identifies the 5p shortfall by counting on from 15p to 20p. In both, the coins/steps show a DIFFERENCE being built, and the child can check by rebuilding the paid amount.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'More coins means more money' — hands back a fistful of small coins and treats having given MANY coins as having given enough, judging by count not value ('I gave you loads, so that's enough').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to value: line up the child's handful against a single 10p+5p and count both totals; show that ten 1p is worth less than one 20p. Rehearse making the SAME value with different coin combinations.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives too many low-value coins for the change, or is satisfied by the NUMBER of coins rather than checking their total value against the 15p gap.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds the two numbers instead of finding the difference — computes 35 + 50 = 85 (or grabs 85p) because 'take away' is the only subtraction they recognise and change isn't seen as subtraction.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Act it out as a shopkeeper: physically count coins UP from 35p into the customer's hand to 50p, and name the total handed over as the change. Contrast 'the shop keeps 35p, you get the rest' with adding.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Combines the price and the amount paid; hands over far too much, or writes 35+50.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counting up but losing the running total when bridging a ten — reaches 40p, then miscounts the second jump (e.g. calls the change 10p or 25p).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach: record each jump on an empty number line so the two jumps (+5, +10) are visible and can be added deliberately; keep amounts bridging a single ten until secure.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Starts a correct counting-on path but the total of the jumps is wrong at the multiple-of-ten boundary.

responseLevels.gap: Grabs coins without matching value, adds the two amounts, or cannot establish the change; judges 'enough' by number of coins.
responseLevels.full: Reliably builds change by counting up from price to paid amount, solves the missing-addend 'how much more' by the same move, checks by rebuilding the paid amount, and transfers to a new price.
responseLevels.partial: Finds the change for the friendly case by counting up, but loses the total when bridging a ten, or can do the change but not the equivalent 'how much more do I need?', treating them as unrelated.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set out a toy labelled 35p and give the child a single 50p coin and a pot of mixed coins. Say: 'Buy the toy and give me the right change — use the coins to show me how you work it out.' Then set a second toy at 20p and say: 'You have 15p. How much more do you need to buy this one?' Watch HOW they work, not just the answer.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands change as a difference counts UP from price to paid amount and the coins record the gap; a child who does not either adds 35+50, grabs a random fistful of coins judging 'enough' by how many, or counts back and loses the total. Correct reasoning yields 15p by a visible counting-on path; the wrong ideas each yield a different, diagnosable move.

pedagogy.summary: Children measure in standard units and then calculate with the measures — adding and subtracting lengths (m/cm/mm), masses (kg/g) and volumes (l/ml). The governing rule is that you can only add or subtract measures that are in the SAME unit, and the answer keeps that unit. At Year 3 the arithmetic is done within a single unit (250 ml + 400 ml = 650 ml); systematic conversion between units (mm–cm–m) comes later, so mixed-unit sums are not yet expected.
bestPractices: Establish 'same unit before you calculate' — line up like units, add, and carry the unit into the answer.
Model length calculations on a number line / tape so adding lengths is combining distances and subtracting is finding a gap.
Always write the unit in the answer; treat a bare number as incomplete.
Keep arithmetic within one unit at this stage; delay formal mm–cm–m conversion (it belongs to a later unit-conversion topic).
Use real measuring-then-calculating tasks (ribbon needed, juice combined) so the operation has a purpose.
keyRepresentations: A number line / tape diagram for combining and comparing lengths
Aligned columns of like units (all in ml, or all in cm) before adding
A measuring bench: measure two quantities, then combine them
An answer frame that always includes the unit (____ ml, ____ cm)
commonMisconceptions: Adds or subtracts across different units as if they were the same number (2 m + 30 cm = 32).
Drops the unit from the answer (250 ml + 400 ml = 650).
Muddles compound units, e.g. reads 3 cm 5 mm as 35 or adds 3 + 5 — not yet knowing 10 mm = 1 cm.
Applies the wrong operation — adds when the problem asks for a difference, or vice versa.

learn.summary: Year 3 children calculate with standard-unit measures: adding and subtracting lengths (m/cm/mm), masses (kg/g) and volumes/capacities (l/ml). The governing rule is 'same unit before you calculate': you only add or subtract measures expressed in the same unit, and the answer keeps that unit (250 ml + 400 ml = 650 ml). Arithmetic stays within a single unit at this stage; systematic mm–cm–m conversion comes later, so mixed-unit sums are not yet expected. A number line / tape model makes combining (stacking) versus differencing (finding the gap) concrete, and every answer must carry its unit.

activities.title: Measure-and-combine bench with a number line
feedback: If the learner writes a bare number (e.g. 650), ask: 'What unit belongs on this answer, and why does it matter?' Treat a measurement answer without a unit as incomplete.

If the learner adds across units (2 m + 30 cm = 32), ask: 'Is 2 metres the same size as 2 centimetres? What has to be true before you can add them?' Line both up on one common scale (2 m lines up as 200 cm) so the mismatch is visible; the goal here is to recognise that the units must match, not to carry out the full conversion, which is a later-stage skill.

If the learner picks the wrong operation, ask: 'Does this problem want you to put the amounts together, or find how much more one is than the other?' and rebuild it on the number line (combine = stack/mark to total, difference = gap).

If the learner muddles a compound unit (writes 3 cm 5 mm as 35 cm, or adds 3 + 5 to get 8), keep the task within a single unit for now; full mm–cm conversion belongs to a later stage. (Note that 35 mm is a correct value for 3 cm 5 mm, so do not mark it as wrong.)
activities.rationale: Representing add/subtract on tape or number-line diagrams follows established measurement progressions where combining and differencing are modelled on a line with equal unit spacing; measuring-then-calculating gives the operation a real purpose. An optional live mechanism — marking measured amounts on the line and a running answer box that always carries the unit — may make the combining idea and the same-unit requirement concrete, but is not the only possible setup.
sourceClaims: Second graders add two lengths to obtain the length of the whole and subtract one length from another to find the difference; length add/subtract problems are represented with tape or number-bond diagrams and equations with a symbol for the unknown, and a number line diagram is a measurement model where consecutive whole numbers are one unit apart.
Unit size is critical in measurement and the unit must always be considered ('what are you counting?' -> the length-units), so a measurement answer is meaningful only with its unit.
Year 3 pupils measure, compare, add and subtract lengths (m/cm/mm), mass (kg/g) and volume/capacity (l/ml) using standard units.
learnerActions: Measure two real quantities of the SAME kind — e.g. two lengths of ribbon in cm, or two beakers of juice in ml (250 ml and 400 ml), or two masses in g.

Combine the two measures on a number line / tape: place lengths end to end to read the total (e.g. 25 cm + 40 cm = 65 cm), or mark the two volumes along the scale to reach the total (250 ml + 400 ml = 650 ml). Write the answer WITH its unit (65 cm; 650 ml).
Switch to a subtraction task: use the same number line to find the difference between the two measures as the gap between them.
Decide for each worded problem whether you are combining the amounts (stack them / mark to the total) or finding how much more one is than the other (find the gap).

Meet the mixed-unit case: a 2 m length and a 30 cm length. Try to total them and notice you cannot simply write 32 — line both up on one common scale (2 m lines up as 200 cm) and say what has to be true (same unit) before adding.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding measures means combining amounts and subtracting means finding a gap; a measurement answer is only meaningful with its unit; and you can only add or subtract measures that are in the same unit.

activities.title: Same-unit calculation check with targeted wrong-answer options
feedback: For the option that drops the unit: 'The arithmetic is right, but what is missing? A measurement answer needs its unit.'

For the option that adds across units: 'Why can't 2 m and 30 cm just be added as 2 + 30? What would make them addable?' Line them up on one common scale (2 m lines up as 200 cm) so the units clearly differ; actually converting and totalling is a later-stage skill, not expected now.
If the learner answers correctly, ask them to generalise: 'What is the rule for when two measures CAN be added together?'
activities.rationale: Short checks that target the specific error patterns (dropping the unit, adding across units) are strongly discriminating for whether the same-unit rule is understood. This format can test and make the rule explicit; recognising a correct option is not the same as producing unit-bearing work, so it complements rather than replaces the number-line sense built on the bench.
sourceClaims: Unit size is critical in measurement and the unit must always be considered ('what are you counting?' -> the length-units), so a measurement answer is meaningful only with its unit.

The systematic relationship among length units (km, m, cm, mm) and conversion between them is placed in Grade 4 (4.MD.1), not Grade 3; expressing larger units in smaller units reinforces place value. This means at the earlier stage children work within a single unit and full mm–cm–m conversion is not yet expected.
learnerActions: Complete fill-in-the-blank sums within one unit, writing the unit in the answer (e.g. 250 ml + 400 ml = ___ ml).
Choose the correct result from options that include one that drops the unit and one that adds across units (e.g. for 2 m + 30 cm, recognise that '32' is wrong).
Explain in words why the across-unit option is wrong before moving on.
activities.intendedInsight: The same-unit rule and the unit-bearing answer can be stated explicitly and recognised in others' work, not just produced on the bench.

activities.title: Reference number-line diagram of a length addition
feedback: Prompt: 'Point to where the total ends on the line — what number is it, and what unit?'
Prompt: 'If this were a subtraction, which part of the picture would be the gap you measure?'
activities.rationale: A fixed diagram cannot be manipulated and does not let the child measure across varied cases or meet the same-unit trap by recomputing, so it works best as a reference or worked example alongside active tasks. It can still clarify the combining idea and unit placement.
sourceClaims: Second graders add two lengths to obtain the length of the whole and subtract one length from another to find the difference; length add/subtract problems are represented with tape or number-bond diagrams and equations with a symbol for the unknown, and a number line diagram is a measurement model where consecutive whole numbers are one unit apart.
learnerActions: Study a labelled number line / tape showing two lengths placed end to end and the total read off the scale.
Trace along the line to see where the first length ends and the second begins, and where the total sits.
Describe in your own words why the total is found by combining distances, and identify where the unit appears in the answer.
activities.intendedInsight: A worked tape/number-line picture shows the combining idea and anchors the vocabulary, as a reference to support the active measure-and-calculate work.

constraints: Keep all arithmetic within a single unit at this stage; delay formal mm–cm–m (and kg–g, l–ml) conversion to a later unit-conversion topic. The mixed-unit trap is used only to reveal that units must match, not to have the child compute a converted total.
Always require the unit in the answer; treat a bare number as an incomplete answer.

Keep length examples (ribbon in cm/mm), capacity examples (juice in ml) and mass examples (in g) coherent — do not label a volume as a 'length' or carry a length action over to a capacity or mass result.
The fill-in/selection check tests and states the same-unit rule but does not by itself build number-line sense; pair it with the measure-and-combine activity.
The reference diagram is a worked example: it cannot let the child measure varied cases or recompute at the same-unit trap, so use it to support, not replace, hands-on measuring and calculating.

Optional interaction examples (marking measured amounts on a line, a subtraction 'gap' mode, a running unit-bearing answer box, lining up mismatched units on one common scale) illustrate the mechanism; they are suggestions, not mandatory features.

When a child muddles a compound unit (e.g. writes 3 cm 5 mm as 35 cm, or adds 3 + 5 to get 8), do not drill conversion now; keep calculations within one unit and let compound-unit fluency arrive with the later conversion topic.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Original inconsistency: the source recommendation text conflated capacity and length examples ('measures two lengths of ribbon (250 ml and 400 ml of juice...)'). 250 ml and 400 ml are capacities (juice/beakers), not lengths of ribbon; ribbon is measured in cm/mm. Activities now keep length (cm), capacity (ml) and mass (g) examples distinct.

Arithmetic checked: 250 ml + 400 ml = 650 ml is correct; 25 cm + 40 cm = 65 cm is correct; 2 m + 30 cm is NOT 32 (2 m = 200 cm, so a converted total would be 230 cm). The mixed-unit item is retained only as a deliberate error to recognise, never as a valid answer; the full conversion to 230 cm is a later-stage skill and is not presented to the child as expected Year 3 work.

The mass strand (kg/g) is named in the objective and evidence but was not exemplified by a dedicated activity; a two-masses-in-g version of the measure-and-combine bench has been offered so this strand can be covered.
The last source (UK National Curriculum, Year 3 measurement) is marked verified:false in the row; the Year 3 scope claim rests on this unverified source and should be confirmed on review.

Original fit field framed some claims as universal ('3D adds nothing', dialogue unsuitable because the skill is 'a watched performance'). These are not established by the cited sources and have been omitted; a conversation or worked demonstration can still support this skill even if it is not the primary vehicle.

probeDeeper: What unit should be on your answer of 650? Why does it matter?
You wrote 2 m + 30 cm = 32 — is 2 metres the same size as 2 centimetres? What has to be true before you can add them?
Show me this addition on the number line — where does the total end up?
Does this problem want you to put the amounts together, or find how much more one is than the other? How can you tell?
assess.correctAnswer: The child adds/subtracts measures that are in the same unit, keeps the unit in the answer (650 ml; 7 cm), chooses the operation that fits the problem, and — faced with the mixed-unit item — recognises the units must match first rather than adding 2 + 30 to get 32.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds/subtracts across different units as bare numbers: treats unlike units as like, e.g. 2 m + 30 cm = 32, or 1 kg + 200 g = 201.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist on a common unit before calculating; show both quantities on one scale so the mismatch is visible; return to attending to the unit when measuring.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Combines the digits of measures in different units without matching them; answer has no coherent unit.

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops the unit from the answer: computes correctly but writes a bare number (250 ml + 400 ml = 650).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Treat a measurement answer without a unit as incomplete; build the habit of writing the unit every time; the calculation itself is sound.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Right arithmetic, no unit on the result; supplies it only when asked.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compound-unit muddle: reads or combines mixed compound units wrongly, e.g. writes 3 cm 5 mm as 35 or adds 3 + 5, not yet knowing 10 mm = 1 cm.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill mm–cm conversion now — systematic conversion belongs to a later stage; keep calculations within a single unit and let compound-unit fluency come with the conversion topic.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats the two parts of a compound measure as one number, or adds them; expected before unit conversion is taught.

errorPatterns.pattern: Wrong operation: adds when the problem asks for a difference, or subtracts when it asks for a total.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Represent the problem on a number line/tape (combine = stack, difference = gap) so the operation follows the model; comprehension, not calculation, is the issue.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct arithmetic but the operation does not match the question's structure.

responseLevels.gap: Adds across different units as bare numbers, or routinely omits the unit, or picks the wrong operation.
responseLevels.full: Calculates with measures in a common unit, carries the unit into every answer, chooses the operation from the problem structure, and recognises that unlike units must be made the same before adding or subtracting.
responseLevels.partial: Adds/subtracts correctly within a single unit and usually keeps the unit, but is caught by the mixed-unit item or an unfamiliar compound unit — the same-unit rule is not yet explicit.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give real quantities to measure and combine: e.g. two lengths of ribbon and two beakers of water, plus a written problem ('250 ml + 400 ml = ?') and a deliberately mixed-unit one ('2 m + 30 cm = ?'). Say: 'Measure these and work out the totals and the difference.' Watch whether they keep like units together, carry the unit into the answer, and choose the right operation.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands calculating with measures produces unit-bearing answers and pauses at the mixed-unit sum; a child who does not writes 650 without a unit, or 2 m + 30 cm = 32, or applies the wrong operation — each visible in the written work.

pedagogy.summary: Children compare how long events last and put several in order by duration, and sequence intervals on a timeline. Because at this age they can't yet calculate elapsed time, comparison rests on measured or timed evidence (stopwatch, sand-timers) and on a common start. The deep hurdle carried from earlier is judging duration by non-time cues — a faster or further event, or the one that FINISHED later, is wrongly thought to have taken longer.
bestPractices: Compare timed events with a stopwatch / sand-timers so duration is measured, not guessed
Use a common start so 'who finished first' fairly shows quicker (a shorter duration)
Explicitly separate 'finished later' from 'took longer' with same-start and different-start cases
Order three durations by lining up their measured lengths (bars / timers)
Sequence intervals on a timeline of the day
keyRepresentations: Stopwatch / sand-timers giving a measured duration
Duration bars laid side by side for ordering
A common start-line for fair comparison
A daily timeline for sequencing intervals
commonMisconceptions: Judges duration by speed or distance (faster/further = longer) — the time-speed-distance confusion
Equates 'finished later / stopped last' with 'took longer', ignoring the start
Orders by how exciting or memorable an event was rather than its measured length
Treats a bigger clock-number at the end as a longer duration

learn.summary: Young children (around ages 6–7) compare how long events last, order several events by duration, and sequence intervals on a daily timeline. Because they are not yet expected to calculate elapsed time, comparison should rest on measured or timed evidence (stopwatches, sand-timers, duration bars). A common start is needed specifically when using finishing order as the evidence of who was quicker; when starts differ, children compare the measured running length of each event instead. The central hurdle is judging duration by non-time cues: thinking the faster, further, more exciting, or later-finishing event 'took longer', or reading a later finishing clock time as a longer duration. (A stopwatch or timer started from zero at the start of each event is different: its end reading is the duration, so a bigger reading there does mean longer.) The strongest teaching separates measured duration from speed, distance, and finishing position.

activities.title: Timed race from a shared start line, then order the duration bars
feedback: If a learner orders by excitement or memorability, re-line-up the measured durations side by side and read the order off the lengths: 'Was the race longest because it FELT long, or because the timer showed the most? Let's check the timers.'
If a learner picks the faster or further event as longest, point back to the shared start: 'We both started together, so whoever stopped first took less time.'
Confirm correct ordering by having the learner trace each bar length and name the order shortest-to-longest.
activities.rationale: Making duration visible as a growing bar from a common start decouples 'how long' from speed and finishing excitement, directly targeting the time-speed-distance confusion. A live, draggable bar lets the child measure and order rather than guess. Comparing and sequencing intervals of time is an explicit Year 2 measurement expectation.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils should 'compare and sequence intervals of time'.
Young children characteristically confuse duration with speed and distance (time-speed-distance confusion), judging that a faster or further-travelling object took more time.

Duration is the weakest area of children's time understanding in Years 3-4 (only about half reaching full understanding), so comparing and ordering durations warrants explicit measured-evidence teaching rather than being assumed.
learnerActions: Run or watch two or three timed events that all begin at the same common start (for example three sand-timers started together, or three classroom activities timed with a stopwatch).
Watch each event's duration grow as a bar (or sand-timer level) and note the moment it stops.
Arrange the finished bars/timers into order from shortest to longest duration — the order is simply the bar lengths.
Explain how you decided, pointing to the measured length rather than how fast or exciting each looked.
activities.intendedInsight: How long an event lasts is read from its measured duration, not from how fast, far, or exciting it was. With a common start, whoever stopped first took the shortest time.

activities.title: Different-start challenge: 'finished last' is not 'took longest'
feedback: If a learner picks whoever stopped last: 'This timer started late but stopped last — did it actually RUN for the most time? How can we tell?'

If a learner points to the later clock time showing when an event stopped and calls it longest, distinguish the two: a later clock time tells you WHEN it ended, not HOW LONG it ran — compare the measured running lengths from each start instead (a timer started from zero at each event's start would show that running length directly).
Reinforce by contrasting with the shared-start case: with a common start, finishing order does show duration; with different starts it does not.
Confirm reasoning when the learner measures each event's running length independently of its stop moment.
activities.rationale: The finished-later-equals-longer error specifically undermines simple duration comparison; deliberately staging a different-start case where the last-to-finish event is shortest confronts that error with measured evidence. Because the last-to-finish event also shows the later finishing clock time, this case likewise addresses reading a later end time as a longer duration (if each event were timed from zero, the shortest event would show the smaller reading). This is the discriminating case between salience/finish-position reasoning and genuine elapsed-time reasoning.
sourceClaims: White Rose Y3 Time (Step 8) documents that 'children may think that an event that ends at a later time must have a longer duration' — the finished-later-equals-longer misconception that also undermines simple duration comparison.
learnerActions: Watch a case where one event starts late but stops last, while its measured duration (bar/timer) is actually the shortest.
Decide which event ran for the most time, and justify using the actual running time rather than who stopped last or whose finishing clock time is later.
Compare a same-start case and a different-start case side by side, and say why the start time changes what finishing order tells you.
activities.intendedInsight: Stopping last only means 'took longest' when everything started together. When starts differ, you must compare how long each event actually ran, not who finished last or whose finishing clock time is later.

activities.title: Compare and sequence from timer readings
feedback: For a 'which took longer?' comparison, if the learner chooses the faster/further event, re-present two events that start together and ask which one is still going after the other stops, so duration is judged by running time rather than speed or distance.
Include a speed/distance counterexample in discussion: 'Both cars started together. The red car went further but the green one was still going after red stopped — which ran for more time?'
Confirm correct answers by having the learner name the measured value they used to decide.
activities.rationale: Comparison and ordering items from timer readings give clear, discriminating practice and check whether the child reasons from measured length. These are recognition/selection tasks, so they verify a decision but do not by themselves require the child to run and measure an event; pair them with the hands-on timing activities above.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils should 'compare and sequence intervals of time'.
learnerActions: Look at two timers and decide which event took longer, explaining how the reading shows it.
Sequence three events by how long they took, using their timer readings or measured lengths.
Match each activity to its measured duration.
Place everyday intervals in order on a timeline of the day to sequence intervals of time.
activities.intendedInsight: Comparing and ordering durations can be read directly from measured values, and intervals of a day can be sequenced in order.

constraints: Learners this age cannot yet calculate elapsed time, so comparison must rest on measured or timed evidence (stopwatch, sand-timers, duration bars); a common start is required only when fair finishing-order reasoning is used to judge who was quicker.

Ordering by how exciting or memorable an event felt is common at this age and often improves with repeated measured evidence; respond by re-lining-up the measured durations side by side and reading the order off the lengths.

A static two-timer picture with tap-to-reveal can label longer/shorter but does not let the child measure and order events live; use it as a scaffold, not a replacement for timing and arranging real durations.
Spoken commentary can invite comparison but does not itself supply the measured evidence that settles which event took longer; pair any discussion with timers or measured lengths.
Timer-reading comparison and matching are recognition tasks: they verify a decision but do not require the learner to independently run and measure events, so include hands-on timing too.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original claimed 3D adds nothing because comparing/ordering durations 'is not a spatial task'; this is a catalog-fit judgement, not an established pedagogical law, so it has been dropped rather than asserted. A 3D format is simply not needed here for the measured-comparison objective.

The original implied the 2D interactive is uniquely able to break the judge-by-speed/finish-position confusion. Measured timing and duration bars support this well, but comparative necessity over other measured-evidence approaches (e.g. real sand-timers) is not established by the cited sources; phrasing has been softened.

The Piaget time-speed-distance claim is marked verified:false in the source row; it is retained in sourceClaims as a well-known developmental observation but should not be treated as freshly verified.

The original's fourth misconception (a bigger end clock-number read as a longer duration) was not explicitly handled in the earlier candidate's learner text; it has been added to the different-start activity's actions and feedback, since the last-to-finish event also shows the larger stop reading.

The summary previously framed a common start as a general requirement for duration comparison; this was corrected to scope it to finishing-order reasoning, matching the different-start activity where events are compared by measured running length without a shared start.

probeDeeper: 'You said the race took longest — was that because it FELT long, or because the timer showed the most? Let's check the timers.'
'We both started at the same time. If I stopped first, did I take more time or less?'
'This timer started late but stopped last — did it actually RUN for the most time? How can we tell?'
'The red car went further but the green one was still going after red stopped — which ran for more time?' (speed/distance counterexample)
assess.correctAnswer: Orders the three by their measured durations; on the common-start pair names the one that ran longer regardless of speed or distance; on the different-start case reasons that stopping last doesn't mean running longest, considering how long each actually ran.

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges duration by speed or distance rather than elapsed time — the faster or further event 'took longer'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare same-start, same-route events with a visible timer so duration is separated from speed; narrate 'we both started together, so whoever stopped first took less time'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the common-start pair picks the faster or further event as the longer one

errorPatterns.pattern: Equates 'finished later / stopped last' with 'took longer', ignoring when each started
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a shared start so finishing order really does show duration, then contrast a different-start case explicitly so the child sees that the start time matters.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the different-start case picks whoever stopped last as the one that ran longest

errorPatterns.pattern: Orders by how memorable or exciting an event was rather than its measured length
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not treat this as a misconception to correct — ordering by salience rather than duration self-corrects with exposure. Instead, re-line-up the measured durations (bars or timers) side by side and read the order off the lengths.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the three-event ordering puts the exciting event as 'longest' regardless of its timer

responseLevels.gap: Orders and compares by speed, distance, finishing position or excitement, not by measured duration.
responseLevels.full: Orders three durations and compares two by measured elapsed time, separating duration from speed, distance and finishing position, and transferring to a new comparison.
responseLevels.partial: Orders and compares correctly for same-start, measured cases, but is caught when starts differ ('stopped last = longest') or by a speed/distance confound.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set comparison and ordering tasks and WATCH how the child decides: (1) Time three classroom activities (or run three sand-timers) from a shared start: 'Put these in order from the one that took the shortest time to the longest, and tell me how you decided.' (2) Two events with a COMMON start where the slower one covers less ground: 'Which took longer?' (3) A different-start case: one timer started late but stopped last — 'Which one ran for more time?' Watch whether they order by measured length or by speed, distance or finishing position.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The different-start case is the discriminator: a child who equates 'stopped last = took longest' gets it wrong, a child who tracks actual elapsed time gets it right. The common-start pair with a slower/shorter event catches judging duration by speed or distance.

pedagogy.summary: Area is the amount of two-dimensional surface inside a bounded region, measured by choosing a unit of area — usually a square — and finding how many unit squares cover the figure with no gaps or overlaps. A unit square has an area of 1 square unit; a figure covered by 12 unit squares has area 12 square units. The concept must be held distinct from perimeter (the distance around) and understood as unchanged when the same squares are rearranged.
bestPractices: Start from covering: which of several shapes covers the most surface, first by cutting/re-composing, then by covering with unit squares.
Name the unit square as '1 square unit' and area as the count of such squares that cover the region without gaps or overlaps.

Deliberately separate area from perimeter — on congruent rectangles, label the unit lengths around the edge of one and draw the square units inside the other, so the two measures are visibly different.
Establish that area is additive and unchanged under rearrangement: the same tiles cover the same area however you move them.
Use square-unit language in every answer ('12 square centimetres', not '12').
keyRepresentations: A single unit square labelled '1 square unit'
A figure on squared paper filled with unit squares, counted
Congruent rectangles: one with unit lengths marked round the perimeter, one with the interior square units drawn
The same set of tiles rearranged into different shapes (area conserved, perimeter changes)
commonMisconceptions: Confuses area with perimeter / length — judges the 'bigger' shape by how far it stretches or the distance around, not the surface covered.
Undifferentiated 'bigger' — calls a longer or taller shape bigger by one dimension without coordinating the 2D covering.
Thinks rearranging the same squares into a new shape changes the amount of area.
Gives area as a bare number without square units, or counts squares with gaps/overlaps.

learn.summary: Area is the amount of two-dimensional surface inside a bounded region, measured by counting how many unit squares (the usual chosen unit of area) cover the figure with no gaps or overlaps. A unit square has area 1 square unit; a figure covered by 12 unit squares has area 12 square units. The concept must be held distinct from perimeter (the distance around) and understood as unchanged when the same squares are rearranged (area is additive and conserved under recomposition). Answers should always carry square-unit language.

activities.title: Cover, count, and separate area from perimeter
feedback: If the squares leave gaps or overlap, say: area is only valid when the squares tile the region with no gaps and no overlaps — line them up edge-to-edge and count again.
If a child gives area as a bare number, prompt: 12 what? Area is counted in square units — say '12 square units' (or '12 square centimetres').

After rearranging, if a child expects the area to change, re-count the tiles together: the same 12 squares still cover 12 square units. Only the shape's outline changed, and the perimeter may or may not have changed, so count it to check.

When area and perimeter are confused, point to the filled interior (area, in square units) versus the traced edge (perimeter, in unit lengths) on the same shape so the two measures are visibly different.
activities.rationale: Building area from physically covering a region with unit squares, then separately tracing the edge, makes 'surface covered' versus 'distance around' concrete, and recomposing the same tiles exhibits conservation of area. An optional live square-unit counter and an AREA/PERIMETER toggle (interior fill vs edge trace) and a rearrange mode can make the distinction and the conservation vivid, but the same learning works with squared paper and physical square tiles.
sourceClaims: Area is the amount of two-dimensional space in a bounded region, measured by choosing a unit of area (often a square); a figure covered by a certain number of squares without gaps or overlaps has an area of that number of square units (3.MD.5, 3.MD.6). Area measurement assumes congruent figures enclose equal areas and that area is additive.
learnerActions: Fill a figure drawn on squared paper with unit squares, snapping them edge-to-edge with no gaps or overlaps, and count them to state the area, e.g. 'area = 12 square units'.

Trace the boundary of the SAME shape separately, stepping round the edge and counting the unit lengths, and record the perimeter in unit lengths. This is a different kind of measure from the area. For a 12-square figure the perimeter number is also different (at least 14), but for some shapes the two numbers can match: a 4-by-4 square has area 16 square units and perimeter 16 units. Even then they measure different things.
Say aloud that the squares INSIDE measure area while the steps AROUND measure perimeter — two different measures of the same shape.

Rearrange the same set of (e.g. 12) tiles, joined edge-to-edge, into a long strip. Re-count the covering squares (still 12), then re-count the perimeter and compare. For example, a 3-by-4 rectangle has perimeter 14 units, but a 1-by-12 strip has perimeter 26 units. The area count stays the same whether or not the perimeter changes.
activities.intendedInsight: Area is the count of unit squares covering a region; it is distinct from perimeter and is unchanged when the same squares are rearranged.

activities.title: Label area on one rectangle, perimeter on its congruent twin
feedback: If a child treats the edge count and the interior count as the same kind of number, highlight the units: one is in square units, the other in unit lengths.
If a child insists a shape with a longer edge must have more area, set up a long-thin shape and a compact shape and count the covering squares to settle it directly.
activities.rationale: Deliberately pairing a perimeter-labelled rectangle with an identical area-filled rectangle addresses the common area/perimeter confusion by making each measure visible on congruent figures.
sourceClaims: Students initially hold undifferentiated views of measurable attributes, calling one object 'bigger' whether it is longer, greater in area, or greater in volume; discussions must clearly distinguish area from length. With strong, distinct concepts of area and perimeter, students differentiate them by drawing rectangles with the same perimeter but different areas (or vice versa) and by labelling unit lengths around the perimeter of one congruent rectangle while drawing the square units inside another.
learnerActions: Take two congruent rectangles.
On the first, mark the unit lengths all the way around the perimeter and total them.
On the second, draw the interior square units and count them for the area.
State in words how the two measurements differ, using square units for area and unit lengths for perimeter.
activities.intendedInsight: Area (surface covered, in square units) and perimeter (distance around, in unit lengths) are distinct attributes even of the very same rectangle.

activities.title: Predict then count: does longer mean bigger area?
feedback: If a child picks the long strip because 'it stretches further', count the squares in both: here the compact Shape A has 12 squares and the strip Shape B has 10, so A has the bigger area despite stretching less (and B even has the longer perimeter).
If a child gets the right answer but justifies it with 'it looks chunkier', push them to count the covering squares so the reason rests on the unit-square count.
For a rearrangement claim that area changed, recompose the identical tiles and re-count — the number of covering squares is unchanged.
activities.rationale: A predict-then-count comparison surfaces and confronts the 'longer/more spread-out is bigger' misconception, and the reasoning prompts distinguish genuine understanding from a lucky choice. Note that in the compact-12 vs strip-10 case the compact shape also has the larger area, so 'bigger area' coincides with 'more compact'; the reasoning tier plus the same-tiles rearrangement probe (same squares, area unchanged) is what truly discriminates. The chosen case does make the shape with the longer perimeter (the strip) the one with the smaller area, so area/perimeter confusion leads to the wrong pick.
sourceClaims: Students initially hold undifferentiated views of measurable attributes, calling one object 'bigger' whether it is longer, greater in area, or greater in volume; discussions must clearly distinguish area from length. With strong, distinct concepts of area and perimeter, students differentiate them by drawing rectangles with the same perimeter but different areas (or vice versa) and by labelling unit lengths around the perimeter of one congruent rectangle while drawing the square units inside another.
learnerActions: Before counting, look at two shapes — a compact block and a long spread-out strip — and predict which has the bigger area and why.
Count the covering unit squares in each shape.
Compare your prediction with the counts and explain any difference.

Answer the follow-ups: What does the area of a shape actually tell you? If you cut a shape apart and rearrange its squares into a long line, does the area change? Why? Shape B is longer than Shape A — so why doesn't 'longer' mean 'bigger area'? How is area different from the distance all the way around the edge?
activities.intendedInsight: 'Bigger area' is decided by counting covering squares, not by how far a shape stretches or how long its edge is; and area is preserved when the same squares are rearranged.

activities.title: Sort statements: about area or about perimeter?
feedback: If a shape with a bigger perimeter is assumed to have a bigger area, revisit the long-thin-vs-compact pair where the bigger-perimeter shape has the smaller area.
Reinforce square-unit language for every area answer.
activities.rationale: Classification and comparison items are discriminating checks of the concept and its distinction from perimeter; they work as a consolidation check after hands-on covering. As a recognition-style check a sort can assess and reinforce the area/perimeter distinction, but it does not by itself require the learner to construct and conserve area, so pair it with the covering and rearranging work.
learnerActions: Read statements and shape comparisons and sort each into 'about area' or 'about perimeter'.
For a long-thin shape and a compact shape, decide which has the bigger area and which has the bigger perimeter, and justify each by counting.
Choose, with reasons, which of several shapes has the bigger area.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can tell which questions concern surface covered (area) versus distance around (perimeter) and justify comparisons by counting.

constraints: Area answers must always be stated in square units (e.g. '12 square centimetres'), not as a bare number.
Unit squares must tile the region with no gaps and no overlaps for the count to be a valid area.

Static reference images (a labelled '1 square unit' and a 12-square figure marked 'area = 12 square units') are useful consolidation but do not let a learner rearrange tiles to experience conservation; pair them with hands-on covering and recomposition.

A sort/multiple-choice check can assess and reinforce the area/perimeter distinction but is a recognition task; it does not by itself require independent construction or demonstrate conservation of area, so use it alongside covering and rearranging activities.
Keep the focus on 2D surface. A 3D setting risks conflating area with volume; if 3D is used, keep the measured attribute explicitly the flat surface.
The optional live counter, AREA/PERIMETER toggle, and rearrange mode are helpful illustrations of the mechanism, not required mechanisms; squared paper and physical tiles achieve the same objective.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Original internal tension: the POE task specifies two shapes with the SAME number of unit squares (to confront conservation), while the diagnostic uses Shape A = 3×4 = 12 squares vs Shape B = 1×10 = 10 squares. The learner activity uses the diagnostic counts (where the strip also has the longer perimeter and smaller area); the reasoning tier and the same-tiles rearrangement probe (area stays 12, perimeter changes) are the stronger discriminators. Both the comparison and the conservation probe are retained.

Categorical catalog judgements that static content, dialogue, or 3D 'cannot' teach the concept are retained only as scoped limits (static images do not support rearrangement; a 3D setting risks volume confusion), not as universal claims about what a medium can teach.
Whether rearranging the 12 tiles changes the perimeter depends on the outline; it is asserted only for the specific 3×4→1×12 strip example used.
Source 'verified:true' flags and 'high' confidence are legacy metadata not re-checked in this rewrite.

assess.poeTask: Before any counting, show two shapes made from the SAME number of unit squares — one a compact block, one a long spread-out strip — and ask the child to predict which has the bigger area and WHY. Then have them count the squares in each. The equal counts confront a 'the longer/more spread-out one is bigger' prediction; the target explanation, given after counting, is that the same squares cover the same amount of surface however they are arranged.
probeDeeper: What does the area of a shape actually tell you?
If I cut Shape A apart and rearrange its 12 squares into a long line, does it still have the same area? Why?
Shape B is longer than Shape A — so why doesn't 'longer' mean 'bigger area' here?
How is the area of a shape different from the distance all the way around its edge?
assess.correctAnswer: Shape A. Area is the number of unit squares that cover a shape with no gaps or overlaps, and A is covered by 12 squares while B is covered by 10 — so A has the bigger area, 12 square units, even though B stretches further.

errorPatterns.pattern: Area/perimeter confusion: judges 'bigger' by how far the shape stretches or the distance around its edge, so chooses the long strip.
errorPatterns.nextMove: On congruent rectangles, mark the unit lengths around the perimeter of one and draw the square units inside the other, so the child sees area (surface covered) and perimeter (distance around) are different measures; then count squares to compare.
errorPatterns.distractor: Shape B, the long strip — it stretches much further, so it covers more.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks Shape B and justifies with 'it stretches further' or 'it has a longer edge/goes further round'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Undifferentiated 'bigger' by one dimension: calls the longer shape bigger from a single dimension without coordinating the two-dimensional covering.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare a single object's several attributes (how long? how much surface?) to distinguish them; count the covering squares to decide area.
errorPatterns.distractor: Shape B, because it is longer than Shape A.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Chooses Shape B 'because it is longer than A', attending only to length.

errorPatterns.pattern: Non-conservation of area: believes rearranging the same squares into a different shape changes the amount of area.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Recompose the identical tiles and re-count — the number of covering squares is unchanged; area is preserved under rearrangement (area is additive).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In the rearrangement probe, says the spread-out shape has more (or less) area than the compact one made from the same squares.

responseLevels.gap: Judges 'bigger' by length, perimeter or how far the shape stretches, choosing the long strip.
responseLevels.full: Defines area as the number of unit squares covering the figure with no gaps or overlaps, compares by counting, holds it distinct from perimeter/length, and knows the area is unchanged when the same squares are rearranged.
responseLevels.partial: Counts unit squares to compare and gets the right answer, but the area/perimeter distinction is shaky — also thinks a longer edge means more area, or is unsure the area stays the same when the squares are rearranged.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show two shapes on squared paper: Shape A is a solid 3-by-4 block (12 squares) and Shape B is a long 1-by-10 strip (10 squares). Ask: 'Which shape has the bigger AREA — and how do you know?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The answer alone can be guessed, so the reason tier carries it: a child who understands area counts the covering squares and picks A; a child who confuses area with length or perimeter picks the long strip B because it 'goes further'. A correct 'A' justified by 'it looks chunkier' rather than by counting squares is caught in the reason.

Area measurement assumes congruent figures enclose equal areas and that area is additive.

pedagogy.summary: Adding and subtracting mixed numbers with like denominators has two viable routes: operate on the whole-number and fraction parts separately, or convert both to improper fractions. The separate-parts route exposes the two signature difficulties — in addition the fraction parts can sum past a whole (2 3/5 + 1 4/5 → 3 + 7/5 needs regrouping to 4 2/5), and in subtraction the minuend's fraction can be smaller than the subtrahend's, forcing a borrow (4 2/6 − 1 5/6: regroup 4 into 3 + 6/6). The convert-to-improper route sidesteps the borrow entirely, which is exactly why it is worth teaching as the fallback. Teach both, let the awkward subtraction MOTIVATE the improper method, and keep the denominator a fixed unit throughout.
bestPractices: Teach BOTH methods and let a subtraction that needs regrouping (4 2/6 − 1 5/6) motivate why converting to improper fractions is often cleaner
Make the borrow physical: exchange one whole for its equivalent in the common unit fraction (1 = 6/6) before subtracting the fraction parts
In addition, always check whether the fraction parts crossed a whole and regroup (7/5 → 1 2/5) so the answer is a proper mixed number
Estimate with the whole numbers first (2 3/5 + 1 4/5 is between 3 and 5, near 4½) to police the result
Hold the denominator as a fixed unit — fifths add to fifths — to block the add-across error carried over from whole-number habits
keyRepresentations: Number line: jump the whole numbers, then the fraction parts, crossing whole boundaries
Bar model with whole tiles plus fraction tiles; a whole tile that shatters into b unit-fractions for the borrow, or b fraction tiles that fuse into a whole
The regroup written as 4 = 3 + 6/6 (or the improper rewrite 26/6)
Improper-fraction form beside the mixed form for comparison
commonMisconceptions: Adds across the fraction parts (3/5 + 4/5 → 7/10), applying whole-number addition to numerator and denominator
Subtracts smaller-from-larger in each column and never borrows (4 2/6 − 1 5/6 → 3 3/6, taking |2−5|=3)
Leaves an improper fraction part in the answer (3 7/5) instead of regrouping to 4 2/5
Miscounts when converting mixed to improper (2 3/5 → 10/5 then forgets the +3/5, or writes 5/5)

learn.summary: Add and subtract mixed numbers with like denominators (ages 9–10). Two routes are worth teaching: (a) operate on whole-number and fraction parts separately, which exposes the two signature difficulties — in addition the fraction parts can sum past a whole (2 3/5 + 1 4/5 → 3 + 7/5, regroup to 4 2/5), and in subtraction the first fraction can be smaller than the second, forcing a borrow (4 2/6 − 1 5/6: regroup 4 into 3 + 6/6); and (b) convert both to improper fractions, which sidesteps the borrow and is worth teaching as the cleaner fallback. Let the awkward subtraction motivate the improper method, keep the denominator a fixed unit throughout, and always tidy an improper fraction part back into a proper mixed number.

activities.title: Trade a whole for unit fractions: make the borrow and carry physical
feedback: If you take |2 − 5| = 3 and write 3 3/6, you subtracted the smaller fraction from the larger without exchanging. Trade one whole for 6 sixths first so you have 8 sixths to subtract from — or convert both to improper fractions (26/6 − 11/6).
If you write 3/5 + 4/5 as 7/10, you added the denominators too. Three fifths and four fifths is seven fifths: the size of the part does not change when you join same-size parts.
If you leave 3 7/5, check: is 7/5 more than a whole? Tidy it into the whole-number part to get 4 2/5. Your addition itself was correct.
activities.rationale: Making the regroup a felt exchange of one whole for its unit fractions targets the add-across and never-borrow misconceptions directly and keeps the denominator as a fixed unit. Locked fraction tiles make the add-across error impossible during the manipulation; the number line offers a parallel view of the same crossing.
sourceClaims: The add-across misconception (adding numerators AND denominators) is a central, documented error in fraction addition/subtraction, arising from misapplying whole-number addition and failing to treat the denominator as the size of the part.

Same-denominator addition items are answered correctly by the large majority (~92%) but a minority of lower-attaining pupils add both numerator and denominator; concrete materials and 'which is bigger' reasoning support remediation.
learnerActions: Work the subtraction 4 2/6 − 1 5/6 using whole tiles and fraction tiles that are locked to sixths so you cannot change the denominator.
Try to take away 5 sixths when you only have 2 — notice you are stuck. Break one whole tile into 6 sixths (the borrow), so you now have 8 sixths, and finish: 8/6 − 5/6 = 3/6, leaving 2 3/6 = 2 1/2.
Work the addition 2 3/5 + 1 4/5 the same way: gather the fifths, and when 5 fifths collect, fuse them into a fresh whole tile, giving 4 2/5.

Optionally model the same two problems on a number line: jump the whole numbers first, then the fraction parts, and watch a jump cross a whole boundary — the same regroup seen as a different representation.
Write each exchange as a number sentence: 4 = 3 + 6/6, and 7/5 = 1 + 2/5.
Say aloud whether the carry and the borrow are the same exchange running in opposite directions.
activities.intendedInsight: Borrowing is not a mysterious digit-move: it is literally trading one whole for its equivalent in the common unit fraction (1 = 6/6), and carrying is the reverse — fusing a whole-worth of unit fractions back into one whole. The denominator stays fixed because fifths only join with fifths.

activities.title: The improper-fraction fallback, side by side
feedback: If your two methods disagree, check the improper conversion: 2 wholes of fifths is 10/5, and you still add the 3/5 on top.
If you write 2 3/5 as 10/5, you forgot to add the 3/5 — it should be 13/5.

Standards expect pupils to add and subtract mixed numbers by replacing each with an equivalent (improper) fraction and/or by using properties of operations, so being fluent in both routes is the goal.
activities.rationale: The subtraction that needs a borrow is the natural motivation for the improper method; running both side by side lets learners compare and self-check. Miscounting during conversion is a known error to guard against.
sourceClaims: Pupils 'add and subtract mixed numbers with like denominators, e.g., by replacing each mixed number with an equivalent fraction, and/or by using properties of operations and the relationship between addition and subtraction' (4.NF.B.3c). In England, adding/subtracting mixed numbers using equivalent fractions is a Year 6 objective.
learnerActions: Rewrite 4 2/6 and 1 5/6 as improper fractions (26/6 and 11/6), subtract to get 15/6, then convert back: 15/6 = 2 3/6 = 2 1/2.
Do the same subtraction by the separate-parts borrow method and check both answers match.
When converting 2 3/5 to improper, count carefully: 2 wholes is 10/5, plus 3/5 is 13/5 — do not drop the +3/5 or stop at 5/5.
Decide which method you found cleaner for the subtraction, and explain why converting to improper removed the borrow.
activities.intendedInsight: Converting to improper fractions avoids the borrow entirely, so it is a reliable fallback when the subtraction needs regrouping; both methods give the same answer when done carefully.

activities.title: Estimate first to police the answer
feedback: If your answer is far from the estimate, re-check for a missed borrow or for added denominators. Separately, check that the fraction part is proper; an untidied part like 3 7/5 has the right value but still needs regrouping to 4 2/5.
3 7/5 is not a tidy mixed number because 7/5 is more than a whole; regroup it to 4 2/5.
activities.rationale: Estimating with the whole numbers and then adjusting for the fraction parts gives learners an independent reasonableness check against value errors such as a missed borrow or added denominators. The proper-fraction check covers un-regrouped answers, which have the correct value.
learnerActions: Before computing 2 3/5 + 1 4/5, estimate using the whole numbers: the sum is between 3 and 5, and since both fraction parts are large, near 4 1/2.
Compute the exact answer and check it sits close to your estimate.

Repeat for 4 2/6 − 1 5/6: whole-number subtraction gives about 3, but because 2/6 is less than 5/6 the fraction part pulls the answer down by about a half, so expect a result between 2 and 3, around 2 1/2 — then confirm 2 1/2 is reasonable.
For each result, ask: is the fraction part proper (numerator less than denominator)? If not, regroup.
activities.intendedInsight: An estimate that starts with the whole numbers and then adjusts for the fraction parts catches value errors such as a missed borrow (3 3/6 instead of about 2 1/2) or added denominators (3 7/10 instead of about 4 1/2), because a wrong answer no longer sits near the estimate. An un-regrouped answer like 3 7/5 has the correct value (it equals 4 2/5), so an estimate cannot catch it; the separate proper-fraction check does that job.

activities.title: Study a worked carry and a worked borrow
feedback: If you cannot say where the extra sixths came from, trace them back to the one whole you broke apart: 1 = 6/6.
A worked example shows the steps but does not let you trigger the exchange on your own numbers — pair it with hands-on or written practice on fresh problems.
Matching mixed numbers to improper forms checks recognition; it does not by itself show you producing every regrouping step, so follow it with a problem you solve in full.
activities.rationale: A worked carry-and-borrow pair with revealable steps supports meaning-making; it is a scaffold, not independent practice, because the learner does not initiate the regroup on their own numbers.
learnerActions: Read a worked addition showing 2 3/5 + 1 4/5 with the step 7/5 revealed as 1 + 2/5, and explain in your own words why the whole-number part becomes 4.
Read a worked subtraction showing 4 rewritten as 3 + 6/6, and answer: why change the 4 into 3 and 6 more sixths?
Match each mixed number to its improper form (e.g. 4 2/6 ↔ 26/6).
activities.intendedInsight: Reading and explaining the regroup steps consolidates the meaning behind the exchange, even without acting it out yourself.

constraints: Lock the denominator as a fixed unit so fifths add to fifths; this blocks the add-across error carried over from whole-number habits.
Always check whether fraction parts crossed a whole and regroup so answers are proper mixed numbers (7/5 → 1 2/5).

Worked-example or revealable-step formats support meaning but do not let the learner trigger the exchange on their own numbers — treat them as scaffolds and follow with independent construction on fresh problems.

Recognition and matching tasks (mixed-to-improper, choosing the right answer) can check understanding but do not elicit the learner's own step-by-step regrouping; include tasks where the learner shows every step.
Teach both methods; do not present the improper route as the only correct one — the separate-parts route is where the borrow and carry become meaningful.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 2 3/5 + 1 4/5 = 4 2/5; 4 2/6 − 1 5/6 = 2 3/6 = 2 1/2 (improper: 26/6 − 11/6 = 15/6 = 2 1/2); 2 3/5 = 13/5. The subtraction's fraction parts give 2/6 − 5/6 = −3/6 = −1/2, so the answer sits about half a whole below the whole-number estimate of 3 (hence around 2 1/2). All consistent. The wrong answers 3 3/6, 3 7/5 and 7/10 appear only as errors to diagnose, never as valid options.

The original quiz design listed answer choices 2 1/2 and 2 3/6 together, which are equal (both correct); this ambiguous multiple-choice set was not reproduced as a learner question — only the genuine distractor 3 3/6 is used, as an error to diagnose.

The original source claimed the topic is 'planar' so '3D adds nothing' and that 'talk cannot enact the borrow'; these are catalog-format judgements, not established facts, and have been dropped rather than asserted. Spoken explanation and physical fraction pieces can both support this learning; no comparative necessity is claimed here.
The number-line representation from the original is included as an optional alternative view in the first activity.

probeDeeper: In the subtraction, why did you turn the 4 into a 3 — where did the extra sixths come from?
Estimate 2 3/5 + 1 4/5 before finishing — should it be above or below 4? How do you know?
Could you do the subtraction by turning both into improper fractions instead? Try it and see if you get the same.
Is 3 7/5 a tidy way to leave a mixed number — why or why not?

errorPatterns.pattern: Never borrows in subtraction: subtracts the smaller fraction from the larger in each column regardless of order — 4 2/6 − 1 5/6 → 3 3/6, taking |2−5| = 3 sixths
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make the exchange physical — trade one whole for 6/6 so there are 8 sixths to subtract from — or switch to improper fractions (26/6 − 11/6), which removes the borrow altogether
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer 3 3/6 (or 3 1/2); the working shows 5/6−2/6 with no exchange of a whole

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds across the fraction parts: 3/5 + 4/5 → 7/10, adding numerators AND denominators
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to fifths as a fixed unit — three fifths and four fifths is seven fifths — on a locked bar; re-establish joining same-size parts before regrouping
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The fraction part of the sum has a changed denominator (7/10 rather than 7/5); the whole numbers may be added correctly

errorPatterns.pattern: Leaves the answer with an improper fraction part: 2 3/5 + 1 4/5 → 3 7/5, not regrouping the 7/5 into 1 2/5
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach — prompt 'is 7/5 more than a whole? then tidy it into the whole-number part'; the child already added correctly
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer written as 3 7/5 (numerator ≥ denominator in a mixed number); the addition itself is sound

responseLevels.gap: Adds across the fraction parts, or never borrows (3 3/6); the denominator is not held as a fixed unit and regrouping is absent.
responseLevels.full: Solves both via a chosen method (separate parts with borrow/carry, or convert to improper), regroups the answer to a proper mixed number, estimates reasonableness with the whole numbers, and transfers to a new mixed-number add/subtract.
responseLevels.partial: Handles cases with no crossing and no borrow, but fails the regrouping subtraction or leaves an improper fraction part; can compute by one method but has no whole-number estimate to check against.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these out, showing every step: first 2 3/5 + 1 4/5, then 4 2/6 − 1 5/6.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The two items are engineered to force the two signature moves: the sum crosses a whole (fraction parts 3/5 + 4/5 = 7/5), so a child who does not regroup leaves 3 7/5; the subtraction needs a borrow (2/6 < 5/6), so a child who subtracts column-by-column takes |2−5| and lands on 3 3/6. Watching the METHOD — not just the answer — reveals which happened, and the add-across error shows up immediately as a changed denominator. A child who regroups both ways, or who converts to improper fractions and gets 4 2/5 and 2 1/2, has the idea; the specific wrong answer names the specific fault.

sources.claim: The add-across misconception (adding numerators AND denominators) is a central, documented error in fraction addition/subtraction, arising from misapplying whole-number addition and failing to treat the denominator as the size of the part.
sources.source: IES / What Works Clearinghouse - Developing Effective Fractions Instruction K-8 (Siegler et al. 2010), Recommendation 2

sources.claim: Same-denominator addition items are answered correctly by the large majority (~92%) but a minority of lower-attaining pupils add both numerator and denominator; concrete materials and 'which is bigger' reasoning support remediation.

sources.claim: Pupils 'add and subtract mixed numbers with like denominators, e.g., by replacing each mixed number with an equivalent fraction, and/or by using properties of operations and the relationship between addition and subtraction' (4.NF.B.3c). In England, adding/subtracting mixed numbers using equivalent fractions is a Year 6 objective.
