pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 6–7 (LANGUAGE): read and write numbers to at least 100 in WORDS — extending the number-word vocabulary to decade words and two-word compounds (fifty-seven), mapping word↔numeral↔quantity.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y2): 'read and write numbers to at least 100 in numerals and in words'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.NBT.3 'read and write numbers to 1000 using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form' (the 0–100 word range sits within this).
• Operational details — building on words to twenty, the child learns the DECADE words (twenty, thirty ... ninety) and the hyphenated compound structure 'tens-word + ones-word' (fifty-seven = 57). The English pattern above twenty is regular and tens-first (unlike the teens), so the main work is (i) the decade spellings, (ii) the fifteen/fifty, thirteen/thirty confusions, and (iii) hyphenation and word↔numeral order.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 6): read 'fifty-seven' and write 57. Tier B (6–7): write 'eighty-three' when shown 83. Tier C (7): read and write all decade words and compound words to 100 correctly, spelling and hyphenating them.
bestPractices: Teach the DECADE words as a set (twenty…ninety) and their link to the tens digit, then the regular compound rule 'decade-word + ones-word' (sixty-four) — above twenty the words are tens-first and regular, a helpful contrast with the teens.
Drill the sound-alike traps directly: thirteen/thirty, fifteen/fifty, etc. — pair each with its numeral and a quantity so meaning disambiguates the near-identical words.
Always connect word ↔ numeral ↔ quantity (read 'seventy-two' → write 72 → show ~72 on a line) so the words carry meaning, not just spelling.
Address orthography explicitly: the hyphen in compounds (forty-five), the tricky spellings (forty not fourty, ninety), coordinating with spelling/handwriting teaching.
Practise both directions and across decade boundaries (seventy-nine → eighty) to cement the compound structure.
keyRepresentations: Decade-word chart (20–90) linked to the tens digit and to bundles of tens.
Word-building frame: [decade word] + [ones word] → compound (sixty + four → sixty-four) beside 64.
Triple-match cards: numeral ↔ word ↔ quantity/number-line position.
Sound-alike contrast pairs (thirteen|thirty, fifteen|fifty) each with a set/numeral.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing '-teen' and '-ty' words by sound and spelling (fifteen vs fifty, thirteen vs thirty).
Misspelling irregular decades (forty as 'fourty', ninety as 'ninty').
Omitting the hyphen or writing compounds as one/many words incorrectly.
Transposing compound numbers back to numerals (writing 'forty-two' as 24) — carrying over the teen ones-first habit.
Writing decade words with extra zeros from the spoken parts (fifty-seven → 507).

learn.summary: For ages 6–7: reading and writing numbers to at least 100 in words, extending from number words to twenty into the decade words (twenty, thirty … ninety) and two-word hyphenated compounds (fifty-seven). The central work is mapping word ↔ numeral ↔ quantity, learning commonly misspelled decade words (forty drops the u of four; ninety keeps the e of nine), fixing the hyphen, and untangling the sound-alike '-teen'/'-ty' pairs (fifteen/fifty, thirteen/thirty). Above twenty the English words follow a regular tens-first pattern (decade word, then ones word), a useful contrast with the teens, although some decade stems (twenty, thirty, fifty, forty) are spelled irregularly.

activities.title: Build compound number words from decade + ones parts
feedback: If a learner writes 'eighty-three' as 803, show that eighty-three means 8 tens and 3 ones: build it and place the 3 into the ones column of a tens/ones frame so it does not trail after 80.
If the compound is run together or missing the hyphen, point to the two parts (decade word + ones word) and show the hyphen joins exactly those two words.
If the order is reversed (writing 'forty-two' as 24), re-read the word tens-first: 'forty' is the tens, '-two' is the ones, so the tens digit comes first (42).
If a decade word is misspelled ('fourty', 'ninty'), flag the correct spelling (forty, ninety) and keep it visible as a reference.
activities.rationale: Composing the word from decade and ones parts and mapping it to both numeral and quantity makes the regular tens-first structure explicit and keeps the words meaningful rather than rote spellings. An optional on-screen builder where tiles snap to the numeral and a number-line position can make this mapping concrete, but the same can be done with word-part cards and a drawn line.
sourceClaims: Number words above twenty are regular tens-first compounds; the persistent difficulties are the -teen/-ty sound-alikes and irregular decade spellings (forty, ninety).
learnerActions: Choose a decade-word part (e.g. 'sixty') and a ones-word part (e.g. 'four') and join them into the compound word 'sixty-four', writing it with the hyphen.

Write the numeral64 beside sixty-four and locate it on a0–100 line. Optionally join on-screen tens and ones word tiles so the compound immediately links to its numeral and line position, with a reverse round asking the learner to assemble or spell the word for83.
Work the reverse direction: shown the numeral 83, say and then correctly spell the word 'eighty-three'.
Write seventy-eight, seventy-nine, eighty, eighty-one, then ninety-nine and one hundred. Notice when a decade changes, when a hyphenated compound is used, and how100 is written.
activities.intendedInsight: For numbers from21 to99 with a nonzero ones digit, the English word is a tens-first compound, such as sixty-four. Exact tens use the decade word alone, and100 is one hundred; connect each form to its numeral and quantity.

activities.title: Sound-alike contrast: '-teen' versus '-ty'
feedback: If a learner uses fifteen and fifty interchangeably, contrast them directly: fifty = 5 tens; fifteen = 1 ten and 5 ones. Say them slowly, stressing -ty vs -teen, and pair each with its base-ten model.
If reading 76 drifts toward a teen word, re-anchor on the tens: seventy is 7 tens, then the ones word -six follows, giving seventy-six.
activities.rationale: The -teen/-ty confusion is a persistent difficulty noted in teaching guidance; attaching each word to its numeral and a concrete quantity disambiguates by meaning. A listen-and-repeat prompt (optional tap-to-hear audio) can help learners hear the ending difference.
sourceClaims: Number words above twenty are regular tens-first compounds; the persistent difficulties are the -teen/-ty sound-alikes and irregular decade spellings (forty, ninety).
learnerActions: Take a minimal pair such as fifteen/fifty and read both aloud, stressing the ending (-teen vs -ty).
Beside each word, write its numeral (fifteen = 15, fifty = 50) and show a matching quantity or base-ten model (fifteen = 1 ten and 5 ones; fifty = 5 tens).
Repeat with thirteen/thirty and other pairs, each time pairing word, numeral and quantity so meaning separates the near-identical sounds.
Answer a quick 'fifteen or fifty?' decision with the set of objects visible, choosing by quantity rather than guessing.
activities.intendedInsight: The '-ty' word names a number of tens (fifty = 5 tens) while the '-teen' word is a teen (fifteen = 1 ten and 5); linking each to a quantity removes the guesswork from the near-identical sounds.

activities.title: Use number words in a real read-and-write task
feedback: If the numeral comes out as 803 (or similarly 507 for fifty-seven), name the error (concatenating the spoken parts as full digits) and rebuild using a tens/ones frame so the ones digit sits in the ones place.
If teen and decade are swapped, return to the contrast pair with quantities before retrying.
Confirm success when the learner produces both directions correctly: 'seventy-six' for 76 and 83 for 'eighty-three'.
activities.rationale: Using the words in a live read/write task, rather than defining them, surfaces the specific slips (teen/decade confusion and the concatenation error) and shows real fluency across both directions. A short matching or fill-the-blank set (e.g. match 'seventy-two' to 72, spell the word for 45) consolidates afterward but checks recognition rather than independent production.
learnerActions: Given a label showing the numeral 76, write the words for a new label a customer could read ('seventy-six'), ordered correctly and hyphenated.
Given the word 'eighty-three' on a card, read it and write the numeral (83).
Check a friend's work: they wrote 803 for 'eighty-three' — decide whether it is right and explain what went wrong.
Compare 40 and 14 (and 'ninety' vs 'nineteen'): read each aloud and write each the other way to confirm you can move both directions.
activities.intendedInsight: A learner who has the system can move fluently in both directions — word to numeral and numeral to word — without concatenating the spoken parts or confusing teen and decade words.

constraints: Teach the decade words (twenty…ninety) as a set linked to the tens digit before drilling compounds, so compounds are built on an understood base.
Always connect word ↔ numeral ↔ quantity; spelling practice alone does not guarantee the words carry meaning.

Address orthography explicitly: the hyphen in compounds, and the commonly misspelled decade words forty (irregular: drops the u of four, not 'fourty') and ninety (regular: keeps the e of nine, not 'ninty'); coordinate with spelling/handwriting teaching.

Matching provided words to numerals checks recognition; independent spelling requires a response in which the word is not supplied. A free-writing or open fill-in task can elicit that production, especially when the learner also explains its quantity.

A static decade-word chart with tap-to-hear audio is a useful reference wall but does not rehearse active spelling/production or sound-alike discrimination; treat it as support, not the main practice.
Practise both directions and across decade boundaries (seventy-nine → eighty) to cement the compound structure.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved research row without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source 1 (the UK curriculum requirement) and the CCSS-M 2.NBT.3 claim support the objective/topic (reading and writing numbers in words in both directions) but not the specific pedagogical principles of the activities; they were therefore not attached as sourceClaims to any activity. Activity 3's diagnostic 'live task surfaces slips' principle comes from the original assessment design, not from the cited sources, so its sourceClaims are [].

The original 'checkpoint' example read 'fifty-seven' for Tier A was preserved; the concatenation example appears in the source as both 803 (eighty-three) and 507 (fifty-seven) — the same error type (inserting the tens as full digits), kept consistently.
The source phrase 'reads 76 as sixteen… territory' is loosely worded and retained only as a symptom description, not as a precise worked example.

Two of the three cited sources are marked unverified in the source row (CCSS-M 2.NBT.3 and the NCETM number-words guidance); the tens-first regularity and -teen/-ty difficulty claims rest on these unverified citations and should not be treated as empirically validated.

probeDeeper: Read these out loud for me: 40 and 14 — which one is which?
Write 'ninety' as a numeral, then 'nineteen'.
Your friend wrote 803 for eighty-three — is that right? What went wrong?
assess.correctAnswer: Writes 'seventy-six' (decade word + ones word, correctly ordered and hyphenated) and writes 83 for 'eighty-three'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses the -ty decade word with the -teen word: reads/writes 'fifteen/50' or 'fifty/15' interchangeably
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast the pair explicitly (fifty = 5 tens; fifteen = 10 and 5). Say them slowly, stressing -ty vs -teen, and pair each with its base-ten model.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child reads 76 as 'sixteen…' territory or writes 15 when the word is 'fifty'; mixes minimal pairs.

errorPatterns.pattern: Concatenates the spoken parts into digits: writes 803 for 'eighty-three' (80 then 3)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that eighty-three means 8 tens and 3 ones — build it, then write it into a tens/ones frame so the 3 lands in the ones place, not after 80.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Words-to-numeral task yields 803, 507, etc.

responseLevels.gap: Confuses teen/decade words or concatenates (803 for eighty-three); cannot reliably move between word and numeral.
responseLevels.full: Reads and writes any number 0–100 in words fluently in context — decade words and hyphenated compounds — and converts both directions without concatenating.
responseLevels.partial: Reads and writes most numbers to 100 in words but slips on the -teen/-ty minimal pairs or on compound numbers under time pressure.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a real task: 'This sweet-jar label shows the numeral 76. Write the words for the new label so a customer can read it.' Then, separately: 'Your friend wrote the card and put the numeral for eighty-three — read the word and write the numeral.' Watch which words and numerals they actually produce and read aloud.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Using the words in a live read/write task — not defining them — exposes the specific slips: the -teen/-ty pair confusion and the concatenation error (writing 803 for eighty-three) only surface when the child must actually produce the form, and a child who has the system produces both directions fluently.

sources.claim: Year 2 pupils read and write numbers to at least 100 in numerals and in words.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (Year 2, Number and place value)

sources.claim: Grade 2 pupils read and write numbers using base-ten numerals and number names (the 0–100 word range sits within reading/writing numbers to 1000).
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, 2.NBT.3

sources.claim: Number words above twenty are regular tens-first compounds; the persistent difficulties are the -teen/-ty sound-alikes and irregular decade spellings (forty, ninety).

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 8–9 (UK Y4, US Grade 3–4). Counting in 6s, 7s, 9s, 25s and 1,000s — the harder skip counts that complete the times-table set and extend into thousands.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y4 'count in multiples of 6, 7, 9, 25 and 1,000', 'find 1,000 more or less than a given number', and 'count backwards through 0 to include negative numbers'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.OA.7 fluent recall of products (the 6s, 7s, 9s underpin those tables); 4.OA.5 generate and analyse number/shape patterns; 4.NBT reading/place value into the thousands.
• Operational details: exploit structure so these are not brute memorised — 6s = doubled 3s; 9s carry a strong pattern (tens digit +1 while ones digit −1 each step, digit sum always 9, a clean diagonal on the hundred square); 7s have the WEAKEST pattern so need the most rehearsal, best built from 5s+2s; 25s are quarters/money/quarter-hours (four 25s = 100); 1,000s extend the place-value step and pair with backward counting through 0 into negatives.
• Checkpoint: skip-count and use structure to self-repair. Tier A (8): count in 6s and 25s from 0 and count in 1,000s. Tier B (8–9): count in 6s, 7s, 9s, 25s, 1,000s from 0 and find 1,000 more/less. Tier C (9): explain 6s as doubled 3s and use the 9s digit pattern (digit sum 9) to check a count, and count in 1,000s backwards through 0 into negatives.
bestPractices: Lead with structure, not brute rote: teach 6s as doubled 3s, and surface the 9s pattern explicitly (each step the tens digit rises by one and the ones digit falls by one, so the digits always sum to 9) so children have a self-check when a count wobbles.

Give the 7s the most rehearsal because they carry the weakest visible pattern — build them from known 5s and 2s (7 = 5 + 2) and from the array, and interleave them with already-secure counts rather than drilling in isolation.
Anchor 25s in quarters and money — four 25s make 100, 25p pieces, quarter-hours — so 25, 50, 75, 100 is felt as building whole hundreds from quarters rather than a memorised list.
Connect every count to its times table and to equal groups/arrays so counting in 6s, 7s and 9s is the fluency route into the ×6, ×7 and ×9 facts, not a parallel skill.

Teach 1,000s alongside 1,000-more/less and backward counting through 0 into negatives, using a number line that extends past 0 so the place-value step and the negative extension are seen on one continuous track.
keyRepresentations: Hundred square with the 9s shaded to reveal the diagonal and the digit-sum-9 pattern (and 6s to show doubled 3s)
Aligned number lines pairing 3s with 6s (doubling) and 5s+2s composing 7s
Equal groups / arrays for 6, 7, 9 linking each count to its multiplication table
Money and clock models for 25s (four quarters = 100, quarter-hours) and an extended number line through 0 for 1,000s and negatives
commonMisconceptions: Counting in 7s (and 6s/9s) as pure rote with no structural anchor, so a single slip cannot be repaired and the count derails.
Missing the 9s pattern and treating each step as '+10 then −1' incorrectly, e.g. writing 9, 18, 27, 37 by adding 10 and forgetting the −1.
Confusing adjacent tables (drifting between 6s and 8s, or 7s and 9s) because the steps feel similar and no pattern flags the error.
Mishandling 25s past 100 (25, 50, 75, 100, 125 becoming …100, 105) by reverting to a smaller or rounder step at the hundred.
Counting in 1,000s but stalling or reversing sign incorrectly when crossing 0 into negatives (…1000, 0, then '1000' again instead of −1000).

learn.summary: Skip counting in6s,7s,9s,25s and1,000s for ages8–9 uses equal groups and number patterns. Build6-jumps from two3-jumps,7-jumps from5+2,25s from four25-unit parts making100, and1,000s on a line through zero. For9,18,…,90 the digits sum to9 and the tens-up/ones-down pattern is visible; it does not extend unchanged to99, whose digits sum to18. Use patterns as checks within their stated range.

activities.title: Step the count and watch the pattern form (pattern explorer)
feedback: For a term in the9-through90 segment, check the tens and ones sum to9. Do not mark99 wrong because its sum is18:99 is also a multiple of9. Beyond that segment, verify the jump or multiplication fact rather than requiring digit sum exactly9.
A common slip is applying '+10' alone (9, 18, 27, 37); point out the missing −1 on the ones digit and that 37's digits sum to 10, not 9.
If the 7s stall, rebuild the next term from the previous one plus 5 plus 2, or derive 7×6 from 7×5+7 (= 35 + 7 = 42) rather than counting on in ones.
At the hundred boundary in 25s (75 → 100 → 125), check the step stayed 25 and did not shrink to a rounder jump such as +5.
When crossing 0 in the 1,000s count, note the sign flips once: ...2000, 1000, 0, −1000, −2000 — not 1000 again.
activities.rationale: Optional controls can shade each multiple and display its actual digit sum. Show the9-through90 tens-up/ones-down pattern, then display99 with digit sum18 rather than keeping a false locked9 meter. Other optional views pair two3-jumps per6-jump,5+2 per7-jump,25-unit parts to100, and1,000-unit jumps across zero.
sourceClaims: Year 4: count in multiples of 6, 7, 9, 25 and 1,000; find 1,000 more or less than a given number; count backwards through 0 to include negative numbers.
The 9s times table shows a digit-sum-of-9 / tens-up-ones-down pattern used as a self-check; 6s are taught as doubled 3s; 7s carry the weakest pattern and need most rehearsal.
learnerActions: Pick a count (6s, 7s, 9s, 25s, or 1,000s) and step it one jump at a time, saying each multiple aloud.

Step0,9,18,…,90. From9 to90, treat9 as09 if comparing tens and ones: the tens digit rises by1, the ones falls by1, and the digit sum is9. Then inspect99: its digits sum to18, so the earlier pattern does not continue unchanged.
For the 6s, show each 6-jump as two 3-jumps (the jump 0→6 is 3+3, and the jump 6→12 is a further 3+3), so each multiple of 6 is reached by pairs of 3-jumps.
For the 7s, build each step as a 5-jump plus a 2-jump (7 = 5 + 2) and rebuild any forgotten term that way.
For25s, partition a100-unit bar or collection into four equal25-unit parts, then continue25,50,75,100,125,150. A quarter-hour clock uses15-minute steps to60, so do not use it to label25-unit steps.
For the 1,000s, step along a number line that continues through 0 into negatives, and find 1,000 more or 1,000 less of a given number.
activities.intendedInsight: Use patterns within a stated range:9 through90 have digit sum9, while99 has digit sum18; each6-jump is two3-jumps;7-jumps can be5+2; four25-unit parts make100; and1,000-unit steps continue through zero.

activities.title: Hundred-square reference with reveal-on-tap structure
feedback: Confirm digit sums from the actual cell:18 through90 sum to9;99 sums to18 and is still a multiple of9. Ask which part of the earlier visual pattern changed.
Use the nested 3s to confirm a 6s term when unsure.
activities.rationale: A laid-out, tap-to-reveal reference surfaces the patterns and serves as a quick check. It does not let the learner generate the count or watch the digit pattern update step by step, so it works best as a reference alongside an activity where the learner drives the count.
sourceClaims: The 9s times table shows a digit-sum-of-9 / tens-up-ones-down pattern used as a self-check; 6s are taught as doubled 3s; 7s carry the weakest pattern and need most rehearsal.
learnerActions: Explore a hundred square with the multiples of 9 and the 6s pattern marked. On a 0–99 square, 9 through 90 form a diagonal. On a 1–100 square, 9 through 81 form the diagonal and 90 sits off it.
Reveal each multiple-of9 cell’s actual digits and sum. Compare18 through90, whose digits sum to9, with99, whose digits sum to18.
Reveal the two 3s nested inside a 6s cell.
Reveal the quarter or coin value behind a 25s cell.
activities.intendedInsight: A reference can show the9s pattern through90 and its change at99, alongside pairs of3-jumps within6-jumps and25-unit quarters of100. Check the actual values rather than extending a visual rule beyond its valid range.

activities.title: Check counts and table links
feedback: For a9s blank in the9-through90 segment, digit sum9 is a useful check. For99 or other ranges, verify the step or multiplication fact rather than requiring a sum of exactly9.
For 1,000 less than 4,200, confirm the answer is 3,200 (reduce the thousands digit by 1).
For the count through 0, confirm the next terms are −1000 and −2000, not a repeat of 1000.
For 'seven groups of 9', confirm 63 and relate it to the 9s count reaching 63 at the seventh step from 0.
activities.rationale: Short, varied questions check these counts and their table links and can surface the specific '+10 only' 9s error and the sign error when crossing 0. Checking is distinct from building the pattern insight, so this complements the generative activity rather than replacing it.
sourceClaims: Year 4: count in multiples of 6, 7, 9, 25 and 1,000; find 1,000 more or less than a given number; count backwards through 0 to include negative numbers.
3.OA.7 fluent recall of products (6s/7s/9s tables); 4.OA.5 generate and analyse number patterns.
learnerActions: Fill a missing term in a sequence, e.g. 6, 12, __, 24.
Fill a 9s blank where a wrong '+10 only' rule would give the wrong answer, then justify using the digit sum.
Order the 25s up to 150.
Match 'seven groups of 9' to 63 and similar table facts.
State 1,000 less than 4,200.
Continue a 1,000s sequence downward through 0 into negatives (e.g. 2000, 1000, 0, __, __).
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent skip counts connect directly to multiplication facts and extend cleanly across the hundred and through 0, and can be checked using structure.

activities.title: Oral rehearsal partner for the weak 7s
feedback: If a 7s term is wrong, prompt rebuilding from the previous term plus 7, or from 5+2 jumps.
Reinforce short daily turns rather than one long chant.
activities.rationale: Spoken turn-taking rehearses the weakest-pattern 7s and prompts structural self-checks aloud. Because the key insight here is visual and structural, oral rehearsal supplements the generative pattern work; it is an oral-rehearsal affordance, not evidence that talk teaches the procedure better than other media.
sourceClaims: The 9s times table shows a digit-sum-of-9 / tens-up-ones-down pattern used as a self-check; 6s are taught as doubled 3s; 7s carry the weakest pattern and need most rehearsal.
learnerActions: Take turns counting in 7s aloud with a partner, each saying the next multiple.
When a term is forgotten, rebuild it from 5s + 2s or from a known fact (7×6 = 7×5 + 7 = 42) rather than counting on in ones.

When a 7s term is uncertain, check it by adding 7 to the previous term or by linking it to the matching ×7 fact (e.g. 7×4 = 28). The digit-sum-9 check belongs to the 9s count, not the 7s: 7s terms such as 14 or 28 do not have digit sum 9.
activities.intendedInsight: The hardest, least rhythmic count (7s) may become more reliable through short, frequent oral rehearsal paired with deriving forgotten terms from known facts.

constraints: Use number structure: pair3-jumps for6, compose5+2 for7, partition100 into four25-unit parts, and continue1,000-unit steps through zero. Scope the9s tens-up/ones-down and digit-sum9 pattern to9 through90;99 has digit sum18.
Give the 7s the most rehearsal because they carry the weakest visible pattern; interleave them with already-secure counts rather than drilling in isolation.
Connect every count to its times table and to equal groups/arrays so counting in 6s, 7s and 9s is the fluency route into ×6, ×7 and ×9, not a parallel skill.

A fixed/reference hundred square can reveal and confirm patterns but cannot let the learner generate the count or watch the digit pattern update step by step; use it as a reference, not the sole teaching vehicle.
Short check questions verify counts and table links but do not by themselves build the pattern insight; pair them with activities where the learner generates the count.
Do not respond to sub-counting by ones with more chanting alone; build fluency through retrieval — derive from known facts, use number-line jumps, and keep practice short and daily.
For the 1,000s crossing 0, the sign flips exactly once (…1000, 0, −1000, −2000); avoid repeating a positive term after 0.

The digit-sum9 check used here applies to9 through90, with9 written as09 for a tens/ones comparison. It does not apply unchanged to99; do not reject a correct multiple of9 just because its digits sum to18.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source claims for CCSS (3.OA.7/4.OA.5) and NCETM were marked verified:false in the original row; only the DfE National Curriculum claim was marked verified:true. Do not treat the unverified claims as established, including the '7s weakest pattern / most rehearsal' heuristic.

Self-audit of facts: 4 quarters = 100 (25, 50, 75, 100) is correct; 1,000 less than 4,200 = 3,200 is correct; 7×6 = 7×5 + 7 = 35 + 7 = 42 is correct; 7×9 = 63; counting 1,000s down through 0 gives 0, −1000, −2000 (sign flips once) — all consistent as used in activities.

Corrected a 6s illustration that previously read '12 = 6+6': that showed 12 as two 6-jumps, contradicting the stated 'two 3-jumps per 6-jump' mechanism. It now shows each 6-jump (0→6 and 6→12) as 3+3.

The original all-terms digit-sum9 rule was inaccurate:9 through90 show the stated pattern, but99 has digit sum18. The activities and reference-square feedback now expose that boundary rather than treating all two-digit multiples the same.

The original claim that these patterns 'read most clearly in flat 2D' and that a 3D scene 'adds nothing' is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law; it has been dropped rather than asserted. A spatial/physical representation (e.g. a number line on the floor) may still support the negative-number extension.
'Count in steps of 1000 up to 10,000' from the evidence pairs with the negative extension; ensure the forward range and the backward-through-0 range are both practised.

probeDeeper: What's the next multiple of 7 after 56?
In the 9s, what do the tens and ones digits do as you go?
How many 25s in 100? And in 200?
Use 7×5 to work out 7×6.
assess.correctAnswer: 0, 6, …, 72; 0, 7, …, 84; 0, 9, 18, …, 90; 0, 25, 50, …, 200; and notices in the 9s the tens digit rises while the ones falls (the digits sum to 9) — using pattern and known facts, not counting on by ones.

errorPatterns.pattern: sub-counts by ones — adds the group in single steps each time, most visibly on 7s: long pauses, finger counting, errors past 49
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT just demand more chanting — fluency comes from retrieval: derive from known facts (7×6 from 7×5+7), use number-line jumps, and keep practice short and daily
errorPatterns.revealedBy: slow, audible sub-counting; 7s markedly weaker than 6s

errorPatterns.pattern: misses the 9s pattern — counts the 9s laboriously without noticing the tens-up/ones-down structure (digits sum to 9)
errorPatterns.nextMove: list the 9s and ring the tens and ones digits to show the mirror pattern and digit-sum; hand it back as a self-check — the counting is there, the structure is the add-on
errorPatterns.revealedBy: no pattern-spotting even when prompted to watch the digits

errorPatterns.pattern: boundary/large-step slips — loses place in the 25s at hundred boundaries (75, 100) or miscounts the 1000s toward 10,000
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT reteach the whole sequence — link 25s to money/quarters and the hundred square, and rehearse the 75→100 and thousands bridges specifically
errorPatterns.revealedBy: boundary errors in the 25s or 1000s runs

responseLevels.gap: Cannot sustain 6s/7s/9s without counting every one in between; no use of pattern or known facts.
responseLevels.full: Skip-counts 6s, 7s, 9s, 25s, 1000s fluently by stepping the group size, and exploits structure (the 9s digit-sum, 25s as quarter-hundreds) to check and extend.
responseLevels.partial: Recites the more familiar sequences but sub-counts on 7s/9s and misses their structure (e.g. the 9s digit pattern).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Count in 6s from 0 to 72. Now the hard one — count in 7s from 0 to 84. Then count in 9s to 90, and count in 25s to 200. As you do the 9s, watch the digits — do you notice anything? (Watch the 7s especially, sub-counting, and whether they spot the 9s tens-up/ones-down pattern.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 6s, 7s and 9s are the least rhythmic multiples and the classic fluency bottleneck (7s hardest), so this is the clearest test of pattern- and fact-based skip counting versus laborious sub-counting. A fluent child steps by the group size and leans on structure (the 9s digit pattern, 25s as quarter-hundreds); a struggling child counts on in ones between terms — reliably slower and error-prone on 7s.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 4-6 (Reception/Y1), CONCEPTUAL. Decompose numbers up to 10 into pairs in MORE THAN ONE WAY (part-part-whole): 5 = 1+4 = 2+3 = 0+5… A high-centrality node (0.26) — flexible decomposition underpins number bonds, bridging-through-ten, and subtraction-as-unknown-part.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1 non-statutory): pupils 'memorise and reason with number bonds to 10 and 20 in several forms'; part-whole reasoning is foundational to bonds.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.OA.3 'decompose numbers less than or equal to 10 into pairs in more than one way… and record with a drawing or equation (e.g. 5 = 2 + 3 and 5 = 4 + 1)'; K.OA.4 finding the missing part to make 10.
• Operational details — Fix the WHOLE, then systematically vary the split, recording each as an equation, so the child sees a number is not one fixed pair but a family of pairs. Work systematically (5 as 0+5, 1+4, 2+3…) to reveal the pattern and build confidence that all pairs have been found. Emphasise the whole staying constant while the parts trade — the conservation idea behind bonds and later regrouping.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 4): find at least two different pairs that make a given number with objects. Tier B (age 5): find several pairs for a number up to 10 and record them as equations. Tier C (age 5-6): work systematically to find ALL pairs for a number and explain that the whole stays the same while the parts change.
bestPractices: Keep the WHOLE fixed and physically trade objects between the two parts, so children see the same total split many ways — the conceptual heart of the topic.
Work systematically (0+5, 1+4, 2+3, …) and record each split as an equation, so the set of pairs is seen as complete and patterned, not random.
Use the part-part-whole frame consistently so 'whole' and 'part' become stable ideas that carry into missing-part subtraction and bonds.
Connect to commutativity gently (2+3 and 3+2 use the same pair) without yet formalising it, and to the emerging idea that knowing one pair gives its partner.
Record with drawings AND equations so the abstract bond is tied to a picture of two parts making a whole.
keyRepresentations: Part-part-whole ('cherry'/bar) model with a fixed whole and two changeable parts
Ten-frame showing a number split by colour into two parts
Bead string or two-colour counters partitioned into two groups
A systematic list/table of all pairs for a number (0+5, 1+4, …) with equations
Rekenrek (arithmetic rack) for showing splits of 5 and 10
commonMisconceptions: Thinking a number has only ONE decomposition (e.g. 5 is 'just' 4 and 1) and not seeing it as a family of pairs.
Losing the whole — changing a part but not compensating the other, so the total drifts (5 becomes 2+4).
Missing pairs or double-counting when not working systematically, so 'all the ways' is never securely established.
Treating 2+3 and 3+2 as entirely unrelated rather than the same pair reordered.
Not connecting decomposition to subtraction — failing to see that if 5 = 2 + 3 then 5 − 2 = 3.

learn.summary: For ages 4-6 (Reception/Y1), build flexible decomposition of numbers up to 10 into part-pairs (part-part-whole): 5 = 0+5 = 1+4 = 2+3, and their reversals. The core insight is that one whole is a FAMILY of pairs — the whole stays constant while the two parts trade. Fix the whole, systematically vary the split, and record each as an equation, connecting to number bonds and missing-part subtraction. Several complementary formats each play a role: concrete manipulatives and a screen part-whole bench both let the child generate pairs and feel the whole conserved, while a static anchor diagram and recognition checks consolidate the bond facts. Physical manipulation is emphasised at this age in line with the curriculum.

activities.title: Part-whole bench: slide the divider, keep the whole
feedback: If the child offers only one split, model several splits of the same 5 and record each as an equation; establish that all are correct and the whole is unchanged.
If a re-split uses more or fewer than 5 counters, anchor that all 5 must be used every time; count the whole before and after each split to see it is conserved.
If splits are found at random with repeats or omissions, scaffold a systematic order (0+5, 1+4, 2+3, …); this is an organisation prompt, not a concept reteach.
Ask: when you split 5 into 1 and 4, how many counters in total? And when it is 2 and 3? — to surface conservation of the whole.
Ask: is 4 and 1 a different way from 1 and 4, or the same? — to gently connect reversals to the same pair.
Ask: have we found all the ways, and how could we be sure? — to motivate systematic searching.
activities.rationale: A movable-divider model with live-updating part numbers and an equation lets the child generate decompositions and watch the two parts change while the whole stays fixed, making conservation and the pair-family idea observable. The found-pairs tally supports systematic searching, and a subtraction toggle links decomposition to missing-part subtraction. The live recolouring, dragging, running tally, and subtraction toggle are optional illustrations of the mechanism, not required product features; equivalent hands-on counters and a written list achieve the same aim.
sourceClaims: Y1 pupils memorise and reason with number bonds within 20 in several forms, resting on part-whole decomposition.
K.OA.3: decompose numbers ≤ 10 into pairs in more than one way, recording with drawings/equations (5 = 2 + 3, 5 = 4 + 1); K.OA.4 make ten.
Systematic part-whole decomposition with a conserved whole underpins number bonds and missing-part subtraction.
learnerActions: Place a fixed whole of counters (e.g. 5) into a single frame, then move a divider across so the counters fall into two parts.
Slide the divider to a new spot and read the two parts aloud (e.g. 1 and 4; then 2 and 3).
Record each split as an equation (5 = 1 + 4, 5 = 2 + 3, …) next to a drawing of the two groups.
Keep a running list of pairs found and check whether every pair has been discovered.
In a 'make 10' mode, fix the whole at 10 and find pairs that make ten.
Flip a found pair to subtraction: having built 5 = 2 + 3, state that 5 − 2 = 3.
activities.intendedInsight: A number is not one fixed pair but a whole family of pairs; the parts trade while the total is conserved, and each known pair also tells a missing-part subtraction fact.

activities.title: Physical trading with counters and a part-whole frame
feedback: If the child thinks only one decomposition is correct, model more splits of the same whole and treat each as valid.
If the total drifts, count all the counters before and after the move to show the whole is conserved.
Prompt 'can you make 5 a different way?' to push a systematic search; pair the talk with the counters so the doing stays concrete.
Note gently that 2+3 and 3+2 are the same pair reordered, without yet formalising commutativity.
activities.rationale: Hands-on trading of concrete objects — keeping the whole fixed while physically moving counters between the two parts — makes conservation tangible at this age. Representations such as ten-frames, bead strings, two-colour counters, and a rekenrek give multiple concrete views; recording with both drawings and equations ties the picture to the abstract bond. Guided talk prompts ('make 5 another way') can prompt a systematic search, but talk alone does not itself provide the physical trading, so use it alongside the manipulatives, which supply the concrete doing.
sourceClaims: Systematic part-whole decomposition with a conserved whole underpins number bonds and missing-part subtraction.
K.OA.3: decompose numbers ≤ 10 into pairs in more than one way, recording with drawings/equations (5 = 2 + 3, 5 = 4 + 1); K.OA.4 make ten.
learnerActions: Lay out a fixed whole of two-colour counters or a bead string and physically move one counter from one part to the other.
After each move, say the two parts and write the matching equation.
Build a systematic list of all pairs for 5, then for 10, recording each with a drawing and an equation.
Explain in your own words why the total stays the same when a counter moves across.
Show that 2+3 and 3+2 use the same two groups reordered.
activities.intendedInsight: Physically trading objects between two parts of a fixed whole makes conservation tangible: the total never changes, only how it is split.

activities.title: Anchor diagram and recognition checks
feedback: For a chosen distractor that is off by one, prompt the child to count both parts together and compare with the target whole.
For a missing-part error, return to the fixed whole and ask how many more are needed to complete it.
Treat the diagram as a ready-made display: if the child has not yet generated pairs themselves, send them back to the counters or the part-whole bench to build pairs first.
activities.rationale: A static anchor diagram offers a clean display of multiple decompositions, and recognition/fill-in tasks are useful consolidation and diagnosis of bond knowledge. These formats check and reinforce the facts; because the pairs are presented ready-made or selected rather than constructed, recognition alone does not by itself elicit independent generation, so use these tasks after generation work (a sequencing proposal, not a verified requirement) so the flexible-decomposition insight is built first.
sourceClaims: K.OA.3: decompose numbers ≤ 10 into pairs in more than one way, recording with drawings/equations (5 = 2 + 3, 5 = 4 + 1); K.OA.4 make ten.
learnerActions: Study a part-whole (cherry/bar) diagram for one number and reveal each pair in turn (tap or lift-the-flap 'another way?').
Fill in the missing part: 5 = 2 + __, and set a slider or write the number to complete the bond.

From a set of candidate pairs that also contains a distractor pair whose total is off by one (so it does not make 5), multi-select only the pairs that make 5; the distractor should be left unselected.
Match given pairs to the correct whole.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing several decompositions laid out and practising missing-part completion consolidates number-bond facts and helps spot pairs that do not make the target whole.

constraints: Primary goal is flexible, systematic generation of multiple pairs with a conserved whole; a child producing only one split or changing the total has not yet met the objective.

Recognition and fill-in tasks (multi-select, slider, matching) consolidate and diagnose bond facts but do not by themselves elicit independent generation of decompositions; use them after construction, not as a substitute for it.

A static anchor diagram presents pairs ready-made; it is a display/anchor and is proposed to follow hands-on or interactive generation so the child feels the whole conserved rather than only reading pairs off.

Guided talk prompts can support searching but do not themselves provide the physical trading or visual comparison, since the generating and comparing is still largely manual and visual at this age; pair them with a manipulative rather than relying on talk alone.

Checkpoints: Tier A (age 4) find at least two different pairs for a given number with objects; Tier B (age 5) find several pairs up to 10 and record as equations; Tier C (age 5-6) work systematically to find ALL pairs and explain the whole stays the same while parts change.

Address known misconceptions: a number having only one decomposition; losing the whole when re-splitting; missing/double-counting pairs when unsystematic; treating 2+3 and 3+2 as unrelated; and failing to connect 5 = 2 + 3 to 5 − 2 = 3.
Treat reversals (1+4 vs 4+1) as the same pair reordered; introduce commutativity only gently, not as a formal rule.
The distractor pair in recognition tasks should over- or under-shoot the target whole (e.g. off by one); never present it as a correct way to make the target.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labels the 3D format as adding 'no conceptual value' and the interactive model's conservation insight as 'impossible in a static picture'; these are catalog-fit judgements, not established necessity or medium-superiority claims. They have been softened: a static diagram can still anchor the facts, and concrete vs screen generation offer complementary experiences.
Two of the three sources (CCSS-M K.OA, NCETM) are marked verified:false in the source row; the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified:true. Evidence strength has not been upgraded here.

The source assessment lists a distractor '5 and 3' (which sums to 8, not 5) for the 'changes the whole' misconception; retained conceptually as 'a pair that over/undershoots the target', never as a stated correct alternative. Arithmetic checked: pairs summing to 5 are 0+5, 1+4, 2+3 and reversals; make-ten pairs sum to 10. No arithmetic errors found in the preserved content.

Comparative-efficacy phrasing about guided talk ('works best alongside/paired') was replaced with narrow affordance/limit wording, since no comparative-efficacy evidence is present in the row. The sequencing recommendation (recognition after generation) is likewise a qualified pedagogical proposal, not a source-verified finding.

probeDeeper: When you split 5 into 1 and 4, how many counters are there in total? And when you split it into 2 and 3?
Is 4 and 1 a different way from 1 and 4, or the same?
Have we found all the ways — how could we be sure?
If the whole were 6 instead of 5, would there be more ways or fewer?
assess.correctAnswer: Several ways — 1+4, 2+3, 0+5 (and their reversals). A child who understands part-part-whole generates more than one split and recognises that the whole (5) stays the same while the parts change.

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes a number has ONE correct decomposition — offers only 2+3 and insists that is 'the' way.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model several splits of the same 5 and record each as an equation; establish that all are correct and the whole is unchanged.
errorPatterns.distractor: There's only one way — 2 and 3.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child cannot produce a second split, or judges other splits as wrong.

errorPatterns.pattern: Changes the WHOLE when re-splitting — the second 'split' uses more or fewer than 5 counters, so the parts no longer sum to 5.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor that all 5 must be used every time; count the whole before and after each split to see it is conserved.
errorPatterns.distractor: 5 and 3.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A later split totals 6 or 4; the child adds/removes counters mid-task.

errorPatterns.pattern: Finds splits unsystematically — repeats or omits some, unsure whether all are found.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold a systematic list (0+5, 1+4, 2+3 …); this is organisation, not a concept gap, so do not reteach part-part-whole.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Produces two or three splits at random and cannot tell if the set is complete.

responseLevels.gap: Produces at most one split, or changes the total when re-splitting.
responseLevels.full: Generates multiple splits (ideally systematically), records them, and states that the whole is conserved while the parts vary.
responseLevels.partial: Finds two or three splits but unsystematically, or is unsure the whole stays the same across splits.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show me a way to split these 5 counters into two groups. Now show me a DIFFERENT way. How many different ways do you think you can make 5?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The behaviour reveals the concept: a child who thinks a number has ONE fixed split stops after one and may call others wrong; a child with part-part-whole flexibly produces several and knows the whole is conserved. Asking 'how many different ways' separates single-split thinkers from flexible decomposers.

sources.claim: Y1 pupils memorise and reason with number bonds within 20 in several forms, resting on part-whole decomposition.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (Year 1 Number: addition and subtraction, non-statutory guidance)

sources.claim: K.OA.3: decompose numbers ≤ 10 into pairs in more than one way, recording with drawings/equations (5 = 2 + 3, 5 = 4 + 1); K.OA.4 make ten.
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Operations & Algebraic Thinking (Kindergarten)

sources.claim: Systematic part-whole decomposition with a conserved whole underpins number bonds and missing-part subtraction.

pedagogy.summary: This is the PROCEDURAL partner to the Angle Sum Rules concept: the child treats angle measure as ADDITIVE (a whole angle equals the sum of its non-overlapping parts, CCSS 4.MD.7) and turns an angle diagram into an EQUATION with a symbol for the unknown, then solves it. The move that matters is representing 'the parts share a fixed whole' as arithmetic — 65° + x° = 180° on a straight line, or 120° + 90° + x° = 360° at a point — and solving by subtraction. Taught well it is not a new fact but a disciplined routine: read the configuration to fix the whole (180° or 360°), write the equation, solve, and sanity-check the answer against the diagram. The diagram is a source of GIVEN facts, not something to remeasure.
bestPractices: Make the equation explicit every time: write 65 + x = 180 (or 120 + 90 + x = 360), name the whole first, then solve — so the reasoning is visible and checkable rather than a mental leap to an answer.
Anchor the whole to the configuration before any arithmetic: straight line → 180°, point → 360°; decide which BEFORE computing, so a point problem is never solved with 180°.
Use a bar/part-whole model of the fixed whole with the unknown as a labelled segment, connecting the algebraic symbol to the shared-whole picture.
Insist the diagram gives facts, not measurements: the answer comes from the marked angles and the rule, NOT from putting a protractor on the printed (often not-to-scale) figure.
Separate a reasoning error (wrong whole, non-additive) from an arithmetic slip (mis-subtracting from 180) when marking — they need different help.
Progress from one unknown on a line, to one unknown among several at a point, to decomposition (two parts making a named whole).
keyRepresentations: Equation with a symbol for the unknown: 65 + x = 180, 120 + 90 + x = 360
Bar / part-whole model of the fixed whole (180° or 360°) with the unknown as a labelled segment
The straight line (180°) and the full point (360°) as the two 'wholes' to subtract from
Decomposition diagram: a large angle split into marked parts that sum to it
commonMisconceptions: Subtracts from the wrong whole — uses 180° at a point or 360° on a straight line because the configuration was not identified first.
Treats angle measure as non-additive — tries to measure the unknown on the diagram instead of computing it from the others.
Reads the diagram as if it were to scale — assumes two angles that 'look equal' are equal (e.g. an isosceles-looking triangle), or measures the printed unknown, rather than using the marked values.
Arithmetic slip when subtracting from 180°/360° (e.g. 180 − 145 gives 45 instead of 35) — the angle reasoning is sound but the subtraction fails.

learn.summary: Learners treat angle measure as additive (a whole angle equals the sum of its non-overlapping parts, CCSS 4.MD.7) and turn an angle diagram into an equation with a symbol for the unknown, then solve by subtraction. The disciplined routine is: read the configuration to fix the whole (straight line = 180°, point = 360°, or a decomposition whole that is either named or found by adding the parts), write the equation, solve, and sanity-check the answer against the diagram. The diagram supplies given facts from its marked values; it is not to be remeasured with a protractor, and it may be drawn not to scale.

activities.title: Name the whole, then build and solve the equation
feedback: If the equation uses the wrong whole (e.g. 120 + 90 + x = 180 for angles at a point, or 360 on a straight line), this is a reasoning error: go back and re-name the whole from the configuration. Sort several diagrams by which whole applies before computing again.

If the equation is correct but the final number is off (e.g. writing 180 − 145 = 45 when the correct result is 35), this is an arithmetic slip, not an angle error: redo the subtraction carefully with a number line or column method; the geometry is already sound.
If no equation appears and a protractor is reached for, point back to the marked values: the other angles plus the rule fix the answer, so cover the figure and solve from the numbers alone.
activities.rationale: Making the equation and the chosen whole explicit every time keeps the reasoning visible and checkable, and lets a reasoning error be separated from an arithmetic slip — which need different help. Anchoring the whole to the configuration before computing prevents solving a point problem with 180°.
sourceClaims: Angle measure is additive: an angle decomposed into non-overlapping parts has a measure equal to the sum of the parts; students solve addition and subtraction problems to find unknown angles on a diagram, using an equation with a symbol for the unknown (4.MD.7).

In diagnostic data on finding a missing angle, some wrong answers are genuine misconceptions (e.g. subtracting from 360 instead of 180) while the most common wrong answer was actually an arithmetic slip in subtracting from 180 by students who knew the rule; another group wrongly assumed the triangle was isosceles because it looked that way — so reasoning errors and arithmetic slips must be distinguished, and 'not drawn to scale' framing helps.
learnerActions: Look at each diagram and first decide and state the whole before any arithmetic: a straight line split by a ray is a half turn (180°); angles meeting at a point make a whole turn (360°); for a decomposed angle, either the whole is named and you find a missing part, or the parts are marked and you add them to find the whole.
For a straight line with one angle marked 65° and the other marked x, write the equation 65 + x = 180, then solve to get x = 115°.
For angles round a point marked 120°, 90° and x, write 120 + 90 + x = 360, then solve to get x = 150°.
For a large angle decomposed into two marked parts, 35° and 40°, write 35 + 40 = w with a symbol for the whole, then solve to get w = 75°.
After solving, check the answer back against the fixed whole (do all the parts add to 180° or 360°, or to the stated decomposition whole?).
activities.intendedInsight: An unknown angle is determined by the marked angles and the fixed whole, so it can be computed with an equation rather than measured. Choosing the correct whole (180° vs 360° vs a decomposition whole) is the first decision, not an afterthought.

activities.title: Part-whole bar model linking the symbol to the shared whole
feedback: If the segments overflow or underfill the bar, the parts do not sum to the chosen whole — recheck either the whole or the arithmetic.
If a learner can fill the bar but not write the matching equation, pair each step: 'the gap' becomes '180 − 65', and 'parts fill the whole' becomes '65 + x = 180'.
activities.rationale: A part-whole/bar model connects the algebraic unknown to the shared-whole picture, supporting learners who treat angle measure as non-additive by showing parts recombining to the whole and a missing part found by subtraction.
sourceClaims: The Progressions develop unknown-angle problems from angle additivity: decomposing an angle and recombining the parts, then finding a missing part by subtraction from the whole.

Angle measure is additive: an angle decomposed into non-overlapping parts has a measure equal to the sum of the parts; students solve addition and subtraction problems to find unknown angles on a diagram, using an equation with a symbol for the unknown (4.MD.7).
learnerActions: Draw or use a bar representing the fixed whole (e.g. a bar labelled 180° for a straight line, or 360° for a point).
Fill the bar with the known angles as labelled segments, leaving a gap for the unknown.
Label the remaining gap as x, and read off that x is what is left when the known parts are taken from the whole.
Connect this to the equation: the gap in the bar is 180 − 65, which is the same as solving 65 + x = 180.
Optionally, use a live model where solving the subtraction makes the x segment snap to exactly fill the bar, so the 'parts complete the whole' idea is visible.
activities.intendedInsight: The algebraic symbol x corresponds to a concrete missing segment of a fixed shared whole; subtraction finds the gap that completes the whole.

activities.title: Decompose and recombine a concrete angle
feedback: If a learner still reaches for a protractor on the missing part, revisit the recombination: since the parts provably sum to the whole, the missing part is fixed by subtraction and does not need measuring.
If the two parts don't sum to the stated whole, check which part is mismarked rather than assuming the rule failed.
activities.rationale: Decomposing and recombining a concrete angle makes additivity tangible before it is used in reverse to find a missing part — the development route described in the K–5 Progressions.
sourceClaims: The Progressions develop unknown-angle problems from angle additivity: decomposing an angle and recombining the parts, then finding a missing part by subtraction from the whole.
learnerActions: Take a concrete angle (e.g. a cut paper wedge, or an angle built from two strips) and split it into two marked parts.
Add the two parts to confirm they equal the whole angle (e.g. 35° + 40° = 75°).
Reverse the process: cover one part and find it by subtracting the known part from the whole.
State in words that non-overlapping parts that exactly fill the angle always sum to the whole, so a missing part can be computed rather than measured.
Note that the paper wedge or strips are physical approximations with slight thickness; the mathematical angle being reasoned about is the idealised figure they represent.
activities.intendedInsight: Angle measure is additive: parts sum to the whole, and reversing this gives a missing part by subtraction. This directly addresses the belief that an unknown angle must be measured.

activities.title: Not-to-scale diagram: reason from marked values, not appearance
feedback: If the answer is close to the printed size rather than 115°, the learner measured or trusted appearance — redo it from the marked values with the figure covered.
If an answer is justified by 'they look the same', point out that only marked or equal-labelled angles can be assumed equal.
activities.rationale: Diagnostic data shows learners who read diagrams as to-scale (e.g. assuming an isosceles-looking triangle) make reasoning errors; 'not drawn to scale' framing and solving from marked values counter this.
sourceClaims: In diagnostic data on finding a missing angle, some wrong answers are genuine misconceptions (e.g. subtracting from 360 instead of 180) while the most common wrong answer was actually an arithmetic slip in subtracting from 180 by students who knew the rule; another group wrongly assumed the triangle was isosceles because it looked that way — so reasoning errors and arithmetic slips must be distinguished, and 'not drawn to scale' framing helps.
learnerActions: Work a diagram labelled 'not drawn to scale' where the printed unknown angle looks smaller than the given 65° angle (for example, drawn acute) but must still equal 115° by the rule.
Cover the figure and solve from the marked numbers and the fixed whole alone (65 + x = 180, x = 115°).
Only then reveal the drawing and notice the picture was misleading.
Discuss a case where two angles 'look equal' but are not marked equal, and explain why you cannot assume equality from appearance.
activities.intendedInsight: A diagram carries stated facts, not scale: answers come from the marked values and the rule, not from measuring the printed figure or assuming look-alike angles are equal.

activities.title: Mixed practice: choose the whole each time
feedback: If one whole is applied to every diagram regardless of configuration, sort the diagrams by which whole applies before solving.
If an impossible answer slips through (e.g. parts exceeding the whole), use the sanity-check step to catch it.
Writing the relationship two ways (65 + x = 180 vs x = 180 − 65) shows flexible understanding; if only one form is possible, revisit the part-whole model.
activities.rationale: Varied configurations force the learner to select the whole and expose a wrong-whole error; requiring a written equation reveals whether the additive structure is understood and distinguishes arithmetic slips from reasoning errors. This volume of varied, feedback-rich practice is how the routine is mastered.
sourceClaims: In diagnostic data on finding a missing angle, some wrong answers are genuine misconceptions (e.g. subtracting from 360 instead of 180) while the most common wrong answer was actually an arithmetic slip in subtracting from 180 by students who knew the rule; another group wrongly assumed the triangle was isosceles because it looked that way — so reasoning errors and arithmetic slips must be distinguished, and 'not drawn to scale' framing helps.

Angle measure is additive: an angle decomposed into non-overlapping parts has a measure equal to the sum of the parts; students solve addition and subtraction problems to find unknown angles on a diagram, using an equation with a symbol for the unknown (4.MD.7).
learnerActions: Work a mixed set that includes a straight-line single-unknown case, a point case with several angles and one unknown, and a decomposition case (adding two marked parts to find the whole, e.g. 35 + 40 = 75°, or finding a missing part from a named whole).
For each item, write the equation first, labelling the whole, before giving a number.
Try writing the same relationship two ways for one diagram, e.g. 65 + x = 180 and x = 180 − 65, to show they describe the same additive structure.

Sanity-check each result: plug the answer back and confirm the parts add to the stated whole (e.g. for two 100° angles and x at a point, 100 + 100 + 160 = 360); ask whether the answer is even possible (e.g. a result of 180° or more for one of two angles on a straight line, or a zero or negative result, means the whole or a value was misread).
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency means choosing the correct whole for each configuration rather than applying one habitual routine, and verifying the answer against the fixed whole.

constraints: This is a procedural skill: learners must actually set up and solve their own equations across varied diagrams, not just watch a labelled worked example. A reveal-the-answer picture can illustrate a worked example but does not let the learner construct and solve, so it is only a scaffold toward independent solving.

Multiple-choice or fill-in-the-blank items (e.g. completing 65 + x = ___, or choosing whether to subtract from 180 or 360) give useful scorable practice and can be used during teaching, but recognition-only responses do not by themselves show independent equation setup; pair them with tasks where the learner writes the whole equation.

Always distinguish a reasoning error (wrong whole, treating measure as non-additive) from an arithmetic slip (mis-subtracting from 180 or 360) when giving feedback — they require different remediation.
Insist that the diagram supplies stated facts, not measurements; include at least one deliberately not-to-scale diagram so measuring or assuming look-alike angles are equal is caught.
Progress from one unknown on a line, to one unknown among several at a point, to decomposition (adding parts to find the whole, or finding a missing part from a named whole).
Physical angle cut-outs and strips are approximations with real thickness; use them to demonstrate additivity, but the represented angle is the idealised figure.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic in the source: 65 + x = 180 → x = 115° ✓; 120 + 90 + x = 360 → x = 150° ✓; 35 + 40 = 75° ✓; 100 + 100 + x = 360 → x = 160° ✓. The illustrative slip 180 − 145 has correct result 35; the value 45 is the deliberately-wrong slip used in feedback to model an arithmetic error, never offered as a learner answer. No errors were propagated into learner-facing correct answers.

The original material asserted that a 3D environment 'gains nothing' and that dialogue cannot deliver this skill; these catalog-style necessity claims are not established by the sources and have been reframed as scoped observations about affordances (procedural fluency needs learner-constructed solving and feedback-rich practice) rather than universal laws.

Activity 5's decomposition wording was corrected to match the worked example (whole found by adding) and activity 1's two sub-cases, resolving a minor internal inconsistency carried from the original 'named whole' progression phrasing.

probeDeeper: 'You wrote 65 + x = 180. Why 180 and not 360 here?' — listen for 'it's a straight line, a half turn' versus a memorised default.
Counterexample: 'This diagram is not drawn accurately. If I told you nothing looks the right size, could you still find x? How?' — checks reliance on the rule over appearance.
'If the two given angles at the point were both 100° instead, what would x be — and is that even possible?' (100+100+x=360 → 160; probes whether they sanity-check against the fixed whole).
'Show me a different equation for the same diagram' — e.g. x = 180 − 65 vs 65 + x = 180 — tests flexible understanding of the additive relationship.
assess.correctAnswer: (1) writes 65 + x = 180 and solves x = 115°; (2) writes 120 + 90 + x = 360 and solves x = 150°; (3) writes 35 + 40 = 75°. Uses the marked values and the correct whole for each configuration, and does NOT try to measure the printed (not-to-scale) angle.

errorPatterns.pattern: Subtracts from the wrong whole — uses 180° for the angles-at-a-point diagram (or 360° on the straight line) because the configuration wasn't identified first.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-establish 'name the whole first': straight line = half turn 180°, point = whole turn 360°; sort diagrams by which whole applies before any arithmetic.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 120 + 90 + x = 180, or gives a point answer that's 180° short; may apply one whole to every diagram regardless of shape.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the diagram as to-scale — measures the printed unknown with a protractor, or assumes two angles that 'look equal' are equal, instead of computing from the marked values.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reinforce that diagrams carry stated facts, not scale; cover the figure and solve from the numbers alone, then reveal that the drawing was misleading.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the not-to-scale diagram gives a value close to the printed size rather than 115°; or justifies an answer with 'they look the same'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats angle measure as non-additive — doesn't believe the unknown is determined, so reaches for a protractor rather than writing an equation.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Decompose-and-recombine a concrete angle to show parts sum to the whole, then reverse it to find a missing part by subtraction; frame the whole as fixed and shared.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cannot start without measuring; produces no equation even though the other angles are given.

errorPatterns.pattern: Arithmetic slip — sets up the correct equation but mis-subtracts from 180°/360° (e.g. 180 − 145 = 45 rather than 35).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the subtraction (number line / column method); no angle reteaching needed — the geometry is held, the arithmetic slipped.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Equation is correct and the method sound, but the final number is off by a computation error, often consistent across items.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot set up or solve: no equation, wrong whole, or measures the diagram; answers bear no reliable relation to the marked angles.
responseLevels.full: Writes and solves the correct equation for line, point and decomposition, choosing the right whole each time, ignores misleading scale by using marked values, sanity-checks the result against the fixed whole, and any error is a clean arithmetic slip rather than a reasoning failure.
responseLevels.partial: Solves the standard single-unknown-on-a-line case and can state 'they add to 180', but is derailed by the point configuration (wrong whole), the not-to-scale diagram (measures/assumes equal), or produces an answer without an equation — applies one routine rather than choosing the whole.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put three diagrams in front of the child. (1) A straight line split by one ray, one angle marked 65°, the other x. (2) Angles round a point marked 120°, 90° and x. (3) A large angle decomposed into two marked parts, 35° and 40°, asking for the whole. Say: 'Find each unknown, and write down the equation you used to get it.' Make diagram (1) deliberately NOT to scale so the printed x looks bigger than 65°. Watch how they set up and solve — do not prompt the rule.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The three configurations force the child to choose the whole (180° vs 360°) rather than apply one habit, so a wrong-whole error is exposed. The not-to-scale diagram separates a child who reasons from the rule from one who measures or trusts appearance. Requiring the written equation shows whether the additive structure is understood or the answer was guessed, and it distinguishes an arithmetic slip (equation right, number wrong) from a genuine reasoning error.
