pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–10y; multiply and divide mentally drawing on known facts, related facts and place-value adjustments (40×60 via 4×6; 7×15 via 7×10+7×5; 360÷9 via 36÷9).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5 'multiply and divide numbers mentally drawing upon known facts'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): builds on 3.OA.7/3.OA.5 (strategies) and 5.NBT.1–2 (place-value scaling) applied to mental calculation.
• Operational details — this extends Y4 mental strategy to LARGER numbers via three moves: (1) scale a known fact by place value (40×60 = (4×6)×100 = 2400; 360÷9 = (36÷9)×10 = 40); (2) partition and use the distributive law (7×15 = 7×10 + 7×5 = 105); (3) derive from a near/related fact. The recurring danger with (1) is the 'append zeros' shortcut applied without place-value understanding — keep it grounded as scaling. Encourage flexible CHOICE of strategy and comparing methods; the aim is efficiency and flexibility, not one prescribed route.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): scale a known fact (30×40 via 3×4). Tier B (age 9–10): use partitioning for 7×15 and place-value scaling for 360÷9. Tier C (age 10): choose and justify the most efficient mental strategy for a mixed set and explain the place-value scaling.
bestPractices: Scale known facts by place value (4×6 → 40×60) understood as ×100, not 'append zeros', so it survives decimals.
Teach partitioning via the distributive law (7×15 = 7×10 + 7×5) with an area-model backing.
Use the ×÷ inverse and related facts to derive division mentally (360÷9 from 36÷9).
Foster flexible strategy CHOICE — compare methods for the same calculation and discuss which is most efficient.
Verbalise the chosen strategy and check reasonableness against an estimate.
keyRepresentations: Known-fact-scaled-by-place-value chains (4×6 → 40×60 = 2400)
Area/partition model for distributive mental multiplication (7×15)
Place-value chart — the scaling behind ×÷ by tens/hundreds
Number line / derived-fact links for division
commonMisconceptions: 'Appending zeros' without place-value understanding, misfiring on decimals or miscounting zeros (40×60 as 240 or 24000).
Partitioning incorrectly (7×15 = 7×10 + 5, dropping the second multiplication).
Not using the inverse/related facts for division, computing from scratch.
Fixating on one strategy rather than choosing the most efficient.
Losing a place value in ÷ scaling (360÷9 as 4 rather than 40).

learn.summary: For ages 9–10, mentally multiply and divide larger numbers by drawing on known facts, related facts and place-value adjustments: scale a known fact by place value (40×60 = (4×6)×100 = 2400; 360÷9 = (36÷9)×10 = 40), partition using the distributive law (7×15 = 7×10 + 7×5 = 105), and derive from related facts. The goal is flexible, efficient strategy CHOICE and reasoning about place value — not a single prescribed route, and not a 'just append zeros' trick.

activities.title: Scaling studio: watch the known fact grow
feedback: If a learner gives 240 for 40×60: ask 'what is a ten times a ten?' Guide to 4 tens × 6 tens = 24 hundreds = 2400 — both numbers contributed a ten, so two zeros.
If a learner gives 24000: have them recount — only one hundred factor arises from tens×tens, so the known fact 24 is scaled by 100, giving 2400 (24000 would be scaling by 1000).
If a learner gives 360÷9 = 4: prompt 'you found 36÷9 = 4; 360 is ten times 36, so the answer is ten times bigger — 40.'
If the digit-sliding helps, confirm: 'the digits moved two places left; each place to the left is worth ten times more, so two places is ×10×10 = ×100.'
activities.rationale: Grounding ×÷ by tens/hundreds as place-value scaling of a known fact keeps the method correct for decimals and helps guard against miscounted zeros, a common misconception at this stage.
sourceClaims: Y5 pupils multiply and divide numbers mentally drawing upon known facts.
Scaling known facts by place value and distributive partitioning are efficient mental strategies; teach flexible strategy choice, not 'append zeros'.
Mental strategies build on properties (3.OA.5) and fluency (3.OA.7) with place-value scaling (5.NBT.1–2).
learnerActions: Take 40×60 and name the known fact hiding inside it (4×6=24).
Place 24 on a place-value chart and scale it by ×100, watching the digits slide two columns to the left to make 2400 — because a ten times a ten makes a hundred, and both numbers contributed a ten.
Explain in units: '4 tens × 6 tens = 24 hundreds = 2400', so the answer has two zeros, not one.
Try the same scaling move on a division: link 360÷9 to the known fact 36÷9=4, then scale by ×10 to get 40.
Contrast with a tricky case where a naive 'add a zero' rule would mislead (e.g. a decimal such as 0.4×60, which is 24, not 240) to feel why scaling by place value is the reliable idea.
Optionally use a live place-value chart where the digits visibly shift columns, rather than zeros simply appearing, to make the scaling felt.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying/dividing by tens and hundreds scales a known fact by place value; tens×tens makes hundreds, so the number of zeros follows from the place-value reasoning, not from a memorised 'append a zero' rule.

activities.title: Partition to make it friendly
feedback: If a learner writes 7×15 = 7×10 + 5 = 75: point to the area model — the second tile is 7×5, not 5. Both parts must be multiplied by 7.
If a learner stalls trying to recall 7×15 whole: prompt 'split 15 into 10 and 5 — which of those are easy to multiply by 7?'
If both tiles are computed but added wrong, have them re-add 70 + 35 and compare to the estimate.
activities.rationale: Partitioning via the distributive law with an area-model backing gives a reliable derived-fact route and directly corrects the common error of dropping the second multiplication.
sourceClaims: Scaling known facts by place value and distributive partitioning are efficient mental strategies; teach flexible strategy choice, not 'append zeros'.
Y5 pupils multiply and divide numbers mentally drawing upon known facts.
learnerActions: Take 7×15 and split 15 into friendly parts: 10 and 5.
Compute 7×10 = 70 and 7×5 = 35, then add: 70 + 35 = 105. State both multiplications explicitly so the second part is not dropped.
Back the partition with an area model: a rectangle 7 wide split into a 7×10 tile and a 7×5 tile, whose areas sum to the whole.
Say the full reasoning aloud and check it against an estimate (7×15 is a little over 100).
activities.intendedInsight: The distributive law lets you break a hard factor into friendly parts and multiply each part, then recombine — so you only need facts you already know.

activities.title: Two routes, same answer: choosing the friendliest
feedback: If both routes give different answers, help locate the slip by re-stating the known fact in each route.
If a learner always uses the same method, ask them to find a second route and compare effort — reinforce that either is correct and efficiency can depend on the numbers.
Praise explicit justification of a choice ('I used scaling because 36÷9 is a fact I know').
activities.rationale: Comparing methods for the same calculation builds flexibility and efficiency, the stated aim of mental calculation at this level.
sourceClaims: Scaling known facts by place value and distributive partitioning are efficient mental strategies; teach flexible strategy choice, not 'append zeros'.
learnerActions: Take 7×15 and solve it two different ways: (a) partition into 7×10 + 7×5, and (b) factor-scaling (15 = 3×5, so 7×15 = (7×5)×3 = 35×3, or 7×3×5 = 21×5).
Confirm both routes land on 105.
Discuss which route felt quicker for this calculation and why.
Repeat the compare-methods habit on a mixed set and justify the most efficient choice for each item.
Optionally present the same calculation in more than one worked form side by side so the alternatives can be compared directly.
activities.intendedInsight: Mental maths is about selecting the friendliest of several valid routes to the same answer, not following one prescribed procedure.

activities.title: Explain-aloud diagnostic and quick checks
feedback: Full response: mentally combines a known fact with correct place-value or partitioning adjustments across × and ÷, explaining the reasoning.
Partial: derives some facts (e.g. 7×15) but mishandles place-value scaling in 40×60, or needs prompting for the division link — revisit the scaling studio.
Gap: appends wrong zero-counts, has no derived-fact strategy, or defaults to a written algorithm — return to known facts and the scaling/partition models.
If the method is right but a single arithmetic slip occurs, do not reteach: have the learner re-state the known fact and re-apply the adjustment; this often lets them self-correct on recheck.
activities.rationale: Listening to the spoken strategy (especially on 40×60) is intended to help distinguish genuine place-value understanding from a memorised zero-count; the quick checks are recognition/fill-in/spot-the-error items, so they consolidate and verify a chosen method but do not by themselves elicit independent strategy construction. Efficacy is not established by this rewrite.
learnerActions: Do 40×60, 7×15 and 360÷9 in your head while explaining your reasoning aloud for each.
Answer a few quick checks to consolidate: choose the quickest way to do 7×15 among options; complete 40×60 = (4×6)×□; find the error in a worked solution where zeros were miscounted.
For each check, re-state the known fact at the core and the place-value or partitioning adjustment you applied.

Answer and justify the probe prompts: how many zeros does 40×60 have and why two not one? how did you break up 15? what small division fact hides inside 360? if you know 4×6=24, what else can you work out quickly?
activities.intendedInsight: A correct mental method pairs a known-fact core with a correct place-value or partitioning adjustment, and you can verify your answer by explaining and estimating.

constraints: Keep ×÷ by tens/hundreds grounded as place-value scaling of a known fact, not 'append zeros' — the latter can lead to miscounted zeros (e.g. when the known fact already ends in zero, as in 50×40 = 2000) and fails on decimals.
When partitioning, require BOTH parts to be multiplied (7×15 = 7×10 + 7×5), not 7×10 + 5.

Recognition/fill-in-the-blank and spot-the-error checks consolidate and verify a chosen strategy but do not by themselves elicit independent strategy construction; pair them with explain-aloud production.
Tap-to-reveal strategy cards anchor the methods but let the learner see rather than try alternatives; use them as a reference scaffold, not as the main practice.
A coaching dialogue ('what known fact helps? is there a quicker route?') can rehearse strategy selection but will not on its own build mental speed or show the place-value scaling visually.
Live-updating place-value charts, draggable area tiles and side-by-side worked routes are optional interaction examples to make the mechanism concrete; they are not required mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source-field correction applied: the topic 'evidence' and one phrasing describe 40×60 as '4×6 then appending zeros'. The scaling studio deliberately reframes this as scaling by ×100 (place value), because 'append zeros' is flagged elsewhere in the same row as the core misconception. The original 'appending zeros' wording is retained here only as a note, not in learner actions.

One source claim (CCSS-M build-on) and the NCETM guidance are marked verified:false in the row; treat their support as legacy/unverified. The DfE Y5 claim is marked verified:true in the row but has not been re-checked in this rewrite.

The legacy 'poor fit for 3D' note was expressed as '3D adds nothing'; omitted as a catalog-style universal claim rather than an established pedagogical law. No claim is made that 3D could not help; it is simply unnecessary for this planar numeric topic.

sourceClaims were trimmed per activity: activity 4 set to [] (no claim supports its diagnostic/consolidation efficacy rationale), and activity 3 kept only the NCETM flexible-strategy-choice claim (the DfE Y5 claim supports the topic, not the comparison/flexibility principle).

Self-audit of arithmetic: 40×60 = 2400 (4×6=24, ×100); 7×15 = 70+35 = 105; 360÷9 = 40 (36÷9=4, ×10); factor-scaling 35×3 = 105 and 21×5 = 105; decimal check 0.4×60 = 24. All consistent. Distractor values 240 and 24000 appear only as errors to be corrected, never as valid answers.

probeDeeper: For 40 × 60, how many zeros does the answer have — and why two, not one?
How did you break up 15 to make 7 × 15 easier?
What small division fact is hiding inside 360 ÷ 9?
If you know 4 × 6 = 24, what else can you work out quickly?
assess.correctAnswer: 2400 (4×6 = 24, then ×100 because tens×tens); 105 (7×10 + 7×5 = 70 + 35); 40 (36÷9 = 4, then ×10). The teacher listens for a known-fact core plus a place-value or partitioning adjustment, done mentally.

errorPatterns.pattern: appends the wrong number of zeros — 40×60 as 240 (one zero) rather than 2400, not seeing tens×tens makes hundreds
errorPatterns.nextMove: reason in units: 4 tens × 6 tens = 24 hundreds = 2400; count that BOTH numbers contributed a ten, so two zeros. Avoid the bare 'add a zero' phrasing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer has too few zeros; child says 'four sixes are 24, add a zero'

errorPatterns.pattern: cannot partition for 7×15 — has no derived-fact route, tries to recall it whole or gives up
errorPatterns.nextMove: model 7×15 = 7×10 + 7×5; rehearse partitioning the harder factor into friendly parts.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child stalls on 7×15 rather than splitting 15 into 10 and 5

errorPatterns.pattern: does not use the inverse/place-value link for 360÷9 — does not see 36÷9 inside it
errorPatterns.nextMove: prompt 'what's 36 ÷ 9? so what's 360 ÷ 9?' — bind the larger division to the known small fact and the place-value shift.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child attempts long division or is stuck rather than using 36÷9 = 4 then scaling

errorPatterns.pattern: right strategy, arithmetic slip in the core fact or the adjustment
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach; have the child re-state the known fact and re-apply the place-value adjustment.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: correct method described, wrong number; self-corrects on recheck

responseLevels.gap: appends wrong zero-counts, has no derived-fact strategy, or defaults to written algorithms.
responseLevels.full: mentally combines a known fact with correct place-value or partitioning adjustments across multiplication and division, explaining the reasoning.
responseLevels.partial: derives some facts (e.g. 7×15) but mishandles the place-value scaling in 40×60, or needs prompting for the division link.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to do these in their head while you listen to their reasoning: 40 × 60, 7 × 15, and 360 ÷ 9. Encourage them to say how they worked each out. Watch whether they draw on a known fact and adjust for place value, rather than reaching for a written algorithm.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The 40×60 case exposes the 'just add the zeros' error: children append only one zero (240) or the wrong number, because tens×tens gives hundreds. Listening to the mental strategy reveals whether they understand the place-value scaling behind derived facts rather than a memorised zero-count.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 7-8. Understand that 100 is a bundle of ten tens (just as a ten is ten ones) — unitising climbs one level. Ten ten-rods fuse into one hundred-flat; 100 becomes a single countable unit.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 3): work in the number system to 1000; 'recognise the place value of each digit in a three-digit number (hundreds, tens, ones)' (this concept is its prerequisite unit).
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.NBT.1a '100 can be thought of as a bundle of ten tens — called a hundred'; foundation for 2.NBT.1.
• Operational details — Re-run the exact bundling story one order of magnitude up, using base-ten flats: count ten tens-rods, physically stack/overlay them onto one hundred-flat, and name the new unit. Stress the self-similar pattern (10 ones→1 ten; 10 tens→1 hundred) so children see place value as a repeating ×10 structure, not a list of separate facts.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 7, emerging): builds 100 from ten tens-rods and says 'ten tens make one hundred'. Tier B (age 7-8, secure): explains 100 = 10 tens = 100 ones and treats a hundred-flat as one unit. Tier C (age 8, extending): articulates the repeating ×10 pattern and predicts the next unit (ten hundreds = one thousand).
bestPractices: Re-tell the SAME unitising story up a level with base-ten flats: ten tens-rods physically become one hundred-flat, mirroring ten ones → one ten.
Name the pattern explicitly: 'each new place is ten of the one before' — make the ×10 self-similarity the headline, not an incidental.
Hold three equivalent views of 100 together: 100 ones (a flat of little squares), 10 tens (ten rods), 1 hundred (one flat) — same quantity, different unit.
Anticipate the next rung (ten hundreds = a thousand) so the pattern is felt as open-ended.
Use the hundred-square (10×10 grid) as the bridge image between 'ten tens' and 'a hundred'.
keyRepresentations: Base-ten hundred-flat (10×10) vs ten tens-rods vs 100 unit-cubes — three views of 100
Hundred-square (10×10 grid) showing ten rows of ten
Gattegno / place-value chart adding the hundreds column
Bundled straws: ten bundles-of-ten wrapped into one bundle-of-hundred
0-1000 number line with hundred markers
commonMisconceptions: Thinking 100 is 'ten' with zeros, not literally ten tens or a hundred ones.
Failing to see the repeating ×10 structure — treating hundreds as an unrelated new idea.
Confusing a hundred-flat with a ten-rod (not tracking which unit is which).
Believing 100 ones and 10 tens are different amounts rather than the same quantity re-unitised.
Counting the little squares one-by-one instead of trusting the unit (no unitising).

learn.summary: For ages 7-8: understand that 100 is a bundle of ten tens, just as a ten is ten ones. The core proposed experience is watching ten ten-rods fuse into one hundred-flat, mirroring the earlier ten-ones-to-one-ten move, so children are intended to experience place value as a repeating ×10 structure rather than a list of separate facts. Hold three equivalent views of 100 together (100 single cubes, 10 rods, 1 flat), and foreshadow the next rung (ten hundreds make a thousand).

activities.title: Fuse ten tens into one hundred on an exchange bench
feedback: When the ten rods snap into one flat, confirm: 'Ten tens just became one hundred — the same move as ten ones becoming one ten, one level up.'
On the three-views toggle, point out the counter never moves: 'Still 100 — same amount, just re-unitised into a different unit.'
If a child treats the flat as unrelated to the rods, re-run the fuse and split slowly so they see the flat come apart into exactly ten rods.
Prompt the prediction: 'If ten tens make a hundred, what do you think ten hundreds make?'
activities.rationale: Performing the fuse/split action is intended to make unitising felt rather than merely stated, and re-running the same story one magnitude up is intended to surface the repeating ×10 structure. The merge animation together with a counter that stays steady at 100 is intended to make the equivalence concrete. Offered as a proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Place value is a self-similar ×10 structure; teaching should surface the repeating unitising pattern across ones/tens/hundreds.
100 can be thought of as a bundle of ten tens — called a 'hundred' (2.NBT.1a).
learnerActions: First re-bundle ten single ones into one ten-rod as a familiar recap, naming what happened: 'ten ones make one ten'.
Gather ten ten-rods into a staging tray; as the tenth rod lands, watch the ten rods merge into a single 10×10 hundred-flat.
Say aloud the pattern that connects the two moves: 'ten of the last unit always makes one of the next'.
Use a 'three views' toggle to flip the same hundred between 100 loose cubes, 10 rods, and 1 flat, while a counter stays steady at 100.
Look at a dimmed 'next level' shelf showing ten flats waiting to become a thousand-cube, and predict what comes next.
activities.intendedInsight: 100 is literally ten tens (and a hundred ones); each new place is ten of the one before, so place value is a self-similar ×10 pattern that keeps going.

activities.title: Bundle physical materials: ten tens into one hundred
feedback: If a child counts the rods and says 'ten', count the ones inside one rod (10), then skip-count the rods in tens to 100, naming 'ten tens, one hundred'.
If a child says 'twenty', distinguish 'ten AND ten' (which is 20) from 'ten LOTS of ten' (which is 100), then skip-count all ten rods to 100.
Reinforce by removing the materials and asking them to say '100 is ten tens' from memory.
activities.rationale: Base-ten equipment is genuinely 3D (cube→rod→flat→large cube), so handling real pieces or straw bundles can support unitising, and the hundred-square grid gives a stable bridge image. Offered as consolidation alongside the interactive fuse, not as evidence that any one medium is superior.
sourceClaims: 100 can be thought of as a bundle of ten tens — called a 'hundred' (2.NBT.1a).
learnerActions: Lay out ten ten-rods (or ten bundles-of-ten straws) and skip-count them: 10, 20, 30 … 100.
Physically stack or wrap all ten together and name the new unit: 'one hundred'.
State the three views in words: 100 ones, 10 tens, 1 hundred — the same quantity.
Overlay ten rods onto a 10×10 hundred-square grid to see ten rows of ten make the hundred.
activities.intendedInsight: A hundred built from real materials is the same quantity whether seen as 100 ones, 10 tens, or 1 hundred; the hundred-square bridges 'ten tens' and 'a hundred'.

activities.title: Match and complete the three views of 100
feedback: For 'ten tens = ___', accept 100 (or '1 hundred' / '100 ones', which name the same amount); for '100 = ___ tens', the answer is 10. If a child writes 100 for the number of tens, point back to the ten rods that made the flat.
If a child picks an option that is not equal to 100, lay the views side by side and count the tens together.
Ask the child to justify a correct match aloud so equivalence is reasoned, not guessed.
activities.rationale: Consolidation that checks the equivalence after the construction work. Recognition and fill-in confirm the stated equivalence but do not by themselves elicit the independent act of unitising, so they follow the hands-on activities.
sourceClaims: 100 can be thought of as a bundle of ten tens — called a 'hundred' (2.NBT.1a).
learnerActions: Match each representation to the others: 100 ↔ 10 tens ↔ 100 ones.
Complete 'ten tens = ___' and '100 = ___ tens'.
Choose which option is the same amount as 100 from a set of choices.
Explain in one sentence why each view is still 100.
activities.intendedInsight: The three views of 100 are equivalent, and the ×10 pattern can be stated, not just built.

constraints: The fuse/split construction should come before matching or fill-in tasks: recognition and completion check equivalence but do not elicit the independent act of unitising.

A static side-by-side reference (flat beside ten rods and 100 cubes with tap-to-reveal equivalences) is a useful anchor for the three views but does not let the child perform the fuse/split; use it to support, not replace, the hands-on move.

Paper, card, straw bundles and base-ten blocks have real (slight) thickness; a 2D screen flat is an idealised picture of the hundred-flat. Treat both as representations of the same quantity and name which unit each piece stands for.
Keep the 'next level' shelf (ten flats → thousand-cube) as an optional teaser to show the pattern is open-ended; do not require mastery of 1000 at this stage.

Diagnostic: show ten tens-sticks and ask what the bundled block is called, how many single ones it is, and how the child knows — the reason reveals ten-tens structure versus rote counting. Discriminating follow-up probes: 'How many single ones are there altogether in ten tens, and how could you be sure without counting them all?'; 'If I take one ten away, how many ones are left in the block now?'; 'Both 10 and 100 use the digits 1 and 0 — how are they different?'
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three cited sources (CCSS-M 2.NBT.1a and NCETM Primary Mastery) are marked unverified in the source row; the DfE Year 3 claim is marked verified. Comparative efficacy of any one medium is not established by these citations.
The DfE Year 3 claim is a curriculum/necessity statement about the objective rather than direct support for a specific teaching principle, so it is not used in activity sourceClaims.

The source row claimed 3D handling 'adds manipulation friction without insight' and that dialogue 'adds little'. These are catalog-fit opinions, not established facts; physical base-ten work is retained as a genuine activity and spoken reasoning (skip-counting aloud, justifying matches) is used within tasks.

Efficacy language in the summary and the interactive activity's rationale was softened to intended/proposed wording because the activities are unvalidated; an invented 'recolouring' visual not present in the original design notes was removed, keeping only the source's merge animation and steady counter.

Self-audit of arithmetic: ten tens = 100 ones (10 groups of 10); '10' tens (not 100) completes '100 = ___ tens', while '100' ones completes 'ten tens = ___'. 'Ten and ten' (20) differs from 'ten lots of ten' (100). These were checked; no erroneous value is left in any question or answer.

probeDeeper: How many single ones are there altogether in ten tens? How could you be sure without counting them all?
If I take one ten away, how many ones are left in the block now?
Both 10 and 100 use the digits 1 and 0 — how are they different?
assess.correctAnswer: One hundred. It is 100 ones altogether, because ten tens is 10 groups of 10, which makes 100.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts the sticks rather than their value: 'there are ten sticks so it's ten'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the ones inside one stick (10), then skip-count the sticks in tens: 10, 20 … 100. Name the new bundle 'one hundred = ten tens = a hundred ones'.
errorPatterns.distractor: It's ten.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child counts 1–10 across the sticks and answers 'ten'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds two tens instead of taking ten of them: 'ten and ten is twenty'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish 'ten AND ten' from 'ten LOTS of ten'. Skip-count all ten sticks in tens to 100.
errorPatterns.distractor: It's twenty.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child answers 'twenty', treating 'ten tens' as 10 + 10.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reaches 100 only by counting every one, with no sense of the ten-tens structure
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the count — attach language to it: each time say '10, 20, 30 … that's ten tens, one hundred'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child laboriously counts all ones to 100 but cannot say '100 is ten tens' when asked again with sticks removed.

responseLevels.gap: Answers 'ten' (counts sticks) or 'twenty' (adds), showing no hundred-as-ten-tens unit.
responseLevels.full: Names the bundle 'one hundred', states it is ten tens and one hundred ones, and moves between the nested units (ones ⇄ tens ⇄ hundred).
responseLevels.partial: Reaches 100 but only by counting all the ones; cannot articulate that a hundred is ten tens.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show ten tens-sticks laid out. Ask: 'If I bundle all ten of these sticks together into one block, what is that block called, and how many single ones is it altogether? How do you know?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has built the nested unit says 'a hundred' and knows it is 100 ones; a child counting only the visible sticks says 'ten' (counts the sticks, not their value), and an additive thinker says 'twenty' (10 + 10). The reason tier reveals whether they reach 100 by the ten-tens structure or by rote.

pedagogy.summary: A polygon is regular only when it meets TWO conditions at once — all sides equal AND all angles equal; failing either makes it irregular. Because the concept is a conjunction, the characteristic error is applying just ONE criterion, usually the more salient 'all sides equal', so a rhombus (four equal sides, unequal angles) gets wrongly called regular; less often a rectangle (four equal angles, unequal sides) does. The square is the pivotal case — the one quadrilateral that satisfies both. Teaching succeeds when children habitually check BOTH sides and angles and can name a shape that passes one test but fails the other. A secondary trap is everyday language: hearing 'regular' as 'ordinary/tidy' and 'irregular' as 'odd-looking'.
bestPractices: State regularity as a conjunction and always check BOTH conditions: equal sides AND equal angles; a shape that fails either is irregular
Use the rhombus and the (non-square) rectangle as the key teaching cases — each satisfies exactly one condition — to break the single-criterion habit
Contrast with the square, the quadrilateral that satisfies both, so children see why it, and not the oblong rectangle or the non-square rhombus, is regular
Include many-sided and non-standard-orientation examples, and avoid only ever showing regular shapes, so 'regular' is not welded to a symmetric-looking prototype (NCETM)
Separate the mathematical meaning of regular/irregular from the everyday meaning
keyRepresentations: A two-column check applied to each shape: sides equal? (tick/cross) | angles equal? (tick/cross)
A regular pentagon/hexagon/equilateral triangle beside their irregular counterparts (an irregular pentagon, a rhombus, an oblong rectangle)
Sorting / Carroll cards: 'regular polygon', 'irregular polygon', 'equal sides but not equal angles', 'at least one right angle' (NCETM)
The rhombus (sides tick, angles cross) and the rectangle (angles tick, sides cross) flanking the square (both tick)
commonMisconceptions: Regular = equal sides only — ignores the equal-angles condition, so a rhombus is wrongly called regular
Regular = equal angles only — so a non-square rectangle is wrongly called regular
'Regular' means an ordinary/symmetrical/tidy-looking shape and 'irregular' means an odd or random-looking one (everyday-language interference)
Assumes a polygon has as many lines of symmetry as it has sides — over-generalised from only ever seeing regular examples (NCETM)

learn.summary: A polygon is regular only when it satisfies TWO conditions simultaneously: all sides equal AND all angles equal. Failing either makes it irregular. The characteristic error is applying only one criterion — usually the more salient 'all sides equal' — so a rhombus (four equal sides, unequal angles) is wrongly called regular; less often a non-square rectangle (four equal angles, unequal sides) is. The square is the pivotal quadrilateral that passes both. Teaching succeeds when children habitually check BOTH sides and angles and can name a shape that passes one test but fails the other. A secondary trap is everyday language: hearing 'regular' as 'ordinary/tidy' and 'irregular' as 'odd-looking'.

activities.title: The two-key lock: checking both conditions on a changing shape
feedback: When a rhombus is placed and only the sides indicator is green: 'All four sides are equal — but look at the angles indicator. Two angles are acute, two obtuse, so the angles are NOT all equal. Failing either condition makes it irregular.'

When a non-square rectangle is placed: 'All four angles are equal right angles — but the sides are not all the same length, so it is still irregular. It mirrors the rhombus, which fails on the other condition.'
When the square passes both: 'Both equal sides AND equal angles — this is the one quadrilateral that turns both keys, so it is regular.'
If a child predicts the rhombus is regular: 'That uses only the sides. Run the angle check too before deciding.'
activities.rationale: The core difficulty is that regularity is a conjunction while learners latch onto a single salient attribute. Letting a learner reshape one figure and watch a rhombus and a rectangle each fail on a DIFFERENT condition makes the two-part rule felt rather than merely recited.
sourceClaims: A regular polygon has sides all of equal length AND each interior angle equal; an irregular polygon has sides that are not all equal OR angles that are not all equal OR both — so failing EITHER condition makes a polygon irregular (hence a rhombus with equal sides but unequal angles, and an oblong rectangle with equal angles but unequal sides, are both irregular)

Children reason from prototypes and impose a single salient attribute as if it defined a category, rather than checking the full set of defining properties — the mechanism behind judging regularity on equal sides alone
learnerActions: Work with an adjustable polygon (3–8 sides) that can be reshaped, with two visible condition indicators overhead — 'all sides equal' and 'all angles equal' — and a 'REGULAR' badge that lights only when BOTH indicators are green.
Start with a square: confirm both indicators are green and the badge reads REGULAR.

Skew the square so it leans into a rhombus — the tool keeps all four sides equal — and watch the sides stay equal (green) while the angles become unequal (red), so the badge drops to IRREGULAR even though every side is still the same length.

Straighten the rhombus back into a square, then stretch it along one direction into a long rectangle: watch the angles stay as four right angles (green) while the sides are no longer all equal (red) — still IRREGULAR.

Take named shapes from a gallery (rhombus, oblong rectangle, square, regular pentagon, irregular pentagon) and place each onto the checker, predicting first whether it will be regular and which condition (if any) it fails.
Attempt a 'make it regular' challenge that only succeeds when both conditions hold at once.
activities.intendedInsight: Regularity is a conjunction: equal sides alone, or equal angles alone, is not enough — the badge is a two-key lock, and only a shape that turns both keys (the square among quadrilaterals) is regular.

activities.title: Sorting with regular/irregular criteria
feedback: If a shape is sorted by look: 'Decide with the two columns, not how neat it looks — a tilted regular pentagon is still regular, and a neat oblong rectangle is still irregular.'
If the rhombus is placed with the regular group: 'Check the angle column. Sides tick, angles cross — it belongs with the irregular shapes.'
Confirm correct discrimination: 'You separated the rhombus (sides only) from the rectangle (angles only) from the square (both) — exactly the three cases that break the single-criterion habit.'
activities.rationale: When continually shown regular shapes, pupils over-generalise (for example assuming the number of lines of symmetry equals the number of sides). Sorting against explicit regular/irregular criteria, and avoiding only-regular examples, directly counters that over-generalisation. A sort can check and build classification but does not itself elicit a spoken explanation or hands-on manipulation.
sourceClaims: Year 4 objective 'Classify polygons ... whether or not they are regular, symmetry properties'; when continually shown regular shapes, pupils over-generalise (e.g. assume the number of lines of symmetry equals the number of sides); remedy = sorting cards with regular/irregular criteria and avoid presenting only regular examples

Children reason from prototypes and impose a single salient attribute as if it defined a category, rather than checking the full set of defining properties — the mechanism behind judging regularity on equal sides alone
learnerActions: Sort a mixed set of polygons into 'regular' and 'irregular' groups, including many-sided shapes and shapes shown in non-standard orientations (e.g. a tilted regular pentagon).

Use a two-way sort with the criteria 'all sides equal?' and 'all angles equal?', giving four groups: 'equal sides but not equal angles', 'equal angles but not equal sides', 'both equal', and 'neither equal'. Place the rhombus, oblong rectangle, square and regular/irregular pentagons.
For each shape, apply a two-column check: sides equal? (tick/cross) | angles equal? (tick/cross), and only call it regular when both columns tick.
Deliberately include an odd-looking regular shape and a tidy-looking irregular shape so that appearance is decoupled from the definition.
activities.intendedInsight: Classifying by explicitly checking both conditions — not by overall appearance or by sides alone — and recognising that 'regular' is not welded to a symmetric-looking prototype.

activities.title: Produce a shape that passes one test but fails the other
feedback: If only one counterexample is produced: 'You have the sides-only case — now make an angles-only case (a long rectangle) to show you can fail either condition.'
If the square/rhombus contrast is explained by sides alone: 'Both do have four equal sides. The difference is the angles: the square's four angles are equal, the rhombus's are not.'
Confirm: 'You produced a shape that passes each test separately and explained the square as the one that passes both — that is the full definition in use.'
activities.rationale: Reciting the criteria without applying them is a common partial state; asking learners to construct cases that pass exactly one condition requires active use of both criteria and surfaces whether the definition is genuinely held. Recognition or sorting alone does not require this independent production.
sourceClaims: A regular polygon has sides all of equal length AND each interior angle equal; an irregular polygon has sides that are not all equal OR angles that are not all equal OR both — so failing EITHER condition makes a polygon irregular (hence a rhombus with equal sides but unequal angles, and an oblong rectangle with equal angles but unequal sides, are both irregular)
learnerActions: Draw a shape with all equal sides that is NOT regular (e.g. a rhombus), and label why: equal sides, unequal angles.
Draw a shape with all equal angles that is NOT regular (e.g. an oblong rectangle), and label why: equal angles, unequal sides.
Explain in words why a square is regular but a rhombus is not, even though both have four equal sides.
State the rule by completing: 'a regular polygon has equal ___ and equal ___', then use it to classify a new shape not seen before.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to construct counterexamples (equal sides only; equal angles only) shows the learner holds and can apply the full two-part definition, not just recite it.

activities.title: Shape inspector dialogue: always ask the second question
feedback: If a verdict is given after one condition: 'Before deciding, say what the angles do. Only then can you call it regular or irregular.'
On everyday-language slips: 'Neat or odd-looking does not decide it — a tilted regular pentagon looks unusual but is regular; a tidy oblong is irregular.'
activities.rationale: Articulating reasoning can surface the single-criterion error, and explicitly separating the mathematical meaning from the everyday meaning addresses language interference. This supports classification work rather than replacing hands-on checking of shapes.
sourceClaims: Children reason from prototypes and impose a single salient attribute as if it defined a category, rather than checking the full set of defining properties — the mechanism behind judging regularity on equal sides alone
learnerActions: Take the role of, or respond to, a 'shape inspector' who accepts 'regular' only after BOTH conditions are confirmed.
When the learner offers 'the sides are equal', the inspector presses: 'The sides are equal — but what about the angles?' before any verdict is reached.
Talk through the rhombus and the rectangle, each time naming which single condition passes and which fails.
Separate the everyday sense ('regular' = ordinary/tidy) from the mathematical sense by discussing a deliberately odd-looking regular shape and a tidy-looking irregular one.
activities.intendedInsight: Verbalising both checks — and resisting a verdict until the second condition is examined — can make the single-criterion habit visible and correctable through talk.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal reference chart of near-twins
feedback: 'The regular pentagon meets both conditions; its irregular twin fails at least one. Name which condition each near-twin fails.'
activities.rationale: A fixed reveal-chart cannot recompute as a learner alters a shape, so it serves as a reference/summary rather than a place to test a shape the learner changes; it is best used alongside the manipulable and construction activities.
sourceClaims: A regular polygon has sides all of equal length AND each interior angle equal; an irregular polygon has sides that are not all equal OR angles that are not all equal OR both — so failing EITHER condition makes a polygon irregular (hence a rhombus with equal sides but unequal angles, and an oblong rectangle with equal angles but unequal sides, are both irregular)
learnerActions: Use a reference chart pairing each regular shape with its irregular near-twin: a regular pentagon beside an irregular pentagon, a square beside a rhombus, a square beside an oblong rectangle.

Reveal for each shape which conditions it meets — e.g. regular pentagon: '5 equal sides AND 5 equal angles'; rhombus: 'equal sides, but NOT equal angles → irregular'; oblong: 'equal angles, but NOT equal sides → irregular'.
Use the chart as a summary to confirm or check answers after sorting or constructing shapes.
activities.intendedInsight: A compact reference reinforces that each irregular near-twin fails a specific named condition, consolidating the conjunction rule.

constraints: Regularity requires checking BOTH conditions together: equal sides AND equal angles. A shape failing either is irregular — do not let 'all sides equal' alone stand as the test.
Use the rhombus (sides only) and the non-square rectangle (angles only) as the discriminating cases, flanking the square (both), so the single-criterion habit is broken from both directions.
Include many-sided and non-standard-orientation examples, and do not present only regular shapes, so 'regular' is not welded to a symmetric-looking prototype.
Explicitly separate the mathematical meaning of regular/irregular from the everyday meaning (tidy vs odd-looking); appearance must not decide classification.
Keep tool manipulations geometrically coherent: a rhombus demonstration must hold all four sides equal (a shear/skew) rather than imply a single-corner drag that would change side lengths.
A reveal/reference chart is a summary scaffold: it does not recompute when a learner changes a shape, so it cannot replace activities where the learner tests shapes they alter.

Sorting or multiple-choice items can check the rule but do not require the learner to construct a counterexample; include production tasks (drawing/labelling a shape that passes one test and fails the other) for full mastery.

Regularity is a planar property of sides and angles; adding a third spatial dimension is not needed to teach it. This is a scope note, not a claim that any representation is incapable of teaching the concept.
Dialogue can surface the single-criterion error and is a useful accompaniment to hands-on checking and sorting of shapes; its efficacy relative to those activities is untested.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support the teaching principle, not the effectiveness of any specific activity.

One listed source (National Curriculum in England, Year 5: 'pupils distinguish between regular and irregular polygons based on reasoning about equal sides and equal angles') was marked verified:false in the row. It was removed from activity sourceClaims and is retained here as curriculum context only; it should be re-checked before being relied upon.

The original design note described 'dragging one corner' of a square to form a rhombus while sides stay equal — geometrically impossible, since moving a single vertex changes side lengths. Activity 1 was reworded to a shear/skew in which the tool keeps all four sides equal, preserving the intended 'sides equal, angles unequal' demonstration.

Geometry self-check: a rhombus has four equal sides with two acute and two obtuse angles (fails the angle condition); a non-square rectangle has four equal right angles with unequal sides (fails the side condition); a square satisfies both. Among quadrilaterals only the square is regular. No arithmetic or force/motion content is present.
'Rhombus' and 'rectangle' are used in the non-square sense throughout, matching the age 9–10 pedagogy; note that technically a square is itself a special rhombus and rectangle.

probeDeeper: You've checked the sides — now check the ANGLES. Are all four angles the same size? So is it regular?
Here is a long rectangle. All four of its angles are equal right angles — is it a regular polygon? Why or why not?
Draw me a shape with all equal sides that is NOT regular. Now draw one with all equal angles that is not regular.
Why is a square regular but this rhombus is not, when both have four equal sides?
assess.correctAnswer: No — it is irregular. A regular polygon must have BOTH all sides equal AND all angles equal; this rhombus has four equal sides but its angles are not all equal (two acute, two obtuse), so it fails the angle condition and is irregular. Only when a rhombus's angles are also all equal — making it a square — is it regular.

errorPatterns.pattern: Regular = equal sides only — 'yes, it's regular, all four sides are the same', ignoring that the angles are not equal
errorPatterns.nextMove: Add the angle check explicitly — run BOTH conditions on the rhombus so the child sees it passes sides but fails angles; contrast with a regular pentagon and with the square. Reteach in place: applying the second criterion IS the target.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — it is regular, because all four sides are equal
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'regular' and, on the reason tier, cites only the equal sides; does not mention the angles

errorPatterns.pattern: Regular = equal angles only — surfaces on a rectangle: 'yes, regular, all four corners are the same', ignoring the unequal sides
errorPatterns.nextMove: Run both conditions on the rectangle — equal angles tick, equal sides cross -> irregular; pair it with the rhombus (the mirror case) and the square (both tick).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Under the rectangle probe, calls an oblong rectangle regular, citing its equal (right) angles

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Regular' means an ordinary/tidy shape and 'irregular' means an odd or random-looking one (everyday-language interference)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the maths meaning from the everyday one; give a deliberately odd-looking but regular example (a regular pentagon tilted) and a tidy-looking irregular one (an oblong rectangle) so appearance is decoupled from the definition.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — it is a neat, even shape, so it is regular
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Justifies by look — 'it's a neat/even/normal shape' or 'it's not a weird shape' — rather than by the sides-and-angles conditions

responseLevels.gap: Calls the rhombus regular citing equal sides only, or judges by look ('it's a normal/diamond shape'); does not use the angle condition and cannot say why a rectangle is irregular.
responseLevels.full: Judges the rhombus irregular because, although its sides are equal, its angles are not — applying BOTH conditions; explains that a regular pentagon has 5 equal sides AND 5 equal angles, identifies the rectangle as irregular (equal angles, unequal sides) and the square as the regular quadrilateral, and can produce a shape that passes one condition but fails the other.
responseLevels.partial: Can recite that a regular polygon needs equal sides 'and equal angles' and gets the rhombus right once prompted to check the angles, but does not apply both conditions spontaneously and cannot handle the rectangle (angles-only) case or explain why the square is the regular quadrilateral — lists the criteria without using them to classify new cases.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show the child a rhombus — a 'diamond' with four equal sides but two acute and two obtuse angles (NOT a square). Ask: 'Is this a regular polygon?' Then, whatever they answer: 'How do you know? What makes a polygon regular?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The rhombus is chosen because it satisfies exactly the salient condition (equal sides) and fails the hidden one (equal angles). A child holding the full two-part definition says 'no, irregular' and cites the unequal angles; a child running the sides-only rule says 'yes, regular — all four sides are equal', exposing the missing angle condition on the reason tier. A 'no' backed only by 'it's a diamond, not a normal shape' reveals the everyday-meaning error rather than mastery.

sources.claim: Year 4 objective 'Classify polygons ... whether or not they are regular, symmetry properties'; when continually shown regular shapes, pupils over-generalise (e.g. assume the number of lines of symmetry equals the number of sides); remedy = sorting cards with regular/irregular criteria and avoid presenting only regular examples
sources.source: NCETM — 'Misconceptions with the Key Objectives' (Shape section, polygon-classification objective)

sources.claim: Children reason from prototypes and impose a single salient attribute as if it defined a category, rather than checking the full set of defining properties — the mechanism behind judging regularity on equal sides alone
sources.source: Yesildag-Hasancebi & Halat (2016), prototype and imposed-attribute obstacles in shape classification, EJMSTE 12(2)

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 10–11y; use parentheses/brackets/braces in numerical expressions and evaluate expressions containing these grouping symbols, including nested ones.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y6 'use their knowledge of the order of operations to carry out calculations involving the four operations' (brackets first).
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 5.OA.1 — 'use parentheses, brackets, or braces in numerical expressions, and evaluate expressions with these symbols.'
• Operational details — grouping symbols OVERRIDE the default order: whatever is inside is computed first, and nested grouping is evaluated inside-out ({2×[3+(7−1)]} → innermost (7−1) first). This is the gateway to full BODMAS. Two skills: EVALUATE grouped expressions (respecting nesting), and INSERT brackets to hit a target value (which shows brackets genuinely change the result, e.g. 2+3×4 = 14 but (2+3)×4 = 20). Colour-coding / bracket-matching and a step-by-step 'collapse the innermost group' routine prevent nesting errors. Note brackets are introduced BEFORE the full BODMAS convention here.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): evaluate a single-bracket expression (3×(4+5)). Tier B (age 10–11): evaluate a nested expression inside-out ({2×[3+(7−1)]}). Tier C (age 11): insert brackets to make an expression equal a target and explain how the brackets changed the value.
bestPractices: Establish that grouping symbols compute first and OVERRIDE default order, evaluating nested groups inside-out.
Use insert-the-brackets-to-hit-a-target tasks to prove brackets genuinely change the result (2+3×4 vs (2+3)×4).
Colour-code / match bracket pairs and rewrite the expression after collapsing each innermost group, to prevent nesting slips.
Introduce different grouping symbols (), [], {} as the same idea at different nesting levels.
Connect to real multi-step calculation and later to formulae and algebra.
keyRepresentations: Colour-matched bracket pairs and inside-out collapse steps
Expression tree / step ladder showing each group evaluated
Target-value insert-the-brackets puzzles
Contrasting expressions with/without brackets on the same numbers
commonMisconceptions: Ignoring brackets and applying only left-to-right or default order.
Evaluating nested brackets outside-in instead of inside-out.
Mismatching bracket pairs in nested expressions.
Believing brackets never change the answer (not seeing they override order).
Dropping a grouping level when rewriting mid-calculation.

learn.summary: For 10–11 year-olds: use and evaluate parentheses, brackets and braces in numerical expressions, including nested grouping. Learners discover that grouping symbols OVERRIDE the default order — whatever is inside is computed first, and nested groups are resolved inside-out — through evaluating grouped/nested expressions, inserting brackets to hit a target value, and explaining why placement changes the result. This sets up the full order-of-operations convention.

activities.title: Bracket playground: move the brackets, watch the value change
feedback: If you leave 2 + 3 × 4 as 14 or add brackets that don't change anything, place them side by side: (2 + 3) × 4 = 20 forces the addition first; 2 + (3 × 4) = 14 does not.
Check your target: (2 + 3) × 4 computes 2 + 3 = 5 first, then 5 × 4 = 20.
Say which operation the brackets made happen first and why that reorders the calculation.
activities.rationale: Grouping is a structural override; inserting/moving brackets and recomputing lets learners feel that brackets change the value, which a stated rule alone may not make equally visible. A live-recompute result and draggable bracket handles make the mechanism concrete, but these are illustrative interactions, not required technology.
sourceClaims: Grouping symbols override default order and nested groups are evaluated inside-out; insert-the-brackets tasks show brackets change the value.
learnerActions: Start with 2 + 3 × 4 and position bracket handles around different parts of the expression.
Compare (2 + 3) × 4 = 20 against 2 + (3 × 4) = 14, reading the result each time.
Given the numbers 2, 3, 4 with + and ×, slide the brackets until the expression equals a target of 20.
State in your own words why where the brackets sit changes the answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Brackets are a genuine structural operation that overrides the default order — WHERE they go determines which operation happens first, so they change the result rather than being optional punctuation.

activities.title: Collapse the innermost group: evaluating nested expressions inside-out
feedback: If you get 17 for 3 × (4 + 5), you multiplied before the bracket — the grouped part must become a single number (9) before anything outside it.

If you multiplied 2 × 3 first in the nested one (getting 6 + 6 = 12), you worked outside-in; always cross out the innermost pair first and rewrite with its value. (Combining 3 + 7 first happens to give the same 18 here, because adding and subtracting can be regrouped, but follow the innermost-first routine.)
A right sequence with a wrong sum inside a bracket is just an arithmetic slip — recompute that one bracket, don't restart the whole routine.
activities.rationale: A step-by-step inside-out collapse with colour-matched bracket pairs anchors the nesting routine and targets the common outside-in and mismatched-pair errors. Tap-to-reveal of each step is an optional way to stage the reveal, not a required format.
sourceClaims: Grouping symbols override default order and nested groups are evaluated inside-out; insert-the-brackets tasks show brackets change the value.
Y6 pupils use the order of operations, including brackets first, to carry out four-operation calculations.
learnerActions: Evaluate 3 × (4 + 5) by computing inside the parentheses first: 4 + 5 = 9, then 3 × 9 = 27.
Evaluate the nested expression 2 × [3 + (7 − 1)] by resolving the innermost pair first: (7 − 1) = 6, then [3 + 6] = 9, then 2 × 9 = 18.
After each step, rewrite the whole expression with the collapsed group replaced by its single value before continuing.
Colour-code or circle matching bracket pairs so you never mismatch or skip a level.
activities.intendedInsight: Nested grouping is resolved from the innermost pair outward; replacing each completed group with its value keeps the calculation tidy and prevents dropping or mismatching a level.

activities.title: Insert brackets to hit a target and explain why
feedback: If you can't reach the target, ask which operation needs to happen first and wrap that part: for 20, the 2 + 3 must be grouped so it becomes 5 before multiplying by 4.
Compare your result against the no-bracket value (14) to confirm the brackets actually changed the order.
State the reorder explicitly: '(2 + 3) × 4 does the addition first, giving 5 × 4 = 20.'
activities.rationale: Target-value insertion tasks discriminate learners who treat brackets as reordering structure from those who ignore them, and require justification rather than a single number. This supports the stated teaching objective of showing brackets change the result.
sourceClaims: Grouping symbols override default order and nested groups are evaluated inside-out; insert-the-brackets tasks show brackets change the value.
learnerActions: Take 2 + 3 × 4 (which without brackets equals 14, using the convention that multiplication is done before addition) and insert parentheses to make it equal 20.
Write out the bracketed version, then evaluate it step by step to confirm it reaches the target.
Explain which operation your brackets forced to happen first, and why that changes the answer from 14 to 20.
Try a second target on a fresh set of numbers and justify your placement.
activities.intendedInsight: Inserting brackets to reach a required value shows that grouping genuinely reorders a calculation: under the convention that multiplication comes before addition, 2 + 3 × 4 is 14, and only grouping (2 + 3) makes it 20. Note that working strictly left to right also gives 20 here, so the learner must write the brackets and explain them; reaching 20 alone does not show the brackets were understood.

activities.title: Checkable practice and spot-the-error
feedback: For the fill-in, check that (7 − 1) = 6 was done before [3 + 6] = 9, then 2 × 9 = 18.
When correcting an error, point to exactly which step used the wrong (outer-first) order.

Choosing a correct option can confirm you recognise the right placement but does not by itself show you can construct bracket placements independently — also do an insertion task where you place the brackets yourself.
activities.rationale: Checkable items verify the routine and surface specific misconceptions (outside-in, ignored brackets). Selecting a correct option confirms recognition but does not elicit independent construction, so pair it with open insertion and evaluation tasks.
learnerActions: Fill in the value of {2 × [3 + (7 − 1)]} and show each inside-out step.
Choose which bracket placement makes 2 + 3 × 4 equal 20 from a set of options.
Spot and correct an expression that was evaluated outside-in instead of innermost-first.
activities.intendedInsight: Grouped and nested evaluations, and bracket-placement choices, can be checked precisely, including incorrect options that reflect outside-in evaluation and ignored brackets.

constraints: Brackets are introduced here BEFORE the full order-of-operations (BODMAS) convention; frame grouping as the gateway to that convention rather than the whole of it.

Selection or multiple-choice items can verify understanding but do not elicit independent construction; include open tasks where the learner evaluates nested expressions and places brackets themselves.

A static collapse diagram can anchor the inside-out routine but cannot let the learner move brackets and watch the value change; use it as a scaffold alongside, not instead of, insertion/manipulation tasks.

Draggable handles, live recompute, tap-to-collapse and colour-matching are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete; the same learning can be done on paper with circled bracket pairs and step-by-step rewriting. Do not treat any one medium as required.
Distinguish an arithmetic slip inside a bracket (recompute that group) from a grouping-order misconception (reteach innermost-first) when responding to errors.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 3 × (4 + 5) = 3 × 9 = 27 (correct). 2 × [3 + (7 − 1)] = 2 × [3 + 6] = 2 × 9 = 18 (correct). (2 + 3) × 4 = 5 × 4 = 20 and 2 + (3 × 4) = 2 + 12 = 14 (correct). Without brackets 2 + 3 × 4 = 14 (correct). All retained as-is.
The legacy '3D adds no value' claim for symbolic expressions was dropped as an unsupported universal; omitted rather than asserted.

The CCSS 5.OA.1 citation is marked verified:false in the row and states only the topic (using/evaluating grouping symbols); it was removed from activity sourceClaims where it supported only the topic and not the specific teaching principle.

The DfE Y6 claim (verified:true in the row) is retained only in activity 2, where it supports the brackets-first/compute-inside-first action; it does not specifically support inside-out nesting, which the NCETM claim (verified:false) covers. No comparative-efficacy or necessity claim is asserted from either source.

probeDeeper: Why did you add 4 and 5 before multiplying by 3?
In the nested one, which bracket did you do first — and why the inner one?
Where did you put the brackets to make 2 + 3 × 4 equal 20, and why does that work?
What would 2 + 3 × 4 be WITHOUT any brackets? How do the brackets change it?
assess.correctAnswer: 3 × (4 + 5) = 3 × 9 = 27. 2 × [3 + (7 − 1)] = 2 × [3 + 6] = 2 × 9 = 18. And (2 + 3) × 4 = 20. The teacher watches for computing the bracketed part first, resolving the innermost bracket before the outer, and correctly placing brackets to force a different order.

errorPatterns.pattern: ignores the brackets and evaluates left to right — 3 × (4+5) done as 3×4 then +5 = 17
errorPatterns.nextMove: name brackets as 'do me first' — the grouping is a wrapper that must be collapsed to a single number before anything outside it; box the bracket and replace it with its value.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer of 17 for 3×(4+5); child processes symbols in reading order

errorPatterns.pattern: for nested grouping, resolves the OUTER bracket before the inner one
errorPatterns.nextMove: always start with the innermost pair; physically cross it out and rewrite with its value, then repeat outward.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: in 2×[3+(7−1)] the child combines 3+7 first or ignores the inner parentheses

errorPatterns.pattern: cannot use brackets to CHANGE a result — does not see that brackets alter which operation happens first (the insertion task defeats them)
errorPatterns.nextMove: compare 2 + 3 × 4 (=14) with (2 + 3) × 4 (=20) side by side so the brackets' power to reorder is felt.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child leaves 2 + 3 × 4 as 14 or brackets it uselessly, not realising (2+3)×4 forces the addition first

errorPatterns.pattern: correct order but an arithmetic slip inside a bracket
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach grouping; have the child recompute the bracket value alone.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: right sequence, wrong sum/product within a bracket

responseLevels.gap: evaluates left to right ignoring brackets; cannot insert brackets to reach a target.
responseLevels.full: resolves grouping innermost-outward, evaluates nested expressions correctly, and inserts brackets deliberately to force a required order, explaining why.
responseLevels.partial: computes single brackets first but muddles nested order (outer before inner), or cannot reliably use brackets to change a result.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to evaluate these, watching the order they compute: 3 × (4 + 5); then a nested one, 2 × [3 + (7 − 1)]; then set a challenge — 'put brackets into 2 + 3 × 4 so that it equals 20'. Watch whether they always compute inside the grouping symbols first and work outward from the innermost.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Brackets exist precisely to OVERRIDE the default order; the insertion task ('make it equal 20') cannot be done by a child who ignores grouping or evaluates strictly left to right. Watching the nested evaluation shows whether they work innermost-outward, which a single answer can mask.

sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 5, Operations & Algebraic Thinking (5.OA.A.1)
