pedagogy.summary: At Y3 'angle' is a genuinely dual idea: it names both the static corner of a shape and the dynamic amount of turn between two lines meeting at a point. Research (Williams & Shuard) argues the dynamic turn/opening conception is the more fruitful one and should be developed first through embodied turning, then bound to the static corners children already see in shapes. The central conceptual hurdle is separating the SIZE of an angle (its opening/turn) from the lengths of the lines that form it — children default to judging by side length.
bestPractices: Begin dynamically: children physically turn (whole body, then arms) and describe quarter/half turns before any corner is named an angle, extending their Y2 turn vocabulary.
Use the 'opening' image — open a book, scissors or a fan and watch the angle grow while the sides stay the same length — so size is felt as opening, not length.
Deliberately vary arm length while holding the opening fixed (and vice versa) so children see the angle stay the same though the lines change, directly confronting the length misconception.
Bind the two meanings explicitly: walk the perimeter of a large floor shape, making a turn at each corner, so every vertex is felt as a turn and seen as a corner.
Consider a fresh, non-length word for the quantity being measured; a novel label helps children stop mapping 'angle' onto the whole figure (Xu et al.).
keyRepresentations: Two hinged arms / geo-strips or a split-pin angle maker — the canonical dynamic model: open and close with arms of fixed length
The opening book, pair of scissors, or fan (opening grows, sides constant)
The child's own body turning (embodied quarter/half turn), then one arm held fixed while the other sweeps
Corners of familiar 2-D shapes with the angle arc marked at the vertex
commonMisconceptions: An angle is bigger when its arms/sides are longer — size judged by line length rather than opening (Askew & Wiliam; Xu et al. length-inconsistent trials near 0%)
An angle is 'the distance between the ends of the lines' — a gap between the tips rather than the opening
The whole-object assumption: 'angle' refers to the entire figure, so the amount-of-turn dimension is never separated out (van Hiele holistic processing)
A corner and a turn are unrelated ideas — the child fails to see a shape's corner as a turn, or a turn as producing a corner

learn.summary: At Year 3, 'angle' is a dual idea: the static corner of a shape AND the dynamic amount of turn/opening between two lines meeting at a point. The central hurdle is separating the SIZE of an angle (its opening/turn) from the LENGTH of the lines forming it — children default to judging by side length. Guidance develops the dynamic turn/opening conception first through embodied turning and 'opening' objects, deliberately varies arm length against a fixed opening to confront the length misconception, then binds turn and corner together explicitly.

activities.title: Turn, then open: building angle as amount of turn
feedback: If a learner says the angle grew 'because the lines got longer' while opening scissors, point out the two blades are the same length throughout — only the opening between them changed.
When a learner opens a book or fan, ask them to track one edge: the edge stays the same length, yet the angle clearly grows, so the growth is in the opening.
Affirm descriptions that use turn/opening language ('I opened the arms further apart') over descriptions that reference the figure's overall size.
activities.rationale: Research cited here argues the dynamic turn/opening conception is the more fruitful one and should be developed first, extending children's earlier turn vocabulary. 'Opening' objects (book, scissors, fan) keep the sides a fixed length while the opening visibly grows, so size is felt as opening rather than length.
sourceClaims: The most common error in comparing angles (from Y3) is judging two identical angles as unequal because the arms differ in length, so children treat an angle as the distance between the ends of the lines; it arises because the arms of taught examples are nearly always equal. Two conceptions — static (corner) and dynamic (amount of turn) — must come together, with the dynamic the more fruitful; remediation uses turning with one arm fixed.
The Year 3 statutory statement is to 'recognise angles as a property of shape or a description of a turn'.
learnerActions: Physically turn your whole body a quarter turn, then a half turn; then do the same with an arm held out, describing each turn aloud.
Open a book, a pair of scissors, or a fan slowly and watch the angle between the parts grow while the two parts themselves stay exactly the same length.
Hold two hinged strips (geo-strips or a split-pin angle maker) pinned at one point; swing one strip open from a small opening to a large one and describe what is changing.
State in your own words what you actually had to do to 'make the angle bigger' (open the lines further apart / turn more).
activities.intendedInsight: An angle is the amount of turn or opening between two lines meeting at a point — something you grow by opening the lines apart, not by making the lines longer.

activities.title: Change the arms, keep the opening: confronting the length rule
feedback: If a learner predicts 'the long one is bigger because its lines are longer', overlay the two equal-opening angles vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned — the second arms land on the same line, showing the openings are identical.
When arms are lengthened with the opening fixed, draw attention to the arc/turn at the vertex staying the same while the arm ends shoot outward.

If a learner judges by the gap between the line tips, draw arcs centred on the vertex at several distances along the arms: arcs further out are longer, just as the gap between the arms widens further out, yet every arc shows the same amount of turn. Lengthening the arms moves the tips further from the vertex, so the tip-gap grows, but the angle is the amount of turn at the vertex, not the distance between the ends.
activities.rationale: Children default to judging angle size by irrelevant properties such as side length, enclosed area, or distance between the tips; on length-inconsistent trials accuracy is very low. Deliberately varying arm length while holding the opening fixed (and vice versa), plus predicting before testing, directly targets this misconception. Overlaying equal-opening angles makes the invariance observable.
sourceClaims: The most common error in comparing angles (from Y3) is judging two identical angles as unequal because the arms differ in length, so children treat an angle as the distance between the ends of the lines; it arises because the arms of taught examples are nearly always equal. Two conceptions — static (corner) and dynamic (amount of turn) — must come together, with the dynamic the more fruitful; remediation uses turning with one arm fixed.

Preschool and elementary children judge angle size by irrelevant properties — side length, enclosed area, distance between the sides; on length-inconsistent trials (larger angle drawn with shorter sides) Chinese 3-6 year olds scored ~3% correct and American 4-5 year olds (Gibson et al. 2015) ~25%, versus near-perfect on length-consistent trials. This reflects a whole-object assumption (van Hiele holistic processing); framing angle as the measure of rotation / opening, or teaching a novel non-length label, helps children separate the size dimension.
learnerActions: Set a hinged angle maker to a fixed opening. Predict aloud whether making both arms twice as long would make the angle bigger, and say why BEFORE testing.
Lengthen (or swap for longer strips) both arms while keeping the opening unchanged; check whether the opening/turn has changed.
Reverse it: hold the arm length fixed and only change the opening, describing which action actually changes the angle.

Compare two drawn angles with the SAME opening but very different arm lengths: predict which is bigger, then overlay them vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned so the second arms fall exactly on top of each other.
activities.intendedInsight: Making the lines longer does not make the angle bigger; only changing the opening/turn changes the angle. Length of the arms and size of the angle are independent.

activities.title: Walking the shape: a corner is a turn
feedback: If a learner says 'a square has corners, it doesn't turn', have them physically walk the perimeter and notice their body turns at each corner before marking the arc there.
If a learner can describe quarter/half turns but cannot point to the angle at a corner, lay the hinge onto the corner so the two sides become the two arms of a turn.
Praise answers that name both the corner and the turn together (e.g. 'this corner is a quarter turn').
activities.rationale: The two conceptions — static corner and dynamic turn — must be bound together explicitly. Walking a square or rectangular perimeter, where each walking turn is a quarter turn matching the right-angled corner, together with laying a hinge along the two sides of any corner, lets corners be felt as turns and seen as corners. This matches the Year 3 aim to recognise angles as a property of shape OR a description of a turn. For non-right corners the walking turn is not the corner's size, so use the hinge for those.
sourceClaims: The Year 3 statutory statement is to 'recognise angles as a property of shape or a description of a turn'.

The most common error in comparing angles (from Y3) is judging two identical angles as unequal because the arms differ in length, so children treat an angle as the distance between the ends of the lines; it arises because the arms of taught examples are nearly always equal. Two conceptions — static (corner) and dynamic (amount of turn) — must come together, with the dynamic the more fruitful; remediation uses turning with one arm fixed.
learnerActions: Walk the perimeter of a large taped square or rectangle, making the turn at each corner and feeling that each turn is a quarter turn.
At each corner, stop and point to the corner where you turned, then mark the arc inside the corner between the two sides, noticing that this square corner and your turn are both a quarter turn.
Place a hinged angle maker onto the corner of a familiar 2-D shape so its arms lie along the two sides; describe the corner as an amount of turn.

Say how much turn a square corner is (a quarter turn), then use the hinge on a narrower (sharper) and a wider corner to say whether each corner is less or more than a quarter turn of one side onto the other.
activities.intendedInsight: A shape's corner is an angle: it is the amount one side would turn about the corner point to lie along the other side, which a hinge laid on the corner can show. At a square or rectangle corner this is a quarter turn, the same as the quarter turn you make walking round it, which links the static and dynamic meanings of 'angle'.

activities.title: A fresh name for the opening (optional scaffold)
feedback: If a learner slips back to describing the whole figure's size, re-point to the opening using the agreed fresh name and vary everything else.
Treat the whole-object framing ('the big one just has more to it') as a normal starting point, not a mistake to confront — keep pointing to the opening over time.
activities.rationale: Children's whole-object assumption (holistic processing) means 'angle' is read as the entire figure. Framing angle as the measure of rotation/opening, or teaching a novel non-length label, is reported to help children separate the size dimension. This is a supportive scaffold layered onto the hands-on work, not a standalone method, and its benefit for an individual learner is not established here.
sourceClaims: Preschool and elementary children judge angle size by irrelevant properties — side length, enclosed area, distance between the sides; on length-inconsistent trials (larger angle drawn with shorter sides) Chinese 3-6 year olds scored ~3% correct and American 4-5 year olds (Gibson et al. 2015) ~25%, versus near-perfect on length-consistent trials. This reflects a whole-object assumption (van Hiele holistic processing); framing angle as the measure of rotation / opening, or teaching a novel non-length label, helps children separate the size dimension.
learnerActions: Agree a fresh, non-length word for the quantity being measured (the 'opening' or 'turn amount') and use it instead of 'angle' for a while.
Each time you compare two angles, point to the opening/turn with the new name while varying arm length, tip distance, or figure size, checking only the opening decides.
Return to the word 'angle' once you can consistently point to the opening as the thing being compared.
activities.intendedInsight: Giving the measured quantity a fresh, non-length name may help stop 'angle' being mapped onto the whole figure, so the size dimension (the opening/turn) can be separated out.

activities.title: Check and discriminate: same opening, different arms
feedback: A judgement justified by the opening/turn is the target. If a learner reaches a correct choice by reasoning about line length instead — even a correct 'same' — re-ground it by overlaying the pair vertex-on-vertex: equal-opening pairs show the openings coinciding, while different-opening pairs show the openings genuinely differ regardless of arm length.
If a learner picks the long-armed angle as bigger when the openings are actually equal, return to the hinge and lengthen the arms with the opening held fixed to show the angle does not change.
Use the reason, not just the choice, to tell a secure understanding from a lucky guess — the mix of equal- and different-opening pairs prevents scoring by always answering 'same'.
activities.rationale: A discrimination task comparing angles with varied arm lengths, including both equal and genuinely different openings, is useful to CHECK whether the opening-versus-length separation has formed; requiring the stated reason distinguishes genuine from lucky correct answers. Recognition/discrimination tasks assess the idea rather than build the felt separation, so this follows the hands-on construction rather than replacing it.
sourceClaims: Preschool and elementary children judge angle size by irrelevant properties — side length, enclosed area, distance between the sides; on length-inconsistent trials (larger angle drawn with shorter sides) Chinese 3-6 year olds scored ~3% correct and American 4-5 year olds (Gibson et al. 2015) ~25%, versus near-perfect on length-consistent trials. This reflects a whole-object assumption (van Hiele holistic processing); framing angle as the measure of rotation / opening, or teaching a novel non-length label, helps children separate the size dimension.
learnerActions: Judge several angle pairs with varied arm lengths — some pairs with EQUAL openings and some with GENUINELY DIFFERENT openings — choosing 'same', 'bigger', or 'smaller' for each, so that each choice is sometimes the correct answer.

For each judgement, state the REASON before confirming — e.g. 'same, because the lines have opened by the same amount', or 'that one is bigger because it has turned further open' — justifying by the opening/turn, not the arm length.
Explain whether two lines that meet but barely open apart make a big or a small angle, and why.
activities.intendedInsight: You can reliably decide whether an angle is the same, bigger or smaller by comparing openings/turns, ignoring arm length and tip distance, and you can say why.

constraints: Develop the dynamic turn/opening conception first, then bind it to the static corners children already see in shapes; the Year 3 aim is to recognise angles as a property of shape OR a description of a turn.

The key conceptual target is separating the SIZE of an angle (opening/turn) from the LENGTH of the lines that form it — activities must vary arm length against a fixed opening (and vice versa), not only present angles with equal arms.

A static reveal that merely labels corners as angles is a limited scaffold: it can name corners but does not let a child vary opening against length, which is where the concept forms. Pair any such display with manipulation.

Recognition or sorting tasks CHECK the discrimination but do not by themselves build the felt invariance of opening under changing arm length; use them after hands-on construction, require the learner's reason (not just the choice), and include both equal- and different-opening pairs so no response can be chosen by default.
Treat the whole-object framing ('angle' means the whole figure) as a normal developmental starting point to grow past over time, not a false belief to confront head-on.

A live hinge with a turn readout and a slider that stretches both arms while the arc/counter stay frozen is an optional interaction example that makes the opening-versus-length mechanism concrete; it is one way to realise the idea, not a required technology. Equivalent physical manipulatives (geo-strips, split-pin angle maker, scissors, book, fan) serve the same purpose.

Physical objects (scissors, books, fans, strips) approximate the mathematical idea: their arms are finite and have thickness, whereas a mathematical angle is the opening between two idealised lines; keep returning attention to the opening at the vertex rather than the ends.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support the underlying teaching principle rather than proving any specific activity was tested.

The legacy row rated a 3D rendering as adding 'little' and a dialogue/conversation as unable to produce the felt invariance. These are catalogue-fit opinions, not established pedagogical laws; they have been reframed as scaffold limits rather than universal claims. An embodied whole-body turn (a spatial, physical action) is retained as valuable, and talking about turns can still support learning even if it does not by itself create the felt opening-versus-length separation.

The legacy claim that a static tap-to-reveal 'cannot deliver the concept' has been softened: a fixed display can still teach by labelling corners, but cannot be manipulated to vary opening against length — stated as a scaffold limit, not an absolute.

Note the physical approximations: scissors, books, fans and strips have real thickness and real ends, whereas a mathematical angle is the opening between two idealised lines of unbounded length; the 'gap between the tips' intuition arises precisely because the drawn/physical arms are finite. This approximation is also addressed directly in activity 2 feedback, not only here.

Quantitative figures in the sources (e.g. ~3% and ~25% correct on length-inconsistent trials) are reproduced verbatim from the source claim text and were not independently checked in this rewrite; the original row's looser 'near 0%' phrasing was not carried through in favour of the more precise sourced figures.

assess.poeTask: Draw two angles with the same opening but very different arm lengths on separate cards. Ask the child to PREDICT which is the bigger angle and to say WHY before you test anything. Then overlay the cards, vertex on vertex with one arm aligned, so the second arms lie exactly on top of each other. A child who predicted 'the long one, because its lines are longer' must confront the second arms falling on the same line — the openings are identical. The reason, stated before observing, is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: You said they're the same. What if I made the lines on this one three times as long — would that change the angle? How do you know?
Show me with your arms: make a small angle, now make it bigger. What did you actually have to do to make it bigger?
Here's a corner of this triangle — where's the turn? If you walked along this side and round the corner, how much would you turn?
If two lines meet but hardly open apart at all, is that a big angle or a small one, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: They are the same size, because an angle is how much the lines have turned or opened apart from each other, and both have opened by the same amount — the length of the lines does not change the angle.

errorPatterns.pattern: The angle with the longer lines is bigger ('these lines are longer, so it's a bigger angle')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay the two angles vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned so the openings coincide; show the arms differ in length but the opening is identical. Return to the hinge model, lengthening the arms with the opening held fixed.
errorPatterns.distractor: The one with the longer lines is bigger
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks the long-armed angle, or answers 'same' but justifies it by talking about the line lengths

errorPatterns.pattern: The angle is the distance between the ends of the two lines ('it's how far apart the tips are')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Mark the arc at the vertex and slide it inward and outward along the arms, showing the opening is the same however far out you look; contrast this with the ever-widening gap between the tips.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Judges by the gap between the endpoints, so a long-armed same-opening angle looks bigger; points at the space between the tips when justifying

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Angle' means the whole corner figure, so its size includes the lines and the space inside ('the big one just has more to it')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT treat this as a false belief to confront — the whole-object framing is a normal starting point (van Hiele holistic processing). Give the quantity a fresh non-length name and repeatedly point to the opening/turn while varying everything else, letting the dimension separate over time.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Talks about the overall size of the figure (arms plus enclosed area) rather than the opening; cannot isolate the turn as a single quantity being compared

errorPatterns.pattern: A corner of a shape and a turn are different, unrelated things ('a square has corners, it doesn't turn')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Walk the perimeter of a large floor shape making the turn at each corner, then mark the arc at that corner — bind the felt turn to the seen corner so the two conceptions are recognised as one.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Can find corners but denies the vertex is a turn, or can describe quarter/half turns but cannot point to the angle at a shape's corner

responseLevels.gap: Judges angle size by the length of the arms or the gap between the tips; picks the long-armed angle as bigger and cannot say what quantity is being compared, treating 'angle' as the whole figure.
responseLevels.full: Explains an angle as the amount of turn/opening between two lines meeting at a point, holds this fixed when arm length changes, and transfers it — recognises a shape's corner as a turn and a turn as an angle, applying the idea to a new figure (relational).
responseLevels.partial: Identifies angles at corners and can echo quarter/half-turn language, but holds these as separate facts — names the corner OR describes a turn without connecting them — and is inconsistent when arm length is varied (multistructural: parts present, relation absent).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put in front of the child two angles with the SAME opening, one drawn with long lines and one with short lines. Ask: 'Which angle is bigger — the one with the long lines, the one with the short lines, or are they the same?' Then, whatever they answer: 'Now tell me how you know.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands angle-as-opening answers 'same' AND justifies it by the amount of turn/opening. A child relying on side length picks the long-armed angle and typically says 'because the lines are longer.' The tier-2 reason is decisive: it separates a genuine 'same' (justified by equal opening) from a lucky 'same', and it exposes the length rule even when a child guesses correctly — right and wrong reasoning give different justifications.

sources.claim: The most common error in comparing angles (from Y3) is judging two identical angles as unequal because the arms differ in length, so children treat an angle as the distance between the ends of the lines; it arises because the arms of taught examples are nearly always equal. Two conceptions — static (corner) and dynamic (amount of turn) — must come together, with the dynamic the more fruitful; remediation uses turning with one arm fixed.

This reflects a whole-object assumption (van Hiele holistic processing); framing angle as the measure of rotation / opening, or teaching a novel non-length label, helps children separate the size dimension.

pedagogy.summary: At 9-10 the modelling situations become scaling, area/perimeter, unit conversion and percentage — and crucially the child now selects among competing representations rather than being handed one. The practice is still the full cycle, but the interpret-back carries real-world stakes: a sale price must come back as pounds and pence a shopper would actually pay, a carpet answer must be an area that a room could hold. The teaching emphasis is (1) choosing a representation that fits the structure (a percentage bar for a discount, a scale diagram for a room, a double number line for a rate) and (2) explaining the final quantity in its own units and checking it is plausible.
bestPractices: Make representation CHOICE explicit: give one situation and ask which model (bar, scale diagram, double number line, table) exposes its structure, and why — the practice at this age is selecting, not just using
Route every percentage answer back to money: '£40 with 25% off is £30 — the £30 is what you actually pay', never leaving a bare 30 or 0.75
For area/perimeter, keep the two quantities distinct and interpret each in its own unit (cm² of carpet vs cm of edging) so the child does not blur area with length
Insist on a reasonableness check tied to the context: a sale price must be less than the original; a scaled recipe more than the original; a converted length the same physical size
Use numberless framing for multi-structure problems so the child models the situation before deciding which numbers to combine
keyRepresentations: Percentage bar model (100% strip partitioned for discount/increase)
Scale diagram / scaled drawing for area and length
Double number line and ratio table for scaling and rates
Area/perimeter rectangle with l, w labelled and formula alongside
commonMisconceptions: Gives the discount amount (£10 off) when asked the sale price (£30), or leaves the answer as a decimal (0.75) never returned to pounds
Confuses area and perimeter — adds sides when the situation needs area, or reports the carpet answer in cm instead of cm²
Applies a percentage as a raw number ('25% is 25') rather than a proportion of the specific amount
Picks a representation by habit rather than fit, so a rate problem gets a single bar that hides the two varying quantities
Scales additively (adds the same amount) instead of multiplicatively when enlarging a recipe or shape

learn.summary: For ages 9-10, real-world maths modelling means running the full cycle — choose a representation that fits the situation's structure, build it, compute, then interpret the result back in the right units with a plausibility check. At this age the new skill is SELECTING among competing models (percentage bar, scale diagram, double number line/ratio table, area rectangle) rather than being handed one. The recurring failure is answering with a by-product of the calculation (the discount £10, or the proportion 0.75) rather than the quantity the situation actually asked for (the £30 a shopper pays), and never sense-checking (a sale price must be below the original).

activities.title: Choose, build, interpret back: a modelling workbench
feedback: If a learner names £10 as the price: draw the percentage bar and shade discount vs part-left — 'you found the bit taken OFF; the price is the bit that STAYS'. Ask 'what does the shopper actually hand over?'

If a learner leaves 0.75 or 75 as the answer: ask '0.75 of WHAT?' and require conversion to £30 stated as money — a percentage answer ends in the unit of the quantity it is a percentage of, which here is pounds

If a learner subtracts 25 ('25% off means take 25') to get £15: anchor the percentage to the bar of £40 — 25% is a quarter OF this strip = £10 — and contrast 25% of £40 (=£10) with 25% of £80 (=£20) to show it depends on the amount

If a learner reports the carpet answer in a length unit (cm or m) or adds the sides for an area question: keep area and length physically distinct — coverage of the floor is a squared unit (m² or cm²), the edge measured is a length (m or cm) — and do not proceed until the unit matches the quantity, with the squared area unit matching the length unit used (a room measured in metres gives m², so 4 m × 3 m = 12 m²)
activities.rationale: Modelling explicitly includes interpreting results in context and reflecting on whether they make sense; a part-whole/percentage bar exposes proportional structure so a child can find and explain a sale price rather than manipulating numbers by rule. Building the situation model before computing, and making representation choice explicit, targets the age-appropriate skill of selecting rather than just using a model.
sourceClaims: Modelling includes interpreting mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflecting on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model
A percentage/part-whole bar exposes proportional structure so children can find a sale price and explain it, rather than manipulating numbers by rule
Keyword strategies backfire and children suspend sense-making; problem-specific supports and building the situation model before computing help children choose the right operation
learnerActions: Take a situation such as 'a £40 jacket has 25% off — what does a shopper pay?' and first choose which representation exposes its structure from a palette: percentage bar, scale diagram, double number line, or ratio table
Build a percentage bar: partition the 100% strip into quarters, shade off one quarter (the discount), and read what remains
State explicitly what each number refers to: £10 is the discount (25% of £40), 0.75 is the proportion of the original price remaining, and £30 is the price paid
Pass an interpret-back gate: state the final answer with its unit (£30) and check it is reasonable — a sale price must be less than £40

Re-run the same process on a room-carpet problem (choose a scale diagram, apply the area formula, and give the area in a squared unit that matches the length unit of the measurements — e.g. a 4 m × 3 m room needs 12 m² of carpet) and a recipe-scaling problem (choose a double number line, answer in grams)
Notice which representation you reach for — if you grab a single bar for a rate problem that has two varying quantities, ask whether it hides structure
activities.intendedInsight: When the question asks what the shopper pays, the answer is the part that STAYS (£30), not the part taken off (£10) nor the bare proportion (0.75); and a model is chosen to fit a situation's structure, with every answer returned to its real units and sense-checked.

activities.title: Defend the answer to a customer or tradesperson
feedback: Reject a bare '10' or '0.75' and ask the learner to say what each number refers to before accepting any answer
If the learner cannot justify plausibility, prompt: 'is the price you pay bigger or smaller than £40, and why must that always be true for a sale?'
activities.rationale: Articulating the interpret-back in words can help the learner attach each number to its referent and defend reasonableness — the discriminating skill, since both wrong answers are genuine by-products of a correct calculation. This is a complementary spoken route to the build task, not a required or superior replacement for it.
sourceClaims: Modelling includes interpreting mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflecting on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model
learnerActions: Work in role with a customer or decorator who only accepts an answer once it is stated as the real quantity they need
Answer the shopkeeper's probe 'you said 30 — is that the discount or what I pay?' by distinguishing the two
Answer the decorator's probe 'is that enough for a 4 m by 3 m room?' by stating an area with its unit (12 m²) and checking it is plausible
Voice the reasonableness check aloud: '£30 — less than £40, so for a sale it makes sense'
activities.intendedInsight: The reflective close of the modelling cycle can be spoken: you name which number is the discount, which is the proportion, and which is the quantity asked for, and you justify that it is sensible.

activities.title: Feel area as coverage, length as edge (optional spatial scaffold)
feedback: If a learner gives a length where an area is needed, or drops the squared unit, return to the physical distinction: coverage fills the floor (a squared unit), the edge runs around it (a length unit), and the squared unit must match the length unit used
activities.rationale: A room may make area-versus-perimeter felt for learners who confuse them, but the core structures at this age (percentage, rate, scale) are planar or numeric, so this remains subordinate to the 2D modelling work and should not displace it. Its benefit for most learners is untested; offer it where the area/length confusion is observed.
learnerActions: Cover the floor of a room to feel area as coverage, reported in a squared unit matching the measurements (e.g. m² of carpet needed for a metre-dimensioned room)
Measure around the edge of the same floor to feel length, reported as a length matching the measurements (e.g. m of skirting or edging)
Say out loud which quantity a given question asks for before computing, and match the unit to it
activities.intendedInsight: Area (coverage) and perimeter (edge length) are physically different quantities with different units; blurring them is the error, not a detail.

constraints: The modelling cycle is the objective: choosing a representation, computing, AND interpreting back with a reasonableness check. A scored step that accepts a bare correct number cannot force or observe the representation-choice and interpret-back, so use such checks only for isolated sub-skills (e.g. percentage of an amount) that feed the real modelling task.

A static labelled percentage bar or scale diagram can prime or remind what a representation shows, but on its own does not let the learner choose, compute, or interpret back; treat it as a reference card, not the teaching vehicle for the practice.

Keep area and length as distinct quantities with distinct units throughout; the area uses a squared unit (m² or cm²) that matches the length unit of the measurements and must not be reported as a length.

Every percentage answer must return to the real quantity the situation asks for, stated with its unit (e.g. the £30 a shopper actually pays when the question asks for the price paid) — never leave a bare 30, 75, or 0.75.
Enlarging a recipe or shape is multiplicative (scale by a factor), not additive (add the same amount); watch for additive scaling.
The room/coverage activity is an optional scaffold for learners who confuse area and perimeter, not a required step for every learner.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Source claims are reproduced exactly from the row and cited only where they support a stated teaching principle; a citation does not establish that any specific activity here was tested for efficacy.

The original framed the 3D room as 'overkill' and the quiz/static image as unable to 'host the modelling cycle'. These are retained as scoped affordance/limit statements (recognition-only checks do not elicit representation-choice or interpret-back) rather than universal claims that such media cannot teach.

The original row stated the room-carpet answer in cm² while giving the room as '4 m by 3 m'. This is an inherited unit inconsistency: 4×3=12 m², and only 120000 in cm². It was corrected so the squared area unit matches the length unit of the measurements (m² for a metre-dimensioned room). The original cm² wording is noted here, not offered to learners as correct.

Self-audit on the worked example: £40 with 25% off gives discount £10 (a quarter of £40), price paid £30, proportion remaining 0.75 — all internally consistent. 25% of £80 would be £20, confirming the percentage depends on the amount. No arithmetic errors found beyond the area-unit inconsistency corrected above, which is now resolved at every occurrence.

probeDeeper: Is the price you pay bigger or smaller than £40? Why must that be true for any sale?
If the discount were 25% of an £80 jacket instead, would the '£10' still be right? What changes?
Someone converts the sale price and writes £3000 — how would you know instantly that's wrong?
Show me on a bar which part is the discount and which part is what you pay — how do the two parts relate to the whole?
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child distinguishing that '10' is the discount (25% of £40) and '0.75' is the fraction/proportion remaining, and that the price PAID is £30; and for a reasonableness check ('£30 is less than £40, which must be true for a sale'). A child who cannot say what 10 and 0.75 each refer to, or who names one of them as the price, is computing without modelling.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reports the discount as the sale price ('it's £10') — computes the change but not the resulting quantity the question asked for
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw the percentage bar and shade the discount vs the part left: 'you found the bit taken OFF; the price is the bit that STAYS'. Route the answer back through 'what does the shopper hand over?'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child names 10 as the price to pay and is untroubled that a £40 jacket now costs £10

errorPatterns.pattern: Leaves the answer as a bare decimal or proportion ('0.75') and never converts it back into pounds and pence in the situation
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist on the return trip: 0.75 of WHAT? Convert to £30 and state it as money. Practise ending every percentage problem in the currency it lives in.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child offers 0.75 (or 75) as the answer with no unit and no sense that a shopper pays in £

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the percentage as a raw number ('25% off means take away 25') rather than a proportion of the specific £40
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor the percentage to the bar of £40: 25% is a quarter OF this strip = £10. Contrast 25% of £40 with 25% of £80 to show it depends on the amount.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child subtracts 25 to get £15, ignoring that 25% must be taken OF the amount

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses which quantity is asked when a situation mixes area and length — reports a carpet answer in cm instead of cm² (or adds sides for an area question)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Keep area and length as physically different things: cover the floor to feel cm² (coverage) vs measure the edge for cm (length). Do not proceed until the unit matches the quantity.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the carpet/room follow-up the child gives a length where an area is needed, or omits the squared unit

responseLevels.gap: Names the discount (£10) or the proportion (0.75) as the final price, or gives a bare number with no unit; cannot say what each number refers to and does not check plausibility.
responseLevels.full: Unprompted, distinguishes discount, proportion-left and price-paid, states £30 with its unit, checks it is below £40 as a sale must be, would reject an out-of-scale result, and transfers the choose-model→interpret→check habit to a fresh scaling, area or rate problem.
responseLevels.partial: Can, when prompted, identify that 10 is the discount and £30 is the price, and states the unit, but does not spontaneously sense-check (that a sale price must be below the original) and needs support to choose the fitting representation.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A £40 jacket has 25% off. A shopper says the answer is 10. Another says it's 0.75. What has each of them worked out, and what is the price the shopper actually pays? How would you know your final answer is sensible?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The two wrong answers are both real by-products of a correct calculation, so arithmetic skill is not the tell — the discriminator is whether the child can attach each number to its referent in the situation and identify which one is the quantity the problem actually asked for, then sense-check it. Only genuine modelling separates 'the discount', 'the proportion left', and 'the price paid'.

pedagogy.summary: Comparing decimals is a place-value skill, not a digit-counting one: the digit in the highest place decides the size, so you compare tenths first, then hundredths, then thousandths — exactly as with whole numbers you compare from the left. The whole difficulty is that decimals invite false analogies with whole numbers. Two opposite faulty rules dominate: 'longer-is-larger' (0.45 > 0.5 'because 45 > 5', treating the tail as a separate whole number) and 'shorter-is-larger' (0.4 > 0.87, either because 0.4 is read like 1/4 versus 1/87, or from the partial truth 'tenths are bigger than hundredths'). Both give correct answers on tidy same-length pairs, so RAGGED decimals (different numbers of places) are essential to expose them. Teach comparison through place-value reasoning and a length model, and establish that annexing zeros (0.7 = 0.70 = 0.700) does not change value.
bestPractices: Compare from the highest place value: line up the points, compare tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths — and reason aloud ('0.38 is 3 tenths and 8 hundredths, which is less than 4 tenths').
Use ragged decimals deliberately (0.4 vs 0.38, 0.5 vs 0.45, 0.9 vs 0.11) because same-length pairs let faulty rules pass undetected.
Establish annexing zeros as value-preserving: 0.7 = 0.70 = 0.700, so you may fill to equal length to compare — but only after the meaning is understood, never as a rote substitute.
Use a length model (Linear Arithmetic Blocks) or a number line where size is shown by length, which is conceptually clearer than area/volume blocks, so 0.38 is visibly shorter than 0.4.

Name the misconception to be resisted (metacognitive approach) and show correct and incorrect comparisons side by side, since the error is partly a failure to inhibit the whole-number rule, not only missing knowledge.
Avoid teaching 'add zeros then compare as whole numbers' as the primary method — rules unsupported by place-value understanding are forgotten and mask the misconception.
keyRepresentations: Place-value chart with decimals aligned on the point
Number line (with zoom) for locating and comparing ragged decimals
Linear Arithmetic Blocks / length model where size = length
10×10 hundredths grids shaded for each decimal to compare area
Side-by-side correct vs incorrect comparison cards for discussion
commonMisconceptions: Longer-is-larger: judging the decimal with more digits as larger (0.45 > 0.5, 0.311 > 0.4), treating the tail as a whole number.
Shorter-is-larger (fraction-thinking): 0.4 > 0.87 because 0.4 is read as 1/4 and 0.87 as 1/87 ('sharing among fewer gives more').
Shorter-is-larger (tenths>hundredths): 0.4 > 0.87 from the over-applied partial truth that a tenth is bigger than a hundredth.
Believing annexing a zero changes value (0.7 ≠ 0.70).
Comparing digit-by-digit from the right, or comparing the fractional parts as isolated whole numbers regardless of place.

learn.summary: Comparing decimals is a place-value skill, not digit-counting. You compare from the highest place: any whole-number part first, then tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths, until the digits differ, reasoning aloud ('0.38 is 3 tenths and 8 hundredths, which is less than 4 tenths'). The core difficulty is false analogy with whole numbers, producing two opposite faulty rules: 'longer-is-larger' (claiming 0.45 > 0.5 'because 45 > 5', treating the tail as a whole number) and 'shorter-is-larger' (claiming 0.4 > 0.87, from reading 0.4 as 1/4 vs 0.87 as 1/87, or from over-applying 'tenths are bigger than hundredths'). Both faulty rules give correct answers on tidy same-length pairs, so RAGGED decimals (different numbers of places) are essential to expose them. Teach through place-value reasoning and a length model, and establish that annexing zeros (0.7 = 0.70 = 0.700) does not change value.

activities.title: Order ragged decimals against a length model
feedback: If the learner ranks 0.312 or 0.38 as largest ('more digits'), draw the bars: 0.38 is plainly shorter than 0.4, and 0.312 is shortest. Say in place value: '0.38 is 3 tenths 8 hundredths, less than 4 tenths.'

If the learner picks the shorter decimal as larger using a sharing/fraction analogy on 0.4 vs 0.87 ('like 1/4 vs 1/87'), separate decimal place value from denominator size: 0.4 is four tenths, 0.87 is eight tenths and seven hundredths, so 0.87 is larger; show both lengths.
If the learner says 'tenths beat hundredths so 0.4 > 0.87', compare from the left: 0.87 already has more tenths than 0.4, so it wins before hundredths matter.

If the learner ranks 0.405 above 0.45 because '405 > 45', line up the points: both have 4 tenths, then 0.45 has 5 hundredths while 0.405 has 0 hundredths, so 0.45 is larger — the extra digits in 0.405 are thousandths, not a bigger whole number.
If the learner says 0.7 and 0.70 differ, show seven tenths equals seventy hundredths and the two lengths are identical.
When the learner reasons highest-place-first and justifies in place-value words, confirm the method and extend to a new thousandths case, for example ordering 3.142, 3.14, 3.2.
activities.rationale: Two opposite, documented misconceptions dominate decimal comparison, and both pass on same-length pairs, so ragged decimals are needed to expose them; a length model and place-value reasoning are recommended over rote 'add zeros and compare as whole numbers'. Predicting-then-checking against visible length is intended to confront the longer-is-larger error at the moment the whole-number rule breaks. The main set already exposes longer-is-larger but can hide shorter-is-larger, so 0.4 vs 0.87 is needed to surface shorter-is-larger, while 0.9 vs 0.11 and 0.45 vs 0.405 give further checks on longer-is-larger.
sourceClaims: Two opposite, well-documented misconceptions dominate decimal comparison — 'longer-is-larger' (more digits taken as larger, treating the tail as a whole number) and 'shorter-is-larger', the latter with two sub-types: confusing decimals with fractions (0.4 read as 1/4 vs 0.87 as 1/87) and over-applying 'tenths are bigger than hundredths'. Faulty strategies can yield correct answers on tidy pairs, so ragged decimals are needed to expose them; a length model (Linear Arithmetic Blocks) and place-value reasoning ('0.38 is 3 tenths and 8 hundredths, less than 4 tenths') are recommended over rote 'add zeros and compare as whole numbers'.
learnerActions: Before using any model, predict the order of ragged decimals from smallest to largest and say why, e.g. for 0.4, 0.38, 0.312, 0.5.
Represent each decimal as a bar or length drawn to a common scale (for example a Linear Arithmetic Block / bar model), then check your predicted order against the lengths.

State the correct order (0.312 < 0.38 < 0.4 < 0.5) and justify it in place-value language: 0.312 and 0.38 both have 3 tenths, so they are smaller than 0.4 (4 tenths) and 0.5 (5 tenths); among the 3-tenths numbers, 0.312 (3 tenths 1 hundredth) is less than 0.38 (3 tenths 8 hundredths).

Also compare the counterexample ragged pairs 0.4 vs 0.87, 0.9 vs 0.11, and 0.45 vs 0.405: predict first, then check each against the length model and in place-value words. These pairs deliberately trip both faulty rules — for example 0.45 vs 0.405 tempts longer-is-larger (405 looks bigger than 45), yet 0.45 (4 tenths 5 hundredths) is larger than 0.405 (4 tenths 0 hundredths 5 thousandths); and on the 0.4/0.38/0.312/0.5 set a shorter-is-larger learner can still land the right order.
Locate the decimals on a number line and, where helpful, zoom between 0.3 and 0.4 to see 0.38 and 0.312 separated in the hundredths.
Compare 0.7 with 0.70 (optionally using an annex-zero toggle or shading) and explain why trailing zeros do not change the value.
activities.intendedInsight: The decimal with more digits is not automatically larger, and the one with fewer digits is not automatically larger either; size is decided by the highest place where the digits differ. A length/number-line model shows that more digits need not mean more length (0.38 is shorter than 0.4, but 0.87 is longer than 0.4). Annexing trailing zeros gives decimals the same number of decimal places without changing their value.

activities.title: Name and resist the whole-number rule (correct vs incorrect cards)
feedback: If the learner cannot name why a wrong card is wrong, re-read both decimals in place-value words and point to where the comparison first decides (the highest differing place).
Praise explicit self-monitoring ('I nearly counted the digits — but I compared tenths first').
If the learner only identifies the right answer without naming the faulty rule, prompt: which rule would make someone pick the wrong card here?
activities.rationale: The greater-digits misconception reflects an overgeneralisation of whole-number knowledge and is partly a failure to inhibit the whole-number rule, so metacognitive approaches that name the misconception and present correct/incorrect examples side by side are recommended.
sourceClaims: The 'greater number of digits means greater magnitude' misconception is among the most common in decimal comparison and reflects an overgeneralisation of whole-number knowledge; it is partly a failure to inhibit the whole-number rule, so metacognitive approaches that name the misconception and present correct/incorrect examples side by side are recommended. Longer-is-larger declines with age while shorter-is-larger persists into adulthood.
learnerActions: Look at side-by-side comparison cards, one clearly labelled correct and one clearly labelled wrong, e.g. '0.45 > 0.5' (labelled wrong) beside '0.45 < 0.5' (labelled correct).
Say out loud which faulty rule produced the wrong card ('longer-is-larger: it counted 45 against 5') and explain why it fails here.
Write or state the place-value reason the correct card holds (0.5 is 5 tenths; 0.45 is 4 tenths 5 hundredths; 5 tenths is more).
Before answering each new pair, flag the rule you must NOT use, then compare correctly.
activities.intendedInsight: The error is partly a failure to inhibit the whole-number rule, not only missing knowledge; naming the misconception and inspecting clearly-labelled correct/incorrect examples side by side helps a learner catch and override it.

activities.title: Show equivalence and area with hundredths grids
feedback: If the learner thinks 0.38 covers more than 0.4 because '38 > 4', count tenths columns: 0.4 fills four full columns (40 squares), 0.38 fills three columns and part of a fourth (38 squares).
If the learner denies 0.7 = 0.70, overlay or count: 7 tenths = 70 hundredths cover the same squares.
On the aligned chart, if the learner compares from the right, redirect to the highest place first.
activities.rationale: Grids and an aligned place-value chart are useful references for area comparison and for making annexing-zeros equivalence concrete; however such references need to be paired with practice across many ragged cases with feedback rather than used alone.
learnerActions: Shade 0.4 and 0.38 each on a 10×10 hundredths grid and compare the shaded areas.
Shade 0.7 on one grid and 0.70 on another, and explain why seven tenths fills the same area as seventy hundredths.
Use an aligned place-value chart (points lined up) to read each decimal digit by digit, starting from tenths, and state which decimal is larger and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Decimals can be compared by area as well as by length, and both representations show that annexing a zero (0.7 = 0.70) preserves value while more digits need not mean more size. (Note: the source synthesis treats length as the clearest magnitude model for this topic; the grid is a complementary reference.)

constraints: Use ragged decimals deliberately (e.g. 0.4 vs 0.38, 0.5 vs 0.45, 0.9 vs 0.11, 0.4 vs 0.87, 0.45 vs 0.405); same-length pairs let both faulty rules pass undetected and should not be the only practice.
On the 0.4/0.38/0.312/0.5 ordering set a shorter-is-larger learner can still reach the right order, so include at least one pair (such as 0.4 vs 0.87) that directly exposes shorter-is-larger.
Teach 'annexing zeros is value-preserving' (0.7 = 0.70 = 0.700) only after the meaning is understood, never as a rote substitute for place-value reasoning.
Avoid teaching 'add zeros then compare as whole numbers' as the primary method; rules unsupported by place-value understanding are forgotten and can mask the misconception.

A length model or number line (where size is shown by length) is the recommended visual here; the source synthesis prefers length over volume/3D models for this topic. This is a stated preference for showing decimal magnitude, not a universal claim that other media cannot teach.

A static aligned chart or single shaded grid is a reference/scaffold: it may support reading or checking a comparison but does not by itself provide the repeated ragged-case practice with feedback that builds the comparison skill.

Multiple-choice/ordering/true-false questions with distractors built from longer-is-larger and shorter-is-larger can diagnose which faulty rule a child uses, but recognising the right option does not by itself build place-value insight; pair any quizzing with construction and justification.
Scope: Year 5 expectation is to read, write, order and compare numbers with up to three decimal places; extend from hundredths to thousandths deliberately.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the worked examples: 0.312 < 0.38 < 0.4 < 0.5 is correct; 0.312 and 0.38 share 3 tenths, and 0.312 (3 tenths 1 hundredth) < 0.38 (3 tenths 8 hundredths); 0.4 and 0.5 have 4 and 5 tenths. 0.7 = 0.70 = 0.700 is correct (seven tenths = seventy hundredths). 0.87 > 0.4, 0.9 > 0.11, and 0.45 > 0.405 are correct. Ordering 3.142, 3.14, 3.2 gives 3.14 < 3.142 < 3.2. Grid counts: 0.4 = 4 columns = 40 squares; 0.38 = 38 squares. No arithmetic errors found.

Coherence fix applied: feedback referring to 0.4 vs 0.87, 0.9 vs 0.11 and 0.45 vs 0.405 now has matching learnerActions in Activity 1, because the main ordering set 0.4/0.38/0.312/0.5 can be ordered correctly by a shorter-is-larger learner and therefore does not reveal that misconception on its own.

Source verification is mixed in the original row: the SMART/Victoria synthesis claim is marked verified; the Durkin & Rittle-Johnson / Roell et al. / Steinle & Stacey synthesis claim and the DfE National Curriculum claim are marked unverified. The Durkin-synthesis claim is reused as a sourceClaim because it directly supports the metacognitive-naming principle, but its verification status was not upgraded here.

The original artefact wording asserting that a conversation or 3D model offers 'no spatial gain' and that a static picture 'cannot' teach has been softened to scoped affordances/limits; comparative necessity is a catalog preference, not established efficacy.
The length-over-volume preference is carried from the source synthesis as a recommendation for this topic, not as proof that volume/3D representations cannot teach decimal comparison.

probeDeeper: You placed 0.38 relative to 0.4 — which has more tenths? Does having more digits always mean bigger?
A friend says 0.9 is smaller than 0.11 because 11 is more than 9. What would you tell them?
Is 0.5 bigger or smaller than 0.45? What about 0.5 and 0.500?
How could you use this number line to check your whole order is right?
assess.correctAnswer: 0.312 < 0.38 < 0.4 < 0.5. Reasoning by place value: 0.312 and 0.38 have 3 tenths (smaller), and 0.312 (3 tenths 1 hundredth) is less than 0.38 (3 tenths 8 hundredths); 0.4 and 0.5 have 4 and 5 tenths. 0.7 = 0.70 — seven tenths equals seventy hundredths; the trailing zero does not change the value.

errorPatterns.pattern: Longer-is-larger: 'more digits means bigger — 0.38 is more than 0.4 because 38 is bigger than 4', treating the digits after the point as a whole number.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the length model — 0.38 is shorter than 0.4 — and reason in place value: '0.38 is 3 tenths 8 hundredths, less than 4 tenths'. Use ragged decimals; name and inhibit the whole-number rule. Reteach comparison of same-length decimals first.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Ranks 0.312 and/or 0.38 as the largest; orders by digit count rather than by tenths.

errorPatterns.pattern: Shorter-is-larger (fraction-thinking): 'the shorter one is bigger — 0.4 beats 0.87 because sharing among 4 gives more than among 87', reading 0.4 as 1/4 and 0.87 as 1/87.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate decimal place value from denominator-size reasoning: 0.4 is four tenths, 0.87 is eight tenths and seven hundredths, so 0.87 is bigger; show both on the length model. Reteach decimal comparison from place value.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks the shorter decimal as larger and justifies with a sharing/denominator analogy.

errorPatterns.pattern: Shorter-is-larger (tenths>hundredths): 'tenths are bigger than hundredths, so 0.4 is bigger than 0.87' — over-applying a partial truth.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare place by place from the left: 0.87 has more tenths than 0.4, so it wins before hundredths matter; grids/length model make it visible. Reteach highest-place-first comparison.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct on pure tenth-vs-hundredth cases but wrong when the hundredths total exceeds the tenths gap (0.4 vs 0.87); may also mis-order fractions by denominator.

errorPatterns.pattern: Annexing a zero changes the value — '0.7 and 0.70 are different, 0.70 is bigger (or smaller)'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show 7 tenths = 70 hundredths on a grid and equal lengths on the line; trailing zeros fill to equal length without changing size. Reteach place-value equivalence.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the tier-2 question, denies 0.7 = 0.70.

responseLevels.gap: Orders by number of digits (longer- or shorter-is-larger) or compares the tails as whole numbers; denies 0.7 = 0.70. Ragged decimals are mis-ordered.
responseLevels.full: Orders ragged decimals correctly by comparing the highest place value first, justifies in place-value language ('0.38 is 3 tenths 8 hundredths, less than 4 tenths'), knows 0.7 = 0.70, and transfers the method to thousandths and to counterexample pairs like 0.9 vs 0.11.
responseLevels.partial: Compares same-length decimals correctly but slips on ragged decimals, or reaches the right order by annexing zeros without explaining place value — executes a rule without the highest-place-first reasoning.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put these in order from smallest to largest and show me how you decided: 0.4, 0.38, 0.312, 0.5. Then tell me — is 0.7 the same size as 0.70, and how do you know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: These are RAGGED decimals, so faulty rules cannot hide. A longer-is-larger child ranks 0.312 or 0.38 as largest ('more digits'). A shorter-is-larger child ranks 0.4/0.5 as largest for the wrong reason and mis-orders 0.312 vs 0.38, or claims 0.4 > 0.5-style errors on other pairs; watching the justification reveals whether it is the fraction-analogy or the tenths>hundredths route. The 0.7 vs 0.70 tier catches the belief that annexing a zero changes value. Same-length pairs would let every faulty rule pass — these do not.

sources.claim: Two opposite, well-documented misconceptions dominate decimal comparison — 'longer-is-larger' (more digits taken as larger, treating the tail as a whole number) and 'shorter-is-larger', the latter with two sub-types: confusing decimals with fractions (0.4 read as 1/4 vs 0.87 as 1/87) and over-applying 'tenths are bigger than hundredths'. Faulty strategies can yield correct answers on tidy pairs, so ragged decimals are needed to expose them; a length model (Linear Arithmetic Blocks) and place-value reasoning ('0.38 is 3 tenths and 8 hundredths, less than 4 tenths') are recommended over rote 'add zeros and compare as whole numbers'.

Longer-is-larger declines with age while shorter-is-larger persists into adulthood.

sources.claim: Pupils should read, write, order and compare numbers with up to three decimal places (Year 5 statutory content).
