pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 7-8 (META). Solve number and practical problems using place value to 1000 — e.g. 'how many tens in 340?', money in pounds and pence, or 'my number has 4 hundreds and 7 ones and no tens, what is it?'. Applying three-digit place value flexibly, not learning it.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 3): 'solve number problems and practical problems involving these ideas' (three-digit place value).
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.NBT / 2.MD.8 apply place value and use it in money and measurement contexts; problem-solving with base-ten reasoning.
• Operational details — Pose varied problems that reward partitioning, 'how many tens/hundreds', missing-digit clues and real contexts (money, measures). Model with part-whole/bar models and place-value counters; think aloud then hand reasoning to the child. Emphasise flexible partitioning (340 = 34 tens = 3 hundreds 4 tens) and inverse/missing-value reasoning.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 7, emerging): solves a one-step place-value problem with a model. Tier B (age 7-8, secure): answers 'how many tens in 340' and missing-digit clues, explaining the strategy. Tier C (age 8, extending): tackles multi-step/real-context problems and reasons flexibly about non-canonical partitions.
bestPractices: Pose genuine problems (how-many-tens, missing-digit clues, money/measures) that reward place-value reasoning, not routine recall.
Model with part-whole / bar models and place-value counters, thinking aloud, then transfer the explaining to the child.
Stress flexible partitioning: 340 is 3 hundreds 4 tens AND 34 tens AND 300 + 40 — choose the useful view.
Use money as a natural place-value context (£/10p/1p mirror hundreds/tens/ones).
Include missing-value / inverse problems to build reasoning beyond direct calculation.
keyRepresentations: Part-whole and bar models for problem structure
Place-value counters and H|T|O chart
Money (pounds/tens of pence/pence) as a place-value context
0-1000 number line for jump/benchmark reasoning
Arrow cards for flexible partitioning
commonMisconceptions: Only seeing canonical partition (340 = 300 + 40) and missing '34 tens'.
Counting in ones instead of using place-value structure.
Mishandling internal zeros in problem numbers (407).
Inverse-blindness on missing-digit/missing-number clues.
Not mapping money/measure contexts onto place-value columns.

learn.summary: For ages 7-8, solve number and practical problems using three-digit place value to 1000, applying it flexibly rather than first learning it. The central objective is flexible re-unitising: seeing that the SAME number can be decomposed many equivalent ways (340 = 3 hundreds 4 tens = 34 tens = 300 + 40) and choosing the view that fits the problem. Children work 'how many tens/hundreds' questions, missing-digit clues (4 hundreds, 0 tens, 7 ones give 407), and money/measure contexts, explaining and checking their reasoning.

activities.title: Place-value problem workbench: re-unitise to answer
feedback: If the child gives only the canonical partition (340 = 3 hundreds 4 tens), prompt: 'Can you exchange each hundred for ten tens? How many tens altogether now?'
When the child exchanges correctly, confirm that 34 tens and 3 hundreds 4 tens are the same number seen two ways.
If the child counts in ones, redirect to the place-value structure: 'Use the hundreds and tens rather than counting each one.'
For 'how many hundreds in 680?', accept 6 hundreds (with 8 tens left over) and discuss why this count is not a whole re-unitising like 340 to 34 tens.
activities.rationale: A manipulable problem bench lets the child physically partition, regroup and read off answers, making the re-unitising move visible rather than guessed. Live recomputation (hundred-flats visibly breaking into ten tens-rods) is intended to make the equivalence concrete. This is one suitable, proposed approach for a problem-solving (META) topic; physical base-ten pieces or arrow cards serve the same purpose without a screen.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils should 'solve number problems and practical problems' involving three-digit place value.
Flexible (non-canonical) partitioning and re-unitising underpin place-value problem solving.
learnerActions: Read a problem card such as 'How many tens are in 340?'
Build 340 with place-value pieces (three hundred-flats, four tens-rods) or arrow cards.
Exchange each hundred-flat for ten tens-rods on an exchange pad and watch 340 reassemble as 34 tens-rods, then read off the answer: 34 tens.
Repeat for another number (e.g. how many tens in 350? how many hundreds in 680?) and say which decomposition you used.
Name the strategy you used each time ('I re-unitised the hundreds into tens').
activities.intendedInsight: The same number can be re-unitised into equivalent decompositions; you pick the view that answers the question, and you can check by rebuilding the original number.

activities.title: Money and measures as place-value columns
feedback: If the child doesn't connect pounds to hundreds, lay the money beside place-value counters so the one-to-one mapping is visible.
For £4.07, check the internal zero: 'There are no 10p coins here — how do we show that in the tens column?'
Confirm answers by rebuilding: '407 pence — can you make that back into pounds and pence?'
activities.rationale: Money is a natural, real context where place-value columns transfer directly, and it surfaces the internal-zero case (£4.07 = 407p). Real contexts reward place-value reasoning over routine recall.
sourceClaims: Place-value reasoning is applied in problem contexts including money and measurement (2.NBT / 2.MD.8).
learnerActions: Solve a money problem such as '£4.07 = how many pence?' using a money tray (pounds, 10p, 1p).
Counting the amount in pence, map pounds onto hundreds (£1 = 100p), 10p onto tens, and 1p onto ones, lining them up in place-value columns.
Work a small shopping total using the same columns you used for whole numbers.
State how the money columns mirror hundreds/tens/ones.
activities.intendedInsight: Money (pounds / 10p / 1p) mirrors the hundreds/tens/ones structure, so a shopping total is solved with the identical place-value reasoning.

activities.title: Missing-digit and missing-value clues
feedback: If the child writes 47 for 'four hundreds, no tens, seven ones', ask: 'Where do the hundreds go? What holds the tens place when there are none?'
For inverse problems, prompt 'what is the number made of?' before any calculation.
Confirm by reading the built number aloud and checking it matches every part of the clue (34 tens and no ones gives 340; 34 tens make 340).
activities.rationale: Missing-digit and inverse problems build reasoning beyond direct calculation and are intended to address inverse-blindness and mishandling of internal zeros, both common difficulties.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils should 'solve number problems and practical problems' involving three-digit place value.
learnerActions: Read a clue such as 'I have 4 hundreds, 0 tens and 7 ones — what number am I?' and build the number (407).
Honour the placeholder: put no tens pieces in the tens column but keep the column, and write a 0 digit there when recording, so the number is written correctly as 407, not 47.
Work an inverse/missing-value problem, e.g. '__ tens make 340' or 'a number has 34 tens and no ones — what is it?'
Explain how you knew where each digit belonged.
activities.intendedInsight: Place value is a two-way tool: you can reason backwards from a description to the number, and internal zeros act as placeholders that must be honoured.

activities.title: Talk-it-through: how did you decide?
feedback: If the child insists '350 IS 3 hundreds and 5 tens, that's it', model several equivalent builds of 350 with base-ten pieces (exchange a hundred for ten tens) and name each as the same number seen differently.
If the child reaches for a taught calculation first, don't supply a procedure — ask 'what is 350 made of?' so composition drives the method.
Treat this as eliciting reasoning, not scoring: surface the thinking rather than grading it.
activities.rationale: Socratic questioning suits a META topic for eliciting strategy. At 7-8, pairing talk with an external model (pieces, arrow cards) is usually more productive than sustained talk alone, so keep manipulatives available during the discussion. A dialogue can elicit and probe reasoning but does not by itself build the hands-on re-unitising move.
sourceClaims: Flexible (non-canonical) partitioning and re-unitising underpin place-value problem solving.
learnerActions: Respond to a riddle or problem and explain, step by step, how you worked it out.

Answer probes such as: 'How many tens are in 350? Is there more than one way to see that?', 'Could 350 also be 35 tens — how would you check?', 'What did you already know about how numbers are built that helped you decide?'
Test whether the same thinking helps for 'how many tens are in 352' and say what changes.
Justify your chosen decomposition and check it by rebuilding the number.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to articulate why a chosen decomposition fits — and to check it — shows place value is held as a flexible strategy, not a single fixed label.

activities.title: Consolidation problems and worked reference
feedback: For a fill-in or multiple-choice item, if wrong, send the child back to build the number and re-unitise rather than restating the answer.
Use the worked example to prompt the next reasoning step, not to supply the result.
Encourage the child to explain the strategy after answering, as the evidence asks for ('explain the strategy used').
activities.rationale: Structured items and a worked-example anchor support consolidation and self-correction. Recognition and recall items assess and reinforce but do not by themselves elicit the independent re-unitising and explanation; use them alongside, not instead of, hands-on construction.
learnerActions: Answer a mix of items: 'how many tens in 340?', '£4.07 = __ pence', 'which number has 4 hundreds, 0 tens, 7 ones?', and match each problem to its useful partition.
Attempt a multi-step word problem in a real context (e.g. money).
Use a worked example of a how-many-tens problem as a reference: step through the reasoning when stuck, rather than copying the answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Varied practice consolidates flexible partitioning and lets the child recognise which decomposition a given problem rewards.

constraints: Target the actual objective — flexible re-unitising and problem solving — not routine recall of 'hundreds, tens, ones'.

Recognition-only items (multiple choice, matching) assess and consolidate but do not by themselves elicit the independent re-unitising and explanation that are the goal; pair them with construction and spoken reasoning.
A worked example is a reference, not varied problem practice; it cannot replace the child working new problems.
Keep money/measure mappings honest: pounds / 10p / 1p mirror hundreds/tens/ones, and the internal-zero case (£4.07 = 407p) must be handled explicitly.
Honour placeholders: a clue like '4 hundreds, 0 tens, 7 ones' must build 407, not 47.

Physical base-ten pieces, arrow cards and screen models all make re-unitising visible; none is uniquely necessary. On-screen live recolouring/exchange is an optional way to show the move, not a requirement.
The evidence expects the child to explain the strategy, so build explanation into every activity.

Where a 'how many hundreds/tens' question does not re-unitise to a whole count (e.g. 680 as hundreds gives 6 hundreds and 8 tens over), treat the remainder honestly rather than forcing a clean single number.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research, not fresh source verification. Sources were NOT re-fetched; activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source lists one US-standards claim and one NCETM claim as verified:false; treat their support as unconfirmed.

The original recommendation framed the interactive bench as the single ideal and rated 3D as having 'no payoff'. These are catalog fit judgements, not established efficacy or necessity claims; alternatives (physical manipulatives, dialogue, quiz, worked example) are preserved here as legitimate approaches with different purposes.
Efficacy-leaning wording in rationales was softened to proposed/intended/narrow-affordance language, as these activities are unvalidated and were not re-verified.

Self-audit checks: 340 = 34 tens (3 hundreds = 30 tens, + 4 tens = 34 tens) is correct; 350 = 35 tens is correct; 352 = 35 tens with 2 ones remaining; £4.07 = 407 pence is correct; '4 hundreds, 0 tens, 7 ones' = 407 is correct; '34 tens and no ones' = 340 is correct; 680 as hundreds = 6 hundreds with 8 tens remaining. No arithmetic errors found in the migrated examples.

probeDeeper: How many tens are in 350? Is there more than one way to see that?
Could 350 also be 35 tens — how would you check?
What did you already know about how numbers are built that helped you decide?
Does that same way of thinking help for 'how many tens are in 352'? What changes?
assess.correctAnswer: Not scored. A rich response recognises 350 can be viewed in several equivalent ways (3 hundreds 5 tens, OR 35 tens, OR 350 ones) and that you choose the view that fits the problem — and can check by rebuilding the number.

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes a number has only ONE correct decomposition ('350 IS 3 hundreds and 5 tens, that's it')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model several equivalent builds of 350 with base-ten pieces (exchange a hundred for ten tens) and name each as the same number seen differently.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child rejects 35 tens as a way to see 350, or cannot regroup to suit the question.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reaches for a taught calculation without first asking what the number is made of
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't supply a procedure — prompt 'what is 350 made of?' first, so place-value reasoning drives the choice of method.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child hunts for an operation to 'do' rather than reasoning about the number's composition.

responseLevels.gap: Treats the number as having one fixed decomposition; looks for a procedure without reasoning about composition.
responseLevels.full: Spontaneously views a number in whichever equivalent decomposition fits the problem, justifies it, and checks by rebuilding.
responseLevels.partial: Regroups when prompted but doesn't yet treat flexible decomposition as a general problem-solving move.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'Someone tells you 350 is made of 3 hundreds and 5 tens. Is that the only way to see what 350 is made of, or are there others? If you got a problem like “how many tens are in 350?”, how would you decide what the number is really made of? Talk me through it.' Surface the thinking — don't grade it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The probe surfaces whether the child sees place value as a flexible tool — a number can be decomposed many ways and you pick the useful one — or as a single fixed label. That stance, not one answer, is what solving place-value problems depends on.

sources.claim: Year 3 pupils should 'solve number problems and practical problems' involving three-digit place value.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (Year 3 Number & place value)

sources.claim: Place-value reasoning is applied in problem contexts including money and measurement (2.NBT / 2.MD.8).
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2

sources.claim: Flexible (non-canonical) partitioning and re-unitising underpin place-value problem solving.
sources.source: NCETM Primary Mastery PD: Place Value (Spine 1)

pedagogy.summary: At 10-11 representation fluency reaches its primary ceiling and turns toward algebra: a child translates a word problem into an algebraic equation AND a bar model, plots table data on a coordinate grid and interprets the relationship, and explains how a pie chart, a fraction and a percentage all show the same proportion (CCSS MP2). Two threads from the verified bank become load-bearing. First, the bar model is now explicitly a precursor to algebra (NCETM): the same part-whole/scaling structure that sized a bar now sizes an equation with a letter for the unknown. Second, the equals sign becomes decisive for algebra — Falkner, Levi & Carpenter show with 4x + 27 = 87 that a child who reads '=' as 'do the calculation' cannot understand why you subtract 27 from both sides, and can only memorise rules to misapply; a RELATIONAL '=' (the two sides name the same amount) is what lets a word problem become a solvable equation. Proportion equivalence (pie chart = fraction = percentage) extends the fraction–decimal–percentage identity of the previous level to a new representation.
bestPractices: Build algebra on the bar model: represent 'a number ×4, add 27, gives 87' as a bar with an unknown part, then as 4x + 27 = 87, mapping each symbol to the bar (NCETM precursor-to-algebra)

Insist on a RELATIONAL equals sign for solving — the two sides are the same amount, so you may do the same to both — not '= means work out the left side'; this is the documented key to moving from arithmetic to algebra (Falkner/Levi/Carpenter)
Ground proportion equivalence: show a pie chart, a fraction and a percentage of the same whole and require the child to explain why they represent one proportion
For coordinate grids, name what each axis and each point's coordinates MEAN in the situation before reading a relationship (MP2 meaning-of-quantities)
Translate in all directions among situation, bar, equation, table, grid and chart, explaining connections at each step
keyRepresentations: Bar model with a labelled unknown mapped to an algebraic equation
Algebraic equation (e.g. 4x + 27 = 87) read relationally as a balance
Coordinate grid plotting ordered pairs from a table
Pie chart / fraction / percentage showing one proportion of a whole
commonMisconceptions: Reads '=' in an equation as 'work out the left-hand side' (operational), so cannot justify doing the same operation to both sides
Treats a bar model and an algebraic equation as unrelated — can draw one but not see it as the other's structure
Treats a pie chart, fraction and percentage as different things rather than one proportion of the whole
Reverses coordinates or reads a point's value without connecting it to the quantity the axis represents

learn.summary: For learners aged 10-11, this guidance builds the bridge from arithmetic representation fluency to algebra. Three connected objectives: (1) translate a word problem into BOTH a bar model with a labelled unknown AND an algebraic equation (e.g. 4x + 27 = 87, where x = 15), mapping each symbol to each part of the bar; (2) read the equals sign RELATIONALLY — the two sides name the same amount, so you may do the same operation to both — rather than as 'work out the left-hand side'; (3) explain why a pie chart, a fraction and a percentage that show the same portion of the same whole all represent one proportion. A supporting objective is plotting ordered pairs from a table onto a coordinate grid and stating what each axis and point MEANS in the situation before reading the relationship. The relational equals sign is the load-bearing idea: research on children's understanding of equality (e.g. Falkner, Levi & Carpenter) reports that many learners read '=' as 'do the calculation'; that reading gives no reason for subtracting 27 from both sides, so learners who hold it may fall back on memorised rules that they can misapply.

activities.title: Build the bar, build the equation, balance it
feedback: If the learner writes the equation but cannot locate x or +27 in the bar, overlay the two and ask 'where is the x in your bar? where is the 27-block?' until each symbol maps to a part.
If the learner subtracts 27 from only one side, ask what happens to the balance — the two sides no longer name the same amount, so the equation is no longer true.
If the learner recites 'move the 27 over, change the sign' without a reason, ask them to justify it using the balance idea: both sides must stay equal.
Target feedback at relational equality and the bar-to-equation mapping, not only at reaching the number for x.
activities.rationale: The bar model is a precursor to symbolic algebra: the same part-whole/scaling structure that sizes a bar sizes an equation with a letter for the unknown. A relational understanding of '=' is a documented foundation for moving from arithmetic to algebra; without it learners tend to rely on memorised solving rules. Constructing both representations and justifying the both-sides move targets this productive core.
sourceClaims: The bar model is a precursor to symbolic algebra: it represents unknowns and exposes the structure that an equation encodes, so a situation can be shown as both a bar and an algebraic equation.

A relational understanding of '=' is a major foundation for algebra: with 4x + 27 = 87, students who see '=' only as 'do something' cannot understand why one subtracts 27 from both sides and can only memorise rules to misapply; understanding '=' as expressing that both sides are the same is what enables equation solving.
learnerActions: Take the word problem: 'I think of a number, multiply by 4, add 27, and get 87.'
Draw a bar model: four equal unknown parts plus a 27-block, all equal in length to an 87-bar.
Write the matching equation 4x + 27 = 87 beneath, and point to where the x, the +27 and the 87 each appear in the bar.

Treat the equation as a balance with two equal sides. Try removing 27 from only one side and say what would go wrong; then remove 27 from BOTH sides (leaving 4x = 60) and explain why the two sides stay equal.
State in your own words why '=' lets you do the same thing to both sides, and finish solving (4x = 60, so x = 15).

If a dynamic model is available, size an unknown bar and watch the equation assemble; in a balance-beam mode, removing weight (such as the 27) from only one pan tips the beam, so removing it from both becomes a felt necessity, and the 27 vanishing on both sides at once mirrors the equation step.
activities.intendedInsight: A bar model and an algebraic equation are the same structure in two forms; the equals sign is a promise that both sides are the same amount, which is exactly why you may apply the same operation to both sides.

activities.title: Argue a classmate out of the operational equals sign
feedback: If the learner merely repeats the rule, prompt: 'Your partner still thinks = means compute the left side — what reason convinces them you can operate on both sides?'
If the learner says the three proportion forms are different, have them show all three on the same whole and name the shared amount.
Reward reasoning that names 'both sides are the same amount' and 'one proportion of the same whole', not just the final verdict.
activities.rationale: Justifying why you may subtract 27 from both sides, and why a pie chart, a fraction and a percentage of the same whole are one proportion, is well suited to dialogue; voicing the operational-equals error and having the learner refute it can surface the relational meaning. This is offered as one effective option, not the only route to the insight.
sourceClaims: A relational understanding of '=' is a major foundation for algebra: with 4x + 27 = 87, students who see '=' only as 'do something' cannot understand why one subtracts 27 from both sides and can only memorise rules to misapply; understanding '=' as expressing that both sides are the same is what enables equation solving.
Fractions, decimals and percentages of the same whole represent one quantity in different forms; equivalence should be understood as sameness of magnitude/proportion.
learnerActions: Respond to a partner (real or role-played) who claims: '= just means work out 4x + 27, and the answer is 87.'
Explain why that reading breaks down when you need to solve for x, using the balance idea that both sides name the same amount.

Respond to the same partner, who points to a pie slice that is 40% of the whole and claims '40% is a different thing from that pie slice' — argue why the slice, the fraction 2/5 (40/100) and 40% of the same whole are one proportion.
Keep the exchange as justification, not a scored answer: push every assertion to a reason.
activities.intendedInsight: Relational equality and proportion equivalence become more convincing when you have to defend them against a plausible wrong view, not just assert them.

activities.title: One proportion, three pictures
feedback: If the learner converts by rule but calls the forms 'different', ask them to point to the same whole in each and name the single proportion.
If the learner reverses or mislabels a percentage, return to the shaded whole and count the proportion directly before converting.
activities.rationale: Proportion equivalence extends the fraction–decimal–percentage identity to the pie-chart representation; when comparing represented portions, equivalence is sameness of magnitude for the same whole, which requires explaining the shared whole, not just converting by rule.
sourceClaims: Fractions, decimals and percentages of the same whole represent one quantity in different forms; equivalence should be understood as sameness of magnitude/proportion.
learnerActions: Look at a pie chart with one quarter shaded.
State the fraction (1/4) and the percentage (25%) it represents.
Explain whether these are the same amount or three different things, pointing to the same whole in each form.
Repeat with another proportion of your choice, converting among pie chart, fraction and percentage and justifying the shared magnitude.
If a linked display is available, change one form (e.g. drag the pie slice) and watch the fraction and percentage update together.
activities.intendedInsight: A pie chart, a fraction and a percentage are different representations of one proportion of the same whole, not three separate quantities.

activities.title: Plot the table and say what the points mean
feedback: If the learner reverses coordinates, re-read the axes' meanings and re-place the point so it matches the situation.
If the learner reads a value without connecting it to the quantity, ask 'what does that number stand for here?' before describing the relationship.
activities.rationale: Attending to the meaning of quantities across representations (decontextualising into symbols and recontextualising by probing referents) is the reasoning target; naming axis and point meaning before reading a relationship enacts it.
sourceClaims: MP2: decontextualize a situation into symbols and contextualize by probing referents; attend to the meaning of quantities across representations.
learnerActions: Take a small table of paired values and plot each pair as an ordered point on a coordinate grid.
Before reading any relationship, name what the horizontal axis means and what the vertical axis means in the situation.
For one point, say what its two coordinates MEAN (e.g. 'at 3 hours the cost is £12'), not just the numbers.
Describe the relationship you see between the quantities, in words tied to the situation.
Check for reversed coordinates by asking whether the point lands where that situation should put it.
activities.intendedInsight: A coordinate point carries situational meaning: naming what each axis and coordinate represents is what turns plotted dots into an interpretable relationship.

constraints: The equation should be CONSTRUCTED and the both-sides step JUSTIFIED by the learner; recognition-only tasks (e.g. 'which equation matches the bar?') can check a match but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of the translation or the relational explanation, so use them only as a warm-up.

A static, tap-to-reveal set linking story, bar, equation and chart can illustrate the connections but cannot let the learner operate on a balance or plot points; treat it as a worked-example scaffold, not the productive activity.

When describing the balance, the required move is to keep the two sides equal (do the same to both); do not let a learner finish having only chanted 'move it over, change the sign' without the balance reason.
For the coordinate work, require the situational meaning of axes and coordinates before any relationship is read, to prevent number-reading without interpretation.

Dynamic recolouring, balance-beam tipping, draggable bars and linked updating displays are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete; they are helpful illustrations, not mandatory, and the reasoning can also be done on paper.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support the underlying teaching principle rather than proving any specific activity was tested.

Arithmetic self-check: 4 × 15 = 60 (partial products 40 + 20), and 60 + 27 = 87, so x = 15 is consistent; the '60' here is the correct value of 4x, not an error. The equation 4x + 27 = 87 is internally sound.

On source scope: the Falkner/Levi/Carpenter claim is attached to the dialogue activity because it supports the relational-equality CONTENT being argued, not because the source endorses dialogue as a medium; efficacy of the dialogic route is stated as proposed/one option, not established.

The source materials lean toward strong single-format and necessity claims (e.g. that an operational equals sign 'cannot' justify both-sides operations, that scored items reward rule-following, that a dynamic linker is uniquely suited). The 'cannot justify' finding is a documented misconception pattern from Falkner/Levi/Carpenter and is stated here as such; the comparative/necessity and medium-superiority framings are not established as universal laws by the cited sources and are retained only as narrowly scoped design observations with stated affordances and limits.
The partner/dialogue activity and the static-linked-set scaffold are preserved as genuine alternatives with distinct purposes, not as inferior copies of one preferred format.

probeDeeper: 'If the equals sign just meant "work out the left side", how would you explain what to do with 4x + 27 = 87? Does that story break down?'
'Point to the x in your bar model. Where is the +27? Where is the 87?'
'Why is it fair to subtract 27 from BOTH sides — what would go wrong if you only did it to one?'
'A pie chart shows one quarter shaded. What fraction and percentage is that — and are they the same amount or three different ones?'
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child rejecting the operational reading and treating '=' relationally (the two sides are the same amount), mapping the word problem to both a bar with an unknown part and 4x + 27 = 87, and justifying 'subtract 27 from both sides' by the balance idea (keeping the two sides equal) rather than by a memorised rule.

errorPatterns.pattern: Operational equals sign blocking algebra: reads '=' as 'compute the left side; the answer follows', so cannot justify operating on both sides — can only memorise rules for solving equations (the documented arithmetic→algebra stumbling block).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild '=' as balance with true/false and open sentences and a balance-beam model until 'same amount both sides' is felt; then re-derive 'subtract from both sides' from it. Reteach in place — relational equality is the new work here.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child endorses 'work out 4x + 27', or 'solves' by a chanted rule ('take 27 over, change the sign') with no reason; can't say why both sides get the same treatment.

errorPatterns.pattern: Bar model and algebraic equation treated as unrelated: can draw the bar or write the equation but not see them as the same structure, so the translation is mechanical.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay the bar and the equation, mapping each part to each symbol ('where is the x in your bar?'); reteach representation fluency connecting bar/equation across situations.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Produces one representation but can't map the unknown part of the bar to the x, or the 27-block to the +27; treats them as two separate tasks.

errorPatterns.pattern: Proportion equivalence not seen: treats a pie chart, a fraction and a percentage of the same whole as different quantities.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show all three on the same whole and require the child to justify the shared proportion; reteach fraction–decimal–percentage equivalence as one magnitude.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the pie slice, the fraction and the percentage are 'different', or can convert by rule but not explain they are one proportion of the whole.

responseLevels.gap: Endorses 'work out the left side', or solves by a rule with no reason; can't connect the bar to the equation or justify operating on both sides.
responseLevels.full: Rejects the operational reading, maps the word problem to both a bar (unknown part) and 4x + 27 = 87, justifies subtracting 27 from both sides by keeping the two equal sides balanced, and explains pie chart/fraction/percentage as one proportion — transferring the relational-equality reasoning to a new equation unprompted.
responseLevels.partial: Produces the bar and the equation, or rejects the operational reading, but can't fully justify 'both sides' by the balance idea — lists the solving steps without the relational reason; or maps bar↔equation but wavers on proportion equivalence.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A classmate is solving 4x + 27 = 87. They say: 'The equals sign means work out 4x + 27, and the answer is 87.' First: do you agree that's what the equals sign is telling us here? Then take this problem — 'I think of a number, multiply it by 4, add 27, and get 87' — show it as a bar model AND as an equation, and explain why you're allowed to subtract 27 from both sides.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with a relational equals sign explains that both sides name the same quantity, so any operation must be done to both to keep them equal; a child with an operational view thinks '=' announces the answer and can only recite 'move the 27 over' without saying why. The prompt is hard to fake: the bar model plus the both-sides justification requires the relational meaning, and a child who truly holds it cannot endorse 'work out the left side'.

sources.claim: MP2: decontextualize a situation into symbols and contextualize by probing referents; attend to the meaning of quantities across representations.
sources.source: CCSS Standards for Mathematical Practice, MP2

sources.claim: The bar model is a precursor to symbolic algebra: it represents unknowns and exposes the structure that an equation encodes, so a situation can be shown as both a bar and an algebraic equation.
sources.source: NCETM, 'The Bar Model'

sources.claim: A relational understanding of '=' is a major foundation for algebra: with 4x + 27 = 87, students who see '=' only as 'do something' cannot understand why one subtracts 27 from both sides and can only memorise rules to misapply; understanding '=' as expressing that both sides are the same is what enables equation solving.
sources.source: Falkner, Levi & Carpenter (1999), Children's Understanding of Equality: A Foundation for Algebra, Teaching Children Mathematics 6(4)

sources.claim: Fractions, decimals and percentages of the same whole represent one quantity in different forms; equivalence should be understood as sameness of magnitude/proportion.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 6–8 (REPRESENTATIONAL): identify, represent and ESTIMATE numbers using different representations — objects, base-ten blocks, drawings, place-value charts and especially the NUMBER LINE — and move flexibly between them.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1–Y3): 'identify and represent numbers using objects and pictorial representations including the number line' (Y1), and 'identify, represent and estimate numbers using different representations' (Y2, Y3).
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.MD.6 (number line as a measurement/position model), 1.NBT/2.NBT representations; the number line as a representation of magnitude runs throughout.
• Operational details — the core is REPRESENTATIONAL FLEXIBILITY: the same number can appear as a set, base-ten blocks, a point on a number line, a numeral, or an expanded form, and the child translates between them. ESTIMATION on a number line (roughly where does 47 sit on 0–100? about how many in this pile?) develops magnitude/number sense, not just exact counting. The number line is the load-bearing representation — it encodes order AND relative size.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 6): place a two-digit number on a 0–100 line in roughly the right position. Tier B (7): represent the same number with base-ten blocks, a number line and a drawing; match a base-ten picture to its numeral. Tier C (7–8): estimate where a three-digit number falls on a 0–1000 line and estimate 'about how many' in a set without counting.
bestPractices: Deliberately represent the SAME number many ways (set, base-ten blocks, number line point, numeral, expanded form) and have children translate between them — representational flexibility, not one favourite model, is the goal.

Use the number line as the anchor representation for MAGNITUDE and estimation: 'about where does 47 go?' builds the sense that numbers have relative size and order, feeding later rounding and decimals.
Teach estimation as a valued skill in its own right ('about how many', 'roughly where') with landmarks/benchmarks (0, 50, 100; halfway) rather than treating every task as exact counting.
Use empty/partially-marked number lines so children reason from benchmarks rather than counting every interval — a key step toward proportional placement.
Connect base-ten-block representations to the place-value the blocks encode (tens rods, ones cubes) so 'representing' reinforces, not bypasses, place value.
keyRepresentations: Number line (marked, then empty with benchmarks) for position, order and estimation of magnitude.
Base-ten blocks (hundreds flats, tens rods, ones cubes) for the same number.
Place-value chart / arrow cards and expanded form (247 = 200 + 40 + 7).
A 'same number, many faces' board linking set ↔ blocks ↔ line ↔ numeral ↔ words.
commonMisconceptions: Treating the representations as unrelated (can build 34 with blocks but can't place it on a line).
Placing numbers on a line by counting marks only, ignoring proportional spacing (47 put just past 0, or bunched near a benchmark).
Believing estimation is 'wrong maths' — wanting to count exactly instead of judging 'about how many/where'.
Misusing an empty number line by assuming equal gaps where none are marked, or ignoring the scale.
Reading base-ten blocks by counting every cube rather than using the tens/hundreds units.

learn.summary: For ages 6–8: children identify, represent and estimate whole numbers across several linked representations — sets of objects, base-ten blocks, drawings, place-value charts, expanded form, numerals and especially the number line — and translate flexibly between them. The number line anchors magnitude and order, supporting benchmark-based estimation ('about where does 47 go?', 'about how many in this pile?') rather than exact counting alone. Progression runs from placing a two-digit number on a 0–100 line (Tier A, age 6), to representing one number as blocks, a line point and a drawing and matching a base-ten picture to its numeral (Tier B, age 7), to estimating a three-digit number on a 0–1000 line and 'about how many' in a set without counting (Tier C, 7–8).

activities.title: Many faces of the same number
feedback: If a child can build 34 with blocks but not place it on a line, pause on translating just those two forms: build 34, then point to roughly where it sits and check they agree.
When blocks and numeral disagree, ask them to recount by tens and ones (rods then cubes) rather than counting every single cube.
Praise correct translations by naming the link: 'Three tens-rods and four cubes IS 34 IS 30 + 4.'

If an interactive linker is available, the optional live cross-updating (change the numeral and watch the blocks, expanded form and line point shift together) makes the 'same number' idea visible; a tap-to-reveal poster showing one number five ways is a lower-tech alternative.
activities.rationale: Representational flexibility — translating the same number across forms, not favouring one model — is the core objective at this stage, and connecting base-ten blocks to the tens/ones they encode keeps representation tied to place value.
sourceClaims: Pupils identify and represent numbers using objects and pictorial representations including the number line, and identify, represent and estimate numbers using different representations.
learnerActions: Pick a number (e.g. 247) and build it several ways: a set or base-ten blocks (2 hundreds flats, 4 tens rods, 7 ones cubes), the numeral 247, the expanded form 200 + 40 + 7, and words.
Place that same number as a point on a number line.
Change one representation and update all the others to match so they always show the same quantity (e.g. add one tens rod to make 257, then fix the numeral, the expanded form and the line point).
Say aloud why these are all the 'same number wearing different clothes'.
Match a mixed set of base-ten pictures to their numerals and to the matching words.
activities.intendedInsight: A single number can appear as a set, base-ten blocks, a point on a number line, a numeral, expanded form or words, and you can translate between them because they all encode the same quantity.

activities.title: Estimate on a benchmarked number line
feedback: If a child counts tick marks or crowds larger numbers toward one end, do not mark positions 'wrong' — linear number-line sense matures with benchmark practice. Keep offering 0/50/100 anchoring and estimation talk.
If they use only the endpoints with no middle reference, establish the midpoint first: find or fold to 50, then reason that 40 sits a little to its left.
Probe with: 'Where would 50 go? How do you know that's the middle?' and 'You placed 40 there — is it nearer 0 or nearer 100?'
Check consistency across representations: 'Show me 40 with base-ten blocks, then point to it on the line — do they agree?'
Check scale awareness: 'If the line went 0 to 1000 instead of 0 to 100, would 40 sit in the same place? Why not?'
A correct response reads the mark as about 70 by proportion (past the middle, most of the way to 100) and places 40 a little below the halfway point, using 0, 50 and 100 as benchmarks.

If a drag-and-drop estimation tool is available, an optional feedback band showing how close the placement is rewards proportional reasoning over mark-counting; the same judgement can be practised on paper with a pencil placement and a reveal of the true position.
activities.rationale: The number line carries both order and relative size, and benchmark-based placement rather than counting every mark develops magnitude sense that later supports rounding and decimals. Early estimates are often compressed, so this is developmental practice, not error to be drilled out.
sourceClaims: The number line is a load-bearing representation for magnitude and estimation; benchmark-based placement (rather than counting every mark) develops number sense and underpins later rounding and decimals.
Pupils represent whole numbers as lengths/points on a number line diagram with equally spaced points corresponding to the numbers.
learnerActions: On a 0–100 line marked only with 0, 50 and 100, place a given number such as 47 or 68 in roughly the right position.
Before placing, decide whether the number is below or above the halfway mark (50) and how far.
Read a mark already placed on a 0–100 line labelled only at its ends (0 and 100, no interior marks) — e.g. a mark at about 70 — and say what number it shows and how you decided.
Scale up: on a 0–1000 line with 0, 500 and 1000 marked, place a three-digit number by proportion.
Explain your placement using the benchmarks: 'past the middle, most of the way to 100.'
activities.intendedInsight: Numbers have relative size and order; you can locate them by reasoning proportionally from benchmarks (0, 50, 100; halfway) instead of counting every tick mark.

activities.title: About how many? — estimating set size
feedback: If a child insists on counting every object, affirm that counting is useful but set a short time or hide the set so they must judge magnitude instead.
Encourage anchoring: 'This looks like about three groups of ten, so around thirty.'
Treat any estimate inside a reasonable band as a success and name the reasoning, not just the number.
activities.rationale: Some children believe estimation is 'wrong maths' and want to count exactly; teaching estimation as a skill in its own right, with benchmarks, builds number sense.
sourceClaims: Pupils identify and represent numbers using objects and pictorial representations including the number line, and identify, represent and estimate numbers using different representations.
learnerActions: Look at a pile or set of 30–50 objects for only a brief moment (too briefly to count every one).
Give a sensible estimate of 'about how many', and say what helped you judge (e.g. comparing to a known group of ten).
Compare your estimate to the actual count and reflect on how close it was.
Discuss that a good estimate within a sensible range is valuable maths, not 'wrong' because it is not exact.
activities.intendedInsight: Estimating 'about how many' is a real, valued skill: judging magnitude quickly using benchmarks is different from, and complements, exact counting.

constraints: A tap-to-reveal poster or a static 'same number five ways' display is a useful reference for the links between representations, but on its own it does not give placement or estimation practice; pair it with actual line placement and 'about how many' tasks.

A slider or matching quiz (place a number on a line, match blocks to numeral, choose an estimate for a flashed set) is suitable for checking representational links and estimation, but recognition/selection responses do not by themselves elicit the independent construction of a number across forms — include tasks where the child builds and translates representations.
Keep base-ten work tied to place value: children should read rods and flats as tens and hundreds, not count every unit cube.

Number lines used for placement and estimation must show their endpoints (e.g. 0–100 or 0–1000) and be drawn to a uniform scale, so equal distances stand for equal differences even where no interior marks are drawn; children should check whether the line runs to 100 or 1000. Open 'empty' number lines used for jottings are not drawn to scale, so do not use them for proportional estimation.

Early number-line estimates are commonly uneven: small numbers are spread too far apart and larger numbers are crowded together toward the upper end. Treat this as developmental and respond with benchmark practice, not by marking placements wrong.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original row marked one source (DfE National Curriculum) as verified and two (CCSS-M 2.MD.6; NCETM guidance) as not verified; the NCETM claim about the number line being 'load-bearing' and underpinning later rounding/decimals reflects legacy guidance and has not been independently confirmed here.

The CCSS 2.MD.6 'equally spaced points' claim supports numbers being represented as points/lengths on a line but not the benchmark-without-counting emphasis; NCETM is the primary support for the proportional-estimation principle.

The source labelled some artefact formats 'poor fit' (open dialogue, 3D) with claims such as '3D adds nothing' and that dialogue 'adds little'; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the evidence and have been dropped rather than propagated. Spoken estimation talk and discussion are retained as useful feedback.

The original claim that an act-and-see-it-update loop 'builds exactly what a static chart cannot' is a catalog preference, not an established efficacy finding; interactive cross-updating is offered here as an optional affordance, not a necessity.

The examples are arithmetically correct: 247 = 200 + 40 + 7 (2 flats, 4 rods, 7 cubes), 247 + 10 = 257, 34 = 30 + 4, and 40 sitting a little below the 50 benchmark. No arithmetic errors found in the source or rewritten examples.

probeDeeper: Where would 50 go? How do you know that's the middle?
You placed 40 there — is it nearer 0 or nearer 100?
Show me 40 with base-ten blocks, then point to it on the line — do they agree?
If the line went 0 to 1000 instead of 0 to 100, would 40 sit in the same place? Why not?
assess.correctAnswer: Reads the mark as about 70 by proportion (past the middle, most of the way to 100) and places 40 a little below the halfway point, using 0, 50 and 100 as benchmarks.

errorPatterns.pattern: Places numbers by counting tick-marks or bunches larger numbers together, treating the line as evenly-spaced steps rather than proportional distance (early estimates are compressed / logarithmic)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill exact positions or mark placements 'wrong' — linear number-line sense matures with benchmark practice, not correction. Keep offering 0/50/100 anchoring games and estimation talk.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child crowds numbers toward one end, or counts ticks to place 40 regardless of where 50 would be.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses only the endpoints with no interior benchmark, so placement is a rough guess with no sense of the middle
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish the midpoint first: fold/find 50, then reason 40 is a little to its left. Build the halfway benchmark before fine placement.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child never references 50; places 40 near an end or arbitrarily.

responseLevels.gap: Reads/places numbers by counting ticks or bunching, with no proportional sense of magnitude.
responseLevels.full: Reads and places numbers using 0/50/100 benchmarks and proportion, and translates the same number across number line, base-ten blocks, and numeral.
responseLevels.partial: Uses the endpoints to place roughly but without anchoring on the midpoint (50), so estimates are unreliable.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a 0–100 number line with a single mark placed at about 70 (only 0 and 100 labelled). Ask: 'What number does this mark show, and how did you decide?' Then give a blank 0–100 line and say: 'Now mark where 40 would go.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Reading a mark AND then producing one, on an unlabelled line, shows whether the child treats the line as proportional magnitude (anchoring on the midpoint) or as ordinal steps to be counted. Translating the same number to base-ten blocks checks the representation is connected to quantity, not just position.

pedagogy.summary: Understanding positive and negative numbers as quantities with opposite DIRECTIONS about a meaningful zero, and operating on them using number-line reasoning. The number line (or thermometer / floors-in-a-building / bank balance) is the central representation: a number's sign is its direction from zero and its magnitude is its distance. Adding a positive moves right/up, adding a negative moves left/down, and subtracting a negative reverses that to move right — so 'subtracting a negative is the same as adding' is derived from direction, not memorised. The recurring difficulty is distinguishing the two meanings of the minus symbol: the sign OF a number versus the operation of subtraction.
bestPractices: Anchor every idea on a number line / thermometer where zero is a real reference (freezing point, ground floor, break-even), not 'nothing'
Keep magnitude (distance from zero) and sign (direction) as separate ideas - counter 'bigger digit = bigger number' for negatives
Use directed-journey language: adding a negative is a move in the negative direction; subtracting a negative reverses direction
Distinguish the operation minus from the negative sign explicitly (colour, gesture, or bracket: 4 + (-7))
Derive 'subtract a negative = add' on the line (removing a debt / turning to face the other way) rather than stating a rule
keyRepresentations: Horizontal number line spanning zero (arrows for direction and length)
Vertical thermometer / floors of a building / sea level
Bank balance and debt (money owed as negative)
Two-colour counters (zero pairs) for combining opposites
commonMisconceptions: Orders negatives by magnitude - thinks -7 > -3 because 7 > 3
Conflates the negative sign with the subtraction operation ('two minuses', reads 4 + (-7) as 4 - 7 or 4 + 7 arbitrarily)
Believes numbers 'stop' at zero, so cannot count or move through zero
Thinks subtracting always makes smaller and adding always makes bigger (fails for negatives)
Treats 'subtract a negative' as more negative rather than as reversing direction

learn.summary: Positive and negative numbers are quantities with opposite DIRECTIONS from a meaningful zero (freezing point, ground floor, break-even), where sign is direction and magnitude is distance. On a number line, adding a positive moves right/up, adding a negative moves left/down, and subtracting a negative reverses direction to move right/up — so 'subtracting a negative is the same as adding' is derived from the direction of travel, not memorised as a sign rule. The central difficulty is distinguishing the two meanings of the minus symbol: the sign OF a number versus the operation of subtraction. Learners should both READ arrows/journeys and PRODUCE their own for new signed calculations, including moves straight through zero.

activities.title: Operate a directed number line: fire and flip the arrow
feedback: If the 1 - (-3) arrow is drawn moving LEFT to -2 ('subtracting a negative makes it more negative'): model on the line and with debt — subtracting a negative reverses direction (removing a -3 is adding 3); walk the arrow flip physically.
If 4 + (-7) is drawn rightward or read as 4 - 7 or 4 + 7: separate 'negative seven' (a directed quantity) from 'subtract' (a move) using brackets, colour and gesture for the two roles.
If the arrow halts at zero: continue the thermometer/lift below zero and count aloud through it (2, 1, 0, -1, -2).
activities.rationale: An operable line where the learner chooses the calculation and watches direction (sign) and length (magnitude) makes the structure of the move the object of attention, rather than a sign rule applied by habit. NCETM advises examining the STRUCTURE of the calculation rather than teaching sign rules; standards frame p+q as a distance |q| from p in a direction set by the sign, and p-q as adding the additive inverse. The through-zero journey for 4 + (-7) (passing 2, 1, 0, -1, -2 on the way to -3) covers an interval across 0 (7 units from 4 to -3), which links to the Year 6 statutory wording on intervals across zero; the 1 - (-3) journey does not cross zero. This is a research-informed design proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Pupils 'understand p + q as the number located a distance |q| from p, in the positive or negative direction depending on whether q is positive or negative' and 'understand subtraction of rational numbers as adding the additive inverse, p - q = p + (-q)', representing these on a horizontal or vertical number line (7.NS.A.1b, 1c).

Hart (1981)/CSMS records that when subtracting a positive integer many students 'simply subtract the numerals and then attempt to determine the sign for the answer', and when subtracting a negative use the rule 'two negatives make a positive'; the misconception is rooted in prior experience that 'addition makes larger and subtraction makes smaller', which breaks down for negatives. NCETM advises examining the STRUCTURE of the calculation rather than teaching sign rules.
Year 6 pupils 'use negative numbers in context, and calculate intervals across 0' (Year 6 Number - number and place value, verbatim statutory wording).
learnerActions: Enter 4 + (-7): start a marker at 4 and draw/trace an arrow 7 units LEFT, landing on -3 — state that the negative sign IS the leftward direction and the 7 is how far.
Enter 1 - (-3): show that the arrow subtraction would send LEFT instead FLIPS to point RIGHT, landing on 4; compare with adding 3 (1 + 3 = 4) and confirm you land in the same place.
Say in words why the arrow reversed: removing a -3 (e.g. clearing a debt of 3) is the same as adding 3.

Replay both journeys vertically on a thermometer/lift mode: for 4 + (-7), count aloud straight down through zero (4, 3, 2, 1, 0, -1, -2, -3); for 1 - (-3), count up from 1 (2, 3, 4) and notice that this journey stays above zero.
activities.intendedInsight: Signed addition and the direction-reversal of subtracting a negative become visible: 'two minuses make a plus' is a direction reversal you can see, not a spell to recall. Numbers do not stop at zero.

activities.title: Zero in context and the two minus signs
feedback: If zero is described as 'nothing': re-anchor on a real context where below-zero values exist (temperature, basement floors, debt).
If the two minus signs are conflated: name 'negative seven' (a directed quantity) separately from 'subtract' (a move), and re-read the calculation aloud with that distinction.
activities.rationale: A fixed reference display supports reading direction, zero-in-context and the sign/operation distinction. It is a reference scaffold: it does not animate a calculation the learner chooses, so it complements rather than replaces the operable line, and it does not by itself show the learner can produce a move.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils 'use negative numbers in context, and calculate intervals across 0' (Year 6 Number - number and place value, verbatim statutory wording).
learnerActions: On a labelled reference line/thermometer, point to a value and state both its sign (direction from zero) and its distance from zero.
Switch contexts (temperature, floors of a building, bank balance) and say what zero means in each (freezing point, ground floor, break-even — not 'nothing').
For a written calculation like 4 + (-7), mark which minus is the negative SIGN of a number and which (if any) is the subtraction OPERATION; use brackets/colour to keep them apart.
activities.intendedInsight: Zero is a meaningful reference point, and the minus symbol carries two distinct meanings that must be read, not guessed.

activities.title: Place, order and interpret signed calculations
feedback: If -7 is placed to the RIGHT of -3 (ordering by magnitude, treating -7 as greater): use the thermometer/line — left of zero is less, and the further left the smaller; contrast -7 and -3 directly.
If the given arrow's calculation is misread: separate direction (sign) from length (magnitude) explicitly and re-read the endpoints.
activities.rationale: Placing, ordering and reading signed calculations target the 'bigger digit = bigger number' error directly and rehearse separating sign from magnitude. The interpret action reads an interval across zero, which the Year 6 statutory wording supports; the ordering focus rests on the separated-ideas teaching principle rather than on that claim. Include a deliberate magnitude-ordering contrast such as -7 versus -3.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils 'use negative numbers in context, and calculate intervals across 0' (Year 6 Number - number and place value, verbatim statutory wording).
learnerActions: Place -7 and -3 on a number line and state which is smaller, explaining via position (the further left, the smaller).
Order a set of negatives from least to greatest.

Interpret a given arrow (e.g. starting at -3, ending at 2): state the calculation it shows (-3 + 5 = 2, or the difference 2 - (-3) = 5, an interval across 0) and what its direction and length tell you.
Decide and justify which way 1 - (-3) moves before drawing it.
activities.intendedInsight: Ordering by position (not by digit size) and reading an arrow's direction and length consolidate that magnitude and sign are separate ideas.

activities.title: Talk through the two meanings of minus
feedback: If the learner says subtracting always sends you left: revisit 1 - (-3) on the line and the debt model to show the reversal.
If the two minuses are described as the same thing: re-draw the calculation distinguishing the directed quantity from the move.
activities.rationale: A probing discussion can surface the two-meanings-of-minus confusion and whether the learner reasons about direction or guesses; it works best alongside the line, where the directional insight is seen, rather than in place of it. Discussion can elicit explanation but does not itself show the learner can construct an arrow for a new calculation.
sourceClaims: Hart (1981)/CSMS records that when subtracting a positive integer many students 'simply subtract the numerals and then attempt to determine the sign for the answer', and when subtracting a negative use the rule 'two negatives make a positive'; the misconception is rooted in prior experience that 'addition makes larger and subtraction makes smaller', which breaks down for negatives. NCETM advises examining the STRUCTURE of the calculation rather than teaching sign rules.
learnerActions: Answer: what is the difference between the minus in 'negative three' and the minus in 'subtract three'?
Explain which way your arrow for 4 + (-7) went and why.
Answer: does subtracting always send you left? What did 1 - (-3) do, and why?
Explain, using the line, which is bigger, -7 or -3.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the two roles of the minus symbol and justifying arrow direction surfaces and tests understanding beyond a correct final answer.

constraints: Anchor every idea on a number line/thermometer/floors/balance where zero is a real reference (freezing point, ground floor, break-even), not 'nothing'.
Keep magnitude (distance from zero) and sign (direction) as separate ideas; counter 'bigger digit = bigger number' for negatives.
Use directed-journey language: adding a negative moves in the negative direction; subtracting a negative reverses direction (right/up on the chosen axis).
Explicitly distinguish the subtraction operation from the negative sign using colour, gesture, or brackets, e.g. 4 + (-7).
Derive 'subtract a negative = add' on the line (removing a debt / turning to face the other way) rather than stating it as a rule.
A fixed reference poster/line supports reading sign, magnitude and zero-in-context but does not animate a learner-chosen operation; use it to complement, not replace, learner production of arrows.

Recognition/placement tasks (ordering, selecting a direction) do not by themselves show the learner can PRODUCE an arrow for a new signed calculation; include tasks where the learner constructs the move themselves.
Two-colour counters (zero pairs) are a useful alternative representation for combining opposites and may be offered alongside the line.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched and legacy 'verified'/'confidence' flags are not independently confirmed. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated a genuine third spatial dimension as adding nothing over a 2D vertical thermometer/lift. This is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law; it is framed here only as a scope note (directed number is one-dimensional, so a vertical 2D thermometer/lift already represents that single directed axis) rather than a universal 'adds nothing' claim.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 4 + (-7) = -3 (7 left of 4); 1 - (-3) = 4 (reverse to move 3 right from 1, matching 1 + 3); -3 + 5 = 2 and 2 - (-3) = 5 — all consistent across the source fields and retained as stated.
The debt analogy ('removing a -3 is the same as adding 3') is a model of direction reversal, not a proof; present it as an illustration alongside the line.

Activity 3's single source claim directly supports its interval-across-zero interpret action; the ordering/magnitude focus rests on the separated-ideas teaching principle rather than on that statutory wording. The Year 6 claim on activity 1 supports the through-zero counting action, not the sign/magnitude-separation principle.

probeDeeper: What is the difference between the minus in 'negative three' and the minus in 'subtract three'?
Your arrow for 4 + (-7) went which way, and why that way?
Does subtracting always send you left? What did 1 - (-3) do - and why?
On the line, which is bigger, -7 or -3, and how does the line show it?
assess.correctAnswer: Interpret: the arrow shows -3 + 5 = 2 (it points right/positive, so something is added; its length 5 is the amount, matching the distance from -3 to 2) - equivalently the difference 2 - (-3) = 5. Translate: 4 + (-7) starts at 4 and moves 7 LEFT to -3; 1 - (-3) reverses direction to move 3 RIGHT (subtracting a negative), landing on 4. Distinguishes the negative sign (direction/position) from the subtraction operation (a move).

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Subtracting a negative just makes it more negative' - draws 1 - (-3) moving LEFT, landing on -2
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model on the line/with debt: subtracting a negative reverses the direction (removing a -3 is the same as adding 3); walk the arrow flip physically.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The translate step: the 1 - (-3) arrow points the wrong way

errorPatterns.pattern: Conflates the negative sign with the subtraction operation - reads 4 + (-7) as 4 - 7 done arbitrarily, or as 4 + 7, unsure which minus is which
errorPatterns.nextMove: Explicitly separate 'negative seven' (a directed quantity) from 'subtract' (a move); use brackets, colour, and gesture for the two roles.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Misreads the calculation the given arrow shows, or draws 4 + (-7) rightward

errorPatterns.pattern: Orders negatives by magnitude, so places -7 to the RIGHT of -3 on the line
errorPatterns.nextMove: Thermometer / left-of-zero-is-less; the further left, the smaller; contrast -7 and -3 directly.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Endpoints placed wrongly; -7 treated as greater than -3

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes numbers 'stop' at zero, so an arrow crossing zero confuses or is halted there
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a thermometer/lift that continues below zero; count aloud through zero (2, 1, 0, -1, -2).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Arrow stops at 0, or the child cannot continue a move through zero

responseLevels.gap: Orders negatives by size, cannot cross zero, or draws arrows in the wrong direction; treats the two minus signs as the same thing.
responseLevels.full: Interprets and produces arrows for adding and subtracting both positive and negative numbers, articulates subtracting a negative as reversing direction (equivalent to adding), and transfers to a new case moving through zero.
responseLevels.partial: Interprets a given arrow correctly and places integers on the line, but cannot reliably PRODUCE an arrow for adding a negative or subtracting a negative - knows the pieces but cannot translate a new signed calculation onto the line.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: First, INTERPRET: here is a number line with an arrow that starts at -3 and ends at 2. What calculation does this arrow show, and what do its direction and length tell you? Then, TRANSLATE: on the number line, draw an arrow to show 4 + (-7) and say where you land; then draw one for 1 - (-3) and say where you land.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Reading the given arrow forces separating direction (sign) from length (magnitude). Producing an arrow for adding a negative (move left) versus subtracting a negative (move right) reveals whether the child understands subtracting-a-negative as a direction reversal or is guessing - and a child who conflates the operation minus with the negative sign draws 4 + (-7) or 1 - (-3) in the wrong direction. Interpreting then producing catches the child who can read a diagram but cannot build one for a new signed calculation.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 8-9. Find 1000 more or less than a number by recognising that only the thousands digit changes (4,562 → 5,562 / 3,562), extending the 10-more/100-more pattern to the next place — unless a boundary forces a roll-over (9,500 + 1000 = 10,500).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 4): count in multiples and find 1000 more or less than a given number (place-value fluency).
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): generalises 2.NBT.8 (±10/±100) into the thousands place; 4.NBT.1 place-value relationships.
• Operational details — Use a place-value chart / Gattegno chart so +1000 steps the thousands digit while others hold; connect to counting in 1000s on a number line. Contrast +10, +100, +1000 side by side so the child tracks which column responds. Teach the roll-over boundary explicitly. Demand the 'which digit changes' reasoning.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8, emerging): finds 1000 more/less with no boundary, using a chart. Tier B (age 8-9, secure): does it mentally, naming the thousands digit as the one that changes. Tier C (age 9, extending): handles roll-overs (9,500+1000) and generalises to numbers beyond 10,000.
bestPractices: Extend the established pattern: +1000 steps the thousands digit, others unchanged — keep asking 'which digit?'.
Contrast +10 / +100 / +1000 side by side so the child locates the responding column.
Use a Gattegno / place-value chart so one digit visibly changes per operation.
Teach roll-over boundaries (9,500 + 1000) as the interesting case.
Insist on place-value reasoning, not counting on, and generalise beyond 10,000.
keyRepresentations: Gattegno / place-value chart (thousands row)
Th|H|T|O place-value counters (add/remove one 1000)
0-10,000 number line with ±1000 hops
Side-by-side ±10/±100/±1000 comparison
Base-ten thousand-cubes for the concrete move
commonMisconceptions: Changing the wrong digit (stepping hundreds instead of thousands).
Boundary errors at 9,000s / crossing 10,000.
Counting on in smaller steps instead of jumping the place.
Confusing 1000 more with 100 more.
Assuming only one digit ever changes, mishandling roll-over.

learn.summary: For ages 8-9: find 1000 more or less than a four-digit number by recognising that normally only the thousands digit changes (4,562 → 5,562 or 3,562), extending the earlier +10/+100 pattern into the next place. The key exceptions are boundary crossings: adding 1000 when the thousands digit is 9 regroups into the ten-thousands place (9,500 + 1000 = 10,500), and subtracting 1000 can remove or reduce a higher digit (1,562 − 1000 = 562; 10,500 − 1000 = 9,500). Learners should justify which digit changes, not count on in smaller steps, and generalise beyond 10,000, where crossings such as 19,500 + 1000 = 20,500 change the ten-thousands digit too.

activities.title: Digit-stepper: which column responds to +1000?
feedback: If the learner expects the hundreds or ones to change, show only the thousands digit ticking and ask them to re-state which column a thousand lives in.
If they confuse 1000 more with 100 more (e.g. answer 4,662), run +100 and +1000 side by side so the differing columns are visible.
Reinforce correct predictions by having the learner say the thousands digit aloud before and after the press.
activities.rationale: Acting on the number and watching a single column respond makes 'which digit changes' concrete and self-correcting; side-by-side comparison with +10/+100 locates the responding column. An interactive stepper is one effective medium, but a place-value chart with counters or a labelled number line can carry the same comparison.
sourceClaims: Mentally adding/subtracting a power of ten changing a single place generalises the Grade 2 ±10/±100 standard.
learnerActions: Start from a four-digit number such as 4,562 shown in a place-value chart or on a number line.
Press +1000 (and −1000) and observe which digit moves: the thousands digit ticks 4→5 for +1000 (giving 5,562) or 4→3 for −1000 (giving 3,562) while hundreds, tens and ones stay locked.
Before each press, predict the result and name the digit that will change; then check against what moves.
Compare +10, +100 and +1000 side by side on the same starting number, saying which column each operation drives.
Use a 0–10,000 number-line view to see ±1000 as equal hops along the line.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding or subtracting 1000 normally changes only the thousands digit, extending the same place-value logic that governs +10 and +100.

activities.title: The roll-over: when a place fills up
feedback: If the answer is 0,300 or stays 9,300, point out that the thousand must be carried; walk through 9 thousands + 1 thousand = 10 thousands = 10,300.
If the answer is 19,300, check that they added exactly one thousand, not ten thousand.
Treat the boundary as a short targeted rehearsal of the single roll, not a re-teach of the whole idea.
activities.rationale: Boundary cases are where place-value reasoning is genuinely tested, so making the carry explicit addresses the common 9,000s/10,000-crossing error directly.
sourceClaims: Boundary roll-overs are the key teaching case for more/less across places.
learnerActions: Start from a boundary number such as 9,500 or 9,300.
Press +1000 and watch the thousands digit pass 9: it rolls 9→0 while a carry moves left, opening a new ten-thousands column (9,500 → 10,500; 9,300 → 10,300).
State in words why the number gains a digit: 9 thousands + 1 thousand = 10 thousands.
Rehearse just the single roll in reasoning: 9 thousands + 1 thousand = 10 thousands, so 9,300 + 1000 = 10,300 — not 0,300, not 9,300, not 19,300.
Try numbers beyond 10,000 to confirm the same place-value rule continues, including crossings such as 19,500 + 1000 = 20,500 and 10,500 − 1000 = 9,500.
activities.intendedInsight: When the thousands digit passes 9, the 'only one digit changes' pattern has a principled exception: the place fills up and regroups into the ten-thousands place (opening a new place for 9,500 → 10,500, or raising an existing ten-thousands digit for 19,500 → 20,500); the reverse crossing happens when subtracting (10,500 − 1000 = 9,500).

activities.title: Scored fluency and boundary checks
feedback: For a plain-case slip, ask which single digit should have moved.
For a boundary slip, redirect to the single-roll rehearsal (9 thousands + 1 thousand = 10 thousands).
Note: scored practice confirms fluency but does not by itself build the conceptual 'which digit' reasoning — pair it with the stepper/chart activities.
activities.rationale: Mixed plain and boundary items discriminate between a learner who only handles the easy case and one who regroups correctly across the thousands boundary.
learnerActions: Answer fill-in items such as '1000 more than 4,562 = __' and '1000 less than 4,562 = __'.
Answer which-digit-changes questions for ordinary cases.
Tackle boundary items deliberately, e.g. 9,500 + 1000 and 9,300 + 1000, writing the full regrouped answer.
Use a slider on a 0–10,000 line to land exactly 1000 away from a given point.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure, quick retrieval of 1000 more/less, including the regrouping boundary, confirms the place-value reasoning is fluent.

constraints: Demand place-value reasoning ('which digit changes, and why') rather than counting on in 1000s.
A static annotated chart is a useful reference but does not let the learner perform the transformation; pair any static image with an action (counters, stepper, or spoken prediction).

Recognition-only items (multiple choice 'which digit changes?') confirm identification but do not elicit independent construction of the answer; include fill-in and boundary items that require producing the regrouped number.
Scored quizzes assess and rehearse fluency; they do not substitute for the comparison work that builds the underlying concept.
Teach the roll-over boundary explicitly as the key case, and generalise to numbers beyond 10,000.
Timed/fluency modes are optional for securing speed, not a prerequisite for understanding.

Arithmetic check: 4,562 + 1000 = 5,562; 4,562 − 1000 = 3,562; 9,500 + 1000 = 10,500; 9,300 + 1000 = 10,300 — all confirmed correct as stated in the source.

probeDeeper: Which digit changes when you find 1000 more? Does any other digit move?
9,300 + 1000 — does it become a five-digit number? Why?
1000 less than 4,562 — did the hundreds/tens/ones change at all?
assess.correctAnswer: 5,562; 3,562; 10,300 — changing only the thousands digit, and rolling into a new place when it passes 9.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adjusts the wrong place — changes the hundreds (or another digit) instead of the thousands
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name the thousands column; add one thousand-block and watch only that column change (unless it overflows).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 1000 more than 4,562 comes out as 4,662 or 4,563.
