pedagogy.summary: Dividing a fraction by a fraction is where the general 'keep-change-flip' (invert-and-multiply) procedure arrives — 2/3 ÷ 4/5 = 2/3 × 5/4 = 5/6. The danger is that it is learned as a meaningless ritual: IES documents that most students (and many teachers) cannot explain why inverting works, and consequently misapply it — not inverting either fraction (→ 8/15), inverting the wrong fraction, or inverting both. The teaching goal is to bind the rule to meaning: keep the measurement reading ('how many 4/5s fit in 2/3?', a bit less than one), model it, and — for the strongest pupils — derive the rule (multiplying dividend and divisor by the reciprocal of the divisor makes the divisor 1). Estimation guards the result.
bestPractices: Anchor the procedure in the measurement meaning — 'how many 4/5s fit in 2/3?' — modelled on a common-denominator bar or number line, so the flipped rule has something to explain
Derive invert-and-multiply rather than assert it (IES): multiply dividend and divisor by the reciprocal of the divisor; the divisor becomes 1, leaving dividend × reciprocal
Drill the STRUCTURE of the rule against its misapplications — flip ONLY the divisor (the second fraction), keep the first, change ÷ to × — by contrasting correct vs 8/15 / wrong-flip worked examples
Estimate first: 2/3 ÷ 4/5 is close to 2/3 ÷ 1, so a little more than 2/3 — catches an inverted-wrong-fraction blunder
Connect to the common-denominator method (2/3 = 10/15, 4/5 = 12/15, so 10 ÷ 12 = 10/12 = 5/6) so pupils see the rule and the meaning agree
keyRepresentations: Common-denominator bar/number line showing how many divisor-lengths fit in the dividend
The reciprocal-derivation chain: (2/3 × 5/4) ÷ (4/5 × 5/4) = (2/3 × 5/4) ÷ 1
Keep-change-flip written with only the SECOND fraction inverted, colour-coded
Estimation number line placing the quotient near 2/3
commonMisconceptions: Does not invert either fraction — just multiplies: 2/3 ÷ 4/5 = 8/15 (IES)
Inverts the wrong fraction — flips the dividend: 2/3 ÷ 4/5 = 3/2 × 4/5 (IES)
Inverts both fractions: 3/2 × 5/4 (IES)
Applies keep-change-flip correctly but as a rote rule — cannot model it, justify the flip, or judge if the answer is reasonable

learn.summary: Dividing a fraction by a fraction is where invert-and-multiply ('keep-change-flip') completes: 2/3 ÷ 4/5 = 2/3 × 5/4 = 5/6. The risk is that it becomes a meaningless ritual — students fail to invert either fraction (→ 8/15), invert the wrong fraction, or invert both. The teaching goal is to bind the rule to meaning: read it as a measurement ('how many 4/5s fit into 2/3?' — a bit less than one), model that, contrast correct and misapplied methods, derive why only the divisor inverts, and use estimation to guard the answer.

activities.title: Measure it and run the rule side by side
feedback: If a learner lays the 4/5 bars and sees more than one fits, re-check the bar lengths against a common-denominator scale (2/3 = 10/15, 4/5 = 12/15): since 12/15 > 10/15, less than one 4/5 fits.
If the rule and the measurement disagree, check which fraction was flipped — only the second (the divisor) should invert; the first stays 2/3.

When the wrong-flip answer 6/5 appears, point out that dividing 2/3 by something only a little less than 1 should give only a little more than 2/3, and the measurement showed less than one whole 4/5 fits (an answer below 1); 6/5 is greater than 1 and nearly double 2/3, so it cannot be right.
activities.rationale: Grounding invert-and-multiply in the measurement meaning and a common-denominator view (10/15 ÷ 12/15 = 10/12) gives the flip something concrete to explain, and making a wrong flip visibly diverge from the measured value targets the exact documented misapplications.
sourceClaims: Students commonly misapply invert-and-multiply: not inverting either fraction (2/3 ÷ 4/5 = 8/15), inverting the wrong fraction (3/2 × 4/5), or inverting both (3/2 × 5/4); such errors reflect a lack of conceptual understanding of why the procedure works

Apply and extend previous understandings of division to divide fractions by fractions, including using visual fraction models and the relationship between multiplication and division (e.g. via common denominators)
learnerActions: Take a bar representing 2/3 and lay 4/5-length bars into it; find that not even one whole 4/5 fits, and read how much of a 4/5 does fit (about 5/6 of one).
Alongside, run keep-change-flip: keep 2/3, change ÷ to ×, flip ONLY the 4/5 to 5/4, and compute 2/3 × 5/4 = 10/12 = 5/6.
Confirm the measured amount (5/6 of a 4/5 fits) and the rule's answer (5/6) agree.
Deliberately flip the wrong fraction (3/2 × 4/5 = 6/5) or both (3/2 × 5/4 = 15/8) and compare each result to the measured 5/6 — notice how far each wrong flip lands from what you measured.
activities.intendedInsight: Inverting the divisor is not an arbitrary trick: the rule's answer matches the measured 'how many 4/5s fit in 2/3', and flipping the dividend or both pulls the answer away from that measured amount.

activities.title: Derive why only the divisor inverts
feedback: If a learner inverts the dividend too, show that doing so changes the value of the dividend, whereas the derivation only ever turns the divisor into 1 and keeps the dividend as it was.
If the step 4/5 × 5/4 = 1 is unclear, have them multiply numerators and denominators: (4×5)/(5×4) = 20/20 = 1.
activities.rationale: The reciprocal derivation gives a justification stronger pupils can own, directly countering the 'it's just a rule' and 'invert both' errors.
sourceClaims: Invert-and-multiply can be DERIVED, not asserted: multiplying dividend and divisor by the reciprocal of the divisor makes the divisor 1, leaving dividend × reciprocal; visual models and estimation should accompany the procedure to make it meaningful
learnerActions: Start from 2/3 ÷ 4/5 and multiply both the dividend and the divisor by the reciprocal of the divisor, 5/4: (2/3 × 5/4) ÷ (4/5 × 5/4).
Compute 4/5 × 5/4 = 1, so the expression becomes (2/3 × 5/4) ÷ 1 = 2/3 × 5/4.
State in your own words why the dividend 2/3 is left untouched and only the divisor is turned into 1.
Explain, using this derivation, why flipping both fractions (3/2 × 5/4) is wrong — the dividend was never inverted.
activities.intendedInsight: Invert-and-multiply can be derived rather than asserted: multiplying dividend and divisor by the reciprocal of the divisor makes the divisor 1, leaving dividend × reciprocal, which is why only the divisor flips.

activities.title: Estimate before you compute
feedback: If a learner accepts 8/15, ask: dividing by something just under 1 should give a bit MORE than 2/3, but 8/15 is LESS than 2/3 (8/15 vs 10/15) — so the method must be wrong.
Reinforce that dividing a positive number by a positive number less than 1 produces a result larger than the dividend.
activities.rationale: Estimation is a documented guard that should accompany the procedure to keep it meaningful and reasonable.
sourceClaims: Invert-and-multiply can be DERIVED, not asserted: multiplying dividend and divisor by the reciprocal of the divisor makes the divisor 1, leaving dividend × reciprocal; visual models and estimation should accompany the procedure to make it meaningful
learnerActions: Before calculating 2/3 ÷ 4/5, note that 4/5 is close to 1, so 2/3 ÷ 4/5 should be close to 2/3 ÷ 1 = 2/3, and a bit more than 2/3 because you are dividing by a little less than 1.
After computing, check whether your answer (5/6) is more than 2/3 (2/3 = 10/15, 5/6 ≈ 12.5/15) — it is.
Use the estimate to reject answers like 6/5 (too big) or 8/15 (less than 2/3, wrong direction).
activities.intendedInsight: A quick estimate of the expected size catches inverted-wrong-fraction and no-flip blunders before they are accepted.

activities.title: Diagnose the method, not just the answer
feedback: Answer 8/15 with no flip: return to the measurement meaning and derivation — ÷ 4/5 must undo multiplying by 4/5, so the divisor inverts.
Answer 6/5 with the dividend flipped: keep the FIRST, flip only the SECOND; use the estimate (answer near but a bit more than 2/3) to flag 6/5 as impossible.
Answer 15/8 with both flipped: only dividing BY the divisor needs undoing, so only the divisor flips — walk the derivation where the dividend is untouched.
Correct 5/6 but a blank or 'that's just the rule' model/story: build the 'how many 4/5s fit in 2/3' model alongside the rule and require an estimate on the next problem.
activities.rationale: Watching the method reveals the precise way invert-and-multiply fails — each wrong answer names a specific documented misapplication — and requiring a model or story elicits a production that recognition alone does not.
sourceClaims: Students commonly misapply invert-and-multiply: not inverting either fraction (2/3 ÷ 4/5 = 8/15), inverting the wrong fraction (3/2 × 4/5), or inverting both (3/2 × 5/4); such errors reflect a lack of conceptual understanding of why the procedure works
learnerActions: Work out 2/3 ÷ 4/5 showing every step of the method.
Then draw a picture or tell a story that shows what 2/3 ÷ 4/5 actually means.
Transfer the method to a new case, e.g. 1/2 ÷ 1/4, and say whether the answer is bigger or smaller than 1/2 and why.
Match each wrong result — 8/15, 6/5, 15/8 — to the mistake that produced it (no flip, wrong fraction flipped, both flipped).
activities.intendedInsight: Owning fraction division means producing the answer, modelling or story-ing the division, justifying why only the divisor flips, and judging the answer's reasonableness — not just reciting the steps.

activities.title: Defend each step to a questioner
feedback: If the learner can only say 'that's the rule', redirect them to the derivation (multiply dividend and divisor by 5/4 so the divisor becomes 1) or the measurement model.
Accept a justification only when it explains why the dividend is left unchanged.
activities.rationale: A questioning dialogue can surface whether a correct answer rests on understanding or ritual, complementing the visual modelling activities; this is a proposed, untested teaching move.
learnerActions: Present each step of 2/3 ÷ 4/5 to a partner or tutor who keeps asking 'why?' and refuses 'because that's the rule' as an answer.
Justify why the division becomes a multiplication, why only the second fraction flips, and why 5/6 is reasonable.
Answer the follow-up: how would the answer change if you flipped the other fraction instead?
activities.intendedInsight: Being pressed for justification can expose a merely rote rule and can push the learner to connect the procedure to the reciprocal derivation and the measurement meaning.

constraints: The target objective is procedural fluency WITH meaning: a learner must model or story the division, justify why only the divisor inverts, and estimate the answer — producing 5/6 alone is not sufficient.
Colour-coding or locking only the second fraction when it flips is a helpful scaffold, but learners must eventually apply the rule without the visual aid.

A matching/selection task can diagnose which misapplication a learner makes and can be used during teaching, but recognising a correct answer does not elicit independent construction of a model or a story — pair it with open working and a modelling demand.

A static worked example (tap-to-reveal steps, 'why only the second flips' flap) supports reading the procedure but does not let the learner test a wrong flip or model a new case; use it as a reference, not the primary task.
Estimation is a check, not the method; use it to flag impossible answers, not to replace exact computation.
Fraction ÷ fraction is a length/quantity comparison that is naturally represented on a bar or number line; a flat model is adequate here, and this is not evidence that any other medium would fail.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The quotient 5/6 is simultaneously a bit LESS than one whole 4/5 (the measurement reading, since 2/3 < 4/5) and a bit MORE than 2/3 (the estimation reading, since dividing by 4/5 < 1 enlarges the dividend); both statements are consistent, not contradictory.

The source labels invert-and-multiply as the general procedure arriving at fraction ÷ fraction; this rewrite presents it as derivable and measurable rather than as the only valid method — the common-denominator route (10/15 ÷ 12/15 = 10/12) is retained as an equivalent approach.

The IES claim is cited as support for the general misapplication pattern and the derivation principle; it does not establish that any specific activity here has been tested for efficacy. The Common Core citation (6.NS.1) is marked verified:false in the source.

The 'Defend each step to a questioner' activity has sourceClaims set to [] because no cited source directly supports Socratic questioning as a teaching/diagnostic method; it is retained only as a conservative, qualified proposal.

probeDeeper: Why does flipping the second fraction and multiplying give the right answer — convince me it isn't just a trick.
Is 5/6 bigger or smaller than 2/3, and does that make sense for dividing by 4/5 (which is nearly 1)?
Try 1/2 ÷ 1/4 with your method — is the answer bigger or smaller than 1/2, and why?
Which single fraction gets flipped, and how would the answer change if you flipped the other one instead?
assess.correctAnswer: 2/3 ÷ 4/5 = 2/3 × 5/4 = 10/12 = 5/6. Meaning: 'how many 4/5s fit into 2/3?' — a bit less than one whole 4/5 fits, namely 5/6 of it. (Or common denominators: 10/15 ÷ 12/15 = 10/12 = 5/6.)

errorPatterns.pattern: Does not invert either fraction — just multiplies straight across: 2/3 ÷ 4/5 = 2/3 × 4/5 = 8/15
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the measurement meaning and the reciprocal derivation — show that ÷ 4/5 must undo multiplying by 4/5, so the divisor is inverted; contrast 8/15 with the measured 5/6
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Working shows a direct multiplication with no flip; answer 8/15

errorPatterns.pattern: Inverts the WRONG fraction — flips the dividend instead of the divisor: 2/3 ÷ 4/5 = 3/2 × 4/5 = 6/5
errorPatterns.nextMove: Colour-lock the rule — keep the FIRST, flip only the SECOND (the divisor) — and use estimation (answer should be near 2/3) to flag 6/5 as impossible; re-derive which fraction inverts
errorPatterns.revealedBy: First fraction is inverted in the working; answer 6/5 (bigger than the dividend, wrong direction)

errorPatterns.pattern: Inverts BOTH fractions: 2/3 ÷ 4/5 = 3/2 × 5/4
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that only the operation of dividing BY the divisor needs undoing, so only the divisor flips; walk the reciprocal derivation where the DIVIDEND is untouched
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Both fractions flipped in the working; answer 15/8

errorPatterns.pattern: Applies keep-change-flip correctly to 5/6 but as pure ritual — cannot draw a model, tell a matching story, or explain why the flip works or whether 5/6 is reasonable
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build the 'how many 4/5s fit in 2/3' model alongside the rule so the procedure gains meaning; require an estimate before computing on the next problem
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct 5/6 but the modelling/story task is blank, wrong, or 'that's just the rule'; no estimation offered

responseLevels.gap: Does not invert, inverts the wrong fraction, or inverts both — the procedure is misapplied and no meaning is available.
responseLevels.full: Computes 5/6 correctly AND grounds it — models or stories 'how many 4/5s fit in 2/3', explains (or derives via the reciprocal) why invert-and-multiply works, estimates the answer's size, and transfers the method reliably to a new fraction ÷ fraction case.
responseLevels.partial: Keeps-changes-flips correctly to 5/6 but purely by rule — cannot model the division, tell a matching story, justify why only the divisor flips, or estimate whether the answer is reasonable.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work out 2/3 ÷ 4/5, showing every step of your method. Then draw a picture or tell a story that shows what 2/3 ÷ 4/5 actually means.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the METHOD catches the exact way the invert-and-multiply rule fails, which a bare answer would hide. A child who does not invert lands on 8/15; one who flips the dividend gets 6/5; one who flips both also errs — each wrong answer names the precise misapplication (all documented by IES). And the demand to MODEL or story the division separates the child who owns the meaning (can show 'how many 4/5s fit in 2/3') from the one running a rote ritual — the latter computes 5/6 but cannot represent it or say why only the second fraction flips.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–10y; generate a number or shape pattern from a given rule; identify features NOT explicit in the rule and explain informally why they occur.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5–Y6 'generate and describe linear number sequences'; reasoning about pattern features.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.OA.5 — 'generate a number or shape pattern that follows a given rule. Identify apparent features of the pattern that were not explicit in the rule itself. For example, given the rule "Add 3" and the starting number 1, generate terms … and observe that the terms appear to alternate between odd and even numbers. Explain informally why the numbers will continue to alternate.'
• Operational details — two intertwined skills: GENERATE (apply a term-to-term rule accurately) and NOTICE-AND-EXPLAIN (spot an emergent feature — alternating odd/even, all even, a repeating units digit — and justify it from the rule's structure). The emphasis, as with times-table patterns, is on the informal EXPLANATION ('add 3 flips parity each time because 3 is odd'), moving from spotting to reasoning. Shape patterns (growing sequences) connect the term number to a count, seeding the position-to-term (nth-term) idea. Use a T-table (term number vs value) and concrete/pictorial growing patterns.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): generate terms from a rule and continue a shape pattern. Tier B (age 9–10): notice an emergent feature (alternating odd/even; always even) and describe it. Tier C (age 10): explain informally WHY the feature must continue, from the rule's structure.
bestPractices: Separate and then connect the two demands: generate accurately, THEN look for a feature the rule didn't state and explain it.
Press for informal explanation grounded in structure ('adding an odd number flips odd↔even'), not restatement of the observation.
Use a T-table (term number vs value) so emergent features and the position-to-value link become visible.
Include growing SHAPE patterns (dots/tiles) alongside number patterns, connecting the picture to the count and seeding nth-term thinking.
Encourage prediction ('what will the 10th term be? will it be odd or even?') and verification.
keyRepresentations: T-table (term number ↔ value) — exposing emergent features
Growing shape/dot pattern — term number as a count
Number line / hundred square — visualising step patterns and parity
Colour-coded terms (odd/even) to make features pop
commonMisconceptions: Applying the rule inconsistently or miscounting steps when generating terms.
'Explaining' a feature by restating it rather than giving a structural reason.
Assuming a short-run feature always holds without justification (over-generalising).
Confusing the term-to-term rule with a position-to-term rule.
Not distinguishing the starting number's role from the step's role in an emergent feature.

learn.summary: For ages 9–10: generate a number or shape pattern from a given rule, then notice a feature the rule did NOT state (alternating odd/even, all-even, a repeating units-digit cycle) and explain informally WHY it must continue from the rule's structure. The teaching goal is to move from spotting a feature to justifying it (e.g. 'adding an odd number flips parity each time'), using a term-number vs value table and growing shape pictures to seed position-to-term thinking.

activities.title: Generate, then colour by parity to spot a hidden feature
feedback: If the differences between your terms aren't all the same (e.g. 1, 4, 7, 9, 12), you added to the wrong term or changed the step partway — mark the +3 jump between every pair to enforce a constant step.

If, when asked what else you notice, you only repeat 'it goes up by 3', look specifically at the last digits (1, 4, 7, 0, 3, 6, 9, 2 …) or at the odd/even pattern — those are features the rule didn't tell you.
Check your 10th term by continuing the sequence; the colour pattern should let you predict its parity before you compute it.
activities.rationale: Separating accurate generation from feature-noticing, and using a term-number vs value table plus parity colouring, makes emergent features and the position-to-value link visible, as the standard requires.
sourceClaims: Y5–Y6 pupils generate and describe linear number sequences and reason about pattern features.
T-tables and growing shape patterns support generate-and-explain reasoning and seed position-to-term thinking.
learnerActions: Take the rule 'start at 1, add 3' and write the first eight terms: 1, 4, 7, 10, 13, 16, 19, 22.
Mark each 'add 3' jump between consecutive terms (on a number line or by an arrow) so the step stays constant.
Colour or mark each term as odd or even and describe what you notice about the sequence of colours.
Record each term in a table with two columns: term number (1st, 2nd, 3rd …) and value, so emergent features line up next to their positions.
Predict whether the 10th term will be odd or even, then generate it and check.
activities.intendedInsight: A rule states a step, but the generated sequence can show a feature the rule never mentioned — here the terms strictly alternate odd, even, odd, even — and a table or parity colouring makes that feature visible.

activities.title: Explain WHY the feature must continue
feedback: If you say a feature 'just is' (e.g. 'the terms are all even because they just are'), push for the reason: even + even = even, so an even start plus an even step stays even.
If you predict odd terms will appear in 'start at 2, add 4', generate a few terms to test the prediction, then reason that adding an even step preserves evenness.
A correct explanation points to the step being odd or even (and, for an all-even or all-odd pattern, to the starting number's parity too) — not simply to the terms you happened to list.
activities.rationale: The objective's heart is informal explanation grounded in structure; pressing past restatement to a parity/digit reason is what distinguishes procedural term-cranking from the intended reasoning.
sourceClaims: 4.OA.5 requires generating a pattern from a rule, identifying features not explicit in the rule, and explaining them informally (e.g. why +3 from 1 alternates odd/even).
Y5–Y6 pupils generate and describe linear number sequences and reason about pattern features.
learnerActions: For 'start at 1, add 3', explain why the odd/even labels keep alternating: adding 3 (an odd number) flips parity every single time, so the alternation must continue forever, not just for the terms you wrote.
For 'start at 2, add 4', predict before writing whether every term will be even, then justify: starting even and adding an even number keeps the result even, because even + even = even.
State a prediction for a step of 2 instead of 3 and explain how the parity pattern would differ (adding an even number leaves parity unchanged).
Give a structural reason, not just a restatement: say WHY it happens from the rule, not merely THAT it happens.
activities.intendedInsight: An emergent feature can be justified from the structure of the rule: an odd step makes the terms alternate (and the starting number fixes which parity the alternation begins with), while an even step keeps every term the same parity (and the start fixes that parity). So the feature must hold for all terms, not just the observed ones.

activities.title: Vary the step to discover the roles of start and step
feedback: If changing only the step also seems to change which parity the terms begin from, check that you really held the starting number fixed — change one thing at a time.

If you can't yet say why the colour locks for an even step, connect it back to the fact that adding an even number never changes parity (even + even = even, odd + even = odd), while adding an odd number flips parity.
activities.rationale: Changing one variable at a time (step, then start) lets learners experimentally separate the two ingredients of the rule and avoid confusing the term-to-term rule with the position-to-term rule.
learnerActions: Keep the start fixed and change the step from 3 (odd) to 4 (even); generate both sequences and compare the parity colouring — alternating for the odd step, locked for the even step.
Now keep the step fixed and change the starting number; notice which feature changes (which parity the terms begin with) and which stays the same (whether they alternate).

Articulate the two distinct roles you discovered: the step's parity decides whether the terms alternate (odd step) or stay a single fixed parity (even step); the start fixes which parity the sequence begins with — the one it stays on for an even step, or the one it starts the alternation with for an odd step.
Test a prediction before computing: for a new rule, say what the hidden feature will be and why, then generate terms to confirm.
activities.intendedInsight: The starting number and the step play different roles in an emergent feature; experimenting by changing one at a time isolates each role.

activities.title: Growing shape patterns and position-to-term
feedback: If you predict later stages only by drawing every one, try using the stage number and the per-step growth to jump ahead, then check by drawing.
If your described rule doesn't reproduce the next term, re-count one stage and recompute the change between stages (it may be constant, or it may itself grow in a pattern, as in square arrangements).
activities.rationale: Including growing shape patterns alongside number patterns connects the picture to the count and seeds nth-term reasoning, as recommended for this objective.
sourceClaims: T-tables and growing shape patterns support generate-and-explain reasoning and seed position-to-term thinking.
Y5–Y6 pupils generate and describe linear number sequences and reason about pattern features.
learnerActions: Continue a growing dot or tile pattern by predicting the next three terms and describing the rule in words.
Count the dots/tiles in each stage and record stage number next to the count in a two-column table.
Link the stage (term) number to its count, and predict a later stage's count, explaining how you used the position rather than drawing every stage.
Notice any hidden feature in the counts (e.g. always even, or a repeating units digit) and explain it from how the shape grows each step.
activities.intendedInsight: Growing shape patterns connect the term number to a count, seeding position-to-term (nth-term) thinking and giving a concrete picture of an emergent numeric feature.

activities.title: Pattern-detective discussion: justify the feature aloud
feedback: For 'would 30 ever appear from start 1, add 3?': the terms are 1, 4, 7, 10, 13, … and each one is one more than a multiple of 3 (it leaves remainder 1 when divided by 3). 30 is itself a multiple of 3 (remainder 0), so it can never appear. Notice that 30 is even and ends in 0 — and terms ending in 0, like 10, 40, 70, do occur — so parity and the units digit alone do NOT settle it; you have to reason from the step, that every term stays one more than a multiple of 3.

If your answer repeats the observation, the detective should ask 'but WHY will that keep happening?' until you name the structural cause — such as the step's parity, the even+even rule, or (for questions like whether 30 appears) the remainder every term leaves when divided by the step.
activities.rationale: A questioning dialogue that refuses restatement and demands a structural reason is well matched to the informal-explanation demand and pairs naturally with a generated sequence and table the learner has built.
sourceClaims: 4.OA.5 requires generating a pattern from a rule, identifying features not explicit in the rule, and explaining them informally (e.g. why +3 from 1 alternates odd/even).
learnerActions: With a partner or adult playing a 'pattern detective', state a feature you noticed and be ready to defend it.
The detective accepts the feature ONLY when you give a structural reason for why it continues (e.g. 'adding an odd number flips parity each time'), not when you restate the observation.

Answer probing questions such as: 'Besides adding 3, what pattern do you see in the numbers?', 'Why do the terms of start-at-2-add-4 stay even?', 'If you start at 1 and add 3, would 30 ever appear — how can you tell?', and 'What changes if the step is 2 instead of 3?'
Revise your explanation if it's only a restatement until it names the structural cause.
activities.intendedInsight: Explaining informally means giving a reason rooted in the rule's structure that shows a feature must persist, not merely reporting what you saw.

constraints: The aim is both skills together: generate accurately AND notice-then-explain a feature not stated by the rule; listing correct terms alone does not meet the objective.
Explanation must be structural (why the feature must continue), not a restatement of the observation.
Distinguish the term-to-term rule (the step) from a position-to-term rule; keep the starting number's role separate from the step's role.

Response formats that only ask a learner to pick the correct explanation from options can check whether they can distinguish a reason from a restatement, but do not by themselves elicit the learner constructing and voicing their own structural justification; use them to assess, and pair with tasks where the learner generates terms and explains in their own words.

A static exemplar table and growing-shape picture can anchor the idea and reveal a feature, but cannot let the learner vary the rule and test how emergent features change; provide that experimentation separately.

Interactive examples (auto-colouring terms by parity, a table filling in as terms are generated, a reveal-the-reason prompt, changing the step to compare) are optional illustrations of the mechanism, not required tools.
Do not over-generalise a short-run observation; require justification before accepting that a feature always holds.

When judging whether a target value can appear in an arithmetic sequence, reason from the step's effect on remainders/divisibility, not from parity or units digit alone, since those surface features can be insufficient (e.g. 30 is even and ends in 0 yet cannot appear in 1, 4, 7, 10, …).

State the role of the step precisely: an odd step makes terms alternate in parity while an even step holds a single parity; the start only sets which parity begins the sequence, so avoid saying terms 'settle/lock to a value' in the alternating (odd-step) case.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original 'poor-fit' note claimed a third dimension 'adds no explanatory power'; this has been dropped as a catalog-preference statement rather than retained as a universal claim. Number/shape sequences are naturally represented in a table and growing picture, but no necessity claim is asserted.
Two of three cited sources were marked unverified in the source row (CCSS 4.OA.5 wording and NCETM guidance); treat their claims as legacy-stated, not independently re-checked here.

Self-audit of worked values: 'start 1, add 3' gives 1, 4, 7, 10, 13, 16, 19, 22 (units digits cycle 1,4,7,0,3,6,9,2); 'start 2, add 4' gives all even terms; the '30' probe is determinate (terms ≡1 mod 3, 30 ≡0 mod 3, so 30 never appears). These were checked and are consistent.

Correction applied this pass: the 'Explain WHY' intendedInsight and the 'Vary the step' action/feedback said the start sets a 'value they lock to / settle on', which is false for the alternating odd-step case; reworded so locking is attributed only to even steps and the start is described as setting the starting parity. The sourceClaims on the 'Vary the step' activity were set to [] because no source claim directly supports the controlled-variation principle.

probeDeeper: Besides 'add 3', what pattern do you see in the numbers you wrote?
Why do the terms of 'start at 2, add 4' stay even every time?
If you started at 1 and added 3, would 30 ever appear? How can you tell?
What would change about the odd/even pattern if the step were 2 instead of 3?
assess.correctAnswer: 1, 4, 7, 10, 13, 16, 19, 22 — the child should notice a feature not in the rule, e.g. the terms alternate odd, even, odd, even, or the ones-digits cycle 1,4,7,0,3,6,9,2. For 'start at 2, add 4': all terms even, because starting even and adding an even number keeps it even. The teacher watches for correct generation AND an informal 'why' for a spotted feature.

errorPatterns.pattern: applies the rule inconsistently — adds the step to the wrong term, or changes the step partway
errorPatterns.nextMove: have the child mark the +3 jump between each pair on a number line so the constant step is enforced.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: terms don't have a constant difference (e.g. 1,4,7,9,12)

errorPatterns.pattern: generates terms correctly but notices NO feature beyond the rule — just re-states 'it goes up by 3'
errorPatterns.nextMove: prompt attention to the ones-digits or odd/even alternation; model 'the rule says add 3, but look — the last digits go 1,4,7,0… why might that repeat?'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: when asked what else they notice, child only repeats the given rule

errorPatterns.pattern: spots a feature but cannot explain informally why it happens (e.g. sees all-even but says 'it just is')
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach pattern generation; scaffold the reason — even + even = even, so starting even and adding even stays even.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: correct observation, no reasoning when asked why

errorPatterns.pattern: predicts wrongly that 'start at 2, add 4' will include odd numbers
errorPatterns.nextMove: generate a few terms to check the prediction, then reason about why even+even stays even.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child predicts odd terms will appear, not seeing that adding an even step preserves parity

responseLevels.gap: cannot generate a consistent pattern, or lists terms but notices/explains no feature.
responseLevels.full: generates the sequence accurately, identifies a feature not given by the rule, and explains informally why it must occur (parity/digit-cycle reasoning), transferring it to a new rule.
responseLevels.partial: generates terms correctly and spots a hidden feature but cannot explain informally why it occurs, or predicts parity incorrectly.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a rule and watch them generate and analyse the pattern: 'Start at 1 and keep adding 3 — write the first eight terms.' Then ask: 'What do you notice about the pattern that the rule didn't tell you?' Then give 'start at 2, add 4' and ask them to predict, before writing, whether all the terms will be even and why. Watch the term generation and the informal explanation of a hidden feature.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Generating terms is routine; the objective's heart is NOTICING a feature the rule didn't state and explaining WHY. Watching whether the child only lists terms versus spots-and-justifies a pattern (alternating parity, digit cycles) separates procedural term-cranking from the intended reasoning.

sources.claim: Y5–Y6 pupils generate and describe linear number sequences and reason about pattern features.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (KS1–2), Years 5–6 Number — algebra/patterns

sources.claim: 4.OA.5 requires generating a pattern from a rule, identifying features not explicit in the rule, and explaining them informally (e.g. why +3 from 1 alternates odd/even).
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 4, Operations & Algebraic Thinking (4.OA.C.5)

sources.claim: T-tables and growing shape patterns support generate-and-explain reasoning and seed position-to-term thinking.
sources.source: NCETM patterns and early algebra guidance

pedagogy.summary: The first fraction operation: adding and subtracting fractions that share a denominator, staying within one whole (5/7 + 1/7 = 6/7). The whole idea is that the denominator NAMES the unit (sevenths) and stays fixed, while the numerators COUNT how many of that unit and are combined like whole numbers. Taught well, it is simply counting like things: two fifths and two fifths make four fifths, exactly as two apples and two apples make four apples — the 'apple' here is the fifth. The denominator is not a number to operate on; it is the label of what is being counted.
bestPractices: Present it as counting like units — use 'dual naming' ('three one-fifths and one one-fifth make four one-fifths' alongside '3/5 + 1/5 = 4/5') so the denominator is heard as the unit being counted, not a second number.
Hold the whole and the unit constant with a single partitioned bar or fraction strip so pieces are visibly the same size and only the count changes.
Keep to same denominators and results within one whole first; establish which of a pair is bigger before adding, per NFER.
Confront the add-across error early and directly (2/5 + 2/5 is not 4/10) using a model where the denominator cannot change.
Do subtraction alongside addition as separating the same units (6/8 − 3/8 = 3/8), keeping the eighth as the fixed unit.
keyRepresentations: Fraction strip / bar partitioned into the fixed unit (sevenths, eighths) where pieces are combined or removed
Number line marked in the unit fraction, counting on/back in that unit
Discrete 'like objects' framing (each piece = one unit fraction) to make combining feel like counting
Paper folded/cut into equal parts (NFER's cut-a-strip-into-sevenths)
commonMisconceptions: Adds (or subtracts) the denominators as well as the numerators: 2/5 + 2/5 = 4/10, misapplying whole-number addition (IES; ~10% of lower-achieving Y6 on an easy same-denominator item, NFER).
Drops the unit and answers a bare whole number: 6/8 − 3/8 = 3, operating only on the numerators as if the denominator weren't there.
Treats the denominator as a quantity to be operated on rather than the name of the unit being counted.

learn.summary: Adding and subtracting fractions with the same denominator within one whole (e.g. 5/7 + 1/7 = 6/7, 6/8 − 3/8 = 3/8). The core idea: the denominator NAMES the unit being counted (sevenths, eighths) and stays fixed, while the numerators COUNT how many of that unit and are combined like whole numbers — 'two fifths and two fifths make four fifths' just as two apples and two apples make four apples, where the 'apple' is the fifth. Teaching targets two misconceptions: adding the denominators too (2/5 + 2/5 → 4/10) and dropping the unit to give a bare whole number (6/8 − 3/8 → 3). For ages 7–8.

activities.title: Locked-unit bar combiner (fixed-denominator model)
feedback: If a learner expects 4/10, have them lay four tenth-pieces next to the built sum. They cover only two fifths, less than the four fifths already on the bar, so 4/10 is too small. Counting the fifths gives 4/5.
If a learner wants to write a bare whole number for 6/8 − 3/8, point back to the eighths bar: three eighth-pieces remain, so the answer is 3/8, measured in eighths, not 3.
Read each piece aloud as 'one fifth' (or 'one eighth') so the denominator is heard as the name of the unit, not a second number.
activities.rationale: Combining visibly same-size pieces on a model where the unit is held constant makes the count change while the unit cannot, directly confronting the add-across error. A placing/snapping interaction with a live running count and spoken piece-naming makes the counting mechanism concrete. (The moment where four tenths visibly cover less than the 4/5 sum is a model affordance; its effectiveness against the misconception is not established by the cited sources.)
sourceClaims: A common mistake is to add or subtract the numerators AND denominators of two fractions, misapplying whole-number addition and failing to recognise that the denominator defines the size of the part; teach why procedures make sense using fixed-unit representations, and use estimation to expose implausible answers.
learnerActions: Work with a bar already partitioned into a fixed unit, e.g. fifths, with the label 'fifths' shown on the bar.
Combine 2/5 and another 2/5 by placing the pieces onto the bar; watch a running count read '4/5' as each piece is read aloud as 'one fifth'.

Test the answer '4/10' by laying four tenth-sized pieces next to the 4/5 you built. Notice that they cover only as much as two fifths, which is less than the four fifths on the bar, so 4/10 is the wrong amount. The pieces you are counting are all fifths.
Switch to subtraction on an eighths bar and remove pieces: start with 6/8 and take away 3/8, reading off 3/8 left.
Try adding one 2/5 too many and watch it run past the end of the bar, foreshadowing sums beyond one whole.
activities.intendedInsight: When denominators are the same, you are counting same-size pieces, so only the count (numerator) changes and the unit (denominator) stays fixed.

activities.title: Dual naming — read fractions as repeated unit fractions
feedback: If a learner starts to combine the denominators, re-voice the sum as 'how many one-fifths altogether?' to pull attention back to counting units.
Praise answers that keep the unit named: 'four one-fifths' is exactly 4/5.
activities.rationale: Hearing the denominator as the unit being counted may reduce the chance of mistakenly operating on it. Dual naming is offered as a supporting verbal routine to accompany the model work; the supporting source is marked unverified in the row.
sourceClaims: Securing that a non-unit fraction is a repeated sum of unit fractions ('three one-fifths'), via dual naming, minimises the chance of children mistakenly operating on the denominator.
learnerActions: Say each fraction two ways: 'three one-fifths' alongside '3/5', and 'one one-fifth' alongside '1/5'.
State the sum both ways: 'three one-fifths and one one-fifth make four one-fifths' alongside '3/5 + 1/5 = 4/5'.
Do the same for subtraction: 'six one-eighths take away three one-eighths leaves three one-eighths', alongside '6/8 − 3/8 = 3/8'.
Point to the denominator each time and name it as the unit being counted.
activities.intendedInsight: A non-unit fraction is a repeated sum of unit fractions, so adding/subtracting is counting those units up or down — the denominator is the label, not a quantity to operate on.

activities.title: Number line counting in the unit fraction
feedback: If the answer comes out as a whole number like 3, re-anchor: 6/8 and 3/8 are points on the line and the gap between them is measured in eighths, so 3/8.
If a sum of two pieces came out smaller than one piece, that's a signal to recheck — adding two pieces should give more, not less.
activities.rationale: A number line re-anchors the fraction as a quantity measured in the unit, specifically countering the 'drop the unit, answer a whole number' error. Estimation (bigger/smaller than a piece) exposes implausible answers.
sourceClaims: A common mistake is to add or subtract the numerators AND denominators of two fractions, misapplying whole-number addition and failing to recognise that the denominator defines the size of the part; teach why procedures make sense using fixed-unit representations, and use estimation to expose implausible answers.
learnerActions: Mark a number line in the unit fraction (e.g. eighths) from 0 to 1.
For 6/8 − 3/8, land on 6/8, count back 3 eighths, and read where you stop (3/8).
For a sum, start at one fraction and count on in the unit, reading each step.
State whether the answer is bigger or smaller than one of the pieces and check your result against that expectation.
activities.intendedInsight: Fractions are quantities/points measured in the unit; combining them is counting on or back in that unit, and the answer is still a count of eighths (6/8 − 3/8 = 3/8, not 3).

activities.title: Paper strip folded/cut into equal parts
feedback: If a learner reaches for a differently-sized piece, compare it against the cut pieces — it isn't a seventh, so it can't be part of this count.
Count the pieces together out loud to confirm the numerator while naming the unit.
activities.rationale: Hands-on cutting and counting of equal paper parts builds part-of-whole understanding through a different concrete medium than a screen model. Real paper pieces have slight thickness and are an approximation of the idealised flat equal parts; neither the paper nor the screen bar is uniquely necessary.
sourceClaims: On an easy same-denominator addition, 92% of Year 6 pupils were correct, but ~10% of lower-achieving pupils added both numerators and denominators (6/7 → 6/14); NFER recommends concrete materials (cut a strip into sevenths) to build part-of-whole understanding.
learnerActions: Fold and cut a paper strip into the fixed unit, e.g. sevenths (or eighths), so every piece is the same size.
Build 5/7 + 1/7 by gathering pieces and counting them: six sevenths, 6/7.
Build 6/8 − 3/8 by setting out six eighth-pieces and removing three, leaving 3/8.
Say aloud what each piece is called and how many there are after combining or removing.
activities.intendedInsight: Physically counting identical cut parts makes clear that combining fractions of the same denominator is counting like units; the piece size (unit) never changes.

activities.title: Fluency practice and error-baiting check (companion)
feedback: If 5/16 is chosen, remind: the denominator names the piece size and stays 8; count the eighths — 5/8.
If 5 is chosen, remind: the answer is measured in eighths, so 5/8, not 5.
Ask the learner to show the answer on a strip to confirm their choice.
activities.rationale: Scored practice is efficient for rehearsing fluency and can probe the misconceptions with targeted distractors, but it elicits recognition/a final answer rather than independent construction of the combining, so it is a companion to the model work.
sourceClaims: A common mistake is to add or subtract the numerators AND denominators of two fractions, misapplying whole-number addition and failing to recognise that the denominator defines the size of the part; teach why procedures make sense using fixed-unit representations, and use estimation to expose implausible answers.
learnerActions: Complete fill-in items such as '2/5 + 2/5 = _/_' and '6/8 − 3/8 = _/_'.
Choose the correct answer to 3/8 + 2/8 from options that include 5/16 (add-across error) and 5 (bare whole number) as distractors, and say why each wrong option is wrong.
Shade pieces on a strip to match each sum or difference.
activities.intendedInsight: Same-denominator sums and differences can be rehearsed to fluency, and deliberately including the add-across and dropped-unit answers as distractors checks whether the unit idea is secure.

constraints: Keep to same denominators with results within one whole first; establish which of a pair is bigger before adding.
Confront the add-across error (2/5 + 2/5 ≠ 4/10) and the dropped-unit error (6/8 − 3/8 ≠ 3) early and directly, using models where the denominator cannot change.
Do subtraction alongside addition as separating the same units, keeping the unit fraction fixed; don't assess only one operation, which lets a learner pass on a lucky case.

A static tap-to-reveal strip (labelling numerator vs denominator, showing one worked sum) can serve as a reference anchor but does not let the learner combine pieces themselves; treat it as a scaffold, not the main doing.
Scored quiz items elicit recognition or a final answer, not independent construction of the combining, so pair them with construction on a model.
Paper/card pieces have real thickness and are an approximation of ideal flat equal parts; a screen bar is an idealised model — both are usable, neither is uniquely necessary.
Compare fractions by holding the common unit (denominator) fixed and counting the numerators; the denominator is a fixed label of the unit, not a quantity that is operated on or 'flipped'.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The legacy source for dual naming (NCETM Spine 3) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its claim as unverified.

The legacy entry asserted depth/3D and in-role dialogue 'add nothing' / 'can't' teach this procedure. These are catalog-fit judgements, not established facts; they are not propagated as universal claims. A 2D model is well-suited here, but other media are not asserted to be incapable.

The legacy 'moment of insight' framing (tenths won't fit the fifths bar, so the error is 'literally impossible') is retained as a model affordance, not as proof the model defeats the misconception; efficacy is not established by the available sources.
The NFER statistic refers to Year 6 pupils, while this micro-topic targets ages 7–8; the figure illustrates the misconception's prevalence but was measured on an older cohort.

The IES claim is attached to the quiz because it names the add-across misconception the distractors target; it does not establish that scored recognition practice teaches the procedure, so the quiz is positioned as a companion only.

probeDeeper: Why does the bottom number stay 5 when you add two fifths?
Show me 2/5 + 2/5 on a strip or number line — where do you land?
A friend says 3/8 + 3/8 = 6/16. Work out what 6/16 is — is it bigger or smaller than 3/8? Can adding two pieces give you the same as just one of them?
If you add two pieces together, should the answer be bigger or smaller than one piece? Check your answer against that.
assess.correctAnswer: 2/5 + 2/5 = 4/5 (denominator stays fifths, add the counts 2 + 2). 6/8 − 3/8 = 3/8 (denominator stays eighths, 6 − 3 = 3).

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds/subtracts the denominators as well: '2 and 2 is 4 on top, 5 and 5 is 10 on the bottom, so 4/10' — operates on the denominator as if it were a second whole number.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to a fixed-unit strip: 2/5 and 2/5 are four SAME-SIZE fifth-pieces, so the answer is fifths; the fifth (denominator) names the piece and can't change when you just count more of them. Contrast tenths physically not fitting the fifths bar.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 4/10 for the sum (or does 8−8 / 6−6 on the bottom in the subtraction); the denominator changes.

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops the unit and gives a whole number: '6 take away 3 is 3' — answers 3, operating only on the numerators and losing the eighths.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor the fraction as a number/quantity on a number line: 6/8 and 3/8 are points, and their difference is still measured in eighths; shade 6 eighths, remove 3, read what's left — 3 eighths, not 3.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Final answer written as a whole number (3) rather than 3/8; the denominator disappears from the answer.

responseLevels.gap: Operates on the denominator too (4/10) or drops the unit and answers a whole number (3); cannot combine same-size parts as a count.
responseLevels.full: Adds and subtracts the numerators while keeping the denominator fixed (4/5, 3/8) and can justify or show it as counting like unit fractions (two fifths and two fifths make four fifths), transferring cleanly to a fresh same-denominator pair.
responseLevels.partial: Gets the same-denominator addition right by rule (4/5) but applies the numerator rule mechanically — falters on the subtraction, can't show it on a model, or is unsure why the denominator stays the same.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are two to work out — show me each step as you go, out loud or on paper: 2/5 + 2/5, and 6/8 − 3/8.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands they are counting like units keeps the denominator fixed and combines only the numerators — 4/5 and 3/8. Watching the working (not just the final number) exposes the two failure modes a correct reasoner never shows: changing the denominator too (4/10, 3/0) reveals the fraction isn't seen as a fixed-size unit, and answering a bare '3' reveals the unit has been dropped entirely. Doing both an addition and a subtraction with the same fixed unit stops a child passing on one lucky case.

sources.claim: A common mistake is to add or subtract the numerators AND denominators of two fractions, misapplying whole-number addition and failing to recognise that the denominator defines the size of the part; teach why procedures make sense using fixed-unit representations, and use estimation to expose implausible answers.
sources.source: IES/WWC Practice Guide, Developing Effective Fractions Instruction for K–8 (Siegler et al., 2010), Recommendations 2 & 3

sources.claim: On an easy same-denominator addition, 92% of Year 6 pupils were correct, but ~10% of lower-achieving pupils added both numerators and denominators (6/7 → 6/14); NFER recommends concrete materials (cut a strip into sevenths) to build part-of-whole understanding.
sources.source: NFER Assessment Hub, 'What are the common mistakes when adding fractions?' (Emily Jones)

sources.claim: Securing that a non-unit fraction is a repeated sum of unit fractions ('three one-fifths'), via dual naming, minimises the chance of children mistakenly operating on the denominator.
sources.source: NCETM Primary Mastery / Spine 3 Fractions, adding & subtracting within one whole (Topic 3.4)

pedagogy.summary: At 8-9 the reasoning practice turns outward: children stop merely explaining their own method and begin CRITIQUING someone else's, and they string more than one fact into a chain ('since 6×10=60 and 6×2=12, then 6×8=60−12=48'). Two moves define the level — building a multi-step argument, and diagnosing why a peer's method fails, not just that its answer is wrong. This is the SMP3 'construct viable arguments AND critique the reasoning of others' pairing made age-appropriate: arguments still lean on concrete referents (fraction bars, place-value equipment) but now demand a because/therefore link between steps. It is best taught not as a solo skill but through structured talk — analysing a deliberately flawed worked example, agreeing whether an argument 'makes sense', and being asked 'which STEP is wrong and why?' rather than 'is the answer right?'
bestPractices: Give children a peer's WRONG-but-plausible worked example (e.g. a column subtraction where the exchange was mis-recorded) and ask them to locate the faulty STEP and say why it breaks — not to redo it and compare answers
Model and require because/therefore connectives so a chain of facts becomes an argument ('since… and… therefore…'), scribing the child's spoken chain when their reasoning outruns their writing
Use 'convince me / convince a doubter' talk routines so an assertion is pushed into a justification; treat 'it just is' as the start, not the end
Anchor arguments in a shared representation (fraction bar, base-ten blocks) both parties can point at, so a critique targets the reasoning and not the person
Teach that finding one clear error and explaining it is worth more than re-solving — error analysis is the practice, per SMP3's 'distinguish correct logic from flawed logic and explain the flaw'
keyRepresentations: Fraction bars / area models for size arguments (more equal parts ⇒ smaller pieces, so 1/3 > 1/5)
Place-value equipment or a written column layout for locating an exchange error
A because/therefore sentence frame turning a list of facts into a chain
Derived-fact number strings (6×10, 6×2 ⇒ 6×8) shown as a linked sequence, not isolated facts
commonMisconceptions: 'It's wrong because the answer's different from mine' — judges a peer's argument by answer-agreement rather than by finding the flawed step
Checking one example and treating the rule as proved for all cases
Restating the method louder instead of giving a reason why it works
Believing a longer fraction/denominator names a bigger piece (1/5 > 1/3)

learn.summary: For ages 8-9, reasoning turns outward: children stop merely explaining their own method and begin critiquing someone else's, and they chain multiple facts into a single argument ('since 6×10=60 and 6×2=12, then 6×8=60−12=48'). Two moves define this level — building a multi-step because/therefore argument, and diagnosing WHY a peer's method fails (which step broke, not just that the answer differs). Arguments still lean on concrete referents (fraction bars, place-value equipment) but now require a because/therefore link between steps. Best taught through structured talk — analysing a deliberately flawed worked example, agreeing whether an argument 'makes sense', and asking 'which STEP is wrong and why?' rather than 'is the answer right?'

activities.title: Convince-me dialogue: catch the broken step
feedback: Name whether the faulty step was correctly located, not whether an answer matches: 'Yes — that flip is the broken line. Now tell me why flipping isn't allowed.'
If the child only announces the right answer ('it's 25'), redirect: 'Don't tell me the right answer yet — show me the first line where their thinking stops being okay, and say why that line breaks.'

If the child senses the error but cannot articulate it, revoice/scribe: offer 'you can't do that because…?' and let the child complete it; point at base-ten equipment so the reason has something to attach to. The reasoning is present even when the telling lags — do not treat this as not-knowing.

If the child agrees you can 'just do 6 take 1' because 'you always take the little one from the big one', this is a genuine false belief about the algorithm: build 71 with base-ten equipment, try to remove 6 ones, and force the exchange before returning to the argument skill.
activities.rationale: The level's core — constructing a chain and critiquing another's — is intrinsically dialogic. An in-role partner that asserts a flawed argument and asks the child to find and explain the broken step exercises SMP3's critique half, and 'how do you know?' pressure pushes the child's own assertions into because-clauses in real time. Children's reasoning frequently runs ahead of their ability to communicate it, so eliciting and scribing is appropriate rather than judging by fluency.
sourceClaims: SMP3: construct viable arguments AND critique the reasoning of others; elementary students construct arguments using concrete referents; they distinguish correct logic from flawed, and if there is a flaw, explain what it is; all grades can listen to others' arguments, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions.

Reasoning develops along a describe→explain→convince→justify→prove ladder, and children's reasoning frequently runs ahead of their ability to communicate it, so a teacher must elicit and scribe the reasoning rather than judge it by fluency of telling.
learnerActions: Listen to or read a plausible-but-wrong worked chain, e.g. a partner says: 'I did 71 minus 46. I couldn't do 1 take 6, so I did 6 take 1, that's 5, then 7 take 4 is 3, so 35.'
Point to the EXACT line where the thinking first goes wrong (the digit-flip), rather than re-solving and comparing totals.
Say WHY that line breaks, grounded in place value: 'you can't flip the digits; the 1 is really part of 71, so you exchange a ten to make 11, and 11 take 6 is 5.'
When challenged with 'how do you know?' or 'why does exchanging fix it?', keep going until the objection becomes a because-chain.
Then construct a correct chain aloud for 71 − 46, starting from what 71 really is (giving 25).
activities.intendedInsight: Critiquing someone else's error forces your own reasoning to become explicit: a vague 'that's not right' can be turned, under questioning, into a because-chain you did not know you had.

activities.title: Build-an-argument workspace: chain the facts, mark the flaw
feedback: Report whether the flaw was correctly located, not whether a final answer matches.
If the child's chain lists facts without connectives, prompt: 'What word joins these two so the second follows from the first?'
If the marked step is wrong, ask the child to read each line aloud and test whether it genuinely follows from the one before.
activities.rationale: A build-an-argument workspace lets the child assemble a chain and mark the exact faulty step, making the 'which step, and why' move concrete and productive. Dragging/snapping tiles and tapping the broken step are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete; they are not required. This complements rather than replaces talk.
sourceClaims: SMP3: construct viable arguments AND critique the reasoning of others; elementary students construct arguments using concrete referents; they distinguish correct logic from flawed, and if there is a flaw, explain what it is; all grades can listen to others' arguments, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions.
learnerActions: Assemble fact tiles ('6×10=60', '6×2=12') into a because/therefore sequence and write the linking reason, e.g. 'since 6×10=60 and 6×2=12, then 6×8=60−12=48.'
In a separate flawed worked example (a column subtraction with a mis-recorded exchange), tap or mark the single broken step and write or pick why it fails.
Check your own chain reads as 'since… and… therefore…', not just a list of true facts side by side.
activities.intendedInsight: A string of true facts only becomes an argument when because/therefore links them; locating 'which step, and why' is a concrete, repeatable move.

activities.title: Fraction-bar size argument: 1/3 > 1/5
feedback: Accept the chain only when it links the number of parts to the size of each part, not just 'the bar looks bigger'.
If the child believes a bigger denominator means a bigger piece, return to the shared bar split from the same whole and count/compare the actual pieces before re-stating the argument.
Treat 'it just is' as the start of a justification, not the end: ask 'convince a doubter'.
activities.rationale: Anchoring an argument in a shared representation lets a critique target the reasoning rather than the person, and directly addresses the common belief that a larger denominator names a bigger piece. For unit fractions the numerator is fixed at 1, so the comparison varies only the number of equal parts of the same whole. Concrete referents are age-appropriate for constructing arguments at this stage.
sourceClaims: SMP3: construct viable arguments AND critique the reasoning of others; elementary students construct arguments using concrete referents; they distinguish correct logic from flawed, and if there is a flaw, explain what it is; all grades can listen to others' arguments, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions.
learnerActions: Using fraction bars or an area model showing the same whole split into 3 and into 5, state and justify which piece is bigger.
Build the chain: 'more equal parts means smaller pieces, so fifths are smaller than thirds, therefore 1/3 > 1/5.'
When a classmate claims '1/5 is bigger because 5 is bigger than 3', find and explain the flaw using the shared bar both of you can point at.
activities.intendedInsight: Splitting the same whole into MORE equal parts makes each part SMALLER, so a unit fraction with the larger denominator is the smaller number — and a representation both parties can point at keeps a critique about the reasoning, not the person.

activities.title: When is a check really a proof? Convince a doubter
feedback: Draw out that 'it works in one example' is evidence to explore, not a proof; ask what a doubter could still object to and what would be needed to be sure for every case.
For the inverse check, point out that 35 + 46 = 81, not 71 — so a careful exact check actually reveals 35 is wrong. 'Close to' only hints at plausibility; it does not prove the answer is right.
If the child treats one checked case as settling a general claim, offer a claim where a second case breaks it, and discuss what changed.
activities.rationale: Empirical/example-based reasoning predominates at this age and the shift to deductive justification is slow and fragile; explicitly surfacing that checking examples does not prove a general claim targets a documented developmental step. The 'close to' inverse-check prompt extends this to verifying a single computation and is an agent-added illustration, conservatively framed as a proposal rather than a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Empirical/example-based reasoning predominates in this age range and the transition to deductive justification is slow and fragile; recognising that checking examples does not prove a general claim is a key developmental step.

Reasoning develops along a describe→explain→convince→justify→prove ladder, and children's reasoning frequently runs ahead of their ability to communicate it, so a teacher must elicit and scribe the reasoning rather than judge it by fluency of telling.
learnerActions: Given a general claim and a single example that fits it, decide whether checking that one example proves the claim for all cases.
Explain why one confirming example is not a proof, and what would be needed to be convinced for every case.
Evaluate a weak check such as: 'A classmate says 71 − 46 = 35 is fine because 35 + 46 is close to 71. Is that a good way to check? What does it actually tell you?'
activities.intendedInsight: Evidence that falls short of a complete argument — a single confirming example, or an approximate 'close to' check — does not establish or verify a claim; distinguishing 'it works here / it's roughly right' from 'it must always work / it is exactly right' is a key step toward justification.

activities.title: Compare-and-annotate launch: sound vs flawed argument
feedback: After the reveal, ask the child to re-explain the flaw without the annotation open.
Move promptly from recognising the flaw to constructing or critiquing a new one, so the productive half is exercised.
activities.rationale: A static correct-vs-flawed pair with tap-to-reveal annotations can seed critique and model reasons, but it shows arguments rather than eliciting the child's own chain or responding to their reasoning; treat it as a launch for talk, not as the assessment. Tap-to-reveal is an optional interaction example, not a required mechanism.
sourceClaims: SMP3: construct viable arguments AND critique the reasoning of others; elementary students construct arguments using concrete referents; they distinguish correct logic from flawed, and if there is a flaw, explain what it is; all grades can listen to others' arguments, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions.
learnerActions: Study a side-by-side pair of worked arguments for the same problem — one sound, one with a hidden error.
Tap each step to reveal the reason it does or does not follow, then say in your own words which argument holds and where the other breaks.
Use this only as a springboard: afterwards, construct your OWN correct chain or critique a fresh flawed example aloud.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing a correct and a flawed argument side by side can seed critique and vocabulary for 'why a step follows', but reading annotations is only a starting point for producing your own argument.

constraints: The productive half of this practice — constructing a multi-step argument and explaining a flaw in the child's own words — requires construction and talk; a scored fixed-answer format can test RECOGNISING a correct argument or spotting a flagged flawed step, but a 'spot the flawed step' multiple-choice item should be used only as a warm-up and its score should not be treated as evidence of the reasoning practice.

Static compare-and-annotate pairs are scaffolds: they can show and label arguments but cannot elicit the child's own chain or respond to their reasoning. Follow them immediately with construction or critique.

Error analysis is the practice: finding one clear faulty step and explaining it is the goal, not re-solving and comparing answers. Keep critique pointed at the shared representation so it targets the reasoning, not the person.
Scribe/revoice a child whose reasoning outruns their words; do not judge reasoning by fluency of telling or score it.

Distinguish an argument-skill gap from a prerequisite gap: if a child endorses 'always take the smaller from the larger', reteach the column-subtraction exchange concept with base-ten equipment before expecting critique of that algorithm.

This guidance is medium-flexible: a live partner, scribed classroom talk, paper worked examples, or a screen workspace can all carry it. Interaction examples (tile snapping, tapping a step, tap-to-reveal) are illustrative, not mandatory.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support the underlying teaching principle rather than proving any specific activity was tested.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 71 − 46 = 25 (correct in the source). The flawed worked example's '35' is explicitly the peer's error to be critiqued, never presented as a valid answer. The exchange explanation (1 becomes 11, 11 − 6 = 5; tens become 6, 6 − 4 = 2, giving 25) is sound and preserved. Note also 35 + 46 = 81 ≠ 71, so the classmate's 'close to 71' inverse check would in fact expose the error; this is surfaced in the weak-evidence activity's feedback.

Self-audit of derived-fact chain: 6×8 = 60 − 12 = 48 is correct (6×10=60, 6×2=12). Note a wording inconsistency in the source: pedagogy and the first evidence item present the chain as 'since 6×10=60 and 6×2=12, then 6×8=60−12=48', but the third evidence item phrases it as 'since 6×8=48 and 6×2=12, then 6×10=60 so 6×8=60−12=48', which assumes the conclusion (6×8=48) as a premise — a circular/garbled ordering. Activities use the sound forward direction (6×10 and 6×2 ⇒ 6×8); the circular phrasing was not propagated.

Self-audit of fraction claim: 1/3 > 1/5 is correct and justified by more equal parts of the same whole meaning smaller pieces; both are unit fractions so only the number of parts varies. No 'denominator rule flips' language is used; same-whole scoping applies to comparing represented portions, while the fractions remain comparable as numbers.

The original labelled a conversation artefact 'ideal' and 3D 'poor/adds nothing'. Those are catalog fit rankings, not established pedagogical laws, and have been removed; the dialogic and workspace activities are presented as complementary options with stated affordances and limits rather than a universal 'only talk teaches this' claim.
Internal identifiers (microTopic and reteach-prerequisite IDs) were stripped from the guidance; the exchange prerequisite is retained conceptually only.

Activity 4 blends example-based generalisation (supported by Hoyles & Küchemann) with critique of an approximate single-computation 'close to' check; the 'close to' strand is an agent extension and is not directly supported by a cited source, though it is conservatively framed and its exact-check correction (35+46=81≠71) is mathematically sound.

probeDeeper: 'Show me the exact line where the thinking first goes wrong — put your finger on it.'
'Why can't you just swap it round and do 6 take away 1? What would you have to do instead?'
'A different classmate says 71 − 46 = 35 is fine because 35 + 46 is close to 71. Is that a good way to check? What does it actually tell you?'
'Now build me a correct chain for 71 − 46 out loud — start with what 71 really is.'
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child locating the specific faulty STEP (flipping 1−6 into 6−1 instead of exchanging a ten) AND giving a reason grounded in place value (the 1 is part of 71, so you take a ten to make 11, then 11−6=5), rather than just announcing that 35 is the wrong answer.

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges the peer's argument by answer-agreement, not by the reasoning: 'it's wrong because I got 25' — re-solves and compares totals without ever locating or explaining the faulty step.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Redirect from answer to step: 'Don't tell me the right answer yet — show me the first line where their thinking stops being okay, and say why that line breaks.' Model once on a different flawed example.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child announces the correct answer or redoes the calculation but cannot point to WHICH step is wrong or WHY; treats 'different answer' as the whole critique.

errorPatterns.pattern: Accepts the smaller-from-larger step as fine — shares the bug: agrees you can 'just do 6 take 1' because 'you always take the little one from the big one.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: This is a genuine false belief about the algorithm — confront it with base-ten equipment: build 71, try to remove 6 ones, force the exchange. Reteach the exchange concept, not the argument skill.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child endorses the flipped subtraction, or hesitates only about the final total, treating column subtraction as digit-by-digit with the smaller digit always subtracted.

errorPatterns.pattern: Sees something is wrong and objects, but the objection stays at 'that's not right' — reasoning outruns communication, no because-clause emerges even though the child clearly senses the flaw.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT treat as not-knowing. Scribe/revoice: offer 'you can't do that because…?' and let the child complete it; point at base-ten blocks so the reason has something to attach to. The reasoning is present; only the telling lags.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Frowns, says 'no you can't do that' or 'it doesn't work like that' but cannot yet articulate the place-value reason when asked 'why not?'

responseLevels.gap: Only evaluates the answer ('it's 25, so they're wrong') or redoes the sum; cannot locate the faulty step or gives no reason.
responseLevels.full: Pinpoints the flipped-subtraction step AND explains the place-value reason it fails (the 1 stands for part of 71, so a ten must be exchanged to make 11−6=5), then reconstructs a correct because/therefore chain — and transfers the 'find the broken step and say why' move to a new flawed example unprompted.
responseLevels.partial: Locates the wrong step (the digit-flip) but explains it as 'that's not the rule' or restates the correct procedure without the place-value reason; can describe the steps but not why the flawed one breaks.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is how a classmate worked out 71 − 46. They wrote: '1 take away 6 — I can't, so I'll do 6 take away 1, that's 5. Then 7 take away 4 is 3. So the answer is 35.' Is their thinking okay? Talk me through what they did, step by step, and tell me where — if anywhere — it goes wrong and why.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who genuinely constructs and critiques arguments identifies the exact broken step and explains the place-value reason it fails; a child who only checks answers will say 'it's wrong, it should be 25' (or redo the sum) without ever naming which step broke or why — same surface verdict, completely different reasoning. Because the error is a real, well-documented one (the 'always take smaller from larger' / smaller-from-larger bug), a child reasoning correctly and one reasoning by answer-agreement give observably different responses.
