pedagogy.summary: Multiplying a fraction by a fraction (and by a whole number), understood as 'a fraction OF a fraction': (a/b) × (c/d) takes a/b of c/d, computed as (a×c)/(b×d) and written in simplest form. The area model makes it visible — shade c/d of a square one way, then a/b of that the other way, and the overlap is the product. The key realisations are that you multiply straight across (no common denominator, unlike addition) and that the product of two proper fractions is SMALLER than either factor, because you are taking part of a part.
bestPractices: Read the product as 'of': 2/3 × 4/5 is two-thirds OF four-fifths, and model it as a fraction of a fraction.
Use the area/'redefine the unit' model (IES Fig 7): shade one fraction vertically, the other horizontally, the crosshatch is the product over the b×d grid.
Establish that you multiply numerators and denominators directly — explicitly contrast with addition, which needs a common denominator, to block the imported rule.
Use estimation/benchmarks so a product smaller than both factors is expected (1/2 of 1/2 is 1/4), refuting 'multiplication makes bigger'.
Simplify products and, where possible, simplify before multiplying; convert improper products to mixed numbers.
Fold in the whole-number case (2/3 × 4 = 8/3) as c/d with d = 1.
keyRepresentations: Area model: unit square partitioned b×d, one fraction shaded each way, product = overlapping tiles
'Fraction of a fraction' bar: take c/d of the whole, then a/b of that piece
Number line for the fraction × whole case
Equation (a×c)/(b×d) aligned with the shaded grid count
commonMisconceptions: Leaves the denominator unchanged (2/3 × 1/3 = 2/3), over-generalising the common-denominator rule from addition to multiplication (IES).
Seeks a common denominator before multiplying, importing the addition procedure unnecessarily.
Believes the product must be bigger than the factors, so distrusts a smaller answer.
Computes the product but leaves it unsimplified (6/12 rather than 1/2).

learn.summary: Multiplying a fraction by a fraction, understood as 'a fraction OF a fraction': (a/b) × (c/d) takes a/b of c/d, computed as (a×c)/(b×d) and written in simplest form. An area model makes it visible — shade c/d of a unit square one way, a/b of that the other way, and the overlap is the product. The key realisations: you multiply straight across (no common denominator, unlike addition), and the product of two nonzero proper fractions is SMALLER than either factor, because you are taking part of a part. The whole-number case (2/3 × 4 = 8/3) folds in as c/d with d = 1: 2/3 of 4 means splitting 4 into 3 equal parts and taking 2 of them, which equals four copies of 2/3. For a whole number greater than 1, the product is larger than the fraction factor (for 1 it is equal, for 0 it is 0).

activities.title: Two-way area shader: a fraction of a fraction
feedback: If the overlap puzzles the learner, point to the two striped strips: the crosshatch is the region that is BOTH two-thirds and four-fifths-shaded — a smaller block inside both.
When a product like 6/12 appears, prompt: 'Can 6/12 be written with smaller numbers?' and check on the grid that 6/12 and 1/2 cover the same region.

A running 'is the answer bigger or smaller than each factor?' readout (where available) shows that for two PROPER fractions, taking part of a part gives a product smaller than either; note that the whole-number case (2/3 × 4 = 8/3) instead grows beyond the fraction factor 2/3, because it is repeated copies rather than a part of a part.
activities.rationale: A fraction of a fraction is exactly the two-way-shaded area model; partitioning both ways and highlighting the overlap makes 'product = crosshatched tiles' and 'smaller than each proper factor' concrete and manipulable. Letting the learner build and vary the shading, rather than view a finished picture, is where the understanding is constructed.
sourceClaims: Students often leave the denominator unchanged in fraction multiplication (e.g. 2/3 × 1/3 = 2/3) by over-generalising the addition procedure; teach the conceptual basis with the area model ('redefine the unit', Fig 7: 1/4 of 2/3) and unit fractions, showing 1/2 × 1/2 = half of a half = 1/4, so the product is smaller than either factor.

Multiply a fraction or whole number by a fraction, interpret (a/b) × q as a parts of a partition of q into b parts, find area of a rectangle with fractional sides by tiling, and write products in simplest form.
learnerActions: Shade 4/5 of a unit square with vertical stripes.
Shade 2/3 of the square with horizontal stripes, over the same region.
Watch the square rule itself into a 3×5 grid of fifteenths; count the crosshatched overlap (8 tiles) and read the product as 8/15.
Repeat for 3/4 × 2/3: see the overlap as 6 tiles out of 12, then use a simplify step to collapse 6/12 to 1/2 on the same picture.
Say each product in words using 'of': '2/3 × 4/5 is two-thirds OF four-fifths.'

Fold in a whole-number case: model 2/3 × 4 (as 2/3 × 4/1) using four unit squares, splitting each into thirds and shading 2/3 of each (equivalently, splitting the 4 wholes into 3 equal parts and taking 2), and read off 8 thirds = 8/3 = 2 2/3; optionally show the same on a number line, jumping 2/3 four times to land on 8/3.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying two proper fractions means taking a part of a part; the crosshatched overlap sits plainly INSIDE both striped regions, so the product is smaller than either proper factor, and the b×d grid gives the denominator automatically (no common denominator needed). The whole-number case is different: 2/3 × 4 is four copies of 2/3, so 8/3 is larger than 2/3.

activities.title: Contrast multiplication with the addition rule
feedback: If the learner keeps a denominator unchanged (2/3 × 1/3 → 2/3), model on the grid that 2/3 of 1/3 is a small block — 2/9 of the whole (2 tiles of 9), not 2/3.

If the learner hunts a common denominator first, ask which operation this is and whether equal-sized parts are needed to combine (that is addition); show the grid gives fifteenths automatically from 3×5 for 2/3 × 4/5.
activities.rationale: The leave-the-denominator and seek-a-common-denominator errors come from importing the addition schema. Explicitly contrasting the two operations on the same visual blocks the imported rule rather than just correcting the symbol manipulation.
sourceClaims: Students often leave the denominator unchanged in fraction multiplication (e.g. 2/3 × 1/3 = 2/3) by over-generalising the addition procedure; teach the conceptual basis with the area model ('redefine the unit', Fig 7: 1/4 of 2/3) and unit fractions, showing 1/2 × 1/2 = half of a half = 1/4, so the product is smaller than either factor.
learnerActions: Work out 2/3 × 1/3 on the area grid: shade 1/3 one way, take 2/3 of it the other way, and count the overlap — 2 tiles out of 9, i.e. 2/9.
State explicitly: the answer is NOT 2/3; two-thirds OF one-third is smaller than one-third.

Compare side by side with an addition problem that needs re-partitioning (e.g. 2/3 + 4/5): notice addition needs same-sized parts (a common denominator) before you can combine, while multiplication splits the unit BOTH ways and the b×d grid supplies the denominator.
Explain in words why you do not need a common denominator to multiply.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplication and addition of fractions run different procedures: addition needs a common denominator to combine like-sized parts; multiplication multiplies across because you are partitioning the unit in two directions.

activities.title: Compute and simplify (practice and self-check)
feedback: For a product that keeps an original denominator (e.g. 8/5 or 8/3 written for 2/3 × 4/5), point back to the grid: the tiles are fifteenths because the square was split 3×5, so the answer is 8/15.
For a correct but unsimplified answer (6/12), do not reteach the multiplication — it is right; only prompt for simplest form.
Use the benchmark 1/2 of 1/2 = 1/4 to confirm that a smaller-than-both answer is expected for two proper fractions, not an error.
activities.rationale: A scorable practice set can deliberately bait the leave-denominator and need-common-denominator errors and can isolate whether the simplifying step is secure. Recognition/fill-in items consolidate and diagnose; they check fluency rather than building the initial 'part of a part' concept, so they follow the construction activities.
sourceClaims: Multiply a fraction or whole number by a fraction, interpret (a/b) × q as a parts of a partition of q into b parts, find area of a rectangle with fractional sides by tiling, and write products in simplest form.
learnerActions: Complete fill-in-the-blank items of the form '2/3 × 4/5 = __/__ = __ (simplest form)'.
Answer a multiple-choice item for 2/3 × 1/3 where '2/3' (denominator left unchanged) is offered as a tempting wrong answer, and choose/justify the correct 2/9.
Finish a problem that yields 6/12 and reduce it to 1/2 as a required step.
Estimate before computing: predict whether each product is bigger or smaller than its factors.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency: multiply numerators and denominators directly, always put the result in simplest form, and expect the product of two proper fractions to be smaller than each factor.

constraints: Read every product as 'of' first (2/3 × 4/5 = two-thirds OF four-fifths) and model it before computing symbolically.
Explicitly contrast with addition: multiplication multiplies straight across and needs no common denominator; raise this whenever a learner tries to find one.
Always put products in simplest form, and where possible simplify before multiplying; convert improper products to mixed numbers (8/3 = 2 2/3).
The practice items check fluency and bait known errors; they do not by themselves build the 'part of a part' meaning, so pair them with the area-model construction rather than substitute for it.

A static finished picture (e.g. tapping to reveal 8/15 on a pre-shaded square) can serve as a reference anchor, but it does not let the learner build the shading or vary the factors, which is where the understanding forms — use it as a supplement, not the main activity.
The area model is planar; a flat grid is the natural representation here and a 3D rendering is not needed for this objective.

The claim 'product is smaller than either factor' is scoped to two nonzero proper fractions; when a proper fraction multiplies a whole number greater than 1, the product (e.g. 2/3 × 4 = 8/3) is smaller than the whole number but larger than the proper fraction factor.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 2/3 × 4/5 = 8/15 (correct); 3/4 × 2/3 = 6/12 = 1/2 (correct); 2/3 × 1/3 = 2/9 (correct); 2/3 × 4 = 8/3 = 2 2/3 (correct). The original row's next-move text said '2/3 of 1/3 is a small block, one-ninth of the whole': that is imprecise — 2/3 OF 1/3 = 2/9 (2 tiles of 9), while 1/9 would be 1/3 of 1/3. Activities use the corrected value 2/9 for 2/3 × 1/3; the mistaken 1/9 is recorded here only, never offered as a learner option.

The 'smaller than either factor' narrative is scoped to proper fractions throughout; activity[0] mixes proper×proper with the whole-number case, so the readout feedback now explicitly flags that 2/3 × 4 = 8/3 grows beyond 2/3 because it is repeated copies.

The original keyRepresentations list includes a number line for the fraction × whole-number case; it is retained as an optional scaffold in the whole-number action (2/3 jumped four times to 8/3) so the distinct representation is not lost.
CCSS/DfE source is marked verified:false in the row; treat it as a standards-alignment reference rather than evidence of efficacy.
Source claims cite the teaching principle (area model, multiply across, simplest form); they do not establish that the specific interactive shader described has been empirically tested.

probeDeeper: Say 2/3 × 4/5 in words using 'of' — what are you taking a part of? Show it on an area picture.
A friend says 2/3 × 1/3 = 2/3. But two-thirds OF one-third — is that bigger or smaller than 1/3? Can it be 2/3?
Do you need a common denominator to multiply? How is that different from adding?
Is 6/12 finished? Write it as simply as you can — how do you know it's the same amount?
assess.correctAnswer: 2/3 × 4/5 = 8/15. 3/4 × 2/3 = 6/12 = 1/2. Multiply numerators and denominators directly (no common denominator), then simplify.

errorPatterns.pattern: Leaves the denominator unchanged: '2/3 × 1/3 = 2/3' or keeps a shared denominator in the answer — imports the addition (common-denominator) rule into multiplication.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model on the area grid: 2/3 of 1/3 is a small block, one-ninth of the whole — not 2/3. Contrast explicitly: addition needs a common denominator, multiplication does not; here you split the unit BOTH ways (b×d).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Product keeps one of the original denominators unchanged; for 2/3 × 4/5 may write 8/5 or 8/3.

errorPatterns.pattern: Finds a common denominator before multiplying, converting 2/3 and 4/5 to fifteenths and then mis-combining — applies the addition setup to a multiplication.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask what operation this is and whether it needs equal-sized parts to combine (no — that's addition). Multiply across; show the grid gives fifteenths automatically from 3×5.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rewrites both fractions over a common denominator as a first step for a multiplication; often then adds or muddles.

errorPatterns.pattern: Multiplies correctly but leaves the answer unsimplified: writes 6/12 and stops.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach multiplying — it's correct. Prompt: 'can 6/12 be written with smaller numbers?' Check on the grid that 6/12 and 1/2 are the same region.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct unsimplified product (6/12); the operation is right, only simplest form is missing.

responseLevels.gap: Leaves the denominator unchanged or seeks a common denominator (importing the addition rule); products don't come from multiplying across.
responseLevels.full: Computes (a/b) × (c/d) = ac/bd, simplifies (6/12 → 1/2), justifies with an area or 'fraction of a fraction' model, recognises the product of proper fractions is smaller than each; transfers to a new pair including a whole number.
responseLevels.partial: Multiplies across correctly for the straightforward case but forgets to simplify, or can't justify with an area model / explain why the product is smaller — procedure without meaning.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these out, showing how (a picture is fine): 2/3 × 4/5, and 3/4 × 2/3. Give each answer in its simplest form.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Multiplying straight across contrasts with the addition habit: a child who leaves the denominator unchanged (2/3 × 1/3 → 2/3) or hunts a common denominator reveals they're running the addition procedure. 3/4 × 2/3 = 6/12 is chosen to require simplifying, isolating whether that final step is secure. Both products are smaller than their factors, probing whether the child accepts 'a fraction of a fraction is smaller'. Watching the method shows which operation's schema is running.

sources.claim: Students often leave the denominator unchanged in fraction multiplication (e.g. 2/3 × 1/3 = 2/3) by over-generalising the addition procedure; teach the conceptual basis with the area model ('redefine the unit', Fig 7: 1/4 of 2/3) and unit fractions, showing 1/2 × 1/2 = half of a half = 1/4, so the product is smaller than either factor.
sources.source: IES/WWC Practice Guide, Developing Effective Fractions Instruction for K–8 (Siegler et al., 2010), Rec 3

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 10–11 — read, write and compare decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form; compare with >, =, < on place-value meaning.
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5 read/write decimal numbers and recognise thousandths; Y6 consolidates comparison and ordering of decimals to three places.
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): 5.NBT.A.3 — 'Read, write, and compare decimals to thousandths. (a) Read and write decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form... (b) Compare two decimals to thousandths based on the meanings of the digits in each place, using >, =, < symbols.'
• Operational details: Read decimals as fractions of the whole ('five and sixty-two thousandths', not 'five point zero six two') to keep place meaning audible. Build expanded form with unit-fraction multipliers (3×(1/10)+9×(1/100)+2×(1/1000)). Compare by aligning place value left-to-right, using equalising trailing zeros (0.38 = 0.380) to defeat the 'longer-is-larger' error.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): 'Write five and sixty-two thousandths as a numeral.' Tier B: 'Compare 0.372 and 0.38 and justify.' Tier C: 'Write 347.392 in expanded form with unit fractions.'
bestPractices: Read decimals using place-value names ('sixty-two thousandths') rather than digit-by-digit 'point zero six two', so the meaning stays audible
Build expanded form with explicit unit-fraction multipliers (×1/10, ×1/100, ×1/1000) to bind each digit to its place
Compare left-to-right by place value, and equalise decimal length with trailing zeros (0.38 = 0.380) to expose 'longer-is-larger' as false
Use a thousandths grid / decimal place-value chart so 0.1, 0.01, 0.001 are seen as nested tenths-of-tenths
Move fluently among numeral, words and expanded form in both directions
keyRepresentations: Decimal place-value chart Ones . tenths hundredths thousandths
Thousandths grid (10×10×10 nesting) or 1000-cube partition of the unit
Three-pane numeral ↔ words ↔ expanded-form translator
Number line to hundredths/thousandths for comparison; trailing-zero alignment tool
commonMisconceptions: 'Longer decimal is larger' (0.372 > 0.38 because it has more digits)
'Shorter decimal is larger' (over-correcting to 'fewer digits = closer to whole')
Reading 0.062 as 'point zero sixty-two' and losing the thousandths meaning
Treating the decimal part as a whole number after the point (comparing 372 vs 38)
Misplacing digits in expanded form — attaching 1/10 to the hundredths digit

learn.summary: Learners aged 10–11 read, write and compare decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form, and compare with >, =, < based on place-value meaning. The central hurdle is the 'longer-is-larger' error (judging 0.372 > 0.38 because it has more digits). Guidance centres on place-value alignment, equalising with trailing zeros, naming decimals by their place ('sixty-two thousandths') to keep place meaning audible, and building expanded form with unit-fraction multipliers.

activities.title: Align and compare on a place-value chart
feedback: If a learner picks 0.372 as larger because '372 > 38', line the decimals up tenths-under-tenths and compare the tenths first (3 vs 3, equal), then the hundredths (7 vs 8), so 0.372 < 0.38. Padding to 0.380 shows equal-length strings so the digit-count argument disappears.
If the grid shading surprises them — the 'shorter' 0.38 shades MORE squares than the 'longer' 0.372 — ask them to restate why: 0.380 > 0.372 because the deciding place (hundredths) has 8 > 7.
Reinforce by naming the deciding place aloud: 'they are equal in the tenths, so the hundredths decides.'
activities.rationale: Comparison to thousandths depends on place-value alignment. Aligning columns, padding trailing zeros and identifying the first differing place makes the >,=,< decision follow from meaning rather than memorised rules, and directly targets the 'longer-is-larger' misconception. A grid and a number line give two further views of the same magnitude relationship.
sourceClaims: 5.NBT.A.3: read, write and compare decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form, comparing with >, =, < based on place-value meaning.
Y5 pupils read and write decimal numbers and recognise thousandths; Y6 consolidates comparing and ordering decimals to three places.
learnerActions: Write two decimals into aligned Ones . tenths . hundredths . thousandths rows, e.g. 0.372 and 0.38.
Pad the shorter decimal with a trailing zero so both have the same length: 0.38 becomes 0.380.
Compare left-to-right, place by place: tenths match (3 = 3), then at the hundredths the 7 and 8 differ, so 0.372 < 0.380.
State the comparison with the correct symbol and say which place decided it.
Shade each value on a thousandths grid (380 squares vs 372 squares) and check which covers more area.
Optionally, mark both decimals on a number line to hundredths/thousandths to see their relative positions as a second representation of the same comparison.
activities.intendedInsight: The length of a decimal does not determine its size; comparison is decided by the first place where the digits differ, read left-to-right. Trailing zeros make equal-length strings without changing value (0.38 = 0.380).

activities.title: Write spoken decimals keeping placeholder zeros
feedback: If a learner writes 5.62 for 'five and sixty-two thousandths', ask which place the word 'thousandths' names (the third place). The 2 must sit there, so 62 becomes 062: 5.062.
Check the reverse: ask them to read 5.62 and 5.062 aloud and notice these are different numbers (sixty-two hundredths vs sixty-two thousandths).
activities.rationale: Reading digit-by-digit ('point zero six two') hides place meaning. Naming the place of the final digit forces correct placement and surfaces the need for placeholder zeros, addressing the dropped-zero error.
sourceClaims: 5.NBT.A.3: read, write and compare decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form, comparing with >, =, < based on place-value meaning.
Y5 pupils read and write decimal numbers and recognise thousandths; Y6 consolidates comparing and ordering decimals to three places.
learnerActions: Read a decimal aloud using place-value names: 'five and sixty-two thousandths' rather than 'five point zero six two'.
Write 'five and sixty-two thousandths' as a numeral, anchoring the last digit in the named place: 'thousandths' means the 2 sits in the third decimal place.
Fill the places: 062 occupies tenths–hundredths–thousandths, giving 5.062.
Explain where the placeholder 0 goes and why it cannot be dropped.
Translate in both directions: given 5.062, say the words; given the words, write the numeral.
activities.intendedInsight: Naming a decimal by its place ('thousandths') tells you which column the last digit must occupy; a placeholder zero may be needed so the digits land in the correct places. 5.062 ≠ 5.62.

activities.title: Build expanded form with unit-fraction multipliers
feedback: If a learner writes 3×10 or 3×1 for the tenths digit, extend the ×10-to-the-left / ÷10-to-the-right pattern through the point: the place right of ones is 1/10, so the tenths digit is multiplied by 1/10.
If a digit is attached to the wrong unit fraction (e.g. 1/10 given to the hundredths digit), re-read the chart left-to-right naming each place in turn.
activities.rationale: Expanded form with explicit unit-fraction multipliers binds each digit to its place and prevents expanding decimal digits with whole-number multipliers. A static labelled number with revealed place values is a useful anchor but does not itself perform the comparison alignment, so pair it with the comparison activity.
sourceClaims: 5.NBT.A.3: read, write and compare decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form, comparing with >, =, < based on place-value meaning.
learnerActions: Tap or point to each digit of a number such as 347.392 and name its place and value.
Write the expanded form binding each digit to its place: 3×100 + 4×10 + 7×1 + 3×(1/10) + 9×(1/100) + 2×(1/1000).
Say what each digit is worth, e.g. 'the 9 is worth 9 hundredths, 9×(1/100)'.
Extend the ×10 pattern rightward through the decimal point: each place is one tenth of the place to its left (1/10, 1/100, 1/1000).
Check a tricky case: the tenths digit is multiplied by 1/10, NOT by 10 or 1.
activities.intendedInsight: Expanded form makes each digit's value explicit. Decimal places continue the base-ten pattern to the right with unit-fraction multipliers (1/10, 1/100, 1/1000), one tenth of the place to the left.

activities.title: Argue and justify a comparison (discussion)
feedback: If the learner argues from digit count, redirect to the tenths-under-tenths alignment and ask which place first differs.
Accept a correct answer only with a place-value justification, not just the right symbol.
activities.rationale: A discussion that baits and corrects the 'longer-is-larger' error can usefully surface a learner's reasoning, though learners should still manipulate aligned place values to resolve the comparison. Treat talk as a complement to the alignment work, not a replacement.
learnerActions: Respond to a prompt such as 'Which is bigger, 0.372 or 0.38, and prove it?'
Make a claim and justify it by aligning place values, not by counting digits.
Defend the claim against the 'longer-is-larger' bait by padding to 0.380 and comparing the hundredths.
Put the comparison into a sentence: '0.38 is bigger because they are equal in the tenths but 8 hundredths beats 7 hundredths.'
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to explain a comparison in words — citing the first differing place — demonstrates place-value understanding rather than rule-following.

activities.title: Check and order several decimals
feedback: For a comparison item, mark a digit-count answer wrong and prompt a place-value re-check with padded zeros.
For the ordering item, have the learner write all values to the same number of places first (0.300, 0.290, 0.305, 0.310), then order the aligned strings.
For the fill-in item, confirm the placeholder zero lands in the tenths place (5.062, not 5.62).
activities.rationale: Comparing, writing from words and ordering mixed-length decimals checks the key skills and misconceptions. This verifies understanding built through manipulation and discussion; it does not by itself build the alignment intuition.
sourceClaims: Y5 pupils read and write decimal numbers and recognise thousandths; Y6 consolidates comparing and ordering decimals to three places.
learnerActions: Compare 0.372 and 0.38 and choose >, = or <, rejecting any answer based purely on digit count.
Complete 'five and sixty-two thousandths = ___' with the correct numeral (5.062).
Order four decimals of unequal length (e.g. 0.3, 0.29, 0.305, 0.31) by padding to equal length and comparing left-to-right, giving 0.29 < 0.3 < 0.305 < 0.31.
Explain each placement rather than only giving the final order.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading, writing and comparing decimals can be verified across numeral and word forms and by ordering, including deliberately mixed-length cases that expose the 'longer-is-larger' trap.

constraints: Read decimals with place-value names ('sixty-two thousandths') rather than digit-by-digit 'point zero six two', so the place meaning stays audible.
Equalise decimal length with trailing zeros (0.38 = 0.380) when comparing; this exposes 'longer-is-larger' as false without changing value.
Watch for over-correction to 'shorter-is-larger' (fewer digits = closer to the whole); length alone decides nothing — only the first differing place does.
5.062 is not 5.62: keep placeholder zeros when a spoken place name requires the final digit to sit further right.

A static labelled number with revealed place values anchors reading and expanded form but cannot carry out the padding/alignment that resolves comparisons; use it alongside the comparison activity, not instead of it.
Recognition or multiple-choice checks verify the skill but do not require the learner to construct alignment reasoning independently; include tasks where they write and justify.

Grid shading, column-highlight tools and a number line to hundredths/thousandths are illustrative, complementary supports for the comparison mechanism, not required equipment; the reasoning can also be carried out on paper by writing values to equal length.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The original row's 'quiz' companion and 'conversation' options were retained as the check/ordering activity and the discussion activity respectively, with product and fit-ranking vocabulary removed.
The source keyRepresentations listed a 'number line to hundredths/thousandths for comparison'; it is reinstated as an optional comparison representation in Activity 1 and the constraints.

The source claimed decimal notation is 'planar and symbolic' so '3D adds no explanatory power' for this topic; this is a reasonable scoping judgement for comparison/notation but is not an established universal law, so it is not asserted as one here.

The original framing that an interactive comparator uniquely makes comparison 'felt, not memorised' is softened: alignment, grid and trailing-zero reasoning can also be done on paper; the interactive example is one concrete medium.
The second CCSS-M source is marked unverified in the row (verified:false); its claim is retained as stated but not treated as independently confirmed.
Activity 5's insight was narrowed to the forms it actually tests (numeral/word forms and ordering); expanded-form checking remains in Activity 3.

probeDeeper: Line up 0.372 and 0.38 by place — which is bigger and why?
Write sixty-two thousandths on its own — where does the 0 go?
In 347.392, what is the 9 worth?

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Longer decimal is larger': says 0.372 > 0.38 because 372 > 38 / it has more digits
errorPatterns.nextMove: Align by place (tenths under tenths); compare tenths first (3 vs 8). Pad with a zero (0.380) to see equal-length strings.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The decimal with more digits is chosen regardless of place value.

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops the placeholder zero in a spoken decimal: writes 5.62 for 'five and sixty-two thousandths'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor the last digit in the named place: 'thousandths' means the 2 sits in the third place, so 062 fills tenths–hundredths–thousandths → 5.062.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Sixty-two thousandths is placed in the tenths/hundredths instead of hundredths/thousandths.

errorPatterns.pattern: Expanded form mishandles the fractional places: writes 3×10 or 3×1 for the tenths instead of 3×(1/10)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Extend the ×10 pattern rightward through the point: each place is 1/10 of the one to its left (1/10, 1/100, 1/1000).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Decimal digits are expanded with whole-number multipliers.

responseLevels.gap: Uses 'longer-is-larger', drops placeholder zeros, or expands decimals with whole-number multipliers.
responseLevels.full: Reads, writes (numerals/words/expanded) and compares decimals to thousandths by place value, keeping placeholder zeros.
responseLevels.partial: Reads/writes tidy decimals but slips on comparisons of unequal length or on spoken thousandths.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Watch across forms. 'Which is bigger, 0.372 or 0.38? Line them up to decide. Write “five and sixty-two thousandths” as a decimal. Then write 347.392 in expanded form.' Watch the comparison reasoning and the placeholder zero in the thousandths write.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 0.372 vs 0.38 is the classic 'longer-is-larger' trap — a child comparing digit-strings picks 0.372. 'Sixty-two thousandths' needs a placeholder zero in the tenths (5.062), catching the child who writes 5.62. Expanded form checks each decimal place carries its unit fraction.

pedagogy.summary: Children find different combinations of coins that make the same total — e.g. 50p as one 50p, or two 20p and a 10p, or five 10p. The valuable skill is doing this SYSTEMATICALLY (starting from the largest coin, or swapping one coin for equivalent smaller ones) rather than at random, and understanding that the sets are equal because their VALUES sum to the same total even though the coins differ. A key constraint: only real denominations exist — there is no 8p coin, but any total can be built from the coins that do exist.
bestPractices: Work with real coins; build one total several different ways
Model a systematic method: start with the largest coin, or swap a coin for equivalent smaller ones (50p to two 20p + 10p)
Ask 'can you find another way?' and record each combination in an organised list
Discuss why the sets are equal — the same total value, different coins
Reinforce that only real denominations exist (no 8p coin), but any total can be made from them
keyRepresentations: Real coins arranged into equal-value sets
A part-whole model (total = these coins / those coins)
An organised list or table of combinations
Swapping one coin for equivalent smaller coins
commonMisconceptions: Uses a non-existent coin (e.g. an '8p') to make a total
Finds combinations unsystematically, repeating some and missing others
Tracks the number of coins rather than their total value
Thinks a set with more coins must be worth more, so two ways can't be equal

learn.summary: Year 2 learners (ages 6-7) find different combinations of real coins that make the same total (e.g. 50p as one 50p, or two 20p + a 10p, or five 10p). The core skill is working SYSTEMATICALLY — starting from the largest coin, or swapping one coin for equivalent smaller ones — and understanding that different coin sets are equal because their VALUES sum to the same total, even though the coins differ. A key constraint: only real denominations exist (there is no 8p coin), but any total can be built from the coins that do exist.

activities.title: Build a target several ways with a live-updating total
feedback: If a learner grabs for a coin that doesn't exist (e.g. an '8p'), note that there is no such coin and ask which real coins could make that part of the total instead.

When a learner finds a new combination, ask 'Can you find another way?' and add it to the organised list. Only ask 'How could you be SURE you've found them all?' when the coins allowed are limited (e.g. only 10p, 20p and 50p for 50p), because with every coin from 1p upwards there are hundreds of ways to make 50p.
If two valid ways look very different, pause on the moment the totals match: 'This set looks completely different but is worth exactly the same — why?'
activities.rationale: The National Curriculum requires Year 2 pupils to find different combinations of coins equal to the same amount. A live total and an organised record support the equal-value idea and encourage systematic enumeration. A live-updating total and an organised board are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete, not a required product; the same work can be done with real coins by hand.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils should 'find different combinations of coins that equal the same amounts of money'.
White Rose Y2 Money teaches making the same amount in different ways using part-whole models, and documents pupils counting the number of coins rather than their value.
learnerActions: Take a target amount (e.g. 50p) and drag or place real-denomination coins into a tray until they reach the total.
Watch a running total so you can see when the tray reaches exactly 50p.
Once a valid way is found, record it on an organised board or list of 'ways to make 50p', then find another distinct way.
Work from the largest coin first, or swap a coin for equivalent smaller ones, so the search is organised rather than random.
Only real coins are available on the shelf (no 8p), so every solution is one that could really be paid.
activities.intendedInsight: Many different coin sets can share the same total value; building each one and watching the total confirm the target makes 'equal value, different coins' directly visible.

activities.title: Swap a coin for equivalent smaller coins without changing the total
feedback: If a learner thinks the five-10p set is 'more' than a single 50p because it has more coins, count the VALUE of each set to the same total and show that more coins can equal fewer coins in value.
Prompt: 'You made 30p with three 10p. Can you make 30p using a 20p? What else do you need?' to rehearse swap reasoning.
Reinforce that the swap did not change the amount, only the coins used.
activities.rationale: Swapping directly targets the misconception that more coins means more money, and models a systematic route between combinations. A live swap action is an optional interaction example; the same reasoning can be done with real coins by hand.
sourceClaims: NCETM guidance notes that a mathematically correct total may use a non-existent coin, and cautions: 'For example, we do not have an 8p coin, but any value can be made of existing denominations of coins'; it also directs attention to making an amount 'in the fewest number of coins', focusing on value rather than count.
White Rose Y2 Money teaches making the same amount in different ways using part-whole models, and documents pupils counting the number of coins rather than their value.
learnerActions: Start with one way of making the total (e.g. a single 50p).
Swap one coin for equivalent smaller coins — lift the 50p and replace it with two 20p and a 10p — and check the total is unchanged.
Try other swaps (e.g. 30p made as three 10p; swap to 20p + 10p) and confirm each keeps the same value.
Describe in words why the new set equals the old one: the coin values still sum to the same amount.
activities.intendedInsight: Exchanging one coin for equivalent smaller coins keeps the total fixed, so a set with more coins can be worth exactly the same as a set with fewer coins.

activities.title: Sort and match coin sets to totals (recognition practice)
feedback: If a learner accepts a set that relies on a non-existent 8p coin, point out there is no 8p coin and ask which real coins could make that value.
If a set is wrongly rejected, re-count its value to the total together.
activities.rationale: Recognition tasks give quick practice judging totals and catching the invented-coin error. As noted in the constraints, selecting from given sets checks judgement of value but does not itself require the learner to construct combinations, so it should accompany building tasks, not replace them.
sourceClaims: NCETM guidance notes that a mathematically correct total may use a non-existent coin, and cautions: 'For example, we do not have an 8p coin, but any value can be made of existing denominations of coins'; it also directs attention to making an amount 'in the fewest number of coins', focusing on value rather than count.
learnerActions: Decide which of several coin sets make a given total (e.g. 'which of these make 50p?').
Sort sets into 'makes 50p' and 'does not make 50p'.
Match a total to a valid coin set.
Spot and reject any set that relies on a non-existent coin, such as an invented 8p.
activities.intendedInsight: Checking whether a coin set reaches a stated total, and rejecting sets that use invented coins, reinforces that value is what matters and that only real denominations may be used.

activities.title: Pay a different way — shopkeeper talk (optional spoken extension)
feedback: If the learner stops after one way, prompt 'Is there another way to make 50p?' and keep a shared list of ways found.
Ask 'Could you make 50p with an 8p coin? Why not?' to surface the real-denominations constraint.
activities.rationale: A spoken prompt can elicit further combinations and their justification. It is best paired with real coins or an organised record, because a spoken exchange alone does not display systematic enumeration as clearly.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils should 'find different combinations of coins that equal the same amounts of money'.
learnerActions: Respond to a shopkeeper asking 'Can you pay 50p a different way?' by naming or laying out another valid coin set.
Explain aloud why the new way is worth the same as the first.
Be challenged to find yet another way, and, when only a few coin types are allowed (e.g. 10p, 20p and 50p), to say how you could be sure you've found them all.
activities.intendedInsight: Explaining and justifying equal-value combinations aloud rehearses the reasoning and the language of 'same total, different coins'.

constraints: Use only real coin denominations; there is no 8p (or 3p) coin, though any total can be built from the coins that do exist.

Systematic enumeration develops with age and practice: treat random searching not as an error to punish but as a cue to model one system (largest coin first, then swap down) and record each way on an organised list.
Recognition and sorting tasks (choosing which given sets make a total) check judgement of value but do not require independent construction of combinations; include building tasks for production.
A static 'ways to make 50p' poster can display combinations but does not let the learner build or swap them; use it as a reference scaffold, not the main activity.

Assess by watching HOW combinations are generated (systematic vs random, real coins vs an invented coin) and by asking why two different sets are equal — this distinguishes secure combining from guesswork and catches the more-coins-means-more-money misconception.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original row rated a 3D interactive 'poor' with the claim '3D adds nothing' and framed the quiz as merely scoring; these are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws, and have been softened or dropped. The source claims do not establish comparative efficacy or necessity of any one medium.
The White Rose source (part-whole models; coin-counting misconception) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its specifics as unconfirmed.

Interaction examples (live total, drag coins, swap tool, organised board) are illustrative of the learning mechanism and optional, not mandatory implementation details. An earlier draft mentioned a 'recolour' action not in the original design notes; it has been removed.

'These two piles look different — one has more coins. Are they really the same amount? How do you know?'
'Could you make 50p with an 8p coin? Why not?'
'You made 30p with three 10p. Can you make 30p using a 20p? What else do you need?' (swap reasoning)

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses a non-existent coin (e.g. an '8p' or '3p') to make a total
errorPatterns.nextMove: Keep only real coins available; check each combination is payable with actual denominations, noting that any total can still be made from the coins that exist.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not treat random searching as an error to correct — systematic enumeration develops with age and practice. Instead, model one system (start from the largest coin, then swap down) and record each way on an organised list so the child sees the pattern.

errorPatterns.pattern: Tracks the number of coins rather than total value — thinks a set with more coins is worth more, so two ways can't be equal
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the VALUE of each set to the same total; show that more coins can equal fewer coins in value.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the five-10p set is 'more' than the single 50p because it has more coins

responseLevels.gap: Uses invented coins or repeats one combination; judges sets by number of coins.
responseLevels.full: Systematically finds multiple valid combinations for a total using real denominations, and explains they are equal because the coin values sum to the same amount.
responseLevels.partial: Finds two or three valid combinations with real coins, but searches at random and can't be sure they are all found, or is unsure why the sets are equal.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set a make-the-total task and WATCH how the child works: (1) 'Show me 50p using these coins. Now make 50p a DIFFERENT way. And another way.' Watch for use of real denominations only, an organised approach, and whether they track value.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching HOW they generate combinations (systematic vs random, real coins vs an invented 8p) separates secure combining from guesswork; asking why two sets are equal catches a child who thinks more coins must mean more money.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 6–7 (Year 2). SKIP COUNTING in 3s, forwards and backwards from 0 — extends the equal-groups idea to a less familiar step size and prepares the 3× table. DfE explicitly links it to understanding 'a third'.
• Standards — UK (DfE): NC Year 2 verbatim 'count in steps of 2, 3, and 5 from 0, and in 10s from any number, forward and backward'; guidance: 'they count in multiples of 3 to support their later understanding of a third.'
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): counting in 3s is not a named CCSS skip-count (US names 5s/10s/100s at 2.NBT.2); it sits within multiplication foundations of Grade 2–3 (2.OA.4 arrays; 3.OA equal groups and 3× facts). The UK names 3s a year earlier than the US formalises the 3× table.
• Operational details: Because 3s don't align to hundred-square columns, the shaded pattern is a DIAGONAL stripe — use it to show 3s still form a regular pattern (defeats 'there's no pattern'). Count backwards from a multiple (30, 27, 24…) as well as forwards. Tie each step to one more group of three (arrays, repeated addition) and forward to the 3× table and to thirds.
• Checkpoint: Tier A counts in 3s from 0 to ~30 forwards. Tier B counts in 3s to at least 36 and backwards from 30. Tier C predicts the next multiple of 3 using the diagonal hundred-square pattern and links 3s to groups of three / the 3× table.
bestPractices: Show 3s as a DIAGONAL pattern on the hundred square so children see 3s are regular even though they don't line up in columns (counters the 'no pattern' feeling).
Insist on backward counting from a multiple (30, 27, 24…) — harder and needed for the full table.
Tie each step to one more group of three (arrays / repeated addition) and forward to the 3× table and 'a third' (the DfE link).
Play spot-the-multiple-of-3 on the hundred square, not only counting up from 0, so multiples are recognised anywhere.
keyRepresentations: Hundred square with multiples of 3 shaded (diagonal stripes).
Number line with equal 3-jumps.
Arrays / groups of three (bridge to the 3× table and thirds).
Backward-count track from 30.
commonMisconceptions: Feeling 3s have 'no pattern' because they don't form neat columns (they form diagonals).
Reciting 3s as isolated rote with no link to groups of three or the 3× table.
Being able to count forward but not backward in 3s.
Losing the step when crossing a decade (…18, 21…) — miscounting the +3 across the ten.

learn.summary: For ages 6–7 (UK Year 2): count in 3s forwards and backwards from 0, extending equal-groups thinking to a less familiar step size and seeding the 3× table and the idea of 'a third'. The central insight is that multiples of 3 still form a regular pattern — a diagonal pattern of repeating parallel lines on a hundred square — even though they do not line up in neat columns like 2s, 5s and 10s. Each step should be tied to one more group of three, and backward counting and mid-sequence continuation practised as skills in their own right.

activities.title: The diagonal reveal: shading 3s on a hundred square
feedback: If a child says 3s have 'no pattern', draw attention to the diagonal lines of shaded squares: the pattern is a slope rather than a column.
If the +3 step is lost crossing a decade — for example adding two and saying 20, or otherwise jumping the step and missing 21 as the next multiple — slow down at the ten and re-anchor: 18 + 3 = 21.
Optional interaction: let the child tap a shaded multiple to reveal its group of three, or watch cells recolour live as they step, so the pattern builds visibly.
activities.rationale: Showing 3s as a diagonal pattern on the hundred square makes their regularity visible and addresses the common sense that 3s are irregular because they don't form columns. Live shading and tap-to-reveal are optional ways to make the pattern concrete.
sourceClaims: Multiples of 3 form a diagonal pattern on the hundred square; showing the pattern counters the sense that 3s are irregular.
Year 2 verbatim: 'count in steps of 2, 3, and 5 from 0, and in 10s from any number, forward and backward'; guidance: 'they count in multiples of 3 to support their later understanding of a third.'
learnerActions: Step forward in 3s from 0 (3, 6, 9, 12…), shading or marking each multiple on a hundred square as you say it.
Notice that, unlike the vertical columns 5s and 10s make, the multiples of 3 march down the grid as repeating parallel diagonal lines (a diagonal pattern).
Use the diagonal pattern to predict the next multiple before you reach it, then check.
Play 'spot the multiple of 3' by pointing to multiples anywhere on the grid, not only counting up from 0.
Pay special attention to crossing each decade (…18, 21… and …27, 30…) so the +3 step is not lost across the ten.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiples of 3 are patterned, not random — the diagonal pattern lets you predict the next multiple and recognise multiples anywhere, countering the feeling that '3s have no pattern'.

activities.title: Number-line 3-jumps and groups of three
feedback: If a child recites 3s with no sense of grouping, lay out the arrays or counters so each jump matches a visible group of three.
Praise linking the jump count to the number of groups (e.g. 'five jumps, five threes, fifteen').
activities.rationale: Tying each skip-count step to an equal group bridges rote counting to multiplicative understanding and to the DfE link with thirds, preventing isolated rote recitation.
sourceClaims: Skip counting builds equal-groups understanding toward the multiplication tables (3.OA); arrays represent groups of three.
Year 2 verbatim: 'count in steps of 2, 3, and 5 from 0, and in 10s from any number, forward and backward'; guidance: 'they count in multiples of 3 to support their later understanding of a third.'
learnerActions: Make equal jumps of 3 along a number line, saying the multiple you land on each time.
For each jump, add one more group of three — show it with an array or counters (three counters per group) alongside the jump.
Connect 'four jumps of 3' to 'four groups of three' (four threes make 12) and to building up the 3× table.
Briefly link three equal groups making a whole to the idea of 'a third'.
activities.intendedInsight: Each step of 3 is one more group of three; stepping in 3s is the foundation of the 3× table and connects to thirds.

activities.title: Counting back and entering mid-sequence
feedback: If backward counting collapses or reverts to forward, slow to short runs with physical hops back along the line — treat it as a distinct skill.
If a child restarts at 3 to continue a mid-sequence, model 'the step is always +3, so add 3 to the last number you were given' and practise from several starting points; do not mark this wrong.

If each next multiple is reached by sub-counting ones under the breath (18… 19, 20, 21), do NOT drill for speed; make the step visible with number-line jumps of 3 and the diagonal pattern, and let fluency grow with exposure.
activities.rationale: Backward counting and mid-sequence entry are harder than the forward chant and are needed for the full table; sub-counting by ones is developmental and is addressed by making the +3 step visible rather than by speed drills.
sourceClaims: Year 2 verbatim: 'count in steps of 2, 3, and 5 from 0, and in 10s from any number, forward and backward'; guidance: 'they count in multiples of 3 to support their later understanding of a third.'
learnerActions: Count backwards in 3s from a multiple: 30, 27, 24… down to 0, using physical or drawn hops back along a number line.
Practise short backward runs (e.g. 12 → 0) as their own skill, not expecting it to come free with forward counting.
Continue a sequence from the middle: given 12, 15, 18, say the next number (and keep going) without restarting from 3.
Say the number just before a given multiple (e.g. what comes before 12 in the 3s).
activities.intendedInsight: Backward counting and continuing from any point are separate skills: the step is always +3 (or −3), so you can add or subtract 3 from the last number rather than restarting.

activities.title: Retrieval and oral fluency
feedback: Correct answers confirm the step; errors signal where to return to the hundred square or number line (e.g. decade crossings or backward runs).
Oral partner counting gives backward-count practice and fluency; pair it with the seen diagonal pattern on a hundred square so the visible pattern reinforces the underlying idea.
activities.rationale: Spaced retrieval and oral partner counting build fluency and expose children who only chant well-patterned sequences; these check and reinforce the understanding built visually rather than replacing it.
learnerActions: Answer quick questions: 'What is the next number in 3s?', fill a missing multiple in a sequence, put multiples of 3 in order, and count back in 3s.
With a partner, count aloud in 3s forwards and backwards, taking turns to say the next number.
Answer 'What's 3 more than 18?' (21) and 'What comes just before 12 in the 3s?' (9).
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency means stepping by three both ways and entering the sequence at any point, not only chanting up from 0.

constraints: Quick-recall questions and recognising/choosing the next multiple check and build fluency but do not by themselves elicit independent counting or the pattern insight; pair them with counting aloud and with the visible diagonal pattern.
Oral partner counting supports fluency and backward practice but does not show the diagonal pattern; combine it with a seen hundred square or number line.
Do not drill for speed when a child sub-counts intervals by ones — treat it as developmental and make the +3 step visible; fluency grows with exposure.
Treat backward counting and mid-sequence continuation as distinct skills to be practised, not as automatically following from forward counting.
The diagonal on the hundred square is a flat 2D pattern; it needs to be seen, but added depth/3D is not required to teach it.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three cited sources were flagged unverified in the source row (the CCSS 3.OA reference and the NCETM diagonal-pattern guidance); the DfE Year 2 claim was marked verified. The diagonal-pattern claim underpins the headline activity but rests on an unverified citation.

On a standard 10-wide hundred square, multiples of 3 form several repeating parallel diagonal lines rather than literally one stripe; the wording was adjusted to 'diagonal pattern/lines' while keeping the original insight that 3s are regular.

The decade-crossing feedback in activity 1 was corrected so it no longer treats sub-counting-by-ones (which still lands on 21) as a decade-crossing error; that developmental pattern is handled in activity 3.

The original row rated a conversation/oral-count approach as only 'possible' and 3D as adding nothing; these were catalog fit rankings. They are reframed here as affordances/limits (oral counting aids fluency but lacks the visible pattern; depth is not needed) rather than universal claims that one medium alone can teach the concept.

The pedagogy section's Tier A/B/C checkpoint descriptions were not carried verbatim into the learner-facing activities; they overlap with the assess gap/partial/full response levels reflected across activities.

probeDeeper: What's 3 more than 18?
Count back: 21, 18, 15…
What number comes just before 12 in the 3s?
How could the hundred square help you see the 3s?
assess.correctAnswer: Recites 3, 6, 9, …, 30 and back 30, 27, …, 0 without sub-counting each interval by ones; continues 12, 15, 18, 21… — stepping by three each time.

errorPatterns.pattern: sub-counts the interval by ones — gets each next multiple of 3 by counting up three ones under the breath rather than knowing the step; slow and error-prone backward
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT drill for speed — fluency grows with exposure; use number-line jumps of 3 and the diagonal 3s stripes on a hundred square to make the step visible
errorPatterns.revealedBy: audible or finger sub-counting between terms; noticeably slower on 3s than on 5s

errorPatterns.pattern: forward-only — counts up in 3s but backward counting breaks down or reverts to forward
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT expect backward to come free with forward — practise short backward runs (12→0) with physical hops on a number line as its own skill
errorPatterns.revealedBy: errors when counting back from 30

errorPatterns.pattern: can't enter mid-sequence — given 12, 15, 18 can't find the next without restarting from 3
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT mark wrong — model 'the step is always +3, so add 3 to the last one' and practise continuing from various points; this matures with practice
errorPatterns.revealedBy: restarts at 3 to work up to the continuation point

responseLevels.gap: Cannot sustain counting in 3s, or only by counting every one in between; backward counting fails.
responseLevels.full: Counts in 3s forwards and backwards fluently, steps by three without sub-counting, and continues the pattern from any given multiple.
responseLevels.partial: Counts up in 3s from 0 but sub-counts by ones for each step, or cannot count back or continue from mid-sequence.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Count in 3s from 0 up to 30. Now count backwards in 3s from 30 down to 0. Then here's part of a sequence — 12, 15, 18, __ — tell me the next number and keep it going. (Watch for sub-counting by ones, whether backward holds, and whether they can continue from mid-sequence.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 3s lack the strong last-digit rhythm of 2s/5s/10s, so this exposes children who only chant well-patterned sequences. A secure child steps by three fluently both ways and enters mid-sequence; a shakier child sub-counts the intervening ones ('18… 19, 20, 21'), especially going backward, or manages the forward chant but collapses in reverse.

pedagogy.summary: Mentally adding or subtracting tens to a three-digit number extends the ones-anchor idea one column up: only the tens digit changes, UNLESS the calculation bridges a hundred (then the hundreds digit changes too). Children reuse decade facts (7 tens ± some tens) while keeping the hundreds and ones fixed. It builds directly on finding 10 more/less and on three-digit place value, taught with a place-value chart and a hundred-marked number line.
bestPractices: Anchor the hundreds and ones; operate only on the tens — 345+40 keeps '3_5' and works 40+40 in the tens
Reuse decade bonds and the make-ten idea at the scale of tens for bridging a hundred (372+40 = 372+28+12... via 380/400)
Contrast a non-bridging case (345+40) with a bridging case (372+40) so the child sees when the hundreds digit moves
Build from '10 or 100 more/less' — adding 40 is four steps of ten
Ask the child to predict which digits change before calculating (DfE evidence)
keyRepresentations: Place-value / Gattegno chart (tens row moves; bridging cascades to hundreds)
Number line marked in tens, around the nearest hundred
Base-ten blocks (add/remove ten-rods, exchange at the hundred)
Hundred-square rows (moving down = +10)
Partitioning jotting (372 = 370 + 2)
commonMisconceptions: Changing the ones digit instead of the tens (345+40 given as 349)
Failing to bridge a hundred: 372+40 given as 3(11)2 or keeping the tens at 11
Smaller-from-larger in the tens when subtracting bridges down (a hundred not decomposed)
Believing 'only the tens digit ever changes', so bridging-a-hundred cases are mishandled

learn.summary: Mentally adding or subtracting multiples of ten to a three-digit number extends the '10 more/less' idea one column up: usually only the tens digit changes, UNLESS the calculation bridges a hundred, in which case the hundreds digit also changes. Children anchor the hundreds and ones, reuse decade facts in the tens (e.g. 7 tens ± some tens), and use make-ten at the scale of tens when crossing a hundred. Teach with a place-value chart and a number line marked in tens around the nearest hundred, deliberately contrasting non-bridging and bridging cases so the exception is visible.

activities.title: Contrast a non-bridging and a bridging case on a place-value chart
feedback: If the child gives 349 for 345 + 40, they treated 40 as 4 and changed the ones. Re-anchor with the chart: 40 is four tens, so it joins the tens; connect it to '10 more' done four times.

If the child leaves eleven tens for 372 + 40 (writing 3(11)2 / 3112) or keeps the hundreds unchanged, show on the tens number line that the jump crosses 400; use make-ten at the scale of tens (add 28 to reach 400, then 12), or exchange ten ten-rods for one hundred with base-ten blocks.
Reinforce correct predictions by asking the child to name the moment the hundreds digit changes and why.
activities.rationale: Year 3 pupils are expected to add and subtract a three-digit number and tens mentally. Bridging a hundred reuses the make-ten strategy at a larger scale, built on finding 10/100 more or less and on unitising tens, so an explicit non-bridging vs bridging contrast isolates when the hundreds digit moves.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils add and subtract mentally a three-digit number and tens.
Bridging a multiple of ten (here a hundred) reuses the make-ten strategy at a larger scale, built on finding 10/100 more or less and on unitising tens.
learnerActions: Start with 345 on a place-value chart and add 40 mentally: before calculating, predict which digits will change and which will stay the same.
Confirm that only the tens change (4 tens + 4 tens = 8 tens), giving 385, with the hundreds (3) and ones (5) unchanged.
Now try 372 + 40, again predicting first: notice the tens reach eleven, so a hundred is composed and the hundreds digit ticks up — resolve to 412 (reach 400 by adding 28, then add the remaining 12).
Say aloud how 372 + 40 is like 7 tens + 4 tens = 11 tens, and point to where the extra hundred comes from.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding or subtracting tens changes only the tens digit UNLESS the running total of tens crosses a hundred, in which case a hundred is composed (or decomposed) and the hundreds digit changes too — the same kind of exception children already met when crossing a ten.

activities.title: Bridge a hundred downwards when subtracting
feedback: If the child keeps the hundreds at 4 for 431 − 50, show on the tens number line that the jump must cross below 400, and decompose a hundred into ten tens with blocks.
If the child does 5 − 3 in the tens (smaller-from-larger, giving 421), check by adding back: 421 + 50 = 471, not 431, and 421 is only 10 less than 431. Then redo by crossing 400.
Confirm 381 and ask the child to explain where the hundred was decomposed.
activities.rationale: Subtraction that bridges down is the same unitising/make-ten idea applied in reverse; an amount check (is the answer exactly 50 less, and does adding 50 back return the start?) and a tens number line expose the common 'smaller-from-larger' and 'hundreds don't move' errors.
sourceClaims: Bridging a multiple of ten (here a hundred) reuses the make-ten strategy at a larger scale, built on finding 10/100 more or less and on unitising tens.
learnerActions: Work out 431 − 50 mentally, first predicting whether the hundreds digit will change.
Check the size: subtracting 50 should make the answer exactly 50 less than 431, which takes it below 400. Is your answer below 400, and does adding 50 back give 431?
Use a number line marked in tens to show the jump crosses below 400 (431 − 31 = 400, then − 19 more = 381).
If using base-ten blocks, decompose one hundred into ten tens before removing five tens.
activities.intendedInsight: Subtracting tens can bridge a hundred downwards, decomposing a hundred into ten tens; the hundreds digit then decreases, and the result must be smaller than the start.

activities.title: Predict and sort: will the hundreds digit change?
feedback: If a bridging item is sorted as non-bridging: for addition items add the tens together (e.g. 7 tens + 4 tens = 11 tens, which exceeds nine tens); for subtraction items check whether the tens removed exceed the tens in the number (e.g. 431 has 3 tens but 5 tens are removed), which forces crossing below a hundred.
Use a mixed-item check with a 3(11)2-style wrong answer for 372 + 40 (shown as 3112, or as 312 when the hundred is dropped) to surface the overgeneralisation, then re-explain via composing a hundred.
Praise reasoning that correctly anticipates the hundreds change, not just correct final digits.
activities.rationale: Asking children to predict which digits change before calculating, and contrasting bridging with non-bridging items, targets the specific misconception that the hundreds never move; recognition/sorting here supports reasoning but should follow, not replace, the mental construction work.
learnerActions: For a mixed set of items (e.g. 345 + 40, 372 + 40, 462 − 30, 431 − 50), predict for each whether the hundreds digit will change before calculating.
Sort the items into 'bridges a hundred' and 'does not bridge a hundred'.
Calculate each mentally, then check your sort against the answers (385, 412, 432, 381).
Explain in your own words the rule: only the tens change unless the calculation crosses a hundred.
activities.intendedInsight: Deciding in advance whether a calculation bridges a hundred builds the discriminating judgement that prevents the over-generalisation 'only the tens digit ever changes'.

constraints: Multiple-choice or sort-and-check tasks can rehearse and surface the bridging over-generalisation, but they check reasoning rather than build the mental method; keep them after the child has constructed answers mentally.

A static tap-to-reveal chart can show which digit changes as a reference, but it cannot animate the cascade of composing a hundred; pair it with number-line or blocks work so the bridging move is actually traced.

Base-ten blocks and chart/number-line models are approximations and representations of the quantities, not the mental calculation itself; the objective is reliable mental computation, so fade the supports as the child becomes secure.
The 'only the tens digit changes' heuristic is explicitly conditional: always make the bridging exception part of the rule, in both addition and subtraction directions.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched, and the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the worked numbers: 345 + 40 = 385; 372 + 40 = 412 (reach 400 by +28, then +12); 462 − 30 = 432 (non-bridging, only tens change); 431 − 50 = 381 (431 − 31 = 400, then − 19 = 381). These check out and are used as stated.
The original source listed the three-item answer as '385, 412, 381' which is correct; retained.

The original 2d-interactive recommendation described the tens wheel for 345 + 40 spinning '4→8' — the tens digit of 345 is 4 and 4+4=8, giving 385, which is consistent. Preserved as a correct example.

The original best practice 'ask the child to predict which digits change before calculating (DfE evidence)' is retained as pedagogy, but neither verbatim source claim directly supports prediction/sorting as a method, so activity 3 lists no source claim.
Independent review trimmed the curriculum claim from activity 2 as topic-only for that activity's method principle; the make-ten/unitising claim remains as the direct support.

Interactive-media design examples (spinning tens wheel cascading to hundreds, number-line-in-tens toggle, live recolouring of changed digits) are retained as optional illustrations of the mechanism, not as mandatory tooling.

probeDeeper: For 345 + 40, which digits changed and which stayed the same? Why?
For 372 + 40, why did the hundreds digit change when it didn't for 345 + 40?
Is 431 − 50 bigger or smaller than 431? Should it be?
How is 372 + 40 like 7 tens + 4 tens? Where does the extra hundred come from?
assess.correctAnswer: 385, 412, 381. 345+40 changes only the tens (385). 372+40 bridges a hundred: tens go 7→9 then over, +12 in tens = 412 (hundreds digit changes). 431−50 bridges down: 431−31 to 400, then −19 more = 381 (hundreds digit changes).

errorPatterns.pattern: Changes the ones digit instead of the tens — '345 + 40 is 349' (adds 4 to the ones)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor with the chart: 40 is four tens, joining the tens. Connect to '10 more' repeated four times.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The ones digit changes rather than the tens; the child treated 40 as 4

errorPatterns.pattern: Fails to bridge a hundred — '372 + 40' leaves eleven tens (3(11)2 / 3112) or keeps the hundreds unchanged
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show on the tens number line that 372+40 crosses 400; make-ten at the scale of tens (add 28 to reach 400, then 12). Exchange ten tens for a hundred with blocks.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 372+40 the tens total reaches eleven but no hundred is composed; hundreds digit unchanged

errorPatterns.pattern: Subtraction bridging down not handled — '431 − 50' keeps the hundreds at 4 or does smaller-from-larger in the tens
errorPatterns.nextMove: On the tens number line show 431−50 must cross below 400; decompose a hundred into ten tens if using blocks. Sanity-check that subtracting makes it smaller.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 431−50 the hundreds digit doesn't drop, or the tens are done as 5−3

responseLevels.gap: Changes the ones instead of the tens, or leaves eleven tens / fails to move the hundreds; believes only the tens digit ever changes.
responseLevels.full: Answers all three mentally, anchoring hundreds and ones, bridges the hundred in both directions, and explains that only the tens change unless the calculation crosses a hundred.
responseLevels.partial: Handles the non-bridging case and can bridge a hundred with a number line or blocks, but not yet reliably in his head; may miss direction on subtraction.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to do these mentally, thinking aloud: 345 + 40, then 372 + 40, then 431 − 50. After each, ask which digits changed. Watch the two that cross a hundred.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 345+40 confirms the child anchors hundreds and ones and operates on the tens. 372+40 and 431−50 bridge a hundred — a child who thinks only the tens digit ever changes leaves eleven tens or fails to move the hundreds, while a correct child cascades to the hundreds. The non-bridging vs bridging contrast isolates the error.
