pedagogy.summary: At 8-9, repeated reasoning becomes explicit generalisation WITH justification: noticing that every fraction equivalent to 1/2 has a numerator half its denominator, seeing 3×4=12, 3×40=120, 3×400=1200 as one scaling pattern and saying WHY, and naming 'derive from a known fact' (8×7 = 8×5 + 8×2) as a general strategy rather than a one-off. CCSS MP8 stresses moving from noticed repetition to a general method while checking reasonableness. Teaching should press beyond 'I see a pattern' to 'why must it happen, and will it always?' — grounding the scaling pattern in place value and the fraction pattern in a visual model.
bestPractices: Lay out a scaling chain (3×4, 3×40, 3×400) and ask the child to explain WHY the product scales by 10 each time using place value, not just append zeros
Show families of equivalent fractions on a bar/number line so the numerator-half-denominator rule for 1/2 is seen to hold and can be tested
Name the derive-from-known-facts move as a reusable general strategy and ask the child to describe it in their own words
Insist on a test case for any stated rule ('does it still work for 3×4000? for 4/8?') to separate a justified generalisation from a guess
keyRepresentations: Place-value scaling chain (×10 shifts) for 3×4 → 3×40 → 3×400
Fraction wall / number line for families of equivalent fractions
Array / area-model split for deriving ×7 from ×5 + ×2
Multiplication grid showing column patterns
commonMisconceptions: Uses 'add a zero' for ×10 scaling with no place-value reason, so it fails on decimals
Notices a pattern but treats it as coincidence, unable to say why it must hold or whether it always will
Over-generalises the 1/2 rule to other fractions, or applies it without testing
Derives a fact but does not recognise the derive-from-known-facts move as a general strategy for other facts

learn.summary: For ages 8-9, press repeated reasoning into justified generalisation: not just noticing that 3×4=12, 3×40=120, 3×400=1200 scale by ten, but saying WHY (place value shifts the digits one place) and testing whether a rule always holds. Similarly, families of equivalent fractions (1/2, 2/4, 3/6) reveal a numerator-half-denominator pattern that should be tested on new cases, not trusted on sight. Name 'derive from a known fact' (8×7 = 8×5 + 8×2) as a reusable strategy the child can describe in their own words. The target is the justification and the extension, not just correct numbers.

activities.title: Scaling machine with a 'why' window
feedback: If the child only says 'add a zero', show the scaling on a place-value chart so the digits visibly shift one column, and contrast a decimal case where 'add a zero' gives the wrong answer: 1.2 × 10 is 12, but writing a zero on the end gives 1.20, which is still 1.2. Use the chart to show that 3×0.4 = 1.2 is a tenth of 12 because the digits shift one column right

If the child gives 120 and 1200 but shrugs at 'will it always work?', don't just assert the rule — ask 'why does times-ten make it ten times bigger?' and work the next case (3×4000 = 12000) together so a justified generalisation forms
Affirm reasoning that connects the shift to place value and confidently extends to 3×4000 for the same reason
activities.rationale: CCSS MP8 stresses moving from noticed repetition to a general method while evaluating reasonableness; grounding the scaling in place value (rather than 'add a zero') supplies the justification and reveals why it generalises. An interactive scaling tool lets the child produce cases and test an extension live, but a place-value chart or written scaling chain achieves the same reasoning on paper.
sourceClaims: MP8: students move from repeated calculations to general methods and shortcuts, and evaluate the reasonableness of results
Pupils should derive facts from known facts, recognise/use structure, and explain why patterns hold using representations that reveal the structure
learnerActions: Start from 3×4 = 12, then produce 3×40 and 3×400 by scaling up by ten each step
For each step, explain WHY the product gets ten times bigger using place value (40 is ten times 4, so the answer is ten times bigger; the digits shift one place left) rather than saying 'add a zero'
Predict 3×4000 and state whether the same reason guarantees it will work, then check
Now test the idea going the OTHER way: 0.4 is a tenth of 4, so is 3×0.4 a tenth of 12? Work it out and explain why the place value, not an added zero, decides this
activities.intendedInsight: The product scales by ten BECAUSE place value shifts the digits one column, so the pattern must keep working (including for 3×4000). Reasoning from place value (not just appending zeros) also handles decimal cases like 3×0.4 = 1.2 — here 0.4 is a tenth of 4, so the product is a tenth of 12, with the digits shifting one column right. The add-a-zero shortcut cannot explain this, and it gives wrong answers for decimals (1.2 × 10 is 12, not 1.20).

activities.title: Equivalent-fraction family tester
feedback: If the child claims a fraction is equivalent to 1/2 on the verbal rule alone when it isn't, check it on the fraction wall/number line (same whole) so the mismatch is visible
If the child says 5/9 is equivalent because 5 is roughly half of 9, prompt them to compare 5/9 and 1/2 exactly on the bar and see they don't line up
Affirm when the child tests a candidate fraction (e.g. confirms 4/8 lines up, 5/9 does not) rather than trusting the rule outright
activities.rationale: EEF guidance recommends explaining why patterns hold using representations that reveal structure; a bar/number line makes the equivalence testable and guards against over-generalisation. A live generator makes testing immediate, but a drawn fraction wall supports the same checking.
sourceClaims: Pupils should derive facts from known facts, recognise/use structure, and explain why patterns hold using representations that reveal the structure
learnerActions: Line up 1/2, 2/4, 3/6 on a fraction bar or number line (same whole) and notice that each numerator is half its denominator
State the candidate rule 'a fraction equals 1/2 when the numerator is half the denominator'
Invent a new fraction and test whether the rule holds by checking it against the bar/number line, not by eyeballing
Try a trap case: is 5/9 equivalent to 1/2 because 5 is 'about half' of 9? How could you be sure?
activities.intendedInsight: A noticed rule must be tested before it is trusted; the numerator-half-denominator pattern for 1/2 can be confirmed on a model, and over-applying it (e.g. to 5/9) is caught by checking rather than guessing.

activities.title: Derive-from-known-facts as a named strategy
feedback: If the child treats 8×7 = 8×5 + 8×2 as a single trick for one fact, ask them to describe it as a general approach and apply it to a new fact
Use an array/area model split into 8×5 and 8×2 parts so the child sees why the parts add to the whole
Watch for the common wrong split 8×5 + 2 (adding 2 instead of 8×2 = 16, which gives 42 not 56); check the split against the model
activities.rationale: EEF recommends deriving facts from known facts and recognising structure; naming the strategy and transferring it to a new fact turns a single derivation into a general method, consistent with MP8's move from repetition to general strategy. An area/array model makes the factor split visible.
sourceClaims: MP8: students move from repeated calculations to general methods and shortcuts, and evaluate the reasonableness of results
Pupils should derive facts from known facts, recognise/use structure, and explain why patterns hold using representations that reveal the structure
learnerActions: Work out 8×7 from facts you already know: 8×5 = 40 and 8×2 = 16, then add to get 56
Explain why splitting 7 into 5 + 2 lets you reuse known facts (an array or area model split into an 8×5 part and an 8×2 part)
Describe the move in your own words as a general strategy for any hard table fact
Try the same strategy on another fact (e.g. 6×7 or 9×6) and say which known facts you'd lean on
activities.intendedInsight: Deriving an unknown fact by splitting a factor and reusing known facts is a reusable general strategy, not a one-off; the child should recognise and name it so they can apply it to other facts.

activities.title: Prove it holds every time
feedback: If the child treats a pattern as coincidence and won't commit to whether it always holds, ask 'why must it happen?' and test the next case together
Praise a reason grounded in structure (place value, the fraction model) over 'it just works'
activities.rationale: MP8 emphasises expressing regularity as a general method and checking reasonableness; insisting on a reason and a test case is how a child moves from 'I see a pattern' to 'it must always happen'.
sourceClaims: MP8: students move from repeated calculations to general methods and shortcuts, and evaluate the reasonableness of results
learnerActions: After extending a scaling chain or stating a fraction rule, answer: how could you convince someone the pattern works every time, not just for these three cases?
Produce a test case for any stated rule ('does it still work for 3×4000? for 4/8?') and report what you find
Distinguish a justified generalisation ('it must, because place value shifts') from a guess ('it just seems to')
activities.intendedInsight: A pattern noticed is not a pattern proven; a reason it must hold, plus a fresh test case, separates a reliable generalisation from a coincidence.

activities.title: Check your generalisation (quick questions)
feedback: If the child picks 5/9 as equivalent to 1/2, send them back to the fraction model to test it
If the child selects 8×5 + 2, point out the second part must be 8×2 = 16, not 2 (so the total is 56, not 42)
Always ask the 'why does it work?' follow-up; a correct pick without a reason is not yet a generalisation
activities.rationale: Recognition questions can check whether a generalisation has formed, but selecting an answer is not the same as constructing a justification; pairing every item with a 'why' step keeps the focus on reasoning. This supplements, not replaces, the construct-and-test activities.
learnerActions: Continue the scaling chain: given 3×4=12 and 3×40=120, give 3×400 and 3×4000
Pick which fractions are equivalent to 1/2 from a set that includes near-misses (e.g. 5/9)
Choose the correct derivation of 8×7 and reject the wrong split 8×5 + 2 in favour of 8×5 + 8×2 = 56
For each choice, say WHY it is correct, not just which answer
activities.intendedInsight: Selecting correct continuations and derivations, paired with a stated reason, confirms the child is generalising with justification rather than pattern-matching.

constraints: The learning target is the justification and the extension, not just correct products or correct fraction picks; accept an answer only when the child can say WHY and whether it always holds.

Recognition/selection questions can check whether a generalisation exists but do not elicit the child's own construction or justification; always pair them with a 'why does it work?' step and treat them as a supplement to construct-and-test work.

A static annotated scaling chain or fraction wall can show and explain the pattern, but cannot let the child generate and test new cases; use it as a reference scaffold, not as the place where testing happens.

Discussion on its own supplies no concrete case or model for the child to test a generalisation against; pair any talk with numbers, a place-value chart, a fraction model, or an array so claims can be checked.
'Add a zero' is an unjustified shortcut that misfires on decimals; require a place-value reason instead.
Scaling chains and fraction families are flat relationships, so a 3D representation is not needed to show their structure.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Arithmetic checked: 8×5=40, 8×2=16, 40+16=56 (8×7); 3×40=120, 3×400=1200, 3×4000=12000, 3×0.4=1.2; the wrong split 8×5+2=42 is only ever presented as an error to reject, never as a valid answer.

Place-value reasoning for ×10 (digits shift one place left on whole numbers) is sound; 3×0.4 is the scaling-DOWN direction (0.4 is a tenth of 4, so the product is a tenth of 12 = 1.2), which is where the 'add a zero' shortcut fails — the activity now flags this is the opposite direction rather than the same leftward shift.
The 5/9 case is a genuine non-equivalence (5 is not half of 9), used to prompt checking rather than eyeballing; 4/8 is a confirming case (4 is half of 8).

The non-preferred 'conversation' and '3D' entries were low-fit in the source; their genuine affordance limits are preserved as narrowly scoped constraints without asserting any universal 'only X can teach this' claim.

probeDeeper: Ask 'you scaled 3×4 up by tens — does the same idea work going the other way, 3×0.4? why or why not?' to test the limits of the generalisation
Counterexample tuned to this topic: 'is 5/9 equivalent to 1/2 because 5 is about half of 9? how could you be sure?' to check the child tests rather than eyeballs
Ask 'you got 8×7 from 8×5 + 8×2 — could you describe that as a general trick for any hard table fact?' to see if the strategy is generalised
Ask 'how could you convince someone the pattern works every time, not just for these three?' to surface justification
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for 120 and 1200 with a place-value justification ('40 is ten times 4, so the answer is ten times bigger; the digits shift a place') and confidence it extends to 3×4000 = 12000 for the same reason. The WHY and the extension, not just the numbers, are the target.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses 'add a zero' with no place-value reason, so cannot justify why the product scales and it would misfire on decimals
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the scaling on a place-value chart so digits shift one column; contrast a decimal case where 'add a zero' fails
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked why, the child says only 'you add a zero' and cannot connect it to ×10 or place value

errorPatterns.pattern: Notices the pattern but treats it as a coincidence, unable to say it must always hold
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT just assert the rule; ask 'why does times-ten make it ten times bigger?' and test the next case together so a justified generalisation forms
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives 120 and 1200 but, asked 'will it always work?', shrugs or won't commit to 3×4000

errorPatterns.pattern: Over-generalises the equivalent-fraction pattern (applies the 1/2 numerator-half-denominator rule to fractions it doesn't fit) without testing
errorPatterns.nextMove: Check the claim on a fraction wall/number line; test candidate fractions rather than trusting the verbal rule
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child claims a fraction is equivalent to 1/2 on the rule alone when it isn't, or won't test

responseLevels.gap: Produces the products by 'add a zero' but cannot justify, treats patterns as coincidence, and over-applies fraction rules without testing
responseLevels.full: Extends the scaling chain with a place-value justification, states the derive-from-known-facts move as a general strategy, and tests fraction generalisations — explaining WHY a rule must hold and transferring it unprompted
responseLevels.partial: States the pattern and can extend it when prompted, but justifies weakly ('you add a zero') and does not reliably test whether a rule always holds

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You know 3 × 4 = 12. What are 3 × 40 and 3 × 400? Explain WHY the pattern works — and would it still work for 3 × 4000?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The products can be produced by 'adding a zero' with zero understanding. What discriminates is the place-value reason and whether the child is sure it generalises. A child with repeated-reasoning insight explains why it must scale and extends confidently; one without recites 'add a zero' and cannot justify or is unsure about 3×4000.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Add and subtract a two-digit number and ones (36 + 7, 52 − 4), mentally and with concrete/pictorial support, bridging through a multiple of ten. Ages 6–7.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2 'add and subtract numbers using concrete objects, pictorial representations, and mentally, including: a two-digit number and ones'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.NBT.4 add within 100 including a two-digit and a one-digit number, using place value and the relationship between addition and subtraction; extended by 2.NBT.5.
• Operational details: the key skill is bridging the tens boundary — partition the ones to reach the next (or previous) decade, then add/subtract the rest (36 + 7 → 36 + 4 = 40, + 3 = 43; 52 − 4 → 52 − 2 = 50, − 2 = 48). Ground in base-ten blocks and the number line so the new ten is seen forming. Contrast with cases that don't cross a ten (43 + 5) so children bridge only when needed.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (age 6) — adds ones without crossing a ten (43 + 5) and with blocks when crossing. Tier B (age 7) — bridges 36 + 7 and 52 − 4 mentally via the decade. Tier C (age 7+) — explains why the tens digit changes and chooses to bridge only when the ones cross a multiple of ten.
bestPractices: Teach bridging explicitly: partition the ones to land on the decade, then add/subtract the remainder.
Use base-ten blocks so ten ones visibly regroup into a new ten (and vice versa when subtracting).
Use the empty number line to show the two-part jump to and past the decade.
Mix bridging and non-bridging items so children decide when a boundary is crossed.
Connect the mental bridging steps to later column methods (regrouping).
keyRepresentations: Base-ten blocks (ones regrouping into a ten)
Empty number line with a jump to the decade then on
Ten-frames / partially filled frames showing the ones
Hundred square (move along a row, drop to next row at the boundary)
Part-whole splitting the ones (7 as 4 + 3)
commonMisconceptions: Adding the ones digits and ignoring the new ten (36 + 7 → 33 or '313').
Counting on/back in ones and slipping by one at the tens boundary.
Failing to change the tens digit when the ones cross a multiple of ten.
Bridging when it isn't needed, or not bridging when it is.
For subtraction, stopping at the decade (52 − 4 → 50) or miscounting past it.

learn.summary: Children aged 6–7 add and subtract a two-digit number and ones by bridging through a multiple of ten: partition the ones to land on the decade, then add or subtract the remainder (36 + 7 → 36 + 4 = 40, + 3 = 43; 52 − 4 → 52 − 2 = 50, − 2 = 48). Core activities use a manipulable number line and base-ten blocks — with ten-frames and a hundred square as alternative views — so the new ten is seen forming and the tens digit updates for a visible reason, with mixed bridging and non-bridging items (43 + 5) so children decide when a boundary is actually crossed. Fluency practice, a static anchor image, and a narrate-your-method conversation are retained as complementary approaches with distinct purposes.

activities.title: Bridge the decade on a number line with a base-ten mat
feedback: If the answer keeps the original tens digit (e.g. 36 + 7 → 33 or '313'), show the ten ones regrouping into one new ten on the mat and re-run the jump through 40 so the tens digit visibly changes.
If the answer is one off (e.g. 42 or 44), point out counting single steps across the boundary; partition the ones to land exactly on 40 first, then add the rest.
For subtraction, if the child stops at 50 or lands on 49/47, model bridging back to 50 first, then taking the remaining 2 to reach 48.
For a non-bridging item like 43 + 5, confirm that the ones do not cross a decade so no bridge is needed, reinforcing when bridging applies.
activities.rationale: Bridging is a two-part jump, and a manipulable number line plus a regrouping mat lets the child reach the decade and then complete the jump while seeing ten ones become a new ten; ten-frames and a hundred square offer the same structure in other concrete/pictorial forms. Live feedback can catch the count-in-ones slip and the ignore-the-new-ten error as they occur. Non-bridging items prevent over-applying the strategy.
sourceClaims: Y2 pupils add and subtract a two-digit number and ones using concrete, pictorial and mental methods.
1.NBT.4 covers adding within 100 including a two-digit and a one-digit number using place value, with regrouping of ten ones into a ten.
Bridging through ten by partitioning is a core mental strategy; digit-separation errors (ignoring the regrouped ten) are common.
learnerActions: Work 36 + 7 by first jumping from 36 to the next decade (40), then completing the jump with the remaining ones (to 43).
On a base-ten mat, watch four loose ones combine with the existing ones to make a whole new ten-stick as the jump reaches 40, so the tens digit change has a visible cause.
Switch to subtraction mode for 52 − 4: jump back to the decade first (52 − 2 = 50), then take the remaining 2 to reach 48.
Mix in non-bridging items such as 43 + 5 and decide for each item whether the ones cross a decade before choosing to bridge.

Optionally view the same bridging in another representation: a ten-frame filling up to a complete ten of ones, or a hundred square where you move along a row and drop to the next row as you cross the decade, so the new ten is seen forming in more than one way.
State out loud which decade you bridge through and why the tens digit does or does not change.
activities.intendedInsight: When adding makes the ones fill up to a whole ten, a new ten is formed and the tens digit increases by one; when subtracting takes away more ones than there are, a ten is broken into ones and the tens digit decreases by one (52 − 4 = 48). Partitioning the ones to reach the decade makes this regrouping explicit for both addition and subtraction.

activities.title: Fluency practice: fill in, draw the jump, choose the decade
feedback: If a learner picks the results distractor that ignores the regrouped ten (e.g. 33 for 36 + 7), return to a regrouping representation to show why the tens digit must change and re-run the jump through 40.
If the drawn jump skips the decade stop, prompt the learner to mark the decade first, then the remainder.
Confirm correct recognition when a non-bridging item is answered without an unnecessary bridge.
activities.rationale: A fixed practice sequence consolidates the method and surfaces the characteristic errors through targeted distractors, but it cannot provide the live regrouping feedback of the manipulative, so it is best used after the hands-on work.
sourceClaims: Bridging through ten by partitioning is a core mental strategy; digit-separation errors (ignoring the regrouped ten) are common.
learnerActions: Complete fill-in results such as 36 + 7 = ___ mentally or with a jotting.
Draw the two-part bridging jump on an empty number line to show reaching the decade and then continuing.
Choose which decade you bridge through for a given calculation, with decade options as the choices (for 36 + 7 the decade is 40).
In a separate results question, identify the correct total, where a distractor such as 33 for 36 + 7 reflects the ignore-the-new-ten error (keeping the original tens digit).
Include at least one non-bridging item so you practise recognising when no bridge is needed.
activities.intendedInsight: Once the bridging strategy is understood, spaced and varied practice builds fluency in partitioning the ones and updating the tens digit accurately.

activities.title: Anchor image: a worked bridging number line
feedback: If the learner cannot say why the jump pauses at 40, highlight that the first jump completes a ten and point to the labelled new ten.
Prompt the learner to connect the picture back to doing their own jump on the manipulative.
activities.rationale: A static worked number line anchors the appearance of bridging and labels the regrouped ten. It supports understanding of the structure, though the count itself still needs to be rehearsed in a doing activity; treat this as a reference rather than practice of the procedure.
learnerActions: Study a number line showing 36 → 40 → 43 with the regrouped ten labelled, revealing each step in turn.
Describe in your own words why the jump stops at 40 before continuing to 43.
activities.intendedInsight: A clear worked picture shows what a bridging jump looks like and names the new ten, giving a reference model for the two-part method.

activities.title: Narrate your method: how did you get across the ten?
feedback: If the explanation describes counting single steps, guide the child to describe partitioning the ones to reach the decade first.
If the child cannot justify why the tens digit changes, revisit the regrouping of ten ones into a new ten.
Confirm reasoning when the child correctly identifies that a non-bridging item needs no bridge.
activities.rationale: A talk-through surfaces the child's method and misconceptions, complementing the hands-on and practice activities; it is a way to assess and reinforce the procedure being practised, though recognition in talk does not by itself guarantee independent production.
learnerActions: Work a bridging item and a non-bridging item, then explain aloud how you got across the ten (or why you did not need to).
Answer questions such as 'Why does the tens digit change here?' and 'For 43 + 5, did you need to cross a ten? How do you know?'
Show 52 − 4 on the number line and say where you stopped on the way.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the decade step and the reason the tens digit changes reveals whether the child is partitioning to bridge or merely counting in ones.

constraints: Ground the strategy in base-ten blocks and the number line (with ten-frames or a hundred square as alternative representations) so the new ten is seen forming (and un-forming when subtracting) before expecting mental calculation.
Always mix bridging and non-bridging items (e.g. 43 + 5) so children learn to bridge only when the ones cross a decade and do not over-apply the strategy.
A fixed practice sequence consolidates fluency but does not provide live regrouping feedback; use it after hands-on manipulative work.
A static worked image anchors what bridging looks like but does not rehearse the count; it is a reference, not a substitute for doing the procedure.

Checkpoint tiers: Tier A (age 6) adds ones without crossing a ten and with blocks when crossing; Tier B (age 7) bridges 36 + 7 and 52 − 4 mentally via the decade; Tier C (age 7+) explains why the tens digit changes and chooses to bridge only when the ones cross a multiple of ten.
Connect the mental bridging steps to later column methods (regrouping) as children progress.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source labels CCSS 1.NBT.4 and the NCETM claims as unverified; do not treat the standards-alignment or misconception-frequency claims as independently confirmed.

The legacy source asserted '3D adds nothing' for this 1-D number-line skill; this comparative/necessity claim is not established by the evidence and has been omitted rather than propagated. A 3D representation is simply not the focus here, not proven worthless.

The legacy source implied a static image 'can't rehearse' the count and that a quiz 'can't give live feedback'; these have been softened to stated-affordance limits (reference vs. practice; delayed vs. live feedback) rather than universal laws.
The ten-frame and hundred-square representations, and the part-whole partitioning of the ones, from the original keyRepresentations are retained within the core activity.

Fixed the fluency activity so the 'which decade?' choice offers decade options while the ignore-the-new-ten distractor (33) belongs to a separate results item; the original design notes had conflated these into one incoherent question.

probeDeeper: How did you get across the ten in 36 + 7?
Why does the tens digit change here?
For 43 + 5, did you need to cross a ten? How do you know?
Show me 52 − 4 on the number line — where did you stop on the way?
assess.correctAnswer: 43; 48; 48. Watch for bridging through the decade on the first two (36 + 4 = 40, + 3 = 43; 52 − 2 = 50, − 2 = 48) and a straightforward ones-addition on the third, which does not cross a ten.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds the ones and ignores the new ten — 36 + 7 becomes 33 (keeps the 3 tens) or '313'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Base-ten blocks: ten ones regroup into a new ten; bridge via 40 and watch the tens digit change.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer keeps the original tens digit; ones handled as if isolated.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts on/back in ones and slips by one crossing the tens boundary (36 + 7 → 42 or 44).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Partition the ones to land on the decade first, then add the rest; track on the number line.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer is one off; observed counting single steps through the decade.

errorPatterns.pattern: For subtraction, stops at the decade or miscounts past it (52 − 4 → 50 or 49/47).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Bridge back to 50 first (− 2), then take the remaining 2; model on the number line.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer is 50, 49 or 47.

responseLevels.gap: Adds/subtracts the digits with no regard to place, or cannot get across the tens boundary.
responseLevels.full: Bridges through the decade by partitioning the ones, updates the tens digit correctly, and recognises when no bridge is needed.
responseLevels.partial: Reaches answers by counting in ones across the boundary — slow and error-prone — without partitioning to bridge.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these out — mentally or on the number line — and talk me through each: 36 + 7; 52 − 4; 43 + 5.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Two items cross a tens boundary and one does not. A child with place-value bridging partitions the ones to hit the decade and updates the tens digit; a child treating the digits separately gives the tell-tale 33 for 36 + 7, and a count-in-ones child slips by one at the boundary. The non-bridging item checks they don't over-apply bridging.

pedagogy.summary: This is the conceptual definition that underpins all percentage work: a percentage is a number of parts PER HUNDRED — a standardised proportion — which is why it can be written equivalently as a fraction (out of 100) and a decimal (45% = 45/100 = 0.45), why the same percentage of different wholes gives different amounts (it is relative to its base, not an absolute quantity), and why percentages can exceed 100% (150% = one and a half times the whole). Standardising 'out of 100' is precisely what makes percentages useful for COMPARING proportions with different totals. Teaching should ground the definition in the 100-grid, hammer the three-way fraction–decimal–percentage equivalence, and repeatedly confront the intuition that a percentage names a fixed amount rather than a proportion of a whole.
bestPractices: Define percentage on a 100-grid: shade 45 of 100 cells — 45% = 45/100 = 0.45 = the shaded proportion; the grid makes 'per hundred' literal.
Stress that a percentage is RELATIVE to its whole: 50% of a small quantity and 50% of a large quantity are different amounts — percentage is a proportion, not a fixed number.
Drill the three-way conversion (fraction ↔ decimal ↔ percentage) in both directions, watching decimal placement (7% = 0.07, not 0.7).
Introduce percentages over 100% deliberately (a 100-grid plus part of a second grid; 150% = 1.5 = one and a half wholes) so 100% is understood as 'the whole', not a ceiling.
Teach 'express A as a percentage of B' as A/B × 100, tying it back to proportion (A out of B, restated out of 100).
Use side-by-side comparison tasks (which class did better: 18/25 or 70/100?) so standardising to 'per hundred' is seen to be the point of percentages.
keyRepresentations: 100-grid (each cell = 1%), shaded to show a percentage as a proportion
Fraction–decimal–percentage equivalence triple (45% = 45/100 = 0.45)
Two differently-sized bars/quantities with the same percentage shaded (relative-to-whole)
A 100-grid plus a partial second grid to show >100% (150% = 1.5 wholes)
'A out of B, restated out of 100' bridge for expressing one quantity as a percentage of another
commonMisconceptions: Treats a percentage as a fixed absolute amount (50% is 'the same amount' regardless of the whole), not as a proportion of its base
Believes percentages cannot exceed 100% (100% is seen as a maximum rather than 'one whole')
Mis-converts between forms: 7% → 0.7 (decimal misplacement), or 0.45 → 4.5%
Confuses 'A as a percentage of B' with 'B as a percentage of A', or which quantity is the whole (the base)

learn.summary: A percentage is a number of parts per hundred — a standardised proportion — so it can be written equivalently as a fraction (out of 100) and as a decimal (45% = 45/100 = 0.45). Because a percentage is relative to its whole (base), the same percentage of different wholes gives different amounts, and percentages can exceed 100% (150% = one and a half wholes). Standardising 'out of 100' is what makes percentages useful for comparing proportions with different totals. Teaching grounds the definition in a 100-grid, drills the three-way fraction–decimal–percentage equivalence, and repeatedly confronts the intuition that a percentage names a fixed amount rather than a proportion of a whole.

activities.title: Shade a 100-grid to define 'per hundred'
feedback: If a learner writes 7% = 0.7, point back to the grid: 7 cells out of 100 is 7 hundredths = 0.07; 0.7 would be 70 out of 100 cells.
If a learner thinks the grid cannot be exceeded, give a second grid and ask them to shade 150 cells in total across the two, naming it as one and a half wholes.
Confirm when all three forms (45%, 45/100, 0.45) are matched to the same shaded region.
activities.rationale: Grounding the definition on a 100-grid makes 'per hundred' literal and ties the fraction and decimal forms to a single visible proportion; a second partial grid shows >100% concretely. Curriculum framing treats fractions, decimals and percentages as different ways of expressing proportions.
sourceClaims: Percentage is 'number of parts per hundred'; pupils interpret percentages as a fraction or decimal, express one quantity as a percentage of another, compare quantities using percentages, and work with percentages greater than 100% (Y5 non-statutory: FDP are 'different ways of expressing proportions').

Translating fluently between percents, decimals and fractions is a key difficulty; a documented error is converting a percent to a decimal incorrectly (treating a small percent as a large decimal, e.g. 7% → 0.7).
learnerActions: On a 10×10 grid (100 cells, each cell = 1%), shade 45 cells and write the result three ways: 45% = 45/100 = 0.45.
State in your own words what '45 out of 100' means by pointing at the shaded and unshaded parts of the grid.
Shade a second grid partly to show more than one whole: fill one full grid and 50 cells of a second, and write 150% = 1.5 = one and a half wholes.
Convert a small percentage carefully: shade 7 cells and record 7% = 7/100 = 0.07 (watch that it is 0.07, not 0.7).
activities.intendedInsight: A percentage literally means parts per hundred, so it is the same quantity expressed as a fraction (out of 100) and as a decimal; 100% is 'one whole', not a ceiling, and percentages can go beyond it.

activities.title: Same percentage, different wholes — 50% of two bags
feedback: If a learner predicts 'the same, because it's 50% of each', have them compute 50% of each whole (10 vs 20) and shade half of each: half of a larger whole is more.

If a learner says 'Bag B gives 20 more, because it has 20 more sweets', compute both halves — the gap is 10, not 20. The halves differ by 50% of the difference in the wholes; reason from 'half of each', not the raw total gap.
If a learner insists 100% must always beat 50%, return to the trap comparison: 100% of 10 = 10 is fewer than 50% of 40 = 20, because the percentages sit on different wholes.
Confirm when the learner both gets 'different amounts' AND justifies it by 'half of each whole, and the wholes differ'.
activities.rationale: The percentage-as-absolute misconception is the central error for this topic; predicting then computing and shading the same percentage on two different wholes directly confronts it, and the trap comparison blocks the shortcut '100% always beats 50%' by showing 50% of a larger whole exceeding 100% of a smaller one. A separate check distinguishes a correct 'no' reasoned proportionally from a 'no' reasoned from the raw total gap.
sourceClaims: Bassan Cincinatus & Sheffet (2016), a peer-reviewed study, documents the percentage-as-absolute misconception: learners treat a percentage as a fixed number added/subtracted regardless of its base — assuming '32% bigger' implies '32% smaller' the other way, and that 32% of one amount equals 32% of a different amount. It states 'a 32% value of one initial amount is not equal to a 32% value of another initial amount — it is important to find out from which whole the percentage is calculated', and that a price +20% then −20% does NOT return to the original.

Per the article abstract (personally fetched), percent is a 'privileged proportion' whose 'extremely concise language has lost its explicit referents, has misleading additive terminology for multiplicative meanings, and has multiple uses for the preposition of', and it 'forms a bridge between real-world situations and mathematical concepts of multiplicative structures' — explaining why learners default to additive schemas. (Abstract verified; full text paywalled.)
learnerActions: Predict first: Bag A has 20 sweets and Bag B has 40 sweets. If you take 50% of each, will you get the same amount from both, or more from one — and why? Write your reason before checking.
Compute 50% of each: 50% of 20 = 10, 50% of 40 = 20.
Shade half of two bars (or grids) sized to represent 20 and 40, and compare the shaded amounts.
Explain in one sentence why the same percentage gave different amounts.

Check a trap comparison: is 100% of a small 10-sweet bag more or fewer sweets than 50% of Bag B (40 sweets)? Compute both (10 and 20): 50% of the larger bag gives MORE than 100% of the smaller bag — so '100% always beats 50%' is false, because each percentage acts on its own whole.
activities.intendedInsight: A percentage is a proportion of its own whole (50% = half of whatever the whole is). Because the wholes differ, equal percentages give different amounts, so a percentage is not a fixed absolute quantity; a larger whole's 50% can even exceed a smaller whole's 100%.

activities.title: Convert fluently between fraction, decimal and percentage
feedback: If 0.45 is written as 4.5%, re-anchor: 0.45 = 45/100 = 45%; 4.5% would be 0.045.
If 7% is converted to 0.7, re-anchor to 7/100 = 0.07.
Confirm when conversions are correct in both directions, including a value over 100%.
activities.rationale: Fluent two-directional conversion, with attention to decimal placement, is a documented difficulty and a stated curriculum requirement. Recognition/matching is a useful check of whether a learner can identify equivalent forms, but it does not by itself show they can produce a conversion; so matching is paired with learner-produced conversions.
sourceClaims: Translating fluently between percents, decimals and fractions is a key difficulty; a documented error is converting a percent to a decimal incorrectly (treating a small percent as a large decimal, e.g. 7% → 0.7).

Percentage is 'number of parts per hundred'; pupils interpret percentages as a fraction or decimal, express one quantity as a percentage of another, compare quantities using percentages, and work with percentages greater than 100% (Y5 non-statutory: FDP are 'different ways of expressing proportions').
learnerActions: Match each percentage to its decimal and its fraction-out-of-100 (e.g. 45% ↔ 0.45 ↔ 45/100; 7% ↔ 0.07 ↔ 7/100; 150% ↔ 1.5 ↔ 150/100).
Go in both directions: given 0.08, write the percentage (8%); given 3/100, write the percentage (3%) and decimal (0.03).
Place a given value on a number line that passes 100%, locating 150% at one and a half wholes.
Explain the decimal-placement rule: converting a percent to a decimal divides by 100, moving two places, so a small percent becomes a small decimal (7% → 0.07).
activities.intendedInsight: The three forms are interchangeable notations for the same proportion; converting reliably in both directions depends on tracking the 'out of 100' divisor and decimal place.

activities.title: Express one quantity as a percentage of another, and compare
feedback: If a learner reports 18/25 as the loser without converting, have them compute 18/25 = 72/100 = 72%, which beats 70%.
If a learner confuses 'A as a % of B' with 'B as a % of A', mark which quantity is the whole in each phrasing and recompute both.
Confirm when the learner identifies the base correctly and uses A/B × 100.
activities.rationale: Expressing one quantity as a percentage of another and comparing via a common 'out of 100' base are explicit curriculum goals; confusing which quantity is the base is a listed misconception, so direction is checked deliberately.
sourceClaims: Percentage is 'number of parts per hundred'; pupils interpret percentages as a fraction or decimal, express one quantity as a percentage of another, compare quantities using percentages, and work with percentages greater than 100% (Y5 non-statutory: FDP are 'different ways of expressing proportions').
learnerActions: Write 'A as a percentage of B' as A/B × 100, and say aloud 'A out of B, restated out of 100'.
Compare two results: one class had 18 out of 25 pass, another 70 out of 100. Convert 18/25 to a percentage (72%) and decide which class did better.
Explain why percentages make this comparison easy: both are restated out of the same total, 100.
Check direction: is 'A as a percentage of B' the same as 'B as a percentage of A'? Try A=10, B=40 (10/40×100 = 25% vs 40/10×100 = 400%) and state which quantity is the whole each time.
activities.intendedInsight: Standardising to 'per hundred' lets you compare proportions with different totals; the base (the 'of B' quantity) is the whole, and swapping A and B changes the question and the answer.

constraints: Keep the base explicit at all times: every percentage is 'of' some whole; when amounts are involved, state the whole before computing.

Matching and multiple-choice checks confirm recognition of equivalent forms but do not, on their own, show the learner can produce conversions or justify the proportional reasoning; pair them with learner-constructed answers and spoken/written explanations.

A static shaded 100-grid is a strong, honest picture of the 'per hundred' definition and the equivalence triple; to let a learner test that the SAME percentage yields different amounts on different wholes, they need to act on at least two different wholes themselves (compute, shade, or physically share), whether with paper grids/bars or an interactive model.

Optional interactive supports — a grid whose fraction and decimal update as cells are shaded, a side-by-side panel shading the same percentage on two differently-sized bars, a drag-past-100% mode onto a second grid, and an 'A as % of B' tool that restates A/B out of 100 — make the mechanism concrete but are not required; the same learning can be reached with paper grids, drawn bars, or shared counters.
Distinguish the diagnostic prediction step from the explanation: the reason given BEFORE observing is what reveals the absolute-vs-proportion view.
Do not teach '100% always beats 50%': supply a counterexample, e.g. 100% of a 10-sweet bag (10) is fewer than 50% of a 40-sweet bag (20), so 50% of a larger whole can exceed 100% of a smaller one.
Percentages compare proportions directly because each one is restated out of a common whole of 100. Comparing the actual amounts still needs each whole: 50% of 40 (20) is more than 100% of 10 (10).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support the underlying teaching principle rather than proving any specific activity was tested.

Scope gap: the objective/evidence includes 'calculate percentage increases and decreases', but no activity builds this (only percentages >100% are represented). The original learn field likewise did not build it, so the rewrite is faithful, but this target is NOT covered and should not be read as taught. The Bassan '+20% then −20%' content is cited for the percentage-as-absolute principle in Activity 2, not for a change-calculation task.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 50% of 20 = 10 and 50% of 40 = 20 (difference 10, not 20); the trap comparison 100% of 10 = 10 is fewer than 50% of 40 = 20; 18/25 = 72% > 70%; 10/40 = 25% and 40/10 = 400%; 7% = 0.07, 45% = 0.45, 0.45 = 45% (not 4.5%), 150% = 1.5, 0.08 = 8%, 3/100 = 0.03 = 3% — all verified consistent.

Trap-comparison restored to the source form: '100% of a 10-sweet bag (10) vs 50% of Bag B (40) = 10 vs 20', which vividly shows 50% of a larger whole exceeding 100% of a smaller one. An equal-case variant reusing only Bags A and B (100% of 20 vs 50% of 40 = 20 vs 20) is also mathematically valid and refutes '100% always beats 50%'; reviewers may prefer it for setup economy.

The second misconception ('reaches no by raw total difference') is subtle: the halves differ by 10, which is 50% of the 20-sweet difference in the wholes — preserved in Activity 2 feedback as stated in the source.

The 'conversation/tutor' alternative and the 'per-hundred static grid' explainer from the source are preserved as approaches within activities and constraints rather than as separate ranked artefacts; comparative-efficacy phrasing was softened because the cited sources do not establish one medium as superior.
Source claims are marked 'verified' in the legacy row, but no re-verification occurred here; evidence strength should not be read as freshly confirmed.

assess.poeTask: Show the child two chocolate bars of clearly different sizes — a small one and a large one. Say you will give them 50% of each. PREDICT before breaking anything: will they get the same amount of chocolate from both, or more from one — and WHY? (A child answering 'the same, because it's 50% of each' is treating the percentage as absolute; the reason given before observing is the diagnostic part.) OBSERVE: break each bar in half — the large bar's half is visibly much more chocolate. EXPLAIN: 50% means half of EACH bar's own whole; because the wholes differ, the halves differ — a percentage is a proportion of its base, not a fixed amount.
probeDeeper: 'Write 50% as a fraction and as a decimal' — checks the parts-per-hundred equivalence (1/2, 0.5), and watch for decimal slips.
'Can you ever have more than 100% of something? Give me an example' — surfaces whether 100% is understood as 'the whole' rather than a ceiling.

Counterexample: 'Bag C has 10 sweets — is 100% of bag C more or fewer sweets than 50% of bag B?' — 100% of 10 (=10) equals 50% of 40 (=20)? No: 10 vs 20 — a child who reasons proportionally computes both; an absolute-view child assumes 100% always beats 50%.
'In one class 18 out of 25 passed; in another 70 out of 100 passed — which did better, and why are percentages useful here?' — tests standardising to 'per hundred' for comparison.
assess.correctAnswer: No. 50% of bag A is 10 sweets and 50% of bag B is 20 sweets. A percentage is a proportion of its OWN whole (50% means half of whatever the whole is), so because the bags have different totals, the same percentage gives different amounts.

errorPatterns.pattern: Percentage-as-absolute: 'Yes, 50% is 50%, so you get the same number of sweets from each bag' — treats the percentage as a fixed amount, not a proportion of the whole
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront with the two bags: compute 50% of each (10 and 20) and shade half of each on a grid; a percentage is half of ITS whole, and the wholes differ. Rebuild percentage as a proportion of the base.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — 50% is 50%, so you get the same number of sweets from each bag
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child answers 'yes, the same', or computes only one bag and assumes it holds for both; the percentage is treated as an absolute quantity

errorPatterns.pattern: Reaches 'no' by the raw difference in totals rather than by proportion: 'bag B gives 20 more, because it has 20 more sweets'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compute both halves (10 and 20, a gap of 10, not 20): the percentage acts on each whole, so the difference in the results is 50% of the difference in the wholes. Anchor to 'half of each'.
errorPatterns.distractor: No — bag B gives 20 more sweets, because it has 20 more sweets than bag A
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says the halves differ by 20 (the difference in the bags) instead of 10; reasons from the absolute gap, not 50% of each whole

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes percentages cannot exceed 100% (100% is a maximum, so 150% is impossible or meaningless)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show 100% = one whole (the full grid); 150% = one and a half wholes on a grid-plus-half-grid. Percentages describe proportions that can exceed the whole (e.g. prices rising to 150% of the original).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked (probe) about 150%, child says 'you can't have more than 100%' or caps it at 100

responseLevels.gap: Treats a percentage as a fixed amount ('50% is the same in both'), or insists percentages cannot exceed 100%; cannot connect percentage to a fraction/decimal of the whole.
responseLevels.full: Defines percentage as parts per hundred / a proportion of its whole, so equal percentages of different wholes give different amounts; converts fluently among fraction, decimal and percentage; interprets and uses percentages greater than 100%; and standardises 'out of 100' to compare proportions with different totals.
responseLevels.partial: Recognises the amounts differ and can compute 50% of each for the practised case, but explains it by the raw difference in totals rather than 'a proportion of each whole', or is shaky on ↔fraction/decimal conversion or on percentages over 100%.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Bag A has 20 sweets and bag B has 40 sweets. Is 50% of bag A the same amount of sweets as 50% of bag B? And — this is the important part — how do you know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The prompt forces the relative-vs-absolute distinction and, via the second tier, the REASON. A child who understands percentage as a proportion of the whole says 'no' and explains it by the different wholes; a child holding the absolute view says 'yes, 50% is 50%'. Crucially the tier-two reason also separates a child who reaches 'no' for the RIGHT reason (proportion of each whole) from one who reaches 'no' for a wrong reason (e.g. 'B has 20 more sweets so its half is 20 more') — hard to answer correctly without the proportional idea.
