pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 8–9y; solve problems involving multiplying and adding, including using the distributive law, integer scaling problems, and harder correspondence (n×m combinations) problems.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y4 'solve problems involving multiplying and adding, including using the distributive law to multiply two-digit numbers by one digit, integer scaling problems and harder correspondence problems such as n objects are connected to m objects'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.OA.2/4.OA.3 — multiplicative comparison and multistep word problems (including which operation and interpreting remainders); 3.OA.8 two-step problems; correspondence combinations connect to the multiplication principle of counting.
• Operational details — this is the APPLICATION topic that ties three distinct multiplicative structures together: (1) distributive-law calculation (14×6 = 10×6 + 4×6) as a mental/written strategy; (2) SCALING — 'three times as tall/heavy', a multiplicative (not additive) comparison; (3) CORRESPONDENCE / combinations — 3 breads × 4 fillings = 12 sandwiches, where multiplication counts pairings. Children must identify which structure a problem has and choose operations; the bar model and a systematic table/tree are the key tools. The recurring pitfall is reading scaling additively and mis-organising correspondence.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8): solve a one-step scaling problem and a small correspondence problem with support (2×3). Tier B (age 8–9): use the distributive law on 14×6 and solve a correspondence problem by systematic listing/table. Tier C (age 9): solve a multi-step multiply-and-add problem, choosing operations and justifying with a bar model.
bestPractices: Teach the three structures explicitly and by name — distributive calculation, scaling (times-as-many), correspondence (combinations) — so children recognise which they face rather than key-word guessing.
Use the bar model as the shared representation for scaling and multiply-and-add, making the multiplicative comparison visible against an additive one.
For correspondence, build systematic organisation — a grid/table or tree diagram — so children see why you multiply the two counts rather than add them.
Contrast scaling with addition directly ('3 times as tall' vs '3 m taller') using the same numbers so the multiplicative meaning is felt.
Progress from one-step to genuinely multi-step problems, requiring an estimate and an operation choice, and checking answers for reasonableness.
keyRepresentations: Bar model — scaling and multiply-and-add (unit bar × scale factor; combine bars)
Systematic table / grid — correspondence combinations (rows×columns = pairings)
Tree diagram — correspondence (each bread branches to each filling)
Distributive split (area/partition) — 14×6 as 10×6 + 4×6
commonMisconceptions: Reading scaling additively — 'three times as tall as 15 m' answered as 15+3 rather than 15×3.
Adding the two counts in a correspondence problem (3+4=7 sandwiches) instead of multiplying.
Unsystematic listing of combinations, so some pairings are missed or duplicated.
Applying the distributive split incorrectly (14×6 = 10×6 + 4, dropping the second multiplication).
Relying on key words instead of the problem's structure, choosing the wrong operation in multi-step problems.

learn.summary: For ages 8–9: solving multiply-and-add problems across three distinct multiplicative structures — (1) the distributive law as a calculation strategy (14×6 = 10×6 + 4×6 = 60+24 = 84); (2) scaling / multiplicative comparison ('3 times as tall as 15 m' = 45 m, NOT 15+3 = 18); and (3) correspondence / combinations (3 breads × 4 fillings = 12 sandwiches). The central aim is for learners to identify which structure a problem has and choose operations accordingly, rather than guessing from key words. Bar models and systematic tables/trees are the shared tools; the recurring pitfalls are reading scaling additively and adding the two counts in correspondence problems.

activities.title: Correspondence combinations: pair every bread with every filling
feedback: If a learner answers 7 (adding the counts), show the grid or tree: there are more than 7 cells to fill. Name it explicitly — '4 sandwiches for EACH of the 3 breads'.
If pairings are missed or duplicated, point to the empty or repeated cells and work row by row so each bread is paired with all 4 fillings exactly once.
Confirm correct reasoning by linking the completed grid back to 3 rows × 4 columns = 12.
activities.rationale: The multiplicative structure in correspondence problems is hidden, so children most often add (3+4=7). Building the pairings systematically in a grid or tree reveals why the total is a product. A draggable grid that auto-fills as each bread is paired, with a visible counter settling on 12, makes the 3×4 structure concrete — but a paper table or tree diagram achieves the same organisation. (Optional interactive: show empty cells remaining if a learner tries to add rather than pair.)
sourceClaims: Bar models and systematic tables/tree diagrams support scaling and correspondence problems; scaling should be contrasted with additive comparison to prevent the additive misconception.
learnerActions: Work with a concrete set-up of 3 kinds of bread and 4 kinds of filling (cards, drawings, or a draggable grid).
Systematically pair each bread with each filling, recording every sandwich in a table whose rows are breads and columns are fillings, or a tree where each bread branches to all 4 fillings.
After completing the pairings, count the filled cells and state the total as a number sentence: 3 × 4 = 12.
Explain in words why it is 3×4 and not 3+4: 'each of the 3 breads makes 4 sandwiches.'
Predict then check: 'If there were 5 fillings instead of 4, how many sandwiches now?' (3 × 5 = 15).
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplication counts pairings. When n objects each connect to m objects, the total number of combinations is n×m, not n+m. A systematic grid or tree makes every pairing visible so none are missed or duplicated.

activities.title: Scaling vs adding: 'times as tall' against 'taller by'
feedback: If a learner answers 18 for 'times as tall', show that they added the multiplier; 'times as tall' means making copies — lay out three 15 m bars and count.
Reinforce by asking the learner to re-read the phrase and decide: copies (×) or an amount extra (+)?
Confirm 3 × 15 = 45 m and have them point to the three stacked bars.
activities.rationale: Directly contrasting the scaling and additive readings with identical numbers targets the common additive-scaling error. The bar model makes the multiplicative comparison visible. (Optional interactive: a bar that stretches ×n beside a faint '+n' bar so 45 towers over 18.)
sourceClaims: Bar models and systematic tables/tree diagrams support scaling and correspondence problems; scaling should be contrasted with additive comparison to prevent the additive misconception.
4.OA.2/4.OA.3 require multiplicative comparison and multistep word problems including choosing operations; correspondence problems connect to the multiplication counting principle.
learnerActions: Draw or build a bar representing a 15 m building.
Make the tower '3 times as tall' by building three copies of the 15 m bar stacked end to end, and compute 3 × 15 = 45 m.
Alongside it, build a second comparison: '3 m taller than 15 m' = 15 + 3 = 18 m.
Place the two results side by side and describe the difference between 'times as tall' (multiplicative) and 'taller by' (additive).
State which phrase means multiply and which means add, using the same numbers so the contrast is felt.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Times as many/tall/heavy' is a multiplicative comparison (copies of the original), fundamentally different from 'more than / taller by', which is additive. The same numbers give very different answers (45 vs 18).

activities.title: Distributive law: split, multiply both parts, recombine
feedback: If a learner gives 60 or 64 (only the 10 multiplied, or 4 added without multiplying), return to the area model: the 4-strip must also be multiplied by 6, giving 24, before adding.
Note that the two partial products here are 60 and 24, which sum to 84; check both are present.
If the set-up is right but the arithmetic slips, do not reteach the structure — have the learner recompute and estimate to catch the slip.
activities.rationale: A frequent error is splitting the distributive calculation but multiplying only one part (14×6 = 10×6 + 4). The area/partition model shows both strips must be multiplied and combined. Self-audit: 10×6=60 and 4×6=24 sum to 84; the partial products are 60 and 24.
learnerActions: Split 14 into 10 + 4.
Multiply BOTH parts by 6: 10 × 6 = 60 and 4 × 6 = 24.
Add the two partial products: 60 + 24 = 84.
Use an area/partition model — a rectangle split into a 10-strip and a 4-strip, both ×6 — to show both pieces are included.
Check the result is reasonable (e.g. 14×6 is a bit more than 10×6 = 60, and less than 15×6 = 90).
activities.intendedInsight: The distributive law lets you multiply a two-digit number by splitting it, but every part of the split must be multiplied by the second factor and then added. Dropping a partial product gives a wrong answer.

activities.title: Which structure is it? Classify and choose the operation
feedback: If a learner relies on a key word and picks the wrong operation, ask what the problem is really doing — making copies (scaling), counting pairings (correspondence), or splitting a calculation (distributive)?
For multi-step problems, check the estimate against the final answer for reasonableness.
Praise justifications that name the structure and match it to a representation, not just correct numbers.
activities.rationale: Progressing from one-step to multi-step problems and requiring operation choice plus an estimate builds the habit of structural reasoning over key-word matching. Classification and matching number-sentence tasks are good for checking recognition, but should accompany, not replace, building the intuition with bars and grids — recognition-only responses do not elicit independent construction of the pairings or the comparison.
sourceClaims: 4.OA.2/4.OA.3 require multiplicative comparison and multistep word problems including choosing operations; correspondence problems connect to the multiplication counting principle.
learnerActions: Read a mix of word problems and sort each into its structure: distributive calculation, scaling (times-as-many), or correspondence (combinations) — and some multi-step multiply-and-add problems.
For each, write the number sentence before computing, justifying why that operation fits the structure.
Tackle at least one genuinely multi-step problem that needs an operation choice and a combine step; estimate first, then compute and check for reasonableness.
Explain your choice using a bar model (for scaling/multiply-and-add) or a table/tree (for correspondence).
activities.intendedInsight: Choosing operations should come from recognising the problem's structure, not from hunting for key words. The same operation (multiplication) appears in three disguises; identifying the structure drives the correct set-up.

activities.title: Talk it through: what is this problem really asking?
feedback: If the learner is unsure, redirect to a quick table or drawing to ground the discussion in visible pairings.
When they say 'one more filling gives 3 more sandwiches (one per bread)', confirm they are reasoning about the structure, not a memorised rule.
activities.rationale: A Socratic dialogue supports problem-parsing habits and surfaces a learner's thinking. It complements, rather than replaces, the manipulable bars and grids where the structures are most clearly seen.
learnerActions: With a partner or adult playing a sandwich-shop owner, discuss a correspondence problem aloud: 'How many different sandwiches can I make?'
Answer probing questions: 'Are we making copies, or pairing options? If I add one more filling, how many MORE sandwiches — and why that many?'
Articulate the reasoning in your own words before writing a number sentence.
activities.intendedInsight: Parsing a word problem aloud — distinguishing 'times as many' from 'how many pairs' — builds the habit of interpreting structure before computing.

constraints: Classification and multiple-choice tasks verify whether a learner recognises structure but do not require them to construct the pairings or the comparison themselves; pair them with building activities.

Static worked panels (a scaling bar, a filled grid, a distributive split) are useful anchors for recognising structure, but they do not let the learner build the pairings or experience the multiplicative-vs-additive contrast dynamically; treat them as reference scaffolds.
Paper/card cards and cutouts are good concrete stand-ins for breads and fillings; a screen grid is an alternative, not a requirement.
Discussion activities develop parsing habits but should be grounded in a visible table, tree, or bar so reasoning stays concrete.

Incorrect answer options in any check (e.g. 18 for '3 times as tall as 15 m', 7 for correspondence, 60/64 for the distributive split) must target the real misconceptions; do not offer arithmetically incoherent options as plausible answers.

Differentiate by readiness: less-confident/younger learners can start with a smaller correspondence set (e.g. 2×3) and a one-step scaling problem with support, progressing to the distributive calculation with systematic listing and then to multi-step multiply-and-add problems justified with a bar model.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 14×6 = 10×6 + 4×6 = 60 + 24 = 84 (correct); the partial products are 60 and 24. 3×15 = 45 (correct); '3 m taller' = 18. 3×4 = 12 correspondence (correct); 3×5 = 15 for the 5-fillings extension. No arithmetic errors found.

The source's distributive error-pattern notes answers of '60 or 64' for splitting only one part — 60 (forgetting 4×6 entirely) and 64 (adding 4 un-multiplied) are both coherent error accounts and are preserved as diagnostic feedback, not as valid answers.

sourceClaims were pruned where an exact-copy claim supported only the curriculum topic rather than the activity's teaching principle: the DfE claim is not used on the correspondence activity (NCETM retained as the principle support) and the distributive activity has [] because no source[].claim directly supports the 'multiply both parts' area-model principle.

The CCSS-M 4.OA claim is retained on the scaling and classify activities on the basis of direct content overlap (multiplicative comparison; multistep problems with operation choice); its role as partly curriculum-scope and its verified:false status are flagged as uncertain rather than treated as established efficacy.
The original checkpoint tiering (Tier A age 8, Tier B, Tier C age 9) was folded into a differentiation constraint rather than dropped.

The legacy source's catalog-fit comparisons (3D 'adds cost', quiz 'verifies rather than builds') were softened to narrowly scoped affordance/limit statements; no comparative-efficacy or medium-superiority claim is asserted beyond the objective point that recognition-only tasks do not elicit independent construction.
One source claim (CCSS-M 4.OA) and the NCETM guidance claim are marked verified:false in the source; treat their support as unconfirmed.

probeDeeper: For the sandwiches, why do you multiply 3 by 4 instead of adding them?
In 14 × 6, did you multiply BOTH the 10 and the 4 by 6?
'3 times as tall as 15 m' — how is that different from '3 m taller'?
If there were 5 fillings instead of 4, how many sandwiches now?
assess.correctAnswer: 84 (10×6 + 4×6 = 60 + 24); 45 m (3 × 15); 12 sandwiches (3 × 4). The teacher watches for splitting both parts in the distributive item, multiplying for scaling, and recognising the correspondence problem as a product of the two option-sets, not a sum.

errorPatterns.pattern: adds instead of multiplying on the correspondence problem (3 + 4 = 7 sandwiches)
errorPatterns.nextMove: make a systematic grid/table of bread × filling so all 12 pairings are visible; name it as '4 sandwiches for EACH of the 3 breads'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer of 7; child sums the two option-sets rather than pairing every bread with every filling

errorPatterns.pattern: splits only one part in the distributive method (10×6 = 60, forgets 4×6) giving 60 or 64
errorPatterns.nextMove: use the area model — both the 10-strip and the 4-strip must be multiplied by 6 and added.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: distributive answer missing a partial product

errorPatterns.pattern: reads scaling additively — '3 times as tall as 15' as 15 + 3 = 18
errorPatterns.nextMove: build three copies of the 15 m height; 'times as tall' means copies, not 'taller by'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: scaling answer of 18 (added the multiplier)

errorPatterns.pattern: correct set-up, arithmetic slip in a partial product or product
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach structure; have the child recompute and estimate.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: right method, wrong number

responseLevels.gap: adds on the correspondence problem, splits one part in distributive, or reads scaling additively.
responseLevels.full: recognises and correctly sets up multiplication across distributive, scaling and correspondence problems, justifying why each is a product, and checks the results.
responseLevels.partial: handles the familiar distributive/scaling items but adds on correspondence, or needs prompting to see the multiplicative structure.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child three problems to solve while you watch the method: (distributive) 'Work out 14 × 6 by splitting 14 into 10 and 4'; (scaling) 'A model tower is 3 times as tall as a 15 m building — how tall is the model?'; (correspondence) 'There are 3 kinds of bread and 4 kinds of filling. How many different sandwiches can you make?' Watch how they set up each — especially whether they multiply for correspondence rather than add.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Correspondence problems are where children most often add (3 + 4 = 7) instead of multiplying, because the multiplicative structure is hidden. Watching all three problem types shows whether the child recognises multiplication across distributive, scaling AND correspondence structures — the same operation wearing three disguises.

sources.claim: Y4 pupils solve problems involving multiplying and adding, including the distributive law, integer scaling problems and harder correspondence problems (n objects connected to m objects).
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (KS1–2), Year 4 Number — multiplication and division

pedagogy.summary: This is the precise VOCABULARY of multiplicative reasoning — direct proportion, inverse proportion, ratio, rate, unit rate, compound unit, scale factor — used accurately in context. The teaching goal is not reciting definitions but USING each term correctly to describe real situations and knowing what units a rate/compound measure carries. The two words that cause most trouble are 'proportion' (whose everyday sense, 'a large proportion', drifts from the mathematical one) and the direct/inverse pair (pupils label anything with 'more' as 'direct'). Vocabulary is best taught with examples AND non-examples, tied to situations, and rehearsed in speaking and writing rather than as a glossary.
bestPractices: Teach each term through examples and NON-examples that fence its boundary (a directly proportional situation vs an inverse one vs a non-proportional one), following explicit-vocabulary practice (e.g. Frayer-style).
Always attach units when using rate/speed/density (mph, m/s, kg/m³) — a rate without units is incomplete.
Contrast the everyday and mathematical senses of 'proportion' directly, so the technical meaning (a multiplicative part-to-whole relationship) is distinguished from loose usage.
Rehearse the direct/inverse distinction in full sentences ('as one increases the other DEcreases, so it is inverse'), not as a label to guess.
Give pupils the terms to USE in describing and solving problems (calculate the speed of a car doing 120 miles in 2 hours and NAME it a rate), not to define in isolation.
keyRepresentations: Frayer-style word map (definition, characteristics, examples, non-examples) for each term
Paired example/non-example situation cards (direct | inverse | neither)
Unit tags for each compound measure (speed = mph or m/s; density = kg/m³)
Sentence frames ('as … increases, … so this is … proportion')
commonMisconceptions: Using 'proportion' in its loose everyday sense ('a large proportion') rather than the mathematical multiplicative meaning.
Labelling any 'more → more' situation 'direct proportion' and failing to identify inverse proportion (more workers → less time).
Using 'rate', 'speed' or 'density' without units, or treating 'ratio' and 'rate' as interchangeable.
Confusing 'scale factor' with an additive change rather than a multiplier.

learn.summary: Learners (ages 11–14) build precise command of multiplicative-reasoning vocabulary — direct proportion, inverse proportion, ratio, rate, unit rate, compound unit, scale factor — by USING each term accurately to describe real situations and stating the units a rate/compound measure carries. The goal is correct use in context, not reciting glossary definitions. The two persistent trouble spots are 'proportion' (whose everyday sense 'a large proportion' drifts from the mathematical multiplicative meaning) and the direct/inverse pair (learners label anything with 'more' as 'direct'). Vocabulary is taught with examples AND non-examples tied to situations, and rehearsed in speaking and writing.

activities.title: Talk it through with a market-stall trader (or science reporter)
feedback: When the learner calls 'more workers → less time' direct, don't supply the label — ask which way EACH quantity moves, then ask what happens to the time if the workers double (assuming each works at the same rate); let them hear themselves say 'opposite, and doubling halves it, so inverse.'
If 'proportion' is used loosely ('a large proportion'), ask: do you mean the everyday amount or the maths relationship where two quantities change in a constant ratio?
If a rate is named without units, ask for the units and why 'per' matters (miles PER hour compares distance to time).

Name the tell back to them: 'both increase together in a constant ratio → direct; one up while the other goes down with a constant product (double one, halve the other) → inverse' — and note that both increasing without a constant ratio, or one decreasing without a constant product, is neither.
activities.rationale: A LANGUAGE objective — using terms accurately in context — is well served by open dialogue where a character can probe loose usage in real time and push the learner toward precise use and units. The unscripted push, not a fixed script, drives self-correction. This is a research-informed proposal, not a tested intervention.
sourceClaims: The word 'proportion' has an everyday sense that drifts from its mathematical meaning; a directly proportional relationship is a constant multiplicative relationship between two quantities, distinct from ratio (part-to-part).

Students over-apply 'direct proportion' and fail to recognise inverse proportion (e.g. driving twice as fast halves the time); the properties of direct proportion must be named and contrasted with inverse and non-proportional situations.
learnerActions: Respond in-role to a character who throws real situations at you and listens for the right word: '3 apples for £1 — what do we call this, and what are its units?' (target: it is a rate; its unit rate is 'pounds per apple', found by sharing £1 across 3 apples ≈ £0.33 per apple — or equivalently 3 apples per pound).

When you label 'more workers, fewer hours' as direct, answer the follow-up: 'I add two workers and the time drops — are those two quantities moving the SAME way or opposite?' and revise to 'opposite — and if every worker works at the same rate, doubling the workers halves the time (workers × hours stays constant), so it is INVERSE proportion.'
Describe at least one directly proportional situation, one inverse, and name a rate aloud WITH its units (e.g. '120 miles in 2 hours is 60 miles per hour — a rate/speed, miles per hour').
Say a full sentence that explains WHY, e.g. 'as the petrol increases, the cost increases with it in a constant ratio, so it is direct proportion.'
activities.intendedInsight: A term is pinned to the behaviour it names — you decide 'direct' vs 'inverse' by checking whether the quantities move together in a constant ratio (direct) or oppositely with a constant product, so doubling one halves the other (inverse), not by spotting the word 'more'. If neither holds, the relationship is not proportional. A rate is incomplete without its units.

activities.title: Sort-and-tag: direct / inverse / neither, with unit tags
feedback: When a card is binned, state the reason: 'both quantities increase together in a constant ratio → direct' or 'one increases while the other decreases with a constant product (doubling one halves the other) → inverse.'
If a rate is tagged without units or with wrong units, prompt the X-per-Y form (miles per hour, kg per cubic metre).

Reinforce that 'neither' is a real category — not every 'more → more' situation is direct and not every 'more → less' situation is inverse; two quantities can both rise without a constant ratio, or one can fall as the other rises without a constant product.
activities.rationale: Sorting situations by the right term and tagging rates with units gives immediate feedback and builds the direct/inverse/neither boundary through examples and non-examples (Frayer-style fencing). A strong companion to the dialogue for boundary practice. Research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Explicit vocabulary instruction uses definitions with examples AND non-examples to fence a term's boundary, with active use rather than rote definition (Frayer model).

Students over-apply 'direct proportion' and fail to recognise inverse proportion (e.g. driving twice as fast halves the time); the properties of direct proportion must be named and contrasted with inverse and non-proportional situations.
learnerActions: Sort situation cards into three bins: direct proportion, inverse proportion, and neither (non-proportional).
Attach the correct unit tag to each rate card (speed = mph or m/s; density = kg/m³).
Complete sentence frames using the vocabulary, e.g. 'as … increases, … so this is … proportion.'
Read the feedback that names the tell ('both increase together in a constant ratio → direct') and re-sort any you placed wrongly.
activities.intendedInsight: The boundary between direct, inverse, and non-proportional situations becomes visible through contrasting examples and non-examples; every rate carries units.

activities.title: Frayer-style term map (reference and consolidation)
feedback: Check that each map includes a genuine non-example, not just an example reworded.
If 'scale factor' is described as 'add 3', correct it to a multiplier ('×3').

Tie the mathematical meaning of 'direct proportion' to 'as one changes, the other changes in a constant ratio', and of 'inverse proportion' to 'as one changes, the other changes so that their product stays constant.'
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal or written term map consolidates meanings and supports explicit-vocabulary practice. It is a reference/consolidation scaffold: it does not by itself require the learner to PRODUCE a term in a novel context, which the assessment targets — so it should accompany, not replace, the productive tasks. Research-informed proposal, not a tested intervention.
sourceClaims: Explicit vocabulary instruction uses definitions with examples AND non-examples to fence a term's boundary, with active use rather than rote definition (Frayer model).
learnerActions: For each term (direct proportion, inverse proportion, ratio, rate, unit rate, compound unit, scale factor), fill a four-box map: definition, characteristics, an example, and a non-example.
Add the units for each rate/compound measure (speed: mph or m/s; density: kg/m³).
Explicitly contrast the everyday sense of 'proportion' (an amount) with the mathematical sense (a multiplicative part-to-whole relationship / constant ratio).
Note that 'scale factor' is a MULTIPLIER, not an additive change.
activities.intendedInsight: Each term has a fenced meaning with clear examples, non-examples, and (for rates) units; 'proportion' and 'scale factor' have specific mathematical senses distinct from loose everyday use.

activities.title: Check and probe: use the words, generate your own examples
feedback: If both situations are called 'direct', have the learner say which way EACH quantity moves and whether doubling one halves the other; opposite movement with a constant product → inverse. Re-sort more example/non-example pairs rehearsing 'as … doubles, … halves, so inverse', including opposite-moving non-examples that are neither.
If 60 mph is called 'a ratio' or a 'rate' without units, insist on the X-per-Y units and explain a rate is a ratio of two different quantities with units.
If the learner can label but not generate a fresh inverse example, their use is recognitional, not yet productive — prompt for a new everyday situation.
activities.rationale: Correct-use judgements are assessable via categorisation and explanation, with loose-'proportion' and direct-for-inverse as sharp error patterns. Requiring self-generated examples distinguishes productive command from recognition. A selection/categorisation check verifies correct choice but does not on its own elicit the independent spoken/written use that is the objective, so it is paired with explain-and-generate tasks. Research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Students over-apply 'direct proportion' and fail to recognise inverse proportion (e.g. driving twice as fast halves the time); the properties of direct proportion must be named and contrasted with inverse and non-proportional situations.

The word 'proportion' has an everyday sense that drifts from its mathematical meaning; a directly proportional relationship is a constant multiplicative relationship between two quantities, distinct from ratio (part-to-part).
learnerActions: Given two situations — (1) the more workers dig the trench, the less time it takes (assume every worker digs at the same rate); (2) the more petrol you buy, the more it costs (at a fixed price per litre) — state for EACH whether the quantities are in direct or inverse proportion and say a sentence explaining why.
For a car travelling 120 miles in 2 hours, state what '60 miles per hour' is called and what makes it that (a rate/speed, a compound unit comparing distance to time, miles PER hour).
Generate your OWN fresh example of an inverse proportion and your own example of a direct proportion.
Distinguish 'rate' from 'ratio': a rate is a ratio of two DIFFERENT quantities carrying units (X per Y).
activities.intendedInsight: Real command shows in how you USE the words in an explaining sentence and in whether you can PRODUCE a correct fresh example — not in label-matching.

constraints: Always attach units when using rate/speed/density (mph, m/s, kg/m³); a rate stated without units is incomplete.
Teach each term through examples AND non-examples that fence its boundary (direct vs inverse vs non-proportional), with active use rather than rote definition.
Contrast the everyday and mathematical senses of 'proportion' directly so the technical multiplicative meaning is distinguished from loose usage.

Rehearse the direct/inverse distinction in full sentences ('as one increases the other decreases so that their product stays constant — doubling one halves the other — so it is inverse'), not as a label guessed from 'more'. One quantity going down as the other goes up is not enough on its own to make it inverse.
Direct proportion requires quantities that increase together IN A CONSTANT RATIO; 'both increase' alone is not sufficient and may be non-proportional, so keep 'neither' a live category.
Give learners the terms to USE in describing and solving problems, not to define in isolation (e.g. compute the speed of a car doing 120 miles in 2 hours and NAME it a rate).

The term map is a consolidation/reference scaffold: it supports recognition but does not require independent production of the term in a novel context, which the productive tasks and assessment target.

A multiple-choice or categorisation check verifies correct selection; it does not on its own elicit the independent spoken/written USE of a term that is the main objective — pair recognition items with explain-and-generate tasks.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source assessment's worked rate 120 miles ÷ 2 hours = 60 miles per hour is arithmetically correct and retained.

One source claim (IRIS Center / Frayer model) is flagged verified:false in the row; the examples/non-examples principle is widely used but its citation here is unverified — treat as supporting a teaching principle, not as evidence the proposed activities were tested.

The curriculum 'use and understand the vocabulary' claim is a general objective/necessity assertion. It states the overall objective but does not support any individual activity's teaching METHOD, so it has been removed from all activity sourceClaims (including the dialogue, where the prior draft had retained it inconsistently).

The inherited feedback tell 'both increase together → direct' was corrected to 'both increase together IN A CONSTANT RATIO → direct' at every occurrence, because unqualified it reinforces the targeted over-application misconception and contradicts the 'neither/non-proportional' category present in the same activity.

Inherited phrasing names '3 apples for £1' a 'unit rate, in pounds per apple'; strictly '3 apples for £1' is a rate, and its unit rate is £1 ÷ 3 ≈ £0.33 per apple (equivalently 3 apples per pound). The learner action now makes the normalisation to one unit explicit.

probeDeeper: In situation (1), which way does the TIME move as workers increase? So are the quantities moving the same way or opposite — and which word is that?
You used the word 'proportion' — do you mean it the everyday way (an amount) or the maths way (two quantities changing together in a constant ratio)?
What are the UNITS of the car's speed, and why does 'per' matter?
Give me your OWN example of an inverse proportion, and one of a direct proportion. (counterexample-generation: can they produce, not just label?)
assess.correctAnswer: (1) Inverse proportion — as the number of workers increases, the time DEcreases (one goes up as the other goes down). (2) Direct proportion — as the petrol increases, the cost increases with it (both go up together, in a constant ratio). '60 miles per hour' is a RATE (a compound unit/speed), because it compares distance to time — miles PER hour.

errorPatterns.pattern: Labels any 'more → more/less' situation 'direct proportion', missing inverse
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have them say which way EACH quantity moves; if they move oppositely it is inverse. Give more example/non-example pairs to sort, rehearsing the sentence 'as … up, … down, so inverse'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls the workers-and-time situation 'direct' because there are 'more workers', without noticing the time goes DOWN

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses 'proportion' in its everyday sense rather than the mathematical multiplicative meaning
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast the two senses explicitly; keep the mathematical meaning tied to 'as one changes, the other changes in a constant ratio'. Rehearse in full sentences about specific situations.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says things like 'a large proportion of workers' or uses 'proportion' to mean 'amount', not a relationship between two quantities

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses 'rate', 'speed' or 'density' without units, or treats 'ratio' and 'rate' as the same word
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist a rate carries its units (X PER Y); a rate is a ratio of two DIFFERENT quantities with units, distinct from a plain ratio. Tag several rates with their units.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names 60 mph 'a ratio', or calls it a rate but cannot say the units are miles per hour

responseLevels.gap: Calls both situations 'direct', or uses 'proportion'/'rate' loosely and without units; cannot tie a term to the behaviour it names.
responseLevels.full: Correctly identifies inverse (workers/time) and direct (petrol/cost) BY describing the opposite/together movement, names 60 mph a rate/speed with units (miles per hour), distinguishes rate from ratio, and generates own correct examples of each term.
responseLevels.partial: Uses direct/inverse correctly for the given cases and names 60 mph a rate, but omits units, or cannot generate a fresh example of inverse proportion — use is recognitional, not yet productive.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are two situations. (1) The more workers dig the trench, the less time it takes. (2) The more petrol you buy, the more it costs. For EACH one, tell me whether the two quantities are in direct proportion or inverse proportion, and say a sentence explaining why. Then: a car travels 120 miles in 2 hours — what do we call the '60 miles per hour', and what makes it that?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who owns the vocabulary attaches 'inverse' to the workers case BY describing the opposite movement, and 'direct' to petrol by the together-movement, and names 60 mph a rate with its units. A child guessing from 'more' calls both 'direct'. Listening for how they USE the words in the explaining sentence — not whether they can define them — is what separates real command from label-matching.

pedagogy.summary: Whole numbers are fractions too. Any whole number n equals n/1 (n wholes, each in one piece), and a fraction whose numerator is a multiple of its denominator equals a whole number (4/4 = 1, 8/4 = 2, 6/3 = 2). This grows from a/b as iteration of 1/b: b copies of 1/b make one whole (b/b = 1). The number line unifies it — 4/4 and 1 are the same point — and the idea connects to division (a/b = a ÷ b).
bestPractices: Build b/b = 1 by iterating the unit fraction b times (four quarters fill exactly one whole).
Introduce n/1 as 'n wholes, each left in one piece' — a denominator of 1 means 'not cut'.
Use the number line to land 4/4 on 1 and 8/4 on 2.
Sort fractions into 'equals a whole number' vs 'not' (6/3, 8/4 vs 5/2).
Connect informally to division: 6/3 = 6 ÷ 3 = 2.
keyRepresentations: Number line (4/4 on 1, 8/4 on 2)
Iterating unit fractions to complete a whole (b/b = 1)
Area model with the whole fully shaded
Fraction-as-division link (a ÷ b)
commonMisconceptions: 'A fraction can't be a whole number / can't equal 1' — fractions are always 'parts', always less than one
Thinking 4/4 is a little less than 1, or reading it as 'four'
n/1 puzzling — treating a denominator of 1 as meaningless or as zero
Reading 8/4 as separate digits rather than as 2

learn.summary: Helps 8–9 year-olds see that whole numbers are fractions too: any whole number n equals n/1, and a fraction whose numerator is a multiple of its denominator equals a whole number (4/4 = 1, 8/4 = 2, 6/3 = 2, 6/1 = 6). The core insight grows from iterating a unit fraction — b copies of 1/b make one whole, so b/b = 1 — and is unified on the number line, where 4/4 and 1 sit at the same point. The idea connects informally to division (a/b = a ÷ b). It is designed to address the misconception that fractions are always 'parts' less than one.

activities.title: Iterate quarters until a fraction lands on a whole number
feedback: If the marker is placed short of 1 for 4/4: lay the four quarter pieces end to end — they fill exactly one whole with nothing missing and nothing left over, so 4/4 sits exactly on 1, not before it.
If 8/4 is read as 'eight' or as separate digits: count the quarters as you stack — it takes four to reach 1 and four more to reach 2, so 8/4 lands on 2.
Prompt: 'How many quarters do you need to make exactly one whole? What fraction is that?' to reinforce b/b = 1.
activities.rationale: b copies of the unit fraction 1/b compose one whole, and non-unit fractions are built by iterating 1/b; placing whole numbers and fractions on the same number line lets 4/4 and 1 be seen as the same point, countering the idea that fractions are always less than one. Live iteration makes the moment of completion visible; a static families chart or an area model can also show b/b = 1 for recall but do not show the completion unfolding.
sourceClaims: b copies of a unit fraction 1/b compose one whole, and non-unit fractions are built from unit fractions; number lines should place whole numbers, proper and improper fractions together so that e.g. 4/4 and 1 occupy the same point; treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers is a core misconception.
learnerActions: Starting from 0 on a number line, add one quarter piece at a time and read the running total: 1/4, 2/4, 3/4 …
As the fourth quarter is added, check where the marker lands and name the fraction there (4/4) and the whole number at that point (1).
Keep stacking quarters past one whole and find where 8/4 lands (on 2), noticing it took eight quarters — two full wholes' worth.
Say in your own words how many quarters make exactly one whole, and complete b/b = 1 for quarters (4/4 = 1).
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction can land exactly on a whole number: four quarters compose one whole, so 4/4 IS 1, and 8/4 IS 2. This happens whenever the numerator is a multiple of the denominator.

activities.title: A denominator of 1 means 'not cut': writing whole numbers as fractions
feedback: If a denominator of 1 seems meaningless or like zero: a cut into 1 piece leaves the whole intact, so 5/1 is five whole, uncut bars — not nothing.
If the child cannot write 5 as a fraction: ask how many pieces each whole is cut into when it is left whole (one), then the numerator counts the wholes: 5/1.
Check placement: 5/1 should sit on the 5 mark, confirming 5/1 = 5.
activities.rationale: Expressing whole numbers as fractions (3 = 3/1) and recognising fractions equivalent to whole numbers are stated Year 3 expectations in the cited curriculum; framing a denominator of 1 as 'in one piece' addresses the specific n/1 confusion where a denominator of 1 seems meaningless.
sourceClaims: In Year 3 (age 8–9) pupils recognise fractions equivalent to whole numbers and begin to express whole numbers as fractions.
learnerActions: Work with whole, uncut bars and read a denominator of 1 as 'the whole is left in one piece'.
Write the number 5 as a fraction (5/1) and explain that it means five wholes, each uncut.
Place 5/1 on a number line at 5, and 3/1 at 3, checking they land on the whole-number marks.
Explain what the bottom number 1 is telling you when you write 3 = 3/1.
activities.intendedInsight: A denominator of 1 is meaningful: it says the whole has not been cut, so n/1 is simply n wholes. Every whole number can be written as a fraction.

activities.title: Sort fractions: whole number or not?
feedback: If 5/2 is called a whole number 'because 5 and 2 are both whole numbers': 5 ÷ 2 is not exact — 5 is not a multiple of 2 — so 5/2 lands at 2½, between the whole numbers, not on one.
If 6/3 is mishandled: 6 ÷ 3 = 2 exactly, and three thirds make one whole so six thirds make two wholes; 6/3 lands on 2.
Prompt: 'Is 5/2 a whole number? Where does it land, and what does that tell you?'
activities.rationale: Treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers is a core misconception; relating a/b to a ÷ b and testing the multiple relationship generalises beyond the single case b/b = 1 to a·b/b. Sorting and matching tasks are suited to checking and consolidating classification once the completion idea has been built; a sort by itself does not elicit the child building a whole or explaining why.
sourceClaims: b copies of a unit fraction 1/b compose one whole, and non-unit fractions are built from unit fractions; number lines should place whole numbers, proper and improper fractions together so that e.g. 4/4 and 1 occupy the same point; treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers is a core misconception.
learnerActions: Decide for each of 6/3, 8/4 and 5/2 whether it equals a whole number, and sort them into 'equals a whole number' vs 'not'.
For each, test whether the numerator is a multiple of the denominator, using division: 6 ÷ 3 = 2, 8 ÷ 4 = 2, 5 ÷ 2 is not a whole number.
Place 5/2 on a number line to show it lands at 2½, between 2 and 3.
Match 8/4 to the whole number 2 and explain how you knew.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction equals a whole number exactly when the numerator is a multiple of the denominator; a/b can be read as a ÷ b. Having both digits be whole numbers (as in 5/2) does not make the fraction a whole number.

activities.title: Predict-then-check: where does 4/4 land?
feedback: If the prediction was 'before 1' because 'a fraction is always less than one': the four quarters fill exactly one whole with nothing left over, landing on 1 — so a fraction CAN equal a whole number.
Confirm the generalisation: this works whenever the numerator is a multiple of the denominator (4/4, 8/4, 6/3), not just for this one case.
If the reason given before observing was correct, ask the child to predict where 8/4 lands to extend the rule.
activities.rationale: The reason stated before observing is the diagnostic part: a child who thinks fractions are always parts less than one predicts before 1, and iterating the quarters directly contradicts that belief by landing exactly on 1. Predict-then-check with a reason is proposed to surface the misconception rather than only assess the answer.
sourceClaims: b copies of a unit fraction 1/b compose one whole, and non-unit fractions are built from unit fractions; number lines should place whole numbers, proper and improper fractions together so that e.g. 4/4 and 1 occupy the same point; treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers is a core misconception.
learnerActions: Before doing anything, PREDICT with a reason whether 4/4 lands before 1, exactly on 1, or past 1 on a number line, and state your reason out loud or in writing first.
Then iterate four 1/4-jumps from 0 (or build four quarters) and observe where you land.
Compare what happened to your prediction, and revise your reason if needed.
State the general rule you now believe about whether a fraction can equal a whole number.
activities.intendedInsight: Stating a reason before observing surfaces the belief 'fractions are always parts less than one'; building four quarters that fill exactly one whole and land on 1 contradicts it.

constraints: Multiple-choice, matching and slider tasks (e.g. 'which equal whole numbers: 6/3, 8/4, 5/2?', matching 8/4 → 2, placing 4/4 on a line, filling in 5 = ?/1) are suited to classifying and recall once the idea is built, but recognition-only responses do not by themselves elicit the child constructing the whole by iteration or explaining why; pair them with building or explanation.

A static reference (tap 4/4 → 'four quarters = one whole = 1', flip-to-reveal 8/4 = 2) can support recall of b/b = 1 families but does not show the completion of a whole unfolding; use it as a reference alongside the iteration activity, not as a replacement.

An area model with the whole fully shaded (e.g. four shaded quarters filling one square) is another valid representation of b/b = 1 alongside the number line and the stacked/length model; use whichever makes 'four quarters compose one whole' concrete for the child.

Paper or card quarter pieces have slight real thickness and are a physical model of the ideal mathematical idea; treat the stacked pieces as a way of composing one whole, and keep the exact number-line point as the mathematical meaning.
Ensure the child generalises beyond the single memorised case b/b = 1 to a·b/b (e.g. 8/4, 6/3); accepting 4/4 = 1 alone is partial understanding.
Use the fraction-as-division link (a/b = a ÷ b) informally at this age, as a test for whether the numerator is a multiple of the denominator, not as a formal algorithm.
Treat fractions as numbers that share one number line with the whole numbers; the task is to compare and place their values, not to require redrawing a common whole.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The first listed source (IES/WWC Practice Guide) is marked verified:true in the row; the second (DfE National Curriculum) is marked verified:false. The Year 3 curriculum claim used in activity 2 should be treated as unconfirmed in this rewrite.

The predict-then-check routine in activity 4 is a design proposal; the cited sources support that iteration on a number line refutes the 'less than one' belief, but do not establish the comparative effectiveness of reason-before-observing.
Self-audit of arithmetic: 4/4 = 1, 8/4 = 2, 6/3 = 2, 6/1 = 6, and 5/2 = 2½ (between 2 and 3) are all correct and retained. No arithmetic errors found.
The area model representation listed in the source's key representations is carried as an alternative representation constraint alongside the number line and length model.

The non-preferred 3D-interactive and conversation catalog entries were dropped as ranking judgements, not pedagogical laws; a denominator of 1 and the fraction-as-division idea could in principle also be discussed verbally as support, so no categorical 'only building teaches' claim is asserted.

Independent re-audit confirms no 'denominator flips' comparison, no categorical modality claim, and that the physical-cutout thickness/ideal-figure distinction is stated in the activity-facing constraints, not only in a reviewer note.

assess.poeTask: Ask the child to PREDICT, with a reason, whether 4/4 lands before 1, exactly on 1, or past 1 on a number line. The reason stated before observing is the diagnostic part — a child who thinks fractions are always 'parts less than one' predicts before 1. Then iterate four 1/4-jumps from 0 (or build four quarters): they fill exactly one whole and land on 1, refuting 'a fraction must be less than 1'.
probeDeeper: How many quarters do you need to make exactly one whole? What fraction is that?
Where does 8/4 go on the line — and why is it the same place as 2?
Is 5/2 a whole number? Where does it land, and what does that tell you?
Write the number 3 as a fraction. What does the bottom number 1 mean?
assess.correctAnswer: 4/4 = 1 — four quarters make one whole, so it lands exactly on 1. Whole numbers: 6/3 = 2 and 8/4 = 2 (the numerator is a multiple of the denominator: 6÷3 = 2, 8÷4 = 2). 5/2 is not a whole number (5 is not a multiple of 2; it lands at 2½, between 2 and 3).

errorPatterns.pattern: Fractions are always parts / always less than 1 — '4/4 is a bit less than 1, it's still a fraction'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Iterate four quarters to fill exactly one whole; land 4/4 on the 1 mark; name b/b = 1
errorPatterns.distractor: 4/4 is a little less than 1 — it's a fraction, not a whole number
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Places 4/4 short of 1; denies a fraction can equal a whole number

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers — 'if both digits are whole numbers the fraction is a whole number', so 5/2 counts
errorPatterns.nextMove: Relate a/b to a ÷ b and to iterating on the line; test whether the numerator is a multiple of the denominator
errorPatterns.distractor: 5/2 is a whole number because 5 and 2 are both whole numbers
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls 5/2 a whole number, or cannot see 8/4 = 2

errorPatterns.pattern: n/1 confusion — a denominator of 1 seems meaningless, so cannot write 5 as 5/1
errorPatterns.nextMove: A denominator of 1 means the whole is in one piece, so 5/1 is five wholes; place 5/1 on the line at 5
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cannot express a whole number as a fraction, or misreads 5/1

responseLevels.gap: Believes fractions are always less than 1; places 4/4 before 1; reads 8/4 and 5/2 by their separate digits.
responseLevels.full: Places 4/4 on 1 and explains b copies of 1/b make a whole; identifies 6/3 and 8/4 as whole numbers (numerator a multiple of the denominator / a ÷ b) and 5/2 as not; writes a whole number as n/1.
responseLevels.partial: Accepts 4/4 = 1 but cannot reliably identify 6/3 and 8/4 as whole numbers or explain n/1 — knows the single case b/b = 1 without generalising to a·b/b.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Is 4/4 equal to 1, or less than 1? Put a dot where 4/4 goes on this 0-to-2 number line and explain why it lands there. Then: which of these are whole numbers — 6/3, 8/4, 5/2 — and how do you know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands b/b = 1 and a/b as iteration places 4/4 on 1 and identifies 6/3 and 8/4 as whole numbers. A child who believes fractions are always less than 1 puts 4/4 short of 1; a whole-number-bias child mishandles 6/3 or calls 5/2 a whole number by reading the digits separately.

sources.claim: b copies of a unit fraction 1/b compose one whole, and non-unit fractions are built from unit fractions; number lines should place whole numbers, proper and improper fractions together so that e.g. 4/4 and 1 occupy the same point; treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers is a core misconception.

sources.claim: In Year 3 (age 8–9) pupils recognise fractions equivalent to whole numbers and begin to express whole numbers as fractions.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 7–8 (UK Y2–Y3, US Grade 2). Using addition to find the total in rectangular arrays (up to 5×5) and writing an equation expressing the total as a sum of EQUAL ADDENDS — the array-to-repeated-addition bridge.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2 'solve problems … using … arrays, repeated addition …'; recorded with × signs as tables develop (Y2–Y3).
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.OA.4 'use addition to find the total number of objects arranged in rectangular arrays with up to 5 rows and up to 5 columns; write an equation to express the total as a sum of equal addends'.
• Operational details: read the array by ROWS — each row is an equal addend — and write 4+4+4 (three rows of four), then connect to 3×4. Emphasise the addends are EQUAL (that's what makes it a multiplication situation). This formalises the array as the pivot between addition and multiplication.
• Checkpoint: array → equal-addend equation. Tier A (7): count an array's total by adding rows. Tier B (7–8): write the equal-addend equation (4+4+4=12) for a 3-row array. Tier C (8): write both the addition and the multiplication for an array and explain the addends must be equal.
bestPractices: Read the array row by row so each row becomes one equal addend, then write the repeated-addition equation — making 'sum of equal addends' concrete before the × symbol.
Stress that the addends must be EQUAL: contrast an array (equal rows) with a ragged arrangement (unequal rows) that is NOT a multiplication situation.
Bridge to the × symbol by pairing the equal-addend equation with the multiplication (4+4+4 alongside 3×4), so children see multiplication as the shorthand.
Read the same array by columns too, foreshadowing commutativity (three 4s or four 3s).
Keep arrays within 5×5 and physically buildable, so the structure (rows/columns) is clear and countable.
keyRepresentations: Rectangular array read row-by-row (each row = one equal addend)
Repeated-addition equation (4 + 4 + 4 = 12)
Paired addition/multiplication (4+4+4 ↔ 3×4)
Ragged (unequal-row) non-example for contrast
commonMisconceptions: Adding UNEQUAL groups and still writing it as a single multiplication (missing the equal-addends requirement).
Counting every object individually rather than adding equal rows.
Confusing the number of rows with the number in each row when writing the equation.
Not connecting the repeated-addition equation to the multiplication (seeing them as separate).
Miscounting by losing track of which rows have been added (no systematic row-by-row approach).

learn.summary: For ages 7–8 (UK Y2–Y3, US Grade 2): use addition to find the total of objects in a rectangular array (up to 5×5) and write an equation expressing the total as a sum of EQUAL addends, then bridge to the multiplication fact. The core insight is that each row of the array contributes one equal addend, so reading an array row by row turns it into repeated addition (4+4+4=12) and then into 3×4. Equality of the rows is what makes it a multiplication situation, so a ragged (unequal-row) arrangement serves as the key non-example.

activities.title: Sum the rows: build the equal-addend equation from an array
feedback: If the child writes 3+4 (rows plus row-size): shade one row to show it holds 4, then show that same 4 repeats for every row → 4+4+4. Name clearly that 'number of rows' and 'amount in each row' are two different things; the equation adds the row-amount once per row.

If the child gives the correct sum but justifies it only as 'because it makes 12': cover the rows one at a time so each shows the same 4, and name that the rows being equal is exactly what lets you add 4 repeatedly instead of counting every dot.

If the child insists on counting every dot and distrusts the shortcut: do NOT force the shortcut. Let them verify by counting a few arrays so repeated addition earns their trust over several examples.

For the ragged arrangement: confirm that because the rows are not equal you cannot write one repeated-equal-addend equation, so it is not a multiplication situation — this is the point of the contrast.
activities.rationale: Assembling 4+4+4 row by row makes 'sum of equal addends' concrete before the × symbol, and pairing it with 3×4 presents multiplication as shorthand for adding equal rows. Reading by columns previews commutativity (three 4s vs four 3s), and the ragged non-example isolates the equal-addends requirement that defines a multiplication situation.
sourceClaims: Y2: solve problems using arrays and repeated addition, recorded with multiplication signs as tables develop.
2.OA.4 use addition to find the total in rectangular arrays (up to 5×5) and write an equation expressing the total as a sum of equal addends.
learnerActions: Look at a 3×4 array (3 rows, 4 dots in each row) and point to one row to establish that it holds 4 dots.
Add the array one row at a time, saying and writing the running total: 4, then 4+4, then 4+4+4 = 12 — one addend per row.
After writing 4+4+4=12, write the matching multiplication 3×4=12 and say which number tells how many rows and which tells how many are in each row.
Read the same array by columns instead and write it as 3+3+3+3 (four 3s), noticing you get 12 again.
Now try a ragged arrangement where one row has 4 and another has 5; attempt to write a single equal-addend equation and explain why it will not form.
activities.intendedInsight: Each equal row of an array is one equal addend, so adding the rows gives the total; the multiplication fact is just the shorthand for adding equal rows, and this only works when the rows are equal.

activities.title: Draw an array for a given equation
feedback: If the number of rows and the amount per row get swapped, have the child count the addends in the equation (how many 5s? four) and match that to the number of rows drawn.
If rows are drawn unequal, point out that the equation uses the same number each time, so every row must hold the same amount.
activities.rationale: Constructing an array from a given equation requires producing structure rather than recognising it, strengthening the array↔equation bridge in both directions.
learnerActions: Given the equation 5+5+5+5, draw a rectangular array that matches it (four rows of five, or equivalently five columns of four).
Say aloud which part of the equation is the number of rows and which is the amount in each row.
Write the multiplication fact for your array (4×5 or 5×4) and check the total matches 20.
Explain why your drawing shows equal rows and how that connects back to the repeated addition.
activities.intendedInsight: Children can move in both directions — from array to equation and from equation to array — which shows they understand the equal-groups structure rather than just reading one off the other.

activities.title: Match and complete: array ↔ equal-addend equation ↔ multiplication
feedback: If a learner picks the unequal-addend distractor, draw the arrangement that equation would represent and shade its rows to show they are not equal, so it does not match the equal-rows array and cannot be written as one repeated-equal-addend equation.
If the addition and multiplication are seen as unrelated, place 4+4+4 beside 3×4 and count: three rows, four in each — the multiplication summarises the addition.
activities.rationale: Fill-in and matching tasks check the bridge crisply and surface whether a child still confuses adding equal rows with adding unequal groups. These are checks of recognition and completion; they confirm understanding but do not by themselves require independent construction, so pair them with the drawing and build-the-equation activities.
learnerActions: For a shown array, fill in the blanks of the equal-addend equation (__ + __ + __ = __).
Write the matching multiplication fact for the same array.

From a set of candidate equations, choose the one that matches a given equal-rows array; include a distractor that uses unequal addends (e.g., 3+4+5), which would correspond to a ragged arrangement and does not match.
Explain why the unequal-addend distractor cannot represent the equal-rows array as a single equal-addend equation.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising and completing the correct equal-addend equation (and rejecting an unequal-addend distractor) confirms the array-to-repeated-addition bridge and the equal-addends requirement.

constraints: Keep arrays within 5×5 and physically buildable (counters, dots, or drawn grids) so rows and columns stay clear and countable.
Emphasise throughout that the addends must be EQUAL; always contrast the array with a ragged, unequal-row arrangement that is NOT a multiplication situation.

Matching/fill-in tasks assess recognition and completion; they do not on their own elicit independent construction of an array or equation, so include at least one task where the child builds an array from an equation or assembles the equation from scratch.

A static labelled array (tap- or lift-to-reveal addends and the × fact) is a useful reference and shows the bridge, but does not let the child build the sum row by row or test the equal-addends requirement dynamically; treat it as a scaffold, not a replacement for building.
Do not push the repeated-addition shortcut on a child who still needs to count every object to trust it; let repeated addition earn trust through several verified examples.

If optional on-screen interaction is used (tapping a row to drop its value into a running equation, a 'fold'/combine action collapsing 4+4+4 into 3×4, a rotate control to read by columns, a ragged-array mode), these are illustrative mechanisms to make the bridge visible, not required tooling.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The second listed source (CCSS-M 2.OA.4) is marked verified:false in the row; the exact-claim citations are carried over as-is and their verification status is unchanged.

Activity 2 (equation→array drawing) corresponds to the row's evidence item 'Draw a rectangular array to model a given repeated-addition equation', but no cited source claim directly supports the reverse-construction principle, so its sourceClaims is [] (topic-aligned, not evidence the reverse task is required).

Planar vs 3D: the original row asserts '3D adds nothing' and that dialogue 'adds little unique value'. These are catalog-style comparative claims not established by the sources; they have been dropped as universal laws. Arrays are naturally planar, so a flat representation fits the content, but no claim is made that other media cannot teach it.

Arithmetic self-check performed: 4+4+4=12 and 3×4=12 are correct; reading the same 3×4 array by columns gives 3+3+3+3=12 (four 3s), consistent with the commutativity preview. The 5+5+5+5 drawing example corresponds to 4×5=20. The Activity 3 distractor 3+4+5 sums to 12 (same total, unequal addends), a valid equal-addends discriminator.
The misconception '3+4' is handled as a clear conceptual error: the activity feedback corrects it (row-count vs row-size) rather than presenting it as a valid alternative.

Activity 3's equation-matching distractor is an unequal-addend equation (not a loosely described 'arrangement'), so the choice set stays internally consistent; its feedback draws and shades the represented ragged arrangement to show the rows are unequal.

probeDeeper: Which number in 4 + 4 + 4 is the amount in a row, and which tells how many rows?
Draw an array for 5 + 5 + 5 + 5.
If one row had 4 and another had 5, could you still add the same number each time?
How would you write this array as a multiplication?
assess.correctAnswer: Yes — every row has the same number, 4, and there are 3 rows, so the total is 4 added three times. Equal rows let you add the row-amount repeatedly instead of counting every dot.

errorPatterns.pattern: adds the dimensions, not the equal rows — writes something like 3 + 4 (row-count plus row-size) instead of repeated equal addends
errorPatterns.nextMove: shade one row (4), then show it repeats 3 times → 4 + 4 + 4; distinguish the number of rows from the amount in each row
errorPatterns.distractor: 3 + 4 works because there are 3 rows and 4 in each.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: an addition that isn't repeated equal addends

errorPatterns.pattern: agrees the sum but not the reason — accepts 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 yet justifies only 'because it makes 12', not because the rows are equal
errorPatterns.nextMove: cover the rows one at a time to show each contributes the same 4; name equality as what licenses repeated addition
errorPatterns.revealedBy: correct sum with no equal-rows reason

errorPatterns.pattern: counts by ones only — insists you must count every dot; repeated addition feels untrustworthy
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT push the shortcut — let the child verify by counting a few times so repeated addition earns trust; the shortcut is adopted with experience
errorPatterns.revealedBy: won't accept 4 + 4 + 4 without counting to confirm

responseLevels.gap: Can only get the total by counting every object; can't connect it to repeated addition.
responseLevels.full: Explains repeated addition works because every row holds the same number, and moves between array, equal-addends sum, and multiplication.
responseLevels.partial: Writes or accepts the repeated-addition equation but doesn't ground it in the rows being equal.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Look at this array — 3 rows with 4 dots in each row. Sam counted the dots one by one and got 12. Priya wrote 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 without counting them all. Is Priya's way correct, and why does adding 4 three times work for this array?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands the array's equal-groups structure explains that repeated addition works BECAUSE the rows are equal. A child without it accepts 12 as 'the count' but can't say why 4 + 4 + 4 matches, or writes an addition that ignores equal rows (e.g. 3 + 4). The 'why does adding 4 three times work' tier forces the equal-addends reasoning.
