pedagogy.summary: Simplifying is the equivalence principle run in reverse: instead of multiplying numerator and denominator by n, you DIVIDE both by a common factor, which regroups the same quantity into fewer, larger pieces without changing its value. Simplest form is reached when numerator and denominator share no common factor but 1 (i.e. you have divided by the HCF). The same machinery — finding a common multiple — lets you rewrite two fractions over a shared denominator. Both skills rest on one idea from Year 5: a/b = (n×a)/(n×b), so a/b = (a÷n)/(b÷n). Teach simplification as 'un-grouping' back to the coarsest partition, not as a memorised rule.
bestPractices: Anchor the procedure to the equivalence principle already learned: show that dividing top and bottom by the same number is the inverse of multiplying by the same number, so the value is unchanged — use a fraction wall or area model where 6/8 and 3/4 occupy identical length.

Connect directly to common factors/multiples work: to simplify, divide by a common factor (fastest via the HCF); to find a common denominator, use a common multiple (efficiently the LCM). Make the number theory visible, not incidental.

Distinguish 'an equivalent, simpler fraction' from 'simplest form' explicitly — a child who writes 6/8 = 3/4 has simplified; a child who writes 6/8 = ... but stops at a form still sharing a factor has not finished. Ask 'can you go further?' every time.
Use dividing-by-HCF as the efficient route but accept repeated division by any common factor (÷2 then ÷2) as valid — the concept, not the shortcut, is the target.
Contrast simplifying with the illegal move of adding or subtracting the same number from top and bottom, which does change the value; have children test 6/8 vs (6-2)/(8-2)=4/6 against the wall.
keyRepresentations: Fraction wall / bar model where equivalent fractions align to identical length (6/8 sits exactly over 3/4)
Area model / grid that can be re-partitioned by merging small cells into larger groups (24 cells shaded 18, re-grouped into 4 columns of which 3 are shaded → 3/4)
Factor pairs and HCF listing beside the fraction (18 = 2×3×3, 24 = 2×2×2×3, common = 2×3 = 6)
Number line showing 18/24 and 3/4 landing on the identical point
Common-multiple ladder for the common-denominator task (thirds and eighths both re-cut into 24ths)
commonMisconceptions: Simplifying by SUBTRACTING a common amount from numerator and denominator (6/8 → 4/6 by taking 2 from each) instead of dividing — treats the fraction additively.
Stopping before simplest form: dividing 18/24 by 2 to get 9/12 and calling it done, not checking for a remaining common factor.
Operating on only one part — dividing the numerator but not the denominator (or renaming only the denominator when finding a common denominator).
Believing simplifying changes the fraction's value ('3/4 is bigger than 6/8 because 4 is fewer pieces') rather than renaming the same quantity.
When finding a common denominator, changing the denominators to match but forgetting to scale the numerators correspondingly.

learn.summary: Teach simplifying as the equivalence principle run in reverse: dividing numerator and denominator by a common factor regroups the same quantity into fewer, larger pieces without changing its value, just as multiplying both by n does. Simplest form is reached when numerator and denominator share no common factor but 1 (you have divided by the HCF). The same number-theory machinery — finding a common multiple — lets two fractions be rewritten over a shared denominator. Anchor to the Year 5 fact a/b = (n×a)/(n×b), so a/b = (a÷n)/(b÷n), and treat simplification as 'un-grouping' back to the coarsest partition, not a memorised rule.

activities.title: Un-grouping a bar: 18/24 back to simplest form
feedback: If the bar length stays fixed while the label changes, the value is unchanged — that non-movement IS the point: same quantity, fewer pieces.
If a chosen divisor leaves leftover cells that won't tile evenly, it is not a common factor of both numbers — that felt 'doesn't fit' is what 'common factor' means.
If you stop at 9/12, ask 'can you go further? do 9 and 12 still share a factor?' — 9/12 is correct but not finished.
Dividing by the HCF (6) reaches simplest form in one step; for 18/24, ÷2 then ÷3 is equally valid and reaches the same place — the concept, not the shortcut, is the target.
activities.rationale: A re-partitionable area/bar model lets the learner perform the regrouping and see the fixed length, making 'same value, fewer pieces' and 'common factor' felt rather than merely told. An optional divisor-snap mechanism (groups form only when the divisor divides both numbers, otherwise leftovers appear) may make the failure of a non-common factor concrete; a 'simplest form' indicator that stays dark until no factor above 1 remains may discourage stopping early. These interaction examples are illustrative proposals, not required and not empirically validated.
sourceClaims: Understanding equivalent fractions — that a fraction can be renamed by multiplying or dividing numerator and denominator by the same number without changing its value — is foundational, and instruction should build simplifying on this principle using visual number-line and area models rather than rote rules.
Pupils should use common factors to simplify fractions and use common multiples to express fractions in the same denomination (Year 6 statutory content).
learnerActions: Start with a bar partitioned into 24 cells with 18 shaded, labelled 18/24.
Choose a number to 'group by' (a divisor) and merge the cells into equal groups of that size, watching the fraction label recompute (e.g. grouping in sixes gives 4 fat groups with 3 shaded → 3/4).

Observe that for each valid grouping of the original 24-cell bar the shaded LENGTH does not move while the label takes an equivalent form (grouping by 2 → 9/12, by 3 → 6/8, by 6 → 3/4) — the quantity is unchanged, only the cut is coarser.
Deliberately try a divisor that is NOT a common factor (e.g. 5): notice the cells will not group evenly and leftovers remain, so that divisor is rejected.
Keep going until no grouping beyond 1 is possible, then state the simplest form and name the HCF (6) that would have reached it in one step.
Also try the valid repeated route (÷2 then ÷3) and confirm it lands on the same 3/4.
activities.intendedInsight: Dividing both parts by a common factor regroups the same quantity into fewer, larger equal pieces, leaving the value (length) unchanged; simplest form is reached only when no common factor above 1 remains.

activities.title: Common denominator by re-cutting to a shared multiple
feedback: If you changed only the denominators (2/24, 5/24) the fractions now mean far less than before — re-cutting the whole into more parts means you must count correspondingly more shaded parts.
Both 24 and 48 are common multiples of 3 and 8, so both give a valid shared denominator; 24 is the smallest (the LCM).
Match the scaling factor: 3→24 is ×8, so 2→16; 8→24 is ×3, so 5→15.
activities.rationale: Re-cutting two bars to a shared grid makes a common multiple visible as a partition both fractions can sit on, and re-shading exposes the classic error of changing denominators without scaling numerators. A ladder of common multiples may make the LCM choice explicit. These are proposed scaffolds, not validated interventions.
sourceClaims: Pupils should use common factors to simplify fractions and use common multiples to express fractions in the same denomination (Year 6 statutory content).
learnerActions: Place bars for 2/3 and 5/8 (or thirds and eighths) side by side.
Find a common multiple of 3 and 8 to use as the shared denominator (24 works; 48 also works — find the smallest, the LCM).
Re-cut BOTH bars into 24ths and rewrite each fraction: 2/3 = 16/24 and 5/8 = 15/24, scaling each numerator by the same factor used on its denominator.
Check: 2/3 becomes 16/24 because both parts were multiplied by 8; 5/8 becomes 15/24 because both were multiplied by 3 — the numerator must scale with the denominator.
Compare using 24 versus 48 and explain why 24 is the smallest denominator that works.
activities.intendedInsight: Expressing fractions over a common denominator uses a common multiple (efficiently the LCM); when you change a denominator you must scale its numerator by the same factor, or you change the quantity.

activities.title: Divide versus subtract: testing the illegal move
feedback: If 4/6 and 6/8 land at different lengths on the wall, the value changed — subtracting from both parts is not simplifying.
If 3/4 and 6/8 land at the same length, dividing both parts preserved the value — that is the legal move.
activities.rationale: Directly testing the additive misconception against a length model lets the learner see the value shift, addressing the common belief that any identical change to both parts is harmless. The wall comparison is the diagnostic surface.
sourceClaims: Understanding equivalent fractions — that a fraction can be renamed by multiplying or dividing numerator and denominator by the same number without changing its value — is foundational, and instruction should build simplifying on this principle using visual number-line and area models rather than rote rules.
learnerActions: Take 6/8 and perform the illegal move of subtracting the same amount from both parts: (6−2)/(8−2) = 4/6.
Lay 6/8 and 4/6 on the same fraction wall or bar and compare their lengths.
Observe that the lengths differ, so subtracting the same number from top and bottom DID change the value.
Contrast with dividing both parts by 2: 6/8 → 3/4, whose length matches 6/8 exactly.
State what the test showed: multiplying or dividing both parts by the same non-zero number keeps the value, but subtracting the same amount from both parts generally changes it (as 6/8 → 4/6 did).
activities.intendedInsight: Simplifying is division of both parts by a common factor, not subtraction of a common amount; the additive move generally changes the value (it keeps it only in special cases such as fractions equal to 1), so it is not a valid equivalence method.

activities.title: Check and explain (assessment of output)
feedback: Only 3/4 among 9/12, 6/8, 3/4, 12/16 is fully simplified; the others still share a factor with their denominator.
9/12 is not wrong, just not finished — 9 and 12 still share a factor of 3, so simplify again to 3/4.

For 18/24, answers like 16/22 or 12/18 (from subtracting a common amount from both parts) or 3/24 (dividing only the numerator) reveal the wrong operation, not just a stopping error — revisit the bar model.
activities.rationale: Short checkable items with distractors built from the subtract-instead-of-divide and stop-early errors make this a diagnostic assessment of the output. Recognition and short-answer items check the result; by themselves they do not elicit the regrouping insight, so this complements rather than replaces the manipulative work.
learnerActions: Write 18/24 in its simplest form and show the working (via HCF 6, or ÷2 then ÷3).
Rewrite 2/3 and 5/8 so they share the same denominator.
Identify which of 9/12, 6/8, 3/4, 12/16 is fully simplified and explain why the others are not.
Explain why dividing both parts by the same non-zero number does not change the value, while subtracting the same amount from both parts generally does.
Answer: your friend simplified 18/24 to 9/12 and stopped — is 9/12 wrong, or just not finished? How do you know?
activities.intendedInsight: Simplest form and common-denominator rewriting can be stated and justified, distinguishing a correct-but-unfinished answer from a wrong operation.

constraints: Build simplifying on the equivalence principle learners met in Year 5 (a/b = (n×a)/(n×b)); do not teach it as an isolated rule.
Make the number theory explicit: divide by a common factor (efficiently the HCF) to simplify; use a common multiple (efficiently the LCM) for a common denominator.
Always ask 'can you go further?' — distinguish 'an equivalent simpler fraction' from 'simplest form'. Stopping at 9/12 is unfinished, not wrong.
Accept repeated division by any common factor (e.g. ÷2 then ÷2 where both divide evenly, or ÷2 then ÷3 for 18/24) as valid; the concept, not the HCF shortcut, is the target.
Simplifying compares and regroups the SAME fraction; no denominator rule 'flips' — dividing both parts by a shared factor is a single consistent operation.

A static tap-to-reveal worked example (e.g. tap to show factor pairs of 18 and 24, highlight the HCF, reveal ÷6 on both parts) can serve as a reference card but does not let the learner try divisors or feel the regrouping; use it alongside, not instead of, hands-on work.
Recognition/short-answer items assess the output (simplest form, common denominator) but do not by themselves elicit the regrouping insight; pair them with construction on a model.
Scale BOTH parts by the same factor: dividing only the numerator, or changing denominators without scaling numerators, changes the quantity.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One listed source (DfE National Curriculum, Year 6 Fractions) is marked verified:false in the source row; treat its claim as unconfirmed.

Arithmetic self-audit: 18/24 ÷ 6 = 3/4 (correct); HCF(18,24)=6 via 18=2×3×3, 24=2×2×2×3, common 2×3=6 (correct). For a shared denominator of 24, 2/3 = 16/24 (×8) and 5/8 = 15/24 (×3) are correct equivalent rewrites, not a sum. 6/8 with the subtract move gives (6−2)/(8−2)=4/6 (a correct depiction of the misconception).

Clarification on the source assessment's additive-misconception examples: subtracting a common amount from 18/24 can correctly yield 12/18 (subtract 6 from each) or 16/22 (subtract 2 from each) — both are legitimate depictions of the subtract-instead-of-divide error, differing only in the amount removed. The source is NOT internally inconsistent here; the divide-vs-subtract activity simply uses the single, cleaner 6/8 → 4/6 example to keep one consistent base fraction.

The source's catalog fit ratings assert that 3D and in-role dialogue add no conceptual value here. These are medium-fit opinions, not established facts; a conversation could still coach and a spatial model could still illustrate. Guidance retains only the narrow observable point (execution and felt regrouping are what the manipulative directly supports) without asserting that other media are impossible.

The 'the concept lives only in the manipulation' and 'a quiz only assesses' framings from the source are softened to narrow affordances: the checking activity is a complementary assessment of output, and recognition alone does not elicit production of the regrouping.

probeDeeper: You wrote 18/24 = 3/4. How do you know 3/4 is as simple as it gets — could you simplify it further? Why not?
Why does dividing the top and bottom by the same number NOT change the fraction's value, when subtracting the same number from both DOES change it?
Your friend simplified 18/24 to 9/12 and stopped. Is 9/12 wrong, or just not finished? How would you know?
To add 2/3 and 5/8 you first put them over 24. Why 24 — would 48 also work? What is the smallest denominator that works, and how did you find it?
assess.correctAnswer: 18/24 = 3/4 (divide both by the HCF 6, or ÷2 then ÷3). Common denominator 24: 2/3 = 16/24 and 5/8 = 15/24.

errorPatterns.pattern: Simplifies by subtracting the same amount from top and bottom ('take 6 off each: 18/24 becomes 12/18') instead of dividing — treats the fraction additively.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Put 18/24 and their subtracted answer on the same bar/wall — the lengths differ, so the value changed. Re-establish that only ×n/n or ÷n/n leaves the quantity unchanged; reteach the equivalence principle.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer like 12/18 or 4/6 for 6/8; when asked to show working, the child subtracts rather than divides.

errorPatterns.pattern: Stops before simplest form ('18/24 = 9/12, done') — divides by a common factor once but does not check whether the result still shares a factor.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach — the operation is sound. Prompt 'can you go further? do 9 and 12 still share a factor?' Build the habit of checking for remaining common factors; suggest dividing by the HCF in one step.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Produces a correct-but-not-final equivalent (9/12 or 6/8) and treats the task as complete.

errorPatterns.pattern: Operates on only one part — divides the numerator but leaves the denominator (or, in the common-denominator task, changes denominators to 24 but leaves the numerators unchanged: 2/24 and 5/24).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the bar: changing the number of parts you count without re-cutting the whole (or vice versa) makes a different quantity. Reteach that equivalence scales BOTH parts by the same factor.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers such as 3/24 for simplifying, or 2/24 and 5/24 for the common-denominator half.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot reach an equivalent simpler fraction, or subtracts from both parts; changes denominators without scaling numerators. Does not connect the action to keeping the value the same.
responseLevels.full: Simplifies to 3/4 by dividing both parts by a common factor (ideally the HCF), verifies no common factor remains, and explains that dividing both parts by the same number regroups the same quantity so the value is unchanged. Rewrites 2/3 and 5/8 as 16/24 and 15/24, scaling numerators with denominators, and can justify the choice of 24 as a common multiple. Transfers the reasoning to a new fraction on request.
responseLevels.partial: Divides both parts correctly to produce an equivalent fraction and can find a common denominator, but stops before simplest form, or can execute the steps without explaining why the value is unchanged — lists the procedure without the relational reason.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is 18/24. Write it in its simplest form, and show how you got there. Then rewrite 2/3 and 5/8 so they share the same denominator.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the child work separates the child who DIVIDES both parts (correct) from the child who subtracts a common amount, who divides only one part, or who stops before simplest form. A child reasoning correctly divides top and bottom by a shared factor and checks nothing divides further; a child with the additive misconception produces 16/22 or 4/6-type answers that look plausible but reveal the wrong operation. The common-denominator half exposes whether they scale numerators when they change denominators — the classic partial-credit trap.

pedagogy.summary: Interpret and construct pie charts as proportions of one whole. Convert each category count to its fraction of the total and then to a sector angle: (frequency ÷ total) × 360°. Recover a count from an angle only when the total is known. Move between the table, fraction/percentage, sector angle and constructed circle; check calculations and drawing rather than relying only on whether the sectors total 360°.
bestPractices: Establish the pie chart as parts of ONE whole: the full circle (360°) is the whole data set, and each sector is that category's fraction of it — so a sector shows a proportion, never a raw count

Teach sector angles as (frequency ÷ total) × 360°, and always check both that the sectors sum to 360° and that each sector matches its table fraction; explicitly contrast with the wrong 'divide 360 by the frequency' and 'multiply frequency by the total' methods
To read an actual quantity from a pie chart, combine the sector (its angle/fraction) with the KNOWN total — make explicit that the raw frequency is not shown on the chart itself
Connect pie-chart angles to percentages and to the angles-at-a-point fact (360°), so children draw on proportion and angle knowledge together
Move fluently in both directions — table → angles → chart to construct, and chart + total → quantities to interpret — so the representation and the data stay linked
keyRepresentations: A circle as the whole (360°) partitioned into sectors, each labelled with its fraction/percentage of the total
The formula (frequency ÷ total) × 360° shown alongside a data table being turned into sectors
A protractor laying off each sector angle from a starting radius (the construction act)
A double representation — same data as a table and as a pie chart — to move between proportion and count
commonMisconceptions: Reading a pie sector as a raw quantity rather than a proportion of the whole — or trying to read an actual count off the chart without using the total
Calculating a sector angle by dividing 360° by the frequency (instead of taking the frequency as a fraction of the total, of 360°)
Calculating a sector angle by multiplying the frequency by the total frequency
Not checking that the sector angles sum to 360°

learn.summary: For ages 10–11, interpret and construct pie charts. The full 360° circle is one data set; each sector angle is the category fraction of the total multiplied by 360°. Recover a count by multiplying the sector fraction by the known total. Compute the angles, draw them with a protractor, label categories, and verify each against the table as well as checking their sum. This topic does not assess line-graph mastery, which belongs to the separate Line graphs topic (mt_HlNSurPVDp).

activities.title: Live pie-chart builder from class data
feedback: If the sectors do not exactly fill the circle (leaving a gap or overlapping), at least one angle is wrong — check the method and the arithmetic: each angle should be the category's fraction of the whole, taken of 360°

360 ÷ 12 = 30° (with 360 ÷ 6 = 60° for the others) makes the sectors total only 150° — less than half the circle — so the circle itself shows the angle must be a fraction of 360°, not 360 divided by the count
After computing, total the sector angles: if they do not make 360°, find the error before drawing
The 'show actual numbers' toggle needs the total because a sector shows only a proportion — an unlabelled sector does not show the raw count on its own
activities.rationale: Construction forces the proportional idea into the open: a live repartitioning circle links the computed angle to a visible share and lets wrong methods fall visibly short of the whole circle, while the protractor step performs the actual construction act. The greyed-out count toggle makes 'sector = proportion, not count' explicit.
sourceClaims: Pie chart sector angles are calculated as (category frequency ÷ total frequency) × 360° and must sum to 360°; two named misconceptions are dividing 360° by the frequency, and multiplying the frequency by the total frequency — both corrected by taking the frequency as a fraction of the total, of 360°

In a pie chart the sectors are proportional to the data; the actual frequency for each sector is usually NOT stated and must be calculated from the sector and the total — a sector shows a proportion, not a raw quantity
learnerActions: Enter a class data table into a tool that repartitions a circle in real time, e.g. favourite pet: dog 12, cat 6, rabbit 6, with 24 children in all
Watch dog's 12-out-of-24 sector swing open to fill exactly half the circle, with a label ticking over to 180° and 50%
Compute each sector angle yourself as (frequency ÷ total) × 360°: dog 12/24 × 360° = 180°, cat and rabbit 6/24 × 360° = 90° each
Add the sector angles and confirm they sum to 360° before drawing

Deliberately try the tempting wrong method 360 ÷ 12 = 30° for dog (and 360 ÷ 6 = 60° for the others) and watch the sectors fall well short of closing, totalling only 150° and leaving 210° of the circle empty
Use a protractor-construction mode to lay off each computed angle from a starting radius
Use a 'show actual numbers' toggle that stays greyed out until the total is entered, making visible that a sector is a proportion, not a count
activities.intendedInsight: A pie sector's angle is the category's share of the whole circle — (frequency ÷ total) × 360° — not 360 divided by the frequency and not frequency times the total; and the sectors must sum to one whole turn, 360°.

activities.title: Recover a count from a sector and the total
feedback: Answering '90 children walk' reads the angle as a count — 90° is the angle, not the number of children
The whole circle is all 40 children; a right angle is a quarter of the circle, so a quarter of 40 = 10
Saying 'you cannot tell' misses that the total lets you recover the count — fraction of the whole × total
activities.rationale: Separating the angle/fraction from the count via the total directly confronts the sector-as-quantity misconception and makes the role of the total explicit.
sourceClaims: In a pie chart the sectors are proportional to the data; the actual frequency for each sector is usually NOT stated and must be calculated from the sector and the total — a sector shows a proportion, not a raw quantity
learnerActions: Read a given pie chart where a sector's angle is stated, e.g. 'the walk sector is a right angle, 90°, and 40 children travel in all — how many walk?'
Work out the sector's fraction of the whole: 90° is a quarter of 360°, so a quarter of 40 = 10 children walk
Try a second: 'a sector is 72° and there are 20 children altogether — how many is that?' (72/360 × 20 = 4)
State explicitly which number came from the chart (the angle/fraction) and which from the given total (the count)
activities.intendedInsight: To get an actual quantity from a pie chart you must combine the sector's fraction with the known total; the raw count is not visible on the chart itself.

activities.title: Compare same-size sectors from different totals
feedback: Equal slice sizes mean equal fractions, not equal counts — apply each chart's own total
Recover each count separately: the same fraction of different totals gives different numbers (a third of 30 = 10, a third of 12 = 4)
When a fraction of a total is not a whole number of people, re-check the data or the fraction; counts of people must be whole
activities.rationale: A counterexample with two totals tests whether the child treats a sector as a proportion rather than an absolute quantity, reinforcing the proportion-plus-total move.
sourceClaims: In a pie chart the sectors are proportional to the data; the actual frequency for each sector is usually NOT stated and must be calculated from the sector and the total — a sector shows a proportion, not a raw quantity
learnerActions: Compare two pie charts: a class of 30 and a class of 12 that both have a 'football' sector of the same size (say 120°, a third of the circle)
Decide whether the equal-size slices mean the same number of children, and justify
Work out the two actual counts using each chart's own total: a third of 30 = 10 versus a third of 12 = 4, noticing that equal fractions give different counts
activities.intendedInsight: A sector is a proportion of ITS OWN total; equal-looking sectors from different totals can represent different counts.

activities.title: Scorable checks on interpret and partial-construct skills
feedback: Choosing the '360 ÷ frequency' option usually gives sectors that do not total 360°, and even when the total happens to come out right it is not the category's fraction of the whole — the fraction-of-360 method, (frequency ÷ total) × 360°, is correct
If the fill-in count is wrong, check whether you used the total and the sector's fraction together
A correct interpretation or angle calculation is a start; construct a complete pie chart to demonstrate the drawing skill
activities.rationale: Short response formats give a scorable check of interpretation and part of construction; because choosing a correct angle is recognition rather than building, pair them with the full builder.
sourceClaims: Pie chart sector angles are calculated as (category frequency ÷ total frequency) × 360° and must sum to 360°; two named misconceptions are dividing 360° by the frequency, and multiplying the frequency by the total frequency — both corrected by taking the frequency as a fraction of the total, of 360°
learnerActions: Complete a fill-in task: 'the bus sector is 120°, there are 36 children, so ___ take the bus' (12)
Compute a sector angle from a table in a single step and enter it
Answer a multiple-choice item that includes the '360 ÷ frequency' answer as a tempting wrong option, and explain why it is wrong
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a sector with the total and computing a sector angle can be checked for accuracy; recognising a correct angle is not the same as constructing a whole chart.

activities.title: Annotated reference charts for reviewing structure
feedback: Use the revealed labels to check your own work, then redo an unlabelled example to confirm you can do it unaided
Reading a labelled chart does not show you can build one — follow up with construction
activities.rationale: A static annotated chart with reveals is a useful reference and worked example, but it does not elicit independent construction or exercise the proportional reasoning that discriminates understanding, so it supports rather than replaces building.
learnerActions: On a labelled pie chart, reveal each sector's angle, fraction/percentage and — given the total — its count, to confirm how the three relate
Use these as worked examples when checking your own constructions or interpretations
activities.intendedInsight: Relating the angle, fraction and count on an annotated pie chart can support review, but independent construction must be checked separately.

constraints: Response-format checks (fill-in, multiple choice, slider) can assess interpretation and approximate construction by choosing a correct angle, but choosing an angle is recognition, not building; pair them with an activity where the child constructs the full chart.
Annotated/static charts with reveals serve as reference and worked examples; they do not elicit independent construction or exercise the proportional reasoning that discriminates understanding.
Use a flat pie chart; 3D perspective or an exploded view can distort the areas learners compare as proportions.

In-role dialogue does not elicit the drawing/construction act — laying off sector angles with a protractor and producing a finished chart to inspect — so it cannot demonstrate the construction skill, even though a child could narrate a calculation in dialogue; it is not a substitute for the compute-and-draw work.
When recovering counts, use data sets and sector fractions that give whole numbers of people where the context is people, so learner answers stay coherent.
Connect pie-chart angles to percentages and to the angles-at-a-point fact (the full turn is 360°) so proportion and angle knowledge reinforce each other.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original counterexample compared a 'football' sector of equal size in classes of 30 and 12 without fixing the angle. A quarter would give 7.5 children for the class of 30 (not a whole number), so the activity now uses a third (120°), giving whole counts of 10 and 4 while still demonstrating that equal fractions of different totals give different counts.

'Show the wrong methods failing' is presented as an observable property of the circle not closing (the wrong angles total 180°, about half the circle); this is a reasonable visual argument, but the claim that watching it fail uniquely corrects the misconception is not established by the cited sources and has been softened.

The claim about in-role dialogue was narrowed from 'cannot verify calculation' to the observable limit that it does not elicit the drawing/construction act or a finished chart; a child could still narrate a calculation in dialogue.

sourceClaims are exact copies of this row's sources where they support the stated teaching principle; the Year 6 statutory curriculum claim was dropped from individual activity sourceClaims because it asserts scope/necessity rather than a teaching principle. No claim of empirical testing of these specific activities is implied.
Taxonomy alignment repair after os-taxonomy PR #30 (2026-10-19). Sources were reused without being re-fetched. Activities are proposals, not empirically validated interventions.

The former combined record has been narrowed to pie charts. Line-graph activities and assessment requirements now belong to mt_HlNSurPVDp; mastery of this pie-chart record is not evidence of line-graph mastery.

probeDeeper: 'Why does apple get 180° when only 10 children chose it?' — pushes the proportion (10 out of 20 is half the whole circle) into words
Two classes have 120° football sectors: one class has 30 children and the other has 12. How many chose football in each class, and why do equal sector angles not imply equal counts?
'A sector is 72° and there are 20 children altogether — how would you find how many that is?' — checks angle → fraction → count via the total
Can sector angles total 360° even if the category shares are wrong? Explain why you must also check every sector against the table.
assess.correctAnswer: The walk sector is 90/360 = 1/4 (25%) of the whole, so 1/4 × 60 = 15 children walk. For the fruit chart: apple 10/20 = 1/2 (50%), so 10/20 × 360° = 180°; banana and orange are each 5/20 = 1/4 (25%), so 5/20 × 360° = 90° each. The angles total 360° and each sector agrees with its table fraction. A completed labelled drawing is required for construction; computing or selecting an angle alone does not demonstrate the full skill.

errorPatterns.pattern: Sector-as-quantity: reads a pie sector's angle as a raw count, or tries to read an actual number off the chart without using the total — not treating the sector as a proportion of the whole
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront in place: the whole circle is all 60 children; a right angle is a quarter of the circle, so a quarter of 60; the sector shows a share, and the count needs the total
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On interpret (a) the child answers '90 children walk' (reading the angle as a count) or says you cannot tell, rather than a quarter of 60 = 15

errorPatterns.pattern: Angle = 360 ÷ frequency: computes each sector angle by dividing 360° by the category's frequency, instead of taking the frequency as a fraction of the total, of 360°
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach the proportion via the percentages/proportion prerequisite: the angle is the category's SHARE of the whole — (frequency ÷ total) × 360° — and the shares must add up to the full circle
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On construction the child writes 360 ÷ 10 = 36° for apple (or multiplies frequency by the total); the sectors do not fill or sum to 360°

errorPatterns.pattern: No 360° check: constructs sectors without verifying they sum to a whole turn, so errors go unnoticed
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, do not reteach: add the checking habit — total the sector angles and confirm 360° before drawing; the proportional idea is intact
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child's method is broadly right but the drawn/calculated sectors sum to more or less than 360° and they do not notice

responseLevels.gap: Treats an angle as a count or cannot relate a category fraction to its share of 360°.
responseLevels.full: Uses the total to recover counts and independently constructs and labels a correct pie chart from a fresh table, checking each fraction and the angle sum.
responseLevels.partial: Interprets a given sector and computes a familiar angle but needs support to calculate, draw or check the entire chart.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: First interpret: a pie chart represents 60 children and its walk sector is 90°. How many children walk? Then construct: a table has apple 10, banana 5 and orange 5, total 20. Calculate every sector angle, draw the pie chart with a protractor, label the categories, and explain how you checked it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The 90° interpretation requires using the total rather than reading the angle as a count. The construction task distinguishes calculation and recognition from producing a correctly partitioned chart. Wrong rules are checked against category shares, not only the angle sum, because an incorrect construction can still total 360°.

sources.claim: Pie chart sector angles are calculated as (category frequency ÷ total frequency) × 360° and must sum to 360°; two named misconceptions are dividing 360° by the frequency, and multiplying the frequency by the total frequency — both corrected by taking the frequency as a fraction of the total, of 360°

pedagogy.summary: This is the pivotal move from recognising shapes by how they LOOK to defining them by their PROPERTIES. A DEFINING attribute is one a shape must have (a triangle: three straight sides, closed; a square: four equal straight sides and four right-angle corners); a NON-DEFINING or 'imposed' attribute is incidental (colour, size, overall orientation, sitting on a horizontal base). Children routinely treat imposed attributes as if they were defining — rejecting a rotated square as a 'diamond', or a long-thin or point-down triangle as 'not a real triangle'. It is taught by explicitly contrasting varied examples with non-examples, foregrounding the invariant defining feature, rotating/resizing the same shape to show identity is preserved, and asking children to explain WHY a shape is or is not a given type.
bestPractices: Explicitly separate 'must-have' (defining) from 'doesn't-matter' (non-defining) attributes: a triangle is ANY closed figure with three straight sides — colour, size and which way it points do not matter.
Contrast varied examples with carefully chosen near-miss non-examples (three sides but one curved; three straight lines that don't quite close) so the defining feature is isolated.
Make non-prototypical and rotated cases the main event — long-thin, right, obtuse and point-down triangles, tilted squares — because these are where imposed attributes get mistaken for defining ones.
Rotate and resize the SAME shape and ask 'is it still a…?' so the child sees the defining attributes stay constant while orientation and size change.

Have children BUILD or DRAW a shape to a defining spec ('draw a triangle that looks different from mine') and JUSTIFY why borderline figures are included or excluded — the reasoning is the assessment.
keyRepresentations: 'Must-have versus doesn't-matter' attribute contrast
Example / near-miss non-example sets (curved side; not closed)
The same shape rotated and resized to show invariance
Tracing each side and checking 'straight' and 'closed'
commonMisconceptions: Treats ORIENTATION as defining (an 'imposed attribute'): a rotated square is a 'diamond'; a triangle 'must' have a horizontal base — about 15% of children reject even a prototypical triangle once it is rotated.
Treats shape type as defined by its image/prototype: only 'regular' triangles or brick-like rectangles count; long-thin, right and obtuse triangles are rejected.
Thinks size or colour can change a shape's identity (a very big or a red triangle is 'a different shape').
Accepts a near-miss non-example (a curved-sided or unclosed 'triangle') because it resembles the prototype — ignoring 'straight' and 'closed'.

learn.summary: Help 6–7 year-olds move from recognising shapes by how they look to defining them by their properties. A defining attribute is one a shape must have (a triangle: three straight sides, closed; a square: four equal straight sides and four right-angle corners); a non-defining ('imposed') attribute is incidental (colour, size, overall orientation, sitting on a horizontal base). Children routinely treat imposed attributes as defining — rejecting a rotated square as a 'diamond', or a long-thin or point-down triangle as 'not a real triangle'. The core moves are: contrast varied examples with carefully chosen near-miss non-examples, foreground the invariant defining feature, rotate/resize the same shape to show identity is preserved, and ask children to explain WHY a shape is or is not a given type.

activities.title: Triangle studio: what can change, what cannot
feedback: When a learner tilts or resizes and still calls it a triangle: 'Yes — you changed how it looks, but you kept three straight sides joined up, so it is still a triangle.'
When a side is bent: 'Now one side is curved, so it is no longer a triangle — a triangle needs every side straight.'
When a corner is pulled open: 'The outline doesn't join up all the way round now, so it is not closed — that's why it stopped being a triangle.'
If a learner expects colour or size to matter: 'Watch the label — making it red or huge changed nothing. Those are "doesn't-matter" attributes.'
activities.rationale: Separating defining from non-defining attributes is learned by observing what CAN change (size, orientation, colour) while the shape stays the same, and what CANNOT (exactly three sides, straightness, closure). A live manipulable where only the invariant features control the label makes that contrast concrete. Live recolouring, size sliders, draggable vertices, and a label that flips with a highlighted broken feature are optional ways to make the mechanism visible, not required components.
sourceClaims: Understanding requires analysing shapes by their DEFINING properties (a triangle must have three sides and be closed; a square is a sub-class of rectangles) and grasping that these properties are invariant over changes in size, orientation and colour — children must be able to explain why a figure is a triangle even when it is not prototypical; over-reliance on prototypical shapes in books and toys is a root cause, so adults should expose children to non-prototypical examples and teach the defining properties explicitly.

Children rely on 'imposed attributes' — attributes that are not formal (sides, corners, lengths) but just match how the prototype looks, e.g. that a triangle has a horizontal base — and treat them as if defining; about 15% failed to identify a prototypical triangle once its orientation changed, non-prototypical triangle TYPES (isosceles, right) were hardest (about half missed), and the remedy is experiencing typical and atypical examples plus non-examples.
learnerActions: Drag the three corners of a triangle to stretch it into different types (long-thin, right, obtuse) and tilt it to any angle, checking after each change whether it is still a triangle and saying why (if the three corners are dragged into one straight line, it flattens and is no longer a triangle).
Use size and colour controls to make the triangle big, small, and recoloured, and confirm the label 'triangle' stays the same because three straight sides and closure have not changed.

Break the shape on purpose: bend one side into a curve, or drag a corner apart so the outline no longer closes, and watch the label flip to 'not a triangle' with the non-straight side or the open gap highlighted.
State in your own words which attributes can be 'thrown around' with no effect (colour, size, orientation) and which changes end it (for example a curved side or an open corner).
activities.intendedInsight: Size, colour and orientation can swing wildly while a shape keeps its identity, but the instant a side curves or a corner opens it stops being a triangle — this makes defining versus non-defining attributes directly visible.

activities.title: Is it or not? — and explain why
feedback: For a correctly accepted point-down triangle: 'Right — turning it upside down didn't change the three straight sides, so it is still a triangle.'
For a correctly rejected curved-sided figure: 'Yes, and the reason matters: one side isn't straight, so it fails the test even though it looks pointy.'
If a learner rejects the long-thin triangle: 'Count the sides — three straight sides, closed. Being long and thin is a "doesn't-matter".'
If a learner calls the tilted square a 'diamond': 'Check the sides and corners — four equal straight sides and four square corners. Turning it didn't change those, so it is still a square.'
activities.rationale: An include/exclude judgement with distractors drawn directly from the orientation and prototype errors targets the misconception, and requiring a stated reason builds recognition on properties rather than prototypes. Note that choosing correctly is easier to elicit than justifying, so the reason should be treated as the main evidence of understanding, not the correct selection alone.
sourceClaims: The Clements & Sarama trajectories use an 'Is it or not? — and explain why' activity in which children decide whether a drawn figure is or is not a given shape and justify it by defining properties (straight sides, corners), building recognition on properties rather than prototypes.

NCETM lists as common errors that children define shapes by their image (only regular triangles / brick-like rectangles count) and by their orientation (a square is only a square with a horizontal base), and recommends ensuring children see a range of examples of the same shape in different orientations, sizes, colours and materials, and can 'recognise a range of triangles and say how they know what they are'.
learnerActions: Decide for each drawn figure whether it is or is not a given shape: non-prototypical positives (long-thin triangle, point-down triangle, tilted square) and near-miss negatives (one curved side, an open/unclosed corner).

For every decision, justify it by naming the defining property — e.g. 'three straight sides, all joined up' or 'that side isn't straight' — rather than 'it looks like one' or 'it points the right way'.
Compare a figure with one resized/recoloured and state whether anything that matters has changed.

Trace a finger along each side of a borderline figure to test 'how many sides?', 'is every side straight?' and 'is it joined up all the way round?' (and, for a square, 'are all four sides equal and all four corners square?')
activities.intendedInsight: Membership of a shape category depends on invariant defining properties, and the reason given — not just the yes/no — shows whether a child is reasoning from properties or from the prototype.

activities.title: Shape detective: argue back
feedback: When the child cites a defining attribute: 'Good argument — four equal sides and square corners. The character gives in.'
If the child relies on how it points: 'The character will keep insisting — which way it points is a "doesn't-matter". Tell them about the sides and corners instead.'
When the child spots a missing feature: 'Exactly — you named what's broken, not just that it looks odd.'
activities.rationale: Because this topic is fundamentally about giving reasons, a dialogue that keeps demanding justification and offers counterexamples can rehearse the explanation skill; a dialogue checks whether a child can produce the reason but does not by itself make the shape change visible. For this age the decision still benefits from seeing the shape change, so pair the discussion with a visible or physical rotation rather than relying on talk alone.
sourceClaims: Understanding requires analysing shapes by their DEFINING properties (a triangle must have three sides and be closed; a square is a sub-class of rectangles) and grasping that these properties are invariant over changes in size, orientation and colour — children must be able to explain why a figure is a triangle even when it is not prototypical; over-reliance on prototypical shapes in books and toys is a root cause, so adults should expose children to non-prototypical examples and teach the defining properties explicitly.
learnerActions: Respond to a character who holds up a rotated square and insists 'that's a diamond, not a square', arguing back from the four equal sides and square corners.
Answer repeated 'how do you know it's a triangle?' challenges, citing a defining attribute each time until the character concedes.
Handle thrown counterexamples — a curved-sided or unclosed figure — by explaining exactly which defining feature is missing.
Defend why size and colour changes do not change the shape's name.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to defend a classification out loud with the defining attribute, against a plausible prototype-based objection, is the goal — the reasoning is what is being learned.

activities.title: Build and draw to a defining spec
feedback: For a valid non-prototypical drawing: 'That looks very different from mine, but you kept three straight sides closed up — so it really is a triangle.'
For an open-cornered build: 'Right now it isn't closed. What would you do to join it up all the way round?'
If the child only draws the tidy prototype: 'Try one that is long and thin or points downward — can you still make it a real triangle?'
activities.rationale: Constructing and drawing to a defining specification, plus justifying borderline cases, requires independent production rather than recognition, and the justification doubles as assessment. A paper or stick build has real thickness and is an approximation of the ideal flat shape; treat the cut-out as standing for the mathematical shape being discussed, not as the shape itself.
sourceClaims: NCETM lists as common errors that children define shapes by their image (only regular triangles / brick-like rectangles count) and by their orientation (a square is only a square with a horizontal base), and recommends ensuring children see a range of examples of the same shape in different orientations, sizes, colours and materials, and can 'recognise a range of triangles and say how they know what they are'.
learnerActions: Draw a triangle that looks completely different from a given one but is still a triangle (e.g. long-thin, right, obtuse, or point-down), then explain why it still counts.
Build shapes from sticks or strips to a spec such as 'three straight sides, joined up all the way round'.
Make a near-miss on purpose (leave a corner open, or use a bendy side) and say what would have to change to fix it.
Turn your own cut-out shape, and compare it with a larger or smaller version, checking aloud that the defining attributes stay the same.
activities.intendedInsight: Producing a novel valid example — and justifying it — shows the child can apply the defining properties rather than only recognise a tidy prototype.

activities.title: Must-have versus doesn't-matter reference
feedback: When a learner places 'orientation' under doesn't-matter: 'Correct — which way it points doesn't change what it is.'
When a learner places 'three straight sides' under must-have: 'Yes — remove that and it stops being a triangle.'
activities.rationale: A clear reference contrasting must-have and doesn't-matter attributes helps children name criteria, and a sort can check whether a child classifies an attribute correctly; a sort does not by itself elicit deciding on NEW borderline figures, which is where the learning happens — so use it alongside judging and building tasks rather than on its own.
learnerActions: Reveal a shape's must-have attributes (three straight sides, closed) and its doesn't-matter attributes (colour, size, orientation) shown greyed out, and read which column each feature belongs to.
Sort a few new attributes into 'must-have' or 'doesn't-matter' using the panel as a guide.
After consulting the panel, decide a fresh borderline case and say which column your reason came from.
activities.intendedInsight: Keeping an explicit two-column picture of defining versus incidental attributes supports children in checking their reasoning against the right criteria.

constraints: Target age 6–7; conceptual geometry about 2-D attributes. Avoid introducing a third dimension/solids for this planar objective, since it adds load and can mislead toward solids.

Treat classification choices (triangle / not a triangle, square / diamond) as scaffolds: the stated reason, not the yes/no, is the real evidence, because a correct choice can come from the prototype alone.
Static reference panels and sorts support but cannot by themselves rehearse deciding on new borderline cases; include tasks where the child decides and justifies fresh figures.
Make non-prototypical and rotated cases the main event (long-thin, right, obtuse, point-down triangles; tilted squares), because these are where imposed attributes get mistaken for defining ones.
Choose near-miss non-examples deliberately: three sides but one curved, or three straight lines that don't quite close, so the defining feature is isolated.

Physical cut-outs and stick builds have real thickness and are approximations of the ideal flat shape; ask about the mathematical shape represented, and distinguish the cut-out from the shape it represents.
Interaction examples (draggable vertices, colour/size controls, a label that flips with the broken feature highlighted) are optional ways to make the mechanism visible, not mandatory mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

sourceClaims are exact copies of this row's sources[].claim and support the stated teaching principles; they do not establish that these specific activities were tested or are comparatively more effective than alternatives.

The claimed figures (about 15% failing a rotated prototypical triangle; about half missing non-prototypical TYPES) come from a single cited study and are reproduced as stated, not independently confirmed here.

The original recommendation implied a 'static image cannot teach' and that only a live 2-D manipulable makes the contrast visible; this has been softened — a fixed panel can still support learning, and physical/paper tasks and dialogue are retained as genuine alternatives with narrow, distinct affordances.

The original row field parentTitle 'Angles in triangles (age 6+)' does not match the stated objective (defining vs non-defining attributes); the original field was not modified, but reviewers should check which title is intended.

Self-check of definitions: triangle = closed figure with three straight sides (any proportions/orientation); square = four equal straight sides and four right-angle corners; the rotated square remains a square, the curved-sided figure fails on straightness, and the unclosed one on closure — these were checked for internal consistency and are correct as used.
Editorial fix applied earlier: several feedback entries had been split mid-sentence into separate array items; these were merged into single coherent feedback strings.
Independent re-audit fix: a learner action asking children to 'resize' a physical cut-out (physically impossible) was changed to turning the cut-out and comparing it with a larger or smaller version.

assess.poeTask: Hold up a triangle resting on its base. Before turning it, ask the child to PREDICT and commit to a reason: 'If I turn it upside down so the point is at the bottom, will it still be a triangle — yes or no, and why?' A prototype/orientation-bound child predicts 'no, it becomes a different shape'. Then slowly rotate it and ask them to explain what they see: the sides and corners are unchanged, so it is still a triangle. The reason stated BEFORE turning is the diagnostic part — it reveals whether orientation is being treated as defining.
probeDeeper: If I make this triangle much bigger, or colour it red, is it still a triangle? Why? (invariance over size and colour)
Here are three straight sticks laid down but not joined at the corners — is that a triangle? Why not? (counterexample — closure)
This shape has one curved side — what would I have to change to make it a real triangle? (counterexample — straightness)
Draw me a triangle that looks completely different from this one but is still a triangle. (transfer / build to a defining spec)
assess.correctAnswer: The long-thin and point-down figures ARE triangles (three straight sides, closed) whatever their proportions or orientation; the curved-sided figure is NOT (a side isn't straight); the rotated square IS still a square (four equal straight sides, four right-angle corners) — turning it does not change what it is. Reasons cite the defining attributes, not the look or the base.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats orientation as defining (an 'imposed attribute'): a rotated square is a 'diamond'; a triangle 'must' sit on a horizontal base
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rotate the SAME cut-out slowly — 'is it still a square now? and now?' — so the child sees the four equal sides and square corners do not change as it turns; name orientation as a 'doesn't-matter'.
errorPatterns.distractor: That one is a diamond, not a square.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rejects the point-down triangle or the tilted square, reasoning from which way it points rather than from its sides and corners.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the prototype image as defining: only a 'regular' triangle counts, so a long-thin, right or obtuse triangle is rejected as 'not a proper triangle'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show many varied triangles and count the three straight sides on each; state that being long, thin or tilted is a 'doesn't-matter' as long as the three straight sides are closed up.
errorPatterns.distractor: It is not a triangle — it is too long and thin.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rejects the long-thin triangle as 'too thin to be a triangle' while accepting only the tidy one.

errorPatterns.pattern: Ignores the defining feature and accepts a near-miss non-example by resemblance — a curved-sided or unclosed 'triangle' is called a triangle because it looks pointy
errorPatterns.nextMove: Put it beside a real triangle and run a finger along each side — 'is EVERY side straight? is it joined up all the way round?' — so straightness and closure become the test.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the curved-sided figure is a triangle; does not check that every side is straight and the figure is closed.

responseLevels.gap: Judges by look or orientation — rejects point-down or long-thin triangles, calls the tilted square a diamond, and/or accepts the curved-sided non-example; reasons from resemblance.
responseLevels.full: Includes non-prototypical and rotated examples, excludes near-miss non-examples, and justifies by the invariant defining attributes (three straight sides and closed; four equal sides and right-angle corners for a square), explaining that size, colour and orientation don't matter — and transfers by drawing a novel valid example.
responseLevels.partial: Accepts varied triangles in familiar orientations and may state 'three sides', but still trips on a strongly rotated or atypical case, OR names the defining feature without applying it to the borderline figure (says 'three sides' yet still rejects the point-down triangle) — has the parts but doesn't yet coordinate them.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show the child three figures in turn: a long, thin triangle; a triangle turned so its point is at the bottom; and a near-miss with one gently curved side. For each ask 'Is this a triangle? How do you know?' Then show a square rotated 45° and ask 'Is this a square, or something else? Why?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has separated defining from imposed attributes accepts the long-thin and point-down triangles, rejects the curved one for the RIGHT reason ('that side isn't straight'), and keeps the rotated square a square. A prototype/orientation-bound child rejects the point-down triangle or the tilted square ('that's a diamond') and may accept the curvy one because it 'looks like' a triangle. The 'how do you know' tier is decisive: 'three straight sides, closed' versus 'it looks like one' or 'it points the right way'.
