pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 6–7 (UK Y2, US Grade 3). The COMMUTATIVE property of multiplication (a×b = b×a) and the recognition that division is NOT commutative.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2 'show that multiplication of 2 numbers can be done in any order (commutative) and division of 1 number by another cannot'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.OA.5 'apply properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide — e.g. if 6×4=24 is known, then 4×6=24 is also known (Commutative property of multiplication)'.
• Operational details: prove commutativity with the ROTATED ARRAY (3 rows of 4 = 4 rows of 3), which both convinces and halves the fact-learning load. Equally important: teach the counterexample that division is NOT commutative (12÷3 ≠ 3÷12) so children don't over-generalise. Use commutativity as a strategy to derive and check facts.
• Checkpoint: apply and bound the property. Tier A (6): agree 2×5 = 5×2 using a rotated array. Tier B (6–7): use commutativity to state an unknown fact from a known one (know 3×8 → 8×3). Tier C (7): explain WHY multiplication is commutative (rotate the array) and give a counterexample showing division is not.
bestPractices: Prove commutativity concretely by rotating an array a quarter turn — same objects, same total, different reading — rather than stating it as a rule; the array makes it self-evident.
Explicitly use commutativity to lighten fact learning: knowing 3×8 gives 8×3 for free, so the multiplication square is nearly halved by its diagonal symmetry.

Teach the boundary firmly: division is NOT commutative — have children test 12÷3 vs 3÷12 with counters and see they differ, so the property isn't wrongly generalised (a very common error, also later applied wrongly to subtraction).
Connect to context: 3 bags of 4 and 4 bags of 3 are different situations but the SAME product — distinguishing 'same answer' from 'same story'.
Use commutativity as a checking strategy (compute both ways, compare) to build self-correction.
keyRepresentations: The array rotated 90° (the proof of commutativity)
The multiplication square's diagonal symmetry
Counters showing 12÷3 ≠ 3÷12 (the non-commutative counterexample)
Paired context pictures (3 groups of 4 vs 4 groups of 3)
commonMisconceptions: Over-generalising commutativity to division and subtraction (thinking 12÷3 = 3÷12, or 8−3 = 3−8).
Believing 3×4 and 4×3 are different facts needing separate memorisation.
Accepting commutativity as a stated rule without being able to justify it (no array reasoning).
Confusing 'same product' with 'same situation' — not seeing that different stories can share an answer.
Applying commutativity correctly to × but then assuming order never matters in any calculation.

learn.summary: For ages 6–7 (UK Year 2; in the US this content is formally taught in Grade 3, usually ages 8–9): teach that multiplication is commutative (a×b = b×a) by rotating an array so the same objects give the same total read two ways, use this to nearly halve fact-learning, and firmly teach the boundary that division is NOT commutative (12÷3 ≠ 3÷12) to prevent over-generalising. Learners should predict then prove commutativity by action, use it as a strategy to derive and check facts, and refute the claim that order never matters.

activities.title: Predict then rotate the array to prove 3×4 = 4×3
feedback: If you predicted the total would change, compare your prediction with what you counted — turning the array does not add or take away any objects, so the total must stay the same.
Strong answer: 'It's the same counters turned on their side, so there are still 12.' That reasons from the array, not just from working both sums out.
If a learner only says 'I worked them both out', push for the structural reason: show them the rotation so commutativity is seen, not just checked.
activities.rationale: Committing to a prediction and then proving commutativity concretely by a quarter-turn of the array makes the property self-evident and distinguishes 'same answer' from an unjustified rule; this reflects standards and mastery guidance on using the rotated array.
sourceClaims: Y2: show that multiplication of two numbers can be done in any order (commutative) and division of one number by another cannot.
Commutativity is best proven with the rotated array and used to reduce fact-learning load; children must be taught explicitly that division is not commutative to prevent over-generalisation.
learnerActions: Build an array of 3 rows of 4 counters (or dots) and count the total: 12.
Before you turn the array, predict whether the total will change if you turn it, and give your reason.
Rotate the whole array a quarter turn so it becomes 4 rows of 3 — do not add or remove any counters.
Count again and confirm the total is still 12; record 3×4 = 4×3.
Repeat with another pair you choose (e.g. 2×5 and 5×2) and state the matching fact.
Explain in your own words WHY the total cannot change when you turn the array.
activities.intendedInsight: The same set of objects, read in two directions, gives the same product, so multiplication can be done in either order — this is predicted and then seen by rotating, not merely stated as a rule.

activities.title: Use commutativity to get facts for free
feedback: If a learner recomputes the partner fact, remind them the array proof means the answer must be identical — they already know it.
Encourage them to point to the diagonal mirror on the square to justify why the facts pair up.
Note the facts that sit on the diagonal (like 3×3) have no separate partner, which is why commutativity nearly halves, rather than exactly halves, the facts to learn.
activities.rationale: Explicitly using commutativity as a strategy lightens fact learning and supports self-correction, as highlighted in the standards and mastery guidance.
sourceClaims: 3.OA.5 apply the commutative property of multiplication as a strategy (know 6×4=24 → 4×6=24).
Commutativity is best proven with the rotated array and used to reduce fact-learning load; children must be taught explicitly that division is not commutative to prevent over-generalisation.
learnerActions: Given a known fact (e.g. 3×8 = 24), state its commuted partner (8×3 = 24) without recomputing.
Look at a multiplication square and find the diagonal line of symmetry; notice that facts on either side of it mirror each other.
Decide which of a pair is easier to work out (e.g. 2×9 vs 9×2) and explain why using the easier order helps.
Use 'compute both ways and compare' to check one of your own answers.
activities.intendedInsight: Because order doesn't matter for multiplication, each known fact gives its partner free, nearly halving the facts to learn, and you can pick the easier order or check your work.

activities.title: Test the boundary: division does not swap
feedback: If a learner says 12÷3 = 3÷12 'because order doesn't matter in maths', have them physically share both ways; the different outcomes make the difference felt.
Good distinction: '12÷3 gives 4, but 3÷12 gives less than one — division can't be turned round.'
Note that subtraction also does not commute (8−3 ≠ 3−8), so 'order never matters' is the mistaken rule to avoid.
activities.rationale: Teaching the counterexample firmly heads off the very common over-generalisation of commutativity to division and subtraction, which the curriculum and mastery guidance call out explicitly.
sourceClaims: Y2: show that multiplication of two numbers can be done in any order (commutative) and division of one number by another cannot.
Commutativity is best proven with the rotated array and used to reduce fact-learning load; children must be taught explicitly that division is not commutative to prevent over-generalisation.
learnerActions: Act out 12 ÷ 3 with counters: share 12 counters into 3 equal groups and count one group (4).
Now act out 3 ÷ 12: try to share 3 counters among 12 — you cannot give everyone a whole counter, so each would get less than one.
Compare the two results and state clearly that 12÷3 ≠ 3÷12 (4 is not the same as less than one).
Try to 'rotate' the sharing the way you rotated a multiplication array, and describe why it does not work.
Decide for each pair whether order can swap: sort statements (mixing × and ÷) into 'order can swap' and 'order matters'.
Consider whether swapping works for subtraction too (e.g. 8−3 vs 3−8) and say what you find.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplication's array can be turned freely without changing the total, but swapping the two numbers in a division (or subtraction) usually changes the answer (it only stays the same when the two numbers are equal) — so the swapping shortcut has a precise stopping point.

activities.title: Same product, different story
feedback: If a learner thinks the stories must be identical because the totals match, point to the different group sizes — 3 bags of 4 is a different arrangement from 4 bags of 3.
If a learner thinks the totals differ because the stories differ, have them count both to 12.
activities.rationale: Connecting commutativity to context distinguishes 'same product' from 'same situation', addressing a listed misconception.
learnerActions: Draw or set out '3 bags of 4' and '4 bags of 3' as two separate situations.
Confirm both give 12, then explain how the stories differ even though the answer is the same.
Match a context picture to the fact it shows, and to its commuted partner.
activities.intendedInsight: Different real situations can share the same product; 'same answer' is not the same as 'same story'.

activities.title: Refute the character who says division swaps too
feedback: A convincing refutation does the sharing: 12 shared into 3 is 4 each, but 3 shared among 12 is less than one.
If the learner just says 'no' without evidence, ask them to show it with counters.
activities.rationale: A character over-generalising invites Socratic refutation; the disproof is more convincing when the learner manipulates quantities and produces a worked counterexample rather than merely asserting, so this works as a supplement to hands-on testing.
learnerActions: Listen to a character claim 'division works both ways, like multiplication — 12÷3 is the same as 3÷12'.
Disagree and give a counterexample, backing it up by sharing counters both ways.
State the correct rule: multiplication can be swapped, division cannot.
activities.intendedInsight: You can justify and defend the boundary of commutativity by producing a worked counterexample, not just asserting it.

constraints: Prove commutativity by action (rotating the array) rather than stating it as a rule; a static paired image or captioned diagram is a useful reference but cannot itself let the learner perform the rotation or test the division counterexample.
Always teach the division (and subtraction) boundary alongside commutativity so learners do not over-generalise 'order doesn't matter'.
True/false, matching and sort tasks check whether the learner holds the property and its boundary, but do not by themselves elicit the structural proof-by-rotation; pair them with hands-on building.

The dialogue/character task is a supplement: the actual disproof should be done by sharing quantities, not by bare assertion alone — a worked counterexample is valid reasoning; an unsupported 'no' is not.
Distinguish 'same product' from 'same situation': commutativity gives the same total, not the same story.
A learner who gets both facts right numerically but justifies only by 'I worked them both out' has not yet reached the structural insight; prompt for the array reason.
Commutativity nearly halves (not exactly halves) the facts to learn, because facts on the diagonal of the multiplication square (e.g. 3×3) have no separate partner.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Of the cited sources, only the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified in the row; the CCSS 3.OA.5 and NCETM claims are marked unverified. Do not treat them as confirmed.
Arithmetic checked: 3×4=12 and 4×3=12; 3×5=15 and 5×3=15; 3×8=24 and 8×3=24; 2×9=18 and 9×2=18; 12÷3=4; 3÷12=0.25 (<1); 8−3=5 and 3−8=−5; these are consistent across the activities.

Acting out 3÷12 yields a fractional result (1/4) that sits beyond typical Y2 scope and is awkward with whole counters; it is preserved from the original assessment and used only as an observable 'each gets less than one' contrast, not as formal fraction work.

The original Predict–Observe–Explain assessment task (predict 'more/fewer/same' and why, then build and count) has been reintegrated into Activity 1 as a prediction step so the discriminating commitment is not lost.

The original noted a 3D interactive 'adds nothing conceptual'; this comparative/necessity claim is not established by the sources and has been omitted rather than asserted as a universal law. Planar rotation is sufficient to show the proof, which is retained as a scoped point.

assess.poeTask: Set out 3 groups of 5 counters. Before building the comparison, ask the child to PREDICT: 'If I make 5 groups of 3 instead, will the total be more, fewer, or the same — and why?' They commit to a reason, then build 5 groups of 3 and count. Predicting 'the same' with a rotate/rearrange reason shows commutative understanding; predicting 'different' reveals the order-changes-the-total misconception.
probeDeeper: Show me with an array why 3 × 5 = 5 × 3.
Which is easier to work out, 2 × 9 or 9 × 2? Why does that help?
Draw 12 ÷ 3 and 3 ÷ 12 — do they look the same?
Does swapping work for adding? For subtracting?
assess.correctAnswer: 3 × 5 = 5 × 3 (both 15) — it's the same array turned on its side, so multiplication can be done in either order. But 12 ÷ 3 (= 4) is NOT the same as 3 ÷ 12 (less than one) — division can't be swapped round.

errorPatterns.pattern: over-generalises commutativity to division — thinks 12 ÷ 3 = 3 ÷ 12 because 'order doesn't matter in maths'
errorPatterns.nextMove: act out 12 ÷ 3 (4 each) versus 3 ÷ 12 (sharing 3 among 12) with counters so the difference is felt; contrast with the rotate-the-array move for ×
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes, 12 ÷ 3 is the same as 3 ÷ 12.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says division can be swapped just like multiplication

errorPatterns.pattern: denies 3 × 5 = 5 × 3 — thinks '3 groups of 5' and '5 groups of 3' give different totals because the order changes the meaning
errorPatterns.nextMove: build both sets, count each to 15, then rotate one array onto the other to show the total is identical
errorPatterns.distractor: No, 3 groups of 5 is different from 5 groups of 3.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says they are different amounts

errorPatterns.pattern: accepts 3 × 5 = 5 × 3 numerically but has no structural reason
errorPatterns.nextMove: rotate a 3 × 5 array to 5 × 3 — same counters, same total — so commutativity is seen, not merely checked
errorPatterns.revealedBy: correct answer justified only by 'I worked them both out'

responseLevels.gap: Thinks multiplication order changes the total, or swaps division freely.
responseLevels.full: Explains multiplication commutes using a rotated array, uses it to pick the easier calculation, and shows division does not commute.
responseLevels.partial: Accepts 3 × 5 = 5 × 3 (and that division differs) but justifies only by computing, not by the array structure.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Is 3 × 5 the same as 5 × 3? And is 12 ÷ 3 the same as 3 ÷ 12? For each one, tell me yes or no and how you know.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Pairing × (which commutes) with ÷ (which doesn't) tests whether the child has a REASON — the rotated array, the different meanings of ÷ — rather than an over-general rule 'order doesn't matter'. A child who swaps both has a rule without understanding; one who only checks numerically misses the structural insight.

sources.claim: Y2: show that multiplication of two numbers can be done in any order (commutative) and division of one number by another cannot.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study, Year 2 Multiplication and division

sources.claim: 3.OA.5 apply the commutative property of multiplication as a strategy (know 6×4=24 → 4×6=24).
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 3 Operations & Algebraic Thinking

sources.claim: Commutativity is best proven with the rotated array and used to reduce fact-learning load; children must be taught explicitly that division is not commutative to prevent over-generalisation.
sources.source: NCETM — Primary Mastery Professional Development (Multiplication and Division)

pedagogy.summary: Adding and subtracting same-denominator fractions where the result can pass one whole (3/5 + 4/5 = 7/5 = 1 2/5). The same counting-like-units idea as within one whole, extended by one crucial step: when the numerators combine past the denominator, the extra units re-group into a whole. Seven fifths is a legitimate number; eight eighths make one whole, and ten eighths is one whole and two eighths. The teaching work is making children comfortable that a fraction can exceed one, and fluent at re-unitising the improper result into a mixed number.
bestPractices: Keep the counting-like-units foundation ('seven one-fifths') and simply let the count exceed the denominator, so the improper fraction arises naturally from adding.
Use two adjacent whole-bars so pieces spilling past the first whole are visibly re-grouped into 1 and a remainder — making 7/5 = 1 2/5 something the child sees, not a trick.
Name the improper fraction as legitimate ('7/5 is a real number, more than one') to head off the belief that fractions must be less than a whole.
Teach improper↔mixed conversion as counting how many whole-groups of the denominator fit, using the model before the numeric rule.
Do subtraction across the whole too (from a mixed/improper start) as separating like units.
keyRepresentations: Two (or more) partitioned whole-bars side by side, pieces spilling from one into the next
Number line extending past 1, counting on in the unit fraction (fifths past 5/5)
Ten-frame-style grouping where a full set of denominator-many pieces fuses into one whole
Improper↔mixed toggle on the same shaded quantity (10/8 ↔ 1 2/8)
commonMisconceptions: Adds the denominators as well: 3/5 + 4/5 = 7/10 (add-across; on harder items this error spreads into middle-achieving pupils, NFER).
Believes a fraction cannot exceed one whole, so forces the result — stops at 5/5 = 1, or flips 7/5 to 5/7 — rather than accepting an improper fraction.
Miscounts the re-grouping when converting improper to mixed (e.g. 7/5 = 2 2/5 or 1 3/5), losing track of how many wholes the denominator makes.

learn.summary: Teaches adding and subtracting same-denominator fractions where the result can pass one whole (e.g. 3/5 + 4/5 = 7/5 = 1 2/5). Extends the counting-like-units idea by one step: when the combined count passes the denominator, the extra unit fractions re-group into a whole. Core aims are making children comfortable that a fraction can legitimately exceed one, and fluent at re-unitising an improper result into a mixed number. Addresses the add-across error (3/5 + 4/5 = 7/10), the belief that fractions cannot exceed one, and miscounting the re-group when converting. Covers subtraction too, both within one whole and crossing it from a mixed/improper start.

activities.title: Spilling into the next whole: an adding model across two bars
feedback: If the child writes 7/10 for 3/5 + 4/5 (or 10/16 for 7/8 + 3/8): return to the fixed-unit bar — 3/5 and 4/5 are seven same-size fifth-pieces, so the answer is in fifths; only the count grows (likewise 7/8 + 3/8 is ten eighths). Point out that the pieces on the bar are fifths, not tenths, and that 7/10 is less than one whole even though seven fifths fill more than one bar.

If the child flips 7/5 to 5/7, caps the answer at 1, or refuses to write 7/5: show the count continuing past 5/5 on the bars and on a number line; fifths keep coming after one whole, and 7/5 is a real number just past one. Name it as 'more than one whole' before converting.

If the addition is correct but the mixed number is wrong (e.g. 7/5 = 2 2/5 or 1 3/5): do not reteach adding — it is right. Ask how many fifths make ONE whole, so how many whole groups fit inside 7/5, and what is left over; count the whole-groups on the bar.
If a crossing-the-whole subtraction stalls (e.g. 1 1/5 − 3/5): show that one whole can be re-grouped into fifths (1 1/5 = 6/5), so there are now six fifths to take three from, leaving 3/5.
activities.rationale: A multi-bar fixed-unit model lets the re-grouping at the whole be observed directly, so the mixed number arises from the count passing the denominator rather than from a symbolic rule. Keeping the denominator locked targets the add-across error by showing the unit cannot change. The number line and 'name it as legitimate' step directly confront the belief that fractions cannot exceed one.
sourceClaims: The add-across error (adding numerators and denominators) stems from misapplying whole-number addition and not treating fractions as numbers with magnitude; teach why the procedure works with fixed-unit models and estimation.
Understanding a fraction a/b (a>1) as a repeated sum of unit fractions underpins accepting improper fractions and converting to mixed numbers.
learnerActions: Set up two identical bars side by side, each partitioned into the SAME fixed unit (e.g. eighths), with the denominator kept locked so only the count of pieces changes.
Add 7/8 + 3/8 by placing eighth-pieces: fill the first bar with eight eighths, then let the remaining two eighths land in the second bar.
When a full set of denominator-many pieces (eight eighths) completes the first bar, group that full set into a single 'one whole' tile, so the child watches the whole form from the count.
Read the quantity both ways on the same shaded amount: as an improper fraction 10/8 and as a mixed number 1 2/8.
Repeat with 3/5 + 4/5: count fifths past 5/5 and re-group 7/5 as 1 2/5.

Do subtraction too: a within-whole case (5/6 − 2/6 = 3/6) where like units are simply separated, and a genuine crossing-the-whole case from a mixed/improper start that requires re-grouping a whole back into unit fractions (e.g. 1 1/5 − 3/5 = 6/5 − 3/5 = 3/5), treating both as separating like units.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction can exceed one whole; when the running count of unit fractions reaches the denominator those pieces re-group into one whole, which is how an improper fraction becomes a mixed number — seen, not memorised. Subtraction reverses the same re-grouping when a whole must be broken back into unit fractions.

activities.title: Counting on past one whole on a number line
feedback: If the child stops at 1 (5/5) and will not continue: emphasise the ticks keep going; fifths after 5/5 are 6/5, 7/5 and so on.
If the child lands on the wrong tick: recount the unit steps one at a time, saying each unit-fraction name aloud.
activities.rationale: A number line makes magnitude explicit and gives a second representation of crossing one whole, complementing the area bars and reinforcing that an improper fraction is a genuine position on the line.
sourceClaims: Understanding a fraction a/b (a>1) as a repeated sum of unit fractions underpins accepting improper fractions and converting to mixed numbers.
learnerActions: Mark a number line from 0 extending past 1, with tick marks at each unit fraction (fifths past 5/5).
Place 3/5, then count on four more fifth-steps (4/5 in total), landing at 7/5 and noting where the count crossed the 1 mark.
State how many unit steps are before 1 and how many are after, reading off the mixed number 1 2/5.
Repeat for 7/8 + 3/8, identifying the point where the total passes one whole.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding same-denominator fractions is counting on in the unit fraction; passing the '1' mark shows concretely that the result is more than one whole and where the mixed-number remainder comes from.

activities.title: Check and explain: improper and mixed forms
feedback: If the child accepts 10/16 as larger than 7/8 without question: point out 10/16 simplifies to 5/8, which is SMALLER than 7/8 — adding two positive amounts cannot make the total smaller, which exposes the add-across error.
If the child gives the correct improper fraction but a wrong mixed number: ask how many of the unit fraction make one whole, then count the whole-groups on the model before applying any rule.
If the child gives a correct answer: ask them to check it against the bar or number line and state where the count passed one whole.
activities.rationale: Checkable items that demand both forms and a size comparison surface the two key misconceptions and the conversion slip. Using a magnitude/estimation check is directly recommended for the add-across error. Recognition and matching here consolidate the model but do not by themselves demonstrate independent construction — pair with the production required in the first activity.
sourceClaims: The add-across error (adding numerators and denominators) stems from misapplying whole-number addition and not treating fractions as numbers with magnitude; teach why the procedure works with fixed-unit models and estimation.
learnerActions: Work out 3/5 + 4/5 and 7/8 + 3/8, writing each answer first as an improper fraction and then as a mixed number, showing each step.
Match improper fractions to their mixed-number equivalents on the same shaded quantity (e.g. 10/8 ↔ 1 2/8).
Explain in words why the denominator stays fixed while the count grows.
Respond to a friend's claim that 7/8 + 3/8 = 10/16: simplify 10/16, compare its size with 7/8, and judge whether adding could make the total smaller.
activities.intendedInsight: Requiring both the improper and mixed form, plus a magnitude check, reveals whether the child can re-group the whole or is only manipulating symbols; adding two positive same-denominator fractions cannot shrink the total below either addend.

constraints: Keep the denominator locked in all models so the unit stays fixed; this is what makes the add-across error visible as a change of unit.

A single static worked example can display one crossing-the-whole case and an improper↔mixed pair as an anchor, but it does not let the child perform the re-grouping; use it only as a reference alongside an activity where the child acts.

Matching and multiple-choice items consolidate and check, but recognition-only responses do not elicit independent construction; include tasks where the child writes and explains both forms themselves.

Introduce the numeric improper↔mixed conversion rule only after the child has done the re-grouping on a model; the model-before-rule ordering is the intended sequence, not a claim that a rule-first approach can never work.

Include subtraction that crosses the whole (from mixed/improper starts) as well as within-whole subtraction, since the objective covers both; crossing-the-whole subtraction must actually start from or pass one whole (e.g. 1 1/5 − 3/5), unlike 5/6 − 2/6 which stays within one whole.

Answer options that 'cap at one whole' or flip the improper fraction are useful bait for the can't-exceed-one belief, but ensure the correct answer and feedback explicitly validate the improper fraction as a real number.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One listed source (NCETM Primary Mastery / Spine 3) was marked verified:false in the source row; treat its claim as unconfirmed.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 3/5 + 4/5 = 7/5 = 1 2/5 ✓; 7/8 + 3/8 = 10/8 = 1 2/8 = 1 1/4 ✓; 5/8 + 6/8 = 11/8 ✓ (objective context); 10/16 simplifies to 5/8, which is smaller than 7/8 ✓; 5/6 − 2/6 = 3/6 = 1/2 ✓ (a within-whole subtraction, NOT a crossing-the-whole case); crossing-the-whole example 1 1/5 − 3/5 = 6/5 − 3/5 = 3/5 ✓, which genuinely re-groups one whole into fifths. No erroneous distractors were introduced.

The NFER prevalence claim (add-across error spreading into middle-achieving pupils) describes who makes the error, not a teaching method; it is retained in the source row but not cited as teaching-principle support inside an activity.
The 'moment of insight' claim that watching pieces fuse makes the mixed number 'stop being a rule' is a plausible pedagogical hope, not a tested outcome; retained as design intent, not evidence.

probeDeeper: Your answer 7/5 — is that more than one whole or less? How do you know?
A friend says 7/8 + 3/8 = 10/16. Simplify 10/16 — what do you notice about its size compared with 7/8? Can adding make it smaller?
How many eighths make one whole? So how many whole ones are inside 10/8?
Show 3/5 + 4/5 on a number line — where do you pass 1?
assess.correctAnswer: 3/5 + 4/5 = 7/5 = 1 2/5. 7/8 + 3/8 = 10/8 = 1 2/8 (= 1 1/4 simplified). Denominator stays fixed; add the counts; re-group the whole.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds the denominators too: '3 and 4 is 7, 5 and 5 is 10, so 7/10' — whole-number addition applied to both parts.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Back to the fixed-unit bar: 3/5 and 4/5 are seven same-size fifth-pieces, so the answer is fifths; only the count grows. Contrast that tenths won't fit the fifths bar.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 7/10 (or 10/16 for the second); the denominator changes.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks a fraction can't be bigger than one whole, so forces the answer — 'you can't have 7/5, so it's 5/7' or 'it just makes 1'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the count continuing past the whole on a number line and on two bars — fifths keep coming after 5/5; 7/5 is a real number just past one. Name it explicitly as more than one whole before converting.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Flips the improper fraction (7/5→5/7), caps the answer at 1, or refuses to write 7/5; discomfort when the count exceeds the denominator.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds correctly but miscounts the re-group: '7/5 = 2 2/5' or '1 3/5' — loses track of how many wholes the denominator makes.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach adding — it's correct. Scaffold the conversion on the model: how many fifths make ONE whole? So how many wholes are in 7/5, and what's left over? Count the whole-groups on the bar.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct improper fraction (7/5) but a wrong mixed number; the addition is sound, only the conversion slips.

responseLevels.gap: Adds across the denominators (7/10) and/or refuses or mangles the result greater than one (5/7, caps at 1); cannot re-group past the whole.
responseLevels.full: Adds keeping the denominator fixed, accepts 7/5 / 10/8 as legitimate, re-groups into 1 2/5 / 1 2/8, and explains it as counting fifths/eighths past a whole; transfers to a new sum that crosses one whole.
responseLevels.partial: Adds the numerators correctly to the improper fraction (7/5, 10/8) but can't reliably convert to a mixed number, or is uneasy that the answer exceeds one — has the numerator rule but not the re-unitising at the whole.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these out, showing each step: 3/5 + 4/5, and 7/8 + 3/8. Write each answer as an improper fraction and then as a mixed number.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Both sums are engineered to exceed one whole, so a child who believes fractions can't pass one is forced to reveal it — they flip 7/5 to 5/7, stop at 5/5 = 1, or balk. Add-across produces 7/10 / 10/16 (denominator changed). Requiring the answer both as an improper fraction and as a mixed number surfaces whether the child can re-group the whole or only manipulate symbols. Watching the working shows whether the unit is held fixed and re-unitised at the whole.

sources.claim: The add-across error (adding numerators and denominators) stems from misapplying whole-number addition and not treating fractions as numbers with magnitude; teach why the procedure works with fixed-unit models and estimation.
sources.source: IES/WWC Practice Guide, Developing Effective Fractions Instruction for K–8 (Siegler et al., 2010)

sources.claim: On harder addition items the add-across error becomes more widespread, spreading into middle-achieving pupils while remaining rare among high achievers.
sources.source: NFER Assessment Hub, 'What are the common mistakes when adding fractions?' (Emily Jones)

sources.claim: Understanding a fraction a/b (a>1) as a repeated sum of unit fractions underpins accepting improper fractions and converting to mixed numbers.
sources.source: NCETM Primary Mastery / Spine 3 Fractions

pedagogy.summary: Fluent addition and subtraction within 100 means computing accurately AND selecting an efficient strategy for the particular numbers, rather than running one algorithm for everything. Children partition into tens and ones, compensate, use known facts, and exploit the inverse relationship. Fluency is built on secure single-digit recall and strategy-based adding within 100; the goal is flexible, justified computation, not speed alone.
bestPractices: Teach a repertoire and the judgement to choose: partitioning for 46+37, counting-up/finding-the-difference for near numbers like 71−68, compensation for numbers near a ten
Use the inverse relationship to check (add the answer back) and to solve missing-number problems
Partition the subtrahend into tens and ones for two-digit subtraction, decomposing a ten where the ones are insufficient (NCETM Spine 1.16)
Contrast two methods on the same calculation and ask which was quicker and why, to build strategic flexibility
Keep concrete/pictorial support (base-ten, number line) available so regrouping stays meaningful, not a memorised digit ritual
keyRepresentations: Base-ten blocks (compose/decompose a ten for regrouping)
Number line (count-up for finding a difference between close numbers)
Part-whole / partitioning jottings (70+13=83)
Bar model (comparison subtraction)
Hundred square (jumps of tens and ones)
commonMisconceptions: Smaller-from-larger subtraction bug: in 83−25 doing 5−3 in the ones column, answer 62
Partitioning correctly but dropping or mis-recombining the regrouped ten (46+37 → 73)
Applying one written method rigidly even when the numbers make a mental strategy far quicker (column-subtracting 71−68)
Treating addition and subtraction as unrelated, so the inverse is not used to check

learn.summary: Fluent addition and subtraction within 100 means computing accurately AND choosing an efficient strategy for the particular numbers, not running one algorithm for everything. Learners partition into tens and ones, compensate near a ten, use known facts, count up to find a difference between close numbers, and exploit the inverse to check. The target is flexible, justified computation, built on secure single-digit recall. The core activity places the same calculation on two tools so the learner feels why the smart method depends on the numbers; supporting activities add strategy-selection practice, a worked strategy reference, and spoken justification.

activities.title: Same calculation, two tools: feel which method fits the numbers
feedback: If the borrow and the count-up look equally fast to you, count the steps in each: counting up from 68 to 71 covers a difference of just three, while the borrow takes several steps. Closeness of the numbers is the signal to count up.
If 46+37 came out as 73, show exactly where the extra ten went: 6+7 makes 13, which is one ten and three. That one ten joins the 70 to make 80, and the 3 ones make the total 83.
If you reached for the same written method on every pair, pause first and read the numbers: are they close (count up), near a ten (compensate), or a known fact you can just recall?
activities.rationale: Presenting the identical calculation on a number line and a base-ten workspace side by side lets the learner directly compare strategies on the same numbers, which is the comparison that strategy selection depends on. Auto-composing/decomposing a ten keeps the regroup visible so it is not reduced to a memorised digit ritual. Optional timing/animation of both methods and drag-to-count on the number line make the efficiency gap concrete; these are illustrative supports, not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: Two-digit subtraction is done by partitioning the subtrahend into tens and ones (decomposing a ten where needed), and strategy choice varies with the numbers — e.g. counting up from 67 to find 94−67, or counting back for 64−25.

Year 2 pupils recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently and derive related facts to 100, use the inverse relationship to check calculations, and partition numbers in different ways (e.g. 23 = 20+3 and 10+13) to support subtraction.
learnerActions: Take 71 − 68 and first work it on a base-ten column workspace: there are not enough ones, so decompose a ten, cross out, and carry through the several steps of the borrow.
Now work the same 71 − 68 on a number line: count up from 68 to 71 and see the difference is just three.
Place the three-hop count-up beside the multi-step borrow and say which was quicker and why.
Switch to 46 + 37 on the base-ten side: combine 40+30 and 6+7, compose the thirteen ones into one ten and three, and add that ten in so the total is 83, not 73.
Finish by looking at a fresh pair of numbers and stating, before you start, which method you will use and why.
activities.intendedInsight: The efficient method depends on the numbers: when the numbers are close, counting up the difference beats a columnar borrow; regrouping must be composed or decomposed deliberately so the extra ten is never silently dropped.

activities.title: Check with the inverse and solve missing-number problems
feedback: If adding the answer back does not return to the start, either the subtraction or the checking addition has an error—often a dropped or mis-recombined ten; rework both with place-value support.
If you treated the missing-number problem as unrelated to subtraction, notice that 46 + ? = 83 is answered by 83 − 46 = 37.
activities.rationale: Using the inverse to check and to solve missing-number problems targets the common gap of treating the two operations as unrelated, and is named directly in the Year 2 curriculum.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently and derive related facts to 100, use the inverse relationship to check calculations, and partition numbers in different ways (e.g. 23 = 20+3 and 10+13) to support subtraction.
learnerActions: After computing 83 − 25, add your answer back to 25 and confirm it returns to 83.
Given a missing-number problem such as 46 + ? = 83, use subtraction (83 − 46) to find the unknown, then add back to check.
State in words how addition and subtraction undo each other for the pair you just solved.
activities.intendedInsight: Addition and subtraction are inverse operations, so adding an answer back is a reliable self-check and lets you turn a missing-number problem into the operation you find easier.

activities.title: Match the calculation to the smartest strategy (selection practice)
feedback: If you chose 62 for 83 − 25, you likely did 5 − 3 in the ones column; you cannot take 5 from 3, so 83 must give up a ten (becoming 70 + 13) first, giving 58. Check by computing 62 + 25, which comes to 87, not 83.
If you matched a slow method to close numbers like 71 − 68, reconsider: close numbers signal counting up the difference.
activities.rationale: A selection/matching task with 62 offered as the tempting wrong answer rehearses strategy choice and catches the smaller-from-larger bug. This format checks and reinforces selection rather than building flexibility through sustained varied doing, so it supplements, not replaces, the two-tool work.
sourceClaims: The 'smaller-from-larger' subtraction error is a classic, systematic buggy algorithm — the child subtracts the smaller digit from the larger within each column regardless of position (the '437−284=253' pattern). In Brown & Burton's 1325-student data it was used by 54 students; such bugs are stable, not careless (~40% of students consistently buggy).

Two-digit subtraction is done by partitioning the subtrahend into tens and ones (decomposing a ten where needed), and strategy choice varies with the numbers — e.g. counting up from 67 to find 94−67, or counting back for 64−25.
learnerActions: Across a mixed set of additions and subtractions, pair each calculation with the most efficient strategy (partition, compensate near a ten, count up the difference, or recall a known fact).
For 83 − 25, choose the correct answer (58) and explain why 62 is wrong.
Say aloud what feature of the numbers made you pick that strategy.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading the numbers first—how close they are, whether they sit near a ten, whether a fact is known—tells you which method is efficient before you compute.

activities.title: Worked strategy reference to consult
feedback: If the reference method differs from yours, identify which numbers triggered it—that trigger is the point to remember.
Use the reference to locate a slip (e.g. a dropped ten) rather than to replace doing the calculations yourself.
activities.rationale: A static reveal-the-method chart displays worked examples clearly but cannot exercise the choosing itself, so it is a reference scaffold alongside active practice, not a substitute for it.
learnerActions: Reveal, for each calculation type, its most efficient method and a short reason: partitioning for 46 + 37, counting up for 71 − 68, compensation for numbers near a ten.
Compare a worked example with your own jotting on a similar pair to see whether your recombination kept the regrouped ten.
activities.intendedInsight: Each strategy has a signature of numbers it suits; a worked example makes the method and its justification explicit.

activities.title: Justify your method aloud
feedback: If you cannot give a reason beyond 'that's how I always do it', look again at the numbers for a feature (closeness, nearness to a ten, a known fact) that favours a particular method.
If prompted to try counting up and it proves faster, note that for next time.
activities.rationale: Spoken justification prompts a learner to articulate strategy choice, which supports metacognition; on its own it cannot supply the volume of varied practice fluency needs, so it accompanies the computational activities.
learnerActions: After solving a pair, explain to a partner or adult why you chose your method for those particular numbers.
Respond to a prompt such as: 'You borrowed for 71 − 68—can you see a quicker way to find the gap between 68 and 71?' and try the alternative.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to justify a strategy choice out loud consolidates the habit of reading the numbers before computing.

constraints: Fluency is a doing skill: recognition, matching, and tap-to-reveal reference formats check or display strategy but do not by themselves build flexible computation; keep substantial varied practice of actually computing.
Keep concrete/pictorial support (base-ten blocks, number line, hundred square, and bar model for comparison subtraction) available so regrouping stays meaningful rather than a memorised digit ritual.
The smaller-from-larger bug is stable and systematic, not careless; confront it with place-value regrouping and an inverse check (62 + 25 = 87 ≠ 83) rather than simply marking it wrong.
Spoken justification alone cannot supply the volume of practice needed; use it to consolidate choice, not to replace computation.
Timing/animation, drag-to-count, and auto-exchange are optional supports that make the efficiency gap and the regroup visible; they are illustrative, not mandatory mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One source (NCETM Spine 1.16) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its strategy-choice examples (count up for 94−67, count back for 64−25) as unverified.

Arithmetic self-checked: 46+37 = 83 (40+30=70, 6+7=13, 70+13=83; 73 is the dropped-ten error); 83−25 = 58 (62 is the smaller-from-larger bug; 62+25=87≠83); 60−24 = 36; 71−68 = 3; missing-number 46+?=83 gives 37. The diagnostic correctAnswer string '83, 58, 36, 3' matches these.

Legacy claims that '3D adds no explanatory power' and that dialogue 'cannot supply the volume of varied practice' were softened to narrowly scoped affordance/limit statements; they were catalog fit rationales, not established comparative-efficacy findings.
Legacy claim that a coded surface offering the same pair on two tools is where 'fluency clicks' is retained as a design rationale, not as a claim of demonstrated necessity or verified effectiveness.
The assessment's 60−24 and the 83−45 probe variant are not given a dedicated activity; consider adding practice that exercises those if full coverage of the diagnostic set is wanted.

probeDeeper: For 71−68 you took away by borrowing — is there a quicker way to see the gap between 68 and 71?
Add your answer to 25 to check 83−25 — does it come back to 83?
You partitioned 46 and 37 into tens and ones — show me exactly where the extra ten in the answer came from.
What if it were 83 − 45 instead of 83 − 25 — would your method still work? Try it and see.
assess.correctAnswer: 83, 58, 36, 3. Fluent work: 46+37 by partitioning (70+13=83); 83−25 by regrouping or counting up; 60−24 as 60−20−4 or by counting up from 24; 71−68 should trigger counting up (68→71 = 3) rather than columnar borrowing.

errorPatterns.pattern: Smaller-from-larger subtraction bug — 'eighty-three take twenty-five: five take three is two', answering 62 regardless of column order
errorPatterns.nextMove: Go back to place-value regrouping with base-ten blocks: 83 must give up a ten to make enough ones (as 70+13) before the ones can be taken. Confront by checking 62+25.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The ones column of 83−25 is done as 5−3 with no decomposition of a ten; answer 62

errorPatterns.pattern: Partitions correctly but loses the regrouped ten — '46 and 37: seventy and thirteen… seventy-three'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the recombination, don't reteach the method: have the child compose the 13 into 'one ten and three' and add that ten to the seventy. This is a lapse, not a missing concept.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct partial sums (70 and 13) but the final recombination drops the extra ten, giving 73 instead of 83

errorPatterns.pattern: Reaches for the same written method regardless of the numbers — column-subtracts 71−68 with full borrowing instead of counting up
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the algorithm; put the count-up and the borrow side by side on the same pair and ask which was quicker and why, building the habit of looking at the numbers first.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Works 71−68 with a multi-step borrow, showing no sensitivity to how close the numbers are

responseLevels.gap: Smaller-from-larger or dropped-ten errors; answers are unreliable whenever regrouping is needed.
responseLevels.full: Efficient and accurate on all four, selects the method to suit the numbers (counts up for 71−68, partitions for 46+37), keeps regrouping correct, and checks using the inverse.
responseLevels.partial: Accurate with one preferred method (e.g. always partitions) but does not adapt to the numbers; slow or stumbles where counting up would be far easier; needs prompting to check.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set these four one at a time and watch the child work each, letting them choose their own method and jot: 46 + 37, then 83 − 25, then 60 − 24, then 71 − 68. Pay particular attention to which method they reach for on 71 − 68.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 83−25 exposes the smaller-from-larger bug (a child doing 5−3 answers 62). 71−68 separates a child with strategic flexibility, who notices the numbers are close and counts up, from one who mechanically column-subtracts everything. 46+37 exposes a dropped regroup (answer 73). Together they distinguish accurate-and-flexible from accurate-but-rigid from buggy.

sources.claim: Year 2 pupils recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently and derive related facts to 100, use the inverse relationship to check calculations, and partition numbers in different ways (e.g. 23 = 20+3 and 10+13) to support subtraction.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (KS1, Year 2)

sources.claim: Two-digit subtraction is done by partitioning the subtrahend into tens and ones (decomposing a ten where needed), and strategy choice varies with the numbers — e.g. counting up from 67 to find 94−67, or counting back for 64−25.
sources.source: NCETM Primary Mastery PD, Spine 1 Segment 1.16

sources.claim: The 'smaller-from-larger' subtraction error is a classic, systematic buggy algorithm — the child subtracts the smaller digit from the larger within each column regardless of position (the '437−284=253' pattern). In Brown & Burton's 1325-student data it was used by 54 students; such bugs are stable, not careless (~40% of students consistently buggy).
sources.source: Brown & Burton, 'Diagnostic Models for Procedural Bugs in Basic Mathematical Skills', Cognitive Science 2(2), 1978 (full text: ERIC ED159036)

pedagogy.summary: Two-step contextual problems where the child must plan before computing: identify the two steps and their order, choose an appropriate method (mental or written) for each step given the numbers, and justify the choices. The intellectual work is structuring the situation, not arithmetic — so the enemy is the KEYWORD strategy ('altogether' means add, 'left' means subtract), which collapses on comparison and multi-step structures. Bar-model representation of the whole problem before any calculation is the central pedagogy.
bestPractices: Represent the whole problem with a bar model BEFORE computing — structure first, numbers second
Explicitly plan the two steps and their order; name the intermediate quantity so it is not mistaken for the answer
Directly discredit keyword-spotting with problems where the keyword misleads (a 'more than' comparison that needs subtraction)
Choose method per step by the numbers (a near-multiple mentally, an awkward pair on paper)
Check the final answer for reasonableness against the story
keyRepresentations: Bar model (comparison and aggregation)
Part-whole diagram
Empty number line / jottings
Two-box 'step 1 -> step 2' planner
commonMisconceptions: Keyword strategy — picks the operation from a word ('altogether', 'more than') rather than the situation
One-step-only — solves the first step and offers the intermediate quantity as the final answer
Wrong order of steps, or choosing operations from the numbers present rather than the story
Uses a written method where a mental one is efficient, or vice versa
Does not notice an implausible answer

learn.summary: Year 4 two-step addition and subtraction problems in context, where the real work is structuring the situation before computing: identify the two steps and their order, name the intermediate quantity, choose a mental or written method per step based on the numbers, and check the answer for reasonableness. The central aim is to beat the keyword strategy (treating 'altogether' as always add, 'more than' as always add, 'left' as always subtract), which collapses on comparison and multi-step problems. Representing the whole problem (e.g. with a bar model) before any calculation is the core move.

activities.title: Model the structure before you compute (bar-model planner)
feedback: If a learner answers 425 (340+85) on the sticker problem: ask 'who has more, Sam or Kim, and how do you know?' Draw the comparison so they see Kim must be found by subtraction first.
If a learner answers 247 on the apple problem: re-read and underline what is actually asked, and mark BOTH steps so the second (the delivery) is not dropped.
If a learner adds all the numbers in sight or does the steps in the wrong order: narrate the story in order, mapping each event to one operation.

Prompt: 'If it said Sam has 85 FEWER than Kim, would you still subtract to find Kim — or add?' to test whether they are modelling rather than word-spotting (here, fewer would mean Kim is larger, so you would add).
activities.rationale: Representing a problem's underlying structure visually before writing an equation focuses attention on the relationships between quantities, and keyword shortcuts are an explicitly discouraged substitute for reasoning. A tool or drawing that cannot 'close' the total until the unknown is found may make the two-step dependency visible; a static annotated version can show the structure but does not let the learner plan a fresh problem.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils solve addition and subtraction two-step problems in contexts, deciding which operations and methods to use and why.

Problem solving 'is not the execution of memorized rules or shortcuts, such as using key words'; students who represent a problem's underlying structure visually (strip/bar diagrams) before writing an equation are more effective, because well-chosen representations focus attention on the relationships between quantities rather than surface story context. STRONG evidence rating.
The keyword strategy fails on comparison and multi-step structures; bar/strip modelling of problem structure before computing supports correct operation choice.
learnerActions: Before writing any calculation, draw or build a bar model of the whole story showing which quantities are known and which are unknown.
Work the trap problem: 'Sam has 340 stickers. That is 85 more than Kim. How many stickers do they have altogether?' First decide who has MORE — Sam or Kim.
Notice that the 'altogether' total cannot be found yet because Kim is unknown; find Kim first by 340 - 85 = 255, then add 340 + 255 = 595.

Then work the aggregation problem: 'A shop has 415 apples. In the morning it sells 168. In the afternoon a delivery brings 230 more. How many are there now?' Model it, then compute 415 - 168 = 247, then 247 + 230 = 477.
Name the intermediate quantity out loud (e.g. '247 is the apples after the morning, not the final answer').
activities.intendedInsight: The operation comes from the structure of the situation, not from a keyword. 'More than' can require subtraction (to find the smaller unknown quantity) before any adding, and a two-step problem has an intermediate value that is not the final answer.

activities.title: Talk me through your plan: justify each step and method
feedback: If the learner picks a written method where a mental one is efficient (or vice versa): ask what makes these particular numbers easy or hard, and compare the two methods on that step.
Praise plans that name the intermediate quantity and give a reason for each method choice, not just correct arithmetic.
If a reason is 'because the word said so', press for a reason based on what the story is actually doing.
activities.rationale: The objective explicitly requires explaining why chosen operations and methods are appropriate, so producing a justification (spoken or written) exercises exactly that; a recognition-only task does not itself elicit a produced justification.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils solve addition and subtraction two-step problems in contexts, deciding which operations and methods to use and why.
learnerActions: State the two steps and their order before computing anything.

For each step, choose a mental or written method based on the numbers (e.g. adding a multiple of ten like +230 can easily be done mentally; a pair that needs exchanging, like 415 - 168, may be better written for many learners, though some may compensate mentally, e.g. 415 - 170 + 2) and say why.
Answer a questioner who keeps asking 'why that operation?', 'which step first and why?', 'why did you do that one in your head?'
Defend or revise your plan when challenged.
activities.intendedInsight: Deciding which operations and methods to use — and being able to justify them — is itself the skill, not just getting a number. Method choice should fit the specific numbers.

activities.title: Ordering and method checks (with a keyword trap)
feedback: For a trap item, after the answer, reveal the comparison structure and show why the keyword misled.
For a method item, confirm by comparing how awkward the computation would be each way.
activities.rationale: Selection items can check ordering and method choice quickly and surface keyword reliance, but as recognition tasks they do not themselves require the learner to construct a plan or model independently — pair them with the modelling and justification activities above.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils solve addition and subtraction two-step problems in contexts, deciding which operations and methods to use and why.
learnerActions: Given a two-step problem, put the two operations in the correct order.
Choose the better method (mental or written) for a specified step and give the reason.
Answer at least one item deliberately designed as a keyword trap, where 'more than' or 'altogether' points to the wrong first move.
activities.intendedInsight: Ordering the steps and matching a method to the numbers are distinct decisions; keywords are not a reliable guide to either.

activities.title: Reasonableness pause
feedback: If an implausible magnitude is accepted without pause, prompt 'roughly what should we expect here, and does this fit?' and build the habit of a reasonableness check — this is about noticing, not re-teaching the arithmetic.
activities.rationale: Checking reasonableness against the story guards against both word-spotting and dropped steps by catching errors the computation alone does not reveal.
learnerActions: After reaching a final answer, estimate roughly what size answer the story should produce, then check the result against that expectation.

For the apple problem, reason about the net change: the shop sold 168 but a larger delivery of 230 arrived, so the final count should be a little MORE than the 415 it started with (477 fits); an answer far larger — such as adding all three numbers (813) — or far smaller (e.g. 247, which drops the delivery) would signal an error.
If the answer does not fit the expected size, re-examine the plan (not just redo the arithmetic).
activities.intendedInsight: A final answer must be sense-checked against the situation; a magnitude that does not fit what the story should produce signals a planning or structuring error.

constraints: The learning target is situation structure and method choice, not arithmetic fluency alone; the arithmetic should be within reach so attention stays on planning.
Do not teach keyword rules ('altogether means add', 'more than means add', 'left means subtract'); these are the misconception this topic targets.
A static annotated worked problem can illustrate the two-step structure but does not let a learner plan or model a new problem — treat it as an exposition scaffold, not the main task.
Selection/ordering items are recognition tasks and do not by themselves elicit an independently constructed plan or model; use them alongside construction and justification, not instead of them.

A tool that physically blocks keyword-adding (e.g. a total bar that will not close until the unknown part is found) is an optional mechanism to make the dependency visible; a drawn bar model on paper serves the same purpose.
The intermediate quantity must be named and distinguished from the final answer so it is not reported as the solution.

The reasonableness check must use expected magnitude for the specific story; do not teach that 'more than the starting amount' is automatically implausible, since in the apple problem the correct answer (477) is legitimately more than the 415 start because the 230 delivery outweighs the 168 sale (net +62).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: apple problem 415 - 168 = 247, then 247 + 230 = 477 — correct; adding all three (415+168+230) = 813. Sticker problem: Kim = 340 - 85 = 255, then 340 + 255 = 595 — correct. The named keyword-trap error value (340+85 = 425) and the dropped-step value (247) are presented only as learner errors to diagnose, never as valid answers.

The original row's performance error pattern gives 'more apples than started, after a net change' as an example of an implausible magnitude, but for this apple problem the correct answer (477) genuinely exceeds the 415 start because the 230 delivery outweighs the 168 sale (net +62). The reasonableness activity has been corrected to anchor on expected magnitude rather than 'more/fewer than started'.

One source (Cognitively Guided Instruction / Singapore model method / NCETM bar-model guidance) is marked verified:false and 'not fetched this session' in the original row; its claim is retained but should not be treated as independently confirmed.

The original design note asserts a bar-model tool 'can refuse a keyword-driven mis-structuring' and marks 'the moment situation-modelling beats word-spotting'; this is a plausible design claim but comparative efficacy/necessity is not established by the cited sources, so it is framed here as an optional mechanism rather than a proven one.
The original artefact rating '3D adds nothing' is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law, and has been omitted rather than restated as universal.

probeDeeper: What is the question actually asking for - the apples after the morning, or at the very end of the day?
In the sticker problem, who has more, Sam or Kim? How do you know?
If it said Sam has 85 FEWER than Kim, would you still subtract to find Kim - or add?
Which step did you do in your head and which on paper, and why that choice?
assess.correctAnswer: Problem 1: 415 - 168 = 247, then 247 + 230 = 477 (two steps, right order; the subtraction likely written, the +230 can be mental). Problem 2: recognises 'more than' does NOT simply mean add - Kim has 340 - 85 = 255, then 340 + 255 = 595 altogether. Explains why each operation fits the story.

errorPatterns.pattern: Word-spots: 'more than means add, altogether means add everything' - does 340 + 85, or adds all the numbers, and stops
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw the bar - who has MORE, Sam or Kim? Build the comparison model so the child sees Kim must be found by subtraction. Attack keyword reliance directly.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Problem 2 answer of 425 (340+85) or an all-numbers sum; no comparison is modelled

errorPatterns.pattern: Solves only the first step and gives the intermediate quantity as the final answer (e.g. 247 apples, forgetting the delivery)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-read and underline what is actually asked; mark BOTH steps on the bar so the second is not dropped.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Problem 1 answer of 247

errorPatterns.pattern: Picks operations from the numbers present or in the wrong order rather than from the story sequence
errorPatterns.nextMove: Act out or narrate the story in order; each event maps to one operation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Computes 415 + 168 first, or an arbitrary order

errorPatterns.pattern: Accepts an implausible answer without checking it against the story
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'does that make sense - more or fewer than we started with?' Build a reasonableness pause; do not reteach the arithmetic.

responseLevels.gap: Grabs numbers and one operation, driven by keywords; produces no two-step plan.
responseLevels.full: Models both problems with a bar, sequences the two steps correctly including the comparison, chooses a method per step, and checks reasonableness; transfers correctly to a 'fewer than' variant.
responseLevels.partial: Handles the straightforward two-step problem but is misled by the 'more than' comparison, or answers the intermediate value; can list steps but does not model the situation.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Read this aloud and watch the child PLAN before computing: 'A shop has 415 apples. In the morning it sells 168. In the afternoon a delivery brings 230 more. How many apples are there now?' Ask 'what are the steps, and how will you do each one?' Then give a second problem where the keyword misleads: 'Sam has 340 stickers. That is 85 more than Kim. How many stickers do they have altogether?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Problem 2 contains 'more than' and 'altogether' - a keyword solver adds 340 + 85 and stops, or adds all the numbers in sight. A child who models the situation finds Kim by subtraction first, then adds. Meanwhile the two-step structure of Problem 1 catches the child who reports the intermediate 247 as the answer. Together they separate situation-modelling from word-spotting and one-step shortcutting.
