pedagogy.summary: Here the fixed-whole idea generalises from lines and points to CLOSED SHAPES: the interior angles of a triangle sum to 180°, of a quadrilateral to 360°, and of any polygon to (n−2)×180° — because every polygon can be cut into (n−2) triangles. The child uses these sums to find a missing angle by subtraction, and for a REGULAR polygon divides the sum equally among the vertices (regular hexagon: 720° ÷ 6 = 120°). The central pedagogical danger is teaching '180° in a triangle' as an isolated fact to memorise; taught well, the triangle sum is DERIVED (torn corners laid on a straight line, or a triangle's angles rearranged to 180°) and the quadrilateral/polygon sums are built by partitioning into triangles — so the whole family hangs together and, crucially, the sum is seen to be INDEPENDENT of the triangle's size.
bestPractices: Derive the triangle sum, don't just state it: tear off the three corners and fit them onto a straight line (180°), or fold them to a point on the base — so 180° is a thing the child has seen happen, not a number to recall.

Build the quadrilateral (360°) and polygon sums by PARTITIONING into triangles — a quadrilateral is two triangles, an n-gon is (n−2) triangles — connecting every polygon back to the triangle rather than memorising separate facts.

Confront size-dependence directly: show that stretching a triangle bigger, or drawing it with longer sides, leaves the angle sum at 180° — many children (and adults) intuitively expect the angles to grow with the triangle.
Use 'not drawn to scale' problems and non-isosceles-looking triangles so children compute from given angles rather than assuming equal angles from appearance.
For regular polygons, separate the two steps clearly: find the total angle sum, THEN divide by the number of (equal) vertices — don't conflate the sum with a single interior angle.
Treat finding a missing angle as subtraction from the known sum, writing the calculation, and sanity-checking (a triangle angle can't exceed 180°).
keyRepresentations: Torn-corners demonstration: three triangle corners rearranged onto a straight line = 180°
Polygon partitioned into triangles: quadrilateral = 2 triangles (360°), n-gon = (n−2) triangles
Angle-sum table: triangle 180°, quadrilateral 360°, pentagon 540°, hexagon 720°
Regular polygon: total sum ÷ number of vertices = one interior angle (hexagon 720° ÷ 6 = 120°)
A stretchable triangle whose angle sum stays 180° as its size changes
commonMisconceptions: Thinks a triangle's angles sum to 360° rather than 180° (documented in diagnostic data), so subtracts from the wrong total.

Believes the angle sum (or a missing angle) depends on the triangle's SIZE — expects a bigger/longer triangle to have larger angles; contradicts the constant 180° sum (documented in children and adults).
Assumes a triangle is isosceles or equilateral because it looks that way on a not-to-scale diagram, so wrongly takes two angles as equal.
Knows '180° in a triangle' only as a disconnected fact and cannot extend it to a quadrilateral or polygon (does not partition into triangles).
For a regular polygon, reports the total angle sum as if it were a single interior angle (forgets to divide by the number of vertices).

learn.summary: Learners find unknown angles in triangles, quadrilaterals and regular polygons using angle-sum properties — but with the triangle's 180° DERIVED (not merely recalled), the quadrilateral/polygon sums BUILT by partitioning into (n−2) triangles, and the crucial fact that the angle sum is INDEPENDENT of the triangle's size made visible rather than asserted. Activities span a hands-on/manipulable derivation of 180° and size-invariance, a partition-to-build-larger-sums task, scorable missing-angle practice (including 'not drawn to scale' and 360°-distractor items), and a two-step regular-polygon calculation (total sum ÷ vertices). The central danger addressed throughout is teaching '180° in a triangle' as an isolated memorised fact.

activities.title: Torn corners make a straight line (deriving 180°)
feedback: If the corners fill the line with no gap or overlap, the angles make a straight angle, 180°. Paper shows this up to small imperfections, and the exact value is the ideal geometric result.
Tearing and folding should give the same result: both arrange the three angles along a straight line.
Try a very differently-shaped triangle: if its corners still fill a straight line, the 180° result is not specific to one triangle.
A paper cutout has slight thickness and torn edges, so expect tiny imperfections; the screen model shows the idealised exact fit for the ideal (zero-thickness) plane figure.
activities.rationale: Deriving the triangle sum by physically rearranging corners onto a straight line — whether by tearing or by folding to a point on the base — connects it to 'angles on a straight line = 180°' and makes 180° an observed outcome rather than a disconnected fact, the pedagogy's central correction. Both paper and an optional drag-and-snap screen model make the mechanism concrete; efficacy relative to simply stating the rule is proposed, not tested.
sourceClaims: Year 5 primary lesson: the interior angles of a triangle sum to 180°, derived from angles on a straight line; a common misconception is that pupils know this only as a disconnected fact, so the recommended approach is to relate the triangle to the quadrilateral by partitioning shapes into triangles.
learnerActions: Cut or tear the three corners off a paper triangle and arrange them side by side so their vertices meet at a single point — observe that together they fill a straight line (180°), with no visible gap or overlap apart from small paper imperfections.

Alternatively derive the same result by using the longest side as the base: fold the top corner down so it touches the base at the foot of the height, then fold the other two corners in to meet it at that point — they again fill a straight line along the base.
Repeat either method with a differently-shaped triangle (e.g. a long thin one and a squat one) and confirm the three corners again fill a straight line.
On a drag-and-drop screen model, drag the three corner-wedges onto a straight line so they snap to fill 180°, with a banner reading the running sum.
activities.intendedInsight: The three interior angles of ANY triangle rearrange to lie on a straight line, so they sum to 180° — this is something you can see happen (by tearing or by folding the corners), not a number to recall.

activities.title: Does the sum change when the triangle changes size?
feedback: If you predicted the sum would grow but it stayed 180°, that is exactly the intuition this task is designed to surface and correct.

Stretching or squashing changes side lengths and individual angles, and simply enlarging the same shape keeps every angle the same. Either way the three angles total 180° (paper measurements may be off by a degree or two).
Making a triangle bigger does NOT make its angles bigger — an enlarged copy of a triangle has exactly the same angles. Work from the given angles, not from how big the triangle looks.
activities.rationale: Both children and educated adults intuitively expect a triangle's angles to scale with its size; confronting this prediction directly, then showing the sum hold constant under reshaping, targets a documented and persistent misconception. An optional live vertex-drag with a sum readout calculated from the current angles (an idealised model) makes the invariance experienceable; its advantage over simply asserting the rule is proposed, not demonstrated.
sourceClaims: Children (6–7) and even educated adults intuitively judge a triangle's missing third angle as scaling with the triangle's overall size — predicting a larger angle when the base is longer — in direct contradiction with Euclid's proposition 32 that the internal angles of a triangle sum to a constant regardless of size; the error reflects mental simulation rather than use of the angle-sum rule, and formal schooling did not predict accuracy.
learnerActions: Predict, before testing: 'If I make this triangle much bigger or stretch it long and thin, will the angle sum get bigger?' Write down your prediction.
Make the triangle larger, then longer and thinner, then squat and wide — on a screen model drag a vertex to reshape it; on paper draw each new triangle.

Each time, re-check the angle sum: read the live sum readout on the screen model, or (on paper) tear or fold the corners of each new triangle, or measure its three marked angles, and record the total.
Compare your prediction with what actually happened to the sum.
activities.intendedInsight: The angle sum stays 180° no matter how big, small, long or stretched the triangle is — side length does not change the angle sum, even though many people expect bigger triangles to have bigger angles.

activities.title: Build the polygon sums by cutting into triangles
feedback: Check: your number of triangles should always be two fewer than the number of sides.
If the quadrilateral gives 360° as two triangles of 180°, you have connected it to the triangle rather than memorised a separate fact.
If you can state WHY a quadrilateral is 360° ('it is two triangles'), you understand the partition, not just the number.
activities.rationale: Partitioning into triangles turns a set of separate memorised sums into one connected system and directly addresses the misconception of knowing '180°' only as an isolated fact that cannot be extended. A tap-to-partition screen mode can make the triangle count visible.
sourceClaims: Year 5 primary lesson: the interior angles of a triangle sum to 180°, derived from angles on a straight line; a common misconception is that pupils know this only as a disconnected fact, so the recommended approach is to relate the triangle to the quadrilateral by partitioning shapes into triangles.
learnerActions: Draw a diagonal inside a quadrilateral to split it into two triangles (in a dented, non-convex quadrilateral, use the diagonal that stays inside); conclude its angle sum is 2 × 180° = 360°.
Partition a convex pentagon (3 triangles) and a convex hexagon (4 triangles) from one vertex, counting the triangles each time.
Record results in an angle-sum table: triangle 180°, quadrilateral 360°, pentagon 540°, hexagon 720°.
State the pattern in words and as a rule: an n-gon splits into (n−2) triangles, so its angle sum is (n−2) × 180°.
activities.intendedInsight: Every simple polygon's (one with no crossing sides) angle sum is built from triangles: an n-sided polygon divides into (n−2) triangles, so its interior angles sum to (n−2) × 180° — the whole family connects back to the triangle.

activities.title: Missing-angle practice, including 'not drawn to scale'
feedback: If you subtracted from 360° for a triangle and got 230°, that exceeds 180° — a sign the wrong total was used; a triangle is 180°.
If a figure looks isosceles but the marked angles differ, trust the numbers: 'not drawn to scale' means both appearance AND measuring the drawing are unreliable — only the marked angles are correct.
Writing the subtraction and checking it is reasonable guards against both the wrong-total error and arithmetic slips.
activities.rationale: Scorable number-entry and multiple-choice practice efficiently rehearses the procedure and catches two documented errors — subtracting from 360° and assuming isosceles from appearance. On a not-to-scale figure, measuring the drawing returns the misleading drawn angles, so only the marked values work. Diagnostic data also notes that the most common wrong answer can be an arithmetic slip by students who DO know the rule, so writing and checking the calculation matters. This practice can check and rehearse the procedure but cannot itself stage the size-invariance discovery, which the manipulable tasks above provide.
sourceClaims: Diagnostic-question data: a documented wrong answer is that angles in a triangle add up to 360° (students subtract from 360 rather than 180); another group assumes the triangle is isosceles because it looks that way; the most common wrong answer was actually an arithmetic slip by students who knew the 180° rule — so reasoning errors must be separated from computation errors.
learnerActions: Find a triangle's third angle given two angles by subtracting from 180° (e.g. 180 − (70 + 60) = 50°); write the calculation.
Find a quadrilateral's missing angle by subtracting the three known angles from 360°.
Answer an item deliberately drawn roughly isosceles though it is NOT to scale: compute only from the marked angles, not from how the figure looks and not by measuring the drawing with a protractor.
Sanity-check each answer (each triangle angle must be more than 0° and less than 180°; the three sum to exactly 180°).
activities.intendedInsight: Missing angles are found by subtracting known angles from the correct total (180° for a triangle, 360° for a quadrilateral), using the MARKED values rather than the picture's appearance or a protractor reading of a not-to-scale drawing.

activities.title: Regular polygons: find the sum, THEN share it out
feedback: If you stopped at 720°, that is the TOTAL of all six angles, not one angle — you still need to divide by 6.
Labelling 'total sum' versus 'one angle' keeps the two steps from collapsing together.
Check scale: one interior angle of a hexagon (120°) should be far smaller than the full 720° total.
activities.rationale: A documented error is reporting the total polygon sum as if it were a single interior angle; explicitly separating the sum step from the divide-equally step addresses this without needing to reteach the sum. An optional regular-polygon panel showing sum ÷ vertices makes the share-equally step concrete.
learnerActions: For a regular hexagon, first find the total interior-angle sum (4 triangles × 180° = 720°).
Then, because all six interior angles of a regular hexagon are equal, divide: 720° ÷ 6 = 120° for one interior angle.
Write the two steps separately and label which number is the TOTAL sum and which is ONE angle.
Repeat for another regular polygon (e.g. regular pentagon: 540° ÷ 5 = 108°).
activities.intendedInsight: For a regular polygon there are two distinct steps: find the total angle sum, then divide equally among the (equal) vertices to get one interior angle — the total sum is not itself a single angle.

constraints: '180° in a triangle' must be derived (e.g. torn corners on a straight line, or corners folded to the foot of the height on the longest side) and connected to the other polygon sums by partitioning into triangles — not taught as an isolated fact to memorise.
Scorable multiple-choice/number-entry practice rehearses and catches distractors but cannot by itself stage the size-invariance discovery; pair it with a manipulable or hands-on reshaping task.
Paper/card triangle cutouts have slight thickness and torn edges; treat them as physical approximations of the ideal zero-thickness plane figure. Label any screen model as an idealisation.

A static picture or table can seed the 180° fact and the angle-sum table but cannot let the learner reshape a triangle to experience the sum staying constant; use it as a scaffold, not a replacement for manipulation.

'Not drawn to scale' problems require computing from marked angles only; do not infer equal angles from an isosceles-looking figure, and do not measure the drawing with a protractor to get the angles.
Separate genuine reasoning errors (wrong total, size-dependence, isosceles assumption) from mere arithmetic slips when interpreting a wrong answer.
Interior-angle sums here concern plane polygons; a 3D setting is not required and could be confused with solid angles.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row framed a 3D or conversation artefact as adding 'no conceptual gain' or being unable to teach the discovery; these comparative-necessity claims are not established by the cited sources and have been softened to scoped affordance/limitation statements in constraints rather than universal laws.
sourceClaims are limited to claims that directly support each principle; the regular-polygon two-step activity has no directly supporting source claim and is marked [].
Arithmetic self-checked: 180−(70+60)=50; wrong-total 360−130=230; quadrilateral 2×180=360; pentagon 3×180=540, 540÷5=108; hexagon 4×180=720, 720÷6=120 — all consistent with the source row.

Edits in this independent review: clarified the size-invariance check method in activity 2 (read the screen sum readout, or tear/fold/measure each fresh paper triangle) because re-tearing the corners of an already-drawn or on-screen triangle is not coherent; retained the earlier restorations of the fold-to-a-point derivation (activity 1) and the 'measuring a not-to-scale drawing misleads' point (activity 4).

probeDeeper: 'You said the missing angle is 50°. If I stretched this triangle to twice as wide but kept these two angles the same, what would the third angle be now?' — counterexample targeting size-dependence (it stays 50°).
'How could you use triangles to work out the angle sum of this hexagon?' — probes whether the polygon sum is derived by partition or just recalled.
'This quadrilateral — why 360° and the triangle only 180°? What's the connection?' — listens for 'a quadrilateral is two triangles'.
'The drawing makes these two angles look equal. Are they? How can you be sure without measuring?' — tests reliance on marked values over appearance.
assess.correctAnswer: (1) third angle = 180 − (70+60) = 50°, using the triangle sum 180°; (2) missing = 360 − (sum of the three), using the quadrilateral sum 360°; (3) one interior angle = 720° ÷ 6 = 120°, having found the hexagon's angle sum (4 triangles × 180°). Computes from the marked/derived sums, not from appearance, and divides the sum for the regular polygon.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks a triangle's angles sum to 360° — subtracts the two known angles from 360 instead of 180.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-derive 180° by tearing the corners onto a straight line; contrast triangle (180°) with quadrilateral (360°) and show the quadrilateral is TWO triangles.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives the triangle's third angle as 360 − (70+60) = 230°, or explains 'a triangle is 360°'; often the rest of the working is correct.

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes the angle sum depends on the triangle's size — expects a bigger or longer-sided triangle to have a larger third angle / larger sum.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the same angles on triangles of very different sizes, and reshape one triangle while the 180° sum holds; make explicit that side length does not change the angle sum.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Judges the missing angle by how big or stretched the triangle looks rather than computing 180 − known; says a wider triangle 'must have a bigger angle there'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Assumes the triangle is isosceles/equilateral from its appearance — takes two angles as equal because the not-to-scale drawing looks that way.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reinforce 'not drawn to scale': compute only from marked angles; show a case where the equal-looking angles are provably unequal from the numbers.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Splits the remaining angle equally, or asserts two angles are equal, with no marking to justify it; relies on how the figure looks.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reports the polygon's total angle sum as a single interior angle — for the regular hexagon gives 720° (the sum) instead of dividing by 6.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the two-step structure: total sum, THEN ÷ number of equal vertices; no reteaching of the sum needed — the final division was dropped.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Finds 720° correctly but stops there, or writes 720° as 'the angle'; the sum step is right, the share-equally step is missing.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot find missing angles reliably: uses the wrong total, judges by appearance or size, or cannot get beyond the triangle; no method for the quadrilateral or hexagon.
responseLevels.full: Computes missing angles in triangle, quadrilateral and regular polygon; derives the polygon sums by partitioning into triangles and divides for a regular polygon; recognises the sum is independent of size; and uses marked values rather than appearance — the 180° rule is a connected tool, not an isolated fact.
responseLevels.partial: Finds a triangle's missing angle using 180° in the standard case, but treats the sums as separate memorised facts — defeated by the regular hexagon (can't partition or forgets to divide), misled by the not-to-scale/isosceles-looking triangle, or shows size-dependence when the shape is stretched. Lists the sums without relating them.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child three figures with angles marked (not to scale). (1) A triangle with two angles 70° and 60°, third unknown — draw it looking roughly isosceles though it isn't. (2) A quadrilateral with three angles marked, one unknown. (3) A regular hexagon, asking for one interior angle. Say: 'Work out each missing angle, and tell me how you got it.' Watch the method — which total they use, whether they partition, whether they trust the picture — without prompting the rules.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Spanning triangle, quadrilateral and regular polygon separates a child who holds a connected system (all sums built from triangles) from one who has a single memorised fact and no way to reach the hexagon. The not-to-scale, isosceles-looking triangle catches trust-the-picture reasoning. Asking 'how did you get it' exposes the 360°-for-a-triangle error and the size-dependence intuition, and separates a genuine reasoning error from a mere arithmetic slip.

sources.claim: Year 5 primary lesson: the interior angles of a triangle sum to 180°, derived from angles on a straight line; a common misconception is that pupils know this only as a disconnected fact, so the recommended approach is to relate the triangle to the quadrilateral by partitioning shapes into triangles.
sources.source: Oak National Academy, 'Angles in triangles' (KS2/Year 5)

sources.claim: Diagnostic-question data: a documented wrong answer is that angles in a triangle add up to 360° (students subtract from 360 rather than 180); another group assumes the triangle is isosceles because it looks that way; the most common wrong answer was actually an arithmetic slip by students who knew the 180° rule — so reasoning errors must be separated from computation errors.
sources.source: Craig Barton / Eedi, 'Angles in a Triangle: Guess the Misconception'

sources.claim: Children (6–7) and even educated adults intuitively judge a triangle's missing third angle as scaling with the triangle's overall size — predicting a larger angle when the base is longer — in direct contradiction with Euclid's proposition 32 that the internal angles of a triangle sum to a constant regardless of size; the error reflects mental simulation rather than use of the angle-sum rule, and formal schooling did not predict accuracy.
sources.source: Hart, Dillon, Marantan, Cardenas, Spelke & Mahadevan (2018), 'The statistical shape of geometric reasoning', Scientific Reports 8:12906

pedagogy.summary: Recognising, finding, naming, and writing 1/3, 1/4, 2/4, and 3/4 of a length, shape, set, or quantity. Two ideas mature here: the DENOMINATOR tells how many equal parts to share the whole into, and the NUMERATOR tells how many of those parts to take (so non-unit fractions like 3/4 are three of the quarter-parts). Fractions of a discrete SET (1/3 of 12 counters) sit alongside fractions of continuous shapes/lengths.
bestPractices: Find a unit fraction by sharing the whole into denominator-many EQUAL parts and taking one; build the non-unit fraction as repeated unit fractions (3/4 = three quarters)
Move between continuous (shade 3/4 of a rectangle) and discrete (1/3 of 12 counters) models
For a set, share into denominator-many equal GROUPS (not groups of that size), then take numerator-many groups
Name and write alongside the action so notation is tied to meaning
Keep the whole explicit and fixed while working
keyRepresentations: A set of counters shared into equal groups (denominator groups; take numerator)
A rectangle/strip partitioned and shaded (e.g. 3 of 4 parts for 3/4)
A length/number line marked into equal parts
Unit-fraction tiles combined to build a non-unit fraction
commonMisconceptions: Reading the denominator as the group SIZE, not the number of groups (1/3 of 12 -> makes groups of 3)
Treating a non-unit fraction like a unit fraction - taking only ONE part for 3/4
Number-vs-quantity: sharing an equal COUNT of unequal-sized items rather than equal amount
Losing track of the whole, or ignoring leftover items when a set doesn't divide evenly

learn.summary: Year 2 pupils (ages 6-7) recognise, find, name, and write the fractions 1/3, 1/4, 2/4, and 3/4 of a length, shape, set of objects, or quantity. Two linked ideas mature: the DENOMINATOR says how many EQUAL parts (or equal groups) to share the whole into, and the NUMERATOR says how many of those parts to take, so a non-unit fraction like 3/4 is three of the quarter-parts, not a single piece. Work moves between continuous wholes (shading part of a rectangle or marking a length) and discrete sets (a third of 12 counters), always keeping the whole explicit and fixed.

activities.title: Fraction-of-a-set bench: share into equal groups, then take some
feedback: If a child makes groups OF three for 1/3 of 12, stop and re-share: the 3 means THREE equal groups; put all 12 into three hoops and take one group (4), not a group of three.
If a child reports 3/4 of 12 as 3, they took only one quarter: build 3/4 as three of the quarter-groups - the numerator counts how many quarters to take, giving 9.
If groups are made unequal, point out that fractions need EQUAL parts before any part can be named.
When toggling to the shaded strip, confirm the child sees the same answer two ways (e.g. 3 of 4 shaded parts match the 3 of 4 groups).
activities.rationale: Finding a fraction of a set or shape is a partition-and-select action; sharing into denominator-many equal groups and selecting numerator-many makes both numbers meaningful, and building 3/4 by taking numerator-many quarter-parts reflects the source principle that non-unit fractions are composed of unit fractions. A live set-and-shape tool with a denominator dial, equal-group enforcement, group selection, and a continuous/discrete toggle can make the share-then-take mechanism and immediate feedback concrete; these are optional interaction examples, not required mechanisms - counters, hoops, and drawn strips achieve the same actions.
sourceClaims: Problems sharing one object yield unit fractions; multiple-object sharing yields non-unit fractions, which are composed of unit fractions (3/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4)
learnerActions: Put out 12 counters as the whole. To find 1/3, share ALL 12 into 3 equal groups (one group per hoop) and take one group - record '1/3 of 12 = 4'.
To find 3/4, share all 12 into 4 equal groups (3 in each) and take THREE of the four groups - record '3/4 of 12 = 9'.
Say aloud 'the bottom number is how many equal groups; the top number is how many groups I take' as you act it out.
Re-show the same fraction as a shaded strip or rectangle divided into the denominator and shaded to the numerator, to see the continuous and discrete versions side by side.

Check a non-dividing case: with a different set of items that does not share evenly (for example 10 counters into 3 groups), notice the leftover. It means the groups cannot all be equal with whole items, so that fraction of the set cannot be found exactly with whole counters (1/3 of 10 is not 3).
activities.intendedInsight: The denominator sets how many EQUAL groups/parts to make; the numerator says how many of those to take - so 3/4 is three quarters, not one piece, and the same fraction describes both a set and a shape.

activities.title: Build a non-unit fraction from unit-fraction parts
feedback: If the child takes only one part for 3/4, count the quarters together: one quarter, two quarters, three quarters - the top number tells how many to take.
If they lose track of the whole, restate what the whole is and re-share it into equal parts before taking any.
activities.rationale: The source principle that non-unit fractions are composed of unit fractions supports building 3/4 as 1/4+1/4+1/4; naming and writing alongside the action ties notation to meaning.
sourceClaims: Problems sharing one object yield unit fractions; multiple-object sharing yields non-unit fractions, which are composed of unit fractions (3/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4)
learnerActions: Find a unit fraction first: share the whole into denominator-many equal parts and take one (e.g. 1/4 of a strip, or 1/4 of 12 counters = 3).
Build 3/4 by repeating that quarter three times (1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4), counting the quarters taken.
State the link: 3/4 means three of the four equal parts, so it is three unit-fractions put together.
Write the fraction next to the action each time so the notation stays tied to the meaning.
activities.intendedInsight: A non-unit fraction is repeated unit fractions: 3/4 is three quarters, built by taking one quarter three times.

activities.title: Same number or same amount? Guarding against the count-vs-quantity trap
feedback: If the whole is an amount of stuff and a child makes equal-count groups of unequal-sized pieces, colour-cue quantity versus count and ask again 'same number of things, or same amount?'
Confirm that for identical counters equal count and equal amount coincide, but for mixed sizes an equal count can leave the amounts unequal.
activities.rationale: The IES guide notes children confuse the number of things shared with the quantity shared, especially with unequal-size items; surfacing this distinction directly - and defining fair sharing as equal amount - targets the misconception.
sourceClaims: Children confuse the number of things shared with the quantity shared, especially with unequal-size items (Roadblock 1.3)
learnerActions: Compare a third of 12 LARGE counters with a third of 12 TINY counters: is the NUMBER of things the same? Is the total AMOUNT the same?

With a mixed set of big and small pieces of the same stuff (e.g. pieces of food to share fairly), check whether equal-COUNT groups also hold an equal AMOUNT. When the whole is an amount of stuff, amount, not count, is what fair sharing must make equal. Exact equal amounts may not be possible without cutting pieces.
Discuss aloud: 'same number of things, or same amount?' to separate the two ideas.
activities.intendedInsight: When the whole is an amount of stuff, fair sharing means giving each share an equal AMOUNT. With identical counters, counting gives equal amounts, but with unequal-sized pieces an equal count is NOT the same as an equal amount, so children must check the amount, not just the number of things. When the question is about the number of objects in a set, the count is what matters.

activities.title: Fraction of a length on a number line or ruler
feedback: If parts along the length are unequal, re-mark so all parts are equal before naming the fraction.
If the child treats 2/4 and 1/4 as the same, count the parts taken: 2/4 takes two of the four equal parts.
activities.rationale: The curriculum requires fractions of a length as well as of shapes and sets; moving between a length, a shape, and a discrete set builds transfer.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils recognise, find, name, and write fractions 1/3, 1/4, 2/4, 3/4 of a length, shape, set of objects, or quantity
learnerActions: Mark a length or strip into denominator-many equal parts and find 1/4 of it.
Compare this with 1/4 of a set of counters: how are the two alike (share into 4 equal parts, take one) and unlike (a length is continuous; counters are separate things)?
Find 2/4 and 3/4 of the same length and notice 2/4 is halfway and 3/4 is three of the four equal parts.
activities.intendedInsight: The same share-then-take rule applies to lengths as to sets and shapes, so fractions transfer across continuous and discrete wholes.

activities.title: Naming and writing practice (recognition and recall check)
feedback: If '1/3 of 12 = 3' is chosen, re-share into THREE equal groups: each group has 4, so a third is 4; a group OF three is a different thing.
Use the denominator-as-group-size wrong answer as a discussion point, not a penalty.
activities.rationale: Naming, matching, and fill-in tasks suit recognition and recall of fractions of amounts and can embed a targeted wrong-answer trap; note that recognition-only responses check recall and do not by themselves elicit the independent sharing action, so pair them with the hands-on bench work.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils recognise, find, name, and write fractions 1/3, 1/4, 2/4, 3/4 of a length, shape, set of objects, or quantity
learnerActions: Match fractions (1/3, 1/4, 2/4, 3/4) to correctly shaded pictures of shapes and sets.
Complete statements such as '3/4 of 12 = __' and '1/3 of 12 = __'.
Spot and reject a tempting wrong answer such as '1/3 of 12 is 3' (which reads the denominator as a group size).
activities.intendedInsight: Fractions of amounts can be named, matched, and written once their meaning is secure, consolidating the link between notation and quantity.

constraints: Fractions require EQUAL parts/groups; share the whole into denominator-many equal parts before taking any.
For a set, share into denominator-many equal GROUPS (not groups of that size), then take numerator-many groups.
Keep the whole explicit and fixed throughout a task.
Non-unit fractions (2/4, 3/4) are repeated unit fractions - take numerator-many parts, not one.

A reference poster or labelled image is reference-only: tapping to highlight parts-taken versus total-parts can support naming but does not have the child do the sharing, so it is a scaffold, not a replacement for partition-and-select practice.
Recognition and matching tasks assess and consolidate naming/writing but do not on their own require the learner to construct the partition; pair them with hands-on sharing.
When a set does not divide evenly, address any leftover explicitly rather than ignoring it.

When the whole is an amount of stuff (e.g. food or material), fair sharing makes the AMOUNT equal; equal COUNT only guarantees this for identical items, so distinguish count from amount when items differ in size. When the whole is the number of objects in a set (e.g. 1/3 of 12 counters), the fraction refers to the count.
Compare fractions as fixed quantities: 2/4 of 12 takes two of the four equal parts, 1/4 takes one; never describe the denominator rule as 'flipping'.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy entry asserted '3D adds nothing' and treated a live interactive bench as uniquely ideal; these are catalog-fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws, and have been softened to affordance-based framing. Hands-on counters, drawn strips, and number lines are equally valid media.
The legacy 'conversation: poor - built by doing' framing was not propagated as a universal claim; discussion ('same number or same amount?') is retained as useful alongside doing.

Arithmetic self-checked: 1/3 of 12 = 4 (three equal groups of 4); 3/4 of 12 = 9 (four equal groups of 3, take three); 1/4 of 12 = 3; 2/4 of 12 = 6; 4/4 of 12 = 12. The wrong answers '1/3 of 12 is 3' and '3/4 of 12 is 3' are retained only as explicitly-labelled misconception traps, never as valid answers.
The probe '4/4 of the 12 counters' correctly resolves to all 12 (the whole); covered by the whole-fixed constraint and preserved worked values.

Editor change: the curriculum source claim was removed from Activity 1, whose rationale is about the partition-and-select mechanism (a topic-level attribution there). It remains in Activities 4 and 5, where the rationale is about length-transfer and naming/writing, which the claim directly supports.

Editor change: Activity 3's intendedInsight and feedback were tightened so fair sharing is defined as equal AMOUNT, with equal count presented only as the method valid for identical items; this avoids reinforcing the count-vs-quantity misconception it targets. No fresh source verification was performed.

probeDeeper: Show me 2/4 of the 12 counters - is that more or less than 3/4?
If I had 12 big counters and 12 tiny ones, is a third of each the same NUMBER? The same AMOUNT?
Find 1/4 of this strip (a length) - how is that like, and unlike, 1/4 of the counters?
What is 4/4 of the 12 counters?
assess.correctAnswer: One-third of 12: share into 3 equal groups (4 in each) -> 4. Three-quarters of 12: share into 4 equal groups (3 in each) and take 3 groups -> 9. The bottom number (denominator) says how many equal groups/parts to make; the top number (numerator) says how many of those parts to take.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the denominator as the group SIZE, not the number of groups - for 1/3 of 12 makes groups of 3
errorPatterns.nextMove: Emphasise the 3 means THREE equal groups; share all 12 into three hoops and take one.
errorPatterns.distractor: One-third of 12 is 3
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reports 1/3 of 12 as 3 (or makes 4 groups of 3 and is unsure which is the answer)

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats a non-unit fraction like a unit fraction - takes only ONE part for 3/4
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build 3/4 as three of the quarter-groups; the numerator counts how many quarters to take.
errorPatterns.distractor: Three-quarters of 12 is 3
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reports 3/4 of 12 as 3 (one quarter) instead of 9

errorPatterns.pattern: Number-vs-quantity: shares an equal COUNT of unequal-sized items rather than an equal amount
errorPatterns.nextMove: Colour-cue quantity vs count (IES); ask 'same number of things, or same amount?'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: With mixed big/small items, makes equal-count groups regardless of amount

responseLevels.gap: Shares by the wrong thing (groups OF n), or takes one part for a non-unit fraction; treats the two numbers as unconnected.
responseLevels.full: Finds 1/3, 1/4, 2/4, 3/4 of sets, lengths, and shapes by sharing into denominator-many equal parts and taking numerator-many, explains the role of each number, and transfers between continuous and discrete wholes.
responseLevels.partial: Finds unit fractions of a set correctly but stumbles on a non-unit fraction (3/4), or works on a shape but not on a discrete set.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put out 12 counters. Ask: 'Find one-third of these counters, then find three-quarters of these counters, and tell me how you worked out each one.' Then ask: 'Why do you share by the bottom number, and what does the top number tell you to do?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: One-third forces the child to make the denominator-many EQUAL GROUPS (a child who makes groups OF three reports the wrong thing). Three-quarters forces them to take NUMERATOR-many parts (a child who treats it like a unit fraction takes only one part and says 3). The two items together separate a secure part-whole reading of the notation from a shallow one.

sources.claim: Problems sharing one object yield unit fractions; multiple-object sharing yields non-unit fractions, which are composed of unit fractions (3/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4)
sources.source: IES/WWC Fractions Practice Guide (Siegler et al., 2010, NCEE 2010-4039), Recommendation 1

sources.claim: Children confuse the number of things shared with the quantity shared, especially with unequal-size items (Roadblock 1.3)
sources.source: IES/WWC Fractions Practice Guide (Siegler et al., 2010), Recommendation 1 roadblocks

sources.claim: Year 2 pupils recognise, find, name, and write fractions 1/3, 1/4, 2/4, 3/4 of a length, shape, set of objects, or quantity
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum, Mathematics Programmes of Study, Year 2 fractions

pedagogy.summary: At age 10-11 children calculate the mean (add the values, divide by how many) AND interpret what it represents: the fair-share or typical value if the total were shared equally among the data points. The pedagogy's whole battle is against learning the rule as an empty procedure. A child who knows only 'add up and divide' makes predictable errors the moment a problem is not transparent — they cannot find a missing value given the mean, they believe adding a score of 0 leaves the mean unchanged, and they cannot say what the mean tells them or accept that it need not equal any actual data value. So the mean should be built as LEVELLING/FAIR SHARE (physically evening out towers of cubes to a common height) before or alongside the algorithm, and taught with the two 'non-transparent' tasks that reveal understanding: the reverse problem (find the missing value from the mean, using total = mean × count) and reasoning about how adding a value shifts the mean.
bestPractices: Build the mean as LEVELLING/FAIR SHARE first — even out unequal towers of cubes to a common height — so the algorithm is seen as sharing the total equally, not just a rule
Always ask 'what does this mean value tell us about the data?' after computing, and accept/expect that the mean need not equal any actual value (nobody scored 82, yet 82 is the mean)
Teach the mean as total = mean × count, so the reverse problem (find a missing value given the mean) is accessible — this is the task that reveals conceptual, not just procedural, knowledge
Probe the effect of changing the data: adding a 0, or an extreme value, MUST change the mean because it is influenced by every value — confront the common belief that a 0 leaves it unchanged
Connect the mean to its properties (it lies between the lowest and highest values; it balances the data) so children can sanity-check an answer that falls outside the data range
Keep the arithmetic (decimal addition and division) reliable so procedural slips don't masquerade as conceptual gaps
keyRepresentations: Towers of cubes / bars levelled to a common height (the fair-share / levelling model of the mean)
A balance-point image on a number line (the mean as the balancing value of the data)
The relationship triangle total = mean × count, used forwards (find mean) and backwards (find a missing value)
A data set with its mean marked, shown falling between the lowest and highest values but equal to none of them
commonMisconceptions: Knowing only the add-and-divide rule with no sense of what the mean represents, so any non-standard problem fails
Believing that adding a data value of 0 does not change the mean (not seeing that the mean is influenced by every value and that the count also rises)
Being unable to find a missing value given the mean — re-averaging the known values instead of using total = mean × count
Expecting the mean to equal one of the data values, or placing it outside the range of the data
Dividing by the wrong count (e.g. ignoring a zero or a repeated value when counting the data points)

learn.summary: Teach 10-11 year olds to calculate the mean (add the values, divide by the count) AND interpret it as the fair-share/levelling value: what each data point would be if the total were shared equally. The central aim is to prevent the mean becoming an empty procedure. Build it as levelling/fair share (evening out towers of cubes to a common height) alongside the algorithm, then use two revealing non-transparent tasks — the reverse problem (find a missing value using total = mean \u00d7 count) and reasoning about how adding a value (including 0) shifts the mean. Reinforce the properties that let children sanity-check: the mean lies between the lowest and highest values, is influenced by every value, and need not equal any actual data value.

activities.title: Level the towers: the mean as fair share
feedback: If a child only restates 'you add them and divide' when asked what the mean tells us, point back to the levelled towers: 'if everyone scored the same, this is the score each would get.'
Mirror the algorithm (sum \u00f7 count) next to the levelled towers so the child sees the two give the same number.
Optional interactive version: let the child drag cubes between towers and watch a read-out show the running mean; a 'balance beam' number line can show the mean as the balancing point of the data.
activities.rationale: Grounding the algorithm in levelling/fair share gives the mean a meaning children can reason from, addressing the misconception of knowing only the bare rule.
sourceClaims: The mean is productively taught as 'fair share' / levelling — evening out the data so each shares the total equally — which grounds the algorithm in a meaning

Knowing the computational rule for the mean does not imply understanding; students with only computational knowledge make predictable errors on all but the most transparent problems, and some believe that adding a value of 0 does not change the mean (though the mean is influenced by every value)
learnerActions: Start with five towers of cubes at different heights (e.g. representing scores), choosing heights whose total is a multiple of 5 so whole cubes can be shared equally, and even them out by moving cubes from the tall towers onto the short ones until every tower is the same height.
State that this common height IS the mean — what each would be if the total were shared equally.
Compute sum \u00f7 count and confirm it equals the levelled height, so the fair-share meaning and the rule are seen as the same thing.
Answer 'if all five pupils had scored the same, what would each have scored?' and 'what does this mean value tell us about the scores?'
activities.intendedInsight: The mean is the value every data point would share if the total were distributed equally; the add-and-divide algorithm computes exactly this fair share, so the rule has a meaning rather than being an arbitrary procedure.

activities.title: The reverse problem: find the missing value
feedback: If the child adds 7+9+6+10 and divides by 4, or divides by 5, point out they have ignored that the mean already describes five scores: ask 'what must all five add up to if their mean is 8?'
Optional interactive version: fix the mean line, hide one tower's height, and let the child drag it up and down until the row levels — discovering the total is fixed at mean \u00d7 count.
Confirm success when the child computes the total first (8\u00d75=40) then subtracts the known 32 to get 8.
activities.rationale: The reverse problem cannot be solved by the add-and-divide rule alone, so it reveals whether a child owns the fair-share meaning rather than just a procedure.
sourceClaims: Knowing the computational rule for the mean does not imply understanding; students with only computational knowledge make predictable errors on all but the most transparent problems, and some believe that adding a value of 0 does not change the mean (though the mean is influenced by every value)
The mean is productively taught as 'fair share' / levelling — evening out the data so each shares the total equally — which grounds the algorithm in a meaning
learnerActions: Given a mean and all-but-one of the values (e.g. four of five spelling scores were 7, 9, 6 and 10; the mean of all five is 8), find the missing value.
Reconstruct the total using total = mean \u00d7 count (8 \u00d7 5 = 40), subtract the known values (40 \u2212 32 = 8) to recover the missing one.
Explain why re-averaging only the known four values is wrong — the mean refers to all five.
activities.intendedInsight: Because the mean is the total shared equally, the total is fixed at mean \u00d7 count; recovering a missing value means finding that total and subtracting what is known, not re-averaging the visible data.

activities.title: Does a zero change the mean?
feedback: If the child says 'you're only adding a zero so it stays the same', recompute with and without the 0 and highlight both that the 0 sits below the current (positive) mean and that the count changed too, so the mean falls.
Optional interactive version: an 'add a new pupil who scored 0' button so the mean visibly shifts and the count updates as the child predicts then watches.
Reinforce that the mean is influenced by every value, so adding a value above the current mean (like 100) moves it up while a value below it (like 0 here) moves it down.
activities.rationale: Directly confronts the documented belief that adding a 0 leaves the mean unchanged, by having the child predict and then recompute on a concrete positive-score case.
sourceClaims: Knowing the computational rule for the mean does not imply understanding; students with only computational knowledge make predictable errors on all but the most transparent problems, and some believe that adding a value of 0 does not change the mean (though the mean is influenced by every value)

Strauss & Bichler's conceptual properties of the average include: it lies between the extreme values, it is influenced by every value, it need not equal one of the values, and it can be a fraction with no physical counterpart — properties children find harder than the bare procedure
learnerActions: Start from a stated data set of positive test scores with a known mean (e.g. 72, 85, 90, 68, 95 with mean 82), predict what happens to the mean when a new value of 0 is added, then recompute to check.
Notice that both the total and the count change (here from 5 values to 6), and that the new 0 still counts as a data point.

State that, because the existing scores are positive, the current mean is positive, so the added 0 lies below it: the mean goes DOWN (e.g. 410 \u00f7 6 \u2248 68.3), pulled toward zero as part of the fair share.
Extend to an extreme value: predict then compute the effect of adding one more score of 100 to the stated set (which, being above the current mean, pulls the mean up).
activities.intendedInsight: Every value — including 0 — influences the mean, and adding a data point also increases the count; for positive scores an added 0 sits below the current mean and lowers it, so it does not leave the mean unchanged.

activities.title: Properties of the mean: sanity-checking an answer
feedback: If a child expects the mean to match one of the scores, show a clear example where it does not and tie it back to fair share.
If a child produces a mean outside the data range, prompt: 'can a fair share be bigger than the biggest value?'

Optional reference: tapping a data set to reveal its total, count and mean, with a note that the mean equals none of the values, can serve as a static check — though it cannot let the child test how a new value moves the mean.
activities.rationale: Knowing the properties lets children detect errors and accept that the mean need not equal a data value, which is harder than the bare procedure.
sourceClaims: Strauss & Bichler's conceptual properties of the average include: it lies between the extreme values, it is influenced by every value, it need not equal one of the values, and it can be a fraction with no physical counterpart — properties children find harder than the bare procedure
learnerActions: For a data set with its mean marked, confirm the mean lies between the lowest and highest values and check it is not greater than every score nor less than every score.
Point out a case where the mean equals none of the actual values (e.g. nobody scored 82, yet 82 is the mean) and explain why that is fine.
Given a computed mean, judge whether it is plausible by checking it falls within the data range.
Answer the counterexample 'could the mean ever be higher than every single score? Why or why not?'
activities.intendedInsight: The mean always lies between the lowest and highest values (inclusive) and need not equal any actual data value (it can even be a fraction with no physical counterpart), so a mean outside the data range signals a computation error.

activities.title: Scorable practice and self-check
feedback: For the zero item, confirm 'down' for the positive-score set and explain the 0 sits below the current mean and the count rises; correct 'stays the same' by recomputing.
For the reverse item, confirm success only when the child uses the total (mean \u00d7 count), not re-averaging.
Keep data sets small and the arithmetic clean so a wrong answer reflects reasoning, not a calculation slip.
activities.rationale: Recognition and short-answer items give a scorable check that targets the specific misconceptions, though they verify less than independent construction and reasoning.
learnerActions: Compute the mean of a small clean data set (fill-in-the-blank).
Solve a reverse item: 'four of five scores are…; the mean is 8; find the fifth.'
Answer a multiple-choice item: 'a new pupil scores 0 — does the mean go up, down, or stay the same?' (for a set of positive scores).
Spot an implausible mean: choose which proposed mean cannot be right because it falls outside the data range.
activities.intendedInsight: Calculating, interpreting, reversing and sanity-checking the mean can each be checked against a correct answer, catching the zero and missing-value errors.

constraints: The levelling/fair-share model and the algorithm must be presented as the same thing, not as two separate topics; always ask what the mean value tells us after computing.

A static annotated data set can label the mean and show it between the extremes, but it cannot let the child level the data or test how a new value moves the mean; use it as reference only, not as the main builder.
Quiz/recognition items give a scorable check but do not elicit independent construction or explanation; pair them with tasks where the child computes, reverses and explains in their own words.
Keep decimal addition and division reliable so procedural slips are not mistaken for conceptual gaps; have the child count the data points first and recheck the arithmetic.
An interactive levelling model is one good way to make the fair-share idea concrete, but cube towers and a number line on paper can carry the same meaning; do not treat any one medium as required.

State direction-of-change predictions against the stated data: for positive scores an added 0 lowers the mean and a value above the current mean raises it; do not present a direction as a rule detached from the data set.
The mean of a one-dimensional data set does not use a third spatial dimension, so a 3D representation adds nothing for this particular content.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic self-audit: 72+85+90+68+95 = 410, 410\u00f75 = 82 (correct). Reverse example: 7+9+6+10 = 32; mean 8 \u00d7 5 = 40; 40\u221232 = 8 (correct). Adding a 0 to the five values (mean 82) gives total 410 over 6 = ~68.3, so the mean falls (consistent with 'down' for positive scores).
The 'adding a 0 lowers the mean' claim is conditioned on positive scores (so the current mean is positive); it is not stated as an unconditional rule for arbitrary data.

The Year 6 statutory curriculum claim establishes only topic and age-appropriateness; it was not cited as support for any specific teaching principle, so it was removed from activity sourceClaims where it only matched the topic.

The legacy framing that an in-role dialogue 'adds no verification' and that a static image 'cannot teach the core of understanding' was softened: these media offer different affordances and limits rather than being universally incapable.

Optional interactive features (drag cubes, balance-beam number line, hide-a-tower reverse mode, add-a-0 button) are presented as examples that make the mechanism concrete, not as mandatory mechanisms.

probeDeeper: 'Your mean is 82 but nobody actually scored 82 — how can that be?' — probes that the mean need not equal a data value
'If all five pupils had scored the same, what would each have scored?' — surfaces the fair-share meaning
Counterexample: 'Could the mean ever be higher than every single score? Why or why not?' — tests the between-the-extremes property
'What happens to the mean if I add one more score of 100? Predict, then work it out.' — checks that every value influences the mean, on a fresh case
assess.correctAnswer: A correct performance: for (1) sums to 410 and divides by 5 to get 82, and describes 82 as a typical / fair-share score that need not equal any actual score; for (2) uses total = mean × count (8×5 = 40), subtracts the known 32, giving 8 — not re-averaging the four; for (3) recomputes and states the mean goes DOWN because the 0 counts and pulls it toward zero (the count also rises). Solving the reverse problem and reasoning correctly about the zero are the marks of conceptual mastery.

errorPatterns.pattern: Mean as bare rule: computes add-and-divide but cannot say what the mean represents, treating it as just the answer to a calculation
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach meaning via the vocabulary/fair-share prerequisite: level cube towers to a common height and ask 'if everyone scored the same, what would each score be?' so the mean carries a meaning, not just a rule
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (1) the child gets 82 but, asked what it tells us, restates 'you add them and divide' rather than describing a typical / fair-share score

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot reverse: given the mean and all-but-one values, re-averages the known values or divides by the wrong count instead of using total = mean × count
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach the mean as the total shared equally: establish total = mean × count on a levelling model, then subtract the known values to recover the missing one
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (2) the child adds 7+9+6+10 and divides by 4 (getting 8) or by 5, rather than computing the total (8×5=40) and subtracting 32 to get 8

errorPatterns.pattern: Zero doesn't count: believes adding a data value of 0 leaves the mean unchanged, not seeing that the mean is influenced by every value and that the count rises too
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront by recomputing with and without the 0 (and note the count changed from 5 to 6); every value, including 0, is part of the fair share
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (3) the child says the mean stays the same because 'you're only adding a zero', rather than recomputing to see it fall

errorPatterns.pattern: Arithmetic slip: uses the right method but makes a decimal addition or division error, or miscounts the data points, giving a wrong mean
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, do not reteach: have the child count the data points first and recheck the addition/division; the concept is intact, only the calculation slipped
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The method is sound (sum then divide by the correct count) but the total or the quotient is wrong

responseLevels.gap: Applies add-and-divide unreliably (divides by the wrong count) or not at all; treats the mean as a real data value and thinks adding a 0 leaves it unchanged
responseLevels.full: Computes the mean, interprets it as the fair-share / typical value that lies between the extremes and need not equal any score, solves the reverse problem via total = mean × count, and reasons correctly that adding a value (including 0) shifts it — transferring to a fresh data set
responseLevels.partial: Computes the mean of a plain list correctly and names it the average, but cannot solve the reverse missing-value problem and cannot explain what the mean represents or that it need not equal an actual value — has the rule, not the fair-share meaning

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set these tasks and WATCH how the child works, saying little. (1) 'Here are five test scores: 72, 85, 90, 68, 95. Work out the mean, and tell me what that number tells us about the scores.' (2) A reverse task: 'Four of five spelling scores were 7, 9, 6 and 10. The mean of all five was 8. What was the fifth score?' (3) 'A new pupil then scored 0 on the spelling test. Does the mean go up, down, or stay the same? Work it out.' (Set the task and WATCH — do not hint at total = mean × count or at what happens with the zero.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Task (1) alone cannot separate rule-following from understanding — both produce 82. Task (2) can only be solved by treating the mean as the total shared equally (total = mean × count); a child with only the add-and-divide rule re-averages the four values or divides by the wrong count. Task (3) directly exposes the well-documented belief that adding a 0 leaves the mean unchanged. The three together separate a child who owns the fair-share meaning from one who has only the procedure.

sources.source: Batanero, Godino, Vallecillos, Green & Holmes (1994), 'Errors and difficulties in understanding elementary statistical concepts'

sources.claim: The mean is productively taught as 'fair share' / levelling — evening out the data so each shares the total equally — which grounds the algorithm in a meaning

sources.claim: Year 6 pupils calculate and interpret the mean as an average (statutory statistics content for this age)

pedagogy.summary: At 8-9, children learn to match the GRAPH TYPE to the DATA TYPE: discrete data (separate categories, counted) belong in a bar chart with gaps between bars; continuous data (measured, changing over time — temperature through a day, plant height over weeks) belong in a time graph whose points are joined because values exist in between. The NC Year 4 step is presenting discrete and continuous data 'using appropriate graphical methods'. The load-bearing ideas are (1) the discrete/continuous distinction drives the representation, (2) a time graph's line carries values BETWEEN the plotted points, and (3) the vertical scale must be checked before judging how big a change is. Teaching should contrast the two graph types on real data and read time graphs both at and between points.
bestPractices: Decide the graph type from the data type: counted categories → bar chart (bars separated); measured-over-time → time graph (points joined)
Read time graphs both at plotted points AND between them, naming that the line shows continuous change (interpolation)
Always read the vertical scale before describing a change, so a steep-looking line isn't over-read
Contrast a bar chart and a time graph of related data side by side so the difference in what each shows is explicit
keyRepresentations: Bar chart with separated bars (discrete categories)
Time graph / line graph with joined points (continuous change)
Paired display: the same context shown both ways to expose which fits
Axis with a clearly marked, even vertical scale
commonMisconceptions: Chooses the wrong representation for the data type — separate bars for continuous time data, or joins discrete category bars into a line
Believes a time graph only tells us the values at the plotted points, not in between (misses continuity)
Reads a steep line as a big change without checking the vertical scale (misleading-scale effect)
Reads the shape of the line as a literal picture of the situation rather than as values against axes

learn.summary: For ages 8-9, learners decide which graph type fits which data type and read time graphs both at and between plotted points. Discrete data (counted, separate categories) belong in a bar chart with gaps between bars; continuous data are measured quantities, and when a measurement changes over time (temperature through a day, plant height over weeks) it fits a time/line graph whose points are joined because real values exist between them. Three load-bearing ideas: (1) the discrete/continuous distinction drives the choice of representation, (2) a joined line gives estimated values BETWEEN the plotted points (interpolation), which assumes the quantity changed fairly steadily between readings, and (3) the vertical scale must be read before judging how big a change is. Teaching contrasts the two graph types on related real data and reads time graphs at AND between points.

activities.title: Dual-view grapher: choose the graph that fits the data
feedback: If a learner joins the tops of the category (pet) bars: ask what a point halfway between cats and dogs would mean; since there is no pet 'between' cats and dogs, the joined line carries no meaning here — separated bars fit counted categories.

If a learner says the temperature at 10:30 cannot be known exactly, agree that it was not measured, then trace along the line between the 10:00 and 11:00 points and read an estimate there; name that temperature changes continuously, so in-between times do have values, and the line gives a sensible estimate if the temperature changed steadily between readings.
If a learner sorts first into counted-categories vs measured-over-time, confirm: counted → bars with gaps, measured-over-time → joined line.
activities.rationale: Contrasting the two graph types on related data and reading a time graph between points makes the discrete/continuous distinction and interpolation concrete. A draggable vertical guide reading any time (including between marks) is an optional interaction that makes continuity visible; a learner-chosen representation forces the data-type decision rather than recognising a given graph.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils interpret and present discrete and continuous data using appropriate graphical methods, including bar charts and time graphs, and begin to relate graphical representation to recording change over time
learnerActions: Take a data set and choose whether to show it as separated bars or a joined line.
For 'favourite pets' (counted categories, e.g. cats and dogs) choose bars with gaps; for 'classroom temperature through the day' choose a joined line.
When tempted to join category values, ask yourself: 'what would a point BETWEEN cats and dogs mean?' and notice there is no sensible answer.
For the temperature line, drag a vertical guide to estimate the value at a time that was never actually recorded, e.g. 10:30, between the plotted points.
Say out loud why the line makes sense for temperature but not for pet categories, using the words discrete and continuous.
activities.intendedInsight: A joined line only makes sense when in-between values are real — that is exactly what continuous data means; counted categories have no in-between, so they go in separated bars.

activities.title: Check the scale before calling a change 'big'
feedback: If a learner calls a change 'huge' from steepness while the axis spans only a few degrees: have them read the axis values and restate the change as an actual amount.
Show the same data on two axes; if the learner sees the lines differ, ask what actually changed (only the scale, not the data).
activities.rationale: Reading the vertical scale first guards against the misleading-scale effect; comparing stretched vs compressed axes of identical data makes the effect explicit.
sourceClaims: Students should be aware that changing the scale of the vertical axis affects the perception of growth — increasing the spacing between increments can make growth appear faster than it was
learnerActions: Look at a temperature line that appears steep and, before describing the change, read the numbers on the vertical axis.
Compare the same temperature data drawn on a stretched (widely spaced) vertical axis and on a compressed one; notice the line looks dramatic or gentle while the data is identical.
Optionally use a scale slider that stretches or shrinks the vertical axis of the same data to feel how the apparent size of the change changes.
State the actual size of the change in degrees, not just 'huge' from the steepness.
activities.intendedInsight: Steepness alone is misleading: the spacing of the vertical scale changes how big a change looks, so you must read the scale before judging the size of a change.

activities.title: Interpret a real time graph at and between points
feedback: If a learner plots plant-growth-over-weeks as unconnected bars, or draws a line through four fruit values, sort the data again as counted-categories vs measured-over-time and reconnect to the discrete/continuous vocabulary.
Probe: 'if I joined the tops of the fruit bars with a line, would the line mean anything?' to test the discrete/continuous boundary.
Probe: 'this line looks steep — what should you check before saying the temperature shot up?' to surface scale-checking.
activities.rationale: Interpreting on an actual time graph plus translating a real data table into the right chart together separate genuine understanding from surface graph-drawing: interpolating on continuous data and choosing bars for discrete data are the two discriminating moves.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils interpret and present discrete and continuous data using appropriate graphical methods, including bar charts and time graphs, and begin to relate graphical representation to recording change over time
learnerActions: Read a time graph of classroom temperature through one day: state the temperature at a marked time, and estimate it at an unmarked time such as 10:30 by reading between points.
Describe what a falling section after 3pm tells you about the situation (temperature getting cooler over time).
Then take a table of how many children chose each of four fruits and decide which graph to draw; draw separated bars against an even scale.
Explain in words why a joined line is right for temperature but a bar chart is right for the fruit choices.
activities.intendedInsight: Interpreting continuous data means estimating values between points and reading rising/falling as change over time; choosing bars for discrete categories and lines for measured-over-time shows the data type drives the representation.

activities.title: Annotated time graph as a reference scaffold
feedback: Use the annotations to confirm vocabulary, then move to a graph where you read an unmarked time yourself.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal annotation supports vocabulary and orientation. As a fixed reference it does not provide a dynamic read-out at an unmarked time or let the learner change the scale (a learner can still estimate between points by eye), so it should precede, not replace, interactive reading.
learnerActions: Tap parts of a static, annotated time graph to reveal what the axes, points and line mean.
Use it to recall the labels for a plotted point, the joined line (continuous change), and the vertical scale.
activities.intendedInsight: A labelled time graph helps name the parts, but as a fixed image it does not give a draggable, precise read-out at an unmarked time or let you restretch the vertical scale; a learner can still estimate a value between points by eye, while an interactive graph makes reading any time and testing scale effects directly manipulable.

constraints: The annotated-graph activity is a reference scaffold: a fixed graph can label the parts but does not provide a dynamic read-out for an unmarked value or let the learner restretch the scale, so pair it with activities where the learner reads between points and compares axes.
Choosing and constructing the representation must stay a learner action: recognising a pre-chosen graph does not elicit the independent decision of which graph fits the data type.
Keep real data types concrete (counted categories vs measured-over-time); the discrete/continuous distinction only lands when learners sort actual data, not abstract definitions.
Interactions such as a draggable vertical guide, a scale slider, or linked stretched/compressed axes are optional ways to make continuity and scale concrete, not required mechanisms.
Keep examples consistent within an activity: use favourite pets (cats/dogs) for the dual-view grapher's discrete case and the four-fruit table for the translating task, rather than blending them.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source listed conversation and 3D artefacts as poor fits with rationales like 'dialogue offers nothing to read' and '3D adds nothing'. These comparative/necessity claims are not established by the cited sources, so they were not carried into guidance as universal laws; the genuine point retained is only that this skill centres on reading and constructing graphs, and that recognition-only tasks do not elicit independent construction.

The source's 'ideal' framing that live manipulation is the best way to learn this is a catalog preference, not established by the cited sources; retained as an interactive proposal with stated affordances, not as proof of superiority.

The reference-scaffold limitation was narrowed: a fixed graph lacks a dynamic read-out and scale-restretching, but a learner can still estimate between-point values by eye — stating a fixed graph 'cannot interpolate' would overstate the limit and undercut the continuity principle.

The original candidate blended 'favourite fruits/pets' and contradicted itself ('value between two fruits' vs 'no fruit between cats and dogs'); this is kept corrected to use pets consistently in the grapher activity, with fruits reserved for the translating task.

probeDeeper: Ask 'why is a joined line right for temperature but not for favourite fruits?' to check the data-type reasoning
Counterexample tuned to this topic: 'we recorded the temperature at 10 and at 11 — can we say anything about 10:30? how?' to test continuity/interpolation
Ask 'this line looks steep — what should you check before saying the temperature shot up?' to surface scale-checking
Ask 'if I joined the tops of the fruit bars with a line, would the line mean anything?' to probe the discrete/continuous boundary
assess.correctAnswer: Interpreting: reads 10:30 by going BETWEEN the plotted points (interpolating) and reads the falling section as the temperature getting cooler over time. Translating: chooses a BAR chart for the discrete fruit categories (separated bars) — not a line — and draws it against an even scale.

errorPatterns.pattern: Chooses the wrong representation for the data type — draws a joined line for discrete categories, or separated bars for continuous time data
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort the data as counted-categories vs measured-over-time first; counted → bars with gaps, measured-over-time → joined line; reconnect to the discrete/continuous vocabulary
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child draws a line through the four fruit values, or plots plant-growth-over-weeks as unconnected bars

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes a time graph only tells the values at the plotted points, not between them (misses continuity)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace the line between two points and read the value there; name that the line shows the value changing continuously
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked the temperature at 10:30 (between marks) the child says it can't be known

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads a steep line as a big change without checking the vertical scale
errorPatterns.nextMove: Read the vertical scale first; compare the same data drawn on a stretched vs compressed axis
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child calls a change 'huge' from steepness while the axis spans only a few degrees

responseLevels.gap: Picks the wrong graph for the data type and reads a time graph only at marked points, ignoring scale
responseLevels.full: Chooses the representation from the data type, reads a time graph at AND between points, and checks the vertical scale before judging the size of a change
responseLevels.partial: Reads a time graph at points and knows bar=discrete/line=continuous when prompted, but doesn't interpolate or check the scale unprompted

assess.diagnosticPrompt: First: here is a time graph of the temperature in our classroom through one day — what was the temperature at 10:30, and what does the falling part after 3pm tell us? Then: here is a table of how many children chose each of four fruits — which kind of graph should you draw for THIS data, and draw it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands reads a time graph between points and picks the representation from the data type; a child who doesn't says the temperature at 10:30 is unknowable, or draws a joined line for the discrete fruit data. The two moves — interpolating on continuous data, and choosing bars for discrete — together separate real understanding from surface graph-drawing.
