pedagogy.summary: At age 9-10 children read and complete real information tables — bus and train timetables and two-way tables (e.g. favourite sport by gender) — and solve one- and two-step problems from them: find a departure time, work out a journey duration, complete a missing cell, compare two values. Two things carry the teaching. First, tracking a value to the intersection of the correct ROW and COLUMN, because dense timetables invite off-by-one-row/column reading. Second, and most characteristically, computing time DURATIONS correctly: children who read '10:50' and '11:20' tend to subtract the digits as if time were decimal (getting 0.70, or calling a 2:23 journey 'two point two three hours'), because minutes are base-60, not base-10. The remedy is to count on in minutes across the hour on a clock or number line, never to subtract clock readings as decimals. Keep every table anchored in a real purpose (catch the bus, plan the journey) so the numbers mean something.
bestPractices: Track every value to the ROW×COLUMN intersection explicitly — finger on the row, finger on the column, meet in the middle — to defeat off-by-one-row/column reading in dense timetables

Teach durations by COUNTING ON in minutes across the hour (10:50 → 11:00 is 10 min, → 11:20 is another 20, so 30 min), using an empty number line or clock face — never by subtracting clock readings as if decimals

Confront the time-as-decimal habit head-on: when a child says a journey takes 0.70 or 2.23 hours, use an analogue clock to show 60 minutes in an hour so the digits after the colon are seen as minutes, not tenths
Underline the question words ('how long', 'how many more', 'how much later') so children compute the DIFFERENCE/DURATION asked for rather than reading a single value off the table
Read two-way tables by naming what each cell, row total and column total MEANS ('this cell is girls who chose football; this end number is all the girls') before doing any arithmetic
Anchor tables in an authentic task — catch the 8:40 bus, work out if you make the connection — so reading is purposeful rather than mechanical
keyRepresentations: A real bus/train timetable grid (services in columns, stops in rows) — the canonical structure for this age
A two-way table (e.g. sport × gender) with row and column totals shown
An empty number line or clock face for counting on the minutes of a duration across the hour
A finger/ruler trace from row and column to their intersection cell
commonMisconceptions: Reading time as a decimal number: giving a journey duration as 0.70 or '2.23 hours' by subtracting or reading clock digits as base-10 rather than counting minutes in base-60
Reading off a single value when a difference or duration is asked ('how many more', 'how much longer') instead of computing it
Off-by-one-row/column reading: taking the value from an adjacent service or stop in a dense grid
In a two-way table, confusing a row/column TOTAL (a margin) with a single cell, or double-counting when categories overlap

learn.summary: For ages 9-10, teach children to read and complete real information tables — bus/train timetables and two-way tables (e.g. favourite sport by gender) — and to solve one- and two-step problems: find a departure time, compute a journey duration, complete a missing cell, compare two values. Two difficulties carry the teaching: tracking a value to the correct ROW×COLUMN intersection (dense grids invite off-by-one reading), and computing time DURATIONS by counting on in minutes across the hour rather than subtracting clock readings as if they were base-10 decimals. Keep every table anchored in an authentic purpose (catch the bus, plan the journey) so the numbers mean something.

activities.title: Live timetable with intersection highlighting
feedback: If the answer belongs to a neighbouring row or column, re-trace: one finger on the row, one on the column, and read only where they meet; use a ruler edge to isolate the row in a crowded timetable.
If a duration comes out as 0.70 or '70', re-count the jumps: to the next o'clock first (10:50→11:00 = 10 min), then past it (→11:20 = 20 min), total 30 minutes.

If the answer is only slightly out (e.g. a jump miscounted, or a boundary minute counted twice when counting minute by minute), the counting-on approach is likely sound — have them re-mark the jumps on a number line and re-add rather than reteaching the concept.
activities.rationale: Tracking to the intersection and counting minutes in base-60 are the two hardest parts of this skill, and making them felt through tracing and counting-on targets the specific off-by-one and time-as-decimal errors. Optional live highlighting and a minute-track are concrete ways to make the mechanism visible, not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: Children read digital/clock times as decimal numbers: from a bus timetable they compute a journey as '2.23' and say it takes 'two point two three hours', interpreting the digits after the point as a decimal fraction rather than minutes; the remedy is an analogue clock and discussing how many minutes are in an hour
learnerActions: Use a real bus/train timetable (often services in columns and stops in rows, but check the headings because layouts vary) to find when a named service reaches a named stop.

Track the stop-row with one finger and the service-column with the other, meeting at the intersecting cell. If a screen model is available, tapping a row and column can light up ONLY the intersecting cell so the off-by-one habit has nowhere to hide.

Find a journey duration by counting on in minutes across the hour: 10:50 → 11:00 is 10 minutes, → 11:20 is another 20, so 30 minutes. If a duration tool is available, drag a marker along a minute-track and watch it tick across the hour.
State out loud why you cannot simply subtract 11:20 − 10:50 and call it 0.70 — the digits after the colon are minutes out of 60, not tenths of an hour.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading tables is a doing skill on a 2D grid: values live at a row×column intersection, and time durations are counted in minutes across the hour, not subtracted as decimals.

activities.title: Confront time-as-decimal with an analogue clock
feedback: If the child still subtracts digits, return to the clock: show the 60 minutes in the hour and count the jumps to and past the o'clock.
Check the 14:45 + 40 min answer: 14:45→15:00 is 15 min, then 25 more to 15:25.
Check the 'next service 25 minutes later' answer: from 10:50, count 10:50→11:00 is 10 min, then 15 more to 11:15, so it leaves at 11:15.
activities.rationale: The source names reading clock times as decimals as a known misconception and names the analogue clock plus 'how many minutes in an hour' as the remedy, so this activity confronts the habit directly and rehearses it across the hour in both directions.
sourceClaims: Children read digital/clock times as decimal numbers: from a bus timetable they compute a journey as '2.23' and say it takes 'two point two three hours', interpreting the digits after the point as a decimal fraction rather than minutes; the remedy is an analogue clock and discussing how many minutes are in an hour
learnerActions: When a journey duration has been found by subtracting clock times as if they were decimals (e.g. 11:20 − 10:50 written as 0.70, or '70 minutes'), look at an analogue clock and state how many minutes are in one hour (60).
Find the correct duration in minutes by counting on from the start time to the end time across the hour on the clock face or an empty number line (e.g. 10:50 → 11:00 → 11:20 = 30 minutes).
Try a journey that crosses the hour in the other direction too — e.g. a train leaving at 14:45 with a 40-minute journey: when does it arrive?
Combine a lookup with a forward duration: if the next service is 25 minutes later than the one shown (say it leaves at 10:50), count on to find its departure time rather than adding digits.
activities.intendedInsight: The digits after the colon are minutes out of 60, not tenths of an hour, so durations must be counted in minutes, not read as decimals.

activities.title: Complete and interpret a two-way table
feedback: If the child reports a single cell (e.g. the number of girls who chose football) when a difference was asked, re-read the underlined 'how many MORE' and point to both values before subtracting.

If a margin total is confused with a single cell, name each number's meaning again before arithmetic. (In a sport-by-gender table the categories do not overlap; keep the double-counting caution for tables where a child could be counted in more than one category.)
activities.rationale: The source names reading off a single value when a difference is asked as a misconception, with underlining the question words as the remedy; naming cells vs totals first targets margin-vs-cell confusion.
sourceClaims: When asked 'how many more' from a chart/table, children read off a single value (e.g. the number one child has) instead of computing the difference; underlining the question words 'how many more' helps direct attention to the required operation
learnerActions: Before any arithmetic, name what each cell, row total and column total MEANS (e.g. 'this cell is girls who chose football; this end number is all the girls').

Complete a missing cell in a two-way table of favourite sport by gender from the given data, checking the filled cell against its row and column totals. If a screen model is available, row and column totals can update live so a filled cell can be checked against its margins.
Answer a 'how many more' question — underline the question words, point to BOTH values, and show the subtraction.
Contrast with a plain 'how many' question so the difference between reading one value and computing a difference is explicit.
activities.intendedInsight: A cell, a row total and a column total mean different things; 'how many more' asks for a difference between two values, not a single read-off.

activities.title: Scorable checks on lookups, durations and cell completion
feedback: A cross-the-hour duration item surfaces decimal subtraction (0.70/'70') versus a correct 30 minutes — if wrong, return to counting on across the hour.
A 'how many more' item surfaces reading a single value instead of a difference — if wrong, point to both values and subtract.
activities.rationale: Lookups, durations and complete-the-cell tasks give a scorable check of the reading procedure; purposely including a cross-the-hour duration and a 'how many more' item catches the two named misconceptions. This format checks a recognition/completion response and does not by itself elicit the child's independent counting-on method, so pair it with the watched performance task.
sourceClaims: Children read digital/clock times as decimal numbers: from a bus timetable they compute a journey as '2.23' and say it takes 'two point two three hours', interpreting the digits after the point as a decimal fraction rather than minutes; the remedy is an analogue clock and discussing how many minutes are in an hour

When asked 'how many more' from a chart/table, children read off a single value (e.g. the number one child has) instead of computing the difference; underlining the question words 'how many more' helps direct attention to the required operation
learnerActions: Find a departure time from a shown timetable (selecting from options).
Complete 'the journey from A to B takes ___ minutes', including at least one item where the arrival crosses the hour (e.g. 10:50→11:20).
Complete or fill a missing cell in a two-way table.
Answer one 'how many more' item that requires a difference, not a single value.
activities.intendedInsight: The reading-and-calculating procedure can be checked against items deliberately chosen to catch time-as-decimal and read-off-instead-of-difference errors.

activities.title: Annotated worked-example timetable (scaffold)
feedback: Once the parts are named confidently, move to a table the child completes and calculates on themselves — this annotated example lets the child recognise structure but does not itself let them perform a duration calculation or complete a table.
activities.rationale: A static annotated grid can label structure and reveal what a cell means, which is a useful orientation, but it pre-bakes answers and does not elicit the duration or completion skill. It is a worked example only, not a substitute for the child doing the calculation.
learnerActions: Study a labelled timetable grid where the structure is annotated: services vs stops and what a single time cell means (and, on a two-way table, a single cell vs a row or column total), with tap-to-reveal explanations of what each part means.
Use it to rehearse naming the parts before doing your own lookups and durations on a live table.
activities.intendedInsight: Understanding the grid structure (services, stops and cells in a timetable; cells and totals in a two-way table) supports accurate reading before the child performs lookups and duration calculations independently.

constraints: Durations must be taught by counting on in minutes across the hour (to the o'clock, then past it) on a clock face or empty number line — never by subtracting clock readings as if they were base-10 decimals.

A static annotated/tap-to-reveal timetable is a worked example only: it orients the child to structure but does not itself let them perform a duration calculation or complete a table, which are the actual skills.
Scorable multiple-choice/fill items check recognition and completion and do not by themselves elicit the child's independent counting-on method; pair them with a watched performance task.
Keep every table anchored in an authentic purpose (catch the bus, make the connection) so reading is meaningful rather than mechanical.
Prerequisites may need reteaching: time conversion/minutes-in-an-hour for duration errors, and careful grid reading for off-by-one-row/column errors.
The double-counting caution applies only to tables where a child could fall into more than one category; a mutually-exclusive table (e.g. sport by gender) does not overlap.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row ranked a conversational format and a third spatial dimension as poor fit for this flat-grid skill and described them as 'adds nothing'. They are dropped rather than asserted as universal pedagogical laws, since the catalog ranking does not establish comparative efficacy or necessity; a flat grid simply does not require a third spatial dimension for this content.

Arithmetic check: 10:50→11:00 = 10 min, →11:20 = 20 min, total 30 min (correct); 14:45 + 40 min = 15:25 (correct); 10:50 + 25 min = 11:15 (correct). The erroneous '0.70'/'70' results are retained only as the misconception to confront, never as valid answers.
Efficacy of optional live-highlight and minute-track interactions is not source-established; they are offered with 'if available'/'may help' wording.

The Year 5 curriculum source claim establishes that completing/reading/interpreting tables is appropriate content for this age but does not evidence any individual activity's mechanism rationale, so it is not cited within the activities; its placement support is reflected in the summary context only.

probeDeeper: 'The bus leaves at 10:50 and arrives at 11:20 — show me how you worked out the 30 minutes.' — forces the method into the open
'A train leaves at 14:45 and the journey is 40 minutes — when does it arrive?' — transfer across the hour in the other direction
'What does this number at the end of the row mean?' (a row total) — probes cell-vs-total understanding
'If the next bus is 25 minutes later than this one, what time does it leave?' — combines reading with a duration in a fresh direction
assess.correctAnswer: A correct performance: for (1) the child tracks the correct row and column to their intersection and reads the right time; for (2) they compute the duration by counting on in minutes across the hour (10:50→11:20 = 30 minutes), not by subtracting the digits; for (3) they complete the cell using the right row and column (checking against a total if available) and give the DIFFERENCE between girls and boys, not a single value. Tracking to the intersection and counting minutes in base-60 are the marks of mastery.

errorPatterns.pattern: Time-as-decimal: computes a duration by subtracting or reading clock times as base-10 numbers — giving 0.70 for 10:50 to 11:20, or calling a journey '2.23 hours' — because minutes are treated as tenths rather than sixtieths
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach duration on the time-conversion prerequisite: use an analogue clock and empty number line, establish 60 minutes in an hour, and count on 10:50→11:00→11:20 so the child sees the answer as minutes, not tenths
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (2) the child subtracts the digits (11:20 − 10:50 → '70' or '0.70'/'0.30') or reports the duration as a decimal number of hours, rather than counting minutes across the hour

errorPatterns.pattern: Read-off-instead-of-difference: when asked 'how many more' or 'how much longer', reads a single value straight off the table rather than computing the difference between two
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront in place: underline the question words 'how many MORE', and have the child point to BOTH values and show the subtraction; contrast with a plain 'how many' question to make the difference explicit
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the 'how many more girls than boys' part of task (3), the child states the number of girls who chose football (a single cell) instead of subtracting the boys' value

errorPatterns.pattern: Off-by-one-row/column reading: in a dense grid, takes the value from an adjacent service or stop — the correct kind of value but from the wrong intersection
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach careful grid reading on the tables prerequisite: track the row with one finger and the column with the other and meet at the intersection; use a ruler/edge to isolate the row in a crowded timetable
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (1) the child gives a plausible but wrong time that belongs to the neighbouring column/row, without tracking row and column to their meeting point

errorPatterns.pattern: Counting-on slip: uses the right count-on method for a duration but miscounts the minutes (e.g. counts the hour boundary twice), giving an answer a few minutes out
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, do not reteach: have them re-mark the jumps on the number line (to the o'clock, then past it) and re-add; the concept is intact, only the count slipped
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (2) the child's method is sound — counting on across the hour — but the total is off by a few minutes

responseLevels.gap: Cannot reliably find a departure time (reads the wrong row/column), and computes durations by treating clock times as decimals
responseLevels.full: Tracks values to the correct row×column intersection, computes durations by counting on in minutes across the hour, finds differences, completes and uses two-way table totals, and transfers the same reading to a fresh timetable unprompted
responseLevels.partial: Reads individual departure times and completes given cells correctly, but computes durations by decimal subtraction, or reads off a single value when a difference/duration is asked — reads the data but not between it

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put a real bus or train timetable (services in columns, several stops in rows) and a partly-completed two-way table (e.g. favourite sport by gender, with some cells and one total missing) in front of the child. Set these tasks and WATCH how they do them, saying little: (1) 'Find the time the 9:15 service reaches [named stop].' (2) 'How long does the journey from [stop A] to [stop B] take on that service?' — choose stops where the arrival crosses the hour (e.g. 10:50 to 11:20). (3) 'Fill in the missing cell in this table, and tell me how many MORE girls than boys chose football.' (Set the task and WATCH — do not model the duration method or point to the right cell.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Task (2) is chosen to cross the hour, so a child treating time as decimal produces a visibly wrong duration (0.70, or '70') while a child counting on gives 30 minutes — the two reason to different answers on the same question. Task (3) pairs a straight lookup with a 'how many more', separating a child who reads the data from one who reads between it; and the two-way structure exposes row/column-total confusion that a single lookup would hide.

sources.claim: Children read digital/clock times as decimal numbers: from a bus timetable they compute a journey as '2.23' and say it takes 'two point two three hours', interpreting the digits after the point as a decimal fraction rather than minutes; the remedy is an analogue clock and discussing how many minutes are in an hour
sources.source: Fen Rivers Academy / The Bridge Trust, 'Misconceptions in Mathematics' (Measurement section)

sources.claim: When asked 'how many more' from a chart/table, children read off a single value (e.g. the number one child has) instead of computing the difference; underlining the question words 'how many more' helps direct attention to the required operation
sources.source: Fen Rivers Academy / The Bridge Trust, 'Misconceptions in Mathematics' (Statistics section)

sources.claim: Year 5 pupils complete, read and interpret information in tables, including timetables (statutory statistics content for this age)

pedagogy.summary: Measuring length with units means covering the object from end to end with same-size units laid with no gaps or overlaps, and reporting the COUNT of those units as the length (CCSS Progression). Two ideas must come together: the units must be identical in size, and they must tile the whole span (endpoint to endpoint) without gaps or overlaps. The classic obstacle is that children treat the task as 'put some objects along it and count them' — counting discrete objects rather than measuring a continuous length — so they leave gaps, mix unit sizes, or start partway along, and still confidently read off a number. Inhelder, Sinclair and Bovet's matches task captures it: children called a row of 6 short matches 'longer' than 5 long ones because it had more units.
bestPractices: Insist units are laid flush end to end, filling the object from one endpoint to the other with no gaps and no overlaps — make full coverage the rule, not decoration
Use a mixed-up puppet who leaves gaps, overlaps units, or starts in the middle, so children diagnose and fix the error (self-checking beats being told)

Confront the same-size-unit principle directly: measure one object with big clips and again with small clips, or run the matches demonstration, so 'more units' is seen NOT to mean 'longer' unless the units match
Emphasise starting flush at one end and that the length is the number of units that SPAN the object, not just the units you happened to place
Ask 'what are you counting?' — the answer is length-units — and count the units (spaces), not the marks or junctions where units meet
Bridge to rulers later by having children build a unit ruler from copies of one unit, so the ruler is understood as iterated units rather than a strip of numerals
keyRepresentations: A book with same-size paper clips laid end to end along it, flush at the start, no gaps
A mixed-up puppet's row with visible gaps/overlaps for the child to correct
Two rows of equal total length — few long units vs many short units — to break 'more units = longer' (the matches task)
A home-made unit ruler built by iterating copies of a single unit
commonMisconceptions: Leaving gaps or overlaps between units but still counting them and reporting a length
Using different-sized units and treating the counts as comparable — concluding the object with MORE units is longer regardless of unit size
Not spanning the whole object — starting the first unit inset from the edge, or stopping before the far end, then counting
Counting the marks/junctions or endpoints rather than the units themselves, producing an off-by-one length

learn.summary: Teaches length measurement as tiling an object end to end with identical units laid flush, no gaps or overlaps, and reporting the COUNT of those units as the length. Two load-bearing ideas must hold together: units are the same size, and they fill the whole span from one endpoint to the other. The core obstacle is treating measurement as 'put some objects down and count them' — so children leave gaps, mix unit sizes, or start partway along and still confidently read off a number. The Inhelder/Sinclair/Bovet matches task captures it: children called a row of 6 short matches 'longer' than 5 long ones because it had more units.

activities.title: Measure a book with paper clips, filling the whole span
feedback: If gaps are left, highlight the uncovered stretch: 'this bit wasn't measured — the clips don't cover all of the book yet'

If the first clip starts inset from the edge or the last stretch is left uncovered, prompt: 'start right at one end and keep going to the other end — the length is the number of clips that SPAN the book'; if the leftover bit is shorter than one clip, agree it is 'about' or 'a bit more than' that many clips
When the span is fully tiled flush with no gaps or overlaps, confirm the count is now an honest length: the number of clips that cover the book end to end
For the home-made ruler, point out that each mark is just where one unit ends and the next begins
activities.rationale: Gaps, overlaps and short spanning are errors of action; letting the child lay and adjust real units and check coverage with a finger makes 'fill the whole length' a rule they enforce rather than are told. An optional interactive version can make gaps glow and withhold a settled count until the span is fully covered, so the consequence of a gap is felt immediately. Building a ruler from iterated copies bridges to standard tools as units-in-a-row.
sourceClaims: Measuring length is choosing a unit and iterating it end to end alongside the object; the length is the number of units required to go from one end to the other WITHOUT gaps or overlaps, using SAME-SIZE units. In the Inhelder/Sinclair/Bovet matches task, children called a row of 6 shorter matches longer than a row of 5 longer matches because it had more units — counting units while ignoring that the units differed in size; first graders can learn that units must be the same size. Students should count the length-units, not the end-points, and learn that '1' on a ruler represents the space to the first mark, not the mark itself.

At the End-to-End Length Measurer level a child lays units end to end to measure an object but may not recognise the need for equal-length units; activities challenge children to fill lengths from endpoint to endpoint without gaps or overlaps, and because children are often not concerned with accuracy the best activities are self-checking (e.g. a mixed-up puppet who makes gap/overlap mistakes for children to correct).

KS1 pupils should measure and begin to record lengths/heights and choose and use appropriate standard units to measure length to the nearest appropriate unit using rulers, developing from measuring with units laid along an object.
learnerActions: Lay identical paper clips along a book, starting flush at one end, so they continue end to end to the far end with no gaps and no overlaps
Run a finger along the book from the very start to the very end to check that the clips cover ALL of it

Report the length as the number of clips that span the book; if the last clip sticks out past the end or a small bit is left that is shorter than a clip, say 'about' or 'a bit more than' that many clips
Repair a row that someone else laid with obvious gaps or overlaps, nudging the clips flush until the whole span is tiled
Build a small ruler by snapping copies of a single clip into a row, to see that a ruler is just units lined up
activities.intendedInsight: A length is the number of equal units that completely fill an object from end to end; gaps, overlaps, or a row that starts inset mean the count does not yet report the true length.

activities.title: Fix the mixed-up puppet's measurement
feedback: If the child accepts a gappy row's count, point to the gap: 'is every bit of the pencil covered? the clips skip this part, so the count isn't the whole length'
Praise diagnosing the specific error ('there's a gap here', 'these overlap', 'it starts too late') over simply restating a number
After repair, have the child re-run the finger-sweep to confirm full coverage
activities.rationale: Self-checking against a deliberately wrong model is better than being told the rule, because children are often untroubled by inaccuracy; diagnosing another's error externalises the principle and makes the child the checker. A puppet or a pre-laid row the child must judge both serve this.
sourceClaims: At the End-to-End Length Measurer level a child lays units end to end to measure an object but may not recognise the need for equal-length units; activities challenge children to fill lengths from endpoint to endpoint without gaps or overlaps, and because children are often not concerned with accuracy the best activities are self-checking (e.g. a mixed-up puppet who makes gap/overlap mistakes for children to correct).
learnerActions: Look at a row laid by a 'mixed-up' puppet that has visible gaps, overlapping units, or units that start in the middle
Explain what the puppet did wrong
Re-lay the units correctly so they fill the span flush, end to end, with no gaps or overlaps, and give the corrected length
Judge a stated count (e.g. 'I measured this pencil and got 6') against a row that has an obvious gap, and say whether the number is right
activities.intendedInsight: A count is only a length when the units completely tile the span; spotting and fixing gaps/overlaps is the child's job, not something to accept on trust.

activities.title: Does 'more units' mean 'longer'? The mixed-size challenge
feedback: If the child says the object with more (smaller) units is longer, lay the two measurements side by side so the equal spans are visible: the object didn't change, only the size of the unit did
If the child mixes big and small clips, ask them to lay one measurement in equal units and compare: 'which count can we trust, and why?'
Confirm the key idea when stated: counts can only be compared when the units are the same size
activities.rationale: Directly confronting the same-size-unit principle by measuring one object with two unit sizes, and by building the wrong mixed count then contrasting it with an equal-unit measure, targets the exact misconception that 'more units = longer'. The matches task is a classic research demonstration of this error.
sourceClaims: Measuring length is choosing a unit and iterating it end to end alongside the object; the length is the number of units required to go from one end to the other WITHOUT gaps or overlaps, using SAME-SIZE units. In the Inhelder/Sinclair/Bovet matches task, children called a row of 6 shorter matches longer than a row of 5 longer matches because it had more units — counting units while ignoring that the units differed in size; first graders can learn that units must be the same size. Students should count the length-units, not the end-points, and learn that '1' on a ruler represents the space to the first mark, not the mark itself.
learnerActions: Measure one object with large clips, then measure the SAME object again with small clips, and compare the two counts
Measure a second object with a jumbled mix of big and small clips, then lay equal-size clips beside it
Answer: 'I measured this ribbon with big clips and got 4, and with little clips I got 8 — did the ribbon get longer? Why did the numbers change?'
Answer: 'Could I measure this with a mix of big and little clips? Why not?'
Optionally run the matches version: compare a row of a few long matches with a row of many short matches that cover the same distance
activities.intendedInsight: More units does NOT mean longer when the units are different sizes; the same object gives a bigger count with smaller units without getting any longer, and mixing unit sizes within one measurement makes the count fail to report a length because each unit covers a different amount.

activities.title: Count the units, not the joins
feedback: If the child counts the points where clips meet (or the clip ends), ask 'what are you counting — the clips, or the joins between them?' and have them touch each clip once
Treat this as a counting slip to tighten, not a conceptual gap — the child who makes it still understands coverage and equal units
Link forward: on a ruler, the number 1 is written at the end of the first unit; it tells us one whole unit has been covered from the 0 end, so we count the spaces covered, not the tick marks
activities.rationale: Distinguishing units from junctions prevents a common off-by-one error and lays groundwork for reading a ruler, where the number at each tick mark tells how many whole units lie between 0 and that mark, so counting tick marks (including 0) gives one too many. This is a precision/counting refinement rather than a reteach of the core concept.
sourceClaims: Measuring length is choosing a unit and iterating it end to end alongside the object; the length is the number of units required to go from one end to the other WITHOUT gaps or overlaps, using SAME-SIZE units. In the Inhelder/Sinclair/Bovet matches task, children called a row of 6 shorter matches longer than a row of 5 longer matches because it had more units — counting units while ignoring that the units differed in size; first graders can learn that units must be the same size. Students should count the length-units, not the end-points, and learn that '1' on a ruler represents the space to the first mark, not the mark itself.
learnerActions: After laying clips along an object, state the count and then point to each thing being counted
Count the units (the clips/spaces), touching each one once, rather than the points where units meet or the end marks
Check a row where the count might be off by one: 'you counted 7 — point to each thing you counted'
activities.intendedInsight: The length is the number of units (the spaces covered), not the number of marks or junctions where units meet; counting the joins gives an off-by-one answer.

activities.title: Pick the correct measurement (recognition check)
feedback: For a chosen gappy or overlapping row, prompt the child to explain whether the whole object is covered
For a mixed-unit distractor, ask whether the units are all the same size and why that matters

If the child says the row with more short units is longer, align the two rows end to end to show the spans match — the object is the same length; only the unit size differs, so the bigger count does not tell us which is longer
When the valid row is chosen, have the child state the two reasons it is valid: equal units AND full end-to-end coverage
activities.rationale: Choosing among correct and flawed rows and counting spanning units checks the concept efficiently. This recognition format confirms whether a child can judge a measurement but does not by itself show they can lay and adjust units independently, so pair it with the hands-on tasks above.
learnerActions: From several rows laid along an object, choose the one that measures it correctly, where distractors have gaps, overlaps, or mixed-size units
Count the units spanning an object and give the number
Compare two rows that cover the SAME span — a few long units versus many short units — and judge whether the row with more (shorter) units is actually longer, explaining your reasoning
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising a valid measurement means checking for full coverage, no gaps/overlaps, and equal units; and when two rows cover the same span, a bigger count made of smaller units does not mean the object is longer.

constraints: This skill is for roughly ages 6–7 (KS1 / first grade); the goal is non-standard units laid end to end, bridging toward rulers later, not yet fluent ruler reading.

The central evidence is the child actually laying units and counting; recognition-only tasks (choosing the correct row) confirm judgement but do not elicit the independent construction and adjustment of a tiled measurement, so they are a check, not a substitute.

A labelled static picture can show why a gappy or mixed row is wrong on tap, but it cannot let the child lay and adjust units; the corrective action stays demonstrated rather than practised, so use it only as a supporting scaffold.

An interactive drag-to-tile tool that flags gaps/overlaps and withholds a settled count is one effective way to make the consequence of a gap immediate; the same learning is achievable with real clips and a finger-sweep check. These are optional illustrations of the mechanism, not a required medium.
Measuring units along an object is a planar task; a 3D handling environment is not needed and adds handling cost without sharpening the gaps/overlaps/equal-unit ideas.
Keep real materials (paper clips, matches, ribbon, books) and physical or screen tiling as approximations of the same idea; neither is universally necessary.

When comparing lengths by their counts, hold the unit size fixed: a bigger count with the same-size unit means longer, but a bigger count made of smaller units on the same span does not. The counts as numbers can still be compared (8 is more than 4); they just do not show which length is longer unless the units are the same size.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support general teaching principles, not that these specific activities were tested.
One source (UK National Curriculum KS1) was marked verified:false in the original row; treat its claim as unconfirmed even where it is cited to support the bridge toward rulers.

Original diagnostic guidance warns against demonstrating before setting tasks when assessing; teaching activities here deliberately include modelling and feedback — keep assessment separate from instruction so a 'watch first' diagnostic remains valid.

The original artefact notes asserted that a static image 'cannot' let the child practise and that a conversation 'cannot render' the measurement; these have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements rather than universal claims about what a medium can teach.

The recognition activity's few-long-vs-many-short comparison is framed so that both equal-span rows are valid measures with their own same-size units; the item asks whether more units means longer (it does not), not which single row is 'valid'.
The mixed-unit reteach in the source links a prerequisite micro-topic ID for unit-size understanding; that routing is an assessment concern and is not reproduced as a learner instruction here.

probeDeeper: 'Run your finger along the book from the very start to the very end — did the clips cover ALL of it?' (surfaces gaps / short spanning)
Counterexample: 'I measured this ribbon with big clips and got 4, and with little clips I got 8. Did the ribbon get longer? Why did the numbers change?' (tests the equal-unit / unit-size idea)
'Could I measure this with a mix of big and little clips? Why not?' (probes the same-size principle directly)
'You counted 7. Point to each thing you counted.' (checks units vs junctions, catching off-by-one)
assess.correctAnswer: (1) Lays identical clips end to end, flush at one end of the book, with no gaps or overlaps, spanning the whole book, and states the length as the number of clips. (2) Uses only same-size clips (or points out that the sizes must match) and explains that mixing sizes makes the counts unfair. (3) Says the gappy measure is wrong because the clips do not cover the whole pencil with no gaps — the count only gives the length when the units fully tile the span.

errorPatterns.pattern: Leaves gaps or overlaps between units but still counts them and reports a length
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the mixed-up puppet who leaves gaps for the child to fix; make 'fill the whole length, no gaps, no overlaps' the explicit rule; have the child run a finger along to check for uncovered bits.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task 1 spaces clips out with gaps or overlaps them, then counts and gives a number; on task 3 accepts the gappy '6'

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses different-sized units and treats the counts as comparable — more units is taken to mean longer regardless of unit size
errorPatterns.nextMove: Run the matches/mixed-clip demonstration — measure one object with big then small units and contrast; establish that units must be the same size for counts to mean anything. Reteach measuring with consistent units.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task 2 mixes big and small clips; or judges the object measured with more (smaller) units to be longer; untroubled by unequal units

errorPatterns.pattern: Does not span the whole object — starts the first unit inset from the edge, or stops before the far end, then counts
errorPatterns.nextMove: Start flush at one endpoint and continue to the other; the length is the number of units that SPAN the object end to end — mark the two endpoints first.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Begins clips partway in or leaves the last stretch uncovered, then reports the count as the length

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts the marks/junctions or endpoints rather than the units, giving an off-by-one length
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, do not reteach: ask 'what are you counting?' — the units, not the joins; touch each unit once as it is counted. This is a counting-slip to tighten, not a conceptual gap.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Counts the points where clips meet (or the clip ends) instead of the clips, arriving one too many or too few

responseLevels.gap: Places units with gaps/overlaps or mixes sizes and counts them anyway; treats measuring as 'put some clips and count', accepting a gappy or mixed measure.
responseLevels.full: Lays identical units flush from one endpoint to the other with no gaps or overlaps, reports the length as the number of units spanning the object, rejects mixed-size units, and explains that gaps, overlaps or unequal units make the count fail to measure the length.
responseLevels.partial: Lays same-size units end to end and counts correctly when the setup is careful, but leaves occasional gaps, starts inset, or does not insist on equal units — and cannot yet explain why gaps or mixed units make the count wrong.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set tasks and WATCH — do not demonstrate first. (1) Give the child a book and a pile of identical paper clips: 'Measure how long the book is.' Watch how they place the clips and how they report the length. (2) Offer a bin that ALSO contains larger and smaller clips mixed in, and ask them to measure a second strip — do they insist on same-size units, or mix them? (3) Show a row you have laid yourself along a pencil with an obvious GAP in the middle (and count aloud a number): 'I measured this pencil and got 6. Is that right?' Watch whether the child spots that gaps/overlaps or mixed units make the count wrong.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A carefully set-up single measurement can be passed by rote. The mixed-unit bin and the pre-laid gappy row force the two load-bearing ideas: a child who is merely counting objects will happily mix unit sizes and accept a gappy row, whereas a child who understands measurement insists on equal units and full end-to-end coverage. Accepting the gappy '6' or mixing clip sizes is the tell.

sources.claim: Measuring length is choosing a unit and iterating it end to end alongside the object; the length is the number of units required to go from one end to the other WITHOUT gaps or overlaps, using SAME-SIZE units. In the Inhelder/Sinclair/Bovet matches task, children called a row of 6 shorter matches longer than a row of 5 longer matches because it had more units — counting units while ignoring that the units differed in size; first graders can learn that units must be the same size. Students should count the length-units, not the end-points, and learn that '1' on a ruler represents the space to the first mark, not the mark itself.
sources.source: Progressions for the Common Core State Standards — K–5 Geometric Measurement (accessible ISBE copy)

sources.claim: At the End-to-End Length Measurer level a child lays units end to end to measure an object but may not recognise the need for equal-length units; activities challenge children to fill lengths from endpoint to endpoint without gaps or overlaps, and because children are often not concerned with accuracy the best activities are self-checking (e.g. a mixed-up puppet who makes gap/overlap mistakes for children to correct).
sources.source: Sarama & Clements, LearningTrajectories.org — Measurement: Length (End-to-End Length Measurer)

sources.claim: KS1 pupils should measure and begin to record lengths/heights and choose and use appropriate standard units to measure length to the nearest appropriate unit using rulers, developing from measuring with units laid along an object.
sources.source: UK Department for Education — National Curriculum in England: Mathematics (KS1 Measurement)

pedagogy.summary: At 9-10 representation fluency is expected across the full spread — real situations, bar models, number lines, multi-digit multiplication, and the fraction–decimal–percentage trio — with the child explaining the connections (CCSS MP2). The signature demand is seeing 0.35, 35/100 and 35% as ONE quantity shown three ways: the IES fractions guide recommends a single representation (a hundredths grid, or one number line with fractions above and decimals/percents below) so the equivalence is a fact of magnitude, not three separate conversion rules. Percentage is the fresh hazard — 'per cent' means 'parts per hundred', and a child who has not internalised that treats 35% as just the number 35 or an unmoored decimal. Scaling problems (bar model ↔ multiplication equation) and reading quantities off a line graph into an equation round out the level; the recurring failure is grabbing visible numbers without asking what quantity each representation is actually showing.
bestPractices: Show 0.35, 35/100 and 35% on ONE representation — a hundredths grid or a single number line with fractions above and decimals/percents below — so equivalence is seen as the same magnitude (IES Rec 2, 4th action step)
Ground percentage in 'parts per hundred' with the hundredths grid before any conversion rule, so 35% is a quantity, not a bare number
Use bar models to expose scaling/multiplicative structure and map each part to the multiplication equation (NCETM structure)
For line graphs, require the child to say what quantity each reading is before choosing an operation — e.g. a difference needs subtraction (MP2 meaning-of-quantities)
Translate in every direction and insist on 'what does each number represent?' at each step
keyRepresentations: Hundredths grid linking fraction, decimal and percentage of the same shaded amount
Single number line carrying fractions, decimals and percentages at shared points
Bar model for scaling/proportion mapped to a multiplication equation
Line graph read into a subtraction/other equation for a difference or change
commonMisconceptions: Treats 0.35, 35/100 and 35% as three different things rather than one magnitude shown three ways
Does not hold 'per cent = parts per hundred', so reads 35% as the number 35 (or a decimal with no meaning)
Grabs both readings off a line graph and adds them instead of asking which quantity and which operation the situation needs
Reads a bar/area model as a separate procedure from the multiplication equation it represents

learn.summary: For ages 9-10, build representation fluency so a child moves between real situations, bar models, number lines, multi-digit multiplication, and the fraction-decimal-percentage trio while explaining the connections and keeping each symbol tied to the quantity it names. The signature demand is seeing 0.35, 35/100 and 35% as ONE quantity shown three ways, located on a single representation (a hundredths grid, or one number line with fractions above and decimals/percents below) so equivalence is a fact of magnitude, not three separate conversion rules. Percentage is the fresh hazard: 'per cent' means 'parts per hundred', and a child who has not internalised that reads 35% as the bare number 35 or an unmoored decimal. Scaling problems (bar model mapped to a multiplication equation) and reading quantities off a line graph into an equation round out the level; the recurring failure is grabbing visible numbers without asking what quantity each representation actually shows.

activities.title: One quantity, three costumes: the linked hundredths grid
feedback: If the child says 35% is bigger than 0.35 'because 35 > nought-point-something', return to the grid: both name the same 35 shaded squares out of 100, so they are the same amount.
If the child converts by a remembered rule without pointing to the shaded region, ask them to show where 35/100, 0.35 and 35% each live on the same grid and the same number-line point.
If the child cannot say what % means, re-ground on '35 out of 100 squares shaded = 35 per hundred = 35%' before touching any conversion rule.
When a new amount is shaded (e.g. 8 squares giving 8/100, 0.08, 8%), confirm the child can state all three forms and tie them back to the shaded area unprompted.
activities.rationale: Locating the same quantity in all three forms on a single hundredths grid or one number line makes equivalence a fact of magnitude and grounds percentage as parts per hundred before any rule. An OPTIONAL live-linker version (shading drives the fraction, decimal and percentage simultaneously and marks the shared number-line point) makes the equivalence vivid by letting the child watch the three notations move together; a static annotated grid can still illustrate the same relationships but does not let the child vary the amount.
sourceClaims: Help students represent fractions as common fractions, decimals and percentages and translate among them; use a single number line (fractions above, decimals/percents below) or a hundredths grid so the same quantity is located and compared in all three forms.
MP2: attend to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute; create a coherent representation and keep symbols tied to their referents across representations.
learnerActions: Shade 35 of 100 squares on a hundredths grid and read off the three labels that name the same shaded region: 35/100, 0.35 and 35%.
Change the shading to a different amount (e.g. 8 squares) and state the fraction, decimal and percentage, explaining why all three must still match the shaded area.
Place the same quantity at a single point on one number line that carries fractions above and decimals/percentages below.
Answer the direct challenge: 'Is 0.35 the same as 35%, or is one bigger?' and justify using the shaded area and the per-hundred meaning, not '35 is bigger than nought-point-something'.
Say aloud what the % symbol means ('parts per hundred') and what the quantity is 35% OF.
activities.intendedInsight: 0.35, 35/100 and 35% were never three numbers to convert between; they are one magnitude shown three ways, and 'per cent' means parts per hundred.

activities.title: Scaling bar mapped to a multiplication equation
feedback: If the child treats the bar and the equation as separate procedures, ask them to map each number in the equation onto a part of the bar.
If the multiplier is wrong, check against the bar: how many times the original length is the scaled bar? (4 to 12 is three times, so ×3.)
Confirm the child can explain why the operation is multiplication (equal-group scaling), not addition.
activities.rationale: The bar model exposes multiplicative/proportional structure and connects a situation to its equation, so scaling can be seen as both a bar and a multiplication equation. An OPTIONAL dragging tool where changing the number of equal parts updates both the bar and the × equation can make the correspondence concrete; the mapping can equally be done with a drawn bar and a written equation.
sourceClaims: The bar model exposes multiplicative/proportional structure and connects a situation to its equation, so scaling problems can be represented as both a bar and a multiplication equation.
MP2: attend to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute; create a coherent representation and keep symbols tied to their referents across representations.
learnerActions: Represent a scaling situation (e.g. a recipe for 4 scaled to 12) as a bar model showing the equal parts.
Write the multiplication equation that matches the bar (here 4×3=12, a scale of ×3), and point to which part of the bar each number in the equation refers to.
If the scale changes, adjust the bar and update the equation together, explaining why the multiplier changes.
State what quantity each number represents before computing.
activities.intendedInsight: A bar model and a multiplication equation describe the same multiplicative/scaling structure; the bar and the symbols are two views of one relationship.

activities.title: Reading a line graph for meaning before choosing an operation
feedback: If the child adds two readings when a difference is wanted, ask: what quantity is each reading, and what is the question actually asking you to find?
If the child can compute but can't justify subtraction, have them describe the change in words first, then pick the matching operation.
Confirm the child names each reading's quantity before selecting an operation.
activities.rationale: Requiring the child to say what quantity each reading is before choosing an operation keeps symbols tied to their referents and counters number-grabbing. A difference between two readings calls for subtraction because of what the situation asks, not because the numbers are visible.
sourceClaims: MP2: attend to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute; create a coherent representation and keep symbols tied to their referents across representations.
learnerActions: On a line graph, name what quantity each point/reading represents before doing any arithmetic.
For a question asking the change or difference between two readings, state which operation the situation needs and why.
Translate the reading into an equation (e.g. a subtraction for a difference) and compute.
Explain why adding the two readings would not give the change.
activities.intendedInsight: Choose the operation from what the situation asks and what each reading means, not by grabbing whichever visible numbers are present.

activities.title: Argue it out: defend equivalence against a doubter
feedback: Accept any correct justification grounded in the shaded quantity and the per-hundred meaning; press for the grid or number-line evidence if the child only asserts 'they're equal'.
If the child agrees with the doubter, go back to the shaded region and the meaning of %.
This dialogue is for reasoning practice and should not be scored.
activities.rationale: Explaining why the forms are the same proportion and what each graph reading means is dialogic, and a doubting partner gives the child something concrete to argue against. This is a reasoning/talk activity, not an assessment; a dialogue can elicit explanation but does not by itself prove the child can construct a representation unaided.
sourceClaims: MP2: attend to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute; create a coherent representation and keep symbols tied to their referents across representations.
learnerActions: Respond to a partner who claims '35% must be bigger than 0.35 — 35 versus nought-point-something!' by proving sameness on the grid.
Explain in your own words why 35/100, 0.35 and 35% are the same proportion.
When the partner reads a line graph aloud and proposes adding two values to find a change, say whether that is right and correct it, giving your reasoning.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to explain and defend why the three forms are one quantity, and why an operation does or doesn't fit, shows understanding beyond rote conversion.

constraints: Show all three notations on ONE representation (a hundredths grid, or one number line with fractions above and decimals/percents below) so equivalence is seen as the same magnitude, not three conversion rules.
Ground percentage in 'parts per hundred' using the grid before introducing any conversion rule, so 35% is a quantity rather than a bare number.
At every step insist on 'what does each number represent?' and translate in every direction.

A static annotated grid or labelled bar model can illustrate equivalence but does not let the child vary the amount or interactively respond to the percentage misconception; treat it as a worked example / scaffold, not the full activity.

Match-the-equivalent exercises test recognition and can reward rote conversion; recognition alone does not elicit independent construction or explanation, so use them only as a warm-up, not as evidence the child can construct the translation or explain the shared magnitude.
The reasoning/argument dialogue is for eliciting explanation and should not be scored.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source claims are cited where they support the teaching principle (single-representation equivalence, bar-model-to-equation structure, MP2 meaning-of-quantities); citation does not establish that these specific activities were empirically tested or that any medium is superior to another.

The legacy entry asserted some comparative/absolute claims (e.g. a quiz tests recognition 'but not constructing', 3D 'conveys nothing better than a grid', a static image 'can't let the child vary the amount'). These have been softened to scoped scaffold limits; the genuine objective limit retained is that recognition-only matching does not elicit independent construction or explanation.

Arithmetic verified: 35% = 0.35 = 35/100 (thirty-five hundredths); 8 squares = 8/100 = 0.08 = 8%; the scaling example 'recipe for 4 scaled to 12' is ×3 because 4×3=12. The 'is 35% bigger than 0.35' hinge is sound — they are equal.

probeDeeper: 'Shade a different amount — say 8 squares. What are the fraction, the decimal and the percentage now, and why do they all match?'
'What does the little % sign actually mean? 35% of what?'
'Is 0.35 the same as 35%, or is one bigger? Prove it on the grid.'
'On this line graph, what quantity is each point? If I want the change between them, what do I do and why?'
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child recognising all three name the SAME shaded quantity (thirty-five hundredths), explaining per cent as parts per hundred, and stating that 35% and 0.35 are the same amount — not that one is larger because '35 > 0.35'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Fraction, decimal and percentage treated as three different things, not one magnitude — picks one as 'the' right label or can't relate them.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the single hundredths grid / one number line with all three notations on the same region until equivalence is a fact of magnitude; reteach fraction–decimal–percentage as the same quantity.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child names only one form as correct, or converts by rote without seeing the shared shaded area; struggles to place all three at one point.

errorPatterns.pattern: Per cent not understood as parts per hundred: reads 35% as the number 35 (so 'bigger than 0.35') or as a meaningless decimal.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to 'per cent = out of 100' on the grid, then connect to 35/100 and 0.35; reteach the meaning of the % symbol before any conversion.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 35% > 0.35 'because 35 is bigger', or cannot say what the % refers to.

errorPatterns.pattern: Number-grabbing off a line graph or bar model: reads values and combines them without asking which quantity or operation the situation needs (e.g. adds two readings when a difference is wanted).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist the child name each reading's quantity first, then choose the operation from the situation; reteach reading representations for meaning before computing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In a graph/scaling task the child pulls the visible numbers and applies an operation without mapping meaning; can't say why subtraction (not addition) gives the change.

responseLevels.gap: Picks one notation as the only right answer or says 35% is bigger than 0.35; treats the forms as separate.
responseLevels.full: Shows all three name the same shaded magnitude, explains per cent as parts per hundred, states 35% = 0.35, and reads graph/scaling representations for their quantities before choosing an operation — transferring the reasoning to a new amount unprompted.
responseLevels.partial: Knows the three forms are 'equal' by a remembered rule but can't ground it in the shaded quantity, or wavers on 35% vs 0.35, or maps FDP but grabs numbers on the graph without meaning.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: On a hundred-square, 35 squares are shaded. One classmate says 'that shows 35/100', another says 'no, it's 0.35', another says 'it's 35%'. Who is right? Explain how these three are related, and show me on the grid. Then tell me: is 35% a bigger amount than 0.35, or the same?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who holds proportion-as-one-magnitude says all three are the same and 35% = 0.35; a child treating notations as separate quantities picks one 'right' answer or claims 35% is bigger. The last question is the hinge: '35 versus nought-point-something' tempts the notation-bound child into 'bigger', while a child who understands per-cent-as-per-hundred sees they coincide. Hard to answer right for the wrong reason — saying 'same' must be backed by the grid and the per-hundred meaning.

sources.claim: MP2: attend to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute; create a coherent representation and keep symbols tied to their referents across representations.
sources.source: CCSS Standards for Mathematical Practice, MP2

sources.claim: Help students represent fractions as common fractions, decimals and percentages and translate among them; use a single number line (fractions above, decimals/percents below) or a hundredths grid so the same quantity is located and compared in all three forms.
sources.source: IES/WWC Practice Guide, Developing Effective Fractions Instruction for K–8 (Rec 2, 4th action step)

sources.claim: The bar model exposes multiplicative/proportional structure and connects a situation to its equation, so scaling problems can be represented as both a bar and a multiplication equation.
sources.source: NCETM, 'The Bar Model'

pedagogy.summary: At 8-9 strategic choice covers mental vs written vs diagrammatic methods, using a second tool to CHECK a result, and selecting the fraction MODEL that fits the task. Two moves are new: reading a calculation to route the method (25×4 mentally by doubling twice; 167×3 in writing), and using a tool to VERIFY — counting unit squares on squared paper against a computed l×w — which is CCSS MP5's 'detect errors' idea made concrete. Choosing the fraction representation matters because different models make different comparisons visible: strips align wholes for 3/8 vs 1/4 in a way a crowded number line does not.
bestPractices: Read the numbers to route the method — sort a mixed set into 'do in your head' vs 'write out' by their features (25×4 vs 167×3)
Teach tools as CHECKERS: after computing l×w, tile the rectangle on squared paper and count to verify — use a second representation and estimation to catch errors (CCSS MP5)
Select the fraction model to fit the comparison (strips align lengths for 3/8 vs 1/4) and discuss why that model helps (EEF: compare representations)
Integrate the calculator for CHECKING, not doing, so mental fluency is not eroded (EEF: less but better)
Name each tool's limitation — a number line crowds when comparing eighths and quarters; strips only help if the wholes are the same length
keyRepresentations: Mental strategies (doubling, partitioning)
Formal written methods
Fraction strips
Number line
Squared paper / arrays for verifying area
Calculator (for checking)
commonMisconceptions: Writes out even friendly calculations like 25×4, missing the mental route
Treats the first answer as final and never checks it with a second tool (CCSS: tools and estimation detect errors)
Grabs a number line to compare 3/8 and 1/4 when strips align the wholes far more clearly — wrong model for the task
Uses the calculator to DO the arithmetic rather than to check it, undermining mental fluency (EEF)

learn.summary: For ages 8-9, this topic builds strategic choice in mathematics: reading a calculation to route the method (mental vs written), using a second tool or representation to VERIFY a result rather than treating the first answer as final, and selecting the fraction model that makes a particular comparison visible. Learners compute a rectangle's area (l×w) and check it by tiling and counting unit squares on squared paper, route friendly calculations like 25×4 to mental strategies while reserving written methods for calculations like 167×3, and compare fractions such as 3/8 and 1/4 by aligning strips against a common whole.

activities.title: Compute the area, then check it by tiling
feedback: When the 24 squares fill the rectangle exactly, name the moment: 'your multiplication and your counting agree, so you can be more confident the area is 24 cm².'
If the tiled count differs from the computed answer (e.g. 25 vs 24), prompt: 'which would you trust, and what would you check first?' Encourage recounting and recomputing rather than guessing.
If the learner computes 24 and will not or cannot check, model tiling the array and counting aloud, then ask them to do the next one themselves.

Optional live mechanism: with an interactive on-screen tool, dragging unit squares onto the rectangle and having it flag a mismatch makes the confirm/catch mechanism concrete — but counting on paper achieves the same check. Note that paper squares have slight physical thickness and model the idealised unit areas.
activities.rationale: Using a second tool and estimation to detect possible errors, and recognising a tool's insight and limits, is the targeted practice. Tiling a computed rectangle makes the 'detect errors' idea concrete for this age.
sourceClaims: Proficient students detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge, and recognise a tool's insight and limitations when deciding whether it is helpful
learnerActions: Find the area of a 6 cm by 4 cm rectangle by computing length times width (6×4 = 24 cm²).
Take 1 cm squared paper, draw or tile the same 6 cm by 4 cm rectangle with 1 cm unit squares, then count the squares.
Compare the count against the computed answer: do 24 squares fill the rectangle exactly?
If the count and the calculation disagree, pause and work out which to trust and what to do next (recount, recompute, re-measure).
Say in your own words how counting squares and multiplying length by width are two views of the same area.
activities.intendedInsight: l×w and counting unit squares are two views of one area, so a second representation can CONFIRM your calculation or catch a slip. Checking is a routine worth doing, not a waste of time.

activities.title: Read the numbers to route the method
feedback: If a learner sets out a column or long-multiplication layout for 25×4, ask them to look at the numbers first and find a mental shortcut; confirm 25×4 = 100.
Ask the learner to give a multiplication where writing it out really IS worth the effort, and discuss what made it so.
Praise the reasoning ('25×4 is friendly because it makes 100'), not just the correct answer.
activities.rationale: Choosing between mental, written and diagrammatic methods by reading the numbers is the core strategic move at this band; justifying the choice develops the judgement rather than just the answer.
learnerActions: Sort a mixed set of multiplications into 'do in my head' and 'write it out' by looking at the numbers first.
Do 25×4 mentally — for example double 25 to 50, double again to 100; or recognise 25×4 = 100.
Choose a written method for 167×3, where the numbers make a written layout worthwhile.
Explain for each one WHY you chose mental or written: what features of the numbers made that choice efficient?
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a calculation's features before starting lets you pick the efficient route; a written layout is worth the effort for some numbers and wasteful for friendly ones.

activities.title: Pick the fraction model that fits the comparison
feedback: If a learner reaches for a number line and struggles, prompt them to align strips over the same whole and compare lengths directly.

Reinforce the limit on the model: strips only let you compare by length when the wholes are the same length; comparing represented portions of different-sized wholes with strips is misleading. The fractions themselves (3/8 and 1/4) are still comparable as numbers — 3/8 > 1/4.
Ask 'why might fraction strips beat a number line for comparing 3/8 and 1/4?' and listen for reasoning about aligned wholes, not just a preference.

Optional mechanism: dragging two strips to a common baseline, or recolouring the shaded parts, makes the length comparison vivid — paper strips cut to the same whole achieve the same alignment, with slight physical thickness standing in for the idealised lengths.
activities.rationale: Representations should be chosen purposefully with a clear rationale, and comparing representations develops conceptual understanding. Matching the model to what must be seen is the skill here.
sourceClaims: Representations must be chosen purposefully with a clear rationale; comparing different representations develops conceptual understanding; and the calculator should be integrated for checking with pupils self-regulating to make less but better use of it
learnerActions: Compare 3/8 and 1/4 using fraction strips, aligning both strips against the same whole length.
Try comparing the same fractions on a number line and notice whether the marks are easy to read; on a short line, eighth and quarter marks can be close together (1/4 sits on the same mark as 2/8).
Decide which representation makes it easiest to see that 3/8 is larger than 1/4, and say why.
State the condition for the strips to work: the wholes being compared must be the same length.
activities.intendedInsight: Different models make different comparisons visible: aligning strips over a common whole shows 3/8 > 1/4 directly, and a number line marked in eighths shows it too (1/4 = 2/8), though a small or crowded line can make it harder to see. The right model depends on what must be seen. 3/8 is larger than 1/4 as numbers regardless of which model is used.

activities.title: Argue your method and model to a partner
feedback: Listen for the learner proposing an independent check (tile and count) rather than re-stating the same calculation.
If the learner cannot justify strips over a number line, revisit aligning strips over a common whole together.
For the calculator question, reinforce: checking a result afterwards is fine; using it to avoid a mental method you already have erodes fluency.
activities.rationale: Explaining and defending a verification habit and a model choice surfaces and consolidates the strategic reasoning that pure computation does not reveal. Dialogue of this kind can elicit the reasoning but does not by itself guarantee the learner will compute or check independently.
sourceClaims: Representations must be chosen purposefully with a clear rationale; comparing different representations develops conceptual understanding; and the calculator should be integrated for checking with pupils self-regulating to make less but better use of it
learnerActions: Work with a partner (or an in-role character) who never checks answers and always reaches for a number line.
When they give an area answer, ask them 'how do you KNOW that is right?' and propose a verification step.
When they compare fractions on a number line, discuss whether strips over a common whole would make this comparison easier to see, and give reasons for the model you prefer.
Decide together when a calculator is a fair checking tool here and when using it would just do the arithmetic for you.
activities.intendedInsight: Verifying with a second tool and choosing a fitting model are habits you can defend out loud; articulating the reasons strengthens them. A calculator is for checking, not for doing the arithmetic you can do yourself.

constraints: This is a strategic/meta skill: a correct final answer alone does not show it. Observe whether the learner verifies with a second tool, routes the method by reading the numbers, and chooses a fitting model — not just whether the answer is 24.

Recognition-only or scored-step formats can test isolated method-choice items but cannot by themselves observe whether a learner spontaneously verifies or justifies a model choice; a correct answer reached without checking still scores full marks. Use such items only to feed richer open work.

Fraction strips only support comparison by length when the wholes are the same length; comparing represented portions of different-sized wholes with strips is misleading. State this condition explicitly, while noting the fractions themselves remain comparable as numbers.
A number line is not 'wrong' in general — it can crowd specifically when comparing eighths and quarters. Keep the limitation scoped to the task rather than dismissing the number line as a tool.
Integrate the calculator for checking a result, not for performing arithmetic the learner can do mentally, so mental fluency is preserved.

Paper strips and squared paper have slight physical thickness; treat them as practical approximations to the idealised mathematical lengths and areas they represent, and treat on-screen strips as an idealised model.

A static reference image can usefully show 'which model shows what' as a support, but cannot host the compute-verify-choose decision-making, which requires the learner to actually calculate, check and select.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source assumes 6×4 = 24 cm² and 25×4 = 100; both are correct. 167×3 = 501 if computed, but the source states only that it merits a written method, so the activity asserts no specific product for it.

The legacy row rated a static image and a quiz as 'poor' partly via universal claims ('a static picture cannot teach this', 'scored steps cannot observe verifying') and judged 3D as adding 'no purchase'. Only the narrow objective limit (recognition/scored-only formats do not by themselves elicit spontaneous verification or justification) is retained in constraints; the categorical 'cannot teach' and '3D adds nothing' framings were softened or dropped as not established by the sources.
The 'number line crowds' claim is an inherited pedagogical judgement, preserved with hedged wording and scoped to eighths-vs-quarters; it was not independently verified.

The non-preferred conversation alternative was preserved as a distinct activity because its pedagogical purpose (defending the verification habit and model choice aloud) differs from the computation/verification activity.
The catalog term 'bench' present in the candidate's area-verification feedback was replaced with a generic 'interactive on-screen tool' to remove product vocabulary from learner-facing text.

probeDeeper: If the squares came to 25 instead of 24, which would you trust, and what would you do next?
Give me a multiplication where writing it out really IS worth the effort.
Why might fraction strips beat a number line for comparing 3/8 and 1/4?
When is it fine to use a calculator here, and when would it just make you lazy?
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for using squared paper to tile and count the 6×4 array as an independent CHECK on the computation (a second representation confirming l×w), and understanding that a check raises confidence or catches an error; and for choosing a MENTAL method for 25×4 (double-double, or 25×4=100) because the numbers are friendly, reserving written work for something like 167×3.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the first answer as final and never checks it — has no habit of verifying with a second tool
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model tiling the array on squared paper and counting; establish that a second representation can confirm a result or catch a slip, and make checking routine.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives 24 and cannot or will not check; the idea of verifying is unfamiliar or seen as pointless

errorPatterns.pattern: Writes out even friendly calculations (25×4) because a written method feels 'proper'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort a mixed set into mental vs written by looking at the numbers first; reserve the written method for calculations whose numbers demand it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Sets out a column or long-multiplication layout for 25×4 rather than seeing 100 mentally

errorPatterns.pattern: Chooses a fraction model that obscures the comparison — a number line where strips would align the wholes for 3/8 vs 1/4
errorPatterns.nextMove: Match the model to what must be seen — same whole, aligned lengths — and reteach the fraction models and equivalence that make comparison visible.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks a model that makes the comparison harder to see, or compares fractions of different-sized wholes

responseLevels.gap: Computes and stops with no verification; writes out friendly calculations, or picks a fraction model by habit regardless of the comparison.
responseLevels.full: Unprompted, verifies the result with a second representation, reads the numbers to choose mental vs written, selects the fraction model that makes the comparison visible, and reserves the calculator for checking.
responseLevels.partial: When prompted, can describe checking with squares or say 25×4 is 'easy', but does not spontaneously verify or read the numbers to route the method.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You worked out that a 6 cm by 4 cm rectangle has an area of 24 cm². A friend says 'you can't be sure — check it.' How could you use squared paper to check, and would you trust 24 more afterwards? And for 25 × 4, would you write it out or do it in your head — why?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who only computes gives 24 and stops; a strategic child uses a second tool to verify (CCSS detect-errors) and reads the numbers to pick the efficient method. 25×4 is deliberately friendly, so choosing to write it out — or being unable to say why checking helps — reveals no strategic judgement, while accuracy alone does not separate the children.

sources.claim: Proficient students detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge, and recognise a tool's insight and limitations when deciding whether it is helpful
