pedagogy.summary: At age 11-13 pupils move from recognising shapes to DERIVING and justifying their properties — the interior angles, diagonals, symmetry and side relationships of triangles, quadrilaterals and circles — and to reasoning about how the shapes relate. The signature idea is hierarchical (class-inclusion) classification: a square is a special case of BOTH a rectangle and a rhombus because it possesses all their defining properties and more. The dominant obstacle, robustly documented, is the prototype phenomenon and partition thinking: pupils who can state definitions still judge by the prototypical picture, so they deny that 'a square is a rectangle' (rectangles are 'long'/slanted parallelograms look a certain way), and even when they accept one direction they miss the 'opposing direction' and transitive inclusions (square ⊆ rhombus ⊆ parallelogram ⇒ square ⊆ parallelogram). For circles, properties are relational and multiplicative — diameter = 2 × radius, circumference = π × diameter — with π a constant ratio independent of the circle's size. Effective teaching derives properties by construction and measurement, works from hierarchical (not partition) definitions, and uses dynamic shapes so pupils see one shape become a special case of another without losing the general properties.
bestPractices: Derive properties rather than assert them: have pupils construct, fold, measure and mark to establish (e.g.) that a parallelogram's diagonals bisect each other, distinguishing this from a rectangle's equal diagonals
Teach hierarchical (inclusion) definitions explicitly and contrast them with partition definitions (de Villiers): a square counts as a rectangle because it meets every rectangle property
Use dynamic shapes to defeat prototype/partition thinking: drag a rectangle until all sides are equal and note that 'square' switches on while 'rectangle' never switches off
Target the opposing-direction and transitive inclusions directly (every square is a rhombus AND a parallelogram; not every rectangle is a square) with always/sometimes/never tasks
For circles, establish diameter = 2r and circumference = πd by measuring several circles, so π emerges as a constant ratio independent of size
keyRepresentations: Dynamic quadrilateral with live name-tags (parallelogram/rectangle/rhombus/square) that light up as properties are met
Quadrilateral hierarchy Venn diagram / family tree
Fold-and-measure derivations of diagonal and symmetry properties
Circle with labelled radius, diameter and circumference and a circumference ÷ diameter ≈ 3.14 readout
Property tables comparing triangles/quadrilaterals for always/sometimes/never reasoning
commonMisconceptions: Partition/prototype classification: denying that a square is a rectangle (or a rhombus) because the shapes 'look different' or a rectangle 'must have two long and two short sides'
One-directional / non-transitive inclusion: accepting square ⊆ rhombus but not square ⊆ parallelogram, or thinking a rectangle cannot share square properties
Judging properties by appearance rather than derivation — e.g. assuming a parallelogram's diagonals are equal (confusing it with a rectangle)
Confusing radius and diameter, or believing π (circumference ÷ diameter) depends on the size of the circle
Treating each named shape as an isolated category with no overlapping membership

learn.summary: For learners aged 11-13, the goal is to move from recognising triangles, quadrilaterals and circles to DERIVING and justifying their properties (interior angles, diagonals, symmetry, side relationships) and reasoning about how shapes relate hierarchically. The signature idea is class-inclusion classification: a square is a special case of BOTH a rectangle and a rhombus because it has all their defining properties and more. The documented core obstacle is prototype/partition thinking — pupils who can state definitions still judge by the prototypical picture, denying 'a square is a rectangle', and often miss the opposing-direction and transitive inclusions (square ⊆ rhombus ⊆ parallelogram ⇒ square ⊆ parallelogram). For circles, properties are relational: diameter = 2 × radius and circumference = π × diameter, with π a constant ratio independent of the circle's size. Effective teaching derives properties by construction and measurement, builds from hierarchical (not partition) definitions, and uses dynamic (or adjustable) shapes so a learner can watch one shape become a special case of another without losing the general properties, with hands-on construction, measurement and comparison supporting the same ideas.

activities.title: Morph a rectangle into a square and watch inclusion persist
feedback: If a learner says the shape 'stopped being a rectangle' when it became a square, ask: which rectangle property did it lose? (It kept four right angles and opposite sides equal/parallel, so it is still a rectangle.)
If a learner insists the shapes 'look different', redirect to checking the square against EVERY rectangle property one by one rather than judging by overall appearance.
activities.rationale: Prototype/partition thinking is robustly documented: learners who know definitions still deny 'a square is a rectangle'. Watching one shape acquire a more general class's name-tags while keeping the general tag makes inclusion visible rather than asserted. The continuous morph requires a dynamic geometry tool (or an adjustable model such as a linkage/geoboard) with name-tags that light up as each shape's properties are met; a set of physical cutouts can support a compare-across-shapes version (holding a long rectangle beside a square and checking shared properties) but cannot show the live transformation, and a static family-tree/Venn reference can support the idea but cannot display the morph itself.
sourceClaims: Hierarchical (class-inclusion) classification means more particular concepts form subsets of more general ones (de Villiers 1994); most learners nevertheless reason by prototype/partition even when they know definitions, denying e.g. that a square is a rectangle ('parallelograms are slanted'), and struggle with the 'opposing direction' and transitive inclusions (accepting square⊆rhombus but not square⊆parallelogram) — a static, inflexible concept image blocking hierarchical reasoning (Fujita 2012 levels; van Hiele informal-deduction level is where class inclusion is understood).

KS3 statutory: pupils 'derive and illustrate properties of triangles, quadrilaterals, circles, and other plane figures (for example, equal lengths and angles) using appropriate language and technologies', 'identify properties of, and describe the results of, translations, rotations and reflections', and know circle parts and that circumference = π × diameter.
learnerActions: Start with a 'long' rectangle and list which names currently fit it: note that, of the names parallelogram, rectangle, rhombus and square, only 'rectangle' and 'parallelogram' apply (it is also a quadrilateral).
Change the shape by moving its corners/sides until all four sides are equal, keeping the four right angles.
Observe that 'rhombus' and 'square' now apply too — while 'rectangle' never stopped applying.
Say in your own words why the square never stopped being a rectangle: it kept every rectangle property and simply gained the extra property of four equal sides.
activities.intendedInsight: A square is a special case of a rectangle (and of a rhombus): it satisfies every defining property of the more general class and adds more, so it belongs to both classes at once.

activities.title: Derive diagonal and symmetry properties by folding and measuring
feedback: If a learner claims a parallelogram's diagonals are equal, ask them to measure both diagonals of a clearly non-rectangular parallelogram — they differ. Equal diagonals belong to the rectangle, not the general parallelogram.
Praise justifications that cite a fold or measurement ('I measured both halves and they matched, so the diagonals bisect') over 'it looks like it'.
activities.rationale: A common error is attributing the wrong property to the wrong class by appearance (e.g. giving a parallelogram equal diagonals by confusing it with a rectangle). Construction and measurement give learners a reliable method to establish and distinguish properties. Paper/card cutouts are approximations with real thickness; treat them as stand-ins for the ideal zero-thickness plane figures.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory: pupils 'derive and illustrate properties of triangles, quadrilaterals, circles, and other plane figures (for example, equal lengths and angles) using appropriate language and technologies', 'identify properties of, and describe the results of, translations, rotations and reflections', and know circle parts and that circumference = π × diameter.
learnerActions: Construct or cut out a parallelogram, a rectangle and a rhombus (paper/card approximations of the ideal flat figures).

Draw the diagonals; fold and measure to test: do the diagonals bisect each other? Are they equal in length? Do they meet at right angles? Also fold along each diagonal and along each line joining midpoints of opposite sides to test which are lines of symmetry.

Record for each shape which diagonal and symmetry properties hold, e.g. a parallelogram's diagonals bisect each other but are NOT generally equal, whereas a rectangle's diagonals ARE equal and a rhombus's diagonals meet at right angles; a non-square rectangle's lines of symmetry join midpoints of opposite sides (its diagonals are NOT lines of symmetry), a non-square rhombus's lines of symmetry are its diagonals, and a parallelogram that is neither has no line of symmetry.
State each property as something you checked by construction/measurement, not something you guessed from the picture.
activities.intendedInsight: Properties should be derived and verified, not read off appearance; different classes have genuinely different diagonal/symmetry properties, which is how you can tell them apart and justify inclusion.

activities.title: Measure several circles to let π emerge as a constant ratio
feedback: If a learner predicted the ratio would be larger for bigger circles, point to their own table: the ratios should be roughly the same for every circle, close to 3.14 apart from measuring error, with no trend by size — the true ratio is fixed, so π is a constant, not size-dependent.
If radius and diameter are confused, have them lay the radius against the diameter and confirm the diameter spans twice the radius across the centre.
Note that small measuring errors make the ratios differ slightly; the pattern 'a bit more than 3 every time' is the point, not a perfectly identical decimal.
activities.rationale: Measuring several circles and comparing the ratio lets π be felt as an invariant rather than memorised, directly confronting the misconception that π depends on circle size. A resizable circle with a live circumference ÷ diameter readout held near 3.14 is an optional model that reinforces the same invariance when physical objects aren't available.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory: pupils 'derive and illustrate properties of triangles, quadrilaterals, circles, and other plane figures (for example, equal lengths and angles) using appropriate language and technologies', 'identify properties of, and describe the results of, translations, rotations and reflections', and know circle parts and that circumference = π × diameter.
learnerActions: Collect several circular objects of different sizes (tins, lids) and some string or tape.
Before measuring, PREDICT how many times the diameter will fit around the circumference, and say WHY — in particular, predict whether the answer changes with the size of the circle.
Wrap and measure the circumference, then measure the diameter, for each object.
Compute circumference ÷ diameter for each and compare: the ratio should come out a little more than 3 (close to 3.14, within measuring error) each time, regardless of the circle's size.
Also check that the diameter is twice the radius (d = 2r) and state circumference = π × diameter in your own words.
activities.intendedInsight: Radius, diameter and circumference are related multiplicatively: d = 2r and C = πd, where π is a constant ratio (≈ 3.14) that does NOT depend on the size of the circle.

activities.title: Always / sometimes / never and the inclusion chain
feedback: If a learner accepts 'a square is a rhombus' but denies 'a square is a parallelogram', walk the chain: a square is a rhombus, every rhombus is a parallelogram, so a square is a parallelogram.
If a learner answers 'a rectangle is a square' as always true, show a long rectangle: it lacks four equal sides, so it is a rectangle but not a square — hence only sometimes.
Encourage justification by which properties are present/absent rather than by appearance.
activities.rationale: Targeting the opposing-direction and transitive inclusions directly addresses the documented one-directional/non-transitive error. Always/sometimes/never items (phrased in singular form so each verdict is well defined), categorisation and matching assess inclusion well, and prototype distractors ('a square is not a rectangle because it looks different') probe the core misconception. Used in teaching, these response formats can also surface reasoning for discussion, though a selection item alone does not elicit a learner's own justification.
sourceClaims: Hierarchical (class-inclusion) classification means more particular concepts form subsets of more general ones (de Villiers 1994); most learners nevertheless reason by prototype/partition even when they know definitions, denying e.g. that a square is a rectangle ('parallelograms are slanted'), and struggle with the 'opposing direction' and transitive inclusions (accepting square⊆rhombus but not square⊆parallelogram) — a static, inflexible concept image blocking hierarchical reasoning (Fujita 2012 levels; van Hiele informal-deduction level is where class inclusion is understood).
learnerActions: Decide for each statement whether it is always, sometimes or never true, and justify by properties: 'A square is a rectangle', 'A rectangle is a square', 'A square is a rhombus', 'A square is a parallelogram'.
Trace the inclusion chain square ⊆ rhombus ⊆ parallelogram and explain why it follows that a square is a parallelogram (transitive reasoning).
Explain why 'a square is a rectangle' is always true but 'a rectangle is a square' is only sometimes true — the two directions are different.
Build or complete a family-tree / Venn diagram of parallelogram, rectangle, rhombus and square, placing each shape in every class it belongs to.
activities.intendedInsight: Inclusion has a direction and is transitive: the more special shape belongs to the more general classes, but not the reverse; chaining inclusions lets you conclude square ⊆ parallelogram.

activities.title: 'Convince me a square is a rectangle' — a reasoning dialogue
feedback: Reward arguments that answer an objection with a property check rather than restating the conclusion.
If the learner concedes to a prototype objection, ask which rectangle property the square actually fails — it fails none.
activities.rationale: A Socratic dialogue that repeatedly asks 'does a square have every property a rectangle needs?' and offers prototype counter-claims can surface and challenge partition reasoning and rehearse justification. It complements, and does not replace, the hands-on derivation and the dynamic morph activities, which can make the inclusion idea visible more directly.
sourceClaims: Hierarchical (class-inclusion) classification means more particular concepts form subsets of more general ones (de Villiers 1994); most learners nevertheless reason by prototype/partition even when they know definitions, denying e.g. that a square is a rectangle ('parallelograms are slanted'), and struggle with the 'opposing direction' and transitive inclusions (accepting square⊆rhombus but not square⊆parallelogram) — a static, inflexible concept image blocking hierarchical reasoning (Fujita 2012 levels; van Hiele informal-deduction level is where class inclusion is understood).
learnerActions: Take the position that a square IS a rectangle and argue it to a partner or teacher who keeps pushing back with prototype objections ('but rectangles are long', 'they look different').
For each objection, answer by checking the square against a specific defining property of a rectangle (four right angles, opposite sides equal and parallel).
Conclude with a property-based statement: a square has every rectangle property and adds four equal sides, so it is a special rectangle.
activities.intendedInsight: A convincing justification of inclusion is built from checking defining properties, and it withstands appearance-based objections.

constraints: Build from hierarchical (inclusion) definitions and explicitly contrast them with partition definitions; a partition definition (e.g. 'a rectangle must have two long and two short sides') is the source of the core misconception and should be surfaced and corrected, not used.

Properties should be explored by construction, folding and measurement, then stated as checked for the shapes tested (within measuring accuracy) and, where possible, justified by reasoning from the definitions so they hold in general — avoid letting learners assert properties from appearance alone.

Paper/card cutouts have real thickness and are approximations of ideal zero-thickness plane figures; a flat screen is also a model. Distinguish the represented ideal shape from its physical or pictured representation.
Measurement of real circles yields ratios near 3.14 with small variation from measuring error; the invariance ('always a bit more than 3') is the learning point, not a perfectly identical decimal.

A static hierarchy/Venn reference is a useful support but cannot display a shape morphing while inclusion persists, and a fixed cutout cannot morph; pair either with a dynamic or adjustable model (or a deliberate compare-across-shapes activity) so inclusion is experienced, not only read.
Recognition-only response formats (picking the right option) do not by themselves elicit a learner's own justification; require them to state property-based reasoning in their own words.

When using always/sometimes/never, phrase items in singular form ('a rectangle is a square') so the verdict is well defined; a universally quantified statement is simply true or false, not 'sometimes'.

Optional interactive features — draggable corners, live name-tags that light up as properties are met, a diagonals overlay toggle, a resizable circle with a fixed C÷d readout — make the mechanism concrete when available, but are not mandatory; paper, string and construction tools serve the same objectives.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support teaching principles rather than proving any specific activity was tested.

The legacy row rated 3D as adding 'nothing essential'. These are plane figures plus one circle ratio, so 2D/physical work is well matched; this is a scope judgement, not evidence that a 3D representation could not help any learner.

The legacy claims that the square/rectangle question 'cannot be answered correctly from the picture alone' and that a static image 'cannot teach' inclusion are comparative claims not established by the cited sources; retained only as the narrow, true point that a static reference and a fixed cutout cannot display the continuous morph, while a dynamic/adjustable model can.

Corrected the morph activity and summary: a fixed paper cutout cannot continuously morph a rectangle into a square, so the continuous transformation is credited to dynamic geometry/adjustable models, with cutouts supporting comparison instead.

The always/sometimes/never activity uses singular-form statements so each a/s/n verdict is well defined; universally quantified statements ('every rectangle is a square') are simply true or false and were not used in learner-facing items.
The objective lists triangle interior angles, but like the original row no dedicated triangle angle-sum derivation activity is included; this is a scope gap to flag, not an introduced error.

Self-audit of mathematical content: d = 2r, C = πd, π ≈ 3.14 constant across sizes, parallelogram diagonals bisect but are not generally equal, rectangle diagonals equal, rhombus diagonals perpendicular, and the inclusion chain square ⊆ rhombus ⊆ parallelogram are all internally consistent and used as stated; no arithmetic or geometric error found to correct.

assess.poeTask: Give the child several circular objects (tins, lids) and string or tape. Ask them to PREDICT how many times the diameter will fit around the circumference — and to say WHY — BEFORE measuring. Then wrap and measure each: the ratio is always a little more than 3 (π), for every size of circle. Whether they predicted the ratio would depend on the circle's size is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: Is every rectangle a square? Why is that direction different from 'every square is a rectangle'?
List the properties of a parallelogram — are its diagonals equal? How could you CHECK rather than guess?
A square is a rhombus and a rhombus is a parallelogram — so is a square a parallelogram? How do you know?
For a circle, how do the radius, diameter and circumference relate — and which stays about 3 times another no matter how big the circle is?
assess.correctAnswer: Yes to both. A square IS a rectangle because it has every defining property of a rectangle — four right angles and opposite sides equal and parallel — and simply adds the extra property that all four sides are equal, so it is a special rectangle. A square IS a rhombus because it has the rhombus's defining property of four equal sides, adding right angles, so it is a special rhombus. The reasoning must be property-based inclusion (the square satisfies all the properties of the more general class), not 'they look different'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Partition/prototype classification — denies a square is a rectangle because rectangles are 'long' (two long, two short sides) or the shapes simply 'look different'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Teach hierarchical vs partition definitions; check the square against EVERY rectangle property; drag a rectangle dynamically until it becomes a square while its rectangle properties persist
errorPatterns.distractor: No — a rectangle must have two long sides and two short sides, so a square is not a rectangle.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'no, a square isn't a rectangle' and justifies it by appearance or by a length restriction on rectangles

errorPatterns.pattern: One-directional / non-transitive inclusion — accepts an easy inclusion (square is a rhombus) but not the transitive or opposing-direction one (square is therefore a parallelogram), or thinks a rectangle cannot share square properties
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make the inclusion chain explicit (square ⊆ rhombus ⊆ parallelogram) and reason transitively; use a Venn/family tree and always/sometimes/never tasks to distinguish the two directions
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On follow-up says a square is a rhombus but denies it is a parallelogram, or accepts every square is a rectangle yet insists a rectangle can never be 'square-like'

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges properties by appearance rather than derivation — e.g. asserts a parallelogram's diagonals are equal (confusing it with a rectangle)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have the pupil derive the property by construction/measurement and compare classes (parallelogram diagonals bisect but are not equal; rectangle diagonals are equal)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: States a property (equal diagonals, right-angle diagonals) from how the figure looks, without constructing or measuring, and attributes the wrong property to the wrong class

responseLevels.gap: Classifies by appearance/prototype, denies a square is a rectangle, states properties only by looking, and treats each shape as an isolated category.
responseLevels.full: Reasons hierarchically from definitions and properties (a square satisfies all rectangle AND all rhombus properties, so is a special case of both), handles opposing-direction and transitive inclusions, derives and verifies properties (parallelogram diagonals bisect; C = πd, d = 2r), and transfers the reasoning to a new shape.
responseLevels.partial: Lists correct properties of each shape and may accept the easier inclusions (square ⊆ rhombus), but cannot handle the opposing-direction or transitive inclusions, or derive/verify a property rather than assert it — knows the parts without the relational hierarchy.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Answer each with yes or no, then explain: Is a square a rectangle? Is a square a rhombus? Use the properties of these shapes in your reasoning.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A pupil who reasons hierarchically from properties answers yes-and-yes and justifies by property inclusion; a pupil reasoning from the prototype answers 'no' because the shapes look different or 'a rectangle must be long'. The square/rectangle question is the classic separator of hierarchical from partition/prototype thinking — it cannot be answered correctly from the picture alone.

pedagogy.summary: Children learn to pick the right standard unit and instrument for what they are measuring — length (m/cm), mass (kg/g), temperature (°C), capacity (l/ml) — and to measure to the nearest sensible unit. The skill has two joined parts: first name the attribute (how long? how heavy? how much fills it?) so the unit family matches, then choose the grain that yields a readable, precise number (a pencil in cm, not m; a drink in ml, not litres).
bestPractices: Name the attribute before choosing a unit — length, mass, temperature or capacity — so the unit family and the instrument match what is being measured.
Teach grain choice explicitly: which unit gives a sensible, readable number for THIS object (cm for a pencil, m for a room), using benchmark sizes to judge.
Establish why standard units at all — contrast two children's hand-spans giving different counts — so children see standard units let everyone compare.
Give a mixed 'measuring station' across all four attributes so choosing (not just reading) is the practised act.
Introduce standard units once the need is understood; the progression warns that heavy early use of many varied non-standard units can actually interfere with grasping why standard units are needed.
keyRepresentations: A measuring station: ruler/tape, kitchen scale, measuring jug, thermometer, with unit dials m/cm, kg/g, l/ml, °C
Benchmark objects for each unit (a metre stick, a 1 kg bag, a 1 litre bottle)
A sorting chart matching everyday objects to their sensible unit
The 'same object, different hand-spans' contrast motivating standard units
commonMisconceptions: Uses a unit or tool from the wrong attribute — e.g. reaches for a ruler to find 'how much water', or gives grams for a length.
Picks the wrong grain — measures a pencil in metres ('0 m') or a room laboriously in centimetres — not choosing to the nearest appropriate unit.
Happily reports a non-standard count ('6 cubes') when a standard measurement is asked for, not seeing why standard units matter.
Reads the instrument carelessly — doesn't measure to the nearest mark, mis-reads the jug's meniscus or the scale.

learn.summary: Children aged 6–7 learn to measure in appropriate standard units: length (m/cm), mass (kg/g), temperature (°C) and capacity (litres/ml). The skill has two joined parts: first name the attribute (how long? how heavy? how much fills it? how hot?) so the unit family and instrument match, then choose the grain of unit that yields a readable, precise number (a pencil in cm, not m; a drink in ml, not litres), and read the instrument to the nearest sensible mark.

activities.title: Measuring station: choose the tool and the unit
feedback: If a learner dials the pencil to metres and reads '0 m', ask: does that number tell us anything useful? Prompt them to choose a smaller unit so the number becomes readable.
If a learner reaches for the ruler to measure the water, ask: does a ruler tell us how MUCH liquid there is, or just how tall the jug is? Redirect to the measuring jug and millilitres.

When a learner picks cm for the pencil and m for the table, confirm: you matched the unit to the size so the number is easy to read and sensible for that object (and if a more exact table length is needed, centimetres can be used too).
If a learner can measure but cannot say why cm rather than m, ask them to compare the two readings and name which is sensible for this object.
activities.rationale: Making the choice of instrument and unit the practised act — and letting a bad choice produce an awkward or impossible reading — is intended to rehearse grain judgement and attribute-matching directly, rather than only reading a pre-chosen tool. An optional interactive version can recompute the readout live as the unit dial turns so the awkward-to-clean transition is immediate; the same learning can be done with real instruments and objects.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils choose and use appropriate standard units to estimate and measure length/height (m/cm), mass (kg/g), temperature (°C) and capacity (litres/ml) to the nearest appropriate unit, using rulers, scales, thermometers and measuring vessels.

Measuring length consists of choosing a unit of measure and iterating it along the object; second graders select and use appropriate tools such as rulers, metre sticks and measuring tapes (2.MD.1). Children may not appreciate the need for identical, standard units and will even measure with a tool subdivided into different-sized units and conclude quantities with more units are larger; establishing why standard units are needed is central.
learnerActions: Set out a mixed set of objects one at a time — a pencil, a table, an apple, a jug of juice, a cup of water (and, if available, something whose temperature matters) — with a ruler/tape, a kitchen scale, a measuring jug and a thermometer all available.
For each object, first say out loud what KIND of measurement this is: how long? how heavy? how much fills it? how hot?
Pick the matching instrument, then choose the standard unit (m or cm, kg or g, litres or ml, °C).
Measure to the nearest mark and state the amount with its unit.

Try a deliberate mismatch — measure the pencil in metres — and notice the number is useless (to the nearest metre a pencil rounds to '0 m'); then switch to centimetres and get a clean reading (a real pencil is usually somewhere between about 10 cm and 19 cm, depending on how much it has been sharpened).
Try reaching for the ruler to measure the jug of juice and notice it cannot give a capacity reading at all.
activities.intendedInsight: You first decide what kind of quantity you are measuring so the unit family and tool fit, then choose a unit grain that gives a sensible, readable number.

activities.title: Why standard units at all — the hand-span contrast
feedback: If a learner is untroubled that the two hand-span counts differ, ask: if you and a friend measured the same table, should you get the same answer? Why didn't you?
If a learner reports a non-standard count ('6 cubes') when a standard unit was asked for, point back to the hand-span contrast and ask which answer another person could check.
activities.rationale: Contrasting two people's hand-spans on the same object is intended to surface the misconception that a personal or non-standard count is sufficient, and to motivate why standard units matter before they are relied on.
sourceClaims: Measuring length consists of choosing a unit of measure and iterating it along the object; second graders select and use appropriate tools such as rulers, metre sticks and measuring tapes (2.MD.1). Children may not appreciate the need for identical, standard units and will even measure with a tool subdivided into different-sized units and conclude quantities with more units are larger; establishing why standard units are needed is central.
learnerActions: Measure the same object (e.g. a table) in hand-spans with two different people and record both counts — for example one person gets 8, another gets 9.
Discuss why the two counts differ for the same table.
Re-measure with a ruler in centimetres and compare: everyone gets the same number.
Explain in your own words why we use standard units like centimetres instead of hand-spans or cubes.
activities.intendedInsight: Standard units let everyone agree and compare, because a non-standard unit changes from person to person.

activities.title: Sort objects to their sensible unit
feedback: If a learner picks kg for an apple, compare the apple against a 1 kg bag benchmark and ask whether the apple is about that heavy.
If a learner sorts a pencil under metres, ask them to picture a metre stick and judge whether the pencil is close to that length.
activities.rationale: Sorting objects to units and choosing the best unit checks the judgement that underlies the choosing skill and is strongly discriminating; it verifies the decision rather than rehearsing the physical act of measuring, so use it alongside hands-on measuring, not instead of it.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils choose and use appropriate standard units to estimate and measure length/height (m/cm), mass (kg/g), temperature (°C) and capacity (litres/ml) to the nearest appropriate unit, using rulers, scales, thermometers and measuring vessels.
learnerActions: Sort a set of everyday objects under the unit you would use: m, cm, kg, g, litres, ml, °C.
Answer targeted questions such as 'Which unit would you use to weigh an apple?' and justify the choice, rejecting a too-big option like kilograms in favour of grams.
Pair each unit with a benchmark object (a metre stick, a 1 kg bag, a 1 litre bottle) and use the benchmark to sanity-check your sorting.
activities.intendedInsight: Each attribute and each sensible size has a matching unit family and grain, which a benchmark size helps you judge.

activities.title: Benchmark reference card
feedback: If a learner is unsure of a unit, direct them to the benchmark and ask: is the object about this big/heavy, or much bigger/smaller?
activities.rationale: A reference chart supports unit choice as a reminder, but it cannot let a learner make and test a choice; it is a scaffold to use alongside active measuring, not a substitute for it.
learnerActions: Keep a reference chart beside your measuring that pairs each unit with a benchmark size and example objects (a metre stick for m, a 1 kg bag for kg, a 1 litre bottle for litres).
Reveal each pairing and use it to check whether your chosen unit looks right for the object in front of you.
activities.intendedInsight: Anchoring each unit to a familiar benchmark size helps you judge which unit gives a readable number.

activities.title: Read the instrument to the nearest mark
feedback: If a learner reads the jug from above or below eye level, show that the line appears to move; have them bring their eyes level with the liquid surface.
If a learner reads off the wrong mark, have them find the nearest marked line and read again. Do not reteach unit choice — that skill is intact here.
activities.rationale: Careless reading is a performance slip separate from unit choice; scaffolding accurate reading addresses it without undoing the choosing skill the learner already has.
learnerActions: With the correct tool and unit already chosen, read a ruler, scale, measuring jug and thermometer carefully.
Read the measuring jug at eye level and find the liquid line (meniscus).
Round to the nearest marked line rather than guessing a whole number.
State the measurement precisely with its unit.
activities.intendedInsight: Even with the right tool and unit, the reading must be taken to the nearest mark and from the correct line to be accurate.

constraints: Introduce standard units once the need for them is understood; heavy early use of many varied non-standard units, before the purpose of measurement is grasped, can interfere with understanding why standard units are needed.
Sorting and targeted-question checks verify the judgement of which unit to use but do not rehearse the physical act of measuring; pair them with hands-on measuring.
A reference card reminds learners of benchmarks but cannot let them make and test a choice; it is a scaffold, not the core activity.
Assessment is best done by watching the learner choose the tool and unit across a mixed set of objects, not by asking them to recite rules.
An interactive live-recompute station is one way to make a bad grain visibly awkward; real instruments and objects achieve the same learning and should not be treated as replaceable by a screen only.

Choosing units is primarily a categorical/attribute judgement; a spatial 3D setting may offer little specific additional leverage for it, and in-role dialogue can discuss but not itself rehearse the watched act of picking a tool — these are observations about fit, not claims that any medium is necessary or impossible.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source row claimed a 3D environment 'adds no insight' and that in-role dialogue 'cannot rehearse' the skill. These were catalogue fit judgements, not established facts, and have been reframed as narrow, qualified affordance observations rather than universal claims of necessity or impossibility.
The '0 m' and ~'13 cm' pencil examples and the 8-vs-9 hand-span counts are illustrative; real measurements vary, so treat specific numbers as examples to be replaced by actual readings.

The UK National Curriculum source claim is marked verified:false in the source row; its content is retained as cited (it is the only claim covering all four attributes) but is not independently confirmed in this rewrite and should not be read as verified.

The Grade 1 interference claim was not attached to the hand-span activity's sourceClaims because it supports the deferral constraint, not that activity's stated rationale; it remains embodied in the constraints.

probeDeeper: Why did you choose centimetres and not metres for the pencil?
If I asked you to measure the length of the playground, would you still use centimetres? What would you use instead, and why?
Which of these tools tells you how HEAVY the apple is, rather than how big it is?
Your friend measured the table in hand-spans and got 9, but you got 8. Who is right — and why do we bother using centimetres?
assess.correctAnswer: For each object the child identifies the attribute and selects a matching instrument, chooses a standard unit of an appropriate grain (cm for the pencil, m for the table/room, g for the apple, ml for the cup, litres for the jug), measures to the nearest unit, and states the amount with its unit — and can say why that unit rather than a much bigger or smaller one.

errorPatterns.pattern: Attribute–unit mismatch: uses a tool or unit from the wrong attribute — reaches for a ruler to find 'how much water', or reports grams for a length — not first asking what kind of quantity this is.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name the attribute first (how long? how heavy? how much fills it? how hot?), then match the unit family; return to hands-on experience with the weak attribute (e.g. filling and pouring for capacity).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks up the ruler for the jug of juice, or answers a 'how heavy?' question in centimetres.

errorPatterns.pattern: Wrong grain — not the nearest appropriate unit: picks a unit far too big or small for the object, e.g. a pencil in metres or a room in centimetres, and doesn't notice the number is unusable.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Discuss which unit gives a sensible, readable number; anchor each unit to a benchmark size and sanity-check the result.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reports '0 m' for a pencil, or sets out to measure the room in centimetres; accepts a nonsense-sized number.

errorPatterns.pattern: Doesn't see the need for standard units: offers a non-standard count ('6 cubes', 'a jug-full') when a standard measurement is asked for, or invents a personal unit.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast two children's hand-spans giving different numbers for the same object; establish that standard units let everyone agree and compare.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives a non-standard answer to 'how many centimetres/grams/millilitres?'; untroubled that another child's count would differ.

errorPatterns.pattern: Careless reading — not to the nearest unit: chooses the right tool and unit but misreads the scale or jug (ignores the meniscus, doesn't round to the nearest mark).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold reading to the nearest mark and reading the jug at eye level; the choosing skill itself is intact, so do not reteach unit choice.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Right instrument and unit, but the number is read off imprecisely or from the wrong line.

responseLevels.gap: Uses a wrong-attribute tool or unit, or reports non-standard counts, or picks a grain that gives a nonsense number without noticing.
responseLevels.full: For each object names the attribute, selects a sensible instrument and an appropriate-grain standard unit, measures to the nearest unit, and justifies the choice (a readable, precise number) and why standard units are used at all.
responseLevels.partial: Matches the right attribute and a standard unit but not to the nearest appropriate grain — measures the room in cm or the pencil in m — succeeding where the unit is obvious but not where scale or precision must be judged.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Lay out a range of objects — a pencil, a table, an apple, a jug of juice, a cup of water (and, if you have one, something whose temperature matters) — with a ruler and tape, a scale, a measuring jug and a thermometer available. Say: 'Measure each of these and tell me the amount.' Do not tell them which tool or unit. Watch which instrument and unit they reach for, whether the grain fits, and how they read it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands unit choice matches the tool to the attribute and dials the grain to a readable, precise number; a child who does not grabs a wrong-attribute tool, reports an awkward '0 m'-type figure without noticing, or offers a non-standard count — each visible in the act, none of which a child with the full concept does. It is watched, never asked about.

sources.claim: Measuring length consists of choosing a unit of measure and iterating it along the object; second graders select and use appropriate tools such as rulers, metre sticks and measuring tapes (2.MD.1). Children may not appreciate the need for identical, standard units and will even measure with a tool subdivided into different-sized units and conclude quantities with more units are larger; establishing why standard units are needed is central.
sources.source: Common Core Progressions — K–5 Geometric Measurement (2012), Grade 2 (2.MD.1) (ISBE mirror)

sources.claim: Early use of a variety of different non-standard length units, before students understand the concepts and usefulness of measurement, may actually interfere with development of the basic measurement concepts required to understand the need for standard units.
sources.source: Common Core Progressions — K–5 Geometric Measurement (2012), Grade 1 note (ISBE mirror)

sources.claim: Year 2 pupils choose and use appropriate standard units to estimate and measure length/height (m/cm), mass (kg/g), temperature (°C) and capacity (litres/ml) to the nearest appropriate unit, using rulers, scales, thermometers and measuring vessels.
sources.source: UK National Curriculum — Mathematics, Key Stage 1 Measurement

pedagogy.summary: Hundredths extend the tenfold structure of place value one level deeper: split each tenth into ten equal parts and you get hundredths, so 1/10 ÷ 10 = 1/100 and 100 hundredths make one whole. The pivotal idea is the NESTING — a hundredth is a tenth of a tenth, ten hundredths rebuild one tenth (10/100 = 1/10). Children must hold that a hundredth is SMALLER than a tenth even though 100 is a bigger number than 10; the whole-number bias that 'more parts means bigger' is the central obstacle. Build hundredths by repeated tenfold partitioning on a length or a 10×10 grid, not by cutting a whole into 100 pieces in one go, so the recursive ten-in-one structure is felt.
bestPractices: Derive hundredths by subdividing a tenth, not the whole: take one tenth of a strip and cut it into ten — each piece is a hundredth — so the child sees 1/10 ÷ 10 = 1/100 and that ten hundredths rebuild the tenth.

Use the 10×10 (hundred) grid and a length/number-line model together: the whole grid = 1, one column/row = 1/10, one small square = 1/100; shading shows 100 hundredths in the whole and 10 in each tenth.
Count in hundredths across the tenth boundary aloud — 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 hundredths — and stop to name 10 hundredths as also 1 tenth, so the 10/100 = 1/10 equivalence is explicit.
Confront the whole-number bias directly: put one tenth beside one hundredth and ask which is bigger and why, surfacing the 'but 100 > 10' intuition so it can be overturned.
Anchor to prior tenths work — just as tenths come from dividing by 10, hundredths come from dividing again by 10 — making place value a repeatable action, not a new fact per column.
keyRepresentations: 10×10 hundred grid (whole = 1, column = 1/10, small square = 1/100)
Length / number line from 0 to 1/10 subdivided into 10 hundredths
A tenth-strip physically cut into ten hundredth-pieces (1/10 ÷ 10 = 1/100)
Place-value nesting diagram: whole → tenths → hundredths, each ten-for-one
Counting sequence in hundredths crossing 10/100 = 1/10
commonMisconceptions: Whole-number bias on the denominator: believing a hundredth is bigger than a tenth 'because 100 is bigger than 10'.
Not coordinating the nesting — treating 10 hundredths and 1 tenth as different, unrelated amounts.
Believing hundredths can only be made by cutting the whole into 100 at once, not by subdividing tenths (missing the recursive ×10 structure).
Losing count across the tenth boundary (after 9 hundredths, not seeing 10 hundredths = 1 tenth).
Thinking 'hundredths' refers to the large number 100 rather than to tiny parts of a whole.

learn.summary: Build hundredths by subdividing a tenth again by ten, so children feel the recursive tenfold nesting: a hundredth is a tenth of a tenth (1/10 ÷ 10 = 1/100), ten hundredths rebuild one tenth (10/100 = 1/10), and 100 hundredths make one whole. The central obstacle is whole-number bias — believing a hundredth is bigger than a tenth 'because 100 > 10' — so comparing a single tenth against a single hundredth is a strongly recommended way to confront it. Derive hundredths by splitting a tenth, not by cutting the whole into 100 at once.

activities.title: Split a tenth into ten hundredths
feedback: When a child counts past 9 hundredths without naming 10 hundredths as 1 tenth, pause at the boundary and watch the ten small pieces reassemble into exactly one tenth; say '10 hundredths = 1 tenth' together.

If a child says the hundredth is bigger 'because 100 is bigger than 10', place the one hundredth against one tenth so the size difference is plain, and explain that splitting the same whole into more equal parts makes each part smaller.
If a child denies the split pieces are hundredths, show that each of the ten tenths would hold ten such pieces, so 100 of them fill the whole, and name the repeatable 'divide by 10 again' action.
activities.rationale: Deriving hundredths by subdividing a tenth (rather than cutting the whole into 100 in one go) makes the recursive ×10 place-value structure an action the child performs, which the curriculum frames as hundredths arising from dividing tenths by ten. Directly comparing one tenth with one hundredth targets the documented whole-number bias.
sourceClaims: Whole-number bias — drawing false analogies with whole numbers, so that a larger number of digits or a larger denominator is taken to mean a larger quantity — is the central, well-documented obstacle when children extend place value to decimal parts such as hundredths; place-value reasoning (a hundredth is a tenth of a tenth) must be built rather than a rule given.
Pupils should count up and down in hundredths and recognise that hundredths arise when dividing an object by one hundred and dividing tenths by ten (Year 4 statutory content).
learnerActions: Start with a strip that is one whole, already partitioned into ten equal tenths.
Take a single tenth and cut (or subdivide) it into ten equal pieces; name one piece 'a hundredth' and write 1/10 ÷ 10 = 1/100.

Work out how many of these small pieces would fill the whole strip: each of the ten tenths holds ten hundredths, so 10 × 10 = 100. Connect this to 'a hundredth is one of a hundred equal parts of the whole'.
Count aloud in hundredths across the tenth boundary — 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 hundredths — and pause at 10 hundredths to say it is also 1 tenth.
Lay one hundredth directly beside one tenth and describe how much smaller the hundredth is.
activities.intendedInsight: Hundredths come from dividing a tenth again by ten; ten hundredths rebuild one tenth and 100 hundredths make one whole. A hundredth is smaller than a tenth even though 100 is a bigger number than 10, because the same whole is split into more equal parts.

activities.title: Count in hundredths across the tenth boundary and place them on a line
feedback: If a child places 7/100 by guessing, have them first mark the ten equal gaps between 0 and 1/10, then count to the seventh.
If the count continues '10 hundredths, 11 hundredths' without recognising 10 hundredths as 1 tenth, stop at the boundary and name both.
If a child treats 10 hundredths and 1 tenth as unrelated amounts, overlay them on the grid or line so they coincide.
activities.rationale: Counting across the 10/100 = 1/10 boundary and placing hundredths on a 0-to-1/10 line are the curriculum's stated evidence behaviours and surface whether the equivalence is coordinated or merely recited.
sourceClaims: Pupils should count up and down in hundredths and recognise that hundredths arise when dividing an object by one hundred and dividing tenths by ten (Year 4 statutory content).
learnerActions: Count up and down in hundredths from 3/100 to 12/100, saying each amount aloud.
When the count reaches 10 hundredths, name the equivalent in tenths (10 hundredths = 1 tenth), and note that the pattern continues (20 hundredths = 2 tenths).
On a number line running from 0 to 1/10, mark the equal gaps needed to show hundredths and place 7/100 in the correct spot.
Explain how many equal gaps lie between 0 and 1 tenth and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Counting in hundredths and placing them between 0 and a tenth reinforces that each tenth holds exactly ten hundredths, so the count crosses cleanly into tenths.

activities.title: Predict and compare: which is bigger, a tenth or a hundredth?
feedback: A child predicting the hundredth is bigger 'because 100 beats 10' reveals whole-number bias; use the side-by-side comparison to overturn it, then restate the meaning of a tenth and a hundredth as one of ten and one of a hundred equal parts.
If a child cannot say how many hundredths make a whole, count ten hundredths into one tenth and ten tenths into the whole (100).
If a child answers 'a thousandth' for splitting a hundredth, affirm the repeatable divide-by-ten action; if unsure, revisit how each place is a tenth of the one before.
activities.rationale: Stating the reason before comparing makes the bias diagnostic, and the direct size comparison confronts it in the moment, consistent with research naming whole-number bias as the central obstacle that must be built past rather than told.
sourceClaims: Whole-number bias — drawing false analogies with whole numbers, so that a larger number of digits or a larger denominator is taken to mean a larger quantity — is the central, well-documented obstacle when children extend place value to decimal parts such as hundredths; place-value reasoning (a hundredth is a tenth of a tenth) must be built rather than a rule given.
learnerActions: Before any cutting, predict which is bigger — one tenth or one hundredth — and state the reason.
Then split one tenth into ten and lay a single hundredth against a tenth.
Explain whether the result matches the prediction and why a hundredth is smaller despite 100 being larger than 10.
Answer: how many hundredths make one whole, and how do you know?
Consider: if one hundredth were split into ten equal parts again, what would each tiny piece be called?
activities.intendedInsight: A hundredth is smaller than a tenth; the whole-number intuition that '100 > 10 so a hundredth is bigger' is wrong because splitting the same whole into more equal parts makes each part smaller. The ÷10 action repeats to make even smaller places.

constraints: A 10×10 hundred grid and a length/number-line model are complementary and are recommended together (whole grid/strip = 1, one column or row = 1/10, one small square or gap = 1/100); pairing the two models is the original's preferred approach, though a single well-chosen model can also support the learning.
Derive hundredths by subdividing a tenth, not by cutting the whole into 100 pieces in one go, so the recursive ten-in-one structure is felt.

Whole-number bias is the central obstacle and must be addressed, not merely stated; directly comparing exactly one tenth against exactly one hundredth is the strongly recommended means (the original's named approach), though it is one effective technique rather than the only possible one.

Paper or card strips have real thickness and are physical approximations of the ideal flat fractional length; a screen model shows the idealised zero-thickness version. Either can support this learning; neither is required.

Recognition or ordering tasks (e.g. picking which is bigger from options, filling '10 hundredths = __ tenth') check outcomes but do not by themselves build the nesting insight; use them alongside subdivision work, not as a substitute for the child performing the split.

Optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete: a live counter that steps in hundredths and snaps to the 1/10 tick with a flipping '10 hundredths = 1 tenth' label; a size-compare mode dropping one hundredth beside one tenth; zooming between 0 and 1/10 to place several hundredths; a tappable column revealing '1 tenth = 10 hundredths'. These are illustrative, not mandatory.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One source (DfE National Curriculum, Year 4 Fractions) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its curriculum-statement citation accordingly.

The source establishes whole-number bias as the obstacle to overcome but does not mandate one particular comparison technique; the side-by-side tenth-vs-hundredth comparison is the original's recommended means, presented as strongly recommended rather than the sole valid method.
Using both the grid and the length/number-line model together is the original's recommended representation pairing, not an absolute requirement; a single model can also build the nesting insight.

The legacy entries asserted a conversation 'adds nothing over a manipulative' and that 3D 'adds no conceptual gain'. These comparative/necessity claims are not established by the sources; a narrated or spatial presentation can still support learning. Preserved here only as the observation that this planar structure is naturally shown on a grid/length and that the key move is the child performing the subdivision, not as a claim that other media cannot teach it.
The row's reteachPrerequisiteId values and the micro-topic id are internal identifiers and were omitted from learner-facing guidance.

Arithmetic/structure audit: 1/10 ÷ 10 = 1/100, 10/100 = 1/10, and 100 hundredths = 1 whole are all consistent; the evidence range 3/100 to 12/100 correctly crosses the 10/100 boundary. No errors found.

assess.poeTask: Before any cutting, ask the child to PREDICT which is bigger, one tenth or one hundredth, and to say WHY. The stated reason is the diagnostic part — a child predicting the hundredth is bigger 'because 100 beats 10' reveals the whole-number bias. Then split one tenth-strip into ten and lay a single hundredth against a tenth: the hundredth is plainly tiny. Have the child explain the mismatch with their prediction.
probeDeeper: You said 10 hundredths is the same as 1 tenth. How many hundredths make one whole, and how do you know?
Which is bigger, 1 tenth or 1 hundredth — and why, when 100 is bigger than 10?
If I split one hundredth into ten equal parts again, what would each tiny piece be called?
Show me 7 hundredths on a line that runs from 0 to 1 tenth — how many equal gaps do you need, and where does 7 hundredths sit?
assess.correctAnswer: After 9 hundredths comes 10 hundredths, which is the same as 1 tenth; then 11, 12 hundredths. Splitting one tenth into ten gives hundredths (1/10 ÷ 10 = 1/100), because each place is a tenth of the one before; 100 hundredths make one whole.

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number bias on the denominator: 'a hundredth is bigger than a tenth because 100 is bigger than 10'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay one hundredth on one tenth so the hundredth is visibly tiny; re-establish that more, smaller parts means each is smaller. Reteach that a tenth is one of ten equal parts of the whole and a hundredth is one of a hundred.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked which is bigger (tier-2 or probe), picks the hundredth; treats a larger denominator as a larger part.

errorPatterns.pattern: Does not coordinate the nesting — counts to 10 hundredths but treats it as unrelated to 1 tenth ('10 hundredths and 1 tenth are different amounts').
errorPatterns.nextMove: On the grid, watch ten hundredths rebuild exactly one tenth; count across the boundary naming 10/100 = 1/10 each time. Reteach the ten-for-one structure from tenths.
errorPatterns.distractor: 10 hundredths is not the same as 1 tenth.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cannot give '1 tenth' as another name for 10 hundredths; counts past the boundary without recognising the equivalence.

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes hundredths can only be made by cutting the whole into 100 directly — 'you can't get hundredths by splitting a tenth' — missing the recursive ×10 structure.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Split a tenth into ten and count how many such pieces fill the whole (100); make the repeatable 'divide by 10 again' action explicit. Reteach the tenfold partition from tenths.
errorPatterns.distractor: You can't make hundredths by splitting a tenth — hundredths only come from cutting the whole into 100 pieces.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the split-a-tenth task, denies the pieces are hundredths or cannot say what they are; sees no link between dividing a tenth and hundredths.

responseLevels.gap: Counts hundredths as a rote sequence but sees no link to tenths, or believes a hundredth is bigger than a tenth. Cannot explain where hundredths come from.
responseLevels.full: Counts across the 10/100 = 1/10 boundary, explains a hundredth as a tenth of a tenth (1/10 ÷ 10 = 1/100) with 100 hundredths in the whole, holds that a hundredth is smaller than a tenth despite 100 > 10, and transfers the ÷10 action to predict thousandths.
responseLevels.partial: Knows 100 hundredths make a whole and can count in hundredths, but cannot explain the tenfold nesting — lists the parts without relating them (does not connect 10 hundredths = 1 tenth or 1/10 ÷ 10 = 1/100).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Start at 8 hundredths and count up in hundredths past ten: what comes after 9 hundredths, and what is another name for it? Then, if I take one tenth and split it into ten equal parts, what is each part called — and why?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands the tenfold nesting counts smoothly across 10/100 and names it as 1 tenth, and explains a hundredth as a tenth of a tenth. A child with whole-number thinking counts '10 hundredths, 11 hundredths' but does not see it equals a tenth, or believes a hundredth is bigger than a tenth because 100 > 10, or insists hundredths can only come from cutting the whole into 100. The second tier ('why') separates a memorised count from grasp of the recursive structure.

sources.claim: Whole-number bias — drawing false analogies with whole numbers, so that a larger number of digits or a larger denominator is taken to mean a larger quantity — is the central, well-documented obstacle when children extend place value to decimal parts such as hundredths; place-value reasoning (a hundredth is a tenth of a tenth) must be built rather than a rule given.
sources.source: Mathematics Developmental Continuum P–10 (Victoria/SMART), 'Comparing Decimal Numbers', synthesising Steinle & Stacey's longitudinal decimal research

sources.claim: Pupils should count up and down in hundredths and recognise that hundredths arise when dividing an object by one hundred and dividing tenths by ten (Year 4 statutory content).
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics Programmes of Study, Year 4 Fractions (including decimals)

pedagogy.summary: The benchmark fractions 1/2, 1/4 and 3/4 have decimal names — 0.5, 0.25, 0.75 — that should be understood, not merely memorised, by routing through hundredths: 1/4 = 25/100 = 0.25, because a quarter of a hundred squares is 25 of them. Grounding the equivalence in an equivalent-fraction step on a hundred square (or a number line where 1/4 and 0.25 mark the same point) prevents the digit-copying error that treats 1/4 as '0.14' or '0.4'. These three equivalents are high-utility landmarks for the whole fraction–decimal–percentage web, so the priority is that children can both recall them and explain WHY they hold.
bestPractices: Derive each equivalent through hundredths on a 10×10 grid: 1/4 of 100 squares = 25 squares = 25/100 = 0.25; 1/2 = 50/100 = 0.5; 3/4 = 75/100 = 0.75.
Use a number line to show 1/4 and 0.25 landing on the SAME point, reinforcing that the fraction and decimal name one value.
Contrast the correct route with the digit-copying trap: 1/4 is NOT 0.14 or 0.4 — check by shading a quarter of the grid (25 squares, not 4).
Build the three as a connected family (1/4, 1/2, 3/4 ↔ 0.25, 0.5, 0.75) and connect to money (£ and quarters) and measures for familiar anchors.
Move both directions — fraction to decimal and decimal to fraction — and ask children to justify with the grid, so recall is backed by reasoning.
keyRepresentations: 10×10 hundred grid with a quarter (25 squares), half (50), three-quarters (75) shaded
Number line where 1/4 and 0.25 share a point (also 1/2 = 0.5, 3/4 = 0.75)
Equivalent-fraction chain 1/4 = 25/100 = 0.25
Money model (£1 = 100p; a quarter = 25p = £0.25)
Fraction↔decimal matching cards for the three landmarks
commonMisconceptions: Digit-copying: writing 1/4 as 0.14 or 0.4 (treating numerator/denominator digits as decimal digits).
Denominator-as-count on the grid: shading 4 squares for 1/4 (reading 1/4 as 4/100 = 0.04).
Believing 0.25 > 0.5 because '25 > 5' (whole-number bias across the decimal).
Treating the fraction and its decimal as different, unrelated values.
Recalling the facts with no grounding, so errors cannot be self-checked.

learn.summary: Children should learn the benchmark decimal names for 1/2, 1/4 and 3/4 (0.5, 0.25, 0.75) by understanding WHY they hold, not just memorising them. The reliable route is through hundredths: 1/4 = 25/100 = 0.25 because a quarter of a hundred squares is 25 of them. Grounding this on a 10×10 grid (and a number line where 1/4 and 0.25 mark the same point) helps counter the digit-copying error (1/4 → '0.14' or '0.4') and the denominator-as-count error (shading 4 squares). These three equivalents are high-utility landmarks across the fraction–decimal–percentage web, so children should be able to both recall them and justify them.

activities.title: Shade a quarter: finding 0.25 on the hundred grid
feedback: If a learner shades 4 squares for 1/4, point out that a quarter means splitting the whole into FOUR equal groups and taking one group; count that group (25 squares), not four single squares.

If a learner writes 1/4 as 0.4, have them shade what 0.4 would be (40 squares) and compare to a shaded quarter (25 squares): 40 is far more than a quarter, so 0.4 cannot be 1/4; the correct name is 0.25.
If a learner writes 1/4 as 0.14, show that the digits of the fraction are not simply copied into the decimal; route through 25/100 to reach 0.25.
When correct, prompt: 'A quarter is 25 of the 100 — how many is a half? And three-quarters? Show it.'
activities.rationale: Shading a fraction of a hundred grid makes the count of squares and the decimal emerge together, grounding the equivalence in place value and equivalent fractions rather than digit manipulation. Testing a wrong guess (0.4 → 40 squares) lets the child see why digit-copying fails. A linked number line reinforces 'same value, two names'.
sourceClaims: Some fractions are easily converted to decimals, and this equivalence is built by converting to a fraction with denominator 100 (e.g. via a hundred square); the hundred square, fraction with denominator 100, decimal and number line are recommended parallel representations for these equivalents.
learnerActions: On a 10×10 grid of 100 squares, split the whole into four equal groups and shade one group to make a quarter.
Count the shaded squares (25) and write the result as 25/100, then as the decimal 0.25.
Repeat for one half (50 squares = 50/100 = 0.5) and three-quarters (75 squares = 75/100 = 0.75), building the three as a connected family.
Mark 1/4 and 0.25 on a number line and check they land on the SAME point; do the same for 1/2 = 0.5 and 3/4 = 0.75.
Work in both directions: given a fraction, find the decimal; given the decimal, shade the grid and name the fraction, justifying each with the grid.
activities.intendedInsight: A quarter of 100 is 25 squares, so 1/4 and 0.25 name one and the same value — a fact the child can rebuild for 1/2 and 3/4 rather than recall blindly.

activities.title: Predict, then check: why isn't a quarter 4 squares?
feedback: A prediction of '4 because of the 4 in 1/4' signals reading the denominator as a number of squares; correct by splitting into four equal groups of 25 and taking one group.
If the prediction was 25, ask the child to articulate the rule: each quarter is 100 ÷ 4 = 25 squares.
After reconciling, ask the child to predict for 3/4 and check (three groups of 25 = 75).
activities.rationale: A predict-then-check routine turns a hidden misconception into a visible, discussable moment and gives the child ownership of the correction. Reading a fraction as two independent whole numbers (the denominator as a count) is a documented error source best countered with area and place-value models such as the grid used here.
sourceClaims: Whole-number bias — treating a fraction as two independent whole numbers, or judging a decimal by the size of its digits — is a central, documented source of error and must be countered with place-value and area models.
learnerActions: Before shading anything, predict how many of the 100 squares you will shade for 1/4, and say WHY.
Then shade a quarter by splitting into four equal groups and taking one; count the squares.
Reconcile the count (25) with your prediction: if you predicted 4, explain what went wrong.
Read off 25/100 = 0.25 and state whether 1/4 and 0.25 are the same value or different.
activities.intendedInsight: Making the prediction explicit surfaces the denominator-as-count error ('4, because of the 4 in 1/4') so the child confronts and corrects it against the actual 25 squares.

activities.title: Which is bigger: 0.25 or 0.5?
feedback: If a learner says 0.25 > 0.5 because 25 > 5, show that 0.5 covers 50 squares and 0.25 covers only 25, so 0.5 is larger; compare tenths first (5 tenths vs 2 tenths).
Reinforce that 0.5 and 0.50 name the same value (50 of 100 squares) to settle the comparison.
activities.rationale: Direct comparison on area models counters whole-number bias across the decimal point, a known persistent error, by making the relative sizes visible.
sourceClaims: Whole-number bias — treating a fraction as two independent whole numbers, or judging a decimal by the size of its digits — is a central, documented source of error and must be countered with place-value and area models.
learnerActions: Shade a quarter (25 squares) and a half (50 squares) on separate hundred grids and compare the shaded areas.
Decide which decimal is larger, 0.25 or 0.5, and explain the choice using the grids rather than the digit strings.
State why '25 is more than 5' does not make 0.25 bigger, referring to tenths and hundredths place value.
Order 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75 and check the order against the grids and the number line.
activities.intendedInsight: Comparing decimals means comparing by highest place value (tenths first), not by treating the digits after the point as whole numbers; a quarter is clearly less than a half on the grid.

activities.title: Connect to money and matching
feedback: If matching relies on guessing, ask the child to justify each pair via the grid or the £1 = 100p anchor.
Recall without justification ('I just know 1/4 is 0.25') is partial: prompt for the 25/100 reasoning so the fact can be self-checked.
If transfer to a new fraction stalls, return to 'how many of 100 squares?' as the anchoring question.
activities.rationale: The fill-in hundredths chain (1/4 = __/100 = 0.__) applies the denominator-100 representation the source recommends and extends to other fractions whose denominators divide 100 exactly. Money and measures add familiar anchors (not drawn from the cited source), and bidirectional matching backed by justification keeps recall grounded in reasoning rather than isolated facts.
sourceClaims: Some fractions are easily converted to decimals, and this equivalence is built by converting to a fraction with denominator 100 (e.g. via a hundred square); the hundred square, fraction with denominator 100, decimal and number line are recommended parallel representations for these equivalents.
learnerActions: Fill in the hundredths chain for each landmark: 1/4 = __/100 = 0.__, 1/2 = __/100 = 0.__, 3/4 = __/100 = 0.__, justifying the denominator-100 step.
Link each equivalent to money as a familiar anchor: £1 = 100p, so a quarter = 25p = £0.25, a half = 50p = £0.50, three-quarters = 75p = £0.75.
Match fraction cards to decimal cards for the three landmarks (1/4↔0.25, 1/2↔0.5, 3/4↔0.75).

Transfer the hundredths route to a new fraction whose denominator divides 100 exactly (for example 1/5 = 20/100 = 0.2 or 1/10 = 10/100 = 0.1), explaining how many of the 100 squares it covers, just as you did for a quarter.
activities.intendedInsight: The three equivalents form a reusable family: the denominator-100 route extends to other fractions whose denominators divide 100 exactly (such as tenths, fifths and twentieths), and familiar contexts like money give extra anchors for recall.

constraints: Target learners are roughly ages 8–9; this is conceptual work on recognising and writing decimal equivalents of 1/4, 1/2 and 3/4. The Year 4 statutory expectation to recognise and write these decimal equivalents is the curriculum anchor (its source was flagged unverified).
Insist that recall is backed by the 25/100 reasoning: a child who recalls 1/4 = 0.25 but cannot justify it on the grid, or grounds one landmark but not the family, has only partial understanding.

A static reference card showing the three shadings with labels is useful for review, but on its own it does not let a child shade, predict, or test wrong answers; use it as a reference scaffold alongside active shading, not as a replacement for it.

Recognition and matching tasks check whether the facts are known and can diagnose digit-copying (0.4/0.14 distractors) and denominator-as-count, but they do not by themselves build the grid-grounded reasoning or elicit the child's own justification.

An interactive grid that recolours as the child shades, counts squares, and shows the linked number-line point is one effective way to make the mechanism concrete, but it is an example, not a required tool; paper hundred grids and a drawn number line serve the same purpose.
Distinguish the mathematical idea (a value named two ways) from any particular display: the number-line point and the grid are representations of the same single value.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The original flagged the DfE National Curriculum (Year 4) source as verified:false; the statutory-content claim is treated as unconfirmed and is NOT used as a supporting sourceClaim.

The source asserted that the grid approach 'directly defeats' the misconceptions and that a conversation 'adds nothing' and 3D 'adds no value'. These are catalog-fit opinions, not established comparative-efficacy findings; they have been softened to scoped proposals and omitted as universal claims.
Money and measures anchors are retained from the original pedagogy but are not supported by any cited source claim; the hundredths chain is the source-backed element of the final activity.

Arithmetic checked: 1/4 of 100 = 25; 1/2 = 50; 3/4 = 75; 0.4 of 100 = 40 squares; 100 ÷ 4 = 25. The comparison 0.5 > 0.25 (5 tenths vs 2 tenths) is correct. No arithmetic errors found in the migrated content.
The reteach prerequisite identifiers from the source (equivalent-fractions and place-value prerequisites) are referenced conceptually in feedback but internal IDs have been removed.

assess.poeTask: Before shading, ask the child to PREDICT how many of the 100 squares they will shade for 1/4 — some say 4, some say 25 — and to say WHY. The reason is diagnostic: '4, because of the 4 in 1/4' reveals denominator-as-count. Then shade a quarter (split into four equal groups, take one) and count 25. Have the child reconcile the 25 with their prediction and read off 25/100 = 0.25.
probeDeeper: You shaded a quarter and got 25 squares. How many squares is a half, and what decimal is that?
Is 1/4 the same value as 0.25, or are they different because one is a fraction and one is a decimal?
Which is bigger, 0.25 or 0.5 — and why, when 25 is more than 5?
What is 3/4 as a decimal? Show it on the grid — how many squares, and how did you get there from a quarter?
assess.correctAnswer: 1/4 = 0.25. On the grid, a quarter of the 100 squares is 25 squares, so 1/4 = 25/100 = 0.25.

errorPatterns.pattern: Digit-copying: writes 1/4 as 0.14 or 0.4, treating the fraction's digits as decimal digits (fraction as two separate whole numbers).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Route through hundredths: 1/4 = 25/100 = 0.25; shade a quarter and count 25 squares. Reteach equivalent fractions so the fraction is seen as one value, not two digits.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives 0.4 or 0.14 for 1/4; on the grid cannot justify it (0.4 would be 40 squares, not a quarter).

errorPatterns.pattern: Denominator-as-count: shades 4 squares for 1/4 (reads 1/4 as 4 out of 100 = 0.04).
errorPatterns.nextMove: A quarter of 100 squares is found by splitting into 4 equal groups of 25, not by taking 4 squares; shade one group. Reteach equivalent fractions (1/4 = 25/100).
errorPatterns.distractor: 1/4 of the hundred grid is 4 squares.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Shades 4 squares on the grid and/or gives 0.04; treats the denominator as a number of squares.

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number bias across the decimal: believes 0.25 > 0.5 because '25 is more than 5'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: On the grid, a quarter (25 squares) is clearly less than a half (50 squares); compare by highest place value. Reteach place value of tenths/hundredths.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a probe, orders 0.25 above 0.5; compares the decimal tails as whole numbers.

responseLevels.gap: Digit-copies (1/4 → 0.14/0.4) or shades 4 squares; cannot connect 1/4 to 25/100. Treats fraction and decimal as unrelated.
responseLevels.full: States 1/4 = 0.25 and explains it as 25/100 by shading a quarter (25 of 100 squares), extends the reasoning to 1/2 = 0.5 and 3/4 = 0.75, treats fraction and decimal as one value on a number line, and transfers the hundredths route to a new benchmark fraction.
responseLevels.partial: Recalls 1/4 = 0.25 (and often 1/2, 3/4) but cannot justify it on the grid, or grounds one but not the family — knows the facts without the 25/100 reasoning.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Write 1/4 as a decimal. Then use this 10×10 grid to explain WHY it equals that decimal.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The decimal alone can be recalled or guessed; the grid explanation separates a child who grounds 1/4 in 25/100 from one who digit-copies (0.14, 0.4) or shades 4 squares (denominator-as-count). A child reasoning correctly shades 25 squares and reads 25/100; the common errors produce a different, self-revealing picture.

sources.claim: Some fractions are easily converted to decimals, and this equivalence is built by converting to a fraction with denominator 100 (e.g. via a hundred square); the hundred square, fraction with denominator 100, decimal and number line are recommended parallel representations for these equivalents.
sources.source: NCETM Mathematics Guidance, Spine 3: Fractions, Segment 3.10 'Linking fractions, decimals and percentages' (Year 6 Teacher Guide)

sources.claim: Whole-number bias — treating a fraction as two independent whole numbers, or judging a decimal by the size of its digits — is a central, documented source of error and must be countered with place-value and area models.
sources.source: Mathematics Developmental Continuum P–10 (Victoria/SMART), 'Comparing Decimal Numbers', synthesising Steinle & Stacey's longitudinal research

sources.claim: Pupils should recognise and write decimal equivalents of 1/4, 1/2 and 3/4 (Year 4 statutory content).
