pedagogy.summary: At 6-7, using structure shifts from noticing a pattern to EXPLOITING it deliberately: reordering 3+9 as 9+3 to count on from the larger number, using place value so 47+10 changes only the tens digit, and seeing that a square is a special rectangle because both have four sides and four right angles. The pedagogy is to make the efficient move and the inefficient move visible side by side, so the child feels why structure pays off — fewer counts, a digit that predictably changes — rather than being told a rule. CCSS MP7 frames this as the step toward the distributive property and flexible use of relationships.
bestPractices: Contrast counting on from the smaller vs the larger addend on the same number line so the child sees three hops beats nine hops and connects that to 'order doesn't change the total'
Use a place-value machine / arrow cards so adding a ten visibly ticks only the tens column, and ask the child to predict which digit will change BEFORE it does
Sort and overlap shape sets (all four-sided, all with right angles) so squares fall inside rectangles, surfacing the structural relationship rather than treating them as separate names
Ask 'is there a quicker way? why does it work?' so the structural strategy is justified, not just performed
keyRepresentations: Number line for count-on-from-larger (comparing hop counts)
Place-value / arrow cards and a tens-and-ones column machine
Venn-style overlapping shape hoops (four sides; four right angles)
Base-ten blocks showing +10 as one added ten-rod
commonMisconceptions: Always counts on from the first number written, not the larger, because order is treated as fixed
Adds 10 by counting in ones or by changing the ones digit (47+10 = 48) rather than seeing the tens digit change
Believes a square is not a rectangle because they look different / have different names (prototype and mutually-exclusive categories)
Applies commutativity to subtraction (34-10 handled like 10-34)

learn.summary: For 6-7 year-olds, using structure shifts from noticing a pattern to deliberately exploiting it: reordering 3+9 as 9+3 to count on from the larger addend, using place value so 47+10 changes only the tens digit, and seeing a square as a special rectangle because both have four sides and four right angles. The core teaching move is to make the efficient and inefficient approaches visible side by side so the child feels why structure pays off — fewer counts, a digit that predictably changes, a shared property — rather than being told a rule, and then justifies why the shortcut is allowed.

activities.title: Choose your start: count on from the larger addend
feedback: If the child says 'both ways are the same / both fine' with no mention of fewer counts, put both counts on one number line so the nine-hop crawl and the three-hop version sit side by side; ask which they'd rather do and why.

If the child insists you must start with the 3 because it is written first, show that starting from 9 still lands on 12, and link the saving to the order-doesn't-change-the-total idea they already know.

If the child reliably picks the larger start for new pairs AND explains it (prompt-free, generalising), extend to larger single-digit pairs; if they can only do it when told 'start from 9', keep comparing hop counts until the choice and reason are their own.
activities.rationale: Comparing hop counts on the same line makes the efficiency payoff felt as the child acts, and ties the shortcut to commutativity instead of presenting it as an arbitrary rule.
sourceClaims: Using structure includes seeing that reordering addends and applying place-value and shape relationships lets students solve efficiently, building toward the distributive property

Pupils should be helped to recognise and use mathematical structure and relationships; manipulatives and representations (e.g. number lines, place-value apparatus) should be chosen to reveal that structure and then faded
learnerActions: For 3 + 9, first count on starting from 3 — draw or hop all nine moves across a number line and watch it crawl from 3 to 12.
Now start from 9 instead and count on three — land on 12 in just three hops.
Say what is the same (both reach 12) and what is different (far fewer hops when you start from the larger number).
Answer: why is swapping the order allowed here? Connect to 'the order you add in doesn't change the total.'
Try the same choice for 2 + 8 and 8 + 2: decide which number to start from and explain your choice before you count.
activities.intendedInsight: Starting the count-on from the larger addend reaches the same total with far less work, and this is allowed because addition can be done in any order (commutativity).

activities.title: Adding ten: predict which digit moves
feedback: If the child adds 10 by changing the ones digit (writing 47 + 10 as 48) or by counting up in ones, return to the ten-rod / tens column: adding one whole ten changes the tens count. Have them predict the column, then check.
Common error to watch for and correct: treating 47 + 10 as 48. The correct result is 57 — only the tens digit increases by one.

If they predict correctly and explain the reason, keep examples within the two-digit range for now (no crossing into the hundreds); a case that crosses into hundreds can come later, once the tens-digit insight is secure.
activities.rationale: A predict-then-check routine with place-value apparatus surfaces the structural reason the tens digit moves, directly confronting the common error of altering the ones digit.
sourceClaims: Using structure includes seeing that reordering addends and applying place-value and shape relationships lets students solve efficiently, building toward the distributive property

Pupils should be helped to recognise and use mathematical structure and relationships; manipulatives and representations (e.g. number lines, place-value apparatus) should be chosen to reveal that structure and then faded
learnerActions: Before adding, predict: when I add 10 to 47, which digit will change and which will stay the same?
Add one ten-rod to a base-ten representation of 47, or move the tens on a place-value / arrow-card setup, and check: the tens change (4→5) and the ones stay the same, giving 57.
Repeat the predict-then-check for 63 + 10, saying which digit changes and why before you do it.
Explain in your own words why adding ten leaves the ones digit alone.
activities.intendedInsight: For two-digit numbers that do not cross into the hundreds, adding ten changes only the tens digit (it goes up by one) because ten is one whole ten; place value, not counting in ones, tells you which column moves.

activities.title: Is a square a kind of rectangle?
feedback: If the child says a square is not a rectangle because they have different names or look different, sort by property so the square lands inside the rectangle set, then name the shared structure.
If the child checks four sides and four right angles to justify the relationship, affirm the property-based reasoning and ask them to find another shape that fits both groups.
Note: the card or paper shapes being sorted are thin physical approximations; focus the child on the mathematical shape represented (its sides and right angles), not on the card itself.
activities.rationale: Sorting and overlapping by property surfaces the structural relationship between squares and rectangles, challenging mutually-exclusive prototype categories.
sourceClaims: Using structure includes seeing that reordering addends and applying place-value and shape relationships lets students solve efficiently, building toward the distributive property

Pupils should be helped to recognise and use mathematical structure and relationships; manipulatives and representations (e.g. number lines, place-value apparatus) should be chosen to reveal that structure and then faded
learnerActions: Sort a mixed set of shapes into groups by property: all shapes with four sides, and all shapes with four right angles.

Overlap the two groups (e.g. two overlapping hoops): the overlap holds every shape with four sides and four right angles, which is the rectangle set. See that squares land there alongside the other rectangles, because they have both properties.
Answer: what is the same about a square and a rectangle, and what is different?
State why a square counts as a special rectangle, pointing to the shared properties rather than the name or how it looks.
activities.intendedInsight: A square is a special rectangle because it has the defining properties of a rectangle (four sides, four right angles); classification should be based on properties, not names or appearance.

activities.title: Does the shortcut still work? Bounding the structure
feedback: If the child applies the swap to subtraction (treats 12 − 4 like 4 − 12), show with objects that you cannot take 12 away from a group of only 4; the order matters for subtraction even though it doesn't for addition.
If the child prefers Maya's way only because '9 is bigger' without mentioning fewer counts or order, prompt them to compare the hop counts and recall why swapping leaves the total unchanged.
activities.rationale: Probing a tuned counterexample reveals whether the child has grasped the structural reason (commutativity of addition) or memorised a surface move, and guards against over-generalising the swap to subtraction.
sourceClaims: Using structure includes seeing that reordering addends and applying place-value and shape relationships lets students solve efficiently, building toward the distributive property
learnerActions: Discuss the diagnostic situation: To work out 3 + 9, Sam started at 3 and counted on nine more; Maya started at 9 and counted on three more. Both got 12. Is one way better, and why?
Say why Maya's way is better (fewer to count on) AND why swapping is allowed (order of adding doesn't change the total).
Test whether the swap idea has limits: does swapping the order also work for 12 take away 4 — could I do 4 take away 12 instead? Explain why not.
Give the general rule you've found: reordering is safe for addition but not for subtraction.
activities.intendedInsight: The reorder-to-the-larger strategy depends on commutativity, which holds for addition but not subtraction; a learner who understands the structure can say where it applies and where it breaks.

constraints: Count-on efficiency should be felt by actually comparing the number of hops for the two starting choices; simply being told 'start from the bigger' performs the move without building the reason.

A scored check or single multiple-choice answer can confirm which start is quicker or which digit changes, but it hides whether the child reasoned structurally or guessed; use it only after the hands-on work and follow with a 'why' question.

Annotated or tap-to-reveal reference pictures (shape hoops, labelled digits) are useful as a reference but do not let the child test the count-on choice or predict a column; they are a scaffold, not the place the strategy is built.
Reordering to count on from the larger addend is justified only for addition; do not let the child extend it to subtraction (12 − 4 is not 4 − 12).
Adding ten changes only the tens digit for two-digit numbers that do not cross into the hundreds; keep examples within that range unless deliberately extending.

Paper/card shape cutouts and base-ten rods are thin physical approximations of ideal figures; direct the child's attention to the mathematical properties (sides, right angles, one whole ten) they represent, not to the physical object.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original source listed '47 + 10 = 48' as a described misconception (changing the ones digit); the correct answer is 57. The activities teach the correct result and use the 48 error only as the error-to-correct, never as a valid option.

No source claim directly supports the subtraction-boundary move in Activity 4 (that commutativity fails for subtraction); it is a conservative inference consistent with the original's counterexample probe and misconception list, not independently verified.

The original counterexample '12 take away 4 / 4 take away 12' is retained to bound the structure to addition; the rewrite makes explicit that subtraction is not commutative, so the swap must not be applied there.

Non-preferred alternatives from the source (reference-only labelled pictures; a scored check of the structural choice) are preserved as a scaffold reference and a follow-up check in the constraints rather than discarded. The original's 'poor' rating of open dialogue was reframed as a narrow affordance (dialogue without a concrete number line gives nothing concrete to reorder/predict for the visual strategy); Activity 4 still uses dialogue legitimately for bounding/reasoning, and no categorical 'dialogue cannot teach' claim is asserted.

The source's gap/partial/full response levels were folded into activity feedback (prompted vs independent reordering; stating why the tens digit moves; extending when the strategy generalises) rather than stated as a separate rubric.
The '3D adds no structural information' comparative claim and internal prerequisite reteach IDs were omitted; the underlying reteach moves are preserved in feedback.

probeDeeper: Ask 'would you start from the larger number for 2 + 8 as well? what about 8 + 2?' to see if the strategy generalises or was a one-off

Counterexample tuned to this topic: 'you said swapping to start from the bigger number is fine — does that also work for 12 take away 4, can I do 4 take away 12?' to test whether the child bounds the structure to addition
Ask 'which digit changes when I add 10 to 63, and which stays the same? why?' to check the place-value structure is understood, not memorised
Ask 'a square and a rectangle — what is the same about them, and what is different?' to surface property-based rather than name-based classification
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child preferring Maya's way because starting from the larger number means fewer to count on, AND justifying that swapping is allowed because the order of adding doesn't change the total.

errorPatterns.pattern: Sees no reason to prefer either method, or prefers starting from the first-written number, because the strategic value of reordering is not grasped
errorPatterns.nextMove: Put both counts on one number line so the nine-hop crawl and the three-hop version sit side by side; ask which they'd rather do and why, connecting the saving to the commutativity they already know
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says 'they're both the same / both fine' with no reference to fewer counts, or insists you must start with the 3 because it is written first

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds ten by changing the ones digit or counting in ones (47+10 treated as 48 or counted one-by-one), missing that place value fixes which digit moves
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to base-ten blocks / place-value machine: adding one ten-rod changes the tens count; predict-then-check which column moves
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked to add 10 to a two-digit number, the child alters the ones column or counts singly rather than ticking the tens

errorPatterns.pattern: Insists a square is not a rectangle because they have different names or look different (mutually-exclusive prototype categories)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort shapes into overlapping hoops by property (four sides; four right angles) so the square lands inside the rectangle set; name the shared structure
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked 'is a square a kind of rectangle? why?' the child says no on the basis of appearance rather than checking four sides and four right angles

responseLevels.gap: Counts on from the first-written number regardless, adds ten by counting in ones, and classifies shapes by name/appearance; treats each task as separate
responseLevels.full: Independently reorders to count on from the larger, predicts the tens digit will change and says why, and justifies a square as a special rectangle by shared properties — transferring the structural move to new numbers/shapes unprompted
responseLevels.partial: Can carry out the efficient move or state the property when prompted ('start from 9', 'only tens change'), but does not choose it independently or explain why it works

assess.diagnosticPrompt: To work out 3 + 9, Sam started at 3 and counted on nine more. Maya started at 9 and counted on three more. They both got 12. Is one way better than the other? Why?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Both children got the right answer, so the number 12 tells you nothing. The discriminating content is WHY one way is better: a child using structure links 'start from the larger' to 'fewer hops' AND to 'order doesn't matter'. A child without it says both are fine or that Sam's is right because 3 comes first.

sources.claim: Using structure includes seeing that reordering addends and applying place-value and shape relationships lets students solve efficiently, building toward the distributive property
sources.source: CCSS Standards for Mathematical Practice, MP7 'Look for and make use of structure'

sources.claim: Pupils should be helped to recognise and use mathematical structure and relationships; manipulatives and representations (e.g. number lines, place-value apparatus) should be chosen to reveal that structure and then faded
sources.source: EEF, 'Improving Mathematics in Key Stages 2 and 3' guidance report (Recommendations 2 and 4)

pedagogy.summary: At 7-8 connecting representations widens to include the NUMBER LINE and to bigger numbers and fractions: a child writes an equation with three-digit numbers to match a measurement or money problem, draws a bar model to represent and solve a fraction problem, and explains how a number-line diagram relates to the quantities in a situation (CCSS MP2). The number line is the pivotal new representation, and the IES fractions practice guide makes it central: it shows a fraction as a NUMBER with a magnitude — a length/position, not two separate whole numbers stacked. This is where the load-bearing misconceptions live: children place 3/4 between 3 and 4 (treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers), or count tick marks/parts without seeing that numerator and denominator together name one quantity. Alongside, the operational equals-sign habit persists into multi-step money/measurement sentences. Good teaching keeps every symbol tied to its referent and uses unmarked number lines and bar models to force attention to the quantity, not the count of parts.
bestPractices: Use the number line as the central tool for fractions-as-numbers: partition 0–1 into equal parts, mark whole numbers as fractions too (e.g. 5/5), and contrast where 3 and 4 sit versus where 3/4 sits (IES Rec 2)
Use unmarked-between-endpoints number lines and 'what quantity is this?' questioning to prevent counting parts without understanding that numerator and denominator name a single number (IES caution)
Keep every number in an equation tied to its referent in the money/measurement story — units included — so translation stays meaningful (MP2)
Draw bar models to expose fraction and multi-step structure before computing (NCETM: reveals structure, precursor to algebra), then map the diagram to the equation
Translate in all directions among situation, bar/number line, and equation, explaining what each representation shows
keyRepresentations: Number line (fractions as lengths/positions; whole numbers labelled as fractions; equivalent fractions stacked above/below)
Bar/strip diagram for fractions and multi-step money/measurement problems
Part-whole and comparison bar models with an unknown
Symbolic equation with three-digit numbers and units tied to the story
commonMisconceptions: Places 3/4 between 3 and 4, reading numerator and denominator as two separate whole numbers
Counts tick marks or parts without seeing that numerator and denominator together name one quantity
Partitions with the wrong number of marks (four hash marks for fourths) or treats the whole line as the unit
Keeps the operational equals-sign habit in multi-step money/measurement sentences and drops units off the numbers

learn.summary: For 7–8 year olds, connecting representations widens to include the NUMBER LINE, bigger (three-digit) numbers, money/measurement, and fractions. The core objective: move fluently among a real situation, a number line, a bar model, and a symbolic equation, explaining what each part represents and keeping every number tied to its referent (including units). The pivotal new representation is the number line, which shows a fraction as a NUMBER with a magnitude — a length/position — not two whole numbers stacked. The load-bearing misconceptions: placing 3/4 between 3 and 4 (reading numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers), and counting tick marks/parts without seeing that numerator and denominator together name one quantity. The operational equals-sign habit (left-to-right compute; drop units) also persists into multi-step money/measurement sentences. Teaching keeps every symbol tied to its referent and uses partitioning on number lines plus bar models to focus on quantity rather than count of parts.

activities.title: Place a fraction on a number line as a length
feedback: Target whether the fraction is placed as ONE magnitude, not whether a point was tapped: 'What single quantity is this point?'
If placed between 3 and 4: contrast directly — 'Locate 3, then 4, then find 3/4 between 0 and 1. Which is less than one whole?'
For partitioning: 'Dividing 0–1 into fourths needs three marks between 0 and 1 — how many marks did you use and why?'
When 5/4 is placed correctly: 'Good — a fraction can be more than one whole; say why the length passes 1.'
activities.rationale: The IES fractions guide makes the number line central for showing fractions as magnitudes and names the between-3-and-4 error as a documented whole-number misapplication; comparing the point's distance from 0 makes magnitude felt. An interactive placer with live length feedback and a whole-number/fraction toggle can make the mechanism concrete, but a fixed, well-drawn number line with the same partitioning task can also teach this — the interactive tool is proposed, not required.
sourceClaims: Fractions are numbers with magnitudes; the number line is a central tool for showing this. Students commonly apply whole-number knowledge — placing 3/4 between 3 and 4 by treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers — and area/strip manipulatives risk children counting parts without understanding numerator and denominator together name a single quantity; unmarked number lines help avoid counting-without-understanding, and partitioning into 1/n requires n−1 marks between whole numbers.
learnerActions: Given a number line that runs 0 to 4, decide where 3/4 belongs before marking it.

If you first place it between 3 and 4, judge how far that point is from 0 — it stretches past 3, far too long for 'three quarters' (an interactive tool can light up this length, but you can equally read the distance on a fixed, accurately drawn line).
Drag or redraw 3/4 back between 0 and 1, partition that first unit into four equal parts, and mark three of those steps from 0.
State the single amount that point names in one sentence (e.g. 'three of four equal parts of one whole, which is less than 1').
Use a whole-number/fraction view to contrast where 3 and 4 sit versus where 3/4 sits.
Extend: place 5/4 and explain how a fraction can be more than 1.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction is a single number with a magnitude — a length/position from 0 — not a numerator and a denominator parked side by side as two whole numbers.

activities.title: Partition an unmarked line and name the quantity
feedback: 'What ONE quantity is this point?' — answers that only recount marks have missed the goal.
If the wrong number of partitions appears (e.g. four hash marks for fourths): 'How many equal parts, and how many marks between 0 and 1 does that take?'
Praise answers that name the point as a single magnitude and justify the number of marks.
activities.rationale: The IES guide cautions that area/strip manipulatives can lead to counting parts without understanding, and suggests unmarked number lines with 'what quantity is this?' questioning; it also notes partitioning into 1/n requires n−1 marks. This activity focuses attention onto the named quantity rather than the count.
sourceClaims: Fractions are numbers with magnitudes; the number line is a central tool for showing this. Students commonly apply whole-number knowledge — placing 3/4 between 3 and 4 by treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers — and area/strip manipulatives risk children counting parts without understanding numerator and denominator together name a single quantity; unmarked number lines help avoid counting-without-understanding, and partitioning into 1/n requires n−1 marks between whole numbers.
learnerActions: Start from a number line with only its endpoints (0 and 1) marked — no interior tick marks.
Cut the space from 0 to 1 into the number of equal parts needed for the fraction you want (e.g. four parts for fourths).
Say how many marks you had to add between 0 and 1 and why that many (fourths need three interior marks).
Point to the exact spot for the fraction and state what single amount that point represents — do not just count marks.
activities.intendedInsight: A point on the line names one quantity; the numerator and denominator together specify a single number, and partitioning into n equal parts needs n−1 interior marks.

activities.title: Build a bar model and equation for a money/measurement story, units attached
feedback: If the child grabs the visible numbers or computes left-to-right: 'Which quantity is the whole here? Map the bar before writing the equation.'
If units are dropped or mismatched: 'Put the unit back on each number and convert to one unit first — what does 3/4 of a metre measure in cm?' (3/4 m = 75 cm).
Check units match (metres vs centimetres) before combining — convert and name both quantities, so 245 cm and 3/4 m are expressed in the same unit, then subtract (170 cm).
Reward explanations that tie each symbol to the story and that identify whole vs part correctly.
activities.rationale: NCETM describes the bar model as revealing problem structure (whole vs parts, where the unknown sits) and bridging concrete to abstract; MP2 requires keeping symbols tied to referents and units, which here includes converting to a common unit before combining. Falkner, Levi & Carpenter document the entrenched operational view of '=' and recommend relational routines to remedy it.
sourceClaims: The bar model reveals problem structure (whole vs parts, where the unknown sits) and is a precursor to algebra; it bridges concrete experience and abstract symbols.
MP2: attend to the meaning of quantities and their units; create a coherent representation and keep symbols tied to their referents when moving between a situation and its representation.

The operational view of '=' ('compute; the answer follows') is entrenched and persists with age; it interferes with writing structurally faithful equations, and is remedied by relational routines (true/false and open number sentences).
learnerActions: Read a measurement or money story, e.g. 'A ribbon is 245 cm long; 3/4 of a metre is cut off.'
Draw a bar model that shows the whole, the parts, and where the unknown sits.
Before combining any numbers, convert so every quantity is in the SAME unit — e.g. 3/4 of a metre = 75 cm — so you are not subtracting 3/4 from 245.

Write a matching equation in which each number keeps its referent and a unit, using the common unit you converted to (for this ribbon, every quantity in cm, e.g. 245 cm − 75 cm = ? cm; use £ or pence consistently when the story is about money).
Say aloud what each number in the equation points back to in the situation, then solve using the bar (245 cm − 75 cm = 170 cm).
Translate in both directions: given an equation, describe the story and draw its bar; given a story, write the equation.
activities.intendedInsight: Equations should be structurally faithful to the situation — each number carries a referent and unit, quantities must share a unit before combining, and '=' means 'the same amount as', not 'compute left to right'.

activities.title: Argue it out: where does 3/4 really live?
feedback: Never scored; push every answer to a because-clause with a reason about magnitude.
If the child guesses 'between 0 and 1' without partitioning: ask the follow-up — 'Show me the exact spot and how many equal parts.'
Accept a correction only when the child names 3/4 as a single quantity less than 1 and justifies the partition.
activities.rationale: Explaining how a number-line diagram relates to quantities is dialogic; presenting the documented misconception and asking the child to argue against it can check whether magnitude is genuinely understood rather than only recognised. MP2's emphasis on coherent, referent-tied representations supports mapping the proposed equation to the story.
sourceClaims: MP2: attend to the meaning of quantities and their units; create a coherent representation and keep symbols tied to their referents when moving between a situation and its representation.

Fractions are numbers with magnitudes; the number line is a central tool for showing this. Students commonly apply whole-number knowledge — placing 3/4 between 3 and 4 by treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers — and area/strip manipulatives risk children counting parts without understanding numerator and denominator together name a single quantity; unmarked number lines help avoid counting-without-understanding, and partitioning into 1/n requires n−1 marks between whole numbers.
learnerActions: Respond to a partner (real or in-role) who places 3/4 between 3 and 4, saying 'because it's got a 3 and a 4 in it.'
Say whether you agree, then show and explain where 3/4 really belongs and how you found its exact spot.
Finish a because-clause: 'It goes between 0 and 1 because…'.
Judge a candidate equation the partner proposes for a money problem, and map each number to the story.
Tackle a follow-up — 'Is 3/4 bigger or smaller than 1?', 'Where would 5/4 go?' — to defend your reasoning.
activities.intendedInsight: Explaining why 3/4 is not between 3 and 4 — and why the numerator/denominator pair names one magnitude — consolidates the concept and can expose shaky reasoning that a correct-looking placement might hide.

activities.title: Linked worked example: one story, four representations
feedback: Use as a worked example, not as evidence of mastery — follow with a construct-it-yourself task.
If the child relies on the highlighting to answer, remove it and ask them to produce the links from scratch.
activities.rationale: A static or tap-to-reveal matched quadruple can illustrate correspondences but does not itself let the child place a fraction, partition a line, or respond to the magnitude misconception; it is a scaffold toward the construction tasks above, not a substitute for them.
sourceClaims: MP2: attend to the meaning of quantities and their units; create a coherent representation and keep symbols tied to their referents when moving between a situation and its representation.
learnerActions: Study a matched set: a story, its bar model, its number line, and its equation side by side.
Highlight (e.g. tap) one part and see the matching parts in the other representations light up.
For each representation, say what it shows that the others make less visible (magnitude on the line; whole/part structure on the bar; the exact relation in the equation).
Then, without the linked view, reconstruct the bar, line, and equation for a new story yourself.
activities.intendedInsight: The four representations describe the same quantities; seeing the correspondences prepares the learner to construct and translate among them independently.

constraints: Reading/placing a correct point on a number line, or selecting a correct equation, is recognition; it does not by itself show the child can CONSTRUCT the translation or explain magnitude/structure. Pair any recognition warm-up (e.g. 'which point is 3/4?') with a construction-and-explanation task.

Illustrations and diagrams that are evocative rather than measured cannot be trusted for precise fraction positions; use tools or drawings where the partition is exact when the point itself is the learning target.

Unmarked number lines and 'what one quantity is this?' questioning are the intended scaffold against counting-without-understanding; if a line is pre-marked, the child may count ticks and bypass the concept.
Area/strip manipulatives remain useful but carry a known risk of children counting parts without seeing a single quantity — pair them with magnitude language and the number line.

Keep units on every number in money/measurement work and confirm units match (m vs cm), converting to a common unit BEFORE combining; the objective includes referent- and unit-faithful equations, not just a numeric answer.

The linked/tap-to-reveal worked example is a scaffold: it shows correspondences but does not require the child to place a fraction, partition a line, or confront the misconception, so it should lead into construction tasks.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit: 'a ribbon 245 cm long, cut off 3/4 of a metre' mixes centimetres and metres; this is a genuine unit-conversion step (3/4 m = 75 cm; 245 cm − 75 cm = 170 cm) kept deliberately as a referent/unit-tracking challenge. The conversion is now an explicit learner action and feedback item, not only a reviewer note, so a child cannot be left subtracting 3/4 from 245 directly.

The original 'the number line's refusal to lie' and 'the recompute makes fraction-as-magnitude felt' are motivational framing for a particular interactive tool; retained as an optional live-length mechanism, not asserted as the only way to teach magnitude.

Claims that fraction magnitude 'is not spatial-3D' and that a quiz 'cannot' show connecting representations were softened: recognition formats have an objective limit (they do not elicit independent construction), but no categorical medium-superiority claim is asserted.
Internal reteach-prerequisite references from the assessment field are left as source-internal data and are not surfaced as learner-facing content.

probeDeeper: 'Is 3/4 bigger or smaller than 1? So which two whole numbers must it sit between? Show me why.'
'Cut the space from 0 to 1 into the right number of parts — how many marks do you need, and why that many?'
'Point to the exact spot for 3/4 and tell me what single amount that point is.'
'Where would 5/4 go — and does that show a fraction can be more than 1?'
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child rejecting the between-3-and-4 placement, treating 3/4 as ONE number with a magnitude less than 1, and locating it by partitioning the unit from 0 to 1 into four equal parts and counting three — explaining that numerator and denominator together name a single quantity, not two whole numbers.

errorPatterns.pattern: Numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers: places 3/4 between 3 and 4 because 'it has a 3 and a 4' — applies whole-number knowledge to a fraction.
errorPatterns.nextMove: This is a documented false belief — confront with contrasting cases (locate 3 and 4, then 3/4 between 0 and 1) and reteach placing unit and non-unit fractions on a number line as lengths from 0.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child agrees with the between-3-and-4 placement, or locates fractions by their digits rather than by magnitude; may say 4/3 'isn't a number'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts tick marks/parts without seeing one quantity: gets a location by counting marks (or draws the wrong number of partitions) rather than treating the numerator/denominator pair as a single magnitude.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use an UNMARKED number line and ask 'what one quantity is this point?'; teach that dividing into 1/n needs n−1 marks between whole numbers and that the point names a single number (IES).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child counts marks to land somewhere, or partitions into the wrong number (four hash marks for fourths), and cannot say what single quantity the point represents.

errorPatterns.pattern: Operational equals sign / number-grabbing in multi-step money/measurement sentences: writes a left-to-right compute or combines the numbers present without preserving the situation's structure or units.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to a bar model to fix which quantity is the whole and keep units on each number; reteach connecting the situation to the representation before symbolising.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In a money/measure story the child produces a compute-then-answer equation, drops units, or grabs the visible numbers without mapping whole vs part.

responseLevels.gap: Places 3/4 between 3 and 4 (or by counting digits/marks); treats numerator and denominator as two whole numbers.
responseLevels.full: Places 3/4 between 0 and 1 by partitioning the unit into four equal lengths and counting three, explains numerator and denominator together name a single number, keeps referents and units when matching the equation — and transfers the magnitude reasoning to a new case (e.g. locating 5/4 beyond 1) unprompted.
responseLevels.partial: Knows 3/4 is less than 1 or belongs between 0 and 1, but locates it by counting marks or can't justify the partitioning — lists the steps without explaining the point as one magnitude; or handles the line but drops structure/units in the money equation.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A classmate is putting fractions on a number line that goes from 0 to 4. They put 3/4 in the space between the 3 and the 4, saying 'because it's got a 3 and a 4 in it.' Do you agree with where they put it? Talk me through where 3/4 really belongs and how you know — and show me how you'd find its exact spot.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands fractions as numbers places 3/4 between 0 and 1 and can justify it by partitioning a unit into a length; a child applying whole-number thinking reads '3' and '4' as separate whole numbers and puts it between them — the two produce visibly different placements and different reasons. The prompt is hard to answer right for the wrong reason: guessing 'between 0 and 1' without the partitioning reason doesn't survive the follow-up, and a child who truly sees magnitude cannot place it between 3 and 4.

sources.claim: The bar model reveals problem structure (whole vs parts, where the unknown sits) and is a precursor to algebra; it bridges concrete experience and abstract symbols.
sources.source: NCETM, 'The Bar Model'

sources.claim: The operational view of '=' ('compute; the answer follows') is entrenched and persists with age; it interferes with writing structurally faithful equations, and is remedied by relational routines (true/false and open number sentences).

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 7–8 (UK Y3, US Grade 3–4). Writing and calculating ×÷ statements using known tables, including two-digit × one-digit, moving from mental methods toward formal written methods.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y3 'write and calculate mathematical statements for multiplication and division using the multiplication tables that they know, including for two-digit numbers times one-digit numbers, using mental and progressing to formal written methods'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.NBT.3 'multiply one-digit whole numbers by multiples of 10'; building toward 4.NBT.5 'multiply … using strategies based on place value … illustrate and explain using … area models'.
• Operational details: the engine is PARTITIONING via the distributive law — 13×4 = (10×4) + (3×4) — made visible with the AREA MODEL / grid method, which is the conceptual bridge to the formal column algorithm. Start mental (partition, known facts) and progress to a recorded grid before the compact written form.
• Checkpoint: partition and calculate. Tier A (7): multiply a teen by a single digit by partitioning (13×4 = 10×4 + 3×4). Tier B (7–8): use a grid/area model to calculate a 2-digit × 1-digit product. Tier C (8): explain how the grid's partial products correspond to the distributive law and combine them correctly.
bestPractices: Anchor two-digit × one-digit in PARTITIONING and the distributive law: split the tens and ones, multiply each, recombine (13×4 = 10×4 + 3×4 = 40+12 = 52).
Use the area model / grid method as the visual of the distributive law — the array grown up — so the formal method later has meaning rather than being a rote procedure.
Progress deliberately from mental partitioning → recorded grid → compact written form, keeping the link between them explicit so children can fall back to meaning.
Use known table facts as the building blocks (10×4 and 3×4 must be secure) and connect × with ÷ (write the matching division statement).
Emphasise place value throughout — the '10' in 13 contributes 10×4=40, not 1×4 — to pre-empt the classic column-multiplication place-value error.
keyRepresentations: Area model / grid method (distributive law made visible)
Partitioning into tens and ones
Arrays scaled up to the area model
Expanded then compact written layout
commonMisconceptions: Place-value error: treating the tens digit as ones (13×4 done as 1×4 + 3×4).
Forgetting to combine ALL partial products (computing 10×4 and 3×4 but not adding them).
Multiplying digit-by-digit without regard to their place value.
Not connecting the grid/area model to the numbers (seeing it as a separate trick).
Losing the link between the mental partition and the written record, so the written method becomes meaningless steps.

learn.summary: For children aged 7–8 (UK Year 3, US Grade 3–4) learning to write and calculate two-digit × one-digit multiplication (and matching division) by partitioning via the distributive law. The core engine is splitting a number into tens and ones, multiplying each part, and recombining — e.g. 13×4 = (10×4)+(3×4) = 40+12 = 52. The area model / grid method makes the distributive law visible as the bridge from mental partitioning to the formal written method. Guidance progresses deliberately: mental partitioning → recorded grid → expanded then compact written layout, keeping the link explicit so the written method carries meaning rather than being memorised as steps.

activities.title: Splitting a rectangle: area model for 13×4
feedback: If a learner multiplies only one piece (e.g. gives 80 for 23×4 and forgets 3×4), point back to the uncounted region of the rectangle: 'This 3×4 part is still inside the rectangle — count it and add it in.'

If a learner treats 20×4 as 8 (multiplying the bare digit 2 and dropping the zero), keep the place-value name attached: '2 tens × 4 = 8 tens = 80', and show the tens region is 20 columns wide, not 2, so its area is ten times the 2×4 = 8 they computed.

If both partial products are correct but the sum slips (e.g. 80 + 12 = 82 instead of 92), do not reteach the method — ask them to re-add carefully and estimate (23×4 is about 100, so 82 looks too small).

Confirm success when a learner partitions by place value, multiplies every part with its correct place value, recombines accurately, can point from each partial product in the expanded form back to the matching grid region, and can explain how the carried ten in the compact form comes from the ones region.
activities.rationale: Anchoring two-digit × one-digit in partitioning and the distributive law, with the area/grid model as its visual, gives the later formal method meaning and pre-empts the classic place-value error of treating the tens digit as ones.
sourceClaims: Y3: write and calculate statements for × and ÷ using known tables, including two-digit × one-digit, using mental and progressing to formal written methods.
The area model / grid method makes the distributive law visible and is the conceptual bridge from partitioning to the formal column algorithm.
learnerActions: Draw or view a rectangle 13 units wide and 4 units tall and cut it with a vertical line at the boundary between the tens and the ones, so it becomes a 10×4 piece and a 3×4 piece.
Work out the product for each piece (10×4 = 40 and 3×4 = 12) and write the number inside each region.
Add the two partial products to find the whole area: 40 + 12 = 52.

Line the grid up next to the expanded written form (40 + 12), saying which partial product matches which region of the grid. Then look at the compact column layout and explain how the 12 from 3×4 becomes 2 ones and a carried ten, which joins the 4 tens from 10×4 to make the 5 tens in 52.
Repeat with 23×4: split into 20×4 = 80 and 3×4 = 12, then combine to 92.
activities.intendedInsight: A two-digit × one-digit product is the sum of the partial products from each place-value part; the '10' in 13 contributes 10×4 = 40 (not 1×4), because you must multiply the whole value of the tens, not just its digit.

activities.title: Moving the split line — the distributive law felt as area
feedback: If a learner thinks a different split gives a different answer, have them recompute both partial products and add again; the totals agree because the whole rectangle is unchanged.
If a learner splits 13 as '1 and 3' rather than '10 and 3', recolour or relabel the tens region to show it is 10 wide, not 1 wide — the area 10×4 = 40 makes the error visible.
Praise reasoning that connects the chosen split to easy known facts, not just a correct number.
activities.rationale: Letting the split point vary while the total holds steady makes the distributive law a felt, general property rather than a one-off trick, and reinforces why place-value partitioning is the convenient choice.
sourceClaims: The area model / grid method makes the distributive law visible and is the conceptual bridge from partitioning to the formal column algorithm.
learnerActions: Starting from a 13×4 rectangle already split at the tens/ones boundary, split the same rectangle (its width of 13) at a different point — for example into a 9×4 piece and a 4×4 piece (note 9 + 4 = 13, so the total width is unchanged) — and compute the two new partial products (36 and 16).
Check that whatever point you split at, the two partial products still add to the same total (52).
Discuss why the split at the tens/ones boundary is the most useful one: it uses known facts (10×4 and 3×4) and lines up with how the number is written.
State the rule in words: splitting the rectangle into parts and adding the parts' areas always gives the whole area.
activities.intendedInsight: The product is unchanged by how you partition — the distributive law — and partitioning by place value is chosen because it lands on known facts and matches the written numerals.

activities.title: Linking multiplication to division with known facts
feedback: If a learner has no strategy for 96÷8 and resorts to slow counting, prompt 'what times 8 is near 96?' and offer the partition 96 = 80 + 16.
If a learner divides only one part, point out the remaining part still needs dividing, just as with multiplication.
Confirm success when the learner reaches the division fluently via known facts and checks it by multiplying back or estimating.
activities.rationale: Connecting × with ÷ and binding division to secure known multiplication facts strengthens both and uses the same partitioning engine, preventing division from being treated as an unrelated procedure.
sourceClaims: Y3: write and calculate statements for × and ÷ using known tables, including two-digit × one-digit, using mental and progressing to formal written methods.
learnerActions: Write the division that matches a multiplication fact you have made (e.g. from 10×4 = 40 write 40÷4 = 10).
Solve 96 ÷ 8 by partitioning: split 96 into 80 + 16, divide each by 8 (80÷8 = 10, 16÷8 = 2) and recombine to get 12.
Alternatively, ask 'what times 8 is near 96?' and use the known fact 8×12 = 96.
Check the answer by multiplying back: 8×12 = 80 + 16 = 96.
activities.intendedInsight: Division can be reached through known multiplication facts and the same place-value partitioning, so multiplication and division are two views of the same relationship.

activities.title: Grid-to-written-method reference and check
feedback: If a learner picks the trap answer 16, return to the grid: the tens region is 10×4 = 40, so the answer cannot be as small as 16.
If a learner computes both partial products but cannot locate them in the written layout, line the grid beside the expanded form and match region to numeral together.
Treat this as a companion consolidation once the model is understood, not a first encounter with the idea.
activities.rationale: A labelled area-model diagram and matching exercises consolidate the correspondence between grid and written method and test the classic place-value pitfall directly; this is reference and consolidation rather than the first interactive build of the concept.
sourceClaims: The area model / grid method makes the distributive law visible and is the conceptual bridge from partitioning to the formal column algorithm.
learnerActions: Given a completed grid, fill in each partial product and then the total, then write the same calculation in the expanded form (e.g. 40 + 12) and the compact column form.
Match a grid diagram to the written calculation that goes with it.
Tackle a check question with the common trap answer present — for 13×4, explain why 16 is wrong (it comes from 1×4 + 3×4, treating the tens digit as ones) and why 52 is right.
Point to each region of a grid and say where its partial product appears in the expanded written method, and how it contributes (including any carry) to the compact form.
activities.intendedInsight: Each step of the written method corresponds to a region of the grid; spotting the place-value trap answer shows understanding of why the tens must be multiplied as tens.

constraints: Known table facts are prerequisites: 10×4 and 3×4 (and similar) must be secure before combining them, and division work relies on known multiplication facts — reteach the relevant facts if they are shaky.

Progress in order — mental partitioning, then recorded grid, then expanded, then compact written form — keeping the link between stages explicit so children can fall back to meaning rather than memorising disconnected steps.
Keep place-value names attached throughout ('2 tens × 4 = 8 tens = 80') to pre-empt the error of multiplying bare digits.

A fixed, labelled diagram can show and teach the correspondence between grid and written method; being able to move the split line and watch partial products recompute is an added affordance for building the distributive insight interactively, not a claim that a static image cannot teach this.

Matching and fill-in checks can confirm whether the method and its pitfalls are grasped, but do not by themselves require the learner to construct the full method from scratch; pair them with building and explaining activities.

An area model is planar; use squared paper, cut-out rectangles, or a screen grid as convenient — none is uniquely necessary, and a paper cutout (which has slight real thickness) approximates the idealised flat area model well enough that this does not affect the mathematics.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 13×4 = 52 via 10×4=40 and 3×4=12 (checks out); 23×4 = 92 via 20×4=80 and 3×4=12 (checks out — the assessment's stated answer 92 and partial products 80 and 12 are correct); 96÷8 = 12 via 80÷8=10 and 16÷8=2, confirmed by 8×12 = 80+16 = 96; the alternate split 9×4=36 and 4×4=16 also sums to 52. No erroneous alternative (e.g. '60' or '82') is presented to learners as valid; these appear only as error patterns to watch for and correct.

The source describes the variable-split activity as a 'killer moment' of dragging a split line; this is retained as an interactive affordance example, not a required mechanism, and the same insight can be reached on paper by comparing different splits.

Source claims for CCSS-M (3.NBT.3 / 4.NBT.5) and the NCETM bridging claim are marked verified:false in the original and should be treated as unconfirmed; the DfE Y3 claim is marked verified:true in the legacy data but has not been re-checked here.

probeDeeper: You split 23 into 20 and 3. Did you multiply BOTH pieces by 4? Show me each.
Why is 20 × 4 equal to 80 and not 8?
For 96 ÷ 8, which times-table fact helped you?
Estimate 23 × 4 roughly — is your answer close to that?
assess.correctAnswer: 23 × 4 = 92 (20×4 = 80, 3×4 = 12, 80 + 12 = 92). 96 ÷ 8 = 12 (e.g. 80÷8 = 10 and 16÷8 = 2, or knows 8×12 = 96). The teacher watches for partitioning by place value, multiplying every part, and recombining — not just multiplying the tens digit.

errorPatterns.pattern: multiplies only one part — does 20 × 4 = 80 and forgets 3 × 4, giving 80; or multiplies the digits as if 2 and 3
errorPatterns.nextMove: use an area model / grid: a 23-by-4 rectangle split into a 20-by-4 and a 3-by-4 region; both regions must be counted and added.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer of 80 (dropped ones) or 8×4-style digit multiplication ignoring place value

errorPatterns.pattern: partitions the tens wrongly — treats 20×4 as 8 (multiplies the digit 2, forgets the zero) so 8 + 12 = 20
errorPatterns.nextMove: reason 2 tens × 4 = 8 tens = 80; keep the place-value name attached ('tens'), not the bare digit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: tens part comes out ten times too small (8 instead of 80)

errorPatterns.pattern: cannot reach the division via known facts — does not connect 96÷8 to a table fact and resorts to slow counting or gives up
errorPatterns.nextMove: prompt 'what times 8 is near 96?'; partition 96 into 80 + 16, divide each by 8, recombine — binding division to known multiplication facts.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child has no strategy for 96÷8, does not try 8×? or partition 96

errorPatterns.pattern: correct method but recombination slip (80 + 12 = 82)
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach; have the child re-add the partial products and estimate (23×4 ≈ 100).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: both partial products right, addition wrong

responseLevels.gap: multiplies only one part, mis-partitions, or has no strategy linking division to known facts.
responseLevels.full: partitions by place value, multiplies every part with correct place value, recombines accurately, and reaches the division fluently via known facts, checking with estimation.
responseLevels.partial: partitions and multiplies both parts for the multiplication but recombines shakily, or solves the division only with heavy support.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to work these while you watch the method: 23 × 4 (encourage partitioning aloud), and 96 ÷ 8 using facts they know. Watch how they break 23 into 20 and 3, whether they multiply BOTH parts, and how they recombine.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The classic partitioning failure is multiplying only one part (20×4 = 80 and forgetting the 3×4), or partitioning the number wrongly (23 = 2 and 3). Watching the child decompose and recombine exposes whether place-value partitioning is understood, which a written answer alone can hide.

pedagogy.summary: This is the shared LANGUAGE of geometric diagrams: a small square means exactly 90°, single and double tick marks mean 'these lengths are equal to each other' (a second, independent equal pair uses double ticks), matching arc marks mean equal angles, arrows mean parallel, and three-letter notation ∠ABC names the angle whose vertex is the MIDDLE letter, B. Fluency is two-way — reading a marked diagram to extract the given information, and producing correct marks when drawing. Crucially the marks encode relationships that are NOT to be read from the picture's appearance: a geometric diagram is a carrier of stated facts, not a scale drawing.
bestPractices: Teach each mark as a statement of a relationship — a tick pair asserts equal lengths, an arc pair asserts equal angles, a square asserts 90° — true regardless of how the picture looks.
Drill the three-letter rule with the vertex in the middle: ∠ABC is the angle at B; point to B first, then trace the two arms BA and BC.
Practise both directions: read a marked diagram aloud ('these two sides are equal, this angle is a right angle') AND mark up a plain diagram to encode given facts.
Stress 'not to scale' — use diagrams whose appearance contradicts the marks so pupils learn to trust the marks over the drawing.
Use double ticks for a second, different pair of equal lengths so pupils see that single versus double distinguishes independent equalities.
keyRepresentations: The mark key: small square = 90°, single/double ticks = equal lengths, single/double arcs = equal angles, arrows = parallel
A triangle or quadrilateral fully marked up and read as a set of statements
∠ABC with B highlighted as the vertex and BA, BC as the arms
A deliberately 'not to scale' diagram whose marks override its look
commonMisconceptions: Reads ∠ABC as the angle at the first (or last) letter rather than the middle letter (the vertex)
Reads tick marks as a measurement or length value rather than 'equal to each other', or treats single and double ticks as equal to one another
Treats the marks as decoration and judges lengths, angles and right angles from the diagram's appearance (assumes it is drawn to scale)
Thinks the small square is just 'a corner' rather than exactly 90°, or misses that unmarked features are unknown

learn.summary: Teach the shared language of geometric diagram markings as statements of relationships, not pictures: a small square asserts exactly 90°, a matching pair of single tick marks asserts 'these two lengths are equal to each other', a second independent equal pair uses double ticks, matching arc marks assert equal angles, and arrows assert parallel lines. Three-letter notation ∠ABC names the angle whose vertex is the MIDDLE letter (B), with arms BA and BC. Fluency runs in two directions — reading a marked diagram to extract the given facts, and adding correct marks when drawing. Critically, a geometric diagram carries stated facts and is not a scale drawing: the marks override the picture's appearance.

activities.title: Mark up a plain figure, then read a 'not to scale' one
feedback: If the learner labels ∠ABC using an arm letter (A or C), rehearse the rule: the middle letter is always the vertex — point to B first, then trace arms BA and BC. An optional interactive can light up the wrong angle when the wrong letter is tapped, making the mismatch visible.

If the learner reads a ticked side as a measurement (e.g. '1 unit') or treats a single-ticked and double-ticked side as equal, restate each mark as a relationship within its own pair and show that double ticks mark a separate, independent equal pair.
If the learner calls a marked-equal pair unequal because one looks longer, insist the marks are the authority on a not-to-scale diagram.

When producing a diagram, check that every stated fact carries its mark and that equal marks are never left on just one side — a stated right angle needs a square, and equal sides need matching ticks on EVERY side in the equal group (both sides of a pair, or all sides if more than two are equal).
activities.rationale: The topic requires fluency in both reading and producing marks, so an activity that has the learner construct marks on a plain four-sided figure and then interpret a not-to-scale marked figure is intended to exercise both directions. A quadrilateral is used for the marking step so the single-tick pair and the independent double-tick pair can both be shown. Using appearance-contradicting diagrams targets the documented error of judging a figure by its look rather than its marked givens. (Proposed design; not empirically validated here.)
sourceClaims: Pupils use conventional markings for parallel lines and right angles (Year 5) and conventional markings and labels for lines and angles (Year 6); at KS3 they describe, sketch and draw using conventional terms and notations for points, lines, parallel lines, perpendicular lines and right angles, and use the standard conventions for labelling the sides and angles of triangle ABC. Misreading these conventions (e.g. the ∠ABC vertex or a tick pair) is therefore a violation of an explicitly stated convention.

A common misconception is trying to MEASURE angles on a diagram that is not drawn accurately: 'When the question states that the diagram is not drawn accurately we cannot simply measure the missing angles using a protractor. We need to use angle facts to calculate the missing angle.' The page also lists 'pairing up the incorrect angles in an isosceles triangle' as a common error — both cases of judging a diagram by its appearance rather than its stated/marked information.

Pupils frequently infer that a triangle is isosceles (and pair up 'equal' base angles) from how the diagram LOOKS rather than from the tick/arc markings — a documented children's-ideas error of trusting appearance over the marks that carry the given information.

Students with an accurate conception of angle read the additivity of angle measure from a diagram and solve for unknown angles using the MARKED given information (right angles and benchmark angles are marked in diagrams), i.e. the marks are the authoritative carriers of the givens.
learnerActions: Starting from a plain quadrilateral (a four-sided figure gives room to show two independent equal-side pairs without overlap), add a small square to the corner stated to be right-angled.

Add a single pair of tick marks to one pair of sides stated to be equal, and a double pair of ticks to a different, independent pair of equal sides — a four-sided figure is needed so the two pairs do not share a side.
Label a stated angle in three-letter notation by identifying its vertex: point to the vertex B first, then trace the two arms BA and BC, so the middle letter B names the angle ∠ABC.
Switch to reading: on a deliberately not-to-scale marked diagram where one side LOOKS longer but carries the matching tick, state which sides are equal from the marks, not the picture.
State aloud what each mark means as a relationship (e.g. 'these two sides are equal to each other', 'this angle is exactly 90°').
activities.intendedInsight: The marks, not the drawing, tell you the truth about a diagram, and the middle letter of three-letter notation is always the vertex.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal the mark key (reading scaffold)
feedback: Confirm correct readings; where the learner's prediction differs from the reveal, name the relationship the mark asserts.
Highlighting the equal sides together reinforces that ticks mean 'equal to each other', not a measurement value.
activities.rationale: Reading conventional markings correctly is an explicit curriculum requirement, and misreading them is a convention violation; a reveal-based tool is intended to build the interpretation half of the skill by linking each symbol to a highlighted feature. It is a scaffold: it supports reading marks but does not ask the learner to produce marks, so it must be paired with construction practice. Its instructional effect is proposed, not empirically validated here.
sourceClaims: Pupils use conventional markings for parallel lines and right angles (Year 5) and conventional markings and labels for lines and angles (Year 6); at KS3 they describe, sketch and draw using conventional terms and notations for points, lines, parallel lines, perpendicular lines and right angles, and use the standard conventions for labelling the sides and angles of triangle ABC. Misreading these conventions (e.g. the ∠ABC vertex or a tick pair) is therefore a violation of an explicitly stated convention.
learnerActions: Tap the small square to reveal 'this angle is exactly 90°'.
Tap a tick pair and see the two equal sides highlight together.
Tap ∠ABC and see the vertex B with its arms BA and BC light up.
Say each meaning aloud before revealing it, then check against the reveal.
activities.intendedInsight: Each symbol in the mark key encodes a specific relationship that can be read off a diagram reliably.

activities.title: Match and select: check interpretation and light production
feedback: If the learner selects the angle at A for ∠ABC, re-state the middle-letter rule and have them trace arms BA and BC from B.
If a single-ticked and double-ticked side are matched as equal, clarify that double ticks denote a separate, independent equal pair.
Choosing 'the angle at point A' for ∠ABC reveals the middle-letter misread; redirect to the vertex B.
activities.rationale: Selection and matching tasks are intended to check interpretation and limited production, and the ∠ABC item specifically targets the middle-letter misconception that source 1 identifies as a convention violation. Recognition tasks are efficient checks but do not require the learner to construct a full marked diagram, so they complement rather than replace hands-on marking.
sourceClaims: Pupils use conventional markings for parallel lines and right angles (Year 5) and conventional markings and labels for lines and angles (Year 6); at KS3 they describe, sketch and draw using conventional terms and notations for points, lines, parallel lines, perpendicular lines and right angles, and use the standard conventions for labelling the sides and angles of triangle ABC. Misreading these conventions (e.g. the ∠ABC vertex or a tick pair) is therefore a violation of an explicitly stated convention.
learnerActions: Answer 'Which angle is ∠ABC?' by selecting the angle at vertex B, not the angle at A or C.
Match each mark (square, single tick pair, double tick pair, arc pair, arrows) to its meaning.
Mark the equal sides on a figure by selecting/drawing the pair that carries matching ticks.
On a not-to-scale item, identify equal sides from the marks even when one side looks longer.
activities.intendedInsight: Both interpreting marks and identifying where marks belong can be checked explicitly, including the middle-letter vertex rule.

activities.title: Probe diagram authority and unmarked features
feedback: Reinforce that two equally-ticked sides are equal regardless of apparent length.
∠BCA has vertex C, so it is a different angle from ∠ABC (vertex B).
If the learner assumes an unmarked corner is a right angle because it looks square, point out that only a drawn square asserts 90°; unmarked features are unknown.
activities.rationale: These prompts target the specific misconceptions of trusting appearance, misplacing the vertex, confusing single/double ticks, and assuming unmarked features. Reasoning about what the diagram does and does not state is intended to deepen the 'marks over appearance' principle.
sourceClaims: A common misconception is trying to MEASURE angles on a diagram that is not drawn accurately: 'When the question states that the diagram is not drawn accurately we cannot simply measure the missing angles using a protractor. We need to use angle facts to calculate the missing angle.' The page also lists 'pairing up the incorrect angles in an isosceles triangle' as a common error — both cases of judging a diagram by its appearance rather than its stated/marked information.

Pupils frequently infer that a triangle is isosceles (and pair up 'equal' base angles) from how the diagram LOOKS rather than from the tick/arc markings — a documented children's-ideas error of trusting appearance over the marks that carry the given information.
learnerActions: Answer: 'This side LOOKS longer than that one, but both carry a single tick — which is actually longer?' (Answer: they are equal.)
Show ∠BCA on the same diagram and decide whether it is the same as ∠ABC or a different angle.
Decide what mark to add for a second pair of equal sides so no one confuses it with the first pair (double ticks).
Answer: 'This corner has no square drawn on it — can you be sure it's a right angle? How would the diagram tell you?' (You cannot assume it; unmarked features are unknown.)
activities.intendedInsight: Marks are authoritative, three-letter names with different middle letters (vertices) denote different angles (though reversing the outer letters, as in ∠ABC and ∠CBA, names the same angle), and an unmarked feature is not a stated fact.

constraints: Cover BOTH directions: reading marked diagrams AND producing marks when drawing. A reading-only reveal tool is a scaffold and does not assess production; pair it with construction tasks.

Recognition and matching tasks check interpretation and light production but do not require constructing a complete marked diagram, so include a production task where the learner draws the square and adds matching ticks in pairs.
Use deliberately not-to-scale diagrams whose appearance contradicts the marks so learners practise trusting the marks over the picture.

Always add equal marks to every member of an equal group, so at least two sides are marked and never just one (e.g. both sides of an equal pair, or all three sides of an equilateral triangle); a stated right angle must carry a drawn square; unmarked features must be treated as unknown.

Reserve double ticks for a second, independent equal pair, and make clear single- and double-ticked sides are NOT equal to each other. Demonstrating two independent equal-side pairs needs a figure with at least four sides (a quadrilateral), not a triangle.

This notation is a convention of 2-D diagrams; a 3-D environment is not required for this objective. Paper-and-pencil marking is an acceptable medium for the production half alongside any interactive tool.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and their efficacy wording is intended/proposed only.

The original row's recommendation described marking two independent equal-side pairs on a TRIANGLE; a triangle has only three sides, so two disjoint equal pairs cannot both be marked. Corrected to a quadrilateral for the marking step so the single- and double-tick pairs are coherent. Logged as an original-row error.

The legacy row claimed a 3-D environment 'has nothing to add' and that open dialogue cannot deliver this skill. These are catalog-fit opinions, not established pedagogical laws; softened to narrowly scoped notes that 2-D marking (including on paper) suffices for this objective and that spoken discussion can support reasoning about marks even if it is not the primary production medium.

Self-audit: verified that ∠ABC has vertex B (middle letter) and ∠BCA has vertex C (a different angle) — consistent throughout. Verified that matching single ticks mean equal lengths and that single vs double ticks denote distinct independent pairs, with single- and double-ticked sides NOT equal to each other. No arithmetic claims present.

Source 1 is cited in the reading/matching activities only to support the convention-reading principle and the fact that misreading a convention is a violation; it is not evidence that any particular interaction format is effective.

probeDeeper: This side LOOKS longer than that one, but they both have a single tick — which is actually longer?
Show me ∠BCA on the same diagram — is that the same angle as ∠ABC or a different one?
If I add a second pair of equal sides, what mark should I use so no one confuses them with the first pair?
This corner has no square drawn on it — can you be sure it's a right angle? How would the diagram tell you?
assess.correctAnswer: Reads the small square as 'this angle is exactly 90°', the tick marks as 'these two sides are equal in length', and identifies ∠ABC as the angle at vertex B (the middle letter); and on the plain diagram draws a small square in a corner to denote 90° and adds a matching pair of tick marks to two sides to denote equal lengths.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads ∠ABC as the angle at A (or C) instead of the vertex B ('ABC, so it's at A')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make the rule explicit and rehearse it — the middle letter is always the vertex; point to it first, then trace the two arms.
errorPatterns.distractor: The angle at point A
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Points to the wrong vertex for ∠ABC, or names an angle using an arm letter rather than the vertex letter

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads tick marks as a measurement or length value, or treats single- and double-ticked sides as equal to each other, rather than 'equal within their own pair'
errorPatterns.nextMove: State each mark as a relationship ('these two are equal to each other') and use double ticks for a separate, independent equal pair.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says a ticked side is '1 unit', or claims a single-ticked and a double-ticked side are equal

errorPatterns.pattern: Ignores the marks and judges lengths, angles and right angles from how the diagram looks (assumes it is drawn to scale)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use deliberately not-to-scale diagrams where the marks contradict the appearance, and insist the marks are the authority.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a not-to-scale diagram, calls a marked-equal pair unequal because one looks longer, or calls an unmarked corner a right angle because it looks square

errorPatterns.pattern: When drawing, omits or misplaces the marks — states a right angle but adds no square, or ticks only one side of an equal pair
errorPatterns.nextMove: Check that each stated fact carries its mark, and that equal marks are added in pairs.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The produced diagram does not encode the stated facts (missing square, a single tick on only one side)

responseLevels.gap: Judges lengths, angles and right angles from the diagram's appearance; misreads the vertex in ∠ABC; treats marks as decoration or as measurements.
responseLevels.full: Reads a marked diagram as a coherent set of stated relationships (trusting the marks over appearance), identifies ∠ABC by its middle-letter vertex, and produces diagrams that correctly encode given facts with square, tick and arc marks, transferring to a new figure (relational).
responseLevels.partial: Reads individual marks correctly in isolation (a square = 90°, a tick pair = equal) but misplaces the vertex in three-letter notation, is swayed by appearance on a not-to-scale diagram, or omits marks when producing a diagram (multistructural).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a triangle marked with a small square at one corner, single tick marks on two of its sides, and one angle named ∠ABC. First (read): 'What does the small square tell you? What do the tick marks tell you? Which angle is ∠ABC — point to it.' Then (produce): 'On this second plain diagram, mark a right angle with the correct symbol, and show that two of its sides are equal in length.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Asking the child both to READ the marks and to PRODUCE them catches the pupil who can recite a meaning but mislabels the vertex or marks equal lengths as measurements. The ∠ABC item specifically catches the middle-letter misread, and requiring production (draw one) is the interpret-translate discriminator — recognition alone hides the gap.
