pedagogy.summary: Children consolidate the use of standard measuring tools — ruler, metre stick, measuring tape — by choosing the right tool for the object, aligning the zero-point with one end (even when the ruler's 0 is not at its physical edge), and reading the result as an accumulation of unit-lengths in centimetres and metres (and inches and feet). The load-bearing idea is that a numeral on the ruler names the amount of space already covered from zero, not the tick mark itself.
bestPractices: Build the ruler from iterated units first — a child-made paper ruler — so the numerals mean 'units so far' rather than labels on tick marks.
Teach zero-point alignment explicitly, including the 'broken ruler' / offset-zero case where the scale starts at 3 and the length is the difference.
Practise tool selection: match the tool to the object (ruler for a pencil, tape for a table, metre stick for a room) and discuss why.
Stress accumulation of distance: reading '8' names the space covered by 8 units, not the 8th mark or line.
Connect unit size to count (the inverse relationship) when switching between centimetres and inches — smaller units give a larger count for the same length.
keyRepresentations: Centimetre / inch ruler
Metre stick and measuring tape
A 'broken ruler' whose scale starts at 3 (offset zero)
A child-made unit ruler built by iterating one unit
An annotated ruler showing 'numeral = units of space covered from 0'
commonMisconceptions: Starts the object at the '1' mark, or reads the last numeral touched — treats numerals as start-signals, not accumulated units.
Cannot cope with an offset or broken ruler; assumes measuring must begin at 0 or the physical edge.
Counts the marks / hash-lines rather than the spaces (unit-lengths) between them, giving a fencepost error of one too many.
Chooses an inappropriate tool — e.g. a short ruler to measure a room by repeated flipping.

learn.summary: Children consolidate measuring length with standard tools (ruler, metre stick, measuring tape) by selecting the right tool for the object, aligning the zero-point with one end — even when the ruler's 0 sits inside the physical edge — and reading the result as an accumulation of unit-lengths (cm/m, inches/feet). The load-bearing idea is that a numeral on the ruler names the amount of space already covered from zero, not the tick mark itself. Key misconceptions targeted: starting at '1', failing with an offset/broken ruler, counting marks instead of spaces (fencepost error), and poor tool choice.

activities.title: Drag-and-align: the chipped-edge ruler
feedback: If the object is aligned at the chipped physical edge, the live readout is wrong — slide the object's end to the actual 0 mark and the reading snaps to the true length (the arbitrary chipped gap is handled by repositioning, not by subtracting a fraction).

If the object's end sits at a whole numeral other than 0 (e.g. the start aligned at '1', or a scale that starts at 3), the length is the end numeral minus the start numeral — not the end numeral read off directly.
For a broken ruler where the object spans from 3 to 12, the length is 12 − 3 = 9 units; prompt: 'this ruler starts at 3 — how long is the object, and how do you know?'
Ask 'does the 8 mean the 8th line, or the space covered up to that mark?' to surface the accumulation idea.
If the same tool is chosen for every object, ask 'which tool fits this length?' — e.g. a short ruler flipped repeatedly across a room accumulates error.
activities.rationale: Allowing misalignment and offset starts, with an immediately recomputed readout, makes the zero-point rule and accumulation-of-distance the felt centre of the task rather than a rule to recite; this is the skill the topic consolidates. The live unit-count and label, the tool-picker, and the offset case are concrete interaction examples, not mandatory mechanisms.
sourceClaims: Second graders measure with rulers, metre sticks and tapes; a key misconception is beginning to count at the numeral '1' — the numerals may signify when to start counting rather than the space already covered, so '1' must be understood as the space from the ruler's beginning to the hash mark, not the mark itself. Correct measuring requires alignment of the zero-point (including when the 0 is not at the ruler's edge) and understanding accumulation of distance; as with all length tasks, students count the length-units, not the end-points. The larger the unit, the fewer units in a given length (inverse relationship).

At the Length Measurer level a child measures knowing the need for identical units, partitions of a unit, the zero point on rulers and accumulation of distance — e.g. aligning each segment of a bent path with the zero endpoint and summing; at the earlier Indirect Comparer level a child may use a ruler but ignores the starting point.
Lower Key Stage 2 pupils measure lengths using rulers, metre sticks and tapes and choose appropriate units and tools.
learnerActions: Drag a ruler to measure a small object such as a leaf or pencil, where the ruler's end is chipped so the 0 mark sits a little inside the physical edge.
Notice that lining the object up with the chipped physical end gives a wrong readout, and that repositioning the object's end to the actual 0 mark gives the true length.
Watch the running unit-count and unit label update as you reposition, so the reading changes live until zero is aligned (or, for a scale that begins at a whole numeral, the offset is accounted for).
Work through a short series of broken-ruler puzzles whose scales start at a numeral other than 0 (e.g. start at 3, end at 12).
Use a tool-picker: match a pencil, a table and a room each to the most suitable instrument (ruler, tape, metre stick) and say why.
activities.intendedInsight: The number read names the units of space covered from zero, not from whatever end you happen to touch, and not the last mark the object reaches; different-sized objects call for different tools.

activities.title: Build a ruler from iterated units
feedback: If marks are counted instead of spaces (giving one too many — a fencepost error), re-sweep and count the spaces between marks; each unit is a length, not a point.
If the smaller unit gives a smaller count, recount: smaller units fit more times into the same length, so the count is larger (the inverse relationship between unit size and count).
Connect back: when reading a manufactured ruler, the numeral still means 'units of space so far', exactly as on the home-made one.
Note: a paper strip has slight thickness and is a physical approximation; the scale it represents is an idealised line of equal unit-lengths.
activities.rationale: Building the scale from units first grounds the meaning of numerals and directly counters the 'mark not space' and 'start at 1' misconceptions, and sets up the inverse relationship when switching units.
sourceClaims: Second graders measure with rulers, metre sticks and tapes; a key misconception is beginning to count at the numeral '1' — the numerals may signify when to start counting rather than the space already covered, so '1' must be understood as the space from the ruler's beginning to the hash mark, not the mark itself. Correct measuring requires alignment of the zero-point (including when the 0 is not at the ruler's edge) and understanding accumulation of distance; as with all length tasks, students count the length-units, not the end-points. The larger the unit, the fewer units in a given length (inverse relationship).

At the Length Measurer level a child measures knowing the need for identical units, partitions of a unit, the zero point on rulers and accumulation of distance — e.g. aligning each segment of a bent path with the zero endpoint and summing; at the earlier Indirect Comparer level a child may use a ruler but ignores the starting point.
learnerActions: Make your own paper ruler by iterating a single chosen unit-length end to end and numbering the accumulated units.
Point out that each numeral names how many whole units of space lie between the start and that mark, not a label stuck on a line.
Measure a few objects with your home-made ruler, finger-sweeping the spaces between marks and counting the spaces (unit-lengths), not the marks.
Compare counts for the same object using a smaller unit versus a larger unit and describe what changes.
activities.intendedInsight: A ruler is iterated identical units; a numeral records units of space accumulated from zero, and the smaller the unit the larger the count for the same length.

activities.title: Broken-ruler and tool-matching diagnostic items
feedback: For an object spanning from 3 to 12 on a broken ruler, the correct length is 9 (end numeral minus start numeral); reporting 12 signals reading the end mark directly.

If the child refuses because 'it doesn't start at 0', affirm that the object's start can line up with any whole-numbered mark, not only 0, and the length is the difference between the end and start readings.
For tool choice, reflect why a tape or metre stick suits a table or room while a short ruler flipped repeatedly accumulates error.
activities.rationale: These items are strongly discriminating checks of the alignment, accumulation and tool-selection skills. A check of this kind confirms the skill more than it builds it, so it is best used alongside the hands-on tasks above, not in place of them.
sourceClaims: Second graders measure with rulers, metre sticks and tapes; a key misconception is beginning to count at the numeral '1' — the numerals may signify when to start counting rather than the space already covered, so '1' must be understood as the space from the ruler's beginning to the hash mark, not the mark itself. Correct measuring requires alignment of the zero-point (including when the 0 is not at the ruler's edge) and understanding accumulation of distance; as with all length tasks, students count the length-units, not the end-points. The larger the unit, the fewer units in a given length (inverse relationship).
learnerActions: Read what a broken/offset ruler reports for an object whose end sits at a numeral other than 0 (e.g. scale starts at 3) and give the length.
Match each object (pencil, table, room) to its most appropriate measuring tool and justify the pairing.
Explain for one item whether a stated reading is the mark number or the units-of-space count.
activities.intendedInsight: The offset-ruler item is a classic discriminator: it separates children who treat numerals as accumulated units from those who treat them as start-signals or labels.

activities.title: Annotated ruler reference card
feedback: Prompt the child to re-state the rule: a numeral names the space already covered from zero, not the mark itself.
If confusion remains, return to the drag-and-align or ruler-building task to rehearse alignment in action.
activities.rationale: A fixed annotated image is a useful reference for the meaning-of-numerals point, but it cannot itself rehearse alignment, repositioning or reading; it supports rather than replaces active measuring.
sourceClaims: Second graders measure with rulers, metre sticks and tapes; a key misconception is beginning to count at the numeral '1' — the numerals may signify when to start counting rather than the space already covered, so '1' must be understood as the space from the ruler's beginning to the hash mark, not the mark itself. Correct measuring requires alignment of the zero-point (including when the 0 is not at the ruler's edge) and understanding accumulation of distance; as with all length tasks, students count the length-units, not the end-points. The larger the unit, the fewer units in a given length (inverse relationship).
learnerActions: Study an annotated ruler that labels, for example, 'this numeral = 3 units of space covered' and '0 starts here'.
Keep the card beside hands-on measuring and point to where the counting of space begins.
Use the annotations to explain in your own words why '8' is not the 8th line.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing numerals explicitly re-described as 'units of space covered from 0' makes the meaning vivid and supports transfer to live measuring.

activities.title: Real-tool measuring performance (diagnostic)
feedback: Probe: 'You lined the pencil up at 1 — where should its end really go? Why 0 and not 1?'
Probe: 'This ruler starts at 3 and the pencil ends at 12 — how long is the pencil? How do you know?' (expected 12 − 3 = 9).
Probe: 'The 8 on the ruler — does it mean the 8th line, or something else?'
Probe: 'Why did you pick the tape and not the little ruler for the table?'
If tool choice is the only weakness and reading is sound, scaffold 'which tool fits this length?' rather than reteaching ruler mechanics.
activities.rationale: Observing the full act — choose, align, read, record, explain — discriminates accumulated-units understanding from treating numerals as labels, and separates appropriate tool matching from one-tool-for-everything, without converting the task into a recognition exercise.
sourceClaims: At the Length Measurer level a child measures knowing the need for identical units, partitions of a unit, the zero point on rulers and accumulation of distance — e.g. aligning each segment of a bent path with the zero endpoint and summing; at the earlier Indirect Comparer level a child may use a ruler but ignores the starting point.
Lower Key Stage 2 pupils measure lengths using rulers, metre sticks and tapes and choose appropriate units and tools.
learnerActions: With a pencil, a table and the whole room to measure, and a ruler, measuring tape and metre stick available plus one 'broken' ruler whose scale starts at 3, measure each object choosing whatever tool seems best.
Align the chosen tool, read the number, and record the result with the correct unit (cm / m, or inches / feet).
Talk through choices when asked: where the object's end should go, why 0 and not 1, and how the broken ruler is read.
activities.intendedInsight: Children apply tool selection, zero-point alignment (or offset subtraction), space-counting and unit recording in a real measuring act, which reveals understanding in performance rather than by being asked.

constraints: Target ages roughly 7–8; procedural skill of selecting and using rulers, metre sticks and measuring tapes in cm/m and inches/feet.
A fixed annotated ruler is a reference scaffold: it conveys the meaning of numerals but cannot rehearse alignment, repositioning, or live reading; pair it with active measuring.
A broken-ruler/tool-matching check is a discriminating assessment of the skill more than a builder of it; use it alongside hands-on tasks, not instead of them.
Reading or recognising a stated value does not itself elicit the independent act of aligning a tool and reading a length; keep genuine construction/measuring in the core tasks.
Live-recompute readouts, running unit-counts, drag-to-align, and tool-pickers are offered as concrete interaction examples to make the mechanism felt, not as required implementations.
When using paper or card unit-strips/rulers, treat them as physical approximations with slight thickness; the represented scale is an idealised line of iterated unit-lengths.
Distinguish the two offset cases: a non-integer chipped edge is handled by repositioning to the 0 mark, while a scale starting at a whole numeral is handled as end numeral minus start numeral.

Match reteaching to the error: a fencepost or 'start at 1' miscount needs reconnecting numerals to iterated units; an ill-fitting tool choice with sound reading needs the tool-to-scale habit, not re-teaching ruler mechanics.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The original row lists the UK National Curriculum claim as verified:false; treat that citation as unconfirmed. It is used only for the uncontroversial tool/unit-selection point.
Arithmetic check: a broken ruler spanning 3 to 12 gives length 12 − 3 = 9 units; this is stated explicitly in feedback to avoid a learner reading the end numeral (12) as the length.
The inverse relationship (smaller unit → larger count) is retained and explicitly guarded against the common reversal in feedback.

Original catalog-fit claims that a 3D environment 'adds spatial overhead without clarifying' and that an in-role dialogue 'cannot align a ruler or catch a fencepost miscount' were softened to scoped suitability judgements; they are not established necessity/efficacy claims.
Original materials referenced internal prerequisite IDs for reteaching unit iteration and tool choice; these have been described functionally rather than by ID.

Feedback keeps the two offset cases distinct: the arbitrary chipped-edge offset is resolved by repositioning to 0, not by subtracting a fractional number, while whole-numeral starts use end-minus-start.

Independent-review change: the chipped-edge drag now uses a ruler (not a measuring tape) for the small leaf/pencil, so it does not clash with the tool-selection lesson; tape/metre stick remain in the tool-picker for larger objects.

The '8' on the ruler — does it mean the 8th line, or something else?
Why did you pick the tape and not the little ruler for the table?
assess.correctAnswer: The child selects an appropriate tool for each object (ruler for the pencil, tape or metre stick for the table and room), aligns the zero-point with one end — or, given the broken ruler, starts at 3 and reads the difference, or repositions to the 0 mark — reads the count of unit-lengths (not the marks), and records the result with the correct unit (cm / m).

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads from '1' — numerals as start-signal: aligns the object's end with the '1' mark, or reports the last numeral crossed, so the count is off by one.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach that 0 is the start and that a numeral names the units of space already covered (the space up to the mark, not the mark); build or annotate a unit ruler to reconnect the numerals to iterated units.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Object lined up at '1' rather than 0, or the final numeral touched read off directly as the length.

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot handle an offset / broken ruler: with the scale starting at 3, reads the final numeral directly (ignoring the offset) or declares the ruler unusable.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Discuss that the zero-point can sit anywhere and the length is end-numeral minus start-numeral; practise deliberately offset starting points.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Given the broken ruler, reports the end numeral as the length, or refuses to measure because 'it doesn't start at 0'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts the marks, not the spaces: counts tick lines (including both endpoints) rather than the unit-lengths between them, a fencepost error giving one too many.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have them finger-sweep and count the spaces / unit-lengths between marks, not the marks; relate back to iterating physical units where each unit is a length, not a point.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Points to and counts the hash marks; answer exceeds the true length by one unit.

errorPatterns.pattern: Inappropriate tool choice: uses one instrument regardless of object — e.g. a 30 cm ruler flipped repeatedly to measure the room, accumulating error.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold 'which tool fits this length?' — the reading skill itself is intact, so do not reteach ruler mechanics; build the habit of matching tool to scale.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reaches for the same tool for pencil, table and room; laborious repeated flipping or an oversized tool for a tiny object.

responseLevels.gap: Aligns the object at '1' or reads the touched numeral, is defeated by the broken ruler, and uses one tool regardless of the object.
responseLevels.full: Chooses a fitting tool, aligns the zero-point (or computes the length from an offset start), reads the accumulated unit-count, records with the correct unit, and can explain that a numeral means units of space measured from zero.
responseLevels.partial: Measures correctly with a normal ruler aligned at zero, but the skill is tied to the standard case — fails the offset/broken ruler, makes a fencepost miscount in a tricky case, or picks an ill-fitting tool; can run the routine but not transfer it.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put out a pencil, a table, and the whole room to measure, with a ruler, a measuring tape and a metre stick available — plus one 'broken' ruler whose scale starts at 3. Say: 'Measure each of these — pick whatever tool you think is best.' Slip the broken ruler in for one object. Watch how they choose the tool, align it, and read off the number.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands the ruler as accumulated units aligns zero and copes with the offset ruler; a child who treats numerals as labels lines up at '1', is defeated by the broken ruler, or counts marks and lands one over. Tool choice separates those who match the instrument to the scale from those who use one tool for everything. All of it is seen in the act, never asked about.

sources.claim: Second graders measure with rulers, metre sticks and tapes; a key misconception is beginning to count at the numeral '1' — the numerals may signify when to start counting rather than the space already covered, so '1' must be understood as the space from the ruler's beginning to the hash mark, not the mark itself. Correct measuring requires alignment of the zero-point (including when the 0 is not at the ruler's edge) and understanding accumulation of distance; as with all length tasks, students count the length-units, not the end-points. The larger the unit, the fewer units in a given length (inverse relationship).
sources.source: Common Core Progressions — K–5 Geometric Measurement (2012), Grades 2–3 (ISBE mirror)

sources.claim: At the Length Measurer level a child measures knowing the need for identical units, partitions of a unit, the zero point on rulers and accumulation of distance — e.g. aligning each segment of a bent path with the zero endpoint and summing; at the earlier Indirect Comparer level a child may use a ruler but ignores the starting point.
sources.source: Sarama & Clements — Learning Trajectories: Measurement (Length): Length Measurer; Conceptual Ruler Measurer

sources.claim: Lower Key Stage 2 pupils measure lengths using rulers, metre sticks and tapes and choose appropriate units and tools.
sources.source: UK National Curriculum — Mathematics, Key Stage 2 Measurement

pedagogy.summary: These word problems apply UNLIKE-denominator addition and subtraction in context, but their defining feature is ESTIMATION WITH BENCHMARKS (0, 1/2, 1) as a reasonableness gate. IES makes this the front-line defence against add-across: 2/5 + 1/2 cannot be 3/7, because 3/7 is less than 1/2 while the sum must EXCEED 1/2; 2/7 cannot be a plausible sum of two positive fractions that reach past a half. Teach pupils to place each fraction against a benchmark and predict the sum's region BEFORE computing with common denominators, then check the exact answer against that estimate — so an implausible result is caught, not accepted.
bestPractices: Estimate with benchmarks first — is each fraction near 0, 1/2, or 1? — and predict whether the sum is above/below 1/2 and 1 before computing (IES)
Compute exactly with common denominators, then CHECK against the benchmark estimate and reject implausible answers (e.g. a sum below 1/2 when it must exceed it)
Model on a number line marked with 0, 1/2, 1 so 'add-across gives too small an answer' is visible
Scale BOTH fractions to the common denominator (not just one) and keep the value unchanged
Use the estimate to explain WHY 2/5 + 1/2 ≠ 3/7, turning reasonableness into a habit
keyRepresentations: Benchmark number line (0, 1/2, 1) with each fraction placed
Bar models recut to a common denominator via equivalent fractions
Estimate-then-compute two-column layout
The comparison 3/7 < 1/2 shown against the true sum region
commonMisconceptions: Adds across (2/5 + 1/3 → 3/8), producing a sum smaller than an addend
Accepts an implausible answer that violates a benchmark (a sum below 1/2 when it must exceed it) because no estimate was made
Partial-scaling to the common denominator — scales one numerator but not the other (2/5 + 1/3 → 6/15 + 1/15)
Treats 'estimate' as optional and computes blind, missing the reasonableness check

learn.summary: Pupils (age 10–11) solve word problems adding and subtracting fractions with unlike denominators, but the defining skill is using benchmark estimation (0, 1/2, 1) as a reasonableness gate. They predict the sum's region BEFORE computing with common denominators, then check the exact answer against that prediction so an implausible result (e.g. an add-across sum that falls below 1/2 when it must exceed it) is caught rather than accepted.

activities.title: Predict the region on a benchmark number line, then compute
feedback: If the learner shades below 1/2: 'Each fraction is more than a quarter — can two amounts that are each bigger than a quarter add up to less than one half?'
If they place 11/15 correctly inside the region: 'Your estimate and your exact answer agree — that is the reasonableness check working.'

If they report 3/8 as the total: 'Both pieces are more than a quarter, so the total must beat a half. 3/8 is less than a half, and even less than 2/5 on its own, so something went wrong — recompute with a common denominator.'
If they rename only one fraction (6/15 + 1/15): 'Check each new fraction still equals the original: does 1/15 equal 1/3? Both fractions must be recut to the same unit.'
activities.rationale: A number line marked at 0, 1/2, 1 makes the benchmark judgement and the reasonableness comparison visible as positions, so an add-across error lands in an obviously wrong place. This supports the estimate-then-compute-then-check habit the standard calls for.
sourceClaims: Estimation with benchmarks is a key tool for judging the reasonableness of fraction sums and catching the add-across error — e.g. recognising a sum must exceed 1/2, so an answer below 1/2 (like 3/7 for 2/5 + 1/2, or 2/7) is impossible
Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions with unlike denominators, using benchmark fractions and number sense to estimate and assess the reasonableness of answers
learnerActions: Read the problem: 'Tara ate 2/5 of a pizza and Sam ate 1/3 of a same-size pizza. How much did they eat together?'
On a 0-to-1 number line marked at 1/4, 1/2 and 3/4, place each fraction: note that both 2/5 and 1/3 sit below 1/2 but above 1/4.

Before computing, shade the region where you predict the TOTAL lands (above 1/2 but below a whole) and say why: each amount is more than 1/4, so together they are more than 1/2; each is less than 1/2, so together they are less than 1.
Rename BOTH fractions to a common denominator (fifteenths): 2/5 = 6/15 and 1/3 = 5/15, then add to get 11/15.
Place 11/15 on the line and check it falls inside your predicted region.
Try an add-across answer (3/8): place it on the line and notice it lands below 1/2 — in the zone you already ruled out as impossible.
activities.intendedInsight: Benchmark estimation predicts a region for the sum; the exact answer must land inside it. Here add-across produces a sum (3/8) smaller than the addend 2/5, which the benchmark exposes as impossible.

activities.title: Argue why an answer is impossible
feedback: If the learner accepts 3/7: 'Compare 3/7 to 1/2. If one of the two parts is already 1/2, can the total be less than 1/2?'
If they explain correctly: 'Exactly — the benchmark catches the error even before you compute.'
If they can reject it but not compute the true answer: 'Now rename both to the same denominator to find what the real total is.'
activities.rationale: Turning the implausible-sum distractor into something the learner must argue against makes reasonableness a habit rather than an optional afterthought. Posing it as a challenge from a character can prompt estimation, though the position judgement benefits from a visual line.
sourceClaims: Estimation with benchmarks is a key tool for judging the reasonableness of fraction sums and catching the add-across error — e.g. recognising a sum must exceed 1/2, so an answer below 1/2 (like 3/7 for 2/5 + 1/2, or 2/7) is impossible

The add-across misconception is far more prevalent on unlike-denominator items (only ~54% correct) than like-denominator ones; 'which is bigger' reasoning and estimation before computing support remediation
learnerActions: A friend proposes that 2/5 + 1/2 = 3/7. Decide whether this can be right.
Place 3/7 and 1/2 on a benchmark line and state where each sits relative to 1/2.
Explain in your own words why 3/7 cannot be the sum: 3/7 is less than 1/2, but adding 1/2 to a positive amount must give more than 1/2.
Give the correct method: rename both to a common denominator and compute the true sum.
Repeat the argument for another proposed value, 2/7: show it is below 1/2, but since one addend here is exactly 1/2, the total must exceed 1/2, so 2/7 cannot be the sum.
activities.intendedInsight: Reasonableness can be used to reject an answer before or without full computation: adding 1/2 to a positive amount must give more than 1/2, and benchmarks make that concrete.

activities.title: Rename both fractions to the common unit
feedback: If a learner leaves one fraction unscaled: 'Does 1/15 equal 1/3? Multiply numerator and denominator of 1/3 by the same number.'
If they rename both correctly: 'Good — each new fraction still has the same value, just a smaller unit.'
If they change the value while renaming: 'Equivalent fractions must point to the same spot on the line — check 6/15 sits exactly where 2/5 does.'
activities.rationale: Partial-scaling is a distinct, common error from add-across; practising renaming both fractions and verifying equivalence targets it directly. Bar models recut to a common denominator can make the shared unit concrete.
learnerActions: For 2/5 + 1/3, find a common denominator (15) and recut both fractions to fifteenths.
Write each equivalent fraction and verify it equals the original: 2/5 = 6/15 (×3/3), 1/3 = 5/15 (×5/5).
Spot the error in a given partial-scaling attempt: 2/5 + 1/3 → 6/15 + 1/15 = 7/15. Identify that 1/15 does not equal 1/3.
Correct it to 6/15 + 5/15 = 11/15.
Check the result against a benchmark estimate (between 1/2 and 1).
activities.intendedInsight: Both fractions must be renamed to the common denominator and each equivalent fraction must keep its original value; changing only one numerator breaks the equivalence.

constraints: Estimation with benchmarks must come BEFORE computing and the reasonableness check must come AFTER; treating estimation as optional removes the gate that catches add-across errors.
Both fractions must be renamed to the common denominator with value unchanged — scaling only one is a distinct error to guard against.

Multiple-choice or recognition items (e.g. 'which answer is impossible?') can diagnose the misconception and prompt estimation, but recognition alone does not show the learner independently predicting a region and constructing the common-denominator computation; include tasks requiring that construction.

A static benchmark line with a worked estimate-then-compute example and tap-to-reveal can illustrate the habit, but does not let the learner predict and test on a fresh problem; use it as a scaffold, not the whole task.

Optional interactive features (dragging fractions onto a line, shading a predicted region, a recutter that scales both fractions together, an 'add-across' toggle) make the mechanism concrete but are illustrative examples, not mandatory. The learning goal is the estimate-then-compute-then-check sequence by any suitable medium.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source listed the Common Core 5.NF.2 claim with verified:false; treat its citation as unverified even though it supports the benchmark-estimation principle.

Arithmetic self-audit: 2/5 + 1/3 = 6/15 + 5/15 = 11/15 (correct); 2/5 = 6/15 and 1/3 = 5/15 (correct). Add-across distractors 3/8 (for 2/5+1/3) and 3/7 (for 2/5+1/2) both fall below 1/2, consistent with the source. Partial-scaling example 6/15 + 1/15 = 7/15 is a consistent error illustration. 2/7 (≈0.29) is below 1/2 and is used ONLY as a separately proposed impossible value, NOT as the add-across result of 2/5 + 1/2 (which is 3/7).

The source's claim that '3D adds nothing' for planar fraction work was removed as unsupported universal boilerplate; a planar representation is well-suited here, but this is a narrow affordance, not a universal law.
Softened the source's framing that estimation 'becomes the alarm' and that 2D is uniquely able to teach this into a narrowly scoped affordance of benchmark number lines.

probeDeeper: Your exact answer — is it bigger or smaller than 1/2? Does that match your estimate?
Why can't 2/5 + 1/2 be 3/7?
Which benchmark (0, 1/2, 1) is 2/5 closest to, and which is 1/3 closest to?
If you renamed only 2/5 to fifteenths but left 1/3 alone, what goes wrong?
assess.correctAnswer: Estimate: 2/5 is a bit less than 1/2 and 1/3 is a bit less than 1/2, so together a bit more than 1/2 but less than 1. Exact: 2/5 + 1/3 = 6/15 + 5/15 = 11/15, which is between 1/2 and 1 — consistent with the estimate.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds across: 2/5 + 1/3 → 3/8, a sum smaller than either sensible estimate
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront with the benchmark — 'both are near a half, so the total must beat a half; 3/8 is less than a half, so something's wrong' — then recompute with a common denominator
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer 3/8 (or 3/7 for 2/5 + 1/2); denominators added; the result sits below 1/2

errorPatterns.pattern: Computes blind and accepts an implausible answer — no estimate made, so a sum that violates a benchmark (below 1/2 when it must exceed it) goes unchallenged
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist on the benchmark prediction first and the check after; make rejecting an impossible answer a required step, not optional
errorPatterns.revealedBy: No estimate offered; an out-of-range answer is reported with no sense that it's impossible

errorPatterns.pattern: Partial-scaling to the common denominator: scales one fraction but not the other (2/5 + 1/3 → 6/15 + 1/15 = 7/15)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that BOTH fractions must be renamed to the common unit — recut both bars to fifteenths — and check each equivalent fraction equals the original
errorPatterns.revealedBy: One numerator changed, the other left as-is; common denominator found but not applied to both

responseLevels.gap: Adds across, makes no estimate, and accepts an impossible answer; benchmarks are not used.
responseLevels.full: Estimates with benchmarks first, computes with a common denominator applied to both fractions, checks the exact answer against the estimate and rejects implausible results, and transfers the estimate-then-check habit to a new unlike-denominator problem.
responseLevels.partial: Computes the exact sum correctly but skips or ignores the benchmark estimate (no reasonableness check), or estimates sensibly but then partial-scales the computation.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Tara ate 2/5 of a pizza and Sam ate 1/3 of the same size pizza. First estimate roughly how much they ate altogether — more or less than a half? more or less than a whole? Then work out the exact amount, showing your method.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Requiring the benchmark estimate BEFORE computing is the discriminator: a child who reasons correctly predicts 'between a half and a whole' and then produces 11/15, which agrees; a child who adds across gets 3/8, which sits BELOW a half and so contradicts a sound estimate — and the telling thing is whether they NOTICE. Watching the estimate-then-compute-then-check sequence (all part of the procedure here, per the topic's own evidence) exposes both the computational error and the missing reasonableness habit, neither visible in a bare answer.

sources.claim: Estimation with benchmarks is a key tool for judging the reasonableness of fraction sums and catching the add-across error — e.g. recognising a sum must exceed 1/2, so an answer below 1/2 (like 3/7 for 2/5 + 1/2, or 2/7) is impossible
sources.source: IES / What Works Clearinghouse — Developing Effective Fractions Instruction K–8 (Siegler et al. 2010), Recommendation 2

sources.claim: The add-across misconception is far more prevalent on unlike-denominator items (only ~54% correct) than like-denominator ones; 'which is bigger' reasoning and estimation before computing support remediation
sources.source: NFER — Common mistakes when adding fractions (Year 6 diagnostic)

sources.claim: Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions with unlike denominators, using benchmark fractions and number sense to estimate and assess the reasonableness of answers
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics — 5.NF.2

pedagogy.summary: The general principle that multiplying the numerator and denominator by the same number n gives an equivalent fraction, and WHY: splitting each of the b parts into n equal pieces makes n×b pieces in the whole and n×a shaded, so the same amount is renamed with a finer counting-unit — the whole and the shaded magnitude are unchanged. This extends to tenths and hundredths (3/10 = 30/100) and is the same as multiplying the fraction by n/n, a name for 1.
bestPractices: Justify with re-partition: each part becomes n parts, so both counts grow ×n while the magnitude is fixed — the point does not move.
Generalise from many worked cases to the statement a/b = (n×a)/(n×b) (IES: any fraction can be written infinitely many equivalent ways).
Frame the move as multiplying by n/n = 1, so the value cannot change.
Apply directly to tenths and hundredths (3/10 = 30/100) as a bridge to decimals.
Confront the additive error head-on — multiplying is repeated re-partitioning; adding a constant is not.
keyRepresentations: Area model re-partitioned (each part → n parts)
Stacked / dual-labelled number lines
Multiplying by n/n (a name for 1)
Ratio table of numerators and denominators
Tenths ↔ hundredths grid
commonMisconceptions: Additive equivalence — adding the same number to top and bottom keeps it equal (IES whole-number thinking)
Whole-number bias — (n×a)/(n×b) 'must be bigger' because the numbers are bigger (4/6 > 2/3)
Multiplying only one part
Believing the value must change because 'you did something to it'

learn.summary: Learners understand WHY multiplying numerator and denominator by the same whole number n (n ≥ 1) gives an equivalent fraction: splitting each of the b parts into n equal pieces makes n×b pieces in the whole and n×a shaded, so the SAME magnitude is renamed with a finer counting-unit. This is the same as multiplying by n/n, a name for 1, so the value cannot change. It extends to tenths and hundredths (3/10 = 30/100). The central contrast is with the additive error: adding a constant to top and bottom is not re-partitioning and in general changes the amount (the only exception is a fraction equal to 1, such as 2/2 → 3/3); for example, adding 1 to the numerator and 1 to the denominator turns 2/3 into 3/4, which is larger, not equal.

activities.title: Rename the same amount: fix the shaded length, change the labels
feedback: If both counts grew but the shaded length stayed put, you have renamed the same amount — that is why 2/3 = 4/6.
If you changed only one part (just the top or just the bottom), re-cut EVERY part instead: splitting each piece changes both the shaded count and the total count together.
If the additive bar (3/4) visibly reached past the 2/3 strip, you have shown that adding 1 to each part is not equivalence — it moves you to a bigger amount.
To check the value is unchanged, ask: did I split each part into equal pieces (keeps the amount), or did I add extra amount (changes it)?
activities.rationale: Equivalence is produced by re-partitioning the same quantity into finer equal parts, so any fraction has infinitely many equivalent names; holding a fixed magnitude while the labels change makes the invariance concrete and directly confronts the additive whole-number error. Paper strips are approximations of ideal flat regions, so the teaching point is the preserved shaded magnitude, not the paper itself.
sourceClaims: Equivalence is produced by re-partitioning the same quantity into finer equal parts (four pizzas among eight children: 4/8 = 2/4 = 1/2), so any fraction has infinitely many equivalent names; the additive 'add the same number to top and bottom' error is whole-number thinking, and treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers underlies errors like 3/8 > 3/5.
learnerActions: Shade 2/3 of a bar (or mark 2/3 as a point on a number line) and keep that shaded length physically fixed — e.g. with a strip of coloured paper laid over the bar.
Subdivide every third into 2 equal pieces, then 3, then 4, and each time count the total pieces and the shaded pieces.
Record the sequence of names for the SAME shaded length: 2/3 → 4/6 → 6/9 → 8/12, and alongside each write the equation ×2, ×3, ×4 applied to both numerator and denominator.
State in your own words why the shaded amount never moved: each part was re-cut into more, smaller pieces, so both counts grew together while the whole and the shaded magnitude stayed the same.

Now test the additive move: change 2/3 by adding 1 to the numerator and 1 to the denominator to get 3/4. Shade 3/4 on an identical bar and lay it against the 2/3 strip. Observe that 3/4 reaches further — it is a different, larger amount.
Explain the difference out loud: multiplying re-cuts the same whole; adding a constant to each part does not re-cut anything, so here (and for any fraction not equal to 1) it lands on a new amount.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying numerator and denominator by a whole number n (n ≥ 1) re-partitions the same whole into finer equal parts, renaming a fixed magnitude; adding the same number to each is not re-partitioning and changes the amount (unless the fraction equals 1). Multiplying by n/n is multiplying by 1.

activities.title: Overlay check: is 4/6 bigger than 2/3?
feedback: If the two marks land on the same point, you have shown 4/6 = 2/3 despite the larger numbers.
If you expected 4/6 to be bigger, count the piece size: sixths are half the size of thirds, so 4 of them equal 2 thirds.
2/2 = 1, and multiplying any amount by 1 leaves it unchanged — that is the whole reason the rule works.
activities.rationale: Directly addresses whole-number bias (that scaled-up numbers 'must be bigger') by making the equal point/length visible on a common whole and tying it to multiplication by 1.
sourceClaims: Equivalence is produced by re-partitioning the same quantity into finer equal parts (four pizzas among eight children: 4/8 = 2/4 = 1/2), so any fraction has infinitely many equivalent names; the additive 'add the same number to top and bottom' error is whole-number thinking, and treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers underlies errors like 3/8 > 3/5.
learnerActions: Place 2/3 and 4/6 on a shared number line (or overlay two identical strips, one cut into thirds with 2 shaded, one cut into sixths with 4 shaded).
Decide whether 4/6 lands on the same point as 2/3 or further along.
Explain why 4/6 is NOT bigger even though 4>2 and 6>3: there are more pieces, but each is smaller, so the total shaded amount is the same.
Connect this to multiplying by 2/2: state what 2/2 equals and why multiplying by it cannot change the value.
activities.intendedInsight: A larger numerator and denominator do not imply a bigger amount when both were scaled by the same factor — the pieces are correspondingly smaller, so the magnitude is unchanged.

activities.title: Generalise and bridge to tenths and hundredths
feedback: If each generated fraction matches 3/5 on your diagram, you have produced genuine equivalents, not just applied a step.
For 3/10 = 30/100, each tenth was cut into 10 hundredths: 10× as many pieces, each a tenth the size, same amount.
If you can say the factor (here 10/10 = 1) and why it preserves value, you understand the rule rather than just the procedure.
activities.rationale: Year 5 pupils identify, name and write equivalent fractions including tenths and hundredths; generalising from several verified cases to the symbolic statement supports durable understanding and the decimal bridge.
sourceClaims: In Year 5 (age 9–10) pupils identify, name and write equivalent fractions of a given fraction, represented visually, including tenths and hundredths.
learnerActions: Generate three fractions equivalent to 3/5 and verify each with a strip or number-line diagram.
State the general rule in words and symbols: a/b = (n×a)/(n×b) for any whole number n ≥ 1, and explain why it holds (re-partition each part into n).
Write 3/10 as hundredths: 3/10 = 30/100. State what you multiplied by (10/10) and why the value does not change.
Explain how this renaming into hundredths helps when working with decimals.
activities.intendedInsight: The equivalence rule generalises to any whole-number factor n ≥ 1 and to the tenths↔hundredths renaming that underpins decimals; the justification (re-partition = multiply by n/n = 1) is the same every time.

activities.title: Predict-then-check: Jo vs Sam
feedback: Jo is right: 2/3 = 4/6. Multiplying both by 2 splits each third into two sixths — twice as many parts, each half the size — so the shaded amount and the whole are unchanged; it is the same point renamed, and ×2/2 is multiplying by 1.
Sam is wrong: adding 1 to the numerator and 1 to the denominator turns 2/3 into 3/4, a different, larger amount, because he is not re-partitioning the same whole.
If you endorsed Sam, place 2/3 and 3/4 on one line: they are different points. Adding shifts the amount; splitting each part keeps it.
If you said 4/6 > 2/3 because the numbers are bigger, overlay them: same point. More pieces, each smaller — same total.
If you only said 'do the same to both' without mentioning re-partitioning or the fixed amount, add the reason: each part is cut into more equal pieces, so the magnitude is preserved.
activities.rationale: A two-tier predict-explain task is proposed to discriminate genuine magnitude-preserving understanding from procedural recall and from the additive and whole-number-bias misconceptions; requiring the reason before observation is the intended diagnostic element. The cited claim supports the misconception content, not the format's efficacy.
sourceClaims: Equivalence is produced by re-partitioning the same quantity into finer equal parts (four pizzas among eight children: 4/8 = 2/4 = 1/2), so any fraction has infinitely many equivalent names; the additive 'add the same number to top and bottom' error is whole-number thinking, and treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers underlies errors like 3/8 > 3/5.
learnerActions: Read the claim: Jo says 2/3 = 4/6 (she multiplied top and bottom by 2); Sam says 2/3 = 3/4 (he added 1 to the numerator and 1 to the denominator). Before drawing, PREDICT with a reason whether 2/3 and 3/4 land on the same point.
Place 2/3, 4/6 and 3/4 on one shared number line (or overlay identical strips) and observe where each falls.
Decide who is right and justify: explain why multiplying keeps the amount but adding does not.

Answer the probes: Why does multiplying both the numerator and the denominator by 2 give twice as many parts but the same amount of chocolate? When you write 2/3 as 4/6, are you multiplying by 2 or by 2/2 — and what is 2/2? Is 3/4 bigger, smaller or equal to 2/3 — prove it on a line?
activities.intendedInsight: Equivalence is renaming a fixed magnitude by re-partitioning (multiplying by a form of 1); adding 1 to each part of 2/3 lands on a different, larger amount (3/4). Stating the reason before checking exposes whether the understanding is genuine.

constraints: A reference display of ×n families (tap 2/3 → 4/6, 6/9, 8/12 with ×n annotations) aids recall but does not let the learner enact the magnitude-preserving re-partition; use it as a support, not the main teaching move.

Recognition/selection tasks (choose which fraction equals 3/5; match ×n pairs; fill in 3/10 = ?/100) are useful for testing the rule and surfacing the additive distractor, but do not by themselves elicit the learner's own re-partition explanation — pair them with a construction or spoken justification.

When using paper strips or cutouts, treat them as approximations of ideal flat regions (real paper has slight thickness); the point is the preserved shaded magnitude, so keep the shaded length physically fixed when comparing names.
Correct the 'multiply only one part' error at the model: both numerator and denominator must change together because every part is re-cut; changing one alone is not equivalence.

A live, draggable subdivision slider with a linked ×n equation and a colour change on the additive move is one way to make the mechanism visible; it is an optional interaction example, not a requirement — the same insight can be reached with paper strips and a number line. Comparative efficacy between these media is not established by the sources.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source diagnostic states Sam adds 1 to the numerator and 1 to the denominator to get 2/3 = 3/4; the audited arithmetic is correct (2/3 ≈ 0.667 < 3/4 = 0.75, so Sam is wrong; 2/3 = 4/6 exactly). No arithmetic error found in the migrated examples.

The source IES claim quotes 'errors like 3/8 > 3/5' as a stated misconception (the true relation is 3/8 < 3/5); it is retained verbatim and framed correctly as an error, never presented to learners as true.
The National Curriculum source is marked unverified in the original; the tenths/hundredths age framing is retained as cited but not independently re-checked here.

The original 'directly defeats'/'cannot animate'/'best grasped not by dialogue' style claims about formats have been softened to scoped affordances; comparative efficacy of any single interaction format is not established by the sources.

The keyRepresentations 'ratio table' is not a standalone activity; the ×n sequence recording in activity 1 captures the same numerator/denominator tabular pattern. A dedicated ratio table could be added if a distinct representation is wanted.

assess.poeTask: Before drawing: Sam claims adding 1 to the top and bottom keeps a fraction the same, so 2/3 = 3/4. Ask the child to PREDICT, with a reason, whether 2/3 and 3/4 land on the same point on a number line. The reason stated before observing is the diagnostic part. Then place both on a shared line (or overlay strips): 3/4 sits to the right of 2/3, refuting the additive rule — while 2/3 and 4/6 coincide exactly.
probeDeeper: Why does multiplying top and bottom by 2 give twice as many parts but the same amount of chocolate?
When you write 2/3 as 4/6, what are you really multiplying 2/3 by — is it 2, or is it 2/2? What is 2/2?
Sam's method turned 2/3 into 3/4. Is 3/4 bigger, smaller, or equal to 2/3? Prove it on a line.
Write 3/10 as hundredths. What did you multiply by, and why doesn't the value change?
assess.correctAnswer: Jo is right: 2/3 = 4/6. Multiplying both by 2 splits each third into two sixths — twice as many parts, each half the size — so the shaded AMOUNT and the whole are unchanged; it is the same point renamed (and ×2/2 is multiplying by 1). Sam is wrong: adding 1 to each turns 2/3 into 3/4, a different, larger amount, because he is not re-partitioning the same whole.

errorPatterns.pattern: Additive equivalence — 'you can add the same number to top and bottom and it stays equal, so 2/3 = 3/4'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Place 2/3 and 3/4 on one number line to show different points; contrast splitting each part (×) with shifting the amount (+)
errorPatterns.distractor: Sam is right too — adding 1 to the top and 1 to the bottom keeps the fraction the same
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Endorses Sam, or says both methods are fine

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number bias — 'Jo changed it: 4/6 is bigger than 2/3 because 4>2 and 6>3'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay 2/3 and 4/6 on strips / a shared line — same length, same point; multiplying by 2/2 is multiplying by 1
errorPatterns.distractor: Jo changed the fraction — 4/6 is bigger than 2/3 because the numbers are bigger
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the value grew after multiplying both parts

errorPatterns.pattern: Multiplying only one part — thinks doubling just the top (or just the bottom) gives an equivalent
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show on the model that splitting each part changes the count of shaded parts AND the total — both numbers must move together
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked to check or generate another case, changes one part only

responseLevels.gap: Endorses the additive method, or says multiplying changes the value (bigger numbers = bigger amount); offers no magnitude-preserving reasoning.
responseLevels.full: Explains ×n as re-partitioning each part into n — both counts grow while the whole and shaded magnitude stay fixed (same point renamed) — shows adding moves the point, and transfers the reasoning to tenths → hundredths.
responseLevels.partial: Knows the ×n rule and picks Jo, but justifies only procedurally ('you do the same to both') without the re-partition / same-magnitude explanation, or cannot say why adding fails — listing the steps without relating parts to the whole.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Jo says 2/3 = 4/6 because she multiplied the top and the bottom by 2. Sam says 2/3 = 3/4 because he added 1 to the top and 1 to the bottom. Who is right? Explain, using a picture or a number line, WHY that method keeps the fraction the same and the other one doesn't.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The correct child links ×n to re-partitioning that preserves magnitude and explains why adding fails. A child with the additive misconception endorses Sam or treats both methods as equally valid; a whole-number-bias child says 4/6 > 2/3 because the numbers are bigger. It is hard to give the magnitude-preserving reason without genuine understanding, and hard to endorse Sam if you hold it.

sources.claim: Equivalence is produced by re-partitioning the same quantity into finer equal parts (four pizzas among eight children: 4/8 = 2/4 = 1/2), so any fraction has infinitely many equivalent names; the additive 'add the same number to top and bottom' error is whole-number thinking, and treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers underlies errors like 3/8 > 3/5.
sources.source: IES/WWC Practice Guide, Developing Effective Fractions Instruction for K-8 (Siegler et al., 2010, NCEE 2010-4039)

sources.claim: In Year 5 (age 9–10) pupils identify, name and write equivalent fractions of a given fraction, represented visually, including tenths and hundredths.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (KS1-2)

pedagogy.summary: At 6-7 the translation becomes three-cornered: a child moves among a real-world situation, a drawing/bar model, and a symbolic number sentence, and — crucially — EXPLAINS how each connects to the others, saying what every number stands for (CCSS MP2's coherent representation and attention to meaning). The bar model now earns its keep: the NCETM stresses it reveals the STRUCTURE of a problem (which quantity is the whole, which are parts) rather than being a way to get the answer, and a single part-whole bar holds a+b, b+a, and both subtractions at once. The load-bearing hazard at this age is the equals sign: Falkner, Levi & Carpenter document that children overwhelmingly read '=' as 'work out the answer' (answering 12 or 17 to 8+4=□+5, at every grade, not fixed by age), so 'write a number sentence to match' can be derailed by an operational, not relational, reading of the symbol. Teaching that builds relational meaning — true/false and open number sentences with the unknown in varied places — is the documented remedy.
bestPractices: Teach the bar model to expose structure, not to compute: which is the whole, which are the parts, and where the unknown sits (NCETM) — then map each part to a referent in the story

Build a RELATIONAL equals sign with true/false sentences (7 = 3 + 4, 8 + 2 = 10 + 4, 8 = 8) and open sentences with the unknown in varied positions (□ = 9 + 5, 7 + □ = 6 + 4), the Falkner/Levi/Carpenter remedy — telling children '= means the same as' is not enough
Require the child to explain the connection ('the 10 in the story is the whole, so it can't be what I add') rather than just producing a sentence
Move in all directions among situation, bar, and equation — not only story→sentence — so representations are read for meaning both ways
Use the bar to show addition and subtraction as one relationship (part-part-whole) so a matching sentence can be written several correct ways
keyRepresentations: Part-whole bar model (whole on top, parts beneath; unknown marked with ?)
Comparison bars for 'how many more' situations
Number sentence with the unknown in varied positions (□ + 5 = 12, 7 + □ = 6 + 4)
True/false number sentences as a relational-equality routine
commonMisconceptions: Reads '=' as 'work out the answer' (operational), so accepts or writes left-to-right computes like 8 + 4 = □ + 5 → 12 regardless of the structure
Grabs the two numbers in a story and adds them without asking which is the whole and which is a part
Ignores 'altogether'/total language when deciding what to combine
Can produce a matching sentence but cannot say what each number represents in the story

learn.summary: For ages 6-7, learners move among three representations of an addition/subtraction situation — a real-world story, a bar or part-whole drawing, and a symbolic number sentence — and explain how each connects to the others, saying what every number stands for. Two priorities drive the design: (1) the bar model is used to expose STRUCTURE (which quantity is the whole, which are the parts, where the unknown sits), not as a computing trick, and a single part-whole bar can be matched by several correct sentences (a=b+c, a=c+b, a−b=c, a−c=b); comparison bars serve the distinct 'how many more' type of situation. (2) The equals sign must be built as RELATIONAL ('the same amount on both sides'), because children very commonly read '=' as 'work out the answer' and will write compute-left-to-right sentences regardless of structure. True/false and open number sentences with the unknown in varied positions are the documented remedy; simply telling children '= means the same as' is reported insufficient on its own.

activities.title: Build the bar from the story, then write the sentence
feedback: If the learner tries to treat 10 (the whole) as a part to add on, prompt: 'Which number is the total of everything? Can the total also be one of the pieces you add together?' In a live builder, sizing a part larger than the labelled whole can be shown overflowing/flagged so the mismatch is visible.
If they write 6 + 10, ask them to point to '10' on the bar: is it the whole bar or a piece of it?
Praise writing a second correct form and ask: 'Why does the take-away sentence match the same bar as the add sentence?'

For the 'how many more' story, check the learner lines the two amounts up to show the difference rather than reusing a part-whole bar; ask 'where on the bar is the extra amount that answers how many MORE?'
activities.rationale: Mapping each number to a referent and building the bar to reveal whole-versus-part structure targets coherent representation and attention to the meaning of quantities; one part-whole diagram legitimately yields several correct sentences, so 'matching' should accept structurally faithful alternatives, and difference situations call for a comparison bar.
sourceClaims: MP2: create a coherent representation of the problem; attend to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute; decontextualize and contextualize, probing the referents for the symbols.

The bar model reveals the mathematical STRUCTURE of a problem (whole vs parts, where the unknown sits) rather than being a method for solving; one part-whole diagram encapsulates a = b + c, a = c + b, a − b = c, a − c = b, so a situation can be matched by several correct sentences.
learnerActions: Read a story such as: '6 red apples, and some green apples, 10 apples altogether.'
Build a part-whole bar: first decide and label which quantity is the WHOLE, then place the known part, then mark the missing part with '?'.
Notice the classic error — putting 6 and 10 side by side as two parts — and correct it by recognising that 10 is the whole, 6 is a part, and the green apples are the missing part.
Write a matching number sentence (6 + ? = 10) and then write at least one other correct form for the same bar (e.g. 10 − 6 = ?).
Say aloud what each number in the sentence stands for in the story.

For a separate 'how many more' story with its own numbers (e.g. 'Tom has 5 stickers and Mia has 8 stickers — how many more does Mia have?'), build a COMPARISON bar instead, lining up the two amounts to show the difference, and write a matching sentence.
activities.intendedInsight: A part-whole bar shows the structure of a situation — which quantity is the whole and which are the parts — so you must identify the whole before deciding what to add, and one bar can be matched by several correct sentences (adding or subtracting). A comparison bar is a different representation that suits 'how many more' situations by lining up two amounts to show the difference between them.

activities.title: True/false and balance: '=' means 'the same as'
feedback: If the learner puts 12 or 17 in 8 + 4 = □ + 5, work both sides out separately: the left side is 8+4=12; if you put 12 in the box the right side becomes 12+5=17, so the two sides are not equal. The box must make the right side equal 12 as well, so the box is 7 (because 7+5=12). A seesaw/balance that tips until both sides are equal can make 'same as' felt.
For true/false items, ask the learner to compute each side separately and compare, rather than reading left to right.
Reinforce correct relational reasoning by asking them to invent their own true sentence with the operation on the right (e.g. 10 = 6 + 4).
activities.rationale: Children very commonly hold an operational view of '=' and answer 12 or 17 to 8+4=□+5; true/false and open number sentences with the unknown in varied places are the reported remedy, and being told '= means the same as' is documented as insufficient on its own.
sourceClaims: Children overwhelmingly hold an operational view of '=' ('carry out the calculation; the answer follows'): given 8 + 4 = □ + 5 the correct answer 7 was given by 0–10% at every grade 1–6 while most answered 12 or 17; the misconception appears as early as kindergarten and is not eliminated by age or by simply telling children '= means the same as' — true/false and open number sentences build the relational meaning.
learnerActions: Decide whether sentences are true or false: 8 = 8; 7 = 3 + 4; 8 + 4 = 12 + 5; 8 + 4 = 7 + 5.
Solve open sentences with the unknown in varied positions: □ = 9 + 5, 7 + □ = 6 + 4, 8 + 4 = □ + 5.
For 8 + 4 = □ + 5, try putting 12 in the box, check whether both sides are really equal, and adjust until they match (7).
Explain for each: how do you decide whether the two sides are the same amount?
activities.intendedInsight: The equals sign means 'the same amount on both sides', not 'the answer comes next'; so you cannot just copy the left-hand total into the box — you must make both sides equal.

activities.title: Explain-why with a study partner
feedback: If the learner only restates the sentence when asked what each number means, point at one numeral at a time and ask 'this one is… which thing in the story?'
If they accept 6 + 10 = 16, ask them to find 10 on a part-whole bar and say whether it is the whole or a piece.
Turn an assertion into a 'because' clause: accept 'it doesn't match BECAUSE 10 is all the apples, so I can't add it to a part.'
activities.rationale: Articulating the mapping and defending a structural judgement against a plausible wrong sentence surfaces whether the mapping is understood rather than implicit; a dialogue can let a learner catch the whole-as-part error and justify a faithful alternative.
sourceClaims: MP2: create a coherent representation of the problem; attend to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute; decontextualize and contextualize, probing the referents for the symbols.
learnerActions: Consider a partner who says: 'The story has 6 red and 10 altogether, so I wrote 6 + 10 = 16 — good match?'
Decide whether this matches the story and say why or why not, naming what 10 is in the story (the whole).
When you write or accept a sentence, point at each number and state what it represents in the story.
Respond to a follow-up: 'Could you match the same story using take-away instead of add? Why does that work too?'
activities.intendedInsight: Explaining the connection out loud — naming the whole, the parts, and what each symbol stands for — is part of understanding, not an extra; a tempting-but-wrong sentence can be rejected with a structural reason.

activities.title: Read the links both ways (worked example / warm-up)
feedback: When the learner matches, ask 'what told you that — which piece of the bar?' rather than accepting the choice alone.
If a warm-up choice is right but unjustified, require a one-sentence reason before moving on.
Treat a tap-to-reveal triple as a worked example to seed the idea, then return to building and explaining.
activities.rationale: A static or tap-to-reveal triple can introduce the mapping and support reading links both ways, but as a worked example it cannot have the learner construct the mapping or respond to an operational-equals error; recognising a matching sentence is a lighter demand than constructing one from structure.
sourceClaims: The bar model reveals the mathematical STRUCTURE of a problem (whole vs parts, where the unknown sits) rather than being a method for solving; one part-whole diagram encapsulates a = b + c, a = c + b, a − b = c, a − c = b, so a situation can be matched by several correct sentences.
learnerActions: Study a matched triple — the story, the bar, and the equation — and tap or point to show which part of the bar and which number corresponds to each part of the story.
Go in more than one direction: not only story→sentence, but bar→story and equation→bar, saying what matches what.
As a quick warm-up, pick which of several sentences matches a given bar, then justify the choice.
activities.intendedInsight: Representations should be read for meaning in both directions, and a correct matching sentence can be recognised and defended by its structure, not by grabbing the visible numbers.

constraints: The bar model must be used to expose structure (whole vs parts, where the unknown sits), not as a procedure for getting the answer.

Provide comparison bars as a distinct representation for 'how many more' (difference) situations alongside the part-whole bar, and give the comparison story its own numbers/context so a value is not simultaneously treated as a whole in one task and a compared quantity in another.

Build the relational equals sign explicitly with true/false sentences and open sentences with the unknown in varied positions; telling children '= means the same as' is reported as insufficient on its own.
Require the learner to say what each number represents and to defend structural judgements with a reason; producing a correct sentence without explanation is a partial outcome to be drawn out.
Accept several structurally faithful sentences for one situation (e.g. 6 + □ = 10 and 10 − 6 = □); do not mark only one form correct.

Recognition-only formats (e.g. multiple-choice 'which sentence matches?') can check recognition but do not require constructing a sentence from structure or explaining the connection, and can be satisfied by the compute-left-to-right habit; use them only as warm-ups, not as the main assessment.

A tap-to-reveal static triple is a scaffold/worked example: it cannot let the learner build the mapping or respond to an operational-equals error, so it should not replace construction and explanation.

Optional interactive mechanisms (a draggable bar builder that flags a part exceeding the labelled whole; a balance/seesaw that tips until both sides are equal) are illustrative ways to make structure and relational equality felt — they are helpful examples, not required mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support the underlying teaching principles, not the specific tasks.

Self-audit of arithmetic/logic: 6 + ? = 10 gives the green apples = 4; 6 + 10 = 16 is arithmetically correct but structurally WRONG for the story (10 is the total, not a part) — the intended discriminating non-example, never endorsed. For 8 + 4 = □ + 5: left side = 12, so □ = 7 (since 7 + 5 = 12); the common wrong answers 12 and 17 reflect the operational-equals misconception and must never be presented as correct. 8 + 4 = 7 + 5 is TRUE (12 = 12); 8 + 4 = 12 + 5 is FALSE (12 ≠ 17); 8 = 8 and 7 = 3 + 4 are TRUE. The comparison example (5 and 8 stickers) gives a difference of 3. These check out.

Comparison bars for 'how many more' situations were absent from the original candidate and have been restored as a distinct representation; they are carried from the objective and the original keyRepresentations, NOT from a quoted source claim, so the activity's sourceClaims cover only the part-whole/meaning core.
The comparison story was given its own numbers/context (previously it reused 6/10 apples, where 10 played contradictory roles) to avoid conflating whole-vs-part with difference.

The original research framed some comparative claims (that 3D 'adds nothing' and that a quiz 'only assesses'). These have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements rather than universal laws; the genuine objective limit retained is that recognition-only responses do not require independent construction or explanation.

The original recommendation's vivid framing ('the insight detonates', 'won't let the total lie') described one specific interactive implementation; retained only as an optional example, not a required mechanism.

probeDeeper: 'Which number in the story is the WHOLE amount? How do you know it can't be something you add on?'
'Point to each number in your sentence and tell me what it is in the story.'
'Is 8 + 4 = 12 + 5 true or false? What about 8 + 4 = 7 + 5? How do you decide?'
'Could you write the story a different correct way — using take-away instead of add? Why does that work too?'
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child recognising that 10 is the WHOLE (not a part to add), mapping 6 and the unknown green apples to the parts, and offering a structurally faithful sentence (6 + □ = 10, or 10 − 6 = □) while reading '=' as 'the same amount on both sides', not 'the answer goes here'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Operational equals sign: reads '=' as 'carry out the calculation, answer follows', so accepts/writes left-to-right computes regardless of structure (the 8+4=□+5⇒12 pattern).
errorPatterns.nextMove: This is a documented, entrenched false belief about the symbol — confront with true/false sentences (8 = 8; 7 = 3 + 4) and a balance model until '=' is felt as 'same as'; reteach reading the +, −, = symbols relationally.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child endorses 6 + 10 = 16, or when asked to fix it writes another 'compute-then-answer' sentence; on 8+4=□+5 puts 12 or 17 in the box.

errorPatterns.pattern: Number-grabbing with no situation model: pulls the two numbers from the story and combines them without asking which is whole and which is part.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild the situation on a part-whole bar — label the whole first, then the known part, then the '?'; reteach moving between the real situation and a representation before writing any symbols.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Justifies 6 + 10 by 'the story has a 6 and a 10'; cannot say which quantity is the total; ignores the word 'altogether'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Gets a correct sentence but cannot explain what each number represents or why the sides match — the mapping is implicit, the reasoning unsaid.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach: point at each numeral and ask 'this one is… in the story?'; have the child narrate the bar. The structure is there; the articulation needs drawing out.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 6 + □ = 10 correctly but, asked 'what does each number stand for?', restates the sentence or goes quiet.

responseLevels.gap: Accepts or writes 6 + 10 (or answers 12 to 8+4=□+5); treats '=' as 'the answer follows' and doesn't distinguish whole from part.
responseLevels.full: Rejects 6 + 10 because 10 is the whole, writes a faithful sentence (6 + □ = 10 or 10 − 6 = □), maps every number to its referent, reads '=' as 'the same amount both sides' — and offers an alternative correct form (add or subtract) explaining why the same structure allows it.
responseLevels.partial: Writes or accepts a structurally correct sentence OR reads '=' relationally, but not both — e.g. rejects 6 + 10 yet still puts 12 in 8+4=□+5, or balances the box but can't say what each number represents in the story.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here's a story: there are 6 red apples and some green apples, and 10 apples altogether. A classmate wrote this to match the story: 6 + 10 = 16. Do you think that matches the story? Talk me through it — what does each number stand for, and if it doesn't match, what would you write instead and why?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with relational understanding and a situation model refuses 6 + 10 because 10 is the total, and writes a sentence whose sides balance; a child with an operational equals sign and no structure grabs the two numbers, adds them, and is satisfied that '=' just precedes the answer. The prompt separates them because the wrong sentence is superficially tempting (both numbers appear) — endorsing it reveals the compute-left-to-right habit, rejecting it with a reason reveals structure plus relational equality. Hard to reject it correctly without meaning; hard to accept it if you truly read '=' as balance.
