pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 10–11 — recognise that a digit represents 10× the place to its right and 1/10 the place to its left (the ×10/÷10 place-value relationship, now extended in BOTH directions across the decimal point).
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5 'recognise the place value of each digit in numbers with up to 3 decimal places' and multiply/divide by 10/100/1000; the reciprocal ÷10 direction underpins Y6 decimal work.
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): 5.NBT.A.1 — 'Recognize that in a multi-digit number, a digit in one place represents 10 times as much as it represents in the place to its right and 1/10 of what it represents in the place to its left.'
• Operational details: Treat place value as a single self-similar structure that continues seamlessly through the decimal point — each step left is unitising (×10), each step right is partitioning (÷10). Contrast digits of equal face value in different places (the 4 in 0.4 vs 0.04 vs 4000) so the child articulates the multiplicative, not additive, gap. Use a Gattegno/place-value chart where a digit physically slides between columns and its value recomputes.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): 'The 4 in 0.4 is ten times the 4 in ___.' Tier B: 'Explain why the 6 in 6000 is a million times the 6 in 0.006.' Tier C: 'A digit moves two places right — what happens to its value and why?'
bestPractices: Present place value as one continuous ×10/÷10 chain that runs unbroken through the decimal point — do not teach whole-number and decimal place value as separate systems
Use a Gattegno chart or place-value slider so a digit physically moves between columns and its value visibly recomputes (×10 left, ÷10 right)
Contrast the SAME face-value digit sitting in different places (4 in 4000 vs 0.4 vs 0.04) and require a multiplicative statement ('ten times', 'one tenth of'), never 'bigger/smaller'
Anchor the ÷10 direction in concrete partitioning — one tenth of a tenth is a hundredth — before abstracting to the rule
Vary the non-example: ask why moving a place is NOT 'add a zero' when decimals are involved, exposing the multiplicative meaning
keyRepresentations: Gattegno / place-value chart (digit slides between columns, value scales ×10 or ÷10)
Place-value chart spanning millions to thousandths with the decimal point fixed and digits mobile
Arrow/relationship cards labelling adjacent columns '×10 →' and '← ÷10'
Base-ten / Dienes extended to decimal flats-longs-units where the 'one' can be reassigned
commonMisconceptions: Believing 'moving a place left just adds a zero' — a rule that breaks for decimals (0.4 → 4, not 0.40)
Treating the decimal point as moving rather than the DIGITS moving relative to a fixed point
Thinking the gap between places is additive (0.4 is '0.36 more than' 0.04) rather than multiplicative (ten times)
Assuming longer decimals are always larger, ignoring place value (0.004 seen as bigger than 0.4)
Losing the self-similar structure at the decimal point — seeing tenths as unrelated to ones

learn.summary: For ages 10–11: understand that each place in a number is worth ten times the place to its right and one tenth of the place to its left, and that this ×10/÷10 structure continues unbroken through the decimal point. The core goal is for a learner to state multiplicative relationships ('ten times', 'one tenth of') between the same digit sitting in different places, and to justify them by position rather than by face value or decimal length.

activities.title: Slide the same digit across the places
feedback: If a learner says the two 4s are 'the same because both are 4', redirect to position: the digit is identical but the places differ, so the worth differs — ask them to read each value aloud (four tenths vs four hundredths).
If a learner counts a single move as ÷100 or ÷2, have them count the columns crossed: tenths to hundredths is ONE step, so ÷10; show 0.004 to illustrate what two steps (÷100) would look like.
Reinforce correct multiplicative language: accept 'ten times' / 'one tenth of', and gently reject 'bigger/smaller' or 'add a zero' as the explanation.
activities.rationale: The concept is a transformation of value by place, so performing the move and reading the recomputed value makes the multiplicative gap concrete rather than merely stated. An optional live readout and a proportional magnitude bar that is ten times longer per leftward step can make the multiplicative (not additive) gap visible.
sourceClaims: 5.NBT.A.1: a digit in one place represents 10 times as much as the place to its right and 1/10 of the place to its left.
The Gattegno chart is a canonical representation for building the ×10/÷10 place-value relationship across whole numbers and decimals.
learnerActions: Work on a place-value chart with columns from millions down to thousandths and a fixed decimal point.
Take a single digit, for example a 4, and place it in the tenths column so it reads 0.4.
Move the same 4 one column to the left to read 4, then 40, then 400, then 4000; each move, say aloud 'ten times as much' and write the ×10 relationship.

Before moving right, split one tenth into ten equal parts and check that each part is one hundredth (and one hundredth into ten parts gives thousandths). Then move the same 4 one column to the right from 0.4 to 0.04 to 0.004; each move, say aloud 'one tenth of' and write the ÷10 relationship.
Park the same 4 three columns apart (for example 4000 and 4, or 4 and 0.004 — each three steps, so ×1000) and state how many times larger one is than the other.
Finish the sentence: '0.4 is ten times 0.04; 0.04 is one tenth of 0.4.'
activities.intendedInsight: A digit's worth changes multiplicatively (×10 each step left, ÷10 each step right) according to its place; the decimal point stays fixed while the digit moves, and the same self-similar rule runs through the decimal point.

activities.title: Why isn't it just 'add a zero'?
feedback: If a learner insists 'add a zero' works, show 0.4 → 4: adding a zero gives 0.40, which is still four tenths, not four.
Confirm understanding when the learner states the rule as '×10 when moving left, ÷10 when moving right' and can apply it to a decimal example.
activities.rationale: Directly contrasting a tempting but faulty shortcut with the multiplicative rule surfaces and addresses the common 'add a zero' misconception.
sourceClaims: Y5 requires recognising the place value of each digit in numbers with up to three decimal places and multiplying/dividing by 10, 100 and 1000.
learnerActions: Consider the claim 'moving a digit one place left just adds a zero.'
Test it on whole numbers: 4 → 40 (works) and then on a decimal: 0.4 → 4 (not 0.40).
Explain in your own words why 'add a zero' fails for decimals but ×10 always works.
Write a corrected rule that holds for both whole numbers and decimals.
activities.intendedInsight: The underlying operation is multiply/divide by ten, not a digit-appending trick; 'add a zero' is a surface pattern that breaks for decimals, exposing the multiplicative meaning.

activities.title: Compare across many places and across zero
feedback: If a learner ranks the 4 in 0.04 as larger because it comes 'further along', use the number line to show 0.04 sits close to zero while 0.4 is near halfway.
If a learner cannot bridge 6,000 and 0.006, have them step through the places one at a time, tagging each ×10 (six steps), to reach a million-fold difference.
activities.rationale: Spanning many places and crossing the decimal point counters the 'longer decimal is larger' and 'face value' errors, and a number line makes the shrinking rightward value visible.
sourceClaims: 5.NBT.A.1: a digit in one place represents 10 times as much as the place to its right and 1/10 of the place to its left.
learnerActions: Compare the 6 in 6,000 with the 6 in 0.006: count how many ×10 steps separate the two places (six steps).
State and justify how many times larger the 6 in 6,000 is (6,000 is 0.006 × 1,000,000).
Place 0.4 and 0.04 on a 0–1 number line (0.4 near the middle, 0.04 close to zero) to see the value shrinking to the right.
Explain which stays the same and which changes when a digit moves place — the digit, or its worth.
activities.intendedInsight: The place-value relationship holds across several steps and across the decimal point; value decreases to the right and increases to the left, regardless of decimal length.

activities.title: Explain and defend your reasoning
feedback: A full response states the ten-times / one-tenth relationship, justifies it by positional value, and applies it in both directions and across several places.
A partial response can order the values and say one is smaller but cannot justify the exact ÷10 factor or muddles it; prompt the learner to count places and name the single ×10/÷10 step.
If the learner says one tenth of a tenth is a twentieth or a tenth, have them partition one tenth into ten equal parts to see each part is a hundredth.
activities.rationale: Requiring a justified comparison rather than a memorised ranking discriminates true positional understanding from surface rules, and asking the learner to explain the partitioning met earlier (one tenth of a tenth is a hundredth) checks that the ÷10 direction rests on concrete meaning rather than a memorised rule.
learnerActions: Answer the prompt: 'Look at the 4 in 0.4 and the 4 in 0.04. How do their values compare, and why?'
Answer a deeper probe: 'Why does moving one place to the right divide the value by ten and not some other number?'
Explain, with reasons, why the 6 in 6,000 is a million times the 6 in 0.006.
Anchor the ÷10 direction in partitioning: explain why one tenth of a tenth is a hundredth.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to justify the exact ÷10/×10 relationship by position — not just order the values — is what demonstrates genuine place-value understanding.

constraints: Present whole-number and decimal place value as ONE continuous ×10/÷10 chain running through the decimal point, not two separate systems.
Require multiplicative language ('ten times', 'one tenth of'); do not accept 'bigger/smaller' or 'add a zero' as the explanation of the relationship.

Recognition-only tasks (for example choosing from multiple options or filling a blank) can consolidate and assess the rule but do not by themselves elicit the learner's own justification; include tasks where the learner states and defends the relationship.

A static annotated chart with reveal cards is a useful reference, but it tells rather than lets the learner perform the slide; treat it as a scaffold, not a substitute for the learner moving a digit and reading the recomputed value.
Partitioning (one tenth of a tenth is a hundredth) should be established concretely before abstracting to the divide-by-ten rule.
Keep worked examples arithmetically exact: columns N apart differ by a factor of 10^N (three columns apart is ×1000, two columns apart is ×100).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic/logic self-audit confirmed: 0.4 = 0.04 × 10 and 0.04 = 0.4 ÷ 10; 6,000 vs 0.006 differ by six ×10 steps (a factor of 1,000,000); one tenth of one tenth = one hundredth; three columns apart = ×1000 and two columns apart = ×100. The example pairs 4000 and 4, and 4 and 0.004, are genuinely three steps apart and consistent with the ×1000 framing.

The original claim that a third spatial dimension 'adds nothing' and 'risks implying value scales with physical size' is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law; a spatial model could still be used — it is simply not required here.

The original framing that manipulation is 'necessary' while dialogue is merely 'possible' reflects catalog fit ranking, not demonstrated comparative efficacy; both a manipulable chart and a Socratic exchange are retained as legitimate approaches serving different purposes.
CCSS-M 5.NBT.A.1 and the NCETM Gattegno-chart claim were marked unverified in the source row; treat their support as unconfirmed.

probeDeeper: Why does moving one place to the right divide the value by ten and not some other number?
How does the 6 in 6,000 compare to the 6 in 0.006 — how many tens apart are they?
If I move the 4 in 0.4 one place LEFT instead, what happens to its value?
What stays the same and what changes when a digit moves place — the digit, or its worth?
assess.correctAnswer: The 4 in 0.04 is worth one-tenth of the 4 in 0.4 (0.04 = 0.4 ÷ 10). A digit one place to the right is worth ten times less, because each place is a tenth of the place to its left.

errorPatterns.pattern: Face value — 'they're the same, both digits are 4', ignoring position.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront with place-value counters or a Gattegno chart: slide the 4 from tenths to hundredths and show its worth divides by ten; the digit is the same but its place is not.
errorPatterns.distractor: They're the same — both digits are 4.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says equal value and justifies by the digit alone.

errorPatterns.pattern: Longer-decimal-is-larger / places grow to the right — thinks the 4 in 0.04 is worth more because it is 'further along'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Place 0.4 and 0.04 on a 0–1 line (0.4 near halfway, 0.04 close to zero) so the shrinking value to the right is visible.
errorPatterns.distractor: The 4 in 0.04 is bigger because it comes further along.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child ranks 0.04's 4 as the bigger value.

errorPatterns.pattern: Right direction, wrong factor — says the 0.04 four is a hundredth (or half) of the other, not a tenth.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the places moved: tenths→hundredths is ONE step, so ÷10; contrast with 0.004 to show what ÷100 would look like.
errorPatterns.distractor: The 4 in 0.04 is one hundredth of the other.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child knows it is smaller and moved one place, but names ÷100 or ÷2.

responseLevels.gap: Compares by the digit or by decimal length; cannot say one value is a tenth of the other.
responseLevels.full: States the ten-times / one-tenth relationship between adjacent places, justifies it by positional value, and applies it in both directions and across several places (e.g. 6,000 vs 0.006).
responseLevels.partial: States the 0.04 four is smaller and can order them, but cannot justify the exact ÷10 relationship or muddles the factor.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Look at the 4 in 0.4 and the 4 in 0.04. How do their values compare, and why?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands positional value says one is a tenth of the other and can say why (the place, not the digit, carries the value). A child stuck on face value says 'same, both are 4'; a child with the longer-is-larger error says the 0.04 one is bigger. The REASON separates true place-value understanding from a memorised comparison.

pedagogy.summary: Children reflect and translate a shape on a squared grid, give the image's coordinates, and articulate that the moved shape is congruent to the original — same size and shape, only its position (and, for reflection, its sense) has changed. The pedagogical heart is that a transformation is a rule for where every point goes, not a vague 'slide it over': reflection sends each vertex perpendicularly across the mirror line to an equal distance on the far side, and translation sends every vertex the same distance in the same direction. Congruence is the invariant that makes both trustworthy.
bestPractices: Build reflection from the point rule, not 'flip it': for each vertex, draw the line to the mirror, note it is PERPENDICULAR to the mirror, count the squares to the line, then count the same number of squares beyond it — the image vertex lands there. Assemble the image vertex by vertex.

Explicitly avoid the language 'straight across' or 'straight down' even for vertical/horizontal mirrors; say 'perpendicular to the mirror line' so the idea generalises when mirror lines later slope (NCETM KS3 6.3).

Draw attention to 'sense': after a reflection the shape reads the mirror-image way round (a clockwise vertex order becomes anticlockwise). This is what distinguishes a true reflection from a shape that has merely been slid across.

Establish translation as 'every point moves the same' — model it by moving ONE vertex '5 right, 2 up', then checking every other vertex followed the identical move; the shape's orientation and sense are unchanged.
Make congruence explicit and testable: trace the original onto tracing paper and lay it over the image to confirm same size and shape; name the word 'congruent'.
Keep coordinate reading disciplined — state the image coordinates as (across, up), guarding against the x-y reversal that surfaces whenever coordinates re-enter.
keyRepresentations: Squared/coordinate grid with a vertical (then horizontal) mirror line
Perpendicular 'joining lines' from each object vertex to its image vertex, crossed at right angles by the mirror line
Tracing paper laid over object and image to demonstrate congruence
A translation vector shown as a 'staircase' arrow (e.g. 5 right then 2 up) applied identically to every vertex
commonMisconceptions: Reflecting by sliding the shape across the mirror unchanged, so its sense is not reversed (translate-instead-of-flip).
Placing the image the wrong distance from the mirror — not equidistant — often by miscounting or letting the shape touch the line.
Believing the shape changes size or becomes a 'different shape' once moved, rather than staying congruent.
Reversing the image coordinates (writing y before x) when reporting where the shape landed.

learn.summary: Year 5 learners reflect and translate a scalene shape on a squared/coordinate grid, state the image coordinates as (across, up), and justify that the moved shape is congruent — same size and shape, with only its position (and, for reflection, its sense) changed. The core idea is that a transformation is a precise rule for where every point goes: reflection sends each vertex perpendicularly across the mirror line to an equal distance on the far side, and translation sends every vertex the same distance in the same direction. Congruence is the invariant that makes both trustworthy.

activities.title: Build a reflection vertex by vertex using the perpendicular-equidistant rule
feedback: If the image reads the same way round as the original (sense not reversed), it is not a reflection. It was most likely slid (or possibly turned) rather than reflected. Rebuild it one vertex at a time using the perpendicular lines so the reversal emerges from the rule. Avoid 'straight across/down' language; say 'perpendicular to the mirror line'.
If the square-counts from the mirror differ between an object vertex and its image, or the image touches the mirror line, recount perpendicular to the line on each side and make the two counts equal.

If coordinates come out as (up, across) — e.g. a corner at (5,3) reported as '(3,5)' while the plotted point is correct — re-anchor 'across first, then up' and recheck one corner together against the grid.
activities.rationale: Teaching reflection from the perpendicular point-rule, and explicitly avoiding 'straight across/down' language, targets the documented misconception that the image stays in the same vertical/horizontal plane and generalises to sloping mirror lines later. Using a scalene shape makes the reversal of sense observable; of the two transformations in this unit, only reflection reverses sense.
sourceClaims: A common reflection misconception is that the image stays in the same vertical/horizontal plane rather than moving perpendicular to the mirror; the remedy is to teach that every line joining a point to its image is perpendicular to the mirror line and to avoid 'straight across/down' language.

Reflection uniquely reverses 'sense' — a feature able to change only under reflection — whereas translation maintains congruence and orientation; this distinguishes a genuine reflection from a shape merely slid across.
The mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of the segments joining object and image vertices (lines joining equivalent points are parallel and the mirror is perpendicular to them).
A recurring coordinate error is reversing the ordered pair (writing/reading the second value before the first); teaching should reinforce reading across before up.
learnerActions: Start with a scalene triangle on a squared grid and a vertical mirror line two squares to its right (choose scalene so a reversal of sense is visible).

For each vertex in turn, draw the line from the vertex to the mirror line that meets the mirror at a right angle (perpendicular to the mirror line); with this vertical mirror it runs along a horizontal grid line. Check the right angle rather than assuming it.
Count the squares from the vertex to the mirror along that perpendicular, then count the SAME number of squares beyond the mirror and mark the image vertex there.
Repeat for every vertex, then join the image vertices to complete the reflected shape.

Compare the vertex order: check that the image reads the mirror-image way round (a clockwise order of corners becomes anticlockwise) — this reversed 'sense' is what makes it a true reflection rather than a slide.
State the coordinates of each image corner as (across, up), reading across first then up.
activities.intendedInsight: A reflection is produced point by point: every line joining an object vertex to its image is perpendicular to the mirror line, and the image vertex is the same distance beyond the mirror as the object is in front. Because this reverses the vertex order, the shape's sense flips — distinguishing a genuine reflection from a shape merely slid across.

activities.title: Translate every point by the same vector and contrast it with reflection
feedback: If only part of the shape moves, or vertices move by different amounts, re-apply the single vector to each vertex in turn until every corner has shifted identically.
If a learner claims the translated shape has 'turned', check the vertex order against the original: a translation leaves it reading the same way round.
Prompt: 'Is your translated triangle congruent to the reflected one as well as to the original? How do you know?' — both transformations preserve size and shape.
activities.rationale: Modelling translation as 'every point moves the same' and directly contrasting it with reflection isolates the invariant (orientation/sense preserved) that separates the two transformations. The curriculum expects Year 5 pupils to translate shapes and recognise the result is congruent.
sourceClaims: Reflection uniquely reverses 'sense' — a feature able to change only under reflection — whereas translation maintains congruence and orientation; this distinguishes a genuine reflection from a shape merely slid across.
Year 5 pupils should reflect and translate shapes and recognise that the translated/reflected shape is congruent (unchanged in size and shape).
learnerActions: Take the original triangle and set a single translation rule, e.g. '5 squares right, 2 squares up', shown as a staircase arrow.
Apply that identical move to ONE vertex first, then check that every other vertex has to follow the exact same move.
Complete the translated shape and confirm its orientation and sense are unchanged (it reads the same way round as the original).
Place the reflected shape and the translated shape side by side and describe the felt difference: the slide keeps sense, the flip reverses it.
Report the translated image coordinates as (across, up).
activities.intendedInsight: A translation moves every point the same distance in the same direction, so orientation and sense are unchanged — the opposite of reflection, which reverses sense. Both leave the shape congruent to the original.

activities.title: Test congruence by tracing and overlaying
feedback: If a learner says the moved shape is bigger, smaller, or 'different', lay the tracing directly over the image (turning it over for a reflection) to show the exact match, then name 'congruent'.
For a reflected image the tracing must be flipped over to match — note that this flip IS the reversed sense, and the shape is still congruent.
If a learner can overlay correctly but resists the word, restate: position changed, size and shape did not — that is what congruent means.
activities.rationale: A direct physical match makes congruence testable rather than asserted, targeting the misconception that moving a shape changes it. Tracing paper or a card cutout is a concrete approximation of the ideal flat figure, which has zero thickness; the demonstration is about the mathematical shape represented, not the physical copy.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils should reflect and translate shapes and recognise that the translated/reflected shape is congruent (unchanged in size and shape).
learnerActions: Trace the original triangle onto tracing paper (or cut out a card copy, noting that real paper/card has slight thickness and only approximates the ideal zero-thickness flat figure it represents).

Lay the tracing directly over the translated image and confirm an exact match in size and shape; for the reflected image, turn the tracing paper OVER to make it match — this flip is itself the reversed sense, and the size and shape are still identical.
Say aloud that the moved shape is congruent to the original: only its position (and, for the reflection, its sense) has changed, not its size or shape.
Answer the challenge 'Is it a new, different triangle now?' — about the mathematical shape represented — by pointing to the exact overlay match.
activities.intendedInsight: Reflection and translation change where a shape is (and reflection changes which way round it reads) but never its size or shape; the technical word for this sameness is 'congruent'.

activities.title: Diagnostic performance task: reflect, translate, and justify
feedback: Watch how the image is built rather than explaining the rule first; a block-shunted image reading the same way round signals a slide-instead-of-reflect error to reteach via the perpendicular rule.

Full response: each reflected vertex perpendicular and equidistant with sense reversed, every translated vertex moved identically, coordinates as (across, up), congruence justified by matching/tracing, and correct transfer when the mirror line or vector changes.

Partial response: carries out both transformations and may name congruence but treats each as a remembered procedure — cannot say WHY the image sits where it does or transfer to a mirror in a new position; reteach the point rule explicitly.
If coordinates are reversed, re-anchor 'across first, then up' and check one vertex together.
activities.rationale: A watch-the-build performance task discriminates genuine understanding of the point rule from imitation, because the two documented misconceptions (unreversed sense; unequal distance from the mirror) show up in how the image is constructed. Probing the perpendicular relationship and congruence surfaces reasoning rather than recall.
sourceClaims: A common reflection misconception is that the image stays in the same vertical/horizontal plane rather than moving perpendicular to the mirror; the remedy is to teach that every line joining a point to its image is perpendicular to the mirror line and to avoid 'straight across/down' language.

Reflection uniquely reverses 'sense' — a feature able to change only under reflection — whereas translation maintains congruence and orientation; this distinguishes a genuine reflection from a shape merely slid across.
The mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of the segments joining object and image vertices (lines joining equivalent points are parallel and the mirror is perpendicular to them).
Year 5 pupils should reflect and translate shapes and recognise that the translated/reflected shape is congruent (unchanged in size and shape).
learnerActions: Given a squared grid showing a scalene triangle and a vertical mirror line two squares to its right, reflect the triangle in the mirror line and state the coordinates of the reflected corners as (across, up).
Back with the original, translate it 5 squares right and 2 squares up, and describe the move made.
Explain whether the new triangle is the same as the first and how you know, using tracing/overlay and the word congruent.

Answer probes: What is the relationship between the line joining a corner to its image and the mirror line? If the mirror moved one square further right, what would happen to the reflected triangle? If a friend slid the triangle across without turning it, is that a reflection, and how can you tell?
activities.intendedInsight: Holding the perpendicular-equidistant rule produces an image that is both the correct distance AND reversed in sense; merely sliding produces the wrong sense (and often the wrong distance). Watching HOW the image is assembled — perpendicular vertex by vertex, or shunted as a whole block — separates understanding from imitation, and the congruence question separates learners who see the shape as invariant from those who think moving changes it.

constraints: Use a scalene shape so the reversal of sense is visible; a symmetric shape can hide whether a learner reflected or merely slid.
Say 'perpendicular to the mirror line' rather than 'straight across/down', even for vertical or horizontal mirrors, so the rule generalises to sloping mirror lines later.
Report image coordinates as (across, up), guarding against the x-before-y / y-before-x reversal.
When using tracing paper to check a reflection, the tracing must be turned OVER to overlay the image; the shape remains congruent and that flip is the reversed sense.

Discrete-item checks (choosing the correctly reflected image among a slid-across distractor and a not-equidistant distractor, filling in image coordinates, true/false on congruence) can diagnose the two misconceptions but, because nothing recomputes, they check rather than build the felt rule; use them alongside, not instead of, construction.

A pre-annotated worked diagram that reveals the perpendicular joining lines, the equal square-counts and the label 'congruent' can illustrate the rule but does not let a learner test their own placement, which is the core skill; treat it as a scaffold, not the assessment.

A live grid where dragging a vertex or the mirror line recomputes the image (with faint perpendicular joining lines, live square-counts that turn green when the two sides match, a sense badge that flips when the reflection is correct, a settable translation arrow applied to all vertices at once, and a ghost of the original for congruence) can make the invariants concrete; these interaction and feedback examples are optional ways to expose the mechanism, not mandatory.

Tracing paper or a card cutout is a concrete approximation of the ideal flat (zero-thickness) figure; use it to demonstrate congruence of the represented mathematical shape while distinguishing that shape from the physical copy.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

One legacy source claim (National Curriculum, Year 5 reflect/translate/congruence) was marked verified:false in the row and is cited in Activities 2, 3 and 4; it directly supports the congruence principle and is the only curriculum source for it, but its evidential status is unconfirmed, so treat its citation accordingly.

The legacy entry framed a 3D rendering and an in-role dialogue as 'poor' for this planar skill. Those are catalog-fit judgements, not universal laws: a planar grid is well suited to square-counting and depth is not used here, but no claim of universal impossibility is made. These alternatives were not carried forward as activities because they do not let the learner construct and verify a reflection; their underlying affordances are noted only as scaffolds/limits.

Legacy phrasing such as 'cannot let the child TEST their own placement' and 'adds nothing' was softened to scoped affordance/limit statements; the exact sources do not establish comparative efficacy or necessity.

The row's evidence statement gives a '3 units right, 2 units up' translation example, whereas the diagnostic and these activities use '5 right, 2 up'; the activities follow the diagnostic consistently.

probeDeeper: Point at one object vertex and its image and ask: 'What can you tell me about the line joining these two corners and the mirror line?' (listen for perpendicular / equal distance, not 'it's across from it').
'If I moved the mirror line one square further right, what would happen to your reflected triangle?' (tests that the image is defined by distance from the mirror, not a fixed spot).
Counterexample: 'Your friend slid the triangle straight across to here without turning it round — is that a reflection? How can you tell?' (listen for sense/orientation reversal being absent).
'You translated it 5 right and 2 up. Is the translated triangle congruent to the reflected one as well as to the original? How do you know?' (congruence is preserved by both transformations).
assess.correctAnswer: The child places each reflected vertex perpendicularly opposite its original at an equal number of squares beyond the mirror line, so the image is equidistant and its sense is reversed (a scalene triangle visibly reads the other way round); reports the image coordinates as (across, up); translates by moving every vertex 5 right and 2 up together; and states the moved shape is congruent — same size and shape — checking by matching or tracing, understanding only position (and, for the reflection, orientation/sense) changed.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reflects by sliding the whole shape across the mirror without reversing it, so its sense is unchanged ('I just moved it over to the other side')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw the line from one vertex to the mirror, show it meets the mirror at a right angle, count the squares and count the same beyond; repeat per vertex so the reversed sense emerges from the rule. Avoid 'straight across' language.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The image reads the SAME way round as the original (vertex order not reversed) — for a scalene triangle the 'point' faces the same direction; the child moves the shape as one block rather than vertex by vertex.

errorPatterns.pattern: Places the image the wrong distance from the mirror — not equidistant — often letting the shape touch the line or miscounting one side
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count squares perpendicular from each vertex to the line, then step the identical count to the far side; mark both counts and compare.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Square-counts from mirror differ between object and image; image sits closer to or on the mirror line.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks the shape changes size or becomes a different shape once moved, so it is no longer 'the same' ('it's a new triangle now')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace the original and lay it over the image to show an exact match; name 'congruent' — position (and sense) changed, size and shape did not.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the moved shape is bigger/smaller or 'different'; cannot justify sameness or resists the word congruent.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses the reported image coordinates, giving the up-value before the across-value
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor 'along the corridor then up the stairs': read across first, then up; check one vertex together against the grid.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: States a landed vertex as (up, across) — e.g. calls (5,3) '(3,5)' — while the plotted point is actually correct.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot place a correct image: slides the shape across with unchanged sense or at an unequal distance, and treats the moved shape as changed or 'new'. Coordinates may also be reversed.
responseLevels.full: Builds both images from the point rule — each reflected vertex perpendicular and equidistant across the mirror with sense reversed, every translated vertex moved identically — reports image coordinates as (across, up), and justifies congruence by matching/tracing, transferring correctly when the mirror line or vector is changed.
responseLevels.partial: Can carry out a reflection and a translation and may name congruence, but treats each as a remembered procedure — e.g. reflects correctly in a vertical mirror yet cannot say WHY the image sits where it does (perpendicular, equidistant), or reports the steps without connecting them to the shape staying congruent. Lists the moves but cannot explain how the point rule forces the image, nor transfer to a mirror in a new position.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Hand the child a squared grid showing a scalene triangle and a vertical mirror line two squares to its right. Say: 'Reflect this triangle in the mirror line, then tell me the coordinates of the reflected corners. Now, back with the original, translate it 5 squares right and 2 squares up and describe the move you made. Last, tell me: is your new triangle the same as the first one, and how do you know?' Set the task and WATCH how the image is built — do not explain the rule.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who holds the perpendicular-equidistant rule produces an image that is both the right distance AND reversed in sense; a child who merely 'slides it across' produces an image that is the wrong sense (and often the wrong distance), so watching HOW the image is assembled — vertex by perpendicular vertex, or shunted whole — separates real understanding from imitation. The congruence question further separates children who see the shape as invariant from those who think moving it changes it.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: The inverse relationship between addition and subtraction — addition and subtraction 'undo' each other, so a known sum yields three related facts and a subtraction can be checked by adding back. Ages 6–7, building on unknown-addend and fact families.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2 'recognise and use the inverse relationship between addition and subtraction and use this to check calculations and solve missing number problems'. Reappears in KS2 for checking with larger numbers.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): builds on 1.OA.4 (subtraction as unknown addend) and 1.OA.6 relationships; supports 2.NBT/3.NBT checking by inverse. Inverse operations are the explicit mechanism for solving □ + 9 = 14 and verifying answers.
• Operational details: teach through the fact family / part-whole triangle — one whole and two parts generate 2 additions and 2 subtractions. Use inverse deliberately for TWO jobs: (a) checking (15 + 7 = 22, so 22 − 7 should give 15) and (b) solving missing-number equations (□ + 9 = 14 → □ = 14 − 9). Emphasise it is a relationship between operations, not a new procedure.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (age 6) — given 6 + 4 = 10 states 10 − 4 = 6 and 10 − 6 = 4. Tier B (age 7) — solves □ + 9 = 14 by subtracting and checks a subtraction by adding back. Tier C (age 7+) — explains that addition undoes subtraction and uses inverse to check a calculation with two-digit numbers.
bestPractices: Anchor on the fact-family triangle / part-whole model so all four related facts come from one whole and two parts.
Make 'checking by the inverse' a routine habit after every calculation, not an add-on.
Use inverse explicitly to convert a missing-number equation into a calculation the child can do (□ + 9 = 14 → 14 − 9).
Keep the SAME three numbers while flipping the operation, so the child sees one relationship rather than four separate facts.
Contrast with situations where inverse reasoning is misapplied, e.g. reminding that order matters in the subtraction facts (10 − 6 vs 6 − 10).
keyRepresentations: Fact-family / part-whole triangle (one whole, two parts, four facts)
Bar model with the whole and two parts, read as add or subtract
Empty number line showing a forward jump and its reversing backward jump
Balance model where adding then subtracting the same amount returns to start
Cuisenaire rods showing a+b and the reverse whole−a
commonMisconceptions: Treating the four fact-family facts as unrelated things to memorise separately.
Believing subtraction facts can also be reversed freely (10 − 6 = 6 − 10), over-extending the 'undo' idea.
Checking a sum by repeating the SAME operation rather than using the inverse.
Solving □ + 9 = 14 by adding 9 and 14, not recognising subtraction as the inverse move.
Thinking 'undoing' requires a different, brand-new procedure rather than the operation they already know.

learn.summary: Help 6–7 year-olds see that addition and subtraction undo each other, so one known sum (e.g. 15 + 7 = 22) generates all four related facts, lets you check a calculation by reversing it, and lets you solve a missing-number equation (□ + 9 = 14) by subtracting. The core aim is to treat these as ONE relationship between operations, not four separate facts to memorise. Builds on fact families and part-whole/unknown-addend ideas.

activities.title: Do and undo it on a number line (with a fact-family triangle)
feedback: If the learner recomputes the subtraction from scratch, point back to the triangle: the whole (22) and two parts (15, 7) already give the subtraction — read it off rather than counting again.
If the learner writes 15 − 7 = 22 or similar, mark on the bar/triangle which number is the whole: you can only take a part away FROM the whole, and 15 and 7 are both parts.

If the learner checks 15 + 7 = 22 by just adding 15 + 7 again, point out that repeating the same calculation can repeat the same mistake. Reversing it (22 − 7 = 15) is a real check, in the same way that adding the parts back (15 + 7) checks the subtraction 22 − 7 = 15.
When the backward jump lands exactly on 15, name it: 'the subtraction undid the addition.'
activities.rationale: A reversible forward/backward action makes 'undo' literal and ties all four facts to a single whole-and-parts structure, directly targeting the misconception that related facts are unrelated. The number-line and triangle are one way to realise this; equivalent reversing can be shown on paper, on a balance model, or with Cuisenaire rods, and none of these media is required over the others.
sourceClaims: Y2 pupils recognise and use the inverse relationship between addition and subtraction to check calculations and solve missing-number problems.
Fact families and the inverse relationship are taught via part-whole structures; children commonly treat related facts as separate and check by repeating rather than reversing.
learnerActions: Start at 15 on a number line and make a forward jump of +7, landing on 22.
Before reversing, predict out loud where a backward jump of 7 will land and why.
Make the backward jump of −7 and confirm you return exactly to 15.
Say in your own words why the subtraction lands back on the start: it is the same jump run in reverse.
Fill in a fact-family triangle with the whole (22) and the two parts (15 and 7), then write all four facts: 15 + 7 = 22, 7 + 15 = 22, 22 − 7 = 15, 22 − 15 = 7.
Check a subtraction by adding the parts back: verify 22 − 7 = 15 by computing 15 + 7.

(Optional) Show the same reversing with another model: a balance that returns to its start after you add then subtract the same amount, or Cuisenaire rods laid as 15 + 7 and then the whole with one part removed.
activities.intendedInsight: Subtraction reverses addition over the SAME three numbers, so taking one part from the whole returns the other part; one sum gives four related facts and a built-in way to check.

activities.title: Solve a missing number by reversing
feedback: If the learner adds 9 and 14, remind them that the box plus 9 already makes 14, so you need to take 9 away from 14 to find the box.
Praise a correct check that substitutes the answer back into the original equation (5 + 9 = 14).
activities.rationale: Turning the equation into a doable subtraction shows inverse operations as the mechanism for solving, not a brand-new procedure.
sourceClaims: Y2 pupils recognise and use the inverse relationship between addition and subtraction to check calculations and solve missing-number problems.
Understanding subtraction as an unknown addend (1.OA.4) and part-whole/fact-family relationships underpins using inverse operations to solve and check.
learnerActions: Look at □ + 9 = 14 and decide what operation would find the missing part.
Explain why subtracting (14 − 9) finds the box: addition and subtraction undo each other.
Compute □ = 14 − 9 = 5 and check by putting it back: 5 + 9 = 14.
Try one or two more missing-number equations, each solved by the inverse and then checked by adding back.
activities.intendedInsight: A missing-addend equation becomes a calculation you can already do by using the inverse operation, and the answer can be confirmed by reversing again.

activities.title: Explain WHY adding back proves a subtraction
feedback: If the learner says 15 − 7 = 22, steer to the whole: 22 is the whole; you subtract a part from the whole, so valid subtractions are 22 − 7 and 22 − 15.
If the learner only recites facts without saying the operations undo each other, ask them to point to the jump that reverses the addition.
Accept a justification that names 22 as the whole and explains the returned part.
activities.rationale: A justification prompt exercises the conceptual 'explain' goal and lets a learner confront the over-generalisation that any pair of the three numbers reverses.
sourceClaims: Fact families and the inverse relationship are taught via part-whole structures; children commonly treat related facts as separate and check by repeating rather than reversing.
learnerActions: Given 22 − 7 = 15, explain how you could be sure it is right WITHOUT redoing the subtraction.
Discuss the difference between reversing (adding the parts back) and simply repeating the same subtraction.
Respond to the claim that 'subtraction undoes too, so 15 − 7 = 22' and explain why that is wrong using which number is the whole.
State a DIFFERENT true subtraction from the same three numbers (22 − 15 = 7) and justify it.
activities.intendedInsight: Checking works because addition reverses subtraction over the same whole and parts; the 'undo' idea applies to taking a part from the whole, not to any rearrangement of the three numbers.

activities.title: Match and consolidate related facts
feedback: For a choice that repeats 15 + 7, explain that a genuine check reverses the operation; an inverse check is 22 − 7 = 15 (or 22 − 15 = 7).
For a mismatched subtraction, return to the whole-and-parts triangle.
activities.rationale: Recognition and fill-in tasks consolidate the four related facts and the inverse check; on their own they confirm familiarity but recognition alone does not require the learner to produce and feel the do-and-undo action.
learnerActions: Match one sum (15 + 7 = 22) to its three related facts.
Fill in blanks in missing-number equations such as □ + 9 = 14, solving by the inverse.
Choose which calculation correctly checks 15 + 7 = 22, distinguishing an inverse check (22 − 7 = 15 or 22 − 15 = 7) from a decoy that just repeats the same addition.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent recall and recognition of the four related facts and the correct inverse check, reinforcing the single relationship.

constraints: Keep the SAME three numbers while flipping the operation so the learner sees one relationship, not four isolated facts.
Make 'check by the inverse' a routine habit after calculating, in line with the objective, rather than an optional afterthought.

Distinguish the whole from the parts explicitly: subtractions take a part from the whole (22 − 7, 22 − 15); a part minus a part (15 − 7) is NOT one of this fact family's four facts (15 − 7 = 8 is a valid operation but a different problem).
Emphasise that subtraction does not reverse 'freely' — order matters, so do not over-extend the undo idea to 15 − 7 = 22.

A fixed/static fact-family picture with tappable corners can anchor the four facts and the checking idea, but it does not let the learner perform the reversing action; it can support rather than stand in for do-and-undo work.

Recognition and matching tasks can check recall of the four related facts and the correct inverse check, but recognition alone does not elicit independent production or the felt experience of reversing; pair them with reversing and explanation work rather than relying on them alone, without mandating a particular medium or strict ordering.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source's correctAnswer field contains self-corrected scratch text ('22 − 6... no — 22 − 15 = 7'); the two valid related subtractions are 22 − 7 = 15 and 22 − 15 = 7. This rewrite uses only the corrected forms and never offers the scratch value as an option.

The original listed a '3D adds nothing' judgement for this numeric relationship; this is a catalog fit opinion, not an established pedagogical law, so it is omitted from learner-facing guidance. A third spatial dimension is simply not needed here, but no universal-necessity claim is made either way.
Two source claims (CCSS-M grade 1; Carpenter et al. CGI) were marked unverified in the original; retained as cited where they support a principle, without upgrading their confidence.

The interactive number-line/triangle, 'undo'/'check' controls, tappable corners, linked panes, balance model, and Cuisenaire rods are optional concrete examples of the same reversing mechanism, not mandatory tooling; the reversing and checking can equally be done on paper. No claim is made that any one medium teaches this better than another.

assess.poeTask: Predict what happens if you start at 15, jump forward 7 on a number line, then jump back 7. Say where you'll land and why BEFORE you move. Then do it — what does landing back on 15 tell you about how adding and subtracting 7 are related?
probeDeeper: Why does taking 7 away from 22 have to give 15 back?
Which of your three numbers is the whole, and how does that decide the subtractions?
If I made a mistake and wrote 22 − 7 = 16, how would the inverse show me I was wrong?
Can you also make a DIFFERENT true subtraction from these three numbers? What is it?
assess.correctAnswer: 22 − 7 = 15 (or 22 − 6... no — 22 − 15 = 7). Either 22 − 7 = 15 or 22 − 15 = 7. Explanation: subtraction undoes addition, so taking back one part from the whole must return the other part — the three numbers form one whole (22) and two parts (15 and 7).

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the facts as separate — recomputes a subtraction from scratch rather than reading it off the relationship.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the fact-family triangle: one whole and two parts generate all four facts; practise reading them off without recalculating.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Starts counting/calculating a subtraction instead of deriving it from 15 + 7 = 22.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Subtraction undoes too, so 15 − 7 also works' — over-extends reversal and offers an invalid subtraction from the wrong pair.
errorPatterns.nextMove: On the bar model, mark which number is the whole (22) — you can only take a part FROM the whole; 15 and 7 are both parts.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives 15 − 7 = 22 or similar, subtracting a part from a part or expecting the whole as the answer.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'To check it, do 15 + 7 again' — checks by repeating the same operation rather than the inverse.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast repeating (same errors reappear) with reversing; establish adding-back as the check.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked to check, re-adds the two numbers instead of subtracting.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot produce a valid related subtraction, or recomputes with no sense of relationship; may give 15 − 7.
responseLevels.full: States a valid subtraction, identifies 22 as the whole, and justifies it by inverse reasoning ('subtraction undoes addition, so the part comes back'), and can use it to check or solve a missing-number equation.
responseLevels.partial: Produces a correct related subtraction but justifies it by calculating, or lists the facts without saying the operations undo each other; doesn't reliably identify the whole.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I worked out that 15 + 7 = 22. Using only those three numbers, tell me a subtraction that must also be true — and explain how you know it is true without working it out from scratch.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has memorised facts separately, or who thinks checking means redoing, will either recompute or offer an invalid rearrangement (e.g. 15 − 7). A child who holds the inverse relationship names a valid subtraction immediately and justifies it by 'undoing' rather than by calculating — the 'without working it out' clause is what forces the relational justification.
