pedagogy.summary: By Year 5 children move from counting squares to using formulae: area of a rectangle = length × width, perimeter = 2 × (length + width), with AREA in square units (cm², m²) and PERIMETER in linear units (cm, m). They apply these both ways (e.g. find a missing side from area and one dimension), compare areas, and estimate the area of irregular shapes on a cm² grid by counting whole and part squares. The central risk is that the formulae are learned instrumentally and area and perimeter get confused; the antidote is to keep each formula anchored to its meaning — area as the number of unit squares covering the surface, perimeter as the distance around the edge.
bestPractices: Keep area tied to covering unit squares and perimeter to the distance around even once formulae are used, so the two are not conflated (relational, not merely instrumental).
Teach area = l × w as an array of unit squares (rows × columns) and perimeter as 2×(l+w); label every answer with correct units (cm² vs cm).
Work both directions: give the area and one side and find the other (area 48 m², length 8 m → width 6 m); express missing-measure problems algebraically, e.g. 4 + 2b = 20.
Estimate irregular area on a cm² grid by counting whole squares and combining part-squares (count a part square if it is at least half), and treat the result explicitly as an estimate.
Use grids, tiles and cut-and-fit activities alongside the formulae so children can see where l × w comes from.
keyRepresentations: cm² grid / squared paper
Unit-square array (rows × columns)
Rectangle with labelled length and width
String-around-the-edge model for perimeter
Algebraic missing-measure equation (e.g. 4 + 2b = 20)
commonMisconceptions: Confuses area and perimeter — uses one formula for the other, or gives the distance around when asked for the covered surface.
Overgeneralises 'area = length × breadth' and reports the answer in linear units (cm) instead of square units (cm²).
When estimating irregular area, counts only whole squares and ignores part-squares (or counts every touched square as a whole).

learn.summary: Year 5 pupils move from counting squares to applying area = length × width and perimeter = 2 × (length + width) for rectangles (including squares), used both forwards and to find a missing side, with area labelled in square units (cm², m²) and perimeter in linear units (cm, m). They also estimate the area of irregular shapes on a cm² grid by counting whole and part squares, treating the result as an estimate. The central risk is instrumental learning that confuses area and perimeter or reports area in linear units; the antidote is keeping each formula anchored to meaning — area as unit squares covering the surface, perimeter as distance around the edge. Activities below range from a hands-on/grid manipulation intended to make the two quantities visibly distinct, through a tap-to-reveal formula scaffold, to a checking quiz, each with its own purpose and limits.

activities.title: Grid playground: reshape a rectangle and watch area and perimeter move apart
feedback: If you used one formula for both, or got the same number by mixing up the methods: shade the whole surface for area (count squares) and run a finger around the edge for perimeter (count length) — rebuild area as covering unit squares before using l × w again. (Getting the same number is not wrong in itself: a 4×4 square really has area 16 cm² and perimeter 16 cm, and the units are still different.)
If you labelled the area in cm instead of cm²: point to one covering square — because area counts squares, it is measured in square units; keep the multiplication, just fix the unit.

For the blob: agree one rule — either 'count a part-square as one if it is at least half, ignore smaller parts' or 'pair up part-squares that together make about one whole' — use it consistently, and say your answer could be a little more or less because it is an estimate.
To check that the two really differ: reshape 6×4 into 12×2 — the area stays 24 cm² but the perimeter changes (from 20 cm to 28 cm), showing they are not the same thing.
activities.rationale: Keeping area tied to covering unit squares and perimeter to distance around — with both counts visible as the shape changes, so one can stay fixed while the other moves — is intended to support relational rather than instrumental understanding and to address the confusion of the two. Live, side-by-side counters in two units (an optional interaction example) can make the distinction concrete; the same can be achieved with physical squared paper, tiles and a finger-trace. Calculating areas and perimeters of rectangles and estimating irregular areas reflect the Year 5 statutory expectations; working backwards to a missing side reflects the non-statutory guidance.
sourceClaims: Year 5 statutory: 'calculate and compare the area of rectangles (including squares), including using standard units, square centimetres (cm²) and square metres (m²), and estimate the area of irregular shapes'; 'measure and calculate the perimeter of composite rectilinear shapes in centimetres and metres'. Y5 non-statutory: missing-measure problems can be expressed algebraically, e.g. 4 + 2b = 20.

Learners confuse area and perimeter because the formulae are taught together without conceptual grounding; they overgeneralise A = l × b to non-rectangles ('most children respond to the word area by saying length times breadth'); they hold instrumental rather than relational understanding (Skemp). Recommendation: shift from teaching formulae to cm² grids and fitting/cutting/folding/counting activities.
learnerActions: On cm² paper (physical squared paper or an on-screen grid), draw or drag the corners of a rectangle and, as it changes shape, keep two counts — tallied by hand on paper or shown live on screen: the squares filling the inside (area, in cm²) and the units traced around the outline (perimeter, in cm).
Compare a 6×4 rectangle (24 cm², 20 cm) with other shapes you make, saying aloud which count is 'squares covering it' (area) and which is 'steps around it' (perimeter).
Switch to a 'missing side' task: with the area fixed at 48 cm² and the length given as 8 cm, find the width (6 cm); then try area 48 m² with length 8 m → width 6 m.
Switch to an 'irregular blob/pond' task: shade whole squares and part-squares on the grid and combine them to estimate the blob's area, stating that it is an estimate.
activities.intendedInsight: Area and perimeter are different quantities with different units: area counts the unit squares covering a surface (cm²); perimeter measures the distance around the edge (cm). One can stay the same while the other changes as a shape is reshaped.

activities.title: Build l × w from an array of unit squares, then express a missing side algebraically
feedback: If you cannot explain why l × w gives area: rebuild the array — each row has 'length' squares and there are 'width' rows, so the total squares = length × width.
If a missing side is wrong: check with the array (does your width, times the length, give the stated area?) or substitute back into your equation.
Always re-check units at the end: a surface answer is square units, an around-the-edge answer is linear units.
activities.rationale: Deriving l × w from a unit-square array is intended to keep the formula meaningful, and reversing it (and expressing it algebraically) matches the Year 5 non-statutory guidance and the worked examples. Tiles/cut-and-fit alongside the formula can show where it comes from rather than relying on instrumental recall.
sourceClaims: Year 5 statutory: 'calculate and compare the area of rectangles (including squares), including using standard units, square centimetres (cm²) and square metres (m²), and estimate the area of irregular shapes'; 'measure and calculate the perimeter of composite rectilinear shapes in centimetres and metres'. Y5 non-statutory: missing-measure problems can be expressed algebraically, e.g. 4 + 2b = 20.

Learners confuse area and perimeter because the formulae are taught together without conceptual grounding; they overgeneralise A = l × b to non-rectangles ('most children respond to the word area by saying length times breadth'); they hold instrumental rather than relational understanding (Skemp). Recommendation: shift from teaching formulae to cm² grids and fitting/cutting/folding/counting activities.
learnerActions: Cover a labelled rectangle with unit-square tiles (or draw the array on squared paper) and count the squares by rows × columns to see where length × width comes from.
Compute the perimeter of the same rectangle as 2 × (length + width), and label each answer with its unit (cm² for area, cm for perimeter).
Find a missing dimension: given area 48 m² and length 8 m, work back to width 6 m; calculate the area of a square with side 7.5 cm (56.25 cm²).
Write a missing-measure problem as an equation, e.g. 4 + 2b = 20, and solve for b.
activities.intendedInsight: The area formula is a shortcut for counting rows × columns of unit squares, and a missing side can be found by reasoning backwards from the area (or as an equation), while perimeter adds the edge lengths.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal formula reference (scaffold)
feedback: Prompt the learner to state which revealed quantity is 'squares covering it' and which is 'distance around', so the formula stays linked to meaning.
Ask the learner to pick the correct unit before revealing it, so they are not just reading the answer.
activities.rationale: A fixed labelled rectangle with tap-to-reveal facts conveys the formulae and units but cannot show area and perimeter varying as the shape changes, so it supports recall rather than building the conceptual distinction. Useful as a reference, best paired with a grid activity.
learnerActions: On a static labelled rectangle, tap the length and width to reveal l × w (area) and 2 × (length + width) (perimeter).
Note the unit each answer takes — cm² for area, cm for perimeter — and say why they differ.
activities.intendedInsight: Recall the two formulae and the correct unit for each as a memory and reference aid.

activities.title: Checking quiz: area, perimeter, missing side and estimate with a units check
feedback: If a units item is wrong, send the learner back to the meaning: area counts covering squares (square units); perimeter measures distance (linear units).

If the blob estimate ignores part-squares or counts every touched square whole, remind them of the agreed part-square rule (either 'at least half counts as one' or pairing part-squares into about one whole) and to apply it consistently.
If area and perimeter are swapped, re-link each formula to its meaning before retrying.
activities.rationale: These tasks map cleanly onto selected-response and slider formats with a units check, making it a useful instrument for checking accuracy and spotting unit confusion. Recognition/selection responses verify application but do not elicit the independent construction and reshaping reasoning of the grid activity, so this complements rather than replaces it.
sourceClaims: Year 5 statutory: 'calculate and compare the area of rectangles (including squares), including using standard units, square centimetres (cm²) and square metres (m²), and estimate the area of irregular shapes'; 'measure and calculate the perimeter of composite rectilinear shapes in centimetres and metres'. Y5 non-statutory: missing-measure problems can be expressed algebraically, e.g. 4 + 2b = 20.
learnerActions: Compute the area and the perimeter of a labelled rectangle, then answer a units question (is the area cm or cm²?).
Find a missing width when given the area and the length.
Estimate the area of a gridded blob, including part-squares.
activities.intendedInsight: Confirm that the learner can apply both formulae accurately, choose correct units, and estimate an irregular area.

constraints: Label every answer with correct units: area in square units (cm², m²), perimeter in linear units (cm, m).

Treat irregular-area counting as an estimate; agree one explicit rule for part-squares — either count a part-square as one if it is at least half and ignore smaller parts, or pair part-squares that together make about one whole — and apply it consistently.
The tap-to-reveal reference supports recall of the formulae and units but cannot show area and perimeter changing as a shape is reshaped; use it alongside, not instead of, grid manipulation.

The checking quiz confirms accurate application and unit choice but its recognition/selection responses do not require the learner to construct and reshape figures or reason about why the two quantities differ.

Keep the formulae anchored to meaning (array of unit squares for area, distance around for perimeter) so they are not learned purely instrumentally; avoid overgeneralising l × w to non-rectangular shapes.

Live counters, dragging corners and a slider estimate are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete; physical squared paper, tiles and finger-tracing achieve the same purpose and neither is mandatory.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support the underlying teaching principle rather than proving any activity was tested.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 8×3 = 24 cm² and 2×(8+3) = 22 cm (diagnostic rectangle); 6×4 = 24 cm² and 2×(6+4) = 20 cm; reshaping 6×4 to 12×2 keeps area 24 cm² (12×2) but changes perimeter to 2×(12+2) = 28 cm — area stays, perimeter changes. Missing-side example: area 48 m², length 8 m → width 6 m (48/8). Square side 7.5 cm → area 56.25 cm². All consistent.

The original row framed the 3D and conversation formats as adding 'no insight'/not applicable; this is a catalog fit judgement, not an established pedagogical law, so it has been omitted rather than asserted as a universal limit. No claim is made that only a dragging grid can teach this distinction.

The 'at least half' counting rule and pairing of part-squares is a reasonable convention for estimation but is an approximation, not an exact method; it is presented explicitly as yielding an estimate.

Efficacy wording in activity rationales was softened to intended/can register because no source proves the proposed activities were tested; affordances (e.g. tap-to-reveal cannot show variation; recognition does not elicit construction) are stated as narrow limits, not medium-superiority claims.

probeDeeper: Point to the part of the rectangle that is its area, and trace the part that is its perimeter — how are they different?
You found area 24 and perimeter 22. If I stretched this into a 12 cm by 2 cm rectangle, would the area stay 24? Would the perimeter stay 22?
Why is the area measured in cm² but the perimeter in cm?
For the blob, how sure are you of your number — could it be a little more or less, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: Computes area 24 cm² (8×3) and perimeter 22 cm (2×(8+3)), keeps the two distinct with correct units, and estimates the blob's area by counting whole squares plus part-squares (roughly counting halves), presenting it as an estimate.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses area and perimeter — uses the wrong formula, or reports the same number for both.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the meanings physically: shade the surface (area = squares) versus run a finger around the edge (perimeter = length). Rebuild area as covering unit squares before returning to the formula.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Computes 2×(8+3) when asked for area, or 8×3 when asked for perimeter, or gives one figure for both.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reports area in linear units (overgeneralising 'length × breadth' without the square-unit meaning).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Connect cm² to one covering square: area counts squares, so it is measured in square units. Do not reteach the multiplication itself — only the unit meaning.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels the area '24 cm' or omits units / mislabels perimeter as cm².

errorPatterns.pattern: Mishandles part-squares when estimating irregular area — counts only whole squares, or counts every touched square as a whole.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Agree a rule (a part square counts if it is at least half) and pair up part-squares into wholes; frame the result explicitly as an estimate.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Ignores part-squares (answer too small) or counts each touched square fully (answer too large), and does not present it as an estimate.

responseLevels.gap: Confuses area and perimeter or applies l×w indiscriminately; units missing or wrong; cannot estimate the irregular area meaningfully.
responseLevels.full: Finds area (24 cm²) and perimeter (22 cm) with correct units, keeps the concepts distinct, estimates the irregular area sensibly from whole and part squares, and explains area as covered squares versus perimeter as distance around.
responseLevels.partial: Computes area and perimeter correctly for the rectangle but muddles units, or handles the rectangle yet cannot estimate the blob's part-squares; runs the formulae without keeping the two meanings distinct.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a rectangle labelled 8 cm by 3 cm drawn on cm² paper and, on the same grid, an irregular blob. Say: 'Find the area of the rectangle, then its perimeter, then estimate the area of the blob — and label each answer with its units.' Then WATCH: which operation they use for each, whether they keep area and perimeter distinct, whether area is cm² and perimeter cm, and how they treat the blob's part-squares.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Setting area, perimeter and an estimate side by side forces the child to keep the two concepts and their units apart; a child with only instrumental knowledge reveals it in the doing — cross-applying a formula, dropping or swapping units, or being unable to handle part-squares — not in what they say about it.

sources.claim: Year 5 statutory: 'calculate and compare the area of rectangles (including squares), including using standard units, square centimetres (cm²) and square metres (m²), and estimate the area of irregular shapes'; 'measure and calculate the perimeter of composite rectilinear shapes in centimetres and metres'. Y5 non-statutory: missing-measure problems can be expressed algebraically, e.g. 4 + 2b = 20.
sources.source: DfE, National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study, Year 5 Measurement

sources.claim: Learners confuse area and perimeter because the formulae are taught together without conceptual grounding; they overgeneralise A = l × b to non-rectangles ('most children respond to the word area by saying length times breadth'); they hold instrumental rather than relational understanding (Skemp). Recommendation: shift from teaching formulae to cm² grids and fitting/cutting/folding/counting activities.
sources.source: Machaba, F.M. (2016), 'The concepts of area and perimeter: Insights and misconceptions of Grade 10 learners', Pythagoras 37(1), a304

pedagogy.summary: At KS3 (ages 11-13) children construct and interpret the full family of statistical displays — frequency tables (including GROUPED tables for continuous/large numerical data), bar charts, pie charts, pictograms and vertical line charts — for both categorical and grouped numerical data, and crucially CHOOSE the representation that fits the data type. Two ideas do the teaching work. First, grouping continuous data into class intervals demands intervals that are equal, non-overlapping and gap-free, so every value falls in exactly one class — which is why inequality notation (e.g. 0≤t<10, 10≤t<20) matters, to fix where a boundary value goes. Second, the representation must match the data: categorical data suits bar charts and pie charts; grouped continuous data suits touching bars/histograms; only genuinely continuous time-series data suits a line graph. The characteristic errors are ambiguous or overlapping class boundaries, and reaching for the wrong chart for the data type (e.g. a line graph joining categories, or a pie chart where the 'whole' is meaningless). Because this is representational, understanding shows in CONSTRUCTING a display, not just reading one.
bestPractices: Group continuous data into equal, non-overlapping, gap-free class intervals that cover the whole range, using inequality notation (0≤t<10, 10≤t<20…) so each value — especially a boundary value — belongs to exactly one class
Use tally marks when counting raw data into a frequency table to avoid miscounts

Teach the representation as a CHOICE driven by data type: categorical → bar chart or pie chart; grouped continuous → touching bars/histogram; proportions of a whole → pie chart; genuine time-series → line graph
Contrast a bar chart (categorical, bars with gaps) with a histogram-style display (continuous, bars touching) so children see why the data type changes the display
Compute pie-chart sector angles as (frequency ÷ total) × 360° and check they sum to 360°
Interpret comparative charts by drawing a CONCLUSION about the difference between data sets, not just reading a single value
keyRepresentations: A grouped frequency table with class intervals in inequality notation and a tally column
A bar chart (categorical, gaps between bars) set beside a histogram-style display (continuous, bars touching) for the same kind of contrast
A pie chart with sectors as (frequency ÷ total) × 360°
A 'which chart?' decision aid keyed to data type (categorical / grouped continuous / proportion / time-series)
commonMisconceptions: Choosing overlapping or ambiguous class intervals (0-10, 10-20) so a boundary value could go in either class, or leaving gaps that omit values
Choosing a representation that doesn't fit the data type — e.g. a line graph joining categorical bars, or a pie chart where the whole is not meaningful
Calculating pie-chart angles by dividing 360° by the frequency instead of taking the frequency as a fraction of the total
Miscounting raw data into the table (helped by tallying), or reading a single value from a comparative chart instead of concluding about the difference

learn.summary: KS3 learners (ages 11-13) construct and interpret the full family of statistical displays — frequency tables (including GROUPED tables for continuous/large numerical data), bar charts, pie charts, pictograms and vertical line charts — and crucially CHOOSE the representation that fits the data type. Two ideas do the teaching work. First, grouping continuous data demands class intervals that are non-overlapping and gap-free, so every value falls in exactly one class — which is why inequality notation (e.g. 0≤t<10, 10≤t<20) matters, to fix where a boundary value goes; equal class widths are the usual KS3 choice so that bar heights can be compared fairly, but equal widths are not what puts each value in exactly one class. Second, the representation must match the data: categorical data suits bar charts, pie charts or pictograms; ungrouped discrete numerical data suits a vertical line chart; grouped continuous data suits touching bars/histograms; proportions of a whole suit a pie chart; genuine time-series data suits a line graph. Because this skill is representational, understanding shows in CONSTRUCTING a display, not just reading one.

activities.title: Grouped-table-and-chart workshop (set intervals, then choose a chart)
feedback: If two intervals share an endpoint without inequality notation (e.g. 0-10 and 10-20), ask where exactly 10 goes; switch to 0≤t<10, 10≤t<20 so it settles into one class.
If any value falls in no class, your intervals have a gap — extend or adjust them so they cover the whole range without gaps.

If you join categorical bars with a line, point out the line implies an order and continuous change between categories that do not exist; grouped continuous data suits touching bars/histogram (or a frequency polygon plotted at class midpoints), and categorical data suits a bar chart with gaps.
For a pie chart, if the sectors do not sum to 360°, recheck each angle as (frequency ÷ total) × 360° rather than 360° ÷ frequency.
activities.rationale: Constructing a table and choosing/building a chart makes the interval and representation decisions consequential rather than abstract, which is where the two discriminating judgements become visible. A live builder where boundary values flag until the notation is unambiguous, and a 'choose the chart' surface that draws the mismatched choice, are optional mechanisms that may make the learning concrete; equivalent work can be done on paper with teacher feedback.
sourceClaims: Numerical data can be organised into grouped data with class intervals; class intervals can be written in different ways and care is needed with the inequalities so an item (especially a boundary/minimum/maximum value) goes into the correct group; tally marks help avoid miscounts when filling in frequencies

Representations should be chosen to fit the data type: categorical data is displayed with bar graphs/pie charts, while numerical (measurement) data uses displays with a measurement scale; distinguishing categorical from numerical data is foundational to choosing a display
Pie chart sector angles are (frequency ÷ total) × 360° and must sum to 360°; a named misconception is dividing 360° by the frequency

KS3 pupils construct and interpret appropriate tables, charts and diagrams, including frequency tables, bar charts, pie charts and pictograms for categorical data, and vertical line (bar) charts for ungrouped and grouped numerical data
learnerActions: Take a strip of raw running times (e.g. 30 runners' times to the nearest second) and set your own class-interval boundaries so the intervals are equal, non-overlapping and gap-free and cover the whole range.
Place each raw value into exactly one class; deliberately try writing intervals as 0-10 and 10-20, then find where a runner who took exactly 10 seconds goes — notice the ambiguity.
Rewrite the intervals using inequality notation (0≤t<10, 10≤t<20…) and confirm the boundary value now has exactly one home.
Choose which chart suits this data — bar chart, pie chart, line graph or histogram-style touching bars — then draw it and check the drawing against the data type.
If you choose a pie chart, compute each sector angle as (frequency ÷ total) × 360° and check the angles sum to 360°.
activities.intendedInsight: Boundary ambiguity is resolved by inequality notation so every value belongs to exactly one class; and the chart must match the data type — a line joining categorical bars implies an order and continuous change between categories that do not exist, whereas grouped continuous data is shown with touching bars (a frequency polygon through class midpoints is a separate, legitimate display for grouped continuous data).

activities.title: Count raw data into a frequency table with tallies
feedback: If your frequencies do not sum to the number of data items, recount the tallies for the disputed rows.
If a value seems to belong to two class rows, your intervals overlap — fix them with inequality notation so each value lands in exactly one class.
activities.rationale: Accurate counting into a table is a prerequisite for every downstream display; tally marks are the standard technique to avoid miscounts.
sourceClaims: Numerical data can be organised into grouped data with class intervals; class intervals can be written in different ways and care is needed with the inequalities so an item (especially a boundary/minimum/maximum value) goes into the correct group; tally marks help avoid miscounts when filling in frequencies
learnerActions: Take a set of raw data (e.g. favourite sports of a class, or heights measured to the nearest cm) and count each value into its row using tally marks.
Convert the tallies to frequencies and check the frequencies sum to the total number of data points.
For continuous or wide-ranging numerical data, group into equal class intervals in inequality notation before tallying.
activities.intendedInsight: Tallying keeps counting accurate and reliable; frequencies should reconcile with the total, catching miscounts.

activities.title: Which chart fits? Decide, justify, and interpret comparatively
feedback: If you pick a line graph for favourite sports, note that categories have no ordering or continuity to join; a bar chart or pie chart fits categorical data.
If you report only one class's value when asked to compare, cite both data sets first, then state the difference as your conclusion.
When naming the modal class, pick the interval with the highest frequency, not the highest boundary number.
activities.rationale: Treating the representation as a choice keyed to data type, and pushing interpretation to a comparative conclusion, targets the two characteristic errors (wrong chart for type; read-off instead of conclusion). A sorting task, a selection item that includes an overlapping-boundary option, and a pie-angle computation contrasted with the 360÷frequency error can give a scorable check when anchored to concrete data sets, but such items do not by themselves elicit independent construction of a display.
sourceClaims: Representations should be chosen to fit the data type: categorical data is displayed with bar graphs/pie charts, while numerical (measurement) data uses displays with a measurement scale; distinguishing categorical from numerical data is foundational to choosing a display

KS3 pupils construct and interpret appropriate tables, charts and diagrams, including frequency tables, bar charts, pie charts and pictograms for categorical data, and vertical line (bar) charts for ungrouped and grouped numerical data
learnerActions: Sort several data sets by which display suits them: categorical → bar chart or pie chart; grouped continuous → touching bars/histogram; proportions of a whole → pie chart; genuine time-series → line graph.
For a categorical case (e.g. pupils' favourite sports), decide whether a line graph would be a good choice and explain why or why not.
Read a bar chart comparing Class A and Class B and state a CONCLUSION about the difference between the two data sets, citing both, not just one bar's value.
Given a grouped frequency table, name the modal class (the interval with the highest frequency).
activities.intendedInsight: Choosing a display is a judgement driven by data type, and interpreting a comparative chart means concluding about the difference between data sets, not reading a single value.

activities.title: Annotated reference: contrast displays side by side
feedback: If you cannot say why one chart's bars touch and the other's have gaps, re-read the data type: grouped continuous data has touching bars; categorical data (and ungrouped discrete values) has gaps between bars or lines.
Check your decision aid matches each data type to its display before using it to choose.
activities.rationale: A worked, annotated contrast is a useful reference and scaffold for the vocabulary and decision rules, though it does not let the learner set intervals or build and judge a representation — the discriminating skills. Use it alongside, not instead of, construction work.
sourceClaims: Representations should be chosen to fit the data type: categorical data is displayed with bar graphs/pie charts, while numerical (measurement) data uses displays with a measurement scale; distinguishing categorical from numerical data is foundational to choosing a display
learnerActions: Study a bar chart of categorical data (bars with gaps) set beside a histogram-style display of grouped continuous data (bars touching) and note what each tells you about the data type.
Examine a grouped frequency table in inequality notation and identify how the boundary value is assigned.
Reveal, for each chart type, which data type it suits and add that to a 'which chart?' decision aid.
activities.intendedInsight: The touching-versus-gapped bars distinction signals continuous versus categorical data; the notation shows where boundary values belong.

constraints: Assessment of understanding should include CONSTRUCTION (building a grouped frequency table and choosing/drawing a display), not only reading given charts; the construction step is what exposes the interval and representation judgements, and the curriculum requires pupils to construct as well as interpret.

Recognition-only or selection items can check interval and chart-choice decisions and catch specific errors (overlapping intervals; 360÷frequency), but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of a display.
Static annotated displays are a reference/worked-example scaffold: they can label and contrast chart types but cannot let the learner set intervals or build and judge a representation.
Boundary values must be assigned by inequality notation (e.g. 0≤t<10, 10≤t<20) so each value belongs to exactly one class; intervals must cover the whole range without gaps.
Pie-chart sector angles are (frequency ÷ total) × 360° and must sum to 360°; dividing 360° by the frequency is a known error.
Reading a single value from a comparative chart is a performance slip to scaffold (underline the comparison, cite both data sets), not necessarily a conceptual gap; the reading skill may be intact.

3D versions of these inherently 2D displays can distort the proportions learners must read (e.g. perspective on a 3D pie chart), so a 2D display is the practical default for this topic. Comparative efficacy of 2D versus 3D is not established by the cited sources.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source's framing that a line-graph-over-categories mismatch 'is seen, not told' and that dialogue/3D formats are unsuitable reflects catalog fit judgements; these have been softened to scoped affordances/limits rather than universal claims. A static image or a dialogue can still support learning; the objective limit retained is that recognition-only responses do not elicit independent construction.
The constraint carrying the source's 3D 'adds nothing' claim was reworded to retain only the narrow distortion caution plus an efficacy caveat, dropping the categorical comparative claim.

Self-audit of worked figures: (frequency ÷ total) × 360° is the correct pie-angle formula and sectors summing to 360° is correct. Inequality-notation interval examples (0≤t<10, 10≤t<20) correctly assign a boundary value of 10 to the second class. No arithmetic errors found in the source examples.
Internal prerequisite identifiers and step-type labels were removed while the underlying reteach intent and comparative-chart diagnostic detail were preserved.

Taxonomy alignment repair after os-taxonomy PR #30 (2026-10-19): chart-choice assessment recovery now points to data presentation (mt_ChjMU2GDJa); the sector-angle recovery remains on pie charts (mt_bESTSBB0wK). Sources and other teaching content were not re-researched.

probeDeeper: 'Your intervals are 0-10 and 10-20 — where does a runner who took exactly 10 seconds go?' — forces the boundary/overlap issue into the open
Counterexample: 'Would a line graph be a good way to show pupils' favourite sports? Why or why not?' — tests chart-to-data-type on a categorical case
'Why did you choose intervals of width 10 rather than uneven widths?' — probes the equal-interval reasoning
'This chart shows Class A and Class B — what is your conclusion about the DIFFERENCE, not just one class?' — pushes interpretation to a comparative conclusion
assess.correctAnswer: Interpretation: names the modal class (the interval with the highest frequency) and draws a comparative CONCLUSION about the two classes, not a single bar's value. Construction: builds a grouped frequency table with equal, non-overlapping, gap-free class intervals in clear inequality notation (e.g. 0≤t<10, 10≤t<20) so each value has exactly one class, and chooses a representation that fits the data type — touching bars/histogram or a bar chart for the grouped frequencies (a pie chart if showing proportions), NOT a line graph joining classes. Unambiguous intervals and a chart matched to the data type are the discriminating moves.

errorPatterns.pattern: Overlapping or ambiguous class intervals: writes classes like 0-10, 10-20 (or leaves gaps) so a boundary value could belong to either class, or some values fall in none
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach on the tables prerequisite: use inequality notation (0≤t<10, 10≤t<20) so each value — especially a boundary — belongs to exactly one class, and check the intervals cover the whole range without gaps
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On construction the child's intervals share endpoints without inequality notation (unsure where a value of exactly 10 goes) or leave gaps that omit values

errorPatterns.pattern: Wrong representation for the data type: chooses a chart unsuited to the data — e.g. a line graph joining categorical bars, or a pie chart where the whole is not meaningful, or draws continuous grouped data as a bar chart with gaps like discrete categories
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach representation choice on the data-presentation prerequisite: match bars to categories, pie sectors to a meaningful whole, and joined lines to appropriately ordered measurements. Address grouped continuous displays here using clearly specified class intervals; do not send all chart-choice errors to the now pie-only topic.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the choose-and-draw step the child selects a line graph for categorical data, or otherwise picks a display that doesn't match whether the data is categorical, grouped continuous, a proportion, or a time-series

errorPatterns.pattern: Pie angle = 360 ÷ frequency: computes each sector angle by dividing 360° by the frequency instead of taking the frequency as a fraction of the total, of 360°
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach the proportion on the pie-chart prerequisite: the angle is (frequency ÷ total) × 360°. Check each sector against its category share, then check that the angles total a full turn; the sum alone does not establish that the shares are correct.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: If a pie chart is chosen, the child writes 360 ÷ frequency for a sector and the sectors do not sum to 360°

errorPatterns.pattern: Read-off instead of conclusion: on a comparative chart reads a single class/bar value where a conclusion about the difference between data sets is asked
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, do not reteach: underline the comparison in the question and have the child cite BOTH data sets before concluding; the reading skill is intact
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On interpret (b) the child states one class's or one bar's value rather than comparing the two data sets and concluding about the difference

responseLevels.gap: Constructs tables with overlapping/gappy or ambiguous intervals; chooses charts unsuited to the data type; reads a single value where a comparison is asked
responseLevels.full: Interprets given representations AND constructs a grouped frequency table with equal, non-overlapping intervals and selects a representation appropriate to the data type, justifying the choice — transferring to a fresh data set
responseLevels.partial: Interprets given tables and charts, and can draw a pie or bar chart when told which to use, but chooses class intervals or the representation unreliably when left to decide — can build a display but not judge which fits the data type

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Two moves. FIRST, interpret given representations: (a) 'Here is a grouped frequency table of pupils' heights — which is the modal class?' (b) 'This bar chart compares Class A and Class B's scores — what can you conclude about the difference?' THEN, translate/construct: 'Here is the raw data — the times, to the nearest second, of 30 runners. Make a grouped frequency table (choose your own class intervals), then decide the best chart to display it and draw it.' Watch especially the class-interval boundaries and the chart choice — that construction step is the discriminator.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The interpret step can be done fairly mechanically; the CONSTRUCT step forces the two judgements into the open. A child who doesn't grasp grouping writes overlapping or gappy intervals and cannot say where a boundary value goes; a child who doesn't grasp representation reaches for a chart that mismatches the data type (a line graph over categories). Both are visible in what they build, separating those who can read a display from those who can design one for the data.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 7–8 (UK Y3, US Grade 3). Solving multiplication/division problems including SCALING ('n times as big/many') and CORRESPONDENCE (n objects each connected to m objects) — multiplicative structures beyond simple equal groups.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y3 'solve problems, including missing number problems, involving multiplication and division, including positive integer scaling problems and correspondence problems in which n objects are connected to m objects'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.OA.3 word problems with equal groups/arrays/measurement; scaling and combinations extend toward 4.OA.2 (multiplicative comparison) and combinatorial reasoning.
• Operational details: SCALING is multiplicative enlargement — 'a tower 3 times as tall' — and must be distinguished from additive '3 taller'. CORRESPONDENCE is systematic pairing — 3 tops each with 4 bottoms = 3×4 = 12 outfits — which naturally forms an array. Bar models represent scaling; organised listing/arrays handle correspondence.
• Checkpoint: recognise the structure and solve. Tier A (7): solve a simple 'n times as many' scaling problem. Tier B (7–8): solve a correspondence problem (3 tops, 4 bottoms) systematically. Tier C (8): explain why '3 times as tall' is ×3 not +3, and represent a correspondence problem as an array.
bestPractices: Distinguish scaling ('3 times as tall/heavy/many' — multiplicative) from additive change ('3 more') explicitly, using bar models where one bar is literally three times the length of the other.
Represent correspondence problems as an array or an organised list so all combinations are found systematically — 3 tops × 4 bottoms fills a 3×4 array of outfits — preventing undercounting.
Use bar models for scaling and comparison so the multiplicative relationship is seen, not just calculated.
Include missing-number and division versions (if the tower is 3 times as tall and 18 cm, how tall is the original?) so scaling and its inverse are both practised.
Connect correspondence to the array/commutativity work so children see it as the same multiplication structure in a new context.
keyRepresentations: Bar model with one bar a multiple of the other (scaling/comparison)
Array or organised list for correspondence/combinations
Correspondence diagram (each of n linked to each of m)
Missing-number equations for the inverse (division) version
commonMisconceptions: Treating scaling additively: reading '3 times as tall' as '3 cm/units taller' rather than ×3.
Undercounting correspondence combinations by not being systematic (missing pairings).
Not recognising a correspondence problem as multiplication at all.
Confusing which quantity is scaled and by how much in comparison problems.
Ignoring the inverse: unable to work backward from the scaled quantity to the original (the division version).

learn.summary: For ages 7–8: solve multiplication/division problems involving SCALING ('n times as big/many', a multiplicative enlargement distinct from additive 'n more') and CORRESPONDENCE (n objects each paired with m objects, e.g. 3 tops × 4 bottoms = 12 outfits, or 4 shirts × 3 trousers = 12), plus the inverse missing-number/division versions. Learners manipulate bars to see scaling as multiplying not adding, build organised pairings or arrays for correspondence, and work backward from a scaled quantity to the original.

activities.title: Stretch the bar: 'times as tall' versus 'taller'
feedback: If a learner answers 11 cm for '3 times as long as 8 cm', they added the multiplier. Build three copies of the 8 cm ribbon end to end so 'times as long' is seen as copies, not 'longer by'.

If the ×3 bar and the +3 bar look similar in a learner's drawing, check the original length: with an 8 cm original, ×3 reaches 24 cm while +3 reaches only 11 cm — and with these operations the gap grows as the original grows.
For the inverse, if a learner multiplies instead of dividing, ask 'three times WHAT gives 18?' and count back in copies.
activities.rationale: Bar models that make one bar literally a multiple of the other let the multiplicative relationship be seen, not just calculated, and directly contrast with an additive bar so the common 'times = more' error is confronted. Including the division version practises scaling and its inverse together.
sourceClaims: Y3: solve problems involving multiplication and division, including positive integer scaling problems and correspondence problems in which n objects are connected to m objects.
learnerActions: Draw or stretch a bar to make it a chosen number of times as long as an 8 cm original bar (e.g. ×3).
Alongside, place a second 'additive' comparison bar that is only 3 units longer than the original, and compare the two end points.
State and solve: 'A blue ribbon is 3 times as long as a red ribbon that is 8 cm — how long is the blue one?' (answer 24 cm).
Then reverse it: given a bar that is 3 times as long and measures 18 cm, find the original length (18 ÷ 3 = 6 cm).
Say aloud why '3 times as long' means three copies, not 'longer by 3'.
activities.intendedInsight: 'n times as big' is multiplicative — it makes that many copies of the quantity — so for this original of 8 cm the ×3 bar (24 cm) ends up well beyond the +3 bar (11 cm); the size of that gap depends on the original (it is not universally true that 'times' exceeds 'plus' for every original and factor), and the inverse of scaling is division.

activities.title: Every outfit: building correspondence as an array
feedback: If a learner answers 7 outfits (4 + 3), they summed the sets instead of pairing. Lay out each shirt with each of the 3 trousers so 4 groups of 3 = 12 becomes visible.
If some combinations are missing, return to the organised list and check every shirt has been paired with every pair of trousers.
Connect to earlier array/commutativity work: 4 rows of 3 and 3 rows of 4 give the same total.
activities.rationale: Representing correspondence as an organised list or array makes all pairings explicit and reveals it as multiplication in a new context, countering both undercounting and the additive error. Drawing or arranging pairings into a grid makes the structure concrete.
sourceClaims: Y3: solve problems involving multiplication and division, including positive integer scaling problems and correspondence problems in which n objects are connected to m objects.
3.OA.3 solve word problems involving equal groups, arrays and measurement; multiplicative comparison develops at 4.OA.1–2.
learnerActions: Solve: 'You have 4 shirts and 3 pairs of trousers — how many different outfits can you make?'
Make an organised list or draw lines pairing each shirt with each of the 3 pairs of trousers, so no pairing is missed.
Arrange the completed pairings into a 4×3 (or 3×4) array and count the cells to confirm 12 outfits.
Change one quantity (e.g. 5 pairs of trousers, giving 4 × 5 = 20) and rebuild to see how the total changes.
Explain why the answer is 4 × 3, not 4 + 3.
activities.intendedInsight: Correspondence (each of n paired with each of m) is the same multiplication structure as an array; working systematically finds all combinations and prevents undercounting.

activities.title: Fill the box: missing factors and the inverse
feedback: If a learner writes 36 (42 − 6) for 6 × □ = 42, they subtracted. Reframe as 'six times what is 42?' and use a times-table fact or 42 ÷ 6.
If a learner guesses without a fact or inverse, model checking by multiplying the guess back.
A correct set-up with a wrong number is a calculation slip, not a structure error — have the learner recompute and verify with the inverse rather than reteaching the concept.
activities.rationale: Practising the inverse (division) version alongside direct multiplication consolidates the multiplicative structure and addresses the common additive attempt to fill missing-number boxes.
learnerActions: Solve the missing-number problem 6 × □ = 42 by asking 'six times WHAT is 42?' and using a known fact or 42 ÷ 6.
Check the answer (□ = 7) by multiplying back: 6 × 7 = 42.
Create and solve a missing-number scaling problem, e.g. 'The tower is 3 times as tall and 18 cm — how tall is the original?' (6 cm).
Explain how multiplication and division undo each other here.
activities.intendedInsight: A missing factor is found with a known fact or by division, not by adding or subtracting; multiplication and division are inverses.

activities.title: Sort and match: which structure is this?
feedback: If a learner is drawn to the additive bait, return to building copies (scaling) or pairing every item (correspondence).
Ask the learner to say why the chosen operation fits the story structure, not just to pick an answer.
activities.rationale: Recognition and sorting tasks make a useful companion check on whether learners identify the structure and spot additive traps; they rehearse and assess choices but do not by themselves require the learner to construct a bar, list or array.
learnerActions: For each word problem, decide whether it is scaling or correspondence, whether the unknown is the result or a missing number (such as the original length or a missing factor), and which operation it needs.
Match a correspondence problem to the array that represents it.
Spot and correct a tempting wrong answer, e.g. choosing '11 cm' for '3 times as long as 8 cm' or '7 outfits' for 4 shirts and 3 trousers.
Justify each choice before solving.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising the multiplicative structure across its varied forms (scaling, correspondence, missing factor, the last solved by division) is an important part of the objective, alongside building representations and solving the problems.

constraints: Scaling must be distinguished explicitly from additive change; '3 times as tall' is ×3, not +3.
Correspondence must be solved systematically (organised list or array) so every pairing is found and undercounting is avoided.
Include both missing-number and division versions so scaling and its inverse are both practised.

Recognition/sorting tasks check whether a learner identifies the structure but do not themselves require constructing a bar, list or array; keep hands-on building of representations as a central route to the concept.

Static illustrations and a posed challenge ('how many outfits?') can introduce or prompt the ideas; manipulating bars and pairings may help learners explore the multiplicative-vs-additive contrast and the systematic count, but this is a proposed approach rather than an evidenced requirement or the only effective route.

Correct the additive errors directly during teaching (copies for scaling, full pairing for correspondence); never present '4+3' or '8+3' as an acceptable answer — show them only as errors to identify and fix.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The CCSS claim (3.OA.3 / 4.OA.1–2) is marked verified:false in the source; treat its standards mapping as unconfirmed.

The original framed a flat/planar representation as having 'no conceptual value' in 3D; this comparative/necessity claim is not established by the source evidence and has been dropped. Bars and arrays are planar here simply because the relationships are naturally represented in two dimensions.

Optional interaction examples (a stretch slider, a ghost additive bar, drag-to-pair lines arranging into a grid, an inverse toggle) are retained as illustrative mechanisms, not as required tooling, and their efficacy is untested.
Arithmetic self-check: 3×8=24; 4×3=12; 4×5=20; 18÷3=6; 6×7=42; 42−6=36; additive traps 8+3=11 and 4+3=7 are shown only as errors to correct.

The multiplicative-over-additive contrast is demonstrated with the chosen numbers (original 8 cm, factor ×3); 'times as big' is not universally larger than 'n more' for every original/factor (e.g. equal for an original of 2 scaled by ×2), so the contrast is tied to the stated example and, for ×3 vs +3, the gap grows with the original.

probeDeeper: Why do you multiply 4 by 3 for the outfits rather than adding them?
'3 times as long as 8 cm' — how is that different from '3 cm longer'?
For 6 × □ = 42, how did you find what goes in the box?
If there were 5 pairs of trousers, how many outfits now?
assess.correctAnswer: 24 cm (3 × 8, scaling); 12 outfits (4 × 3, correspondence); □ = 7 (missing factor, via 42 ÷ 6 or knowing 6×7). The teacher watches for multiplication on the scaling and correspondence problems and use of a known fact / inverse for the missing number.

errorPatterns.pattern: adds on the correspondence problem (4 + 3 = 7 outfits) instead of pairing every shirt with every trouser
errorPatterns.nextMove: lay out the pairings systematically (each shirt with each of 3 trousers) so 4 groups of 3 = 12 becomes visible.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer of 7 outfits; child sums the sets

errorPatterns.pattern: reads scaling additively — '3 times as long as 8' as 8 + 3 = 11
errorPatterns.nextMove: build three copies of the 8 cm ribbon; 'times as long' means copies, not 'longer by'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer of 11 cm; child adds the multiplier

errorPatterns.pattern: cannot handle the missing-number box — tries to add or subtract to fill it, not seeing the missing factor
errorPatterns.nextMove: reframe 6 × □ = 42 as 'six times WHAT is 42' and use the known fact or 42÷6.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child writes 36 (42−6) or guesses without using a fact/inverse

errorPatterns.pattern: correct operation, calculation slip
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach structure; have the child recompute and check with the inverse.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: right set-up, wrong number

responseLevels.gap: adds on correspondence, reads scaling additively, or cannot fill the missing-number box.
responseLevels.full: chooses multiplication for scaling and correspondence and uses a fact/inverse for the missing number, justifying each set-up and checking results.
responseLevels.partial: handles one or two structures but slips on correspondence or the missing number, or needs prompting to see the multiplication.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child these to solve while you watch the set-up: (scaling) 'A blue ribbon is 3 times as long as a red ribbon that is 8 cm — how long is the blue one?'; (correspondence) 'You have 4 shirts and 3 pairs of trousers. How many different outfits can you make?'; (missing number) 'Fill in the box: 6 × □ = 42.' Watch which operation they choose for each.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Correspondence is where children add (4 + 3 = 7 outfits) instead of multiplying, and scaling is where they add the multiplier (8 + 3). Watching the operation chosen across the three structures shows whether the child recognises multiplication in its varied disguises — the point of the objective.

pedagogy.summary: Because area is additive, a rectilinear figure (an L- or T-shape) can be cut into non-overlapping rectangles, each area found by multiplying, then summed. The two hard steps are partitioning cleanly (no gaps, no overlaps) and deriving a sub-rectangle's missing side from the outer measurements. It is a direct application of area-as-additive and of finding rectangle areas by multiplying.
bestPractices: Physically cut or draw the figure into rectangles before calculating, so the decomposition is concrete
Show that more than one valid decomposition gives the SAME total — the point of additivity
Teach how to derive missing internal lengths from the given outer lengths (e.g. 5 − 3 = 2)
Insist the two pieces are non-overlapping — shade them different colours and check no tile is both
Keep square units on every sub-area and the total
keyRepresentations: An L/T-shape with dashed decomposition lines
A grid overlay for counting/checking sub-rectangles
The two sub-rectangles pulled apart and labelled
A figure with some sides blank, prompting missing-length reasoning
commonMisconceptions: Treats the figure as one big rectangle — multiplies the outer bounding dimensions as if the notch weren't there
Overlaps the two sub-rectangles and double-counts the shared corner
Cannot find a sub-rectangle's side when it isn't printed
Adds side lengths / a perimeter-like total instead of areas, or drops the square unit

learn.summary: Teaches children to find the area of compound rectilinear shapes (L- and T-shapes) by decomposing them into non-overlapping rectangles, finding each rectangle's area by multiplying, and summing. The two hard steps are partitioning cleanly (no gaps, no overlaps) and deriving a sub-rectangle's missing internal side from the given outer measurements. This rests on two prior ideas: area is additive, and rectangle area is found by multiplying rows by columns. For the worked example, a 3 m × 5 m rectangle gives 15 m² and a 2 m × 4 m rectangle gives 8 m², summing to 23 m². The sub-areas are ADDED (not multiplied) because area is additive.

activities.title: Cut the L-shaped floor plan into rectangles
feedback: If a cut leaves the corner region inside both pieces, that overlap is double-counted — shade the two pieces in different colours and check that no tile is both colours.
If the child multiplies the two sub-areas (e.g. 15×8) instead of adding, point back to the grid: each rectangle covers a separate set of tiles, so the tile counts are summed, giving 15 + 8 = 23.
If the total differs after a second split, re-check for a gap or overlap: valid non-overlapping splits must give the same total.
If the answer is written as '23 m' rather than '23 m²', relabel: area is counted in square units, not length units.
activities.rationale: Decomposing is a spatial act with concrete consequences: an overlapping cut double-counts the shared corner, and a different valid cut lands on the same total. Drawing and re-cutting makes additivity something the child discovers, and prompting why the pieces are added (not multiplied) names the additive principle explicitly.
sourceClaims: For 3.MD.7d, real-world area problems involve figures that are not all rectangular but decomposable into rectangles (e.g. an 'L-shaped' room); students recognise area as additive and find such areas by decomposing and adding.
Area is additive: the area of the union of two regions that overlap only at their boundaries is the sum of their areas; area is measured by tiling without gaps or overlaps.
Pupils find the area of rectilinear/compound shapes by counting or by splitting into rectangles at Key Stage 2.
learnerActions: Look at an L-shaped room on a grid with its outer measurements labelled.
Draw a cut line to split the shape into two non-overlapping rectangles.
Find each sub-rectangle's area by multiplying its sides (e.g. 3×5 = 15 m² and 2×4 = 8 m²).
Add the two areas to get the total, keeping square-metre units (23 m²).
Say why the two areas are ADDED rather than multiplied: each rectangle covers a separate part of the floor, and area is additive.
Re-cut the same shape a different valid way and confirm the total is still 23 m².
activities.intendedInsight: A rectilinear figure can be split into non-overlapping rectangles whose areas ADD to the whole; the pieces are summed (not multiplied) because area is additive, and any valid split gives the same total.

activities.title: Find the hidden internal side
feedback: If the child stalls at the blank side, prompt: 'Which outer measurements tell you this hidden length?'
If a number is invented rather than computed, show the subtraction that produces it (e.g. 5 − 3 = 2 for that illustrative figure, or 5 − 2 = 3 / 7 − 3 = 4 for the 23 m² plan).
activities.rationale: Deriving missing internal lengths is a distinct hurdle from partitioning; isolating it as a strategy prompt (not a concept reteach) targets children who freeze at an unprinted side.
sourceClaims: For 3.MD.7d, real-world area problems involve figures that are not all rectangular but decomposable into rectangles (e.g. an 'L-shaped' room); students recognise area as additive and find such areas by decomposing and adding.
learnerActions: Look at a compound shape (which may be a separate illustrative figure, not the earlier floor plan) where one internal side is left blank and only the outer measurements are printed.

Work out which outer measurements determine the missing internal length by subtracting; for example, 5 − 3 = 2 is a generic illustration of taking one printed outer length from another, not the derivation of a hidden side in the 23 m² floor plan (whose hidden sides come from 5 − 2 = 3 and 7 − 3 = 4).
Mark the derived length on the figure.
Complete the decomposition and compute the total area.
activities.intendedInsight: A sub-rectangle's unlabelled side can be derived by reasoning about the outer lengths, not guessed or taken only from printed numbers.

activities.title: Spot the whole-rectangle error
feedback: If the child accepts 35 m², overlay a grid and count the corner tiles that are missing from the figure.
If the child multiplies every printed number, ask which rectangle each number belongs to; the shape is two separate rectangles, not one product.
Reinforce: cut the figure into rectangles, then multiply each piece, then add.
activities.rationale: The whole-rectangle error (treating a compound shape as one big rectangle, or multiplying all numbers) is the signature misconception; confronting it on a fresh case surfaces and corrects it. Grid counting grounds the point concretely.
sourceClaims: Spatial structuring (seeing a region as rows and columns of squares) is the key hurdle and must be built with many array activities; discussions must distinguish area from length — grounding the overlap and add-the-edges errors.
learnerActions: Examine a worked solution where someone multiplied the outer bounding dimensions (e.g. 5×7 = 35 m²) as if the notch weren't there, or multiplied every printed number together.
Explain what that person forgot about the shape.
Overlay or imagine a grid and count: the tiles in the missing corner are not there.
Give the correct total by decomposing first (15 + 8 = 23 m²).
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying the outer bounding dimensions — or multiplying all the printed numbers together — counts tiles the shape does not contain; the missing notch must be accounted for, and here we do that by decomposing the shape into rectangles before multiplying each piece.

activities.title: Covering versus going around
feedback: If the child sums the edges, tile a sub-rectangle and have them count the square units inside instead.
If the square unit is dropped, relabel the total with m².
activities.rationale: Some children add side lengths or drop the square unit, conflating area with perimeter. Contrasting covering with going around, and counting actual tiles, distinguishes the two quantities.
sourceClaims: Spatial structuring (seeing a region as rows and columns of squares) is the key hurdle and must be built with many array activities; discussions must distinguish area from length — grounding the overlap and add-the-edges errors.
learnerActions: Tile one sub-rectangle and count the square units inside it.
Contrast that with tracing around the edges of the whole figure.
State whether the task asks for area (tiles inside) or perimeter (distance around), and answer with the correct square units.
activities.intendedInsight: Area counts the squares covering the inside and is reported in square units; adding up the edges gives a perimeter-like total, which is a different quantity.

constraints: Insist the two pieces are non-overlapping — shade them different colours and check no tile belongs to both; non-overlapping is exactly what lets the areas add.
Keep square units on every sub-area and on the total.

A static tap-to-reveal figure (reveal the dashed split, then each sub-area, then a lift-the-flap total) can explain the method, but does not let the child attempt their own cut or catch an overlap they created; use it as an explanatory scaffold, not as the main construction task.
Keep the figures flat rectilinear plans. Adding a third dimension drifts toward volume and obscures the decomposition, so a 3D treatment is not suited to this specific objective.

A scripted in-role dialogue does not itself elicit the child drawing a cut, computing each sub-area and summing; if used, let it frame or discuss the task rather than replace the hands-on construction. This is a scope note, not a claim that dialogue is inherently unable to teach the procedure.

Recognition-only formats (matching a shape to a valid decomposition, picking the 35 m² distractor) can assess and reinforce, but do not by themselves elicit the child independently drawing a cut and deriving a missing length.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic checked: 3×5 = 15, 2×4 = 8, 15+8 = 23 m²; the whole-rectangle distractor 5×7 = 35 m² is intentionally the wrong answer and must never be presented as correct. The 23 m² figure is self-consistent with a 5 m × 7 m bounding box (35 m²) and a 3 m × 4 m notch (12 m²), since 35 − 12 = 23.

The derived length '5 − 3 = 2' is a generic illustration only. In the specific 23 m² figure the hidden internal sides derive as 5 − 2 = 3 or 7 − 3 = 4, so if 'Find the hidden internal side' is deployed on the same shape its numbers must be relabelled for consistency.

Teachers should ensure the printed outer measurements of any specific figure are self-consistent with the intended decomposition, the one blank internal side, and the bounding box used for the distractor before use.
The objective covers both L- and T-shapes; the activities use an L-shape as the representative worked figure, and a T-shaped plan is an equally valid example to vary with.
One cited claim (National Curriculum KS2) was marked unverified in the source; it is retained as supporting the general splitting-into-rectangles approach, not as independent evidence of efficacy.

probeDeeper: 'You split it into these two rectangles — could you split it a different way and still get 23 m²? Show me.' (additivity / conservation across decompositions)
'How did you work out this side when it wasn't written on the plan?'
'Someone got 35 m² by doing 5×7. What did they forget about the shape?' (surfaces the whole-rectangle error on a fresh case)
'Why do we ADD the two areas together, and not multiply them?'
assess.correctAnswer: Draws a decomposition into two non-overlapping rectangles, derives the unlabelled internal length from the given outer lengths, computes 3×5 = 15 m² and 2×4 = 8 m², sums to 23 m² keeping square-metre units, and can show that a different valid split gives the same 23 m².

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the whole figure as one rectangle — multiplies the outer bounding dimensions (e.g. 5×7) as if the notch weren't there, or multiplies all the given numbers together
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay a grid and count — the tiles in the missing corner aren't there; then cut the figure into rectangles before multiplying.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives 35 m² (5×7) for the L-shape, or multiplies every printed number

errorPatterns.pattern: Overlaps the two sub-rectangles and double-counts the shared corner, so the total comes out too big
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't just correct the number — have them shade the two pieces in different colours and check that no tile is both colours; non-overlapping IS what makes the areas add. This coordinates with spatial-structuring practice and self-corrects.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The two rectangles the child draws share a strip or corner, and that region gets counted in both areas

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot find a sub-rectangle's side when it isn't printed — guesses or freezes rather than deriving it from the outer lengths
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold: 'Which outer measurements tell you this hidden length?' and mark the derived length on the figure — a strategy prompt, not a concept reteach.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Stalls at the blank internal side, or invents a number instead of computing (e.g. 5 − 3)

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds side lengths / gives a perimeter-like total instead of areas, or drops the square unit (answers in m not m²)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast covering (tiles inside) with going around (edges); tile one sub-rectangle so the child counts square units and re-labels the answer.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Sums the edges around the figure, or writes the total as '23 m' rather than '23 m²'

responseLevels.gap: Treats the figure as one rectangle or overlaps the pieces; cannot decompose it into non-overlapping rectangles.
responseLevels.full: Partitions into non-overlapping rectangles (deriving missing internal lengths), sums the areas with correct square units, and recognises that a different valid decomposition yields the same total.
responseLevels.partial: Decomposes into rectangles and finds each area when every dimension is given, but lists the pieces without reliably summing, or stalls when an internal side must be derived — can't yet transfer to a figure needing a worked-out length.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set the task and watch how the child decomposes. Present an L-shaped room drawn on paper with the outer measurements labelled — overall it is a 3 m × 5 m rectangle with a 2 m × 4 m rectangle joined on, and one internal length is left blank so it must be worked out. Say: 'Find the total area of this room. Show me how you split it up.' Watch them partition, find each area, sum, and handle the missing side; then ask them to split it a different way.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching HOW the child cuts catches overlaps and gaps that a bare answer would hide; the blank internal side catches whether they reason about hidden lengths or just use printed numbers; asking for a second split catches whether they trust additivity or believe the total depends on how you cut.
