pedagogy.summary: Two fractions are equivalent when they mark the SAME point / the same magnitude on the number line (or the same length on a strip), even though they are written with different numerators and denominators. Families such as 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6 arise because re-partitioning each unit part into finer equal parts leaves the position unchanged. Stacked and aligned number lines, and dual labels above/below one line, make the coincident points visible.
bestPractices: Use stacked 0–1 number lines (halves, thirds, fourths … tenths — IES Figure 4) and read off the points that line up.
Label one set of fractions above a single line and another set below it, pointing to 1/2 and 4/8 at the same spot (IES fix for Roadblock 2.3).
Measure equal lengths with different fraction strips (IES Figure 5) to feel 'same size'.
Practise the documented hard case: find an equivalent on a differently-partitioned line (e.g. 1/2 on a line divided into sixths).
Insist that 'same point = same number', directly countering the belief that different symbols must mean different amounts.
keyRepresentations: Stacked / aligned 0–1 number lines (IES Figure 4)
One line with dual labels above and below (1/2 above, 4/8 below at one point)
Fraction strips of different unit sizes compared by length
Fraction wall
commonMisconceptions: Cannot accept two differently-written fractions as the same point (IES Roadblock 2.3)
Cannot locate an equivalent on a differently-partitioned line (e.g. finding 1/2 as 3/6 on a sixths line)
'Different numbers can't name the same amount' — denies equivalence altogether
Additive drift — thinks 1/2 and 2/3 are equivalent because you 'add 1 to each'
Whole-number bias — 2/4 must be bigger than 1/2 because the numbers are larger

learn.summary: Two fractions are equivalent when they mark the SAME point (same magnitude) on a number line or the same length on a strip, even though they are written with different numerators and denominators. Families such as 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6 arise because re-partitioning each unit part into finer equal parts leaves the position unchanged. Stacked/aligned 0–1 number lines, dual labels above and below one line, and length-matched fraction strips make the coincident points visible. The documented hard cases are (a) accepting two differently-written fractions as the same point and (b) finding an equivalent on a differently-partitioned line (e.g. locating 1/2 as 3/6 on a line divided into sixths). Re-partitioning only produces a new name when the finer parts subdivide evenly all the way to the point.

activities.title: Plumb-line on stacked thirds and sixths lines
feedback: If a learner reads off 4/6 for the point under 2/3, confirm the shared point and ask them to measure both lengths from 0 to check they match.
If a learner insists 2/3 and 4/6 differ because the numbers differ, dual-label the single point (2/3 above, 4/6 below) and measure both lengths from 0 to show they coincide.
Probe: 'How many sixths make one half? Show me the jumps on the line.' (Answer: three sixths reach the midpoint, so 3/6 = 1/2.)
activities.rationale: Aligning lines and reading off coincident points directly addresses the documented difficulty of accepting two equivalent fractions as the same point. A live plumb-line and dual labels make the mechanism concrete; a static stacked diagram can serve the same role but cannot be re-aligned by the learner. Efficacy over other media is not established by the cited sources.
sourceClaims: Equivalent fractions are those representing the same numerical value; number lines and stacked/dual-labelled lines are the recommended tools, and students find it hard to see two equivalent fractions as the same point (Roadblock 2.3) or to find an equivalent on a differently-partitioned line. Recommendation 2 is rated moderate evidence.
learnerActions: Stack a 0–1 line divided into thirds directly above a 0–1 line divided into sixths, carefully aligned at 0 and 1.
Point to 2/3 on the thirds line and drop a vertical plumb-line straight down to the sixths line.
Name the fraction on the sixths line that sits at exactly the same point (4/6), and state in words: two different names, one position.
Repeat for other target points and record each equivalent pair you find.
Say aloud why the shared point means the two fractions are equal in size.
activities.intendedInsight: Equivalent fractions are different names for the SAME point on the number line; same position means same magnitude.

activities.title: Re-partition toggle: the point that does not move
feedback: Ask: 'When you split each third into two to make sixths, did the 2/3 mark move? Why not?' (It stays put; subdividing parts does not change position.)
If a learner claims 'there is no 1/2 on the sixths line', have them split each half into three and count the three sixths to the midpoint, then mark 3/6 on the 1/2 point.

Ask: 'Is there a fraction written in fifths that equals 1/2? Why or why not?' Use this to surface that 1/2 cannot be written as a whole number of fifths (1/2 = 2.5/5), so no fifths mark lands on it — re-partitioning only renames a point when the parts divide evenly to reach it.
activities.rationale: Explicitly re-partitioning while watching the mark stay put addresses the crux difficulty of finding an equivalent on a differently-partitioned line, and explains WHY families arise rather than just listing them. Live subdivision makes the invariance visible; a prepared sequence of printed lines can approximate it.
sourceClaims: Equivalent fractions are those representing the same numerical value; number lines and stacked/dual-labelled lines are the recommended tools, and students find it hard to see two equivalent fractions as the same point (Roadblock 2.3) or to find an equivalent on a differently-partitioned line. Recommendation 2 is rated moderate evidence.
learnerActions: Start on a thirds line with 2/3 marked.
Split each third into two equal parts to create a sixths line, keeping the 0–1 ends fixed.
Observe whether the 2/3 mark moves, and add the new label 4/6 to that same point.
Explain in your own words why subdividing each part does not shift the position, only adds a finer-grained name.
Now locate 1/2 on a line divided into sixths by splitting each half into three (not two): count three sixths to the midpoint and mark 3/6 at the 1/2 point.
activities.intendedInsight: Re-partitioning each unit part into finer equal parts preserves a fraction's position, which is why equivalent families exist. When the finer partition subdivides evenly all the way to the point, that same point simply gains a new name (1/2 becomes 3/6 on a sixths line); when the partition does not reach the point (e.g. fifths for 1/2), no such name exists.

activities.title: Measuring equal lengths with different fraction strips
feedback: If a learner lists 2/4 and 3/6 but cannot explain why, link back to the re-partition reasoning: each half splits evenly into the finer parts, so the endpoint does not move.
Ask the learner to produce one fraction that is NOT equal to 1/2 but lands near it, and one that IS equal to it, then justify each on the strip or line.
activities.rationale: A length model gives a second sense of 'same size' that complements the point model and supports generating a full equivalent family, meeting the curriculum expectation to show families of equivalents using diagrams. Physical strips and card cutouts are approximations to the idealised zero-thickness lengths they represent.
sourceClaims: Pupils recognise and show, using diagrams, families of common equivalent fractions in KS2 (Years 3–4).
learnerActions: Lay a 1/2 strip, a 2/4 strip and a 3/6 strip along the same 0–1 length.
Check by eye and by measuring that they reach the same endpoint (allowing for the slight thickness and cutting error of physical strips).
State that 'same length = same number' even though the pieces and labels differ.
Find and record at least three fractions equal to 1/2 using the strips and/or a number line (e.g. 2/4, 3/6, 5/10).
activities.intendedInsight: Equivalence can also be felt as equal length: differently-partitioned strips that reach the same point name the same amount.

activities.title: Contrast renaming with 'add one to each'
feedback: If a learner names 3/4 as equal to 2/3, place both on the shared line and show 3/4 (0.75) lies further right than 2/3 (about 0.667), then contrast the +1 shift with even subdivision.

If a learner says 2/4 must be bigger than 1/2 'because the numbers are larger', return to the shared point/length to show the two coincide; larger numerator and denominator here do not mean a larger amount.
activities.rationale: Juxtaposing additive drift and whole-number-bias errors against the same-point model lets learners see why these shortcuts fail on the line, rather than only being told they are wrong.
sourceClaims: Equivalent fractions are those representing the same numerical value; number lines and stacked/dual-labelled lines are the recommended tools, and students find it hard to see two equivalent fractions as the same point (Roadblock 2.3) or to find an equivalent on a differently-partitioned line. Recommendation 2 is rated moderate evidence.
learnerActions: On a shared 0–1 line with 2/3 marked, predict where 3/4 (from 'add 1 to top and bottom') would land.
Place 3/4 on the line and observe it sits to the RIGHT of 2/3, at a different point.
Compare this +1 shift with splitting each part into finer pieces, which did not move the mark.
Explain why adding the same number to numerator and denominator is NOT the same as finding an equivalent.
activities.intendedInsight: Equivalence is a shared point produced by re-partitioning; adding the same amount to numerator and denominator is not a valid way to find equivalents, because for any fraction other than one whole it moves the point (2/3 -> 3/4 is further right), so the new fraction is not equivalent. (The only exception is a fraction equal to 1, such as 2/2 -> 3/3, which stays at 1.)

activities.title: Verify and sort equivalents (practice and check)
feedback: For each decision, require the learner to point to the position or length that justifies it, not just a symbolic rule.
If a sorting error appears, return to the shared line to locate both fractions before correcting.
activities.rationale: Verification and sorting consolidate and check the concept after it has been constructed and apply the same-value definition directly (e.g. 'do 2/3 and 4/6 land on the same point?'); this is practice/assessment support, so it should follow, not replace, the construction activities above. A sort can check classification but does not itself elicit the physical re-partitioning or the explanation of why the point does not move.
sourceClaims: Equivalent fractions are those representing the same numerical value; number lines and stacked/dual-labelled lines are the recommended tools, and students find it hard to see two equivalent fractions as the same point (Roadblock 2.3) or to find an equivalent on a differently-partitioned line. Recommendation 2 is rated moderate evidence.
learnerActions: Decide for pairs such as 'do 2/3 and 4/6 land on the same point?' and justify using a line or strip.
Match equivalent fractions to a target fraction.
Sequence a set of fractions in order along a number line.
Sort cards into 'equivalent to 1/2' and 'not equivalent to 1/2', explaining each placement.
activities.intendedInsight: Once the same-point idea is built, learners can reliably verify, match and sort equivalents and justify their decisions by position or length.

constraints: Target understanding (REPRESENTATIONAL): learners should locate, generate and explain equivalents, not just recognise them.

A fraction wall or stacked-line reference that only highlights a family (e.g. tap 1/2 -> highlights 2/4, 3/6, 4/8) is a useful recall/reference scaffold but does not let the learner re-partition, so it cannot by itself build the crux differently-partitioned case; use it alongside, not instead of, re-partitioning work.

Verification/matching/sorting tasks consolidate and assess classification but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of a family or an explanation of why the point does not move; pair them with construction activities.

Full understanding requires generating a correct family for 1/2 AND explaining equivalence as re-partitioning that preserves position AND correctly rejecting a non-equivalent (e.g. recognising that no fraction written in fifths equals 1/2, since no fifths mark lands on it). Reading off a single aligned equivalent is only partial.
Fraction strips and card cutouts have slight physical thickness; treat them as approximations to the ideal zero-thickness lengths and points on an idealised number line.

Re-partitioning only yields an equivalent when each unit part subdivides evenly to the point: 1/2 can be named in sixths (3/6, each half split into three) but cannot be written as any whole number of fifths, so no fifths mark lands on 1/2. Keep this condition explicit — never describe a half as simply 'absent from the line'.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row claimed 3D 'adds nothing' and that dialogue/conversation could not teach this because equivalence 'is planar' and 'built by aligning and re-partitioning, not by in-role dialogue'. These are catalog-fit judgements, not established comparative-efficacy findings, and have been softened/omitted: a number-line/length focus is well justified here, but universal necessity or medium-superiority claims are not asserted.
The IES claim is marked verified in the source row; the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified:false. Treat the curriculum citation as an expectation statement, not as efficacy evidence.

Arithmetic checked: 1/2 = 2.5/5 is not a fifths gridpoint, so no fifths-partition mark equals 1/2; applying +1 to top and bottom of 2/3 gives 3/4 = 0.75 > 2/3 (about 0.667), correctly further right; 2/4, 3/6 and 5/10 all equal 1/2; three sixths reach the midpoint (3/6 = 1/2); halves become sixths by splitting each half into three, thirds become sixths by splitting each third into two.

Editorial correction (no new source check): the original row's 'full' level and discriminator phrased the fifths non-example as '1/2 is not a point on a fifths line'. This was tightened to 'no fraction written in fifths equals 1/2 / no fifths mark lands on it', since 1/2 is a magnitude present on any 0–1 line and only its fifths-partition naming is impossible.

probeDeeper: When you split each third into two to make sixths, did the 2/3 mark move? Why not?
Is 1/2 on a line divided into fifths? Why or why not?
Give me a fraction that is NOT equal to 1/2 but lands near it, and one that IS equal to it.
How many sixths make one half? Show me the jumps on the line.
assess.correctAnswer: 4/6 is at the same point as 2/3 — same position means same magnitude, so 2/3 = 4/6 (each third splits into two sixths, the point does not move). Three fractions equal to 1/2: e.g. 2/4, 3/6, 5/10, each marking the midpoint of 0–1.

errorPatterns.pattern: Same-point denied — 'the dots are in the same place but the numbers are different, so they can't be equal'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Dual-label the single point (2/3 above, 4/6 below) and measure both lengths from 0 to show they match
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Refuses to accept 2/3 = 4/6 despite the shared point

errorPatterns.pattern: Additive equivalence — offers 3/4 (or treats 1/2 ≈ 2/3) as equal by 'adding 1 to top and bottom'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Place both on the shared line; show 3/4 sits to the right of 2/3; contrast the +1 shift with splitting each part
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names 3/4 as equal to 2/3, or places supposed equivalents at different points

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot find an equivalent on a differently-partitioned line — 'there is no 1/2 on the sixths line'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count sixths to the midpoint (three of them) and mark 3/6 on the 1/2 point
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Locates 1/2 among halves but says it is absent from a sixths line

responseLevels.gap: Treats differently-written fractions as necessarily different amounts; cannot find an equivalent on a differently-partitioned line.
responseLevels.full: Identifies same-point equivalence, generates a correct family for 1/2, explains equivalence as re-partitioning that preserves position, and correctly rejects a non-equivalent (e.g. 1/2 is not a point on a fifths line).
responseLevels.partial: Reads off an aligned equivalent (4/6 = 2/3) from stacked lines but cannot generate a family independently or explain why the point does not move — lists 2/4, 3/6 without the re-partition reasoning.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show stacked 0-to-1 number lines, one divided into thirds and one into sixths, lined up. Point to 2/3 on the thirds line and ask: 'Which fraction on the sixths line is at exactly the same point, and how do you know they are equal?' Then ask: 'Show me on these lines three fractions that are all equal to 1/2.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who reads equivalence as same-point identifies 4/6 and generates a correct family. The Roadblock-2.3 child insists 2/3 and 4/6 differ because the numbers differ; the additive child offers 3/4 ('2/3 plus one to each'); the whole-number-bias child says 4/6 is bigger. Both moves — interpret the aligned point and produce a family — are required.

sources.claim: Equivalent fractions are those representing the same numerical value; number lines and stacked/dual-labelled lines are the recommended tools, and students find it hard to see two equivalent fractions as the same point (Roadblock 2.3) or to find an equivalent on a differently-partitioned line. Recommendation 2 is rated moderate evidence.
sources.source: IES/WWC Practice Guide, Developing Effective Fractions Instruction for K-8 (Siegler et al., 2010, NCEE 2010-4039)

sources.claim: Pupils recognise and show, using diagrams, families of common equivalent fractions in KS2 (Years 3–4).
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (KS1-2)

pedagogy.summary: The bar model (tape diagram) is the workhorse representation of the whole ratio-and-proportion strand: a ratio like 3:2 becomes 3 equal blocks beside 2 equal blocks, and once ONE block's value is known, every ratio, sharing, scaling and percentage problem is read straight off the picture. The key idea children must build is that each block is an equal unit, and that solving is a three-move routine — draw the bars to match the relationship, find the value of one block, then read off what's asked. Teaching should establish the equal-block convention firmly, move from concrete (cubes/counters) to the drawn bar, and always draw the diagram BEFORE calculating so the structure of the problem is made visible rather than guessed from key words.
bestPractices: Establish the equal-unit convention explicitly: every block in the bars is the SAME size and stands for the same amount — the model breaks if blocks are drawn unequal.
Teach the three-move routine: (1) draw bars matching the ratio/parts, (2) find the value of one block (total ÷ number of blocks), (3) read off the required quantity — make step 2 the pivot.
Contrast part-to-part (two separate bars, e.g. 3 and 2) with part-to-whole (one bar of 5, or a whole bar split) so children pick the right layout for the question.
Progress concrete → pictorial → abstract: build the ratio with coloured cubes, then draw the labelled bar, then connect to the numeric calculation.
Label the bars fully — the total (a brace over the whole), the known value, and the '?' — so the diagram carries the problem's information.

Compare the bar model with double number lines and ratio tables on the same problem so children can say when each is most useful (bar for sharing a fixed total; double number line/table for scaling up a rate).
keyRepresentations: Part-to-part twin bars (e.g. 3 equal blocks : 2 equal blocks) with a brace showing the total
Part-to-whole single bar split into the total number of parts, one section shaded
Cubes/counters as the concrete precursor to drawn blocks
Ratio table and double number line as complementary models to contrast
One labelled block annotated with its value (the pivot of the three-move routine)
commonMisconceptions: Draws blocks of unequal size, so the model no longer represents equal units
Sets up part-to-whole when the problem is part-to-part (draws a bar of 3 for a 3:2 ratio and treats the 2 as part of it), or vice versa
Jumps to arithmetic without finding the value of one block, so the diagram is decorative rather than a solving tool
Maps the wrong quantity to the wrong bar, or forgets which bar is which after drawing

learn.summary: Teach the bar model (tape diagram) as the workhorse for ratio and proportion. A ratio like 3:2 becomes 3 equal blocks beside 2 equal blocks; once the value of ONE block is known, every share, scaling and percentage answer is read off the picture. Build three habits: (1) draw bars matching the relationship, (2) find the value of one block (known amount ÷ number of blocks it covers — e.g. total ÷ all blocks when the total is given, or one share ÷ that share's blocks when a part is given), (3) read off what is asked — with the equal-unit convention (every block the same size) made firm first. Progress from concrete cubes/counters to a drawn, labelled bar to the numeric calculation, and always draw before calculating so problem structure is visible rather than guessed from key words. Constructing a model is the core objective; reading a prepared model is a valuable scaffold toward it.

activities.title: Build the tape diagram: draw, find one block, read off
feedback: If a learner draws blocks of unequal size, return to physical cubes: every block is one identical cube. Rebuild the diagram with equal units before drawing again — with unequal blocks you cannot say what one block is worth.

If a learner maps the total to just one bar (e.g. treats £20 as belonging only to the 3-block bar, giving £20 ÷ 3), point to the brace: it spans the WHOLE, so count every block under it (5) before dividing.

If a learner draws a reasonable diagram but guesses the shares without finding one block's value, scaffold only the pivot: 'What is one block worth?' (total ÷ number of blocks), then read the shares from that — the picture and the answer must connect.
When shares correctly add back to the total, confirm that the equal-unit structure is what made the reading possible.
activities.rationale: A representation is learned by constructing and manipulating it, not only by viewing it. Building the bars, assigning a total and deriving one-block-value turns the three-move routine into deliberate action, and the add-back check helps catch errors such as dividing the total by only one part's blocks (though it cannot catch every error, e.g. swapped shares still add back to the total).
sourceClaims: Ratio and proportion (unequal sharing, 'for every', recipes, scale) are represented with simple pictures/bars at upper KS2, drawing the model to expose problem structure before calculating.
A part-to-part relationship ('for every 1 concentrate, 4 water') is illustrated by drawing equal rectangles/parts side by side; counters or cubes are an equivalent concrete representation.
learnerActions: Given '£20 shared in the ratio 3:2', build two bars — 3 equal blocks beside 2 equal blocks — keeping every block the same width.
Place a brace spanning all 5 blocks and label it with the total, £20.
Find the value of one block by dividing the total by the number of blocks: £20 ÷ 5 = £4.
Fill every block with £4, then read off the two shares: 3 × £4 = £12 and 2 × £4 = £8; check they add back to £20.
Toggle the same ratio between part-to-part twin bars (3 and 2) and a part-to-whole single bar of 5, and say which layout the question needs.
Repeat independently for a new problem: share £18 in the ratio 5:1 — six equal blocks in two bars (5 and 1), brace £18, one block = £3, shares £15 and £3.
Re-read one of your diagrams as a proportion: 'what fraction of the money is the shaded bar?' (e.g. 3 out of 5).
activities.intendedInsight: Each block is an equal unit standing for the same amount; dividing the whole by the number of blocks gives one block's value, and from that single fact every share and proportion can be read straight off the picture without a memorised rule.

activities.title: Concrete first: build the ratio with cubes, then draw it
feedback: If the drawn blocks no longer match the cube counts, re-pair each block with one cube and recount.
If a learner cannot say what one block represents, return to the cubes and name the unit aloud before drawing.
activities.rationale: A concrete-to-pictorial-to-abstract progression grounds the equal-unit convention in a manipulable object before it becomes a drawn abstraction, which guidance presents as an equivalent concrete representation of the same relationship.
sourceClaims: A part-to-part relationship ('for every 1 concentrate, 4 water') is illustrated by drawing equal rectangles/parts side by side; counters or cubes are an equivalent concrete representation.
learnerActions: Lay out coloured cubes or counters for a part-to-part ratio — e.g. 1 cube of concentrate for every 4 cubes of water.
Count the total cubes and share a given total across them so each cube (block) gets an equal value.
Redraw the same arrangement as a labelled bar diagram, matching one block to one cube.
State in words what each block stands for before doing any arithmetic.
activities.intendedInsight: The drawn block is a shorthand for an equal physical unit; moving from cubes to the drawn bar preserves the equal-unit meaning rather than inventing a new rule.

activities.title: Read a worked bar model (scaffold)
feedback: If a learner reads the brace as belonging to one bar rather than the whole, re-point to its span across all blocks.
Confirm understanding only once the learner can restate the total ÷ blocks step unprompted.
activities.rationale: Because a bar model is itself a picture, a labelled worked example with staged reveals supports interpreting the convention. This is a reading scaffold: it does not itself require the learner to build a model for a new problem, so it should lead into construction rather than replace it.
learnerActions: Study a labelled '£20 shared 3:2' diagram and, part by part, state what each feature means: a single block, the 3-section, the 2-section, the brace, any shading.
Reveal and confirm: one block = £20 ÷ 5 = £4; the 3-section = £12; the brace shows the whole = £20.
Explain back, in your own words, how the one-block value was found and how each share follows from it.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent reading of a prepared diagram — knowing what every block, brace and shaded section stands for — supports constructing your own model, which this scaffold then leads into.

activities.title: Match, read and sketch (assessment-style practice)
feedback: For a wrong match, ask which feature of the diagram (number of blocks, brace span) contradicts the chosen problem.
For an unequal-block choice, restate that every block must be the same size.
Note that selecting a correct answer here is recognition; follow it with a sketch so the learner constructs, not just identifies.
activities.rationale: Translating between representations tests well as scored items, and the included sketch step moves beyond recognition toward construction, where shaky understanding surfaces.
sourceClaims: Ratio and proportion (unequal sharing, 'for every', recipes, scale) are represented with simple pictures/bars at upper KS2, drawing the model to expose problem structure before calculating.
learnerActions: Match bar diagrams to the worded problems they represent.
Read a quantity off a labelled bar, watching for traps: a distractor assuming unequal blocks, and a distractor confusing part-to-part with part-to-whole.
Sketch the blocks for a given ratio (e.g. draw the layout for sharing a stated total in a stated ratio).
activities.intendedInsight: Interpreting and translating between words and bar models — and noticing where equal-unit or part/whole choices go wrong — shows command of the representation beyond surface recognition.

activities.title: Compare the bar model with tables and double number lines
feedback: If a learner always reaches for one tool, pose a problem where the other is clearly more efficient and ask them to justify the switch.
Verbal explanation checks reasoning; pair it with building or reading a model so the visual-spatial structure is also constructed, not only described.
activities.rationale: Comparing models on the same problem lets learners articulate when each is most useful. Dialogue is useful for verbalising the reading and judging representations; it complements, rather than replaces, building and seeing the diagram.
learnerActions: Solve the same problem with a bar model and then with a ratio table or double number line.
For a fixed-total sharing problem and for a scaling-up-a-rate problem, decide which representation is most useful and say why.
Discuss with a mentor or partner: 'What does each block stand for? What is the total? Which tool fits this question best?'
activities.intendedInsight: Different representations often suit different questions — bar models are especially clear for sharing a fixed total, while tables and double number lines are often convenient for scaling a rate (though each can solve both) — and being able to choose and justify a representation shows flexible understanding.

constraints: Every block in the bars must be the same size and stand for the same amount; the model breaks if blocks are drawn unequal.
Distinguish part-to-part (two separate bars, e.g. 3 and 2) from part-to-whole (one bar of 5, or a whole split), and choose the layout the question needs.
Always draw the diagram before calculating so problem structure is made visible rather than guessed from key words.
Label the diagram fully — the total (a brace over the whole), the known value and the '?' — so it carries the problem's information.
Make 'find the value of one block' the pivot: a diagram that is drawn but never used to find one block's value is decorative, not a solving tool.
Reading a prepared model (tap-to-reveal, worked example) is a scaffold toward constructing one; it does not by itself require the learner to build a model for a new problem.
Matching and multiple-choice items assess recognition; independent construction requires the learner to draw a correct model for a new ratio.
The bar model is planar; a flat layout keeps the equal-unit comparison clear. Added depth is not needed for this representation (this is a scope note, not a claim about 3D teaching generally).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Arithmetic checked: £20 ÷ 5 = £4, shares £12 and £8 (sum £20); £18 ÷ 6 = £3, shares £15 and £3 (sum £18); proportion reading 3 out of 5 for the 3-block bar. All consistent.

The reading-scaffold activity (worked model) carries no sourceClaim: the available claim supports drawing/constructing bars to expose structure, not the reading-reveal principle, so [] is used to avoid topic-only attribution.
The assessment-style activity's attached drawing/structure claim rests on its single sketch (construction) sub-step, not on its matching/reading components; retained on that narrow basis.

The legacy entry asserted depth 'adds nothing' to a bar model; this has been softened to a scope note about keeping the layout planar for clear comparison, as catalog ratings do not establish a universal claim about 3D.

The legacy entry stated a tap-to-reveal image 'cannot' let a child build one for a new problem; retained as a scaffold limit (reading does not itself elicit construction) rather than a claim that static images cannot teach construction.

Optional interaction examples from the design notes (snapping blocks to equal width, dropping a total onto the brace, value propagating into every block at once, a part-to-part/part-to-whole toggle, a compare-view) are preserved as illustrative mechanisms, not mandatory tooling.

probeDeeper: 'What is one block worth, and how did you get it?' — checks the total ÷ number-of-blocks pivot is understood, not copied.
'Show me on your diagram where the £18 is' — forces the total to be mapped to the whole (the brace), catching the map-to-one-bar error.

Counterexample: 'If I shaded one bar and asked what PROPORTION of the money it is, could you use the same diagram?' — a child who owns the model re-reads it as part-to-whole (e.g. 5 out of 6); a child who memorised 'sharing' stalls.
'Which is more useful here — this bar model or a ratio table — and why?' surfaces whether the child can judge the representation, the top response level.
assess.correctAnswer: The diagram shows a quantity of £20 shared in the ratio 3:2 — 5 equal blocks in total, each worth £20÷5 = £4, so the shares are £12 and £8. For the new one: six equal blocks in two bars (5 and 1), brace £18, one block = £3, shares £15 and £3.

errorPatterns.pattern: Draws unequal blocks: makes the 5-bar blocks a different size from the 1-bar block, so the blocks no longer represent equal units
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to cubes: every block is one identical cube. Rebuild the given diagram with physical equal units before drawing again.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The new diagram has mismatched block sizes; the child cannot then say 'one block = £3' because the blocks aren't equal

errorPatterns.pattern: Maps the total to one bar instead of the whole: reads '£20' as belonging to the 3-block bar (or draws the £18 over only the 5-bar)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point to the brace: it spans the WHOLE — count every block under it (5) before dividing. Distinguish part-to-part bars from the part-to-whole brace.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says the 3 blocks are worth £20 (so one block = £20÷3), ignoring that the brace spans all 5 blocks

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the diagram as decorative: draws bars but never finds the value of one block, guessing shares from the numbers in the problem
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach drawing — scaffold the pivotal move only: 'what is one block worth?' (total ÷ number of blocks), then read the shares from that.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child produces a reasonable-looking diagram but reads no value off it — the picture and the answer are disconnected

responseLevels.gap: Cannot say what the given diagram shows, or draws a new one with unequal blocks, the wrong number of blocks, or the total mapped to a single bar; the picture does not represent the ratio.
responseLevels.full: Reads the given model, faithfully constructs a new one with equal blocks and the total mapped to the whole, uses one-block-value to read off any required quantity, re-reads the same diagram as part-to-part or part-to-whole as needed, and can say when a bar model beats a table or double number line.
responseLevels.partial: Reads the given diagram correctly and reproduces the layout, but treats it as illustration — does not use 'one block = total ÷ blocks' to read off a share, or mis-handles the part-to-whole reading, or needs prompting to map the total to the whole.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a bar model: two bars, one made of 3 equal blocks and one made of 2 equal blocks, with a brace over all of them labelled '£20'. First, tell me what this diagram is showing. Then draw me a new bar model for sharing £18 in the ratio 5:1.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Reading THEN constructing separates surface recognition from genuine command of the representation. A child who understands the model reads the total-over-blocks structure and reproduces it faithfully for the new ratio, with equal blocks and the total mapped to the whole. A child who does not either mis-reads the given bars (thinks the £20 belongs to one bar, or blocks are unequal) or, more tellingly, cannot construct the new diagram — draws unequal blocks, the wrong number of blocks, or a part-to-whole layout. The translate step (draw a new one) is where shaky understanding shows.

sources.claim: Ratio and proportion (unequal sharing, 'for every', recipes, scale) are represented with simple pictures/bars at upper KS2, drawing the model to expose problem structure before calculating.
sources.source: National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (Year 6 ratio and proportion; non-statutory guidance)

sources.claim: A part-to-part relationship ('for every 1 concentrate, 4 water') is illustrated by drawing equal rectangles/parts side by side; counters or cubes are an equivalent concrete representation.
sources.source: NRICH (University of Cambridge) — 'Ratio or Proportion?' article

pedagogy.summary: This is the vocabulary foundation for the whole ratio-and-proportion strand: children must use ratio, proportion, percentage, scale, equivalent, relative size, part-to-part, part-to-whole and 'out of' precisely, and grasp the central distinction that a RATIO compares part to part (3 red : 2 blue) while a PROPORTION compares a part to the whole (3 out of 5 are red = 3/5). Because these words are used loosely in everyday speech and are often taught as an inseparable phrase ('ratio and proportion'), the teaching goal is to differentiate them through repeated use in concrete contexts — mixing paint or squash, recipes, sharing — rather than through memorised definitions. Language precision here prevents the classic error of reading a part-to-part ratio as if it were a part-to-whole fraction.
bestPractices: Introduce terms through a concrete mixing/sharing context (e.g. squash: '1 part concentrate to 4 parts water') and the 'for every' phrasing before any notation — 'for every 1 concentrate there are 4 water' makes part-to-part audible.

Contrast ratio and proportion side by side on the SAME situation: 'the ratio of concentrate to water is 1:4' vs 'the proportion that is concentrate is 1 out of 5' — so children hear part-to-part against part-to-whole.

Attach each term to a representation: ratio → two coloured bars side by side; proportion/percentage → one bar (the whole) with a shaded part; scale → an enlargement pair. Language and picture reinforce each other.
Use 'out of' deliberately as the bridge to fractions and percentages: 3 out of 5 = 3/5 = 60%, all describing the same proportion.
Elicit and require the vocabulary in pupils' own explanations (talk moves) rather than accepting a right numeric answer with vague words — the objective IS the language.
Draw scale/equivalent language from enlargement examples ('every length is 3 times as big — a scale factor of 3') so 'scale' and 'equivalent' are grounded in action.
keyRepresentations: Two side-by-side coloured bars (part-to-part) contrasted with one part-shaded whole bar (part-to-whole / proportion)
'For every ___ there are ___' sentence frame linking language to the ratio
Squash/paint mixing jugs or coloured counters (concrete part-to-part)
A double-headed 'same proportion' triple: fraction 3/5 = 60% = 3 out of 5
An enlargement pair of shapes labelled with the scale factor
commonMisconceptions: Uses 'ratio' and 'proportion' interchangeably, as if they mean the same thing
Reads a part-to-part ratio as a part-to-whole fraction: hearing 'red to blue is 2:3' and saying '2/3 are red' (should be 2/5)
Treats 'proportion' only as everyday 'a large proportion' (a vague amount) rather than a comparison of part to whole
Confuses 'scale' / 'scale factor' with a difference (adds a fixed amount) rather than a multiplicative enlargement

learn.summary: Language foundation for ratio and proportion (ages 9–11): children must use ratio, proportion, percentage, scale, equivalent, relative size, part-to-part, part-to-whole and 'out of' precisely, and grasp the central distinction that a RATIO compares part to part (3 red : 2 blue) while a PROPORTION compares a part to the whole (3 out of 5 are red = 3/5 = 60%). Because these words are used loosely in everyday speech and are often taught as the inseparable phrase 'ratio and proportion', the objective is to differentiate them through repeated use in concrete mixing/sharing/recipe contexts rather than through memorised definitions. The payoff is preventing the classic error of reading a part-to-part ratio as if it were a part-to-whole fraction.

activities.title: Squash-mixing bench: one mixture, two descriptions
feedback: If a child writes the proportion as '1 out of 4', point to the single whole-bar: it visibly shows five parts in the whole, not four, so the 4 cannot be the whole — count all parts first (1 + 4 = 5), then name the proportion as 1 out of 5.

If a child gives the same numbers for both (e.g. 1:4 for the ratio AND '1 out of 4' for the proportion), have them re-describe each from its own picture using the matching word: the twin-bar for ratio, the whole-bar for proportion.
When both frames are correct, prompt the 'say it another way' link: 1 out of 5 = 1/5 = 20%, all naming the same proportion.

When the recipe is scaled to 2 concentrate and 8 water, work it through: the ratio 2:8 is equivalent to 1:4, and to find the proportion count the whole first (2 + 8 = 10), so the proportion that is concentrate is 2 out of 10 = 1 out of 5 — unchanged from the 1:4 mixture even though the numbers grew.
activities.rationale: A LANGUAGE objective is met when the child manipulates a situation and NAMES what changes; showing part-to-part and part-to-whole pictures simultaneously lets the learner attach each term to a distinct representation and makes the wrong denominator visibly contradicted rather than corrected by a rule. The live twin-bar/whole-bar pairing and the completion frames are offered as a concrete mechanism for this language work, not as the only possible medium.
sourceClaims: Ratio compares part to part while proportion compares a part to the whole; the 'for every' phrasing and simple pictures (rectangles/counters) are recommended for first teaching, and proportion is related to fractions.
learnerActions: Build a mixture by adding whole 'parts' of concentrate and water into a jug (for example 1 part concentrate to 4 parts water).

As each part is added, read two pictures that update together: a twin-bar showing concentrate beside water (part to part) and a single stacked bar showing the whole mixture with the concentrate shaded (part to whole).
Complete two sentence frames about the SAME mixture: 'the RATIO of concentrate to water is __ : __' and 'the PROPORTION that is concentrate is __ out of __'.
Then 'say it another way': express the proportion as a fraction, a percentage and an 'out of' phrase (for 1 part in 5: 1/5 = 20%).
Change the recipe and say whether the ratio and the proportion change.
activities.intendedInsight: The same mixture is described two different ways depending on which picture you read: for 1 concentrate to 4 water, the 1 sits against the 4 in the twin-bar (ratio 1:4) and against the whole of 5 parts in the single bar (proportion 1 out of 5). Ratio compares part to part; proportion compares part to whole; the whole = the sum of the parts.

activities.title: 'For every' spoken frame before notation
feedback: If the child jumps straight to '1 out of 5' when asked 'for every', redirect: 'for every' compares the two amounts to each other (1 to 4), not to the whole.
If the child says 'for every 1 there are 5', count the water parts only (4) — the whole (5) is a separate idea named by proportion, not by the 'for every' comparison.
activities.rationale: Grounding language in 'for every' speech before notation is explicitly recommended for first teaching and keeps part-to-part distinct from part-to-whole from the start.
sourceClaims: Ratio compares part to part while proportion compares a part to the whole; the 'for every' phrasing and simple pictures (rectangles/counters) are recommended for first teaching, and proportion is related to fractions.

At upper KS2 percentages, decimals and fractions are taught as different ways of expressing proportions; pupils meet ratio informally via 'for every' and unequal sharing, and 'scale factor' describes multiplicative enlargement.
learnerActions: Describe a mixture aloud using 'for every' before any colon notation: 'for every 1 concentrate there are 4 water'.
Then translate the spoken frame into the ratio 1:4.
State separately how much of the WHOLE drink is concentrate: 1 out of 5.
Repeat with coloured counters or paint instead of squash to hear the same structure in a new context.
activities.intendedInsight: 'For every ___ there are ___' makes part-to-part audible before symbols are introduced, so the ratio notation is read as a comparison of parts rather than copied as a rule.

activities.title: In-role recipe talk that requires precise words
feedback: If the child swaps the terms, the partner asks which comparison they mean and points back to the two amounts (part to part) versus the whole (part to whole).
Accept a correct numeric answer only when it is paired with the matching word; the goal is the language, not just the number.
activities.rationale: A responsive partner can require precise term use and gently challenge everyday blurred usage; this targets the language objective through genuine use rather than recited definitions. Offered as one route; a human conversation partner serves the same purpose.
learnerActions: Describe recipes and drink orders to an in-role partner (for example a smoothie-bar owner), using 'ratio' and 'proportion' correctly.
When the partner challenges a loose statement — 'you said proportion; did you mean part to part or part to whole?' — re-say it with the matching word.
Explain a part-to-part comparison and a part-to-whole comparison for the same order.
activities.intendedInsight: Correct USE of the vocabulary in unscripted dialogue is the actual objective; being asked to clarify loose usage forces the part-to-part vs part-to-whole reference to become explicit.

activities.title: Sort and complete: ratio vs proportion across contexts
feedback: If a child reads 'red to blue is 2:3' as '2/3 are red', count the whole: 2 + 3 = 5 parts, so 2 out of 5 are red — the 3 is the other part, not the whole.
If a statement is miscategorised, ask: does it compare two parts to each other (ratio) or a part to the whole (proportion)?
activities.rationale: A scored sorting and fill-in set can check whether the child selects the right term and distinguishes part-to-part from part-to-whole across contexts; it checks recognition and discrimination but does not by itself require the child to generate descriptions unprompted, so pair it with the spoken/building tasks.
sourceClaims: Ratio compares part to part while proportion compares a part to the whole; the 'for every' phrasing and simple pictures (rectangles/counters) are recommended for first teaching, and proportion is related to fractions.
learnerActions: Sort statements about mixtures, recipes and beads into 'this is a ratio' vs 'this is a proportion'.
Fill in sentence frames: 'the ratio of red to blue is __ : __' and 'the proportion that is red is __ out of __'.
For a described situation such as 'red to blue is 2:3', state what proportion are red (2 out of 5) and explain why '2/3 are red' is wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: Across varied contexts the same structural distinction holds: the ratio uses the part counts; the proportion uses the whole (sum of the parts).

activities.title: Labelled mixing glossary (reference scaffold)
feedback: Reveals the correct label on tap; because it does not require the child to produce or choose the word, use it as a glossary alongside, not instead of, tasks that demand use.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal labelled example is a useful reference, but a LANGUAGE objective is met by using the words, which a reveal-only artefact does not require; hence it is a support, not the main activity.
learnerActions: On a worked mixing example, tap the concentrate to reveal 'part', tap the jug to reveal 'whole', and tap the pair to reveal 'ratio 1:4 / proportion 1 out of 5'.
Use it to look up which word names which comparison while doing the building or talking tasks.
activities.intendedInsight: Each term is anchored to a concrete feature of the mixture: parts, the whole, and the two comparisons built from them.

activities.title: Scale factor from an enlargement pair
feedback: If a child says the shape got '2 cm bigger' on each side, check a second length that was a different length on the original shape (e.g. a 1 cm side and a 2 cm side enlarged by 3 become 3 cm and 6 cm, adding 2 cm and 4 cm): the added amount differs between those sides while the multiplier stays the same — scale factor is the multiplier. (If every side starts the same length, as in a square, the added amounts will match, so compare sides of different original lengths.)
Confirm by checking that each length of the new shape equals the matching original length times the scale factor.
activities.rationale: Grounding 'scale' and 'equivalent' in an enlargement action connects the words to a multiplicative relationship, addressing the common confusion of scale with additive difference.
sourceClaims: At upper KS2 percentages, decimals and fractions are taught as different ways of expressing proportions; pupils meet ratio informally via 'for every' and unequal sharing, and 'scale factor' describes multiplicative enlargement.
learnerActions: Compare an original shape with its enlargement and find how many times bigger every length is ('every length is 3 times as big').
State the scale factor as that multiplier ('a scale factor of 3') and check it is multiplicative, not an added amount.
Describe a reduction the same way (for example a scale factor of 1/2).
activities.intendedInsight: 'Scale'/'scale factor' names a multiplicative enlargement or reduction — every length is multiplied by the same number — not a fixed amount added on.

constraints: The objective is linguistic and relational: require the vocabulary in the child's own explanations rather than accepting a correct number with vague words.
Introduce terms through a concrete mixing/sharing context and 'for every' speech before any colon notation.

Reveal-only labelled examples and sort/fill-in tasks are scaffolds: they support recognition and reference but do not by themselves require the child to generate correct descriptions unprompted; pair them with building and spoken tasks.
Keep ratio and proportion contrasted on the SAME situation so the part-to-part vs part-to-whole difference is heard and seen, not memorised.
The whole used for a proportion is the SUM of the parts (1 concentrate + 4 water = 5), so the proportion that is concentrate is 1 out of 5, not 1 out of 4.

Scaling the amounts (e.g. 1:4 to 2:8) leaves the ratio equivalent (2:8 = 1:4) and the proportion unchanged once the whole is recomputed (2+8=10, so 2 out of 10 = 1 out of 5); use this to test real command of the language.
'Scale factor' is multiplicative (every length times the same number), not an added difference.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row's '3D adds nothing' judgement about this being spatial-only has been removed as a universal claim; a spatial model is simply not the proposed route here, which is a narrow design choice, not an established law.

Independent re-audit confirmed the scaled-mixture feedback is now correct: for 2:8 the whole is 2+8=10 and the proportion of concentrate is 2 out of 10 = 1 out of 5 (unchanged), derived rather than carried as a fixed denominator; no residual '1 out of 10' error remains.

Self-audit of central numbers: 1 concentrate to 4 water gives ratio 1:4 and proportion 1 out of 5 = 1/5 = 20% (concentrate); water is 4 out of 5 = 4/5 = 80%. 'red to blue is 2:3' gives 2 out of 5 red, not 2/3. Scale factor 3 and reduction 1/2 are multiplicative. All consistent.
Coverage note: the vocabulary terms 'relative size' and 'unequal' from the stated objective are only lightly exercised; consider an explicit task if full vocabulary coverage is required.

probeDeeper: 'Say the same thing as a fraction and as a percentage' — checks the 'out of'/proportion link to 3/5, 60% style equivalence.

Counterexample: 'If I made it 2 cups concentrate to 8 cups water, would the ratio change? Would the proportion that is concentrate change?' — a child with the language sees ratio 2:8 = 1:4 and proportion still 1 out of 5 (unchanged); a child without it thinks bigger numbers mean a different drink.
'Point to what the ratio compares, and what the proportion compares' — forces the part-to-part vs part-to-whole reference to be made explicit.
'A recipe says the ratio of sugar to flour is 2:3 — what proportion of the mixture is sugar?' checks transfer of the whole = 2+3 = 5 idea to a new context.
assess.correctAnswer: The RATIO of concentrate to water is 1:4 (or 'for every 1 concentrate there are 4 water') — a part-to-part comparison; and the PROPORTION of the drink that is concentrate is 1 out of 5 (1/5, 20%) — a part-to-whole comparison. The two numbers (4 vs 5) differ because ratio compares part to part and proportion compares part to whole.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses 'ratio' and 'proportion' as if identical: 'the proportion of concentrate to water is 1:4' — applies part-to-part language to a part-to-whole comparison and vice versa
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront with the twin picture: 'ratio compares these two bars; proportion compares this part to the whole bar' — have the child re-describe each from its own picture, using the matching word.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child swaps the terms freely, or uses only one of them for both comparisons; the everyday blurred usage carries over

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the part-to-part ratio as a part-to-whole fraction: gives the proportion as '1 out of 4' (using the water count as the whole) instead of 1 out of 5
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the single whole-bar: count all the parts in the whole drink (5) before naming the proportion. Reinforce 'out of' = out of the whole.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child keeps the 4 as the denominator for the proportion, not seeing that the whole is 1+4=5 parts

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats 'proportion' only in its vague everyday sense ('a big proportion is water') rather than as a numerical part-to-whole comparison
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the precise sense: 'proportion means how many parts out of the whole — how many of the 5 parts are water?' Bridge to fraction/percentage (4/5, 80%).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives a qualitative amount ('mostly water') and cannot attach a number-out-of-the-whole to 'proportion'

responseLevels.gap: Uses ratio and proportion interchangeably or vaguely; cannot separate the part-to-part comparison from the part-to-whole one; gives the same numbers for both.
responseLevels.full: Spontaneously and correctly uses ratio (part-to-part), proportion (part-to-whole) and 'out of' across new contexts, connects proportion to fraction and percentage, and recognises that scaling the amounts leaves the ratio and the proportion unchanged.
responseLevels.partial: Uses the terms correctly for the practised squash example and can state the ratio 1:4, but slips when the context changes (recipe, beads), or lists the terms without reliably matching ratio→part-to-part and proportion→part-to-whole, or needs prompting to find the whole (5).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here's a jug of orange squash made with 1 cup of concentrate and 4 cups of water. Tell me about this drink using the words 'ratio' and 'proportion' — describe how much concentrate there is compared with the water, and how much of the whole drink is concentrate.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The context forces the child to USE both words about the same situation, so the part-to-part vs part-to-whole distinction shows itself in whether they say 1:4 for the ratio but 1 out of 5 for the proportion. A child who has the language keeps the two comparisons separate; a child who does not either uses the words interchangeably or gives the same denominator for both (1:4 and '1 out of 4'), revealing the part-to-part-as-part-to-whole confusion. Because it asks for USE, not a definition, it distinguishes real command of the vocabulary from a recited gloss.

sources.claim: Ratio compares part to part while proportion compares a part to the whole; the 'for every' phrasing and simple pictures (rectangles/counters) are recommended for first teaching, and proportion is related to fractions.
sources.source: NRICH (University of Cambridge) — 'Ratio or Proportion?' article

sources.claim: At upper KS2 percentages, decimals and fractions are taught as different ways of expressing proportions; pupils meet ratio informally via 'for every' and unequal sharing, and 'scale factor' describes multiplicative enlargement.

pedagogy.summary: Venn diagrams organise outcomes into regions defined by set membership: elements outside both circles, in one circle only, and in the overlap (intersection). Students learn to CONSTRUCT the diagram (fill the intersection FIRST, then subtract to find the 'only' regions, then account for the 'neither' universal-set remainder) and to INTERPRET it (read region frequencies and translate them into probabilities over the correct denominator). The intersection A∩B is 'in both', the union A∪B is 'in either', and probability is always the region count over the total number in the universal set (unless a conditional restricts the denominator). Systematic listing and the product rule generate the full outcome set that the diagram then organises.
bestPractices: Fill the INTERSECTION first, then subtract it from each set total to get the 'only-A' and 'only-B' regions — this prevents double-counting the overlap
Always place the 'neither' elements inside the rectangle (universal set) but outside both circles, and check all regions sum to the total
Name each region in words before writing set notation — 'likes both', 'likes cricket but not football' — then attach A∩B, A∪B, A only
Compute probability as region-frequency ÷ universal-set total; only restrict the denominator when the question conditions on a subset
Use systematic listing / the product rule to build the complete outcome set, then sort it into the diagram so favourable ÷ total rests on genuine outcomes
keyRepresentations: Two-circle Venn diagram inside a labelled rectangle (universal set)
Three-circle Venn diagram for three-set problems (seven internal regions)
Intersection-first fill order: overlap, then 'only' regions by subtraction, then 'neither'
Two-way table as an alternative organiser mapping to the same four regions
commonMisconceptions: Confusing intersection and union — shading 'in either' when asked for 'in both', or vice versa
Double-counting the overlap — adding the two circle totals for A∪B without subtracting A∩B
Forgetting the 'neither' region, so the diagram's regions do not sum to the universal-set total
Using a circle total (or the whole universal set) as the denominator for a probability that is actually conditional on a restricted subset

learn.summary: Students learn to CONSTRUCT a Venn diagram (fill the intersection first, then subtract to find the 'only' regions, then account for the 'neither' remainder inside the universal-set rectangle) and to INTERPRET it (read region frequencies and translate them into probabilities over the correct denominator). A∩B is 'in both', A∪B is 'in either', and probability is region-count over the universal-set total unless a conditional restricts the denominator. Systematic listing and the product rule generate the full outcome set the diagram then organises. The discriminating skill is construction on a fresh case, which exposes intersection/union confusion and wrong-denominator errors that reading a pre-labelled diagram can hide.

activities.title: Build a two-circle Venn from student data, then shade and read probabilities
feedback: If a learner shades both whole circles for A∪B, point out the overlap has been counted twice and the running total passes 30 — the middle six can only be counted once, so the union count is A + B − A∩B.

If they shade the entire cricket circle (14) for 'cricket but NOT football', return to region naming: the overlap is 'both'; 'cricket but not football' is the cricket circle MINUS the overlap — the crescent only (8).
If they write P(cricket only) = 8/14, ask 'out of how many students altogether?' — an unconditional probability is over the whole 30, so 8/30.
If they answer 'the probability is 8' (a count), restate that a probability is a part of the whole between 0 and 1 — the region count over the total: 8 out of 30 is 8/30.
On the conditional, if they keep 30 as the denominator, ask who is being considered now — only the cricket-lovers, so the denominator is 14, not 30.
activities.rationale: Venn regions are spatial partitions of the outcome set; constructing the diagram from raw data (intersection-first, then subtraction, then 'neither') prevents double-counting and makes the correct denominator concrete. Construction on a fresh description is the move that distinguishes genuine understanding from parroting region labels.
sourceClaims: On a Venn diagram the intersection A∩B is the region 'in both sets' and the union A∪B is 'in either set'; to find the union you cannot simply add the two circle totals because that double-counts the overlap, and a conditional probability restricts the denominator to the relevant subset rather than the whole universal set.
learnerActions: Place 30 student tokens into a two-circle Venn (football / cricket) inside a rectangle; fill the intersection first (likes both), then the 'only' crescents (by subtracting the overlap from each set total when only totals are given), then the 'neither' region outside both circles — e.g. 12 football-only, 6 both, 8 cricket-only, 4 neither.
Check that all regions sum to 30 before reading anything off.
Name each region in words BEFORE writing notation: 'likes both' = A∩B, 'football only' = A only, 'likes either' = A∪B, 'neither' outside both.
Shade 'likes cricket but NOT football' (the cricket-only crescent, 8 students) and write its probability as 8/30 = 4/15 over the total of 30.
Shade A∪B and find its COUNT two ways: by adding region counts (12 + 6 + 8 = 26), and by checking 18 + 14 − 6 = 26 to see why the overlap is subtracted; the probability is then 26/30.
Switch to a conditional: 'among the cricket-lovers, what fraction also like football?' — identify the new denominator (14, all who like cricket) and compute 6/14.
activities.intendedInsight: The overlap counts once, so the union COUNT is A + B − A∩B; and the denominator is the whole universal set unless a question conditions on a restricted subset, in which case the denominator shrinks to that subset.

activities.title: Generate the full outcome set, then sort it into the diagram
feedback: If a probability looks wrong, check whether every outcome was listed — a missing outcome changes both the region count and the total.

If the learner struggles to coordinate regions with individual outcomes, have them tag each listed outcome with its region before counting, so region totals are built from real outcomes rather than guessed.
activities.rationale: Research highlights that children's core difficulty is coordinating aggregated regions with the underlying equally-likely outcomes; building the outcome set first and sorting it addresses that directly.
sourceClaims: Correctly enumerating and counting outcomes over unions and intersections requires representing the complete set of outcomes systematically (tables, grids, Venn diagrams); the difficulty children face is coordinating aggregated regions with the underlying equally-likely outcomes.
learnerActions: For a combined-events scenario, use systematic listing or the product rule to enumerate every possible outcome before sorting.
Place each enumerated outcome into the correct Venn region (or a two-way table as an alternative organiser mapping to the same four regions).

Confirm that favourable ÷ total rests on the genuine, fully-listed outcomes, and that those listed outcomes are equally likely (e.g. ordered pairs from a fair coin and a fair die, not just the possible totals of two dice). Then count the region, count the universal set and form the fraction.
Compare the Venn diagram and a two-way table of the same data to see that both encode the four regions (both, A only, B only, neither).
activities.intendedInsight: Probabilities read off a diagram are only trustworthy when the complete set of equally likely outcomes has been enumerated and sorted correctly; the diagram organises outcomes but does not create them.

activities.title: Explain why the overlap is not counted twice (reasoning talk)
feedback: If a learner adds the two circle totals for the union, ask them to point to who gets counted twice and why that inflates the total.
If they say adding 'neither' students changes no probabilities, remind them the universal-set total grew, so every probability over the whole set changes even though the circle counts did not.
activities.rationale: Dialogue can probe why the overlap is not double-counted and why denominators shift, but the core skill is constructing and reading the spatial diagram, so talk is best used alongside construction, not instead of it.
sourceClaims: On a Venn diagram the intersection A∩B is the region 'in both sets' and the union A∪B is 'in either set'; to find the union you cannot simply add the two circle totals because that double-counts the overlap, and a conditional probability restricts the denominator to the relevant subset rather than the whole universal set.
learnerActions: Justify each region count aloud: how many like football altogether (18, not 12), how many like cricket altogether (14), how many like both (6).

Explain in your own words why the number who like football OR cricket is 12 + 8 + 6 = 26 — and NOT 18 + 14 = 32 — because the 6 who like both are already included in each circle total; the probability is then 26/30.

State what changes and what stays the same if four more 'neither' students join: the universal-set total rises to 34, so every probability taken over the universal set changes, while the region counts for football and cricket stay fixed (and a probability taken only among cricket-lovers, like 6/14, is unaffected).
activities.intendedInsight: Verbal justification surfaces the double-counting logic and the role of the denominator, reinforcing the construction skill rather than replacing it.

activities.title: Interpretation and sorting practice (scaffold)
feedback: If a learner selects 6/18, ask what the denominator should be — the universal-set total of 30, not a circle total.
If they select the bare count 6, restate that a probability is a fraction of the total: 6/30.
activities.rationale: Tap-to-reveal and sorting tasks teach the region vocabulary and interpretation efficiently, but they are recognition-level: they do not require the learner to construct a diagram from raw data or decide a denominator on a fresh case. Use them before, not instead of, the construction activity.
sourceClaims: On a Venn diagram the intersection A∩B is the region 'in both sets' and the union A∪B is 'in either set'; to find the union you cannot simply add the two circle totals because that double-counts the overlap, and a conditional probability restricts the denominator to the relevant subset rather than the whole universal set.
learnerActions: On a pre-authored Venn, reveal region labels: tap the overlap for 'likes both — 6 students — A∩B', a circle-only crescent for 'football only — 12', outside for 'neither — 4'; answer 'What fraction like both?' → 6/30.
Sort described students into the four regions (drag-to-region sorting).
Match region names (A∩B, A∪B, A only) to shaded pictures.
Read a probability off a completed diagram, watching for a wrong-denominator option such as 6/18 (circle-total denominator) or an unnormalised count such as 6.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising region meanings and reading probabilities off a completed diagram builds the vocabulary that construction then applies.

constraints: Fill the intersection first, then subtract to get the 'only' regions, then place 'neither' inside the rectangle but outside both circles — and check all regions sum to the universal-set total.

When one member of the universal set is chosen at random (each equally likely), compute probability as region-frequency ÷ universal-set total; restrict the denominator only when the question conditions on a subset.
Keep probabilities and counts distinct: a union COUNT may exceed 1 (e.g. 26), but the probability is that count over the total (26/30) and always lies between 0 and 1.

Recognition and sorting tasks (tap-to-reveal, matching, categorization, multiple choice) assess and build vocabulary but do not elicit independent construction of a diagram from raw data or an independently chosen denominator; keep a genuine construct-from-description task in the sequence.
A completed/pre-authored Venn is a scaffold: it teaches what each region means but cannot test whether the learner can build a diagram or choose the correct denominator on a new case.

Interactive features (drag tokens into regions, tap-to-shade with live set-notation and probability recompute, a conditional mode that greys out the rest and switches the denominator, a flag when the union overlap is selected twice) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete — they are illustrative, not required.
A two-way table is a valid alternative organiser mapping to the same four regions; do not treat the circle layout as the only representation.
Three-circle Venn diagrams (seven internal regions) extend the same logic for three-set problems.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic on the worked example (30 students: 12 football-only, 6 both, 8 cricket-only, 4 neither): football total 12+6=18, cricket total 8+6=14, union 12+8+6=26 = 18+14−6, neither 4, grand total 18+8+4=30 (or 12+6+8+4=30) — all consistent. P(cricket only)=8/30=4/15 and P(both)=6/30=1/5 check out. The conditional P(football | cricket)=6/14 uses denominator 14 (all cricket-lovers), which is correct.

The union work distinguishes the union COUNT (26) from its probability (26/30). The original assessment probe ('What is P(likes football OR cricket)? ... do you add 12 + 8 + 6, or 18 + 14?') had conflated the count with the probability; this is kept distinct in the learner-facing actions.

The original source row claimed a 3D representation 'adds nothing' to a flat categorical partition. This is a catalog-style universal claim not established by the cited sources; it has been dropped rather than propagated. A flat partition is well-suited here without asserting a third dimension is universally useless.
The original also framed dialogue as something 'talk alone cannot deliver'; rescoped to a narrow point that verbal justification complements, rather than replaces, construction.
Original assessment distractor '6/18' uses a circle-total denominator (football total 18); retained as a diagnostic distractor, not as a valid answer.

The Bryant & Nunes claim was removed from Activity 1's sourceClaims (it supports the systematic-enumeration principle of Activity 2, not Activity 1's construction/double-counting principle) and retained where it directly applies.

probeDeeper: You said the middle is 6 — if I ask how many like football ALTOGETHER, is it 12 or 18? Why?
What is P(likes football OR cricket)? Talk me through it — do you add 12 + 8 + 6, or 18 + 14? Why can't you just add the two circle totals?
Suppose I only look at the students who like cricket — among THEM, what fraction also like football? What's the denominator now, and why did it change?
If four more students who like neither sport joined, which probabilities would change and which would stay the same?
assess.correctAnswer: Tier 1 (interpret): the middle region is the intersection — students who like both football AND cricket — 6 students, so P(both) = 6/30 = 1/5. Tier 2 (construct): shades ONLY the cricket-only crescent (the part of the cricket circle outside the overlap), 8 students, and writes P = 8/30 = 4/15 over the universal-set total of 30.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses intersection and union when shading — shades the whole cricket circle (overlap included) for 'cricket but NOT football', or the reverse
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to region-by-region naming: the overlap is 'both'; 'cricket but not football' is the cricket circle MINUS the overlap — shade the crescent only
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the construct move, shades the entire cricket circle (14) rather than the cricket-only crescent (8), or shades the overlap when 'only' was asked

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses a wrong denominator — divides by a circle total (or, for a conditional, by the whole universal set) instead of the total in the correct set
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'out of how many?' — an unconditional probability is over the whole 30; only a conditional ('among cricket-lovers') restricts the denominator to that subset
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes P(cricket only) = 8/14 (cricket-circle denominator) instead of 8/30, or on a conditional keeps 30 as the denominator

errorPatterns.pattern: Reports a region frequency as the probability — writes P = 8 or P = 6, not a fraction of the total
errorPatterns.nextMove: A probability is a part of the whole between 0 and 1 — the region count over the universal-set total; 8 students out of 30 means 8/30
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'the probability is 8' or 'the probability is 6', giving a count rather than count/total

responseLevels.gap: Cannot reliably name the overlap as 'both', shades union when intersection is asked, or reports counts instead of probabilities; construction fails
responseLevels.full: Constructs the region accurately (cricket-only crescent), writes the probability over the correct denominator (8/30 = 4/15), computes A∪B by subtracting the double-counted overlap, and shifts the denominator correctly when a question is conditional — transferring the region logic to a new description
responseLevels.partial: Interprets a labelled diagram correctly and reads P(both) off it, but the construct move slips — shades the whole circle for a 'not' region, or uses a circle total as the denominator; can name regions but cannot yet coordinate 'only', union, and the correct denominator on a fresh case

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show the child a completed two-circle Venn inside a rectangle: 12 in 'football only', 6 in the overlap, 8 in 'cricket only', 4 outside both (30 students total). FIRST ask: 'Point to the middle region — what does it mean, and how many students like BOTH sports? What is the probability a random student likes both?' THEN hand them a blank Venn and this fresh description and ask them to CONSTRUCT it and answer: 'Shade the region for students who like cricket but NOT football, and write the probability as a fraction.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Interpreting a given region is easier than constructing one: a child can parrot 'the middle is both' yet still shade the whole cricket circle (including the overlap) for 'cricket but NOT football', or divide by a circle total instead of 30. The construct move is the discriminator — it exposes intersection/union confusion and denominator errors that reading a labelled diagram hides.

sources.claim: On a Venn diagram the intersection A∩B is the region 'in both sets' and the union A∪B is 'in either set'; to find the union you cannot simply add the two circle totals because that double-counts the overlap, and a conditional probability restricts the denominator to the relevant subset rather than the whole universal set.
