pedagogy.summary: Adding and subtracting within 1000 extends the compose/decompose-a-ten idea to a second boundary — composing a hundred from ten tens and decomposing a hundred into ten tens. It is taught concretely and pictorially (base-ten blocks, place-value counters, drawings) BEFORE the compact column algorithm, so that 'carrying' and 'borrowing' across two columns are understood as exchange, not digit rituals. The DfE places this in Year 3 as the conceptual foundation for formal columnar methods.
bestPractices: Work concrete→pictorial→written for the SAME calculation so the recording mirrors the exchange (NCETM Spine 1.17: strategies across the hundreds boundary combine bridging-ten with unitising)
Make both boundaries explicit: ten ones → one ten, and ten tens → one hundred; and the reverse for subtraction
Use place-value counters or base-ten on a H-T-O mat so an exchanged unit physically moves one column left/right
Deliberately include 'exchange across a zero' cases (e.g. 402−137) since these are the hardest and most error-prone
Check with estimation and the inverse operation (DfE Year 3)
keyRepresentations: Base-ten blocks (ones, ten-rods, hundred-flats) on a place-value mat
Place-value counters on a H-T-O grid
Part-whole / partitioning drawings (256 = 200+50+6)
Number line for count-up subtraction across hundreds
Expanded written layout bridging to compact columns
commonMisconceptions: Smaller-from-larger subtraction across any column (e.g. ones done as larger-minus-smaller)
Failing to compose a hundred: ten or more tens left in the tens place (170+80 recorded with 15 in the tens column)
Borrow-across-zero errors: decomposing when the adjacent column is 0 (402−137) done incorrectly
Treating each column independently with no exchange, so carried/borrowed units vanish

learn.summary: Year 3 learners add and subtract within 1000 by extending the compose/decompose-a-ten idea to a second boundary: ten tens make a hundred, and a hundred can be broken back into ten tens. Taught concretely then pictorially then in writing for the SAME calculation, so 'carrying' and 'borrowing' across two columns are understood as exchange, not digit rituals. Across-a-zero subtraction (e.g. 402−137) is the hardest, most error-prone case and deserves deliberate attention.

activities.title: Double exchange on a place-value mat: 256 + 167
feedback: If twelve tens are left sitting in the tens column, prompt: 'You have twelve tens — can you swap ten of them for a hundred? Show me on the mat.' Physically swap ten ten-rods for one hundred-flat and watch it slide to the hundreds column.
If a carried unit disappears, point back to the rod/flat that moved and ask where its mark is in the written record.
Check with estimation: 260+170 is about 430, so 423 is reasonable.
activities.rationale: Working concrete→pictorial→written for one calculation lets the recording mirror the physical exchange; making BOTH boundaries explicit (ten ones→one ten and ten tens→one hundred) addresses the compose-a-hundred misconception directly.
sourceClaims: Strategies for calculating across the tens boundary combine with unitising to calculate across the hundreds boundary; exchange (ten ones for one ten, ten tens for one hundred) is the unifying structure.

Year 3 pupils add and subtract numbers with up to three digits using formal written methods, add/subtract mentally, estimate and use inverse operations to check, and apply partitioning related to place value (e.g. 146 = 100+40+6, 146 = 130+16).
learnerActions: Lay out 256 and 167 with base-ten blocks (or place-value counters) on a H-T-O mat.
Combine the ones: 6+7=13. Exchange ten ones for one ten and move that ten into the tens column (leave 3 ones).
Combine the tens: 5+6+1(carried)=12 tens. Exchange ten tens for one hundred and move it into the hundreds column (leave 2 tens).
Combine the hundreds: 2+1+1(carried)=4. Read the result: 423.
Record the matching written steps beside the blocks — first in an expanded layout, then in compact columns — so each written mark names a physical exchange.
activities.intendedInsight: Carrying across two columns is the same exchange move repeated at a second boundary: ten ones become one ten, and ten tens become one hundred.

activities.title: Cascade across a zero: 402 − 137
feedback: If the child does 7−2 ('seven take two is five') instead of exchanging, return to decomposition within 100 first (the same move one column up), then rebuild 402−137 so a unit must be broken open before subtracting.

If the child fabricates a digit (9 or 0) at the zero column without decomposing, model the two-step cascade with blocks: a hundred becomes ten tens, THEN a ten becomes ten ones. Slow it down and have the child narrate each step.
Compare: 'What if it were 452−137 instead of 402−137 — which is easier, and why?' to surface why the zero is the hard part.
activities.rationale: Across-a-zero cases are deliberately included because they are the hardest and expose borrow-across-zero and smaller-from-larger bugs; building and narrating the cascade shows why the procedure works rather than rehearsing a ritual.
sourceClaims: Borrow-across-zero and smaller-from-larger are classic systematic subtraction bugs.

Year 3 pupils add and subtract numbers with up to three digits using formal written methods, add/subtract mentally, estimate and use inverse operations to check, and apply partitioning related to place value (e.g. 146 = 100+40+6, 146 = 130+16).
learnerActions: Build 402 with blocks on the mat (4 hundreds, 0 tens, 2 ones).
Try to subtract the ones (2−7): there aren't enough, and there are no tens to borrow — notice the empty tens column.
Break one hundred into ten tens (now 3 hundreds, 10 tens, 2 ones).
Break one of those tens into ten ones (now 3 hundreds, 9 tens, 12 ones). This is 402 written as 300+90+12.
Narrate each exchange aloud before recording it, so the two-step cascade is spoken and written in order.
activities.intendedInsight: When a column is empty you cannot borrow directly; you must first decompose the next higher unit to fill it, then decompose again — a cascade, not a one-step borrow.

activities.title: Annotated worked example: reveal each exchange step
feedback: If a prediction is wrong, ask the learner to redo the step with physical blocks before moving on, since this format shows the exchange but does not let the child perform it.
Reinforce naming: 'ten tens is one hundred, exactly as ten ones is one ten.'
activities.rationale: A step-revealing worked example gives a reference model and prompts prediction, but it is a scaffold: it does not let the child perform the double regroup, so it should follow or accompany hands-on work.
learnerActions: Study a worked addition and a worked across-zero subtraction with each exchange step hidden until requested.
Before revealing, predict what happens to a pile of ten tens, or where a borrowed ten in an empty column comes from.
Reveal the step (e.g. the tens pile becoming one hundred and some tens; the zero column being fed from a decomposed hundred) and compare it with your prediction.
Explain in your own words why the unit moved one column over.
activities.intendedInsight: Each written exchange step corresponds to a specific regrouping of units; a step-by-step reference makes the structure of the double regroup visible.

activities.title: Consolidation practice with across-zero and compose-a-hundred checks
feedback: If '15 tens' is left uncomposed, return to the mat and swap ten ten-rods for one hundred-flat.
If an across-zero answer is wrong, rebuild that one with blocks and narrate the cascade.
Use estimation to flag unreasonable answers before checking the detail.
activities.rationale: Practice consolidates and catches borrow-across-zero and compose-a-hundred errors; it rehearses the skill rather than building the initial exchange insight, so it belongs after concrete and pictorial work.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils add and subtract numbers with up to three digits using formal written methods, add/subtract mentally, estimate and use inverse operations to check, and apply partitioning related to place value (e.g. 146 = 100+40+6, 146 = 130+16).
Borrow-across-zero and smaller-from-larger are classic systematic subtraction bugs.
learnerActions: Work a mixed set of three-digit additions and subtractions, including several across-a-zero subtractions.
For 170+80, choose the correct result and explain why '15 tens' (a two-digit entry in the tens column) is wrong — ten of those tens must become a hundred (250).
Fill in the decomposition of 402 as 300+90+12 and use it to complete 402−137.
Check each answer by estimating and, where possible, by the inverse operation.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent recording still depends on composing a hundred and decomposing across a zero; checking with estimation and inverse catches slips.

constraints: Work concrete→pictorial→written for the SAME calculation so the written recording mirrors the physical exchange.
Make both boundaries explicit in both directions: ten ones↔one ten and ten tens↔one hundred.
Deliberately include across-a-zero subtraction (e.g. 402−137); do not treat it as an afterthought.
A step-revealing worked example is a reference scaffold: it shows exchange steps but does not let the child perform the double regroup, so pair it with hands-on work.
Practice items consolidate and diagnose errors but rehearse rather than build the exchange insight; use them after concrete and pictorial work, not instead of it.
Place-value counters or base-ten blocks on a labelled H-T-O mat should be arranged so an exchanged unit physically moves one column, and the written record should name that move.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The Brown & Burton (1978) / VanLehn (1990) source on subtraction bugs is marked unverified in the original row; treat the borrow-across-zero / smaller-from-larger bug framing as plausible but unconfirmed here, even though its claim text is cited to support the relevant rationales.

Arithmetic self-audit: 256+167 → ones 13 (carry 1), tens 5+6+1=12 (carry 1), hundreds 2+1+1=4 → 423 ✓. 402−137 → 402 as 300+90+12; 12−7=5, 90−30=60, 300−100=200 → 265 ✓. 170+80=250, and leaving '15 tens' (15 in the tens column) is the error to avoid ✓.

The original rated conversation 'poor' with the claim talk 'cannot supply the repeated hands-on exchange'; narrated explanation is included here as a supporting move within hands-on activities rather than asserted as incapable of teaching. The original 3D 'poor' rating is noted but not framed as a universal law.

The original claim that the animated across-zero case 'is exactly the case that defeats children on paper' is softened to 'hardest and most error-prone'; no comparative efficacy of any one medium over another is asserted.

Activity 3 (annotated worked example) carries sourceClaims [] because its rationale is a pedagogical scaffold-limitation claim that no original source directly supports; the underlying exchange mathematics is nonetheless consistent with the NCETM unitising claim cited elsewhere.

probeDeeper: You had twelve tens in 256+167 — can you swap some of those for a hundred? Show me on the mat.
For 402 − 137 there were no tens to take from — where did you get them?
Check 256+167 by estimating first: roughly 260+170 is about 430 — is your answer close?
What if it were 452 − 137 instead of 402 − 137 — which is easier, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: 423 and 265. For 256+167: ones 6+7=13 (compose a ten), tens 5+6+1=12 (compose a hundred), hundreds 2+1+1=4 → 423. For 402−137: no tens to give ones, so decompose a hundred into ten tens then a ten into ten ones (402 as 300+90+12), 12−7=5, 90−30=60, 300−100=200 → 265.

errorPatterns.pattern: Smaller-from-larger across a column — in 402−137 does 7−2 in the ones ('seven take two is five') rather than exchanging
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to concrete decomposition within 100 first (this exchange is the same move one column up), then rebuild 402−137 with blocks so the child must break a unit open before subtracting.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The ones (or tens) column is done as larger-digit-minus-smaller regardless of which is on top; no decomposition attempted

errorPatterns.pattern: Fails to compose a hundred — leaves ten or more tens in the tens place (records '12' in the tens column of 256+167)
errorPatterns.nextMove: On the mat, physically swap ten ten-rods for one hundred-flat and watch it move into the hundreds column; name that ten tens is one hundred, exactly as ten ones is one ten.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The tens total reaches twelve but no hundred is composed; the written answer has a two-digit entry in one column

errorPatterns.pattern: Borrow-across-zero error — in 402−137 tries to take a ten from the empty tens column, so writes 9 or 0 there without first decomposing a hundred
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model the two-step cascade with blocks: a hundred becomes ten tens, THEN a ten becomes ten ones. Slow it down and have the child narrate each exchange before recording.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child stalls or fabricates a digit at the zero column; the hundred is never decomposed to feed the tens

responseLevels.gap: Columns handled independently; leaves twelve tens uncomposed, or stalls/fabricates at the zero, or does smaller-from-larger; answers unreliable when a boundary is crossed.
responseLevels.full: Composes a ten and a hundred, decomposes across a zero, records the exchanges, relates the drawing to the written method, and checks with estimation or the inverse.
responseLevels.partial: Exchanges correctly with blocks in front of them but cannot yet carry it into a written record, or manages the single exchange in 256+167 but not the across-zero decomposition in 402−137.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child base-ten blocks (or place-value counters) and paper and set two calculations to work with the apparatus and record: 256 + 167, then 402 − 137. Watch what happens at each column, and especially at the zero in 402.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 256+167 forces exchange at BOTH the ten and hundred boundaries; a child who leaves twelve tens in the tens place, or drops a carry, is exposed. 402−137 requires decomposing across a zero — the classic borrow-across-zero bug and smaller-from-larger both surface here, and neither can be faked by treating columns independently.

pedagogy.summary: Children learn that there are 60 seconds in a minute, the names and lengths of the twelve months, and that a leap year has 366 days occurring every four years. The second/month facts are usually recalled well; the conceptual depth is the irregular month-length pattern, the non-decimal 60-grouping for seconds and minutes, and — hardest — WHY a leap year exists: the Earth takes about 365¼ days to orbit the Sun, so a day is added every four years. Most children do not connect time units to the Earth's motion at all.
bestPractices: Anchor the months and their lengths on a real calendar with a mnemonic (knuckles, or '30 days hath September'), revisiting the irregular 31/30/28 pattern
Count seconds into minute-groups on a timer so the 60-grouping (not 100) is felt
Explain the leap year through the Earth's orbit — the extra ~quarter-day each year accumulating into one whole day every four years — rather than as an arbitrary rule
Use the four-year cycle concretely (which recent years were leap years? when is the next?)
keyRepresentations: A wall calendar / year-strip divided into 12 months
The knuckle mnemonic for month lengths
A stopwatch or number line marked in seconds
A four-year calendar cycle showing February gain a 29th day
An Earth-orbit model linking the year to one revolution
commonMisconceptions: Assumes all months are the same length (e.g. 30 days each)
Treats the leap-year rule as arbitrary, unconnected to the Earth's orbit
Over-applies base-10 to seconds and minutes (90 seconds = 0.9 of a minute; 1 minute 30 seconds = 130 seconds)
Thinks February always has 28 days

learn.summary: For 7-8 year olds learning time-unit and calendar facts: 60 seconds in a minute, the names and irregular lengths of the twelve months, and that a leap year has 366 days and usually comes every four years. Factual recall of seconds/minutes and month names is usually a strength; the conceptual depth lies in (1) the uneven 31/30/28 month-length pattern (February has 29 days in a leap year), (2) the non-decimal grouping of 60 for seconds and minutes, and (3) WHY leap years exist - the Earth takes about 365 and a quarter days to orbit the Sun, so the leftover quarter-days add up to about one extra day every four years. (Because the true leftover is slightly less than a quarter, a few century years such as 1900 and 2100 are not leap years; this detail is beyond the core objective.) Research reports most children do not connect time units to the Earth's motion at all.

activities.title: Advance a four-year calendar cycle and watch February change
feedback: If a learner expects every February to have 29 days, replay the cycle slowly and have them count: three turns at 28, only the fourth at 29.
If a learner says all months are the same length, have them read off the popped lengths and group them into 31-day, 30-day, and 'other' (February) piles.
If a learner can state '366 every four years' but not why, pair this with the orbit activity so the extra day has a cause, not just a count.
activities.rationale: Showing the extra day appear only on the fourth cycle makes the four-year period concrete rather than a recited rule; revealing each month's length makes the irregular pattern visible. A live dial lets the learner advance year-by-year and watch February change - an optional interaction that makes the cycle observable. This is a proposed design, not a measured intervention.
learnerActions: Step through four years one at a time on a calendar dial or a strip showing four Februaries in a row.
On years one, two and three, note that February has 28 days; on the fourth year watch a 29th day appear and the year-counter go from 365 to 366.
Say aloud what changes and what stays the same across the four years, then predict which upcoming calendar year will be the next leap year.
Tap or reveal each month in turn to pop up its length, and sort or describe the uneven 31/30/28 pattern as a shape, not just a list.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Every four years' is not an arbitrary rule to memorise - the extra day actually appears only on the fourth turn, and February is the month that gains it, while month lengths follow a lumpy repeating pattern.

activities.title: Build the leap day from the Earth's orbit
feedback: If a learner says the extra day is added 'to make the number even' or 'just because', show the four quarter-days accumulating so the day has a physical source.
If a learner thinks the quarter-day disappears each year, point to the set-aside tokens: the leftover is saved, not lost, until four of them make a whole day.
activities.rationale: Research reports that about 78% of Years 3-4 students did not connect time with the Earth's revolution around the Sun, even though a calendar year is based on one revolution of the Earth around the Sun (while a day comes from one spin of the Earth); building the quarter-day accumulation is intended to address this documented gap. The stated topic is the fact and cycle rather than full orbital mechanics, so keep the model simple and focused on the leftover-day accumulation. Proposed design, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: In a Years 3-4 interview study, 78% of students did not connect the notion of time with the Earth rotating on its axis or revolving around the Sun — even though calendars measure days from one revolution — while basic facts such as the number of seconds in a minute and the months of the year were largely a strength (>90% correct).
learnerActions: Using an orbit model, card tokens, or a tally, give each year its length as 'about 365 and a quarter days' and set aside the leftover quarter each year.
After four years, snap the four leftover quarter-days together into one whole extra day.
Explain in your own words where the extra day came from and why we only add it roughly every four years, then name the day we add it to (29 February).
activities.intendedInsight: The leap day exists because the Earth's orbit takes about 365 and a quarter days; the leftover quarter-day each year builds up to one whole day about every four years, which we add to February.

activities.title: Group seconds into minutes at exactly 60
feedback: If a learner writes '1 minute 30 seconds = 130 seconds', have them count the first minute as 60 seconds on the timer, then add 30 to get 90.
If a learner says 90 seconds is 0.9 of a minute, show that a full minute closes only at 60, so 90 seconds is one minute (60) plus 30 more - i.e. one and a half minutes, not 0.9.
Reinforce that the minute 'closes' at 60 before any leftover seconds are counted into the next minute.
activities.rationale: Research reports children apply discrete whole-number and base-10 reasoning to time and struggle to coordinate the non-standard grouping of 60, so the difficulty lies in converting rather than recalling the fact. Counting seconds into minute-groups on a stopwatch or number line is intended to make the 60-grouping felt before it is applied to conversions. Proposed design, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Children apply discrete whole-number reasoning to time and struggle to coordinate the non-standard grouping of 60, so converting between seconds and minutes (rather than recalling the fact) is where difficulty lies.
learnerActions: Count seconds on a stopwatch or a number line marked in seconds, and mark where a full group of 60 closes into one minute.
Work out how many seconds are in one and a half minutes, saying why it is 90 (60 + 30) and not 150 - rather than applying base-10 place value (treating 1.5 minutes as 1.5 x 100 = 150 seconds).
Convert a two-way example such as '1 minute 30 seconds = [ ] seconds' and '90 seconds = [ ] minute [ ] seconds', regrouping at 60 each time.
activities.intendedInsight: Seconds and minutes group in 60s, not 100s, so conversions require regrouping at 60 rather than applying base-10 place value.

activities.title: Recall and sort the facts
feedback: If month lengths are muddled, anchor them on a real wall calendar and revisit the irregular 31/30/28 pattern with the mnemonic.
If a learner thinks February always has 28 days, connect back to the four-year cycle where it gains a 29th.
Fact recall alone does not show the learner understands why a leap year happens; follow correct recall with a 'why' question.
activities.rationale: Naming, sorting and stating facts consolidate the statutory recall content, which research reports children generally find to be a strength (>90% correct). A sort or fact item can check classification and recall but does not by itself elicit the explanation of cause or the regrouping skill, so it is a foundation, not the whole objective. Proposed design, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils should 'know the number of seconds in a minute and the number of days in each month, year and leap year' (statutory Measurement content).

In a Years 3-4 interview study, 78% of students did not connect the notion of time with the Earth rotating on its axis or revolving around the Sun — even though calendars measure days from one revolution — while basic facts such as the number of seconds in a minute and the months of the year were largely a strength (>90% correct).
learnerActions: Name the months in order and state how many days each has.
Sort the months into 31-day, 30-day, and 'other' (February) groups.
Answer fact questions: '1 minute = [ ] seconds', 'how often is a leap year?', 'how many days in a leap year?'
Use a mnemonic such as knuckles or '30 days hath September' to recall which months are shorter.
activities.intendedInsight: The core recall facts - 60 seconds, month names and lengths, and that a leap year has 366 days and usually comes every four years - need to be fluent so attention can go to the harder conceptual links.

constraints: Fact-recall items (naming months, stating '60 seconds', multiple-choice on leap-year frequency) check recall and classification but do not by themselves elicit the causal explanation of leap years or the regrouping skill for seconds/minutes; always pair recall with a 'why' or a conversion task.

A static calendar or year-strip with tap-to-reveal month lengths can name the facts and show the irregular pattern, but cannot run the four-year cycle or demonstrate the 60-grouping dynamically; use it as a naming scaffold, not as the full objective.

A character explaining months and leap years can introduce the facts; the four-year cycle and the 60-grouping may be easier to follow through a worked or observed sequence, though the cited sources do not establish this comparison. Treat the character as an introduction scaffold.
Keep the orbit model focused on the quarter-day accumulation; the objective is the leap-year fact and cycle, not full orbital mechanics.
Mnemonics (knuckles, '30 days hath September') aid recall of month lengths but do not teach why leap years occur; treat them as memory aids only.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and no empirical effectiveness is claimed.

The leap-year rule is an approximation: a year is about 365.2422 days and the full civil rule skips some century leap years (e.g. 1900 is not a leap year, 2000 is). The '365 and a quarter days, one extra day every four years' framing matches the source material and is age-appropriate for 7-8 year olds, but is a simplification; flagged for awareness, not corrected in the learner-facing activities.

Self-audit of conversions: 1 minute 30 seconds = 90 seconds (60 + 30); 2 and a half minutes = 150 seconds (60 + 60 + 30). The source assessment's probe answer '250' and distractors '130'/'0.9 of a minute' are intentional wrong-answer examples addressed as misconceptions, never taught as correct. In the seconds activity the '0.9' misconception is confined to the reverse-direction feedback (90 seconds read as 0.9 of a minute), and '150' is used only as a base-10 distractor for 'one and a half minutes', which is genuinely wrong for that quantity.

The original source labelled a 3D calendar as adding 'nothing' and a static image as unable to 'run' the cycle, and called telling inferior to showing; these are reframed as scaffold affordances/limits with hedged wording rather than universal claims about what any medium can or cannot teach.

reteachPrerequisiteId mt_2XDGT5tei1 in the source is tied to the seconds-regrouping misconception and is a catalog reference retained in assessment data, not surfaced in learner-facing guidance; it could not be independently verified here.

The statutory curriculum claim was removed from the four-year-dial activity's sourceClaims because it did not directly support that activity's design rationale; it is retained on the recall activity, whose rationale explicitly consolidates statutory recall content.

probeDeeper: 'If a year were exactly 365 days with nothing left over, would we ever need a leap year? Why or why not?'
'Where does the leftover time each year go until we use it?'
'How many seconds is two and a half minutes — and why isn't it 250?'
'Which months have fewer than 31 days, and how do you remember which ones?'
assess.correctAnswer: (A) The Earth takes about 365 and a quarter days to go once round the Sun; the leftover quarter-days build up to one whole day roughly every four years, which we add to February. (B) 90 seconds, because 60 seconds make one minute, so one and a half minutes = 60 + 30. Names the shorter months (Feb; the 30-day months).

errorPatterns.pattern: Knows a leap year is 366 days but treats the extra day and 'every four years' as an arbitrary rule, with no link to the Earth taking about 365¼ days to orbit the Sun
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't just restate the rule: build the ~quarter-day-per-year leftover with an orbit model or four-year tally so the accumulation into one extra day is seen, then name that day (29 Feb).
errorPatterns.distractor: The extra day is added to make the total number of days even, for no special reason
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the 'why' tier says 'just because' or 'to make the number even', and cannot connect it to the length of a year / the Earth's orbit

errorPatterns.pattern: Doesn't coordinate the group of 60 for seconds and minutes — applies base-10/discrete reasoning, so 1 minute 30 seconds is read as 130 seconds, or 90 seconds as 0.9 of a minute
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count seconds into minute-groups on a stopwatch/number line so a full 60 closes into one minute before applying it to conversions.
errorPatterns.distractor: 130 seconds
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the seconds item fails to regroup at 60 (gives 130 seconds, 0.9, or similar)

responseLevels.gap: Cannot reliably state 60 seconds in a minute or the months and their lengths, and has no idea why a leap year happens.
responseLevels.full: States the facts AND explains the leap year as ~quarter-day-per-orbit accumulating into one day every four years, handles the irregular month lengths, and converts seconds ↔ minutes using the 60-grouping, transferring to a new case.
responseLevels.partial: States 60 seconds, names the months and the leap-year facts (366, every four years), but recites them as isolated facts — cannot explain the leap year via the Earth's orbit or regroup seconds and minutes at 60.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the fact, then the reason. (A) 'A leap year has 366 days instead of 365 — one extra day. Where does that extra day come from, and why do we only add it every four years?' (B) 'How many seconds is one and a half minutes, and how do you know?' Also, in passing: 'Which months have fewer than 31 days?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The leap-year 'why' tier separates a child who has memorised '366 / every four years' from one who links it to the Earth's ~365¼-day orbit — a connection ~78% of children in the research did not make; the seconds item catches base-10 over-application even in a child who can state '60 seconds in a minute'.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Subtraction as an unknown-addend problem — understanding that 10 − 8 = ? is the same question as 8 + ? = 10, so subtraction can be solved by finding the missing part / counting on. Ages 6–7, a key bridge from take-away to the additive structure.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): supports Y1–Y2 'represent and use number bonds and related subtraction facts' and 'recall and use addition and subtraction facts', where subtraction facts are derived from known addition bonds; underpins missing-number problems like 7 = □ − 9.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.OA.4 'Understand subtraction as an unknown-addend problem. For example, subtract 10 − 8 by finding the number that makes 10 when added to 8.'
• Operational details: reframe the take-away picture as a missing-part picture on a part-whole model — whole known, one part known, find the other part. Encourage counting on from the subtrahend to the minuend, especially when the parts are close (12 − 9 by counting up 9→10→11→12). This is the efficiency insight, not just an alternative.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (age 6) — given 9 + □ = 13, matches it to 13 − 9 and finds 4. Tier B (age 7) — chooses to count on for 12 − 9 because the numbers are close, and explains why. Tier C (age 7+) — states that every subtraction can be rewritten as an addition with a missing part and uses it to solve/check.
bestPractices: Anchor on the part-whole model: subtraction reveals a missing PART when the whole and one part are known.
Teach counting-up (shopkeeper's method) explicitly as the efficient strategy when subtrahend and minuend are close.
Pair each subtraction with its unknown-addend twin (13 − 9 = ? ↔ 9 + ? = 13) so the equivalence is repeatedly seen.
Use missing-number equations in varied positions to force the additive reading rather than a take-away action.
Delay pure take-away drilling; contrast 'how many are left' with 'how many more to reach' so difference/missing-part meanings are established.
keyRepresentations: Part-whole (cherry) diagram with the missing part as the unknown
Bar model: total bar with one part shaded and the gap to find
Empty number line showing a count-on jump from subtrahend to minuend
Double ten-frame with one frame filled and the gap to ten visible
Fact-family triangle linking the whole and its two parts
commonMisconceptions: Believing subtraction can only mean 'take away / count back', so refusing to count up.
Not seeing 8 + ? = 10 and 10 − 8 = ? as the same question.
Counting back inefficiently for close numbers (12−11 counted back eleven steps) and making errors.
Confusing which quantity is the whole and which is a part in the part-whole model.
Treating the answer to 8 + ? = 10 as 10 (writing the whole) rather than the missing part.

learn.summary: Help 6–7 year-olds understand subtraction as an unknown-addend problem: 12 − 9 = ? asks the same question as 9 + ? = 12 — find the missing PART of a known whole. Anchor the equivalence on a part-whole model, teach counting up from the subtrahend when the numbers are close, and repeatedly pair each subtraction with its addition twin. A linked part-whole/number-line display can make the 'same gap, two routes' insight concrete; dialogue draws out the justification; matching and missing-number tasks consolidate; a static part-whole picture (with a double ten-frame and fact-family triangle as further representations) anchors both equations against one diagram.

activities.title: Two routes, one gap: linked part-whole and number line
feedback: When both routes land on the same gap, say: 'Taking away and counting up reached the same number — because they are the same question asked two ways.'
If the child gets 4 on 12 − 9 by counting back including the start (or by counting up starting on 9), replay the count-up: 9→10→11→12 is three jumps; count them together on the line.
If the child writes the whole (12) as the missing addend, point to the gap on the bar: 'We already know this part is 9; we are looking for the piece that fills the rest up to 12.'
activities.rationale: Showing the same situation two ways at once — take-away and count-on landing on one gap — can make the unknown-addend equivalence visible from a single action, and close-number cases let the child feel why counting up is often more efficient. Dragging to remove, hopping up the line, and the two equations updating together are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete, not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: 1.OA.4 requires understanding subtraction as an unknown-addend problem, e.g. subtract 10−8 by finding the number that makes 10 when added to 8.

Missing-addend problems are conceptually harder than take-away and children often solve subtraction by counting back even when counting up is more efficient; deriving subtraction from known addition facts is a documented strategy.
Y1–Y2 pupils represent and use number bonds and related subtraction facts and solve missing-number problems, deriving subtraction facts from addition bonds.
learnerActions: Look at a part-whole bar with whole 10 and known part 8, and a number line beside it.
First try to count BACK from the whole by the known part (back 8 from 10) to find the missing part; notice this is fiddly for some pairs.
Then start at the known part (8) and hop UP to the whole (8→9→10), counting the jumps to find the gap.
See both routes highlight the SAME gap of 2, and read the two printed sentences 10 − 8 = 2 and 8 + 2 = 10 together.
Repeat with a close-number case such as 12 − 9: count back nine steps, then instead start at 9 and hop up 9→10→11→12 (three easy jumps), and see 12 − 9 = 3 printed above 9 + 3 = 12.
activities.intendedInsight: A subtraction and its unknown-addend twin ask the same question — the missing part of a whole — and counting up from the subtrahend is often the shortcut, especially when the numbers are close.

activities.title: Explain why counting up works
feedback: If the child says the two are 'different sums', put 12 as the whole and 9 as a known part on a part-whole model and show the single missing part answers BOTH questions.
Affirm reasoning that names the missing part: 'Yes — the number you add to 9 to reach 12 is the same as the number left when you take 9 from 12.'
activities.rationale: The equivalence is a reasoning insight, so inviting the child to explain why counting up works and to state the addition twin targets the conceptual 'understand as' objective. Responsive spoken discussion lets a tutor probe the justification directly; recognition-only tasks would not elicit this spoken justification.
sourceClaims: 1.OA.4 requires understanding subtraction as an unknown-addend problem, e.g. subtract 10−8 by finding the number that makes 10 when added to 8.
learnerActions: Solve a close-number subtraction such as 12 − 9 using whatever method you choose.
Answer aloud: 'You could take 9 away — but is there a quicker way to get from 9 up to 12?'
State the matching addition sentence (9 + ? = 12) for the subtraction.
Explain in your own words why 12 − 9 and 9 + ? = 12 are the same question.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to justify the equivalence — not just produce the number — shows the child reads subtraction additively rather than only as take-away.

activities.title: Match, fill, and choose the quicker route
feedback: For 9 + □ = 13: the missing part is 4, not 13 — 13 is the whole; underline the gap being asked for.
For the 'quicker route' choice, affirm counting up for 12 − 9 because 9 and 12 are close (three jumps) while counting back nine steps invites errors.
If the child reverses whole and part, restate: the whole is the total; the two parts add to it.
activities.rationale: Matching, missing-number and strategy-choice tasks consolidate an already-built idea. A fixed sequence of items consolidates and checks recognition and strategy choice rather than letting the child freely toggle representations, so it is best used after the linked model and paired with an explanation prompt.
sourceClaims: Y1–Y2 pupils represent and use number bonds and related subtraction facts and solve missing-number problems, deriving subtraction facts from addition bonds.

Missing-addend problems are conceptually harder than take-away and children often solve subtraction by counting back even when counting up is more efficient; deriving subtraction from known addition facts is a documented strategy.
learnerActions: Match each subtraction to its unknown-addend twin, e.g. 13 − 9 ↔ 9 + □ = 13.
Fill in the missing addend: 9 + □ = 13 (answer 4), then write the matching subtraction 13 − 9 = 4.
Decide which is quicker for 12 − 9 — counting up or counting back — and give a reason.
Given a known fact such as 8 + 5 = 13, write a subtraction you can now answer straight away.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidate the pairing of subtraction with its addition twin and the strategic choice of counting up when numbers are close.

activities.title: One diagram, both equations (anchor)
feedback: Point at the gap: 'This is the part we are finding — it completes 8 up to 10.'
If the child names the whole as the answer, re-point to the known part and the gap.
On the ten-frame, the empty cells show the same gap (2 empty cells when 8 of 10 are filled); on the triangle, the whole sits apart from its two parts.
activities.rationale: A static part-whole picture can present both equations against one diagram and reveal the missing part, which anchors the equivalence; a double ten-frame and fact-family triangle offer the same structure in other forms. It does not let the child act out take-away and count-on as the same gap, so use it as an anchor or for learners who need a settled reference rather than as the primary builder.
sourceClaims: 1.OA.4 requires understanding subtraction as an unknown-addend problem, e.g. subtract 10−8 by finding the number that makes 10 when added to 8.
learnerActions: Look at a part-whole diagram with a tappable whole and one known part.
Tap or lift a flap to reveal the missing part.
Read both equation forms shown side by side against the same diagram, e.g. 10 − 8 = 2 and 8 + 2 = 10.
Name which number is the whole and which are the parts.

Compare the same whole and parts in other representations — a ten-frame with 8 cells filled and the gap of 2 to ten visible (use a double ten-frame for wholes above 10, e.g. 9 filled plus 3 more to reach 12), and a fact-family triangle linking the whole and its two parts — and read how each shows the missing part.
activities.intendedInsight: Both the subtraction and its addition twin describe the same part-whole picture, and the answer is the missing part.

constraints: Target ages 6–7; this bridges take-away toward the additive structure of subtraction.

The static part-whole picture and the matching/missing-number tasks consolidate or anchor; they do not let the child freely toggle between the take-away and count-on views, which the linked model provides.

Matching and multiple-choice items check recognition and strategy choice; they do not by themselves elicit the child's own spoken or written justification of why the two questions share an answer — pair them with an explanation prompt.

Teach counting up explicitly as the efficient strategy when subtrahend and minuend are close; do not present it as universally faster — for a pair like 12 − 3, counting back three is quicker, so prompt strategy choice by how near the numbers are.
Delay pure take-away drilling; contrast 'how many are left' with 'how many more to reach' so both difference and missing-part meanings are established.

Watch the count-up step count: 9→10→11→12 is three jumps; starting the count on the subtrahend itself (or counting back including the start) produces an off-by-one error (answer 4). This is a procedural slip, not a conceptual one — model the count rather than reteaching the concept.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source marks the DfE National Curriculum claim as verified:true and the CCSS 1.OA.4 and Cognitively Guided Instruction claims as verified:false; these flags were not re-checked here.
The double ten-frame (gap-to-ten) and fact-family triangle representations from the original keyRepresentations are preserved in the anchor activity.

The recommendation narrative for 12 − 9 uses a gap of 3 (9→10→11→12), while the worked example for 10 − 8 uses a gap of 2 (8→9→10); both are arithmetically correct. Confirmed 9 + 3 = 12 and 8 + 2 = 10, and 9 + 4 = 13.

The off-by-one answer of 4 for 12 − 9 arises from miscounting the up-jumps (counting the start) or counting back including the start; handled as a strategy/counting fix, not a conceptual reteach, consistent with the source.

probeDeeper: You found 3. In this story, is 3 a part or the whole? How do you know?
What's your evidence that 9 + 3 and 12 − 9 have the same answer?
What if it were 12 − 3 instead? Would counting up still be the quick way, or would counting back be quicker — and why?
If I tell you that 8 + 5 = 13, what subtraction could you answer straight away?
assess.correctAnswer: 3 — and explains that 12 − 9 asks the same question as 9 + ? = 12: the number you add to 9 to reach 12 is the same as the number left when you take 9 from 12, so both give 3. Often solved by counting up from 9.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Subtraction just means take away, so it isn't an adding question' — gets 3 by counting back but insists 12−9 and 9+?=12 are different, unrelated sums.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach in place on a part-whole model: put 12 as the whole and 9 as a known part, and show the single missing part answers BOTH questions; do not drill more take-away.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: solves the subtraction yet cannot connect it to the addition, or calls them 'different sums'.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The answer to 9 + ? = 12 is 12' — writes the whole (or adds the visible numbers) instead of the missing part.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the part-whole diagram to name which piece is the whole and which is the unknown part; point at the gap that is being asked for.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked the addition twin, says 12 (the total) rather than 3.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts back for close numbers and slips by one (starts the count on 9 rather than the first step), giving 4.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the concept — model counting UP for close numbers and prompt strategy choice by how near the numbers are; check the count with fingers or a number line.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 4; on watching, counts '9, 10, 11, 12' as four steps or counts back including the start.

responseLevels.gap: Solves only by counting back (or not at all) and treats 12−9 and 9+?=12 as unrelated; cannot state the matching addition.
responseLevels.full: Explains that 12−9 and 9+?=12 ask the same thing (the missing part of a whole), chooses to count up when the numbers are close, and uses a known addition fact to answer a new related subtraction.
responseLevels.partial: Gets 3 and, when prompted, can state 9+3=12, but treats it as a separate fact — cannot explain why the two questions share an answer and does not transfer to a new pair.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a subtraction: 12 − 9. Work out the answer. Then tell me how this is the same as the addition 9 + ? = 12.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who holds only a take-away conception can still reach 3 by counting back, but stalls or denies the link on the second tier — they cannot say why 9 + ? = 12 gives the same result. A child with the unknown-addend concept answers the 'why' immediately and frequently prefers counting up because the numbers are close. The REASON tier separates the two even when both produce the numeric answer.

pedagogy.summary: At 6-7 the modelling cycle becomes explicit at both ends: represent a measurement or money problem with a number sentence, bar model, or diagram, AND interpret the numerical answer back in context ('15 cm means the ribbon is 15 centimetres long') (CCSS MP4). Bar models now carry two-step and comparison structures. The defining new demand — and the one teachers most often skip — is the return trip: a bare '5' is not an answer to 'how much is left?'; the answer is '5p change'. This is exactly where 'suspension of sense-making' (CDE) does its damage: children compute and stop, without asking whether the number is reasonable or what it means. The CDE guide warns that stripping problems down to numbers and keywords ('take away means subtract') actively reinforces the habit; the remedy is to reason about the situation first and always interpret and sense-check the result.
bestPractices: Insist on the return trip: every numerical answer is interpreted in context with its unit ('5p change', '15 cm long') — the interpret-in-context half of MP4
Reason about the situation before computing; resist keyword-stripping, which the CDE guide identifies as a cause of suspension of sense-making
Use bar models to expose two-step and comparison structure so the child models the relationships, not just grabs numbers (NCETM)
Build the reasonableness check: 'could you have MORE money after spending some?' — sense-check the answer against the situation
Ask 'what does this number mean here?' at the end of every problem, not just 'what's the answer?'
keyRepresentations: Part-whole and comparison bar models for two-step problems
Number sentence with units attached to the quantities
Number line for measurement/money jumps
Simple diagrams of the situation (coins, ribbon lengths)
commonMisconceptions: Stops at a bare number without interpreting it in context or attaching a unit
Grabs the numbers and applies the operation a keyword suggests, without modelling the situation
Doesn't sense-check — accepts an answer that can't be true in the situation (change larger than the money paid)
Reports the wrong quantity (gives the total when the question asks for what's left)

learn.summary: For ages 6-7, this topic develops the full mathematical modelling cycle: represent a money or measurement word problem with a number sentence, bar model, or diagram, AND complete the 'return trip' by interpreting the numerical answer back in context with its unit ('5p change', '15 cm long') and checking whether it is reasonable. The defining new demand is that a bare number is not an answer; the remedy to 'suspension of sense-making' is to reason about the situation before computing and always interpret and sense-check the result afterwards.

activities.title: Model a shop story, then make the return trip
feedback: If the child stops at a bare '5': ask 'five what? what is that for Sam?' — the calculation is right, only the interpretation needs prompting.
If the child endorses 35: 'you gave 20p and want 35p back — can you get more money by spending some?' Let them catch and reject the impossibility, then state the real change as '5p change'.
Direct feedback at the interpretation and the sense-check, not only at whether the arithmetic was correct.
activities.rationale: Building and then being required to interpret and sense-check makes the situation-answer link explicit; an optional live reasonableness gate (a slider or thumbs that flags impossible answers such as change > amount paid) and a required 'what does it mean?' step make the return trip concrete rather than skippable.
sourceClaims: MP4: represent a situation with an equation/diagram and interpret the mathematical result in the context of the situation, reflecting on whether it makes sense.

Suspension of sense-making leads students to compute without checking realism; stripping problems to numbers and keywords reinforces this, and problem-specific supports (explain why the answer makes sense, draw it, consider a contrasting answer) promote reasoning — whereas a general 'these are tricky' warning does not.
learnerActions: Read a shop story, e.g. 'Sam has 20p in his purse and buys a sticker costing 15p. How much change does he get?'
Build a bar model of the situation: 20 as the whole, split into a 15 part and a mystery (change) part; or write a matching number sentence.
Work out the missing part to land on 5.
Complete a mandatory 'what does your 5 mean?' step: attach the unit and quantity, finishing the sentence '5p change'.
Pass a reasonableness check before the answer is accepted: decide whether a candidate answer could possibly be true in the story (e.g. flag that change greater than the amount paid is impossible).
activities.intendedInsight: A calculation is not finished when the number appears; it is finished when the number is read back into the story and checked for whether it could possibly be true. You cannot end up with MORE money after spending some.

activities.title: Argue with the shopkeeper: catch the impossible change
feedback: Keep this dialogic and unscored — the aim is reasoning and interpretation, not a mark.
If the child accepts 35p untroubled, prompt them to picture the purse: 'show me how Sam could end up with more than 20p.'
Praise rejecting the impossible answer AND naming the unit of the real one ('5p change').
activities.rationale: Saying what an answer means and defending its reasonableness is naturally dialogic; a partner offering a bare or impossible number lets the child practise interpreting and sense-checking, which the CDE guide names as problem-specific supports. This is a proposed activity; the dialogic format's effectiveness is not independently verified.
sourceClaims: Suspension of sense-making leads students to compute without checking realism; stripping problems to numbers and keywords reinforces this, and problem-specific supports (explain why the answer makes sense, draw it, consider a contrasting answer) promote reasoning — whereas a general 'these are tricky' warning does not.
learnerActions: Talk with a shopkeeper character (role-played by a partner, teacher, or on-screen character) who offers a plausible-sounding but impossible answer: 'You gave me 20p for a 15p sticker, so your change is 35p, right?'
Decide out loud whether 35p can be right, and explain why change cannot be larger than the money paid.
State the correct change in context ('5p change') and justify it.
Respond to a follow-up: 'If the sticker cost 25p, could Sam buy it with his 20p? How do you know?'
activities.intendedInsight: Defending why an answer does or does not make sense out loud strengthens the reasonableness habit; a contrasting impossible answer provokes the check that compute-and-stop skips.

activities.title: Bar models for part-whole and comparison problems
feedback: If the child adds the two numbers because a keyword suggested it, pause before any operation and model the situation on the bar first (e.g. 20 as the whole, 15 as a part).
Check that each number on the bar carries a unit and matches a real quantity in the story.
Ask 'what does this number mean here?' at the end, not just 'what's the answer?'
activities.rationale: Drawing part-whole and comparison bar models, and number-line models, for one-step and comparison problems builds the habit of modelling the relationships before computing, then attaching units and interpreting the result (NCETM/MP4).
sourceClaims: Bar models expose two-step and comparison structure so children model the relationships in a situation rather than grabbing numbers.
MP4: represent a situation with an equation/diagram and interpret the mathematical result in the context of the situation, reflecting on whether it makes sense.
learnerActions: Draw a part-whole bar model for a word problem, labelling which part is the known quantity, which is the whole, and which is the unknown.
Use a comparison bar model to show two quantities side by side for a comparison problem (e.g. one ribbon longer than another).
Use a number line to represent money or measurement jumps when that fits the story better.
Attach units to each quantity on the model and to the final answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Bar models expose the structure of a situation — including part-whole and comparison relationships — so the child models the relationships rather than grabbing numbers and applying a keyword operation.

constraints: Every numerical answer must be interpreted in context with its unit ('5p change', '15 cm long') — the interpret-in-context half of MP4 is the core objective, not an optional extra.
Reason about the situation before computing; resist keyword-stripping ('take away means subtract'), which the CDE guide identifies as a cause of suspension of sense-making.

A static worked example (story, bar, answer, and a 'what it means' flap) can illustrate the return trip but does not let the child model or sense-check for themselves; use it as a scaffold, not the main task.

Recognition-only scored items check getting the number rather than interpreting it in context or judging reasonableness, and can reward the compute-and-stop habit; a short 'is this answer reasonable?' item can still be useful during teaching, but keep the modelling and interpretation work open and constructive.

A reasonableness gate, slider, or shopkeeper character are optional ways to make the sense-check concrete, not mandatory mechanisms; the required learning is the interpretation and the check themselves.

Where a learner shows number-grabbing errors, reteach by modelling the real situation on a bar before any operation; this connects to the prerequisite skill of representing the situation rather than grabbing numbers/keywords (CDE).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Arithmetic checked: 20p - 15p = 5p change is correct; 20 + 15 = 35 is the keyword-grabbing error and must only ever appear as the impossible candidate to be rejected, never as a valid answer.

The source's claim that scored/quiz items only test getting the number and reward compute-and-stop was softened: a response format can be used reasonably during teaching, so it is framed as a limitation of recognition-only items rather than a universal law.
The 3D 'poor fit' entry carried no teaching content (money/measurement modelling here is not spatial), so it was omitted rather than converted into guidance.

An internal prerequisite/catalog ID present in the source has been removed from learner-facing text; only the pedagogical reteach move it pointed to is retained, and its identifier was not re-verified.

Independent re-audit confirms the three previously logged issues (internal ID in a constraint, internal ID in a preservation entry, and blended rationale in the bar-model activity) are resolved at every occurrence; no catalog IDs, fit labels, or quiz-step vocabulary remain in learner-facing text.

probeDeeper: 'Sam only had 20p. Can his change be 35p? Why not?'
'What should the answer be — and 5 WHAT?'
'Draw me a bar for this: which part is the 20, which is the 15, which is the change?'
'If the sticker cost 25p, could Sam buy it with his 20p? How do you know?'
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child rejecting 35 as impossible (you can't have more money after spending), finding 5, and interpreting it as '5p change', not a bare number.

errorPatterns.pattern: Number-grabbing / keyword operation: adds the two numbers (or applies the operation a word suggests) without modelling the situation — gets 35.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model the situation on a bar (20 as the whole, 15 as a part) before any operation; reteach representing the real situation rather than grabbing numbers/keywords (CDE).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child endorses 35, justifying it by 'there's a 20 and a 15'; cannot say why change should be less than 20.

errorPatterns.pattern: Suspension of sense-making: doesn't check the answer against the situation — accepts a number that can't be true (change bigger than the money paid).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build the habit of asking 'could this be true here?'; use contrasting/impossible answers to provoke checking (CDE problem-specific supports).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reaches 35 (or any impossible value) and is untroubled; no reasonableness check.

errorPatterns.pattern: Bare number, no interpretation: finds 5 but doesn't say it is 5p of change.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the return trip: 'five what? what is that for Sam?'; the calculation is right, the interpretation needs prompting.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers '5' and stops; asked what it means, restates '5'.

responseLevels.gap: Accepts 35 (or another impossible value); no sense-check and no interpretation.
responseLevels.full: Rejects 35 as impossible because change can't exceed the money paid, finds 5, interprets it as '5p change', and can locate the quantities on a bar — transferring the reasonableness check to a new case unprompted.
responseLevels.partial: Rejects 35 or finds 5, but not both fully — e.g. computes 5 without noticing 35 is impossible, or says 'it should be less' without interpreting '5p change'.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Sam has 20p. He buys a sticker that costs 15p. A friend worked it out and said the answer is 35. Does 35 make sense as Sam's change? Talk me through it — what should the answer be, and what does that number mean for Sam?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who models and sense-checks rejects 35 because change can't exceed the money you had, and interprets the answer with its unit and meaning; a child who computes-and-stops or keyword-adds accepts 35 or gives '5' with no meaning. The impossible candidate answer is the hinge: sense-making children reject it instantly, compute-and-stop children don't. Hard to reject it for the wrong reason; hard to accept it if you're really picturing the situation.

pedagogy.summary: At 7-8, using structure extends place value to three digits (adding hundreds changes only the hundreds digit), turns the multiplication/division link into a fact-deriving tool (6×4=24 gives 4×6, 24÷4 and 24÷6), and makes shape classification property-based (sort by number of sides, right angles, parallel lines rather than by look). The teaching aim is a habit: before computing or naming, ask 'what do I already know that this is like?' CCSS MP7 marks this as the run-up to the distributive property (7×8 = 7×5 + 7×3) and to reasoning about geometric figures by their structure.
bestPractices: Use a single array to show a whole fact family at once (6 rows of 4) so 6×4, 4×6, 24÷4 and 24÷6 are read off one structure, not learned as four separate facts
Use a three-digit place-value machine / arrow cards and predict-then-check which column moves when adding 100, 10 or 1
Classify shapes with property checklists and overlapping sets (sides, right angles, parallel pairs) so classification survives rotation and odd examples
Ask 'which fact that you already know helps here?' to build the transfer habit rather than fresh computation
keyRepresentations: Rectangular array / area model for the multiplication-division fact family
Three-digit place-value apparatus and arrow cards
Property checklists and Venn-style overlapping shape sets
Distributive splits (7×8 as 7×5 + 7×3) shown on a partitioned array
commonMisconceptions: Treats multiplication and division as unrelated, recomputing 24÷4 from scratch despite knowing 6×4
When adding 100 to a three-digit number, changes the wrong column or mis-carries
Classifies shapes by orientation/appearance (a rotated square becomes a 'diamond'; only a 'pointing-up' triangle is a triangle)
Thinks a derived fact must be checked by counting because facts feel separate rather than connected

learn.summary: For ages 7-8, build the habit of looking for structure before computing or naming: ask 'what do I already know that this is like?' Three strands: (1) read a whole multiplication/division fact family off one array (6×4, 4×6, 24÷4, 24÷6 from the same 6 rows of 4); (2) use three-digit place value so adding 100/10/1 changes only the matching column, barring a carry into the next place; (3) classify shapes by properties (sides, right angles, parallel pairs) so the classification survives rotation. This is the run-up to the distributive property (7×8 = 7×5 + 7×3) and to reasoning about figures by structure.

activities.title: One array, four facts
feedback: If the child pauses to count or skip-count for the divisions, return to the one array and physically read all four facts from it (rows, columns, sharing, grouping) so the single structure is seen to hold them all; name division as undoing multiplication.
If they treat 24÷4 as unrelated to 6×4, cover a factor on the array they just built and ask 'how many fours are hidden here?' so the quotient is read, not recalculated.
Probe scaling: 'you knew 6×4 — does that also help with 6×8, or 60×4? how?' to check the structural link transfers.
Counterexample check: 'division undoes multiplication — so does 24÷5 come out as neat as 24÷4? why not?' to test understanding beyond the slogan.
activities.rationale: A single manipulable array makes the shared structure of a fact family visible as the child acts, supporting the deriving habit rather than four separately memorised facts; well-chosen representations such as arrays expose structure and can later be faded.
sourceClaims: Teaching should help pupils recognise and use mathematical structure and relationships, using well-chosen representations (e.g. arrays, place-value apparatus) that expose structure and are then faded
Students using structure see e.g. 7×8 = 7×5 + 7×3 (distributive property) and recognise significant structure in figures — the run-up to reasoning by structure rather than recomputation
learnerActions: Lay out 24 counters as 6 rows of 4 and state the multiplication it shows (6×4=24).
Rotate the whole array a quarter turn and read it again as 4 rows of 6; say why 6×4 and 4×6 are the same 24 dots seen two ways.
Cover one factor: with 24 shared into 4 rows, read off how many are in each row (6) to get 24÷4; then read 24÷6 the same way.
Say in your own words how knowing 6×4=24 means you already know 24÷4 and 24÷6 without counting.
Try a second fact family (e.g. 5 rows of 3) and derive all four facts from the single array.
activities.intendedInsight: One rectangular array holds a whole fact family; multiplication and division are the same structure read different ways, so a known product gives the related quotients without recomputing.

activities.title: Partition to derive a harder product
feedback: If the parts don't recombine, re-count each sub-array (7×5 and 7×3) separately before adding, and check the split covers all 8 columns with none missing.
Audit the arithmetic together: 35+21=56; if a child suggests another total, recount one part on the array rather than accepting the number.
Ask them to split the same product a second way (e.g. 7×4 + 7×4, where each part is 28 and the total is again 56) and confirm it reaches the same total, reinforcing that the whole is conserved.
activities.rationale: Showing the distributive split on a partitioned array connects the fact-deriving habit to standard structural reasoning named in the practice standards.
sourceClaims: Students using structure see e.g. 7×8 = 7×5 + 7×3 (distributive property) and recognise significant structure in figures — the run-up to reasoning by structure rather than recomputation
learnerActions: Take a product you don't know by heart, e.g. 7×8, and lay it as 7 rows of 8.
Split the 8 columns into 5 and 3, drawing a line through the array.
Work out the two easier parts (7×5=35 and 7×3=21) and add them (35+21=56).
State the rule you used: 7×8 = 7×5 + 7×3, then try splitting a different product your own way.
activities.intendedInsight: A large product can be built from easier known products by partitioning the array — this is the distributive property seen concretely.

activities.title: Predict which column moves
feedback: If the child names or alters the wrong column when adding 100, predict-then-check on the place-value machine and watch only the hundreds count move.
If a carry occurs (e.g. adding 100 to 970 → 1070), treat it explicitly: the hundreds column fills and rolls into thousands — note this is still the hundreds place acting, not a random digit changing.
Probe directly: 'which digit changes when I add 100 to 470, and which stay the same? why those?'
activities.rationale: Predict-then-check with place-value apparatus makes the column structure something the child reasons about rather than a procedure to copy; such representations expose structure and can be faded.
sourceClaims: Teaching should help pupils recognise and use mathematical structure and relationships, using well-chosen representations (e.g. arrays, place-value apparatus) that expose structure and are then faded
learnerActions: Using a three-digit place-value apparatus or arrow cards, build a number such as 253 (or 470).
Before adding, predict out loud which digit will change and which will stay the same when you add 100.
Add one hundred-flat (or spin the +100 wheel) and check: for 253 and 470 only the hundreds count moves, with no carry.

Repeat for +10 and +1, each time predicting first, then stating why only that one column changed (true for 253 or 470; if the column being added to holds a 9, notice that a carry also changes the next place).
activities.intendedInsight: Place value is structured by columns; adding 100 changes only the hundreds, 10 only the tens, and 1 only the ones, unless the addition causes a carry into the next place (e.g. 259+1=260, 295+10=305, 970+100=1070).

activities.title: Classify by properties, not by how it looks
feedback: If the child says a rotated square is a 'diamond' and no longer a square, or that only a point-up triangle is a triangle, run the property checklist while rotating the shape so they see the properties are unchanged by orientation.
If they justify by appearance, ask 'count the sides and right angles — did any change when it tilted?' to redirect to properties.
Include odd and rotated examples deliberately so classification does not depend on a standard pose.
activities.rationale: Property checklists and overlapping sets make classification depend on structure rather than orientation, addressing the common misconception that a rotated square becomes a 'diamond' and is no longer a square; recognising significant structure in figures is the aimed-for habit.
sourceClaims: Students using structure see e.g. 7×8 = 7×5 + 7×3 (distributive property) and recognise significant structure in figures — the run-up to reasoning by structure rather than recomputation
learnerActions: Pick a shape and run a property checklist: count the sides, mark the right angles, find any parallel pairs.
Classify it from the checklist (e.g. square: 4 equal sides, 4 right angles, 2 pairs of parallel sides — also a rectangle).
Rotate the shape 45° and re-run the checklist; confirm the same properties, so the classification does not change.
Sort several shapes into overlapping sets (e.g. 'has a right angle', 'has parallel sides') and place a rotated square and an upside-down triangle correctly.
Justify one classification aloud by citing properties, not orientation.
activities.intendedInsight: A shape's class comes from its properties (sides, angles, parallel lines), which stay the same under rotation — a tilted square is still a square; calling it a 'diamond' does not make it a different shape (a square is also a special rhombus).

constraints: The teaching aim is the transfer habit 'which fact that I already know helps here?' — reaching the right numbers is not enough; the child should explain why one fact yields the others.

A fixed reference diagram of a fact family or distributive split can annotate and explain, but cannot be rotated or re-covered by the learner; a manipulable array lets the child test that a turned array re-reads and that covering a factor reveals a quotient. Use static diagrams as support, not as the sole route to the deriving habit.

Matching or derive-the-answer tasks (from 6×4=24, give 24÷6) can check whether facts are treated as connected, but a correct answer may be a recomputed one; always pair with 'which known fact did you use?' to distinguish deriving from recalculating.

Carrying is an exception to 'only one column changes': when adding 100/10/1 causes a carry, the named column fills and rolls into the next place. Address this explicitly rather than teaching 'the other columns never change'.

Fact families and three-digit place value are quantitative; 2D shape classification by property needs the 2D figure and its properties. These do not require 3D models, though a 3D context is not forbidden where genuinely useful.

Optional interaction examples (tap to highlight 6×4, rotate the array to read 4×6, cover a factor to reveal a division, a predict-then-check place-value wheel, live recolouring of a checklist while rotating a shape) make the mechanism concrete; they are illustrative, not mandatory.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support general principles rather than proving any specific task was tested.

The original claimed adding 100 'only changes the hundreds digit'; this holds except when a carry occurs. The summary, Activity 3 and the constraints now qualify the generalisation, and the child predicts and checks, so it is not taught as absolute.

The original artefact notes asserted a dialogue 'lacks the array and columns the child needs' and that these topics 'do not need 3D'. These are catalog-fit opinions, not established necessity claims; softened to scoped affordances/limits in constraints.
Arithmetic self-audit: 6×4=24; 24÷4=6; 24÷6=4; 5×3=15; 7×5=35, 7×3=21, 35+21=56 (=7×8); alternative split 7×4+7×4 = 28+28 = 56; 970+100=1070. All checked and consistent as used in activities.
Source claims as written describe general guidance (recognise/use structure; use and fade representations) and do not establish comparative efficacy or necessity of any particular artefact type.

probeDeeper: Ask 'you knew 6×4 — does knowing 6×4 also help with 6×8, or 60×4? how?' to test whether the structural link scales to new facts
Counterexample tuned to this topic: 'you said division undoes multiplication — so does 24÷5 come out as neat as 24÷4? why not?' to check the child understands the relationship, not a slogan
Ask 'which digit changes when I add 100 to 470, and which stay the same? why those?' to probe the place-value structure directly
Rotate a square 45° and ask 'is it still a square? how can you be sure?' — a structural thinker checks sides and angles, not the tilt
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child deriving all three from the one fact and explaining the link: 4×6 is the same array turned round; 24÷4 asks how many fours in 24 (six), 24÷6 asks how many sixes (four) — division undoes the multiplication.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats multiplication and division as unrelated operations, recomputing 24÷4 from scratch despite just stating 6×4=24
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to one array and physically read all four facts from it (rows, columns, sharing, grouping) so the single structure is seen to hold them all; name division as undoing multiplication
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child pauses to count or skip-count for the divisions rather than reading them off the known fact

errorPatterns.pattern: When adding hundreds, changes the wrong column (253+100 alters tens or ones) because three-digit place-value structure is insecure
errorPatterns.nextMove: Predict-then-check on a three-digit place-value machine; add one hundred-flat and watch only the hundreds count move
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked which digit changes when adding 100 to a three-digit number, the child names or alters the wrong column

errorPatterns.pattern: Classifies shapes by orientation or appearance — a rotated square becomes a 'diamond', or only checks how it looks rather than its sides/angles/parallel lines
errorPatterns.nextMove: Run a property checklist (sides, right angles, parallel lines) while rotating the shape so the child sees the properties are unchanged by orientation
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked to justify a classification, the child cites how the shape looks or which way it points rather than counting sides/right angles/parallel pairs

responseLevels.gap: Recomputes divisions from scratch, mis-places the changing digit when adding hundreds, and classifies shapes by look; each task handled in isolation
responseLevels.full: Reads all four facts off the one array and explains the inverse relationship, predicts and justifies which digit changes, and classifies by properties despite rotation — and reuses 'what do I already know that this is like?' on new problems unprompted
responseLevels.partial: Derives the related facts or names the right column/property when prompted, but cannot clearly explain why one fact gives the others or reverts to counting under pressure

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You know that 6 × 4 = 24. Without counting anything out, what does that tell you about 4 × 6, and about 24 ÷ 4 and 24 ÷ 6? How does the one fact give you the others?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Reaching the numbers is easy; the discriminating content is the EXPLANATION of why one fact yields the others. A child using structure narrates the array/inverse relationship; a child without it treats each as a separate fact to recompute or recall, or gets the divisions but cannot say why they follow.

sources.claim: Students using structure see e.g. 7×8 = 7×5 + 7×3 (distributive property) and recognise significant structure in figures — the run-up to reasoning by structure rather than recomputation
sources.source: CCSS Standards for Mathematical Practice, MP7 'Look for and make use of structure'

sources.claim: Teaching should help pupils recognise and use mathematical structure and relationships, using well-chosen representations (e.g. arrays, place-value apparatus) that expose structure and are then faded
