pedagogy.summary: Equivalent fractions are different names for the same amount: holding the whole constant, splitting each part into more (smaller) pieces multiplies both numerator and denominator without changing the quantity, so 2/3 = 4/6 = 6/9. The load-bearing insight, best seen on a fraction wall or bar, is that MORE pieces each SMALLER can total the same amount — which directly confronts the whole-number bias that '4/6 must be more than 2/3 because 4 > 2'. Teach the multiplicative structure with diagrams before any 'times top and bottom' rule.
bestPractices: Build equivalence by SPLITTING each part of a fixed bar (2/3 → split each third in two → 4/6) so the shaded amount visibly never changes
Use a fraction wall / stacked bars so equal rows align and equivalents line up
Confront the additive error explicitly — show that '+1 to top and bottom' (2/3 → 3/4) shifts the shaded amount
Confirm on a number line that equivalent fractions land on the SAME point
Compare shaded AREAS of identical wholes, never different-sized wholes, when judging equivalence
keyRepresentations: Fraction wall / stacked equal-length bars (canonical equivalence reference)
A single bar re-partitioned by splitting each part (2/3 → 4/6)
Number line with dual labelling (thirds above, sixths below) showing the same point
Area model (identical rectangles shaded to the same amount)
commonMisconceptions: Whole-number bias — 4/6 judged more than 2/3 'because 4 > 2 and there are more pieces'
Different numbers must mean different amounts (denies equivalence)
Makes 'equivalents' by ADDING the same number to top and bottom (2/3 → 3/4)
Compares shaded amounts across different-sized wholes
Thinks changing only the numerator or only the denominator keeps the value

learn.summary: Equivalent fractions are different names for the same amount. Holding the whole constant, splitting each part into more (smaller) pieces multiplies both numerator and denominator without changing the quantity, so 2/3 = 4/6 = 6/9. The load-bearing insight, best seen on a fraction wall or bar, is that MORE pieces each SMALLER can total the same amount, which confronts the whole-number bias that '4/6 must be more than 2/3 because 4 > 2'. Teach the multiplicative structure with diagrams before any 'times top and bottom' rule.

activities.title: Split each part of a fixed bar (2/3 becomes 4/6)
feedback: If the child says the second bar has more chocolate, lay the 2/3 bar directly over the 4/6 bar so the shaded lengths coincide; the pieces are smaller but the shaded strip is identical.

If the child changes only the numerator or only the denominator and expects the same amount, shade that fraction on an identical bar and compare: the shaded length differs, so both parts must be multiplied by the same number.
If the child offers 3/4 as equal to 2/3, shade 3/4 on an identical bar and align it with 2/3: the shaded length is clearly longer, so adding is not the same as splitting.
Prompt: 'Did the amount of chocolate change when you drew the splitting lines? What changed and what stayed the same?'
Reinforce: both the number of parts and the number shaded were multiplied by the same number, so the fraction's value did not change.
activities.rationale: Making and watching the split while the shaded length stays fixed lets equivalence be felt as 'same amount, more cuts', and directly contrasts changing one part, and the additive error, with the multiplicative structure. An interactive version (a 'split every part into ___' control that cleaves each part live while the symbol updates 4/6, 6/9, with an 'add 1 to top and bottom' button that visibly shifts the strip) may make the mechanism more concrete, but drawing the splits on paper serves the same purpose.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils recognise and show, using diagrams, equivalent fractions with small denominators.
learnerActions: Shade two of three equal parts of a bar to show 2/3.
Split every third into two equal pieces by drawing a line through each part; count that four of six parts are now shaded and write 4/6.
Describe what happened to the length of shaded strip: it did not grow or shrink, there are just more lines.
Keep splitting to generate the family: split each part into three for 6/9, into four for 8/12; each time check the shaded strip stays the same length.

Test changing only one number: on an identical bar change only the bottom number (2/3 to 2/6) or only the top number (2/3 to 3/3) and shade it; check that the shaded amount changes, so changing just one part does NOT make an equivalent fraction.
Try the trap: add one to the top and one to the bottom (2/3 to 3/4) and shade 3/4 of an identical bar; compare the shaded length with the original 2/3.
activities.intendedInsight: Splitting each part (multiplying numerator and denominator by the same number) makes more, smaller pieces that cover exactly the same amount; for fractions like 2/3, changing only one of the two numbers, or adding one to each, shifts the amount, so neither is a way to make an equivalent fraction.

activities.title: Fraction wall: which rows line up
feedback: If the child reads only the numbers, redirect attention to where each bar ends relative to the shared vertical line.
Ask: 'These have different numbers but reach the same line. What does that tell you about the amount?'
If the child cannot see why rows align, connect back to splitting: a third split into two gives two sixths, which is why 2/3 and 4/6 reach the same line.
activities.rationale: The fraction wall is the canonical static reference for equivalence; tapping or tracing a row shows which fractions align. It shows the result rather than generating the split-each-part mechanism, so pair it with the splitting activity.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils recognise and show, using diagrams, equivalent fractions with small denominators.
learnerActions: Use a fraction wall of stacked equal-length rows (halves, thirds, quarters, sixths, ninths) and find where rows end at the same vertical line.
Identify equivalents by alignment: 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6, and 2/3 = 4/6.
Explain in words why two fractions that reach the same line are equal (they cover the same length of the identical whole).
Check a non-example: does 2/3 line up with 3/4? Note it does not, so they are not equivalent.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction wall is a reliable reference: fractions that cover the same length of the identical whole name the same amount, regardless of how many pieces.

activities.title: Same point on the number line
feedback: If the child expects two different points, count the sixths across to 4/6 and the thirds across to 2/3 and show the marks fall together.
Ask: 'If they are at the same point, how much of the distance from 0 to 1 does each cover?'
Connect to the bar: the same length on the bar becomes the same point on the line.
activities.rationale: Showing equivalents coinciding at one point addresses whole-number bias, where a child compares numerators and denominators separately, by making magnitude the object of attention. Dual labelling (thirds above, sixths below) makes the shared point concrete.
sourceClaims: Whole-number bias leads students to compare fractions by their separate numerators/denominators (e.g. thinking 3/8 > 3/5 by comparing denominators); the guide recommends showing equivalent fractions occupy the same magnitude/point using number lines and dividing a 0-1 line into halves and quarters so 1/2 and 2/4 coincide.
learnerActions: Draw a number line from 0 to 1 and mark thirds above it (1/3, 2/3).
On the same line, mark sixths below it (1/6, 2/6, 3/6, 4/6, 5/6, including 4/6 against 2/3).
Place 2/3 and 4/6 and check whether they land on the same point or different points.
Repeat with 1/2 and 2/4 (marking halves and quarters) to confirm they coincide.
activities.intendedInsight: Equivalent fractions occupy the same magnitude and land on the same point of a number line, independent of how the line is partitioned.

activities.title: Sort, match and complete equivalents
feedback: If 3/4 is placed with the equivalents, ask the child to shade 3/4 and 2/3 on identical bars and compare the lengths.
For a missing-value error, return to splitting: 2/3 with each part split into two gives 4/6, so the numerator is 4.
Note: these matching and completion tasks check classification and completion; they do not by themselves build the multiplicative structure, so use them after the diagram work above.
activities.rationale: Recognition and completion tasks assess equivalence and can catch the additive error, but they test rather than construct the underlying structure. Keep them as consolidation, not as the primary teaching.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils recognise and show, using diagrams, equivalent fractions with small denominators.
learnerActions: Match pairs of equivalent fractions (for example 1/2 with 2/4, 2/3 with 4/6), justifying each with a quick diagram.
Complete the missing value: 2/3 = __/6, and explain how the splitting gives the answer.
Sort a set into 'equivalent to 2/3' and 'not equivalent', deliberately including the additive trap 3/4, and explain why 3/4 does not belong.
When comparing shaded amounts, always use identical-sized wholes, never different-sized wholes.
activities.intendedInsight: Identifying and completing equivalents consolidates the idea; the additive trap, together with a required explanation, checks whether the child multiplies both parts rather than adding.

activities.title: Predict, overlay, explain (diagnostic)
feedback: If the prediction is '4/6 is more because 4 > 2', after overlaying the bars, split each third in front of the child to show four smaller sixths covering the same length.
If the child says the two 'just look the same', push for the mechanism: each third was split in two, so the amount could not change.
If the child denies they can be equal because the numbers differ, show them landing on the same number-line point and name both as one amount.

A full response states 2/3 = 4/6, justifies by holding the whole constant and splitting each part, rejects the additive error, generates another equivalent, and confirms the same point on a number line. A partial response agrees the shaded amounts match but explains it only as 'they look the same' or by counting, without the split-each-part mechanism. A gap response says the fraction with bigger numbers is more or denies equivalence is possible.
activities.rationale: A predict-then-check task with a required reason surfaces whole-number bias, no-equivalence and additive misconceptions even when a rehearsed child guesses 'same'. Comparing only identical wholes keeps the portion comparison valid; the number-line step confirms shared magnitude.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils recognise and show, using diagrams, equivalent fractions with small denominators.

Whole-number bias leads students to compare fractions by their separate numerators/denominators (e.g. thinking 3/8 > 3/5 by comparing denominators); the guide recommends showing equivalent fractions occupy the same magnitude/point using number lines and dividing a 0-1 line into halves and quarters so 1/2 and 2/4 coincide.
learnerActions: Look at two identical bars held apart: one shaded 2/3, one shaded 4/6.
Predict whether 4/6 shades MORE than, LESS than, or the SAME as 2/3, and state a reason BEFORE checking.
Slide the second bar onto the first and observe whether the shaded regions coincide.
Respond to a claim: 'Mia says 4/6 is more because 4 > 2 and there are more pieces.' Explain why she is wrong.
Generate one further fraction equal to 2/3 using a diagram and justify it.
activities.intendedInsight: The stated reason, not just the final answer, reveals whether the child holds the whole constant and compares the shaded amount, or falls into whole-number or additive thinking.

constraints: When comparing represented portions (shaded areas or bar lengths), always use identical-sized wholes; comparing shaded amounts across different-sized wholes invalidates the equivalence judgement. As numbers on a number line, equivalent fractions remain comparable and coincide at one point.
Teach the multiplicative structure (splitting each part, multiplying numerator and denominator by the same number) with diagrams BEFORE introducing any 'times top and bottom' rule.

Both numerator and denominator must be multiplied by the same number: for fractions less than one, such as 2/3, adding one to each (2/3 to 3/4) or changing only one of the two numbers shifts the shaded amount and does not make an equivalent fraction. (Adding one to each keeps the amount the same only when the fraction is a whole, e.g. 3/3 to 4/4, so it is not a valid rule.)
Matching, sorting and fill-in-the-blank tasks consolidate and check classification/completion but do not on their own build the underlying structure; use them after diagram-based construction.
A fraction wall shows which fractions align but does not itself demonstrate the split-each-part mechanism; pair it with active splitting.
Suitable for ages 7-8 (small denominators); the goal is recognising and showing equivalence with diagrams, not symbolic manipulation in isolation.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original catalog rated a conversation/persona format as 'adds little' and a third dimension as 'decorative' for this planar area/length idea. These were catalog fit judgements and are not asserted here as universal claims: a discussion may still support reasoning and a 3D model is simply not needed for a planar length/area concept; the stated objective is diagram-based construction of equivalence.

Arithmetic check: 2/3 = 4/6 = 6/9 = 8/12 (multiplying both parts by 2, 3, 4); 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6. The additive trap 2/3 to 3/4 is correctly presented as NOT equivalent (3/4 = 0.75 > 2/3 approximately 0.667). No numerical errors found.

The source pedagogy also listed the misconception that changing only the numerator or only the denominator preserves value; this is now explicitly addressed in the splitting activity (e.g. 2/3 to 2/6), alongside the additive trap.

The IES source claim quotes the student misconception 'thinking 3/8 > 3/5' (in reality 3/8 < 3/5); it is retained verbatim only as a description of the misconception in sourceClaims and is never offered to a learner as a valid comparison.
The source row referenced internal prerequisite reteach ids for the whole-number and no-equivalence misconceptions; these are internal identifiers and have been omitted from learner-facing guidance.

sourceClaims are exact copies of this row's sources[].claim, cited only where they support the stated teaching principle (showing/recognising with diagrams; number-line magnitude). Citation does not establish that any specific activity was empirically tested or human-reviewed.

assess.poeTask: Show the two fractions un-overlaid: a bar shaded 2/3 and an identical bar shaded 4/6, held apart. Ask the child to predict whether 4/6 shades MORE than, LESS than, or the SAME amount as 2/3, and to say why before checking. A whole-number-biased child predicts '4/6 is more, because 4 > 2'. Then slide the second bar onto the first — the shaded regions coincide exactly. The pre-observation reason is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: Draw a line splitting each of the three parts of the first bar in half. What fraction is shaded now, and did the amount of chocolate change?
Is 2/3 the same as 3/4? Someone got 3/4 by adding one to the top and one to the bottom — what would you say?
Find another fraction equal to 2/3 using a diagram. How do you know it's equal?
On a number line from 0 to 1, would 2/3 and 4/6 land on the same point or different points? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: They are equal — 2/3 = 4/6. The same amount of chocolate is shaded on both bars; the second bar just has each third split into two, so four smaller sixths cover exactly the same length as two thirds. Mia is wrong: more pieces are each smaller, so the total amount is the same.

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number bias — the fraction with bigger numbers/more pieces is judged to be more (4/6 > 2/3 because 4 > 2 and 6 > 3)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay the two identical bars so the shaded lengths coincide; split each third to generate the sixths in front of the child so the amount is seen not to change
errorPatterns.distractor: 4/6 is more, because 4 is more than 2 and it has more pieces.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 4/6 is more chocolate and points to the larger numbers or the greater number of shaded pieces

errorPatterns.pattern: No-equivalence — different numbers must name different amounts, so 2/3 and 4/6 'can't be the same'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show 2/3 and 4/6 landing on the same point on a number line and covering the same length on the wall; name both as one amount
errorPatterns.distractor: They must be different — the two fractions have different numbers.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Insists they must differ because the fractions are written with different numbers

errorPatterns.pattern: Additive equivalence — makes 'equivalents' by adding the same number to top and bottom (2/3 = 3/4)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast +1-to-each (shifts the shaded strip) with split-each-part (leaves it fixed); establish that both parts must be MULTIPLIED
errorPatterns.distractor: 2/3 = 3/4 — I added one to the top and one to the bottom.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Generates an equivalent by +1 to each, or agrees 2/3 = 3/4

responseLevels.gap: Says the fraction with bigger numbers is more (4/6 > 2/3), or denies that two differently-written fractions can be equal.
responseLevels.full: States 2/3 = 4/6 and justifies by holding the whole constant and splitting each part (multiplicative), rejects the additive error, generates a further equivalent, and confirms on a number line that they share the same point.
responseLevels.partial: Agrees 2/3 and 4/6 shade the same amount when shown the diagram, but explains it as 'they just look the same' or by counting, without the split-each-part mechanism; may still make equivalents by adding, or falter when the whole isn't drawn.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are two identical chocolate bars. The first is split into three equal parts with two of them shaded (2/3). The second is split into six equal parts with four of them shaded (4/6). Mia says 4/6 is more chocolate, because 4 is more than 2 and there are more pieces. Is she right? How much of each bar is shaded, and WHY are they the same or different?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A whole-number-biased child says 4/6 > 2/3 'because 4 > 2 / more pieces'. Correct reasoning holds the identical whole constant and compares shaded amount, recognising that splitting each part (multiplying numerator AND denominator) leaves the amount unchanged — the reason (tier 2) exposes the bias and the additive error even when a rehearsed child guesses 'same'.

sources.claim: Whole-number bias leads students to compare fractions by their separate numerators/denominators (e.g. thinking 3/8 > 3/5 by comparing denominators); the guide recommends showing equivalent fractions occupy the same magnitude/point using number lines and dividing a 0-1 line into halves and quarters so 1/2 and 2/4 coincide.

pedagogy.summary: Children learn to compare and sort a mixed collection of 2-D shapes, 3-D solids and everyday objects by their geometric PROPERTIES — number of sides, number/type of faces, flat vs curved surfaces, number of vertices — and to articulate the criterion they used. The procedural goal is a consistent, property-based sort: choosing one attribute, applying it to every item, and being able to re-sort the same collection a different way. It builds directly on knowing the properties (2-D sides, 3-D faces/edges/vertices) and pushes children off the van Hiele visual level, where they group by overall look, colour or size. Best taught with real shapes to handle, 'is/is not' two-set sorting, and 'guess my rule' games.
bestPractices: Sort a physical, mixed collection into two sets on an 'is / is not' criterion (e.g. has a curved surface / has no curved surface), then challenge children to re-sort the SAME set a different way.
Play 'guess my rule': present a set already sorted by someone else and have children infer the property used — this makes the criterion explicit.
Insist the rule is a geometric property; when a child groups by colour or size, restrict the set to one colour/size so appearance cannot be the criterion.
Hand children real solids to handle and mark faces/edges/vertices with a wipe-clean pen as they count, so a sort by 'number of faces' rests on an accurate count.
Model articulating the rule aloud ('all of these have a triangular face') and ask 'does EVERY shape in this group follow your rule?' to check consistency.
keyRepresentations: A mixed tray of handleable 2-D shapes and 3-D solids plus everyday objects
Two sorting hoops / Carroll or Venn two-set frame labelled with an 'is / is not' criterion
Wipe-clean pen for marking faces/edges/vertices while counting
'Guess my rule' pre-sorted sets
commonMisconceptions: Sorts by a non-defining feature — colour, size or overall look — rather than a geometric property.
Groups shapes by holistic resemblance ('these look the same') and cannot state a single consistent rule, letting the rule drift mid-sort.
Miscounts sides, faces or vertices — losing track of where counting started — so shapes end up in the wrong group.
Can sort one way but cannot re-sort the same collection by a different property, or cannot infer the rule of a set sorted by someone else.

learn.summary: Children aged 6-7 learn to compare and sort a mixed collection of 2-D shapes, 3-D solids and everyday objects by geometric PROPERTIES — number of sides, number/type of faces, flat vs curved surfaces, number of vertices — and to articulate the criterion used. The procedural goal is a consistent, property-based sort: choose one attribute, apply it to every item, then re-sort the SAME collection a different way. This builds on knowing the properties and pushes children off the van Hiele visual level, where they group by overall look, colour or size. Best taught with real shapes to handle, 'is / is not' two-set sorting, and 'guess my rule' games.

activities.title: Sort a real tray two ways on an 'is / is not' rule
feedback: If a child groups by colour, size or 'the pretty ones', restrict the collection to a single colour and size so appearance cannot be the criterion, forcing attention to a property.

When a placement breaks the chosen rule (e.g. a cone, which has a curved surface, dropped into 'no curved surface'), point to the mismatch and ask which property decides membership — the property, not the look.
Prompt consistency: 'Does every shape in this group follow your rule?' If membership drifts for a borderline shape, revisit the stated rule.

Watching a shape such as a triangular prism move to the other hoop when the rule changes — it has no curved surface but does have triangular faces, so it belongs in a different group under each rule — is the moment 'a sort needs one property' becomes concrete. (A cube would stay put, since it has neither a curved surface nor a triangular face.)
activities.rationale: 'Is / is not' two-set sorting with a required second re-sort of the same set targets the flexible, property-based sorting that distinguishes a child reading shapes by property from one grouping by overall look. Restricting colour/size removes appearance as a possible criterion.
sourceClaims: Children should sort shapes into two sets on 'is / is not' criteria and be able to guess a sorting rule from how shapes have been sorted; a common misconception is failing to recognise a shape in a different orientation, remedied by handling and rotating cut-outs.

Young children at the van Hiele visualization level group shapes holistically by appearance, colour and orientation rather than defining properties; the instructional goal is to analyse shapes by properties (e.g. number of sides), invariant to colour, size and orientation.
learnerActions: Take a physical, mixed tray of handleable 2-D shapes, 3-D solids and everyday objects.

Choose ONE geometric property as the rule (e.g. 'has a curved surface / has no curved surface') and place every item into one of two sorting hoops or a labelled two-set frame. Check that the rule makes sense for every item in the tray: a flat 2-D shape such as a circle has a curved side (edge) but no curved surface, so either agree how 2-D shapes are judged or pick a rule that fits both 2-D and 3-D items (e.g. 'has a curved edge or surface / has none').
Say the rule aloud ('all of these have a curved surface') and check: does EVERY shape in this group follow my rule?
Now scatter the SAME shapes and re-sort them by a different property (e.g. 'has a triangular face / has no triangular face'); notice which shapes move to a different hoop and why.
activities.intendedInsight: A sort rests on one geometric property held constant and applied to every item; the same collection can be grouped validly in more than one way depending on which property you choose.

activities.title: Guess my rule
feedback: If a child cannot state a single rule that every group member satisfies, model one aloud ('these all have a triangular face') and check each member against it.

If the inferred rule is a non-geometric feature such as colour or size, point to two members of the SAME group that differ in that named feature (e.g. two different colours) yet were grouped together, so the child sees appearance cannot be the rule and looks for the shared geometric property.
Confirm success when the child's continuation placements all satisfy the same stated property.
activities.rationale: Inferring someone else's rule separates a child who reads shapes by property from one who grouped by holistic resemblance; it makes the criterion explicit rather than letting it drift.
sourceClaims: Children should sort shapes into two sets on 'is / is not' criteria and be able to guess a sorting rule from how shapes have been sorted; a common misconception is failing to recognise a shape in a different orientation, remedied by handling and rotating cut-outs.
learnerActions: Look at a set someone else has already sorted into two groups, with the rule hidden.
Infer and state the geometric property that was used to make the two groups.
Continue the sort by placing a few more shapes into the correct group, keeping the rule constant.
Then set your own 'guess my rule' challenge for a partner.
activities.intendedInsight: Making the hidden criterion explicit forces attention onto defining properties and shows that a good sort rests on one rule every member satisfies.

activities.title: Count faces, edges and vertices accurately before sorting
feedback: If recounts give different totals, ask how to be sure each side/face is counted once and model marking each one as it is counted — scaffold the counting, do not reteach the whole topic.
If a shape lands in the wrong group, check whether its faces/vertices were miscounted rather than whether the rule was wrong.
activities.rationale: Miscounting sides, faces or vertices from losing track of the starting point is a known error that makes count-based sorts inconsistent; handling real solids and marking each feature addresses the difficulty of counting features from an image.
sourceClaims: 3-D shapes can be sorted by their properties (faces, edges, vertices; e.g. curved surface / no curved surface, 6-or-more vertices, no triangular faces); the stated common misconception is that children find it hard to count faces, vertices and edges from an IMAGE of a solid; remedy is to hand children real solids to handle and mark each feature with a wipe-clean pen as they count.

A common misconception is that children miscount sides or vertices because they lose track of where they started counting; the remedy is to ask how to count each side/vertex once and model marking each one as it is counted.
learnerActions: Hold a real solid and mark each face, edge or vertex with a wipe-clean pen as you count it, so you count each one exactly once.
Record the count, then use it as the sorting rule (e.g. 'sort solids by number of faces' or 'six or more vertices / fewer than six vertices').
Recount a solid a second way and check you get the same total; if not, find where you lost track.
Place each solid in the correct group based on the verified count.
activities.intendedInsight: A count-based sort is only as reliable as the count; marking each feature once prevents losing track and keeps the sort consistent.

activities.title: Inspect 3-D solids for flat vs curved surfaces
feedback: If a child decides from one view only, prompt them to turn the solid right over to check the other surfaces.
Confirm when the flat-vs-curved judgement matches every surface inspected (e.g. a cylinder has two flat circular faces and one curved surface).
activities.rationale: Handling and rotating solids helps children judge flat-vs-curved surfaces that are hard to read from a static image. An on-screen rotatable solid may supplement this for the 3-D portion, though the sorting action itself is a flat grouping task; efficacy relative to handling is untested here.
sourceClaims: 3-D shapes can be sorted by their properties (faces, edges, vertices; e.g. curved surface / no curved surface, 6-or-more vertices, no triangular faces); the stated common misconception is that children find it hard to count faces, vertices and edges from an IMAGE of a solid; remedy is to hand children real solids to handle and mark each feature with a wipe-clean pen as they count.
learnerActions: Pick up and rotate each solid to inspect every surface, feeling and looking for flat versus curved surfaces.
Sort the solids into 'has a curved surface / has no curved surface' based on what you found.
Explain for a tricky solid (e.g. a cylinder) which surfaces are flat and which are curved.
activities.intendedInsight: Rotating a solid to inspect all its surfaces reveals properties that a single view hides, supporting an accurate flat-vs-curved sort.

constraints: The skill is doing: placing shapes, testing a criterion, and re-sorting. A view-only tap-to-reveal illustration does not let the child perform or switch a sort, so it does not build the procedure on its own.

A fixed, scored categorization (sort by a GIVEN rule) can check sorting against a supplied criterion, but because the rule is provided it does not require the child to choose, articulate or switch the criterion; use it to check rather than to build the flexible re-sort.
Insist the rule is a geometric property; when a child groups by colour or size, restrict the set to one colour/size so appearance cannot be the criterion.
Require a SECOND, different sort of the same collection plus a 'guess my rule' inference — these are what best separate property-based sorting from grouping by overall look.

Paper or card cut-outs and real solids have slight thickness and can be held and turned; treat them as physical representations of the mathematical shapes, and ask children about the shape REPRESENTED, not whether the object can be picked up. A rotatable on-screen solid is a model that may supplement, not replace, handling where handling is available.

When naming a specific solid in an example, make sure it fits the property claimed (e.g. use a triangular prism/pyramid when illustrating 'has a triangular face', and only call a solid a cube when it is cube-shaped); do not assume a generic box is a cube.

An optional on-screen drag-into-two-loops sorter with a swappable rule tile and immediate feedback (a shape springing back with a red outline when it breaks the rule) can make the mechanism concrete; this is one possible interaction, not a required one, and its benefit over physical sorting is untested.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy 'poor / ideal / possible' artefact rankings and the claim that a conversation 'adds nothing' were catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical facts; they have been reframed as scoped affordances/limits (e.g. view-only media do not support the active sorting that is the objective). No claim of medium superiority is asserted beyond these narrow affordances.

The original research narrative used a CUBE as the shape that 'moves to the other hoop' when switching from 'has a curved surface' to 'has a triangular face'. A cube has neither a curved surface nor a triangular face, so under the natural relabelling it stays in the 'no' group for both rules and does not move. This has been corrected in the activity to a shape that genuinely moves (e.g. a triangular prism).
'Six or more vertices' as a sorting band is taken from the source example; confirm the solids provided actually make this discrimination meaningful for the specific collection used.
The first 'guess my rule' set must itself be sorted by a valid single geometric property, or the inference task is unsound; check the pre-sorted example before use.

probeDeeper: You put these together — tell me your rule. Does EVERY shape in this group follow it?
Can you sort exactly the same shapes a completely different way?
I'll add this shape [a large, differently-coloured triangle] — which group does it go in, and why?
Here is a set I sorted into two groups. What was my rule?
assess.correctAnswer: Sorts by a stated geometric property — e.g. 2-D shapes by number of sides, or 3-D solids by flat-vs-curved faces or number of faces/vertices — applies it consistently to every shape, articulates the rule ('these all have a curved surface'), re-sorts the same collection by a different property, and infers the property behind a set sorted by someone else.

errorPatterns.pattern: Sorts by a non-defining feature — colour, size or 'the pretty ones' — rather than a geometric property.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Restrict the collection to a single colour and size so appearance cannot be the criterion, forcing attention to a property; model a property rule aloud ('I'm putting all the ones with a curved surface here').
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The two groups differ by colour or size, not by sides/faces; when asked the rule, the child names a non-geometric feature.

errorPatterns.pattern: Groups by holistic resemblance ('these look the same') without an explicit criterion, and the rule drifts as more shapes are added.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Play 'guess my rule' with a pre-sorted set, then have the child continue that sort — modelling that a sort rests on one explicit property held constant.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cannot state a single rule that every group member satisfies; membership changes when asked to justify a borderline shape.

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscounts sides, faces or vertices because they lose track of where they started, so a count-based sort is inconsistent.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach: ask how to be sure each side/face is counted once, and model marking each one with a wipe-clean pen as it is counted.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Recounts give different totals; a shape lands in the wrong group because its sides/faces were miscounted.

responseLevels.gap: Sorts by a non-geometric feature (colour, size) or by holistic resemblance, cannot state a consistent rule, or miscounts so the sort is wrong.
responseLevels.full: Sorts by a stated geometric property applied consistently to every shape, re-sorts the same collection by a different property, and infers the rule of a set sorted by someone else — treating number of sides / flat-vs-curved faces / number of vertices as the basis for grouping (SOLO relational, with transfer).
responseLevels.partial: Sorts correctly by one property and states that rule, but cannot re-sort the collection a different way, applies the rule inconsistently to some shapes, or cannot infer the rule of a pre-sorted set (SOLO multistructural — one criterion, not coordinated).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a mixed tray of 2-D shapes and 3-D solids. Set the task and watch: 'Sort these into two groups so that everything in a group shares something. When you are done, tell me your rule.' Then: 'Now sort the same shapes a completely different way.' Finally, hand them a set you have already sorted and say: 'What was my rule?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the sort (rather than asking the child to describe sorting) reveals whether the criterion is a defining property applied consistently, or an appearance feature / a rule that drifts. Requiring a SECOND, different sort of the same shapes and a 'guess my rule' inference separates a child who reads shapes by property from one who grouped by overall look — the latter can rarely re-sort or name someone else's rule.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–11y; find all factor pairs for numbers 1–100; identify common factors and common multiples of two numbers; use these to solve problems.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5 'identify multiples and factors, including finding all factor pairs of a number, and common factors of two numbers'; Y6 extends to common factors/multiples.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.OA.4 (all factor pairs 1–100, factor vs multiple, prime/composite) and 6.NS.4 (common factors and multiples, GCF/LCM).
• Operational details — the concepts interlock: FACTORS divide into a number (found systematically in pairs, stopping at the square root); MULTIPLES are in a number's times table (infinite). COMMON factors/multiples are shared between two numbers — the intersection. The key discriminations are factor vs multiple (goes-into vs times-table) and the systematic search that guarantees completeness. Represent factors as rectangle dimensions and multiples as number-line hops; common factors/multiples as the overlap of two such sets (a Venn/two-column tool). This is the direct foundation for simplifying fractions (common factors), common denominators (common multiples), HCF/LCM and ratio.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): list all factor pairs of a number to ~50 systematically. Tier B (age 9–10): find common factors and the first common multiples of two numbers. Tier C (age 10–11): use common factors/multiples to solve a problem and explain factor-vs-multiple precisely.
bestPractices: Search factor pairs systematically (1,2,3… pairing each), stopping at the square root, using commutativity to know the set is complete.
Sharply distinguish factors (divide into the number; finite; rectangle side-lengths) from multiples (times table; infinite; number-line hops).
Represent common factors/multiples as the OVERLAP of two sets (two lists or a Venn diagram) so 'common' means shared.
Ground the work in problems — arranging rows, coinciding events (common multiples), sharing into equal groups (common factors) — not just listing.
Explicitly link to downstream use: common factors simplify fractions; common multiples give common denominators; both feed HCF/LCM and ratio.
keyRepresentations: Rectangle/array — factors as side lengths (factor rainbow for completeness)
Number line / multiplication-grid rows — multiples as skip-count hops
Two-set overlap / Venn diagram — common factors and common multiples
Factor and multiple lists side by side to spot the intersection
commonMisconceptions: Confusing factors with multiples (factor of 12 vs multiple of 12).
Missing factor pairs through unsystematic searching, especially middle ones and the number itself/1.
Thinking there is a 'largest multiple' or a 'smallest factor other than 1' confusion.
Treating 'common' loosely rather than as shared between BOTH numbers.
Forgetting 1 is a common factor of every pair, or that the numbers themselves are factors.

learn.summary: For ages 9–11, build the interlocking ideas of factors (numbers that divide into a whole), multiples (a number's times table), and what two numbers share in common (common factors and common multiples). Learners search factor pairs systematically (pairing 1,2,3… and stopping near the square root), sharply distinguish factor from multiple, and treat 'common' as the overlap of two sets. Work is grounded in problems and linked downstream to simplifying fractions, finding common denominators, and later HCF/LCM and ratio. A manipulable sets-and-overlap tool is proposed as the core builder, with a two-tier probe and a static reference/quiz as complementary assessment and scaffolds.

activities.title: Factors-and-multiples explorer (three linked modes)
feedback: If a middle factor pair is missed (e.g. forgetting (4,9) of 36), prompt: 'Have you tried making a rectangle with 4 along one side?' and point to the gap in the rainbow.
If the child keeps checking past the square root, show that each new pair just repeats one already found — that is why you can stop near √N.
If the child slides a non-shared factor into the Venn overlap, ask: 'Is that number in BOTH lists?' and highlight the two source lists.
When the 6-hops and 8-hops coincide, name the meeting points: '24 is the first common multiple of 6 and 8; 48 and 72 are the next two.'
When the largest number in the overlap glows (12 for 24 and 36, and again for 36 and 48), name it as the highest common factor and ask how it could help simplify a fraction like 24/36.
activities.rationale: Direct manipulation and comparison of sets lets completeness and shared-ness be discovered rather than told; representing factors as rectangles and common factors/multiples as set overlaps supports the meaning of 'common' and is foundational for fractions and ratio. Live number-line hops make the first common multiple visible as a collision.
sourceClaims: Representing factors as rectangles and common factors/multiples as set overlaps supports completeness and the meaning of 'common', foundational for fractions and ratio.
learnerActions: Factor mode: for a chosen number N (e.g. 36), form every possible rectangle (array) of N counters and log each pair of side-lengths as a factor pair on a factor rainbow — e.g. (1,36), (2,18), (3,12), (4,9), (6,6).
Explain how you know you have found them all: pairs are logged from the outside in, and once you reach the square root the pairs repeat, so the set is complete.

Multiple mode: set one number line to skip-count in 7 and read off the first five multiples (7,14,21,28,35); then set two adjustable number lines to skip-count in 6 and 8, watch where the hops coincide, and record the first THREE common multiples (24, 48, 72) — the first collision is at 24.

Common mode: set two numbers (e.g. 24 and 36), pour each factor list into a two-set Venn diagram, slide the shared factors into the overlap, and identify the largest shared factor (12) as the highest common factor; then repeat with 36 and 48 (shared factors 1,2,3,4,6,12, highest common factor 12).
State in words what 'common' means here: a factor or multiple shared by BOTH numbers — the intersection of the two sets.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Common' literally means the overlap of two sets; completeness of a factor list comes from systematic pairing around the square root; and the first common multiple is the first place two skip-counts collide. Factors are finite and divide into a number (rectangle side-lengths), while multiples are infinite times-table hops.

activities.title: Factor detective: prove the list is complete
feedback: If the child stops arbitrarily, ask them to show that every remaining number to test would only repeat a pair already found.
If the child claims a shared factor without checking both numbers, ask them to point to it in each list.
Reinforce vocabulary when it slips: factors divide INTO the number; multiples are the number counted up.
activities.rationale: A Socratic 'have we found them all? what do these two numbers share?' builds the systematic-search habit and the meaning of 'common'. It complements the visual tool by forcing explicit justification.
learnerActions: For a given number, argue aloud or in writing that no factor has been missed: test divisibility in order (1, 2, 3, …) and pair each factor with its partner.
Justify why you can stop checking near the square root: if N = a×b, one of a or b is at most √N, so any larger factor has already appeared as a partner.
Identify what two chosen numbers share and defend your answer: which factors (and which early multiples) belong to BOTH?
activities.intendedInsight: Systematic searching plus the square-root stopping point guarantees a complete factor list, and 'common' must be justified as membership in both sets.

activities.title: Is it prime? Decide and justify the stopping point
feedback: If the child says '97 is prime because it is odd', counter: 9 is odd but 3×3 (not prime), and 2 is even but prime — parity does not decide primeness.
If the child calls 1 prime, restate the exactly-two-distinct-factors definition: 1 has only one factor.
If the child lists 97, 194, 291…, re-anchor: those are multiples of 97; primeness is about what divides INTO 97.
If the child checks every number up to 96, show that factors pair up so testing primes to ~10 suffices.
activities.rationale: Asking why a learner can stop checking exposes whether they understand that factors come in pairs around the square root — the deep idea — and distinguishes a reasoner from a guesser. Common errors (prime = odd, 1 is prime, confusing factors with multiples) are directly addressed with counterexamples.
learnerActions: Decide whether a given number (e.g. 97) is prime.
Test divisibility only by primes up to the square root (for 97: 2, 3, 5, 7, since √97 ≈ 9.8) and record the results.
Explain WHY you can stop at about 10: beyond √97 any factor would pair with one already checked.
Conclude using the definition: a prime has exactly two distinct factors (1 and itself); 1 is neither prime nor composite because it has only one factor.
activities.intendedInsight: Primeness is about the NUMBER of factors, not about being odd; factor-pairing around the square root tells you when it is safe to stop checking.

activities.title: Static reference and checking quiz
feedback: For sorting errors, remind: factors divide into the number; multiples are in its times table.
For a wrong first-common-multiple choice, return to the two skip-counts and find the first collision (24 for 6 and 8).
Use the tap-to-reveal Venn to confirm which factors are truly shared.
activities.rationale: Listing all factors, first multiples, and common factors/multiples is crisply checkable with distractors targeting the classic factor-vs-multiple confusion; a static rainbow and Venn make completeness and overlap visible as a reference. A sort of this kind can check the factor/multiple classification but does not itself require the learner to perform the systematic search or vary the two numbers from scratch.
learnerActions: Study a factor rainbow of 36 and an adjacent Venn of the factors of 24 and 36, tapping to reveal the common factors.
Sort items into 'factor of 24' vs 'multiple of 24' to rehearse the core discrimination.
Fill in a missing factor pair of 36.
Choose the first common multiple of 6 and 8 from options and explain the choice.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidates and checks the factor/multiple distinction, completeness, and the meaning of overlap once the ideas have been built.

constraints: Target age 9–11; coverage: all factor pairs for numbers 1–100, common factors and common multiples of two numbers, and using these to solve problems, with prime/composite as a related discrimination.
Search factor pairs systematically (1,2,3… pairing each) and stop near the square root, using commutativity to confirm the set is complete.
Sharply distinguish factors (divide into the number; finite; rectangle side-lengths) from multiples (times table; infinite; number-line hops).
Treat 'common' strictly as shared between BOTH numbers (the intersection of two sets), not loosely.
Remember 1 is a common factor of every pair, the number itself is a factor, and there is no 'largest multiple'.
Define prime as exactly two distinct factors; 1 is neither prime nor composite.

Ground work in problems (arranging rows, coinciding events, sharing into equal groups), not just listing, and link explicitly to simplifying fractions (common factors), common denominators (common multiples), and later HCF/LCM and ratio.

The static rainbow/Venn and the quiz are scaffolds and checks: they let a learner read off or recognise answers but do not themselves require the learner to perform the systematic search or vary the two numbers. Use them after, or alongside, active construction.

The interactive examples (dragging counters into rectangles, adjustable number lines whose hops light up on coincidence, factor lists pouring into a Venn with the largest shared factor highlighted) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete; equivalent results can be reached with paper factor rainbows, two written multiple lists, and a hand-drawn Venn.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated a 3D interactive 'poor' with the claim '3D adds cost without insight'; this universal claim is not established by catalog ratings and has been dropped rather than propagated. A manipulable 2D/physical set representation is proposed on its affordances, not on a claim that other media cannot teach the topic.

The legacy 'ideal/strong/possible/poor' fit rankings and the single 'recommended' format were catalog preferences; they are not treated as pedagogical laws. The static reference and quiz are preserved as genuine complementary tools with their stated scaffolding limits.

Worked example checked: factor pairs of 36 are (1,36),(2,18),(3,12),(4,9),(6,6) — correct and complete; √36 = 6, so (6,6) is the natural stopping pair. First five multiples of 7 are 7,14,21,28,35. First three common multiples of 6 and 8 are 24,48,72. Factors of 24 and 36 share 1,2,3,4,6,12 (HCF 12); factors of 36 and 48 share 1,2,3,4,6,12 (HCF 12). 97 is prime; testing primes up to √97 (≈9.8): 2,3,5,7 — correct stopping set.

Source 'claim' fields citing CCSS 4.OA.4/6.NS.4 and NCETM guidance are marked verified:false in the row; the DfE curriculum claim is marked verified:true. CCSS requirement claims and the DfE topic claim were removed from sourceClaims where they supported only coverage rather than the stated teaching principle; the NCETM representational claim is retained where it directly backs the principle, though it too is unverified. No efficacy or comparative-superiority claim is asserted for any proposed activity.

The diagnostic probe set (including 'Is 1 a prime number?', '9 is odd — is it prime?') and reteach prerequisite IDs belong to the assessment field and were not modified; relevant reasoning was surfaced into the prime activity's feedback without altering assessment design, and no internal IDs were carried into the learner-facing guidance.

probeDeeper: Why could you stop checking at about 10 instead of going all the way to 96?
Is 1 a prime number? Why or why not?
9 is odd — is it prime? What does that tell you about 'odd means prime'?
Find all the common factors of 24 and 36 — how do you make sure you get them all?
assess.correctAnswer: Yes, 97 is prime. A child reasoning correctly checks for factors other than 1 and 97 by testing divisibility by primes up to √97 (≈ 9.8) — 2, 3, 5, 7 — finds none divide it, and concludes it has exactly two factors. The key reasoning is WHY they can stop at ~10 (beyond that, a factor would pair with one already checked).

errorPatterns.pattern: thinks all odd numbers are prime (or all primes are odd) — calls 97 prime 'because it's odd', and would call 9 or 15 prime too
errorPatterns.nextMove: counterexample: 9 is odd but 3×3, so not prime; and 2 is even but prime. Primeness is about number of factors, not parity.
errorPatterns.distractor: 97 is prime because it is an odd number
errorPatterns.revealedBy: justification rests on oddness; child also calls 9, 15, 21 prime

errorPatterns.pattern: believes 1 is prime (or is unsure), miscounting factors
errorPatterns.nextMove: define prime as EXACTLY two distinct factors; 1 has only one factor, so it is neither prime nor composite.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child includes 1 as prime or reasons about factors including a phantom extra

errorPatterns.pattern: checks divisibility unsystematically and stops arbitrarily (or checks every number up to 96), not knowing the √n stopping point
errorPatterns.nextMove: show factors pair up (if 97 = a×b, one of them is ≤√97); so testing primes to ~10 suffices — that is why you can stop.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child either stops too early with no justification or laboriously tests far too many divisors

errorPatterns.pattern: confuses factors with multiples when justifying — lists multiples of 97 instead of testing its factors
errorPatterns.nextMove: re-anchor vocabulary: factors divide INTO 97; multiples are 97 counted up. Primeness is about factors.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child writes 97, 194, 291… rather than checking what divides 97

responseLevels.gap: equates prime with odd, thinks 1 is prime, or checks divisibility with no system; cannot justify certainty.
responseLevels.full: defines prime as exactly two factors, tests primes up to the square root systematically, justifies the stopping point via factor-pairing, and finds common factors/multiples reliably.
responseLevels.partial: correctly identifies 97 as prime by testing divisors but checks unsystematically or cannot explain the √n stopping point; shaky on the factor/multiple distinction.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Is 97 a prime number? Decide, and then explain how you know for certain — what did you have to check, and how did you know when you could stop checking?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Many children think prime means 'odd', or check only a few small numbers unsystematically, or believe 1 is prime. Asking WHY they can stop checking exposes whether they understand that factors come in pairs around the square root — the deep idea. A guesser cannot justify certainty.

pedagogy.summary: At 10-11, the most advanced problems span ratio, proportion, algebra, negative numbers, and all four operations with fractions and decimals. The child analyses given and unknown quantities, plans a solution pathway, sets up equations, and evaluates reasonableness with estimation and inverse operations. A specific, well-documented obstacle sharpens here: the compulsion to calculate interferes with the algebraic thinking these problems demand — students rush to combine the given numbers instead of representing the unknown and the relationships. The keyword strategy remains unreliable and estimation remains the reasonableness anchor (e.g. vetting a decimal-division answer). Teaching centres on analysing known/unknown and representing relationships before computing, on estimation and inverse checks, and on modelled self-questioning to monitor a long, multi-representation solution.
bestPractices: Analyse given vs unknown and represent the relationship (equation, bar, ratio table) BEFORE computing — resist the compulsion to combine numbers immediately
Estimate to check reasonableness, especially for decimal division and proportion answers; verify with inverse operations
Teach structure/schema over keywords — keyword matching fails badly on complex multi-step problems
Use bar models and ratio tables to expose proportional structure and keep the unknown explicit (WWC Rec 3)
Model self-questioning to plan and monitor across a multi-step, multi-representation solution (WWC Rec 2)
Interpret the result back in context (e.g. a negative or fractional answer's meaning) rather than stopping at a number

Equation with a letter for the unknown
Double number line for proportional reasoning
Estimation/rounding and inverse-operation checks for reasonableness
Known/unknown analysis frame

Keyword strategy on complex problems — operations chosen from words, wrong order
No estimate/reasonableness check on decimal-division or proportion answers
Stopping at a number without interpreting what it means in context (e.g. a negative or non-integer answer)

learn.summary: For 10-11 year olds tackling the most advanced multi-step problems (ratio, proportion, algebra, negative numbers, and all four operations with fractions and decimals), the central teaching move is to represent the relationship between known and unknown quantities BEFORE computing. A well-documented obstacle at this age is the compulsion to calculate: students grab the given numbers and combine them immediately instead of representing the unknown and the structure. Teaching centres on analysing known/unknown, building a representation (ratio table, bar model, double number line, or equation with a letter for the unknown), estimating to vet reasonableness (especially decimal-division and proportion answers), checking with inverse operations, modelled self-questioning across a long solution, and interpreting the result back in context (including what a negative or fractional answer means).

activities.title: Set it up before you solve
feedback: If the child starts multiplying/dividing the given numbers at once and cannot say what quantity each step finds, require a represent-the-relationship step first (ratio table, bar, double number line, or equation with a letter), then discuss why jumping to arithmetic loses the structure.

If the child picks an operation from a cue word and produces a plan the structure does not support, have them map the problem onto a ratio table or equation so operation choice follows from the structure, not the words.

If the child finalises a decimal or scaled answer with no estimate and cannot say what it means, scaffold estimate-then-inverse-check and ask 'what does this answer mean here?' — do not reteach the underlying arithmetic.
If the child stops at a number, prompt interpretation: what does a fractional or negative result represent in this situation?
activities.rationale: Analysing known vs unknown and representing the relationship before computing directly targets the compulsion-to-calculate obstacle; student-built visual representations of problem structure and estimation/inverse reasonableness checks are the levers for multi-step problem solving.
sourceClaims: The compulsion to calculate can interfere with the algebraic thinking usually needed to solve word problems; teachers should focus on the relationship between knowns and unknowns and not rush to compute.
Self-questioning to monitor and reflect (Rec 2) and student-built visual representations of problem structure (Rec 3) each have strong evidence for improving multi-step problem solving.
Proficient solvers analyse givens, constraints and goals, plan a pathway rather than jumping in, and check answers by a different method, asking 'Does this make sense?'.
learnerActions: Read a ratio, proportion, or algebra problem, e.g. 'Flour and sugar are mixed in the ratio 3:2. A baker uses 750 g of flour. How much sugar? Then she scales the whole recipe by 1.5 — how much of each?'
Before touching any numbers, label what is KNOWN and what is UNKNOWN in the problem

Build a representation of the relationship first: a ratio table, a bar model, a double number line, or an equation with a letter for the unknown (e.g. 3 parts flour = 750 g, so 1 part = 250 g, sugar = 2 parts = 500 g)
Only after the relationship is represented, carry out the computation to find the missing quantity

State an estimate for the answer as a benchmark (e.g. scaling by 1.5 means each quantity ends up about half again — one and a half times — as large, so flour becomes roughly 1100-1150 g and sugar roughly 750 g)
Check the result with an inverse operation and compare it to the estimate
Say what the answer means back in the problem's context, including what a negative or fractional result would represent
activities.intendedInsight: When you represent the relationship first, the structure shows which computation will find the missing quantity: a ratio table or bar model makes clear what one part is worth and how many parts are needed, so you resist the pull to simply combine the given numbers.

activities.title: Teach structure, not keywords
feedback: If the child defends an operation by pointing to a cue word, show a case where the same word implies a different operation, and redirect to the ratio table/equation.
If the plan does not match the structure, ask the child to trace each step back to a known/unknown quantity rather than a word.
activities.rationale: Keyword matching fails badly on complex multi-step problems; teaching schema/structure is the recommended alternative.
sourceClaims: Keyword-to-operation matching is unreliable and collapses on multi-step problems; teach problem structure (schema) instead.
learnerActions: Take a complex multi-step problem and resist choosing an operation from a cue word (e.g. 'altogether', 'left', 'share')
Instead, map the problem onto a ratio table or equation so the operation choice follows from the structure
Compare a keyword-driven plan with a structure-driven plan and identify where the keyword approach would choose the wrong operation or wrong order
Justify the final set-up by explaining which quantity each step finds
activities.intendedInsight: Keyword-to-operation matching is unreliable and collapses on multi-step problems; the structure of the problem, not its words, determines the operations and their order.

activities.title: Think-aloud partner: what's known, what's unknown, how are they related?
feedback: If the child wants to compute before articulating the relationship, the partner withholds approval and re-asks the known/unknown/relationship question.
If the child skips the estimate or the context interpretation, prompt both explicitly before accepting the answer.

On the painters probe, if the child answers 3 hours (6÷2) they have just combined the numbers; guide them to reason that each painter alone is slower than the pair, so one alone takes MORE than 6 hours (with equal rates, 12 hours) — the pair finishing faster is the key relationship.
activities.rationale: Modelled self-questioning to plan and monitor across a multi-step, multi-representation solution has strong evidence, and speaking the set-up and reasonableness check aloud rehearses planning before computing.
sourceClaims: Self-questioning to monitor and reflect (Rec 2) and student-built visual representations of problem structure (Rec 3) each have strong evidence for improving multi-step problem solving.
Proficient solvers analyse givens, constraints and goals, plan a pathway rather than jumping in, and check answers by a different method, asking 'Does this make sense?'.
learnerActions: Work through a ratio/algebra problem with a partner (real or in-role) who asks 'What is known? What is unknown? How are they related?' before allowing any computation
Articulate the relationship aloud and describe the chosen representation before computing
State an estimate aloud and justify it, then run an inverse check and say whether the answer is reasonable
Explain what the answer means in context, including a negative or fractional result

Reason aloud about a counterexample: 'Two painters together take 6 hours to paint a room; how long would one painter take alone — is it more or less than 6 hours, and why?' — decide whether you are reasoning about the situation or just combining the numbers
activities.intendedInsight: Monitoring your own solution by self-questioning — stating known/unknown, planning, estimating, and checking — keeps a long multi-representation solution on track and rehearses the antidote to the compulsion to calculate.

activities.title: Match the problem to its set-up (supporting check)
feedback: If a match is wrong, return to the known/unknown analysis and ask which quantity the chosen set-up would actually find.
If a reasonableness judgement lacks a benchmark, prompt the child to state an estimate first.
activities.rationale: 'Which set-up represents this problem?' and estimation-reasonableness items suit this age and reinforce structure and reasonableness; recognising a correct set-up or a reasonable answer size does not by itself elicit the generative planning and representation of a full multi-step algebraic/ratio solution, so this is a supporting check rather than a standalone measure of production.
sourceClaims: Keyword-to-operation matching is unreliable and collapses on multi-step problems; teach problem structure (schema) instead.
Proficient solvers analyse givens, constraints and goals, plan a pathway rather than jumping in, and check answers by a different method, asking 'Does this make sense?'.
learnerActions: Given a problem, choose which equation or ratio table correctly represents it from several options
Answer estimation-reasonableness items: given a decimal-division or proportion result, judge whether it is about the right size and why
Explain the reason for each match or judgement, not just the selection
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising the correct structural representation and the reasonable size of an answer reinforces represent-first and reasonableness habits, though recognising a set-up does not by itself elicit the independent planning and construction of a full solution.

activities.title: Walk through a worked set-up (scaffold)
feedback: If the child can follow the worked stages but cannot reproduce the set-up unaided, return to the 'set it up before you solve' task where they build the representation themselves.
Prompt the child to compare their own next-stage prediction with the revealed stage and explain any difference.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal worked example can show the set-up and the estimate that vets the answer, but the child does not do the representing or checking, so it is a scaffold toward independent construction rather than a substitute.
learnerActions: Step through a worked ratio/algebra problem, revealing one stage at a time: first the known/unknown analysis, then the representation, then the estimate, then the computation and inverse check
At each revealed stage, predict what comes next before uncovering it
Afterwards, attempt a fresh problem doing the representing and checking yourself
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing a fully modelled represent-first-then-check sequence can clarify the routine, but the learning transfers only when the child next does the representing, estimating, and checking independently.

constraints: Represent the relationship (ratio table, bar model, double number line, or equation with a letter for the unknown) before computing; an optional design is to keep the compute/number pad locked until a relationship is represented, so the child cannot grab and combine numbers immediately. The lock is one optional way to enforce represent-first, not a required mechanism.

Always estimate a benchmark and verify with an inverse operation, especially for decimal-division and proportion answers; a reasonableness gauge comparing the answer to the estimate is a useful optional cue.
Always interpret the result back in context (what a negative or fractional answer means) rather than stopping at a number.

Worked-example and match-the-set-up tasks are scaffolds/checks: they do not require the child to independently plan and construct a full multi-step solution, so pair them with tasks where the child does the representing, estimating, and checking.

A scored selection format can check recognition of a correct set-up or a reasonable answer size, but does not by itself elicit the generative planning and representation of a multi-step algebraic/ratio solution; use it as a supporting reasonableness check alongside production tasks.
Avoid teaching keyword-to-operation matching as a strategy; it fails on complex multi-step problems.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support the underlying teaching principle, not that these specific activities were tested.

Worked example of the flour/sugar problem checked: 3 parts flour = 750 g gives 1 part = 250 g, so sugar = 2 parts = 500 g; scaling by 1.5 gives flour 1125 g and sugar 750 g. These are internally consistent and match the source's stated values (1 part = 250 g, sugar = 500 g).

The source's estimate phrasing was 'a bit more than half again'. Because 1.5x is exactly half again (one and a half times) and the exact scaled values are precisely 1.5x the originals, the benchmark was corrected to 'about half again / one and a half times' to avoid wrongly flagging the correct answer as below the estimate.

The 'two painters take 6 hours together; how long does one take alone?' counterexample is a work-rate problem: because the pair finishes faster than either alone, the single-painter time is MORE than 6 hours (12 hours under the equal-rate assumption). It is retained as a learner-facing proportional-reasoning probe; facilitators must confirm the answer is greater than 6 hours and must not treat the naive 6/2 = 3 hours as correct. The exact 12-hour value only holds if the two painters work at equal rates.
The locked-compute-panel design is presented as an optional interaction example, not a mandatory mechanism; a fixed worked example or a conversation partner can also enforce represent-first.

The 'match the problem to its set-up' activity (activity 4) had the CCSS MP1 claim added to its sourceClaims so the estimation-reasonableness half of its rationale is directly source-supported; the keyword/schema claim supports the structure-recognition half.
Source verification flags ('verified:true') are legacy metadata and are not re-confirmed here.

probeDeeper: 'What is known and unknown here — how are the quantities related?' (surfaces represent-first vs number-grabbing)
'Set it up before you compute — could a ratio table or a bar help?' (represent the relationship)
'Your answer is a decimal — about what size should it be, and what does it mean in the recipe?' (reasonableness + interpretation)

Counterexample: 'Two painters take 6 hours together; the problem asks how long one takes alone — is the answer more or less than 6 hours? Why?' — does the child reason proportionally about the situation, or just combine numbers?
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for a child who first identifies known/unknown and represents the relationship (ratio table or bar: 3 parts = 750 g, so 1 part = 250 g, sugar = 500 g), then scales, and checks reasonableness by estimation (1.5× should make each a bit more than half again) and by an inverse. Representing the relationship before computing, and checking reasonableness, are the targets.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Require a represent-the-relationship step first (ratio table, bar, or equation with a letter for the unknown); discuss why jumping to arithmetic loses the structure.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Given a ratio/algebra problem the child starts multiplying/dividing the numbers at once and cannot articulate what quantity each step finds; no set-up or equation appears.

errorPatterns.pattern: Keyword strategy on a complex problem — operations chosen from words and applied in the wrong order.

errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child picks an operation from a cue word and produces a plan the structure does not support; keyword matching fails on complex multi-step problems.

errorPatterns.pattern: No reasonableness check on a decimal/proportion answer, and stopping at a number without interpreting it in context.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold estimate-then-inverse-check and always ask 'what does this answer mean here?'; do not reteach the arithmetic.

responseLevels.gap: Jumps straight to combining the numbers with no set-up, picks operations from words, offers no estimate, and cannot interpret the answer in context.
responseLevels.full: Analyses known/unknown and represents the relationship (ratio table/equation) before computing, plans the pathway, estimates and inverse-checks a decimal answer, interprets it in context, and transfers the represent-then-check routine to a new complex problem unprompted.
responseLevels.partial: Can, when prompted, state known/unknown or build a representation and estimate — but does not spontaneously represent the relationship before computing, nor use estimation/inverse to catch an error, nor interpret the result.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Pose a ratio/algebra problem, e.g. 'Flour and sugar are mixed in the ratio 3:2. A baker uses 750 g of flour. How much sugar? Then she scales the whole recipe by 1.5 — how much of each?' Before any computing ask: 'What is known and what is unknown here? How would you set this up before working out numbers? Once you have a decimal answer, how would you check it is reasonable?' Discuss the reasoning; do not score the number.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child thinking algebraically pauses to represent the relationship (parts, a ratio table, or an equation) before touching numbers, and can estimate to vet a decimal answer. A child gripped by the compulsion to calculate immediately combines 750, 3, 2 and 1.5 in some order with no set-up and no estimate, and cannot say whether the result is reasonable. The presence or absence of a represent-first step, and of a reasonableness check, is the discriminator — hard to fake.
