pedagogy.summary: Rounding a one-decimal-place number to the nearest whole means deciding which of the two neighbouring whole numbers it is closest to on the number line — the tenths digit tells you which half you are in. The 'round up at 5' rule is a CONVENTION for the exact midpoint (x.5), which is genuinely equidistant. It is best taught as 'nearest' on a number line, from which the digit rule is derived, not as a first-move recipe for chopping or bumping digits.
bestPractices: Put the decimal on a number line between its two whole neighbours and ask 'which is it nearer?' before any rule
Mark the halfway point (e.g. 3.5) and treat 'round up at the midpoint' as an agreed convention introduced only once 'nearest' is secure
Distinguish rounding from truncating: 3.7 rounds to 4, it is not chopped to 3
Round to the NEAREST — resist teaching 'if there's anything after the point, go up' (that sends 3.2 to 4)
Have children round a set and articulate the rule as a consequence of distance, then check by estimating
keyRepresentations: Number line 3–4 with 3.7 plotted and 3.5 marked as halfway
Bead string / hundred square segment between two wholes
A 'rounding hill' where a ball rolls to the nearer whole
Place-value chart
commonMisconceptions: Truncates — drops the decimal and always rounds down (3.7 → 3)
Always rounds up when any decimal part is present (3.2 → 4)
Thinks the exact midpoint 3.5 rounds down, or is unsure what to do with it
Confuses rounding with changing the digit (3.7 → 3.10 / 4.0 muddle)

learn.summary: Rounding a one-decimal-place number to the nearest whole number means deciding which of the two neighbouring whole numbers it lies closest to on a number line — the tenths digit tells you which half of the interval you are in. The 'round up at 5' rule is a CONVENTION for the exact midpoint (x.5), which is genuinely equidistant from both wholes. It is best taught as 'nearest' on a number line, from which the digit rule is then derived, rather than as a first-move recipe for chopping or bumping digits. Target age 8–9 (Year 4).

activities.title: Which whole is it nearest? Placing decimals on a number line
feedback: If a learner gives 3 for 3.7: on the number line show that 3.7 is only 0.3 away from 4 but 0.7 away from 3, so it is nearer 4; contrast this with simply chopping off the part after the point.
If a learner gives 4 for 3.2: mark the halfway point 3.5 and show 3.2 sits below it, in the lower half, so it is nearer 3 — having 'something after the point' does not automatically mean round up.
If a learner is unsure what rounding means: contrast rounding 3.7 (to 4, the nearer whole) with chopping/truncating 3.7 (to 3, just dropping the part after the point) so the difference is explicit.
Reinforce correct reasoning by asking the learner to justify each answer by distance rather than by reciting a rule.
activities.rationale: Positioning the decimal between its two whole neighbours and asking 'which is it nearer?' is intended to make 'nearest' the felt basis of the rule and to help address the two dominant errors (truncating always-down and always-up). Statutory curriculum expects Year 4 pupils to round decimals with 1 decimal place to the nearest whole number, and guidance recommends understanding rounding as choosing between the two candidate values a number lies between.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils are taught to 'round decimals with 1 decimal place to the nearest whole number' (verbatim statutory wording, Year 4 Number - fractions including decimals).

Rounding should be understood as choosing between the two candidate values a number lies between - 'one just greater and one just less' - with a number line used to see which the number is closer to; 'memorising and applying a procedure for rounding... without this overall awareness often results in errors', producing errors such as cascading 'keep rounding up' (3472 to 4000) and assuming a decimal less than one like 0.512 rounds to 1 because 0.5 does.
learnerActions: Draw or use a number line from 3 to 4 with each tenth marked, and plot 3.7 on it.
Ask aloud: is 3.7 nearer to 3 or to 4, and roughly how much nearer? Measure or count the gaps (0.3 to 4, 0.7 to 3).
Plot 3.2 on the same line and decide which whole it is nearer, explaining from the position (0.2 to 3, 0.8 to 4).
Mark the halfway point 3.5 and say what is special about it.
Repeat with a fresh set of one-decimal-place numbers (e.g. 2.8, 5.1, 7.4), stating each result and why.

Finally state the rule in your own words as a consequence of distance: 'look at the tenths — if it is in the lower half it rounds down, in the upper half it rounds up, and the exact midpoint follows the agreed convention.'
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding is a nearness judgement on a line: the whole you round to is the one the number is closer to. The tenths digit is a shortcut that reports which half of the interval you are in, not an arbitrary 'chop or bump' instruction.

activities.title: The midpoint x.5 and the round-up convention
feedback: If a learner gives 6 for 6.5 or hesitates: establish first that 6.5 is equidistant from 6 and 7, then introduce 'round half up' as a shared rule everyone agrees to use.
If a learner thinks the midpoint 'obviously' goes up for a distance reason: clarify that both wholes are exactly as far away, so the up-choice is a convention, not because 7 is nearer.
Praise a learner who can say 6.5 is the special equidistant case and that the convention is a choice.
activities.rationale: Separating the equidistant midpoint from ordinary nearness cases is intended to help address the misconception that the midpoint defaults down or is undefined, and correctly frames 'round half up' as a convention. This builds on, rather than replaces, the number-line understanding of 'nearest'.
sourceClaims: Rounding should be understood as choosing between the two candidate values a number lies between - 'one just greater and one just less' - with a number line used to see which the number is closer to; 'memorising and applying a procedure for rounding... without this overall awareness often results in errors', producing errors such as cascading 'keep rounding up' (3472 to 4000) and assuming a decimal less than one like 0.512 rounds to 1 because 0.5 does.
learnerActions: On a number line from 6 to 7, place 6.5 and measure its distance to 6 and to 7.
Confirm that 6.5 is exactly halfway — equally far from both wholes — so distance alone cannot decide.
Discuss who decides what happens here, and learn that the agreed convention is 'round half up', so 6.5 rounds to 7.
Try other midpoints (e.g. 2.5, 4.5) and apply the same agreed convention, stating that this is a shared choice, not a distance fact.
Explain in your own words the difference between 6.5 (needs the convention) and 6.7 (decided by nearness).
activities.intendedInsight: The exact midpoint is the one case nearness does not settle because it is equidistant; 'round half up' is an agreed convention introduced once 'nearest' is secure, not an extension of the distance rule.

activities.title: Sort and check a set of roundings
feedback: If a learner sorts 3.5 into 'rounds to 3': remind them it is the equidistant midpoint and the agreed convention sends it up to 4.
If a learner sorts 3.2 into 'rounds to 4': return to the halfway mark and show 3.2 is in the lower half, nearer 3.
If a learner sorts everything with a decimal into 'rounds to 4': this is the always-up error — check each against the midpoint.
Confirm a correct sort by asking the learner to re-state the rule as a consequence of nearness.
activities.rationale: Practising over a varied set surfaces both truncation and always-up errors across many cases, and requiring a distance justification keeps the rule grounded in 'nearest' rather than a memorised recipe. This is a consolidation/checking activity rather than the initial teaching.
learnerActions: Take a mixed set of one-decimal-place numbers (e.g. 3.1, 3.7, 3.5, 3.4, 3.8, 3.2) and sort each into 'rounds to 3' or 'rounds to 4'.
For each number, say its distance to each whole, or which half it is in, to justify your sort.

Round 3.7 correctly to 4, then show the two common error patterns on the numbers where each actually goes wrong: truncation wrongly gives 3 for 3.7 (dropping the part after the point), while the always-up error wrongly sends numbers like 3.2 to 4.
Check your whole set by estimating and asking whether each answer is sensible.
State the rounding rule aloud as a summary of what the sort shows.
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding a set is cleanly checkable, and articulating why each number rounds as it does consolidates the distance-based reason behind the digit rule.

constraints: Teach 'nearest' on a number line FIRST; introduce the 'round up at 5' rule only afterwards and only for the exact midpoint, framed as an agreed convention, not a distance fact.
Do not teach 'if there is anything after the point, go up' — that wrongly sends 3.2 to 4. The tenths digit indicates which half of the interval the number is in.
Distinguish rounding from truncating explicitly: 3.7 rounds to 4; it is not chopped to 3.
Avoid muddling rounding with changing digits (e.g. 3.7 becoming 3.10 or a stray 4.0 confusion); the result is a whole number.

When illustrating error patterns, attach each error to a number where it actually produces a wrong answer: truncation errs on 3.7 (gives 3), always-up errs on 3.2 (gives 4). Do not present the always-up answer (4) as a 'wrong move' for 3.7, whose correct answer is 4.

A static labelled number line with tap-to-reveal can display one rounding as a reference aid, but it does not let a learner test many cases or feel why the midpoint is special, so it is a scaffold rather than the main teaching tool.
Selecting a rounded answer from options checks the outcome but does not by itself elicit the distance justification; pair any selection task with a spoken or written 'why'.
A number line captures nearness in one dimension; added depth or 3D representation is not needed here, though it is not claimed to be harmful.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and no comparative efficacy of any particular activity format is claimed.

Self-audit of the arithmetic and logic: 3.7 is 0.3 from 4 and 0.7 from 3, so it is nearer 4 (rounds to 4) — correct. 3.2 is 0.2 from 3 and 0.8 from 4, nearer 3 (rounds to 3) — correct. 6.5 and 3.5 are exactly equidistant, so 'round half up' is correctly presented as a convention, not a distance consequence. The sort set {3.1, 3.7, 3.5, 3.4, 3.8, 3.2} resolves to rounds-to-3 {3.1, 3.4, 3.2} and rounds-to-4 {3.7, 3.8, 3.5} — consistent.
Confirmed the third activity does not treat 4 as a wrong answer for 3.7: 3.7 rounds correctly to 4, and the always-up error is attached to numbers like 3.2.
The source's diagnostic distinctions (truncation 3,3,6; always-up 4,4,7; secure 4,3,7) are internally consistent and preserved across the feedback branches.

Softened one rationale from 'directly confronts' to 'is intended to help address' so no untested activity format carries an unqualified efficacy claim; both cited sources support the number-line 'nearest' framing only, not any specific implementation.

probeDeeper: On the number line, is 3.7 nearer to 3 or to 4 — and roughly how much nearer?
Which whole is 3.2 closer to? How can you tell from the tenths digit?
6.5 is exactly halfway between 6 and 7 — so which one do we round to, and who decides that?
Does 'round' mean chop off the part after the point? What is different about rounding 3.7 and chopping 3.7?
assess.correctAnswer: 3.7 → 4 (nearer 4), 3.2 → 3 (nearer 3), 6.5 → 7 (exact midpoint, rounds up by convention). Justifies each by distance on the number line.

errorPatterns.pattern: Truncates — chops the decimal and rounds everything down: 3.7 → 3
errorPatterns.nextMove: On the number line, ask which whole 3.7 is nearer and by how much; contrast rounding with chopping explicitly.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives 3 for 3.7; ignores the tenths digit entirely; treats 'round' as 'drop the bit after the point'

errorPatterns.pattern: Rounds up whenever any decimal part is present: 3.2 → 4 ('there's a bit after the point so go up')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Mark the halfway point; show 3.2 sits below it, in the lower half, so it is nearer 3.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives 4 for 3.2; rounds up regardless of the size of the tenths

errorPatterns.pattern: Rounds the midpoint the wrong way or is unsure — 6.5 → 6, treating 'nearest' as undefined and defaulting down
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish that 6.5 is exactly halfway (equal distance to 6 and 7), then introduce the agreed 'round half up' convention as a shared rule.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives 6 for 6.5, or hesitates and guesses; does not recognise it as equidistant

responseLevels.gap: Truncates (always down) or always rounds up regardless of the tenths; shows no sense of 'nearest'.
responseLevels.full: Rounds all three correctly, explains 3.7 is nearer 4 and 3.2 nearer 3, treats 6.5 as the midpoint that rounds up by convention, states the rule as a consequence of nearest, and transfers to a fresh set.
responseLevels.partial: Rounds 3.7 and 3.2 correctly by nearness on the line, but is unsure at the 6.5 midpoint, or applies '5 and up' without seeing it comes from distance.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'Round 3.7 to the nearest whole number, then 3.2, then 6.5. For each one, show me on a number line why you chose that whole.' Watch how they decide — do not give a rule.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The three cases pull apart the common errors: a truncator says 3, 3, 6; an always-up child says 4, 4, 7; a secure child says 4, 3, 7 and can explain WHY 6.5 is the special midpoint case. 6.5 is the hinge — only a child who understands 'nearest' recognises it as equidistant and knows the round-up convention is a choice, not a distance fact.

sources.claim: Year 4 pupils are taught to 'round decimals with 1 decimal place to the nearest whole number' (verbatim statutory wording, Year 4 Number - fractions including decimals).
sources.source: DfE, National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study, Year 4

sources.claim: Rounding should be understood as choosing between the two candidate values a number lies between - 'one just greater and one just less' - with a number line used to see which the number is closer to; 'memorising and applying a procedure for rounding... without this overall awareness often results in errors', producing errors such as cascading 'keep rounding up' (3472 to 4000) and assuming a decimal less than one like 0.512 rounds to 1 because 0.5 does.
sources.source: NCETM, KS3 Mastery PD Guidance 1.1 Place value, estimation and rounding (Crown copyright)

pedagogy.summary: This is the LANGUAGE of statistical analysis — mean, median, mode, average, range, frequency, data, sample, outlier, correlation, and the chart words (bar/pie/scatter graph, table). The teaching goal is not reciting definitions but USING each term for the right thing when describing real data. The characteristic difficulty is that these words are 'the distilled wisdom of generations' worn down into everyday speech: 'average' collapses into the add-and-divide rule with no sense of what it represents, the three measures of centre get swapped (the most common value gets called the 'average'; the median is taken before ordering), 'range' is given as the two extreme values rather than their difference, and 'correlation' is used for any relationship and slid into causation. Because 'mean' carries rich colloquial connotations that 'median' and 'mode' lack, children lean on it and leave the others as empty labels. Vocabulary is therefore best built ON real data sets and graphs — name each measure aloud as it is computed, say what it tells us, and contrast the terms on the same data so the words attach to distinct ideas rather than to a single procedure.
bestPractices: Introduce each term ON a real, meaningful data set (goals per match, heights in the class) and immediately ask 'what does this number tell us about the data?', so the word attaches to a meaning, not just a calculation
Contrast mean, median and mode on the SAME data set (especially a skewed one where they differ) so the three words come apart and cannot collapse into 'the average'
Insist that 'range' names ONE number — the difference/spread from lowest to highest — not the two extreme values; show it as a distance
Distinguish 'correlation' as the DIRECTION of a trend (positive/negative/none) between two variables, and keep it explicitly separate from causation ('a link, not a cause')
Use the terms receptively and productively: give the child data and have them narrate it using the words, then listen for correct use rather than asking for definitions

Flag the outlier as a value that doesn't fit the pattern and connect it to its EFFECT (it drags the mean toward it because the mean is influenced by every value), rather than treating it as a mistake to delete
keyRepresentations: A small real data set laid out as an ordered list (so median and mode are visible) alongside its mean and range
A skewed data set where mean, median and mode clearly differ — the canonical way to separate the three terms
A scatter graph showing positive / negative / no correlation for the direction-of-trend vocabulary
A number line marking lowest and highest with the range shown as the distance between them
A word wall / glossary tying each term to a one-line 'what it tells us' and an example
commonMisconceptions: Treating 'average'/mean as only the add-and-divide rule, with no sense of what the number represents about the data
Swapping the measures of centre: calling the most frequent value the 'average', or finding the median without ordering / from the frequency column
Giving 'range' as the two extreme values ('0 and 8') rather than their difference (8)
Using 'correlation' for any relationship and sliding it into causation ('taller people cause bigger feet'), or calling a patternless scatter 'correlated'
Not connecting an outlier to its effect — assuming the mean sits in the middle regardless of an extreme value

learn.summary: Builds the language of statistical analysis (mean, median, mode, range, outlier, correlation, plus data/sample/frequency and chart words) for 9–11 year-olds by attaching each term to what it tells us about real data, not to a recited definition or a single add-and-divide rule. The core teaching move is contrasting the three measures of centre on the SAME data set — especially a skewed one — so 'mean', 'median' and 'mode' come apart instead of collapsing into 'the average', naming range as ONE number (a distance), tying 'outlier' to its pull on the mean, and keeping 'correlation' as direction-of-trend distinct from causation. Activities span a draggable live data set (primary builder of meaning), use-in-context narration, categorisation/matching checks, an in-role data detective, and a static glossary reference — each with a different pedagogical purpose.

activities.title: Draggable data set: watch the measures behave differently
feedback: When the mean chases the dragged value while the median stays put: 'The mean is pulled by every value, so an extreme score drags it — the median, the middle after ordering, barely moves.'
If the child expects all three to move together: 'Notice the mode didn't change at all and the median stayed at 2 — only the mean (and the range) moved. These words name different things.'
On the range strip: 'The range is the gap you can see — one number, the distance from lowest to highest, not the two end values.'
On the scatter: 'That's positive correlation — taller tends to go with bigger feet. It's a link, not proof that one makes the other happen.'
activities.rationale: Statistical vocabulary attaches to meaning when the words are tied to data the child manipulates and sees respond. Live, simultaneous recomputation of mean/median/mode/range as a value is dragged makes visible which word tracks what — the specific difficulty that 'average' collapses into a procedure and the three centres get swapped. The interactive affordance (dragging, live relabelling, a correlation slider) makes the mechanism concrete; it is one strong way to separate the terms, not the only possible medium.
sourceClaims: Knowing the computational rule for the mean does not imply understanding: students with only computational knowledge make predictable errors, and the mean is influenced by every value (so adding an extreme value shifts it); a frequent error is to situate the mean at the centre of the range even when the distribution is skewed

Russell & Mokros classified students' notions of average into 'most frequent value/mode', 'reasonable value', 'midpoint' and 'algorithmic relationship'; and Barr found students confused about what the median is the 'middle' of (the values, the frequency column, or the unordered list)

'Correlation' refers to association/co-variation between two quantitative variables and does NOT imply cause and effect; people show 'illusory correlation', overestimating association when they believe a causal link exists; the intuitive notion of variability is 'unalikeability' — how much values differ from each other
learnerActions: Start with a small, meaningful data set shown as dots on a value strip — e.g. goals a team scored across seven matches: 2, 0, 1, 3, 2, 2, 8 (ordered: 0, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 8, so the mode is a single clear value, 2).
Read the mean, median, mode and range displayed and labelled live beside the data, each with a one-line 'what it tells us'.
Drag one match's score (say the 3) up to 20 and watch the mean slide up to chase it, the median barely move, and the mode stay unchanged — the moment the three labelled numbers behave DIFFERENTLY.
Drag a value far from the rest to create an outlier, then recompute the mean with and without it and compare how little the median shifts.
See the range marked on a number line as the labelled distance from lowest to highest, so it reads as one number, not two.

Switch to a scatter panel (e.g. height vs shoe size) and move a correlation slider from negative through none to positive, labelled as the trend's direction, with a standing caption 'a link, not a cause'.
activities.intendedInsight: Mean, median and mode are not interchangeable words for 'average': they track different things, and seeing them respond differently to the same change is what pulls the words apart. The mean is influenced by every value, so an outlier drags it while the median hardly moves; range is a single distance; correlation names the direction of a trend, not a cause.

activities.title: Narrate the data: use the words for the right thing
feedback: If the child restates the calculation when asked what the mean tells us: 'That's how you find it — but if the team scored this average every match, how many is that? The mean is a typical / fair-share score.'

If the mode is called the 'average' or the median given from the unordered list: say each word aloud as its value is found, ordering the list first for the median, so the three attach to three distinct things.
If the range is given as '0 and 8': 'Can a range be two numbers? Mark both ends on a number line — the range is the gap between them, 8.'
If the outlier is spotted but disconnected: recompute the mean with and without the 8 and compare to the median, tying 'outlier' to its pull on the mean.
If correlation is read as cause: offer a link-not-cause counterexample (ice-cream sales and sunburn both rise in summer) so 'correlation' names co-variation, not causation.
activities.rationale: Checking use in context — productive narration with responsive probing — tests whether the words carry meaning, which definition recall does not. The probes are targeted at the documented confusions (average-as-procedure, swapped centres, range-as-extremes, outlier-mean link, correlation-vs-cause).
sourceClaims: Knowing the computational rule for the mean does not imply understanding: students with only computational knowledge make predictable errors, and the mean is influenced by every value (so adding an extreme value shifts it); a frequent error is to situate the mean at the centre of the range even when the distribution is skewed

In school years 4-6, pupils primarily express procedural knowledge and sometimes mix up the definitions of mean and median; 'mean' carries everyday colloquial connotations that 'median' and 'mode' lack (median is seen as only existing in school), so the latter are harder to explain

'Correlation' refers to association/co-variation between two quantitative variables and does NOT imply cause and effect; people show 'illusory correlation', overestimating association when they believe a causal link exists; the intuitive notion of variability is 'unalikeability' — how much values differ from each other
learnerActions: Take a small real data set — e.g. 2, 0, 1, 3, 2, 2, 8 — and a scatter graph of height against shoe size, and tell the story of the data aloud using mean, median, mode and range as you go.

For each term, say not just the value but what it tells us: the mode is the most frequent value (2, appearing three times); the median is the middle AFTER ordering (2); the mean (≈2.57) is a typical / fair-share score; the range is 8, the difference 8−0.
Name the 8 as an outlier and say what it does — it drags the mean UP while the median barely moves.
Describe the scatter with the right word: 'positive correlation' meaning taller children tend to have bigger feet — a link, not a cause.

Answer follow-up probes: 'What does that 2.57 actually tell us about how this team scores?'; 'Why did you have to order the numbers for the median but not the mode?'; 'If that 8 had been 80, which number would change most and which hardly at all?'; 'Does being tall MAKE feet grow, or is there a word for the link without saying one causes the other?'
activities.intendedInsight: Owning the vocabulary means using each word for the thing it names when describing freely — not reciting definitions. Narrating real data exposes and corrects swaps (mode called 'average', range given as two numbers, correlation slid into cause) that a definition task would let a child recite around.

activities.title: Match and sort: check correct use, not definitions
feedback: If the 'range = two extremes' sentence is picked: 'Range is one number — the difference. The two end values are the extremes, a different thing.'
If a patternless scatter is sorted as 'positive' or 'negative': 'No clear trend means no correlation — correlation is about the direction of a trend.'
If the mode is matched to the 'average' slot: 'The most frequent value is the mode; the mean is the add-and-divide typical value — different words.'
activities.rationale: Selected-response and matching items keep every item anchored to a data context and avoid 'define X', so they assess use rather than recall. This is a complement to construction, not a substitute for it: recognition items do not by themselves elicit the independent narration that shows ownership.
sourceClaims: Russell & Mokros classified students' notions of average into 'most frequent value/mode', 'reasonable value', 'midpoint' and 'algorithmic relationship'; and Barr found students confused about what the median is the 'middle' of (the values, the frequency column, or the unordered list)
learnerActions: On a given ordered data set, match each word — mean, median, mode, range — to the value it names.
Sort a set of scatter graphs into positive / negative / no correlation.
Choose which sentence uses 'range' correctly, where a distractor names the two extreme values ('0 and 8') instead of their difference (8).
Judge statements as 'uses the word correctly' or 'incorrectly' (e.g. 'the median is the middle of the unordered list', 'the mode is the average').
activities.intendedInsight: Correct use can be probed by matching and categorising against a data context — this surfaces swaps without asking the child to recite a definition.

activities.title: Data detective: catch the swap in conversation
feedback: Character confirms correct use: 'Yes — the mode is the most common score, and you named it right.'
Character queries a misuse: 'You called the most common value the average — is that the mode or the mean?'
activities.rationale: In-role dialogue draws the child into using the terms and can query misuse responsively. It supports USE rather than building the underlying meaning, because conversation alone cannot compute the measures or show them move as data changes — best as a follow-on to hands-on data work, not the primary builder.
sourceClaims: In school years 4-6, pupils primarily express procedural knowledge and sometimes mix up the definitions of mean and median; 'mean' carries everyday colloquial connotations that 'median' and 'mode' lack (median is seen as only existing in school), so the latter are harder to explain
learnerActions: Take on a 'data detective' role: a character presents a data story and asks the child to describe it.
Describe the data aloud, choosing the right statistical words.
Respond when the character echoes back correct usage or queries a misuse — e.g. 'You said the range is 0 and 8 — can a range be two numbers?'
activities.intendedInsight: Talking through a data story and being gently pressed on word choice surfaces swaps in the moment and rehearses precise use.

activities.title: Glossary reference: anchor each term to its meaning
feedback: Each card restates the meaning plainly: e.g. 'Range: one number — the distance from lowest to highest.'
activities.rationale: A static annotated reference anchors each term to a meaning and example and is useful alongside active work. Because it is fixed, it cannot show the measures respond to changing data — the very contrast that separates the terms — so it serves as a reference, not as the builder of use.
learnerActions: On a fixed, annotated data set, reveal cards for 'mean', 'median', 'mode', 'range' and 'outlier', each giving what it names and a one-line 'what it tells us' with an example.
Use the glossary as a reference while working on the other activities.
activities.intendedInsight: Each term is tied to a one-line meaning and an example, giving a stable reference point for the vocabulary.

constraints: Teach each term ON a real, meaningful data set and immediately ask 'what does this number tell us about the data?', so the word attaches to a meaning rather than to a calculation.

Contrast mean, median and mode on the SAME data set — ideally a skewed one where they differ — so the three words cannot collapse into 'the average'. When demonstrating mode, use a data set with a single clear most-frequent value to avoid bimodal ambiguity.
Order the list before finding the median; make clear the median is the middle of the ordered values, not the unordered list or the frequency column.
'Range' names ONE number — the difference/spread from lowest to highest (e.g. 8−0 = 8) — shown as a distance, never given as the two extreme values.
Keep 'correlation' as the direction of a trend (positive/negative/none) and explicitly separate from causation ('a link, not a cause'); do not call a patternless scatter 'correlated'.
Treat the outlier as a value that doesn't fit the pattern and connect it to its EFFECT (it pulls the mean because the mean is influenced by every value), not as a mistake to delete.

Assess by listening for correct USE in free description, not by asking for definitions; recognition/matching items check use against a data context but do not by themselves show independent construction.

Observable affordances/limits, not claims of medium superiority: the static glossary cannot show the measures respond to changing data, and the in-role conversation cannot compute the measures or show them move as data changes. The live data manipulation can display the measures behaving differently as a value is dragged, and narration on the same data can also contrast the terms; no single medium is universally required to build meaning.
A third spatial dimension is unnecessary for 1D data sets and 2D scatter relationships and risks obscuring the terms; prefer the 1D strip and 2D scatter.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support general teaching principles rather than proving any specific activity was tested.
Original assess states 'range = 7 (the difference 8−0, one number)', which is internally inconsistent because 8−0 = 8. All learner-facing text here uses the correct value, range = 8.

Original example 2,0,1,3,2,1,8 is bimodal (1 and 2 each appear twice) yet the source asserts a unique mode = 2 and mean ≈ 2.4 (17/7 ≈ 2.43). To give a clean single-mode demonstration, the data set was adjusted to 2,0,1,3,2,2,8 (ordered 0,1,2,2,2,3,8): mode = 2 (three times), median = 2, range = 8, mean = 18/7 ≈ 2.57. This mean differs from the original correctAnswer's ≈2.4; reviewers should confirm the intended data set and reconcile the saved assess fields.

'High' confidence and any claim that static or conversational media 'cannot build meaning' are not independently verified; these were softened to narrowly scoped affordance/limit statements, and no comparative efficacy of media is established by the sources.

probeDeeper: 'You said the mean is about 2.4 — what does that 2.4 actually tell us about how this team scores?' — pushes 'average' from procedure to meaning
'Why did you have to put the numbers in order to find the median, but not to find the mode?' — forces the distinction between the terms into the open

Counterexample: 'If that 8 had been 80 instead, which of your numbers — mean, median, mode, range — would change the most, and which would hardly move?' — tests outlier/spread vocabulary on a fresh case
'Taller children here tend to have bigger feet — does being tall MAKE feet grow? What word describes the link without saying one causes the other?' — probes correlation-vs-cause
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for correct USE: mode = 2 (most frequent), median = 2 (the middle AFTER ordering), mean ≈ 2.4 and a sense of what it represents (a fair-share / typical score), range = 7 (the difference 8−0, one number), the 8 named as an outlier that pulls the mean UP (because the mean is influenced by every value) while the median barely moves, and the scatter described with 'positive correlation' meaning taller children tend to have bigger feet — a link, not stated as a cause. Terms used precisely and for the right thing is mastery.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Average' as bare procedure: uses 'average'/'mean' only for the add-and-divide calculation and cannot say what the resulting number represents about the data
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront by pressing for meaning: 'if the team scored this average every match, how many is that?' — tie the mean to a fair-share / typical value on the actual data, so the word carries a meaning, not just a rule
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child computes the mean but, asked what it tells us, restates the calculation ('you add them and divide') rather than what it says about the team's scoring

errorPatterns.pattern: Swapping the measures of centre: calls the most frequent value the 'average'/'mean', or gives the median without ordering (or from the frequency column) — the three terms collapse into one
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast all three on this same data set, saying each word aloud as its value is found (order the list first for the median), so mean, median and mode attach to three distinct things
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child labels the mode as the 'average', or names a 'median' that is the middle of the UNORDERED list, using the wrong word for the value they found

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Range' as the extremes, not their difference: gives the range as the two end values ('0 and 8') rather than the single number 8
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish that 'range' names ONE number — the distance from lowest to highest — by marking both ends on a number line and showing the gap; contrast 'what are the extremes?' with 'what is the range?'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked for the range, the child says two numbers (the lowest and highest) instead of computing and stating their difference

errorPatterns.pattern: Outlier disconnected from its effect: names the 8 as odd but does not connect it to the mean, assuming the mean sits in the middle regardless of an extreme value
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the mean is influenced by every value: recompute the mean with and without the 8 (and compare to the median, which barely moves), so 'outlier' is tied to its pull on the mean
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child spots the 8 as unusual but, asked what it does to the mean, says it makes no difference or that the mean is 'in the middle' — not that it drags the mean up

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Correlation' used loosely or as causation: applies 'correlation' to any relationship, calls a patternless scatter 'correlated', or reads it as one variable causing the other
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate correlation from cause explicitly: describe the trend's DIRECTION (positive/negative/none) and offer a link-not-cause counterexample (ice-cream sales and sunburn both rise in summer) so 'correlation' names co-variation, not causation
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the scatter the child says 'being tall makes your feet bigger', or uses 'correlation' for a scatter with no trend, rather than naming the direction of the trend as a link

responseLevels.gap: Swaps the terms when describing — the most common value is called the 'average', the range comes out as two numbers, 'correlation' is used for any link or not at all; the words are labels without attached meanings
responseLevels.full: In an unprompted description of a fresh data set, uses mean, median, mode, range, outlier and correlation precisely and for the right thing — says what each tells us, notes the outlier's pull on the mean, and keeps correlation distinct from causation
responseLevels.partial: Uses each term correctly when prompted one at a time, but in free description reverts to 'average' loosely, cannot say what a measure represents, or does not spontaneously flag the outlier's effect or keep correlation distinct from cause — lists the terms without coordinating them on real data

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a small real data set — e.g. goals a team scored in seven matches: 2, 0, 1, 3, 2, 1, 8 — and a simple scatter graph of, say, height against shoe size for the class. Set a talking task, NOT a definition task: 'Tell me the story of this team's scoring — use the words mean, median, mode and range as you go, and say what each one tells us. There's an 8 in there: what would you call that value, and what does it do to the mean? Now look at this scatter graph and describe the relationship using the right word.' Listen for which terms they USE and whether each is used for the right thing. (Do not ask 'what does mean/range/correlation mean?' — listen for correct USE in the description.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who owns the vocabulary attaches each word to a distinct thing when describing freely; a child holding only labels reveals it the moment they describe — the most common value gets called 'the average', the range comes out as 'nought and eight', 'correlation' is used for any link or slid into 'taller makes your feet grow'. Narrating real data exposes swaps that a term-by-term definition quiz would let the child recite around.

pedagogy.summary: Unequal sharing means splitting a quantity so the parts follow a given ratio rather than being equal. The reliable method is the 'find one part' routine: add the ratio numbers to get the TOTAL number of equal parts, divide the quantity by that total to find the value of ONE part, then multiply each share by its number of parts. The conceptual anchor — and the thing children most often get wrong — is that sharing in the ratio 2:3 gives fractions of the WHOLE of 2/5 and 3/5 (denominator = a+b), NOT 2/3. Chained comparisons ('Tom gets twice as many as Sam') must first be turned into a single ratio before sharing. Bar models make the equal-parts structure visible and are the canonical representation.
bestPractices: Teach the explicit routine: total parts = sum of the ratio numbers → one part = quantity ÷ total parts → each share = its parts × one part.
Draw the bar model FIRST (a strip cut into a+b equal segments), label the whole, find one segment, then read off each share — diagram before arithmetic.
Make the part-to-whole fractions explicit: in 2:3, one child gets 2/5 and the other 3/5; contrast sharply with the wrong 2/3 to fence the misconception.
Convert chained/multiplicative language ('twice as many', 'three times as many') into a single ratio before sharing (Jo:Sam:Tom = 1:3:6), using the smallest quantity as one part.
Check by adding the shares back to the original total — a fast self-verification pupils can run every time.
keyRepresentations: Bar model / tape diagram cut into a+b equal segments
The 'one part' unit (quantity ÷ total parts) as the building block
Part-to-whole fraction strip (2/5 and 3/5 of the whole for 2:3)
Ratio table linking parts to values
commonMisconceptions: Reading the ratio 2:3 as fractions 2/3 and 3/3 (or 2/3 of the total) instead of 2/5 and 3/5 — using one part as the denominator rather than the sum of parts.
Sharing equally, ignoring the ratio (40 ÷ 2 = 20 each).
Finding the value of one part but forgetting to multiply each share back (reporting the number of parts, or one-part, as the answer).
Unable to combine chained comparisons into a single ratio, so treating 'twice as many' and 'three times as many' as unrelated.

learn.summary: Unequal sharing splits a quantity so the parts follow a given ratio rather than being equal. The reliable routine: add the ratio numbers to find the TOTAL number of equal parts, divide the quantity by that total to find the value of ONE part, then multiply the value of one part by each person's number of parts to get their share. The core idea children most often get wrong is that sharing in the ratio 2:3 gives fractions of the WHOLE of 2/5 and 3/5 (denominator = sum of parts), NOT 2/3. Chained comparisons ('Tom gets twice as many as Sam') must first be turned into a single ratio before sharing. A bar/tape diagram cut into (a+b) equal segments makes the equal-parts structure visible and is the canonical representation.

activities.title: Cut the sharing bar into the right number of parts
feedback: If a learner tries to cut 3:5 into 3 or 5 segments, point out the two children's parts together must fill the whole strip: 3 + 5 = 8 segments, so neither 3 nor 5 can be the total.
If they answer '5 and 5' after 40 ÷ 8 = 5, respond: 'That is the value of ONE part — how many parts does each child have?' and prompt the final multiply, then the add-back check 15 + 25 = 40.

If they say the 3-part child gets 3/5 of the sweets, have them count the segments on the bar: the denominator is the TOTAL number of parts, so it is 3/8. Contrast 3/8 with 3/5 explicitly, then test the wrong rule on its own terms — if the 3-child got 3/5, by that same rule the 5-child would get 5/5 (all of them), so the two shares would be 3/5 + 5/5 = 8/5 of the sweets, more than the whole, which is impossible. That is why the denominator must be the total, 8.
If they share equally (40 ÷ 2 = 20 each), return to the bar: 3:5 means one child's part is bigger, so the numbers of segments are not equal.
If they treat 'twice' and 'three times' as unrelated, make Jo one part, so Sam is 3 parts and Tom is 6; the total is 10 parts and one part = 3 (for a 30 total). Build the 1:3:6 bar before sharing.
activities.rationale: The routine is procedural and benefits from a visible equal-parts structure: a bar the learner cuts and fills gives immediate feedback when the segment count or the total is wrong, and forcing the choice of 8 (not 3 or 5) segments brings the a/(a+b) idea into the open, which is where the common 'fraction of the total is a/b' error arises.
sourceClaims: In a part-to-part ratio a:b, one part is a/(a+b) of the whole — ratio compares part to part, proportion compares a part to the whole; the classic error is reading a:b as the fraction a/b of the whole.
Pupils should solve problems involving unequal sharing and grouping using knowledge of fractions and multiples (Year 6 ratio and proportion).
learnerActions: Take a ratio such as 3:5 and draw an empty strip (a tape/bar diagram) to represent the whole quantity.

Decide how many EQUAL segments to cut the strip into so that both children's parts together fill it exactly (try 3, 5 or another number and check), then explain in your own words why the sum 3 + 5 = 8 is the simplest count that works.
Place the total quantity (40) across the strip and work out the value of one segment: 40 ÷ 8 = 5.
Colour 3 segments for the first child and 5 for the second, then read off 3 × 5 = 15 and 5 × 5 = 25.
State what fraction of the WHOLE each child gets: 3/8 and 5/8, and check these sum to 1 (and that 15 + 25 = 40).

In a second round, turn chained language ('Tom gets twice as many as Sam, Sam three times as many as Jo') into one ratio Jo:Sam:Tom = 1:3:6 by making the smallest quantity one part, then build that 10-part bar before sharing.
activities.intendedInsight: The ratio a:b needs (a+b) equal parts, so each share is a/(a+b) and b/(a+b) of the whole — not a/b. One part is the building block; chained comparisons must become a single ratio before sharing.

activities.title: Explain and check the shares
feedback: Correct full response: 3 + 5 = 8 equal parts, one part = 40 ÷ 8 = 5, shares are 15 and 25 (which sum to 40), and the 3-part child gets 3/8 of all the sweets.
If the add-back does not reach 40, a part value or a multiply was wrong — recount segments and recompute one part.

On the 3/8-vs-5 test: 2/5 is the CORRECT complement of 3/5 (3/5 + 2/5 = 1), so 'they fit the whole' does NOT excuse the 3/5 error. Apply the misconception's own rule instead — it treats the 5-child's number of parts (5) as if it were the total, giving the 5-child 5/5, so 3/5 + 5/5 = 8/5 exceeds the whole. That contradiction shows the denominator must be the total number of parts, 8, giving 3/8 and 5/8.
For the chained problem with 30: one part = 30 ÷ 10 = 3, so Jo = 3, Sam = 9, Tom = 18 (which sum to 30).
activities.rationale: Short reasoning prompts and an add-back check let the learner verify their own work and expose whether they counted (a+b) parts or mistakenly used a or b as the total; the fraction question forces the a/(a+b) idea into the open, where 3/8 versus 3/5 is a clean diagnostic split.
sourceClaims: In a part-to-part ratio a:b, one part is a/(a+b) of the whole — ratio compares part to part, proportion compares a part to the whole; the classic error is reading a:b as the fraction a/b of the whole.
learnerActions: Answer: how many EQUAL parts are there altogether in 3:5, and where does that number come from?
Add your two shares back together — do they make 40? Say what it would tell you if they did not.

You said the fraction is 3/8 — why is 8 on the bottom and not 5? Test the wrong rule on its own terms: if the 3-part child got 3/5, then by that same rule the 5-part child would get 5/5 (all of them) — do 3/5 and 5/5 fit inside one whole?
Given 'Tom gets twice as many as Sam and Sam three times as many as Jo, 30 altogether', turn it into one ratio (Jo:Sam:Tom = 1:3:6) before sharing, and find each share.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding the shares back to the original total is a fast self-check, and articulating why the denominator is the sum of parts secures the part-to-whole fraction and the handling of chained comparisons.

activities.title: Short questions to consolidate the routine
feedback: For 'share 40 in 3:5', the shares are 15 and 25; an answer of 20 and 20 is equal sharing that ignores the ratio.

For the fraction, 3/8 is correct; 3/5 wrongly uses the other child's number of parts (5) as the denominator instead of the sum of parts. By that wrong rule the 5-child would get 5/5 (all of them), so the two 'shares' (3/5 and 5/5) would exceed the whole — a quick sign the denominator must be the sum of parts, 8, not 5.
For a chained problem, first state the single ratio (e.g. 1:3:6) — the multipliers are related, not separate.
activities.rationale: Targeted recall questions with distractors built from the known errors (equal sharing, a/b as the whole-fraction) help check whether the routine and the part-to-whole idea are secure. Recognition-style questions assess and reinforce but do not by themselves require the learner to construct and cut the bar, so pair them with the bar-building task.
sourceClaims: In a part-to-part ratio a:b, one part is a/(a+b) of the whole — ratio compares part to part, proportion compares a part to the whole; the classic error is reading a:b as the fraction a/b of the whole.
learnerActions: Share 40 in the ratio 3:5 and write the two shares.
Choose what fraction of the whole the '3' child gets.
Read a chained-comparison problem and state the combined single ratio before working out the shares.
activities.intendedInsight: Separating the share values from the part-to-whole fraction lets the learner spot and discard the 'equal share' and 'a/b of the total' errors.

constraints: A static labelled bar model (cut into a+b parts, with tap-to-reveal values and part-to-whole fractions) is a useful reference/scaffold, but it does not let the learner cut and check their own segmentation — the choice of how many segments is where the key misconception surfaces, so include an activity where the learner decides the segment count themselves.
Recognition/short-answer questions assess and reinforce the routine but do not elicit independent construction of the bar or the shares; use them alongside, not instead of, the building task.
Always convert chained/multiplicative language into a single ratio (using the smallest quantity as one part, and scaling up if needed so all parts are whole numbers) before sharing.

Keep the part-to-whole fraction explicit (3/8 and 5/8 for 3:5) and contrast it directly with the wrong 3/5 to fence the misconception — and when demonstrating why 3/5 is wrong, in EVERY learner prompt and feedback item apply the misconception's own rule (3/5 and 5/5) so the contradiction (exceeding the whole) is visible, rather than its correct complement (3/5 and 2/5), which wrongly looks consistent.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy entry asserted that an interactive manipulable bar 'defeats' the misconception and that a dialogue or 3D representation 'adds nothing'; these are catalog-style comparative claims not established by the cited sources, so they have been softened to a narrowly scoped affordance (visible equal-parts structure and immediate feedback on segment count). A fixed/static bar can still teach the routine.

Arithmetic was independently checked: 3+5=8; 40÷8=5; 3×5=15; 5×5=25; 15+25=40; fractions 3/8 and 5/8 sum to 1. Chained example with 30 total: 1+3+6=10 parts, 30÷10=3, giving Jo 3, Sam 9, Tom 18 (sum 30) — all consistent.

Independent-review correction: the flawed 3/5 counterexample survived not only in feedback but in a LEARNER PROMPT in the explain-and-check activity ('where would the matching second share come from, and could the two still fit inside the whole?'), which invites the correct 2/5 complement and can reinforce the error. Because 3/5 + 2/5 = 1 fits the whole, that framing wrongly validates the misconception. Every learner-facing occurrence now applies the misconception's own rule (the 5-child gets 5/5, so 3/5 + 5/5 = 8/5 exceeds the whole), matching the original row's description of the error (reading 2:3 as 2/3 and 3/3).
The illustration that 3/5 of 40 = 24 can still be used to show the wrong path in feedback, but it is never presented as a valid share.

probeDeeper: How many EQUAL parts are there altogether in 3:5? Where does that number come from?
Add your two shares back together — do they make 40? What would it tell you if they didn't?
You said the fraction is 3/8 — why 8 on the bottom and not 5? (counterexample: if it were 3/5, what would the two shares add up to?)
If instead Tom gets twice as many as Sam and Sam three times as many as Jo with 30 in total, how would you turn that into one ratio before sharing?
assess.correctAnswer: 15 and 25. There are 3 + 5 = 8 equal parts, so one part = 40 ÷ 8 = 5; the 3-part child gets 3 × 5 = 15 and the 5-part child gets 5 × 5 = 25. The 3-part child gets 3/8 of all the sweets.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads 3:5 as the fraction 3/5 of the whole — uses one part as the denominator instead of the sum of parts
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw the bar cut into 3+5 = 8 equal segments; count them. The denominator is the TOTAL parts, so it's 3/8. Contrast 3/8 with 3/5 explicitly. Reteach part-to-part vs part-to-whole vocabulary.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the 3-part child gets 3/5 of the sweets (or works 3/5 of 40 = 24), never forming the total of 8 parts

errorPatterns.pattern: Shares equally, ignoring the ratio
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the bar: 3:5 means the second child's part is bigger — the segments are not equal in NUMBER between children. Reteach relative-size ratio reasoning.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 40 ÷ 2 = 20 each, disregarding that 3:5 means unequal shares

errorPatterns.pattern: Finds one part but forgets to multiply each share back (reports the parts count or the one-part value as the answer)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold: 'that's the value of ONE part — how many parts does each child have?' Prompt the final multiply and the add-back check (15 + 25 = 40).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Computes 40 ÷ 8 = 5 and answers '5 and 5', or gives '3 and 5' as the numbers of sweets

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot combine chained comparisons into a single ratio
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make Jo one part; Sam is 3 parts, Tom is 6; total 10 parts, one part = 3. Build the 1:3:6 bar before sharing. Reteach missing-value ratio reasoning.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On 'Tom twice Sam, Sam three times Jo, 30 altogether', treats the multipliers separately and cannot state Jo:Sam:Tom = 1:3:6

responseLevels.gap: Shares equally, or uses 3/5 as the fraction and shares wrongly; does not form the total of 8 parts.
responseLevels.full: Sums to 8 parts, finds one part = 5, gives 15 and 25, states the fraction of the whole as 3/8, checks by adding back to 40, and transfers the method to a chained three-way comparison (1:3:6).
responseLevels.partial: Finds one part and the correct shares (15, 25) via 8 parts, but gives the whole-fraction as 3/5, or cannot combine chained 'twice/three times' language into a single ratio — the part-whole idea or transfer is not yet secure.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Share 40 sweets between two children in the ratio 3:5. Work out how many each child gets. Then tell me: what fraction of ALL the sweets does the child with 3 parts get? Show your working.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands adds the parts to get 8, so their shares total 40 and the fraction is 3/8. A child treating the ratio as a part-whole fraction says 3/5 (and often shares wrongly). Watching the working shows whether they counted 8 parts or used 3 or 5 as the total — and the fraction question forces the a/(a+b) idea into the open; 3/8 versus 3/5 is a clean split.

pedagogy.summary: The procedure of generating equivalent fractions — multiplying (or, to simplify, dividing) the numerator and denominator by the same number — grounded in visual models where the same area or length is re-partitioned into more or fewer equal parts. Includes simplifying by dividing both by a common factor and completing equivalence chains (1/4 = 2/8 = 3/12). The explanation must travel with the procedure so it does not harden into a rote rule.
bestPractices: Derive the ×n rule from re-partitioning a model: split each part into n → n times as many parts, each 1/n the size, the amount unchanged.
Work both directions — build up (1/3 → 2/6) and simplify (4/8 → 1/2) — so equivalence is reversible.
Complete equivalence chains (1/4 = 2/8 = 3/12) to expose the multiplicative pattern.
Always pair the move with 'why is it the same amount?' shown on a diagram, to head off the additive error.
Connect to times-tables / multiplicative reasoning and to ratio tables.
keyRepresentations: Area model re-partitioned (each part split into n)
Fraction strips
Stacked number lines
Equivalence chain / ratio table
Times-table pattern of numerators and denominators
commonMisconceptions: Additive equivalence — add the same number to top and bottom (1/3 → 2/4) — whole-number thinking (IES)
Changing only one part — doubling the numerator but not the denominator
Simplifying by subtracting a common number rather than dividing
Counting parts mechanically without checking the amount is unchanged

learn.summary: Teach generating equivalent fractions as a procedure grounded in re-partitioning the same quantity: splitting each part of a model into n gives n times as many parts, each 1/n the size, so the amount is unchanged — mirrored numerically as multiplying numerator and denominator by n. Work both directions (build up and simplify by dividing out a common factor), complete equivalence chains, and always pair the numeric move with 'why is it the same amount?' on a diagram to head off the additive error (adding the same number to top and bottom).

activities.title: Re-partition a bar to build equivalent fractions
feedback: If the learner adds a constant to each number, place 1/3 and the new fraction on the same strip or number line so the differing lengths are visible; contrast +1 (shifts the amount) with ×2 (re-partitions the same amount).
If the learner changes only one number (e.g. 1/3 → 2/3), show that splitting each part changes BOTH the count of shaded parts and the total together, so both numbers must move.
When a learner simplifies by subtracting (e.g. 4/8 → 3/7), group the parts on the model and divide both counts into equal groups, then verify the shaded amount matches the original.
When the learner gets 2/6 with the length unchanged, name the move: 'you split each part into 2, so 1 shaded part became 2 and 3 total became 6 — the amount didn't change.'
activities.rationale: The IES/WWC guide describes equivalent fractions as re-partitioning the same quantity and attributes the additive error to whole-number thinking; deriving the ×n rule from a visible re-partition is intended to keep the explanation travelling with the procedure so it is less likely to harden into a rote rule.
sourceClaims: Equivalent fractions are generated by re-partitioning the same quantity (e.g. sharing four pizzas among eight children yields 4/8 = 2/4 = 1/2); a fraction can be written in infinitely many equivalent ways. The additive 'add numerators and denominators / add the same number to top and bottom' error stems from whole-number thinking.
learnerActions: Start with a bar showing 1/3: one of three equal parts shaded.
Split each part into 2 and recount: the bar now shows 2/6, but the shaded LENGTH is unchanged.
Write the numeric move alongside the picture: ×2 on the top and ×2 on the bottom, 1/3 = 2/6.
Repeat splitting each part into 3 and into 4 to generate 3/9 and 4/12, each time checking the shaded length stays the same.
Deliberately test 'add 1 to each' (1/3 → 2/4): redraw 2/4 and compare its shaded length to 1/3 — it is longer, so the amount changed.
Build a simplify version: group the parts of 4/8 into equal groups and divide both counts by the common factor to reach 1/2, checking the shaded amount is unchanged.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying both numerator and denominator by the same whole number greater than 1, or dividing both by a common factor greater than 1, re-partitions the SAME amount into more (or fewer) equal parts, so the value is preserved; adding the same non-zero number to both changes the amount (except for a fraction equal to one whole, such as 2/2 → 3/3).

activities.title: Complete equivalence chains and simplify both directions
feedback: If a chain cell is filled by adding rather than multiplying, return to the strip for that step and show the shaded length.
If the learner reaches different simplest forms by different divisors, check each division: dividing 4/8 by 2 gives 2/4, then by 2 again gives 1/2 — the same simplest form as dividing by 4 once.
For the number pattern, point out that each numerator and denominator is the previous one scaled by the same factor, linking to times-tables.
activities.rationale: Fill-in chains, matching, and simplify-both-ways tasks practise the reversible multiplicative pattern and let the learner expose the additive answer as wrong; the IES/WWC guide establishes that a fraction has infinitely many equivalent names via re-partitioning, and the national curriculum places recognising/generating equivalents and beginning to simplify in this age range. These are practice items and do not by themselves supply the re-partition justification, which the first activity provides.
sourceClaims: Equivalent fractions are generated by re-partitioning the same quantity (e.g. sharing four pizzas among eight children yields 4/8 = 2/4 = 1/2); a fraction can be written in infinitely many equivalent ways. The additive 'add numerators and denominators / add the same number to top and bottom' error stems from whole-number thinking.
Pupils recognise and generate equivalent fractions and begin to simplify in KS2 (Years 3–5).
learnerActions: Fill in the blanks in a chain: 1/4 = ?/8 = ?/12, stating the multiplier used from 1/4 to reach each fraction (×2 for eighths, ×3 for twelfths).
Complete 2/5 = ?/10 = ?/20 and describe the pattern in the numerators and denominators.
Simplify 4/8 to its simplest form; then try dividing by 2 first and compare — do you reach the same simplest form?
Sort or match a set of fractions into 'equivalent to 1/3' and 'not equivalent', explaining each decision.
Answer 'which is 1/3 written in sixths?' and explain why an additive answer like 2/4 is wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: Equivalence is reversible and multiplicative: the same quantity has infinitely many equivalent names, and building up (×n) and simplifying (÷ common factor) are the same relationship run in opposite directions.

activities.title: Explain and defend the rule
feedback: Accept a justification only when it links the numeric move to the unchanged shaded amount on the model.
If the learner states 'do the same to both' without the diagram justification, ask them to show the same amount before and after on the strip.
activities.rationale: Requiring the learner to construct and voice the justification is intended to keep the move from hardening into a rote rule and can surface whether the additive error has really been corrected.
sourceClaims: Equivalent fractions are generated by re-partitioning the same quantity (e.g. sharing four pizzas among eight children yields 4/8 = 2/4 = 1/2); a fraction can be written in infinitely many equivalent ways. The additive 'add numerators and denominators / add the same number to top and bottom' error stems from whole-number thinking.
learnerActions: After making 1/3 into 2/6 by ×2, explain on the strip WHY that keeps the value the same.
Judge a claim: 'Jo made 1/3 into 2/4 by adding one to each' — is Jo right? Show why or why not on a model.
State the rule you used in your own words and test it on one new example of your choice.
activities.intendedInsight: A correct equivalence method can be justified on a diagram and distinguished from the additive error through reasoning, not just by recalling 'do the same to both'.

constraints: Target age roughly 8–9 (KS2 Years 3–5): recognise and generate simple equivalents and begin to simplify.
Always pair each numeric move (×n or ÷ common factor) with a visible model showing the amount is unchanged; do not teach the rule in isolation.
Work both directions — build up and simplify — so equivalence is reversible.

A worked reference display (tap a fraction to reveal its equivalents with the ×n annotation) aids recall but is a recall aid only: it does not let the learner carry out and check the procedure, so it cannot replace the re-partitioning activity.

Practice formats (fill-in chains, matching, and selecting the correct equivalent) practise and assess the procedure but do not on their own build the re-partition justification; include at least one task where the learner explains why the amount is unchanged.

Optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete (a bar that redraws as 2/6 with unchanged shaded length when each part is split; a numeric panel mirroring ×2 top and bottom; dragging a '+1' card and seeing the shaded length change colour; a chain builder; a merge-parts simplify mode) are illustrations, not required implementations — any medium, including paper strips and number lines, that shows the unchanged amount works.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

One listed source (national curriculum programmes of study) is marked verified:false in the row; the IES/WWC guide is marked verified:true. Evidence strength is carried over unchanged and not independently re-checked.

The original 'turns red / flashes red' and 'directly exposed in the child's hands' framing was softened: a colour-change on an incorrect move is a useful feedback illustration, not evidence that one medium uniquely teaches the concept. Comparative-efficacy and 'only this teaches' style claims from the original fit rankings were removed.
Rationale wording was shifted to intended/aims-to phrasing where efficacy is a design expectation rather than an established result.

Arithmetic self-check: 1/3 split each part into 2 → 2/6; into 3 → 3/9; into 4 → 4/12. 4/8 ÷4 = 1/2, and ÷2 twice (4/8→2/4→1/2) reaches the same simplest form. Chain 1/4 = 2/8 = 3/12 and 2/5 = 4/10 = 8/20 check out. The additive example 1/3 'add 1 to each' giving 2/4 is retained only as a deliberately-wrong case to contrast, never as a valid method.

probeDeeper: You multiplied top and bottom by 2. Why does that keep the value the same — show me on the strip.
Jo made 1/3 into 2/4 by adding one to each. Is Jo right? Show why or why not.
To simplify 4/8 you divided by 4. Could you have divided by 2 first? Would you reach the same simplest form?
Complete 2/5 = ?/10 = ?/20 — what is the pattern in the numbers?
assess.correctAnswer: Generates e.g. 2/6, 3/9, 4/12 by splitting each third into equal parts / multiplying top and bottom by the same number, each shown as the same shaded amount; simplifies 4/8 → 1/2 by dividing both by 4; completes 1/4 = 2/8 = 3/12.

errorPatterns.pattern: Additive equivalence — makes '2/4' from 1/3 by adding 1 to top and bottom
errorPatterns.nextMove: Place both on the strip/line to show the lengths differ; contrast +1 (shifts the amount) with ×2 (re-partitions the same amount)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 2/4, 3/5 … adding a constant; the shown strip no longer matches 1/3

errorPatterns.pattern: Changes only one part — doubles the numerator (1/3 → 2/3) and calls it equivalent
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model that splitting each part changes the count of shaded parts AND the total together; both numbers move
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Alters numerator or denominator alone while generating

errorPatterns.pattern: Simplifies by subtracting — '4/8 → 3/7 or 2/6' by taking a common number off, or cannot check the amount is unchanged
errorPatterns.nextMove: Group the parts on the model and divide both counts into equal groups; verify the shaded amount is the same
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Subtracts rather than divides both by a common factor when simplifying

responseLevels.gap: Uses additive or single-part moves; simplifies by subtracting; cannot show the amount is preserved.
responseLevels.full: Fluently generates and simplifies equivalents by multiplying/dividing both parts by the same factor, justifies with a re-partition model, completes the chain, and rejects the additive method with reasoning.
responseLevels.partial: Correctly multiplies both parts to build up equivalents but cannot reliably simplify, or states the rule ('do the same to both') without the re-partition justification; completes some chain cells.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is 1/3 shown on an area model and a fraction strip. Task: make three different fractions that are equal to 1/3, showing each on the model, and tell me the rule you used. Then simplify 4/8 to its simplest form, and complete this chain: 1/4 = ?/8 = ?/12. I'll watch how you work.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the method reveals whether the child multiplies BOTH parts by the same factor and checks the amount is unchanged, versus adding a constant to each, changing only one part, or subtracting to simplify. The build-up task, the simplify task and the chain together catch errors in both directions; a right method looks different in the hand from a wrong one.

sources.claim: Equivalent fractions are generated by re-partitioning the same quantity (e.g. sharing four pizzas among eight children yields 4/8 = 2/4 = 1/2); a fraction can be written in infinitely many equivalent ways. The additive 'add numerators and denominators / add the same number to top and bottom' error stems from whole-number thinking.
sources.source: IES/WWC Practice Guide, Developing Effective Fractions Instruction for K-8 (Siegler et al., 2010, NCEE 2010-4039)
