pedagogy.summary: Proportional relationships are represented with double number lines (two parallel scales aligned at 0), ratio tables, and coordinate graphs — and the defining graphical signature is a STRAIGHT LINE THROUGH THE ORIGIN. The representational skills are (1) plotting proportional pairs and drawing that line, (2) explaining WHY it must pass through (0,0) — because zero of one quantity means zero of the other — and (3) reading off an unknown value from the line or table (if 3 kg costs £6, find 5 kg). The key idea to build is that the three representations show the SAME constant multiplier: the gap between rungs on a double number line, the column multiplier in a ratio table, and the gradient of the line are one and the same. The persistent error is thinking any straight line (or any rising graph) shows proportion, ignoring the origin.
bestPractices: Connect the three representations explicitly — double number line, ratio table, and graph — as views of one constant multiplier, moving between them on the same example.
Foreground the origin: ask 'what does it cost for 0 kg?' so pupils reason that a proportional graph MUST pass through (0,0), and use that as a test.
Align double number lines at 0 and keep the scales consistent, so equivalent ratios sit at matching positions.
Read unknowns both by scaling on the table/number line and by reading off the graph, checking the two agree.
Contrast a proportional line (through origin) with a straight line that misses the origin (e.g. a fixed charge plus a rate) so 'straight' alone is not mistaken for 'proportional'.
keyRepresentations: Double number line (two parallel scales aligned at 0)
Ratio table with a constant column multiplier
Coordinate graph: straight line through the origin (gradient = the rate)
Overlay contrasting a through-origin line with a not-through-origin line
commonMisconceptions: Thinking any straight line — or any rising graph — shows direct proportion, ignoring whether it passes through the origin.
Not aligning the double number line at 0, so equivalent ratios don't correspond.
Reading a graph as isolated points and being unable to interpolate an unknown, or swapping the axes when reading off.
Believing the graph need not start at (0,0) — missing that zero of one quantity means zero of the other.

learn.summary: Pupils aged 11–14 learn to represent direct proportion across three linked views — a double number line (two parallel scales aligned at 0), a ratio table in which every kg entry is multiplied by the same constant to give its £ entry, and a coordinate graph whose signature is a STRAIGHT LINE THROUGH THE ORIGIN. The core insight is that the factor linking each pair of matching marks on the double number line (e.g. 1 kg ↔ £2, 3 kg ↔ £6), the kg-to-£ multiplier in each pair in the table, and the gradient of the line (£ per kg) are ONE AND THE SAME constant multiplier. Learners plot proportional pairs and draw the line, explain why it must pass through (0,0) (zero of one quantity means zero of the other), and read off unknowns (if 3 kg costs £6, find 5 kg → £10). The persistent error to confront is treating any straight or rising line as proportional while ignoring the origin.

activities.title: Linked board: one rate, three views that move together
feedback: If a drawn line misses (0,0), ask 'what does it cost for 0 kg?' — it must be £0, so the line has to start at the origin.
If the double number line is not aligned at 0, highlight that equivalent ratios then fail to sit at matching positions; realign at 0.
If axes are swapped when reading off, prompt: read UP from the weight on the x-axis to the line, then ACROSS to the cost on the y-axis.
When the fixed-charge toggle lifts the line off the origin, name it: still straight, but no longer proportional because 0 kg no longer costs £0.
activities.rationale: Plotting pairs, drawing the line, and reading off unknowns are direct-manipulation tasks; moving between the three views on one example is intended to make the shared multiplier concrete, and the fixed-charge contrast separates 'straight' from 'proportional'. Live linking and dragging are offered as examples of how to make the shared multiplier visible, not as the only possible medium.
sourceClaims: A directly proportional relationship graphs as a straight line through the origin; properties include that doubling one quantity doubles the other and that if one quantity is zero the other is zero.

Pupils should use double number lines and ratio tables, and recognise that proportional relationships are represented by straight-line graphs through the origin, relating the multiplicative relationship to linear functions.
learnerActions: Enter or accept a rate such as 3 kg → £6 and watch a ratio table, a double number line, and a coordinate graph populate for the SAME example.
Plot the proportional pairs on the graph and draw the line; confirm it passes through the origin.
Drag a point to 5 kg and read £10 simultaneously on the table, the number line, and the graph.

Point to where the constant '×2' appears in each view: the gradient of the line (£2 per kg), the multiplier from each kg entry to its £ entry in the table (3 → 6, 5 → 10), and the factor linking each pair of matching marks on the double number line (1 kg ↔ £2, 3 kg ↔ £6).
Flip a 'fixed charge' toggle (e.g. add a standing £2) and observe the whole line lift OFF the origin while staying perfectly straight; state whether it is still proportional and why not.
activities.intendedInsight: All three representations encode the SAME constant multiplier, and the origin — not mere straightness — is the test of proportionality.

activities.title: Annotated proportion graph: reveal the origin, the rate, and a read-off
feedback: If the learner calls the not-through-origin line proportional, return to the origin: at 0 kg the fixed-charge line already costs £2, so it fails the origin test.
If the rate is misread, trace one unit along x and read the matching rise on y to recover the constant multiplier.
activities.rationale: A proportion graph is largely a fixed object; annotating it with tap-to-reveal on origin, gradient, and read-off, plus a contrasting line, is intended to rehearse the recognition cues at low cost. A fixed image here cannot be freely manipulated but can still surface these cues for inspection; it complements rather than replaces the interactive board.
sourceClaims: A directly proportional relationship graphs as a straight line through the origin; properties include that doubling one quantity doubles the other and that if one quantity is zero the other is zero.
learnerActions: Examine a proportion graph and reveal, at the origin, that 'at 0 kg, cost is £0'.
Reveal along the line the constant multiplier (the rate, e.g. £2/kg).
Reveal at a chosen point its read-off (e.g. 5 kg → £10).
Compare a companion line that is straight but does NOT pass through the origin (a fixed £2 charge plus £2/kg) and decide, with reasons, that it is not proportional.
activities.intendedInsight: The recognition cues of a proportional graph are the origin crossing and a single constant rate; a straight line that misses the origin is a direct counterexample to 'straight means proportional'.

activities.title: Identify, read, and produce proportional lines
feedback: If a produced line misses (0,0), it is the key discriminator: recognition alone will not place the line; re-anchor using 'at 0 kg, cost £0'.
If an unknown is only found when the weight is an already-plotted point, stress that the line gives a value for EVERY weight, so interpolate between plotted points.
If axes are swapped during read-off, label both axes first, then read up-then-across.

If a £2/kg line is drawn as if it were separate from the given line, point out that equal rates give the SAME line through the origin; a genuinely different rate (e.g. £1/kg through (3,3)) gives a shallower distinct line.
activities.rationale: Identifying the proportional graph, reading off values, matching a table to a line, and drawing a new line are cleanly assessable, with 'any straight line' and axis-swap as sharp distractors. The draw step elicits independent construction, which recognition-only items do not.
sourceClaims: Pupils should use double number lines and ratio tables, and recognise that proportional relationships are represented by straight-line graphs through the origin, relating the multiplicative relationship to linear functions.
learnerActions: Choose which of several graphs shows direct proportion, where a straight not-through-origin line is a deliberate trap.
Given a ratio table, plot the points and draw the matching line through the origin.
Read an unknown off a line through (3,6) (e.g. find the cost of 5 kg → £10), stating which axis you read up from and which you read across to.

On the same axes, DRAW a line for a DIFFERENT fruit's price: note that a £2/kg fruit would COINCIDE with the given £2/kg line through (3,6), whereas a shallower £1/kg line passes through (3,3) — and check your line is anchored at the origin.
activities.intendedInsight: Interpreting a point, interpolating an unknown, and independently producing an origin-anchored line together show whether the learner sees the graph as a constant-multiplier relationship rather than a picture.

constraints: Multiple-choice identification and tap-to-reveal items assess or rehearse recognition of cues; they do not by themselves elicit the independent production of an origin-anchored line, so include a draw/plot task for full mastery.
An annotated fixed graph cannot be freely manipulated; pair it with a task where learners plot, drag, or draw so the constant multiplier is explored, not just viewed.
Always keep double number lines aligned at 0 and scales consistent, or equivalent ratios will not correspond.
When introducing the fixed-charge contrast, state the setup explicitly (e.g. £2 standing charge plus £2/kg) so learners attribute the lifted line to the non-zero start, not to a changed rate.

When asking learners to draw a 'different' line, ensure the chosen rate is genuinely different from any line already on the axes (£1/kg, not £2/kg, against a given £2/kg line), so the task is coherent.

In-role dialogue and 3D manipulation were judged poor fits here: the relationship is inherently 2D (two quantities, one plane), and drawing/reading a graph is a visual-spatial task; these are design judgements for this topic, not universal rules.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic and geometry: at £2/kg, 3 kg → £6 and 5 kg → £10 are consistent; a £1/kg line through the origin passes through (3,3); the fixed-charge example (£2 + £2/kg) correctly gives £2 at 0 kg and so misses the origin. The original's note that a £2/kg drawn line coincides with the given (3,6) line has been preserved and the 'different rate' wording kept coherent (£1/kg used as the genuinely different, shallower line).

The source claims support the mathematical signature (straight line through the origin; zero maps to zero; use of double number lines and ratio tables) but do not establish the comparative efficacy of any particular interface (linked board, tap-to-reveal, drag). Efficacy of specific media is not asserted; medium wording has been kept to proposed/intended.
The original judgement that conversation and 3D 'add nothing' has been softened to a scoped design decision for this 2D topic rather than a universal law.

probeDeeper: What would this fruit cost for 0 kg? Where must the line be at x = 0, and why?
How did you find the cost of 5 kg from the line — which way did you read, and how do you know it isn't, say, £, from the other axis?

Here is a line that is straight but does NOT go through the origin (a fixed £2 charge plus £2/kg) — is THAT one directly proportional? How can you tell? (counterexample separating 'straight' from 'proportional'.)
Show me this same relationship as a ratio table — where is the '×2' that the graph's steepness shows?
assess.correctAnswer: (a) 3 kg costs £6 (so this fruit is £2 per kg). (b) 5 kg costs £10 — read up from 5 on the x-axis to the line and across to £10. (c) A straight line through the origin passing through (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6)… — in fact the SAME line here, since £2/kg matches; if asked for, say £1/kg would be a shallower line through the origin, e.g. (3, 3).

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks any straight (or rising) line shows proportion; draws or accepts a line that misses the origin
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'what does this fruit cost for 0 kg?' — it must be £0, so the line has to start at the origin. Contrast with a fixed-charge line that misses it. Rehearse the origin test.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In (c) draws a line not through (0,0), or when shown a not-through-origin line calls it proportional

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the graph as isolated points and cannot interpolate an unknown, or swaps the axes
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model reading up from the x-value to the line and across to the y-axis; the line gives a value for EVERY weight, not just plotted ones. Label axes before reading.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 5 kg, only answers if 5 is a plotted point, or reads across-then-up the wrong way giving the wrong coordinate

errorPatterns.pattern: Does not connect the graph to the double number line / ratio table — treats them as unrelated
errorPatterns.nextMove: Put the three side by side for the same example; show the gradient, the column multiplier, and the number-line gap are the same number. Align the number line at 0.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Can read the graph but cannot say how the same relationship looks as a ratio table, or does not align the double number line at 0

responseLevels.gap: Misreads the axes or cannot interpolate; draws a line that misses the origin and treats any straight line as proportional.
responseLevels.full: Reads (3,6) as '3 kg for £6', interpolates 5 kg → £10 by reading the line, DRAWS a new proportional line through the origin, explains why it must pass through (0,0), and links the graph to the ratio table/double number line as the same constant multiplier.
responseLevels.partial: Interprets the given point and reads off 5 kg → £10 correctly, but draws a new line without anchoring it at the origin, or cannot translate the graph into a ratio table / double number line — recognition without full production or cross-representation.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a graph: a straight line through the origin passing through the point (3, 6), where the x-axis is weight in kg and the y-axis is cost in pounds. (a) What does the point (3, 6) tell you? (b) Use the line to find the cost of 5 kg. (c) Now, on the same axes, DRAW the line for a different fruit that costs £2 per kg.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Interpreting a point, reading off an unknown, and then PRODUCING a proportional line all test whether the child sees the graph as a constant-multiplier relationship, not a picture. A child who has it reads (3,6) as '3 kg for £6', interpolates 5 kg → £10, and draws a new line THROUGH THE ORIGIN. A child who hasn't reads the axes the wrong way, cannot interpolate, or draws a line that misses (0,0). The 'now draw one' step is the discriminator — recognition alone won't produce a correct origin-anchored line.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 10–11y; divide up to 4-digit ÷ 2-digit using formal SHORT division where appropriate, interpreting remainders according to context; and CHOOSE short vs long division.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y6 'divide numbers up to 4 digits by a two-digit whole number using … short division where appropriate, interpreting remainders according to the context'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 6.NS.2 fluent multi-digit division; 5.NBT.6 division by 2-digit divisors — method choice is a UK curriculum emphasis.
• Operational details — the distinctive skill is METHOD SELECTION: short division by a 2-digit divisor is efficient when the divisor is 'friendly' (e.g. 16, or a divisor whose multiples the child knows/can derive quickly, 3648÷16), doing the multiply-subtract mentally at each place; long division is safer when the divisor is awkward and mental multiples are hard. This is exemplary of strategic tool choice. Children need both methods secure, then judgement about which fits. Remainder interpretation (as decimal/fraction in measurement contexts) carries over. Estimate first and check by multiplying back.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): short division by a friendly 2-digit divisor (e.g. ÷12, ÷15). Tier B (age 10–11): 3648÷16 by short division and interpret the remainder in context. Tier C (age 11): justify choosing short vs long division for given calculations and explain the trade-off.
bestPractices: Teach method CHOICE explicitly — short division when the divisor's multiples are easy to hold mentally; long division when they aren't — as a case of strategic tool selection.
Secure both methods first, then give mixed sets where the child must decide and justify the method.
Support mental multiples of the divisor (derive 16×3 etc.) so the compressed short-division steps are reliable.
Carry over flexible remainder interpretation (decimal/fraction in measurement, round by context).
Estimate first and check by multiplying the quotient back; compare efficiency of the two methods on the same calculation.
keyRepresentations: Short-division ('bus stop') layout with a 2-digit divisor
Side-by-side short vs long division of the same calculation (efficiency comparison)
Divisor multiples list to support the mental steps
Bar model / number line for remainder interpretation
commonMisconceptions: Forcing short division with an awkward divisor and making mental-multiple errors (should choose long division).
Carry/remainder errors in the compressed steps because the mental multiplication is insecure.
Not interpreting the remainder appropriately for the context.
Believing one method is always 'better' rather than choosing by the numbers.
Place-value slips when the divisor doesn't fit into a leading digit.

learn.summary: For ages 10–11: divide numbers up to 4 digits by a two-digit divisor using formal short division where appropriate, choose between short and long division based on how 'friendly' the divisor is, and interpret remainders according to context (as a whole number, fraction, or decimal). The core new skill is strategic METHOD SELECTION once both methods are secure, supported by mental multiples of the divisor and by estimating and checking with multiplication.

activities.title: Method-chooser: the same division, two ways
feedback: 3648÷16 = 228 exactly; if your answer isn't near your estimate of ~225, recheck a step.
If a short-division step went wrong, check whether your mental multiple of the divisor was correct (e.g. 16×3=48) — insecure multiples are a common cause of carry errors.

Once the quotient has started, if the divisor doesn't fit into the current part, write a zero in that place of the quotient and carry any amount on; otherwise the quotient will have the wrong number of digits (4080÷17 = 240 is a good example — the zero in the ones place matters because 17 does not go into the final 0).
If you found short division error-prone with ÷17, that friction is the point: it shows why an awkward divisor often calls for long division.
activities.rationale: Method choice may be learned effectively by doing the same division both ways and experiencing the efficiency/reliability trade-off, with support for the mental multiples that short division compresses. Securing both methods first, then giving mixed problems where the learner decides and justifies, is proposed to build the judgement the Year 6 standard targets.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils divide up to 4 digits by a two-digit number using short division where appropriate, interpreting remainders according to the context.
Choosing short vs long division by the divisor's friendliness is a case of strategic tool selection; both methods should be secure first.
learnerActions: Solve 3648÷16 using short division ('bus stop' layout), using a list of multiples of 16 (16, 32, 48, 160, 1600, …) to support the multiply-subtract step at each place.
Solve the SAME calculation 3648÷16 using long division, writing out each multiply-subtract step.
Compare the two side by side and state which was quicker for THIS divisor and why.
Now try a divisor many learners find awkward, e.g. 4080÷17, by short division; notice whether and where holding multiples of 17 mentally becomes error-prone.
Solve 4080÷17 again by long division and compare how reliable each felt.
State a rule of thumb in your own words: when the divisor's multiples are easy to hold, short division is efficient; when they are hard, long division is safer.
Estimate first (e.g. 3600÷16 ≈ 225) and check the final answer by multiplying the quotient back (228×16 = 3648?).
activities.intendedInsight: Whether short or long division is the better tool depends on how friendly the divisor is, not on habit — and you can experience this trade-off by doing the same calculation both ways. Both methods are legitimate; the skill is choosing and justifying.

activities.title: Justify the method for a mixed set
feedback: A good justification names the divisor's friendliness, e.g. 'multiples of 15 are easy (15, 30, 45…), so short division is efficient.'
If you claimed one method is always best, revisit the awkward divisor (e.g. ÷17 or ÷29) — that case shows why judgement beats a fixed rule.
Always estimate first so a slipped step is caught (e.g. 2925÷15 ≈ 3000÷15 = 200, 5887÷29 ≈ 6000÷30 = 200; the exact answers are 195 and 203).
activities.rationale: Mixed sets requiring a decision plus justification target the distinctive UK curriculum emphasis on method selection, rather than execution alone. A Socratic 'which method suits these numbers, and why?' framing is proposed to build selection judgement.
sourceClaims: Choosing short vs long division by the divisor's friendliness is a case of strategic tool selection; both methods should be secure first.
6.NS.2 requires fluent multi-digit division; 5.NBT.6 develops 2-digit-divisor division — UK adds explicit short/long method choice.
learnerActions: For each calculation in a mixed set (e.g. 3648÷16, 4080÷17, 2925÷15, 5887÷29), decide whether short or long division suits it before computing.
Write one sentence explaining your choice, referring to whether the divisor's multiples are easy to derive.
Carry out the division with your chosen method, then estimate and check by multiplying back.
Answer: is any ONE method always 'better'? Explain why not, using an example from your set.
activities.intendedInsight: Strategic tool choice means matching the method to the numbers; no single method is universally superior, and whether a divisor is 'friendly' depends on which multiples you can derive quickly.

activities.title: Interpreting the remainder in context
feedback: 5 m ÷ 16 gives each piece = 5/16 m = 0.3125 m; writing '0 m r5' misses what the leftover means when sharing a length.
Ask 'what does the leftover stand for here?' — sharing the remainder equally means each share gets remainder ÷ divisor more units (e.g. 5/16 m each); convert to a decimal for a length.
In a 'how many buses?' context the remainder usually forces rounding UP; in a 'how many full boxes?' context it forces rounding DOWN.
activities.rationale: Flexible remainder interpretation (decimal/fraction in measurement, rounding by context) is an explicit standard requirement and a common failure point; a bar model or number line makes the meaning of the leftover concrete.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils divide up to 4 digits by a two-digit number using short division where appropriate, interpreting remainders according to the context.
learnerActions: Solve a measurement problem where the remainder must be expressed appropriately, e.g. '5 m of ribbon is shared into 16 equal pieces — how long is each piece?'
Share the leftover too: remainder over divisor gives the fraction of a metre added to each piece (here 5/16 m), then convert it to a decimal length.
For a different context (e.g. buses needed to carry people, or full boxes that can be filled), decide whether to round up, round down, or keep a remainder, and explain why.
Use a bar model or number line to show what the leftover represents before writing it as a fraction/decimal.
activities.intendedInsight: A remainder is not always written as 'r n' — the context dictates whether it becomes a fraction, a decimal, or forces rounding, so you must interpret what the leftover means.

activities.title: Check your understanding
feedback: For method choice, the reason matters as much as the answer: short division often fits ÷16 because its multiples are easy for many learners to hold; ÷17 is often awkward because many learners find its multiples harder to derive mentally.
For the fill-in step, verify your mental multiple of the divisor and that the quotient has the right number of digits.
For the remainder item, pick the fraction/decimal form when a measurement context demands it, not 'r n'.
activities.rationale: Selected-response and fill-in items efficiently check method appropriateness, procedural execution, and remainder interpretation. These verify recognition and single-step execution; they do not by themselves show the learner can independently choose and carry out a method on a fresh problem, so pair them with an unaided performance task.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils divide up to 4 digits by a two-digit number using short division where appropriate, interpreting remainders according to the context.
learnerActions: Choose: for 3648÷16 versus 4080÷17, which calculation better suits short division, and give the reason.
Fill in the missing step of a partially worked short-division ('bus stop') layout, including writing a zero in the quotient where the divisor doesn't fit a place.
Select the correctly interpreted remainder for a measurement context (e.g. the length of each piece as a fraction or decimal) rather than a whole-number 'r' form.
activities.intendedInsight: You can recognise the appropriate method, execute a short-division step correctly, and interpret a remainder for its context.

constraints: Secure BOTH short and long division before asking learners to choose between them; method selection presupposes fluent execution of each.
Support mental multiples of the divisor (e.g. deriving 16×3) so the compressed short-division steps are reliable; carry/remainder errors often trace back to insecure multiplication.

Do not teach that one method is universally 'better'; the objective is choosing by the numbers. Equally, do not frame a divisor's 'friendliness' as a fixed property — it depends on which multiples the individual learner can derive quickly.

Recognition-only and fill-in items assess method appropriateness and single steps but do not elicit independent choice-and-execution on new problems; pair them with a performance task where the learner chooses and carries out a method unaided.
A static side-by-side worked comparison is a useful reference for the trade-off but cannot let the learner choose and execute on new numbers; treat it as a scaffold, not the full objective.

When interpreting remainders, the correct written form depends on the context (fraction/decimal for measurement; round up or down for discrete grouping); do not apply one remainder convention universally.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three cited sources carry verified:false in the source row (the CCSS-M comparison claim and the NCETM strategic-tool-selection claim); treat the 'UK adds explicit short/long method choice' and 'friendliness dictates method' framings as informed curriculum interpretation, not independently verified fact.

Arithmetic self-check: 3648÷16 = 228 exactly (228×16 = 3648); estimate 3600÷16 = 225. 5÷16 = 0.3125 = 5/16 m. Added comparison/mixed-set divisors: 4080÷17 = 240, 2925÷15 = 195, 5887÷29 = 203 — all checked here but introduced by this rewrite and not part of the verified source; re-confirm before classroom use.

The source's claim that short division 'wins here' for ÷16 is efficiency-relative and depends on the learner's fluency with multiples of 16; retained as a learner-observed comparison, not an established comparative-efficacy result.
The original 'is best learned by doing' efficacy framing was softened to proposed/qualified wording, as no source establishes the comparative effectiveness of any medium or activity format.
The original 'possible'/static worked-comparison and Socratic conversation alternatives were preserved as scaffolds and as a justification activity respectively, each with its stated limit.

probeDeeper: How did you decide how many 16s go into the first part of 3,648?
In the ribbon problem, what does the leftover mean — and how do you write it as a length?
Estimate 3,648 ÷ 16 roughly — is your answer close?
How could you check your division answer using multiplication?
assess.correctAnswer: 3,648 ÷ 16 = 228 (exact). For 5 m ÷ 16, each piece is 0.3125 m (or 5/16 m). The teacher watches for a workable division method (chunking known multiples of 16, or short/long division) and correct interpretation of the remainder as a fraction/decimal rather than 'r something' when the context demands it.

errorPatterns.pattern: has no strategy for a two-digit divisor — stalls because 16 isn't a known table, or guesses digits of the quotient
errorPatterns.nextMove: build a short menu of easy multiples first (16, 32, 160, 1600) and subtract chunks; a two-digit divisor needs known multiples, not a memorised table.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child cannot start, or writes quotient digits with no relation to multiples of 16

errorPatterns.pattern: expresses the remainder as 'r n' when the measurement context requires a fraction/decimal
errorPatterns.nextMove: ask 'what does the leftover mean when we're sharing metres?' — the remainder over the divisor is a fraction of a piece; convert to decimal for length.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer given as '0 m r5' or similar rather than 5/16 m or 0.3125 m

errorPatterns.pattern: place-value slip in short division — mishandles a digit that the divisor doesn't go into (forgets the zero in the quotient)
errorPatterns.nextMove: insist on writing a zero in the quotient when the divisor doesn't fit that place, carrying the amount on; check the quotient's magnitude by estimation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: quotient has the wrong number of digits; e.g. drops a place when 16 won't divide a leading part

errorPatterns.pattern: correct method, arithmetic slip in a multiplication/subtraction step; caught by estimation
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach; have the child check with multiplication (228×16 = 3648?) and estimate.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: one step wrong; estimate (3600÷16 ≈ 225) flags it

responseLevels.gap: has no method for a two-digit divisor, or leaves a measurement remainder as 'r n'.
responseLevels.full: divides by the two-digit number using a secure method, interprets the remainder as a whole number, fraction, or decimal according to context, and checks with multiplication/estimation.
responseLevels.partial: completes the whole-number division with support but mishandles the remainder's interpretation, or omits a quotient zero.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to compute 3,648 ÷ 16 while you watch, letting them choose their method. Then give a measurement division whose remainder must be expressed as a fraction or decimal (e.g. '5 m of ribbon shared into 16 equal pieces — how long is each?') and watch how they handle the remainder. Notice whether they lean on multiples of the divisor and how they interpret what's left over.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Dividing by a two-digit number tests whether the child can build up or use multiples of an unfamiliar divisor, and the measurement item tests remainder interpretation as fraction/decimal (not whole-number rounding). Watching the method reveals whether they have a strategy for a non-table divisor or are stuck without a times-table.

pedagogy.summary: Expanding a single bracket applies the distributive law: the multiplier outside acts on EVERY term inside, and its sign travels with it. It is best taught through the area/grid model — a rectangle of width equal to the multiplier and length equal to the sum inside splits into one region per inside term, so 3(2x+5) is visibly 3×2x plus 3×5. The two persistent errors are distributing over only the first term (3(2x+5)→6x+5) and mishandling the sign of a negative multiplier; the area model and a substitution check defeat both.
bestPractices: Use the area/grid model: the multiplier is one side, each inside term a separate region, so every term must be multiplied.
Draw an arrow from the multiplier to EACH inside term to force full distribution.
Handle the sign explicitly — write −2(x−4) as (−2)×x + (−2)×(−4); a negative times a negative gives +8.
Check by substituting a value: 3(2x+5) and 6x+15 must agree at, say, x=1 (both 21).
Then combine with collecting like terms, e.g. 3 + 2(x+1) → 3 + 2x + 2 → 2x + 5, stressing that only the bracket is expanded first (order of operations).
keyRepresentations: Area/grid rectangle split into one region per inside term
Arrows fanning from the multiplier to each term
Number substitution check (evaluate both forms at x=1)
Signed-multiplier annotation (−2 × −4 = +8)
commonMisconceptions: Multiplies only the first term inside: 3(2x+5) → 6x+5 (documented as 2(n+3)=2n+3 being judged correct).
Sign error with a negative multiplier: −2(x−4) → −2x−8 (fails to flip the second sign).
Confuses × with +: 3(2x+5) → 3+2x+5, or adds the outside number to the coefficient (3×2x → 5x).
Leaves the expression unexpanded or unsimplified after multiplying.

learn.summary: Teach expanding a single bracket as the distributive law: the multiplier outside acts on EVERY term inside, and its sign travels with it. An area/grid model makes this visible — a rectangle whose width is the multiplier and whose length is the sum inside splits into one region per inside term, so 3(2x+5) is seen as 3×2x plus 3×5. Target the two persistent errors directly: distributing over only the first term (3(2x+5)→6x+5) and mishandling the sign of a negative multiplier (−2(x−4)→−2x−8, instead of the correct −2x+8). A substitution check and factoring back give learners independent ways to verify.

activities.title: Split the rectangle: area model of a bracket
feedback: If only one region is multiplied: draw an arrow from the multiplier to EACH inside term — the multiplier's side borders BOTH regions, so both must be multiplied. 3(2x+5) = 3×2x + 3×5.

If the −4 keeps its sign (−2x−8): write the second product with brackets, (−2)×(−4) = +8, and connect to 'two negatives make a positive'. At x=0 this slip shows up (correct −2(0−4)=8, but −2x−8 gives −8); confirm at a non-zero value too, e.g. −2(1−4)=6 and −2×1+8=6.

If the outside number is added instead of multiplied (3+2x+5) or folded into the coefficient (3×2x=5x): rewrite as 3×(2x+5), and recall that a number against a bracket means multiply, not add; 3×2x means three lots of 2x, which is 6x.
activities.rationale: The area/grid model represents each inside term as a distinct region, making 'multiply everything inside' something learners can see and reconstruct rather than memorise. An optional interactive version (tapping the '+' to slice the length, regions auto-labelling their area, a toggle that recolours regions and flips signs when the multiplier becomes negative) makes the mechanism concrete, but the reasoning also works with a drawn and hand-labelled rectangle. This model is one effective route and need not be the only one.
sourceClaims: Students commonly mis-expand a single bracket by multiplying only the first term — e.g. judging 2(n+3)=2n+3 to be correct — whereas 2(n+3)=2n+6; the lesson uses area representations to address this distributive-law error.
learnerActions: Draw (or manipulate) a rectangle labelled width 3 and length (2x + 5).
Split the length at the '+' into two parts, producing two regions: a 3-by-2x region and a 3-by-5 region.
Label each region with its own area: 3×2x = 6x and 3×5 = 15.
Gather the two areas to write the total: 3(2x+5) = 6x + 15.

Now take a new example with a negative multiplier, −2(x−4), and split it into one part for each term inside the bracket. A length of −2 is not a real side length, so treat the grid as a signed diagram, not a literal area: write it as (−2)×x + (−2)×(−4), reasoning that a negative times a negative gives +8, so the result is −2x + 8.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing the bracket as TWO regions answers 'why does the +5 not just come along unchanged?' — the multiplier covers every region, so every inside term must be multiplied, and the sign of a negative multiplier is applied to each term.

activities.title: Expand, then check by substitution
feedback: If both forms disagree at the chosen value, the expansion is wrong — re-check that every inside term was multiplied and that signs were handled.
If the check passes, note that agreement at one value is supporting evidence but not conclusive for a linear expression; test a second value and factor back to confirm the structure.
Avoid picking x=0 as the only check when a constant term could mask an error in the x-term — try a non-zero value such as x=1 or x=2, or use more than one value.
activities.rationale: A worked procedure with sign handling is consolidated by doing expansions and verifying them with feedback. Substitution and factoring back are genuine self-checking strategies learners can carry to any expansion. Scored fill-in or sort-the-terms tasks can give practice, provided they require learners to construct the expansion rather than only recognise a correct answer.
learnerActions: Expand 3(2x+5) and write the result (6x + 15).
Choose a value, say x=1, and evaluate both the original and the expansion: 3(2×1+5)=3×7=21 and 6×1+15=21 — they agree.
Expand −2(x−4) and check at x=1: −2(1−4)=−2×−3=6 and −2×1+8=6 — they agree.
Try to verify a second way by factoring the answer back to the bracket form.
Decide whether each expansion is correct, correcting any that disagree.
activities.intendedInsight: Substituting a value gives a learner an independent way to confirm or refute their expansion, so correctness is not dependent on the teacher's say-so; an expansion and its original must agree for every value.

activities.title: Expand within a larger expression (order of operations)
feedback: If the 3 is also multiplied by 2: point out that the 3 stands alone and is added, not part of the product 2(x+1); only 2 multiplies the bracket.
If terms are left uncombined (3 + 2x + 2): remind the learner to collect like constants, 3+2=5, giving 2x+5.
Confirm by substitution: at x=1, 3+2(1+1)=7 and 2(1)+5=7.
activities.rationale: Transferring expansion into a multi-term expression tests whether learners apply distribution selectively and then simplify, which is the National Curriculum expectation for manipulating algebraic expressions.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should simplify and manipulate algebraic expressions by multiplying a single term over a bracket.
learnerActions: Take 3 + 2(x+1) and expand only the bracket first: 3 + 2x + 2.
Collect like terms to simplify fully: 2x + 5.
Explain why the +3 is not multiplied by 2 — only the term attached to the bracket is expanded first.
Check the simplified form by substituting a value into both the original and the final expression.
activities.intendedInsight: Only the multiplier attached to the bracket is distributed; other terms are combined afterwards by collecting like terms, respecting the order of operations.

constraints: Expansion with sign handling is a procedure built through practice with feedback; recognition-only tasks (choosing a correct answer from options) can diagnose errors but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of an expansion — include tasks where learners write the full working.

A static labelled area diagram can show the split and support reasoning, but it does not let the learner carry out expansions across varied cases; pair any fixed diagram with learner-produced expansions to build fluency.
The area/grid model is inherently planar — the two dimensions represent multiplier and sum. Keep it in 2D; introducing a third dimension would misleadingly suggest volume.
The correct results to preserve are 3(2x+5) = 6x + 15 and −2(x−4) = −2x + 8 (NOT −2x−8). Any practice item or distractor must treat 6x+5 and −2x−8 as errors to be caught, never as acceptable answers.

When checking by substitution, prefer a non-zero value (e.g. x=1) or use more than one value so that a correct constant term cannot mask an error in the variable term; x=0 is acceptable only when the error being caught lives in the constant term.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source lists one citation as not verified (the CSMS/ICCAMS sign-error claim); treat its evidential strength as unconfirmed.

The legacy entry asserted that a third dimension 'adds nothing' and that dialogue is unsuitable; these have been softened to scoped claims (keep the model planar to avoid implying volume; a conversation alone may be less suited than practice with feedback for consolidating a multiplicative procedure, efficacy untested) rather than universal laws.

Self-audit on arithmetic and signs: 3×2x=6x, 3×5=15, total 6x+15 correct; (−2)×(−4)=+8 so −2(x−4)=−2x+8 correct; substitution checks 3(2×1+5)=21=6+15, −2(1−4)=6=−2×1+8, and 3+2(1+1)=7=2×1+5 verified. The legacy misconception example −2(x−4)→−2x−8 is retained only as an error to correct, never as a valid answer.

Editor adjustments: substitution checks harmonised to prefer non-zero values (removing an internal contradiction where x=0 was both used and discouraged); the self-check activity's sourceClaims set to [] because no source claim directly supports substitution/factoring as a verification strategy; the KS3 curriculum-necessity claim removed from the area-model activity's sourceClaims because it supports the topic only, not the area-model principle; single-value substitution reworded as supporting-but-not-conclusive evidence.

probeDeeper: Draw me a rectangle that shows why 3(2x+5) has two parts — what is each part's area?
In −2(x−4), what is −2 × −4, and how sure are you? (counterexample targeting the sign)
Is 3(2x+5) the same as 3×2x + 5? Put x=1 into both and check.
How could you convince someone your expansion is right — without me telling you? (expect: substitute a value, or factorise back)

errorPatterns.pattern: Distributes over the first term only — 3(2x+5) → 6x+5 — the second inside term is copied across unchanged (documented: students judge 2(n+3)=2n+3 to be correct).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw the rectangle: the multiplier is one side and covers BOTH regions; draw an arrow from the 3 to each inside term. Show 3(2x+5) = 3×2x + 3×5.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Only the first inside term is multiplied; the constant (or second term) appears unchanged in the answer.

errorPatterns.pattern: Sign error with a negative multiplier — −2(x−4) → −2x−8 — the sign of the second term is not flipped.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Write the multiplication with brackets and signs shown: (−2)×(−4) = +8; connect to two-negatives-make-a-positive; check by substituting x=0.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second term keeps its inside sign, or a negative multiplier is applied to only the first term's sign; −2×−4 is written as −8.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses multiplication with addition — 3(2x+5) → 3+2x+5, or folds the multiplier into the coefficient as 3×2x = 5x.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-establish that a number against a bracket means multiply; rewrite 3(2x+5) as 3×(2x+5); check by substitution.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The outside number is added to inside terms, or coefficients are added rather than multiplied.

responseLevels.gap: Multiplies only the first term, or adds instead of multiplies; the second inside term is lost or unchanged so the expansion is wrong.
responseLevels.full: Distributes over every term with correct signs including negative multipliers, simplifies the result, checks by substitution or by factorising back, and transfers to 3 + 2(x+1)-type expressions where the bracket must be expanded before adding.
responseLevels.partial: Expands correctly with a positive multiplier over both terms, but slips on the negative multiplier's sign, or does not simplify/collect afterwards — the routine case works but a rule-exposing case fails.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child this card and say 'expand each of these, showing your working': 3(2x + 5), and then −2(x − 4). Say nothing about method. Watch whether the multiplier reaches BOTH inside terms, and how they handle the sign on the −4.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The two cases isolate the two errors without any question being asked: 3(2x+5) → 6x+5 exposes distributing over the first term only, while −2(x−4) → −2x−8 exposes the negative-multiplier sign failure. A child who is sound multiplies both terms and gets +8 from two negatives; the written line tells the teacher which, if either, is missing.

sources.claim: Sign errors when a negative term is distributed over a bracket are a recurrent, documented algebra-manipulation difficulty.
sources.source: Küchemann/Hart CSMS tradition, as summarised in Hodgen et al. RME 11(2) (ICCAMS)

pedagogy.summary: Given two rules (e.g. 'start at 0, add 3' and 'start at 0, add 6'), the child generates both sequences, lines up CORRESPONDING terms (1st with 1st, 2nd with 2nd, …), and notices the relationship between the two is MULTIPLICATIVE: each Rule-B term is twice the corresponding Rule-A term — because the step 6 is twice the step 3 and both start at 0 — not merely 'more'. They form ordered pairs from corresponding terms, plot them in the first quadrant, and see the points fall on a straight line through the origin. It is a deliberate bridge from Grade 4/Year 5 pattern work toward proportional relationships (y = 2x) and functions. Crucially, pupils generate each pattern from a GIVEN rule; they are not required to guess a hidden rule.
bestPractices: Line the two sequences up in a two-row table so pupils compare column-by-column (corresponding terms), not within a single row
Press for a MULTIPLICATIVE description ('twice', '___ times as much') and an explanation of WHY — the step 6 is twice the step 3, and both start at 0
Explicitly contrast additive ('6 more') with multiplicative ('twice') using the corresponding pairs, showing the difference grows while the ratio stays constant
Form ordered pairs as (Rule-A term, Rule-B term), respecting the (x, y) order, and plot in the first quadrant
Notice the points lie on a straight line through the origin and connect this to y = 2x, previewing proportional reasoning
Keep both rules GIVEN — the task is to generate from the rules and then spot the relationship, not to infer a secret rule
Use tape/bar diagrams to make 'twice as much' visible
keyRepresentations: Two-row table of corresponding terms (positions aligned in columns)
The (x, y) ordered-pair notation drawn from corresponding terms
First-quadrant coordinate grid with points on a ray through the origin
Tape / bar diagram showing one quantity as twice the other
commonMisconceptions: Describes the relationship additively ('the second is 6 more') instead of multiplicatively ('twice') — defaulting to additive comparison, which only fits the first pair because the difference actually grows (3, 6, 9, …)
Compares term-to-term WITHIN one sequence (the +3 or +6 step) instead of between the corresponding terms of the two sequences
Reverses the ordered pair, plotting (6, 3) instead of (3, 6), or counting up-then-across
Tries to guess a single hidden rule underlying both sequences rather than generating each from its given rule
Assumes the 'twice' relationship comes from the steps alone, and keeps applying it even when the two sequences do not both start at 0

learn.summary: Pupils (age 10–11) generate two numerical sequences from two GIVEN rules (e.g. 'start at 0, add 3' and 'start at 0, add 6'), line up corresponding terms in a two-row table, and discover the relationship is multiplicative — each Rule-B term is twice the corresponding Rule-A term — because the step 6 is twice the step 3 and both start at 0. They explain why, contrast additive ('6 more') with multiplicative ('twice'), form ordered pairs (x, y) from corresponding terms, and plot them to see the points fall on a straight line through the origin (y = 2x). This bridges earlier pattern work toward proportional reasoning. Both rules are given; pupils are not asked to guess a hidden rule.

activities.title: Generate, align, and compare two sequences
feedback: If a pupil says 'B is 6 more than A', ask them to check a later pair — e.g. position 4, where A=9 and B=18, a gap of 9. The difference between corresponding terms is not constant but grows (3, 6, 9, 12…), so 'add 6' is not the relationship; the ×2 ratio, by contrast, stays constant — compare 'how many times' not 'how many more'.

If a pupil compares within one row (the +3 or +6 step), point to a single column (say position 3) and ask: 'what is B here, what is A here, how do they compare?' — the comparison is vertical across the two rows.
If a pupil hunts for a single hidden rule joining both sequences, remind them the rules are GIVEN: generate each sequence directly from its own rule, THEN look for the relationship between them.
Confirm the full reasoning: B is twice A at every corresponding position because 6 = 2×3 and both start at 0.
activities.rationale: Grade 5 pattern work asks pupils to generate two numerical patterns from given rules, examine relationships between corresponding terms, and prepare for proportional relationships. Distinguishing additive comparison (what is added) from multiplicative comparison (what factor multiplies) is a known conceptual hurdle, so explicitly contrasting the growing difference with the constant ratio targets the core discrimination.
sourceClaims: In Grade 5 (5.OA.3) students work with two numerical patterns that can be related, examine the relationships within sequences of ordered pairs and in first-quadrant graphs, and this prepares them for proportional relationships and functions; pupils generate a pattern from a GIVEN rule and are not required to infer or guess the underlying rule.

Additive versus multiplicative comparison (Grade 4): in an additive comparison the question is what amount would be ADDED to one quantity to get the other; in a multiplicative comparison the question is what FACTOR would multiply one to get the other; multiplicative Compare situations must be carefully distinguished from additive Compare problems.

CCSS 5.OA.B.3 canonical example: from 'Add 3' and 'Add 6' starting at 0, students observe that the terms in one sequence are twice the corresponding terms in the other and explain informally why (because 6 is twice 3).
learnerActions: Write out the first six terms of Rule A (start at 0, add 3): 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15
Write out the first six terms of Rule B (start at 0, add 6): 0, 6, 12, 18, 24, 30
Line the two sequences up in a two-row table so position 1 sits above position 1, position 2 above position 2, and so on
For each column, compare Rule B's term with Rule A's term in the SAME position (vertical comparison across the two rows, not along one row)
State the relationship multiplicatively: 'B is twice (×2) A in every column' and explain why — Rule B adds 6, which is twice the 3 Rule A adds, and both start at 0
Check what happens to the difference between corresponding terms down the columns (6−3=3, 12−6=6, 18−9=9…): it is not constant but grows, while the ×2 ratio stays the same in every column
activities.intendedInsight: The two sequences are related by a constant factor (×2) at corresponding positions. 'B is 6 more' does not describe the relationship, because the difference between corresponding terms is not constant but grows (0, 3, 6, 9, …) — so no single 'add a number' rule fits every column. 'B is twice A' holds in every column instead, and here this works because the step 6 is twice 3 and both sequences start at 0.

activities.title: Make ordered pairs and plot them
feedback: If points sit on the wrong side of or below the intended line, check the (x, y) order: the first number moves across (Rule A, x), the second moves up (Rule B, y). Re-plot one pair together — e.g. ask the pupil to point to where (3, 6) goes and say which number moves across and which moves up.
If a pupil plots (6, 3) instead of (3, 6), re-establish the convention and re-plot.
Confirm that all points lie on one straight ray climbing through (0, 0), matching the constant ×2 in the table.
activities.rationale: Forming ordered pairs from corresponding terms and graphing them in the first quadrant is the explicit objective of this standard and the bridge to seeing a proportional relationship as a line through the origin. Respecting (x, y) order is a common error point worth rehearsing in the plotting itself.
sourceClaims: In Grade 5 (5.OA.3) students work with two numerical patterns that can be related, examine the relationships within sequences of ordered pairs and in first-quadrant graphs, and this prepares them for proportional relationships and functions; pupils generate a pattern from a GIVEN rule and are not required to infer or guess the underlying rule.
learnerActions: Turn each column into an ordered pair as (Rule-A term, Rule-B term): (0,0), (3,6), (6,12), (9,18)…
For each pair, use the first number to move ACROSS (x, Rule A) and the second number to move UP (y, Rule B)
Plot the first four pairs in the first quadrant of a coordinate grid
Describe the shape the points make, and notice they lie on a straight line through the origin
Connect this to y = 2x, linking the table, the pairs, and the line as one object
activities.intendedInsight: Corresponding terms of two proportional sequences form ordered pairs whose points lie on a straight line through the origin; the constant ×2 ratio is the same thing as the equation y = 2x and the slope of that ray.

activities.title: Test whether the ×2 depends on the starting number
feedback: If a pupil still says 'twice' after changing the start, work one column numerically: with A starting at 1, position 2 gives A = 4 and B = 6, and 6 is not 2×4 — the ratio is no longer constant.
Draw out the general point: the ×2 held cleanly because the starting numbers fitted it too (both were 0), not just because one step was twice the other.
activities.rationale: A listed misconception is assuming the 'twice' relationship comes from the steps alone and keeping it even when a changed starting number breaks it (e.g. A starting at 1 while B starts at 0). Varying the start deliberately exposes this and deepens understanding of the condition behind the proportional relationship.
sourceClaims: CCSS 5.OA.B.3 canonical example: from 'Add 3' and 'Add 6' starting at 0, students observe that the terms in one sequence are twice the corresponding terms in the other and explain informally why (because 6 is twice 3).
learnerActions: Keep Rule B as 'start at 0, add 6' but change Rule A to 'start at 1, add 3' (1, 4, 7, 10, …)
Generate both sequences and line them up by position
Check each column: is B still exactly twice A now?
Explain what broke and why — the clean ×2 relationship relied on the starting numbers as well as the steps (in the original rules, both started at 0), not on the steps alone
activities.intendedInsight: The multiplicative relationship between corresponding terms comes from the steps AND the starting numbers; in the original rules both start at 0. When A starts at 1 but B starts at 0, 'twice' no longer holds in every column even though one step is still twice the other — so pupils should not assume 'twice' from the steps alone.

activities.title: Tape diagram for 'twice as much'
feedback: If a pupil focuses on the extra length (the gap) rather than the number of copies, redirect to 'how many A-tapes make a B-tape?' — the answer stays 2 in every column, while the extra length grows.
Confirm the two-copies structure matches the ×2 in the table and the slope of the line.
activities.rationale: A tape/bar diagram is a standard representation for making multiplicative comparison concrete and is specifically suggested as support for pupils defaulting to additive comparison. It offers a visual route to 'twice' alongside the numerical table.
sourceClaims: Additive versus multiplicative comparison (Grade 4): in an additive comparison the question is what amount would be ADDED to one quantity to get the other; in a multiplicative comparison the question is what FACTOR would multiply one to get the other; multiplicative Compare situations must be carefully distinguished from additive Compare problems.
learnerActions: For a chosen column (e.g. position 3: A = 6, B = 12), draw a tape/bar for the Rule-A term
Draw the Rule-B tape beside it and lay out how many copies of the A tape fit the B tape
Confirm the B tape is exactly two A tapes long, making 'twice as much' visible
Repeat for another column to check the two-copies relationship holds across positions
activities.intendedInsight: 'Twice as much' is a length/quantity relationship that can be seen directly: the larger bar is made of exactly two copies of the smaller, reinforcing multiplicative comparison over additive comparison.

activities.title: Check and sort: additive vs multiplicative, table-to-graph
feedback: If a pupil selects the additive answer ('B is 6 more than A'), return to a later column (e.g. position 4, where A=9 and B=18, a gap of 9) and show the difference between corresponding terms is not constant but grows, so 'add 6' does not describe the relationship — whereas ×2 holds in every column.
If a pupil reverses a plotted point, restate: first number across (x), second up (y).
Confirm correct matches by tracing one column from table to ordered pair to point on the line.
activities.rationale: Short checks (fill-in-the-blank, sort, match, plot) verify the skill and surface the common additive misconception ('B is 6 more') and the (y, x) reversal. These confirm mastery rather than build the generate-and-compare reasoning, so they belong after the construction activities.
learnerActions: Complete 'B term = __ × A term' for a given pair of sequences starting at 0
Given a described relationship, sort it as additive ('6 more') or multiplicative ('twice'), and say which one holds in every column
Match a two-row table to its correct straight-line graph
Plot a specified pair (e.g. (3, 6)) on the grid, deliberately avoiding the (6, 3) reversal
activities.intendedInsight: Pupils can apply the multiplicative relationship, choose it over the tempting additive description, and coordinate table, pairs, and graph correctly.

constraints: Keep both rules GIVEN; the task is to generate each sequence from its own rule and then find the relationship, not to guess a hidden rule.
Compare CORRESPONDING terms column-by-column (vertical, across the two rows), not term-to-term within a single sequence.

The clean ×2 relationship between corresponding terms depends on the starting numbers as well as the steps: here it works because 6 = 2×3 and both start at 0 (in general, Rule B's start must be twice Rule A's start). Do not present 'twice' as following from the steps alone.

The difference between corresponding terms is not constant — it grows (0, 3, 6, 9, 12…); do not present 'B is 6 more' as a true relationship that holds for a specific early pair. It coincides at most at a single column, and the honest contrast is 'difference grows' versus 'ratio stays ×2'.
Respect (x, y) order when forming and plotting pairs: Rule-A term across (x), Rule-B term up (y).

Recognition and sort/match/fill-in checks confirm the skill but do not, on their own, elicit the independent construction of generating two sequences and coordinating them into pairs and a graph; use them after construction.

A consolidation summary (a two-row table beside a pre-plotted line with the ×2 annotated and facts revealed on tap) can tidily review the result, but a fixed display does not let the learner generate the terms or watch the growing difference against the constant ratio themselves; treat it as a review aid, not the main task.

Optional interactive supports that make the mechanism concrete: taps that fill each row ('add 3' / 'add 6') with corresponding terms locked in columns; a toggle between a '+' view (drawing the growing difference 3, 6, 9…) and a '×' view (showing the constant ×2 in every column); auto-plotting each column as an ordered pair that lands on the ray through the origin; and a 'change the starting number' control to reveal that the ×2 breaks when the starts no longer fit it (e.g. A starts at 1 while B starts at 0), and holds only when B's start is twice A's start. These are illustrative, not required mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source for the canonical 'Add 3 / Add 6, terms are twice the corresponding terms' example (CCSS 5.OA.B.3) is marked verified:false in the row; the two Progressions claims are marked verified:true. Treat the canonical-example claim as unverified.

Arithmetic self-check: Rule A 0,3,6,9,12,15 and Rule B 0,6,12,18,24,30; corresponding ratios all ×2; differences between corresponding terms are 0,3,6,9,12,15 (equal to Rule A's values), confirming the difference grows and is NOT constant. This means 'B = A + 6' coincides at exactly one column (A=6, B=12); the original row's phrasing that the additive claim is 'true only for the first pair' / 'fails from the second pair on' is arithmetically imprecise and was corrected in the guidance to 'the difference grows' with ×2 holding everywhere. The 'change the start' case A:1,4,7,10 vs B:0,6,12,18 correctly shows ×2 fails (e.g. 6 ≠ 2×4).

The original row's 3D and conversation 'poor' ratings carried universal phrasing ('adds nothing', dialogue 'does not build' the procedure). These catalog preferences were not propagated as pedagogical laws; the procedural, construction-based nature of the objective is instead captured in constraints without asserting any medium is universally incapable.

probeDeeper: You said B is 6 more than A. Check the pair at position 4 — is B still exactly 6 more? What is happening to the gap as you go down?
Why does B come out as twice A — what is it about the two rules that makes that happen?
What if Rule A started at 1 instead of 0 (1, 4, 7, …) while Rule B still started at 0 and added 6? Would B still be exactly twice A?
Point to where (3, 6) goes on the grid, and tell me which number moves you across and which moves you up.
assess.correctAnswer: A: 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15. B: 0, 6, 12, 18, 24, 30. Each Rule-B term is TWICE (×2) the corresponding Rule-A term, because Rule B adds 6 each step which is twice the 3 that A adds, and both start at 0. Ordered pairs (0,0), (3,6), (6,12), (9,18) plotted give points on a straight line through the origin (y = 2x).

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares the two sequences additively — 'Rule B is 6 more than Rule A' — instead of multiplicatively ('twice')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Line up several corresponding pairs and ask 'is the gap the same or growing?'; the ×2 ratio is constant while the difference grows — compare 'how many times' not 'how many more', supported by a tape diagram
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes the relationship as an added amount, usually read off the first pair; it fails later because the gap grows (3, 6, 9, 12)

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares WITHIN one sequence (the +3 or +6 step) rather than between the corresponding terms of the two sequences
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point to a single column (say position 3): 'what is B here, what is A here, how do they compare?' — the comparison is vertical across the two rows, not horizontal
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The answer is about how one sequence grows down its own row, not how B relates to A at the same position

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses the ordered pair — plots (6, 3) instead of (3, 6), or counts up-then-across
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-establish the convention: the first number moves you ACROSS (Rule A, x), the second moves you UP (Rule B, y); re-plot one pair together
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Points sit on the wrong side of / below the intended line; the (x, y) order is not respected

errorPatterns.pattern: Hunts for a single hidden rule connecting both sequences instead of generating each from its given rule
errorPatterns.nextMove: The rules are GIVEN — generate each sequence directly from its own rule, THEN look for the relationship between them; you are not hunting a secret rule
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Invents a rule or looks for 'the pattern' rather than applying the two rules as given, then comparing

responseLevels.gap: Cannot generate both sequences reliably from the rules, or describes only how one sequence grows; gives no relationship between corresponding terms; pairs and plot are missing or reversed.
responseLevels.full: Generates both, states B is twice A at every corresponding position and explains why from the steps (6 = 2×3, both start at 0), forms correctly ordered pairs, plots them on the ray through the origin, and recognises that the additive gap grows while the ×2 ratio stays constant — transferring to predict the relationship for a new pair or a changed start.
responseLevels.partial: Generates both sequences and lines them up, but describes the relationship additively ('6 more') or only for the first pair, and/or plots pairs mechanically without connecting the constant ×2 to the straight line — has the parts (two sequences, some pairs) but not the multiplicative structure joining them.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Use two rules. Rule A: start at 0, add 3. Rule B: start at 0, add 6. Write out the first six numbers of each, lined up underneath one another. Then tell me how a number in Rule B compares with the number in the SAME position in Rule A — and why it works out that way. Finally, turn the first four matching pairs into points and plot them.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with the multiplicative structure says B is TWICE A in every position and explains it from the steps (6 = 2×3, both start at 0); the ×2 holds in every column. A child comparing additively says 'B is 6 more' — true only for an early pair, and decisively wrong because the DIFFERENCE grows (3, 6, 9, …), so 'plus 6' fails from the second pair on. Whether they compare corresponding terms across the two rows (vertical) or just read a within-row step (+3, +6) exposes the corresponding-terms confusion; and plotting (3,6) versus (6,3) exposes the ordered-pair order.

sources.claim: In Grade 5 (5.OA.3) students work with two numerical patterns that can be related, examine the relationships within sequences of ordered pairs and in first-quadrant graphs, and this prepares them for proportional relationships and functions; pupils generate a pattern from a GIVEN rule and are not required to infer or guess the underlying rule.
