sources.claim: Additive versus multiplicative comparison (Grade 4): in an additive comparison the question is what amount would be ADDED to one quantity to get the other; in a multiplicative comparison the question is what FACTOR would multiply one to get the other; multiplicative Compare situations must be carefully distinguished from additive Compare problems.
sources.source: Progressions for the CCSS in Mathematics, K-5 Operations and Algebraic Thinking (Grade 4, p.29; Grade 3, p.22)

sources.claim: CCSS 5.OA.B.3 canonical example: from 'Add 3' and 'Add 6' starting at 0, students observe that the terms in one sequence are twice the corresponding terms in the other and explain informally why (because 6 is twice 3).
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, 5.OA.B.3

pedagogy.summary: At 6-7, repeated reasoning turns into deriving and rule-describing: using a known double to get a near-double (6+7 = 6+6+1 = 13), noticing that subtracting 10 always drops the tens digit by one, and stating a rule for a sequence ('add 5 each time, so the ones digit alternates 0, 5'). The MP8 habit is to notice the repeated step, articulate it as a rule, and use it to predict — while checking it actually holds. Teaching should make the known fact and the derived one adjacent (a double and its near-double side by side) and press for the rule in the child's words, then test it on a fresh case.
bestPractices: Put a doubles fact next to its near-double (6+6 and 6+7) so the '+1' adjustment is seen, not computed from scratch
Ask the child to state the rule ('what's happening each time?') and then test it on the next case to guard against a rule taken from too few examples
Use a hundred square / place-value cards so −10 visibly drops the tens digit each time
Record a sequence and its step so the repeating structure and its rule are both on show ('+5, +5, +5')
keyRepresentations: Doubles and near-doubles on ten-frames / cubes (double + 1)
Hundred square and place-value cards for ±10
Number line marked with equal repeated steps (+5)
Bead strings for repeated addition patterns
commonMisconceptions: Recomputes 6+7 from one, not seeing it as the known double 6+6 plus 1
Applies the near-double adjustment wrongly (adds 2, or doubles the larger number)
States a rule from one or two cases and assumes it holds without testing
Subtracts 10 by changing the ones digit or counting back in ones instead of dropping the tens digit

learn.summary: For ages 6-7, this topic builds the habit of looking for and expressing regularity in repeated reasoning (MP8): deriving a near-double from a known double (6+7 = 6+6+1 = 13), noticing that subtracting 10 from a two-digit number drops the tens digit by one, and stating a sequence rule ('+5 each time starting from 5, so the ones digit alternates 5, 0') — then TESTING that rule on a fresh case rather than trusting it from one or two examples. Core teaching moves: place a known fact adjacent to the derived one so the adjustment is seen not recomputed, press for the rule in the child's own words, and always test the generalisation on a new case.

activities.title: Near-doubles builder: the double plus one
feedback: If the child counts up from 6 (or from 1) rather than referring to 6+6, put 6+6 and 6+7 side by side so the single extra cube is visible, and name 6+7 as 'the double and one more'.
If the child says 6+7=14 (added two) or doubles the 7, use the two rows to show exactly ONE cube was added — steady the adjustment; no need to reteach doubles.
Probe flexibility: 'you used 6+6 to get 6+7 — could you use 7+7 instead (one less than 14)? which double is handiest here?'
activities.rationale: Making the known fact and the derived one physically adjacent lets the '+1' be observed rather than computed, which is the derive-from-known-facts habit the guidance describes and keeps the derivation visible before fading support; repeating the adjustment across 6+7, 6+8 and 7+8 begins the repeated-reasoning shortcut.
sourceClaims: Pupils should derive number facts from known facts and use structure/relationships; representations should make the derivation visible and be faded over time
MP8 involves noticing repeated reasoning to reach general methods and shortcuts, while continually evaluating the reasonableness of results
learnerActions: Set out two rows of 6 cubes (or two ten-frames of 6) and confirm the double: 6+6=12.
Add exactly ONE more cube to one row and say the new total: 6+7=13. State it as 'the double I know, and one more'.
Repeat for 6+8 ('two more than the double, so 14') and for another double you know, e.g. 7+7=14 so 7+8=15.
Say aloud which double you used and how many you adjusted by, before giving the total.
activities.intendedInsight: A near-double can be derived from an adjacent known double by adjusting, instead of counting up from one.

activities.title: State a rule, then test it
feedback: If the child announces 'it's add 5' after two terms and won't check, do not simply confirm or correct it — ask 'how could we be sure? test the next one' so the checking habit forms.
If a later term surprises the child, treat the surprise as the lesson: a rule from too few cases can be wrong; revise and re-test.
Ask 'your rule is add 5 — what will the ones digit of the next three terms be? how do you know?' to check the rule predicts, not just describes.
activities.rationale: Recording the sequence and its step together — on a number line or bead string as well as in writing — puts the repeating structure and its rule both on show (representations making the structure visible), and requiring a test on the next case guards against a generalisation drawn from too few examples.
sourceClaims: MP8 involves noticing repeated reasoning to reach general methods and shortcuts, while continually evaluating the reasonableness of results
Pupils should derive number facts from known facts and use structure/relationships; representations should make the derivation visible and be faded over time
learnerActions: Lay out the first few terms of a sequence (e.g. 5, 10, 15, 20) and say the repeating step out loud: '+5, +5, +5'. Optionally show the equal +5 jumps on a number line or bead string so the repeating structure is visible.
State the rule in your own words: 'each time we add 5'. Predict the NEXT term before extending.
Predict the ones digit of the next three terms (25, 30, 35) and say why ('they alternate 5, 0, 5').

TEST it: have the adult reveal the next term of the given sequence (e.g. uncover a hidden card or the next group on the bead string) and compare it with your prediction; if it does not match, revise the rule. Extending the sequence yourself with your own rule is not a test.
Then say how you could be sure a rule is right before trusting it.
activities.intendedInsight: A rule guessed from a couple of cases should be tested on fresh cases before we rely on it: a passing test makes us more confident (it does not prove the rule), while one failing case shows the rule needs revising — this is the MP8 discipline of checking a generalisation.

activities.title: Subtracting 10 on a hundred square — and bounding the rule
feedback: If the child subtracts 10 by changing the ones digit or counting back in ones, use the hundred square to show the move is one whole row back (straight up on a square with 1 in the top row; straight down on a square numbered from the bottom) — the ones digit does not change.
Counterexample to bound the rule: 'you said take away ten drops the tens digit — does take away ONE do that to 45?' (45−1=44) to check the child limits the rule to −10.
Confirm by reading the place-value cards: the tens card goes down one, the ones card is untouched.
activities.rationale: A hundred square or place-value cards make the −10 move structural rather than counted, and testing whether −1 behaves the same teaches the child to bound a generalisation to its conditions and evaluate reasonableness.
sourceClaims: MP8 involves noticing repeated reasoning to reach general methods and shortcuts, while continually evaluating the reasonableness of results
Pupils should derive number facts from known facts and use structure/relationships; representations should make the derivation visible and be faded over time
learnerActions: On a hundred square (or with place-value cards), start at a two-digit number such as 45 and subtract 10; land on 35 and notice the tens digit dropped by one while the ones digit stayed the same.
Repeat from two or three other starting numbers to see the same pattern each time; state the rule: 'take away 10 drops the tens digit by one'.
Test the boundary: does taking away ONE do the same thing? Try 45−1 (which gives 44) and see it does not — so the rule is only for −10.
Say the rule in your own words AND what it does NOT cover.
activities.intendedInsight: Subtracting 10 from a two-digit number lowers the tens digit by one and leaves the ones digit unchanged — and a good rule is stated with the conditions under which it holds.

activities.title: Check-in: which fact did you use?
feedback: A correct number alone does not show repeated-reasoning insight — follow up with 'which fact did you use?' because a scored blank does not reveal whether the rule was reasoned or guessed.
If the child recomputes from one, redirect to the adjacent known double before accepting the answer.
activities.rationale: Fill-in and sequence-continuation items can confirm a correct answer, but because scoring alone cannot reveal whether a derivation occurred or whether a rule was reasoned or guessed, pair every item with a 'how did you get it?' question. This is a check, best used after hands-on work; it verifies recall and continuation without by itself eliciting the child's reasoning.
learnerActions: Answer short derivation prompts such as '6+6=12, so 6+7=__' and 'continue the sequence 5, 10, 15, __'.
For each answer, say WHICH known fact or rule you used to get it, not just the number.
Try at least one where you explain how you'd check your answer is reasonable.
activities.intendedInsight: Getting the right number is not enough; the target is reusing a known fact or rule and being able to justify it.

constraints: This is a META/mathematical-thinking topic for ages 6-7: the goal is the derive-and-check habit, not just correct totals. Listen for reuse of a known fact and the adjustment, not just the answer 13.

Fill-in or sequence-continuation checks can show whether a correct answer was produced but cannot by themselves reveal whether a derivation occurred or whether a rule was reasoned, recalled or guessed; always pair with 'which fact did you use?' and treat them as a follow-up to hands-on building, not a replacement.

A static near-doubles card or annotated −10 column can illustrate the move for reference, but does not let the child adjust the quantity or test a self-stated rule; use it as a reference scaffold, not the main task.
Bound the −10 rule explicitly: it lowers the tens digit by one and leaves the ones digit unchanged — this specific 'drop the tens by one' rule does not generalise to −1 or other amounts.
Do not confirm or correct a child's sequence rule for them when the aim is building the checking habit; prompt them to test the next case instead.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original recommendation leaned on a specific interactive 'near-doubles builder' and 'sequence machine' and rated conversation and 3D artefacts 'poor'. Those comparative/necessity ratings are catalog preferences, not established efficacy; the concrete affordances (live total update when a cube is added, a machine flagging a wrong predicted term) are preserved here as optional ways to make the mechanism visible, achievable with physical cubes, ten-frames, number lines, bead strings, hundred squares, or screen tools.

The original claims that '3D adds no structural information' and that 'open dialogue gives nothing concrete' were omitted as unsupported universal statements; spoken explanation of which fact was used is in fact central to assessing this reasoning habit, while a sort or fill-in check alone verifies classification/recall without eliciting that explanation.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 6+6=12, 6+7=13, 6+8=14, 7+7=14, 7+8=15, 45−10=35, 45−1=44 all check out; the sequence 5,10,15,20 continuing 25,30,35 has ones digits alternating 5,0,5. Independent re-review found no arithmetic or logic errors to correct.
The number-line (+5) and bead-string representations from the original keyRepresentations are retained as optional supports in the sequence activity.

Independent re-review adjusted only source attribution: the EEF visible-representation claim was added to Activity 2 because its rationale directly invokes representations making the repeating structure visible. No learner-facing error was found.

probeDeeper: Ask 'you used 6+6 to get 6+7 — could you use 7+7 to get 6+7 as well? which double is handiest?' to test flexible reuse of known facts
Counterexample tuned to this topic: 'you said take away ten drops the tens digit — does taking away ten from 45 give 35? what about taking away ONE?' to check the child bounds the rule to −10
Ask 'your rule is add 5 — what will the ones digit of the next three terms be? how do you know?' to probe whether the rule predicts, not just describes
Ask 'how could you check your rule is right before trusting it?' to surface the MP8 habit of testing a generalisation
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child deriving from the known double: '6+7 is one more than 6+6, so 13; 6+8 is two more, so 14.' The reuse of the known fact and the adjustment, not just 13, is the target.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Put 6+6 and 6+7 side by side on ten-frames so the single extra cube is visible; name 6+7 as 'the double and one more'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child counts up from 6 (or from 1) rather than referring to 6+6

errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold with the two ten-frames to see exactly ONE cube was added; do not reteach doubles, just steady the adjustment

errorPatterns.pattern: States a sequence rule from one or two cases and assumes it holds without testing further
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT simply confirm or correct the rule; ask 'how could we be sure? test the next one' so the habit of checking a generalisation forms

responseLevels.gap: Recomputes each sum from one, mis-adjusts near-doubles, and states rules without testing; each result treated as new
responseLevels.full: Independently derives from known facts (double ± 1, −10 drops the tens digit), states a sequence rule AND tests it on a fresh case, and predicts confidently — transferring the derive-and-check habit unprompted
responseLevels.partial: Derives a near-double or continues a sequence when prompted, but does not reuse known facts independently or check that a stated rule holds

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You know 6 + 6 = 12. Use that to work out 6 + 7 quickly, without counting from one. Then tell me how it would help with 6 + 8.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Reaching 13 by counting up shows no repeated-reasoning insight; deriving it as 'the double plus one' does. A child using the structure adjusts the known fact and extends the idea to 6+8; a child without it recounts each sum from the start.

pedagogy.summary: Algebraic vocabulary (expression, equation, inequality, term, coefficient, factor) is best taught not as definitions to memorise but as language the child USES while doing and justifying maths. The load-bearing distinction is expression vs equation, which turns on the equals sign: an expression represents a value; an equation is a statement that can be true or false and therefore tested; an inequality uses <, >, ≤, ≥ instead. Teach the '=' relationally (sameness/balance) rather than operationally ('work out the answer'), and name terms/coefficients/factors on real expressions, including negative signs.
bestPractices: Contrast minimal pairs aloud: 2a+3 (expression) vs 2a+3=11 (equation) vs 2a+3<11 (inequality) — the child must say which is which and why, pointing to the =, <, or > as the deciding feature.
Use an Always/Sometimes/Never-true card sort so students must TEST statements by substitution rather than 'solve' them — this forces the relational meaning of the equals sign.
Insist on justification ('how do you know it's an equation and not an expression?') rather than accepting the label alone.
Teach '=' as balance/sameness (both sides name the same value), explicitly challenging the 'makes/gives the answer' reading, e.g. accept and discuss 7 = 3 + 4 and 3 + 4 = _ + 2.
Name terms, coefficients and factors on genuine expressions including signs, e.g. in 5x − 2y + 7 there are three terms, the coefficient of x is 5, of y is −2, and 7 is a constant.
keyRepresentations: Card sort into Expression / Equation / Inequality bins (and Always/Sometimes/Never true)
Balance scale for the equals sign as sameness
Colour-coded term boxes that isolate each term with its sign
Number line for representing inequalities
commonMisconceptions: Calls any algebra string an 'equation' and expects to 'solve' it, even with no equals sign (writes an expression when asked for an equation).
Reads '=' operationally ('= means work out the answer'), so rejects 8 = 3 + 5 or treats an equation as an instruction rather than a statement.
Conjoins terms / treats a letter as an object, so miscounts terms or reads 3a + 2b as a single quantity (or '5ab').
Treats an inequality as if it were an equation with a single answer, ignoring the range of values it describes.

learn.summary: Teach algebraic vocabulary (expression, equation, inequality, term, coefficient, factor) as language a learner USES while doing and justifying maths, not as definitions to memorise. The load-bearing distinction is expression vs equation, which turns on the equals sign: an expression names a value; an equation is a statement that can be true or false, so it can be tested by substitution; an inequality uses <, >, ≤, ≥ and is also a statement that can be tested; at this level it is typically true for a whole range of values (e.g. 2a + 3 < 11 for a < 4), though some inequalities are true for all values or for none. Teach '=' relationally (both sides name the same value / balance), explicitly challenging the operational 'work out the answer' reading, and name terms, coefficients and factors on genuine expressions including negative signs.

activities.title: Build an equation from an expression (card-sort workspace)
feedback: If a learner labels the bare 2a + 3 an equation and starts hunting for a value of a, put 2a + 3 and 2a + 3 = 11 side by side and ask: what changed, and what can you do now that you could not before? Draw out that the '=' is what creates a statement to test.
If a learner tries to 'solve' an inequality for a single answer, ask how many values of a make 2a + 3 < 11 true, and have them check several values to see it holds for a whole range (a < 4).

Optional interaction that makes the mechanism concrete: a greyed-out 'Test it' button that only lights once an '=' is present, and a truth-lamp that flips red↔green as a candidate value is slid in — these illustrate testability, they are not required for the lesson.
activities.rationale: A felt expression→equation transformation targets the documented error of writing/treating an expression as an equation, and substitution-based testing is intended to require the relational meaning of the equals sign rather than an operational 'find the answer' reading.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should use and interpret the vocabulary of expressions, equations, inequalities, terms and factors, and substitute numerical values into formulae and expressions.

In trials, students commonly write an expression (e.g. 'y+3') when asked for an equation, and fail to include a variable; the lesson requires them to TEST statements by substitution rather than assume, and highlights that some assume different letters must take different values.

Children frequently interpret the equals sign operationally ('do something / write the answer') rather than relationally (a statement that the two sides are equal), which underlies difficulty with equations.
learnerActions: Start with 2a + 3 sitting on its own and say aloud whether there is anything to 'test' or 'solve' — establish that it just names a value.
Drag an '=' and the number 11 alongside it to form 2a + 3 = 11, and say what has now changed.

Sort a set of six cards into Expression / Equation / Inequality bins (e.g. 2a + 3, 2a + 3 = 11, 2a + 3 < 11), pointing each time to the =, <, >, ≤ or ≥ as the deciding feature, or saying that no such sign is present for an expression.
Substitute candidate values of a into 2a + 3 = 11 to test whether the statement is true or false; confirm it is true only at a = 4.

Also do an Always / Sometimes / Never true card sort, TESTING each statement by substitution rather than trying to 'solve' it, and recognising that one counterexample rules out 'always' (and one true case rules out 'never'), but checking a few values alone cannot prove 'always' or 'never' — give a reason for those.
activities.intendedInsight: The equals sign turns an inert value (expression) into a statement that can be true or false (equation) and therefore tested; an inequality is also a testable statement, and here (2a + 3 < 11) it is true across a whole range of values (a < 4) rather than at a single answer.

activities.title: Read '=' as balance and sameness
feedback: If a learner reads 2a + 3 = 11 as 'do 2a + 3 and the answer is 11', recast it as 'the two sides are the same value' and use the balance image to make sameness visible.
If a learner rejects 8 = 3 + 5 as 'the wrong way round', present it and 3 + 4 = ___ + 2 deliberately and discuss why both are legitimate statements about sameness.
activities.rationale: Addresses the well-documented operational reading of the equals sign by having learners accept and justify relationally-formatted equalities.
sourceClaims: Children frequently interpret the equals sign operationally ('do something / write the answer') rather than relationally (a statement that the two sides are equal), which underlies difficulty with equations.
learnerActions: Using a balance scale (physical or depicted), show that both sides of an equation name the same amount.
Judge and discuss statements written in unfamiliar orders, e.g. 7 = 3 + 4 and 3 + 4 = ___ + 2, deciding whether each is legitimate and what goes in the blank.
Explain to a partner why 3 + 4 = 7 and 7 = 3 + 4 are NOT different statements despite one looking 'backwards'.
activities.intendedInsight: The equals sign asserts that both sides have the same value; it is not an instruction to 'produce the answer on the right', so reversed and two-sided equalities are perfectly valid.

activities.title: Name terms, coefficients and factors — keeping the signs
feedback: If a learner counts one or two terms in 5x − 2y + 7 or merges 3a + 2b, have them box each term with its sign and count the boxes; contrast with 3a + 2a to show when combining is valid.
If a learner gives the coefficient of y as 2 rather than −2, point to the minus sign immediately in front and have them read the term as a whole, sign included.
activities.rationale: Letter-as-object and conjoining of unlike terms are persistent interpretations among 11–16 year-olds; isolating each signed term and contrasting like with unlike terms targets these directly.
sourceClaims: Letter-as-object and the conjoining of unlike terms are persistent, well-documented interpretations of algebraic letters among 11–16 year-olds.
KS3 pupils should use and interpret the vocabulary of expressions, equations, inequalities, terms and factors, and substitute numerical values into formulae and expressions.
learnerActions: On 5x − 2y + 7, box each term WITH its sign and count the boxes (three terms).
State the coefficient of x (5) and of y (−2), being explicit that the minus sign belongs to the coefficient, and name 7 as the constant.
Contrast 3a + 2b (two terms, cannot be combined) with 3a + 2a (like terms that can) to resist conjoining and the '5ab' error.
On 2(a + 3), identify it as an expression whose factors are 2 and (a + 3), and state what would turn it into an equation.
activities.intendedInsight: Terms are the parts separated by + and − (each carrying its own sign); a coefficient is the number multiplying a letter, signs included; factors are what is multiplied together — and a letter stands for a number, not a labelled object, so unlike terms cannot be merged.

activities.title: Justify the word you chose ('convince me')
feedback: Accept a label only with a reason; if the reason is 'it just looks like one', redirect the learner to point to the =, <, or > AND say what it does to the statement.
If a learner cannot say what is missing from an expression, pair it with the matching equation so the added '=' and right-hand side are visible.
activities.rationale: Insisting on justification rather than the bare label is intended to surface whether the learner is relating the symbol to its meaning or merely matching surface features; spoken challenge can rehearse precise usage alongside the manipulation-based work.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should use and interpret the vocabulary of expressions, equations, inequalities, terms and factors, and substitute numerical values into formulae and expressions.
learnerActions: After labelling a card, answer 'how do you know it's an equation and not an expression?' by pointing to the deciding symbol and saying what it does.
Respond to a sceptical questioner who challenges sloppy usage, e.g. 'you called that an equation — convince me', and defend or correct the label.
Explain, for an expression you chose, what you would add to make it an equation and what you could then do that you cannot do now.
activities.intendedInsight: Precise algebraic language is a tool for reasoning: being asked to justify a label is intended to push the learner past surface pattern-matching to state what the deciding symbol (=, <, >) actually means — that an equals sign makes a testable statement of sameness, not just that a particular symbol is present.

constraints: This is a LANGUAGE objective for ages 11–12: the goal is precise USE and justification of vocabulary, not memorised definitions; always require the learner to say which category and why.

Categorization/matching/multiple-choice checks (sort statements into expression/equation/inequality; match term to coefficient; 'which change turns 2a+3 into an equation?') assess the distinction efficiently but do not by themselves elicit the independent construction of an equation from an expression — use them after, not instead of, the build-and-test activity.

A static labelled 'anatomy' (tap the =, a term, a coefficient to reveal its name) works as a reference glossary but does not stage the expression↔equation transformation that carries the key insight; this is a limitation of a glossary-style reference, not an impossibility of static media.

Optional interactive features (greyed-out 'Test it' button, truth-lamp, value sliders, balance scale, colour-coded signed term boxes, number line for inequalities) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete; none is mandatory and they should not replace the learner's own stating and justifying.
A balance scale and value substitution are approximations of 'both sides name the same value'; keep the represented idea (sameness/testability) in focus rather than the prop.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support teaching principles, not the tested effectiveness of any specific activity.

Self-audit (arithmetic/logic checked): for 2a + 3 = 11, a = 4 is correct (8 + 3 = 11). For 2a + 3 < 11, the solution is a < 4, correct. In 5x − 2y + 7 there are three terms; coefficient of x = 5, of y = −2, constant = 7 — correct and signs preserved. 3 + 4 = 7 and 7 = 3 + 4 are the same relational statement — correct. 2(a + 3) has factors 2 and (a + 3).

Two source claims (Kieran 1981 on the operational/relational equals sign, and Hodgen et al. 2009 on letter-as-object/conjoining) carry verified:false in the original row; they are cited here to support teaching principles only, with no upgrade of their confidence or evidence status.

The original framing that 3D 'adds nothing' to a symbolic distinction has been softened to a scope note (a static or non-spatial representation can still teach the parts; manipulation additionally stages the transformation) rather than asserted as a universal law.
Removed the original claim that a static reveal 'cannot stage' the transformation, restating it as a limitation of a glossary-style reference rather than an impossibility.

Independent-review correction: activity 4's intendedInsight previously treated 'point to the =, <, > feature' as the goal while opposing it to 'surface appearance', which is contradictory because the symbol is itself a surface feature; reworded so justification goes beyond symbol-spotting to the symbol's relational meaning, consistent with the partial/full response levels.
Efficacy verbs ('forces', 'surfaces') in activity rationales/insights were softened to intended-effect wording to avoid asserting proven outcomes of untested proposals.

probeDeeper: You said this one is an expression — what would you have to add to make it an equation, and what could you then do that you can't do now?
Point to the terms in 5x − 2y + 7. How many are there, and what is the coefficient of x? Of y?
Your friend says 3 + 4 = 7 and 7 = 3 + 4 are different, because the second one is 'backwards'. What would you tell them? (counterexample probing the relational equals sign)
Is x + 2 > 10 an equation? If not, what is it, and how many values of x make it true?
assess.correctAnswer: 2a + 3 is an expression — it has no equals sign, so there is nothing to test; it just represents a value. 2a + 3 = 11 is an equation — a statement that can be true or false, so you can solve it (a = 4). 2a + 3 < 11 is an inequality — true for a range of values (a < 4). To turn the expression into an equation you set it equal to something.

errorPatterns.pattern: Calls an expression an equation and expects to 'solve' it — 'it's an equation, so a = something' — cannot say what is missing (documented as students writing expressions when asked for equations).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Put the matched pair 2a+3 and 2a+3=11 side by side; ask what changed and what you can now do that you could not before. Establish that the '=' is what turns a value into a statement to test.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels the bare 2a+3 an equation and starts trying to find a value of a, or cannot point to the equals sign as what an equation must have.

errorPatterns.pattern: Operational reading of the equals sign — '= means work out the answer' — so treats an equation as an instruction and is uneasy with 8 = 3 + 5 or 3 + 4 = _ + 2.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a balance scale: both sides name the same amount. Deliberately present 7 = 3 + 4 and 3 + 4 = _ + 2 and discuss why they are legitimate.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes 2a+3=11 as 'do 2a+3 and the answer is 11' rather than 'the two sides are the same'; rejects a reversed or two-sided equality as 'backwards' or 'wrong way round'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Conjoins terms / treats letters as objects, so miscounts terms or reads 3a + 2b as one quantity (or '5ab').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Box each term WITH its sign; count the boxes. Contrast 3a+2b (two terms, cannot combine) with 3a+2a (like terms). Re-establish that a letter stands for a number, not a labelled object.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked how many terms are in 5x − 2y + 7, gives one or two, or merges 3a+2b; misreads the coefficient of y as 2 rather than −2 (drops the sign).

responseLevels.gap: Uses 'equation' as a catch-all for any string of algebra; cannot point to the equals sign as the distinguishing feature; tries to 'solve' an expression or reads '=' as 'gives the answer'.
responseLevels.full: Distinguishes all three AND explains that the equals sign makes a statement that can be true or false (relational), identifies terms, coefficients and factors correctly including signs, and transfers to a new case — e.g. recognises 2(a+3) as an expression whose factor is 2, and states what would turn it into an equation.
responseLevels.partial: Correctly sorts expression/equation/inequality by spotting the =, <, > symbols, but cannot yet articulate WHY it matters (that an equation is a testable statement) or slips on terms/coefficients when negative signs are involved — lists the surface features without relating them.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put three cards in front of the child: 2a + 3, then 2a + 3 = 11, then 2a + 3 < 11. Say: 'You and a partner are checking work. Your partner wrote 2a + 3 and called it an equation. Talk me through whether that's the right word, what you'd actually call each of these three, and what you could DO with each one.' Then listen — do not offer the words yourself.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child holding the relational meaning of '=' names 2a+3 an expression, cites the MISSING equals sign, and says an equation is something you can test/solve. A child with the operational reading calls everything an 'equation to solve', tries to 'find a' from the bare expression, and cannot say what distinguishes the three — the same context separates the two reasoners because only correct use references the =, <, > signs as the deciding feature.

sources.claim: KS3 pupils should use and interpret the vocabulary of expressions, equations, inequalities, terms and factors, and substitute numerical values into formulae and expressions.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (KS3)

sources.claim: In trials, students commonly write an expression (e.g. 'y+3') when asked for an equation, and fail to include a variable; the lesson requires them to TEST statements by substitution rather than assume, and highlights that some assume different letters must take different values.
sources.source: Mathematics Assessment Project — 'Sorting Equations and Identities' Classroom Challenge (Common Issues table & activity)

sources.claim: Children frequently interpret the equals sign operationally ('do something / write the answer') rather than relationally (a statement that the two sides are equal), which underlies difficulty with equations.
sources.source: Kieran, C. (1981). Concepts associated with the equality symbol. Educational Studies in Mathematics, 12(3), 317–326.

sources.claim: Letter-as-object and the conjoining of unlike terms are persistent, well-documented interpretations of algebraic letters among 11–16 year-olds.
sources.source: Hodgen, Küchemann, Brown & Coe (2009). Children's understandings of algebra 30 years on. Research in Mathematics Education, 11(2).

pedagogy.summary: A metacognitive topic: using rounding/estimation as an INDEPENDENT check on the reasonableness of a calculation, and judging the appropriate degree of accuracy for a context. Two ideas intertwine — (1) an estimate sets a ballpark that can DISPROVE an exact answer in seconds (if 47,832 + 23,156 is about 71,000, an answer of 3,988 must be wrong), and (2) the right level of accuracy depends on purpose (a stadium crowd is honestly '52,000'; a shop bill must be exact). The habit being built is 'is this answer sensible?', not another calculation.
bestPractices: Teach estimation as a CHECK done independently, before or after the exact calculation - never by repeating the exact method
Round to a level that keeps useful discrimination (nearest 1,000 for five-digit sums, not nearest 10,000)
Use deliberately wrong answers and ask 'how can you tell this is impossible without redoing it?'
Discuss real contexts where precision is spurious (crowd sizes, distances) vs essential (money, counts that must balance)
Frame accuracy as a decision with reasons, not 'more digits = better'
keyRepresentations: Number line showing the estimate as a bracket/ballpark around the true value
Rounded-vs-exact comparison ('about 71,000' beside 70,988)
Context cards (crowd / money / distance) ranking needed precision
Order-of-magnitude 'gauge' (is the answer in the right zone?)
commonMisconceptions: Thinks a good estimate should EQUAL the exact answer (so treats the small difference as an error)
Checks by recomputing exactly rather than estimating - defeating the purpose
Believes more accuracy is always better; cannot see when rounding is appropriate
Rounds to an unhelpful level (too coarse to discriminate, or too fine to be an estimate)
Treats the estimate itself as the required answer

learn.summary: Learners build the habit of asking 'is this answer sensible?' by using rounding/estimation as an INDEPENDENT check on a calculation, and by judging the level of accuracy a context actually needs. Two intertwined ideas: (1) an estimate sets a ballpark that can disprove an exact answer in seconds (if 47,832 + 23,156 is about 71,000, an answer of 3,988 must be wrong), and (2) the right precision depends on purpose (a stadium crowd is honestly '52,000'; a shop bill must be exact). The two ideas are one habit, not separate tricks, and the check is deliberately NOT a re-computation of the same sum.

activities.title: The estimate as a lie-detector: prove an answer wrong without redoing it
feedback: If a learner says 71,000 is 'wrong' because the exact answer is 70,988: an estimate is meant to be near, not equal; being close is exactly what you want, and its job is to catch big errors, not to match digit for digit.

If a learner reaches for the full algorithm to check: redoing the same method can easily repeat the same mistake (especially if it comes from how you do the method), so the error may go undetected; a quick, independent estimate can catch large errors that repeating the method might miss.

If a learner rounds a five-digit sum to the nearest 10,000: that grain is often too coarse to catch errors of a few thousand (50,000 + 20,000 = 70,000 would still expose 3,988, but would not show up an answer like 74,000 as suspicious) - match the rounding grain to the question, coarse enough to be quick but fine enough to still discriminate.
When an answer IS close to the estimate, note that 'close' does not guarantee correctness; the estimate rules out large errors, not small ones.
activities.rationale: Treating estimation as a check done independently of the exact method targets the core misconception of recomputing to verify, and the use of a deliberately wrong answer makes 'how can you tell without redoing it?' concrete; choosing between nearest 100 and nearest 1,000 practises matching the grain to the context.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils use rounding to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, levels of accuracy
Computational estimation is a distinct competence used to judge reasonableness (order-of-magnitude checking), and appropriate precision is context-dependent
learnerActions: Take a completed sum with its answer, e.g. 47,832 + 23,156 = 3,988.
Round each number to a useful grain (nearest 1,000: about 48,000 and about 23,000) WITHOUT recomputing the exact sum.
Add the rounded numbers to get a ballpark of about 71,000.
State whether the given answer is possible: 3,988 is nowhere near 71,000, so it must be wrong - perhaps a place-value, alignment or copying slip; the estimate shows that it is wrong, not why.
Decide, for a stated context, whether a nearest-100 or a nearest-1,000 estimate is the better grain, and justify which keeps enough discrimination to be a useful check.
Repeat with other answers, including one that is close to the estimate (e.g. 70,988) and judge whether 'close' is enough to trust.
Explain, in your own words, why this check catches the error faster than redoing the full algorithm.
activities.intendedInsight: An estimate is an independent order-of-magnitude check: it can PROVE an answer impossible in seconds without ever doing the exact calculation. An estimate is a deliberate ballpark, not a rival exact answer.

activities.title: Honest precision: choosing the right level of accuracy for the purpose
feedback: If a learner insists the exact figure is always best: ask who the figure is for and what they'll do with it; nobody counted every head in a crowd, so extra digits imply a certainty that doesn't exist.
If a learner accepts 'about 52 pounds' for a shop bill: money must balance exactly, so here precision is the point, not a preference.
If a learner rounds too coarsely or too finely: match the grain to the purpose - '50,000' may erase a meaningful difference, while rounding a crowd to the nearest 10 is pointlessly precise.
activities.rationale: Directly addresses the 'more accuracy is always better' misconception by framing accuracy as a justified choice across contrasting real contexts where precision is either spurious or essential.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils use rounding to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, levels of accuracy
Computational estimation is a distinct competence used to judge reasonableness (order-of-magnitude checking), and appropriate precision is context-dependent
learnerActions: Consider a context, e.g. a newspaper reporting a football crowd. Decide whether it should print '52,000' or '51,847', and say why.
Argue that a crowd figure is inherently approximate, so '52,000' communicates the scale honestly while '51,847' implies a false precision nobody actually counted.
Contrast with a shop totting up a customer's bill: decide whether 'about 52 pounds' is acceptable and explain why money (and any count that must balance) needs exactness.
Rank several context cards (crowd / money / distance / stock count) by how much precision each honestly needs, giving a reason for each.
Identify a case where rounding a crowd to '50,000' would be TOO rough - when might that coarse figure hide something that matters?
activities.intendedInsight: The right level of accuracy is a decision with reasons tied to purpose and audience - not 'more digits is always better'. Spurious precision can be misleading; appropriate rounding can be more honest.

activities.title: Convince the sceptic (spoken reasoning)
feedback: Reward reasoning that separates the ballpark role of the estimate from the exact answer, and that ties precision to purpose.
Press any claim that an estimate 'failed' because it wasn't equal, or that exactness is universally better.

If a learner treats estimate-checking and choosing accuracy as unrelated tricks, prompt them to see both as one question - 'is this number sensible for its purpose?' - so they can transfer the habit to a new context.
activities.rationale: Reasonableness and appropriate-accuracy judgements are genuinely dialogic; an in-role 'convince me' exchange exercises the justification directly, surfaces thinking for discussion, and targets the partial-level state of holding the two ideas apart.
sourceClaims: Computational estimation is a distinct competence used to judge reasonableness (order-of-magnitude checking), and appropriate precision is context-dependent
learnerActions: In role with a sceptical editor/partner, justify out loud why a proposed answer must be impossible, using only an estimate.
Argue, when challenged, why '52,000' is the honest figure to print for a crowd and why a bill demands exact pounds and pence.
Respond to follow-up challenges: 'Could an answer be close to your estimate and still be wrong?' and 'How close is close enough to trust?'
Explain how the estimate check and the accuracy choice are the same underlying habit - asking whether a number is sensible for its purpose.
activities.intendedInsight: Judging reasonableness and defending a level of accuracy is reasoning you can articulate and defend, not just a computed value; the two moves are one habit, not separate tricks.

activities.title: Quick checks: spot the impossible answer and sort by needed precision
feedback: For a correct selection, ask the learner to say how they knew without the exact sum.
A recognition response shows which option was chosen but does not by itself show the learner could build the estimate or justify the accuracy level, so always ask for the 'why'.
activities.rationale: Selection items make the curriculum skills (rounding to check, choosing accuracy) assessable, but recognition-only responses do not elicit the independent construction of an estimate or a justified accuracy choice, so pair them with brief reasoning.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils use rounding to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, levels of accuracy
learnerActions: Given an estimate, select which of several proposed answers is impossible (e.g. an answer near 4,000 when the estimate is about 71,000).
Sort contexts into 'needs an exact figure' vs 'a rounded figure is honest'.
For each choice, briefly state the reason rather than only choosing the option.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising impossible answers and matching precision to context are checkable skills; adding a short reason connects them to the underlying judgement.

constraints: Estimation must be taught as a CHECK performed independently of the exact method - never by repeating the exact calculation, which can easily repeat the same error (especially a misunderstanding of the method) and so may not catch it.

Round to a level that keeps useful discrimination (e.g. nearest 1,000 for five-digit sums, not nearest 10,000); choosing between nearest 100 and nearest 1,000 is itself a reasoned, context-dependent decision.
An estimate is a deliberate ballpark; being near the exact answer is correct, not an error. 'Close to the estimate' rules out large errors but does not guarantee the exact answer is right.
Accuracy is a decision justified by purpose and audience, not 'more digits = better'; both spurious precision and over-coarse rounding are wrong for their context.

Recognition/selection tasks confirm a choice but do not by themselves show the learner can independently generate an estimate or justify a precision level - pair them with spoken or written reasoning.

Scaffolds such as a gauge, dial, number-line bracket, or tap-to-reveal poster are aids to make the mechanism visible; the objective is the learner's own judgement, so fade them as learners articulate the reasoning unaided.
Treat estimate-as-check and accuracy-by-purpose as one connected habit; a learner who performs each in isolation but cannot link them has only a partial grasp.
Context-dependent precision claims (e.g. whether '50,000' is too rough) depend on the specific purpose and must be reasoned per case, not applied as a fixed rule.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 47,832 + 23,156 = 70,988 (exact); 48,000 + 23,000 = 71,000 (estimate) - consistent across the source. The impossible answers 3,988 and 3,421 each sit well over an order of magnitude below 71,000 and ~50,000 respectively, consistent with a place-value/alignment slip; retained as given.

The source's evidence line 'Identify that a calculated answer of 3,421 cannot be correct because the estimate gives approximately 50,000' names no addends, so the ~50,000 estimate cannot be independently checked here; used only as a generic 'order of magnitude out' illustration and kept out of any learner-facing option.

Interactive examples from the original (answer-checker 'bench', gauge swinging to a red IMPOSSIBLE zone, context dial for money/crowd/distance, number-line bracket, tap-to-reveal poster) are preserved as optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not as mandatory mechanisms.

Original 'poor fit' claim that a 3D/spatial treatment 'adds nothing' was not carried over as a universal law; the topic is simply judgement about number, so spatial manipulation is not the focus here.
The source's partial response level (treating estimate-as-check and accuracy-by-purpose as separate tricks) is addressed in the dialogic activity's actions and feedback.

Activity 4's cited curriculum claim supports naming the assessed skills only; the recognition-only limitation is stated as an objective affordance, not as claimed source-backed efficacy of any medium.

probeDeeper: Your estimate was about 71,000 and the real answer is 70,988 - does that small difference mean your estimate was wrong?
Could an answer be close to your estimate and still be wrong? How close is 'close enough' to trust it?
When would rounding a crowd to '50,000' be TOO rough - when might that hide something that matters?
For a shop totting up a customer's bill, would 'about 52 pounds' be an acceptable level of accuracy? Why not?
assess.correctAnswer: Strong reasoning rounds each number (about 48,000 + 23,000 = 71,000), so any answer near 4,000 is impossible - it is an order of magnitude out, probably a place-value or alignment slip - and this is spotted WITHOUT the exact sum. On accuracy: a crowd figure is inherently approximate, so '52,000' communicates the scale honestly and '51,847' implies a false precision nobody counted; but for money, or counts that must balance, exactness is the point. The right level of accuracy depends on the PURPOSE, not on having more digits.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks a good estimate should equal the exact answer, so calls 71,000 'wrong' because the real answer is 70,988
errorPatterns.nextMove: Discuss: an estimate is a deliberate ballpark, not a rival answer; its job is to catch big errors, and being near (not equal) is exactly right.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Objects that the estimate 'doesn't match'; treats the estimate as a failed exact calculation

errorPatterns.pattern: Insists on recomputing the sum exactly to check it, rather than estimating
errorPatterns.nextMove: Discuss why an independent quick estimate catches errors that redoing the same method would just repeat; contrast the two as checks.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reaches for the full algorithm again when asked how to tell the answer is wrong

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes exact is always better - insists the newspaper print 51,847 and cannot see when rounding is appropriate
errorPatterns.nextMove: Discuss audience and purpose; surface spurious precision (nobody counted every head); contrast with a shop bill where exactness matters.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rejects '52,000' as 'not accurate enough' regardless of purpose

errorPatterns.pattern: Rounds to an unhelpful level - checks a five-digit sum to the nearest 10,000 (losing all discrimination) or rounds a crowd to the nearest 10
errorPatterns.nextMove: Discuss matching the rounding grain to the question: coarse enough to be quick, fine enough to still tell a right answer from a wrong one.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Chooses a rounding grain that is far too coarse or too fine for the question

responseLevels.gap: Can only check by recomputing exactly; treats accuracy as 'more digits is better'; cannot use an estimate to judge an answer.
responseLevels.full: Uses the estimate as an independent order-of-magnitude check AND justifies the level of accuracy by purpose/audience, transferring to a new context (money exact, crowd rounded) and explaining why.
responseLevels.partial: Can produce an estimate and see 3,988 is wrong, OR can say a crowd figure is approximate - but treats these as separate tricks; lists the ideas without connecting estimate-as-check to accuracy-fits-purpose, and cannot choose the right grain for a new context.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A pupil works out 47,832 + 23,156 and writes 3,988. Without doing the exact sum yourself, how could you tell straight away that this answer must be wrong? Then a different question: if a newspaper reports the crowd at a football match, should it print '52,000' or '51,847' - and why? Talk me through your thinking on both.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who can only compute must redo the sum to judge it; strong reasoning uses the estimate as an independent order-of-magnitude check and recognises accuracy as purpose-dependent. This is surfaced for DISCUSSION - it reveals how the child thinks about number, not a single right/wrong mark.

sources.claim: Year 5 pupils use rounding to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, levels of accuracy
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum, Mathematics Programmes of Study, Year 5 Number - addition and subtraction

sources.claim: Computational estimation is a distinct competence used to judge reasonableness (order-of-magnitude checking), and appropriate precision is context-dependent
sources.source: Sowder, 'Estimation and number sense' in Grouws (ed.) Handbook of Research on Mathematics Teaching and Learning (1992); NCTM number-sense standards

pedagogy.summary: A quarter is ONE OF FOUR EQUAL parts of a whole. It extends halving: fold in half and half again gives four equal parts (the IES 'powers of two' route). Quarters apply to single objects, lengths, and sets (a quarter of 12 = share into four equal groups, take one). Four quarters recompose the whole, and two quarters make a half — the seed of equivalence.
bestPractices: Reach quarters by repeated halving (halve, then halve each half) before free four-way partitioning — IES powers-of-two progression
Insist on four EQUAL parts; check by matching/overlaying
Work quarters of sets by sharing into four equal groups (not making groups of four)
Name and count: 'four quarters make one whole', 'two quarters make a half'
Use continuous and discrete models so 'a quarter' is not tied to one shape
keyRepresentations: A shape folded in half then half again into four matching parts
A strip/length marked into four equal parts
12 counters shared into four equal groups
Four quarters reassembling into the whole; two quarters overlaying a half
commonMisconceptions: Any four pieces count as quarters regardless of size (equal-parts missing)
Muddling the names — calling a quarter 'a half', or vice versa
A quarter of a set found by making groups OF four rather than four equal groups
Thinking a quarter is bigger than a half because 'four is more than two' (whole-number bias, developing here)

learn.summary: A quarter is one of FOUR EQUAL parts of a whole. Reach quarters by repeated halving (fold in half, then halve each half, giving four matching parts in total), work them on single objects, lengths, and sets (a quarter of 12 = share into four equal groups and take one), and show that four quarters recompose the whole while two quarters make a half — seeding equivalence. The core learner actions are partitioning/folding to make equal parts and sharing a set into four equal groups, with naming and counting attached to the number of equal parts.

activities.title: Halve, then halve again: making four equal quarters
feedback: If a learner accepts any four pieces as quarters, have them overlay the pieces: unequal pieces do not match, so they are not quarters.
When all four parts match after folding twice, confirm: 'Four equal parts — each one is a quarter, and all four make the whole.'
If two quarters joined line up exactly with the other two quarters (or with a half of the same shape), name it: 'Two quarters make a half.'
Use overlaying as a practical check — real paper folds have slight thickness and are only approximate, so look for parts that clearly match rather than treating the overlay as an exact proof.
activities.rationale: The IES/WWC powers-of-two route builds fourths by halving then halving again before free four-way partitioning, and insisting on equal parts (checked by matching) targets the common error of counting pieces regardless of size. A live fold/partition lets the child test equality rather than take it on trust; a static poster of quartered objects can show the result but does not let the child verify equality themselves.
sourceClaims: Quarters/fourths are reached via a halving (powers-of-two) strategy - halve then halve again - before partitioning into other numbers of parts
Year 1 pupils recognise, find, and name a quarter as one of four equal parts of an object, shape, or quantity
learnerActions: Fold (or partition) a symmetrical shape such as a square, rectangle or circle in half, then fold each half in half again so the shape opens into four matching parts.
Check the four parts are equal by matching or overlaying them; only equal parts count as quarters.
Count aloud: 'four quarters make one whole'.
Join two of the quarters to make a half, then place that pair over the other two quarters (or over an identical shape folded once into halves) to see that 'two quarters make a half'.
Compare with a shape cut into four UNEQUAL pieces and explain why those are not quarters.
activities.intendedInsight: A quarter is one of four EQUAL parts; repeated halving is a reliable way to produce them, four quarters rebuild the whole, and two quarters together make a half.

activities.title: A quarter of a set: sharing 12 into four equal groups
feedback: If a learner makes groups of four (ending with three groups) or hands over four objects, redirect: the 4 in 'a quarter' means FOUR equal groups — share all 12 into four hoops and take one.
When the four groups are equal, confirm the count: 'Each group has 3, so a quarter of 12 is 3.'
If groups are unequal, prompt: 'Are all four groups the same? Move counters until they match.'
activities.rationale: Working quarters of discrete sets by equal sharing (not grouping-of-four) addresses a specific documented confusion and supports finding a quarter of a quantity as required by the Year 1 curriculum. Discovering 3 by sharing rather than guessing makes the division meaning concrete. An optional set mode that flags unequal groups until they match makes the equal-sharing requirement visible.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils recognise, find, and name a quarter as one of four equal parts of an object, shape, or quantity
learnerActions: Take 12 counters and share them, one at a time, into four equal groups (four hoops or circles).
Keep going until all 12 are placed and every group has the same number.
Report how many are in one group — 'a quarter of 12 is 3'.
Contrast with making groups OF four and notice that gives three groups, which is a different question.
activities.intendedInsight: A quarter of a set is found by sharing the whole set into four equal groups and taking one group — not by making groups of four.

activities.title: Naming by counting equal parts: halves vs quarters
feedback: If a learner calls a quarter 'a half' (or vice versa), count the equal parts together and re-attach the name to the count.
If a learner thinks a quarter is bigger than a half because 'four is more than two', overlay a quarter on a half of the SAME shape to show the quarter is smaller.
Confirm correct naming by restating the count: 'Four equal parts, so each is a quarter.'
activities.rationale: Explicit naming of quarters is needed because some children call all fractional parts 'one-half'; linking the name to the count and connecting half-to-quarters by halving addresses both the naming muddle and the whole-number-bias idea that more pieces means a bigger piece.
sourceClaims: Some children think all fractional parts are called 'one-half', so explicit naming of quarters is needed
learnerActions: Partition one shape into two equal parts and name each a 'half'; partition another into four equal parts and name each a 'quarter'.
Count the equal parts aloud and attach the name to the count: two equal parts = halves, four equal parts = quarters.
Use halve-then-halve-again on the same shape to see how a half becomes two quarters.
Decide, for a correctly-made part, whether it is a half or a quarter and justify by counting the equal parts.
activities.intendedInsight: The fraction name follows the number of equal parts: two equal parts are halves, four equal parts are quarters; of the SAME whole, a quarter is smaller than a half.

activities.title: Sorting quarters from not-quarters
feedback: If a learner marks a four-way UNEQUAL cut as 'quarters', point to the pieces: 'Count them — four pieces, but are they all the same size? If not, they are not quarters.'
Reinforce the fix: for a shape, fold in half and then in half again so all four parts match; for a set, share it into four groups with the same number in each.
For the quarter-of-12 question, confirm by sharing 12 into four equal groups to check the answer is 3.
activities.rationale: A recognition/sorting task that pairs the correct NUMBER of pieces (four) with unequal sizes discriminates children who merely count pieces from those who require equal parts. A sort of this kind can check and prompt discussion of classification, but on its own it does not require the child to independently construct four equal parts or share a set, so pair it with the folding and sharing activities.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils recognise, find, and name a quarter as one of four equal parts of an object, shape, or quantity
learnerActions: Look at several shapes and sets, some divided into four EQUAL parts and some into four UNEQUAL parts.
Sort each into 'quarters' or 'not quarters', including a tricky case cut into four clearly unequal pieces.
For each 'not quarters' case, say what is wrong (the parts are not equal) and how to fix it (fold in half then half again, or divide into four equal parts).
Answer: 'A quarter of 12 is ___' and explain how you know.
activities.intendedInsight: Having four pieces is not enough — the four parts must be equal to be quarters.

constraints: Insist on four EQUAL parts; check by matching or overlaying rather than by eye alone, treating the overlay as a practical check (real paper folds have slight thickness and are approximate), not an exact mathematical proof.
Work quarters of sets by sharing into four equal groups, not by making groups of four.
Use both continuous models (shapes, strips/lengths) and discrete models (sets of counters) so 'a quarter' is not tied to one shape or layout.

Sorting/recognition tasks can check whether a child requires equal parts and prompt discussion, but do not by themselves require the child to generate four equal parts or share a set; use them alongside hands-on folding and sharing.
A reference poster of quartered objects can show the result but does not let the child test equality; use it as support, not as the main way to learn.
Introduce the half/quarter link ('two quarters make a half', 'four quarters make a whole') as the seed of equivalence at an age-appropriate level, not as formal equivalent-fraction rules.

When comparing the SIZE of a quarter and a half as portions, compare them of the SAME whole — of that same whole a quarter is smaller than a half; as numbers, fractions remain comparable and a quarter is always less than a half.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labelled a conversation artefact 'poor' ('built through folding and sharing, not dialogue, at this age') and a 3D artefact 'poor' ('planar partitioning; 3D adds nothing'). These are catalog-fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws, and are not asserted here as universal claims. Talk/naming remains valuable alongside hands-on work, and planar partitioning is the most natural model, not proof that other media add nothing.

Self-audit: a quarter of 12 is 3 (12 shared into four equal groups); making groups OF four instead yields three groups — these are different operations, correctly distinguished in the activities. A quarter is smaller than a half of the SAME whole; the 'four is more than two' reasoning is explicitly corrected rather than propagated.

Fraction-of-area idealisation assumes exactly equal parts; paper/card folds have slight thickness and real folds are approximate, so 'matching/overlaying' is a practical equality check (stated in the folding activity and constraint), not an exact proof.

The 'snap green when parts match' and 'refuse done until groups are equal' behaviours are retained as optional feedback mechanisms that make equality visible; they are examples, not mandatory tooling.

probeDeeper: How many quarters make one whole?
Is a quarter bigger or smaller than a half of the same shape - how do you know?
Show me a quarter of these 12 counters - how did you split them?
If I fold the paper in half and then in half again, what have I made?
assess.correctAnswer: No - the pieces are not equal, so they are not quarters. Quarters are four EQUAL parts; fold in half and then in half again (or divide into four equal parts) so all four match. Four equal quarters make the whole square.

errorPatterns.pattern: Any four pieces are quarters - 'there are four pieces, so they're quarters' - equal-size ignored
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fold two identical squares, one into equal quarters and one unequally, and overlay to show only equal parts match.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes - there are four pieces, so they're quarters
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says each piece of the unequal four-way cut is a quarter

errorPatterns.pattern: Muddles the fraction names - calls a quarter 'a half' or a half 'a quarter'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the equal parts aloud and attach the name to the count (two equal parts = halves; four = quarters); halve-then-halve to link them.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Uses the wrong name for a correctly-made part

errorPatterns.pattern: A quarter of a set found by making groups OF four, not four equal groups
errorPatterns.nextMove: Emphasise the 4 means FOUR equal groups; share all 12 into four hoops and take one.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For a quarter of 12, makes groups of four (getting three groups) or hands over four objects

responseLevels.gap: Counts four pieces as quarters regardless of equality, or confuses the name with 'half'.
responseLevels.full: States a quarter is one of FOUR EQUAL parts, makes them by halving twice, knows four quarters make a whole (and two make a half), and finds a quarter of a set by sharing into four equal groups.
responseLevels.partial: Knows quarters must be equal for a shape but cannot find a quarter of a set, or cannot reliably make four equal parts.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a square divided into four pieces that are clearly different sizes. Ask: 'Is each of these pieces a quarter of the square? How do you know?' Then ask: 'How could you fold a square to be sure of making four quarters, and how many quarters make the whole square?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The right NUMBER of pieces (four) with unequal sizes separates children who count pieces from children who require equal parts. Tier 2 checks they can generate quarters (via halving) and know four quarters make the whole - not just recognise a picture.

sources.claim: Quarters/fourths are reached via a halving (powers-of-two) strategy - halve then halve again - before partitioning into other numbers of parts
sources.source: IES/WWC Fractions Practice Guide (Siegler et al., 2010, NCEE 2010-4039), Recommendation 1

sources.claim: Year 1 pupils recognise, find, and name a quarter as one of four equal parts of an object, shape, or quantity

sources.claim: Some children think all fractional parts are called 'one-half', so explicit naming of quarters is needed
