pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 10–11 — read, write, order and compare numbers up to 10,000,000 and determine the value of each digit.
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y6 'read, write, order and compare numbers up to 10 000 000 and determine the value of each digit.'
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): 4.NBT.A.2 (read/write multi-digit whole numbers using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form; compare with >, =, <) extended by 5.NBT place value; CCSS does not name a 10,000,000 ceiling explicitly.
• Operational details: Group digits into three-digit PERIODS (ones, thousands, millions) separated by commas/spaces; read each period as a three-digit number followed by its period name. Stress that the comma structure, not the raw digit count, drives reading. Handle placeholder zeros within and between periods (7,045,200). Order by scanning from the most significant digit; align by periods.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): 'Write 4,302,561 in words.' Tier B: 'State the value of the 7 in 7,045,200.' Tier C: 'Order four seven-digit numbers and justify using the leading digits.'
bestPractices: Teach reading by three-digit periods (ones/thousands/millions): read the period as a 3-digit number, then say its name — the comma grouping is the reading tool
Foreground internal and cross-period placeholder zeros (7,045,200) as the main difficulty; require the child to hold empty places
Order by a most-significant-digit-first scan with periods aligned, resolving ties one place at a time
Move fluently between numeral, words and expanded form, and value-of-a-digit statements ('the 7 is worth seven million')
Use real 7-digit contexts (populations, distances, view counts) so magnitude is meaningful, not just symbol-copying
keyRepresentations: Period-grouped place-value chart with Millions | Thousands | Ones panels
Three-pane translator: numeral ↔ words ↔ expanded form
Comma/space separators as period boundaries
Number line / magnitude bar for ordering seven-digit values
commonMisconceptions: Misreading placeholder zeros — reading 7,045,200 as 'seven hundred forty-five thousand two hundred' by dropping empty places
Losing period boundaries and reading digit-by-digit for very large numbers
Confusing face value with place value (the 7 as 'seven' not 'seven million')
Assuming more digits always means larger without aligning periods when digit counts match
Inserting or omitting 'and' / mis-segmenting when writing in words

learn.summary: For ages 10–11: read, write, order and compare whole numbers up to 10,000,000 and state the value of each digit. The core difficulty is the three-digit PERIOD structure (ones, thousands, millions) and holding placeholder zeros (e.g. 7,045,200). Learners should build numbers, translate fluently between numeral, words and expanded form, state digit values as place value (the 7 in 7,045,200 is 'seven million'), and order by a most-significant-digit-first scan with periods aligned, resolving ties one place at a time.

activities.title: Period builder with live three-way echo
feedback: If the words and the numeral stop corresponding (e.g. reading 7,045,200 as 'seven hundred forty-five thousand two hundred' by dropping the internal zero), rebuild in the period-labelled grid and read each three-digit group, then attach its period name.

If a digit's value is misnamed (e.g. the 7 as 'seven' or 'seven hundred thousand'), count columns from the right in threes to find the period, or read the whole number aloud so the 7 is heard as 'seven million'.
Point out explicitly that the internal zero in 7,045,200 is doing a job: it holds a place even though it is not spoken.
activities.rationale: A live builder that groups digits into periods and simultaneously echoes numeral, words and expanded form is intended to make the period structure and placeholder-zero handling operative as the child constructs numbers, rather than only described. Linked numeral/words/expanded panels and live recomputation are optional interaction examples that make the reading mechanism concrete. The cited standards describe the content and the numeral/number-name/expanded-form representations being practised; they are not evidence that this interaction is more effective than another medium.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils read, write, order and compare numbers up to 10,000,000 and determine the value of each digit.
4.NBT.A.2: read and write multi-digit whole numbers using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form; compare using >, =, <.
learnerActions: Set each digit onto a place-value chart labelled Millions | Thousands | Ones, grouped into three-digit periods.

As each digit is placed, watch the number appear three ways at once: the comma-grouped numeral (e.g. 7,045,200), the words read period by period ('seven million, forty-five thousand, two hundred'), and the expanded form.

Deliberately build numbers with internal and cross-period placeholder zeros (e.g. set the hundred-thousands place — the leading digit of the thousands period — to 0, as in 7,045,200) and observe how the words panel skips the empty place without dropping the period boundary.
State aloud, for a chosen digit, its full place value (e.g. 'the 7 is worth seven million').
activities.intendedInsight: The comma/period grouping — not the raw digit count — is what lets you read a large number aloud; each nonzero three-digit period is read as a number then given its period name (the ones period has no spoken name, and a period that is all zeros, as in 7,000,200, is skipped entirely), and an internal zero silently holds a column without being spoken.

activities.title: Write, value and order on paper (consolidation)
feedback: If ordering is done by length or first digit only, align the numbers vertically by place and compare digit by digit; with equal leading digits, keep comparing rightward until a difference appears — here 3,204,000 and 3,240,000 agree until the ten-thousands digit (0 vs 4) within the thousands period.
After writing in words, re-check the period breaks: 'How did you know where to put the comma/period breaks?'
Probe the placeholder zero: 'What is the value of the 0 in 7,045,200 — does it do anything?' and extend with 'Write the number that is one more than 4,302,561 in words.'
activities.rationale: These read/write/value/order tasks are directly assessable and consolidate the notation-heavy procedure. The near-identical ordering set (same leading digits, differing in the thousands period) discriminates place-by-place comparison from shortcuts like length or first digit. These are proposed consolidation tasks, not validated interventions.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils read, write, order and compare numbers up to 10,000,000 and determine the value of each digit.
learnerActions: Write 4,302,561 in words (answer: four million, three hundred two thousand, five hundred sixty-one).
State the value of the 7 in 7,045,200 (answer: seven million).
For the ordering, align the numbers by place and compare left-to-right, moving right only when digits tie; say which digit finally decided between 3,204,000 and 3,240,000.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading, writing, valuing and ordering seven-digit numbers all rely on the same period structure and on place-by-place comparison, including when leading digits agree.

activities.title: Labelled reference number with tap-to-reveal periods
feedback: If a learner relies only on this fixed example, move them to constructing their own numbers so they practise assembling arbitrary values and resolving orderings themselves.
activities.rationale: A fixed, labelled example with tap-to-reveal period names and digit values is a useful reference anchor; it supports recognition and recall but does not by itself require the learner to assemble arbitrary numbers or resolve orderings. Pair it with build/write tasks.
learnerActions: Study a labelled seven-digit number (e.g. 4,302,561) and tap each three-digit period to reveal its name and read-out.
Tap an individual digit to reveal its place value.
Use this as a reference anchor while writing or ordering other numbers.
activities.intendedInsight: A clearly period-labelled example makes the millions/thousands/ones structure and per-digit place values visible as a stable reference.

activities.title: Dictation and 'why isn't the zero spoken?' discussion
feedback: If the dictated number is written with wrong grouping (especially around an internal zero), rebuild it in the period grid and align each spoken group to a period.
Prompt the learner to justify comma/period placement rather than count digits.
activities.rationale: Spoken dictation plus responsive discussion can probe the reasoning behind placeholder zeros and period breaks; it may complement, rather than replace, interactive construction of the notation. This is a proposed activity, not a validated intervention.
learnerActions: Listen to a mentor dictate a large number in words and write it as a comma-grouped numeral.
Explain why a placeholder zero (e.g. in 7,045,200) is not spoken yet must still be written.
Discuss how the comma/period breaks map to the spoken words.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating why an internal zero holds a place without being spoken is intended to support and strengthen the learner's grasp of the period structure.

constraints: Target objective: read, write, order and compare whole numbers up to 10,000,000 and determine each digit's value, including numbers with internal and cross-period placeholder zeros.
State digit values as place value (e.g. 'seven million'), not face value ('seven').
Order by scanning most-significant-digit-first with periods aligned, resolving ties one place at a time; do not order by digit count or first digit alone when lengths/leading digits match.

The tap-to-reveal labelled number is a reference scaffold: it supports recognition but does not elicit independent construction of arbitrary numbers or ordering decisions; pair it with build/write tasks. This is a narrow affordance limit, not a claim that reference examples cannot teach.

Recognition-only responses (e.g. multiple-choice value-of-digit) can assess but do not by themselves require the learner to construct words or resolve an ordering; include production tasks (writing in words, assembling numbers, ordering).
Use real seven-digit contexts (populations, distances, view counts) so magnitude is meaningful rather than symbol-copying.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source marks the UK DfE National Curriculum claim as verified=true and the CCSS 4.NBT.A.2 claim as verified=false; retained as provided without re-checking.
The source observes that CCSS does not explicitly name a 10,000,000 ceiling; the upper bound comes from the UK Y6 standard. Treated as a scope note, not a universal claim.

The legacy row rated 3D as 'poor' and framed a quiz as only a 'co-consolidator'; these are catalog fit judgements, not pedagogical laws, and have been expressed as affordance/limit statements rather than claims that any medium cannot teach.

The original correct answer writes 'three hundred two thousand' without 'and'; UK convention often inserts 'and' (e.g. 'three hundred and two thousand, five hundred and sixty-one'). Retained as given; the pedagogy notes mis-insertion/omission of 'and' as a known writing error.

The curriculum source claims attached to the builder activity support the content and representations (numeral/number name/expanded form), not the effectiveness of the interactive medium; efficacy wording is kept conservative throughout.

probeDeeper: How did you know where to put the commas when writing it in words?
What is the value of the 0 in 7,045,200 — does it do anything?
For the ordering, which digit finally decided between 3,204,000 and 3,240,000?
Write me the number that is one more than 4,302,561 in words.
assess.correctAnswer: (1) four million, three hundred two thousand, five hundred sixty-one. (2) seven million. (3) 3,024,000; 3,204,000; 3,240,000; 3,420,000.

errorPatterns.pattern: Period/grouping error — misreads 4,302,561 (e.g. 'four hundred thirty thousand...') or writes it as digits with wrong grouping, especially around the internal zero.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild the number in a period-labelled place-value grid (millions | thousands | ones); read each three-digit group then attach its period name.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Words and digits do not correspond; the millions or thousands period is mislabelled.

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscounts the place when valuing a digit — gives the 7 in 7,045,200 as 'seven hundred thousand' or just 'seven'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count columns from the right in threes to name the period, or read the whole number aloud so the 7 is heard as 'seven million'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Digit value is off by one or more powers of ten; child counts columns unreliably.

errorPatterns.pattern: Orders by length or first digit only — with equal leading digits, compares wrongly or guesses, ignoring later place values.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Align the numbers vertically by place and compare left-to-right digit by digit, moving right only when digits tie.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Ordering breaks on the near-identical numbers; child stops comparing once early digits match.

responseLevels.gap: Misgroups periods, misvalues digits by powers of ten, or orders by length/first digit.
responseLevels.full: Reads, writes, values and orders seven-digit numbers reliably, using period structure and left-to-right place comparison, including numbers with internal zeros.
responseLevels.partial: Reads and writes most seven-digit numbers but stumbles on internal zeros or on comparing numbers that agree in the leading digits.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Three tasks on paper. (1) Write 4,302,561 in words. (2) State the value of the 7 in 7,045,200. (3) Order these smallest to largest: 3,240,000; 3,204,000; 3,024,000; 3,420,000.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watch how the child handles the periods and the internal zeros. Reading to millions requires grouping digits into millions/thousands/ones periods and holding placeholder zeros; the near-identical ordering set (same leading digits, differing in the thousands period) exposes whether comparison is done place-by-place or by a shortcut like length or first digit.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 8–9y; understand division as an unknown-factor problem: 32 ÷ 8 = ? is the same as 8 × ? = 32 — division and multiplication are inverse operations.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y3 'write and calculate mathematical statements for multiplication and division using the multiplication tables'; Y2 established using the inverse and that ×÷ are related; children use known × facts to answer ÷.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.OA.6 — 'Understand division as an unknown-factor problem, e.g., find 32 ÷ 8 by finding the number that makes 32 when multiplied by 8.'
• Operational details — the goal is that children STOP treating ÷ as a separate skill and reach for a known × fact instead: to find 32÷8 they ask 'eight times what is 32?'. This is the engine of division fluency and rests on fact families / the multiplication–division inverse. Use the array/rectangle (one side known, other unknown) and the fact-family triangle (8, 4, 32 generating 8×4=32, 4×8=32, 32÷8=4, 32÷4=8) as the core models.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8): rewrite 32÷8=? as 8×?=32 and solve using a known fact. Tier B (age 8–9): given a fact-family triangle, write all four related ×÷ facts. Tier C (age 9): explain WHY knowing 6×7=42 instantly gives both 42÷6 and 42÷7, using the inverse relationship.
bestPractices: Teach the fact-family triangle (three numbers → two × and two ÷ facts) so children experience × and ÷ as one linked system, not two.
Reframe every division as a missing-factor question aloud: '32÷8' → 'eight times what is 32?' — make this verbal move the default strategy.
Use the array with one dimension hidden: 32 dots in 8 rows, cover the columns, and ask how many per row — the unknown factor is literally the missing side.
Practise the inverse both directions with the same trio so children check division by multiplying back (8×4=32 confirms 32÷8=4).
Deliberately connect to fluency: as × tables are memorised, harvest the ÷ facts for free rather than learning them separately.
keyRepresentations: Fact-family triangle (the 8/4/32 trio generating all four ×÷ statements)
Array/rectangle with one side unknown — division as finding the missing dimension
Bar model — whole 32 split into 8 equal parts, each part the unknown factor
Number line — how many 8-hops reach 32 (unknown number of jumps)
commonMisconceptions: Seeing ÷ and × as unrelated, so learning division facts from scratch instead of deriving them from known products.
Writing the fact family wrongly by treating ÷ as commutative (32÷4 and 4÷32 as the same).
Getting the missing-factor direction confused (solving 8×?=32 as 8×32).
Not using multiplication to check division answers, so errors go uncaught.
Believing the unknown must be the largest number in the trio.

learn.summary: For ages 8–9, build the understanding that division is an unknown-factor problem: 32 ÷ 8 = ? is the same question as 8 × ? = 32, because multiplication and division are inverse operations. The core move is to reframe every division aloud as a missing-factor multiplication ('eight times what makes 32?') and to use known times-table facts to derive division answers rather than learning division separately. Core models are the fact-family triangle, the array with one dimension hidden, the bar model, and the number line of equal hops.

activities.title: Fact-family array: grow the eights until you reach 32
feedback: If a learner grows past 32 (e.g. to 40, which is 5 columns), ask them to look at the total and step back one column to land exactly on 32.
When all four statements appear, prompt: 'Point to the multiplication you used and the division it just answered — how are they the same picture?'
If they treat 8×4 and 32÷8 as separate problems, cover the columns again and ask them to predict the division answer before revealing.
activities.rationale: Letting the learner physically grow groups of 8 and watch the missing dimension and the four fact-family statements appear together ties division concretely to a known multiplication, directly targeting the misconception that × and ÷ are unrelated. The slider/shutter updating together is an optional interaction example that makes the inverse concrete; a hidden-dimension array drawn on paper with counters works similarly.
sourceClaims: 3.OA.6 requires understanding division as an unknown-factor problem (find 32÷8 by finding the number that makes 32 when multiplied by 8).
Fact families and the multiplication–division inverse should be used so division facts are derived from known products, supporting fluency.
learnerActions: Face the question '32 ÷ 8 = ?' alongside a grid showing 8 rows whose columns are hidden behind a shutter.
Instead of dividing, add columns of 8 one at a time, tracking the running total: 8, 16, 24, 32.
Stop when the total reaches 32 and count how many columns you added (4).
Reveal the full array and read off all four related facts together: 8×4=32, 4×8=32, 32÷8=4, 32÷4=8.
Say aloud what you just did: 'I found 32÷8 by asking how many 8s make 32.'
activities.intendedInsight: Division answers the question 'how many of this factor fit into the whole?' — it is multiplication with a missing factor, and the same array simultaneously shows the multiplication and its inverse division.

activities.title: Fact-family triangle: four facts from three numbers
feedback: If a learner writes '4÷32', point out that division is not commutative: the whole (32) is the amount being divided, so it comes first — the family gives 32÷4 and 32÷8, not 4÷32.

If a learner writes '32÷32', explain that the fact family for 8, 4 and 32 uses all three different numbers; the whole 32 is divided by one of its factors (8 or 4), not by itself, so 32÷32 is not one of these four facts.

If a learner assumes the hidden number must be the largest in the trio, show the triangle: here the whole 32 sits at the top and is the largest, yet when a base corner is hidden the missing number is a smaller factor (4 or 8) — the unknown is only the biggest when the top number itself is covered.
If they can state 8×4=32 but stall on 32÷4, prompt: 'The triangle has the same three numbers — which number is now hidden?'
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal or lift-the-flap triangle is a clean, memorable anchor for the four related facts and the inverse idea that learners can carry as a mental model. It consolidates structure but does not let learners vary the trio and watch the inverse hold across many cases, so pair it with the array activity.
sourceClaims: Fact families and the multiplication–division inverse should be used so division facts are derived from known products, supporting fluency.
Y3 pupils write and calculate mathematical statements for multiplication and division using the tables they know, using the inverse relationship established in Y2.
learnerActions: Draw or view a triangle with the product 32 at the top and the factors 8 and 4 at the base corners.
Cover one corner (say the 4) and say how you would find the hidden number using the other two.
Write all four related facts from the trio: 8×4=32, 4×8=32, 32÷8=4, 32÷4=8.
Repeat with a new trio, e.g. 6, 7, 42, writing all four statements (6×7=42, 7×6=42, 42÷6=7, 42÷7=6).
activities.intendedInsight: Three different numbers in a fact family (like 8, 4 and 32) give two multiplications and two divisions, so knowing one product gives you both divisions for free. When the two factors are the same (like 4, 4 and 16), there is just one multiplication and one division.

activities.title: Rewrite and check: division as missing factor
feedback: If a learner chooses a reversed form like 4÷32, ask which number is the whole being divided — that must come first in the division, so it should be 32÷4.
If a learner inverts to 8×32, prompt: 'Does 8 times 32 give 32? 8×32 is 256. We need the number that, times 8, makes 32 — that is 4.'

If a learner fills 8×?=32 by adding (e.g. '8 and 24 more makes 32'), restate it as 'how many eights are in 32?' and count equal groups — 8, 16, 24, 32 is four hops — so they build groups of 8, not a sum.
Praise multiplying back as a check: 'You confirmed 32÷8=4 by showing 8×4=32 — that catches mistakes.'
activities.rationale: These crisply checkable tasks consolidate the strategy and target the commutativity, wrong-direction, and additive misconceptions with specific prompts (4÷32, 8×32, adding to reach 32). This format verifies and consolidates the idea rather than building it from scratch, and does not show the array's missing side, so it follows the manipulation activities.
sourceClaims: Y3 pupils write and calculate mathematical statements for multiplication and division using the tables they know, using the inverse relationship established in Y2.
learnerActions: Rewrite each division as a missing-factor multiplication, e.g. 32÷8=? ↔ 8×□=32, then solve using a known fact.
Match each division fact to the multiplication fact that solves it.
Check each division answer by multiplying back (8×4=32 confirms 32÷8=4).
Spot the trap: decide whether '32÷8 = 8×32' is correct, and explain your reasoning.
activities.intendedInsight: Rewriting ÷ as missing-× and checking by multiplying back makes the inverse relationship a reliable, self-correcting strategy.

activities.title: Maths-detective talk: which fact helps?
feedback: If a learner starts counting or sharing, redirect: 'Before counting — what times 8 gives that number?'
If they explain the inverse clearly for 42, invite them to transfer it to a fresh trio to show it generalises.
activities.rationale: A Socratic partner can nudge the missing-factor move and make the verbal reframing habitual, which the pedagogy names as the default strategy. The underlying structure is best carried by the array/triangle, so dialogue supports but does not replace manipulation.
learnerActions: When given a division, answer the prompt 'which times-table fact you already know could help here?' before computing.
State the division as a spoken missing-factor question: '32÷8' becomes 'eight times what gives 32?'
Explain in your own words why knowing 6×7=42 instantly gives both 42÷6=7 and 42÷7=6.
activities.intendedInsight: Verbalising the missing-factor question makes reaching for a known multiplication the default first move for any division.

constraints: The rewrite-and-match-and-check format mainly verifies and consolidates; it does not elicit construction of the array model or show the missing dimension, so use it after hands-on work, not as the first exposure.
The static triangle anchors the four facts but does not let learners vary the trio and watch the inverse hold across many cases — pair it with the variable array.
Dialogue prompts support the verbal missing-factor habit but should accompany, not replace, manipulation of the array and triangle.

Division is not commutative: the whole (e.g. 32) must be the number being divided, so guard against the commutativity error 4÷32; also guard against 32÷32, which reuses one number and is not part of the 8/4/32 family.
The slider/shutter and tap-to-reveal are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete; the same learning can be done with counters, drawn arrays, and paper triangles.
Keep the missing-factor direction explicit: 8×?=32 is solved by finding the factor (4), not by computing 8×32 (=256) or by adding to reach 32.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One source claim (3.OA.6) is marked verified:false and two NCETM/standards claims are unverified in the original row; treat cited standards wording as legacy, not re-checked.

The original assessment reteach note 'the answer to a division is always SMALLER-or-equal to what you started with when sharing among many' is only true for dividing by a whole number greater than 1 and could mislead if generalised; it was not carried into learner-facing actions. Prefer rebuilding the fact triangle (product on top, factors at corners) to fix wrong-direction errors.
Arithmetic self-check: 8×4=32, 32÷8=4, 32÷4=8, 8×32=256, 5×8=40, and 6×7=42 with 42÷6=7, 42÷7=6 all verified correct as used in activities and feedback.

probeDeeper: You used 8 × 4 = 32. How does knowing that multiplication tell you the division answer?
If I change it to 32 ÷ 4, which fact helps now — and what will the answer be?
Write the whole fact family for 8, 4 and 32. Which two are multiplications and which two are divisions?
Someone says 32 ÷ 8 must be 8 × 32. Why is that not right?
assess.correctAnswer: 4. The child reframes 32 ÷ 8 as 'eight times WHAT makes 32?' — 8 × 4 = 32, so 32 ÷ 8 = 4 — because division asks for the missing factor, and multiplication and division are inverse operations that undo each other.

errorPatterns.pattern: finds the answer only by dealing out / repeated subtraction and cannot connect it to a multiplication fact — sees ÷ and × as unrelated procedures
errorPatterns.nextMove: lay out the same 32 in a 8×4 array; show the ONE array answers both 8×4=? and 32÷8=?; build a fact-family triangle so the inverse link is explicit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child solves 32÷8 by sharing counters but, asked which times-table fact helps, shrugs or starts a fresh count

errorPatterns.pattern: inverts the unknown-factor relationship — for 32÷8 reaches for '32 × 8' or picks the wrong fact family member
errorPatterns.nextMove: anchor on 'the answer to a division is always SMALLER-or-equal to what you started with when sharing among many' and rebuild the fact triangle: the product 32 sits at the top, 8 and the missing 4 at the corners.
errorPatterns.distractor: 8 (because 8 × 4 = 32, so I picked the 8)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child names a multiplication whose product is not 32 (e.g. 8×32) or multiplies the two given numbers

errorPatterns.pattern: reads the missing-factor equation 8 × ? = 32 but then adds to reach 32 (8 + 24) rather than multiplies
errorPatterns.nextMove: restate the box as 'how many EIGHTS in 32', count the eights (8,16,24,32 = four jumps) on a number line to bind it to groups, not addition.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child says '8 and then 24 more makes 32' when filling the box

responseLevels.gap: reaches an answer only by sharing/counting or gets it wrong; treats × and ÷ as unconnected; cannot supply a linked multiplication.
responseLevels.full: reframes the division as an unknown-factor multiplication, justifies it via the inverse relationship, generates the full fact family, and transfers to a new division using the same product.
responseLevels.partial: states 8 × 4 = 32 gives 4 for this item but cannot generalise — does not produce the reciprocal division (32÷4) from the same fact or articulate 'division finds the missing factor'.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a division: 32 ÷ 8 = ?. Solve it, but instead of sharing or counting, use a multiplication fact you already know. Which multiplication did you use, and why does that give you the answer to the division?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child can get 4 by skip-counting or sharing without seeing the inverse relationship; the demand to name the multiplication fact and explain WHY it answers the division exposes whether they hold division as an unknown-factor problem. A child who only knows division as 'sharing out' can compute but cannot state the linked multiplication as a reason.

pedagogy.summary: Tree diagrams (and sample-space grids and systematic listing) generate the full set of equally-likely outcomes for single and combined events, from which theoretical probability is favourable ÷ total. Students list outcomes (e.g. the 36 ordered results of two dice), draw trees with probabilities on the branches, MULTIPLY along a path (the AND rule) and ADD across paths (the OR rule), and adjust probabilities for without-replacement (dependent) events. The recurring conceptual hazard is assuming aggregated outcomes — like the eleven dice totals — are equally likely.
bestPractices: Build the complete sample space first (grid or list), respecting ORDER, so favourable/total rests on genuinely equally-likely outcomes
Confront the two-dice trap head-on: the eleven totals 2–12 are NOT equally likely; there are 36 equally-likely ordered outcomes
Teach the AND rule (multiply along a branch) and OR rule (add across paths) explicitly, and the complement shortcut for 'at least one'
For without-replacement problems, recompute the second-level branch probabilities from the reduced situation (dependent events)
Leave fractions uncancelled until the end so common denominators are available for adding paths
keyRepresentations: Sample-space grid / two-way table (e.g. 6×6 for two dice)
Systematic ordered listing of outcomes
Probability tree with values on branches; multiply along, add across
Reduced-denominator second branches for dependent events
commonMisconceptions: Assuming aggregated outcomes are equally likely — treating the eleven totals of two dice as each 1/11 (equiprobability bias)
Ignoring order when listing — counting 3+4 and 4+3 as one outcome, undercounting the sample space
Adding probabilities along a branch instead of multiplying (misapplying AND/OR)
Reusing the first-event probabilities on the second branch of a without-replacement (dependent) event

learn.summary: Students build complete, equally-likely sample spaces (ordered lists or grids) for single and combined events, then compute theoretical probability as favourable ÷ total. They draw probability trees, multiply along a single path (AND), add across separate, mutually exclusive complete paths (OR), use the complement for 'at least one', and recompute second-level branches for without-replacement (dependent) events. The central hazard is assuming aggregated outcomes — such as the eleven dice totals — are equally likely, when it is the 36 ordered outcomes that are equally likely.

activities.title: The two-dice grid: why totals are not equally likely
feedback: If a learner writes P(7) = 1/11: there are eleven possible totals, but they do not occur equally often. Count the shaded cells — seven has six ways, two has just one — so the totals cannot each be 1/11.

If a learner counts 3+4 and 4+3 as one outcome (getting three ways to make 7, or 21 outcomes total): treat the dice as an ordered pair, first then second; (3,4) and (4,3) are genuinely different results, giving 36 outcomes and six ways to make 7.
Confirm success when the full grid is filled, six cells are identified for total 7, and the learner can say the ordered outcomes — not the totals — are what is equally likely.
activities.rationale: Theoretical probability only equals favourable ÷ total when the counted outcomes are genuinely equally likely; the two-dice grid makes the distinction between elemental equally-likely outcomes and aggregated events visible and countable.
sourceClaims: Children (and adults) show an equiprobability bias in the two-dice problem, assuming all the possible totals are equally probable; the difficulty is distinguishing elemental equally-likely outcomes from aggregated events, which requires representing the full sample space.
learnerActions: On paper or a 6×6 grid, write the total in every one of the 36 cells for (first die, second die), keeping the two dice as an ordered pair so 3+4 and 4+3 are separate cells.
Shade all cells where the total is 7 and count them (6 cells: 1+6, 2+5, 3+4, 4+3, 5+2, 6+1), then shade cells where the total is 2 (1 cell: 1+1).
State P(total = 7) = 6/36 = 1/6 and P(total = 2) = 1/36.
Explain in a sentence why P(7) is NOT 1/11, referring to the 36 equally-likely ordered outcomes.
activities.intendedInsight: The 36 ordered (die1, die2) outcomes are equally likely; the eleven totals 2–12 are NOT, because different totals arise from different numbers of ordered outcomes.

activities.title: Trees: multiply along a path, add across paths
feedback: If a learner computes P(tail and 6) = 1/2 + 1/6: along a single path use the AND rule and multiply (1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12). Adding is only for OR across separate, mutually exclusive complete paths.
If a learner cancels fractions early and then struggles to add paths: keep denominators uncancelled until the end so paths can be added over a common denominator.
Confirm success when the learner multiplies along a path for a combined event and adds across separate paths for an 'or' event, and can say which operation goes with AND and which with OR.
activities.rationale: Explicitly separating multiply-along (AND) from add-across (OR) addresses the common error of applying the wrong operation, and delaying cancellation keeps path addition tractable.
sourceClaims: In tree diagrams, probabilities on each set of branches sum to 1, you multiply along the branches for the AND rule (P(A and B) = P(A)×P(B)) and add across paths for OR; for dependent (without-replacement) events the second set of branch probabilities changes with the first outcome; and fractions should not be cancelled too early.
learnerActions: Draw a probability tree for a coin flip followed by a die roll, writing the probability on each branch and checking each set of branches sums to 1.
Find P(tail and 6) by multiplying along the single path: 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12.
Find a two-path 'OR' probability by computing each separate complete path's product, then adding the path products together (the paths are mutually exclusive, so adding is valid).
Leave fractions uncancelled until the final step so paths share common denominators when added.
activities.intendedInsight: Along one path, combined events use AND and you multiply; across separate complete paths that each satisfy the question, you use OR and add. These are different operations for different situations.

activities.title: Without replacement: the second branch changes
feedback: If a learner keeps the original probabilities on the second branches: after removing a counter there are fewer counters in total and one fewer of the colour drawn — recompute each second branch from what is actually left.
Confirm success when every second-level branch reflects the reduced totals and the path product uses those updated values.
activities.rationale: Recomputing second-level branches from the reduced situation is the core procedure for dependent events and directly targets the misconception of reusing first-event probabilities.
sourceClaims: In tree diagrams, probabilities on each set of branches sum to 1, you multiply along the branches for the AND rule (P(A and B) = P(A)×P(B)) and add across paths for OR; for dependent (without-replacement) events the second set of branch probabilities changes with the first outcome; and fractions should not be cancelled too early.
learnerActions: Set up a bag problem, e.g. 3 red and 2 blue counters, and draw a tree for taking two counters without replacing the first.

Write the first-draw probabilities (3/5 red, 2/5 blue), then recompute each second-draw branch from the reduced situation — one fewer counter in total, and one fewer of whatever was drawn (e.g. after a red: 2/4 red, 2/4 blue).

If an optional tool offers a 'replace / don't replace' switch, toggle it and watch the second-level branch probabilities change (with no replacement) or stay the same (with replacement) to see the dependency.
Find a combined probability, e.g. P(two reds) = 3/5 × 2/4 = 6/20 = 3/10, multiplying along the path with the updated second branch.
activities.intendedInsight: For dependent (without-replacement) events, the second draw's probabilities depend on the first outcome, so they must be recomputed from the reduced contents rather than reused.

activities.title: Drill and check: rules and the equiprobability trap
feedback: For the P(7) item, 1/11 is incorrect: counting ordered outcomes gives 6/36 = 1/6; 1/11 wrongly assumes the eleven totals are equally likely.
For the fill-in, the AND rule gives 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12.
For the without-replacement item, the second branch uses the reduced totals; keeping the original values is the error to catch.
activities.rationale: Targeted recognition and fill-in items reinforce the rules and surface the equiprobability distractor; they consolidate procedures but do not by themselves require constructing a full fresh sample space, so they supplement — and do not replace — the construction activities. Efficacy of the format is proposed, not demonstrated.
learnerActions: Answer a short-answer item: P(total = 7) with two dice — write the fraction and justify it, explaining why the common answer 1/11 is wrong.
Complete a fill-in: P(tail and 6) = 1/2 × ___ = ___.
Solve a without-replacement item where the second branch must be recomputed, and explain why it differs from the first.
Where available, tap grid cells to reveal their totals or tap a tree path to reveal its product, using these only to self-check after you have reasoned.
activities.intendedInsight: Quick recognition and fill-in checks can reinforce the AND/OR rules and resurface the equiprobability trap, but learners should reason first and use any reveal only to confirm; such items check and consolidate the procedures and do not by themselves build a full fresh sample space.

constraints: Sample spaces must be built on genuinely equally-likely outcomes; for two dice that means the 36 ordered (die1, die2) pairs, not the eleven totals.
Order must be respected when listing: (3,4) and (4,3) are distinct outcomes; ignoring order undercounts the sample space.
For dependent (without-replacement) events, every second-level branch must be recomputed from the reduced contents; first-event probabilities cannot be reused.
The OR (add-across) rule applies only to separate, mutually exclusive complete paths; the AND (multiply-along) rule applies within a single path.
Leave fractions uncancelled until the end so paths can be added over a common denominator.

Short-answer, fill-in and tap-to-reveal items can reinforce and self-check the rules, but do not require a learner to independently construct a complete fresh sample space; pair them with construction tasks.

Tap-to-reveal grids/trees and a replace/don't-replace toggle are optional supports to make the mechanism visible; they are not required, and should be used after the learner has reasoned, not instead of reasoning.
Rolling physical or 3D dice can add realism and generate data, but the counting and branch arithmetic are carried by the grid and tree; feed any physical results back into the grid/tree.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: two-dice total 7 has six ordered ways (1+6,2+5,3+4,4+3,5+2,6+1) → 6/36 = 1/6; total 2 has one way (1+1) → 1/36; P(tail and 6) = 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12; without-replacement example P(two reds from 3R,2B) = 3/5 × 2/4 = 6/20 = 3/10 (first draw 3/5 red, 2/5 blue). All consistent with the source row.
The '1/11' value appears only as a misconception to be corrected, never as a valid answer offered to learners.
The complement shortcut for 'at least one' is named in the pedagogy summary but is not given a worked activity here; a reviewer may wish to add one.

Activity 4 (drill) carries empty sourceClaims: the Nuffield equiprobability-bias claim documents the bias but its principle (resolving the bias requires building the full sample space) does not support a drill rationale that avoids full construction, and no source establishes the efficacy of recognition/fill-in drill.

Source claims cited support the underlying principles (tree rules; equiprobability bias) but do not establish that these specific activities or any particular interactive/toggle/tap-to-reveal feature were tested for efficacy; efficacy of any medium is therefore left as proposed/intended, not demonstrated.

probeDeeper: You flip a coin AND roll a die — what is P(heads and a 6)? Do you add or multiply the branch probabilities, and why?
Are the totals 2 to 12 equally likely? How many ways can you make 7, and how many ways to make 2?
If you draw two counters from a bag WITHOUT replacing the first, do the second-branch probabilities stay the same? Why not?
Why is 3+4 counted separately from 4+3 in the grid?
assess.correctAnswer: A correct performance: builds the sample space of 36 equally-likely ordered (die1, die2) outcomes — via a grid or systematic list — finds 6 ways to total 7 (1+6, 2+5, 3+4, 4+3, 5+2, 6+1) giving P(7) = 6/36 = 1/6, and 1 way to total 2 (1+1) giving P(2) = 1/36. The student recognises the 36 ordered outcomes are equally likely but the totals are not.

errorPatterns.pattern: Assumes aggregated outcomes are equally likely — treats the eleven totals 2–12 as each 1/11
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build the 6×6 grid of the 36 equally-likely ordered outcomes; count how many make each total — seven has six ways, two has one — so the totals are not equally likely
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives P(7) = 1/11 (or P(2) = 1/11) without building the sample space of ordered outcomes

errorPatterns.pattern: Ignores order when listing, undercounting the sample space
errorPatterns.nextMove: Treat (die1, die2) as ordered pairs — 3+4 and 4+3 are different cells on the grid; there are 36 outcomes, six of which total 7
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Counts 3+4 and 4+3 as one outcome, giving 21 outcomes or only three ways to make 7

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds probabilities along a branch instead of multiplying (misapplies the AND rule)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Along a single path use the AND rule: multiply (1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12); adding is for OR across separate paths
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a follow-up combined event computes P(A and B) as P(A) + P(B) — e.g. P(tail and 6) = 1/2 + 1/6

errorPatterns.pattern: Reuses the first-event probabilities on the second branch of a without-replacement (dependent) event
errorPatterns.nextMove: For dependent events recompute the second branch from the reduced situation — one fewer item, and one fewer of whatever was drawn
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a 'draw two without replacing' probe, keeps the original probabilities on the second set of branches

responseLevels.gap: Assumes the totals are equally likely (P(7) = 1/11); no systematic sample space; adds branch probabilities for combined events
responseLevels.full: Builds the complete 36-outcome ordered sample space, counts favourable outcomes correctly (6 ways to 7 → 1/6), multiplies along branches and adds across paths, and recomputes probabilities for without-replacement events
responseLevels.partial: Builds some of the sample space and multiplies along branches for simple independent cases, but undercounts by ignoring order, or keeps probabilities fixed for without-replacement events — computes without a complete, ordered sample space

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child paper and this task: 'Two fair dice are rolled and the two numbers are added together. Work out the probability the total is 7. Then work out the probability the total is 2.' (Set the task and WATCH — watch whether they treat all totals 2–12 as equally likely or systematically build the 36-outcome sample space, whether they respect order when counting the ways to make 7, and how they express and simplify the answers.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching separates the student who lays out all 36 ordered outcomes and counts six ways to make 7 from one who assumes the eleven totals are equally likely (P(7) = 1/11), or ignores order and undercounts (three ways to 7, or 21 outcomes). The two-dice sample space is the classic exposer of assuming aggregated outcomes are equally likely.

pedagogy.summary: This extends whole-unit line plots to a scale subdivided into halves and quarters. The demanding new part is the SCALE: the intervals between 2, 2¼, 2½, 2¾, 3 must be equal, the fraction marks correctly ordered, and the child must measure to the nearest quarter inch on a ruler whose subdivisions they can actually read and name. It is best taught by measuring to the nearest ¼ inch with a clearly subdivided ruler, then transferring onto a number line already partitioned into quarters — keeping the ruler's quarter-inch ticks aligned with the plot's quarter marks so the subdivision of the tool and the subdivision of the axis are seen to be the same thing.
bestPractices: Use a ruler with clearly marked and (at first) labelled quarter-inch subdivisions so children can name the value of the tick they round to
Pre-partition the plot's scale into quarters to scaffold correct ordering and equal spacing, then fade the scaffold
Keep the ruler's ¼-inch tick spacing aligned with the ¼ spacing on the plot so tool and axis share one subdivision
Maintain the one-X-per-object rule established with whole units
Check ordering and equivalence explicitly: 2¼ < 2½ < 2¾, and ½ sits at the same place as 2/4
keyRepresentations: A ruler subdivided (and labelled) in quarter-inches
A number line partitioned into equal quarters
A fraction strip or bar linking ¼, ½, ¾ to show equal parts and order
Stacked X marks, one per object
commonMisconceptions: Spacing the fraction marks unequally or out of order — placing ½ midway but crowding or mis-ordering ¼ and ¾
Measuring 'to the nearest line' on the ruler without knowing the fraction that line represents, so a tick position is recorded rather than a measured value
Carrying over the value-vs-frequency habit — reading stack height as length
Treating ½ and 2/4 as different positions on the scale

learn.summary: Children generate measurement data by measuring objects to the nearest half inch and to the nearest quarter inch on a ruler whose subdivisions they can read and name, then display the data on a line plot whose horizontal scale is partitioned into equal quarter-inch intervals (…2, 2¼, 2½, 2¾, 3…). The demanding new skill is the SCALE: equal spacing, correct fraction ordering (2¼ < 2½ < 2¾), and recognising that 2½ sits at the same position as 2 2/4 (because ½ = 2/4). A guiding practice is drawing the axis to true inch scale and keeping the ruler's quarter-inch ticks aligned with the plot's quarter marks so the subdivision of the tool and the subdivision of the axis are seen as the same partition of one unit. One X per object, and stack height means frequency, not length.

activities.title: Measure to the nearest quarter and build the fractional scale
feedback: If the quarter marks are unevenly spaced or out of order (e.g. 2¼, 2¾, 2½): reteach partitioning one unit into equal parts with a fraction strip; align each ¼ tick under the ruler and check the order 2¼ < 2½ < 2¾.

If the child records a tick position like 'the third line' but cannot name the fraction it represents: label the quarter ticks with their fraction values and practise naming ¼, ½, ¾ on the ruler before plotting.
If the child answers 'how long is one?' with a stack's count: align the ruler under the plot and separate 'how many objects' (stack height) from 'how long is one object' (axis position).

Probe: 'Show me where 2½ is — why exactly there, and not closer to 2 or to 3?' and 'Is ½ the same place as 2/4 on your line? Why?' and 'If an object measured 2¾, would its X go left or right of the 2½ stack?'
activities.rationale: The grade-level objective is to generate measurement data with a ruler marked in halves and fourths and display it on a line plot scaled appropriately. Building the equal-interval fractional scale is a construction skill, so the activity has learners physically measure, partition, and place marks rather than only interpret a given plot. Aligning the ruler under the axis is intended to make the shared subdivision concrete.
sourceClaims: Grade 3 standard: generate measurement data by measuring lengths using rulers marked with halves and fourths of an inch; show the data by making a line plot where the horizontal scale is marked off in appropriate units — whole numbers, halves, or quarters.
learnerActions: Measure a set of ribbons or objects (about 5–6) against a ruler whose quarter-inch ticks are clearly marked and, at first, labelled with their fraction values (¼, ½, ¾).

For each object, name the quarter inch it rounds to out loud or in writing — e.g. 'this one is 2¾ inches', not 'the third line'; for one or two objects, also name the nearest half inch and notice that the two answers can be different.

Using the ruler to mark it, draw a number line at true scale (1 inch per whole number) that covers every measured length, and partition it into equal quarters between the whole numbers, so the marks run e.g. 2, 2¼, 2½, 2¾, 3 in correct order and with equal spacing.
Place one X per object at its fractional value on the line.

Align the ruler directly under the true-scale plot, with the ruler's whole-inch marks under the matching whole numbers on the axis, so each ¼ tick on the ruler sits beneath the matching ¼ mark on the axis.
(Optional, on screen) Measure a ribbon that is 2¼ inches: drop its X and watch it settle one quarter-tick past 2, directly beneath the same tick on the ruler, making the shared subdivision visible.
Check ordering and equivalence explicitly: confirm 2¼ < 2½ < 2¾, and that 2½ lands at the same position as 2 2/4 (because ½ = 2/4).
Read the finished plot: e.g. 'how many objects were 2½ inches?' and 'how many were shorter than 2½?'
activities.intendedInsight: The subdivision on the ruler and the subdivision on the plot's axis are the same partition of one unit into equal quarters; a measured length maps to a position on an equal-interval scale, and ½ = 2/4 is one position, not two.

activities.title: Separate frequency from length
feedback: If the child reads stack height as length: physically align the ruler under the plot, then ask them to trace the axis position for length and separately count Xs for frequency, naming which answers which question.
Reinforce with the probe 'How many objects were shorter than 2½? How can you tell?' so counting across stacks is tied to axis position.
activities.rationale: Research reports that students transfer a bar-graph habit of reading bar/stack height as a data value, confusing frequency with the value of the variable on the axis, and this confusion can persist after instruction even in simple dot plots. Explicitly separating the two questions aims to address this documented error; its effectiveness here is not independently established.
sourceClaims: Students transfer the bar-graph habit of reading bar height as a data value, confusing frequency (stack height) with the value of the variable (axis position); the axis confusion persists after instruction and appears even in simple dot plots.
learnerActions: On a completed fractional line plot, point to the axis position that gives an object's LENGTH and separately count the stacked Xs that give the FREQUENCY at that length.
Answer paired questions: 'How long is this object?' (read axis) versus 'How many objects were this long?' (count the stack).
Explain in your own words why a taller stack does not mean a longer object.
activities.intendedInsight: On a line plot the horizontal axis position is the measured value, while the height of a stack of Xs is how many objects share that value — these are two different quantities.

activities.title: Interpret and order a given fractional plot
feedback: If ordering is wrong, return to a fraction strip to compare ¼, ½, ¾ as equal parts of one unit.
If the child treats ½ and 2/4 as different positions, mark both on the same strip and show they coincide.
activities.rationale: Reading a given plot tests interpretation, ordering, and equivalence. It is a useful complement to construction, though on its own it does not show whether a child can build a correctly spaced quarter scale from scratch — so it should accompany, not replace, the measuring-and-plotting task.
learnerActions: Given a finished fractional line plot, order the marked values 2¼, 2½, 2¾ from least to greatest.
Count how many objects fall at a given value (e.g. 'how many were 2½?').
Compare: how many objects were shorter than 2½, and how many were longer.
Confirm that 2½ and 2 2/4 name the same position on the scale (because ½ = 2/4).
activities.intendedInsight: A correctly built fractional scale can be read for order, counts, and comparisons, and equivalent fractions occupy the same position.

activities.title: Reference: name each quarter mark and show ½ = 2/4
feedback: If the child cannot name a tick, return to the labelled reference and say the value aloud before plotting.
Fade the labels once the child reliably names and orders the quarters without them.
activities.rationale: A labelled reference scaffolds correct naming and ordering of quarter marks and makes the ½ = 2/4 equivalence explicit. It is a support, not a substitute for measuring to the nearest quarter or constructing the scale, so it is faded as competence grows.
learnerActions: Study a labelled fractional line plot or fraction strip where each quarter mark is named (¼, ½, ¾).
Reveal or confirm that ½ equals 2/4 and that the half mark sits midway between adjacent whole numbers.
Use this as a reference while measuring and plotting, then set it aside once the scale can be built independently.
activities.intendedInsight: Each quarter tick has a nameable fraction value, and equivalent fractions (½ = 2/4) share one position; this naming supports accurate measuring and plotting.

constraints: Use a ruler with clearly marked quarter-inch subdivisions, labelled at first, so children can name the fraction value of the tick they round to rather than recording 'the nearest line'.
Keep the ruler's ¼-inch tick spacing aligned with the plot's ¼ spacing so the tool and the axis share one subdivision.
Maintain the one-X-per-object rule established with whole-unit plots.
Check ordering and equivalence explicitly: 2¼ < 2½ < 2¾, and 2½ at the same position as 2 2/4 (because ½ = 2/4).

A labelled reference image or tap-to-reveal plot is a scaffold for naming marks; being fixed, it does not by itself exercise measuring to the nearest quarter or constructing the scale, so pair it with hands-on measuring and plotting and fade it.

Reading-only tasks (ordering, counting on a given plot) assess interpretation but do not show whether a child can build a correctly spaced, correctly ordered quarter scale; include a construction task to cover that.

Snap-to-equal-spacing or tick-alignment feedback (whether on screen or via physically aligning a ruler under the plot) is an optional way to make the shared subdivision visible; it is not the only way to teach equal intervals.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original row claimed a third dimension 'adds nothing' and that a measuring-and-plotting construction 'has no dialogic content' for a conversational format; these are catalog-fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws, and have been dropped rather than asserted. Different media (tactile ruler, screen model, discussion of why order holds) offer different affordances.

The original claim that a static picture or quiz 'cannot deliver' the insight has been softened: a fixed reference can still teach naming and equivalence; it simply cannot be manipulated to practise measuring or building the scale. Only the objective limit (recognition/reading does not elicit independent construction) is retained.
Example values (2, 2¼, 2½, 2¾, 3) and the equivalence ½ = 2/4 were checked and are correct; ordering 2¼ < 2½ < 2¾ is correct.

Two reteach prerequisite links (one for partitioning, one for frequency-vs-value) and a micro-topic identifier were present in the source; their IDs are internal catalog references and are described by purpose rather than ID here.
The original diagnostic specified 6 objects while the evidence list specified five objects; 'about 5–6' is used and the minor discrepancy is left for human review rather than silently resolved.
The optional 3¼ snap interaction is an unvalidated design proposal from the original note; it is offered as an optional illustration and its efficacy is not asserted by the cited sources.

probeDeeper: Show me where 2½ is — why exactly there, and not closer to 2 or to 3?
Is ½ the same place as 2/4 on your line? Why?
How many objects were shorter than 2½? How can you tell?
If an object measured 2¾, would its X go to the left or the right of the 2½ stack?
assess.correctAnswer: Subdivides the axis into equal quarter-inch intervals in correct order (…2, 2¼, 2½, 2¾, 3…), measures each object to the nearest quarter inch by reading the ruler's subdivisions, places one X per object at its fractional value, and can read the plot (e.g. 'how many were 2½ inches').

errorPatterns.pattern: Spaces the fraction marks unequally or out of order — puts ½ midway but crowds ¼ and ¾, or orders 2¼, 2¾, 2½
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach partitioning one unit into equal parts with a fraction strip; align each ¼ tick under the ruler and check order 2¼ < 2½ < 2¾
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The quarter ticks on their axis are not evenly spaced, or the fractions run out of order

errorPatterns.pattern: Measures 'to the nearest line' on the ruler but cannot say the fraction that line represents, recording a tick position rather than a measured value
errorPatterns.nextMove: Label the quarter ticks with their fraction values; practise naming ¼, ½, ¾ on the ruler before plotting
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Records marks like 'the third line' or mis-names the quarter it rounded to

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the height of a stack as the length, carrying the bar-graph habit over to the fractional plot
errorPatterns.nextMove: Align the ruler under the plot and separate 'how many objects' from 'how long is one'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'how long?' with a stack's count rather than its position

responseLevels.gap: Cannot build a correct fractional scale — unequal or mis-ordered quarter marks, or cannot read the ruler to the nearest ¼.
responseLevels.full: Subdivides the axis into equal, correctly-ordered quarter intervals, measures to the nearest ¼ reading true fraction values, places one X per object, and compares and reads fractional positions, transferring to a new measurement.
responseLevels.partial: Measures and places Xs but the spacing is imperfect, or cannot justify fraction order and equivalence (½ vs 2/4); reads counts but not fractional comparisons.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a ruler marked in quarter-inches and 6 objects. Say: 'Measure each to the nearest quarter inch and show them all on this line.' Provide an unmarked horizontal line. Watch how they subdivide the scale into quarters, whether the fraction marks are equally spaced and correctly ordered, and how they read the ruler to the nearest ¼.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The equal-interval demand exposes whether the child treats the axis as a true measurement scale — quarters evenly spaced, ½ at 2/4 — or as a row of ordered labels. Mis-spaced or mis-ordered ticks reveal a partitioning gap that a whole-unit plot would hide, and reading 'to the nearest line' without naming its value shows the ruler subdivision was never understood.

sources.claim: Students transfer the bar-graph habit of reading bar height as a data value, confusing frequency (stack height) with the value of the variable (axis position); the axis confusion persists after instruction and appears even in simple dot plots.

pedagogy.summary: Adding within 100 is taught as strategy work grounded in place value, not as an early column algorithm. Children partition, use known number bonds, and bridge tens: 46+7 becomes 46+4+3, 38+40 adds tens to tens leaving ones untouched. The concrete-pictorial-abstract progression (base-ten blocks, bead strings, number lines → jottings) makes the tens boundary visible before it is recorded symbolically.
bestPractices: Extend within-20 'make ten' bonds to numbers within 100 — 46+7 uses the same partition of 7 into 4+3 that 6+7 does (NCETM Spine 1.13: known within-ten facts applied to a two-digit + single-digit number)
Keep tens and ones distinct: for 38+40, add the multiple of ten to the tens and leave the ones alone, so the child feels tens land on tens
Use multiple connected representations for the same calculation — bead string, part-whole diagram, number line, and symbolic jotting — so the strategy transfers
Secure fluent partitioning of numbers to ten first; it is the explicit prerequisite for independent bridging
Ask the child to relate the mental strategy to a written record and justify it, not just state the answer (curriculum: explain the reasoning)
keyRepresentations: Bead string / 100-bead frame (bridging a ten made visible)
Base-ten blocks (tens rods and ones)
Number line with jumps (partition the added amount into a jump to the next ten, then the rest)
Part-whole model (partition the addend, e.g. 7 = 4 + 3)
Hundred square (move along for ones, down for tens)
commonMisconceptions: Treating a multiple of ten as ones: 38+40 done as 38+4=42
Not bridging the ten: 46+7 done as 6+7=13, keeping the 3 and losing the extra ten (answer 43), or concatenating to 413
Adding the added amount to the wrong part (ones added to the tens digit)
Persisting with count-all/count-on-in-ones instead of using place value

learn.summary: Children aged 6-7 add within 100 using place-value strategies, not a column algorithm. They partition addends, use known number bonds to bridge a ten (46+7 as 46+4+3), and add tens to tens leaving the ones untouched (38+40=78). A concrete-pictorial-abstract progression (bead strings, base-ten blocks, number lines, then jottings) makes the tens boundary visible before it is recorded symbolically. The crossing-a-ten moment and the tens-onto-tens move are the two insights to build and check.

activities.title: Watch a ten compose when you cross the boundary
feedback: If the child computes the ones as 13 but writes only the 3 (answer 43) or strings digits as 413, return to make-ten within 20 on a bead string so the extra ten is seen composing, then carry that exact move up to 46+7. The crossed ten must not disappear.

If the child counts on in ones (54, 55, ... 62 for 53+9), do not ban the counting or penalise slowness: it is valid and matures as make-ten becomes automatic. Model the make-ten jump alongside their count so the efficient move becomes the natural one.
Praise relating the spoken strategy to the partition: 'you split 7 into 4 and 3 to land exactly on the ten'.
activities.rationale: Known within-ten facts and partitioning transfer to a two-digit-plus-single-digit sum; the make-ten bridging strategy depends on fluent partitioning of numbers to ten, and letting the child act on the boundary turns bridging into something observed rather than told. A live manipulative where loose ones visibly compose a ten (with a running count) makes the regroup concrete; this is one effective way to expose the structure, not the only possible one. Equivalent physical bead strings or base-ten blocks serve the same purpose.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils add and subtract using concrete objects, pictorial representations and mentally, including a two-digit number and ones, a two-digit number and tens, and two two-digit numbers; recall facts to 20 and derive related facts to 100.

Known within-ten facts and partitioning are applied to add a single-digit number to a two-digit number; the make-ten bridging strategy requires fluent partitioning of numbers to ten, and strategies are connected across multiple representations (tens frames, part-whole, number line, symbolic).
Unitising (treating one ten as a single entity) and exchange are the ideas children must grasp to calculate with numbers beyond ten; a digit's value depends on its position.
learnerActions: Start with 46 shown on a bead string or in a base-ten workspace
Add single ones one at a time, saying the running total aloud (47, 48, 49, 50, 51, 52, 53)

When the added one makes ten loose ones, see that they complete a ten (on a bead string, the next block of ten beads is filled; with base-ten blocks, swap the ten ones for a ten-rod), so the count goes 49, then 50, then on to 53
Re-tell what happened: 'I added 4 to reach 50, then 3 more to make 53', and link it to the partition 7 = 4 + 3
Repeat for 53 + 9 (bridge to 60 by adding 7, then +2)
activities.intendedInsight: Bridging a ten is not an arbitrary rule: the extra ten is physically composed from ten ones, and the make-ten partition (7 = 4 + 3) is the same move used within 20 applied at 46.

activities.title: Tens land on tens: add a multiple of ten
feedback: If the child gives 38 + 40 = 42 (adding 4 to the ones, saying 'four tens is a four'), rebuild with ten-rods: forty is four tens and joins the three tens already there. Confront the size mismatch — 42 is only just above 38, so it cannot be right after adding forty.
Reinforce order-independence: adding the 8 first or the 40 first both give 78.
activities.rationale: The curriculum expects adding a two-digit number and a multiple of ten; keeping tens and ones distinct prevents the common error of adding a multiple of ten as if it were ones. Base-ten rods make the place-value distinction tangible.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils add and subtract using concrete objects, pictorial representations and mentally, including a two-digit number and ones, a two-digit number and tens, and two two-digit numbers; recall facts to 20 and derive related facts to 100.
Unitising (treating one ten as a single entity) and exchange are the ideas children must grasp to calculate with numbers beyond ten; a digit's value depends on its position.
learnerActions: Start with 38 shown with three ten-rods and eight ones
Add four ten-rods, watching them join the tens while the eight ones stay untouched
State the total as 70 + 8 = 78, and say why the ones did not change
Check by a different order: add 30 + 40 = 70 first, then the 8 — confirm it gives the same 78
Contrast with the wrong move: 'is 38 + 40 the same as 38 + 4? why not?' — notice 42 is only 4 more than 38, far too small after adding forty
activities.intendedInsight: A multiple of ten joins the tens, not the ones; four tens combine with three tens to make seven tens, leaving the ones unchanged.

activities.title: Partition the addend with a part-whole picture
feedback: If the child splits 7 into something that does not reach 50 (e.g. 2 and 5), ask which part gets them exactly to the next ten from 46.
A labelled picture shows the structure but does not let the child perform the regroup themselves; pair it with hands-on bridging (first activity) so the felt move and the structure connect.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal or labelled part-whole diagram makes the partition and the ten-crossing explicit. It teaches the structure of the strategy; because the learner does not act on the boundary, it works best alongside, not instead of, hands-on regrouping.
sourceClaims: Known within-ten facts and partitioning are applied to add a single-digit number to a two-digit number; the make-ten bridging strategy requires fluent partitioning of numbers to ten, and strategies are connected across multiple representations (tens frames, part-whole, number line, symbolic).
learnerActions: Look at 46 + 7 with 7 shown in a part-whole model
Split the 7 into 4 (the amount needed to reach the next ten) and 3 (the rest)
Mark where the calculation crosses a ten (at 50) and label it 'this is where we cross a ten'
Say the two jumps: 46 + 4 = 50, then 50 + 3 = 53
activities.intendedInsight: Choosing the partition that lands exactly on the next ten is what makes bridging efficient; the structure of the strategy can be seen even before acting it out.

activities.title: Connect the strategy to a written record and explain it
feedback: Efficient work: 46+7 by partitioning 7 into 4+3 (46+4=50, then +3=53); 38+40 by adding tens (30+40=70, then +8=78) leaving the ones untouched; 53+9 by bridging (53+7=60, then +2=62) or 53+10-1.
If the child only states answers, ask them to link the jotting to the number line and say why each step works.
activities.rationale: The curriculum asks pupils to relate the strategy to a written method and explain their reasoning; using multiple connected representations for the same calculation helps the strategy transfer. Consolidation items (fill-the-blank partitions such as 46 + ? = 50, 50 + ? = 53, and choosing the correct partition of 38+40 rather than the common 42 error) check retention after the insight is built.
sourceClaims: Known within-ten facts and partitioning are applied to add a single-digit number to a two-digit number; the make-ten bridging strategy requires fluent partitioning of numbers to ten, and strategies are connected across multiple representations (tens frames, part-whole, number line, symbolic).
learnerActions: For each of 46+7, 38+40, 53+9, carry out the mental strategy and write a matching jotting (e.g. 46 + 4 = 50, 50 + 3 = 53)
Show the same calculation as a number-line jump (a jump to the next ten, then the rest)
Explain aloud why the method works, not just the answer
Answer probes: 'Show on the number line why 46 + 7 lands on 53'; 'For 38+40, would adding the 8 first give the same answer? How do you know?'; 'What changes if it were 46 + 40 instead of 46 + 4?'
activities.intendedInsight: The mental strategy, the number-line jump, and the written jotting are the same story told three ways; being able to justify the reasoning is part of the objective.

constraints: Teach as strategy work grounded in place value, not as an early column algorithm.
Secure fluent partitioning of numbers to ten first; it is the explicit prerequisite for independent bridging.

Fill-the-blank and multiple-choice items rehearse, check and consolidate the strategy and suit practice after the insight is built; they do not let the child enact the ten-crossing regroup by hand, so pair them with the hands-on activity (and the part-whole scaffold) rather than using them to first build the strategy.
A labelled or tap-to-reveal part-whole picture shows the structure but does not let the child perform the regroup; it is a scaffold to pair with hands-on bridging, not a replacement.
Do not ban counting-on in ones or penalise slowness; it is a valid developmental strategy that matures as make-ten becomes automatic. Model the efficient jump alongside the child's count.

Optional interactive supports (dragging ones that compose a ten at the boundary, a running count, sliding ten-rods onto the tens, a toggle mirroring the action as a number-line jump and jotting) make the mechanism concrete but are examples, not required mechanisms; equivalent physical bead strings and base-ten blocks serve the same purpose.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources have NOT been re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The NCETM Spine 1 source (Segments 1.11 & 1.13) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its claim with corresponding caution.

The source row rated a third spatial dimension and in-role dialogue as poor fits with reasoning that extra dimensions 'add nothing' and 'talk is not the bottleneck'. These are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws, and are not asserted here. Addition within 100 is a quantity-and-place-value idea that does not require a third spatial dimension, and spoken explanation remains valuable for the 'explain your reasoning' objective.

Arithmetic self-check performed: 46+7=53, 38+40=78, 53+9=62, 30+40=70, 70+8=78, 53+7=60, 60+2=62 all correct. The error patterns 42 (for 38+40) and 43/413 (for 46+7) are named only as misconceptions to diagnose and correct, never as valid answers.

The 'explain your reasoning' objective is drawn from the broader DfE curriculum; the specific quoted DfE claim does not state it, so its support rests mainly on the multiple-representations claim rather than a direct quotation.
The prerequisite reteach IDs in the original assessment (e.g. mt_THl9GLxwoL, mt_m1W6nTQJ2b) are internal identifiers and have been omitted from learner-facing guidance.

probeDeeper: Show me on this bead string (or number line) why 46 + 7 lands on 53.
You added the 40 first for 38+40 — would you get the same answer if you added the 8 first? How do you know?
Which of these three was easiest for you, and what was it about the numbers that made it easy?
What if it were 46 + 70 instead of 46 + 7 — what changes about how you'd do it?
assess.correctAnswer: 53, 78, 62. Efficient work: 46+7 by partitioning 7 into 4+3 (46+4=50, then +3=53) or make-ten; 38+40 by adding the tens (30+40=70, +8=78) leaving the ones untouched; 53+9 by bridging (53+7=60, +2=62) or 53+10−1.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats a multiple of ten as ones — 'thirty-eight plus forty is forty-two' (adds the 4, not 40)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild with ten-rods: forty is four tens, and it joins the three tens already there. Confront the size mismatch — 42 is barely more than 38.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 38+40 the child adds 4 to the ones rather than 40 to the tens, giving 42; explains 'four tens is a four'

errorPatterns.pattern: Doesn't bridge the ten — '46 plus 7: six and seven is thirteen, so forty-three' (keeps the 3, loses the extra ten) or concatenates to 413
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to make-ten within 20 on a bead string so the extra ten is seen composing, then carry that exact move up to 46+7.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 46+7 the child computes the ones as 13 but writes only the 3, or strings digits together; the crossed ten disappears

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts on in ones by finger or tally rather than using place value — accurate but slow, and fragile when the count is long
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT ban the counting or penalise the slowness — it is a valid strategy that matures as make-ten becomes automatic. Model the make-ten jump alongside their count so the two line up and the efficient move becomes the natural one.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 53+9 the child counts 54,55,…62 one by one instead of jumping to 60 then +2

responseLevels.gap: Combines digits without regard to place value (38+40→42) or gives 46+7 as 43/413; cannot reliably cross a ten.
responseLevels.full: Uses place-value partitioning or make-ten fluently on all three, keeps tens and ones distinct, bridges the ten correctly, and can relate the jotting to a number-line or written record and say why it works.
responseLevels.partial: Reaches answers by counting on in ones, or handles 38+40 but stumbles whenever a ten must be bridged; the method works on some items but not dependably across the boundary.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put these three in front of the child one at a time and ask them to work each out, thinking aloud and jotting if they wish: 46 + 7, then 38 + 40, then 53 + 9. Watch closely what happens on the two that cross a ten.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The two items that cross a ten (46+7, 53+9) separate a child who bridges using place value from one who mishandles the boundary and drops or concatenates the extra ten; 38+40 separates a child who adds tens to tens from one who adds the '4' of forty to the ones. A child using place value gets all three cleanly; a child guessing digit-by-digit fails predictably at the boundary.
