pedagogy.summary: This KS3 synthesis topic asks pupils to apply formal written methods for all four operations across integers (including negatives), decimals, and proper/improper fractions and mixed numbers. The central difficulty is not any single algorithm but KEEPING THEM APART: IES documents that students — and even many teachers — confuse the procedures, e.g. importing the common-denominator step of addition into multiplication, or leaving the denominator unchanged in multiplication because they meet more addition problems. Add to this negative-number sign handling and the need to convert mixed numbers to improper fractions before multiplying or dividing. Teach by contrasting the four operations on the SAME operands so pupils see WHEN a common denominator is needed and when it is not, always estimating for reasonableness.
bestPractices: Contrast all four operations on the same pair (e.g. 3/4 and 2/3) so pupils see addition/subtraction need a common denominator while multiplication/division do not
Require an estimate before every calculation to catch mis-applied algorithms and sign errors
Convert mixed numbers to improper fractions before multiplying or dividing; keep the meaning (measurement/partition) attached to division
Handle negative signs explicitly on a number line and with stated rules, separating 'combining signed quantities' from 'multiplying/dividing signs'
Confront algorithm confusion directly (IES): show a correctly and an incorrectly chosen method side by side and discuss why each is right or wrong
keyRepresentations: A comparison table of +, −, ×, ÷ applied to the same two fractions, exposing which needs a common denominator
Number line for signed-integer addition/subtraction
Improper-fraction rewrites for × and ÷ of mixed numbers
Estimation with benchmarks / whole-number bounds
commonMisconceptions: Applies the wrong algorithm for the operation — finds a common denominator to multiply, or multiplies across to add
Leaves the denominator unchanged in multiplication, or seeks a common denominator in multiplication/division
Sign errors with negatives (e.g. −5 + 3 treated as −(5+3), or confusing −×− with −+−)
Multiplies or divides mixed numbers without first converting to improper fractions (distributes incompletely)

learn.summary: KS3 pupils apply formal written methods for all four operations across integers (including negatives), decimals, and proper/improper fractions and mixed numbers. The central difficulty is not any single algorithm but keeping them apart: students (and even some teachers) confuse the procedures — importing addition's common-denominator step into multiplication, or leaving a denominator unchanged in multiplication. Add negative-sign handling and the standard step of converting mixed numbers to improper fractions before multiplying or dividing, since working on the mixed form directly is only correct if every part is fully distributed. Teach by contrasting the four operations on the SAME operands so pupils see when a common denominator is needed and when it is not, always estimating for reasonableness.

activities.title: Same two fractions, four operations
feedback: If a learner finds a common denominator to multiply (3/4 × 2/3 recut to 9/12 × 8/12 first), point out that this step is unnecessary. It only gives a wrong answer if the shared denominator is kept (72/12 instead of 72/144 = 1/2). Contrast it directly with the standard method on the same pair and name the principle: multiplication scales, so you multiply numerators and multiply denominators (4×3 = 12).
If a learner multiplies across to add (3/4 + 2/3 → 6/12), re-establish that addition combines same-size parts, which first requires recutting to a common denominator.
If the estimate and exact answer disagree (e.g. an answer less than 1 for 3/4 + 2/3), treat the mismatch as a signal to recheck which method was used.
activities.rationale: Running the same operands through contrasting operations makes method-selection visible and structural rather than memorised; a side-by-side comparison exposes the documented algorithm confusion.
sourceClaims: Students and even many teachers confuse the algorithms for adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing fractions, and over-generalise a rule that fits one operation to another (e.g. leaving the denominator unchanged in multiplication, or seeking a common denominator where multiplication does not need one); the panel recommends confronting these confusions directly.
learnerActions: Fix two operands, e.g. 3/4 and 2/3, and work all four operations on this same pair, writing out each method.
For addition and subtraction, recut both to a common denominator (9/12 and 8/12) before combining: 3/4 + 2/3 = 9/12 + 8/12 = 17/12 = 1 5/12.
For multiplication, multiply across without a common denominator: 3/4 × 2/3 = 6/12 = 1/2 — notice a common denominator is NOT needed here.
State out loud or in writing when a common denominator is required and when it is not, and say why (addition combines same-size parts; multiplication scales).
Before each calculation, estimate: should 3/4 + 2/3 be more or less than 1? Check your exact answer agrees.
activities.intendedInsight: Whether a common denominator is needed is a structural feature of the OPERATION, not a ritual applied to every fraction calculation: addition/subtraction combine same-size parts (need a common denominator) while multiplication/division scale (do not, in the standard methods).

activities.title: Spot the wrong method
feedback: When a learner catches a common-denominator step inside a multiplication, confirm it and have them restate why multiplication does not need one.
When a learner catches an add-across in an addition, confirm it and have them restate why same-size parts must be made first.
If a learner cannot spot the error, return to the same-operands comparison and let them rebuild the correct method before re-attempting.
activities.rationale: Directly confronting the misconception — showing a correctly and an incorrectly chosen method side by side — is the recommended response to algorithm confusion.
sourceClaims: Students and even many teachers confuse the algorithms for adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing fractions, and over-generalise a rule that fits one operation to another (e.g. leaving the denominator unchanged in multiplication, or seeking a common denominator where multiplication does not need one); the panel recommends confronting these confusions directly.
learnerActions: Examine worked examples where an algorithm has been mis-applied: a multiplication where the common denominator was kept (e.g. 9/12 × 8/12 written as 72/12), or an addition done straight across.
Catch the error, name which operation's method was wrongly imported, and redo the calculation correctly.
Match each incorrect worked example to the specific error it contains.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to diagnose a wrongly chosen method gives evidence that the pupil distinguishes the procedures, though it should be confirmed by the pupil producing correct methods; it confronts the exact confusion documented as tripping up students and teachers alike.

activities.title: Signed integers on a number line
feedback: If a learner gives −8 for −5 + 3, they have treated it as −(5+3); walk the move of 3 to the right from −5 to land at −2.
If a learner gives 8, the sign has been dropped; re-model the starting point at −5 and the direction of the move to land at −2.
Reinforce by distinguishing −×− (sign rule for multiplication) from −+− (combining on the line).
activities.rationale: A number line makes the direction and magnitude of combining signed quantities concrete and separates it from sign-rule arithmetic for multiplication and division.
learnerActions: Model −5 + 3 as a move of 3 to the right starting from −5, landing at −2.
Answer: is −5 + 3 bigger or smaller than −5, which direction do you move, and why?
Separate 'combining signed quantities' (addition/subtraction) from 'multiplying/dividing signs', stating the rule for each.
Estimate and check: does combining a negative with a positive of smaller magnitude (e.g. −5 + 3) stay negative?
activities.intendedInsight: Adding a positive to a negative moves right along the number line, toward zero and past it if the positive has the larger magnitude (e.g. −5 + 8 = 3); the sign is not simply inherited and magnitudes are not simply summed. Combining signed quantities is a different process from multiplying/dividing signs.

activities.title: Convert mixed numbers before × and ÷
feedback: If a learner multiplies/divides only the whole-number part, show how the fractional part is dropped and return to the improper-fraction rewrite.

If a learner keeps only one denominator when multiplying the improper forms (e.g. 5/2 × 2/3 → 10/2 instead of 10/6), return to the area meaning: both denominators partition the unit, so both are multiplied (2×3 = 6).
activities.rationale: Converting to improper fractions first and anchoring division in its measurement/partition meaning prevents incomplete distribution and keeps the computation meaningful.
learnerActions: Rewrite a mixed number as an improper fraction before multiplying or dividing, e.g. 2 1/2 = 5/2.
Divide: 2 1/2 ÷ 1/2 by working from the improper form 5/2 ÷ 1/2.
Keep the meaning of division attached — for example reading a division as 'how many halves fit?' — and check the answer makes sense.
Estimate first so an incomplete distribution (multiplying only the whole part) is caught.
activities.intendedInsight: Converting mixed numbers to improper fractions before multiplying or dividing is the standard, reliable method; working on the mixed form directly often leads to incomplete distribution (e.g. operating on only the whole part) unless every part is distributed.

constraints: Scored multiple-choice or sorting tasks (e.g. 'which method does this need?', sorting calculations into needs/does-not-need a common denominator, matching a wrong worked example to its error) may efficiently check which method a pupil selects and surface algorithm confusion, but recognition of a method is not the same as producing one: such tasks do not themselves require a pupil to construct and justify a full written method, so pair them with pupils writing out and explaining their own working.

A static comparison chart of the four operations on one pair (tap-to-reveal each worked method, lift-the-flap 'why does × not need a common denominator?') supports the contrast but cannot let a pupil test method-selection on new operands; use it as a reference scaffold, not the main task.
Always require an estimate before each calculation to catch mis-applied algorithms and sign errors.
Watch and discuss the written method, not just the final answer, since the imported procedure is where the confusion shows.

A tutor-style 'which method and why?' dialogue can press past 'because that's the rule' and surface a pupil's reasoning, but the computation and the signed/mixed manipulations need a visual or symbolic working surface alongside it.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 3/4 + 2/3 = 9/12 + 8/12 = 17/12 = 1 5/12 ✓; 3/4 × 2/3 = 6/12 = 1/2 ✓; −5 + 3 = −2 ✓; 2 1/2 = 5/2 ✓; 5/2 ÷ 1/2 = 5 ✓; 5/2 × 2/3 = 10/6 ✓. The listed misconception endpoints (−8, 8, 10/2, keeping one denominator) are labelled as errors, not as valid answers.

Multiplication (and standard division) 'not needing' a common denominator is correct as a standard-method statement; an equivalent-fractions or common-denominator-division route can incidentally share a denominator but is never required. Kept scoped to the required method.

The KS3 curriculum source claim establishes the overall synthesis requirement (all four operations across integers, decimals, proper/improper fractions and mixed numbers, positive and negative) but is not attached to any activity's sourceClaims, because no individual activity rationale depends on that requirement specifically rather than on the method-contrast principle.

sourceClaims on the signed-integer and mixed-number activities are [] because the two available sources address fraction algorithm confusion and the KS3 curriculum requirement, not number-line sign handling or conversion efficacy specifically.

The decimals strand of the objective is named in the summary but has no dedicated activity; a formal-written-method decimals task would complete coverage and could reuse the estimate-first and show-your-method constraints.

probeDeeper: Why does the addition need a common denominator but the multiplication doesn't?
Is −5 + 3 bigger or smaller than −5 — which way do you move on the number line, and why?
Turn 2 1/2 into an improper fraction — how would you then divide it by 1/2?
Estimate 3/4 + 2/3 — should it be more or less than 1, and does your exact answer agree?

errorPatterns.pattern: Imports the wrong algorithm: finds a common denominator to MULTIPLY (3/4 × 2/3 → recuts to twelfths first), or multiplies across to ADD (3/4 + 2/3 → 6/12)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast the two on the same operands and name the principle — addition combines same-size parts (needs a common denominator), multiplication scales (does not); re-establish the ± common-denominator method
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The method for (b) shows a common-denominator step, or (a) shows a straight-across multiplication; the two operations are handled by the same ritual

errorPatterns.pattern: Leaves a denominator unchanged in multiplication: 3/4 × 2/3 → 6/4 (or 6/3), multiplying numerators but keeping one denominator
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the area meaning of fraction multiplication — both denominators partition the unit — so both are multiplied; recompute on a tiled square
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Product keeps an original denominator rather than 4×3 = 12

errorPatterns.pattern: Sign error combining signed integers: −5 + 3 treated as −(5+3) = −8, or the sign dropped to give 8
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model −5 + 3 as a move of 3 to the right from −5 on a number line, landing at −2; separate combining signed quantities from multiplying signs
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer −8 or 8; the 3 is added to the magnitude or the sign is mishandled

responseLevels.gap: Confuses the algorithms (common denominator in ×, or add-across in +) and/or makes sign errors; no reliable method-selection.
responseLevels.full: Selects and applies the correct method for each operation fluently across fractions, mixed numbers and signed integers, converts to improper fractions for ×/÷, handles signs on a number line, estimates for reasonableness, and transfers to unfamiliar mixed cases.
responseLevels.partial: Each operation is correct in isolation but the child hesitates or slips when operations are interleaved, does not convert mixed numbers to improper before ×/÷, and offers no estimate to check.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these out, showing your method for each: (a) 3/4 + 2/3; (b) 3/4 × 2/3; (c) −5 + 3.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Pairing addition and multiplication of the SAME fractions is the trap for algorithm confusion: a child who genuinely distinguishes the methods finds a common denominator for (a) and multiplies straight across for (b); a confused child either seeks a common denominator in (b) or multiplies across in (a). The signed item (c) separates 'combining signed quantities' from magnitude arithmetic — −2 versus −8 or 8. Watching the written method, not just the answers, shows exactly which procedure was imported where.

sources.claim: Students and even many teachers confuse the algorithms for adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing fractions, and over-generalise a rule that fits one operation to another (e.g. leaving the denominator unchanged in multiplication, or seeking a common denominator where multiplication does not need one); the panel recommends confronting these confusions directly.
sources.source: IES / What Works Clearinghouse — Developing Effective Fractions Instruction K–8 (Siegler et al. 2010), Recommendations 3 & 5

sources.claim: KS3 Number programme of study requires pupils to 'use the 4 operations, including formal written methods, applied to integers, decimals, proper and improper fractions, and mixed numbers, all both positive and negative' — the exact synthesis this topic assesses.
sources.source: DfE, National curriculum in England: mathematics programmes of study, Key Stage 3 — Number (statutory; Crown copyright)

pedagogy.summary: At 9-10, problems become genuinely complex — three or more steps spanning large numbers, fractions, decimals, and percentages, often with unit conversion. The child analyses what is known and unknown, plans a multi-step strategy, and — crucially — evaluates reasonableness through estimation and inverse operations (e.g. estimating 4,832 × 7 as ≈ 35,000 to vet a computed 33,824; recognising that a percentage over 100% cannot represent part of a whole in context). The keyword strategy and the compulsion to calculate remain the dominant threats, now compounded by weak magnitude sense with decimals and percentages. Teaching centres on estimation-as-benchmark, student-built representations that expose sub-structure, and modelled self-questioning to monitor a long solution.
bestPractices: Estimate first with rounding to set a magnitude benchmark, then compute, then check against the estimate; verify with inverse operations
Analyse known vs unknown explicitly before planning; represent the unknown (letter or bar) rather than rushing to combine numbers
Teach magnitude sense for percentages and decimals: a part cannot exceed 100% of the whole; sense-check the size of decimal answers
Build the student's own diagram (bar/double-number-line for percentages, strip for fractions) to expose sub-structure (WWC Rec 3)
Model self-questioning to monitor progress across three or more steps (WWC Rec 2)
Teach structure/schema over keywords — keyword matching is unreliable and collapses on multi-step problems
keyRepresentations: Rounding/estimation to a benchmark (≈ 5,000 × 7) for reasonableness
Bar model and double number line for percentages/decimals
Strip diagram for fraction sub-steps
Inverse-operation check (work backwards)
Known/unknown analysis with a letter for the unknown
commonMisconceptions: Keyword strategy on complex problems — operations chosen from words, wrong order
No estimate/reasonableness check — accepting a computed answer that rounding would flag as wrong (compulsion to calculate)
Weak magnitude sense — accepting a percentage over 100% or a 'part' larger than the whole as a valid answer in context
Losing track across three or more steps — not monitoring what has been found versus what remains

learn.summary: For 9-10 year olds tackling complex problems of three or more steps that span large numbers, fractions, decimals, and percentages (often with unit conversion), the goal is to make estimation-as-benchmark, inverse-operation checking, and magnitude sense into trusted, routinely-used tools. The dominant threats are the keyword strategy (choosing operations from cue words), the compulsion to calculate (computing without checking reasonableness), and weak magnitude sense (accepting a percentage over 100%, or a 'part' larger than the whole, as a part of a fixed group). Activities centre on: estimate-first routines that set a magnitude band before computing, student-built representations (bar models, double number lines, strip diagrams) that expose problem structure, explicit known/unknown analysis, and modelled self-questioning to monitor long solutions.

activities.title: Estimate-first complex-problem solver
feedback: If a computed answer lands outside the estimate band the child set, flag it and ask them to recheck that step rather than supplying the number: 'Your estimate said about 35,000 — does 338,240 fit inside your band?' (4,832 × 7 is actually 33,824, which does fit near 35,000; an answer like 338,240 is about ten times too big and should be flagged.)

OPTIONAL interaction example: a reasonableness gauge can do two jobs — light up when a computed answer falls outside the child's own estimate band, and light up on an impossible context such as working that yields '130% of the pupils' with a prompt like 'more than everyone?'. Offer this as a support, not a required mechanism.

When the child reaches an over-100% 'part' of a fixed group (e.g. pupils who passed), prompt: 'Could more than everyone have passed? What does that tell you about your working?' rather than correcting it directly.
When a step is complete, point to the tracker: 'What have you found, and what is still unknown?'
activities.rationale: Estimation-as-benchmark, inverse checking, and percentage/decimal magnitude sense are act-and-recompute skills best rehearsed by doing them on a live problem. Student-built representations expose sub-structure and self-questioning supports monitoring across multiple steps.
sourceClaims: Self-questioning to monitor and reflect (Rec 2) and student-built visual representations of problem structure (Rec 3) each have strong evidence for improving multi-step problem solving.
The compulsion to calculate leads students to compute without evaluating reasonableness; teachers should focus on relationships and reasonableness before and after computing.
Proficient solvers analyse givens and goals, monitor and evaluate progress, and check answers by a different method, continually asking 'Does this make sense?'.
learnerActions: Take a three-step problem, e.g. finding a percentage of a large quantity that also requires a unit conversion, and lay it out as separate sub-step cards so each step is visible.
Build your own representation for the key step: a double number line or bar model for the percentage step, a strip diagram for a fraction step.
Before computing, round each number and place an estimate into a benchmark band (e.g. round 4,832 to about 5,000, so 4,832 × 7 should be about 35,000).
Compute each sub-step, then compare the computed answer against your own estimate band, and against what makes sense in context (e.g. a 'part' of a fixed group cannot be more than everyone in it).
Keep a running 'found so far / still to find' tracker so you don't lose your place across the steps.
Work backwards with an inverse operation to confirm or fix the answer.
activities.intendedInsight: An answer can be rejected by your own estimate and by plain context, not just by a teacher. Estimation and magnitude sense become tools you trust, and a long problem stays manageable when its sub-structure is laid out and monitored.

activities.title: Known/unknown analysis before computing
feedback: If the child picks an operation from a single word, ask them to lay out known vs unknown first and justify the step order from the relationships.
Praise plans that name what is unknown and defer computing until the structure is clear.
activities.rationale: Keyword matching is unreliable and collapses on multi-step problems; teaching structure/schema and explicit known/unknown analysis gives a dependable basis for planning.
sourceClaims: Keyword-to-operation matching is unreliable and collapses on multi-step problems; teach problem structure (schema) instead.
Self-questioning to monitor and reflect (Rec 2) and student-built visual representations of problem structure (Rec 3) each have strong evidence for improving multi-step problem solving.
learnerActions: Before touching the numbers, write down what is known and what is unknown in the problem.
Represent the unknown explicitly — with a letter or a bar — rather than rushing to combine numbers.
State a plan for the order of steps, explaining why that order, based on how the quantities relate rather than on cue words.
Discuss why a cue word (e.g. 'altogether', 'left') can point to the wrong operation on a multi-step problem.
activities.intendedInsight: The plan should come from the structure of the problem, not from matching keywords to operations, which is unreliable and breaks down on multi-step problems.

activities.title: Reasoning partner that prompts (does not supply)
feedback: The partner should never supply the steps; if the child stalls, narrow the prompt (e.g. 'round each number first') rather than give the answer.
When the child verbalises a correct magnitude rejection with a reason, affirm the reasoning, not just the conclusion.
activities.rationale: Prompting known/unknown analysis, an estimate, and an inverse check across a long problem rehearses the monitoring routine and forces the child to justify magnitude reasoning aloud.
sourceClaims: Self-questioning to monitor and reflect (Rec 2) and student-built visual representations of problem structure (Rec 3) each have strong evidence for improving multi-step problem solving.
Proficient solvers analyse givens and goals, monitor and evaluate progress, and check answers by a different method, continually asking 'Does this make sense?'.
learnerActions: Work through a long problem with a partner (teacher, peer, or in-role coach) who asks, not tells.
Answer prompts aloud: 'What's known and unknown? What's your estimate? Could that percentage be right — more than everyone? Can you check it a different way, working backwards?'
Justify your magnitude reasoning aloud, e.g. explain why 130% of the pupils cannot be a valid part of a fixed whole group.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the monitoring routine — analyse, estimate, sense-check magnitude, verify by inverse — makes it habitual and portable to new problems.

activities.title: Estimation and magnitude-sense targeted items
feedback: Use these items alongside richer problem-solving work, not as a substitute: a scored linear format can check estimation and magnitude judgements but does not itself elicit the independent planning or monitoring a long solution requires.
If a child rejects 250% of a jug as nonsense, probe: a jug is a unit you can need more than one of, so 250% means 2.5 jugs — distinguish 'part of a fixed group' from 'multiples of a reference unit'.
activities.rationale: Estimation and magnitude-sense recognition items suit this age and give useful diagnostic signal on reasonableness, but recognition-only formats do not themselves elicit the independent planning and monitoring a full solution requires.
sourceClaims: Proficient solvers analyse givens and goals, monitor and evaluate progress, and check answers by a different method, continually asking 'Does this make sense?'.
The compulsion to calculate leads students to compute without evaluating reasonableness; teachers should focus on relationships and reasonableness before and after computing.
learnerActions: Answer short targeted questions such as 'Which computed answer must be wrong by estimation?' and 'Can 130% of the class pass?'
For a counterexample like 'A jug holds 2 litres; a recipe needs 250% of the jug — what does that mean?', decide whether it is nonsense or a sensible 2.5 jugs, and explain your reasoning.
Explain in each case how rounding or the 100%-is-the-whole idea drove your judgement.
activities.intendedInsight: Estimation brackets a calculation and magnitude sense tells whether a percentage or decimal result is possible in context — and over-100% is not automatically impossible (2.5 jugs is fine) when the whole is a reference unit you can need more than one of, rather than a fixed group.

activities.title: Worked complex problem with reveal of estimate and inverse check
feedback: Make clear this is a worked example to study: the child does not perform the planning or checking here, so always pair it with an attempt where they do.
Prompt transfer: 'Now set your own estimate band before computing this new problem.'
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal worked example can display the estimate and inverse check to make the routine explicit, but because the child does not carry out the checking, it is a scaffold toward independent solving rather than a full task. No cited source claim directly supports passive worked-example modelling for this objective.
learnerActions: Study a complete worked three-step problem where each step can be revealed one at a time.
At each step, reveal the estimate benchmark that was set, and the explanation of why an over-100%-of-a-fixed-group answer would be impossible.
Then attempt a fresh problem yourself, applying the estimate-then-check routine without the reveals.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing how an experienced solver sets an estimate and reasons about magnitude models the routine before the child performs it independently.

constraints: Scored, linear question formats and recognition-only items can probe estimation and magnitude judgements but do not themselves elicit the planning or monitoring of a long solution; use them alongside full problem-solving work, not as a substitute.

A tap-to-reveal worked example shows the estimate and inverse check but the child does not perform the planning or checking; treat it as a modelling scaffold and always follow with an independent attempt.
In the reasoning-partner activity the partner must prompt and never supply the steps, or the monitoring routine is not rehearsed.

A percentage over 100% is impossible only as a 'part' of a fixed whole group (e.g. pupils who passed). It is perfectly valid when the whole is a reference unit that can be exceeded (e.g. 250% of a jug = 2.5 jugs). Do not teach 'over 100% is always wrong'; teach the distinction.
Optional interface features (reasonableness gauge, benchmark band, running found/to-find tracker, double number line) make the mechanism concrete but are examples, not mandatory components.
Complex numerical problem solving here is not inherently spatial; a 3D spatial treatment was judged a poor fit for this objective, though this is a design judgement rather than a general rule.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support teaching principles, not the specific activities' effectiveness.

Self-audit of the estimation example: rounding 4,832 up to 5,000 gives 5,000 × 7 = 35,000, a reasonable benchmark for the exact product 4,832 × 7 = 33,824 (33,824 is below but close to 35,000, consistent with rounding up). The example is sound.

The source materials frame 'a percentage over 100% cannot represent part of a whole' as a magnitude-sense target. This is correct for a part of a fixed group, but the row's own counterexample (250% of a 2-litre jug = 2.5 jugs) shows over-100% is valid for a reference unit. The rewrite preserves both and scopes the distinction in every relevant activity and in constraints to avoid teaching an over-general rule.
The original assessment flagged the risk of a child wrongly rejecting 250% of a jug as nonsense; this nuance is retained in the magnitude-sense activity feedback.

The worked-example activity's sourceClaims were set to [] because no source claim directly supports passive worked-example modelling; the activity remains qualified as a scaffold toward independent solving.

Reteach-prerequisite and micro-topic identifiers from the source (place-value and percentage prerequisites) were dropped as internal catalog references; the underlying reteach moves (anchor percentages to a bar/number line, scaffold estimate-first) are preserved as feedback.

probeDeeper: 'About how big should 4,832 × 7 be? How does that help you trust or doubt 33,824?' (estimation benchmark)
'Could 130% of the pupils really have passed? Why not?' (percentage magnitude sense)
'Check the multiplication a different way — can you work backwards?' (inverse verification)

Counterexample: 'A jug holds 2 litres. A recipe needs 250% of the jug. What does that mean you need?' — does the child reinterpret sensibly (2.5 jugs) or reject it as nonsense wrongly, and can they explain?
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for a child who estimates 4,832 × 7 as about 5,000 × 7 = 35,000 and uses that to vet a computed 33,824, and who immediately recognises 130% of the pupils is impossible because a part cannot exceed the whole. Estimation as a benchmark and percentage/decimal magnitude sense are the targets.

errorPatterns.pattern: Keyword strategy on a complex multi-step problem — operations chosen from words and applied in the wrong order.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have the child analyse known/unknown and build their own diagram so the plan comes from structure; discuss why a cue word misleads.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child seizes on a word to pick an operation and cannot lay out a coherent plan for a three-step problem; keyword matching is known to fail on multi-step problems.

errorPatterns.pattern: No estimation/reasonableness check — computes without a rounding benchmark and accepts an answer that estimation would flag as wrong.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold estimate-first (round each number) as a benchmark and an inverse check after; revisit the estimation-and-check routine if needed.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives a product with no sense of its size and, when asked, cannot say roughly how big it should be; does not check by inverse.

errorPatterns.pattern: Weak magnitude sense with percentages/decimals — accepts a percentage over 100% (or a part larger than the whole) as a valid answer in context.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor percentages to a bar/double number line where 100% is the whole group; revisit percentage–decimal–fraction equivalents so magnitude is felt.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child carries '130% of the pupils' forward without flagging it, or accepts a fraction/decimal 'part' bigger than the whole.

responseLevels.gap: Picks operations from words, computes with no estimate, and accepts impossible answers (e.g. over-100% of a group) without noticing.
responseLevels.full: Analyses known/unknown, plans, sets an estimation benchmark, monitors across all steps, rejects impossible magnitudes with a reason, verifies by inverse, and transfers the estimate-then-check routine to a new complex problem unprompted.
responseLevels.partial: Can plan the steps and, when prompted, estimate or flag the percentage — but does not spontaneously use estimation to catch an error or reject an impossible magnitude, and loses track across three steps.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Pose a complex problem such as: 'Work out 4,832 × 7' followed by a context question like 'In a school of 240 pupils, a report says 130% passed. Could that be right?' Ask: 'Before computing the multiplication, about how big should it be? After, how do you know your answer is sensible? And what does the 130% tell you?' Discuss the reasoning; do not score the number.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with reasonableness reasoning brackets the multiplication by rounding and rejects the 130% on sight with a reason. A child on the keyword/compulsion habit computes without estimating and treats 130% as just another number to carry forward, noticing nothing. The magnitude-sense judgement and the estimation bracket are where correct and incorrect reasoning separate — hard to fake either.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 5–6 (UK Y1–Y2, US Grade 2). Using ARRAYS (rows and columns) to represent both multiplication and division — the canonical model that carries commutativity, the ×÷ inverse, and later the area model.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y1 'calculating the answer using … arrays with the support of the teacher'; Y2 'solve problems … using materials, arrays, repeated addition …'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.OA.4 'use addition to find the total number of objects arranged in rectangular arrays with up to 5 rows and up to 5 columns; write an equation to express the total as a sum of equal addends'; feeds 3.OA.1/3.
• Operational details: an array is a rectangle of objects in equal rows and columns. Read it two ways (3 rows of 4 = 4 columns of 3) to see COMMUTATIVITY; read it as repeated addition (each row is a group); cover part to see DIVISION (total ÷ rows = columns). The array is the single most reusable representation in the domain — it becomes the area model for written multiplication.
• Checkpoint: build and read arrays. Tier A (5): make a 2×3 array and count the total. Tier B (5–6): write the multiplication for an array (3 rows of 4 = 12) and rotate it. Tier C (6): from one array write two multiplications and a division (3×4=12, 4×3=12, 12÷4=3).
bestPractices: Build arrays physically in equal rows and columns and describe them precisely as 'rows of' and 'columns of' before recording — the regular structure is what makes the total computable without counting every object.
Rotate the array a quarter turn to reveal commutativity concretely: 3 rows of 4 becomes 4 rows of 3, same total — the array makes 3×4=4×3 obvious rather than asserted.
Read the SAME array as repeated addition (row by row) and as multiplication, so the array ties the two together.
Use the array to introduce division as the inverse: cover the total and ask 'if 12 objects make 3 equal rows, how many in each row?' — one picture yields the whole fact family.
Treat the array as the seed of the area model — keep rows/columns aligned in a rectangle so the later transition to area and the grid/expanded written methods is continuous.
keyRepresentations: The rectangular array of counters/dots (rows × columns)
The array rotated 90° to show commutativity
Fact-family link: one array → two × facts + two ÷ facts
The array as precursor to the area model / grid method for written multiplication
commonMisconceptions: Confusing rows with columns and so mis-describing the array (though the total is the same, the language matters for later).
Counting every object one-by-one instead of using the row/column structure (missing the point of the array).
Not seeing that a rotated array has the same total — treating 3×4 and 4×3 as needing separate counts.
Building arrays with unequal rows (ragged rectangles) — breaking the equal-groups structure.
Not recognising the array as a division picture as well as a multiplication one.

learn.summary: For ages 5–6 (roughly UK Year 1 into early Year 2; US Kindergarten–Grade 1, noting that US standards formally introduce arrays in Grade 2, ages 7–8), use rectangular arrays (equal rows and columns) as a central model for multiplication and division. Learners build arrays, read them two ways to see commutativity, read them as repeated addition, and cover part to reveal division — so one picture yields a whole fact family and seeds the later area model.

activities.title: Build and read an array
feedback: If a learner counts all 12 by ones, model skip-counting each row aloud ('4, 8, 12') and point to each row as you go; the structural view develops with repeated exposure to equal grouping, so do not drill it.
If rows are different lengths (a ragged arrangement), line up the columns and check every row has the same number before reading it — only then is it a true array.
Prompt: 'How could you count the total quickly using the rows?'
activities.rationale: Describing arrays precisely as 'rows of' and 'columns of' before recording makes the regular structure explicit, which is what lets the total be computed from the factors rather than counted individually. If using physical counters, note the counters sit in a flat grid: the array represents a 2D arrangement.
sourceClaims: Y1 use arrays (with teacher support); Y2 solve problems using materials, arrays and repeated addition.
2.OA.4 find the total of objects in rectangular arrays (up to 5×5) and express as a sum of equal addends.
The array is the key representation linking repeated addition, commutativity and the inverse relationship, and is the precursor to the area model for formal multiplication.
learnerActions: Lay out counters (or draw dots) in equal rows and columns to make an array, e.g. 3 rows of 4.
Say aloud exactly what you made: '3 rows of 4' — then also read it as columns: '4 columns of 3'.
Find the total WITHOUT counting every object: skip-count each row, '4, 8, 12'.
Write the multiplication the array shows: 3 × 4 = 12.
Try building another array to order as an extension, e.g. 'Show me 2 × 5 as an array', and state its total.
activities.intendedInsight: An array has a regular row/column structure, so you can find the total by using the rows rather than counting every object one by one.

activities.title: Rotate the array to see commutativity
feedback: If a learner re-counts from scratch after rotating and is surprised the total matches, revisit that the same counters were only turned, none added or removed.
If a learner treats 3×4 and 4×3 as needing separate counts, have them physically rotate the same array rather than build a new one.
Prompt: 'If I turned the array on its side, what multiplication would it show then?'
activities.rationale: Physically rotating one array a quarter turn demonstrates commutativity concretely rather than asserting it, because the same objects are rearranged and the total is preserved. In a screen model this can be an interactive rotate control with the product shown updating live; on paper, physically turning the layout serves the same purpose.
sourceClaims: The array is the key representation linking repeated addition, commutativity and the inverse relationship, and is the precursor to the area model for formal multiplication.
learnerActions: Build 3 rows of 4 and record the total (12).
Turn the whole array a quarter turn so it becomes 4 rows of 3.
Count or check the total again and notice it is still 12.
Write both multiplications from the one array: 3 × 4 = 12 and 4 × 3 = 12.
activities.intendedInsight: Rotating an array turns 3 rows of 4 into 4 rows of 3 while the total stays the same — so 3 × 4 = 4 × 3 is something you can see, not just a rule to remember.

activities.title: Find the division in the same array
feedback: If a learner builds rows of 4 but can't name a division, point to each 'group of 4', count the groups, and name that as 12 ÷ 4 = 3 — bridging both operations on one array.
Prompt: 'What division does your rows-of-4 array show?'
activities.rationale: Using the array to introduce division as the inverse — covering the array, stating the total and the number of rows, and asking how many are in each row — lets a single picture yield the whole fact family, linking multiplication and division. A cover action (physical card or an interactive mask) makes the 'unknown' concrete.
sourceClaims: Y1 use arrays (with teacher support); Y2 solve problems using materials, arrays and repeated addition.
The array is the key representation linking repeated addition, commutativity and the inverse relationship, and is the precursor to the area model for formal multiplication.
learnerActions: Start from a total, e.g. 12 loose counters.
Arrange them into an array with rows of 4; count how many rows you made.
State the division the array shows: 12 ÷ 4 = 3 (12 grouped into rows of 4 makes 3 rows).
Cover the array, tell a partner the total (12) and the number of rows (3), and ask how many are in each row (12 ÷ 3 = 4); then uncover to check.
activities.intendedInsight: One array is a division picture as well as a multiplication picture: the rows and columns are the two factors, and reading the total the other way reveals the inverse fact.

activities.title: Write the whole fact family from one array
feedback: If a learner writes only one multiplication, have them rotate (or re-read) the array to find the second.
If the division facts are missing, link each factor to a dimension: 'how many rows?' and 'how many in each row?'

A tap-to-reveal reference array (callouts for rows, columns, total and the facts) can support learners as a check — but reading and writing the facts themselves, not just recognising them, is the goal.
activities.rationale: Reading the SAME array as repeated addition and as multiplication, and deriving both × and ÷ facts, connects the representations so one picture supports the whole fact family and keeps the rows/columns aligned for the later area/grid method.
sourceClaims: The array is the key representation linking repeated addition, commutativity and the inverse relationship, and is the precursor to the area model for formal multiplication.
learnerActions: Look at a single array (e.g. 3 rows of 4).
Write both multiplication facts: 3 × 4 = 12 and 4 × 3 = 12.
Write both division facts: 12 ÷ 4 = 3 and 12 ÷ 3 = 4.
Also write the array as repeated addition, row by row: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
activities.intendedInsight: A single array ties together repeated addition, two multiplication facts and two division facts — it is a key, highly reusable representation, and the same rectangle later becomes the area model for written multiplication.

constraints: Keep rows and columns equal and aligned in a rectangle; ragged arrangements break the equal-groups structure the array depends on.

Learners should construct and build arrays (from counters, drawing, or a drag-to-set builder), not only recognise or match pre-made ones — recognition/matching tasks check array-reading but do not elicit independent construction.
Keep the rows/columns aligned as a rectangle so the transition to the area model and grid/expanded written methods stays continuous.

Checkpoint tiers: Tier A (age 5) make a 2×3 array and count the total; Tier B (5–6) write the multiplication for an array and rotate it; Tier C (6) from one array write two multiplications and a division.

A static labelled array (e.g. a fixed on-screen image) is a useful reference and can show the fact family, but the learner cannot resize or rebuild it, and a fixed screen image cannot be rotated. Pair it with building/rotating work when the commutativity-by-rotation insight is the aim.

An array is a flat 2D rectangular arrangement; distinguish the grid from any physical counters used to build it. A 3D rendering is not required for this 2D objective and adds handling cost — this is a design judgement for this task, not a claim that 3D provides no learning value in general.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source rated a 'conversation/dialogue' artefact as poor-fit on the grounds it 'adds little' and 3D as adding 'no insight'; these are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws. They have been softened throughout to scoped notes about the 2D representation and the value of construction; comparative efficacy of any medium is not asserted.

The original pedagogy called the array 'the single most reusable representation in the domain'; this superlative exceeds the cited source claims (which say 'key representation') and has been reduced to a sourced 'key, highly reusable representation' framing.
Source worked examples use 3 rows of 4 = 12 (3×4=12, 4×3=12, 12÷4=3, 12÷3=4) and 2×3=6; arithmetic checked and correct.
Source marks CCSS-M 2.OA.4 and the NCETM claim as verified:false; treat those citations as unverified. The DfE NC claim is marked verified:true in the source but has not been re-checked here.

sourceClaims in Activity 1 attach the DfE and CCSS-M curriculum claims (building arrays with materials; equal-addend/repeated-addition basis) alongside the NCETM structural claim; the NCETM claim most directly supports the precise-structure rationale, while DfE/CCSS support the array-and-repeated-addition basis rather than the specific language principle.

probeDeeper: How could you count the total quickly using the rows?
What division does your rows-of-4 array show?
If I turned the array on its side, what multiplication would it show then?
Show me 2 × 5 as an array.
assess.correctAnswer: The array shows 3 × 4 = 12 (3 rows of 4). Arranging 12 into rows of 4 makes 3 rows — that same picture shows 12 ÷ 4 = 3. The rows and columns match the two factors.

errorPatterns.pattern: doesn't use the array structure — counts every counter one at a time instead of rows × per-row
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT drill — model skip-counting each row ('4, 8, 12'); the structural view of arrays develops with repeated exposure to equal grouping
errorPatterns.revealedBy: counts all 12 by ones with no use of the rows

errorPatterns.pattern: builds a non-rectangular arrangement — makes rows of different lengths so it isn't a true array
errorPatterns.nextMove: align the columns and check every row has the same number before reading it
errorPatterns.revealedBy: ragged, unequal rows when building

errorPatterns.pattern: can't read the division from the array — reads 3 × 4 but doesn't see 12 ÷ 4 = 3 in the same picture
errorPatterns.nextMove: point to the 'groups of 4', count the groups, and name that as 12 ÷ 4 — bridging both operations on one array
errorPatterns.revealedBy: builds rows of 4 but can't state the number of rows as a division

responseLevels.gap: Miscounts arrays by counting one-by-one and cannot build an equal-rows arrangement; rows/columns aren't linked to the factors.
responseLevels.full: Reads an array as a multiplication and total, builds an array to match a grouping/division situation, and connects the same array to both operations.
responseLevels.partial: Reads or builds an array for multiplication but doesn't connect it to the matching division, or needs support to keep the rows equal.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is an array — 3 rows with 4 counters in each row. Tell me a multiplication this array shows and what the total is. Now here are 12 loose counters — arrange them into an array with rows of 4, and tell me how many rows you made.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who reads arrays maps rows-and-columns to the factors and the total, both when reading a given array and when building one from a situation. A child without it counts one-by-one (missing the row structure and often mis-totalling), says only 'lots' rather than 3×4, or builds a ragged arrangement with unequal rows. Requiring both an INTERPRET (read the array) and a TRANSLATE (build from a grouping) exposes exactly where the mapping breaks.

sources.claim: Y1 use arrays (with teacher support); Y2 solve problems using materials, arrays and repeated addition.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 8–9y; interpret products of whole numbers: 5 × 7 means 5 groups of 7 (equal-groups structure made explicit and named).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y3 pupils develop reliable methods and 'solve problems, including missing number problems, involving multiplication', building on Y2 recall of 2/5/10 tables and the equal-groups meaning of ×.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.OA.1 — 'Interpret products of whole numbers, e.g., interpret 5 × 7 as the total number of objects in 5 groups of 7 objects.'
• Operational details — the first factor is the number of groups, the second the group size (adopt one convention explicitly, but show children the answer is the same either way — a bridge to commutativity). Move deliberately from repeated addition (7+7+7+7+7) to the compact product 5×7, so × is seen as a shorthand for equal groups, not a brand-new operation. Use the three canonical models in parallel: equal groups (collections), arrays (rows×columns), and number-line hops of equal size.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8): given 4 × 6, say/draw 4 groups of 6 and give the total. Tier B (age 8–9): match a × expression to the correct equal-groups word problem and to an array. Tier C (age 9): write a × expression for a picture AND explain what each factor represents (groups vs group size).
bestPractices: Bridge explicitly from repeated addition: write 7+7+7+7+7 alongside 5×7 so the product is felt as a compression of equal groups, not a new fact to memorise.
Use the three-model triangle — equal groups, array, equal-hops on a number line — and have children translate one representation into the others; fluency in switching is the concept.
Insist on language: read 5 × 7 as 'five groups of seven', and always name what each factor means, so children do not treat × as a meaningless symbol between two numbers.
Follow CPA: concrete counters into hoops → pictorial array/bar → abstract expression, keeping the equal-groups meaning visible at each step.
Contrast equal-groups situations with unequal-groups ones (3+5+4 is NOT multiplication) so children abstract the 'equal' in equal groups.
keyRepresentations: Equal groups (counters in hoops / bags of sweets) — the primary meaning of a product
Rectangular array (rows × columns) — makes the total structured and countable, and previews commutativity and area
Number line with equal-sized hops — links × to skip counting and to scaling
Bar model / repeated-addition strip — 5 equal bars of 7 bridging + to ×
commonMisconceptions: Reading 5 × 7 as '5 and 7' or adding the factors (5+7=12) rather than seeing groups.
Confusing which factor is the number of groups vs the group size, then drawing 7 groups of 5 for '5 groups of 7' — harmless for the product but a sign the structure isn't understood.
Believing the groups need not be equal — counting any collection as multiplication.
Thinking × always makes a 'much bigger' number and being surprised by ×1 or (later) ×0 and fractional factors.
Treating × as an unrelated new operation rather than a shorthand for repeated equal addition.

learn.summary: For 8–9 year olds, build the meaning of a product as equal groups: 5 × 7 means 5 groups of 7, totalling 35. Move deliberately from repeated addition (7+7+7+7+7) to the compact product, naming what each factor represents (number of groups vs group size), and translate between equal-groups collections, rectangular arrays, and equal-sized number-line hops. The central idea to establish is that the groups must be equal, and that × is a shorthand for repeated equal addition, not a brand-new operation.

activities.title: Equal-groups builder: set the groups and the group size
feedback: If a child makes the groups unequal, point out the arrangement can't be written as one × expression until every group matches — this is the 'equal' in equal groups.
When a child writes 5 × 7, have them point to the five hoops and to the seven counters inside one hoop, naming each factor's job.
If a child reads 5 × 7 as '5 and 7' or expects 5+7=12, set the array and the sum 7+7+7+7+7 side by side and count the total (35) together to show it is not simple addition of the two numbers.
activities.rationale: Letting quantity drive a linked visual — hoops, array, and repeated-addition sum updating together — is intended to let 'groups of' be felt rather than told, and surfacing the equal-groups constraint directly addresses the misconception that any collection counts as multiplication. Live recolouring/relinking of the three representations is an optional interaction example that makes the mechanism concrete, not a required feature.
sourceClaims: Equal-groups, array, and number-line models should be used in parallel and translated between to build the meaning of multiplication (CRA/CPA progression).
learnerActions: Choose how many groups and how many in each group (for example, 5 groups of 7), then place that many counters into each hoop.
Watch an array of rows × columns assemble beside the hoops and a running repeated-addition sum (7+7+7+7+7) build underneath, all three reading the same total.
Collapse the long sum into the product by writing it as 5 × 7, and read it aloud as 'five groups of seven'.
Deliberately drag one extra counter into a single hoop so the groups become unequal, and notice the arrangement can no longer be written as a single product until all groups match again.
Vary the two quantities and say, each time, which number is the number of groups and which is the size of each group.
activities.intendedInsight: A product is equal groups counted efficiently: the total recomputes as you change how many groups and how many per group, and the groups must be equal for a single multiplication to describe them. Repeated addition and the product are two forms of the same quantity.

activities.title: Concrete to pictorial to symbol with real counters
feedback: If a child draws 6 groups of 4 for 'four baskets of six', agree the total is the same (24) but map the story precisely: 4 baskets (groups), each holding 6.
If a drawing is correct but the equation is hesitant, label the array's rows and columns and read both factors off the picture to bridge drawing to symbols.
If the number-line hops are unequal, point out each hop must be the same size (6) precisely because the groups are equal.

For the unequal example, ask what single number is in every group as the groups stand; show that there isn't one, so no single × expression describes these groups. (If a child notices the 12 counters could be shared out again into 3 groups of 4, agree: that is a new, equal grouping, so it can be written as 3 × 4.)
activities.rationale: A concrete-pictorial-abstract progression keeps the equal-groups meaning visible at each step, and explicitly contrasting equal with unequal groups helps children abstract the 'equal' requirement. Paper, counters, drawn arrays and a number line are welcome concrete media here, and the number-line hops realise the third canonical model.
sourceClaims: Equal-groups, array, and number-line models should be used in parallel and translated between to build the meaning of multiplication (CRA/CPA progression).
learnerActions: Put physical counters into hoops or bags to make, say, 4 groups of 6, and count the total.
Redraw the same situation as a rectangular array of 4 rows of 6 (or 6 rows of 4) and as a repeated-addition strip of 4 equal bars of 6.
Show the same four groups of six as four equal hops of 6 along a number line (0 → 6 → 12 → 18 → 24), landing on the total.
Write the matching expression and label which factor is the number of groups and which is the group size.
Contrast with an unequal collection such as 3 + 5 + 4 and explain why, as the groups stand, it cannot be written as a single multiplication.
activities.intendedInsight: The same equal-groups quantity can be shown concretely, pictorially, on a number line and symbolically, and only equal groups can be written as a single product; unequal groups cannot.

activities.title: Labelled reference diagram with reveal callouts
feedback: If a child can state the total but not what each factor means, direct them back to the specific callout for that factor.
Accept any wording for the 'why 5 × 7' question that expresses 'seven added five times' or 'five equal groups of seven'.
activities.rationale: A static labelled diagram with tap-to-reveal callouts is a clean vocabulary anchor. It names the structure well but does not let the child vary the numbers, so it supports reference and language rather than building the varying-quantity intuition; pair it with a manipulable activity.
learnerActions: Study a labelled picture of 5 groups of 7 (or a 5×7 array) and reveal callouts naming each part: '5 = number of groups', '7 = size of each group', '35 = total'.
Answer the prompt 'Why can we write 5 × 7 instead of 7+7+7+7+7?' in your own words.
Use the diagram as a reference while naming the factors in a new expression.
activities.intendedInsight: Each factor in a product has a distinct meaning — number of groups versus group size — and the product is the total of equal groups.

activities.title: Match, sort and consolidate (checking understanding)
feedback: If a child matches a '4 + 6' story to 4 × 6, build the four groups of six, count 24, and set it beside 4 + 6 = 10 so the difference between joining two numbers and making four equal groups is visible.
If a match is right but the reason is 'there's a 4 and a 6', ask them to point to the four groups and the six in each before accepting it.
activities.rationale: Matching and sorting tasks are highly checkable and good for consolidation and diagnosis, including a deliberate add-the-factors wrong option (a '4 + 6' story). A sort can check or reinforce classification of situations as equal-groups or not, but does not by itself elicit the child's own construction or explanation, so use it after hands-on construction.
learnerActions: Link an expression such as 4 × 6 to its array, its equal-groups picture, and a matching word problem.
Build or order the repeated-addition sum (6+6+6+6) that corresponds to a given product.
Decide whether a given story shows equal groups (multiplication) or just two numbers joined (addition), explaining the choice.
Spot and reject a tempting wrong match, such as a '4 + 6' story offered for 4 × 6, explaining why it does not fit.
activities.intendedInsight: Interpreting a product means connecting an expression to its equal-groups structure, its array, its repeated-addition form and a real situation — and distinguishing it from merely adding the two numbers seen.

activities.title: Explain equal groups to a puzzled partner
feedback: If the explanation only restates the numbers, ask the partner's follow-up 'how many groups, and how many in each?' to push toward structure.
If a story has unequal groups, ask whether every bag has the same number, and have them adjust it.
activities.rationale: Spoken explanation and responsive questioning can surface a child's own language for 'groups of' and probe factor meaning. A conversation on its own cannot display a recomputing array or collection, so use talk alongside a picture or array that shows the total.
learnerActions: Take the role of explaining to a younger friend (or a market stall-holder counting bags of apples) what 5 × 7 means.
Answer the partner's probing questions: 'How many bags, and how many in each?' and 'What does the 5 mean here?'
Tell a short story that matches a given product such as 3 × 5, naming the groups and the group size.
activities.intendedInsight: Putting equal-groups meaning into your own words can reveal and strengthen understanding of which factor is the number of groups and which is the group size.

constraints: Adopt one convention for reading the factors (first = number of groups, second = group size), but show that the total is the same either way as a bridge to commutativity; do not treat a right total with swapped factors as a product error.

Groups must be equal for a situation to be written as a single product; unequal collections as given (e.g. 3+5+4) cannot be described by one product and should be used as explicit non-examples, while acknowledging that regrouping the counters into equal groups (e.g. 3 groups of 4) creates a new equal-groups situation.

Reference diagrams and recognition/matching/sorting tasks check or anchor vocabulary and classification; they do not by themselves elicit independent construction or explanation, so pair them with activities where the child builds groups and writes the expression.
Spoken-explanation activities are a supplement: keep a visible array or collection alongside so the total and structure are shown, not only described.
Keep repeated addition visible next to the product at each step so × is experienced as a compression of equal addition, not a separate memorised fact.
Avoid implying × always makes a 'much bigger' number; this prepares for later ×1, ×0 and fractional factors without surprise.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit: 5 × 7 = 35 and 4 × 6 = 24 confirmed; repeated-addition forms (7 five times; 6 four times) are consistent, and the number-line hops 0→6→12→18→24 equal 24. 4 + 6 = 10 correctly contrasted with 4 × 6 = 24 in the misconception feedback.

Swapping factors (6 groups of 4 vs 4 groups of 6) gives the same total but a different match to a story; this is a matching/structure issue, not a wrong product — preserved as such, not framed as an arithmetic error.
Efficacy wording in the rationales uses intended/may because the activities are unvalidated proposals.

The equal-sized number-line hop model is now instantiated as a learner action and feedback item within the concrete-to-pictorial activity; it remains lighter than the equal-groups and array strands, so a dedicated skip-counting activity could further strengthen the three-model triangle.

Two of the three cited sources (3.OA.1 CCSS and the NCETM/CPA guidance) are marked verified:false in the source row; the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified:true. Cited claims support general teaching principles only and do not establish that these specific activities were tested or are comparatively more effective. The 3.OA.1 claim was not cited on any activity because it names the objective rather than any activity's specific teaching mechanism.

The non-preferred 3D option was omitted because its content was a ranking rationale (that a third spatial dimension adds no new information for planar equal-groups work) rather than a distinct teaching activity; this is a scoped observation, not an established universal law.
Quiz-step vocabulary (including 'distractor') and internal artefact-type labels were removed from learner-facing text per the brief.

probeDeeper: Draw me 4 × 6 — what does each part of your drawing show?
Is 4 × 6 the same total as 4 + 6? Why not?
Tell me a story that matches 3 × 5.
If each basket had 6 eggs and there were 5 baskets, how would the expression change?
assess.correctAnswer: 4 × 6 (and 6 + 6 + 6 + 6) — it's 4 groups of 6, so it's 6 added four times, total 24. 4 + 6 would just be one 4 and one 6 joined, not four groups of six.

errorPatterns.pattern: adds the two numbers — reads a multiplication story as 'combine the numbers I see' (4 + 6 = 10) rather than four groups of six
errorPatterns.nextMove: build the four groups of six with counters or an array, count the total, and set it beside 4 + 6 so the difference between joining two numbers and making equal groups is visible
errorPatterns.distractor: 4 + 6, because there's a 4 and a 6.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: chooses 4 + 6, or answers 10

errorPatterns.pattern: mis-maps which factor is the number of groups and which is the group size — draws 6 groups of 4 for 'four baskets of six'
errorPatterns.nextMove: agree the total is the same, then map the story precisely — 4 baskets (groups) each holding 6 — and discuss how the two factors play different roles in context
errorPatterns.revealedBy: draws 6 rows of 4 (right total, wrong match to the story)

errorPatterns.pattern: draws equal groups correctly but can't connect them to the expression — can't say which number is the groups and which the size
errorPatterns.nextMove: label the array's rows and columns and read off both factors, bridging drawing to symbols — the group idea is there, only the link to notation is missing
errorPatterns.revealedBy: a correct drawing paired with a wrong or hesitant equation

responseLevels.gap: Interprets the multiplication story additively (4 + 6) or spots the two numbers without the groups-of structure.
responseLevels.full: Explains 4 × 6 as four groups of six, draws or reads an array to match, and connects the equal-groups structure to both the repeated-addition form and a word problem.
responseLevels.partial: Identifies 4 × 6 and can draw equal groups, but is shaky about which factor is the number of groups versus the group size, or links to the expression only with support.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here's a problem: 'There are 4 baskets with 6 eggs in each basket.' Which of these could you write for it — 4 × 6, or 4 + 6, or 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 — and tell me why it means the same as the story.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who grasps multiplication as equal groups picks 4×6 (and the repeated-addition form) and explains it as four groups of six. A child with only a vague sense picks 4 + 6 (adds the two numbers they see), or picks 4×6 but justifies it by 'there's a 4 and a 6' rather than the groups-of structure. The 'why it means the same as the story' tier separates structural understanding from number-spotting.

sources.claim: Y3 pupils solve problems including missing-number problems involving multiplication, building on the equal-groups meaning established in Y2.
