pedagogy.summary: Systematic listing enumerates all combinations of two categories (e.g. 3 starters × 4 mains) so that none is missed and none repeated, by working in a fixed order: hold the first choice constant, run through every second choice, then move on. Organising the combinations into a table or tree makes completeness checkable, and reveals that the total equals the PRODUCT of the number of options in each category (3 × 4 = 12) — an early foundation of multiplicative counting.
bestPractices: Model a fixed order — hold starter 1 and pair it with every main in turn, then starter 2, and so on — rather than listing haphazardly
Record in a two-way grid or tree so gaps and repeats are visible and completeness can be argued
Ask 'how do you know you've found them all?' and value the answer 'I worked systematically'
Draw out that the total = rows × columns = the product of the options (3 × 4), not the sum (3 + 4)
Start from sorting/ordering the child's random attempts to expose what is missing, then move to generating in order
Offer the tree diagram as an alternative systematic structure to the grid
keyRepresentations: Two-way grid / table (one category on the rows, the other on the columns)
Tree diagram (a branch per first choice, a sub-branch per second choice)
An ordered list generated by holding one choice fixed
The multiplication statement 3 × 4 = 12 read off the grid
commonMisconceptions: Lists haphazardly, so combinations are missed or duplicated and completeness cannot be judged
Cannot tell whether all the combinations have been found
Predicts the total by ADDING the options (3 + 4 = 7) instead of multiplying (3 × 4 = 12)
Changes both choices at once (e.g. only the diagonal S1M1, S2M2, S3M3), losing track of the rest
Believes there are only a handful, stopping before the set is complete

learn.summary: Learners enumerate every combination of two categories (e.g. 3 starters × 4 mains) systematically — holding the first choice fixed and running through every second choice before moving on — so that none is missed or repeated. Recording the combinations in a two-way grid or tree makes completeness arguable and reveals that the total equals the PRODUCT of the options in each category (3 × 4 = 12), not their sum (3 + 4 = 7). This is an early foundation of multiplicative counting for Year 6.

activities.title: Pair and light the grid: building every meal in order
feedback: If the predicted total was 7, point out: each of the 3 starters makes 4 meals, so 4 + 4 + 4 = 3 × 4 = 12; the count is the grid's area (rows × columns = 3 × 4), whereas 3 + 4 just adds the two side counts and does not count the meals.

If the list is unordered with gaps or repeats, prompt: 'How do you know you've found them all?' and guide to the answer 'I worked systematically' — hold one category fixed and run through the other fully before changing it.

If only the diagonal (S1M1, S2M2, S3M3) was produced, note that both choices changed at once; show that a full ROW must be filled — fix starter 1 and vary the main across all four before moving to starter 2.
When the grid is complete and ordered, affirm that completeness can now be argued from the system itself, and that the whole row-by-row fill makes 3 × 4 = 12 visible as the grid's area.
activities.rationale: Starting from the learner's own random attempts and then sorting them exposes what is missing, motivating the move to systematic generation; a two-way grid makes completeness checkable and surfaces the product structure directly. A 'predict first' step confronts the add-versus-multiply error before building.
sourceClaims: Children first find all possibilities in a random way and cannot see which cases are missing; sorting their attempts exposes the gaps and teaches them to generate systematically, because having a system ensures no options are left out ('how do you know you've found them all?' — 'I worked systematically').
learnerActions: Start with 3 starters and 4 mains and first PREDICT how many different meals you think are possible before listing any — write down your prediction and say whether you think it is 3 + 4 or 3 × 4.

Begin by pairing starters and mains in any order you like, recording each meal you make in a two-way grid (starters down the side as rows, mains across the top as columns) by marking the matching cell.
Look at the grid: check whether random pairing has left scattered marked cells with empty gaps, or whether you tried to mark any meal twice. Ask yourself: have I found them all? Can I be sure?
Now switch to a fixed order: hold starter 1 and pair it with every main in turn (filling a whole ROW), then starter 2's row, then starter 3's row, until every cell is marked with no gaps.
Count the completed grid as rows × columns = 3 × 4 = 12, and compare this with your earlier prediction.
Explain how you know you have found every meal, and why the total is 3 × 4 rather than 3 + 4.
activities.intendedInsight: Working in a fixed order — fix one choice, run through every option of the other — guarantees no combination is missed or repeated, and the complete set fills a grid whose total is rows × columns, the product of the options.

activities.title: The tree-diagram route to the same complete set
feedback: If a starter branch is missing a sub-branch, point out that every starter must be paired with every main, so each branch sprouts all 4 mains.
If the child counts branches by adding (3 + 4), reconnect to the grid: 3 starters each with 4 mains is 3 × 4 = 12 end-points.
activities.rationale: Offering the tree as an alternative systematic structure to the grid gives a second representation of the same completeness-and-product idea; when every starter branch is given a sub-branch for every main, the tree ensures no options are left out. Whether it transfers better than the grid is not established, so both are offered as equivalent structures.
sourceClaims: Children first find all possibilities in a random way and cannot see which cases are missing; sorting their attempts exposes the gaps and teaches them to generate systematically, because having a system ensures no options are left out ('how do you know you've found them all?' — 'I worked systematically').
learnerActions: Draw a tree: one branch for each starter, then from each starter branch draw a sub-branch for every main.
Read each complete path from left to right as one meal (e.g. starter 1 → main 3).
Count the end-points of the tree and check it matches the grid total of 12.
Explain why each starter branch must sprout the same 4 sub-branches, so the total is 3 lots of 4 = 3 × 4.
activities.intendedInsight: A tree diagram is a second systematic structure that enumerates the same complete set; the repeated identical sub-branching is the product 3 × 4 made visible a different way.

activities.title: Check and extend: how many if a category grows?
feedback: If the total is given as 7, revisit the row-by-row fill: 3 rows of 4 is 3 × 4 = 12; the additive answer counts the individual options (starters plus mains), not the combinations.
If extending to a 4th starter yields an added rather than multiplied answer, prompt: one more starter adds one more full row of 4 mains, so 4 rows of 4 = 4 × 4 = 16.
If a missing combination is overlooked, ask which starter still needs pairing with which main — the empty grid cell names it.
activities.rationale: A short set of targeted checks (count with the common additive answer of 7 against the correct 12, a missing-combination fill, and a transfer prediction) probes product-versus-sum reasoning and completeness; such checks verify the skill but do not themselves build the systematic method, so they follow the building activities.
learnerActions: Answer 'How many meals are there altogether?' and justify whether it is 3 + 4 or 3 × 4.
Fill in a deliberately missing combination given a partly-completed grid or list.
Predict, WITHOUT listing them all, how many meals there would be if the café added a 4th starter (4 × 4 = 16), explaining your reasoning from the product structure.
Match each listed meal to its grid cell to confirm the set is complete and non-repeating.
activities.intendedInsight: The product structure lets you predict the count when a category grows without enumerating every case, confirming the skill transfers beyond the original numbers.

constraints: A completed grid or tree with reveal-on-tap can SHOW the organised set and the product, but if the learner does not build it or test completeness themselves, the systematic search and the product structure are presented rather than discovered — use it as a worked example, not as the main learning activity.

Recognition or matching checks (e.g. selecting the total, filling one missing combination) verify the skill but do not elicit the learner's own systematic enumeration method; keep an open construction task where the learner generates and orders the combinations themselves.
The structure here is inherently a flat two-dimensional grid or tree; a third spatial dimension is not needed and can obscure the rows × columns count.

A role-play dialogue may discuss the systematic method, but on its own it does not require the learner to generate and order the combinations themselves; if used, pair it with actual listing and grid-building so the learner produces the enumeration.

The additive error (3 + 4 = 7) must be confronted directly, ideally by a predict-before-building step and by reading the total as the grid's area (rows × columns), not merely noted as a possible slip.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit (arithmetic): 3 × 4 = 12 is correct and 3 + 4 = 7 is the common additive wrong answer to be avoided as the true total; 4 × 4 = 16 for the 4-starter extension is correct. No erroneous alternatives were carried into learner questions.

The 'grid's area' framing is accurate because each cell is exactly one combination, so rows × columns counts the meals; the earlier 'not the perimeter' wording was corrected because 3 + 4 = 7 is not the grid's perimeter and the contrast should be area versus the sum of the side counts.

Source citations support the general teaching principles (systematic generation; Year 6 enumeration objective) but do not establish the comparative efficacy of any specific interactive build, of the predict-first step, or of the tree versus grid; no claim of tested effectiveness is made. The DfE objective claim establishes the topic only and was not used as an activity sourceClaim where it did not support the specific teaching principle.

probeDeeper: How do you know you have listed every meal — could there be one you've missed?
How many meals are there altogether — is it 3 + 4 or 3 × 4, and why?
If the café added a 4th starter, how many meals would there be then, without listing them all?
You listed S1M1, S2M2 and S3M3. Which meals have you left out?
assess.correctAnswer: 12 meals — each of the 3 starters paired with each of the 4 mains (S1M1, S1M2, S1M3, S1M4, S2M1, …, S3M4), found by holding each starter and running through all four mains. The total is 3 × 4 = 12 (the product of the options), complete because every starter has been paired with every main.

errorPatterns.pattern: Lists haphazardly — random pairings, so meals are missed or duplicated and completeness cannot be judged
errorPatterns.nextMove: Hold one category fixed and run through the other in order; record in a grid so gaps show — 'found them all because I worked systematically'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: An unordered list with gaps or repeats; cannot answer 'have you found them all?'

errorPatterns.pattern: Predicts the total by ADDING the options — 3 + 4 = 7 — rather than multiplying, 3 × 4 = 12
errorPatterns.nextMove: Each of the 3 starters generates 4 meals, so 4 + 4 + 4 = 3 × 4 = 12; the filled grid's area is the count
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives the total as 7 and does not connect it to the rows × columns of the grid

errorPatterns.pattern: Changes both choices at once (e.g. only the diagonal S1M1, S2M2, S3M3), losing track of the remaining pairings
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fix one choice and vary the other FULLY before changing the fixed one; the grid shows the whole row must be filled
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Produces one combination per starter and stops, missing the other pairings

responseLevels.gap: Lists a few combinations at random with gaps or repeats; cannot say whether the list is complete; gives the total by adding or by guessing.
responseLevels.full: Enumerates all combinations by holding one category fixed and running through the other in order, records them so completeness is evident, justifies 'all of them' by the system, and gives the total as the product 3 × 4 = 12 explaining why — transferring to predict the count when a category grows.
responseLevels.partial: Lists many combinations and senses there is a full set, but works unsystematically (misses or repeats) or cannot justify completeness, and/or finds the total by counting one-by-one rather than as 3 × 4 — has combinations but not the systematic and multiplicative structure.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A café offers 3 different starters and 4 different mains. List every possible meal of one starter and one main, and show me how you know you have listed them all. Then tell me how many meals there are altogether, and why.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child working systematically holds one category fixed and runs through the other, produces all 12 in order, and gives the total as 3 × 4 = 12 explaining the product; a child listing haphazardly misses or repeats meals, cannot justify completeness, and often predicts the total by ADDING (3 + 4 = 7). Both the 'how do you know you've got them all?' question and the total separate systematic, multiplicative reasoning from random listing.

sources.claim: Year 6 pupils should 'enumerate possibilities of combinations of 2 variables'.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (Year 6 Algebra)

sources.claim: Children first find all possibilities in a random way and cannot see which cases are missing; sorting their attempts exposes the gaps and teaches them to generate systematically, because having a system ensures no options are left out ('how do you know you've found them all?' — 'I worked systematically').
sources.source: NRICH — Encouraging primary children to work systematically (Liz Woodham)

pedagogy.summary: Area with fractional side lengths is where the area model of fraction multiplication becomes a proof: a rectangle 2/3 unit by 3/4 unit, tiled with small squares, contains squares each worth 1/12 of a unit square (because the unit is cut into 3 columns and 4 rows → 12 tiles), and the shaded 2×3 = 6 of them give 6/12 = 1/2. The representational demand is to READ such a tiled diagram — say what one tile is worth and what multiplication the whole shows — and to PRODUCE one for a new product. The load-bearing insight is that the unit square is REDEFINED by the two partitions: denominators multiply because the tile count per unit is b×d, and numerators multiply because a×c tiles are shaded. This grounds (a/b)×(c/d) = ac/bd in an area a child can count.
bestPractices: Start from a whole unit square and partition it in TWO directions (vertical thirds, horizontal quarters) so the child sees 12 tiles appear and names each as 1/12 — the redefinition of the unit is the whole lesson
Connect the tile count to the symbols explicitly: 3×4 = 12 in the denominator is the tiles-per-unit; 2×3 = 6 in the numerator is the shaded tiles
Have children both interpret a given tiling AND draw their own for a fresh product, so reading and producing the representation are both secured
Use the area model to make simplification visible — 6/12 of the unit square is literally half of it, seen by eye
Extend to a mixed-number side (1 1/2 × 2/3) by tiling more than one unit square, so the model scales beyond proper fractions
Keep the unit square explicit and labelled throughout — the commonest failure is losing track of what '1' is
keyRepresentations: Two-way partitioned unit square (area model) with a×c tiles shaded out of b×d
Single unit-fraction tile labelled 1/(b×d) as the counting unit
Grid extended across several unit squares for mixed-number sides
Side-by-side diagram and equation (a/b)×(c/d) = ac/bd with the tiles that justify each factor
commonMisconceptions: Reads the tile as 1/(b+d) — e.g. 1/7 for a 3-by-4 partition — adding the partitions instead of multiplying (area treated additively)
Confuses area with perimeter — measures the boundary of the shaded rectangle rather than counting interior tiles
Partitions in only one direction, so the two-dimensional tile is never formed and denominators are not multiplied
Loses the unit square: counts shaded tiles as a whole number (6) rather than 6 of 12 of ONE unit
Believes area must be larger than the sides, so distrusts an area (1/2) smaller than either side length

learn.summary: Teaches area of a rectangle with fractional side lengths as a visual demonstration of fraction multiplication: a unit square cut in two directions (e.g. thirds one way, quarters the other) forms b×d tiles each worth 1/(b×d), and shading the a×c corner block gives ac/bd of the unit. The core insight is that the unit square is REDEFINED by the two partitions — denominators multiply because there are b×d tiles per unit, numerators multiply because a×c tiles are shaded. Learners must both READ a given tiled diagram (naming one tile's value and the multiplication it shows) and PRODUCE one for a fresh product. Worked example: 2/3 × 3/4 gives 3×4=12 tiles, 2×3=6 shaded = 6/12 = 1/2 — an area smaller than either side because both sides are less than 1.

activities.title: Build the area and watch the tiles appear
feedback: If a learner names the tile 1/7 (3 columns + 4 rows), pause and count the tiles in one unit square out loud together: 3 across, 4 down — the grid makes 12 tiles, not 7. The number of columns and the number of rows multiply (3 × 4 = 12); they do not add.
If a learner reports the edge of the shaded rectangle instead of the interior, distinguish 'how far around' from 'how much surface': point to and count the filling tiles, not the boundary.

If a learner is unsettled that 1/2 is smaller than both 2/3 and 3/4, show that taking a fraction (less than 1) OF another fraction gives a part of a part, so here it is smaller than either factor — the whole unit square is the reference, and the shaded block spans 2/3 of the width and 3/4 of the height, so it covers only half the whole square. (This 'smaller than both' result holds because both side lengths are less than 1; a mixed-number side such as 1 1/2 can give a larger product.)
Confirm success when the learner links 3×4 to the tile count/denominator and 2×3 to the shaded count/numerator, keeping the unit square as the named whole throughout.
activities.rationale: Partitioning a unit square in two directions and counting the resulting tiles makes the redefinition of the unit visible and countable, grounding the symbolic rule in an area the learner can see and count. A live two-way tiler (vertical slider for thirds, horizontal slider for quarters, auto-labelled 1/12 tile, a shaded region reporting 6/12 = 1/2, and a 'show the whole unit' toggle that greys the other tiles) makes the recompute itself the proposed proof; such interactivity is one possible approach, not the only way to teach this.
sourceClaims: The area model — partitioning a unit square in two directions so the unit is redefined into b×d tiles and a×c are shaded — is the recommended representation for developing understanding of fraction multiplication ((a/b)×(c/d) = ac/bd)

Find the area of a rectangle with fractional side lengths by tiling it with unit squares of the appropriate unit fraction side lengths, and show that the area is the same as would be found by multiplying the side lengths
learnerActions: Start from one whole unit square. Partition it in two directions — cut it into 3 columns one way and 4 rows the other way — to model 2/3 × 3/4.
Count the small tiles that appear in the whole unit square (3 across × 4 down = 12) and name the value of ONE tile: 1/12 of the unit square.
Shade the 2-by-3 corner block (2 of the 3 columns, 3 of the 4 rows) and count the shaded tiles: 2×3 = 6, so 6 tiles = 6/12 = 1/2.
Compare the shaded rectangle against the whole unit square and confirm it is exactly half of it — an area smaller than either side length (because each side is less than 1).
Say aloud which number in the picture gives the denominator (3×4 = 12 tiles per unit) and which gives the numerator (2×3 = 6 shaded tiles).
activities.intendedInsight: Cutting the unit square in two directions redefines the unit into b×d equal tiles (so denominators multiply) and the shaded a×c block gives the numerator — this is why (a/b)×(c/d) = ac/bd, and why the product can be smaller than both sides when both sides are less than 1.

activities.title: Read a tiled diagram and justify each number
feedback: If a learner reads the whole as an addition or reads the boundary, re-ask what multiplication the SHADED interior shows and have them count filling tiles.

A lift-the-flap or tap interaction ('tap a tile → 1/12'; 'tap the shaded block → 6 tiles = 6/12 = 1/2'; 'tap the axes → 3 columns × 4 rows = 12') can confirm each justification; the 'why 1/12 and not 1/7?' flap targets the additive error directly.

This reading task secures recognition; recognising a correct diagram does not itself show the learner can build one, so follow it immediately with a drawing task where the learner constructs the representation.
activities.rationale: Interpreting a given tiling isolates the READ half of the representational goal and lets tappable layers tie each visible feature to its symbol. This is a scaffold: recognising a correct diagram does not show the learner can build one, so it should be paired with a production task.
sourceClaims: Find the area of a rectangle with fractional side lengths by tiling it with unit squares of the appropriate unit fraction side lengths, and show that the area is the same as would be found by multiplying the side lengths
learnerActions: Look at a fully tiled 2/3 × 3/4 diagram. Point to one tile and state its value, then state the multiplication the whole shaded rectangle shows.
Answer: why is one tile 1/12 and not 1/7? Trace the two-way cut that creates the grid to justify your answer.
Point to the part of the picture that gives the 12 (3 columns × 4 rows) and the part that gives the 6 (the 2×3 shaded block).
Match the diagram to its equation (a/b)×(c/d) = ac/bd, identifying the tiles that justify each factor.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a tiled area diagram means naming the counting unit (1/(b×d)) and recognising the shaded block as the product — the two-directional grid of 3 columns × 4 rows, not adding the columns and rows (3 + 4), is what makes each tile a twelfth.

activities.title: Produce your own diagram for a fresh product
feedback: If the drawing has parallel strips (cut in one direction only), prompt: 'the OTHER side also has to be cut — how many pieces that way?' Have the learner lay the second set of cuts and re-count the grid before reading the area.
If the learner writes 4/5 or 1/2 as the answer, point back to the tile value: there are 10 tiles per unit, so each is 1/10 and 4 of them is 4/10 = 2/5.
For the 1 1/2 × 2/3 extension, check that the grid spans a full unit plus a half-unit wide (and 2/3 tall), so tiles are counted across both unit squares; with tiles of 1/6 the area comes to 6/6 = 1.

A produce-mode on a two-way tiler (blank grid; learner builds the product; it checks tile worth and shaded count) or offline drawing both work; the point is that the learner constructs the two cuts, not selects from options.
activities.rationale: Producing a fresh diagram exposes whether the two-directional partition genuinely transferred or was only recognised; a learner who cuts in one direction only, or cannot choose the cuts, reveals that the unit-redefinition idea did not stick. Extending to a mixed-number side confirms the model scales beyond proper fractions. A fixed grid or recognition-only response cannot verify a freely produced diagram, so independent drawing is needed here.
sourceClaims: Find the area of a rectangle with fractional side lengths by tiling it with unit squares of the appropriate unit fraction side lengths, and show that the area is the same as would be found by multiplying the side lengths
learnerActions: On a blank unit square, DRAW a rectangle showing 1/2 × 4/5: choose the two cuts yourself — partition into 2 one way and 5 the other way.
Name what one tile is worth (1/10) and explain why: 2×5 = 10 tiles fill the unit.
Shade a 1-by-4 block (4 tiles) and read the area: 4/10 = 2/5.
Say which cuts produced the 10 and which shaded tiles produced the 4, pointing to each number in your own drawing.

Extend the model: tile across more than one unit square to find the area of a rectangle with sides 1 1/2 and 2/3 (here the product is 1, larger than the 2/3 side — a useful check that the 'smaller than both' intuition only applies when both sides are less than 1).
activities.intendedInsight: Choosing both partitions yourself — not just one — is what shows you own the idea that two cuts redefine the unit; the model scales to mixed numbers by tiling more than one unit square.

constraints: Keep the unit square explicit and labelled throughout — losing track of what '1' is is the commonest failure.

A static or tappable tiled diagram supports reading (naming the tile, identifying the multiplication) but cannot host the produce half; pair it with an actual drawing task where the learner chooses both cuts.

Recognition-only responses (multiple choice on tile value, shading on a pre-partitioned grid) can check specific points — e.g. distinguishing 1/12 from 1/7 — but do not require the learner to construct or explain the representation, and cannot verify a freely produced diagram. Use them as checks, not as the main task.

Rectangular area here is a planar (flat) idea; a thin cutout or screen grid only approximates the represented ideal unit square (ideal figures have zero thickness, while real paper or card has slight thickness). Avoid 3D/volume renderings, which can misframe the unit-square idea being taught.
Start each build from the whole unit square and partition in TWO directions; a one-direction cut never forms the two-dimensional tile and does not multiply the denominators.

Interpreting and producing a tiled diagram is visual-spatial work; talk alone cannot display the two-way partition or capture the learner's drawing, though discussion can support the reasoning alongside the diagram.
The 'product is smaller than either side' intuition applies only when both side lengths are less than 1; do not state it unconditionally, since the mixed-number extension (1 1/2 × 2/3 = 1) breaks it.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source lists CCSS 5.NF.4b as verified:false; treat that citation as unconfirmed.

The original framed several claims as absolutes ('a dialogue cannot show the two-way partition', '3D would misframe', a quiz 'rewards the answer over the reasoning'). These have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements; the catalog ratings do not establish comparative efficacy or necessity.

Corrected learner-facing wording: an earlier draft claimed the shaded block is 'less than half-width', but 2/3 of the width is more than half; it now reads 2/3 of width and 3/4 of height. The 'smaller than both sides' claim is scoped to proper-fraction sides, since the lesson's own 1 1/2 × 2/3 extension yields 1.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 2/3 × 3/4 → 3×4=12 tiles, 2×3=6 shaded = 6/12 = 1/2; 1/2 × 4/5 → 2×5=10 tiles, 1×4=4 shaded = 4/10 = 2/5; 1 1/2 × 2/3 → 3 halves × 2 thirds = 6 tiles of 1/6 = 6/6 = 1. No arithmetic errors remain.
The claim 'the recompute IS the proof' is a design rationale, not established efficacy; retained only as a proposed teaching mechanism.
Prerequisite reteach IDs (from the assessment field) are preserved as concepts (multiplying partitions for the denominator; area = length × width as filling tiles) without the internal IDs.

probeDeeper: Your shaded area came out as 1/2, which is smaller than either side (2/3 and 3/4). How can the area be smaller than both sides — is that a mistake?
Point to just ONE tile and tell me its value again — how do you know it's a twelfth and not a seventh?
If the rectangle had been 2/3 by 3/4 but I'd only cut the unit into thirds one way and not cut it the other way, could you still count the area? Why not?
On your 1/2 × 4/5 drawing, which cuts give the 10 and which shaded tiles give the 4 — show me each number in the picture.
assess.correctAnswer: One tile is 1/12 of the unit square (the unit is cut into 3 columns and 4 rows, 3×4 = 12 tiles). The shaded rectangle shows 2/3 × 3/4, covering 2×3 = 6 tiles = 6/12 = 1/2. For 1/2 × 4/5: partition the unit into 2 (one way) and 5 (the other) → 10 tiles each 1/10; shade a 1-by-4 block = 4 tiles = 4/10 = 2/5.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads one tile as 1/7 (or 1/(b+d)): 'three cuts and four cuts, that's seven pieces' — adds the partitions instead of multiplying them
errorPatterns.nextMove: Go back to the physical grid: count the tiles in ONE unit square out loud (3 across, 4 down → 12) before naming any tile; connect 3×4 to the tile count and to the denominator of the product in mt_AabJisinfi
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names the tile 1/7 rather than 1/12, or gives the product as 5/7 / 5/12; treats the two-way grid as if the cuts combine additively

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses area with perimeter / reads the boundary: counts or measures the edge of the shaded rectangle instead of the interior tiles, or reports side lengths rather than tile count
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate 'how far around' from 'how much surface': shade and count the INTERIOR tiles explicitly; re-anchor area = l × w as tiles-that-fill from mt_eiB3-6pu6a before returning to fractional tiles
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives an answer tied to the outline (e.g. adds the sides) rather than 6 tiles; when producing, draws the rectangle's edge but does not tile/fill it

errorPatterns.pattern: Partitions in one direction only when producing: cuts the unit into halves (or fifths) but not both, so the two-dimensional 1/10 tile is never formed for 1/2 × 4/5
errorPatterns.nextMove: Prompt 'the OTHER side also has to be cut — how many pieces that way?'; have them lay the second set of cuts and re-count the grid tiles before reading the area
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The drawn diagram has parallel strips, not a grid; the child cannot say what one tile is worth or gives 4/5 / 1/2 rather than 4/10

responseLevels.gap: Cannot connect the tiling to a product: names the tile 1/7 or by whole-number count, reads the boundary instead of the interior, or cannot begin the produce task; the unit square is not held as the reference whole.
responseLevels.full: Reads the tile as 1/12 and the whole as 2/3 × 3/4 = 6/12 = 1/2, AND produces a correct two-way partition for 1/2 × 4/5 (10 tiles, 4 shaded = 2/5), explaining that the two partitions multiply to give tiles-per-unit and the shaded count gives the numerator; transfers the model to a new product and accounts for an area smaller than both sides.
responseLevels.partial: Reads the given 2/3 × 3/4 diagram correctly (tile = 1/12, 6 tiles = 1/2) but cannot cleanly PRODUCE the fresh 1/2 × 4/5 diagram — partitions one direction, or gets the picture right yet cannot explain WHY tiles-per-unit is 3×4; recognises the representation without owning it.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a rectangle drawn 2/3 of a unit wide and 3/4 of a unit tall, tiled with small equal squares. First, tell me: what fraction of one whole unit square is ONE small tile, and what multiplication does the whole shaded rectangle show? Then, on this fresh unit grid, DRAW a rectangle that shows 1/2 × 4/5, and use your drawing to find the area.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The two moves — READ then PRODUCE — catch different failures. Reading the tile as 1/12 versus 1/7 separates the child who multiplies the partitions from the one who adds them; naming the multiplication as 2/3 × 3/4 (not, say, an addition or a perimeter) tests that the diagram is read as area. Then producing a fresh diagram for 1/2 × 4/5 exposes whether the two-directional partition is genuinely understood or was only recognised — a child who cuts in one direction only, or who cannot choose the cuts, reveals that the unit-redefinition idea did not transfer.

sources.claim: The area model — partitioning a unit square in two directions so the unit is redefined into b×d tiles and a×c are shaded — is the recommended representation for developing understanding of fraction multiplication ((a/b)×(c/d) = ac/bd)

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–10y; recognise and use square and cube numbers and the notation ² and ³ (49 = 7² = 7×7; 4³ = 64 = 4×4×4).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5 'recognise and use square numbers and cube numbers, and the notation for squared (²) and cubed (³)'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): connects to 5.NBT.2 (whole-number exponents for powers of 10) and 6.EE.1 (evaluate expressions with whole-number exponents); square/cube language is developed through area and volume.
• Operational details — the notation must be tied to its GEOMETRIC meaning: n² is the area of an n×n square (a genuinely square array), n³ is the volume of an n×n×n cube. This is where 'squared' and 'cubed' get their names — not arbitrary labels. The dangerous misconception is reading n² as n×2 (7² as 14) and n³ as n×3; anchoring to the square/cube array blocks it. Square numbers are the diagonal of the multiplication table (products of equal factors) and have an odd number of factors. Cubes require the genuinely 3D step. Recall the first ~10 squares and small cubes.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): read/write ² and ³ and compute small cases (5², 2³) as repeated equal multiplication. Tier B (age 9–10): list the first ten square numbers and explain 7² as a 7×7 square. Tier C (age 10): explain why n²≠n×2, connect squares to the multiplication-table diagonal, and cubes to volume.
bestPractices: Anchor ² and ³ to their geometric meaning — n² as an n×n square's area, n³ as an n×n×n cube's volume — so the names and notation make sense.
Confront the n² = n×2 misconception directly by showing 7² (a 7×7 array of 49) next to 7×2 (14).
Locate square numbers on the multiplication-table diagonal (equal factors) and note their odd factor count.
Build cubes with unit cubes / a 3D model so 'cubed' is genuinely spatial, distinct from squares.
Memorise the first ten squares and the small cubes, and use correct notation (49 = 7², not 7×7 only).
keyRepresentations: n×n square array — area meaning of n²
n×n×n cube of unit cubes — volume meaning of n³
Multiplication-table diagonal — the square numbers
Notation cards linking 7² = 7×7 = 49 and 4³ = 4×4×4 = 64
commonMisconceptions: Reading n² as n×2 (7²=14) and n³ as n×3 (4³=12).
Confusing squared and cubed, or the notation ²/³.
Thinking of square/cube numbers as arbitrary lists rather than areas/volumes.
Believing squaring always makes a much bigger number without the geometric picture (surprised by 1²=1).
Not recognising square numbers as products of a number with itself (table diagonal).

learn.summary: For 9–10 year-olds learning to recognise and use square and cube numbers and the notation ² and ³ (e.g. 49 = 7² = 7×7; 4³ = 64 = 4×4×4). The central aim is to tie the notation to its geometric meaning: n² is the area of an n×n square and n³ is the volume of an n×n×n cube — this is where 'squared' and 'cubed' get their names. The most important misconception to defeat is reading the exponent as a multiplier (7² as 7×2 = 14, or 4³ as 4×3 = 12); anchoring to the square and cube arrays blocks it. Square numbers also lie on the diagonal of the multiplication table (products of equal factors) and have an odd number of factors. Learners should recall the first ~10 squares and the small cubes and use correct notation.

activities.title: Growing squares: why 7² is not 7×2
feedback: If a learner writes 7² = 14, place the 7×7 array (49 cells) next to a 7×2 rectangle (14 cells): the square obviously holds far more. Rename the exponent as 'how many 7s are multiplied', so 7² = 7×7.
If a learner is surprised that 1² = 1, show the 1×1 square — a single cell — and confirm squaring does not always make a much bigger number.
When a learner notices the gaps 3, 5, 7, affirm it: each new square adds an L-shaped border of odd size, which is why the differences are consecutive odd numbers.
activities.rationale: Building the array and comparing n² against n×2 side by side makes the area meaning concrete and directly addresses the dominant exponent-as-multiplier error. Locating squares on the multiplication-table diagonal connects the notation to equal factors.
sourceClaims: Square and cube notation should be anchored to the area of a square and volume of a cube to prevent the n²=n×2 error; squares lie on the multiplication-table diagonal.
Y5 pupils recognise and use square and cube numbers and the notation ² and ³.
learnerActions: Build or draw an n×n square array for a chosen n and count the total cells, writing it as n².
Start small and step n up: 1 (1 cell), 2 (a 2×2 of 4), 3 (a 3×3 of 9), 4 (a 4×4 of 16). Write each as 1², 2², 3², 4².
Build a 7×7 square (49 cells) and, beside it, a separate 7×2 rectangle (14 cells); compare the two by eye — note that 7² = 49 is far larger than 7×2 = 14.
Say out loud what the little 2 means: 'how many 7s are multiplied together', i.e. 7×7, NOT 'multiply 7 by 2'.
Notice how much is added each time n grows by one: the totals jump 1, 4, 9, 16, and the gaps are 3, 5, 7 — successive odd numbers.
Plot each square number onto the diagonal of a multiplication table (where the row number equals the column number) and see that square numbers are the products of a number with itself.

Optionally notice that a square number has an odd number of factors — e.g. 9 has factors 1, 3, 9 (three of them) — because its square root is a repeated factor that pairs with itself instead of a different partner.
activities.intendedInsight: n² means an n×n square array (its area), not n×2. The notation is a picture of a square, and square numbers are the products of equal factors that lie on the multiplication-table diagonal.

activities.title: Building a cube: what 'cubed' really means
feedback: If a learner writes 4³ = 12, build the cube by layers so the 64 cubes are visible and unmistakably more than 12; rename the exponent as 'how many 4s multiplied', giving 4×4×4.
If a learner gives 16 for both 4² and 4³, set the flat 4×4 square (16) next to the 4×4×4 solid (64): two equal factors for square, three for cube. The exponent tells which.
When a learner builds layer by layer and states 4 layers × 16 = 64, affirm the link between the stacking and n×n×n.
activities.rationale: Cube numbers are genuinely spatial, so constructing an n×n×n cube from unit cubes makes 'cubed' meaningful and clearly distinct from 'squared'. Contrasting the flat square with the solid cube separates the two operations by their number of equal factors.
sourceClaims: Square and cube notation should be anchored to the area of a square and volume of a cube to prevent the n²=n×2 error; squares lie on the multiplication-table diagonal.
Whole-number exponent notation is developed in 5.NBT.2 (powers of 10) and 6.EE.1 (evaluate expressions with exponents); square/cube meaning connects to area and volume.
learnerActions: Using unit cubes (physical or a build-it model), assemble an n×n×n cube for a chosen n, stacking it layer by layer (each layer is n×n). Keep a running total, and when all n layers are in place write the final total as n×n×n = n³.
Build 4³ specifically: make four layers, each a 4×4 square of 16 cubes, to reach 64 cubes total; write 4³ = 4×4×4 = 64.
Rotate or turn the cube to see all its faces and confirm it is genuinely three-dimensional.
Place a flat 4×4 square (16) beside the 4×4×4 cube (64) and describe the difference: squared uses two equal factors (a flat area), cubed uses three (a solid volume).
Say what the little 3 means: 'how many 4s are multiplied together' — 4×4×4 — not 'multiply 4 by 3'.
activities.intendedInsight: n³ means an n×n×n cube built from unit cubes (its volume), using three equal factors. 'Cubed' is spatial and distinct from 'squared'; the exponent counts how many equal factors are multiplied.

activities.title: Reading and recalling the notation
feedback: If a learner picks 14 for 7², treat it as the key trap: point back to the 7×7 array of 49 and restate the exponent's meaning.
If recall of a square or cube is shaky, rebuild it as repeated equal multiplication (e.g. 4³ = 4×4×4) rather than guessing.
Correct notation matters: encourage writing 49 = 7², not only 7×7, so the symbol becomes familiar.
activities.rationale: Recall and reading of notation are checkable and benefit from the exponent-as-multiplier distractor; pairing each symbol with its array/cube keeps the geometric meaning attached rather than treating the numbers as an arbitrary list. Recognition and recall practice consolidates but does not by itself build the area/volume meaning — pair it with the building activities.
sourceClaims: Y5 pupils recognise and use square and cube numbers and the notation ² and ³.
learnerActions: Match notation to meaning and value: 7² ↔ a 7×7 array ↔ 49; 4³ ↔ a 4×4×4 cube ↔ 64. For each, first predict, then reveal the picture and the value.
Answer the question 'why is 7² not 14?' in your own words, referring to the 7×7 square.
List the first ten square numbers (1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100) and write each with its notation (e.g. 49 = 7²).
Recall the small cubes (1³=1, 2³=8, 3³=27, 4³=64, 5³=125) and write each as repeated equal multiplication.
Write a value using correct notation, e.g. record 49 as 7² (not only as 7×7).
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent recall and correct reading of ² and ³ rest on the array/cube meaning; the notation is shorthand for repeated equal multiplication, not a multiplier.

constraints: Tie ² and ³ to geometric meaning: n² as an n×n square's area, n³ as an n×n×n cube's volume, so the names and notation make sense rather than being arbitrary labels.
Directly confront the exponent-as-multiplier error by showing 7² (a 7×7 array of 49) alongside 7×2 (14), and 4³ (64) rather than 4×3 (12).
Distinguish squared from cubed by number of equal factors (two vs three) and by shape (flat area vs solid volume).

Recognition/recall practice (matching, fill-in, multiple choice) tests and consolidates but does not by itself build the area/volume meaning — use it after or alongside construction, not instead of it.
Include 1² = 1 so learners see squaring does not always make a much larger number.

Expectations by stage: at age 9, read/write ² and ³ and compute small cases as repeated equal multiplication; by age 9–10, list the first ten squares and explain 7² as a 7×7 square; by age 10, explain why n² ≠ n×2, connect squares to the multiplication-table diagonal, and cubes to volume.

Physical unit cubes and build-it screen models offer different experiences; either can make 'cubed' spatial. A flat drawing can still show and teach the square meaning even though it cannot be dragged to vary n.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original flagged two sources as unverified (Common Core connection to 5.NBT.2/6.EE.1, and the NCETM guidance on anchoring to area/volume and the table diagonal); only the DfE National Curriculum claim was marked verified. Treat the unverified claims accordingly.

The odd-number-of-factors property of square numbers (present in the original operational details) was restored as an optional enrichment in the squares activity; no source directly asserts it, so it is framed as a mathematical observation.

A legacy suggestion to preview a cube as stacked 2D layers was retained only as the layer-by-layer building description within the cube activity; genuine 3D construction (physical cubes or a rotatable model) is preferred so 'cubed' is truly spatial. The 2D-layer preview is a scaffold, not the main picture.

The claim that dialogue 'can't render' square/cube growth was softened: spoken explanation is useful for naming the exponent and for the probing questions, though it does not replace building or drawing the arrays.

Arithmetic checked: first ten squares 1,4,9,16,25,36,49,64,81,100; small cubes 1,8,27,64,125; 7²=49, 7×2=14; 4²=16, 4³=64, 4×3=12 — all consistent with the source. The distractor values (7²=14, 4³=12, 4²/4³ both 16) are presented only as errors to correct, never as valid answers.

probeDeeper: The little 2 in 4² — what is it telling you to do? How is that different from 4 × 2?
Why is 16 called a 'square' number? Show me with tiles.
What would 5² be — and if someone said it's 10, what mistake did they make?
How many small cubes are in a 4×4×4 block, and how does that match 4³?
assess.correctAnswer: 4² = 16 and 4³ = 64. A child reasoning correctly reads 4² as 4 × 4 (four rows of four — a square) and 4³ as 4 × 4 × 4 (a 4-by-4-by-4 cube), explaining the exponent as HOW MANY times the base is used as a factor — not as multiply-by-2 or multiply-by-3.

errorPatterns.pattern: reads the exponent as a multiplier — 4² as 4×2 = 8, 4³ as 4×3 = 12 ('squaring means doubling')
errorPatterns.nextMove: build the square: 4² is a 4×4 array = 16 tiles, visibly not 8; contrast with 4×2 = a 4×2 rectangle of 8. Name the exponent as 'how many 4s are multiplied', not 'multiply by the little number'.
errorPatterns.distractor: 4² = 8 (the 2 means times 2)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child answers 8 for 4² (or 12 for 4³), and explains 'the 2 means times 2'

errorPatterns.pattern: confuses square and cube — uses 4×4 for 'cubed' or does not distinguish the two operations by the exponent
errorPatterns.nextMove: tie the words to shape: square = flat 4×4 tile grid, cube = solid 4×4×4 block; the exponent counts the dimensions/factors (2 for square, 3 for cube).
errorPatterns.distractor: 4³ = 16 (same as four squared)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child gives 16 for both 4² and 4³, or is unsure which raised number means which

errorPatterns.pattern: computes correctly but attaches no geometric meaning — cannot say why 16 is called a 'square number' or 64 a 'cube number'
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach the calculation; arrange 16 tiles into the 4×4 square and 64 cubes into the 4×4×4 block so the names connect to the shapes they already computed.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child gets 16 and 64 via repeated multiplication but, asked why they're 'square'/'cube' numbers, has no answer

responseLevels.gap: reads the exponent as a multiplier (4² = 8, 4³ = 12) or confuses square with cube; no factor meaning.
responseLevels.full: reads 4² as 4×4 and 4³ as 4×4×4, explains the exponent as the number of equal factors, links the names to the square array and cubic block, and applies it correctly to a new base (e.g. 5² = 25).
responseLevels.partial: gets 16 and 64 but explains them as doubling/tripling for this case, or computes correctly yet cannot connect 'square'/'cube' to the shapes — no transfer to a new base.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: What does 4² (four squared) equal? And what does 4³ (four cubed) equal? For each, explain what the little raised number is telling you to do — not just the answer.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The classic error is reading the exponent as a multiplier: 4² = 4×2 = 8 and 4³ = 4×3 = 12. A child who answers 16 and 64 but explains 'I doubled / I tripled' has the right numbers for the wrong reason and will fail on other bases. The meaning tier catches this; the number alone does not.

pedagogy.summary: Having seen that tiling a rectangle equals the product of its side lengths, children now compute area directly by multiplying the side lengths (7 cm × 9 cm = 63 cm²) and work the relationship backwards — representing a whole-number product as a rectangle of that area. The multiplication carries meaning from the array (squares in a row × rows), and the answer is in square units.
bestPractices: Compute area as side × side, keeping the array meaning (one side = squares in a row, the other = number of rows) in view.
Insist on square units in the answer (cm², m²), tying the unit back to unit squares.
Work the reverse: given an area like 36 square units, find rectangles that have it (factor pairs) and label their sides.
Use real contexts (a garden 8 m by 5 m) so the multiplication solves a problem.
Contrast multiplying for area with adding for perimeter so the two are not conflated.
keyRepresentations: A rectangle labelled 7 cm × 9 cm with area 63 cm²
An area model linking multiplication to a rectangle of squares
Several rectangles all of area 36 (2×18, 3×12, 4×9, 6×6) with sides labelled
A word-problem sketch (garden 8 m × 5 m)
commonMisconceptions: Adds the side lengths (perimeter) instead of multiplying for area.
Gives the answer in linear units (cm) rather than square units (cm²).
Cannot reverse the relationship — struggles to draw a rectangle of a given area or to find its factor-pair sides.
Multiplies unrelated numbers or applies l×w to a non-rectangle.

learn.summary: Children compute the area of a rectangle by multiplying its side lengths (7 cm × 9 cm = 63 cm²), keeping the array meaning in view (squares in a row × number of rows) and answering in square units. They also work the relationship backwards: given a target area such as 36 square units, they construct rectangles whose side lengths multiply to that area (2×18, 3×12, 4×9, 6×6) and label the sides. Multiplying for area is explicitly contrasted with adding for perimeter so the two measures are not conflated.

activities.title: Build and compute: side × side = area
feedback: If a learner adds the sides (7 + 9 = 16), return to the tiled array: area is rows of squares, so it is squares-in-a-row × rows. Re-derive 7 × 9 from the tiling before using the formula.
If the number is right but the unit is linear (63 cm), tie the unit to the unit square: each tile is 1 cm², so the count is in square centimetres — always write the squared unit.

For the garden, if a learner answers 13, ask 'what did 8 + 5 actually measure?' (the length of two touching sides, which is only half the distance around: the perimeter is 8 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 26 m) to separate edge lengths from the surface covered (8 × 5 = 40 m²).
activities.rationale: Multiplying side lengths to find rectangle area rests on understanding area as covering with unit squares arranged in rows; keeping the array meaning visible lets the formula carry the counting meaning, and insisting on square units guards against the common linear-unit slip.
sourceClaims: Students learn to multiply length measurements to find the area of a rectangular region, understanding this as a multiplicative relationship of the number of square units in a row and the number of rows; they explain why multiplying the side lengths gives the same area as counting the tiles, and represent whole-number products as rectangular areas (3.MD.7).
Year 4 pupils find the area of rectilinear shapes by counting squares and multiply side lengths to find areas of rectangles.
learnerActions: Choose two side lengths for a rectangle (e.g. 7 and 9) and draw it on squared paper or with a grid overlay.
Count the squares as rows of squares (squares-in-a-row × number of rows) and confirm this equals multiplying the side lengths: 7 × 9 = 63.
Write the answer with square units: 63 cm².
Change one side (e.g. 7 → 8) and recompute, noticing the rectangle re-tiles and the area becomes 8 × 9 = 72 cm².
Solve a real context: a garden 8 m by 5 m — find its area (8 × 5 = 40 m²).
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying the two side lengths gives the same total as counting all the unit squares, because the rectangle is a number of equal rows; the result is measured in square units.

activities.title: Reverse the relationship: many rectangles, one area
feedback: If a learner draws a rectangle that is not 36 (e.g. sides that don't multiply to 36), find factor pairs of 36 together and match each pair to a rectangle, using the grid to verify.
If a learner finds only one option and stops, prompt systematically: 'Does 2 divide 36? 3? 4? 6?' to surface more factor pairs (and note 1×36 is also valid).
Confirm 6×6 counts as a valid rectangle (a square) with area 36.
activities.rationale: Representing a whole-number product as a rectangular area and finding factor-pair sides deepens the product–area link and addresses the common difficulty of reversing the relationship.
sourceClaims: Students learn to multiply length measurements to find the area of a rectangular region, understanding this as a multiplicative relationship of the number of square units in a row and the number of rows; they explain why multiplying the side lengths gives the same area as counting the tiles, and represent whole-number products as rectangular areas (3.MD.7).
learnerActions: Given a fixed area of 36 square units, find rectangles whose sides multiply to 36 and draw each, labelling the sides.
List the factor pairs discovered: 2×18, 3×12, 4×9, 6×6 — all have area 36 (and 1×36 is also valid).
Check each rectangle against a grid to confirm it really covers 36 squares.
State what stays the same across all of them (the product/area = 36) and what changes (the shape).
activities.intendedInsight: One area can be made by many different rectangles; it is the product of the side lengths, not the shape, that is fixed.

activities.title: Area versus perimeter: surface versus edge
feedback: If a learner uses the perimeter value as the area, ask them to shade the surface and trace the edge separately so the two quantities are visibly different.
Reinforce that area answers end in square units (cm², m²) while perimeter answers end in linear units (cm, m).
activities.rationale: Contrasting the two measures directly addresses the frequent misconception of adding side lengths when area is required and of mislabelling units; the distinction between surface (square units) and distance around (linear units) must be maintained.
sourceClaims: Area formulas must rest on a firm conceptual foundation about what area is (covering with unit squares); the distinction between area (surface, square units) and perimeter (distance around, linear units) must be maintained, guarding against adding side lengths when area is required.
learnerActions: For a 7 × 9 rectangle, work out both the area (multiply: 63 cm²) and the perimeter (add the sides around: 7 + 9 + 7 + 9 = 32 cm).
Say in words what each measures: area covers the surface in square units; perimeter is the distance around in linear units.
Given a mixed set of problems, decide for each whether to multiply (area) or add the edges (perimeter) and justify the choice.
Explain why a friend who did 8 + 5 = 13 for the garden's area has found something other than the area.
activities.intendedInsight: Area (surface, square units) and perimeter (distance around, linear units) are different measures computed differently; multiplying finds area, adding the edges finds perimeter.

activities.title: Check your understanding: compute, select, and label units
feedback: If a distractor equal to the perimeter is chosen, revisit the area-versus-perimeter contrast so the surface (multiply) and the edge (add) are kept distinct.
If the unit is linear, link back to the unit square (1 cm² per tile).
For wrong products, re-derive the multiplication from the array of rows.
activities.rationale: Targeted recognition and short-answer items can surface the add-vs-multiply error and the unit error during practice; recognition alone does not, however, elicit independent construction of a rectangle of a given area (see constraints), so pair these with open drawing/building tasks.
learnerActions: Compute the area of a given rectangle and write it with correct square units (fill-in or short answer).
From several rectangles, select the one(s) with area 36, including a distractor whose perimeter is 36 (an 'add the sides' trap) but whose area is not 36.
Choose the correct unit for an area (cm vs cm²) and explain why.
Solve a word problem: a garden 8 m by 5 m — give the area with units (40 m²).
activities.intendedInsight: Applying area-as-product fluently means multiplying (not adding), using square units, and recognising correct rectangles for a target area.

constraints: Keep the array meaning in view: one side = squares in a row, the other = number of rows; the formula should carry the counting meaning, not replace it.
Always require square units (cm², m²) in area answers, tied back to the unit square.

A static labelled rectangle (e.g. '7 cm × 9 cm, area 63 cm²') is a useful reference for illustrating one calculation, but on its own it cannot have the learner compute across varied cases or perform the reverse construction; pair it with tasks where the learner computes and builds.

Recognition/selection items (choosing which rectangle has area 36, choosing cm vs cm²) can check understanding during teaching, but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of a rectangle of a given area; include open drawing/building tasks for that objective.
This content is for planar rectangular area; avoid presenting it with volume/solid contexts that could confuse area with volume.

Interactive supports — e.g. a live-updating 'l × w = area' label, an optional unit-square grid overlay, a reverse mode that fixes the area while the learner adjusts dimensions, and a perimeter toggle — are helpful optional illustrations of the mechanism, not required mechanisms; the same learning can be done on squared paper.

probeDeeper: Why do you multiply the two sides rather than add them to get the area?
You got 63 — 63 what? Why is the unit 'square centimetres'?
Can you draw a different rectangle that also has an area of 36? How many can you find?

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds the side lengths instead of multiplying: gives 7 + 9 = 16 (or a perimeter) as the area.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the tiled array — the area is rows of squares, so it is squares-in-a-row × rows; re-derive 7×9 from tiling before using the formula.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 7 + 9, or answers 16 or 32; treats area like distance around.

errorPatterns.pattern: Linear units instead of square units: computes 63 but labels it '63 cm' rather than '63 cm²'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Tie the unit to the unit square — each tile is 1 cm², so the count is in square centimetres; always write the squared unit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct number, wrong unit — no 'square' in the unit for an area.

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot reverse: struggles to draw a rectangle of a given area or to find factor-pair sides, giving a shape whose sides don't multiply to the target.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Find factor pairs of the area together (2×18, 3×12, 4×9, 6×6) and match each to a rectangle; use the grid to check.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 'area 36', draws a rectangle that isn't 36, or can only think of one option and gets stuck.

responseLevels.gap: Adds the sides (perimeter), or gives linear units, or cannot construct a rectangle of a given area.
responseLevels.full: Computes area as the product of the side lengths in square units, solves area word problems, and reverses the relationship to draw and label rectangles of a given area.
responseLevels.partial: Multiplies the sides correctly for a given rectangle but slips on units (cm not cm²) or cannot reliably reverse to build a target area.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Pose three tasks: 'Find the area of a 7 cm by 9 cm rectangle'; 'Draw a rectangle with an area of 36 square units and label its sides'; and 'A garden is 8 m by 5 m — what is its area?' Watch whether they multiply (not add) the sides, whether they use square units, and whether they can reverse the relationship to construct a given area.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands area-as-product multiplies and gives square units, and can build a rectangle of a target area; a child who does not adds the sides (perimeter), gives linear units, or cannot reverse to find factor-pair sides — each visible in the work.
