pedagogy.summary: At age 12-14 pupils learn that a pair of parallel lines cut by a transversal produces a structured set of equal and supplementary angles: corresponding angles are equal, alternate (interior) angles are equal, and co-interior (same-side interior) angles are supplementary (sum 180°). The goal is to REASON with these relationships to find unknown angles and to justify WHY they hold — ideally by translating one crossing's four-angle cluster along the transversal onto the other, so equality is grounded in transformation, not in a memorised 'F' or 'Z' shape. Two documented obstacles dominate: pupils over-generalise to 'angles on parallel lines are equal', missing that co-interior angles are supplementary; and they confuse alternate with corresponding angles, unable to pick them out in any but the simplest diagrams. A subtler difficulty is perceptual — pupils accept lines as parallel only when they are similar in length and position, so off-set lines are not seen as parallel and the rules go unapplied. Teaching therefore stresses structural reasoning, precise language over mnemonics, and non-standard, off-set diagrams.
bestPractices: Ground equality in transformation: use tracing paper to translate the four-angle cluster at one crossing along the transversal so it lands exactly on the other, showing corresponding/alternate angles are equal
Distinguish equal pairs (corresponding, alternate) from supplementary pairs (co-interior) explicitly, e.g. colour-code the two 'families' so the 70°/110° split is visible
Insist on precise language and full reasons ('x = 45° because alternate angles are equal') rather than 'F' and 'Z' angle mnemonics, which do not support reasoning
Use non-standard and off-set diagrams so pupils learn to identify pairs in rotated figures and still perceive off-set lines as parallel
Build multi-step angle-chasing on secure basic angle facts (straight line 180°, vertically opposite, angles at a point) and require a stated reason at each step
keyRepresentations: Parallel lines + transversal with all eight angles, the two crossings' clusters colour-linked
Tracing-paper / translation-along-the-transversal overlay demonstrating equal angles
Colour-coded equal vs supplementary angle families
Off-set and rotated parallel-line diagrams (non-prototypical)
Angle-chase worked example with a reason justifying each step
commonMisconceptions: Over-generalising 'angles on parallel lines are equal', so treating co-interior (supplementary) angles as equal
Confusing alternate and corresponding angles, and failing to identify them in non-standard diagrams
Relying on 'F'/'Z' mnemonics that give the answer without supporting reasoning
Not perceiving off-set lines (little overlap) as parallel, so not applying the angle rules
Applying parallel-line angle rules to lines that are not actually parallel

learn.summary: Pupils aged 12-14 learn that when a transversal crosses a pair of parallel lines it produces a structured set of equal and supplementary angles: corresponding angles are equal, alternate (interior) angles are equal, and co-interior (same-side interior) angles are supplementary (sum to 180°). The aim is to REASON with these relationships to find unknown angles and to justify WHY they hold — grounding equality in the translation of one crossing's four-angle cluster along the transversal onto the other, rather than in a memorised 'F' or 'Z' shape. Teaching must separate the equal family (corresponding, alternate) from the supplementary family (co-interior), insist on precise language and full reasons, and use off-set and rotated diagrams so pupils still perceive genuinely parallel lines as parallel and apply the rules.

activities.title: Translate the angle cluster along the transversal
feedback: If the slid copy lands on the lower cluster (within tracing accuracy), the translation shows that corresponding angles are equal; then use vertically opposite angles to explain why alternate angles are equal too.
If a pupil relies on the 'F'/'Z' look, ask them to describe what MOVEMENT maps one angle onto the other, so the reason is the translation, not the letter shape.
When the lines are not parallel, point out that the copy no longer fits and the readings diverge — this is the evidence that parallelism is the condition for the equalities.
activities.rationale: Grounding equality in the translation of the four-angle cluster along the transversal gives a structural reason for the result and directly addresses the over-generalisation and parallel-perception obstacles; tracing paper makes the transformation concrete.
sourceClaims: Students often confuse alternate and corresponding angles and cannot pick them out in any but the simplest diagrams; 'F' and 'Z' angle mnemonics do not support reasoning (use precise language and full reasons instead); a further difficulty is that students accept lines as parallel only if similar in length/position, so off-set lines are not perceived as parallel; equality is best shown by translating the four-angle cluster along the transversal with tracing paper. The parallel-line/transversal image contains all the structure needed to deduce the angle sum of a triangle.
learnerActions: Draw (or use a prepared diagram of) two parallel lines crossed by a transversal, marking the parallels with matching arrows.
Trace the four-angle cluster at the upper crossing onto tracing paper, then slide the tracing straight down along the transversal until it lands on the lower crossing.

Observe that every angle in the slid copy lands on the matching angle at the lower crossing (as closely as tracing allows; in the ideal diagram the fit is exact). State which pairs this shows are equal: corresponding angles directly, and alternate angles by combining this with vertically opposite angles at the same crossing.
Now draw a second diagram where one line is deliberately NOT parallel to the other; trace and slide again, and record where the copy fails to fit and how the readings differ.
Write a one-sentence conclusion: equality of these angle pairs depends on the lines being parallel.
activities.intendedInsight: Corresponding angles are equal because one crossing's angle cluster can be translated along the transversal onto the other, which is a transformation, not a shape to recognise. Alternate angles are then equal because each one is vertically opposite a corresponding partner. These equalities break when the lines are not parallel.

activities.title: Sort angle pairs into equal and supplementary families
feedback: If a pupil labels the co-interior angle 70°, ask them to check it against a straight line: the co-interior angle and the adjacent equal angle together make 180°, so it must be 110°.
Correct colouring with the 70°/110° split visible shows the two families are being kept apart — exactly the distinction the over-general rule erases.
activities.rationale: Explicitly separating the equal family from the supplementary family with a worked 70°/110° split targets the dominant over-generalisation that 'angles on parallel lines are equal'.
learnerActions: In a given parallel-lines-and-transversal diagram, point to one marked angle (e.g. 70°) and name its corresponding, alternate, and co-interior partners.
Colour the equal family (corresponding and alternate) in one hue and the supplementary family (co-interior) in another.
For a 70° starting angle, label each partner with its value: the equal partners read 70°, and the co-interior partner reads 110° because co-interior angles sum to 180° (180 − 70 = 110).
Explain in words why the co-interior angle is 110° and not 70°, referring to the straight line or to the equal angle that sits on a straight line with it.
activities.intendedInsight: Not all angles made with parallel lines are equal: corresponding and alternate angles are equal, while co-interior angles are supplementary, so a 70° angle produces both 70° partners and a 110° partner.

activities.title: Identify pairs in off-set and rotated diagrams
feedback: If a pupil says the rules 'don't apply because the lines don't look parallel', redirect them to the arrow marks: matching arrows mean parallel, so the rules do apply.
If a pupil applies equality to an unmarked, non-parallel diagram, point out there is no parallel condition shown, so the equalities are not guaranteed.
activities.rationale: Non-standard, off-set, and rotated diagrams counter the perceptual error that only similar-looking lines are parallel and the inverse error of applying the rules to non-parallel lines.
sourceClaims: Students often confuse alternate and corresponding angles and cannot pick them out in any but the simplest diagrams; 'F' and 'Z' angle mnemonics do not support reasoning (use precise language and full reasons instead); a further difficulty is that students accept lines as parallel only if similar in length/position, so off-set lines are not perceived as parallel; equality is best shown by translating the four-angle cluster along the transversal with tracing paper. The parallel-line/transversal image contains all the structure needed to deduce the angle sum of a triangle.
learnerActions: Work with diagrams where the parallel lines overlap only a little, are off-set, or are rotated away from the usual horizontal layout, with the parallels marked by arrows.
Before applying any rule, check the arrow marks to confirm the lines really are parallel.
Pick out and name each requested angle pair (corresponding, alternate, co-interior) despite the unusual orientation.
Also examine a diagram whose lines are NOT marked parallel and explain why the equal/supplementary rules may not apply there.
activities.intendedInsight: Parallelism is judged by the marking arrows and definition, not by how similar the lines look; the angle relationships hold in rotated and off-set diagrams whenever the lines are genuinely parallel, and must not be assumed when they are not.

activities.title: Multi-step angle chase with a stated reason at each step
feedback: Accept an answer only when each step carries a correct, precise reason; 'because of the F shape' is not a reason — name the relationship.
If a step is unjustified or a basic fact is misused, isolate that step and ask which angle fact licenses it before continuing.
activities.rationale: Requiring a stated reason at every step and resting multi-step work on secure basic angle facts develops the structural reasoning that mnemonics bypass.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory: pupils 'understand and use the relationship between parallel lines and alternate and corresponding angles' and 'apply the properties of angles at a point, angles at a point on a straight line, vertically opposite angles' to derive and use angle results.

Students often confuse alternate and corresponding angles and cannot pick them out in any but the simplest diagrams; 'F' and 'Z' angle mnemonics do not support reasoning (use precise language and full reasons instead); a further difficulty is that students accept lines as parallel only if similar in length/position, so off-set lines are not perceived as parallel; equality is best shown by translating the four-angle cluster along the transversal with tracing paper. The parallel-line/transversal image contains all the structure needed to deduce the angle sum of a triangle.
learnerActions: Given a diagram combining parallel lines, a transversal, and other lines, find an unknown angle that requires two or more steps.
At each step, write the angle fact used as a full reason, e.g. 'x = 45° because alternate angles are equal' or 'y = 180 − 45 = 135° because angles on a straight line sum to 180°'.
Use secure basic facts where needed: angles on a straight line sum to 180°, vertically opposite angles are equal, and angles at a point sum to 360°.
Check the final answer by an independent route (e.g. a different pair of angles) where possible.
activities.intendedInsight: Unknown angles are found by chaining relationships, each justified by a stated reason, building on secure basic angle facts rather than by pattern-matching a letter shape.

activities.title: Predict, reason, then check (diagnostic)
feedback: A pupil answering 110° with a supplementary/straight-line justification shows secure understanding of the two families.

A pupil answering 70° with 'angles on parallel lines are equal' reveals the over-generalisation — separate the equal family from the supplementary family and use straight-line reasoning to show the co-interior angle is 110°.
If a pupil only states that the relationship holds without saying why, press for the structural reason (translation or straight line).
activities.rationale: A predict-reason-check task makes the stated reason the diagnostic focus, surfacing whether a pupil holds a blurred 'all equal' rule or genuinely distinguishes equal from supplementary pairs. The stated correct value 110° follows from 180 − 70 = 110.
learnerActions: Look at two parallel lines cut by a transversal with one angle marked 70°; the teacher points to its co-interior (same-side interior) angle.
PREDICT whether that angle is equal, bigger, or smaller than 70°, and state WHY before checking.
Check by sliding a tracing-paper copy of the 70° angle (or an equal partner) along the transversal and reasoning via the straight line: the co-interior angle is 180 − 70 = 110°.
Answer the follow-up: would the answer still hold if the lines were not quite parallel, and why does parallelism matter?
activities.intendedInsight: Co-interior angles between parallel lines are supplementary (110° here), distinct from the equal alternate/corresponding pairs; a correct justification distinguishes the two families and depends on the lines being parallel.

constraints: Pupils must produce full reasons, not just answers: 'x = 45° because alternate angles are equal', not 'F angle'. 'F'/'Z' mnemonics give an answer without supporting the reasoning and should not stand in for a stated relationship.

Keep the equal family (corresponding, alternate) explicitly distinct from the supplementary family (co-interior); a single 'angles on parallel lines are equal' rule is a misconception to correct, not a shortcut to accept.

The angle rules apply only when the lines are genuinely parallel; require pupils to check the parallel marking before applying equalities, and do not apply the rules to unmarked or non-parallel lines.

A static labelled reference diagram (with tap-to-reveal partners and relationships) is a useful lookup aid but cannot animate the translation that justifies equality or let pupils un-parallel the lines; treat it as a scaffold, not the full lesson.

Tracing-paper cutouts have slight thickness and are physical approximations of the ideal zero-thickness lines and angles they represent; use them to demonstrate the translation while noting the idealisation.

Matching and multiple-choice items (e.g. sort pairs into 'equal' vs 'supplementary', find a missing angle, with a co-interior item offering a tempting but wrong '70° (equal)' option and a non-standard diagram) can probe the core over-generalisation and assess identification, but a recognition-only format does not by itself elicit the pupil's own constructed reasoning or the felt translation — pair it with tasks that require a written or spoken reason.
Multi-step angle-chasing depends on secure basic angle facts (straight line 180°, vertically opposite, angles at a point); shore these up first.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Self-audit arithmetic: for a 70° marked angle, co-interior partner = 180 − 70 = 110° (correct); the equal (corresponding/alternate) partners = 70°. These are consistent throughout.

Neither cited source claim explicitly states that co-interior angles are supplementary or names the 'angles on parallel lines are equal' over-generalisation; the equal-vs-supplementary family-separation activity (activity 2) and the predict-reason-check diagnostic (activity 5) therefore carry an empty sourceClaims, resting on the curriculum/pedagogy description. Activity 5's translation check-step is nonetheless consistent with the source's recommended tracing-paper technique, but no source claim directly supports its stated rationale.

The source material does not establish comparative efficacy or necessity of any particular medium; the original catalog fit judgements ('3D adds nothing', a dynamic model is 'ideal', a quiz 'cannot deliver' understanding) have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements.

A dynamic sliding model with live readouts and an un-parallel control is an optional, helpful way to make the translation and the parallel-condition visible; it is presented as an interaction example, not a mandatory mechanism — tracing paper on paper achieves the same reasoning.

The original 'correctAnswer' noted an equivalent framing: the 70° angle equals the alternate/corresponding angle that lies on a straight line with the co-interior angle; this is retained as an alternative justification route and is mathematically sound.

assess.poeTask: Draw two parallel lines cut by a transversal and mark one angle. Ask the child to PREDICT whether a specified alternate angle will be equal, bigger, or smaller — and to say WHY — before checking. Then slide a tracing-paper copy of the first angle along the transversal onto the second: it fits exactly, showing they are equal by translation. The stated reason for the prediction is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: Which angle in this diagram IS equal to the 70° — and how do you know it's equal rather than supplementary?
Slide a tracing-paper copy of the 70° angle along the transversal — where does it land, and what does that prove?
If I drew the two lines so they weren't quite parallel, would your answer still hold? Why does parallelism matter?
Explain WHY alternate angles are equal — not just that they are.
assess.correctAnswer: 110°. Co-interior (same-side interior) angles between parallel lines are supplementary — they add to 180° — so 180 − 70 = 110°. (Equivalently, the 70° angle is equal to the alternate/corresponding angle that sits on a straight line with the co-interior angle, and angles on a straight line sum to 180°.) The reasoning must distinguish co-interior/supplementary from the equal alternate/corresponding pairs.

errorPatterns.pattern: Over-generalises 'angles on parallel lines are equal', so treats the co-interior angle as equal (70°) rather than supplementary (110°)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the equal family (corresponding, alternate) from the supplementary family (co-interior); use straight-line reasoning and colour-coding to show why co-interior sums to 180°
errorPatterns.distractor: 70° — angles made with parallel lines are always equal.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 70° and justifies with 'angles made with parallel lines are equal'

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses alternate and corresponding angles, so pairs the wrong angles as equal — especially in non-standard diagrams
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reason from structure via translation along the transversal rather than 'F'/'Z' mnemonics; practise identifying pairs in non-standard diagrams with precise language
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels a corresponding pair 'alternate' (or vice versa), or cannot pick out the pairs once the diagram is rotated

errorPatterns.pattern: Does not perceive off-set lines as parallel (little overlap), so does not apply the rules — or applies parallel-line rules to lines that are not parallel
errorPatterns.nextMove: Mark parallels with arrows and check the parallel condition before applying rules; use off-set/non-standard diagrams so parallelism is judged by the marks, not the look
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the angle relationships 'don't apply' because the lines 'don't look parallel', or uses equality on a diagram whose lines are not marked parallel

responseLevels.gap: Applies a single 'angles on parallel lines are equal' rule to everything, cannot tell equal from supplementary, and cannot identify pairs in non-standard diagrams.
responseLevels.full: Finds unknown angles by combining relationships, distinguishes equal (alternate/corresponding) from supplementary (co-interior), justifies equality by translation along the transversal, and reasons correctly in non-standard and off-set diagrams.
responseLevels.partial: Uses corresponding/alternate/co-interior correctly in standard diagrams and gets 110°, but reverts to 'F'/'Z' pattern-matching, mis-identifies pairs in rotated or off-set diagrams, or can only say that the relationship holds, not why — names the pairs without reasoning from structure.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In this diagram two parallel lines are crossed by a transversal. One angle is marked 70°. The angle I point to is its co-interior (same-side interior) angle. What is that angle, and explain how you know.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A pupil who understands the structure knows co-interior angles are supplementary (110°) and justifies it via the straight line or translation; a pupil carrying a blurred 'angles on parallel lines are equal' rule answers 70°. The correct answer requires distinguishing equal pairs from supplementary pairs and cannot be reached from a single over-general rule.

sources.claim: Students often confuse alternate and corresponding angles and cannot pick them out in any but the simplest diagrams; 'F' and 'Z' angle mnemonics do not support reasoning (use precise language and full reasons instead); a further difficulty is that students accept lines as parallel only if similar in length/position, so off-set lines are not perceived as parallel; equality is best shown by translating the four-angle cluster along the transversal with tracing paper. The parallel-line/transversal image contains all the structure needed to deduce the angle sum of a triangle.

pedagogy.summary: Y4 extends the right-angle benchmark into naming and ordering: an acute angle is less open than a right angle, an obtuse angle is more open (up to a straight line, i.e. two right angles). Children classify angles as acute / right / obtuse and order them by openness. The persistent obstacle is comparing and ordering when arm lengths differ — the exact task where the arm-length misconception bites (Askew & Wiliam locate the most common error here). Naming should follow secure less-than / greater-than-a-right-angle comparison, not precede it.
bestPractices: Anchor both names to the right angle: acute = less open than a right angle, obtuse = more open (but less than a straight line); compare every angle to the checker before naming it.
Order by superimposing openings, not by eyeballing the tips: overlay angles vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned so only the opening is compared — this defeats the arm-length and area traps.
Use a dynamic opening (hinge or fan) to sweep from acute through right to obtuse, naming each zone as it is passed.
Hunt for and colour-sort the acute, right and obtuse angles inside real triangles and quadrilaterals.
Keep mnemonics subordinate to meaning — 'a cute little angle' is a memory hook, not the definition, which is the comparison to a right angle.
keyRepresentations: The right-angle checker as the dividing benchmark, and an 'openness' scale from nothing to a straight line with the right angle marked in the middle
A hinge / fan sweeping through acute → right → obtuse
Overlay (vertex-on-vertex) comparison for ordering by opening
Acute / right / obtuse angles picked out and colour-sorted within shapes
commonMisconceptions: Ordering angles by arm length or by the distance between the tips rather than by the opening (Askew & Wiliam; Xu et al. list side length, enclosed area and distance between the sides as the irrelevant properties children use)
Judging by the space or area enclosed between the arms rather than the opening
Naming by appearance rather than by comparison to a right angle — a long-armed acute angle called obtuse because it 'looks big', or the two names simply swapped
Naming before comparing: applying acute/obtuse labels without checking against the right angle

learn.summary: Year 4 learners identify acute and obtuse angles and compare/order angles up to two right angles by size. Both names are anchored to the right angle: acute is less open than a right angle, obtuse is more open (but less than a straight line, i.e. two right angles). The persistent obstacle is comparing and ordering angles when the arm lengths differ — children tend to judge by arm length, enclosed area, or the distance between the tips rather than by the opening. The proposed core teaching move is vertex-on-vertex overlay comparison, with naming intended to follow secure less-than/greater-than-a-right-angle comparison rather than preceding it.

activities.title: Order the baited angles, then overlay to check
feedback: If a learner orders by arm length and places the long-armed narrow angle as largest, overlay that trapped pair vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned so the narrow opening visibly folds inside the wide one; then re-sort by opening.
If a learner asks whether shortening the long arms would change its place, let them test it — shortening the arms does not change the opening, so the order stays the same.
Confirm correct orderings that are justified by comparing openings, overlaying, or relating each angle to a right angle, rather than by line length.
activities.rationale: A common comparison error is treating an angle as the distance between the ends of its lines, judging the angle with longer lines as larger; this may be reinforced when taught examples mostly use equal-length arms. Deliberately anti-correlating arm length with opening and then providing an overlay comparison is proposed to target exactly this misconception. An optional overlay tool that snaps two angles vertex-on-vertex, and a seeded four-angle task where the smallest opening has the longest arms, are intended to make the mechanism concrete.
sourceClaims: When comparing angles (from Year 3) the most common error is judging two identical angles as unequal because the arms differ in length, treating an angle as the distance between the ends of the lines; it arises because taught examples nearly always use equal-length arms.

When comparing angle size, elementary (and even middle-school) students are confused by irrelevant properties — the length of the sides, the area within the sides, and the distance between the sides — and mistakenly judge that the angle formed by longer lines is larger; this reflects a whole-object assumption, and framing angle as the measure of opening/rotation helps separate the size dimension.
Year 4 pupils should identify acute and obtuse angles and compare and order angles up to two right angles by size.
learnerActions: Receive four angles to drag into order from smallest to largest, where the smallest opening is deliberately drawn with the longest arms and the largest opening with the shortest arms.
State out loud, before moving anything, which angle you think is biggest and why.
Overlay any two angles vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned, so only the openings are compared.

Overlay the longest-armed angle on the shortest-armed one and watch the long-armed 'big-looking' angle's opening fall INSIDE the short-armed angle's opening, then compare the other pairs the same way and re-sort all four by opening.
Re-state the rule you now use to decide the order.
activities.intendedInsight: An angle's size is its opening, not the length of its arms, the distance between the tips, or the area enclosed. Overlaying vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned isolates the opening, so an angle with longer arms but a narrower opening is seen to be the smaller angle.

activities.title: Sweep a hinge through acute, right and obtuse
feedback: If a learner names an angle in a way that contradicts its comparison to a right angle, return to the checker: less open than a right angle is acute, more open (but less than a straight line) is obtuse — test before labelling.
Confirm that obtuse 'stops' at a straight line (two right angles); an angle that is exactly a straight line, or more open than one, is not obtuse.
Treat mnemonics such as 'a cute little angle' as a memory hook only, not the definition — the definition is the comparison to a right angle.
activities.rationale: A dynamic opening that sweeps continuously through the three named zones, with the right angle marked as the dividing benchmark, is intended to attach names to degrees of openness rather than to how a shape looks, supporting naming by comparison rather than by appearance. The live label and small-square snap-in are optional feedback examples that make the benchmark visible.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should identify acute and obtuse angles and compare and order angles up to two right angles by size.

When comparing angle size, elementary (and even middle-school) students are confused by irrelevant properties — the length of the sides, the area within the sides, and the distance between the sides — and mistakenly judge that the angle formed by longer lines is larger; this reflects a whole-object assumption, and framing angle as the measure of opening/rotation helps separate the size dimension.
learnerActions: Open a hinge or fan slowly from nearly closed to a straight line.

Watch (or control) a label that ticks through acute → right → obtuse as the opening grows, with a small square snapping in at the right angle, and that changes to 'straight line (not obtuse)' when the opening reaches a straight line.
Pause the sweep and name the zone the opening is currently in.
Identify where obtuse stops — at a straight line, which equals two right angles.
activities.intendedInsight: The names acute, right and obtuse are zones of openness defined relative to the right-angle benchmark: acute is less open than a right angle, right is exactly a right angle, and obtuse is more open but less than a straight line (two right angles).

activities.title: Hunt and colour-sort angles inside shapes
feedback: If a learner labels an angle by appearance (e.g. calls a long-armed acute angle obtuse because it 'looks big'), return the naming to the checker and have them test the angle against a right angle before labelling.
Confirm classifications that are justified by comparison to the right angle rather than by overall size or orientation of the figure.
activities.rationale: Hunting for and colour-sorting the acute, right and obtuse angles inside triangles and convex quadrilaterals applies classification in a relational context — finding all angles of a type in a new shape — which is a more demanding application than classifying isolated angles. It is also intended to guard against naming by appearance when orientation or arm length is misleading.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should identify acute and obtuse angles and compare and order angles up to two right angles by size.

When comparing angle size, elementary (and even middle-school) students are confused by irrelevant properties — the length of the sides, the area within the sides, and the distance between the sides — and mistakenly judge that the angle formed by longer lines is larger; this reflects a whole-object assumption, and framing angle as the measure of opening/rotation helps separate the size dimension.
learnerActions: Examine a given triangle or convex quadrilateral (one with no inside angle more open than a straight line).
Find every angle and decide whether it is acute, right or obtuse by comparing each to a right angle.
Colour-sort the angles by type (e.g. one colour for acute, one for right, one for obtuse).
Explain, for a tricky angle, how you checked it against the right angle rather than guessing from its appearance.
activities.intendedInsight: Acute, right and obtuse angles occur inside real shapes, and each is classified by comparison to a right angle — not by the orientation of the shape or the length of its sides.

activities.title: Predict-then-check: short wide angle vs long narrow angle
feedback: If a learner predicts the long-armed angle is bigger because of its line lengths, overlay the pair vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned so the narrow opening folds inside the wide one, then relate each back to the right-angle benchmark.

If a learner judges by the gap between the tips or the enclosed space, mark an arc at the vertex and slide it in and out along the arms to show the opening is the same however far out you look; then overlay to compare the opening alone, ignoring the shaded region.
Confirm answers that order by opening and justify by overlaying or comparing to a right angle, not by line length.
activities.rationale: Asking for a prediction and a reason before any movement is intended to surface whether the learner is using the length rule or comparing openings; the overlay then provides the disconfirming evidence. Marking and sliding an arc at the vertex addresses the related area/tip-distance misconception by showing the opening is invariant to how far out along the arms you look.
sourceClaims: When comparing angles (from Year 3) the most common error is judging two identical angles as unequal because the arms differ in length, treating an angle as the distance between the ends of the lines; it arises because taught examples nearly always use equal-length arms.

When comparing angle size, elementary (and even middle-school) students are confused by irrelevant properties — the length of the sides, the area within the sides, and the distance between the sides — and mistakenly judge that the angle formed by longer lines is larger; this reflects a whole-object assumption, and framing angle as the measure of opening/rotation helps separate the size dimension.
learnerActions: Look at two angles: A with short arms and a wide opening, B with long arms and a narrow opening.
Predict which is the bigger angle and say why, before anything is moved.
Overlay them vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned so B's second arm falls inside A's.
Reconcile your prediction with what the overlay shows, and restate the rule for comparing angles.
Answer the probe: if the long arms were made much shorter, would the angle's place in the order change? Why? And could a short-armed angle ever be bigger than a long-armed one — can you draw one?
activities.intendedInsight: The reason a learner gives first is the diagnostic part: a learner who predicts B is bigger 'because its lines are longer' is asked to reconcile that with the wider opening of A winning once the angles are overlaid.

constraints: Anchor both names to the right angle: compare every angle to a right-angle checker before naming it. Acute = less open than a right angle; obtuse = more open but less than a straight line (two right angles).

Order by superimposing openings, not by eyeballing the tips: overlay angles vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned so only the opening is compared. Because the overlay compares the openings alone, differences in arm length, enclosed area and tip distance cannot drive the comparison.
Naming should follow secure less-than/greater-than-a-right-angle comparison, not precede it.
Keep mnemonics subordinate to meaning — 'a cute little angle' is a memory hook, not the definition.

A static picture that reveals labels when tapped supports recognition and classification of clear cases, but it cannot carry out the overlay comparison or the dynamic sweep; treat it as a scaffold for classification only, not a replacement for the overlay work.

Classification and ordering practice (classifying angles as acute/right/obtuse, ordering them by size, and finding all of a type in a shape) is useful for assessment and practice, but recognising and ordering angles does not by itself build the overlay intuition for the length trap; pair it with hands-on overlay work.

If learners manipulate physical paper/card angle cutouts, note that cutouts have slight real thickness and can be held and overlaid, whereas the on-screen or ideal figure is a zero-thickness model of the mathematical angle; the comparison is about the represented angle, not the physical card.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated 3D and in-role dialogue formats as poor fits and asserted a static image cannot build overlay intuition. These are presented here as narrowly scoped affordance/limit observations (a static reveal cannot perform the dynamic overlay or live sweep), not as universal claims about what any medium can teach; the cited sources establish the misconception and curriculum content, not comparative efficacy between media.

Self-audit of the geometry: an angle's measure is its opening and is invariant to arm length and to how far out along the arms you look; the 'slide the arc in and out' demonstration is consistent with this. Obtuse angles are those strictly between a right angle and a straight line; a straight line (two right angles) is the upper bound for this Year 4 topic. No arithmetic or force/motion content was present to correct.

The legacy attribution of this four-angle ordering task as 'Askew & Wiliam's documented diagnostic task' and the phrase that the overlay 'defeats' the trap have been softened to proposed/geometric wording; the sources support the misconception's prevalence and the curriculum objective but not comparative efficacy of this specific design.

The colour-sort method itself is not evidenced by the cited sources; its supporting claims cover the identify-acute/obtuse content and the appearance-naming misconception it addresses, not the recolouring technique's effectiveness.

assess.poeTask: Show two angles: A with short arms and a wide opening, B with long arms and a narrow opening. Ask the child to PREDICT which is the bigger angle and WHY before anything is moved. Then overlay them vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned so B's second arm falls inside A's. A child who predicted B 'because its lines are longer' must confront the wider opening winning; the reason stated first is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: You put this one first as the smallest, and it has the longest lines. If I made its lines much shorter, would it change its place in the order? Why?
Show me how you'd check, without measuring, whether this angle is acute or obtuse.
Is it possible for an angle with short little lines to be bigger than an angle with long lines? Can you draw me one?
How open can an angle get and still be called obtuse — where does obtuse stop?
assess.correctAnswer: Orders the angles by their opening, ignoring arm length (so the long-armed narrow angle goes first and the short-armed wide angle last), and justifies by comparing openings, overlaying, or relating each to a right angle — not by how long the lines are.

errorPatterns.pattern: The angle with the longest lines is the biggest ('longer arms mean a bigger angle')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay the trapped pair vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned so the narrow opening visibly folds inside the wide one; re-sort by opening and return to the right-angle benchmark.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Orders by arm length, placing the long-armed narrow-opening angle as the largest, and justifies by mentioning the line lengths

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges by the space or gap between the arms — the angle that encloses more area, or whose tips are further apart, is the bigger angle
errorPatterns.nextMove: Mark the arc at the vertex and slide it in and out along the arms to show the opening is the same however far out you look; overlay to compare opening alone, ignoring the shaded region.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Ranks a short-armed wide angle below a long-armed narrow one because it 'takes up less space' or its tips are closer together

errorPatterns.pattern: Names by appearance, not by comparison to a right angle — a long-armed acute angle called obtuse because it 'looks big', or acute and obtuse swapped
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return every naming to the checker — less open than a right angle is acute, more open is obtuse — and have the child test before labelling.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels an angle acute or obtuse in a way that contradicts its comparison to a right angle, especially when arm length or orientation is misleading

responseLevels.gap: Orders and names angles by arm length, tip-distance, or enclosed space; swaps acute and obtuse or names by appearance; cannot separate the opening from the overall figure.
responseLevels.full: Orders and classifies purely by opening — overlaying or comparing to a right angle regardless of arm length — explains acute as less and obtuse as more open than a right angle (up to a straight line / two right angles), and finds all the acute and obtuse angles in a new shape (relational).
responseLevels.partial: Classifies clear acute / right / obtuse cases and recalls the names, and orders angles correctly when the arms are the same length, but is misled when arm length is anti-correlated with opening, or names an angle without comparing it to a right angle (multistructural).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child four angles to order from smallest to largest, with arm length deliberately anti-correlated with opening — the smallest opening is drawn with the longest arms and the largest opening with the shortest arms. Say: 'Put these four angles in order, from the smallest angle to the biggest.' Then: 'Tell me how you decided the order.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Anti-correlating arm length with opening means a child using the length rule produces a specifically reversed order on the trapped pair, while a child comparing openings orders correctly; the tier-2 reason reveals which method was used. This is Askew & Wiliam's documented diagnostic task for the misconception.

pedagogy.summary: This is the first sustained problem-solving procedure of the strand: given a ratio and one known quantity, find the missing one using multiplication and division ('red:blue is 3:5, there are 15 blue — find red'). The reliable method is to find the multiplier that maps the known ratio-part to the actual amount (15 ÷ 5 = 3, so ×3), then apply it to the other part (3 × 3 = 9), or equivalently to find the value of one 'share' via a bar model. The central teaching battle is against ADDITIVE reasoning — children who reason 'blue went up by 10, so red goes up by 10' (a constant difference) instead of scaling by a constant multiplier. Teaching must make the multiplicative relationship explicit and visible, using bar models, ratio tables and 'for every' language so that scaling, not adding, becomes the natural move.
bestPractices: Draw a bar model first: equal blocks for each part make 'find one block' (the multiplier/share value) the obvious pivot, and expose the structure before any arithmetic.
Name the multiplier explicitly: 'what do we multiply the ratio by to get the real amounts?' (15 = 5 × 3, so ×3 everywhere) — this directly counters additive thinking.
Use a ratio table so equivalent ratios (3:5, 6:10, 9:15) are seen as scalings of the same relationship, and the constant multiplier is visible down the columns.

Confront the additive error head-on with a comparison task: show that 'add 10 to both' changes the relationship (3:5 vs 13:15 are different mixtures) whereas multiplying keeps it — ideally with a concrete mixing/colour context where the change is perceptible.
Keep 'for every' language central ('for every 3 red there are 5 blue') so scaling up in whole groups feels natural before formal multiplier work.
Vary which quantity is known and use non-unit and non-integer multipliers so children cannot rely on simple build-up alone.
keyRepresentations: Bar model with equal blocks per part (find one block = the share/multiplier)
Ratio table showing the constant multiplier down the columns (3:5, ×3 → 9:15)
Double number line aligning the two quantities at 0
'For every a there are b' grouping with counters/cubes
Arrow diagram showing '×3' mapping ratio to real amounts
commonMisconceptions: Additive/constant-difference reasoning: 'blue rose by 10, so red rises by 10' (or 'the difference is 2, keep it') instead of scaling by a constant multiplier
Applies the multiplier to only one quantity, or adds the multiplier instead of multiplying
Uses the wrong direction (multiplies when should divide to find the multiplier, or vice versa)
Build-up strategy that works for whole-number cases but collapses when the multiplier is non-integer

learn.summary: Learners solve missing-value ratio problems (given a ratio and one known quantity, find the other) by finding and applying a constant multiplier, e.g. 'red:blue is 3:5, there are 15 blue — find red' (15÷5=3, so ×3, red = 3×3 = 9). The central challenge is overcoming ADDITIVE reasoning — 'blue rose by 10, so red rises by 10' or 'keep the same difference' — by making the multiplicative relationship visible through bar models, ratio tables and 'for every' language, and by letting learners see that adding the same amount to both unequal parts changes the relationship while multiplying both parts by the same factor preserves it.

activities.title: Scale a mixture and compare adding versus multiplying
feedback: If the learner adds the difference (e.g. 15−5=10, then red = 3+10 = 13): show that 13:15 produces a different mixture/shade from 3:5, then ask 'what do we multiply 5 by to get 15?' and apply that same factor to red.
If the learner finds ×3 but applies it to only one part: highlight that both bar/table columns move together, so the same multiplier acts on red and blue.
If the learner multiplies when they should divide (or the reverse): ask 'is 15 bigger or smaller than 5? so are we scaling up or down?' before choosing the operation.
When correct: name the multiplier explicitly ('5 became 15, that is ×3, so red 3 becomes 9') and connect it to one 'share' on the bar model.
activities.rationale: A live outcome that visibly changes under adding but stays the same under multiplying can make the multiplicative structure perceptible, which may help with additive-strategy interference. Ratio tables and bar/double-number-line models that move both parts together are commonly recommended supports for this error.
sourceClaims: NCETM documents that in scaling/missing-value problems 'students often assume that relationships are additive... in situations where the actual relationship is multiplicative' — e.g. for '5 miles = 8 km, how many km is 7 miles?' students say 'two more miles means two more km', and for a ratio 2:5 assume a constant £3 difference rather than scaling. The remedy is to find the constant multiplier (functional/scalar) using ratio tables and bar/double-number-line models that move both parts together.

Year 6 pupils 'solve problems involving the relative sizes of two quantities where missing values can be found by using integer multiplication and division facts', and recognise proportion when quantities are in the same ratio (recipes, similar shapes).
learnerActions: Meet the problem 'red:blue is 3:5 and there are 15 blue — how many red?' alongside a visible outcome such as rows of beads or a paint shade produced by the ratio.
Scale the ratio up a ratio table (3:5, 6:10, 9:15) and watch two bars (one per part) grow together, stating the multiplier that turns 5 into 15 (×3) and applying the same ×3 to red to get 9.

Try two contrasting moves on the mixture: 'add 10 to each part' (giving 13:15) and 'multiply each part by 3' (giving 9:15), and observe which move keeps the mixture/shade the same and which changes it.
Say in words why multiplying by 3 keeps the same relationship but adding 10 to both does not.

As an optional extension beyond the integer-fact objective, keep red:blue 3:5 but switch to a measurable paint mixture: with 12 ml blue the multiplier is 12÷5 = 2.4, so red = 3×2.4 = 7.2 ml. This shows that building up in whole groups of 3:5 cannot reach the answer. (A bead count could not be 7.2, so use continuous amounts here.)
activities.intendedInsight: The two quantities in a ratio are linked by a constant multiplier, not a constant difference: scaling both parts by the same factor preserves the relationship, while adding the same amount to both breaks it whenever the two parts are unequal.

activities.title: Build a bar model to find one share
feedback: If the learner cannot start: cover the arithmetic and ask 'if these 5 equal blocks hold 15 altogether, how much is in one block?'
If a learner gives one block the whole known total: remind them the known amount is shared equally across its blocks, not placed in one.
When correct: link the 'per block' value to the multiplier so the two methods are seen as the same idea.
activities.rationale: Drawing equal blocks first exposes the structure and makes 'find one block' the obvious pivot, giving a route to the answer via equal shares that supports multiplicative reasoning.
sourceClaims: NCETM documents that in scaling/missing-value problems 'students often assume that relationships are additive... in situations where the actual relationship is multiplicative' — e.g. for '5 miles = 8 km, how many km is 7 miles?' students say 'two more miles means two more km', and for a ratio 2:5 assume a constant £3 difference rather than scaling. The remedy is to find the constant multiplier (functional/scalar) using ratio tables and bar/double-number-line models that move both parts together.
learnerActions: Draw a bar model with equal blocks for each part of the ratio (3 blocks red, 5 blocks blue).
Match the known quantity to its blocks and work out the value of one block (15 blue ÷ 5 blocks = 3 per block).
Multiply the value of one block by the number of blocks in the unknown part (3 × 3 = 9 red).
Explain, pointing at the model, why the red count is that number because every block holds the same amount.
activities.intendedInsight: Finding the value of a single equal 'share' or block reveals the constant multiplier and makes the equal-grouping structure of a ratio explicit before any symbolic arithmetic.

activities.title: Solve varied missing-value problems and catch the additive trap
feedback: If the learner answers 17 for the apples: that is 2 + (20−5), adding the difference; show that 5 scaled to 20 is ×4, so apples go 2 × 4 = 8.

If the learner stalls on the non-integer case: extend build-up by asking 'how many groups of 5 is 20?' to turn counting-in-groups into ×4. Then note that 12 is 2 groups of 5 and 2 more, i.e. 2 and 2/5 = 2.4 groups, and apply ×2.4.
If the learner inverts the direction: compare the sizes of the two known amounts to decide scale up or down before computing.
When correct across varied cases: confirm the multiplier is found by division of matching parts and applied by multiplication to the other part.
activities.rationale: Varying which quantity is known and including non-integer multipliers prevents reliance on simple build-up and makes the constant-multiplier method the robust strategy; additive distractors are diagnostic of the core misconception.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils 'solve problems involving the relative sizes of two quantities where missing values can be found by using integer multiplication and division facts', and recognise proportion when quantities are in the same ratio (recipes, similar shapes).

NCETM documents that in scaling/missing-value problems 'students often assume that relationships are additive... in situations where the actual relationship is multiplicative' — e.g. for '5 miles = 8 km, how many km is 7 miles?' students say 'two more miles means two more km', and for a ratio 2:5 assume a constant £3 difference rather than scaling. The remedy is to find the constant multiplier (functional/scalar) using ratio tables and bar/double-number-line models that move both parts together.
learnerActions: Solve a set of missing-value problems where the known quantity varies between the two parts and multipliers are sometimes non-integer, e.g. 'for every 2 apples there are 5 oranges; with 20 oranges, how many apples?' (×4 → 8 apples).
For each, state the multiplier and show it applied to both parts.

Compare a tempting additive answer with the correct scaled answer and explain which relationship each uses, e.g. for 2 apples : 5 oranges with 20 oranges, the additive move gives 2+15 = 17 while the correct scaled answer is 2×4 = 8.

As an optional extension, tackle one non-integer case using measurable quantities (e.g. 2 cups juice : 5 cups water with 12 cups water → ×2.4 → 4.8 cups juice) to test that the method still works when whole-group build-up cannot reach the number.
activities.intendedInsight: The same constant multiplier applies to both parts regardless of which quantity is known, and multiplicative reasoning works even when the multiplier is not a whole number — unlike repeated adding.

activities.title: Talk it through: is it still the same drink?
feedback: If the learner accepts 'add 10 to each': ask them to compare the mixture before and after and notice that, because the two parts are unequal, the taste/shade would change (e.g. 3:5 becomes 13:15).
If the learner scales correctly: prompt them to state the multiplier explicitly and connect 'for every' groups to multiplication.
activities.rationale: Posing 'for every' problems and probing additive suggestions keeps scaling language central; discussion can surface a learner's reasoning, though the preserving-versus-breaking contrast is often clearer when the outcome can be seen as well as discussed.
sourceClaims: NCETM documents that in scaling/missing-value problems 'students often assume that relationships are additive... in situations where the actual relationship is multiplicative' — e.g. for '5 miles = 8 km, how many km is 7 miles?' students say 'two more miles means two more km', and for a ratio 2:5 assume a constant £3 difference rather than scaling. The remedy is to find the constant multiplier (functional/scalar) using ratio tables and bar/double-number-line models that move both parts together.
learnerActions: Take on a recipe or juice-bar scenario where orders must be scaled up while keeping the same taste/mixture.
When a character suggests 'just add 10 more of each', decide and explain whether the drink stays the same, then propose the correct scaling.
Use 'for every' language ('for every 3 red there are 5 blue') to justify scaling up in whole groups before naming the formal multiplier.
activities.intendedInsight: Keeping a ratio the same means scaling both parts by the same factor; 'for every' grouping language supports this before formal multiplier notation.

constraints: This is procedural problem-solving: learners should construct and solve problems and state the multiplier, not merely recognise a correct answer from options.

Build-up (repeatedly adding the ratio unit) is a valid stepping stone and should be extended toward the multiplier ('how many groups of 5 is 20?'), not discouraged. Non-integer multipliers, where whole-group build-up fails, are an optional extension beyond the integer-fact objective and should use measurable (continuous) quantities.

A worked example that only reveals one scaling (e.g. tap to show ×3) is a reference scaffold; it does not by itself give practice solving varied problems or confronting the additive alternative, so pair it with learner-constructed solutions.

Scored item sets with additive distractors (e.g. 17 for 2:5 with 20 known) can check and diagnose the additive misconception, but selecting a correct option does not by itself require the learner to produce the method or justify why the multiplier applies to both parts, so pair them with learner-constructed, explained solutions.

Vary which quantity is known, include non-unit multipliers and scaling down, and offer non-integer multipliers only as an optional extension with measurable quantities (or ratios not in simplest form that give whole answers, e.g. 4:6 with 15 → ×2.5 → 10), so correctness does not depend on whole-number build-up alone.
Keep each activity's ratio consistent within its own worked examples (e.g. activity 1 stays 3:5), so learners are not silently switched between different ratios mid-task.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 15÷5=3 and 3×3=9 (red beads) correct; for 2 apples:5 oranges with 20 oranges, 20÷5=4 and 2×4=8 (correct), additive error 2+(20−5)=17 (correctly labelled as the misconception, not a valid answer); non-integer case in activity 1 keeps 3:5 so 12÷5=2.4 and 3×2.4=7.2, and in activity 3 uses 2:5 so 12÷5=2.4 and 2×2.4=4.8 (both correct). These values are presented as intended.

The non-integer answers 7.2 (beads, activity 1) and 4.8 (apples, activity 3) are mathematically correct from their stated setups but are not whole-object counts; treat them as numerical scaling exercises, or choose a context where fractional values make sense.

The claim that a visible interactive contrast 'directly defeats' the misconception is a design rationale only; the cited sources establish the misconception and recommend ratio-table/bar/number-line remedies but do not establish comparative efficacy of a particular interactive outcome. Stated here as a proposal with its affordance, not as proven superiority.

probeDeeper: 'How did you decide to multiply by 4?' — checks the multiplier comes from 20÷5, not a guess.
'Does adding the same number to both parts keep the same relationship? Why or why not?' — directly surfaces additive vs multiplicative thinking.

Counterexample: 'What if there were 12 oranges instead of 20 — how many apples?' (multiplier ×2.4) — a child with true multiplicative reasoning scales to 4.8; a build-up-only or additive child stalls or mis-adds.
'Show me on a bar model why the apples are 8' — forces the equal-share structure to justify the answer.
assess.correctAnswer: 8 apples. The oranges scaled from 5 to 20, which is ×4, so the apples scale the same way: 2 × 4 = 8. (Equivalently, one 'share' logic via a bar model gives 8.)

errorPatterns.pattern: Additive / constant-difference reasoning: 'oranges went up by 15, so apples go up by 15' (→ 17), or 'the difference stays 3' — uses a constant difference instead of a constant multiplier
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront additively vs multiplicatively on a perceptible mixture: show 'add the difference' makes a different mixture, while scaling keeps it. Rebuild via 'what do we multiply 5 by to get 20?' and a bar model. This is documented additive-strategy interference, not carelessness.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child computes 20−5 = 15 (or the 3 gap) and adds it to the apples rather than finding ×4; answer 17 (or a gap-preserving value)

errorPatterns.pattern: Scales only one quantity, or adds the multiplier instead of multiplying: finds ×4 for oranges but leaves apples at 2, or does 2+4
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reinforce that the SAME multiplier acts on both parts (the ratio table columns move together); use the bar model where every block scales identically.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child finds the multiplier but applies it to one part only, or treats ×4 as +4 (giving 6)

errorPatterns.pattern: Wrong direction of scaling: divides when should multiply (or vice versa), e.g. treats 20 as the small amount
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach ratio — scaffold 'which is bigger, 5 or 20? so are we scaling up or down?' before choosing the operation. A set-up lapse.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child sets up 5 ÷ 20 or scales apples down; the multiplier is inverted

errorPatterns.pattern: Build-up that only works for whole-number multipliers: repeatedly adds the ratio unit (2,5 → 4,10 → ...) but cannot cope when the multiplier is non-integer
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT discourage build-up — it is a sound stepping stone; extend it toward the multiplier by asking 'how many groups of 5 is 20?' so counting-in-groups becomes ×4. It matures into multiplicative reasoning.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child successfully counts up in 2s-and-5s to reach 20 oranges but is stuck if asked about, say, 12 oranges

responseLevels.gap: Uses additive reasoning (adds the difference) or cannot set up the problem; gets 17 and defends it, or scales the wrong quantity/direction with no self-correction.
responseLevels.full: Finds the constant multiplier and applies it to both parts (or reasons via equal shares/bar model), explains why adding a constant would break the relationship, and transfers reliably to non-integer multipliers and either-quantity-known problems.
responseLevels.partial: Solves whole-number cases by build-up or by finding the multiplier for the practised numbers, but the reasoning is fragile — reverts to additive or stalls when the multiplier is non-integer or the known quantity changes; can find a multiplier but not always justify why it applies to both parts.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: For every 2 apples in a fruit bowl there are 5 oranges. A bigger bowl keeps the same relationship and has 20 oranges. Work out how many apples are in the bigger bowl — however you like, I'll watch.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The numbers are chosen so the additive and multiplicative strategies give clearly different answers: a child scaling multiplicatively finds ×4 and gets 8; a child reasoning additively sees oranges rose by 15 (from 5 to 20) and adds 15 to the apples, giving 17 — or keeps the difference of 3 and gives 17. Watching the method (do they seek a multiplier/scale the bars, or do they add the difference?) reveals which relationship the child is using, which is the entire conceptual hinge of ratio.

The remedy is to find the constant multiplier (functional/scalar) using ratio tables and bar/double-number-line models that move both parts together.
