pedagogy.summary: At age 10-11 (UK Y6) children construct 2-D shapes to a specification using a ruler and protractor — e.g. a triangle from two sides and an included angle, or a regular polygon from side length and interior angle. This is a precision motor-and-procedure skill layered on angle-measuring: the accuracy of the final figure exposes whether the sub-skills are secure. The dominant failure points are protractor-specific — reading the wrong scale on a dual-scale protractor (drawing the supplement of the intended angle), and misplacing the protractor's centre on the vertex or its zero-line along the drawn side — plus the ruler habit of measuring from the ruler's physical end instead of its zero mark. The remedy is a disciplined routine (estimate the angle first to choose the right scale; centre-on-vertex, zero-line-on-line; ruler zero on the endpoint) taught explicitly and rehearsed, alongside checking that the figure closes and sides are equal.
bestPractices: Estimate before measuring: decide whether the target angle is bigger or smaller than a right angle, then pick the protractor scale whose reading agrees — the single most reliable guard against the dual-scale supplement error

Drill the placement routine explicitly: protractor centre-hole on the vertex dot, zero-line exactly along the existing side, count up from the 0 on the arm you laid down; a single-scale or numberless protractor removes the scale ambiguity while the routine is learned
Teach ruler measurement from the zero mark, not the end of the ruler; mark the point then join, rather than eyeballing a length

Sequence the construction: draw the base first with the ruler, then set each given angle at its endpoint, then rule the rays to meet — and check the figure CLOSES; a non-closing triangle signals an accumulated placement/scale error
For regular polygons, connect side length and the (interior or exterior) turn angle so children construct by repeating an equal side and an equal turn, checking equal sides and equal angles
keyRepresentations: Protractor with the estimate-first rule (is it more or less than 90°?) to disambiguate the two scales
Single-scale or numberless protractor for the placement-learning phase
The 'centre-on-vertex, zero-on-line' placement diagram
Base-then-angles construction sequence for a triangle (SAS-style)
Side-and-turn model for constructing regular polygons
commonMisconceptions: Reads the wrong scale on the dual-scale protractor, drawing the supplement (e.g. 60° instead of 120°)
Places the protractor's centre off the vertex or its zero-line off the side, so every angle is a few degrees out or the ray does not start at the vertex
Measures length from the physical end of the ruler rather than the zero mark, adding the end-margin to each length
Treats a 'nearly closing' triangle as correct rather than a signal of accumulated error
Draws sides to look right rather than to the measured length, or turns an inconsistent amount at each corner of a regular polygon

learn.summary: For children aged 10-11 (UK Year 6) learning to construct 2-D shapes to a specification with a ruler and protractor: a triangle from a base and the two angles at its ends (Angle-Side-Angle), a triangle from two sides and an included angle (Side-Angle-Side), a rectangle from length and width, or a regular polygon from side length and turn angle. This is a precision procedural skill layered on angle measuring. The accuracy of the finished figure is itself the evidence: measuring its sides and angles against the specification (and, for rectangles and regular polygons, checking whether it closes) exposes whether the sub-skills are secure; an ASA or SAS triangle will close even when it is inaccurate, so closure alone proves little there. There are three dominant, well-documented failure points — two protractor-specific plus one ruler habit: reading the wrong scale on a dual-scale protractor (so the supplement is drawn, e.g. 140° for 40°), and misplacing the protractor (centre off the vertex, zero-line off the drawn side); and, separately, measuring length from the ruler's physical end rather than its zero mark. The remedy taught here is a disciplined, rehearsed routine: estimate the angle first to choose the right scale, centre-on-vertex with zero-line-on-line, ruler zero on the endpoint, then check the finished figure by measuring its sides and angles (and closure, for rectangles and polygons).

activities.title: Construct a triangle from a base and two base angles (ASA-style)
feedback: If the triangle fails to close or looks badly wrong, check whether you read the supplement (e.g. 140° where 40° was wanted): re-estimate 'bigger or smaller than a square corner?' and choose the scale whose number agrees.
If every angle is a few degrees out or a ray does not start at the vertex, re-seat the protractor: centre hole on the dot, zero-line exactly on the line.
If the base comes out systematically long, check you measured from the ruler's zero mark and not its physical end (the other two sides are set by the angles, so check those angles too).

A triangle whose measured angles (40°, 65° and a third angle of about 75°) and 7 cm base all match within tolerance is good evidence the routine held together; closing alone proves little, because the two rays will meet for almost any guessed angles that add up to less than 180°.
activities.rationale: Construction is a procedural doing-skill: building placement-and-scale judgement requires the child to actually set the angles and measure the sides, and re-measuring the finished triangle (the two set angles, the 7 cm base and a third angle of about 75°) turns the figure into immediate self-assessment of the coordinated routine.
sourceClaims: UK Y6 statutory: pupils 'draw 2-D shapes using given dimensions and angles'; the wider programme expects accurate use of a ruler to the nearest millimetre and measuring/drawing angles with a protractor.

Documented protractor difficulties: on a dual-scale protractor pupils struggle with WHICH scale to read (drawing the supplement), and with placing the vertex and baseline correctly; a numberless/single-scale protractor and estimate-first strategies reduce these errors (Exeter 2002 work cited).
learnerActions: Rule a base exactly 7 cm long, placing the ruler's zero mark (not its physical end) on the starting point, then mark and join.
At the left endpoint, before reading, decide: is the 40° angle smaller or bigger than a square corner (right angle)? Use that estimate to pick which of the two protractor scale numbers to read.
Place the protractor with its centre hole on the vertex dot and its zero-line exactly along the base, count up from the 0 on the arm laid along the base, mark 40°, and rule the ray.
Repeat at the right endpoint to set a 65° angle and rule the second ray so the two rays meet.

Check the triangle against the specification: re-measure the 40° and 65° angles and the 7 cm base, then measure the third angle, which should be about 75° (the angles of a triangle add up to 180°). If an angle is out by more than about 2°, or the two rays spread apart and never meet (a sign that a supplement such as 140° was drawn), find where the placement or scale error crept in.
activities.intendedInsight: The two scales of a dual-scale protractor offer supplementary numbers (e.g. 40 and 140); your own estimate of whether the angle is bigger or smaller than a right angle is what picks the correct one. Careful placement and measuring from zero are what make the figure match its specification. (A base with an angle set at each of its two ends is an angle-side-angle construction.)

activities.title: Isolate placement with a single-scale or numberless protractor
feedback: If angles are consistently off by a small amount, the zero-line is probably not flush with the side or the centre hole is off the dot — re-seat and remeasure.
When placement feels automatic, test yourself by switching back to the dual-scale tool and estimating first.
activities.rationale: Removing scale ambiguity isolates the placement routine so it can be rehearsed deliberately; the cited misconception work notes numberless/single-scale protractors reduce these specific errors while the routine is learned.
sourceClaims: Documented protractor difficulties: on a dual-scale protractor pupils struggle with WHICH scale to read (drawing the supplement), and with placing the vertex and baseline correctly; a numberless/single-scale protractor and estimate-first strategies reduce these errors (Exeter 2002 work cited).
learnerActions: Using a numberless or single-scale protractor, practise seating it: centre hole on the vertex dot, zero-line exactly along the existing side, every time.
Measure and draw several given angles, focusing only on placement while the scale-reading ambiguity is removed.
Once placement is automatic, return to a dual-scale protractor and reintroduce the estimate-first scale choice.
activities.intendedInsight: Separating the placement sub-skill from the scale-reading sub-skill lets each become secure before they must be coordinated.

activities.title: Construct a regular polygon by repeating an equal side and an equal turn
feedback: If the pentagon does not close, check whether you turned an inconsistent amount at some corners or drew a side to look right rather than measuring it.
If sides differ in length, re-measure each from the ruler's zero mark rather than judging by eye.
activities.rationale: Connecting side length to a repeated turn gives children a constructive model of regularity and a built-in check (equal sides, equal turns, closure).
sourceClaims: UK Y6 statutory: pupils 'draw 2-D shapes using given dimensions and angles'; the wider programme expects accurate use of a ruler to the nearest millimetre and measuring/drawing angles with a protractor.
learnerActions: Draw a regular pentagon with sides of 4 cm by ruling an equal side, then setting an equal turn at each corner, and repeating.

Use the same angle at every corner: for a regular pentagon each interior angle is 108° (equivalently an exterior turn of 72°, since 360° ÷ 5 = 72°); with a protractor, measure 108° inside the shape from the side just drawn. The side length (4 cm) does not change these angles.
After drawing, check that all five sides are equal in length and all corners turn by the same amount, and that the figure closes back to the start.
activities.intendedInsight: A regular polygon is built from a repeated equal side and an equal turn; keeping both consistent is what makes it regular and makes it close.

activities.title: Knowledge check on scale choice and placement (supporting check)
feedback: If you pick the supplement, re-apply 'bigger or smaller than a square corner?' and choose the number that agrees.
Correctly spotting a misplaced protractor means you know the placement rule; now apply it with real tools on paper.
activities.rationale: A recognition check can surface whether the scale and placement rules are understood, but it cannot by itself elicit or assess actual drawing accuracy; use it alongside, not instead of, hands-on construction.
sourceClaims: Documented protractor difficulties: on a dual-scale protractor pupils struggle with WHICH scale to read (drawing the supplement), and with placing the vertex and baseline correctly; a numberless/single-scale protractor and estimate-first strategies reduce these errors (Exeter 2002 work cited).
learnerActions: Given an angle, state which of the two protractor scale readings is correct and why (estimate against a right angle first).
Spot a misplaced protractor in a picture (centre off the vertex, or zero-line off the side) and say what is wrong.
Estimate an unlabelled angle as bigger or smaller than a right angle before any reading is given.
activities.intendedInsight: The decisions behind a correct construction — scale choice and correct placement — can be reasoned about explicitly, which supports but does not replace actual drawing.

constraints: This is a hands-on motor-and-procedure skill: it must be practised with real ruler-and-protractor construction on paper (as the Y6 programme requires). Recognition-only checks (which scale, spot the misplacement) support reasoning but do not elicit the actual drawing accuracy that is the target skill.
A labelled picture or reference card can display the placement routine but cannot by itself build the placement-and-scale judgement; treat it as a reminder, not the main teacher.

A draggable on-screen ruler and protractor is an optional scaffold for the judgement (scale choice, placement, closure check) and should be paired with real tools so the physical motor skill develops alongside; it is not a substitute for drawing on paper.
Accept an accuracy tolerance of roughly ±2° and ±2 mm for a successful construction at this age.

The estimate-first rule ('bigger or smaller than a right angle?') resolves the supplement ambiguity only when the target angle is not itself close to 90°; for angles near a right angle, placement and careful reading carry more of the load.

A triangle built from a base plus an angle at each of its ends is an angle-side-angle (ASA) construction; a triangle built from two sides and the angle between them is side-angle-side (SAS). Name the construction accurately rather than conflating the two.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original row labelled the base-and-two-angles construction 'SAS-style' in its keyRepresentations; this is incorrect — a base with an angle at each end is an angle-side-angle (ASA) construction. The activity and summary have been corrected to ASA; SAS is retained only to describe the separate two-sides-and-included-angle evidence item.

An optional interactive scaffold was described in the source (protractor snaps/glows when centred, both scale numbers ghost-appear with a 'bigger or smaller than a square corner?' prompt, ruler enforces measuring from zero, green tick when the figure closes). These are retained as illustrative affordances, not mandatory mechanisms.

The source asserted '3D adds nothing' and that a static image 'cannot teach' the skill; these have been softened to scoped limits (planar construction; a picture is a reminder not a teacher) rather than universal claims, since catalog ratings do not establish necessity or comparative efficacy.

The example triangle (base 7 cm, 40° and 65°) and pentagon (4 cm sides) are internally consistent: 40+65+75=180, so the third angle is 75°, a valid closing triangle. No arithmetic errors found in the migrated examples.
Two error patterns in the original row routed to a reteach prerequisite; prerequisite routing is a platform concern and is not reproduced in learner-facing guidance.

probeDeeper: Before you read the protractor — is this angle going to be more or less than 90°? So which of the two numbers can it be?
Your triangle didn't quite close — where do you think the error crept in?
Why did you start measuring from there and not from the very end of the ruler?
For the pentagon, how did you know how far to turn at each corner to keep the sides and angles equal?
assess.correctAnswer: Lays the ruler's zero (not its end) on the start point and rules a 7 cm base; places the protractor centre on each base endpoint with the zero-line along the base, reads the correct scale to mark 40° and 65°, and rules the two rays to meet, producing a closed triangle accurate to about ±2° / ±2 mm; constructs the pentagon with equal 4 cm sides and an equal turn at each corner.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the wrong scale on the dual-scale protractor, drawing the supplement of the intended angle
errorPatterns.nextMove: Install the estimate-first rule: 'is this bigger or smaller than a square corner?' then choose the scale whose number agrees; rehearse on a single-scale/numberless protractor until scale choice is automatic
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Marks 140° where 40° was asked (or 120° for 60°), so the angle drawn is the supplement and the triangle is badly wrong or fails to close

errorPatterns.pattern: Misplaces the protractor — centre off the vertex or the zero-line off the drawn side — so angles are consistently a few degrees out or the ray does not start at the vertex
errorPatterns.nextMove: Explicit 'centre-hole on the dot, zero-line on the line' routine, checked each time; use a numberless protractor to isolate placement from scale-reading
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Each measured/drawn angle is off by a small consistent amount, or the ray begins away from the vertex; the triangle nearly-but-not-quite closes

errorPatterns.pattern: Measures length from the physical end of the ruler rather than the zero mark, adding the end-margin to each side
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reground ruler use: align the zero mark (not the end) with the endpoint, mark, then join; verify a couple of lengths back against the ruler
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Sides come out systematically long by the ruler's end-margin, or lengths are judged by eye rather than measured from zero

responseLevels.gap: Cannot place the protractor or ruler reliably — reads whichever scale, measures from the ruler end — and the figures do not close or match the given dimensions.
responseLevels.full: Constructs the specified figure accurately and repeatably: estimates before reading to pick the right scale, aligns centre-on-vertex and zero-on-line, measures from the ruler's zero, and self-checks that the triangle closes and the polygon's sides and angles are equal.
responseLevels.partial: Draws each element correctly in isolation but with recurring slips — sometimes the wrong scale, or the triangle nearly closes — able to measure but not yet to coordinate the whole construction to the given spec (has the parts but not their relational assembly).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put a ruler and a protractor in front of the child. Say: 'Draw a triangle with a base of 7 cm, an angle of 40° at the left end of the base and an angle of 65° at the right end. Then draw a regular pentagon with sides of 4 cm.' Watch how they place the protractor, which scale they read, where they start the ruler, and whether the triangle closes — do not talk them through it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The finished figure is the evidence: a child with the skill produces a closing, correctly-scaled triangle because they estimated-then-read the right scale and aligned centre-on-vertex, zero-on-line; a child without it draws the supplementary angle (wrong scale) or a non-closing, mis-sized figure. You cannot fake a closing triangle by guessing.

pedagogy.summary: Fluency within 1000 is NOT just 'do columnar faster' — it is the flexible, adaptive choice of the most efficient method for THESE particular numbers (Threlfall; NCETM 'intelligent practice'). The child should have three tools in play — the standard columnar algorithm, mental strategies (compensation, near-doubles, place-value partitioning), and counting up on an empty number line for close subtractions — and pick well. Efficiency and the add/sub inverse relationship (checking) are the goals, not a single rote procedure.
bestPractices: Contrast strategies explicitly: put the same problem up and ask 'clever way vs plod way?' — build adaptive expertise rather than defaulting to the algorithm
Use counting-up on an empty number line for close subtractions (300-298, 401-399) so difference-as-distance is felt
Teach compensation for near-multiples (525+199 = 525+200-1) alongside the algorithm
Always link subtraction to addition for checking (inverse), not re-counting
Reserve the standard columnar algorithm for problems where no shortcut helps (456+287)
keyRepresentations: Place-value columns / base-ten exchange (the algorithm's meaning)
Empty number line (counting up for difference)
Part-whole bar model
Hundred square / place-value chart for +/-10, +/-100 jumps
commonMisconceptions: Reaches for the column algorithm for every problem even when counting up or compensating is far quicker (strategy inflexibility)
Smaller-from-larger subtraction bug — subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in a column regardless of position
Cannot decompose to subtract when a column is zero (borrow-across-zero)
Treats subtraction as unrelated to addition — re-counts to check instead of using the inverse

learn.summary: Fluency within 1000 is adaptive strategy choice, not just faster column arithmetic: pupils match the most efficient method to the particular numbers. The child should hold three tools and pick well — the standard columnar algorithm (for problems where no shortcut helps, e.g. 456+287), mental strategies (compensation 525+199 = 525+200-1, near-doubles, place-value partitioning), and counting up on an empty number line for close subtractions (300-298, 401-399). Subtraction is linked to addition for checking (inverse), not re-counting. Learners also need to handle known systematic subtraction bugs: smaller-from-larger, and borrow/decompose across a zero.

activities.title: Two-track strategy bench: match the method to the numbers
feedback: If the child reaches for columns on 300-298: put the two numbers on an empty number line and ask 'how far apart are they?'; contrast the steps each method took. Build the habit of glancing at the numbers before choosing.
If the child uses the algorithm well on 456+287: affirm that this is exactly where the column method earns its place.
When checking, if the child re-does the subtraction: prompt them to add the answer back using the item's own numbers — for 300-298, does 2 + 298 return 300? — to make the inverse-check routine.
activities.rationale: Running two tracks side by side lets the child feel the cost of a poor method choice and the payoff of a good one; reversing with 456+287 keeps the algorithm valued rather than discarded. A live recomputing bench with a visible timer is one concrete way to make the cost of the choice visible; a paper version (solve both ways, compare, time with a clock) can serve the same purpose.
sourceClaims: The defining standard for fluency within 1000 is strategic, not rote: pupils 'fluently add and subtract within 1000 using strategies and algorithms based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction' — a range of algorithms may be used.

Adaptive expertise — choosing a strategy suited to the specific numbers (e.g. counting up for close subtractions, compensation for near-multiples) — is a distinct, teachable goal beyond executing the standard algorithm.
learnerActions: Meet a problem such as 300-298. Before computing, glance at the numbers and predict which method will be quickest.
Solve it two ways side by side: an empty-number-line track (count up from 298 to 300) and a column-algorithm track (set up and exchange across the zero). Time or step-count both.
Compare: on 300-298 the number line jumps the gap in one hop of 2 while the column track is still exchanging across the zero (and may trip over it).
Now try 456+287 the same way and compare: no obvious shortcut stands out for these numbers, so the column algorithm is a sensible, efficient choice here.

Add a check step using the inverse, with this activity's own numbers: for 300-298, add your answer (2) back to 298 and confirm you reach 300; for 456+287 (=743), subtract one addend from the total to recover the other.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency means matching the method to the numbers, not grinding one algorithm; close numbers favour counting up, near-multiples favour compensation, and messy numbers favour the column algorithm.

activities.title: Sort first, then solve: which method would you choose?
feedback: If a problem is mis-sorted, ask the child to say how far apart the numbers are, or how close one is to a round number, then re-sort.
If the child sorts correctly but reverts to one method when computing, point back to their own sort and ask them to honour the chosen method.
For 502-5, if the child tries to count up the whole gap or reaches for column borrowing, point out that only 5 is subtracted, so counting back 5 or compensating is far quicker.
activities.rationale: A categorise-then-compute task drills adaptive selection explicitly and makes the selection step visible. Sorting and justifying is recognition-plus-reasoning; it checks classification but does not itself elicit the computation, so pair it with actual calculation so selection is tested against real arithmetic.
sourceClaims: Adaptive expertise — choosing a strategy suited to the specific numbers (e.g. counting up for close subtractions, compensation for near-multiples) — is a distinct, teachable goal beyond executing the standard algorithm.
learnerActions: Sort 8 problems into three piles: 'count up' (close numbers), 'compensate' (near a multiple like +199), and 'column' (no shortcut helps).
For each problem, state in one phrase why it belongs in that pile ('these two are close, so I count up').
Then compute the answers.

Transfer: given a new pair such as 502-5, decide which method is quickest — note the two numbers are far apart but only 5 is taken away, so counting back 5 or compensation beats a column borrow across the zero.
activities.intendedInsight: Strategy selection is a distinct, assessable skill: you can name and justify why a particular method fits particular numbers before doing any arithmetic.

activities.title: Fix the subtraction bugs: smaller-from-larger and borrow across zero
feedback: If the child writes 265 (smaller digit taken from larger in the ones and tens): return to concrete base-ten exchange on the failing columns, showing that 8 cannot be taken from 3 and 6 cannot be taken from 0 without exchanging, and that the hundreds must then drop from 7 to 6.
If the child stalls at the zero, writes 0 in the tens, or borrows incorrectly: model exchanging one hundred into ten tens first (703 = 6 hundreds, 9 tens, 13 ones) with blocks before the digits.
Finish with the inverse check: add the answer (135) back to 568 and confirm you reach 703.
activities.rationale: Smaller-from-larger and borrow-from-zero are documented, stable subtraction bugs, so targeted concrete exchange work on the exact failing column addresses a known error source rather than a one-off slip.
sourceClaims: Smaller-from-larger and borrow-from-zero are systematic, documented, STABLE subtraction bugs: borrow-from-zero (change a 0 to 9 but fail to keep borrowing left) is the single most common bug in Brown & Burton's data (107/1325); smaller-from-larger was used by 54; ~40% of students showed consistently buggy behaviour.
learnerActions: Work 703-568 with base-ten materials (or place-value chips) before writing digits: exchange one hundred into ten tens, then one ten into ten ones, so 703 becomes 6 hundreds, 9 tens, 13 ones.
Check each column: confirm you cannot take 8 from 3 in the ones without exchanging — you do not simply subtract the smaller digit from the larger.
Complete the written algorithm, keeping the borrow moving left across the zero (the answer is 135).

Compare your answer with a wrong answer like 265 and explain which columns were mishandled (265 comes from taking the smaller digit from the larger in each column: the ones (3 take 8) and tens (0 take 6) skipped their exchanges, so the hundreds was never reduced from 7 to 6; the ones digit 5 matches the correct answer only by coincidence).
activities.intendedInsight: Column subtraction requires exchanging by place value; a top digit smaller than the bottom digit means you must decompose, and when a zero column must give to the column on its right (as in 703-568), it first needs an exchange from the hundreds — not leaving the column as 0.

activities.title: Strategy-menu reference and 'convince me' justification
feedback: If the child cannot justify a choice beyond 'that's how you do it', ask them to compare the number of steps their method took with an alternative.
Use the menu wall as a reference, not a crutch: encourage the child to predict the pick before consulting it.
activities.rationale: A static menu offers a useful reference but cannot by itself let the child experience the cost of a choice; a justification exchange surfaces reasoning. Both support, rather than replace, actually doing and comparing the methods in the bench activity.
sourceClaims: Adaptive expertise — choosing a strategy suited to the specific numbers (e.g. counting up for close subtractions, compensation for near-multiples) — is a distinct, teachable goal beyond executing the standard algorithm.
learnerActions: Build or use a strategy-menu wall with three worked examples, one per method (count up, compensate, column), each labelled with when it is the smart pick.
After solving a problem, explain to a partner or coach why your chosen method was quickest for those numbers.
Respond to a challenge ('convince me your method was quickest') by pointing to the number features that made your choice efficient.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to articulate why a method fits particular numbers consolidates adaptive expertise and exposes whether a choice was reasoned or habitual.

constraints: The goal is efficient, adaptive method choice plus the add/sub inverse for checking — not speed at a single rote procedure.
A static strategy-menu poster is a reference only: it cannot let the child experience the choice or feel its cost, so pair it with activities that involve actually doing and comparing methods.
A sort/categorise step checks selection reasoning but should be paired with real computation so pupils also execute the chosen method correctly.
A justification dialogue surfaces reasoning but does not replace actually doing and comparing the methods; keep real computation central.
Subtraction checking should use addition (inverse), not re-counting the subtraction, and each check should use the numbers of the problem actually solved.
Reserve the standard column algorithm for problems where no shortcut helps (e.g. 456+287); do not treat it as the default for every problem.
Base-ten cutouts/blocks are concrete approximations of place-value structure; use the exchange physically before the written digits for borrow-across-zero.
Computation within 1000 is planar place-value work; the proposed number-line and column representations are sufficient here — a third spatial dimension is not required for this topic.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched this session. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source marks the Threlfall/NCETM 'intelligent practice' claim as not fetched this session (verified:false); treat the adaptive-expertise principle as plausibly supported but unverified here.

Worked arithmetic check: 300-298 = 2 (one hop of 2 by counting up); 525+199 = 525+200-1 = 724; 456+287 = 743; 703-568 = 135 (703 = 6 hundreds, 9 tens, 13 ones; the buggy 265 arises from smaller-from-larger/flip errors). These arithmetic facts were verified during this rewrite; no source effectiveness claims were verified.

The original 'only a live 2D bench can let the child pick a method and FEEL the cost', 'dialogue cannot provide', and '3D adds nothing' claims were softened to narrowly-scoped affordances with limits; the comparative-necessity wording is not established by the cited sources. Stopwatch timing is likewise one concrete scaffold, not a requirement.

502-5 is used as a transfer item; it is a 'small takeaway from a round-ish number' where counting back or compensation is quick, NOT a close-numbers/difference-as-distance case. The original gap note's 'these are close' phrasing is loose; confirm the intended discriminating feature when authoring.

Inverse checks are scoped to each activity's own problem numbers: the 300-298/456+287 bench uses its own numbers, and the 703-568 inverse check (135+568=703) sits in the subtraction-bug activity where that problem is actually worked.

probeDeeper: Which of those four was quickest for you, and why?
Could you have done 456 + 287 a cleverer way, or was the column method best there?
What about 502 - 5 - column method, or something quicker?
Show me how you'd check the 703 - 568 answer without redoing the subtraction.
assess.correctAnswer: Flexible and fluent: solves 300-298 by counting up / difference of 2 (not columnar borrowing), adds 199 by 525+200-1 (compensation), uses the columnar algorithm for 456+287 where no shortcut helps, and handles 703-568 with a correct exchange across the zero. Justifies each choice by the numbers ('these two are close, so I counted up').

errorPatterns.pattern: Sets up 300-298 in columns and grinds a borrow-across-zero instead of noticing the two numbers are almost the same ('you just do the column method for take-aways')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Put the two numbers on an empty number line and ask 'how far apart are they?'; contrast the time each method took. Build the habit of glancing at the numbers before choosing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reaches for the algorithm on 300-298 and 525+199 and never counts up or compensates, even when prompted to find a quicker way

errorPatterns.pattern: In 703-568 subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in each column regardless of which is on top (smaller-from-larger bug)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to concrete base-ten exchange on the specific failing column; show that you cannot take 8 from 3 without exchanging.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes an answer like 265; the tens/ones are 'flipped' where the top digit is smaller

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot decompose to subtract in 703-568 because the tens column is 0 (borrow-across-zero)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model exchanging one hundred into ten tens first (703 = 6 hundreds, 9 tens, 13 ones) with base-ten blocks before the digits.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Stalls at the zero, writes 0 in the tens, or borrows incorrectly

errorPatterns.pattern: Having answered, re-counts the subtraction to check instead of adding the answer back (inverse not linked)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, do not reteach: 'add your answer to 568 - do you get back to 703?' Make the inverse-check routine.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked to check, redoes the same subtraction rather than using addition

responseLevels.gap: Reaches for one method for all four (usually columnar), misapplies it on the near-numbers, and cannot say why that method was chosen.
responseLevels.full: Selects an efficient method per item and justifies it by the numbers, and checks via the inverse; transfers the 'are these close?' judgement to a new pair such as 502-5.
responseLevels.partial: Computes all four correctly but uses the same method throughout - can name a method but does not match it to the numbers, and cannot transfer the 'these are close' idea to 502-5.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put these four in front of the child one at a time and say: 'Solve each one however you think is best, and tell me why you chose that way.' 300 - 298; 525 + 199; 456 + 287; 703 - 568. Watch WHICH method they reach for each time and listen to the 'why'.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 300-298 and 525+199 punish a child who owns only one tool: a rote columnar solver laboriously borrows across the zero on 300-298 (and often errs), whereas a flexible child sees the difference is just 2. 456+287 conversely rewards the algorithm. The mix separates true fluency (right method for these numbers) from mere procedure.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 6–7 (UK Y2, US Grade 2–3). Recall and use multiplication AND division facts for the 2, 5 and 10 tables — the first fact set, built on the 2s/5s/10s skip counting.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2 'recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 2, 5 and 10 multiplication tables, including recognising odd and even numbers'; non-statutory 'connect the 2, 5 and 10 tables to each other' and 'use commutativity and inverse relations (4×5=20 and 20÷5=4)'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.OA.7 'fluently multiply and divide within 100 … by end of Grade 3 know from memory all products of two one-digit numbers' (the 2s/5s/10s are the earliest-secured, from 2.OA skip counting).
• Operational details: derive rather than only chant — 10s from place value, 5s as half of the 10s, 2s as doubles. Crucially include the DIVISION facts and out-of-sequence recall (not just reciting). Use commutativity and the inverse to get four facts from one (2×5, 5×2, 10÷5, 10÷2).
• Checkpoint: quick recall + inverse. Tier A (6): recall 2s and 10s facts in order. Tier B (6–7): recall any 2, 5 or 10 fact out of order and its division fact. Tier C (7): explain that the 5s are half the 10s and state the full fact family for 5×4.
bestPractices: Build the three tables on structure, not rote: 10s from place value, 5s as exactly half of the matching 10s fact, 2s as doubles — so a forgotten fact can be re-derived.
Teach the DIVISION facts alongside the multiplication facts as fact families (5×4=20 → 20÷5=4, 20÷4=5), and use commutativity so learning one fact delivers its partner — halving the memory load.
Rehearse out of sequence and in mixed contexts once the count is secure, so recall is genuine fluency rather than a chant that only works from the start.
Exploit hundred-square and multiplication-square patterns (5s and 10s in columns, 2s in even columns) to make the facts a connected web — building on the skip-counting patterns already learned.
Connect the three tables to each other and to odd/even (the 2s table = even numbers) so the fact sets reinforce rather than compete.
keyRepresentations: Multiplication square / times-table grid (patterns and commutative symmetry)
Hundred square with 2s, 5s, 10s shaded (columns/even-number pattern)
Arrays for each fact (and the fact family)
Number line with equal jumps (bridge from skip counting)
commonMisconceptions: Being able to chant the table from the start but not recall a fact out of order — mistaking the chant for fluency.
Knowing the multiplication fact but not the corresponding division fact.
Treating 5×4 and 4×5 as separate facts to memorise (not using commutativity).
Confusing 'the 2 times table' with 'counting in 2s starting anywhere' — or muddling doubling with adding 2.
Not connecting 5s to 10s (missing that 5s are half the 10s), so each table is learned in isolation.

learn.summary: For ages 6–7 (UK Y2, US Grade 2–3): recall and USE multiplication AND division facts for the 2, 5 and 10 tables, out of order and as fact families, built on structure rather than rote chanting. Derive 10s from place value, 5s as exactly half of the matching 10s fact, and 2s as doubles, so a forgotten fact can be re-derived. Teach division facts alongside multiplication (5×4=20 → 20÷5=4, 20÷4=5) and use commutativity so one learned fact delivers its partner. Connect the three tables to each other and to odd/even (the 2s = even numbers).

activities.title: Shade the table: derive the 5s from the 10s
feedback: If a child treats the 5s and 10s as unrelated, pair the two shaded columns side by side and ask 'what is half of 40?' to reveal 5×4 = 20.
If a child doubles wrongly or adds 2 instead, show 2×6 as two groups of 6 (or 6 doubled = 12), distinct from 6+2 = 8.
Reinforce the end-digit pattern as a self-check: 5s end in 5 or 0; 10s end in 0.
Optional live display: when the learner taps a grid cell, pop out the array for that fact and write its whole fact family so the derivation stays visible.
activities.rationale: Building facts on structure (place value, halving, doubling) lets a learner re-derive a forgotten fact and connects the tables rather than learning each in isolation; a visible, manipulable grid makes the 'half the 10s' relationship directly observable, and the number line links it to the skip-counting already secured.
sourceClaims: Y2: recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 2, 5 and 10 tables, including odd/even; connect the tables and use commutativity and inverse relations.
Tables should be derived from structure (10s from place value, 5s as half of 10s, 2s as doubles) and learned with their division facts as fact families, not by rote chanting alone.
learnerActions: On a multiplication grid or hundred square, shade the 10s column (10, 20, 30, 40, 50…) and read them as place-value facts: 10×3 = 3 tens = 30.

Beside it, shade the 5s (5, 10, 15, 20, 25…) and line each 5s value up against the matching 10s value. On a multiplication grid this is the 5s column; on a hundred square the 5s fill two columns, the numbers ending in 5 and those ending in 0.
Notice and say aloud that each 5s value sits exactly halfway to the 10s value: 5×4 = 20 is half of 10×4 = 40.

Shade the 2s (on a multiplication grid, the 2s column; on a hundred square, every column ending in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8) and state that the answers in the 2s table are even numbers, and that 2×n is the double of n.
Pick one fact per table and write it as a derivation: '10×6 = 60, so 5×6 = 30 (half), and 2×6 = 12 (double of 6).'
Optionally, show the same facts as equal jumps on a number line (counting in 2s, 5s or 10s) to connect the shaded columns back to the skip-counting the child already knows.
activities.intendedInsight: The 2, 5 and 10 tables are a connected web, not three separate lists: 10s come from place value, 5s are half the matching 10s, 2s are doubles — so any fact can be rebuilt if forgotten.

activities.title: Four facts from one array: multiplication and its inverse
feedback: If division lags, return to the SAME array and count the rows/columns to show 20÷5 and 20÷4 directly.
If a child treats 5×4 and 4×5 as two separate things to memorise, rotate the array a quarter turn to show it is the same 20.
Use a fact-family triangle (20 at top, 5 and 4 below) so the child can cover any one number and state it from the other two.
activities.rationale: Fact families on a single array link multiplication with its inverse division and exploit commutativity, directly targeting the common gap where multiplication is fluent but division or the commutative partner is not.
sourceClaims: Tables should be derived from structure (10s from place value, 5s as half of 10s, 2s as doubles) and learned with their division facts as fact families, not by rote chanting alone.
Y2: recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 2, 5 and 10 tables, including odd/even; connect the tables and use commutativity and inverse relations.
learnerActions: Build or look at an array for one fact, e.g. 5 rows of 4 (= 20).
Write the two multiplication facts the array shows using commutativity: 5×4 = 20 and 4×5 = 20.
Write the two division facts from the same array: 20÷5 = 4 and 20÷4 = 5.
Repeat for several 2/5/10 facts, each time producing the full fact family of four facts from one picture.
Say why 20÷5 = 4 'has to be' true given 5×4 = 20 (sharing 20 into 5 equal rows gives 4).
activities.intendedInsight: One array holds a whole fact family; using commutativity and the inverse means learning one fact delivers its partners, so division facts are not extra memorising.

activities.title: Mixed quick-recall, out of order, with a derive-it fallback
feedback: Correct answers for the prompts above: 5×3 = 15, 10×4 = 40, 2×7 = 14; 20÷5 = 4, 30÷10 = 3, 14÷2 = 7.
On a miss, respond with the array AND the derive-it prompt (find the ten fact and halve it; double for twos), not just the right number.

For a near-miss count error such as 5×3 answered as 20, note that 20 still ends in 0, so the basic end-digit check (5s end in 5 or 0) will not catch it. Use the derive-it route instead (10×3 = 30, half of 30 is 15), or the sharper pattern that 5 times an odd number ends in 5. Then re-count one step at a time to check. The correct answer is 15.
Do NOT drill under heavy time pressure if a child reconstructs by skip-counting; keep skip-counting as a backup while spaced, meaningful retrieval moves facts into memory.
Optional quick-fire mode: present facts in random order with instant array feedback on misses.
activities.rationale: Out-of-order mixed × and ÷ practice distinguishes true recall from skip-count reconstruction and exposes lagging division facts; pairing every miss with a structural derivation keeps fluency resting on recoverable structure.
sourceClaims: Y2: recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 2, 5 and 10 tables, including odd/even; connect the tables and use commutativity and inverse relations.
learnerActions: Once skip-counting is secure, answer facts asked OUT of sequence, mixing × and ÷: 5×3, 10×4, 2×7, then 20÷5, 30÷10, 14÷2.
For each, notice whether you knew it instantly or had to count, and say which.
On any fact you did not just know, use the derive-it route aloud: for a 5s fact, find the matching 10s fact and halve it; for a 2s fact, double the number.
Keep skip-counting available as a backup check, not as the main method.
activities.intendedInsight: Genuine fluency is recall out of order (including division), not a chant that only works from the start; when memory fails, a structured derivation recovers the fact.

activities.title: Trade-a-fact oral rehearsal
feedback: Keep the derive-it prompt handy so a miss ends with a reconstructed fact, not just the answer.
If division is slower than multiplication, pair every × question with its ÷ inverse so the family is rehearsed together.
activities.rationale: Oral rehearsal adds low-stakes retrieval practice and reinforces fact families; a spoken partner does not itself display the shaded columns or arrays that make the halving relationship visible, so it works best alongside the grid and array tasks rather than replacing them.
sourceClaims: Tables should be derived from structure (10s from place value, 5s as half of 10s, 2s as doubles) and learned with their division facts as fact families, not by rote chanting alone.
learnerActions: Take turns with a partner: one asks a 2, 5 or 10 fact (× or ÷), the other answers, then they swap.
On a miss, the asker prompts the derivation: 'What's the ten fact? Now halve it' for 5s, or 'double it' for 2s.
Include inverse pairs deliberately, e.g. ask 5×6 then immediately 30÷5.
activities.intendedInsight: Spoken back-and-forth rehearsal gives extra meaningful retrieval and keeps the derive-it route verbal and quick.

constraints: Secure skip-counting in 2s, 5s and 10s is a prerequisite; if a child can only reconstruct every fact by counting from the start, strengthen that skip-counting first rather than drilling under time pressure.
Answer-giving/recall checks measure whether facts are fluent but do not by themselves build the structure; use them alongside the deriving and fact-family tasks, not in place of them.
A fixed poster or static grid is a good pattern reference but cannot run out-of-order recall practice or generate arrays on demand; combine it with spoken or interactive mixed-fact practice.
Out-of-order, mixed × and ÷ recall is the target; a chant that only works from the beginning of the table is not yet fluency.
Keep the halving relationship explicit: 5×n is half of 10×n (e.g. 5×4 = 20 is half of 40), and 2×n is the double of n, distinct from n+2.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic in prompts/feedback: 5×3 = 15, 10×4 = 40, 2×7 = 14, 20÷5 = 4, 30÷10 = 3, 14÷2 = 7, 5×4 = 20, 5×6 = 30, 2×6 = 12, 10×6 = 60 — all verified correct. The near-miss example '5×3 = 20' is presented explicitly as an error to correct (correct value 15), never as a valid option.
The source claim that '5s are half the 10s' and '2s are doubles' is mathematically sound and retained as the derivation backbone.

CCSS 3.OA.7 (verified:false) states the fluency objective but was not cited as method-level support for out-of-order practice; its comparative/efficacy weight should not be overstated. NCETM mastery guidance is also marked unverified in the row.

Original row asserted that a talking partner 'adds little' and that 3D 'adds no conceptual value'; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the available sources and have been removed or recast as narrow affordance-and-limit statements.
The number-line-with-equal-jumps representation from the original row was restored as an optional action in the shading activity to preserve the stated bridge from skip counting.

probeDeeper: How did you work out 5 × 3 — did you know it or count it?
What's 5 × 6? How could 5 × 5 help?
Which of these tables feels easiest? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: 15, 40, 14; 4, 3, 7 — answered from memory (or by very rapid skip-count), with the division facts as secure as the multiplication.

errorPatterns.pattern: reconstructs every fact by skip-counting — to answer 5 × 3 counts '5, 10, 15' rather than recalling; accurate but slow
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT drill under time pressure — recall builds from repeated meaningful use; keep skip-counting as a backup while spaced retrieval moves facts into memory
errorPatterns.revealedBy: audible or finger counting-up before each answer

errorPatterns.pattern: division facts lag multiplication — fluent on 5 × 3 but stalls on 20 ÷ 5; the ÷ fact isn't linked to the same fact family
errorPatterns.nextMove: teach fact families on one array/triangle — 5 × 4 = 20, so 20 ÷ 5 = 4 and 20 ÷ 4 = 5
errorPatterns.revealedBy: quick on ×, slow or guessing on ÷

errorPatterns.pattern: near-miss count error — says 5 × 3 = 20 (miscounts a step) or muddles the 5s and 10s
errorPatterns.nextMove: anchor the pattern (5s end in 5 or 0; 10s end in 0) and re-count to self-check
errorPatterns.revealedBy: an answer one step off, or a 5s/10s mix-up

responseLevels.gap: Cannot produce the facts, or only by counting from the start each time with errors.
responseLevels.full: Answers 2/5/10 multiplication and division facts from memory (or near-instantly), using fact families to link × and ÷.
responseLevels.partial: Recalls 2s/5s/10s multiplication but reconstructs by skip-counting, or the division facts lag behind.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I'll ask some facts quickly — answer as fast as you can, and I'll watch whether you count to get there. 5 × 3? 10 × 4? 2 × 7? Now the division ones: 20 ÷ 5? 30 ÷ 10? 14 ÷ 2? (Watch whether recall is instant or reconstructed by skip-counting, and whether the division facts are as secure as the multiplication.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Asking multiplication and its inverse division side by side, and watching HOW the child answers, separates true recall from skip-count reconstruction, and reveals the common gap where multiplication is fluent but the matching division facts are not.

sources.claim: Y2: recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 2, 5 and 10 tables, including odd/even; connect the tables and use commutativity and inverse relations.

sources.claim: 3.OA.7 fluently multiply and divide within 100 and know from memory all products of two one-digit numbers by end of Grade 3.

sources.claim: Tables should be derived from structure (10s from place value, 5s as half of 10s, 2s as doubles) and learned with their division facts as fact families, not by rote chanting alone.

pedagogy.summary: At 10-11 this is the capstone of using structure: reading algebraic form (3(n+5) = 3n+15) via the distributive property, treating a shape hierarchy as a deduction engine (all rectangles are parallelograms, so parallelogram properties transfer), and moving fluently across 1/8 = 0.125 = 12.5% and ratio structures to solve proportions efficiently. The child should see a complex expression as a single object composed of parts — CCSS MP7's own example is seeing x²+9x+14 as (x+2)(x+7) via 14=2×7 and 9=2+7, and reading 5−3(x−y)² as '5 minus a non-negative amount'. The teaching aim is deliberate structural reading before manipulation, backed by the area model for distribution.
bestPractices: Ground 3(n+5) = 3n+15 in an area rectangle n+5 wide and 3 tall, split into 3n and 15, so distribution over BOTH terms is seen not memorised
Use the shape hierarchy as a reasoning tool: 'this is a rectangle, therefore it is a parallelogram, therefore…' to deduce unknown properties without measuring
Keep FDP and ratio equivalences fluent (1/8=0.125=12.5%; 3:5 as 3/8 and 5/8 of the whole) so the child picks the form that makes the comparison trivial
Prompt 'what is this expression made of? can you see it as one object?' to build structural reading before symbolic manipulation
keyRepresentations: Area / grid model for the distributive law with a letter (n+5 by 3)
Shape hierarchy tree (quadrilateral → parallelogram → rectangle/rhombus → square)
FDP equivalence bar and ratio/double number line
Algebra tiles for expressions as composed objects
commonMisconceptions: Distributes over the first term only: 3(n+5) = 3n+5 (multiplier not applied to the second term)
Treats the letter as an object or label ('n is a name') rather than a number, or conjoins 3n+5 into 8n
Denies category links in the hierarchy (a rectangle is 'not' a parallelogram), blocking property transfer
Sticks to one FDP/ratio form and converts laboriously instead of choosing the efficient equivalent

learn.summary: For ages 10-11, the aim is deliberate structural reading before manipulation: seeing a complex expression as a single object made of parts, grounding the distributive law 3(n+5)=3n+15 in an area model, using the 2-D shape hierarchy as a deduction engine (all rectangles are parallelograms, so parallelogram properties transfer), and moving fluently among fraction/decimal/percentage and ratio forms (1/8=0.125=12.5%) to make comparisons trivial. The activities span a hands-on area-model build, a shape-hierarchy reasoning task, flexible FDP/ratio comparison, and a diagnostic probe requiring justification.

activities.title: Build the distributive law with a lettered area rectangle
feedback: If the learner writes 3n+5: point to the empty 3×5 region of the rectangle that their answer ignores, and ask what area it represents.
If they accept 3n+5 as plausible, have them substitute n=2: 3n+5 gives 11 but 3×(2+5) gives 21, so the forms disagree.

To probe generality, ask whether it still holds for a fraction such as n=1/2; another matching value is consistent with the rule but does not prove it, while the area split (3 lots of n plus 3 lots of 5 for any width n) shows why it holds for every n.
If correct, ask them to describe the rectangle in words: '3 lots of (n+5) is 3 lots of n plus 3 lots of 5.'
activities.rationale: An area model that the learner partitions makes distribution over both terms visible and lets the classic 3n+5 error produce a concrete missing block, supporting structural reading backed by a representation that reveals structure.
sourceClaims: Older students using structure see an expression as composed of parts and as a single object, e.g. x²+9x+14 via 14=2×7 and 9=2+7, and read 5−3(x−y)² as 5 minus a non-negative amount
Pupils should recognise and use mathematical structure, including reading expressions as descriptions of relationships, and use representations that reveal structure
learnerActions: Draw or display a rectangle that is 3 tall and (n+5) wide.
Split the width into an n-part and a 5-part, making two strips: a 3-by-n strip and a 3-by-5 strip.
Label the strips 3n and 15 (because 3×5=15) and write the whole area as 3(n+5)=3n+15.
Deliberately try the tempting wrong answer 3n+5 by multiplying only the n-strip, then look for what area is left unaccounted for.
Identify the missing 3×5 block as the reason 3n+5 is wrong, and state why the 3 must act on BOTH terms.
Check with a number: let n=2, so 3×(2+5)=21, 3n+15=21, but 3n+5=11.
activities.intendedInsight: Distribution multiplies every term inside the bracket, not just the first; the area of the whole rectangle equals the sum of the two strips, so 3(n+5)=3n+15 is built, not memorised.

activities.title: Use the shape hierarchy as a deduction engine
feedback: If the learner denies a link ('a rectangle is not a parallelogram'), place the rectangle inside the parallelogram set and ask which part of the parallelogram definition it fails — it fails none.
If they can state a link but not use it, prompt: 'opposite sides of a parallelogram are parallel; is a rectangle a parallelogram? so what about its opposite sides?'
Reward chained reasoning: 'square → rectangle → parallelogram' means all parallelogram AND rectangle properties apply to the square.
activities.rationale: Treating the hierarchy as a reasoning tool turns classification into deduction, letting learners transfer properties and justify facts structurally instead of measuring; the hierarchy diagram is a representation that reveals this structure.
sourceClaims: Pupils should recognise and use mathematical structure, including reading expressions as descriptions of relationships, and use representations that reveal structure
learnerActions: Draw or arrange a hierarchy: quadrilateral → parallelogram → rectangle/rhombus → square.
Place a rectangle inside the parallelogram set and state 'this is a rectangle, therefore it is a parallelogram.'
List the parallelogram properties the rectangle must inherit (e.g. opposite sides parallel and equal) WITHOUT measuring.
Extend the chain: a square is a rectangle and a rectangle is a parallelogram — say what that lets you conclude about a square's sides and angles.
Use an inherited property to deduce a missing angle or side fact in a given rectangle.
activities.intendedInsight: Category membership lets properties transfer down the hierarchy, so you can deduce facts by reasoning about what a shape IS rather than by measuring each case.

activities.title: Choose the efficient fraction-decimal-percentage or ratio form
feedback: If the learner converts laboriously in one fixed direction, ask which single conversion would have made the comparison immediate.
For 1/8 vs 12% of the same amount: converting 1/8 to 12.5% allows a direct percentage comparison showing 12.5% > 12%, so 1/8 is the larger.
If a ratio is treated as two separate unrelated numbers, prompt them to find the whole (3+5=8) so each part becomes a fraction of the whole (3/8 and 5/8).
activities.rationale: Flexible FDP and ratio equivalence lets learners pick the representation that makes a comparison trivial, reinforcing structural choice over rote conversion; equivalence representations reveal the shared quantity.
sourceClaims: Pupils should recognise and use mathematical structure, including reading expressions as descriptions of relationships, and use representations that reveal structure
learnerActions: Record the equivalences 1/8=0.125=12.5% and explain how each is obtained from the others.
Given a comparison such as 'which is larger, 1/8 or 12% of the same amount?', decide which form (1/8, 0.125, or 12.5%) makes the comparison easiest and say why.
Rewrite a ratio such as 3:5 as fractions of the whole (3/8 and 5/8) and use that to solve a proportion.
Solve a short proportion problem by first choosing the most convenient form, then justify the choice.
activities.intendedInsight: The same quantity has several equivalent forms; fluently switching to the form that makes a comparison or calculation trivial is itself a structural skill.

activities.title: Diagnose and justify: is 3(n+5)=3n+5?
feedback: Full reasoning: rejects 3n+5, gives 3n+15 justified by the area split AND a numerical check, and reads the expression as a composed object unprompted.
Partial: corrects to 3n+15 when prompted but justifies only by a remembered rule — push for an area picture or a substitution check.

Gap: accepts 3n+5, or conjoins 3n+5 into 8n — return to the area rectangle to expose the missing 3×5, then substitute a value to show the forms disagree (at n=2, 3n+5 gives 11, 3n+15 gives 21, and 8n gives 16).
If the learner treats n as a label ('n stands for an apple'), substitute several values to show n is a number that varies, and that 3n and 5 are unlike terms that cannot be combined.
activities.rationale: An open probe requiring both a corrected answer and a justification (picture plus substitution) discriminates structural understanding from a rote rule and surfaces the specific distribute-over-first-term and conjoining errors.
sourceClaims: Older students using structure see an expression as composed of parts and as a single object, e.g. x²+9x+14 via 14=2×7 and 9=2+7, and read 5−3(x−y)² as 5 minus a non-negative amount
learnerActions: Consider: 'A friend writes 3 × (n + 5) = 3n + 5. Is that right? If not, what should it be?'
Decide whether the statement is correct and give the corrected form if not.
Convince the friend using a picture (the area rectangle splitting into 3n and 15) AND an example (substitute a value for n).
Substitute n=2 to check: 3×7=21 matches 3n+15=21, not 3n+5=11.
Test with a fraction such as n=1/2 to see that 3(n+5)=3n+15 also holds there, then use the area picture to explain why it holds for every n, since examples alone cannot prove a general rule.
activities.intendedInsight: A correct thinker sees the 3 must act on both terms and can justify 3(n+5)=3n+15 in general with the area model; substitution is decisive for rejecting 3n+5, because one counterexample is enough to disprove it, and in fact 3n+5 and 3n+15 differ by 10 for every value of n.

constraints: A multiple-choice or true/false check using the 3(n+5)=3n+5 wrong-answer option and hierarchy items can surface and check classification errors, but a correct selection can mask shaky reasoning; always pair it with a 'why' justification step, since recognition alone does not elicit the learner's own construction or explanation.

A tap-to-reveal poster or pre-built annotated split is a reference scaffold only: it does not let the learner produce the wrong 3n+5 split and see the missing block, so it should supplement, not replace, learner-constructed partitioning.

Dialogue alone provides no written symbols or diagram for the learner to partition; structural reading of expressions is better supported when the symbols and a structure-revealing representation (such as the area model) are visible to act on — an affordance observation, not a claim that dialogue can never contribute.

The optional interactive version (a lettered area-model splitter where dragging a divider cleaves the rectangle into a labelled 3n strip and a 3×5 strip, plus a linked hierarchy tree that highlights inherited properties on selection) is one proposed way that may make the mechanism concrete (efficacy untested), not a required medium; paper rectangles and a drawn hierarchy can achieve the same reasoning.

Any physical rectangles or cut shapes used are representations of the ideal mathematical region or figure, not the figure itself; the reasoning concerns the mathematical shape represented, and physical thickness is not a criterion in this 2-D work.
Keep n explicitly as a number that varies, not as an object or label, so unlike terms (3n and 5) are not conjoined.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The two cited sources (CCSS MP7; EEF KS2-3 maths) support the general principle of reading expressions structurally and using structure-revealing representations; they do not establish the comparative efficacy or necessity of any specific activity or medium. Their attachment to the shape-hierarchy and FDP/ratio activities is general-principle support only (via 'recognise and use mathematical structure' and 'use representations that reveal structure'), not activity-specific or topic-specific evidence.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 3×(2+5)=21; 3n+15 at n=2 = 6+15=21 (match); 3n+5 at n=2 = 6+5=11; 8n at n=2 = 16 (both correct disagreements); 3×5=15; 1/8=0.125=12.5% (so 1/8 > 12%); 3:5 gives parts 3/8 and 5/8 of a whole (sum 8). All consistent as used.

The original's claim that '3D adds load, not insight' for this topic has been reduced to a scoped observation: 2-D area and hierarchy representations are the natural fit and a flat area model suffices; this is not asserted as a universal law about 3-D representations.
The fraction comparison 1/8 vs 12% is scoped to 'of the same amount'; as numbers these remain directly comparable, and no denominator 'rule-flipping' language is used.

probeDeeper: Ask 'check your answer by letting n = 2 — does 3(n+5) equal 3n+15 or 3n+5?' to see whether the child uses substitution as a structural check
Counterexample tuned to this topic: 'does 3(n+5) = 3n+15 still hold if n is a fraction, like 1/2? test it' to probe whether the distributive structure is general, not number-specific
Ask 'a square is a rectangle and a rectangle is a parallelogram — what does that let you say about a square's sides without measuring?' to test chained property inheritance
Ask 'to compare 1/8 and 12% of the same amount, which form makes it easiest — 1/8, 0.125 or 12.5%? why?' to probe flexible FDP structure
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child rejecting 3n+5 and giving 3n+15 with a structural justification: the 3 multiplies BOTH the n and the 5 (area rectangle 3 by n+5 splits into 3n and 15), and/or a numerical check (n=2: 3×7=21, and 3n+15=21 while 3n+5=11).

errorPatterns.pattern: Distributes the multiplier over the first term only: 3(n+5) = 3n+5, leaving the 5 un-multiplied
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the area rectangle so the un-multiplied 3×5 block is visible; confirm with a numerical substitution that 3n+5 gives the wrong total
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child endorses 3n+5, or writes it themselves, and cannot see the missing 3×5

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the letter as an object/label or conjoins terms (3n+5 collapsed to 8n), because n is not held as a number
errorPatterns.nextMove: Substitute several values for n to show 3n+5 and 8n disagree; name n as a number that varies, and 3n and 5 as unlike terms
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child combines unlike terms or talks about n as a thing ('n stands for an apple') rather than a quantity

errorPatterns.pattern: Denies a hierarchy link (a rectangle is 'not' a parallelogram), blocking property transfer used to deduce angle/side facts
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the hierarchy tree to place the rectangle inside the parallelogram set; reason that it inherits parallel opposite sides
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked 'is a rectangle a parallelogram? so are its opposite sides parallel?' the child refuses the category link

responseLevels.gap: Accepts 3(n+5)=3n+5 or conjoins terms, denies hierarchy links, and converts FDP forms rigidly; no structural reading of the expression
responseLevels.full: Rejects 3n+5, gives 3n+15 justified by area AND a numerical check, chains hierarchy properties to deduce unknowns, and picks efficient FDP/ratio forms — reading each expression as a composed object unprompted
responseLevels.partial: Corrects to 3n+15 or states a hierarchy/FDP fact when prompted, but justifies by a remembered rule rather than the area model or a substitution check, and doesn't transfer

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A friend writes 3 × (n + 5) = 3n + 5. Is that right? If not, what should it be, and how would you convince your friend using a picture or an example?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child reasoning correctly sees the 3 must act on both terms and can prove it by area or by substituting a number; a child reasoning incorrectly accepts 3n+5 (distributes over the first term only) or cannot justify beyond a rule. Substituting a value is decisive — 3n+5 and 3n+15 disagree for every n, so a correct thinker's check exposes the error while a rote one has no check.
