pedagogy.summary: These word problems apply multiplication of a fraction by a whole number in context — 5 people each eating 3/8 of a pizza, four 2/3-metre ribbon pieces. The core idea is a/b × n as n copies of a/b (repeated addition of a unit-fraction multiple), and the practical twist is interpreting an improper-fraction product back in context: 5 × 3/8 = 15/8 = 1 7/8 pizzas eaten, but you must BUY 2 whole pizzas. Teach it as repeated groups on a bar or number line, estimate between whole numbers (6 × 3/4 lies between 4 and 5), convert the improper result to a mixed number, and round or interpret according to the situation.
bestPractices: Model as repeated equal groups — n copies of a/b — accumulating on a bar or number line so the product is built, not just computed
Multiply only the numerator by the whole number (n × a/b = na/b); keep the denominator as the unchanged unit
Estimate between which whole numbers the product lies before computing (6 × 3/4 is between 4 and 5)
Convert the improper product to a mixed number and INTERPRET it in context (round pizzas needed up to a whole)
Distinguish 'how much is eaten' (exact mixed number) from 'how many must be bought' (rounded up)
keyRepresentations: Number line with repeated fraction jumps of a/b
Repeated-groups bar (n copies of the fraction) accumulating past wholes
Improper → mixed conversion of the product
Context interpretation card (eaten vs needed)
commonMisconceptions: Multiplies the denominator too (4 × 2/3 → 8/12), scaling the unit as well as the count
Adds the whole number to the fraction instead of multiplying (3/8 + 5)
Leaves the answer as an improper fraction with no contextual meaning, or fails to round 'pizzas needed' up
Chooses the wrong operation because the repeated-groups structure is not read

learn.summary: Learners solve word problems that multiply a fraction by a whole number (n × a/b = na/b) by treating the product as n copies of the unit-fraction multiple, accumulating them on a bar or number line, converting the improper result to a mixed number, and interpreting that result in context — distinguishing exactly how much is used (e.g. 1 7/8 pizzas eaten) from how many whole units must be bought (2 pizzas). Core examples: 5 people each eating 3/8 of a pizza; four ribbon pieces of 2/3 metre; estimating that 6 × 3/4 lies between 4 and 5.

activities.title: Build the product by stacking repeated fraction groups
feedback: If the denominator changed (e.g. 4 × 2/3 written as 8/12), return to the groups: 2/3 + 2/3 + 2/3 + 2/3 — only the number of thirds grows, each piece is still a third.
If the whole number was added instead (3/8 + 5), redraw the five groups of 3/8 and name it aloud as 'five lots of 3/8' before writing ×.
If the answer was left improper, prompt: how many whole bars and how much extra does 15/8 make?
activities.rationale: Modelling multiplication as accumulating repeated groups on a visual model builds na/b concretely and confronts the documented error of scaling the denominator; keeping the denominator fixed shows the unit is unchanged.
sourceClaims: Understanding a/b as a multiple of 1/b and multiplying a fraction by a whole number (n × a/b = na/b) is built with visual models of repeated groups; multiplying the denominator as well is a documented error to confront
Solve word problems involving multiplication of a fraction by a whole number using visual fraction models and equations (e.g. n × a/b), and interpret the resulting product
learnerActions: Take a catering problem: 5 friends, each eats 3/8 of a pizza — work out the total eaten by building copies, not by jumping to a rule.
Stack five copies of a 3/8 bar (or draw five jumps of 3/8 on a number line) and track the running total: 3/8, 6/8, 9/8, 12/8, 15/8, noting when the total crosses a whole.
Record the result as the improper fraction 15/8 and convert it to the mixed number 1 7/8.
State in words: the top number (count of eighths) grows while the denominator stays eighths — the unit does not change.
Repeat the build for 4 × 2/3 (thirds accumulating to 8/3 = 2 2/3) to generalise.
If a live builder is available, set the fraction and the count and watch copies stack with a running total snapping the whole-number boundaries; otherwise draw each jump by hand.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying a fraction by a whole number is repeatedly adding that fraction: n copies of a/b accumulate to na/b, so only the numerator (count of unit fractions) grows while the denominator stays the fixed unit.

activities.title: Interpret the result: eaten versus bought
feedback: If 15/8 or 1 7/8 is given as the number to buy, ask: 'You can't buy 7/8 of a pizza — how many whole ones cover 1 7/8?' The multiplication is correct; only the interpretation is missing.
If rounding is applied where it isn't needed (ribbon length), point out that 2 2/3 metres is a valid measurement — rounding depends on whether the unit can be partial.
Reinforce estimating first: if 6 × 3/4 was expected to be a whole number, note that 18/4 = 4 1/2 lies between 4 and 5, as the estimate predicts, so the product is not a whole number.
activities.rationale: Interpreting the improper product in context — distinguishing the exact amount from the whole quantity a situation demands — is the real purpose of the word problem; estimating between whole numbers provides a reasonableness check.
sourceClaims: Solve word problems involving multiplication of a fraction by a whole number using visual fraction models and equations (e.g. n × a/b), and interpret the resulting product
learnerActions: Using the computed total 1 7/8 pizzas eaten, decide how many whole pizzas must be ordered, given you cannot buy part of a pizza.
Explain why 1 7/8 rounds UP to 2 here, and why the question 'how much is eaten' keeps the exact 1 7/8.
Answer a contrast pair: 'How much pizza is eaten?' (1 7/8, exact) and 'How many whole pizzas must be bought?' (2, rounded up).
For the ribbon problem, state 4 × 2/3 = 8/3 = 2 2/3 metres and decide whether rounding is needed (it is not — a length can be a mixed number).
Before computing another problem, estimate between which two whole numbers the product lies, e.g. 6 × 3/4 is between 4 and 5.
activities.intendedInsight: An improper-fraction product must be read back into the situation: the exact mixed number answers 'how much', but 'how many whole units are needed' may require rounding up — and some quantities (like length) sensibly stay as mixed numbers.

activities.title: Check and consolidate with targeted questions
feedback: A product with a changed denominator (8/12), often then 'simplified' to 2/3, reveals the denominator-scaling error — reteach via repeated groups.
A correct computation but a fractional buy-quantity shows a missing interpretation step, not a broken method.
An answer near 5 3/8 or an addition of whole and fraction signals the wrong operation was chosen — redraw the groups and name them before writing ×.
activities.rationale: A short set of discriminating items separates computational slips, the denominator misconception, and interpretation gaps, and checks transfer to a new context. Recognition items check reasoning but do not by themselves show independent construction, so pair them with an end-to-end solve.
sourceClaims: Understanding a/b as a multiple of 1/b and multiplying a fraction by a whole number (n × a/b = na/b) is built with visual models of repeated groups; multiplying the denominator as well is a documented error to confront
learnerActions: Answer: 4 × 2/3 = ? Choose and justify from 8/12, 8/3, 2 2/3, explaining why 8/12 is wrong (denominator scaled) and showing that 8/3 and 2 2/3 are the same value.
Fill in the blank: n × a/b = __/b, stating the rule in your own words.
Estimate on a scale 'between which two whole numbers is 6 × 3/4?' and place it.
Solve a fresh word problem (e.g. a new fraction × whole context) end to end: build, compute na/b, convert, and interpret whether to round.
Explain in a sentence what a party host should order for a group, separating 'eaten' from 'bought'.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent learners compute na/b (numerator only), convert to a mixed number, interpret in context, estimate between whole numbers, and transfer the method to a new word problem.

constraints: Enforce or emphasise numerator-only scaling: when multiplying, the denominator (unit) stays fixed; a builder that makes multiplying the denominator impossible is a scaffold, but learners must also be able to state and apply the rule without the tool.

Recognition/multiple-choice items (e.g. choosing 8/3 over 8/12) check whether the learner can judge answers but do not on their own demonstrate independent construction; include at least one full build-and-interpret task.
A tap-to-reveal static worked pair illustrates the accumulation and interpretation but cannot let the learner vary the count — use it as an example, not as the main practice where varying n matters.
Rounding up applies to quantities that must be whole (pizzas to buy); it is not universal — lengths and similar measures can remain mixed numbers. Always tie rounding to the situation.
A conversational/role-play framing (party-planning host) can pose the 'eaten vs bought' question well, but the accumulation itself benefits from a visual surface (bar or number line).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic audit (independently re-checked): 5 × 3/8 = 15/8 = 1 7/8; 4 × 2/3 = 8/3 = 2 2/3; 6 × 3/4 = 18/4 = 4 1/2, which lies between 4 and 5. The original candidate draft had written '18/4 = 4 2/3' in the interpret activity's estimation feedback; this is incorrect and now reads 4 1/2 at every occurrence.

The source row rated a 3D/physical representation as a 'poor fit' with the claim that '3D adds nothing' for planar repeated groups; this categorical modality claim is not an established pedagogical law and has been dropped. A 3D or physical representation is simply a different, non-required experience, not evidence that one medium is superior.

CCSS source is marked verified:false in the row; no new verification was performed. The IES/WWC source is marked verified:true in the row — this reflects legacy metadata, not a re-check during this rewrite.

probeDeeper: In (a), 15/8 pizzas are eaten — can you buy 15/8 of a pizza? How many whole ones do you need?
Between which two whole numbers does 6 × 3/4 lie, without computing exactly?
Show 4 × 2/3 as jumps on a number line — how many thirds altogether?
Estimate (b) — more or less than 2 metres? more or less than 3?
assess.correctAnswer: (a) 5 × 3/8 = 15/8 = 1 7/8 pizzas eaten; you must buy 2 whole pizzas. (b) 4 × 2/3 = 8/3 = 2 2/3 metres.

errorPatterns.pattern: Multiplies the denominator as well: 4 × 2/3 → 8/12 (scales the unit along with the count)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to repeated groups — four lots of 2/3 is 2/3 + 2/3 + 2/3 + 2/3 — on a number line so only the count of thirds grows; the third stays the unit
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Product has a changed denominator (8/12 rather than 8/3); often then 'simplified' to 2/3

errorPatterns.pattern: Leaves the answer as an improper fraction with no contextual meaning, or fails to round 'pizzas needed' up: reports 15/8 or 1 7/8 as the number to buy
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold — 'you can't buy part of a pizza; how many whole ones cover 1 7/8?' — the multiplication is sound, only the interpretation is missing
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Computation correct but the buy-quantity is given as a fraction/mixed number rather than 2 whole pizzas

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds instead of multiplies, or chooses the wrong operation: 3/8 + 5, because the repeated-groups structure is not read
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw the groups first — 5 people each with 3/8 — and name it as 5 lots of 3/8 before writing ×
errorPatterns.revealedBy: An addition of the whole and the fraction, or an answer near 5 3/8; no repeated-groups working

responseLevels.gap: Multiplies the denominator, or adds instead of multiplies; no repeated-groups model.
responseLevels.full: Multiplies correctly (numerator only), converts to a mixed number, interprets in context (rounds pizzas needed up to 2), estimates between whole numbers, and transfers to a new fraction × whole word problem.
responseLevels.partial: Computes na/b correctly (15/8, 8/3) but cannot convert/interpret the improper result in context — leaves it improper or fails to round the buy-quantity up.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Solve these, showing your working: (a) Each person eats 3/8 of a pizza and there are 5 people — how much pizza is eaten in total, and how many whole pizzas must be bought? (b) A ribbon is cut into pieces each 2/3 of a metre long — how long are 4 pieces altogether?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the method catches the two faults a bare answer hides: whether the denominator was wrongly scaled (4 × 2/3 → 8/12 instead of 8/3) and whether the improper product was interpreted in context. Part (a) is engineered to separate 'how much is eaten' (1 7/8, exact) from 'how many to buy' (2, rounded up) — a child who reports 1 7/8 pizzas to buy has computed correctly but not interpreted. A child who multiplies the denominator, or adds instead, reveals a broken model of a/b × n.

sources.claim: Understanding a/b as a multiple of 1/b and multiplying a fraction by a whole number (n × a/b = na/b) is built with visual models of repeated groups; multiplying the denominator as well is a documented error to confront
sources.source: IES / What Works Clearinghouse — Developing Effective Fractions Instruction K–8 (Siegler et al. 2010), Recommendation 3

sources.claim: Solve word problems involving multiplication of a fraction by a whole number using visual fraction models and equations (e.g. n × a/b), and interpret the resulting product
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics — 4.NF.4c

pedagogy.summary: Subtracting multiples of ten (70−30) is taught through unitising: a decade number is a count of tens, so 70−30 is seven tens minus three tens, and the answer is four tens. The known single-digit fact (7−3=4) is reused at the scale of tens. Ten-rods, bead strings and number lines that jump in tens make this visible, so the '0' in the answer carries meaning rather than being appended as a trick.
bestPractices: Build on 'the multiples of ten represent one-to-nine tens': treat 70−30 as 7 tens − 3 tens (NCETM Spine: derived facts, e.g. 30+70 from 3+7)
Reuse the known within-ten fact explicitly — connect 7−3 to 70−30 so the child sees the same subtraction at a larger unit
Represent with ten-rods and with a number line that jumps in tens, so subtraction of tens is a small number of large jumps
Ask the child to explain that subtracting tens is like subtracting the tens digits because each unit is a ten — meaning behind the zero
Contrast 70−3 with 70−30 to expose whether the child is tracking the unit
keyRepresentations: Ten-rods / base-ten tens (remove whole rods)
Bead string in tens or 100-bead frame
Number line with jumps of ten
Hundred square (move up in tens)
Place-value chart showing the tens column
commonMisconceptions: Dropping the ten-unit: subtracting 7−3=4 and answering 4 instead of 40
Treating the zero as a spelling trick ('add a zero') with no unit meaning
Counting back in ones (70,69,68…) and losing track
Confusing 70−3 with 70−30 because the unit isn't tracked

learn.summary: Teach subtracting multiples of ten (e.g. 70−30) through unitising: a decade number is a count of tens, so 70−30 is seven tens minus three tens = four tens. The known fact 7−3=4 is reused at the scale of tens, so the '0' in 40 carries real place meaning rather than being appended as a trick. Removable tens-materials, bead strings, and number lines that jump in tens make this visible; contrasting 70−3 with 70−30 exposes whether the child is tracking the unit.

activities.title: Removing whole tens from a tens-only mat
feedback: If the child answers 4 for 70 − 30, point to the four rods and ask 'is each of these one, or ten?' — rebuild the answer as four tens = 40.
If the child says 'you just add a zero', ask them to show the four tens on the mat and explain why the answer is four tens and not four ones.
Confirm good reasoning by asking the child to check: add the three removed rods back and see that seven tens (70) returns.
activities.rationale: Unitising — treating 'one lot of ten' as a single object that can be removed whole — is the crux of calculating with numbers larger than ten, and removable tens-materials let the child act on tens as units while watching the count change in ten-steps. An optional linked number line jumping in tens can mirror the rod action.
sourceClaims: Unitising — engaging with 'one lot of ten' as a single entity operated on as one object — is essential for calculating with numbers larger than ten.
learnerActions: Lay out seven ten-rods (or ten-sticks/strips of ten) to represent 70.
For 70 − 30, physically remove three whole rods and say the running count aloud: 70 → 60 → 50 → 40.
Name what is left as 'four tens, which is 40', pointing at the four rods rather than counting individual cubes.
Say the matching single-digit fact: 'seven tens minus three tens is four tens, just like 7 − 3 = 4.'
Repeat for 80 − 50 (eight rods, remove five, leaving three = 30) and 90 − 60 (nine rods, remove six, leaving three = 30), each time removing whole rods and stating the answer in tens.
activities.intendedInsight: Subtracting multiples of ten is the same subtraction as the known single-digit fact, spoken in units of ten; the zero in the answer is a real placeholder showing zero ones, which keeps the 4 in the tens place. It is not decoration.

activities.title: Contrasting 70 − 3 with 70 − 30
feedback: If the child gives the same answer for both, ask them to lay the two removed amounts side by side (three rods vs three cubes) and compare.
Praise reasoning that references the unit: 'three tens is thirty, three ones is only three.'
activities.rationale: Contrasting 70−3 with 70−30 exposes whether the child is tracking the unit rather than mechanically subtracting digits, directly addressing the confusion between the two.
sourceClaims: Unitising — engaging with 'one lot of ten' as a single entity operated on as one object — is essential for calculating with numbers larger than ten.
learnerActions: Work 70 − 30 by removing three whole ten-rods; record the answer (40) and the running count.
Rebuild 70 with seven ten-rods, then unbundle (or exchange) one ten-rod for ten single cubes; use these to work 70 − 3 by removing three single cubes.
Compare the two results: 70 − 30 = 40 (a big change) versus 70 − 3 = 67 (a small change).
Explain in words why removing three tens changes the number far more than removing three ones.
activities.intendedInsight: The size of the unit being removed matters: subtracting tens and subtracting ones are different because each ten is worth ten ones.

activities.title: Linking the known fact on a reference chart
feedback: If the child writes the answer but reads it as ones, re-read it together as 'four tens'.
Reinforce by asking which single-digit fact each decade subtraction is 'borrowing'.
activities.rationale: A reference layout that pairs the within-ten fact with the decade fact makes the reuse of known facts explicit. This is a scaffold for consolidation and does not by itself let the child act on removing tens, so it works best after hands-on removal.
sourceClaims: Derived-fact reasoning for decade calculations reuses known within-ten facts at the scale of tens (e.g. 86−50 via 80+6−50 = 30+6).
Year 2 pupils derive facts to 100 from facts to 20, e.g. using 3+7=10 to calculate 30+70=100 and 100−70=30; they understand multiples of ten and the value of each digit.
learnerActions: Look at 70 and state that it is '7 tens'.
Alongside 7 − 3 = 4, write 7 tens − 3 tens = 4 tens = 40.
Do the same for other decade pairs (e.g. 8 − 5 = 3 beside 80 − 50 = 30), reading each as a statement about tens.
activities.intendedInsight: Each decade subtraction reuses a single-digit fact at the scale of tens, so the known fact gives the answer directly.

activities.title: Decade subtraction practice with the dropped-unit trap
feedback: If 4 is chosen, return to the rods: four tens, not four ones.
If the correct answer (40) is chosen but the explanation is 'add a zero', ask them to justify it in tens.
activities.rationale: A short practice set rehearses the strategy and surfaces the dropped-unit error with a targeted trap; it is best placed after hands-on and reference work, which do more to first build the underlying idea.
learnerActions: Complete a short sequence of decade subtractions (e.g. 70−30, 60−40, 90−50), writing each answer.
For 70 − 30, choose the correct answer from options that include 4 as a tempting wrong answer, and explain why 4 is wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidate the tens strategy and catch the common error of dropping the ten-unit.

activities.title: Optional: rhythmic count-back in tens
feedback: Keep this chant focused on jumping in tens for fluency; counting back in ones is still a valid strategy and should not be marked wrong, but for this particular chant gently restart in tens so the ten-jump becomes automatic.
activities.rationale: Rhythmic chanting can reinforce the decade count-sequence and support fluency. It supports but does not build the unitising insight, so it is a supplement to the hands-on work rather than the primary teaching.
learnerActions: Chant the tens count-back sequence aloud with a rhythm: '70, 60, 50, 40' for 70 − 30.
Match the number of jumps to the number of tens being removed.
activities.intendedInsight: The tens count-sequence becomes fluent and the 'jump in tens' becomes a natural move.

constraints: The reference chart and reveal-style layouts are consolidation scaffolds: they link 7−3 to 70−30 but do not let the child remove tens and watch the count change, so they do not by themselves build the unitising action.

Practice sequences and choice items rehearse the strategy and can surface errors such as the dropped ten-unit, so they are well suited to consolidation and checking, and are less likely than hands-on removal to first establish the unitising idea.
Chanting supports the count-sequence; on its own it does not establish why the answer is four tens.

Paper strips, rods, or card tens have slight physical thickness and are approximations of abstract tens; keep attention on 'each piece is worth ten', and an idealised on-screen counter is a model of the tens count, not the tens themselves.
Do not forbid or mark wrong a child who counts back in ones — it is a valid strategy that matures; model the ten-jump alongside it.
Keep the 'subtract the tens digits, keeping the ten-unit' shortcut scoped to decade−decade subtraction; it is not a general rule for cases needing regrouping.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated 3D as 'adding nothing' and framed dialogue as unable to build the insight; these have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements rather than universal superiority claims, since the sources do not establish comparative efficacy or necessity.
One source claim (NCETM derived-fact reasoning, used in Activity 3) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its specific worked example as unconfirmed and do not rely on it as proven.

The legacy assessment/correctAnswer uses 'subtract the tens digits keeping the ten-unit' as an efficient method; this is sound for pure multiples of ten but should not generalise to cases requiring regrouping — kept narrowly scoped to decade minus decade.
The value 4 appears in Activity 4 only as a deliberately labelled wrong answer that the child must identify and explain, not as a potentially valid option.

probeDeeper: You said 80 − 50 = 30. Show me with the ten-rods why it's 30 and not 3.
How is 8 − 5 like 80 − 50? How is it different?
What about 80 − 5 — is that the same as 80 − 50? Work it and tell me the difference.
Can you check your answer by adding 50 back to 30?
assess.correctAnswer: 40, 30, 30. Efficient: treat each as tens — seven tens minus three tens is four tens, 40 — or subtract the tens digits keeping the ten-unit (the zero). With rods, remove five ten-rods from eight, leaving three ten-rods = 30.

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops the ten-unit — 'seven take three is four, so 70 take 30 is 4' — or gets 40 only by 'adding a zero' with no reason
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild with ten-rods so the answer is seen as four tens; name that each digit counts tens, so the zero is a real ten's place, not decoration.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives a single-digit answer, or writes 40 but explains it purely as a zero trick with no sense that the digits are tens

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts back in ones — works 70−30 by counting 69,68,67… thirty steps, often losing the count
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT forbid the count-back or mark it wrong — it is a valid strategy that matures. Model 'these are whole tens, so jump in tens' alongside the child's count so the ten-jump becomes the natural move.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child counts back one at a time rather than removing three tens; slow and error-prone on the longer counts

responseLevels.gap: Answers 4 for 70−30, or counts back in ones and loses track; treats the zero as a spelling trick.
responseLevels.full: Answers in tens immediately, explains that subtracting tens is like subtracting the tens digits because each is one ten, and checks by adding back.
responseLevels.partial: Reaches answers with ten-rods in front of them or by counting back, but cannot yet reason 'seven tens minus three tens' without the materials.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set these to work one at a time and watch how the child does them: 70 − 30, 80 − 50, 90 − 60. Then hand them ten-rods and ask them to build 80 − 50 and tell you the answer and how they know.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who unitises answers in tens almost instantly and explains '7 tens minus 3 tens'. A child who has lost the ten-unit either counts back thirty ones (and may lose track) or subtracts the digits and drops the ten, saying 70−30=4, or can only justify the zero as 'you add a zero'.

sources.claim: Year 2 pupils derive facts to 100 from facts to 20, e.g. using 3+7=10 to calculate 30+70=100 and 100−70=30; they understand multiples of ten and the value of each digit.

sources.claim: Unitising — engaging with 'one lot of ten' as a single entity operated on as one object — is essential for calculating with numbers larger than ten.
sources.source: NRICH, place-value articles (unitising)

pedagogy.summary: At 9-10, using structure is about choosing the most efficient form or route by exploiting relationships: rewriting 25×16 as 25×4×4 = 100×4 = 400 via factor pairs, treating 0.75, 3/4 and 75% as one quantity in three dresses and picking whichever makes the problem easy, and deploying angle facts (angles on a line sum to 180°) as deductive tools instead of measuring. The pedagogy is to make the strategic saving visible — compare the clever route against the grind — and to build fluency moving between fraction/decimal/percentage forms so the child reaches for the handiest one.
bestPractices: Show 25×16 both ways — the column algorithm and the 25×4×4 = 100×4 regrouping — so the factor-pair route is felt as a shortcut, not a trick
Use a triple number line / double-sided cards linking 0.75 = 3/4 = 75% so the forms are interchangeable and the child selects by convenience
Present missing-angle problems where measuring is awkward so the child must deduce from 180°/360°/vertically-opposite facts
Ask 'which form / which route makes this easiest, and why?' so structure use is a deliberate choice
keyRepresentations: Factor trees and factor-pair regrouping (16 = 4×4; 25×4 = 100)
Triple representation of FDP (bar, number line, and 0.75 / 3⁄₄ / 75% cards)
Angle diagrams with a straight line / point as the structural constraint
Area/array models linking factors to products
commonMisconceptions: Runs the standard column algorithm for 25×16 without looking for factor pairs that make it a mental step
Converts laboriously every time instead of recognising 0.75, 3/4 and 75% as the same number
Measures a missing angle with a protractor rather than deducing it from an angle fact
Picks the fraction/decimal/percentage form by habit rather than by which is efficient for the task

learn.summary: For ages 9-10, 'using structure' means deliberately choosing an efficient route or form by exploiting relationships rather than grinding: rewriting 25×16 as 25×4×4 = 100×4 = 400 via factor pairs; treating 0.75, 3/4 and 75% as one quantity and picking whichever form makes a task a one-step job; and deducing missing angles from facts (angles on a straight line sum to 180°, around a point 360°, vertically opposite angles equal) instead of measuring. The core teaching move is to make the strategic saving visible — run the clever route alongside the grind — and to build fluent movement between fraction/decimal/percentage forms so the child reaches for the handiest one and can say why.

activities.title: Factor-pair regrouping run beside the column method
feedback: If the child runs column multiplication without regrouping, explore the factor pairs of 16 (4×4, 2×8) and the fact 25×4 = 100; lay it out on an array so the friendly 100 appears visibly.
If the child cannot name why 25 and 16 are a convenient pair, prompt: 'What times 25 gives 100? Can 16 be split to hand you that factor?'

For 23×16, affirm that there is no clean pairing to a hundred here: 23 is prime, so its only factor pair is 1×23, and neither 23 nor 16 is a factor of 100. 23 can still be split by adding (20 + 3) for a different method, but no factor pair builds 100 — this explains why 25×16 is a special case, not a universal trick.
activities.rationale: Showing the shortcut and the long method side by side lets the saving be felt rather than asserted, and testing a non-example checks the child understands the condition that enables the structure, supporting deliberate choice of efficient methods.
sourceClaims: Proficient students look for and make use of structure, e.g. rewriting expressions and seeing composed objects, to solve efficiently rather than by brute computation
Pupils should recognise and use mathematical structure and relationships and choose efficient methods; teaching should compare representations and strategies for efficiency
learnerActions: Work out 25×16 without the column algorithm, splitting 16 into 4×4, then pairing one 4 with 25 to make 100, so the product collapses to 100×4 = 400 in two moves
Carry out the column method for 25×16 as well, and compare how many steps each route took
State the 'hinge' that made the shortcut work (25×4 = 100) and explain why spotting it saved effort
Try the same thinking on 50×16 and 25×24: regroup each to a friendly round number (50×2×8 = 100×8 = 800; 25×4×6 = 100×6 = 600) and show the route
Test a non-example, 23×16: try to find a neat factor pair to a hundred and explain why 25×16 is 'luckier'
activities.intendedInsight: A hard-looking multiplication can dissolve when you spot a factor pair that builds a friendly round number (here 25×4 = 100); recognising WHAT makes a shortcut available is the skill, not just reaching the answer.

activities.title: One quantity in three forms: choose the handiest
feedback: If the child converts 75% to 0.75 and multiplies laboriously, show the 3/4 route (£80 ÷ 4 = £20, ×3 = £60) and ask which took fewer steps.
If the child always uses the same form, pose numbers where each form wins in turn so the 'it depends on the numbers' idea surfaces.
Praise reasoning that names why a form fits — e.g. '3/4 suits £80 because 80 divides by 4 cleanly.'
activities.rationale: Lining the three forms up as one point and asking for a justified choice targets flexible, efficient selection rather than rote conversion, matching the aim of choosing efficient methods and comparing representations.
sourceClaims: Pupils should recognise and use mathematical structure and relationships and choose efficient methods; teaching should compare representations and strategies for efficiency
learnerActions: Look at a single amount shown at once as 3/4, 0.75 and 75% (on a bar or number line marking the same point) and confirm they are one number
Find 75% of £80 and decide whether to use 75%, 0.75 or 3/4; show that 3/4 gives ÷4 then ×3 = £60 in one line
For 30% of £90, decide between 0.3, 3/10 or 30% and justify the choice (3/10 of £90 = £27)
Then try 12.5% of £80 and notice whether the handiest form changes (e.g. 1/8 of 80 = £10), explaining why the best form depends on the numbers
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction, decimal and percentage can name the same quantity, so a flexible solver selects whichever form makes the particular numbers easiest instead of converting by habit.

activities.title: Deduce missing angles instead of measuring
feedback: If the child reaches for a protractor, present a diagram drawn not-to-scale or with an angle off the page so measuring fails and the fact must be used.
Prompt 'What do these angles add up to, or which pair must be equal?' to surface the structural constraint before working it out.
If a regular polygon is involved, draw attention to the repeated equal angles so one deduction covers several.
activities.rationale: Posing problems where measurement is impractical forces reliance on the angle fact as a structural tool, building deductive reasoning over measurement.
sourceClaims: Proficient students look for and make use of structure, e.g. rewriting expressions and seeing composed objects, to solve efficiently rather than by brute computation
learnerActions: Given a diagram where measuring is awkward or impossible, find the missing angle by using a fact (angles on a straight line sum to 180°, around a point 360°, or vertically opposite angles equal)
Name which fact you leaned on and show the working (e.g. 180° − known angle, or 'these two are vertically opposite so they are equal')
Explain how you know the answer is right without a protractor

Extend to a regular polygon: use its equal angles/sides with a known fact (e.g. one given angle, or the equal angles at the centre adding up to 360°) to find unknown angles systematically rather than measuring each one
activities.intendedInsight: Angle facts are deductive tools: depending on the fact you either subtract the given parts from a known total (180° on a line, 360° around a point) or set vertically opposite angles equal — both give an exact answer, unlike the approximation of measuring.

activities.title: Explain the choice: a tap-to-reveal and short explanation
feedback: Accept any correct route, but press for the reason: a strong response names the hinge (25×4 = 100) or the fitting form (3/4 for a ÷4-friendly number).
If the explanation is missing, replay the two routes side by side and ask which took fewer steps and why.
A reference card and angle-fact diagram can consolidate recall, but follow with a problem that requires choosing a route so the child demonstrates selection, not just recognition.
activities.rationale: A reveal/match format and a short explanation question consolidate equivalences and surface the reasoning behind the chosen route; because both 400 and £60 are reachable by grinding, articulating the reason is what distinguishes structural from procedural work.
learnerActions: Match or reveal FDP equivalents (0.75 = 3/4 = 75%) and annotate a worked angle diagram to consolidate the facts
After solving, answer 'which route/form did you choose and why was it quickest?' in your own words
Compare your chosen route against a slower alternative and state what made the difference
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to state WHY a route is efficient — not just getting the answer — is the sign of structural thinking; the answer alone can be reached by grinding.

constraints: Reference cards, FDP match tasks and static angle-fact posters consolidate recall but do not let the child test alternative routes or feel the efficiency difference; pair them with problems that require choosing a method and explaining the choice.

Scored matching or 'which route is quickest?' items can check the structural choice but can mask whether efficiency was actually reasoned; always ask the child to say why, so recognition is not mistaken for independent construction.

The 25×4 = 100 factor-pair shortcut is specific: it works because 25 is a factor of 100 and 16 splits to supply the needed 4. State this condition and include non-examples (e.g. 23×16) so the move is not over-generalised as a universal trick.
The best FDP form is numbers-dependent (3/4 suits £80, 1/8 suits 12.5% of £80); do not teach a single 'always use' form.

Factor regrouping, FDP equivalence and these angle facts live in number lines, arrays and 2D diagrams; a 3D model is not needed here, though this reflects the topic's flat content rather than a general rule about 3D.

Open discussion alone gives the child no numbers, bars or diagrams to regroup or manipulate; these activities need those representations present, which does not imply dialogue cannot support the reasoning.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy source framed open conversation and 3D as 'poor' and claimed a quiz 'hides' reasoning; these are reframed as scoped limits (the tasks need concrete numbers; this topic's content is flat; scores can mask reasoning so pair with an explanation probe) rather than universal laws about media.

The 23×16 non-example is retained as a check on the shortcut's condition: 23 is prime and neither it nor 16 is a factor of 100, so no clean pairing to a hundred exists — this is the intended teaching point.

Activity 3's intended insight covers both deduction types so vertically opposite angles (found by equality) are not misdescribed as 'total minus parts', keeping the stated insight consistent with every method the child uses.

Independent re-audit: arithmetic, units, the FDP equivalences, angle facts and the factor-pair condition were re-checked and are internally consistent; no categorical medium-superiority claims remain and efficacy wording stays qualified.

probeDeeper: Ask 'would the factor-pair trick help for 25×24 or 50×16 too? how would you regroup those?' to test whether the structure generalises
Counterexample tuned to this topic: 'for 23×16 is there a neat factor pair to a hundred? why is 25×16 luckier?' to check the child understands WHAT makes the shortcut available
Ask 'to find 30% of £90 would you use 0.3, 3/10 or 30%? does your choice change if it's 12.5% of £80?' to probe deliberate form selection
Ask 'how do you know the missing angle without measuring? what fact are you leaning on?' to surface the structural constraint
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for exploiting factor pairs (25×16 = 25×4×4 = 100×4 = 400 because 25×4 makes 100) and for choosing 3/4 of £80 as easiest (÷4 then ×3 = £60) with a reason about which form suits the number. The reasoning about WHY the route is efficient is the target.

errorPatterns.pattern: Does not spot the factor pair and runs the standard algorithm for 25×16, because 16 is not seen as 4×4 or 25 as a quarter of 100
errorPatterns.nextMove: Explore factor pairs of 16 and the fact 25×4=100; regroup on an array so the friendly 100 appears
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child sets out column multiplication rather than regrouping; cannot say what makes 25 and 16 a convenient pair

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats 0.75, 3/4 and 75% as separate things to convert each time rather than one number, so no efficient form is chosen
errorPatterns.nextMove: Line up the three forms on one bar/number line as the same point; practise picking the form that fits the given number
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child laboriously converts 75% to a decimal and multiplies, unaware 3/4 gives a one-line answer for £80

errorPatterns.pattern: Reaches for a protractor to find a missing angle instead of deducing it from angles on a line summing to 180°
errorPatterns.nextMove: Pose diagrams where measuring is awkward or impossible so the angle fact must be used as a tool; subtract from the known total
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Given a missing-angle diagram, the child measures rather than subtracting from 180°/360°

responseLevels.gap: Column-multiplies 25×16, converts every FDP form from scratch, and measures missing angles; no structural shortcut sought
responseLevels.full: Spontaneously spots the factor pair and names the hinge (25×4=100), selects the handiest FDP form with a reason, and deduces angles from facts — transferring 'what structure makes this easy?' to new numbers and diagrams
responseLevels.partial: Can use a factor pair, switch FDP form, or apply an angle fact when prompted, but does not choose the efficient route independently or explain why it is efficient

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work out 25 × 16 in the cleverest way you can — no column method — and tell me how you spotted the shortcut. Then: to find 75% of £80, would you rather work with 75%, 0.75 or 3/4, and why?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Both 400 and £60 are reachable by grinding; what discriminates is whether the child SPOTS the factor pair / chooses the handy form and can articulate why. A structural thinker names 25×4=100 as the hinge and picks 3/4 for a ÷4-friendly number; a non-structural one column-multiplies and converts 75% laboriously.

pedagogy.summary: Construct and interpret line graphs for a measured quantity changing over time. Build from the earlier line-graph problem-solving topic: select a scale, label axes and units, plot pairs accurately and connect observations in time order. Distinguish observations from straight-line estimates, and point height from change or rate. Require an independently produced graph as well as verbal interpretation.
bestPractices: Begin with a small familiar table and discuss the variables, units and observation times before drawing.
Choose evenly spaced numerical scales that include the data; label each axis and unit.
Plot every time/value pair, checking both coordinates before joining points in time order.
Introduce unequal time intervals only after equal intervals, preserving the numerical spacing of time.
Ask for a trend and a numerical difference, then for an intermediate estimate with its assumption.
keyRepresentations: A paired table and a pupil-constructed time/temperature graph.
Axes with equally spaced numerical intervals and visible units.
A straight segment between two observations labelled as a model-based estimate.
Two intervals showing why total change and change per hour can differ.
commonMisconceptions: Treats rows as equally spaced times when the time gaps differ.
Uses a changing numerical scale along an axis.
Swaps coordinates or reads graph height without the time/value units.
Treats a line segment as an exact record of every unmeasured value.
Names the highest point when asked for the largest change or fastest increase.

learn.summary: For ages 10–11, construct a complete line graph from a table of continuous measurements and use it to answer questions. Choose labelled numerical scales, preserve actual time spacing, plot paired readings and join in order. Read observations, describe trends, compute differences and estimate between observations under an explicit straight-line assumption. With unequal intervals, distinguish total change from change per hour.

activities.title: Build a line graph from a table
feedback: If the points are equally spaced in value because each occupies a new row, read the temperature scale rather than counting rows.
If a label or unit is missing, ask what another reader would need to recover a table value.
If a plotted point disagrees with the table, check its two coordinates before redrawing the whole graph.
activities.rationale: The task elicits the construction performance required by the updated objective. The topic description and evidence statements establish scope; the activity is an editorial proposal, not a tested intervention.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils interpret and construct pie charts and line graphs and use these to solve problems (statutory statistics content for this age)
learnerActions: Use temperatures at 09:00 12°C, 10:00 16°C, 11:00 18°C, 12:00 17°C and 13:00 19°C. Name time as the horizontal variable and temperature as the vertical variable.
Choose equal-hour spacing and a vertical scale covering 12–19°C; a 0–20°C axis with equal 2°C intervals and clear minor divisions is one option. Label time and temperature (°C).
Plot each pair yourself, check its horizontal and vertical coordinates, join points in time order, and add an informative title.
Compare your plotted points with the table before viewing a worked answer.
activities.intendedInsight: A line graph is a constructed mapping between paired measurements and labelled numerical axes, not a copied silhouette.

activities.title: Read, compare and estimate on your graph
feedback: The highest point is 19°C at 13:00, but the largest hourly rise is 4°C from 09:00 to 10:00.
The 10:00–11:00 rise is 2°C; the straight-line estimate for 10:30 is 17°C, not a measurement.
Actual unmeasured temperature could have differed; a useful estimate is not an exact observation.
activities.rationale: Reading values before comparing or inferring moves from observation to interpretation and uses common height/shape confusions as teaching targets; it is a proposed activity, not an evaluated intervention.
sourceClaims: Graph-as-picture error: students treat the graph as a literal picture of the problem situation (drawing/reading a hill shape for a speed-vs-time graph over a hill), with two subtypes — global correspondence (whole scene matched to whole graph) and feature correspondence (a local visual feature matched to a graph feature); this occurs even when the student can describe the changes verbally

Slope-height confusion and related substitutions (height-for-slope, slope-for-height, height-for-difference, slope-for-curvature): students use the wrong graphical feature for the quantity asked; McDermott et al. found as many as half of students used height instead of slope to judge speed

Curcio's three hierarchical levels of graph comprehension — reading the data (literal lift), reading between the data (compare/combine/find differences), reading beyond the data (predict/infer) — students must read the data before they can read between or beyond it; framework adopted by NCTM for assessment
learnerActions: Identify the highest recorded temperature and the interval with the largest increase.
Find the 10:00–11:00 change, then estimate 10:30 using the straight segment and state the assumption.
Explain a flat or falling segment in terms of the measured quantity; distinguish the line from a picture of a journey or landscape.
activities.intendedInsight: Point height, change and estimated intermediate values answer different questions.

activities.title: Keep unequal time intervals honest
feedback: If the three points are equally spaced along time, check the clock times and re-space them.
Compute both the change and elapsed time; 6 ÷ 2 = 3°C per hour.
activities.rationale: This transfer task extends the height-versus-change distinction to the rate-of-change evidence. It is proposed practice, not an evaluated lesson.
sourceClaims: Slope-height confusion and related substitutions (height-for-slope, slope-for-height, height-for-difference, slope-for-curvature): students use the wrong graphical feature for the quantity asked; McDermott et al. found as many as half of students used height instead of slope to judge speed
learnerActions: Plot a second table: 09:00 10°C, 10:00 14°C and 12:00 20°C. Make the 10:00–12:00 gap twice the 09:00–10:00 gap.
Compare the first rise, 4°C in one hour, with the later rise, 6°C in two hours. Calculate change per hour before saying which interval warmed faster.
Explain why the larger total increase is not necessarily the steeper rise when time intervals differ.
activities.intendedInsight: Numerical time spacing determines the plotted rate: 4°C per hour is faster than 3°C per hour although 6°C is the larger total rise.

activities.title: Explain when a line is useful
feedback: Joining unordered categories does not define a useful interpolation.
Time-ordered observations can support a line-based estimate only under a stated assumption about what happened between them.
activities.rationale: The bar/line contrast is used only to clarify when joining points is meaningful, without claiming that one representation is always superior; it is a proposed activity.
sourceClaims: KS2 line-graph teaching: line graphs are used for continuous data where points between plotted points carry meaning; a rising line means an increase, a falling line a decrease, a flat line no change; pupils read values and find differences from the graph
learnerActions: Compare a temperature table indexed by time with favourite-fruit counts by unordered category. Choose a line graph for the former and bars for the latter.
Explain what an intermediate time means, and why halfway between apple and banana has no corresponding ordered category value.
Check that your own graph could be read by someone who did not see the original table.
activities.intendedInsight: Graph choice depends on the variables and their ordering; connecting points does not manufacture meaningful intermediate data.

constraints: Build on mt_H6LlpWgEYS for reading and problem-solving, and mt_u5HkSxZECM for graph vocabulary; assess actual construction separately.
Keep numerical scales uniform and elapsed time spacing accurate, including unequal intervals.
A correct trend description or selection of a ready-made graph does not demonstrate independent construction.
Interpolation estimates depend on the joining assumption and do not recover exact unmeasured observations.
Avoid 3D decoration that adds no measured variable.

Why is the largest hourly rise not at the highest point?
What assumption makes 17°C a defensible estimate for 10:30?
With 09:00 10°C, 10:00 14°C and 12:00 20°C, which interval has the greater total rise and which the faster rise per hour?
assess.correctAnswer: The pupil constructs a graph with time and temperature units, equal numerical scale intervals and all five correctly paired points joined in order. Highest: 13:00, 19°C. Largest hourly rise: 09:00–10:00, 4°C. The 10:00–11:00 change is +2°C and the straight-line 10:30 estimate is 17°C; the actual value is not known. For 09:00, 10:00, 12:00 the last horizontal gap is twice the first.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats table row order as equal elapsed time even when time gaps differ.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Mark clock intervals on a number line and make two hours occupy twice the space of one hour.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Places 09:00, 10:00 and 12:00 at equal horizontal distances.

errorPatterns.pattern: Substitutes the highest point for the largest increase.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare consecutive values on the earlier line-graph problem-solving topic, marking changes over equal intervals.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names 13:00 rather than 09:00–10:00 for the largest hourly rise.

errorPatterns.pattern: Misplots a coordinate or omits a scale label despite explaining the graph correctly.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a two-coordinate checking routine and ask the learner to correct the point or label without reteaching the whole concept.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: One point disagrees with the table or an axis lacks units.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot map the paired readings onto numerical axes or uses inconsistent spacing.
responseLevels.full: Independently constructs and checks the graph, interprets height and change correctly, explains the interpolation assumption and handles unequal time intervals.
responseLevels.partial: Reads a supplied graph but needs scaffolding to choose scales, plot or label the complete construction, or explain an estimate.

Then ask how the horizontal positions should change for readings at 09:00, 10:00 and 12:00.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Independent construction reveals scale, labelling and coordinate errors that choosing a finished graph would conceal. The same data separate the highest point from the greatest rise; the estimate and unequal-time transfer expose observation/model and row/time-spacing confusions.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 10–11 — explain the pattern in zeros when multiplying by powers of 10 and in decimal-point placement when ×/÷ by a power of 10; use whole-number exponents for powers of 10 (10³ = 1000).
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5/Y6 multiply and divide whole numbers and decimals by 10, 100 and 1000; exponent notation is a US-forward extension of the same ×10 structure.
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): 5.NBT.A.2 — 'Explain patterns in the number of zeros of the product when multiplying a number by powers of 10, and explain patterns in the placement of the decimal point when a decimal is multiplied or divided by a power of 10. Use whole-number exponents to denote powers of 10.'
• Operational details: Build exponent as a COUNT of factors of 10 (10³ = 10×10×10), then connect the exponent to both the zero-count in whole-number products AND the number of places the digits shift. Emphasise that DIGITS shift, the point stays; the exponent tells you how many places. Predict-then-check with a place-value chart before generalising.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): 'Write 10⁴ as an ordinary number and say how many zeros.' Tier B: 'Explain why 3.4 × 10² = 340 using the digit shift.' Tier C: 'Predict 2.56 × 10³ without calculating and justify the pattern.'
bestPractices: Define an exponent as the number of factors of 10 (10³ = 10×10×10), never as 'the number of zeros' — the zero-count is a CONSEQUENCE for whole numbers that breaks for decimals
Tie the exponent simultaneously to zeros in a whole-number product and to the number of places the digits shift, so the child sees them as the same pattern
Insist that the digits move and the decimal point stays fixed — explicitly reject 'move the decimal point'
Use predict-then-check on a place-value chart before stating the generalisation
Include ÷ by powers of 10 alongside × so the pattern is bidirectional and exponents are seen to shift digits the other way
keyRepresentations: Place-value chart with digits sliding N columns for ×10^N (point fixed)
Expanded factor strings: 10³ = 10×10×10 = 1000 with zeros tallied
Exponent stepper linking 10¹, 10², 10³ to 10, 100, 1000 and their zero counts
Arrow cards showing 3.4 → 34 → 340 with '×10' per hop
commonMisconceptions: 'Multiplying by a power of 10 just adds zeros' — fails for decimals (3.4 × 100 ≠ 3.400)
Reading 10³ as 10×3 = 30 (confusing exponent with a factor)
Believing the decimal point moves rather than the digits
Miscounting the shift — shifting by the base (10) rather than the exponent (3)
Assuming the exponent equals the number of digits in the result rather than factors of ten

learn.summary: For ages 10–11: explain the patterns in zeros when multiplying whole numbers by powers of ten, and the decimal-point placement when multiplying or dividing decimals by a power of ten, using whole-number exponents (10³ = 1000). The central idea is that an exponent counts factors of ten (10³ = 10×10×10) and equals the number of place-value columns the digits shift; the digits move while the decimal point stays fixed. The 'add zeros' shortcut is a consequence for whole numbers only and breaks for decimals (3.4 × 100 = 340, not 3.400); any zeros that do appear are placeholders for emptied whole-number columns, not zeros glued onto the original digits.

activities.title: Sweep the exponent on a place-value chart
feedback: If a learner writes 3.400 for 3.4 × 100, show on the chart that each ×10 slides the digits one column left: 3.4 → 34 → 340. The answer is 340, not 3.400 — the digits moved into larger columns and a single zero fills the now-empty ones place, rather than zeros being appended after the decimal point.

If the digits move the wrong way, anchor direction: multiplying a positive number by 10, 100 or 1000 makes it bigger, so digits travel to larger (left-hand) columns; dividing by these makes it smaller, so they move right.
If a learner shifts by 10 instead of by 3 for 10³, re-read the exponent: the little 3 is how many columns, not the base.

Confirm success when the learner predicts the number of columns from the exponent before moving any digit and explains that any zero appearing in the product is a placeholder for an emptied column, not a zero appended to the original digits.
activities.rationale: A live, predict-then-check representation lets the learner see the exponent, the zero-count and the shift-distance change together, which is what can turn a rule into a visible pattern. Including division makes the pattern bidirectional.
sourceClaims: Y5/Y6 pupils multiply and divide whole numbers and decimals by 10, 100 and 1000.
5.NBT.A.2: explain patterns in zeros and decimal-point placement for ×/÷ by powers of 10 and use whole-number exponents to denote powers of 10.
learnerActions: Place a number — e.g. 3.4 — on a place-value chart with the decimal point marked in a fixed position.

Set a power of ten (10¹, then 10², then 10³) and, for each, slide every digit left by the number shown in the exponent; the column count is the total shift from 3.4 and equals the exponent: 3.4 → 34 (10¹, one column) → 340 (10², two columns) → 3400 (10³, three columns), keeping the point pinned.
Alongside, write the power in expanded form (10³ = 10×10×10 = 1000) and tally its zeros.
State in words: 'The exponent tells me how many columns the digits jump.'
Repeat with division by powers of ten (shifting digits the other way, e.g. 3.4 ÷ 10 = 0.34) and with a whole number like 7 (7 × 10 = 70) to compare where zeros appear.
activities.intendedInsight: The exponent equals the number of place-value columns the digits shift, so 'powers of ten' and 'place-value shift' are the same idea. For a decimal like 3.4, multiplying by 10 does not append a zero (3.4 × 10 = 34, not 3.40); any zeros appearing in larger products such as 340 or 3400 are placeholders filling emptied whole-number columns, not zeros glued onto the original number — so the 'add-a-zero' rule is not the real pattern.

activities.title: Reference ladder of powers of ten
feedback: If a learner reads 10³ as 30, unpack it as repeated multiplication 10×10×10 = 1000 and set it beside 10×3 = 30.

If a learner says the exponent is 'the number of zeros' as a definition, restate it as the number of factors of ten — the zero-count of the power is a result, and using it as an 'add that many zeros' rule fails for decimals (3.4 × 100 = 340, not 3.400).
This ladder is a static reference; pair it with the moving chart so the digit shift is seen as an action, not only read.
activities.rationale: A revealable ladder is a strong anchor for the factor-string meaning of exponents and directly targets the 10³ = 30 confusion, though on its own it shows values rather than the shifting action.
sourceClaims: 5.NBT.A.2: explain patterns in zeros and decimal-point placement for ×/÷ by powers of 10 and use whole-number exponents to denote powers of 10.
learnerActions: Reveal each power from 10¹ to 10⁶ one at a time, writing its expanded factor string and ordinary value (e.g. 10⁴ = 10×10×10×10 = 10000).
For each, state the number of factors of ten and the number of zeros, and note that they match for these whole-number powers.
Contrast 10³ = 10×10×10 = 1000 with 10×3 = 30 aloud, so the exponent is not mistaken for a plain multiplier.
activities.intendedInsight: An exponent is a count of factors of ten, and for a power of ten written on its own the zero-count equals that factor count — while 10³ is emphatically not 10×3.

activities.title: Defend it against the 'add zeros' rule
feedback: If the learner cannot explain beyond the rule, ask them to say where each digit lands column by column.
Press for 'how many times bigger/smaller' to connect the exponent to the factor (100 for 10², 1000 for 10³).
activities.rationale: Requiring a spoken or written justification, not just an answer, discriminates understanding of the pattern from mimicry of a shortcut.
learnerActions: Face a prompt such as: 'A classmate says 3.4 × 10² = 3.400. Explain why that is wrong and give the correct answer.'
Justify using the digit shift: each ×10 moves the digits one column left, so 3.4 → 34 → 340.
Answer and explain 2.56 × 10³ (= 2560) and 2.56 ÷ 10³ (= 0.00256), saying how multiplication and division differ in shift direction.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the place-value shift exposes why 'add a zero' only looks right when the point sits at the end of a whole number, and why it fails for decimals; the zeros that do appear are placeholders for emptied columns.

activities.title: Predict-and-check consolidation
feedback: For 2.56 × 10³ the answer is 2560; 2.56000 just glues zeros on without shifting; 0.00256 divides instead of multiplies; 76.8 treats 10³ as 30.
Use any wrong choice as a cue to return to the place-value chart for that case.
activities.rationale: Short selected- and filled-response items can efficiently consolidate the pattern and surface the three named misconceptions as distractors; this checks that the pattern holds rather than demonstrating why it holds, so keep a task that requires a constructed explanation alongside it.
learnerActions: Complete items such as: fill in 10³ = ____; and choose the correct value of 2.56 × 10³ from options that include the add-zeros error 2.56000, the wrong-direction error 0.00256, and the exponent-as-multiplier error 76.8.
Put 10¹, 10², 10³, 10⁴, 10⁵ in order and match each to its zero count.
For each item, write one sentence saying why the chosen answer is right.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure recall that each power of ten corresponds to a fixed number of place-value shifts, with common error patterns ruled out explicitly.

constraints: Define an exponent as the number of factors of ten (10³ = 10×10×10), never as 'the number of zeros' — the zero-count of the power of ten is a consequence, and the 'add that many zeros' rule works only for whole-number products and breaks for decimals.

Distinguish appended zeros from placeholder zeros: multiplying a decimal does not append zeros after its decimal point to the original digits, but placeholder zeros may legitimately fill emptied whole-number columns (e.g. 340, 3400, 2560). Do not tell a learner 'no zeros appear' when the displayed product contains them.
Insist that the digits move and the decimal point stays fixed; avoid teaching 'move the decimal point' as the primary idea, though it can be mentioned as an equivalent description.
Include division by powers of ten alongside multiplication so the shift is seen as bidirectional.
The reference ladder is a static anchor: on its own it does not show the digit shift as an action, so pair it with the moving chart.
Selected-response consolidation checks the pattern but does not elicit the learner's own explanation; keep a task that requires constructing a justification.
Live recolouring/highlighting, digit sliding, a mobile exponent dial, zero tallies and a divide toggle are offered as optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not as required mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source lists one US standard citation as not verified (verified:false for 5.NBT.A.2); treat that citation's status as unconfirmed.

Clarified the lead activity's column-count wording so each total shift is tied to its exponent (10¹→one column, 10²→two columns, 10³→three columns), avoiding a reading where a single ×10 hop is labelled two columns.

Corrected the original 'the columns fill without any zeros being added' framing: 3.4 × 100 = 340 and 3.4 × 1000 = 3400 do contain placeholder zeros, and 34 → 340 appends a placeholder; the guidance distinguishes zeros appended after the decimal point (the 3.400 error) from placeholder zeros filling emptied columns.

The source's correct-answer phrasing 'the decimal point moves three places right' is retained only as an equivalent secondary description, subordinated to the 'digits move, point fixed' framing per the pedagogy's own best practice.

probeDeeper: Why does the answer get bigger, and by how many times exactly?
What does the little 3 in 10³ actually tell you to do?
Would 'add three zeros' work for 2.56 × 10³? Why or why not?
What is 2.56 ÷ 10³, and how is it different from multiplying?
assess.correctAnswer: 2,560. Multiplying by 10³ means ×1000, so every digit becomes worth a thousand times more and shifts three places to the left (equivalently the decimal point moves three places right, and a zero fills the empty ones place).

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Add three zeros' rule — appends zeros to the written digits, giving 2.56000 for 2.56 × 10³.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that ×10 shifts every digit one place left (2.56→25.6→256→2560); the 'add a zero' shortcut only works for whole numbers because the point sits at the end.
errorPatterns.distractor: 2.56000 — you add three zeros.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Zeros are stuck onto the decimal without the point moving; answer keeps the decimal in place.

errorPatterns.pattern: Moves the point the wrong way — divides instead of multiplies, giving 0.00256.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor direction: multiplying makes it bigger, so digits move to larger places (left); rehearse on a place-value chart with the point fixed and digits sliding.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer is smaller than the start; point moved left for a multiplication.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the exponent as a plain multiplier — reads 10³ as 30, so 2.56 × 10³ becomes 2.56 × 30 = 76.8.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Unpack 10³ = 10×10×10 = 1000; contrast with 10×3 = 30 so the exponent is seen as repeated multiplication.
errorPatterns.distractor: 76.8 — you multiply by 30.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child multiplies by 30 (or says 10³ = 30), confusing exponent with base×exponent.

responseLevels.gap: Appends zeros, moves the point the wrong way, or treats 10³ as 30.
responseLevels.full: Predicts the result via place-value shift, explains the exponent as repeated ×10, and handles decimals and both × and ÷ by powers of ten consistently.
responseLevels.partial: Gets whole-number cases right by rule but the pattern breaks with a decimal like 2.56, or cannot explain why the point moves.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Without calculating it out, what is 2.56 × 10³? Explain why the digits or the decimal point move the way they do.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands the pattern explains it by place-value shift (×10 three times moves digits left) and correctly gets 2,560. A child running the 'add three zeros' rule writes 2.56000; one who thinks the exponent is a multiplier gets 76.8 (×30). The explanation, not just the answer, reveals whether the zero-pattern is understood or mimicked.
