pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 7-8. Determine whether a quantity (initially up to 20) is odd or even by pairing objects: even = every object has a partner (no leftover); odd = one left over. Even numbers can be written as two equal addends (8 = 4 + 4).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): counting in 2s and recognising odd/even patterns support number-structure work (KS1→Y3).
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.OA.3 'determine whether a group of objects (up to 20) has an odd or even number of members, e.g. by pairing objects or counting them by 2s; write an equation to express an even number as a sum of two equal addends'.
• Operational details — Build odd/even from the concrete pairing action (line up objects in twos; is there a lone one?), link to skip-counting in 2s, and connect to the doubles fact (even = double of something). Later generalise the digit rule (look at the ones/last digit) but ground it first in the pairing structure so the rule is understood, not memorised.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 7, emerging): pairs objects to decide odd/even up to ~10. Tier B (age 7-8, secure): decides odd/even to 20 by pairing or counting in 2s and writes an even number as n + n. Tier C (age 8, extending): states and justifies the last-digit rule (0,2,4,6,8) and predicts odd/even for larger numbers.
bestPractices: Anchor in the pairing action first: arrange in twos and check for a leftover — the definition, not a memorised list.
Link to counting in 2s and to doubles (even numbers are doubles), connecting three ideas.
Have children write even numbers as equal addends (8 = 4 + 4) to formalise 'made of pairs'.
Introduce the last-digit shortcut only AFTER the pairing meaning is secure, and justify it via the pairs in the ones.
Use two-column / ten-frame arrangements so 'paired vs one sticking out' is visually obvious.
keyRepresentations: Objects arranged in two rows / pairs (leftover = odd)
Ten-frame (pairs in columns; a lone counter shows odd)
Number track coloured by odd/even (alternating pattern)
Counting-in-2s hops on a number line
Doubles facts (n + n) linked to even numbers
commonMisconceptions: Thinking odd/even is about being 'big/small' or arbitrary, not about pairing.
Confusing odd/even with the count of digits or with multiples of other numbers.
Believing 0 is odd, or being unsure whether 0/2 are even.
Memorising the last-digit rule with no grasp of why (can't justify).
Miscounting pairs and so misclassifying near-boundary numbers.

learn.summary: For ages 7-8: build the meaning of odd/even from the pairing action — line up objects two-by-two and check for a leftover (even = everything pairs, odd = one left over). Ground the concept in pairing, counting in 2s, and doubles (even = n + n) before introducing the last-digit shortcut, so the rule is understood rather than memorised.

activities.title: Pair-them-up frame
feedback: If the learner thinks odd/even depends on the number being big or small, show a small odd number and a large even number side by side so size is decoupled from parity.
When a counter is stranded, highlight it (e.g. it glows or wobbles alone) and name it 'the leftover with no partner — that's what odd means'.
When the slider ticks up, prompt: 'Did adding one make a new pair, or leave one stranded? What does that make the number now?'
When a child writes 8 = 4 + 4, connect it to the frame: 'four pairs, or two equal groups of four — that's why it's even.'
activities.rationale: Odd/even is defined by the pairing action, so letting the child change the count and watch the parity flip makes the alternating structure and the doubles link concrete. The live recolouring, lone-counter highlight, slider, and equal-addends strip are optional interaction examples that make the pairing mechanism visible; they are not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: Determine whether a group of objects (up to 20) is odd or even by pairing or counting by 2s, and write an even number as a sum of two equal addends (2.OA.3).
Odd/even should be grounded in the pairing structure and doubles before the last-digit rule is introduced.
learnerActions: Choose a number of counters (start up to 10, then up to 20) and drop them into a two-row frame so they arrange into pairs.
Look at the result: if one counter is left with no partner the number is ODD; if every counter is matched the number is EVEN.
Use a slider or counter to add one and remove one, watching whether the lone counter appears or disappears each time.
Say out loud what changes each step: adding one either strands a single counter (makes it odd) or creates a new pair (makes it even).
Use an 'equal addends' strip to write each even number as n + n (e.g. 8 = 4 + 4).
activities.intendedInsight: A number is even when its objects pair with none left over and odd when exactly one is left over; because adding one either completes a pair or strands a single, odd and even alternate, and every even number is a double (n + n).

activities.title: Predict then check with real counters
feedback: If a child says 13 is even because 'you can split it into 7 and 6', have them line the 7 and 6 up in pairs and show that one is stranded — even means pairs with none left over, so the two groups must be equal.
If a child answers instantly from size ('even because it's big'), show small and large numbers of each parity so size is clearly not the rule.
If the reasoning is right ('one left over means odd') but the count slips, slow the one-to-one matching and recount the leftover pile — the concept is intact; support the counting.
For 0: there is nothing left unpaired, so 0 is even — invite the child to articulate this with the 'none left over' definition.
activities.rationale: A predict-then-check task with a stated reason exposes whether a child treats 'odd' as an unpairable leftover or just as a label, and separates conceptual misunderstanding (unequal-split or size rules) from simple miscounting.
sourceClaims: Determine whether a group of objects (up to 20) is odd or even by pairing or counting by 2s, and write an even number as a sum of two equal addends (2.OA.3).
learnerActions: Take a pile of counters (e.g. 13). Before touching them, predict whether they will all get a partner or whether one will be left over, and say why.
Pair them two-by-two to check your prediction.
Discuss: why is 13 odd but 12 even — what changes when you add one more?
Tackle a friend's claim that 'zero is odd because there's nothing to pair', and decide whether 0 is odd or even.
Try reasoning about a large number (e.g. 100 or 24 or 47): how could you tell odd or even without pairing every one?
activities.intendedInsight: Parity is about whether everything pairs with nothing left over, not about size or whether the number can be split into any two groups; this reasoning generalises to larger numbers.

activities.title: Counting in 2s and the last-digit rule
feedback: If a child recites the last-digit rule but cannot justify it, pair up a ten to show it makes 5 pairs with none left over, then return to pairing in the ones and ask why those digits leave no leftover.
If skip-counting and pairing give different answers, recount together — both methods should agree for the same number.
Link each even result back to a double (n + n) to reinforce that even numbers are made of pairs.
activities.rationale: The last-digit shortcut is introduced only after the pairing meaning is built, so it is understood and justifiable rather than memorised; counting in 2s and the coloured number track connect three representations of the same idea. This activity targets the extending tier (Tier C) where children justify the rule and predict for larger numbers.
sourceClaims: Odd/even should be grounded in the pairing structure and doubles before the last-digit rule is introduced.
Counting in 2s and recognising odd/even number patterns are part of the primary number curriculum.
learnerActions: Count a group by 2s (hop along a number line in twos) to decide if the total is even, and compare this with the pairing result for the same number.
Colour a number track by odd and even to reveal the alternating pattern.
After the pairing meaning is secure, look at the ones digit of several numbers (e.g. 20, 12, 24, 16, 18, 47, 53) and notice which digits (0,2,4,6,8) go with even.

State and justify the last-digit rule by reasoning that every ten makes 5 pairs with none left over, so whether there is a leftover depends only on the ones; then use it to predict the parity of a larger number.
activities.intendedInsight: Counting in 2s, the alternating number-track pattern, and the last-digit rule all describe the same pairing structure; the digit shortcut is a justified consequence of pairing, not a memorised fact.

constraints: Anchor the concept in the pairing action first; introduce the last-digit shortcut only after the pairing meaning is secure and have children justify it: every ten splits into 5 pairs with none left over, so only the ones can leave a leftover.
'Even' means pairs with none left over — equal pairing. Splitting a number into any two groups (e.g. 13 as 7 and 6) does not make it even; the groups must be equal.
0 is even (nothing is left unpaired); address the 'zero is odd' claim explicitly rather than leaving it ambiguous.
Decouple parity from size: deliberately show small odd numbers and large even numbers so children do not infer parity from magnitude.

A sorting/categorising or multiple-choice task (sort into odd/even bins, fill 8 = __ + __, choose and explain) is suitable for consolidation once the pairing meaning is built; such a task can check or reinforce classification but does not by itself elicit the independent pairing construction and explanation.

A static paired-vs-leftover illustration with tap-to-reveal is a useful reference, but it cannot be manipulated by the child; the alternation insight is stronger when the learner changes the count and watches the parity flip.
Use two-column / ten-frame arrangements so 'paired vs one sticking out' is visually obvious; these can be physical counters or an on-screen model.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three cited sources (CCSS 2.OA.3 and the NCETM pairing-before-rule claim) are marked verified:false in the source row; the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified:true. Do not treat the unverified claims as confirmed.

The source material frames open dialogue and 3D manipulatives as 'poor' fits for this concept. Those are catalog fit rankings, not evidence of universal inefficacy — discussion is used productively here in the predict-then-check and zero-is-even reasoning, and the planar nature of pairing is a specific reason 3D adds little for this particular task, not a universal law.

Self-audit: pairing/parity logic checked — adding one to an even number strands a single (odd); adding one to an odd number completes a pair (even); alternation holds. 0 is even. 8 = 4 + 4 is correct. Ones digits of 20/24 are even, 47/53 are odd. The 'split into 7 and 6' example is correctly flagged as a misconception (unequal groups), not taught as valid.
The source misconception 'confusing odd/even with the count of digits or with multiples of other numbers' is only implicitly addressed; a dedicated probe could be added if desired.

assess.poeTask: Give the child 13 counters. Before touching them, ask: 'If you pair these two-by-two, will they all get a partner, or will one be left over?' Have them commit to a prediction and say why, THEN pair to check. The pre-observation reason exposes whether 'odd' is understood as an unpairable leftover or just a label.
probeDeeper: Why is 13 odd but 12 even — what changes when you add one more?
What if it had been 100 counters — how could you tell odd or even without pairing every one?
A friend says 'zero is odd because there's nothing to pair.' What would you say?
Show me with these counters what 'one left over' looks like.
assess.correctAnswer: Odd — if you pair the 13 up (two by two), there is one left over that has no partner; a number is even only when everything pairs with nothing left over.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'It's even because you can make two groups — 7 and 6.' Treats 'can be split into two groups' as the definition of even, ignoring that the groups must be equal.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront with counters: make the two groups, then line them up in pairs — show 7 and 6 do not match and one is stranded. Define even as 'pairs with none left over'.
errorPatterns.distractor: Even — you can split it into a group of 7 and a group of 6.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child calls 13 (or 7, 9) even and justifies with any two-way split rather than pairing into twos.

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges odd/even by how big the number is or whether it 'looks like' a counting-by-twos number, e.g. thinks large numbers are even.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ground the judgement in the ones digit and in pairing; show small and large numbers of each parity so size is decoupled from parity.
errorPatterns.distractor: Even — thirteen is a biggish number so it's even.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child answers instantly from the size of 13 with no pairing reasoning, or says 'even because it's big'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Has the pairing idea but miscounts the counters and reports the wrong leftover, e.g. pairs 12 and forgets the 13th.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the count — slow the one-to-one, recount the leftover pile — do not reteach the odd/even concept, which is intact.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reasoning is correct ('one left over means odd') but the count of counters or of leftovers slips.

responseLevels.gap: Answers from size or an unequal-split rule; calls 13 even, or gives 'odd' with no pairing reason.
responseLevels.full: States odd because pairing leaves one over, generalises to 'even = pairs with none left / ends in 0,2,4,6,8', and predicts parity of a new number (e.g. 24, 47) by rule.
responseLevels.partial: Says odd and can pair counters to show the leftover for 13, but cannot yet state the general rule or predict a new number without laying it out.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Is 13 odd or even? How do you know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with the pairing/grouping idea says 'odd, because one is left over'. A child who only knows a size rule or a 'split into two groups' rule will accept 13 as even (7 and 6 are two groups) or guess from magnitude, so the REASON — not the answer alone — separates them.

pedagogy.summary: Comparing two fractions that share a numerator or a denominator, by reasoning about the SIZE of the parts rather than the size of the digits. Same denominator: the parts are the same size, so more of them is more (5/6 > 2/6). Same numerator: the same COUNT of parts, but a larger denominator makes each part smaller, so the fraction is smaller (3/8 < 3/4). Both fractions must refer to the same whole. Comparisons are recorded with >, =, <.
bestPractices: Anchor same-numerator reasoning in sharing: the more people share, the smaller each share — 1/3 of an object is greater than 1/4 (IES Rec 1).
Reason about part SIZE and count, never the digits alone: 'the same number of parts, but each eighth is smaller than each fourth'.
Insist both fractions refer to the SAME whole before comparing.
Use fraction strips/bars aligned to one whole and a single number line.
Confront whole-number bias with contrasting cases (3/8 vs 3/4, where the bigger denominator gives the smaller fraction).
Read the >/</= symbol as opening toward the larger amount.
keyRepresentations: Aligned fraction strips / bars on one whole
Single 0–1 number line
Same-whole area models
Equal-sharing scenario (more sharers = smaller share)
commonMisconceptions: Whole-number bias — a larger denominator means a larger fraction (1/8 > 1/3 because 8 > 3; 3/8 > 3/4 by comparing denominators) (IES)
Comparing across different wholes (3/4 of a small bar vs 1/2 of a large bar)
Treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers
Over-applying 'bigger bottom = smaller' so blindly it mis-fires on same-denominator pairs

learn.summary: Compare two fractions that share a numerator or a denominator by reasoning about the SIZE and COUNT of the parts, not the size of the digits. Same denominator: parts are equal-sized, so more of them is more (5/6 > 2/6). Same numerator: the same count of parts, but a larger denominator makes each part smaller, so the fraction is smaller (3/8 < 3/4). When comparing by shaded models, both fractions must be drawn on the SAME whole for the picture to be fair; comparisons are recorded with >, =, <.

activities.title: Lock the numerator, grow the denominator: watch the parts shrink
feedback: If a learner writes 3/8 > 3/4 because 8 > 4, point back to the shaded bars on the same whole: 'You have three pieces on each bar. Which single piece is bigger, an eighth or a fourth? So which set of three covers more?'
If correct, extend: 'If you cut into sixteenths instead, would one piece be bigger or smaller than an eighth? What does that tell you about 3/16 versus 3/8?'
If a learner compares bars of different lengths, stop and insist both fractions be drawn on identical wholes before deciding.
activities.rationale: Same-numerator reasoning follows from sharing: the more sharers, the smaller each share (1/3 > 1/4). Making the fixed count of parts visibly shrink as the denominator grows directly confronts whole-number bias, a documented misconception addressed by contrasting cases.
sourceClaims: Same-numerator comparison follows from sharing (more sharers = smaller share; 1/3 > 1/4); whole-number bias (e.g. 1/8 > 1/3 because 8 > 3, or 3/8 > 3/5 by comparing denominators) is a documented misconception addressed by contrasting cases; children must grasp that a part's size decreases as the denominator increases.
learnerActions: Set up two bars (strips, drawn area models, or an interactive tool) pinned to the SAME whole.
Set both bars to 3/4 to start (numerator 3 and denominator 4 on each), so the two shaded amounts are identical.
On the first bar, raise the denominator from 4 to 8 so it shows 3/8; keep the second at 3/4.
Describe what happens to each part as the bottom number grows from 4 to 8, then state which shaded amount is larger.
Write the correct symbol between them (3/8 __ 3/4) with the sign opening toward the larger amount.
Say aloud: 'Same number of parts (3), but each eighth is smaller than each fourth, so 3/8 is less than 3/4.'
activities.intendedInsight: When the numerator is held fixed, a larger denominator cuts the whole into more, smaller parts, so the fraction gets SMALLER, not bigger. The digits '8 > 4' do not mean '3/8 > 3/4'.

activities.title: Same denominator: count the equal parts
feedback: If a learner reverses this (says 2/6 > 5/6) by over-applying a 'bigger number means smaller' idea carried over from same-numerator pairs, clarify when each rule applies: 'The bottoms are the same here — sixths are sixths. So just count: is five pieces more or less than two?'
If correct, ask them to read the symbol aloud and confirm it opens toward the larger amount.
activities.rationale: Learners who memorise 'bigger denominator means smaller' can blanket-apply it and mis-fire on same-denominator pairs. Pairing this case with the same-numerator case forces attention to WHEN each line of reasoning is valid, rather than to the digits alone.
learnerActions: On one whole, shade 5/6 and 2/6 on aligned bars or on a single 0–1 number line.
State that the sixths are all the same size on both.
Decide which is larger by counting how many equal parts are shaded, then write 5/6 __ 2/6.
Explain: 'Same-size sixths, and five of them is more than two, so 5/6 > 2/6.'
activities.intendedInsight: When the denominator is shared, the parts are identical in size, so the fraction with more parts (larger numerator) is larger. This is a DIFFERENT comparison from the same-numerator case and must not be solved by 'bigger bottom = smaller'.

activities.title: Does 3/4 always beat 3/8? The same-whole rule
feedback: If a learner concludes 3/8 > 3/4 from mismatched drawings, ask: 'Were both bars the same size to begin with? Redraw them the same length and look again.'
If correct, challenge: 'Can you make two fractions where the one with the bigger bottom number is actually the smaller fraction, and show why on equal wholes?'
activities.rationale: Comparing the shaded regions of fractions drawn on different wholes is a distinct misconception from whole-number bias and needs its own explicit confrontation; drawing on a shared whole keeps the picture fair, a precondition stressed in the pedagogy.
learnerActions: Draw 3/4 on a short bar and 3/8 on a long bar, deliberately mismatched.
Compare the shaded regions by eye and notice the drawing can be misleading.
Redraw both fractions on identical wholes and compare again.
State in your own words why, when you compare by shaded pictures, both fractions must be drawn on the same whole for the comparison to be fair.
activities.intendedInsight: When you judge which fraction is larger by looking at shaded regions, both must be drawn on the same whole for the picture to be fair; 3/4 of a small bar can look smaller than 3/8 of a large bar, even though, as numbers, 3/4 > 3/8.

activities.title: Practise and sort comparisons
feedback: Accept an answer only when the learner can justify it by part size or count; a right symbol with a digit-only reason ('8 is bigger') should prompt 'bigger what — bigger number, or bigger piece?'
Mix same-numerator and same-denominator items so learners must select the right reasoning each time, not run one rule blindly.
activities.rationale: Practice and ordering consolidate comparison once part-size reasoning is built; interleaving the two pair types guards against mechanically applying a single rule. Recognition/selection tasks consolidate and check classification but do not by themselves elicit the independent construction and justification that the modelling activities require.
learnerActions: Decide the correct sign for same-numerator pairs (e.g. 3/8 vs 3/4) and same-denominator pairs (e.g. 5/6 vs 2/6).
Order short sets of same-numerator fractions and, separately, same-denominator fractions from smallest to largest.
Sort pairs into >, =, and < groups and, where used, match a fraction pair to its symbol.
For each answer, state the reason in part-size/count language rather than quoting digits.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency in applying the two lines of reasoning across varied pairs, with the correct rule chosen for the structure of each pair.

activities.title: Reference fraction wall (support)
feedback: Use this to jog memory, then ask the learner to reconstruct the comparison on their own same-whole model and explain it.
activities.rationale: A fixed fraction wall supports recall of relative sizes but does not let the learner vary a denominator or test a new comparison, so it is a reference scaffold rather than the main investigation.
learnerActions: Line up two rows of a fraction wall, e.g. place 3/8 under 3/4 on the same whole, to see relative sizes.
Use a lift-the-flap or note to recall 'eighths are smaller, so 3/8 is less than 3/4'.
Return to the drawing/building activities to test and justify an actual comparison.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction wall helps recall relative sizes of common fractions as a reference aid.

constraints: When comparing by shaded models/pictures, both fractions must be drawn on the same whole; a picture drawn on a different-sized whole can mislead. (As numbers, fractions such as 3/4 and 3/8 remain comparable regardless of any drawing.)
Reason about the SIZE and COUNT of parts, never the digits alone (e.g. 'the same number of parts, but each eighth is smaller than each fourth').
Read > and < as opening toward the larger amount; = means the two amounts are equal.

The same-numerator and same-denominator cases are DIFFERENT comparisons: with a shared denominator compare numerators (more same-size parts is more); with a shared numerator compare part sizes (larger denominator = smaller parts). Do not let a learner apply 'bigger bottom = smaller' to a same-denominator pair.
The fraction wall is a recall aid only; it cannot let the learner vary the denominator or test a comparison, so it should not replace the modelling/building activities.
Recognition and sorting tasks consolidate and check classification but do not on their own elicit independent construction of a model and a justification.
This microtopic targets same-numerator and same-denominator comparisons for age 8–9; general comparison of fractions with different numerators AND denominators is beyond this scope.

Physical fraction strips and card models have slight real thickness and are approximations of ideal equal parts; treat any paper or on-screen model as a model of the same-whole comparison, not the ideal figure itself.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The IES/WWC claim is marked verified in the source row; the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked unverified (verified:false) and is not cited in any activity's sourceClaims.

Interactive examples (two bars pinned to one whole, locking numerators, dragging the denominator, auto-drawn comparison symbol, mismatched-whole warning, tapping fraction-wall rows, lift-the-flap) are preserved as OPTIONAL ways to make the mechanism concrete; equivalent results can be reached with paper strips, drawn area models, or a single number line.

Original source rated a third dimension and an in-role conversation as poor-fit for this planar comparison task; these are retained as observations about this task's nature, not as universal claims that such media can never teach fraction comparison.

The original row states the common-whole requirement without qualification; it has been scoped here to comparing represented (shaded) portions, since fractions as numbers remain comparable irrespective of the drawn whole.

The source's whole-number-bias illustration '3/8 > 3/5 because 8 > 5' is retained only inside the cited misconception claim; it is a wrong belief to confront (correctly 3/8 < 3/5), never offered as a valid comparison in a learner task.

probeDeeper: You said 3/8 is smaller. If I cut the whole into even more parts — sixteenths — would one part be bigger or smaller than an eighth?
Which is bigger, 3/4 of this bar or 3/4 of that longer bar? Does 3/4 always beat 3/8?
Write the correct sign between 5/6 and 2/6 — which way does it point, and why?
Make up two fractions where the one with the bigger bottom number is actually the smaller fraction.
assess.correctAnswer: 3/8 < 3/4 (same number of parts, but eighths are smaller than fourths, so three eighths is less than three fourths); 5/6 > 2/6 (same-size sixths, and five of them is more than two). Both drawn on the same whole.

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number bias — '3/8 is bigger than 3/4 because 8 is bigger than 4'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Align both bars on the same whole; show each eighth is smaller than each fourth; use contrasting cases so the bigger denominator gives the smaller fraction
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Orders the same-numerator pair by denominator size

errorPatterns.pattern: Over-corrected rule — 'bigger bottom always means smaller', mis-fired so 2/6 beats 5/6
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach the concept; clarify WHEN each rule applies — same denominator means compare the numerators (more same-size parts is more)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reverses or freezes on the same-denominator control set

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares across different wholes — draws 3/4 on a small bar and the other on a large bar and compares the shaded regions directly
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist both fractions be drawn on identical wholes before any comparison
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Uses mismatched-size wholes for the two fractions

responseLevels.gap: Orders by comparing digits (denominator or numerator alone); says 3/8 > 3/4; may reverse the same-denominator pair.
responseLevels.full: Writes 3/8 < 3/4 and 5/6 > 2/6, justifies each on a same-whole model by reasoning about part size and count, and recognises the whole must be the same for a fair comparison.
responseLevels.partial: Gets the same-denominator comparison right but falters on the same-numerator pair (whole-number bias), or gets both by a rule without a same-whole model or part-size reasoning.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Task: using bars drawn on the same whole (or a number line), show which is larger and write >, <, or = — first for 3/8 and 3/4, then for 5/6 and 2/6. I'll watch how you build and decide each one.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The same-numerator pair (3/8 vs 3/4) triggers whole-number bias — a child ordering by denominator writes 3/8 > 3/4. The same-denominator control (5/6 vs 2/6) catches a child who has memorised 'bigger bottom = smaller' and blanket-reverses, wrongly making 2/6 > 5/6. Only part-size reasoning gets both right.

sources.claim: Same-numerator comparison follows from sharing (more sharers = smaller share; 1/3 > 1/4); whole-number bias (e.g. 1/8 > 1/3 because 8 > 3, or 3/8 > 3/5 by comparing denominators) is a documented misconception addressed by contrasting cases; children must grasp that a part's size decreases as the denominator increases.
sources.source: IES/WWC Practice Guide, Developing Effective Fractions Instruction for K-8 (Siegler et al., 2010, NCEE 2010-4039)

sources.claim: Pupils compare and order unit fractions and fractions with the same denominators in Year 3 (age 7–8); fraction comparison develops across KS2.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (KS1-2)

pedagogy.summary: Children read and write time to five minutes — including quarter past and quarter to — and draw the hands. Two representational hurdles: reading the minute hand in fives (the minute hand on the 5 means 25 past, not 5), and the 'to' side, where times after half past belong to the NEXT hour and the hour hand sits over halfway toward it. 'Quarter to' is new and easily confused with 'quarter past'. Taught by counting round the clock in fives and using a past/to (right/left) split.
bestPractices: Count the minute intervals in fives round the clock so each number stands for a multiple of 5
Split the clock: right-hand side = 'past', left-hand side = 'to'
Teach that after half past, times are 'minutes to' the NEXT hour and the hour hand is over halfway between the two numbers
Contrast quarter past (hour hand just past a number) with quarter to (hour hand nearly at the next number)
Read AND write — analogue ↔ words ↔ digital (quarter past 9 / 9:15) — and draw the hands
keyRepresentations: A clock with the 5-minute counts marked around it
A past/to split clock (right = past, left = to)
A geared clock for the hour-hand position
Triple cards: words / analogue / digital (quarter past 9 – 9:15)
commonMisconceptions: Reads the minute-hand number directly (minute hand on 5 → '5 past' not 25 past; on 2 → '2 past' not 10 past)
Confuses quarter past and quarter to
After half past, keeps counting 'past' (35 minutes past) instead of switching to 'to' (25 to)
Names the wrong hour for a 'to' time, or puts the hour hand on a number instead of partway toward the next

learn.summary: Children aged 6–7 read and write time to five minutes — including quarter past and quarter to — and draw the clock hands. Two representational hurdles dominate: reading the minute hand in fives (the minute hand on the 5 means 25 past, not 5), and the 'to' side, where times after half past are named in relation to the NEXT hour (although the digital hour stays as the earlier hour, e.g. quarter to 4 = 3:45) and the hour hand sits over halfway toward it. 'Quarter to' is new and easily confused with 'quarter past'. The core teaching moves are counting round the clock in fives and splitting the clock into a 'past' (right) and 'to' (left) side.

activities.title: Count round the clock in fives
feedback: If a learner reads 3:25 as 'five past three', pause and recount the fives aloud from the 12 to the 5 (5, 10, 15, 20, 25) and ask them to land on the number the hand actually reaches.
Confirm: minute hand on the 5, counted in fives, is 25; the hour hand sitting between the 3 and the 4 (not yet halfway) tells us the hour is still 3, so it is twenty-five past three.
For a minute hand on the 2, recount: 5, 10 — that is ten past, not two past.
activities.rationale: Counting the intervals in fives directly targets the most common error — reading the minute-hand numeral as the minutes — by making each number stand for its five-count before any real time is read.
sourceClaims: White Rose Year 2 Time teaches quarter past/to and time to five minutes, and lists as 'things to look out for': children confuse 'quarter past' and 'quarter to'; keep the hour hand on a number instead of partway between; say the number the minute hand points to (e.g. '1 minute past' instead of '5 minutes past'); and after half past continue 'past' (35 past) instead of 'to' (25 to). It teaches right = past / left = to, and that times after half past relate to the next hour with the hour hand over halfway between the numbers.

The hour hand is significantly harder to position than the minute hand, and children frequently use 'Number Matching' (matching a digit to a clock numeral, accurate only ~half the time) and treat hour and minute units separately — the mechanism behind reading the minute-hand numeral directly and mis-placing the hour hand.
learnerActions: Starting at the 12, count the minute marks in fives round the clock, saying the running total at each number: 1→5, 2→10, 3→15, 4→20, 5→25, and so on.
Label (or tap, if using an interactive clock where each number lights its running five-count) each number with its minute value.
Then read a real clock showing 3:25: minute hand on the 5, hour hand between the 3 and the 4 but not yet halfway, so the hour is still 3. State the minutes as twenty-five, not five.
Repeat with other 'past' times to five minutes.
activities.intendedInsight: The number the minute hand points to is NOT the number of minutes — each number stands for its multiple of five, so the minute hand on the 5 means 25 minutes, not 5.

activities.title: The 'past' to 'to' switch at the bottom of the clock
feedback: If a learner gives a '35 past three' style answer for a left-side time, remind them they have crossed the bottom of the clock onto the 'to' side, and count the minutes back to the next hour (to four).
Check the named hour: on the 'to' side, we name the hour the hands are heading toward, not the one just left behind.

If an interactive clock is available, moving the minute hand across the 6 and watching 'twenty-five past' flip to 'twenty-five to' — with the named hour advancing — makes the switch visible; otherwise trace it with a finger on a geared clock.
activities.rationale: The right/past–left/to split and counting back from the 6 directly address the error of continuing to count 'past' after the half hour and naming the wrong hour.
sourceClaims: White Rose Year 2 Time teaches quarter past/to and time to five minutes, and lists as 'things to look out for': children confuse 'quarter past' and 'quarter to'; keep the hour hand on a number instead of partway between; say the number the minute hand points to (e.g. '1 minute past' instead of '5 minutes past'); and after half past continue 'past' (35 past) instead of 'to' (25 to). It teaches right = past / left = to, and that times after half past relate to the next hour with the hour hand over halfway between the numbers.
learnerActions: Split the clock down the middle: the right-hand side is 'past', the left-hand side is 'to'.
Watch (or move the minute hand) as it travels from twenty-five past across the 6 and up the left side. As it crosses the bottom, start counting the minutes BACK to the next hour instead of forward.
Note that once past the half hour, the named hour becomes the NEXT hour, and the hour hand moves over halfway between the two numbers toward it.
Read twenty-five to four: minute hand on the 7, hour hand over halfway from 3 to 4 — and say why it is 'to four' and not '35 past three'.
activities.intendedInsight: After half past, we count the minutes remaining until the NEXT hour and name that next hour; the hour hand sits over halfway between the current and next number to show this.

activities.title: Quarter past versus quarter to, and placing the hour hand
feedback: If a learner draws twenty to four with the hour hand on the 3, point out the hour hand should be over halfway toward the 4 because it is nearly the next hour.
If quarter to 4 is read as quarter past 4, check which side of the clock the minute hand is on: the 9 is on the 'to' side, so it is quarter to.
Reinforce: quarter past = hour hand just past the number; quarter to = hour hand nearly at the next number.
activities.rationale: Explicitly contrasting the two quarters and showing the hour hand's gradual position between numbers addresses the confusion of the two quarters and the habit of placing the hour hand on a number.
sourceClaims: White Rose Year 2 Time teaches quarter past/to and time to five minutes, and lists as 'things to look out for': children confuse 'quarter past' and 'quarter to'; keep the hour hand on a number instead of partway between; say the number the minute hand points to (e.g. '1 minute past' instead of '5 minutes past'); and after half past continue 'past' (35 past) instead of 'to' (25 to). It teaches right = past / left = to, and that times after half past relate to the next hour with the hour hand over halfway between the numbers.

The hour hand is significantly harder to position than the minute hand, and children frequently use 'Number Matching' (matching a digit to a clock numeral, accurate only ~half the time) and treat hour and minute units separately — the mechanism behind reading the minute-hand numeral directly and mis-placing the hour hand.
learnerActions: Contrast two clocks: quarter past 9 (minute hand on the 3, hour hand just past the 9) and quarter to 4 (minute hand on the 9, hour hand nearly at the 4).
Say which side of the clock each is on (quarter past = right side; quarter to = left side) and which hour is named.

For a 'to' time, draw the hour hand over halfway toward the next number — NOT resting on a number. For quarter to 4, place the hour hand nearly at the 4; for twenty to four, place the hour hand over halfway from the 3 to the 4 with the minute hand on the 8.
Check: is the hour hand closer to the current number or the next number?
activities.intendedInsight: 'Quarter to' and 'quarter past' are different sides of the clock with different named hours; the hour hand moves gradually and, for 'to' times, sits part-way toward the next number rather than on a number.

activities.title: Translate between words, clock face, and digital
feedback: Check that drawn hands match: the minute hand lands on the correct number for the five-count and the hour hand is placed appropriately (on the 'to' side it should be part-way toward the next number).

When writing quarter past 9 as a digital time, confirm 15 minutes past, so 9:15; for quarter to, the minutes are 45 and the hour is still the earlier numeral (quarter to 4 = 3:45) — flag this as a point to watch when introducing digital 'to' times.

If an activity only asks learners to recognise or match a given answer, follow it with drawing or writing so the learner produces the time independently (recognition alone does not show they can produce it).
activities.rationale: Reading, writing, and drawing times on analogue clocks (production, not just recognition) is what the objective requires; linking these to the digital form is an extra connection that consolidates the representational links.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils should 'tell and write the time to five minutes, including quarter past/to the hour and draw the hands on a clock face to show these times' (statutory Measurement content).
learnerActions: Match or build triple sets linking the same time across three forms: words ('quarter past 9'), an analogue clock face, and digital ('9:15').
Given a time in words, draw the hands on a blank clock to show it (e.g. draw twenty to four: minute hand on the 8, hour hand over halfway from 3 to 4).
Given an analogue clock, write the time in both words and digits.
Fill in the digital form of a worded time: 'quarter past 9 = 9:15'.
activities.intendedInsight: The same moment in time can be read, spoken, written in words, and written in digits, and the learner can move fluently between all of these forms including drawing the hands themselves.

activities.title: Rehearse saying times aloud
feedback: If a spoken time is wrong, return to the clock face and recount or re-split before saying it again.
Encourage full relative phrases ('quarter to four') rather than bare digits, since the wording is part of the objective.
activities.rationale: Spoken rehearsal supports the relative language of time, and the form of a time expression can shape how children reason about the clock. This is a supporting activity — spoken rehearsal alone does not elicit the reading, writing, and drawing of actual clock hands, which the objective requires.
sourceClaims: The FORM of a time expression shapes reasoning: relative expressions ('half past 11', 'quarter to') elicited part-whole/fraction descriptions of the clock while precise times (2:30) elicited whole-number descriptions, in interviews with Grades 2 and 4 (corroborated across Grades 2-5).
learnerActions: Say target times aloud in words as you point to or build them on a clock, e.g. 'twenty-five past three', 'quarter to four'.
Explain in your own words why a time is 'to' rather than 'past', and which hour you name.
Pair the spoken form with pointing to the hands so speech stays tied to what the hands show.
activities.intendedInsight: Putting time-telling into one's own spoken words helps rehearse the relative 'past'/'to' language, but it should stay anchored to reading, writing, and drawing actual clock hands.

constraints: The objective requires pupils to both tell AND write time to five minutes including quarter past/to, and to draw the hands — so recognition-only matching tasks must be followed by independent construction (drawing hands, writing the time).

A static labelled clock can show the five-counts but cannot demonstrate the 'past'→'to' switch dynamically or check a learner's drawn hour hand; use it as a reference, and still have learners draw and move hands.
A geared or movable clock is valuable for showing the hour hand's gradual position between numbers, which a fixed picture cannot be adjusted to demonstrate.
Spoken rehearsal of times supports the language but does not replace reading, writing, and drawing on actual clock faces.

When introducing the digital form of 'to' times, note that the hour numeral stays as the earlier hour (quarter to 4 = 3:45) even though we name 'four' when speaking — a common point of confusion to handle explicitly.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the four cited sources are marked verified:false in the source row (Earnest & Chandler 2021 on expression form; and the National Curriculum statutory content citation). Treat their claims with corresponding caution; the exact claim strings are retained only where they directly support a stated teaching principle.

Self-audit of time arithmetic (all consistent): quarter past = 15 minutes (9:15); quarter to 4 = 45 minutes past the hour = 3:45; twenty to four = minute hand on the 8 (5×8=40, i.e. 20 minutes to the next hour); twenty-five to four = minute hand on the 7 (35 minutes, i.e. 25 to); 3:25 = minute hand on 5. The source's diagnostic places 'twenty to four' minute hand on the 8 and 'quarter to 4' minute hand on the 9 (45 minutes), both correct.

Editor refinement: the 3:25 hour-hand position was changed from the original 'just past 3' to 'between 3 and 4 but not yet halfway'. At 25 minutes the hour hand is close to halfway, so 'just past 3' was imprecise and risked reinforcing the 'hour hand stays by the number' misconception; the still-3 hour point is preserved and now mirrors the 'over halfway' description used for twenty-five to four.
The original row's 3D rationale ('the clock face is planar; 3D adds nothing') was dropped as a catalog-ranking judgement rather than an objective pedagogical limit; it is not asserted here.

Editor change: the Earnest & Chandler (2021) claim is kept only in the spoken-rehearsal activity, whose principle is the relative language of time; it is not attached to the translation activity, whose principle is statutory production/translation. No efficacy comparison between media is claimed.

probeDeeper: 'The minute hand points to the 5. Why is that twenty-five minutes and not five?'
'You crossed the bottom of the clock — should this be "past" or "to" now, and which hour do we name?'
'For quarter to 4, is the hour hand closer to the 3 or the 4? Draw where it goes.'
'Write "quarter past 9" two ways — in words and in numbers.'
assess.correctAnswer: Reads 3:25 (twenty-five past three) — minute hand on 5 counted in fives is 25, hour hand just past 3; reads quarter to 4 — minute hand on 9 is 15 minutes to the next hour, hour hand nearly at 4. Draws twenty to four with the minute hand on 8 and the hour hand over halfway from 3 to 4; writes quarter past 9 as 9:15.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the number the minute hand points to as the minutes — minute hand on 5 → 'five past' instead of twenty-five past; on 2 → 'two past' instead of ten past
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the intervals in fives round the clock and mark each number with its 5-count before reading real times.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reads 3:25 as 'five past three'

errorPatterns.pattern: After the half hour, keeps counting 'past' instead of switching to 'to' — reads twenty-five to four as 'thirty-five minutes past three'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Split the clock right = 'past' / left = 'to'; after the 6, count the minutes back to the next hour.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives a '35 past' style answer for a left-side (to) time

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses 'quarter to' with 'quarter past' and/or draws the hour hand on a number rather than over halfway toward the next for a 'to' time
errorPatterns.nextMove: On a geared clock contrast quarter past (hour hand just past the number) with quarter to (over halfway to the next), and name the next hour for 'to' times.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws twenty to four with the hour hand on the 3 (or reads quarter to 4 as quarter past 4), or muddles which quarter is which

responseLevels.gap: Reads the minute-hand numeral as the minutes; cannot use 'to'; puts the hour hand on a number.
responseLevels.full: Reads and writes times to five minutes on both sides (past and to), including quarter past/to, places the hour hand correctly between numbers, names the correct hour for 'to' times, and translates analogue ↔ words ↔ digital for a new time.
responseLevels.partial: Reads 'past' times to five minutes correctly, but keeps counting past after the half hour, confuses quarter to/past, or mislocates the hour hand for 'to' times.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Interpret, then translate. (Interpret) Show a clock at 3:25 — minute hand on 5, hour hand just past 3: 'What time is this? What is each hand telling you?' Then a clock at quarter to 4 — minute hand on 9, hour hand nearly at 4: 'And this one?' (Translate) Blank clock: 'Draw the hands to show twenty to four. Then write quarter past 9 in numbers.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The 3:25 item catches reading the minute-hand numeral directly ('five past'); the quarter-to-4 and twenty-to-four items catch the 'to' switch, the next-hour rule, and the hour-hand position — a child can read o'clock and half past yet fail all of these.

It teaches right = past / left = to, and that times after half past relate to the next hour with the hour hand over halfway between the numbers.

pedagogy.summary: Children complete the missing half of a symmetric figure across a given mirror line — finishing a butterfly, a pattern on squared paper, or a shape — and verify it by folding. The skill is applied reflection: every point of the drawn half has a partner the same perpendicular distance on the other side of the mirror, and joining these partners reconstructs the whole. Done well it is point-by-point and checkable by folding; done poorly it is a freehand 'looks about right' sketch. The fold test is both the method's justification and its self-check.
bestPractices: Complete the figure point by point, not by eye: for each corner or key point of the given half, count the squares perpendicular to the mirror line, then count the same number on the far side and mark the partner point; join the partners in the same order.
Insist every partner point is EQUIDISTANT from the mirror line — the reflected feature is the same distance out, not roughly opposite; use the squared grid to count exactly.
Make sure the completed half is a mirror image (sense reversed), not a slid copy — a butterfly's second wing points the opposite way; contrast reflecting with translating.
Handle points that sit ON the mirror line explicitly: they stay put (distance zero), so they are not duplicated or shifted.
Always check by folding along the mirror line so the two halves coincide (or use a mirror/Mira on the line); this both proves correctness and defines what symmetry means (NCETM).
Progress from patterns and vertical mirrors to horizontal and, later, sloping mirror lines, keeping the 'perpendicular and equidistant' rule constant so it generalises (NCETM KS3 6.3).
keyRepresentations: Squared grid with a marked mirror line and the given half of the figure
Perpendicular counting arrows from each point of the given half to its partner on the far side
Fold test / Mira mirror placed on the line to verify the halves coincide
Butterfly or letter half as an intuitive 'complete the other side' context
commonMisconceptions: Completing the figure by eye so the reflected points are not equidistant from the mirror line.
Sliding a copy of the half across (translating) rather than reflecting, so the completed shape is not a true mirror image.
Miscounting the squares, so individual partner points land the wrong distance from the mirror.
Duplicating or shifting points that lie on the mirror line instead of leaving them fixed.

learn.summary: Children complete the missing half of a symmetric figure across a given mirror line (a butterfly, a pattern on squared paper, or a shape) point by point, and verify by folding along the line so the halves coincide. The core idea: every point of the drawn half has a partner the same perpendicular distance on the other side of the mirror; joining these partners in the same order reconstructs the whole as a true mirror image (sense reversed, not a slid copy). The fold test is both the construction method's justification and its self-check. Progress from vertical to horizontal and later sloping mirror lines, holding the 'perpendicular and equidistant' rule constant.

activities.title: Build the butterfly's missing wing, point by point
feedback: If the second half is sketched freehand and roughly opposite, return to counting squares: the reflected feature must be the SAME distance out, not approximately mirrored. Then fold to confirm.
If one or two points are a square off, don't reteach reflection — just re-count that point, mark the equal perpendicular squares on both sides, and fold to self-correct.

If the completed half folds onto the original everywhere (allowing for small folding inaccuracies), that is good evidence the figure is symmetric; the equal square-counts on both sides are what justify it.
activities.rationale: Completing a symmetric figure is itself a point-by-point reflection with an immediate fold check; doing it by hand on a grid with physical folding makes the perpendicular-equidistant relationship concrete and gives a built-in verification. The curriculum expects Year 4 pupils to complete a simple symmetric figure about a specific line of symmetry.
sourceClaims: Reflection sends each point perpendicular to the mirror line to an equal distance on the far side (the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining a point to its image); teaching should avoid 'straight across' language so the rule generalises to sloping mirrors.

Suggested symmetry activities include completing half a symmetrical shape using the line of symmetry and checking by drawing round, cutting out and folding so the halves coincide (careless cutting can affect results).
Year 4 pupils should complete a simple symmetric figure with respect to a specific line of symmetry.
learnerActions: Start from half a butterfly drawn on squared paper beside a clearly marked vertical mirror line.
For each key point of the given half (e.g. a wingtip), count the squares perpendicular from the mirror line to that point.
Count the SAME number of squares straight out on the far side, perpendicular to the mirror, and mark the partner point.
Repeat for every corner/key point, then join the partners in the SAME order as the original half.

Fold the paper along the mirror line (holding it up to the light if needed), or stand a mirror/Mira on the line and compare the reflection of the given half with your drawn half. Check that the two halves line up, allowing for small inaccuracies in drawing and folding.
If the fold misses anywhere, find the slipped point, re-count its squares on both sides, and correct it.
activities.intendedInsight: Reflection sends each point perpendicular to the mirror line to an equal distance on the far side; building partner-by-partner (counting equal perpendicular distances) and folding to check turns a 'looks about right' sketch into a construction you can justify and check.

activities.title: Reflect, don't slide: spot the difference
feedback: If a learner accepts the slid copy as symmetric, point to the two wings pointing the SAME way, then fold: the halves fail to coincide, so it is not a reflection.
Contrast the words: 'reflect' flips the sense; 'slide' keeps it. Rebuild one feature by the perpendicular-equidistant rule to see the reversal emerge.
activities.rationale: A classic error is translating rather than reflecting; explicitly contrasting the two, with a fold test as arbiter, targets the sense-reversal property directly.
sourceClaims: Reflection uniquely reverses 'sense', distinguishing a true mirror image from a shape merely slid (translated) across.

Suggested symmetry activities include completing half a symmetrical shape using the line of symmetry and checking by drawing round, cutting out and folding so the halves coincide (careless cutting can affect results).
learnerActions: Look at two completions of the same half-butterfly: one where the second wing points the opposite way, one where a copy of the left wing has been slid across so both wings point the same way.
Decide which is truly symmetric and explain how you can tell.
Fold each along the mirror line and watch which one's halves coincide.
Say what folding reveals about the slid copy (the wingtips miss).
activities.intendedInsight: Reflection reverses 'sense' — a true mirror image faces the opposite way, unlike a shape merely slid (translated) across, which keeps the same orientation and, for a lopsided half like a butterfly wing, will not fold onto the original half.

activities.title: Points on the line, and new mirror directions
feedback: If a learner duplicates or shifts an on-the-line point, note its distance from the line is zero, so its partner is itself.
If horizontal or sloping mirrors cause trouble, re-state the rule as 'perpendicular to the mirror, equal distance' rather than 'straight across', so it transfers to any direction.
A fold that fails for a sloping mirror helps show where a partner point was misplaced, so you can re-count that point's perpendicular distance.
activities.rationale: Avoiding 'straight across' language and handling on-the-line points explicitly lets the rule generalise beyond vertical mirrors, which the misconception list flags as a common failure point.
sourceClaims: Reflection sends each point perpendicular to the mirror line to an equal distance on the far side (the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining a point to its image); teaching should avoid 'straight across' language so the rule generalises to sloping mirrors.
learnerActions: Work a figure that has a key point sitting right ON the mirror line; decide where its partner goes (it stays put — distance zero, not duplicated or shifted).
Complete a figure whose mirror line is HORIZONTAL, counting squares perpendicular to that line (now up/down).

Later, try a figure with a SLOPING mirror line (on squared paper, a diagonal line at 45°), keeping the same rule: each partner the same perpendicular distance from the line, counted in corner-to-corner diagonal steps across the squares.
Fold (or imagine the fold) along each mirror line to check the halves coincide.
activities.intendedInsight: The 'perpendicular and equidistant' rule is constant whatever the mirror's orientation; points on the line are fixed, and the method generalises from vertical to horizontal and sloping lines.

activities.title: Check and choose: deciding if a completion is correct
feedback: If you choose the slid (same-orientation) copy, notice both halves face the SAME way, so it cannot be a reflection; fold it and the wingtips miss.
If you choose the version with a point one square off, re-count that point's perpendicular distance from the mirror on both sides; a fold would fail just at that point.

Recognising correct completions and predicting whether a fold would match confirm your understanding, but they do not by themselves make you build and fold your own figure, so pair them with at least one hands-on completion.
activities.rationale: Recognition and fold-prediction questions are efficient for checking whether learners can distinguish correct reflections from the two characteristic errors, provided they complement rather than replace construction-and-fold work.
sourceClaims: Reflection uniquely reverses 'sense', distinguishing a true mirror image from a shape merely slid (translated) across.
learnerActions: On a grid, complete a given half by marking the partner points and joining them.
From several completed figures, pick the correctly reflected one, rejecting a wrong version that is the half slid across (same orientation) and another where a point is one square off.
Decide whether folding a figure along the mirror line would make the halves match, and say yes or no.
Justify each choice by counting squares or by predicting the fold.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to recognise correct reflections — and name exactly why the slid-copy and one-square-off versions are wrong — consolidates the perpendicular-equidistant and sense-reversal rules.

constraints: The task should require the learner to construct and fold-check their OWN figure; recognition-only questions (pick the right completion, or judge whether a fold would match) confirm discrimination but do not elicit independent construction of a symmetric figure.

A static or tap-to-reveal worked example (showing each partner point's square-count and a fold overlay) can demonstrate the method, but on its own does not let the learner complete and fold-test their own figure, which is the skill; use it as a scaffold, not the whole task.
Keep the language 'perpendicular to the mirror, equal distance' rather than 'straight across', so the rule transfers to horizontal and sloping mirror lines.
Handle on-the-line points explicitly: they are fixed (distance zero), not duplicated or shifted.
Paper cutouts and folds have real thickness and careless cutting/folding can affect results; treat the fold as an approximate physical check of an ideal reflection.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source rated planar (2D) construction the best fit and marked 3D and conversation formats 'poor' with claims that 3D 'distracts' and a character 'cannot supply' plotting/fold verification. These are scoped as 'this planar grid task fits 2D construction best'; they are not universal laws. A discussion could still support reasoning, and a physical/tactile fold is one effective check among others — not claimed as the only way.

The source's framing that only live/interactive manipulation turns a guess into a tested construction has been softened: physical paper-and-fold work achieves the same construct-and-check loop; interactive recolouring/snapping are optional aids, not the only mechanism.
The Year 4 National Curriculum claim is marked verified:false in the source; it is retained (including in activity 1 sourceClaims) as stated but remains unverified.

An author-facing instruction in the check-and-choose activity ('design a wrong option so...') was rewritten as learner-facing feedback, and question-format jargon was removed from learner-facing text.

probeDeeper: Point at one wingtip and its partner: 'How far is each from the mirror line? What has to be true about those two distances?' (listen for equal perpendicular distance).
'If I fold your finished figure along the mirror line, what should happen? Try it — does it?' (fold as the self-check; a mismatch localises the error).
Counterexample: 'Your friend just traced the left half and slid it to the right without turning it round. Is that symmetrical? How can you tell?' (elicits that a slid copy is not a reflection).
'This point sits right on the mirror line — where does its partner go?' (tests that on-the-line points stay fixed).
assess.correctAnswer: The child builds the missing half point by point — each partner point the same number of squares perpendicular from the mirror line as its original, joined in the same order — so the completed figure is a true mirror image (sense reversed), leaves any on-the-line points fixed, and works for the horizontal mirror as well as the vertical. The child verifies by folding along the mirror line (or imagining the fold) so the halves coincide.

errorPatterns.pattern: Completes the figure by eye, so reflected points are not equidistant from the mirror line
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to counting: for each point, count squares perpendicular to the mirror and mark the same count on the far side; then fold to confirm. Revisit what a line of symmetry means.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The second half is drawn freehand and roughly opposite; partner points are the wrong distance out; a fold would not line up.

errorPatterns.pattern: Slides a copy of the half across the mirror (translates) instead of reflecting, so the completed shape is not a true mirror image
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the fold does not match; rebuild one feature by the perpendicular-equidistant rule so the reversal emerges. Contrast 'reflect' with 'slide'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The two halves face the SAME way (a butterfly's wings both point right); sense is not reversed even if the copy is neatly placed.

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscounts the squares for some points, so individual partners land the wrong distance from the mirror
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach reflection — have the child re-count the slipped point, marking the perpendicular squares on both sides, and fold to self-correct.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Most of the figure is correct but one or two points are a square off; the overall shape is nearly right and the child is surprised when the fold misses there.

responseLevels.gap: Completes the figure by eye or by sliding a copy across; halves are not equidistant or not reversed, and a fold would not match; does not self-check.
responseLevels.full: Builds the missing half point by point — every partner equidistant and perpendicular, sense reversed, on-the-line points fixed — for vertical and horizontal mirrors, and verifies by folding so the halves coincide, self-correcting any slipped point.
responseLevels.partial: Reflects roughly correctly for a vertical mirror by counting most points, but slips on some distances, struggles when the mirror is horizontal, or does not fold-check unprompted. Can carry out the steps but cannot reliably justify equidistance or transfer the method to a new mirror orientation.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child squared paper showing half a simple symmetric figure (say the left half of a butterfly or a simple flag pattern) with a clearly marked vertical mirror line, plus one figure whose mirror line is horizontal. Say: 'Complete each figure so the whole thing is symmetrical about the mirror line. When you have finished, check your work.' Set the task and WATCH how the second half is built and whether the child checks by folding — do not explain the method.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who holds the reflection rule places every partner point at an equal perpendicular distance and produces a figure that folds onto itself; a child who works by eye or slides a copy produces a half that is not equidistant or not reversed, and a fold would not match. Watching HOW the half is constructed — counting squares versus sketching — and whether they fold-check reveals the difference directly.
