pedagogy.summary: The nth-term (position-to-term) rule expresses the structure of EVERY term directly from its position, so you can jump to the 100th term without listing. For an arithmetic sequence it is (common difference)×n + (zero term): the coefficient of n IS the constant difference, and the constant is the 'zeroth term' one step before the first. The nth term is new learning at KS3 and must be built from — and sharply distinguished from — the term-to-term rule, which only tells you how to get the NEXT term. Fluency means deriving it, using it to reach far terms, and testing membership by solving a linear equation.
bestPractices: Build the rule from growing shape / matchstick patterns so the coefficient of n is SEEN as the repeated group and the constant as the fixed starting part; rewrite terms to expose structure (4 = 1+3, 7 = 1+3+3, 10 = 1+3+3+3)
State explicitly that the coefficient of n equals the common difference, and that the constant is the zeroth term (step back one before the first term) — not the first term
Use the shared sentence 'As the value of n increases by one, each term increases (or decreases) by ___' to tie the difference to the coefficient of n
ALWAYS verify a proposed rule by substituting n = 1, 2, 3 and checking it regenerates the actual terms
Plot the terms and read the common difference as the steepness, but do not join the points (non-integer positions have no meaning)
Test membership by setting the nth term equal to the target and solving the linear equation, accepting the number only if n is a whole number
Deliberately include decreasing and decimal/fraction sequences so the rule generalises beyond positive-integer, increasing cases
keyRepresentations: Growing shape / matchstick patterns (the repeated group = coefficient of n, the fixed start = constant)
Position-vs-term table with an explicit '0th term' column
The 'as n increases by one, the term changes by d' sentence frame
Plotted terms on a graph (steepness = common difference; points not joined)
'Set the rule equal to the target and solve' for membership testing
commonMisconceptions: Uses the common difference as the WHOLE rule: writes n + 4 (or just 'add 4') for 3, 7, 11, 15 instead of 4n − 1
Confuses 'multiples of 3' with 'increases by 3' — assumes a sequence going up by 3 must contain multiples of 3
Whole-object method: finds the 100th term by taking the 10th term × 10, or claims the 10th term is twice the 5th (only true when the line passes through the origin)
Gets the sign wrong for decreasing sequences: writes 4n + 6 for 10, 6, 2, −2 instead of −4n + 14
Attends to the term-to-term rule instead of position, so cannot reach a far term without listing
Over-generalises from only-increasing examples, treating decreasing sequences as a different kind

learn.summary: Learners derive and apply the nth-term (position-to-term) rule for an arithmetic sequence, sharply distinguishing it from the term-to-term 'add d' rule. The core structure: the coefficient of n is the common difference, and the constant is the 'zeroth term' one step before the first term (not the first term itself). Fluency means deriving the rule from structure, verifying it by substituting n=1,2,3, jumping to far terms (e.g. the 100th) without listing, and testing membership by solving rule=target and accepting only whole-number positions. Include decreasing and decimal/fraction sequences so the rule generalises.

activities.title: Build the rule from a growing pattern
feedback: If a learner writes n + 4 (or 'add 4') for 3, 7, 11, 15, have them substitute n=1,2,3: it gives 5, 6, 7, which steps by 1 and starts wrong. Contrast with 4n (right step, wrong start), then adjust the constant to reach 4n − 1.

If a learner writes 4n (forgetting the −1) or 4n + 3 (using the first term as the constant), point out that 4n gives 4, 8, 12 (each value 1 too big) and 4n+3 gives 7, 11, 15 (the real terms shifted one position along). Step back before the first term to find the zeroth term: 3 − 4 = −1.
Reinforce: the constant is the value at n = 0, found by going one step before the first term, not the first term itself.
activities.rationale: Building the coefficient as a seen repeated group and the constant as a stepped-back zeroth term ties each part of the rule to visible structure; the NCETM guidance links the coefficient to the common-difference meaning and documents the n+3-instead-of-3n+1 error that this derivation targets.
sourceClaims: The nth term is new learning at KS3; the coefficient of n represents the common difference (as n increases by one, the term increases by that amount); documented misconceptions include writing n+3 instead of 3n+1, confusing 'multiples of three' with 'increases by three', the whole-object method (100th term = 10th term ×10; 10th = twice 5th, only valid through the origin), and wrong sign for decreasing sequences (4n+6 for 10,6,2,−2).
learnerActions: Work through an illustrative growing shape or matchstick example such as 4, 7, 10, … and rewrite each term to expose structure: 4 = 1+3, 7 = 1+3+3, 10 = 1+3+3+3. Here the fixed start 1 is the zeroth term and the repeated +3 is the coefficient, giving the rule 3n + 1.
Apply the same technique to the target sequence 3, 7, 11, 15: identify the repeated group (+4) as the coefficient of n and the fixed starting part (the zeroth term) as the constant.
Find the zeroth term by stepping back one step before the first term (for 3,7,11,15: 3 − 4 = −1), and state the rule as 4n − 1.
Complete the sentence frame 'As the value of n increases by one, each term increases (or decreases) by ___' and connect that difference to the coefficient of n.
activities.intendedInsight: The nth-term rule reads structure directly from position: the coefficient of n IS the common difference, and the constant is the term at position zero — found by stepping back one before the first term, not the first term itself.

activities.title: Position machine: test a rule and jump to far terms
feedback: Always verify a proposed rule by substituting n=1,2,3 and checking it regenerates the actual terms before trusting it.

For a decreasing sequence, if a learner writes 4n + 6 for 10, 6, 2, −2, note the coefficient of n is the signed difference: a decreasing sequence needs a negative coefficient (−4n + 14). The wrong rule may give the first term by luck (4×1+6 = 10) but fails at later positions (4×2+6 = 14, not 6) — substitute n=1,2,3 to catch it.

Live interaction examples (optional, not required): drag an n slider to assemble each term as n copies of a difference-block on a fixed start-block; a 'test all' button that lights cells green/red; a 'jump to n=100' button. These make the mechanism concrete but are not the only way to run the activity — a table or pencil-and-paper substitution works just as well.
activities.rationale: Substitution-based verification and leaping to a far term directly target the whole-object misconception and the habit of attending only to the term-to-term rule; the signed-coefficient check addresses the documented wrong-sign error for decreasing sequences.
sourceClaims: The nth term is new learning at KS3; the coefficient of n represents the common difference (as n increases by one, the term increases by that amount); documented misconceptions include writing n+3 instead of 3n+1, confusing 'multiples of three' with 'increases by three', the whole-object method (100th term = 10th term ×10; 10th = twice 5th, only valid through the origin), and wrong sign for decreasing sequences (4n+6 for 10,6,2,−2).
KS3 national curriculum requires pupils to 'recognise arithmetic sequences and find the nth term' and to generate terms from a position-to-term rule.
learnerActions: Type a candidate rule into a 'test all' box that substitutes n=1,2,3,4,5 and marks each term green (matches the real sequence) or red (does not).

Watch a wrong rule fail visibly: n+4 turns every cell red (it gives 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 instead of 3, 7, 11, 15, 19), while 4n−1 lights every cell green — so the term-to-term rule and the position rule are seen to differ, not just told apart.
Use a 'jump to n=100' control to produce the 100th term instantly (399 for 4n−1) and feel why listing is absurd.
Repeat the derive-then-verify cycle for a decreasing sequence (10, 6, 2, −2 → −4n + 14) and a decimal/fraction sequence so the rule generalises beyond increasing positive-integer cases.
activities.intendedInsight: A position rule can be tested against the real terms and used to leap straight to any position; a rule written as 'n + d' from the term-to-term 'add d' rule generally fails substitution, and the coefficient carries the SIGNED difference, so a decreasing sequence needs a negative coefficient.

activities.title: Membership testing by solving an equation
feedback: If a learner judges 101 to be in the sequence because it is odd like the real terms, do not reteach the whole concept — scaffold the method: set 4n−1 = 101 and solve; a term exists only when n comes out a whole number.
Emphasise that surface features (odd/even, 'looks similar') are not evidence of membership; only the solved whole-number position is.
activities.rationale: Solving rule=target with a whole-number-position check directly replaces surface-judging of membership — the performance error flagged in the source material. This uses the KS3 position-to-term rule but is an inverse application not asserted by the cited claims, so no source claim is attached.
learnerActions: Given a target number, set the nth-term rule equal to it and solve the linear equation for n.
Accept the target as a term only when n is a whole number; reject it when n is non-integer.
Work the deliberately misleading case: for 3,7,11,15,… test 101 by solving 4n−1 = 101 → 4n = 102 → n = 25.5 → not a whole position → not a term; then test 99 → n = 25 → yes.
When a target is rejected, find the nearest actual terms (99 at n=25 and 103 at n=26) to show which values really belong.
activities.intendedInsight: Membership is decided by solving rule=target and checking for a whole-number position, not by whether a number 'looks like' the others (e.g. being odd).

activities.title: Graph the terms and read the difference
feedback: If a learner claims the 100th term equals the 10th term × 10 (or the 10th is twice the 5th), use the plot: doubling the position does not double the term unless the graph passes through (0,0). Use the position rule and substitute instead.
Remind learners not to join the plotted points: only whole-number positions exist, so a continuous line would imply meaningless in-between terms.
activities.rationale: Plotting ties the coefficient to steepness and exposes why the whole-object/multiply-a-term method fails except through the origin; the 'do not join points' caution preserves the integer-position idealisation.
sourceClaims: The nth term is new learning at KS3; the coefficient of n represents the common difference (as n increases by one, the term increases by that amount); documented misconceptions include writing n+3 instead of 3n+1, confusing 'multiples of three' with 'increases by three', the whole-object method (100th term = 10th term ×10; 10th = twice 5th, only valid through the origin), and wrong sign for decreasing sequences (4n+6 for 10,6,2,−2).
learnerActions: Plot the sequence terms against their position numbers.
Read the common difference as the steepness between successive plotted points, and connect this to the coefficient of n.
Do NOT join the points with a line — positions are whole numbers, so non-integer positions have no meaning here.
Use the graph to challenge the whole-object claim: check whether doubling the position doubles the term, and notice this only holds if the plotted line would pass through (0,0).
activities.intendedInsight: Steepness on the position-term graph matches the common difference, and multiplying a term's value in step with its position only works when the line passes through the origin.

activities.title: Check and consolidate fluency
feedback: For membership items, require the solved whole-number position before accepting an answer; a number that merely resembles the sequence's terms is not thereby a member.

A static annotated card (coefficient highlighting the repeated +4 group; tap/reveal the 0th term) is a useful summary reference, but on its own it does not let a learner test a candidate rule against the real terms — use it after learners have derived and tested rules themselves.
activities.rationale: Recognition and selected-response items efficiently check fluency and surface specific misconceptions (n+4 vs 4n−1, whole-object, surface-membership); by design they verify recognition rather than elicit independent construction of the rule, so they follow the building activities.
learnerActions: Complete fill-the-blank items (e.g. 'nth term of 3,7,11 is __n__') and choose between distractors that pit n+4 against 4n−1.
Answer a multiple-choice item whose distractor is the whole-object claim '100th term = 10th term × 10', explaining why it is wrong.
Decide a membership item where the target (e.g. 101) is odd but not in the sequence, so surface-checking fails and only solving succeeds.
Use a labelled reference card: the sequence with +4 arrows, the rule 4n−1 annotated, and the zeroth term revealed (3−4 = −1) as a consolidation summary after the main work.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can recognise the correct position rule, reject the whole-object shortcut, and settle membership by solving rather than by appearance.

constraints: The nth term is new learning at KS3 and must be built from — and sharply distinguished from — the term-to-term rule, which only gives the next term.
State explicitly that the coefficient of n equals the common difference and the constant is the zeroth term (one step back before the first term), not the first term.

Keep any term decomposition consistent with its own sequence: 4=1+3, 7=1+3+3, 10=1+3+3+3 illustrates 4,7,10,… (rule 3n+1, zeroth term 1); for 3,7,11,15 the repeated group is +4 and the zeroth term is 3−4=−1, giving 4n−1.
Always verify a proposed rule by substituting n=1,2,3 before accepting it; a rule that gives the first term correctly can still fail later (common for wrong-sign decreasing cases).
Deliberately include decreasing and decimal/fraction sequences; the coefficient of n is the SIGNED difference, so decreasing sequences have a negative coefficient.
Membership must be decided by solving rule=target and accepting only a whole-number position, never by surface features such as parity or resemblance.
When plotting, read steepness as the common difference but do not join the points — non-integer positions have no meaning.

A static annotated diagram is a consolidation/reference scaffold: it does not let a learner test a wrong rule against the real terms or independently jump to a far term, so it should follow, not replace, derivation and verification.
Recognition/selected-response items check fluency but do not elicit independent construction of the rule; use them after building activities, not instead of them.

Live-manipulation features (sliders, test-all lights, jump-to-n, membership solver) are helpful ways to make the mechanism concrete but are optional; equivalent work can be done with tables, graphs, and pencil-and-paper substitution.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One cited claim (DfE KS3 Mathematics programmes of study, position-to-term requirement) is marked verified:false in the source row; treat its evidential weight accordingly.

The candidate had merged the difference-3 decomposition (4=1+3, 7=1+3+3, 10=1+3+3+3) into the difference-4 sequence 3,7,11,15, which contradicted its own stated rule 4n−1 (the decomposition implies start 1 / rule 3n+1). This is corrected by presenting 4,7,10,… as a distinct illustrative example before applying the technique to 3,7,11,15.

The membership activity previously cited the DfE position-to-term claim; membership-by-solving is an inverse application not asserted by either source claim, so its sourceClaims has been set to [] with the KS3 link kept only as context.

Self-audit of arithmetic/logic: for 3,7,11,15 the rule 4n−1 gives 3,7,11,15 (correct); zeroth term 3−4=−1 (correct); 100th term 4×100−1=399 (correct); 101 → 4n−1=101 → 4n=102 → n=25.5 (not a term), 99 → n=25 (term). For 10,6,2,−2 the rule −4n+14 gives 10,6,2,−2 (correct); the distractor 4n+6 is wrong and is used only as an error to catch, never as a valid option. For 4,7,10,… the rule 3n+1 gives 4,7,10,13 (correct), zeroth term 1. All checked consistent.
The non-preferred 3D entry's claim that rendering a flat concept in 3D 'adds no depth' was treated as a catalog preference, not a universal law, and omitted rather than asserted.

The source framed the 2d interactive as 'ideal' and the static image/quiz/conversation as weaker; these fit rankings were removed and the useful content from each (reference card, assessment items, Socratic 'convince me 4n−1 not n+4' challenge) was preserved as distinct activities.

probeDeeper: Your rule is 4n − 1. Show me where the −1 comes from — what is the term at position zero?
Without listing, how do you know the 100th term? Convince me that finding the 10th term and multiplying by ten would NOT work here.
If the sequence had been 10, 6, 2, −2, … instead, what would change in your rule and why?
You said 101 is not in the sequence. What is the nearest number that IS in it, and how did you find it?
assess.correctAnswer: nth term = 4n − 1; 100th term = 399 (4×100 − 1); 101 is NOT a term because 4n − 1 = 101 gives n = 25.5, not a whole-number position (the terms either side are 99 at n=25 and 103 at n=26).

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses the common difference as the whole rule: writes n + 4 (or 'add 4') for the nth term because each term goes up by 4
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have them substitute n = 1, 2, 3 into n+4 and see it starts at 5 and steps by 1; contrast with 4n (right step, wrong start) then adjust the constant to −1
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Their rule gives 5, 6, 7, … at n = 1, 2, 3 rather than 3, 7, 11 — but they typically do not substitute to check

errorPatterns.pattern: Right coefficient, wrong constant: writes 4n (forgets the −1) or 4n + 3 (uses the FIRST term as the constant instead of the zeroth term)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Find the zeroth term by going back one step before the first (3 − 4 = −1); the constant is the term at n = 0, not the first term
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 4n gives 4, 8, 12; 4n+3 gives 7, 11, 15 (off by one position) — they never step back to the zeroth term

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-object / multiply-a-term: finds the 100th term by taking the 10th term and multiplying by ten, or claims the 10th term is twice the 5th
errorPatterns.nextMove: Plot the terms — doubling the position does not double the term unless the graph passes through (0,0); use the position rule and substitute
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Their 100th term does not match the rule's value; the method only works when the line passes through the origin (0,0)

errorPatterns.pattern: Wrong sign for a decreasing sequence: for 10, 6, 2, −2 writes 4n + 6 (difference read as +4) instead of −4n + 14
errorPatterns.nextMove: The coefficient of n is the SIGNED difference; a decreasing sequence has a negative coefficient; verify by substituting n = 1, 2, 3
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The rule generates the first term correctly but not subsequent terms; they treat the difference as positive because they see '4' between terms

errorPatterns.pattern: Decides membership by how the number looks (it is odd, or 'looks like the others') instead of solving the rule = target equation
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, do not reteach the concept: set the rule equal to the target and solve; a term exists only when n comes out a whole number
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 101 is in the sequence without solving; performs no whole-number-position check

responseLevels.gap: Cannot produce a position rule; continues by adding 4 repeatedly and would list all 100 terms to reach the 100th; decides membership by how the number looks.
responseLevels.full: Derives 4n − 1 explaining coefficient = common difference and constant = zeroth term, jumps to the 100th by substitution, settles membership by solving 4n−1 = 101 → n = 25.5 → not a whole position → not a term, and transfers the method to a decreasing or decimal sequence.
responseLevels.partial: Finds 4n − 1 and the 100th term by substituting, but treats it as a remembered procedure — cannot say why the coefficient is the common difference or the constant is the zeroth term, and reverts to listing or surface-judging when the sequence decreases or when membership is asked.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a sequence: 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, … Find a rule that gives you any term straight from its position number, and use it to work out the 100th term without listing them all. Then tell me: is 101 in this sequence — and how do you know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who holds the position-to-term structure writes 4n−1, reaches the 100th by substitution, and settles membership by solving to a whole-number position. A child who only has the term-to-term rule cannot get the 100th without listing, tends to write n+4 or 4n, and judges membership by surface features. The target 101 is deliberately ODD (like every real term) so 'the terms are odd and 101 is odd, so yes' fails — only solving 4n−1=101 reveals n=25.5. And n+4 versus 4n−1 diverge immediately at n=1 (5 vs 3), so the wrong rule is caught the moment it is checked.

pedagogy.summary: Children learn that a line of symmetry is a fold line: a line about which one half of a figure maps exactly onto the other. They find ALL such lines in a shape, recognise shapes that have none, and — crucially — do this whatever the shape's orientation. The defining idea is the fold-and-match test, not a counting rule: a rectangle has two lines of symmetry (through the midpoints of opposite sides), not four, and its diagonals are NOT lines of symmetry because folding along a diagonal leaves the halves misaligned. Symmetry is a structural property to be tested, never read off the number of sides.
bestPractices: Define a line of symmetry operationally — fold along it and the two halves must coincide exactly; teach children to check by drawing round a shape, cutting it out and folding (mindful that careless cutting distorts the result) (NCETM).

Actively confront the 'lines of symmetry = number of sides' over-generalisation: because early examples are usually regular shapes, children conclude a rectangle has 4 lines — give many NON-regular shapes and have them test each candidate line by folding (NCETM).
Use the rectangle as the anchor counterexample: its 2 real lines (vertical and horizontal through side-midpoints) versus its 2 falsely-assumed diagonals, disproved by folding corner-to-corner.

Present shapes in varied orientations — tilted and rotated, not just upright — so symmetry is judged by structure, not by whether a mirror line happens to be vertical; move the mirror line around (geoboard + elastic band) rather than always drawing it on upright pictures (NCETM).
Teach patterns before shapes — children recognise symmetry in patterns more readily — then progress to naming and drawing lines on shapes (NCETM).
Sort shapes by symmetry (Carroll/Venn: 'no lines', 'exactly one line', 'more than one line') to build precise vocabulary and expose non-symmetric cases.
keyRepresentations: Fold test — physically folding a cut-out shape so halves coincide (the definition made concrete)
Geoboard with an elastic band as a movable mirror line
Mira/mirror placed on a candidate line to see if the reflection completes the shape
Rectangle-versus-square comparison showing 2 lines vs 4
Carroll/Venn sorting by number of lines of symmetry
commonMisconceptions: Assuming the number of lines of symmetry equals the number of sides — so a rectangle is given 4 lines instead of 2 (over-generalised from regular shapes).
Treating a diagonal of a rectangle (or other non-square) as a line of symmetry, when folding along it shows the halves do not match.
Only recognising a line of symmetry when it is vertical/upright, missing symmetry in tilted or rotated shapes.
Thinking every shape must have at least one line of symmetry (not recognising asymmetric shapes).

learn.summary: Children learn that a line of symmetry is a fold line: a line about which one half of a figure maps exactly onto the other. The defining idea is an operational fold-and-match test, not a counting rule. A non-square rectangle has two lines of symmetry (through the midpoints of opposite sides), not four, and its diagonals are NOT lines of symmetry because folding corner-to-corner leaves the halves misaligned (a square, the special rectangle, has 4 lines including its diagonals). Children find ALL lines in a shape, recognise shapes with none, and judge symmetry whatever the shape's orientation. The activities use physical folding of cut-out shapes and movable mirror lines to confront the common 'lines = number of sides' over-generalisation, with item-based and tappable-image formats as complementary assessment and illustration.

activities.title: Fold-and-match test with a drawn candidate line
feedback: When halves coincide exactly, the line is a true line of symmetry; where corners or edges miss, it is not — e.g. an optional green overlay for a match and red where halves fail to meet makes this vivid.
If a learner marks 4 lines on the rectangle, have them fold each: the two diagonals fail, leaving 2 true lines.

If a learner says a diagonal 'cuts it in half so it counts', fold corner-to-corner and look at the corners — 'cuts in half' is not the same as 'folds onto itself'; the two triangles are congruent but do not land on each other under the fold.
If a learner only finds symmetry when a line is upright, keep the shape tilted and fold along the sloping line to show symmetry belongs to the shape, not the page.

A paper or card cut-out has slight thickness and may be imperfectly cut; treat the fold result as testing the ideal flat shape it represents, and re-check a near-miss in case it is only a cutting artefact.
activities.rationale: The misconception lives in the child's own proposed line, so letting them test their OWN candidate lines by folding gives the felt refutation of the counting rule. Physical cut-and-fold, or a model that folds across a drawn line, makes the operational definition concrete; varied orientations prevent the 'symmetry must be upright' habit.
sourceClaims: A key symmetry misconception is that the number of lines of symmetry equals the number of sides — 'when continually faced with regular shapes, pupils will draw the conclusion that number of lines of symmetry is equal to the number of sides – and nearly always assume 4 lines of symmetry for [a] rectangle'.

Children find recognising symmetry easier with patterns than with shapes (teach in that order); teaching should avoid finding lines of symmetry only on regular polygons and give varied experiences — geoboards with an elastic-band mirror line, completing half a shape, and checking by drawing round, cutting out and folding (mindful careless cutting distorts results).
Year 4 pupils should complete a simple symmetric figure with respect to a specific line of symmetry, and identify lines of symmetry in 2-D shapes presented in different orientations.
learnerActions: Start with a cut-out or on-screen rectangle. Draw where you think each fold line (line of symmetry) should be, and say why before testing.
Fold (or let a screen model fold) one half across each drawn line and check whether the two halves land exactly on top of each other.
Deliberately try a diagonal corner-to-corner: fold along it and watch the far corners — they miss each other, so it is NOT a line of symmetry.
Confirm the vertical and horizontal lines through the side midpoints: these fold to an exact match, so the rectangle has 2 lines, not 4.
Tilt or rotate the shape (e.g. 30-40 degrees) and re-check the same lines are still there without turning the page upright.
Progress to non-regular polygons and a few asymmetric shapes (answer: 0 lines), testing every candidate line by folding.
activities.intendedInsight: A line of symmetry is whatever survives the fold-and-match test, not whatever a count-the-sides rule predicts; symmetry is a structural property of the shape independent of its orientation.

activities.title: Movable mirror line on a geoboard or with a mirror
feedback: If the reflected image does not line up with the existing half, the mirror is not on a line of symmetry — move it and try again.
When completing a half-shape, check the finished figure folds onto itself along the given line.
Careless cutting distorts a cut-out, so a near-miss fold may be a cutting artefact — re-check with a mirror or a cleaner cut-out.
activities.rationale: A movable mirror line decouples symmetry from page orientation and lets children explore many candidate positions; starting from patterns matches the reported ease ordering. Completion tasks rehearse the Year 4 objective of completing a symmetric figure about a specific line.
sourceClaims: Children find recognising symmetry easier with patterns than with shapes (teach in that order); teaching should avoid finding lines of symmetry only on regular polygons and give varied experiences — geoboards with an elastic-band mirror line, completing half a shape, and checking by drawing round, cutting out and folding (mindful careless cutting distorts results).
Year 4 pupils should complete a simple symmetric figure with respect to a specific line of symmetry, and identify lines of symmetry in 2-D shapes presented in different orientations.
learnerActions: Use a geoboard with an elastic band (or a Mira/mirror laid on a candidate line) as a movable mirror line.
Move the mirror line around the shape rather than always drawing it on an upright picture; check whether the reflection completes the shape.
Begin with symmetric patterns before moving to named shapes, recognising symmetry in patterns first.
Complete the missing half of a shape given a specific line of symmetry.
activities.intendedInsight: A mirror line can sit anywhere, and reflection across the right line reproduces the shape; recognising symmetry in patterns builds toward naming and drawing lines on shapes.

activities.title: Sort shapes by number of lines of symmetry
feedback: A shape with no line of symmetry is a valid answer — not every shape is symmetric.

If a learner says the rectangle has 4 lines like the square because both have 4 sides, test the rectangle's diagonals by folding to show it has exactly 2 lines (still in 'more than one line', like the square, but with a different count).
Use the regular hexagon (6 lines, 6 sides), equilateral triangle (3 lines, 3 sides) and rectangle (2 lines, 4 sides) side by side to pin down exactly when the side-count rule works.
When a learner justifies a placement only by counting sides, ask them to fold a candidate line — the regular cases and the rectangle then separate clearly.
activities.rationale: Sorting builds precise vocabulary and brings non-symmetric and non-regular cases into view, which supports attacking the over-generalisation from regular shapes; a sort checks classification but does not itself elicit folding, so each placement is justified by the fold-and-match test. Comparing triangle, square, rectangle and hexagon isolates why the counting rule is only sometimes valid.
sourceClaims: A key symmetry misconception is that the number of lines of symmetry equals the number of sides — 'when continually faced with regular shapes, pupils will draw the conclusion that number of lines of symmetry is equal to the number of sides – and nearly always assume 4 lines of symmetry for [a] rectangle'.

Children find recognising symmetry easier with patterns than with shapes (teach in that order); teaching should avoid finding lines of symmetry only on regular polygons and give varied experiences — geoboards with an elastic-band mirror line, completing half a shape, and checking by drawing round, cutting out and folding (mindful careless cutting distorts results).
learnerActions: Sort a set of shapes into 'no lines', 'exactly one line', and 'more than one line' using a Carroll or Venn arrangement.
Include non-regular and asymmetric shapes so cases with zero lines appear.
For each shape, justify its placement by the fold-and-match test rather than by counting sides.
Compare an equilateral triangle (3 lines), a square (4 lines), a rectangle (2 lines) and a regular hexagon (6 lines), and discuss when 'lines = sides' holds and when it breaks.
activities.intendedInsight: Symmetry must be tested per shape; 'lines = number of sides' holds only for regular shapes, so the equilateral triangle, square and regular hexagon match their side counts while the (non-regular) rectangle has fewer lines than its 4 sides.

activities.title: Check items and tappable-line illustration (assessment and support)
feedback: For the rectangle item, the answer is 2; choosing 4 signals the count-the-sides rule and choosing the diagonals signals the 'cuts in half' error — both are refuted by folding.

On a tilted shape that does have a line of symmetry, a 'no symmetry' answer usually means the learner is only looking for upright lines; re-test by folding along a sloping line (a tilted asymmetric shape genuinely has 0 lines).
The tappable overlay shows which fixed lines match, but it reveals pre-drawn lines rather than the learner's own guess, so pair it with hands-on folding of a candidate line the learner proposes.
activities.rationale: Items offering 4 and the diagonals as tempting wrong answers help separate the heuristic from the method, because the two give different answers for a rectangle. A tappable fold-reveal illustrates the idea and supports learners, but because it presents fixed lines it does not let the child test their own proposed line, where the misconception actually lives. Recognition items assess the concept but do not themselves generate the fold-and-match evidence the learner must produce.
sourceClaims: A key symmetry misconception is that the number of lines of symmetry equals the number of sides — 'when continually faced with regular shapes, pupils will draw the conclusion that number of lines of symmetry is equal to the number of sides – and nearly always assume 4 lines of symmetry for [a] rectangle'.
Year 4 pupils should complete a simple symmetric figure with respect to a specific line of symmetry, and identify lines of symmetry in 2-D shapes presented in different orientations.
learnerActions: Answer short items: 'How many lines of symmetry does this rectangle have?' (with 4 and 'the diagonals' as tempting wrong options), draw all lines on a given figure, decide whether a statement about a tilted shape is true or false, and sort shapes by number of lines.
Include at least one tilted shape and one asymmetric shape in any set.
As a lighter support, tap each drawn line on a static shape to reveal a fold overlay showing match or mismatch, and open a flap asking 'does the diagonal work?' answered by the mismatched fold.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising and drawing correct lines of symmetry — especially rejecting the rectangle's diagonals and spotting tilted symmetry — demonstrates the fold-and-match concept rather than a counting habit.

constraints: Define a line of symmetry operationally: fold along it and the two halves must coincide exactly. Teach checking by drawing round a shape, cutting it out and folding — but note careless cutting distorts the result, so a near-miss may be a cutting artefact.
Actively confront the 'lines = number of sides' over-generalisation with many NON-regular shapes; do not rely only on regular shapes, which breed the misconception.

Use the rectangle as the anchor counterexample (2 real lines vs 2 falsely assumed diagonals) and contrast with equilateral triangle (3), square (4) and regular hexagon (6) to show the side-count rule holds for regular shapes only.
Present shapes in varied orientations (tilted and rotated), judging symmetry by structure, not by whether a mirror line happens to be vertical.

A paper or card cut-out has slight thickness and can be imperfectly cut; treat it as an approximation of the ideal flat shape whose exact halves coincide, and reason about the mathematical shape it represents rather than the physical card.
Recognition and multiple-choice items assess the concept but do not, by themselves, generate the fold-and-match evidence the learner must produce; pair them with hands-on or learner-proposed folding.

A tappable-line reveal shows fixed, pre-drawn lines; it illustrates the idea but does not let a child test their own candidate line, so use it as support alongside active folding, not as a replacement.
This is planar (line/reflective) symmetry of 2-D shapes; keep away from 3-D planes of symmetry and depth, which are a different topic.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source marks the two NCETM claims as verified:true and the National Curriculum (Year 4) claim as verified:false; this status was not re-checked here, and the Year 4 claim is used only to support orientation/completion items.

The original artefact-fit entries asserted that 'no static picture can deliver' the diagonal refutation and that a conversation 'cannot provide the fold-and-match evidence'. These comparative-necessity claims are not established by the cited sources and have been softened to affordance/limit statements: a static image or dialogue can still teach, but does not let the learner test their own proposed line.

Arithmetic/geometry self-audit: rectangle = 2 lines (vertical and horizontal through side midpoints), square = 4, equilateral triangle = 3, regular hexagon = 6; the diagonals of a non-square rectangle are not lines of symmetry. These are consistent across the source and retained. The '4 lines' and 'diagonals' appear only as labelled tempting wrong options/misconceptions, never as correct answers.
Internal catalog IDs and fit rankings, plus the reteach-prerequisite ID, were removed; the Year-2 vertical-symmetry revisit is retained as an orientation re-test without the ID.

assess.poeTask: Give the child a paper rectangle. Ask them to PREDICT how many lines of symmetry it has and to mark where, saying WHY before folding. Then have them fold along each marked line and OBSERVE which folds make the halves coincide. The prediction of 4 (or of a working diagonal) is violated when the diagonal fold leaves the corners apart — the child then EXPLAINS that only the vertical and horizontal folds match, so there are 2.
probeDeeper: 'You folded along the vertical line and the halves matched. Now fold along a diagonal — what happens to the corners?' (counterexample that refutes the diagonal directly).
'A square has 4 lines of symmetry. Why does this rectangle have fewer, even though both have 4 sides?' (forces reasoning about equal vs unequal sides, not the counting rule).

'A regular hexagon has 6 lines of symmetry — the same as its number of sides. So is "lines = sides" a good rule? When does it work and when does it break?' (tests understanding of WHY the rule holds for regular shapes only).
Rotate the rectangle 40°: 'Does it still have lines of symmetry? Show me where, without turning the page.' (orientation-independence).
assess.correctAnswer: Two lines of symmetry — one vertical and one horizontal, each through the midpoints of opposite sides. The child justifies each by the fold-and-match test (folding along the line, the two halves land exactly on each other) and explains that the diagonals are NOT lines of symmetry because folding corner-to-corner leaves the halves misaligned.

errorPatterns.pattern: Assumes the number of lines of symmetry equals the number of sides, so a rectangle 'has 4' ('four sides, four lines')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fold the rectangle along each proposed line; the diagonals fail. Contrast with the square (4) and a regular hexagon (6) to show the rule holds ONLY for regular shapes, and have the child test many non-regular shapes.
errorPatterns.distractor: 4 lines of symmetry — one for each side
errorPatterns.revealedBy: States 4 lines for the rectangle; applies a counting rule rather than folding; often confident because it worked on squares and regular shapes.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats a diagonal of the rectangle as a line of symmetry (fold corner-to-corner)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fold along the diagonal and look at the corners — they do not meet; the two triangles are congruent but reflected the wrong way. Establish that 'cuts it in half' is not the same as 'folds onto itself'.
errorPatterns.distractor: The two diagonals are also lines of symmetry
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws one or both diagonals as lines of symmetry and claims the halves 'match'; has not actually tested the fold, or judges by the line 'splitting it in two' rather than by congruent reflection.

errorPatterns.pattern: Only recognises a line of symmetry when it is vertical/upright, missing symmetry in a tilted or rotated shape
errorPatterns.nextMove: Keep the shape tilted and use a mirror/fold along a sloping line; show symmetry is a property of the shape, not of the page orientation. Revisit vertical-only symmetry from Year 2.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a rotated shape (surfaced by a follow-up), finds no line or only a would-be vertical one; needs to turn the shape upright before spotting symmetry.

responseLevels.gap: Counts lines of symmetry as the number of sides (rectangle = 4), includes diagonals, and/or only looks for a vertical line; cannot justify by folding.
responseLevels.full: Identifies all and only the true lines of symmetry by the fold-onto-itself test, rejects the rectangle's diagonals with a corner-mismatch justification, finds symmetry regardless of orientation, and explains that 'lines = sides' holds for regular shapes only — transferring correctly to non-regular and asymmetric shapes.
responseLevels.partial: Finds the two true lines by folding on an upright shape but cannot fully justify why the diagonals fail, or reverts to the counting rule on an unfamiliar shape, or misses symmetry when the shape is tilted. Can list lines but not explain the fold-and-match criterion or transfer it to rotated/non-regular cases.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show an upright rectangle (clearly not a square). Ask: 'How many lines of symmetry does this rectangle have? Draw each one. Then tell me: how do you KNOW each line you drew is a line of symmetry — and how would you decide whether a line is NOT one?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The rectangle is the decisive shape: a child using the 'lines = number of sides' rule answers 4 (adding the two diagonals), while a child using the fold-and-match test answers 2 — the heuristic and the correct method give DIFFERENT answers here, so the response separates them. The reason tier is essential: some children draw 2 lines by imitation but cannot say why the diagonals fail, revealing a fragile concept.

sources.claim: A key symmetry misconception is that the number of lines of symmetry equals the number of sides — 'when continually faced with regular shapes, pupils will draw the conclusion that number of lines of symmetry is equal to the number of sides – and nearly always assume 4 lines of symmetry for [a] rectangle'.
sources.source: NCETM 'Misconceptions with the Key Objectives' (Shape strand, Year 3/Year 4 symmetry objectives)

sources.claim: Children find recognising symmetry easier with patterns than with shapes (teach in that order); teaching should avoid finding lines of symmetry only on regular polygons and give varied experiences — geoboards with an elastic-band mirror line, completing half a shape, and checking by drawing round, cutting out and folding (mindful careless cutting distorts results).
sources.source: NCETM 'Misconceptions with the Key Objectives' (Shape strand teaching activities)

sources.claim: Year 4 pupils should complete a simple symmetric figure with respect to a specific line of symmetry, and identify lines of symmetry in 2-D shapes presented in different orientations.
sources.source: UK National Curriculum, Mathematics KS2 (Year 4 geometry: properties of shapes)

pedagogy.summary: Four-quadrant coordinates extend first-quadrant plotting by carrying each axis through zero into the negatives. The key move is reading a position as an ordered pair — the FIRST coordinate on the x-axis (horizontal), the SECOND on the y-axis (vertical) — and coordinating each sign with a direction. It is best taught by building the plane as two perpendicular number lines the child can already order, teaching the axis-order convention structurally rather than by a first-quadrant rhyme, and working in all four quadrants together rather than bolting negatives on afterwards.
bestPractices: Build the plane as a horizontal and a vertical number line crossing at the origin, so negative coordinates simply inherit the ordering the child already knows from the number line.

Teach the convention structurally: the first coordinate is read on the x-axis, the second on the y-axis; rehearse against the origin (0,0). Treat 'along the corridor, up the stairs' as a first-quadrant crutch ONLY — it breaks down for negatives (to plot (4,-5) you go along then DOWN the stairs), so prioritise 'x-axis first' once negatives appear.
Use points in all four quadrants from the start; have children name the quadrant from the sign pair (+,+), (-,+), (-,-), (+,-) rather than memorising quadrant numbers.
Work both directions — plot from given coordinates AND read coordinates off a plotted point — including negative and fractional values, so fluency is not one-way.

Surface the reversal error deliberately with a compare-correct-and-incorrect task (one child says a point is (8,6), another says (6,8) — who is right and why?), and state the scale of each axis before reading or plotting, especially when grid lines represent 2, 5 or 10.
keyRepresentations: Two perpendicular number lines forming the Cartesian plane, origin labelled
'x-axis first, then y-axis' read against the origin (the 'corridor/stairs' rhyme holds only in the first quadrant)
Sign-by-quadrant grid: (+,+) | (-,+) | (-,-) | (+,-)
commonMisconceptions: Reverses the ordered pair, plotting/reading (y, x) — takes the vertical value first (the single most common coordinate error).
Sign/direction error: counts the wrong way for a negative value, landing a point in the wrong quadrant.
Misreads the scale: assumes each grid line is one unit when it is 2, 5 or 10, or reads two differently-scaled axes as if identical.
Over-relies on the 'along the corridor, up the stairs' mnemonic and is stranded when a coordinate is negative (goes 'up the stairs' for a negative y).

learn.summary: Learners plot and read positions in all four quadrants of the Cartesian plane using positive and negative x- and y-values. The core idea: a position is an ordered pair whose FIRST coordinate is read along the horizontal x-axis and whose SECOND is read along the vertical y-axis, with each sign tied to a direction. Build the plane as two perpendicular number lines crossing at the origin so negatives inherit the ordering the child already knows, teach the axis-order convention structurally (not via a first-quadrant rhyme), and work across all four quadrants together rather than adding negatives afterwards.

activities.title: Plot and read on a four-quadrant grid
feedback: If a point lands in the wrong quadrant, mirrored across the diagonal — for example aiming for (-3, 2) but landing where (2, -3) belongs — the pair has been reversed: re-read the first number along the horizontal x-axis, then the second up or down the vertical y-axis.

If the horizontal step is right but a negative y was counted upward (or a negative x the wrong way), rebuild the axis as a number line through zero, count the negative on that line first, then transfer the direction onto the grid.

If a read-back value comes out as half (or a fraction) of the true value, the scale was ignored: ask 'what is one grid line worth on this axis?' and count in those units — a point 3 lines right and 2 lines up on axes rising in 2s is (6, 4), not (3, 2).

When comparing (-3, 2) with (2, -3), if the learner expected a near-identical point, draw attention to the different quadrant as evidence that the order of the numbers matters, because each sign is read on the axis its position assigns.
activities.rationale: Placing a point and seeing where it lands makes the horizontal-then-vertical sequence and the sign-to-direction link concrete, and deliberately contrasting a pair with its reversal targets the most common coordinate error directly. A live grid with on-target feedback, a read-back mode, and a scale control (lines worth 1, 2, 5) makes each sub-skill visible; these interaction examples are optional illustrations, not required mechanisms — equivalent work can be done on squared paper.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should 'work with coordinates in all four quadrants'.

Misreading the axis scale (e.g. failing to notice the axis goes up in 2s/5s/10s rather than 1s, or that two axes use different scales) is a documented student difficulty when reading coordinates and graphs.

The most common coordinate error is reversing the ordered pair / reading the axes in the wrong order (one pupil says a point is (8,6), another (6,8)); the 'along the corridor, up the stairs' mnemonic works only in the first quadrant and breaks down for negatives (e.g. plotting (4,-5) requires going along then DOWN), so pupils should be taught explicitly that the first coordinate is read on the x-axis and the second on the y-axis, and the reversal is best remediated with a compare-correct-vs-incorrect reasoning task.
learnerActions: Given a target coordinate such as (-3, 2), place a point by first moving horizontally along the x-axis to -3, then vertically along the y-axis to 2, and check whether it lands on target.

Immediately after plotting (-3, 2), plot (2, -3) and compare where the two points land: note that swapping the order of the two numbers (each keeping its own sign) sends the point to a visibly different quadrant.
Switch to reading: a point is shown already marked on the grid, and the learner states its coordinates as (x, y) with correct signs.
Repeat with on-axis points such as (0, 2) and with negative and fractional values so plotting and reading are both rehearsed.
State what one grid line is worth before each plot or read, practising with grids where each line represents 1, then 2, then 5.
activities.intendedInsight: The order of the two numbers and the sign of each carry independent meaning: (-3, 2) and (2, -3) are different points in different quadrants, and the interval each grid line represents must be checked before counting.

activities.title: Name the quadrant from the signs
feedback: If a point is placed in a quadrant whose signs don't match (e.g. a (-,-) point put where (+,-) belongs), check each sign against its axis direction separately.
For (0, 2), reinforce that one coordinate being zero means the point lies exactly on an axis — here the y-axis, 2 above the origin — so it belongs to no quadrant.
activities.rationale: Naming quadrants from the sign pair reinforces the sign-to-direction link structurally and avoids rote memorisation of quadrant numbering, while still realising the curriculum expectation to work across all four quadrants. A reference layout that reveals each quadrant's sign pair and labels the axes ('x first, horizontal'; 'y second, vertical') can support this as a reference, though it does not by itself rehearse plotting or reading.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should 'work with coordinates in all four quadrants'.
learnerActions: For a given point, state its quadrant by its sign pair: (+,+), (-,+), (-,-), (+,-), rather than recalling an abstract quadrant number.
Rehearse the convention against the origin (0,0): confirm that the first coordinate is read on the horizontal axis and the second on the vertical.
Classify on-axis points such as (0, 2): explain why a point with a zero coordinate sits on an axis and is not inside any quadrant.
activities.intendedInsight: The combination of signs locates which region of the plane a point lies in, and a zero coordinate places a point on an axis rather than inside a quadrant.

activities.title: Compare correct and incorrect readings
feedback: If the learner picks the reversed reading, trace each coordinate back to its axis: the first number is the horizontal position, the second the vertical.
If the learner still relies on 'up the stairs' for a negative y, show that a negative second coordinate means moving DOWN, and restate the axis-first convention that covers every case.
For the prediction, confirm A(3,-2) lands in the fourth quadrant (3 right, 2 down) while A(-2,3) lands in the second (2 left, 3 up) — a different point, reflected across the line y=x.
activities.rationale: A compare-correct-and-incorrect reasoning task is a documented way to remediate the reversal error, and explicitly flagging the corridor/stairs rhyme as first-quadrant-only prevents learners being stranded by negatives.
sourceClaims: The most common coordinate error is reversing the ordered pair / reading the axes in the wrong order (one pupil says a point is (8,6), another (6,8)); the 'along the corridor, up the stairs' mnemonic works only in the first quadrant and breaks down for negatives (e.g. plotting (4,-5) requires going along then DOWN), so pupils should be taught explicitly that the first coordinate is read on the x-axis and the second on the y-axis, and the reversal is best remediated with a compare-correct-vs-incorrect reasoning task.
learnerActions: Consider a dispute about a point plotted 8 units right of the origin and 6 units up: one person says it is (8, 6), another says (6, 8). Decide who is right and explain why, pointing to which number belongs on which axis.

Explain, using a case like plotting (4, -5), why 'along the corridor, up the stairs' is unreliable for negatives — here you go along then DOWN — and why 'read the first coordinate on the x-axis' always holds.
Predict where A(3, -2) and A(-2, 3) each land and justify whether they are the same point or different.
activities.intendedInsight: Reasoning about why a reading is right or wrong fixes the ordered-pair convention more durably than a first-quadrant mnemonic, which fails once the y-coordinate is negative.

activities.title: Accuracy check across all four quadrants
feedback: Expected placements: A in the fourth quadrant (3 right, 2 down); B in the second (4 left, 1 up); C in the third (2 left, 3 down); D on the y-axis, 2 above the origin.
For the sign-change question, B(-4,1) to B(-4,-1) moves straight down by 2 units, keeping the same horizontal position (4 left of the origin).

If A and B land mirrored across the diagonal, the pair was reversed; if a negative lands in an adjacent quadrant, a sign direction was miscounted; if a read-back is a fraction of the true value, the scale was read as units.
activities.rationale: Procedural accuracy across both directions, including negative and on-axis values and non-unit scales, confirms the convention has transferred. Draw-a-path plotting and short read-back responses can score accuracy well, but such checking tasks confirm the skill rather than build the underlying sequence.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should 'work with coordinates in all four quadrants'.

Misreading the axis scale (e.g. failing to notice the axis goes up in 2s/5s/10s rather than 1s, or that two axes use different scales) is a documented student difficulty when reading coordinates and graphs.
learnerActions: Plot and label a set of points spanning every quadrant plus an on-axis case, e.g. A(3, -2), B(-4, 1), C(-2, -3), D(0, 2).
Read back the coordinates of points already marked on the grid, including on a non-unit scale (axes rising in 2s).
Describe how a point moves when a coordinate changes sign, e.g. B from (-4, 1) to (-4, -1): which direction and how far.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency means plotting from coordinates AND reading coordinates from a plotted point reliably, including negative, on-axis, and non-unit-scale cases (fractional values are practised in the first activity).

constraints: Work in all four quadrants from the start rather than adding negatives after first-quadrant practice.

Treat 'along the corridor, up the stairs' as a first-quadrant crutch only; once negatives appear, prioritise 'first coordinate on the x-axis, second on the y-axis', because the rhyme breaks for a negative y (plotting (4,-5) means along then DOWN).
Always state the scale of each axis before reading or plotting, especially where grid lines represent 2, 5 or 10, or where the two axes use different scales.
Rehearse both directions — plot from given coordinates and read coordinates off a plotted point — so fluency is not one-way.

A static labelled plane or reference card can help name quadrants and locate the origin but does not rehearse the act of plotting or reading, where the procedure lives; use it as a reference alongside active plotting.
Recognition-only or read-back-only responses confirm accuracy but do not by themselves build the plotting sequence; pair them with active placement.
Squared paper and drawn axes are a fully adequate substitute for any on-screen grid; the interactive examples are illustrative, not required.
A third spatial dimension is unnecessary for this planar ordered-pair concept and risks adding load without clarifying the two-axis sign-direction link.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the diagnostic cases: A(3,-2) is 3 right, 2 down (fourth quadrant); reversed to (-2,3) it is 2 left, 3 up (second quadrant), i.e. mirrored across the line y=x — matching the stated reversal error. B(-4,1) to (-4,-1) is a downward move of 2 units with unchanged horizontal position. A point 3 lines right and 2 lines up on axes rising in 2s is (6,4), confirming the halved read-back pattern. Activity 1 feedback now uses only the activity's own (-3,2)/(2,-3) pair to avoid switching example pairs mid-feedback.

The legacy reteach note phrased the fix as 'x is the corridor, count that first, then y up or down the stairs'; this rewrite keeps the corridor/stairs phrasing only as an explicitly first-quadrant crutch and leads with the axis-first convention, to avoid reintroducing the mnemonic's failure for negatives.

A non-preferred alternative (an in-role dialogue) was judged in the source as unable to rehearse the physical placement of points; this is retained only as the narrow objective point that dialogue does not itself exercise the plotting action, not as a universal claim that dialogue cannot teach coordinate reasoning.

The KS3 'work with coordinates in all four quadrants' claim is a curriculum requirement used to ground the all-quadrant scope of activities 1, 2 and 4; no source directly addresses the specific principle of naming quadrants from sign pairs, so that pedagogical choice is carried from the original pedagogy notes rather than from a cited source.

probeDeeper: You plotted A at (3, -2). Where would A(-2, 3) go — the same place or a different one? Show me.
Point D is (0, 2). What is special about where it sits, and why isn't it inside a quadrant?
If I changed B from (-4, 1) to (-4, -1), which way would it move, and how far?
assess.correctAnswer: A sits in the fourth quadrant (3 right, 2 down); B in the second (4 left, 1 up); C in the third (2 left, 3 down); D on the y-axis, 2 above the origin. The read-back point is named as (x, y) with correct signs and read against the '2s' scale (e.g. a point 3 lines right and 2 lines up is (6, 4)).

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses the ordered pair, plotting (y, x): counts the vertical value first, so A(3,-2) lands where (-2,3) belongs — second quadrant instead of fourth
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach the convention against the origin — 'x is the corridor, count that first, then y up or down the stairs' — using the horizontal number line the child already orders.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Watch the order of counting: A and B land in the wrong quadrants, mirrored across the diagonal from where they belong.

errorPatterns.pattern: Sign/direction error for negatives: right-count is correct but counts up instead of down for a negative y (or left/right wrong for negative x), landing the point in the wrong side
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild the axes as two number lines through zero and count the negative on the line first, then transfer that direction onto the grid.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: B(-4,1) or C(-2,-3) lands in an adjacent quadrant; the negative is counted in the positive direction.

errorPatterns.pattern: Misreads the scale: on the read-back, states (3, 2) for a point that is 3 and 2 grid-lines along axes that go up in 2s (true value (6, 4)) — treats each line as one unit
errorPatterns.nextMove: Before reading, ask 'what is one grid line worth on this axis?' Scaffold the count in the correct units; the concept is intact, only the scale was overlooked.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Read-back value is exactly half (or a fraction) of the true value; child ignores the axis interval.

responseLevels.gap: Plots points into wrong quadrants, reverses pairs, or cannot read a marked point back; treats negatives inconsistently and ignores scale.
responseLevels.full: Plots and reads all four points accurately including the on-axis and negative cases, self-checks order and sign, and correctly reads back a point on a non-unit scale — transferring the ordered-pair convention to a new point.
responseLevels.partial: Plots positive and first-quadrant points correctly and reads simple points, but slips on sign/direction for negatives or reads a non-unit scale as units — can place the parts but does not yet coordinate sign with direction reliably across all four quadrants.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a coordinate grid showing all four quadrants, with each square worth one unit. Plot and label these four points: A(3, -2), B(-4, 1), C(-2, -3), D(0, 2). When you have finished, I will point to a fifth point already marked on the grid (drawn on axes that go up in 2s) and you tell me its coordinates.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who holds the ordered-pair convention and the sign-to-direction link places every point in the correct quadrant on the first attempt. A child who reverses the pair sends A and B into wrong quadrants in a way a correct plot never produces; D(0,2) separates those who treat 0 as a genuine coordinate sitting on the axis from those who drift off it; and the read-back on a non-unit scale exposes anyone assuming one line equals one unit.

pedagogy.summary: At 7-8 precision consolidates into consistent conventions: always specifying units in measurement answers ('35 cm', not '35'), using fraction vocabulary precisely (numerator, denominator, equivalent), and writing equations with correct notation (£/p, >, <, =, and fraction symbols). The teaching emphasis is that a written mathematical statement must be readable by anyone without guesswork — '£3.5' is ambiguous where '£3.50' is not, and calling the top number 'the denominator' confuses a listener. Precision here is about shared, agreed conventions that carry meaning, in line with CCSS MP6's call to communicate precisely and use clear definitions.
bestPractices: Require the unit as part of every measurement answer and money to be written to two decimal places (£3.50), because a bare or truncated number can be misread (CCSS: specify units, appropriate precision)
Attach each fraction term to its role — numerator counts the parts we have (top), denominator names how many make the whole (bottom) — and use 'equivalent' only for fractions of equal value
Have children proofread statements for a reader: 'could someone misunderstand this?' — turning precision into an act of communication
Read notation aloud in words (>, <, =, ¾) so the symbol and its meaning stay linked (CCSS: state the meaning of symbols)
Model correct money and fraction notation consistently and correct drift promptly, so conventions become automatic
keyRepresentations: Measurement answers written with units (35 cm, 2 kg, 500 ml)
Money notation to two decimal places (£3.50)
Fraction written with numerator and denominator labelled
Comparison and equation notation (>, <, =)
Fraction bars / number line linking symbol to quantity
commonMisconceptions: Omits or is inconsistent with units — writes '35' for 35 cm (CCSS)
Writes money imprecisely — '£3.5' for £3.50, or mixes symbols as '£3.50p'
Swaps or avoids fraction vocabulary — calls the top number the denominator, or says 'the bottom number' rather than denominator
Uses 'equivalent' loosely for any related fractions rather than only equal-value ones

learn.summary: For ages 7-8, the objective is communicating with mathematical precision: always specifying units in measurement answers ('35 cm', not '35'), using fraction vocabulary accurately (numerator for the top that counts the parts, denominator for the bottom that names how many make the whole, 'equivalent' only for equal-value fractions), and writing notation correctly (money in pounds with £ and two decimal places, e.g. £3.50, or in pence with p, e.g. 350p, but not both symbols; >, <, =, fraction symbols). The core insight is that a written mathematical statement should be readable by anyone without guesswork: '£3.5' invites misreading where '£3.50' does not, and the equals sign must mean 'is the same as' so that false statements like 7+5=12+3 are rejected. Precision here is treated as an act of communication grounded in shared, agreed conventions.

activities.title: Maths proofreader's bench: fix the almost-right statements
feedback: For '£3.5', point out that amounts in pounds are written to two decimal places: without the trailing convention a reader could take '£3.5' to mean three pounds and five pence (£3.05) rather than three pounds fifty, so writing '£3.50' makes the amount unambiguous. (Note that in strict decimal £3.5 equals £3.50; the point is that dropping the convention invites a reader's misreading, not that £3.5 literally equals £3.05.)

If a length is written as '35', ask '35 of what? Could someone read this as 35 metres?' and have the unit added so the meaning is fixed (contrast 35 cm, 35 m and 35 mm to show how the unit changes the meaning).
When the fraction sentence is corrected, link each word to the bar: the numerator (top) counts the parts we have; the denominator (bottom) names how many make the whole.

For '7 + 5 = 12 + 3', work out each side (left is 12, right is 15); because the two sides are not the same value the statement is false, and the equals sign always means the two sides are equal in value.
activities.rationale: Showing a reader act on imprecise notation makes the cost of ambiguity concrete and turns correction into communication rather than rule-following; the equals-sign item targets a documented tendency to read '=' operationally and accept false statements. The misreading of '£3.5' is used as an illustrative communication device about convention, not as a claim that £3.5 equals £3.05 or about any specific real till.
sourceClaims: Proficient students specify units of measure, express answers with a degree of precision appropriate to the context, state the meaning of the symbols they use, and use clear definitions and vocabulary to communicate precisely

The equal sign must be used consistently to mean 'is the same as'; children who read it operationally accept false statements like 7+5=12+3 — evidence that notation must carry an agreed, precise meaning
learnerActions: Work through a set of statements that are almost right and repair each one: '£3.5' (a price), '35' (a length), 'the top number is the denominator', and '7 + 5 = 12 + 3'.

Submit each statement first as it is written — the sloppy version — to a reader that acts only on what is written and may misread nonstandard notation, then submit the repaired version and compare what the reader does with each. For example, when the two-decimal-place convention is dropped, a reader could misread '£3.5' as three pounds and five pence (£3.05) and short-change the customer; writing '£3.50' removes that ambiguity.

Repair the price to '£3.50', add 'cm' to the 35, and rewrite the fraction sentence as 'the top number is the numerator', checking it against a fraction bar where the numerator counts the shaded parts.
Decide whether '7 + 5 = 12 + 3' is true, and state why the equals sign means 'is the same as' rather than 'here comes the answer'.
Proofread each finished statement by asking 'could someone misunderstand this?'
activities.intendedInsight: A written mathematical statement should be readable by anyone without guesswork; a dropped unit, a missing decimal place, or a swapped term can change the meaning a reader takes from it, so following shared conventions is an act of communication, not a nitpick.

activities.title: Dialogue with a literal reader
feedback: If the character shows a possible misreading of the money, prompt: 'You wrote £3.5 — amounts in pounds are written to two decimal places, so write £3.50, and use £ or p, not both,' which makes the amount unambiguous.

If the child says 'the bottom number' or swaps the terms, ask them to attach each word to its role against a fraction bar — numerator counts the parts (top), denominator names how many make the whole (bottom) — before continuing.
Reinforce correct statements by having the character act correctly, confirming the notation was unambiguous.
activities.rationale: A responsive in-role listener can produce the repair through back-and-forth and may surface the child's reasoning about why the convention matters; this supports the precision objective and complements, rather than replaces, written practice.
sourceClaims: Proficient students specify units of measure, express answers with a degree of precision appropriate to the context, state the meaning of the symbols they use, and use clear definitions and vocabulary to communicate precisely
learnerActions: Give notation to a character (a shopkeeper or robot) who acts only on what is written and may misread nonstandard notation: writing '£3.5' lets the character show how it could be misread as three pounds five pence (£3.05), even though £3.5 strictly equals £3.50, and writing '35' with no unit leaves the character unable to tell whether cm, m or mm is meant, so it cannot act correctly.
Correct the notation in response to what the character does: fix £3.5 to £3.50, add the missing unit, and name the numerator and denominator correctly when asked for fraction words.
Explain to the character why the corrected version removes the confusion.
activities.intendedInsight: Precision repairs can come from seeing a listener try to act on exactly what was written or said; the child supplies the convention that prevents the misreading and says why it matters.

activities.title: Spot-the-error and write-it-correctly screener
feedback: Confirm correct rewrites; for a missed item, show the precise form and name the convention (units as part of the answer, pounds to two decimal places and only one of £ or p, numerator/denominator by role).
Where a child only recognises but does not rewrite, follow up with an open task that asks them to construct the corrected statement and say why it matters.
activities.rationale: Spot-the-error items efficiently screen for which conventions need work, but they target recognition and rewriting; they do not on their own elicit the child's full reasoning about why a convention carries meaning, so pair them with the bench or dialogue for that.
sourceClaims: Proficient students specify units of measure, express answers with a degree of precision appropriate to the context, state the meaning of the symbols they use, and use clear definitions and vocabulary to communicate precisely
learnerActions: Work through short items that present units, money, and fraction-vocabulary slips (e.g. '35' for a length, '£3.5', '£3.50p', 'the top number is the denominator') and either flag the error or rewrite the statement correctly.
For each flagged item, write the corrected version.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising and rewriting common notation slips builds fluency and shows which conventions are not yet automatic.

constraints: Precision tasks should have the child produce or repair notation (write/say the corrected statement), not merely recognise a correct label; a static labelled example or reference card can support but cannot accept the child's input to host the production/repair practice.
Recognition-only or spot-the-error items screen for slips efficiently but do not by themselves elicit the child's reasoning about why a convention matters — use open prompts for that.

Keep fraction vocabulary tied to roles: numerator counts the parts we have (top); denominator names how many make the whole (bottom); 'equivalent' applies only to fractions of equal value, not to any related fractions.
Money in pounds is written with £ and two decimal places, and money in pence is written with p and no decimal point (e.g. '£3.50' or '350p'); never use both symbols ('£3.50', not '£3.5' or '£3.50p').
A fraction bar or number line that links the symbol to the quantity helps keep the term attached to its meaning; this is a representation choice, not a required mechanism.

In strict decimal '£3.5' equals '£3.50'; the till/character device illustrates how dropping the two-decimal-place convention invites a reader's MISREADING (e.g. as £3.05), and must not be stated as £3.5 literally equalling £3.05.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Mathematically '£3.5' = '£3.50'; the original's 'till reads £3.5 as £3.05' was reframed in all learner-facing text as a possible human misreading when the convention is dropped, so the guidance does not teach a false decimal equivalence.

The legacy row rated a static labelled example and 3D as 'poor' with claims like '3D adds nothing' and that a static example 'cannot host the practice'; these are catalog-fit judgements. Retained only the genuine, narrowly scoped limit (a static display cannot accept input, so recognition does not elicit independent construction) and softened the rest.

The MP6 claim supports the precision objective the dialogue and screener activities teach but does not independently evidence that any one medium outperforms another; medium efficacy is left as proposed/may.
reteachPrerequisiteId and quiz-step/screener-feeding-the-bench vocabulary were internal routing details and were not carried into learner-facing guidance.

probeDeeper: You wrote 35 — 35 of what? Could I think you meant 35 metres?
Is '£3.5' the same as '£3.50'? What might someone think '£3.5' means?
In ¾, which is the numerator and which the denominator — and what does each one tell you?
Why does it matter that we all use 'denominator' to mean the same thing?
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child correcting '£3.5' to '£3.50' (money to two decimal places / pounds and pence) and correcting 'the top number is the denominator' to numerator (the top counts the parts; the bottom, the denominator, names how many make the whole), and for saying why the conventions matter (£3.5 could be misread; the wrong word confuses the listener). Surfaced for discussion, not scored.

errorPatterns.pattern: Omits or is inconsistent with units — writes '35' for a length that is 35 cm
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist the unit is part of the answer; contrast 35 cm with 35 m and 35 mm so the unit visibly changes the meaning. Reteach calculating with standard units.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives bare numbers for measurements and is untroubled by '35 what?'

errorPatterns.pattern: Writes money imprecisely — '£3.5' for £3.50, or '£3.50p' mixing the symbols
errorPatterns.nextMove: Money is written to two decimal places, and £ OR p not both; show how £3.5 could be read as £3.05. Reteach in place — a convention, not a gap.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Produces £3.5 or £3.50p and does not see how a reader could misinterpret it

errorPatterns.pattern: Swaps or avoids fraction vocabulary — names the top number the denominator, or says 'the bottom number' instead of denominator
errorPatterns.nextMove: Attach each term to its role against a fraction bar — numerator counts the parts (top), denominator names the size of the whole (bottom). Reteach fraction notation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Mislabels numerator/denominator or avoids the terms altogether

responseLevels.gap: Gives bare numbers, writes money loosely (£3.5), and mislabels or avoids fraction vocabulary, without noticing a reader could misunderstand.
responseLevels.full: Unprompted, specifies units and correct money notation, uses fraction vocabulary precisely, writes equations with correct symbols, and can explain why shared, exact conventions are needed to be understood.
responseLevels.partial: When prompted, adds units, corrects to £3.50, and can name numerator and denominator, but does not apply the conventions consistently or spontaneously.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A child wrote the price as '£3.5', and said 'in three-quarters, the top number is the denominator.' Are these written and said correctly? Fix anything that isn't quite right, and tell me why it matters.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child attending to precision spots BOTH the money-notation slip and the swapped fraction term and can say what goes wrong; a child who is loose reads straight past them. Both are almost-right on the surface, so only genuine attention to convention — not arithmetic — separates the children.
