pedagogy.summary: The inverse-size relationship: cutting a whole into MORE equal shares makes each share SMALLER. A quarter of a pizza is smaller than a half of the same pizza, and an eighth smaller still. This directly confronts the whole-number bias by which children read a bigger denominator as a bigger amount ('4 > 2 so a quarter is bigger'). It rests on comparing unit fractions of the SAME whole, and is the seed of later fraction comparison (1/3 > 1/4).
bestPractices: Compare unit fractions of IDENTICAL wholes (same pizza, same bar) so the only thing changing is the number of shares
Use predict-then-check: ask which piece is bigger before cutting, then overlay to test (surfaces the whole-number-bias reason)
Increase the number of sharers and have children watch each share shrink (IES: link to names, 1/3 of it > 1/4 of it)
Name the pattern explicitly: more equal shares of the same whole = smaller pieces
Stress that the comparison only holds when the wholes are the same size
keyRepresentations: Two identical circles/bars, one halved and one quartered, pieces overlaid
A share-counter with a slider for number of shares, one piece highlighted shrinking
A fraction wall (1 whole, halves, quarters, eighths) aligned to the same length
commonMisconceptions: Larger denominator = larger fraction / whole-number bias ('a quarter is bigger than a half because 4 is more than 2'; 1/8 > 1/3) - documented in IES
Comparing fractions of DIFFERENT-sized wholes without noticing the whole matters
Confusing the number of pieces with the amount in one piece ('4 pieces is more than 2 pieces')

learn.summary: Help 6-7 year olds grasp the inverse-size relationship: cutting the SAME whole into more equal shares makes each share smaller. A quarter of a pizza is a smaller amount than a half of the same pizza, and an eighth smaller still. This directly confronts the whole-number bias by which children read a bigger denominator as a bigger amount ('4 > 2 so a quarter is bigger'). When comparing the actual amounts, the comparison relies on the wholes being identical, and it seeds later unit-fraction comparison (1/3 > 1/4).

activities.title: Predict-then-check with two identical pizzas
feedback: If the child predicts the quarter is bigger 'because 4 is more than 2', let the overlay settle it: the half visibly covers the quarter and more, so the bigger denominator did NOT make the bigger piece.
If the child says the 4-piece pizza has 'more' because it has more pieces, refocus on one single slice versus one single slice, not the count of pieces.
When they state the pattern themselves after watching the shrink, confirm it and restate: sharing one whole among more people gives each person less.
Keep attention on the amount of pizza each piece represents; the paper is just a model of the flat region being shared.
activities.rationale: Predicting before overlaying surfaces the whole-number-bias reasoning out loud, then the physical overlay of identical wholes contradicts it, so the correction is something the child sees happen rather than a rule they are told. Keeping the wholes identical means the number of shares is the only variable.
sourceClaims: As the number of people sharing a whole increases, each share decreases; teachers link this to fraction names (1/3 of an object is greater than 1/4 of it)
Children commonly view fractions with larger denominators as larger (e.g. they think 1/8 > 1/3) - the whole-number bias
Year 2 pupils compare and understand the size of fractions such as halves and quarters
learnerActions: Give the child two identical paper 'pizzas' of exactly the same size (the paper stands in for the flat region being shared - what matters is the amount each piece represents, not the paper itself).
Before cutting, ask them to predict: if one pizza is cut into 2 equal pieces and the other into 4 equal pieces, whose single piece will be bigger, and why? Record the stated reason.
Cut both pizzas and lay one half on top of one quarter so the child can see the half blankets the quarter with room to spare.
Then cut (or imagine cutting) the same-size whole into 8, then more, and have the child watch a single piece keep getting smaller.
Name the pattern out loud together: 'more equal shares of the same whole means smaller pieces.'
activities.intendedInsight: A single share gets smaller as the same whole is split among more sharers, so a half of a pizza is a bigger amount than a quarter of the same pizza even though 4 is more than 2.

activities.title: Live share-slider: watch one piece shrink
feedback: If the child expects the piece to grow as shares increase, let them watch the highlighted slice shrink and ask them to revise their prediction.
Prompt them to connect the moving slider to the earlier paper activity: more equal shares of the same whole, smaller piece, every time.
activities.rationale: A live, adjustable number of shares with one highlighted piece lets the child generate the shrink and overlay to test a prediction, which a fixed diagram cannot be manipulated to do. An interactive model is offered as one concrete way to make the mechanism visible; it is not the only route and complements the physical paper work.
sourceClaims: As the number of people sharing a whole increases, each share decreases; teachers link this to fraction names (1/3 of an object is greater than 1/4 of it)
Children commonly view fractions with larger denominators as larger (e.g. they think 1/8 > 1/3) - the whole-number bias
learnerActions: Show two identical circular pizzas side by side, each with a control that sets the number of equal shares.
Have the child set one pizza to 2 shares and the other to 4, highlight one piece on each, then drag the highlighted pieces together to overlay them.
Ask the child to describe what happens to the overlapped pieces: the half covers the quarter with space left over.
Have the child push the share control higher (8, 10, 12) on one pizza and describe how a single highlighted piece keeps shrinking.
activities.intendedInsight: As the number of equal shares rises, one share visibly shrinks, making the inverse relationship between number of shares and size of each share concrete.

activities.title: Order and compare unit fractions of the same whole
feedback: If a child orders by the denominator digit (treating 1/8 as biggest), return to overlay or the shrinking slice to re-anchor the size order.

If a child says a quarter is 'always' a smaller amount than a half regardless of the cakes, contrast a quarter of a large cake with a half of a small one to show the two wholes must be equal for that amount comparison to hold.
Reward reasoning that names that the wholes must be the same AND that more shares means each piece is smaller.
activities.rationale: Ordering and choosing between unit fractions of the same whole consolidates the pattern and lets you check whether the child reasons from piece size or reverts to the digit. The explicit 'different-sized wholes' question guards against over-generalising the amount comparison, and the 'biggest number on the bottom' prompt confronts the whole-number bias by name.
sourceClaims: As the number of people sharing a whole increases, each share decreases; teachers link this to fraction names (1/3 of an object is greater than 1/4 of it)
Year 2 pupils compare and understand the size of fractions such as halves and quarters
learnerActions: Show pictures of 1/2, 1/3, 1/4 and 1/8 of the SAME cake and ask the child to order them largest to smallest.
Ask the child to explain why the order goes that way in terms of sharing.
Ask the child directly: 'Why doesn't the biggest number on the bottom mean the biggest piece?'
Pose a comparison question such as: 'Who has more, someone with a half of a cake or someone with a quarter of the same cake?' and ask for the reason.
Ask the trap question: 'Could a quarter ever be a bigger amount than a half? What would have to be true about the two cakes?'
activities.intendedInsight: Unit fractions of the same whole can be ordered by size (1/2 > 1/3 > 1/4 > 1/8); when comparing the actual amounts in the pieces, the comparison relies on the wholes being the same size.

activities.title: Aligned fraction wall as a reference
feedback: If the child cannot see the comparison, draw attention to one tile per row rather than the whole row.
Note that this wall shows the sizes but does not let them generate the shrink themselves; pair it with the paper or slider activity for the 'why'.
activities.rationale: A static aligned wall is a useful reference for the size order of halves, quarters and eighths, but it shows the result rather than letting the child produce the shrink or test their own prediction, so it works best as a support alongside the hands-on comparisons.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils compare and understand the size of fractions such as halves and quarters
learnerActions: Show a fraction wall with rows for 1 whole, halves, quarters and eighths, all aligned to the same total length.
Have the child point to and compare a single tile in each row against the whole and against each other.
Ask them to find which single tile is biggest and which is smallest, and to say why.
activities.intendedInsight: A single piece gets shorter as the whole is divided into more equal parts, shown against a common length.

constraints: When comparing the actual amount in a piece, use IDENTICAL wholes (same pizza, same bar) so the only thing changing is the number of shares. This is a requirement for comparing represented portions; it is NOT a claim that fractions as numbers are incomparable (as numbers, 1/2 is always greater than 1/4).

Stress that 'a quarter is a smaller amount than a half' is guaranteed only when the two physical wholes are the same size; with different-sized wholes it can go either way, for example a quarter of a large whole can be a larger amount than a half of a small whole.

The aligned fraction wall and other fixed diagrams show the size order but do not let the child generate the shrink or test a prediction; use them as supports, not as the main mechanism for confronting the misconception.

Ordering/multiple-choice tasks can check whether the child selects the right size order, but selection alone does not show the child constructing the reasoning, so pair selection tasks with 'explain why' prompts.
Keep the focus on the amount in ONE single piece, not the number of pieces, when confronting the 'more pieces = more to eat' confusion.
Paper pizzas and cards are physical stand-ins for the ideal flat regions being shared; compare the amounts they represent rather than any property of the paper itself.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original source rated a 3D manipulation as adding 'nothing' and plain conversation as 'poor' because the misconception 'yields to physical comparison, not to talk'. These are catalog fit judgements, not established facts; they have been softened. Physical comparison is well suited here, but talk and discussion can still support reasoning, and this rewrite does not assert any format is universally useless or uniquely necessary.

The claim that an interactive slider is uniquely able to teach the inverse relationship was softened: a fixed diagram cannot be manipulated, but can still support learning; the slider is presented as one concrete option.
The 1/2 > 1/3 > 1/4 > 1/8 size ordering, the overlay demonstration, and the whole-number-bias description are internally consistent and arithmetically sound.

The common-whole requirement is scoped to comparing the represented amounts; as numbers, fractions remain comparable (1/2 > 1/4 always), which is a nuance beyond the explicit scope of the cited sources for this age.

assess.poeTask: Give the child two identical paper 'pizzas'. BEFORE cutting, ask them to predict: if one is cut into 2 equal pieces and the other into 4, whose single piece will be bigger, and WHY - record the reason. Then cut both and lay one half on top of one quarter. Observe the half covers the quarter and more. The pre-cut REASON is the diagnostic part: a '4 is bigger than 2' justification reveals whole-number bias, which the overlay then contradicts.
probeDeeper: If Bea cut hers into 8 pieces instead, would her piece be bigger or smaller than a quarter?
Could a quarter ever be bigger than a half? What would have to be true about the two pizzas?
Order these for size: a half, a third, and a quarter of the same cake.
Why doesn't the biggest number on the bottom mean the biggest piece?
assess.correctAnswer: Ali has more - a half is bigger than a quarter of the same pizza. Cutting the same whole into more equal pieces makes each piece smaller, because one whole is being shared among more parts. (Tier 2: the more sharers, the less each one gets.)

errorPatterns.pattern: Larger denominator means larger fraction - 'a quarter is bigger because 4 is more than 2' (whole-number bias)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Predict-then-overlay two identical wholes (see poeTask); name the pattern 'more shares = smaller piece'.
errorPatterns.distractor: Bea - a quarter is bigger because 4 is more than 2
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Chooses Bea and justifies with the size of the denominator digit

errorPatterns.pattern: More pieces means more to eat - confuses the NUMBER of pieces with the AMOUNT in one piece
errorPatterns.nextMove: Focus on the size of a single piece; overlay one slice on one slice.
errorPatterns.distractor: Bea - she cut hers into more pieces, so she has more
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Chooses Bea 'because she has 4 pieces and Ali only has 2', even though each eats one piece

errorPatterns.pattern: Ignores that the wholes must be the same size to compare
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast 1/4 of a large pizza with 1/2 of a small one; the whole must be equal for the rule to hold.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Later claims 'a quarter is always smaller than a half' regardless, or cannot see why 'same size pizza' was stated

responseLevels.gap: Picks the larger-denominator fraction as bigger and reasons from the digits ('4>2').
responseLevels.full: States that more equal shares of the same whole means smaller shares, orders 1/2 > 1/3 > 1/4 and explains why, recognises the wholes must be identical, and transfers to 1/8.
responseLevels.partial: Orders unit fractions of the same whole correctly when shown a picture, but reverts to 'bigger number = bigger' without the model, or overlooks that the wholes must be the same size.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Two children each have a whole pizza, exactly the same size. Ali cuts hers into 2 equal pieces and takes one piece. Bea cuts hers into 4 equal pieces and takes one piece. Ask: 'Who has more pizza to eat - and how do you know?' Then ask: 'Why does cutting the same pizza into MORE pieces make each piece smaller?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A whole-number-bias child reasons '4 is more than 2, so Bea's quarter is bigger' and gives the wrong answer with a confident, articulable wrong reason - exactly the tell we want. A child who understands sharing picks Ali and explains that more pieces from the same whole means smaller pieces. Identical pizzas remove the 'it depends on the pizza' escape, so the denominator size is the only thing in play.

pedagogy.summary: An inequality compares expressions and, unlike an equation, its solution is a RANGE (a set) of values, not a single value. On a number line that range is shown by a circle at the boundary — open/hollow for strict < or > (boundary excluded), closed/filled for inclusive ≤ or ≥ (boundary included) — with an arrow or segment covering the values that satisfy it. Solving uses the same inverse operations as equations. The representational competence is translating fluently among worded constraint, inequality symbol and number-line diagram; it is best taught by tying the circle style to boundary inclusion, the arrow to the satisfying set, and rehearsing worded phrases such as 'at least' and 'at most'.
bestPractices: Distinguish strict from inclusive explicitly: open circle = boundary NOT included (<, >), closed circle = boundary included (≤, ≥), tied to whether the boundary value itself satisfies the statement.
Represent the solution as a SET (arrow/segment), not a point; test a value inside and outside the range to confirm which side to shade.
Rehearse worded-constraint translation: 'at least 12' → x ≥ 12, 'at most'/'no more than' → ≤, 'more than' → strict >.
Solve inequalities with the same inverse operations as equations (for KS3 cases like 3x + 1 < 10) and read the result back onto the number line.
(KS4 extension) flag that multiplying or dividing both sides by a NEGATIVE reverses the inequality, while keeping the KS3 focus on the representation.
keyRepresentations: Number line with open vs closed circle at the boundary plus an arrow for the solution set
The symbol quartet <, ≤, >, ≥ mapped to circle style and direction
Worded constraint ↔ inequality symbol ↔ number-line diagram triple
A test value checked inside and outside the range
commonMisconceptions: Confuses strict (<, >) with inclusive (≤, ≥): uses the wrong circle style (open for ≥, filled for <).
Shades or points the arrow the wrong way (reads the symbol direction backwards).
Treats the solution as a single boundary value (x < 5 means x = 4) rather than a whole set.
Worded-boundary error: renders 'at least 12' as x > 12 (strict) instead of x ≥ 12.

learn.summary: An inequality compares expressions and, unlike an equation, its solution is a RANGE (a set) of values rather than a single value. On a number line that range is shown by a circle at the boundary — open/hollow for strict < or > (boundary excluded), closed/filled for inclusive ≤ or ≥ (boundary included) — with an arrow or segment covering the values that satisfy it. Solving uses the same inverse operations as equations, except that multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number reverses the inequality sign (an extension point). The core skill is translating fluently among a worded constraint, the inequality symbol and the number-line diagram, tying circle style to boundary inclusion, the arrow to the satisfying set, and rehearsing worded phrases such as 'at least' and 'at most'.

activities.title: Build and test a number-line inequality
feedback: If a value exactly on the boundary is marked as satisfying under > or <, ask: 'does the boundary value itself make the statement true?' For strict < or >, it does not, so the circle is open.
If the arrow covers values that fail the test, pick one value on each side (e.g. is −5 ≥ −2? is 0 ≥ −2?) to decide which side belongs to the solution.
If only the boundary point is marked, prompt that an inequality's solution is EVERY value in the range — mark several, then the whole arrow or segment; contrast with an equation's single answer.
activities.rationale: A live builder plus a 'does this value satisfy it?' tester makes boundary inclusion and solution-as-a-set directly observable, and letting the symbol switch recolour the boundary value ties the open/closed convention to a fact about solutions. Testing values on each side addresses reading direction backwards.
sourceClaims: Students have difficulty distinguishing > from ≥ and < from ≤ (whether the boundary is included) — shown graphically by whether a boundary line is dashed or solid, the coordinate-grid analogue of an open vs closed circle on a number line; they also shade/read the wrong side, and reason about the solution as isolated points rather than a whole region/set.
learnerActions: Choose an inequality symbol (<, ≤, >, ≥) and a boundary value, then draw the matching number line: decide whether the boundary circle is open or closed and which way the arrow points.
Test several sample values by asking of each, 'does this value satisfy the inequality?', and mark those that satisfy it (e.g. in one colour) and those that do not (another colour).

Switch the symbol from ≥ to > (or ≤ to <) on the same boundary and observe what changes: the boundary circle hollows, and a value sitting exactly on the boundary flips from satisfying to not satisfying.
Deliberately draw the arrow the wrong way, then test values along it to see that a whole stretch of the line fails the check — confirming direction matters.
Read a given diagram (e.g. a filled circle at −2 with a right-pointing arrow) back into symbols and words.
activities.intendedInsight: Inclusion is not an arbitrary drawing convention: whether the circle is filled depends on whether the boundary value itself is a solution. The arrow/segment represents the whole set of satisfying values, and its direction is fixed by what the symbol means.

activities.title: Translate worded constraints into symbols and diagrams
feedback: If 'at least 1' is rendered as x > 1 or an open circle, ask whether 1 itself is allowed — 'at least' includes the boundary, so x ≥ 1 with a closed circle.
If 'less than 4' is drawn with a closed circle at 4, check whether 4 satisfies 'less than 4' — it does not, so the circle is open.
Confirm the compound case by testing x = 1, x = 4 and a value between: 1 should satisfy, 4 should not, and the between-value should satisfy.
activities.rationale: Worded-constraint translation is the part of the representational skill most prone to slips between strict and inclusive phrasing; rehearsing the phrase→symbol mapping and checking the boundary against the words targets that error directly.
sourceClaims: Students have difficulty distinguishing > from ≥ and < from ≤ (whether the boundary is included) — shown graphically by whether a boundary line is dashed or solid, the coordinate-grid analogue of an open vs closed circle on a number line; they also shade/read the wrong side, and reason about the solution as isolated points rather than a whole region/set.
learnerActions: Translate worded constraints into inequality symbols: 'at least 12' → x ≥ 12, 'at most'/'no more than' → ≤, 'more than' → strict >, 'less than' → strict <.
Build a phrase→symbol reference table and, for each phrase, test the boundary value against the words ('is 12 allowed if you must be at least 12?').
Draw the number-line diagram for a compound statement such as 'x is at least 1 and less than 4' (closed circle at 1, open circle at 4, segment shaded between).
Check your diagram by reading it back into words and comparing with the original statement.
activities.intendedInsight: Everyday boundary phrases map precisely onto strict or inclusive symbols, and testing whether the boundary value is allowed decides between an open and closed circle.

activities.title: Solve a simple linear inequality and plot its solution set
feedback: If the solution is given as a single value, remind that solving an inequality yields a range — plot the whole arrow or segment, not a point.
If a test value inside the range fails the original inequality, recheck the inverse operations step by step.
For the negative-multiplier extension: test an actual value in both the original and transformed inequalities to see that the direction must flip for the solutions to agree.
activities.rationale: The curriculum requires solving linear inequalities and representing the solution set on a number line; tying the solved result back to the diagram reinforces that the solution is a set. The negative-multiplier rule is flagged as an extension rather than the KS3 focus.
sourceClaims: Pupils should 'solve linear inequalities in one variable ... ; represent the solution set on a number line' — this is the Key Stage 4 Algebra statutory statement (at KS3 pupils use the symbols =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥ and inequality notation a < x ≤ b).
learnerActions: Solve a one-step or two-step inequality such as 3x + 1 < 10 using the same inverse operations as an equation (subtract 1, then divide by 3, giving x < 3).
Represent the resulting solution set on a number line with the correct open or closed circle and arrow.
Check the solution by testing a value inside the range and a value outside it.
(Extension) Explore what happens when both sides are multiplied or divided by a negative number, using test values to discover that the inequality direction reverses.
activities.intendedInsight: Solving an inequality mirrors solving an equation, but the answer is a set shown on the number line; special care is needed when multiplying or dividing by a negative because the direction reverses.

activities.title: Reference card: symbols, circles and directions
feedback: If a mapping is wrong (e.g. open circle paired with ≥), re-derive it from the question 'is the boundary value a solution?' rather than memorising.
Encourage pairing the card with an actual drawn example so the reference supports, rather than replaces, building the diagram.
activities.rationale: A static symbol-to-diagram reference supports recall but cannot by itself rehearse constructing or translating an inequality, so it is positioned as a check alongside the building activities.
learnerActions: Match each of <, ≤, >, ≥ to its circle style (open for strict, closed for inclusive) and, for inequalities written with the variable on the left (e.g. x < 3), to the direction of its arrow; notice that 3 > x means the same as x < 3, so the arrow still points left.
Use the card as a check when building or reading diagrams, confirming each choice against whether the boundary value is itself a solution.
activities.intendedInsight: The four symbols map systematically onto circle style; they map onto arrow direction once the inequality is written with the variable on the left (e.g. x ≥ a points right), giving a quick self-check reference.

constraints: A static reference card mapping symbols to circle style and arrow direction supports recall but does not rehearse building, translating or reading inequalities independently; pair it with construction tasks.

Matching, multiple-choice and fill-in-the-blank items can check the representation (e.g. 'open or closed circle for x ≥ 3?', 'at least 12 → x __ 12') but recognition-style responses do not elicit independent construction of a diagram or translation; include tasks where the learner draws the number line and states the inequality themselves.
This content lives on a one-dimensional number line, so a three-dimensional representation carries no extra spatial payload for it; a 2D line with circle, arrow and test values is sufficient.
The negative-multiplier direction-reversal rule is a KS4 extension; keep the KS3 focus on the representation and translation.
Keep the solution-as-set idea explicit: an inequality's answer is every value in the range, contrasted with an equation's single value.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The two cited sources support the existence of the boundary-inclusion/direction/set misconceptions and the curriculum requirement to represent solution sets on a number line; they do not establish the comparative efficacy of any specific activity format, interaction, or medium.

The curriculum source labels the solve-and-represent statement as KS4 Algebra (KS3 covers the symbols/notation); activity 3 treats the full solving plus negative-multiplier reversal as an extension beyond the KS3 representation focus, consistent with the source.

Self-audit: the worked values (x ≥ −2 with closed circle and right arrow; compound 1 ≤ x < 4 with closed circle at 1, open at 4) are internally consistent, and 3x + 1 < 10 solves to x < 3 via one-/two-step inverse operations. The negative-multiplier reversal is genuine inequality mathematics, not a spurious denominator-style 'flip'. No arithmetic or logic errors were found in learner-facing text.

probeDeeper: You showed x ≥ −2. Is −2 itself a solution? What about −2.5? How does your diagram say so?
If the circle at −2 were hollow instead of filled, what would change about the inequality?
In your diagram for 'at least 1 and less than 4', is x = 4 included? Is x = 1? How can you tell from the circles?
Are 'you must be more than 12' and 'you must be at least 12' the same inequality? Show each on a number line.
assess.correctAnswer: The diagram shows x ≥ −2 (closed circle = boundary included; arrow to the right = values greater than or equal to −2). The produced number line has a CLOSED circle at 1, an OPEN circle at 4, and the segment between them shaded: 1 ≤ x < 4.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses strict with inclusive circle style — reads the filled circle as x > −2, or draws an OPEN circle at 1 for 'at least 1' / a closed circle at 4 for 'less than 4'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'does −2 itself count as a solution?' — if yes, fill the circle; translate the symbol into words to separate > from ≥.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The wrong circle style appears on read or draw; the boundary's inclusion does not match the symbol/words.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the direction backwards — takes a closed circle with a right arrow as x ≤ −2, or shades the wrong side of the boundary
errorPatterns.nextMove: Test a value on each side (is −5 ≥ −2? is 0 ≥ −2?) to fix which side belongs to the solution.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The arrow/shading covers the values that do NOT satisfy the inequality.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the solution as a single value, not a set — marks only a dot at the boundary, or gives one number for x ≥ −2
errorPatterns.nextMove: An inequality's solution is EVERY value in the range — mark several, then the arrow/segment; contrast with an equation's single answer.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws a point with no arrow/segment, or answers 'x = 1'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Worded-boundary translation error — renders 'at least 1' as x > 1 (strict) rather than x ≥ 1, or 'less than 4' as ≤ 4
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build a phrase→symbol table ('at least'→≥, 'at most'→≤, 'more/less than'→ strict) and test the boundary value against the words.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Uses strict symbols/open circles for 'at least/at most', or inclusive for 'more/less than'.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot read the circle/arrow, uses the wrong circle style, or marks a single point instead of a set.
responseLevels.full: Reads the diagram as x ≥ −2, produces the compound 1 ≤ x < 4 with correct open/closed circles and a shaded set, and justifies each boundary's inclusion against the words — translating fluently in both directions and to a new, compound case.
responseLevels.partial: Reads and draws simple one-boundary inequalities with the correct circle style, but slips on direction, on the 'at least/at most' wording, or on the compound two-boundary case — handles single translations without coordinating symbol, words and diagram across the whole set.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a number line with a FILLED (closed) circle at −2 and an arrow pointing to the right. First: what inequality does this diagram show? Then, on a fresh number line, show the solution to the statement 'x is at least 1 and less than 4'.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Reading the diagram tests whether the child maps a filled circle to ≥ (not >) and a right arrow to 'greater'; producing the compound diagram reverses the translation and exposes both the strict/inclusive choice (closed at 1 for 'at least', open at 4 for 'less than') and whether the solution is drawn as a set (a shaded segment) rather than isolated points. A child who confuses the circle styles or marks a single point cannot produce the correct diagram.

sources.claim: Students have difficulty distinguishing > from ≥ and < from ≤ (whether the boundary is included) — shown graphically by whether a boundary line is dashed or solid, the coordinate-grid analogue of an open vs closed circle on a number line; they also shade/read the wrong side, and reason about the solution as isolated points rather than a whole region/set.

pedagogy.summary: This topic turns coordinate reading into PRODUCING: given coordinates, plot the point on the grid; and given a shape's structure, work out and plot a missing vertex, then draw the sides. It is a two-way translation between the symbolic pair (x, y) and the spatial mark on the grid — reading a pair to place a point, and reading a placed configuration to generate a new coordinate. Completing a polygon (find the 4th vertex of a square, the 3rd of a triangle) is where coordinates meet shape properties: the missing vertex of a rectangle/square shares one known vertex's x-value and another's y-value. The dominant error, as in reading, is reversal (plotting up-then-across); the second is completing a shape 'by eye' from appearance rather than reasoning from the coordinates.
bestPractices: Plot with the same along-then-up discipline as reading: find the x-line first, travel up to the y-line, mark the intersection — count from the origin against numbered lines.

For a missing vertex, reason from coordinates and shape properties, not appearance: the 4th vertex of a rectangle takes its x from one neighbour and its y from the other; verify sides are the right lengths.
Have children state the missing coordinate BEFORE plotting it, so the reasoning is explicit and checkable.
Draw the sides in order and check the result is the intended polygon (right angles for a rectangle, equal sides for a square), catching mis-plotted vertices.
Contrast a correctly completed square with a plausible-looking wrong one to show that 'looks right' is not the test — the coordinates are.
Use the reversal distractor deliberately: plot (5,4) and (4,5) to show they are different, reinforcing order in the act of plotting.
keyRepresentations: Numbered coordinate grid with origin, points plotted as line-intersections
Along-then-up plotting path from the origin to each point
Partly-drawn polygon with given vertices and one missing, to be completed
The missing vertex sharing one neighbour's x and another neighbour's y (rectangle/square)
Completed shape with all vertex coordinates labelled
commonMisconceptions: Reversal when plotting — going up before across, so the point lands in the mirror position (e.g. plots (5,4) at 4-across-5-up).
Completing a polygon by eye/appearance rather than reasoning from coordinates and shape properties, giving a wrong missing vertex.
Counting squares instead of numbered lines when plotting, producing off-by-one positions.
Joining vertices in the wrong order, producing a crossed or incorrect polygon even when the points are right.

learn.summary: This topic moves children from reading coordinates to PRODUCING them: given a pair (x, y), plot the point; given a partly-drawn polygon, reason out and plot a missing vertex, then draw the sides. The key reasoning is that the missing vertex of a rectangle or square whose sides run along the grid lines shares one neighbour's x-value and another neighbour's y-value, so completion is derived from coordinates and shape properties rather than guessed by eye. The two dominant errors are reversal (plotting up-then-across) and completing 'by eye' from appearance instead of reasoning from the coordinates.

activities.title: Plot-and-complete on a numbered grid
feedback: If a plotted point lands reversed, return to along-then-up plotting from the origin, tie the first number to the across axis, and plot (5,1) and (1,5) together to show they differ.
If the fourth vertex is placed by eye (near but not at the target), ask the child to say which neighbour's x and which neighbour's y it must share, then check side lengths and right angles.
If points land one line off, anchor at the origin (0,0) and count the numbered line labels aloud while placing the point, rather than counting cells crossed.

When the drawn sides form a leaning or lopsided quadrilateral, point out that the coordinates, side lengths and right angles, not the appearance, are the test — four equal sides and four right angles for a square, equal opposite sides and four right angles for a rectangle.
activities.rationale: Plotting and completing a polygon is a produce-and-check action: entering a point and drawing the sides gives spatial feedback that exposes reversal (the point visibly lands wrong) and by-eye completion (the figure fails to close into the named shape, or the side lengths are unequal). Stating the coordinate before plotting makes the reasoning explicit and checkable.
sourceClaims: Students graph points in the first quadrant to represent problems and interpret coordinate values, locating each point by an ordered pair measured from the origin along the two axes (5.G.1, 5.G.2).
Year 4 pupils should plot specified points and draw sides to complete a given polygon.

A common documented misconception is putting the y-coordinate before the x, giving an incorrectly placed point; the Year 4 objective works on a grid where the lines are numbered (reading numbered lines rather than counting squares). Sample key questions ask for the missing fourth vertex of a square given three vertices.
learnerActions: Plot a given point by finding the x-line first, travelling up to the y-line, and marking the intersection, counting from the origin against the numbered lines.
Plot (5,4) and then (4,5) and compare: show they land in different places to make the along-then-up order explicit.

Given three vertices of a genuine square, e.g. (1,1), (1,4) and (4,4) (whose fourth vertex is (4,1), a 3-by-3 square with four equal sides), STATE the fourth coordinate aloud before plotting it, then plot it and draw the sides; check all four side lengths are equal and all four corners are right angles so the figure is genuinely a square.
Check the completed figure is the intended polygon: right angles and matching opposite sides for a rectangle, right angles and four equal sides for a square.

Repeat with three vertices of a rectangle, e.g. (1,1), (1,4), (5,4) whose fourth vertex is (5,1), giving a 4-by-3 rectangle, so the shared-x / shared-y reasoning transfers and children see that unequal sides (4 and 3) make a rectangle, not a square.
activities.intendedInsight: A point's location is fixed by reading x (across) then y (up) from the origin, and the missing vertex of a rectangle or square whose sides run along the grid lines can be reasoned out because it shares one neighbour's x and another neighbour's y; 'looks right' is replaced by 'is right' when the drawn sides form the named shape, with right angles at every corner and matching side lengths — four equal sides for a square, equal opposite sides for a rectangle.

activities.title: Which coordinate completes the shape? — diagnostic choices
feedback: If the reversed pair is chosen, revisit along-then-up order and compare the swapped pair with the correct one on a grid.
If the by-eye value is chosen, ask which neighbour supplies the x and which supplies the y for the missing corner, then check the side lengths.
If points are joined in the wrong order producing a crossed figure, draw the sides in vertex order and check the shape closes correctly.
activities.rationale: Choosing the correct missing vertex is cleanly scorable and useful for diagnosis, with the reversed pair and the by-eye value as targeted distractors. On its own this recognition format does not elicit the child independently plotting and drawing to see the sides close, so pair it with a grid where the child produces and checks.
sourceClaims: A common documented misconception is putting the y-coordinate before the x, giving an incorrectly placed point; the Year 4 objective works on a grid where the lines are numbered (reading numbered lines rather than counting squares). Sample key questions ask for the missing fourth vertex of a square given three vertices.
learnerActions: Choose which coordinate completes a given genuine square, e.g. three vertices (1,1),(1,4),(4,4) whose correct fourth vertex is (4,1), from options that include the reversed pair and a plausible but wrong by-eye value.
Explain WHY the chosen coordinate is correct in terms of shared x and shared y, not appearance.
Match a set of plotted points to their coordinate labels.
Plot a given set of points to form a rectangle and join them in order.
activities.intendedInsight: Identifying the correct missing vertex, and rejecting the reversal and by-eye distractors, shows that the vertex is determined by the coordinates and shape structure, not by how the figure looks.

activities.title: Reveal how a completed shape's coordinates relate
feedback: If a prediction is wrong, show which neighbour supplies the x and which supplies the y and re-trace the plotting path.
Prompt the child to state the shared-value reasoning before revealing the answer so the pattern, not the picture, is used.
activities.rationale: A static or worked grid can display the structural relationship between vertices and let the child predict before revealing, which supports the shared-x/shared-y reasoning. It is a scaffold: a fixed figure cannot be re-plotted or tested by the child, so the producing that defines this topic still needs an interactive or paper grid where the child plots their own points and draws the sides.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should plot specified points and draw sides to complete a given polygon.
learnerActions: On a completed rectangle with all vertices labelled, tap each corner to reveal how its coordinates relate to its neighbours (which x it shares, which y it shares).
Before a 'where must the fourth corner go?' answer is revealed, predict the coordinate and give a reason based on the shared values.
Trace the along-then-up path from the origin to each labelled vertex.
activities.intendedInsight: Even on a worked, labelled figure the child can see the structural pattern — each vertex shares an x with one neighbour and a y with another — which is the reasoning needed to complete a polygon.

constraints: Plot with along-then-up discipline: find the x-line, travel up to the y-line, mark the intersection; count from the origin against the numbered lines, not by counting squares.

Completion must be reasoned from coordinates and shape properties (shared x and shared y of neighbours, for shapes whose sides run along the grid lines), not from appearance; verify side lengths and right angles — four equal sides with four right angles confirm a square, equal opposite sides with four right angles a rectangle.
Have children state the missing coordinate before plotting it so the reasoning is explicit and checkable.

Recognition-only formats (choosing the missing vertex, matching labels) are good for diagnosis but do not by themselves show the child independently plotting and drawing the sides to see the figure close; pair them with a produce-and-draw task.
A worked, labelled figure is a scaffold: it shows the relationship but cannot be re-plotted or tested by the child, so include a grid (interactive or paper) where the child plots and draws.
First-quadrant plotting and completing plane polygons is a 2D task; include the zero-coordinate/axis case, e.g. compare (3,0) and (0,3) as distinct points.

When a point set is named a square, confirm it actually has four equal sides; a set like (1,1),(1,4),(5,4),(5,1) has unequal sides (4 and 3) and is a rectangle, so use it as a rectangle example and reserve 'square' for equal-sided sets such as (1,1),(1,4),(4,4),(4,1).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Optional interaction examples retained from the source (type a coordinate to drop a point with an along-then-up trail, snap-to-numbered-lines with origin highlighted, a complete-the-polygon mode that draws the sides and names the resulting shape, (5,4) vs (4,5) order check) are illustrative of the learning mechanism and are not mandatory.

The source's '3D adds no value' and 'dialogue cannot teach plotting' claims were not propagated as universal laws; 2D plotting is the natural medium for this content, but no comparative-efficacy claim is asserted.

Corrected original error: the point set (1,1), (1,4), (5,4) with fourth vertex (5,1) forms a RECTANGLE 4 units wide and 3 units tall (sides 4 and 3), NOT a square. The derivation is sound — the fourth vertex shares x=5 with (5,4) and y=1 with (1,1) — but the original row's diagnostic prompt and correctAnswer mislabel the resulting figure a 'square' (its own evidence list correctly calls the identical set a rectangle). Guidance now treats this set as a rectangle example and supplies a genuine square example (1,1),(1,4),(4,4),(4,1), a 3-by-3 square with four equal sides.

probeDeeper: 'How did you know the fourth corner was (5,1) and not somewhere else?' — listen for 'it shares this x and that y', not 'it looked right'.
Counterexample: 'If I move this corner from (5,1) to (5,2), is it still a square? Why not?' — tests that the coordinates, not appearance, define the shape.
'Here are three corners of a rectangle instead of a square — where does the fourth go?' — checks the shared-x/shared-y reasoning transfers.
'Plot (3,0) and (0,3) — are they the same point?' — surfaces order and the zero-coordinate/axis case during producing.
assess.correctAnswer: READ: each point is located across (x) then up (y) from the origin — e.g. (5,4) is 5 across, 4 up. PRODUCE: the fourth vertex is (5,1) — it shares the x-value (5) of (5,4) and the y-value (1) of (1,1); plotted at 5-across-1-up, completing the square with vertical and horizontal sides.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reversal when plotting — plots the fourth vertex (or reads a given one) up-before-across, placing (5,1) at 1-across-5-up.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to along-then-up plotting from the origin, tying the first number to the x (across) axis; plot (5,1) and (1,5) together to show they differ.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The plotted point is the coordinate-swap of the correct one; the drawn figure is not a square; reading of the given vertices may also swap across and up.

errorPatterns.pattern: Completes the polygon by eye — places the fourth vertex where it 'looks right' rather than reasoning from the coordinates and the square's properties.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reason from structure: the missing vertex of a rectangle/square shares one neighbour's x and the other's y; check side lengths and right angles rather than trusting appearance.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The fourth point is near but not at (5,1); the child can't say it should share (5,4)'s x and (1,1)'s y; the drawn shape is a rough quadrilateral, not a square.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts squares not numbered lines — plots off-by-one, or starts from 1 instead of the origin.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor at the origin (0,0) and plot on the numbered lines; count line labels aloud while placing the point.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Points land one line off; the child counts cells crossed rather than reading the line labels.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot plot given points reliably or complete the polygon: points land reversed or off-by-one, no missing vertex, or a shape that isn't the target.
responseLevels.full: Reads each given vertex as (across, up), derives the missing vertex from the shared x and y of its neighbours, plots it accurately on the numbered lines, and draws sides that form the correct polygon — reading and producing coordinates fluently in both directions.
responseLevels.partial: Plots the given vertices correctly (can read the marks) but cannot PRODUCE the missing vertex by reasoning — guesses by eye, or reverses when plotting the new point — so the completed figure is not a true square; reads but does not fully translate to producing.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a grid with three vertices of a square marked and labelled: (1,1), (1,4) and (5,4). First (READ): 'Point to each marked vertex and tell me what its two numbers mean.' Then (PRODUCE): 'Plot the fourth vertex to complete the square, write its coordinates, and draw the sides.' Watch both the reading and the plotting.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The task requires BOTH translating a symbol to a location (reading the given vertices) and generating a new symbol from a spatial/structural constraint (the missing vertex). A child who can read but not produce plots by eye and misses (5,1); a child who reverses lands the fourth vertex at (1,5); a child reasoning correctly derives it from the shared x and y. Drawing the sides then exposes whether the figure is actually a square, catching by-appearance completion.

Sample key questions ask for the missing fourth vertex of a square given three vertices.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Add and subtract a two-digit number and tens (45 + 30, 82 − 40) mentally and with concrete/pictorial support, recognising that only the tens digit changes. Ages 6–7.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2 'add and subtract numbers using concrete objects, pictorial representations, and mentally, including: a two-digit number and tens'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.NBT.5/1.NBT.6 (mentally find 10 more/less; subtract multiples of 10) and 2.NBT.8; adding/subtracting a multiple of ten changes only the tens.
• Operational details: build directly from '10 more/10 less' — adding 30 is three jumps of ten, so the ones stay fixed and the tens digit changes by 3. Use base-ten blocks (add/remove ten-sticks, ones untouched) and a hundred square (move vertically). The insight is that the ones digit is invariant.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (age 6) — finds 45 + 10 then 45 + 30 by repeated tens. Tier B (age 7) — computes 45 + 30 and 82 − 40 mentally in one step. Tier C (age 7+) — explains that only the tens digit changes and predicts the result before calculating.
bestPractices: Build from '10 more/10 less' to adding/subtracting several tens at once.
Use base-ten blocks: add or remove ten-sticks while the ones pile stays untouched.
Use a hundred square with vertical moves (down = +10, up = −10).
Draw attention to the invariant ones digit as the key check.
Contrast with adding ones (which changes the ones) so children don't confuse the two.
keyRepresentations: Base-ten ten-sticks added/removed beside a fixed ones pile
Hundred square with vertical jumps
Empty number line with jumps of ten
Place-value (Gattegno) chart sliding the tens
Arrow cards separating tens and ones
commonMisconceptions: Changing the ones digit as well as the tens when adding tens.
Adding the tens digit to the ones (45 + 30 → 48 or 75... e.g. treating 30 as 3 ones).
Miscounting the number of tens jumps.
Confusing add-tens with add-ones procedures.
For subtraction, borrowing into the ones unnecessarily.

learn.summary: For ages 6–7: add and subtract a two-digit number and a multiple of ten (e.g. 45 + 30, 82 − 40) mentally and with concrete/pictorial support, building from '10 more/10 less'. The key insight is that adding or subtracting whole tens leaves the ones digit fixed and, while the answer stays between 0 and 99, changes only the tens digit (crossing 100, e.g. 85 + 30 = 115, also changes the hundreds). The classic error is treating the added tens as ones (45 + 30 → 48) or changing both digits. A deliberate contrast with adding ones (45 + 3) keeps the two procedures distinct.

activities.title: Add and remove tens while the ones stay put
feedback: If a learner answers 48 for 45 + 30, show that 30 is three ten-sticks, not three single ones: place the three ten-sticks with the tens and leave the ones pile of five untouched, so 45 + 30 = 75.
If the ones digit changes after adding tens (e.g. 45 + 30 → 70 or 78), point to the ones column on the hundred square and confirm it stays 5 through every vertical jump.
If the tens digit is off by one ten (65 or 85 for 45 + 30), count the ten-jumps aloud together and track them on fingers so exactly three tens are added.
When the learner correctly keeps the ones fixed, ask them to predict the next item before acting to confirm the reasoning, not just the answer.
activities.rationale: A manipulable base-ten mat and hundred square make the invariant ones digit visible as tens are added or removed, which targets the common place-value confusion between adding tens and adding ones. A 'predict then act' step shifts focus from counting to reasoning about place value.
sourceClaims: Y2 pupils add and subtract a two-digit number and tens using concrete, pictorial and mental methods.
Adding multiples of ten leaves the ones digit invariant; confusing add-tens with add-ones is a common place-value error.
learnerActions: Start with a base-ten representation of 45: four ten-sticks and five single ones, with the numeral 45 shown alongside.
Before acting, predict the answer to 45 + 30 and say which digit you think will change.
Add three more ten-sticks one at a time for +30, saying the running total aloud: 45 → 55 → 65 → 75, and notice that the five single ones never move.
Switch to subtraction: start from 82 (eight ten-sticks, two ones) and remove four ten-sticks for 82 − 40, reaching 42, with the two ones untouched.

Repeat the same moves on a hundred square numbered with 1 at the top: for +30 move three rows straight down (45 → 55 → 65 → 75); for −40 move four rows straight up (82 → 72 → 62 → 52 → 42), watching that the ones column stays the same.
Immediately afterwards do 45 + 3 with single ones to feel the difference: now the ones pile changes and the tens stay the same.

Optionally, show the same tens move on other representations of place value — an empty number line with jumps of ten, a Gattegno place-value chart where the tens row slides while the ones stay, or arrow cards that separate the tens and ones — to reinforce that only the tens change.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding or subtracting a multiple of ten moves only the tens; the ones digit is invariant. Adding ones is a different move that changes the ones instead.

activities.title: Fluency practice: one-step add/subtract tens
feedback: If a fluency answer alters the ones digit, send the learner back to the base-ten or hundred-square representation to re-see the fixed ones before continuing.
Reinforce correct one-step answers by asking the learner to state which digit changed and why.
activities.rationale: Speeded recall practice is proposed to help cement the one-step move once the invariant-ones insight is secure; it practises fluency rather than building the underlying place-value understanding, so it is best used after the manipulative work.
learnerActions: Complete fill-in items such as 45 + 30 = ___ and 82 − 40 = ___, aiming to answer in one step.
Answer 'which digit changes?' questions for an add-tens item, resisting a distractor answer that alters the ones digit.
Work through a short sequence of +10 steps (e.g. 45, 55, 65, 75) and then a −10 sequence, saying each total.
Mix in an occasional add-ones item (45 + 3) so you have to decide which digit changes each time.
activities.intendedInsight: The one-step mental move for adding/subtracting tens can become more automatic, while deliberate contrast with adding ones keeps the two procedures from merging.

activities.title: Explain and predict the invariant digit
feedback: If the learner cannot explain the invariance but gets answers by repeated +10 steps, name what they are doing: each +10 is one step down the hundred square (with 1 at the top) with the ones unchanged, so adding three tens keeps the ones fixed.
If the learner confuses the add-tens and add-ones items, revisit the deliberate 45 + 30 versus 45 + 3 contrast with concrete materials.
activities.rationale: Prompting prediction and explanation surfaces the place-value reasoning and can distinguish a learner who understands invariance from one relying only on repeated counting; the contrast item is the discriminating check.
sourceClaims: Adding multiples of ten leaves the ones digit invariant; confusing add-tens with add-ones is a common place-value error.
learnerActions: Work out 45 + 30; 82 − 40; and 45 + 3 mentally and state which digit changed each time.
Explain why only the tens change when adding or subtracting tens, and why the ones change for 45 + 3.
Predict the ones digit of 82 − 40 before calculating, then check.
Show 45 + 30 on a hundred square and describe which way you move and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to articulate why the ones stay fixed (because whole tens are being added) demonstrates secure place-value reasoning beyond getting the right number.

constraints: Build from an existing '10 more/10 less' skill: adding 30 is three jumps of ten, so the ones stay fixed and, when the total stays below 100, the tens digit goes up by three.

Include a contrast with adding ones (e.g. 45 + 3) so learners do not merge the add-tens and add-ones procedures; this contrast is strongly recommended and is the basis of the diagnostic discrimination between the two moves.
Fluency/fill-in practice reinforces speed but does not by itself build the invariant-ones understanding; use it after concrete and pictorial work.
A static highlighted hundred square can anchor the idea but does not let the learner practise the move; treat it as an anchor, not the main activity.
Live digit updates, dragging ten-sticks, and vertical hundred-square jumps are helpful ways to make the mechanism concrete but are optional illustrations, not required mechanisms.
Base-ten sticks and hundred squares are pictorial/concrete models of place value; keep attention on what each represents (tens vs ones) rather than the material itself.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Checked arithmetic: 45 + 30 = 75, 82 − 40 = 42, 45 + 3 = 48 are all correct as stated across the source fields.

The source listed 48 as the correct answer for 45 + 3 (not for 45 + 30); this is consistent, and 48 is used only as the correct answer to the add-ones contrast item and as a named misconception for 45 + 30, never as a valid alternative answer to 45 + 30.

Two CCSS/NCETM source claims are marked verified:false in the original; comparative, necessity or efficacy claims should not be inferred from them. The CCSS claim was removed from the fluency activity's sourceClaims because it supports topic coverage, not the efficacy of speeded practice.

The DfE claim retained in the first activity provides curriculum/method-level support (concrete, pictorial, mental methods are expected for this skill); it is not evidence that the manipulative is more effective than any other medium.

The original rated 3D interactive as 'poor' because it 'adds nothing' — this comparative/necessity framing was not retained as a universal law; adding tens is a one-dimensional place-value move and alternative media may still illustrate it.
Additional source representations (empty number line, Gattegno chart, arrow cards) are retained as optional representations rather than required mechanisms.

probeDeeper: Which digit changed in 45 + 30, and why only that one?
How is 45 + 30 different from 45 + 3?
Predict the answer to 82 − 40 before you work it out — what will the ones digit be?
Show me 45 + 30 on the hundred square — which way do you move?
assess.correctAnswer: 75 (tens change, ones stay 5); 42 (tens change, ones stay 2); 48 (ones change — this one adds ONES, not tens). Watch that the child keeps the ones digit fixed when adding/subtracting tens and correctly switches to changing the ones on the last item.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the added tens as ones — 45 + 30 handled as 45 + 3, giving 48.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Base-ten blocks: 30 is three ten-sticks, not three ones; add them to the tens while the ones pile is untouched.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 48 for 45 + 30; adds to the ones place.

errorPatterns.pattern: Changes the ones digit as well as the tens when adding/subtracting tens.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Highlight the invariant ones digit; use the hundred square vertical move where the ones column stays constant.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Ones digit differs from the start number after adding tens (e.g. 45 + 30 → 70 or 78).

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscounts the number of tens jumps (adds 20 or 40 instead of 30).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the ten-jumps aloud with the blocks or hundred square; track with fingers.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Tens digit off by one ten (65 or 85 for 45 + 30).

responseLevels.gap: Adds tens to the ones place or changes both digits arbitrarily; cannot keep the ones fixed.
responseLevels.full: Adds/subtracts multiples of ten in one step, keeps the ones digit fixed with justification, and correctly switches procedure when ones are added instead.
responseLevels.partial: Gets add/subtract-tens right by repeated +10 steps but is unsure why the ones stay fixed, or confuses it with adding ones.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these out mentally and tell me which digit changed each time: 45 + 30; 82 − 40; 45 + 3.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Two items add/subtract tens (ones must stay fixed) and the third adds ones (ones must change) — a deliberate contrast. A child who confuses the two procedures, or who alters the ones when adding tens, is exposed: 45 + 30 → 48 or an altered ones digit is the tell. Asking 'which digit changed?' makes the place-value reasoning visible.

pedagogy.summary: Writing algebraic equations means translating a situation — a 'think of a number' process or a comparison — into symbols, with letters standing for the NUMBER of things (not the things themselves) and an equals sign expressing genuine equality. The two documented traps are the reversal error (mapping words left-to-right onto symbols, so '4 times as many cats as dogs' becomes 4c=d instead of c=4d) and treating letters as object-labels. Both are defeated by anchoring translation to quantities and always testing the finished equation with real numbers.
bestPractices: Model the quantity, not the word order: before writing, ask 'if there were 3 dogs, how many cats?' and build the equation to fit the numbers.
Insist letters stand for the NUMBER of things ('c = the number of cats'), never the object ('c = cats') — the label reading drives reversal.
Build process ('think of a number...') equations step-by-step with a function machine, so operations and their order are captured faithfully.
Always check the finished equation by substituting a value — 4c=d with d=3 predicts three-quarters of a dog, exposing the reversal.
Read the equation back in words and compare it to the original statement (Clement's self-check).
keyRepresentations: Bar model (a cats-bar made of 4 copies of the dogs-bar)
Function machine for 'think of a number' processes
Table of values to test a candidate equation
Two-way word↔symbol translation cards
commonMisconceptions: Reversal error via word-order matching: '4 times as many cats as dogs' → 4c=d, mapping words directly to symbols instead of modelling the relationship.
Letter-as-object/label (static comparison): treats c as 'cats' and reads 4c=d as 'four cats for each dog', with '=' meaning correspondence not equality.
Writes an expression with no equals sign when an equation is required.
Mis-orders operations in a process translation ('double it and add 5' written wrongly), ignoring order of operations.

learn.summary: Writing algebraic equations means translating a situation — a 'think of a number' process or a comparison — into symbols, where each letter stands for the NUMBER of things (not the thing itself) and the equals sign expresses genuine equality. Two documented traps recur: the reversal error (mapping words left-to-right onto symbols, so '4 times as many cats as dogs' becomes 4c=d instead of c=4d) and reading letters as object-labels. Anchor every translation to quantities, and always test the finished equation by substituting real numbers.

activities.title: Bar-model translator with a numerical reality check
feedback: If the learner writes 4c = d: substitute d = 3. The equation then claims c = 0.75 — three-quarters of a cat, and fewer cats than dogs, though the picture shows 12 cats. Ask 'can there be three-quarters of a cat? Should there be more cats or more dogs? What does that tell you about the equation?'
If c = 4d survives the substitution (d = 2 gives c = 8, matching the picture), confirm: the equation agrees with real counts.
Read the finished equation aloud in words and compare it to the original story: does 'the number of cats is four lots of the number of dogs' match?

For the process mode, if operations are misread or mis-ordered (e.g. n² + 5, which squares instead of doubling, or 2(n + 5), which adds before doubling), rebuild one step at a time and name each operation in turn.
activities.rationale: The reversal error is defeated when a wrong equation is tested against real quantities; building the situation with a bar first, then checking with numbers, makes the collision visible. An interactive slider that recolours the picture and recomputes the count as the learner sets the number of dogs is one way to make the check concrete, but the same cycle works on paper with a table of values.
sourceClaims: The reversal error is the dominant mistake in translating comparison statements to equations: Clement, Lochhead & Monk (1981) found 37% of engineering freshmen wrote 6S=P instead of S=6P, and ~68% of the incorrect responses were reversals; it stems from word-order matching (direct left-to-right mapping) or a static-comparison/letter-as-label reading, not carelessness.
learnerActions: Read a comparison statement such as '4 times as many cats as dogs'.
Before writing anything, answer 'if there were 3 dogs, how many cats?' (12) and build the picture: a cats-bar made of 4 copies of the dogs-bar.
Write the equation that fits the picture: c = 4d (equivalently 4d = c), where c = the number of cats and d = the number of dogs.
Test it: set d = 2, check that the equation gives c = 8, and confirm the picture agrees.

Deliberately try the reversed equation 4c = d, set d = 3, and see that it demands c = 0.75 — three-quarters of a cat, not the 12 cats the picture shows, and fewer cats than dogs. Notice that d = 4 gives c = 1, a whole number but still fewer cats than dogs, so compare with the picture rather than only checking for a whole number. Explain why this shows word-order matching is wrong.
In a second mode, turn a 'think of a number' process into an equation step by step, e.g. 'think of a number, double it, add 5, get 17' → 2n + 5 = 17.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading words straight into symbols left-to-right is NOT the same as modelling the relationship; testing an equation against counts built from the situation (3 dogs → 12 cats) reveals a reversed equation, which predicts fewer cats than dogs and sometimes even a non-whole count such as three-quarters of a cat.

activities.title: Function machine for process equations
feedback: If the learner writes operations in reading order regardless of the process, step through the machine box by box and rebuild the expression.
After solving, substitute the value back through the machine to confirm it produces the stated result.
activities.rationale: Building process equations step-by-step with a function machine captures operations and their order faithfully, addressing the mis-ordering misconception; connecting to order of operations supports correct notation.
learnerActions: Take a 'think of a number' process, e.g. 'think of a number, treble it, subtract 4, and you get 20'.
Feed the unknown through a function machine one operation at a time: n → ×3 → −4 → 20.
Write the equation capturing the operations in order: 3n − 4 = 20.
Find the value of n that works (n = 8), and check by substituting it back (3×8 − 4 = 20).
Contrast with a mis-ordered attempt and explain why operation order matters.
activities.intendedInsight: A process translates faithfully only when each operation and its order are captured in turn; the letter is an unknown number flowing through the machine.

activities.title: Match stories to equations, including reversal traps
feedback: When a reversal distractor is rejected, confirm with the counterexample: 4c = d with d = 3 would give three-quarters of a cat instead of 12 cats, which is fewer cats than dogs, the opposite of the story.
When a match is made, require the number check so the choice is defended, not guessed.
activities.rationale: A scored matching and fill-in-the-blank check targets the exact errors (reversal, mis-ordering) efficiently, but recognition alone does not require the learner to construct and defend an equation from scratch.
sourceClaims: The reversal error is the dominant mistake in translating comparison statements to equations: Clement, Lochhead & Monk (1981) found 37% of engineering freshmen wrote 6S=P instead of S=6P, and ~68% of the incorrect responses were reversals; it stems from word-order matching (direct left-to-right mapping) or a static-comparison/letter-as-label reading, not carelessness.
learnerActions: Connect comparison statements to the correct equation, with reversal distractors present (e.g. 4c = d offered alongside c = 4d for '4 times as many cats as dogs').
Fill in the blanks of a process equation, e.g. 'think of a number, treble it, subtract 4, get 20' → __n − __ = __.
For any match you make, justify it by substituting a value — and for any distractor you rejected, say which number exposes it.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising correct translations and spotting reversal distractors sharpens the distinction between word-order matching and modelling; justification by substitution turns recognition into reasoning.

activities.title: Puzzle-setter dialogue: write, read back, and defend
feedback: If the read-back does not match the story — e.g. 4c = d read faithfully as 'four lots of the number of cats equals the number of dogs' (four dogs for every cat), whereas the story 'four times as many cats as dogs' means four cats for every dog — that mismatch signals a reversal; test it with a value.
If a letter is described as the object ('c = cats'), restate it as 'the number of cats' and substitute a value to show the letter behaves like a number.
activities.rationale: Posing situations and probing 'read it back — does it match?' rehearses the self-check and surfaces reasoning; the numerical-collision insight is made sharper when paired with an actual substitution rather than discussion alone.
learnerActions: A puzzle-setter poses a situation (process or comparison) and asks you to write an equation for it.
Read your equation back in words and judge whether it matches the original statement (Clement's read-back self-check).
When challenged ('someone wrote 4c = d for 4 times as many cats as dogs — are they right?'), argue your case using specific numbers.
State plainly what each letter stands for, e.g. 'c is the number of cats', and confirm the equals sign means equality.
activities.intendedInsight: Spoken justification and reading the equation back out loud can catch reversal and letter-as-label errors that a silent write-down may hide.

activities.title: Annotate a worked translation
feedback: After the annotation, require the learner to translate a new statement and substitute a value — the example is a model, not a substitute for constructing and testing an equation.
activities.rationale: A fixed worked example does not itself run the try-and-test cycle that corrects reversal, but it can make one correct translation explicit; it is a scaffold toward independent construction, not a replacement for it.
learnerActions: Examine a finished translation such as 2n + 5 = 17.
Reveal which words of the original statement each symbol came from (n ← 'a number', ×2 ← 'double it', +5 ← 'add 5', =17 ← 'to get 17').
Then write your own equation for a fresh statement and run the number check yourself.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing the word-to-symbol mapping of a correct example clarifies what faithful translation looks like, before attempting the full try-and-test cycle independently.

constraints: Letters must stand for the NUMBER of things ('c = the number of cats'), never the object ('c = cats'); the object-label reading drives the reversal error.

Always close translation with a numerical test: substitute a value and check the equation gives the count you predicted from the situation (e.g. 3 dogs → 12 cats). A non-whole count of objects is a warning sign, but a whole answer alone does not prove the equation is right (4c = d with d = 4 gives c = 1).
An equation requires an equals sign expressing equality; an expression alone is not an equation and the equals sign does not mean correspondence.

Matching and fill-in-the-blank checks are recognition tasks: they assess and rehearse but do not by themselves require the learner to construct and defend an equation independently — pair them with construction.
A fixed annotated example is a scaffold; it does not itself run the try-and-test cycle, so follow it with learner-generated translations that are tested with numbers.
For comparison statements, build the quantities (e.g. 'if 3 dogs, then 12 cats') before writing the equation, rather than mapping words left-to-right.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The MacGregor & Stacey (1993) source is marked unverified in the row (>50% reversals among 9th graders on 'y is eight times z'); treat its figures cautiously and verify before citing.

Self-audit of the reversed-equation counterexample: for 4c = d with d = 3, the equation gives c = 3/4, i.e. three-quarters of a cat (a valid fraction but not a whole count of animals). The original text said '4c=d with d=3 predicts three-quarters of a dog' in one place and 'half a dog' in another — these conflate which animal is fractional and are inconsistent. The correct reading is that c (cats) becomes fractional; activities state three-quarters of a cat for d = 3. The 'half a dog' phrasing (from d = 2 in the recommendation) is dropped as inconsistent.

Self-audit of process arithmetic: 'double it, add 5, get 17' → 2n + 5 = 17 gives n = 6; 'treble it, subtract 4, get 20' → 3n − 4 = 20 gives n = 8; '4 times as many cats as dogs' with 3 dogs gives 12 cats — all consistent.
The claim that a 3D/spatial environment 'adds nothing' to symbolic translation was removed as a non-established universal; it is simply not developed here because the learning target is symbolic.

The DfE curriculum claim was removed from activity-level sourceClaims because it supports the objective/topic and curriculum necessity, not the specific teaching principles (numerical reality check; function-machine ordering). It remains part of the row's evidence base for the objective overall.

probeDeeper: If there are 3 dogs, how many cats — and does your equation give that when d = 3? (a numerical counterexample to the reversal)
Read your equation out loud in words. Does it match the story exactly? (Clement's read-back check)
In 2n + 5 = 17, can n be any number, or is it one particular number? How would you find it?
Someone wrote 4c = d for '4 times as many cats as dogs.' Are they right? Convince me using numbers. (counterexample confronting the reversal head-on)
assess.correctAnswer: Interpret: n is the number I first thought of; doubling it and adding 5 gives 17 (so n = 6). Translate: c = 4d (equivalently 4d = c) — there are four times as many cats, so the number of cats is four lots of the number of dogs.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reversal error by word-order matching — writes 4c = d for '4 times as many cats as dogs', mapping the words straight onto symbols left-to-right.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor to quantities: 'if there are 3 dogs, how many cats?' (12). Does 4c = d give that? Build a small table of values BEFORE writing the equation, then read the equation aloud to check it matches.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 'four times as many cats as dogs' the child writes 4c = d, and reads it back as 'four cats for every dog'; the equation fails a numerical test.

errorPatterns.pattern: Letter-as-object / static comparison — treats c as 'cats' and the equals sign as correspondence, not the NUMBER of cats and equality.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Restate every letter as 'the number of ___'; substitute a value to show the letter behaves like a number, not a name.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Interprets 2n+5=17 as involving a thing called n rather than an unknown number; in translation uses letters as units/labels ('c cats').

errorPatterns.pattern: Mis-orders operations when translating a process — 'double it and add 5' written with the operations in the wrong order or notation reversed.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild the expression one step at a time with a function machine, capturing each operation in turn; connect to order of operations.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes something like n2+5, or applies the operations in reading order regardless of the process described.

responseLevels.gap: Maps words directly to symbols (4c=d) or treats letters as object-labels; the equation does not survive a numerical check, and interpreting a given equation is vague or thing-based.
responseLevels.full: Translates both process and comparison statements so they survive a numerical check, interprets a given equation back into a matching story, treats letters as numbers of things, and self-corrects by substituting values or reading the equation back.
responseLevels.partial: Translates simple one-operation and process statements correctly and interprets a given equation's operations, but reverses or mis-models comparison ('times as many') statements, or is inconsistent about whether the letter is a number.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Two parts. First (interpret): show the child 2n + 5 = 17 and ask 'in words, what is this saying, and what does n stand for?' Then (translate): 'Now write an equation for this — At the shelter there are 4 times as many cats as dogs. Use c for the number of cats and d for the number of dogs.' Listen and watch what they write; offer no options.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The translate direction separates the reasoners: a child who models quantities writes c = 4d and can justify it with numbers; a child using word-order matching writes 4c = d ('4 times cats as dogs', straight off the sentence) and reads it back as 'four cats per dog'. The interpret direction exposes letter-as-label — saying n is the tag 'number' rather than a particular unknown number to be found.

sources.claim: Year 6 pupils should express missing number problems algebraically and use simple formulae (algebra introduced as a language for solving problems).

sources.claim: The reversal error is the dominant mistake in translating comparison statements to equations: Clement, Lochhead & Monk (1981) found 37% of engineering freshmen wrote 6S=P instead of S=6P, and ~68% of the incorrect responses were reversals; it stems from word-order matching (direct left-to-right mapping) or a static-comparison/letter-as-label reading, not carelessness.
