pedagogy.summary: Partitioning a shape into equal parts means parts of equal AREA — the same amount of the whole — not parts of the same SHAPE. A square can be split into 4 equal parts as four strips, four small squares, or four triangles, and each is 1/4 because the areas are equal. The denominator counts how many equal-area pieces the whole is cut into, and each piece is 1/b of the whole. Equal shares of the same whole need not look alike.
bestPractices: Define equal parts as equal AREA, and show several correct partitions of one shape that look different but cover the same amount
Contrast valid equal-area partitions with tempting invalid ones (four pieces of different sizes) so 'four pieces' does not automatically mean 'quarters'
Use overlay/rearrangement or a squared grid to check that differently-shaped parts really have equal area
When reading a pre-partitioned shape, count the equal REGIONS (not the cut lines) and check they are equal before writing 1/b
Connect to the unit-fraction meaning: each equal-area part is 1/b of the whole
keyRepresentations: A square partitioned several ways into 4 (strips, quadrants, both diagonals)
Squared/grid paper to measure and compare areas
Overlay or cut-and-rearrange to prove two differently-shaped parts are equal
Area-model rectangle labelled in unit fractions
commonMisconceptions: Believes equal parts must be the same SHAPE (rejects a valid differently-shaped 1/4)
Counts pieces without checking equal area — calls any shape cut into 4 pieces 'quarters', even unequal ones
Writes the unit fraction from the number of cut lines rather than the number of regions
Thinks only the 'standard' partition (e.g. four small squares) is correct

learn.summary: Equal parts of a shape means parts of equal AREA — the same amount of the whole — not parts of the same SHAPE. A square can be split into four equal parts as strips, as quadrants, or as four triangles (both diagonals), and each is 1/4 because the areas are equal. The denominator counts how many equal-area regions the whole is cut into, and each region is 1/b of the whole. Learners should partition shapes several ways, check equal area by cutting and rearranging or by counting grid squares, contrast valid partitions with unequal 'four-piece' traps, and read a pre-partitioned shape by counting equal regions rather than cut lines.

activities.title: Quarter a square two different ways
feedback: If the learner makes only look-alike splits, prompt: 'Can you quarter it a way that does NOT make four identical pieces?' Offer the both-diagonals triangle split.
When four triangles and four strips both read 1/4, highlight: 'These look nothing alike, yet each is one quarter — because each covers the same AREA.'

If a learner rejects the triangle-quarter, verify equal area: cut the triangle into pieces and reassemble them to fill a strip, or count grid squares, putting the half squares cut by the diagonal together, to show the triangle and the strip cover the same number of squares (for example, 4 each on a 4-by-4 grid). A bare overlay of the two different shapes does not by itself prove equal area.
activities.rationale: Producing and comparing genuinely different equal-area partitions targets the belief that equal parts must be congruent, and grounds the unit fraction in area. An interactive version where the learner draws cut lines and each region's area is reported as a fraction of the whole would make 'equal area, any shape' directly checkable; a challenge mode asking for TWO valid ways reinforces that the standard partition is not the only correct one.
sourceClaims: CCSS 2.G.A.3 requires students to 'recognize that equal shares of identical wholes need not have the same shape.'

CCSS 3.G.A.2 requires partitioning shapes into parts with EQUAL AREAS and expressing the area of each part as a unit fraction of the whole (e.g. partition a shape into 4 parts with equal area and describe each part as 1/4 of the shape's area) — grounding 'equal parts = equal area'.

NCETM lists as a common error 'children thinking that equal means they must look identical'. It teaches that a square's four parts can each have the same area (1/4 of the whole) yet be non-congruent (not look identical), and recommends starting with congruent partitions then deliberately varying examples (including non-straight cut lines, different ways to quarter a square) to expose the misconception.
A unit fraction 1/b is one part of a whole partitioned into b equal parts; the area model represents fractions as equal-area regions of a shape.
learnerActions: Take a square and cut (or draw cut lines) to make 4 equal parts.
Now make 4 equal parts a DIFFERENT way — e.g. four vertical strips, then four quadrants, then four triangles using both diagonals.

For each attempt, check that every part covers the same amount: cut and rearrange the parts to see if they match, or draw the square on grid paper and count the squares (putting half squares together) in each part.
Label each part 1/4 and state in words why it is one quarter.
Compare a set of four triangles with a set of four strips: confirm both read 1/4 even though they look nothing alike.
activities.intendedInsight: Parts that look completely different can each be 1/4 as long as their AREAS are equal and together they cover the whole.

activities.title: Spot the trap: four pieces vs four equal parts
feedback: If the learner calls a shape with four unequal pieces 'quarters', compare the areas on a grid: 'These pieces are different sizes, so they can't each be one quarter.'
Reinforce: 'A quarter means one of four EQUAL parts — same amount each — not just one of four pieces.'
activities.rationale: Contrasting valid equal-area partitions with tempting unequal ones breaks the 'four pieces = quarters' shortcut and forces an area check before naming the fraction. A sorting task with distractors built from congruence-required and count-the-pieces errors makes the judgement explicit and checkable, though it rehearses the decision rather than eliciting the learner's own partitioning.
sourceClaims: CCSS 3.G.A.2 requires partitioning shapes into parts with EQUAL AREAS and expressing the area of each part as a unit fraction of the whole (e.g. partition a shape into 4 parts with equal area and describe each part as 1/4 of the shape's area) — grounding 'equal parts = equal area'.
A unit fraction 1/b is one part of a whole partitioned into b equal parts; the area model represents fractions as equal-area regions of a shape.
learnerActions: Look at a square cut into four pieces of clearly different sizes. Decide: is each piece a quarter? Explain.
Check by comparing the areas — on squared/grid paper, or by cutting and rearranging the pieces to see if they match.
State whether 'four pieces' is the same as 'four equal parts', and why.
Sort several partitioned shapes into 'shows quarters' and 'does not': include an equal-area-but-different-shape example (YES) and a four-unequal-pieces example (NO).
activities.intendedInsight: Counting four pieces is not enough — a quarter must be one of four EQUAL-area parts. Unequal pieces are not quarters even though there are four of them.

activities.title: Read a pre-partitioned shape: count regions, not lines
feedback: If the learner writes 1/3 for a shape with three parallel cut lines and four regions, say: 'Count the PARTS, not the lines — three cuts make four parts, so each is 1/4.'
If the learner names a fraction without checking the regions are equal, prompt: 'Are all these regions the same amount? Check before you write the fraction.'
activities.rationale: Reading pre-partitioned shapes is a distinct skill from making partitions, and the off-by-one cut-line error and the skip-the-equality-check error are common. Requiring both an equality check and region-counting addresses both errors.
sourceClaims: A unit fraction 1/b is one part of a whole partitioned into b equal parts; the area model represents fractions as equal-area regions of a shape.
learnerActions: Given a shape already cut into equal parts, first check the regions really are equal in area.
Count the number of equal REGIONS (the parts), not the number of cut lines.
Write the unit fraction for one part, e.g. 1/5 for one of five equal regions.
Check your reasoning on a case with three parallel cut lines: three cuts make four parts, so each is 1/4 — not 1/3.
activities.intendedInsight: The denominator is the number of equal regions the whole is cut into, so you count the parts, not the cuts; and the regions must be equal in area before you name the fraction.

activities.title: Prove two different shapes are equal area
feedback: To show a triangle-quarter and a strip-quarter are the same amount, cut one into pieces and reassemble them to fill the other, or check they cover the same number of grid squares, putting the half squares cut by the diagonal together; then name it: 'Same amount, different shape — both are one quarter.' A bare overlay of two different shapes does not by itself prove equal area.
If the learner cannot justify beyond appearance, steer toward an area check: 'Cut it up and fit the pieces into the other shape, or count grid squares, to see if the amounts match.'
If using paper or card cutouts, note they are approximations of the ideal flat figure: their slight thickness is not part of the area being compared — only the flat region matters.
activities.rationale: Giving learners a concrete method to verify equal area turns the abstract claim 'equal parts = equal area' into something they can test, and supports the deeper justification tier where understanding shows rather than rote production of two partitions.
sourceClaims: NCETM lists as a common error 'children thinking that equal means they must look identical'. It teaches that a square's four parts can each have the same area (1/4 of the whole) yet be non-congruent (not look identical), and recommends starting with congruent partitions then deliberately varying examples (including non-straight cut lines, different ways to quarter a square) to expose the misconception.
CCSS 2.G.A.3 requires students to 'recognize that equal shares of identical wholes need not have the same shape.'
learnerActions: Pick a differently-shaped candidate quarter (a triangle, an L-shape, a strip) and a square.
Use cut-and-rearrange to test whether the candidate covers the same area as a known quarter, or place both on squared/grid paper and count squares, putting any half squares together.
Decide whether the candidate really is 1/4 and justify by area.
Try the diagnostic: show two DIFFERENT ways to split a square into 4 equal parts, label each part, and explain how you know each is 1/4 even when the parts are different shapes.
activities.intendedInsight: Equal area can be verified by cutting pieces and reassembling them to fill the other shape, or by measuring on a grid — so you can confirm a differently-shaped part is genuinely 1/4.

constraints: Define equal parts as equal AREA throughout; the shape of a part may differ as long as it covers the same amount of the whole.

Start with congruent (look-alike) partitions, then deliberately vary examples — including non-straight cut lines and multiple ways to quarter a square — to expose the 'must look identical' misconception.
Require an equal-area check (cut and reassemble to fill, or count grid squares) before naming any fraction; do not let 'four pieces' or a count of cut lines determine the denominator.
A bare overlay of two differently-shaped parts does not prove equal area; use cutting-and-reassembling or grid-square counting to demonstrate it.

A static gallery of partitioned shapes with tap-to-reveal areas can illustrate the idea and serve as a reference, but it does not let the learner partition a shape or test their own cuts; use it as a scaffold, not as the main activity.

A sort or multiple-choice judgement (shows quarters vs not, 'is the triangle a quarter?') can rehearse and check the decision but does not itself elicit the learner constructing their own partitions; pair it with hands-on partitioning.
This is a 2D area idea; introducing a third dimension is unlikely to help and may distract from equal-area partitioning of a flat shape.

When using paper/card cutouts to cut, reassemble and compare, treat them as approximations of the ideal flat regions — their thickness is not part of the area being compared; state this to the learner in the activity.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated conversation and 3D as 'poor' and asserted a third dimension 'confuses rather than clarifies' and that insight comes 'not from in-role dialogue'. These are catalog-fit judgements, not established efficacy claims; they have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements in constraints.

The off-by-one cut-line example is sound for parallel straight cuts: three parallel cuts producing four equal regions gives 1/4, not 1/3. No arithmetic or geometric errors were found in the source examples; the equal-area-by-decomposition reasoning is valid for the flat-figure idealisation.

Verification of equal area between a triangle-quarter and a strip-quarter requires cutting one into pieces and reassembling (or grid-square counting); a single uncut piece will not coincide with a differently-shaped piece. Feedback wording was corrected accordingly.

The legacy 'area meter refuses to call them quarters' framing is an optional interactive feedback example (live area reporting, flagging unequal pieces); it is preserved as an optional mechanism, not a required one, and its learner-testing status is unknown.

assess.poeTask: Show the child a square split into 4 parts of clearly different SHAPES but equal AREA (e.g. one large right-triangle and several strips that together equal it). Before any measuring, ask: 'Are these four parts equal? Is each one a quarter?' Have them predict and say why. A child judging by appearance predicts 'no, they're different sizes'. Then check by overlaying/rearranging on a grid — the areas match — refuting the shape-based prediction and revealing that equal parts are about area, not looks.
probeDeeper: I've split this square into a big triangle and some strips — is the triangle a quarter? How could we check the areas are equal?
Here is a shape already cut into 5 equal parts — what fraction is one part, and how do you know it is 1/5?
If I cut a square into 4 pieces but they are different sizes, is each one 1/4? Why not?
Can two quarters of the same square look completely different and still both be 1/4?
assess.correctAnswer: Two distinct equal-area partitions (e.g. four vertical strips, and four triangles by both diagonals), each part labelled 1/4. Each part is 1/4 because the four parts have EQUAL AREA and together make the whole — the shape of a part can differ as long as it covers the same amount.

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes equal parts must be the same shape — 'those aren't quarters because they don't look the same'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay or rearrange a triangle-quarter and a strip-quarter to show they cover the same area; equal parts means equal amount, not identical shape.
errorPatterns.distractor: The parts must all be the same shape, or they aren't quarters
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Can produce only congruent-looking splits; rejects a valid differently-shaped 1/4 (e.g. a triangle) as 'not a quarter'

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts pieces without checking equal area — 'four pieces, so each is a quarter', even when the pieces are different sizes
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare the areas on a grid; unequal pieces are not quarters. A quarter must be one of four EQUAL-area parts.
errorPatterns.distractor: Any shape split into 4 pieces shows quarters, even if the pieces are different sizes
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels an unequally-cut shape as quarters; counts regions but never compares their areas

errorPatterns.pattern: Writes the unit fraction from the number of cut LINES rather than the number of regions (off by one)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the equal REGIONS, not the lines: three cuts make four parts, so each is 1/4.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a pre-partitioned shape, counts the cuts (e.g. 3 lines) and writes 1/3 for what are actually 4 regions

responseLevels.gap: Insists equal parts must be identical in shape, or labels unequal pieces as fractions by counting them; cannot produce a second valid partition.
responseLevels.full: Produces two genuinely different equal-area partitions, labels each 1/4, justifies by equal area covering the whole regardless of shape, reads a pre-partitioned shape by counting equal regions, and rejects unequal partitions.
responseLevels.partial: Produces equal-area partitions and labels 1/b, but only congruent-looking ones, or cannot articulate that equal AREA (not shape) is what matters, or is unsure about a differently-shaped quarter.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a square. Show me two DIFFERENT ways to split it into 4 equal parts, and label each part. Then tell me: how do you know each part really is 1/4, even when the parts are different shapes?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Tier 1 (produce two partitions) can be done by rote. Tier 2 — justifying that differently-shaped parts are still 1/4 because their AREAS are equal — is where understanding shows. A child judging by appearance offers only look-alike splits, rejects a valid triangle-quarter, or accepts four unequal pieces as quarters by counting them. A secure child produces genuinely different partitions and appeals to equal area.

pedagogy.summary: Comparing decimals with the SAME number of decimal places uses exactly the same process as comparing whole numbers: work from the highest place value down, and decide at the first place where the digits differ. Because the numbers are the same length, there is no ragged-length trap, so this is the foundational easy case — the whole-number strategy and correct place-value reasoning happen to agree. The genuine misconceptions (longer-is-larger, shorter-is-larger) only surface with unequal-length decimals and belong to the next topic.
bestPractices: Compare the highest place value first (whole number, then tenths, then hundredths) and stop at the first place where they differ — for 3.72 vs 3.27 the wholes tie, so tenths (7 vs 2) decides
Align the decimal points vertically so equal places line up in columns
Read every digit by its place-value name ('4 tenths 5 hundredths'), never as a bare digit string
Use a number line and a length model (linear blocks, LAB) rather than area/volume blocks, because length shows relative size directly
Flag that reading the decimal part as a whole number ('72 beats 27') happens to work here but will fail on ragged decimals like 0.4 vs 0.15 — build the place-value habit now
keyRepresentations: Number line marked in hundredths (0–1, and 3–4 for the 3.72/3.27 pair)
Place-value columns aligned on the decimal point
LAB / linear arithmetic (length) blocks
10×10 hundredths grid for area backup
commonMisconceptions: Reads the decimal part as a whole number ('72 > 27') — lands the right answer here but is a fragile, non-place-value strategy
Compares from the right (last digit first) as if column-adding
Ignores or misreads the whole-number part when it is present

learn.summary: Comparing decimals that have the SAME number of decimal places (up to two) uses the same process as comparing whole numbers: work from the highest place value down and decide at the first place where digits differ. Because the numbers are equal length here, there is no ragged-length trap — correct place-value reasoning and an (incorrect) read-it-as-a-whole-number strategy happen to agree, so this is the foundational easy case. The genuine longer-is-larger / shorter-is-larger misconceptions only surface with unequal-length decimals (a later topic). The teaching aim is to build the place-value habit now, before it is tested by ragged decimals.

activities.title: Order decimals on a number line and a length bar
feedback: If a child reads '72 beats 27', accept the right answer but push the reasoning: rebuild each number as tenths and hundredths on the line and ask what the 7 and the 2 are actually worth.
If a child compares from the right (last digit first), use the number line to show the biggest place decides size; practise reading left-to-right and naming the highest place first.
Reinforce correct reasoning by having them re-voice it: '3.72 and 3.27 — the wholes are equal at 3, so the tenths decide, and 7 tenths is more than 2 tenths.'

Probe transfer: 'Would "fifteen beats four" still work for 0.4 vs 0.15? Why or why not?' to flag that the whole-number trick breaks on ragged decimals (here 0.4 > 0.15, so the 'fifteen beats four' trick fails).
activities.rationale: Ordering is a spatial act; placing cards on a line and seeing the winner settle furthest right, backed by a length-bar view, is intended to turn 'compare the highest place first' into something felt. A length model may show relative size more directly than an area or volume model, but the cited source does not establish this comparative efficacy — treat it as a design preference. The 3.72/3.27 pair adds the check that learners establish equal wholes before moving to tenths.
sourceClaims: Comparing decimals uses the same highest-place-value-first process as whole numbers; comparisons between EQUAL-LENGTH decimals are a weak diagnostic because a correct place-value strategy and an (incorrect) treat-as-whole-number strategy produce the same answer — the longer-is-larger and shorter-is-larger misconceptions require ragged-length decimals to reveal.
learnerActions: Take three cards — 0.45, 0.54, 0.39 — and place each on a number line ticked every 0.1 with minor ticks every 0.01, smallest to largest.
Say aloud why 0.54 lands furthest right and 0.39 nearest the start, naming the tenths: 'five tenths beats four tenths beats three tenths'.
View each number also as a growing length bar so the relative sizes are visually clear (0.54 is the longest bar).
Then place 3.72 and 3.27 on a 3–4 number line, first checking the whole-number parts tie at 3, then deciding on the tenths (7 vs 2).
State the order and justify by comparing the highest differing place first.
activities.intendedInsight: Decimal size can be read as position on a line: ordering is decided by the highest place at which the digits differ, read left to right, not by the raw digit string or the rightmost digit.

activities.title: Align place-value columns and read every digit by its name
feedback: If a learner says 0.60 is bigger than 0.6 'because it has more digits', align the columns and read the hundredths place: 0 hundredths adds nothing, so 0.60 = 0.6.
If they name digits as bare numbers ('sixty'), re-prompt for the place-value name ('six tenths').
Praise stopping at the first differing column rather than reading all the way to the end.
activities.rationale: Column alignment and place-value naming build the durable strategy that will survive ragged-length decimals later, where reading the decimal part as a whole number fails.
sourceClaims: Comparing decimals uses the same highest-place-value-first process as whole numbers; comparisons between EQUAL-LENGTH decimals are a weak diagnostic because a correct place-value strategy and an (incorrect) treat-as-whole-number strategy produce the same answer — the longer-is-larger and shorter-is-larger misconceptions require ragged-length decimals to reveal.
learnerActions: Write a pair such as 3.72 and 3.27 one above the other with the decimal points aligned vertically so equal places line up in columns.
Read each digit by its place-value name — 'three ones, seven tenths, two hundredths' — never as a bare digit string.
Scan from the highest place downward and circle the first column where the digits differ; declare that column the decider.
Compare 0.6 and 0.60: first write 0.6 as 0.60 by appending a trailing zero so both have two decimal places, then read the places (6 tenths and 0 hundredths in each) to show they are equal in value.
activities.intendedInsight: Aligning on the decimal point and naming each digit by its place makes the comparison a place-value decision, and shows a trailing zero can be appended (0.6 = 0.60) to equalize length without changing the value.

activities.title: Pairwise comparison and placement practice (scorable check)
feedback: Correct order: 0.39 < 0.45 < 0.54 (decided on the tenths: 3, 4, 5).
Correct comparison: 3.72 > 3.27 (wholes tie at 3, so tenths 7 > 2 decide).
A right answer with 'seventy-two beats twenty-seven' reasoning is fragile — follow up with the number-line rebuild and a ragged pair (e.g. 0.4 vs 0.15) to make place value explicit.
activities.rationale: Ordering and pairwise comparison map cleanly onto scorable items and give quick practice, but they confirm the answer more than the method. Because equal-length pairs are a weak diagnostic, pair every scored item with a request for the reasoning. Keep all items equal length to stay within this topic.
sourceClaims: Comparing decimals uses the same highest-place-value-first process as whole numbers; comparisons between EQUAL-LENGTH decimals are a weak diagnostic because a correct place-value strategy and an (incorrect) treat-as-whole-number strategy produce the same answer — the longer-is-larger and shorter-is-larger misconceptions require ragged-length decimals to reveal.
learnerActions: Order 0.45, 0.54, 0.39 from smallest to largest.
Choose which is larger: 3.72 or 3.27, and give the reason.
Place a given two-decimal-place value at the right spot on a 0–1 line.
For each item, say which digit you looked at first and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Equal-length comparisons can be done quickly and correctly by comparing the highest differing place, and the reasoning (not just the answer) should be stated.

constraints: Keep all practised and scored comparisons the same length (up to two decimal places) within this topic; teaching the ordering of unequal-length / ragged decimals, which reveal longer-is-larger and shorter-is-larger, belongs to the next topic. Two exceptions are allowed: appending a trailing zero to show equivalence (writing 0.6 as 0.60 so 0.6 = 0.60) as an equal-value demonstration, and a single brief, unscored verbal transfer probe (e.g. 0.4 vs 0.15) used only to show that the read-it-as-a-whole-number trick breaks.

Equal-length comparisons are a weak diagnostic on their own: a correct place-value strategy and a read-it-as-a-whole-number strategy give the same answer, so always elicit the reasoning, not just the ordering.
A static number line with tap-to-reveal place values is useful as a reference card, but ordering should remain an active decision the child makes, not a result they read off.

Prefer a number line and a length (linear) model for showing relative size; a 10×10 hundredths grid can serve as an area backup. Depth/volume models are not needed for this one-dimensional size idea (a design preference, not a proven ranking of media).
Watch for the specific error of comparing from the right (last digit first) as if column-adding, and for ignoring or misreading a present whole-number part.
Optional interaction examples (drag-and-snap cards, a colour-the-winner cue, a growing length bar, slider placement, tap-to-reveal place values) make the mechanism concrete but are not mandatory.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the single source was not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source supports that equal-length decimal comparisons are a weak diagnostic (place-value and whole-number strategies agree); it does not establish comparative efficacy of number-line vs other media, so claims that a length model 'shows relative size more directly' are presented as a design preference, not proven necessity.

The non-preferred 'static image / reference card' option is retained as a scaffold note and the 'conversation' option as an omission; the original rated the conversation format poor ('no persona or open inquiry'), which is a fit judgement, not an established pedagogical law.

Trailing-zero equivalence (0.6 = 0.60) appears in the assessment probes and response levels, so it is included here as a reading/naming equivalence check within scope, framed as appending a trailing zero to equalize length rather than as ragged ordering.

probeDeeper: Which digit did you look at first, and why that one?
In 3.72, what is the 7 worth? And what is the 2 worth in 3.27?
What about 0.6 and 0.60 — are those the same size or different? How do you know?
If I gave you 0.4 and 0.15, would 'fifteen beats four' still work? Why or why not?
assess.correctAnswer: 0.39 < 0.45 < 0.54 (decided on the tenths: 3, 4, 5), and 3.72 > 3.27 (wholes tie at 3, so the tenths 7 > 2 decide). Justifies by comparing the highest place first.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the decimal part as a whole number: 'point-seventy-two is bigger than point-twenty-seven because 72 beats 27'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Accept the answer but push the reasoning: rebuild each number as tenths and hundredths on the number line, then show a ragged pair (0.4 vs 0.15) where the whole-number trick fails — make the place-value habit explicit now.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Justifies by the digit string rather than place value; says 'seventy-two' not 'seven tenths'; lands the right answer here but for the wrong reason

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares from the right, starting at the last digit as if adding in columns
errorPatterns.nextMove: On the number line, show that the biggest place decides size; practise reading left-to-right and naming the highest place first.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Points to the hundredths digit first, or hesitates about which end to start from; mis-orders when the whole-number part carries the decision

responseLevels.gap: Orders by the raw digit string or from the right and cannot justify by place value; mis-orders when the whole part matters.
responseLevels.full: Compares the highest differing place first, articulates 0.54 = 5 tenths > 0.45 = 4 tenths, places numbers correctly on a line, recognises 0.6 = 0.60, and transfers cleanly to a new equal-length set.
responseLevels.partial: Gets equal-length comparisons right and can say 'more tenths wins', but relies on the numbers being the same length and cannot yet explain place value or handle a trailing-zero case like 0.6 vs 0.60.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child these cards: 0.45, 0.54, 0.39. Say: 'Put these in order, smallest to largest, and tell me how you decided.' Then hand them 3.72 and 3.27 and ask which is larger. Watch which digit they look at first and listen to the reason — do not prompt a method.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Because all three cards are the same length, a correct place-value strategy and a treat-it-as-a-whole-number strategy give the SAME order (per Steinle & Stacey, equal-length pairs are a weak diagnostic on their own). So this task is not trying to catch longer-is-larger — that lives in the ragged-decimal topic (mt_933BohS9BH). What it discriminates is HOW the child reasons: a secure child names tenths and compares from the highest place; a fragile child says 'seventy-two beats twenty-seven' or starts from the right — a right answer reached by a method that will break the moment lengths differ. The 3.72/3.27 pair adds the check that they establish the wholes are equal before moving to the tenths.

pedagogy.summary: This topic extends percentages to CHANGE: increasing and decreasing by a percentage, finding the original value after a change (reverse percentages), and simple interest. The single most powerful idea — emphasised by the research — is that every percentage change is a MULTIPLICATION by a scale factor: a 15% increase is ×1.15, a 20% decrease is ×0.8. This reframing replaces error-prone add-on/subtract-off methods and makes reverse problems tractable (divide by the multiplier) and reveals why an increase then a decrease by the same percentage does NOT return to the start (the multipliers are not reciprocals: 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96). Teaching should build the decimal multiplier explicitly, show increases and decreases as ×(1 ± r), teach reverse percentages as dividing by the multiplier, and confront the 'it cancels out' intuition head-on. Simple interest is then repeated addition of a fixed percentage of the ORIGINAL each period (contrast with compound).
bestPractices: Teach every percentage change as a single multiplier: increase by r% is ×(1 + r/100), decrease by r% is ×(1 − r/100) — e.g. +15% is ×1.15, −20% is ×0.8.
Explicitly correct the multiplier: a 5% increase is ×1.05, NOT ×1.5; a 6% amount is ×0.06, not ×0.6 — decimal placement is the classic slip.
Teach reverse percentages as the inverse operation: if the new value is the original ×0.8, then original = new ÷ 0.8 — never 'add the percentage back onto the new value'.

Confront 'increase then decrease by the same % returns to the start' directly: show 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96, and the classic case that a price up 50% must then fall by 33⅓% (not 50%) to return — because the base has changed.
Distinguish simple interest (a fixed percentage of the ORIGINAL principal each period, so total = P × r × t) from compound (interest on a growing balance); keep the base fixed for simple interest.
Use a bar/100-grid and pair decimal multipliers with their reverse (×1.25 pairs with ×0.8) so the reciprocal relationship of reverse percentages is visible.
keyRepresentations: Decimal-multiplier form of change: ×(1 + r/100) and ×(1 − r/100)
Paired multiplier cards showing reverse = reciprocal (×1.25 ↔ ×0.8, product 1)
Bar model where the original is 100% and the change adds/removes a shaded strip
Reverse-percentage arrow: original →(×0.8)→ new, so new →(÷0.8)→ original
Simple-interest table: same interest (r% of P) added each year for t years
commonMisconceptions: Treats a percentage change as addition/subtraction rather than a single multiplication (e.g. 240 + 0.15 or 240 + 1.15 rather than ×1.15)
Reverse-percentage error: to find the original before a 20% discount, adds 20% of the SALE price back on (64 + 20% of 64) instead of dividing by 0.8
Assumes an increase then a decrease by the same percentage returns to the original (subtracts percents: 20% up then 20% down = no change), not seeing the base has changed
Builds the wrong multiplier: 5% increase as ×1.5, or 6% as ×0.6 (decimal misplacement)
Computes simple interest on a growing balance (compound) or forgets to multiply by the number of years

learn.summary: Percentage change taught as a single multiplication by a scale factor: increase by r% is ×(1 + r/100), decrease by r% is ×(1 − r/100). This reframing makes reverse percentages tractable (divide by the multiplier), exposes why an increase then an equal-percentage decrease does not return to the start (1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96, because the second change acts on a changed base), and distinguishes simple interest (a fixed percentage of the original principal each period) from compound. Learners build the decimal multiplier explicitly, solve forward and reverse problems, confront the 'it cancels out' intuition with computation, and compute simple interest on a fixed base.

activities.title: The price-changer: every change is a multiplier
feedback: If a learner writes £240 + 15 = £255, or ×1.5 (£360), or ×0.15 (£36): rebuild the multiplier — +15% means 100% + 15% = 115% = ×1.15; check the decimal, 15% = 0.15 so the multiplier is 1 + 0.15 = 1.15.
If a learner confuses ×1.15 with ×1.5: point out ×1.5 is a 50% increase; put ×1.15 and ×1.5 side by side on the same value to show the gap.
Confirm a correct multiplier by reading the bar: ×1.15 on £240 is £276, which is 15% more than £240.
activities.rationale: Treating every percentage change as a single multiplier by (1 ± r/100) replaces error-prone add-on/subtract-off methods; the classic slip is decimal misplacement, which explicit contrast of ×1.05 vs ×1.5 targets. A live bar/multiplier display may make the scale factor and resulting value visible together, but the multiplier can equally be built on paper; the display is one optional medium, not a requirement.
sourceClaims: All percentage changes are multiplications by a scale factor; documented student errors include treating percent change as addition/subtraction, mis-converting the multiplier, dividing by the wrong base, and assuming an increase then decrease by the same percent cancels out (0.8 × 1.25 = 1; the inverse of a percent increase is not a decrease by the same percent) — e.g. a price up 50% must fall 33⅓% to return.
KS3 pupils solve problems involving percentage change (increase, decrease and original-value problems) and simple interest in financial mathematics, and interpret percentages as operators.
learnerActions: Start with a value shown as a bar (drawn on paper or on screen), e.g. £240, apply a 15% increase, write the change as a single multiplication ×1.15, and read off the new value (£276).
Apply a 20% decrease to a value and write it as ×0.8; write a 6% decrease as ×0.94 (100% − 6% = 94%).
Deliberately contrast ×1.15 with ×1.5 and ×0.15 for a 15% increase, stating which is correct and why (100% + 15% = 115% = 1.15).
Match pairs of multiplier cards and check which pairs multiply to 1 (e.g. ×1.25 ↔ ×0.8), noticing the multiplier that UNDOES a change is its reciprocal.
OPTIONAL interaction if a live tool is available: drag or set the percentage and watch the bar grow/shrink while the displayed multiplier and new value update together.
activities.intendedInsight: A percentage increase or decrease is one multiplication by (1 ± r/100), not an add-on or subtract-off, and the decimal multiplier must be built carefully: a 5% increase is ×1.05, not ×1.5; and finding 6% OF a value is ×0.06, not ×0.6 (distinct from a 6% decrease, which is ×0.94).

activities.title: Reverse percentages: undo by dividing
feedback: If a learner computes 20% of £64 and adds it (£76.80), or otherwise treats £64 as the base: reframe as a multiplier — sale price = original ×0.8, so original = £64 ÷ 0.8. Show that 20% of the true original £80 is £16, confirming £80 → £64; the percentage is of the ORIGINAL.
Reinforce the self-check: a correct original survives 'reduce by 20%' and lands back on £64; the add-back answer (£76.80) does not, falling to £61.44.
activities.rationale: The reverse problem is the key discriminator between an additive model and a multiplicative model of percentage change; teaching it as the inverse operation (divide by the multiplier) and requiring a reversal check directly confronts the documented add-back error.
sourceClaims: All percentage changes are multiplications by a scale factor; documented student errors include treating percent change as addition/subtraction, mis-converting the multiplier, dividing by the wrong base, and assuming an increase then decrease by the same percent cancels out (0.8 × 1.25 = 1; the inverse of a percent increase is not a decrease by the same percent) — e.g. a price up 50% must fall 33⅓% to return.
KS3 pupils solve problems involving percentage change (increase, decrease and original-value problems) and simple interest in financial mathematics, and interpret percentages as operators.
learnerActions: Given a sale price of £64 that is already 20% off, find the original price by recognising sale = original ×0.8, so original = £64 ÷ 0.8 = £80.
Check the answer: reduce the found original by 20% and confirm it returns to the sale price (20% of £80 is £16, so £80 → £64).
Explicitly compare the correct method (÷0.8) with the common wrong method (£64 + 20% of £64 = £76.80) and check which one survives the reversal test (£76.80 reduced by 20% gives £61.44, not £64).
Draw a reverse arrow: original →(×0.8)→ new, so new →(÷0.8)→ original.
activities.intendedInsight: To find an original value before a percentage change, divide by the multiplier that produced the change; the percentage is taken of the original, not of the new/sale value, so adding the percentage back onto the new value is wrong.

activities.title: Does it cancel out? Chaining changes on a changing base
feedback: If a learner says the price returns to the start: compute ×1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96 and track £100 → £120 → £96; point out the 20% decrease is taken from the larger £120 base.
If a learner assumes the restoring fall equals the rise: show the £20 → £30 case needs a 33⅓% fall, because 33⅓% is taken of £30, not £20.
activities.rationale: The 'it cancels out' belief is a documented, seductive misconception; confronting it with direct computation and a visibly changed base, rather than assertion, lets learners see the multiplicative structure. Prediction-before-computation surfaces the belief so it can be challenged.
sourceClaims: All percentage changes are multiplications by a scale factor; documented student errors include treating percent change as addition/subtraction, mis-converting the multiplier, dividing by the wrong base, and assuming an increase then decrease by the same percent cancels out (0.8 × 1.25 = 1; the inverse of a percent increase is not a decrease by the same percent) — e.g. a price up 50% must fall 33⅓% to return.
learnerActions: Predict first: if a price goes up 20% and then down 20%, is it back where it started?
Compute the chain as multipliers: ×1.2 then ×0.8 = ×0.96, a 4% net fall; test on a concrete value, e.g. £100 → £120 → £96.
Identify why: after the increase the base is larger (£120), so the 20% decrease removes more (£24) than the 20% increase added (£20).
Explore the classic case: a £20 item up 50% becomes £30; find what percentage fall returns it to £20 (£10 off £30 is 33⅓%, not 50%).
OPTIONAL interaction if a chain tool is available: apply +20% then −20% and watch the bar land short of the start, with the post-increase base highlighted.
activities.intendedInsight: Equal up-then-down percentages do not cancel, because each percentage acts on whatever base is current; the two multipliers are not reciprocals (1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96, not 1), so the net result is a fall. (Note this differs from the reciprocal pair that UNDOES a single change, e.g. ×1.25 then ×0.8 = 1.)

activities.title: Simple interest on a fixed base
feedback: If a learner gives one year's interest (£15) only: remind them to multiply by the number of years, £15 × 4 = £60.
If a learner grows the balance each year (compounds): clarify that simple interest keeps the base at the ORIGINAL £500 every year; interest = £500 × 0.03 × 4 = £60.
activities.rationale: A frequent error is computing interest on a growing balance (compound) or omitting the time factor; keeping the base fixed and tabulating equal yearly additions makes the structure of simple interest explicit and separates it from compound. The cited curriculum source establishes simple interest as a KS3 objective; the specific error pattern is drawn from the inherited misconception analysis and was not re-verified here.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils solve problems involving percentage change (increase, decrease and original-value problems) and simple interest in financial mathematics, and interpret percentages as operators.
learnerActions: Compute simple interest on £500 at 3% per annum for 4 years: find one year's interest (£500 × 0.03 = £15), then multiply by the number of years (£15 × 4 = £60).
Build a year-by-year table showing the same £15 added each year because it is always 3% of the original £500.
Contrast briefly with compound: ask whether year 2's interest would still be £15 if interest were added to the balance each year (under compound it would not, because the base grows).
activities.intendedInsight: Simple interest is a fixed percentage of the ORIGINAL principal each period, so total interest = P × r × t; it must be multiplied by the number of periods, and the base stays fixed (unlike compound interest, which grows the base).

constraints: A scored set of items (fill-in-the-multiplier, a reverse-percentage selection item with the '£64 + 20%' add-back as a distractor, a true/false on 'up 20% then down 20% returns to start' where the misconception is the incorrect option, and a simple-interest item with a compound distractor) can diagnose which model a learner holds, but selecting among options does not by itself elicit the independent construction of a multiplier or a dividing-by-the-multiplier method; include tasks where the learner writes or builds the method.

A static worked example or tap-to-reveal diagram (e.g. tap +15% to reveal ×1.15, tap a reverse problem to reveal ÷0.8) can present the method as a reference, but it is fixed and cannot be re-based by the learner, so the 'base changes under you' insight is better met by actually applying a sequence of changes and tracking the new base.

A shop/bank persona dialogue can pose sale and interest problems and raise the 'does it cancel' challenge, but learners still need to carry out the multiplier computation themselves rather than only hear it explained.
Keep the base fixed for simple interest; do not let it drift into compound unless deliberately contrasting.

When checking reverse-percentage answers, require a reversal test (apply the original percentage change to the found original, e.g. reduce it for a sale or increase it for a price rise, and confirm it returns to the given value) rather than accepting the numeric answer alone.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit (arithmetic, confirmed correct): £240 × 1.15 = £276; £64 ÷ 0.8 = £80, and 20% of £80 = £16 so £80 − £16 = £64; add-back error £64 + 20%×£64 = £76.80, and £76.80 × 0.8 = £61.44; chain ×1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96 so £100 → £120 → £96 (4% net fall); £20 × 1.5 = £30, and to return to £20 the fall is £10/£30 = 33⅓%; simple interest £500 × 0.03 × 4 = £60 with £15 per year; 6% decrease = ×0.94. All internally consistent.

Subtle distinction preserved from the source: ×1.25 and ×0.8 ARE reciprocals (product 1), so a ×0.8 undoes a ×1.25 (a 20% decrease undoes a 25% increase); but applying the SAME percentage up then down is NOT reciprocal (1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96; 1.25 × 0.75 = 0.9375). The card-matching concerns undoing the same change, whereas the 'cancels out' misconception concerns the same percentage in opposite directions — these are different comparisons and must not be conflated.

The source states the inverse of a percentage increase is not a decrease by the same percent; this is a mathematical fact (demonstrated by computation) and is retained as such, not as an untested effectiveness claim.

The simple-interest misconceptions (compounding the balance, omitting the time factor) come from the legacy row's misconception list; neither cited source claim documents them, so activity 4 cites only the curriculum-objective claim.

Efficacy of the optional live tool, quiz set, tap-to-reveal diagram and persona dialogue is not established; they are proposed scaffolds with scoped affordances and limits, not evidenced as superior to one another.

probeDeeper: 'You got £80 — check it: what is £80 reduced by 20%?' — a correct method survives the check (→£64); the add-back error does not (£76.80 reduced by 20% is £61.44).
'A price goes up 20% and then down 20% — is it back to what it was? Why?' — directly surfaces the cancels-out misconception and the changing base.
'Write the 15% increase as a single multiplication' — checks the ×1.15 scale-factor idea rather than an add-on method.
Counterexample for interest: 'What if it were compound interest instead — would year 2's interest still be £15?' — tests whether the fixed-base of SIMPLE interest is understood.
assess.correctAnswer: Original jacket price = £64 ÷ 0.8 = £80 (since sale price = original ×0.8). Increase: £240 × 1.15 = £276.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverse-percentage error: to undo a 20% discount, adds 20% of the SALE price back (64 + 20% of 64 = £76.80), treating the new value as the base
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reframe as a multiplier: sale price = original ×0.8, so original = £64 ÷0.8. Show 20% of £80 (the true original) is £16, confirming £80 → £64; the percentage is of the ORIGINAL, not the sale price.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child computes 20% of £64 and adds it, or otherwise works from £64 as the original; answer £76.80 rather than £80

errorPatterns.pattern: Add/subtract instead of multiply, or wrong multiplier: does 240 + 15, or ×1.5, or ×0.15, instead of ×1.15
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build the multiplier explicitly: +15% means 100% + 15% = 115% = ×1.15; contrast ×1.15 with ×1.5. Check the decimal (15% = 0.15).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The increase answer is £255 (+15 flat), £360 (×1.5), or £36 (×0.15) rather than £276

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes an increase then a decrease by the same percentage returns to the original (subtracts percents / 'it cancels out')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compute it: ×1.2 then ×0.8 = ×0.96, a 4% net fall; show the second percentage acts on the larger base. Use the £20 blouse (+50% then must fall 33⅓% to return).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked (probe), child says a price up 20% then down 20% is back to the start; does not see the base changed

errorPatterns.pattern: Simple interest computed on a growing balance (compound) or without multiplying by the number of years
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach percentages — clarify simple interest is r% of the ORIGINAL each year, kept constant: interest = £500 × 0.03 × 4. Contrast briefly with compound.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For £500 at 3% for 4 years, child gives one year's interest (£15), or compounds the balance, instead of £15 × 4 = £60

responseLevels.gap: Uses add/subtract for changes and the add-back method for reverse problems; believes same-percentage up-then-down cancels; cannot form the multiplier.
responseLevels.full: Treats every percentage change as ×(1±r), solves reverse problems by dividing by the multiplier and checks the result, explains why equal up/down percentages don't cancel (changed base), and computes simple interest as a fixed percentage of the original per period.
responseLevels.partial: Handles a straightforward increase/decrease with a multiplier for practised numbers, but reverts to add-back on reverse problems, mis-forms awkward multipliers, or is unsure whether up-then-down cancels; simple interest sometimes compounded or missing the time factor.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A jacket was reduced by 20% in a sale and now costs £64. Find its original price before the sale. Then, separately, increase £240 by 15%. Do both however you like — I'll watch.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The reverse problem is the discriminator: a child who understands percentage change as a multiplier sees £64 = original ×0.8 and divides (£80); a child using add/subtract intuition adds 20% of £64 back (£64 + £12.80 = £76.80) — the documented reverse-percentage error — giving a wrong answer that is itself diagnostic. The increase task reveals the multiplier: ×1.15 (correct) versus +15 flat, ×1.5, or ×0.15. Watching the method shows which model of percentage change the child holds.
