pedagogy.summary: Comparing and ordering unit fractions (1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5) and same-denominator fractions (2/5, 4/5) is the procedure that operationalises fraction magnitude. Two rules that FEEL contradictory must be held together: for unit fractions a larger denominator means a SMALLER fraction (more equal parts, each smaller), while for same-denominator fractions a larger numerator means a LARGER fraction (more of the same-sized part). Teach both with bars/number lines so the direction of each rule is grounded in piece size, and so children don't over-generalise a blanket 'bigger bottom = smaller'.
bestPractices: Order unit fractions against a common whole using aligned bars so 1/5 is visibly the smallest and 1/2 the largest
Use a 'cut into more pieces' action so children feel each piece shrink as the denominator grows
Order same-denominator fractions by counting how many of the SAME piece, keeping the piece size fixed
Place fractions on a shared number line so both comparisons are read as position
Make explicit WHY the denominator direction flips between the two cases (piece size vs how many pieces)
keyRepresentations: Aligned equal-length bars for unit fractions (a fraction wall column)
Number line locating the fractions being compared
Same-denominator strip where only the count of shaded parts changes
'Cut into more' animation shrinking each unit fraction
commonMisconceptions: Whole-number bias — orders unit fractions 1/5, 1/4, 1/3, 1/2 (bigger denominator judged bigger)
Over-correction — after learning 'bigger bottom = smaller', reverses same-denominator fractions too (1/5 > 2/5 > 3/5)
Compares numerators and denominators independently rather than as one quantity
Cannot place the fractions consistently on a number line to check the order
Ignores that the whole must be the same when comparing

learn.summary: Year 3 learners (age 7-8) compare and order unit fractions (1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5) and same-denominator fractions (1/5...4/5). Two directions that feel contradictory must be held together: for unit fractions a LARGER denominator means a SMALLER fraction (the whole is cut into more, smaller pieces), while for same-denominator fractions a LARGER numerator means a LARGER fraction (more of the same-sized piece). These are not one rule reversing; they compare different varying quantities. Ground both in piece size using aligned bars and a shared number line so children do not over-generalise a blanket 'bigger bottom = smaller'.

activities.title: Order unit fractions under one shared whole
feedback: If a learner puts 1/5 first and 1/2 last (whole-number bias), lay the unit fractions as aligned bars against ONE whole so 1/5 is visibly the shortest; ask them to point to which piece is largest.
Probe: 'You put 1/2 first. Show me on the bars (for example, equal pizzas cut into halves and fifths) WHY one half is bigger than one fifth.'
If pieces are not aligned to a common whole, redraw them under the same '1 whole' rule before comparing, and remind that the represented whole must be the same to compare the portions.
activities.rationale: Grounding fraction magnitude in part size against a common whole targets whole-number bias when ordering unit fractions.
sourceClaims: Students frequently show whole-number bias when ordering fractions, viewing those with larger denominators as larger (e.g. 1/8 > 1/3); this can be diagnosed by having them label and compare fractions, and remedied by grounding magnitude in the number line and part size.
Year 3 pupils compare and order unit fractions, and fractions with the same denominators.
learnerActions: Take fraction cards 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5 and arrange them from largest to smallest.

Represent each card as a bar the same length as a single common '1 whole' bar, split into that many equal parts with one part shaded, and line the bars up beneath that '1 whole' so the shaded pieces can be compared by length.
State and check the order: 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5 from largest to smallest, confirming 1/5 is the shortest and 1/2 the longest.
Explain out loud why 1/2 is bigger than 1/5 by pointing at the piece lengths against the same whole.
activities.intendedInsight: When the whole is the same, a unit fraction with a larger denominator is smaller because the whole is split into more, smaller pieces.

activities.title: Cut into more pieces and feel each one shrink
feedback: Probe: 'Which is bigger, 1/3 or 1/4? If I cut a cake into more and more pieces, what happens to the size of each piece?'
If a learner still judges more pieces as bigger, slow the cutting down and compare one piece before and after an extra cut on the same whole.
An optional 'cut into more' action or animation that adds a slice and visibly shrinks every piece makes the shrinking concrete; this is one way to show it, not the only way.
activities.rationale: An enacted partitioning action ties the abstract denominator rule to a felt change in piece size, reinforcing more-parts-means-smaller.
sourceClaims: Students frequently show whole-number bias when ordering fractions, viewing those with larger denominators as larger (e.g. 1/8 > 1/3); this can be diagnosed by having them label and compare fractions, and remedied by grounding magnitude in the number line and part size.
learnerActions: Start with one whole and partition it into 2, then 3, then 4, then 5 equal pieces, each time comparing the size of a single piece to the previous one.
Describe what happens to the size of each piece as more cuts are added.
Connect the action back to the cards: more pieces (bigger denominator) means each piece, and so each unit fraction, is smaller.
activities.intendedInsight: Cutting a fixed whole into more equal parts makes each part smaller, so more pieces means a smaller unit fraction.

activities.title: Order same-denominator fractions by counting the same-sized piece
feedback: If a learner reverses the fifths (1/5 > 2/5 > 3/5 > 4/5) after learning 'bigger bottom = smaller' (over-correction), fix the piece size at one fifth and count how many are shaded; show 4/5 covers more of the bar than 2/5.

Probe: 'Why does "more fifths" mean MORE, but a bigger bottom number mean LESS?' Separate 'how big each piece is' from 'how many pieces there are' — the unit-fraction case varies the piece size, this case varies the count.
Reinforce that here the piece size does NOT change; only the count of shaded pieces does.
activities.rationale: Holding the piece fixed while varying the count isolates the numerator's meaning and guards against over-generalising the denominator rule to same-denominator sets.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils compare and order unit fractions, and fractions with the same denominators.
learnerActions: Take fifths fractions 1/5, 2/5, 3/5, 4/5 and order them from largest to smallest, keeping the piece size (one fifth) fixed.
Represent each as a bar where only the number of shaded fifths changes, and check that 4/5 covers more of the bar than 2/5.
State the order 4/5, 3/5, 2/5, 1/5 and explain that more fifths means more because each piece is the same size.
activities.intendedInsight: When the denominator is fixed, the numerator counts how many of the same-sized piece, so a larger numerator means a larger fraction.

activities.title: Place and read the fractions on a shared number line
feedback: Probe: 'Where would 3/5 sit compared to 1/2 on the line, bigger or smaller? How could the number line help you decide?'
If a learner compares numerators and denominators independently (component comparison), insist on one quantity per card and order by position on the line.
If 1/5 is placed furthest right, revisit the unit-fraction bars before returning to the line.
activities.rationale: A shared number line represents each fraction as a single quantity, countering component comparison and letting learners self-check both orderings against position.
sourceClaims: Students frequently show whole-number bias when ordering fractions, viewing those with larger denominators as larger (e.g. 1/8 > 1/3); this can be diagnosed by having them label and compare fractions, and remedied by grounding magnitude in the number line and part size.
learnerActions: Place each fraction from both sets onto one shared number line between 0 and 1, consistent with its order.
Decide where 3/5 sits compared with 1/2 and judge whether it is bigger or smaller.
Use position on the line to check that the unit-fraction order and the fifths order agree with where each fraction lands.

Try a mixed set (e.g. 1/5, 1/2, 3/5) and use positions on the number line, together with the two rules, to order it; note that neither rule on its own can compare fractions such as 3/5 and 1/2, where both the numerator and the denominator differ.
activities.intendedInsight: Both comparisons can be read as position on one number line, which unifies the unit-fraction and same-denominator cases into a single idea of magnitude.

activities.title: Practise and check the orderings
feedback: For 2/5 vs 4/5, confirm 4/5 is larger because it has more fifths; if a learner instead picks 2/5 (over-applying 'bigger bottom = smaller' where the denominators are equal), return to the fixed-piece bar and count the shaded fifths.

Checking whether the order is correct is useful, but build the underlying magnitude sense first with bars and the number line, since simply recognising the right answer does not by itself elicit the reasoning.
Ask the learner to justify each answer so correct ordering is backed by the piece-size explanation, not a memorised rule.
activities.rationale: Targeted practice can consolidate ordering and reveal whole-number bias or over-correction. Ask for a piece-size or number-line explanation alongside the selected or ordered answer.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils compare and order unit fractions, and fractions with the same denominators.
learnerActions: Order 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5 from largest to smallest as an ordering task.

Compare 2/5 and 4/5 and choose the larger, explaining the choice; be alert to the tempting wrong answer of picking 2/5 by over-applying 'bigger bottom = smaller' to a comparison where only the numerator differs.
Place a given fraction at the right spot on a number line as a final check.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent, correct ordering of both fraction types, with the reasoning articulated, confirms the magnitude idea has taken hold.

constraints: When comparing fractions with bars or area representations, the represented whole must be the same; aligned bars and number-line placements only work when they share one unit. As numbers, fractions still have comparable magnitudes (e.g. by position on a shared number line).
A static fraction wall or reference image lets children read off comparisons but does not let them enact the ordering, so use it as a reference scaffold alongside, not instead of, hands-on ordering.
Recognition or multiple-choice practice checks whether the order is correct but does not by itself require the learner to construct and justify the ordering; pair it with explanation.

Keep the two cases explicitly connected: unit-fraction comparison varies the denominator (numerator fixed at 1), while same-denominator comparison varies the numerator (denominator fixed) — explain that they compare different quantities, which is why 'bigger bottom = smaller' must not be over-generalised to same-denominator sets. This is not a single rule flipping.
Fraction comparison here uses lengths of bars and positions on a number line (or areas of equal wholes); for this objective a third spatial dimension adds no comparative information.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row claimed a static image 'can't let them ACT the ordering' and that dialogue is poor for this procedure; these have been softened to scoped limits (a static reference supports reading-off but not enacting) rather than universal laws, since the sources do not establish comparative efficacy or necessity.

Optional interaction examples (drag-to-unfurl bars, a 'cut into more' action, fifths bars growing, placement on a line) are retained as concrete ways to make the mechanism visible; they are illustrative, not mandatory.

The original pedagogy and quiz task described the denominator rule as 'flipping' between the two cases and referenced a 'larger-denominator distractor' for 2/5 vs 4/5; both are incoherent (the cases vary different quantities; 2/5 and 4/5 share denominator 5) and have been corrected rather than reproduced.

Self-audit of the arithmetic and ordering logic found the source orderings correct: unit fractions largest-to-smallest 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5; fifths largest-to-smallest 4/5, 3/5, 2/5, 1/5; 4/5 > 2/5. No conceptual errors were introduced into learner-facing actions.

probeDeeper: You put 1/2 first. Show me on the pizzas WHY one half is bigger than one fifth.
Which is bigger, 1/3 or 1/4? If I cut a cake into more and more pieces, what happens to the size of each piece?
You ordered the fifths 1/5, 2/5, 3/5, 4/5. Why does 'more fifths' mean MORE, but a bigger bottom number mean LESS?
Where would 3/5 sit compared to 1/2 on the line — bigger or smaller? How could the number line help you decide?
assess.correctAnswer: Unit fractions largest→smallest: 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5 (larger denominator = smaller piece). Same-denominator fractions largest→smallest: 4/5, 3/5, 2/5, 1/5 (more fifths = more). Each card placed consistently on the number line matching its order.

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number bias on unit fractions — orders 1/5 > 1/4 > 1/3 > 1/2, treating the larger denominator as the larger fraction
errorPatterns.nextMove: Lay the unit fractions as aligned bars against one whole so 1/5 is visibly smallest; cut a whole into more pieces to feel each shrink; reteach more-parts-means-smaller
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Puts 1/5 first and 1/2 last, or places 1/5 furthest right on the number line

errorPatterns.pattern: Over-correction — having learned 'bigger bottom = smaller', reverses the same-denominator set too (1/5 > 2/5 > 3/5 > 4/5)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fix the piece size (a fifth) and count how many are shaded; show 4/5 covers more of the bar than 2/5; separate 'how big each piece' from 'how many pieces'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Orders the fifths backwards, treating a bigger numerator as smaller

errorPatterns.pattern: Component comparison — compares numerators and denominators independently instead of as one quantity, muddling any set that mixes denominators
errorPatterns.nextMove: Represent each fraction as a length on a common number line and order by position; insist on one quantity per card
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Orders a mixed set by looking only at the top numbers (or only the bottom), ignoring the relationship

responseLevels.gap: Orders unit fractions by denominator size (1/5 largest), or reverses the same-denominator set — whole-number bias runs throughout.
responseLevels.full: Orders both sets correctly and fluently, places them consistently on a number line, and articulates the unifying idea — the denominator sets the piece size (more pieces → smaller each), the numerator counts how many of that piece — transferring to a novel comparison.
responseLevels.partial: Orders unit fractions correctly (1/2…1/5) and same-denominator fractions correctly when each set is done separately, but treats them as two unconnected rules — cannot explain why the denominator direction flips, or falters when sets are mixed or placed on one line.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are four fraction cards: 1/2, 1/5, 1/3, 1/4. Put them in order from LARGEST to smallest. Now here are four more: 3/5, 1/5, 4/5, 2/5 — put these in order from largest to smallest too. As you go, place each fraction on this number line. [Watch how the child orders each set and where they place the cards.]
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Whole-number bias makes a child order the unit fractions 1/5, 1/4, 1/3, 1/2 — the exact reverse of correct — so watching the direction on the unit set exposes it instantly. The same-denominator set is the control: it is ordered by numerator (bigger IS more), so a child who has merely memorised 'bigger bottom = smaller' and reverses everything is caught, distinguishing genuine magnitude reasoning from a reversed rote rule.

sources.claim: Students frequently show whole-number bias when ordering fractions, viewing those with larger denominators as larger (e.g. 1/8 > 1/3); this can be diagnosed by having them label and compare fractions, and remedied by grounding magnitude in the number line and part size.
sources.source: IES/WWC Practice Guide 'Developing Effective Fractions Instruction K-8' (Siegler et al. 2010, NCEE 2010-4039), Recommendations 2 and 5

sources.claim: Year 3 pupils compare and order unit fractions, and fractions with the same denominators.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (KS2, Year 3 fractions)

pedagogy.summary: Likelihood language gives children words — impossible, unlikely, even chance, likely, certain — to describe how probable everyday events are, before any numbers. The teaching aim is correct USE in context: mapping each word onto the composition of a situation (how many of each outcome), and reserving 'certain'/'impossible' for the true endpoints while using the graded middle for everything else. It is the gateway to the 0-to-1 scale and to comparing likelihoods.
bestPractices: Anchor a physical 'likelihood line' (a washing line / strip labelled impossible → even chance → certain) and have children peg real events onto it, justifying placements aloud

Start from everyday, personally-meaningful events ('it will get dark tonight', 'it will snow in July') then move to structured chance devices (bags of counters, spinners) where the composition can be inspected
Deliberately contrast 'likely' with 'certain' and 'unlikely' with 'impossible' using a mostly-red bag: red is likely but a blue draw is still possible, so red is not certain
Insist children give a reason grounded in the numbers ('most of them are red') rather than personal desire ('I want red')
Use unequal situations early (7 red, 3 blue; a spinner with one big section) so 'even chance' is not over-generalised to any two-outcome case
keyRepresentations: Likelihood line / probability word-scale strip (impossible ↔ certain)
Bags of coloured counters with visible, countable composition
Spinners with equal vs unequal sections
Everyday-event cards to sort and order
commonMisconceptions: Treating 'even chance' as meaning 'any situation with two possible outcomes' (e.g. calling a 1-red / 5-blue draw 'even chance' because there are two colours)
Collapsing the graded words to guarantees — 'likely' taken to mean it will definitely happen, 'unlikely' that it definitely won't
Confusing 'impossible' (cannot happen, probability 0) with 'very unlikely' (rare but possible) — e.g. calling a rare draw 'impossible'
Judging likelihood by personal preference or wishful thinking rather than by how many of each outcome there are

learn.summary: Likelihood Language (ages 9-10, Mathematics/Probability): children learn to USE and justify the words impossible, unlikely, even chance, likely, certain to describe how probable everyday events and chance-device outcomes are, before any numbers. The teaching aim is correct use in context — mapping each word onto the composition of a situation (how many of each outcome), reserving 'certain'/'impossible' for the true endpoints and using the graded middle for everything else. This is the gateway to the 0-to-1 scale and to comparing likelihoods. Core activity is open dialogue where the child generates and repairs their own wording against outcomes that push back; a live likelihood line/strip and sorting tasks are strong supports, and a tap-to-reveal reference scene can accompany them.

activities.title: The Chance-master's bag: say it, then watch it happen
feedback: If the child says 'red is certain', take out and show a blue counter (pick one deliberately, or keep drawing until one comes out, since a single random draw is usually red): 'Certain? But look, here is a blue I could pull. So is red certain, or only likely?' — let the over-strong word fail against a real possible outcome.

If the child says 'even chance' because there are two colours, count together: '7 red vs 3 blue is not equal, so it is not an even chance — what would the bag need for red and blue to be an even chance?' (equal numbers).
If the child accepts '7 on a 1–6 die is very unlikely', ask 'could it EVER come up? Which faces are on the die?' — since there is no 7, it cannot happen, so it is impossible, not merely rare.
If the child calls a green draw 'very unlikely', ask 'could it EVER happen? Show me a green counter.' There is none, so it is impossible, not merely rare.
If the child treats blue (unlikely) as 'impossible', point out some blue counters are present, so it can still happen — contrast 'rarely' with 'never'.
Affirm reasons grounded in counts ('most are red, so likely') and press on reasons grounded in desire ('I want red') by asking what the counters show.
activities.rationale: This is a LANGUAGE objective whose mastery is producing and justifying the words in context, so an open, unscripted dialogue that makes the child generate (not select) the vocabulary and repair it against real outcomes is intended to target the objective directly. Using unequal compositions guards against over-generalising 'even chance'; drawing the rare outcome and probing the impossible endpoint confront the guarantee and impossible-vs-unlikely misconceptions.
sourceClaims: Likelihood words (certain, likely, even chance, unlikely, impossible) map onto the 0-to-1 scale, and a key misconception is treating any two-outcome situation as an even chance — a cube with 1 red and 5 blue faces has two outcomes but probabilities 1/6 and 5/6, not even.

Even young children can register that the more numerous of two outcomes is more likely (additive 'more/less' reasoning), and the equiprobability bias — assuming all outcomes are equally likely — is a documented misconception in children's probabilistic reasoning.
learnerActions: Look into a bag you can see holds mostly red counters (e.g. 7 red and 3 blue) with the composition visible.
Before any draw, say in words how likely a red draw is and WHY, grounding the reason in the numbers ('most of them are red') rather than wanting red.

When you declare red 'certain', watch the game-master take out and show a blue counter (picked on purpose, or by drawing until one appears, because a single random draw will usually be red), then repair your word: was red certain, or only likely? Explain the difference.

Answer the opposite trap: the game-master suggests 'landing on 7 with this ordinary 1–6 die is only very unlikely, isn't it?' — decide whether 7 is very unlikely (rare but possible) or impossible (cannot happen at all), and say why.
Describe a green draw ('there are no green counters'), and a 'red or blue' draw ('only those two colours exist'), choosing and justifying a word for each.
Reject vague answers: if you say '50-50', be ready for 'but there are 7 red and 3 blue — is that even?' and recount to decide.
activities.intendedInsight: Each likelihood word corresponds to how many of each outcome there are; 'likely' is not a guarantee and 'impossible' (cannot happen at all) is stronger than 'very unlikely' (rare but possible). 'Even chance' requires equal numbers, not merely two possible outcomes.

activities.title: Physical likelihood line: peg real events and justify
feedback: If every event lands at the extremes or at 'even chance', ask for a reason tied to counts or frequency, and nudge toward the graded middle only for events that are not truly all-or-none or equally balanced.
If an unequal spinner/bag is called 'even chance', compare the total size or count for the outcome against the total for everything else: if those two totals are unequal, it cannot be an even chance.
Praise placements justified by 'most/few/none' rather than by what the child hopes happens.
activities.rationale: Anchoring a physical scale and pegging real events makes the ordering concrete and the reasoning public; starting from everyday events before structured devices connects the words to meaning, and insisting on number-grounded reasons addresses wishful-thinking and equiprobability errors.
sourceClaims: Even young children can register that the more numerous of two outcomes is more likely (additive 'more/less' reasoning), and the equiprobability bias — assuming all outcomes are equally likely — is a documented misconception in children's probabilistic reasoning.
learnerActions: Set up a washing line or paper strip labelled impossible → unlikely → even chance → likely → certain.

Peg everyday, personally-meaningful events onto it, saying your placement aloud: 'it will get dark tonight', 'it will snow in July', 'I'll flip heads', 'the sun will rise tomorrow' (for the weather and daylight events, think about where you live: snow in July is likely in some southern places, and near the poles there are times with no sunset or no sunrise).
Move to structured chance devices where composition is inspectable — bags of counters, spinners with equal and unequal sections — and peg outcomes from those.
Place at least one deliberately unequal situation (7 red/3 blue; a spinner with one big section) and justify why it is NOT an even chance.
Say out loud the reason for each placement, referring to how many of each outcome there are.
activities.intendedInsight: Events can be ordered along a graded scale from impossible to certain, and placement is decided by composition, not by preference — unequal situations sit away from 'even chance'.

activities.title: Live likelihood strip with an adjustable bag
feedback: If the child relies on the suggested-word zone without reasoning, cover it and ask them to predict the word before revealing.
When blue counters are removed, prompt: 'has red become certain yet? Is there still any blue left?' to tie 'certain' to zero alternatives.
activities.rationale: A live, manipulable strip makes the mapping from composition to word felt and correctable in real time, while still requiring the child to produce the word. The recolouring/slider and suggested-word zone are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory features.
sourceClaims: Likelihood words (certain, likely, even chance, unlikely, impossible) map onto the 0-to-1 scale, and a key misconception is treating any two-outcome situation as an even chance — a cube with 1 red and 5 blue faces has two outcomes but probabilities 1/6 and 5/6, not even.
learnerActions: Drop an event card onto a 0-to-1 likelihood strip and SAY the word that fits before confirming.
Change the number of red vs blue counters (e.g. with a slider) and watch which word best fits shift as the composition changes.
Remove the blue counters one at a time and predict, then say, which word changes and why ('likely' sliding toward 'certain' as blue is removed).
Always voice the word yourself rather than only reading the suggested-word zone.
activities.intendedInsight: The word that fits a situation depends on and moves with the composition; as favourable outcomes dominate, the likelihood slides toward 'certain', and only when none of the other outcome remains is it 'certain' (and the absent outcome 'impossible').

activities.title: Sort and order events (recognition check)
feedback: If the child accepts '1-vs-5 as even chance', have them count and compare: two colours is not enough; the counts must be equal.
If sorting is correct but reasons are missing, ask 'why does this one go here?' and require a count-based justification, since a correct label alone does not show the reasoning behind it.
activities.rationale: Categorisation and sequencing test recognition of the words and can surface misconceptions through targeted distractors, but selecting from options checks recognition rather than the child's own justified use; pairing each placement with a spoken reason partly bridges this gap.
sourceClaims: Likelihood words (certain, likely, even chance, unlikely, impossible) map onto the 0-to-1 scale, and a key misconception is treating any two-outcome situation as an even chance — a cube with 1 red and 5 blue faces has two outcomes but probabilities 1/6 and 5/6, not even.
learnerActions: Sort event cards into five groups: impossible, unlikely, even chance, likely, certain.
Order a set of events along the scale from least to most likely.
Judge deliberately tricky distractors, e.g. a two-colour but 1-vs-5 draw offered as 'even chance', and decide whether the label is right.
For each card you place, add a spoken or written reason comparing how many of each outcome there are.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising which word fits is a useful step, but the real target is correct, justified use — distractors built from common misconceptions reveal whether the word is being applied for the right reason.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal reference scene (worked examples)
feedback: Encourage self-prediction before revealing so the scene supports, rather than replaces, the child's own wording.
Point out that each revealed reason refers to how many of each outcome there are — the same justification the child should give.
activities.rationale: A static tap-to-reveal scene can present the vocabulary and worked reasons clearly, but being pre-baked it does not by itself elicit the child producing or comparing language; it works best as a reference alongside the dialogue or physical line, not as the sole activity.
learnerActions: Browse events arranged along a likelihood line and tap each to reveal the correct word and the numeric reason behind it.
Use this as a reference or worked-example companion when checking your own reasoning after attempting an event yourself.
Try to name the word yourself first, then tap to compare with the revealed answer and reason.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing worked reasons (why red is likely but not certain, why green is impossible) models the count-based justification expected of the child's own answers.

constraints: The objective is correct USE and justification of the five words in context; activities must make the child produce and justify the vocabulary, not merely select it.
Justifications must be grounded in the composition (how many of each outcome), not in personal preference or wishful thinking.

Reserve 'certain' and 'impossible' for the true endpoints (all favourable / zero favourable) and use the graded middle for everything else; do not let 'likely' become a guarantee or 'unlikely' become 'impossible'.

Keep 'impossible' (cannot happen at all, e.g. 7 on a 1–6 die or a green draw when none are present) distinct from 'very unlikely' (rare but possible); never present a strictly impossible outcome as a graded-middle case.

Use unequal compositions early (e.g. 7 red/3 blue, a spinner with one big section) so 'even chance' is not over-generalised to any two-outcome case; when comparing two represented outcomes, 'even chance' requires equal numbers.

Sorting/sequencing and the tap-to-reveal scene are recognition or reference scaffolds: they can assess classification or model reasoning but do not on their own elicit the child's independent, justified use of the words — pair them with spoken/written reasons or follow with open dialogue.
The live strip's slider/recolouring and suggested-word zone are optional illustrative interactions, not required mechanisms; the child must still voice the word themselves.

A spatial/3D environment is not required for this vocabulary-focused objective, which centres on producing and justifying words rather than spatial reasoning; the source judged it to add little over a flat scale and dialogue, but treat this as a scoped, untested design judgement, not a universal claim that 3D media add nothing.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support general teaching principles rather than proving any specific activity was tested.

Self-audit of worked examples: for a visible 7 red / 3 blue bag — red draw = likely (most but not all), blue = unlikely (few but present), green = impossible (none), red-or-blue = certain (only those two colours). These are internally consistent. 'Even chance' for red vs blue would require equal counts (e.g. 5 red / 5 blue); the 7/3 and 1/5 cases are correctly flagged as NOT even chance.

The 'die lands on 7' example is used to contrast impossible vs very-unlikely; landing on 7 on a standard 1–6 die is strictly impossible (cannot happen), so the dialogue has the character offer the under-strong 'very unlikely' for the child to correct to 'impossible'. The original source phrasing ('the die can land on 7 — very unlikely?') is preserved in intent but reframed so the prompt does not pre-answer it.

The source's judgement that a 3D environment adds little conceptual leverage here has been softened to a scoped, untested design judgement per guidance; it should not be read as a universal claim that 3D media add nothing.
No arithmetic, fractions, or force/motion content requiring further correction was identified in this row.

probeDeeper: You said red is likely — is it certain? Could you ever pull out a blue instead?
Why is that not an 'even chance'? What would the bag have to look like for red and blue to be an even chance?
Is 'impossible' the same as 'very unlikely'? Give me one event that is impossible and one that is only very unlikely.
If I took out all the blue counters, which word would change, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for correct USE: 'red' = likely (most but not all are red), 'blue' = unlikely (some but few), 'green' = impossible (there are none), 'red or blue' = certain (only those two colours exist). Justifications should refer to how many of each colour there are, and the strip should order them impossible(green) → unlikely(blue) → likely(red) → certain(red-or-blue).

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses 'even chance' for any situation with two outcomes ('it's 50-50, there's red and blue') regardless of how many of each there are
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront directly: count them together — 7 red vs 3 blue is not equal, so it is not an even chance; ask what the bag would need for 'even chance' to be true (equal numbers)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls the 7-red/3-blue draw 'even chance' or '50-50' because two colours are present, without comparing the counts

errorPatterns.pattern: Collapses graded words into guarantees — 'likely' means it will happen, 'unlikely' means it won't
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw the rare blue in front of them to show likely is not certain and unlikely is not impossible; contrast 'most of the time' with 'always/never'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says a red draw is 'certain' or 'will happen' because most are red, and treats blue as effectively impossible

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses 'impossible' (cannot happen, 0) with 'very unlikely' (rare but possible)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'could it EVER happen?' to separate the endpoints (impossible/certain) from the graded middle (how often); show there is no green counter at all, so it truly cannot happen
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls the green draw 'very unlikely' rather than impossible, or calls a rare-but-present outcome 'impossible'

responseLevels.gap: Uses only 'maybe / will / won't' or blanket '50-50' for everything; no graded vocabulary; treats any two-outcome situation as even chance
responseLevels.full: Uses all five words correctly across varied events AND justifies each by comparing favourable to total outcomes (red is likely-not-certain because most but not all are red), and cleanly distinguishes impossible from very-unlikely
responseLevels.partial: Uses the five words but unreliably in the middle — conflates likely with certain or impossible with very-unlikely; can label single events but justifies by preference or by naming colours rather than comparing how many of each

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put in front of the child a bag holding 7 red and 3 blue counters (composition visible), and read out four events: 'I pull out a red', 'I pull out a blue', 'I pull out a green', 'I pull out a red or a blue'. Ask them to describe each using probability words — certain, likely, even chance, unlikely, impossible — and to say WHY for each. Then ask them to place the four events on a strip from impossible to certain. Listen for the words used correctly and justified by the composition; do not offer options or expect a number.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child mapping words to composition calls red 'likely' (not certain, because a blue is still possible), blue 'unlikely', green 'impossible' (zero in the bag), and red-or-blue 'certain'. A child reasoning from surface features says 'even chance' for red-vs-blue because there are two colours, calls blue 'impossible' (confusing rare with can't-happen), or calls red 'certain' (likely taken as a guarantee). The justification, not the label, reveals which.

sources.claim: Likelihood words (certain, likely, even chance, unlikely, impossible) map onto the 0-to-1 scale, and a key misconception is treating any two-outcome situation as an even chance — a cube with 1 red and 5 blue faces has two outcomes but probabilities 1/6 and 5/6, not even.
sources.source: Third Space Learning — Describing Probability

sources.claim: Even young children can register that the more numerous of two outcomes is more likely (additive 'more/less' reasoning), and the equiprobability bias — assuming all outcomes are equally likely — is a documented misconception in children's probabilistic reasoning.
sources.source: Bryant & Nunes, Children's Understanding of Probability: A Literature Review (Nuffield Foundation, 2012)

pedagogy.summary: Dividing a unit fraction by a whole number is the PARTITION (sharing) meaning of division: 1/3 ÷ 4 asks 'if one-third is shared among 4, how big is each part?' — splitting the third into 4 pieces cuts the whole into 3 × 4 = 12, so each piece is 1/12. This is the natural PARTNER and CONTRAST to whole ÷ unit-fraction: here the answer gets SMALLER (which matches intuition), and the denominator grows because the whole is re-partitioned more finely. Teach it on an area/bar model by splitting an already-shaded third, connect the double-partition (3 then 4) to the 12, and verify with the inverse 1/12 × 4 = 1/3.
bestPractices: Split a physically-shaded 1/3 into 4 equal parts on a bar and extend the cuts across the whole, so the child SEES the whole become twelfths and reads one new piece as 1/12
Make the double-partition explicit: 3 parts, each cut into 4, gives 3 × 4 = 12 — the denominator arithmetic is the picture, not a rule
Contrast with the sibling operation (4 ÷ 1/5) so children distinguish 'share it out, gets smaller' from 'how many fit, gets bigger' — the commonest confusion in this pair
Verify every result with the inverse: 1/3 ÷ 4 = 1/12 because 1/12 × 4 = 1/3
Use a story context ('share 1/6 of a pizza between 3') so the sharing structure is grounded
keyRepresentations: Area/bar model: a shaded 1/3 sub-divided into 4, with the whole re-ruled into 12
Number line where the 0–1/3 segment is split into 4 sub-segments of 1/12
The double-partition grid (3 × 4) tying the 12 to the two cuts
Inverse equation 1/12 × 4 = 1/3 beside the picture
commonMisconceptions: Over-generalises the just-learned 'dividing by fractions makes bigger' and inverts: 1/3 ÷ 4 = 1/3 × 4 = 4/3 (confuses partition with measurement division)
Gets 1/12 by a rule but cannot say why the pieces are twelfths — thinks they are still thirds
Treats numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers, dividing the wrong part (e.g. 1 ÷ 4 over 3)
Adds the whole number to the denominator: 1/3 ÷ 4 → 1/7

learn.summary: Teach dividing a unit fraction by a whole number (e.g. 1/3 ÷ 4 = 1/12) as the sharing/partition meaning of division: 'if one-third is shared among 4, how big is each part?' Splitting the shaded third into 4 pieces re-rules the whole bar into 3 × 4 = 12 equal parts, so each new piece is a twelfth — smaller than a third. Build the double-partition (3 then 4) visually on a bar or number line, verify with the inverse 1/12 × 4 = 1/3, and deliberately contrast with the sibling operation (whole ÷ unit fraction, e.g. 4 ÷ 1/5) so learners distinguish 'share it out — gets smaller' from 'how many fit — gets bigger', the commonest confusion in this pair.

activities.title: Share a third four ways on a bar
feedback: If the piece is named a 'smaller third', re-extend the cut lines across the whole bar and count all 12 equal parts — the whole has been re-ruled, so the new unit is a twelfth.
If the learner cannot say where 12 comes from, point to the 3 original parts and the 4 cuts in each: 3 × 4 = 12.
Confirm by reassembling: 4 twelfths placed side by side exactly cover the original third, so 1/12 × 4 = 1/3.
A number line gives the same result: the 0–1/3 segment splitting into 4 sub-segments of 1/12 mirrors the bar being re-ruled into twelfths.
activities.rationale: Partitioning the fraction into equal parts on an area/bar model or number line and justifying the result by the inverse multiplication relationship is the recommended way to model dividing a fraction by a whole number; seeing the denominator become 12 as a direct consequence of the second cut makes the computation meaningful rather than rule-bound.
sourceClaims: Dividing a fraction by a whole number is modelled by partitioning/splitting the fraction into equal parts, using area models and number lines; the result is justified by the inverse relationship with multiplication and by visual models that reflect the computation process
Interpret and compute quotients of unit fractions by non-zero whole numbers (e.g. 1/3 ÷ 4 = 1/12) using visual models and the relationship between multiplication and division
learnerActions: Start with a whole bar that has one-third shaded.
Apply a '÷4' cut to the shaded third so it splits into 4 equal parts.

Re-rule the WHOLE bar the same way: if your cuts run along the bar (crossing the third-lines), extend them across the whole bar; if they run across the bar like the third-lines, cut each of the other two thirds into 4 equal parts too. Count: the whole is now ruled into 12 equal parts.
Read off one little shaded piece and name it: it is one-twelfth, not a smaller third.
Say out loud where 12 comes from: 3 original parts, each cut into 4, gives 3 × 4 = 12.
Gather 4 of the twelfths back together to remake the original third, confirming 1/12 × 4 = 1/3.
Optionally repeat on a number line: split the 0–1/3 segment into 4 equal sub-segments and see each is 1/12 of the whole 0–1 line.
activities.intendedInsight: Sharing one-third among 4 cuts the whole into twelfths because the second cut (into 4) multiplies the first partition (into 3): 3 × 4 = 12. The answer is smaller than 1/3, and the denominator grows because the whole is re-partitioned more finely — this is the picture, not a memorised rule.

activities.title: Share vs. how-many-fit: the sibling contrast
feedback: If a learner inverts 1/3 ÷ 4 to 1/3 × 4 = 4/3, ask them to describe in words what is being shared and into how many parts — sharing a third cannot give each person more than a third, let alone more than a whole.
If stories are mismatched, re-read each for the action word: 'share among' signals splitting (smaller); 'how many fit' signals counting (bigger).
Re-use one bar for both questions so the two actions sit on the same picture.
activities.rationale: Over-generalising a rule that fits one operation to another is a documented interference error that instruction must confront directly; placing the two meanings on one representation and having the child state which applies targets exactly this confusion.
sourceClaims: Treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers, and over-generalising a rule that fits one operation to another, are documented interference errors instruction must confront directly
learnerActions: Work two questions side by side on bars: 'share 1/3 among 4' (1/3 ÷ 4) and 'how many fifths fit in 4?' (4 ÷ 1/5).
For each, say aloud which action is happening: splitting one piece into more pieces, or counting how many pieces fit.
Predict before computing whether each answer is bigger or smaller than the starting number, and why.
Match short stories ('share this third between four of you' / 'how many 1/5 cups fill 4 cups?') to the correct ÷ expression.

State the rule-of-thumb in meaning terms for these cases: sharing among 2 or more makes each part smaller than the amount shared; counting how many unit fractions (smaller than 1) fit into a whole number gives an answer larger than that whole number.
activities.intendedInsight: Dividing a unit fraction by a whole number (sharing) and dividing a whole number by a unit fraction (measuring how many fit) are different meanings with opposite size effects. Naming which is happening HERE prevents over-generalising 'dividing by fractions makes it bigger'.

activities.title: Build and solve your own sharing story
feedback: If a learner writes 1/6 ÷ 3 = 1/9, show that sharing multiplies the parts (6 parts each cut into 3 = 18), it does not add 3 to the bottom.
If the story describes 'how many fit' instead of sharing, rewrite it so one amount is split among a number of people.
Always close by reassembling the m pieces to recover the original fraction as a check.
activities.rationale: Creating a story context and verifying via the inverse are both named practices for this objective; generating a fresh case tests transfer beyond the worked example.
sourceClaims: Dividing a fraction by a whole number is modelled by partitioning/splitting the fraction into equal parts, using area models and number lines; the result is justified by the inverse relationship with multiplication and by visual models that reflect the computation process
Interpret and compute quotients of unit fractions by non-zero whole numbers (e.g. 1/3 ÷ 4 = 1/12) using visual models and the relationship between multiplication and division
learnerActions: Take a new case such as 1/6 ÷ 3 and write a short sharing story for it (e.g. 'share one-sixth of a pizza between 3').

Draw a bar with one-sixth shaded and split that sixth into 3 equal parts, then re-rule the whole the same way (extend cuts that cross the sixth-lines across the bar, or cut every other sixth into 3 too).
Count the total equal parts the whole is now cut into (6 × 3 = 18) and name one piece (1/18).
Verify with the inverse: 1/18 × 3 = 1/6.
Explain how you found the bottom number, referring to the two cuts, not an added-on rule.
activities.intendedInsight: The partition method generalises: for any unit fraction 1/n ÷ m, splitting each of the n parts into m re-rules the whole into n × m parts, so each piece is 1/(n×m). Whenever the fraction is shared among 2 or more (m ≥ 2) the piece is smaller than the original; sharing among 1 would leave it unchanged.

activities.title: Check understanding with targeted distractors
feedback: 4/3 comes from multiplying instead of dividing (1/3 × 4 = 4/3), possibly from over-applying 'dividing with fractions makes bigger'; but sharing a third among 4 must give something smaller than a third, so 4/3 cannot be right.
1/7 treats ÷4 as '+4 on the bottom'; sharing multiplies the parts (3 × 4 = 12), so re-cut and count the 12 pieces.
The answer 1/12 only counts as secure when the learner can name why the pieces are twelfths — if they call them 'thirds', rebuild the partition and count the 12 parts.
activities.rationale: The partition result and the bigger-vs-smaller contrast are checkable, and the specific wrong answers 4/3 (inversion) and 1/7 (added-to-denominator) map onto documented misconceptions, so they make useful distractors. A recognition item checks the result but does not by itself show the learner can construct the partition, so pair it with drawing and explanation.
sourceClaims: Treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers, and over-generalising a rule that fits one operation to another, are documented interference errors instruction must confront directly
learnerActions: Answer: 1/3 ÷ 4 = ? choosing from 1/12, 4/3, 1/7.
For the chosen answer, state in one sentence whether it is bigger or smaller than 1/3 and why.
On a blank bar, draw the split of a shaded third into quarters and re-rule the whole bar the same way (extend cuts that cross the third-lines, or cut each third into 4) to show the twelfths.
Answer the second-tier probe: 'Point to one small piece — how do you know it is a twelfth and not a smaller third?'
activities.intendedInsight: A secure answer is 1/12 WITH an explanation that the whole is cut more finely into twelfths; the characteristic errors are 4/3 (multiplying instead of dividing, possibly from over-applying 'dividing with fractions makes bigger') and 1/7 (adding the whole number to the denominator).

activities.title: Talk-through sharing (optional discussion scaffold)
feedback: If the learner cannot name the piece, invite them to describe or sketch the cuts — the naming follows from counting all equal parts of the whole.
Steer talk back to 'is it bigger or smaller than a third, and why' to keep the sharing meaning central.
activities.rationale: Discussion can elicit reasoning about the sharing meaning and the size comparison, but the cutting and re-ruling that generate the twelfths need a visual surface (bar or number line), so talk complements rather than replaces the model.
learnerActions: Take on a sharing-story role: 'split this third fairly between four of you'.
Discuss aloud whether each person's piece is bigger or smaller than a third, and justify it.
Explain how the pieces get their name (twelfths) by describing the cuts you would make.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the sharing structure and the size comparison in words reinforces the partition meaning and can surface rule-following when a learner cannot name why the pieces are twelfths.

constraints: A multiple-choice or recognition item confirms the result (1/12) but does not show the learner can independently construct the partition or explain why the pieces are twelfths; pair any recognition item with drawing the split and stating the inverse.

A static or fixed bar figure can teach the partition meaning if it is read and explained, but it does not let the learner vary the sharer to generalise; include at least one case the learner partitions themselves (e.g. 1/6 ÷ 3).

The partition can also be shown on a number line (split the 0–1/3 segment into 4 sub-segments of 1/12), a representation named in the research alongside area models; offer it as an additional representation, not a replacement for the bar.

Interactive splitting (dragging a '÷4' cutter, cut lines auto-extending across the whole, auto-labelling 1/12, an inverse panel reassembling the pieces, a contrast switch to 4 ÷ 1/5) is offered as an optional way to make the mechanism concrete, not a required mechanism.
Partitioning a fraction of a bar is a planar task; a 3D treatment is not needed here and could invite a volume misreading — kept as a noted limitation, not a claim that 3D can never help.
Always ground the answer in meaning: require the learner to state whether the result is smaller than the original fraction and why, not just produce the numeral.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 1/3 ÷ 4 = 1/12 (3 × 4 = 12) and inverse 1/12 × 4 = 1/3 are correct; 1/6 ÷ 3 = 1/18 (6 × 3 = 18) and 1/18 × 3 = 1/6 are correct; 4 ÷ 1/5 = 20. Distractors 4/3 (inversion, from 1/3 × 4) and 1/7 (add-to-denominator) are intentional wrong answers, labelled as such, never offered as valid.
The 4/3 distractor is attributed to inverting 1/3 ÷ 4 to 1/3 × 4 (not to 4 ÷ 1/3, which equals 12); this is now stated consistently in activities 2 and 4.
Qualified the generalisation 'each piece is 1/(n×m)' so it is described as smaller than the original fraction only when shared among 2 or more (m ≥ 2); dividing by 1 leaves the fraction unchanged.

The contrast activity uses 4 ÷ 1/5 (= 20); the original row uses both 4 ÷ 1/5 and 4 ÷ 1/3 (= 12) in different fields. Both are valid 'how-many-fit' sibling cases; either is acceptable as the contrast example.

Restored the number-line representation (0–1/3 segment split into 4 sub-segments of 1/12), which the candidate had dropped; it is an alternative to the bar model and is named in the supporting IES claim.
One source claim (Common Core 5.NF.7a) is marked verified:false in the row; it is retained as cited but its verification status is unconfirmed and was not re-checked here.

The original strong claim that the partition meaning is 'FELT' only via live recompute, and that 3D 'adds nothing', has been softened to scoped affordances/limits; comparative necessity between media is not established by the sources provided.

probeDeeper: How is 1/3 ÷ 4 different from 4 ÷ 1/3 — which one gets bigger and which gets smaller, and why?
Point to one of your small pieces — how do you know it is a twelfth and not a smaller third?
If you shared 1/6 among 3 instead, what would each piece be, and how did you get the bottom number?
Prove your 1/12 is right using multiplication.
assess.correctAnswer: 1/12. Sharing one-third among 4 means splitting the third into 4 equal parts; cutting each third into 4 cuts the whole into 3 × 4 = 12, so each part is 1/12 — smaller than 1/3. Check: 1/12 × 4 = 1/3.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Dividing by fractions makes it bigger' — over-applies the whole ÷ unit-fraction result and inverts: 1/3 ÷ 4 = 1/3 × 4 = 4/3
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the two meanings on one bar — 'how many fifths fit in 4' (counting, bigger) versus 'share a third among 4' (splitting, smaller) — and have the child say aloud which is happening HERE before recomputing
errorPatterns.distractor: 4/3 — dividing by a fraction makes the answer bigger
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer 4/3 (bigger than 1/3); working shows a multiplication/inversion; second tier claims the answer should be bigger

errorPatterns.pattern: Gets 1/12 but cannot justify it — says the four pieces are still 'thirds', or cannot explain where 12 comes from (rule without the double-partition meaning)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build the partition physically — cut a shaded third into 4, extend the cuts across the whole, count the 12 — and connect 3 × 4 = 12 to the fraction-as-division meaning of the pieces
errorPatterns.revealedBy: First tier correct (1/12) but second tier empty or wrong: names the pieces thirds, or 'you just times the bottom by 4' with no picture

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds the whole number to the denominator: 1/3 ÷ 4 → 1/7 (treats ÷4 as '+4 on the bottom')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that sharing MULTIPLIES the parts (each of 3 becomes 4, giving 12), not adds; re-cut the bar and count the total pieces rather than guessing the bottom number
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer 1/7; the 4 is bonded to the denominator additively

responseLevels.gap: Inverts to 4/3, or answers 1/7, or cannot start; no sharing meaning and the answer is thought to grow.
responseLevels.full: Answers 1/12 and explains it as sharing/splitting the third into 4 so the whole becomes twelfths, states clearly that the result is smaller than 1/3 and why, verifies with 1/12 × 4 = 1/3, and distinguishes it from 4 ÷ 1/3; transfers to a fresh unit-fraction ÷ whole case.
responseLevels.partial: Produces 1/12, likely by 'times the bottom by 4', but cannot picture the split or explain why the pieces are twelfths, and muddles this with the how-many-fit direction when the sibling case appears.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work out 1/3 ÷ 4. Then explain why, using a picture or words — what is being shared or split, and is your answer bigger or smaller than 1/3?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child holding the partition meaning gives 1/12 AND explains it as splitting the third, naming why the pieces become twelfths (the whole is cut more finely). The telling failure is the child fresh from 4 ÷ 1/5 who over-applies 'dividing by fractions makes bigger' and inverts to 4/3 — exactly the sibling-confusion this topic must separate. The second tier also catches the child who recalls 1/12 by rule but calls the pieces 'thirds' or cannot say where 12 comes from.

sources.claim: Dividing a fraction by a whole number is modelled by partitioning/splitting the fraction into equal parts, using area models and number lines; the result is justified by the inverse relationship with multiplication and by visual models that reflect the computation process
sources.source: IES / What Works Clearinghouse — Developing Effective Fractions Instruction K–8 (Siegler et al. 2010), Recommendation 3

sources.claim: Treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers, and over-generalising a rule that fits one operation to another, are documented interference errors instruction must confront directly
sources.source: IES / WWC Fractions Practice Guide — misconception step, Recommendation 3

sources.claim: Interpret and compute quotients of unit fractions by non-zero whole numbers (e.g. 1/3 ÷ 4 = 1/12) using visual models and the relationship between multiplication and division
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics — 5.NF.7a

pedagogy.summary: At age 10-11 children make a LINE PLOT of measurement data in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8) and then OPERATE on that data with fractions — totalling measurements, finding differences, and redistributing a total equally among the data points. Two ideas carry the teaching. First, a line plot is not a bar graph: its horizontal axis is a genuine MEASUREMENT SCALE (a number line), so every position on it exists whether or not a measurement falls there ('64 inches is not a category like spiders'), and gaps between observed values must be shown. Second, the signature problem — 'if the total were shared equally, how much would each have?' — is an informal, hands-on route to the MEAN (fair share), and to solve it children total the fractions (often re-labelling the scale in a common unit such as eighths to get like denominators) and then divide by the count. So the topic fuses data display with fraction arithmetic, and the equal-redistribution task quietly previews averaging.
bestPractices: Draw the horizontal axis as a proper measurement scale (a number line marked in the fractional unit), and include every position — mark unobserved values too, because unlike categories, measurement values have gaps that must be shown
Distinguish the line plot from a bar graph explicitly: the axis is a measurement scale you could read off a ruler, not a set of separate categories
Re-label the scale in a common fractional unit (e.g. eighths) so that totalling and comparing measurements produces like denominators
Treat 'redistribute the total equally' as a fair-share problem — pour everything together, then share among the data points — making the link to the mean concrete before it is named
Keep the fraction arithmetic (adding unlike denominators, dividing by the count) reliable, since the data questions depend on it
Attend to precision when measuring and recording to the nearest 1/2, 1/4 or 1/8, and place each mark carefully at its scale position
keyRepresentations: A number-line measurement scale marked in eighths, with an X (or dot) stacked above each measured value — the line plot itself
The same measurements re-expressed over a common denominator (eighths) for totalling
A 'pour together then share equally' image for the equal-redistribution (fair-share/mean) task
A ruler marked in halves/quarters/eighths, showing where the scale of the plot comes from
commonMisconceptions: Treating a line plot like a bar graph — showing only the values that occur, side by side as categories, with no continuous scale and no gaps for unobserved values
Adding the measurement fractions by combining numerators and denominators instead of finding a common denominator
Not seeing 'redistribute equally' as total ÷ count (the fair share / mean) — giving a middle value or leaving the data unchanged
Placing marks imprecisely on the scale, or mis-reading the fractional interval (e.g. an eighth for a quarter)

learn.summary: Learners aged 10-11 make a line plot of measurement data in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8), then operate on that data with fractions: totalling measurements, finding differences, and redistributing a total equally among the data points. Two ideas carry the teaching. First, a line plot is not a bar graph: its horizontal axis is a genuine measurement scale (a number line), so every position on it exists whether or not a measurement falls there, and gaps between observed values must be shown. Second, the signature problem — 'if the total were shared equally, how much would each have?' — is an informal, hands-on route to the mean (fair share): learners total the fractions (often re-labelling the scale in a common unit such as eighths to get like denominators) and then divide by the count. The topic fuses data display with fraction arithmetic, and the equal-redistribution task (using identical containers so equal volume reads cleanly) previews averaging before it is named.

activities.title: Place-and-share: build the plot, then pour the total
feedback: If a mark lands on the wrong fractional interval (e.g. at 3/8 when the value is 1/2 = 4/8), point to a labelled position and count the eighths across to re-place it; the plot's structure is fine, only the placement slipped.
If observed values are drawn as adjacent bars with no empty positions between them, show a ruler: every eighth exists on the scale, so unobserved positions must stay visible as gaps.
If fractions are added by combining numerators and denominators (e.g. 1/2 + 3/4 = 4/6), re-label both in eighths first (4/8 + 6/8 = 10/8 = 1 2/8) and check the sum against the scale.

If the fair share is answered with an unchanged amount, or by picking a middle or most common value without working, pour everything together to get the total, then share it among all the containers: equally means total ÷ count. (For 3/4, 1/2, 1/4, 1/2 the middle value happens to equal the fair share of 1/2, so ask to see the total-and-divide working rather than judging by the answer alone.)
activities.rationale: Placing marks on a real fractional scale and physically pouring-then-sharing is proposed to make the fill-the-gaps and fair-share ideas concrete and operable, rehearsing both the display skill and the fraction arithmetic the data questions depend on. An optional interactive version may let the learner drag each X onto the scale, auto-re-label amounts in eighths when totalling, and animate the pour-and-share so each container settles at the shared amount; these are illustrative mechanisms, not requirements — paper, a ruler and real identical beakers achieve the same work and may be preferable for measuring precision.
sourceClaims: A line plot displays measurement data on a number-line diagram whose scale corresponds to the measuring tool; unlike categorical data on a bar graph, measurement values have gaps that must be shown ('64 inches is not a category like spiders'), and a value not present is still written in its proper position on the scale

Standard 5.MD.2: make a line plot in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8) and use fraction operations to solve problems, e.g. given different measurements of liquid in identical beakers, find how much each would hold if the total were redistributed equally — which Grade 6 students later see as the MEAN of the data set; solving such problems may require re-labelling the scale in eighths to produce like denominators
Adding fractions with unlike denominators requires replacing them with equivalent fractions over a common denominator (a well-documented error is adding numerators and denominators directly)
learnerActions: Measure (or use given) several lengths to the nearest 1/8 and place a mark (an X or dot) above each value on a horizontal scale marked in eighths.
Keep every eighth-position on the scale visible, including positions where no measurement falls, so the gaps are shown (for example, if nothing lands on 4 5/8, that spot stays on the number line).
Say aloud why an unobserved value still has a place on the scale: it is a measurement value on a ruler-like scale, not a separate category.

For a fair-share task, start with four identical (same-size) containers holding 3/4, 1/2, 1/4 and 1/2 cup. Combine all the liquid into one larger container that can hold at least 2 cups, and write the sum, re-labelling each amount in eighths: 6/8 + 4/8 + 2/8 + 4/8 = 16/8 = 2 cups.
Pour the combined 2 cups equally back into the four identical containers and record how much each now holds; connect the result (1/2 cup each) to total ÷ count = 2 ÷ 4.
Total the two shortest measurements and find a difference between two values, re-expressing over a common denominator first.
activities.intendedInsight: A line plot's axis is a continuous measurement scale with gaps for unobserved values, not a row of categories; and 'share the total equally' means total ÷ count — the fair share, which previews the mean made physical.

activities.title: Check the operations on a given plot
feedback: For an answer that adds tops and bottoms (e.g. 1/2 + 3/4 giving 4/6), re-express both in eighths and recompute; 4/8 + 6/8 = 10/8 = 1 2/8.
For a fair-share answer that is the most common amount or an unchanged value, re-total all amounts and divide by the number of containers.
If a difference is found without first making like denominators, re-express both values in eighths before subtracting, then check the result against the scale.
activities.rationale: A scorable check of totals, differences and the equal-share item verifies the fraction operations and the fair-share interpretation. This is a focused check on given data; it does not by itself require the learner to construct a plot from raw measurements, so pair it with the construction activity. As a design choice for this check, keep data sets small with clean fraction sums so the arithmetic stays reliable and the reasoning stays visible.
sourceClaims: Standard 5.MD.2: make a line plot in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8) and use fraction operations to solve problems, e.g. given different measurements of liquid in identical beakers, find how much each would hold if the total were redistributed equally — which Grade 6 students later see as the MEAN of the data set; solving such problems may require re-labelling the scale in eighths to produce like denominators
Adding fractions with unlike denominators requires replacing them with equivalent fractions over a common denominator (a well-documented error is adding numerators and denominators directly)
learnerActions: From a provided small line plot, write the total of the two shortest measurements, showing the common-denominator step.
Answer a fair-share question such as 'If all the liquid were shared equally between identical containers, how much would each hold?' by totalling then dividing by the count.
Compare two values to find a difference, re-expressing over eighths first.
Watch for and avoid two traps: adding numerators and denominators together, and reporting a middle value instead of total ÷ count.
activities.intendedInsight: Totals, differences and fair shares read off a line plot all depend on correct like-denominator fraction arithmetic and on reading 'equally' as total ÷ count.

activities.title: Explain and stretch the fair-share idea
feedback: If the learner says the empty spot should be removed, return to the ruler image: a measurement value is not a category, so its position exists regardless of whether data falls there.

If adding the zero container does not change the learner's answer, recompute total ÷ count with the new count (2 cups ÷ 5 = 2/5 cup each): the fair share is sensitive to how many are sharing, even when the added amount is zero.
If the fruit bar chart and the line plot are treated as the same, point out that fruit names are categories with no scale, while lengths sit on a measurement number line.
activities.rationale: Explanation and counterexample probes surface whether understanding is robust and transfer the fair-share reasoning to a new case, including sensitivity to the count. Verbal explanation complements, but does not replace, the hands-on construction and computation; explaining a procedure is not the same as performing it.
sourceClaims: A line plot displays measurement data on a number-line diagram whose scale corresponds to the measuring tool; unlike categorical data on a bar graph, measurement values have gaps that must be shown ('64 inches is not a category like spiders'), and a value not present is still written in its proper position on the scale

Standard 5.MD.2: make a line plot in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8) and use fraction operations to solve problems, e.g. given different measurements of liquid in identical beakers, find how much each would hold if the total were redistributed equally — which Grade 6 students later see as the MEAN of the data set; solving such problems may require re-labelling the scale in eighths to produce like denominators
Adding fractions with unlike denominators requires replacing them with equivalent fractions over a common denominator (a well-documented error is adding numerators and denominators directly)
learnerActions: Answer: 'You didn't measure any item at 4 5/8 — should that spot still be on your scale? Why?' to put the measurement-scale-vs-category distinction into words.
Explain why you changed both fractions into eighths before adding them.
Tackle a counterexample: 'If one more identical container with 0 cups joined the sharing, how much would each get now?' and state why the answer changes.
Contrast this line plot with a bar chart of favourite fruits and say what makes the axes different.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating why unobserved positions remain on the scale, why common denominators are needed, and how the fair share responds to the count (including a zero) consolidates both the display and the averaging ideas.

constraints: Reliable fraction arithmetic (adding unlike denominators, dividing by a count) is a prerequisite the data questions depend on; shore it up if it is shaky.

The horizontal axis must be drawn as a proper measurement scale (an evenly spaced number line marked in the fractional unit) with every position present, including unobserved values shown as gaps — not a set of separate bar-graph categories.

A static annotated line plot can display the scale and label totals and fair shares as a reference or worked example, but it does not let the learner place data, show gaps, or carry out the pour-and-share, so it is a support rather than the main task.

An interactive drag/pour tool is one way to make the mechanism concrete; paper plots, a real ruler, and physical identical beakers accomplish the same learning and may be preferable for precision in measuring and recording. A 2D scene suffices for this measurement scale and its data.
A recognition-only or multiple-choice check can verify answers but does not by itself elicit construction of a plot from raw measurements; combine it with a construction task.
Role-play or in-character dialogue does not confirm that the learner can accurately place marks or perform the fraction arithmetic, so it is not a substitute for a do-and-calculate task.

Attend to precision: measure and record to the nearest 1/2, 1/4 or 1/8 and place each mark carefully at its scale position; distinguish a placement slip (scaffold) from a conceptual bar-graph error (reteach).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 3/4 + 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/2 = 6/8 + 4/8 + 2/8 + 4/8 = 16/8 = 2 cups; shared among 4 gives 1/2 cup each (2 ÷ 4); adding a zero container gives 2 ÷ 5 = 2/5 cup each. The source example 4 3/8 + 4 1/2 = 8 7/8 inches also checks out (3/8 + 4/8 = 7/8), with 4 3/8 and 4 1/2 being the two shortest of the source pencil set. 1/2 + 3/4 = 4/8 + 6/8 = 10/8 = 1 2/8. These were checked during this review but not independently re-verified against the original sources.
'Identical beakers' was restored from the source so that equal redistribution reads as equal volume per container; the arithmetic is unchanged.

The original artefact-fit note that a third spatial dimension 'adds nothing' is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law; it has been removed and reframed only as 'a 2D scene suffices here' within constraints, without asserting 3D is useless in general.
The original 'a static image cannot teach this / only a live tool can' framing was softened: a fixed diagram still teaches as a reference even though it cannot be manipulated.

The reteach-prerequisite links in the source assessment (unlike-denominator and line-plot prerequisites) are retained as pedagogical intent but internal prerequisite identifiers were removed as non-portable.
The efficacy of hands-on construction over other media is stated as proposed/intended, not as a verified empirical result.

probeDeeper: 'You didn't measure any pencil at 4⅝ — should that spot still be on your scale? Why?' — probes the measurement-scale (fill-the-gaps) idea versus categories
'Why did you change both fractions into eighths before adding them?' — forces the common-denominator reason into words
Counterexample: 'If one more beaker with 0 cups joined the sharing, how much would each get now?' — tests that the fair share is total ÷ count and is sensitive to the count and to a zero
'How is this line plot different from a bar chart of favourite fruits?' — checks the measurement-vs-categorical distinction on a fresh case
assess.correctAnswer: A correct performance: for (1) draws a number-line scale marked in eighths and stacks a mark above each measured value, leaving the positions with no data visible as gaps (not a row of bars); for (2) adds the two fractions using a common denominator (e.g. 4⅜ + 4½ = 8⅞ inches); for (3) totals ¾+½+¼+½ = 2 cups and divides by 4 to get ½ cup each (fair share). A genuine measurement scale with gaps shown, like-denominator addition, and reading 'share equally' as total ÷ count are the marks of mastery.

errorPatterns.pattern: Line-plot-as-bar-graph: treats the distinct measurement values as categories — shows only the values that occur, side by side, with no continuous scale and no gaps for unobserved values
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach on the line-plot prerequisite: the axis is a measurement scale like a ruler — every eighth-position exists and must be shown, even where no pencil falls, because a measurement value is not a category
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (1) the child draws the observed lengths as separate adjacent bars/columns with no evenly-spaced number-line scale, omitting the empty positions between values

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds fractions by combining numerators and denominators instead of finding a common denominator
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach on the unlike-denominators prerequisite: re-label all the measurements in a common unit (eighths) before adding, and check the result against the scale
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (2) or (3) the child writes something like ½ + ¾ = 2/6 (or 2/4), adding tops and bottoms rather than re-expressing over eighths first

errorPatterns.pattern: Redistribute-not-as-fair-share: does not read 'share the total equally' as total ÷ count — gives a middle value, one of the amounts, or leaves the data unchanged
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront by pouring together and sharing out: combine all the liquid (the total), then share it among the four beakers; 'equally' means total ÷ count — the fair share
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (3) the child reports ½ because it is the most common amount, or picks a beaker's value, rather than totalling to 2 cups and dividing by 4

errorPatterns.pattern: Placement/interval slip: places a mark at the wrong fractional interval or miscounts eighths, though the plot's form is right
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, do not reteach: have the child re-read the scale mark and count the eighths from a labelled point; the understanding of the plot is intact, only the placement slipped
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The line plot is structurally correct but a mark sits at ⅜ where the value is ½, or an eighth is read as a quarter

responseLevels.gap: Builds a bar-graph-like display (observed values as adjacent categories, no measurement scale or gaps); adds the fractions by combining numerators and denominators; treats 'share equally' as choosing a value
responseLevels.full: Constructs a proper line plot on a fractional measurement scale with gaps shown, totals and differences measurements using common denominators, solves the equal-redistribution problem as total ÷ count (the fair share), and transfers the same reasoning to a fresh measurement set
responseLevels.partial: Constructs a correct line plot on a measurement scale and reads it, and adds fractions with like denominators, but stumbles when denominators differ or does not connect 'redistribute equally' to total ÷ count — displays and reads the data but cannot fully operate on it

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a set of measurements to the nearest 1/8 (e.g. eight pencils: 4½, 4¾, 4½, 5, 4⅜, 4¾, 4½, 5 inches) and set these tasks, WATCHING how they work. (1) 'Make a line plot to show these lengths.' (2) 'What is the combined length of the two shortest pencils?' (3) 'Four beakers hold ¾, ½, ¼ and ½ of a cup. If all the liquid were shared equally between the four beakers, how much would each hold?' (Set the task and WATCH — do not tell them to use a common denominator or hint that sharing equally is total ÷ count.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Task (1) exposes whether the child treats the axis as a measurement scale (gaps present, evenly spaced) or as bar-graph categories (only observed values, side by side). Task (3) cannot be solved by reading the plot — it requires totalling unlike fractions and dividing by the count, so it separates a child who can operate on the data from one who can only display it, and previews the mean. The two together distinguish display-only competence from full fraction-operation competence.
