pedagogy.summary: Rounding a two-decimal-place number extends 'nearest' to a chosen precision: to the nearest whole, decide between the two neighbouring wholes; to one decimal place, decide between the two neighbouring tenths. The digit ONE place to the right of the target place is the decider. Two traps carry the topic: double rounding (3.47 → 3.5 → 4 when the true nearest whole is 3) and the boundary carry (12.95 to 1dp → 13.0, where the rounded-up tenth ripples into the whole). Rounding is the everyday tool for ESTIMATION (4.83 + 2.17 ≈ 5 + 2 = 7).
bestPractices: Round in ONE step from the original number — never round an already-rounded value; to the nearest whole, only the tenths digit decides (3.47 has 4 tenths, so it rounds to 3)
Identify the single deciding digit: the one immediately to the right of the place you are rounding to
Handle the carry explicitly on a number line: 12.95 lies between 12.9 and 13.0 and is nearer 13.0, so the whole number changes
Keep the target place value: rounding 3.47 to 1dp gives 3.5, and 12.95 to 1dp is written 13.0, not 13
Use rounding to estimate and sense-check (4.83 + 2.17 ≈ 7), and judge whether the estimate is above or below
keyRepresentations: Number line zoomed to the target precision (wholes; then tenths)
Place-value chart marking the target place and the deciding digit
Estimation on a number line for sums like 4.83 + 2.17
Boundary number line 12.9–13.0 for the carry case
commonMisconceptions: Double rounding: 3.47 → 3.5 → 4 to the nearest whole
Uses the wrong deciding digit — looks at the hundredths (or a chain of digits) when rounding to a whole
Drops the boundary carry: 12.95 → 12.10 or 12.9 instead of 13.0
Omits the trailing zero / place: writes 13 when 1dp is asked, or truncates

learn.summary: Teaches rounding two-decimal-place numbers to the nearest whole and to one decimal place, treating rounding as choosing between two neighbouring values at a chosen precision, decided by the single digit immediately to the right of the target place. Two central traps: double rounding (3.47 → 3.5 → 4 when the nearest whole is 3) and the boundary carry (12.95 to 1dp → 13.0, where the rounded tenth ripples into the whole). Rounding is linked to estimation (4.83 + 2.17 ≈ 5 + 2 = 7); for this particular pair the rounding errors cancel, so the estimate equals the true sum. A zoomable number line is the lead activity because the same number can be rounded to different precisions and the carry can be watched; a set of checkable questions, a static annotated line, and diagnostic prompts are preserved as complementary tools.

activities.title: Zoomable number line: one-step rounding and the visible carry
feedback: If a learner reaches 4 for 3.47 to the nearest whole via 3.5, show on the line that 3.47 never reaches 3.5; round once, straight from the original, and only the tenths digit (4) counts.

If a learner writes 12.9 for 12.95 to 1dp, show on the 12.9–13.0 line that 12.95 sits exactly halfway between 12.9 and 13.0, and that the usual rule (a deciding digit of 5 rounds up) gives 13.0; when the tenth rounds up past 9 it carries into the whole, just like 9 + 1 in whole-number columns.
Reinforce keeping the target place: 12.95 to 1dp is written 13.0, not 13.

For the estimate, accept 'exactly equal': rounding 4.83 up by 0.17 and 2.17 down by 0.17 cancels, so 7 is neither above nor below 7.00 for this pair — a good moment to see that rounding errors can offset.
activities.rationale: A number line that can be re-zoomed lets the same number be rounded to different precisions so the deciding digit changes visibly, and the 12.95 carry can be watched rather than asserted. The optional zoom control, the midpoint marking, the side-by-side wrong-path comparison, and the 'ticking up' animation make the mechanism concrete; these are illustrative, not mandatory. Source guidance frames rounding as choosing between a just-greater and just-less number located on a number line, and warns that applying a procedure without this awareness produces cascading/double rounding and boundary-carry (trail-of-9s) errors.
sourceClaims: Rounding to a chosen precision is 'choosing between two numbers, one just greater and one just less', decided by locating the number on a number line; 'memorising and applying a procedure... without this overall awareness often results in errors', including sequential/cascading rounding up (rounding an already-rounded value rather than in one step) and the 'trail of 9s' boundary carry (e.g. 9999 rounds to 10000), where a rounded digit ripples into the next place.
Year 5 pupils are taught to 'round decimals with 2 decimal places to the nearest whole number and to 1 decimal place' (verbatim statutory wording).
learnerActions: Plot 3.47 on a number line showing whole numbers 3 and 4; mark the 3.5 midpoint and judge that 3.47 sits just below it, so it is nearer 3.

Deliberately try the tempting wrong path: round 3.47 to 3.5 first, then watch 3.5 round up to 4 — the WRONG whole. Compare side by side with going straight from 3.47 (tenths digit 4, below half) which gives 3.
Zoom the line to tenths and round 3.47 to one decimal place (3.5).

Switch to a 12.9–13.0 view and round 12.95 to one decimal place; notice it sits exactly halfway, so by the usual rule (a deciding 5 rounds up) it snaps to 13.0, and watch the whole-number digit tick from 12 to 13 as the carry ripples in.

Use an estimation view to round 4.83 and 2.17 each to the nearest whole and add (5 + 2 = 7); then compare with the true sum (7.00) and say whether the estimate is above, below, or exactly equal — here rounding 4.83 up and 2.17 down cancel, so the estimate equals the true total.
activities.intendedInsight: Round in ONE step from the original number; to the nearest whole only the tenths digit decides, so 3.47 → 3. The boundary carry (12.95 → 13.0) is a real event where a rounded-up tenth ripples into the whole, not a rule failure.

activities.title: Identify the deciding digit on a place-value chart
feedback: If a learner rounds 3.47 to a whole using the 7 (→ 4), re-establish the target place and show the single digit to its right is the only decider; have them point to it first.
If a learner rounds up 'because there are digits after', clarify that only that one deciding digit matters, not the presence of further digits.
activities.rationale: Explicitly locating the target place and its single deciding digit targets the wrong-deciding-digit misconception. A static or tap-to-reveal chart serves as a reference aid; it labels the deciding digit for one case but does not itself animate precision-switching or the carry, so it supports rather than replaces the number-line activity.
learnerActions: Place a number such as 3.47 in a place-value chart and name the place you are rounding to.
Point to the ONE digit immediately to the right of that place as the sole decider before rounding — for rounding to a whole, the tenths digit (4); for rounding to 1dp, the hundredths digit.
Explain why the 7 (hundredths) does NOT decide the nearest whole of 3.47.
activities.intendedInsight: The deciding digit is exactly the one place to the right of the target place (the tenths when rounding to a whole, the hundredths when rounding to 1dp) — never a chain of digits.

activities.title: Checkable rounding and estimation questions
feedback: Answer 4 for 3.47 to the nearest whole signals double rounding — revisit the one-step number-line comparison.
Answer 12.9 for 12.95 to 1dp signals a dropped carry; 12.10 signals a mishandled carry — revisit the 12.9–13.0 line.
Answer 13 (without the .0) signals a lost trailing place — the question asked for 1dp, so write 13.0.
For the estimate, 'exactly equal' is correct here: the +0.17 and −0.17 rounding errors cancel, so accept it rather than requiring above/below.
activities.rationale: Rounding to a stated precision and estimation are cleanly checkable, and targeted distractors (4 from double rounding, 12.9 from a dropped carry, 13 from a lost place) surface specific misconceptions. This checkable format is well suited to practising and checking the procedure and surfacing these specific errors; it does not itself animate the precision-switching or carry that the number line makes visible, so it works best following the number-line work.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils are taught to 'round decimals with 2 decimal places to the nearest whole number and to 1 decimal place' (verbatim statutory wording).
learnerActions: Round 3.47 to the nearest whole number (answer 3).
Fill the blank: 12.95 to 1dp = ___ (answer 13.0).

Estimate 4.83 + 2.17 by rounding each to the nearest whole (5 + 2 = 7) and say whether the estimate is above, below, or exactly equal to the true total (7.00) — for this pair the rounding errors cancel, so it is exactly equal.
Round 3.47 to one decimal place (3.5).
activities.intendedInsight: A learner can round correctly to a stated precision in one step and use rounding to estimate and sense-check a sum.

activities.title: Diagnostic sequence and probing questions
feedback: 3.47 to the nearest whole is the double-rounding hinge: a secure learner reads the tenths (4 < 5) and says 3 in one step; a double-rounder gets 3.5 then 4.
12.95 to 1dp is the carry hinge: secure → 13.0; dropped carry → 12.9; wrong carry → 12.10.

For the estimate, accept 'exactly equal' as the correct relationship for 4.83 + 2.17: the rounding errors (+0.17 and −0.17) offset exactly, so the estimate 7 equals the true sum 7.00 — do not require above/below.
Finish by asking the learner to transfer the method to a new two-decimal-place number.
activities.rationale: These prompts come directly from the assessment design and separate the three error patterns (double rounding, carry-handling, truncation) while requiring the learner to articulate reasoning, supporting transfer to a new number. The estimate relationship is left open in the prompt so it genuinely diagnoses the learner's reasoning, with the 'errors cancel' explanation reserved for feedback.
learnerActions: Round 3.47 to the nearest whole number, then round 3.47 to one decimal place; say which single digit tells you each answer and why not the 7.
Round 12.95 to one decimal place and explain what happens to the whole-number part and why.
Estimate 4.83 + 2.17 by rounding each to the nearest whole; then say whether the estimate is above, below, or exactly equal to the real total.
If you said 3.5 and then 4 for the nearest whole, redo it going straight from 3.47 — which whole is it actually nearer?
activities.intendedInsight: Explaining the deciding digit and the carry, in one step from the original, distinguishes secure rounding from double rounding, dropped/mishandled carry, and truncation.

constraints: Round in ONE step from the original number — never round an already-rounded value.
Keep the target place value: rounding to 1dp requires the trailing place (write 13.0, not 13).
The static annotated number line and place-value chart are reference/scaffold aids: they can label the deciding digit for one case but do not demonstrate precision-switching or the carry dynamically.

The set of checkable questions checks answers and surfaces misconceptions via distractors; this format does not itself animate the precision-switching or carry that the number line shows, so pair it with the number-line work rather than treating it as the sole route to the nearness concept.
For the estimation example 4.83 + 2.17, the estimate (7) equals the true sum (7.00); do not require learners to pick 'above' or 'below' — accept 'exactly equal'.
Prerequisite reteach for double rounding and wrong-deciding-digit errors is flagged to an earlier place-value micro-topic in the source assessment.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Original-row error corrected: the assessment's probe 'estimate 4.83 + 2.17 — is your estimate above or below the real total?' has no above/below answer, because rounding 4.83 up (+0.17) and 2.17 down (−0.17) cancel, giving estimate 7 = true 7.00. All learner-facing actions now allow 'exactly equal'; the diagnostic prompt is left open with the explanation in feedback. The original binary phrasing is noted here and in preservationAudit.uncertain, not reproduced as a required answer.

Arithmetic/logic self-audit: 3.47 to nearest whole = 3 (tenths 4 < 5), to 1dp = 3.5 (hundredths 7 ≥ 5); 12.95 to 1dp = 13.0 (carry correct); 4.83 → 5, 2.17 → 2, estimate 7 vs true 7.00 (equal). Distractors '4' (3.47) and '12.9'/'12.10'/'13' (12.95) are intentional wrong options and must never be presented as correct.

The source's 'poor fit' claims that depth 'adds nothing' and that a mechanical procedure offers no worthwhile dialogue are catalog preferences, not established pedagogical laws; omitted from learner-facing guidance rather than asserted as universal.

The source 'possible' claim that a static line 'cannot show precision-switching or the carry dynamically' is retained narrowly as a scaffold limitation, not as a claim that static images cannot teach.
Catalog artefact vocabulary ('quiz') was replaced with neutral descriptions ('set of checkable questions') in the summary and constraints.

probeDeeper: To round 3.47 to the nearest whole, which single digit tells you the answer — and why not the 7?
You said 3.5 and then 4 — what do you get going straight from 3.47? Which whole is it actually nearer?
Round 12.95 to one decimal place — what happens to the whole-number part, and why?
Estimate 4.83 + 2.17 by rounding each — is your estimate above or below the real total?
assess.correctAnswer: 3.47 → 3 (nearest whole; tenths digit is 4) and 3.5 (to 1dp); 12.95 → 13.0 (to 1dp, the carry ripples into the whole); 4.83 + 2.17 ≈ 5 + 2 = 7.

errorPatterns.pattern: Double rounding: rounds 3.47 to 3.5 first, then rounds 3.5 up to 4 for the nearest whole
errorPatterns.nextMove: Round once, straight from the original: to the nearest whole only the tenths digit (4) counts, so 3.47 → 3. Show on the line it never reaches 3.5.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 4 for 3.47 to the nearest whole, and explains it by first getting 3.5

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops or mishandles the boundary carry: 12.95 → 1dp gives 12.9 or 12.10 instead of 13.0
errorPatterns.nextMove: On a 12.9–13.0 line, show 12.95 is nearer 13.0; when the tenth rounds up past 9 it carries into the whole, just like 9 + 1 in whole-number columns.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rounds the tenths up but leaves the whole unchanged (12.9), or writes an impossible 12.10

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses the wrong deciding digit — looks at the hundredths (7) when rounding 3.47 to a whole, or rounds up because 'there are digits after'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Identify the place being rounded to and the ONE digit immediately to its right as the sole decider; practise pointing to it before rounding.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rounds 3.47 to a whole by the 7 (→ 4), or cannot say which single digit decides

responseLevels.gap: Truncates or rounds by the wrong digit; cannot round to a stated precision.
responseLevels.full: Rounds to the nearest whole and to 1dp in ONE step from the original, handles the 12.95 → 13.0 carry, uses rounding to estimate 4.83 + 2.17 ≈ 7, explains which digit decides at each precision, and transfers to a new number.
responseLevels.partial: Rounds correctly to one precision but double-rounds when finding the nearest whole, or mishandles the 12.95 carry, or drops the trailing .0.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'Round 3.47 to the nearest whole number, and then round 3.47 to one decimal place. Next, round 12.95 to one decimal place. Finally, estimate 4.83 + 2.17 by rounding.' Watch each step — especially whether they go via 3.5 for the whole, and what happens to 12.95.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 3.47 to the nearest whole is the double-rounding hinge: a secure child reads the tenths (4 < 5) and says 3 in one step; a double-rounder rounds to 3.5 first, then up to 4 — a different, wrong answer. 12.95 to 1dp is the carry hinge: a secure child gets 13.0, while others write 12.9 (ignored the carry) or 12.10 (carried wrongly). Together they separate double rounding, carry-handling, and truncation.

pedagogy.summary: Children solve elapsed-time word problems in both directions — find the END time given a start and a duration, and find the DURATION between two times — using a blank number line. They count on in convenient jumps (to the next o'clock, whole hours, then minutes). The persistent errors are treating time as base-10 (adding minutes past 60 without rolling the hour), column subtraction that fails across the hour boundary, and counting in the wrong direction.
bestPractices: Use a blank number line for both problem types; count on in jumps (next o'clock, whole hours, minutes)
Decide the direction first: adding a duration forwards vs finding the gap between two times
Bridge the o'clock rather than subtracting in columns
Represent the story on the line before calculating (start, jumps, end)
Check the answer against a clock face
keyRepresentations: Blank number line with labelled jumps
Clocks marking start and end
The 'bridge to the next o'clock' jump
commonMisconceptions: Adds the duration to the minutes only, ignoring the hour roll-over past 60 (2:15 + 47 -> '2:62')
Column subtraction of the two times, failing across the hour boundary
Counts in the wrong direction (subtracts a duration instead of adding, or vice versa)
Overshoots or undershoots the o'clock bridge (base-10 slip)

learn.summary: Children solve elapsed-time word problems in both directions — finding the END time from a start and a duration, and finding the DURATION between two times — using a blank number line and counting on in convenient jumps (to the next o'clock, then whole hours, then minutes). The core teaching move is showing that the SAME number line solves both 'when does it end?' and 'how long is it?', so elapsed time becomes one count-on method rather than two mysterious sums. Persistent errors to target: treating time as base-10 by writing minutes past 60 without rolling the hour over (2:15 + 47 -> '2:62'), column subtraction that fails across the hour boundary, and counting in the wrong direction.

activities.title: Count on along a number line to find the end time
feedback: If a learner writes an end time with 60 or more minutes (e.g. '2:62' or '3:75'), ask: 'Can a time have 62 minutes? What happens at 60?' Then bridge to the next o'clock first (2:15 -> 3:00) and add the rest.
If the first jump overshoots or undershoots the o'clock, ask 'How many minutes from 2:15 to the next whole hour?' before adding the remaining minutes.
Confirm success by checking: 3:40 + 35 = jump +20 to 4:00 then +15 = 4:15, with the hour correctly rolled over.
activities.rationale: A blank number line lets children bridge to the next o'clock rather than add minutes past 60, directly addressing the base-10 slip. Research documents that children apply base-10 whole-number reasoning to time and struggle to coordinate its base-60 groupings, which produces minutes-past-60 errors; a published scheme of learning uses the blank number line with jumps to whole hours and minutes for exactly this purpose.
sourceClaims: White Rose Y4 Time (Step 3) documents using a blank number line to find durations and start/end times (e.g. jumps of +1 hour and +10 minutes), and warns that children may attempt to calculate durations using column subtraction, leading to inaccuracies when hours are crossed.

Children apply base-10 whole-number reasoning to time and cannot easily coordinate its base-60 groupings, explaining minutes-past-60 errors (2:15 + 47 -> '2:62') and column-subtraction failures across the hour boundary.
learnerActions: Read a word problem such as: 'A film starts at 2:15 and lasts 47 minutes — when does it end?'
Draw a blank number line and mark the start time (2:15).
Make a first jump that bridges to the next o'clock: +45 minutes to reach 3:00.
Make a second jump with the remaining minutes: +2 to reach 3:02; label each jump and read off the end time.
Repeat with a harder bridge: 'Swimming starts at 3:40 and lasts 35 minutes — when does it finish?' Jump +20 to 4:00, then +15 to reach 4:15.
Check the end time on a clock face.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding a duration means counting FORWARD from the start; bridging to the next o'clock first makes the hour roll over correctly, so you never write an impossible time like 2:62 or 3:75.

activities.title: Fill the gap to find a duration
feedback: If a learner sets out 10:05 minus 9:20 in columns and borrows in base-10, show that this fails across the hour boundary; model counting on in jumps to the o'clock then the minutes instead.
If a learner adds 9:20 and 10:05 together, ask 'Are you finding how LONG it is or adding two moments? Which jumps fill the gap?'
Reinforce that the two jumps (+40 then +5) sum to the answer the same way the end-time jumps did.
activities.rationale: Modelling a duration as a filled gap counteracts the column-subtraction error that fails across the hour boundary, which a published scheme of learning explicitly warns about, and which research links to base-10 reasoning applied to base-60 time.
sourceClaims: White Rose Y4 Time (Step 3) documents using a blank number line to find durations and start/end times (e.g. jumps of +1 hour and +10 minutes), and warns that children may attempt to calculate durations using column subtraction, leading to inaccuracies when hours are crossed.

Children apply base-10 whole-number reasoning to time and cannot easily coordinate its base-60 groupings, explaining minutes-past-60 errors (2:15 + 47 -> '2:62') and column-subtraction failures across the hour boundary.
learnerActions: Read a problem such as: 'How many minutes are there between 9:20 and 10:05?'
On a blank number line, mark both times (9:20 and 10:05).
Jump from the earlier time to the next o'clock: +40 minutes to reach 10:00.
Jump the remaining minutes: +5 to reach 10:05.
Add the jumps together (40 + 5) to get the total duration of 45 minutes.
Check against a clock face, and explain why adding 9:20 and 10:05 together would be nonsense.
activities.intendedInsight: Finding a duration means filling the GAP between two times with jumps and summing them — not subtracting in columns and not adding the two clock times together. Bridging the o'clock keeps the base-60 boundary correct.

activities.title: Decide the direction before you jump
feedback: If a learner counts backward on a 'find the end' problem, or forward on a 'find the start', pause and re-ask: 'Is the unknown an end time, a start time, or how long it lasted? Which way do the jumps go?'
If a learner adds 9:20 and 10:05 when asked for a gap, restate that a gap is filled with jumps between the two times, never a sum of the clock readings.
Praise correct identification of the unknown and direction before any arithmetic begins.
activities.rationale: Explicitly rehearsing whether the unknown is an end time, start time, or duration addresses the directional/performance error where children subtract a duration that should be added, or add two clock times. Using the one number line for all three cases shows elapsed time as a single jump-counting method, counting forward or backward and bridging the o'clock.
learnerActions: Before calculating any problem, state out loud whether the unknown is an END time (jump forward from the start by the duration), a START time (jump backward from the end by the duration) or a GAP (fill the space between two given times).
Solve a mixed set, e.g. 'A show ends at 10:05 and lasted 45 minutes — when did it START?' by counting BACKWARD: -5 to 10:00, then -40 to 9:20.
Compare a forward problem and a backward problem side by side, labelling which way the jumps go.
Say which number is unknown and which direction the jumps travel before marking the line.
activities.intendedInsight: Choosing the direction first — forward to find an end, backward to find a start, or filling the gap to find a duration — prevents counting the wrong way or adding two clock times together.

constraints: Pupils should already read and record time in seconds, minutes and hours and compare durations before tackling these word problems; if they write times with 60+ minutes, revisit how 60 minutes rolls the hour over before continuing.

Multiple-choice or fill-in-the-blank items about elapsed time can check whether answers are correct, but they do not show whether the child built the jumps or bridged the o'clock; pair them with a 'show your jumps' task so the method is visible.
A fixed worked-example diagram can illustrate the jumps but does not let the child build them in either direction; use it as a reference, not as the main practice.
A spoken or dialogue format can pose word problems and prompt reasoning, but still needs the child to actually draw and label jumps so the method is practised, not just discussed.

An interactive number line where jumps are dragged and a clock rolls over as each jump lands can make the hour roll-over visible in real time; this is one helpful presentation, not a requirement — the same learning can happen with pencil-and-paper number lines and a physical clock face.
Always state the known times explicitly (the start time for end-time problems, both times for duration problems, and the end time for start-time problems) so the direction of counting is unambiguous.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original source row rated a 3D interactive as adding nothing and a static image/conversation as unable to let the child build jumps. These catalog-style comparative claims have been softened into scoped notes about affordances and limits rather than universal pedagogical laws.

Arithmetic self-check: 2:15 + 47 min = +45 to 3:00 then +2 = 3:02 (correct); 3:40 + 35 = +20 to 4:00 then +15 = 4:15 (correct); 9:20 to 10:05 = +40 then +5 = 45 min (correct); backward 10:05 − 45 = −5 to 10:00 then −40 = 9:20 (correct). The erroneous learner outputs '2:62' and '3:75' are retained only as misconceptions to diagnose and correct, never as valid answers.
The original row listed a prerequisite reteach id for base-60/hour-crossing; that internal identifier has been dropped in favour of the plain-language prerequisite stated in constraints.

The 'decide the direction' activity targets a performance error (wrong-direction counting) that had no directly supporting source claim in the original row, so its sourceClaims is left empty; the number-line method itself is sourced on the first two activities.

probeDeeper: 'Show me your first jump — where did you land?' (o'clock bridge)
'Your answer says 2:62 — can a time have 62 minutes? What happens at 60?'
'Are you finding when it ENDS, or how LONG it is? Which way do the jumps go?'
'A show ends at 10:05 and lasted 45 minutes — when did it START?' (backward count-on)
assess.correctAnswer: For the film, counts on 2:15 to 3:00 (+45) then +2 = 3:02 (or +47 bridging correctly); for 9:20 to 10:05 counts +40 to 10:00, +5 = 45 minutes; for 3:40 + 35 bridges to 4:00 (+20), +15 = 4:15 — rolling the hour over rather than writing 3:75.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds the duration to the minutes only, ignoring the hour roll-over past 60 (2:15 + 47 -> '2:62')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the number line to bridge to the next o'clock first (2:15 -> 3:00), then add the rest; show that 60 minutes rolls the hour over.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes an end time with minutes of 60 or more; doesn't bridge to the next hour

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses column subtraction of the two times, failing across the hour boundary
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model counting on to fill the gap (jumps to the o'clock, then minutes); make the base-60 boundary explicit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 10:05 minus 9:20 in columns and borrows base-10, getting a wrong gap

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts in the wrong direction — subtracts a duration when it should be added on, or adds the two clock times together when finding a gap
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold: decide first whether the unknown is an end time (jump forward by the duration) or a gap (fill between the two times); rehearse choosing the direction before jumping.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On 'find the end' counts backwards; on 'find the gap' adds 9:20 and 10:05

responseLevels.gap: Adds minutes past 60 or subtracts in columns; counts the wrong direction; can't cross the hour.
responseLevels.full: Solves both elapsed-time directions on a number line, bridging the o'clock, rolling the hour over correctly, and choosing the right direction for the unknown.
responseLevels.partial: Solves within-hour problems and one direction reliably, but slips crossing the hour or on the reverse (find-start / find-duration) case.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set both problem types and WATCH: (1) 'A film starts at 2:15 and lasts 47 minutes — when does it end? Show me your jumps.' (2) 'How many minutes between 9:20 and 10:05?' (3) A crossing-the-hour end-time: 'Swimming starts at 3:40 and lasts 35 minutes — when does it finish?' Watch whether they count on with a number line (bridging the o'clock) or add minutes past 60, subtract in columns, or go the wrong direction.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The hour-crossing items catch the child who adds minutes past 60 (2:15 + 47 -> '2:62'; 3:40 + 35 -> '3:75') or subtracts in columns; a child bridging the o'clock on a number line rolls the hour correctly. Doing both directions catches counting the wrong way.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 10–11 (META): use estimation to CHECK answers to calculations, and judge, in context, an appropriate degree of accuracy. This is a monitoring/self-regulation skill layered over computation, not a new calculation method.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y6): 'use estimation to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, an appropriate degree of accuracy'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.OA.3 'assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies including rounding'; supported by 5.NBT.4 rounding and SMP MP1 (make sense) / MP6 (attend to precision).
• Operational details — the child rounds each number to a convenient value (487×23 → 500×20 = 10000), computes the easy estimate, then compares it to the exact answer to catch gross errors (misplaced digit, wrong operation). Separately, they judge how precise the answer needs to be (money to 2dp, people rounded up, a fair 'about' for a crowd). Emphasis on whether the estimate is above/below and why.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): estimate 487×23 by rounding to 500×20 and use it to sanity-check a given answer. Tier B (10–11): spot an unreasonable answer (e.g. decimal point misplaced) by comparing with a quick estimate. Tier C (11): decide whether an exact answer or an estimate is appropriate for a given real context and justify the degree of accuracy.
bestPractices: Teach estimation as a HABIT that brackets the real calculation — estimate first (what should it be about?), compute, then compare — so it becomes automatic self-checking, not an extra chore done only when asked.

Make the purpose catching ERRORS: give calculations with planted mistakes (decimal-point slips, wrong operation, digit dropped) and have children use an estimate to flag the unreasonable ones — the estimate's job is to be roughly right, fast.
Discuss DIRECTION of rounding: rounding both factors up over-estimates, both down under-estimates — so children can say whether the true answer should be a bit more or less than the estimate.

Separate 'estimate to check' from 'degree of accuracy in context': explore contexts where over/under-estimating matters (buying enough paint = round up; sharing money = exact) so accuracy is a contextual judgement.

Value a good estimate even when 'wrong': stress it need not match the exact answer — it must be close enough to reveal a blunder; discourage children from 'estimating' by computing exactly then rounding.
keyRepresentations: Rounded-calculation shorthand: 487 × 23 ≈ 500 × 20 = 10000, written above the exact working as a check line.
Number line showing the estimate and the exact answer as nearby points — a wildly distant exact answer flags an error.
'Reasonable / unreasonable' sorting frame comparing computed answers against a quick estimate.
Up/down rounding arrows on each factor to reason whether the estimate is an over- or under-estimate.
commonMisconceptions: Computing the exact answer first and then 'rounding it' — defeating the purpose of a quick independent check.
Believing an estimate is 'wrong' unless it equals the exact answer, so distrusting the whole method.
Rounding to unhelpful values (rounding 23 to 23, or over-rounding so the estimate is useless).
Not using the estimate to actually CHECK — producing it then ignoring an exact answer that clearly conflicts.
Confusing 'appropriate accuracy' — giving money to 3dp, or rounding a count of buses down when you need enough for everyone.

learn.summary: For ages 10–11: use estimation as a habit for checking calculations and judging an appropriate degree of accuracy in context. This is a monitoring/self-regulation skill layered over computation — estimate first, compute, then compare to catch gross errors (misplaced decimal points, wrong operation, dropped digit) and decide how precise an answer needs to be for the real situation.

activities.title: Estimate Detective: flag the unreasonable answer
feedback: If the learner computes the exact answer first then rounds it, point out this defeats the purpose — the check must be a fast, independent estimate made before or instead of trusting the exact product.
When a proposed answer sits far from the estimate, confirm that the gap itself is the signal: they can flag the error without finishing the exact calculation.
If they distrust an estimate because it does not equal the exact answer, reassure that a good estimate need only be close enough to reveal a blunder.

Handle direction carefully: here 487 rounds UP to 500 but 23 rounds DOWN to 20, so this mixed-direction estimate leans both ways and its direction is not predetermined. In fact the true answer 11201 lands ABOVE the estimate 10000 (the down-rounding of 23 outweighed the up-rounding of 487), which shows why you should not assume 'rounded up means over-estimate' for a mixed case — use a both-up or both-down example when you want a clean over- or under-estimate.
activities.rationale: Estimation-to-check is a predict-then-compare loop; letting the learner set rounded factors, generate an estimate, and compare it against a proposed answer rehearses the checking habit directly. Planted errors (decimal slips, wrong operation) make the catching purpose concrete.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils use estimation to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, an appropriate degree of accuracy.
Pupils assess the reasonableness of answers to multistep problems using mental computation and estimation strategies including rounding.
learnerActions: Face a calculation with a proposed answer, e.g. 487 × 23 with a candidate answer shown — some candidates are correct, others sabotaged by a misplaced decimal point or a wrong operation.
Round each number to a convenient, friendly value (e.g. 487 → 500, 23 → 20) and compute the easy estimate (500 × 20 = 10000).
Place the estimate and the proposed answer as points on the same number line, then judge whether the proposed answer is 'reasonable' or 'unreasonable' by how far it sits from the estimate.

State the general direction rule — rounding BOTH factors up over-estimates (so the true answer is a bit less than the estimate) and rounding BOTH down under-estimates (so the true answer is a bit more) — then notice that the 500 × 20 example is MIXED (487 rounds up, 23 rounds down), so its direction is NOT cleanly predetermined; for a mixed case rely on the estimate's MAGNITUDE to catch gross errors rather than declaring a precise over- or under-estimate.
Rule each proposed answer reasonable or not WITHOUT computing the exact product first.
activities.intendedInsight: A quick independent estimate shows roughly what size the answer should be, so an answer sitting far from the estimate is visibly wrong (487 × 23 cannot be 1121 when the estimate is ~10000). The estimate's job is to be roughly right, fast — not to match exactly.

activities.title: How accurate does it need to be?
feedback: If a learner always prefers exact answers, raise a context (roughly enough seats? approximate cost?) where speed and a ballpark beat spurious precision.
If they round a count down when more is needed, walk through the real consequence (not enough buses/paint) so the direction of rounding is tied to purpose.
Praise reasoning that fits precision to purpose, e.g. money kept to 2dp but a crowd quoted to the nearest hundred.
activities.rationale: Separating 'estimate to check' from 'degree of accuracy in context' lets learners treat accuracy as a judgement driven by the situation and its consequences rather than a mechanical rule.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils use estimation to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, an appropriate degree of accuracy.
learnerActions: Meet real contexts — buying enough paint, sharing money fairly, counting a crowd, working out how many buses are needed — and decide whether an exact answer or an estimate is appropriate.
Choose the sensible precision for each: money to 2 decimal places, the number of buses or tins of paint needed rounded UP so there is enough, a fair 'about' for a crowd size.
Explain the consequence of choosing wrongly, e.g. rounding the number of buses down leaves people without a seat; giving money to 3 decimal places is spurious precision.
Name a situation where a rough estimate is actually more useful than an exact answer (when a ballpark is enough, or when speed matters more than precision).
activities.intendedInsight: Appropriate accuracy is a contextual judgement, not a fixed rule: the purpose of the answer sets how precise it must be, and sometimes a fast ballpark beats an exact figure.

activities.title: Does that seem about right? — reasoning aloud
feedback: If a learner says 'the estimate was 10,000 and I got 11,201 so it's definitely correct', discuss the limit: an estimate rules out gross errors but cannot confirm exactness — pair it with an inverse check when exactness matters.

If a learner dismisses estimation as pointless once the exact answer exists, show a worked example with a slipped digit (e.g. a wrong result of 1,120 offered for 487 × 23, whose true value is 11,201) that the estimate instantly flags; estimation guards against your own errors.
There is no single scored answer here — surface and value the child's reasoning rather than marking it right or wrong.
activities.rationale: The objective is metacognitive — the child's stance toward estimation as a checking tool and toward appropriate accuracy, not a computed value. Socratic prompting suits surfacing and challenging that stance; it works alongside, not instead of, the active predict/compare drill.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils use estimation to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, an appropriate degree of accuracy.
learnerActions: Be presented with suspicious proposed answers and, before any reveal, say whether each seems about right and why.
Answer probing questions: 'If your estimate was 10,000 and your worked answer was 1,150, which do you trust — and what do you do next?'
Explain whether an estimate can ever PROVE an exact answer is 100% correct, and why not.
Describe how you would round 487 × 23 to check it, and justify why you rounded that way.
activities.intendedInsight: Estimation is a stance toward reasonableness and its limits: it can rule out place-value-sized errors but cannot verify the last digits, so it complements — not replaces — an exact or inverse check.

constraints: This is a META/self-regulation objective layered over computation, not a new calculation method — learners should already be able to perform the underlying multiplication/division.

Multiple-choice or matching tasks ('is this answer reasonable?', match calculations to best estimates, pick appropriate accuracy for a context) can assess the judgement, but recognition-only formats do not elicit the estimate-FIRST habit; include tasks where the learner generates the estimate independently.

A static annotated worked check (≈ line above the exact working, with reveal of how it exposes a decimal-point error) is a useful reference, but the checking habit is rehearsed through an active compare loop rather than by reading a fixed example.
Discourage 'estimating' by computing the exact answer and then rounding it — the check must be fast and independent.
Avoid rounding to unhelpful values (e.g. leaving 23 as 23, or over-rounding so the estimate is useless); the estimate must be both easy and close enough to reveal a blunder.

The both-factors-up/both-factors-down over/under rule only applies cleanly when both factors round the SAME way; a mixed-direction rounding (e.g. 500 × 20, where 487 rounds up and 23 rounds down) does not predetermine whether the true answer is above or below the estimate, so use magnitude for error-catching there.
An estimate rules out gross errors but cannot verify exactness; do not teach it as a guarantee of a correct answer.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source worked example '487 × 23 = 1,120' appears in an error-pattern as a planted slipped-digit mistake; the true product is 11,201. This is intentional in the diagnostic context (an unreasonable answer to be flagged), so it is retained only as an error-to-catch, never presented as correct.

Self-audit of the estimate: 500 × 20 = 10,000 is correct; the exact 487 × 23 = 11,201. Because 487 rounds up but 23 rounds down, the estimate is mixed-direction; here it lands about 11% BELOW the true value, so the simple 'rounded up ⇒ over-estimate' inference does not hold for this example. The candidate values 1,121/1,150/1,120 are correctly characterised as unreasonable.

Asking a 10–11 learner to determine which rounding 'dominates' in a mixed case was reframed to recognising that mixed roundings do not predetermine the direction; this keeps the point age-appropriate and avoids implying a clean over/under verdict for 500×20.
The second cited US standard (CCSS-M 4.OA.3) is marked verified:false in the source; do not treat its support as independently confirmed.

Optional interaction examples from the source (dial/spinner to set rounded factors, auto-computed estimate, number-line comparison, up/down arrows tinting over/under-estimate, context-consequence mode) are retained as illustrative affordances, not mandatory mechanisms.

probeDeeper: If your estimate was 10,000 and your worked answer was 1,150, which do you trust — and what does that tell you to do next?
Can an estimate ever prove your exact answer is 100% correct? Why or why not?
Give me a real situation where a rough estimate is actually better than an exact answer.
How would you round 487 × 23 to check it, and why round that way?
assess.correctAnswer: There is no single right answer to score — surface the child's thinking. Strong reasoning: round to 500 × 20 = 10,000, so a calculated answer near 11,000 is plausible but 1,100 or 110,000 is definitely wrong; the estimate can't confirm exactness but can catch place-value-sized errors. And an estimate is more useful than exactness when a ballpark is enough (is there enough money? roughly how many buses?) or when speed matters more than precision.

errorPatterns.pattern: sees estimation as pointless once an exact answer exists — 'why estimate if I can just work it out?'
errorPatterns.nextMove: surface, don't score: discuss a worked example with a slipped digit (487×23 = 1,120) that the estimate instantly flags; estimation guards against your own errors.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child dismisses estimation, treating the exact calculation as self-evidently trustworthy

errorPatterns.pattern: thinks an estimate can CONFIRM an answer is exactly right, not just flag it as reasonable
errorPatterns.nextMove: discuss the limit of estimation: it rules out gross errors but cannot verify the last digits; pair it with an inverse check for exactness.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child says 'the estimate was 10,000 and I got 11,201 so it's definitely correct'

errorPatterns.pattern: believes an exact answer is always preferable — no sense that context sets the needed accuracy
errorPatterns.nextMove: raise contexts (roughly enough seats? approximate cost?) where speed and a ballpark beat spurious precision; accuracy should fit the purpose.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child cannot name a situation where a rough answer suffices or is better

responseLevels.gap: dismisses estimation as pointless, or cannot use it to judge whether an answer is reasonable.
responseLevels.full: uses estimation to flag unreasonable answers (while recognising it can't verify exactness), and judges when a ballpark versus an exact answer fits the context, explaining the reasoning.
responseLevels.partial: uses estimation to get a ballpark but treats it as confirming exactness, or cannot articulate when approximate accuracy is more appropriate than exact.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You worked out 487 × 23 and got an answer. Before we trust it — how could a quick estimate tell you whether the answer is probably right or definitely wrong? And when is a rough estimate actually MORE useful than an exact answer? Talk me through your thinking.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: This META objective is about the child's stance toward estimation as a checking TOOL and toward appropriate accuracy — not a computed value. The probe surfaces whether they see estimation as a way of judging reasonableness (and its limits) versus treating it as just 'a rough sum' or as pointless once you have the exact answer.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 8–9y; interpret whole-number quotients: 56 ÷ 8 can mean the number in each share (partitive/sharing) OR the number of equal groups of 8 (quotitive/grouping).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y3 'solve problems, including missing number problems, involving … division', building on Y1–Y2 sharing and grouping and the fact that division is NOT commutative.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.OA.2 — 'Interpret whole-number quotients of whole numbers, e.g., interpret 56 ÷ 8 as the number of objects in each share when 56 objects are partitioned equally into 8 shares, or as a number of shares when 56 objects are partitioned into equal shares of 8 objects each.'
• Operational details — the load-bearing idea is that ONE division expression models TWO different actions: sharing (partitive: 56 shared among 8 → how many each) and grouping (quotitive: 56 put in groups of 8 → how many groups). Both give 7, but the story and the drawing differ. Teach both explicitly and have children label which is which; this dual meaning is the single hardest and most neglected point. Keep division tied to multiplication and to its two prerequisite actions from Y1.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8): share 12 counters among 3 plates and among groups of 3; give both answers. Tier B (age 8–9): match a ÷ expression to a sharing story AND a grouping story and draw each. Tier C (age 9): write a ÷ expression for a picture and state whether it shows sharing or grouping, and why the answer means different things.
bestPractices: Teach BOTH structures deliberately and by name — partitive/sharing ('how many in each?') and quotitive/grouping ('how many groups?') — using the same numbers so children see one ÷ expression modelling two actions.

Use contrasting stories for the same expression (56÷8: '56 sweets shared between 8 children' vs '56 sweets into bags of 8') and have children draw each differently — the drawings expose which structure they hold.
Anchor division to multiplication from the start (56÷8 relates to 8×?=56) so division is not learned as an isolated procedure.
Follow CPA: physically share/group counters → draw the sharing/grouping → write the ÷ expression, keeping the action visible.
Introduce remainders informally through the same actions (15 shared among 4 leaves 3 over) so the meaning of a remainder is grounded before written methods.
keyRepresentations: Sharing model — dealing counters one-by-one into a fixed number of plates (partitive: answer = per plate)
Grouping model — repeatedly taking a fixed group size until the pile is gone (quotitive: answer = number of groups)
Array / rows×columns — shows ÷ as the inverse of × (56 in 8 rows → 7 per row)
Number line — equal backward hops of 8 from 56 to 0 (grouping) counts the number of jumps
commonMisconceptions: Believing division has only one meaning (sharing), so grouping/quotitive word problems are misread or mis-drawn.
Thinking division is commutative — that 56÷8 and 8÷56 are the same — by analogy with ×.
Sharing unequally or forgetting shares must be equal.
Believing the answer must always be smaller and being confused by remainders or by dividing a smaller by a larger number.
Divorcing ÷ from × and treating it as a standalone symbol rather than the inverse operation.

learn.summary: For ages 8–9: interpret whole-number quotients so that one division expression (e.g. 56 ÷ 8 = 7) models TWO different actions — partitive/sharing ('56 shared among 8 → how many each?') and quotitive/grouping ('56 put into groups of 8 → how many groups?'). Both reach 7, but the story, the drawing, and what the 7 counts differ. Teach both structures explicitly by name, keep division tied to multiplication (8 × ? = 56), follow a concrete→pictorial→abstract progression, and introduce remainders informally through the same actions.

activities.title: Share-and-group the same pile
feedback: If a learner says only the sharing action 'is really dividing', have them act out both with counters — deal-one-each versus make-a-group-then-another — and point out both reach 7 and both are written 56 ÷ 8.
If a learner writes 8 ÷ 56, anchor that the whole amount (56) is the thing being broken up, so it is written first (the dividend); connect to starting with the whole set before sharing.

If a learner reaches 7 both ways but cannot explain the difference, have them label each drawing — 'number of groups' versus 'size of each group' — and narrate the two stories; do not reteach the operation, just make the roles explicit.
When a remainder appears (e.g. 58 ÷ 8 = 7 r2), ask why some counters are left over: can they still give every one of the 8 plates one more counter, or make another full bag of 8?
activities.rationale: Division's dual meaning can be made concrete by performing both actions on the same quantity and comparing. A sharing mode and a grouping mode on identical counters let a learner watch two different processes land on the same quotient, making partitive-versus-quotitive concrete and letting remainders emerge naturally. This aligns with teaching both structures by name and with a concrete-pictorial-abstract progression. A live surface that re-deals or re-groups and relabels the answer can make this tangible, but counters and plates/bags on a table achieve the same comparison.
sourceClaims: 3.OA.2 requires interpreting quotients as both the number in each share (partitive) and the number of shares/groups (quotitive).
Division should be taught through both partitive (sharing) and quotitive (grouping) structures using concrete-pictorial-abstract progression.
learnerActions: Start with one pile of 56 counters.
First, SHARE: deal the counters one at a time, round-robin, into 8 plates until the pile is empty. Count how many landed on each plate (7).
Then, GROUP: from a fresh pile of 56, repeatedly scoop a group of 8 counters into a bag until the pile is empty. Count how many bags you made (7).
Write 56 ÷ 8 = 7 beside BOTH actions, then say aloud what the 7 means in each: '7 on each plate' versus '7 bags'.

Repeat both actions with 58 counters. When sharing, deal only full rounds (one to every plate) and stop when there are too few left to give all 8 plates one more. When grouping, stop when fewer than 8 counters remain. Notice the 2 leftover counters that cannot complete another round of equal shares or another group of 8. These are the remainder (58 ÷ 8 = 7 r2).
activities.intendedInsight: One division expression encodes two different questions. Doing both actions on the same quantity shows that 56 ÷ 8 lands on 7 either way, yet the 7 means 'number in each share' when sharing and 'number of groups' when grouping. Leftovers that cannot complete a share or a group are a remainder.

activities.title: Two panels, same expression
feedback: If a learner thinks the two pictures are different sums, point out both total 56 and both are written 56 ÷ 8 — only what the 7 counts changes.
Reinforce the labels: 'sharing — answer = how many in each share' and 'grouping — answer = how many groups'.
activities.rationale: A clear two-panel contrast with reveal-the-label callouts is a strong anchor for the dual-meaning vocabulary. A fixed diagram cannot let the learner perform the actions and discover the equivalence, so it works best alongside hands-on sharing/grouping rather than instead of it.
sourceClaims: 3.OA.2 requires interpreting quotients as both the number in each share (partitive) and the number of shares/groups (quotitive).
learnerActions: Look at two side-by-side pictures: LEFT shows 8 plates of 7 counters; RIGHT shows 7 bags of 8 counters.
For the left picture, state what the answer counts ('how many on each plate'); for the right, state what it counts ('how many bags').
Write the single expression 56 ÷ 8 = 7 under both and answer: 'Both say 56 ÷ 8 = 7 — so what does the 7 count in each?'
Name each structure: left = sharing/partitive, right = grouping/quotitive.
activities.intendedInsight: The same expression and the same answer attach to two distinct meanings; naming each structure fixes the vocabulary of sharing versus grouping.

activities.title: Arrays and number lines: division as the inverse of multiplication
feedback: If a learner treats 56 ÷ 8 as unrelated to multiplication, point to the array: the same 8 rows of 7 give both 8 × 7 = 56 and 56 ÷ 8 = 7.
If a learner miscounts hops on the number line, check that every hop is exactly 8 and that they count the hops, not the points landed on (56→48→40→32→24→16→8→0 is 7 hops).
activities.rationale: Arrays make the inverse relationship between multiplication and division visible, and equal backward hops on a number line represent the quotitive/grouping meaning as repeated subtraction. These anchor division to multiplication — a load-bearing idea in the original research — rather than teaching it as a standalone procedure.
learnerActions: Arrange the 56 counters as an ARRAY — 8 rows of 7 (or 7 rows of 8) — and write 8 × 7 = 56 alongside 56 ÷ 8 = 7 to see division as the inverse of multiplication.
Read the same array both ways: 8 rows of 7 counters, or 7 columns of 8 counters, each totalling 56.
On a NUMBER LINE, start at 56 and make equal backward hops of 8 until you reach 0; count the hops (7) — this is the number of groups of 8, the grouping/quotitive meaning.
Say how 8 × 7 = 56, 56 ÷ 8 = 7 and 56 ÷ 7 = 8 are all related through the same array.
activities.intendedInsight: An array makes division visible as the inverse of multiplication (8 × 7 = 56 ↔ 56 ÷ 8 = 7), and equal backward hops on a number line model the grouping meaning as repeated subtraction. Both keep division connected to multiplication rather than treated as an isolated symbol.

activities.title: Sort and match the stories
feedback: A tempting wrong match is a story like '6 shared among 24' or '6 ÷ 24' — use it to catch the belief that division is commutative, then return to the whole-gets-broken-up idea.
If a learner only ever picks 'sharing', revisit the hands-on grouping action to establish that making equal groups of a fixed size is also division.
activities.rationale: Sorting and matching are highly checkable and can pinpoint the single-meaning misconception and the commutativity error. This consolidates and reveals understanding rather than building it, so it is best used after learners have performed both actions. It elicits classification and explanation, not independent construction of the actions themselves.
learnerActions: Sort a set of word problems into two bins: 'sharing' and 'grouping'.
For 24 ÷ 6, choose which written story matches it as a GROUPING situation (making groups of 6) and explain your choice.
Explain why a story such as '6 shared among 24' (i.e. 6 ÷ 24) is NOT the same as 24 ÷ 6 — division is not commutative.
For each story you sort, say what each number stands for — the whole, the number of groups or the group size, and the answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Classifying and matching stories surfaces whether a learner holds only the sharing meaning and exposes the commutativity error (treating 24 ÷ 6 and 6 ÷ 24 as the same).

activities.title: The baker's choice
feedback: If the learner cannot state the difference, pair the talk with counters so the two physical processes are visible while they explain.
Prompt: 'In your story, what does the 6 tell you — the number of groups, or how many in each group?'
activities.rationale: Spoken explanation and story-making can prompt a learner to put the structure into words and expose confusion. Discussion is proposed to work best when coupled to concrete sharing/grouping, since talk alone does not have the learner carry out the two physical actions; it is not a substitute for them.
learnerActions: Take the role of helping a baker split 56 rolls.
Decide and say aloud: do you want 8 boxes with the same number in each (sharing), or boxes that each hold 8 (grouping)?
Describe what changes between the two choices and what the answer 7 means in each.
Invent your own grouping story for 24 ÷ 6 and tell it to a partner.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the choice out loud prompts a learner to distinguish sharing from grouping and to say what each number represents, strengthening the language of the two structures.

constraints: Teach both structures deliberately and by name — partitive/sharing ('how many in each?') and quotitive/grouping ('how many groups?') — using the SAME numbers so one expression models two actions.
Keep division tied to multiplication (56 ÷ 8 relates to 8 × ? = 56, and arrays show the inverse relationship) so it is not learned as an isolated procedure.
Follow concrete → pictorial → abstract: physically share/group, then draw/array/number-line, then write the expression, keeping the action visible.
Division is NOT commutative: 56 ÷ 8 and 8 ÷ 56 are different. Address this explicitly, including using a correctly reversed-story distractor (e.g. 6 ÷ 24 as the reversal of 24 ÷ 6).

Sorting, matching, and multiple-choice tasks verify and reveal understanding (including recognition-only responses) but do not by themselves have the learner independently perform the sharing and grouping actions; use them after hands-on work.
A fixed two-panel diagram anchors vocabulary but cannot be manipulated to let the learner discover the equivalence; pair it with hands-on actions.
Introduce remainders informally through the same actions (leftovers that cannot complete a share or a group) before any written method.
Shares must be equal; guard against sharing unequally and against the belief that a quotient must always be smaller or that one cannot divide a smaller number by a larger one.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit: 56 ÷ 8 = 7 is correct both as 8 shares of 7 and as 7 groups of 8; 58 ÷ 8 = 7 remainder 2, consistent with the leftover-counters description; 24 ÷ 6 = 4 (used for classification/story-making). Array check: 8 rows of 7 = 56, giving 8 × 7 = 56, 56 ÷ 8 = 7 and 56 ÷ 7 = 8. Number-line check: 56→48→40→32→24→16→8→0 is 7 hops of 8.

The source's diagnostic treats the 8 as the number of shares/groups in the sharing Story A and as the group size in the grouping Story B; this is preserved consistently in the activities and feedback.

The original row's grouping distractor for 24 ÷ 6 was given as an '8 ÷ 24 story', which does not reverse 24 ÷ 6 and cannot illustrate commutativity; it was an error and has been corrected to the proper reversal 6 ÷ 24. The erroneous original value is recorded here only, not offered to learners.

The array (division as the inverse of multiplication) and number-line (equal backward hops = number of groups) representations from the original key representations were missing from the candidate's activities; they have been restored as a dedicated activity to preserve the tie-to-multiplication idea.

Source claims for CCSS 3.OA.2 and NCETM are marked verified:false in the row; the DfE claim is marked verified:true. No efficacy or comparative-necessity claims are asserted beyond what the standards/guidance state.

The original research asserted the dual meaning 'is only felt' by the interactive mode, that 'no static picture can' build it, and that the concept 'lives in the two physical processes which talk can't render'; these categorical necessity/modality claims have been softened to scoped proposals, since catalog fit ratings do not establish such necessity.

probeDeeper: In Story A, what does the 8 tell you? In Story B, what does the 8 tell you?
Draw 56 ÷ 8 for the sharing story.
Could 56 ÷ 8 ever leave something over? When?
Make up your own grouping story for 24 ÷ 6.
assess.correctAnswer: Yes — both are 56 ÷ 8. In Story A you know the number of groups (8 children) and find the size of each share (7 each); in Story B you know the group size (8 per bag) and find the number of groups (7 bags). Same division, two meanings.

errorPatterns.pattern: only sharing counts as division — thinks division means sharing into a known number of groups, so making groups of 8 (Story B) isn't 'really' dividing
errorPatterns.nextMove: act out both with counters — deal-one-each (sharing) versus make-a-group-then-another (grouping) — showing both reach 7 and both are 56 ÷ 8
errorPatterns.distractor: Only Story A is 56 ÷ 8; Story B is a different sum.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says only Story A is 56 ÷ 8 and treats Story B as a different operation

errorPatterns.pattern: reverses the dividend and divisor — writes 8 ÷ 56 for these stories
errorPatterns.nextMove: anchor that the whole (56) gets broken up, so it is the dividend; connect to the equal-sharing model where you start with the whole set
errorPatterns.revealedBy: records the division the wrong way round

errorPatterns.pattern: solves both to 7 but the quotient's meaning is opaque — can't say the 8 is the number of groups in A and the group size in B
errorPatterns.nextMove: label each drawing (number of groups vs size of group) and narrate the two stories — do not reteach the operation, just make the roles explicit
errorPatterns.revealedBy: correct answers with no account of what each number represents

responseLevels.gap: Recognises only one meaning of division (usually sharing) and treats grouping as a different operation, or reverses the ÷ sentence.
responseLevels.full: Explains both the sharing and grouping meanings of 56 ÷ 8, says what each number represents in each, and matches stories to the expression.
responseLevels.partial: Solves both stories to 7 but cannot articulate that the 8 is the number of groups in one and the group size in the other.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are two stories. Story A: '56 sweets shared equally among 8 children — how many each?' Story B: '56 sweets put into bags of 8 — how many bags?' Can they BOTH be written as 56 ÷ 8? Explain how each one is 56 ÷ 8.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands division holds BOTH the sharing (partitive) and grouping (quotitive) meanings and can say what the 8 and the 7 stand for in each. A child with only one model insists just one story 'is really dividing' (usually the sharing one), or reaches 7 for both but can't explain why the 8 plays a different role in each. The two-story tier forces the dual structure into the open.

pedagogy.summary: At 7-8 modelling covers measurement, money and time, with multi-step problems and a choice of representation (bar model, number line, or equation), and the interpretation demand sharpens: the final answer must be read as the RIGHT quantity — 'is this the total cost or the change?' (CCSS MP4). Multi-step money is the signature context: a child must carry an interim result forward and then interpret the final number correctly. The persistent hazard remains suspension of sense-making (CDE) — computing to a number without asking whether it is reasonable or which quantity the question actually wants. Good teaching has the child choose and justify a representation, keep units throughout, interpret the final answer in context, and sense-check it; line plots from measurement data extend modelling to reading answers off a data display.
bestPractices: Have the child choose AND justify a representation for the problem (bar model / number line / equation), matching tool to structure (MP4 identify and map quantities)
For multi-step money, name each interim result ('that's the total cost') before the next step, and interpret the final answer as the quantity asked (change vs total)
Keep units attached throughout and sense-check the final answer against the situation (CDE)
Use line plots so children read answers off a data display back into the real-world question
Reason about the situation before computing; avoid reducing the problem to keywords (CDE)
keyRepresentations: Bar model for multi-step and comparison money/measurement problems
Number line for time and measurement jumps
Equation with units for total cost / change
Line plot of measurement data
commonMisconceptions: Reports the wrong quantity — gives the total cost when the question asks for the change
Stops after the first step of a multi-step problem
Computes without sense-checking whether the answer is reasonable in context
Drops or muddles units (mixing pounds and pence, or minutes and hours)

learn.summary: For ages 7-8, model real-world measurement, money, and time problems by choosing and justifying a representation (bar model, number line, or equation), carrying multi-step calculations with units attached, and crucially interpreting the final number as the RIGHT quantity (total cost vs change). The signature hazard is suspension of sense-making: computing to a number without naming which quantity the question asked for or checking its reasonableness. Line plots extend modelling to reading answers off a data display.

activities.title: Multi-step money modeller: name the quantity, then check it
feedback: When the child labels 85p as 'change', separate the quantities on the bar — the £1 whole, the 85p cost part, the change part — and label each, then ask which quantity the question wants
If the child stops at 85p, prompt: 'you found the cost — what does the question still want?'
If the child accepts 85p as change without checking, ask: 'could your change be 85p if you spent 85p from a pound?' to build the sense-check habit
Confirm when the child names 85p as cost, computes 15p change, attaches the unit, and checks that 85p + 15p makes the £1 paid
activities.rationale: Live build-and-check lets the child choose a representation, track interim results with units, and label the final number as the correct quantity with a reasonableness gate, directly targeting the interim-vs-final confusion. A linked bar panel that tracks the running parts with units and a prompt asking 'what is this number so far?' makes the interim-vs-final distinction concrete.
sourceClaims: MP4: identify important quantities and map their relationships with diagrams/tables/equations; interpret results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether they make sense.

Suspension of sense-making leads students to produce a number without checking realism; problem-specific supports that make students reason about the situation help, and reasoning about relationships should precede computing.
Bar models expose multi-step and comparison structure, helping children track which quantity is which through a problem.
learnerActions: Set up a shopping problem: two items at 65p and 20p, paying with £1
Choose a representation and say why it fits (e.g. a bar model with a £1 whole, an 85p part for the shopping, and a mystery part)
Pause at the interim number and label it: 'that 85p — what is it?' Answer: the total cost (65p + 20p = 85p)
Carry on to the second step: change £1 into 100p, then work out 100p − 85p = 15p as the change
Interpret the final number with its unit ('15p change') and sense-check it: the cost and the change together should make the £1 paid (85p + 15p = 100p = £1)
Transfer: re-run the model paying with £2 instead and describe what changes
activities.intendedInsight: In a multi-step problem each number along the way means something specific; the answer is only right when you name the quantity the question actually asked for and check it is reasonable in context.

activities.title: Shopkeeper who tries it on (spoken correction)
feedback: If the child accepts the shopkeeper's framing, ask them to point to where the cost ends and the change begins
Prompt the child to restate the final quantity with its unit and say how they know it is reasonable
This dialogue is never scored — treat it as thinking-out-loud practice
activities.rationale: Interpreting which quantity the answer is and reasoning about the situation is dialogic; a partner offering the total cost as if it were the change invites the child to reason about the relationships, sort out the quantities, and verbalise the distinction.
sourceClaims: Suspension of sense-making leads students to produce a number without checking realism; problem-specific supports that make students reason about the situation help, and reasoning about relationships should precede computing.
learnerActions: Play out a shop exchange where a shopkeeper rings up two items and states the subtotal as if it were the change
Catch and correct the error out loud, explaining which quantity the stated number actually is
Keep units straight (pounds and pence) while justifying the fix
Explain aloud how a bar or equation would separate the cost from the change
activities.intendedInsight: Distinguishing which quantity the answer names is a reasoning skill you can articulate and defend, not just compute.

activities.title: Worked multi-step walkthrough (scaffold)
feedback: After each revealed meaning, ask the child to predict what the next step computes and why
Prompt the child to restate which quantity is the final answer the question wanted
activities.rationale: A static worked example with revealable interim/final interpretations illustrates the process and the interim-vs-final distinction. As a scaffold it does not elicit the child's own representation choice or an independent sense-check, so pair it with a build-and-check task.
sourceClaims: MP4: identify important quantities and map their relationships with diagrams/tables/equations; interpret results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether they make sense.
learnerActions: Step through a worked multi-step money or measurement problem
Reveal what each step's number means (e.g. tap a step to show 'this is the total cost', 'this is the change')
Describe in your own words what the interim number means before seeing the next step
activities.intendedInsight: Each number in a worked solution carries a meaning; following the labels shows how an interim quantity differs from the final answer.

activities.title: Line plot from measurement data
feedback: If the child reads a value but doesn't tie it to the question, ask 'what does this number tell you about the objects you measured?'
Prompt a units and reasonableness check on the answer read from the plot
activities.rationale: Line plots extend modelling to reading answers off a data display and interpreting them in context, matching the measurement-data strand of the objective.
sourceClaims: MP4: identify important quantities and map their relationships with diagrams/tables/equations; interpret results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether they make sense.
learnerActions: Collect or receive measurement data (e.g. lengths of objects)
Create a line plot displaying the data
Use the plot to answer a real-world question, reading the answer off the display back into the situation
State what quantity your answer represents and whether it is reasonable
activities.intendedInsight: A data display is a representation you read answers from; the answer must be interpreted back into the real-world question with its units.

constraints: Keep units attached throughout every calculation (don't mix pounds and pence, or minutes and hours) and sense-check the final answer against the situation
Have the child reason about the situation before computing; avoid reducing the problem to keywords

The worked-example walkthrough is a scaffold: it illustrates the process but does not elicit the child's own representation choice or an independent sense-check, so it should not replace build-and-check practice
The dialogue/shopkeeper activity should never be scored
A scored 'which is the change?' item can serve at most as a warm-up; a recognition-only response does not elicit the child's own representation choice, interim interpretation, or reasonableness check

This objective involves money/measurement/time, which is not spatial-3D, so a 3D build is not specifically matched to it; this is a fit note for this objective, not a claim that 3D media teach nothing in general
Arithmetic check: 65p + 20p = 85p (the interim total, which is the COST), and since £1 = 100p, 100p − 85p = 15p is the CHANGE; keep these two quantities distinct in every representation

probeDeeper: 'What does the 85 tell you — is it the cost or the change? How do you know?'
'You paid £1. What do you still need to work out, and how?'
'Is 15p a sensible change for spending 85p from a pound? Check it.'
'If you'd paid with £2 instead, what would change in your model?'
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child recognising 85p is the TOTAL COST (an interim quantity), computing the change as 100 − 85 = 15p, interpreting it as '15p change', and sense-checking that the change is less than the £1 paid.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reports the wrong quantity: gives the total cost (85p) as if it were the change — confuses which quantity the question asks for.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the quantities on a bar (the £1 whole; the 85p cost part; the change part) and label each; reteach interpreting which quantity the answer names.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says the change is 85p; treats the subtotal as the final answer.

errorPatterns.pattern: Stops after the first step: computes the total cost and doesn't carry on to the change.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the step structure: 'you found the cost — what does the question still want?'; the child can do both steps but didn't monitor the goal.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reaches 85 and stops, as if the problem is done; no second operation.

errorPatterns.pattern: Suspension of sense-making: doesn't check the final answer against the situation (change ought to be less than the £1 paid, and 85p change from spending 85p is suspicious).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Prompt 'could your change be 85p if you spent 85p from a pound?'; build the habit of sense-checking against the context (CDE).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Accepts 85p change without noticing it equals the spend and leaves nothing sensible; no reasonableness check.

responseLevels.gap: Gives 85 as the change; stops after one step and doesn't sense-check.
responseLevels.full: Names 85p as the total cost, computes 100 − 85 = 15p as the change, interprets it with its unit, and sense-checks it against the £1 paid — choosing/justifying a representation and transferring the interim-vs-final distinction to a new multi-step problem.
responseLevels.partial: Recognises 85 is the cost OR computes 15 as the change, but not both cleanly — e.g. finds 15 without naming 85 as the cost, or names the cost but doesn't finish/sense-check.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In a shop you buy two things: one costs 65p and one costs 20p. You pay with a £1 coin. A friend works it out and says 'the answer is 85'. Is 85 the change? Talk me through the problem — what does 85 mean, what is the change, and how do you know your change makes sense?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who models the multi-step situation and interprets quantities sees that 85 is the cost, not the change, and finishes the second step; a child who computes-and-stops offers 85 as the answer. The prompt separates them because 85 is a real, correct interim number — accepting it as the change reveals stopping early and confusing quantities, while rejecting it reveals full modelling. Hard to get right without carrying the situation through both steps.
