pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 8–9y; multiply a one-digit number by a multiple of 10 (10–90) using place value and properties (7×30 = 7×3 tens = 21 tens = 210).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y3–Y4 use place value and known facts to multiply mentally; underpins Y4 short multiplication and estimation.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.NBT.3 — 'multiply one-digit whole numbers by multiples of 10 in the range 10–90 (e.g. 9×80, 5×60) using strategies based on place value and properties of operations.'
• Operational details — the reasoning, not the trick, is the objective: 7×30 = 7×(3×10) = (7×3)×10 = 21×10 = 210 (associativity + place value). The '×10 shifts digits one place left' understanding must replace the dangerous 'just add a zero' rule (which breaks for decimals later). Use place-value counters/columns and the known fact 7×3=21 scaled by ten. This is the engine of estimation (234×5 ≈ 200×5) and a stepping-stone to × multiples of 100/1000 and to long multiplication.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8): 3×40 via 3×4 tens with counters. Tier B (age 8–9): any 1-digit × multiple of 10 mentally, explaining via the known fact and place value. Tier C (age 9): explain why the product gains a zero in terms of ten-times-larger, and use the skill to estimate a larger product.
bestPractices: Reason from the known fact scaled by ten: 7×30 = (7×3) tens = 21 tens = 210, using associativity and place value explicitly.
Teach 'ten times larger → digits shift one place left', NOT 'add a zero', so the idea survives the move to decimals.
Use place-value counters and columns so 21 tens visibly becomes 210 (regrouping ten tens into a hundred).
Connect immediately to estimation — rounding a factor to a multiple of ten to bound a larger product.
Extend the same reasoning to multiples of 100/1000 once secure, keeping the place-value story constant.
keyRepresentations: Place-value counters / columns — 21 tens regrouped to 210
Known-fact-×-ten chain (7×3=21 → 7×30=210)
Gattegno/place-value chart — the leftward digit shift for ×10
Number line in tens — skip counting by 30
commonMisconceptions: Over-relying on 'add a zero' as a rule without understanding, which later misfires with decimals (0.7×30).
Multiplying the wrong part (7×30 as 21 rather than 210) — losing the place-value scaling.
Adding an extra or too few zeros through miscounting places.
Not connecting 7×30 to the known fact 7×3, so it's computed from scratch.
Confusing multiplying by a multiple of ten with adding tens.

learn.summary: For ages 8–9: multiply a one-digit number by a multiple of 10 (10–90) by reasoning from a known fact scaled by ten — 7×30 = 7×(3×10) = (7×3)×10 = 21 tens = 210 — using place value and the associative property. The objective is the reasoning, not the 'add a zero' trick: learners should understand multiplying by 10 as making a number ten times larger so its digits shift one place left, which is why 210 ends in a zero (the ones place empties). This understanding survives the later move to decimals, where 'add a zero' fails (0.7×10 = 7, not 0.70), and powers estimation (234×5 ≈ 200×5) and multiplication by multiples of 100/1000.

activities.title: Scaling a known fact by ten with place-value counters
feedback: If a learner writes 7×30 = 21, point back to the rods: 'You took three tens seven times, not three ones. Count the tens — 21 tens is 210.'
If a learner gives 210 but only explains 'you add a zero', ask them to show it with the rods: 'Where did that zero come from? Watch the ones column empty when everything grows ten times bigger.'
If a learner miscounts zeros (e.g. 2100), have them regroup the tens carefully onto the place-value chart and reread each column.
Affirm reasoning that names the known fact: 'Yes — knowing 7×3 = 21 let you get 7×30 without starting over.'
activities.rationale: Place-value counters and regrouping make '21 tens = 210' a visible exchange rather than a memorised rule, and tie the standard's required place-value/property strategy directly to the known single-digit fact.
sourceClaims: 3.NBT.3 requires multiplying one-digit numbers by multiples of 10 (10–90) using place-value and property strategies.
Y3–Y4 pupils use place value and known facts to multiply mentally, underpinning short multiplication and estimation.
learnerActions: Build the known fact 7×3 as an array of 21 single counters (or draw them).
Replace each single counter with a rod of ten, stating aloud 'now there are 21 tens'.
Regroup the 21 tens: exchange ten tens for one hundred, repeat, ending with 2 hundreds and 1 ten.
Record the result on a place-value chart (hundreds | tens | ones) and read it as 210.
Say the full reasoning chain: '7×3 = 21, so 7×30 = 21 tens = 210, because 30 is 3 tens.'
Repeat for 5×60 (5×6 = 30, so 5×60 = 30 tens = 300) and 3×40 (3×4 = 12, so 3×40 = 12 tens = 120), each time naming the known single-digit fact first.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying by a multiple of 10 is multiplying by the single-digit fact and then by ten; the extra zero in the product is the result of every digit shifting one place left as the amount becomes ten times larger, not a zero 'stuck on the end'.

activities.title: Why 'add a zero' is not the real rule
feedback: If a learner says 0.7×10 = 0.70, show the shift on the chart: 'Sliding left makes 7, not 0.70. The zero rule breaks here — but the shift still works.'
If a learner adds too many or too few zeros for the 7×300 extension, count the place shifts together: '×100 means shifting two columns left.'
Encourage precise language: 'ten times larger' and 'shifts one place left' rather than 'add a zero'.
activities.rationale: Deliberately contrasting the whole-number case with a decimal case targets the misconception that 'add a zero' is the underlying rule, replacing it with the place-value shift that generalises.
sourceClaims: Teach multiplying by ten as a place-value shift (ten times larger) rather than 'adding a zero', which fails for decimals.
learnerActions: On a place-value chart, place 7 in the ones column, then slide it one column left to make 70; describe what happened to the digit.
Do the same with 21: slide it one column left so the ones place becomes empty and a 0 fills it, giving 210.
Now try 0.7×10 on the same chart: slide 0.7 one column left to get 7 — notice no zero was added.
State in your own words why '×10 shifts digits one place left' is safer than 'add a zero'.
(Optional extension, once the tens pattern feels secure) Predict and check 7×300 using the same idea: 7×3 = 21, shifted two places = 2100.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying by ten always shifts digits one place to the left; for whole numbers this shows up as a trailing zero, but the shift — not the zero itself — is the real rule, which is why it still works for decimals.

activities.title: Using tens facts to estimate
feedback: If a learner rounds the wrong way or forgets to scale, revisit the known-fact chain: '6×4 = 24, so 6×40 = 240.'
If a learner treats the estimate as exact, prompt: 'Is 6×43 more or less than 6×40? By about how much?'
Praise clear connections between the rounded factor and the place-value reasoning.
activities.rationale: Multiplying by multiples of ten is a useful tool for estimation (the standard itself only names place-value and property-based strategies for products in the range 10–90); applying it keeps the place-value story in a purposeful context.
sourceClaims: Y3–Y4 pupils use place value and known facts to multiply mentally, underpinning short multiplication and estimation.
learnerActions: Estimate 6×43 by rounding 43 to 40 and computing 6×40 = 240 (6×4 = 24, so 6×40 = 24 tens = 240), explaining the reasoning.

(Optional extension, once the tens case is secure) Estimate 234×5 by rounding 234 to 200 and computing 200×5 = 1000 (2×5 = 10, so 200×5 = 10 hundreds = 1000), using the same known-fact-then-scale reasoning.
Compare each estimate to the exact answer (6×43 = 258; 234×5 = 1170) and say whether the estimate is high or low and roughly by how much.
Make up one estimation of your own using a multiple of ten and justify it.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying by a multiple of ten (and, by the same reasoning, a multiple of a hundred) lets you quickly bound or approximate a larger product, which checks whether an exact answer is reasonable.

activities.title: Spot and explain the error
feedback: For '7×30 = 21': 'The 30 is three tens, so the answer must be 21 tens = 210 — ten times bigger than 21.'
For '8×40 = 32': 'That's just 8×4. Scale by ten: 32 tens = 320.'
Confirm the correct ones (5×60 = 300 and 9×80 = 720) and ask the learner to articulate the reasoning, not just the verdict.
activities.rationale: Identifying and repairing errors consolidates the reasoning and surfaces whether a learner can justify answers rather than apply a rote appendage; this is a consolidation/check activity that tests fluency rather than a substitute for building the scaling intuition with counters.
learnerActions: Decide whether each worked example is correct: 7×30 = 21; 5×60 = 300; 8×40 = 32; 9×80 = 720.
For any that are wrong, say exactly what went wrong (e.g. multiplied the tens as ones, or dropped/added a zero).
Rewrite each incorrect one with the full reasoning chain to make it correct.
Explain in words why 5×60 = 300 ends in a zero.
activities.intendedInsight: Common slips — multiplying the tens digit as ones, or miscounting zeros — can be caught by checking against the known-fact-times-ten chain.

constraints: The learning objective is the reasoning (known fact × ten via associativity and place value), not a memorised 'add a zero' step; any activity must require the learner to explain where the zero comes from.
Teach 'ten times larger → digits shift one place left' explicitly, because 'add a zero' misfires for decimals (0.7×10 = 7).
Secure the underlying single-digit fact (e.g. 7×3) first; if it is shaky, the whole derivation is unreliable.

Recognition/multiple-choice and fill-in-the-blank checks test fluency but do not by themselves build the scaling intuition; use them for consolidation alongside construction with counters and spoken reasoning.
Physical base-ten equipment and a drawn or on-screen place-value chart are both suitable; manipulatives make the regrouping of ten tens into a hundred concrete.
Extend the identical place-value story to multiples of 100/1000 only once the tens case is secure; the 7×300 step is presented as an optional extension for this reason.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 7×3=21 so 7×30=210; 5×6=30 so 5×60=300; 3×4=12 so 3×40=120; 6×4=24 so 6×40=240; 8×4=32 so 8×40=320; 9×8=72 so 9×80=720; 7×3=21 so 7×300=2100; 6×43=258; 234×5=1170; 2×5=10 so 200×5=1000 — all check out. The 'spot the error' items 7×30=21 and 8×40=32 are intentionally incorrect for learners to catch, with corrected values (210, 320) supplied in feedback.
Decimal check: 0.7×10=7 (not 0.70); the shift-left framing is correct and the 'add a zero' rule correctly fails here.
Source note: the CCSS 3.NBT.3 and NCETM claims are marked unverified (verified:false) in the original row; retained as cited without upgrading their evidence status.

Original source row legacy vocabulary describing specific interactive formats (e.g. a 'scaler' widget, tap-to-reveal, lift-the-flap) has been generalised into medium-independent learner actions while preserving the live-regrouping mechanism as an optional illustration.

The decimal example (0.7×10), the 200×5 estimation step and the 7×300 extension may exceed the typical age-band comfort zone; all are retained from the original design but flagged as needing teacher judgement/support.

probeDeeper: What does 7 × 30 have to do with 7 × 3?
Why does the answer end in a zero — where does that zero come from?
How could 6 × 40 help you estimate 6 × 43?
If you know 7 × 3 = 21, what is 7 × 300?
assess.correctAnswer: 210 and 240. The teacher watches for the child reasoning '7 × 3 tens = 21 tens = 210' — using the single-digit fact and scaling by ten — rather than a disconnected zero-adding rule.

errorPatterns.pattern: multiplies the tens digit as ones — 7×30 treated as 7×3 = 21, forgetting the ten (answer 21)
errorPatterns.nextMove: reason 7 × 3 TENS = 21 tens = 210; use base-ten equipment to show three tens taken seven times.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer is ten times too small; child computes 7×3 and stops

errorPatterns.pattern: 'adds a zero' as a rote rule with no meaning — works here but cannot say why, and will misapply it to decimals later
errorPatterns.nextMove: tie the zero to 'ten times bigger': multiplying by 30 is multiplying by 3 then by 10, and ×10 shifts digits one place, showing up as a zero for whole numbers.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child gets 210 but explains only 'you add a zero'; cannot connect to 7×3

errorPatterns.pattern: not fluent in the underlying single-digit fact, so the whole derivation is shaky
errorPatterns.nextMove: shore up the single-digit fact before layering the tens reasoning.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child hesitates or errs on 7×3 itself

responseLevels.gap: multiplies the tens digit as ones (answer ten times too small), or has no reasoning at all.
responseLevels.full: reasons via the known fact scaled by ten ('7 × 3 tens = 21 tens'), explains the zero as the result of ×10, and uses the skill to estimate larger products.
responseLevels.partial: gets the right answer via 'add a zero' but cannot connect it to the single-digit fact or explain why the zero appears.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to work out 7 × 30 and 6 × 40 in their head, saying how they did it. Watch whether they use the known fact (7×3) and reason about tens, or whether they just 'add a zero' without understanding — then probe by asking what 7 × 30 has to do with 7 × 3.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Multiplying by a multiple of ten is the first place the 'add a zero' shortcut appears; watching HOW the child reasons (does the zero come from 'ten times', or is it a rote appendage?) reveals whether place-value understanding underpins the shortcut — essential because the same rule misfires later on decimals.

pedagogy.summary: Volume is introduced as an attribute of 3D solids — the amount of space a solid takes up — measured by packing it with unit cubes. A unit cube (side 1 unit) has 'one cubic unit' of volume; a solid packed with n unit cubes without gaps or overlaps has volume n cubic units. The conceptual work is distinguishing volume (space filled, counted in cubes) from area and surface area (surface covered, counted in squares), and grasping that the count includes HIDDEN interior cubes, not just the visible faces. Research by Battista & Clements shows the real difficulty is spatial structuring — organising the cubes into iterable units (rows, columns, layers) — rather than mere formula recall, and that it is NOT simply confusion between volume and surface area.
bestPractices: Build volume from packing real unit cubes into open boxes, counting with no gaps or overlaps, before any formula.
Explicitly contrast volume (cubes filling space, cubic units) with area/surface area (squares covering a surface, square units).
Draw attention to hidden interior cubes: predict how many cubes fill a solid, then unpack to check, so children account for what they cannot see.
Encourage organising the count into rows/columns/layers rather than counting one cube at a time (spatial structuring).
Use 'cubic unit' language and correct notation from the outset.
keyRepresentations: Unit cube (1×1×1)
Open box packed with unit cubes
Layer / row / column structuring of a solid
Predict-then-unpack activity
Isometric 3D cube diagram (with hidden cubes)
commonMisconceptions: Confuses volume with area or surface area (counts faces or squares rather than the space filled).
Counts only the visible/outside cubes and misses hidden interior cubes (Battista & Clements Strategy C).
Double-counts cubes along shared edges and triple-counts corners when reading a 3D drawing.

learn.summary: Volume is the amount of space a 3D solid takes up, measured by packing it with unit cubes (side 1 unit = one cubic unit of volume); a solid packed with n unit cubes without gaps or overlaps has volume n cubic units. The core difficulty is spatial structuring — organising cubes into rows, columns and layers and accounting for HIDDEN interior cubes you cannot see from any face — not merely recalling a formula or confusing volume with surface area. Learners should distinguish volume (cubes filling space, cubic units) from area/surface area (squares covering a surface, square units).

activities.title: Predict, then unpack: how many cubes fill the block?
feedback: If a learner gives about 21, they have counted the cubes on the three shown faces (front, top and side), typically double-counting shared edges, while missing the back and interior cubes that also fill space — the three faces in fact show 19 distinct cubes. Peel the layers to reveal the hidden cubes and recount by layer.
If a learner gives 26, ask: 'Is there a cube that no face touches?' Unpack to expose the single centre cube, then rebuild layer by layer so the buried cube is included.
Correct total: 27 cubic units — a 3×3 layer (9 cubes) repeated 3 times, including the back cubes and the one completely inside.
Reinforce layer structuring: once one layer is counted, the rest follow by iterating, which guards against double-counting edges and triple-counting corners when reading a 3D drawing.
activities.rationale: Battista & Clements (as summarised by Olkun & Knaupp) locate the difficulty in spatial structuring — students conceptualise the cubes in terms of faces, account only for visible/outside cubes (Strategy C), double-count edges and triple-count corners, and fail to count invisible interior cubes; the most viable strategy is organising the array into iterable layers. Predict-then-unpack with real cubes confronts a visible-only guess with the physically revealed total.
sourceClaims: Battista & Clements found the difficulty is spatial structuring, not confusion between volume and surface area: students conceptualise the set of cubes in terms of faces and account only for visible/outside cubes (Strategy C), double-count cubes along edges and triple-count corners, and fail to count invisible interior cubes; the most viable strategy is organising the array into iterable layers.

5.MD.C.3: 'Recognize volume as an attribute of solid figures and understand concepts of volume measurement.' 3.a: 'A cube with side length 1 unit, called a unit cube, is said to have one cubic unit of volume, and can be used to measure volume.' 3.b: 'A solid figure which can be packed without gaps or overlaps using n unit cubes is said to have a volume of n cubic units.'
learnerActions: Look at a solid built from unit cubes — e.g. a 3×3×3 block shown so only three faces are visible — and PREDICT how many unit cubes make it up, stating your reasoning before building or unpacking.
Build the solid from real unit cubes (or take an existing one apart), peeling off one layer at a time to expose the middle.
Count by structuring: find how many cubes are in one layer (a 3×3 layer = 9), then how many layers (3), reaching 3 layers of 9 = 27.
Identify any cube touched by no outside face — the one hidden dead-centre — and say where it is and how many such hidden cubes there are.
Compare your first prediction with the unpacked total, and explain what you missed if they differ.
activities.intendedInsight: Volume counts EVERY cube that fills the solid, including cubes hidden at the back and buried in the interior — not just the cubes whose faces you can see. Organising the count into iterable layers lets you neither miss nor double-count cubes.

activities.title: Explore occlusion with a rotatable, sliceable solid
feedback: When the first guess counts only visible faces, reveal the hidden cubes by rotation and layer-peeling so the gap between guess and total is visible.
When a learner counts outside squares (e.g. 9 on each of 6 faces = 54), overlay the squares and then pack with cubes to show that area covers the surface while volume fills the inside.
Use 'cubic unit' language and correct notation (e.g. cm³) consistently.
activities.rationale: The crux difficulty is spatial — cubes are hidden behind others — so rotating, slicing and toggling transparency directly surface the occluded interior cubes a single fixed view does not show. Interactive recolouring/transparency and a predict-then-reveal counter make the mechanism concrete; these are optional illustrative supports, not required apparatus, and their effectiveness relative to physical cubes is untested.
sourceClaims: Battista & Clements found the difficulty is spatial structuring, not confusion between volume and surface area: students conceptualise the set of cubes in terms of faces and account only for visible/outside cubes (Strategy C), double-count cubes along edges and triple-count corners, and fail to count invisible interior cubes; the most viable strategy is organising the array into iterable layers.
learnerActions: Rotate a solid built from unit cubes to see it from every side, noticing that cubes hidden behind others from one angle become visible from another.
Peel the solid into layers and toggle transparency on the outer shell to reveal and count the interior cubes that no face shows.
Use a predict-then-reveal counter: log your first visible-only guess, then reveal the true total and compare.
Toggle an overlay of the outside squares to contrast the surface (counted in squares = area) with the cubes that fill the solid (counted in cubes = volume).
activities.intendedInsight: Rotating and slicing a 3D solid makes occlusion concrete: the cubes you could not see are really there and must be counted. Volume (filling, cubes) and surface area (covering, squares) measure different things.

activities.title: Build and fill with an isometric builder
feedback: If the learner counts one cube at a time, prompt them to find one layer first and then iterate it.
Note that a flat isometric drawing can still hide back and interior cubes; cross-check with a built or rotatable model when the hidden count is in doubt.
activities.rationale: An isometric builder with a live count supports layer structuring, the strategy Battista & Clements identify as most viable. It is offered as an alternative with a different affordance; because it lacks true rotation, the hidden-cube insight is weaker and benefits from a 3D or built cross-check.
sourceClaims: Battista & Clements found the difficulty is spatial structuring, not confusion between volume and surface area: students conceptualise the set of cubes in terms of faces and account only for visible/outside cubes (Strategy C), double-count cubes along edges and triple-count corners, and fail to count invisible interior cubes; the most viable strategy is organising the array into iterable layers.
learnerActions: Build or fill an isometric solid by placing unit cubes, watching a live count update as you add each cube.
Use a layer tool to group the cubes into rows, columns and layers, then read off how many layers of how many cubes.

State the total as a structured product (layers × cubes-per-layer) when every layer is identical, as in a rectangular box; if layers differ, add the layer counts. Either way, use layers rather than a one-by-one tally.
activities.intendedInsight: Even in a flat isometric view, structuring the solid into layers and iterating the layer count is the reliable way to find volume and avoid miscounting.

activities.title: Count, explain and diagnose the reasoning
feedback: 27 cubic units — three layers of 9 (a 3×3 layer repeated 3 times), including the back cubes and the one completely inside; volume is the space filled (cubes), not the surface area (the squares on the outside).

About 21 means the three shown faces were counted — with shared edges double-counted — while the back and interior cubes were missed (a non-double-counted visible count is 19); reveal the hidden cubes by layer.
26 means the single buried centre cube was missed — ask which cube is touched by no face.
54 means outside squares (9 per face × 6 faces) were counted — that is a surface measure, not the cubes filling the solid.
activities.rationale: Four distinct answers (about 21, 26, 54, 27) with their stated reasons discriminate the underlying conception, letting teaching target the specific error. Asking for the reason before building reveals whether the learner pictures the hidden interior.
sourceClaims: Battista & Clements found the difficulty is spatial structuring, not confusion between volume and surface area: students conceptualise the set of cubes in terms of faces and account only for visible/outside cubes (Strategy C), double-count cubes along edges and triple-count corners, and fail to count invisible interior cubes; the most viable strategy is organising the array into iterable layers.
learnerActions: Given an isometric drawing of a 3×3×3 cube (only three faces visible) and a pile of real unit cubes, predict the total and explain WHY before building.

Answer probe questions: Is there a cube you cannot see from any side — how many and where? If I asked for the AREA of the outside instead, would you count the same things — what is different? How can you organise your count into layers so you neither miss nor double-count a cube?
Diagnose a peer: 'A friend counted 54 by counting squares on the faces — what did they measure instead of volume?'
activities.intendedInsight: A correct volume answer pairs the total (27 cubic units) with a reason that accounts for hidden/interior cubes and distinguishes volume from surface area — the reasoning, not just the number, shows the conception.

constraints: Build volume from packing real unit cubes into open boxes, counting with no gaps or overlaps, before introducing any formula.
Explicitly contrast volume (cubes filling space, cubic units) with area/surface area (squares covering a surface, square units).
Use 'cubic unit' language and correct notation (e.g. cm³, m³) from the outset.

A fixed/static isometric picture can introduce and assess the idea but cannot be manipulated to reveal occluded cubes; use a built model, rotatable solid, or predict-then-unpack to make the hidden interior accountable when the hidden count is the learning target.

Count-the-cubes recognition items (e.g. multiple choice or slider) can assess the skill but do not by themselves elicit the learner's structuring strategy or independent account of hidden cubes; pair with explain-your-reasoning or build tasks.
Recognition-only responses do not require the learner to construct or justify the layer structure; include construction and explanation for the conceptual objective.

Interactive transparency, layer-peeling and predict-then-reveal counters are optional illustrative supports, not mandatory apparatus; real cubes that can be built and unpacked can serve the same roles, while a clear isometric drawing can introduce or assess the idea but cannot by itself reveal hidden cubes.
Keep the ~21 figure only as a learner misconception (edge double-counting); the distinct visible count for a 3×3×3's three shown faces is 19, and this must never be offered as a correct answer.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Independent arithmetic check of the 3×3×3: the three shown faces contain 19 distinct cubes (27 total minus an 8-cube hidden corner block), not 21; the source's 'about 21' reflects a typical learner over-count that double-counts shared edge cubes, consistent with the Strategy C error, so it is retained only as a learner misconception answer, never as a correct count. Buried interior count is exactly 1 (centre cube), surface-square count is 54 (9 × 6), surface-cube count is 26, and total volume is 27 = 3 × 9 — all verified.

The source framing that a flat picture 'cannot provide' the needed representation and that a quiz 'only assesses' has been softened to narrowly scoped affordances/limits, since catalog ratings do not establish comparative necessity or efficacy.
Assessment-method/quiz-step vocabulary ('two-tier') has been removed from learner-facing titles.

Cited standards (5.MD.C.3; DfE Year 6) support the volume concept and unit-cube definition; the Olkun & Knaupp claim summarises Battista & Clements on spatial structuring. These support the teaching principles but do not demonstrate that any specific activity here was tested.

Then build and unpack it: 27, as three layers of 9, including the hidden centre cube. A prediction that counts only visible cubes (or surface squares) is contradicted by the build; the reason stated first reveals whether they picture the hidden interior.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts only the visible outside cubes on the faces shown, missing hidden cubes (and often double-counting edges).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Structure the solid into layers and predict-then-unpack real cubes so the hidden cubes are physically revealed; count one layer, then iterate.
errorPatterns.distractor: About 21 cubes (the ones I can see on the three faces)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives about 21, adding up the cubes showing on the front, top and side.

errorPatterns.pattern: Misses the fully interior cube(s) — counts all surface cubes but forgets the buried one.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask whether any cube is touched by no face; unpack to expose the centre cube, then rebuild by layers so the interior is accounted for.
errorPatterns.distractor: 26 cubes (I missed the one hidden right in the middle)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives 26, having counted every visible and back cube but not the one hidden in the middle.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses volume with surface area — counts the squares on the outside faces.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast covering (squares on the surface = area) with filling (cubes inside = volume); pack the solid with cubes to show volume counts the inside.
errorPatterns.distractor: 54 (the squares on the outside — 9 on each of the 6 faces)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives 54, counting 9 squares on each of the 6 faces.

responseLevels.gap: Counts only visible cubes, or counts face-squares (surface), with no sense of hidden cubes or that volume is the space filled.
responseLevels.full: Structures the solid into layers (three layers of 9 = 27), explicitly accounts for hidden and interior cubes, and distinguishes volume (cubes filling space, cubic units) from surface area (squares on the outside).
responseLevels.partial: Knows volume is about the cubes filling the solid and may reach 27 by unsystematic counting, but cannot reliably account for hidden cubes or cleanly separate it from surface area; lists cubes without structuring into layers.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show an isometric drawing of a cube built from unit cubes, 3 cubes along each edge (a 3×3×3), so only three faces are visible. Ask: 'How many unit cubes make up this solid, and how do you know you have counted the ones you cannot see?' Then ask: 'Is the volume the same as the area of its outside surface — why or why not?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who conceives volume as space-filling reaches 27 and can point to the hidden cubes; a child stuck on faces gives about 21, one confusing volume with surface gives 54, and one who misses only the buried cube gives 26 — four distinct answers whose stated reasons expose the underlying conception.

pedagogy.summary: At 9-10 the choices sharpen: mental (25×40) vs long multiplication (347×26); a protractor to VERIFY an estimated angle rather than trusting the eye; and choosing between a full common-denominator method and a quicker BENCHMARK comparison (against 1/2) for ordering fractions, with a reason. The strategic advance is recognising when a shortcut beats the general algorithm — and, crucially, when it does NOT (two fractions the same side of 1/2 and close together defeat the benchmark). Estimation and measuring tools work together: estimate first, then measure to check.
bestPractices: Read the numbers to route (25×40 mentally as 25×4×10; 347×26 by long multiplication)

Teach benchmark comparison (is it below, at, or above 1/2?) as an efficient alternative to common denominators, and discuss which fractions each method suits (EEF: efficiency, comparing representations)
Use the protractor to VERIFY an estimate, not replace it — estimate the angle, then measure to check (CCSS: detect errors)
Prize the justification of the choice as much as the answer, since competing methods reach the same order
Name the benchmark's limitation: when fractions sit the same side of 1/2 and close together it cannot separate them, so a common denominator earns its keep

learn.summary: For ages 9-10, build the strategic judgement of choosing an efficient method and knowing when a shortcut beats the general algorithm — and when it fails. Learners read the numbers to route a multiplication (25×40 mentally as 25×4×10 vs 347×26 by long multiplication), estimate an angle then measure with a protractor to verify, and order fractions by benchmarking against 1/2 versus finding a common denominator. The key insight: a 1/2 benchmark is fast and sufficient when fractions fall on different sides of 1/2 (e.g. 3/8 below, 5/8 above), but cannot separate two fractions on the same side of 1/2 (e.g. the close pair 5/8 vs 4/7), where another method such as equivalent fractions or a common denominator is needed. Estimation and tools work together: estimate first, then measure to confirm or correct. Prize the justification of the choice as much as the answer, since competing methods reach the same order.

activities.title: Estimate then verify an angle
feedback: If the learner skips the estimate and reads straight off the protractor, prompt: 'Before you measure, what's your best guess? Now check — were you close?'
If the estimate is far off (e.g. 'about 70°' for a 38° angle), ask them to compare against a right angle (90°) as a reference and re-estimate.

If they say estimating was a waste because they measured anyway, point out that a big gap between your estimate and your reading warns you that you may have misread the protractor scale (protractors carry two scales, so a good estimate guards against reading the wrong one).
activities.rationale: MP5 describes proficient students detecting possible errors using estimation and making sound decisions about when a tool helps, recognising its insight and limits — so pairing estimate-then-measure develops exactly that disposition. Presented as a proposed activity, not a tested intervention.
sourceClaims: Proficient students detect possible errors using estimation and other knowledge, and make sound decisions about when a tool is helpful, recognising its insight and limitations
learnerActions: Look at a drawn angle and state an estimate aloud, e.g. 'about 40°'.
Place a protractor on the angle and read the actual measure, e.g. 38°.
Compare the estimate with the measurement and say whether the estimate was close.
Explain why estimating first was not wasted even though you measured afterwards.
activities.intendedInsight: The eye gives a ballpark; the tool confirms or corrects it. Estimating first makes you more likely to catch a measuring slip, and measuring checks the estimate — the two work together rather than one replacing the other.

activities.title: Benchmark versus common denominator for ordering fractions
feedback: If the learner uses common denominators even for 3/8 vs 1/2, prompt: 'Is 3/8 below or above a half? Does that already settle it?'
If the learner says 5/8 and 4/7 are 'both above a half so about the same', point out that both being above 1/2 does not tell you which is larger, and ask them to find a common denominator.
Confirm the equivalence check: 5/8 = 35/56 and 4/7 = 32/56, so 4/7 is smaller — the 1/2 benchmark alone could not reveal this.
Praise reasons given for the choice, not just the correct final order, since both methods reach the same order.
activities.rationale: EEF recommends pupils make considered decisions about when different methods are appropriate and efficient, and that comparing representations develops conceptual understanding — this task has learners compare the benchmark and common-denominator representations and judge fit. Proposed activity, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Pupils should make considered decisions about when different methods are appropriate and efficient, and comparing representations of an idea develops conceptual understanding
learnerActions: Order 3/8, 1/2, 5/8 by comparing each to 1/2 (below, at, or above a half) and write the order.
Order the same three fractions by finding a common denominator, and check the two methods agree.
Compare how long each method took and say which was quicker here.
Now try to order 5/8 and 4/7: test whether the 'compare to a half' check separates them (both are above 1/2).
When the 1/2 benchmark cannot separate them, find a common denominator (or equivalent fractions) to order them exactly, e.g. 5/8 = 35/56 and 4/7 = 32/56, so 4/7 < 5/8.
State a rule for yourself about which method fits which fractions.
activities.intendedInsight: Benchmarking against 1/2 instantly sorts fractions that fall on different sides of a half, but when both fractions sit on the same side of 1/2 the 1/2 benchmark cannot separate them — then a common denominator earns its keep. The skill is matching the method to the fractions' features, not always using one method.

activities.title: Route the multiplication by reading the numbers
feedback: If the learner sets up long multiplication for 25×40, ask: 'Can you see a quicker way using 25×4 and then ×10?'
If a mental attempt at 347×26 goes astray, suggest the written algorithm and check the partial products line up by place value (for reference 347×20 = 6940 and 347×6 = 2082, giving 9022).
Ask the learner to name the number feature (round factor, small digits) that triggered their choice, reinforcing the routing habit.
activities.rationale: EEF's efficiency recommendation covers choosing when different methods are appropriate and efficient; routing between mental and written multiplication is a direct instance. Proposed activity, not a tested intervention.
sourceClaims: Pupils should make considered decisions about when different methods are appropriate and efficient, and comparing representations of an idea develops conceptual understanding
learnerActions: Look at 25×40 and decide whether a mental method or long multiplication is quicker.
Compute 25×40 mentally, e.g. as 25×4×10 = 100×10 = 1000.
Look at 347×26 and decide on a method.
Compute 347×26 by long multiplication and show the partial products.
For each, say what feature of the numbers made you choose that method.
activities.intendedInsight: Friendly numbers (round factors, easy regroupings) invite a mental route; awkward multi-digit numbers call for the written algorithm. Reading the numbers before starting saves effort.

activities.title: Argue with a shortcut-happy partner
feedback: If the learner cannot generate counter-cases, prompt them to find two fractions on the same side of 1/2 that are close together.
If the learner lets the eye-only angle claim stand, remind them that estimation is for checking and a protractor confirms the actual measure.
Praise clear justifications that name the fractions' features, not just correct answers.
activities.rationale: Explaining and defending when a method fits, including the limits of a shortcut, aligns with EEF's point that comparing representations and making considered method decisions builds understanding. A dialogue can rehearse this reasoning; it is offered as one route, not the only way. Proposed activity, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Pupils should make considered decisions about when different methods are appropriate and efficient, and comparing representations of an idea develops conceptual understanding
learnerActions: Work with a partner (real or role-played) who benchmarks every fraction comparison and trusts the eye for every angle.
When the partner benchmarks 5/8 vs 4/7 and declares them 'about the same', supply the counter-case: both are above a half, so the 1/2 benchmark cannot order them.
Show the partner how a common denominator settles 5/8 vs 4/7 exactly (35/56 vs 32/56).
When the partner reads an angle from the eye alone, insist on a protractor check and explain why.
Give the partner two fraction pairs where benchmarking is smart and two where it is not.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to say when a shortcut works and when the algorithm is required — and defending a verification step — shows genuine fit judgement rather than rote method use.

constraints: The learning objective is the judgement of matching method to problem features, so prize the justification of the choice as much as the final answer — both methods reach the same order, so a correct answer alone does not show strategic understanding.
Estimation and measurement are complementary: estimate first, then measure to check. Do not frame the protractor as replacing estimation or estimation as replacing the tool.

Selected-response or single-step scored checks can verify an isolated method choice but do not, on their own, reveal the efficiency judgement or the estimate-then-verify habit, because a correct order reached by the laborious method still counts as fully correct; use them only to feed richer method-choice work.

The benchmark's limitation must be made explicit: a single 1/2 benchmark cannot separate two fractions on the same side of 1/2, so for a same-side (and close) pair a common denominator or equivalence is warranted.

A static reference chart of 'benchmark vs common denominator' is at most a supporting scaffold; it does not let the learner estimate, measure, compare timings, or justify, which is where the decision-making becomes visible.
Angle measurement and fraction ordering are planar tasks; a three-dimensional representation is not needed for this objective (stated as a scope note for this content, not a universal claim).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 25×40 = 1000 (via 25×4×10) is correct. For 5/8 vs 4/7 with common denominator 56: 5/8 = 35/56 and 4/7 = 32/56, so 4/7 < 5/8 — correct, and both lie above 1/2 (28/56), confirming the 1/2 benchmark cannot separate them. 347×26 was left for the learner; for reference 347×26 = 9022 (347×20=6940, 347×6=2082, sum 9022).

Precision clarification on the benchmark limit: a single 1/2 benchmark never orders two fractions on the same side of 1/2, whether near or far apart. The 'same side and close together' framing (retained from the source) is where no other simple benchmark (e.g. 1 whole or 3/4) helps either, so a common denominator or equivalence is the reliable tool; this is true, not merely true for 'close' pairs.

The legacy entries asserted 'a static picture cannot teach this', 'scored steps cannot observe the judgement', and '3D adds nothing'. These comparative-necessity claims are not established by the cited sources; they have been softened into scoped scaffold/scope limits in constraints rather than presented as universal pedagogical laws.

The source carried reteach-prerequisite links and diagnostic/assessment fields that are not learner-facing activity content; they were not altered. Their internal identifiers have been omitted from this guidance.

The source lists benchmark fractions as 1/2 and 1 whole; the activities focus on 1/2 because it separates the given examples. Benchmarking against 1 whole remains a valid technique but is not exercised here.

probeDeeper: For 5/8 and 4/7, why doesn't 'compare to a half' settle it — and what would?
Give me two fractions where benchmarking is the smart move, and two where it isn't.
You estimated an angle as 40° and the protractor says 38° — was estimating a waste of time? Why not?
When is long multiplication worth the effort over a mental method?
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for recognising the benchmark (compare to 1/2) is quicker and sufficient for 3/8, 1/2, 5/8, while 5/8 and 4/7 both sit above 1/2 and close together so the benchmark cannot separate them and a common denominator or equivalence is warranted — a judgement about which method fits which fractions.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses common denominators for every comparison, even 3/8 vs 1/2, never reaching for a benchmark
errorPatterns.nextMove: Teach the 'compare to a half first' check and reserve the full algorithm for when benchmarks cannot separate — a self-regulation issue, reteach in place.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Grinds a common-denominator computation where 'below/above a half' would settle it instantly

errorPatterns.pattern: Applies a benchmark to two close, same-side fractions (5/8 vs 4/7) where it cannot separate them, and guesses
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the benchmark's limitation for same-side-close fractions and reteach finding a common denominator / equivalence to order them exactly.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the two are 'both above a half so about the same' or guesses the order

errorPatterns.pattern: Relies on visual inspection for angles and skips the protractor check
errorPatterns.nextMove: Estimate then MEASURE to check; treat the protractor as the verifier of the estimate, not an optional extra. Reteach measuring angles with a protractor.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: States an angle from the eye alone and resists measuring to verify

responseLevels.gap: Uses one method for everything (common denominators or long multiplication throughout), or trusts the eye for angles; gives no efficiency or verification reasoning.
responseLevels.full: Unprompted, matches method to the fractions (benchmark when it separates, common denominator when it cannot), estimates then verifies angles with a protractor, justifies each choice by efficiency and fit, and transfers the judgement to mental vs long multiplication.
responseLevels.partial: When prompted, says benchmarking is 'quicker' for the first set, but does not notice that 5/8 vs 4/7 needs the algorithm, or checks angles only when told.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: To put 3/8, 1/2 and 5/8 in order, one child finds a common denominator for all three; another just says '3/8 is below a half, 5/8 is above, so it's 3/8, 1/2, 5/8'. Who chose the smarter method here, and why? Would your advice change for ordering 5/8 and 4/7?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Both methods order 3/8, 1/2, 5/8 correctly, so accuracy is not the tell; the discriminator is whether the child sees the benchmark suffices here AND recognises the second pair as a case where it fails, matching method to the fractions' features (EEF's efficiency point) rather than applying one method blindly.

pedagogy.summary: At 10-11 this is the capstone of repeated reasoning: abstracting an algebraic rule from a run of cases and VERIFYING it. The child builds the interior-angle-sum rule (n−2)×180° from triangle/quadrilateral/pentagon, writes the nth-term rule of a linear sequence to predict any term, and generalises structural facts — always testing the generalisation on a specific case. CCSS MP8's own high examples live here: abstracting slope into (y−2)/(x−1)=3, and spotting the cancelling pattern in (x−1)(x+1), (x−1)(x²+x+1)… to reach a general formula. Teaching should organise cases in a table so the regularity is visible, press for the general rule in symbols, and demand a verifying case — the difference between a conjecture and a checked generalisation.
bestPractices: Tabulate a family of cases (polygon sides vs angle sum; position vs term) so the constant step and the offset are visible before the rule is written
Move from 'what's the pattern?' to 'write the rule for the nth/any case' in words then symbols
Always verify a stated generalisation on a fresh specific case (test (n−2)×180 on a hexagon) before trusting it
Decompose the geometric case (split a polygon into n−2 triangles) so the rule is explained, not just fitted
keyRepresentations: Polygon triangulation (an n-gon splits into n−2 triangles)
Position-vs-term tables and the nth-term expression
Linear-sequence graphs/number lines showing constant difference and offset
Algebra tiles / area models for operation-property generalisations
commonMisconceptions: Uses a term-to-term rule and cannot produce an nth-term rule for a far term
Assumes direct proportion — e.g. angle sum is n×180° or the 20th term is 20×(first term) — ignoring the −2 offset / start value
States a generalisation but never verifies it on a specific case, so errors go uncaught
Fits a rule to the given cases that fails to generalise (a pattern that works for 3, 4, 5 sides but wasn't reasoned from structure)

learn.summary: For ages 10-11, this is the capstone of 'look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning': abstract a general algebraic rule from a run of specific cases AND verify it on a fresh case. Learners build the interior-angle-sum rule (n−2)×180° from triangle/quadrilateral/pentagon, write the nth-term rule of a linear sequence to predict any term, and generalise structural facts about operations — each time testing the generalisation on a specific case. The core discrimination is twofold: (a) capturing the −2 offset / start value instead of assuming direct proportion (n×180°, or 20th term = 20×first term), and (b) treating verification on a new case as a reflex, not an afterthought. Teaching should tabulate the cases so the constant step and offset are visible, press for the rule in words then symbols, decompose the geometric case so the rule is explained rather than curve-fitted, and always demand a verifying case.

activities.title: Polygon angle-sum explorer: build, tabulate, abstract, verify
feedback: If the learner writes n×180° (e.g. 6×180 = 1080° for a hexagon), triangulate the hexagon together and count: there are 4 triangles, not 6. Test the n×180 rule against the known pentagon (it gives 900°, not 540°) and watch it fail — a convex n-gon triangulated from one vertex always yields exactly n−2 triangles, so the sum is (n−2) lots of 180°, not n.

If the learner states a rule and stops, do not confirm it; ask 'does it give the pentagon's 540°? Now test the hexagon, which you held back and did not use to build the rule.' Make the verifying case a required step every time.
If the learner reaches (n−2)×180° with the triangle reasoning and checks the hexagon at 720°, affirm both the structural justification AND the check as the target — the formula alone is not enough.
activities.rationale: Tabulating a family of cases makes the constant step (+180°) and the offset (−2) visible before the rule is written; decomposing the polygon into n−2 triangles explains the rule structurally so it generalises instead of merely fitting 3,4,5 sides; demanding a fresh verifying case separates a conjecture from a checked generalisation.
sourceClaims: Pupils should recognise and use mathematical structure to generalise and should reason about why relationships hold, using representations that reveal the structure
learnerActions: Start with a triangle (angle sum 180°). Add one side at a time to make a quadrilateral, then a pentagon (convex shapes); for each, split the polygon into triangles by drawing diagonals from one vertex. Keep the hexagon back as a fresh test case.
Record in a running table: number of sides, number of triangles, and angle sum. Notice the sum climbs by a steady +180° each time while the triangle count stays at (sides − 2).

Explain WHY: in a convex polygon, from one vertex you can reach the n−3 non-adjacent vertices by diagonals, so an n-sided polygon splits into exactly n−2 triangles, and its angle sum is (n−2) lots of 180° — reason the rule from the structure, don't just fit it to the numbers.
Write the general rule in words ('two fewer than the number of sides, times 180°') then in symbols: (n−2)×180°.

Verify on a case you did not build the rule from: test a hexagon — (6−2)×180° = 720° — and check it matches the measured/added angles. Then stretch it: a decagon (10 sides, 1440°) and a 100-gon — does it still make sense?
activities.intendedInsight: The angle sum is (n−2)×180° BECAUSE the polygon decomposes into n−2 triangles — a rule explained by structure, and confirmed by testing a new polygon rather than trusted on faith.

activities.title: nth-term rule tester for a linear sequence
feedback: If the learner extends the sequence step by step instead of writing a rule, tabulate position against term and ask for the 100th term — continuing by hand becomes impractical, motivating the nth-term rule.

If the learner writes 20 × (first term) for the 20th term, test that rule against a known term (does term = position × first term give the 2nd term correctly? 2×5 = 10, but the 2nd term is 9) and see it fail; locate the missing offset.

If the learner writes 4n + 1, checks it against the listed terms and then confirms it on a fresh term such as the 5th (21), affirm that testing a case not used to build the rule is how you move from a conjecture to a checked generalisation.
activities.rationale: Position-vs-term tables reveal the difference and offset; requiring prediction of a far term forces a genuine nth-term rule rather than term-to-term iteration; checking the rule against a listed term builds verification into the habit and exposes the direct-proportion misconception.
sourceClaims: Pupils should recognise and use mathematical structure to generalise and should reason about why relationships hold, using representations that reveal the structure
learnerActions: Take a linear sequence such as 5, 9, 13, 17, … and tabulate position (1, 2, 3, 4) against term so the constant difference (+4) and the start value are visible.
Move from the term-to-term rule ('add 4') to a position-to-term rule: difference × n + offset. For 5, 9, 13, 17 this is 4n + 1.
Predict a far term you cannot easily count to — the 20th term (81) and the 100th term (401) — using the rule, not step-by-step continuation.

Verify: first check your rule reproduces every listed term (e.g. the 4th term should give 4×4+1 = 17), then test a fresh case not used to build it — extend the sequence by one step to get the 5th term (21) and check that 4×5+1 = 21. If a conjectured rule breaks any term, it is wrong — fix it.
Explain why direct proportion fails here: the 20th term is NOT 20 × the first term, because the sequence does not pass through zero at position zero (the rule 4n+1 gives 1 at n=0, not 0).
activities.intendedInsight: A general nth-term rule lets you jump to any term directly, and the offset (start value) matters — direct proportion from the first term is a classic error that verification against a known term catches.

activities.title: Generalise a structural fact and find the case that disproves a false rule
feedback: If a learner cannot say what the −2 corresponds to, return to the triangulation of a convex polygon: from one vertex you can draw diagonals only to the n−3 non-adjacent vertices, which splits the polygon into exactly n−2 triangles (a hexagon gives 4). Each side not touching the chosen vertex is the base of one triangle; the 2 sides that meet at the chosen vertex do not get a triangle of their own, which is where the −2 comes from.
If a learner accepts a false rule, ask them to find one polygon (or one sequence term) where it breaks; a single counterexample is enough to reject it.
Affirm a response that states the rule, grounds it in structure, and can name a disproving case for a false alternative.
activities.rationale: Reasoning about why a relationship holds (not just that it fits cases) is what makes a generalisation reliable; practising counterexample selection trains the verification habit the assessment targets. Algebra tiles/area models are offered as optional representations that may make the structure visible for simpler products.
sourceClaims: MP8's advanced examples: abstracting slope into an equation from repeated checks, and noticing the cancelling regularity across (x−1)(x+1), (x−1)(x²+x+1)… to reach a general formula — generalising from repeated reasoning
Pupils should recognise and use mathematical structure to generalise and should reason about why relationships hold, using representations that reveal the structure
learnerActions: Generalise an operation property with a reason, e.g. 'any whole number m divided by a non-zero whole number n can be written as the fraction m/n, so dividing by n gives a denominator of n (before any simplifying)' — state it, then justify why it holds, not just that it works on examples.

Explore the cancelling regularity in products like (x−1)(x+1), (x−1)(x²+x+1), … and describe the general pattern that emerges; an area model or algebra tiles may help visualise the simpler binomial product (x−1)(x+1), but are harder to apply to the cubic case, so treat them as an optional aid rather than a required method.

Practise verification-by-counterexample: given a false claim such as 'a polygon's angle sum is n×180°', name the specific polygon that shows it is wrong and state what it gives versus the true value (e.g. pentagon: rule gives 900°, truth is 540°).
Answer the discriminating prompt: 'Why n−2 and not n — what does the −2 correspond to in the shape?'
activities.intendedInsight: Generalising means stating a rule, justifying why it holds from structure, and being able to produce the single case that would disprove a false version — all three are part of mathematical reasoning.

constraints: Verification is not optional: every stated generalisation must be tested on a fresh specific case before it is trusted. Do not let a learner stop at a rule, and do not simply confirm a rule for them — ask for the verifying case.
Guard against the direct-proportion misconception explicitly: n×180° for angle sums and 20×(first term) for the 20th term are the key errors to surface and refute, not avoid.

The rule must be reasoned from structure (a convex n-gon triangulated from one vertex is n−2 triangles), not merely curve-fitted to 3, 4, 5 sides; a pattern that happens to fit the given cases but wasn't reasoned may not generalise.

A static triangulation diagram or a pre-filled table is a useful reference for showing the decomposition, but by itself it does not let the learner conjecture a rule and test it on a new case — pair any static display with an actual conjecture-and-check task.

An interactive explorer or a well-designed quiz (deriving the rule, finding a far term, and selecting the case that disproves a false rule) can each be used during teaching, not only for assessment; choose by what the learner needs to do, not by assuming one medium alone can teach generalisation.

3D representation is unlikely to be needed here because polygon angle sums, linear sequences and operation properties are flat/symbolic; it may add handling load rather than insight for this specific content. This is a scoped judgement about this topic, not a universal or verified claim about 3D.
Area models/algebra tiles are an optional representation whose fit is strongest for simple binomial products; do not present them as a verified or required method for the cubic cancelling pattern.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and the legacy 'verified' flags were not independently re-checked.

Self-audit of the examples used: triangle 180°, quadrilateral 360°, pentagon 540°, hexagon (6−2)×180° = 720°, decagon (10−2)×180° = 1440° — all consistent with (n−2)×180°. The n×180 distractor gives pentagon 900° and hexagon 1080°, correctly shown as wrong. Sequence 5,9,13,17 has rule 4n+1: 4th term 4×4+1 = 17 ✓, 20th term 81, 100th term 401 — consistent.

The legacy 'possible'/'poor' fit entries carried universal-sounding claims (a tap-to-reveal 'cannot' let the child conjecture; 'open talk gives nothing to test'; '3D adds load, not insight'). These have been softened to scoped, qualified observations with stated affordances/limits in the constraints; catalog fit rankings and quiz-step vocabulary were removed.

The operation-property example was tightened to 'any whole number m divided by n can be written as the fraction m/n'; the exact source wording ('dividing by n always gives a denominator of n') was looser and reviewers may wish to confirm the intended statement.

The original source listed an algebra-tile/area-model representation for operation-property generalisations and for the (x−1)(x+1)… cancelling pattern; the applicability of area models to the polynomial-factoring (cubic) example is plausible but not established by the cited sources and is now scoped as optional and reviewable.

Counterexample tuned to this topic: 'a classmate says the angle sum is n×180° — which polygon would show that's wrong, and what does it give versus the true value?' to probe verification by counterexample

Ask 'write the rule for the nth term of 5, 9, 13, 17… and prove it gives the 4th term correctly' to link generalisation with verification
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for (n−2)×180° reached by reasoning (each extra side adds 180° / an n-gon is n−2 triangles), and a verification on the hexagon giving (6−2)×180 = 720°. The reasoned rule AND the check are the target, not the formula alone.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Triangulate the polygon to show it is n−2 triangles, not n; test the n×180 rule against the known pentagon and see it fail

responseLevels.gap: Spots '+180°' or 'add 4' but writes no general rule, or uses n×180 / direct proportion, and does not verify
responseLevels.full: Abstracts (n−2)×180° (and nth-term rules) with a structural justification and verifies on a new case, catching direct-proportion errors — generalising AND checking unprompted
responseLevels.partial: Produces a general rule when prompted (often needing the table) but omits the offset reasoning or does not test it on a fresh case

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A triangle's angles add to 180°, a quadrilateral's to 360°, a pentagon's to 540°. What is the rule for the angle sum of a polygon with n sides? How did you get it — and test your rule on a hexagon.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Spotting '+180° each time' is easy; the discriminating parts are (a) capturing the −2 offset in a general rule rather than n×180, and (b) verifying on a new case. A child reasoning correctly explains the n−2 triangles and checks the hexagon; a child reasoning incorrectly writes n×180 (direct proportion) or states a rule without testing it.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 7-8. Find 10 more/less and 100 more/less than any number to 1000, mentally, by recognising WHICH digit changes: +10 changes the tens, +100 changes the hundreds, and the other digits stay — except when a boundary forces a carry/exchange (e.g. 190 + 10 = 200).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 3): mental methods and place value to 1000 (find 10/100 more or less).
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.NBT.8 'mentally add 10 or 100 to, and mentally subtract 10 or 100 from, a given number 100-900'.
• Operational details — Extend the two-digit '10 more' vertical-move idea to a place-value chart / Gattegno chart where +10 steps the tens digit and +100 steps the hundreds digit while others hold. Explicitly teach the boundary cases where a column 'fills up' and rolls over (190+10, 950+100). Demand the explanation of which digit changes and why.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 7, emerging): finds 10/100 more/less with no boundary crossing, using a chart. Tier B (age 7-8, secure): does it mentally for any number to 1000 and names the changing digit. Tier C (age 8, extending): handles roll-over boundaries (190+10, 890+100) and explains the exchange.
bestPractices: Extend the two-digit pattern: +10 steps the tens digit, +100 steps the hundreds digit, others unchanged — make the 'which digit?' question explicit.
Use a Gattegno / place-value chart so the child selects a new tens- or hundreds-row and physically sees one digit change.
Teach boundary roll-overs deliberately (190+10=200, 950+100=1050 later) as the interesting cases, not exceptions to memorise.
Contrast +10 vs +100 side by side so the child tracks different columns.
Insist on the reasoning ('the hundreds digit goes up by one, tens and ones stay') to keep it place-value based, not counting.
keyRepresentations: Gattegno / place-value chart (change one row = change one digit)
H|T|O place-value counters (add/remove one 10 or one 100)
0-1000 number line with ±10 and ±100 hops
100-square generalisation / number grid
Base-ten flats/rods for the concrete +100 / +10 move
commonMisconceptions: Changing the wrong digit (adding 100 but stepping the tens).
Failing at boundaries — 190 + 10 giving '1100' or '190' unchanged instead of 200.
Counting on in ones instead of jumping the place.
Confusing 10 more with 100 more.
Assuming only one digit ever changes, so mishandling the carry when a column rolls over.

learn.summary: For ages 7-8: find 10 more/less and 100 more/less than any number up to 1000, mentally, by reasoning about which digit changes. +10 steps the tens digit, +100 steps the hundreds digit, and the other digits stay the same \u2014 except at a boundary where a column 'fills up' and rolls over (e.g. 190 + 10 = 200, where the tens roll 9\u21920 and carry into the hundreds). Learners should name which digit changes and explain why, keeping the method place-value based rather than counting in ones.

activities.title: Digit stepper: watch one column respond
feedback: If the wrong column is predicted: name explicitly which column '10 more' and '100 more' act on, add the matching base-ten piece (one ten or one hundred), and watch only that column move.
If a learner counts on in ones to reach the answer, prompt: 'Can you jump straight to the column that changes instead of counting?'
Reinforce correct reasoning by restating it: 'The hundreds digit goes up by one; tens and ones stay.'
activities.rationale: Making the 'which digit?' question explicit and showing exactly one column respond to one operation builds place-value reasoning rather than rote counting. An interactive chart where the affected digit highlights and ticks while others are locked can make the mechanism concrete; a number-line view showing \u00b110/\u00b1100 hops is an optional alternative representation. These interaction examples illustrate the mechanism and are not required mechanisms \u2014 base-ten counters or a paper chart reach the same insight.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils develop mental place-value methods to 1000, including finding 10 or 100 more or less.
learnerActions: Start with a three-digit number shown in an H|T|O place-value chart (e.g. 638).
Predict which digit will change before pressing +100, then press it and check: only the hundreds digit ticks up (638\u2192738) while tens and ones stay fixed.
Repeat with +10, -10, -100 on several numbers, each time saying aloud which column changes and which stay the same.
Contrast +10 and +100 side by side on the same starting number to track that they act on different columns.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding/subtracting 10 acts on the tens column and adding/subtracting 100 acts on the hundreds column; when no column rolls over (as with 638), the other digits hold still. This is a place-value jump, not counting on in ones. Boundary cases such as 190 + 10 come in the next activity.

activities.title: Boundary roll-overs: when a column fills up
feedback: If a learner writes a malformed number (190+10 = '1100' or '190' unchanged; 10 more than 695 = '6,105'): don't reteach the whole idea \u2014 rehearse the single roll on a number line or base-ten mat, e.g. 305\u2192295 (a ten taken by exchanging one hundred for ten tens), 695\u2192705 (9 tens + 1 ten = 10 tens make a new hundred, hundreds 6\u21927, ones stay 5).
If a learner assumes only one digit ever changes: show them the carry/borrow so they see a second column move when a column overflows.
Confirm correct regrouping: '950 + 100 fills the hundreds, so it rolls into a new thousands column: 1050.'
activities.rationale: Boundary roll-overs are the key teaching case and are best met deliberately rather than treated as exceptions. Seeing or physically working a cascade \u2014 the tens rolling 9\u21920 while a carry moves leftward, or exchanging base-ten pieces \u2014 makes the carry/borrow visible. Base-ten counters and a 0-1000 number line give concrete and linear views of the same jump.
sourceClaims: Boundary roll-overs (e.g. 190+10) are the key teaching case and should be made explicit rather than treated as exceptions.
learnerActions: Start at 190 and find 10 more. Watch (or work out on a base-ten mat/number line) the tens roll 9\u21920 and a ten carry up to make one more hundred, so 190 becomes 200.
Find 10 less than 305: the tens are 0, so a hundred must be exchanged for ten tens before removing one \u2014 305, 295.
Find 10 more than 695: the tens fill up (9 tens + 1 ten = 10 tens), which rolls over to make a new hundred, so the hundreds go 6\u21927 and the ones stay 5 \u2014 695 becomes 705.
Find 100 more than 950 and decide whether the answer is still a three-digit number (it becomes 1050, which rolls into a new thousands column).

For each, say which digits moved and why, e.g. for 190 + 10: 'the tens filled up, so they rolled to 0 and added one to the hundreds'; for 305 - 10: 'there were no tens, so I exchanged a hundred for ten tens and took one away'; for 950 + 100: 'the hundreds filled up, so they rolled to 0 and made one thousand.'
activities.intendedInsight: The rule 'only one digit changes' has a meaningful exception: when a column reaches its limit (a 9 going up, or a 0 going down), it rolls over and carries/borrows into the next column. These boundary cases are the interesting core of the skill, not exceptions to memorise.

activities.title: Fluency practice with boundary items
feedback: For plain-case errors adjusting the wrong place (100 more than 456 \u2192 466): re-name which column the operation acts on and redo with the matching base-ten piece (the answer is 556).
For boundary errors: rehearse just the single roll, not the whole concept.

Use probing questions to check reasoning, e.g. '10 less than 305 \u2014 what happens to the tens and the hundreds?', 'Which digit changes when you find 100 more? Does any other digit move?', '100 more than 950 \u2014 is the answer still a three-digit number?'
activities.rationale: Scored practice can consolidate a fluency skill after understanding is built, and deliberately mixing boundary items checks that learners handle regrouping rather than mechanically bumping one digit. Practice items assess and reinforce; they should follow, not replace, the conceptual work above.
learnerActions: Answer quick fill-in items: '100 more than 638 = __', '10 less than 305 = __', '100 more than 950 = __'.
Answer 'which digit changes?' when finding 100 more (or 10 less) for a given number.
Mix plain cases (456 + 100) with boundary cases (190 + 10, 695 + 10, 305 - 10) so the two are not predictable.
Optionally use a slider on a 0-1000 line to land on answers and self-check.
activities.intendedInsight: Once the place-value reasoning is understood, the skill can become quick mental recall, applied reliably even when a boundary forces a regroup.

constraints: Fill-in and multiple-choice practice consolidates and checks fluency but should follow conceptual work with a chart, counters, or number line; recognition-only responses do not by themselves build the place-value reasoning or the explanation of which digit changes.

A static annotated chart can serve as a reference for which digit +10/+100 changes, but learners need to carry out the transformation (physically, with counters, or interactively) to experience the roll-over; treat a fixed image as a reference scaffold, not the whole lesson.
Always require learners to explain which digit changes and why, so the method stays place-value based rather than counting on in ones.

Interactive highlights, locked digits, animated carries, number-line toggles, timed rounds, and sliders are optional illustrations of the mechanism; the same insight can be reached with base-ten counters, a Gattegno/place-value chart, or a paper number line.

Tier the work: emerging learners find 10/100 more/less with no boundary crossing using a chart; secure learners do it mentally for any number to 1000 and name the changing digit; extending learners handle genuine roll-over boundaries (190+10, 950+100) and explain the exchange.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Of the three cited sources, the CCSS 2.NBT.8 claim and the NCETM boundary-roll-over claim are marked verified:false in the source row; the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified:true. Treat citation strength accordingly.

The source's parentTitle and standards describe numbers up to 1000, but 950 + 100 = 1050 crosses into the thousands; this is used intentionally as an extending example, framed as 'does the answer stay three digits?' rather than contradicting the 'to 1000' scope.

The original Tier C checkpoint listed '890+100' as a roll-over boundary, but 890+100=990 does not cross any boundary (hundreds 8\u21929, no overflow). This non-rolling example was corrected out of the learner-facing guidance; a genuine tens roll-over in that region would be e.g. 890+10=900.

The original assessment feedback contained a garbled phrase for 695\u2192705 ('ten ones... a ten makes the next hundred'); it was corrected in both the learner action and feedback to describe a tens roll-over (9 tens + 1 ten = 10 tens \u2192 new hundred, hundreds 6\u21927, ones stay 5), with the regrouping intent preserved.
CCSS 2.NBT.8 is a Grade 2 US standard while the UK Year 3 placement is ages 7-8; the age framing (7-8) was retained from the row but the cross-standard age mapping is approximate.
Standards citations establish the skill/objective but do not themselves evidence the efficacy or necessity of any particular medium; efficacy wording is kept as proposed/optional.

Which digit changes when you find 100 more? Does any other digit move?

assess.correctAnswer: 556; 295; 705; 1,050 — changing only the right digit unless a boundary forces a regroup, and regrouping correctly across it.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adjusts the wrong place — adds 100 to the tens digit, or adds 10 to the hundreds
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name which column '10 more' and '100 more' act on; add the matching base-ten piece and watch only that column (until it overflows).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 100 more than 456 comes out as 466 or 1,456; 10 more changes the hundreds.

errorPatterns.pattern: Fails to regroup across a boundary: 10 less than 305 → 315 or 300; 10 more than 695 → 6,105 or 605
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the whole idea — rehearse the single roll on a number line or base-ten mat: 305, 295 (a ten borrowed from the hundred) and 695, 705 (ten ones... a ten makes the next hundred).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The boundary cases give a malformed number or don't roll into the next place.

responseLevels.gap: Adjusts the wrong place or cannot cross a boundary.
responseLevels.full: Finds 10/100 more or less for any number to 1000, adjusting the correct place and regrouping across boundaries, and names which digit changes.
responseLevels.partial: Handles plain cases (456 + 100) but stumbles when a zero/nine forces a regroup.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask quickly and watch the method: '100 more than 456? ... 10 less than 305? ... 10 more than 695? ... 100 more than 950?' The last three cross a boundary — watch what happens to the neighbouring digits.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 456 checks the plain case (one digit changes); 305 (10 less) and 695 (10 more) force a roll across a zero/nine into the next place; 950 + 100 crosses into thousands. Watching reveals whether the child adjusts the right place and handles the carry/borrow, versus mechanically bumping one digit.
