pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 7–8 (UK Y3, US Grade 2–3). Skip counting in 4s, 8s, 50s and 100s — extending equal-step counting into the multiplication-facts that underpin the times tables.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y3 'count from 0 in multiples of 4, 8, 50 and 100'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.NBT.2 'skip-count by 5s, 10s, and 100s'; 3.OA.7 recall of products (the 4s and 8s underpin the ×4 and ×8 tables); 3.NBT.3 multiply one-digit by multiples of 10.
• Operational details: teach 4s and 8s through the DOUBLING CHAIN — 2s doubled give 4s, 4s doubled give 8s (each 8-step is two 4-steps is four 2-steps). 50s are half-hundreds/money (two 50s make 100) and 100s extend the place-value step. Counting in 4s and 8s is explicitly the equal-groups on-ramp to the 4 and 8 times tables.
• Checkpoint: skip-count fluently and connect to equal groups. Tier A (7): count in 4s and 100s from 0 with a number-line/hundred-square prop. Tier B (7–8): count in 4s, 8s, 50s, 100s from 0 and state the matching equal-groups fact (three 4s = 12). Tier C (8): explain 8s as doubled 4s and 4s as doubled 2s, and count 50s to 500 linking two 50s = 100.
bestPractices: Build 4s and 8s from the DOUBLING relationship rather than as separate chants: stack a 2s number line, a 4s line and an 8s line so the child sees each 4-jump spans two 2-jumps and each 8-jump spans two 4-jumps.

Tie every skip count to equal groups and the array — counting 4, 8, 12, 16 is one group, two groups, three groups of four — so skip counting is experienced as repeated addition and the direct route into the ×4 and ×8 tables.
Anchor 50s in money and half-hundreds: two 50p coins make £1, two 50s make 100, so counting 50, 100, 150 is felt as pairing up to hundreds rather than a new memorised list.
Use the hundred square to expose the visual pattern of each count (the 4s and 8s make regular diagonal/column patterns; 50s and 100s march down rows) so the pattern is seen, not just heard.

Rehearse forwards and backwards and from non-zero starts once the forward count is secure, and connect back to previously mastered 2s/5s/10s so the new counts join a coherent web rather than standing alone.
keyRepresentations: Stacked/aligned number lines (2s, 4s, 8s) showing the doubling of jump size
Equal groups and arrays (groups of 4, groups of 8) linking the count to repeated addition and multiplication
Hundred square with each multiple shaded to reveal the pattern (4s, 8s columns/diagonals; 50s and 100s down the rows)
Coins and a money line (50p, £1) anchoring the 50s count in half-hundreds
commonMisconceptions: Treating 4s and 8s as unrelated rote lists and never noticing 8s are doubled 4s — so a slip in one count cannot be repaired from the other.
Adding the wrong step (drifting into 2s when counting 4s, or 5s when counting 50s) because the step size isn't held steady.
Miscounting 50s as 'fifties are like fives with a zero' and producing 50, 100, 150, 250 — losing a step or mis-pairing to hundreds.
Not connecting the skip count to groups, so the child can chant 4, 8, 12 but cannot say how many groups of four make 12 — the count stays verbal and never becomes multiplicative.
Boundary slips crossing hundreds while counting in 50s or 100s (150→200, 950→1000) when the hundreds digit must roll.

learn.summary: For ages 7–8 (UK Y3, US Grade 2–3): counting from 0 in multiples of 4, 8, 50 and 100, built on the doubling chain (2s doubled are 4s, 4s doubled are 8s) and tied explicitly to equal groups so skip counting becomes the on-ramp to the ×4 and ×8 tables. 50s are anchored in money/half-hundreds (two 50s make 100). The central insight to teach is the relationship between step sizes — that each 8-jump spans two 4-jumps spans four 2-jumps — and the connection between a verbal count and 'how many groups'.

activities.title: The doubling chain: stacked number lines for 2s, 4s and 8s
feedback: If a learner sub-counts (audibly counting 4-by-4 or one-by-one to reach the next 8), do not drill for speed. Point to the known 4s fact and prompt 'double it' — fluency grows through repeated jumps on the number line, not pressure.
If a learner treats 4s and 8s as unrelated, write out the 4s from 0 and ring every second number (0, 8, 16…) to reveal the 8s: 'the 8s take a jump twice as big.'
When a learner lands correctly, ask them to show which smaller jumps live inside the big jump, so the doubling is explained, not just recited.
activities.rationale: The target relationship is between step sizes, which becomes visible when the counts are laid against each other and the jumps aligned. Building 4s and 8s from doubling rather than as separate chants gives learners a repair strategy and links directly to the ×4 and ×8 tables. Optional interactive versions (buttons that advance each line, with smaller jumps ghosting in beneath each larger step) may make the nesting more manipulable; a paper version with three aligned strips achieves the same alignment.
sourceClaims: Skip counting in 4s and 8s is developed via the doubling relationship and as the equal-groups route into multiplication tables.
learnerActions: Lay out (or display) three aligned number lines starting at 0: one marked in 2s, one in 4s, one in 8s, with the same spacing so matching numbers sit directly above one another.
Step along the 8s line one jump at a time. For each 8-jump, mark the two 4-jumps directly beneath it, and the four 2-jumps beneath those.
Say aloud as you go: 'one jump of 8 is the same distance as two jumps of 4, which is four jumps of 2.'
Count the 4s aloud (0, 4, 8, 12, 16…) and ring every other number starting from 0 — notice the circled numbers are exactly the 8s count (0, 8, 16…).
Count backwards in 8s from 96, checking each step against the 4s line.
Repeat from a non-zero start once the forward count is secure (e.g. count on in 4s from 24).
Link the new counts back to the 2s, 5s and 10s you already know, so 4s/8s/50s/100s join a coherent web rather than standing alone.
activities.intendedInsight: 8s are doubled 4s and 4s are doubled 2s; a slip in one count can be repaired using the other, because the step sizes nest inside each other.

activities.title: From skip count to equal groups and arrays
feedback: If a learner can chant '4, 8, 12' but cannot say how many groups of four make 12, rebuild with physical groups so each number names one more group.
If a learner answers 'how many fours in 20' by guessing, have them step the number line and tally the jumps.
Confirm success when the learner moves fluently between the count, the groups and the product.
activities.rationale: Tying every skip count to equal groups and the array makes the count multiplicative rather than purely verbal, and matching items test the count-to-groups connection directly. This is the bridge from counting to table recall.
sourceClaims: 2.NBT.2 skip-count by 5s, 10s and 100s; 3.OA.7 fluently multiply and recall products — counting in 4s and 8s underpins the ×4 and ×8 tables.
Skip counting in 4s and 8s is developed via the doubling relationship and as the equal-groups route into multiplication tables.
learnerActions: Build groups of four with counters: one group, two groups, three groups, saying the running total (4, 8, 12) and the matching fact ('three fours = 12').
Arrange the same counters into an array (rows of four) so each skip-count step adds one row.
Match skip-count totals to equal-groups statements, e.g. pair 'three groups of 8' with 24, 'five fours' with 20.
Answer group-count challenges in both directions: 'How many fours in 20?' (five) and 'What is four groups of eight?' (32).
Repeat the build for groups of eight, noticing each group of eight is two groups of four.
activities.intendedInsight: A skip count is repeated addition of equal groups; knowing the count lets you say how many groups make a total, which is exactly the multiplication fact.

activities.title: Counting in 50s and 100s with money and the hundred square
feedback: If a learner says 50, 100, 150, 250 (losing a step), do not reteach the whole sequence — rehearse the specific boundary bridge (…, 150, 200) with coins or a number line.
If a learner loses place crossing a hundred, slow down at the boundary and name the rolling hundreds digit aloud.

If a learner uses '50s are like 5s with a zero', accept it as a valid pattern (each 50s number is ten times the matching 5s number), and also build meaning by pairing coins to hundreds so they can explain why 150 + 50 = 200.
activities.rationale: Anchoring 50s in money and half-hundreds makes the count felt as pairing to hundreds rather than a new memorised list, and the hundred square and number line expose the visual pattern so it is seen, not only heard. Targeting boundary crossings addresses a common place-value slip. No cited source directly supports this money-anchoring approach, so it is offered as a research-informed proposal.
learnerActions: Pair up 50p coins (or £50 notes) to make pounds/hundreds: two 50s make 100, so count 50, 100, 150, 200… pairing as you go.
Count on in 50s from 0 to 1000, deliberately slowing at each hundred boundary (…, 450, 500, 550; …, 950, 1000) and checking the hundreds digit rolls correctly.

On a 1–100 hundred square, shade the 4s and 8s to see their column/diagonal patterns; then on a number line or track to 1000, mark the 50s and 100s to see them step evenly, with 50s landing twice as often as 100s.
Count in 100s from 0 to 1000 and compare with the 50s on the same number line.
State explicitly: 'how many 50s make 1000?' and check by pairing (two 50s = 100, so twenty 50s = 1000).
activities.intendedInsight: Counting in 50s can be understood as pairing up to hundreds (two 50s make 100); it also matches the 5s count with each number ten times bigger (5, 10, 15 → 50, 100, 150), but the pairing view carries the meaning. Boundary crossings require the hundreds digit to roll, and shading/marking makes each count's pattern visible.

activities.title: Oral fluency and self-check with a counting partner
feedback: If totals disagree between the 8s and 'two lots of 4s' check, find the step where they diverge and re-jump it.
Praise self-correction that uses the 4s to repair the 8s rather than restarting.
activities.rationale: Spoken rehearsal with responsive prompting may support oral fluency and keeps the doubling link active; it is intended to complement the visual/structural work rather than replace it, and is best used once the structure is understood rather than as the first route in. Its effectiveness relative to the manipulative is untested.
sourceClaims: Skip counting in 4s and 8s is developed via the doubling relationship and as the equal-groups route into multiplication tables.
learnerActions: Count in 8s aloud with a partner, taking turns on each step.
Check an 8s count against the 4s count, confirming that each 8s step equals two 4s steps (e.g. two jumps of 4 reach 8, four jumps of 4 reach 16).
Have the partner pose doubling prompts: 'If four fours are 16, what are four eights?'
Count forwards and backwards from non-zero starts to build flexibility, and relate the counts to the already-known 2s, 5s and 10s.
activities.intendedInsight: Oral rehearsal and self-checking against a related count build fluency and reinforce that the 4s and 8s support each other.

constraints: Counting in 4s and 8s is best built from the doubling relationship, not taught as separate rote chants, so learners can repair one count from the other.
Every skip count should be tied to equal groups/arrays so the count becomes multiplicative, not merely verbal.
Do not drill for speed when a learner is sub-counting; connect to the known related count and let fluency grow through repeated jumps and retrieval.

Sequence, fill-in-the-blank and matching exercises can check these counts but do not by themselves build the doubling structure — use them to check mastery after the relationship has been taught; a sort/match verifies classification without eliciting an explanation of why 8s are doubled 4s.

A pre-shaded pattern reference (static or tap-to-reveal) supports pattern spotting and the equal-groups link but does not let the learner drive the count or see the doubling animate; treat it as a reference, not the primary build.

Interactive overlays (advancing lines, ghosted smaller jumps, live shading) and physical coins are optional concrete aids to make the mechanism visible; they are means, not required mechanisms — aligned paper strips and real coins work too.
A standard 1–100 hundred square displays the 4s/8s patterns; use a number line or track for 50s and 100s up to 1000.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources have not been re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the counts: 4s from 0 to 48 (0,4,8,12,16,20,24,28,32,36,40,44,48), 8s from 0 to 96 (0,8,…,96), and 50s to 1000 (twenty steps of 50) are all arithmetically consistent. 'Every second multiple of 4, counting from 0, is a multiple of 8' is correct (0,8,16… are the even-indexed 4s). Equal-groups facts used are correct: three fours = 12, five fours = 20, three eights = 24, four eights = 32, twenty fifties = 1000.
The source's erroneous example sequence '50, 100, 150, 250' (used to illustrate a learner error) is preserved only as a misconception to correct, never presented as a valid count.

Two of three cited sources are marked verified:false in the source row (the CCSS-M and NCETM claims); treat their specific wordings as unconfirmed, and the doubling/equal-groups pedagogy as a recommended rather than empirically proven approach.

Activity 3 (50s/100s money and boundary work) has sourceClaims set to [] because none of the cited claims directly supports its money-anchoring/boundary-roll teaching principle; it is a research-informed proposal only.

The original research rated a 3D environment as adding 'no conceptual gain' for these planar patterns. That is a catalog fit judgement, not a pedagogical law; flat aligned views are proposed because the doubling overlay and hundred-square pattern read clearly in 2D, without claiming 3D cannot teach it.

The original keyRepresentation referred to a 'hundred square' for 50s/100s; a 1–100 square cannot show these to 1000, so a number line/track is used instead for those counts. The 4s/8s remain on the hundred square.

probeDeeper: What's the next multiple of 8 after 56?
How is counting in 8s like counting in 4s?
Count in 50s — how many 50s make 1000?
What's 4 more than 44? And 8 more than 88?
assess.correctAnswer: 0, 4, 8, …, 48; 0, 8, 16, …, 96; 0, 50, 100, …, 1000; and notices 8s are the 4s doubled (every second multiple of 4) — each step adds the group size.

errorPatterns.pattern: sub-counts by smaller steps — builds the 8s by counting on in 4s (or ones) each time rather than stepping by 8; slow and breaks under load
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT drill for speed — use number-line jumps of 8 and connect to the known 4s ('double it'); fluency grows with practice and retrieval
errorPatterns.revealedBy: audible intermediate counting between the multiples of 8

errorPatterns.pattern: no link between 4s and 8s — treats them as two separate lists, doesn't see 8s as doubled 4s
errorPatterns.nextMove: write out the 4s and ring every other one to reveal the 8s — 'a jump twice as big' — making the doubling relationship explicit
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says the sequences are unrelated, or can't use the 4s to get the 8s

errorPatterns.pattern: 50s/100s digit slip — loses place in the 50s (…, 450, 500, 550) or miscounts at boundaries

responseLevels.gap: Cannot sustain 4s/8s beyond a few terms without counting every one, and treats each sequence as unrelated.
responseLevels.full: Skip-counts 4s, 8s, 50s, 100s fluently, steps by the group size without sub-counting, and uses the 4s-doubled-are-8s relationship.
responseLevels.partial: Recites 4s, 8s, 50s from 0 but sub-counts for each step, or cannot exploit the 4s↔8s doubling link.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Count in 4s from 0 to 48. Now count in 8s from 0 to 96. Then count in 50s to 1000. And as you do the 8s, tell me — how could counting in 4s help you count in 8s? (Watch fluency, sub-counting, and whether they see 8s as double the 4s.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 4s and 8s have weaker rhythmic support than 2s/5s/10s, so this exposes children who chant only well-patterned sequences. The 'how do 4s help 8s' question tests whether the child sees the doubling relationship — a bridge to the 4× and 8× tables — rather than treating the sequences as unrelated. Sub-counting by ones/fours, or no link between 4s and 8s, marks a fragile grasp.

pedagogy.summary: This topic builds from the triangle angle sum (180°) to the general interior-angle sum of any polygon, (n−2)×180°, DERIVED by splitting the polygon into n−2 triangles, and to the interior/exterior angle relationship (they sum to 180° at each vertex; all exterior angles sum to 360° for any polygon). Best taught by deriving the formulas from structure — partitioning into triangles, walking the perimeter to feel the 360° of turning — rather than memorising them, and by carefully separating the two 'totals' pupils confuse: interior + exterior = 180° at ONE vertex, versus all exterior angles = 360° for the WHOLE polygon. For regular polygons each angle is the sum divided by n, but this division applies ONLY when the polygon is regular.
bestPractices: Derive (n−2)×180° by splitting the polygon into triangles from one vertex (a hexagon → 4 triangles → 720°); don't present the formula as a rule to memorise
Distinguish demonstration from proof: tearing off a triangle's corners to form a straight line DEMONSTRATES 180° but is not a proof — pupils should also meet the deductive argument
Keep the two exterior-angle totals apart: interior + exterior = 180° at a single vertex; the sum of ALL exterior angles is 360° for any polygon, however many sides

Attach the word 'regular' to every ÷n formula: each interior angle = sum ÷ n and each exterior = 360 ÷ n hold ONLY for regular polygons; for an irregular one, find a missing angle by subtracting known angles from the sum
Use the 'walking the perimeter' turning model to make the 360° total of exterior angles concrete
Stress that the angle sum depends on the NUMBER OF SIDES, not on the size of the polygon
keyRepresentations: Polygon partitioned into triangles from one vertex (n sides → n−2 triangles)
Torn-off triangle corners arranged on a straight line (demonstration of 180°)
A marker 'walking the perimeter', turning through 360° in total (exterior angles)
Interior and exterior angle pair at a vertex sitting on a straight line (sum 180°)
A regular polygon with equal angles beside an irregular one with the same sum but unequal angles
commonMisconceptions: Thinking a triangle's angles sum to 360°
Confusing interior and exterior angles
Dividing 360° (or the interior sum) by n for an IRREGULAR polygon, or assuming all its angles are equal
Believing a bigger polygon has a bigger angle sum (angle scales with size)
Reporting the interior-angle SUM as though it were one interior angle (forgetting to divide by n)

learn.summary: Pupils (ages 11–14) derive the interior-angle sum of a polygon by splitting it into n−2 triangles from one vertex ((n−2)×180°), feel the exterior-angle total of 360° by walking the perimeter, and carefully separate the two 'totals' they confuse: interior + exterior = 180° at ONE vertex, versus all exterior angles = 360° for the WHOLE polygon. Dividing by n (sum÷n for each interior, 360÷n for each exterior) gives each angle ONLY when all the angles are equal. This is true of every regular polygon (the KS3 focus), and also of equal-angled shapes such as a non-square rectangle. The angle sum depends on the number of sides, not the polygon's size. The strongest route is proposed to be a construction the child performs (triangulate, walk the perimeter, toggle regular/irregular); fixed diagrams and scored questions are useful support with stated limits.

activities.title: Triangulate to build the angle sum
feedback: If a learner says the sum should be bigger for a physically larger polygon, enlarge the same shape with its angles unchanged and ask whether any angle changed — the sum depends only on the number of sides.

If a learner counts n triangles instead of n−2, ask them to look at the two sides meeting at the chosen vertex and check whether every side became the base of its own triangle; the two sides at the chosen vertex do not, which is why the count is n−2.
An optional running tally showing '(n−2)×180' as diagonals are drawn makes the link between triangle count and total concrete; this is a support, not a requirement.
activities.rationale: Deriving the formula from triangulation rather than memorising it targets the topic's core structure and the documented size-independence misconception. Learner-performed partitioning with immediate confirmation is proposed as the strongest route; fixed diagrams can show one split but cannot let the child vary n.
sourceClaims: The interior angle sum of an n-sided polygon is (n−2)×180°, derived by splitting the polygon into n−2 triangles each summing to 180° (quadrilateral 360°, pentagon 540°, hexagon 720°); an exterior angle is on a straight line with its interior angle so they sum to 180°; the sum of all exterior angles is 360° (from 180n − (n−2)×180 = 360); students often confuse a demonstration for a proof

Children (and educated adults) tend to judge a triangle's missing angle as scaling with the triangle's size, contradicting the size-independent angle sum — they reason by mental simulation rather than by the rule
KS3 pupils should derive and use the sum of interior angles of a polygon and the fact that the exterior angles of a polygon sum to 360°
learnerActions: Start with a polygon whose number of sides you can change. Before calculating, predict: what do all its interior angles add to?
Split the polygon into triangles by drawing diagonals from one corner. Count the triangles: a pentagon gives 3, a hexagon gives 4.
Record the running total as (number of triangles)×180°: pentagon 3×180 = 540°, hexagon 4×180 = 720°.
State the general pattern in your own words: splitting from one corner, a convex n-sided polygon always makes n−2 triangles, so the interior sum is (n−2)×180°.
Add two more sides and confirm the sum GROWS with the number of sides — not with the polygon's size.
activities.intendedInsight: The interior-angle sum (n−2)×180° is a consequence of how many triangles the polygon decomposes into, and it depends on the number of sides, not the size.

activities.title: Walk the perimeter: exterior angles total 360°
feedback: If a learner says more sides should give a bigger exterior total, have them walk two different polygons and compare: both complete exactly one full turn (360°).
If a learner reports 360° at a single vertex, point to the straight line at that corner: the interior and its exterior together make 180° there.
An optional mode that accumulates each turn as the marker strides round makes 'one full turn = 360°' concrete; keep it as an illustration, not the only way to reach the result.
activities.rationale: The perimeter-walk turning model makes the 360° exterior total tangible and directly separates the two totals pupils confuse. The exterior sum of 360° regardless of sides is supported by sources (convex KS3 case); the single-vertex 180° pairing is a distinct relationship.
sourceClaims: The interior angle sum of an n-sided polygon is (n−2)×180°, derived by splitting the polygon into n−2 triangles each summing to 180° (quadrilateral 360°, pentagon 540°, hexagon 720°); an exterior angle is on a straight line with its interior angle so they sum to 180°; the sum of all exterior angles is 360° (from 180n − (n−2)×180 = 360); students often confuse a demonstration for a proof

Students commonly confuse interior and exterior angles; they wrongly assume all exterior angles are equal or that more sides means a bigger exterior sum (it is always 360° regardless of the number of sides); the formula 360÷n gives each exterior angle ONLY for a regular polygon — irregular polygons still total 360° but each angle must be found individually
KS3 pupils should derive and use the sum of interior angles of a polygon and the fact that the exterior angles of a polygon sum to 360°
learnerActions: Imagine (or move a marker) walking around the outside of the polygon, turning at each corner to follow the next side.
Add up all the turns you make to get back to your starting direction.
Repeat for convex polygons with different numbers of sides and confirm the turns always total exactly 360°, however many sides there are.
At a single chosen corner, mark the interior angle and the exterior angle sitting together on a straight line, and check they sum to 180°.
Say aloud the difference between the two totals: interior + exterior = 180° at ONE vertex; ALL exterior angles together = 360° for the whole polygon.
activities.intendedInsight: Walking the perimeter of a convex polygon means turning through one full 360° in total, so the exterior angles sum to 360°, regardless of the number of sides — a separate fact from the 180° interior/exterior pair at a single vertex.

activities.title: Regular or irregular: when may you divide by n?
feedback: If a learner divides an irregular polygon's sum by n, point to two visibly different angles in the figure and ask whether they could both equal the quotient; contrast directly with the regular hexagon of the same 720° sum where every angle really is 120°.

If a learner reports 540° as a single interior angle of the pentagon, ask 'is 540° a sensible size for ONE angle in a pentagon?' and prompt the final ÷5 — the method is sound, only the last step was dropped.
An optional regular/irregular toggle where the '÷n' button is available only in regular mode makes the boundary visible; the greying-out illustrates the condition, it does not prove it.
activities.rationale: The equal-angles condition, which every regular polygon meets, is the distinction the topic hinges on. Holding the sum fixed (same-sided regular vs irregular hexagon) and keeping the subtract-from-sum method alongside the ÷n method prevents over-generalising ÷n and separately addresses the forget-to-divide lapse.
sourceClaims: Students commonly confuse interior and exterior angles; they wrongly assume all exterior angles are equal or that more sides means a bigger exterior sum (it is always 360° regardless of the number of sides); the formula 360÷n gives each exterior angle ONLY for a regular polygon — irregular polygons still total 360° but each angle must be found individually
learnerActions: Take a regular pentagon: find the interior sum by triangulation (3×180 = 540°), then find EACH interior angle by dividing by n (540÷5 = 108°).
Find each exterior angle two ways and check they agree: 180 − 108 = 72° and 360÷5 = 72°.

Compare two hexagons that have the SAME interior sum of 720°: a regular hexagon, where ÷6 gives each angle = 720÷6 = 120°, and an irregular hexagon, where the angles are visibly unequal so no single quotient describes them all.

For the irregular hexagon, divide 720 by 6 to get 120°, then compare with the figure: its angles are not all equal, so 120° cannot be each angle — ÷n does not give each angle of a polygon whose angles are unequal (even if one angle happened to equal the quotient).
Instead, find ONE missing angle of the irregular hexagon by subtracting the five known angles from 720°.

Write the rule: you may divide the sum by n to get each angle ONLY when every angle is equal, as in every regular polygon (a rectangle shows that equal angles are enough, even if the sides differ); the sum itself is the same for any hexagon.
activities.intendedInsight: Dividing the interior sum by n (or using 360÷n for exterior) gives each angle ONLY when all the angles are equal, as in a regular polygon. Two polygons with the same number of sides share the same interior sum, but for one with unequal angles a missing angle is found by subtracting the known angles rather than by dividing.

activities.title: Triangle angle sum: 180°, not 360°
feedback: If a learner gives 360 − 70 − 60 = 230°, they are treating the triangle's angles as going 'all the way round' to 360° — re-derive 180° from the torn corners on a straight edge and contrast with a full turn.

Note for the teacher: tearing corners DEMONSTRATES the 180° sum but is not a proof; pupils should also meet the deductive argument (e.g. draw a line through one vertex parallel to the opposite side and use alternate angles).
activities.rationale: The 'triangle sums to 360°' error is documented, and this activity both corrects it and distinguishes demonstration from proof as the pedagogy requires. The torn-corner task is concrete physical evidence; its status as demonstration (not proof) is stated.
sourceClaims: A common documented misconception on a triangle missing-angle item is that the angles sum to 360° (subtracting the known angles from 360)

The interior angle sum of an n-sided polygon is (n−2)×180°, derived by splitting the polygon into n−2 triangles each summing to 180° (quadrilateral 360°, pentagon 540°, hexagon 720°); an exterior angle is on a straight line with its interior angle so they sum to 180°; the sum of all exterior angles is 360° (from 180n − (n−2)×180 = 360); students often confuse a demonstration for a proof
learnerActions: Find the third angle of a triangle whose other two angles are 70° and 60° by subtracting from 180°: 180 − 70 − 60 = 50°.
Tear the three corners off a paper triangle and arrange them against a straight edge; observe they fit along a straight line (180°).
Contrast this straight-line 180° with a full turn of 360° so the two 'wholes' are kept apart.
Explain why you subtracted from 180° and not 360°.
activities.intendedInsight: A triangle's interior angles sum to 180° (a straight line), which is a different whole from the 360° of a full turn; a missing angle is found by subtracting the known angles from 180°.

activities.title: Check and consolidate with mixed questions
feedback: If a learner picks the option that divides an irregular polygon's sum by n, revisit the regular/irregular distinction: ÷n needs equal angles.
If a learner selects an exterior angle when asked for an interior one, return to the straight-line pair at a vertex (they sum to 180°).

Scored questions confirm whether the facts and distinctions are secure, but on their own they do not show the learner deriving the sum by triangulation or reasoning openly about interior/exterior — pair them with the construction activities.
activities.rationale: Structured questions check fluency and surface the exact distractors (irregular ÷n, interior/exterior swap) the topic targets. They are proposed as a complement to, not a replacement for, the derivation work.
sourceClaims: Students commonly confuse interior and exterior angles; they wrongly assume all exterior angles are equal or that more sides means a bigger exterior sum (it is always 360° regardless of the number of sides); the formula 360÷n gives each exterior angle ONLY for a regular polygon — irregular polygons still total 360° but each angle must be found individually
learnerActions: Give the interior-angle sum of a named polygon (e.g. octagon → (8−2)×180 = 1080°).
For a regular polygon, give BOTH an interior angle and its matching exterior angle, and state how they relate (sum to 180° at a vertex).
Answer a question that contrasts interior versus exterior angles, and identify why a tempting wrong option (dividing the sum by n for an irregular polygon whose angles are unequal) is invalid.
Order several polygons by their interior-angle sum and explain what the ordering depends on (number of sides).
activities.intendedInsight: Named-polygon sums, interior/exterior relationships and the regular-only condition can be recalled and applied fluently and distinguished from common distractors.

constraints: Division by n (sum÷n for each interior, 360÷n for each exterior) gives each angle ONLY when all the angles are equal. Every regular polygon has equal angles, and regular polygons are the KS3 focus, but some irregular shapes do too: a non-square rectangle has four 90° angles (360÷4). For polygons with unequal angles, find a missing angle by subtracting the known angles from the sum. Never present ÷n as giving each angle of a polygon whose angles are unequal.

Two polygons with the same number of sides have the same interior-angle sum. Whether all the angles are equal (as in any regular polygon) affects only whether each angle equals sum÷n, not the sum itself.
Keep the two totals distinct: interior + exterior = 180° at ONE vertex; ALL exterior angles together = 360° for the whole polygon.
Tearing off triangle corners onto a straight line DEMONSTRATES the 180° sum; it is not a proof. Pupils should also meet the deductive argument.
The angle sum depends on the number of sides, not on the polygon's size; an enlarged copy of the same shape has the same angles.

When a convex polygon is split from one vertex, an n-sided polygon yields n−2 triangles (not n); diagonals are drawn only from the single chosen vertex, and the two sides meeting at that vertex do not each form a separate triangle base.
The perimeter-walk 'one full turn = 360°' model applies to convex (non-reflex) polygons, the intended KS3 case; the interior-sum (n−2)×180° and subtract-from-sum methods hold for any simple polygon.

Fixed diagrams (tap-to-reveal) can show one triangle split and label interior/exterior at a vertex but cannot let the child vary n or test the regular/irregular boundary; treat them as support, not as inferior in every respect.
Scored/recognition questions assess facts and distinctions but do not by themselves elicit the learner's own triangulation or open interior/exterior reasoning; pair them with construction work.
Polygon angle sums are planar; polyhedron angle defect is a different, later topic and is not needed here.

Optional interactive features (running sum as diagonals are drawn, perimeter-walk accumulator, regular/irregular toggle with ÷n button enabled only in regular mode) are illustrations of the mechanism, not mandatory tools and not evidence that the rules hold.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source lists the KS3 national curriculum citation as verified:false; its claim is used only to describe curriculum expectations, not to assert efficacy.

Self-audit (arithmetic/geometry) checks passed and were retained: triangle 180−70−60=50°; pentagon 3×180=540°, 540÷5=108°, exterior 180−108=72°=360÷5; hexagon 4×180=720°, regular hexagon 720÷6=120°; octagon (8−2)×180=1080°; exterior-sum identity 180n−(n−2)×180=360.

Corrected an overstated claim in the regular/irregular activity: dividing an irregular hexagon's 720° by 6 need not differ from EVERY angle (one angle could coincidentally be 120°); the valid point is that a single quotient cannot describe unequal angles, so ÷n does not apply.

The perimeter-walk one-full-turn model assumes convex polygons; learner examples here are convex, which is the standard KS3 case. The (n−2)×180° interior-sum derivation and the subtract-from-sum method remain valid for any simple polygon.

Original row asserts '3D adds nothing' and that unscripted dialogue 'neither performs the triangulation nor checks the arithmetic' as fit rationales; these are catalog-fit judgements, not established comparative claims, and have been softened to narrowly scoped limits in constraints rather than propagated as universal laws.
The Hart et al. (2018) source concerns triangle size-independence specifically; it is extended here to polygon size-independence, which the source does not directly establish for all polygons.

Retained the original key representation of a regular polygon beside an irregular one with the SAME sum but unequal angles (regular vs irregular hexagon at 720°); no mathematical error was found in that content.

probeDeeper: 'If I made this pentagon twice as big, would each angle change? Why or why not?' — a counterexample targeting size-dependence
'You split the hexagon into 4 triangles — why 4 and not 6?' — pushing the (n−2) structure into a reason
'This hexagon is irregular — can you still divide 720 by 6 to get each angle? Why not?' — a counterexample on the regular-only division
'At this corner, how are the interior and exterior angles related, and how do you know?' — pressing the 180°-at-a-vertex link
assess.correctAnswer: (a) 180 − 70 − 60 = 50°. (b) The hexagon splits into 4 triangles from one vertex, so the interior sum is 4×180 = 720°; a missing angle is 720 minus the other five. (c) Regular pentagon interior sum = 3×180 = 540°, so each interior angle = 540÷5 = 108°; each exterior angle = 180 − 108 = 72° (equivalently 360÷5 = 72°). The child derives the sum by triangulation and divides by n only because the pentagon is stated to be regular.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks a triangle's angles sum to 360° — subtracts the known angles from 360 ('shapes go all the way round to 360')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-derive triangle = 180° from the straight line (tear the three corners onto a straight edge); contrast with the 360° of a full turn so the two wholes are kept apart
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On (a) gives 360−70−60 = 230°, or any answer built on a 360° whole for the triangle

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses interior and exterior angles — gives the exterior when asked for the interior (or vice versa), or treats them as unrelated rather than summing to 180° at the vertex
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the interior and exterior angle at one vertex sitting on a straight line so they must sum to 180°; label both on the same diagram before calculating
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On (c) reports 72° as 'the interior angle' or 108° as 'the exterior', or cannot connect the two at a vertex

errorPatterns.pattern: Divides by n for an IRREGULAR polygon, or assumes all its angles are equal — applies 360÷n or sum÷n without checking regularity
errorPatterns.nextMove: Stress that ÷n gives each angle ONLY when the polygon is regular; for an irregular one, find a missing angle by subtracting the known angles from the sum
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On (b) divides 720 by 6 to 'find each angle' of the irregular hexagon, though its angles differ

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes the angle sum depends on the polygon's SIZE — a bigger triangle/polygon has bigger angles ('the longer side makes a wider angle')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the same-shape polygon enlarged with its angles unchanged; make explicit that the sum depends only on the number of sides, not the size
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Judges or adjusts an angle according to side length or overall size rather than using the fixed sum

errorPatterns.pattern: Reports the interior-angle SUM as if it were a single interior angle — forgets to divide by n for the regular polygon
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'is 540° a sensible size for ONE angle in a pentagon?'; prompt the final ÷5 — the method is right, only the last step was dropped, so scaffold rather than reteach
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On (c) gives 540° as 'each interior angle' of the pentagon instead of 540÷5 = 108°

responseLevels.gap: Cannot find the angles reliably — sums a triangle to 360°, cannot derive a polygon's angle sum, or divides an irregular polygon's sum by n; interior and exterior are confused
responseLevels.full: Derives the interior-angle sum by splitting into n−2 triangles, calculates interior and exterior angles keeping the two distinct, divides by n only for regular polygons, and explains that the sum depends on the number of sides not the size — transferring the method to a polygon with a new number of sides
responseLevels.partial: Uses 180° for the triangle and can recall or apply (n−2)×180° for the sum, but cannot derive it by triangulation, forgets to divide by n (or divides when the polygon is irregular), or confuses interior with exterior — has the formulas as isolated rules, not a connected structure, and cannot transfer to a new polygon or justify why

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child three figures and a pencil: (a) a triangle with two angles marked 70° and 60°; (b) an IRREGULAR hexagon; (c) a regular pentagon. Set them to: (a) find the third angle; (b) find the sum of the interior angles of the hexagon, showing how — invite them to split it up — then find one missing angle given the other five; (c) find EACH interior angle and EACH exterior angle of the regular pentagon. Watch whether they subtract from 180 (not 360) for the triangle, whether they split the hexagon into triangles to get (n−2)×180, whether they divide by n only because the pentagon is regular, and whether they keep interior and exterior angles distinct.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands subtracts the triangle's angles from 180 and derives the hexagon sum by triangulating; a child with the classic error subtracts from 360 (a visibly different answer) or divides the irregular hexagon's sum by 6. Asking for EACH angle of the regular pentagon and its exterior angle exposes interior/exterior confusion and the forget-to-÷n lapse; the irregular hexagon exposes those who apply ÷n indiscriminately.

sources.claim: The interior angle sum of an n-sided polygon is (n−2)×180°, derived by splitting the polygon into n−2 triangles each summing to 180° (quadrilateral 360°, pentagon 540°, hexagon 720°); an exterior angle is on a straight line with its interior angle so they sum to 180°; the sum of all exterior angles is 360° (from 180n − (n−2)×180 = 360); students often confuse a demonstration for a proof
sources.source: NCETM KS3 Subject Knowledge Audit 6.1 'Geometrical Properties'

sources.claim: Students commonly confuse interior and exterior angles; they wrongly assume all exterior angles are equal or that more sides means a bigger exterior sum (it is always 360° regardless of the number of sides); the formula 360÷n gives each exterior angle ONLY for a regular polygon — irregular polygons still total 360° but each angle must be found individually
sources.source: Third Space Learning, 'Sum of Exterior Angles of a Polygon'

sources.claim: Children (and educated adults) tend to judge a triangle's missing angle as scaling with the triangle's size, contradicting the size-independent angle sum — they reason by mental simulation rather than by the rule
sources.source: Hart, Dillon, Marantan, Cardenas, Spelke & Mahadevan (2018), 'The statistical shape of geometric reasoning', Scientific Reports 8:12906

sources.claim: A common documented misconception on a triangle missing-angle item is that the angles sum to 360° (subtracting the known angles from 360)
sources.source: Craig Barton / Eedi, 'Angles in a Triangle: Guess the Misconception'

sources.claim: KS3 pupils should derive and use the sum of interior angles of a polygon and the fact that the exterior angles of a polygon sum to 360°
sources.source: National curriculum in England: mathematics programmes of study (KS3)

pedagogy.summary: 'Finding a fraction or percentage OF an amount' is the operator interpretation of multiplication: 'of' means multiply. The prior 'a/b of q' work becomes fully general here — 3/4 of 200 = 3/4 × 200 = 150; 20% of 60 = 0.2 × 60 = 12. The pedagogical crux is that children fluent in unit-fraction-of (÷ by denominator) must generalise to non-unit fractions and to percentages, and must accept that multiplying can make a quantity SMALLER. Teach it as one operator acting on a quantity — bar/hundred-grid partition first, then the ×-as-operator equation — and anchor it in real contexts (discounts, tax, portions) where the operator chains.
bestPractices: Build from the known unit-fraction case: to find 3/4 of 200, first find 1/4 (÷4 = 50) then take 3 of them (×3 = 150); make the two-step structure explicit before compressing to 3/4 × 200
Represent the amount as a whole bar or a hundred-grid and physically partition it, so 'of' is seen as partition-then-take, matching the (a/b)×q meaning
Convert percentages to fractions/decimals deliberately (20% = 20/100 = 0.2) so 'percentage of' reuses the identical operator, not a separate rule
Use realistic multi-step contexts — 20%-off a £45 jacket, VAT, tips, recipe portions — so the operator is chained and the answer's reasonableness can be judged
Contrast a scaling-up operator (150% of, 5/4 of) with a scaling-down one so children see 'of' is not tied to 'gets smaller'
keyRepresentations: Bar model of the whole amount partitioned into b equal parts, a of them shaded
Hundred-grid / percentage bar for percentage-of
Double number line pairing the amount with 0-100% for percentage-of
The operator equation a/b × q, written beside the partition it summarises
commonMisconceptions: Finds the unit fraction and stops (200÷4 = 50 offered as '3/4 of 200'), forgetting to take a copies
Converts the percentage wrongly — 25% treated as ÷25 or ×25, or 20% as 0.02 / 2.0
Believes 'of'/multiplication must enlarge, so distrusts a correct smaller answer
Adds/subtracts the percentage directly to the amount instead of operating (20% of 60 read as 60+20 or 60-20)

learn.summary: Teach 'a fraction/percentage OF an amount' as one multiplicative operator: 'of' means multiply. Build from the known unit-fraction case (3/4 of 200 = find 1/4 by ÷4 = 50, then take 3 = 150), make percentage-of reuse the identical operator via conversion (20% = 20/100 = 0.2, so 20% of 60 = 0.2×60 = 12), and anchor it in real discount/tax/portion contexts. The conceptual crux is accepting that multiplying can make a quantity smaller when the operator is below 1, while an operator above 1 grows it. Visual partition (bar, hundred-grid, double number line) should precede and sit beside the ×-as-operator equation.

activities.title: Operator machine: set an amount, set an operator, watch it partition
feedback: If a learner stops at the unit fraction (gives 50 for 3/4 of 200), re-shade ONE quarter (50) then ask 'how many quarters is three-quarters?' and shade the other two before recompressing to 3/4 ×.
If a learner expects the answer to always be bigger, direct them to flip the operator past 1 and back under 1 and compare each result with the starting amount.
If '20% off £45' is answered as 45 − 20 = £25, insist the operator acts ON the price: find 20% OF 45 first (= £9), shade it, then take it away.
activities.rationale: Setting the amount, choosing the operator and seeing the live partition makes the partition-then-take meaning concrete and lets the learner test the 'does of always shrink?' question directly; chaining a real discount shows the operator applied in context. The shrink/grow toggle and live recolouring are offered as one interaction example to make the mechanism visible, not as the only valid medium.
sourceClaims: Finding a fraction of a fraction / of a quantity is fraction multiplication, and multiplying can produce a result smaller than the starting amount — a documented source of student surprise the operator interpretation must confront
Fractions and ratios function as operators/multipliers on quantities (a/b of q = a/b × q); percentage of a quantity is the same operator via decimal conversion

By age 11 pupils solve problems involving the calculation of percentages (e.g. of measures and money) and find fractions of amounts using multiplication; 'of' as an operator is a Year 6 / KS3 expectation
learnerActions: Enter an amount shown as a whole bar or hundred-grid (e.g. 200).

Work one example at a time, each with its own entered amount: with 200 in the bar apply the fraction 3/4; then re-enter 60 and apply the percentage 20% — watch the same machine partition into equal parts and shade the taken portion each time.
Read the equation printed beside each partition: 3/4 × 200 = 150; and separately 20% = 20/100 = 0.2, so 0.2 × 60 = 12.
Move the operator above 1 (e.g. 150% of 200 = 300, or 5/4 of 200 = 250) and below 1, and describe in words whether the result grew or shrank from the starting amount and why.

Second stage — a shop: start from a £45 price, apply '20% off' so 20% of £45 = £9 is shaded (a double number line pairing £0–£45 with 0–100% can show where 20% sits), then subtract to reach the £36 paid; state the two separate moves — find 20% OF the price, THEN take it away.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Of' is one action — partition the whole into equal parts, then take a copies — whether it wears a fraction hat or a percent hat. Whether the result is bigger or smaller than you started is decided by the operator's size, not by multiplication 'always enlarging'.

activities.title: Worked bar in stages: make the two-step structure inspectable
feedback: If only the ÷denominator step appears, ask what the numerator tells you to do with the unit parts you found.
If the 'why smaller' prompt stalls, point to how many of the four parts were taken versus how many make the whole.
activities.rationale: A staged, revealable worked example exposes the hidden two-step structure that fluent learners often compress, and a parallel percentage bar shows the operator reused. A fixed worked example of this kind supports inspection of structure; it does not let the learner vary the operator themselves, so pair it with exploratory or production work.
sourceClaims: Finding a fraction of a fraction / of a quantity is fraction multiplication, and multiplying can produce a result smaller than the starting amount — a documented source of student surprise the operator interpretation must confront
Fractions and ratios function as operators/multipliers on quantities (a/b of q = a/b × q); percentage of a quantity is the same operator via decimal conversion
learnerActions: On a whole bar for 3/4 of 200, split it into four equal parts and name one part (1/4 = 50).
Take (shade) three of those parts and record the second move explicitly (×3 → 150).

Repeat the same staged partition on a hundred-grid for 20% of 60, reading '20 of the hundred parts' and reaching 12; a double number line pairing 60 with 0–100% can sit alongside to show 20% as a position.
Answer the prompt 'why is the answer smaller than 200?' in your own words.
activities.intendedInsight: Finding a non-unit fraction of an amount is two linked steps — divide to find the unit part, then multiply to take a copies — and percentage-of is the same partition read out of a hundred.

activities.title: In-role market trader: reasoning about more-or-less
feedback: If the learner detaches the percentage from the price, ask 'twenty percent OF what?' before any subtraction.
If they claim the £-off stays the same when the price doubles, have them compute 20% of £90 (= £18) and compare with 20% of £45 (= £9).
activities.rationale: Spoken reasoning and responsive challenge can elicit and probe the shrink/scale intuition and the reasonableness judgement; keep numbers small enough for mental work. Discussion complements rather than replaces the visual partitioning and written computation, which benefit from a visual surface. No source establishes dialogue as superior to another medium here, so this is a qualified proposal.
learnerActions: Take on a market-trader/shopkeeper exchange where you compute successive small-number discounts and portions mentally.
Before each calculation, answer the trader's probe: 'is that more or less than you started with?'
Explain to the trader what the money taken off actually is — e.g. '£9 is 20% OF the £45 price'.
Reason about a what-if: if the price doubled from £45 to £90, would the £-off double? Justify (20% of £90 = £18, double the £9).
activities.intendedInsight: The operator is applied to a specific quantity, so the amount taken off scales with that quantity; judging reasonableness ('more or less than I started') is part of operating correctly.

activities.title: Mixed operator check with targeted distractors
feedback: Choosing 50 flags the missing ×numerator step — return to taking three of the quarters.
Landing on 3, 120 or 1.2 flags a conversion fault — rebuild 20% = 20/100 = 0.2 on a hundred-grid.
Landing on £25 flags subtracting the raw percentage — find 20% OF 45 (= £9) first, then subtract.
activities.rationale: A scored check with distractors built from the documented error patterns (unit-fraction-stop, percentage mis-conversion, operate-vs-subtract confusion) surfaces which specific operator move is broken. Such a check verifies fluency and diagnoses faults; selecting a correct option does not itself elicit independent construction, so it should follow the construction and visual activities rather than replace them.
learnerActions: Set 1/4 of 200, then choose 3/4 of 200 from options that include the unit-fraction-stop value 50.
Complete the conversion 20% = 0.__ then compute × 60, with options reflecting common mis-conversions (3, 120, 1.2) alongside the correct 12.
Solve a discount word step for the £45 jacket with distractors £25 (from 45−20) and other near-value options alongside the correct £36, showing the 20%-of-45 = £9 step.
Read the feedback given after each item, which names which operator move was right or wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: Operating correctly means completing BOTH the divide and the take-a-copies step, converting the percentage cleanly, and operating-then-subtracting in a discount — not pattern-matching to a single rule.

constraints: Build from the known unit-fraction case before compressing: make the two-step structure (÷denominator to find the unit part, then ×numerator to take a copies) explicit for non-unit fractions.
Convert percentages deliberately (20% = 20/100 = 0.2) so percentage-of reuses the identical operator rather than becoming a separate rule.
Deliberately contrast an operator below 1 (shrinks) with one above 1 (grows, e.g. 150% of, 5/4 of) so learners do not glue 'multiply' to 'gets bigger'.

Keep each operator example's amount explicit so the printed equation matches the amount actually set (e.g. 3/4 of 200, 20% of 60, 20% of £45) — do not silently change the amount between a stated setup and its result.
Use realistic multi-step contexts (discount, VAT, tips, recipe portions) and require judging the answer's reasonableness.

The staged worked bar is a scaffold: it makes structure inspectable but the learner cannot vary the operator, so it must not be the only format — pair it with activity where the learner sets the operator and with production tasks.
The scored check assesses and diagnoses fluency; it does not by itself build the operator meaning and should follow, not replace, the constructive work.
Recognition/multiple-choice responses do not elicit independent construction; include tasks where the learner computes and shows method, not only selects an answer.
Discount tasks require two distinct moves — find the percentage OF the amount, then subtract — and both should be stated separately.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The original listed one source as verified (IES/WWC Practice Guide) and two as unverified (DfE National Curriculum, Common Core); verification status is carried as-is and not upgraded.

Arithmetic self-audit passed: 3/4 of 200 = 150 (1/4 = 50, ×3 = 150); 20% of 60 = 0.2×60 = 12; 20% of £45 = £9, £45 − £9 = £36; 20% of £90 = £18 (doubles, consistent with the probe); 150% of 200 = 300; 5/4 of 200 = 250. Distractor values (50, 3, 120, 1.2, £25) are intended wrong answers and are labelled as such.

Fixed an internal inconsistency in Activity 1: the machine's single '200' amount was being paired with a 20%-of-60 equation (20% of 200 would be 40). Each operator example now states its own amount so setup and printed result agree.

The DfE curriculum claim is retained only in Activity 1, where it names the operator/multiplication content directly; it is a curriculum-expectation statement and is not used as evidence of any medium's efficacy.

The market-trader (conversation) activity has no source claim attached: the available sources support the mathematical content/curriculum expectation but do not establish that spoken dialogue elicits the more-or-less/scaling intuition better than another medium, so efficacy is left as a qualified proposal.

The original 3D 'poor-fit' entry asserted '3D adds nothing' — this is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law, so it was dropped rather than propagated as a universal claim. Fraction/percentage-of is treated as a planar partition operation, kept only as a narrow affordance rationale.
The 'shrink-toggle/operator machine' is preserved as an optional interaction example that makes the mechanism concrete; it is not asserted as the only medium that can teach this.

probeDeeper: Your answer to 3/4 of 200 is smaller than 200 — is that allowed? Why or why not?
How would 150% of 200 be different from 3/4 of 200 — bigger or smaller than 200, and how do you know before calculating?
The jacket dropped by £9. What was that £9 — nine of what?
If the jacket had been £90 instead of £45, would the £-off double? Explain.

errorPatterns.pattern: Finds the unit fraction and stops: '3/4 of 200? 200 ÷ 4 is 50' — takes one part, not three ('it's quarters, so I divide by four')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the two-step structure on a bar: shade ONE quarter (50), then ask 'how many quarters is three-quarters?' and shade the other two; make 'a copies of the unit part' explicit before recompressing to 3/4 ×
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 50 for 3/4 of 200 (or divides by the numerator), method shows the ÷denominator step but not the ×numerator step

errorPatterns.pattern: Mis-converts the percentage: treats 20% as ×20, ÷20, 2.0 or 0.02 rather than 0.2 — 'per cent means out of a hundred' not carried into the operator ('20% of 60 is 60 ÷ 20 = 3' or '× 20 = 1200')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild 20% = 20/100 = 0.2 on a hundred-grid and read '20 of the hundred parts of 60'; connect back to percentage-as-fraction before re-attempting
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer to 20% of 60 is 3, 1200, 120 or 1.2 rather than 12; the conversion line shows the wrong place-value or wrong operation

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds or subtracts the percentage as a raw number instead of operating: '20% off £45' read as 45 − 20 = £25 (the % detaches from the amount it acts on)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist the operator acts ON the price: 'find 20% OF 45 first — how much money is that?' shade it on the price bar, then take it away; separate the two moves
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Jacket answer is £25 (or 60−20=40 for the second part); no 20%-of-45 = £9 step appears

responseLevels.gap: Cannot connect 'of' to multiplication: gives 50, or subtracts the percentage as a number, or cannot start the discount; treats each item as an unrelated rule.
responseLevels.full: Operates fluently across fraction-of, percentage-of and the multi-step discount, converting the percentage cleanly and judging the answer's reasonableness; explains that 'of' = × and that an operator below 1 shrinks and above 1 grows, transferring the same machine to an unfamiliar context.
responseLevels.partial: Operates correctly on straightforward cases (3/4 of 200 = 150, 20% of 60 = 12) but the method is a memorised procedure — cannot say why the answer may be smaller, or stumbles on the discount because operate-then-subtract is not seen as the SAME operator applied to a context.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these out and show your method for each: first, 3/4 of 200; then 20% of 60. Now a real one — a jacket costs £45 and it has 20% off in a sale. What do you pay?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the METHOD separates the child who genuinely operates from the one who pattern-matches: the 3/4 case exposes whether they take all three quarters or stop at the unit fraction; the 20% case exposes their percentage-to-operator conversion; and the discount forces them to operate THEN subtract, so a child who just does 45−20 or 45−9-without-the-9-being-20%-of-45 reveals a broken operator. A child reasoning correctly produces 150 / 12 / £36 by partition-then-take; a child reasoning wrongly lands on 50, or 1.2/120, or £25, and the wrong number names the exact fault.

pedagogy.summary: Simple chance experiments are the child's hands-on entry to probability: flip a coin, roll a die, or draw counters many times, record each trial in a tally chart, and compare what happened with what was expected. The procedural goal is disciplined trial-by-trial recording and a sensible read of the results — seeing that outcomes cluster near the expected split without matching it exactly, and that each trial is independent of the last.
bestPractices: Have children predict the expected outcome first ('about half heads'), then run and record, so the comparison is theirs to make
Enforce one-tally-per-trial recording as the trial happens, not reconstruction from memory, and total the marks against the number of trials
Pool results across the class to show a larger sample landing closer to the expected split than any one child's 20 trials
Explicitly discuss why 13 heads out of 20 does NOT mean the coin is broken — short runs vary
Confront 'it's due' / 'heads again' talk on the spot: the coin has no memory, each flip is independent
keyRepresentations: Tally chart / frequency table (one row per outcome)
Coins, dice, and bags of counters as trial-generators
Bar or block chart of observed frequencies against the expected line
Prediction-vs-result comparison
commonMisconceptions: Expecting the experiment to match the theoretical split exactly, and concluding the device is biased when it does not (law of small numbers)
Recency thinking — predicting the next trial from the recent run ('it's been heads four times, so tails is due', or 'heads is on a streak')
Recording carelessly — backfilling tallies or losing count so the total does not match the number of trials
Treating the result of a small experiment as the true probability rather than an estimate

learn.summary: Children aged 9–10 learn probability through hands-on chance experiments: predict an expected outcome, flip a coin / roll a die / draw counters many times, record each trial one-tally-at-a-time in a tally chart, and compare what happened with what was expected. Core insights: a fair device produces outcomes that cluster near but rarely exactly match the expected split, so expecting an exact match and concluding the device is biased from too few trials is the law-of-small-numbers error; each trial is independent of the last (no 'it's due' recency thinking); and a small experiment estimates rather than proves the true probability. With a fair device, running or pooling many more trials usually brings the observed proportion closer to the expected split, though not to an exact match.

activities.title: Predict, flip, tally: run and read a coin experiment
feedback: If a child gets 13 heads and 7 tails and says the coin is rigged or that they 'did it wrong', don't reteach the mechanics — explain that 20 trials is too few to judge fairness and short runs vary. Pool their flips with classmates' to reach 100+ and see whether the proportion moves nearer to half (with a fair coin it usually does, though not exactly).

If the tally total doesn't equal 20, or marks were backfilled from memory, this is an execution lapse: support a one-mark-immediately-per-flip routine with a running count rather than reteaching the concept.
If the child did get close to half, affirm reading it as 'about half, but not exactly ten' — close to the expected split rather than an exact match.
activities.rationale: Conducting and recording is a procedure best learned by doing it, so the child owns the prediction-versus-result comparison. Predicting first makes the comparison theirs; one-tally-per-trial enforces disciplined recording; totalling against the trial count catches miscounts. Sources note that a small sample need not match the theoretical probability and that concluding bias from too few trials is a documented mistake.
sourceClaims: A small sample need not match the theoretical probability, and concluding bias from too few trials is a documented mistake: '20 times is not enough trials' — the more trials, the closer relative frequency gets to the theoretical probability.
learnerActions: Before flipping, predict the expected number of heads in 20 flips (about 10) and write it down.
Set up a tally chart with one row per outcome (heads, tails).
Flip the coin 20 times, marking exactly one tally per flip AS it happens — not reconstructing from memory afterward.
Total the marks and check the total equals the number of flips (20).
Describe what you notice: was it about half? Exactly ten? How close to your prediction?
activities.intendedInsight: A fair device produces outcomes clustered near the expected split but not exactly matching it; disciplined one-tally-per-trial recording is part of the procedure, and the total must reconcile with the number of trials.

activities.title: Watch the proportion settle: scale up the number of trials
feedback: If a child thinks 20 trials already proved the coin fair or unfair, draw attention to how much the proportion still wobbles at 20 versus how it usually steadies by a few hundred — the gap between the proportion of heads and one-half tends to narrow with more trials (even though the difference in raw counts of heads and tails can grow).
Name explicitly that the result of a small experiment is an estimate of the probability, not the true probability itself.
activities.rationale: Pooling to a larger sample and watching the proportion steady confronts the law of small numbers concretely — children typically see short-run variation give way to proportions close to (not exactly at) the expected split. A live tally with a running relative-frequency bar (that wobbles then steadies) and a 'run 20' versus 'run 500' contrast make this mechanism visible; manual single-trial mode preserves one-tally-per-trial experience before auto-running. These interaction examples are optional illustrations of the mechanism, not required tooling.
sourceClaims: A small sample need not match the theoretical probability, and concluding bias from too few trials is a documented mistake: '20 times is not enough trials' — the more trials, the closer relative frequency gets to the theoretical probability.
learnerActions: After a lopsided small sample (e.g. 13 heads in 20), keep going: pool results across the class, or keep flipping toward 100, 200, 500 trials.
Track both the growing tally AND the running proportion of heads as more trials accumulate.
Compare a 'small run' (20) against a 'large run' (hundreds): notice which lands closer to the expected half (usually, but not always, the large run).
State what the larger sample tells you that the small one couldn't.
activities.intendedInsight: For a fair coin, as the number of trials grows the observed proportion tends to move toward the expected split and steady; a lopsided 20-trial result can easily happen by chance with a fair coin, so on its own it is not evidence of bias. The small experiment gives an estimate, not the true probability.

activities.title: The coin has no memory: confront recency thinking
feedback: If the child predicts the next flip from the recent run ('it's been heads four times, tails is due') or seems surprised a streak 'kept going', state plainly that the coin has no memory and each flip is independent, then test it by predicting-then-flipping several times.
Reinforce: with a fair coin, a run of heads is just as likely to be followed by heads as by tails.
activities.rationale: Recency errors — both negative recency ('a tail is due') and positive recency (expecting a streak to continue) — reflect a failure to treat trials as independent and are documented across childhood. Predict-then-flip repetition surfaces the belief and tests it against outcomes so the child confronts it directly.
sourceClaims: Recency errors — both 'a tail is due' (negative recency, from the representativeness heuristic) and expecting a streak to continue (positive recency) — reflect a failure to treat successive trials as independent, and are documented across childhood.
learnerActions: After a run of several heads in a row, predict the next flip (or say it cannot be predicted) and say WHY.
Flip again and check; repeat the predict-then-flip several times.
Explain whether a streak of heads makes tails any more 'due' on the next flip.
State in your own words why each flip stays 50-50 regardless of what came before.
activities.intendedInsight: Successive trials are independent: the coin has no memory, so neither 'tails is due' (negative recency) nor 'heads is on a streak' (positive recency) is correct — each flip remains 50-50 whatever preceded it.

activities.title: Interpretation check: does a small sample prove bias?
feedback: If a child answers that 13–7 proves bias, point back to short-run variation and the need for more trials to judge fairness.

If a child says the next flip is 'due' to be tails (or that heads is 'hot'), restate that each flip is independent, so the streak does not change the odds; for a fair coin, heads and tails stay equally likely at 50-50.
activities.rationale: A recognition or multiple-choice format can test interpretation of a completed tally and reasoning about bias and independence, but it cannot deliver the hands-on conducting-and-recording practice; use it as a check alongside, not instead of, performing an experiment. This supports interpretation only — it does not elicit independent construction of the experiment.
sourceClaims: A small sample need not match the theoretical probability, and concluding bias from too few trials is a documented mistake: '20 times is not enough trials' — the more trials, the closer relative frequency gets to the theoretical probability.
learnerActions: Read a completed tally showing 13 heads and 7 tails out of 20 flips.
Decide whether this proves the coin is unfair, and explain your reasoning.
Say how you could check whether the coin is actually biased.
Given a streak of four heads, say whether the next flip is more likely to be heads, more likely tails, or neither — and explain why.
activities.intendedInsight: Judging fairness and independence from a completed record: 13 of 20 heads does not prove bias because 20 trials is too few; checking requires many more trials; and no run of heads changes the next flip's odds — for a fair coin, heads and tails remain equally likely.

constraints: The child must actually perform and tally the experiment; a recognition-only or reading-a-completed-tally task does not elicit the independent conducting-and-recording skill the topic requires.
Enforce one-tally-per-trial recording as the trial happens, not reconstruction from memory; total the marks against the number of trials so a mismatch is caught.
Have children predict the expected outcome before running, so the prediction-versus-result comparison is theirs to make.

Distinguish an execution lapse (careless recording, miscounting) from a conceptual error (expecting an exact match, recency thinking) — support the recording habit for the former, confront the belief for the latter.
A completed-tally interpretation check supports reasoning about bias and independence but is a supplement; it does not replace conducting the experiment.

Physical tossing (coin/die) and on-screen simulators offer different experiences — tactile realism versus the ability to scale rapidly to hundreds of trials; recording and comparing frequencies is not a spatial task, so neither is universally required. Treat the choice as a trade-off, not a ranking.
A small experiment yields an estimate of the probability, not the true probability; make this explicit to avoid treating a 20-trial result as definitive.
Live-tally, running proportion bar, 'run 20 vs run 500' contrast, and manual single-trial mode are optional illustrations of the mechanism, not mandatory tooling.
After any run, each flip of a fair coin stays 50-50 and heads is exactly as likely as tails next — never present one outcome as 'most likely' following a streak.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and the cited claims support teaching principles rather than proving any specific activity was tested.

Self-audit of the probability logic: for a fair coin, each flip is independent and stays 50-50 regardless of prior outcomes; a run of heads makes neither heads nor tails more likely next. The expected value in 20 flips is 10 heads, but the actual result varies and clustering near (not exactly at) 10 is normal — all consistent across the source fields.

Correction confirmed: the summary names 'law of small numbers' as the misconception (expecting a small sample to match / inferring bias from too few trials), consistent with the original pedagogy, not as a label for the correct clustering fact.

Correction confirmed: the interpretation-check action asks whether the next flip after a streak is more likely heads, tails, or neither, so 'neither — equally likely' is available; the recency-activity opening action also allows 'cannot be predicted' as a valid response.

Independent re-audit found the probability logic coherent from first action through every feedback item; no further errors or contradictions were introduced, and the two prior corrections hold at every learner-facing occurrence.

The source framing that a linear quiz 'cannot' deliver the conducting skill and dialogue 'cannot' deliver recording practice was softened to scoped affordances/limits rather than universal impossibility claims; the genuine objective limit (recognition-only tasks do not elicit independent construction) is retained.

The claim that a 3D toss 'buys little' over a 2D simulator was reframed as a trade-off (tactile realism vs rapid scaling) rather than a ranking, since comparative efficacy is not established by the sources.

probeDeeper: You got 13 heads and 7 tails — does that prove the coin is unfair? How could you check?
It just landed heads four times in a row. What do you think the next flip will be, and why?
If you flipped it 200 times instead of 20, what would you expect the tally to look like?
Did you get exactly 10 heads? Should you have expected to? Why or why not?
assess.correctAnswer: A correct performance: the child predicts about half (roughly 10 heads), sets up a tally with one row per outcome, marks exactly one tally per flip AS it happens, totals 20 marks for 20 flips, and reads the result sensibly — 'about half, but not exactly ten' — treating it as close to the expected split rather than an exact match, and does not claim the next flip is 'due' to be a particular side.

errorPatterns.pattern: Expects the small experiment to match the theoretical split exactly and concludes the coin is biased when it does not
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach the mechanics — pool their flips with others' to reach 100+ and show the proportion settling near half; name that 20 trials is too few to judge fairness (the seed of the experimental-vs-theoretical topic)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On getting 13 heads and 7 tails, declares the coin unfair or that they 'did it wrong'

errorPatterns.pattern: Recency thinking — predicts the next trial from the recent run ('it's been heads four times, tails is due', or 'heads is hot')
errorPatterns.nextMove: State plainly that the coin has no memory — each flip is independent and stays 50-50 regardless of what came before; test it by predicting-then-flipping several times
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Announces a prediction for the next flip based on the previous outcomes, or seems surprised the streak 'kept going'

errorPatterns.pattern: Records carelessly — backfills tallies or loses count so the total does not match the number of trials
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold a one-mark-immediately-per-flip routine and a running count; this is an execution lapse, so support the recording habit rather than reteaching the concept
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Tally total ≠ 20, or the child reconstructs marks from memory after flipping rather than marking each in turn

responseLevels.gap: Records unsystematically (miscounts, backfills) or treats the outcome as predictable/exact; uses recency to predict the next flip; cannot relate the result to the prediction
responseLevels.full: Records systematically one-per-trial, predicts about half, reads the outcome as close-to-but-not-exactly expected, attributes the gap to too few trials, and treats each flip as independent of the last
responseLevels.partial: Records accurately and states an expectation, but reads any deviation as the coin being unfair, expects an exact match, or shows recency thinking — lists results without linking short-run variation to the small number of trials

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a coin and a blank tally chart and say: 'Before you start, tell me roughly how many heads you expect in 20 flips. Now flip the coin 20 times, recording each result, then tell me what you notice.' (Set the task and WATCH — do not tell them how to record or how to interpret. Watch how they tally, whether they predict the next flip from the last few, and how they explain the gap between 'about 10' and what they actually got.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching separates the child who tallies one-mark-per-trial and reads roughly-half sensibly from one who backfills or miscounts, declares the coin broken on getting 13–7, or says 'tails is due' mid-run. The doing exposes law-of-small-numbers and recency beliefs that a written answer would hide.

pedagogy.summary: At 10-11 the reasoning practice reaches its primary-school ceiling: formal, multi-step arguments and their sharpest tool, the counter-example. A child chains angle facts to PROVE a given angle must be 60° (not measure it), finds and explains an error in a peer's fraction division, and — the signature move — disproves a false conjecture such as 'multiplying always makes bigger' with a single case (×1/2 makes smaller). This is where the empirical→deductive asymmetry Hoyles & Küchemann document becomes explicit content: one counter-example kills a universal claim, while no number of confirming examples establishes it. SMP3's critique half is now central — arguments span fractions, ratio, algebra and geometry, and a competent Y6 reasoner locates a flawed step, explains why it fails, and offers a correct alternative. Teaching aims at the felt logic of implication: 'if… then…', the difference between a claim and its converse, and why a counter-example is decisive.
bestPractices: Make the counter-example a taught tool: give false 'always/sometimes/never' conjectures ('multiplying makes bigger', 'the more sides, the bigger the angles') and reward the single case that breaks them, per Hoyles & Küchemann's finding that a counter-example reveals WHY a claim is false

Require proof by chained fact, not measurement: to show an angle is 60°, insist on a logical progression of angle facts ('angles on a line sum to 180°, and these two are 60° and 60°, therefore…'), reserving measuring for checking
