Use peer critique across arenas — a flawed fraction division ('invert the first fraction'), a mis-added ratio, a misaligned calculation — and demand 'which step, why, and what's the correct method' (SMP3 explain-the-flaw plus alternative)
Draw the claim/converse distinction with concrete cases so 'if it's a square then it has four right angles' is not confused with its converse
Keep pressing convince→justify: a confident explanation that has gaps is convincing; a correct, complete because/therefore chain is justifying — name which one the child has produced
keyRepresentations: A single well-chosen counter-example as a disproof object (e.g. 6 × 1/2 = 3 against 'multiplying makes bigger')
Chained angle-fact diagrams (angles on a line / in a triangle / vertically opposite) building to a proved value
Scaling picture of multiplication (× less than 1 shrinks, × 1 keeps, × more than 1 grows) to reason about product size without computing
A because/therefore proof frame linking givens through steps to conclusion
commonMisconceptions: 'Multiplication always makes bigger / division always makes smaller' — the whole-number generalisation that fails for factors below 1
Confirming a conjecture with examples and calling it proved (empirical proof scheme)
Confusing a statement with its converse ('if square then 4 right angles' ⇒ 'if 4 right angles then square')
Inverting the wrong fraction in division, or 'dividing straight across', and critiquing only by the odd-looking answer rather than the faulty step
Believing a proved geometric result holds only for the specific diagram drawn

learn.summary: For 10-11 year-olds, this builds formal, multi-step mathematical argument and its critique half: constructing proofs by chaining facts (not measuring), finding and explaining errors in a peer's working, and the signature move of disproving a false 'always' conjecture with a single counter-example. Learners meet the proof asymmetry — one honest counter-example kills a universal claim, while confirming examples cannot establish it unless every possible case is checked (impossible for claims about all numbers) — and the logic of implication, including the claim/converse distinction. Activities span fractions, ratio, algebra and geometry, with a live adversarial dialogue as the primary vehicle and a manipulable conjecture/proof workspace, static critique cards, and a recognition warm-up as complementary alternatives serving different purposes.

activities.title: The confident conjecture champion (adversarial dialogue)
feedback: Revoice and extend the learner's chain rather than scoring it; when they offer only confirming examples, press 'so is it proved, or could there still be a breaker?'
If they name a counter-example, ask them to say exactly why that one case is enough to sink the whole 'always' rule.

When they repair the champion's fraction-division flip, ask them to state which step was wrong and what the correct step is (inverting the divisor, not the first fraction), not just that the answer looked odd.
Separate convincing from justifying: if an explanation sounds confident but has gaps, name it as convincing; if it is a complete because/therefore chain, name it as justifying.
activities.rationale: Defending a proof against a skeptic and disproving a confident false claim are naturally real-time exchanges; a responsive adversary can press on the learner's specific gaps and adapt to a patched claim or a converse in a way a fixed artefact cannot — an affordance of responsiveness, not a claim that only dialogue can teach this logic (the workspace activity also makes the if/therefore structure tangible). This is a research-informed proposal, not a tested intervention.
sourceClaims: SMP3: construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others; make conjectures; use counterexamples; distinguish correct logic from flawed and explain the flaw; older students can compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments.

A general counter-example gives insight into WHY a statement is false; empirical/example-based reasoning predominates and the shift to understanding logical implication (and the claim/converse distinction) is slow and fragile, so one counter-example being decisive is a hard-won idea.

Primary proof types include proof by counter-example; specific confirming examples do not constitute a watertight proof, and recognising this is a key step on the describe→explain→convince→justify→prove ladder.
learnerActions: Face an in-role character who asserts a universal claim with total confidence: 'Multiplying ALWAYS makes a number bigger — I've tried 3×4, 5×6, 10×10, works every time. So it's proved, right?'
Decide whether piling up more agreeing examples settles it, or whether you must HUNT for a case that breaks the claim.
Produce and state a decisive counter-example, e.g. '6 times a half is three — that's smaller, so it's not always,' and explain why that single case is enough.

When the champion patches the claim ('okay, multiplying always makes bigger OR the same') test the patch again: × 1/2 still shrinks it (so it breaks the patch), while × 1 only reaches the 'same' boundary the patch now allows.

When the champion defends a flawed fraction division ('just flip the FIRST fraction') locate the faulty step, say why it fails, and give the correct method (invert the divisor — the second fraction — then multiply).
Answer the champion's probes: 'Is that a proof or just examples?' and 'Does the opposite — the converse — also hold?'
activities.intendedInsight: A universal claim is destroyed by one honest counter-example, while confirming cases cannot prove it unless every possible case is checked (impossible for claims about all numbers); constructing arguments and critiquing flawed ones are the same reasoning practice, and a claim is not the same as its converse.

activities.title: Conjecture-testing and proof-building workspace
feedback: Report whether the chosen counter-example truly breaks the claim as scoped (for 'multiplying makes bigger': is the product actually not bigger, either smaller as with × 1/2 or equal as with × 1?), not merely whether a value was placed.
Report whether the proof chain is complete — every step justified from givens to conclusion — rather than answer-matching the final angle.
On the fraction-division panel, confirm whether the tapped step is the genuinely faulty one (inverting the first fraction instead of the divisor) and whether the selected method is correct.
activities.rationale: A manipulable workspace makes the decisive-single-case logic and the if/therefore structure tangible: dragging a value to watch a claim collapse and snapping facts into a chain externalise the reasoning. The live recolouring/collapse and drag interactions are illustrative mechanisms, not required tooling. Research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: A general counter-example gives insight into WHY a statement is false; empirical/example-based reasoning predominates and the shift to understanding logical implication (and the claim/converse distinction) is slow and fragile, so one counter-example being decisive is a hard-won idea.

SMP3: construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others; make conjectures; use counterexamples; distinguish correct logic from flawed and explain the flaw; older students can compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments.
learnerActions: Sort 'always / sometimes / never' claims and use a counter-example finder: drag values and watch a claim collapse when, say, × 1/2 makes the product shrink. Use claims whose truth value is determinate — e.g. 'multiplying makes bigger' (an 'always' claim broken by a factor below 1 such as × 1/2). If including 'the more sides a shape has, the bigger its angles', state inside the task which angle is meant (e.g. each interior angle): for regular polygons each interior angle does grow with the number of sides, but it fails for irregular shapes, so it sorts as 'sometimes' — do not present it as a straightforwardly false 'always' claim.

Build an angle-fact proof chain: snap facts ('angles on a line sum to 180°', 'angles in a triangle sum to 180°', 'vertically opposite angles are equal') into an if/therefore track to reach a proved angle such as 60°, reserving measuring only to check — and only when the chosen givens genuinely force that value.
Critique a peer's fraction division: tap the mis-inverted step and select the correct method, then state in your own words why the flawed step fails.
activities.intendedInsight: Chaining established facts yields a proved value that holds generally, not just for the drawn diagram; a well-chosen single case breaks an 'always' claim; and locating a faulty step is more productive than rejecting an answer for looking odd.

activities.title: Annotated sound-vs-flawed proofs and conjecture cards
feedback: Prompt talk around each revealed card: 'Does this one case prove the rule, or just this instance?'

Draw the claim/converse contrast with a concrete pair, e.g. 'if it's a square then it has four right angles' versus 'if it has four right angles then it's a square' — the second is false because a non-square rectangle also has four right angles.
activities.rationale: Static annotated examples and reveal cards are a scaffold that can launch discussion and model what a flaw and a counter-example look like. They cannot respond to a learner's own implication errors or elicit a learner-constructed proof or hunted counter-example, so they support rather than replace the dialogue and workspace activities.
sourceClaims: Primary proof types include proof by counter-example; specific confirming examples do not constitute a watertight proof, and recognising this is a key step on the describe→explain→convince→justify→prove ladder.

SMP3: construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others; make conjectures; use counterexamples; distinguish correct logic from flawed and explain the flaw; older students can compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments.
learnerActions: Compare an annotated correct fraction division with a flawed one side by side, and discuss where and why the flawed one goes wrong (it inverts the first fraction rather than the divisor).
Work through a set of true/false conjecture cards; tap a card to reveal either a counter-example that breaks it or a short proof sketch that supports it.
Use these as a springboard for talk: say aloud whether each revealed case is a proof or just an example, and whether the converse of a true claim also holds.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing a flawed step laid out beside a correct one, and cards that reveal breakers or sketches, can seed critique vocabulary and prime the claim/converse distinction before learners construct their own arguments.

activities.title: Pick-the-breaker warm-up
feedback: Confirm whether the chosen case genuinely makes the product NOT bigger than the starting number: either smaller (e.g. a positive starting number times a factor below 1, or times 0) or equal (e.g. × 1). Then ask the learner to articulate the reason.
Do not treat a correct selection as evidence that the learner can construct a proof chain or explain a flaw independently.
activities.rationale: A recognition task can quickly surface whether a learner can spot a counter-example and serve as a warm-up, but it rewards fast selection over constructed reasoning and so must not stand in for the productive core. Research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Primary proof types include proof by counter-example; specific confirming examples do not constitute a watertight proof, and recognising this is a key step on the describe→explain→convince→justify→prove ladder.
learnerActions: From several candidate cases, pick the one that disproves a stated 'always' claim (e.g. which case breaks 'multiplying makes bigger'?).
After choosing, say aloud why that case is decisive and why the other candidates do not break the claim.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising which case is a counter-example is a useful entry step, but choosing from options does not itself elicit a constructed proof or a flaw explained in one's own words.

constraints: Insist on proof by chained fact, not measurement: measuring is only for checking a value, never for establishing that an angle MUST be a given size.
A proved geometric result holds generally, not only for the specific diagram drawn — make this generality explicit so learners do not think the proof applies only to one picture.

Reward finding the single breaker over listing confirming cases; explicitly name the asymmetry (one counter-example disproves an 'always'; no number of confirming cases proves it unless every possible case has been checked, which is impossible for claims about all numbers).
Keep the claim/converse distinction concrete: 'if square then four right angles' is not the same as 'if four right angles then square' (a non-square rectangle breaks the converse).

Recognition and selection tasks (pick-the-breaker, tap-the-step) are scaffolds; they do not elicit a learner-constructed proof chain or a flaw explained in the learner's own words, so do not treat a correct selection or score as evidence of the full reasoning practice.

If a learner endorses 'multiplication always makes bigger', treat it as a genuine false belief: reteach multiplication as scaling (for a positive starting number: × less than 1 shrinks, × 1 keeps, × more than 1 grows) with a picture, not only the argument skill.

When a learner suspects a rule is false but cannot yet find the counter-example, prompt the search ('what if a number were less than 1? try a half') without handing over the answer — the deductive instinct is forming.

The flawed fraction-division cue is 'invert/flip the first fraction'; it must always be presented as the error to find and critique, never as a method to follow — the correct method inverts the divisor (second fraction) then multiplies.

Any conjecture used in a sort must have a determinate truth value as stated; if a claim's truth depends on scope (e.g. 'more sides, bigger angles' depends on angle type and regular vs irregular), state that scope inside the activity so the sort is fair.
Static annotated examples and reveal cards cannot respond to a learner's own implication errors; pair them with dialogue or discussion.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified, and all activities are research-informed proposals rather than validated interventions.

Self-audit of worked examples: 6 × 1/2 = 3 is correct and is a valid counter-example to 'multiplying always makes bigger'; 8 × 0 = 0 is also valid. For the strict claim 'makes bigger', × 1 is also a breaker (6 × 1 = 6 is not bigger). The angle proof target of 60° is used illustratively and depends on the specific givens in a diagram — ensure the chained facts actually force 60° before presenting it to learners.

Comparative necessity over other media is NOT established by the sources provided; the original's 'only live dialogue teaches this' framing has been reduced to the narrow affordance of real-time responsiveness to the learner's gaps.

The patched claim 'multiplying always makes bigger OR the same' remains false for 0 < factor < 1 (× 1/2 shrinks), so × 1/2 is still a valid breaker; × 1 only reaches the 'same' boundary the patch allows and no longer breaks the patched claim. Keep the two tests distinct when guiding learners.

The flawed fraction-division cue 'flip/invert the first fraction' is a deliberate error to be critiqued (the divisor, i.e. the second fraction, is the one inverted); ensure it is always framed as the error to find, never as a method to follow.

The conjecture 'the more sides a shape has, the bigger its angles' is now scoped in-activity as a 'sometimes' claim: each interior angle of a regular polygon does grow with sides (triangle 60°, square 90°, pentagon 108°, hexagon 120°...), but it fails for irregular shapes and for exterior angles. The original pedagogy's treatment of it as flatly false is imprecise; specify the intended angle type before using it.

probeDeeper: 'How many examples where it works would it take to PROVE the rule always holds? And how many where it fails to prove it doesn't?'
'You found 6 × 1/2 = 3. Say exactly why that one case is enough to sink the whole rule.'
'The classmate now says "okay, but multiplying always makes it bigger OR the same". Is that fixed, or can you still break it? Try × a half again — and try × 1.'
'Is "multiplying makes bigger" the same claim as "if the answer is bigger then you multiplied"? Give me a case that separates them.'
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child producing a counter-example with a factor less than 1 (e.g. 6 × 1/2 = 3, or 8 × 0 = 0) AND recognising that ONE such case is enough to disprove the 'always' claim, rather than adding more confirming examples or hedging.

errorPatterns.pattern: Multiplication-makes-bigger generalisation: endorses the rule because every whole-number case tried confirms it — the classic over-extension of whole-number multiplication to all numbers.
errorPatterns.nextMove: This is a genuine false belief about multiplication — confront with scaling: 'what is 6 lots of a half?' Reteach multiplication as scaling (× less than 1 shrinks) using a picture, not just the argument skill.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child agrees the rule is true, or tests only whole numbers and confirms it; when nudged, cannot see why a fraction would behave differently.

errorPatterns.pattern: Empirical proof scheme: responds to 'prove it's wrong' by trying MORE examples, or judges the rule 'usually/mostly true', not grasping that one counter-example is decisive and confirming cases never prove an 'always'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name the asymmetry explicitly: 'How many YES examples would prove an ALWAYS? How many NO examples to disprove it?' Elicit that one counter-example is enough; celebrate finding the breaker over listing confirmers.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child piles up examples on either side, or says 'it's right most of the time' — treats proof as accumulation of cases rather than a single decisive breaker.

errorPatterns.pattern: Suspects the rule is false and rejects the example-piling, but cannot yet find or articulate the counter-example — the deductive instinct is present but the productive step lags.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT read as not-knowing. Prompt the search without giving the answer: 'you think there's a case — what if one of the numbers were less than 1? Try a half.' Let the child produce and state the breaker; the logic of implication is already forming.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 'I don't think it's always true' or 'there might be a case where it's not' but stalls when asked to produce one; may hover near fractions without landing 6×1/2.

responseLevels.gap: Endorses the rule, or tries only whole numbers and confirms it, or says 'mostly true'; does not produce a counter-example.
responseLevels.full: Produces a factor-below-1 counter-example (6 × 1/2 = 3, or ×0) AND states that a single such case disproves the 'always' claim while no number of confirming cases could prove it — then applies the same counter-example strategy unprompted to a repaired or new conjecture (e.g. the converse or the '≥' patch).
responseLevels.partial: Suspects or states the rule is false, or even offers a fractional case, but cannot explain why one counter-example is DECISIVE — may still want more cases to be sure, or gets the verdict without the sufficiency reason.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A classmate is sure of this rule: 'When you multiply two numbers, the answer is always bigger than both of them — I've tried loads and it always works.' Are they right? Talk me through how you'd decide, and if you think the rule is wrong, show me the most convincing way to prove it's wrong.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands proof-by-counter-example knows that a single case with a factor below 1 settles it decisively, and reaches for one; a child in the empirical scheme keeps testing whole numbers, confirms the rule, or says 'mostly true' — never grasping that one breaker overturns 'always'. The prompt is hard to answer right for the wrong reason: guessing 'wrong' isn't enough; the discriminating act is generating the decisive case AND stating that one is sufficient. It's hard to answer wrong for the right reason because a correct reasoner cannot help but see the ×1/2 case once looking for a breaker.

sources.claim: SMP3: construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others; make conjectures; use counterexamples; distinguish correct logic from flawed and explain the flaw; older students can compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments.
sources.source: CCSS Standards for Mathematical Practice, MP3

sources.claim: A general counter-example gives insight into WHY a statement is false; empirical/example-based reasoning predominates and the shift to understanding logical implication (and the claim/converse distinction) is slow and fragile, so one counter-example being decisive is a hard-won idea.
sources.source: Hoyles & Küchemann (2002), Students' Understandings of Logical Implication, Educational Studies in Mathematics 51(3)

sources.claim: Primary proof types include proof by counter-example; specific confirming examples do not constitute a watertight proof, and recognising this is a key step on the describe→explain→convince→justify→prove ladder.
sources.source: NRICH, 'Reasoning: The Journey From Novice to Expert' (Cambridge)

pedagogy.summary: A coordinate pair names ONE location on a grid with an ORDERED pair of numbers: the first says how far to travel across from the origin (horizontal, the x-direction), the second how far up (vertical, the y-direction). The whole idea rests on two things children must hold together — that the order is a fixed convention (so (2,4) and (4,2) are different points), and that you read against the NUMBERED LINES from the origin (0,0), not by counting squares. The single most documented error is reversal: writing the vertical number before the horizontal. Taught well, coordinates are built on prior position language (along/across then up) and grounded in the physical act of travelling from the origin — 'along the corridor, then up the stairs' — before being abstracted to the (x, y) notation.
bestPractices: Fix the read as a two-step journey from the origin: ALONG first (how far across), THEN UP (how far up) — the 'along the corridor and up the stairs' image, with x = across (NCETM).
Make the order matter visibly: plot (2,4) and (4,2) on the same grid so children SEE they are different points, defeating the belief that order is arbitrary.
Read against the numbered LINES from the origin (0,0), not the squares — anchor counting at zero to avoid off-by-one errors.
Name the axes and connect names to coordinates (x-axis ↔ x-coordinate, first number; y-axis ↔ y-coordinate, second number), so reversal has a rule to fall back on ('x comes before y').
Move fluently between reading a plotted point and stating a shape's vertices, so a coordinate is seen as a location, not two loose numbers.
Build on Year 3/earlier position and direction vocabulary (left/right, up/down, across) before introducing the formal pair.
keyRepresentations: Numbered coordinate grid with the origin (0,0) marked
'Along the corridor, then up the stairs' journey from the origin (across before up)
Two contrasting points (2,4) vs (4,2) shown together to make order matter
The (x, y) ordered pair with axes labelled x (across) and y (up)
A shape plotted on the grid with each vertex's coordinates read off
commonMisconceptions: Reversal — putting the y-coordinate before the x (reading/plotting up before across), giving an incorrectly placed point (documented, NCETM).
Believing the order is arbitrary — treating (2,4) and (4,2) as the same location.
Counting squares/cells instead of reading the numbered grid lines, producing off-by-one positions.
Not anchoring to the origin — starting the count at 1 rather than 0, or from the wrong corner.

learn.summary: A coordinate pair names ONE location on a grid with an ORDERED pair of numbers: the first tells how far ACROSS from the origin (horizontal, x-direction), the second how far UP (vertical, y-direction). Two ideas must be held together: the order is a fixed convention (so (2,4) and (4,2) are different points), and you read against the NUMBERED LINES from the origin (0,0), not by counting the squares. The most documented error is reversal — writing the vertical number before the horizontal. Coordinates are well supported by prior position vocabulary (along/across, then up) and grounded in the physical image of travelling from the origin — 'along the corridor, then up the stairs' — before abstracting to (x, y) notation. Activities below range from an interactive place-and-see grid, through diagnostic reading tasks, to static reveal scaffolds; each has a distinct purpose and its own limits.

activities.title: Coordinate-journey grid: place the point and watch the path
feedback: When a placement is reversed, show the along-then-up trail and the target point together so the child sees it landed in a different place and why.
Use the compare mode to display (2,4) and (4,2) at once so 'order matters' is seen rather than told.
If the child starts counting at 1 or from the wrong corner, highlight the origin and the numbered line labels while re-counting from 0.
activities.rationale: Live tracing of the across-then-up journey and immediate placement feedback make the convention concrete, and plotting reversed pairs together surfaces the reversal and order-arbitrary misconceptions in the act of placing. Interaction such as path-tracing, the compare control, and glowing numbered lines are optional ways to make the mechanism visible, not required features.
sourceClaims: A common documented misconception is 'putting the y co-ordinate before the x, resulting in incorrectly placed position', caused by lack of knowledge of the order or of the names of the axes; suggested remedies include 'x comes before y' and 'along the corridor and up the stairs' (x is across). The Year 4 objective uses a grid where the lines are numbered, distinguishing reading numbered lines from counting squares.

A point in the plane is located by an ordered pair of numbers (its coordinates) measured from the origin along two perpendicular axes; the first number is travel along one axis and the second along the other, with the axis names and coordinate names corresponding (x-axis/x-coordinate, y-axis/y-coordinate); points are graphed in the first quadrant (5.G.1, 5.G.2).
learnerActions: Given a target pair such as (4,2), place the point on a numbered first-quadrant grid.
Watch the tool trace the journey from the origin — along 4, then up 2 — and drop the marker where you placed it.
If you read 'up before across', notice your point lands at 2-across-4-up, a clearly different point (a different gridline crossing) from the target (4,2), with the along-then-up trail showing why.
Press a compare control to drop (2,4) and (4,2) side by side so you SEE they are two different points.
Count against the glowing numbered lines starting from the origin (0,0), not the squares between them.
activities.intendedInsight: The order of the pair fixes the point — reading up before across lands you somewhere else — and counting is read from the numbered lines starting at the origin, not by counting squares.

activities.title: Read the point: diagnose reversal and off-by-one
feedback: If a child picks (4,2) for a point at 2-across-4-up, point out they read up before across and re-run the along-then-up read.
For an off-by-one answer such as (3,5) or (1,3) where (2,4) was intended, re-count against the numbered line labels from the origin, not the squares.
If a child names some vertices but not all, return to reading each corner as a single location.
activities.rationale: Reading a plotted point is cleanly scorable and the reversed pair makes a precise distractor that catches children who read up before across; an off-by-one option catches square-counting. This format is good for practice and diagnosis but, on its own, does not stage the place-and-watch-it-land-wrong moment — pair it with construction work. Recognising a correct option does not by itself show the child can independently construct a point.
sourceClaims: A common documented misconception is 'putting the y co-ordinate before the x, resulting in incorrectly placed position', caused by lack of knowledge of the order or of the names of the axes; suggested remedies include 'x comes before y' and 'along the corridor and up the stairs' (x is across). The Year 4 objective uses a grid where the lines are numbered, distinguishing reading numbered lines from counting squares.

A point in the plane is located by an ordered pair of numbers (its coordinates) measured from the origin along two perpendicular axes; the first number is travel along one axis and the second along the other, with the axis names and coordinate names corresponding (x-axis/x-coordinate, y-axis/y-coordinate); points are graphed in the first quadrant (5.G.1, 5.G.2).
learnerActions: Read the coordinates of a plotted point on a numbered grid and write them as an ordered pair, e.g. (3,5).
Answer 'which of these is (2,4)?' with (4,2) also offered, choosing the correct point.
Match and name the coordinates of all vertices of a plotted shape.
Explain which number is 'across' and which is 'up' for each answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a plotted point as (across, up) can be checked reliably, and a reversed or off-by-one answer indicates which misconception is likely at work.

activities.title: Labelled-grid reveal: seed the convention and the axis names
feedback: When a reading is revealed, restate it as across-first, up-second so the order is reinforced.
Tie the first number to the x-axis by name so reversal has a rule to correct it.
activities.rationale: Connecting axis names to coordinate names and surfacing the across-first reading seeds the convention and supports recall of the order; the 'x comes before y' mnemonic is a documented remedy for reversal. This is a seeding/reference scaffold: it presents fixed examples to read and name, so on its own it does not let the child test a placement or experience order mattering through their own action — follow it with construction and reading tasks.
sourceClaims: A common documented misconception is 'putting the y co-ordinate before the x, resulting in incorrectly placed position', caused by lack of knowledge of the order or of the names of the axes; suggested remedies include 'x comes before y' and 'along the corridor and up the stairs' (x is across). The Year 4 objective uses a grid where the lines are numbered, distinguishing reading numbered lines from counting squares.

A point in the plane is located by an ordered pair of numbers (its coordinates) measured from the origin along two perpendicular axes; the first number is travel along one axis and the second along the other, with the axis names and coordinate names corresponding (x-axis/x-coordinate, y-axis/y-coordinate); points are graphed in the first quadrant (5.G.1, 5.G.2).
learnerActions: Tap a point on a labelled grid to reveal its along-then-up reading (across first, then up).
Tap the x- and y-axes to reveal 'x = across, first number' and 'y = up, second number'.
Lift a flap comparing (2,4) and (4,2) to see they name different points.
Say aloud the rule 'x comes before y' and connect each axis name to its coordinate.
activities.intendedInsight: Each number in the pair has a fixed meaning tied to a named axis, giving a rule ('x comes before y') to fall back on when unsure of the order.

activities.title: Name the corners: coordinates as locations of a shape
feedback: If a vertex is reversed, re-run the along-then-up read for that corner.
For the (0,3) case, confirm a zero across is still a valid coordinate read from the origin.
If a child says A and B are the same, plot both and show the two distinct points (A at (2,4), B at (4,2)).
activities.rationale: Reading vertices and probing the origin and zero-coordinate cases tests coordinates as locations across several points and forces the order-matters distinction. Aligned to the topic evidence of reading points, explaining horizontal/vertical, and identifying all vertices of a plotted shape.
sourceClaims: A point in the plane is located by an ordered pair of numbers (its coordinates) measured from the origin along two perpendicular axes; the first number is travel along one axis and the second along the other, with the axis names and coordinate names corresponding (x-axis/x-coordinate, y-axis/y-coordinate); points are graphed in the first quadrant (5.G.1, 5.G.2).
learnerActions: Read aloud the coordinates of every corner of a rectangle (or other shape) plotted on the grid.
Decide whether a point sitting on the up-line at height 3 with nothing across is (0,3).
Judge a claim such as 'B was written as (2,4), the same as A' when the grid shows A at 2-across-4-up and B at 4-across-2-up — show on the grid why it is right or wrong.
Explain how you remember which number comes first.
activities.intendedInsight: A coordinate is a single location, not two loose numbers; moving between a plotted point, a vertex, and the origin consolidates reading and justifies the order.

constraints: Scope is the first quadrant with a numbered grid for ages 8–9; whole-number coordinates read from the origin (0,0).

The static labelled-grid reveal seeds the convention and axis names but does not let a child test a placement or experience order mattering through their own action; use it alongside construction and reading tasks, not as the sole experience.
Reading/selected-response items diagnose and give practice but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of a point; pair them with place-the-point work.
Build on Year 3/earlier position vocabulary (left/right, up/down, across) before introducing the formal (x, y) pair.
Counting must be anchored at the origin and read against the numbered lines, not the squares between them, to avoid off-by-one errors.

Interaction examples (path tracing, compare control, glowing numbered lines, tap-to-reveal, lift-the-flap) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete and should not be treated as mandatory mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source rated 3D and conversation formats as poor for this topic. These catalog fit judgements are not treated as universal laws: a discussion can still support recall of the 'x comes before y' rule, so the claim that order is 'grasped by locating points, not by discussion' was softened and spoken justification was retained as a supporting step in the corners activity.
The legacy claim that a third dimension 'adds confusion, not insight' is a scope decision for this age/first-quadrant topic, not an established general finding; kept only as a scope constraint.

The DfE claim establishes the Year 4 first-quadrant objective (topic/scope) but does not support any specific activity's teaching principle, so it is reflected in the scope constraint rather than attached as a per-activity sourceClaim.
Source claims cite curriculum standards and a documented misconception; they support the teaching principles but do not demonstrate that these specific activities were tested for efficacy.

probeDeeper: 'Point to (0,0). If a point sits right on the up-line at height 3, what are its coordinates?' — checks the origin anchor and a zero x-coordinate.
Counterexample: 'A friend wrote B as (2,4), the same as A. Is that right? Show me on the grid why or why not.' — forces the order-matters distinction.
'Which number tells you how far across, and which tells you how far up? How do you remember which comes first?' — surfaces the rule versus a guess.
'Read me the coordinates of every corner of this rectangle' — tests reading a coordinate as a location across several vertices.
assess.correctAnswer: A = (2,4), B = (4,2). The first number is how far ACROSS (horizontal, x) and the second is how far UP (vertical, y), counted from the origin (0,0); A and B are DIFFERENT points because the order matters.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reversal — reads/writes the vertical number before the horizontal ('up before across'), so A is given as (4,2) and B as (2,4).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reinstate 'along the corridor, then up the stairs' (x = across, first); tie the first number to the x-axis by name; practise placing a point and checking the along-then-up path.
errorPatterns.distractor: A is (4,2) and B is (2,4)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A and B are swapped; or the child counts up first then across; justification appeals to no rule about which axis is first.

errorPatterns.pattern: Order treated as arbitrary — says (2,4) and (4,2) name the same point, so A and B are 'the same'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Plot (2,4) and (4,2) together so the two different squares are seen; stress that a coordinate is an ORDERED pair — the order fixes the point.
errorPatterns.distractor: A and B are the same point
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Claims A and B are the same location, or that swapping the numbers makes no difference; may write the pairs correctly but see no distinction.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts squares instead of the numbered lines — reads off-by-one, or starts counting from 1 rather than the origin.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor counting at the origin (0,0) and read the NUMBERED lines, not the squares between them; point to the line labels while counting.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives A as (3,5) or (1,3); counts the cells crossed rather than reading the line labels; does not start at 0.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot reliably read a point's coordinates: reverses, counts squares, or cannot say which number comes first; no notion that order fixes the point.
responseLevels.full: Reads any first-quadrant point as (across, up) from the origin, explains the first number is horizontal (x) and the second vertical (y), knows (2,4)≠(4,2), and reads off all the vertices of a plotted shape correctly.
responseLevels.partial: Reads a point correctly in a clear case and knows the pair has two numbers, but reverses when the two values are confusable, or reads correctly yet cannot justify the order (treats it as arbitrary), or is off-by-one from counting squares — cannot yet read all of a shape's vertices dependably.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a first-quadrant grid with numbered lines. Plot two points: A at 2 across and 4 up, B at 4 across and 2 up. Ask: 'Write the coordinates of A and of B.' Then: 'How do you decide which number to write first — and are A and B the same point or different?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Two points that are coordinate-reversals of each other mean a child who reverses x and y will swap A and B — the error is unmissable. The second tier separates a child who happened to write the right pair from one who understands WHY: a child who says 'the order doesn't matter' or 'you go up first' reveals the misconception even if one label came out right. A correct answer for the right reason names across-then-up from the origin.

sources.claim: A point in the plane is located by an ordered pair of numbers (its coordinates) measured from the origin along two perpendicular axes; the first number is travel along one axis and the second along the other, with the axis names and coordinate names corresponding (x-axis/x-coordinate, y-axis/y-coordinate); points are graphed in the first quadrant (5.G.1, 5.G.2).
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 5 Geometry

sources.claim: A common documented misconception is 'putting the y co-ordinate before the x, resulting in incorrectly placed position', caused by lack of knowledge of the order or of the names of the axes; suggested remedies include 'x comes before y' and 'along the corridor and up the stairs' (x is across). The Year 4 objective uses a grid where the lines are numbered, distinguishing reading numbered lines from counting squares.
sources.source: NCETM, Misconceptions with the Key Objectives (Position, Direction, Movement and Angle)

sources.claim: Year 4 pupils should describe positions on a 2-D grid as coordinates in the first quadrant.
sources.source: UK Department for Education, Mathematics programmes of study: Key Stages 1 and 2 (Year 4 geometry — position and direction)

pedagogy.summary: At 9-10, repeated reasoning is used to build general METHODS and predict beyond the drawn cases: seeing that ×25 can be done as ×100 then ÷4 and explaining why, building 35% from 10% (÷10) and 5% (half of 10%) as a reusable percentage toolkit, and describing a sequence's general rule to predict the 20th term without listing all twenty. The pivotal MP8 shift here is from a term-to-term (recursive) view to a position-to-term (functional) rule that lets you jump straight to any term. Teaching should force the 'jump' — ask for the 20th or 100th term — so the recursive habit becomes insufficient and a general rule is needed.
bestPractices: Derive percentage facts from 10% (÷10) and build others by halving/scaling, naming it as a general method for any percentage
Ask for a FAR term (20th, 100th) so listing becomes impractical and a position-to-term rule is needed
Justify equivalent methods (×25 = ×100 ÷4) by why they work, not as isolated tricks
Have the child state the general rule and verify it against a known term before trusting it
keyRepresentations: Percentage bar / double number line (100% → 10% → 5% → 35%)
Sequence tables pairing position (n) with term to expose the position-to-term rule
Equivalent-fraction and factor models for ×25 = ×100 ÷4
Ratio tables for scaling methods
commonMisconceptions: Predicts the 20th term by extending term-by-term (or drawing all terms) instead of a position-to-term rule
Uses only a term-to-term rule ('add 4') and cannot jump to a far term efficiently
Treats each percentage as a separate conversion rather than building from 10% and 5%
States a general rule from a few cases without verifying it on a known term

learn.summary: Help 9-10 year-olds shift from term-to-term (recursive) reasoning to position-to-term (functional) rules so they can jump straight to any term, and build a reusable percentage toolkit from 10% and 5%. The core move is forcing the 'jump' — asking for a far term (20th, 100th) so listing becomes impractical and a general rule is needed — then insisting the rule be verified against a known term. Equivalent calculation methods (×25 = ×100 then ÷4) should be justified by why they work, not memorised as tricks.

activities.title: Sequence machine: force the jump to a far term
feedback: If the child writes 21, 25, 29… or says 'just keep adding 4', note that this term-to-term habit works but won't reach the 100th term efficiently — tabulate position against term so the relationship (4×position + 1) is visible, then ask for the 100th term.

If the child scales a known term by the position ratio (e.g. says the 20th term = 4×the 5th term), test that shortcut against a known term: does 4×(the 1st term) give the 4th term correctly? (4×5 = 20, but the 4th term is 17.) Use the position table to show that scaling multiplies the constant start-offset too, so the result is too big.
If the child announces a rule but won't check it, ask 'does your rule give the 3rd term correctly? check it' so verification becomes a habit rather than an afterthought.
activities.rationale: Asking for a far term rather than the next one is what forces the distinction between recursive and functional thinking; a position table reveals the structure (difference × position + offset) and makes the general method efficient. An optional interactive form — a position slider that tempts listing alongside a 'rule' box that leaps straight to the chosen term and checks against the listed value — can make the contrast concrete, but the learning works on paper with a table too.
sourceClaims: MP8: by attending to repeated calculations students abstract general rules (e.g. abstracting a formula) and look for general methods and shortcuts, checking reasonableness
Pupils should recognise and use structure to find efficient general methods and choose efficient strategies; representations should reveal the relationship
learnerActions: Look at a sequence such as 5, 9, 13, 17, … and notice the constant difference of 4.
Try to reach the 20th term by extending term-by-term and feel how slow and error-prone this gets.
Make a table pairing position (n) with term so the relationship becomes visible.
State a position-to-term rule (e.g. term = 4×position + 1) and use it to jump straight to the 20th term (81).
Check the rule against a known early term (does it give the 3rd term correctly?) before trusting it.
Then be asked for the 100th term, where listing is clearly impractical, so the general rule proves its worth.
activities.intendedInsight: A position-to-term rule lets you reach any term in one step, which counting-on cannot do efficiently; a rule is only trustworthy once checked against a known term.

activities.title: Build a percentage toolkit from 10% and 5%
feedback: If the child treats each percentage as a separate calculation, prompt them to start from 10% (÷10) and 5% (half of 10%) and ask which combination of those parts makes the target.
If the child assembles 35% correctly, ask whether the same approach gives 65% so they generalise the method rather than memorising one case.
An optional 'builder' where 10% and 5% tiles snap together to make 35% can make the part-whole structure tangible, but a drawn percentage bar or a ratio table serves the same purpose.
activities.rationale: Deriving unknown facts from known facts and naming the reusable method embodies the repeated-reasoning target; a percentage bar, double number line or ratio table reveals the part-whole and scaling relationship.
sourceClaims: MP8: by attending to repeated calculations students abstract general rules (e.g. abstracting a formula) and look for general methods and shortcuts, checking reasonableness
Pupils should recognise and use structure to find efficient general methods and choose efficient strategies; representations should reveal the relationship
learnerActions: Find 10% of an amount by dividing by 10.
Find 5% by halving the 10% value.
Assemble 35% of an amount by combining three 10% parts and one 5% part (e.g. 35% of £80 = 24 + 4 = 28).
Explain that this is a general method: name which parts you'd combine to make a different percentage such as 65%.
Use a percentage bar or double number line (100% → 10% → 5% → 35%) to see how the parts make up the whole.
Use a ratio table to scale the 10% and 5% parts to a different total amount, showing the method generalises across amounts, not just one figure.
activities.intendedInsight: Any multiple of 5% can be built by combining derived facts (10% and 5%) rather than treated as a separate one-off conversion. Other percentages, such as 37%, need further derived facts like 1%. This gives a reusable method that scales to any amount.

activities.title: Justify an equivalent calculation method
feedback: If the child only states the shortcut, ask them to explain why ×100 then ÷4 equals ×25, using 25 = 100 ÷ 4.
If the child's explanation holds, ask them to check it against a direct calculation to confirm reasonableness.
activities.rationale: Justifying equivalent methods rather than memorising them is central to MP8 and to choosing efficient, structurally-grounded strategies.
sourceClaims: MP8: by attending to repeated calculations students abstract general rules (e.g. abstracting a formula) and look for general methods and shortcuts, checking reasonableness
Pupils should recognise and use structure to find efficient general methods and choose efficient strategies; representations should reveal the relationship
learnerActions: Work out why multiplying any number by 25 can be done by multiplying by 100 then dividing by 4.
Use a factor/equivalent-fraction model (25 = 100 ÷ 4) to explain the equivalence, not just assert it.
Try the method on a worked example and check the result matches the direct multiplication.
Explain in words why the two routes must give the same answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Equivalent methods and shortcuts are reliable because of structure (25 = 100 ÷ 4), not because they are isolated tricks; understanding why lets you judge when a shortcut applies.

activities.title: Probe and discuss the generality of a rule
feedback: Listen for a position-to-term rule (term = 4×position + 1, so the 20th is 81) reached by linking the constant difference 4 to the position, plus a check against a known term — using the rule to jump rather than counting on is the target.

If the child uses a proportional shortcut (scaling a known term by the position ratio), have them test it on an early known term so the mishandled start-offset is exposed — e.g. 4×(the 5th term) gives 4×21 = 84, whereas the true 20th term is 81. The gap of 3 appears because scaling multiplies the +1 offset by 4 as well (4×1 = 4 instead of 1), so the answer is 3 too big.
There is no single scored answer here; the goal is reasoning that is general and self-checked.
activities.rationale: Open probing distinguishes genuine functional understanding from recursive habits and surfaces the proportional-reasoning trap of treating the sequence as proportional, which wrongly scales the constant offset. These prompts also require learners to construct and justify, not merely recognise.
sourceClaims: MP8: by attending to repeated calculations students abstract general rules (e.g. abstracting a formula) and look for general methods and shortcuts, checking reasonableness
learnerActions: Answer 'how would you find the 100th term — does your method still work?' to test whether a rule is genuinely general.
Evaluate a classmate's claim: 'the 20th term is 4×(the 5th term) — is that right? check it on the 2nd term' and explain the flaw.
Explain how to build 35% of £80 from 10% and 5%, and whether the same method gives 65%.
Explain why ×25 equals ×100 then ÷4.
activities.intendedInsight: Stating a rule is not enough; its generality must be tested against far cases and known terms, and proportional shortcuts that wrongly scale the constant offset along with the term fail these checks.

constraints: A static percentage bar or sequence table can display the relationship but cannot force the far-term jump or test a learner's stated rule; use it as a reference scaffold, not as the task that elicits independent generalisation.

Recognition-only formats (picking the correct method or the 20th term from options) can test the general method, but should be paired with a 'why/how' step so they elicit justification rather than guessing; on their own they do not require the learner to construct and verify a rule.
Include a term-by-term distractor (one that gives only the next term) when testing sequences, to catch recursive-only thinking.
Verification against a known term should be required, not optional: a rule stated from a few cases is not yet trusted.

Percentages and linear sequences are numeric relationships; manipulable numbers, tables, ratio tables or bars support the work. 3D representation is not needed here, though this is a judgement about this content, not a universal claim.

Open discussion without a concrete referent gives the learner nothing to manipulate or test; pair any discussion with an actual sequence, number or percentage to reason about (as the probing activity does).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the worked examples: sequence 5, 9, 13, 17 has first term 5 and common difference 4, giving term = 4n + 1; the 20th term is 4×20 + 1 = 81 (consistent with the source). 35% of £80 = (10% = 8)×3 + (5% = 4) = 24 + 4 = 28; the source's part-structure is correct. ×25 = ×100 ÷ 4 is valid since 25 = 100 ÷ 4. No arithmetic errors found in migrated examples.

The original 'force the jump / only this teaches why the rule beats counting on' framing is retained as a pedagogical rationale but softened: a static table, ratio table or paper task can also teach the position-to-term rule; the interactive contrast is one effective way, not the only way.
The claim that '3D adds no structure' was reframed as a scoped judgement about this numeric content rather than a universal law.

The proportional-shortcut misconception (20th term = 4×5th term = 4×21 = 84, rather than the correct 81) ignores the start-offset; retained as an error to probe and critique, never offered as a valid method or answer.

probeDeeper: Ask 'how would you find the 100th term — does your method still work?' to test whether the rule is genuinely general
Counterexample tuned to this topic: 'a classmate says the 20th term is 4×(the 5th term) — is that right? check it on the 2nd term' to probe the proportional-reasoning trap
Ask 'to find 35% of £80, how do you build it from 10% and 5%? would the same method give 65%?' to test the general percentage method
Ask 'why does multiplying by 25 equal multiplying by 100 then dividing by 4?' to surface justification of an equivalent method
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for a position-to-term rule (term = 4×position + 1, so the 20th is 81) reached by linking the constant difference 4 to the position, and a check against a known term. Using the rule to jump, not counting on, is the target.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses only a term-to-term rule ('add 4') and extends term-by-term, unable to jump to the 20th efficiently
errorPatterns.nextMove: Tabulate position against term so the relationship (4×position + 1) is visible; ask for the 100th term to make listing clearly impractical
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child starts writing 21, 25, 29… or says 'keep adding 4' with no position rule

errorPatterns.pattern: Builds a position rule but uses a proportional shortcut wrongly (e.g. 20th = 4×(5th term)), ignoring the constant offset
errorPatterns.nextMove: Test their shortcut against a known term (does it give the 4th term correctly?); expose the offset with the position table
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child scales a known term by the position ratio rather than using term = difference×position + start-offset

errorPatterns.pattern: States a general rule from a few cases without verifying it on a known term
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT just accept or correct; ask 'does your rule give the 3rd term correctly? check it' so verification becomes habitual
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child announces a rule and won't check; is surprised if it fails an early term

responseLevels.gap: Extends term-by-term, cannot reach a far term without listing, and treats each percentage as a separate conversion
responseLevels.full: Derives a position-to-term rule and jumps to the 20th/100th term, verifies it on a known term, and builds any percentage from 10%/5% — stating and checking general methods unprompted
responseLevels.partial: Finds a far term or builds a percentage when prompted, but relies on term-to-term steps or an unverified rule and doesn't justify the general method

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A sequence starts 5, 9, 13, 17, … What is the 20th term? Don't write out all twenty — tell me the general rule you'd use and how you found it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Counting on 'add 4' sixteen more times can also reach 81, but shows a recursive, not general, grasp. A child with repeated-reasoning insight builds a position-to-term rule and jumps; a child without it extends term-by-term or cannot handle '20th' without listing. Asking for the 20th (not the 5th) is what forces the distinction.

sources.claim: MP8: by attending to repeated calculations students abstract general rules (e.g. abstracting a formula) and look for general methods and shortcuts, checking reasonableness
sources.source: CCSS Standards for Mathematical Practice, MP8 'Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning'

sources.claim: Pupils should recognise and use structure to find efficient general methods and choose efficient strategies; representations should reveal the relationship
sources.source: EEF, 'Improving Mathematics in Key Stages 2 and 3' guidance report (Recommendations 2 and 4)

pedagogy.summary: At KS3 (age 11-13) accurate drawing and measuring with ruler and protractor is extended in two directions: constructing a triangle from a given specification (e.g. two sides and the included angle, SAS) to the nearest degree and millimetre, and interpreting scale drawings to extract real measurements. The construction half carries forward the protractor hazards of Y6 — chiefly reading the wrong scale on a dual-scale protractor and misplacing vertex/baseline — now under a tighter accuracy demand. The scale-drawing half introduces a distinct and heavily-documented conceptual hazard: children reason ADDITIVELY about scale (adding a constant) instead of MULTIPLICATIVELY (multiplying by a scale factor), and drop or muddle units when converting between drawing and reality. Effective teaching keeps the placement/estimate-first routine for construction, and for scale makes the multiplicative structure explicit — 'each 1 cm on the drawing stands for so many metres, so I multiply' — with pictorial models, precise language about dimensions, and reasonableness checks.
bestPractices: Keep the estimate-first protractor routine (is the angle bigger or smaller than a right angle? then choose the scale that agrees) and centre-on-vertex / zero-on-line placement, now to nearest-degree accuracy

Sequence SAS-style construction: rule one side from the ruler's zero, set the included angle at its endpoint, measure the second side, rule the third to close; treat a non-closing triangle as a signal of accumulated error
Teach scale as a MULTIPLIER: write 'real = drawn × scale factor' (and drawn = real ÷ factor), draw children's attention explicitly to the multiplicative and away from the additive relationship
Keep units explicit and precise — say 'each 1 cm represents 2 m' and carry the units through the conversion; avoid the vague word 'size', which conflates length with area
Use pictorial/scale-plan models, which research shows reduce the tendency toward additive strategy, and demand a reasonableness check on the real length
keyRepresentations: Protractor with the estimate-first rule to disambiguate the two scales (to nearest degree)
Base-then-included-angle-then-side SAS construction sequence
Scale statement 'real = drawn × scale factor' with a worked ratio (e.g. 1 cm : 2 m)
Scale plan / map with a stated scale for measuring and converting real lengths
Double number line or ratio table linking drawn cm to real m (to make the multiplier visible)
commonMisconceptions: Reasons additively about scale — adds a constant difference rather than multiplying by the scale factor — the classic additive-strategy error, most common in the ratio/proportion literature
Drops or muddles units in a scale conversion, or treats 'size' loosely (confusing length scale with area scale)
Reads the wrong scale on the dual-scale protractor, measuring/drawing the supplement of the intended angle
Misplaces the protractor centre or zero-line, so measured angles are consistently a few degrees out
Accepts a nearly-closing constructed triangle as accurate rather than as evidence of accumulated placement/measurement error

learn.summary: KS3 (age 11-13) learners extend accurate ruler-and-protractor work in two directions: constructing a triangle from a specification (e.g. two sides and the included angle, SAS) to the nearest degree and millimetre, and interpreting scale drawings to extract real measurements. Construction carries forward the protractor hazards of earlier years — reading the wrong scale on a dual-scale protractor (drawing the supplement) and misplacing vertex/baseline — now under a tighter accuracy demand. Scale drawing introduces a well-documented conceptual hazard: reasoning ADDITIVELY about scale (adding a constant) instead of MULTIPLICATIVELY (multiplying by a scale factor), and dropping or muddling units when converting. Effective teaching keeps the estimate-first placement routine for construction, and for scale makes the multiplicative structure explicit — 'each 1 cm on the drawing stands for so many metres, so I multiply' — with pictorial models, precise language about dimensions, and reasonableness checks.

activities.title: SAS construction with the estimate-first protractor routine
feedback: If your measured third side or remaining angles differ noticeably from about 6.7 cm, 47° and 78°, do not accept them as 'close enough'. This is evidence of accumulated error: recheck the protractor centre on the vertex, the zero-line along the side, and which scale you read
If you set 125° where 55° was asked, you read the wrong scale and drew the supplement; re-estimate 'bigger or smaller than a square corner?' and pick the scale that agrees

If the sides or angle drift from 6 cm / 8 cm / 55°, rehearse the base-then-included-angle-then-side sequence on another figure. Use the self-check of measuring the third side and the remaining angles against their expected values
activities.rationale: On a dual-scale protractor, pupils struggle with which scale to read and with vertex/baseline placement. Estimate-first strategies reduce these errors. Comparing the measured third side and remaining angles with expected values reveals accumulated inaccuracy; closure alone is not a check, because an SAS triangle always closes when the endpoints are joined. An interactive canvas can make this routine concrete: the protractor shows both scale numbers with a 'bigger/smaller than a square corner?' lock, the ruler measures from zero, and a tick confirms that the measured third side and angles are within tolerance. The same routine works with a physical ruler, protractor and paper.
sourceClaims: On a dual-scale protractor pupils struggle with which scale to read (drawing the supplement) and with vertex/baseline placement; estimate-first strategies and numberless/single-scale protractors reduce these errors.
learnerActions: Construct a triangle from two sides of 6 cm and 8 cm with an included angle of 55° between them: rule the first side from the ruler's zero, place the protractor with its centre on the endpoint vertex and zero-line along the side, set the 55° angle, measure and mark the second side, then rule the third side to close the triangle

Before reading the protractor, estimate first: 'Is 55° bigger or smaller than a right angle (a square corner)?' Smaller, so choose the scale that gives a value under 90°, not the 125° on the other scale

Because you finish by joining the two free endpoints, an SAS triangle always closes, so closing does not show it is accurate. Instead, measure the third side and the other two angles and compare them with the expected values. For 6 cm, 8 cm and 55°, the third side should be about 6.7 cm and the other angles about 47° and 78°, and all three angles add up to 180°. A clear mismatch signals placement or measurement error: recheck the vertex placement, the zero-line and the scale you chose
Aim for accuracy to about the nearest degree and nearest millimetre
activities.intendedInsight: Accurate construction depends on a disciplined sequence (base → included angle → side → join the endpoints) and on choosing the right scale on a dual-scale protractor by first estimating against a right angle. Joining the endpoints always closes an SAS triangle, so accuracy is checked by comparing the measured third side (about 6.7 cm) and remaining angles (about 47° and 78°) with the expected values, not by whether the triangle closes.

activities.title: Scale conversion as a multiplier, not an addition
feedback: If you added a constant (e.g. treated '1 cm represents 2 m' as '+2'), compare 4.5 + 2 = 6.5 with 4.5 × 2 = 9: the scale says every 1 cm is 2 m, so you multiply
If you dropped the units and just wrote '9', restate it as 9 m and carry 'm per cm' through the working so the result has the right units
Avoid the vague word 'size': say which dimension (side-length) you mean, since length scale and area scale are different
Check against reality for the actual object and scale given: does the converted length make sense for what the plan depicts?
activities.rationale: The additive strategy — computing a difference and applying it rather than a common multiplier — is the most commonly reported erroneous strategy in the ratio/proportion literature, geometric-figure problems are the most vulnerable, and pictorial models reduce it. Scale factor is a multiplier and teaching should draw attention to the multiplicative relationship and away from the additive one, refer precisely to 'dimensions (side-length)', and avoid the imprecise word 'size'. A live converter bar and a scale slider that shows the real length multiply while the drawn length stays put can make the multiplicative structure felt, but a ratio table, double number line, or physical scale map serve the same purpose.
sourceClaims: The additive strategy — computing the difference between terms and applying it, rather than a common multiplier — is the most commonly reported erroneous strategy in the ratio/proportion literature; geometric-figure problems are the most vulnerable to additive errors, non-integer scale factors most strongly trigger it, and pictorial models reduce it. Builds on Hart/CSMS (1981/1985).

Scale factor is a multiplier: teaching should 'ensure children's attention is drawn to the multiplicative relationship between side-lengths and not to the additive relationship'; shapes are similar only when every dimension is scaled by the SAME factor (adding a constant to each dimension does not produce a similar shape); refer precisely to 'dimensions (side-length)' and avoid the imprecise word 'size', which can be confused with area.
learnerActions: On a printed or on-screen scale plan labelled 'Scale: 1 cm represents 2 m', measure a wall to the nearest millimetre (e.g. read 4.5 cm)

Convert to the real length by multiplying: write 'real = drawn × scale', so 4.5 cm × 2 m per cm = 9 m, carrying the units through the whole conversion. Equivalently, with the unitless scale factor of 1:200, 4.5 cm × 200 = 900 cm = 9 m
State the scale in words: 'each 1 cm on the drawing is 2 m in real life, so I multiply'
Use a double number line or ratio table linking drawn cm to real m to keep the multiplier visible
Check the real length is reasonable for the object (e.g. a 9 m wall in a room)

Explore what happens when the scale changes, as a thought experiment about the scale factor: imagine the same drawn length read at a different scale — if 1 cm represented 5 m (a 1:500 scale) instead of 2 m (a 1:200 scale), the real length multiplies, so the same 4.5 cm would stand for 22.5 m while the drawn length on the plan stays the same. Apply the reasonableness check to whatever object and scale are actually given — at 1:500 the plan would depict a correspondingly larger space
activities.intendedInsight: Scale is a multiplicative relationship: real length = drawn length × scale factor (and drawn = real ÷ factor). Changing the scale factor multiplies the real length while the drawing is unchanged; adding a constant does not model scale.

activities.title: Feeling the scale factor by zooming from plan to real room
feedback: If the expansion feels surprising, it is because scale multiplies: each small step on the plan stands for a much larger real distance
Always come back to the numeric conversion — the zoom builds intuition, but the answer still comes from drawn × scale factor with units
activities.rationale: The spatial 'zoom from plan to real room' is an optional enrichment that can make a scale factor feel concrete; the core conversion remains numeric and planar, so this supports rather than replaces the measuring-and-multiplying work. Offered as an alternative with a different (intuition-building) purpose, not as the main vehicle. Its intuition-building efficacy is untested.
learnerActions: Starting from a floor-plan with a stated scale (e.g. 1 cm represents 2 m), zoom from the plan into a representation of the actual-size room to experience how a small drawn length corresponds to a large real one
Connect the visual expansion back to the number: a 4.5 cm wall on the plan becomes a 9 m wall in reality at 1 cm : 2 m
Return to the plan and do the measuring and conversion numerically
activities.intendedInsight: A scale factor can be made viscerally real by seeing a drawn length expand to its actual size, reinforcing that the real object is the drawing multiplied by the factor.

activities.title: Check scale reasoning and protractor scale choice (recognition practice)
feedback: If you picked the additive option (6.5 m), recall that each 1 cm represents 2 m, so the relationship multiplies: 4.5 × 2 = 9 m
If you picked the answer with no units, remember the real length is in metres (9 m)
For the scale item, estimate the angle against a right angle first, then pick the agreeing scale
activities.rationale: Fixed-response items can test scale conversions and scale-choice decisions with targeted distractors. This is recognition practice and consolidation; on its own it does not elicit or assess a learner's actual construction accuracy or their independent assembly of the conversion, which require doing and explaining.
sourceClaims: The additive strategy — computing the difference between terms and applying it, rather than a common multiplier — is the most commonly reported erroneous strategy in the ratio/proportion literature; geometric-figure problems are the most vulnerable to additive errors, non-integer scale factors most strongly trigger it, and pictorial models reduce it. Builds on Hart/CSMS (1981/1985).

On a dual-scale protractor pupils struggle with which scale to read (drawing the supplement) and with vertex/baseline placement; estimate-first strategies and numberless/single-scale protractors reduce these errors.
learnerActions: Answer a conversion item such as: a wall measures 4.5 cm on a plan at 1 cm : 2 m — what is the real length? Choose from options that include an additive distractor (6.5 m from adding) and a units-dropped distractor ('9' with no units) alongside the correct 9 m
Answer a 'which scale reads this angle?' item: given an angle estimated smaller than a right angle, decide which of the two protractor scales to read
Explain in words why you multiply rather than add, and why the units matter
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising additive and units-dropped distractors and choosing the correct protractor scale reinforces the multiplicative structure and the estimate-first habit; recognising the right answer among options is not the same as independently constructing or converting, so this consolidates rather than replaces the full task.

constraints: Construction accuracy is a doing skill within the KS3 curriculum: it is built by actually ruling sides, placing a protractor, and measuring. A static diagram or tap-to-reveal picture can serve as a reference for the scale statement and protractor routine but does not itself elicit placement accuracy or the learner performing the multiplicative conversion.

Recognition-only items (choosing among options, naming the right scale) do not elicit independent construction of the triangle or independent assembly and explanation of the scale conversion; use them to consolidate, and assess the full skill through a performance task.
A zoom-from-plan-to-real-room experience is optional enrichment for intuition; the core conversion is numeric and should still be carried out and explained with units.
Keep units explicit throughout a conversion; avoid the vague word 'size', which conflates length with area — length scale and area scale differ.

Interactive affordances (ghosted dual-scale numbers, a 'bigger/smaller than a square corner?' lock, a live converter bar, a scale slider from 1:200 to 1:500, a green tick when the constructed triangle's measured third side and angles are within tolerance) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete. They are helpful options, not required, and the same learning is achievable with a physical ruler, protractor, paper, scale maps, ratio tables and double number lines.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated a static image and conversation as 'poor' and a 2D interactive as 'ideal' / the only way to 'defeat' the two hazards. These are catalog fit preferences; the exact sources support the teaching principles (estimate-first routine, multiplicative scale, pictorial models) but do not establish the comparative efficacy or necessity of any one medium. Medium-specific necessity claims have been softened to scoped proposals.

Arithmetic/logic self-audit: 4.5 cm × 2 m/cm = 9 m is correct. The 22.5 m figure is also correct — 1:500 denotes 1 cm : 5 m, so 4.5 cm × 5 m/cm = 22.5 m, consistent with 1:200 denoting 1 cm : 2 m. It is presented in activity 2 as a scale-factor thought experiment (same drawn length, different scale) illustrating that the real length multiplies while the drawn length is unchanged, not as a graded item or a claim about a specific room's wall. 55° is less than a right angle and its supplement is 180 − 55 = 125°, matching the dual-scale hazard. The additive distractor 4.5 + 2 = 6.5 m is one plausible incorrect-strategy illustration.

The KS3 statutory source claim was removed from the activity sourceClaims arrays because it states the curriculum objective/topic rather than the specific teaching principle in each rationale; the objective itself is preserved in the activity content. Legacy reteach prerequisite IDs and quiz-step vocabulary were removed per rewrite rules, with the underlying reteach moves preserved as feedback.

probeDeeper: Your drawing shows 4.5 cm here — how do you turn that into a real length? Why multiply and not add?
If the scale were 1 cm to 5 m instead, would this wall be longer or shorter in real life? By how much?
Before you read the protractor — is 55° bigger or smaller than a right angle? So which of the two numbers is it?
How do you know your triangle is accurate — what would you check?
assess.correctAnswer: Constructs the SAS triangle accurately (side ruled from the ruler's zero, 55° set with centre-on-vertex and the correct protractor scale, second side measured, third side ruled to close) to about ±2° / ±2 mm; measures the wall on the plan to the nearest millimetre and converts by multiplying by the scale factor (drawn length × 2 m per cm), keeping units, and explains 'each 1 cm on the drawing is 2 m in real life, so I multiply.'

errorPatterns.pattern: Reasons additively about scale — adds a constant difference instead of multiplying by the scale factor when converting between drawing and reality
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make the multiplier explicit — 'real = drawn × scale factor' on a ratio table / double number line; draw attention to the multiplicative relationship and away from the additive one; use pictorial models, which reduce additive responses
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For a 4.5 cm wall at 1 cm:2 m gives an answer got by adding (e.g. treats the '2' as +2, or scales dimensions inconsistently), rather than 4.5 × 2 = 9 m; on 'similar shape' checks accepts adding the same amount to each side as an enlargement

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the wrong scale on the dual-scale protractor, drawing or measuring the supplement of the intended angle
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reinstate the estimate-first rule ('bigger or smaller than a square corner?') then pick the agreeing scale; rehearse on a single-scale/numberless protractor until scale choice is automatic
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Sets 125° where 55° was asked (or reports an angle as its supplement), so the SAS triangle is wrong or fails to close

errorPatterns.pattern: Constructs by eye rather than to the given spec, so the triangle does not close or the sides/angle are off — a lapse of the drawing skill under the tighter accuracy demand
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach from scratch: rehearse the base-then-included-angle-then-side sequence and the 'does it close?' self-check on a couple of figures
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The triangle nearly-but-not-quite closes, or sides/angle drift from 6 cm / 8 cm / 55°, despite the child knowing the routine

responseLevels.gap: Cannot construct to the given spec and converts scale by adding or with no units; reads whichever protractor scale.
responseLevels.full: Constructs the SAS triangle accurately to the nearest degree/millimetre, measures precisely, and converts drawing↔real by the multiplicative scale factor with units, explaining the scale and checking the real length is reasonable — and transfers correctly to a different scale.
responseLevels.partial: Constructs the triangle and can measure on the plan, but converts scale inconsistently — adds instead of multiplies, or drops units — or slips on the protractor scale; has the component moves (measure, multiply) without reliably assembling and explaining the conversion (lists parts without the relational whole).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a ruler, a protractor, and a printed scale drawing of a room or map labelled 'Scale: 1 cm represents 2 m'. Say: 'First, draw a triangle accurately with two sides of 6 cm and 8 cm and an angle of 55° between them. Then, on this plan, measure this wall and tell me its real length, and explain the scale you used.' Watch the construction and how they convert — do not talk them through it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The constructed triangle and the stated real length together reveal the reasoning: a child who thinks multiplicatively converts by × scale-factor with units intact; a child who thinks additively adds a constant or muddles units, and a dual-scale slip yields the supplementary angle and a triangle that will not close. Right answers are hard to reach by an additive route — the numbers diverge.
