pedagogy.summary: Adding and subtracting decimals to hundredths, understood as the SAME place-value system as whole numbers continued rightward past the point. The algorithm is identical — align by place value, compose ten hundredths into a tenth on carrying and decompose a tenth into ten hundredths on borrowing — the only new hazard is that alignment must be by the DECIMAL POINT (tenths under tenths), not by right-edging the digits, and 'ragged' decimals (3.4 + 2.78) must be equalised with a placeholder zero. Children should relate the strategy to the written method and explain WHY it works from place value.
bestPractices: Align by the decimal point; write in placeholder zeros so both numbers have the same number of places (3.4 -> 3.40)
Use base-ten blocks re-scaled (flat = 1, rod = 0.1, small = 0.01) so ten-hundredths-make-a-tenth mirrors ten-ones-make-a-ten
Estimate first (3.45 + 2.78 is about 6) to catch a misplaced point
Explicitly connect the decimal algorithm to the whole-number one - 'same exchange, new columns'
Ask the child to explain why lining up the points (not the digits) is necessary
keyRepresentations: Place-value columns with a fixed, aligned decimal point (Th... O . tenths hundredths)
Re-scaled base-ten blocks (1 / 0.1 / 0.01)
Number line for counting up (5.03 - 2.67)
Money and metric-measure contexts (pounds.pence, metres.cm)
commonMisconceptions: Aligns the digits by the right edge instead of by the decimal point (3.4 + 2.78 set up wrongly)
Treats the digits after the point as a separate whole number ('longer decimal is bigger', so mis-orders/mis-sets)
Loses or misplaces the decimal point in the answer
Fails to borrow across the tenths, especially with a zero (5.03 - 2.67)
Thinks appending or dropping a trailing zero changes the value

learn.summary: Add and subtract decimals to hundredths by treating the decimal point as the fixed marker of where the same place-value columns continue rightward. The written algorithm is identical to whole-number column arithmetic — align by place value, compose ten hundredths into a tenth when carrying, decompose a tenth into ten hundredths when borrowing — with one new hazard: columns must be aligned by the DECIMAL POINT (tenths under tenths), not by right-edging the digits, and 'ragged' decimals such as 3.4 + 2.78 must be equalised with a placeholder zero (3.40). Learners should estimate first to place the point, compute correctly in both directions including across a zero, and explain WHY lining up the points (not the digits) is necessary.

activities.title: Decimal exchange bench: aligning by the point and trading ten-for-one
feedback: If a learner right-edges 3.4 under 2.78 (lining the 4 under the 8), stop and insist on lining up the decimal points and inserting a placeholder zero (3.40); a highlighted empty hundredths slot can prompt this, and the re-scaled blocks show tenths sitting under tenths.
If a learner cannot take 7 hundredths from 3 hundredths in 5.03 − 2.67, model the exchange with blocks first (one whole → ten tenths, one tenth → ten hundredths) before working the digits.
If the point is lost or misplaced in the answer, anchor it with the estimate: for 3.4 + 2.78, 'about 6, so it's 6.18, not 61.8 or 0.618'.
Confirm the carry explicitly: ten hundredth-pieces fuse into one tenth-piece, which slides one column left — the same move as ten ones making one ten.
activities.rationale: A fixed-point column layout with re-scaled base-ten blocks makes 'align by the point' and the hundredths→tenths exchange concrete and connects the decimal procedure to the whole-number regrouping learners already know, supporting the standard's call to use concrete models and place-value strategies and to relate the strategy to a written method.
sourceClaims: Pupils 'add, subtract, multiply, and divide decimals to hundredths, using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used' (5.NBT.B.7, cluster: perform operations with decimals to hundredths).

Decimal addition/subtraction is formally established in Year 5: pupils 'practise adding and subtracting decimals, including a mix of whole numbers and decimals, decimals with different numbers of decimal places, and complements of 1' (Year 5 fractions/decimals notes and guidance).
learnerActions: Set up 3.4 + 2.78 in place-value columns with the decimal point fixed in a central column; notice that 3.4 has an empty hundredths slot (to the right of the 4, above the 8), and add the placeholder zero so it becomes 3.40 with tenths under tenths and hundredths under hundredths.

Compute 3.45 + 2.78: the hundredths total 13, so fuse ten hundredth-pieces into a single tenth-piece and carry it one column left — exactly the ones-to-tens carry already known. Record the answer 6.23.
Solve 5.03 − 2.67 by decomposing: exchange one whole into ten tenths and one tenth into ten hundredths so you can take 7 hundredths from 3 hundredths; record 2.36.
Before each calculation, estimate roughly (3.45 + 2.78 is about 6) and use the estimate to check the point is in the right place afterward.
Re-scale base-ten blocks so a flat = 1, a rod = 0.1, and a small cube = 0.01, and physically trade ten small cubes for one rod to mirror ten-ones-make-a-ten.
activities.intendedInsight: Decimals are not a new arithmetic: the point just marks where the columns keep going, and the ten-for-one exchange across every boundary (hundredths→tenths, tenths→ones) is unchanged from whole numbers. You must line up tenths under tenths and hundredths under hundredths because you can only add like to like.

activities.title: Confronting 'longer-is-larger' with ragged decimals
feedback: If a learner judges 4.11 larger than 4.9 because it has more digits, rebuild the comparison with equal places (4.11 vs 4.90) on a number line or with hundredths blocks, reading tenths and hundredths explicitly.

If a learner claims 2.78 is larger than 3.4 because it has more digits or a bigger part after the point, compare the ones first (2 ones vs 3 ones). Then rewrite with equal places (2.78 vs 3.40) and show on a number line or with blocks that 2.78 is smaller, even though 0.78 is more than 0.40. If they treat .45 and .4 as 45 and 4, compare 0.40 versus 0.45 (forty versus forty-five hundredths).
If a learner believes 6.180 differs from 6.18, establish directly that the extra zero adds zero thousandths, so the values are identical.
activities.rationale: 'Longer-is-larger' is a documented decimal misconception that is exposed specifically by ragged decimals of unequal length, and above all by cases where the longer decimal is actually the smaller one (e.g. 4.11 vs 4.9); equalising places and comparing on a shared model directly targets it, whereas a case where the longer decimal is also larger would let the misconception pass undetected.
sourceClaims: 'Longer-is-larger' is a well-documented decimal misconception in which children treat the digits after the point as a separate whole number (e.g. '4.11 is larger than 4.9 as it is longer'); it is exposed only by 'ragged' decimals of unequal length, and about half of Year 5 students make such errors. The classification traces to Sackur-Grisvard & Leonard (1985), Nesher & Peled (1986) and Resnick et al. (1989).
learnerActions: Decide which is larger, 4.11 or 4.9. Many children wrongly pick 4.11 because it 'looks longer' — but 4.9 is larger. Rewrite with equal places (4.11 vs 4.90) and read them as eleven hundredths versus ninety hundredths to see why.

Decide which is larger, 0.4 or 0.45, and whether 0.4 and 0.40 are equal or different. Then rewrite 0.4 as 0.40 (forty hundredths) to compare the same number of places directly (forty hundredths versus forty-five hundredths).
Build or mark both numbers with hundredths blocks or on a number line, lining up equal place values, and state which is larger and why.
Check the claim 'is 6.18 the same as 6.180?' and justify the answer from place value (appending a trailing zero adds zero in the next place, so the value is unchanged).

Explain in your own words why 2.78 is smaller than 3.4 even though it has more digits and a larger part after the point (0.78 vs 0.40): compare the ones first (2 < 3). Explain why you cannot judge decimal size by counting digits.
activities.intendedInsight: The digits after the point are not a separate whole number, so a 'longer' decimal is not automatically larger — 4.9 (nine tenths) is larger than 4.11 (eleven hundredths) despite having fewer digits, while 0.45 (forty-five hundredths) is larger than 0.4 (forty hundredths). You must compare the same place values. Trailing zeros do not change value because they add nothing to any place.

activities.title: Explain why the points must line up
feedback: A strong response aligns by the point using placeholder zeros, regroups correctly in both directions including across a zero, uses the estimate to place the point, and explains WHY the points must align; probe further if the learner solves equal-length items but cannot yet state the reason.

If a learner solves 3.45 + 2.78 but mis-aligns the ragged 3.4 + 2.78 or fails the borrow across the zero in 5.03 − 2.67, return to the exchange bench for that specific hazard before re-asking for the justification.
activities.rationale: Articulating why alignment follows from place value is the standard's 'explain the reasoning' strand and distinguishes procedural fluency from genuine understanding; dialogue can elicit and check this justification alongside the computation.
sourceClaims: Pupils 'add, subtract, multiply, and divide decimals to hundredths, using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used' (5.NBT.B.7, cluster: perform operations with decimals to hundredths).
learnerActions: Answer the question 'why must the decimal points line up — what goes wrong if they don't?' in your own words, referring to place value.
Work 5.03 − 2.67 and explain what you did to be able to take 7 hundredths from 3 hundredths (decomposing across the tenths and the zero).
Estimate 3.45 + 2.78, 3.4 + 2.78, and 5.03 − 2.67 (about 6, 6, and 2) and describe how each estimate tells you where the point belongs in the exact answer.
Transfer the reasoning to a fresh ragged or zero case you have not seen, setting it up, computing it, and justifying the alignment.
activities.intendedInsight: You can only add tenths to tenths and hundredths to hundredths, so aligning by the point keeps like place values together; estimating first lets you catch a misplaced point. Full mastery means justifying the algorithm from place value, not just following steps.

constraints: The computation is a doing skill: learners must actually set up, regroup, and compute, not merely recognise correct setups. Fill-in-the-blank or slider-estimate items can assess column setup, regrouped digits, and estimates, but recognition-only responses do not elicit independent construction of the algorithm.

Always include at least one ragged-decimal item (e.g. 3.4 + 2.78) and one borrow-across-a-zero item (e.g. 5.03 − 2.67); clean equal-length items alone confirm only the basic algorithm and hide the decimal-specific hazards.

When checking 'longer-is-larger', include at least one comparison where the longer decimal is the smaller value (e.g. 4.11 vs 4.9); a comparison where the longer decimal is also larger (e.g. 0.4 vs 0.45) does not discriminate the misconception on its own.

A tap-to-reveal worked example (tap the point to reveal 'tenths under tenths'; tap the carry to reveal ten hundredths = one tenth) is useful as fixed reference, but a fixed example cannot be re-set by the learner, so pair it with hands-on setup and computation.
Re-scaled base-ten blocks (1 / 0.1 / 0.01) are an approximation: the physical pieces have thickness and the scaling is a convention, so keep the mapping (flat = 1, rod = 0.1, cube = 0.01) explicit.
Money (pounds.pence) and metric-measure (metres.cm) contexts are helpful, but watch that the two-place convention of money does not reinforce 'always two digits after the point'.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Arithmetic checked: 3.45 + 2.78 = 6.23; 3.4 + 2.78 = 6.18 (via 3.40); 5.03 − 2.67 = 2.36. Estimates about 6, 6, and 2 are consistent. These match the source's stated correct answers.

Activity 2 keeps the discriminating comparison 4.11 vs 4.9 (the longer decimal 4.11 is actually smaller), taken from the source's own misconception example. The original candidate's 0.4 vs 0.45 does not expose 'longer-is-larger' because there the longer decimal is genuinely larger; it is retained only for the trailing-zero/equal-places teaching.

Activity 2 feedback was corrected so the remediation numbers match the learner's actual error: the '2.78 bigger after the point than 3.4' confusion is rebuilt as 0.78 vs 0.40, while '.45 and .4 as 45 and 4' is rebuilt as 0.40 vs 0.45.

The source assessment's reteach note phrased a comparison as an ambiguous question ('0.4 = 0.40 = forty hundredths, larger than 0.45? No'); the intended point is that 0.40 equals forty hundredths and is NOT larger than 0.45 (forty-five hundredths). The activity states this plainly.

The original artefact-fit notes claimed a third dimension 'adds nothing' to this planar place-value work; this is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law, so it is omitted rather than asserted. A 3D representation is simply unlikely to be necessary here, not proven worthless.
The 'glowing empty hundredths slot' and 'blocks fusing/sliding' are retained as optional, illustrative concrete feedback, not mandatory implementations.

The DfE Year 5 claim is kept on Activity 1 because that activity practises ragged and mixed whole/decimal cases ('decimals with different numbers of decimal places'); it supports the activity content rather than the choice of concrete representation.

probeDeeper: Roughly what should 3.45 + 2.78 come to, before you work it out exactly?
Why do the decimal points have to line up - what goes wrong if they don't?
In 5.03 - 2.67, what did you do to be able to take 7 hundredths from 3 hundredths?
Is 6.18 the same as 6.180 - how do you know?
assess.correctAnswer: 3.45 + 2.78 = 6.23 (composes ten hundredths into a tenth, ten tenths into a one). 3.4 + 2.78 = 6.18, aligning by the point with a placeholder zero (3.40). 5.03 - 2.67 = 2.36, decomposing across the tenths (and the zero). Estimates about 6, 6, and 2. Explains that the points align because you can only add tenths to tenths and hundredths to hundredths.

errorPatterns.pattern: Aligns the numbers by their right-hand digits instead of by the decimal point, so 3.4 + 2.78 lines the 4 under the 8
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist on lining up the points and adding a placeholder zero (3.40); use the re-scaled base-ten bench so tenths sit under tenths.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The written setup - columns do not share a vertical decimal point; answer like 3.4+2.78 = 6.22 or 0.622

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the decimal part as a separate whole number ('longer is bigger'), mis-ordering or mis-setting the numbers
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare on a number line / with hundredths blocks; 0.4 = 0.40 = forty hundredths, larger than 0.45? No - build the direct comparison with equal places.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reasoning that 2.78 is 'bigger after the point' than 3.4, or handling .45 and .4 as 45 and 4

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot decompose across the tenths to subtract, especially with a zero, in 5.03 - 2.67
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model exchanging one whole -> ten tenths, one tenth -> ten hundredths with re-scaled blocks before the digits.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Wrong tenths/hundredths digits, or smaller-from-larger within the decimal places

errorPatterns.pattern: Loses or misplaces the decimal point in the answer, or thinks adding/dropping a trailing zero changes the value
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor the point with the estimate ('about 6, so it's 6.18 not 61.8'); establish 6.18 = 6.180.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer with the point in the wrong place, or 6.18 written as 6.180 believed to be different/larger

responseLevels.gap: Right-edges the digits, mis-sets ragged decimals, or loses the point; no sense of the answer's size.
responseLevels.full: Aligns by the point (using placeholder zeros), regroups correctly in both directions including across a zero, estimates to place the point, and justifies the algorithm from place value; transfers to a new ragged/zero case.
responseLevels.partial: Solves the equal-length item and can describe the steps, but mis-aligns the ragged decimal or fails the borrow across the tenths/zero, and cannot yet say WHY the points must line up.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child these to set out and solve on paper, watching how they align them: 3.45 + 2.78; 3.4 + 2.78; and 5.03 - 2.67. Ask them to estimate each answer first, and for 5.03 - 2.67 to explain why the algorithm works.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 3.4 + 2.78 is the ragged-decimal trap: a child who right-edges the digits lines the 4 under the 8 and gets nonsense, while a child who aligns by the point (and adds the placeholder zero) succeeds. 5.03 - 2.67 forces a decimal borrow across a zero. The clean 3.45 + 2.78 confirms the basic algorithm, so failures localise to the decimal-specific hazards.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 10–11: understand and APPLY the conventional order of operations (BODMAS/PEMDAS) across the four operations, so a multi-operation string has one agreed value.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y6): 'use their knowledge of the order of operations to carry out calculations involving the four operations'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 5.OA.1 evaluate expressions with these symbols; the full precedence convention is assumed from Grade 6 onward (6.EE.1–2) once exponents enter.
• Operational details — establish the hierarchy Brackets → Orders/exponents → Multiplication & Division (equal rank, left→right) → Addition & Subtraction (equal rank, left→right). Stress that ×/÷ share a tier and +/− share a tier — you do NOT do all × before all ÷; you sweep left→right within the tier. It is a social CONVENTION for removing ambiguity, not a law of nature; brackets let you override it.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): 8 + 2 × 5 = 18 not 50, and can say why (multiply first). Tier B (10–11): evaluate 12 ÷ 3 + 4 × 2 = 12 correctly, handling two same-tier operations. Tier C (11): evaluate a bracketed multi-tier string e.g. 3 × (4 + 2) − 10 ÷ 5 and justify each step in order.
bestPractices: Motivate the NEED first: give the class 8 + 2 × 5 and collect the different answers (18 and 50) before naming the rule — the convention exists precisely to end that disagreement, so let them feel the ambiguity.

Teach ×÷ as one equal-rank tier and +− as one equal-rank tier, always swept left→right, to pre-empt the dominant 'do all × before any ÷' error; use worked pairs like 12 ÷ 2 × 3 (=18, not 2) that break if you reorder within the tier.

Underline operations tier-by-tier in colour before computing — first circle brackets, then underline the ×÷ tier, then the +− tier — so the child sees the STRUCTURE of the expression before touching a single number.

Connect to already-secured brackets work (mt_8jFSnXxqQD): brackets are the top of the hierarchy and are the tool for overriding default precedence, so writing 8 + 2 then ×5 as (8 + 2) × 5 makes the intended order explicit.

Avoid over-reliance on the mnemonic: BODMAS/PEMDAS wrongly suggests D before M and A before S. Reinforce the two equal-rank tiers explicitly and rehearse counterexamples so the acronym doesn't cement the misconception.
keyRepresentations: A tiered 'staircase' or ladder diagram: Brackets on the top step, Orders next, ×÷ on one shared step, +− on the bottom shared step — visually encoding that same-step operations are equal and read left→right.
Colour-coded expression annotation (circle brackets, underline ×÷, box +−) applied to the live expression before evaluation.
Step-by-step rewrite chains where the expression shrinks one line at a time (12 ÷ 3 + 4 × 2 → 4 + 8 → 12), each line showing exactly one tier resolved.
Number line / equal-groups callback for WHY 8 + 2 × 5 = 18: the 2 × 5 is one chunk of ten added to 8, not (8+2) copied five times.
commonMisconceptions: Strict left-to-right computation ignoring precedence: reading 8 + 2 × 5 as 50 because they add first.
Treating the acronym literally: doing Division before Multiplication (or Addition before Subtraction) because D/A come first in BODMAS, e.g. 12 ÷ 2 × 3 wrongly done as 12 ÷ 6 = 2.
Believing multiplication ALWAYS beats division rather than sharing a tier resolved left→right.
Ignoring or mis-scoping brackets — evaluating outside a bracket first, or dropping the bracket once opened.
Thinking the convention is a deep mathematical truth rather than an agreed notation choice, which blocks understanding of why brackets can override it.

learn.summary: For ages 10–11, learners understand and apply the conventional order of operations (BODMAS/PEMDAS) across the four operations so that a multi-operation string has one agreed value. The core insight is structural: brackets sit at the top, then orders/exponents, then multiplication and division as one equal-rank tier swept left→right, then addition and subtraction as one equal-rank tier swept left→right. It is a social convention for removing ambiguity, not a law of nature, and brackets exist to override it. Activities build and check the sequencing skill, pre-empt the dominant 'do all × before any ÷' error, and surface why the convention is needed.

activities.title: Two paths, two answers: feeling why we need a rule
feedback: If a learner resolves 8 + 2 × 5 as 50 by adding first, show the string as 8 added to a single group '2 × 5'; the multiplication binds its two numbers together first. Contrast 8 + 2×5 with (8+2)×5 to show the convention matters.
If a learner gets 18 but cannot say why, prompt: 'What came out to 10 here, and why did you combine those two numbers first?'

When a learner justifies the order by 'multiplication gives a bigger answer' or 'is more powerful', redirect: it is an agreed convention to avoid ambiguity, not because × is stronger; brackets can override it.
activities.rationale: Collecting the conflicting answers 18 and 50 before naming the rule lets learners feel the ambiguity the convention resolves. A surface that visibly collapses sub-parts one step at a time makes the sequence felt rather than memorised, and a live comparison of the two paths targets the most common error directly. An optional tier-highlighter that shades ×÷ versus +− before any number is touched makes the structure of the expression visible first.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils should use knowledge of the order of operations to carry out calculations involving the four operations.
learnerActions: Meet a live multi-operation string such as 8 + 2 × 5 and decide which operation to resolve next by selecting it.
Follow the path when you choose '+' first: watch 8 + 2 become 10, then × 5 become 50.
Place a second copy of the same string beside it and resolve it the agreed way: 2 × 5 = 10 first, then + 8 = 18.
Compare the two: identical symbols, two different answers — then state in your own words why an agreed order is needed.
Try other ambiguous strings and predict both the 'reading-order' answer and the conventional answer before resolving.
activities.intendedInsight: The order of operations is an agreed convention that removes genuine ambiguity: the same symbols can yield different values unless everyone resolves them the same way, with multiplication/division taken before addition/subtraction.

activities.title: Same tier, left to right
feedback: If a learner mis-orders the ×÷ tier — for example doing the multiplication first in 12 ÷ 2 × 3 to get 12 ÷ 6 = 2 instead of sweeping left→right to 12 ÷ 2 = 6 then × 3 = 18 — clarify that ×÷ are one tier taken left to right, and + − are one tier taken left to right; the BODMAS/PEMDAS letters name tiers, not a strict queue.
Worked pairs like 12 ÷ 2 × 3 (= 18, not 2) break if you reorder within the tier — use them to make the left→right sweep concrete.
If a learner mis-orders 10 − 4 + 2, show that subtraction and addition are equal rank and must be taken in reading order.
activities.rationale: The letter order of the acronyms can mislead: BODMAS lists Division before Multiplication, PEMDAS lists Multiplication before Division, and both list Addition before Subtraction. Rehearsing counterexamples where reordering within a tier changes the answer pre-empts this common error so the acronym does not cement the misconception.
sourceClaims: The BODMAS/PEMDAS acronym commonly induces the error of doing division before multiplication and addition before subtraction; ×÷ and +− should be taught as equal-rank tiers resolved left-to-right.
learnerActions: Evaluate 12 ÷ 2 × 3 by sweeping left→right within the ×÷ tier: 12 ÷ 2 = 6, then 6 × 3 = 18.
Try resolving it the wrong way (× before ÷: 2 × 3 = 6, then 12 ÷ 6 = 2) and compare the two answers.
Do the same for 10 − 4 + 2 within the +− tier: 10 − 4 = 6, then 6 + 2 = 8, and show why doing 4 + 2 first gives the wrong answer.
Evaluate 12 ÷ 3 + 4 × 2: resolve both multiplications/divisions in reading order, then add, reaching 4 + 8 = 12.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplication and division share one equal-rank tier and are resolved left→right (not all × before all ÷); addition and subtraction likewise share one tier resolved left→right.

activities.title: See the structure before you compute
feedback: A tiered 'staircase' can anchor the hierarchy: brackets on the top step, orders next, ×÷ on one shared step, +− on the bottom shared step — same-step operations are equal and read left→right.
If a learner evaluates outside a bracket first or drops the bracket once opened, re-emphasise that brackets are resolved first and must be kept until their contents are a single value.
A number-line / equal-groups callback shows what 8 + 2 × 5 = 18 means under the agreed convention: the 2 × 5 is one chunk of ten added to 8, not (8 + 2) copied five times.
activities.rationale: Annotating operations tier-by-tier before computing lets the child see the structure of the expression first, and step-by-step rewrite chains make each tier resolution explicit, supporting accurate evaluation of longer multi-tier strings.
learnerActions: Before calculating, annotate the expression by tier: circle brackets, underline the ×÷ operations, box the +− operations.
Build a rewrite chain that shrinks one line at a time, each line resolving exactly one tier, e.g. 12 ÷ 3 + 4 × 2 → 4 + 8 → 12.
For 3 × (4 + 2) − 10 ÷ 5, resolve the bracket first (4 + 2 = 6), then the ×÷ tier (3 × 6 = 18 and 10 ÷ 5 = 2), then the +− tier (18 − 2 = 16), justifying each step.
Explain the resolution of each line aloud so the order is stated, not just performed.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading the structure of an expression tier-by-tier before touching numbers makes the correct sequence clear and keeps multi-tier, bracketed strings manageable.

activities.title: Brackets override the default order
feedback: Connect to earlier brackets work: writing 8 + 2 then × 5 as (8 + 2) × 5 makes the intended order explicit.
If a learner treats the convention as a deep mathematical truth, stress that it is an agreed notation choice — which is exactly why brackets are allowed to override it.
Dropping brackets into an expression and watching the value change lets override-by-brackets be something the learner does, not just something they are told.
activities.rationale: Treating the convention as a law of nature blocks understanding of why brackets override it. Letting learners place brackets to force a different value connects the override to the structure and reinforces that the order is a convention.
sourceClaims: Grade 5 pupils use parentheses/brackets/braces in numerical expressions and evaluate expressions with these symbols; full precedence with exponents follows in Grade 6.
learnerActions: Take 8 + 2 × 5 (= 18) and add brackets to force the other value: write (8 + 2) × 5 and evaluate it to 50.
Given a target answer, decide where brackets must go to reach it, then check by evaluating.
Explain how brackets changed which operation you resolved first and why that overrode the usual precedence.
Make up your own bracketed string for a partner and challenge them to justify each step in order.
activities.intendedInsight: Brackets sit at the top of the hierarchy and are the tool for overriding default precedence; placing them is a deliberate act that changes the agreed order.

activities.title: Why is this right? A questioning discussion
feedback: Press for justification: 'Why does multiplication go first here — and would it still if there were brackets?'
If a learner justifies the order by the size of the result rather than by convention, redirect to ambiguity-removal as the reason.
Accept answers that correctly separate 'knowing the rule' from 'saying why 18 is right and 50 wrong'.
activities.rationale: A Socratic questioning format can probe why the convention exists and press for justification, which suits the 'it is a convention, not a law' insight. This may complement procedural practice: the core skill is evaluation, which is likely well supported by active manipulation, so the discussion is intended to accompany rather than replace hands-on evaluation.
learnerActions: Respond to a prompt such as: 'For 8 + 2 × 5, my scientific calculator says 18, my friend says 50 — who is right and why?' (Note: many basic calculators work out each step as it is keyed in and would show 50.)
Justify your answer by naming which operation is resolved first and why, not by which answer 'looks bigger'.
Argue why an agreed order of operations is needed at all, using an ambiguous string as evidence.
Say where you would add brackets to deliberately make 8 + 2 × 5 equal 50.
activities.intendedInsight: The order of operations is a convention for ending disagreement over a string's value, not a law about which operation is stronger — and learners should be able to justify it, not just apply it.

constraints: Motivate the need for the rule first by collecting the conflicting answers (18 and 50) before naming it, so learners feel the ambiguity the convention resolves.

Teach ×÷ as one equal-rank tier and +− as one equal-rank tier, always swept left→right; explicitly rehearse counterexamples (e.g. 12 ÷ 2 × 3 = 18, where doing the × first wrongly gives 2) so the acronym's letter order does not cement 'division before multiplication' (BODMAS), 'multiplication before division' (PEMDAS) or 'addition before subtraction' (both).
Frame the order as an agreed convention for removing ambiguity, not because multiplication is 'stronger' or gives bigger answers; brackets are the legitimate override.

A static reference staircase or chart anchors the hierarchy well but does not let the learner evaluate a live expression or feel the left→right sweep; use it alongside active evaluation, not instead of it.

Recognition-only or outcome-only checks (e.g. picking the first operation, or a final-value answer) can confirm the result but do not by themselves require the learner to state or justify the order; pair them with tasks that ask for the sequence and the reasoning.
This is a flat symbolic/notational concept with no spatial dimension, so a 3D/spatial setting is unlikely to add value for it; keep attention on the structure of the expression.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three cited sources carry verified:false in the source row (the US CCSS 5.OA.1/6.EE.1–2 mapping and the NCETM order-of-operations guidance); treat their claims as unconfirmed pending review.

Checkpoint example 3 × (4 + 2) − 10 ÷ 5 evaluates to 16 (bracket 6, then 3×6=18 and 10÷5=2, then 18−2=16); the source row did not state its value, so the worked value here is supplied for correctness and should be confirmed.

The original row's commonMisconceptions labelled '12 ÷ 2 × 3 wrongly done as 12 ÷ 6 = 2' as 'division before multiplication', but reaching 2 requires doing the multiplication (2 × 3) first; the corrected feedback labels this accurately as a multiplication-before-division / tier mis-ordering error. BODMAS can still mislead on ×÷ and +− ordering in general, which the activity addresses.

Assessment correctAnswer states multiplication is done before addition 'by convention — not simply left to right'; this is the intended discrimination and is preserved. Source arithmetic (8+2×5=18; 12÷3+4×2=12; 12÷2×3=18) was checked and is correct.

Activity 5 (Socratic discussion) was left with no sourceClaims: none of the three cited claims directly support its convention-justification teaching principle, so [] is used rather than borrowing the NCETM tier claim from Activity 2.

probeDeeper: Why is 8 + 2 × 5 equal to 18 and not 50?
Where would you put brackets to MAKE it equal 50?
In 12 ÷ 3 + 4 × 2, which parts do you do first, and in what order?
Why do we need an agreed order of operations at all?
assess.correctAnswer: 18. A child reasoning correctly does the multiplication first (2 × 5 = 10) then adds 8, and explains that multiplication is done before addition by convention — not simply left to right. They recognise 50 would come from wrongly adding first.

errorPatterns.pattern: evaluates strictly left to right, ignoring operation priority — 8 + 2 = 10, × 5 = 50
errorPatterns.nextMove: show the expression as 8 plus a group '2 × 5'; the multiplication binds its numbers together first. Contrast 8 + 2×5 with (8+2)×5 to show the convention matters.
errorPatterns.distractor: 50 (add 8 and 2 first, then multiply by 5)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer of 50; child explains 'I just went along the line'

errorPatterns.pattern: treats BODMAS too rigidly — always does ALL division before ANY multiplication, or all addition before subtraction, rather than left-to-right within a tier
errorPatterns.nextMove: clarify × and ÷ share a tier (do them left to right), as do + and −; BODMAS letters are tiers, not a strict queue.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: on 12 ÷ 3 + 4 × 2 or on 10 − 4 + 2 the child mis-orders within the same tier

errorPatterns.pattern: believes multiplication is done first because it is 'more powerful' / always gives a bigger answer, a faulty rationale
errorPatterns.nextMove: stress it is an agreed convention to avoid ambiguity, not because × is 'stronger'; brackets can override it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child justifies the order by size of result rather than by convention

responseLevels.gap: evaluates left to right (50), or gives 18 with no valid reason.
responseLevels.full: applies the tiered convention correctly (incl. left-to-right within a tier), evaluates multi-step expressions accurately, and explains the order as a convention that removes ambiguity and can be overridden by brackets.
responseLevels.partial: gets 18 and cites 'multiply before add' but mis-handles same-tier left-to-right cases, or justifies the order by result-size rather than convention.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: What does 8 + 2 × 5 equal? Once you've given your answer, explain why it comes out that way and not the other way.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The single most common error is evaluating strictly left to right (8 + 2 = 10, ×5 = 50). Asking WHY separates a child who has internalised the operation-priority convention from one who read the answer off in reading order or who 'knows the rule' but can't say why 18 is right and 50 wrong.

pedagogy.summary: Children measure the SAME object in two different units and discover the inverse relationship: the smaller the unit, the more of them it takes, so the larger the number. Measuring a desk gives ~120 in centimetres but only ~47 in inches — the desk hasn't changed; the count is bigger because a centimetre is smaller than an inch. This is the conceptual bridge from 'counting units' to understanding that a measurement is a number relative to a unit.
bestPractices: Measure one object in two units side by side and put the two numbers next to each other to provoke 'why are they different?'
Make explicit that the object did not change — only the size of the unit did — so a bigger number does not mean a bigger object.
Name the relationship as inverse: smaller unit → more units → bigger number; larger unit → fewer units → smaller number.
Use a same-number/different-unit case (A is 10 small paperclips, B is 10 jumbo paperclips) to show equal counts can mean different lengths.
Ask children to PREDICT which unit will give the bigger number before measuring, so the counterintuitive result confronts a naive prediction.
keyRepresentations: The same desk measured with a cm ruler and an inch ruler, the two counts side by side
Two rows of the same length tiled with small vs large units (many small / few large)
Regular vs jumbo paperclip chains (same count, different length)
A statement frame: 'smaller unit → ____ units → ____ number'
commonMisconceptions: Bigger-unit-bigger-number: believes the larger unit (inch) gives the larger number because inches are 'bigger'.
Thinks the object itself is longer when the number is bigger — the cm measurement 'makes the desk longer'.
Smaller-unit-smaller-number: reasons a centimetre is small so it must give a small number, landing on inches.
Treats equal counts as equal lengths regardless of unit size (10 small clips = 10 jumbo clips).

learn.summary: Children measure the SAME object in two different units and discover the inverse relationship: the smaller the unit, the more of them it takes, so the larger the number. A desk measures about 120 in centimetres but only about 47 in inches — the desk hasn't changed; the count is bigger because a centimetre is smaller than an inch. This bridges from 'counting units' to understanding that a measurement is a number relative to a unit. The ~120/~47 figures are illustrative of one real desk, not fixed for every object.

activities.title: One desk, two rulers: watch the counts differ
feedback: If a learner predicted inches would give the bigger number because 'inches are bigger', re-measure and count both aloud so they watch the smaller centimetre produce MORE units than the inch.
If a learner says the desk is longer in centimetres because the number is bigger, lay both counts against the one unchanged edge and ask what actually changed — only the unit, not the desk.
If a learner reasons 'a centimetre is small so it gives a small number', count centimetres aloud so they feel small units pile up to MORE, not fewer, landing on about 120 vs 47 for this desk.
Confirm success when the learner states centimetres give the bigger number BECAUSE each centimetre is smaller, and predicts metres give a smaller number than centimetres.
activities.rationale: Measuring one unchanged object in two units side by side, with a predict-first step, confronts the naive 'bigger unit means bigger number' prediction against the actual counts; a live tally and a third-unit toggle are proposed to make the inverse relation concrete and generalisable. The draggable rulers, filling tally and metres toggle are optional interaction examples that may make the mechanism visible; they are not required mechanisms, and the approximate counts illustrate one real desk rather than fixed values.
sourceClaims: Second graders learn the inverse relationship between the size of the unit of length and the number of units required: the larger the unit, the fewer units in a given measurement. For example it takes more centimetre lengths than inch lengths to cover a distance because the inch is the larger unit. This is the productive time to measure the same object with different units, both standard and non-standard.

At the Length Unit Relater and Repeater level a child relates the size and number of units (inverse relationship), e.g. 'if you measure with centimeters instead of inches, you'll need more of them, because each one is smaller.'
learnerActions: Before measuring, PREDICT: which number will be bigger when you measure the desk in centimetres versus inches? Say WHY.
Lay the inch ruler along the desk edge and count units as a tally climbs to about 47.
Lay the centimetre ruler along the very same edge and watch the tally race past to about 120.
Point to what actually changed between the two measurements — and confirm the desk itself did not change.
Toggle to a third, larger unit (metres) and watch the count shrink; say whether that fits the rule.
Complete the statement frame: 'smaller unit → ____ units → ____ number' and 'larger unit → ____ units → ____ number'.
activities.intendedInsight: A measurement is a number relative to a unit: the smaller the unit, the more of them fit, so the larger the number — even though the object is unchanged.

activities.title: Same count, different length: the paperclip chains
feedback: If a learner says 10 clips equals 10 clips so the lengths match, lay the chains side by side so the jumbo chain is visibly longer, then name why: each jumbo clip is bigger.
Confirm success when the learner explains the lengths differ because the units differ in size even though the count is the same.
activities.rationale: A same-number/different-unit case directly targets the 'more units = longer' / 'counting means size doesn't matter' bias noted in the progressions, reinforcing that a measurement depends on the unit, not the count alone.
sourceClaims: Students can use the concept of unit to infer relative size: if object A is 10 regular paperclips long and object B is 10 jumbo paperclips long, the number of units is the same but the units differ in size, so the lengths differ. Counting discrete items often convinces students that the size of what is counted does not matter, whereas in measurement unit size is critical, producing a 'more units = longer' bias.
learnerActions: Compare object A, measured as 10 regular paperclips, with object B, measured as 10 jumbo paperclips.
Decide whether the two objects are the same length, and explain why or why not.
Lay the two chains alongside each other to check the prediction.
activities.intendedInsight: Equal counts do NOT mean equal lengths when the units differ in size — unit size is critical in measurement, unlike in counting discrete items.

activities.title: Check and consolidate the inverse relation
feedback: A correct answer with the wrong reason should be probed: a child who truly has the concept says 'centimetres, because a centimetre is smaller so more of them fit', whereas 'inches, because inches are bigger' reveals the direct-relation misconception.
For the metres item, confirm the learner links the larger unit to fewer units and a smaller number, showing the relation generalises in both directions.
Use the labelled side-by-side only as consolidation after the hands-on measuring; on its own it states the idea but does not let the learner generate the counts or predict.
activities.rationale: Predict-and-explain items plus a same-count/different-length item are discriminating checks of the inverse relation because the reason tier catches a correct answer reached by wrong reasoning. The static labelled reference consolidates after generation but cannot elicit prediction or count-generation on its own. The reason-tier discrimination reflects the assessment design rather than a separately source-verified effect.
sourceClaims: Second graders learn the inverse relationship between the size of the unit of length and the number of units required: the larger the unit, the fewer units in a given measurement. For example it takes more centimetre lengths than inch lengths to cover a distance because the inch is the larger unit. This is the productive time to measure the same object with different units, both standard and non-standard.
learnerActions: Answer: which gives the bigger number for the same desk — centimetres or inches — and say why.
Answer: measure the desk in metres instead of centimetres — will the number be bigger or smaller? Why?
Answer the paperclip item: object A is 10 small clips, object B is 10 jumbo clips — same length or not, and why?
Review a side-by-side reference of the desk labelled '120 cm / 47 in' (illustrative of one real desk) and reveal the rule: 'smaller unit → more of them → bigger number'.
activities.intendedInsight: The learner can predict and justify measurement outcomes from unit size across new units, not just recall the desk result.

constraints: The learner must GENERATE the two counts and make a prediction first; a static labelled image (e.g. '120 cm / 47 in' with a tap-to-reveal rule) states the idea but does not let the learner produce the counts or predict, so it belongs as post-activity consolidation rather than the core experience. This describes the affordance of each format, not a claim that other media cannot teach the idea.
Multiple-choice and slider checks can assess the relation, but the reason/explanation must be elicited — a 50/50 answer alone does not show the concept; require the justification tied to unit size.
Make explicit that the object did not change — only the size of the unit did — so a bigger number does not mean a bigger object.
The approximate counts (~120 cm, ~47 in) depend on the specific desk; treat them as illustrative of a real desk, not fixed facts for every object.
Use at least two units spanning different sizes (e.g. inch vs centimetre, then metres) so the relation can be seen to work in both directions.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy entry rated a 3D interactive as 'adding nothing' and framed dialogue as unable to teach the insight. These are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws; they are omitted as universal claims. A 2D side-by-side measuring experience is proposed on its narrow affordance (showing two counts on one object), without asserting other media cannot teach this.

Arithmetic/logic self-audit: the inverse relation as stated is correct — a centimetre is smaller than an inch (1 inch ≈ 2.54 cm), so a fixed length yields more centimetres than inches, and metres (larger) yield fewer units than centimetres. The example counts (~120 cm vs ~47 in) are mutually consistent for a desk of roughly 120 cm ≈ 47 in (47 × 2.54 ≈ 119). No arithmetic errors requiring correction were found.

The prerequisite reteach references in the source assessment remain in the assessment field and are not surfaced to learners; they are internal references and should not appear in learner-facing guidance.

The progressions' 'two rows tiled with small vs large units' representation is folded into the measuring activity rather than built as a separate panel; this substitution was not independently re-verified against the source.

assess.poeTask: Before measuring, ask the child to predict which number will be bigger when the desk is measured in centimetres versus inches, and to say WHY. Then have them measure it both ways. The result (about 120 cm but only about 47 inches for the same desk) confronts a 'bigger unit gives a bigger number' prediction; the target explanation, given after observing, is that the centimetre is the smaller unit so it takes more of them.
probeDeeper: You said centimetres gives about 120 and inches about 47 — did the desk get bigger? So what actually changed?
If we measured the same desk in metres instead, would the number be bigger or smaller than the centimetre number? Why?
Object A is 10 small paperclips long and object B is 10 jumbo paperclips long — same number, 10. Are they the same length? Why or why not?
Why does it take MORE centimetres than inches to cover the very same desk?
assess.correctAnswer: The centimetres give the bigger number, because a centimetre is smaller than an inch, so it takes MORE centimetres than inches to cover the same desk (smaller unit → more units → bigger number).

errorPatterns.pattern: Bigger-unit-bigger-number (direct relation): matches the size of the number to the size of the unit, so says inches give the bigger number because an inch is bigger.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-measure one object with different-sized units and count aloud, watching the smaller unit produce more; make the inverse relation explicit.
errorPatterns.distractor: Inches — an inch is bigger than a centimetre, so you get a bigger number.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Chooses inches and justifies it with 'inches are bigger, so a bigger number'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Object-changed / more-units-means-longer: reads the bigger number as meaning the desk itself is longer in centimetres, applying discrete counting to a fixed length.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Stress the desk never changed — only the unit did; lay both counts against the one unchanged edge and discuss what actually changed.
errorPatterns.distractor: The desk is longer when you measure it in centimetres, because that number is bigger.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the desk is longer when measured in centimetres because 'the number is bigger'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Smaller-unit-smaller-number: reasons that because a centimetre is small it must give a small number, so lands on inches for the bigger number.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront with the actual counts (120 cm vs 47 in) and count small units aloud to feel that smaller units pile up to MORE, not fewer.
errorPatterns.distractor: Inches — a centimetre is smaller, so it must give a smaller number.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Chooses inches with the reasoning 'a centimetre is smaller, so it gives a smaller number'.

responseLevels.gap: Says the bigger unit gives the bigger number, or believes the desk is longer when the number is bigger (object changed).
responseLevels.full: States centimetres give the bigger number BECAUSE the centimetre is smaller so more are needed, generalises the inverse relation to a new unit (metres → smaller number), and recognises the object's length is unchanged.
responseLevels.partial: Knows centimetres give the bigger number, from experience or rote, but cannot explain it through unit size — states the two numbers without linking 'more units' to 'smaller unit', or cannot predict for a new unit.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a desk. If you measure it in centimetres you get one number, and if you measure the SAME desk in inches you get a different number. Which measurement will be the BIGGER number — the centimetres or the inches? And why?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The answer alone can be guessed 50/50, so the reason tier carries the discrimination: a child who has the concept says 'centimetres, because the centimetre is smaller so more of them fit', while common wrong reasoning ('inches, because inches are bigger' or 'inches, because a centimetre is small so it gives a small number') is hard to hold alongside a correct inverse relation. A correct answer with the wrong reason is caught.

pedagogy.summary: Using a simple formula means reading what it tells you to do — in words or symbols — substituting the given values, and computing with the correct order of operations, applying EVERY operation the formula specifies. The signature pitfalls are ignoring the bracket in P = 2(l + w) (doubling only the length), omitting the ½ in the area of a triangle, confusing the perimeter and area formulae, and mismatched units. Connecting each formula to the shape it describes keeps the computation meaningful.
bestPractices: Read the formula first and say what it computes and what each letter means before substituting.
Do the bracket first: for P = 2(l + w), add length and width, THEN double — not 2×l + w.
Apply every operation in the formula, including the ½ for a triangle; link it to the triangle being half its enclosing rectangle.
Distinguish perimeter (distance round, in cm) from area (space inside, in cm²) and attach the correct units.
Substitute carefully and check the result is sensible for the shape.
keyRepresentations: The shape itself with the formula overlaid (perimeter traced round the edge)
Triangle drawn inside its enclosing rectangle (why ½)
Function machine for the sequence of operations
Worded-formula ↔ symbol-formula matching cards
commonMisconceptions: Ignores the bracket / order of operations: P = 2(l + w) computed as 2×l + w (e.g. 2×5+3 = 13 instead of 2×8 = 16).
Omits the ½ in a triangle's area, giving b×h (24) instead of ½×b×h (12).
Confuses perimeter and area formulae, or uses the wrong measurements.
Attaches wrong units (perimeter in cm², or no units).
Reads a worded formula incorrectly and mis-sequences the operations.

learn.summary: Year 6 learners use simple formulae (in words or symbols) to calculate values, substituting given numbers and applying EVERY operation in the correct order. The signature pitfalls are ignoring the bracket in P = 2(l + w) and doubling only the length (2×l + w), omitting the ½ in the area of a triangle, confusing perimeter with area, and mismatched units (cm vs cm²). Connecting each formula to the shape it describes keeps the computation meaningful.

activities.title: Formula-on-a-shape: watch the bracket do its work
feedback: If the 'double first' trace fails to close, point out that it counts both lengths but only one width, so it falls short by one width — the bracket (add first) is what makes the boundary close.

For the triangle, if the ½ is treated as optional, show that the leftover pieces of the same-base, same-height rectangle exactly cover the triangle (for a right-angled triangle, two identical copies form the rectangle): base × height is the whole rectangle, so the triangle's area is half of that. With a paper cut-out, treat it as a model of the ideal flat triangle.
When the answer looks wrong, prompt: 'read the formula again — have you done every operation it lists, in the order it lists them?'
activities.rationale: Seeing the bracket and the ½ act on an actual shape links symbolic order of operations to the quantity being measured, countering the instrumental, ungrounded learning that research associates with area/perimeter confusion and over-generalising the rectangle formula to triangles. Live recolouring, the perimeter trace, the function machine, and the 'double first' toggle are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete; a static or paper version (tracing with a pen, cutting and rearranging a paper triangle against a rectangle with the same base and height) can carry the same idea, with the paper cut-out understood as an approximation of the ideal plane figure.
sourceClaims: Students writing/evaluating expressions apply operations left-to-right and mishandle the order of operations implied by symbolic form and parentheses — the same error that produces 2(l+w) -> 2*l+w.

Learners confuse area and perimeter because the formulae (A = l x b and P = 2(l + b)) are taught at about the same time and learned instrumentally, without conceptual grounding (Van de Walle et al.; Dickson 1989: confusion is 'nearly always due to inadequate preparation... given the formulae without adequate explanation'); and they over-generalise the rectangle area formula, extending A = l x b to non-rectangular figures such as triangles (Olivier 1989) — the mechanism behind applying base x height to a triangle without the halving adjustment the triangle requires.
learnerActions: Set the length and width of a rectangle (for example with sliders), and evaluate P = 2(l + w) step by step: add length and width inside the bracket FIRST, then double.
Trace the perimeter round the edge of the rectangle as the formula computes, and check the traced path closes back on itself.
Toggle a 'double first' version that shows what 2×l + w would do — a path that traces both lengths but only one width, so it stops one side short and never closes round the shape.

Flip to a triangle whose top vertex lies above its base and place it on a rectangle with the same base and height (on screen or with a paper/card cut-out). Cut or drag the leftover pieces of the rectangle to show they exactly cover the triangle (for a right-angled triangle, two identical copies make the rectangle), so the ½ in A = ½ × b × h is seen as the triangle being half that rectangle. (A paper cut-out has slight thickness and stands in for the ideal flat, zero-thickness triangle; it still shows the half-area relationship.)
Optionally lay the formula out as a function machine so the sequence of operations the formula specifies is explicit.
State, in your own words, what each formula computes and what each letter means before substituting.
activities.intendedInsight: The bracket's order is not arbitrary here: adding-then-doubling walks the whole boundary and closes it, while doubling-then-adding misses one width and does not. The ½ for a triangle is the visible fact that a triangle has half the area of a rectangle with the same base and height.

activities.title: Substitute and compute with feedback
feedback: If 13 appears for P (from 2×5 + 3), show that this doubles only the length; add length and width first, then double, to get 16 cm.
If 24 appears for the triangle, point to the ½ written in the formula — every operation must be carried out, so halve 24 to 12 cm².
If units are wrong (area with no square units, or perimeter in cm²), re-read what the formula computes: distance round (cm) versus space inside (cm²).
activities.rationale: Choosing formulae, substituting, and attaching units are cleanly checkable, and distractors built from the bracket and ½ errors make the characteristic mistakes visible for correction. A recognition/fill-in item checks substitution and formula choice but does not by itself require the learner to construct and justify a full method; pair it with the step-showing and explanation actions above.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils should use simple formulae (expressed in words or symbols) to calculate values.
Students writing/evaluating expressions apply operations left-to-right and mishandle the order of operations implied by symbolic form and parentheses — the same error that produces 2(l+w) -> 2*l+w.
learnerActions: Fill in the blank: P = 2(5 + 3) = __, showing the bracket step (2 × 8 = 16 cm) before the answer.
Choose the area of a triangle with base 6 cm and height 4 cm from options including 12 cm² and the ½-omission result 24 cm²; explain why 24 is wrong.
Match each worded formula to its symbol form (e.g. 'multiply the base by the height, then halve' ↔ A = ½ × b × h).
Attach the correct units to each answer and say why perimeter is in cm but area is in cm².
Work an unfamiliar simple worded formula end-to-end, naming each operation as you do it.
activities.intendedInsight: Substituting into a given formula and picking the right formula/units is a procedure built by doing and checking; the common slips are the bracket and the dropped ½, so each is targeted directly.

activities.title: Label the shape and reveal the steps
feedback: If a learner cannot predict the next step, return to naming what each letter measures on the shape.
Use the revealed steps to confirm whether the bracket was handled first.
activities.rationale: A static labelled shape with step-reveal shows the parts of a formula clearly and supports reading it (in words or symbols) before use. It is a scaffold: because the numbers are fixed it does not let the learner compute across changing values, which is where the bracket and ½ errors actually surface, so follow it with the substitution and formula-on-a-shape activities.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils should use simple formulae (expressed in words or symbols) to calculate values.
learnerActions: On a labelled rectangle, tap or point to the perimeter formula and reveal each step of the calculation in turn.
Say what each letter in the formula stands for on the drawing before any numbers are substituted.
Predict the next step before revealing it, then check your prediction against the shown calculation.
activities.intendedInsight: Connecting each symbol to the part of the shape it measures keeps the formula meaningful before computing.

constraints: Perimeter and triangle area here are planar (2D) quantities; a third dimension is not needed and can mislead toward surface area or volume, so keep the representation flat.

A paper or card triangle cut out and rearranged against a rectangle with the same base and height has slight thickness and is an approximation of the ideal plane figure; use it to show the half-area relationship, not as a literal zero-thickness shape. This is also noted in the activity where the paper model is proposed.
The static label-and-reveal task is a scaffold: fixed numbers mean it cannot elicit computing across different values, which is where the characteristic errors live.

Recognition/multiple-choice items check substitution and formula/unit selection but do not on their own require the learner to construct and justify a full method; include step-showing and explanation to assess independent procedure.
Always apply every operation the formula specifies, in order: bracket first in P = 2(l + w), and include the ½ for a triangle.
Describe triangle area as half the base times the (perpendicular) height; avoid calling base and height 'two side lengths', since the height is a perpendicular distance, not necessarily a side.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: P = 2(5 + 3) = 2 × 8 = 16 cm (bracket-ignoring slip gives 2×5 + 3 = 13); triangle area = ½ × 6 × 4 = 12 cm² (½-omission gives 6×4 = 24). All checked and consistent across the summary, activities, feedback, and constraints.

The source row's 3D-unsuitable and conversation-unsuitable ratings were catalog fit judgements; retained only the genuine, narrowly scoped point that a third dimension risks shifting toward surface area/volume for a planar quantity. No universal 'only this teaches' or 'dialogue cannot teach procedures' claim is asserted.

Source claim attributions were tightened: the curriculum-scope claim was removed from activity 1 because that activity's principle is conceptual grounding of order of operations/½, supported by the order-of-operations and area/perimeter claims rather than by curriculum scope.

The inherited worded formula 'multiply the two side lengths, then halve' loosely treated base and height as 'side lengths'; the learner-facing matching task was corrected to 'multiply the base by the height, then halve', since height is a perpendicular distance, not a triangle side. The original phrasing is recorded in the preservation audit for fidelity.

The cited sources support curriculum scope and the mechanisms of the order-of-operations and area/perimeter errors; they do not establish the comparative efficacy of any particular activity or medium.

probeDeeper: In part (a), why add before you double? What do you get if you double first, and does it match the shape? (order-of-operations reasoning)
Your triangle sits inside a 6-by-4 rectangle — how do their areas compare, and why the ½? (counterexample/derivation for the half)
What units should each answer have, and why is area measured differently from perimeter?
Here is a formula in words: 'multiply the two side lengths, then halve.' Which is it — area of a triangle or perimeter of a rectangle? (interpreting a worded formula)

errorPatterns.pattern: Ignores the bracket / order of operations — computes 2(l + w) as 2×l + w, doubling only the length.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Bracket first — add length and width, THEN double; connect to perimeter as two lengths plus two widths traced round the shape.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 2×5 + 3 = 13 (or similar); only one dimension is doubled before the other is added.

errorPatterns.pattern: Omits the ½ in a triangle's area — computes base × height and stops, giving the rectangle's area.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the triangle as exactly half its enclosing rectangle by cutting/folding; stress that every operation written in the formula must be carried out.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer is 24 (6×4) rather than 12; the ½ in the formula is not applied.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses perimeter and area, or the units — uses the wrong formula/quantity, or labels perimeter in cm².
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the two ideas — perimeter is the distance round (cm), area is the space inside (cm²); read what the formula computes before using it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Adds where the formula multiplies (or vice versa), or gives area with no square units / perimeter with cm².

responseLevels.gap: Ignores brackets/order or omits an operation (drops the ½), or selects the wrong formula; the calculation does not follow the formula as written.
responseLevels.full: Interprets worded or symbolic formulae, applies every operation in the correct order (bracket first, includes the ½), attaches correct units, and transfers the approach to an unfamiliar simple formula.
responseLevels.partial: Substitutes and computes a single-operation formula correctly, but slips on the bracket in 2(l + w), forgets the ½, or muddles units — manages the routine case but not reliably.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child this card and say 'work these out, showing your steps': (a) A rectangle has length 5 cm and width 3 cm — use P = 2(l + w) to find its perimeter. (b) A triangle has base 6 cm and height 4 cm — use A = ½ × b × h to find its area. Say nothing about method. Watch whether they do the bracket first in (a) and include the ½ in (b), and whether the units are right.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Each item isolates an error in the written steps: (a) exposes ignoring the bracket (2×5+3 = 13) versus adding first then doubling (16); (b) exposes omitting the ½ (24) versus halving (12). Units (cm vs cm²) further separate a child who knows what each formula computes. Watching the steps, not asking, shows which operation was dropped or mis-ordered.
