pedagogy.summary: Children find the area of a rectangle by tiling it with unit squares arranged in rows and columns, and discover that the count equals the product of the side lengths: the number of squares in a row times the number of rows. The multiplication must GROW out of seeing the array structure — one side tells how many squares are in a row, the other tells how many rows — not be applied as a rote length-times-width rule.
bestPractices: Tile the rectangle in complete rows and columns, then count — first one by one, then skip-counting by rows, then multiplying.
Draw the array structure explicitly: line segments forming rows and columns, so the child anticipates the full grid.
Make the equivalence explicit — explain WHY rows × (squares in a row) gives the same number as counting all the tiles.
Rotate the rectangle to show area is preserved and 4×6 = 6×4 (commutativity from the array).
Use squared paper: draw a rectangle, tile it, and write the matching multiplication.
Contrast with adding the sides (perimeter) so multiplication-for-area is not confused with addition.
keyRepresentations: A rectangle tiled with unit squares showing rows and columns
A 4×6 array with '6 in each row, 4 rows' annotated and 4×6 = 24
Row-strips (cut-outs) repeated to fill the rectangle
A rectangle rotated 90° to show 4×6 = 6×4
commonMisconceptions: Adds the side lengths (4 + 6 = 10) instead of multiplying — confusing area with perimeter.
Cannot structure the array — counts squares one by one with no sense of rows × columns, so never reaches the multiplication.
Multiplies the sides as a rote rule but cannot explain why it equals the tile count.
Miscounts rows or columns, especially when the grid is only partly drawn.

learn.summary: Children find the area of a rectangle by tiling it with unit squares arranged in complete rows and columns, then discover that the count equals the product of the side lengths: number of rows × squares in each row (for example, 4 rows of 6 is 4 × 6 = 24 square units). The key is that multiplication GROWS from seeing the array — one side tells how many squares are in a row, the other tells how many rows — rather than being applied as a rote length-times-width rule. Work should distinguish this from going around the edge (perimeter), and show that rotation preserves area so 4×6 = 6×4.

activities.title: Build the array and watch the multiplication grow
feedback: If the total jumps by six as each row is added, point out that this skip-counting by rows is exactly what 4 × 6 means.
If a learner still counts every tile one by one, slow down and highlight one full row, then count on by that row size instead of by ones.
After rotating, if the learner expects the area to change, re-count: the same squares are present, just turned, so the area is unchanged and 4×6 = 6×4.
If asked, show that going once around the edge (4 + 6 + 4 + 6 = 20) measures the border, not the covered surface — area is the squares inside.
activities.rationale: Interpreting rectangular area as a multiplicative relationship between the number of squares in a row and the number of rows, with arrays drawn and skip-counted before multiplying, is how children come to explain why side-length multiplication matches the tile count. Rotating arrays and seeing area preserved supports commutativity.
sourceClaims: To make sense of multiplying side lengths for area, students first interpret rectangular area as a multiplicative relationship of the number of square units in a row and the number of rows, relying on spatial structuring; they draw arrays, skip-count the number in each row, then multiply, and learn to explain why multiplying the side lengths gives the same area as counting the tiles — one length is how many squares in a row, the other is how many rows (3.MD.7).

Students rotate rectangular arrays physically and mentally and understand their areas are preserved under rotation, so 4 × 7 = 7 × 4 (commutative property). Spatial structuring — seeing a rectangle as decomposable into rows and columns of squares — precedes meaningful use, is difficult, and needs many array activities; the incomplete-array case shows children struggle to coordinate rows and columns.
learnerActions: Set up a rectangle 4 rows tall and 6 squares wide, adding one complete row of six unit squares at a time.
As each row is added, count on by six: 6, 12, 18, 24, and notice the running total jump by six each time.
Alongside the growing grid, build the matching statement '4 × 6' and connect it to 'four rows of six'.
Rotate the rectangle so it becomes 6 rows of 4; check that the total is still 24, showing 4 × 6 = 6 × 4.
Say in your own words why you do NOT have to count all 24 squares — each new row simply adds another six.
activities.intendedInsight: The multiplication IS the array: one factor is how many squares are in a row and the other is how many rows, so rows × squares-in-a-row gives the same total as counting every tile. Rotation preserves area, which is why 4×6 = 6×4.

activities.title: Tile and label on squared paper
feedback: If the grid is only partly drawn and the count seems off, mark the unit ticks on opposite sides and join them to complete every row and column, then recount carefully.
If the learner writes 4 × 6 but cannot explain it, ask them to shade one row and count how many squares it holds, then how many such rows fill the shape.
Praise an explanation that names 'six in each row, four rows' rather than just the right number.
activities.rationale: Finding area by counting squares and relating it to multiplying side lengths for rectangles is a curriculum expectation at around this age in some curricula (for example, US Common Core Grade 3; in England, counting squares to find area appears in Year 4 and calculating the area of rectangles in Year 5); constructing and labelling the array, not just reading it, builds the spatial structuring that makes the formula meaningful.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils find the area of rectilinear shapes by counting squares and relate this to multiplying side lengths for rectangles.

To make sense of multiplying side lengths for area, students first interpret rectangular area as a multiplicative relationship of the number of square units in a row and the number of rows, relying on spatial structuring; they draw arrays, skip-count the number in each row, then multiply, and learn to explain why multiplying the side lengths gives the same area as counting the tiles — one length is how many squares in a row, the other is how many rows (3.MD.7).
learnerActions: On squared paper, draw a rectangle (for example 4 by 6) and tile it by marking off every complete row and column so no squares are missing.
Count the squares — first by ones to confirm, then by skip-counting whole rows.
Write the matching multiplication (4 × 6 = 24 square units) beside the rectangle.
Point to which side tells 'how many squares in a row' and which tells 'how many rows'.
activities.intendedInsight: Drawing and tiling your own rectangle, then writing the multiplication, cements that the two side lengths are the per-row count and the number of rows, and that their product is the area in square units.

activities.title: Area is not the distance around (spot the error)
feedback: If a learner accepts 4 + 6 = 10 as area, re-establish area by counting the covering squares (24) and contrast it with tracing along the edge.
Note that 4 + 6 = 10 is only two sides, and even the full perimeter 4 + 6 + 4 + 6 = 20 is the distance around the border, not the area — neither 10 nor 20 is the covered surface.
Confirm the correct area only once the learner shows the filled rows and columns giving 24.
activities.rationale: Confusing area with going around the edge by adding side lengths is a common misconception; directly contrasting covering the surface with following the border, then rebuilding the array, re-links the count to multiplication.
sourceClaims: To make sense of multiplying side lengths for area, students first interpret rectangular area as a multiplicative relationship of the number of square units in a row and the number of rows, relying on spatial structuring; they draw arrays, skip-count the number in each row, then multiply, and learn to explain why multiplying the side lengths gives the same area as counting the tiles — one length is how many squares in a row, the other is how many rows (3.MD.7).
learnerActions: Look at a worked attempt where a child wrote 4 + 6 = 10 as the 'area' of a 4-by-6 rectangle.
Decide what 4 + 6 actually measures, and correct the method to find the true area.
Trace the border of the rectangle to see that adding sides follows the edge, while tiling covers the surface.
Rebuild the array and state the correct area, 24 square units, with its multiplication.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding two side lengths (4 + 6 = 10) measures along the edge, not the covered surface; even the full border (4 + 6 + 4 + 6 = 20) is still a length around, not area. Area is the count of unit squares that fill the rectangle, found by multiplying squares-in-a-row by number-of-rows.

activities.title: Row-strips that fill the rectangle
feedback: If a learner cannot yet see the row structure, do NOT impose a length×width rule — practise laying and skip-counting row-strips first, as spatial structuring develops with repeated array work.
If strips overlap or leave gaps, re-lay them edge to edge so every square is covered exactly once before counting.
Reinforce that each strip adds another six, which is why multiplying by the number of strips works.
activities.rationale: Spatial structuring — seeing a rectangle as decomposable into rows and columns — is difficult and needs many array activities; row-strip cut-outs and skip-counting by rows support children who otherwise count one by one.
sourceClaims: Students rotate rectangular arrays physically and mentally and understand their areas are preserved under rotation, so 4 × 7 = 7 × 4 (commutative property). Spatial structuring — seeing a rectangle as decomposable into rows and columns of squares — precedes meaningful use, is difficult, and needs many array activities; the incomplete-array case shows children struggle to coordinate rows and columns.
learnerActions: Take strips of six joined unit squares (row-strips) and lay them to fill a 4-by-6 rectangle with no gaps or overlaps.
Count how many strips are needed (4), and how many squares each strip holds (6).
Skip-count the strips — 6, 12, 18, 24 — to find the total.
Write and say the multiplication: four rows of six is 4 × 6 = 24 square units.
activities.intendedInsight: Repeated equal row-strips make the 'rows × number-in-each-row' structure physical, so the multiplication is felt as grouping equal rows rather than a memorised rule.

activities.title: Check and justify the link
feedback: A full response names the two meanings of the factors and explains that rotation keeps the same squares, so area is unchanged.
If the learner multiplies correctly but cannot explain why, return to a drawn array and have them show which side is the per-row count and which is the number of rows, then skip-count the rows.
Treat a '4 by 6' area answer of 10 (two sides) or 20 (the full border/perimeter) as a confusion with distance around the edge, and reteach area as the covering squares (24).
activities.rationale: Explaining why multiplying side lengths equals counting the tiles is the stated learning goal; prompting for justification and for the rotation argument distinguishes genuine structuring from rote multiplication.
sourceClaims: To make sense of multiplying side lengths for area, students first interpret rectangular area as a multiplicative relationship of the number of square units in a row and the number of rows, relying on spatial structuring; they draw arrays, skip-count the number in each row, then multiply, and learn to explain why multiplying the side lengths gives the same area as counting the tiles — one length is how many squares in a row, the other is how many rows (3.MD.7).
learnerActions: Answer why 4 × 6 gives the same number as counting all the tiles one by one, pointing to 'squares in a row' and 'number of rows'.
Complete a statement such as '4 × 6 = __ square units' and explain the unit.
Compare a 4×6 and a rotated 6×4 rectangle and state whether the area changes, with a reason.
Explain what a classmate measured if they wrote 4 + 6 = 10 for the area.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to justify the multiplication — not just compute it — is the sign the array structure has become the reason for the formula.

constraints: Multiplication for area must grow out of the array: one side is squares-in-a-row, the other is number-of-rows. Do not introduce length×width as a rote rule before the child can structure rows and columns.
Keep the figure planar. Avoid moving to 3D blocks here, which can blur rectangular area with volume; area is a covering of flat unit squares.
Tile in complete rows and columns with no gaps or overlaps. Partly-drawn grids cause miscounts; complete the grid before counting.
Always use square units for area and distinguish them from the linear units used for the border/perimeter.

A static labelled array (e.g. '6 in each row, 4 rows, 4×6 = 24') is a useful reference, but on its own it does not let a child build rows or rotate to feel commutativity; pair it with hands-on tiling or construction.

A conversation or verbal explanation can discuss the array and check understanding, but does not by itself get the child to construct, tile and count the rows; pair any discussion with hands-on tiling or array construction.
Items that only ask the child to select or fill in an answer can check the link but do not by themselves build the array sense; include construction, tiling and explanation.
For a child who cannot yet see rows and columns, prioritise spatial-structuring practice (row-strips, drawing rows/columns, skip-counting) over imposing the formula.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The UK National Curriculum claim is marked verified:false in the source row; its Year 4 framing is used only with qualification and is unconfirmed.

Numbers checked in this rewrite: 4 rows of 6 gives 6, 12, 18, 24 = 24; 4 × 6 = 6 × 4 = 24; the full perimeter of a 4-by-6 rectangle is 4 + 6 + 4 + 6 = 20, while 4 + 6 = 10 is only two sides — both are border measures, not area. The common wrong answers 10 and 20 are addressed as border/perimeter confusions, not offered as valid area options.

The original row's 'add the sides' comparison uses 4 + 6 = 10 and labels it 'the perimeter'; 10 is actually a two-side sum, not the full perimeter (20). This is the original's error and is corrected in the activities so 10 is not presented as the complete perimeter.
Whether 'spatial structuring must precede the formula' holds as strongly as the progressions source states has not been independently re-verified here.

probeDeeper: Why does 4 times 6 give the same answer as counting all the tiles one by one?
If I rotate the rectangle so it's 6 by 4, does the area change? Why or why not?
Where are the 'rows' in your rectangle, and where is 'the number in each row'?
Your friend added 4 + 6 and got 10 for the area — what did they actually measure instead?
assess.correctAnswer: The child tiles the rectangle in complete rows and columns with no gaps, finds the area (24) by counting or skip-counting rows, writes 4 × 6 = 24, and explains that one side gives the number of squares in a row and the other gives the number of rows — so multiplying them gives the same total as counting all the tiles.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds the side lengths instead of multiplying: gives 4 + 6 = 10 (the perimeter) as the area.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-establish area as the covering squares by counting the tiles; contrast with the once-around edge; then rebuild the array and connect the count to multiplication.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 4 + 6, or answers 10 or 20; treats area like the distance around.

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot structure the array: counts squares one by one with no sense of rows and columns, so never connects the count to multiplication.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT impose the length×width formula yet — spatial structuring develops with practice; use row-strip cut-outs, draw the rows and columns, and skip-count by rows before multiplying.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Counts every tile individually, often miscounting; shows no rows×columns structure and does not offer a multiplication.

errorPatterns.pattern: Rote multiplication without understanding: multiplies the sides and gets 24 but cannot explain why it matches counting the tiles.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the array — have the child show which side is the number in a row and which is the number of rows, and skip-count the rows to see the product build.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives 4 × 6 = 24 but, asked why, cannot point to 'squares in a row' and 'number of rows'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscounts rows or columns: correct multiplicative method but an off-count, especially when the grid is only partly drawn.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw the unit marks on opposite sides and join them to complete the grid; recount rows and columns carefully.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Right approach, wrong factor — e.g. counts 5 rows on a 4-row grid because the array isn't fully drawn.

responseLevels.gap: Adds the side lengths (perimeter), or counts one by one with no array structure and no multiplication.
responseLevels.full: Tiles in rows and columns, connects the area to number-in-a-row × number-of-rows, writes and justifies the multiplication, and sees that rotation preserves the area (4 × 6 = 6 × 4).
responseLevels.partial: Tiles and counts correctly and even writes 4 × 6 = 24, but cannot explain why the multiplication matches the count — the rows×columns structure is not yet the reason.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a rectangle (e.g. 4 by 6) on squared paper or with unit-square tiles and say: 'Tile this, find its area, and show me why the area equals the side lengths multiplied together.' Watch whether they build rows and columns or count one by one, whether they multiply or add the sides, and whether they can explain the link.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has structured the array multiplies rows by squares-in-a-row and can justify it; a child who has not counts one by one with no multiplication, or adds the sides for a perimeter answer, or multiplies by rote but cannot say why — each visible in how they tile, compute and explain.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 9-10. Read, write, order and compare whole numbers to at least 1,000,000 in numerals, number names, expanded form and via place value — e.g. write 403,072 in words/expanded form; compare 548,301 and 543,801. The system now spans six digits and the thousands-grouping (comma every three places) becomes essential to reading magnitude.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 5): 'read, write, order and compare numbers to at least 1,000,000 and determine the value of each digit'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.NBT.2 read/write/compare multi-digit numbers in multiple forms (Grade 4 to 1,000,000).
• Operational details — Extend the place-value chart to six columns grouped in threes (thousands | ones periods); teach reading by GROUPS ('four hundred and three thousand, and seventy-two') rather than digit by digit. Keep numeral/words/expanded synced. Prioritise multi-zero numbers (403,072; 500,006) and comparison by highest-place scan. Ground large numbers in real contexts (populations, distances) so the magnitudes mean something.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9, emerging): reads/writes six-digit numbers with clear groups, no awkward zeros. Tier B (age 9-10, secure): translates among registers incl. multi-zero (403,072) and compares/orders six-digit numbers. Tier C (age 10, extending): reads/writes tricky zero-laden numbers fluently and justifies ordering by place value.
bestPractices: Teach reading by three-digit GROUPS (thousands period, ones period), using the comma as the group marker, not digit-by-digit.
Extend the six-column place-value chart and keep numeral / words / expanded form synchronised.
Prioritise multi-zero numbers (403,072; 500,006) — the dominant error source at six digits.
Compare/order using the highest-place-first scan generalised to six digits, aligning by place.
Anchor to real large-number contexts (city populations, distances) for meaning.
keyRepresentations: Six-column place-value chart grouped in threes (periods)
Numeral with comma grouping | number name | expanded form
Place-value counters / Gattegno chart to millions
0-1,000,000 number line for magnitude
Real data (populations) as reading/ordering material
commonMisconceptions: Reading digit-by-digit instead of by groups (misreading 403,072).
Dropping or misplacing internal zeros (403,072 → 43,072 or 4,372).
Misplacing the thousands comma so the group boundary and magnitude are wrong.
Ordering by digit count or left-alignment rather than place value.
Saying 'and' in the wrong place / mangling the thousands word.

learn.summary: For ages 9-10: read, write, order and compare whole numbers to at least 1,000,000 across numerals, number names and expanded form, determining each digit's value. The central skill is reading by three-digit GROUPS (periods) using the comma as a group marker, with special attention to placeholder zeros (403,072; 500,006) and to comparing by scanning from the highest place first. Large numbers should be grounded in real contexts (populations, distances) so magnitudes carry meaning.

activities.title: Periods-based number translator to a million
feedback: If 403,072 is read as 'forty-three thousand...', the ten-thousands column was skipped: point to that empty column and say its 0 holds the place so the number is four hundred AND three thousand.
If 'four hundred thousand and seven' is written 400,700 or 4,000,007, rebuild it period by period (400 | 007) and count that each period has exactly three digits.
Dictating zero-heavy numbers and asking the learner to place the placeholder 0 themselves surfaces the empty-column error directly.
When forms are linked, changing the numeral should make the words and expanded form update; a mismatch shows a group or zero was read wrongly.
activities.rationale: Acting on a grouped place-value chart where registers stay synchronised lets group-reading and placeholder-zero placement become visible and self-correcting; a live highlight of the active period models reading by chunks. Optional interactions (highlighting the period being read, dictation mode, speaking a chunk aloud, a number-line context) make the mechanism concrete but are not mandatory.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils should 'read, write, order and compare numbers to at least 1,000,000 and determine the value of each digit'.
Reading large numbers by three-digit periods and explicit multi-zero work reduce reading/writing errors.
learnerActions: Build a six-column place-value chart split by a comma into a thousands period and a ones period (e.g. 403 | 072), and add a millions column when showing 1,000,000, which needs seven digits.

Enter or read a number and keep three linked forms in sync: the grouped numeral (403,072), the number name ('four hundred and three thousand and seventy-two') and expanded form (400,000 + 3,000 + 70 + 2).
Read the number by chunks, one period at a time, rather than reciting single digits.
Work deliberately on zero-heavy numbers: write 500,006; write 'four hundred thousand and seven' as a numeral (400,007); read 403,072 aloud.
Place each number on a 0-1,000,000 number line and tie it to a real quantity such as a city's population.
activities.intendedInsight: A six-digit number is read and built as two three-digit groups; internal zeros are placeholders that hold a column empty, and that empty column still needs its 0 so the magnitude stays correct.

activities.title: Compare and order six-digit numbers from the highest place
feedback: If 543,801 is called larger because 801 > 301, redirect to the first place that differs when scanning from the left: the thousands place decides it (8 > 3).

If ordering is done by the first digit alone, or numbers with different digit counts are compared by lining up their left ends, align the numbers by place value (right-aligned) and compare column by column from the highest place until a difference appears. Comparing digit counts first is valid for whole numbers: more digits means larger.
Reading each number aloud by periods first helps confirm which place is which before comparing.
activities.rationale: Highest-place-first comparison generalises the standard place-value comparison to six digits; using pairs that differ only in a middle place prevents learners from relying on the first or last digit.
sourceClaims: Read and write multi-digit whole numbers using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form; compare using >, =, < (4.NBT.2).
Year 5 pupils should 'read, write, order and compare numbers to at least 1,000,000 and determine the value of each digit'.
learnerActions: Compare pairs such as 548,301 and 543,801, aligning them by place and scanning from the highest place first.
State which single place decides the comparison and stop there (here the thousands digit: 8 > 3, so 548,301 > 543,801).
Order a set of four six-digit numbers from smallest to largest, justifying each step by place value.
Include pairs that differ only in a middle place so the deciding digit is not at either end.
activities.intendedInsight: When numbers are aligned by place value (right-aligned), magnitude is decided by the highest place at which two numbers differ, not by left-alignment, the first digit alone, or the final digits. For whole numbers written without leading zeros, a number with more digits is always larger (100,000 > 99,999), and this is the same rule applied to an extra highest place.

activities.title: Expanded form by place value, not face value
feedback: If a tens digit is expanded as 7 instead of 70, name its place aloud and add the parts: 400,000 + 3,000 + 7 + 2 rebuilds to 403,009, not 403,072.
Always sum the expanded parts to confirm they reconstruct the original numeral.
activities.rationale: Explicitly adding expanded parts back to check reconstruction catches face-value errors that are invisible when expansion is treated as mere copying of digits.
sourceClaims: Read and write multi-digit whole numbers using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form; compare using >, =, < (4.NBT.2).
learnerActions: Decompose a six-digit number into place-value parts, naming each digit with its place ('7 tens = 70', not '7').
Rebuild the number by adding the parts back and check it matches the original numeral.
Compare a correct expansion (400,000 + 3,000 + 70 + 2) with a face-value error (400,000 + 3,000 + 7 + 2) and explain which digit is wrong and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Each digit's contribution equals its face value times its place value; dropping the place multiplier changes the number.

activities.title: Read big numbers aloud in a real context
feedback: If the spoken reading is correct but the written numeral drops a zero, compare the two period-by-period to find the missing placeholder.

If your class's naming convention uses 'and' (as in 'four hundred and three thousand and seventy-two'), say it only within a period's value, not as a substitute for a missing group. Many US curricula leave 'and' out of whole-number names, so follow the convention your materials use.
activities.rationale: Oral reading has a genuine spoken element; pairing it with written capture elicits production in both registers rather than recognition alone, so the placeholder-zero skill is actually written and practised.
sourceClaims: Reading large numbers by three-digit periods and explicit multi-zero work reduce reading/writing errors.
learnerActions: Hear or read a real large quantity (a city's population, a distance) and read the numeral back aloud by periods.
Then write the numeral you heard, placing any internal zeros as placeholders.
Discuss what the number means at that magnitude using the number line.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent oral reading by groups and accurate written capture of the same number reinforce each other, and real contexts make the magnitude meaningful.

constraints: Reading-aloud alone does not capture written numerals; pair oral work with written production so placeholder zeros are actually practised.
A fixed reference display showing one number across all registers is a useful anchor, but two-way production (building and writing numbers) needs an input surface, not just a picture.

This is a notation and language task with no inherent spatial content, so a 3D/depth representation offers no specific advantage for THIS objective (an objective limit here, not a general claim that 3D cannot teach).
Recognition exercises (e.g. pairing a numeral with its number name) check translation but do not by themselves elicit independent writing of a numeral from dictation; include construction tasks.
Prioritise multi-zero numbers (403,072; 500,006) and middle-place comparisons, since these are common error sources at six digits.
Teach reading by three-digit groups with the comma as the group marker, not digit-by-digit.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The CCSS-M 4.NBT.2 and NCETM claims are marked unverified in the source row; the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified. Evidence strength was not independently confirmed here.

Self-audit: the source's 'correctAnswer' expands 403,072 as 400,000 + 3,000 + 70 + 2 (correct). The face-value error example in assess, 400,000 + 3,000 + 7 + 2, reconstructs to 403,009; it is retained only as a deliberate non-example, never as correct guidance.

probeDeeper: How do you group 403,072 to read it aloud?
Which single place decides between 548,301 and 543,801?
Write 'four hundred thousand and seven' — where do the zeros go and why?
assess.correctAnswer: 'Four hundred and three thousand and seventy-two'; 400,000 + 3,000 + 70 + 2; 548,301 > 543,801 (decided at the thousands digit, 8 vs 3); 400,007.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads/writes ignoring placeholder zeros or period grouping: 403,072 read as 'forty-three thousand...', or 'four hundred thousand and seven' written 400,700 / 4,000,007
errorPatterns.nextMove: Group digits into three-digit periods (thousands | ones) and read period by period; use a place-value chart so each zero holds its column.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The numeral has the wrong number of digits or the zeros land in the wrong places.

errorPatterns.pattern: Expanded form uses face value not place value: 400,000 + 3,000 + 7 + 2 (tens digit as 7)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name each digit with its place ('7 tens = 70') and add the parts back to check they rebuild the number.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A digit is expanded without its place multiplier.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares from the wrong end: judges 548,301 vs 543,801 by the later digits (301 vs 801)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare from the highest place; stop at the first differing place (thousands: 8 > 3).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 543,801 is called larger because 801 > 301.

responseLevels.gap: Loses placeholder zeros, expands by face value, or compares from the wrong end.
responseLevels.full: Reads, writes (numerals/words/expanded), orders and compares numbers to 1,000,000 using period grouping and highest-place-first reasoning.
responseLevels.partial: Handles numbers without awkward zeros but slips on placeholders or on comparisons that turn on a middle place.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Watch across forms. 'Read 403,072 aloud, then write it in expanded form. Now compare 548,301 and 543,801 with < or >. Then write “four hundred thousand and seven” as a numeral.' Watch the placeholder zeros and which place the comparison turns on.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 403,072 and 'four hundred thousand and seven' both hinge on placeholder zeros, exposing period-reading and concatenation errors; the comparison 548,301/543,801 differs only at the thousands place, so a child scanning from the wrong end picks wrongly.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 8-9. Recognise the place value of each digit in a four-digit number (thousands, hundreds, tens, ones): in 7,345 the 7 is 7 thousands (7000). Partition and recompose four-digit numbers (3000 + 400 + 50 + 2 = 3,452). The ×10 column structure extends one more place, and the thousands separator/comma enters.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 4): 'recognise the place value of each digit in a four-digit number (thousands, hundreds, tens, and ones)'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.NBT.1/4.NBT.2 generalise place-value understanding and read/write multi-digit whole numbers using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form.
• Operational details — Extend the H|T|O bench to Th|H|T|O with base-ten (thousand-cube), place-value counters and arrow cards; keep build + numeral + expanded form synced. Introduce the thousands-cube as the next unitising rung (ten hundreds = one thousand) and the comma/space grouping. Attend to multi-zero numbers (3,006; 4,050; 7,000) as the key difficulty.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8, emerging): states each digit's value in a four-digit number using a chart. Tier B (age 8-9, secure): partitions/recomposes any four-digit number incl. one internal zero. Tier C (age 9, extending): handles multi-zero numbers (3,006) and explains the thousands place as ten hundreds.
bestPractices: Extend the column bench to Th|H|T|O so the thousands place is 'the same ×10 idea, one more column'.
Introduce the thousand-cube as the next unitising step (ten hundred-flats = one thousand-cube), reinforcing the repeating pattern.
Keep build, numeral (with comma/space grouping) and expanded form (3000+400+50+2) synchronised.
Prioritise multi-zero numbers (3,006; 4,050) — the biggest source of four-digit errors.
Use place-value counters for larger numbers where physical thousand-cubes become unwieldy, keeping the column meaning.
keyRepresentations: Th|H|T|O place-value chart with base-ten (thousand-cube/flat/rod/cube) or counters
Arrow / place-value cards (3000 + 400 + 50 + 2 → 3,452)
Expanded form and numeral with thousands separator
Gattegno chart extended to the thousands row
0-10,000 number line for magnitude
commonMisconceptions: Mishandling multi-zero numbers (writing 'three thousand and six' as 3006 wrong-length, or 3,600).
Losing a placeholder in 4,050 or 7,000.
Assigning the wrong value (the 7 in 7,345 read as 7 hundreds).
Concatenation of expanded parts (3000+400+50+2 written as 3000400502).
Misplacing or ignoring the thousands comma so magnitude is misread.

learn.summary: Four-digit place value for ages 8-9: recognise the value of each digit in a four-digit number (in 7,345 the 7 is 7 thousands = 7000), partition and recompose (3000 + 400 + 50 + 2 = 3,452), understand that thousands extend the same ×10 column pattern one place further, and handle multi-zero numbers (3,006; 4,050; 7,000) with correct placeholders and comma/space grouping. Building and recomposing numbers in a Th|H|T|O structure is the central activity for this objective; checking-style and reference activities support but are not a substitute for construction.

activities.title: Build and recompose in the Th|H|T|O bench
feedback: When ten hundred-flats fuse into a thousand-cube, confirm: 'Ten hundreds became one thousand — the same trade as ten tens for a hundred, just one column further left (and the same as ten ones for a ten, two columns further left).'

If a learner thinks 3,452 and 3,542 are the same size because they use the same digits, rebuild both and compare: the 5 is worth 50 in one but 500 in the other, so the totals differ — the column, not the digit, sets the worth.

If a learner builds 'three thousand and six' as a wrong-length numeral, point to the empty hundreds and tens columns: 'Nothing here and nothing here — but we still write a 0 in each, so it reads 3,006, not 36 or 3,600.'
If the expanded parts get concatenated (3000400502), rebuild from blocks and arrow cards and show 3000 + 400 + 50 + 2 lining up under the correct columns, then overlapping into 3,452.
When emptying a column changes the numeral, ask the learner to predict the new numeral and comma position before revealing it.
activities.rationale: Constructing numbers and recomposing them from parts, with blocks, arrow cards, numeral and expanded form kept synchronised, lets learners experience place value as a repeating structure and see placeholders arise from genuinely empty columns rather than as a rule to memorise. Swapping digits between columns surfaces the 'order doesn't matter' misconception directly. A number line adds a magnitude check that guards against comma/grouping misreads. Multi-zero numbers are the principal difficulty and benefit from explicit placeholder work.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'recognise the place value of each digit in a four-digit number (thousands, hundreds, tens, and ones)'.
Generalise place-value understanding and read/write multi-digit whole numbers using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form (4.NBT.1-2).
The ×10 place-value structure repeats into thousands; multi-zero numbers are the principal difficulty and need explicit placeholder work.
learnerActions: Extend the familiar H|T|O column bench to Th|H|T|O and assemble a number such as 3,452 using thousand-cubes, hundred-flats, ten-rods and ones.
Drag ten hundred-flats into a tray and watch them fuse into one thousand-cube, saying aloud 'ten hundreds make one thousand' — the same unitising move one column up.
Keep three things in view at once as you build: the blocks, the numeral with its comma (3,452), and the expanded form 3000 + 400 + 50 + 2.
Use arrow (place-value) cards to lay out 3000 + 400 + 50 + 2, then slide them together so they overlap into the single numeral 3,452, linking the expanded form to the compact numeral.
Place the finished number on a 0-10,000 number line to check its rough magnitude, noticing how the comma/grouping helps you read size at a glance.

Swap two digits in your built number — for example exchange the 4 and the 5 in 3,452 to make 3,542 — and compare both on the bench and on the number line to see that moving a digit into a different column changes its value and the whole number's size.
Empty one column at a time (3,452 → 3,402 → 3,002) and describe what happens to the numeral and the expanded form.

In a reverse mode, listen to or read a spoken number such as 'three thousand and six' and build it; leave the hundreds AND tens columns empty so two bold placeholder 0s appear and the numeral resolves to 3,006 (not 36 or 3,600).
activities.intendedInsight: A digit's worth is set by its column, not by the digit itself — so swapping digits between columns changes the number; thousands repeat the ×10 pattern (ten hundreds = one thousand); and empty columns must still be written as 0 so magnitude and the comma are correct.

activities.title: Reference wall: one number decoded
feedback: If a learner reads the 7 in 7,345 as 7 hundreds, point to its column position and count from the ones: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands.
For 3,006, confirm that the two 0s mark empty hundreds and tens so the 3 stays in the thousands column.
activities.rationale: A fixed worked example gives a stable visual anchor and a quick reference for digit values and the hardest multi-zero case. It cannot build arbitrary numbers, so it supports rather than substitutes for hands-on construction.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'recognise the place value of each digit in a four-digit number (thousands, hundreds, tens, and ones)'.
The ×10 place-value structure repeats into thousands; multi-zero numbers are the principal difficulty and need explicit placeholder work.
learnerActions: Study a single four-digit number displayed in a Th|H|T|O chart and tap each digit to reveal its blocks and its value (the 7 in 7,345 → 7 thousands = 7000).
Open a dedicated 3,006 anchor and use a flap or note that explains why the two internal zeros must both be written.
Use this wall as a lookup reference while working on other construction tasks.
activities.intendedInsight: Each digit's value can be read directly from its column, and internal zeros are placeholders that hold a column's place.

activities.title: Check digit values and expanded form
feedback: For 4,050 = 4000 + ___ + 50 + ___, confirm the hundreds blank is 0 and the ones blank is 0 — the empty columns still count.

If 'three thousand and six' is read as 3,600 (or 36), contrast the candidate forms digit by digit in a column chart to show where each digit sits, making clear that only 3,006 keeps the 3 in the thousands column with 0s holding the empty hundreds and tens.
activities.rationale: Targeted checking items confirm that value-of-digit, expanded-form and multi-zero knowledge is secure. These items use recognition responses: they assess and reinforce but do not themselves elicit independent construction of a number from parts, so they are best used after construction work.
sourceClaims: Generalise place-value understanding and read/write multi-digit whole numbers using base-ten numerals, number names and expanded form (4.NBT.1-2).
learnerActions: Answer 'value of the digit' questions, e.g. state the value of the 7 in 7,345 (7000, not 7 or 700).
Complete fill-in-the-blank expanded forms: 3,452 = 3000 + ___ + 50 + 2 (blank is 400); 4,050 = 4000 + ___ + 50 + ___ (both blanks are 0).
Match numerals to their expanded forms and spoken number names.
For 'three thousand and six', identify the correct written form 3,006 and explain why the incorrect forms 36 and 3,600 must be rejected.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can reliably read off a digit's value by its place and write/complete expanded forms, including where a column is zero.

activities.title: Spot the place-value detective's mistake
feedback: When the learner corrects the character, prompt them to point to the specific empty columns that need a 0.
Ask the learner to generate a second tricky number (e.g. 7,000 or 4,050) and explain its zeros.
activities.rationale: Explaining and correcting a worked error prompts learners to verbalise the placeholder principle. Because it elicits explanation and checking rather than building the column structure with blocks, it works best alongside hands-on construction rather than as the main route.
sourceClaims: The ×10 place-value structure repeats into thousands; multi-zero numbers are the principal difficulty and need explicit placeholder work.
learnerActions: Work with a character who keeps mis-sizing numbers such as 3,006 (writing 36 or 3,600).
Explain, using a column chart, why the character is wrong and correct the number together.
Say back the rule in your own words: empty hundreds and tens still need a 0 so the thousands digit keeps its place.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating why a multi-zero number must be written a particular way deepens understanding of placeholders.

constraints: Multi-zero numbers (3,006; 4,050; 7,000) are the main source of four-digit errors and should be prioritised, with explicit placeholder work.

Keep build, numeral (with comma/space grouping) and expanded form synchronised so learners connect the three representations; arrow cards and a number line are useful extra links to the numeral and to magnitude.
The reference-wall and checking activities assess or anchor understanding but do not let learners construct arbitrary numbers; use them to support, not replace, hands-on building and recomposition.
Checking/matching items use recognition responses and do not by themselves elicit independent construction of a number from parts.
Use place-value counters for larger numbers where physical thousand-cubes become unwieldy, while keeping the column meaning explicit.

Address common slips directly: reading a digit off the wrong column, concatenating expanded parts (3000400502), losing a placeholder, misplacing or ignoring the thousands comma, and assuming digit order doesn't matter.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original row rated a 3D interactive 'poor' and argued a 3D thousand-cube 'doesn't make the idea spatial'. This comparative/necessity claim is not established by the cited sources; it has been treated as a design preference, not asserted as a universal law. Base-ten blocks (physical cubes or on-screen models) can each support the concept.

The auto-fuse and placeholder-snap interactions are retained as concrete, optional mechanisms that make the unitising and placeholder ideas visible; they are not the only way to teach this and should not be read as mandatory.
The CCSS and NCETM source claims are marked verified:false in the original row; confidence should not be upgraded on migration.

The source assessment's digit-swap / order-matters comparison (value of the 5 in 3,452 vs 3,542; whether swapping the 4 and 5 changes size) and the 'digit order doesn't matter' misconception have now been incorporated into Activity 1's construction and feedback; a further comparison/ordering extension could still be added.
The Gattegno chart extended to the thousands row was not carried into the activities; it remains an available alternative representation for displaying the repeating ×10 row structure.

probeDeeper: What is the value of the 3 in 3,452 — and why is it so much more than the 4?
Build 3,452 for me from thousands, hundreds, tens and ones.
If I swap the 4 and the 5, does the number get bigger or smaller? Why?
Which is worth more, the 5 in 3,452 or the 5 in 3,542?
assess.correctAnswer: In 3,452 the 4 is worth 4 hundreds (400). In 3,542 the same digit 4 is worth 4 tens (40). The value changes because the digit's place — not the digit itself — determines its worth.

errorPatterns.pattern: Face value — 'the 4 is just 4', the same in both numbers, ignoring its column.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Partition 3,452 with base-ten blocks or a place-value chart; show the 4 as four hundred-flats, then move it to the tens column to see its worth become 40.
errorPatterns.distractor: The 4 is worth 4 in both.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child states the value as the bare digit and says it does not change.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads value off the wrong column — names the 4 in 3,452 as 4 tens rather than 4 hundreds.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Label the four columns (thousands, hundreds, tens, ones) and point to where the 4 sits; count from the ones rather than guessing.
errorPatterns.distractor: The 4 in 3,452 is 4 tens.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct idea that place matters, but the column is miscounted by one.

errorPatterns.pattern: Digit order doesn't matter — thinks 3,452 and 3,542 are the same size because they use the same digits.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compose both from place-value parts (3000+400+50+2 vs 3000+500+40+2) and compare totals to show swapping columns changes the number.
errorPatterns.distractor: 3,452 and 3,542 are the same size.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says the value is unchanged AND the two numbers are equal.

responseLevels.gap: Gives the digit's face value and denies it can change across positions.
responseLevels.full: States each digit's value by its place, explains that position (not the digit) sets the worth, and predicts how swapping digits changes the number.
responseLevels.partial: Knows position matters and can partition, but miscounts a column or is unsure why swapping digits changes the number.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In the number 3,452, what is the value of the 4? Would that value change if I wrote 3,542 instead? Why?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands place value says the 4 is worth 400 here but 40 there, and grounds it in position. A child on face value says '4' or '400' in both and insists it can't change; asking whether it changes across the two numbers forces the positional idea into the open.
