pedagogy.summary: Year-1 children make the leap from comparing lengths to quantifying them: laying identical units (cubes, paper clips) end to end and counting them, then beginning to read a centimetre ruler. The concept underneath the procedure is that a measurement is a count of equal-sized length-units tiling the object with no gaps or overlaps, always recorded as a number WITH a unit.
bestPractices: Begin with non-standard units (interlocking cubes, paper clips) laid end to end; count and record the result before any ruler is introduced.
Insist the units are identical in size — deliberately contrast a row measured with mixed-size units so children see why equal units matter.
Make iteration self-checking: units abut with no gaps and no overlaps; have children build their own paper ruler by marking off one repeated unit, tying the ruler back to iteration.
Always attach a unit to the number ('8 cubes', '12 cm') and ask 'what are you counting?' so the number stays tied to length, not to how many objects.
Introduce the centimetre ruler as a tool that simply counts the same iterated units, with the start of the object aligned to the beginning of the ruler.
keyRepresentations: Interlocking / unit cubes laid end to end along an object
Paper-clip chains as a non-standard unit
A child-made paper ruler with a single unit marked off repeatedly
Centimetre ruler
A recording strip: '____ cubes' / '____ cm'
commonMisconceptions: Leaves gaps between units or overlaps them, treating measuring as 'placing things along' rather than covering the length.
Uses mixed-size units yet counts them as one total.
Counts the number of discrete objects (cardinality) rather than the length covered — e.g. a row of 6 short matches is called 'longer' than an equal row of 5 longer matches.
Begins counting the ruler at the numeral '1' instead of the zero/start.

learn.summary: Year-1 children move from comparing lengths to quantifying them: laying identical units (cubes, paper clips) end to end, counting them with no gaps or overlaps, and then beginning to read a centimetre ruler. The core concept is that a measurement is a count of equal-sized length-units tiling the object completely, always recorded as a number WITH a unit.

activities.title: Tile the length with identical cubes
feedback: If there is a gap between cubes, run a finger along the uncovered stretch and ask: is that length being counted? Close the gap and re-count.
If two cubes overlap, point out that the same stretch is being counted twice; separate them so they just abut.
When the row is clean and gap-free, confirm the count and always restate it with the unit: 'about 8 cubes long.'

In a digital version the running counter can redden or refuse to total a gappy or overlapping row, and only count a cleanly tiled row — so the no-gaps/no-overlaps rule is felt, not just told. This live recompute is one optional way to make the rule self-checking.
activities.rationale: Year-1 children often slide units without abutting them exactly and are not concerned about accuracy, so self-checking iteration (abutting units, finger-check, or a recompute that only counts a clean row) targets the actual procedural leap of covering the length rather than merely placing units along it.
sourceClaims: Measuring length means iterating a chosen unit end to end with no gaps or overlaps and counting the units; Grade 1 children may initially leave gaps or overlaps, treating measuring as placing units along a path rather than covering the length; units must be the same size; children may count discrete objects (cardinality) and call a row with more, smaller items 'longer'; a measurement is a number assigned relative to a unit and must be recorded with its unit.

In the Length Unit Relater and Repeater level children iterate a single unit and understand the need for equal-length units; children often are not concerned about accuracy when iterating (sliding a unit without abutting it exactly), so the best activities are self-checking.
learnerActions: Place a pencil or book in front of you and a tub of same-size cubes beside it.
Lay cube after cube along the pencil, end to end, from one end of the pencil.
Nudge the cubes so each one touches the next with no gaps and no overlaps.
Count the cubes and say the result as a number with its unit, e.g. '8 cubes'.
Run a finger along the pencil to check no uncovered stretch is left between cubes.
activities.intendedInsight: A length-count only means the length when identical units cover the object completely, with no gaps and no overlaps.

activities.title: Why the units must all be the same size
feedback: If the child counts mixed sizes as one total, pause on the '3 large and 4 small' challenge: are these 7 of the same thing? Establish that the units must all match before the count means anything.
After re-measuring with one size, confirm the total and connect it back to the clean, equal-unit row.
Ask 'would bigger units give you more or fewer?' to check they expect a larger unit to give a smaller count.
activities.rationale: Deliberately contrasting equal versus mixed units exposes the equal-unit rule directly; this addresses the documented misconception of counting mixed-size units as a single total.
sourceClaims: Measuring length means iterating a chosen unit end to end with no gaps or overlaps and counting the units; Grade 1 children may initially leave gaps or overlaps, treating measuring as placing units along a path rather than covering the length; units must be the same size; children may count discrete objects (cardinality) and call a row with more, smaller items 'longer'; a measurement is a number assigned relative to a unit and must be recorded with its unit.

In the Length Unit Relater and Repeater level children iterate a single unit and understand the need for equal-length units; children often are not concerned about accuracy when iterating (sliding a unit without abutting it exactly), so the best activities are self-checking.
learnerActions: Measure the book again, but this time use a bin that has a few oversized blocks mixed in with the small cubes.
Report the total and check whether it makes sense.
Try the challenge: '3 large blocks and 4 small blocks laid in a row — is the book 7 blocks long?' Explain your answer.
Re-measure the book using only one size of unit and compare.
activities.intendedInsight: A measurement is only meaningful when every unit is the same size; mixing sizes makes the count nonsense.

activities.title: Length is extent, not how many pieces
feedback: If the child says the 6-match row is longer because it has more pieces, lay the two rows side by side aligned at one end so they can see whether the extents match.
When asked 'what are you counting?', steer from 'the matches' toward 'the length' — the number of pieces alone does not tell you the length unless the pieces are the same size.
If the child lines the rows up and finds they reach the same point, confirm they are the same length and ask how aligning at one end let them tell.
activities.rationale: Children often judge length by cardinality, calling a row of more, smaller items 'longer'. The two rows are set up to be the same total length (an off-stage setup condition the child is not told); direct side-by-side comparison re-anchors length as extent independent of the number of pieces.
sourceClaims: Measuring length means iterating a chosen unit end to end with no gaps or overlaps and counting the units; Grade 1 children may initially leave gaps or overlaps, treating measuring as placing units along a path rather than covering the length; units must be the same size; children may count discrete objects (cardinality) and call a row with more, smaller items 'longer'; a measurement is a number assigned relative to a unit and must be recorded with its unit.
learnerActions: Look at two rows of matches: one row made of 6 short matches and one row made of 5 longer matches.
Decide which row is longer, or whether they are the same length, and say what you are counting.
Lay the two rows directly side by side, aligned at one end, to check your answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Length is how far something extends, not how many pieces make up the row; more pieces does not mean longer.

activities.title: Build a paper ruler and read a centimetre ruler
feedback: If the child lines the object up with '1', show that the stretch from 0 to '1' is already one unit, so reading the numeral at the far end gives one centimetre too many; realign to 0 and re-read.
If they read off the last numeral the object touches without aligning the start, go back to the paper ruler to re-connect numerals to counted units.
Confirm the recorded result always carries its unit ('15 cm'), not a bare number.
In a digital version a virtual ruler can be required to align at 0 before it reads out, linking the tiled units to the tool. This is one optional way to make the zero-start concrete.
activities.rationale: Building a paper ruler from a single repeated unit ties the ruler back to iteration, and keeps ruler work light at this age. Starting at '1' or reading the last numeral touched are common Year-1 errors the zero-alignment work addresses.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils measure and begin to record lengths and heights using non-standard and then standard units, and begin to use a ruler.

Measuring length means iterating a chosen unit end to end with no gaps or overlaps and counting the units; Grade 1 children may initially leave gaps or overlaps, treating measuring as placing units along a path rather than covering the length; units must be the same size; children may count discrete objects (cardinality) and call a row with more, smaller items 'longer'; a measurement is a number assigned relative to a unit and must be recorded with its unit.
learnerActions: Take a strip of paper and mark off one chosen unit over and over, end to end, to make your own ruler.
Use your paper ruler to measure a short object, counting the units.
Now take a centimetre ruler and line its start (the 0) up with one end of the object, not the '1' mark.
Read off how many centimetres long the object is and record it as a number with its unit, e.g. '15 cm'.
activities.intendedInsight: A ruler is just a tool that counts the same iterated units; you start from zero because the numerals name the units of space already covered.

activities.title: Spot-the-gap and how-many checks
feedback: For a 'spot the gappy row' choice, name exactly what is wrong with each rejected row — a gap, an overlap, or mixed-size units.
For a how-many answer that is off by one, check where the count started: for a cube row, the first cube is counted as 1; for a ruler picture, the object should start at the 0 mark.
Use these as checks after hands-on practice, not instead of it.
activities.rationale: Recognition items and sliders can check the idea and a spot-the-gap step is discriminating, but recognition-only responses do not elicit the hand-action of building a clean row; keep these as post-practice checks.
learnerActions: Look at several pictured rows and pick which one has been measured correctly (no gaps, no overlaps, equal units).
For a tidy row of cubes, say or set a slider to how many cubes long it is.
For a ruler picture, say how many centimetres long the object is.
activities.intendedInsight: You can recognise a correctly measured row and read a count, but recognising one does not by itself build the skill of producing a clean row yourself.

constraints: Begin with non-standard units (interlocking cubes, paper clips) laid end to end; count and record before any ruler is introduced.
Always attach a unit to the number ('8 cubes', '12 cm') and ask 'what are you counting?' so the number stays tied to length, not to how many objects.
Keep ruler work light at this age; a child-made paper ruler tying the ruler back to a single repeated unit is the bridge to the centimetre ruler.

Recognition/selection items (spot-the-gap, how-many sliders) check understanding but do not by themselves build the hand-action of iterating and fixing a gappy row; use them as post-practice checks, not the main activity.

A static tap-to-reveal of a cube-row or ruler ('each cube = one length-unit', '0 starts here') can clarify the meaning of the marks as a reference, but a fixed image cannot be re-tiled by the child; pair it with hands-on or interactive iteration.

Physical cubes and an on-screen model offer different experiences; neither is claimed as the only way to learn iteration. Prefer whichever lets the child iterate units and get honest feedback on gaps, overlaps and mixed sizes.
When probing cardinality-vs-length, present or compare rows by aligning the objects side by side at one end; reteaching may require returning to direct length comparison as a prerequisite.

The matches example only demonstrates cardinality-vs-length if the two rows are genuinely the same total length; set the rows to be physically equal but do NOT tell the child they are equal, so the comparison stays open and is discovered by aligning them.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original rated 3D as 'poor' because length is one-dimensional, and dialogue/conversation as 'poor' for a procedural skill. These catalog fit-rankings are not retained as universal pedagogical laws; the relevant objective limit (recognition-only responses do not elicit independent construction) is kept, but claims that a static image or a conversation 'cannot teach' are softened or dropped.
The UK National Curriculum source is marked verified:false in the row; treat the Year-1 ruler claim accordingly.

Self-audit of the matches example: a row of 6 shorter matches and a row of 5 longer matches must be set to the same total length to illustrate cardinality-vs-length. This equality is a setup condition kept off-stage; the child-facing prompt no longer states the rows are equal (that would give away the answer) and instead offers 'same length' as one allowed answer the child can reach by aligning the rows.

Self-audit of ruler logic: aligning the object end with 0 (not '1') is correct — the space before the '1' mark is already one unit — so reading from '1' loses a unit; this correction is retained in the activity.

Corrected the cardinality activity on independent review: the prior feedback 'end to end' (which joins rows lengthwise) was already changed to side-by-side alignment, and the learner-facing setup that revealed the rows as 'the same total length' has now been removed so the probe is neither leading nor self-answering; the equality remains only as an off-stage setup condition in the constraints and rationale.

probeDeeper: You said 8 — 8 what? Point to one of them.
If I measured this same book with these bigger blocks instead, would I get more than 8 or fewer than 8? Why?
Watch — I'll lay them like this (place with a gap). Is that measuring properly? What's wrong with it?
Can you start the ruler somewhere other than the end and still get the right length?
assess.correctAnswer: The child lays identical units end to end from one end of the book with no gaps or overlaps, counts the length-units (not the objects at random), states and records the count WITH a unit ('about 12 cubes' / '15 cm'), and — when they reach for the ruler — aligns its start (0) with the end of the book rather than the '1' mark.

errorPatterns.pattern: Gaps or overlaps: lays units with spaces between them or overlapping, as if measuring is 'putting things along' the object rather than covering its whole length with no holes.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach in place: have them run a finger along the object to feel the uncovered length between cubes; use abutting, self-checking units and re-count.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cubes placed with visible gaps or overlapping; the child still counts them and offers a number.

errorPatterns.pattern: Mixed-size units counted as equal: combines cubes and larger blocks and reports one total, not noticing the units differ.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Pose the '3 large blocks and 4 small blocks — is it 7 blocks long?' challenge; establish that measuring units must all be the same size, then re-measure with one size.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A row of different-sized objects counted as a single number.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts discrete objects, not length (cardinality): judges length by how many pieces there are, so a row of more, smaller units is called 'longer' than an equal-length row of fewer, larger units.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the matches-experiment discussion and to direct length comparison so length is re-anchored as extent independent of the number of pieces.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Shown two equal-length rows, the child says the one with more items is longer; answers 'what are you counting?' with 'the cubes' not 'the length'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Ruler read from '1': treats the numerals as signals for where to start counting, so lines the book up with the '1' mark or reports the last numeral touched.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that 0 is the start and that a numeral names the units of space already covered; keep ruler work light at this age and build a paper ruler by iterating a single unit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Object aligned to the '1' on the ruler, or the final numeral crossed read off as the length; answer off by one.

responseLevels.gap: Lays units with gaps/overlaps or mixes sizes, or gives a bare number with no unit, or judges length by how many pieces there are regardless of the actual extent.
responseLevels.full: Lays identical units with no gaps or overlaps from one end, counts the length-units, records the number with its unit, aligns the ruler's zero, and can say a bigger unit would give a smaller count.
responseLevels.partial: Lays equal units end to end and counts them, but the procedure is fragile: e.g. iterates cubes cleanly yet starts the ruler at '1', or omits the unit unless prompted — succeeds in the practised case but does not transfer to the ruler.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set out a book, a tub of same-size cubes with a few larger blocks mixed in, and a centimetre ruler. Say: 'Measure how long this book is and tell me the number.' Do not tell them how. Watch how they lay the units, whether they mix sizes, and where they start the ruler; then ask them to write the result down.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who holds the concept produces a clean, gap-free row of equal units and a number-with-unit, and starts the ruler at zero. A child who lacks it reveals precisely which sub-idea is missing in the way they lay and read — gaps/overlaps, mixed units, counting objects, or starting at 1 — none of which a child with the full concept does. The performance is watched, never asked about.

pedagogy.summary: Dividing by 10 (or 100) makes every digit ten (or a hundred) times smaller, so each digit slides one place (or two places) to the RIGHT on a place-value chart while the digits themselves and their order stay the same. 37 ÷ 10 = 3.7 (the 3 moves from tens to ones, the 7 from ones to tenths); 4 ÷ 100 = 0.04 (the 4 moves to hundredths and a zero must hold the empty tenths place). It is emphatically NOT 'move the decimal point' or 'add/remove a zero' — those rules mislead as soon as a placeholder is needed.
bestPractices: Use a place-value chart and physically slide digit cards one column right per division by 10 — the digits move, the point stays put
Forbid the 'just add/cross off a zero' shortcut; it only works for multiples of ten and breaks on 37 ÷ 10
Make the placeholder zero explicit: for 4 ÷ 100 the tenths column is empty, so a 0 must hold it to give 0.04, not 0.4
Anchor in money and metric (£4 ÷ 100 = 4p = £0.04; 37 cm ÷ 10) so the shrinking is meaningful
Read every result back by place value ('3 ones and 7 tenths') rather than as a digit string
keyRepresentations: Place-value chart with sliding/draggable digit cards
Gattegno (tenths/hundredths) chart
Base-ten blocks with exchange (a rod is a tenth of a flat)
Number line and money/metric contexts
commonMisconceptions: Applies 'move the decimal point' by rote and gets the magnitude wrong (37 ÷ 10 → 0.37 or 370)
Omits the placeholder zero: 4 ÷ 100 → 0.4
Over-generalises 'divide by 10 = take a zero off', which fails on numbers without a trailing zero

learn.summary: Dividing by 10 or 100 makes every digit ten or a hundred times smaller, so each digit slides one or two places to the RIGHT on a place-value chart while the digits and their order stay the same. 37 ÷ 10 = 3.7 (the 3 moves from tens to ones, the 7 from ones to tenths); 4 ÷ 100 = 0.04 (the 4 moves to hundredths and a 0 must hold the empty tenths place). The reliable idea is that digits shift and shrink. 'Add/remove a zero' fails for numbers like 37, which have no trailing zero, and 'move the decimal point' gives the same answer but hides why the values change and can lead to errors when a placeholder is needed.

activities.title: Slide the digits right on a place-value chart
feedback: If a learner writes 0.37 or 370 for 37 ÷ 10, return to the chart and slide each digit exactly one column right; show the point stays put and the digits move, and ask 'ten times smaller than 37 — is that near 3 or near 300?'

If a learner writes 0.4 for 4 ÷ 100, show the 4 landing in hundredths with the tenths column empty; ask what must hold the empty tenths place, and establish that without the 0 the value would be ten times too big.
When a learner reads results by digit string, prompt them to name each digit's place value instead ('what is the 7 worth now?').
activities.rationale: The concept is literally a movement of digits across columns, so enacting the slide and naming each landing place targets magnitude and placeholder reasoning directly, rather than a memorised symbol rule.
sourceClaims: Errors in decimal place value stem from over-generalising whole-number rules (e.g. 'add/remove a zero', 'move the point') rather than reasoning about the size of each digit's place; secure understanding requires reasoning about place value, not memorised digit-manipulation rules.
learnerActions: Set up a place-value chart with columns labelled hundreds, tens, ones, then a decimal point, then tenths and hundredths.
Place digit cards for 37 (3 in tens, 7 in ones) and predict what dividing by 10 will do.
Divide by 10 by sliding each digit card one column to the RIGHT: the 3 moves from tens to ones, the 7 moves from ones to tenths, giving 3.7. Notice the decimal point itself does not move.
Read the result back by place value: '3 ones and 7 tenths'.
Now place a single digit card for 4 in the ones column and divide by 100 by sliding it two columns right, so the 4 lands in hundredths.
Notice the tenths column is now empty and write a 0 to hold that place, giving 0.04. Say why, without the 0, you would wrongly read 0.4.

Optionally model the same shrink with another representation — base-ten blocks with exchange (letting a flat be one whole so a rod is a tenth of a flat and a small cube a hundredth), a Gattegno tenths/hundredths chart, or a number line — to see the quantity becoming ten or a hundred times smaller.
activities.intendedInsight: Dividing by 10 (or 100) shifts every digit one (or two) places right and makes it ten (or a hundred) times smaller; a placeholder zero is needed whenever a column between the point and a digit is left empty.

activities.title: Confront the 'take a zero off' rule
feedback: If a learner stalls trying to remove a zero from 37, point to the pair 40 ÷ 10 (works) versus 37 ÷ 10 (fails) and rebuild using the digit slide.
If a learner keeps 37 unchanged, ask 'is your answer ten times smaller than 37?' to expose the error.
activities.rationale: Directly comparing a case where the shortcut appears to work against one where it breaks helps dislodge the over-generalised whole-number rule, which is the documented source of error.
sourceClaims: Errors in decimal place value stem from over-generalising whole-number rules (e.g. 'add/remove a zero', 'move the point') rather than reasoning about the size of each digit's place; secure understanding requires reasoning about place value, not memorised digit-manipulation rules.
learnerActions: Work out 40 ÷ 10 and notice that 'take a zero off' happens to give 4.
Now try the same rule on 37 ÷ 10 and show it fails — there is no trailing zero to remove, and leaving 37 unchanged (or writing 370) is wrong.
Redo 37 ÷ 10 on the place-value chart by sliding digits right to get 3.7, and state in your own words why the shortcut only worked for 40.

Test 'move the decimal point' similarly and check it against the chart result. Notice that, done correctly, it agrees with the chart, but it does not show that each digit has become ten times smaller.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Remove a zero' only works when there is a trailing zero to remove, and 'move the point' gives the right result only when it is applied carefully but does not explain why it works. Sliding each digit one place right and reading place value always works and shows why.

activities.title: Anchor the shrink in money and measurement
feedback: If a learner gives £0.4 for £4 ÷ 100, relate it to coins: 4p is four hundredths of a pound, so a 0 must hold the tenths (ten-pence) place.
Have the learner read each answer by place value to confirm the magnitude is sensible.
activities.rationale: Familiar money and metric contexts make the shrinking meaningful and give a concrete check on magnitude and placeholder placement.
learnerActions: Work out £4 ÷ 100 and connect it to 4p, writing it as £0.04; check the 4 sits in the hundredths (pence-of-a-pound) place.
Work out 37 cm ÷ 10 and express the result as 3.7 cm, checking which column each digit lands in.
For each context, say which digit moved and what it is now worth.
activities.intendedInsight: Dividing by 10 or 100 means a quantity becomes ten or a hundred times smaller, and the place-value result matches real money and metric amounts.

activities.title: Check placeholder and magnitude with targeted questions
feedback: If 0.4 is chosen for 4 ÷ 100, show on the chart that the 4 belongs in hundredths and the tenths place needs a 0.
If 0.004 is chosen, check how many columns the 4 moved: dividing by 100 moves it two places, not three.
Confirm understanding by asking the learner to name each digit's place value, not just the numeral.
activities.rationale: Well-chosen distractors (0.4 for the missing placeholder, 0.004 for over-shifting) surface the exact magnitude and placeholder errors; this checks whether a result is correct and should follow, not replace, the hands-on slide work.
learnerActions: Complete 37 ÷ 10 = ___ and state what each digit is worth.
Choose the correct value of 4 ÷ 100 from 0.4, 0.04, and 0.004, and justify the choice by naming where the 4 lands.
Match each digit in your answers to its place value (ones, tenths, hundredths).
activities.intendedInsight: A correct answer must place every digit in the right column, using a placeholder zero where a column is emptied; the 0.4-versus-0.04 distinction is the sharpest test.

activities.title: Static chart as a reference label
feedback: If a learner can label landing places but cannot produce them, return to physically sliding the digits so the movement is performed, not just read.
activities.rationale: A still reference supports vocabulary and recall; because it does not enact the slide, it works best alongside an activity where the learner carries out the movement.
learnerActions: Beside the moving chart, keep a labelled still chart and point to where each digit of 37 starts and where it lands after ÷10.
Use it to look up and name the place value of any digit in a result (for example, the hundredths place in 0.04).
activities.intendedInsight: A fixed chart names where digits land and supports recall of place-value labels, as a companion to enacting the movement.

constraints: Teach digits-shift-right with the decimal point staying fixed; do not teach 'add/remove a zero' as a rule, since it fails for any number without a trailing zero (e.g. 37 ÷ 10), and do not teach 'move the decimal point' as the main rule, since it gives the same result but hides why each digit's value changes and can lead to errors when a placeholder zero is needed (e.g. 4 ÷ 100).
Always make the placeholder zero explicit: 4 ÷ 100 = 0.04, not 0.4; require learners to say why the tenths place needs a 0.
Have learners read results by place value ('3 ones and 7 tenths'), not as a bare digit string, so magnitude is checked.
A static chart labels landing places but does not perform the movement; use it as a reference beside activities where the learner actually slides the digits.
Recognition/selection questions check whether a result is correct but do not by themselves elicit the learner independently constructing the movement; pair them with hands-on chart work.

Alternative representations (base-ten blocks with exchange, Gattegno chart, number line) are optional supports, not requirements; when using base-ten blocks, fix which block is the whole so a rod reads as a tenth.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The single cited source supports that decimal place-value errors arise from over-generalising whole-number rules and that place-value reasoning is needed; it does not establish the comparative efficacy of any specific activity or medium here.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 37 ÷ 10 = 3.7 and 4 ÷ 100 = 0.04 are correct; £4 ÷ 100 = £0.04 = 4p and 37 cm ÷ 10 = 3.7 cm are correct. The 0.004 distractor corresponds to an over-shift of three places (effectively ÷1000) and is retained only as an incorrect option, never as a valid answer.
The legacy source rated depth/3D and dialogue formats as adding nothing; that is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law, so it has been dropped rather than asserted as universal.
The legacy reteach-prerequisite links for the error patterns use internal topic identifiers and were not migrated into learner-facing guidance.

The original keyRepresentations listed a Gattegno chart, base-ten blocks with exchange (a rod is a tenth of a flat), and a number line; these had been dropped by the candidate and have been restored as optional alternative representations.

probeDeeper: When you divide by 10, does each digit get bigger or smaller — and by how much?
In your answer 3.7, what is the 7 worth now, and where was that digit before?
For 4 ÷ 100, why can't we just write 0.4? What has to go in the tenths place, and why?
Some people say 'to divide by 10, take off a zero'. Does that work for 37 ÷ 10? Why not?
assess.correctAnswer: 37 ÷ 10 = 3.7 (3 ones, 7 tenths); 4 ÷ 100 = 0.04 (4 hundredths, with 0 holding the tenths place). Explains that dividing by 10 shifts every digit one place to the right.

errorPatterns.pattern: Moves the decimal point by rule without place-value meaning, landing the wrong magnitude: 37 ÷ 10 → 0.37 or 370
errorPatterns.nextMove: Go to the place-value chart and slide the digits one column right; show the point stays and the digits move. Rebuild what 'ten times smaller' means.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Talks about 'moving the point' rather than 'each digit gets smaller'; answer is off by a factor of ten or a hundred

errorPatterns.pattern: Omits the placeholder zero: 4 ÷ 100 → 0.4 because they 'put the 4 after the point'
errorPatterns.nextMove: On the chart, show the 4 landing in hundredths with the tenths column empty; a 0 must hold that place or the value is ten times too big.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 0.4 for 4 ÷ 100; cannot say what belongs in the tenths column

errorPatterns.pattern: Over-generalises 'to divide by 10 just take a zero off' and is stuck or invents a zero when the number has none (37)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront the rule directly: show 40 ÷ 10 where it seems to work and 37 ÷ 10 where it fails; replace it with digits-shift-right on the chart.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Tries to remove a zero from 37 and stalls, or writes 37 unchanged / 3.70

responseLevels.gap: Moves the point by rote or adds/removes zeros, producing the wrong magnitude, and cannot name the digits' place values.
responseLevels.full: Divides by 10 and 100 fluently with correct placeholder zeros, states each digit's new place value, and explains that dividing by 10 shifts every digit one place right; transfers to a fresh number.
responseLevels.partial: Gets 37 ÷ 10 = 3.7 but fumbles 4 ÷ 100 (omits the placeholder or is unsure), or can name new place values only when prompted.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a place-value chart and say: 'Work out 37 ÷ 10, then 4 ÷ 100. For each answer, tell me what each digit is worth.' Watch how they get the answer — do not tell them a method.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands slides the digits right and keeps them, using a placeholder zero where a column is emptied (4 ÷ 100 = 0.04). A child running a rote 'move the point' or 'add/remove a zero' rule produces 0.37, 370, or 0.4. The 4 ÷ 100 case is the sharpest: it forces a placeholder zero that a rule-follower typically omits, and it asks for digit values, exposing whether place value is understood or just recited.

sources.claim: Errors in decimal place value stem from over-generalising whole-number rules (e.g. 'add/remove a zero', 'move the point') rather than reasoning about the size of each digit's place; secure understanding requires reasoning about place value, not memorised digit-manipulation rules.

pedagogy.summary: Thousandths continue the tenfold nesting one place further: split a hundredth into ten and each piece is a thousandth, so 1/100 ÷ 10 = 1/1000, and the places march ones → tenths → hundredths → thousandths, each a tenth of the one before. The coordinating facts are 10 thousandths = 1 hundredth, 100 thousandths = 1 tenth, and 1000 thousandths = 1 whole. In notation, 25 thousandths is 25/1000 = 0.025, where the leading placeholder zero holds the empty tenths place. The recurring obstacle is again whole-number bias — believing a thousandth is bigger than a hundredth 'because 1000 > 100' — and the placeholder error 25/1000 → 0.25. Build thousandths by repeated ÷10 subdivision and by zooming in on the number line between two hundredths.
bestPractices: Derive thousandths by subdividing a hundredth into ten, making 1/100 ÷ 10 = 1/1000 an action the child performs, so the recursive tenfold structure is felt rather than told.
Coordinate two levels of nesting explicitly: 10 thousandths = 1 hundredth AND 100 thousandths = 1 tenth, so children compose the ×10 steps instead of applying a single one.
Zoom the number line: locate 0.345 by zooming between 0.34 and 0.35 and splitting into ten, so a thousandth is seen as a tenth of the gap between hundredths.
Drill the placeholder in notation: 25/1000 = 0.025 (two leading places filled), contrasting 25/100 = 0.25 and 25/10 = 2.5, so place governs the number of zeros.
Confront whole-number bias directly — compare 0.05 and 0.005, or one hundredth against one thousandth — so 'more parts, smaller each' overturns 'bigger denominator, bigger part'.
keyRepresentations: Place-value chart: ones | tenths | hundredths | thousandths
Number line with zoom between two hundredths, split into ten thousandths
Recursive subdivision model (whole → tenth → hundredth → thousandth, ten-for-one each step)
Comparison pair 0.05 vs 0.005 to break whole-number bias
commonMisconceptions: Whole-number bias: a thousandth taken as bigger than a hundredth or tenth 'because 1000 > 100'.
Placeholder error: writing 25 thousandths as 0.25 (or 0.0025), not 0.025.
Miscoordinating the nesting: saying 10 thousandths = 1 tenth (one ×10 step) instead of 100 thousandths = 1 tenth.
Treating the digits after the point as a whole number, so 0.025 is read as 'twenty-five' and mis-sized.
Thinking the number line 'runs out' at hundredths, so not subdividing further to place a thousandth.

learn.summary: Thousandths continue the tenfold nesting one place further: split a hundredth into ten and each piece is a thousandth, so 1/100 ÷ 10 = 1/1000, and the places march ones → tenths → hundredths → thousandths, each a tenth of the one before. The coordinating facts are 10 thousandths = 1 hundredth, 100 thousandths = 1 tenth, and 1000 thousandths = 1 whole. In notation, 25 thousandths = 25/1000 = 0.025, where the leading placeholder zero holds the empty tenths place. The recurring obstacles are whole-number bias (believing a thousandth is bigger than a hundredth 'because 1000 > 100') and the placeholder error (writing 25/1000 as 0.25). Build thousandths by repeated ÷10 subdivision and by zooming in on the number line between two hundredths.

activities.title: Zoom the number line to place 0.345
feedback: If a learner says the line stops at hundredths, prompt: 'The gap between 0.34 and 0.35 can itself be cut into ten — what is each new piece called?'
If they place 0.345 at the wrong mark, have them count the ten equal steps aloud and check that 0.345 sits on the fifth mark (5 thousandths past 0.34).
If a learner thinks a thousandth is the smallest piece possible, invite them to split it into ten again and name the ten-thousandth, reinforcing that the ÷10 subdivision can always continue.
Confirm success when they can name each step as one thousandth and justify the position of 0.345 by counting thousandths.
activities.rationale: Locating a thousandth by zooming between two hundredths and subdividing into ten makes the recursive tenfold structure an action the child performs, rather than a rule stated to them. If a live number line is used, dragging a zoom control and watching the gap split into ten labelled steps makes the mechanism concrete; a drawn paper number line zoomed and re-divided on a fresh strip serves the same purpose.
sourceClaims: Whole-number bias — treating a larger denominator or more digits as a larger quantity — is the central obstacle as children extend place value to thousandths, and place-value reasoning built by subdivision and number-line work (rather than a stated rule) is needed; faulty digit-based rules can pass easy items, so placeholder and comparison cases must be used.
Pupils should recognise and use thousandths and relate them to tenths, hundredths and decimal equivalents (Year 5 statutory content).
learnerActions: Start with a number line showing just 0.34 and 0.35, with nothing marked between them, and predict aloud roughly where 0.345 should go.
Zoom into the gap between 0.34 and 0.35 and divide it into ten equal steps; name what each single step is worth (one thousandth, a tenth of the gap between two hundredths).
Count the steps and place 0.345 exactly on the fifth mark (the midpoint of the gap), then state why: it is 5 thousandths past 0.34.
Repeat the zoom-and-split for another thousandth, e.g. place 0.347, so the subdivision becomes a repeatable action, not a one-off.
Extend the action one level further: split a single thousandth into ten equal parts and name each tinier piece a ten-thousandth, illustrating that the ÷10 subdivision can always be repeated again.
activities.intendedInsight: A thousandth is a tenth of the gap between two hundredths; the number line never 'runs out' — you can always subdivide one more time by ten to locate a finer value (a tenth of a thousandth is a ten-thousandth).

activities.title: Split a hundredth and compare sizes to break whole-number bias
feedback: If the learner predicts the thousandth is bigger 'because 1000 beats 100', do not just correct — have them physically lay one thousandth against one hundredth so the size difference is visible, then restate the rule 'more parts means each is smaller'.
For 0.05 vs 0.005, if they pick 0.005, point to the split: 0.005 is 5 thousandths while 0.05 is 50 thousandths (ten times larger); have them count how many thousandths are in each.
Confirm success when the learner states that a thousandth is smaller than a hundredth and can explain why the larger number 1000 does not make the part larger.
activities.rationale: Directly predicting, then confronting the prediction with a visible length comparison, targets whole-number bias in the moment the child commits to a wrong reason. Showing one thousandth beside one hundredth makes 'more parts, smaller each' concrete; a live splitter that recolours or relabels each new piece, or a paper strip cut into ten, both make the subdivision tangible. A paper strip cut into ten has slight thickness, so treat it as a model of the ideal zero-thickness partition, not identical to it.
sourceClaims: Whole-number bias — treating a larger denominator or more digits as a larger quantity — is the central obstacle as children extend place value to thousandths, and place-value reasoning built by subdivision and number-line work (rather than a stated rule) is needed; faulty digit-based rules can pass easy items, so placeholder and comparison cases must be used.
learnerActions: Before comparing, predict which is bigger, one hundredth or one thousandth, and say WHY in words.
Take one hundredth and split it into ten equal parts; identify each part as one thousandth.
Lay a single thousandth beside a whole hundredth and describe what you see — the thousandth is tiny next to the hundredth.
Reconcile this with your prediction: even though 1000 is a bigger number than 100, a thousandth is a smaller amount because it comes from cutting into more, smaller parts.
Compare 0.05 and 0.005 directly and state which is bigger and why, when both use the digit 5.
activities.intendedInsight: More, smaller parts means each part is smaller: a thousandth is smaller than a hundredth despite 1000 > 100, overturning 'bigger denominator, bigger part'.

activities.title: Write thousandths and justify the placeholder zero
feedback: If the learner writes 0.25 for 25 thousandths, return to the chart: thousandths is the third place after the point, so 25 must occupy hundredths and thousandths, leaving tenths empty and needing a 0.
If they write 0.0025, check column by column: the 5 should sit in thousandths (third place), not further right.
Confirm success when they both write 0.025 correctly and explain, using the chart, why the zero after the point is needed and why 25/100 and 25/1000 differ.
activities.rationale: Writing thousandths within an explicit place-value chart and contrasting 25/10, 25/100, 25/1000 makes the placeholder error visible and correctable by reasoning about place rather than digit-copying. A running chart that updates as the learner fills each column, or a hand-drawn chart, both make the empty tenths cell explicit.
sourceClaims: Whole-number bias — treating a larger denominator or more digits as a larger quantity — is the central obstacle as children extend place value to thousandths, and place-value reasoning built by subdivision and number-line work (rather than a stated rule) is needed; faulty digit-based rules can pass easy items, so placeholder and comparison cases must be used.
Pupils should recognise and use thousandths and relate them to tenths, hundredths and decimal equivalents (Year 5 statutory content).
learnerActions: Using a place-value chart with columns ones | tenths | hundredths | thousandths, write 25 thousandths: place the 2 in hundredths and the 5 in thousandths.
Fill the empty tenths column with a 0 and write the decimal 0.025, then explain that the zero holds the empty tenths place.
Contrast the set 25/10 = 2.5, 25/100 = 0.25, 25/1000 = 0.025, and describe how the place of the value decides where the digits land and how many leading places are filled.
Write a second example, e.g. 35 thousandths = 35/1000 = 0.035, and say why there is one placeholder zero straight after the decimal point (in the tenths place).
activities.intendedInsight: The place a value occupies, not just the digits, fixes the written decimal; the placeholder zero in 0.025 holds the empty tenths position so the 2 lands in hundredths and the 5 in thousandths.

activities.title: Compose two tenfold steps: 10 and 100 thousandths
feedback: If the learner says 10 thousandths = 1 tenth, build it in stages: 'How many thousandths in a hundredth? And how many hundredths in a tenth? So how many thousandths in a tenth?'
Have them count on a subdivided line through both levels to see the two steps accumulate to 100.
Confirm success when they answer 100 thousandths per tenth and can name both tenfold steps that compose it.
activities.rationale: Explicitly coordinating two levels of nesting addresses the miscoordination error (saying 10 rather than 100 thousandths per tenth) by having the child compose the steps instead of applying one. Counting through the levels on a subdivided line or stacking the facts on a chart both make the two steps visible.
sourceClaims: Whole-number bias — treating a larger denominator or more digits as a larger quantity — is the central obstacle as children extend place value to thousandths, and place-value reasoning built by subdivision and number-line work (rather than a stated rule) is needed; faulty digit-based rules can pass easy items, so placeholder and comparison cases must be used.
Pupils should recognise and use thousandths and relate them to tenths, hundredths and decimal equivalents (Year 5 statutory content).
learnerActions: State and show that 10 thousandths make 1 hundredth (one ÷10 subdivision).
Then show that 10 hundredths make 1 tenth, so composing the two steps gives 100 thousandths = 1 tenth.
Continue the chain to 1000 thousandths = 1 whole, naming each tenfold step.
Answer the trap question 'How many thousandths are in one tenth?' and justify 100 (two tenfold steps), explaining why 10 is wrong (it skips a step).
activities.intendedInsight: Getting from thousandths to tenths is two tenfold steps, not one: 10 thousandths = 1 hundredth and 100 thousandths = 1 tenth; the nesting composes rather than applying a single ×10.

activities.title: Check and diagnose with targeted questions
feedback: For the comparison item, if the learner selects 0.005 citing 1000 > 100, route back to the split-and-compare activity to re-establish 'more parts, smaller each'.
For 25/1000, if they omit the placeholder zero, return to the place-value chart activity.
Treat the 'why' answers as diagnostic: a learner who answers correctly but cannot explain the two-step nesting or the placeholder still needs the composing and notation activities.
activities.rationale: These checkable items with distractors (the 1000 > 100 comparison, the missing placeholder) surface whole-number bias and placeholder errors diagnostically. Checks assess outcomes rather than build the nesting insight, so they complement, not replace, the subdivision and zoom activities.
sourceClaims: Whole-number bias — treating a larger denominator or more digits as a larger quantity — is the central obstacle as children extend place value to thousandths, and place-value reasoning built by subdivision and number-line work (rather than a stated rule) is needed; faulty digit-based rules can pass easy items, so placeholder and comparison cases must be used.
learnerActions: Complete 25/1000 = 0.0__ and justify where the 2 and 5 sit and why the zero is there.
Complete '100 thousandths = __ tenth' and explain the two-step reasoning.
Decide which is bigger, 0.05 or 0.005, and give a reason that does not rely on 'more digits means bigger'.
Place 0.345 between 0.34 and 0.35 by stating how many equal steps are in the gap and which step 0.345 is.
activities.intendedInsight: Correct answers plus a stated reason distinguish genuine grasp of the recursive tenth-of-a-tenth-of-a-tenth structure from a memorised conversion or digit-copying.

constraints: Target age roughly 9–10 (Year 5): recognise and use thousandths and relate them to tenths, hundredths and decimal equivalents.
Build thousandths by subdivision and zooming as actions the child performs, so the recursive tenfold structure is felt, not merely asserted.

A reference chart or diagram with tappable nesting facts and a notation flap can communicate the structure as a reference, but on its own it does not let the child perform the subdivision or the zoom; use it as a reference scaffold alongside, not instead of, hands-on subdivision.

Checkable question formats with distractors assess outcomes and can diagnose errors (whole-number bias, placeholder) but do not by themselves elicit the construction of the nesting; use them to check and route, not as the sole means of teaching the insight.
Always use placeholder cases (25/1000 = 0.025) and comparison cases (0.05 vs 0.005) because faulty digit-based rules can pass easy items.
Address whole-number bias directly by making 'more, smaller parts means each is smaller' visible, rather than by rule assertion.
Treat any physical paper split as a model of the ideal zero-thickness partition: real card has slight thickness and only approximates the mathematical subdivision.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The second listed source (DfE National Curriculum) is marked verified:false in the source row; it is cited only for the Year 5 scope/content statement, not for comparative efficacy.

Self-audit of arithmetic and place value: 25/1000 = 0.025 (2 in hundredths, 5 in thousandths, 0 placeholder in tenths); 25/100 = 0.25; 25/10 = 2.5; 35/1000 = 0.035 — all consistent. The ten-for-one chain 10 thousandths = 1 hundredth, 100 thousandths = 1 tenth, 1000 thousandths = 1 whole is internally consistent. Dividing 0.34–0.35 into ten equal steps puts 0.345 on the fifth mark, i.e. the midpoint and 5 thousandths past 0.34; 0.05 = 50 thousandths and 0.005 = 5 thousandths — consistent.

The original 'conversation' and '3D' fit entries asserted a character/depth 'adds nothing'; these universal-dismissal claims were dropped rather than propagated, since the source ratings do not establish such necessity/impossibility claims. No source establishes that the 2D interactive is superior to any other medium; the medium preference is a pedagogical proposal only.

The source probeDeeper and responseLevels.full extend the ÷10 action to ten-thousandths; this was restored as an action and feedback in the zoom activity so the 'never runs out' claim is enacted, not merely asserted.

Physical paper cut into ten parts is an approximation with thickness; it represents the ideal zero-thickness partition and should be treated as a model of it, not identical to it (noted in the relevant activity, not only here).

assess.poeTask: Before comparing, ask the child to PREDICT which is bigger, one hundredth or one thousandth, and to say WHY. The reason is diagnostic: predicting the thousandth is bigger 'because 1000 beats 100' reveals the whole-number bias. Then split one hundredth into ten and lay a single thousandth beside a hundredth — the thousandth is plainly tiny. Have the child reconcile this with their prediction.
probeDeeper: You wrote 25 thousandths as 0.025. Where does the 2 sit, and where does the 5 sit — and why the zero right after the point?
Which is bigger, 0.05 or 0.005 — and why, when the digits are both 5?
If I split one thousandth into ten equal parts again, what would each tiny piece be called?
Show me where 0.345 goes between 0.34 and 0.35 — how many equal steps are in that gap, and which one is 0.345?
assess.correctAnswer: 10 thousandths in one hundredth; 100 thousandths in one tenth. 25 thousandths = 25/1000 = 0.025; the placeholder zero holds the empty tenths place so the 2 lands in hundredths and the 5 in thousandths (each place a tenth of the one before).

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number bias: 'a thousandth is bigger than a hundredth because 1000 is bigger than 100'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Lay one thousandth against one hundredth so the thousandth is visibly tiny; re-establish 'more, smaller parts means each is smaller'. Reteach the tenfold place structure from tenths/hundredths.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a comparison probe (0.05 vs 0.005, or 'which is bigger, a hundredth or a thousandth') picks the thousandth; treats a larger denominator as a larger part.

errorPatterns.pattern: Placeholder error: writes 25 thousandths as 0.25 (or 0.0025) rather than 0.025.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the place-value chart — thousandths is the third place, so 25 occupies hundredths and thousandths with a zero in tenths; contrast 25/100 = 0.25 with 25/1000 = 0.025. Reteach place-fixes-the-value.
errorPatterns.distractor: 25 thousandths is written 0.25.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 0.25 for 25/1000; does not fill the tenths place with a zero.

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscoordinates the nesting: says there are 10 thousandths in a tenth (one ×10 step) instead of 100 (two steps).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build it in stages — 10 thousandths make a hundredth, and 10 hundredths make a tenth, so 100 thousandths make a tenth; count on the subdivided line. Reteach composing tenfold steps.
errorPatterns.distractor: There are 10 thousandths in one tenth.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers '10' for thousandths in a tenth; applies a single tenfold step instead of composing two.

responseLevels.gap: Believes a thousandth is bigger than a hundredth, writes 25/1000 as 0.25, or gives 10 thousandths per tenth. No coordinated nesting.
responseLevels.full: Coordinates the nesting (10 thousandths = 1 hundredth, 100 = 1 tenth, 1000 = 1 whole), writes 25/1000 = 0.025 with the placeholder and justifies it, holds that a thousandth is smaller than a hundredth despite 1000 > 100, places 0.345 by zooming between hundredths, and extends the ÷10 action to ten-thousandths.
responseLevels.partial: Can write 0.025 and recite that 1000 thousandths make a whole, but cannot explain the two-step nesting (100 thousandths = 1 tenth) or why the placeholder is needed — lists facts without relating them.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: How many thousandths are in one hundredth, and how many thousandths are in one tenth? Then write 25 thousandths as a fraction and as a decimal, and tell me why it is written that way.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 'How many thousandths in a tenth' checks whether the child composes two ×10 steps (100) or applies just one (10). Writing 25/1000 exposes the placeholder — a digit-copier writes 0.25. The tier-2 'why' separates a memorised conversion from grasp of the recursive tenth-of-a-tenth-of-a-tenth structure and of a thousandth being smaller than a hundredth despite 1000 > 100.
