pedagogy.summary: This is deductive reasoning from a rectangle's defining properties: because a rectangle has four right angles and two pairs of equal opposite sides, a child can DEDUCE unknown facts — a missing angle must be 90°, an opposite side equals the given one, and a missing side follows from the perimeter (P = 2(l+w)) or the area (A = l×w). The work is reasoning, not measuring: the diagram is usually not drawn to scale, so lengths and angles must come from the stated properties and given numbers, not from the picture. The dominant obstacle is confusing area and perimeter (and their inverse operations); a second is reading unknown lengths off the not-to-scale drawing; a third is forgetting that opposite sides are equal, so a single given side already fixes its opposite.
bestPractices: Reason from the definition: all four angles are 90° and opposite sides are equal, so a given side determines its opposite — mark the equal sides and squared corners on the diagram before calculating
Keep perimeter and area distinct: perimeter is the distance round (P = 2(l+w), cm), area is the space inside (A = l×w, cm²); read which one the problem gives before choosing the inverse step
Work the inverse deliberately: from a perimeter, halve to get l+w then subtract the known side; from an area, divide by the known side — model each as 'undoing' the formula
Treat the diagram as NOT to scale — use the marked and given information, never a ruler on the picture (a side that looks longer may be the equal one)
Attach correct units throughout (cm for length, cm² for area) and sense-check the answer against the rectangle
keyRepresentations: The rectangle with opposite sides tick-marked equal and all four corners squared (90°), given values labelled and the unknown as a box
P = 2(l+w) and A = l×w overlaid on the shape, with 'undo' arrows for the inverse step
A bar / part-whole model for perimeter showing l+w as half the perimeter
Deliberately not-to-scale rectangles where the marks and numbers override the look
commonMisconceptions: Confuses area and perimeter, or their formulae/units — e.g. divides by a side when the problem gave the perimeter, or halves the area (Machaba: taught together, learned instrumentally)
Short-cuts the perimeter inverse — subtracts the known side straight from the whole perimeter instead of from half of it
Reads unknown lengths or angles off the not-to-scale diagram instead of deducing them from the properties and givens
Forgets that opposite sides are equal, so treats all four sides as unknown even after one is given, or doubts that the fourth angle is 90°

learn.summary: Year 5 pupils (age 9-10) learn to DEDUCE missing lengths and angles of a rectangle from its defining properties (four right angles; two pairs of equal opposite sides) and the given numbers, rather than measuring the diagram. Core work: find a missing side from a given side and the perimeter (P = 2(l+w): halve, then subtract) or from a given side and the area (A = l×w: divide); state that the fourth angle must be 90°; attach correct units (cm, cm²). The deliberately not-to-scale drawing forces reliance on numbers and properties. The dominant obstacle is confusing area with perimeter (and their inverse operations); others are reading lengths/angles off an inaccurate picture, short-cutting the perimeter inverse (subtracting from the whole perimeter instead of from half), and forgetting that one given side already fixes its opposite.

activities.title: Deduce the missing side: perimeter then area, from a not-to-scale rectangle
feedback: If the child types the missing perimeter side correctly, an optional boundary-trace can run a pen round all four sides and click shut at exactly 28, confirming the sides total the perimeter; for the area task, an optional interior-tiling can fill the inside exactly with a 6-by-8 region — these visual confirmations are supportive, not required to validate the reasoning.

If the child writes 28 - 8 = 20, point out that 28 is the whole way round (two lengths plus two widths); undo P = 2(l+w) by halving to 14 first, then subtract the known 8 — a bar or part-whole model showing l+w as half the perimeter makes the halving step visible.

If the child divides 28 by 8 (applying the area method to a perimeter), or halves 48 (applying the perimeter method to an area), ask which quantity the problem gave — distance round or space inside — before choosing the step.
If the child measures or eyeballs the picture, remind them the drawing is not to scale: a side that looks longer may be the equal one; trust the marked and given numbers.
If the child leaves two sides unknown, point back to the tick marks — one given side already fixes its opposite because opposite sides are equal.
If the child says the fourth angle 'looks like' 90°, press that it must be 90° because every rectangle angle is a right angle.
activities.rationale: Deducing missing lengths and angles from rectangle properties is the stated Year 5 objective, and the common error of measuring an inaccurate diagram is addressed by making the figure not-to-scale so facts, not the picture, must be used. Pairing perimeter and area tasks targets the well-documented area/perimeter confusion by forcing a deliberate choice of inverse operation.
sourceClaims: Year 5 statutory content: pupils use the properties of rectangles to deduce related facts and find missing lengths and angles

Learners confuse area and perimeter because the formulae A = l×b and P = 2(l+b) are taught at about the same time and learned instrumentally, without conceptual grounding; they over-generalise the rectangle area formula to other figures

A common error is trying to MEASURE a diagram that is not drawn accurately: 'when the question states that the diagram is not drawn accurately we cannot simply measure ... we need to use [the] facts to calculate' — i.e. deduce from given information rather than read lengths/angles off the picture
learnerActions: Work with a rectangle labelled '8 cm' on one side and 'perimeter = 28 cm', drawn deliberately almost square so measuring is useless; one side is a blank box.
Before calculating, mark the equal opposite sides (tick marks) and the four squared (90°) corners so the given 8 cm is seen on its opposite side too.
Reason the perimeter case aloud or in writing: two sides are 8; the four sides total 28; half the perimeter is 14; 14 - 8 = 6, so the missing side is 6 cm.
Switch to an area task: '48 cm², one side 8 cm' — divide 48 ÷ 8 = 6 to find the missing side, and note the inside is filled by a 6-by-8 region.
State the size of the fourth angle (90°) and justify it from the definition, not the picture.
Attach units throughout: cm for sides, cm² for area.
Transfer to a fresh rectangle with different numbers, choosing halve-then-subtract for perimeter and divide for area.
activities.intendedInsight: Missing facts about a rectangle are deduced from its properties and the given numbers, not read off the drawing; 'going round' (perimeter: halve, then subtract) and 'filling in' (area: divide) are different inverse operations that must be chosen by what the problem gives.

activities.title: Short-answer deductions with targeted wrong-answer options
feedback: For an answer of 28 - 8 = 20: the subtraction was from the whole perimeter; halve to 14 first, then subtract 8.

For an answer found by halving the area: halving 48 cm² only gives 24 cm², which is half the area, not a side. Halving is the first step for undoing a perimeter, not an area. To undo A = l×w, divide by the known side: 48 ÷ 8 = 6 cm.
If a length is labelled cm² (or an area cm), re-link the unit to the quantity: lengths are cm, areas cm².
If the child picks the misleading pictured proportion, restate that the figure is not to scale.
activities.rationale: Fixed items can score the deductions cleanly and present carefully chosen wrong-answer options (halved-area; subtract-from-whole-perimeter) that reveal the specific misconceptions. This format checks recognition and single-answer production but does not let the child watch the boundary close as the inverse lands, so it complements rather than replaces the constructive task.
sourceClaims: Learners confuse area and perimeter because the formulae A = l×b and P = 2(l+b) are taught at about the same time and learned instrumentally, without conceptual grounding; they over-generalise the rectangle area formula to other figures
learnerActions: Given one side and the perimeter, construct the other side (e.g. side 8 cm, perimeter 28 cm → fill in 6 cm) and show the halve-then-subtract working.
Given the area and one side, find the other side (e.g. 48 cm², one side 8 cm → 6 cm) and show the division.
Answer a units item: decide whether a given answer should be in cm or cm².
Face a not-to-scale figure whose proportions mislead, and justify the answer from the numbers rather than the look.
When choosing among options, reject the halved-area answer and the subtract-from-whole-perimeter answer (28 - 8 = 20) and explain why each is wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: The child can reliably select and carry out the correct inverse operation and attach the correct unit, resisting the area/perimeter confusion and the not-to-scale picture.

activities.title: Rectangle properties reference card
feedback: If asked whether a rectangle can have only three right angles, reason that the angles of a quadrilateral sum to 360°, so three right angles force the fourth to be 90° too — it cannot have exactly three.
When comparing a square and a rectangle, note both have four right angles and opposite sides equal; a square additionally has all four sides equal.
activities.rationale: A properties reference supports recall of the definitions that underpin the deduction and seeds NCETM reasoning discussion. It is a static reference: the child does not perform the deduction here, so it is a scaffold beside active practice, not the skill itself.
sourceClaims: Year 5 objective on the properties of rectangles; suggested probes include 'tell me some facts about rectangles', 'is it possible for a rectangle to have only three right angles?', and 'what is the same and what is different about a square and a rectangle?' — reasoning from properties (opposite sides equal, four right angles); the area of a right-angled triangle can be seen as half its enclosing rectangle
learnerActions: Consult a labelled rectangle: each corner reveals '90°', each side reveals 'equals its opposite', and the formulae P = 2(l+w) and A = l×w reveal their undo steps.
Use it alongside practice to recall the defining properties before calculating.

Answer NCETM-style reasoning probes: 'Tell me some facts about rectangles'; 'Is it possible for a rectangle to have only three right angles?'; 'What is the same and what is different about a square and a rectangle?'
activities.intendedInsight: A rectangle's defining properties — two pairs of equal opposite sides and four right angles — are the authority for deduction, and holding them in mind prevents treating sides or the fourth angle as unknown.

constraints: The task is reasoning and calculation with feedback, not measuring: diagrams should be marked as not to scale so lengths and angles come from stated properties and given numbers.
Keep perimeter and area (and their inverse operations and units) explicitly distinct; present both side by side so the child must choose the correct step rather than apply one method by default.
The reference/tap-to-reveal card is a recall scaffold only — it does not require the child to perform a deduction, so it should sit alongside active practice, not replace it.

Fixed-item practice (single-answer construction and multiple-choice) checks recognition and single-answer production and can present diagnostic wrong-answer options, but it does not let the child construct and visually confirm the inverse step; use it to complement constructive practice.
Boundary-trace and interior-tiling animations are optional confirmations of a correct answer, not the mechanism the child must use to reason.

Keep the work planar: length, area and perimeter of a rectangle are two-dimensional; adding a third dimension risks drifting toward surface area and volume, which is a different objective at this stage.
The perimeter inverse is halve-then-subtract (28 → 14 → 14 - 8 = 6); do not subtract the known side from the whole perimeter.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The National Curriculum source (Year 5 'use the properties of rectangles to deduce related facts and find missing lengths and angles') is marked verified:false in the source row; treat its support as unconfirmed.

Legacy claims that open dialogue and 3D are 'poor' fits were framed as near-universal in the source. Retained only as narrowly scoped affordance notes: open dialogue suits reasoning probes but not step-by-step compute-and-deduce practice with feedback, and a third dimension can mislead toward volume for a planar objective. No comparative efficacy is asserted.

Arithmetic self-audit: perimeter 28 cm with one side 8 cm → half is 14, 14 - 8 = 6 cm (correct); area 48 cm² ÷ 8 = 6 cm (correct); the value 28 - 8 = 20 is deliberately wrong and must appear only as a flagged misconception, never as a valid answer.

The NCETM claim also mentions 'the area of a right-angled triangle can be seen as half its enclosing rectangle'; this is beyond the current missing-side objective and was not built into an activity to avoid scope creep.

probeDeeper: This problem gives the PERIMETER — why do you halve it before subtracting? What would 28 - 8 give you, and is that a side?
The picture looks almost square, but the numbers say one side is 8 cm and the perimeter 28 cm — which do you trust, and why?
You found one side is 6 cm — what are the other three sides, and how do you know without measuring?
The second rectangle gives an AREA — why do you divide here, but halve-and-subtract for the first one?
assess.correctAnswer: First rectangle: reasons that opposite sides are equal, so half the perimeter is 14 cm and the missing side = 14 - 8 = 6 cm; states that all angles, including the fourth, are 90°. Second rectangle: missing side = 48 ÷ 8 = 6 cm. Uses the given numbers and rectangle properties (not the drawing), with correct units (cm and cm²).

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses area and perimeter, or their inverse operations — e.g. divides when the problem gave the perimeter, or halves the area to find a side
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the two ideas: perimeter is the distance round (halve to l+w, then subtract), area is the space inside (divide by the side); read which is given before choosing the step (Machaba: the two are taught together and confused when learned instrumentally).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Applies the area method to the perimeter task or vice-versa (divides 28 by 8, or halves 48), or labels a length in cm²

errorPatterns.pattern: Short-cuts the perimeter inverse — subtracts the known side straight from the whole perimeter (28 - 8 = 20) instead of from half of it
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model P = 2(l+w) as two lengths plus two widths; undo by halving to get l+w, then subtract the known side — a bar model showing the half-perimeter helps.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 28 - 8 = 20 (or similar) rather than halving to 14 first

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the missing length or angle off the not-to-scale drawing instead of deducing it — measures or eyeballs the picture
errorPatterns.nextMove: State that the diagram is not to scale — the numbers and the rectangle's properties are the authority; use the marks, not the picture (Third Space: when a diagram is not drawn accurately you cannot measure, you must use the facts).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reports a length close to what the wrong-proportioned picture shows, or reaches for a ruler; says the fourth angle 'looks like' 90° rather than knowing it must be

errorPatterns.pattern: Forgets opposite sides are equal — treats the given side as fixing only itself, so tries to solve with all sides unknown, or is unsure that the fourth angle is 90°
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reground the defining properties — a rectangle has two pairs of equal opposite sides and four right angles; mark the equal sides and squared corners before calculating.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Does not use '8 also appears on the opposite side'; leaves two sides unknown, or hesitates over the fourth angle

responseLevels.gap: Applies the wrong operation (divides the perimeter, halves the area, or subtracts from the whole perimeter), or reads the length off the not-to-scale picture; cannot reliably state that the fourth angle is 90°.
responseLevels.full: Deduces each missing side from the rectangle's properties and the given numbers — halving the perimeter then subtracting, and dividing for the area — states that the fourth angle is 90° from the definition, ignores the not-to-scale drawing, attaches correct units, and transfers to a new rectangle problem.
responseLevels.partial: Handles one type — say the area division — but slips on the perimeter inverse (subtracts from 28 rather than 14), or gets the numbers but muddles the units, or needs prompting to use opposite-sides-equal; manages the routine case but not both reliably.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a rectangle drawn deliberately NOT to scale (make it look almost square), with one side labelled 8 cm, the perimeter labelled 28 cm, and one side left blank — plus a second rectangle with area 48 cm² and one side 8 cm. Say: 'Find the missing side of each, and tell me the size of the fourth angle. Show your working.' Say nothing about method; watch how they get the missing sides and whether they measure the picture or reason from the numbers.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The perimeter and area problems sit side by side so the child must pick the right inverse, and the not-to-scale drawing means measuring the picture gives a wrong answer — exposing the child who reads lengths off the diagram. A child reasoning from properties halves the perimeter before subtracting and divides for the area; a child confusing the two divides the perimeter or subtracts from the whole 28; a child trusting the picture reports the wrong measured length. Watching the working — not asking 'what is the difference between area and perimeter?' — shows which.

sources.claim: Learners confuse area and perimeter because the formulae A = l×b and P = 2(l+b) are taught at about the same time and learned instrumentally, without conceptual grounding; they over-generalise the rectangle area formula to other figures
sources.source: Machaba, F.M. (2016), 'The concepts of area and perimeter: Insights and misconceptions of Grade 10 learners', Pythagoras (peer-reviewed; ERIC full text)

sources.claim: Year 5 objective on the properties of rectangles; suggested probes include 'tell me some facts about rectangles', 'is it possible for a rectangle to have only three right angles?', and 'what is the same and what is different about a square and a rectangle?' — reasoning from properties (opposite sides equal, four right angles); the area of a right-angled triangle can be seen as half its enclosing rectangle
sources.source: NCETM — 'Misconceptions with the Key Objectives' (Shape section, Year 5 rectangles objective; Area & Perimeter discussion)

sources.claim: A common error is trying to MEASURE a diagram that is not drawn accurately: 'when the question states that the diagram is not drawn accurately we cannot simply measure ... we need to use [the] facts to calculate' — i.e. deduce from given information rather than read lengths/angles off the picture
sources.source: Third Space Learning — GCSE Maths, Angles (Common misconceptions)

sources.claim: Year 5 statutory content: pupils use the properties of rectangles to deduce related facts and find missing lengths and angles
sources.source: National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (Year 5 Geometry — properties of shapes)

pedagogy.summary: At 6-7, with teacher prompting, the child moves from merely showing a method to EXPLAINING and beginning to JUSTIFY it — using drawings, number sentences, or words to say not just what they did but why the answer is right, including confirming it by an alternative method and spotting an error in a worked example. On the NRICH ladder this spans explaining and convincing. The characteristic gap here is between convincing and justifying: a child at this stage is often confident ('I reckon it's right') with an argument that does not yet hang together as a complete because-chain. Teaching supplies the logical connectives and sentence stems that turn a confident assertion into a reasoned justification, uses alternative-method agreement as a form of justification, and treats error-finding as reasoning practice.
bestPractices: Prompt 'why does that work?' and 'how do you know it's right?' — not just 'what did you do?'
Teach logical connectives and sentence stems ('because', 'so', 'therefore', 'this can't be right because…') to move confident asserting toward complete justification
Use an alternative method that gives the same result as a justification ('the other way also gives 13, so it makes sense')
Use worked examples containing errors and ask children to find and EXPLAIN the mistake
Keep concrete/visual support (drawings, number sentences) as the backbone of the explanation
Distinguish, for yourself and the child, confident-but-incomplete (convincing) from a correct complete chain (justifying), and push gently toward the latter
keyRepresentations: Drawings and number sentences as the medium of explanation
Alternative-method check (two routes to the same answer)
Sentence stems with connectives (because / so / therefore)
True-or-false equation judgements
The explain → convince → justify steps of the NRICH ladder
commonMisconceptions: Confident assertion ('I reckon it's right') offered as justification, with an incomplete or incoherent chain (convincing mistaken for justifying)
Describing the method but stopping short of saying WHY it gives the right answer unless heavily prompted
Spotting that a worked example is wrong but being unable to explain the flaw
Treating 'justify' as 'do the sum again' rather than giving a reason

learn.summary: For ages 6-7, with adult prompting, children move from showing a method to EXPLAINING and beginning to JUSTIFY it — using drawings, number sentences, or words to say not just what they did but WHY the answer is right. The characteristic gap is between convincing (confident but with an incomplete chain, 'I reckon it's right') and justifying (a correct, complete because-chain). Teaching supplies logical connectives and sentence stems, uses alternative-method agreement as a form of justification, and treats finding and explaining errors in worked examples as reasoning practice.

activities.title: The 'convince me' partner
feedback: When the child only asserts confidently: 'You've convinced me you're sure — now tell me WHY, starting with because…'
When they narrate steps but no reason: 'You made ten first — but why does making ten give the right answer?'
When an alternative method agrees: 'The other way also gives 13, so it makes sense — two routes, same answer.'
When they spot a flawed example only by the odd-looking answer: 'What should have happened at this step? Is each side really the same?'
When they produce a complete chain: name it back so they hear their reasoning hold together.
activities.rationale: Explaining and justifying with prompting is naturally a guided dialogue: a responsive partner can ask 'why does that work?', supply because/so stems, accept an alternative method as evidence, and fold error-critique into the same conversation. Reasoning and its communication develop separately and both benefit from explicit support such as sentence stems and modelling.
sourceClaims: Proficient students justify their conclusions and communicate them, and can distinguish correct reasoning from flawed reasoning and explain what the flaw is; all students can decide whether others' arguments make sense.

Convincing (confident, possibly inaccurate, incomplete chain) is a distinct rung below justifying (a correct, complete chain using because/therefore/so); reasoning and its communication develop separately and both need explicit support (sentence stems, modelling).
learnerActions: Pose the child a within-20 calculation (e.g. 8 + 5) and ask them to explain HOW they worked it out.
Then ask 'why does that work?' and 'how do you know it's right?' — not just 'what did you do?'.
When the child stalls or only asserts ('I just know', 'I reckon it's right'), hand over a sentence stem: 'Start with because…' and prompt for the missing link.
Have the child upgrade a confident hunch into a chain, e.g. 'because 5 is 2 and 3, and 8 and 2 make 10, so 10 and 3 more is 13'.
Ask the child to show the same calculation a different way and check whether it also gives the answer ('the other way also gives 13 — what does that tell us?').
Present a worked example containing a slip (e.g. a number bond that doesn't actually make ten) and ask 'Is this right? How can you tell?' — pushing for WHICH step is wrong and WHY.
activities.intendedInsight: A confident answer is not the same as a justification; a reason that works can be built by linking steps with 'because' and 'so', and an alternative method that agrees is supporting evidence that backs up the reason, though it does not replace explaining why.

activities.title: Build an explanation you can test
feedback: If the chain skips a link: 'Something's missing between here and here — what goes in between, starting with because?'
If the second method disagrees: 'Two routes gave different answers — one of them has a slip; let's find it.'
On a correctly identified and explained error: confirm the step AND the reason, not just the flag.
If the child flags an error without a reason: 'You're right it's wrong — now which step, and what should have happened?'
activities.rationale: Arranging steps and connective words (because/so/therefore) and running an alternative-method or error check can make justification a concrete thing the child constructs and tests, rather than a phrase to recite; the explicit support of sentence stems and modelling is what the research emphasises. Draggable step cards, connective tiles, an 'check it another way' tool and a tap-the-wrong-step error mode are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not required.
sourceClaims: Convincing (confident, possibly inaccurate, incomplete chain) is a distinct rung below justifying (a correct, complete chain using because/therefore/so); reasoning and its communication develop separately and both need explicit support (sentence stems, modelling).
learnerActions: Give the child step cards (number sentences / method steps) and connective tiles ('because', 'so', 'therefore') to arrange into an argument chain for why a calculation is right.
Have the child read the assembled chain aloud to check it actually hangs together and establishes the claim.
Check the answer a second way (an alternative method) and compare — do the two routes agree?
In an error-spotting task, give a worked example and have the child point to the wrong step AND say why it is wrong.
Keep drawings and number sentences as the backbone of the explanation throughout.
activities.intendedInsight: Justification is something you assemble and test, not just a confident feeling: steps linked with connectives form a chain; a second method checks whether the answer agrees, and checking each step tests whether the chain really holds.

activities.title: Model a complete because-chain (scaffold)
feedback: After modelling: 'Now you say it for a new sum — start each step with because…'
If the child only copies the words: ask them to explain why one of the steps is needed.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal justified example models a complete because-chain and gives a reference point, but it is a scaffold: while only viewing, the child does not construct their own argument, so it must lead into independent construction.
learnerActions: Show a justified worked example where each step is paired with its 'because' reason, e.g. reveal one step at a time so the child sees what a full chain looks like.
After viewing, ask the child to re-tell the chain in their own words, then produce one for a fresh calculation themselves.
activities.intendedInsight: A worked justification shows the TARGET: every step has a reason, and the reasons connect to establish the answer.

activities.title: Critique items: real reason or just saying it's right? (complement)
feedback: After a choice, ask the child to say WHY the chosen reason is the proper one, so selection leads back to constructing their own explanation.
On the counterexample: 'The answer is right — but does the reasoning always work?'
activities.rationale: Selected-response critique items can probe whether a child recognises flaws and distinguishes reasons from assertions, but a recognition/selected-response format cannot assess a child BUILDING their own justification, so it complements rather than replaces the dialogue and construction activities. No comparative efficacy of this format over others is claimed.
sourceClaims: Proficient students justify their conclusions and communicate them, and can distinguish correct reasoning from flawed reasoning and explain what the flaw is; all students can decide whether others' arguments make sense.
learnerActions: Present short 'find the error' items where the child selects the faulty step in a worked example, then says why it is faulty.
Present 'which is a proper reason vs just saying it's right?' items where the child picks the genuine justification over a confident restatement.
Use an open discussion counterexample (child must explain, not just pick): 'Someone got the right answer with a method that only works because these numbers are small — is their reasoning good?'
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising the difference between a reason and a confident assertion, and between good reasoning and a lucky right answer, may help a child see what a proper justification needs; recognising a good reason does not by itself produce one, so these items complement — not replace — the construction tasks.

constraints: Target the gap between convincing and justifying: confident-but-vague is a normal developmental rung, NOT wrong reasoning — hand over connectives and ask for the missing link rather than marking it wrong.
Do not accept 'do the sum again' or 'because it's right' as justification; the target is a reason WHY the method gives the right answer.
Keep concrete/visual support (drawings, number sentences) as the backbone of explanation at this age.
Modelled/tap-to-reveal justified examples are scaffolds: the child sees a chain but does not build one, so always follow with independent construction.

Selected-response critique items assess recognition of flaws and reasons, not the child's own construction of a justification; use them to complement, not replace, dialogue and building tasks. Recognising a good reason does not by itself elicit producing one.
Error-finding should require naming the faulty step AND why it is faulty, anchored on the meaning of equality (is each side really the same?), not just flagging that the answer looks off.
Alternative-method agreement is used here as a form of justification ('two routes, same answer') — frame it as supporting the reason, not as a substitute for explaining why the method works.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The claim that 'explaining arithmetic reasoning is not spatial' (used to dismiss a 3D format) is a catalog fit judgement, not an established pedagogical law; it has been omitted rather than asserted as universal.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 8 + 5 = 13 via make-ten (8 + 2 = 10, then 10 + 3 = 13) is correct and preserved. The flawed-worked-example task deliberately contains an error for the child to find — ensure any wrong step shown is clearly labelled as the item to critique, not presented as a correct model.

The source claims support the general principles (justifying vs convincing; distinguishing correct from flawed reasoning) but do not establish the comparative efficacy or necessity of any specific format (dialogue, step-card builder, critique items, etc.); efficacy wording is kept qualified (proposed/may/intended).

Independent review confirms activity 4's intended insight and rationale are consistent with the limit that recognition does not elicit production; the embedded counterexample is now explicitly an open explain-why probe, not a scored selection.

probeDeeper: 'Why does making ten first give the right answer — start with because…' (pushes assertion into a reason)
'Show it a different way — does that also give 13? What does that tell us?' (alternative method as justification)
'This worked example is wrong — which step, and why?' (explain a flaw, not just flag it)
Counterexample: 'Someone got the right answer using a method that only works because these numbers are small — is their reasoning good?' (reasoning vs a lucky answer)
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for a child who explains the method AND gives a reason it works ('because 8 and 2 make 10, then 3 more is 13'), uses an alternative method as confirmation, and, shown the flawed example, says it is wrong and points to WHY. A complete because-chain and the ability to explain an error are the targets, not the arithmetic.

errorPatterns.pattern: Convincing mistaken for justifying — confident assertion ('I reckon it's right', 'definitely') with an incomplete or incoherent chain of reasoning.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not treat confident-but-vague as wrong reasoning; hand over connectives ('because… so…') and ask for the missing link. This is a normal rung below justifying and firms up with modelling.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child is sure and fluent but the argument skips steps or does not actually establish the claim; confidence outruns the logic.

errorPatterns.pattern: Describes the method but stops short of WHY it works, unless heavily prompted.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Prompt 'why does making ten work?' and use the alternative-method check ('the other way also gives 13 — what does that tell us?') to surface a reason.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child narrates 'I made ten first' but, asked why that gives the right answer, restates the steps rather than giving a reason.

errorPatterns.pattern: Spots that a worked example is wrong but cannot explain the flaw.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point to the step and ask 'what should have happened here?'; anchor on the meaning of equality (is each side really the same?) and model naming the flaw.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says 'that's wrong' because the answer looks off, but cannot identify the faulty step or say why it is faulty.

responseLevels.gap: Restates the answer or 'because it's right'; no reason; can flag the flawed example only by the wrong answer, if at all.
responseLevels.full: Gives a complete because/so chain for why the method works, uses an alternative method as genuine confirmation, explains precisely why the worked example is wrong, and does so with only light prompting.
responseLevels.partial: Explains the method and, prompted, is confident it is right and may check another way — but the justification is asserted rather than reasoned (convincing), and the error is spotted without a clear why.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Pose a calculation such as 8 + 5. Ask: 'Explain how you'd work it out — and why is your answer right? Can you show it a different way to check?' Then show a worked example with an error (e.g. a bond that doesn't make ten) and ask: 'Is this right? How do you know?' Discuss the reasoning; do not mark a number.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who justifies produces a connected because/so chain and can say why the error is an error. A child who only convinces asserts confidently ('I reckon it's right') with gaps, and on the flawed example can say 'it's wrong' (answer mismatch) but not name the faulty step. The presence of a complete reasoned chain, and of an explained flaw, is the discriminator.

sources.claim: Proficient students justify their conclusions and communicate them, and can distinguish correct reasoning from flawed reasoning and explain what the flaw is; all students can decide whether others' arguments make sense.
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Standard for Mathematical Practice 3

sources.claim: Convincing (confident, possibly inaccurate, incomplete chain) is a distinct rung below justifying (a correct, complete chain using because/therefore/so); reasoning and its communication develop separately and both need explicit support (sentence stems, modelling).
sources.source: NRICH (University of Cambridge), Reasoning: The Journey From Novice to Expert

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 6-7 (Y2), META. Use place-value understanding AND known number facts together to solve problems: knowing 34 = 30 + 4 and a bond like 3+2=5 lets you reason 34 + 20 = 54, or work backwards ('add 10 to my number and I get 45'). This is the application layer that turns tens-and-ones knowledge into a problem-solving tool.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y2): 'use place value and number facts to solve problems'; recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently and derive related facts to 100.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.NBT.4/5/6 and 2.NBT.5–9 — add/subtract within 100 using strategies based on place value and properties of operations; mentally find 10 more/less.
• Operational details — Keep it strategy-based, not algorithm-based at this stage: partition (34 = 30 + 4), operate on the parts, recombine. Model missing-number and 'I think of a number' problems that demand working backwards. Emphasise that a known fact (3+2) plus place value (these are TENS) generates a new fact (30+20). Use concrete/pictorial support and expect children to explain WHICH fact and WHICH partition they used.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 6): use 34 = 30 + 4 to add a multiple of ten (34 + 20) with blocks. Tier B (age 6-7): solve a one-step missing-number problem ('__ + 10 = 45') by reasoning about the tens. Tier C (age 7): solve a two-step or unfamiliar-context problem, choosing a partition and a known fact, and explain the reasoning.
bestPractices: Teach partition–operate–recombine explicitly: split into tens and ones, act on the relevant part, put it back together — making the place-value structure the engine of the strategy.
Connect a known bond to its place-value scaling out loud: 'I know 3 + 2 = 5, and these are tens, so 30 + 20 = 50' — so number facts and place value are used together, not in isolation.
Use missing-number and 'think of a number' problems to force flexible, backwards reasoning rather than one-directional calculation.
Insist on explanation/justification ('which fact did you use? how did you split it?') so the META goal — choosing and applying structure — is assessed, not just the answer.
Support with concrete/pictorial models (blocks, part-whole diagrams, number lines) while the strategy forms, then fade them as reasoning becomes secure.
keyRepresentations: Part-whole (cherry) diagram splitting a number into tens and ones
Base-ten blocks for partition–operate–recombine
Empty/marked number line for jumps of tens and ones
Bar model for missing-number and comparison problems
Fact-family / derived-fact chains (3+2=5 → 30+20=50 → 34+20=54)
commonMisconceptions: Reaching for a counting-in-ones or column method instead of using place-value structure, because the number-fact link was never made.
Applying a known bond but forgetting the unit — saying 30 + 20 = 5 (using 3+2 but dropping the tens).
Unable to work backwards — treating 'think of a number' problems as if they can only be solved forwards.
Partitioning incorrectly under a problem's wording (mis-splitting 34 as 3 + 4 rather than 30 + 4).
Focusing on getting an answer without checking it fits the problem, so an unreasonable result goes unquestioned.

learn.summary: For ages 6-7 (Y2), help children use place-value structure together with known number facts to solve problems — e.g. knowing 34 = 30 + 4 and 3 + 2 = 5 to reason that 34 + 20 = 54, and to work backwards on 'I think of a number' problems. The core strategy is partition–operate–recombine: split a number into tens and ones, act on the relevant part, then put it back together, saying aloud which fact and which partition were used. Keep it strategy-based (not column algorithm) at this stage, support with concrete and pictorial models, and insist on explanation so the META goal — choosing and justifying structure — is what develops.

activities.title: Problem playground: partition, operate, recombine
feedback: If the child counts all 54 from one, prompt 'what do you already know that's close?' and show the shortcut (30 + 20) beside the count rather than reteaching the bonds.

If the child refuses to attempt because 'we haven't done this one', think aloud how a known fact generates a new one, name derivation as real mathematics, and invite them to build the next step themselves.
If they say 30 + 20 = 5, point back to the blocks: these are tens, so the answer is 50, not 5 — the unit must be kept.
If they split 34 as 3 + 4, re-anchor on the part-whole diagram: the 3 stands for 30 (three tens).
For the work-backwards mode, if they treat it as only solvable forwards, invite them to test a value and check whether '+10' lands on 45, adjusting up or down.
activities.rationale: Making partition–operate–recombine visible and generative lets the place-value structure act as the engine of the strategy; auto-generating fresh problems supports transfer, and a work-backwards mode forces flexible reasoning. Linked fact-chains and live recombination (e.g. a fact ribbon lighting up, number-line testing) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not required.
sourceClaims: Y2 pupils use place value and number facts to solve problems, and derive/use addition and subtraction facts to 100.
Partition–operate–recombine and deriving new facts from known bonds are core mastery strategies for using place value in calculation.
learnerActions: Take a problem such as 34 + 20 and split 34 into a 30-part and a 4-part (using base-ten blocks, a part-whole 'cherry' diagram, or drawing).
Add the 20 onto the tens part only, saying aloud 'I know 3 + 2 = 5, and these are tens, so 30 + 20 = 50'.
Recombine the parts: 50 + 4 = 54, and state the full chain 3+2=5 → 30+20=50 → 34+20=54.
Try a 'mystery number' / work-backwards problem such as '__ + 10 = 45': cover or guess the start number and test candidate values on a number line until the equation holds.
Repeat with fresh problems (e.g. 34 + 30, 56 + 20) so the strategy — not one answer — is what transfers.
activities.intendedInsight: A number bond you already own (like 3 + 2) can do the heavy lifting on tens, so an unfamiliar calculation can be derived by partitioning and recruiting a known fact rather than counted out from one.

activities.title: Socratic coaching: which fact and which split?
feedback: If the child reverts to counting, nudge toward place value: 'what known fact is hiding in here?'
If they cannot say why splitting 34 into 30 and 4 is legitimate, revisit the part-whole model to show the whole is unchanged.
Affirm reasoning that names both the partition and the fact, even if the final arithmetic needs a small correction.
activities.rationale: Because this is a META skill about choosing and justifying, dialogue that asks the child to state and defend a method can develop the reasoning and respond to the child's chosen approach. This is offered as one effective format alongside hands-on work, not as the only way to teach justification.
sourceClaims: Partition–operate–recombine and deriving new facts from known bonds are core mastery strategies for using place value in calculation.
learnerActions: Face a posed problem (e.g. 34 + 20 or a two-step unfamiliar-context problem) and explain the method you would choose before calculating.

Answer probes: 'What did you already know that you leaned on?', 'How could you use what you already know to solve this?', 'Which fact helped, and why?', 'Is it allowed to split 34 into 30 and 4 — why doesn't that change the answer?'
Compare cases: 'Could you solve 34 + 30 the same way? What changes?' and 'Would this splitting trick help for 34 + 9, or would you do something different there?'
Justify out loud which partition and which known bond you used.
activities.intendedInsight: Choosing and justifying a strategy — recognising that partitioning preserves the total and that known facts can be scaled by place value — is the real mathematical work, beyond getting a single answer.

activities.title: Consolidation problems, including missing-number and trap items
feedback: For a dropped-unit choice (30 + 20 = 5), reconnect to blocks: twenty added to thirty is five tens, i.e. 50.
If a missing-number item is only attempted forwards, encourage testing values or using the bar model to work backwards from the whole (45) and the known part (10) to reach 35.
Ask the child to check the answer fits the problem's wording so an unreasonable result is questioned.
activities.rationale: Problem sets consolidate application and let specific misconceptions (dropping the unit, forwards-only thinking) be surfaced by targeted items, with a bar model making the missing-part structure visible. This format presents problems rather than coaching the forming strategy, so it suits practice after the strategy has been modelled.
sourceClaims: Y2 pupils use place value and number facts to solve problems, and derive/use addition and subtraction facts to 100.
learnerActions: Solve missing-number and 'think of a number' problems (e.g. '__ + 10 = 45', 'I think of a number, add 10, and get 45 — what was my number?'), using a bar model to show the known part, the unknown part, and the whole.
Decide which partition would help a given problem before solving it.
Spot and reject the trap answer where the unit is dropped (e.g. recognise that 30 + 20 is 50, not 5).
Explain, for each item, which fact and which partition were used.
activities.intendedInsight: Place value and known facts can be applied across varied problem types, and keeping track of the unit (tens vs ones) is essential.

activities.title: Worked-example reference anchor
feedback: If a child treats the anchor as the only problem they can do, hand them a fresh problem and ask them to apply the same three steps — naming that deriving a new result is itself mathematics.
activities.rationale: A fixed worked example is a useful reference for the structure of the strategy. Because problem-solving is generative, a single static example should be paired with new problems the child generates or attempts; it anchors rather than replaces practice.
learnerActions: Study one fully worked derived-fact chain (partition–operate–recombine on a single problem), revealing each step: split, operate on the relevant part, recombine.
Retell the steps in your own words before tackling a new problem of your own.
activities.intendedInsight: A clear model of the full chain (e.g. 3+2=5 → 30+20=50 → 34+20=54) gives a template children can imitate on new problems.

constraints: Keep the work strategy-based (partition–operate–recombine), not column-algorithm based, at this stage.
Always name the unit: a known bond like 3 + 2 scales to 30 + 20 = 50 only because these are tens; dropping the unit (saying 5) is the error to catch.
Partition correctly: 34 = 30 + 4, not 3 + 4 — the leading digit stands for tens.

Recognition/selection-only items (choosing which partition, spotting a trap answer) assess application but do not by themselves elicit independent construction or spoken justification; pair them with building, writing, or explaining.
Support with concrete/pictorial models (blocks, part-whole diagrams, number lines, bar models) while the strategy forms, then fade them as reasoning becomes secure.
Insist on justification ('which fact? how did you split it?') so the META goal is assessed, not just the final answer.
A single static worked example cannot pose or respond to new problems; use it as an anchor alongside generative practice.

The original rated a 3D format 'poor' claiming '3D adds nothing' and said a static image 'cannot pose or respond to new problems'; these catalog-style comparative claims are not established by the sources and have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements rather than universal laws.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 34 + 20 = 54 and 30 + 20 = 50 are correct; the derived chain 3+2=5 → 30+20=50 → 34+20=54 is consistent. Fresh examples check out: 34 + 30 = 64 and 56 + 20 = 76. The '30 + 20 = 5' statement appears only as a labelled misconception/distractor, never as a valid answer. The missing-number example '__ + 10 = 45' correctly resolves to 35.
The bar model (an original key representation for missing-number problems) is present in the consolidation/missing-number activity's learner actions, so the preservation claim is now accurate.
Both assessment error patterns are now reflected in feedback (the refusal/myth in the hands-on and anchor activities; defaulting to counting in the hands-on and Socratic activities).
Two source claims (CCSS-M and NCETM) are marked verified:false in the row; retained verbatim only where they directly support a rationale, with no upgrade of their evidence status.

probeDeeper: What did you already know that you leaned on?
Could you solve 34 + 30 the same way? What changes?
Is it allowed to split 34 into 30 and 4? Why doesn't that change the answer?
Would this splitting trick help for 34 + 9 too, or would you do something different there?
assess.correctAnswer: Not scored. A rich response reasons that you can split 34 into 30 and 4, use a fact you know (30 + 20 = 50), then recombine (50 + 4 = 54) — and can say why breaking a number up and leaning on known facts is a legitimate move.

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes each calculation must be taught or memorised as its own item: 'I can't do it, we haven't done that one'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Think aloud how a known fact generates a new one; name derivation as real mathematics and invite the child to try building the next one themselves.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child refuses to attempt an untaught combination or waits to be shown the method.

errorPatterns.pattern: Defaults to counting everything from one even when a known bond would shortcut the work
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the bonds — prompt 'what do you already know that's close?' so the known fact gets recruited; make the shortcut visible next to the count.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child has the bonds but counts all 54 rather than recruiting 30 + 20.

responseLevels.gap: Insists the sum must be counted out or taught first; does not recruit any known fact.
responseLevels.full: Spontaneously reasons that unfamiliar calculations can be derived by partitioning and leaning on known facts, and explains why partitioning preserves the total.
responseLevels.partial: Uses a known fact when prompted but treats it as a one-off, not as a general way to reach untaught answers.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'Here's 34 + 20. Suppose you'd never been shown this exact one before. Is there something you already know that could help you work it out without counting it all? Talk me through how you'd decide.' Surface the thinking for discussion — don't grade it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The probe reveals the child's belief about where answers come from: whether calculations must be individually taught/memorised, or can be DERIVED from facts already held. That epistemic stance — not the single answer — is what is being surfaced.

pedagogy.summary: Compound units measure one quantity PER another — speed (distance per time), density (mass per volume), unit price (cost per gram/item), flow rate. Fluency means (1) computing the rate by dividing the right way round, (2) using the rate to scale up or down and to compare (best-buy, faster-of-two), and (3) converting units correctly, including two-stage conversions like km/h ↔ m/s. The recurring procedural trap is average speed: it is TOTAL distance ÷ TOTAL time, NOT the mean of two speeds. Teaching should build the rate from a double number line or ratio table so 'per one' is visible, and treat the formula triangle with caution because it lets pupils get answers without proportional understanding.
bestPractices: Derive every compound measure as a UNIT RATE first ('how much for exactly one?') using a double number line or ratio table, before any formula.
For best-buy comparisons, insist on a common basis — cost per 100 g for both products — rather than comparing raw price to raw size.
Teach average speed as total distance ÷ total time by working a two-leg journey where the naive mean-of-the-two-speeds answer is demonstrably wrong.
Do km/h↔m/s as a deliberate two-step chain (×1000 m per km, ÷3600 s per hour) with units tracked through each step, not a memorised single factor.
Prefer double number lines / ratio tables over the formula 'magic triangle', which can block proportional reasoning by reducing it to symbol-shuffling (NCETM).
keyRepresentations: Double number line pairing the two quantities (e.g. km against hours, cost against grams)
Ratio table for scaling a rate up and down and for unit conversion
Unit-rate label ('£ per 100 g', 'm per s') as the object of comparison
Distance–time context for average speed (total over total)
commonMisconceptions: Averaging two speeds directly (60 and 40 → '50') instead of using total distance ÷ total time.
Dividing the wrong way round when forming a rate (time ÷ distance for speed, or cost basis inverted).
Comparing unit prices on different bases (price of the big pack vs unit price of the small) and concluding the cheaper total is the better value.
Botching km/h↔m/s by using a single wrong factor (e.g. ×60 or ÷60) instead of the ×1000÷3600 chain.
Treating the formula triangle as the concept — getting a number without knowing whether it should be bigger or smaller.

learn.summary: Compound units measure one quantity PER another: speed (distance per time), density (mass per volume), unit price (cost per gram/item), flow rate. Fluency means (1) computing the rate by dividing the right way round, (2) using the rate to scale up/down and to compare (best-buy, faster-of-two), and (3) converting units correctly, including two-stage chains like km/h↔m/s. The recurring trap is average speed: it is TOTAL distance ÷ TOTAL time, not the mean of two speeds. Build every rate as a visible 'per one' using a double number line or ratio table before any formula, and treat the formula triangle cautiously because it can reduce proportional reasoning to symbol-shuffling. The activities below span an interactive rate workshop, a paper performance task, a short check, and a consolidation reference card, each with a distinct purpose.

activities.title: Rate workshop: best-buy, two-leg journey, and km/h↔m/s converter
feedback: If the pupil writes (60+40)÷2 = 50, show the two leg times (1 h vs 1.5 h) and ask which speed the cyclist spent more time at; more time at 40 pulls the average below 50. Rebuild on a double number line, total over total.

If a division is done the wrong way round (e.g. 40÷60 instead of 60÷40 for the time of a 60 km leg at 40 km/h, or size÷price for a unit price), anchor 'per one': 40 km/h means 40 km in ONE hour, so 60 km takes 60÷40 = 1.5 h. Track units so km ÷ km/h leaves hours. For a unit price, cost goes on top so the result is £ per g (or per item), not g per £.
If the converter uses a single ×60 or ÷60, redo the chain as two labelled steps with units cancelling, and apply the magnitude check (36 km/h ≈ 10 m/s).
If best-buy is decided on total price or pack size, require both products as cost per 100 g (or per item) first; only same-basis figures are comparable.
When the prediction '50' differs from the computed 48, name the gap as the insight: equal distances covered at unequal speeds cannot be averaged by taking the mean of the speeds.
activities.rationale: Compound measures are procedural and comparative, so the learner should perform the rate calculation and get immediate feedback on best-buy, faster-of-two, and unit conversion, with a double number line that recomputes as they scale. Deriving the unit rate first and comparing on a common basis follows guidance to secure the meaning of 'per' and reason multiplicatively via the unit rate. A recomputing double number line, drag-onto-shared-line, a plotted distance-time graph, and on-screen unit cancelling are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory features.
sourceClaims: KS3 Ratio, proportion and rates of change requires pupils to 'use compound units such as speed, unit pricing and density to solve problems' and to 'change freely between related standard units'; KS4 adds 'convert between related compound units (speed, rates of pay, prices, density, pressure) in numerical and algebraic contexts'.

NCETM treats compound measures (speed = distance÷time, density = mass÷volume) as multiplicative comparisons and names as a common misconception that 'compound measures are different from other forms of proportional relationship' when they follow the same multiplicative rules; it stresses securing the meaning of 'per', recommends double number lines and ratio tables, and raises formula triangles as a practice to scrutinise for whether they promote understanding.
Reasoning about rate multiplicatively via unit rate (per one) rather than additively underpins best-buy and speed comparisons.
learnerActions: Best-buy station: compare two shelf tags (e.g. 400 g for £1.80 vs 250 g for £1.20). Put both onto a shared 'cost per 100 g' line and state which is cheaper.
Two-leg journey station: assemble a journey of 60 km at 60 km/h then 60 km at 40 km/h, and — before doing any arithmetic — predict the average speed for the whole journey.

Now compute it: write down the time each leg takes (60÷60 = 1 h and 60÷40 = 1.5 h), then total distance (120 km) and total time (2.5 h), then average speed (120 ÷ 2.5 = 48 km/h). Compare this with your prediction and explain the gap.
Converter station: turn a km/h figure into m/s as two visible steps — ×1000 (km→m), then ÷3600 (per hour→per second) — tracking units so they cancel on screen.
Sanity-check magnitude: 36 km/h should come out as about 10 m/s — a fast cycling/sprinting pace, well above a walk — not 0.6 or 600.
activities.intendedInsight: A rate is 'how much for exactly one', computed by dividing the right way round; average speed is total distance ÷ total time (not the mean of speeds) because more time spent at the slower speed pulls the average down; conversions are a tracked chain, not a single memorised factor; and fair comparisons need a common per-unit basis.

activities.title: Average-speed performance task: work the journey on paper
feedback: Correct answer: 48 km/h. First leg 60÷60 = 1 h; second leg 60÷40 = 1.5 h; total 120 km over 2.5 h gives 120÷2.5 = 48 km/h.
If the answer is 50 from (60+40)÷2, have them find each leg's time first and ask which speed was ridden longer; more time at 40 drags the average below 50.

For the equal-times variant (1 h at 60 then 1 h at 40): total 100 km over 2 h = 50 km/h — here the mean IS correct because equal times are spent at each speed. Use this as a contrasting counterexample, not the general rule.

Full response: produces 48 via leg times → total÷total, forms rates the right way round, converts km/h↔m/s as a correct two-step chain with sensible magnitude, compares best-buys on a common per-unit basis, and transfers to an unfamiliar rate.
Partial response: computes total÷total correctly but slips on a related procedure (inverts a division or botches the conversion) — method not yet secure across compound units.
activities.rationale: Asking the pupil to work the journey on paper discriminates between those computing average speed as total distance ÷ total time and those averaging the speeds, because the equal-distance, unequal-speed setup makes 48 and the naive 50 genuinely different numbers. The equal-times counterexample is mathematically precise: the mean equals the true average speed only when equal times are spent at each speed.
sourceClaims: Average speed is total distance ÷ total time, which equals the arithmetic mean of the two speeds ONLY when equal TIMES are spent at each; for equal DISTANCES the average is the harmonic mean 2uv/(u+v). The page proves the harmonic mean is ≤ the arithmetic mean (difference factorises to (u−v)²/[2(u+v)]), so averaging the two speeds overestimates the true average speed on equal-distance legs — the exact 48-vs-50 trap in this record.
learnerActions: Work out: a cyclist rides 60 km at a steady 60 km/h, then another 60 km at a steady 40 km/h. Find the average speed for the whole journey, showing every step on paper.
Find each leg's time first (60÷60 = 1 h; 60÷40 = 1.5 h), then total distance (120 km), total time (2.5 h), and average speed (120 ÷ 2.5 = 48 km/h).
Answer probes: which leg took more time, so should the average be nearer 60 or nearer 40 — does 50 fit? Then redo with equal TIMES (1 h at 60, 1 h at 40) and explain why the average is 50 this time.
Convert your 48 km/h into metres per second, talking through each step and the units.

Compare two products (e.g. 400 g for £1.80 vs 250 g for £1.20): put both on a cost-per-100 g basis (45p vs 48p), say which is the better buy, and explain what would go wrong if you just compared their prices.
activities.intendedInsight: Watching the pupil compute (rather than recite a rule) reveals whether they use total÷total or average the speeds; because equal distances are covered at unequal speeds, the correct 48 cannot be reached by the mean method, so the method is visible in the number produced. The equal-TIMES counterexample shows the mean is correct only when equal times are spent at each speed.

activities.title: Short check on rates, best-buy and conversion
feedback: If the mean-of-speeds option is chosen, route back to computing leg times and total÷total.
If the 'bigger pack is automatically cheaper' option is chosen, require both products on a common per-100 g basis before deciding.
For a wrong conversion, prompt the two-step ×1000 then ÷3600 chain and the magnitude check.

Use this check to confirm or challenge mastery; it records which answer was produced but does not by itself show the pupil can construct the full method independently — pair it with the paper performance task.
activities.rationale: Rate computation, best-buy choice, and conversion are cleanly checkable in short formats, and the characteristic errors make strong tempting wrong options. A recognition/short-answer format is efficient for surfacing specific slips but does not elicit the independent step-by-step construction that the performance task requires; it is a complement, not a replacement.
learnerActions: Work out and type the cost per 100 g for a product given its price and weight.
Choose the better buy between two differently sized packs where the smaller pack is actually cheaper per unit, so that 'the bigger pack must be cheaper per unit' is a tempting but wrong option.
Choose the average speed of a two-leg equal-distance journey, with the mean-of-the-two-speeds value (e.g. 50) offered as the key trap.
Give a km/h→m/s conversion as a typed value, then check its magnitude.
activities.intendedInsight: The mean-of-speeds error and wrong-way-round division make sharp, diagnostic wrong options, so a quick check can surface whether these specific slips persist after teaching.

activities.title: Consolidation reference card: 'per one' facts and the average-speed warning
feedback: Use the card to remind yourself what 'per one' means for each measure, then go and perform an actual calculation to check you can apply it.
Treat the revealed 'total distance ÷ total time' statement as a prompt to redo a worked journey, not as the whole lesson.
activities.rationale: A static labelled double number line or reference card with tap-to-reveal facts consolidates the idea and keeps the key warning visible. It cannot let the learner perform and check a calculation, which is the heart of this procedural topic, so it functions as a consolidation aid alongside the workshop and performance task rather than as the main teaching activity.
sourceClaims: NCETM treats compound measures (speed = distance÷time, density = mass÷volume) as multiplicative comparisons and names as a common misconception that 'compound measures are different from other forms of proportional relationship' when they follow the same multiplicative rules; it stresses securing the meaning of 'per', recommends double number lines and ratio tables, and raises formula triangles as a practice to scrutinise for whether they promote understanding.
learnerActions: Tap a shelf tag to reveal its unit price (e.g. cost per 100 g) and restate it in words: 'this much for one hundred grams'.
Tap 'average speed' to reveal 'total distance ÷ total time, NOT the average of the two speeds'.
Tap density, speed, and unit-price entries to reveal the 'per one' meaning behind each formula before using it in a calculation.
activities.intendedInsight: A labelled double number line and tap-to-reveal 'per one' facts consolidate the meaning of each compound unit and keep the average-speed warning salient.

constraints: Derive every compound measure as a unit rate first ('how much for exactly one?') using a double number line or ratio table before introducing any formula.
For best-buy, insist on a common basis (cost per 100 g, or per item for both products) rather than comparing raw price to raw size.

Teach average speed as total distance ÷ total time by working a two-leg journey where the naive mean-of-speeds answer is demonstrably wrong; include the equal-TIMES counterexample where the mean IS correct, so pupils learn the precise condition rather than a blanket 'never average speeds'.
Do km/h↔m/s as a deliberate two-step chain (×1000 m per km, ÷3600 s per hour) with units tracked, not a single memorised factor; include a magnitude sanity check (e.g. 36 km/h ≈ 10 m/s).
Prefer double number lines / ratio tables over the formula 'magic triangle', which can reduce proportional reasoning to symbol-shuffling; use the triangle only with care if at all.
The reference card is a consolidation scaffold: it holds facts but does not let the learner perform or check a calculation, so it must not be the sole activity for this procedural skill.

The short check records which answer was produced and surfaces specific slips, but recognition-only responses do not elicit independent construction of the full method; pair it with the paper performance task.
Density and unit price follow the same multiplicative 'per one' structure as speed; comparisons and conversions should be modelled on that shared structure rather than treated as separate rules.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support teaching principles, not the tested effectiveness of these specific activities.

Self-audit (arithmetic): 60÷60 = 1 h; 60÷40 = 1.5 h; total 120 km over 2.5 h = 48 km/h — confirmed. Equal-times variant: 100 km over 2 h = 50 km/h — confirmed; the arithmetic mean is exact only for equal times, matching the harmonic-mean argument in the sources. Conversion: 36 km/h = 36000 m / 3600 s = 10 m/s — confirmed.

Self-audit note on framing: the equal-distance case gives the harmonic mean 2uv/(u+v) = 2·60·40/100 = 48, consistent with the computed answer; the activities state the correct method (total÷total) and present the mean only as the trap, so no erroneous instruction is taught.

The original row described 10 m/s as 'walking-fast'; this is inaccurate (10 m/s ≈ 36 km/h, a fast cycling/sprinting pace), so the activity now describes it as a fast cycling/sprinting pace while keeping the numeric magnitude check.

The original row contained non-preferred-format rationales asserting '3D adds nothing' and that an in-role dialogue 'cannot exercise' the required doing-and-checking. These comparative/necessity claims are not established by the sources and have been softened or dropped; the short check and reference-card activities are retained with scoped affordances and stated limits rather than universal exclusions.

The original 'formula triangle blocks proportional reasoning' claim is retained as a cautious preference (prefer number lines/tables; use the triangle with care), consistent with the practitioner source scrutinising rather than universally banning it.

probeDeeper: Which leg did the cyclist spend more time on — the fast one or the slow one? So should the average be nearer 60 or nearer 40? Does 50 fit that?

Redo it with the two legs the same TIME instead of the same distance (1 hour at 60, then 1 hour at 40). Now what is the average speed — and why is it 50 this time? (counterexample: equal times DO give the mean.)
Show me how you'd turn 48 km/h into metres per second — talk me through each step and what the units are.
For the best buy, how did you make the two products comparable? What would go wrong if you just compared their prices?
assess.correctAnswer: 48 km/h. First leg takes 60÷60 = 1 hour; second leg takes 60÷40 = 1.5 hours. Total distance = 120 km, total time = 2.5 hours, so average speed = 120÷2.5 = 48 km/h.

errorPatterns.pattern: Averages the two speeds directly — (60+40)÷2 = 50 km/h — instead of total distance ÷ total time
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have them find the TIME for each leg first (1 h and 1.5 h). Ask 'which speed did the cyclist spend more time at?' — more time at 40 pulls the average below 50. Rebuild on a double number line, total over total.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes (60+40)÷2 or otherwise combines the speeds without ever computing the two times; answer is 50

errorPatterns.pattern: Divides the wrong way round when forming a rate (time÷distance for speed, or inverts a unit price)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor 'per one': speed is 'km for ONE hour', so distance goes on top. Track units through the division so km/h falls out, not h/km.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Computes 60÷60 correctly by luck but on a leg like 60 km at 40 km/h writes 40÷60, or forms cost-per-pound as size÷price

errorPatterns.pattern: Mishandles the km/h↔m/s conversion, using a single wrong factor (×60 or ÷60) instead of the ×1000 then ÷3600 chain
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do the chain as two labelled steps with units cancelling: km→m (×1000), then per hour → per second (÷3600). Check magnitude: 36 km/h should be a walking-fast 10 m/s, not 0.6 or 600.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a follow-up conversion, multiplies or divides by 60 once, or forgets one of the two steps, giving an answer out by a factor of 60 or 1000

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares best-buys on different bases — assumes the bigger pack or the lower total price is automatically better value
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist both are expressed as cost per 100 g (or per item) before deciding; only same-basis figures are comparable.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a best-buy task picks the cheaper total or the bigger pack without reducing both to a common per-unit basis

responseLevels.gap: Answers 50 by averaging the speeds; does not compute the leg times or total÷total, and cannot correctly form or convert a rate.
responseLevels.full: Produces 48 km/h via leg times → total distance ÷ total time, forms rates the right way round, converts km/h↔m/s as a correct two-step chain with sensible magnitude, and compares best-buys on a common per-unit basis — and can transfer to an unfamiliar rate.

Because equal DISTANCES are covered at unequal speeds, the correct answer (48) differs from the naive mean (50) — a pupil cannot land on 48 by the mean method, so the procedure is visible in the number they produce.
