pedagogy.summary: Placing fractions on a number line is the move from 'fraction = part of a shape' to 'fraction = a number with a magnitude', locatable, orderable and equivalence-checkable. The load-bearing idea is that a fraction 1/b is made by splitting ONE unit (the distance between two whole numbers) into b equal SEGMENTS — needing b−1 marks between them — and the point at the a-th mark is a/b. Teach with the unit held visible so children stop treating the whole line as the unit and stop placing 3/4 'between 3 and 4'.
bestPractices: Start from pre-segmented 0-to-1 lines, then minimally-labelled lines with landmarks (0, 1/2, 1, 1½, 2), then unmarked lines to force interval thinking (IES Rec 2)
Teach fourths as four equal SEGMENTS between 0 and 1 made by THREE marks; generalise 1/n needs n−1 marks
Use contrasting cases to kill 'between 3 and 4': locate 3 and 4 on a 0-to-4 line, then 3/4 within 0-1, and discuss why each sits there
Reason with landmarks and distance ('is 1/12 closer to 1/4 or to 0?') so magnitude, not counting, drives placement
Use dual labelling (fifths above the line, tenths below) to show equivalent fractions land on the same point
keyRepresentations: 0-to-1 number line partitioned into equal segments (the core model)
Minimally-labelled landmark line (0, 1/2, 1)
Dual-labelled line (two fractional-unit sequences) for equivalence
Fraction strip laid alongside the line to link area-model and length-model
commonMisconceptions: Treats the number line like a ruler — counts tick marks (or draws 4 marks for fourths) instead of equal segments (IES Roadblock 2.1)
Places 3/4 between 3 and 4, treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers (IES Roadblock 2.2)
Treats the whole line as the unit — e.g. locates 3/4 three-quarters of the way across a 0-to-5 line
Sees a fraction only as part of a shape, not as a single number that has a place on a line
Larger-denominator-is-larger — places 1/8 further from 0 than 1/3

learn.summary: Help 7-8 year olds move from 'fraction = part of a shape' to 'fraction = a number with a place on the line'. The load-bearing idea: a fraction 1/b is made by splitting ONE unit (the distance between two whole numbers) into b equal SEGMENTS, which needs b−1 marks between them, and a/b is the point at the end of the a-th equal segment counted from 0 (for a less than b, this is the a-th interior mark). Keep the unit visible so children stop treating the whole line as the unit and stop placing 3/4 'between 3 and 4'. Core model is a 0-to-1 line partitioned into equal segments; progress to landmark lines and then unmarked lines to force interval thinking, and use dual labelling to show equivalence as the same point.

activities.title: Three marks make fourths: partition and place on an interactive line
feedback: If the child draws or expects four interior marks for fourths, point out four interior marks make FIVE parts; count the equal segments together and confirm three marks give four parts.
If the bead is read as 4/4 or 4/5, recount the equal segments from 0 and name the end of the third segment as 3/4.
If 3/4 is placed between 3 and 4 on the longer line, locate 3 and 4 first, then ask 'is 3/4 bigger or smaller than 1?' and relocate it within the first unit.
When 1/2 lands on 5/10, name it: 'same point, two names — that's what equivalent means.'
activities.rationale: Partitioning a unit into equal segments and reading the end of the a-th segment directly targets the ruler-counting error (Roadblock 2.1) and the 'between 3 and 4' error (Roadblock 2.2); dual-labelled lines show equivalent fractions occupying the same point. Live controls (cut-into-parts dial, draggable bead that reports its fraction, length toggle, tenths track) make the segment-counting mechanism and the fixed unit concrete, but are optional ways to realise the task and the same learning can be done on paper.
sourceClaims: Recommendation 2 (Moderate Evidence): use number lines to teach fractions as numbers. Dividing a number line into 1/n units needs n-1 marks between two whole numbers; students err by drawing 4 marks for fourths or treating the whole line as the unit (Roadblock 2.1), and by placing 3/4 between 3 and 4, treating the fraction's numbers as separate whole numbers (Roadblock 2.2).

Students often view fractions with larger denominators as larger (e.g. 1/8 > 1/3), diagnosable by having them label hatch marks on a 0-to-1 number line; equivalent fractions can be shown to occupy the same point using dual-labelled lines.
learnerActions: On a 0-to-1 line, set a 'cut this unit into ___ parts' control to 4 and watch exactly THREE marks drop in, splitting the line into four equal segments.
Say aloud how many marks made four parts (three, not four), and colour each of the four segments, counting SEGMENTS rather than marks.
Drop a bead on the third mark; if the line reports a fraction, check it announces '3/4' and explain why that point is 3/4.

Extend the line from 0-to-1 to 0-to-4, keeping each whole-number unit the same length (or redraw it that way), and notice the 3/4 bead stays three-quarters of the way from 0 to the first '1', nowhere near the '3'.
On a second track below, lined up with the same 0 and 1 and labelled in tenths, slide a 1/2 bead until it lands exactly on 5/10, and state that the two labels name the same point.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction 1/b comes from cutting one unit into b equal segments (needing b−1 interior marks), and a/b is the point at the end of the a-th segment. The unit stays 'one whole' even when the line gets longer, so 3/4 lives between 0 and 1, not between 3 and 4. Equivalent fractions are the same point under different labels.

activities.title: Place and reason on paper lines: pre-marked, landmark, then unmarked
feedback: If a child drifts toward whole-number placement on the longer or unmarked line, return to naming the unit (0 to 1) and ask how many equal parts the denominator calls for.
For 'is 1/12 closer to 1/4 or 0?', prompt: twelfths are small, so compare how far 1/12 sits from 0 against how far it sits from 1/4, rather than which number looks bigger.
If an unmarked line is partitioned unequally, fold or measure to check the segments are the same length before placing the point.
activities.rationale: Fading from pre-segmented to landmark to unmarked lines forces interval thinking and shifts the child from counting to magnitude reasoning (IES Rec 2). Contrasting 3 and 4 with 3/4 on the same 0-to-4 line directly confronts the separate-whole-numbers error. Landmark distance questions support ordering fractions and address larger-denominator-is-larger.
sourceClaims: Recommendation 2 (Moderate Evidence): use number lines to teach fractions as numbers. Dividing a number line into 1/n units needs n-1 marks between two whole numbers; students err by drawing 4 marks for fourths or treating the whole line as the unit (Roadblock 2.1), and by placing 3/4 between 3 and 4, treating the fraction's numbers as separate whole numbers (Roadblock 2.2).
learnerActions: On a 0-to-1 line already divided into four equal segments (fourths), place 1/2, 1/4 and 3/4 by counting equal segments from 0.

On a minimally-labelled line showing only 0, 1/2, 1, 1½ and 2, place a concrete fraction such as 1¾ using landmarks — reasoning that it sits just below 2 (between 1½ and 2) — rather than counting every mark.
On an UNMARKED 0-to-1 line, decide how many segments you need, make the b−1 marks yourself, then place the fraction.
Answer landmark-reasoning questions such as 'Is 1/12 closer to 1/4 or to 0?' and 'Is 3/4 closer to 0 or to 1?', explaining using distance.
On a 0-to-4 line, place both 3 and 4, then separately place 3/4, and say in your own words why 3/4 does not go between 3 and 4.
activities.intendedInsight: Placement is driven by magnitude and distance from landmarks, not by counting ticks. Children who can partition an unmarked line themselves have internalised that the unit is divided into equal segments, and they keep fractions within the correct whole-number interval.

activities.title: Bridge from the shape model and compare unit fractions
feedback: If the child says a line 'isn't a shape so you can't do fractions on it', use the strip-along-the-line bridge until the shaded part and the point coincide, then name the point.
If 1/8 is placed further from 0 than 1/3, compare one eighth-segment with one third-segment of the same unit: more parts, shorter parts, so 1/8 sits nearer 0.
If a reference point is misnamed, recount the equal segments from 0 and describe the point as 'the end of the a-th of b equal parts'.
activities.rationale: Linking the area model to the length model addresses children who see fractions only as parts of shapes and refuse or randomise line placement. Comparing segment lengths of the same unit partitioned differently reteaches 'more parts means smaller' before ordering, targeting the larger-denominator-is-larger misconception. A labelled reference line supports reading, but being fixed it cannot by itself make the child confront miscounting — pair it with the partitioning task.
sourceClaims: Students often view fractions with larger denominators as larger (e.g. 1/8 > 1/3), diagnosable by having them label hatch marks on a 0-to-1 number line; equivalent fractions can be shown to occupy the same point using dual-labelled lines.
learnerActions: Shade 3/4 of a fraction strip exactly as long as the 0-to-1 unit, starting the shading at one end, then lay that end at 0 along the line so the shaded part reaches a point; name that point as the number 3/4.
Partition one unit into thirds, then partition an identical unit into eighths, and compare the lengths of a single segment in each.
Place 1/3 and 1/8 on the same 0-to-1 line and decide which is further from 0, explaining using segment length.
State in your own words whether a fraction such as 3/4 is 'a number' or 'just a piece of a shape', and point to where it lives on the line.
Reference check: label 0, 1/4, 1/2, 3/4, 1 on a line and explain for each point which segment's end it marks.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction names one number and has a single location on the line; the area (shape) model and the length (line) model agree. More equal parts of the same unit means each part is smaller, so 1/8 is closer to 0 than 1/3 — the denominator counts how many parts split ONE whole.

constraints: Hold the unit (the 0-to-1 distance) visible and fixed so children do not treat the whole line as the unit; test transfer on a 0-to-4 or unmarked line, not only on a pre-segmented 0-to-1 line.
Teach fourths as four equal SEGMENTS made by THREE interior marks; generalise that 1/n needs n−1 interior marks. Insist on counting segments, not tick marks.

A fixed labelled reference line can teach and be used while teaching, but on its own it does not require the child to construct segments or re-place a point on a longer line; combine reference-reading with active partitioning and placement.

Fraction strips and paper cutouts have real slight thickness and only approximate the ideal flat model; use them to bridge area and length, and treat any on-screen line as a model of the idealised (zero-thickness) number line.

When comparing unit fractions such as 1/8 and 1/3, keep the SAME whole and compare how one segment's length changes as the denominator changes; describe this as 'more parts means smaller parts', never as a denominator rule that 'flips'.

Placing and comparing points is a construct-and-check task: recognition-only or matching responses can check placement but do not by themselves elicit the child independently partitioning a unit and justifying a location. Include at least one task where the child makes the marks and states the reasoning.

Live controls (cut-into-parts dial, snapping/announcing bead, length toggle, tenths track) are optional illustrations of the mechanism, not required equipment; the same learning can be done on paper with careful partitioning.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original claimed the two headline errors are 'refuted on contact' and 'die on sight' with a dynamic line, and that a static image 'can't let the child confront miscounting', a dialogue 'can't substitute', and 3D 'adds nothing'. These are catalog-fit assertions, not established efficacy claims; softened here to scoped affordances/limits. Comparative medium superiority is not asserted by the cited Moderate-Evidence source.
Geometry self-audit: a fraction's point on the number line is the END of the a-th equal segment, and b−1 interior marks produce b equal segments; four interior marks would produce five segments.

Landmark question audit: 1/12 ≈ 0.083 and 1/4 = 0.25, so 1/12 is closer to 0 than to 1/4; and 1/8 = 0.125 is closer to 0 than 1/3 ≈ 0.333. These are kept as reasoning prompts for the child to work out, not pre-stated answers. The added example 1¾ = 1.75 sits between 1½ and 2, just below 2.

The Year 3 'count up and down in tenths' curriculum claim was removed from the paper-lines activity (which contains no tenths) to avoid citing a source that supports only the topic context rather than that activity's teaching principle.
Edit this pass: the second activity's landmark-placement action was made concrete (place 1¾ using the 1½/2 landmarks) so it models landmark reasoning rather than leaving the fraction unspecified.

probeDeeper: Is 3/4 closer to 0 or closer to 1? How do you know?
Point to where 1/8 would go and where 1/3 would go. Which is further from 0, and why?
Someone put 3/4 in the space between the 3 and the 4 on this line. What would you tell them?
Is a fraction like 3/4 a number, or just a piece of a shape? Where does that show up on the line?
assess.correctAnswer: The dot is at 3/4, because 0-to-1 is divided into four equal parts (segments) and the dot sits at the end of the third part. On the 0-to-4 line, 3/4 goes three-quarters of the way from 0 towards 1 (just below 1, NOT between 3 and 4) and 1/2 goes halfway between 0 and 1; each is a single number between 0 and 1 because its denominator splits ONE unit.

errorPatterns.pattern: Rules-the-line like a ruler — counts tick marks (or draws 4 marks for fourths) instead of equal segments, so the point is misread or the unit is mis-partitioned
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show fourths as four equal SEGMENTS made by THREE marks between 0 and 1; have the child colour each segment and count segments, not marks (IES Roadblock 2.1)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reads the 3/4 point as 4/4 or 4/5, counts the 0 mark as one, or when drawing puts four interior marks to make fourths

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number placement — treats the numerator and denominator as two separate whole numbers and puts 3/4 between the 3 and the 4 on the 0-to-4 line
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrasting cases: locate 3 and 4, then 3/4 as a number between 0 and 1; reteach fraction as a single quantity of one whole before returning to the line (IES Roadblock 2.2)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the 0-to-4 line marks 3/4 in the interval from 3 to 4

errorPatterns.pattern: Fraction-as-part-of-shape only — can shade 3/4 of a pizza but insists a line 'isn't a shape, you can't do fractions on it' or places it arbitrarily
errorPatterns.nextMove: Bridge the area model to length: lay a fraction strip along the 0-1 line so the shaded part reaches the same point; name the point as the number
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Refuses the task, treats the line as decoration, or places the fraction with no relation to the unit

errorPatterns.pattern: Larger-denominator-is-larger — places 1/8 further from 0 than 1/3
errorPatterns.nextMove: Partition the same unit into thirds then eighths and compare segment lengths; reteach more-parts-means-smaller before ordering on the line
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked to place unit fractions, puts the one with the bigger denominator further to the right

responseLevels.gap: Counts tick marks, draws four marks for fourths, places 3/4 between 3 and 4, or says a line can't show fractions — treats the two numbers separately.
responseLevels.full: Interprets the marked point as 3/4 by segments, produces 3/4 and 1/2 on a fresh 0-to-4 line both within 0-1 and reasoned by landmarks, and explains a fraction is a single number whose denominator partitions one unit — transferring to locate or compare a new fraction.
responseLevels.partial: Reads and places 3/4 and 1/2 on a pre-marked 0-to-1 line by counting equal segments, but on a 0-to-4 or unmarked line loses the unit (miscounts or drifts toward whole-number placement) and cannot yet say a fraction is one number located relative to landmarks.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: First, look at this number line from 0 to 1. There are three marks spaced equally between 0 and 1, and I have put a dot on the third mark. What number is at the dot, and how do you know? Now here is a fresh line labelled from 0 to 4. Put 3/4 on it, and put 1/2 on it, and tell me why each one goes where you put it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Interpreting the marked point separates ruler-counting (reads it as 4/4 or miscounts marks) from interval thinking (end of the third equal segment). The 0-to-4 placement is the decisive translate move: a child who treats numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers puts 3/4 between 3 and 4, which a part-of-a-shape understanding alone cannot avoid, whereas seeing a fraction as one number keeps it inside the first unit.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 6-7. Mentally find 10 more or 10 less than a two-digit number WITHOUT counting on in ones — 10 more than 56 is 66, 10 less is 46 — by recognising that adding/subtracting a ten changes only the tens digit (the ones stay put).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 1/2): 'given a number, identify one more and one less'; Year 2 place-value and mental strategies building toward 'add and subtract … a two-digit number and tens'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.NBT.5 'given a two-digit number, mentally find 10 more or 10 less than the number, without having to count; explain the reasoning used'; extended by 2.NBT.8.
• Operational details — Use the 100-square (move straight DOWN a row for +10, UP for -10) and base-ten rods (add/remove one rod) so the child SEES the ones column untouched and only the tens change. Move quickly from concrete to the mental generalisation and demand the explanation ('the ones stay the same, the tens go up by one'). Watch the decade boundary and the ones-digit-unchanged rule.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 6, emerging): finds 10 more/less using a 100-square, moving a row. Tier B (age 6-7, secure): states 10 more/less of any two-digit number mentally and explains the tens digit changes. Tier C (age 7, extending): does it fluently across decade boundaries and justifies why the ones digit never changes.
bestPractices: Exploit the 100-square structure: +10 is one row DOWN, -10 is one row UP, in the same column — the visual makes 'ones unchanged, tens ±1' obvious.
Use tens-rods: add or remove exactly ONE rod and narrate that the cubes (ones) never moved.
Insist on the generalised explanation, not just the answer, so it becomes reasoning rather than counting.
Contrast with '1 more/1 less' so the child distinguishes changing the ones from changing the tens.
Rehearse across decade boundaries to build fluency and flag where the pattern needs care.
keyRepresentations: 100-square (vertical moves = ±10) — the canonical model
Base-ten tens-rods and ones-cubes (add/remove one rod)
0-100 number line with hops of 10
Place-value chart showing only the tens digit changing
Gattegno chart (change the tens-row selection, keep the ones)
commonMisconceptions: Counting on in ones (56, 57, 58…66) instead of jumping a ten — no place-value shortcut.
Changing the ones digit as well, or changing the wrong digit (56 → 57 for '10 more').
Confusing 10 more with 1 more.
Miscounting on the 100-square by moving diagonally or the wrong direction.
Struggling at decade boundaries because the pattern is memorised without understanding the tens digit's role.

learn.summary: For ages 6-7: mentally find 10 more or 10 less than a two-digit number without counting on in ones, by recognising that adding/subtracting a ten changes only the tens digit while the ones digit stays the same (10 more than 56 is 66; 10 less is 46). The core objective is reasoning plus fluency: the child should both produce the answer instantly and explain why only the tens digit changes. Concrete models (100-square vertical moves, base-ten rods) build the insight; timed recall practice consolidates it once understanding is secure. Keep examples within the two-digit range where only the tens digit changes by one.

activities.title: The 100-square vertical jump
feedback: If the child moves diagonally or sideways, point out that +10/-10 keeps the SAME column — only the row changes.

If the child moves in the wrong direction, link 'more' to the direction in which the numbers get bigger (down the grid on a top-down 100-square) and 'less' to the direction in which they get smaller (up).
Ask the child to compare the ones digit before and after: it should be identical every time.
When the child traces the vertical stripe, highlight that the move looks the same for every jump, which is why the shortcut always works.
activities.rationale: The 100-square's vertical structure makes 'ones unchanged, tens ±1' directly visible, so the child can see the pattern rather than memorise it. An optional interactive version — tap a number, press +10/-10, the highlight slides one row and the ones digit locks/glows while the tens digit ticks — may make the mechanism concrete, but a paper 100-square with a finger works for the move itself.
sourceClaims: The 100-square's vertical structure is a canonical model for ±10, making the unchanged ones digit visible.
Pupils are given a number and identify one more and one less, and develop mental place-value strategies including adding/subtracting tens.
learnerActions: Point to a starting number on a 100-square (for example 56).

On a 100-square numbered from the top (1-10 in the top row), to find 10 more, move straight DOWN exactly one row, staying in the same column; to find 10 less, move straight UP one row in the same column. (On a bottom-up 100-square the directions are reversed. Check which way the numbers grow on your grid.)
Say the new number aloud (56 → 66 for 10 more, 56 → 46 for 10 less).
Repeat the +10 jump several times to trace a straight vertical stripe down the grid: 56 → 66 → 76 → 86.
Each time, name the ones digit and the tens digit and state what changed: 'the ones stayed 6, the tens went up by one.'
activities.intendedInsight: Adding or subtracting ten is always the same move — straight down or up one row — and the ones digit never moves because only a whole ten is added or removed.

activities.title: Add or remove one ten-rod
feedback: If the child disturbs the cubes, reset and emphasise that only a rod is added or removed.
Ask: 'How many cubes before? How many after?' to confirm the ones are unchanged.
Connect back to the written number: the tens digit changed by one, the ones digit is identical.
activities.rationale: Physically adding/removing a single rod narrates the place-value reason the ones stay put, reinforcing the 100-square move with a different, hands-on representation. An optional screen toggle can grey out the ones-cubes to show they didn't move, but real rods give the same narrative through handling.
sourceClaims: Pupils are given a number and identify one more and one less, and develop mental place-value strategies including adding/subtracting tens.
learnerActions: Lay out a two-digit number with base-ten tens-rods and ones-cubes (for example 5 rods and 6 cubes for 56).
To add 10, place exactly ONE more rod; to subtract 10, take exactly ONE rod away.
Watch the ones-cubes the whole time and say aloud that they did not move.
Read the new total and state which digit changed (the tens) and which stayed the same (the ones).
activities.intendedInsight: Adding ten means adding a single ten-rod, which changes the tens count by one and leaves the ones completely untouched.

activities.title: Ten more versus one more
feedback: If the child answers '10 more than 56 is 57,' show that 57 is only ONE more — use the rods or 100-square to add a full ten and reach 66.
Reinforce: '1 more adds one cube; 10 more adds one rod.'
activities.rationale: A common error is confusing 10 more with 1 more or altering the wrong digit. Deliberately contrasting the two operations helps the child distinguish changing the ones from changing the tens.
sourceClaims: Pupils are given a number and identify one more and one less, and develop mental place-value strategies including adding/subtracting tens.
learnerActions: For the same starting number (for example 56), find 1 more and then 10 more; then find 1 less and 10 less.
Say which digit changes each time: 1 more changes the ones (56 → 57); 10 more changes the tens (56 → 66).
Explain in your own words how '10 more' is different from '1 more.'
activities.intendedInsight: Changing the ones digit (±1) and changing the tens digit (±10) are distinct moves; the child must adjust the correct digit for the correct operation.

activities.title: Mental fluency and explanation
feedback: If the child reaches the answer by counting (57, 58 … 66) with fingers or whispering, don't just reteach the answer — return to adding one ten-rod and show only the tens column changed, then rebuild toward saying it without counting.
If one direction (more) is reliable but the other (less) is not, practise the weaker direction with the 100-square move first.
Always ask the child to explain: 'Which digit changed? Why only that one?'

If the child meets a case like 10 more than 90, note it becomes 100 — a three-digit number where a hundreds digit appears, so it sits beyond the two-digit 'only the tens digit changes' pattern; treat it as a separate extension, not a routine check.
activities.rationale: This is a fluency skill, so timed/scored practice is appropriate once the concept is built. Watching the method (instant vs counting) is as important as the answer; requiring the explanation keeps it reasoning rather than rote. Formats such as fill-in-the-blank, multiple choice spotting the wrong-digit error, ordering a +10 sequence, or a ±10 slider on a 0-100 number line are all suitable.
sourceClaims: Given a two-digit number, mentally find 10 more or 10 less without counting, and explain the reasoning (1.NBT.5).
Pupils are given a number and identify one more and one less, and develop mental place-value strategies including adding/subtracting tens.
learnerActions: Answer rapid spoken or written items: 10 more than 73? (83) 10 less than 40? (30) 10 more than 56? (66) 10 less than 56? (46).
Give each answer without fingers or counting on in ones.
Complete a +10 chain by filling blanks: 46 → 56 → 66 → __ (76).
After answering, state which digit changed and why the ones digit did not.
Rehearse items that cross a decade boundary while the result stays a two-digit number (for example 10 more than 85 is 95, 10 less than 40 is 30) to check the pattern holds.
activities.intendedInsight: Once the place-value reason is understood, 10 more/10 less becomes instant recall produced by a single tens-digit change rather than by counting, for results that remain two-digit numbers.

constraints: Move from concrete models (100-square, rods) to the mental generalisation fairly quickly, and demand the explanation ('the ones stay the same, the tens go up/down by one'), not just the answer.

A static annotated 100-square is a useful reference for the pattern, but it does not let the child perform the jump and watch the ones hold still; use it alongside, not instead of, an activity where the child makes the move.

Scored/timed practice consolidates recall but assesses output; it is best used AFTER the place-value concept is built, and it does not on its own reveal whether the child is counting or jumping — watch the method during practice.
Multiple-choice/recognition items can spot wrong-digit errors but do not elicit independent construction of the answer or the explanation; include production items too.
Keep practice within the two-digit range where only the tens digit changes by one; 90→100 introduces a hundreds digit and is an extension case, not a routine item for this objective.
Rehearse decade crossings (e.g. 10 less than 40 = 30) deliberately, since a pattern memorised without understanding often breaks down there.
Distinguish '1 more / 1 less' explicitly from '10 more / 10 less'; confusing 10 more with 1 more is a common error.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Of the cited sources, the DfE National Curriculum claim was marked verified in the source row; the CCSS-M 1.NBT.5 claim and the NCETM 100-square claim were marked not verified. Treat the latter two as unconfirmed.

The legacy row framed open dialogue and 3D models as 'poor' and a picture as unable to let the child perform the jump. These are reasonable fit observations for this specific dynamic skill but have been softened to narrow affordances: a static image can still support the pattern as a reference, and conversation can be used to elicit the required explanation. They are not universal claims about medium superiority.

Arithmetic check: 10 more than 56 = 66, 10 less than 56 = 46, 10 more than 73 = 83, 10 less than 40 = 30, +10 chain 46→56→66→76 — all correct, all two-digit results where only the tens digit changes by one. The '10 more than 90' example is excluded from routine practice because 90+10=100 leaves the two-digit range and introduces a hundreds digit, so the 'only the tens digit changes by one' rule does not cleanly hold; it is retained only as an explicitly flagged extension case.
Independent re-audit confirms the two-digit scope fix is applied at every learner-facing occurrence (activity[3] actions, feedback, summary, and constraints).

probeDeeper: Which digit changed when you added 10? Why only that one?
10 more than 73 — did the ones digit change at all?
10 less than 40 — what happens to the ones digit?
assess.correctAnswer: 66, 46, 83, 30 — produced instantly by changing the tens digit by one, without counting on in ones.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts on or back in ones (fingers/whispering) instead of jumping a whole ten
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the answer — make the ten visible: add a tens rod on a base-ten mat and show only the tens column changed. Build toward saying it without counting.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child reaches 66 but by counting 57, 58 … 66; slow, with fingers.

errorPatterns.pattern: Changes the ones digit instead of the tens: '10 more than 56 is 57'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast 'one more' vs 'ten more' on a base-ten model; ten more adds a ten (tens digit +1), the ones stay put.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer differs from the given number by 1, not 10.

responseLevels.gap: Alters the wrong digit, or can only reach the answer by counting on in ones.
responseLevels.full: Instantly gives 10 more/less by adjusting the tens digit and explains the ones digit is unchanged.
responseLevels.partial: Gets answers by counting a ten in steps, or is reliable one direction (more) but not the other (less).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask quickly and watch how they get the answer (fingers? counting? or instant?): '10 more than 56? ... 10 less than 56? ... 10 more than 73? ... 10 less than 40?' Watch whether the tens digit jumps in one move.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The task is timed against counting: a child who understands 10-more as a single tens-jump answers immediately and can say only the tens digit changed; a child without it counts on ten ones (fingers, whispering) or alters the wrong digit. Watching the METHOD, not just the answer, is the point.

pedagogy.summary: Algebraic notation is a compact convention that pupils must READ and WRITE fluently: juxtaposition means multiply (ab = a×b), 3y means y+y+y (= 3×y), a² means a×a (not 2a), a/b means a÷b, and brackets group operations. The deep idea is that a letter stands for a NUMBER, so the notation obeys the same order of operations as arithmetic — you cannot read an expression left to right like a sentence. The two persistent hazards are (1) writing/reading expressions left-to-right and so mangling order of operations (writing '4 + n × 5' for 'add 4 to n, then multiply by 5', which should be 5(n+4)), and (2) misreading the symbols themselves — 3y as 3+y, a² as 2a, ab as a two-digit number — often because the letter is treated as a label rather than a number.
bestPractices: Establish that a letter is a NUMBER (a 'hidden number'), so every notation convention is just shorthand for an arithmetic operation — test by substituting a value and checking the reading makes sense.
Read notation aloud precisely and translate both ways: symbols→words and words→symbols ('3y' ↔ 'three lots of y' ↔ 'y+y+y'), so the meaning is rehearsed, not guessed.

Confront the left-to-right error directly: contrast 'add 4 then multiply by 5' (= 5(n+4)) with 'multiply by 5 then add 4' (= 5n+4) and show they give different values — order of operations, not word order, decides.
Separate the coefficient from the power explicitly (3y vs y³, 2a vs a²) by unpacking each into repeated addition or repeated multiplication.
Use area/array models and word↔symbol card matching so the same expression is met in multiple representations (following Swan/MAP).
keyRepresentations: Repeated-operation unfolding (3y → y+y+y; a² → a×a)
Word ↔ symbol ↔ area-model card sets (Swan/MAP translation task)
Substitution check (replace the letter with a number to test a reading)
Bracket-as-grouping diagram contrasting 5(n+4) with 5n+4
commonMisconceptions: Reading/writing expressions left-to-right, ignoring order of operations (writing '4 + n × 5' for 'add 4 then multiply by 5' instead of 5(n+4)).
Misreading the symbols: 3y as 3+y (or a two-digit number), a² as 2a or a×2, ab as a concatenated number rather than a×b.
Treating the letter as an object/label ('a' = apple) rather than a number, which blocks operating on it.
Mis-grouping with brackets — reading 5(n+4) as 5n+4, or (n+3)² as n²+3².

learn.summary: Pupils (ages 11–12) learn to READ and WRITE algebraic notation fluently, grounded in the idea that a letter stands for a NUMBER. Core conventions: juxtaposition means multiply (ab = a×b), 3y means y+y+y (= 3×y), a² means a×a (not 2a), a³ means a×a×a, a²b means a×a×b, a/b means a÷b, coefficients can be written as fractions, and brackets group operations. The two persistent hazards are (1) reading/writing expressions left-to-right and so mangling order of operations (writing '4 + n × 5' for 'add 4 to n, then multiply by 5', which should be 5(n+4)), and (2) misreading the symbols themselves (3y as 3+y, a² as 2a, ab as a two-digit number), often because the letter is treated as a label rather than a number. Guidance centres on a build-and-evaluate translator where misreadings produce visibly different values, supported by word↔symbol↔area-model matching, a tap-to-reveal reference, and oral reading rehearsal.

activities.title: Expression translator: build, read, and evaluate
feedback: If a learner reads 'add 4 then multiply by 5' as '4 + n × 5', substitute n=5 into both: show 45 (brackets) versus 29 (no brackets) and name that word ORDER does not set the order of operations — brackets do.
If a learner reads 3y as 3+y, evaluate both at y=4: 3y = 12 but 3+y = 7, so they cannot be the same.
If a learner reads a² as 2a, substitute a=3: a² = 9 but 2a = 6; unfold a² into a×a and 2a into a+a to separate power from coefficient.
activities.rationale: Translating live between words, symbols and a value lets a left-to-right slip or symbol misreading produce a visibly different number, so the convention is rehearsed against arithmetic rather than guessed. The word tiles, substitution box, and tap-to-unfold panel are illustrative mechanisms, not a required product; the same contrast can be reached with paper and spoken substitution.
sourceClaims: Students write expressions left to right showing little understanding of the order of operations implied by the symbols (e.g. '4 + n × 5' for what should be 5(n+4)), and mis-handle brackets (2(n+3)=2n+3; (n+3)² = n²+3²); the lesson builds meaning by translating between words, symbols, tables and area models.
KS3 pupils should use and interpret algebraic notation, including ab for a×b, 3y for y+y+y and 3×y, a² for a×a, a³ for a×a×a, a²b, a/b for a÷b, coefficients written as fractions, and brackets.
learnerActions: Build an expression from word tiles such as 'the number', '×5', '+4', and 'brackets', and watch the symbolic form assemble alongside.

Enter the two readings 'add 4 then multiply by 5' and 'multiply by 5 then add 4', and substitute n=5 into each using a substitution box: confirm 5(n+4) = 45 and 5n+4 = 29, so the two readings land on different numbers.
Use a tap-to-unfold panel to open 3y into y+y+y and y² into y×y, then substitute y=4 to check (3y = 12, y² = 16), distinguishing coefficient from power.
Test a deliberate misreading: enter 3y as 3+y and let the tool evaluate both to expose the mismatch.
activities.intendedInsight: Notation obeys the same order of operations as arithmetic, decided by brackets and structure rather than left-to-right word order; a letter is a hidden number, so '3y' and 'a²' are shorthand for repeated operations, not new symbols read like a sentence.

activities.title: Word↔symbol↔area-model matching and targeted multiple choice
feedback: For a wrong match between 5(n+4) and 5n+4, substitute n=5 and compare 45 with 29 to show which reading needs brackets.
If a learner chooses 10 for a² at a=5, remind that a² = a×a = 25, whereas 2a = a+a = 10.
If a learner chooses 3+y for 3y, unfold 3y into y+y+y and test with a value (at y=4, 3y=12 but 3+y=7).
activities.rationale: A matching and multiple-choice format surfaces whether a learner's reading is secure and uses the common errors as distractors, while the area/array model meets each expression in a second representation. This format checks recognition and discrimination; on its own it does not require the learner to construct an expression independently, so pair it with the build-and-evaluate task.
sourceClaims: Students write expressions left to right showing little understanding of the order of operations implied by the symbols (e.g. '4 + n × 5' for what should be 5(n+4)), and mis-handle brackets (2(n+3)=2n+3; (n+3)² = n²+3²); the lesson builds meaning by translating between words, symbols, tables and area models.
learnerActions: Match word descriptions to their expressions, e.g. connect 'four more than the number, all multiplied by five' to 5(n+4) and 'five times the number, then add four' to 5n+4, plus n² and 3n.
Match the same expression across representations — a word description, its symbolic form, and an area/array model — so each expression is met in more than one representation (following Swan/MAP).
Answer: what does 3y mean? (Correct: y+y+y; distractors: 3+y, and '3y read as a two-digit number'.)
Answer: what is the value of a² when a=5? (Correct: 25; distractor: 10, which is 2a.)
Translate 'the number divided by 5, then add 4' and 'add 4 to the number, then divide the whole thing by 5' into symbols and explain how the notation shows the difference.
activities.intendedInsight: Matching words, symbols and an area/array model makes the coefficient/power/grouping conventions explicit, with left-to-right and symbol-misreading answers as sharp contrasts to the correct reading.

activities.title: Annotated expression reference card
feedback: Each revealed part restates the convention and gives a substitution example so the reading is tied to a number.
activities.rationale: A fixed annotated card consolidates the conventions and serves as a reference. Because it does not let the learner build an expression or watch a misreading evaluate wrongly, it is a scaffold used alongside the build-and-evaluate work, not a replacement for it.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should use and interpret algebraic notation, including ab for a×b, 3y for y+y+y and 3×y, a² for a×a, a³ for a×a×a, a²b, a/b for a÷b, coefficients written as fractions, and brackets.
learnerActions: Tap each part of a labelled expression to reveal its meaning, e.g. 'ab means a×b', '3y means y+y+y', 'a² means a×a', 'a³ means a×a×a', 'a²b means a×a×b', 'a/b means a÷b', and that a coefficient can be written as a fraction, with a worked substitution example for each.
Return to the card as a quick reference while attempting the translator or matching tasks.
activities.intendedInsight: The standard conventions can be consolidated and recalled: juxtaposition is multiplication, a coefficient multiplies the letter (a whole-number coefficient such as 3y can be read as repeated addition, y+y+y, while a fractional coefficient such as ½y means ½×y = y/2), a power is repeated multiplication, a/b is division, and brackets group.

activities.title: Read it aloud: oral rehearsal of precise reading
feedback: When a learner says '3 plus y' for 3y, substitute y=4 and ask whether 3y is 12 or 7, then restate '3y is three lots of y'.
activities.rationale: Reading aloud and responsive challenge rehearse precise reading and expose misreadings through substitution. Reading aloud rehearses interpretation but does not by itself elicit written symbolic construction, so treat it as secondary to the build-and-evaluate task.
sourceClaims: Children commonly treat a letter as an object/label or as a specific unknown rather than a generalised number, and misread notation such as coefficients and powers (letter-usage levels).
learnerActions: Read expressions aloud precisely, e.g. say '3y' as 'three lots of y' and 'y²' as 'y times itself'.
Respond when challenged on a misreading: 'you said 3 plus y — if y is 4, is 3y twelve or seven?' and resolve it by substituting.
Translate both ways in speech: symbols→words and words→symbols.
activities.intendedInsight: Saying the notation precisely rehearses meaning rather than guessing, and a substitution challenge exposes a slip immediately.

activities.title: The letter is a hidden number
feedback: If a learner talks about n as 'the letter' or a label and is unsure it can be added or multiplied, reassert that n is a hidden number and substitute a value to show the operation working. A review of using letters for unknowns from earlier work may help.
activities.rationale: The object/label misconception blocks operating on the symbol, so reasserting that the letter is a number and substituting a value grounds every convention. This diagnostic distinction follows the cited letter-usage research.
sourceClaims: Children commonly treat a letter as an object/label or as a specific unknown rather than a generalised number, and misread notation such as coefficients and powers (letter-usage levels).
learnerActions: State that each letter is a hidden NUMBER, then substitute a chosen value to make operations on it concrete.
Rewrite an answer that keeps the letter as a tag/label into one that treats the letter as a number that can be added and multiplied.
Check a reading by substituting a value and asking whether the reading makes sense.
activities.intendedInsight: Because a letter stands for a number, expressions can be operated on and evaluated like arithmetic; treating the letter as an object/label ('a' = apple) blocks this.

constraints: A letter stands for a NUMBER; every notation convention is shorthand for an arithmetic operation, testable by substituting a value.

Word ORDER does not set the order of operations — brackets and structure do: 'add 4 then multiply by 5' is 5(n+4) (=45 at n=5) and 'multiply by 5 then add 4' is 5n+4 (=29 at n=5); keep these distinct.
Separate coefficient from power explicitly: 3y = y+y+y (so 3y=12 at y=4) while y² = y×y (=16 at y=4); 2a = a+a while a² = a×a (so at a=3, 2a=6 but a²=9).
Juxtaposition means multiply (ab = a×b, not a concatenated two-digit number); a/b means a÷b; brackets group, so 5(n+4) ≠ 5n+4 and (n+3)² ≠ n²+3².
The matching/multiple-choice format checks recognition and discrimination but does not by itself elicit independent construction of an expression; pair it with a build-or-write task.

The annotated reference card and read-aloud dialogue are scaffolds: the card cannot let a learner build an expression or watch a misreading evaluate, and reading aloud rehearses interpretation but does not by itself elicit written symbolic construction.
Interactive panels, substitution boxes and tap-to-unfold reveals are illustrative mechanisms, not mandatory; the same learning can be reached with paper, cards, and spoken substitution.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support teaching principles rather than proving any activity was tested.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 5(n+4) at n=5 = 5×9 = 45 and 5n+4 at n=5 = 29 (correct); 3y at y=4 = 12 and y²=16 (correct); a² at a=5 = 25 and 2a=10 (correct); a² at a=3 = 9 and 2a=6 (correct); 3+y at y=4 = 7 (correct). These values are used in learner-facing feedback.

The original claimed '3D adds nothing' for this topic; this universal-necessity phrasing was removed rather than propagated. The topic is symbolic, so a 3D model offers no clear affordance here, but no comparative-efficacy claim is asserted.
The Küchemann/CSMS source is marked unverified (verified:false) in the row; its claim is used only to support the letter-as-number and misreading principles and is flagged as unverified.

The area/array-model representation (a keyRepresentation and Swan/MAP practice in the original) is carried in the matching activity; a³, a²b and coefficients-as-fractions were added to the reference card to retain the full NC convention list.

probeDeeper: Check your (a) and (b) by putting n = 5 into each — do they give the same answer or different? Which one needed brackets, and why?
You wrote/read 3y — if y = 4, what is 3y? Is that 12 or 7? What does that tell you about '3 plus y'?
How is 2a different from a² — put a = 3 into both. (counterexample separating coefficient from power: 6 vs 9.)
Write in symbols: 'the number divided by 5, then add 4' and 'add 4 to the number, then divide the whole thing by 5' — how does the notation show the difference?
assess.correctAnswer: (a) 5n + 4; (b) 5(n + 4); (c) n² (or n×n). And: 3y means 'three lots of y', i.e. y + y + y (or 3×y); y² means 'y times itself', i.e. y×y.

errorPatterns.pattern: Writes/reads expressions left-to-right, ignoring order of operations (‘add 4 then multiply by 5’ written as 4 + n × 5 rather than 5(n+4))
errorPatterns.nextMove: Substitute n = 5 into both readings and compare the values (45 vs 29). Show word ORDER doesn't set the order of operations — brackets do. Contrast 5(n+4) with 5n+4 explicitly.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For (b) writes 4 + n × 5 (or n + 4 × 5) and treats it as the same as (a); cannot say the two need different bracketing

errorPatterns.pattern: Misreads the symbols: 3y as 3+y (or a two-digit number), a² as 2a or a×2
errorPatterns.nextMove: Unfold each: 3y = y+y+y, y² = y×y; check by substituting y = 4 (3y = 12, y² = 16, NOT 7 or 8). Separate coefficient (multiplies) from power (repeated multiply).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reads 3y as 'three plus y' or 'thirty-y'; reads y² as 'two y' or 'y times two'

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the letter as an object/label ('n' = a name or thing) rather than a number, so cannot operate on it
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reassert 'the letter is a hidden NUMBER'; substitute a value to make the operations concrete. Reteach letters-for-unknowns from KS2.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Talks about n as 'the letter' or a label and is unsure it can be added/multiplied like a number; writes answers that keep the letter as a tag

responseLevels.gap: Reads/writes left-to-right (4 + n × 5 for (b)), or misreads 3y as 3+y and y² as 2y; treats letters as labels.
responseLevels.full: Writes 5n+4 and 5(n+4) distinctly, reads 3y as y+y+y and y² as y×y, treats the letter as a number (checks by substitution), and translates fluently both ways between words and symbols including division and brackets.
responseLevels.partial: Handles simple notation (writes 5n+4, reads 3y as y+y+y) but slips on grouping (cannot correctly bracket 'add then multiply' as 5(n+4)) or on power-vs-coefficient (a² vs 2a) — conventions not yet secure across cases.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I'm thinking of a number — call it n. Write an expression for each: (a) five times the number, then add four; (b) four more than the number, and then all of that multiplied by five; (c) the number multiplied by itself. Then read these two aloud and tell me what each means: 3y and y².
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A pupil who reads notation as numbers writes 5(n+4) with brackets for 'add then multiply', keeps 5n+4 distinct from it, and reads 3y as y+y+y and y² as y×y. A pupil reading left-to-right writes '4 + n × 5' for (b) and cannot separate it from (a); one treating letters as labels reads 3y as 3+y and y² as 2y. Listening to how they WRITE and READ in context — not whether they can recite a rule — splits these cleanly, and the (a)/(b) pair specifically exposes the order-of-operations reading.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 8–9y; apply the commutative, associative and distributive properties as STRATEGIES to multiply and divide (not as formal named laws to memorise).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y4 'recognise and use factor pairs and commutativity', 'multiply … three numbers' (associativity), and use the distributive law within written/mental methods; Y3 begins distributive partitioning.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.OA.5 — 'Apply properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide' (commutative: 6×4=4×6; associative: 2×(3×5) via (2×3)×5; distributive: 8×5+8×2 = 8×7). Note CCSS says pupils need not know the property names.
• Operational details — the point is flexible, efficient calculation: commutativity halves facts to learn and lets you reorder; associativity lets you regroup three factors into an easy pair (2×3×5 → 6×5 or 2×15); distributivity is the big one — split a hard fact/large factor into friendly parts (8×7 = 8×5 + 8×2) and it is the conceptual seed of the area model and ALL formal written multiplication. Show each property in the array/area model where it is visibly true, then use it to make calculation easier. Division is NOT commutative or associative — make that explicit.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8): use commutativity (know 4×6 → 6×4) and split a fact distributively with support (7×6 = 5×6 + 2×6). Tier B (age 8–9): use all three to simplify a calculation and justify with an array. Tier C (age 9): choose the most efficient property for a given calculation and explain why division isn't commutative.
bestPractices: Prove each property visually first — rotate an array for commutativity, regroup counters for associativity, split an array for distributivity — then use it to make a calculation easier, so properties are tools not vocabulary.

Lead with the distributive property as the highest-value strategy: it turns unknown facts into known ones (8×7 = 8×5 + 8×2) and is the direct bridge to the area model and formal written multiplication.
Use the area model as the shared home of all three properties so the later written algorithm is 'properties made compact', not a new trick.
Explicitly contrast × (commutative/associative) with ÷ (neither) using counterexamples so children don't overgeneralise.
Prioritise strategy CHOICE — give calculations where different properties are most efficient and discuss which to pick.
keyRepresentations: Rotatable array — commutativity (same array, two orientations, same total)
Split area model — distributivity (8×7 as 8×5 + 8×2 two sub-rectangles)
Regroupable groups-of-groups — associativity (2×3×5 rebracketed)
Bar model / number sentence chains showing the equivalent forms
commonMisconceptions: Overgeneralising commutativity/associativity to division (32÷8 = 8×32; (24÷4)÷2 = 24÷(4÷2)).
Applying the distributive split incorrectly — e.g. 8×7 = 8×5 + 2 (forgetting to multiply the second part) or splitting the wrong factor.
Treating the properties as names to memorise rather than strategies to use, so they aren't deployed in calculation.
Not seeing that the area model IS the distributive law, so written multiplication later feels disconnected.
Thinking reordering changes the answer, or conversely that any reordering is always allowed.

learn.summary: For ages 8–9, teach the commutative, associative and distributive properties as calculation STRATEGIES (not named laws to memorise) that leave a total invariant. Prove each property visibly in an array/area model first, then use it to make a hard calculation easy. Centre the distributive split (8×7 = 8×5 + 8×2) as the highest-value strategy and the direct bridge to the area model and formal written multiplication. Explicitly contrast × (commutative/associative) with ÷ and − (neither), and prioritise strategy choice — which property is most efficient for a given calculation.

activities.title: Property playground: rotate, split, regroup on one array
feedback: If a learner writes 8×7 = 8×5 + 2 = 42, draw 8 rows of 7, cut into 8 rows of 5 and 8 rows of 2, and ask how many squares are in the second block: it is 8×2 = 16, not 2, so 40 + 16 = 56. Make the split visible before returning to symbols.

If a learner distrusts regrouping and recomputes (2×3)×4 and 2×(3×4) separately each time, build both with cubes (e.g. 4 lots of a 2-by-3 group, which is 6 taken 4 times, versus 2 lots of 12, where 12 is 3×4), count once each (24 both times), and name associativity as 'regrouping a multiplication never changes the total'.

If a learner says order 'doesn't matter' for division or subtraction (e.g. 8−7 = 7−8), show quick counterexamples such as 10−3 = 7 while 3−10 cannot be done with whole numbers (it goes below zero on a number line), and 12÷3 = 4 while 3÷12 is less than 1, so the property stays bound to × and + specifically.
Prompt justification: 'You said 8×5 + 8×2 — why is that the same as 8×7 and not more or less?' and 'Could you use 8×5 to help work out 8×9? Show me the split.'
activities.rationale: For multiplication, these properties are transformations that leave the total invariant, so letting a learner rotate, split and regroup while a live total holds is intended to help them discover each property rather than be told it, and immediately use it to simplify a calculation. A visible split-array is the area model, which embodies the distributive property and bridges to written multiplication. A division mode in which swapping the numbers changes the answer directly addresses the common overgeneralisation of commutativity to division. Dragging, live recolouring and the equal-total display are concrete examples of how the mechanism is made felt, not required implementations.
sourceClaims: Y4 pupils recognise and use factor pairs and commutativity, multiply three numbers, and use distributive partitioning within methods.
3.OA.5 requires applying commutative, associative and distributive properties as strategies to multiply and divide; pupils need not know the property names.
The area model embodies the distributive law and bridges to formal written multiplication; properties should be shown in arrays before being used as calculation strategies.
learnerActions: On an array/area canvas, meet an 'ugly' fact like 8×7. Drag a divider through the 7 to carve the array into 8×5 and 8×2; watch the two sub-rectangles light up as 40 and 16 and combine to 56.
Rotate the same array 90° and confirm the total does not change (8×7 = 7×8) — commutativity as 'same array, two orientations, same total'.
For three factors (2×3×5), toggle or drag the bracket between (2×3)×5 and 2×(3×5), and confirm the total holds — associativity as regrouping into an easier pair (6×5 or 2×15).

Switch to a division mode: swap the two numbers in a ÷ calculation (e.g. 32÷8 = 4 becomes 8÷32, which is less than 1) and see that the answer changes, then say in your own words why division is not commutative (32÷8 is not 8÷32).
Choose your own split for a new ugly fact (e.g. 8×9 = 8×5 + 8×4) and check the partial products add to the whole (40 + 32 = 72).
activities.intendedInsight: In multiplication, reordering, regrouping and splitting change how a calculation is written without changing its total; a hard multiplication fact can be cut into two friendly facts and reassembled. This 'cut-the-hard-one-into-two-easy-ones' move is the distributive property, and it is the same move that formal written multiplication later makes compact. Division and subtraction are not commutative or associative, so swapping or regrouping their numbers can change the answer.

activities.title: Split-area anchor for the distributive fact
feedback: If the learner cannot explain the invariance, point to the shared height (8) across both parts and the widths adding to 7 (5 + 2), so no squares are added or lost.
Connect the picture back to symbols: the whole rectangle's area is the sum of the two parts' areas.
activities.rationale: A fixed, pre-split area diagram is a clean anchor for the distributive idea and the area-model bridge. Because it cannot be moved to vary the split, it shows one case rather than invariance across many, so it supports rather than replaces manipulable exploration; use it as a static anchor or consolidation after the playground.
sourceClaims: The area model embodies the distributive law and bridges to formal written multiplication; properties should be shown in arrays before being used as calculation strategies.
learnerActions: Study an area rectangle for 8×7 that is pre-split into 8×5 and 8×2.
Reveal the labels: left part '8×5 = 40', right part '8×2 = 16', whole '= 56'.
Answer the prompt 'Why does splitting the 7 into 5 and 2 not change the total?' before moving on.
activities.intendedInsight: The distributive split keeps the whole fixed because the two sub-rectangles together are exactly the original rectangle; 8×7 and 8×5 + 8×2 name the same quantity.

activities.title: Consolidate and sort: valid forms and the division trap
feedback: For the fill-in, if the learner writes anything other than 2, return to the array: the second part must be 8 rows of 2, i.e. 8×2.
If the learner picks a division distractor for 6×4, remind them commutativity is about reordering the SAME operation, and test the division claim with small numbers (e.g. 6÷4 ≠ 4÷6).
When sorting, have the learner give a counterexample for each 'not true for ÷' statement (e.g. 32÷8 = 4 but 8÷32 is less than 1; (24÷4)÷2 = 3 but 24÷(4÷2) = 12).
activities.rationale: Completing a split, selecting the correct equivalent form and sorting always-true versus division statements target the overgeneralisation misconception. These checks assess and consolidate property USE; they do not by themselves build the invariance intuition, so pair them with the manipulable or anchor activities.
learnerActions: Complete a distributive split: 8×7 = 8×5 + 8×□.
Choose which expression equals 6×4, with 4×6 correct and 6÷4 and 4÷6 offered as tempting wrong choices.
Sort statements into 'always true' versus 'not true for division', e.g. is 32÷8 = 8÷32? Is (24÷4)÷2 = 24÷(4÷2)?
activities.intendedInsight: Property use can be checked and the overgeneralisation to division can be caught: reordering and regrouping hold for × but not for ÷.

activities.title: The lazy mathematician: justify the easiest strategy
feedback: Push for reasons, not just answers: 'Is there an easier way to work that out, and how do you know it gives the same total?'
If the learner accepts an invalid division or subtraction reorder, ask them to test it with a concrete counterexample.
activities.rationale: A Socratic 'is there an easier way?' dialogue prompts strategy choice and verbal justification, which supports deployment of the properties. Discussion complements rather than substitutes for seeing the properties as visual transformations, so use it alongside the array work.
learnerActions: Talk with a 'lazy mathematician' character who always wants the easiest split or reorder for a given calculation.
When the character proposes a move (e.g. regroup 2×3×5 to 6×5, or split 7×6 into 5×6 + 2×6), explain why it gives the same answer.
Decide together which property is most efficient for different calculations and say why.
Catch the character out when it tries to 'reorder' a division or subtraction.
activities.intendedInsight: Choosing the most efficient property and justifying it out loud is part of fluent calculation; not every operation permits reordering.

constraints: Teach these as strategies for efficient calculation, not as formal named laws to memorise; CCSS-M notes pupils need not know the property names.
Make explicit that division is NOT commutative or associative, and that subtraction is not either; use counterexamples so learners do not overgeneralise.
Guard against the additive-split error (8×7 = 8×5 + 2): both parts must be multiplied by the shared factor (8×5 + 8×2).

The static split-area anchor and the sort/fill tasks check and consolidate property use, but a fixed diagram cannot vary the split or regrouping across many cases; manipulable exploration across varied cases can let learners meet the invariance across many instances, so pair the static anchor and check tasks with it.
Recognition and fill-in tasks assess property use; they do not themselves elicit the learner independently choosing and justifying a strategy, which the dialogue and open splits target.
Three-factor associativity can suggest a cuboid, but that belongs to volume; keep properties-as-strategies work in planar arrays/area to avoid added manipulation cost and off-topic meaning.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labels a 3D treatment as adding 'no invariance insight'; this rewrite keeps the planar focus as a scoped design choice (arrays/area are where these properties are most directly visible) rather than a universal claim that 3D cannot teach anything here.

Arithmetic checked: 8×7 = 56; 8×5 = 40, 8×2 = 16, 40+16 = 56; 8×9 = 72 via 8×5 + 8×4 = 40 + 32; 2×3×5 = 30 via 6×5 or 2×15; 6×4 = 24 = 4×6; (24÷4)÷2 = 3 but 24÷(4÷2) = 12; 32÷8 = 4 but 8÷32 < 1. The additive-split error 8×5 + 2 = 42 appears only as a misconception to correct, never as a valid alternative.
The source mentions 'double 8×3.5' in passing for 8×7; this involves a non-integer partial and is not appropriate for this age group, so it is omitted from learner-facing actions.
The assessment's responseLevels, diagnosticPrompt and probe questions were not altered by this rewrite; they inform but are not restated as separate guidance fields.

Efficacy wording in constraint 4 was softened from 'is what lets learners feel the invariance' to a qualified affordance, since no source establishes manipulation as the necessary mechanism for building the invariance intuition.

probeDeeper: You said 8×5 + 8×2. Why is that the same as 8×7 and not more or less?
What if it had been 8 × 9 — could you use 8 × 5 to help? Show me the split.
Does this trick also work for 8 − 7? Why or why not?
Someone says 6 × 7 = 6×5 + 2. What went wrong in their thinking?
assess.correctAnswer: 8 × 7 = 56. A child reasoning correctly splits the 7: 8 × 7 is 8 × 5 plus 8 × 2, so 40 + 16 = 56 — because seven groups of eight is the same as five groups of eight and two more groups of eight (distributive property). Any valid split (8×7 = 8×6+8, or double 8×3.5 is not expected here) counts if the REASON is about decomposing one factor into parts that are added.

errorPatterns.pattern: treats distributive split additively on both parts: '8×7 = 8×5 + 2 = 42' — adds the leftover 2 instead of 8×2
errorPatterns.nextMove: draw the array: 8 rows of 7, cut it into 8 rows of 5 and 8 rows of 2; ask how many squares are in the second block — it is 8×2=16, not 2. Make the split visible before returning to symbols.
errorPatterns.distractor: 8 × 7 = 42 (I did 8×5 then added 2)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child gets 42 and, when probed, says 'I had 8×5 then added the 2 more'

errorPatterns.pattern: believes changing the grouping changes the answer — does not trust that (2×3)×4 = 2×(3×4); recomputes each time as if they could differ
errorPatterns.nextMove: build both groupings with cubes (2 stacks of 3, taken 4 times vs 2 stacks of 12) and count once each; name associativity as 'regrouping never changes the total'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: when asked if reordering/regrouping factors is 'allowed', child hedges or checks by full recomputation rather than asserting it must be equal

errorPatterns.pattern: over-generalises commutativity/associativity to subtraction or division: 'if 8×7=7×8 then 8−7=7−8'
errorPatterns.nextMove: confront with a quick counterexample (10−3 vs 3−10 using a number line) so the property is bound to × and + specifically, not to all operations.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child asserts order 'doesn't matter' for a subtraction or division example

responseLevels.gap: gives 56 only by recomputing or recall, or gets 42 via the additive-split error; cannot explain why decomposing a factor is valid.
responseLevels.full: decomposes a factor and adds the partial products, justifies it as breaking the groups into parts that recombine to the whole (distributive), and transfers the strategy to a new fact (e.g. 8×9 via 8×5+8×4); correctly refuses to apply it to subtraction.
responseLevels.partial: correctly derives 56 from 8×5 and 8×2 for this case but treats it as a one-off trick — cannot generalise the split to a new factor or name why it must work.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I know that 8 × 5 = 40. Without working out 8 × 7 the long way, can you use what you already know to figure it out? Tell me what you did and why it works.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who merely memorises facts can state 56 but cannot justify deriving it and will say 'I just know it' or recompute from scratch. A child who holds the property explains WHY 8×5+8×2 must equal 8×7 — the split of the factor, not luck. The reason-tier separates fact-recall from structural understanding, and the classic distributive error (adding to the wrong factor, or 8×7 = 8×5+2) surfaces here.

sources.claim: Y4 pupils recognise and use factor pairs and commutativity, multiply three numbers, and use distributive partitioning within methods.

sources.claim: 3.OA.5 requires applying commutative, associative and distributive properties as strategies to multiply and divide; pupils need not know the property names.
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 3, Operations & Algebraic Thinking (3.OA.B.5)

sources.claim: The area model embodies the distributive law and bridges to formal written multiplication; properties should be shown in arrays before being used as calculation strategies.
