pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 8-9 (REPRESENTATIONAL). Identify, represent and estimate numbers to 10,000 across MULTIPLE representations — place-value counters, base-ten, expanded form, numeral, and crucially position on a 0-10,000 number line — and move between them. Estimation on the line makes four-digit magnitude concrete.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 4): 'identify, represent and estimate numbers using different representations'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.NBT.2 read/write/compare multi-digit numbers in multiple forms; number-line reasoning about magnitude.
• Operational details — Teach representations as interchangeable views of one number, with the number line as the magnitude spine: locate/estimate a four-digit number on 0-10,000 using benchmark landmarks (halfway = 5000, quarters, thousands). Move both ways: given a numeral, place it; given a point, name it. Connect estimation to rounding and to reasoning about 'about how big'.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8, emerging): places a four-digit number roughly on a landmarked 0-10,000 line. Tier B (age 8-9, secure): translates among numeral/expanded/counters and estimates position using benchmarks. Tier C (age 9, extending): estimates on a sparsely-marked line and justifies using nearest landmarks.
bestPractices: Use the 0-10,000 number line as the magnitude spine, with benchmark landmarks (5000 halfway, thousands, 2500/7500) to anchor estimation.
Treat numeral / expanded form / counters / number-line point as interchangeable views and translate in all directions.
Practise both directions on the line: place a given number, and name a marked point.
Progress from densely-marked to sparsely-marked lines so estimation relies on proportional reasoning, not counting ticks.
Link estimation to rounding ('4,367 is about 4,000') and to sense-checking calculations.
keyRepresentations: 0-10,000 number line with benchmark landmarks (the magnitude spine)
Place-value counters and Th|H|T|O chart
Expanded form and numeral (with comma)
Base-ten thousand/hundred/ten/one pieces
Bar/strip model for proportional estimation on the line
commonMisconceptions: Placing numbers by leading digit only (putting 4,900 and 4,100 at the same spot).
Treating the number line as evenly-spaced counting rather than proportional magnitude.
Ignoring landmarks and guessing position.
Confusing representations (reading expanded form as separate numbers).
Mis-scaling: putting 5,000 not at the halfway point of 0-10,000.

learn.summary: For ages 8-9, teach four-digit numbers (to 10,000) as one quantity seen through interchangeable views — numeral, expanded form, place-value counters/base-ten, and a point on a 0-10,000 number line — and have learners translate in every direction. The number line acts as the magnitude spine: estimate and place numbers using benchmark landmarks (halfway = 5,000, quarters at 2,500/7,500, thousands), so four-digit magnitude becomes a felt distance rather than a string of digits. A bar/strip model can support proportional reasoning about position. Link estimation to rounding and sense-checking.

activities.title: Linked-representations estimator on a 0-10,000 line
feedback: If the marker is placed by leading digit only (6,300 near a '6' tick on a miscounted scale), reveal the true position lit against the 5,000 halfway and 7,500 three-quarter landmarks so the learner sees 6,300 sits a little past 6,000, past halfway but not yet three-quarters, about midway between 5,000 and 7,500.

When a learner bunches numbers at one end or spaces them evenly regardless of value, build the landmarks together — locate 5,000 first, then 2,500 — and let them self-adjust rather than marking it wrong; proportional sense is still forming at this age.
When one view disagrees with another, translate back and forth explicitly: point to a digit and ask what term it contributes to the expanded form, and where that moves the marker.
activities.rationale: Estimation and multi-representation can be made concrete by acting — moving a marker and seeing proportional feedback, or changing one view and watching the others recompute. Linked, recompute-on-action panels (numeral, expanded, counters, line marker), a bar/strip model, and a fading-ticks estimation game are optional ways to make the mechanism visible; the essential element is the learner acting on the line and reasoning from benchmarks, which is achievable on paper too.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'identify, represent and estimate numbers using different representations'.
Read, write and compare multi-digit numbers in multiple forms (4.NBT.2); number-line reasoning supports magnitude.
The number line as a proportional magnitude model, with benchmark landmarks, is central to estimation and to number sense.
learnerActions: Work with four synced views of one number: numeral, expanded form, place-value counters (Th|H|T|O), and a draggable marker on a 0-10,000 number line.
Change any one view (e.g. add/remove counters) and watch the others, including the marker's position on the line, update to match.
Play an estimation round: a target such as 6,300 appears; drag the marker to where you think it sits, then compare with the revealed true position and your error.

Use landmark hints — find 5,000 (halfway) first, then 2,500 and 7,500 — and decide where the number falls: ask yourself 'is 6,300 past halfway? is it yet past three-quarters?' and justify your answer before checking.
Optionally use a bar/strip model alongside the line to reason about proportion (e.g. shade roughly 6,300 out of a 10,000 strip) and relate the shaded length to where the marker should sit.
As you improve, work on lines where tick marks are removed so placement must come from proportional reasoning, not counting ticks.
Say aloud what you found first on the line and why the number lands where it does (e.g. '6,300 is past the middle but not yet at three-quarters, about halfway between 5,000 and 7,500').
activities.intendedInsight: The same number can be expressed as a numeral, expanded form, and counters, and these all correspond to one proportional position on the number line; magnitude is a distance anchored by landmarks, not the leading digit alone.

activities.title: Three-view translation with a placeholder zero
feedback: If a learner drops the empty hundreds column or misplaces digits (342, 3,42, or 30,042), return to the columns and show that removing the zero slides the 3 down into the hundreds place (342), while an extra zero pushes it up into the ten-thousands place (30,042); either way its value changes. The zero holds the hundreds place open.

If the expanded form or line placement contradicts the numeral just written (e.g. writing 3,000 + 400 + 2 for 3,042), translate explicitly: point to the 0 in 3,042 and ask what term it contributes (none — that is why there is no hundreds term).

Probe with: 'Why is there no "+ something hundred" in the expanded form?', 'If I take the zero out and write 342, what happened to the 3?', and 'How did you decide where on the line to put it — what did you find first?'
activities.rationale: A number with an internal zero forces learners to reveal whether they treat position as value. Requiring three representations (numeral, line, expanded) from one source exposes whether the views are genuinely linked or memorised separately.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'identify, represent and estimate numbers using different representations'.
Read, write and compare multi-digit numbers in multiple forms (4.NBT.2); number-line reasoning supports magnitude.
learnerActions: Read place-value counters such as 3 thousands, 0 hundreds, 4 tens, 2 ones and write the numeral (3,042).
Write the same number in expanded form (3,000 + 40 + 2) and explain why there is no hundreds term.
Show roughly where 3,042 sits on a 0-10,000 line — a little above the 3,000 mark, just under a third of the way along.
Translate in the reverse directions too: given a marked point, name the number; given expanded form, build the counters.
Explore what changes if a column changes: e.g. 3 thousands, 4 hundreds, 0 tens, 2 ones gives 3,402 — and discuss how moving the counts between columns shifts the number's value and its line position.
activities.intendedInsight: Position determines value: the zero in the hundreds column is a placeholder that must be kept, and the numeral, expanded form, and line position must all agree because they describe one number.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal reference poster (scaffold)
feedback: Use the highlighted links to confirm or correct your own translation; for estimation, you still need to place the marker yourself to build proportional judgement.
activities.rationale: A static or tap-to-reveal reference clarifies the links between the different representations of one number and is a useful reference. As an observable affordance, it shows correspondences rather than requiring the learner to estimate or construct, so independent line placement still needs separate learner action.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'identify, represent and estimate numbers using different representations'.
learnerActions: Study one number shown simultaneously as numeral, expanded form, counters, and a point on the line.
Tap a representation to highlight the matching parts in the others and the matching line position.
Use it as a reference check after attempting a translation yourself, not as a substitute for acting on the line.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing the correspondences across representations highlighted together reinforces that they are views of one quantity.

activities.title: Quick-check items for placement and matching
feedback: For 'which point is 4,900?', if 4,900 and 4,100 are placed at the same spot (leading-digit error), re-anchor on the nearest thousand and halfway landmarks to separate them.
Use mismatches between a chosen match and the line position to prompt a re-check in both directions.
activities.rationale: Short recognition and slider items efficiently sample matching and placement across many numbers. As an observable limit, selection-based items confirm fluency but do not by themselves elicit the independent construction and reasoning that the translation and estimator activities require.
sourceClaims: Read, write and compare multi-digit numbers in multiple forms (4.NBT.2); number-line reasoning supports magnitude.
learnerActions: Place a given number (e.g. 6,300) on a 0-10,000 line using a slider.
Match a numeral to its expanded form and to a counter/base-ten depiction.
Choose which marked point on the line is 4,900 (distinguished from 4,100).
Supply a missing representation given one of the others.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent movement between representations and benchmark-based placement can be demonstrated across short, varied prompts.

constraints: Treat numeral, expanded form, counters/base-ten, and the number-line point as interchangeable views of one number and practise translating in all directions, not just one way.

Use the 0-10,000 line as the magnitude spine with benchmark landmarks (5,000 halfway, 2,500/7,500 quarters, thousands); progress from densely-marked to sparsely-marked lines so estimation relies on proportional reasoning rather than counting ticks.
Link estimation to rounding ('4,367 is about 4,000') and to sense-checking calculations.

The tap-to-reveal poster and selection/slider quick-checks are scaffolds and samples: they show or test correspondences but do not require the learner to construct or estimate independently; include construction and line-placement tasks for that.

Address common errors directly: placing by leading digit only, treating the line as even counting rather than proportional magnitude, ignoring landmarks, reading expanded form as separate numbers, and mis-scaling (5,000 not at the halfway point).

For the developmental error of bunching/even spacing, do not mark it wrong or drill in isolation — co-build landmarks and let the learner self-adjust, as proportional sense is still forming at ages 8-9.

Linked live-recompute panels, draggable markers, fading tick marks, landmark hints, and a bar/strip model for proportional estimation are optional illustrative mechanisms, not mandatory tools; the learning goal is learner action and benchmark reasoning on the line, achievable on paper too.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Source list marks the DfE National Curriculum claim as verified; the CCSS-M 4.NBT.2 and NCETM number-line claims are listed as not verified in the original row — treat their support as unconfirmed.

sourceClaims on the scaffold (poster) and quick-check activities support the representational/number-line CONTENT being shown or sampled; they do not evidence the affordance LIMITATIONS stated in those rationales, which are objective/pedagogical observations (recognition/selection does not itself elicit independent construction), not sourced findings.

The original rated open dialogue and 3D as 'poor' with rationales like 'open dialogue can't capture line placement' and 'magnitude on a line is planar'. These are reframed as narrow affordance notes (selection/discussion does not by itself elicit independent line placement) rather than universal claims that such media cannot teach; no catalog ranking is asserted as a pedagogical law.

Arithmetic/representation self-audit: 3 thousands, 0 hundreds, 4 tens, 2 ones = 3,042 = 3,000 + 40 + 2, placed just above the 3,000 mark (3,042/10,000 ≈ 0.304, a little under a third) — consistent. The variant 3 thousands, 4 hundreds, 0 tens, 2 ones = 3,402. 6,300/10,000 = 0.63 — past halfway, not yet three-quarters.
The bar/strip model (an original keyRepresentation omitted from the prior candidate) has been restored as an optional proportional-estimation representation.
Error-pattern examples (342, 3,42, 30,042, and 3,000 + 400 + 2) are retained as diagnostic signs of dropping/concatenating the placeholder or detaching representations, not as correct answers.

probeDeeper: Why is there no '+ something hundred' in the expanded form?
If I take the zero out and write 342, what happened to the 3?
How did you decide where on the line to put it — what did you find first?
What if the counters were 3 thousands, 4 hundreds, 0 tens, 2 ones — how does the number change?
assess.correctAnswer: 3,042 — placed just under a third of the way along the line (a little above the 3,000 mark) — expanded as 3,000 + 40 + 2.

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops the empty hundreds column or concatenates the counts — writes 342, or writes 3,42 / 30042, because the zero 'has nothing so it doesn't count'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the columns: show that removing the zero slides the 3 out of the thousands place and changes its value; the zero holds the hundreds place open.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Numeral has the wrong number of digits or a missing placeholder; child cannot say why a zero is needed.

errorPatterns.pattern: Bunches numbers at one end of the number line or spaces them evenly regardless of value — places 3,042 near the middle or crams small-thousands together.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT mark it wrong or drill placement in isolation; build the line's landmarks together (find 5,000 first, then 2,500) and let the child self-adjust — the sense of proportional position is still forming.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Number-line placement ignores relative magnitude (e.g. 3,042 put at the halfway mark).

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the three representations as unrelated tasks — can write the numeral but the expanded form or line does not match it (e.g. writes 3,000+400+2).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Translate back and forth explicitly: point to the 0 in 3,042 and ask what term it contributes to the expanded form (none — that is why there is no hundreds term).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Expanded form or line contradicts the numeral the child just wrote; no cross-checking.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot produce a correct numeral from the counters; loses the placeholder or the digit order.
responseLevels.full: Produces all three consistently, uses the zero as a placeholder deliberately, places on the line by proportional reasoning, and can translate from any one representation to the others.
responseLevels.partial: Writes 3,042 correctly but one representation is detached — expanded form or line placement does not agree with the numeral, or cannot translate back.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are place-value counters: 3 in the thousands column, none in the hundreds, 4 in the tens, 2 in the ones. Write this as a number. Then show me roughly where it sits on a 0-to-10,000 number line, and write it in expanded form.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The empty hundreds column forces the child to reveal whether they treat position as value: a child who understands place value writes 3,042 and holds the zero as a placeholder, while a child who reads columns as a running total writes 342 or 3,42 or 30,042. Requiring three representations (numeral, line, expanded) exposes whether they are linked or memorised separately.

pedagogy.summary: By Y6 children should reach van Hiele level 3 (informal deduction): not just that a square is a special rectangle, but a full quadrilateral hierarchy where attributes flow downward — anything true of a parallelogram is automatically true of a rhombus, rectangle and square, because each is a special parallelogram. The two load-bearing ideas are (a) attribute inheritance (a subcategory has every property of its parents plus extra) and (b) the ASYMMETRY of class inclusion: all squares are rectangles but not all rectangles are squares. Persistent obstacles are exclusive/oblong-prototype thinking carried up from KS2, and treating 'all A are B' as if it were symmetric ('so all B are A'). Teaching succeeds when children build and defend the hierarchy from properties rather than from appearance.
bestPractices: Make attribute inheritance explicit: a rhombus is a parallelogram with all sides equal, a rectangle is a parallelogram with right angles, a square is both — so a square inherits every parallelogram property (opposite sides parallel, diagonals bisect each other) automatically
Draw the hierarchy as a family tree / nested sets and have children justify each subset link ('why is every rectangle a parallelogram?') from properties
Confront the asymmetry directly with the two statements 'all squares are rectangles' vs 'all rectangles are squares' and demand the reason for which is true
Use everyday class-inclusion analogies (every spaniel is a dog and an animal, but not every dog is a spaniel) to make the one-directional logic intuitive
Ask for defining vs shared properties: what do ALL parallelograms share, and what EXTRA property makes each special case — forcing the necessary/sufficient distinction
keyRepresentations: Quadrilateral hierarchy diagram (family tree) with quadrilateral ⊃ parallelogram ⊃ {rhombus, rectangle} ⊃ square
Nested Venn sets showing rhombus and rectangle overlapping, with square in the intersection
Property table: rows = shapes, columns = properties (opposite sides parallel, all sides equal, right angles, equal diagonals) showing how ticks accumulate down the hierarchy
A parallelogram with adjustable angles and side lengths that becomes a rhombus, rectangle, or square as constraints are added
commonMisconceptions: Treating 'all squares are rectangles' as symmetric — concluding 'so all rectangles are squares' (or that both are equally true/false)
Reversing the subset direction — thinking a rectangle is a special square rather than a square a special rectangle
Exclusive/oblong prototype persisting from KS2: a 'real' rectangle must be longer than it is wide, so a square is not a rectangle at all
Not applying inheritance: agreeing a rhombus is a parallelogram in words, but not granting that it therefore has all parallelogram properties (e.g. opposite sides parallel, diagonals bisecting)

learn.summary: Year 6 learners (ages 10-11) build the quadrilateral hierarchy from properties rather than appearance, grasping two load-bearing ideas: attribute inheritance (a subcategory has every property of its parents plus an extra constraint) and the asymmetry of class inclusion (all squares are rectangles, but not all rectangles are squares). The target understanding is the van Hiele informal-deduction level (level 3 when levels are numbered from 1, level 2 when numbered from 0): learners justify and defend subset links from properties, overcoming the exclusive/oblong prototype formed in earlier school years and the tendency to treat 'all A are B' as symmetric.

activities.title: Build the shape by adding properties
feedback: If a learner builds a square but denies it is a parallelogram, point back to the property table: it has opposite sides parallel, so it meets the parallelogram definition.

If a learner expects removing 'right angles' from a rectangle to leave it a rectangle, show that the 'rectangle' label depends on that very property — removing it moves the shape up to plain parallelogram.

When a learner sees the reverse challenge is impossible, name the insight: 'all rectangles are parallelograms but not all parallelograms are rectangles' (just as all squares are rectangles but not all rectangles are squares) is something you bumped into, not a rule to memorise.
activities.rationale: Adding and removing defining properties and watching a shape's position in the hierarchy change makes attribute inheritance and the one-directional asymmetry concrete and reasoned rather than memorised. A live constraint model with linked hierarchy diagram, nested Venn sets and a ticking property table is an optional way to make the mechanism visible; the same reasoning can be done with paper cut-outs and a drawn family tree.
sourceClaims: Attributes of a category belong to all its subcategories (5.G.3); classify two-dimensional figures in a hierarchy based on properties (5.G.4)
At van Hiele level 3 (informal deduction) students can explain why all squares are rectangles; the levels progress from visual to descriptive to relational reasoning
A square is a subclass of rectangle; children must learn class inclusion and often resist inclusive membership
learnerActions: Start with a general 'floppy' quadrilateral and switch on one property at a time: make opposite sides parallel, add right angles, make all sides equal.

Watch how the shape changes and where it belongs: making opposite sides parallel turns it into a parallelogram; adding right angles makes it a rectangle; instead making all sides equal makes it a rhombus; doing both makes it a square.

After each change, record in a property table which properties the shape now has (opposite sides parallel, all sides equal, right angles, equal diagonals), noticing that these ticks accumulate as you go down each branch of the family tree.

Attempt the reverse challenge: try to make a rectangle that is NOT a parallelogram, and explain why you cannot — four right angles force each pair of opposite sides to be parallel (two sides that are both perpendicular to the same side are parallel), so every rectangle automatically meets the parallelogram definition.
Place the finished square, rhombus and rectangle onto a family-tree (hierarchy) diagram and into nested Venn sets, saying why the square sits inside BOTH the rhombus and rectangle regions.
activities.intendedInsight: A square inherits every property of the parallelogram, rhombus and rectangle because it is a special case of each; adding an extra constraint moves a shape DOWN the hierarchy, and the inheritance runs one way only — removing the extra property moves back up, but you cannot have a rectangle that is not also a parallelogram.

activities.title: Defend the asymmetry: which statement is true?
feedback: If a learner picks statement (2), use nested sets: the square set sits INSIDE the rectangle set, so square→rectangle always holds but rectangle→square does not.

If a learner rejects statement (1) because 'a rectangle must be longer than it is wide', show rectangles ranging from very long to square and test each against the definition (right angles, parallel opposite sides) rather than its typical look.
If a learner treats both statements as equally true or false, return to the spaniel/dog/animal analogy to feel the direction of the inclusion.
activities.rationale: Directly confronting the two statements and demanding a property-based reason surfaces whether the learner treats inclusion as symmetric, reverses the direction, or holds the oblong prototype — each error leads to a distinct, identifiable answer, so this both teaches and discriminates reasoning.
sourceClaims: 'All squares are rectangles, but not all rectangles are squares'; guiding questions 'Is a square a special rectangle? Is a rectangle a special parallelogram? Is a rhombus a special kite?'
Children impose non-defining attributes and reason from prototypes, causing them to reject inclusive relationships between quadrilaterals
A square is a subclass of rectangle; children must learn class inclusion and often resist inclusive membership
learnerActions: Consider two statements: (1) all squares are rectangles, (2) all rectangles are squares. Decide which is true and which is false.

Justify the choice from properties: a square has every property a rectangle needs (four right angles, opposite sides equal and parallel) PLUS all four sides equal, so every square qualifies as a rectangle; a rectangle only becomes a square when it also has equal sides, which most do not.
Test the everyday analogy: every spaniel is a dog and every dog is an animal, but not every animal is a dog — explain how this one-directional logic matches squares and rectangles.
Attempt counterexamples: draw a rectangle that is NOT a square, a parallelogram that is NOT a rectangle, and try to draw a square that is NOT a rectangle (explaining why the last is impossible).
activities.intendedInsight: Class inclusion is one-directional: 'all A are B' does not mean 'all B are A'. The subset asymmetry follows from the extra defining property, not from which shape is more familiar.

activities.title: Shared versus extra properties across the parallelogram family
feedback: If a learner agrees in words that a rhombus is a parallelogram but lists its properties in isolation, build the property table so the shared parallelogram properties are seen carrying down to every special case.
If a learner cannot name the EXTRA property for a rhombus or rectangle, prompt: 'What does this shape have that a general parallelogram need not have?'
Praise reasoning that distinguishes a property ALL members share from the extra property that makes a case special.
activities.rationale: A property table makes inheritance visible and forces the necessary/sufficient distinction, addressing the misconception where learners grant category membership in name but withhold the inherited properties. A tap-to-reveal hierarchy with properties highlighted in parent nodes is one optional consolidation reference once the idea is understood.
sourceClaims: Attributes of a category belong to all its subcategories (5.G.3); classify two-dimensional figures in a hierarchy based on properties (5.G.4)
A square is a subclass of rectangle; children must learn class inclusion and often resist inclusive membership
learnerActions: List the properties that ALL parallelograms share (opposite sides parallel and equal, diagonals bisect each other).

For each special case, state the extra property that defines it compared with a general parallelogram: a rhombus adds all sides equal, a rectangle adds right angles, and a square adds both (or just one extra property compared with a rhombus or a rectangle).
Fill a property table (rows = shapes, columns = properties) and confirm that each subcategory keeps every shared parallelogram property and adds its extra constraint.
Transfer the reasoning to a new or less familiar shape: given its properties, say where it belongs in the hierarchy and why, and which properties it inherits.
Justify a subset link in words, e.g. 'why is every rectangle a parallelogram?', using shared properties rather than appearance.
activities.intendedInsight: Every special parallelogram inherits all the shared parallelogram properties and adds extra defining constraints (one for a rhombus or a rectangle; two for a square, which is one more than a rhombus or a rectangle); this separates necessary/shared properties from the extra property or properties that name each shape.

activities.title: Convince the shape sceptic
feedback: If the learner argues from appearance ('it just looks like one'), the sceptic should ask which defining properties are met.
If the learner accepts the reverse ('every rhombus is a square'), ask for a rhombus that is not a square as a counterexample.
Reward justifications that cite shared and extra properties explicitly.
activities.rationale: Dialogue that demands property-based justification can surface reasoning and press the asymmetry, and can complement structural work done with diagrams and manipulatives.
sourceClaims: At van Hiele level 3 (informal deduction) students can explain why all squares are rectangles; the levels progress from visual to descriptive to relational reasoning
learnerActions: Respond to a sceptic who accepts a hierarchy claim only when it is justified from properties: 'Convince me a square belongs inside the rhombus family.'
Answer the follow-up pressure: 'Then is every rhombus a square?' — explaining why the reverse does not hold.
State, for each claim, which properties make it true and which extra property the reverse would require.
Use a counterexample when the sceptic over-generalises (e.g. produce a rhombus that is not a square).
activities.intendedInsight: Being made to articulate and defend each subset link, and to expose the reverse as false, consolidates property-based justification over appearance-based classification.

activities.title: Classify and check the hierarchy
feedback: If a shape is misplaced, ask which defining property is missing or extra for the region chosen.
For the true/false item, if the reversal is chosen, revisit the nested sets showing the square set inside the rectangle set.
activities.rationale: Categorisation, matching and a well-built true/false item check that reasoning is secure and are well suited to confirming the hierarchy and asymmetry. Recognition and correct placement alone do not require the learner to construct the inheritance, so use these alongside or after construction and reasoning work.
sourceClaims: Attributes of a category belong to all its subcategories (5.G.3); classify two-dimensional figures in a hierarchy based on properties (5.G.4)
learnerActions: Drag or place a set of quadrilaterals into nested regions of a hierarchy, putting the square in the intersection of the rhombus and rectangle sets.
Match each shape (parallelogram, rhombus, rectangle, square) to its extra defining property.
Answer a true/false question on the asymmetry — 'Which is true: all squares are rectangles, or all rectangles are squares?' — and spot the reversal as a wrong option.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure recall and correct placement confirm the hierarchy is stable, including the asymmetry and each shape's extra defining property.

constraints: Build and defend the hierarchy from properties, not from appearance; the oblong/prototype view ('a rectangle must be longer than it is wide') must be directly confronted, not reinforced.

Classification, matching and true/false items check that the hierarchy is secure but do not by themselves require the learner to construct the inheritance insight; use them to confirm understanding alongside or after construction and reasoning work.

A tap-to-reveal hierarchy/property table is a useful reference once the idea is understood, but it does not let the learner add or remove constraints to feel a shape descend the hierarchy; pair it with construction activities.
Dialogue with a sceptic supports property-based justification; the structural subset relationships can be seen clearly in a diagram, nested sets or manipulative, so pair dialogue with those.

Optional interactive features (live constraint handles, animated descent down the tree, updating nested Venn sets, a ticking property table, tap-to-reveal nodes) make the mechanism concrete but are not required; paper cut-outs and a drawn family tree can serve the same reasoning (a paper cut-out has slight thickness and only approximates the ideal flat quadrilateral it represents).
Keep class-inclusion attention one-directional: contrast 'all squares are rectangles' with 'all rectangles are squares' as genuinely different claims, not as a reversible rule.

Use 'equal diagonals' (true of rectangles and squares, not of general parallelograms or rhombuses) as the distinguishing property-table column so ticks genuinely accumulate; keep 'diagonals bisect each other' as a shared parallelogram property, not as an accumulating column.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original rated a 2D constraint sandbox as 'ideal' and dismissed a third spatial dimension as 'adds nothing'; this comparative/necessity claim is a catalog preference not established by the cited sources, so it has been softened to an optional affordance rather than a universal law.

The original claimed a scored linear quiz 'tests the reasoning rather than building the inheritance insight' and that dialogue 'supports rather than delivers'; these have been reframed as narrow affordances/design cautions, not proven efficacy or medium-superiority claims.
The National Curriculum (Year 6 Geometry) source is marked verified:false in the row; treat that citation with caution.

If using physical cut-outs to model quadrilaterals, note that paper has slight thickness and only approximates an ideal plane figure; discuss the represented flat shape, not whether the card can be handled.

The property-table column was changed from 'diagonals bisect each other' (a shared parallelogram property that does not accumulate) to 'equal diagonals' (parallelogram ✗, rhombus ✗, rectangle ✓, square ✓) so the accumulation observation stays coherent; the bisecting property is retained as a shared parallelogram property.

probeDeeper: 'What do ALL parallelograms have in common? What extra property makes a rhombus special? A rectangle?' (tests inheritance and the necessary/sufficient distinction)
'A spaniel is a dog and every dog is an animal — is every animal a dog? How is that like squares and rectangles?' (class-inclusion analogy pushing the one-directional logic)
'You said a square is a rectangle — is a square also a rhombus? Is it a parallelogram? Why?' (transfer down two branches of the hierarchy)

'Can you draw a rectangle that is NOT a square, and a parallelogram that is NOT a rectangle? Could you ever draw a square that is NOT a rectangle?' (counterexamples; the last is impossible — the asymmetry made concrete)
assess.correctAnswer: Statement (1) is true, statement (2) is false. A square has every property a rectangle needs (four right angles, opposite sides equal and parallel) plus the extra property that all four sides are equal, so every square qualifies as a rectangle. A rectangle only becomes a square when it gains that extra property of equal sides, which most rectangles do not have — so not every rectangle is a square.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses the subset direction — picks 'all rectangles are squares' as the true one (treats the more familiar/larger category as the special case)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use nested-set and property-table work to show which set contains which: the square set sits INSIDE the rectangle set, so going square→rectangle always holds but rectangle→square does not. Revisit classifying by parallel/perpendicular-line properties.
errorPatterns.distractor: Statement (2) is the true one — all rectangles are squares
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Chooses statement (2) and, on the reason tier, argues that a rectangle 'is a kind of square' or that the two claims are interchangeable

errorPatterns.pattern: Oblong-prototype exclusion persisting from KS2 — 'a square isn't a rectangle at all because a rectangle has to be longer than it is wide', so (1) is judged false
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate defining properties from typical appearance; show rectangles ranging from very long to square and test each against the definition. Reground in property-based classification.
errorPatterns.distractor: Neither is true — a square is not a rectangle
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rejects statement (1) and, on the reason tier, defines a rectangle by its unequal-sides look rather than its right angles and parallel opposite sides

errorPatterns.pattern: Inheritance not applied — agrees a rhombus/rectangle is a parallelogram in name, but does not grant that it therefore has all parallelogram properties, and describes rhombus/rectangle as unrelated to the parallelogram family
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build the property table so shared parallelogram properties (opposite sides parallel and equal, diagonals bisect) are seen to carry down to every special case, with each subcategory adding exactly one extra constraint.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Under the parallelogram probe, lists a rhombus's or rectangle's properties in isolation and cannot say what EXTRA property each adds to a shared parallelogram base

responseLevels.gap: Picks the wrong statement or says both are equally true/false; or rejects 'all squares are rectangles' on appearance. Cannot use defining properties to reason about inclusion.
responseLevels.full: Picks statement (1) and explains the asymmetry from properties — a square has all a rectangle's properties plus equal sides, so every square is a rectangle but only equal-sided rectangles are squares; places quadrilaterals correctly in a hierarchy, states the properties all parallelograms share, and explains rhombus and rectangle as parallelograms each adding one extra property, transferring the reasoning to a new shape.
responseLevels.partial: Picks statement (1) and can say a square is a special rectangle, but lists shared/defining properties without using them to explain the asymmetry, and cannot apply inheritance to the parallelogram family (does not identify what extra property makes a rhombus or rectangle special, or transfer to a new case).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Tell the child: 'Here are two statements — (1) all squares are rectangles, and (2) all rectangles are squares. One is true and one is false.' Ask: 'Which one is true? And how do you know — what makes it true and the other one false?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands one-directional class inclusion picks statement (1) and explains the asymmetry via the extra property. A child treating inclusion as symmetric, or reversing the direction, picks (2) or says both are true/false. A child still holding the oblong prototype rejects (1) outright ('a square isn't a rectangle'). Each faulty reasoning route lands on a different, identifiable answer, and the reason tier separates a memorised 'square is a special rectangle' from genuine grasp of WHY the reverse fails.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–10y; multiply and divide whole numbers AND decimals by 10, 100 and 1000, understanding the digit shift.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5 'multiply and divide whole numbers and those involving decimals by 10, 100 and 1000'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 5.NBT.2 — 'explain patterns in the number of zeros of the product when multiplying a number by powers of 10, and … in the placement of the decimal point when a decimal is multiplied or divided by a power of 10'; 5.NBT.1 place-value ten-times relationship.
• Operational details — the essential understanding is that ×/÷ by a power of ten SHIFTS every digit left/right across the place-value columns — the digits move, the decimal point stays put (or equivalently the point moves relative to the digits). This must replace the false 'add a zero / move the decimal point' rule, which breaks for decimals (3.45×100 is 345, not 3.4500). Use a place-value chart / Gattegno chart where digits physically slide. ×1000 = three places left; ÷1000 = three places right, introducing tenths/hundredths/thousandths. This underpins metric conversions and powers-of-ten notation.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): × and ÷ whole numbers by 10/100 with digit-shift language. Tier B (age 9–10): 3.45×100, 72÷1000 correctly, explaining the shift. Tier C (age 10): explain why 'add a zero' fails for decimals and connect to metric conversion.
bestPractices: Teach as a digit SHIFT across place-value columns (digits move left for ×, right for ÷), not 'add a zero' or 'move the point', which mislead with decimals.
Use a place-value/Gattegno chart where digits physically slide the correct number of places, with the decimal point fixed.
Introduce tenths/hundredths/thousandths through ÷10/100/1000 so the columns to the right of the point are meaningful.
Link the number of places to the power of ten (×1000 → 3 places) and later to exponent notation.
Connect to metric conversions (m↔cm↔mm, kg↔g) as an authentic application.
keyRepresentations: Place-value / Gattegno chart with sliding digits (point fixed)
Arrow/shift diagram showing 1/2/3 places for 10/100/1000
Decimal place-value columns (tenths, hundredths, thousandths)
Metric conversion tables as an application
commonMisconceptions: 'Add a zero' rule misapplied to decimals (3.45×100 wrongly written as 3.4500).
'Move the decimal point' causing confusion about direction or number of places.
Shifting the wrong number of places for the power of ten.
Forgetting to fill empty places with zeros as placeholders when needed (e.g. 72÷1000 = 0.072).
Thinking dividing always makes the digits smaller in value without understanding the place shift.

learn.summary: For ages 9–10: multiply and divide whole numbers and decimals by 10, 100 and 1000 by understanding that each digit SHIFTS across the place-value columns — digits move left for multiplying and right for dividing, while the decimal point stays fixed. This replaces the fragile 'add a zero' rule, which breaks for decimals (3.45×100 is 345, not 3.4500), and the memorised 'move the point' rule, which gives the same numerical result but hides why the value changes and is easily misapplied (for example where to put the point in a whole number, or forgetting placeholder zeros). The skill underpins metric conversions and powers-of-ten notation.

activities.title: Sliding digits on a place-value chart
feedback: If a learner appends zeros to a decimal (3.45×100 → 3.4500): on the chart, multiplying by 100 makes every digit worth 100× more, so each digit moves two columns left — the '3' becomes 3 hundreds. The point does not move; the digits do. The correct answer is 345.

If 72÷1000 comes out as 720 or 7.2: dividing makes each digit worth a thousandth as much, so the digits move exactly three columns to the RIGHT. 720 has moved them left (the wrong direction), and 7.2 has moved them only one place right instead of three.
If 72÷1000 is written as 0.72 (too few decimal places): count every column each digit crosses and drop a zero into each empty one so 72 lands correctly as 0.072.

If the place count is off by one under speed: this may be a counting slip rather than a misunderstanding. Recount the zeros in 10/100/1000, match them to the places shifted, and check whether the error comes back on similar items.
activities.rationale: The target concept is itself a digit shift across place-value columns, so watching digits slide while the point stays fixed makes the mechanism visible and exposes why the memorised 'add a zero' rule fails for decimals. Labelling the columns tenths/hundredths/thousandths gives meaning to the places opened up by division.
sourceClaims: 5.NBT.2 requires explaining patterns in zeros and decimal-point placement when ×÷ by powers of ten; 5.NBT.1 the ten-times place-value relationship.
Teach ×÷ by powers of ten as a place-value digit shift, not 'add a zero'/'move the point', which mislead with decimals.
learnerActions: Set up a place-value chart with labelled columns from hundreds down to thousandths (… H  T  O • t  h  th) and a fixed decimal point.
Place 3.45 in the columns, then multiply by 100: slide every digit TWO columns to the LEFT so the 3, 4 and 5 become 345. Note that nothing was appended — the digits moved.
Now test the tempting 'just add two zeros' shortcut on 3.45 and compare: it gives 3.4500, which is wrong. Discuss why the shortcut fails for decimals.
Divide 72 by 1000: slide every digit THREE columns to the RIGHT, and fill each empty column it crosses with a placeholder zero, giving 0.072 (including the leading 0).
Compute 6 × 10 by sliding one place left (giving 60), and connect the number of places shifted to the number of zeros in 10/100/1000 (×1000 → 3 places).
Optionally switch the chart to a metric mode so the same kind of shift is reread as a conversion: metres → centimetres is ×100 (two places left) and centimetres → millimetres is ×10 (one place left).
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying or dividing by a power of ten changes what each digit is worth, so the digits shift the matching number of place-value columns; the decimal point does not move, and empty columns must be filled with placeholder zeros.

activities.title: Reference chart with reveal-able shift arrows
feedback: If the direction is reversed: multiplying moves digits LEFT (larger value), dividing moves them RIGHT (smaller value).
If the count is wrong: match the number of places to the number of zeros in the power of ten.
activities.rationale: A static annotated chart is a clean, reusable reference that consolidates the direction-and-count rule, though it cannot itself let a learner slide digits through many cases — pair it with active manipulation for the shift intuition.
sourceClaims: Teach ×÷ by powers of ten as a place-value digit shift, not 'add a zero'/'move the point', which mislead with decimals.
learnerActions: Study a place-value chart annotated with arrows that show the shift for ×10 (one place), ×100 (two places) and ×1000 (three places), and the reverse for division.
Answer the prompt 'why isn't 3.45 × 100 = 3.4500?' and check your reasoning against a revealed explanation.
State in your own words how many places each power of ten shifts the digits and in which direction.
activities.intendedInsight: A clear reference links each power of ten to a fixed number of places and direction, reinforcing that the direction and count — not zero-appending — determine the result.

activities.title: Spot-the-error and fill-in consolidation
feedback: For the 3.45×100 choice: 3.4500 keeps the point fixed and tacks on zeros, leaving the value unchanged — wrong. Sliding each digit two places left gives 345.
For 72÷1000: a missing placeholder zero gives 0.72; count the crossed columns to reach 0.072.
An off-by-one place error may be a counting slip, so recount and see whether it happens again; a wrong direction signals the digit-shift idea needs revisiting.
activities.rationale: Checkable items that deliberately include the decimal trap and placeholder cases let a learner apply and test whether the shift understanding transfers; such items consolidate, check and diagnose but do not themselves provide the digit-sliding manipulation, so use them after active manipulation.
learnerActions: Complete 72 ÷ 1000 = ___ , writing all placeholder zeros.
Choose the correct value of 3.45 × 100 from options including the trap value 3.4500, and explain why the trap is wrong.
Find and fix the mistake in a worked example where a digit has been shifted the wrong number of places.
Explain, for one of your answers, how the value of each digit changed.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidation surfaces the specific decimal trap (3.4500) and the placeholder-zero requirement (0.072), confirming whether digit-shift reasoning is secure rather than a fragile trick.

activities.title: Testing the 'just add a zero' claim out loud
feedback: If the learner defends 'add a zero': ask what each digit is now worth — in 345 the 3 is 3 hundreds, so the digits moved, they were not padded.
If they are unsure how to express it: 'multiplying by 100 makes every digit worth 100 times more, so each slides two columns left.'
activities.rationale: A Socratic dialogue can draw out and challenge the misconception by prompting the learner to test it; it works best alongside a chart where the shift can be seen, since discussion alone does not let the learner manipulate the digits.
sourceClaims: Teach ×÷ by powers of ten as a place-value digit shift, not 'add a zero'/'move the point', which mislead with decimals.
learnerActions: Respond to a character who insists you can always 'just add a zero' to multiply by ten.
Test the claim on a whole number (6 × 10 = 60) where it seems to work, then on a decimal (3.45 × 100) where it produces 3.4500.
Argue, using place value, why the claim is unsafe and what actually happens to the digits.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating why 'add a zero' works for whole numbers but fails for decimals turns a half-learned rule into reasoned understanding of the digit shift.

constraints: Teach the operation as a digit shift across place-value columns (left for ×, right for ÷), not as 'add a zero' or 'move the decimal point': 'add a zero' gives wrong answers for decimals, and 'move the decimal point', although it gives the same numerical result, hides the change in place value and is easily misapplied to whole numbers and placeholder zeros.
Always fill empty columns crossed by a shift with placeholder zeros, including leading zeros (e.g. 72 ÷ 1000 = 0.072).
Introduce tenths/hundredths/thousandths through dividing by 10/100/1000 so the columns to the right of the point are meaningful before relying on them.
Link the number of places shifted to the number of zeros in the power of ten (×1000 → 3 places) and, later, to exponent notation.

Reference charts and multiple-choice / fill-in items consolidate, check and diagnose whether digit-shift reasoning transfers, but do not themselves provide the sliding manipulation; pair them with active manipulation rather than treating them as sufficient alone.

A manipulable sliding chart, a static annotated chart, a dialogue, and consolidation items each serve a different observable purpose; none is inherently sufficient alone, and no claim is established here that only one medium can teach this.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic checked: 3.45×100=345, 72÷1000=0.072, 6×10=60. The original assessment 'correctAnswer' listed '345; 0.072; 60'; the '60' corresponds to the 6×10 diagnostic item and is correct, so it is retained — it is not an erroneous alternative.

One source (DfE National Curriculum) is marked verified; two (CCSS-M 5.NBT and NCETM place-value guidance) are marked unverified in the source row. The DfE claim attests only curriculum topic coverage, so it is not carried as support for a digit-shift teaching rationale. No comparative-efficacy or medium-superiority claims are asserted beyond what the sources support.

The original row rated a 3D treatment as 'poor'/'adds no insight'; this catalog rating is kept only as a narrow note rather than carried as a universal claim, since a catalog rating does not establish that 3D can teach nothing here.
Categorical phrasing that static/quiz media 'cannot build intuition' was softened to the observable affordance that they do not provide the digit-sliding manipulation themselves.

probeDeeper: When you multiplied 3.45 by 100, did the decimal point move or did the digits move? Which is it really?
Why does 72 ÷ 1000 need those zeros after the point?
Explain what multiplying by 10 does to the value of each digit.
Someone got 3.4500 for 3.45 × 100. What did they do wrong?
assess.correctAnswer: 345; 0.072; 60. The teacher watches for the child moving each digit the correct number of places (two places left for ×100, three places right for ÷1000) with the decimal point staying put and zeros filling empty places — not a memorised 'add two zeros' trick that breaks on decimals.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'add zeros' rule — for 3.45 × 100 appends zeros to give 3.4500 instead of 345
errorPatterns.nextMove: use the place-value chart: multiplying by 100 makes every digit worth 100× more, so each digit SHIFTS two columns left; the '3' becomes 3 hundreds. The point does not move — the digits do.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer keeps the decimal point in place and tacks on zeros; magnitude unchanged

errorPatterns.pattern: 'move the decimal point' with the wrong direction or count — moves it right for division, or by the wrong number of places
errorPatterns.nextMove: reframe as digits shifting: dividing by 1000 makes each digit worth a thousandth as much, so digits move three columns RIGHT; fill empty places with zeros, including leading 0.0…
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 72 ÷ 1000 comes out as 720 or 7.2 rather than 0.072

errorPatterns.pattern: forgets to insert zeros as placeholders — 72 ÷ 1000 written as 0.72 (only shifts what's visible)
errorPatterns.nextMove: count the columns crossed and insert a zero in each empty one so 72 lands in the correct places (0.072).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: too few decimal places; digits shifted but empty columns not filled

errorPatterns.pattern: shifts correctly but miscounts places by one under speed
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach; have the child recount the number of zeros in 10/100/1000 and match to places shifted.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer off by a factor of ten; self-corrects when recounting columns

responseLevels.gap: relies on 'add zeros', gives 3.4500, or moves the point the wrong way/amount; no place-value reasoning.
responseLevels.full: shifts digits the correct number of places in both directions for whole and decimal numbers, fills placeholders, keeps the point fixed, and explains each digit's changed value.
responseLevels.partial: handles whole-number cases by shifting but slips on decimals or forgets placeholder zeros in division.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to work these while you watch, using a place-value chart if they wish: 3.45 × 100, 72 ÷ 1000, and 6 × 10. Watch whether they SHIFT the digits across the place-value columns or whether they just 'add/remove zeros' or 'move the decimal point' as a rule.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The 'add a zero' rule works for whole numbers but fails on 3.45 × 100 (gives 3.4500, wrong) — so watching a decimal case exposes whether the child understands digit-shift or has memorised a fragile trick. 72 ÷ 1000 forces filling in leading zeros (0.072), catching those who only shuffle visible digits.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 10–11 — identify the value of each digit in numbers given to three decimal places (in 4.378 the 7 represents 7 hundredths).
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5 recognise place value of digits in numbers with up to 3 decimal places; Y6 applies this to determine each digit's value.
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): 5.NBT.A.1 and 5.NBT.A.3a — understanding the value of each digit in a decimal to thousandths, with each place one tenth the place to its left.
• Operational details: For each digit, state its value as digit × place-unit (7 in 4.378 = 7 × 1/100 = 7 hundredths). Reinforce the ten-times-smaller relationship between adjacent decimal places. Reverse the task — given digit values, reconstruct the number — to prove flexible understanding and to surface placeholder-zero handling (4 ones, 0 tenths, 7 hundredths, 3 thousandths = 4.073).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): 'In 2.635 what is the value of the 3?' Tier B: 'Explain the relationship between adjacent decimal places.' Tier C: 'Write the number with 4 ones, 0 tenths, 7 hundredths, 3 thousandths.'
bestPractices: Require each digit's value as digit × place-unit ('7 hundredths', '7 × 1/100'), not just its place name
Explicitly state and re-derive that each place is one tenth of the place to its left (the ÷10 chain through decimals)
Run the task in reverse — give digit values, reconstruct the numeral — to force placeholder-zero handling (0 tenths → 4.073)
Contrast identical digits in different places within one number (the two 3s' values differ) to separate face value from place value
Use a decimal place-value chart so each column's unit is explicit as the child reads a digit
keyRepresentations: Decimal place-value chart Ones . tenths hundredths thousandths with unit labels 1, 1/10, 1/100, 1/1000
Digit-value cards: '7 → 7 hundredths → 0.07'
Thousandths grid showing each place as ten of the next-smaller
Reverse-build slots (digit-into-place) with a live numeral readout
commonMisconceptions: Naming the place but giving the wrong value (the 7 is 'in the hundredths' but stated as '7' or '0.7')
Reading the decimal part as one whole number (378) rather than digit-by-place values
Confusing tenths and hundredths (off-by-one place), especially with a leading zero
Dropping placeholder zeros when reconstructing (writing 4.73 for 4 ones/0 tenths/7 hundredths/3 thousandths)
Believing adjacent places differ additively rather than by a factor of ten

learn.summary: For ages 10–11: identify the value of each digit in numbers given to three decimal places (e.g. in 4.378 the 7 represents 7 hundredths, 7 × 1/100 = 0.07). Learners state each digit's value as digit × place-unit, re-derive that each decimal place is one tenth of the place to its left, and reconstruct a numeral from given digit-values to surface placeholder-zero handling (4 ones, 0 tenths, 7 hundredths, 3 thousandths = 4.073). A key discrimination is that 3 tenths is worth more than 7 hundredths even though 7 is the larger digit.

activities.title: Reveal each digit's value (digit × place-unit)
feedback: If a learner gives just the digit or just the place name ('7' or 'hundredths'), ask them to finish the sentence '7 × 1/100 = ___' so the value is named, not only the place.
If they say the 7 is worth 7, rebuild the chart and read 4.378 aloud as '4 ones, 3 tenths, 7 hundredths, 8 thousandths', anchoring each digit to its fraction.
If they miscount by one column (calling the 7 tenths or thousandths), count columns aloud left-to-right from the point — tenths, hundredths, thousandths — landing deliberately on the 7.
Confirm the two 3s in 2.335 differ because one sits in the tenths column, worth ten times the adjacent hundredths column — separating face value from place value.
activities.rationale: Requiring value as digit × place-unit (not just the place name) and contrasting identical digits in adjacent columns directly targets the common error of naming the place but stating the wrong value, and separates face value from place value. An optional interactive form — tapping a digit to bloom its value with the column highlighted and ÷10/×10 arrows to neighbours — can make the ten-times relationship concrete, but a labelled chart with spoken/written values teaches the same idea.
sourceClaims: Y5 pupils recognise the place value of each digit in numbers with up to three decimal places.
5.NBT.A.1/A.3a: understand the value of each digit in a decimal to thousandths, each place one tenth of the place to its left.
learnerActions: Write or display a number to three decimal places, e.g. 4.378, above a place-value chart with columns labelled Ones . tenths hundredths thousandths and units 1, 1/10, 1/100, 1/1000.
For each digit, say and write its value as digit × place-unit: the 7 is 7 × 1/100 = 7 hundredths = 0.07; the 8 is 8 × 1/1000 = 8 thousandths = 0.008.
State explicitly how adjacent places relate: the hundredths place is one tenth of the tenths place (÷10 moving right, ×10 moving left).

Within a single number containing two identical digits in adjacent decimal columns, e.g. 2.335 (2 ones, 3 tenths, 3 hundredths, 5 thousandths), compare the two 3s and explain why their values differ (3 tenths = 0.3 versus 3 hundredths = 0.03) even though the digit is the same.
activities.intendedInsight: A digit's worth is its face value times the unit of the column it sits in; adjacent decimal places differ by a factor of ten, not by addition, so the same digit can mean very different amounts.

activities.title: Reverse build: reconstruct the numeral from given values (placeholder zeros)
feedback: If a learner writes 4.73, point out that the 7 has slid from the hundredths column into the tenths column (and the 3 from thousandths into hundredths) — ask which column each digit now occupies and whether that matches the given values.

If they omit the zero, have them read both numbers aloud — 4.73 as '4 and 73 hundredths' and the correct 4.073 as '4 and 7 hundredths 3 thousandths' (73 thousandths) — to hear that these are different numbers.
Confirm success when they keep the 0 to hold the tenths column and can say why the zero is not optional.
activities.rationale: Running the task in reverse forces explicit placeholder-zero handling, which the forward 'name the value' task can hide. This addresses the documented error of dropping placeholder zeros when reconstructing. A drag-and-assemble interface with a live numeral readout is one effective way to make the empty column visible, but the same learning occurs by writing digits into chart cells on paper.
sourceClaims: Y5 pupils recognise the place value of each digit in numbers with up to three decimal places.
5.NBT.A.1/A.3a: understand the value of each digit in a decimal to thousandths, each place one tenth of the place to its left.
learnerActions: Given a set of digit-values — 4 ones, 0 tenths, 7 hundredths, 3 thousandths — place each into its column on a place-value chart and read off the numeral.
Write the resulting number: 4.073.
Deliberately try leaving the empty tenths column blank and read what you get: 4.73. Compare 4.073 with 4.73 and explain why they are different numbers.
Repeat with another set that includes a zero in a middle place (e.g. 3 ones, 0 tenths, 0 hundredths, 5 thousandths = 3.005) and justify each zero's job.
activities.intendedInsight: A placeholder zero is worth 0 itself, but it does real work by holding a column open; omitting a zero that comes before other digits shifts every later digit into the wrong place and produces a different number. Reconstruction proves flexible, two-way understanding of place value.

activities.title: Which is worth more — the smaller digit or the larger?
feedback: If a learner ranks 7 hundredths above 3 tenths, place 0.3 and 0.07 on a 0–1 line so the sizes of the chunks are visible.
If they say the 7 is worth more because it comes later (further right), re-anchor each digit to its fractional unit and compare the units, not the positions.
Confirm when they justify 3 tenths > 7 hundredths by comparing place-units rather than digits.
activities.rationale: This comparison is the discriminating task: it exposes 'bigger-digit-is-bigger-value' and 'later-is-larger' misconceptions and demands reasoning from place-units. A spoken, responsive discussion lets a mentor probe why the values differ; a 0–1 number line gives a concrete size check.
sourceClaims: 5.NBT.A.1/A.3a: understand the value of each digit in a decimal to thousandths, each place one tenth of the place to its left.
learnerActions: Compare the value of the 3 and the 7 in 4.378: state the 3 is 3 tenths (0.3) and the 7 is 7 hundredths (0.07).
Decide which is worth more and justify it — the 3, because tenths are ten times bigger chunks than hundredths, so 3 tenths outweighs 7 hundredths even though 7 is the larger digit.
Mark 0.3 and 0.07 on a 0–1 number line to see that 3 tenths is a bigger portion than 7 hundredths.
Discuss: when 4.378 becomes 4.387, whose value changed — the 7's or the 8's? Explain using the columns: both changed, since the 7 and 8 swapped between the hundredths and thousandths places.
activities.intendedInsight: Place, not face value, determines worth in a decimal: reasoning about the column must override the surface impression that the bigger digit is worth more or that a digit further right is larger.

constraints: Learners must state each digit's value as digit × place-unit (e.g. '7 hundredths', '7 × 1/100 = 0.07'), not only name the place.
Include the reverse reconstruction task; naming values forward alone can hide the placeholder-zero error, so reconstruction from values is needed to prove two-way understanding.

Multiple-choice or fill-in-the-blank items (e.g. 'value of the 3 in 2.635', 'reconstruct 4 ones/0 tenths/7 hundredths/3 thousandths = ___') can consolidate and check understanding but do not themselves build the place-unit link; pair them with construction and explanation.

A fixed labelled diagram with revealed per-digit values is a strong reference for the reveal step but cannot host the reverse-build that tests placeholder zeros, so it is a partial scaffold for this objective.

Optional interactive affordances (tap-to-reveal, drag value tiles into columns, live numeral readout, ÷10/×10 arrows) make the mechanism concrete but are not required; equivalent learning is possible with a paper chart and spoken reasoning.

When contrasting identical digits, use a number where the repeated digit appears in genuinely different places and state the correct factor between those places (adjacent columns = ten times; non-adjacent columns differ by a larger power of ten).
Checkpoint tiers: age-10 'In 2.635 what is the value of the 3?'; explain 'the relationship between adjacent decimal places'; write 'the number with 4 ones, 0 tenths, 7 hundredths, 3 thousandths'.

One listed source (DfE National Curriculum) was marked verified in the original row and one (CCSS-M) was marked unverified; verification status was not re-checked here.

The original candidate's identical-digits example 3.303 contained three 3s (not two) and had a 'ten times' feedback that was false for its non-adjacent columns; it was replaced with 2.335, which has exactly two 3s in adjacent columns (tenths and hundredths) so the ten-times relationship holds.

In this independent review, activity 2's zero-dropping feedback was corrected: both read-aloud phrases previously named 4.073, so the intended contrast failed; the feedback now reads 4.73 as '73 hundredths' versus 4.073 as '7 hundredths 3 thousandths'.

Original diagnostic/answer text uses 4.378 with digits 3 tenths, 7 hundredths, 8 thousandths; one checkpoint/compare example uses 2.635 (6 tenths, 3 hundredths, 5 thousandths). These are internally consistent and preserved as distinct examples.

The original 'possible'/'poor' fit framing (conversation and 3D) was converted to pedagogical notes: dialogue is retained as a genuine teaching option for the comparison task rather than dismissed; no universal 'static image cannot teach' or '3D adds nothing' claim is asserted.

probeDeeper: Which is worth more, the 3 or the 7 — and why isn't it just 'the bigger digit'?
What is the value of the 8 in 4.378, and how does it relate to the 7?
Write me a number with 4 ones, 0 tenths, 7 hundredths and 3 thousandths.
If I change 4.378 to 4.387, whose value changed — the 7's or the 8's?
assess.correctAnswer: The 7 represents 7 hundredths (0.07); the 3 represents 3 tenths (0.3). The 7's place is worth ten times less than the 3's place, so the 3 is worth more even though 7 is the larger digit.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the decimal part as a whole number — 'the 7 is worth 7', treating .378 like three hundred seventy-eight.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild the places with a decimal place-value chart; read 4.378 as '4 ones, 3 tenths, 7 hundredths, 8 thousandths', anchoring each column to a fraction.
errorPatterns.distractor: The 7 is worth 7.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Values are stated as bare digits with no fractional place named.

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscounts the place by one — calls the 7 'tenths' or 'thousandths' instead of hundredths.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count columns aloud left-to-right from the point (tenths, hundredths, thousandths), landing deliberately on the 7; do not just supply the name.
errorPatterns.distractor: The 7 is 7 thousandths.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct idea of fractional places but the label is off by one column.

errorPatterns.pattern: Longer/later-is-larger — thinks the 7 is worth more than the 3 because it comes further right.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare 0.3 and 0.07 on a 0–1 line; show tenths are bigger chunks than hundredths so 3 tenths outweighs 7 hundredths.
errorPatterns.distractor: The 7 is worth more than the 3 because it comes later.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child ranks 7 hundredths above 3 tenths.

responseLevels.gap: Reads decimal digits as whole numbers or cannot name fractional places.
responseLevels.full: Names each digit's fractional value, states the ten-times relationship between adjacent places, and correctly judges 3 tenths > 7 hundredths with justification.
responseLevels.partial: Names 7 hundredths correctly but defaults to 'bigger digit = bigger value' when comparing with the 3, or is off by one place under pressure.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In the number 4.378, what is the value of the 7? And how does that compare with the value of the 3?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who reads decimal place value names 7 hundredths and sees the 3 is worth more despite being the smaller digit — the reasoning must override the surface 'bigger digit'. A child reading the decimal as a whole number, or miscounting places, or applying longer-is-larger gives a different answer and a revealing reason.
