pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 4–6 (UK Reception–Y1, US K–Grade 2, formalised Grade 3). Division as equal SHARING (partitive: share 12 among 3 → how many each?) and equal GROUPING (quotitive: how many groups of 3 in 12?) — the domain's most central concept (centrality 0.43, highest in Maths).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y1 'solve one-step problems involving multiplication and division, by calculating the answer using concrete objects, pictorial representations and arrays with the support of the teacher'; non-statutory 'through grouping and sharing small quantities, pupils begin to understand … division'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): concept seeded in K–Grade 2; formalised at 3.OA.2 'interpret whole-number quotients — e.g. 56 ÷ 8 as the number of objects in each share when 56 are partitioned into 8 equal shares, OR as the number of shares when partitioned into groups of 8'.
• Operational details: teach BOTH structures explicitly — sharing (deal out one-to-each) meets children's fairness intuition first; grouping (make groups of a fixed size) links division to repeated subtraction and to the multiplication tables/inverse. Same equation, two different pictures. Keep quantities small, concrete, and initially remainder-free.
• Checkpoint: model and distinguish the two meanings. Tier A (4–5): fairly share a small set one-to-each and say how many each got. Tier B (5–6): solve both a sharing and a grouping story for the same numbers with counters. Tier C (6): explain that 12÷3 can mean '3 equal shares' OR 'groups of 3', and that both give 4.
bestPractices: Teach BOTH division structures deliberately, not just sharing: sharing (partitive — 'share 12 among 3 plates, how many each?') and grouping (quotitive — 'how many groups of 3 can I make from 12?'). Children default to sharing; grouping must be taught because it is the bridge to repeated subtraction and to reading a times-table fact as a division.
Start fully concrete with a 'one for you, one for me' dealing action for sharing, and a 'scoop groups of n' action for grouping, before any symbol — the physical act carries the meaning.
Show the SAME numbers under both stories so children see one division fact (12÷3=4) can be pictured two ways — this prevents them treating sharing and grouping as unrelated.
Link division to multiplication as its inverse from the start using the array/equal groups (3 groups of 4 is 12, so 12 shared into 3 is 4) — builds the fact-family idea early.
Use fair-sharing language to connect to early fractions (sharing 1 cake among 2 = a half), and keep first examples exact (no remainder) so the core idea is secure before remainders complicate it.
keyRepresentations: Equal-sharing model — dealing counters one-at-a-time into plates/hoops (partitive)
Equal-grouping model — scooping a set into groups of a fixed size (quotitive)
Arrays and equal groups linking division to its inverse multiplication
Bar model (whole split into equal parts) and number line (equal jumps back for grouping/repeated subtraction)
commonMisconceptions: Believing division only means sharing-out (partitive), so a 'how many groups of 3?' problem is not recognised as division at all.
Treating sharing and grouping as different operations rather than two meanings of the same ÷ — not seeing they give the same answer.
Thinking division is commutative: that 12÷3 and 3÷12 are the same (they are not).
Confusing which number is shared and which is the number of groups/size of group (dividend vs divisor) when moving to symbols.
Assuming every sharing must come out exactly and being thrown by leftovers, or sharing unequally and still calling it 'fair'.

learn.summary: For ages 4–6 (roughly UK Reception–Y1, US Pre-K–Grade 1; division with symbols is formalised later, e.g. US Grade 3), build division from two concrete meanings on the same quantity: equal SHARING (partitive: share 12 among 3 plates → how many each?) and equal GROUPING (quotitive: how many groups of 3 fit in 12?). Children default to sharing, so grouping must be taught deliberately — it is the bridge to repeated subtraction and to reading a times-table fact as a division. Keep quantities small, concrete, and initially remainder-free, and show the same numbers under both stories so children see one division fact (12÷3=4) pictured two ways.

activities.title: Share-and-group the same pile
feedback: If a learner makes groups of 3 when asked to share among 3 plates, act out both situations separately side by side — 'share between 3 plates' (3 shares) versus 'make groups of 3' — and name the difference out loud.
If shares come out unequal, model round-robin dealing ('one for you, one for you'), then count both piles and compare, so 'fair' is pinned to 'equal'.
When a total does not divide evenly, simply name 'there's one left over, it won't share fairly' and move on — do not treat the leftover as an error to reteach; remainders come later.
Reinforce the link to multiplication: '3 groups of 4 make 12, so 12 shared into 3 gives 4' — the actions are inverses.
activities.rationale: The curriculum expects division to be met through both grouping and sharing of small quantities using concrete objects, pictorial representations and arrays, and standards describe interpreting a quotient as either the number in each share or the number of equal groups. Enacting both structures on one quantity makes the two meanings concrete and comparable.
sourceClaims: Y1: solve one-step problems involving multiplication and division using concrete objects, pictorial representations and arrays; through grouping and sharing small quantities pupils begin to understand division.
3.OA.2 interpret whole-number quotients as the number in each share (partitive) OR the number of equal groups (quotitive) — the two structures of division.
Division should be taught through both sharing (partitive) and grouping (quotitive) structures; grouping links division to repeated subtraction and to multiplication facts.
learnerActions: Take 12 counters and 3 plates (or hoops). Deal counters out one at a time — 'one for this plate, one for this plate, one for this plate' — until the pile is gone, then count how many each plate got (4).
On the SAME 12 counters, now scoop them into groups of 3, setting each group aside until none remain, then count how many groups you made (4).
Say the matching division sentence for both actions: 12÷3=4. Notice the same answer arrived from two completely different actions — sharing among 3, and making groups of 3.
Try a total that will not share evenly (e.g. 13 counters among 3 plates): deal fairly until you cannot give everyone one more (4 each), and name the leftover (1 left over).

Optional with an interactive counters tool: toggle between a SHARE mode (choose number of plates, tap 'deal', watch counters distribute one at a time) and a GROUP mode (choose a group size, lasso groups); flip modes on the identical pile to see the same equation form on screen.
activities.intendedInsight: Division has two meanings — equal shares and equal groups — and the same numbers can be pictured both ways, giving the same answer; this is the twin meaning children most often miss.

activities.title: Fair-share check with teddies
feedback: Correct full answer for the 2-teddy share: '6 each — it's fair because both teddies have the same number with none left over; I gave them out one at a time until they were gone.'
If a learner offers unequal piles and is untroubled by the difference, model one-for-you dealing, then count and compare both piles so equality becomes the test of fairness.
If a learner shares equally but never checks the piles match, prompt them to count both and confirm they are the same before calling it fair.
With an odd total (e.g. 13 between 2), name the leftover plainly rather than reteaching; noticing 'one left over, won't share evenly' is the goal, not resolving the remainder.
activities.rationale: A 'share fairly and justify' prompt discriminates children who use equality as the governing idea (deal one-to-one, verify equal shares) from those who split unevenly or call it fair without checking. Asking 'how do you know it's fair' surfaces whether 'equal' rather than 'everyone got some' is the constraint. The share-among-3 and groups-of-3 follow-ups revisit 12÷3 under both meanings.
learnerActions: Share 12 counters fairly between 2 teddies so each gets the same. Say how many each teddy gets (6) and explain how you know it is fair.
Count each teddy's pile and compare — are they the same, with none left over?
Describe your method: 'I gave them out one at a time to each teddy until they were gone.'
Now share the same 12 counters among 3 teddies and say how many each gets (4); then answer the matching grouping question: how many groups of 3 can you make from 12? (4) — both are 12÷3.
Try 13 counters: can you still share them fairly between the 2 teddies? What happens? (6 each with 1 left over — it won't share evenly).
activities.intendedInsight: Fairness here means everyone gets an equal amount. When the total shares evenly there are none left over, and when it does not (e.g. 13 between 2), the leftover is simply named. A child shows understanding by checking the groups match, not just by giving everyone 'some'.

activities.title: Sort the stories: sharing or grouping?
feedback: If a learner does not recognise a 'how many groups of 3?' problem as division, act it out with counters alongside a sharing version and name both as division.
If a learner thinks 12÷3 and 3÷12 are the same, show with counters that sharing 12 among 3 differs from sharing 3 among 12 — division is not commutative.
This sorting and matching can check whether the child holds both meanings; it checks classification rather than eliciting the physical dealing/scooping, so use it after hands-on sharing and grouping.
activities.rationale: Categorising stories and matching a division sentence to both picture types can verify that a learner holds both meanings and does not treat sharing and grouping as unrelated operations. It checks classification and is best used after concrete work; it does not itself elicit the physical handling that builds the concept.
sourceClaims: 3.OA.2 interpret whole-number quotients as the number in each share (partitive) OR the number of equal groups (quotitive) — the two structures of division.
Division should be taught through both sharing (partitive) and grouping (quotitive) structures; grouping links division to repeated subtraction and to multiplication facts.
learnerActions: Read or hear short word problems and sort each into 'sharing' (share a total among a number of people/plates) or 'grouping' (make groups of a fixed size).
Match a division sentence like 12÷3=4 to BOTH a shared picture (3 plates with 4 each) and a grouped picture (4 groups of 3).
Fill in the answer to simple remainder-free division sentences, using counters to check.
activities.intendedInsight: Both wordings — 'share among 3' and 'how many groups of 3' — are division, and a single division fact matches both a sharing picture and a grouping picture.

activities.title: Correct the unfair sharer
feedback: If a learner accepts the unequal shares, hand them the counters and have them redeal one-to-one, then count each friend's share.
Use fair-sharing language to connect to early fractions — sharing 1 cake between 2 is a half — keeping first examples exact with no remainder.
A talking partner cannot move the counters for the child, so make sure the child physically redistributes the quantity rather than only talking about it.
activities.rationale: A fair-share dilemma can prompt reasoning about equality, but a talking character cannot let the child manipulate the quantity, so dialogue works best paired with hands-on dealing. Fair-sharing language also seeds early fraction ideas.
learnerActions: A puppet or story character shares a set unfairly on purpose (gives one friend 'a lot'). Fix it so every friend gets an equal share.
Explain to the character why the new sharing is fair and the old one was not.
Pose and solve a fair-share dilemma aloud: 'We have 12 sweets and 4 friends — what's fair?' (3 each).
activities.intendedInsight: Talking through fairness reinforces that equal shares are the rule, while actually moving the counters is what lets the child make and check the equal shares.

constraints: Keep totals small, concrete, and initially remainder-free so the core idea is secure before leftovers complicate it.

Teach BOTH structures deliberately: sharing meets the fairness intuition first, but grouping must be explicitly taught because children default to sharing and grouping is the bridge to repeated subtraction and to multiplication facts.
Treat leftovers gently at this age: name 'there's one left over' and move on; do not reteach remainders as a misunderstanding — remainder work comes later.
Start fully concrete (dealing and scooping actions) before introducing symbols; the physical act carries the meaning.
Sorting/matching and fill-in-the-answer tasks can check classification but do not themselves elicit the physical dealing/scooping — use them after hands-on sharing and grouping, not instead of it.
A talking character or puppet cannot let the child manipulate quantity, so keep dialogue as a supplement to concrete dealing.

Watch for the dividend/divisor confusion as symbols appear: be clear which number is the total being shared and which is the number of groups or the size of each group; division is not commutative (12÷3 ≠ 3÷12).

The source claims for 3.OA.2 and NCETM are marked unverified in the source row; the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified. Confidence levels were not independently re-checked.

probeDeeper: Count each teddy's pile — are they the same?
Now share the same 12 between 3 teddies — how many each?

What if you had 13 counters — could you still share them fairly?
assess.correctAnswer: 6 each — it's fair because both teddies have the same number with none left over. I gave them out one at a time to each teddy until they were gone.

errorPatterns.pattern: shares unequally — makes two piles that aren't equal or hands 'a lot' to one teddy; equality isn't yet the constraint
errorPatterns.nextMove: model round-robin dealing ('one for you, one for you'), then count both piles and compare so 'fair' is pinned to 'equal'
errorPatterns.distractor: One teddy gets more because that pile looks big.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: offers unequal piles as the answer and is untroubled by the difference

errorPatterns.pattern: confuses sharing-between with grouping-into — asked to share between 2 teddies, instead makes groups of 2
errorPatterns.nextMove: act out the two situations separately — 'share between 2 teddies' (2 groups) versus 'make groups of 2' — and name the difference
errorPatterns.revealedBy: builds sets of 2 rather than 2 equal shares

errorPatterns.pattern: mishandles a leftover — with a number that won't share evenly, quietly gives one teddy extra
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT treat as a misunderstanding to reteach — remainder understanding comes later; simply name 'there's one left over, it won't share fairly' and move on

responseLevels.gap: Splits into unequal piles or stops before all are shared; equality is not the governing idea.
responseLevels.full: Deals out one-to-one into equal groups, verifies the shares are equal with none left over, and handles both sharing-between and grouping-into forms.
responseLevels.partial: Shares equally by dealing but doesn't check the groups match, or handles sharing-between but not the 'how many groups of' form.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are 12 counters. Share them out fairly between these 2 teddies so each teddy gets the same. How many does each teddy get — and how do you know it's fair?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands equal sharing deals out one-to-one and checks the two groups are equal, justifying fairness by equal amounts. A child without it splits unevenly (a big pile and a small one), stops before all are shared, or calls it fair without checking. The 'how do you know it's fair' tier surfaces whether 'equal' is the governing idea rather than just 'everyone got some'.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 10–11: use written division where the answer has up to two decimal places — divide decimals to hundredths by whole numbers (e.g. 14.76 ÷ 4 = 3.69), and continue division past the decimal point.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y6): 'use written division methods in cases where the answer has up to two decimal places'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 5.NBT.7 — divide decimals to hundredths using place-value strategies, models, and relating to a written method; 6.NS.3 fluency with decimal division.
• Operational details — the key move is continuing short/long division past the decimal point, carrying the remainder to the next place: 14.76 ÷ 4 proceeds 14÷4 = 3 r2, bring down 7 (as 27 tenths), 27÷4 = 6 r3, bring down 6 (36 hundredths), 36÷4 = 9 → 3.69, keeping the point aligned. Where a whole number doesn't divide exactly, annex zeros after the point (18.6 → 18.60) to continue. Context problems (sharing £18.60 among 5) motivate decimal quotients and connect to money/measures.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): compute 14.76 ÷ 4 = 3.69 keeping the point aligned. Tier B (10–11): explain how to continue past the decimal point / annex a zero when a place won't divide. Tier C (11): solve a context problem needing decimal division (share £18.60 among 5) and interpret the answer as money.
bestPractices: Teach the decimal point in the quotient as ALIGNED with the point in the dividend — place it first, then divide place by place — so the point's position is structural, not an afterthought.

Show that continuing past the point is the SAME process as whole-number division: the remainder is regrouped into the next-smaller place (tenths, then hundredths), which children already know from long division of whole numbers (mt_WsM4EmdOLe).
Use annexing zeros deliberately: when there is a remainder at the last given place, adding a zero (13 ÷ 4 → 13.00 ÷ 4 = 3.25) lets division continue — grounded in equivalence, not a trick.
Anchor in context and estimation: sharing money/measures makes decimal quotients meaningful, and an estimate (14.76÷4 ≈ 15÷4 ≈ 3.7) sanity-checks the point placement.
Connect to ×÷ by powers of ten and place value (mt_wPgpMJ0-PA): dividing regroups a unit into ten of the next-smaller unit, exactly the place-value structure underpinning the method.
keyRepresentations: Short/long division layout (bus stop) with the quotient's decimal point drawn directly above the dividend's point before dividing.
Place-value regrouping picture: a leftover one 'exchanged' into ten tenths, a leftover tenth into ten hundredths, mirroring the carry.
Money/measure context model (£18.60 shared into 5 equal parts) that names the tenths and hundredths as 10p and 1p.
Annexing-zeros illustration: 13 = 13.00 shown as equivalent, enabling the division to continue to 3.25.
commonMisconceptions: Misplacing or omitting the decimal point in the quotient (getting 369 or 36.9 for 14.76÷4).
Stopping at a remainder instead of continuing past the point or annexing a zero (13÷4 = 3 r1 left unfinished rather than 3.25).
Treating the tenths/hundredths digits as separate whole-number divisions without carrying the remainder down.
Writing the remainder as a whole number when the context calls for a decimal (money answer given as '3 remainder 2').
Losing place-value alignment so digits drift into the wrong column.

learn.summary: For ages 10–11: divide decimals to hundredths by whole numbers using written division, continuing past the decimal point. The central insight is that the quotient's decimal point sits directly above the dividend's point (structural, not guessed), and that continuing past the point is the SAME regrouping used in whole-number division — each leftover is exchanged into ten of the next-smaller place. Worked anchor: 14.76 ÷ 4 = 3.69; and annexing zeros (13 → 13.00 ÷ 4 = 3.25) lets division continue when a remainder is left after the dividend's last digit (a place where the divisor doesn't fit instead gets a 0 in the quotient). Context problems (sharing £18.60 among 5 = £3.72) motivate decimal quotients and connect to money and measures.

activities.title: Step-by-step divider: walk 14.76 ÷ 4
feedback: If the answer comes out as 369 or 36.9, the point was misplaced — line the quotient's point directly above the dividend's point and check the magnitude: 14.76 ÷ 4 is about 15 ÷ 4 ≈ 3.7, so 3.69 is sensible.
If a leftover is dropped instead of exchanged, show the counters: 2 leftover ones become 20 tenths and join the next column before dividing again.
Verify the result by multiplying back: 3.69 × 4 = 14.76.
activities.rationale: Decimal division is a step-by-step regrouping procedure whose critical insight is point alignment; animating each remainder being exchanged into ten of the next-smaller unit and locking the quotient point above the dividend point makes both the process and its place-value structure felt. Optional supports — counters that visibly exchange one unit into ten of the next, and an estimate strip that flags a mis-placed point — make the mechanism concrete.
sourceClaims: Aligning the quotient's decimal point with the dividend's and regrouping remainders into the next-smaller place makes decimal division continuous with whole-number division.
Y6 pupils use written division methods in cases where the answer has up to two decimal places.
Pupils divide decimals to hundredths using place-value strategies and models, relating the strategy to a written method and explaining the reasoning.
learnerActions: Before finding any digit, place the quotient's decimal point directly above the point in 14.76 — establish that its position is fixed by the dividend, not guessed.
Work left to right: 14 ÷ 4 = 3 remainder 2. Show the leftover 2 ones being EXCHANGED into 20 tenths, which join the 7 tenths to make 27 tenths.
Continue: 27 tenths ÷ 4 = 6 remainder 3. Exchange the leftover 3 tenths into 30 hundredths, joining the 6 hundredths to make 36 hundredths.
Finish: 36 hundredths ÷ 4 = 9, giving 3.69 with the point aligned.
Narrate at each step: continuing 'past the decimal point' is the same regrouping already used for whole numbers.
activities.intendedInsight: The decimal point in the quotient is aligned structurally with the dividend's point, and dividing past the point is the familiar regrouping of a leftover into ten of the next-smaller place.

activities.title: Annex a zero to continue the division
feedback: If the child stops at '3 r1', remind them the leftover can be shared further: extend the dividend with a zero and keep dividing past the point.
If a decimal place is skipped when the divisor doesn't fit, insist that every brought-down decimal digit yields a quotient digit — write a 0 in the quotient for that place rather than omitting it.
Check 3.25 × 4 = 13 to confirm.
activities.rationale: Annexing zeros deliberately — grounded in equivalence rather than as a memorised rule — resolves the common error of stopping at a whole-number remainder, and reinforces that the written method continues place by place.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils use written division methods in cases where the answer has up to two decimal places.
Aligning the quotient's decimal point with the dividend's and regrouping remainders into the next-smaller place makes decimal division continuous with whole-number division.
learnerActions: Try 13 ÷ 4 and reach 3 remainder 1; notice the division is not finished.
Rewrite 13 as 13.00 (an equivalent value) and place the quotient point above it.
Continue dividing: carry the remainder 1 as 10 tenths, 10 ÷ 4 = 2 remainder 2, carry 2 as 20 hundredths, 20 ÷ 4 = 5, giving 3.25.
Conclude that there was no real remainder — just more decimal places to find.
Repeat with 18.6 ÷ 5: annex a zero (18.60), continue to 3.72.
activities.intendedInsight: Annexing zeros after the decimal point is grounded in equivalence (13 = 13.00), not a trick; it lets division continue until it terminates or reaches the required number of places.

activities.title: Money and measures context: £18.60 shared among 5
feedback: If the answer is given as '3 remainder 3', ask what happens to the leftover money — it is shared further into 10p and 1p coins, so the division continues.
Estimate first: £18.60 ÷ 5 is about £20 ÷ 5 = £4, so £3.72 is sensible; an answer like £37.2 or £0.372 should be questioned by sense.
Confirm by multiplying back: £3.72 × 5 = £18.60.
activities.rationale: Context and estimation anchor decimal quotients and make the point placement checkable by sense; naming tenths and hundredths as 10p and 1p coins connects the abstract regrouping to money.
sourceClaims: Pupils divide decimals to hundredths using place-value strategies and models, relating the strategy to a written method and explaining the reasoning.
Y6 pupils use written division methods in cases where the answer has up to two decimal places.
learnerActions: Set up £18.60 ÷ 5 as a written division, aligning the quotient point above the point in 18.60.

Divide: 18 ÷ 5 = 3 remainder 3; exchange 3 leftover pounds into tenths (as 10p coins) with the 6 to make 36 tenths; 36 ÷ 5 = 7 remainder 1; exchange into hundredths (1p coins) with the 0 to make 10 hundredths; 10 ÷ 5 = 2, giving £3.72.
Name the tenths as 10p coins and the hundredths as 1p coins so the regrouping is meaningful.
Interpret the answer as money: each person gets £3.72.
Check with multiplication: £3.72 × 5 = £18.60.
activities.intendedInsight: Decimal quotients are meaningful in context: sharing money or measures requires continuing past the point, and the answer must be interpreted (e.g. as pounds and pence), not left as a whole-number remainder.

activities.title: Place-the-point and finish-the-division practice
feedback: For the point-placement choice, reason from magnitude: 14.76 ÷ 4 ≈ 3.7, so 3.69 is right and 369 or 36.9 are off by powers of ten.
If the ordering omits annexing a zero where a remainder persists, point back to the equivalence 13 = 13.00.
These checks test the result; still ask the child to carry out an unaided written division to show the regrouping is understood, not guessed.
activities.rationale: Recognition and ordering items give efficient practice and expose the signature point-placement error, but they check results more than they build the regrouping procedure, so they supplement rather than replace independent written working.
learnerActions: Fill in the missing quotient digits for a partly-worked 14.76 ÷ 4.
Decide where the decimal point belongs, choosing between answers like 369, 36.9 and 3.69, and justify the choice by magnitude.
Put a set of division steps in order, including the step of annexing a zero to continue.
Match each quotient to the context problem it answers (e.g. a money-sharing problem).
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising a correct point placement and ordering the steps consolidates the procedure; estimation justifies the choice rather than guesswork.

activities.title: Talk it through: the leftover money problem
feedback: If the child says 'there's a remainder and we stop', prompt: can the £2 be shared as coins? Lead them to tenths (10p) and hundredths (1p).
Follow the discussion with written working so the verbal idea is grounded in the actual procedure.
activities.rationale: A spoken prompt about a leftover can probe whether the child sees that division continues past the point, but the procedural walk is better carried out through written working and manipulation, so this is a lead-in, not the main teaching.
learnerActions: Consider a scenario: money is shared equally but there is £2 left over — what now?
Explain aloud how to divide the leftover further into smaller coins (tenths and hundredths).
State where the decimal point goes in the answer and why.
Then carry out the full written division to confirm the spoken reasoning.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating what to do with a leftover surfaces the idea of continuing past the decimal point before formalising it in symbols.

constraints: The learning objective is carrying out written division past the decimal point: learners must produce the quotient digit by digit with correct point alignment, not merely recognise a correct answer.
Recognition and ordering tasks check results and expose point-placement errors, but they do not elicit independent construction of the regrouping procedure; pair them with unaided written division.
Tap-to-reveal worked examples are a reference model only — they do not let the child drive the division or annex zeros themselves, so follow them with learner-driven working.
Annexing zeros must be justified by equivalence (13 = 13.00), not presented as a memorised trick.

Prerequisite links: regrouping a unit into ten of the next-smaller place draws on long division of whole numbers and on ×÷ by powers of ten / place value; reteach these if the point drifts or leftovers are dropped.
Every brought-down decimal place must yield a quotient digit, including a 0 when the divisor does not fit that place, to avoid losing place value.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three cited sources (CCSS-M 5.NBT.7/6.NS.3 and the NCETM decimal-division guidance) were marked unverified in the source row; treat the point-alignment/regrouping principle as guidance, not established comparative efficacy.

The source row claimed 3D 'adds nothing' for symbolic column procedures; this is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law, and has been dropped rather than asserted. A non-spatial symbolic procedure simply has limited need for a spatial model here.

Optional interaction examples (exchanging counters, annex-a-zero control, money skin naming coins, estimate strip) are retained as concrete illustrations of the mechanism, not as mandatory implementations.

The Y6 written-division curriculum claim is the governing method standard and is cited on the construction activities (1–3) whose core action is carrying out written division to two decimal places; it is omitted from the recognition/ordering practice activity, whose recognition-supplements-construction rationale it does not support.

Independent editorial re-review conducted afresh: all quotients, remainders, exchanges, money interpretations, estimates and multiply-back checks confirmed consistent; no categorical medium-superiority claims, internal IDs, or quiz-step vocabulary remain in learner-facing text; no new unresolved learner-facing errors found.

probeDeeper: Where does the decimal point go in your answer, and how did you decide?
When you had a remainder, what did you do to keep going past the decimal point?
Estimate 14.76 ÷ 4 — is 3.69 sensible?
How could you check £18.60 ÷ 5 = £3.72 using multiplication?
assess.correctAnswer: 14.76 ÷ 4 = 3.69. £18.60 ÷ 5 = £3.72. The teacher watches for the decimal point in the answer placed directly above the point in the dividend, and for the child continuing the division into the decimal places (bringing down the tenths/hundredths, or annexing zeros) rather than stopping at a whole-number remainder.

errorPatterns.pattern: misplaces or ignores the decimal point in the quotient — divides the digits as if whole, giving 369 or 36.9
errorPatterns.nextMove: line the quotient's decimal point directly above the dividend's; reason about magnitude (14.76÷4 is about 3.7, so 3.69 not 369).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer off by a power of ten; point not aligned above the dividend's point

errorPatterns.pattern: stops at a whole-number remainder instead of continuing into decimals — e.g. 18.60÷5 as '3 r3' rather than 3.72
errorPatterns.nextMove: show that the leftover can be shared further: bring down the tenths and hundredths (or annex zeros) and keep dividing past the point.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child leaves a remainder where a decimal quotient is expected; does not bring down/annex to the hundredths

errorPatterns.pattern: loses place value of a digit after the point — forgets a zero in the quotient when the divisor doesn't go into a decimal place
errorPatterns.nextMove: insist every brought-down decimal digit yields a quotient digit — write a 0 in the quotient when the divisor doesn't fit that place.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: quotient missing a decimal place (e.g. 3.9 instead of 3.09-type errors)

errorPatterns.pattern: correct method, arithmetic slip; caught by estimation
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach; have the child estimate and check with multiplication (3.69×4 = 14.76?).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: one step wrong; estimate (15÷4 ≈ 3.75) flags it

responseLevels.gap: misplaces the decimal point or stops at a whole-number remainder; answer off by a power of ten.
responseLevels.full: divides accurately into the decimal places with the point correctly aligned, continues past a remainder by annexing zeros, and checks the result by estimation/multiplication.
responseLevels.partial: places the point correctly on straightforward cases but stops early on a remainder, or drops a decimal-place zero.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to compute 14.76 ÷ 4 using a written method while you watch, and then to share £18.60 equally among 5 people. Watch how they handle the decimal point in the quotient and whether they continue dividing past the point (adding zeros) when there is a remainder.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The signature errors are dropping/misplacing the decimal point in the quotient and stopping at a whole-number remainder instead of continuing past the point. Watching the process exposes both; a correct final answer alone can't show whether the point placement was understood or lucky.

pedagogy.summary: These real-world problems multiply fractions AND mixed numbers in context — scaling a recipe (2 1/3 cups × 1 1/2 batches), with estimation used to judge reasonableness. The signature difficulty is mixed-number multiplication: pupils who multiply the whole parts and the fraction parts separately and add (2 1/3 × 1 1/2 → 2 + 1/6) omit the cross terms and get a badly wrong answer. The fix is to convert both mixed numbers to improper fractions before multiplying (7/3 × 3/2 = 21/6 = 3 1/2) or to use an area model that shows ALL four partial products. Reasonableness via scaling (2 1/3 × 1 1/2 ≈ 2.3 × 1.5 ≈ 3.5) is the check that catches the incomplete-distribution error.
bestPractices: Convert mixed numbers to improper fractions before multiplying (2 1/3 = 7/3), avoiding incomplete distribution
Or use an area model for mixed × mixed that lays out ALL four partial products so none is dropped
Estimate by scaling before computing (about 2.3 × 1.5 ≈ 3.5 cups) and check the exact answer against it
Use the scaling meaning — more than one batch means MORE than 2 1/3 cups — to sense-check direction
Draw a fraction/area model of the context so the computation is grounded, not rote
keyRepresentations: Area model of mixed × mixed with four partial-product regions
Improper-fraction rewrite of both mixed numbers
Recipe/scaling bar showing the ingredient stretched by the batch factor
Estimation with rounded decimals or whole numbers
commonMisconceptions: Incomplete distribution: multiplies whole × whole and fraction × fraction, omitting the cross terms (2 1/3 × 1 1/2 → 2 1/6)
Multiplies without converting mixed to improper, mishandling the parts
Leaves the denominator unchanged / seeks a common denominator (importing add/subtract habits into ×)
Skips the reasonableness check, so an implausible product goes unnoticed

learn.summary: Pupils (ages 10–11) solve real-world problems multiplying fractions and mixed numbers, e.g. scaling a recipe of 2 1/3 cups by 1 1/2 batches. The signature error is incomplete distribution: multiplying whole×whole and fraction×fraction separately and adding (2 1/3 × 1 1/2 → 2 + 1/6 = 2 1/6), which drops the two cross-term contributions. Fixes are converting both mixed numbers to improper fractions before multiplying (7/3 × 3/2 = 21/6 = 3 1/2) or using an area model that shows ALL four partial products; a scaling estimate (≈2.3 × 1.5 ≈ 3.5) catches the error.

activities.title: Recipe scaler with a four-region area model
feedback: If the learner answers 2 1/6, point to the rectangle: the 2×1/2 and 1/3×1 strips — the biggest contributions after the main block — were left out. Ask them to add those regions in.
If a common-denominator step appears, note that this is a multiplication: both denominators multiply (3×2=6) and no common denominator is needed; contrast with how addition of fractions works.

If an out-of-range answer is accepted without doubt, ask: 'More than one batch means more or less than 2 1/3 cups?' — since 1 1/2 batches is more than one, the answer must exceed 2 1/3, so 2 1/6 is impossible.
Confirm success when the area total, the improper-fraction result, and the estimate all agree on about 3 1/2 cups.
activities.rationale: The incomplete-distribution error is literally a missing piece of an area, so an area model that displays and sums all four partial products is intended to make the omission visible and to tie the recipe context to the computation. An optional interactive version can light up or flash the two cross-term regions as uncounted when the shortcut is attempted, with a parallel improper-fraction panel and an estimate slider rounding to 2.3 × 1.5 ≈ 3.5 — these are illustrative mechanisms, not required ones.
sourceClaims: Solve real-world problems involving multiplication of fractions and mixed numbers using visual fraction models or equations, converting mixed numbers to improper fractions (or using the area model) to compute completely

The misconception that multiplication always makes numbers bigger, and the need to check reasonableness (e.g. multiplying by a factor less than 1 gives a smaller product), must be confronted; real/personalised contexts and visual models improve fraction multiplication problem-solving
learnerActions: Take a recipe needing 2 1/3 cups of flour and a goal of 1 1/2 batches, and first estimate by scaling (about 2.3 × 1.5 ≈ 3.5 cups) before doing any exact computation.
Draw or build a rectangle 2 1/3 wide and 1 1/2 tall to represent the product.
Tile the rectangle into its four regions: the 2×1 block, the 2×1/2 strip, the 1/3×1 strip, and the 1/3×1/2 corner; label each region's value (2, 1, 1/3, 1/6) and add them to get 3 1/2 cups.
Alongside, rewrite both mixed numbers as improper fractions and compute 7/3 × 3/2 = 21/6 = 3 1/2, checking it matches the area total.
Check the exact answer (3 1/2 cups) against your earlier scaling estimate of about 3.5 cups.
activities.intendedInsight: Mixed × mixed produces four partial products; the shortcut of only multiplying wholes and fractions omits the two large cross-term strips (2×1/2 and 1/3×1), so the answer 2 1/6 is far too small. Converting to improper fractions or counting all four regions gives the complete product, and a scaling estimate confirms direction and magnitude.

activities.title: Spot the forgotten pieces (static area diagram)
feedback: If the learner picks the small 1/3×1/2 corner as the 'forgotten' piece, point out the two long strips (2×1/2 and 1/3×1) are the usually-dropped and far larger contributions.
Confirm when they name both cross-term strips and show the running total reaching 3 1/2.
activities.rationale: A static annotated diagram supports reading complete distribution and naming the typically omitted terms. It is a scaffold for interpretation; it does not by itself let the learner build a new product or catch their own omission while working, so it should precede or accompany independent construction rather than replace it.
sourceClaims: Solve real-world problems involving multiplication of fractions and mixed numbers using visual fraction models or equations, converting mixed numbers to improper fractions (or using the area model) to compute completely
learnerActions: Study a labelled area diagram of 2 1/3 × 1 1/2 split into four regions.
Reveal each region's partial product in turn and keep a running total to 3 1/2 cups.
Answer: 'Which two pieces do people most often forget?' and explain why leaving them out gives 2 1/6.
activities.intendedInsight: Complete distribution means all four regions are counted; the commonly forgotten pieces are the two cross-term strips (2×1/2 and 1/3×1), which together are large enough that omitting them wrecks the answer.

activities.title: Chef scaling challenge (reasonableness in role)
feedback: If the learner assumes any multiplication increases the amount, use the 1/2-batch case: half a batch needs less than 2 1/3 cups, so the product is smaller.
Prompt them to state the direction before arithmetic so an out-of-range answer stands out.
activities.rationale: A spoken/role scenario is well suited to rehearsing the direction-of-scaling and reasonableness judgement and to confronting the 'multiplication makes bigger' misconception, including a less-than-one factor. The precise four-region computation still benefits from a visual surface, so pair this with the area or improper-fraction work rather than relying on discussion alone.
sourceClaims: The misconception that multiplication always makes numbers bigger, and the need to check reasonableness (e.g. multiplying by a factor less than 1 gives a smaller product), must be confronted; real/personalised contexts and visual models improve fraction multiplication problem-solving
learnerActions: Work with a chef scenario that scales recipes up and down.
Before computing, answer 'more or less than 2 1/3 cups?' for a given batch factor and justify it.
Also tackle a shrinking case, e.g. making 1/2 a batch, and predict whether the flour needed is more or less than 2 1/3 cups.
Then compute the exact amount and check it against your prediction.
activities.intendedInsight: Scaling by more than one gives more than the original amount; scaling by a factor less than one gives less — so multiplication does not always make a number bigger. The reasonableness prediction is a check that catches implausible products.

activities.title: Targeted practice: convert, distribute, estimate
feedback: If 2 1/6 is chosen, revisit the two omitted cross-term strips (2×1/2 and 1/3×1) and add them back in.
If 3 is chosen, point out it ignores or rounds away part of the fractional contributions; the full four-region total is 3 1/2, not 3.
If the conversion is wrong, remind them 2 1/3 = (2×3+1)/3 = 7/3.
Confirm when the learner selects 3 1/2, justifies it, and their estimate (≈3.5) supports it.
activities.rationale: Short-answer and matching items can probe whether conversion and complete distribution happened and whether an estimate was used, using the error patterns as sharp distractors. Such recognition-and-fill items assess and rehearse components but do not by themselves elicit the independent building of the area reasoning, so use them alongside the construction activities.
learnerActions: After first estimating the product by rounding (about 2.3 × 1.5 ≈ 3.5), choose the correct value of 2 1/3 × 1 1/2 from 2 1/6, 3, and 3 1/2, and explain why the others are wrong.
Fill in the improper-fraction conversions: 2 1/3 = 7/3 and 1 1/2 = 3/2.
Match each of the four area regions to its partial product.
Estimate the product by rounding before carrying out the exact calculation.
activities.intendedInsight: The distractor 2 1/6 is exactly the incomplete-distribution result; 3 is a plausible wrong answer whose likely origin (rounding 2 1/3 down to 2, or dropping part of the fractional contribution) is not pinned down by the source, so it is used only as an explicitly-wrong option. Recognising why each is wrong reinforces complete distribution and the reasonableness check.

constraints: Target age 10–11; procedural real-world fraction and mixed-number multiplication.
Convert both mixed numbers to improper fractions before multiplying, OR lay out all four partial products in an area model; do not multiply whole×whole and fraction×fraction and add.
This is multiplication: both denominators multiply and no common denominator is required — do not import addition/subtraction habits.

Require a scaling estimate before computing and check the exact answer against it; include at least one less-than-one (shrinking) factor so learners meet a case where the product is smaller than the original.

The static diagram and the recognition/matching items are scaffolds or checks: they support interpretation but do not by themselves require the learner to construct a new product or catch their own live omission.
The area model is a 2D representation of the product (cups × batches), not a physical area: cups of flour are actually a volume measure, but a 3D volume model is unnecessary and could mislead here.
Interactive touches (flashing uncounted regions, estimate slider, tappable regions) are optional illustrative mechanisms, not mandatory.
The '3' option is an explicitly-wrong distractor only; do not present it or 2 1/6 as a valid answer, and do not assert a certified origin for the '3' error beyond plausible rounding/omission.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the arithmetic: 2 1/3 × 1 1/2 = 7/3 × 3/2 = 21/6 = 3 1/2. The four partial products are 2×1=2, 2×1/2=1, 1/3×1=1/3, 1/3×1/2=1/6, summing to 2+1+1/3+1/6 = 3 3/6 = 3 1/2 — consistent. The incomplete-distribution result 2 + 1/6 = 2 1/6 is the stated misconception and is used only as an explicitly-wrong distractor, never as a valid answer.

The distractor '3' from the original quiz is retained as a plausible wrong option; its likely origin (rounding or dropping a term) is not specified in the source, so its exact diagnostic meaning is uncertain and is not asserted as fact.
One source (Common Core 5.NF.6) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its citation as a standards reference, not as evidence of empirical effectiveness.

The source claim that visual models and real contexts 'improve' fraction multiplication problem-solving describes general research findings and does not establish that any specific activity here was tested or is superior to alternatives.
Efficacy language in activity rationales was kept to intended/illustrative wording, as none of these proposed activities has been empirically validated.

probeDeeper: Estimate first — roughly how many cups? Does your exact answer match?
If you made only 1/2 a batch instead of 1 1/2, would you need more or less than 2 1/3 cups — why?
Draw the recipe as a rectangle — how many pieces are there, and did you count all of them?
Turn both mixed numbers into improper fractions — does multiplying them give the same answer as your method?
assess.correctAnswer: Estimate: about 2.3 × 1.5 ≈ 3.5 cups (a bit more than one batch's 2 1/3). Exact: 2 1/3 × 1 1/2 = 7/3 × 3/2 = 21/6 = 3 1/2 cups.

errorPatterns.pattern: Incomplete distribution: multiplies the whole parts and the fraction parts only — 2 1/3 × 1 1/2 → (2×1) + (1/3×1/2) = 2 1/6 — omitting the two cross terms
errorPatterns.nextMove: Lay out the area with all four regions (or convert both to improper fractions) so the two large cross-term strips are counted; check against the scaling estimate
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer 2 1/6 (or similar too-small value); working shows only two products, no conversion to improper fractions

errorPatterns.pattern: Multiplies without converting mixed to improper, or leaves a denominator unchanged / seeks a common denominator (importing add-subtract habits into multiplication)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Convert to improper fractions first (7/3 × 3/2) and recall that multiplication multiplies both denominators and needs no common denominator; contrast with addition
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A common-denominator step appears in a multiplication, or the mixed numbers are multiplied part-wise with a kept denominator

errorPatterns.pattern: Skips the reasonableness check — no estimate, so an implausible product (2 1/6, or a value below one batch) is accepted
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the scaling estimate — 'more than one batch, so more than 2 1/3 cups' — and require it before computing; the check, not the arithmetic, is what's missing
errorPatterns.revealedBy: No estimate offered; an out-of-range answer reported without doubt

responseLevels.gap: Incomplete distribution (2 1/6) or leaves a denominator unchanged; no estimate and no sense that the answer is wrong.
responseLevels.full: Estimates by scaling, computes 3 1/2 via improper fractions or a complete area model, checks the exact answer against the estimate, and transfers to a new real-world product including a shrinking-factor (less-than-one) case.
responseLevels.partial: Converts to improper fractions and computes 3 1/2 but purely by rule — no estimate or reasonableness check — or estimates sensibly yet distributes incompletely in the exact working.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Solve this, showing your working and giving a rough estimate first: a recipe needs 2 1/3 cups of flour, and you want to make 1 1/2 batches — how much flour do you need?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Mixed × mixed is the exact place the incomplete-distribution error bites: a child who converts to improper fractions (or lays out all four partial products) gets 3 1/2; a child who multiplies whole×whole and fraction×fraction and adds gets 2 1/6 — and the estimate (≈3.5) instantly flags 2 1/6 as impossible. Requiring an estimate first plus the full working reveals both whether the distribution was complete and whether the answer was sense-checked, neither visible from a bare number.

pedagogy.summary: Children operate transformations as rules on coordinates: translating a shape changes every vertex by adding/subtracting the horizontal and vertical moves (right +x, left −x, up +y, down −y), while reflecting in an axis changes the sign of exactly ONE coordinate — reflection in the x-axis sends (x, y) to (x, −y), reflection in the y-axis sends (x, y) to (−x, y). The conceptual anchor is that the axis you reflect IN is the mirror, points move PERPENDICULAR to it, and so the coordinate measuring distance from that mirror flips sign while the other is unchanged. Fluency means predicting image coordinates from the rule and explaining why each rule takes the form it does.
bestPractices: Derive the sign rules from the geometry, not memorised swaps: reflecting in the x-axis flips the shape VERTICALLY, so the vertical (y) coordinate changes sign and x stays; reflecting in the y-axis flips it HORIZONTALLY, so x changes sign and y stays.
Tie the rule to equal distance: the image is the same distance from the axis as the original, on the opposite side — (x, y) and (x, −y) are both |y| from the x-axis (Oak National Academy).

Explicitly separate the two axis rules with worked pairs — e.g. (−4, 1) reflects to (4, 1) in the y-axis but to (−4, −1) in the x-axis — so pupils feel which single coordinate changes each time (Oak).

Confront reflection-as-translation head-on with examples and non-examples: a slid shape keeps its orientation, a reflected shape is reversed; use real mirrors as a scaffold, then move to reasoning with coordinates (Oak).
For translation, treat each direction as a signed change to the matching coordinate — '2 down' subtracts 2 from y — and have pupils PREDICT image coordinates before plotting.
Avoid 'straight across/down' language; say points move perpendicular to the mirror line, so the correct coordinate change is understood rather than transposed (NCETM KS3 6.3).
keyRepresentations: Four-quadrant coordinate grid with the x- and y-axes as mirror lines
Coordinate mapping notation: translation (x, y) → (x+a, y+b); reflection in x-axis (x, y) → (x, −y); in y-axis (x, y) → (−x, y)
Real mirror / Mira placed on an axis to check the image, as a scaffold
Paired worked example showing the same vertex reflected in each axis to contrast which coordinate changes
commonMisconceptions: Reflecting in the x-axis but changing the sign of the WRONG coordinate (negating x instead of y), effectively reflecting in the other axis.
Reflecting by sliding/translating the shape rather than reflecting it, so the image is not reversed.
Getting the translation sign wrong — adding when the move is left or down instead of subtracting.
Reversing the coordinate pair (writing the y-value before the x-value) when stating image vertices.

learn.summary: Year 6 pupils learn to translate shapes on a four-quadrant coordinate grid (adding/subtracting signed amounts to matching coordinates) and to reflect shapes in the x- or y-axis by negating exactly one coordinate. The goal is to DERIVE the sign rules from geometry — points move perpendicular to the mirror axis, so the coordinate measuring distance from that axis flips sign while the other stays — rather than memorise a swap. Core errors: changing the wrong coordinate (reflecting in the wrong axis), sliding instead of reflecting (no reversal), wrong translation signs for left/down moves, and reversing the ordered pair.

activities.title: Predict, then reflect: watch the single coordinate flip
feedback: If a predicted point lands in the wrong quadrant, diagonally opposite the true image (e.g. (4, 1) in the first quadrant instead of (−4, −1) in the third for an x-axis reflection), you likely negated the wrong coordinate — ask which direction the shape actually moves and which coordinate measures distance from that axis.
If the image keeps facing the same way (not mirrored), you slid/translated instead of reflecting; rebuild one vertex at an equal perpendicular distance on the opposite side so the reversal appears.
Check the image and original are the same distance from the axis and the same size and shape — e.g. (x, y) and (x, −y) are both |y| from the x-axis.
activities.rationale: Acting on a shape and watching the coordinate table update makes the single-coordinate sign change visible, and predicting first surfaces the wrong-coordinate and slide-not-reflect misconceptions as a visibly misplaced point. Contrasting the SAME vertex reflected in each axis separates the two rules by reasoning rather than memorised swap. A live table, ghost original, and predict-mode are optional supports that make the mechanism concrete.
sourceClaims: The most common mistake pupils make when reflecting is to flip/translate the shape rather than reflect it; the reflection and original should be the same distance from the axis and the same size and shape, and real mirrors help pupils notice the direction the reflection faces.

Reflecting a vertex at (−4,1) in the y-axis gives (4,1) (only x changes sign) while reflecting it in the x-axis gives (−4,−1) (only y changes sign); reflecting in both axes gives (4,−1). Distractor answers that change the wrong coordinate correspond to the classic 'wrong coordinate / wrong axis' error.

Reflection should be taught via the perpendicular structure — every line joining a point to its image is perpendicular to the mirror line — avoiding 'straight across/down' language, so the correct coordinate change is derived rather than memorised; examples should span all quadrants and the axes.
learnerActions: On a four-quadrant grid, start with a triangle plotted in the second quadrant and its vertices labelled with coordinates.
Before anything moves, choose 'reflect in the x-axis' and write down what you predict each vertex will become.
Run the reflection: watch each vertex move perpendicular to the x-axis (vertically, to the opposite side) while, in a coordinate table, only the y-value changes sign and x stays the same.
If a real mirror or Mira is available, stand it on the x-axis to check the image faces the opposite way and sits the same distance from the axis.
Now, starting from the SAME triangle, reflect in the y-axis instead and predict again: this time the shape flips sideways (perpendicular to the y-axis) and only x changes sign.
Compare the two results on the same vertex, e.g. (−4, 1) → (−4, −1) in the x-axis but (−4, 1) → (4, 1) in the y-axis.
activities.intendedInsight: Reflecting in the x-axis flips the shape vertically, so the y-coordinate (vertical distance from the x-axis) negates and x is unchanged; reflecting in the y-axis flips it horizontally, so x negates and y is unchanged. The axis you reflect IN is the mirror and points move perpendicular to it.

activities.title: Translate by signed changes — predict before plotting
feedback: If a '2 down' move made the y-value increase, you added instead of subtracted — down and left reduce the coordinate; re-predict then check one vertex on the grid.
If the whole shape moved but didn't reverse, that is correct for a translation — a translation never produces a mirror image.
Check each vertex against the grid before trusting the rule.
activities.rationale: Predicting signed coordinate changes before plotting targets the add-when-it-should-subtract error and distinguishes a slide (orientation preserved) from a reflection (orientation reversed).
learnerActions: Take a triangle on the grid and a translation instruction such as '3 squares right and 2 squares down'.
Treat each direction as a signed change to the matching coordinate: right adds to x, left subtracts from x, up adds to y, down subtracts from y. So '3 right, 2 down' gives (x, y) → (x+3, y−2).
Predict the new coordinates of every vertex BEFORE plotting, then plot and check against the grid.
Say back how the whole shape kept its orientation (a slide does not reverse the shape).
activities.intendedInsight: Translation adds or subtracts a signed amount to the matching coordinate and preserves orientation; left and down are negative changes, not additions.

activities.title: Contrast slide versus reflect, and keep the pair in order
feedback: If you reported a vertex as (y, x) though the plotted point looks right, re-anchor 'x before y, along then up/down' and recheck.
If an on-axis point moved, remember a point on the mirror is already on it, so its distance from the axis is zero and it does not move.
Use examples and non-examples (and a real mirror on the axis) to confirm the reflection faces the other way.
activities.rationale: Pairing reflection against translation on the same shape elicits the reversal/equidistance idea versus a straight slide, and explicit (x, y) ordering guards against the common pair-reversal interference error. The on-axis fixed-point case is a useful boundary check.
sourceClaims: The most common mistake pupils make when reflecting is to flip/translate the shape rather than reflect it; the reflection and original should be the same distance from the axis and the same size and shape, and real mirrors help pupils notice the direction the reflection faces.
A recurring coordinate error is reversing the ordered pair (stating the second value before the first); guard against it with 'x before y / along then up'.
learnerActions: Reflect a triangle in the x-axis and separately translate the same triangle 'down' by a fixed amount; place the two results side by side.
Describe how they differ: the reflected image is reversed and equidistant on the opposite side of the axis; the translated image faces the same way and simply slid.
Find a vertex that sits ON the mirror axis, e.g. (0, 4) on the y-axis, and reflect in that axis: note it stays fixed.
When listing every image vertex, write x before y ('along then up/down') and check one plotted point matches the pair you wrote.
activities.intendedInsight: Reflection reverses sense and is equidistant across the mirror; translation preserves sense. Points on the mirror axis map to themselves. Ordered pairs are always (x, y).

activities.title: Diagnose with paired axis items (assessment)
feedback: Choosing (4, 1) for an x-axis reflection means you changed x instead of y — you effectively reflected in the y-axis; re-anchor to the vertical flip.
Choosing (−1, −4) means you swapped the coordinate order of the correct image (−4, −1); apply 'x before y'.
A correct choice or plot with no 'why' is not yet secure — ask for the perpendicular/equidistance reason.
activities.rationale: Multiple-choice items whose distractors ARE the misconceptions diagnose cleanly, and the draw-and-list step adds some image construction. However, selecting among options does not by itself build the felt derivation of why one coordinate changes, so pair this assessment with the predict-and-construct activities above.
sourceClaims: Reflecting a vertex at (−4,1) in the y-axis gives (4,1) (only x changes sign) while reflecting it in the x-axis gives (−4,−1) (only y changes sign); reflecting in both axes gives (4,−1). Distractor answers that change the wrong coordinate correspond to the classic 'wrong coordinate / wrong axis' error.
learnerActions: Answer items such as '(−4, 1) reflected in the x-axis = ?' where the correct answer is (−4, −1), the wrong-coordinate answer (4, 1) and the reversed-pair answer (−1, −4) are offered as options.
Complete fill-in-the-blank image coordinates after a stated translation.
Plot a reflection by drawing the image, then list its vertices.
Explain in words why only one coordinate changed for each reflection.
activities.intendedInsight: Picking the correct image while rejecting wrong-axis and reversed-pair distractors, plotting the image correctly, and explaining why only one coordinate changes together show the rule is reasoned rather than guessed.

constraints: Reflection and translation here are 2-D coordinate operations on the plane; a third dimension (z-values, planes of reflection) is not needed and distracts from the (x, y) sign rules.

Avoid 'straight across / straight down' as a generic rule; say points move perpendicular to the mirror axis so the correct coordinate change is understood rather than transposed (for the x-axis this motion happens to be vertical, for the y-axis horizontal).

Recognition/multiple-choice items diagnose and check but do not themselves elicit independent construction of an image or an explanation; use them alongside tasks where the child predicts, plots and justifies.
A real mirror or Mira is a helpful scaffold for noticing reversal and equidistance, but pupils should progress to reasoning directly with coordinates.

A static annotated grid can label a vertex's image and its coordinate change on tap, but it cannot let the child predict and test their own image, which is where the sign confusion lives — treat it as a supporting illustration, not the main task.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of worked coordinates: (−4, 1) reflected in x-axis → (−4, −1); reflected in y-axis → (4, 1); in both → (4, −1); these are internally consistent across pedagogy, assess and sources. '3 right, 2 down' maps (x, y) → (x+3, y−2) — consistent with the diagnostic.
Reversed-pair distractor: the order-swap of the correct image (−4, −1) is (−1, −4); an earlier draft listed (1, −4), which is not a reversed pair and was fixed in activity 4.

Activity 4 contains both recognition (multiple-choice) and production (draw-and-list) steps; its stated limitation is scoped to the multiple-choice selection only, not to the whole activity, to avoid implying the activity never elicits construction.
The 'reflect in the x-axis flips vertically so y changes' reasoning is sound geometrically; retained as derivation, not as an unverified claim of comparative teaching efficacy.

The UK National Curriculum source is verified:false in the row and only establishes the curriculum expectation that Year 6 pupils translate and reflect shapes; it does not support the teaching principle in activity 2, so activity 2's sourceClaims is [].

On-axis fixed-point case ((0,4) reflected in the y-axis stays fixed) was present only in the assessment probes; added as a boundary check in an activity because it is mathematically correct and pedagogically useful.

probeDeeper: 'You reflected in the x-axis and the y-coordinates changed sign. Why that coordinate and not the x?' (listen for vertical flip / perpendicular-to-the-axis reasoning, not a recited rule).
Counterexample: 'Now reflect the SAME triangle in the y-axis instead. What changes this time?' (tests that the child does not apply the x-axis rule to both).
'Reflecting in the x-axis moves the triangle downward, and translating 2 down also moves it downward. How are the two results different?' (elicits reversal/equidistance versus a straight slide).
'One vertex sits at (0, 4), on the y-axis. Where does it go when you reflect in the y-axis?' (points on the mirror axis stay fixed).
assess.correctAnswer: For the translation, each vertex gains 3 on x and loses 2 on y (right +x, down −y). For the reflection in the x-axis, each vertex keeps its x and negates its y — (x, y) → (x, −y) — so the image sits the same distance below the axis as the original is above, reversed in sense. The child explains that translating adds/subtracts to the coordinates while reflecting in the x-axis changes the sign of the y-coordinate only (and reflecting in the y-axis would change x only), because points move perpendicular to the mirror axis.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reflects in the x-axis but changes the sign of the wrong coordinate — negates x instead of y — effectively reflecting in the other axis
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor to the geometry: reflecting in the x-axis flips the shape vertically, so the vertical (y) coordinate changes; move each vertex perpendicular to the axis and read off (x, −y). Contrast with a y-axis reflection on the same shape.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives (−x, y) for an x-axis reflection (e.g. maps (−4,1) to (4,1) instead of (−4,−1)); the image appears on the wrong side/quadrant; the child recites 'x-axis so change x'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reflects by sliding/translating the shape across the axis rather than reflecting it, so the image is not reversed
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use examples and non-examples and a real mirror on the axis to show the reflection faces the other way; rebuild one vertex by equal perpendicular distance so the reversal emerges.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The image keeps its orientation (not a mirror image) and/or is not equidistant from the axis; the child moves the whole shape as a block.

errorPatterns.pattern: Gets the translation sign wrong — adds instead of subtracts for a left or down move (treats every move as increasing the coordinate)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rehearse each direction as a signed change on a signed axis — down subtracts from y, left subtracts from x; predict the coordinate before plotting and check against the grid.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For '2 down' the y-value increases (or for 'left' the x increases); the translated image goes the wrong way on one axis.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses the coordinate pair, stating the y-value before the x-value, when listing image vertices
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor 'x before y, along then up/down'; check one image vertex together against the grid.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reports an image vertex as (y, x) though the plotted point is right; e.g. writes (−1,−4) for a point at (−4,−1).

responseLevels.gap: Changes the wrong coordinate when reflecting (or reflects by sliding), and/or gets translation signs wrong; cannot say why a coordinate changes.
responseLevels.full: Translates with correct signed changes, reflects in either axis by negating the correct single coordinate with an equal-distance/perpendicular justification, keeps on-axis points fixed, states image coordinates as (x, y), and explains the add/subtract (translation) versus sign-change (reflection) rules — transferring correctly between the two axes.
responseLevels.partial: Reflects in the x-axis and translates by rule in familiar cases but cannot justify why the y-coordinate (not x) changes, slips on the y-axis reflection or on a 'down/left' translation sign, or reverses a pair. Executes the steps but cannot connect the sign change to the perpendicular flip or transfer to the other axis.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give a four-quadrant grid with a small triangle plotted in the second quadrant (vertices labelled with their coordinates). Say: 'First, translate this triangle 3 squares right and 2 squares down, and write the new coordinates of each vertex. Then, starting from the original, reflect it in the x-axis and list the reflected vertices. Finally, tell me how the coordinates changed in each case, and why.' Set the task and WATCH which coordinate the child changes and whether the reflected image is reversed — do not state the rules.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Reflecting in the x-axis, a child who grasps the perpendicular structure negates y and keeps x, landing the image in the correct quadrant; a child who has memorised a swap negates x instead — effectively reflecting in the WRONG axis — and the image lands in a visibly different place. A child who translates instead of reflecting produces an un-reversed image. Watching which single coordinate changes, and whether sense reverses, separates true understanding from rule-transposition; the 'why' further exposes memorisation.
