pedagogy.summary: The capstone add/subtract problem-solving node: multi-step problems in real contexts with numbers up to 10,000,000 and decimals, where the child decides which operations AND which method — mental, written, or calculator — to use for each step, and justifies the choice. Beyond the multi-step reasoning inherited from earlier years, the distinctive demands are (1) choosing the calculator wisely (for genuinely awkward large/decimal computation, not for steps doable mentally) and (2) checking calculator/written output for reasonableness with an estimate, because a single keying or place-value slip is now worth millions.
bestPractices: Model the whole problem (bar model) and plan every step before computing
Choose method per step by the numbers: mental for round/near steps, written for structured ones, calculator for awkward large/decimal arithmetic - and say why
ALWAYS estimate the expected result so a calculator keying error (missed digit, misplaced point) is caught
Track intermediate quantities and re-read the actual question so the final step is not dropped
Interpret the answer back in context (units, sense, magnitude)
keyRepresentations: Multi-bar / running-total model
Step-and-method planner (step | operation | method | why)
Estimate strip for the reasonableness check
Real contexts: populations, money, distances, measures (decimals)
commonMisconceptions: Offers an intermediate quantity as the final answer, or drops a step
Word-spots operations rather than modelling the situation
Over-relies on the calculator (keys in steps doable mentally) or refuses it for genuinely awkward computation
Trusts the calculator display without an estimate, so a keying/place-value error goes unnoticed
Loses track of the decimal point or a period (thousands/millions) in large or decimal numbers

learn.summary: Year 6 capstone for add/subtract multi-step problem solving in real contexts with numbers up to 10,000,000 and decimals. The distinctive demands beyond multi-step reasoning are: choosing a method per step (mental, written, or calculator) and justifying it, and checking any calculator/written output against an estimate so a keying or place-value slip (now worth millions) is caught. Learners must model the whole situation, track intermediate quantities, and answer the actual question rather than report a running total.

activities.title: Charity accounts mission planner
feedback: If a learner keys 345,000 where about 3,450,000 was expected, prompt: 'that's ten times too small - check the place value: have you missed a zero or put the decimal point in the wrong place?'
If the final answer equals an intermediate (e.g. the post-March figure), prompt: 're-read the question; which steps are still marked on your bar? Is the April-costs step included?'
If a learner keys in +2,000,000 on a calculator, ask: 'could you do this one in your head?' - discuss method fit without reteaching the arithmetic.
If a learner hand-grinds the awkward 675,450.75 subtraction unnecessarily, ask whether a calculator would suit that step and why.
activities.rationale: The national curriculum requires pupils to solve addition and subtraction multi-step problems in contexts, deciding which operations and methods to use and why, and to use estimation to check answers and judge an appropriate degree of accuracy. Making method choice and a reasonableness gate the core loop targets exactly this content. An optional interactive version can hold the estimate and flash a magnitude warning when the entered result is an order of magnitude off, and can feed each result into a visible running bar; these are illustrative mechanisms, not requirements - the same loop works on paper with a planner grid and an estimate strip.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils should be taught to 'solve addition and subtraction multi-step problems in contexts, deciding which operations and methods to use and why' and to 'use estimation to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, an appropriate degree of accuracy'; Year 6 place value covers reading and ordering numbers up to 10,000,000 (verbatim statutory wording).
Estimation is essential for judging the reasonableness of calculator/written output; sensible calculator use is a taught competence.
learnerActions: Read a real multi-step problem, e.g. 'A charity had 3,450,000 pounds. In March it spent 1,280,000 pounds and received donations of 2,000,000 pounds. In April its costs were 675,450.75 pounds. How much does it have at the end of April?'
Before computing, model the whole problem with a running-total bar and mark every event as a signed change on the bar.

Build a running estimate first: estimate each step's expected result as well as the final total (about 3.45m - 1.28m + 2m - 0.68m is roughly 3.5m, with intermediate ballparks of about 2.17m then 4.17m along the way).
For each step, choose mental, written, or calculator, carry out the computation, and write one sentence saying WHY that method fits those numbers.
After any calculator or written step, compare that result's order of magnitude against your estimate for that same quantity before accepting it.
Re-read the original question and give the end-of-April balance (3,494,549.25 pounds), interpreted back in context, not an intermediate total.
activities.intendedInsight: A calculator does not free you from thinking: the estimate is what tells you whether to trust the display, and the final answer must answer the question asked, not report a running total.

activities.title: Defend your plan and tool choices
feedback: If justification is vague ('it just seemed right'), press for the specific feature of the numbers that makes the chosen method fit.
If the learner cannot say the expected ballpark, send them back to build the estimate before defending the tool choice.
activities.rationale: The topic explicitly requires justifying which operations and methods to use and why; an in-role defence dialogue exercises that judgement directly. A spoken, responsive defence can surface reasoning that a written answer alone may not reveal.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils should be taught to 'solve addition and subtraction multi-step problems in contexts, deciding which operations and methods to use and why' and to 'use estimation to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, an appropriate degree of accuracy'; Year 6 place value covers reading and ordering numbers up to 10,000,000 (verbatim statutory wording).
learnerActions: After solving a multi-step problem, explain the plan aloud to a partner or character who challenges it.
Answer probing challenges: 'Why calculator there but mental here? Roughly what should this step come to? Does that final answer make sense in the context?'

Justify each method choice by reference to the specific numbers (for example, round or near-round steps often suit mental methods, structured ones written methods, and awkward large or decimal ones a calculator - but the choice is a reasoned judgement, not a fixed rule).
State the ballpark estimate and say how it would have exposed a mis-keyed result about ten times too small or too large, such as 349,454.93 or 34,945,492.50.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to justify which operations and methods you used - and what the answer should roughly be - is part of competent problem solving, not an optional extra.

activities.title: Sequence, method, and spot the impossible answer
feedback: If an impossible answer is accepted (e.g. one order of magnitude off), prompt the learner to compare it digit-by-place against the estimate.
If the wrong final step is chosen, ask whether the selected figure is an intermediate or the balance the question requests.
activities.rationale: Sequencing, method selection, and identifying an unreasonable result are useful checks of understanding. This format mainly assesses recognition and ordering; it does not require the learner to independently construct the plan and computation, so pair it with the planner activity for production.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils should be taught to 'solve addition and subtraction multi-step problems in contexts, deciding which operations and methods to use and why' and to 'use estimation to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, an appropriate degree of accuracy'; Year 6 place value covers reading and ordering numbers up to 10,000,000 (verbatim statutory wording).
learnerActions: Put the steps of a given multi-step problem into the correct order.
For each step, select the best method (mental / written / calculator) and give a reason.
Given an estimate for a step, identify which of several candidate calculator answers is impossible because it is the wrong order of magnitude.
Flag any answer that reports a running total instead of answering the actual question.
activities.intendedInsight: Checking an answer against an estimate lets you reject results that are impossible by magnitude, and the correct final answer is the one that matches the question asked.

activities.title: Walk through an annotated worked example
feedback: Prompt learners to explain in their own words why each annotated method was chosen before moving on, so the walkthrough does not become passive reading.
activities.rationale: A worked example displays the structure of a good solution, the bar-model representation, and the role of the estimate. As a scaffold it does not by itself require the learner to generate their own plan or method choices, so it should precede or support independent problem solving rather than replace it; comparing it to the learner's own attempt can, however, prompt reflection on method choice.
sourceClaims: Teaching students to use visual representations (Recommendation 3, rated STRONG evidence) improves problem solving; the guide frames problem solving as reasoning about structure, 'not the execution of memorized rules or shortcuts, such as using key words'.
learnerActions: Study a complete multi-step worked example; reveal, for each step, the operation used, the method chosen, and the reasonableness check applied.
Identify where the estimate was built and how it confirmed (or would have caught an error in) each computed result.
Compare the annotated plan to your own attempt and note any step you dropped or any method you would change.
activities.intendedInsight: A well-structured solution makes its operation, method choice, and reasonableness check explicit at every step.

constraints: Numbers up to 10,000,000 and decimals (e.g. pounds-and-pence) must appear so the magnitude stakes of a keying/place-value slip are real.
Problems must be modelled from the situation, not solved by word-spotting operations from keywords.
The estimate should be built before or alongside computing, not after, and as a running/per-quantity estimate so it can actually gate each calculator/written result.

Recognition and ordering tasks assess understanding but do not elicit independent construction of the plan and computation; include at least one task where the learner builds and justifies the whole solution.

The worked-example walkthrough is a scaffold: it displays structure but does not by itself require the learner to generate their own plan and method choices; pair it with a task where the learner constructs and justifies the whole solution.
Interactive magnitude-warning gates, running bars, and live checks are optional illustrative mechanisms; the same learning works on paper with a planner grid and estimate strip.
Method fit is a reasoned choice about the numbers, not a fixed rule; do not teach 'always use a calculator' or 'never use a calculator'.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources have NOT been re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic self-audit of the source example: 3,450,000 - 1,280,000 = 2,170,000; + 2,000,000 = 4,170,000; - 675,450 = 3,494,550. This matches the stated correct answer 3,494,550 and the ~3.5m estimate. The distractors 349,455 (ten times too small) and 34,945,500 (ten times too large) are correctly characterised as order-of-magnitude errors.
The source claim on estimation and sensible calculator use (Sowder 1992; NCTM) is marked verified:false in the row; treat it as supporting guidance, not established efficacy evidence.

The IES/WWC visual-representations claim is rated STRONG for visual representations and reasoning-about-structure generally; it does not independently establish the efficacy of the worked-example walkthrough format, which is proposed as a scaffold.

The original catalog rationale implied non-interactive formats 'cannot' let the child plan or make method choices; this has been softened to scope-limited statements about what each format exercises, without asserting universal necessity of the interactive format.

probeDeeper: Roughly how much should be left at the end - before you calculate exactly?
Which step did you use the calculator for, and why not that one?
Is the question asking for the balance after March, or at the end of April?
If your calculator showed 349,455, would you believe it - how would you know it was wrong?
assess.correctAnswer: Plans the steps: 3,450,000 - 1,280,000 + 2,000,000 - 675,450 = 3,494,550. Chooses methods per step (the +2,000,000 mental; the 675,450 subtraction written or calculator), estimates (about 3.45m - 1.28m + 2m - 0.68m is roughly 3.5m) and checks the final figure against it. Answers the end-of-April balance, not an intermediate, and reads it back in context.

errorPatterns.pattern: Gives a running total (e.g. the post-March figure) as the final answer, or drops the April-costs step
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-read the question; mark all steps on the bar so the last subtraction is not dropped.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Final answer equals an intermediate; a step is missing from the working

errorPatterns.pattern: Word-spots operations or applies them in the wrong order rather than modelling the situation
errorPatterns.nextMove: Narrate the story in sequence; each event maps to one signed change on the bar.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Adds a cost or subtracts a donation; steps out of order

errorPatterns.pattern: Trusts the calculator display without an estimate, so a keying or place-value slip (missed digit, misplaced point) goes unnoticed
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build the estimate FIRST; teach the display is only trustworthy if it matches the ballpark.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Accepts an answer an order of magnitude off (e.g. 349,455 or 34,945,500) without pause

errorPatterns.pattern: Over-relies on the calculator for steps doable mentally, or grinds by hand an awkward computation a calculator suits - no reasoned method choice
errorPatterns.nextMove: Discuss method fit step by step; scaffold 'could you do this one in your head?' Do not reteach the arithmetic.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Keys in +2,000,000, or laboriously hand-computes the pence figure, without justifying

responseLevels.gap: Grabs numbers and operations by keywords; drops steps or reports an intermediate; trusts any result without checking.
responseLevels.full: Models the problem, sequences all steps, chooses and justifies a method per step, estimates and checks the result for reasonableness, and answers the actual question in context; transfers to a differently-structured large-number/decimal problem.
responseLevels.partial: Completes the chain and can use a calculator, but with no reasoned method choice, or stops at a running total, or does not estimate to check; lists steps without modelling.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Read this aloud and watch the child plan, choose methods, and check: 'A charity had 3,450,000 pounds. In March it spent 1,280,000 pounds and received donations of 2,000,000 pounds. In April its costs were 675,450 pounds. How much does it have at the end of April?' Ask which steps, in what order, which method for each and why, and whether the final figure is sensible.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The four steps, mixed magnitudes and a decimal-scale pence figure catch the child who drops a step, offers a running total as the answer, or word-spots operations. Requiring an estimate exposes whether the child would notice an unreasonable (e.g. calculator-mis-keyed) result, and the per-step method choice separates thoughtful tool use from blanket calculator reliance.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 6-7 (Y1/Y2). Add and subtract within 20 using STRATEGIES — making ten (8+6 = 8+2+4 = 14), decomposing to bridge ten (13−4 = 13−3−1 = 9), and using known facts. A high-centrality strategy hub (0.17): bridging through ten is the reasoning that later powers column carrying/borrowing.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1/Y2): represent/use bonds and related facts within 20; Y2 derive and use related facts; bridging-ten strategies are core KS1 mental methods.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.OA.6 add/subtract within 20 using 'making ten… decomposing a number leading to a ten… and relationship between addition and subtraction'; 2.OA.2.
• Operational details — Teach making-ten explicitly on the ten-frame/rekenrek: to add 8+6, fill the first frame to 10 by moving 2 from the 6, leaving 4, so 10+4. For subtraction across ten, decompose to reach ten first (13−4 → 13−3 to 10, then −1). Emphasise ten as a friendly landmark. This is about REASONING to a fact, bridging the gap between counting and full recall (within-20).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 6): use a ten-frame to make ten when adding a bridging fact (8+6). Tier B (age 6-7): explain a making-ten or decompose-to-ten step for a within-20 fact. Tier C (age 7): choose flexibly between making-ten, near-doubles and known facts, and derive subtractions from additions.
bestPractices: Teach making-ten physically on two ten-frames/a rekenrek: children MOVE counters to complete the first ten, seeing why 8+6 becomes 10+4.
For subtraction bridging ten, model decomposing to land on ten first (13−4 = 13−3−1), so ten is the landmark in both directions.
Frame ten as a 'friendly number' and connect making-ten to the bonds-to-10 facts children already know.
Encourage strategy flexibility — near-doubles, known facts and making-ten — and discuss which is efficient for a given calculation.
Use the empty number line to record bridging jumps (+2 to 10, then +4), linking strategy to a spatial model that scales to larger numbers.
keyRepresentations: Two ten-frames showing one filled to 10 and the extra spilling into the second
Rekenrek for shifting beads to make ten
Empty number line with a jump to 10 then beyond
Part-whole model decomposing the second addend (6 = 2 + 4)
Bead string of 20 partitioned at the ten
commonMisconceptions: Counting on/back in ones across ten instead of using ten as a landmark (slow and error-prone at the boundary).
Splitting the wrong addend or splitting it wrongly when making ten (e.g. taking 4 not 2 from the 6 to fill an 8).
For subtraction, decomposing incorrectly across ten (13−4 done as 13−4 in ones with a boundary error).
Not connecting making-ten to known bonds to 10, so the strategy feels arbitrary.
Applying making-ten rigidly even when a known fact or near-double would be quicker.

learn.summary: For ages 6-7 (Y1/Y2): add and subtract within 20 using strategies — making ten (8+6 = 8+2+4 = 14), decomposing to bridge ten (13−4 = 13−3−1 = 9), and deriving from known facts. The core insight is treating ten as a friendly landmark reached in both directions; this bridging reasoning later underpins column carrying and borrowing. The focus is the method, not just a correct answer, since counting all by ones can reach 14 without showing the intended understanding.

activities.title: Make ten by moving counters on a double ten-frame
feedback: If the leftover is wrong (answer 12 or 16), count exactly how many counters spill past ten and rehearse partitioning the second addend: 6 = 2 + 4, so only 2 cross to the 8.
If a child takes the wrong amount (e.g. 4 from the 6 to fill an 8), ask: how many empty cells does the first frame have? Move exactly that many.
Connect the move to bonds they know: 8 needs 2 to make 10, which is the pair 8+2 they already recognise.
If a child counts on in ones across ten, model the make-ten move on two frames so ten becomes the landmark rather than a boundary counted through.
activities.rationale: Physically completing the first ten and watching the second addend split lets children perform and see the partition-and-recombine, linking the strategy to bonds-to-10 they already know. The number line records the bridging jump in a spatial model that scales to larger numbers.
sourceClaims: Y1/Y2 pupils use and derive number facts within 20; bridging-through-ten mental strategies are core KS1 methods.
1.OA.6: add and subtract within 20 using making ten, decomposing a number leading to a ten, and the relationship between addition and subtraction.
Making-ten and decompose-to-ten strategies, taught on ten-frames/rekenreks with the empty number line, build bridging reasoning that underpins later column methods.
learnerActions: Set out 8 counters in the first ten-frame (two cells empty) and 6 in the second to add 8 + 6.
Move 2 counters from the 6 across to fill the first frame to 10, and notice the 6 has broken into 2 and 4.
Read the result as 10 + 4 = 14, and say aloud which part you moved and why.
Record the same move on an empty number line as a jump of +2 to reach 10, then +4 to reach 14.
Repeat with other bridging facts (e.g. 7+5, 9+6), each time completing the first ten first.
activities.intendedInsight: Making ten is a MOVE: reorganising an awkward fact around the friendly ten (8+6 becomes 10+4) shows WHY the strategy works, not just that it gives 14.

activities.title: Bridge down to ten for subtraction
feedback: A common error is subtracting to ten and then ADDING the remainder (13 − 3 = 10, then +1 → 11). Both parts must be subtracted: after reaching 10, take the remaining 1 away, not add it, so 13 − 4 = 9.
If a child answers 11, track the 4 explicitly as 3-then-1 BOTH removed, using number-line jumps backward to and past ten.
If a child subtracts in ones and makes a boundary slip, slow down at ten and say the two jumps separately.
activities.rationale: Modelling subtraction as decompose-to-ten makes ten the landmark in both directions and prevents the frequent boundary error of losing track of how much is left to subtract.
sourceClaims: Y1/Y2 pupils use and derive number facts within 20; bridging-through-ten mental strategies are core KS1 methods.
1.OA.6: add and subtract within 20 using making ten, decomposing a number leading to a ten, and the relationship between addition and subtraction.
learnerActions: To work out 13 − 4, start at 13 and first subtract enough to land on 10: 13 − 3 = 10.
Then subtract the rest: the 4 was split into 3 and 1, so take the remaining 1, giving 10 − 1 = 9.
Show both jumps back on a number line — back to 10, then one more past it.
Check you have subtracted the whole amount (3 + 1 = 4), not just part of it.
Try more subtractions that cross ten (12−5, 15−7), each time stepping onto ten first.
activities.intendedInsight: Ten is a landmark in BOTH directions: decomposing the number being subtracted so you land on ten first keeps the calculation accurate across the boundary.

activities.title: Explain and compare strategies aloud
feedback: If a child applies make-ten rigidly where a known fact or near-double is quicker, acknowledge their method then ask whether another way would be faster here.
If the strategy feels arbitrary, link it back to bonds to 10 the child already knows so making ten feels purposeful.
Praise a correct method even when the arithmetic needs a nudge, and separately correct the number slip.
activities.rationale: Socratic questioning may elicit and refine a child's bridging method and probe flexibility, and relating additions to subtractions reflects the 1.OA.6 emphasis on the relationship between the two operations.
sourceClaims: 1.OA.6: add and subtract within 20 using making ten, decomposing a number leading to a ten, and the relationship between addition and subtraction.
learnerActions: Talk through how you worked out 8 + 6, step by step: which number did you split, and what did that make?
Answer probing questions: 'Why did you take 2 across to the 8 — what does that make?' and 'For 13 − 4, why break the 4 into 3 and 1?'
Offer a second method for 8 + 6 (e.g. treat it as a near-double: move 1 from the 8 to the 6 to make the double 7 + 7 = 14, or use 6 + 6 + 2, or a known fact) and say which felt quicker.
Use a known addition fact to derive a subtraction: if 8 + 4 = 12, explain how that gives 12 − 8 = 4.
Describe how a ten-frame shows what is happening in your method.
activities.intendedInsight: Because this is a reasoning strategy, explaining and comparing methods builds flexibility — children learn to choose making-ten, a near-double or a known fact according to the calculation, and to see addition and subtraction as related.

activities.title: Fill the bridging step
feedback: This checks the recorded steps; it does not by itself build the reorganisation insight, so pair it with hands-on making-ten first.
If the blank is wrong, return to moving counters to see exactly how the second number splits.
activities.rationale: Fill-in-the-step items can assess whether a child can carry out and articulate the intermediate bridging step, as a complement to hands-on construction rather than a replacement for it.
learnerActions: Complete the make-ten decomposition: 8 + 6 = 8 + 2 + ___ , then give the total.
Complete a subtraction decomposition: 13 − 4 = 13 − 3 − ___ , then give the answer.
Say which number got split and why that amount was chosen.
activities.intendedInsight: Recording the intermediate bridging step makes the strategy's structure explicit and checkable.

constraints: Assess the METHOD, not just the answer: a correct 14 reached by counting all by ones does not demonstrate making-ten. Watch how the child reaches the answer.
Reaching ten first requires splitting the correct number: for 8 + 6 only 2 (not 4) crosses to the 8, matching the first frame's two empty cells.
In subtraction bridging, both parts of the decomposed amount must be SUBTRACTED (13 − 3 then − 1 = 9); subtracting to ten and then adding the remainder gives the wrong answer 11.
Fill-in-the-step and recognition tasks check recorded steps but do not elicit the hands-on reorganisation; use them after children have performed the move with counters.
A static worked example of a bridging split anchors the strategy but does not let a child perform the move on varied facts; treat it as a scaffold, not the whole lesson.
Counters, paper ten-frames, bead strings and number lines are all suitable concrete media; an on-screen draggable version is one option, not a requirement.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

For 8+6, a near-double route uses 7+7=14 (adjusting from the double of 7); if offering near-doubles to a child, state the double explicitly so the adjustment is clear. 'Near-double' is used loosely here for a balancing step and is not established as superior to making-ten by the cited sources.

The legacy entry asserted a static image 'can only show the finished regrouping' and that '3D adds nothing'; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the cited sources and have been softened to scope-limited notes about what each medium affords.
Two CCSS/NCETM sources are marked unverified in the source row; treat their claims as cited standards, not as evidence that any specific activity above was tested.

The dialogue activity's sourceClaims were trimmed to the CCSS 1.OA.6 claim, which supports the relating-addition-to-subtraction principle; the NCETM ten-frame/number-line claim is retained only on the ten-frame activity it directly describes.

probeDeeper: Why did you take 2 across to the 8 — what does that make?
For 13 − 4, why break the 4 into 3 and 1?
Is there another way you could work out 8 + 6?
How does a ten-frame show what is happening?
assess.correctAnswer: 8 + 6 = 14 via make-ten (8 + 2 = 10, then + 4 → 14); 13 − 4 = 9 via decomposing to ten (13 − 3 = 10, then − 1 → 9). Any valid bridging strategy is fine — the point is a strategy, not counting all.

errorPatterns.pattern: Partitions the wrong amount when bridging — e.g. 8 + 6: takes 2 to make ten but then adds 6 again, or miscombines 8 + 2 + 4.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a ten-frame to see exactly how many spill past ten; rehearse partitioning the second addend (6 = 2 + 4).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Make-ten attempted but the leftover is wrong (answer 12 or 16).

errorPatterns.pattern: No bridging — counts on or all by ones; the make-ten strategy is absent.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model make-ten explicitly with two ten-frames; here counting-all is not the target, so make the strategy the focus.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Fingers and no use of a ten landmark.

errorPatterns.pattern: Decomposes subtraction the wrong way — 13 − 4 as 13 − 3 = 10 then + 1 → 11, losing track of how much is left to subtract.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Track the 4 as 3-then-1 both subtracted, using number-line jumps back to and past ten.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 13 − 4 answered 11.

responseLevels.gap: Counts all by ones or misbridges so the answer is wrong; no reliable strategy.
responseLevels.full: Applies make-ten and decomposing-through-ten fluently to both addition and subtraction within 20, and explains the steps.
responseLevels.partial: Uses make-ten / decomposition on addition but not subtraction, or needs support to partition correctly.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show me how you work out 8 + 6 — talk me through your steps. Now do 13 − 4 and tell me how.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: This topic is about the STRATEGY, so watch the method, not just the answer. Making-ten / decomposing-through-ten shows the intended understanding; a correct answer reached by counting all by ones does not demonstrate it. The subtraction reveals whether decomposition is tracked correctly.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 7–8 (UK Y2→Y3, US Grade 2). Counting within 1,000, including skip-counting by 5s, 10s and 100s and understanding what changes as you cross into the hundreds.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2 'count in steps of 2, 3, and 5 from 0, and in tens from any number' and use of <, >, =; Y3 'count from 0 in multiples of 4, 8, 50 and 100' and 'find 10 or 100 more or less than a given number', with fluent order and place value to 1,000.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.NBT.2 'Count within 1000; skip-count by 5s, 10s, and 100s'; 2.NBT.8 'mentally add/subtract 10 or 100 to a given number 100–900'.
• Operational details: the leap from within-100 to within-1000 is a PLACE-VALUE leap, not just a longer chant — +10 rolls the tens digit, +100 rolls the hundreds digit, and the child must see WHICH digit changes. Skip from non-round starts (e.g. 5s from 315, 100s from 240). The reliable stall is crossing hundred boundaries (190→200, 995→1000) where a digit carries.
• Checkpoint: skip-count aloud and predict the crossing. Tier A (7): count on in 10s and 100s from a round number within 1000 with a hundred-square/number-line prop. Tier B (7–8): skip-count by 5s/10s/100s from any start and state 10-more/100-more without counting. Tier C (8): cross 190→200 and 970→1000 explaining which digit rolls and why.
bestPractices: Frame within-1000 counting as PLACE VALUE in motion: use base-ten materials (hundreds flats, tens rods, unit cubes) so +10 physically adds a rod and +100 adds a flat — the child sees the digit that changes rather than reciting.

Make crossing a hundred boundary the explicit teaching event: pause at 190, ask 'what comes next in 10s?', and show the ten tens rods trading for one hundred flat so the roll from 190→200 is felt, not mysterious.
Skip-count from non-round and 'ragged' starts (5s from 315, 10s from 268, 100s from 240) so the pattern is a rule about which digit moves, not a memorised round-number chant.

Sync three representations of the same skip count — hundred/thousand grid highlights, equal jumps on a number line, and equal groups of counters — so 100s counting is seen as repeated equal groups (the multiplication/place-value bridge).
Separate '10 more' from 'count on ten by ones': ask for 10-more and 100-more instantly and check the child is rolling a digit, not counting 1,2,3… to prove the place-value idea has landed.
keyRepresentations: Scalable number line marked to 1,000 with equal jumps (jumps of 10 and of 100) to show constant step size and boundary crossings
Thousand grid / linked hundred squares where each skip count lights a column or diagonal, exposing the 5s, 10s and 100s patterns
Base-ten blocks (unit cubes, tens rods, hundreds flats) with regrouping — ten rods trade for one flat at the hundred boundary
Place-value columns (H T U) with digit-rollers so a step by 10 or 100 visibly advances one column and carries into the next
commonMisconceptions: Hundred-boundary stall — reaching 190 the child says '191, 192…' or '100-ten', not knowing 200 comes next; the decade/hundred bridge is the classic breakdown point.
'+10 means add a zero' / '+100 means add two zeros' — over-generalised from round numbers, so 268+10 becomes 2680 or 26810.
Treating the count as a longer rote chant and losing track of which digit changes, so skip-counting from a non-round start collapses.
Confusing tens and hundreds steps (counting 240, 250, 260 when asked to skip in 100s) because the difference between which column moves is not yet secure.
Losing the ones digit when skip-counting by 10s or 100s from a ragged start (315→320 instead of 325) because the child re-rounds to a decade.

learn.summary: For ages 7–8 (UK Y2→Y3, US Grade 2), skip-counting within 1,000 by 5s, 10s and 100s is a place-value event, not a longer chant: the learner must see WHICH digit rolls when adding 5, 10 or 100, and why a carry happens when crossing a hundred (190→200) or thousand (995→1000) boundary. Core activities drive a live place-value counter from round and ragged starts, with static reference and checking tasks as supports. Non-round starts (5s from 315, 100s from 150/240, 10s from 268) are emphasised so the learner holds the other digits fixed rather than re-rounding to a decade.

activities.title: Place-value skip-count playground (drive the carry)
feedback: If the learner predicts '2680' for 268+10 (the 'add a zero' error), pause the counter and show only the tens column advancing 6→7 to give 278; name that +10 moves one column, it does not append a digit.
If a ragged start collapses to a decade when counting on in 10s (315→320 instead of the correct 325), highlight the fixed ones digit (5) and replay the jump so the learner sees the ones stay put.
At the boundary, if the learner hesitates, show the ten tens-rods snapping into one hundred-flat so the carry is seen rather than recited.

When a '10 more' answer is produced instantly and correctly, confirm by rolling the tens digit (plus the regrouped next digit if a boundary is crossed), reinforcing that this is a place-value move, not counting on by ones.
activities.rationale: The classic stall is at hundred/thousand boundaries and from non-round starts; a learner-driven counter that synchronises grid, number line and place-value columns lets the child predict then see the exact digit that rolls, targeting the 'add a zero' and re-rounding misconceptions directly.
sourceClaims: 2.NBT.2: Count within 1000; skip-count by 5s, 10s, and 100s. 2.NBT.8: mentally add 10 or 100 to, and subtract 10 or 100 from, a given number 100–900.
Skip counting is a bridge to multiplicative reasoning and place value, not rote chanting; regrouping at ten/hundred boundaries is a core mastery checkpoint.
learnerActions: Set a start number — round (e.g. 240) or ragged (e.g. 315, 268) — and choose a step of +5, +10 or +100.
Before tapping, predict aloud the next number and say which digit you think will change.

Tap the step and watch three linked views move together: a thousand grid lights the landed number, a number line draws one equal jump, and place-value columns (H-T-U, with a Th column that appears when you reach 1000) roll the digit or digits that change.
Stop deliberately at 190 and predict 'what comes next in 10s?', then tap +10 and watch ten tens-rods trade for one hundred-flat while the hundreds digit rolls 1→2 and the tens resets to 0.
Repeat the boundary move by counting in 5s up to 995→1000 and describe, in your own words, which columns carried.

Switch to a '10 more / 100 more instantly' challenge: state the answer without counting on by ones, then tap to check which digit rolled (just one digit unless the step crosses a hundred or thousand boundary, e.g. 195 → 205).
activities.intendedInsight: Adding 10 rolls the tens digit and adding 100 rolls the hundreds digit; if no boundary is crossed, the other digits stay the same. When a hundred/thousand boundary is crossed (e.g. 190 → 200), the next place up also changes because of regrouping (ten of one place trading for one of the next), not a mysterious jump.

activities.title: Hands-on regrouping with base-ten materials
feedback: If the learner counts 150, 250, 350 but drops the 50 to say 100, 200, 300, point to the five tens rods still sitting on the mat and ask what should have stayed the same.
If the learner recites a number but adds the wrong piece, map the spoken digit to the matching column of blocks before continuing.
activities.rationale: Base-ten materials make +10/+100 a concrete regrouping action, so the child can see which digit changes rather than reciting a longer chant; this grounds the live on-screen counter.
sourceClaims: Skip counting is a bridge to multiplicative reasoning and place value, not rote chanting; regrouping at ten/hundred boundaries is a core mastery checkpoint.
learnerActions: Build a start number with hundreds flats, tens rods and unit cubes (e.g. 190 as one flat and nine rods).
To add 10, physically add one tens rod; to add 100, add one hundreds flat — and say which digit changed.
At 190, add the tenth rod, then trade ten rods for one hundreds flat to make 200, and say 'the tens rolled to 0 and the hundreds went up by one'.
Skip-count by 100s from 150 using flats, keeping the five tens and nothing in the ones fixed, to reach 250, 350 … 950.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding 10 or 100 physically adds a rod or a flat, and crossing a boundary is the concrete act of trading ten rods for one flat — making the digit that changes something the learner can handle and see, not just recite.

activities.title: Annotated thousand-square and place-value reference
feedback: If the learner names the wrong column for a step, point back to the lit pattern and the H-T-U labels so the step size maps to a single column.
Use the boundary flap as a reminder that the join between 190 and 200 is a trade, to be practised live with the counter or blocks.
activities.rationale: A static annotated reference is a strong support for recognising patterns and naming columns, but recognition alone does not enact the carry or recompute from a ragged start, so it accompanies rather than replaces the manipulable counter.
learnerActions: Study a thousand grid / linked hundred squares where a 10s count lights one column, a 5s count lights two columns, and a 100s count lights the same position in each hundred square, and name the pattern you see.
Tap a highlighted 100s column to reveal the note 'each step adds one hundred — the hundreds digit changes', and name the H, T, U columns.
Open the flap at the 190→200 join to read how ten tens trade for one hundred.
activities.intendedInsight: The 5s/10s/100s patterns fall in predictable places (columns for 5s and 10s, the same position in each hundred square for 100s), and naming the place-value columns helps the learner say which digit each step advances.

activities.title: Checking and diagnostic skip-count tasks
feedback: Expected: 150, 250 … 950; 480, 485 … 520 crossing 500 correctly; 1000, 990, 980 …; and 620, 720, 820, 920, 1020 crossing the thousand boundary cleanly. (985, __, 1005 fills to 995.)
'10 more than 268' = 278; if a learner offers 2680, that is the 'add a zero' error — show the tens digit rolling 6→7 instead. ('100 more than 613' = 713.)
If the learner snaps 100s-from-150 to 100, 200, 300, name the dropped 50 and re-run keeping tens and ones fixed.

If an error appears precisely at 495→500 or at 1000 while mid-run counting is fine, treat it as a boundary-bridge gap: rehearse just 490, 495, 500, 505 and 980, 990, 1000, 1010 on a number line, naming the regrouping — do not re-drill the whole sequence.
If backward counting breaks only at boundaries, practise short backward runs across each boundary as its own skill; do not assume backward fluency arrives with forward.
activities.rationale: Boundary-crossing and ragged-start items probe the key misconceptions crisply and separate secure three-digit place value from a learner who snaps to pure multiples or re-rounds; placed after the constructive activities they primarily verify the insight, while their feedback can reteach when an error appears.
sourceClaims: 2.NBT.2: Count within 1000; skip-count by 5s, 10s, and 100s. 2.NBT.8: mentally add 10 or 100 to, and subtract 10 or 100 from, a given number 100–900.
Skip counting is a bridge to multiplicative reasoning and place value, not rote chanting; regrouping at ten/hundred boundaries is a core mastery checkpoint.
learnerActions: Order a set of 100s cards from 240 and fill blanks in sequences that cross a boundary, e.g. 985, __, 1005.
Answer '100 more than 613' and '10 more than 268', writing the single digit that changed.
Count on in 100s from 150 up to 950; count in 5s from 480 up to 520; count back in 10s from 1000; count on in 100s from 620 and say what happens when the count passes 1000 (920 → 1020).
Explain for each: which digit changed and which stayed the same.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency means changing only the relevant place and crossing hundred and thousand boundaries cleanly, from non-round starts and in both directions.

activities.title: Count-with-me partner rehearsal (spoken practice)
feedback: If the learner supplies a wrong boundary number, pause and return to a number line or blocks to show the regrouping before resuming the count.
Reward a correct boundary supply by having the learner name the digit that changed.
activities.rationale: Spoken turn-taking rehearses the sequence orally and prompts boundary crossings; it adds oral practice alongside the visual/place-value work rather than replacing the manipulable or concrete activities.
learnerActions: Take turns skip-counting aloud with a counting buddy, alternating each number in a 10s or 100s run.
When the buddy hesitates at 190 in a 10s run, supply the next number (200) and say which digits rolled.
Say each number clearly and, at boundaries, state what carried before moving on.
activities.intendedInsight: Rehearsing the count aloud, especially at the deliberate hesitation at a boundary, builds oral fluency and the habit of naming the carry.

constraints: The annotated thousand-square and place-value reference is a scaffold: it shows patterns and names columns but does not itself enact the carry or recompute from a ragged start, so pair it with a manipulable counter or base-ten materials.

Checking/diagnostic tasks are primarily for verifying the pattern and catching misconceptions; their feedback can also prompt reteaching, but they are best placed after the constructive activities rather than being the sole means of building the place-value insight.
Spoken partner practice rehearses the sequence orally but does not by itself make the digit-rolling visible; keep it alongside visual/concrete work.

Base-ten cutouts and rods are physical approximations of the ideal place-value idea: use the trade of ten rods for one flat to represent regrouping, and connect the concrete piece to the spoken digit and the written column.
Practise backward counting across boundaries as its own skill rather than assuming it transfers automatically from forward fluency.
When crossing a boundary during a ragged-start count, keep the ones/tens that should stay fixed in view so the learner does not re-round to a decade.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched and the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row claims a talking character 'adds little the manipulative doesn't do better' and that a 3D scene 'adds spatial overhead with no conceptual payoff'; these comparative-efficacy/necessity claims are not established by the cited sources, so the conversation activity is retained as optional spoken practice and the 3D option is omitted rather than asserting it has no value.

The legacy 'strong' quiz note says it 'verifies rather than builds' the insight; this has been scoped to a placement limit (checking tasks follow constructive work; their feedback can still reteach), not retained as a universal claim that such tasks cannot teach.
One source (CCSS-M 2.NBT) is marked verified:false and the NCETM claim is unverified; confidence should not be upgraded on that basis.

Diagnostic answer sequences and expected errors (150→250…950; 480→520 crossing 500; 620→1020 crossing 1000; blank 995 in 985,__,1005; 2680 as the add-a-zero error; 268+10=278; 613+100=713) were checked for arithmetic consistency and carried through to learner-facing feedback.

The original misconception example '315→320 instead of 325' is only an error when counting on in 10s (315+10=325); 315→320 is correct under a +5 step, so the step is named explicitly in the feedback to avoid ambiguity.

probeDeeper: What digit changes when you count in 100s from 150? What stays the same?
What comes after 995 in 5s?
Count back in 100s from 1000.
What's 100 more than 940?
assess.correctAnswer: 150, 250, …, 950; 480, 485, …, 520 (crossing 500 correctly); 1000, 990, 980…; and 620, 720, 820, 920, 1020 — changing only the relevant place and crossing the thousand boundary cleanly.

errorPatterns.pattern: snaps to pure multiples — counting in 100s from 150 drops the 50 and gives 100, 200, 300
errorPatterns.nextMove: use a place-value chart or bead string so only the hundreds digit ticks while the 50 stays fixed; name what stays and what changes
errorPatterns.revealedBy: loses the tens/ones and recites round hundreds

errorPatterns.pattern: hundred/thousand boundary break — 5s or 10s stall or err when crossing 500 or 1000 (e.g. 495→'400', or can't pass 1000)
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT re-drill the whole sequence — rehearse just the bridges (490, 495, 500, 505; 980, 990, 1000, 1010) on a number line, naming the regrouping
errorPatterns.revealedBy: an error precisely at the boundary while mid-run counting is fine

errorPatterns.pattern: backward collapse over boundaries — counts back in 10s fine until a hundred or the thousand, then errs
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT expect backward to arrive with forward — practise short backward runs across each boundary on a number line as its own skill
errorPatterns.revealedBy: backward errors that appear only at boundaries

responseLevels.gap: Reverts to pure multiples (100, 200…) instead of keeping the other digits; breaks down at hundred/thousand boundaries.
responseLevels.full: Counts within 1000 by 5s/10s/100s forwards and backwards from any start, changing only the relevant place and crossing hundred and thousand boundaries cleanly.
responseLevels.partial: Skip-counts within 1000 from standard starts but falters counting from a non-multiple, or when crossing 500/1000, or backwards.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Count on in 100s starting from 150: 150, 250, 350… up to 950. Now count in 5s from 480 up to 520. Then count backwards in 10s from 1000 for a bit. Last, count on by 100s from 620 — what happens at 1000? (Watch counting in 100s from a non-multiple, crossing 500 in 5s, and crossing 1000.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Counting in 100s from 150 (a non-multiple of 100) tests holding tens and ones constant while moving hundreds; the 5s run 480→520 tests crossing a hundred boundary; going through 1000 tests the thousand boundary. A child with three-digit place value handles all; a weaker child snaps 100s-from-150 to 100, 200, 300, mis-crosses 495→500, or stalls at 1000.

sources.claim: Y2: count in steps of 2, 3 and 5 from 0, and in tens from any number; Y3: count from 0 in multiples of 4, 8, 50 and 100 and find 10 or 100 more or less than a given number.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (KS1/KS2), Year 2 & Year 3 Number

sources.claim: 2.NBT.2: Count within 1000; skip-count by 5s, 10s, and 100s. 2.NBT.8: mentally add 10 or 100 to, and subtract 10 or 100 from, a given number 100–900.
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 2 Number & Operations in Base Ten

sources.claim: Skip counting is a bridge to multiplicative reasoning and place value, not rote chanting; regrouping at ten/hundred boundaries is a core mastery checkpoint.
sources.source: NCETM — Primary Mastery Professional Development (Number, Place Value)

pedagogy.summary: Children measure several real objects to the nearest whole unit and display them on a line plot: a horizontal number line marked in equal whole-number intervals with one X stacked above each measured value. The line plot is where measuring, counting and the number line meet — the horizontal axis is a true measurement scale (equal intervals, every value shown even when no data lands there), height tells you HOW MANY objects, position tells you HOW LONG. The procedure is best taught by having children generate their OWN data, then build the plot on a pre-scaled line, keeping the ruler physically aligned under the axis so 'position = length' is felt, not just told.
bestPractices: Have children measure real objects they care about and record the data first, then plot — the plot should display data they generated
Provide a pre-drawn horizontal line and stress that the scale is a ruler: equal intervals, every whole-number value present even if no X sits above it
Keep an actual ruler aligned beneath the plot so the X's position reads as a length on the same scale
Explicitly separate the two questions the plot answers: 'how many?' (count the Xs) versus 'how long?' (read the position)
Bridge from earlier tally/categorical work but flag the key shift — the axis is now a measurement scale, not arbitrary categories
keyRepresentations: The horizontal number line as a measurement scale (equal whole-unit intervals)
Stacked X marks, one X per object
A ruler aligned under the plot linking measured length to axis position
A tally / frequency table as a bridge from raw measurements to the plot
commonMisconceptions: Reading the height of a stack as the length ('the tallest stack is the longest object')
Drawing only the values that occurred and spacing them evenly, so a value with no data is omitted and the intervals become unequal
Measuring from the 1 mark or the ruler's end instead of zero, so every length is off by a unit
Treating each X as one unit of length rather than one object

learn.summary: Children generate their own measurement data by measuring several real objects to the nearest whole unit, then display the data on a line plot: a horizontal number line marked in equal whole-number intervals with one X stacked above each measured value. The horizontal axis is a true measurement scale (equal intervals, every value shown even when no data lands there); height tells you HOW MANY objects, position tells you HOW LONG. Teaching works best when children measure first, then build the plot, with a ruler kept physically aligned under the axis so 'position = length' is felt. A line may be pre-scaled as an early scaffold, but constructing the scale on a plain line is the fuller skill the objective targets. A tally or frequency table can bridge from raw measurements, but the axis is an ordered measurement scale, not the reorderable categories of earlier tally/category charts. Core activity: a measure-and-plot build (hands-on or on-screen). Supporting activities: interpreting a given plot, and a reference/reveal of a finished plot for the meaning of each X and position.

activities.title: Measure your own objects, then build the line plot
feedback: If a child reads a tall stack as a long object, slide the real ruler under the plot and ask them to point to where an object of that length would actually sit; hold the two questions apart — 'how many objects?' versus 'how long is one?'

If a child treats each X as a unit of length (e.g. 'three Xs means 3 cm long'), clarify that each X stands for one object placed at its measured position; the length is read from the horizontal scale, not from how many Xs are stacked.

If a child leaves out a value nothing measured (e.g. axis reads 3,4,6,7 with 5 missing), reteach the axis as a ruler — every unit is present whether or not data lands on it; overlay a real ruler and mark the empty value together.

If a child reorders or evenly spaces only the values that occurred (as in a category chart), remind them the axis is an ordered measurement scale where position means length, so every unit must appear in order.
If every measurement is off by one unit, pause the plotting and reteach measuring from zero with gap-free unit iteration before returning.

When a child notices a whole-number value on the scale with no X above it, confirm that the empty spot is meaningful: it shows no object had that length, and the scale keeps it open. If a child has put an X at a value nothing measured, have them check their recorded data and remove it.
If a second object also measures 6, confirm its X stacks above the first at the same position — the stack grows upward (count) while the position stays fixed (length).
activities.rationale: The standard describes a procedure — generate measurement data, then show it on a line plot with a horizontal whole-number scale — so children should actually measure and build rather than only read. Learners who carry over bar/case-value habits confuse stack height (frequency) with the variable value (position); pairing the ruler with the axis targets that specific confusion.
sourceClaims: Grade 2 standard: generate measurement data by measuring lengths of several objects to the nearest whole unit; show the measurements by making a line plot with a horizontal scale marked off in whole-number units.

Students familiar with bar / case-value graphs transfer the habit of reading bar height as a data value, confusing frequency (y-axis / stack height) with the value of the variable (x-axis / position); even after instruction nearly 20% report the frequency at the centre rather than the variable value, and this axis confusion appears in simple dot plots too.
learnerActions: Collect 6-8 small real objects (pencils, crayons, leaves, blocks) and measure each to the nearest whole centimetre, measuring from the ruler's zero mark, not from 1 or the end.
Record each measurement in a simple tally or frequency table as a bridge from raw measurements to the plot.

Notice how a line plot differs from earlier tally or category charts: here the horizontal axis is an ordered measurement scale with equal whole-number intervals and every value present, not a set of arbitrary categories you could reorder or leave out.

On a horizontal line, mark the scale as equal whole-number intervals across the full range of your data, including any whole-number value that nothing measured. Early on a line that is already pre-scaled can be provided as a scaffold so you focus on plotting; building the scale yourself afterwards is the fuller skill this topic is aiming at.
Place exactly one X above each object's measured value; when two objects share a length, stack a second X on top of the first.

If your scale marks are spaced 1 cm apart, keep an actual ruler aligned directly beneath the line, with its numbers matching your scale labels, so each X's horizontal position reads as a length on the same scale.
Answer two separate questions from your finished plot: 'How many objects were 6 cm?' (count the Xs in that stack) and 'How long is the longest object?' (read its position on the scale).
activities.intendedInsight: On a line plot the sideways position of an X answers 'how long?' while the upward height of a stack answers 'how many?'. Unlike reorderable categorical charts, the axis is a ruler-like measurement scale: equal intervals with every whole-number value staying on it even when no object landed there, so the gaps stay equal.

activities.title: Interpret a given line plot: how many versus how long
feedback: If a child answers 'how long is the longest?' with a stack's count, redirect them to the horizontal scale and ask them to read the position of the rightmost X.
If a child ignores an empty scale value, ask what it tells them about objects of that length.
Confirm that adding an object changes the count of a stack but not the positions already on the plot.
activities.rationale: Interpreting a given plot isolates the value-versus-frequency distinction that learners commonly collapse. This supports but does not replace the generative build, since reading a finished plot does not require constructing the scale or measuring.
sourceClaims: Students familiar with bar / case-value graphs transfer the habit of reading bar height as a data value, confusing frequency (y-axis / stack height) with the value of the variable (x-axis / position); even after instruction nearly 20% report the frequency at the centre rather than the variable value, and this axis confusion appears in simple dot plots too.
learnerActions: Study a completed line plot and answer count questions such as 'How many objects were 6 cm long?' by counting the Xs in a stack.
Answer position questions such as 'How long is the longest object?' by reading the scale, not the stack height.
Explain what an empty whole-number value on the scale means (no object had that length).
Predict what changes if one more object measuring 6 cm were added (one more X on the 6 stack; the position is unchanged).
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a line plot means deliberately choosing between counting (height) and reading position (length); the same plot answers both kinds of question in different ways.

activities.title: Reference reveal: what each X and each position means
feedback: If a child confuses the two, pair each reveal with the question it answers ('how many' at a stack, 'how long' at a position).
Note that this reference shows meaning but does not by itself let a child generate data or feel the measure-then-plot link.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal or point-and-name reference clarifies the meaning of marks and positions and can scaffold self-checking. It is a reference, not a substitute for building the plot from one's own measurements.
learnerActions: Point to (or tap) a stack and state 'how many' objects it represents.
Point to (or tap) a position on the scale and state 'how long' that is.
Use the finished plot as a reference while checking a plot you built yourself.
activities.intendedInsight: Each X stands for one object, placed at its measured length; a stack's height is a count, its position is a length.

constraints: The core objective is a procedure: children must actually measure objects and construct the scale and marks, not only read or recognise a finished plot. A pre-scaled line is an acceptable early scaffold, but children should reach the point of building the scale themselves.
Children should generate and record their own data before plotting, so the plot displays data they produced.

The horizontal axis must be an ordered measurement scale: equal whole-unit intervals across the full range, with every whole-number value present even where no data lands — unlike reorderable categorical/tally charts.

Measure from zero with gap-free unit iteration; measuring from the 1 mark makes every length one unit too long, and measuring from the ruler's physical end can make lengths wrong by the size of any gap before the zero mark.
One X per object; two equal-length objects produce a stack of two at the same position. Each X represents an object, not a unit of length.

Interpreting a given plot and reveal-the-meaning references are supporting scaffolds: they can assess or clarify interpretation but do not exercise the generative measure-and-scale skill, so do not rely on them alone.
Keeping a real ruler aligned under the axis is a concrete device to link length to position; it is one effective option, not the only way to teach the link.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original row asserts that a static picture or a quiz 'cannot teach' the position-from-height separation and empty-value requirement. This comparative-necessity claim is not established by the cited sources; it has been softened to scope each format's affordances and limits. A fixed/reveal reference or an interpretation quiz can still support learning, though neither elicits independent construction of the scale.

The original marked 3D and conversation formats as 'poor' with claims like '3D adds nothing' and 'dialogue has no purchase'; these universal claims are not supported by the sources and have been omitted rather than propagated. The planar nature of a line plot is noted as a reason 2D construction fits the task without asserting other media teach nothing.

The original is internally mixed on whether the line is pre-scaled (its pedagogy best practice) or plain/unmarked for the child to scale (its assessment diagnostic). Both are retained here as phase-appropriate options; the fuller skill and the objective require the child to construct the scale.

The optional on-screen mechanics (draggable ruler, X snapping to the measured value, live recompute, flagging a mis-positioned X or skipped scale value) are preserved as example interaction mechanisms, not mandatory requirements; the same objective can be met with physical ruler, objects, and paper.
The ~20% figure and bar-graph transfer claim derive from a single cited study (Kaplan et al. 2014) applied here to a grade-2 line-plot context; not independently re-verified.

probeDeeper: Point to a spot on your scale where you didn't measure anything — what does it mean that there's no X there?
How many objects were 6 cm long? How do you know?
If I measured one more object at 6 cm, what changes on your plot?
Which object is the longest — show me on the ruler, not just the stack.
assess.correctAnswer: Marks the horizontal axis in equal whole-unit intervals spanning the full range INCLUDING values with no data; measures each object from zero; stacks exactly one X per object at its measured value (two same-length objects give a stack of two); can then read 'how many' by counting Xs and 'how long' by reading position.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the height of a stack as the length — 'this object is 3 long' because three Xs sit above it
errorPatterns.nextMove: Slide the actual ruler under the plot and ask them to point to where an object of that length would sit; hold the two questions apart — 'how many objects' vs 'how long is one'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked 'how long is the longest object?', answers with the tallest stack's count; or builds the plot treating bar height as length

errorPatterns.pattern: Draws only the values that occurred, spaced evenly, so a value nothing measured is left off and the intervals become unequal
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach the axis as a ruler — every unit is present whether or not data lands on it; overlay a real ruler and mark the empty value together
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Axis reads e.g. 3, 4, 6, 7 with 5 missing and equal gaps between the marks

errorPatterns.pattern: Measures from the 1 mark or the ruler's end instead of zero, so every recorded length is off by a unit
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach zero-point, gap-free unit iteration with the ruler before returning to the plot
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A systematic +1 or -1 error across all measurements before the plot is even built

responseLevels.gap: Cannot build a correct scale — leaves out empty values or spaces marks unequally, or reads stack height as length; the plot does not faithfully represent the measurements.
responseLevels.full: Generates data by measuring from zero, scales the axis in equal whole units including empty values, places one X per object, and reads BOTH how-many (count) and how-long (position), transferring correctly to a new object added to the plot.
responseLevels.partial: Builds a correct scale and places one X per object, but treats the plot as a picture — can say how many Xs are in a stack yet cannot fluidly switch to 'how long', or is thrown by a scale value with no data; lists the marks without connecting count and position.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a ruler and 6-8 small objects. Say: 'Measure each of these to the nearest whole centimetre, then show all your measurements on this line.' Provide a plain, unmarked horizontal line. Watch how they scale the axis, place the Xs, handle two objects that share a length, and handle a value in the range that nothing measured.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands the plot answers 'which is longest?' by position and keeps empty scale values open; a child running the familiar bar-graph habit answers by stack height and omits the values nothing measured. The two produce visibly different plots and different answers to the same question, so watching the build — not asking about it — separates them.

sources.claim: Grade 2 standard: generate measurement data by measuring lengths of several objects to the nearest whole unit; show the measurements by making a line plot with a horizontal scale marked off in whole-number units.
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, 2.MD.D.9

sources.claim: Students familiar with bar / case-value graphs transfer the habit of reading bar height as a data value, confusing frequency (y-axis / stack height) with the value of the variable (x-axis / position); even after instruction nearly 20% report the frequency at the centre rather than the variable value, and this axis confusion appears in simple dot plots too.
