pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–10y; divide up to 4-digit ÷ 1-digit using short division (with place-value/array support), and interpret remainders appropriately for the context.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5 'divide numbers up to 4 digits by a one-digit number using the formal written method of short division and interpret remainders appropriately for the context'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.NBT.6 / 5.NBT.6 — 'find whole-number quotients … using strategies based on place value, the properties of operations, and/or the relationship between multiplication and division; illustrate and explain using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models.'
• Operational details — short division ('bus stop') processes the dividend left-to-right by place value: at each digit ask 'how many divisors fit?', record the quotient digit, and CARRY the remainder to the next place. Understanding rests on place-value partitioning (4932÷6 = 4000+900+30+2 shared) and the ×÷ inverse (checking by multiplying back). The distinctive Y5 demand is interpreting the remainder in context: round up (minibuses needed), round down (full bags), keep as a remainder, or express as a fraction/decimal — the SAME calculation yields different answers by context. Estimate first (4932÷6≈5000ö5≈1000).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): 3-digit ÷ 1-digit short division, no remainder. Tier B (age 9–10): 4-digit ÷ 1-digit with a remainder, and state it correctly. Tier C (age 10): interpret the remainder three ways for three different contexts of the same division and check via multiplication.
bestPractices: Build short division on place-value partitioning — exchange/carry the remainder to the next column — using place-value counters so 'carrying the remainder' is understood as regrouping.
Teach remainder interpretation as context-dependent: round up, round down, keep, or express as fraction/decimal — using the same calculation in different stories.
Always check the answer with the inverse (quotient×divisor + remainder = dividend) and against an estimate.
Connect to the array/area (division as finding the missing dimension) so short division isn't a rootless ritual.
Handle the 'won't go' case explicitly (a leading digit smaller than the divisor → 0 in that place and carry), a common stumbling point.
keyRepresentations: Short-division ('bus stop') layout with carried remainders
Place-value counters/columns — exchanging the remainder into the next place
Array/area with an unknown dimension — division as inverse of ×
Number line / bar model for remainder interpretation in context
commonMisconceptions: Mishandling the remainder carry — not moving it to the next place or adding it wrongly.
Interpreting the remainder wrongly for the context (rounding down when you must round up, e.g. minibuses).
Dropping a place when the digit is smaller than the divisor (not writing the 0 and carrying).
Not checking with multiplication, so errors persist.
Treating short division as digit-manipulation divorced from place value/sharing meaning.

learn.summary: For learners aged 9–10: divide numbers up to 4 digits by a one-digit number using the short-division ('bus stop') method, grounded in place-value exchange, and interpret the remainder according to the context (round up, round down, keep as a remainder, or express as a fraction/decimal). The central insight is that the same calculation can yield different correct answers depending on the story, and that answers should be checked by multiplying back and against an estimate.

activities.title: Share the columns: short division with place-value counters
feedback: If a learner divides each digit independently with no carry, model the exchange explicitly: the leftover from a column becomes ten counters of the next place; write the small carried digit before dividing the next place.
If the quotient has too few digits because a place was skipped, point to the column where the divisor wouldn't go and insist on writing 0 there and carrying the whole amount on.
Confirm correct work by linking each written carry digit back to the physical exchange the learner just performed.
activities.rationale: Building the algorithm on visible place-value exchange helps 'carrying the remainder' be understood as regrouping rather than an unexplained ritual, and makes the dropped-zero error addressable at its source. Dragging/exchanging counters with live quotient digits recording above is one concrete way to make the regrouping felt; a physical set of counters serves the same purpose.
sourceClaims: 4.NBT.6/5.NBT.6 require finding quotients using place value, properties and the ×÷ relationship, illustrated with arrays/area models.
Short division should be grounded in place-value exchange; remainders must be interpreted according to context (round up/down/keep/fraction).
learnerActions: Lay out 4932 as place-value counters: 4 thousands, 9 hundreds, 3 tens, 2 ones.

Share each column left to right into 6 equal groups, starting with the thousands (4 thousands won't make a group of 6, so that place gives 0 — exchange the 4 thousands for 40 hundreds and carry them on).

When a column won't share evenly, exchange each leftover counter for ten counters of the next-lower place and add them to that column (e.g. a spare hundred becomes ten tens that join the tens column).
Record the quotient digit for each place above the bus-stop layout as you go, and write the carried amount beside the next digit.
When the divisor won't go into a place at all, write 0 in the quotient for that place and carry the whole amount onward — do not skip the place.
Finish with 4932 ÷ 6 = 822 and note there is no remainder here; then repeat with a dividend that leaves a remainder.
activities.intendedInsight: The 'carried remainder' of the written short-division method is the same idea as regrouping/exchanging place-value counters: a leftover in one column is worth ten of the next place down. Every place of the dividend produces a quotient digit, including a 0 when the divisor won't go.

activities.title: One division, three answers: interpreting the remainder in context
feedback: If a learner stops at 'r5' without interpreting it, ask what the leftover represents here (5 sweets, not enough for another full bag) and tie the number to the situation.

If a learner rounds inappropriately for the context, re-read the story together: 'Can leftover children travel with no minibus?' pushes toward rounding up; 'Is a half-full bag a full bag?' pushes toward rounding down.
Acknowledge when the learner gives different, correctly justified answers for different stories about the same calculation — that is exactly the point.
activities.rationale: Treating remainder interpretation as context-dependent, using one calculation across several stories, targets the common error of reading the remainder wrongly for the situation. A live context switcher that reframes the same leftover is one way to make this vivid; spoken stories or written word problems work too.
sourceClaims: Y5 pupils divide up to 4 digits by a one-digit number using formal short division and interpret remainders appropriately for the context.
Short division should be grounded in place-value exchange; remainders must be interpreted according to context (round up/down/keep/fraction).
learnerActions: Take a single division that leaves a remainder and solve it once — for example, 125 ÷ 8 = 15 remainder 5.

Read that SAME result (15 remainder 5) inside three different stories about 125 items: 'containers that each hold 8 — how many containers are needed for 125 items?' (round the quotient UP to 16, because the 5 left over still need a container), 'full bags of 8 — how many full bags from 125 sweets?' (round DOWN to 15, with 5 left over), and 'share 125 cm of ribbon fairly among 8 groups — how much each?' (the leftover can be split, so express it as a fraction, giving 15 and 5/8 cm each).
State in words what the leftover of 5 means in each story (e.g. '5 sweets are not enough to fill another full bag').
Decide, for each story, whether the right answer rounds up, rounds down, or keeps the remainder — and justify why.
For extra practice with the round-up case, try 52 children into minibuses of 9: 52 ÷ 9 = 5 remainder 7, which rounds UP to 6 minibuses because the 7 leftover children still need transport.
activities.intendedInsight: The same calculation gives different legitimate answers depending on what the leftover represents in the situation; interpreting the remainder is a decision about the context, not a fixed rule applied to the number.

activities.title: Estimate first, check by multiplying back
feedback: For a correct method with a single-digit arithmetic slip, do not reteach the method — have the learner verify with multiplication and estimation and locate the wrong digit (e.g. a quotient of 812 gives 812 × 6 = 4872, not 4932, which flags an error).
If an estimate is far from the result, prompt the learner to recheck which place values were shared and whether the estimate itself was rounded sensibly.
Reinforce the inverse relationship by writing the check equation alongside the division each time.
activities.rationale: Routine estimation and inverse checking address the misconception that short division is digit-manipulation divorced from meaning, and stop arithmetic slips from persisting unnoticed. A check panel that multiplies the quotient back is one convenient support; doing the multiplication by hand achieves the same check.
sourceClaims: 4.NBT.6/5.NBT.6 require finding quotients using place value, properties and the ×÷ relationship, illustrated with arrays/area models.
learnerActions: Before dividing, make a rough estimate by rounding to friendly numbers (round 4932 to about 4800, then 4800 ÷ 6 = 800), so expect a quotient near 800 — about three figures. Avoid rounding the divisor down (e.g. 6 to 5), which would inflate the estimate.
Carry out the short division to get a quotient and any remainder.
Check with the inverse: compute quotient × divisor (+ remainder) and confirm it equals the dividend, e.g. 822 × 6 = 4932.
Compare the answer with the estimate and ask whether it is sensible; if the check fails, find and fix the slip rather than re-learning the method.
activities.intendedInsight: Division and multiplication are inverses: quotient × divisor (+ remainder) = dividend. An estimate and an inverse check catch arithmetic slips and keep the quotient's size reasonable.

activities.title: Talk it through: does the leftover change the answer?
feedback: If the learner cannot justify the choice, ask a sharpening question: 'What happens to the children who don't fit on the full minibuses?'
Draw out the distinction between the arithmetic (how the division ran) and the decision (what the leftover means here).
activities.rationale: A Socratic exchange may build remainder interpretation by prompting the learner to reason about meaning; it is proposed to complement, rather than replace, the visual algorithm work, since discussion alone does not rehearse the written layout. Efficacy is untested here.
sourceClaims: Y5 pupils divide up to 4 digits by a one-digit number using formal short division and interpret remainders appropriately for the context.
learnerActions: With a partner or guide, discuss a solved division in a real story: 'We have a remainder of 5 — do we need another minibus, or is 5 left over fine?'
Argue for rounding up or down and give the reason in terms of the story.
Explain to the other person what the remainder means and why the chosen answer fits the situation.
activities.intendedInsight: Deciding what to do with a remainder is a reasoned choice about the context that can be defended out loud, not an automatic operation.

constraints: Short division must be grounded in place-value exchange: present 'carrying the remainder' as regrouping a leftover into ten of the next-lower place, not as an isolated digit trick.
Every digit of the dividend must yield a quotient digit, including writing 0 (and carrying the whole amount) when the divisor won't go into a place — explicitly teach this 'won't go' case.

Interpret the remainder according to the context (round up, round down, keep as a remainder, or express as a fraction/decimal); the same calculation can give different correct answers in different stories, so demonstrate all three readings on ONE division.
Always check with the inverse (quotient × divisor + remainder = dividend) and against an estimate; estimates should round to friendly numbers without deflating the divisor.

Multiple-choice or spot-the-error items can assess procedure and interpretation (e.g. '52 children, minibuses of 9 — how many buses?'), but recognition responses do not by themselves elicit the learner independently running their own division or exchanging counters; pair them with learner-produced working.
Discussion-only activities may support remainder interpretation but do not themselves rehearse the written layout, so combine them with worked division.
Place-value counters (physical or on-screen) are an approximation that makes exchange concrete; the written bus-stop layout is the target notation the learner must ultimately produce.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 4932 ÷ 6 = 822 exactly (822 × 6 = 4932), no remainder — confirmed. 125 ÷ 8 = 15 remainder 5 (15 × 8 = 120, +5 = 125); as a round-up container count it becomes 16 (16 × 8 = 128 ≥ 125); as a fair share, 15 and 5/8 — confirmed. 52 ÷ 9 = 5 remainder 7, so 'minibuses of 9 for 52 children' rounds up to 6 (6 × 9 = 54 ≥ 52) — confirmed.

Corrected an internal contradiction: the 'one division, three answers' activity previously used two different divisions (52÷9 and 125÷8) across its three stories, defeating its own point; it now uses 125 ÷ 8 for all three readings, with 52 ÷ 9 kept as a separate round-up example.

The source estimate '4932 ÷ 6 ≈ 5000 ÷ 5 ≈ 1000' is misleading: 1000 is far from the true quotient (~822) because rounding 6 down to 5 and 4932 up to 5000 both inflate the estimate. The activity replaces it with a closer estimate (4800 ÷ 6 = 800); the loose original wording should not be reused in learner text.
One source claim (CCSS 4.NBT.6/5.NBT.6) and the NCETM guidance are marked verified:false in the source row; the DfE claim is marked verified:true. Evidence strength is unchanged by this rewrite.
The original '3D adds nothing' framing was removed as an unsupported universal claim; no activity relies on it.

probeDeeper: When 6 didn't divide evenly into a digit, what did you do with the leftover?
What does the remainder 5 mean if these are sweets going into bags of 8?
How could you check 4,932 ÷ 6 = 822 using multiplication?
Estimate 4,932 ÷ 6 roughly — is 822 sensible?
assess.correctAnswer: 4,932 ÷ 6 = 822. 125 ÷ 8 = 15 remainder 5 (15 full bags, 5 sweets left over). The teacher watches for correct short-division bookkeeping — carrying the remainder into the next digit — and a sensible contextual reading of the final remainder.

errorPatterns.pattern: does not carry the remainder into the next column — divides each digit independently
errorPatterns.nextMove: model the carry explicitly: the leftover from each column becomes tens of the next; write the small carried digit before dividing the next place.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: quotient digits computed per-digit with no carry; answer wrong from the second column on

errorPatterns.pattern: omits a zero in the quotient when the divisor doesn't go into a place
errorPatterns.nextMove: insist every digit of the dividend yields a quotient digit — write 0 and carry the whole amount on.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: quotient has too few digits (e.g. a place skipped when 6 won't divide a small carried value)

errorPatterns.pattern: leaves the answer as 'r5' with no contextual interpretation, or rounds inappropriately for the context
errorPatterns.nextMove: ask what the leftover represents HERE (5 sweets not enough for another full bag); tie the remainder to the situation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child reports '15 r5' but cannot say what the 5 means for the bags

errorPatterns.pattern: correct method, arithmetic slip; caught by inverse check
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach; have the child verify with multiplication and estimation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: one digit wrong; check 822×6 = 4932 flags it

responseLevels.gap: fails to carry remainders between columns, omits quotient zeros, or cannot interpret the remainder.
responseLevels.full: carries remainders correctly through all columns, handles quotient zeros, interprets the final remainder in context, and checks with multiplication/estimation.
responseLevels.partial: executes short division correctly on the clean case but slips on carrying or the quotient-zero case, or leaves the remainder uninterpreted.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to compute 4,932 ÷ 6 by short division while you watch, then 125 ÷ 8 and tell you what the remainder means if these were sweets going into bags of 8. Watch how they carry the remainder from one column to the next and whether they interpret the final remainder in context.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Short division's characteristic errors are failing to carry the remainder to the next column and mishandling a place the divisor won't go into (dropping a zero). Watching the carry process, plus asking for the remainder's meaning, distinguishes procedural bookkeeping and interpretation from a merely correct-looking answer.

sources.claim: Y5 pupils divide up to 4 digits by a one-digit number using formal short division and interpret remainders appropriately for the context.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (KS1–2), Year 5 Number — multiplication and division

sources.claim: 4.NBT.6/5.NBT.6 require finding quotients using place value, properties and the ×÷ relationship, illustrated with arrays/area models.
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grades 4–5, Number & Operations in Base Ten (4.NBT.B.6, 5.NBT.B.6)

sources.claim: Short division should be grounded in place-value exchange; remainders must be interpreted according to context (round up/down/keep/fraction).

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 8-9. Read and write Roman numerals to 100 (I, V, X, L, C and combinations, incl. subtractive pairs like IV, IX, XL) and convert to/from Hindu-Arabic. The deeper aim: appreciate BY CONTRAST that our system has place value and a zero, which Roman numerals lack — illuminating why place value is powerful.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 4): 'read Roman numerals to 100 (I to C) and know that over time the numeral system changed to include the concept of zero and place value'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): not a CCSS-M topic; taught in some US curricula as enrichment/history of number.
• Operational details — Teach the symbol values and the additive rule (XVII = 10+5+1+1), then the subtractive rule (IV = 5−1, IX, XL, XC) as the tricky exception. Convert both directions. Crucially, run the CONTRAST explicitly: try 'writing' large or zero quantities in Roman and feel the absence of place value and a placeholder — making our base-ten system's efficiency vivid.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8, emerging): reads/writes additive numerals (XVII, LX). Tier B (age 8-9, secure): handles subtractive pairs (XLIV = 44) both directions. Tier C (age 9, extending): explains why Roman has no zero/place value and why that makes calculation harder.
bestPractices: Teach symbol values, then the additive rule, then subtractive pairs (IV, IX, XL, XC) as the key exception.
Practise conversion in both directions with real artefacts (clocks, dates, chapter numbers).
Run the explicit contrast: attempt a large number or 'zero' in Roman to FEEL the missing place value and placeholder.
Use the contrast to deepen appreciation of base-ten (position carries value; zero holds a place).
Watch the subtractive-notation errors (IIII vs IV, or invalid forms like IL).
keyRepresentations: Roman symbol→value reference (I,V,X,L,C)
Additive decomposition (XVII = 10+5+1+1) vs subtractive (IX = 10−1)
Side-by-side Roman | Hindu-Arabic conversion chart
Real artefacts: clock faces, monument dates, book chapters
Place-value chart as the contrast (what Roman lacks)
commonMisconceptions: Pure additive thinking, writing 4 as IIII or 9 as VIIII instead of IV/IX.
Inventing invalid subtractive forms (IL for 49 instead of XLIX).
Misordering symbols or ignoring the subtractive-position rule.
Thinking Roman numerals have a zero or place value.
Reading a subtractive pair additively (IX as 11).

learn.summary: For ages 8-9: read and write Roman numerals to 100 (I, V, X, L, C and their combinations, including subtractive pairs like IV, IX, XL, XC) and convert both ways to Hindu-Arabic numbers. The deeper aim is to appreciate BY CONTRAST that our base-ten system carries value by position and uses zero as a placeholder, which Roman numerals lack — making vivid why place value is powerful. Teach symbol values, then the additive rule (XVII = 10+5+1+1), then the subtractive rule (IV = 5-1) as the tricky exception, and run the contrast explicitly by trying to write numbers that need many repeated symbols, a very large number, and zero in Roman.

activities.title: Build-a-numeral bench with a contrast challenge
feedback: If IIII or VIIII is built, show the standard subtractive fix (IV = 5-1, IX = 10-1) and explain that a smaller symbol placed before a larger one in one of the allowed pairs (IV, IX, XL, XC) means subtract.
If an invalid form like IL is built for 49, show the valid XLIX and explain which subtractive pairs are allowed (IV, IX, XL, XC).

During the contrast challenge, place the Roman form beside the tidy base-ten numeral and name the real limits: unwieldy strings of repeated symbols (long for 88, far longer for a number like 3,000 within the taught set, with conventional large-number symbols like M lying beyond the taught set), and genuinely no symbol at all to put where our zero sits.
activities.rationale: Building and converting numerals by action with immediate correction surfaces the subtractive exception at the moment of error, and staging the 'write a long numeral / write zero' challenge lets the learner feel the absence of place value and a placeholder rather than just be told about it. A live value display and invalid-form flagging make the additive-versus-subtractive mechanism concrete; these are optional illustrations of the mechanism, not required technology.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'read Roman numerals to 100 (I to C) and know that over time the numeral system changed to include the concept of zero and place value'.
Contrasting Roman numerals with base-ten deepens appreciation of place value and the placeholder role of zero.
learnerActions: Place or drag symbol tiles (I, V, X, L, C) into a row and read the value aloud as you build, e.g. XVII = 10+5+1+1 = 17.
When you write 4 as IIII or 9 as VIIII, notice it is flagged and rewrite it the valid subtractive way (IV = 5-1, IX = 10-1).
Convert both directions: given 44, build XLIV; given XLIV, read it as 40 + 4.

Take the contrast challenge: write 88 (LXXXVIII) and notice how many repeated symbols it needs; then try a very large number like 3,000 and see how unwieldy it becomes — within the taught symbols you would need a huge string of C's, and the usual Roman form MMM uses M, a symbol beyond those you are taught; then try to write zero and find there is NO symbol at all — each shown beside the compact base-ten numeral.
activities.intendedInsight: Roman numerals combine fixed symbol values by adding (and sometimes subtracting the smaller-before-larger pair); because they have no place value and no zero placeholder, numbers with many repeats become unwieldy, very large numbers become enormous strings or need symbols beyond the basic set, and zero cannot be written at all — which is exactly why position-carries-value and a placeholder zero are powerful inventions.

activities.title: Talk to a Roman accountant about why the system changed
feedback: If the learner thinks the Roman system just needs a zero symbol added, point out that position must also carry value for zero to do its placeholder job.
Prompt the learner to connect the accountant's difficulty adding large numbers to the missing place value, not just unfamiliar symbols.
activities.rationale: A responsive dialogue may suit the history-of-number objective because the 'why did the system change?' story invites questioning and discussion; recognition tasks alone do not require the learner to articulate the reason. This is a proposed affordance rather than established superiority over other media, and it complements the building activity by foregrounding the reason behind the contrast.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'read Roman numerals to 100 (I to C) and know that over time the numeral system changed to include the concept of zero and place value'.
Contrasting Roman numerals with base-ten deepens appreciation of place value and the placeholder role of zero.
learnerActions: In role, interview a Roman merchant or scholar about how they wrote numbers and did sums.
Ask them to add two large numbers using only Roman numerals and notice where it gets hard.
Probe: why was there no way to write zero, and why did the world later adopt place value and zero?
Summarise in your own words what base-ten gives us that Roman numerals do not.
activities.intendedInsight: The history-of-number aim — that the numeral system changed over time to include zero and place value — can become meaningful through an unscripted 'why is this so hard?' exchange that carries the contrast the curriculum emphasises.

activities.title: Consolidate conversion with real artefacts and validity checks
feedback: If XLIV is read additively as 66, show that a smaller symbol before a larger one in an allowed pair (IV, IX, XL, XC) means subtract: XL = 50-10 = 40, IV = 5-1 = 4, so XLIV = 44.

If the learner says the first symbol 'is in the tens place', contrast directly: in 44 position sets value, but in XLIV each symbol keeps its own value and we add or subtract — Roman has no place value and no zero.
Reinforce the standard subtractive forms (IV, IX, XL, XC), reject invalid ones like IL, and treat IIII as a non-standard clock-face variant rather than the standard way to write 4.
activities.rationale: Conversion in both directions, validity-of-form checks and real artefacts anchor the skill in genuine contexts. Recognition and matching tasks are useful for consolidation and checking but do not by themselves require the learner to construct a full explanation, so pair them with the spoken 'how do the two 4s differ?' prompt.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'read Roman numerals to 100 (I to C) and know that over time the numeral system changed to include the concept of zero and place value'.
learnerActions: Read Roman numerals on real artefacts — clock faces, monument or building dates, book chapter numbers — and write their Hindu-Arabic values (note that many clocks show 4 as IIII, a traditional variant; the standard written form is IV).
Write given numbers (e.g. 44, 49, 88) in Roman numerals, choosing valid subtractive forms.
Decide which of several forms is valid for a number like 49 (XLIX, not IL) and explain why.
Explain aloud how the two 4s in 44 differ (40 and 4 by position) and why XLIV instead uses subtraction.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent two-way conversion and recognising valid versus invalid forms consolidate the reading/writing skill, while explaining the two 4s in 44 reinforces the place-value contrast.

activities.title: Reference chart and annotated clock face
feedback: When a learner uncovers a numeral's make-up, confirm whether it is additive (VII = 5+1+1) or subtractive (IX = 10-1).
Use the adjacent place-value chart to point out there is no column or symbol in Roman that behaves like our zero placeholder.
activities.rationale: A fixed chart or annotated image is a valuable reference and can teach symbol values, though it cannot itself be manipulated to compute values or stage the contrast — so it supports rather than replaces the building and dialogue activities.
learnerActions: Keep a symbol-to-value reference to hand (I=1, V=5, X=10, L=50, C=100).
Tap or point to each clock numeral to reveal its value and whether it is built additively or subtractively.
Use a side-by-side Roman | Hindu-Arabic chart to check your conversions, and a place-value chart alongside to see what Roman lacks.
activities.intendedInsight: A clear reference supports recall of symbol values and makes the additive/subtractive make-up of familiar numerals (like clock numbers) explicit.

constraints: The deeper objective is conceptual appreciation of place value and zero by contrast, not just symbol decoding; the contrast must be run explicitly (try to write a long numeral, a very large number, and zero in Roman).

Recognition and matching tasks consolidate and check the skill but do not by themselves elicit an independent spoken or written explanation of why our system differs; include a construct-an-explanation prompt.
A static chart or annotated image teaches symbol values and make-up but cannot be manipulated to compute values live or stage the balloon/zero contrast; treat it as a reference scaffold.

Valid subtractive forms are IV, IX, XL, XC; when writing, treat IIII and VIIII as non-standard (use IV and IX), noting that IIII is a traditional variant still seen on many clock faces, and reject invalid forms such as IL (for 49, use XLIX).
Roman numerals genuinely have no zero symbol and no positional place value — present this as the real system contrast, not as a claim about any particular teaching medium being uniquely necessary.

This topic teaches symbols I to C only; large numbers (e.g. 3,000) should be used to show how numerals become unwieldy within the taught set and that conventional large-number symbols such as M lie beyond those taught — not presented as part of the required symbol set, and not framed as literally 'running out' of symbols.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the arithmetic and logic: XVII = 10+5+1+1 = 17 (correct); XL = 50-10 = 40 and IV = 5-1 = 4, so XLIV = 44 (correct); LXXXVIII = 88 (correct); XLIX = 49 is the valid form, IL is invalid. The legacy additive misreading 'XLIV = 66' is retained only as an error pattern to correct, never as a valid answer.

The row's contrast example '3,000' is conventionally MMM (uses M, outside the taught I–C range); within the taught set it would require roughly thirty C's, i.e. an unwieldy ballooning string. It is therefore treated as a ballooning/beyond-taught illustration, NOT as a case of 'running out of symbols'. The only genuine 'no symbol at all' case is zero.

Two cited sources (CCSS-M absence note and NCETM place-value PD) are marked verified:false in the source row; the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified:true. Evidence strength is not upgraded here.
Comparative-efficacy wording about dialogue versus recognition has been softened to proposed/may phrasing; the source row does not establish superiority of any medium.

probeDeeper: In 44, how is the first 4 different from the second 4?
Does the Roman system have a symbol for zero? Why does our system need one?
Read XLIV and split it into its chunks.
assess.correctAnswer: XLIV = 44 (XL = 40 by subtraction, IV = 4 by subtraction). It differs because Roman numerals combine symbols by value with no place value and no zero, whereas in 44 the two 4s mean different amounts (40 and 4) because of their POSITION, and we use 0 to hold empty places.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads Roman numerals additively, ignoring subtractive order: XLIV = 10 + 50 + 1 + 5 = 66
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show smaller-before-larger means subtract: XL = 50 − 10 = 40, IV = 5 − 1 = 4. Re-read XLIV as 40 + 4.
errorPatterns.distractor: XLIV = 66.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child sums all symbols regardless of a smaller-before-larger pair.

errorPatterns.pattern: Imports place value into Roman numerals — thinks a symbol's position gives it a tens/ones value
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast directly: in 44 position sets value; in XLIV each symbol keeps its own value and we add/subtract. Roman has no zero and no place value.
errorPatterns.distractor: In XLIV the symbols get tens/ones values from their position, just like 44.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says the first symbol 'is in the tens place' or that our 44 and XLIV work the same way.

responseLevels.gap: Reads Roman numerals additively (XLIV = 66) or claims they work like place value.
responseLevels.full: Reads/writes Roman numerals to 100 with subtraction and explains that Roman lacks place value and zero, unlike our positional system.
responseLevels.partial: Converts simple Roman numerals but cannot articulate why our place-value system (with zero) differs.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask: 'Read XLIV for me. Now tell me: how is the Roman way of writing forty-four different from the way we write 44? How do you know?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Contrasting XLIV with 44 forces the child to articulate what place value actually does. A child who understands names position (the two 4s differ) and the role of zero; a child who doesn't either reads Roman additively (66) or wrongly imports place value into the Roman symbols. The reason tier exposes the systems contrast.

sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (Year 4 Number & place value)

sources.claim: Roman numerals are not a CCSS-M topic but appear as history-of-number enrichment in various curricula.
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics (absence of Roman numerals in the standards)

sources.claim: Contrasting Roman numerals with base-ten deepens appreciation of place value and the placeholder role of zero.
sources.source: NCETM Primary Mastery PD: Place Value (Spine 1); history-of-number pedagogy

pedagogy.summary: The right angle is the benchmark angle of Y3: a quarter turn, the corner of a square, marked with a small square. Children learn to identify it with a right-angle checker (folded paper / L-shape) and to classify other angles relative to it — less open or more open. The turn facet is quantitative: two right angles make a half turn, four make a complete turn (360°). The pedagogical goal is that the right angle becomes a reusable UNIT of comparison whose identity is independent of orientation and of arm length.
bestPractices: Make the checker: fold paper (or a circle) twice to build a right-angle tester and have children place it into real corners to test — a concrete, self-checking tool (NCETM 'Monster Right Angle Measurer').
Build right angles from turns: a quarter turn is one right angle, two quarter turns make a half turn (a straight line), four bring you back to the start; link to the four compass points.
Classify by comparison before naming: is this corner more open or less open than my checker? — establishing the less-than / greater-than idea informally ahead of the words acute/obtuse.
Vary orientation on purpose — rotate and mirror right angles off the upright — so 'right angle' is not tied to a standard L.
Connect the two facets: a quarter turn LEAVES a right angle between the start arm and the finish arm.
keyRepresentations: The right-angle checker / folded-paper tester, and the small-square right-angle mark
The clock face and compass rose showing quarter, half, three-quarter and full turns
Body turns and a hinge / geo-strip opened exactly to a right angle
The four right-angled corners of squares and rectangles
commonMisconceptions: A right angle must be 'upright' like a standard L; a rotated or mirrored one is not recognised as a right angle (orientation dependence)
A right angle drawn with long arms is 'bigger' or 'more than' one with short arms (the arm-length misconception carried over)
Any sharp-looking corner is a right angle — labelling corners by rough appearance rather than testing against the checker
Miscounting right angles in a turn — e.g. two right angles make a full turn, or a half turn returns you to the start

learn.summary: Year 3 children learn the right angle as a reusable benchmark unit: a quarter turn, the corner of a square, marked with a small square. They build and use a right-angle checker (folded paper / L-shape) to test real corners, classify other angles as less open or more open than a right angle, and compose turns from right angles (two make a half turn, four a complete turn / 360°). Key goal: the right angle's identity is independent of orientation and arm length.

activities.title: Make and use a right-angle checker
feedback: If the checker sits flush, it is a right angle — stamp the small square; a rectangular window corner should fit exactly.
If the corner is more open than a right angle, the checker's arm cannot reach the corner's other side and leaves a gap between them.

If the corner is less open than a right angle, the checker's arm overhangs past the corner's side — a pizza slice tip is usually less open than a right angle when the pizza is cut into more than four equal slices, but test it to check.
For the tilted right angle, turn the checker to match its orientation: it still fits exactly, so it is still a right angle — being 'on its side' does not change it.
For the long-armed corner, place the checker on both the long-armed and a short-armed right angle: both fit, so arm length does not make a corner 'bigger'.
(Adult note: the more-open case is an obtuse angle and the less-open case an acute angle; keep the child's language to 'more open' / 'less open' at this stage.)
activities.rationale: A concrete, self-checking tester lets children test rather than eyeball corners, intended to counter the 'sharp-looking = right angle' habit. Seeding tilted and long-armed right angles aims at the orientation-dependence and arm-length misconceptions; framing angle as opening (fit of the checker) rather than side length addresses the whole-object/side-length misconception, which the cited source notes is countered by framing angle as turn/opening.
sourceClaims: Recommended teaching reinforces that an angle is an amount of turn shown by two adjoining lines (one for the start, one for the finish); children make and use a right-angle tester (a 'Monster Right Angle Measurer') to find right angles in shapes and objects, and make right-angled turns between the four compass points.

Children judge angle size by irrelevant properties including the length of the sides (a same-size angle drawn with longer sides is judged bigger), a misconception robust from preschool through elementary years; it stems from a whole-object assumption and is countered by framing angle as the measure of turn/opening.
learnerActions: Fold a piece of paper (or a paper circle) in half and in half again to make a right-angle tester with a crisp square corner.
Place the checker into real corners around the room and on shapes — a window frame, a book corner, a slice of pizza, an open pair of scissors.
For each corner, decide: does the checker fit flush (a right angle), or is the corner less open / more open than the checker?
Mark each confirmed right angle with a small square symbol.
Deliberately test corners that are tilted off-upright and corners drawn with very long arms, turning the checker to match each corner before reading the fit.
activities.intendedInsight: A right angle is one reusable unit of comparison; a corner is a right angle only if it fits the checker exactly, regardless of how it is turned or how long its arms are.

activities.title: Build turns from right angles
feedback: If you predicted two turns to get home, notice that after two quarter turns in the same direction from your stated starting direction you are facing backwards — it takes four quarter turns in the same direction to return home.
After each quarter turn, confirm one right angle has been added; two make a half turn / straight line, four make 360°.
If you lose count, mark each quarter position on the floor or compass rose so the right angles stack visibly.
activities.rationale: Physically composing turns, with a prediction stated first against a named starting direction, surfaces the common miscount (that two right angles make a full turn, or that a half turn returns you to the start). Connecting the quarter turn to the static square corner joins the two facets of the concept.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils should identify right angles, recognise that 2 right angles make a half-turn, 3 make three-quarters of a turn and 4 a complete turn, and identify whether angles are greater than or less than a right angle.

Recommended teaching reinforces that an angle is an amount of turn shown by two adjoining lines (one for the start, one for the finish); children make and use a right-angle tester (a 'Monster Right Angle Measurer') to find right angles in shapes and objects, and make right-angled turns between the four compass points.
learnerActions: Stand facing a chosen landmark (e.g. the window). Predict: how many quarter turns will bring you back to facing exactly the way you started? Say why before turning.
Make the turns one quarter at a time, always turning the same way (e.g. all clockwise), counting one right angle each time and noticing which way you face after each.
Pause after two quarter turns: notice you are facing backwards (a half turn / straight line), not home.
Link to the four compass points and a clock face: a quarter turn is one right angle, two a half turn, three a three-quarter turn, four a full turn (360°).
With a hinge or two geo-strips, open exactly to a right angle and connect: a quarter turn leaves a right angle between the start arm and the finish arm.
activities.intendedInsight: Turns are composed of right angles: two right angles make a half turn (facing back), three make a three-quarter turn, and four make a complete turn (360°) back to the start.

activities.title: Sort and classify mixed angles
feedback: You should select the tilted and long-armed right angles as well as the upright one — all three fit the checker exactly.
Leave out the just-less and just-more angles: the checker will not sit flush on them.
Justify by fit / quarter turn / square corner, not by which way the angle points or how long its arms are.
If you missed the tilted right angle, turn the checker to match its orientation and re-test.
activities.rationale: A mixed set including a tilted and a long-armed right angle lets the task discriminate a child who tests against the benchmark from one who recognises only an upright L or judges by arm length. Asking for the reason exposes whether 'right angle' means a quarter-turn / square-corner benchmark or merely a familiar picture.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils should identify right angles, recognise that 2 right angles make a half-turn, 3 make three-quarters of a turn and 4 a complete turn, and identify whether angles are greater than or less than a right angle.

Children judge angle size by irrelevant properties including the length of the sides (a same-size angle drawn with longer sides is judged bigger), a misconception robust from preschool through elementary years; it stems from a whole-object assumption and is countered by framing angle as the measure of turn/opening.
learnerActions: Look at a set of about five angles laid out in mixed orientations: a true right angle tilted off-upright, a true right angle with very long arms, one angle just less open than a right angle, one just more open, and one obvious upright right angle.
Point to every right angle you can find, testing each with your checker rather than judging by appearance.
Sort the remaining angles into 'less open than a right angle' and 'more open than a right angle'.
Pick one angle you called a right angle and explain how you know — 'it fits my checker / it's a quarter turn / it makes a square corner'.
Order a few angles from least open to most open.
activities.intendedInsight: Classifying angles relative to the right-angle benchmark (less / equal / greater) establishes the less-than and greater-than idea informally, ahead of the words acute and obtuse, and relies on testing not appearance.

constraints: The right-angle concept is planar; turning in space or testing real 3D object corners can add interest but is not required to establish the benchmark idea.

Classification/counting questions (right / less / greater, order by openness, count right angles in a turn) can reliably assess understanding but do not by themselves elicit the hands-on testing of fitting a checker or the physical composing of turns — pair any such assessment with hands-on testing and turning.

A static picture that reveals 'right angle / not' when corners are tapped can support recognition and the small-square notation, but does not let a child test corners or compose turns; treat it as a partial scaffold for one facet only.
Deliberately include rotated/mirrored and long-armed right angles in any task so the benchmark is not tied to a standard upright L or to arm length.
When children predict turns, have them state the result relative to a stated starting direction (e.g. 'facing the window') so the count of right angles is unambiguous.
Keep child-facing language to 'less open' / 'more open' than a right angle at this stage; introduce acute/obtuse only as later vocabulary, not within these Year 3 prompts.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Removed the formal terms acute/obtuse from child-facing feedback to stay consistent with the stated goal of establishing less-open/more-open informally ahead of those words; retained them only as an adult note.

An optional on-screen version could use a draggable checker that glows green and stamps a small square on an exact fit (showing 'less open' / 'more open' otherwise) and a turn dial that adds quarter turns while a counter shows right angles (2 = facing back, 4 = home / 360°). These are illustrative interaction examples, not required mechanisms.

The source claimed 3D 'adds cost without deepening' and that an in-role dialogue 'cannot deliver' the felt fit of a checker; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the cited evidence and have been softened to scoped notes about affordances.

The source framed a quiz as assessing but 'not building checker intuition' — retained only as an objective limit that recognition/selection tasks do not themselves elicit hands-on testing; a selected-response format can still be used during teaching.
Efficacy phrasing in activity rationales was kept as 'intended/aims to' because these are unvalidated proposals; only the side-length-as-opening framing is directly supported by sources[2].claim.

assess.poeTask: Ask the child to PREDICT how many right-angle (quarter) turns it takes to end up facing exactly the way they started, and to say WHY, before doing it. Then have them make the turns one quarter at a time, counting a right angle each time and noticing where they face after two. A child who predicts two must confront landing facing backwards after two turns; the stated reason is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: This corner is tilted over on its side. Is it still a right angle? How could you check?
If you stand facing me and make two quarter turns, which way are you facing now, and how many right angles was that?
I drew this right angle with really long arms and this one with short arms. Is the long one a bigger angle? Why?
How is a right angle different from this one that's just a little bit more open than your checker?
assess.correctAnswer: Selects the true right angles regardless of orientation or arm length (including the tilted one and the long-armed one), leaves out the just-less and just-more ones, and justifies by 'it's a quarter turn / it fits my right-angle checker / it makes a square corner' rather than by how it looks or which way it points.

errorPatterns.pattern: A right angle must point up like an L; a tilted or mirrored one is not a right angle ('that one's on its side, so it's different')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rotate the checker itself onto the tilted corner so it still fits exactly — show the right angle is preserved under rotation; have the child re-test each corner with the checker turned to match.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Misses the tilted right angle and selects only upright ones

errorPatterns.pattern: The right angle with long arms is bigger / 'more than' a right angle ('its lines are longer so the corner is bigger')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Place the checker on the long-armed and the short-armed right angles in turn — both fit exactly; return to opening-not-length with the hinge.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rejects the long-armed right angle as too big, or ranks it as more open than the checker

errorPatterns.pattern: Any sharp-looking corner is a right angle ('that looks about square to me')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist on the checker — place it and read 'more open' or 'less open'; build the habit of testing rather than eyeballing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Selects the just-less and just-more angles as right angles without testing them

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscounts right angles in a turn — two right angles make a full turn, or a half turn brings you back to the start
errorPatterns.nextMove: Physically make the turns, one right angle per quarter, marking each: two land you facing backwards (a half turn / straight line), four bring you home.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked to count right angles in a turn, says two make a full turn, or cannot say four make 360°

responseLevels.gap: Recognises only the upright L as a right angle, or labels corners as right angles by appearance without testing; miscounts right angles in a turn.
responseLevels.full: Uses the right angle as an orientation- and length-independent benchmark: tests any corner against it, classifies less/greater confidently, and explains a turn as built from right angles (two make a half turn, four a full turn / 360°), transferring to new corners and turns (relational).
responseLevels.partial: Identifies upright right angles, uses the checker on standard cases, and can recall that four right angles make a full turn, but treats these as separate skills — fails on the tilted or long-armed right angle, or cannot connect the quarter turn to the static square corner (multistructural).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Lay out about five angles in mixed orientations: a true right angle tilted off-upright, a true right angle drawn with very long arms, one angle just less open than a right angle, one just more open, and one obvious right angle. Ask: 'Point to every right angle you can find.' Then: 'Pick one you chose and tell me how you know it's a right angle.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Including a tilted right angle and a long-armed right angle separates a child who tests against the quarter-turn/checker benchmark from one who recognises only an upright L or judges by arm length. The tier-2 reason exposes whether 'right angle' means a quarter-turn / square-corner benchmark or merely a familiar picture.

sources.claim: Year 3 pupils should identify right angles, recognise that 2 right angles make a half-turn, 3 make three-quarters of a turn and 4 a complete turn, and identify whether angles are greater than or less than a right angle.
sources.source: National curriculum in England: mathematics programmes of study (gov.uk)

sources.claim: Recommended teaching reinforces that an angle is an amount of turn shown by two adjoining lines (one for the start, one for the finish); children make and use a right-angle tester (a 'Monster Right Angle Measurer') to find right angles in shapes and objects, and make right-angled turns between the four compass points.
sources.source: NCETM, Misconceptions with the Key Objectives

sources.claim: Children judge angle size by irrelevant properties including the length of the sides (a same-size angle drawn with longer sides is judged bigger), a misconception robust from preschool through elementary years; it stems from a whole-object assumption and is countered by framing angle as the measure of turn/opening.
sources.source: Xu, Chen, Ma, Zhao, Jiao & Xin (2020), Frontiers in Psychology 11:568388

pedagogy.summary: Year 4 (age 8–9) draws the measures strands together: pupils ESTIMATE, COMPARE and CALCULATE across different measures — length, mass, capacity and money in pounds and pence. Three distinct skills sit here. Estimation means producing a reasoned rough value (and using it to sense-check exact work). Comparison across units requires converting to a common unit first (1.5 kg vs 1200 g → 1500 g > 1200 g). Calculation with money now uses decimal £.p as one quantity. The recurring hazard across all three is treating a measure as two separate whole numbers (2 m 30 cm, £3.47) or comparing raw digits while ignoring units.
bestPractices: Teach estimation as a deliberate step BEFORE exact calculation — round each price/measure to something friendly (£2.45 ≈ £2, 1.30 ≈ £1), get an approximate total, then compute exactly and CHECK the exact answer against the estimate.
For comparison, always convert to a common unit first and make the conversion explicit (1.5 kg = 1500 g); use double number lines or a bar to show why the digits alone can't be compared.
Use benchmarks/referents for estimation (a metre stick, a 1 kg bag, a 1-litre bottle, a £1 coin) so estimates are anchored, not guessed.
Handle money totals as single decimal quantities, aligning by the decimal point and exchanging 100p→£1; connect £.p place value to metric decimals (2.30 m, £2.30).
Make 'is this answer reasonable?' a routine — an unreasonable exact answer signals an error to find.
keyRepresentations: Benchmark referents (metre stick, 1 kg mass, 1 litre, £1 coin) for anchoring estimates
Double number line / bar model for comparing across units
Place-value columns aligned by the decimal point (metric measures and money)
Rounding number line for estimation before exact calculation
commonMisconceptions: Compares across units by digits alone, ignoring the unit ('1200 g > 1.5 kg because 1200 > 1.5').
Skips estimation and so cannot judge whether an exact answer is reasonable.
'String-length thinking' persists in totals — treats £2.45 or 2 m 30 cm as two separate whole numbers when adding.
Rounds after calculating rather than before, or rounds the wrong way, so the estimate is useless as a check.

learn.summary: Year 4 (age 8–9) learners estimate, compare and calculate across measures — length, mass, capacity and money in pounds and pence. Three distinct skills sit together: estimation (producing a reasoned rough value and using it to sense-check exact work), comparison across units (converting to a common unit first, e.g. 1.5 kg = 1500 g > 1200 g), and calculation with money as a single decimal £.p quantity. The recurring hazard across all three is treating a measure as two separate whole numbers (2 m 30 cm, £3.47) or comparing raw digits while ignoring units.

activities.title: Measure bench: estimate first, then check
feedback: If the learner skips the estimate and goes straight to an exact total: ask 'Before you worked it out exactly, what did you EXPECT the answer to be about — and does your exact answer match that?' Build the habit of rounding and adding for a ballpark first.

If an out-of-range exact answer is accepted without comment (e.g. £45 or £0.45 for the three items): point back to the estimate of about £4 and ask whether the result is plausible, then help locate the error.
If rounding happens after calculating or the wrong way, so the estimate cannot act as a check: practise rounding each amount before computing and comparing the two.
activities.rationale: Research cited here (NCETM, unverified in this row) suggests learners often skip estimating before calculating and so may lack a sense of a sensible answer, leaving errors undetected; committing the estimate before the exact value is revealed is intended to make reasonableness-checking a routine. A live estimate→reveal→gap loop (committing an estimate, then revealing the exact value and showing the error) is a proposed way to make the check concrete, not a tested intervention.
sourceClaims: Pupils rarely estimate before calculating and so lack a sense of a sensible answer, leaving errors undetected.
learnerActions: Face a task: three priced items (£2.45, £1.30, £0.75) to total, or two measures to compare.

Round each amount to something friendly (£2.45≈£2, £1.30≈£1, £0.75≈£1) and commit a rough estimate BEFORE seeing any exact answer — for example drag a slider or write the estimate down and lock it in.
Keep benchmark referents in view while estimating (a £1 coin, a metre stick, a 1 kg bag, a 1-litre bottle) so the estimate is anchored rather than guessed.
Only after the estimate is committed, reveal/compute the exact total (£4.50) and look at the gap between estimate and truth.
Decide out loud whether the exact answer is reasonable: does it land near the estimate (about £4)? If not, treat that as a flag to find an error.
activities.intendedInsight: An exact answer that lands far from a sensible estimate signals a likely error; landing near it makes the answer plausible, though it cannot catch every small slip (e.g. £4.40 instead of £4.50). Estimation is a deliberate step before calculation and a checkable habit afterwards, not an afterthought.

activities.title: Convert before you compare: the balance that tips
feedback: If the learner picks the larger NUMBER regardless of unit ('1200 g is heavier because 1200 > 1.5'): ask 'What is 1.5 kg in grams? Now which is more?' and make converting to a common unit the first step every time.
Offer the counterexample 'What if the bag were 1.5 kg and the other were 1500 g — which is heavier then?' to show they are equal once converted.
If conversion is shaky, rehearse on a double number line or balance that you can only compare like with like.
activities.rationale: Comparison across units requires converting to a common unit first; making the conversion explicit (and, optionally, physically felt on a balance or number line) targets the digits-only misconception. A 3D balance or filling a container can add physicality to mass/capacity work, though the core reasoning is numeric rather than inherently spatial.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should estimate, compare and calculate different measures, including money in pounds and pence; non-statutory guidance says they build on place value and decimal notation to record metric measures including money, and use multiplication to convert from larger to smaller units.
learnerActions: Take two measures in different units, e.g. 1.5 kg and 1200 g.
Before deciding which is larger, convert both to a common unit: 1.5 kg = 1500 g (using multiplication by 1000 from larger to smaller unit), or convert 1200 g = 1.2 kg.
Compare only once the units match: 1500 g > 1200 g, so 1.5 kg is heavier.

Optionally use a double number line or bar model to show why the raw digits (1.5 vs 1200) cannot be compared directly; a balance-scale tool that rewrites 1.5 kg as 1500 g and tips against 1200 g lets the comparison be seen rather than asserted.
Order a short set across units, e.g. 1.5 kg / 1200 g / 900 g, after converting all to grams (1500 g, 1200 g, 900 g).
activities.intendedInsight: To compare two measures reliably, first express them in the same unit; comparing the raw digits while ignoring the units can give the wrong answer (1200 > 1.5, yet 1200 g < 1.5 kg).

activities.title: Money as one quantity: totalling £.p
feedback: If the total has three digits after the point, or pounds and pence are added independently, or amounts are not lined up by the decimal point: return to £.p as one quantity, realign by the decimal point and exchange 100p for £1.
Connect back to metric decimals (2.30 m) so the same place-value reasoning transfers across measures.
Self-check the three items: pence 45+30+75 = 150p = £1.50, pounds 2+1+0 = £3, giving £4.50 — use this to confirm the total.
activities.rationale: The 'two separate whole numbers' error affects measurement as well as money (using '2 m and 30 cm' as two whole numbers instead of 230 cm), driven by whole-number language; competence with two-place money amounts does not guarantee wider decimal understanding, so handling money as a single aligned decimal quantity is deliberately taught.
sourceClaims: The 'two separate whole numbers' error affects measurement as well as money — e.g. using '2 m and 30 cm' as two whole numbers instead of 230 cm — driven by whole-number language; competence with two-place money amounts does not guarantee wider decimal understanding.
learnerActions: Total three amounts such as £2.45, £1.30 and £0.75.
Treat each amount as a single decimal quantity, not as two separate whole numbers; align the amounts by the decimal point.
Add, exchanging 100p for £1 where the pence exceed 99, to get £4.50.
Check the result reads place-value-honestly: two digits after the point, not three (£3.150 would signal pence added past 100 without exchanging).
Connect £.p place value to metric decimals written the same way, e.g. 2.30 m alongside £2.30.
activities.intendedInsight: Money totals are single decimal quantities: aligning by the decimal point and exchanging 100p→£1 avoids 'string-length thinking' that adds pounds and pence as independent whole-number columns.

activities.title: Benchmark estimation across length, mass and capacity
feedback: Ask 'Estimate the length of this classroom in metres. What did you use to help you decide — a metre stick? a stride?' to surface whether the estimate is anchored.
If an estimate seems arbitrary, point to a concrete referent (metre stick, 1 kg bag, 1-litre bottle, £1 coin) and re-anchor.
Prompt transfer: having estimated a length, ask the learner to use the same rounding-then-check move on a money total or a mass.
activities.rationale: The DfE programme of study expects pupils to estimate across different measures and to transfer the routine between measure types; anchoring estimates to physical benchmarks/referents is a pedagogy-level recommendation (from the row's best practice) rather than a directly cited finding, so it is offered as a reasoned proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should estimate, compare and calculate different measures, including money in pounds and pence; non-statutory guidance says they build on place value and decimal notation to record metric measures including money, and use multiplication to convert from larger to smaller units.
learnerActions: Estimate the length of the classroom in metres before measuring, stating what referent you used (a metre stick, a stride).
Estimate a mass against a known 1 kg bag, or a capacity against a 1-litre bottle.
Say the estimate aloud and the reasoning behind it, then measure or compute the exact value and compare.
Transfer the estimate→convert→calculate routine across length, mass, capacity and money rather than only within one measure type.
activities.intendedInsight: Good estimates come from anchoring to physical benchmarks you know, and the same estimate-then-check routine works across every measure.

constraints: Estimation must be committed BEFORE the exact value is revealed or calculated — otherwise it cannot serve as a check and becomes an afterthought.

A labelled picture or benchmark image can show what a metre, 1 kg or £1 looks like, but on its own cannot run the estimate-then-check loop or a unit conversion; use it as a referent, not as the full activity.

Recognition/ordering formats (choose-the-heavier, order these) can rehearse and check each skill crisply but do not by themselves elicit the learner's own free reasoning; pair them with prompts asking the learner to state and justify the estimate and the conversion.

A 3D balance or container adds physicality to mass/capacity comparison but is optional; the core reasoning (convert, compare, estimate) is numeric and not inherently spatial, and is not needed for money or estimation.

Interaction examples (slider to commit an estimate, a balance that rewrites 1.5 kg as 1500 g and tips, double number lines, decimal-aligned place-value columns) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory tools.

Role-play dialogue does not by itself require the learner to carry out the estimation or unit conversion this objective targets, so on its own it may not elicit the procedural steps; if used, direct it to prompt the learner to state and justify an estimate rather than relying on it to teach the procedure.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Arithmetic self-check: £2.45 + £1.30 + £0.75 = £4.50 (pence 45+30+75 = 150p = £1.50; pounds 2+1+0 = £3). This confirms the stated exact total.
Unit check: 1.5 kg = 1500 g > 1200 g, so 1.5 kg is correctly the heavier mass; the digits-only reading (1.5 < 1200) is the misconception, not a valid comparison.

One source (NCETM, 'Misconceptions with the Key Objectives') is marked verified:false in the row; its claim about learners rarely estimating is retained but treated as unverified, and the rationale wording was softened accordingly. Treating estimation-before-calculation as a habit is pedagogically reasonable but its efficacy is not independently established here.
Benchmark anchoring of estimates is drawn from the row's best-practice/pedagogy notes rather than from a directly cited source claim; it is retained as a reasoned recommendation.

The original framing that a live 2D interaction is 'exactly' the ideal and static/dialogue formats are 'poor' reflects a catalog preference, not established comparative efficacy; retained as design suggestions with stated affordances/limits rather than universal laws.

probeDeeper: 'Before you worked it out exactly, what did you EXPECT the answer to be about — and does your exact answer match that?'
'You said 1200 g is heavier — what is 1.5 kg in grams? Now which is more?'
'What if the bag were 1.5 kg and the other were 1500 g — which is heavier then?' (counterexample: equal once converted).
'Estimate the length of this classroom in metres. What did you use to help you decide — a metre stick? a stride?'
assess.correctAnswer: Gives a reasoned estimate first (≈£2 + £1 + £1 = £4, or 'about £4.50') THEN the exact £4.50, and uses the estimate to check it. For the masses: 1.5 kg is heavier because 1.5 kg = 1500 g, which is more than 1200 g — stated by converting to a common unit, not by comparing 1.5 with 1200.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares across units by the digits, ignoring the unit — 'the 1200 g is heavier because 1200 is bigger than 1.5' (or bigger than 15).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make units common first, every time: convert 1.5 kg → 1500 g (or 1200 g → 1.2 kg) on a double number line or balance, then compare; rehearse that you can only compare like with like.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks the item with the larger NUMBER regardless of unit; does not convert 1.5 kg to 1500 g before deciding.

errorPatterns.pattern: Skips estimation and cannot judge reasonableness — goes straight to an exact calculation, produces an unreasonable total (e.g. £45 or £0.45 for the three items) and doesn't notice it's wrong.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach in place: build the habit of rounding each amount and adding for a ballpark BEFORE calculating, then checking the exact answer against it — an exact answer far from the estimate flags an error to find.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: No rough answer offered before calculating; an out-of-range exact answer accepted without comment.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'String-length thinking' in the money total — treats £2.45, £1.30, £0.75 as separate whole-number columns, adding pence past 100 without exchanging (e.g. £3.150) or misaligning the decimal points.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to £.p as one quantity: align by the decimal point, exchange 100p for £1, and read the total place-value-honestly; connect to metric decimals (2.30 m).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A total with three digits after the point, or pounds and pence added independently, or amounts not lined up by the decimal point.

responseLevels.gap: Compares raw numbers ignoring units, offers no estimate, and cannot total £.p reliably; accepts unreasonable answers.
responseLevels.full: Estimates before calculating and uses the estimate to check; converts to a common unit before comparing; totals money as a single quantity; and transfers the estimate–convert–calculate routine across length, mass, capacity and money.
responseLevels.partial: Calculates exactly and/or converts for a friendly case, but does not estimate to check, or can compare only when the units already match — lists results without judging reasonableness or transferring across measure types.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put three price tags in front of the child — £2.45, £1.30, £0.75 — and say: 'First tell me ROUGHLY what these cost altogether, then work out the exact total.' Then show a 1.5 kg bag and a 1200 g bag and ask: 'Which is heavier — and how do you know?' Watch whether they estimate before calculating, and whether they convert before comparing.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has the idea estimates first (rounding sensibly) and converts to a common unit before comparing, so 1.5 kg is correctly heavier; a child who lacks it dives straight to an exact calculation with no reasonableness check, and/or judges 1200 g heavier because 1200 > 1.5 (or > 15). Estimating-before and converting-before each produce a visibly different move from the wrong ideas.
