pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 8-9. Order and compare numbers beyond 1000 with >, <, = by scanning from the highest place value down (thousands first, then hundreds, tens, ones). Directly generalises the three-digit most-significant-digit-first procedure to four digits and beyond.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 4): 'order and compare numbers beyond 1000'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.NBT.2 'compare two multi-digit numbers based on meanings of the digits in each place, using >, =, and < symbols'.
• Operational details — Reinforce the general rule 'compare the highest place first; drop to the next place only on a tie' with aligned numerals/place-value charts and number-line placement. Stress-test with same-leading-digit pairs (4,562 vs 4,526), mixed-length comparisons (987 vs 1,024) and multi-zero numbers (4,050 vs 4,005). Progress from pairs to ordering sets, using real contexts (populations, distances).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8, emerging): compares four-digit numbers with different thousands. Tier B (age 8-9, secure): orders a set beyond 1000 and states the scan rule. Tier C (age 9, extending): resolves same-leading-digit, mixed-length and multi-zero cases with place-value justification.
bestPractices: Generalise the scan: compare the highest place first, descend only on a tie — identical logic, more columns.
Align numerals/charts so digits stack by place and the deciding column is visible.
Use same-leading-digit (4,562/4,526), mixed-length (987/1,024) and multi-zero (4,050/4,005) traps.
Anchor to the number line for magnitude and connect to real large-number contexts.
Progress pair → ordered set, justifying each comparison by place value.
keyRepresentations: Aligned numerals / place-value charts stacked by place
0-10,000+ number line for magnitude
>, =, < symbols (open to larger)
Ordered card rails (smallest→largest)
Real-context data (populations, distances) as numbers to order
commonMisconceptions: Comparing by number of digits incorrectly, or by the largest single digit.
Not descending to the next place on a tie (declaring equal too early).
Mishandling multi-zero numbers (4,050 vs 4,005).
Aligning numbers to the left instead of by place value (mixed lengths).
Reversing the symbol or binding it to reading order.

learn.summary: For ages 8-9: order and compare numbers beyond 1000 using >, <, = by scanning from the highest place value down (thousands, then hundreds, tens, ones), descending to the next place only when a place ties. This generalises the three-digit most-significant-digit-first procedure to four digits and beyond, in line with the Year 4 objective to 'order and compare numbers beyond 1000'. Core moves: right-align numbers by place, compare the highest place first, and justify each decision by place value. Stress-test with same-leading-digit pairs (4,562 vs 4,526), mixed-length pairs (987 vs 1,024), and multi-zero numbers (4,050 vs 4,005). Progress from single comparisons to ordering whole sets using real contexts such as populations and distances.

activities.title: Place-aligned comparison bench
feedback: For 4,562 vs 4,526: thousands tie, hundreds tie, then the tens decide — 6 beats 2, so 4,562 > 4,526. The decision is made at the first differing place.

For 987 vs 1,024: once aligned by place, 1,024 reaches the thousands place and 987 does not, so 1,024 is larger. For whole numbers, more digits does mean larger because the number reaches a higher place; the error comes from left-aligning and comparing 9 with 1.
For 4,050 vs 4,005: thousands tie, hundreds tie, then the tens decide — 5 beats 0, so 4,050 > 4,005. Zeros still hold a place and must be compared in their column.
If the symbol was placed by scanning from the right or by picking the number with the biggest single digit, re-align the columns and restart from the leftmost place.
activities.rationale: Comparison beyond 1000 is a left-to-right place-value decision. Acting on aligned numbers and resolving the deciding place—with explicit attention to ties, zeros, and mixed lengths—targets the common errors of left-alignment, judging by the biggest single digit, and declaring equality too early. An optional interactive version can auto-align the two numbers into a stacked chart, animate the highest-place-first scan (pulsing 'tie — keep going' until the deciding column lights), swing the symbol toward the larger number, and offer a live 'order the set' rail plus number-line placement for magnitude; these examples make the mechanism concrete but are not required.
sourceClaims: Compare two multi-digit numbers based on the meanings of the digits in each place using >, =, < (4.NBT.2).
Aligning by place value and scanning most-significant-digit-first, with mixed-length and multi-zero cases, addresses the core comparison errors.
learnerActions: Take two numbers (including different lengths like 987 and 1,024) and write or place them so the digits stack by place value, right-justified into a place-value chart.
Starting at the highest place, compare column by column; mark each tied place and move down one place only when the current place is equal.
Place a > or < symbol between the numbers based on the first place that differs, and say which place decided it; use = only if every place ties.
Work the trap pairs: 4,562 vs 4,526 (same thousands and hundreds), 4,050 vs 4,005 (multi-zero), and 987 vs 1,024 (mixed length).
Then order a set of 5 numbers from smallest to largest using real data such as city populations, justifying each neighbouring comparison by place value.
activities.intendedInsight: Once two numbers are lined up by place, the larger number is decided at the first (highest) place where they differ, not by which number has a big digit somewhere. On a tie you keep going down to the next place; if every place ties, the numbers are equal. For whole numbers written without leading zeros, the number with more digits is always larger, because it reaches a higher place.

activities.title: Number-line placement for magnitude
feedback: If 999 is placed to the right of 1,001, note that 1,001 crosses into the thousands and sits further right, so 1,001 is larger even though 999 shows big 9s.
When line positions are close (e.g. 8,901 vs 8,910), fall back to the column scan: thousands and hundreds tie, then the tens decide — 1 beats 0, so 8,910 > 8,901.
activities.rationale: Anchoring comparison to magnitude on a number line connects the symbolic rule to quantity and guards against treating comparison as a symbol game detached from size. This magnitude-anchoring link is a research-informed proposal rather than a claim backed by the cited sources.
learnerActions: Place given numbers (e.g. 8,091; 8,901; 8,910) at their approximate positions on a 0–10,000 number line.
Use the positions to read off the order from smallest to largest.
Check the line ordering against the place-value scan and resolve any disagreement by column comparison.
activities.intendedInsight: Ordering reflects magnitude on the number line, and the place-value scan should agree with where numbers sit on the line.

activities.title: Convince-me: rebut the big-digit claim
feedback: A strong rebuttal: 'Line them up by place — 1,024 has a digit in the thousands and 987 does not, so 1,024 is larger. Big digits in a lower place can't beat a filled higher place.'
If the rebuttal only restates the answer, push for the reason: which place decided, and why do we start there?
activities.rationale: The skill is procedural, but a brief justification/rebuttal task reinforces place-value reasoning and is useful alongside, not instead of, hands-on comparison practice. Its efficacy over other formats is not established by the cited sources.
sourceClaims: Aligning by place value and scanning most-significant-digit-first, with mixed-length and multi-zero cases, addresses the core comparison errors.
learnerActions: Read a character's claim such as '987 > 1,024 because it has more big digits'.
Write or say a rebuttal that aligns the numbers by place and names the deciding place.
Give a second example (e.g. 999 vs 1,001) that shows why a big single digit does not make a number larger.
activities.intendedInsight: Justifying a comparison out loud forces the most-significant-place reasoning to the surface and exposes big-digit and left-alignment shortcuts as faulty.

activities.title: Annotated worked scan (reference)
feedback: Each 'tie' means keep going; the first place that differs fixes the answer — for example thousands equal, then hundreds decide.
activities.rationale: A static or tap-through worked example gives a clear reference for the scan. It supports understanding of the procedure but does not by itself provide varied practice, so pair it with the comparison bench and ordering tasks.
learnerActions: Step through a worked comparison where thousands are equal, then hundreds decide, noting at each step whether the place ties or decides.
Use this as a reference model before attempting fresh pairs independently.
activities.intendedInsight: The procedure is: compare highest place first, descend only on a tie, stop at the first differing place.

constraints: Right-align by place value, not to the left; left-alignment causes mixed-length errors such as judging 987 larger than 1,024.
On a tie at any place, descend to the next lower place rather than declaring the numbers equal; only if every place, including the ones, ties are the numbers equal.
Treat zeros as place-holders that must be compared in their column (4,050 vs 4,005 is decided in the tens).

Recognition-only formats (choosing a symbol from options) consolidate and assess but do not by themselves require the learner to construct the aligned comparison or state the deciding place; include tasks where the learner lines up numbers and justifies the order.
A worked/annotated scan is a reference scaffold, not varied practice; learners still need to compare and order fresh numbers themselves.

Interactive auto-alignment, animated scans, and live 'order the set' checking are optional illustrations of the mechanism; the same learning is achievable with aligned numerals on paper and a drawn number line.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Of the three cited sources, only the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified in the source row; the CCSS 4.NBT.2 claim and the NCETM claim are marked unverified. Treat the NCETM statement about which practices 'address the core comparison errors' as a legacy claim, not independently confirmed effectiveness evidence.

The DfE claim ('order and compare numbers beyond 1000') is a curriculum objective/topic and is reflected in the summary; it is not attached as sourceClaims support for any activity's specific teaching principle (which concerns the place-value scanning method), consistent with the number-line activity carrying [].

The legacy source asserted that a static image 'can't provide varied practice' and that magnitude ordering is 'planar' (rejecting 3D); these are catalog-fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws, and have been softened to narrowly scoped scaffold limits.

Worked example arithmetic was re-checked: 4,562 vs 4,526 decided in the tens (6>2); 4,050 vs 4,005 decided in the tens (5>0); 8,091 < 8,901 < 8,910; 8,910 vs 8,901 decided in the tens (1>0). No arithmetic errors found.
The number-line magnitude-anchoring principle and the rebuttal-task efficacy are agent proposals not directly backed by any cited source claim.

probeDeeper: Which place did you compare first? Why start there?
3,472 and 3,427 have the same digits — which is bigger and how do you know?
Order 999 and 1,001 — what makes 1,001 bigger even though 9 is a big digit?
assess.correctAnswer: 3,472 > 3,427; order 8,091 < 8,901 < 8,910; comparing from the highest place value down.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares digit-by-digit from the right, or by which number has a bigger digit somewhere, instead of from the highest place
errorPatterns.nextMove: Right-align the numbers in place-value columns and compare from the leftmost place, stopping at the first place that differs.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 3,472 vs 3,427 is judged by the ones/tens rather than the hundreds; ordering is scrambled.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses digit-count carelessly, misaligning numbers of different lengths (999 vs 1,001)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Line numbers up by columns; a number reaching a higher place (thousands) beats one that doesn't. Contrast 999 and 1,001.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A shorter number is called larger, or numbers aren't lined up by place before comparing.

responseLevels.gap: Compares by digit-count or a stray big digit; ordering ignores place value.
responseLevels.full: Compares from the highest differing place, orders numbers to 10,000 reliably, and justifies with place-value reasoning.
responseLevels.partial: Orders clearly different numbers but errs on same-digit or different-length cases.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Watch them compare and order beyond 1000. 'Put a symbol between 3,472 and 3,427. Now order these: 8,910; 8,091; 8,901. Tell me which place you looked at and why.' The 3,472/3,427 pair (same digits) forces highest-place-first reasoning.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Same-digit and near-identical numbers cannot be ordered by digit-count or first-glance size — only by scanning from the most significant differing place. Watching where the child starts (highest place) versus scanning from the right exposes the method.

pedagogy.summary: Children come to see that area and perimeter are INDEPENDENT: two shapes can share an area yet have different perimeters, and share a perimeter yet have different areas. The work is systematic — fix one quantity (say area 24 cm²) and generate rectangles that differ in perimeter (a long thin 1×24 has a large perimeter; a squarer 4×6 a smaller one). The misconception to dislodge is the intuitive 'Same A – Same B' rule (same area must mean same perimeter, and vice versa). It is best taught by having children build many shapes with a fixed area or perimeter and tabulate the other, so the variation is SEEN, not asserted — and by probing reasoning, since a correct answer can still come from the faulty intuition.
bestPractices: Fix one quantity and vary the shape systematically (all rectangles of area 24; all shapes of perimeter 20), tabulating the other so children see it change.
Confront the 'Same A – Same B' intuition head-on with counterexamples (a 3×4 and a 2×6 rectangle both have area 12 but perimeters 14 and 16).
Use squared paper and tiles so children construct and count rather than rely on a remembered rule.
Probe reasoning beyond correct answers — a right answer can come from the intuitive rule, so always ask 'why' (Tsamir & Mandel).
Link to practical intuition: a long thin field and a square field can hold the same crop area but need very different lengths of fence.
keyRepresentations: Squared paper / tile arrangements at fixed area
Table of dimensions versus perimeter (or perimeter versus area)
Long-thin-versus-square rectangle pair with equal area
Fence/string model for perimeter around a fixed area
commonMisconceptions: 'Same A – Same B': believes shapes with equal area must have equal perimeter (or that changing sides by equal-and-opposite amounts leaves both unchanged).
Conflates area and perimeter, so cannot hold one fixed while varying the other.
Thinks making a shape 'bigger' must increase area and perimeter together.

learn.summary: Children learn that knowing one of area or perimeter does NOT determine the other: two shapes can share an area yet have different perimeters, and share a perimeter yet have different areas. (They are not completely unrelated, though: for example, a fixed perimeter limits how large the area can be.) The core work is systematic — fix one quantity (e.g. area 24 cm²) and generate shapes that differ in the other, tabulating so the variation is SEEN, not asserted. The target misconception is the intuitive 'Same A – Same B' rule (same area must mean same perimeter, and vice versa). Because a correct answer can come from the faulty intuition, always probe the reasoning.

activities.title: Lock the area, watch the perimeter change
feedback: If the perimeter is reported as unchanged, re-count the edge units of the 1×24 and compare with the 4×6 — the long thin shape needs far more edge.
Prompt: 'The surface still covers 24 squares. Why does the distance around keep growing?'
A 'fence/string' overlay makes it concrete: the same crop area (24 squares) needs a longer and longer fence as the rectangle gets thinner.
activities.rationale: Fixing one quantity and tabulating the other lets children watch independence happen rather than be told it; squared paper supports constructing and counting over recalling a rule. The fence/string overlay and auto-filling table are optional supports that make the mechanism concrete.
sourceClaims: Year 6 statutory: 'recognise that shapes with the same areas can have different perimeters and vice versa'.

Year 6 Mastery PD develops the generalisations 'Shapes can have the same perimeter but different areas' and 'Shapes can have the same area but different perimeters' through matchstick/squared-paper tasks (e.g. four shapes of area 16 units² with perimeters 34, 20, 16 and 26 units), reminding children that perimeter is measured in length units and area in square units.
learnerActions: Start from a 4×6 rectangle on squared paper (or a drag-to-reshape grid) that reads 'Area 24 cm², Perimeter 20 cm'.
Reshape it to 3×8, 2×12, then 1×24, keeping the area pinned at 24 cm² each time.
After each shape, count the squares to confirm the area is still 24, then count the edge units to find the new perimeter (20, 22, 28, 50 cm).
Record each rectangle's dimensions and perimeter in a table so the growing perimeter is visible alongside the unchanged area.
Say aloud what stays the same and what changes.
activities.intendedInsight: Keeping area fixed while reshaping shows the perimeter climbing even though the covered surface is unchanged, so same area does NOT force same perimeter.

activities.title: Lock the perimeter, watch the area change
feedback: If a child expects the areas to match, compare the 5×5 (area 25) with the 1×9 (area 9) — same perimeter 20 cm, very different area.
Prompt: 'Same length of fence every time — why does the amount of ground inside change?'
activities.rationale: Showing the 'vice versa' direction (fixed perimeter, varying area) prevents a one-sided understanding and reinforces independence both ways, matching the statutory 'and vice versa'.
sourceClaims: Year 6 statutory: 'recognise that shapes with the same areas can have different perimeters and vice versa'.

Year 6 Mastery PD develops the generalisations 'Shapes can have the same perimeter but different areas' and 'Shapes can have the same area but different perimeters' through matchstick/squared-paper tasks (e.g. four shapes of area 16 units² with perimeters 34, 20, 16 and 26 units), reminding children that perimeter is measured in length units and area in square units.
learnerActions: Fix a perimeter (e.g. 20 cm) and build several rectangles that all have that perimeter: 1×9, 2×8, 3×7, 4×6, 5×5.
For each, count the squares to find the area (9, 16, 21, 24, 25 cm²) and record it in a table.
Note which shape gives the largest area and which the smallest for the same perimeter.
activities.intendedInsight: With perimeter held constant, the area varies — so same perimeter does NOT force same area either; in both directions, fixing one quantity does not fix the other (although the fixed perimeter does cap the area: here the 5×5 square gives the most).

activities.title: The string test (predict, then check)
feedback: If the prediction was 'same area so same distance around', treat that stated reason as the thing to revisit: count the edges of each before and after testing with the string.
If a child argues 3×4→2×6 'takes off one and adds on, so it evens out', compute both perimeters explicitly (14 vs 16) — the changes do NOT cancel; the perimeter changed even though the area did not.
If area and perimeter are reported as a single number, re-separate the meanings: area is the squares covered, perimeter is the distance around.
activities.rationale: A predict-observe-explain task with an actual counterexample surfaces the reasoning that produced the answer, so a lucky correct area is not mistaken for understanding. Asking for a fresh example checks that the child can generalise rather than treat it as a one-off.
sourceClaims: Many learners hold the intuitive 'Same A – Same B' rule (same perimeter → same area; same area → same perimeter). Counterexample: a 3×4 and a 2×6 rectangle both have area 12 but perimeters 14 and 16. Learners believe increasing one pair of sides and decreasing the other by the same amount leaves area and perimeter unchanged ('is like you did nothing'). Correct answers found via an intuitive rule do not reflect understanding (Tsamir & Mandel 2000), so teachers must probe further.
learnerActions: Look at a 3×4 rectangle and a 2×6 rectangle on squared paper; confirm both have area 12 cm² by counting squares.
PREDICT whether one loop of string will go exactly around both, and say WHY before testing.
Lay the string around each and measure: the 3×4 needs 14 cm, the 2×6 needs 16 cm.
Draw a THIRD rectangle with area 12 but yet another perimeter, and find the largest perimeter you can make for area 12 (with whole-number sides, the thinnest 1×12 gives 26 cm).
activities.intendedInsight: Both rectangles cover the same area (12 cm²) but their perimeters differ (14 cm and 16 cm) — a direct counterexample to 'Same A – Same B'.

activities.title: Convince the sceptic
feedback: If the child only states the answer, push for the justification tied to a specific pair (e.g. 3×4 vs 2×6, or 1×9 vs 5×5).

If the child agrees 'bigger area always means bigger perimeter', give a direct counterexample: a 5×5 square (area 25 cm², perimeter 20 cm) has a LARGER area than a 1×24 rectangle (area 24 cm², perimeter 50 cm) yet a much SMALLER perimeter — so a bigger area does not force a bigger perimeter.
activities.rationale: Requiring the child to construct an argument and generate counterexamples targets the reasoning the misconception rule hides. This dialogue form builds explanation but, on its own, does not provide the visual variation the construction tasks do, so pair it with them.
sourceClaims: Many learners hold the intuitive 'Same A – Same B' rule (same perimeter → same area; same area → same perimeter). Counterexample: a 3×4 and a 2×6 rectangle both have area 12 but perimeters 14 and 16. Learners believe increasing one pair of sides and decreasing the other by the same amount leaves area and perimeter unchanged ('is like you did nothing'). Correct answers found via an intuitive rule do not reflect understanding (Tsamir & Mandel 2000), so teachers must probe further.
learnerActions: Respond to a character who insists 'same area must mean same perimeter' and 'bigger area always means bigger perimeter'.
Build or draw counterexamples and use them to explain, in your own words, why the character is wrong.
Answer the follow-up: 'If two shapes have the same perimeter, must they have the same area? Show me two that don't.'
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the reason — that area and perimeter vary separately — consolidates understanding beyond producing a correct answer.

constraints: Perimeter is measured in length units (cm) and area in square units (cm²); keep these distinct when recording and comparing.
A correct answer can still come from the faulty 'Same A – Same B' intuition, so always ask 'why' and require a justification or a fresh example.

Multiple-choice or sequencing items can diagnose the misconception via distractors but do not by themselves produce the 'aha'; pair any recognition task with construction (drawing/building and counting).
A single static equal-area pair with revealed perimeters gives one counterexample but does not let the child vary the shape; use it as a starter, not the whole lesson.
Use squared paper or tiles so children construct and count rather than rely on a remembered rule.

To refute 'bigger area always means bigger perimeter', use a pair where the larger-area shape has the smaller perimeter (e.g. 5×5 area 25, P 20 vs 1×24 area 24, P 50); an equal-area pair alone does not address a 'bigger area' claim directly.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

All quantitative examples were re-checked: area-24 rectangles 4×6 (P=20), 3×8 (P=22), 2×12 (P=28), 1×24 (P=50) are correct; perimeter-20 rectangles 1×9 (A=9), 2×8 (A=16), 3×7 (A=21), 4×6 (A=24), 5×5 (A=25) are correct; the 3×4 (A=12, P=14) and 2×6 (A=12, P=16) counterexample is correct; the 5×5 (A=25, P=20) vs 1×24 (A=24, P=50) counterexample for 'bigger area' is correct.

The original 'possible: 3D adds nothing' claim was dropped as an unsupported universal; the topic is planar so 2D construction is the natural medium, but this is a scope note, not a proven claim about 3D's inability to teach.

The non-preferred conversation and static-image approaches are retained as 'Convince the sceptic' and a starter scaffold respectively, with their limitations noted in constraints rather than as universal laws.

The 'largest perimeter for area 12' answer (1×12 → 26 cm) holds only for whole-number-sided rectangles as used in these Year 6 tasks; for arbitrary shapes perimeter is unbounded, so frame the question within the rectangle context.

assess.poeTask: Show the two rectangles (3×4 and 2×6) and a length of string. Ask the child to PREDICT whether the same loop of string will go exactly around both — given they cover the same area — and to say WHY before testing. Then lay the string around each: the 3×4 needs 14 cm, the 2×6 needs 16 cm. The reason given before observing (typically 'same area so same distance around') is the diagnostic part; the string makes the independence undeniable.
probeDeeper: You said the areas are equal — count the squares to check. Now count the edge lengths. Are the perimeters equal?
Can you draw a THIRD rectangle with area 12 but a different perimeter again? What is the largest perimeter you can make?
If two shapes have the same perimeter, must they have the same area? Show me two that don't.
A friend says 'bigger area always means bigger perimeter.' Is that always true?
assess.correctAnswer: Both have area 12 cm² (same area), but their perimeters are 14 cm and 16 cm (different) — so the same area can have different perimeters; area and perimeter are independent.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Same A – Same B': because the areas are equal, concludes the perimeters must be equal too.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the edge units of each on squared paper; tabulate several equal-area rectangles and their differing perimeters so the independence is seen, then re-ask.
errorPatterns.distractor: Same area and same perimeter — if the area is the same, the distance around must be the same too.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the perimeters are the same 'because the areas are the same'.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'It balances out': reasons that shrinking one side and growing another leaves both area and perimeter unchanged.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compute both quantities for each rectangle explicitly and show the perimeter changed even though the area did not; stress the changes do not cancel.
errorPatterns.distractor: The perimeter stays the same because one side got shorter while the other got longer.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Argues going from 3×4 to 2×6 'takes off one and adds on, so it evens out' and both stay equal.

errorPatterns.pattern: Conflates area and perimeter, computing one and reporting it as both.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-separate the meanings — area as covered squares, perimeter as distance around — before comparing the two rectangles.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives a single number for 'area and perimeter', or measures the distance around when asked about area.

responseLevels.gap: Asserts that equal area forces equal perimeter (Same A – Same B) with no checking.
responseLevels.full: Shows the areas equal and perimeters different, explains that area and perimeter vary independently, and generates further shapes with fixed area and changing perimeter (or vice versa).
responseLevels.partial: Correctly finds both quantities for the given pair but treats it as a one-off, or reaches the right answer via 'it balances out' without seeing area and perimeter as independent; cannot generate a new example.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are two rectangles: one is 3 cm by 4 cm, the other 2 cm by 6 cm. Do they have the same area? Do they have the same perimeter? Explain your reasoning.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child holding 'Same A – Same B' and a child who understands independence give OPPOSITE answers to 'same perimeter?'. The reason they state — areas equal therefore perimeters equal, versus area and perimeter vary separately — exposes which, so a lucky correct area is not mistaken for understanding.

pedagogy.summary: Children extend rectangle area to parallelograms (A = base × perpendicular height) and triangles (A = ½ × base × perpendicular height). The formulae are best DERIVED, not told: a parallelogram is cut and rearranged into a rectangle of equal area, and two identical triangles join to make a parallelogram or rectangle, so a triangle is half of it — which is why we divide by two. The load-bearing ideas are that the height must be the PERPENDICULAR distance to the base (not a slant side), that any side can serve as the base with its matching perpendicular height, and that the halving step follows from the dissection rather than being an arbitrary rule.
bestPractices: Derive each formula by dissection: rearrange a parallelogram into a rectangle; join two copies of a triangle into a parallelogram so the triangle is half of it.
Insist the height is perpendicular to the chosen base; have children mark the right angle and show non-examples of lines that are NOT the perpendicular height.
Include shapes in varied orientations so children see the base need not be horizontal and any side can be the base with its own perpendicular height.
Deliberately give diagrams with a decoy slant length (e.g. base 7, height 6, slant 8) so children practise selecting the perpendicular height and ignoring unnecessary numbers.
Tie the ÷2 to the two-triangles-make-a-parallelogram image so halving is meaningful and not forgotten.
keyRepresentations: Parallelogram cut-and-rearranged into a rectangle
Two congruent triangles joined into a parallelogram/rectangle
Right-angle mark showing base–height perpendicularity
Rotated shapes with base and perpendicular height labelled
Decoy-slant diagrams (extra unnecessary length shown)
commonMisconceptions: Uses the slant side instead of the perpendicular height, partly from believing every number given must be used.
Forgets to halve for a triangle (computes base × height and stops).
Thinks the base must be the horizontal or bottom side, so cannot identify base and height in rotated or obtuse triangles.

learn.summary: Year 6 learners derive and apply area formulae for parallelograms (A = base × perpendicular height) and triangles (A = ½ × base × perpendicular height) through dissection rather than being told the rules. A parallelogram is cut and rearranged into an equal-area rectangle; two congruent triangles are joined into a parallelogram so a triangle is seen to be exactly half (justifying the ÷2). The load-bearing ideas are: the height must be the PERPENDICULAR distance to the chosen base (not a slant side), any side can be the base with its own matching perpendicular height, and the halving step follows from the dissection rather than being an arbitrary rule. Decoy slant lengths teach that a 'given' number is not always a 'needed' number.

activities.title: Dissection workbench: rearrange to reveal the formulae
feedback: If the rearranged pieces form a rectangle of equal area, confirm that base × perpendicular height must therefore be the parallelogram's area.
When two congruent triangles snap into a parallelogram, point out that one triangle is exactly half, so we halve the product — this is why the ÷2 is there, not an arbitrary rule.
If a learner uses the slant side, mark the right angle and show the height must meet the base at 90°; the slant is longer and does not measure the perpendicular distance.

If a learner is stuck because the base is not at the bottom, rotate the shape and show any side can serve as the base with its own perpendicular height: for a triangle, this runs to the opposite vertex (or meets the extended base line if the triangle is obtuse); for a parallelogram, it runs to the opposite side.
activities.rationale: The national curriculum expects pupils to relate rectangle area to parallelograms and triangles by dissection and to understand the formulae, and the NCETM spine derives the ÷2 from joining two congruent triangles. A hands-on or on-screen rearrangement makes the derivation and the perpendicular-height requirement visible rather than told.
sourceClaims: Year 6 statutory: 'calculate the area of parallelograms and triangles'. Non-statutory: pupils 'relate the area of rectangles to parallelograms and triangles, for example, by dissection, and calculate their areas, understanding and using the formulae (in words or symbols) to do this'.

Area of parallelogram = base × perpendicular height; triangle = base × perpendicular height ÷ 2. Teachers must 'include examples of lines that are not the perpendicular height' and 'remind children that the line must be at 90° to the base'; show the base 'is not necessarily from the horizontal plane, and that any of the sides can be used as the base'; a 'who is right?' task uses a triangle with sides 8, 6 (perpendicular height) and 10 (slant); the ÷2 is derived because 'two triangles that are the same can be joined to make a parallelogram'; 'children may forget to halve after multiplying the base and the perpendicular height'.
learnerActions: Take a parallelogram whose perpendicular height from a top corner lands on the base. Cut along that height to remove a right-angled triangle, then slide it to the other end so it forms a rectangle of the SAME area. Confirm that base × perpendicular height is the area, because the rectangle's length and width are the parallelogram's base and perpendicular height.
Take a triangle, duplicate and rotate the copy, and fit the two copies together into a parallelogram; observe that the single triangle is exactly HALF, so its area is base × perpendicular height ÷ 2.
Place or drag the height line so it meets the base at 90°, marking the right angle; check a line that is NOT perpendicular and explain why it is not the height.
Rotate the shape so the base is no longer horizontal, then identify which side is now the base and where its perpendicular height falls.
Work with a diagram that includes a decoy slant length (e.g. base 7, perpendicular height 6, slant 8) and deliberately ignore the slant when computing the area.
activities.intendedInsight: The area formulae are consequences of rearranging shapes: a parallelogram is a rectangle in disguise, and a triangle is half a parallelogram, which is where the ÷2 comes from. The height is always perpendicular to whichever side is chosen as the base, and not every given number is needed.

activities.title: Paper-and-scissors dissection (hands-on alternative)
feedback: Because the rectangle is made from exactly the same pieces with no gaps or overlaps, it has the same area as the parallelogram; if the measured rectangle length and width match the parallelogram's base and perpendicular height (allowing for small measuring and cutting errors), that shows why base × perpendicular height gives the area.
If a learner draws the height to a slanted side rather than perpendicular to the base, have them use a right-angle check and redraw to the opposite vertex.
activities.rationale: Paper dissection achieves the same curriculum-specified derivation as an on-screen workbench and offers a tactile route; both make the rearrangement something the learner performs rather than watches. Paper cutouts have slight real thickness, so treat them as approximations of the ideal flat (zero-thickness) figures they represent.
sourceClaims: Year 6 statutory: 'calculate the area of parallelograms and triangles'. Non-statutory: pupils 'relate the area of rectangles to parallelograms and triangles, for example, by dissection, and calculate their areas, understanding and using the formulae (in words or symbols) to do this'.
learnerActions: Cut out a paper parallelogram, draw its perpendicular height, snip along it to remove a right-angled triangle and slide it across to physically make a rectangle; measure the rectangle's length and width and compare them with the parallelogram's base and perpendicular height.
Cut two identical paper triangles and fit them together to make a parallelogram or rectangle; state in words why one triangle is half.
Physically turn a triangle so a different side is the base, then draw the perpendicular height from the opposite vertex to that base and mark the right angle.
activities.intendedInsight: Physically cutting and rearranging makes the equal-area and 'half of a parallelogram' relationships concrete, and turning the paper shape shows the base does not have to be horizontal.

activities.title: 'Who is right?' and calculation practice with decoy lengths
feedback: If a learner reaches for the 8 cm slant, point to the right-angle mark: only the length perpendicular to the base measures the height; the slant is extra information.
If a learner stops at 7 × 6 = 42 for a triangle, send them back to the two-triangles image: one triangle is half, so halve to get 21 cm².
If a learner halves a parallelogram, show that a parallelogram IS the whole rectangle-equivalent, so no halving — the ÷2 belongs only to the triangle.
activities.rationale: Calculation items with decoy slants and 'who is right?' prompts directly surface the slant-height and forgot-to-halve errors flagged in the curriculum guidance. This activity checks and consolidates fluency; it is weaker at building the dissection insight, so it should follow the derivation work.
sourceClaims: Area of parallelogram = base × perpendicular height; triangle = base × perpendicular height ÷ 2. Teachers must 'include examples of lines that are not the perpendicular height' and 'remind children that the line must be at 90° to the base'; show the base 'is not necessarily from the horizontal plane, and that any of the sides can be used as the base'; a 'who is right?' task uses a triangle with sides 8, 6 (perpendicular height) and 10 (slant); the ÷2 is derived because 'two triangles that are the same can be joined to make a parallelogram'; 'children may forget to halve after multiplying the base and the perpendicular height'.
learnerActions: Compute the area of a triangle given a base, a marked perpendicular height and a decoy slant length, choosing the correct length and halving (e.g. base 7, perpendicular height 6, slant 8 → 7 × 6 ÷ 2 = 21 cm²).
Compute the area of a triangle with base 12 cm and perpendicular height 7 cm, halving the product: 12 × 7 ÷ 2 = 42 cm².
Decide in a 'who is right?' task which of two learners picked the correct length for the height, and justify the choice using the right-angle mark.

Complete a worked step that forces the ÷2 explicitly, and separately compute a parallelogram area without halving (e.g. base 8, perpendicular height 5 → 40 cm²) to show that ÷2 is NOT applied to parallelograms.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency in selecting the perpendicular height, ignoring unnecessary numbers, and applying the ÷2 only to triangles, while being able to justify each choice.

activities.title: Diagnostic: two shapes with decoy slants
feedback: Correct responses: triangle = 7 × 6 ÷ 2 = 21 cm²; parallelogram = 8 × 5 = 40 cm². Probe with 'why divide by two for the triangle but not the parallelogram?' and 'why didn't you use the 8 cm?'
Ask 'if I turn this triangle so the 7 cm side is at the top, does its area change? Which side is the base now?' The area is unchanged; this checks that the base need not be horizontal.
Invite the learner to show, by cutting or drawing, why a triangle is half a parallelogram, to test whether the ÷2 is understood or merely memorised.
activities.rationale: Requesting both shapes with a decoy slant separates a child who applies the formula relationally from one who plugs in whatever numbers appear; the wrong-length choice and a missing (or wrongly applied) ÷2 become visible in the working.
sourceClaims: Area of parallelogram = base × perpendicular height; triangle = base × perpendicular height ÷ 2. Teachers must 'include examples of lines that are not the perpendicular height' and 'remind children that the line must be at 90° to the base'; show the base 'is not necessarily from the horizontal plane, and that any of the sides can be used as the base'; a 'who is right?' task uses a triangle with sides 8, 6 (perpendicular height) and 10 (slant); the ÷2 is derived because 'two triangles that are the same can be joined to make a parallelogram'; 'children may forget to halve after multiplying the base and the perpendicular height'.
learnerActions: Given a triangle labelled base 7 cm, perpendicular height 6 cm (right angle marked to the base) and slant side 8 cm, find its area.
Given a parallelogram with base 8 cm, perpendicular height 5 cm and a longer slant side shown, find its area.
Explain aloud which lengths were used and why: why the triangle is halved and the parallelogram is not, and why the 8 cm slant was ignored.
activities.intendedInsight: Demonstrates relational understanding: selecting the perpendicular height, ignoring the decoy, halving only the triangle, and justifying the ½ via two-triangles-make-a-parallelogram.

constraints: The height must always be the PERPENDICULAR distance to the chosen base (meeting it at 90°), never a slant side; have learners mark the right angle and examine lines that are NOT the perpendicular height.

Any side can serve as the base with its own matching perpendicular height; include shapes in varied orientations (including rotated and obtuse triangles) so learners do not assume the base is horizontal or at the bottom.
Tie the ÷2 to the two-congruent-triangles-make-a-parallelogram image so halving is meaningful; apply ÷2 only to triangles, not parallelograms.
Include decoy slant lengths so learners practise selecting needed lengths: a 'given' number is not always a 'needed' number.
Calculation/'who is right?' practice checks and consolidates fluency but does the least to build the dissection insight; it should follow, not replace, the rearrangement work.

Tap-to-reveal static diagrams can show the dissection steps but do not let the learner perform the rearrangement; a live on-screen manipulation or physical paper cutting lets the learner carry out the cut-and-rearrange themselves.
Paper cutouts have slight real thickness and are approximations of the ideal flat (zero-thickness) figures; distinguish the represented plane shape from its physical model.
Re-secure rectangle and parallelogram area first, as a prerequisite, if a learner has no sense of perpendicular height.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy source labelled the 2D interactive 'ideal' and rated 3D and conversation formats 'poor' ('3D adds nothing'); these are catalog fit rankings, not established pedagogical laws. The parallelogram and triangle derivation is genuinely planar, so 3D offers no obvious affordance here, but this is not asserted as a universal necessity, and a dialogue or static image can still support the ideas even if less suited to the hands-on rearrangement.

The two cited sources list different example dimensions (the NCETM 'who is right?' triangle uses sides 8, 6 perpendicular height, 10 slant; the diagnostic uses base 7, height 6, slant 8). Both are preserved as distinct decoy examples. Self-audit confirms 7 × 6 ÷ 2 = 21 cm², 8 × 5 = 40 cm², and 12 × 7 ÷ 2 = 42 cm² are arithmetically correct.

The diagnostic's slant 8 with base 7 and perpendicular height 6 is a decoy figure (7, 6, 8 do not form a right triangle), which is pedagogically fine as an 'ignore the extra number' task; it is not presented as a Pythagorean triple and should not be treated as a geometrically exact scale drawing.
An internal prerequisite catalog ID present in the source row was removed from learner-facing guidance; the prerequisite concept (re-securing rectangle/parallelogram area) is retained.

probeDeeper: Why do you divide by two for the triangle but not the parallelogram?
The 8 cm was written on the triangle — why didn't you use it?
If I turn this triangle so the 7 cm side is at the top, does its area change? Which side is the base now?
Show me, by cutting or drawing, why a triangle is half a parallelogram.
assess.correctAnswer: Triangle area = 7 × 6 ÷ 2 = 21 cm² (uses the perpendicular height, ignores the 8 cm slant, halves); parallelogram area = 8 × 5 = 40 cm² (base × perpendicular height, not the slant).

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses the slant side instead of the perpendicular height, believing every number given must be used.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Mark the right angle and show the height must meet the base at 90°; give tasks with unnecessary numbers so 'given' does not mean 'needed'. Re-secure rectangle/parallelogram area first.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Computes 7×8÷2 or 8×5, reaching for the 8 cm slant rather than the marked perpendicular height.

errorPatterns.pattern: Forgets to halve for the triangle.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to two-congruent-triangles-make-a-parallelogram so the child sees the triangle is half; do not simply tell them to divide — make the halving mean something.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives 7 × 6 = 42 cm² for the triangle, with no ÷2.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks the base must be horizontal/bottom, so cannot identify base and height in a rotated or obtuse triangle.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rotate the shape physically; show any side can be the base and the height is the perpendicular distance to the opposite vertex from THAT base.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a rotated shape, measures a slanted side as the height, or is stuck because the base is not at the bottom.

responseLevels.gap: Grabs any two numbers (often the slant) and multiplies; no sense of perpendicular height and no halving.
responseLevels.full: Selects the perpendicular height, ignores the decoy slant, halves for the triangle, handles rotated shapes, and justifies the ½ via two-triangles-make-a-parallelogram.
responseLevels.partial: Uses the perpendicular height OR halves but not both reliably, or succeeds only when the base is horizontal; applies the formula without connecting it to the dissection.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Hand the child a triangle labelled base 7 cm, perpendicular height 6 cm (right angle marked to the base) and a slant side 8 cm, plus a parallelogram with base 8 cm, perpendicular height 5 cm and a longer slant side shown. Say: 'Find the area of each.' Then WATCH which lengths they choose, whether they use the perpendicular height rather than the 8 cm slant, whether they halve for the triangle, and whether they can say why.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The decoy slant (8 cm) plus a request for both shapes separates a child who knows the formula relationally from one who plugs in whatever numbers appear: the wrong-number choice and a missing ÷2 are visible in the working, and the parallelogram checks whether 'divide by two' is applied blindly to it as well.

pedagogy.summary: Children learn to describe 3-D solids by three distinct properties — faces, edges and vertices — and to count each for common solids (canonically: a cube has 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices). The two teaching challenges are (1) keeping the three properties distinct (a face is a flat 2-D surface, an edge is the straight line where two faces meet, a vertex is the point where edges meet) rather than blurring them under everyday words like 'side' and 'corner', and (2) counting reliably including the hidden features on the far side. It is best taught by handling real solids and counting each property by touch in a fixed order, marking features as they are counted, and being explicit about how curved solids are described.
bestPractices: Count by touch in a fixed order — colour or number each face, trace each edge, dot each vertex — so the three properties stay distinct and nothing is double-counted or missed.
Hand children the real solid to turn while looking at pictures of it, so hidden faces, edges and vertices are included in the count rather than only the visible ones.
Define each term against the object: a face is a flat surface (itself a 2-D shape), an edge is the straight line where two faces meet, a vertex is the corner where edges meet.

Be explicit about curved solids: a curved surface is described as a 'curved surface', not a face, and the curved boundary is not an edge — and note that schemes differ, so state the convention being used.
Connect faces to 2-D shapes and (later) to nets, where each face appears as a separate flat shape, reinforcing the face count.
keyRepresentations: Handleable solids (cube, cuboid, pyramid, sphere, cylinder, cone) counted by touch
Colour-a-face / trace-an-edge / dot-a-vertex marking system while counting
Nets that fold up into the solid, showing each face as a separate 2-D shape
A cube-vs-cylinder pair to contrast flat faces with a curved surface
commonMisconceptions: Blurs faces, edges and vertices under everyday words, calling edges 'sides' and vertices 'corners' so the three properties run together when counting.
Counts only the faces/edges/vertices that are visible, missing the hidden ones on the far side (gives a cube 3 faces, 9 edges or 4 corners).
Counts a curved surface as a 'face' and the curved boundary line as an 'edge' (e.g. says a cylinder has 3 faces).
Treats the whole solid as if it were the 2-D shape of a face, not distinguishing the flat face from the 3-D object.

learn.summary: Children aged 6-7 learn to describe common 3-D solids by three distinct properties — faces (flat surfaces, each itself a 2-D shape), edges (the straight line where two faces meet) and vertices (the corner where edges meet) — and to count each reliably for solids such as a cube (6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices). The two core challenges are keeping the three properties distinct rather than blurring them under everyday words like 'side' and 'corner', and counting the hidden features on the far side rather than only those visible. A well-supported route for this age is handling real solids (including while looking at a flat picture of the same solid), counting each property by touch in a fixed order with a marking system, and being explicit about how curved solids are described.

activities.title: Count a real cube by touch in a fixed order
feedback: If a child calls an edge a 'side' or a vertex a 'corner' and runs the properties together, pause and name each property against the object as they touch it: 'This flat part is a face; this straight line where two faces meet is an edge; this point where edges meet is a vertex.'
If the recount from a different starting face gives a different total, the marking slipped — re-mark systematically so each feature is counted exactly once.
If a child reaches only 3 faces or 9 edges, prompt: 'Turn the cube over — are there features round the back you haven't marked yet?'
activities.rationale: Faces, edges and vertices are spatial properties; counting by touch in a fixed order with a marking system keeps the three distinct and ensures hidden features are included. Handling the real solid while naming each property is a recommended approach for this age.
sourceClaims: A curved surface is NOT a face and the curved line where a curved surface meets a flat face is NOT an edge; each face of a 3-D shape is a 2-D shape; an edge is the straight line where two faces meet and a vertex is the corner where edges meet; handling solids while viewing images supports counting faces, edges and vertices. Curved solids are described with a 'curved surface' (e.g. cylinder = two circular faces + one curved surface).
KS1/early-years practice: attend to 3-D properties (edges, faces, vertices), handle real objects, and count by physically tracking features; each face relates to a 2-D shape.
learnerActions: Hold a real cube and turn it in your hands.
Count the faces first: colour or number each flat surface as you touch it, saying 'face' each time, until every face is marked. Record the total.
Then trace each edge with a finger, marking each traced edge (e.g. a gold line or sticker), saying 'edge' each time, until all are traced. Record the total.
Then dot each vertex (corner) with a sticker, saying 'vertex' each time. Record the total.
Recount starting from a different face to check your totals stay the same (6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices).
activities.intendedInsight: A face, an edge and a vertex are three different things; counting each property separately in a fixed order, and marking features as you go, keeps them distinct and makes sure nothing hidden is missed or double-counted.

activities.title: Predict then count the hidden features
feedback: A child who predicts around 9 edges (the most you can see at once, when three faces are showing) is reasoning only about the visible faces — celebrate noticing the gap when the far-side edges bring the total to 12. (The '9' is a rough illustrative expectation, not a measured value; from one view you see at most 3 faces, 9 edges and 7 vertices.)

If a child reads all the information straight from the flat picture, prompt them to turn the real solid to check for features the picture hides; the point is linking the 2-D view to the full 3-D object.
If a friend's claim is used ('a cube has 3 faces because they can only see 3'), ask the child to explain, turning the cube, why that friend missed some.
Reinforce that recounting from a different face should reach the same total once hidden features are included.
activities.rationale: Under-counting arises specifically from representing only the visible side of a 3-D figure and difficulty translating a 2-D representation into the full 3-D structure; a predict-then-count routine that pairs a flat picture with the real solid and forces attention to the hidden back is intended to target this error.
sourceClaims: Students represent only the visible side of a 3-D figure and under-count features that are not directly visible, reflecting difficulty translating a 2-D representation into the full 3-D structure — grounds the hidden-feature under-count when counting faces/edges/vertices.
learnerActions: Before counting, look at a cube and predict out loud how many edges it has altogether, saying your number first.
Look at a flat picture or drawing of the cube next to the real cube, and point out which edges, faces and corners in the picture are hidden from view.
Now trace and mark every edge on the real cube together, turning it so the far side comes into view and you find the hidden features from the picture.
Compare your prediction with the counted total of 12, and talk about the edges 'round the back' you could not see at first.
Repeat the routine for vertices and faces: each time, predict the visible-only number aloud first, then turn the real solid to reach the full totals (8 vertices, 6 faces).
activities.intendedInsight: A solid has features on its hidden far side that a flat picture does not show directly; a count based only on what you can see is too small, so you must turn the real object to catch every feature.

activities.title: Flat face versus curved surface
feedback: If a child says a cylinder has 3 faces, have them feel the round wall and ask whether it is flat like a face — then introduce 'curved surface' for it.
State explicitly which convention you are using, because schemes differ in how they describe curved solids; tell the child the rule you are following so they are not confused by other wording.
Reinforce by linking each flat face to the 2-D shape it matches (the circular faces of the cylinder, the square faces of the cube).
activities.rationale: The curved-surface distinction is an explicit curriculum convention that must be taught directly and stated, since schemes differ; feeling flat versus curved on real solids makes the distinction concrete.
sourceClaims: A curved surface is NOT a face and the curved line where a curved surface meets a flat face is NOT an edge; each face of a 3-D shape is a 2-D shape; an edge is the straight line where two faces meet and a vertex is the corner where edges meet; handling solids while viewing images supports counting faces, edges and vertices. Curved solids are described with a 'curved surface' (e.g. cylinder = two circular faces + one curved surface).
learnerActions: Hold a cylinder and run a hand over the round wall and over the flat ends.
Count the flat faces — the two circles on a cylinder — and mark them.
Decide whether the round wall is a face: feel that it is not flat, and name it a 'curved surface' rather than a face.
Check the circle-to-curve boundary: is it a straight line where two flat faces meet? Under the convention we are using, if not, it is not counted as an edge (some schemes call it a curved edge).
Say the full description: a cylinder has two flat (circular) faces and one curved surface.
Then repeat with a cone and note it has one flat circular face, one curved surface, and a single pointed apex; say whether your scheme calls the apex a vertex, since no edges meet there.
Compare the solids directly with the cube to contrast flat faces with a curved surface.
activities.intendedInsight: Under the convention used here, a face is a flat surface and an edge is a straight line where two flat faces meet; the round part of a cylinder or cone is described as a curved surface, not a face, and its curved boundary is not counted as an edge, while a cone has a pointed apex that many schemes call a vertex even though no edges meet there.

activities.title: Faces as 2-D shapes and nets
feedback: For a flat-faced solid, if the number of shapes in the net does not match the touch-count of faces, recount both and find the discrepancy together; for curved solids, expect one extra piece that forms the curved surface.
Emphasise that the whole solid is not the same as one of its flat faces — the solid is a 3-D object, each face is a flat 2-D shape.

Note for the adult: a paper or card net has a slight real thickness and is a physical model of the ideal flat faces, which mathematically have no thickness. Ask the child about the flat 2-D shape the card represents (a square, a circle), not whether the card itself can be held or how thick it is.
activities.rationale: Connecting faces to 2-D shapes and to nets, where each face appears as a separate flat shape, reinforces the face count and addresses treating the whole solid as if it were a 2-D shape; the card is an approximation of the ideal flat face and this is made explicit in the activity.
sourceClaims: A curved surface is NOT a face and the curved line where a curved surface meets a flat face is NOT an edge; each face of a 3-D shape is a 2-D shape; an edge is the straight line where two faces meet and a vertex is the corner where edges meet; handling solids while viewing images supports counting faces, edges and vertices. Curved solids are described with a 'curved surface' (e.g. cylinder = two circular faces + one curved surface).
learnerActions: For a solid you have counted (e.g. a cube), name the 2-D shape of each face (a square).
Unfold a net that folds up into the solid, laying out each face as a separate flat shape.

For a solid with only flat faces (e.g. a cube), count the flat shapes in the net and check the number matches the face count you found by touch; for a cylinder or cone, notice that one piece of the net becomes the curved surface, not a face.
Fold the net back into the solid to see each flat shape become a face.
Talk about the shape each face represents — a square, a circle — rather than about the card itself.
activities.intendedInsight: Each face of a 3-D solid is a 2-D shape; seeing the faces laid out flat in a net, each as its own shape, reinforces the face count and links 3-D solids to 2-D shapes.

activities.title: Check and explain the counts
feedback: Recall questions check the totals but do not by themselves build the counting strategy — if a count is wrong, return to handling and marking the real solid rather than just stating the right number.
A child who can give numbers but cannot say how a face differs from an edge may be reciting; probe the distinction and reteach by touch if needed.
activities.rationale: Direct questions and matching can check recall of counts but do not by themselves build the counting strategy or the face/edge/vertex distinction; they are best used as an end-check alongside asking the child to articulate the difference. This is a research-informed proposal, not a tested design.
learnerActions: Answer direct questions such as 'How many edges does a cube have?' and match a solid to its face count.
Explain in your own words what makes a face different from an edge, and an edge different from a vertex.
Respond to a friend's wrong claim (e.g. 'a cube has 3 faces because I can only see 3') by explaining and demonstrating the correct count.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to state the counts and articulate the difference between the three properties shows the properties are genuinely held apart, not just recited.

constraints: Tap-to-reveal or labelled-model activities that show a feature's name and definition on tap can teach vocabulary, but they display the answer rather than requiring the child to build the count or feel the flat-versus-curved distinction; use them to introduce terms, not to replace counting.

A flat-screen tally that colours each tapped face/edge/vertex can build the keep-them-distinct skill, but a flat screen makes it harder to reveal hidden features on the far side — a main source of miscounting; pair it with a solid the child can turn.

A rotatable on-screen 3-D model lets a child turn the solid to catch hidden features and can toggle to a cylinder for the curved-surface convention; it is one good way to surface the hidden-feature error, but real solids in the hand should confirm what the screen shows, and the on-screen model should be understood as a model of the solid, not the solid itself.
Scored recall questions check whether a child remembers counts; they do not on their own build the counting strategy or the property distinction, so use them as an end-check.
Always state explicitly which convention you are using for describing curved solids, because schemes differ.

Paper nets and card cutouts have a slight real thickness and are approximations of the ideal flat faces, which have no thickness; use them to represent faces but keep attention on the flat 2-D shape represented rather than on picking up or handling the card as a definition of the shape.
Recognising or recalling counts is not the same as producing a reliable count by handling and tracking features; expect production, not only recognition.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The cited study on under-counting hidden features (Sudirman et al., 2023) used a junior-high sample and documents the general obstacle, not the 6-7 age group specifically; treat its applicability to this age as indicative, not established.

The legacy source material asserted in places that no flat medium can target these challenges and that a 3-D interactive is uniquely necessary; this comparative-necessity claim is not established by the sources and has been softened to scoped affordances and limits.
The 'typically predicts around 9' figure for visible cube edges, and the 'stall at 3 or 4', are illustrative expectations, not measured results; use them as rough guides only.
The hypothetical friend's claim of '4 faces' is a child-level undercount used only as a wrong claim to refute; the correct cube total is 6 faces.

assess.poeTask: Hold up a cube. 'Predict how many edges this cube has altogether. Say your number before we trace them.' A child who counts only what they see typically predicts around 9 (the visible edges). Then trace and mark every edge together, turning the cube. The gap between the predicted number and the counted 12 — and their reaction to the edges 'round the back' — is the diagnostic: it exposes whether they reasoned about the whole solid or only its visible face.
probeDeeper: Here is a cylinder. How many flat faces does it have? Is the round curved part a face? How can you tell?
You counted the corners you can see. Turn the cube over — did you miss any? How many are there altogether?
Show me an edge. Now show me a vertex. What is the difference between them?
A friend says a cube has 4 faces because they can only see 4. What would you tell them?
assess.correctAnswer: 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices. A face is a flat surface (itself a 2-D shape — here a square); an edge is the straight line where two faces meet; a vertex/corner is the point where edges meet. The child counts systematically — turning the cube and tracking the hidden features — rather than counting only what faces them.

errorPatterns.pattern: Blurs the three properties, using 'side' or 'corner' loosely so face, edge and vertex run together when counting.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count by touch in a fixed order — colour each face, trace each edge, dot each vertex — naming the property each time, so the three stay distinct.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cannot say what makes a face different from an edge, calls edges 'sides', and gives inconsistent counts when asked to recount.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts only the visible faces/edges/vertices and misses the hidden ones — gives a cube 3 faces or 4 corners.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Hand them the solid to turn, marking each feature as it is counted (sticker on vertices, line on edges) so hidden ones are included; recount from a different face to confirm the total is stable.
errorPatterns.distractor: A cube has 3 faces and 4 corners.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: States fewer than 6 faces / 8 vertices / 12 edges; on questioning, admits counting only what faced them.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts a curved surface as a 'face' and the curved boundary line as an 'edge' — e.g. says a cylinder has 3 faces.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Feel the solids: a face is FLAT and an edge is a straight line where two flat faces meet; adopt 'curved surface' language for the round part, and state the scheme's convention explicitly since schemes differ.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a cylinder or cone, counts the curved surface as a face or calls the circle-to-curve boundary an edge.

responseLevels.gap: Blurs faces, edges and vertices (calls edges 'sides', cannot distinguish them) or counts only the visible features, giving inconsistent counts.
responseLevels.full: Distinguishes face (flat 2-D surface), edge (line where two faces meet) and vertex (corner where edges meet), counts all three correctly including hidden features by tracking systematically, and transfers the distinction to a new solid — e.g. correctly says a cylinder has two flat faces and a curved surface (SOLO relational, with transfer).
responseLevels.partial: Counts the faces, edges and vertices of a cube correctly when handling it and can define each, but lists the three counts without coordinating them, miscounts hidden features on a less familiar solid, or wrongly counts a curved surface as a face (SOLO multistructural).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a real cube. Ask: 'Count the faces, then the edges, then the corners (vertices). Now tell me — what makes a face different from an edge?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The three counts together with the face-vs-edge distinction separate a child who genuinely holds the three properties apart from one who blurs them (calling edges 'sides', miscounting because the properties run together) or who counts only the visible half. Reaching 12 edges in particular requires tracking hidden edges, so it is hard to fluke by looking; the second tier exposes whether the child can articulate the difference or is just reciting numbers.

Curved solids are described with a 'curved surface' (e.g. cylinder = two circular faces + one curved surface).
