pedagogy.summary: Extending the formal columnar algorithm from three to four digits. The mathematics is unchanged — align by place value, and compose (carry) or decompose (exchange/borrow) between adjacent columns — but four digits add a thousands column and, crucially, harder exchange chains, including borrowing across one or more zeros (4002-1367). The DfE also requires checking with estimation (rounding) and the inverse, so approximate reasonableness is taught alongside exact procedure.
bestPractices: Keep the base-ten exchange rationale explicit — a carry is 'ten of these make one of those', a borrow is the reverse — do not let it become a symbol-pushing trick
Estimate first by rounding (4002-1367 is about 4000-1400 = 2600) so a place-value slip is caught
Deliberately include one across-zero subtraction — it is the most diagnostic and most-failed case
Use place-value column headers / grid paper so digits of unequal length align correctly (878 under 3456)
Check every answer with the inverse operation
keyRepresentations: Place-value columns with Th/H/T/O headers
Base-ten blocks including the thousand cube (exchange made physical)
Part-whole bar model
Empty number line for the rounding estimate
commonMisconceptions: Borrow-across-zero failure — cannot decompose when the adjacent column is 0 (4002-1367)
Smaller-from-larger bug — subtracts the smaller digit from the larger regardless of position
Misaligns digits when the two numbers have different lengths (right-aligning wrongly, or lining up under the wrong column)
Fails to compose — leaves a two-digit result in a column instead of carrying
Treats checking as redoing the sum rather than estimating or using the inverse

learn.summary: Year 4 pupils extend the formal columnar algorithm from three to four digits: aligning by place value, composing (carrying) when a column total reaches ten or more, and decomposing (borrowing/exchanging) when a top digit is too small — including the hardest case, borrowing across one or more zeros (e.g. 4002-1367). The DfE also requires checking answers by rounding to estimate and by using the inverse operation, so approximate reasonableness is taught alongside the exact procedure. The exchange rationale must stay explicit (a carry is 'ten of these make one of those'; a borrow is the reverse) rather than becoming a symbol-pushing trick.

activities.title: Cascade the thousand: borrow across two zeros with base-ten quantities
feedback: If the child stalls at the zeros or writes a garbled middle (e.g. 3745 or 2735), model exchanging one thousand downward through the columns with base-ten blocks (thousand to ten hundreds to ten tens to ten ones) BEFORE touching the written digits.
If they change the 0 to a 9 but stop borrowing from the next column left, show that the thousand being broken up is what supplies those nines — the 9s and the final 12 all come from one thousand.
If the estimate and exact answer disagree wildly, check for a place-value misalignment rather than redoing blindly.
Confirm success when they treat 4002 as 3 thousands, 9 hundreds, 9 tens, 12 ones and reach 2635 with both checks agreeing.
activities.rationale: Borrow-from-zero is the single most common systematic subtraction bug in a large diagnostic dataset, and multi-zero minuends compound it across adjacent columns; making the exchange a visible movement of grouped quantities targets exactly where a symbol-only procedure tends to break down. A dynamic or hands-on model lets the child observe the cascade as the thousand-block splits into ten hundreds, then ten tens, then ten ones — the regrouping seen in motion rather than only as a finished state, while a printed worked example can still serve as a static reference.
sourceClaims: Borrow-from-zero is the single most common systematic subtraction bug in Brown & Burton's 1325-student data (107 occurrences): when borrowing from a column whose top digit is 0, the student changes the 0 to a 9 but fails to continue borrowing from the next column left; related zero bugs include STOPS/BORROW/AT/ZERO and MOVE/OVER/ZERO/BORROW. Smaller-from-larger (54 students) and these zero-borrow bugs are stable, not careless — ~40% of students showed consistently buggy behaviour. Multi-zero minuends (e.g. 4002) compound the zero-borrow bug across adjacent columns.
Composing/decomposing tens, hundreds and thousands (exchange) is the conceptual basis of the columnar algorithm; DfE Appendix 1 sets out the formal written methods this progression cross-references.
learnerActions: Set up 4002 - 1367 in place-value columns with Th/H/T/O headers, aligning from the ones column on the right.
Build 4002 physically (or on a screen model): four thousand-blocks and two ones, with empty hundreds and tens.
Try to subtract 7 ones from 2 ones; notice there is nothing in the hundreds or tens to exchange from, so the exchange must come from the thousands.

Exchange one thousand-block into ten hundred-blocks, then one hundred into ten tens, then one ten into ten ones — watching the single thousand ripple down through the two empty columns until the ones column holds 12.
Record each changed digit in the written algorithm in step with the blocks (4002 becomes 3 thousands, 9 hundreds, 9 tens, 12 ones) and finish the subtraction to reach 2635.
Round both numbers to make an estimate (about 4000 - 1400 = 2600). Ideally do this before the exact working in the steps above. Then compare the estimate with the exact answer 2635.
Check with the inverse: confirm 2635 + 1367 = 4002.
activities.intendedInsight: Borrowing across zero is not a special rule: when an adjacent column is empty you continue the exchange one column further left, and a single thousand can cascade down through the zeros to free up ones. The written digits are a record of quantities actually regrouped.

activities.title: Align and compose: mixed-length columnar addition and subtraction
feedback: If the child lines 878 under the left of 3456, or 483 under the wrong columns of 6250, reinstate place-value headers or grid paper and anchor every number from the ones column on the right.
If they write a two-digit entry such as 14 in the ones column of 3456+878, show that ten ones make one ten carried to the next column.

If they subtract the smaller digit from the larger regardless of position (e.g. treat the ones 0-3 as 3 and the tens 5-8 as 3 in 6250-483), stop and exchange concretely: you cannot take 3 ones from 0 ones without exchanging a ten. After that exchange only 4 tens are left, and you cannot take 8 tens from 4 tens without exchanging a hundred.
Confirm success when the ones sit under the ones, carries and exchanges are shown, 3456+878=4334 and 6250-483=5767, and both the estimate and the inverse support each answer.
activities.rationale: Mixed-length alignment and the compose/smaller-from-larger errors are distinct, stable bugs from the borrow-across-zero case, so they deserve their own practice; grid paper and place-value headers give a concrete anchor, and estimation plus inverse checking are statutory.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils are taught to 'add and subtract numbers with up to 4 digits using the formal written methods of columnar addition and subtraction where appropriate' and to 'estimate and use inverse operations to check answers to a calculation' (statutory).

Borrow-from-zero is the single most common systematic subtraction bug in Brown & Burton's 1325-student data (107 occurrences): when borrowing from a column whose top digit is 0, the student changes the 0 to a 9 but fails to continue borrowing from the next column left; related zero bugs include STOPS/BORROW/AT/ZERO and MOVE/OVER/ZERO/BORROW. Smaller-from-larger (54 students) and these zero-borrow bugs are stable, not careless — ~40% of students showed consistently buggy behaviour. Multi-zero minuends (e.g. 4002) compound the zero-borrow bug across adjacent columns.
learnerActions: Set out 3456 + 878 using place-value headers or grid paper, placing the 8 of 878 under the ones column (not under the left of 3456).
Add column by column; when the ones make 14, write 4 and carry one ten to the tens column rather than writing a two-digit entry in the ones.
Set out 6250 - 483, anchoring the 3 under the ones column, and subtract, exchanging from the next column left wherever the top digit is too small.
For each answer, round both numbers to estimate first, then check the exact result with the inverse operation.
activities.intendedInsight: Digits are added or subtracted by matching place value, anchored from the ones column on the right regardless of how many digits each number has; a column result of ten or more is carried, and a column that is too small to subtract requires exchanging from the next column left.

activities.title: Check it two ways: estimate and inverse
feedback: If the child simply redoes the original subtraction, scaffold the estimate (round both numbers) and the inverse addition separately; do not reteach the algorithm itself.
If the estimate is far from the exact answer, treat that as a signal to re-check alignment or an exchange, not to accept the exact answer anyway.
Confirm success when the child produces a rounded estimate near 2600 AND an inverse sum that returns the original minuend 4002.
activities.rationale: Pupils commonly treat checking as re-running the sum, which cannot catch a systematic procedural bug; the DfE requires both estimation and inverse operations, and separating these from the algorithm keeps them as genuine independent checks.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils are taught to 'add and subtract numbers with up to 4 digits using the formal written methods of columnar addition and subtraction where appropriate' and to 'estimate and use inverse operations to check answers to a calculation' (statutory).
learnerActions: After solving 4002 - 1367, round both numbers (about 4000 - 1400 = 2600) on a number line or strip and say whether 2635 is reasonable.
Check the same answer a second, independent way by adding the result to the number subtracted: 2635 + 1367 should return 4002.
Answer: 'What if it had been 4000 - 1367 instead — does that change how you borrow?' and explain.
Compare the two forms of checking and say what each one catches that the other might miss.
activities.intendedInsight: Checking is not redoing the same subtraction: estimation catches place-value-scale slips, and the inverse addition independently confirms the exact answer. They are complementary, not repetition.

constraints: Keep the base-ten exchange rationale explicit throughout — a carry is 'ten of these make one of those', a borrow is the reverse — so the algorithm does not become a symbol-pushing trick.
Deliberately include at least one across-zero subtraction (e.g. 4002-1367): it is the most diagnostic and most-failed case.
Use place-value column headers or grid paper so digits of unequal length align correctly (e.g. 878 under the right-hand end of 3456), anchoring from the ones column on the right.
Estimate first by rounding so a place-value slip is caught, and check every answer with the inverse operation.

A fill-in-the-column or reveal-the-exchange practice format can assess and rehearse the carried/borrowed digits and the rounded estimate, but it cannot verify a child's handwritten column ALIGNMENT, so include some set-it-out-on-paper work where the child chooses the layout.

A tap-to-reveal worked-example reference can show the ten-for-one exchange behind each carry/borrow mark, but it does not let the child perform the exchange, so it supplements rather than replaces active regrouping.

Screen-based base-ten models and physical blocks offer different experiences; either can make the exchange visible, and neither is required over the other. Physical cubes have thickness and can be handled; a screen model is an idealised representation of the same grouped quantities.

The source attributes '4002-1367 is the single most diagnostic subtraction case' to VanLehn in the assessment field, but the cited full-text source is Brown & Burton (1978); the VanLehn attribution is not backed by a fetched source here and should be checked before asserting it.

One source (NRICH place-value / DfE Appendix 1) is marked verified:false and 'not fetched this session'; it is used to support the exchange rationale in activity 1, so treat that support as unverified.

Original source fields contained comparative-necessity phrasing ('which no static picture can', 'a genuine third dimension adds nothing', open dialogue 'cannot exercise' the task). These have been softened to scoped affordances/limits; no comparative efficacy of one medium over another is established by the available sources.
The original pedagogy listed a part-whole bar model representation that is not used in these activities; it was a non-central representation, not an error.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 4002-1367=2635 (regrouping 4002 as 3 thousands, 9 hundreds, 9 tens, 12 ones) is correct; 2635+1367=4002 confirms. 3456+878=4334 (ones 6+8=14, write 4 carry 1). 6250-483=5767. Rounded estimate 4000-1400=2600 is close to 2635. All checked consistent.

probeDeeper: Roughly what should the answer be, before you work it out exactly?

What if it had been 4000 - 1367 instead - does that change how you borrow?
How could you use addition to check your subtraction is right?
assess.correctAnswer: Aligns each sum by place value (878 under the right-hand end of 3456; 483 under the ones/tens/hundreds of 6250), composes tens/hundreds/thousands when carrying, and exchanges correctly across BOTH zeros in 4002-1367 (treating 4002 as 3 thousands, 9 hundreds, 9 tens, 12 ones) to get 2635. Estimate approx 4000-1400 = 2600, close to 2635; inverse 2635+1367 = 4002.

errorPatterns.pattern: Subtracts the smaller digit from the larger regardless of which is on top (smaller-from-larger bug), e.g. in 6250-483 does 3-0 or 0-3 as 3

responseLevels.gap: Misaligns the digits or breaks down at the zeros; has no sense of whether the answer is reasonable.
responseLevels.full: Solves all three including the double-zero borrow, aligns correctly, AND verifies with both an estimate and the inverse; transfers the method to 4000-1367.
responseLevels.partial: Gets the clean items right and can describe the column steps, but fails the across-zero exchange, or checks only by redoing the sum and never estimates.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child three to set out and solve on paper, watching how they line the digits up: 3456 + 878; 4002 - 1367; 6250 - 483. Then ask them to check the 4002 - 1367 answer two ways - by estimating and by the inverse.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 4002-1367 forces a double borrow across two zeros - the single most diagnostic subtraction case (VanLehn). 3456+878 forces multi-column composing, and 6250-483 forces alignment of a three-digit number under a four-digit one. A shallow procedure fails visibly at the zeros or the alignment while sailing through the clean addition.

pedagogy.summary: At 7-8 the strategic choice widens to METHODS — mental, jottings, formal written algorithm, calculator — and to measuring tools chosen by the object. The defining act is READING the numbers first and picking a method that fits their features, rather than defaulting to the column algorithm for everything: 345+200 is a mental case (add two hundreds, other digits unchanged), while 345+278 (with regrouping) is where a written method earns its keep. EEF's guidance is explicit that pupils should learn a range of mental, written and calculator methods and make considered decisions about when each is appropriate and efficient, self-regulating so they make less but better use of any one method.
bestPractices: Teach pupils to look at the numbers before choosing — sort calculations into 'do in your head', 'jot', 'write out', 'use a calculator' — so method follows the numbers (EEF Rec 4)
Present a range of methods and ask 'when is each appropriate and efficient?', building considered decision-making rather than a single default
Integrate the calculator as a checking tool and teach reasonableness checks, so pupils self-regulate ('less but better') rather than reaching for it or the algorithm reflexively (EEF)
Match measuring tools to the object's size and precision — ruler for a pencil, metre stick/tape for a room — and name why the wrong-scale tool fails
Prize the justification: two methods may both reach 545, so the assessable skill is the reason for the choice, not the answer
keyRepresentations: Mental methods (partitioning, known facts)
Jottings / empty number line
Formal columnar algorithm
Calculator (for checking and awkward numbers)
Measuring tools: ruler, metre stick, tape
commonMisconceptions: Applies the formal written method to everything, even 345+200 or 300+300, because it is the 'proper' way — missing the faster mental route (EEF: not self-regulating)
Attempts a regrouping calculation like 345+278 in the head and drops a carry, misjudging when a written method is needed
Trusts a calculator answer without a reasonableness check
Chooses a measuring tool that doesn't fit the object — a 30 cm ruler for a room — ignoring range and cumulative error

learn.summary: For 7-8 year olds, the target skill is choosing a calculation method (mental, jottings, formal written algorithm, or calculator) and measuring tools by first READING the numbers or the object, rather than defaulting to the column algorithm for everything. 345+200 is a mental case (add two hundreds, tens and ones unchanged), while 345+278 involves regrouping and is where a written method earns its effort. The assessable skill is the justification for the choice, not just the answer — since two methods can both reach 545. Learners also decide which representation fits (for example when an empty number line helps more than base-ten blocks), integrate a calculator as a checking tool with a reasonableness judgement, and match measuring tools to an object's size and precision.

activities.title: Method chooser: route each calculation
feedback: If a learner sets out columns for 345+200, ask what the numbers let them SEE — point to the +200 and that only the hundreds digit changes; invite them to say 545 without writing.

If a learner reaches the right answer by an inefficient method, acknowledge the correct answer but ask 'could you have done that one a faster way? What in the numbers tells you?' — the reason for the choice is the point.

If a learner tries 345+278 in their head and drops the carry, don't reteach the algorithm; ask the meta-question 'is this one to hold in your head, or one to write down?' and let them choose the written method with a reason.
activities.rationale: EEF Recommendation 4 advises teaching a range of mental, written and calculator methods and building considered decisions about when each is appropriate and efficient; an interactive routing task where the effort of each method is visible is one proposed way to make the strategic payoff felt rather than told. An optional interactive 'bench' can reflect the effort of a slow column build versus an instant mental route to make efficiency concrete.
sourceClaims: Pupils should be taught a range of mental, calculator and pencil-and-paper methods and encouraged to make considered decisions about when each is appropriate and efficient, integrating the calculator and self-regulating so they make less but better use of it
Proficient students consider available tools and make sound decisions about when each is helpful, recognising its insight and limitations
learnerActions: Work through a stream of mixed calculations (e.g. 345+200, 300+300, 345+278), and for each one first decide out loud which method fits: do it in your head, jot it down, write it out as columns, or use a calculator.
For each, state WHY that method fits before solving — e.g. 'I can see +200, so the tens and ones don't change, so I'll do it in my head.'
Compare the effort: deliberately set out columns for 345+200 and notice how many steps that takes versus saying 545 straight away.
Deliberately choose the written column method for 345+278 and name why (there is regrouping / a carry to track) it is worth the extra effort.

For a given problem, also decide which representation would help most — for example when an empty number line is clearer than base-ten blocks — and say what about the problem makes that representation fit.
Sort a mixed set of calculations into two piles: 'do in your head' and 'worth writing down', and explain what feature of the numbers put each one where it went.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading the numbers first and spotting their features (round hundreds vs messy regrouping) lets you pick the method or representation that costs least effort; the column algorithm is worth its effort precisely for the messy cases, not for every calculation.

activities.title: Calculator check: is that sensible?
feedback: If a learner accepts the calculator answer without any check, prompt 'how big should the answer roughly be? Does 623 fit near 630?'
If a learner only trusts the calculator by redoing it exactly, point out that an estimate is faster and still a valid check.
Praise a learner who rounds to check (≈350+280≈630) and concludes 623 is in range, so the calculator's answer is confirmed sensible.
activities.rationale: EEF advises integrating the calculator and self-regulating so pupils make less but better use of it, which requires reasonableness checks rather than reflexive trust. MP5 emphasises recognising a tool's insight and limitations. Here 623 is the correct answer, so the task teaches confirming reasonableness, not rejecting a right result.
sourceClaims: Pupils should be taught a range of mental, calculator and pencil-and-paper methods and encouraged to make considered decisions about when each is appropriate and efficient, integrating the calculator and self-regulating so they make less but better use of it
Proficient students consider available tools and make sound decisions about when each is helpful, recognising its insight and limitations
learnerActions: A calculator returns 623 for 345+278. Decide whether that answer is sensible WITHOUT redoing the exact calculation.
Estimate instead: 345 is about 350, 278 is about 280, so the total should be around 630 — use that to judge the calculator's answer.

Say aloud a quick reasonableness check for the result: rounding to size (≈630), and the last-digit check (5+8=13, so the ones digit should be 3 — 623 ends in 3). Confirm these checks ratify 623 rather than flag an error.
Practise choosing when a calculator is the sensible tool (awkward numbers, checking) versus when a mental or written method is faster.
activities.intendedInsight: A calculator answer should be checked for reasonableness rather than trusted blindly; estimating the rough size and the expected last digit is a quick way to show an answer is sensible or catch a wrong one, though passing these checks does not prove the answer is exactly right (for example, 633 would also pass both).

activities.title: Fit the measuring tool to the object
feedback: If a learner picks the 30 cm ruler for a room, ask how many times they'd have to move it and what happens to the small errors each time.
If a learner picks a tool correctly, ask them to say the feature of the object (its size) that made that tool fit.
Confirm that there isn't one 'proper' tool — the right choice depends on what is being measured.
activities.rationale: The topic couples arithmetic method choice with tool selection as a single strategic habit of reading the situation before choosing; naming cumulative error from repeated placement makes the limitation concrete, though its size depends on the specific tool and method. MP5 supports making sound decisions about when a tool is helpful and recognising its limitations.
sourceClaims: Proficient students consider available tools and make sound decisions about when each is helpful, recognising its insight and limitations
learnerActions: Decide which tool to use to measure a pencil versus a room: a 30 cm ruler, or a metre stick / tape measure.
Explain why a 30 cm ruler is a poor choice for a room — it needs many placements, and each placement can add a little error that accumulates.
Match a few objects (book, desk, corridor, pencil) to the tool whose range and precision suits them, and name the reason each time.
activities.intendedInsight: The same 'read the job, then choose the tool' habit used for arithmetic applies to measuring: match the tool's range and precision to the object, and recognise that repeated placement of a short ruler can accumulate error.

activities.title: Argue the choice with a method-defaulting partner
feedback: If the learner cannot say why 345+278 is a written-method case, prompt them to point at the regrouping / carry they'd have to track mentally.
If the learner can only say a mental method is 'quicker' when prompted but doesn't choose it spontaneously, give more mixed examples and ask them to route first, solve second.
Reward a clear 'because the numbers...' reason over a correct answer with no explanation.
activities.rationale: A dialogue partner who over-writes everything and springs a regrouping case is one proposed way to pull out the self-regulating rationale EEF says pupils need; justification is the discriminating evidence because both methods reach the same answer. This is one way to elicit the reasoning, not the only way.
sourceClaims: Pupils should be taught a range of mental, calculator and pencil-and-paper methods and encouraged to make considered decisions about when each is appropriate and efficient, integrating the calculator and self-regulating so they make less but better use of it
learnerActions: Work with a partner (or in-role tutor) who writes out columns for EVERYTHING, including 345+200, and argue the case for when a mental method is enough.
Respond when the partner springs a regrouping calculation (345+278): decide whether to upgrade to a written method and give your reason.

Answer prompts like: 'Give me a calculation where the column method really IS the best choice, and one where it would be silly', and 'For 345+278, why does writing it down help more than doing it in your head?'
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to justify a method choice — including when to upgrade to a written method for regrouping — is the self-regulating reasoning the skill is really about.

constraints: The assessable skill is the REASON for the method choice, not the answer: 345+200 and 345+278 can both be checked, but a correct answer reached by an inefficient method does not demonstrate strategic judgement.

Treat a learner who holds 345+278 in their head and drops a carry as a judgement issue about when to deploy a written method, not a gap in the algorithm — do not reteach the algorithm, tune the choice.
623 is the correct answer for 345+278; the reasonableness-check task must confirm it is sensible (≈630, ones digit 3), never lead a learner to reject it.

A scored 'which method?' item can assess recognition of an efficient choice but does not by itself show the self-regulation or reasonableness-checking; use such items to feed into, not replace, a task where the learner routes and justifies.

A static reference chart of 'which method when' is a useful reminder but does not itself let the learner route calculations, feel the efficiency difference, or justify a choice — treat it as a reference alongside, not instead of, the routing task.
Estimation-for-checking (≈350+280≈630) is an approximation used to judge reasonableness, not an exact recalculation.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic self-audit: 345+200=545 (correct); 345+278=623 (correct). The calculator value 623 used in the checking task is the correct answer, so the 'is it sensible?' task confirms reasonableness (≈630, ones digit 3) rather than hunting a planted error; no activity asks a learner to reject a correct result.

The legacy source rated 3D as 'adding nothing' and a static image/quiz as unable to teach the practice; these comparative-efficacy/necessity claims are not established by the cited sources and have been narrowed to scoped affordances/limits (a static chart as a reference; a scored item as recognition-only).
The number-line vs base-ten-blocks representation-choice example from the original evidence was restored into the method-chooser activity.
The measuring-tool cumulative-error point is qualitatively reasonable but its magnitude depends on the specific ruler, object and method; presented qualitatively, not as a quantified absolute.

The formal objective (description) spans multi-digit numbers, decimals and fractions, but all worked examples here are whole-number — consistent with the source's own examples, but decimals/fractions method-choice is not exemplified and would need separate material to cover the full stated scope.
Legacy 'high' confidence and 'verified' source flags were not re-checked in this rewrite.

probeDeeper: Give me a calculation where the column method really IS the best choice, and one where it would be silly.

responseLevels.gap: Defaults to one method (usually the column algorithm) for all calculations, or mismatches measuring tools; does not read the numbers to inform the choice.
responseLevels.full: Unprompted, reads the numbers and matches the method to their features (mental for +200, written for +278), justifies by efficiency and the numbers' structure, checks a calculator answer for reasonableness, and selects measuring tools by the object's size and precision.
responseLevels.partial: Can say a mental method is 'quicker' for 345+200 when prompted, but does not spontaneously choose it, or cannot articulate what makes 345+278 a written-method case.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Two children work out 345 + 200. One sets out the column method and carries carefully; the other just says '545' straight away. Who chose the better method for THIS calculation, and why? Now what about 345 + 278 — would your advice change?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Both methods reach 545, so accuracy is not the tell — the discriminator is whether the child reads the numbers and matches the method to their features (round hundreds → mental; messy regrouping → written). A child who says 'columns is the proper way' for 345+200 reveals no strategic judgement; the second calculation checks they can also justify UPGRADING to a written method.

sources.claim: Proficient students consider available tools and make sound decisions about when each is helpful, recognising its insight and limitations
sources.source: CCSS Standards for Mathematical Practice — MP5 Use appropriate tools strategically

sources.claim: Pupils should be taught a range of mental, calculator and pencil-and-paper methods and encouraged to make considered decisions about when each is appropriate and efficient, integrating the calculator and self-regulating so they make less but better use of it
sources.source: EEF — Improving Mathematics in Key Stages 2 and 3 (Recommendation 4: choose between mathematical strategies)

pedagogy.summary: Composing 2-D shapes — combining triangles, squares, trapezoids and half-/quarter-circles into composite shapes and finding new shapes within them — develops through Clements & Sarama's trajectory from unsystematic Piece Assembly, through trial-and-error Picture Making, to composing WITH ANTICIPATION and substituting equivalent pieces. It is taught best with outline (puzzle) tasks engineered so each successive level of thinking is required, prompting children to choose pieces by side length and angle rather than general appearance, and asking them to decompose a composite and name the simpler shapes that make it up.
bestPractices: Use outline puzzles engineered to require the next level of thinking (e.g. remove one internal guide line to push from Piece Assembler to Picture Maker).
Nudge from trial and error to anticipation: 'Can you see which shape will fit before you place it?'
Have children choose pieces by attributes — matching side lengths and angles — and use turns and flips intentionally.
Ask children to decompose the composite ('what smaller shapes make this up?') and to find new shapes within it (two triangles make a square; two half-circles make a circle).
Pitch tasks one level beyond the child's current level and fade support — this out-performed jumping straight to the target level (Clements et al. 2019, effect size .55).
keyRepresentations: Pattern blocks and tangram pieces
Outline puzzle cards of increasing difficulty
Two triangles composing a square or larger triangle; half-circles composing a circle
Angle-and-side-length matching between a gap and a piece
commonMisconceptions: Assembles by trial and error with no advance plan and does not anticipate the new shape (an expected early trajectory level, not a fault).
Chooses pieces by general shape only, not by matching angles and side lengths, so pieces do not fit the gap.
Sees the composite as one whole and cannot decompose it into the simpler shapes it is made from.

learn.summary: Children compose 2-D shapes — combining triangles, squares, trapezoids, and half-/quarter-circles into composite shapes and finding new shapes within them. The goal is to move along Clements & Sarama's trajectory: from unsystematic trial-and-error assembly (Piece Assembler), through trial-and-error picture making, to composing WITH ANTICIPATION — choosing a piece because its angle and side length will fit, using turns and flips intentionally, and decomposing a composite back into the simpler shapes that make it up. The core teaching medium is manipulating flat pieces into outline (puzzle) tasks engineered so each successive level of thinking is required, with immediate fit/misfit feedback.

activities.title: Fill the outline with the right pieces
feedback: If the child places pieces at random until one fits and cannot say in advance which will fit: this is an expected early trajectory level, not an error — do NOT mark it wrong. Offer a puzzle just one step ahead (for example, remove a single internal guide line) and ask 'Can you see what will fit before you place it?'
If the child grabs a triangle of the wrong size or angle that won't fit: say 'This gap has a slanted edge — which piece has an edge that matches it?' and compare edges and corners before placing.
When a piece snaps into place because its angle and side matched, name it: 'You picked that because its edge was the same length as the gap.'
activities.rationale: Outline puzzles engineered to require the next level of thinking, with pieces chosen by angle and side length and intentional rotation/reflection, are the tasks through which this trajectory was researched. Pitching one level beyond the child's current level and fading support is the recommended progression.
sourceClaims: Shape composition progresses from the Piece Assembler and Picture Maker levels (building by unsystematic trial and error, choosing pieces by general shape or side length) to the Shape Composer level (composing with anticipation, choosing pieces by angle as well as side length and using rotations and reflections intentionally); outline puzzles are engineered so each successive level of thinking is required, and instruction one trajectory level ahead out-performed skipping to the target level (effect size .55).
learnerActions: Give the child flat shape pieces (for example, pattern blocks, tangram pieces, or cut-out triangles, squares, rectangles, trapezoids, half-circles and quarter-circles) and an outline puzzle card that those pieces can cover exactly. Standard pattern blocks and tangrams do not include half-circles or quarter-circles, and tangrams have no trapezoid, so add cut-out pieces for any shapes the set lacks.
As they work, ask them to say which shape they are using and why.
Before each placement, prompt: 'Will this piece fit this gap? How do you know?' — encouraging a prediction from the gap's edges and corners.
When a piece doesn't fit, have them compare the gap's edge length and corner angle to the piece, then choose one that matches.
Let them use turns and flips to make a piece fit, naming what they did ('I flipped it so the slanted edge lines up').
activities.intendedInsight: A piece can be chosen in advance by matching its side length and angle to the gap, rather than by trying pieces at random until one happens to fit.

activities.title: Same pieces, different shapes
feedback: If the child treats each arrangement as unrelated, overlay or re-join the same two right-angled triangles in front of them to show the square and the larger triangle come from the same pieces.
Praise the moment they predict a new shape before building it: that is composing with anticipation.
activities.rationale: Composing new shapes from the same component pieces, using rotation and reflection intentionally, is explicitly required by the trajectory and the grade-1 standard. The square/larger-triangle example only holds for congruent right-isosceles triangles, so pieces are chosen accordingly.
sourceClaims: Grade 1 geometry requires pupils to compose two-dimensional shapes (rectangles, squares, trapezoids, triangles, half-circles and quarter-circles) to create a composite shape, and to compose new shapes from the composite shape.

Shape composition progresses from the Piece Assembler and Picture Maker levels (building by unsystematic trial and error, choosing pieces by general shape or side length) to the Shape Composer level (composing with anticipation, choosing pieces by angle as well as side length and using rotations and reflections intentionally); outline puzzles are engineered so each successive level of thinking is required, and instruction one trajectory level ahead out-performed skipping to the target level (effect size .55).
learnerActions: Using two congruent right-isosceles (tangram-style) triangles, have the child join them along their long (hypotenuse) edges to form a square. Then have them rejoin the same two triangles along one of the shorter equal edges, mirrored so the two right-angle corners sit side by side, to form a larger triangle instead. Joining them along a shorter edge with one triangle turned the other way makes a parallelogram, which is another new shape worth naming. (Note for the adult: two equilateral pattern-block triangles would instead make a rhombus, not a square, so choose right-isosceles triangles for this square example.)
Have them put two half-circles together to form a circle, and explore what else the pieces can make.
Ask: 'You made a square from two triangles — can you make a different shape with those same two pieces?'
activities.intendedInsight: The same pieces can compose different shapes depending on how they are turned and joined — composing is a deliberate, reversible act.

activities.title: Find the shapes hiding inside
feedback: If the child names only the whole composite and cannot show its parts, lift and overlay the pieces to reveal the two right-angled triangles inside the square, then hunt together for 'shapes hidden within shapes'.
Confirm when they both name a part and show where it sits in the whole.
activities.rationale: Decomposing the composite and naming its component shapes is a listed objective in the row's own evidence and directly addresses the misconception that a composite is one undifferentiated whole. Neither cited source claim directly attests to decomposition, so no source claim is attached here.
learnerActions: Show the child a completed composite shape and ask 'Which smaller shapes are hiding inside this?'
Have them lift and separate the pieces to reveal, for example, that the square is made of two right-angled (right-isosceles) triangles or the circle of two half-circles.
Ask them to name each component shape as they take the composite apart, then rebuild it.
activities.intendedInsight: A composite shape is built from — and can be pulled apart into — simpler named shapes; seeing the whole does not mean you can only see the whole.

activities.title: Reference and post-check (supporting activities)
feedback: If a child can match or name parts but still fits pieces by trial and error, return to the hands-on outline puzzles — matching checks recognition, not the composing action.
Use the spoken prediction to surface anticipation, then have the child actually place the piece to confirm.
activities.rationale: A static decomposition display supports naming parts but does not exercise the act of fitting pieces; a matching/sequence check can verify which pieces make a shape but not the composing action; a spoken prediction can prompt anticipation but the manipulative act carries the learning. These supports are useful alongside, not instead of, hands-on composition.
learnerActions: As a reference, show a composite alongside a reveal of its decomposition ('this is made of two triangles') to support naming the parts.
As a post-check after hands-on building, have the child match composites to the component pieces that make them, or sequence which pieces make a given shape.
Use a short spoken prediction before a build: 'Which piece will fit here, and why?'
activities.intendedInsight: Naming and matching parts consolidates vocabulary and checks understanding, but the composing skill itself is built through the hands-on fitting activities above.

constraints: The core skill is a manipulative, spatial act: children must physically (or on-screen) fit, turn, and flip pieces into outlines. Recognition-only tasks (matching a composite to its parts, naming shapes) check understanding but do not elicit the independent act of composing.
A static composite with a tap/reveal of its decomposition is a reference and naming aid; it cannot exercise choosing and fitting pieces.
This is a planar concept; it needs a flat working surface (physical blocks or a 2-D screen). A 3-D rendering is not needed and can distract from the flat composition being learned.
Spoken prediction ('which piece will fit?') is valuable for eliciting anticipation but should accompany actual placement, not replace it.
Trial-and-error assembly with no advance plan is an expected early trajectory LEVEL, not a fault to be marked wrong; respond by offering a puzzle one step ahead and fading support.

Engineer puzzles to require the next level of thinking (e.g. remove one internal guide line at a time) and pitch one level beyond the child's current level; the cited study reports this out-performed jumping straight to the target level (effect size .55).
For the 'two triangles make a square' example, use congruent right-isosceles (tangram-style) triangles; two equilateral pattern-block triangles form a rhombus, not a square.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source claims support the learning-trajectory principle and the grade-1 composition standard; they do not establish that these specific activity designs were tested, nor do they establish comparative efficacy of any particular medium.

Decomposition ('find the shapes hiding inside') is drawn from the row's objective, evidence and misconception list; neither sources[].claim directly attests to decomposition, so the decomposition activity carries no source claim.

The legacy row asserted that 3-D 'adds nothing and can mislead' and that dialogue 'cannot carry' composing. These have been softened to narrowly scoped affordance/limit statements (planar concept needs a flat surface; spoken prediction supports but does not replace placement), since the cited sources do not establish such necessity or medium superiority.

The original row's keyRepresentations/evidence stated 'two triangles compose a square' without specifying triangle type; standard equilateral pattern-block triangles cannot make a square (they make a rhombus), so the corrected activity specifies congruent right-isosceles (tangram) triangles for that example.

Overlaying/separating pattern-block pieces assumes idealised flat shapes; physical blocks have slight thickness, which is acceptable as an approximation of the planar shapes represented and need not be treated as an error.

probeDeeper: Before you place that piece — will it fit this gap? How do you know?
You made a square from two triangles — can you make a different shape with those same two triangles?
Which smaller shapes are hiding inside this composite?
This gap has a slanted edge — which piece has an edge that matches it?
assess.correctAnswer: Selects pieces by their attributes and places them to fill the outline exactly, choosing pieces with anticipation rather than only trial and error; combines two triangles into a square (and, e.g., two half-circles into a circle); and decomposes and renames the composite by its component shapes.

errorPatterns.pattern: Assembles by trial and error with no advance plan and does not anticipate the composite shape being made
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT mark this 'wrong' — it is an expected level; offer a puzzle one step ahead (remove just one internal guide line) and prompt 'can you see what will fit before you place it?'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Places pieces at random until one fits and cannot say in advance which piece will fit the gap

errorPatterns.pattern: Chooses pieces by general shape only, not by matching angles and side lengths, so the piece does not fill the gap
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare the gap's edges and corners to the piece before placing — match by side length and angle
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Grabs a triangle of the wrong size or angle that will not fit the space

errorPatterns.pattern: Sees the composite as one undifferentiated whole and cannot find the simpler shapes within it
errorPatterns.nextMove: Lift and overlay the pieces to show the square is two triangles; hunt for shapes hidden within shapes
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names the whole composite but cannot show the two triangles inside the square

responseLevels.gap: Places pieces by trial and error with no plan and cannot decompose the composite into simpler shapes.
responseLevels.full: Selects pieces by side length and angle with anticipation, fills the outline efficiently, and decomposes and recomposes the composite (two triangles make a square; two half-circles make a circle), naming the parts.
responseLevels.partial: Fills the outline, often by trial and error, and names some pieces, but does not choose by matching angles and sides or reliably find new shapes within the composite.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are pattern-block pieces — triangles, squares, trapezoids and some half-circles and quarter-circles. Cover this outline puzzle exactly using the pieces, and as you work tell me which shapes you are using. Then show me two triangles making a square, and tell me one other shape you could make from the pieces.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the build separates the Shape Composer, who picks a piece knowing from its sides and angles that it will fit, from the Piece Assembler, who tries pieces at random until one happens to fit. Asking the child to make a square from two triangles and to name another composable shape exposes whether they see composites as built from — and decomposable into — simpler shapes.

sources.claim: Shape composition progresses from the Piece Assembler and Picture Maker levels (building by unsystematic trial and error, choosing pieces by general shape or side length) to the Shape Composer level (composing with anticipation, choosing pieces by angle as well as side length and using rotations and reflections intentionally); outline puzzles are engineered so each successive level of thinking is required, and instruction one trajectory level ahead out-performed skipping to the target level (effect size .55).
sources.source: Clements, Sarama, Baroody, Joswick & Wolfe (2019), 'Evaluating the Efficacy of a Learning Trajectory for Early Shape Composition', American Educational Research Journal 56(6) (ERIC ED594902)

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 5-6 (Y1). Add and subtract one-digit and two-digit numbers to 20, INCLUDING zero (14+5=19, 17−3=14, and the +0/−0 case). The procedural application of within-20 bonds; also where the identity role of zero is established.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1): 'add and subtract one-digit and two-digit numbers to 20, including 0'; non-statutory: pupils 'realise the effect of adding or subtracting 0'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.OA.5/6 relate counting to addition/subtraction and add/subtract within 20; the additive identity (n+0=n) is an early property.
• Operational details — Use bonds and within-20 strategies to calculate, not counting-all. Give the +0/−0 case explicit attention because young children often assume every operation must change the number — model with objects that adding or taking nothing leaves the quantity unchanged. Keep to the 0-20 range including the teen boundary (crossing ten), reinforcing making-ten. Record with number sentences.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 5): add/subtract within 20 using bonds or a fast strategy for non-bridging cases (14+5). Tier B (age 5-6): handle bridging cases (8+7) and correctly compute +0/−0. Tier C (age 6): calculate fluently within 20 and explain why adding/subtracting 0 leaves the number unchanged.
bestPractices: Calculate using known bonds and making-ten rather than counting all, so this procedural work reinforces the fact base.
Give +0 and −0 explicit, concrete treatment (adding/taking nothing) to establish zero as the additive identity and dispel 'every operation changes the number'.
Attend to the teen boundary: bridging-ten cases (8+7, 15−7) need the making-ten strategy, not ones-counting.
Record calculations as number sentences and connect to the child's representations to keep meaning attached.
Vary which quantity is unknown lightly to connect with missing-number work.
keyRepresentations: Ten-frames / rekenrek for within-20 sums and bridging
Empty number line for jumps (including a 0 jump that stays put)
Part-whole model linking the calculation to bonds
Objects demonstrating 'add nothing / take nothing' for the zero case
Number track 0-20
commonMisconceptions: Assuming +0 or −0 must change the number (giving 5+0=6 or 5−0=4).
Counting all/counting on in ones across the ten boundary instead of making ten.
Errors at the teen boundary (miscounting when crossing 10).
Ignoring the operation and just combining the two numbers seen.
Reversing subtraction to keep the larger number first without noticing the meaning changes.

learn.summary: For ages 5-6 (UK Y1), learners add and subtract one-digit and two-digit numbers within 20, including the +0/−0 case, using known number bonds and making-ten rather than counting all. Core aims: fluent within-20 calculation, correct bridging across ten (e.g. 8+7), and understanding that adding or subtracting zero leaves a quantity unchanged. Activities centre on acting out calculations with ten-frames and number lines, with a concrete treatment of the zero case to dispel the belief that every operation must change the number.

activities.title: Drive a ten-frame and number-line calculator
feedback: If the learner counts all from one, prompt: hold the first number in mind and count on only the second (hold 14, count on 5 more).
For a bridging case, ask how many more are needed to fill the frame to ten, then how many are left over (8 needs 2 more to make ten, leaving 5, so 15).
If the answer is off by one on the number line, have them name the first jump aloud and check they didn't count the starting number itself as a jump (17 − 3: start at 17, jump back 3 to 14).
activities.rationale: Acting out a calculation on a ten-frame and number line keeps the procedure tied to meaning and reinforces the making-ten strategy at the teen boundary, where ones-counting is error-prone. A live, re-drivable calculation where counters move and a number sentence forms makes the strategy visible; a fixed worked example cannot be re-driven with new numbers.
sourceClaims: Explicit concrete treatment of the +0/−0 case dispels the common belief that every operation must change the number; bridging-ten cases need making-ten not ones-counting.
learnerActions: Build the first number on a double ten-frame (two ten-frames, since one frame holds only 10) (e.g. place eight counters on the first frame for 8+7).

Add or subtract the second number by moving counters, and for bridging cases split the second number to fill the frame to ten first (slide two counters over to complete ten, leaving five, to reach 15).
Show the same calculation as a jump on a 0-20 number line.
Write the matching number sentence alongside the action (e.g. 8 + 7 = 15).
Repeat with a non-bridging case (14 + 5) and a take-away (17 − 3).
activities.intendedInsight: Within-20 sums and differences can be found by using bonds and making ten, not by counting all in ones; bridging reorganises the quantity around ten.

activities.title: Add nothing, take nothing: the zero case
feedback: If the learner changes the number (e.g. 12 + 0 = 13), act out physically putting zero more counters on, then recount to show the quantity is the same.
Ask directly: when you added nothing, did any counter move? So what is the answer?
Reinforce the contrast: taking 3 away changes the number, taking 0 away does not.
activities.rationale: Young children often assume every operation must change the number, producing errors like 5+0=6 or 5−0=4. Concretely acting out 'add nothing / take nothing' and seeing the quantity unchanged targets this directly and establishes zero's identity role. A side-by-side contrast with a non-zero operation sharpens the point.
sourceClaims: Explicit concrete treatment of the +0/−0 case dispels the common belief that every operation must change the number; bridging-ten cases need making-ten not ones-counting.
1.OA.5/6: relate counting to add/subtract and add/subtract within 20; the additive identity n + 0 = n is a foundational property.
Y1 pupils add and subtract one-digit and two-digit numbers to 20, including 0, and realise the effect of adding or subtracting 0.
learnerActions: Build a number on a double ten-frame (e.g. 12: one full frame and 2 on the second frame).
Choose 'add 0' and watch that no counters move and the number stays 12.
Choose 'subtract 0' from another number (e.g. 16) and confirm it stays 16.
Show the same on the number line as a jump of length zero that stays on the spot.
Say or write why the number did not change: adding or taking nothing leaves the quantity exactly as it was.
Contrast with a nearby case that does change (17 − 3 vs 17 − 0).
activities.intendedInsight: Adding or subtracting 0 leaves a number unchanged (n + 0 = n, n − 0 = n); not every operation changes the quantity.

activities.title: Spoken probe: what happens if we add zero?
feedback: If the explanation is 'it just stays', press for why: because no amount was added or taken away.
Accept correct reasoning expressed in the child's own words; follow a wrong prediction by acting it out with objects.
activities.rationale: A short dialogue may surface the identity idea and let the child articulate reasoning, which the top checkpoint tier expects. Discussion complements, but is not itself calculation practice; the hands-on activities remain the vehicle for building and rehearsing the procedure. Efficacy of the dialogue as a standalone is proposed, not evidenced.
learnerActions: Discuss: 'What happens to 12 when you add nothing to it?'
Explain in your own words how 17 − 3 is different from 17 − 0.
Predict and justify the answer to a new zero case before checking it with objects.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to state why adding or subtracting zero leaves a number unchanged shows understanding beyond getting the answer.

activities.title: Mixed within-20 practice set
feedback: For an answer like 14 + 5 = 64, show that the 5 ones are added to the 4 ones, not to the ten; make place value visible with tens-and-ones.
For a changed zero answer, re-act adding/taking nothing.
For an off-by-one slip with a sound method, scaffold the count aloud rather than reteaching the strategy.
activities.rationale: Varied practice is needed to build procedural fluency and to probe specific errors (the zero misconception, adding to the wrong part, crossing-ten slips). Including missing-number items lightly connects to later algebraic work. A practice set drills the procedure but relies on the making-ten strategy having been built elsewhere (for example, in the hands-on calculator activity); it does not by itself teach that strategy.
sourceClaims: Explicit concrete treatment of the +0/−0 case dispels the common belief that every operation must change the number; bridging-ten cases need making-ten not ones-counting.
learnerActions: Work a varied set spanning non-bridging sums (14 + 5), bridging sums (8 + 7), take-aways (17 − 3, 15 − 7), and several +0/−0 items (12 + 0, 16 − 0).
Occasionally solve a missing-number item (e.g. 14 + ? = 19) to vary which quantity is unknown.
Jot a number line or ten-frame when helpful.

For non-bridging items, say which digit changed and which stayed the same (14 + 5 → the ones change, 4 + 5 = 9 → 19); notice that in bridging items like 8 + 7 the tens change too, and in ±0 items no digit changes.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency comes from applying bonds and making-ten across the full 0-20 range, including the zero cases and the teen boundary.

constraints: Keep calculations within the 0-20 range, including the teen boundary (crossing ten).
Use bonds and making-ten rather than counting all; the procedural work should reinforce the fact base.
Give +0 and −0 explicit, concrete attention — it is where zero's identity role is established and a common misconception lives.
Record calculations as number sentences and connect them to the child's own representations to keep meaning attached.
A fixed worked example can anchor the ideas but cannot supply the varied, re-drivable practice the procedure needs; use it as an anchor, not the main vehicle.

A practice set drills and assesses the procedure but does not by itself build the making-ten strategy; discussion surfaces reasoning but is not calculation practice. The hands-on calculation is the proposed primary vehicle for building the strategy here, with efficacy stated as proposed rather than proven.

Tiered expectations: at age 5, non-bridging cases via a fast strategy; age 5-6, bridging cases and correct +0/−0; age 6, fluent within-20 calculation with an explanation of why ±0 leaves the number unchanged.

Distinguish subtraction meaning when ordering: 17 − 3 is not the same as 3 − 17; do not reorder subtraction to keep the larger number first without noting the meaning changes (and 3 − 17 lies outside the Y1 within-20 range).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Two of the three cited sources are marked unverified in the source row (CCSS-M 1.OA.5/6 and the NCETM mastery claim); treat citations accordingly and do not infer tested efficacy.

Self-audit of worked examples: 14 + 5 = 19, 17 − 3 = 14, 8 + 7 = 15, 15 − 7 = 8, 12 + 0 = 12, 16 − 0 = 16, and 14 + ? = 19 → 5 — all checked correct. The diagnostic answer string in the source (19, 14, 12, 16) is consistent.
The source states 14 + 5 'stays within the decade' with 'no crossing of ten'; 14 + 5 = 19 is within the teens with no bridge, so this is correct as stated.

The error-pattern example '14 + 5 given as 64 (added to the tens)' is retained only as a feedback/diagnostic target with corrected framing (ones add to ones); no wrong instruction is presented to the learner.

sourceClaims were trimmed where a cited claim supported only the topic/scope rather than the activity's teaching principle: the DfE scope claim was removed from the ten-frame calculator and mixed-practice activities, and the spoken-probe activity carries no sourceClaims because no source directly supports dialogue efficacy. The DfE claim is retained on the zero-case activity because it explicitly includes 'realise the effect of adding or subtracting 0'.

Medium-superiority language was softened: the practice set's reliance on prior strategy-building is scoped to 'elsewhere' rather than asserting hands-on is the only route, and 'Neither replaces hands-on calculation' was reworded to a proposed primary vehicle, consistent with the untested efficacy of the specific interaction.
The 3D/spatial 'skip' framing was dropped as a catalog judgement rather than an established pedagogical law; within-20 calculation is simply better served by the ten-frame/number-line medium here.

probeDeeper: For 14 + 5, which digit changes and which stays the same? Why?
What happens to 12 when you add nothing to it?
How is 17 − 3 different from 17 − 0?
Show me on the number line how you got 19.
assess.correctAnswer: 19, 14, 12, 16 — the first two stay within the decade (add/subtract to the ones), and adding or subtracting 0 leaves the number unchanged.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds/subtracts to the wrong part, or counts all from one instead of counting on from 14.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use tens-and-ones or a number line — hold 14, count on 5, adding ones to the ones; make the place value visible.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 14 + 5 given as e.g. 64 (added to the tens) or laboriously counted from one.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks ± 0 must change the number — 12 + 0 = 13 (or 120), 16 − 0 = 15.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Act out adding nothing / taking nothing away to establish that zero leaves the quantity unchanged.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child alters the number when adding or subtracting zero.

errorPatterns.pattern: Method right but counting-on/back slips by one (off-by-one).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold count-back, naming the first jump aloud; the strategy is sound, so do not reteach it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 17 − 3 given as 15 (counted the starting number as the first jump).

responseLevels.gap: Adds to the wrong part, counts all from one, or changes the number when adding/subtracting zero.
responseLevels.full: Adds/subtracts ones within the teens by place value, counting on/back efficiently, and treats ± 0 as leaving the number unchanged.
responseLevels.partial: Calculates within the decade correctly but slowly by counting, or is unsure about the zero cases.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these out (you can jot or use a number line): 14 + 5? … 17 − 3? … 12 + 0? … 16 − 0?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: These stay within the teens with no crossing of ten, so a child who understands place value adds the ones to the ones digit (14 + 5 → 4 + 5 = 9 → 19). Watch for adding to the wrong part or counting all from one; the ± 0 items catch the belief that an operation must change the number.

pedagogy.summary: Mental addition and subtraction with increasingly large numbers, driven by place-value knowledge and derived facts rather than a visualised written algorithm. The core move is to SCALE a known small-number fact by place value (4 + 8 = 12, so 40,000 + 8,000 relates to 45,000 + 8,000 = 53,000) and to choose an efficient strategy — partitioning, compensation, near-doubles, and counting up for subtraction from round numbers (10,000 - 3,200). Fluency here means flexible, place-value-based mental strategies, not doing the column algorithm in one's head.
bestPractices: Build from known facts scaled by place value ('you know 6 + 4 = 10, so 6,000 + 4,000 = 10,000') and watch the zeros
Teach counting up (shopkeeper's method) for subtraction from round numbers (10,000 - 3,200 = count up 6,800)
Use near-doubles and compensation as first-choice mental strategies
Encourage jottings (empty number line) to support, not replace, mental method
Discuss strategy choice: which numbers make which strategy smart
keyRepresentations: Empty number line (counting up, bridging)
Place-value chart / Gattegno chart (scaling a fact by ×10)
Part-whole partitioning diagram
Known-fact 'family' cards scaled up
commonMisconceptions: Fails to scale a bond correctly - misplaces zeros (45,000 + 8,000 given as 125,000 or 5,300)
Tries to visualise the full column algorithm mentally and loses track of the exchanges
Subtracts from a round number by decomposing in the head instead of counting up, and errs
Treats +/- of large numbers as fundamentally harder rather than the same facts scaled
Ignores an efficient strategy (counting up, compensation) and grinds digit by digit

learn.summary: Year 5 mental addition and subtraction with increasingly large numbers, built from place-value knowledge and derived facts rather than running a written column algorithm in the head. The central move is to scale a known small-number fact by place value (knowing 6 + 4 = 10 lets you reach 6,000 + 4,000 = 10,000; knowing 45 + 8 = 53 gives 45,000 + 8,000 = 53,000) while tracking the zeros, and to choose an efficient strategy for the numbers at hand: partitioning, compensation, near-doubles, and counting up from the smaller to the larger number for subtraction from round numbers (10,000 - 3,200 = 6,800). Fluency means flexible, place-value-based mental strategies and the ability to explain the choice, not silent reproduction of column working.

activities.title: Scaling bench: a small fact with zeros bolted on
feedback: If the digits are right but the magnitude is wrong (e.g. 5,300 or 53,00 for 45,000 + 8,000), name it as a place-value slip: re-slide 45 + 8 = 53 up the chart saying the unit each step so '53' becomes '53 thousand'.
If the learner recomputes from scratch at each scale instead of reusing the known fact, pause and ask 'which small fact is hiding inside this one?' before continuing.
activities.rationale: Deriving new facts from known facts scaled by place value is an explicit mental-calculation strategy; making the scaling literal (chart row by row, watching zeros) targets the common zero-misplacement error directly.
sourceClaims: Subtraction can be done by complementary addition ('shopkeeper's method') - counting up from the smaller to the larger number, bridging through round-number 'landmarks'; 'many children find it easier to subtract by counting up rather than by counting back', and the answer is the total of the jumps, not a point on the line. Mental calculation rests on deriving new facts from known facts scaled by place value (e.g. 140 + 150 = 290 via 14 + 15 = 29; 680 + 430 via 68 + 43).
learnerActions: State a known small fact first, e.g. 6 + 4 = 10, then scale it up a place-value row at a time: 60 + 40 = 100, 600 + 400 = 1,000, 6,000 + 4,000 = 10,000, saying aloud how many zeros the answer gains.
Repeat the scaling with a fact that bridges, e.g. 45 + 8 = 53, to reach 450 + 80 = 530 and 45,000 + 8,000 = 53,000; say the unit explicitly ('45 thousand plus 8 thousand is 53 thousand').

Check each scaled answer keeps '53' as its non-zero digits and changes only in magnitude, matching the size of the numbers being added (530 is 53 tens; 53,000 is 53 thousands); flag an answer that loses that digit pattern (e.g. 125,000) or that keeps the digits but lands at the wrong magnitude (e.g. 5,300 instead of 53,000) as a scaling slip, not a new sum.
activities.intendedInsight: A 'big' calculation is often a small fact the learner already owns, with place value shifting the whole fact up predictably; the zeros are bookkeeping, not extra arithmetic.

activities.title: Counting up from a round number
feedback: If the learner gives the landing point instead of the total of the jumps, remind them the answer is the sum of the hops (800 + 6,000 = 6,800), not 10,000.
If the learner describes 'borrowing' across the zeros and pauses or errs, model the gap on a number line instead: frame it as measuring the distance between the two numbers.
For 20,000 - 19,850, if the learner starts a full decomposition, prompt 'how far apart are these two numbers?' to surface the single small jump of 150.
activities.rationale: Complementary addition (counting up through round-number landmarks) is documented as a mental subtraction strategy many children find easier than counting back, and it sidesteps the exchange-tracking error that arises when picturing the column method across zeros.
sourceClaims: Subtraction can be done by complementary addition ('shopkeeper's method') - counting up from the smaller to the larger number, bridging through round-number 'landmarks'; 'many children find it easier to subtract by counting up rather than by counting back', and the answer is the total of the jumps, not a point on the line. Mental calculation rests on deriving new facts from known facts scaled by place value (e.g. 140 + 150 = 290 via 14 + 15 = 29; 680 + 430 via 68 + 43).
learnerActions: Subtract 3,200 from 10,000 by counting up on an empty number line: jump +800 from 3,200 to 4,000, then +6,000 from 4,000 to 10,000; the answer is the TOTAL of the jumps, 6,800 (not the point you land on).
Try 20,000 - 19,850 the same way: notice the numbers are close, count up +150 from 19,850 to 20,000, and decide this gap is tiny so counting up is clearly quicker than decomposing.
Say aloud whether counting up or taking away felt easier for each, and why the numbers made that choice sensible.
activities.intendedInsight: Subtraction from a round number is a short journey measured by adding the jumps; counting up avoids the error-prone mental 'borrowing' across a string of zeros, and the size of the gap signals when it is the smart choice.

activities.title: Choosing a strategy to fit the numbers
feedback: If the learner reaches a correct answer by one slow default method throughout, accept the answer but ask 'what did you notice about these two numbers?' to prompt near-doubles or counting up.
If the learner cannot name any strategy, work one example together and have them re-explain it in their own words before the next item.
activities.rationale: The target is flexible strategy choice (scaled fact, counting up, near-doubles, compensation), so activities should require naming and justifying the method, since a correct answer by an inefficient route still signals strategy inflexibility. Sorting a strategy can check that a learner classifies it, though classification alone does not require independently constructing and carrying out the calculation, so the main work stays learner-generated.
learnerActions: Look at 2,500 + 2,600 and spot the near-double: double 2,500 = 5,000, then add 100 to get 5,100, rather than partitioning digit by digit.
Sort a mixed set of calculations into 'count up' versus 'partition' versus 'near-double/compensate', saying what feature of the numbers triggered each choice.
After solving each item, explain the method used; compare a partitioning route and a near-doubles/counting-up route side by side for the same item to see which was fewer steps.
activities.intendedInsight: Efficient mental calculation is about reading the numbers and picking a strategy that fits them, not applying one default method to everything.

activities.title: Explain your mental shortcut
feedback: If the explanation reveals an inefficient route despite a correct answer, affirm the answer then model the more efficient strategy for comparison.
Use 'talk me through it' to catch a right answer reached by mentally running the column algorithm, and redirect to scaling or counting up.
activities.rationale: Asking the learner to articulate a strategy is a design proposal intended to support metacognition and to help distinguish an efficient, place-value-based method from a laborious one; the counting-up and derived-fact strategies being explained are themselves documented, but the source does not establish that explaining them aids learning. Explanation is intended to support fluency and does not replace repeated practice.
learnerActions: After doing a calculation in your head, talk a listener through HOW you did it, step by step, so the method is audible, not just the answer.

Answer prompts such as: 'How does knowing 45 + 8 help with 45,000 + 8,000?', 'For 10,000 - 3,200, did you take away or count up, and which was easier here?', and 'What did you notice about 2,500 and 2,600 that let you use a double?'
Transfer the explained method to a fresh case (e.g. 20,000 - 19,850) and predict which strategy will be quickest before solving.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the strategy aims to consolidate it and to expose whether a right answer came from an efficient, place-value-based method or a laborious one.

constraints: These are mental strategies: the aim is flexible place-value reasoning, not reproducing the written column algorithm in the head.
Jottings such as an empty number line should support the mental method, not replace it with full written working.

Sorting tasks and fill-in-the-blank recall can rehearse and check scaled facts and strategy classification, but recognising or categorising a strategy is not the same as independently constructing and carrying out the calculation; keep the main work learner-generated and spoken/explained.

A reference poster or tappable fact-family display is useful as a lookup, but on its own it does not require the learner to perform the scaling or the counting up; use it alongside active calculation.

A linked place-value chart that slides a fact up a row while the answer gains zeros, and a number line showing counting-up hops that total the answer, are helpful ways to make the mechanism concrete; they are optional supports, not required apparatus.
Do not ban or time-pressure a child who still counts on in ones for parts of a calculation; this matures as derived-fact fluency grows. Keep modelling place-value jumps and let the counting recede.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic in the source was checked and is correct: 45,000 + 8,000 = 53,000; 10,000 - 3,200 = 6,800 (800 + 6,000); 2,500 + 2,600 = 5,100 (double 2,500 = 5,000, +100); 20,000 - 19,850 = 150 (count up +150). The listed wrong answers (125,000; 5,300; 53,00) are preserved only as error patterns to diagnose, never as valid options.

The source's catalog judgement that mental place-value calculation 'is not spatial' and that a 3D treatment adds nothing is a fit ranking, not an established pedagogical law; it has been dropped rather than asserted. No comparative-efficacy or necessity claim between media is made here.
The counting-up answer must be the TOTAL of the jumps, not the number landed on; this is emphasised in the activity to pre-empt a known slip, consistent with the source claim.

Activity 4 (explain your shortcut) cites no source: the source documents counting-up and derived-fact strategies but does not establish that having learners explain them improves learning, so that efficacy framing is left as a design proposal.

probeDeeper: How does knowing 45 + 8 help you with 45,000 + 8,000?
For 10,000 - 3,200, did you take away or count up - which was easier here and why?
What did you notice about 2,500 and 2,600 that let you use a double?
What about 20,000 - 19,850 - would you take away, or count up?
assess.correctAnswer: 45,000 + 8,000 = 53,000 (scales 45 + 8 = 53, keeps the thousands). 10,000 - 3,200 = 6,800, ideally by counting up from 3,200 (to 4,000 is 800, to 10,000 is 6,000, total 6,800). 2,500 + 2,600 = 5,100 via near-doubles (double 2,500 = 5,000, add 100). Explains the strategy chosen.

errorPatterns.pattern: Misplaces the zeros when scaling a bond - '45,000 + 8,000' given as 125,000, 5,300, or 53,00
errorPatterns.nextMove: Slide the fact up the place-value chart (45 + 8 = 53, so 45 thousand + 8 thousand = 53 thousand); make the unit explicit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer has the right digits but wrong magnitude

errorPatterns.pattern: Tries to picture the full column algorithm in the head for 10,000 - 3,200 and loses track of the exchanges across the zeros
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model counting up on an empty number line; frame subtraction from a round number as measuring the gap.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Long pause then a wrong answer; describes 'borrowing' rather than counting up

errorPatterns.pattern: Ignores the efficient strategy - grinds digit by digit or counts in small steps instead of using near-doubles / counting up
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare strategies side by side; ask 'what do you notice about these two numbers?' to prompt near-doubles.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gets there slowly by an inefficient route; cannot name a strategy

errorPatterns.pattern: Still counts on in ones for parts of the calculation rather than using place value
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT ban or time-pressure the counting - it matures with derived-fact fluency; keep modelling place-value jumps and let it recede.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Whispered counting; slow single-unit steps

responseLevels.gap: Cannot do them mentally, or misplaces zeros; no strategy beyond counting.
responseLevels.full: Selects an efficient, place-value-based strategy per item (scaled fact, counting up, near-doubles), explains the choice, and transfers to a new case such as 20,000 - 19,850.
responseLevels.partial: Reaches correct answers but by one default method throughout (e.g. always partitioning), misses counting-up on 10,000 - 3,200 or near-doubles on 2,500 + 2,600, and cannot transfer to 20,000 - 19,850.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to do these in their head and talk you through HOW: 45,000 + 8,000; 10,000 - 3,200; and 2,500 + 2,600. Listen for the strategy, not just the answer.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 10,000 - 3,200 rewards counting up and punishes a child who tries to run the column algorithm mentally across the zeros. 45,000 + 8,000 exposes whether a known bond is scaled correctly or the zeros are misplaced. 2,500 + 2,600 invites near-doubles - a child who partitions laboriously reveals strategy inflexibility. The 'talk me through it' makes the method visible, so a right answer by an inefficient route is still caught.
