pedagogy.summary: Writing simple fractions of quantities (1/2 of 6 = 3) and recognising the first equivalence: 2/4 = 1/2. Equivalence means two differently-written fractions name the SAME amount (the same-sized piece, cut into a different number of parts). This is the child's first encounter with the idea that a fraction has many names, and the natural place to confront the whole-number bias that '2/4 must be more than 1/2 because the numbers are bigger'.
bestPractices: Establish equivalence by overlaying identical wholes cut two ways (two quarters exactly cover one half)
Derive equivalence from sharing (four pizzas among eight children = 4/8 = 2/4 = 1/2 - IES)
Write the fraction sentence alongside the model (1/2 of 6 = 3) so notation records a known amount
Confront the 'bigger numbers = more' intuition head-on with a predict-then-check comparison
Ask for more than one name for the same amount to normalise many-names-one-value
keyRepresentations: Two identical bars, one halved and one quartered, with two quarters overlaid on one half
A fraction wall aligning 1/2 with 2/4
A set of 6 shared into two equal groups (1/2 of 6 = 3)
Number line with 1/2 and 2/4 landing on the same point
commonMisconceptions: 2/4 is more than 1/2 because the numbers are bigger (whole-number bias)
Two fractions written with different numbers cannot name the same amount (no concept of equivalence)
Errors computing a unit fraction of a quantity (1/2 of 6) by not sharing equally

learn.summary: Year 2 children (ages 6-7) write simple fractions of quantities (e.g. 1/2 of 6 = 3) and meet their first fraction equivalence: 2/4 = 1/2. Equivalence means two differently-written fractions name the same amount - the same-sized piece, cut into a different number of parts. This is the natural place to confront the whole-number bias that '2/4 must be more than 1/2 because the numbers are bigger'. The core teaching move is predict-then-check: the child predicts a comparison, then overlays two quarters onto one half to see them coincide exactly.

activities.title: Overlay check: proving 1/2 = 2/4 by covering
feedback: If the child predicts 2/4 is more because '2 pieces is more than 1' or 'the numbers are bigger', let them do the overlay: the two quarters cover the half exactly, so the amounts are equal despite the larger numbers.
If the pieces don't line up, check that both bars were the same size to start and that each bar was cut into equal pieces; re-cut and overlay again.
Reinforce correct work: 'You found two names for the same amount - 1/2 and 2/4 are equal.'
When they find a further equivalent such as 3/6, confirm that it too covers one half, so the same amount can have many names.
activities.rationale: Overlaying identical wholes cut two ways lets the child see directly that two quarters coincide with one half. Starting from a prediction makes the whole-number bias explicit before it is contradicted. Using identical-sized wholes removes any 'it depends on the bar' escape, keeping attention on the fractions themselves.
sourceClaims: Children view fractions with larger denominators/numbers as larger (whole-number bias), which obstructs seeing 2/4 = 1/2
Year 2 pupils write simple fractions (e.g. 1/2 of 6 = 3) and recognise the equivalence of 2/4 and 1/2
learnerActions: Take two identical chocolate bars (or paper strips of the same length). Cut one into 2 equal pieces and the other into 4 equal pieces.
Before moving anything, predict and say aloud: are 2 pieces from the four-piece bar MORE, LESS, or the SAME as 1 piece from the two-piece bar? Give your reason.
Place the two quarter-pieces exactly on top of the one half-piece and check whether they cover it with nothing left over and no overlap.
Write the result as a fraction sentence: 1/2 = 2/4, and say in words 'the same amount, cut into a different number of parts'.
Find at least one more name for the same amount (for example cut another identical bar into 6 and check that 3/6 also covers one half).
activities.intendedInsight: Two quarters cover exactly one half, so 2/4 and 1/2 name the same amount even though 2/4 uses bigger numbers. A fraction has many names for one value. The prediction step surfaces the 'bigger numbers = more' intuition so the overlay can confront it directly.

activities.title: Equal sharing: deriving equivalent fractions
feedback: If the child treats 4/8 and 1/2 as different amounts, lay the shares side by side so they see each child's portion is identical.
Confirm when they connect the sharing result to equivalence: 'Each child gets half a pizza - that's why 4/8 = 2/4 = 1/2.'
activities.rationale: Equal-sharing scenarios with common factors give a meaningful route into equivalence, complementing the overlay model.
sourceClaims: Equivalence can be developed from equal-sharing scenarios with common factors (e.g. four pizzas among eight children give 4/8 = 2/4 = 1/2)
learnerActions: Share 4 pizzas equally among 8 children by drawing or using counters; work out how much each child gets.
Write the share each child receives as a fraction (4/8), then show by grouping that this is also 2/4 and 1/2.
Explain in your own words why 4/8, 2/4 and 1/2 all describe the same share.
activities.intendedInsight: Equivalent fractions arise naturally from equal sharing: the same real share can be written with different numbers, and these names are equal.

activities.title: Finding a fraction of a quantity by equal sharing
feedback: If the child gives a wrong value for 1/2 of 6, check that the counters were shared into two EQUAL groups before counting one group.
If the child struggles to make four equal groups from 6 whole counters, point back to the equivalence 2/4 = 1/2 so they can compute 1/2 of 6 = 3 instead; both routes give 3.
Confirm correct sentences: 'Half of 6 is 3, and because 2/4 is the same as 1/2, 2/4 of 6 is also 3.'
activities.rationale: Grounding 'fraction of a quantity' in equal sharing addresses the error of not dividing into equal groups and links computation back to the written notation. The final answer 2/4 of 6 = 3 is a whole number, but making four equal groups of whole counters is awkward (6 shared four ways is 1.5 each), so routing through the known equivalence 2/4 = 1/2 keeps young learners on whole-counter sharing while reinforcing why equivalent fractions give equal results.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils write simple fractions (e.g. 1/2 of 6 = 3) and recognise the equivalence of 2/4 and 1/2
learnerActions: Take a set of 6 counters. Share them into 2 equal groups and count one group to find 1/2 of 6.
Write the sentence 1/2 of 6 = 3 next to your groups.
Try 1/2 of 10 by sharing 10 into 2 equal groups, and write 1/2 of 10 = 5.

Now find 2/4 of 6. Sharing 6 counters into 4 equal groups does not give whole counters (each group would be one and a half), so use the equivalence 2/4 = 1/2: since 1/2 of 6 = 3, we know 2/4 of 6 is also 3.
activities.intendedInsight: A unit fraction of a quantity is found by sharing equally into the number of parts named by the denominator and taking one group. Because 2/4 = 1/2, taking 2/4 of a quantity gives the same result as taking 1/2 of it.

activities.title: Many names on one point: number line and matching
feedback: If the fractions land on different points, check the line was divided into equal parts; re-measure.
If the child matches by digit size rather than value, return to the overlay or number line to show the true equal pairs.
Confirm: 'Both sit on the same point, so 1/2 and 2/4 are the same amount.'
activities.rationale: A number-line view and matching/recognition tasks consolidate equivalence after the hands-on overlay. Matching and choosing answers check recognition of equivalent pairs; they do not by themselves show the child can construct or explain an equivalence, so pair them with the explaining and overlay work.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils write simple fractions (e.g. 1/2 of 6 = 3) and recognise the equivalence of 2/4 and 1/2
learnerActions: Mark 0 and 1 at the ends of a strip or line. Fold or measure to place 1/2, then divide the same line into quarters and place 2/4.
Check that 1/2 and 2/4 land on exactly the same point.
Match written fractions to their equal partners (for example pair 1/2 with 2/4), explaining why each pair is equal and why a 'bigger numbers' pairing would be wrong.
Say or write a short justification: 'They are at the same point, so they are the same amount.'
activities.intendedInsight: Equivalent fractions occupy the same position on the number line, giving another way to see that different names can mean one value. Matching tasks let the child rehearse recognising equivalent pairs and rejecting 'bigger-number' traps.

constraints: Use identical-sized wholes (same-length bars or strips) when demonstrating equivalence by overlay; different-sized wholes let the child escape with 'it depends on the bar' and break the comparison. This common-whole requirement applies to comparing the represented portions; as numbers, 1/2 and 2/4 remain comparable (indeed equal).
Every whole must be cut into EQUAL parts before counting or sharing; unequal parts invalidate both the fraction-of-a-quantity work and the overlay.

Matching and multiple-choice tasks assess recognition of equivalent pairs; they do not elicit independent construction or explanation, so include tasks where the child builds a model and states why in words.

A printed fraction wall or equivalence poster is a useful reference but is fixed: the child cannot test the overlay on it. Pair reference images with an activity where the child actually cuts and overlays pieces.
Keep the prediction step before the check: recording the child's reason first is what makes the whole-number bias visible and the overturning meaningful.

When a quantity does not share cleanly into the number of groups named by a denominator (e.g. sharing 6 whole counters into four equal groups), route the task through an equivalent unit fraction (2/4 of 6 via 1/2 of 6) rather than forcing fractional counters.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support teaching principles rather than proving any specific activity was tested.

The original probeDeeper prompt '1/2 of 6 is 3 - what is 2/4 of 6?' invites forming four equal groups of 6, which does not give whole counters (6 shared four ways is 1.5 each). The activity now computes 2/4 of 6 via the equivalence 2/4 = 1/2, giving 3. The final value (3) is correct either way; only the intermediate whole-counter grouping is awkward. Original phrasing retained here for reviewer awareness.
Arithmetic checks: 1/2 of 6 = 3 and 1/2 of 10 = 5 are correct; 4/8 = 2/4 = 1/2 and 3/6 = 1/2 are correct equivalences; 2/4 of 6 = 3.

The equal-sharing example (4 pizzas among 8 children) and whole-number-bias framing come from the IES/WWC guide claims; efficacy or necessity of any one representation is not asserted beyond what those claims state.

Independent re-audit found no new learner-facing errors, contradictions, or unsupported categorical modality claims; removed catalogue rankings and the '3D adds nothing'/'dialogue is poor' dismissals were not reintroduced.

assess.poeTask: Show two identical chocolate bars. Ask the child to predict and justify: is 2 pieces from the four-piece bar MORE, LESS, or the SAME as 1 piece from the two-piece bar? Record the reason. Then place the two quarter-pieces exactly on top of the one half-piece; observe they cover it exactly. The pre-observation reason is diagnostic - a 'bigger numbers / more pieces' justification reveals the whole-number bias that the overlay then contradicts (2/4 = 1/2).
probeDeeper: Can you find another fraction that is the same amount as 1/2?
Is 2/4 always equal to 1/2, even for a bigger bar?
1/2 of 6 is 3 - what is 2/4 of 6?
Why can two fractions that look different be the same amount?
assess.correctAnswer: The same amount. 1/2 and 2/4 are equivalent - they name the same-sized piece, just cut into a different number of parts. Two quarters cover exactly one half. (Tier 2: 1/2 = 2/4.)

errorPatterns.pattern: 2/4 is more than 1/2 - 'two pieces is more than one', or 'the numbers are bigger' (whole-number bias)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Predict-then-overlay two quarters onto one half (see poeTask); they coincide, so the amounts are equal.
errorPatterns.distractor: The second one - 2/4 is more than 1/2 because 2 is more than 1
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Chooses the four-piece bar as more and justifies by piece-count or digit size

errorPatterns.pattern: Two fractions written with different numbers cannot be the same amount - no concept of equivalence
errorPatterns.nextMove: Same amount, different name: overlay the pieces and show one point on a number line; collect other names for 1/2.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Insists 1/2 and 2/4 must differ because they are written differently

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot compute a unit fraction of a quantity (e.g. 1/2 of 6) reliably
errorPatterns.nextMove: Share 6 into two equal groups; write 1/2 of 6 = 3 alongside.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives a wrong value for 1/2 of 6 by not sharing into two equal groups

responseLevels.gap: Says 2/4 and 1/2 differ because the numbers differ, or picks 2/4 as more; no equivalence idea.
responseLevels.full: Recognises 2/4 = 1/2 as the same amount with different names, explains it with a model, computes unit fractions of quantities, and finds or tests a further equivalent (e.g. 3/6).
responseLevels.partial: Accepts 2/4 = 1/2 when shown a diagram but cannot generate another equivalent name or explain why, or cannot compute 1/2 of a quantity.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show two identical chocolate bars. One is cut into 2 equal pieces and you take 1 piece; the other is cut into 4 equal pieces and you take 2 pieces. Ask: 'Do you have the same amount of chocolate, more, or less? How do you know?' Then ask: 'So what can you say about the fractions 1/2 and 2/4?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A whole-number-bias child says the 2/4 bar is more 'because 2 pieces / bigger numbers', giving a clear wrong reason; a child with the equivalence idea says 'the same' and names 1/2 and 2/4 as equal. Identical bars remove any 'depends on the bar' escape, so the judgement is purely about the fractions.

pedagogy.summary: At 8-9 precision spans fraction/decimal vocabulary, naming angle types (acute, obtuse) accurately, specifying units in measurement and money, and using notation (=, <, >, ÷, ×) correctly. Two strands become load-bearing: area answers need a SQUARE unit ('63 square centimetres', not '63' or '63 cm', because area counts unit squares), and time in 24-hour notation (15:45) must be kept distinct from 12-hour am/pm ('15:45 pm' is a contradiction). Following EEF's KS2 guidance, the teacher rephrases vague pupil language into precise mathematical language rather than merely marking it wrong.
bestPractices: Tie the unit to what is being measured — area counts squares, so it is cm²; contrast 63 cm (a length) with 63 cm² (an area) so the unit carries meaning (CCSS: specify units)
Keep number systems distinct: 24-hour time (00:00–23:59) has no am/pm; show 15:45 and 3:45 pm as the same moment via subtracting 12
Name angles against a right angle — acute is smaller, obtuse is larger — rather than 'big/small angle' (CCSS: clear vocabulary)
Rephrase vague responses into precise mathematical language, modelling the correct term rather than only correcting (EEF KS2/3)
Read notation aloud and have pupils explain, so terms and symbols stay linked to meaning
keyRepresentations: Unit-square tiling to justify cm² for area
Dual 24-hour / 12-hour clock display
Angles compared to a right-angle template (acute/obtuse)
Measurement and money answers written with units
Fraction words matched to symbols (three quarters = ¾)
commonMisconceptions: Gives an area with no unit or a length unit — '63' or '63 cm' instead of '63 cm²'
Mixes 24-hour and 12-hour notation — writes '15:45 pm', or cannot relate 15:45 to 3:45 pm
Names angle types imprecisely — swaps acute and obtuse, or says 'big angle'
Treats 'three fourths' and 'three quarters' as different amounts rather than two correct names for the same value

learn.summary: Mathematical precision for ages 8-9: tie units to what is measured (area counts unit squares, so it is cm², not a bare number or a length unit), keep 24-hour time distinct from 12-hour am/pm (15:45 is the same moment as 3:45 pm, but '15:45 pm' is a contradiction), name angle types against a right angle (acute smaller, obtuse larger and less than a straight angle), and treat 'three fourths' and 'three quarters' as two names for the same value. The teaching move throughout is to rephrase vague language into precise mathematical language and ask the child to say why the exact unit or notation matters, rather than only marking an answer wrong.

activities.title: Tiling to find the unit for area
feedback: If the child writes '63' with no unit, ask: '63 what? Is 63 cm the same as 63 cm²?' and point to the tiled squares.
If the child writes '63 cm', show that cm measures a length along an edge, while the squares filling the rectangle each cover an area, so the count of squares is cm².
When the child supplies '63 cm²' and explains it counts unit squares, confirm that the unit now carries the meaning of the answer.
activities.rationale: Letting the child see area built from counting unit squares makes the square unit come from the structure of the quantity rather than being an arbitrary label; EEF advises rephrasing vague responses into precise mathematical language and using contrasting non-examples (63 cm vs 63 cm²).
sourceClaims: Proficient students specify units of measure, use clear definitions and vocabulary, and state the meaning of the symbols they use to communicate precisely

Teachers should support pupils to use language reflecting mathematical structure by rephrasing vague, non-mathematical responses into appropriate mathematical language, and address misconceptions with counterexamples and non-examples
learnerActions: Enter or write the area of a rectangle, e.g. '63'.
Fill (or draw) the rectangle with unit squares that tile it exactly, counting the squares.
Revise the answer to carry a square unit: '63 cm²' or '63 square centimetres'.
Contrast an edge length of 63 cm (a length measured along one side) with an area of 63 cm² (unit squares covering the inside), and say why they are different quantities.
Answer the prompt: 'why does the unit have to be square?'
activities.intendedInsight: Area counts how many unit squares cover a region, so its unit is a square unit (cm²); a bare number says how many but not of what, and a plain length unit (cm) describes a distance, not a covering.

activities.title: One moment, two clocks: 24-hour vs am/pm
feedback: If the child writes '15:45 pm', ask: 'What does the pm add, or clash with? Does 24-hour time use am/pm?'
If the child cannot relate 15:45 to 3:45 pm, model the subtraction 15 − 12 = 3 and show both naming the same instant.
Confirm success when the child keeps the systems separate and converts between them fluently with a reason.
activities.rationale: Showing the same instant two ways makes the contradiction in '15:45 pm' concrete and gives a conversion method for afternoon and evening times (subtract 12 for 13:00–23:59), with the noon and midnight hours handled separately; this reflects attending to precision in notation.
sourceClaims: Proficient students specify units of measure, use clear definitions and vocabulary, and state the meaning of the symbols they use to communicate precisely
learnerActions: Read a time written in 24-hour notation, e.g. 15:45.

Convert it to 12-hour am/pm: for times from 13:00 to 23:59, subtract 12 from the hour and write pm (15 − 12 = 3, giving 3:45 pm); 12:00–12:59 stays 12 and is pm, 00:00–00:59 becomes 12 am, and 01:00–11:59 keep their hour and are am. Check both show the same moment on a dual clock display.
Decide whether '15:45 pm' can be correct, and explain what the 'pm' clashes with.
Write the same time correctly in each system and state that 24-hour time runs 00:00–23:59 with no am/pm.
activities.intendedInsight: 24-hour and 12-hour are two complete, separate ways of naming the same moment; 'pm' belongs only to the 12-hour system, so stamping it onto a 24-hour time mixes two systems and contradicts itself.

activities.title: Naming angles against a right angle
feedback: If the child says 'big angle' or 'small angle', ask them to compare it to a right angle and attach the term acute or obtuse to that comparison.
If acute and obtuse are swapped, re-anchor on the right-angle template: acute is smaller, obtuse is larger.
Confirm when the child names the type and can say how they are sure.
activities.rationale: Anchoring vocabulary to a right-angle comparison replaces vague size words with a precise, checkable criterion, consistent with using clear mathematical vocabulary.
sourceClaims: Proficient students specify units of measure, use clear definitions and vocabulary, and state the meaning of the symbols they use to communicate precisely
learnerActions: Place or overlay a right-angle template on a given angle.
Decide whether the angle is smaller than a right angle (acute), exactly a right angle (right angle), or larger than a right angle but less than a straight angle (obtuse).
State the angle type using the correct term and justify it by the comparison, avoiding 'big angle' or 'small angle'.
Repeat for several angles, including some close to a right angle.
activities.intendedInsight: Angle names are defined by comparison to a right angle (acute < right < obtuse), so the right angle is the reference that makes the vocabulary precise and reliable.

activities.title: Two names, one value: fraction vocabulary
feedback: If the child treats 'three fourths' and 'three quarters' as different, show both pointing to the same ¾ and the same shaded region.
When the child reads a symbol aloud and explains its meaning, confirm the term and symbol are linked to meaning.
activities.rationale: Linking words, symbols and meaning keeps notation tied to understanding; reading aloud and explaining supports precise mathematical language.
sourceClaims: Proficient students specify units of measure, use clear definitions and vocabulary, and state the meaning of the symbols they use to communicate precisely

Teachers should support pupils to use language reflecting mathematical structure by rephrasing vague, non-mathematical responses into appropriate mathematical language, and address misconceptions with counterexamples and non-examples
learnerActions: Match fraction words to symbols, e.g. 'three quarters' = 'three fourths' = ¾.
Explain that 'three fourths' and 'three quarters' name the same amount, not two different amounts.
Read notation aloud (=, <, >, ÷, ×) and state what each symbol means in a given statement.
activities.intendedInsight: A value can have more than one correct name; 'quarter' and 'fourth' are two words for the same part, and symbols carry fixed meanings that should be read and explained, not just copied.

activities.title: In-role questioner who takes answers literally
feedback: The character should accept an answer only once the unit or notation is unambiguous, prompting 'specify and repair' until it is.
If the child repairs without reason, ask them to say what the original was missing.
activities.rationale: Dialogue that queries bare numbers and mixed time systems draws out the precise unit and notation and lets the child practise repairing their own language, matching EEF's rephrasing-into-precise-language guidance. Offered as an alternative route; this is a proposal, not a claim that dialogue is required or superior to other media.
sourceClaims: Teachers should support pupils to use language reflecting mathematical structure by rephrasing vague, non-mathematical responses into appropriate mathematical language, and address misconceptions with counterexamples and non-examples
learnerActions: Give answers to a character (e.g. a robot or timetable clerk) who queries anything imprecise: '63 what — is that a length or an area?', 'you can't put pm on a 24-hour time'.
Specify the missing unit or repair the mixed notation in response to each query.
State in your own words why the correction matters.
activities.intendedInsight: Precision is what lets another reader interpret an answer correctly; a bare number or mixed notation leaves the meaning ambiguous.

activities.title: Fix-the-notation screener
feedback: Correct responses supply the square unit and spot the 24-hour/pm contradiction; use misses to route the child to the tiling or dual-clock activity.
Because recognition and completion items confirm the fix but not the reasoning, follow up by asking the child to explain why.
activities.rationale: Short items screen efficiently for the units slip and 24-hour errors, but a screener on its own checks the correction rather than eliciting the reasoning behind the convention, so it is best used to feed the richer activities.
learnerActions: Complete items that add the missing unit to an answer (e.g. turn '63' into '63 cm²').
Convert between 24-hour and am/pm (e.g. 15:45 ↔ 3:45 pm) and flag a mixed form like '15:45 pm' as wrong.
Identify a diagnostic case: 'A child wrote the area as 63 and a time as 15:45 pm — fix anything that isn't right and say why the missing or wrong part matters.'
activities.intendedInsight: Quick items can reveal who leaves units off or mixes time systems, pointing to where fuller teaching is needed.

constraints: Area answers must carry a square unit (cm²/square centimetres): a bare number or a length unit (cm) is not an acceptable area, because area counts unit squares.
24-hour time runs 00:00–23:59 and uses no am/pm; '15:45 pm' is a contradiction and must be either 15:45 or 3:45 pm.
Angle names are defined relative to a right angle (acute < right < obtuse, with obtuse less than a straight angle); 'big'/'small angle' is not precise naming.

A static labelled reference can show correct units and time formats but does not itself let the child tile an area, convert a time, or repair notation, so pair any reference with activities that require the child to produce and correct.
Recognition/completion items confirm whether a fix is applied but do not on their own elicit the child's explanation of why the convention matters; follow them with a 'say why' prompt.

Interactive feedback examples (a rectangle that fills with unit squares, a dual clock lighting 15:45 and 3:45 pm together, an error on '15:45 pm', a right-angle overlay) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory tooling; the same insights can be reached with paper tiling, drawn clocks, and a paper right-angle corner.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and the cited claims support general principles (attend to precision; rephrase into precise language) rather than proving any specific activity was tested.

The source framed 24-hour vs 12-hour and angle naming as 'not spatial in a way 3D would illuminate' and a static image as unable to teach these strands. These are catalog-fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws; they have been softened to scope limits (observable affordances) rather than universal claims.

The source held reteach prerequisite links for area-by-counting-squares and for acute/obtuse identification (none given for time); these were internal catalog identifiers, were never surfaced to learners, and have been removed from this guidance.

probeDeeper: You wrote 63 for the area — 63 what? Is 63 cm the same as 63 cm²?
Can '15:45 pm' be right? What does the 'pm' add, or clash with?
What's the same and what's different about 'three fourths' and 'three quarters'?
Is this angle acute or obtuse — and how can you be sure?
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for correcting '63' to '63 cm²' / '63 square centimetres' (area is measured in square units because it counts unit squares, not a bare number or a length unit) and recognising '15:45 pm' is wrong because 24-hour time uses no am/pm — it is 15:45, the same as 3:45 pm — and for saying why (63 alone doesn't say how much or of what; 15:45 pm mixes two systems). Surfaced for discussion, not scored.

errorPatterns.pattern: Gives an area with no unit, or a length unit — '63' or '63 cm' — instead of '63 cm²'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show area as tiled unit squares so the unit must be square; contrast 63 cm (a length) with 63 cm² (an area). Reteach measuring area by counting unit squares.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: States an area as a bare number or with cm, untroubled by 'is 63 cm the same as 63 cm²?'

errorPatterns.pattern: Mixes 24-hour and 12-hour notation — writes '15:45 pm' or cannot relate 15:45 to 3:45 pm
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish that 24-hour time runs 00:00–23:59 with no am/pm, and 15:45 = 3:45 pm (15−12=3). Reteach in place with a dual clock.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Stamps am/pm on a 24-hour time or mis-converts between the systems

errorPatterns.pattern: Names angle types imprecisely — swaps acute and obtuse or says 'big/small angle'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare each angle to a right angle — acute is smaller, obtuse is larger — and attach the term to the comparison. Reteach identifying acute and obtuse angles.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Mislabels an obtuse angle as acute or avoids the terms

responseLevels.gap: Gives areas with bare or length units, muddles 24-hour and 12-hour time, and uses imprecise angle words.
responseLevels.full: Unprompted, uses correct square units, keeps 24-hour and am/pm distinct and converts fluently, names angle types precisely, and explains why the exact unit or notation is needed.
responseLevels.partial: When prompted, adds cm² and converts 15:45 to 3:45 pm, but not consistently or spontaneously, and still occasionally confuses acute and obtuse.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A child measured a rectangle and wrote its area as '63'. Another wrote a time as '15:45 pm'. Are these written with enough precision? Fix anything that isn't right, and say why the missing or wrong part matters.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child attending to precision supplies the square unit and spots the 24-hour/pm contradiction; a loose child leaves 63 bare and sees nothing wrong with 15:45 pm. Both slips look fine on the surface and neither is exposed by arithmetic — only attention to convention separates the children.

pedagogy.summary: Children measure and calculate the perimeter of composite (rectilinear) shapes — figures with only straight sides and right angles, like an L-shape, that look like rectangles joined together. The distinctive skill is DEDUCING unmarked side lengths from the labelled ones (opposite sides of the whole must match, adding or subtracting known lengths) before totalling, and adding every boundary side exactly once. The main hazards are forgetting to find the missing sides and adding only the numbers given, mis-deducing a missing length, including internal split-lines, double-counting, and confusing perimeter with area.
bestPractices: Define a rectilinear/compound shape (straight sides, right angles; rectangles joined) and use both terms.
Deduce unmarked sides from labelled ones: the two shorter sides along a direction sum to the opposite longer side (add or subtract known lengths).
Mark each side as it is added so none is missed or counted twice, and check every side is included.
Distinguish the boundary (perimeter) from internal split-lines, which are not part of the perimeter.
Keep perimeter (length, cm) distinct from area (cm²).
keyRepresentations: L-shaped / rectilinear figure with some sides unmarked
Missing-side deduction (opposite sides equal)
Tick-each-side-as-counted method
Boundary-versus-internal-line contrast
commonMisconceptions: Forgets to find the unmarked sides and adds only the given numbers.
Cannot see that the two shorter sides equal the opposite longer side, so mis-deduces a missing length.
Includes internal lines, double-counts a side, or confuses perimeter with area.

learn.summary: Year 5 pupils measure and calculate the perimeter of composite rectilinear shapes (straight sides, with every corner made by sides meeting at right angles — rectangles joined, e.g. an L-shape). The distinctive skill is DEDUCING unmarked side lengths from the labelled ones: in each direction, the side lengths on one side of the shape add up to the side lengths on the opposite side. In an L-shape this means the two shorter sides along one direction add up to the opposite longer side (so a missing length is found by adding the two shorter sides, or by subtracting a known shorter side from the longer one); other shapes, such as U- or T-shapes, may have more than two parts on one side. Pupils then total every boundary side exactly once. Chief hazards: adding only the given numbers (forgetting missing sides), working out a missing length wrongly, including internal split-lines, double-counting a side, and confusing perimeter (a length in cm or m) with area (cm2 or m2).

activities.title: Trace-the-boundary L-shape with live missing-side reveal
feedback: If you reached an unmarked side and guessed, line it up against the opposite side(s) of the whole shape and add or subtract the known lengths — the total length across the shape in each direction must match.
If your total is too large, check whether you added an inside line or counted a side twice; a side should tick off only once as you trace.
If you added only the printed numbers, ask: have I found every unmarked side first? Mark each side before adding anything.
activities.rationale: Tracing the boundary while deducing unmarked sides is intended to make the deduction step — the crux of the topic — concrete, and ticking each side as it is added directly guards against the miscounting and double-counting the curriculum flags. An OPTIONAL interactive version can light and tick each side as the finger passes, keep the internal line greyed out, and pulse the two opposite labelled sides so their sum snaps onto the blank; these are illustrative mechanisms, not requirements, and the same work can be done on cm paper by hand.
sourceClaims: A rectilinear/compound shape has only straight sides and right angles (rectangles joined). Things to look out for: 'children may miscount when adding the sides of rectilinear shapes'; 'if children do not have a secure understanding of addition and subtraction, they may struggle when finding missing sides'; 'children may find it difficult to see that the two shorter sides are equal to the longer opposite side'. A reasoning task shows a character whose total wrongly 'includes sides that are inside the shape'. Children are 'encouraged to mark sides that they have already included in their total, to avoid counting sides more than once'.

Year 5 statutory: 'measure and calculate the perimeter of composite rectilinear shapes in centimetres and metres'. Y5 non-statutory: 'Pupils calculate the perimeter of rectangles and related composite shapes, including using the relations of perimeter or area to find unknown lengths.'
learnerActions: Trace a finger (or pen) all the way around the boundary of an L-shaped figure, naming or ticking each side as you pass it so no side is counted twice and none is missed.

When you reach an unmarked side, work out its length from the labelled sides: the two shorter sides along a direction add up to the opposite longer side, so find a missing longer side by adding the two shorters, or find a missing shorter side by subtracting the known shorter length from the longer. Write the deduced length on the blank.
Keep a running total as you go; when every side is ticked, read off the perimeter in cm.
Notice the internal 'fold' line where the rectangles join: leave it out — it is not part of the boundary.
activities.intendedInsight: A hidden side length is not missing information: it can be recovered from the labelled sides, because the shorter sides along a direction add up to the opposite longer side. Perimeter is the total distance around the boundary, each side counted exactly once, excluding internal lines.

activities.title: Find-the-missing-side, total, and spot-the-mistake
feedback: If you included a line inside the shape, remember perimeter is only the outer boundary — trace it to check.
If you gave a cm2 answer, you have found area, not perimeter; perimeter is a length in cm, the total of the sides.
For a missing side, point to the opposite side(s) of the whole shape: the total length across in that direction must balance.
activities.rationale: Compute-perimeter, find-missing-side and spot-the-mistake items probe the skill and its characteristic errors directly. A recognition (multiple-choice) spot-the-mistake item checks diagnosis but does not by itself require the pupil to construct a full perimeter from scratch, so pair it with an open compute task.
sourceClaims: A rectilinear/compound shape has only straight sides and right angles (rectangles joined). Things to look out for: 'children may miscount when adding the sides of rectilinear shapes'; 'if children do not have a secure understanding of addition and subtraction, they may struggle when finding missing sides'; 'children may find it difficult to see that the two shorter sides are equal to the longer opposite side'. A reasoning task shows a character whose total wrongly 'includes sides that are inside the shape'. Children are 'encouraged to mark sides that they have already included in their total, to avoid counting sides more than once'.
Learners commonly confuse area and perimeter, often because the concepts and their formulae are met together without conceptual grounding.
learnerActions: Given an L-shape with some sides labelled and some blank, find each unmarked side by adding or subtracting the labelled lengths along that direction, then total the whole perimeter.

Examine a worked solution where a character has made an error — e.g. included an internal join-line, or omitted an unmarked side — and say exactly which side is wrong and what the correct total should be.
Decompose the shape into rectangles to see why the two shorter sides add up to the opposite longer side.
activities.intendedInsight: The method has two stages — deduce all unknown sides, then add every boundary side once — and the common errors (adding only given numbers, including inside lines, double-counting, giving area instead) are specific and checkable.

activities.title: Draw a composite shape to a target perimeter
feedback: If your total isn't 40 cm, re-trace the boundary and re-add, ticking each side once.
Check your shape only has right angles and straight sides; a diagonal or curve changes the task.
Make sure the lengths across the shape in each direction agree with each other.
activities.rationale: Production (drawing and labelling to a constraint) elicits independent construction that a recognition item does not by itself require, and the draw-and-check task still exercises the curriculum skill of calculating the perimeter of a composite shape; it matches the stated evidence of drawing a composite shape with a given perimeter.
sourceClaims: Year 5 statutory: 'measure and calculate the perimeter of composite rectilinear shapes in centimetres and metres'. Y5 non-statutory: 'Pupils calculate the perimeter of rectangles and related composite shapes, including using the relations of perimeter or area to find unknown lengths.'
learnerActions: On cm paper, draw a composite rectilinear shape (rectangles joined, straight sides that always meet at right angles) whose perimeter is exactly 40 cm.
Label every side and check that the total length across the shape in each direction balances.
Add all the boundary sides to confirm the total is 40 cm, ticking each side once.
activities.intendedInsight: Constructing a shape to a given perimeter — not just reading one — requires the pupil to control which sides are boundary, how deduced sides relate, and to keep length (cm) distinct from area.

constraints: Define rectilinear/compound shape explicitly (only straight sides, with sides always meeting at right angles, including the inward corner of an L-shape; rectangles joined) and use both terms.

Include figures with unmarked sides so the deduction step is genuinely required; fully-labelled shapes given to read off only practise addition, not the distinctive skill (the draw-your-own task, where the pupil labels all sides they create, is a separate production activity).
Mark/tick each side as it is added to prevent missing or double-counting a side.
Distinguish the boundary (perimeter) from internal split/join lines, which are excluded.
Keep perimeter (length, cm) distinct from area (cm2); address the common area/perimeter confusion explicitly.
Secure addition and subtraction underpin missing-side deduction; reteach these prerequisites if the pupil cannot combine the known lengths.

Tap-to-reveal or lit-side animations are optional scaffolds that illustrate the method but do not by themselves give the pupil tracing or counting practice — follow them with pupil-constructed working.
A spot-the-mistake multiple-choice item checks error-diagnosis but does not require constructing a full perimeter; include at least one open compute or draw task.

State the relationship precisely: in each direction, the side lengths on one side of the shape SUM to the side lengths on the opposite side. In an L-shape, the two shorter sides along a direction SUM to the opposite longer side, and other composite shapes may have more than two parts on one side. Subtraction is only how a missing shorter side is recovered (longer minus a known shorter), not a restatement that the shorter sides 'equal' the longer.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy 'poor fit' claims that 3D 'adds nothing' and that the learning 'is not a dialogue' were removed as catalog-preference boilerplate; a 2D/paper representation suits planar shapes well, but no source establishes that other media could not also support aspects of the task.

Geometric idealisation note: a drawn or screen figure represents an idealised plane shape; cm-paper cutouts have real thickness and only approximate the ideal figure. This does not affect the perimeter arithmetic but is worth flagging if physical cutouts are used.

Diagnostic example in the source (outer 8 cm and 6 cm with a notch and two unmarked sides) was retained conceptually; exact numeric consistency of any specific L-shape used should be checked so that opposite directions genuinely balance before giving it to a learner.

The White Rose source phrases the relationship as the two shorter sides being 'equal to' the opposite longer side; the accurate statement is that they SUM to it. Learner-facing text uses 'add up to', and subtraction is described only as the operation for recovering a missing shorter side, not as a restatement of the relationship. The verbatim source wording is preserved only within sourceClaims.

Activity 3's DfE sourceClaim grounds the perimeter-calculation content the drawing task exercises; the production-over-recognition point is treated as a narrow objective affordance, not as source-proven efficacy.

probeDeeper: Which sides weren't labelled? How did you work out their lengths?
Trace the perimeter with your finger — did you include any line inside the shape?
How do you know you counted every side exactly once?
If I asked for the area instead, would you do the same thing?
assess.correctAnswer: Deduces the two unmarked sides from the labelled ones (opposite sides of the whole are equal, found by adding or subtracting known lengths), adds all boundary sides exactly once, and gives the perimeter in cm.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds only the labelled numbers and forgets to find the unmarked sides.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Mark every side of the shape; deduce each unmarked side from the opposite labelled sides before adding anything.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Sums the given lengths and stops, omitting the two unmarked sides.

errorPatterns.pattern: Mis-deduces a missing side — does not see that the two shorter sides equal the opposite longer side.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Line up the shape's opposite sides and add or subtract the known lengths to find the missing one; use the decomposition into rectangles to see the relationship.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Guesses or mislabels an unmarked side rather than adding/subtracting the known lengths.

errorPatterns.pattern: Includes an internal split-line, double-counts a side, or confuses perimeter with area.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace the boundary with a finger (perimeter is the distance around) and tick each side once; contrast cm (length) with cm² (area).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Adds a line inside the shape, counts a side twice, or multiplies to give an area instead.

responseLevels.gap: Adds only the given numbers, or includes internal lines / confuses with area; no missing-side reasoning.
responseLevels.full: Deduces unmarked sides from the labelled ones, adds every boundary side exactly once (excluding internal lines), and gives the perimeter in cm, keeping it distinct from area.
responseLevels.partial: Finds the perimeter when all sides are labelled but cannot reliably deduce unmarked sides, or occasionally double-counts; the method is present but not secure.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child an L-shaped figure on cm paper with only some sides labelled (e.g. an outer 8 cm and 6 cm, and a notch with two sides given but two sides left unmarked). Say: 'Find its perimeter.' Then WATCH whether they deduce the unmarked sides from the labelled ones, whether they add every boundary side exactly once (and not the internal line), and whether they confuse it with area.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: An L-shape with unmarked sides forces the deduction step, so a child who only adds the visible numbers is exposed at once; whether they trace the boundary (excluding internal lines) and avoid double-counting is visible in the working, which is why the task is set and watched.
