pedagogy.summary: Converting tenths to hundredths applies the equivalent-fraction principle (×10/×10) so that tenths and hundredths share a common denominator and can be added. It rests on place value: one tenth IS ten hundredths, so 3/10 is 30 hundredths, and 3/10 + 4/100 becomes 30/100 + 4/100 = 34/100. The whole point is that you cannot combine the two until they are the same-sized pieces.
bestPractices: Anchor every conversion on a 10×10 hundredths grid: one full column of ten small squares is one tenth, making '1 tenth = 10 hundredths' visible rather than a rule
Convert BEFORE combining — shade the tenths as whole columns, then the extra hundredths as single squares, then count all the small squares
Connect to place-value columns (tenths | hundredths) and to money/metric (£0.30 = 30p, 3/10 m = 30 cm) so the ×10 relationship is felt in familiar units
Insist the answer is read back in hundredths and, when ready, as a decimal (34/100 = 0.34) to bridge to decimal notation
Contrast a correct conversion with the '7/110' error out loud so children can articulate why you never add the denominators
keyRepresentations: 10×10 hundredths grid (column = tenth, square = hundredth)
Place-value chart with tenths and hundredths columns
Number line 0–1 marked in hundredths
Base-ten flat/rod (rod = tenth of the flat, small cube = hundredth)
commonMisconceptions: Adds across both denominators: 3/10 + 4/100 = 7/110 (adds tops and bottoms)
Treats 3/10 as 3 hundredths, shading three single squares, and reports 7/100
Thinks the denominators can be added because 'they are close', ignoring that the pieces are different sizes

learn.summary: Converting tenths to hundredths rests on place value and the equivalent-fraction principle (×10/×10): one tenth is ten hundredths, so 3/10 = 30/100, and 3/10 + 4/100 becomes 30/100 + 4/100 = 34/100. Learners cannot combine tenths and hundredths until the pieces are the same size, so the conversion must happen before adding. A 10×10 hundredths grid (each column = one tenth = ten small squares) makes this relationship concrete; a base-ten flat/rod model, place-value columns, number lines, money (£0.30 = 30p) and metric (3/10 m = 30 cm) anchor it in familiar units, and the decimal form (34/100 = 0.34) bridges to decimal notation.

activities.title: Build 3/10 + 4/100 on a hundredths grid
feedback: If three columns are shaded, confirm: 'One column is ten small squares, so three columns is thirty hundredths — 3/10 = 30/100.'

If only three single squares are shaded for 3/10, lay a tenth-column (strip of ten) beside one single square and ask how many small squares fit in the column; rebuild the column-of-ten before returning to the sum.
When the total is reported, prompt the learner to read it back in hundredths (34/100) and, when ready, as the decimal 0.34.
activities.rationale: The concept is a transformation that becomes undeniable when seen: shading three tenths and watching them occupy thirty small squares makes '1 tenth = 10 hundredths' concrete rather than a memorised rule. An optional live tally that counts '30 hundredths' as the columns land, and shows 30/100 + 4/100 = 34/100 with the decimal 0.34, can make the recomputation visible; letting the learner first shade three lone squares turns the common error into a self-correcting moment. A base-ten flat/rod set offers the same ×10 structure in a different medium, and a static labelled grid (tap a column to reveal 'this column = 10 hundredths') works as a reference companion, though a fixed picture is not manipulable and so does not let the learner carry out the conversion themselves.
sourceClaims: Creating a common denominator via the equivalent-fraction principle (multiplying numerator and denominator by the same number) is the foundation for adding fractions with unlike denominators, and adding numerators AND denominators is a documented, high-frequency error.
learnerActions: Take a blank 10×10 hundredths grid where each full column of ten small squares represents one tenth.
Shade 3/10 by filling three whole columns, then count the small squares covered to confirm it is 30 hundredths.
Add 4/100 by shading four more single squares.
Count all the shaded small squares and report the total as hundredths (34/100), then, when ready, write it as a decimal (0.34).
Deliberately try shading just three lone single squares for 3/10 first, notice that this is only 3/100, then correct it to three full columns.

Optionally model the same amounts with base-ten blocks, where the flat is one whole, a rod is one tenth, and a small cube is one hundredth, to see the same ×10 relationship in a different manipulative.
activities.intendedInsight: Three tenths covers the same shaded area as thirty hundredths, so tenths must be converted to hundredths before they can be added to hundredths.

activities.title: Explain why 5/10 = 50/100 and challenge the 7/110 error
feedback: If the learner says 5/10 = 5/100, ask them to count the squares in five full columns on the grid to see it is 50.
If they write 7/110, return to the grid: one column is ten squares, so 3/10 covers thirty squares; you can only add once the pieces are the same size — rebuild 3/10 = 30/100 first.
Confirm correct reasoning: 'A tenth is ten hundredths, so you scale both the top and bottom by ten — the amount does not change, only the size of the pieces.'
activities.rationale: Articulating why the add-across-both-denominators error is wrong, and distinguishing which addends already share a denominator, strengthens the equivalence rather than the mechanical count. Checkable prompts (rewrite 7/10 = 70/100; choose between 34/100, 7/110 and 7/100 where the last two are distractors to reject; sort by whether conversion is needed) surface the add-across error directly. Response-selection formats like these can be used during teaching to prompt reasoning, though on their own they check recognition rather than eliciting independent construction.
sourceClaims: Creating a common denominator via the equivalent-fraction principle (multiplying numerator and denominator by the same number) is the foundation for adding fractions with unlike denominators, and adding numerators AND denominators is a documented, high-frequency error.
learnerActions: On a hundredths grid, show 5/10 and explain why it covers 50 small squares, not 5.
Rewrite 7/10 as an equivalent fraction over 100 (70/100).
Respond to a classmate who claims 3/10 + 4/100 = 7/110: explain out loud why you never add the denominators, using the idea that the pieces are different sizes until converted.
When offered answer choices such as 34/100, 7/110 and 7/100, pick 34/100 and say explicitly why each of the other two is wrong.
Sort several sums into 'already hundredths' versus 'convert a tenth first' before solving them.
activities.intendedInsight: Equivalent tenths-to-hundredths conversions come from multiplying numerator and denominator by ten; denominators are never added because they name the size of the pieces, which must match before combining.

activities.title: Connect to place value, money and metric, then to decimals
feedback: If a learner cannot yet convert on paper without the grid, that is partial mastery — return to the grid to re-anchor '1 tenth = 10 hundredths', then retry on paper.

If the method is sound but the square count slips (e.g. 33 or 35), scaffold the count ('ten, twenty, thirty… thirty-one, thirty-two, thirty-three, thirty-four') rather than reteaching the concept — the idea is held, the count slipped.
Confirm the money/metric link: '30p out of 100p is 30 hundredths of a pound, just like 30/100.'
activities.rationale: Anchoring the conversion in money, metric units and the place-value chart lets the ×10 relationship be felt in familiar quantities, and reading answers back as decimals builds the bridge to decimal notation. Transfer to a new pair without the grid distinguishes fluent understanding from grid-dependent success.
learnerActions: Place tenths and hundredths into a place-value chart with labelled tenths and hundredths columns and read the conversion from the columns.
Match each fraction to a familiar unit: 3/10 = £0.30 = 30p, and 3/10 m = 30 cm, noting the ×10 relationship.
Mark 0.34 on a 0–1 number line divided into hundredths and relate it to 34/100.
Write a converted answer such as 34/100 as the decimal 0.34 and say why they are the same quantity.
Transfer to a fresh pair, e.g. 6/10 + 7/100 (= 67/100), aiming to convert without needing the grid.
activities.intendedInsight: The tenth-to-hundredth ×10 relationship is the same structure seen in place value, money and metric measures, and it bridges directly to decimal notation.

constraints: Convert before combining: shade tenths as whole columns, then extra hundredths as single squares, then count all the small squares — do not add until the pieces are the same size.
Never add denominators; 3/10 + 4/100 is not 7/110, and 3/10 is not 3/100. These are the two priority errors to surface and correct, not merely caveat.
A static labelled grid or tap-to-reveal image is a reference scaffold: it can show 7/10 = 70/100 but is not manipulable, so it supports rather than replaces active grid or base-ten work.

Paper or card grid cutouts have slight thickness and can be handled; a drawn or on-screen grid is a flat model of the same quantity — in every case the question is about the fractional amount represented, not the physical object.
Response-selection and sorting tasks can prompt reasoning during teaching but, used alone, check recognition rather than eliciting independent construction of the conversion.

An optional live-tally/snap-counting grid makes the recomputation visible but is one way to realise the activity, not a required mechanism; the same learning works with a drawn grid, base-ten blocks, or spoken counting.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified, and the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The single cited source supports the equivalent-fraction/common-denominator principle and the add-across error as high-frequency; it does not establish the comparative efficacy of the grid, the base-ten model, the live tally, or any specific response format.

An earlier version asserted that spatial depth 'adds nothing' and that dialogue 'adds no value'. These are unsupported categorical claims, not pedagogical laws, and have been softened to affordance statements; the flat grid is well-suited to this planar, quantitative concept but is not proven uniquely necessary.
The earlier claim that a static image 'cannot let the child do the conversion' is retained only as an objective scaffold limit (a fixed image is not manipulable), not as a claim that it cannot teach.
The base-ten flat/rod representation from the original was restored as an optional alternative manipulative; its comparative effectiveness is not independently established.

Arithmetic self-audit: 3/10 = 30/100; 30/100 + 4/100 = 34/100 = 0.34; 7/10 = 70/100; 5/10 = 50/100; 6/10 + 7/100 = 67/100 — all consistent. The erroneous values 7/110 and 7/100 appear only as misconceptions to be corrected or as distractors to reject, never as valid answers in learner-facing tasks.

probeDeeper: How many small squares are in one whole column? So how many hundredths is 3/10?
If a friend told you 3/10 + 4/100 = 7/110, what would you say to them?
What about 5/10 — how many hundredths is that? Show me on the grid why it is 50 and not 5.
Could you write your answer of 34/100 as a decimal as well?
assess.correctAnswer: Shades three full columns for 3/10 (recognising that is 30 small squares / 30 hundredths), adds four single squares for 4/100, and reports 34/100 (may also say 0.34).

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds across both denominators: 'three tenths plus four hundredths is seven over a hundred-and-ten' — combines numerators and denominators as if they were whole numbers
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the grid and count: one column is ten squares, so 3/10 covers thirty squares. You can only add once the pieces are the same size. Rebuild the equivalence 3/10 = 30/100 before re-adding.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 7/110 (or 7/100) without converting; on the grid, shades correctly but then ignores the shading and just adds the written numbers

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats 3/10 as three hundredths — shades three single squares for 3/10 and reports 7/100
errorPatterns.nextMove: Lay a tenth-strip beside a single hundredth-square and ask how many small squares fit in the strip; rebuild the column-of-ten before returning to the sum.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Shades three tiny squares (not three columns) for 3/10; treats a tenth and a hundredth as the same-sized piece

errorPatterns.pattern: Converts correctly but miscounts the squares when tallying (loses track counting in tens then ones)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the count ('ten, twenty, thirty… thirty-one, two, three, four'); do not reteach the concept — the idea is held, the count slipped.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Method is sound — three columns plus four squares — but the reported total is off by a small amount (e.g. says 33 or 35)

responseLevels.gap: Adds numerators and/or denominators directly (7/110 or 7/100), or shades three lone squares for 3/10 — no conversion happens and tenths and hundredths are treated as the same size.
responseLevels.full: Converts 3/10 → 30/100 fluently, combines to 34/100, explains that a tenth is ten hundredths, writes 0.34, and transfers to a fresh pair such as 6/10 + 7/100 without needing the grid.
responseLevels.partial: Converts 3/10 to 30/100 when working on the grid and reaches 34/100, but cannot yet do it fluently on paper without the grid, or lists the steps without being able to say why one column is ten hundredths.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put a blank 10×10 hundredths grid in front of the child. Say: 'Show me 3/10 on this grid, then show me 4/100 as well, and tell me how much you have altogether written as hundredths.' Then watch — say nothing about how to do it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands turns the tenths into hundredths physically — three columns become thirty squares — before combining, so the answer is 34/100. A child who does not either shades three lone squares for 3/10 (reporting 7/100) or writes 7/110 by adding tops and bottoms. The grid forces the tenth-as-ten-hundredths relationship into the open, so the error is visible in what they shade, not just what they write.

sources.claim: Creating a common denominator via the equivalent-fraction principle (multiplying numerator and denominator by the same number) is the foundation for adding fractions with unlike denominators, and adding numerators AND denominators is a documented, high-frequency error.
sources.source: IES/WWC Practice Guide: Developing Effective Fractions Instruction for Kindergarten Through 8th Grade

pedagogy.summary: A fraction a/b is understood as a copies of a unit fraction 1/b, where 1/b is the quantity made by one part when the whole is cut into b EQUAL parts. Teach the unit fraction first as an amount (a specific length/area), then build a/b by iterating (counting) that unit: 3/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4. The pivotal idea is that the denominator names how many equal parts the whole is split into — and therefore the SIZE of each part — while the numerator counts how many of those parts we take. Hold the whole fixed and insist the parts be equal.
bestPractices: Introduce the unit fraction 1/b as a quantity (a definite amount/length), naming it, before non-unit fractions a/b (IES Rec 1 equal-sharing progression).
Build a/b by iterating the unit fraction — 'three-quarters is three one-quarters' — counting unit fractions the way you count objects.
Keep the whole fixed and require parts equal in AREA; accept differently-shaped pieces if they are treated as equal-area.
Vary the whole (bar, circle, length, set) and vary b so children see that the denominator controls the size of each part.
Guard against mechanical part-counting: ask 'how big is ONE part?' not only 'how many are shaded?' (IES caution that strips/circles can mislead if counted without meaning).
Link the area model, the length/number-line jump, and the set model for the same fraction so a/b is not tied to one picture.
keyRepresentations: Area model — a bar or circle partitioned into b equal parts, a shaded
Fraction strips of a single unit size
Length / number-line jump of size 1/b iterated a times
Set model — a of every b·k objects
Cuisenaire rods where a rod is chosen as the whole
commonMisconceptions: Equal-parts ignored — any b pieces are called bths regardless of size (IES Roadblock 1.2)
Counting shaded parts mechanically without grasping that numerator and denominator together name one quantity (IES caution)
Reading the denominator as a group SIZE ('thirds = groups of three') rather than the number of equal parts
Whole-number bias — a bigger denominator means a bigger part or a bigger value
Non-unit fraction taken as a unit fraction — for 3/4 shading just one part
Calling every fractional part 'a half'

learn.summary: Teach a/b as a copies of the unit fraction 1/b, where 1/b is the definite amount made by ONE part when a whole is cut into b EQUAL parts. Build the unit fraction first as a quantity, then iterate it (3/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4). The pivotal insight is that the denominator names how many equal parts the whole is split into — and so, for a given whole, fixes the SIZE of each part — while the numerator counts how many such parts are taken. Within any comparison keep the whole fixed and insist parts be equal (equal area in area models, equal length on lengths/number lines, equal number in sets); vary b on a fixed whole so part-size visibly depends on the denominator, and vary the kind of whole across separate tasks so the idea is not tied to one picture.

activities.title: Cut it fair, then count the unit
feedback: If a learner shades without equalising the parts, ask: 'Are these parts the same size? If not, is one really one-sixth?' Have them re-cut until the parts are equal before naming any as 1/6.
If a learner says 2/6 and 2/4 are 'the same, both are 2', ask 'How big is ONE part in each bar?' and have them overlay a sixth on a fourth to see the sixth is thinner.
If a learner says 2/6 is more 'because 6 is bigger than 4', return to the overlay of one sixth on one fourth; once they see the sixth is the smaller piece, re-ask the comparison.
Reinforce correct reasoning by having them restate: 'the bottom number says how many equal parts, so it sets how big each part is.'
activities.rationale: Introducing the unit fraction as an amount and iterating it to build a/b follows the equal-sharing-before-notation progression and directly confronts whole-number bias and equal-parts errors. Requiring learners to check and re-cut until the parts are equal before labelling any as a fraction, and letting them iterate and overlay the unit themselves, is proposed to make equal-parts and unit-size felt rather than told. The side-by-side 2/6 vs 2/4 comparison with overlay targets the specific misconception that matching numerators mean equal amounts.
sourceClaims: A fraction should be understood as built from unit fractions (a/b as a copies of 1/b), taught via equal-sharing before formal notation; part-whole tools can mislead if children count parts corresponding to numerator and denominator without understanding they together name a single quantity.
Whole-number bias / larger-denominator-is-larger and equal-parts errors are documented children's fraction misconceptions.
learnerActions: Take one whole bar (a chocolate bar works well) and cut it into equal parts, e.g. 6, checking that the parts are genuinely equal in area before accepting them.
Shade ONE part and name it as a quantity: 'this is one-sixth, 1/6'.
Build 2/6, then 3/6, by copying that single 1/6 piece and counting as you go, saying 'two one-sixths, three one-sixths' and writing the label each time.
Reset the sixths bar to show 2/6, then set an identical bar beside it, cut into 4 equal parts, and shade 2 parts on it (so you have 2/6 next to 2/4).
Slide the two shaded regions over one another to compare how much chocolate each shows, and state which is more and why.
activities.intendedInsight: a/b is a copies of an equal part whose size is fixed by the denominator; shading the same NUMBER of parts does not give the same amount, because sixths are smaller than fourths of the same whole (so 2/6 < 2/4).

activities.title: How big is ONE part? (vary the whole and the denominator)
feedback: If a learner counts shaded pieces mechanically, redirect with 'how big is one part?' before accepting the answer.
If a learner thinks 1/8 > 1/4 because 8 > 4, have them cut the SAME whole into 4 then into 8 and compare one piece of each.
Accept differently-shaped pieces as equal if the learner can show they are equal in area; praise reasoning that focuses on amount rather than appearance.
activities.rationale: Linking area, length/number-line, set and Cuisenaire-rod models for one fraction prevents the concept being tied to a single representation, and varying b while holding the whole fixed makes the denominator-controls-size idea visible. Asking 'how big is one part?' guards against mechanical part-counting.
sourceClaims: A fraction should be understood as built from unit fractions (a/b as a copies of 1/b), taught via equal-sharing before formal notation; part-whole tools can mislead if children count parts corresponding to numerator and denominator without understanding they together name a single quantity.
Whole-number bias / larger-denominator-is-larger and equal-parts errors are documented children's fraction misconceptions.
learnerActions: Build the SAME fraction across different wholes — a bar, a circle, a fraction strip, a length/number line, a set of objects (e.g. 2 of every 6), and Cuisenaire rods with one chosen rod as the whole.
On a number line, make the fraction by repeating a jump of size 1/b, a times, instead of shading an area.
Re-cut one bar into 8 equal parts and name one part (1/8); compare its size to one quarter of that same bar and state which is bigger and why.
Draw a given fraction, e.g. 2/6, of the SAME whole a DIFFERENT way — differently shaped parts but the same amount.
For each model, answer not just 'how many are shaded?' but 'how big is ONE part?'
activities.intendedInsight: The same fraction names the same relationship to its whole (and the same number) whatever picture is used, but the amount it shows depends on the size of the whole; for any given whole the denominator controls how many equal parts it is cut into (regardless of that whole's shape), and more equal parts of the SAME whole means each part is smaller (1/8 < 1/4).

activities.title: Predict, then check: comparing same-numerator fractions
feedback: If the stated reason is 'the same, both are 2', after the overlay ask them to explain why 2/4 covers more despite both counting two parts.
If the reason is '6 is more so sixths-bar is more', use the overlay of one sixth on one fourth, then have them re-state the rule about part size.

For the small-bar/big-bar trap, clarify that comparing the ACTUAL amounts of chocolate requires equal wholes, while as numbers 3/4 is still greater than 1/2; praise learners who notice the wholes differ.
activities.rationale: A predict-then-check routine with a reason stated before observing surfaces whole-number and part-counting reasoning diagnostically, and the physical overlay refutes both 'they're the same' and 'more parts means more'. The whole-size caveat protects against over-generalising when comparing physical amounts, without denying that fractions as numbers are comparable.
sourceClaims: Whole-number bias / larger-denominator-is-larger and equal-parts errors are documented children's fraction misconceptions.

A fraction should be understood as built from unit fractions (a/b as a copies of 1/b), taught via equal-sharing before formal notation; part-whole tools can mislead if children count parts corresponding to numerator and denominator without understanding they together name a single quantity.
learnerActions: Before cutting, look at two identical bars. Predict and give a REASON: if 2 parts are shaded on a bar cut into 4, and 2 parts on an identical bar cut into 6, which shows more chocolate — or the same? State the reason out loud BEFORE observing.
Then cut both bars and slide the shaded regions over each other to check.
Revise or confirm your prediction, explaining what the comparison showed.
Build 3/4 from single pieces and say how many quarters and how big each one is.
Tackle the trap question: could 3/4 of a small bar be LESS chocolate than 1/2 of a big bar? State what must be true about the wholes to compare the amounts fairly.
activities.intendedInsight: With the whole held fixed, more equal parts means each part is smaller, so 2/4 > 2/6 and 3/4 > 3/6 even though the counts match; comparing the AMOUNTS shown by two models is only fair when the wholes are the same size, though the fractions themselves, as numbers, remain comparable (3/4 > 1/2 always).

activities.title: Identify, match and construct across models (consolidation)
feedback: For the unequal-pieces item, if a learner accepts it as quarters, overlay or measure the pieces to show they are not equal, so cannot be quarters.
A sort into equal-parts vs not can check classification, but it does not by itself show the learner can build and justify a fraction — follow matching with a construct-and-explain step.
Use evocative illustrations for recognition, but return to a measured/equal-area model whenever size is in question.
activities.rationale: Retrieval, matching and categorisation consolidate the concept once it is built, and the explicit equal-parts-vs-not sort targets the equal-parts misconception by checking classification. This supports, rather than replaces, hands-on partitioning and iterating.
sourceClaims: A fraction should be understood as built from unit fractions (a/b as a copies of 1/b), taught via equal-sharing before formal notation; part-whole tools can mislead if children count parts corresponding to numerator and denominator without understanding they together name a single quantity.
Whole-number bias / larger-denominator-is-larger and equal-parts errors are documented children's fraction misconceptions.
learnerActions: Identify the fraction shaded in a given model, e.g. one shaded part of a shape in 5 equal parts named as 1/5.
Match a written fraction a/b to the model that shows it.
Sort models into 'equal parts' vs 'not equal parts', and judge whether a bar cut into 4 UNEQUAL pieces with one shaded really shows a quarter.
Construct a requested fraction yourself — draw it, or choose/colour the right number of equal parts.
Explain in words what the denominator and numerator each tell you for one chosen example.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure, flexible recognition and construction of a/b across representations, with equal parts as the non-negotiable criterion.

constraints: Always hold the whole fixed and require parts to be equal when naming fractions: equal in AREA for area models, equal in length for length/number-line models, equal in number for set models; differently-shaped pieces of an area model are acceptable only if they are genuinely equal in area.
Introduce the unit fraction 1/b as a named quantity before non-unit fractions a/b.

When comparing the AMOUNTS two models show by counting shaded parts, this is only valid when the wholes are the same size; state this explicitly, especially in trap questions mixing a small and a large whole. Note that fractions as numbers remain comparable regardless (3/4 > 1/2).

A static reference such as a fraction wall can label parts ('one of six equal parts = 1/6') but does not let the learner enforce equal parts or iterate the unit themselves; treat it as a reference layer alongside active partitioning, not a substitute for it.

Recognition-only tasks (identify/match) and sorts confirm classification/fluency but do not by themselves elicit independent construction or justification; pair them with a construct-and-explain step.

Keep the work in the plane (area/length/set); a third spatial dimension is not needed for this planar concept and can obscure equal-area partitioning. This is a scoped limitation here, not a universal claim about 3D media.
Guard against mechanical part-counting: routinely ask 'how big is ONE part?', not only 'how many are shaded?'
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source assessment's worked comparison is sound: with the whole fixed, 3/6 < 3/4 and 2/6 < 2/4 because more equal parts makes each part smaller. These were preserved as the target reasoning.

The whole-size 'fair comparison' caveat applies to comparing physical amounts across different-sized wholes; the fractions themselves as numbers remain comparable (3/4 > 1/2). This scoping was added to avoid implying fractions are not comparable, and Activity 2's part-size claim was tightened to a FIXED whole to match it.
Cuisenaire rods and fraction strips from the source key representations were restored in Activity 2, which an earlier draft had dropped.
The England National Curriculum Year 3 placement claim is marked verified:false in the source; treat the age mapping (ages 8–9 / Year 3) as unconfirmed.

Source claims about equal-sharing progression and documented misconceptions support the general teaching principles cited; they do not establish the comparative efficacy of any specific activity or interactive format proposed here.

The original research rated non-interactive and 3D/dialogue formats as poor fit with strong wording (e.g. 'adds nothing', 'where the learning happens'); these were softened to scoped affordance/limit statements in constraints rather than treated as universal pedagogical laws.

assess.poeTask: Before cutting, show two identical bars. Ask the child to PREDICT and give a REASON: if I shade 2 parts of a bar cut into 4, and 2 parts of an identical bar cut into 6, which shows more chocolate — or the same? The reason stated before observing is the diagnostic part. Then cut and slide the two shaded regions over each other: 2/4 covers more than 2/6, refuting both 'the same, both are 2' and '6 is more'.
probeDeeper: Build 3/4 for me from single pieces — how many quarters, and how big is each one?
If I cut the same bar into 8 equal parts instead of 4, what is one part called, and is it bigger or smaller than one quarter?
Could 3/4 of this small bar be less chocolate than 1/2 of that big bar? What has to be true about the wholes for us to compare fairly?
Draw 2/6 a different way — a different shape, but the same amount.
assess.correctAnswer: 3/4. The 4 (denominator) tells how many EQUAL parts the whole is cut into, so each part is 1/4; the 3 (numerator) counts how many of those parts we take, i.e. 3/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4. The second bar shows 3/6, which is LESS than 3/4: both have 3 shaded parts, but each sixth is smaller than each fourth because the same whole is cut into more pieces.

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number bias — 'the second one is more because it has sixths and 6 is bigger than 4'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to identical wholes; overlay one sixth on one fourth so the child sees the sixth is the smaller piece; only then re-ask the comparison
errorPatterns.distractor: 3/6 is more — it's in sixths and 6 is more than 4
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 3/6 > 3/4, pointing to the larger denominator as the larger amount

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts shaded parts and ignores their size — 'they're the same, both have 3 pieces shaded'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'how big is ONE part in each bar?'; overlay a sixth on a fourth; establish that same count of different-sized parts is not the same amount
errorPatterns.distractor: They're the same — both have 3 pieces shaded
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says equal because the numerators match, without attending to part size

errorPatterns.pattern: Equal-parts ignored — describes the denominator as 'cut into 4 pieces' with no requirement they be equal
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show a bar cut into 4 UNEQUAL pieces with one shaded and ask if that shaded piece is a quarter; establish equal-area as the criterion
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When explaining what the 4 means, omits 'equal'; would accept a 4-unequal-piece bar as showing quarters

responseLevels.gap: Reads numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers; counts shaded pieces; says 3/6 equals or beats 3/4; cannot say how big one part is.
responseLevels.full: Names 3/4 as three copies of 1/4, explains the denominator sets the equal-part SIZE while the numerator counts them, and concludes 3/6 < 3/4 because sixths are smaller than fourths of the same whole; transfers by redrawing 2/6 a different way.
responseLevels.partial: Names 3/4 correctly and says '4 parts, 3 shaded', but handles the comparison by counting or whole-number reasoning, or can name the parts without explaining that each 1/b's size depends on b — listing the parts without relating part-size to the whole.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a bar cut into 4 equal parts with 3 shaded. Ask: 'What fraction is shaded? In your own words, what does the 4 tell us and what does the 3 tell us?' Then show an identical bar cut into 6 equal parts with 3 shaded and ask: 'Is this more chocolate, less, or the same as the first — and why?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands a/b as a copies of a unit whose size is set by b will say 3/6 < 3/4 and justify by part size; a child using whole-number or part-counting reasoning will call them equal ('both have 3') or say 3/6 is more ('6 is bigger'). It is hard to answer 'less, because sixths are smaller' for the wrong reason, and hard to answer 'equal/more' if you truly grasp unit-part size.

sources.claim: A fraction should be understood as built from unit fractions (a/b as a copies of 1/b), taught via equal-sharing before formal notation; part-whole tools can mislead if children count parts corresponding to numerator and denominator without understanding they together name a single quantity.
sources.source: IES/WWC Practice Guide, Developing Effective Fractions Instruction for K-8 (Siegler et al., 2010, NCEE 2010-4039)

sources.claim: Whole-number bias / larger-denominator-is-larger and equal-parts errors are documented children's fraction misconceptions.
sources.source: IES/WWC Practice Guide, Developing Effective Fractions Instruction for K-8 (Siegler et al., 2010)

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 8-9. Round any number to the nearest 10, 100 or 1000 by deciding which multiple it is CLOSER to on the number line (4,367 → 4,370 / 4,400 / 4,000), using the midpoint as the tipping point and the convention 'halfway rounds up'.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 4): 'round any number to the nearest 10, 100 or 1000'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.NBT.3 'use place-value understanding to round multi-digit whole numbers to any place'.
• Operational details — Teach rounding as a nearness decision on the number line FIRST: mark the two bounding multiples, find the midpoint, and see which side the number sits. Only then formalise the 'look at the next digit' rule, justified by the midpoint. Emphasise that the target place determines the bounding multiples, and handle the halfway convention and cascade cases (e.g. 4,970 to nearest 100). Link to estimation.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8, emerging): rounds to the nearest 10 using a number line. Tier B (age 8-9, secure): rounds to 10/100/1000 and explains via nearer multiple / midpoint. Tier C (age 9, extending): handles halfway and cascade cases and uses rounding to estimate calculations.
bestPractices: Teach rounding as a nearness decision on the number line before any digit rule — the line gives the meaning.
Always mark the two bounding multiples and the midpoint; the midpoint is the tipping point.
Derive the 'look at the next digit' rule FROM the midpoint so it is understood, not memorised.
Make explicit that the target place chooses the bounding multiples (nearest 100 → bound by hundreds).
Teach the halfway-rounds-up convention and cascade cases (4,970 → 5,000 to nearest 100) deliberately; link to estimating calculations.
keyRepresentations: Number line with the two bounding multiples and midpoint (the canonical model)
Place-value chart to identify the rounding digit and the decider digit
'Rounding hill'/rollercoaster midpoint image
0-10,000 line for rounding to 1000
Estimation contexts (sensible approximations)
commonMisconceptions: Rounding by the wrong digit or to the wrong place (ignoring which place is the target).
Always rounding down (truncating) or always up.
Chained/successive rounding (rounding the ones then tens then…) instead of one decision.
Mishandling the halfway case or the cascade (4,970 to nearest 100 → 4,900 not 5,000).
Treating rounding as a rule with no sense of 'nearer to', so unable to check reasonableness.

learn.summary: For ages 8-9: round whole numbers to the nearest 10, 100 or 1000 by treating rounding as a nearness decision on a number line FIRST — mark the two bounding multiples, find the midpoint, and see which side the number sits — then formalise the 'look at the next digit' rule as a shortcut justified by the midpoint. Core worked example: 4,367 rounds to 4,370 (nearest 10), 4,400 (nearest 100), 4,000 (nearest 1000). Deliberately teach the halfway convention (half rounds up) and cascade/carry cases (4,970 → 5,000 to nearest 100). Includes a number-line manipulation activity, a consolidation assessment with targeted traps, and a static reference image as a scaffold.

activities.title: Number-line rounding bench: snap to the nearer multiple
feedback: If a learner rounds 4,367 to 4,300, drag the marker and point to the midpoint 4,350: 4,367 is past it, so it is nearer 4,400.

If a learner uses the wrong digit for nearest 100 (inspecting the 7, which is the ones digit, or the 3, the hundreds digit itself, instead of the 6, the tens digit that decides), name the decider digit — one place to the right of the rounding place — mark it, and look only at that.
If a learner keeps trailing digits (4,367 → 4,467, or keeps the 67), show on the line that the rounded value must be a multiple of 100, so everything after the hundreds becomes zero.
For the cascade 4,970 → 5,000, walk the single carry rather than reteaching everything: 4,970 is 49 hundreds and 70, so 49 hundreds + 1 = 50 hundreds = 5,000; rehearse near the boundary.
activities.rationale: Grounding rounding in number-line nearness and the midpoint before formalising the digit rule builds understanding and helps avoid rote truncation errors; dragging across the midpoint makes the decision rule concrete and visible. The place selector and cascade animation are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism tangible, not mandatory implementation.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'round any number to the nearest 10, 100 or 1000'.
Use place-value understanding to round multi-digit whole numbers to any place (4.NBT.3).
Rounding should be grounded in number-line nearness and the midpoint before the digit rule is formalised, to avoid rote truncation errors.
learnerActions: Place or drag the target number (e.g. 4,367) as a marker on a number line between its two bounding multiples — 4,300 and 4,400 when rounding to the nearest 100 — with the midpoint 4,350 clearly flagged.
See that 4,367 sits PAST the midpoint, so it is nearer to 4,400; watch the marker snap to 4,400 (an arc or snap animation makes the 'nearer multiple' choice visible rather than recited).

Drag the marker back and forth across the midpoint and watch the rounded result flip at 4,350: whole numbers below 4,350 (e.g. 4,349) round down to 4,300, while 4,350 itself and anything above round up to 4,400. This shows that the midpoint is the tipping point, and that the half-rounds-up convention decides the exact-halfway case.
Use a target-place selector (10/100/1000) that rescales the line and changes the bounding multiples, so you feel how the target place chooses which multiples bound the number.
Work a cascade case: round 4,970 to the nearest 100 and watch the roll up to 5,000 — the hundreds carry over (49 hundreds + 1 = 50 hundreds = 5,000).
After the line meaning is built, name the 'decider' digit — the one immediately to the right of the place you are rounding to — and connect it to which side of the midpoint you are on.
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding means choosing the nearer multiple of the target place; the midpoint is the tipping point, and the 'look at the next digit' rule is just a quick way of telling whether the number is below halfway (decider 0-4, round down) or at or past halfway (decider 5-9, round up, with exactly halfway going up by the agreed convention).

activities.title: Consolidation across places with targeted traps
feedback: For a halfway case like 2,650 to the nearest 100, if the learner always rounds down (2,600), state the agreed convention (half rounds up, so 2,650 → 2,700) and mark the midpoint on the line so they see 2,650 is exactly halfway and the rule decides.
For 1,970 to the nearest 100, the carried answer is 2,000; if they produce 1,900 or a malformed value, walk the single carry: 1,970 is 19 hundreds and 70, so 19 hundreds + 1 = 20 hundreds = 2,000.
If a rounded answer is not a clean multiple of the target place, return to the number line to show the rounded value must land exactly on a multiple.
activities.rationale: After the line meaning is built, varied practice across places with specific traps consolidates the procedure and surfaces the remaining failure mechanisms (wrong decider digit, halfway habit, carry past 9). A recognition/fill format is useful for consolidation and checking; note it does not by itself elicit independent construction of the number-line justification, which the first activity provides.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'round any number to the nearest 10, 100 or 1000'.
Use place-value understanding to round multi-digit whole numbers to any place (4.NBT.3).
learnerActions: Round given numbers to the nearest 10, 100 and 1000 (e.g. round 4,367 to each place) via fill-in or multiple choice.
First select the target place, then round, so the two steps stay distinct.
Tackle deliberately chosen trap cases: the halfway case 2,650 to the nearest 100 (which rounds up to 2,700), and the cascade case 1,970 to the nearest 100 (which carries to 2,000).
Match numbers to their rounded values across places.
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding can be applied reliably across different target places, including the halfway (5) and nine-cascade cases, once the nearness meaning is secure.

activities.title: Rounding-hill reference image (scaffold)
feedback: If a learner cannot say why a number rounds a certain way, point to the midpoint on the hill and ask which side the number is on.
Prompt the learner to then carry out the nearness decision themselves on a live number line, not just read it off the poster.
activities.rationale: A static image or 'roll to nearer multiple' tap is a helpful reference and reminder, but the nearness decision is best made by the learner acting on a line; treat this as a scaffold that supports, rather than replaces, active rounding.
sourceClaims: Rounding should be grounded in number-line nearness and the midpoint before the digit rule is formalised, to avoid rote truncation errors.
learnerActions: Use a static rounding-hill / number-line poster showing the two bounding multiples and the marked midpoint as a reference while rounding.
Optionally tap a number on the hill to watch it roll to the nearer multiple, with the midpoint marked, as a reminder of the nearness decision.
activities.intendedInsight: A visual 'hill' with a marked midpoint reminds learners that rounding goes to the nearer multiple and that the midpoint decides direction.

constraints: Teach rounding as a number-line nearness decision FIRST; only then formalise the 'look at the next digit' rule, justified by the midpoint, so it is understood rather than memorised.
Always mark the two bounding multiples and the midpoint; the target place chooses the bounding multiples (nearest 100 → bound by hundreds).

Deliberately teach the halfway-rounds-up convention and cascade/carry cases (e.g. 4,970 → 5,000 to nearest 100); state the convention explicitly since 'half rounds up' is a chosen convention, not a mathematical necessity.
The rounded value must be a multiple of the target place: all digits after the rounding place become zero.
Avoid chained/successive rounding (rounding ones, then tens, then hundreds); rounding to a target place is a single decision from the original number.

The static hill/poster is a reference scaffold; its limit is that it shows rather than requires the learner's own nearness decision. A fill/multiple-choice format consolidates and checks but does not by itself require the learner to construct the number-line justification.
When assessing, watch the working (which digit decides and what happens to trailing digits), not only the final number, to reveal which rule the child is running.

The decider digit for a target place is the digit one place to the RIGHT of it (for 4,367 to nearest 100 the decider is the tens digit 6, not the hundreds digit 3, the ones digit 7, or the thousands digit 4).
Carry arithmetic must match the actual number: 4,970 → 49 hundreds + 1 = 50 hundreds = 5,000; 1,970 → 19 hundreds + 1 = 20 hundreds = 2,000.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The candidate originally miscomputed the 4,970 cascade carry as '19 hundreds + 1 = 20 hundreds = 2,000' (reasoning that belongs to 1,970). Corrected to 49 hundreds + 1 = 50 hundreds = 5,000 at every learner-facing occurrence.

The source's wrong-decider-digit misconception listed 'the 7 or the 4' for 4,367 to the nearest hundred; the 4 is the thousands digit and contradicts the pattern's own description (hundreds digit itself or ones digit). Corrected to the 7 (ones) or the 3 (hundreds digit itself), with 6 (tens) as the correct decider.

The source assessment includes a double-rounding probe (4,347): rounding to the nearest ten gives 4,350, then to the nearest hundred (half-up) gives 4,400, whereas rounding straight to the nearest hundred gives 4,300 — these differ. Any demonstration must make clear the straight-to-hundred answer (4,300) is correct and chained rounding is the error being exposed.

The source correctAnswer '4,400; 2,000; 2,700' maps to the diagnosticPrompt cases (4,367 / 1,970 / 2,650 to nearest hundred), not the probeDeeper prompts (e.g. 2,999 to nearest ten is 3,000); these probe numbers were not reconstructable and were not propagated into learner-facing material. Reviewers should confirm intended probe numbers and answers.

The original row's '3D adds nothing' / 'open dialogue adds little' fit judgements were catalog preferences and are not propagated as universal claims. A number line is naturally planar, but this does not establish that other media cannot support rounding.

Two of three sources are marked unverified in the source row; comparative efficacy or necessity of the number-line-first approach is not independently established here beyond the cited claim about grounding rounding in nearness.

probeDeeper: Round 2,999 to the nearest ten — what happens to the other digits?
Show me on a number line why 4,367 rounds to 4,400 and not 4,300.
Round 4,347 to the nearest ten, then round THAT to the nearest hundred. Now round 4,347 straight to the nearest hundred — do you get the same? (double-rounding)
assess.correctAnswer: 4,400; 2,000; 2,700 — deciding by the digit one place to the right of the hundreds, then replacing all digits after the hundreds place with zero.

errorPatterns.pattern: Decides using the wrong digit — the hundreds digit itself, or the final (ones) digit — instead of the digit one place to the right of the rounding place
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name the 'decider' digit: the one immediately to the right of the place you're rounding to. Mark it, then look only at that. Reground with place-value columns.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 4,367 to the nearest hundred the child inspects the 7 or the 4, not the 6.

errorPatterns.pattern: Rounds the target digit but leaves the trailing digits unchanged (4,367 → 4,467, or keeps the 67)
errorPatterns.nextMove: On a number line, show the rounded value must be a multiple of 100 — so everything after the hundreds becomes zero.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The rounded answer still carries the original tens/ones.

errorPatterns.pattern: Always rounds a 5 down (or always up) regardless of convention: 2,650 → 2,600
errorPatterns.nextMove: State the class convention (half rounds up) and mark the midpoint on a number line so they see 2,650 is exactly halfway and the rule decides.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Halfway case is resolved by a fixed 'down' habit rather than the agreed rule.

errorPatterns.pattern: Fails to carry when rounding up past a 9: 1,970 → 1,900 or 1,1000 instead of 2,000
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the whole procedure — walk the single carry: 19 hundreds + 1 = 20 hundreds = 2,000. Rehearse on a number line near the boundary.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The nine-cascade case gives a malformed or non-carried answer.

responseLevels.gap: Uses the wrong decider digit or leaves trailing digits in place; rounded value is not a clean multiple.
responseLevels.full: Rounds to nearest 10/100/1000 accurately including the 5 and 9-cascade cases, zeroes trailing digits, and justifies by nearer multiple on a number line.
responseLevels.partial: Rounds clear cases correctly but mishandles the halfway 5, the carry past 9, or which place to look at.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set the task and watch the working: 'Round 4,367 to the nearest hundred. Now round 1,970 to the nearest hundred. Now round 2,650 to the nearest hundred.' Ask them to show it on a number line for at least one. Watch which digit they use to decide and what they do to the digits after it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The three cases are chosen to trip specific mechanisms: 4,367 checks whether trailing digits are zeroed; 1,970 forces a carry past 9 into the thousands; 2,650 is the halfway (5) case. Watching the working — not the final number alone — reveals which rule the child is running.
