pedagogy.summary: Collecting like terms means combining terms that share the SAME letter AND the same power, keeping each term's sign, and leaving unlike terms uncombined. The deep obstacle is not the procedure but 'acceptance of lack of closure' (Collis): children see 3a + 2b as an instruction to be finished rather than an answer in its own right, so they force it closed — conjoining to 5ab, or reaching for a single number. Teach it as sorting a mixed pile into groups, using quantities ('the number of a's') rather than objects, and make explicit that a fully-simplified expression can be several terms.
bestPractices: Treat collecting as sorting: group a-terms, b-terms and constants separately; only terms in the same group combine.
Insist on same letter AND same power — 3a and 2a² are NOT like terms; contrast a (length) with a² (area).
Keep each term's sign attached to it: in 4a − b + 2a, the − belongs to the b; collect signed coefficients.
Directly confront lack of closure: rehearse that 3a + 2b IS the answer and cannot be made shorter — an expression is an object, not an unfinished sum.
Prefer 'number of apples' over 'a = apple': the object/fruit-salad analogy breeds the letter-as-object error and licenses conjoining (a+b='ab').
keyRepresentations: Algebra tiles (an x-tile, a y-tile, a unit tile — only identical tiles stack)
Sorting groups / columns by term type
Area square for a² vs a bar for a (why powers differ)
Signed-coefficient bar model
commonMisconceptions: Conjoins unlike terms to 'close' the expression: 3a + 2b → 5ab or one number, because an open sum feels unfinished (lack of closure, Collis).
Combines terms with the same letter but different powers: 3a + 2a² → 5a² or 5a³.
Loses or mishandles a sign when collecting: treats −b as +b, or 5a − 3a as 8a.
Drops the variable when combining: 3a + 5a → 8 instead of 8a.
Letter-as-object thinking (a = apple) that makes a + b feel like it should be 'ab'.

learn.summary: Collecting like terms means combining only terms that share the SAME letter AND the same power, keeping each term's sign, and leaving unlike terms uncombined. The deep obstacle is 'acceptance of lack of closure' (Collis): learners treat 3a + 2b as an instruction to be finished rather than as an answer in its own right, so they force it closed by conjoining to 5ab or reaching for a single number. Teach collecting as sorting a mixed pile into groups, talk in quantities ('the number of a's') rather than objects, and make explicit that a fully-simplified expression can be several terms.

activities.title: The sort that refuses to merge (algebra-tile bench)
feedback: If a learner forces an a-tile onto a b-tile, point to the refusal: different tiles cannot pool, so 3a + 2b stays as two terms.
When three tidy stacks remain, confirm explicitly: '3a + 2b + 5 is finished — it does not need to become one number or one term.'
In negative mode, if a red tile is ignored, show the cancellation: one anti-b removes one b, so 3b − b = 2b, not 4b.
activities.rationale: Tiles that physically refuse to combine give a concrete counter to the closure urge, and sorting mirrors the 'group a-terms, b-terms and constants' structure of the procedure. A manipulative lets learners rehearse the comparison directly; this is a proposed design, not evidence that tiles outperform other media.
sourceClaims: Children are reluctant to 'accept lack of closure' (Collis): asked what e+f+g is when e+f=8, only ~41% of Year 9 gave 8+g in 1976 and there was no improvement 30 years later; interviews show '8g' feels like a finished answer while '8+g' feels like an unfinished sum to be worked out — the drive that produces conjoining.
learnerActions: Start with a jumbled heap of a-tiles, b-tiles and unit-tiles mixed together.
Drag identical tiles together so they stack and label themselves (three a-tiles become '3a', two b-tiles become '2b', five unit-tiles become '5').
Deliberately try to press an a-tile onto a b-tile — notice it will not fuse and springs apart; you cannot build an 'ab' tile this way.
State the finished result as three separate stacks: 3a, 2b, 5, and say aloud that this is fully simplified.
Switch on a negative-coefficient mode where red 'anti-tiles' cancel matching tiles, e.g. show how 3b − b leaves 2b.
activities.intendedInsight: Unlike terms genuinely cannot be merged, and the leftover collection of separate terms IS the complete answer — an expression is an object, not an unfinished sum.

activities.title: Sort and complete the expression
feedback: If 'a' and '2b' land in the same bin, remind: same letter AND same power required to share a group.
If 5ab is chosen, respond that a-terms and b-terms are different piles and cannot pool — the answer keeps both.
If the − is dropped from 2b, re-attach the sign to its term before combining.
activities.rationale: A categorisation and completion check surfaces conjoining and sign errors through learners' own responses. This response format can both assess and, used while teaching, rehearse the sort; recognising a correct form does not by itself show a learner can independently construct a simplified expression, so learner-produced simplifications are also required.
learnerActions: Drag each term of 4a − 2b + 3 + a into the correct bin: 'a-terms', 'b-terms', or 'numbers' (the − stays attached to the 2b).
Complete the simplification: 4a − 2b + 3 + a = ____ (answer: 5a − 2b + 3).
Choose the correct simplified form from options that include the closure-driven trap '5ab' and a sign-error option — and give a one-line reason for rejecting 5ab.
activities.intendedInsight: Correctly sorted, signed terms simplify to several terms; conjoining to a single term or number is wrong, and each sign travels with its own term.

activities.title: Name the parts of a term
feedback: If a learner groups a with a², contrast the bar (length a) with the square (area a²): visibly different objects that do not combine.
Prefer 'the number of a's' over 'a = apple'; the object analogy encourages a + b feeling like it should be 'ab'.
activities.rationale: A labelled, tappable reference builds term vocabulary and the length-vs-area contrast for powers. It is a glossary scaffold: because the example is fixed it cannot be rearranged by the learner, so it does not elicit independent sorting — pair it with the construction activities.
sourceClaims: Letter-as-object interpretations of algebraic letters (a = apple), which license conjoining unlike terms, are a long-documented CSMS-tradition difficulty among secondary students.
learnerActions: Given a pre-sorted expression such as 3a + 2b + 5, tap each term to reveal its type (a-term, b-term, constant) and its signed coefficient.
Say in words what each term counts: 'the number of a's is 3', 'the number of b's is 2', '5 is a constant on its own'.
Explain why 2a and a² are different terms: a can stand for a length (a bar) and a² for an area (a square), so they are different objects and 3a + 2a² cannot be collected.
activities.intendedInsight: The vocabulary of terms, coefficients and powers, and why same-letter-different-power terms (a vs a²) are unlike and cannot pool.

activities.title: Confront lack of closure in words
feedback: If a learner insists on one number, affirm that 6a + 2b + 5 is itself the answer — there is nothing further to do.

If 7ab is accepted, talk in quantities: the number of a's (4) and the number of b's (3) stay in different groups. Substituting a = 2, b = 5 gives 23 for 4a + 3b but 70 for 7ab, so they are not equivalent.
If the − is attached to the wrong term, re-read 4a − b + 2a as 'take away one b', so the b-total is −b and the result is 6a − b.
activities.rationale: Explicit discussion targets the closure belief head-on and rehearses sign handling, which a silent sort may leave implicit. Discussion is one route to articulating the reasoning and complements the manipulative; it is not claimed here to be more effective than other media.
sourceClaims: Children are reluctant to 'accept lack of closure' (Collis): asked what e+f+g is when e+f=8, only ~41% of Year 9 gave 8+g in 1976 and there was no improvement 30 years later; interviews show '8g' feels like a finished answer while '8+g' feels like an unfinished sum to be worked out — the drive that produces conjoining.
learnerActions: Decide whether 6a + 2b + 5 is finished or whether there should be a single number at the end, and explain how you know.

Answer: is 4a + 3b equivalent to 7ab, meaning equal for every value of a and b? Test a = 2, b = 5 (23 vs 70) and explain why they are not equivalent, even though a few special values (such as a = b = 1) happen to give equal numbers.
Use quantity language to test conjoining: say 'the number of a's is 4 and the number of b's is 3', then explain why these two counts stay separate instead of becoming 7 of a new thing called 'ab'.
Track a sign: in 4a − b + 2a, say where the minus sign belongs and simplify (answer: 6a − b).
activities.intendedInsight: A multi-term expression can be the complete answer; conjoining unlike terms is never valid, and each sign belongs to its own term.

constraints: Insist on same letter AND same power: 3a and 2a² are not like terms; contrast a (length) with a² (area).
Keep each term's sign attached before combining: in 4a − b + 2a the − belongs to the b; collect signed coefficients.
Prefer 'the number of a's' over 'a = apple'; the object/fruit-salad analogy breeds letter-as-object thinking and licenses conjoining (a + b = 'ab').
Make explicit that a fully-simplified expression can be several terms — an expression is an object, not an unfinished instruction.

The tap-to-reveal labelled expression is a vocabulary scaffold: its fixed example cannot be rearranged by the learner, so it does not elicit independent sorting or construction. Pair it with tasks where learners build and sort.

The categorisation/selection check uses recognition and selection; recognising a correct form does not guarantee a learner can independently construct a simplified expression, so also require learner-produced simplifications.
Algebra tiles and discussion offer different experiences (manipulation vs articulation); neither is claimed here to be the only way to fix the closure misconception.
Watch written working rather than only final answers: a merged single term, a wrong sign, or a dropped variable each show as a distinct final line.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original source row asserted the tile 'directly defeats the closure urge', that a third spatial dimension 'adds nothing', and that a static image 'cannot stage' the merge experience. These are catalog-style comparative/necessity claims not established by the cited sources; they have been softened to scoped proposals with stated affordances and limits.

The Küchemann/Hart CSMS claim is marked verified:false in the source and should be checked before relying on it; the two DfE and Hodgen et al. claims are marked verified:true in the legacy data but were not re-verified in this rewrite.

The source row's own error examples '5a − 3a as 8a' and '3a + 5a → 8' are listed as misconceptions to detect, not as correct arithmetic; correct values are 5a − 3a = 2a and 3a + 5a = 8a. These appear only in diagnostic/feedback framing, never as valid learner answers.

The KS3 DfE claim is a topic/curriculum statement and does not directly support any activity's teaching-principle rationale, so it is not attached as sourceClaims to the tile or sort activities; the scored-sort activity likewise has sourceClaims set to [].

probeDeeper: Is 6a + 2b + 5 finished, or should there be a single number at the end? How do you know? (probes lack of closure head-on)
Could 4a + 3b ever be written as 7ab? If so, when — if never, why not? (counterexample confronting conjoining)
What is the difference between 2a and a² — and can you collect 3a + 2a²? (powers)
When you dealt with − b, where did the minus sign go, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: 6a + 2b + 5. (4a + 2a = 6a; 3b − b = 2b; the 5 is a constant on its own; nothing else combines.)

errorPatterns.pattern: Conjoins unlike terms to force closure — '3a + 2b must make 5ab' or 'there has to be a proper answer' — because an open expression feels unfinished (documented: only ~41% of Year 9 accept e+f+g = 8+g; 'ab feels finished, a+b feels like an unfinished sum').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a quantities context (4 apples + 3 bananas is not '7 abananas') and tiles that refuse to merge; establish explicitly that 6a + 2b + 5 IS the answer — an expression can be an object, not an instruction.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Merges a-terms and b-terms into a single term (5ab), or insists on reducing to one number; says the expression 'isn't finished' until it is one item.

errorPatterns.pattern: Combines same-letter, different-power terms — treats 3a and 2a² as like, giving 5a² or 5a³.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Like terms need the SAME letter AND the same power; contrast a (a bar) with a² (a square) so they are visibly different objects that cannot pool.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Adds coefficients of a and a² together; groups a with a² when sorting.

errorPatterns.pattern: Loses a sign when collecting — reads −b as +b, or mishandles a negative coefficient, e.g. 3b − b → 4b.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach collecting — attach each sign to its own term first (the − belongs to the b), then combine signed coefficients; rehearse directed-number addition in place.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The sign attached to a term is dropped or flipped in the working; b-total comes out too large.

responseLevels.gap: Merges unlike terms into one term or a single number, or cannot begin; treats the expression as a sum to be 'worked out' to one answer.
responseLevels.full: Collects a-terms, b-terms and constants separately with correct signs, leaves the answer as several terms without unease (accepts lack of closure), rejects 3a+2b=5ab with a reason, and transfers to unfamiliar variables and powers.
responseLevels.partial: Collects like terms correctly when coefficients are positive and single-variable, but slips on the negative term, on the lone constant, or on same-letter-different-power — combines the parts it recognises but not reliably, and may still be uneasy leaving several terms.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Hand the child this card and say 'simplify this as far as you can, showing your working': 4a + 3b + 2a − b + 5. Say nothing about method. Watch whether they keep a-terms, b-terms and the constant separate, how they treat the −b, and whether they try to force everything into a single term.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Because the teacher watches the written working rather than asking, each error shows as a different final line: a child driven to close writes one merged term (e.g. 15ab, or a single number); a child who mishandles the sign gets 4b instead of 2b; a child who drops variables gets a bare number; a sound child leaves three separate terms with correct signs and shows no unease that the answer 'isn't one number'.

sources.claim: KS3 pupils should simplify and manipulate algebraic expressions by collecting like terms.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (KS3)

sources.claim: Children are reluctant to 'accept lack of closure' (Collis): asked what e+f+g is when e+f=8, only ~41% of Year 9 gave 8+g in 1976 and there was no improvement 30 years later; interviews show '8g' feels like a finished answer while '8+g' feels like an unfinished sum to be worked out — the drive that produces conjoining.
sources.source: Hodgen, Küchemann, Brown & Coe — Children's understandings of algebra 30 years on (ICCAMS, BSRLM Proceedings 28(3)/RME 11(2))

sources.claim: Letter-as-object interpretations of algebraic letters (a = apple), which license conjoining unlike terms, are a long-documented CSMS-tradition difficulty among secondary students.
sources.source: Küchemann/Hart, CSMS (Children's Understanding of Mathematics: 11–16), as summarised in Hodgen et al. RME 11(2)

pedagogy.summary: Locating a/b on a number line by partitioning the unit interval 0–1 into b equal parts (each of length 1/b) and iterating a of them from 0. The number line recasts a fraction as a NUMBER with a magnitude and a position, not a shaded region. The critical shift is to count equal INTERVALS (lengths from 0), not tick marks or dots, and to treat the 0–1 segment as the unit.
bestPractices: Partition the 0–1 interval into b equal parts and emphasise the LENGTH from 0 (the magnitude) rather than the tick mark.
Iterate the unit fraction: 3/4 is three 1/4-jumps from 0.
Make explicit that b equal parts need b−1 marks inside the interval (fourths = 3 interior marks), countering the tick-counting error.
Use lines that extend past 1 so a/b sits among the numbers and cannot be pushed 'between 3 and 4' (IES Roadblock 2.2).
Do both moves — read the fraction at a given point (interpret) AND place a given fraction on a blank line (produce).
Contrast with the area model and stress that the same fraction is 'the same size / the same point'.
keyRepresentations: Single 0–1 number line partitioned into b equal intervals
Unit-fraction 'jump' iterated a times from 0
Stacked 0–1 number lines (IES Figure 4, halves through tenths)
Fraction strips measured against the line (IES Figure 5)
commonMisconceptions: Counting tick marks instead of intervals / drawing b marks rather than b−1 interior marks (IES Roadblock 2.1)
Whole-number placement — putting 3/4 between 3 and 4, treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers (IES Roadblock 2.2)
Treating the whole drawn segment (0 to the far end) as the unit rather than 0–1
Reading a point by matching to marks with no sense of the unit-fraction length

learn.summary: Help children locate a/b on a number line by partitioning the 0–1 interval into b equal parts (each of length 1/b) and iterating a of them from 0. The number line recasts a fraction as a NUMBER with a magnitude and a position, not a shaded region. The key shift is counting equal INTERVALS (lengths from 0), not tick marks or dots, and treating the 0–1 segment — not the whole drawn line — as the unit. Learners should both read a fraction at a given point and place a given fraction on a blank line.

activities.title: Build fourths: three cuts, not four marks
feedback: If 3/4 is placed too far from 0, count the equal jumps from 0: 'how many jumps of the same size?' — three quarter-jumps, landing before 1.

If fourths are drawn with 4 interior marks, shade each piece and count LENGTHS, not marks: four interior marks make five parts (fifths if equally spaced), but four equal parts need only 3 cuts inside.
If a point is read off by one (e.g. calling it 4/5), re-count the equal intervals from 0 rather than the ticks.
activities.rationale: Partitioning into b equal parts with b−1 interior marks and iterating the unit fraction directly attacks the common tick-counting error; letting the child see that four marks produce fifths, not fourths, makes the correction concrete.
sourceClaims: Number lines should be used to teach fractions as numbers with magnitude; students commonly count tick marks rather than intervals (Roadblock 2.1) and apply whole-number knowledge by placing e.g. 3/4 between 3 and 4 (Roadblock 2.2). Recommendation 2 (number lines) is rated moderate evidence.
learnerActions: Start with a bare line labelled only 0 and 1 — the 0–1 segment is the unit.

To make 'fourths', first try the common mistake: drop FOUR equally spaced marks inside the 0–1 segment. Notice this cuts the unit into FIVE equal parts, each one a fifth (1/5) — the far interior mark sits at 4/5. So you have actually made fifths, not fourths: a sign something has gone wrong.
Correct to THREE interior marks so the unit is cut into exactly four equal parts (quarters); the marks land at 1/4, 2/4, 3/4, and a fourth quarter-length jump lands exactly on 1 (4/4).
State the rule in your own words: b equal parts need b−1 interior marks.
Place 3/4 by jumping the quarter-length three times from 0, landing one quarter-length short of 1.
activities.intendedInsight: Four equal parts require three interior cuts (b equal parts need b−1 interior marks); a/b is measured as a LENGTH from 0 (a jumps of 1/b), not as a count of tick marks. Drawing four equally spaced interior marks cuts the unit into five equal parts (fifths), so calling them fourths mislabels the pieces — making the tick-counting error visible so the child can correct it.

activities.title: Read the point, then place the fraction
feedback: If the point is read as 4/5, re-count the equal intervals from 0 — the marks are not the count; the lengths are.
If 3/4 is placed beyond 1, ask 'where is 1? must 3/4 be less than 1 or more than 1?' and place it inside 0–1.
If a child can read on a marked line but struggles on a blank one, rebuild the partition step by step before placing.
activities.rationale: Doing both moves — interpret a shown point and produce a placement on a blank line — consolidates the magnitude idea and exposes whether the child relies on pre-drawn marks.
sourceClaims: Number lines should be used to teach fractions as numbers with magnitude; students commonly count tick marks rather than intervals (Roadblock 2.1) and apply whole-number knowledge by placing e.g. 3/4 between 3 and 4 (Roadblock 2.2). Recommendation 2 (number lines) is rated moderate evidence.
Pupils are taught to recognise and use fractions as numbers and to place them on a number line during KS2 (Years 3–4, ages 8–9).
learnerActions: On a 0–1 line already divided into 6 equal parts, with a dot on the 4th mark from 0, say what fraction the dot shows and explain how you know (four 1/6-lengths from 0 = 4/6).
On the same line, find and mark 1/2 (the 3rd mark, i.e. 3/6) and explain why it sits halfway.
Then take a blank 0–1 line and place 3/4 yourself: partition into 4 equal parts, count 3 parts from 0, land three-quarters of the way to 1.
Talk through each step aloud as you place it.
Also try ordering several fractions along one line to compare their positions.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a given point (interpret) and placing a given fraction on a blank line (produce) are both needed; a fraction is the same size / the same point however it is represented.

activities.title: Which segment is the unit?
feedback: If 3/4 lands at three-quarters of the entire drawing, find and mark 1 first, then measure the quarter-length against the 0–1 segment only.
If a child says 3/4 would move when the line reaches 2, point back to the fixed 0–1 unit — the quarter-length is unchanged.
activities.rationale: Explicitly locating 1 and using lines that run past 1 help expose and address both the whole-segment-as-unit error and the whole-number placement of 3/4 beyond 1.
sourceClaims: Number lines should be used to teach fractions as numbers with magnitude; students commonly count tick marks rather than intervals (Roadblock 2.1) and apply whole-number knowledge by placing e.g. 3/4 between 3 and 4 (Roadblock 2.2). Recommendation 2 (number lines) is rated moderate evidence.
learnerActions: On a line that extends past 1 (to 2 or beyond), first find and mark where 1 is.
Place 3/4 and check it sits below 1, NOT at three-quarters of the whole drawn line.
Answer: if this line went all the way to 2 instead of 1, would 3/4 move? Explain why not.
State that everything is measured against the fixed 0–1 length, whatever the drawing shows.
activities.intendedInsight: The unit is the 0–1 segment, not the whole drawn picture; with 0 and 1 kept in place, a/b keeps its position no matter how far the line is drawn. Lines extending past 1 let children show, and teachers address, errors such as placing 3/4 at or beyond 1, or 'between 3 and 4'.

activities.title: Compare with the area model
feedback: If the child treats the area-model and line versions as different fractions, lay a fraction strip whose whole matches the 0–1 length against the line so the shaded length and the marked point coincide.
Prompt: 'Is 3/4 a different amount on the line than in the rectangle? Why or why not?'
activities.rationale: Contrasting the area model with the line while stressing identical magnitude links prior representational knowledge to the number-line view and guards against seeing them as unrelated.
learnerActions: Shade 3/4 of a rectangle using the area model, then place 3/4 on a number line.
Explain how both show the same fraction — 'the same size, the same point'.
Measure a fraction strip against the line, using strips whose whole is the same length as the line's 0–1 segment, so the length and the position match (e.g. the 1/6 strip against sixths on the line).
activities.intendedInsight: The same fraction has one magnitude whether shown as a shaded region or as a point/length on a line; connecting the two representations reinforces that a fraction is a single number.

constraints: A pre-labelled reference line (tap a point → 'this is 3/4, three quarter-jumps from 0') supports recall but does not let the child partition or iterate, where the learning lives; use it as a scaffold only, not as the main task.
Both interpret (read a shown point) and produce (place on a blank line) are required; recognition alone does not elicit the independent partitioning and placement that demonstrate understanding.

A number line is one-dimensional; the unit-interval idea lives on a single line, so added dimensions are not needed for this particular objective (this is a scope note, not a claim that other media cannot teach).
Children aged ~8–9 (KS2 Years 3–4) are the intended audience; keep lines and partitions simple (halves through tenths).

When an interactive builder is used, optional feedback such as rejecting an unequal drag, a 'hopper' that jumps the unit fraction and lands on a/b, a draggable point that reports the nearest fraction and turns green on the exact spot, and a mode showing the line running past 1 can make the mechanism concrete — these are illustrative, not mandatory or proven superior to other media.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One source (DfE National Curriculum) was marked verified:false in the original; treat its curriculum-placement claim with that caveat.

Arithmetic correction made during review: drawing four interior marks cuts the 0–1 unit into FIVE equal parts (fifths, each 1/5), with the far interior mark at 4/5 — it does NOT overshoot past 1. Three interior marks make four quarters (marks at 1/4,2/4,3/4), and a fourth quarter-length jump lands exactly on 1 (4/4).

The original recommendation's claim that the far mark 'lands on 5/4' when four marks are dropped is a confused/erroneous original detail: 5/4 would require five quarter-length jumps (keeping the interval at 1/4), not four interior marks. It is recorded in uncertainty notes and not presented to learners.

Verified examples after correction: 4/6 reads as four 1/6-lengths from 0; 1/2 = 3/6 sits at the 3rd mark; 3/4 sits three-quarters toward 1, just before 1; three interior marks make four equal quarters; four interior marks make five equal fifths (far mark 4/5).

The original error-pattern note 'reads the 4th mark... calls the point 4/5' is retained only as a plausible tick-counting slip used in feedback as an off-by-one example to re-count, not taught as a fact; it has not been independently verified.

probeDeeper: How many equal parts did you make, and how many marks did you draw inside — why is that one fewer than the number of parts?
Where is 1 on your line? Is 3/4 before or after 1, and how do you know?
This point is 4/6. Can you find and mark 1/2 on the same line?
If this line went all the way to 2 instead of 1, would 3/4 move? Why not?
assess.correctAnswer: The dot is 4/6 — four 1/6-lengths from 0. To place 3/4: partition 0–1 into 4 equal parts (3 marks inside), then count 3 parts from 0, so 3/4 sits three-quarters of the way to 1, just before 1.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts tick marks not intervals — reads the 4th mark as if the marks were the count, or makes 4 interior marks to show fourths
errorPatterns.nextMove: Shade each interval and count LENGTHS from 0 ('how many jumps of the same size?'); make explicit that b equal parts need b−1 interior marks
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Off-by-one reading of the point, or partitions with the wrong number of marks when producing

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number placement — puts 3/4 between 3 and 4, treating the fraction as two separate whole numbers
errorPatterns.nextMove: Firmly label 0 and 1; ask 'where is 1? must 3/4 be less than 1 or more?'; place it inside 0–1
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the blank line places 3/4 beyond 1, near where 3 or 4 would be

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the whole drawn segment as the unit — ignores the 0–1 labelling and measures a/b as a fraction of the entire picture
errorPatterns.nextMove: Find and mark 1 first; establish that the unit is 0–1, and everything is measured against that fixed length whatever the drawing shows
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a line drawn past 1, places 3/4 at three-quarters of the total drawn length rather than of 0–1

responseLevels.gap: Counts tick marks or places 3/4 beyond 1 / at three-quarters of the whole drawing; cannot identify the 0–1 unit interval.
responseLevels.full: Reads the point as 4/6 by counting equal intervals from 0, and independently partitions 0–1 into b equal parts and iterates a of them to place 3/4 correctly below 1, explaining the unit interval and the interval length.
responseLevels.partial: Reads or partitions correctly on a marked line but falters when producing on a blank line, or gets the position without articulating that each interval is 1/b and the unit is 0–1.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a 0-to-1 number line already divided into 6 equal parts, with a dot on the 4th mark from 0. Ask: 'What fraction is this dot, and how do you know?' Then give a blank 0-to-1 line and ask: 'Mark 3/4 on this line, and talk me through how you place it.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who treats the 0–1 segment as the unit and counts equal intervals reads 4/6 and places 3/4 correctly below 1. The tick-counting child miscounts marks (calls the point 4/5, or draws 4 marks for fourths); the whole-number-placement child pushes 3/4 out beyond 1 (toward '3 to 4') or places it at three-quarters of the whole drawing. Both moves — interpret and produce — are needed to pass.

sources.claim: Number lines should be used to teach fractions as numbers with magnitude; students commonly count tick marks rather than intervals (Roadblock 2.1) and apply whole-number knowledge by placing e.g. 3/4 between 3 and 4 (Roadblock 2.2). Recommendation 2 (number lines) is rated moderate evidence.
sources.source: IES/WWC Practice Guide, Developing Effective Fractions Instruction for K-8 (Siegler et al., 2010, NCEE 2010-4039)

sources.claim: Pupils are taught to recognise and use fractions as numbers and to place them on a number line during KS2 (Years 3–4, ages 8–9).
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (KS1-2)

pedagogy.summary: Dividing a quantity in a given ratio is the formal KS3 procedure: for a ratio a:b (or a:b:c), the TOTAL number of parts is a+b(+c); one part = quantity ÷ total parts; each share = its parts × one part. Two things distinguish this from earlier unequal-sharing work: it extends cleanly to THREE-part ratios (divide 180 in 1:2:3), and it goes both ways — pupils must also express a completed division back AS a ratio in simplest form (10 and 14 becomes 5:7), and read off a part as a fraction of the whole. The persistent hazard is using a part rather than the SUM of parts as the denominator; the fix is the same find-one-part routine, kept visible on a bar model.
bestPractices: Standardise the routine explicitly: total parts = sum of all ratio numbers → one part = quantity ÷ total → multiply each ratio number by one part.
Extend to three-part ratios immediately (1:2:3 → 6 parts) so the 'sum ALL the parts' step is generalised, not tied to two shares.
Practise the reverse direction: given the actual shares, write them as a ratio and simplify (10:14 → 5:7), and state a share as a fraction of the whole.
Keep the bar model as the check: the number of equal segments equals the sum of the ratio numbers; adding the shares must return the original quantity.
Distinguish part-to-part (a:b) from part-to-whole (a out of a+b) in the notation, since the same numbers appear in both.
keyRepresentations: Bar model / tape diagram with a+b(+c) equal segments
The 'one part' unit (quantity ÷ total parts)
Ratio table (parts | value) extended to three columns for three-part ratios
Simplest-form ratio from actual shares (divide by the HCF)
commonMisconceptions: Dividing by a single part rather than the sum of parts (÷3 or ÷5 instead of ÷8), or in a 3-part ratio forgetting to include every part in the total.
Sharing the quantity equally among the number of terms (180 into three equal 60s for 1:2:3).
When reversing, writing the shares as a ratio without simplifying (10:14 left un-reduced), or reversing the order.
Confusing part-to-part with part-to-whole — stating a share as a/b of the whole rather than a/(a+b).

learn.summary: Divide a quantity in a given ratio using the find-one-part routine: total parts = sum of ALL ratio numbers; one part = quantity ÷ total parts; each share = its ratio number × one part. The guidance generalises this to three-part ratios (divide 180 in 1:2:3 = 6 parts, not 3) and works both directions: express a completed division back as a simplest-form ratio (10 and 14 → 5:7) and state a share as a fraction of the whole. The persistent hazard is using one part, rather than the sum of parts, as the denominator; a bar/tape model with the correct number of equal segments keeps the correct total visible as a check.

activities.title: Ratio-divider on a tape diagram (forward direction)
feedback: If the strip is cut into three segments for 1:2:3, flag it: count that 1+2+3 = 6 segments are needed before the fill unlocks.

If the learner divides by the number of ratio terms or by a single term instead of the sum of parts (e.g. 180 ÷ 3 = 60) or shares equally (60, 60, 60), show the six-segment bar and recompute one part = 180 ÷ 6 = 30.
If the learner finds one part but stops (answers '30', or '1, 2, 3'), prompt that 30 is only ONE part: ask how many parts each share has, then multiply (1×30, 2×30, 3×30 → 30, 60, 90).
If the shares don't sum to the original quantity, prompt a recount of segments — the total must return 180.
activities.rationale: An optional interactive tape diagram that refuses an incorrect number of segments can make the '÷ total parts' step explicit and give immediate feedback; because the learner segments and fills the bar, the task lets them produce the working rather than only recognise a finished answer. The refusal mechanism is one illustrative design, proposed rather than required or uniquely effective, and its efficacy is not source-verified; it teaches the National Curriculum objective of dividing a quantity in a given ratio.
sourceClaims: Pupils should divide a given quantity into two (or more) parts in a given part:part or part:whole ratio, and express a division as a fraction of the whole (KS3 ratio, proportion and rates of change).
learnerActions: Enter a ratio such as 1:2:3 and cut the strip into the SUM of the parts — six equal segments for 1:2:3, not three.
Let the quantity (e.g. 180) distribute across the equal segments and read off one part = 180 ÷ 6 = 30.
Colour 1, 2 and 3 adjacent segments to read the shares 30, 60 and 90, then add them to check they return 180.
Repeat with a two-part ratio (e.g. share £60 in 2:3: 5 parts, one part = 12, shares 24 and 36, summing to 60).
activities.intendedInsight: A three-part ratio 1:2:3 needs six equal parts, not three; dividing once by the total number of parts and then scaling each term is the whole routine, and the shares must add back to the original quantity.

activities.title: Reverse station: write shares as a simplest-form ratio
feedback: If the learner leaves 10:14 un-simplified, prompt: what common factor divides both? Divide by 2 to get 5:7.
If the order is reversed to 14:10, point back to which share came first (10) and restore the matching order.
activities.rationale: The forward division task does not test simplification, so a separate reverse task is needed to secure it. Casting simplification as dividing both terms by the HCF connects to prior fraction work.
sourceClaims: In a part-to-part ratio a:b(:c), a part is a/(a+b(+c)) of the whole; ratio compares part to part and must be reduced to simplest form — the classic error is reading a:b as a/b of the whole.
learnerActions: Take two actual shares (e.g. 24 sweets shared as 10 and 14) and write them as a ratio 10:14.
Simplify by dividing both terms by their highest common factor (÷2) to reach 5:7, keeping the order matching the shares as stated.
Explain how this is like simplifying a fraction, and check you have not reversed the order (14:10 is wrong for 10 then 14).
activities.intendedInsight: A completed division can be expressed back as a ratio, and a ratio must be reduced to simplest form by dividing by the common factor — directly analogous to simplifying a fraction.

activities.title: Part of the whole as a fraction
feedback: If a learner writes the middle share of 1:2:3 as 2/3, point to the six segments: the denominator is the total parts, so it is 2/6 = 1/3.
Compare 2/6 and 2/3 side by side so the distinction between part-to-part and part-to-whole is visible.
activities.rationale: Confusing a:b with a/b of the whole is a documented classic error; anchoring the denominator to the counted total parts on the bar addresses it directly.
sourceClaims: In a part-to-part ratio a:b(:c), a part is a/(a+b(+c)) of the whole; ratio compares part to part and must be reduced to simplest form — the classic error is reading a:b as a/b of the whole.
Pupils should divide a given quantity into two (or more) parts in a given part:part or part:whole ratio, and express a division as a fraction of the whole (KS3 ratio, proportion and rates of change).
learnerActions: For 1:2:3, state what fraction of the whole each share is: 1/6, 2/6 (=1/3) and 3/6 (=1/2), using the TOTAL of 6 parts as the denominator.
Contrast part-to-part with part-to-whole explicitly: the middle share is 2 parts out of 6 total, so 2/6, NOT 2/3.
Optionally toggle a colour band to light each part and reveal its fraction of the whole.
activities.intendedInsight: When stating a share as a fraction of the whole, the denominator is the SUM of all parts (a+b+c), not another single term; part-to-part and part-to-whole use the same numbers differently.

activities.title: Checks for understanding (written/selected response)
feedback: For 60, 60, 60: that divides equally rather than in 1:2:3 — re-form the total of 6 parts and scale each term.
For 10:14 chosen as final: it is not yet simplified — divide both terms by 2 to reach 5:7.
For 2/3: the denominator should be the total of 6 parts, giving 2/6 = 1/3.
activities.rationale: Selected/short responses efficiently reveal the equal-share and un-simplified-ratio errors, but they confirm recognition and recall rather than requiring the learner to build the segmented bar and produce the working; use alongside the construction tasks.
learnerActions: Fill in: divide 180 in 1:2:3 → __, __, __ (answer 30, 60, 90; the equal-share response 60, 60, 60 is a common error).
Choose the simplest-form ratio for shares of 10 and 14 (answer 5:7; the un-simplified 10:14 is a distractor).
State what fraction of the whole the middle share of 1:2:3 is (answer 2/6 = 1/3).
activities.intendedInsight: Three-part division, reverse-to-ratio, and part-of-whole can each be checked, with 'shared equally' and 'un-simplified ratio' as the diagnostic error responses; add a two-part item (e.g. £60 in 2:3) if two-part division is also to be checked.

constraints: Treat the forward division and the reverse (shares → simplest-form ratio) as distinct objectives: the forward task does not exercise simplification, so include a separate reverse task.

A static segmented reference bar (e.g. six equal segments for 1:2:3) with tap-to-reveal 'one part = total ÷ sum of parts' can consolidate the routine but does not let the learner segment, fill, or reverse a division themselves — it is a reference card, not a substitute for construction.
Selected-response checks confirm recognition/recall; they do not require the learner to build the bar or produce the working, so pair them with construction tasks for full evidence.
Always re-include every term in the total: a three-part ratio must sum all parts (1+2+3 = 6), and the shares must add back to the original quantity as a check.
Keep part-to-part (a:b) and part-to-whole (a out of a+b+c) distinct in notation, since the same numbers appear in both.
After finding one part, scale each term (×1, ×2, ×3) — reporting one part alone, or '1, 2, 3', is incomplete.
