Self-audit (arithmetic/logic checked): 180 ÷ 6 = 30; shares 30+60+90 = 180 ✓. £60 in 2:3 → 5 parts, 60 ÷ 5 = 12, shares 24 and 36, sum 60 ✓. 10:14 ÷2 = 5:7 ✓. Middle share of 1:2:3 = 2/6 = 1/3 ✓; largest share 3/6 = 1/2 ✓.

The legacy entry asserted a dividing procedure 'gains nothing' from dialogue and that 3D 'adds nothing' because partitioning is one-dimensional. These comparative-necessity claims are not established by the sources and have been dropped rather than propagated as universal laws; the tape/bar model is retained as a well-fitted representation without claiming other media cannot teach this.
The 'refusal to cut into three segments' is preserved as one optional, illustrative feedback mechanism, not a mandatory or uniquely effective design; its efficacy is untested.

Restored the original assessment's 'performance' error pattern (finds one part but forgets to multiply each term back) as explicit feedback in the forward-division activity, as it was missing from the source candidate.

The original probeDeeper listed '3/3, 3/6, or 3/1' as candidate answers for the largest share; only the correct 3/6 = 1/2 is used, and the erroneous options were not migrated as learner-facing choices.

probeDeeper: How many equal parts are there altogether in 1:2:3? Why 6 and not 3?
Add your three amounts together — do they make 180? What would it mean if they didn't?
What fraction of the whole 180 is the largest share? (counterexample: is it 3/3, 3/6, or 3/1 — and why?)
For 10:14, how did you get 5:7 — what did you divide by, and how is that like simplifying a fraction?
assess.correctAnswer: For 180 in 1:2:3: total parts = 1 + 2 + 3 = 6, so one part = 180 ÷ 6 = 30; the shares are 30, 60 and 90 (which add to 180). For the reverse: 10:14 simplifies (÷2) to 5:7.

errorPatterns.pattern: Divides by a single part or by the number of terms rather than the SUM of all parts
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw the bar cut into 1+2+3 = 6 equal segments and count them; one part = 180 ÷ 6. Check the shares add back to 180. Reteach ratio notation and the total-parts idea.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 180 ÷ 3 = 60 and gives 60, 60, 60 (equal), or 180 ÷ 1 / ÷2 / ÷3 separately; total parts of 6 never formed

errorPatterns.pattern: When reversing, writes the shares as a ratio without simplifying (or reverses the order)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Treat it like simplifying a fraction: divide both by the common factor (2). Keep the order matching the shares as stated. Reteach ratio simplification.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives 10:14 as the final answer, or writes 14:10, not dividing by the HCF to 5:7

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses part-to-part with part-to-whole — states a share as a/b of the whole rather than a/(a+b+c)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point to the six segments: the denominator is the TOTAL parts. Contrast 2/6 with 2/3 explicitly. Reteach the vocabulary of part-to-part vs part-to-whole.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a follow-up, says the middle share of 1:2:3 is 2/3 of the whole rather than 2/6 = 1/3

errorPatterns.pattern: Finds one part correctly but forgets to multiply each term back
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold: 'that's ONE part — how many parts does each share have?' Prompt the multiply and the add-back check.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Computes 180 ÷ 6 = 30 and answers '30' or '1, 2, 3' rather than 30, 60, 90

responseLevels.gap: Shares equally (60,60,60) or divides by one part; cannot form the total of 6 parts, and leaves a reversed ratio un-simplified.
responseLevels.full: Sums all parts to 6, finds one part = 30, gives 30/60/90 checked to 180, simplifies 10:14 to 5:7, and correctly states a share as its fraction of the whole (e.g. 2/6 = 1/3) — handling both directions and three-part ratios.
responseLevels.partial: Divides 180 correctly via 6 parts to 30/60/90, but leaves 10:14 un-simplified, or states a share as part-of-part not part-of-whole — the reverse direction or the fraction interpretation is not yet secure.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Divide 180 in the ratio 1:2:3. Work out the three amounts, and show your working. Then, separately: 24 sweets were shared as 10 and 14 — write that sharing as a ratio in its simplest form.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A pupil who has the routine sums all three parts to 6, divides once, and scales — shares total 180. A pupil dividing by the number of terms shares equally (60, 60, 60) or divides by one part; a pupil who cannot reverse leaves 10:14 un-simplified. Watching the working shows exactly which step fails, and the reverse task separately tests simplification, which the forward task does not.

sources.claim: Pupils should divide a given quantity into two (or more) parts in a given part:part or part:whole ratio, and express a division as a fraction of the whole (KS3 ratio, proportion and rates of change).
sources.source: UK National Curriculum, Mathematics programmes of study

sources.claim: In a part-to-part ratio a:b(:c), a part is a/(a+b(+c)) of the whole; ratio compares part to part and must be reduced to simplest form — the classic error is reading a:b as a/b of the whole.
sources.source: NRICH, 'Ratio or Proportion?'

pedagogy.summary: At Key Stage 3 children use faces, edges, vertices and cross-sections to reason about solids and solve problems. The ideas are best taught by physically slicing solids (clay, play-doh, food) at different orientations so the cut face is seen to CHANGE, insisting that a cross-section is a new surface distinct from a pre-existing face, and scaffolding straight (orthogonal) cuts before slanted (oblique) ones. Linking a prism's constant cross-section to its 'base times height' structure connects properties to measurement.
bestPractices: Physically slice solids at parallel, perpendicular and oblique orientations; predict-then-cut so a naive prediction can be violated.
Name the cut as a NEW surface — the shape where the slicing plane meets the solid — distinct from an outer face the solid already had.
Scaffold orthogonal cuts before oblique ones: straight slices can be solved by recognising a shape, slanted slices need more precise reasoning (Cohen & Hegarty; Munns et al.).
Count faces, edges and vertices on the solid handled in the round, not on the 2-D picture, so hidden elements are included.
Treat a prism as a constant cross-section swept along its length, linking to volume as area of base times height.
keyRepresentations: Sliced play-doh or food solids showing the fresh cut face
The cylinder's three cuts: circle (parallel), rectangle (perpendicular), ellipse (oblique)
A prism shown as its cross-section swept through a height
A face/edge/vertex tally taken from the solid in the round
commonMisconceptions: A solid has one fixed cross-section — a cylinder is 'always a circle' whatever the slice.
Confuses the cross-section with a pre-existing outer face, reporting a surface the solid already had.
Assumes a 2-D shape extends orthogonally into 3-D, so a slanted cut of a cylinder is judged a circle rather than an ellipse (over-applying 'the slice looks like the base').
Counts only the faces and edges visible in a 2-D drawing, missing hidden ones.

learn.summary: Learners build the idea that a cross-section is a NEW surface created where a slicing plane meets a solid, so its shape depends on the direction of the cut, not just on the solid. Core work is predict-then-slice on real solids (play-doh, carrot, food) at parallel, perpendicular and oblique orientations, naming the cut as distinct from any outer face the solid already had, scaffolding straight cuts before slanted ones, transferring the idea to a new solid such as a cone, counting faces/edges/vertices on the solid handled in the round, and linking a prism's constant cross-section to area-of-base-times-height.

activities.title: Predict, then slice: a cylinder gives more than a circle
feedback: If you answered 'circle' for the top-to-bottom cut too, slice the cylinder both ways and lay the two fresh faces side by side: the parallel cut is a circle, the perpendicular (top-to-bottom) cut is a rectangle — the shape tracks the direction of the cut.

If you named the cylinder's flat end or curved outer surface, hold up the freshly cut face and note: 'this surface did not exist before the cut' — the cross-section is new, not a face the solid already had.

The pre-stated reason is the diagnostic part: a mismatch between your justification and the real cut is exactly what shows the idea shifting from 'the solid has one cross-section' to 'the shape depends on how you slice it'.
activities.rationale: Predicting then violating a naive prediction targets the dominant misconception that a solid has a single fixed cross-section; students are documented to find identifying cross-section shapes difficult, so making the slice-dependence concrete addresses that difficulty directly.
sourceClaims: Identifying the shape of a solid's cross-section is difficult for middle and high school students (Davis 1973); students blend surface-area and volume ideas for the cylinder (e.g. doubling the circular base), reflecting a failure to grasp volume as area of the base (a cross-section) times height.
learnerActions: Hold a play-doh or carrot cylinder and a plastic knife.
BEFORE cutting, predict AND justify the shape of a straight top-to-bottom slice through the middle; write or say the reason.

Cut and compare the fresh cut face to your prediction (for a true cylinder a rectangle appears, not a circle; a real carrot that tapers gives a near-trapezium, an approximation to the ideal rectangle).
Make a second cut parallel to the circular ends and check that this one does give a circle.
State in your own words why the two cuts give different shapes.
activities.intendedInsight: A cross-section is the shape where the slicing plane meets the solid, so one solid yields many cross-sections depending on how it is sliced; a cylinder is only 'a circle' when sliced parallel to its base.

activities.title: Tilt the cut: straight before slanted
feedback: If you insisted the tilted cut is still a circle, overlay it on a traced circle: the cut face is longer in one direction. If the cut crossed only the curved surface it is an ellipse, not a circle; if it also clipped a flat end, it is part of an ellipse with a straight edge.

Notice the pattern: straight (orthogonal) cuts can often be solved by recognising a familiar shape, but slanted (oblique) cuts need you to reason about how the plane passes through the solid, so tackle the straight cuts first and build up to slanted ones.
On the cone, a vertical cut through the apex gives a triangle, not a circle — the same lesson that the shape depends on how the plane passes through the solid.
activities.rationale: Oblique cutting planes produce more errors than orthogonal ones because people assume 2-D shapes extend orthogonally into 3-D; scaffolding from orthogonal to oblique sections, and transferring to a fresh solid, is an evidence-based ordering.
sourceClaims: Oblique cutting planes produce more errors than orthogonal ones; people tend to assume a 2-D shape extends orthogonally into 3-D even for oblique sections, so orthogonal slices can be solved by recognising a shape while oblique slices need metric reasoning — interventions should scaffold from orthogonal to oblique cross-sections.
learnerActions: After solving the parallel and perpendicular cuts, tilt the knife and cut the cylinder at a slant.
Predict first: is the slanted cut face still a circle? Name the shape you expect.
Cut, then lay the slanted cut face over a traced circle of the same cylinder to compare.

Describe how the oblique cut stretches the circle into an ellipse when the slanted plane crosses only the curved surface. If your cut also runs through a flat end, the face is part of an ellipse with a straight edge, so note which case you got.
Transfer the idea to a new solid: predict then check the cross-section of a cone sliced vertically through its apex (a triangle), to test slice-dependence on a different shape.
activities.intendedInsight: Assuming a 2-D shape extends straight up into 3-D leads to calling a slanted cut a circle; oblique cuts need more careful reasoning than straight ones, a slanted slice of a cylinder that crosses only the curved surface is an ellipse (one that also cuts an end is an ellipse cut off by a straight edge), and the slice-dependence idea transfers to other solids such as a cone.

activities.title: The sweep that makes a prism
feedback: If you expected the shape to change along the prism, your repeated cuts parallel to the end show the same triangle each time. A constant polygonal cross-section like this is the defining feature of a prism.
Connect this to measurement: because the cross-section (the base) is the same all the way through, the volume is the area of that base multiplied by the length.
activities.rationale: Linking the constant cross-section of a prism to base-area-times-height connects spatial properties to volume and addresses the documented blending of surface-area and volume ideas.
sourceClaims: Identifying the shape of a solid's cross-section is difficult for middle and high school students (Davis 1973); students blend surface-area and volume ideas for the cylinder (e.g. doubling the circular base), reflecting a failure to grasp volume as area of the base (a cross-section) times height.
learnerActions: Take a triangular prism (or model one in play-doh).
Slice it parallel to its triangular end, then slice again further along its length.
Compare the cut faces: check whether the cross-section ever changes along the length.
Explain why a polygonal cross-section that never changes (for slices parallel to the end) is what makes the solid a prism, and connect this to volume as area of the end (base) times the length.
activities.intendedInsight: A prism is a constant polygonal cross-section swept along its length; this constancy (which a cylinder shares, with a circle as its cross-section) links the solid's properties to volume = area of base x height.

activities.title: Count faces, edges and vertices in the round
feedback: If you gave a triangular prism four faces, or missed the back edges, you were counting only what the picture shows — turn the solid over and mark each face as you count to include the hidden ones (a triangular prism has 5 faces, 9 edges, 6 vertices).
Use the solid itself, not the drawing, as your source of truth for counting.
activities.rationale: Spatial visualisation and property-based reasoning must be coordinated to overcome the 'look' of a 2-D diagram, which underlies counting only the visible faces and edges of a pictured solid.
sourceClaims: Spatial visualisation and property-based reasoning must be coordinated by domain knowledge to overcome the 'look' of a 2-D diagram, which underlies counting only the visible faces/edges of a pictured solid.
learnerActions: Hold the actual solid (triangular prism, square-based pyramid) and turn it over in your hands.
Count faces, edges and vertices, marking each face as you tally it so you do not miss hidden ones.
Compare your in-the-round count with what you would have counted from a flat 2-D picture of the same solid.
State how many elements the drawing would have hidden.
activities.intendedInsight: Counting from the solid handled in the round includes hidden faces, edges and vertices that a 2-D drawing conceals, so property-based reasoning must override the 'look' of a diagram.

activities.title: Explore slicing on a rotatable 3-D model (optional scaffold)
feedback: Watch the moment the circle stretches into an ellipse as you tilt the plane away from flat (parallel) towards a slant. The shape is responding continuously to the plane, so 'a cylinder is always a circle' cannot hold.

If a live 3-D model is unavailable, a side-view slider that redraws the cut face as you tilt a cutting plane, or a static reference image of a cylinder's three labelled cuts (circle/rectangle/ellipse) with each cut tappable to reveal its shape, can serve as lighter-weight versions — these summarise the idea but do less to build the felt slice-dependence than hands-on cutting.

Any on-screen or modelled cut face represents an idealised zero-thickness surface; the real play-doh or card slice has slight thickness, so treat it as an approximation to the mathematical cross-section.
activities.rationale: Cross-sections are inherently spatial, and a continuously morphing cut face makes orientation-dependence explicit; a rotatable model complements physical cutting. This is offered as a proposal, not as evidence that any one medium is uniquely necessary.
learnerActions: On a 3-D model, grab a translucent cylinder and a rotatable slicing plane.
Rotate the plane from flat (parallel) to upright (perpendicular) to a slant, watching the cut face render in real time.

Observe how the cut face changes continuously as the plane tilts. Going from flat to upright, the circle stretches into ellipses, then into ellipses cut off by straight edges once the plane meets the ends, and finally becomes a rectangle when the plane is upright.
Keeping the plane parallel to the prism's end, sweep it along the prism's length and watch the cross-section stay constant.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing the cut face morph continuously as a plane tilts makes the slice-dependence vivid: one solid, many cross-sections, the shape tracking the tilt of the plane.

constraints: Hands-on cutting is the core method; the 3-D model, 2-D slider and labelled reference image are scaffolds or summaries, useful for illustration but not a replacement for predicting and cutting real solids.

A static or interactive picture can illustrate the three cuts but does not let the learner vary the slice themselves; a quiz that matches cuts to orientations or counts elements of pictured solids checks recognition only and does not itself elicit the independent prediction-and-justification that reveals the misconception.
Scaffold straight (orthogonal) cuts before slanted (oblique) ones; oblique cuts are harder and should not be the entry point.
Always require counting from the solid handled in the round (or a model that can be rotated), not from a single 2-D drawing, so hidden elements are included.

Paper or card cutouts and play-doh slices have real thickness; treat them as approximations to the ideal zero-thickness cross-section, and label any on-screen cut face as a model of that idealised surface. Ask about the mathematical surface represented, not whether the physical slice can be held.
Insist the cross-section is named as a NEW surface where the plane meets the solid, distinct from any pre-existing outer face.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit: a triangular prism has 5 faces, 9 edges and 6 vertices; the legacy error-pattern example of 'four faces' is the mistaken answer, not the correct count — the correct count is stated in activity feedback and the mistaken one is kept only as a diagnostic signal.

Self-audit: a perpendicular (top-to-bottom through the middle) cut of a right cylinder gives a rectangle; a cut parallel to the circular ends gives a circle; a slanted cut across the body gives an ellipse (an oblique cut that reaches a circular end can give part of an ellipse/stadium, but for the straightforward body slant an ellipse is correct for this age group). A vertical cone cut gives a triangle only when it passes through the apex; off-apex it is a hyperbola.

Activity 1's rationale was tightened to cite only the documented difficulty of identifying cross-section shapes; the National Curriculum claim had already been removed from its sourceClaims because it establishes KS3 placement of cross-sections (topic), not the predict-then-slice teaching principle. The volume/surface-area blending content is carried by Activity 3 where the source directly supports it.
Transfer to a cone/new solid was restored (from responseLevels 'full' and the evidence statement) to preserve testing of slice-dependence on a second solid.

The source claims support general teaching principles (difficulty of cross-section identification, orthogonal-before-oblique scaffolding, coordinating spatial and property reasoning); they do not establish that any specific medium (3-D model vs physical cutting) is comparatively more effective, so no such comparative-efficacy claim is asserted.

The legacy row marked a 3-D interactive as 'ideal' and dialogue as unable to convey spatial slicing; these catalog fit rankings have been removed and the 3-D model reframed as an optional scaffold rather than a necessity.

assess.poeTask: Give the child a play-doh (or carrot) cylinder and a plastic knife. BEFORE any cut, ask them to predict and JUSTIFY the shape of a straight top-to-bottom slice through the middle. Most predict 'a circle' because a cylinder 'is' a circle. Then cut: a rectangle appears. The pre-stated reason is the diagnostic part — the mismatch forces the shift from 'the solid has one cross-section' to 'the shape depends on how you slice it'.
probeDeeper: Now I tilt the knife and cut the cylinder at a slant — is the cut face still a circle? What is it?
Is the shape you named a face the cylinder already had, or a new surface the cut made?
A triangular prism is sliced parallel to its triangular end all along its length — does the cut shape ever change? Why does that make it a prism?
How many faces does this prism have altogether, including the ones you cannot see in the picture?
assess.correctAnswer: The parallel cut gives a circle; the top-to-bottom (perpendicular) cut gives a rectangle. A cross-section is the shape where the slicing plane meets the solid, so it depends on the direction of the cut, not just on the solid — the cylinder is not 'a circle' by nature, only when sliced parallel to its base.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks a solid has a single fixed cross-section — 'a cylinder is a circle', so any cut is a circle regardless of direction
errorPatterns.nextMove: Slice a play-doh cylinder both ways so the rectangle appears; name the slicing plane and vary its direction explicitly
errorPatterns.distractor: A circle — the same shape as the flat slice
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'circle' for the perpendicular cut too and cannot explain the difference

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses the cross-section with a pre-existing outer face — reports a surface the solid already has rather than the newly cut shape
errorPatterns.nextMove: Cut a solid and hold up the fresh face: 'this surface did not exist before the cut'; contrast it with the outer faces
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names the cylinder's flat end or curved surface instead of the cut face

errorPatterns.pattern: Assumes a 2-D shape extends straight (orthogonally) into 3-D, so a slanted cut of a cylinder is judged a circle rather than an ellipse — over-applying 'the slice looks like the base'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Slice at a slant and lay the ellipse over a traced circle; scaffold from straight cuts to slanted ones
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the oblique probe insists the tilted cut is still a circle

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts only the faces, edges and vertices visible in the 2-D drawing, missing the hidden ones
errorPatterns.nextMove: Hand the child the solid to turn over and count, marking each face as it is tallied
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives a triangular prism four faces, or misses the back edges, when counting from a picture

responseLevels.gap: Gives one shape for every cut ('a circle'), or names an existing face; treats the cross-section as a fixed property of the solid.
responseLevels.full: Explains a cross-section as the intersection of the slicing plane with the solid, so its shape depends on the cut's direction; predicts circle, rectangle and ellipse for the three orientations and links a prism's constant cross-section to its structure, transferring to a cone or a new solid.
responseLevels.partial: Gets the parallel (circle) and perpendicular (rectangle) cuts and can count faces, edges and vertices, but lists these as separate facts — cannot yet say the cut depends on the slicing plane and fails the oblique case (calls it a circle).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A solid cylinder — like a tin of beans — is cut straight across, parallel to its circular ends: what 2-D shape is the freshly cut face? Now the same cylinder is cut straight down through the middle, from top to bottom: what shape is that cut face? Explain why the two cuts give different shapes.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands a cross-section as slice-dependent gives two different shapes and can say why; a child holding 'a cylinder's cross-section is a circle' answers 'circle' for both and cannot justify a difference. The reason-tier is essential — answering 'rectangle' by luck without the slicing-plane idea is exposed by the oblique probe, where they revert to 'circle'.

sources.claim: Identifying the shape of a solid's cross-section is difficult for middle and high school students (Davis 1973); students blend surface-area and volume ideas for the cylinder (e.g. doubling the circular base), reflecting a failure to grasp volume as area of the base (a cross-section) times height.
sources.source: Dorko & Speer (2013), 'Calculus Students' Understanding of Volume', Investigations in Mathematics Learning 6(2) (ERIC EJ1052960)

sources.claim: Oblique cutting planes produce more errors than orthogonal ones; people tend to assume a 2-D shape extends orthogonally into 3-D even for oblique sections, so orthogonal slices can be solved by recognising a shape while oblique slices need metric reasoning — interventions should scaffold from orthogonal to oblique cross-sections.
sources.source: Munns, He, Topete & Hegarty (2023), 'Visualizing Cross-Sections of 3D Objects', Journal of Intelligence 11(11):205 (reporting and replicating Cohen & Hegarty 2007, 2012)

sources.claim: Spatial visualisation and property-based reasoning must be coordinated by domain knowledge to overcome the 'look' of a 2-D diagram, which underlies counting only the visible faces/edges of a pictured solid.
sources.source: Fujita, Kondo, Kumakura, Kunimune & Jones (2020), Mathematics Education Research Journal 32(2)

sources.claim: Using properties of 3-D shapes including visualising cross-sections is a Key Stage 3 geometry objective in the English National Curriculum.
sources.source: National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (gov.uk)

pedagogy.summary: Children establish that packing a right rectangular prism with unit cubes gives the same volume as multiplying the edge lengths: V = l × w × h, equivalently base area × height (V = B × h). The formula must be DERIVED from the layer structure — one layer is the base area (l × w) in cubes, and the height tells how many layers — so that l × w × h is understood, not just recalled (Battista & Clements: rote V = LWH without layer structure is a documented failure). They apply the formula to real-world problems, estimate, and compare volumes in cm³ and m³.
bestPractices: Derive V = l × w × h from layers: l × w cubes in the base layer, repeated h times (V = B × h).
Connect the formula to the counting-cubes work so l × w × h is meaningful, not memorised.
Apply to real contexts (boxes, tanks) and compare volumes; estimate before calculating.
Watch that all three dimensions are multiplied (not added) and that the answer is in cm³.
keyRepresentations: Base layer (l×w) iterated h times
V = l × w × h and V = B × h
Labelled cuboid
Real containers (box, tank)
commonMisconceptions: Uses V = l×w×h rotely with no sense of layers (Strategy D), so cannot adapt to B×h or explain why it works.
Adds the edge lengths (l+w+h) instead of multiplying, or multiplies only two of the three dimensions.
Confuses volume with surface area, or records cm² instead of cm³.

learn.summary: Learners derive the volume formula for a right rectangular prism from its layer structure: with whole-number edge lengths in centimetres, the base layer holds l × w unit cubes (an area of l × w cm²), and the height h tells how many identical layers stack up, so V = l × w × h = base area × height (B × h). The goal is understanding why multiplying three edge lengths counts the cubes, not reciting a string. Learners then apply both V = l × w × h and V = B × h to real contexts (boxes, tanks), estimate, compare volumes, and record answers in cm³ or m³.

activities.title: Build the prism layer by layer
feedback: If a learner sets 4 × 3 × 5 and reads 60 cm³ but cannot say why, pause the stack mid-build: 'That one layer is 4 × 3 = 12 cubes covering 12 cm². How many layers tall is the box? So how many cubes altogether?'
When the height doubles from 5 to 10 and the learner expects the volume unchanged, point to the visibly doubled stack: the layer count doubled, so the volume doubled.
If the learner describes the answer only as '4 times 3 times 5', ask them to point to the base layer and the number of layers, then write it as 12 × 5 to connect l × w × h with B × h.
activities.rationale: Seeing a base layer replicate up the height makes l × w × h mean 'base area × number of layers' rather than a memorised string. Battista & Clements documented that some students apply V = LWH with no layer structure and cannot adapt or explain it; structuring the array into iterable layers is what makes the formula meaningful. A dynamic 3D build lets the learner set dimensions and watch terms assemble (B, then × h); a 2D side view with l/w/h sliders and an animating layer stack conveys the same derivation, and a tank/box skin ties it to real capacity. The 3D-versus-2D presentation choice is a design option, not a claim of proven superiority.
sourceClaims: 5.MD.C.5.a: 'Find the volume of a right rectangular prism with whole-number side lengths by packing it with unit cubes, and show that the volume is the same as would be found by multiplying the edge lengths, equivalently by multiplying the height by the area of the base.' 5.b: 'Apply the formulas V = l × w × h and V = b × h for rectangular prisms to find volumes... in the context of solving real world and mathematical problems.'

Battista & Clements found some students use V = LWH with no indication they understand it in terms of layers (Strategy D, rote memorisation without intuitive understanding); for the formula to be meaningful, numerical reasoning must come out of structuring the array into iterable layers (base iterated through the height).
learnerActions: Set a box to 4 × 3 × 5 and watch the base layer tile in as 4 × 3 = 12 unit cubes, which cover a base area of 12 cm²; name this base area B.
Stack that identical 12-cube layer upward 5 times to fill the box, tracking the readout as it builds '12 × 5 = 60 cm³' alongside '4 × 3 × 5'.
Change the height from 5 to 10 and predict, then check, what happens to the number of layers and the total volume.
Switch to a tank skin and relate the same count to how much water fills the container.
Re-express the result as B × h and say in words: 'one base layer, repeated so many times high.'
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying the three edge lengths counts cubes because l × w is one layer and h is how many identical layers there are; V = l × w × h is the same idea as V = base area × height.

activities.title: Apply and compare prism volumes
feedback: If a learner writes 4 + 3 + 5 = 12, return to one layer of 4 × 3 and five layers: adding gives an edge total, not a cube count — all three dimensions must be multiplied.
If a learner computes 4 × 3 = 12 and stops, ask how many layers tall the box is; the height is still needed.

If the answer is written as 60 cm², link cm³ to a single filling unit cube and distinguish filling a space (volume, cm³) from covering faces (surface area, cm²); the multiplication itself may be correct.
For a missing-edge task, check the learner divides the volume by the product of the two known edges rather than guessing.
activities.rationale: Applying V = l × w × h and V = B × h to real and mathematical problems is a stated objective, and the add-vs-multiply slip and the unit error surface directly in written working. A response-format task (compute, find missing edge, choose unit, compare) can be used during teaching as well as for checking, with distractors targeting l + w + h and cm². This recognition/computation work complements but does not replace the layer-structure derivation.
sourceClaims: 5.MD.C.5.a: 'Find the volume of a right rectangular prism with whole-number side lengths by packing it with unit cubes, and show that the volume is the same as would be found by multiplying the edge lengths, equivalently by multiplying the height by the area of the base.' 5.b: 'Apply the formulas V = l × w × h and V = b × h for rectangular prisms to find volumes... in the context of solving real world and mathematical problems.'
learnerActions: Compute the volume of several labelled cuboids using V = l × w × h, writing the unit as cm³ each time.
Find a missing edge length when given a prism's volume and two of its dimensions.
Given the base area B and height h (instead of three separate edges), compute V = B × h.
Compare two cuboids and decide which holds more, estimating before calculating.
Spot and correct worked examples that add the dimensions (l + w + h) or multiply only two of the three.
activities.intendedInsight: The formula is a tool for real problems: you can run it forwards (edges to volume), backwards (volume and two edges to the third), and in the B × h form, and you must use all three dimensions and the cubic unit.

activities.title: Explain why packing equals multiplying
feedback: If the learner gets 60 but cannot explain it, or stalls when given the base area and height instead of three edges, rebuild from cubes: base area × height means 'one layer, so many times high.'
If the learner cannot connect their answer to layers, lay out one 4 × 3 layer and stack five to show the identical layer repeating.
For 'twice as tall', expect the volume to double because the number of identical layers doubles — check they reason from layers, not just recompute.
activities.rationale: Asking 'why does it work' and probing the B × h form separates relational understanding (base layer × height) from rote V = LWH. A static labelled cuboid with tap-to-reveal layer reasoning can present the idea, but on its own offers no manipulation, so pair it with the manipulable build or with hands-on cubes. This is best watched — observe whether the learner multiplies all three dimensions, connects to layers or B × h, and writes cm³.
sourceClaims: Battista & Clements found some students use V = LWH with no indication they understand it in terms of layers (Strategy D, rote memorisation without intuitive understanding); for the formula to be meaningful, numerical reasoning must come out of structuring the array into iterable layers (base iterated through the height).
learnerActions: Take a labelled 4 cm × 3 cm × 5 cm cuboid with a real prompt ('a tank 4 cm by 3 cm by 5 cm — how much water fills it?') and find its volume.
In words or on a diagram, reveal the base layer (12 cubes), the number of layers (5), and the product l × w × h, explaining why they match.

Answer the probing questions: Why does multiplying the three edge lengths give the number of cubes? What is the base area, and how many layers high? If the tank were twice as tall, what happens to the volume? Why cm³ and not cm²?
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to justify V = l × w × h via base-layer × height — not just produce 60 — is the mark of relational understanding, and it transfers to the B × h form and to real capacity questions.

constraints: Derive V = l × w × h from the layer structure (l × w cubes in the base layer, covering l × w cm², repeated h times = B × h) so the formula is understood, not memorised.

A static labelled image or a recognition/compute task can present or check the idea but does not by itself elicit the learner building and explaining the layer structure; pair it with manipulation (physical cubes or an interactive build).

Physical unit cubes and a screen model offer different experiences of the same cube-packing derivation; learners should connect the cube-packing to the multiplication, in line with the standard's packing-with-unit-cubes method.
Watch that all three dimensions are multiplied (not added) and that none of the three is left out; distinguish volume (cm³, filling) from surface area (cm², covering).
Record volumes in the correct cubic unit (cm³ or m³) and estimate before calculating in real-context problems.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The two cited sources (Common Core 5.MD.C.5 and Olkun & Knaupp 1999 summarising Battista & Clements) support the standard's content and the layer-structure principle; they do not establish comparative efficacy of any specific artefact format (3D vs 2D vs static vs cube manipulatives). Claims that layer-iteration 'reads most clearly in 3D' are design opinions, not established findings, and are kept out of learner-facing text.

Arithmetic self-check: base layer 4 × 3 = 12 cubes covering 12 cm²; 12 × 5 = 60; 4 × 3 × 5 = 60 cm³ — consistent. The l + w + h distractor (4 + 3 + 5 = 12) is retained only as an error pattern to diagnose, never as a valid answer.

probeDeeper: Why does multiplying the three edge lengths give the number of cubes?
What is the base area here, and how many layers high is it? (B × h)
If the tank were twice as tall, what happens to the volume?
Why cm³ and not cm²?
assess.correctAnswer: 60 cm³ = 4 × 3 × 5, explained as a base layer of 12 cubes repeated 5 times (B × h); records the answer in cm³.

errorPatterns.pattern: Applies V = l×w×h rotely with no sense of layers (Strategy D).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild from layers with cubes — base area × height — so the formula means 'one layer, so many times high'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gets 60 but cannot say why, or is stuck when asked for B×h or given the base area and height instead of three edges.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds the dimensions or multiplies only two of the three.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to packing cubes: one layer is 4×3, and there are 5 layers, so all three dimensions are needed.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Computes 4+3+5 = 12, or 4×3 = 12 and stops, forgetting the height.

errorPatterns.pattern: Records the wrong unit or computes surface area instead of volume.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Link cm³ to a filling cube and distinguish filling (volume) from covering (surface); do not reteach the multiplication.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 60 cm², or works out the area of the faces.

responseLevels.gap: Adds dimensions or multiplies only two; wrong units; no layer or base reasoning.
responseLevels.full: Finds 60 cm³, explains it as base area × height (a base layer iterated), adapts to B×h and real contexts, and uses cm³.
responseLevels.partial: Computes l×w×h correctly but cannot explain it via layers or convert to B×h; applies the formula rotely.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give a labelled cuboid (4 cm × 3 cm × 5 cm) with a real-world prompt ('a tank 4 cm by 3 cm by 5 cm — how much water fills it?'). Say: 'Find its volume, and explain why your method works.' Then WATCH whether they multiply all three dimensions, whether they can connect it to layers (base 12, five layers) or to B×h, and whether they write cm³.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Asking 'why does it work' and probing B×h separates relational understanding (base layer × height) from a rote V=LWH; the add-versus-multiply slip and the unit error surface directly in the working, so the task is watched rather than asked about.

sources.claim: 5.MD.C.5.a: 'Find the volume of a right rectangular prism with whole-number side lengths by packing it with unit cubes, and show that the volume is the same as would be found by multiplying the edge lengths, equivalently by multiplying the height by the area of the base.' 5.b: 'Apply the formulas V = l × w × h and V = b × h for rectangular prisms to find volumes... in the context of solving real world and mathematical problems.'
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 5 Measurement & Data (5.MD.C.5.a–b)

sources.claim: Battista & Clements found some students use V = LWH with no indication they understand it in terms of layers (Strategy D, rote memorisation without intuitive understanding); for the formula to be meaningful, numerical reasoning must come out of structuring the array into iterable layers (base iterated through the height).
sources.source: Olkun & Knaupp (1999) (ERIC ED428954), summarising Battista & Clements (1996 JRME 27(3); 1998)

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 5–7 (Year 1 → Year 2). SKIP COUNTING in 2s, 5s and 10s — the first move beyond counting by ones into counting equal GROUPS. The gateway to multiplication (equal groups / repeated addition), even numbers, telling time (5s) and place value (10s).
• Standards — UK (DfE): NC Year 1 'count in multiples of 2s, 5s and 10s'; guidance: 'counting in 2s, 5s and 10s from different multiples to develop their recognition of patterns in the number system (for example, odd and even numbers).'
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.CC.1 'count … by tens'; Grade 2 extends — 2.NBT.2 'Count within 1000; skip-count by 5s, 10s, and 100s.' Skip counting underpins the multiplication foundations of 2.OA.3–4 and Grade 3 OA.
• Operational details: Teach as counting equal GROUPS, not a new chant — each 'step' is one more group of 2/5/10 (link to repeated addition, the multiplication seed). Use the HUNDRED SQUARE (shade 5s → two columns; 10s → one column; 2s → even columns) and the NUMBER LINE (equal jumps landing on multiples) so the pattern is seen. Count from different starting multiples, not only 0. Anchor 2s↔even, 5s↔clock/tallies/fingers, 10s↔place value.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (5–6) counts in 10s to 100 and 2s to 20 from 0. Tier B (6) counts in 5s to 50 and links 2s to even numbers. Tier C (6–7) counts in 2s/5s/10s from a non-zero multiple and explains each step adds a group ('5s go up by five each time = one more group of five').
bestPractices: Teach each skip count as adding one equal GROUP (repeated addition), not a disconnected chant — this is the multiplication seed.
Shade multiples on a hundred square so the visual pattern (columns/diagonals) makes the sequence predictable rather than memorised.
Use a number line with equal-sized jumps landing on multiples — the jump size IS the step, making 'counting in 5s' concrete.
Count from different starting multiples and in both directions so it is flexible, not a fixed rote song.
Anchor to real contexts: 2s (pairs, even numbers), 5s (fingers, tally marks, clock minutes), 10s (tens, money).
keyRepresentations: Hundred square with multiples shaded (pattern by column/diagonal).
Number line with equal jumps (the jump = the step size).
Equal groups / arrays of 2, 5, 10 (the bridge to multiplication).
Fingers (5s/10s), tally marks (5s), coins (5s/10s).
commonMisconceptions: Reciting the multiples as a chant with no sense that each step is +one group — so it doesn't transfer to multiplication.
Thinking the multiples are the ONLY numbers that 'exist', or that skip counting removes the in-between numbers (7 isn't 'skipped away').
Only able to start from 0 — can't skip-count from a different multiple or backwards.
Confusing 'counting in 2s' with 'counting to 2', or losing the pattern at decade boundaries (5s: '…45, 50, 55').

learn.summary: Skip counting in 2s, 5s and 10s for ages 5–7, taught as counting equal GROUPS (one more group of 2/5/10 each step) rather than a memorised chant — the bridge to multiplication, repeated addition, even numbers, clock minutes and place value. Core representations are the hundred square (on a standard 10-wide square, shaded multiples of 2, 5 and 10 form straight column patterns) and the number line (equal-sized jumps landing on multiples). Learners should count from different starting multiples and in both directions, not only forward from 0.

activities.title: One hop, one group: linking jumps, counters and the hundred square
feedback: If a learner recites fluently from 0 but can't say what comes after 40 in 10s, bring them back to one jump: 'each hop adds ten — show me the next group.'
When the shaded 10s form a single straight column and the 5s two columns, prompt: 'what do you notice about where they are?' so the pattern, not memory, drives the next number.

If a learner sub-counts the in-between numbers under their breath, that is a normal developing step — let the equal jump and the shaded pattern gradually make it feel like one move; do not mark it wrong.
If starting at 30 they restart from 0, say 'start here and keep hopping' and practise entering mid-sequence from several multiples.
activities.rationale: Showing the jump, the stacked group of counters and the shaded hundred-square cells together makes 'counting in fives' concrete as repeated equal groups rather than a chant, and counting from varied multiples and in both directions keeps it flexible. Linked, simultaneously-moving views (number line + counters + hundred square) are offered as one way to make the group structure visible; the panels moving together is an optional interaction example, not a required mechanism.
sourceClaims: Year 1: 'count in multiples of 2s, 5s and 10s'; guidance: counting in 2s, 5s and 10s from different multiples to develop recognition of number patterns (e.g. odd and even).
2.NBT.2 'Count within 1000; skip-count by 5s, 10s, and 100s'; skip counting underpins multiplication foundations (equal groups / repeated addition).
Skip counting is taught as counting equal groups (the multiplication bridge) using the hundred square and number line to make patterns visible.
learnerActions: Pick which step size you are counting in: 2, 5 or 10.
Take one step forward on a number line, making an equal-sized jump (a jump of 5 for 5s) that lands on the next multiple.
For each jump, add a GROUP of that many counters into a new stack/tower, so you see the jump as 'one more group of five'.
Shade or light up the cells you land on (5, 10, 15 …) on a hundred square as you go.
Say aloud what each step adds: 'each hop adds five — one more group of five.'
Try starting from a non-zero multiple (e.g. start at 30 and count on in 10s: 30, 40, 50 …).
Try counting in the other direction too (e.g. count back in 10s from 50: 50, 40, 30 …).
activities.intendedInsight: Each step of skip counting adds (or, going back, removes) one equal group, so the next multiple can be predicted from the pattern and from 'one more group' instead of recited — this is the seed of multiplication and repeated addition.

activities.title: Spotting the pattern on a multiples chart
feedback: If a learner says the multiples are the 'only numbers that exist' or that in-between numbers are 'skipped away', point to the chart: 7 is still there, we are just landing on every second/fifth/tenth number.
At a decade boundary, if they lose the pattern (…45, 50, 55), have them trace the column to confirm the next landing cell.
activities.rationale: A pre-marked multiples chart is a genuinely useful reference whose pattern is visible even when static; it supports recognising multiples and crossing decade boundaries. It shows the pattern but does not itself require the learner to generate each step, so pair it with tasks where the learner constructs and explains steps.
sourceClaims: Year 1: 'count in multiples of 2s, 5s and 10s'; guidance: counting in 2s, 5s and 10s from different multiples to develop recognition of number patterns (e.g. odd and even).
learnerActions: Look at a hundred square or multiples chart with the 2s, 5s or 10s already marked.
Tap or point to a multiple to reveal it and the group it stands for (e.g. 15 = three groups of five).
Describe the visual pattern: 10s make one straight column, 5s make two columns, 2s shade the even columns.
Use the chart as a reference to answer 'what comes next in 5s after 45?' across a decade boundary.
activities.intendedInsight: The multiples sit in a predictable visual pattern, so you can find the next one by reading the pattern rather than restarting the chant — and the pattern survives decade boundaries like 45, 50, 55.

activities.title: Anchoring 2s, 5s and 10s to real things
feedback: If a learner confuses 'counting in 2s' with 'counting to 2', re-ground in pairs: each new pair adds two to the total.
Use fingers and tally marks to re-establish the fives if the 5s pattern slips.
activities.rationale: Anchoring each step size to familiar contexts gives meaning to the groups and supports transfer to even numbers, telling time and place value.
sourceClaims: Year 1: 'count in multiples of 2s, 5s and 10s'; guidance: counting in 2s, 5s and 10s from different multiples to develop recognition of number patterns (e.g. odd and even).
learnerActions: Count pairs of objects in 2s and connect to even numbers (2, 4, 6 …).
Count hands/fingers and tally marks in 5s (5, 10, 15 …) and clock minutes in 5s.
Count groups of ten — tens blocks or 10p coins — in 10s and link to place value (how many tens).
Say how each context shows 'one more group': one more pair, one more hand of five, one more ten.
activities.intendedInsight: Skip counting describes real repeated groups — pairs, fives and tens — so 2s↔even, 5s↔clock/tallies/fingers, 10s↔place value make the counts meaningful and memorable.

activities.title: Fluency practice: fill, continue, match
feedback: A 'next multiple' or 'fill the gap' task checks fluency but, on its own, may let a learner answer by recognition; follow up with 'how did you know?' to check for group reasoning.
In the oral partner game, use the caught slip to prompt 'how did you know that was wrong?' rather than just correcting.
activities.rationale: These tasks give targeted fluency practice and the array-matching links sequences back to equal groups. Fill/continue tasks check recall and recognition but do not by themselves show the learner is reasoning from groups, so pair them with the construction and explanation tasks. The oral call-and-response gives fluency and listening practice but lacks a seen pattern, so it complements rather than replaces the visual work.
learnerActions: Fill in a missing multiple in a sequence (…, 10, __, 20 in 5s).
Say what comes next in 2s/5s/10s from a given number, including across a decade boundary.
Put a set of multiples in order.
Match a skip-count (e.g. 5, 10, 15) to an array or picture of equal groups.
Do an oral count-in-5s with a partner as call-and-response, and catch a deliberate slip in the other person's count.
activities.intendedInsight: Repeated varied practice — including continuing from non-zero starts and matching counts to equal-group arrays — builds fluency while keeping the count tied to groups.

constraints: Teach skip counting as adding one equal group each step (repeated addition), not as a disconnected chant — this is the multiplication seed.
Count from different starting multiples (not only 0) and in both directions, so the skill is flexible rather than a fixed rote song.

A pre-marked multiples chart and fill/continue practice items are references and recognition checks; they show or test the pattern but do not require the learner to independently construct each step, so pair them with tasks where the learner generates and explains steps.

Reverting to counting the in-between numbers by ones, and difficulty starting from a non-zero multiple, are developmental stages that improve with practice — do not mark them as errors; scaffold with equal jumps and hundred-square patterns.
Do not imply that only the multiples 'exist' or that in-between numbers are removed; the full number sequence is still present, we just land on every 2nd/5th/10th number.
Watch decade boundaries in 5s (…45, 50, 55) where the pattern is easily lost.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labels the CCSS 2.NBT.2 and NCETM claims as verified:false; only the DfE Year 1 claim is marked verified. Treat the standards-alignment and 'taught as equal groups' statements as unverified; they are retained only where they directly support the equal-groups principle.

The legacy note that a third dimension 'adds nothing' to a grid/line pattern was removed as a catalog-fit judgement, not an established pedagogical law; a planar hundred square and number line are well-suited here, which is sufficient without the universal claim.

The legacy framing of one interactive as 'the killer move' / 'the insight clicks' was softened: the linked number-line/counters/hundred-square views are presented as one effective way to make equal groups visible, not as uniquely necessary.

The oral call-and-response and static chart are described by narrow affordances (fluency/listening practice; visible but non-generative reference); no categorical 'only this teaches' or 'cannot teach' claim is asserted.
Catalog/product vocabulary ('quiz', artefact-fit rankings) was removed from learner-facing text; where mentioned in these notes it only documents the removal.

probeDeeper: What comes after 16 when counting in 2s?
Count in 10s but start at 30.
Look at the 5s you tapped — what do you notice about where they are?
How is counting in 2s like counting groups of 2?
assess.correctAnswer: Recites 2s, 5s, 10s accurately to the stated limits; the hundred-square taps fall in a straight column (10s) and a regular pattern (5s, 2s); continues 30, 40, 50… when started at 30 — treating skip counting as counting equal groups, not a fixed jingle.

errorPatterns.pattern: skip-counting-as-chant — recites the sequence as a memorised rhyme but can't say what comes after a given multiple without restarting, and can't map it to the numbers
errorPatterns.nextMove: link each step to a group — a jump of 2 on the number line, a column of 10 on the square — saying 'each hop adds two' so the sequence carries meaning
errorPatterns.revealedBy: fluent from 0 yet stuck on 'what's after 40 in 10s?' or unable to point the sequence out on the hundred square

errorPatterns.pattern: reverts to counting by ones — gets the next multiple by counting the ones in between under their breath rather than stepping by the group size
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT treat as an error — the group-step speeds up with practice; use number-line equal jumps and hundred-square patterns to make the step feel like one move
errorPatterns.revealedBy: pauses and sub-counts between multiples

errorPatterns.pattern: can't start from a non-zero multiple — counts in 10s only from 0; asked to start at 30, restarts at 0 or 10
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT correct as a mistake — practise 'start here and keep hopping' from various multiples on a number line; entering mid-sequence develops with exposure
errorPatterns.revealedBy: restarts rather than continuing from 30

responseLevels.gap: Cannot sustain a skip-count sequence, or produces it only as a memorised chant with no link to the numbers on a track or square.
responseLevels.full: Skip-counts 2s, 5s, 10s to the limits, continues from any multiple, and connects each step to adding an equal group (jumps on a number line, patterns on a hundred square).
responseLevels.partial: Recites 2s/5s/10s from 0 fluently but reverts to counting by ones for the next multiple, or can't start from a non-zero multiple — the equal-group structure isn't yet seen.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Count out loud in 2s from 0 up to 20. Now count in 10s up to 100. Now count in 5s up to 50, and this time point to each number as you say it on this hundred square. Then start at 30 and count on in 10s. (Watch fluency, whether the taps land in the right pattern, and whether they can start from a non-zero multiple.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Reciting from 0 is the baseline; the pointing-on-the-square and start-at-30 tasks reveal whether the child sees skip counting as adding equal groups or is just chanting. A chant-only child can say '5,10,15,20' but can't point to them correctly, can't start from 30, or drops back to counting by ones to get the next number.
