pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 8–9y; recognise and use factor pairs and commutativity in mental calculations (e.g. list factor pairs of 24; reorder a product for easier calculation).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y4 'recognise and use factor pairs and commutativity in mental calculations'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.OA.4 — 'find all factor pairs for a whole number in the range 1–100 … recognize that a whole number is a multiple of each of its factors' (leads into prime/composite); 3.OA.5 commutativity as a strategy.
• Operational details — a factor pair is two numbers that multiply to give a target (24: 1×24, 2×12, 3×8, 4×6). The two skills interlock: commutativity means 3×8 and 8×3 are the SAME pair, so you find pairs systematically and stop when they meet in the middle (avoiding duplicates). Factor pairs are found via known table facts and the ×÷ inverse ('what times what makes 24?'). The mental-calculation payoff: reorder/regroup using pairs (e.g. 25×16 = 25×4×4 = 100×4 = 400). Represent each pair as a rectangle (24 dots as 1×24, 2×12, 3×8, 4×6 rectangles) so factors ARE the possible rectangle dimensions — the direct bridge to arrays/area and later to primes (a prime makes only the 1×n rectangle).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8): find factor pairs of a small number with an array (12). Tier B (age 8–9): list ALL factor pairs of a number to ~50 systematically, using commutativity to avoid repeats. Tier C (age 9): use factor pairs to simplify a mental calculation and explain why you stop searching at the square root.
bestPractices: Search for factor pairs systematically — 1, 2, 3, … in order, pairing each with its partner — and use commutativity to know you've found them all when the pair 'meets in the middle'.
Represent each factor pair as a rectangle of the target number, so a factor is literally a side length and children see the finite set of rectangles a number allows.
Find factors through known table facts and the ×÷ inverse, reinforcing that factor-finding is division/known-fact work.
Use factor pairs and commutativity as mental-calculation tools (reorder/regroup for easy pairs like ×5×2=×10), not just as a listing exercise.
Seed prime/composite intuition: numbers with only the 1×n rectangle (one factor pair) hint at primes; square numbers have a repeated factor (the square).
keyRepresentations: Rectangle/array for each factor pair — factors as side lengths of all rectangles of that number
Systematic factor-pair list (1×24, 2×12, 3×8, 4×6) with the 'meet in the middle' stopping point
Factor 'rainbow' arcs pairing 1–24, 2–12, 3–8, 4–6 — shows commutativity and completeness
×÷ fact family — factor-finding as division
commonMisconceptions: Listing 3×8 and 8×3 as different pairs (not applying commutativity), inflating the count.
Missing factor pairs by searching unsystematically, especially the middle ones.
Confusing factors with multiples (factors go INTO the number; multiples are in its times table).
Forgetting 1 and the number itself are always a factor pair.
Not knowing when to stop — continuing past the square root and re-finding pairs in reverse.

learn.summary: Teaching factor pairs and commutativity to 8–9 year-olds: a factor pair is two whole numbers that multiply to a target (24: 1×24, 2×12, 3×8, 4×6). Commutativity means 3×8 and 8×3 are the SAME unordered pair, so pairs are searched systematically from 1 upward and the search stops when the two factors 'meet in the middle' (near the square root). Each pair corresponds to a rectangle the number can form, which bridges to arrays/area and previews primes (a whole number greater than 1 with only the 1×n rectangle). Factor pairs also pay off as a mental-calculation tool via reordering/regrouping (e.g. 25×16 = 25×4×4 = 100×4 = 400). Manipulable rectangle-building is the core; static diagrams, checking tasks, and Socratic questioning serve distinct supporting roles.

activities.title: Rectangle hunt: build every rectangle of a number
feedback: If a rectangle has gaps, it is not a valid arrangement — the dimensions only count as a factor pair when every counter fills a complete rectangle.
When a learner records 3×8 and 8×3 separately, show the same rectangle rotated: same counters, same two factors, so it is one pair, not two.
If a learner is unsure when to stop, point out that once the two sides of the rectangle cross over (near 4 and 6 for 24), every larger factor has already appeared as the partner of a smaller one.
With 23, prompt: 'Can you make any rectangle other than a single line? What does that tell you about 23?'
activities.rationale: Building rectangles makes the abstract list a felt, discovered structure, ties factor-finding to arrays/area (the total count equals the number), and lets completeness and the stopping point emerge from running out of rectangles rather than from a memorised rule. Contrast with a prime previews prime/composite ideas. Optional live feedback (logging dimensions, drawing rainbow arcs, rotating a rectangle to show 3×8 = 8×3) makes the mechanism concrete but is not required — paper, tiles, or dots work.
sourceClaims: Representing factor pairs as rectangles/arrays and searching systematically (stopping at the square root) supports completeness and previews prime/composite numbers.
4.OA.4 requires finding all factor pairs for a whole number 1–100 and recognising multiples, leading into prime/composite.
learnerActions: Take 24 counters (or squared paper, tiles, or dots) and arrange them into complete, gap-free rectangles, recording the dimensions of each as a factor pair.
Work systematically: ask 'does 1 fit? does 2 fit? does 3 fit?...' in order, logging each rectangle you can make (1×24, 2×12, 3×8, 4×6).
After making 3×8, try to make 8×3 and observe it is the SAME rectangle turned a quarter-turn — record it as one pair already found, not a new one.
Keep going (5 does not fit; 6 gives 6×4, the same rectangle as 4×6) and notice that no NEW rectangles appear once the two sides meet in the middle; explain why you can stop there.
Repeat with 23 counters and discover only a single 1×23 line forms — a whole number greater than 1 that makes only a single 1×n line is prime.
Draw a 'factor rainbow': arcs pairing 1–24, 2–12, 3–8, 4–6 to show each pair and completeness.
activities.intendedInsight: Factors are the possible side-lengths of all rectangles a number can form; commutativity collapses 3×8 and 8×3 into one pair; a systematic search can stop where the factors meet in the middle because every larger factor has already appeared as the partner of a smaller one; and a whole number greater than 1 that makes only the 1×n rectangle is prime.

activities.title: Factor pairs as a mental-calculation tool
feedback: Check the regrouping preserves the product: 25×4×4 uses the same factors as 25×16 (because 16 = 4×4), so the answer must match (400).
If a learner cannot find a factor, prompt them to use a known table fact or division: 'what number times 4 gives 16?'
activities.rationale: The curriculum goal names mental calculation explicitly; applying factor pairs to real regrouping connects the skill to its payoff and reinforces factor-finding as division/known-fact work.
sourceClaims: Y4 pupils recognise and use factor pairs and commutativity in mental calculations.
learnerActions: Rewrite a multiplication by regrouping convenient factors: turn 25×16 into 25×4×4, then compute 100×4 = 400.
Find a factor pair that makes a product easy (e.g. pairing ×5 with ×2 to make ×10), and explain why reordering is allowed.
Find factors using known times-table facts and the multiplication/division inverse: 'what times what makes 24?'
activities.intendedInsight: Commutativity (changing the order) and regrouping (choosing which factors to multiply first, e.g. 25×(4×4) = (25×4)×4) let you use factor pairs to turn a calculation into easier steps, so factor-finding is a practical mental-maths tool, not just a listing exercise.

activities.title: Prove the list is complete (systematic-search reasoning)
feedback: If the justification is 'I think that's all', model checking each counting number in order from 1 up to the point where the factor pairs meet (e.g. 1 to 6 for 36), recording each result so completeness is demonstrated, not guessed.
For the odd-count question, show that a square's two equal factors (5×5 for 25) count as one factor, so the total is odd.
activities.rationale: A Socratic 'how do you know?' exchange can build the systematic-search and completeness habit and targets the 'stop too early' and 'don't know when to stop' errors. It works alongside, not instead of, the visual rectangle work.
sourceClaims: Representing factor pairs as rectangles/arrays and searching systematically (stopping at the square root) supports completeness and previews prime/composite numbers.
learnerActions: List all factor pairs of a number such as 36, then explain how you know none is missing.
Respond to a challenge — 'Have we found them all? How do you know?' — by describing your sweep from 1 and your stopping point.

Explain why 24 has an even count of factors (8) but a square number like 25 has an odd count (3: 1, 5, 25), because one pair uses the same factor twice (5×5, the square root), so that factor is counted only once.
activities.intendedInsight: Completeness comes from a systematic sweep that pairs each small factor with its partner and stops where they meet, not from feeling finished; in a square number, one pair uses the same factor twice (e.g. 6×6 for 36), so that factor is counted once and the number of factors is odd.

activities.title: Check and sort: factors, pairs, and multiples
feedback: 24 has four distinct factor pairs. If a learner answers eight, they are counting reversed versions (8×3 as separate from 3×8) — these are the same pair.
If a learner lists a multiple (e.g. 48) as a factor of 24, remind them a factor goes INTO 24; a multiple is 24 times something.
Always include 1 and the number itself (1×24) — these form a pair every whole number has.
activities.rationale: Short checkable tasks can verify the duplicate/commutativity and factor-versus-multiple distinctions. A sort or fill-in checks classification but does not itself build the rectangle intuition or elicit the hands-on discovery of the stopping point, so it best follows the hands-on work.
sourceClaims: 4.OA.4 requires finding all factor pairs for a whole number 1–100 and recognising multiples, leading into prime/composite.
learnerActions: Fill in the missing factor pair of 36 given a partial list.
Sort numbers into 'factor of 24', 'multiple of 24', 'both' (24 itself) or 'neither' to distinguish the two ideas.
State how many DISTINCT factor pairs 24 has (four: 1×24, 2×12, 3×8, 4×6), treating each unordered pair once.
activities.intendedInsight: Factors divide into the number while multiples lie in its times table; distinct factor pairs are counted once because commutativity makes reversed versions the same pair.

constraints: Count a factor pair once: 3×8 and 8×3 are the same unordered pair. The common error of listing them separately (giving 24 '8 pairs') must be corrected in teaching, not presented as a valid option.

Checking/sorting tasks verify understanding and check classification; they do not by themselves build the rectangle intuition or let a learner discover the meeting-in-the-middle point, so they are well placed after hands-on exploration (not a universal requirement).

A static factor-rainbow diagram is a useful reference and can show completeness and commutativity, but it does not let the learner search for pairs or discover the meeting-in-the-middle point themselves.

Physical counters, tiles, or dots have slight thickness and stand in for the ideal flat rectangle; treat the arrangement as a representation of the number's structure where side-lengths = factors and the total count = the number — this legitimately bridges to arrays and area, so preserve (do not deny) the array/area interpretation.
Factor pairs are planar (two factors, rectangles). A three-factor/volume (cuboid) treatment belongs to a different topic and should not be introduced here.
Always include the 1×n pair; every number has 1 and itself as a factor pair.
The 'one rectangle = prime' observation applies only to whole numbers greater than 1; 1 forms only 1×1 but is not prime.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original materials describe stopping 'at the square root'. For these learners this is framed concretely as 'the two sides of the rectangle meet in the middle'; the exact square-root rule is the underlying reason and can be stated by older/more confident learners.
Source claims for CCSS-M 4.OA.4 and the NCETM guidance were marked unverified in the original row; do not treat them as independently confirmed.

The original counted 24 as having four distinct factor pairs; one legacy error-pattern distractor stated '24 has 8 factor pairs' — this is included only as a misconception to correct, never as a correct answer.

The original framed primes as 'numbers with just one rectangle'; this converse is inaccurate for 1, so the learner-facing wording was qualified to whole numbers greater than 1 while keeping the correct direction (a prime makes only the 1×n rectangle).

probeDeeper: How did you know 5 is not a factor of 24?
You wrote 3×8. Is 8×3 a different pair or the same one — why?
How did you know when to stop checking numbers?
24 has an even number of factors but 25 has an odd number. Why might that be?
assess.correctAnswer: 1×24, 2×12, 3×8, 4×6 (and their commutative partners 24×1, 12×2, 8×3, 6×4, which are the same pairs). A child reasoning well works UP from 1 checking each number in turn, stops when the factors meet in the middle (after 4×6, since 5 doesn't divide 24 and 6 has already appeared), and uses commutativity to know 3×8 and 8×3 are one pair, not two.

errorPatterns.pattern: searches unsystematically and stops early — lists 1×24, 2×12, 4×6 and misses 3×8, with no way to know a pair is missing
errorPatterns.nextMove: model checking every counting number in order (does 1 go in? 2? 3? …) and recording each result, so completeness comes from the systematic sweep, not from feeling done.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child offers an incomplete set and, asked how they know it's complete, says 'I think that's all' with no method

errorPatterns.pattern: counts 3×8 and 8×3 as two different factor pairs, inflating the list — not treating commutativity as making them one pair
errorPatterns.nextMove: show 3×8 and 8×3 as the same array rotated a quarter turn — same rectangle, same factors; a factor PAIR is one unordered pair.
errorPatterns.distractor: 24 has 8 factor pairs (3×8 and 8×3 are different)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child lists eight 'pairs' and treats reversed versions as new

errorPatterns.pattern: does not know when to STOP — keeps testing numbers past 24 or is unsure why the search ends, missing that factors pair up around the square root
errorPatterns.nextMove: point out that once the two factors in a pair cross over (here after 4 and 6), every larger factor has already appeared as the partner of a smaller one, so the search is complete.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child keeps trying numbers like 7, 9, 10 aimlessly or asks 'how far do I go?'

responseLevels.gap: finds a few pairs by trial with gaps, no method for completeness, and/or double-counts commutative reversals.
responseLevels.full: sweeps systematically from 1, uses commutativity to pair factors and avoid duplicates, stops correctly where factors meet, and justifies that the list is complete.
responseLevels.partial: finds all four pairs but only by luck or exhaustive guessing — cannot justify completeness or explain the stopping point; may still treat reversals as distinct.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Find ALL the factor pairs of 24 — every pair of whole numbers that multiply to make 24. When you have them, tell me how you knew you had found them all and hadn't missed any.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Unsystematic children find some pairs and guess they are done; the reason tier ('how do you know you have them all?') separates a random search from a systematic sweep up to the square-root turning point. Whether they double-count 3×8 and 8×3 reveals if commutativity is being used to organise the search.

sources.claim: Y4 pupils recognise and use factor pairs and commutativity in mental calculations.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (KS1–2), Year 4 Number — multiplication and division

sources.claim: 4.OA.4 requires finding all factor pairs for a whole number 1–100 and recognising multiples, leading into prime/composite.
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 4, Operations & Algebraic Thinking (4.OA.B.4)

sources.claim: Representing factor pairs as rectangles/arrays and searching systematically (stopping at the square root) supports completeness and previews prime/composite numbers.
sources.source: NCETM factors and multiples guidance

pedagogy.summary: A mixed number (2¾) and an improper fraction (11/4) name the SAME quantity in two forms; converting between them rests on 'how many wholes fit', because b/b = 1 whole. So 11/4 = 8/4 + 3/4 = 2 wholes and 3/4 = 2¾; reversing, 3⅖ = 3 wholes = 15 fifths, plus 2 fifths = 17/5. It is grounded in iterating unit fractions past the whole (counting quarters past 4/4) and in recognising that b copies of 1/b rebuild one whole.
bestPractices: Build from unit-fraction iteration on a number line or bar — count quarters past 4/4 = 1 whole — so the child SEES wholes forming inside an improper fraction
Make 'b bths = 1 whole' explicit, so 11/4 groups into wholes and 3 wholes = 15 fifths is understood, not memorised
Teach mixed→improper as 'each whole is b bths' (3 wholes × 5 = 15 fifths, add the 2) rather than a bare '× then add' trick; keep the denominator unchanged
Always verify by converting back (17/5 → 3⅖) so the two forms are seen as equal
Treat improper fractions as legitimate numbers, not mistakes to be 'fixed'
keyRepresentations: Number line with unit-fraction jumps continuing past 1 whole
Fraction bars/tiles where b pieces fuse into one whole tile
Area circles showing 11/4 as two full circles plus three quarters
Improper fraction and mixed number marked at the SAME point
commonMisconceptions: Mixed→improper adds the whole to the numerator: 3⅖ → (3+2)/5 = 5/5
Multiplies but forgets to add the numerator (15/5), or concatenates the digits (32/5)
Improper→mixed miscounts the wholes (e.g. 11/4 → 3¾)
Believes an improper fraction is 'not allowed' and must always be written as a mixed number
Changes the denominator during conversion

learn.summary: A mixed number (2¾) and an improper fraction (11/4) name the same quantity in two forms. Converting between them rests on 'how many wholes fit', because b copies of 1/b rebuild one whole (b/b = 1). So 11/4 = 8/4 + 3/4 = 2 wholes and 3/4 = 2¾; reversing, 3⅖ = 3 wholes = 15 fifths, plus 2 fifths = 17/5. Ground the work in iterating unit fractions past the whole (counting quarters past 4/4) rather than a bare rule, and treat improper fractions as legitimate numbers.

activities.title: Stamp quarters past the whole and watch wholes form
feedback: If a learner writes 3⅖ = 5/5, rebuild the 3 wholes as fifths on the bar: one whole is 5 fifths (not 1), so 3 wholes = 15 fifths, then add the 2 → 17/5.
If a learner writes 15/5, praise the ×b step (three wholes make fifteen fifths) and prompt the missing step: 'now add the two more fifths'.
If a learner writes 32/5, point out that gluing the 3 and 2 together ignores what the digits count; ask how many fifths are in 3 wholes.
If a learner reads 11/4 as 3¾ or subtracts 11 − 4, group the eleven quarters into fours on the bar: two complete groups of four (2 wholes) with three quarters left.

As an alternative representation, show 11/4 as area circles: two fully shaded circles plus three quarters of a third circle give the same 2¾ — another way to see the wholes already sitting inside the improper fraction.
Always close by converting back (17/5 → 3⅖, or 2¾ → 11/4) to confirm the two forms are equal.
activities.rationale: Building from unit-fraction iteration lets the child SEE wholes forming inside an improper fraction, so conversion is understood as regrouping rather than a half-remembered digit trick. Making 'b bths = 1 whole' explicit is intended to target the add-to-numerator error by showing a whole becoming b pieces rather than one.
sourceClaims: Improper fractions are legitimate numbers locatable on the number line (values greater than one); a fraction a/b (a>1) is b copies of the unit fraction 1/b, so b of them rebuild one whole — the basis for mixed↔improper conversion.
learnerActions: On a number line marked in quarters, add one quarter at a time, counting aloud: 1/4, 2/4, 3/4, 4/4.
At the 4th quarter, group the four quarters into one whole unit; do the same again at the 8th quarter.
Keep going to the 11th quarter and read off what you have: two whole units with three quarters sitting past them, so 11/4 = 2¾.
Now work the other way for 3⅖: break each of the 3 wholes into fifths (one whole = 5 fifths, so 3 wholes = 15 fifths), then add the 2 extra fifths to get 17/5.
Keep the denominator unchanged throughout, and say the running total in both forms as you go.
activities.intendedInsight: The improper form and the mixed form mark the SAME point: every b copies of 1/b fuse into one whole, and each whole breaks back into b pieces. This is why you multiply 3 × 5 (each whole is 5 fifths) and then add the 2, not add the whole to the numerator.

activities.title: Convert both directions and verify by reversing
feedback: Answers: 11/4 = 2¾ (8/4 = 2 wholes, 3/4 left over); 3⅖ = 17/5 (3 wholes = 15 fifths, plus 2 fifths), denominator unchanged.
If a learner insists 7/4 must become 1¾ to be 'allowed', confirm 7/4 and 1¾ are the same size and that a top-heavy fraction is a legitimate number sitting past 1.
If a learner changes the denominator during conversion, stop and ask what size the pieces are — the piece size (the denominator) does not change, only how they are grouped.
Probe with: 'How many quarters make one whole? So how many quarters are in 2 wholes?' and 'For 3⅖, why work out 3 × 5 before adding the 2 — what does the 15 count?'
activities.rationale: Bidirectional conversion with a built-in reverse-check makes the equality of the two forms explicit (grounded in b copies of 1/b rebuilding a whole) and surfaces the distinct add-to-numerator (5/5), forgot-to-add (15/5), and concatenate (32/5) errors as visibly different wrong answers to diagnose.
sourceClaims: Improper fractions are legitimate numbers locatable on the number line (values greater than one); a fraction a/b (a>1) is b copies of the unit fraction 1/b, so b of them rebuild one whole — the basis for mixed↔improper conversion.
learnerActions: Convert 11/4 to a mixed number and 3⅖ to an improper fraction, showing your working for each.
For the improper→mixed task, state how many wholes you found and how many pieces are left over.
For the mixed→improper task, say out loud what the first product counts (e.g. '15 counts the fifths in 3 wholes') before adding the leftover pieces.
Check each answer by converting it back to the other form and confirming you return to where you started.
Also write 6/5 + 4/5 = 10/5 as both an improper fraction and a whole number (2).
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent two-way conversion with a reverse-check confirms the forms are equal and that improper fractions such as 7/4 or 17/5 are valid answers, not mistakes to be 'fixed'.

activities.title: Reveal the wholes hidden inside an improper fraction (support)
feedback: If the learner marks the wrong number of groups, re-count: four quarters per whole, so eleven quarters give two full groups with three left.

This labelled picture is a reference aid; follow it up by actually performing the grouping and the reverse (breaking wholes back into pieces) so the conversion is practised as a reversible action, not only recognised.
activities.rationale: A labelled static bar helps a learner who needs to first SEE the wholes inside 11/4 before enacting the regrouping; it is a stepping stone toward independent conversion. The source supports the underlying content (whole groups sit inside an improper fraction); the scaffold itself is an unvalidated design choice.
sourceClaims: Improper fractions are legitimate numbers locatable on the number line (values greater than one); a fraction a/b (a>1) is b copies of the unit fraction 1/b, so b of them rebuild one whole — the basis for mixed↔improper conversion.
learnerActions: Look at a bar showing 11/4 drawn as individual quarters.
Circle or mark off the complete groups of four quarters, naming each group as one whole.
Read what is left after grouping and write the mixed number: 2 wholes + 3 quarters = 2¾.
activities.intendedInsight: An improper fraction already contains whole groups; finding them is a matter of grouping b pieces at a time, with the leftover pieces naming the fraction part.

constraints: Keep the denominator unchanged during conversion — only the grouping of equal-sized pieces changes.
Teach mixed→improper as 'each whole is b bths' (3 wholes × 5 = 15 fifths, then add 2), not as a bare '× then add' trick, so the first product is understood as counting pieces.
Treat improper fractions as legitimate numbers, not errors that must always be rewritten as mixed numbers.

The labelled static-bar activity is a scaffold: it can show and name the wholes inside an improper fraction but does not require the learner to enact the reversible grouping, so pair it with hands-on or line-based conversion.

Multiple-choice or fill-in tasks using the distractors 5/5, 15/5 and 32/5 can surface misconceptions, but watching the learner's working (grouping pieces vs. manipulating digits) is what discriminates understanding from a half-remembered rule; a recognition-only response does not by itself show independent construction.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified, and the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Depth/3D and open-dialogue formats were noted in the source as weak fits for this quantitative, procedural topic; this was retained as a design observation only and not asserted as a universal pedagogical law.

Worked arithmetic was independently checked: 11/4 = 8/4 + 3/4 = 2¾; 3⅖ = 15 fifths + 2 fifths = 17/5; 6/5 + 4/5 = 10/5 = 2. The distractors 5/5, 15/5, 32/5 are deliberately WRONG answers for diagnosis and must never be presented as correct.
The audible 'click'/'snap' fusing effect from the original recommendation is an optional interaction detail; it is offered as an example of making the grouping concrete, not as a required mechanism.

The area-circle model (two full circles plus three quarters for 11/4) is reinstated from the original key representations as an alternative to the number line/bar; efficacy of any one representation over another is not independently measured here.

The IES/WWC source directly supports the mathematical basis of conversion (b copies of 1/b rebuild one whole; improper fractions as legitimate numbers), not the comparative effectiveness of the specific scaffolds proposed; scaffold choices remain unvalidated.

probeDeeper: How many quarters make one whole? So how many quarters are in 2 whole ones?
For 3⅖, why do we work out 3 × 5 before adding the 2 — what does the 15 count?
Is 7/4 a proper answer, or must it be written as a mixed number? Are 7/4 and 1¾ the same size?
Check your 17/5 by turning it back into a mixed number — what do you get?
assess.correctAnswer: 11/4 = 2¾ (8/4 = 2 wholes, 3/4 left over); 3⅖ = 17/5 (3 wholes = 15 fifths, plus 2 fifths = 17/5), denominator unchanged.

errorPatterns.pattern: Mixed→improper adds the whole number to the numerator: 3⅖ → (3 + 2)/5 = 5/5
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild 3 wholes as fifths on the bar: one whole is 5 fifths, not 1, so 3 wholes = 15 fifths. Then add the 2.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 5/5 (or 5 over 5) for 3⅖; adds 3 + 2

errorPatterns.pattern: Multiplies the whole by the denominator but forgets to add the numerator (15/5), or concatenates the digits (32/5)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the two steps ('three wholes make fifteen fifths… now add the two more fifths'); the method is nearly there — do not reteach the concept.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 15/5 (dropped the +2) or 32/5 (glued 3 and 2); the × b step is present but the +a step is missing or mis-executed

errorPatterns.pattern: Improper→mixed miscounts the wholes: 11/4 → 3¾, or subtracts (11 − 4) to get the numerator
errorPatterns.nextMove: Group the eleven quarters into fours on the bar: two complete groups (2 wholes) with three quarters left.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reports the wrong number of wholes, or manipulates 11 and 4 by subtracting rather than grouping into fours

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes an improper fraction is 'not allowed' — calls 11/4 a mistake or insists everything must be written as a mixed number
errorPatterns.nextMove: Iterate unit fractions past the whole on a number line to show 11/4 is a real, legitimate number that simply sits past 1.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says a top-heavy fraction is wrong, or refuses to accept 17/5 as a valid answer

responseLevels.gap: Adds the whole to the numerator or miscounts the wholes; treats improper fractions as invalid; changes the denominator.
responseLevels.full: Converts both directions fluently, explains each step from b/b = 1 whole, verifies by converting back, and accepts improper fractions as legitimate numbers; transfers to a new pair.
responseLevels.partial: Converts one direction reliably but stumbles on the other, or reaches the answer by a rule without being able to explain the × b step as 'each whole is b bths'.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'Convert 11/4 into a mixed number, and convert 3⅖ into an improper fraction. Show me how you work each one out.' Watch the method for each — do not tell them a rule.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the working shows whether the child groups b bths into wholes (understanding) or manipulates digits by a half-remembered rule. 3⅖ is the hinge for mixed→improper: adding the whole to the numerator gives 5/5, multiplying but forgetting to add gives 15/5, concatenating gives 32/5 — three visibly different wrong answers — while a secure child gets 17/5 and can say why (3 wholes = 15 fifths). The 11/4 direction checks whether they count the wholes correctly.

sources.claim: Improper fractions are legitimate numbers locatable on the number line (values greater than one); a fraction a/b (a>1) is b copies of the unit fraction 1/b, so b of them rebuild one whole — the basis for mixed↔improper conversion.
sources.source: IES/WWC Practice Guide: Developing Effective Fractions Instruction (Recommendation 1, unit-fraction iteration and fractions on the number line)

pedagogy.summary: At 6-7, problem solving grows from single-step sense-making into planning a pathway through a two-step or more complex problem: the child, with teacher guidance, identifies what is known and what must be found, decides which information is relevant, chooses and sequences operations, and checks the answer for reasonableness. Two documented habits work against this. First, keyword/number-grabbing: choosing an operation from a cue word or simply using every number present, ignoring which information is relevant. Second, the compulsion to calculate: rushing to an answer without an estimate or sense-check. The most effective supports are teacher-modelled self-questioning (strong evidence) and teaching children to build visual representations — strip/bar diagrams — that map the relevant quantities and reveal the sequence of steps (strong evidence).
bestPractices: Model self-questioning aloud and give a short prompt list: 'What do I know? What must I find? What shall I do first?' (WWC Rec 2, strong evidence)
Teach children to build their OWN visual representation (bar/strip diagram) that maps knowns to the unknown — building it beats being handed one (WWC Rec 3, strong evidence)
Use the representation to keep the WHOLE multi-step situation visible so the child does not stop after step one
Include problems with an irrelevant number so 'identify relevant information' is actually exercised, not assumed
Estimate first to set a reasonableness benchmark, then compute, then ask 'does this make sense?' and check by a different method
Encourage strategy-switching: if the first approach stalls, represent it a different way rather than abandoning — name this as normal
keyRepresentations: Bar / strip diagram mapping known parts to the unknown
Part-part-whole and comparison ('more than') structures
Number line for two-step jumps
Numberless staged reveal to build relationships before numbers appear
A prompt list / four-move frame: understand → plan → solve → check
commonMisconceptions: Answering only the first step of a two-step problem (treating multi-step as single-step)
Using every number in the problem, including an irrelevant one, because 'they must all be needed'
Choosing the operation from a cue word rather than the problem's structure
Computing an answer and stopping, with no estimate or reasonableness check (compulsion to calculate)

learn.summary: For 6-7 year olds, help children plan a pathway through two-step and more complex word problems: identify what is known and what must be found, decide which information is relevant (setting aside any red-herring number), choose and sequence operations, estimate first, and check the answer for reasonableness. Two documented habits work against this: keyword/number-grabbing (choosing an operation from a cue word or using every number present) and the compulsion to calculate (rushing to an answer with no estimate or sense-check). The strongest supports in the sources are teacher-modelled self-questioning and children building their OWN visual representations (strip/bar diagrams, or a number line for two-step jumps) that map relevant quantities and reveal the sequence of steps. Several activities below address the same objective through different media (a build-your-own workspace, a planning dialogue, a worked-example companion, and a reasonableness-judgement item); keep more than one because they exercise construction, talk, and recognition respectively.

activities.title: Build-your-own 'plan-it' workspace with a red herring and an estimate-first step
feedback: When the computed answer strays far from the estimate, flag it with a reasonableness gauge and invite a re-check by a different method rather than supplying the answer.
If the child incorporates the irrelevant number, prompt: 'Which numbers do you actually need here, and which one can you ignore? Why?'

On a genuinely two-step problem (e.g. two successive departures), if the child gives the intermediate result (16) as the final answer, keep both parts of the representation visible and ask 'Have we answered what it asked?'
activities.rationale: Building and using one's own visual representation that maps problem quantities, and modelling a self-questioning monitoring routine, are both reported as strong-evidence levers; estimating and checking by a different method and planning before jumping in are part of proficient problem solving. An estimate slider, draggable bar-model or number-line canvas, staged reveal, and a reasonableness gauge are concrete examples of these mechanisms, not mandatory implementations.
sourceClaims: Teaching students to build and use their own visual representations (e.g. strip/schematic diagrams) that map problem quantities has strong evidence of improving problem solving; modelling a self-questioning monitoring routine also has strong evidence.

The 'compulsion to calculate' — rushing to compute rather than reasoning about knowns and unknowns — undermines problem solving; teachers should push back by focusing on relationships before computing and using numberless word problems.

Proficient solvers analyse givens, constraints and goals, plan a solution pathway rather than jumping in, monitor and change course if necessary, and check answers with a different method asking 'Does this make sense?'.
learnerActions: Meet a problem revealed a piece at a time: first the story, then the question, then the numbers (a staged, numberless-to-numbered reveal).
Build your OWN representation by dragging parts onto a canvas to map the known parts to the unknown — a bar/strip diagram, or a number line to show the jumps — rather than using a pre-made diagram.

Identify and physically set aside the irrelevant number. For example, in 'There are 24 children and 3 teachers; 8 children go home. How many children are left?' the 3 teachers are not needed (this one is a single step, 24 − 8 = 16, chosen to practise spotting a red herring).

Practise the sequencing on a genuinely two-step version, e.g. '8 children go home in the morning and 6 more go home at lunch; how many are left?' — here finding 16 is only step one (24 − 8), and 10 is the answer (16 − 6).
Before computing, set an estimate ('about how big will the answer be?') to create a reasonableness benchmark.

Compute, then compare the answer to your own estimate; when the answer lands far from the estimate, re-check — did you stop after step one, use the spare number, or (in problems where order matters) do the steps in the wrong order?
Return to the still-visible model to complete or fix the second step.
activities.intendedInsight: Planning, relevance-sorting, and self-checking become things the child does and watches on a live representation, rather than rules they are told. Keeping the whole situation visible helps the child notice when they have stopped after step one on multi-step problems, and comparing to a self-made estimate can make an unreasonable answer stand out.

activities.title: Planning dialogue with a 'detective partner' that models self-questioning
feedback: The partner helps plan a pathway without giving the steps away, and explicitly asks which information is a red herring.
If the child stalls, the partner suggests representing the problem a different way and names strategy-switching as normal, not failure.
Always prompt an estimate before computing and a 'does this make sense?' check at the end.
activities.rationale: Modelling a self-questioning monitoring routine has strong evidence, and proficient solvers plan a pathway, monitor, and check with a different method; a conversational partner can rehearse exactly this talk. Dialogue is one route to the routine; it does not replace the child building their own representation.
sourceClaims: Teaching students to build and use their own visual representations (e.g. strip/schematic diagrams) that map problem quantities has strong evidence of improving problem solving; modelling a self-questioning monitoring routine also has strong evidence.

Proficient solvers analyse givens, constraints and goals, plan a solution pathway rather than jumping in, monitor and change course if necessary, and check answers with a different method asking 'Does this make sense?'.
learnerActions: Work with an in-role partner who models self-questioning aloud and asks you to answer: 'What do I know? What must I find? What shall I do first? Does that make sense?'
Say which information is needed and which is a red herring, and justify your plan aloud before computing.
Before computing, estimate ('about how big should the answer be?'), then close every problem by sense-checking the result against that estimate.
When your first approach stalls, try 'let's show it another way' — represent the problem differently (for example, swap a bar model for a number line) rather than abandoning it.
activities.intendedInsight: Rehearsing the monitoring routine in talk — planning the pathway, naming relevant versus irrelevant information, and sense-checking — builds the habit of reasoning about structure before numbers.

activities.title: Worked-example companion: reveal a good solver's self-questions and why a number was ignored
feedback: Each revealed phase names the self-question and the reason, not just the arithmetic step.
Follow with a problem the child plans themselves so the worked example is a model, not the whole task.
activities.rationale: A worked example can make the self-questioning and relevance-sorting frame visible. This is a scaffold: because the child watches rather than plans, it must be paired with the child doing their own planning and representation to build the skill; recognition of a good solver's moves does not by itself elicit the child's own production.
sourceClaims: Teaching students to build and use their own visual representations (e.g. strip/schematic diagrams) that map problem quantities has strong evidence of improving problem solving; modelling a self-questioning monitoring routine also has strong evidence.
learnerActions: Work through a tap-to-reveal worked two-step problem, uncovering each phase: understand → plan → solve → check.
At each phase, reveal the self-question a good solver asks and why the irrelevant number was ignored.
After viewing, retell the plan in your own words and then try a fresh problem where YOU do the planning and relevance-sorting.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing the plan-then-check frame and the reasoning for discarding a spare number makes the usually-invisible monitoring moves explicit before the child performs them independently.

activities.title: 'Which answer is unreasonable, and why?' judgement item
feedback: Credit the reasoning ('smaller than the start because some left'), not just the verdict.
If the child cannot say why, prompt an estimate first: 'About how big should it be?'
activities.rationale: A reasonableness-judgement item targets the 'does this make sense?' check. A recognition/judgement format can be used during teaching to surface reasoning, but on its own it does not elicit the child's independent planning or construction of a representation, so use it sparingly and avoid a battery of two-step sums.
sourceClaims: Proficient solvers analyse givens, constraints and goals, plan a solution pathway rather than jumping in, monitor and change course if necessary, and check answers with a different method asking 'Does this make sense?'.

The 'compulsion to calculate' — rushing to compute rather than reasoning about knowns and unknowns — undermines problem solving; teachers should push back by focusing on relationships before computing and using numberless word problems.
learnerActions: Read a 'take away' story and an offered answer that is larger than the starting amount.
Decide whether the answer is reasonable, and explain WHY using the situation (e.g. 'fewer than 24 should be left because some children went home').
Where possible, state roughly how big the answer should be before judging it.
activities.intendedInsight: Judging reasonableness against the situation — not re-computing — rehearses the estimate-and-sense-check habit and can surface the compulsion-to-calculate pattern.

activities.title: Replace keyword cues with problem-structure reasoning
feedback: If the child picks an operation from a word, ask them to retell the situation and build the strip diagram first.
Discuss explicitly why a cue word pointed the wrong way in the trap problem.
activities.rationale: The keyword strategy ties a word to an operation without understanding the text and is unreliable because keywords are not exclusive to one operation; teaching problem structure (schema) is the recommended replacement.
sourceClaims: The keyword strategy ties a word to an operation without understanding the text and should be replaced by teaching problem structure (schema); it is unreliable because keywords are not exclusive to one operation.

Teaching students to build and use their own visual representations (e.g. strip/schematic diagrams) that map problem quantities has strong evidence of improving problem solving; modelling a self-questioning monitoring routine also has strong evidence.
learnerActions: Retell a word problem in your own words before touching any numbers.
Decide the operation from the problem's structure (part-part-whole, comparison/'more than', two-step change), not from a cue word.
Map the relevant quantities onto a part-part-whole or comparison bar so the structure, not a keyword, drives the plan.
Test a trap problem where a 'more than' phrase does not mean 'add', to see that keywords are unreliable.
activities.intendedInsight: Keywords are not tied to one operation; reasoning from the problem's structure (schema) is more reliable than grabbing an operation from a cue word.

constraints: This is guided problem solving: at 6-7 the teacher scaffolds by modelling self-questioning and keeping the whole situation visible; holding both steps of a two-step problem in mind is still emerging.
Include at least one irrelevant number so 'identify relevant information' is actually exercised, not assumed.

When illustrating multi-step work and stop-after-step-one, use a genuinely two-step problem (two operations); a single-operation problem with a distractor exercises relevance-sorting but not step sequencing.
Build-your-own representations are the target; being handed a pre-made diagram or watching a worked example are scaffolds and must be followed by the child planning and building independently.
Avoid teaching keyword rules; reason from problem structure instead.

Scoring final answers rewards fast computing and does not assess planning, relevance-sorting, or reasonableness reasoning. A reasonableness-judgement item can be used during teaching, but a battery of two-step sums should be avoided and recognition-only items do not elicit independent construction of a plan or representation.
When a child solves only the first step, do not simply supply step two or drill two-step sums; keep both parts represented and ask 'have we answered what it asked?'
When a child computes with no check, make an estimate the opening move and 'does this make sense?' the closing move, and check by a different method.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original row's canonical example ('24 children, 3 teachers, 8 go home → 16 left') is labelled a two-step problem but is a single operation (24 − 8) with a distractor. It is retained to practise relevance-sorting, and a genuinely two-step variant (two successive departures, 24 − 8 − 6 = 10) was added so the stop-after-step-one feedback is coherent.

Worked arithmetic check: 24 − 8 = 16; in the two-step variant 16 − 6 = 10; both results are less than 24, consistent with 'some went home'. The original framing 'a bit less than 24' is a loose estimate; the essential reasonableness check is 'fewer than 24'.

The carpenter counterexample (4 planks, each 1 metre, how many half-metre pieces) correctly yields 8 pieces (4 metres ÷ 0.5 m); it is intended to test situation reasoning versus number-combining, so keep it as a discussion probe, not a scored item.

Worked-example and reasonableness-judgement items were reframed from the legacy 'quiz/interactive-image can only assess' phrasing to narrow objective limits: a recognition or judgement format can support teaching but does not on its own elicit independent planning; no comparative-efficacy claim is asserted beyond the cited sources.

The legacy '3-D adds nothing / no pedagogical return' claim was dropped as catalog boilerplate rather than migrated as a universal law; planning a pathway is simply not a spatial task, so a 3-D manipulative is not indicated here, but no universal necessity claim is made.

The number line for two-step jumps was reinstated as an explicit alternative representation in the workspace and dialogue activities, since it is a distinct keyRepresentation and objective evidence point in the original row.
The WWC strong-evidence claims are drawn from a Grades 4-8 guide; applying them to 6-7 year olds is a research-informed extension not directly evidenced for this age band.

probeDeeper: 'Which numbers do you actually need here, and which one can you ignore? Why?' (forces relevance reasoning)
'You found 16 after one step — have we answered the whole question yet?' (surfaces the stop-after-step-one signature)
'About how big should the answer be, before you work it out exactly?' (estimate as a reasonableness benchmark)
Counterexample: 'A carpenter has 4 planks. Each is a metre long. How many half-metre pieces can she cut?' — does the child reason about the situation, or just combine the numbers?
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for a child who identifies the relevant numbers (24 and 8) and sets aside the 3 teachers as not needed, plans a pathway (start with 24, take away 8), estimates it will be 'a bit less than 24', gets 16, and checks it makes sense (fewer than 24 because some went home). The planning, relevance-sorting and reasonableness talk are the targets, not the subtraction itself.

errorPatterns.pattern: Solves only the first step of a two-step problem — stops once one operation is done, treating the multi-step problem as single-step.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT simply supply step two or drill two-step sums. Keep the whole situation represented (a bar model showing both parts) so the unfinished second step stays visible; ask 'have we answered what it asked?' It consolidates with guided exposure.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a two-step problem the child produces the intermediate result as the final answer and is satisfied; holding both steps in mind is still emerging at this age.

errorPatterns.pattern: Number-grabbing / keyword: uses every number given (including an irrelevant one) or picks an operation from a cue word, rather than reasoning about which information is relevant.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have the child retell the situation and build their own strip diagram, mapping only the relevant quantities; discuss why the spare number is not needed. Avoid keyword rules.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child incorporates the 3 teachers into the calculation, or chooses add/subtract from a word, ignoring the situation's structure.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compulsion to calculate: computes and stops with no estimate or reasonableness check, accepting an answer even when it is clearly too big or too small.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make estimate-first routine ('about how big?') and 'does this make sense?' the closing move; check by a different method. Help the child notice the feeling of an answer not adding up.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives an answer larger than the starting amount for a 'take away' story and is untroubled; offers no estimate.

responseLevels.gap: Uses all numbers or a cue word; computes with no estimate; answers only the first step or accepts an unreasonable answer without noticing.
responseLevels.full: Plans the pathway explicitly, sets aside the irrelevant number with a reason, estimates the answer's size, completes both steps, and uses the estimate/situation to confirm reasonableness — then transfers the same routine to a new problem unprompted.
responseLevels.partial: Can list the plan and, when prompted, identify the relevant numbers or estimate — but does the steps in sequence without connecting them: does not spontaneously use the estimate to catch an error or notice an unfinished second step unless asked.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give a two-step problem within 100 that contains one irrelevant number, e.g. 'There are 24 children and 3 teachers. 8 children go home. How many children are left?' Before any answer ask: 'How do you decide what to do first? Which numbers do you actually need? Show me your plan.' Then: 'About how big should the answer be — and once you have it, how would you know it makes sense?' Discuss the thinking; do not mark the number right or wrong.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A guided planner reasons about STRUCTURE before numbers: they say what must be found, ignore the irrelevant 3, and can justify roughly how big the answer should be. A child running on keyword/number-grabbing uses all three numbers (or picks an operation from a word) and computes with no estimate; a child who treats multi-step as single-step answers only the first sub-step. The tells are in relevance-sorting and the reasonableness benchmark, not the arithmetic.

pedagogy.summary: The coordinate system is built from two perpendicular NUMBER LINES — the x-axis (horizontal) and the y-axis (vertical) — crossing at the origin (0,0). An ordered pair (x, y) names ONE unique point by two distances from the origin: the first number is how far ALONG the x-axis (horizontal), the second how far UP the y-axis (vertical). The order is a convention that carries meaning, so (2,4) and (4,2) are different points. The dominant error is reversal — reading or writing the pair in the wrong order (y before x, 'up before across'); a second is treating the axes as blank space rather than number lines, so the child counts squares instead of reading the numbered lines and/or loses the origin as the (0,0) anchor.
bestPractices: Build the axes as two number lines the child already knows, laid perpendicular and meeting at 0 (the origin); a point's coordinates are just readings on those two number lines
Fix the order with a memorable rule — 'x is a-cross, then up', 'along the corridor, then up the stairs', x before y — and always read horizontal first
Contrast (2,4) with (4,2) explicitly so the child sees that changing the order changes the point
Read from the numbered LINES, not by counting squares, and anchor every reading at the origin (0,0)
Name and point to the x-axis, y-axis and origin repeatedly so the vocabulary is secure
keyRepresentations: Two perpendicular number lines meeting at the origin, each labelled; the point reached by reading along then up
The 'corridor then stairs' / 'a-cross then up' journey traced from the origin to the point
(2,4) and (4,2) plotted together to show the order matters
A grid with numbered lines (not just squares) to read off directly
commonMisconceptions: Reversal — gives/reads the pair as (y, x): up before across (NCETM: 'putting the y-coordinate before the x')
Treats order as arbitrary — thinks (2,4) and (4,2) are the same point
Counts squares/gaps from the edge instead of reading the numbered lines from the origin (off-by-one)
Loses the origin as the (0,0) start, or thinks the axes are just the borders of the grid rather than number lines

learn.summary: Teach the coordinate pair as an ORDERED address read off two perpendicular number lines (x-axis horizontal, y-axis vertical) that meet at the origin (0,0). The first number is distance ALONG the x-axis, the second is distance UP the y-axis, so (2,4) and (4,2) are different points. Target the two dominant errors: reversal (writing/reading y before x) and counting squares from a grid edge instead of reading the numbered lines from the origin. Core activities use a plotting/journey task where swapping the same two numbers lands on different points; alternatives include a labelled reference grid and a navigator-talk task that each serve a narrower purpose.

activities.title: Along then up: the swapped-pair journey
feedback: If both markers landed in the same place, check whether you moved along the x-axis FIRST for both — the first number is always the across move.
Use 'x is a-cross, then up' or 'along the corridor, then up the stairs' to fix the order.

Read the numbered LINES, not the squares: start at 0 (the origin) and find the line by READING its printed label — the line labelled 4 is the one printed with a 4 — rather than counting squares or gaps from the edge.
If you reversed a pair, re-trace from the origin saying the first number aloud as the across move.
activities.rationale: Plotting both reversed pairs and seeing them land on different points is intended to target the reversal error and the 'order is arbitrary' misconception; starting every journey from the origin and reading numbered lines targets the count-squares/off-by-one error. Fixing the order with a stated mnemonic is a commonly used remedy.
sourceClaims: A coordinate system uses two perpendicular number lines (axes) meeting at the origin; an ordered pair locates a point by distances travelled from the origin along each axis in the given order, with the first number relating to the first axis

Common coordinate error = 'putting the y-coordinate before the x, resulting in incorrectly placed position' from a lack of knowledge of the order or names of the axes; also counting squares rather than numbered lines; remedies = 'x is a-cross', 'along the corridor then up the stairs'
learnerActions: On a numbered coordinate grid (first quadrant), first point to and name the x-axis, the y-axis and the origin. Then start at the origin (0,0) and plot (4,2): move 4 ALONG the x-axis first, then 2 UP, tracing the corridor-then-stairs path and marking the point where the lines cross.
Now plot (2,4) from the origin the same way (2 along, then 4 up) and mark that point too.
Compare: describe out loud where each marker landed and why the two points are in different places on the grid even though they use the same two numbers.
Write a sentence: 'The order matters because ___.'
Check your work: point to and name the x-axis, the y-axis and the origin again, and confirm that both journeys started at the origin (0,0).
activities.intendedInsight: The pair is an ordered address, not just two numbers: swapping the order sends you to a different place, and every reading starts from the origin and is read off the numbered lines.

activities.title: Read it back: name the pair for a given point
feedback: Correct order: horizontal (x) reading first, then vertical (y).
The origin is (0,0) because it is where both number lines read zero — the start of every journey, not the first square.
For 'same or different', (2,4) and (4,2) are DIFFERENT points because the across and up amounts are swapped.
activities.rationale: Producing the pair for a shown point (rather than only recognising it) checks the convention in the reverse direction and is intended to surface reversal and origin-naming errors; making reversal and origin-naming the discriminating cases keeps the items focused on the core convention.
sourceClaims: Common coordinate error = 'putting the y-coordinate before the x, resulting in incorrectly placed position' from a lack of knowledge of the order or names of the axes; also counting squares rather than numbered lines; remedies = 'x is a-cross', 'along the corridor then up the stairs'
learnerActions: Look at a point shown on a numbered grid and state its coordinate pair, saying the across reading first then the up reading.
For a point such as the one at 3 across and 5 up, write (3,5) and complete: '(3,5) means 3 along the ___-axis and 5 up the ___-axis.'
Decide for a 'same or different' pair such as (2,4) and (4,2) and justify your choice.
Point to the origin and state its coordinates, explaining why it is (0,0).
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a point back into an ordered pair uses the same across-then-up convention and the origin as the zero start; naming the axes and origin secures the vocabulary.

activities.title: Labelled grid reference (scaffold)
feedback: Match each label to the move: first number = along the x-axis, second = up the y-axis.
Confirm the origin reading is (0,0) before reading any other point.
activities.rationale: A labelled reference can secure vocabulary and the reading convention, best used after active plotting. Because it is fixed, it supports consolidation but does not by itself let the learner vary the order and see the point change; it is a useful reference, not a replacement for active plotting.
learnerActions: Study a labelled grid where tapping or pointing to the origin reveals '(0,0), where the axes cross' and a point reveals 'along 3, up 5'.
Use it as a reference to check your own readings after plotting.
Name the x-axis, y-axis and origin from the labels.
activities.intendedInsight: A clearly labelled grid consolidates the vocabulary (x-axis, y-axis, origin) and the along-then-up reading as a reference.

activities.title: Navigator talk: give the pair before I move (alternative)
feedback: If the navigator does not reach your target, check that your first number is the across amount.
Say the order aloud: 'across first, then up.'
activities.rationale: A talk-based task may surface the reversal misconception through explanation and self-correction; it complements, rather than replaces, plotting on the grid where the effect of the order is seen directly.
sourceClaims: Common coordinate error = 'putting the y-coordinate before the x, resulting in incorrectly placed position' from a lack of knowledge of the order or names of the axes; also counting squares rather than numbered lines; remedies = 'x is a-cross', 'along the corridor then up the stairs'
learnerActions: Direct a navigator to a target point you have been shown by giving its coordinate pair, saying the across move first; the navigator moves exactly as told (first number across, second number up), so check whether it reaches the target.
When the navigator asks 'across or up first?', answer and explain before it moves.
Re-state a pair correctly if the navigator queries the order.
activities.intendedInsight: Because the navigator always moves the first number across and the second number up, a reversed pair sends it to a different point than the target, which is intended to make the reversal error audible and visible and to prompt self-correction.

constraints: This microtopic is a first-quadrant, 2-D coordinate idea; a third axis is a much later topic and would distract from the ordered-pair convention here.

Recognition/matching items (which point is (3,5)?) check the convention but do not require the learner to construct the pair or watch the order change the point; pair them with plotting or spoken production.

A labelled reference grid is a consolidation scaffold: it is fixed, so the learner cannot themselves vary the order on it — use it after active work; this is a limitation of that one reference, not a claim that fixed images cannot teach.
Always read from the numbered lines and anchor at the origin (0,0); counting squares/gaps from a grid edge invites off-by-one errors.
If a learner cannot name x-axis/y-axis/origin at all, reteach that prerequisite (naming the axes and establishing the origin as (0,0)) before coordinate reading.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One cited source (National Curriculum in England mathematics programmes of study) is marked verified:false in the row; treat the Year 5/Year 6 placement detail as unconfirmed.

The original 'read-mode' interactive, the animated along-then-up trail, the side-by-side (2,4)/(4,2) comparison toggle, and tap-to-reveal labels are preserved as optional interaction/feedback examples, not mandatory mechanisms.

The source's framing that a static reference 'cannot test the order for themselves' is retained only as a scoped limitation (it is fixed), not as a claim that fixed images cannot teach the convention.

Independent re-review confirmed the two previously flagged items (feedback line-labelling risk and navigator-insight efficacy overclaim) are resolved; no learner-facing contradictions or unsupported categorical claims remain.

probeDeeper: Point to the origin. What are its coordinates, and why (0,0)?
In (2,4), what does the 2 tell you to do, and what does the 4 tell you?
If I gave you (4,2) instead, would the point be in the same place? Show me.
Which axis is the x-axis — and does the first number go with it or the second?
assess.correctAnswer: A is (2,4) and B is (4,2) — they are DIFFERENT points. In each pair the first number is the distance ALONG the x-axis (horizontal) from the origin and the second is the distance UP the y-axis (vertical); because the order is swapped, A is 2 across and 4 up while B is 4 across and 2 up, so they land in different places.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reversal — reads/writes the pair as (y,x): up before across
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fix the order with 'x is a-cross, then up' / 'along the corridor then up the stairs'; always read horizontal first (NCETM). Reteach in place — the order convention is the core of this topic.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives A as (4,2), or reads B as (2,4); on the reason tier says the first number is 'how far up'

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats order as arbitrary — thinks (2,4) and (4,2) name the same point
errorPatterns.nextMove: Plot both together so the child sees two different squares; stress that the pair is an ordered address, not a set of two numbers.
errorPatterns.distractor: A and B are the same point
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says A and B are the same, or that 'it doesn't matter which way round the numbers go'

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts squares/gaps from the edge instead of reading the numbered lines from the origin (off-by-one)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Read the numbered LINES and anchor at the origin (0,0) — the origin is the zero start, not the first square.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reads A as one out (e.g. (3,5) or (1,3)) by counting squares rather than lines, or by starting the count at 1 instead of 0

errorPatterns.pattern: Loses the origin / treats the axes as borders — starts counting from a grid corner rather than (0,0), or cannot name x-axis/y-axis/origin
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish the origin as (0,0) where the two number lines cross; name and point to the x-axis, y-axis and origin before reading any point.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Counts from the top-left or a grid corner; cannot point to the origin or name the axes

responseLevels.gap: Reverses the pair, or says (2,4) and (4,2) are the same point; counts squares from a grid corner; cannot name the axes or the origin.
responseLevels.full: Reads (2,4) and (4,2) as different points, explains the first number as distance along the x-axis and the second as up the y-axis from the origin, names the x-axis/y-axis/origin, and reads from the numbered lines anchored at (0,0).
responseLevels.partial: Reads a point correctly in a standard case and names the axes, but reverses under pressure, reads by counting squares (off-by-one), or is shaky on why the origin is (0,0) — has the procedure without the ordered-address concept.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: On a coordinate grid, mark point A at (2,4). Ask: 'What are the coordinates of A?' Then plot a second point B at (4,2) and ask: 'And what about B? Are A and B the same point or different — and how do you know? What does each number in the pair tell you?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A and B are reversals of each other, so a child who reads the order correctly gives (2,4) and (4,2) and calls them different, explaining across-then-up; a child who reverses gives A as (4,2); a child who thinks order is arbitrary says A and B are the same point. Each faulty route lands on a distinct, identifiable answer, and the reason tier ('what does each number tell you?') separates a correct-by-luck reading from real understanding.
