pedagogy.summary: Mentally adding or subtracting ones to a three-digit number rests on one insight: only the ones digit changes, UNLESS the calculation bridges a ten (then the tens digit changes too, and possibly the hundreds). Children apply their secure within-20 bonds at the end of a larger number, keeping the hundreds and tens as an untouched 'anchor'. It is taught with place-value apparatus and a number line so the local change is visible against the stable larger part.
bestPractices: Anchor the hundreds/tens and operate only on the ones — 345+7 keeps '34_' fixed and works 5+7
Reuse within-20 make-ten bonds for the bridging cases (345+7 = 345+5+2 = 350+2)
Contrast a non-bridging case (345+3) with a bridging case (345+7) so the child notices when more than the ones digit changes
Use a marked number line / hundred-square segment to show the small jump near a decade
Ask the child to predict which digits will change before calculating (DfE evidence: explain that only the ones digit changes unless bridging)
keyRepresentations: Place-value chart / Gattegno chart (only the ones row moves; bridging cascades)
Number line segment around the nearest ten
Base-ten blocks (add/remove ones, exchange at the ten)
Bead string near a decade
Partitioning jotting (345 = 340 + 5)
commonMisconceptions: Changing the wrong digit (adding the ones to the tens or hundreds digit)
Failing to bridge: 345+7 given as 342 or 3412 (keeps 2, drops the extra ten) instead of 352
Smaller-from-larger on the ones when subtracting bridges down (462−5 given as 463: does 5−2)
Believing 'only the ones digit ever changes', so bridging cases are mishandled

learn.summary: Year 3 pupils mentally add or subtract ones to a three-digit number. The core insight: only the ones digit changes UNLESS the calculation bridges a ten, in which case the tens digit (and possibly the hundreds) also changes. Children anchor the hundreds and tens as a stable 'larger part' and operate only on the ones, reusing secure within-20 make-ten bonds for the bridging cases. Contrasting a non-bridging case directly with a bridging case is what refines the rough rule 'only the ones change' into the accurate 'only the ones change unless we cross a ten'.

activities.title: Anchor the larger part, spin only the ones
feedback: If the child changes the wrong digit (e.g. gives 345+3 as 375, adding to the tens): re-anchor with the chart — the 3 is three ones, so it joins the ones. Name the value of each digit before adding.
Reinforce by asking which column the added amount belongs to, every time, until anchoring is automatic.
activities.rationale: Anchoring the larger part and operating only on the ones makes the local nature of the change explicit; naming place value directly counters the wrong-digit error. A coded or physical chart where only the ones row moves makes this concrete, while base-ten blocks, a bead string or a partitioning jotting (345 = 340 + 5) show the same stable-anchor idea in other media.
learnerActions: Show 345 on a place-value chart (e.g. a Gattegno chart) with the hundreds, tens and ones rows visible.
Work 345 + 3: change only the ones from 5 to 8, keeping '34_' fixed, and say aloud which digits stayed the same and which changed.
Name the value of each digit before adding (the 3 you add is three ones, so it joins the ones), to guard against adding to the wrong column.
Predict, before calculating, which digits will change.
activities.intendedInsight: A change to the ones stays local: the hundreds and tens act as an untouched anchor, so for a non-bridging case only the ones digit moves.

activities.title: Bridge a ten with make-ten bonds
feedback: If the child fails to bridge (e.g. 345+7 given as 342, keeping the 2 and dropping the extra ten, or strings digits as 3412): rebuild with make-ten on the number line — 345 to 350, then +2 — and connect it to the within-20 bond they already know.
Highlight that keeping the tens digit at 4 cannot be right because the answer passed 350.
activities.rationale: Bridging reuses within-ten make-ten bonds, and multiple representations (number line, hundred-square, place value, symbolic) connect the mental strategy. Showing the ones filling to the decade then the remainder makes visible why the tens digit moves. The cascading chart and number-line toggle are optional illustrations of the mechanism, not required apparatus.
sourceClaims: Bridging a ten reuses within-ten 'make ten' bonds; multiple representations (number line, place value, symbolic) connect the mental strategy.
learnerActions: Work 345 + 7 on a marked number line (or a hundred-square segment near the decade): jump +5 to land on 350, then +2 more to reach 352.
Connect this to the within-20 bond already known: split 7 into 5 + 2, so 345 + 7 = 345 + 5 + 2.
Notice the moment the tens digit changes (4 becomes 5 as you cross 350) — this is the exception to 'only the ones change'.
Optionally watch a place-value chart where the ones roll past 9 and cascade a carry of +1 into the tens, with a number-line toggle showing the same jump onto 350 then stepping to 352.
activities.intendedInsight: When a calculation crosses a ten, the ones 'fill up' to the next decade and the tens digit also changes; make-ten bonds the child already knows handle the split.

activities.title: Contrast non-bridging and bridging side by side
feedback: If the child insists only the ones can ever change, point to the bridging case where the tens visibly moved past a decade, and ask them to re-predict.
Praise correct predictions that name the crossing of a ten as the reason the tens digit changes.
activities.rationale: Contrasting a non-bridging case with a bridging case isolates exactly when more than the ones digit changes, which is the heart of this skill. Prediction-before-calculation surfaces the misconception for discussion. Rapid mixed items can rehearse and check the skill but mainly confirm rather than build the insight.
learnerActions: Place 345 + 3 and 345 + 7 next to each other and predict, for each, which digits will change before calculating.
Calculate both, then state which digits actually changed and why they differed.
Articulate the refined rule: 'only the ones change, unless we cross a ten'.
Try a mixed set of items sorted by whether they bridge, predicting each time.
activities.intendedInsight: Directly comparing a case where only the ones change with one that bridges turns the rough rule into the accurate rule and exposes the 'only the ones ever change' overgeneralisation.

activities.title: Bridge downwards when subtracting
feedback: If the child does 'five take two is three' and gives 463 (subtracting the smaller from the larger within the column): show on the number line that 462 − 5 must move down past 460 — take 2 to reach 460, then 3 more. Sanity-check that subtracting makes the number smaller.
Reinforce the direction check as the first move on any subtraction that bridges.
activities.rationale: The smaller-from-larger error can produce an answer larger than the start, as with 462 − 5 → 463, though not always (464 − 7 → 463). A number-line model travelling down past the decade corrects it. A direction check, plus a check that the tens digit dropped, catches it. Answers across the set: 345+3 = 348 (only ones change), 345+7 = 352 (bridges up, tens change), 462−5 = 457 (bridges down, tens change).
sourceClaims: Bridging a ten reuses within-ten 'make ten' bonds; multiple representations (number line, place value, symbolic) connect the mental strategy.
learnerActions: Work 462 − 5 on a number line (or hundred-square segment near the decade), moving DOWN: take 2 to reach 460, then 3 more to land on 457.
Check direction first: subtracting should make the answer smaller than 462, so an answer above 462 is wrong.
State which digits changed (the tens digit drops from 6 to 5) and why.
Thinking aloud, do 345 + 3, 345 + 7 and 462 − 5 in turn, saying which digits change after each.
activities.intendedInsight: Subtracting across a decade moves the number down past the ten, so the tens digit drops. A direction check catches the smaller-from-larger error when it gives an answer above the start (462 − 5 → 463), but it cannot catch every case. Checking that the tens digit dropped, because the answer passed below 460, makes the check complete.

constraints: The target is mental calculation: apparatus (place-value/Gattegno chart, number line, hundred-square segment, base-ten blocks, bead string, partitioning jottings) are scaffolds to make the local-versus-bridging change visible, to be faded as the child calculates reliably in their head.

Multiple-choice or rapid mixed items (e.g. 345+7 with a 342 distractor) chiefly check whether the child bridges and catch the 'only ones change' overgeneralisation; they do not by themselves build the bridging insight, which needs the child to construct and explain the steps.
A static tap-to-reveal chart can show which digit changes but does not let the child follow the carry cascade; pair it with a number line or manipulation if the bridging mechanism is the goal.
Prerequisites: secure within-20 make-ten bonds and confident place-value naming of hundreds/tens/ones digits; reteach these if the wrong-digit or no-bridge errors persist.
Partial mastery looks like handling the non-bridging case and bridging only with a number line or apparatus, not yet reliably in the head, and possibly missing direction on subtraction.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The second listed source (NCETM make-ten bonds / multiple representations) is marked verified:false in the source row; treat its support as provisional.

sourceClaims were trimmed so each cites a source only where it supports the teaching principle: the DfE claim establishes the Year-3 objective/topic but does not support the specific anchoring, contrast or direction-check techniques, so those activities carry []. The NCETM claim is retained on the two bridging activities; note its support for the subtraction direction-check specifically is partial (it backs bridging via number line, not the direction heuristic itself).

The source row's worked subtraction note contained a garbled fragment ('462−52 wait — take 2 to reach 460, then 3 more = 457'); the intended method is take 2 to reach 460 then 3 more to 457. The corrected steps are used in the activity; the original garble is recorded here only.
Self-audit of arithmetic: 345+3=348, 345+7=352, 462−5=457 all confirmed. The distractors named (342, 3412, 463, 467) are explicitly error patterns, not valid answers.
The source claim '3D adds nothing' for this topic has been omitted as a catalog-ranking judgement rather than an established pedagogical law; this rewrite neither asserts nor relies on it.

probeDeeper: For 345 + 3, which digits changed and which stayed the same? Why?
For 345 + 7, why did the tens digit change when it didn't for 345 + 3?
Is your answer to 462 − 5 bigger or smaller than 462? Should it be?
What would 345 + 7 be if it were 345 + 70 instead — which digit changes then?
assess.correctAnswer: 348, 352, 457. 345+3 changes only the ones (348). 345+7 bridges: ones fill to 350 then +2 = 352 (tens digit also changes). 462−5 bridges down: 462−52 wait — take 2 to reach 460, then 3 more = 457 (tens digit changes).

errorPatterns.pattern: Changes the wrong digit — adds the ones amount to the tens or hundreds ('345 + 3 is 375')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor with the place-value chart: the 3 is three ones, so it joins the ones. Name the value of each digit before adding.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The altered digit is not the ones; the child adds to the wrong column

errorPatterns.pattern: Fails to bridge — '345 + 7: five and seven is twelve, so 342' (keeps the 2, drops the extra ten) or 3412
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild with make-ten on the number line (345+5 to 350, then +2); connect to the within-20 bond they already know.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 345+7 the answer keeps 2 in the ones but the tens digit is unchanged, or digits are strung together

errorPatterns.pattern: Smaller-from-larger when subtracting bridges down — '462 − 5: five take two is three, so 463'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show on the number line that 462−5 must move DOWN past 460; take 2 to reach 460, then 3 more. Sanity-check direction: subtracting makes it smaller.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 462−5 the child does 5−2 and the answer is larger than the start, or the tens digit doesn't drop

responseLevels.gap: Changes the wrong digit, or gives 342/3412 and 463; believes only the ones digit ever changes.
responseLevels.full: Answers all three mentally, anchoring the larger part, bridges the ten in both directions, and explains that only the ones change unless the calculation crosses a ten.
responseLevels.partial: Handles the non-bridging case and can bridge with a number line or apparatus, but not yet reliably in his head; may miss the direction on subtraction.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to do these mentally, thinking aloud: 345 + 3, then 345 + 7, then 462 − 5. After each, ask which digits changed. Watch the two that bridge a ten.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 345+3 confirms the child anchors the larger part. 345+7 and 462−5 both bridge a ten — a child who believes only the ones digit ever changes gives 342/3412 or 467/463, while a child who bridges correctly adjusts the tens. The contrast between the non-bridging and bridging items isolates the misconception.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: The equals sign means 'is the same value as' — a statement of balance between two expressions, not a 'do the answer' operator. Includes judging equations true or false (e.g. 7 = 3+4, 5+2 = 6+1, 8 = 8) for ages 6–7.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): supports Y1–Y2 'solve one-step problems... using concrete objects and pictorial representations, and missing number problems such as 7 = □ – 9', which require reading '=' relationally rather than as a signal to compute leftward.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.OA.7 'Understand the meaning of the equal sign, and determine if equations involving addition and subtraction are true or false. For example, which of the following are true and which are false? 6 = 6, 7 = 8 – 1, 5 + 2 = 2 + 5, 4 + 1 = 5 + 2.'
• Operational details: deliberately VARY the equation form — answer on the left (8 = 5+3), operations both sides (5+2 = 6+1), bare identity (8 = 8) — to defeat the 'operator/answer-comes-next' reading. Use balance language and a physical balance model. True/false judging (relational thinking) beats always solving.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (age 6) — judges 4+1 = 5 and 5 = 4+1 both true, and 4+1 = 6 false. Tier B (age 7) — judges 5+2 = 6+1 true WITHOUT computing both sides fully, using compensation. Tier C (age 7+) — fills a missing number to make each side balance (8+3 = 9+□) and explains using 'the same as'.
bestPractices: Read '=' aloud consistently as 'is the same value as' / 'balances', never 'makes' or 'gives you'.
Present equations in varied, non-standard forms early (answer-left, operations-both-sides, identity) so children never fix on left-to-right computing.
Use a pan balance or balance-beam model so equality is felt as physical equilibrium, not a finish line.
Prioritise true/false judging and relational thinking (compensation: 5+2 = 6+1 because one more here, one less there) over always calculating both sides.
Include missing-number-in-any-position tasks (□ = 7−5, 8 = □+3) to force the relational reading.
keyRepresentations: Pan balance / balance beam with equal masses or cubes on each side
Number balance (bucket balance) where hanging weights on numbered pegs balance
Part-whole bar with the same total shown two ways
Double ten-frame showing both expressions holding equal counts
Equation cards in varied layouts with a true/false sorting mat
commonMisconceptions: Reading '=' as 'work out the answer' / 'the total goes here' (operator misconception) — so 8 = 5+3 looks 'backwards' or wrong.
Rejecting bare identities like 8 = 8 as 'not a sum' or incomplete.
In a+b = c+□, writing the running total of the left side into the box (e.g. 8+4 = 12+□ → box = 12 or 12+? = to next), the classic Falkner/Carpenter error.
Believing there can only be one number after the '='.
Thinking both sides must LOOK identical rather than share a value.

learn.summary: For ages 6–7, teach that the equals sign means 'is the same value as' / 'balances' — a statement of balance between two expressions, not an instruction to 'work out the answer'. Deliberately vary equation form (answer on the left like 8 = 5+3, operations on both sides like 5+2 = 6+1, bare identity like 8 = 8) and prioritise judging true/false and relational reasoning (compensation) over always computing both sides. A physical or on-screen balance model anchors equality as equilibrium rather than a finish line.

activities.title: Balance beam: build both sides and watch it level
feedback: If the learner expects a single answer to follow '=', show the beam settling level for 8 = 5+3 and read it aloud as 'eight is the same value as five plus three'.
When two different-looking sides balance (5+2 and 6+1), prompt: 'Both pans hold 7 — one more here, one less there — so they balance.'
For the missing-number pan, name the blank as 'what makes this side the same value as the other', not 'the total of the first side'.
activities.rationale: A balance model makes equality a felt state of equilibrium rather than a rule, letting children test their own expressions and directly confront the operator ('answer comes next') misconception. If a live balance is unavailable, a pan balance with cubes achieves the same targeting; a screen version with draggable tiles and a tipping beam is an optional way to give immediate corrective feedback.
sourceClaims: Children commonly read '=' as an operator ('do the answer') and mis-solve a+b=c+□ by placing the running total in the box; varied equation forms and relational thinking remediate this.
learnerActions: Set an expression on the left pan and another on the right (for example 5+2 on the left, 6+1 on the right) using identical cubes on a physical pan balance (5 cubes and 2 cubes on one side, 6 cubes and 1 cube on the other), or number/operation tiles on an on-screen balance that weighs each side by its value.
Predict whether the beam will tip or settle level, and say why, before releasing it.
Watch whether the beam tips or settles level: with identical cubes (or an on-screen balance that weighs by value), it sits level only when both sides share the same value.
Try a case where the sides look different but balance: put 8 on the left and 5+3 on the right and observe that the beam still sits level.
Try a missing-number challenge: add to one pan to level the beam, e.g. make 8+3 balance 9+□ (the blank is 2, since both sides then make 11).
activities.intendedInsight: The equals sign is the pivot/balance point: two sides are equal when they share the same value, regardless of how each side looks or which side 'the answer' is on. '=' is not a direction to compute leftward.

activities.title: True or false across varied forms
feedback: If a learner calls 8 = 8 false or 'unfinished', say: 'Both sides are 8 — the same value — so it is true. = does not need a sum after it.'
If a learner calls 5 + 2 = 4 + 3 false because 'the numbers are different', have them find each side's value (7 and 7): equal value matters, not identical appearance.
For 5 + 2 = □ + 3, if the learner writes 7 (the left total), ask what the box must be so the right side equals 7; guide to 4, not the running total.
activities.rationale: Judging equations true/false across varied forms is exactly the relational task targeted by this objective, and it consolidates and surfaces reasoning. Missing-number problems in varied positions also require reading '=' relationally. A true/false response format can be used during teaching as well as for checking; on its own, recognition judging does not require the learner to construct and feel the balancing, so pair it with construction and explanation.
sourceClaims: 1.OA.7 requires understanding the equal sign and judging equations true or false, e.g. 6=6, 7=8−1, 5+2=2+5, 4+1=5+2.
Y1–Y2 pupils solve missing-number problems such as 7 = □ – 9, which require reading '=' relationally.
Children commonly read '=' as an operator ('do the answer') and mis-solve a+b=c+□ by placing the running total in the box; varied equation forms and relational thinking remediate this.
learnerActions: Judge whether each sentence is true or false and say how you decided: 6 = 6; 7 = 8 − 1; 5 + 2 = 2 + 5; 4 + 1 = 5 + 2.
Judge 4 + 1 = 5 and 5 = 4 + 1 (both true) and 4 + 1 = 6 (false).
For 5 + 2 = 6 + 1, decide true or false WITHOUT fully computing both sides, using compensation (one more on one side, one less on the other).
Sort a set of equation cards into 'balanced / true' and 'not balanced / false' piles.
Fill a missing number to make the sentence true: 8 = □ + 3 (blank is 5); 8 + 3 = 9 + □ (blank is 2); □ = 7 − 5 (blank is 2).
activities.intendedInsight: A number sentence is true when both sides have the same value, in any layout — identity, answer-left, or operations on both sides — and relational reasoning can decide this without always calculating.

activities.title: Static balance picture to anchor 'the same as'
feedback: If a learner says 8 = 5+3 looks 'backwards', reveal both values are 8 and read '=' as 'is the same value as'.
activities.rationale: A fixed balance picture can anchor the 'is the same value as' meaning and explain why answer-left sentences are true. Because it does not respond to the child's own expressions, it cannot give the corrective tipping feedback of a manipulable balance, so use it as a scaffold alongside hands-on or responsive work.
learnerActions: Look at a level balance with an expression on each pan (e.g. 8 on one side, 5+3 on the other).
Tap or point to each side to reveal its value.
Say why the balance stays level: 'both sides are 8, so they balance — that is what = means'.
activities.intendedInsight: Both sides of a true equation share one value even when they look different; a level balance pictures this meaning of '='.

activities.title: Talk it through: why is this true?
feedback: If the learner rejects 8 = 8, ask what each side's value is and whether they are the same.
If the learner insists only one number can follow '=', offer 7 = 5 + 2 and ask whether both sides are 7.
activities.rationale: Spoken questioning elicits the misconception verbally and builds explanation. Discussion alone does not provide the visual balancing many children benefit from, so combine it with a balance model or construction task.
learnerActions: Answer a partner's or tutor's questions about varied-form equations: 'Is 8 = 5 + 3 true? How do you know?'
Explain why 8 = 8 counts as a true number sentence.
Explain whether 5 + 2 = 6 + 1 is true and how you can tell without adding both sides fully.
Read the '=' sign aloud in words and make a true number sentence with 8 on its own on one side.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating why a sentence balances makes a child's reading of '=' explicit and lets 'answer-comes-next' thinking be noticed and corrected.

constraints: Read '=' aloud consistently as 'is the same value as' / 'balances', never as 'makes' or 'gives you'.
Present answer-left, operations-both-sides and identity forms early so children do not fix on left-to-right computing.
Prioritise true/false judging and relational (compensation) reasoning over always calculating both sides, but still ensure learners can construct and complete equations, not only recognise them.

A fixed balance picture and recognition-only true/false items do not require the learner to construct equations or feel the beam respond to their own expressions; use them as scaffolds alongside hands-on or constructive tasks.

Checkpoints: age 6 — judges 4+1 = 5 and 5 = 4+1 true, 4+1 = 6 false; age 7 — judges 5+2 = 6+1 true without fully computing, using compensation; age 7+ — fills a missing number to balance each side (8+3 = 9+□) and explains using 'the same as'.
Address the running-total error directly: in a + b = □ + c the blank is 'what makes this side the same value as the other', solved by balancing, not by writing the left-hand total.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the running-total error: for 5 + 2 = □ + 3 the erroneous answer is 7 (the left total); the correct value for the box is 4, since both sides must equal 7. Learner-facing feedback here guides to 4, not 7.

Self-audit of worked balances: 5+2 = 4+3 (7=7), 5+2 = 6+1 (7=7) and 8 = 5+3 (8=8) are all true as stated; 4+1 = 5+2 (5≠7) is false as stated; 8 = □+3 gives 5, 8+3 = 9+□ gives 2, □ = 7−5 gives 2; these are consistent.

Two source claims (CCSS-M 1.OA.7 and the Carpenter/Franke/Levi relational-equals research) are marked unverified in the legacy row; the DfE curriculum claim is marked verified. Evidence strength was not re-checked and is carried forward unchanged.

Source claims support the general value of varied forms, missing-number tasks and relational thinking; they do not establish comparative efficacy of any particular medium (balance beam vs. picture vs. discussion). Claims of one medium being necessary were softened to scoped proposals.

Independent re-audit found no arithmetic, logic, or categorical-claim errors requiring correction; evidence-strength uncertainty remains the only open limitation and is conservatively qualified above.

assess.poeTask: Set 5 + 2 on one pan of a balance and 4 + 3 on the other. Predict whether it will tip or stay level, and say why. Then release it and explain what the balance shows about the '=' sign.
probeDeeper: How would you read the '=' sign out loud, in words?
Can a true number sentence have the answer on the left, like 7 = 5 + 2? Why?
Is 5 + 2 = 6 + 1 true? How could you tell without adding up both sides fully?
Make me a true number sentence that has 8 on its own on one side.
assess.correctAnswer: Both are TRUE. 5 + 2 = 4 + 3 because both sides have the value 7; 8 = 8 because both sides are the same value. Reason: '=' means 'is the same value as' / both sides balance — it is not an instruction to write an answer.

errorPatterns.pattern: '= means work out the answer, and the answer goes after it' — so 8 = 8 looks unfinished or wrong.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Read '=' aloud as 'is the same value as'; use a pan balance and present answer-left and identity forms until they stop expecting an answer to follow.
errorPatterns.distractor: 8 = 8 is false because there is no sum to work out.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls 8 = 8 false/incomplete, or wants to write a single number after 5 + 2 =.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Both sides must look the same' — judges 5 + 2 = 4 + 3 false because the numbers are different.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compute the value of each side and show equal VALUE is what matters, not identical appearance; introduce compensation (one more here, one less there).
errorPatterns.distractor: 5 + 2 = 4 + 3 is false because the numbers on each side are different.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says false and points to the different digits rather than comparing values.

errorPatterns.pattern: Running-total error: in a + b = □ + c the child puts the left-hand total in the box.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the balance to name the box as 'what makes this side the same value as the other'; solve by balancing, not by totalling the left.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Given 5 + 2 = □ + 3, writes 7 (the left total) in the box.

responseLevels.gap: Treats '=' as 'answer comes next', rejects 8 = 8 or answer-left forms, and judges by appearance of the digits.
responseLevels.full: Reads '=' as 'same value / balance', judges any form true or false including identities and operations-both-sides, sometimes using compensation rather than full computation.
responseLevels.partial: Correctly judges standard-form sentences and accepts identities when prompted, but still expects a single number after '=' or cannot judge operations-both-sides by reasoning.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: True or false: 5 + 2 = 4 + 3? And true or false: 8 = 8? Tell me how you decided each one.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The operator-misconception child rejects 8 = 8 ('there's no sum to do / it's not finished') and expects a single answer after '='; the relational child accepts both and explains balance. The bare identity 8 = 8 is the sharpest tell — it looks 'wrong' to anyone reading '=' as 'work out the answer'.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 6–7 (Year 2). COUNTING IN TENS FROM ANY NUMBER (not just multiples of 10) — e.g. 7, 17, 27, 37… A place-value insight: adding/subtracting 10 changes only the TENS digit; the ones digit stays the same. The foundation for mental +10/−10 and column place value.
• Standards — UK (DfE): NC Year 2 'count … in 10s from any number, forward and backward'; Year 3 'find 10 or 100 more or less than a given number'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.NBT.5 'Given a two-digit number, mentally find 10 more or 10 less than the number, without having to count'; extends to 2.NBT.8. Directly parallel to the UK statement.
• Operational details: Teach on the HUNDRED SQUARE as a VERTICAL move — straight DOWN a column = +10, straight UP = −10 — so the child SEES the tens digit tick while the ones digit is fixed; contrast with counting in ones (a horizontal move). Use base-ten blocks (add a ten-rod; ones untouched) for the concrete why. Say the rule aloud: 'the ones stay the same'. Practise forwards and backwards from non-multiples (83, 73, 63…).
• Checkpoint: Tier A counts in 10s from a non-multiple forward (4, 14, 24…). Tier B counts in 10s forward and backward from any two-digit number and states that the tens digit changes. Tier C explains WHY only the tens digit changes (one more ten, ones unchanged) and does it mentally.
bestPractices: Teach it as a VERTICAL move on the hundred square (down = +10, up = −10) so the tens-digit change and the fixed ones-digit are seen.
Use base-ten blocks: add one ten-rod while the ones pile is untouched — the concrete 'why' behind the digit rule.
Say the rule aloud — 'the ones stay the same, the tens go up by one' — and test it from many non-multiple starts.
Practise backward (−10) from any number; connect to mental 10-more / 10-less.
keyRepresentations: Hundred square (vertical move = ±10; ones digit fixed down a column).
Base-ten blocks / Dienes (add or remove a ten-rod).
Place-value chart (tens column changes, ones column unchanged).
Number line with 10-jumps from a non-round start.
commonMisconceptions: Changing the ones digit too (e.g. 27 → 38) — not isolating the +10 to the tens.
Only able to add 10 to multiples of 10 (can't start from 7 or 23).
Treating +10 as 'just add a 0' — which fails for non-round numbers (27 ≠ 270).
Losing the column on the hundred square (drifting sideways instead of straight down).

learn.summary: For ages 6–7 (Year 2): counting in tens from ANY number, not just multiples of ten (e.g. 7, 17, 27, 37…). The core place-value insight is that adding or subtracting 10 keeps the ones digit the same while the tens digit changes by one — and at a hundred boundary such as 96 → 106 the tens roll from 9 to 0 and a new hundred appears (backwards, 106 → 96, they roll from 0 to 9), while the ones digit still does not move. This is the foundation for mental +10/−10 and later column place value. It is best made visible as a vertical move on a hundred square (on a standard square numbered from 1 at the top, straight down = +10 and straight up = −10; check the direction on squares numbered from the bottom), with concrete support from base-ten blocks (add/remove a ten-rod, ones untouched). Practise forwards and backwards from non-multiples and say the rule aloud.

activities.title: Down a column, ones frozen — the +10/−10 move on the hundred square
feedback: If a learner recites decade names (7 → 10, 20, 30) and drops the 7: on the hundred square move straight DOWN the column from 7 to show 7, 17, 27 keep the ones digit; name aloud what stays (the 7) and what changes (the tens).

If the ones digit drifts (7, 17, 28, 38): do NOT reteach counting — highlight that the ones column stays the same, using place-value arrow cards or adding one ten-rod each time so the +10-only structure is felt.

If a learner stalls at the hundred boundary (fine to 97, then stuck or says 100, 110): extend the square past 100 and rehearse just the 97 → 107 → 117 bridge, pointing out the ones digit (7) still stays while the tens roll from 9 to 0 and a new hundred appears. Saying 100 means the ones digit has changed, so revisit what stays the same and give more practice crossing 100.

If a learner says +10 means 'add a 0' (27 → 270): compare 27+10 on the grid with the actual answer 37. Show that adding a 0 multiplies by ten, so it never gives +10, even for round numbers (20 with a 0 added is 200, but 20+10 = 30).
activities.rationale: A vertical hop on the hundred square keeps all numbers in a column sharing the same ones digit, so the fixed ones and ticking tens are seen directly. An optional linked panel updating the numeral — ones digit staying lit while the tens change — and a synchronised base-ten rod can make the mechanism concrete, though a printed hundred square with a counter supports the same move.
sourceClaims: Counting in tens from any number is a place-value move best shown as a vertical move on the hundred square (tens change, ones fixed).
learnerActions: Start on a non-multiple, e.g. 27, on a hundred square.
Make a +10 move by dropping straight DOWN one row: 27 → 37 → 47 → 57, saying each number aloud.
Each step of this 27 → 57 run, point to the ones digit (the 7) and say 'the ones stay the same'; point to the tens digit and say 'the tens go up by one' (true while you stay inside a hundred).
Reverse it: make −10 moves by going straight UP one row: 83 → 73 → 63 → 53, saying what stays (the ones) and what changes (the tens).
Watch for drifting sideways — keep the move strictly vertical so you stay in the same ones-digit column.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding or subtracting ten never touches the ones digit; it is the same single downward (or upward) step on the hundred square whatever number you start from. '+10' is not 'add a zero' — it is 'one row down'.

activities.title: Concrete why: add a ten-rod with base-ten blocks
feedback: If a learner changes the ones to make +10, point out the ones pile should not have been touched and rebuild it.
Connect the blocks back to the digits: the number of ten-rods is the tens digit, the ones pile is the ones digit.
activities.rationale: Manipulating ten-rods gives a physical cause for the digit rule, complementing the grid picture with hands-on structure.
learnerActions: Build a two-digit number with base-ten blocks, e.g. 23 as two ten-rods and three ones.
To add 10, bring in ONE more ten-rod and leave the ones pile untouched; read the new number (33).
To subtract 10, take one ten-rod away and leave the ones pile untouched; read the new number.
Say the rule as you go: 'one more ten, the ones don't change'.
Link each action to its numeral and, if available, to the hundred-square move.
activities.intendedInsight: Physically, +10 is just one extra ten-rod; the ones stay as they are. This is the concrete reason the ones digit never changes.

activities.title: Say-it and spot-the-slip practice
feedback: If a learner finds 10 more only by counting on in ones, encourage the direct 'one row down' move instead.
When a learner spots the wrong digit, ask them to correct it and state the rule.
Recognising a wrong sequence is a check; it does not by itself show the learner can produce a correct one, so also ask the learner to generate their own sequences aloud.
activities.rationale: Mixed forward/backward retrieval and error-spotting consolidate the rule and surface misconceptions. This reinforces, rather than replaces, the grid and blocks work where the insight is first seen.
learnerActions: Answer quick questions: 'What is 10 more than 47?' and 'What is 10 less than 47?'
Fill in a tens sequence from a non-multiple, e.g. 4, 14, __, __, 44.
Look at a wrong sequence (e.g. 7, 17, 28, 38) and say which digit changed that shouldn't have.
Count aloud forwards from a non-multiple and backwards from a two-digit number, stating each step is +10 or −10.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent +10/−10 from any starting number, with the ability to notice when the ones digit has wrongly moved.

activities.title: Explain the pattern out loud
feedback: Accept explanations like 'you add one more ten, so the ones don't move'.
For ten more than 96, let the learner use the extended grid to see 96 → 106: point out that the ones digit (6) still does not move, while the tens roll from 9 to 0 and a new hundred appears.
activities.rationale: Explaining the structure distinguishes a child who understands tens-and-ones from one who is reciting a memorised sequence.
learnerActions: Count in tens from a non-multiple, then answer: 'What stays the same each time, and what changes?'
Answer in your own words why the ones digit stays the same each time and what happens to the tens.
Try harder prompts: ten less than 43 (33); ten more than 96 (106, crossing 100).
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to articulate that each step adds or removes one ten — so the ones digit always stays the same while the tens digit changes by one, rolling over into a new hundred at a boundary like 96 → 106 where the ones (6) still does not move — shows place-value reasoning rather than just the chant.

constraints: Always practise from NON-multiples (7, 23, 83…), not just 10, 20, 30 — multiples can be done by chanting decade names without the place-value insight.
Include backward (−10) as well as forward counting; backward from a two-digit number additionally tests subtraction of ten.

State the robust invariant to children: the ones digit always stays the same. The tens digit normally goes up (or down) by one, but at a hundred boundary it rolls over: forwards (96 → 106) it goes from 9 to 0 and a new hundred appears; backwards (106 → 96) it goes from 0 to 9 and the hundred goes. The ones digit is unchanged either way.
A hundred-square counter or screen model shows the move but is a representation; pair it with base-ten blocks for the concrete 'why' when a learner only mimics the grid.
Error-spotting and 'which digit is wrong' tasks check recognition; also require the learner to produce sequences and explanations independently.
Do not teach '+10 means add a 0' — adding a 0 multiplies by ten, so it never gives +10 (27+10 = 37, not 270; 20+10 = 30, not 200).
Keep the move strictly vertical on the hundred square; drifting sideways reverts to counting in ones.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original flagged a 3D representation as 'adding nothing'; this universal comparative claim has been dropped. A planar hundred square is well suited here, but no comparative-efficacy claim against other media is asserted.

The original rated an oral back-and-forth as only 'possible' because the ones-fixed insight is 'best seen on the grid'. Spoken practice is retained as useful consolidation; the categorical claim that the grid is uniquely able to teach the insight is softened to a scoped affordance (the grid makes the fixed ones/ticking tens visible).

The original summary and probe phrase the rule as '+10/−10 changes only the tens digit'. This holds within a hundred but not across a hundred boundary (96+10=106: the ones digit 6 is unchanged, but the tens roll 9→0 and a new hundred appears). Learner-facing text foregrounds the always-true invariant — the ones digit stays fixed — while describing the tens roll-over; the original simplification is noted here only.

The 'number line with 10-jumps from a non-round start' listed in the source representations is not implemented as a dedicated activity; it is compatible but was not carried into the learner-facing tasks.

Arithmetic checked: 27+10=37,47,57; 83−10=73,63,53; 23+10=33; 96+10=106; 97+10=107, 107+10=117; 43−10=33; 4,14,24,34,44 is consistent. Decade-snapping error (7→10,20,30) and ones-drift (7,17,28,38) are preserved as learner errors to diagnose, not as instructions to follow.

probeDeeper: What stays the same each time, and what changes?
Count back in tens from 83 — what's ten less than 43?
What's ten more than 96?
Why does only the tens digit change?
assess.correctAnswer: 7, 17, 27, 37, …, 97, 107… and 83, 73, 63, …, 13, 3 — keeping the ones digit fixed and changing only the tens digit by one each step.

errorPatterns.pattern: snaps to multiples of ten — asked to count in tens from 7, produces 10, 20, 30, ignoring the ones digit and reciting the decade names instead
errorPatterns.nextMove: on a hundred square move straight DOWN the column from 7 to show 7, 17, 27 keep the ones digit; name aloud what stays (the 7) and what changes (the tens)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: drops the 7 and recites 10, 20, 30…

errorPatterns.pattern: ones digit drifts — changes the ones as well ('7, 17, 28, 38'), not holding the +10-only rule
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT reteach counting — highlight that the ones column stays the same, using place-value arrow cards or adding one ten-rod (Dienes) each time so the +10-only structure is felt
errorPatterns.revealedBy: the ones digit wanders across steps

errorPatterns.pattern: hundred-boundary break — fine to 97 then stalls or says '100, 110' wrongly, or can't pass 100
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT treat as a place-value failure — extend the hundred square past 100 and rehearse just the 97, 107, 117 bridge; it comes with exposure
errorPatterns.revealedBy: breakdown specifically at 97→107

responseLevels.gap: Reverts to reciting multiples of ten (10, 20, 30) instead of keeping the ones digit; cannot count in tens from a non-multiple.
responseLevels.full: Counts forwards and backwards in tens from any number, holding the ones digit fixed and changing only the tens, and articulates that each step is +10/−10.
responseLevels.partial: Counts on in tens from a non-multiple but the ones digit occasionally drifts, or breaks at a hundred boundary, or cannot go backwards.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Start at 7 and count on in tens: 7, 17, 27… keep going as far as you can. Now start at 83 and count backwards in tens. (Watch whether only the tens digit changes while the ones stays fixed, and whether they cross the hundred boundary cleanly.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Counting in tens from a NON-multiple (7, not 10) can't be done by chanting the decade names — the child must hold the ones digit constant and move only the tens. A child with tens-and-ones place value keeps the 7 and marches the tens; a child without it drifts to multiples of ten (7, 10, 20…), lets the ones digit wander, or breaks at the hundred boundary. Backward from 83 additionally tests −10.

pedagogy.summary: Angle sum rules are the first place children use angle facts to REASON rather than measure: because a full turn is 360° and a straight line is a half turn (180°), the angles that fill a point must total 360° and the angles on a straight line must total 180°, and vertically opposite angles are equal. The load-bearing idea underneath is ADDITIVITY — an angle decomposed into parts has a measure equal to the sum of the parts (CCSS 4.MD.7). Taught well, the child sees a straight line or a point as a fixed 'whole' (180° / 360°) that the parts share out, so a missing part can be found by subtraction without a protractor. The conceptual jump is from 'measure each angle' to 'the whole is fixed, so the parts are constrained'.
bestPractices: Ground the two totals in turn: a straight line is a half turn (180°), a full point is a whole turn (360°) — connect directly to the degrees-as-fraction-of-a-turn idea rather than presenting 180/360 as arbitrary.
Build additivity concretely: decompose an angle into two parts, measure each and the whole, and show the parts sum to the whole; then reverse it to FIND a missing part by subtraction.
Use the fixed-whole framing explicitly — 'these angles share out 180° (or 360°); if one takes 110° the rest must be 70°' — so children reason instead of reaching for the protractor.
Contrast the two rules deliberately (line = 180° vs point = 360°) so they are not confused; anchor 270° as three right angles and 360° as four.
Derive vertically opposite = equal from the straight-line rule (both share the same partner angle to make 180°), rather than asserting it as a separate fact to memorise.
keyRepresentations: Straight line as a half turn = 180°; full point as a whole turn = 360°
The fixed 'whole' shared out among parts (bar-like partition of 180° or 360°)
Right angle as the 90° quarter unit: two make a straight line, four make a point, three make 270°
Decompose-and-recombine diagram showing angle measure is additive
Vertically opposite pair derived from two straight-line sums
commonMisconceptions: Confuses the two totals — uses 360° for angles on a straight line or 180° for angles at a point.
Angle measure treated as non-additive / not conserved — insists on measuring every angle separately and does not believe a missing angle is determined by the others.
Does not recognise a straight line as an angle of 180° (a straight/half-turn angle 'doesn't look like an angle'), so cannot apply the rule.
Thinks vertically opposite angles are supplementary (add to 180°) rather than equal, confusing them with the adjacent straight-line pair.
Assumes the parts must be equal (splits 180° as 90° + 90° by default) regardless of the given angle.

learn.summary: Teach children that a straight line is a half turn (180°) and a full point is a whole turn (360°), so the angles filling each are parts that share out a fixed whole. The load-bearing idea is additivity: an angle split into non-overlapping parts has a measure equal to the sum of the parts. Once the whole is seen as fixed, a missing part is found by subtraction without a protractor, and vertically opposite angles can be derived as equal rather than memorised. The conceptual jump is from 'measure each angle' to 'the whole is fixed, so the parts are constrained.'

activities.title: The shared-whole angle bench
feedback: If a learner expects the total to change as they drag, pause and point to the banner: the parts trade size but their sum stays locked — that is exactly why one part fixes the other.
When a learner first says 'the other one must be 70° without measuring', confirm this is the key move: 70° is simply 180° − 110°.

In the crossing-lines view, if a learner expects the opposite angles to add to 180°, show the two measures staying equal as the lines turn — the pair that always adds to 180° is the adjacent pair on the straight line; the opposite pair adds to 180° only when the lines are perpendicular (90° each).
activities.rationale: Letting one angle grow as the other shrinks while the sum stays visibly locked makes the invariant-sum relationship concrete and lets the child predict a hidden part rather than be told the rule. A live, draggable model makes the constrained sum observable; a static picture can state the totals but cannot show them staying constant as the parts change.
sourceClaims: Angle measure is additive: when an angle is decomposed into non-overlapping parts, the whole's measure is the sum of the parts' measures; solve addition/subtraction problems to find unknown angles on a diagram (4.MD.7). The whole turn is 360° and degrees are a fraction of that turn (4.MD.5).

The Progressions develop angle additivity from decomposing angles and relate benchmark degrees to fractions of a turn (right angle = quarter turn = 90°, straight = half turn = 180°, full = 360°), the basis for angle-sum reasoning at a point and on a line.
learnerActions: Watch a ray that pivots on a straight line, with two angle wedges filling it; each wedge shows its degrees and a banner reads the running total, e.g. '110° + 70° = 180°'.
Drag the pivoting ray and notice that one wedge swells while the other yields, but the total never moves off 180°.
Say aloud the moment you realise you no longer need to measure the second angle: it is whatever is left of 180°.
Switch to a point version where three or four wedges share 360°, and drag to see the total stay locked at 360°.
Open a crossing-lines view: drag the lines and watch the vertically opposite pair stay equal as everything turns.
activities.intendedInsight: The whole (180° on a line, 360° at a point) is fixed, so the parts are constrained; a missing part is whatever is left of the whole, and vertically opposite angles are equal because each pair shares the same partner angle to make 180°.

activities.title: Hide and predict the missing angle
feedback: If a learner says 'you can't tell without measuring', decompose and recombine first: measure two parts and the whole to show the parts sum to the whole, then reverse it to find the missing part by subtraction.
If a learner answers 90° by assuming an equal split, show the ray redrawn so the angles are visibly unequal yet still total 180° — the equal case is just one of many.
If a learner subtracts from 360° on a straight-line diagram, place a line diagram and a point diagram side by side and re-derive from turn: a line is a half turn (180°), a point a whole turn (360°).
activities.rationale: Predicting before revealing forces reasoning from the fixed whole rather than measurement, and directly confronts the non-additive, equal-split, and wrong-whole errors by making the correct subtraction explicit.
sourceClaims: Angle measure is additive: when an angle is decomposed into non-overlapping parts, the whole's measure is the sum of the parts' measures; solve addition/subtraction problems to find unknown angles on a diagram (4.MD.7). The whole turn is 360° and degrees are a fraction of that turn (4.MD.5).
UK national curriculum Year 5 expects pupils to know angles at a point total 360°, angles on a straight line total 180°, and to identify 270° as three right angles / other multiples of 90°.
learnerActions: On a straight-line diagram with one angle given (e.g. 110°), state the other angle before any reveal and say why it must be that size.
Explain the reason in words: 'the two angles sit on a straight line, which is a half turn of 180°, so together they make 180° and 180 − 110 = 70.'
Repeat for a point where three or four angles share 360°, finding the missing one by subtracting the others from 360°.
Try a case where the ray is clearly not up the middle, so the two parts are visibly unequal yet still total 180°.
activities.intendedInsight: A missing angle is determined by the others through subtraction from the fixed whole; the parts need not be equal.

activities.title: Contrast the line and the point, anchor on right angles
feedback: If a learner confuses the two totals, re-anchor on turn: a straight line is half of a full turn, so 180° is half of 360°.
If a learner marks vertically opposite angles as adding to 180°, revisit the crossing-lines model: the pair sharing a straight line adds to 180°, the opposite pair is equal.
Praise correctly identifying 270° as three right angles and connect it to 360° as four right angles.
activities.rationale: Deliberately contrasting line and point prevents the two rules being muddled, and anchoring on the right-angle unit grounds 180°, 270°, and 360° in a shared quarter-turn benchmark rather than arbitrary numbers. Recognition and sorting tasks give scorable practice; they consolidate application but do not by themselves build the fixed-whole intuition that the live, draggable model provides.
sourceClaims: UK national curriculum Year 5 expects pupils to know angles at a point total 360°, angles on a straight line total 180°, and to identify 270° as three right angles / other multiples of 90°.

The Progressions develop angle additivity from decomposing angles and relate benchmark degrees to fractions of a turn (right angle = quarter turn = 90°, straight = half turn = 180°, full = 360°), the basis for angle-sum reasoning at a point and on a line.
learnerActions: Sort a set of diagrams by which whole applies: 180° for angles on a straight line, 360° for angles at a point.
Tap a straight-line diagram to reveal '180° = half turn' and a point to reveal '360° = whole turn'.
Build the benchmarks: two right angles make a straight line (180°), four make a point (360°), and three make 270°.
Answer practice items that find a missing angle on a line and at a point, including an item that checks whether vertically opposite angles are equal (not that they add to 180°).
activities.intendedInsight: The two totals come from half-turn versus whole-turn; 270° is three right angles; vertically opposite angles are always equal, but they add to 180° only in the special case where the lines are perpendicular (both 90°), whereas adjacent angles on a straight line always add to 180°.

constraints: Ground both totals in turn (straight line = half turn = 180°, point = whole turn = 360°) rather than presenting the numbers as arbitrary facts to memorise.
Derive vertically opposite = equal from two straight-line sums sharing a partner angle, rather than asserting it as a separate memorised fact.

Recognition, sorting, and fill-in items consolidate applying the rules but do not elicit the independent reasoning that predicting a hidden part before revealing it requires; use them as practice, not as the sole check of understanding.
A static diagram can reveal and label the totals but cannot show the sum staying constant as the parts change, so the reasoning move stays told rather than discovered with it alone.
Always include cases where the two parts are unequal, so children do not infer that angles on a line must be 90° each.
Angles at a point and on a line are planar; a three-dimensional setting is not needed and can distract from the fixed-whole idea.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched, and the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The cited standards and curriculum documents support angle additivity, benchmark turns, and the Year 5 angle facts; they do not establish the comparative efficacy of any specific interactive design, so claims of one medium being uniquely able to teach this have been softened to scoped affordances.

The core subtraction (180 − 110 = 70) and benchmark facts (two right angles = 180°, three = 270°, four = 360°) were checked and are correct. The original row's wrong-whole distractor printed '290°' while labelling it 360 − 110; this is an original error, since 360 − 110 = 250°. Neither the inconsistent 290° nor the corrected 250° is reproduced in any learner-facing item here; the wrong-whole pattern is taught abstractly as 'subtracting from 360° instead of 180°.'

assess.poeTask: Draw a straight line with a point on it and one ray up, making two angles; mark one as 110°. Ask the child to PREDICT the other angle and — before any measuring — say WHY it must be that size. Then measure both and add them. The reason given before measuring is the diagnostic part: a child who predicts 70° 'because it looks about right' but cannot say the two must total 180° (a straight line = half turn) reveals the additive straight-line rule is not yet there, even if the number happens to be close.
probeDeeper: 'If I'd told you the first angle was 30° instead of 110°, what's the other one? How did you get it so quickly?' — a rule-holder answers instantly by subtraction; a measurer stalls.
'Now there are THREE angles sitting on the straight line, not two. What do all three add up to?' — tests that additivity generalises beyond two parts.
Counterexample: 'A friend says these two angles must be equal, 90° each. Is that always true? Show me a case where it isn't.' — confronts the equal-split assumption.
'Angles at a point make 360° but on a straight line only 180° — why the difference?' — surfaces the half-turn vs whole-turn reasoning.
assess.correctAnswer: 70°, because the two angles sit on a straight line, which is a half turn of 180°, so together they must make 180° and 180 − 110 = 70. (The reason — a straight line is 180° and the parts share it — is the part that matters.)

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses the wrong whole — subtracts from 360° instead of 180° because the two rules (line = 180°, point = 360°) are confused.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast the two configurations side by side and re-derive from turn: a straight line is a HALF turn (180°), a full point a WHOLE turn (360°); sort diagrams by which whole applies.
errorPatterns.distractor: 290°, because the angles around the point add up to 360°
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 290°, or explains 'angles round a point make 360°' for a straight-line diagram; may give 180° for angles at a point on other items.

errorPatterns.pattern: Angle measure treated as non-additive — does not believe the second angle is determined by the first, so insists it must be measured.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Decompose-and-recombine: measure two parts and the whole to show the parts sum to the whole, then reverse to FIND a missing part by subtraction; frame the straight line as a fixed 180° shared out.
errorPatterns.distractor: You can't tell — you'd have to measure the other angle
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reaches for a protractor, or says 'you can't know without measuring'; cannot compute the missing angle even though 110° is given.

errorPatterns.pattern: Assumes an equal split — halves the whole regardless of the given angle, answering 90°.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that the ray is not up the middle; drag/redraw it so the two angles are visibly unequal yet still total 180°; the equal case is just one of many.
errorPatterns.distractor: 90°, because the line is split into two equal angles
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 90° and justifies with 'they're the same' or 'it's split in the middle', ignoring the 110°.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot find the missing angle without measuring, or uses the wrong whole; treats each angle as independent and gives no valid reason.
responseLevels.full: Gets 70° and justifies it by the straight line being a half turn (180°) whose parts are additive; distinguishes it cleanly from the 360° point rule, transfers to three-part sums and angles at a point, and derives vertically opposite angles as equal rather than supplementary.
responseLevels.partial: States and uses the fact ('they add to 180°') to get 70°, but cannot explain WHY 180° (does not connect it to a straight line being a half turn) and does not transfer to a point, to three-angle sums, or to vertically opposite equality — lists the rules without relating them.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a straight line with a point on it and one ray going up, making two angles. Mark one angle as 110° and leave the other blank. Ask: 'What is the other angle?' — and then, whatever they say: 'How do you know it has to be that, without measuring it?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has only pattern-matched a number can sometimes land on 70°, but the second tier forces the reason: only a child who holds the straight-line-is-180°-and-additive idea can say WHY. A child using the wrong whole says 290° (360−110); a child who doesn't believe the sum is fixed says 'you can't tell without measuring'; a child assuming equal split says 90°. Each wrong route reveals a distinct, documented misunderstanding, and a right answer for the wrong reason is caught by the second tier.

The whole turn is 360° and degrees are a fraction of that turn (4.MD.5).

pedagogy.summary: Children learn to estimate lengths in standard units by building a 'mental ruler' — anchoring a guess to a known referent (a fingernail ≈ 1 cm, a big stride ≈ 1 m, a doorway height ≈ 2 m) and iterating that image — then measuring to check and revise. Estimation comes AFTER hands-on measuring, and research favours explicit strategy (benchmarks, mental iteration) over unstructured guess-and-check.
bestPractices: Teach personal benchmarks/referents (fingernail ≈ 1 cm, hand-span, a stride ≈ 1 m, doorway ≈ 2 m) so estimates are anchored, not blind guesses.
Require a committed estimate BEFORE measuring, so estimation is a real prediction, not a post-hoc guess.
Model the mental-ruler strategy: iterate the image of a unit along the object, or compare it to a known length.
Always follow up by measuring and evaluating closeness ('were you over or under? by how much?') to recalibrate the mental ruler.
Choose the appropriate unit for the scale being estimated (cm for a book, m for the playground).
keyRepresentations: Personal benchmark referents: fingernail ≈ 1 cm, hand-span, stride ≈ 1 m, doorway ≈ 2 m
A 'mental ruler' / mental number line of length magnitudes
An estimate–measure–difference recording strip
Everyday reference objects (an inch-long piece of gum, a metre stick)
commonMisconceptions: Wild guessing with no referent — numbers untethered to any known length, often off by an order of magnitude.
Unit/scale confusion — estimating a book at '20 m' or a room at '300 cm', muddling centimetres and metres.
Not committing before measuring — treats estimation as pointless and reaches straight for the ruler.
Never recalibrating — measures but doesn't compare with the estimate, so the mental ruler never improves.

learn.summary: Children estimate lengths in standard units (inches, feet, centimetres and metres) by building a 'mental ruler' — anchoring a guess to a known referent (a fingernail ≈ 1 cm, a US quarter ≈ 1 inch across, a 12-inch ruler = 1 foot, a metre stick = 1 m, a doorway ≈ 2 m tall) and mentally iterating that image along an object — then measuring to check and revise. The core cycle is: commit an estimate BEFORE measuring, measure, then judge how close ('over or under? by how much?') and adjust the next estimate. Estimation follows hands-on measuring, and research-informed practice favours explicit strategy (benchmarks, mental iteration) over unstructured guessing. The unit and benchmark must fit the scale (cm or inches for a book, m or feet for a playground).

activities.title: Estimate–measure–revise with a benchmark referent
feedback: If a number is given with no basis ('a hundred?') and is wildly off, prompt: 'What could you compare it to? Your fingernail is about 1 cm — how many of those fit along the book?'
If the number is sensible but the unit is wrong-sized (a book at '20 m', a pencil at '15 feet'), ask: 'Is a book really as long as 20 metre sticks? What unit matches something this size?'
After measuring, always ask 'Were you over or under? By how much? What will you change next time?' so the estimate and measurement are related, not treated separately.
When the scene jumps to a large distance, prompt switching referent: 'A fingernail won't help here — what about a metre stick, or a foot-long ruler?'
activities.rationale: After experience with measuring, Grade 2 learners estimate lengths; skilled estimators move between measurements and magnitudes on a 'mental ruler', and research suggests explicitly teaching strategies (iterating a mental image of the unit, comparing with a known measurement) and benchmark lengths rather than relying on unstructured guess-and-check. Committing before measuring makes estimation a genuine prediction, and the compare-and-revise step with a recording strip is what improves the mental ruler.
sourceClaims: After experience with measuring, second graders learn to estimate lengths (2.MD.3). Skilled estimators move between measurements and magnitudes on a 'mental ruler'. Although 'guess and check' can be useful, research suggests explicitly teaching estimation strategies (iterating a mental image of the unit, comparing with a known measurement) and learning benchmark lengths (e.g. an inch-long piece of gum, a 6-inch dollar bill, a metre ≈ floor to a doorknob, 'tall as a doorway') to build mental rulers.

Personal benchmarks such as 'tall as a doorway' build students' intuitions for amounts of a quantity; a combination of internalized units and measurement processes lets students develop increasingly accurate estimation competencies.
Year 3/4 pupils estimate lengths using units of inches, feet, centimetres and metres and check by measuring.
learnerActions: Before measuring, commit an estimate for a given object in an appropriate unit and say how you worked it out (e.g. 'my fingernail is about 1 cm, so this book is around 20 cm').

Anchor the estimate to a personal benchmark — fingernail ≈ 1 cm, US quarter ≈ 1 inch across, hand-span, 12-inch ruler = 1 foot, metre stick = 1 m (check your own stride against it; a child's stride is usually shorter than 1 m), doorway ≈ 2 m tall — and mentally iterate that unit along the object.
Measure the object and compare to your estimate: were you over or under, and by how much?
Record each estimate, the measured length and the difference on an estimate–measure–difference strip, so the gap is visible and comparable across objects.
State what you would change for the next estimate, then try the next object and check whether your estimates get closer.
Work across different scales (book → desk → whiteboard → playground) and switch benchmark and unit to match the scale.
activities.intendedInsight: A good estimate is a reasoned prediction anchored to a known length, not a blind guess; measuring then recalibrates the mental ruler, and the benchmark and unit must suit the object's scale.

activities.title: Interactive estimate-then-reveal loop (optional digital scaffold)
feedback: The revealed gap (e.g. estimate 25 cm, true 22 cm) shows over/under directly; prompt the learner to say how they will adjust next round.
If the slider estimate ignores the ghost referent, prompt comparing against it before locking in.
When the fingernail referent becomes useless at playground scale, confirm the switch to a metre-scale benchmark and appropriate unit.
activities.rationale: An estimate-commit-reveal loop with a benchmark referent and a closeness score across scales may make the commit–measure–revise pedagogy concrete and interactive. The slider, benchmark 'ghost', animated ruler sweep and running score are offered as optional interaction examples that make the feedback mechanism tangible, not as required or proven-superior mechanisms.
sourceClaims: After experience with measuring, second graders learn to estimate lengths (2.MD.3). Skilled estimators move between measurements and magnitudes on a 'mental ruler'. Although 'guess and check' can be useful, research suggests explicitly teaching estimation strategies (iterating a mental image of the unit, comparing with a known measurement) and learning benchmark lengths (e.g. an inch-long piece of gum, a 6-inch dollar bill, a metre ≈ floor to a doorknob, 'tall as a doorway') to build mental rulers.
learnerActions: Set an estimate on a slider for the displayed object and lock it in.
Use a faint benchmark referent shown alongside (e.g. a 1 cm fingernail, a 1-foot ruler or a 1 m metre stick) to anchor the estimate before locking.
Watch a ruler sweep across the object to reveal the true length and the gap between it and your estimate.
Play successive rounds across scales (book → desk → playground), aiming to make estimates closer; switch to a metre-stick (1 m) or foot-ruler referent when a small benchmark no longer fits.
Optionally track a running closeness score to see whether estimates tighten across rounds.
activities.intendedInsight: Repeatedly anchoring to a referent, committing, and then seeing the measured gap makes the recalibration of the mental ruler visible and rewards getting closer over rounds.

activities.title: Benchmark reference cards (supporting scaffold)
feedback: If a learner cannot name a referent for a unit, revisit the matching card and physically check it (e.g. look at a real fingernail, pace a real stride).
Use the cards to challenge unit/scale errors: 'Which card matches something the size of a book?'
activities.rationale: Tap-to-reveal or printed benchmark cards support the referent strategy by making the internalized units explicit and available. This is a reference scaffold: it supplies the benchmarks but does not by itself run the estimate–measure–revise cycle, so it is best used alongside actual measuring.
sourceClaims: Personal benchmarks such as 'tall as a doorway' build students' intuitions for amounts of a quantity; a combination of internalized units and measurement processes lets students develop increasingly accurate estimation competencies.
learnerActions: Study benchmark cards linking a unit to a vivid referent: fingernail ≈ 1 cm, US quarter ≈ 1 inch across, hand-span, 12-inch ruler = 1 foot, metre stick = 1 m (compare your own stride with it), doorway ≈ 2 m tall.
Match each everyday object or scale to the benchmark and unit that fits it before estimating.
Keep a benchmark card beside you as a reference while doing the estimate–measure–revise activity.
activities.intendedInsight: Having a small set of well-rehearsed personal referents gives every estimate something concrete to anchor to and helps sanity-check the unit.

constraints: Estimation should come AFTER hands-on measuring experience, so learners have felt real unit sizes.
Learners must commit a real estimate BEFORE measuring; reaching straight for the ruler turns estimation into a post-hoc guess.

Always include the compare-and-revise step (over/under and by how much), recorded on an estimate–measure–difference strip; measuring without relating it to the estimate does not improve the mental ruler.
Choose the unit and benchmark appropriate to the scale (cm for a book, m for the playground); the same referent will not serve all scales.
Benchmark reference cards are a supporting scaffold: they provide referents but do not supply measured feedback, so pair them with real measuring.

A fixed scored slider practice of 'estimate this length' items scored on closeness can exercise and assess the estimating skill, but on its own it lacks benchmark scaffolding and the explicit compare-and-revise loop; add these around it rather than relying on scored items alone.
Recognition-only or score-only formats do not by themselves elicit the learner's reasoning; include prompts for how the estimate was derived.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The UK National Curriculum claim (Year 3/4 estimate and check by measuring) is marked verified:false in the source row; treat the KS2 citation as unverified even though it is retained as a supporting sourceClaim.

Length estimation is a one-dimensional task, so a 3D scene adds spatial load without supporting the mental-ruler strategy; this is a task-fit observation, not a claim that another medium 'cannot teach'. Likewise, spoken discussion can still support estimation reasoning but does not by itself supply the measured feedback that recalibrates a guess. The legacy row's absolute 'dialogue cannot supply the measured feedback' and '3D adds nothing' phrasings are not established by the sources and have been narrowed to these observable limits.

Efficacy of the interactive slider/ghost/score scaffold is untested; sourceClaims attached to it support the underlying benchmark/mental-iteration strategy, not the effectiveness of any specific interaction.

Example consistency check: a book estimated at 25 cm measuring 22 cm is a plausible small gap; a book at '20 m' or '1000 cm' and a room at '300 cm' are used only as misconception illustrations in feedback, never as correct answers.

probeDeeper: How did you get that estimate — what did you compare it to?
You said the book is about 30 cm — is that longer or shorter than your hand-span? Does that seem right?
Your estimate was 30 and it measured 22 — were you over or under, and what would you change next time?
Would you estimate the playground in centimetres? What unit would you use instead, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: The child gives a committed estimate in an appropriate unit BEFORE measuring, grounded in a referent or mental ruler ('the door is about 2 m — a bit taller than me'; 'my fingernail is about 1 cm so the book is around 20 cm'), lands in the right order of magnitude, then measures and judges how close, adjusting the next estimate.

errorPatterns.pattern: Wild guess with no referent: produces a number untethered to any known length, often off by an order of magnitude, and cannot say how they got it.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Teach and rehearse personal benchmarks (fingernail ≈ 1 cm, stride ≈ 1 m, doorway ≈ 2 m) and 'iterate the unit in your head' before guessing; scaffold rather than reteach measuring.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Blurts an estimate with no basis ('a hundred?'), wildly off; when asked how, has no referent to name.

errorPatterns.pattern: Unit/scale confusion: right number sense but wrong unit magnitude — estimates a book at '20 m' or a room at '300 cm', muddling centimetres and metres.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor each unit to a vivid benchmark (cm = fingernail, m = big stride) and sanity-check the unit; more hands-on measuring to feel unit sizes.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Estimate is a reasonable figure attached to the wrong-sized unit for the object.

errorPatterns.pattern: Doesn't recalibrate: measures but never compares the result with the estimate, or says 'close' regardless, so the mental ruler never improves.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build the compare-and-revise habit — 'were you over or under? by how much? what will you change next time?' — across several objects.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats estimate and measurement as unrelated; no reflection on over/under; next estimate no better.

responseLevels.gap: Guesses with no referent and a wildly wrong magnitude, or uses a nonsensical unit, and does not relate the estimate to the measured result.
responseLevels.full: Anchors estimates to referents/mental ruler across scales in appropriate units, commits before measuring, then compares and adjusts — estimates get closer over successive objects.
responseLevels.partial: Gives a reasonable estimate for familiar objects using a benchmark, but the mental ruler is shaky — right for a book yet wildly off for a large distance, or does not recalibrate after measuring.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Point to a few objects at different scales — a book, the width of the doorway, the length of the whiteboard. Say: 'Before you measure, estimate how long each one is — tell me your estimate and how you worked it out — then measure and see how close you were.' Watch whether they anchor to a referent or guess blindly, whether the unit fits the scale, and whether they use the result to adjust.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with a mental ruler anchors the estimate to a known length and lands in the right ballpark with a sensible unit; a child without one guesses wildly (a book at '1000 cm'), uses no referent, or picks a silly unit, and doesn't recalibrate after measuring — all visible in the doing.

Although 'guess and check' can be useful, research suggests explicitly teaching estimation strategies (iterating a mental image of the unit, comparing with a known measurement) and learning benchmark lengths (e.g. an inch-long piece of gum, a 6-inch dollar bill, a metre ≈ floor to a doorknob, 'tall as a doorway') to build mental rulers.
