pedagogy.summary: This is the procedural workhorse of percentages: finding a percentage of an amount (15% of 360) and using percentages to COMPARE quantities. At this age the reliable, meaning-preserving method is to build any percentage from friendly known facts — 10% (divide by 10), 5% (half of 10%), 1% (divide by 100) — and combine them (15% = 10% + 5%), which keeps the calculation grounded in 'parts per hundred' rather than a memorised rule. The second, subtler skill is comparison: a percentage is always relative to its base, so comparing two percentages of DIFFERENT amounts requires calculating the actual amounts, not just comparing the percentages. Teaching should anchor percentages to a 100-grid or bar, drill the 10%/5%/1% building blocks, and force explicit attention to 'percent of WHAT' whenever comparing.
bestPractices: Build percentages from benchmark facts: 10% (÷10), 1% (÷100), 5% (half of 10%), 25% (÷4), 50% (÷2), then combine (15% = 10% + 5%; 35% = 25% + 10%).
Anchor to a 100-square or a bar split into ten 10% chunks so 'parts per hundred' stays visible and 10% of 360 = 36 is seen, not just computed.

Make 'percent of what?' explicit in every comparison problem: a bigger percentage of a smaller amount can be less than a smaller percentage of a bigger amount — always compute the actual amounts to compare.
Connect the three forms fluently — 15% = 15/100 = 0.15 — and check the decimal is placed correctly (15% = 0.15, not 1.5), since misplacing it is a common source of tenfold errors.
Use bar models for percentage-of-amount: the whole bar is 100%, partition and shade to read off the required percentage.
Progress from friendly percentages (multiples of 5) to any percentage, and to a single-multiplier method (×0.15) once the benchmark method is secure.
keyRepresentations: 100-square (each cell = 1%) and a bar split into ten 10% chunks
Benchmark fact ladder: 10%, 5%, 1%, 25%, 50% and how to combine them
Percentage bar model (whole = 100%, shade the required part)
The equivalence triple 15% = 15/100 = 0.15
Two labelled bars of different totals for comparison (percent of WHICH base)
commonMisconceptions: Compares two percentages while ignoring their different bases (assumes 30% off always saves more than 25% off, whatever the prices)
Misplaces the decimal when converting: treats 15% as 1.5 (or 6% as 0.6), giving a tenfold error
Cannot assemble a percentage from benchmarks, or takes 5% as 10% ÷ 5 instead of 10% ÷ 2
Treats a percentage as a fixed absolute amount rather than a proportion of the given whole

learn.summary: Year 6 pupils learn to find a percentage of an amount (e.g. 15% of 360) by building from benchmark facts — 10% (÷10), 5% (half of 10%), 1% (÷100) — and combining them (15% = 10% + 5%), keeping the calculation grounded in 'parts per hundred'. The subtler skill is comparison: because a percentage is always relative to its base, comparing two percentages of DIFFERENT amounts requires computing the actual amounts, not just comparing the percentages. Anchoring to a 100-grid or bar, drilling the benchmark building blocks, and forcing explicit attention to 'percent of WHAT' when comparing are the core moves.

activities.title: Build a percentage from benchmark chunks
feedback: If 10% of 360 is given as 3.6 or 360, return to 'parts per hundred': 10% means one of ten equal chunks, i.e. ÷10, so 10% of 360 = 36. Rebuild the triple 10% = 10/100 = 0.1.
If 5% is computed as 360÷5 = 72, point out that dividing the whole by 5 gives a fifth, which is 20%, not 5%. 5% is HALF of 10%, so 5% of 360 = 36 ÷ 2 = 18.
If the pupil cannot combine, show that 15% = 10% + 5%, so £36 + £18 = £54.

A running total shown as chunks snap together is one way to let the pupil watch £36 + £18 = £54 build up rather than only computing it (an optional illustration of the mechanism, not a required tool).
activities.rationale: Building percentages from benchmarks keeps the meaning (proportion of a hundred) in view and is treated here as the reliable, meaning-preserving method at this age; the equivalence triple and decimal-placement work directly target the documented percent-to-decimal conversion errors. An interactive bar with a live running total is a proposed way to make the build-and-combine action concrete; efficacy of the specific interaction is not established by the sources, which also note that benchmark-then-combine can be inefficient relative to a single multiplier.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils solve problems involving the calculation of percentages (e.g. of measures, such as 15% of 360) and the use of percentages for comparison.

Documented common student errors include converting a percent to a decimal incorrectly (e.g. treating 6% as 0.6) and using inefficient benchmark-then-combine methods; the underlying idea is percentage as a proportion, and translating fluently between percents, decimals and fractions is a key difficulty.
learnerActions: Treat a bar as the whole amount (e.g. £360 = 100%) and partition it into ten equal 10% chunks.
Find 15% of £360 by taking one 10% chunk (£36) and half of another (5% = £18), then combining them to read £54.
Say aloud how each benchmark is found: 10% = ÷10, 1% = ÷100, 5% = half of 10%, 25% = ÷4, 50% = ÷2, and combine (e.g. 35% = 25% + 10%).
Record the matching equivalence each time: 15% = 15/100 = 0.15, and check the decimal point is in the right place (0.15, not 1.5).
Progress from friendly multiples of 5 to any percentage, and later to a single multiplier (×0.15) once the benchmark method is secure.
activities.intendedInsight: Finding a percentage of an amount is assembling friendly known pieces, not recalling an opaque rule; 'parts per hundred' stays visible on the bar.

activities.title: Compare mode: percent of WHICH base?
feedback: If the pupil picks the 30% deal with no calculation, ask 'percent of WHAT?' and have them compute both actual savings on the two labelled bars.
If they compute one base and assume it applies to both, draw attention to the different bar totals and have them compute the second separately.
Two bars of different totals shown side by side, with each discount slice drawn to scale, can let the pupil SEE the 25%-of-£80 slice (£20) come out taller than the 30%-of-£60 slice (£18).
activities.rationale: The comparison is deliberately rigged so the smaller percentage gives the larger saving, which directly addresses the base-ignoring misconception; the underlying principle is that a percentage is a proportion of its own base. Drawing both slices to scale on different-height bars is a proposed way to make the relationship visible; its comparative efficacy over other formats is not established.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils solve problems involving the calculation of percentages (e.g. of measures, such as 15% of 360) and the use of percentages for comparison.

Documented common student errors include converting a percent to a decimal incorrectly (e.g. treating 6% as 0.6) and using inefficient benchmark-then-combine methods; the underlying idea is percentage as a proportion, and translating fluently between percents, decimals and fractions is a key difficulty.
learnerActions: Look at two bars of different totals side by side, e.g. an £80 coat at 25% off and a £60 jacket at 30% off.
First predict which deal saves more, then compute both actual savings: 25% of £80 = £20 and 30% of £60 = £18.
State the result: the COAT saves more (£20 > £18) even though its percentage is smaller, because the two percentages are taken of different prices.
Test the base explicitly: if the jacket had cost £100 instead of £60, recompute — 30% of £100 = £30 would now win — to show that the base matters.
Finish by writing a one-sentence explanation of why a smaller percentage can give a larger amount.
activities.intendedInsight: A percentage is relative to its own base; to compare two percentages of different amounts you must compute the actual amounts, not compare the percentages.

activities.title: Scored practice set with a base-ignoring distractor
feedback: Mark the 'bigger-percentage-wins' choice as a base error and prompt recomputation of both actual amounts.
If an answer is out by a factor of ten (e.g. 15% of 360 given as 5.4 or 540), flag the decimal/place-value slip and rebuild 15% = 0.15.
If the build-up blanks are inconsistent (10% right but 15% wrong), show 15% = 10% + 5%.
activities.rationale: A scored set can check percentage-of-amount and comparison cleanly, and a base-ignoring option is diagnostic; it consolidates and diagnoses rather than being the main place the comparison concept is constructed. Recognition-style items can check whether an answer is correctly classified but do not by themselves elicit the independent build-and-combine construction.
sourceClaims: Documented common student errors include converting a percent to a decimal incorrectly (e.g. treating 6% as 0.6) and using inefficient benchmark-then-combine methods; the underlying idea is percentage as a proportion, and translating fluently between percents, decimals and fractions is a key difficulty.
learnerActions: Complete fill-in build-ups: 10% of 360 = ☐, 5% of 360 = ☐, so 15% of 360 = ☐.
Answer a multiple-choice comparison of two discounts on differently-priced items, where one option is the 'bigger percentage must win' answer.
Use a slider to estimate a percentage on a 0-to-amount scale as a proportional sanity check before computing exactly.
Convert between forms in short items: write 15% as a fraction and a decimal and check decimal placement.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency with benchmark build-up and correct decimal conversion, plus recognising when a percentage-only comparison is wrong.

activities.title: 100-grid reference and shop-context discussion
feedback: If the pupil answers the shopkeeper by percentage alone, challenge with the rigged case where the smaller percentage wins and ask them to compute both actual amounts.

For '15% is 54 — roughly what fraction of 360 is that, and does that seem about right?', prompt a proportional check: 54 lies between a tenth of 360 (36) and a fifth (72), not 540 or 5.4. It is one and a half times 36 because 15% is one and a half times 10%.
activities.rationale: A static grid can anchor one worked percentage as a reference, and a conversational shop context can surface the base question and check reasoning; a conversation of this kind may prompt justification but does not itself drill computation, so repeated practice across cases is still needed for fluency.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils solve problems involving the calculation of percentages (e.g. of measures, such as 15% of 360) and the use of percentages for comparison.
learnerActions: On a 100-square where the whole grid is 360 and each cell = 1% (worth 3.6), reveal 10 cells (10% = 36), then a further 5 cells (5% = 18), then read 15 cells (15% = 54), as a benchmark reference.
Discuss a shopkeeper's competing deals on differently-priced items: 'which saves more?', and justify by computing actual amounts rather than comparing percentages.
Answer probing questions: 'How did you get 10% of 360 — and how do you know it isn't 3.6?'; 'Give me a quick way to find 5%, and 1%, of any amount.'
activities.intendedInsight: The 100-grid keeps 'parts per hundred' concrete, and talking through a real comparison forces 'percent of what?' into the reasoning.

constraints: 5% is HALF of 10% (÷2). It is not the amount ÷ 5, which gives 20%, and it is not 10% ÷ 5, which gives 2%. These are common slips to pre-empt.
Always make 'percent of what?' explicit in comparison problems — a bigger percentage of a smaller amount can be less than a smaller percentage of a bigger amount, so compute the actual amounts.
Check decimal placement: 15% = 0.15, not 1.5; misplacement gives tenfold errors.
The static 100-grid is a benchmark reference, not the main practice: fluency and comparison require the pupil to compute across multiple cases, not just view one worked example.

The scored set consolidates and diagnoses; recognition-style items can check whether an answer is right but do not by themselves elicit the independent build-and-combine construction, so they supplement rather than replace the bar work.

Bar/grid models are representations of proportion; keep the numeric meaning (parts per hundred) explicit so pupils do not treat the picture as the whole method. Percentages and fractions are comparable as numbers (e.g. 0.15 < 0.30) irrespective of any base; it is the actual amounts they produce that depend on the base, so when comparing represented portions use a common whole.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and the interactive mechanisms are optional illustrations of the learning mechanism, not mandatory tools or product features.

Self-audit of the worked numbers: 10% of 360 = 36, 5% = 18, 15% = 54 (correct). 25% of £80 = £20; 30% of £60 = £18, so the coat saves more (£20 > £18) — the comparison is correctly rigged. 30% of £100 = £30 (correct for the counterexample). No arithmetic errors found.

Tension in source claim 2: it describes 'benchmark-then-combine' as an inefficient method and a documented difficulty, whereas the pedagogy recommends it as the reliable Year 6 method. The claim is retained because it also supports percentage-as-proportion and decimal-conversion errors; it is NOT treated as evidence that benchmark-then-combine is efficient or best. Progression to a single multiplier (×0.15) once benchmarks are secure is kept to acknowledge the efficiency point.

Comparative efficacy of the interactive bar over static grid or quiz formats is not asserted; sources establish the curriculum objective and document misconceptions but do not establish necessity or superiority of any medium.

probeDeeper: 'How did you get 10% of 360 — and how do you know it isn't 3.6?' — checks the place-value meaning of 10%.
'You said 15% is 54 — roughly what fraction of 360 is that, and does that seem about right?' — checks a proportional sanity check (15% ≈ a bit more than a tenth).

Counterexample: 'If the jacket had been £100 instead of £60, would your answer change?' — a child who understands base recomputes (30% of £100 = £30 now wins); a percentage-only reasoner does not see why it would matter.
'Give me a quick way to find 5%, and 1%, of any amount' — surfaces whether the benchmark toolkit is fluent.
assess.correctAnswer: 15% of 360 = 54 (10% is 36, 5% is 18, total 54). Coat saving = 25% of £80 = £20; jacket saving = 30% of £60 = £18; so the COAT saves more (£20 > £18) even though its percentage is smaller, because the amounts are percentages of different prices.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares the percentages and ignores the different bases: 'the jacket, because 30% is more than 25%' — without working out the actual savings
errorPatterns.nextMove: Force 'percent of WHAT?' — compute both actual amounts on two labelled bars of different heights; show the smaller percentage taking the bigger slice. Reinforce percentage as relative to its own base.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child picks the bigger percentage as the bigger saving with no calculation, or calculates one base and assumes it applies to both

errorPatterns.pattern: Misplaces the decimal / mis-converts the percentage: takes 10% of 360 as 3.6 or 360, or treats 15% as 1.5, giving a tenfold error
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the 100-grid / 'parts per hundred': 10% means ÷10 (one whole chunk of the ten), 1% means ÷100; check 15% = 0.15 not 1.5. Rebuild the equivalence triple.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The percentage-of-amount answer is out by a factor of ten (e.g. 15% of 360 given as 5.4 or 540)

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot assemble the percentage from benchmarks, or takes 5% as 10% ÷ 5 instead of half of 10%
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach percentages — scaffold the benchmark relationships: 5% is HALF of 10%; 15% = 10% + 5%. A lapse in assembling, not a conceptual gap.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child finds 10% correctly but computes 5% as 360÷5 = 72, or cannot combine 10% and 5% into 15%

responseLevels.gap: Cannot find a percentage of an amount reliably (tenfold errors, faulty benchmarks) and compares discounts by percentage alone, ignoring the base.
responseLevels.full: Fluently builds any percentage of an amount from benchmarks (or a single multiplier), places decimals correctly, and when comparing always computes the actual amounts relative to each base, explaining why a smaller percentage can give a larger amount.
responseLevels.partial: Finds friendly percentages of an amount via 10%/5% build-up for the practised case, but the method is fragile (place-value slips, awkward percentages) or still compares percentages without consistently computing both bases when they differ.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Two things, do them however you like and I'll watch. First, find 15% of 360. Second, two shops: a coat that normally costs £80 has 25% off, and a jacket that normally costs £60 has 30% off — work out which sale saves you more money.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The comparison is rigged so the SMALLER percentage (25%) gives the LARGER saving (£20 vs £18): a child who understands that a percentage is relative to its base computes both actual amounts and picks the coat; a child who treats the percentage as the whole story picks the jacket (30% > 25%) without computing. And 15% of 360 exposes the build-up method and the decimal placement — whether 10% is read as 36 (correct) or 3.6/360 (place-value slip). Watching, not asking, surfaces both.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Use counting on and counting back as strategies for addition and subtraction (8 + 3 by counting on 9,10,11; 12 − 3 by counting back 11,10,9). Ages 6–7, the bridge from counting-all to more efficient calculation.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y1 'add and subtract one-digit and two-digit numbers to 20, including zero' and count on/back; underpins Y2 mental strategies.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.OA.5 'Relate counting to addition and subtraction (e.g. by counting on 2 to add 2)'; a stepping stone toward 1.OA.6 strategies.
• Operational details: teach counting ON from the larger number (start at 8, not 1) as more efficient than counting-all, and counting BACK for subtraction, tracking the number of steps. Best supported on a number line/track so the steps are visible and the child doesn't count the start as a step. This is a transitional strategy — valued, then increasingly replaced by known facts and derived facts.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (age 6) — adds 8 + 3 by counting on from 8. Tier B (age 7) — counts back accurately for 12 − 3 and starts count-on from the larger addend for 2 + 9. Tier C (age 7+) — explains counting on as adding and chooses count-on vs count-back sensibly.
bestPractices: Teach counting ON from the larger addend, not counting all from one, as the efficiency step.
Use a number line or number track so jumps are visible and the start number isn't miscounted as a step.
Track the number of steps with fingers or marks to prevent off-by-one errors.
Model counting back for subtraction and connect it to 'one less each time'.
Treat counting on/back as a transitional strategy — celebrate it, then nudge toward known and derived facts for efficiency.
keyRepresentations: Number line / number track with hops
Fingers used to keep track of the count of steps
Hundred square for later extension
Bead string showing jumps
'Start big, count on' prompt card
commonMisconceptions: Counting all from one instead of counting on from a number (a normal earlier stage).
Counting the starting number as the first step (8 + 3 → 8,9,10 = 10), an off-by-one error.
Counting on from the first-written number rather than the larger one, making more steps than needed.
Counting in the wrong direction for subtraction.
Over-relying on counting for facts that should become instant recall.

learn.summary: For ages 6–7, teach counting on for addition and counting back for subtraction as the efficiency step beyond counting-all. The core skills: start from the larger number (e.g. begin at 8 for 8+3), say the NEXT number as the first count ('9'), and track the number of steps so the start isn't miscounted. Best anchored on a visible number line/track where hops are seen and counted, then gradually replaced by known and derived facts. Target sums: 8+3=11 (count on), 12−3=9 (count back), 2+9 (start from the larger addend, 9).

activities.title: Hop along the number line: count on and count back
feedback: If a child counts the start number as the first step (8+3 → '8,9,10' = 10), point out that 8 is where you START, and the first hop lands on 9 — count the landings, not the starting spot.
If a child starts at 1 and counts everything, gently cover the first group, say '8', and count on from there; this earlier stage matures with number sense, so model rather than drill.
For subtraction going the wrong way, link counting back to 'one less each time' and track the backward hops with fingers.
If a child always starts from the first-written number (2 for 2+9), ask which number gives fewer hops and why starting at 9 is quicker.
activities.rationale: Counting on/back is literally movement along a number line, so a track where hops are visible and counted is intended to make the strategy and the off-by-one error observable, so the child can self-correct. A live track that counts each landing (and does not count the start as a step) is intended to target the classic '8,9,10'=10 slip. Starting-number highlighting, count-on/count-back modes, and a 'start from the bigger number' prompt for commutative pairs are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete. Efficacy of this interaction is a proposal, not a tested result.
sourceClaims: Y1 pupils add and subtract one- and two-digit numbers to 20 including zero, using counting strategies.
1.OA.5 relates counting to addition and subtraction, e.g. counting on 2 to add 2.
Children progress from counting-all to counting-on; counting the start number as a step is a common off-by-one error, and counting-on from the larger addend is the efficiency goal.
learnerActions: On a number line or number track, set the start at the larger number (8 for 8+3) and make three hops forward, saying the number you LAND on each time: '9, 10, 11' — not '8'.
Keep track of how many hops you have made using fingers or marks, so you take exactly three.
Switch to count-back mode for 12−3: start at 12 and hop backward three times, saying '11, 10, 9'.
For 2+9, decide which number to start from and explain why you start at 9, not 2.
Narrate out loud where you start and how many steps you take.
If it helps, show the same forward hops on a bead string; a hundred square can be used later to extend counting on and back to larger numbers.
activities.intendedInsight: Starting AT the larger number and taking just a few hops lands on the same answer as counting everything from one, but is faster; the first count is the next number along from the start (9 for 8+3; 11 when counting back from 12 for 12−3), not the start number.

activities.title: Spaced practice: draw the hops and choose the start
feedback: Watch for an off-by-one answer (10 for 8+3): the result is 11 — recount the landings, not the start.
If the chosen start for 2+9 is 2, note that starting at 9 means only two hops instead of nine.
For 6+2, start at 6 and count on '7, 8' — two hops lands on 8.
activities.rationale: Fixed items give good spaced consolidation but cannot correct the count as it happens, so they work best after the live hopping activity rather than instead of it.
sourceClaims: Children progress from counting-all to counting-on; counting the start number as a step is a common off-by-one error, and counting-on from the larger addend is the efficiency goal.
learnerActions: Draw the jumps on a number line for 8+3 and for 12−3, labelling each landing number.
Answer: 'Which number should you start counting from for 2+9?' and justify the choice.
Fill in results for several count-on and count-back sums (for example 6+2), checking you did not count the start as a step.
activities.intendedInsight: Repeated, varied practice consolidates counting on from the larger addend and counting back accurately, reinforcing where the count begins.

activities.title: Talk it through: why start at the bigger number?
feedback: If the explanation defends counting all from one, model covering the first group and counting on, and ask which took fewer counts.
Praise explanations that connect counting on to adding and counting back to 'one less each time'.
activities.rationale: Spoken reasoning reveals the underlying strategy and lets a tutor probe the counting-all habit; it complements, rather than replaces, watched practice where the procedure is performed and tracked.
sourceClaims: Children progress from counting-all to counting-on; counting the start number as a step is a common off-by-one error, and counting-on from the larger addend is the efficiency goal.
learnerActions: Work out a sum and narrate where you start and how many steps you take.
Answer questions like 'Why did you start at 8 and not at 1?' and 'Which is quicker for 8+3 — counting everything or counting on? Why?'.
Explain in your own words how counting on is a way of adding.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating why you start from the larger number and that counting on is adding surfaces (and helps move past) a counting-all habit.

constraints: Counting on/back is a transitional strategy: celebrate it, then nudge toward known and derived facts so it isn't over-relied on for instant-recall facts.

Counting-all from one is a normal earlier developmental stage; model counting on but do not drill it as an error — children typically move beyond it as number sense grows with experience and modelling.
A static worked number line can anchor what counting on looks like but gives no practice tracking one's own steps, where the errors occur; use it as an anchor, not the main practice.
Recognition/multiple-choice items can check the choice of start number but do not elicit the child independently performing and tracking the count; pair them with doing and narrating.
Watching HOW the child counts is central: the overt count reveals strategy and off-by-one errors that the final answer alone can hide.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Source row flagged the US CCSS 1.OA.5 claim and the Cognitively Guided Instruction claim as verified:false; treat their cited support as unconfirmed even though they are topically relevant.

The original rated a 3D treatment 'poor' asserting '3D adds nothing'; this universal claim is not established by the row and has been dropped. A number line is naturally one-dimensional, which is a sufficient rationale without claiming 3D is universally useless.
Arithmetic checked: 8+3=11, 12−3=9, 2+9=11, 6+2=8; the off-by-one distractor (10 for 8+3) is correctly flagged as an error, not a valid answer.

probeDeeper: Why did you start counting at 8 and not at 1?
Show me on the number line how you got 12 − 3.
Which is quicker for 8 + 3 — counting everything, or counting on? Why?
For 2 + 9, which number would you start from, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: 11; 9; 8. Watch for the child counting ON from the larger number (starting at 8, saying '9, 10, 11'), counting BACK for the subtraction, and NOT counting the start number as a step.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts all from one rather than counting on from a number.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill or correct as an error — this stage self-resolves with number sense; gently model covering the first set, saying '8', and counting on, and let it mature.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 8 + 3, starts at 1 and counts out all eight then all three.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts the starting number as the first step (8 + 3 → '8, 9, 10' = 10).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Start the count on the NEXT number; use a number line and fingers so the start isn't a step. Not a concept reteach.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 10; observed saying the start number as step one.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts back unreliably or in the wrong direction for subtraction.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model back-counting on a number line and link to 'one less each time'; track steps with fingers.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 12 − 3 counts up, or miscounts the backward steps.

responseLevels.gap: Counts all from one, or cannot track the count reliably; frequent errors.
responseLevels.full: Counts on from the larger addend and counts back accurately, tracking the number of steps, and explains counting on as a way of adding.
responseLevels.partial: Counts on/back but with off-by-one slips, or always starts from the first-written number rather than the larger.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these out and show me how you count each one: 8 + 3; 12 − 3; 6 + 2.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching HOW the child counts is the whole test: a counting-all child starts at 1 and counts every item; a counting-on child starts at 8. An off-by-one child audibly counts the start number as step one and lands on 10. The overt count reveals the strategy and the classic error in a way the answer alone cannot.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 11–12 — understand and use place value for decimals, measures and integers of ANY size; extend the number system so all positive/negative integers, decimals and fractions sit on a single number line.
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics, KS3): 'understand and use place value for decimals, measures and integers of any size' and 'order positive and negative integers, decimals and fractions' on one line.
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): 6.NS.C.6 (position integers and rationals on the number line, opposites) and 6.NS.C.7 (understand ordering of rational numbers).
• Operational details: Consolidate the ×10/÷10 place-value structure as UNBOUNDED in both directions — no largest, no smallest place — and unify previously separate representations (whole numbers, decimals, negatives, fractions) onto ONE number line. Stress that every number, however written, names a single point; the line is the common ground where mixed forms can be compared.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 11): 'State the value of the 7 in 4,700,000 and in 0.007.' Tier B: 'Place −3/4, 0.6, −2 and 1.25 on one number line.' Tier C: 'Explain why the place-value system has no largest and no smallest place.'
bestPractices: Present place value as a single unbounded ×10/÷10 structure — no largest or smallest place — rather than a table that stops at millions or thousandths
Unify whole numbers, decimals, negatives and fractions onto ONE number line so mixed forms share a common reference for comparison
Insist every representation (numeral, fraction, decimal) names a single POINT on the line
Convert between forms to a common representation (usually decimal or a common denominator) before comparing across types
Use magnitude/scale reasoning ('the value of a digit is its face value times its place') for numbers of any size
keyRepresentations: Single number line hosting integers, decimals, negatives and fractions together
Place-value chart extended arbitrarily far left and right of the decimal point
Zoomable number line to locate decimals/fractions between integers
Form-conversion cards (fraction ↔ decimal) feeding points onto the line
commonMisconceptions: Thinking place value 'runs out' at a largest place (millions) or smallest place (thousandths)
Treating whole numbers, decimals, negatives and fractions as living on separate scales rather than one line
Placing negatives as if their magnitude sets their order (−3/4 to the left of −2)
Assuming a fraction and its decimal (3/4 and 0.75) are different points rather than the same point
Comparing mixed forms by surface features (digit count) rather than converting to a common form

learn.summary: For ages 11–12: extend place value as an unbounded ×10/÷10 structure (no largest or smallest place) and unify whole numbers, decimals, negatives and fractions onto ONE number line, where every number — however written — names a single point. Learners locate and order mixed forms by position relative to zero and to integer landmarks, recognising that a fraction and its decimal (e.g. 3/4 and 0.75) are the SAME point, and that on a standard (left-to-right) line ordering follows leftmost-is-smallest across all number types.

activities.title: Many forms, one line
feedback: If a fraction is placed by its visible digits (e.g. 1/2 put near the 2), convert it to a decimal or locate it between integer landmarks: 1/2 = 0.5 sits halfway between 0 and 1, not near 2.
If negatives are ordered by magnitude (e.g. −3/4 placed left of −2), anchor zero: on a standard line every point further left is smaller, so −2 < −3/4 because −2 is further from zero on the left.
If 3/4 and 0.75 are placed at different points, convert 3/4 to 0.75 and confirm both describe three-quarters of the way from 0 to 1 — they are literally one point.
activities.rationale: Placing mixed representations on a single line forces a common measure of size and confronts the misconceptions that different number types live on separate scales and that notation digits dictate position. This supports ordering integers, decimals and fractions on one line.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils understand and use place value for decimals, measures and integers of any size and order integers, decimals and fractions on a number line.
6.NS.C.6/C.7: position integers and rational numbers on the number line and understand ordering of rational numbers.
learnerActions: Draw a single number line and place each of these numbers on it: −3/4, 0.6, −2, and 1.25. Then, on a separate zoomed-out view using an appropriate scale, mark a large integer such as 4,700,000, noting that the same ×10/÷10 structure governs both views.
For each number, say in words where it sits relative to zero and to the nearest whole-number landmarks (e.g. '1.25 is a quarter of the way from 1 to 2').
Place 3/4 and 0.75 separately, then check that both land on exactly the same point; write one sentence explaining why they must coincide.

Write all the numbers in order from smallest to largest, treating 3/4 and 0.75 as one point, and justify the order using position on the line, not the digits (−2 < −3/4 < 0.6 < 3/4 = 0.75 < 1.25 < 4,700,000).
activities.intendedInsight: Whole numbers, decimals, negatives and fractions all belong to one number line governed by a single ×10/÷10 structure; each names a single point and equivalent forms name the same point. On a standard (left-to-right) line, size is read as position (leftmost is smallest) across every type, even when very large and very small values must be shown at different scales.

activities.title: Zoom in — is there a smallest place?
feedback: If the line is treated as discrete ('the next number', only a few slots between landmarks), zoom one segment and mark finer divisions to show more and more numbers fit — any fraction or decimal has a place.
If the learner claims place value 'runs out' at thousandths or at millions, point to the column-naming continuing with each zoom: the pattern is ×10/÷10 repeated, with no final column.
activities.rationale: Progressive subdivision makes the unbounded ×10/÷10 place-value structure concrete, addressing the misconception that place value stops at a largest or smallest place; it also illustrates (informally) that the line keeps subdividing so any decimal or fraction has a place.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils understand and use place value for decimals, measures and integers of any size and order integers, decimals and fractions on a number line.
learnerActions: Take the segment from 0 to 1 and subdivide it into tenths; label 0.6 among them.
Zoom into a tenth (e.g. between 0.6 and 0.7) and subdivide into hundredths; place a value such as 0.65.
Zoom again into hundredths and mark thousandths; keep a note of which place column you are in at each step (tenths → hundredths → thousandths…).
Argue in writing whether this subdividing ever stops, and state what that means for a 'smallest place' in the place-value system.
Repeat the reasoning outward: explain why there is likewise no largest place as the ×10 structure grows.
activities.intendedInsight: The ×10/÷10 place-value structure continues without end in both directions — there is no smallest place and no largest place. Informally, between any two points more numbers can always be found, so any decimal or fraction has a location between landmarks.

activities.title: Value of a digit at any scale
feedback: If only the face value (7) is given, prompt for the place: the 7 in 4,700,000 is 7 hundred-thousands = 700,000; the 7 in 0.007 is 7 thousandths = 0.007.
If columns are miscounted on the decimal side, count rightward from the decimal point: tenths, hundredths, thousandths.
activities.rationale: Magnitude/scale reasoning for digits of any size consolidates place value as a single unbounded structure rather than a table that stops at millions or thousandths.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils understand and use place value for decimals, measures and integers of any size and order integers, decimals and fractions on a number line.
learnerActions: State the value of the 7 in 4,700,000 and the value of the 7 in 0.007.
For each, say which place column the 7 occupies and compute face value × place value.
Explain in one or two sentences why the same digit can represent vastly different amounts depending on its place.
Optional extension: explain to a partner (or in writing) why the place-value system has no largest and no smallest place.
activities.intendedInsight: A digit's value is its face value times its place value, and this scaling reasoning works for numbers of any size, large or small.

activities.title: Which is smaller, and why
feedback: Correct ordering: −3 < 1/2 < 2.75. −3 is smallest because it is furthest left of zero, regardless of number type.
If 1/2 is ranked below −3 ('it's less than one'), anchor zero: every negative lies left of every positive, so −3 < 1/2 whatever the digits suggest.
If 2.75 is ranked by '275', relocate it as three-quarters of the way from 2 to 3 and compare positions.
activities.rationale: This diagnostic comparison exposes ordering-by-magnitude-of-negatives and reading-by-digits, and the justification for '−3 smallest' reveals whether the learner reasons by position across types.
sourceClaims: 6.NS.C.6/C.7: position integers and rational numbers on the number line and understand ordering of rational numbers.
learnerActions: Place −3, 1/2 and 2.75 on one number line relative to zero and to each other.
Order them from smallest to largest.
Explain how you know −3 is the smallest, referring to its position rather than the size of the digit 3.
Name a number between 1/2 and 2.75, and then another number between those two, to show many values lie between any pair.
activities.intendedInsight: On a standard (left-to-right) number line, across all number types the leftmost position (furthest below zero) is smallest; a negative can be smaller than a small positive fraction even though its digit looks large. Informally, infinitely many numbers also lie between any two points.

constraints: Learners should construct placements and justifications themselves; multiple-choice or slider checks can consolidate the unified-line idea afterwards, but recognition-only responses do not elicit the independent placing, converting and justifying that evidences full understanding.

When comparing mixed forms, convert to a common representation (decimal or common denominator) or locate each between integer landmarks before ordering; do not compare by surface features such as digit count. Fractions remain comparable numbers; the common-reference requirement is about positioning represented portions consistently.

A static, annotated line showing several forms on one axis can illustrate the unification and is a useful scaffold, but it cannot be re-scaled by the learner, so pair it with hands-on subdividing/zooming when demonstrating that the structure is unbounded and that more numbers always fit between landmarks.

Treat large integers and sub-unit decimals at appropriate separate scales when a single drawn line cannot show both; the point is that the same ×10/÷10 structure governs each, so the unification is conceptual even when two views are used.
The number system here is one-dimensional, so a single line is the correct representation; avoid adding extra spatial dimensions that would misrepresent ordering.

'Leftmost is smallest' assumes the conventional left-to-right orientation of the number line; use that standard orientation and make it explicit rather than treating it as an intrinsic property of the numbers.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the two cited standards were marked verified:false in the source and have not been re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Source value-of-digit example checked: the 7 in 4,700,000 is 700,000 (7 hundred-thousands) and the 7 in 0.007 is 7 thousandths; both are internally consistent and retained.

Ordering checked: −3 < 1/2 < 2.75 and −2 < −3/4 < 0.6 < 1.25 < 4,700,000 are correct; the source's own stated misconception 'placing −3/4 left of −2' is correctly treated as an error to correct, not taught.

The subdividing/zoom demonstration illustrates (does not formally prove) the unbounded place-value structure and that numbers always lie between any two points; density is a true mathematical property but is not attributed to the cited standards, which support ordering and place value rather than density.
Optional interaction examples (zoomable/subdividing line, slider placement, snapping equivalent forms to one point, place-value read-out) are preserved as illustrative, not mandatory mechanisms.

probeDeeper: Why is −3 to the left of 1/2 when 3 is bigger than a half?
How did you decide exactly where 2.75 goes between the whole numbers?
Is 1/2 the same point as 0.5 on this line? How do you know?
Name a number between 1/2 and 2.75 — and another between those two.
assess.correctAnswer: −3 sits three to the LEFT of zero; 1/2 halfway between 0 and 1; 2.75 three-quarters of the way from 2 to 3. Ordered: −3 < 1/2 < 2.75. −3 is smallest because it is furthest left / below zero, regardless of the type of number.

errorPatterns.pattern: Orders negatives by magnitude — argues 1/2 is the smallest 'because it's less than one', and −3 is not really small because 3 is a decent-sized number.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor zero on the line; show every negative lies left of every positive, so −3 < any positive including 1/2, whatever the digits say.
errorPatterns.distractor: 1/2 is the smallest, because it's less than one.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child ranks 1/2 below −3, or is surprised −3 is least.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads a fraction/decimal by its visible digits — places 1/2 near 2, or ranks 2.75 by '275'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Convert to a common frame (all as decimals, or all located between integer landmarks) so 1/2 = 0.5 lands between 0 and 1, not near 2.
errorPatterns.distractor: 1/2 goes near the 2 on the line.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Placement or ordering tracks a digit in the notation rather than the number's value.

errorPatterns.pattern: Consecutive-number thinking — believes there is a 'next' number and only a few values sit between landmarks, so a fraction has one fixed slot with gaps around it.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Zoom a segment (0 to 1) and mark tenths, then hundredths, to show the line is dense — any decimal or fraction has a place.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child treats the line as discrete, unsure where non-integers 'fit' or claims spots are 'taken'.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot place mixed types on one line; orders by digits or by magnitude of negatives.
responseLevels.full: Locates and orders integers, fractions and decimals on a single line by position relative to zero and to integer landmarks, and justifies size by leftmost-is-smallest across all types.
responseLevels.partial: Places and orders correctly when types are separated, but muddles when integers, fractions and decimals must be compared together, or reverts to magnitude for the negative.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: On one number line you have to place −3, 1/2 and 2.75. Where does each go relative to zero and to each other — and how do you know −3 is the smallest?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Placing mixed representations on ONE line forces a common measure of size. A child with full place-value/number-system understanding orders across integers, fractions and decimals by position. A child who orders negatives by magnitude, or who cannot locate a fraction/decimal without a whole-number cue, is exposed — and the reason for '−3 smallest' is the tell.

pedagogy.summary: At 7-8, mathematical argument becomes multi-step: the child constructs and follows a chain of reasoning (e.g. why columnar addition works, step by step), finds and explains errors, and — the new and demanding move — argues for why a GENERAL statement is true (e.g. 'adding two even numbers always gives an even number'). This is where the empirical proof scheme first bites: children tend to 'prove' a general claim by checking a few confirming examples, not realising that examples illustrate but do not establish a claim for all cases. Research shows this reliance on example-based justification is strong and the shift to structural/deductive argument is hard and slow. Teaching accepts examples as a starting point but explicitly models the move to a general (often visual/generic) argument, uses counterexamples to disprove, and keeps building the because-chain with connectives.
bestPractices: Model the move from examples to a general argument: 'it works for these — but how do we know it works for EVERY even number?'
Use generic/visual proofs accessible at this age (an even number as pairs with none left over; two evens make pairs with none left over, so the total is even)
Teach disproof by counter-example — one case that breaks a statement is enough to show it is false
Use worked examples with errors (e.g. wrong regrouping) and require an explanation of which step is wrong and why, grounded in place value
Build multi-step because/therefore chains and check each link follows from the last
Accept examples as illustration but name explicitly that a few examples are not a watertight proof — this is a key development, not a failing to be punished
keyRepresentations: Generic/visual proof (even number as pairs; place-value columns)
Counter-example as a disproof tool
Multi-step because/therefore chain
Worked examples containing deliberate errors
The justify → prove steps of the NRICH ladder
commonMisconceptions: Empirical proof scheme — treating a few confirming examples as proof that a general statement is always true
Convincing-not-justifying — a confident argument with missing steps, close to but not yet a complete chain
Identifying an error only as 'the answer is different' rather than naming the faulty step and why
Not realising that one counter-example is enough to disprove a general statement

learn.summary: For 7-8 year olds learning to justify mathematical reasoning: help children move from checking a few examples toward arguing why a GENERAL statement must be true for all cases (the empirical-to-structural shift). Core moves: build multi-step because/therefore chains, use generic/visual proofs (an even number as pairs with none left over), disprove a universal claim with a single counter-example, and locate and explain the faulty step in a worked example grounded in place value. Accept examples as a starting point but explicitly name that examples illustrate rather than prove — treat this as a developmental milestone, not a mistake to punish.

activities.title: Convince the friendly skeptic
feedback: When the child keeps offering examples: 'Those are all even, I agree — but could there be ANY two evens, somewhere, that don't work? How could you be sure without trying them all?'
When the child reaches for the pairs structure: affirm it — 'Now you've given a reason that covers every even number at once, not just the ones you tried.'
If the child says examples settle it: 'Examples show it works THIS time; let's find a reason it must work EVERY time.' — name that this move is a big step forward, not a failing.
For the disproof task: 'Just one case breaks it, doesn't it? One counter-example is enough to show an "always" statement is false.'
activities.rationale: The signature move at this age — sensing examples are not enough and reaching for a general reason — is well provoked by a skeptic who accepts each example yet keeps asking 'what about a pair you haven't tried?'. Dialogue is a proposed way to make the empirical-to-structural shift felt rather than merely told, consistent with 'convince yourself/friend/enemy' framing in the reasoning literature; efficacy here is not independently validated.
sourceClaims: Students strongly tend to validate conjectures with empirical, example-based reasoning (often a single example) rather than deductive argument, and the shift from empirical to structural/deductive reasoning is difficult and slow; a general counter-example gives insight into WHY a statement is false.

Specific examples are helpful for illustration but do not constitute a watertight proof; moving children beyond specific examples to a general argument (including generic and visual proofs, and disproof by counter-example) is a key development in primary reasoning.
learnerActions: State a general claim, e.g. 'adding two even numbers always gives an even number', and offer an example such as 4 + 6 = 10
Respond to a partner (an adult or a role-play) who cheerfully agrees each example is even but keeps asking: 'Can you give me another? And another?'
Face the key question: 'I believe every pair you've tried — but even numbers go on forever, so you could never check them all. How do you KNOW there isn't one pair that breaks it?'
Reach for a reason that covers all cases at once, e.g. 'every even number is made of pairs with none left over, so two of them still make complete pairs, so the total is even'
Then take a FALSE statement from the partner (e.g. 'adding two numbers always gives an even number') and topple it with a single counter-example such as 2 + 3 = 5
activities.intendedInsight: When there are endlessly many cases, as with even numbers, no pile of examples can establish a claim for every case, but a structural reason can — and a single counter-example is enough to disprove a general ('always') statement even though many examples cannot prove one.

activities.title: Build and test an argument workspace
feedback: When a case-tester stays unsatisfying no matter how many cases pass: 'That's the point — it never turns into certainty. What reason would cover every case?'
When the pairs argument is built: 'You've used how even numbers are made, not just examples — that's a general argument.'
On a sort: 'Good — to reject an "always" claim show one case that breaks it; to reject a "never" claim show one case where it does happen; for a "sometimes" statement show one case each way.'
If a chain skips a step: 'What's the missing step between here and here?'
activities.rationale: Making the empirical-to-general shift visible — cases that never suffice, a manipulable pairs structure, an always/sometimes/never sorter and a counter-example slot — operationalises disproof and generic proof. Interactive elements such as a case-tester that never turns green, a pair-grouping manipulative, and a counter-example slot are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not required tools.
sourceClaims: Specific examples are helpful for illustration but do not constitute a watertight proof; moving children beyond specific examples to a general argument (including generic and visual proofs, and disproof by counter-example) is a key development in primary reasoning.
Proficient students make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements, justify conclusions, use counter-examples, and can distinguish correct from flawed reasoning and explain the flaw.
learnerActions: Take a statement such as 'two evens → even' and run it against several cases, noticing that no number of green ticks ever proves it for all cases
Use a grouping tool (physical counters, drawn dots, or an on-screen manipulative) to split a number into pairs with none left over, then show that two such numbers still make complete pairs

Sort statements into always / sometimes / never true. To reject a claim that something is ALWAYS true, give one counter-example that breaks it; to reject a claim that something is NEVER true, give one case where it does hold; for a statement that is genuinely SOMETIMES true, show both a case where it holds and a case where it does not
Build the argument as a chain: 'every even number splits into pairs, SO two evens are pairs plus pairs, THEREFORE the total is even' — and check each link follows from the last
activities.intendedInsight: Testing cases can suggest a conjecture, but a generic argument built from how numbers are structured is what establishes it for every case. Always/sometimes/never sorting sharpens disproof: one counter-example rejects a claimed 'always', one confirming case rejects a claimed 'never', while a 'sometimes' claim needs a case each way.

activities.title: Spot and explain the faulty step
feedback: If the child says only 'the answer's wrong': 'Point to the exact step — what should have happened in the tens column?'
When the child names the regrouping step: 'Yes — that's the broken link, and here's the place-value rule it breaks.'
Keep the focus on explaining the flaw; this is not an occasion to reteach addition from scratch.
activities.rationale: Critique of worked examples with errors, anchored in place value, develops the ability to locate and justify a flaw rather than flag a discrepancy. A tap-to-reveal companion (reveal why a regrouping step is wrong, or why two evens must sum to an even) can model the target, but note its limit: revealing does not require the child to construct the explanation.
sourceClaims: Proficient students make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements, justify conclusions, use counter-examples, and can distinguish correct from flawed reasoning and explain the flaw.
learnerActions: Examine a worked columnar addition that contains a deliberate error (e.g. incorrect regrouping between the ones and tens columns)
Locate the exact step that is wrong — not just notice the final answer differs from your own
Explain WHY it is wrong in terms of place value, e.g. 'the ten that should have been carried into the tens column was dropped'
Say what should have happened in that column to make it correct
activities.intendedInsight: Finding an error means naming the specific faulty step and the place-value rule it breaks, not merely observing that the answer looks different.

constraints: Accept examples as legitimate illustration and a starting point; explicitly name that a few examples do not prove a general claim. This empirical-to-structural shift is a known developmental milestone and is hard and slow — treat it as development, not as a failing to be corrected sharply.

Distinguish 'convincing' from 'justifying': a confident multi-step argument with a missing link is close to proof. Don't dismiss it — ask 'what's the missing step between here and here?' and offer because/therefore stems to complete the chain.

Keep always/sometimes/never logic precise: a single counter-example disproves an 'always' claim and a single confirming case disproves a 'never' claim, but a genuine 'sometimes' classification requires both a case where the statement holds and a case where it fails.

Tap-to-reveal / worked-example companions model a general argument or flaw but do not require the child to construct the argument; use them to illustrate, then move to tasks where the child builds and states the reasoning.

Always/sometimes/never items, 'is this a proof or just examples?' items, and spot-the-error items probe critique and discrimination well, but a recognition-only response cannot show a child independently constructing a general argument; use these to complement, not replace, construction tasks.
When critiquing the flawed worked example, keep the focus on naming the faulty step and the place-value rule; do not reteach the addition procedure itself.
The error-spotting task assumes the child can already perform columnar addition with regrouping; if that prerequisite is shaky, address it separately rather than inside the justification task.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support general principles rather than proof that any specific activity here was tested.

The original row rated spatial/3D work 'poor' with the rationale 'arguing about number properties is not spatial.' This is a reasonable fit judgement for this topic but is not an established pedagogical law; it is reframed as 'number-property argument is not inherently spatial' context rather than a universal claim, and the 3D option was omitted as adding no distinct learning purpose here.

The even-number generic proof is sound as stated (an even number = pairs with none left over; sum of two such = pairs with none left over = even). Arithmetic in examples checked: 4 + 6 = 10 (even), 2 + 8 = 10 (even), 2 + 3 = 5 (odd, a valid counter-example to 'any two numbers sum to even'). No errors found.

The deliberate-error worked example is described generically (incorrect regrouping, a dropped carried ten); no specific flawed computation was supplied in the source, so facilitators should construct one and verify its intended error before use.

probeDeeper: 'You've checked some pairs — how do you know there isn't a pair somewhere that breaks it?' (surfaces the empirical scheme)
'Can you show why it must be even using how even numbers are built, not just examples?' (pushes toward a generic/structural argument)
'Which exact step in this worked example is wrong, and why?' (explain a flaw, not just flag it)
Counterexample: 'Someone says "adding two numbers always gives an even number." True? Can you find one case that breaks it?' (2 + 3 = 5 — one counter-example disproves)
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for a child who is not satisfied by examples alone and reaches for a general reason (e.g. every even number splits into pairs with none left over, so two evens still make complete pairs, so the total is even), and who, on the worked example, names the specific faulty step and why it breaks (place-value regrouping). Moving beyond examples to a structural argument, and explaining a flaw, are the targets.

errorPatterns.pattern: Empirical proof scheme — treats a few confirming examples as proof that a general statement holds for all cases.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Accept examples as illustration, then explicitly model the move to a general/generic argument ('how do we know for a pair we haven't tried?'); use the pairs structure of even numbers. Name that examples illustrate but do not prove — a key development, not a failing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked how they know it is always true, the child gives examples ('4+6=10, 2+8=10, see?') and, pressed for certainty about every case, offers more examples rather than a reason.

errorPatterns.pattern: Convincing-not-justifying — a confident multi-step argument with missing links, close to but not a complete chain.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not dismiss it — it is almost proof; ask 'what's the missing step between here and here?' and supply because/therefore stems to complete the chain.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child has the right idea (pairs) but skips steps, so the chain does not quite establish the claim; sure of the conclusion but the logic has gaps.

errorPatterns.pattern: Identifies an error only as 'the answer is different', not by naming the faulty step and why.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point to the step and ask 'what should have happened in the tens column?'; anchor the explanation in place value; do not reteach addition itself.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the flawed columnar example the child senses it is wrong but cannot point to the incorrect regrouping or say what place-value rule it breaks.

responseLevels.gap: Offers examples as proof and, pressed, just adds more; flags the flawed example only by its wrong answer; does not see that one counter-example disproves.
responseLevels.full: Argues from structure that the statement must hold for all cases (a complete because-chain), uses a single counter-example to disprove a false statement, names precisely why the worked example is wrong, and transfers this to a new general claim unprompted.
responseLevels.partial: Constructs a multi-step argument or a generic idea (pairs) but with gaps, or checks several examples while sensing they are not conclusive; spots the error without fully naming the faulty step (the convince/justify boundary).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask: 'Someone says, "If you add two even numbers you always get an even number." Is that true? How do you KNOW it is true for every pair of even numbers, not just the ones you tried?' Then show a columnar addition with a regrouping error and ask: 'Find the mistake and explain why it's wrong.' Discuss the reasoning as a whole; do not score a single answer.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who is beginning to prove treats examples as illustration and knows they must argue for ALL cases — and can name why the error is an error. A child on the empirical proof scheme offers a few examples as if they settle it and, pressed, just supplies more; on the error task they say 'the answer's wrong' without locating the step. Whether the child sees that examples are not enough, and can name a flaw, is the discriminator — hard to fake either way.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 5–6 (UK Y1–Y2, US K–Grade 2). Multiplication as repeated addition of EQUAL groups — the entry model for ×, built directly on the equal-groups skip counting from Counting & Cardinality.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y1 non-statutory 'make connections between arrays, number patterns, and counting in 2s, 5s and 10s'; Y2 'solve problems involving multiplication … using materials, arrays, repeated addition, mental methods and multiplication facts'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.OA.4 'use addition to find the total number of objects arranged in rectangular arrays … express the total as a sum of equal addends'; 3.OA.1 'interpret products — 5×7 as the total in 5 groups of 7 objects each'.
• Operational details: multiplication starts as 'a groups of b' — 3 groups of 4 = 4+4+4. Anchor in the skip-counting bridge (count 4, 8, 12 = one, two, three fours). IMPORTANT caveat for later: repeated addition is the entry MODEL, not the whole meaning (scaling and continuous quantities come later) — but for this age equal-groups/repeated addition is the correct foundation.
• Checkpoint: connect groups, repeated addition and count. Tier A (5): make 3 groups of 2 and count the total. Tier B (5–6): write 4+4+4 for '3 groups of 4' and give the total. Tier C (6): say '3 groups of 4 is 12' and skip-count 4, 8, 12 to match, recognising it as three fours.
bestPractices: Introduce × as 'groups of' with equal groups the child physically makes, and always stress the groups must be EQUAL — the defining feature children most often drop.
Bridge explicitly from the skip counting already mastered: counting 4, 8, 12 IS one four, two fours, three fours — so multiplication is met as something familiar (equal jumps) not brand new.
Move along the concrete–pictorial–abstract path: real objects in groups → pictures/arrays → the repeated-addition sentence 4+4+4 → later the × symbol; keep the group structure visible at each step.
Use the number line with equal jumps alongside grouped objects so repeated addition and skip counting are seen as the same thing in two representations.

Distinguish the two numbers in 'a groups of b' (number of groups vs size of group) with consistent language, so children don't muddle 3 groups of 4 with 4 groups of 3 even before commutativity is formalised.
keyRepresentations: Equal groups of concrete objects ('3 groups of 4')
Number line with equal jumps (linking to skip counting)
Repeated-addition number sentence (4 + 4 + 4)
Arrays (rows of equal size) as the bridge to the × symbol
commonMisconceptions: Adding groups that are not equal and still calling it multiplication — losing the 'equal groups' defining property.
Reading 3 × 4 as 3 + 4 (confusing multiplication with a single addition).
Counting the number of groups when asked for the total, or vice versa — muddling the two roles.

Believing multiplication is ONLY repeated addition (a seed of later trouble with fractions/decimals/scaling) — at this age fine, but teachers should model equal-groups language, not 'times means add lots'.
Miscounting the total by losing track of which groups have been counted (no systematic skip count).

learn.summary: For 5–6 year olds (roughly UK Y1, US K–Grade 1), introduce multiplication as repeated addition of EQUAL groups ('a groups of b'): 3 groups of 4 = 4+4+4. Build on the skip counting children are learning at this age (counting in 2s, 5s and 10s, e.g. 2, 4, 6 = one, two, three twos); when using groups of 4, introduce counting in fours alongside the groups (4, 8, 12 = one, two, three fours) rather than assuming it is already known. Keep the group structure visible from real objects → pictures/arrays → the repeated-addition sentence → later the × symbol. Stress that the groups must be equal (the defining feature children most often drop) and keep the two numbers distinct (how many groups vs how many in each). Repeated addition is the correct entry model at this age, but it is a model, not the whole meaning of multiplication.

activities.title: Equal-groups builder: watch groups, sentence and number line move together
feedback: When the jumps land on 4, 8, 12, point out that these are the numbers we say when counting in fours, so 'three fours' and 'count in fours three times' coincide; with groups of 2, 5 or 10, point out that the landing numbers are the skip-count numbers already learned.
If a learner adds an unequal group, note that this isn't multiplication yet: multiplication needs the SAME number in every group; help them make the groups equal again.
Ask which number says how many groups and which says how many in each group, to keep the two roles separate.
activities.rationale: Building the groups and watching the repeated-addition sentence, number-line jumps and total update in lockstep makes the equivalence of grouping, repeated addition and skip counting concrete and lets the child vary the number of groups and feel the pattern. Live sentence growth, number-line jumps, the collapse control and the unequal-group flag are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism visible, not required features.
sourceClaims: Y1 connect arrays and number patterns to counting in 2s, 5s and 10s; Y2 solve multiplication problems using materials, arrays, repeated addition, mental methods and facts.

Multiplication is introduced via equal groups/repeated addition and connected to skip counting; repeated addition is the entry model but multiplication is more than repeated addition (scaling comes later).
learnerActions: Set a group size, e.g. 4.

Add groups one at a time. With each group added, watch three things update together: a new '+4' joins a running repeated-addition sentence (4, then 4+4, then 4+4+4), a jump advances along a number line (4→8→12), and a total counter climbs.

Notice where each number-line jump lands (4, 8, 12) and say these numbers as counting in fours; also try a group size of 2, 5 or 10 and compare where the jumps land with the skip counting you already know.
Use a collapse control to fold '4+4+4' into '3 groups of 4', then expand it back.
Try adding an unequal group (e.g. a group of 3 among the fours) and see it flagged as 'not equal groups yet'; fix it so all groups match.
activities.intendedInsight: '3 groups of 4', '4+4+4', and 'counting in fours three times' are three views of one and the same thing, and the groups must be equal for it to be multiplication.

activities.title: Make the groups yourself with real objects
feedback: Have the learner map each addend back to a specific group ('point to where this 2 is').
If the child counts by ones without grouping, separate the groups physically and count each group, writing one addend per group.
activities.rationale: Concrete, child-made equal groups anchor the concrete–pictorial–abstract path and keep the group structure visible as the repeated-addition sentence is written.
sourceClaims: Y1 connect arrays and number patterns to counting in 2s, 5s and 10s; Y2 solve multiplication problems using materials, arrays, repeated addition, mental methods and facts.
learnerActions: Physically make, for example, 3 groups of 2 counters.
Count the total.
Write the matching repeated-addition sentence 2+2+2 and point to where each '2' is in your groups.
Rebuild with a different number of groups (e.g. 4 groups of 2) and write the new sentence.
activities.intendedInsight: Each addend in the repeated-addition sentence corresponds to one equal group of objects.

activities.title: Number line and grouped objects side by side
feedback: If jumps are unequal, note that equal jumps correspond to equal groups; help resize them.
Ask the child to connect the last number landed on to the total of all the groups.
activities.rationale: Showing equal jumps alongside grouped objects links the two representations the Y1 curriculum connects (arrays/number patterns and counting in 2s, 5s, 10s).
sourceClaims: Y1 connect arrays and number patterns to counting in 2s, 5s and 10s; Y2 solve multiplication problems using materials, arrays, repeated addition, mental methods and facts.
learnerActions: Place grouped objects (e.g. three groups of 4) next to a number line.
Draw equal jumps of 4 on the number line, landing on 4, 8, 12.
Say the totals as you jump and match each jump to a group.
activities.intendedInsight: Skip counting on a number line and repeated addition of equal groups are the same idea shown two ways.

activities.title: Match, sequence and fill in — a companion check
feedback: For the unequal-groups item, confirm that multiplication needs equal groups and ask the child to say why the offered picture fails.
If a match is wrong, return to grouped objects and rebuild the sentence addend by addend.
activities.rationale: Matching, sequencing and fill-in-the-blank crisply test the picture–sentence–total connection and the equal-groups property; this checks understanding rather than constructing and varying the groups, so use it alongside the hands-on work.
learnerActions: Match an equal-groups picture to its repeated-addition sentence (e.g. three groups of 4 ↔ 4+4+4).
Put skip-count totals in order (4, 8, 12).
Fill in the blank: 4+4+4 = ?
Spot and reject a picture of unequal groups offered as if it were '3 groups of 4'.
activities.intendedInsight: A matching/sequencing/fill-in task shows whether the picture–sentence–total link holds and whether unequal groups are correctly rejected; recognition here does not by itself build or vary the concept.

activities.title: Talk it through: 'how many wheels on 3 cars?'
feedback: When the partner makes groups unequal, prompt the child to notice and fix it.
Encourage the full phrase '3 groups of 4 is 12', not just the total.
activities.rationale: Spoken, responsive discussion rehearses equal-groups language; because the insight is visual and quantitative, pair talk with objects or the builder rather than using it alone.
learnerActions: Answer an equal-groups question such as 'how many wheels on 3 cars with 4 wheels each?' by counting groups aloud.
Correct a partner who 'forgets' to keep the groups equal (e.g. gives one car 3 wheels).
Say the matching sentence, e.g. 4+4+4, and give the total.
activities.intendedInsight: Equal-groups language ('3 groups of 4') describes real situations and must keep every group the same size.

constraints: Groups must always be EQUAL; adding unequal groups and calling it multiplication is the defining error to prevent.
Keep the two numbers in 'a groups of b' distinct: how many groups vs how many in each group. Do not let '3 groups of 4' blur into '4 groups of 3' even before commutativity is formalised.
Do not read 3 × 4 as 3 + 4; multiplication is repeated addition of equal groups, not a single addition of the two numbers.

Repeated addition is the entry model for this age, not the full meaning of multiplication; avoid 'times just means add lots'. Scaling and continuous quantities come later. Model equal-groups language instead.
Matching/sequencing/fill-in tasks check the connection but do not by themselves have the child construct and vary equal groups; keep hands-on building central.
A static picture or tap-to-reveal caption can introduce equal groups but does not let the child vary the number of groups; treat it as an introduction or scaffold, not the main concept-builder.
Interaction examples (live sentence growth, number-line jumps, collapse control, unequal-group flag) are illustrative options, not mandatory mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic/logic: 3 groups of 2 = 2+2+2 = 6 ✓; 4+4+4 = 12 with number-line landing on 4,8,12 ✓; 3 cars of 4 wheels = 4+4+4 = 12 ✓; 4 groups of 2 = 2+2+2+2 = 8 ✓. The diagnostic distractor '5 cakes' arises from erroneously doing 3+2 (groups + size) and is presented only as an error pattern, never as a valid answer.

Among the listed curriculum/professional standards, the CCSS-M (2.OA.4/3.OA.1) and NCETM claims carry verified:false in the original; the DfE claim is marked verified. All are treated as unverified in this rewrite since sources were not re-checked, and the specific US standard codes were not reproduced in the learner guidance.
The original cites 3.OA.1, a Grade 3 standard, alongside the stated 5–6 / US K–Grade 2 scope; this pre-existing tension is left unaltered as an original-row framing rather than rewritten.

The original 'equal groups and repeated addition are planar... a 3D environment adds no conceptual value' was a catalog fit judgement; it has been dropped rather than asserted as a universal law. A flat representation is sufficient here, but this is a scoped design preference, not evidence that 3D can teach nothing.

The original curriculum objective 'recognise an array as showing equal rows' is carried only lightly (via the CPA progression and matching pictures); an explicit array-focused activity could strengthen coverage but was not present as a separate scaffold in the original.

The original's age-tiered checkpoint (Tier A/B/C) is covered informally across activities (make groups and count → write the sentence → say and skip-count) but its explicit per-age tiering was condensed out; reinstating differentiated tiers could aid assessment.

probeDeeper: Which number tells us how many plates, and which tells us how many cakes on each?
Can you point to where each '2' in 2 + 2 + 2 is on the plates?
If there were 4 plates with 2 cakes, what would the adding-up look like?
What if one plate had 3 cakes and another had 1 — could we still say 2 + 2 + 2?
assess.correctAnswer: 6 cakes. A child reasoning correctly sees the three plates as three EQUAL groups of 2 and connects '3 groups of 2' to the repeated addition 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 — explaining that each plate contributes one 2 to the sum.

errorPatterns.pattern: counts all the cakes by ones with no sense of the equal groups — cannot connect to 2 + 2 + 2
errorPatterns.nextMove: physically separate the plates and count each group of 2, writing 2 + 2 + 2; make each addend a plate.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child gets 6 by counting each cake but, asked to show 2+2+2, cannot map each 2 to a plate

errorPatterns.pattern: adds the numbers seen rather than repeating the group — does 3 + 2 = 5
errorPatterns.nextMove: clarify 3 is HOW MANY groups, 2 is HOW MANY in each; act out three lots of two, not 'three and two'.
errorPatterns.distractor: 5 cakes (3 plates and 2 cakes, so 3 + 2)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer of 5; child adds the count of plates to the count on a plate

errorPatterns.pattern: does not require the groups to be EQUAL — accepts unequal plates as the same kind of situation
errorPatterns.nextMove: contrast equal vs unequal plates; repeated addition of the SAME number is what multiplication captures.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child treats plates with 2, 3, 1 cakes as also '3 groups' for multiplication

responseLevels.gap: counts by ones only, or adds 3 + 2; no equal-groups structure.
responseLevels.full: identifies the equal groups, maps each addend to a group, connects '3 groups of 2' to 2 + 2 + 2 = 6, and recognises the groups must be equal.
responseLevels.partial: gets 6 and links it to 2 + 2 + 2 for this case but doesn't clearly require the groups to be equal or generalise to a new number of groups.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are 3 plates with 2 cakes on each. How many cakes altogether? After the child answers, ask: can you show me why that's the same as 2 + 2 + 2?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child can count 6 by ones without grasping the equal-groups structure. Asking them to connect it to 2 + 2 + 2 reveals whether they see multiplication as repeated addition of EQUAL groups, or merely counted a pile. The reason tier separates counting from grouping structure.
