pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–10y; multiply up to 4-digit × 1-digit AND 2-digit × 2-digit using formal long multiplication, illustrated with the area model.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5 'multiply numbers up to 4 digits by a one- or two-digit number using a formal written method, including long multiplication for two-digit numbers'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 5.NBT.5 — 'fluently multiply multi-digit whole numbers using the standard algorithm'; 4.NBT.5 covers up to 4-digit × 1-digit with area/place-value strategies.
• Operational details — the new challenge over Y4 short multiplication is the TWO-DIGIT multiplier: 34×27 requires multiplying by both the ones (7) and the tens (20), then adding partial products. The area model (45×23 as four sub-rectangles 40×20, 40×3, 5×20, 5×3) is the conceptual scaffold that shows WHY there are two rows of partial products and why the second row is shifted (it's ×20, not ×2). The classic error — forgetting the placeholder zero on the second partial product — is precisely a lost-place-value error the area model prevents. Estimate first (34×27≈30×30=900) to bound the answer.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): 4-digit × 1-digit (2347×6) securely. Tier B (age 9–10): 2-digit × 2-digit long multiplication (34×27) with correct partial-product placement. Tier C (age 10): draw the matching area model and explain why the second partial product is shifted / carries a zero.
bestPractices: Anchor long multiplication in the area model: 2-digit×2-digit as four sub-rectangles, so the two partial-product rows and the shift are seen as ×ones and ×tens.
Make the placeholder zero meaningful — the second row is ×20 (tens), not ×2 — rather than a rule to 'put a zero down'.
Estimate first by rounding both factors to bound the answer and catch magnitude errors.
Progress grid method → expanded partial products → compact long multiplication, keeping the area link visible.
Check with the inverse or by comparing to the estimate; watch carrying across multiple columns.
keyRepresentations: Area/grid model with four sub-rectangles (the home of the partial products)
Expanded partial-products layout bridging grid to compact form
Compact long-multiplication layout with the placeholder zero
Estimation (rounding both factors) to bound the product
commonMisconceptions: Omitting the placeholder zero on the second partial product (treating ×20 as ×2).
Multiplying only by the ones digit of the two-digit multiplier and forgetting the tens.
Carrying errors across several columns, or adding carries into the wrong place.
Misaligning partial products when adding them.
Not connecting the algorithm to the area model, so errors can't be self-diagnosed.

learn.summary: For 9–10 year-olds learning formal long multiplication (up to 4-digit × 1-digit and 2-digit × 2-digit), anchor the written algorithm in the area model so the two partial-product rows and the placeholder zero become meaningful place-value facts rather than memorised rules. The central objective: the child sees that the second partial-product row is '×20 (tens)', not '×2', and that the four sub-rectangles of an area model sum to the same total as the two added partial products. Estimation by rounding both factors bounds the answer and catches magnitude slips.

activities.title: Bridge the area model to the written method (34 × 27)
feedback: If the second partial product comes out as 68 instead of 680: you multiplied by 2 instead of 20. Look at the 34×20 region of your grid — it is twenty rows worth 680, not 68. Write the zero first to reserve the ones place, saying 'we are multiplying by twenty'.

If you only computed 34 × 7 and stopped: every part of 27 (both the 20 and the 7) must multiply every part of 34. Check your grid has all four regions — a missing region means a missing partial product.
If you wrote 34×2 + 34×7: you split 27 into digits 2 and 7 without place value. The tens digit is worth 20, so draw the ×20 regions explicitly.
If 238 + 680 doesn't total 918, recheck your column alignment and any carries — your estimate of ~900 tells you the answer should be near there.
activities.rationale: Coupling a partitioned area model to the columnar layout makes the place value of each partial product (and the meaning of the placeholder zero) visible, so a lost place value can be self-diagnosed. A live split-screen where partitioning tiles fill the long-multiplication frame, with tiles sliding together to show 600+210+80+28 = 918 matching the two added partials, is one concrete way to make this mechanism visible; a running estimate panel can flag magnitude slips.
sourceClaims: The area model should scaffold long multiplication, making partial products and the placeholder zero (× tens) meaningful.
learnerActions: Estimate first by rounding both factors: 34 × 27 ≈ 30 × 30 = 900, and keep this estimate in view as you work.
Draw an area model for 34 × 27 and partition it into four labelled sub-rectangles: 30×20, 30×7, 4×20, 4×7.
Alongside, set up the long-multiplication layout and compute the first partial product 34 × 7 = 238 (which is the 30×7 and 4×7 tiles: 210 + 28).
Compute the second partial product 34 × 20 = 680, writing a 0 in the ones place FIRST because this whole row is ×20, i.e. tens (this is the 30×20 and 4×20 tiles: 600 + 80).
Add the two partial products: 238 + 680 = 918, and confirm it matches the sum of all four area tiles (600 + 210 + 80 + 28 = 918).
Check the result against your estimate of 900 — are they close?
activities.intendedInsight: The second partial-product row is shifted and carries a placeholder zero because it is ×20 (tens), not ×2; the four area sub-rectangles are exactly the same quantities as the two written partial products broken apart, so the algorithm and the area model are two views of the same calculation.

activities.title: Secure 4-digit × 1-digit short multiplication (2,347 × 6)
feedback: If a carry is added into the wrong column, recheck each step and compare with your estimate. Note that rounding 2,347 DOWN (to 2,000 or 2,300) gives an underestimate, so the true answer should sit a little above those figures — 14,082 (just over 13,800) is reasonable.
If any column is skipped, remember every digit of 2,347 must be multiplied by 6.
activities.rationale: This activity enacts the Y5 curriculum requirement to multiply a number up to four digits by a one-digit number using a formal written method; it also secures the carrying and place-value fluency that two-digit long multiplication builds on, forming a sensible progression before the two-row layout.
sourceClaims: Y5 pupils multiply numbers up to 4 digits by a one- or two-digit number using a formal written method, including long multiplication for two-digit numbers.
learnerActions: Estimate first: 2,347 × 6 ≈ 2,000 × 6 = 12,000 (or 2,300 × 6 = 13,800 for a tighter bound).
Compute 2,347 × 6 in formal written layout, carrying across each column: 7×6=42 (write 2 carry 4), 4×6=24 plus 4 = 28 (write 8 carry 2), 3×6=18 plus 2 = 20 (write 0 carry 2), 2×6=12 plus 2 = 14.
Read off the answer 14,082 and check it against your estimate.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying a multi-digit number by a single digit requires multiplying every digit and correctly handling carries across several columns; estimation bounds the magnitude.

activities.title: Map each written partial product to its area region (45 × 23)
feedback: If a region is missing or a partial product doesn't account for the full value of a digit, redraw the grid so every part of 23 (20 and 3) multiplies every part of 45 (40 and 5).
If the ×20 partial product lacks its placeholder zero, link it to the 800 + 100 = 900 tens regions: the row lives in the tens.
If the two totals (region sum and partial-product sum) disagree, recheck each region's arithmetic against the matching partial.
activities.rationale: Explicitly connecting the four area regions to the two partial products is the discriminating task that separates understanding from rote execution, and it directly targets the common error of omitting partial products.
sourceClaims: The area model should scaffold long multiplication, making partial products and the placeholder zero (× tens) meaningful.
learnerActions: Draw an area model for 45 × 23 with four regions: 40×20, 40×3, 5×20, 5×3.
Add all four regions to get the product: 800 + 120 + 100 + 15 = 1,035.
Now compute 45 × 23 by long multiplication and point to which area regions make up each partial product: 45×3 = 135 (= 120 + 15) and 45×20 = 900 (= 800 + 100).
Confirm the two partial products 135 + 900 = 1,035 equal the sum of the four area regions.
activities.intendedInsight: Each written partial product is a sum of two area sub-rectangles, so a child who can map regions to partials understands WHY there are two rows rather than following steps by rote.

activities.title: Consolidation: spot-the-error and estimate checks
feedback: For the spot-the-error item: the second row is ×20, so it must occupy the tens — the 0 marks the empty ones place, meaning '×20 not ×2'.
For the estimate item: rounding 48 to 50 and 52 to 50 gives 2,500, close to the true product 2,496, so it is a good magnitude check.
activities.rationale: Procedural consolidation with error-spotting and estimation tests and reinforces the procedure efficiently. This recognition/fill-in format checks the procedure rather than independently eliciting construction of the area link, so it is best used after the construction activities, not in place of them.
learnerActions: Examine a worked 34 × 27 in which the placeholder zero is missing from the second partial product; identify the error and explain why the zero belongs there.
Fill in a missing second partial product in a given long-multiplication layout.
Choose or state the best estimate for 48 × 52 by rounding both factors (≈ 50 × 50 = 2,500).
activities.intendedInsight: The missing placeholder zero and estimation are the quickest self-checks for magnitude; recognising the error reinforces the place-value reasoning behind the shifted row.

constraints: Recognition and fill-in/spot-the-error tasks consolidate the procedure but do not elicit the child independently constructing an area model and mapping it to the written method; use them after, not instead of, the bridging construction work.

Annotated static worked examples (area model above, written method below, tap to reveal each partial product's region) are useful reference scaffolds, but a fixed example cannot give feedback on a child's own fresh calculation or their own placeholder-zero error — pair them with tasks the child computes.

Spoken dialogue alone lacks a shared visible written layout, so it cannot display aligned columns or reliably catch column-placement errors in this spatial, multi-step procedure; keep a written/drawn layout at the centre rather than relying on talk alone (this is a layout-affordance limit, not a claim that dialogue can never support the procedure).

The area model is a conceptual scaffold for place value; the goal is eventual fluent compact long multiplication with the area link available for self-diagnosis, not permanent dependence on drawing grids.
Treat carrying/alignment slips as performance errors (re-estimate and recheck the flagged column) rather than reteaching the whole method.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic self-audit (all confirmed correct): 34×7=238, 34×20=680, 238+680=918; area tiles 600+210+80+28=918; 2,347×6=14,082; 45×23 regions 800+120+100+15=1,035 and partials 135+900=1,035; 48×52=2,496 with estimate 50×50=2,500. The source's correctAnswer states the 45×23 region sum as 1,035 — matches.

The source's 3D-interactive dismissal ('3D adds cost without insight') was removed as a catalog-fit judgement rather than an established pedagogical law; the planar area model is simply the natural representation for this place-value procedure, stated without claiming 3D could teach nothing.
CCSS 5.NBT.5/4.NBT.5 and the NCETM/IES area-model guidance are marked verified:false in the row; they are retained as cited but their evidence strength is not independently confirmed here.

The original prerequisite reteach IDs (mt_18fK9sQdIz, mt_AQo4u7O4sM) are catalog-internal and have been dropped from learner-facing guidance; the underlying reteach moves are preserved in the feedback.

For 2,347 × 6 both rounding choices (2,000 and 2,300) are underestimates, so the true answer exceeds them; feedback states this explicitly so the estimate is not mistaken for a bracket that must contain the answer.

The Y5 curriculum claim attached to the 2,347×6 activity directly supports the content requirement the activity enacts; the progression/sequencing point stated in that rationale is an editorial judgement the claim does not itself assert.

probeDeeper: Why did you write a zero before the second row of the multiplication?
In your grid, which region equals 40 × 20, and how much is it?
Estimate 34 × 27 roughly — is 918 reasonable?
How does adding the four grid regions match adding your two partial products?
assess.correctAnswer: 34 × 27 = 918 (34×7 = 238, 34×20 = 680, sum 918). 2,347 × 6 = 14,082. Area model for 45×23 has four regions 40×20=800, 40×3=120, 5×20=100, 5×3=15, sum 1035. The teacher watches for the placeholder zero when multiplying by the tens digit, correct partial products, and the child mapping each grid region to a partial product.

errorPatterns.pattern: omits the placeholder zero — multiplies by the tens digit as if it were ones (34×2 recorded as 68, not 680)
errorPatterns.nextMove: connect to the area model: the 34×20 region is twenty rows, worth 680, not 68; write the zero first to reserve the ones place, saying 'we are multiplying by twenty'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: second partial product is ten times too small; final total far too low

errorPatterns.pattern: treats 34×27 as 34×2 + 34×7 (adds tens and ones digits without place value), or only multiplies by one digit
errorPatterns.nextMove: draw all four regions of the grid so every part of 27 (20 and 7) multiplies every part of 34; nothing may be left out.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: partial products do not account for the full value of each digit; area model has missing regions

errorPatterns.pattern: carrying error within a partial product or misaligned column addition
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach the method; have the child estimate first and recheck the flagged column.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: one partial product or the final addition wrong; often caught by estimate (34×27 ≈ 30×30 = 900)

responseLevels.gap: omits the placeholder zero, multiplies by only one digit, or cannot link the method to the area model.
responseLevels.full: executes long multiplication with correct placeholders and partial products, maps each partial to an area region, and checks against an estimate.
responseLevels.partial: completes 4-digit × 1-digit correctly but slips on the 2-digit × 2-digit placeholder, or draws the grid without connecting regions to partial products.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to compute 34 × 27 by long multiplication while you watch, and separately to compute 2,347 × 6. Then ask them to draw an area (grid) model for 45 × 23 and point to where each partial product sits. Watch the placeholder zero on the tens row and whether the partial products match the area regions.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Long multiplication's signature failure is the missing placeholder zero on the second partial product (multiplying by 2 tens but recording as 2 ones). Connecting the written partials to the four area regions distinguishes a child who understands WHY there are partial products from one following steps by rote.

pedagogy.summary: Estimating and checking is a habit of mind, not a calculation: before working something out, round to get a ballpark; after, judge whether the exact answer is reasonable against that ballpark, and verify using the inverse operation. The point is epistemic — how do I know my answer is sensible? — so estimation must come BEFORE calculating (to be a genuine check, not a rationalisation) and the inverse must be understood as an independent re-derivation, not a repeat of the same sum.
bestPractices: Estimate FIRST by rounding (to the nearest 10/100), then calculate, then compare — order matters or it isn't a check
Teach the inverse as a genuinely independent check: add the answer back to test a subtraction (and vice versa), rather than redoing the identical operation
Use deliberately wrong 'answers' and ask 'sensible or silly?' so the estimate earns its keep by catching nonsense
Discuss reasonableness openly — why 121 can't be right for 412+389 — rather than marking it
Build on the inverse relationship (add undoes subtract) and place-value rounding
keyRepresentations: Number line / rounding scale (which ten or hundred is it nearest?)
Bar model showing the inverse (whole minus part returns the other part)
'Sensible or silly?' answer cards to judge
Estimate-then-exact two-column jotting
Fact-family triangle (linking + and − for the inverse check)
commonMisconceptions: Treating estimation as pointless — 'you can't know until you do the real sum'
Estimating AFTER calculating, bending the estimate to match the answer already found (confirmation)
'Checking' by repeating the identical operation (which reproduces the same error) instead of using the inverse
Rounding erratically so the estimate isn't a fair ballpark

learn.summary: Estimation and checking are habits of mind for judging whether an answer is sensible, not extra calculations. Learners round FIRST to get a ballpark, then calculate, then compare; and they check using the inverse operation (adding the answer back to test a subtraction) understood as an independent re-derivation, not a repeat of the same sum. Aimed at ages 7-9 working with sums and differences of two- and three-digit numbers.

activities.title: Sensible or silly? Judge before you compute
feedback: If a learner refuses to judge without computing exactly, prompt: 'You don't need the exact answer — about how big should it be? Could 121 possibly be right for 412 + 389?'
When they correctly flag 121 as silly, name what they did: 'You rounded to about 800 and saw 121 was far too small — that's the check working.'
If they only estimate after seeing the exact answer, discuss why the estimate must come first to be a real check rather than a confirmation of what they already found
activities.rationale: Estimation is a distinct competency from exact calculation, and ordering it before the calculation is what makes it a genuine check rather than a rationalisation. Deliberately wrong candidate answers force the estimate to earn its keep by catching nonsense, and the two-column jotting makes the estimate-versus-exact comparison explicit.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils estimate the answer to a calculation and use inverse operations to check answers, and identify unreasonable answers by comparing to an estimate.

Computational estimation and judging reasonableness are distinct competencies from exact calculation; effective checking uses the inverse operation as an independent verification rather than repeating the original procedure.
learnerActions: Look at a calculation paired with a proposed answer, e.g. 412 + 389 = 121, and decide quickly whether it is 'sensible' or 'silly' BEFORE working out the exact answer
Say aloud the rounded ballpark you used: '400-and-something plus about 390 is roughly 800, so 121 can't be right'
Judge a batch of items, some with reasonable answers (e.g. 801) and some deliberately wrong, flagging the silly ones
Record your estimate and the exact answer side by side in two columns, so you can compare the ballpark against the worked result
Only after committing to your judgement, work out or reveal the exact answer and see whether your estimate caught the nonsense
activities.intendedInsight: A rounded ballpark, formed before calculating, is enough to catch a wildly wrong answer — so estimation is a genuine check, not busywork or a guess made after the fact.

activities.title: Check by adding back: the inverse as an independent test
feedback: If a learner 'checks' by subtracting again, ask: 'If you made a slip the first time, would doing exactly the same thing catch it? What could you do instead that works a different way?'
When they add the answer back and reach the start number, affirm: 'Getting back to 623 shows the subtraction was right — you tested it a different way.'
If the inverse relationship itself is shaky, revisit how add undoes subtract using the bar model and fact-family triangle before returning to checking
activities.rationale: Effective checking uses the inverse as an independent verification; understanding it as a different route (not a repeat) is the conceptual core. The bar model and fact family make the inverse relationship concrete.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils estimate the answer to a calculation and use inverse operations to check answers, and identify unreasonable answers by comparing to an estimate.

Computational estimation and judging reasonableness are distinct competencies from exact calculation; effective checking uses the inverse operation as an independent verification rather than repeating the original procedure.
learnerActions: Take a completed subtraction, e.g. 623 − 178 = 445, and check it by adding the answer back: 445 + 178
Confirm that the sum returns to the starting number (623) — if it does, the subtraction is verified
Contrast this with simply redoing 623 − 178 again, and explain why repeating the identical operation can easily repeat the original mistake, while adding back tests the answer a different way
Use a bar model (the whole minus one part returns the other part) and a fact-family triangle linking the three numbers to see how addition and subtraction undo each other
activities.intendedInsight: Checking with the inverse operation is an independent re-derivation of the answer, whereas repeating the same subtraction just reproduces the same potential error.

activities.title: How do you KNOW it's right? Reasoning discussion
feedback: Draw out reasoning rather than marking: value 'about 800, so 121 is far too small' over a bare right/wrong label
If a learner says 'you can't know until you do the real sum', surface that a rounded ballpark already rules out 121 — you knew without the exact calculation
Probe the limit honestly: an answer near the estimate (e.g. 790 vs ~800) could still be slightly off, so the estimate narrows the range rather than proving exactness
activities.rationale: The topic is epistemic — how do I know my answer is sensible? — so open discussion that probes justification suits it and exposes the misconception that only exact recomputation can establish correctness. This is explicitly a discussion to elicit reasoning, not a scored task.
sourceClaims: Computational estimation and judging reasonableness are distinct competencies from exact calculation; effective checking uses the inverse operation as an independent verification rather than repeating the original procedure.
learnerActions: Respond to a prompt such as: 'A friend adds 412 + 389 and gets 121; another gets 801. Without working out the exact sum, how could you tell which answer must be wrong?'
Explain how to check a subtraction like 623 − 178 WITHOUT just doing the same subtraction again
Discuss: if your estimate and your exact answer disagree, which do you trust, and what do you do next?
Consider whether an answer could be close to the estimate but still wrong — so what does an estimate tell you, and what does it not?
activities.intendedInsight: An estimate bounds roughly how big an answer should be and flags gross errors, but it does not guarantee exactness; the inverse gives a separate confirmation. Knowing an answer is sensible is a matter of reasoning, not only recomputation.

activities.title: Rounding to a fair ballpark
feedback: If rounding is inconsistent, point to the number line: 'Is 178 nearer 170 or 180? Round both numbers the same careful way.'
Reinforce that the goal is a quick, fair approximation — not another exact sum
Note that rounding choices (nearest 10 vs nearest 100) change how tight the estimate is; a looser estimate still catches a wildly wrong answer
activities.rationale: Place-value rounding is the prerequisite skill that makes estimation a fair check; a static rounding scale is useful reference, and practising consistent rounding addresses the 'erratic rounding' misconception.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils estimate the answer to a calculation and use inverse operations to check answers, and identify unreasonable answers by comparing to an estimate.
learnerActions: Round two- and three-digit numbers to the nearest 10 and the nearest 100, e.g. 412 → 410 (nearest 10) or 400 (nearest 100); 389 → 390 (nearest 10) or 400 (nearest 100); 178 → 180 (nearest 10) or 200 (nearest 100)
Use a number line or rounding scale to see which ten or hundred a number is nearest to
Form an estimate for a sum or difference by rounding each number to the SAME place, e.g. 623 − 178 ≈ 620 − 180 ≈ 440 (both to nearest 10)
Compare estimates formed with consistent rounding against erratic rounding to see why fair, consistent rounding gives a trustworthy ballpark
activities.intendedInsight: A reliable estimate depends on rounding each number fairly to the same place; erratic rounding produces a ballpark you can't trust.

constraints: Estimation must come BEFORE calculating to function as a genuine check; estimating afterwards invites bending the estimate to match the answer already found (confirmation).

The inverse check must be understood as an independent re-derivation; repeating the identical operation is a weak check because it can easily repeat the original error (especially a misunderstanding of the method), even though it sometimes catches a careless slip.

An estimate bounds how big an answer should be and catches gross errors, but does NOT prove exactness — an answer close to the estimate can still be slightly wrong. Do not teach 'close to the estimate = correct'.
Treat the reasoning probes as discussion to surface thinking, not as scored right/wrong items; what matters is the quality of the epistemic reasoning.
A static rounding scale, bar model or fact-family triangle is a useful reference but does not by itself exercise the judging habit — pair reference tools with active judging and checking.

A timed 'buzz silly before the answer reveals' format is an optional motivational scaffold (short time pressure forces rounding over computing); it is not required, and the core objective is the estimate-first reasoning, which can also be done untimed on paper or aloud.
Prerequisite: the inverse relationship (add undoes subtract) and place-value rounding should be reteachable if shaky before checking work can succeed.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic self-audit: 412 + 389 = 801 (so 121 is correctly 'silly'); rounded 400 + 390 = 790, or 400 + 400 = 800 — both ballparks correctly expose 121. 623 − 178 = 445, and 445 + 178 = 623 confirms the inverse check. 620 − 180 = 440 as an estimate. 412→410/400, 389→390/400, 178→180/200 all check out. All original examples hold.

One source (NCTM/Sowder-based claim on estimation as a distinct competency and inverse as independent verification) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its support as research-informed, not established efficacy.
The legacy 'possible' entry asserted a static rounding scale 'cannot exercise the judging habit'; this has been softened to a scoped limit (reference vs active judging) rather than a universal claim.
The legacy '3D is poor because not spatial' ranking was dropped as catalog boilerplate; no pedagogical loss, as the topic is genuinely non-spatial.
The original recommendation implied there 'isn't time to compute' as the mechanism; retained only as an optional time-pressure scaffold, since estimation-first reasoning can be taught untimed too.

The bar model and the estimate-then-exact two-column jotting representations from the original were restored into the inverse-check and judging activities respectively, having been dropped in an earlier draft.

Independent recheck confirmed the prior corrections are present at every learner-facing occurrence (four-misconception count, restored bar model and two-column jotting, removed internal reteach ID). The only new change is clarifying the rounding example in the rounding activity so the per-number nearest-10/100 options do not conflict with the 'round to the same place' instruction for estimates.

probeDeeper: Why is 121 obviously too small for 412 + 389?
If your estimate and your exact answer disagree, which do you trust — and what do you do next?
Why is adding the answer back a better check than just doing the subtraction again?
Could an answer be close to the estimate but still wrong? So what does an estimate actually tell you — and what does it not?
assess.correctAnswer: Strong reasoning rounds to estimate — about 400 + 390 ≈ 800 — so 121 is obviously wrong and 801 is sensible; and checks the subtraction by adding the answer back to 178 to see if it returns 623 (the inverse), or by estimating 620 − 180 ≈ 440. It treats an answer as unreasonable when it is far from the estimate.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'You can't know until you do the real sum' — estimation dismissed as guessing with no value
errorPatterns.nextMove: In discussion, surface that a rounded ballpark is enough to catch a wildly wrong answer; play 'sensible or silly?' so estimation demonstrably earns its keep. Do not score — draw out the reasoning.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child refuses to judge without computing exactly, or treats the estimate as just another guess

errorPatterns.pattern: Estimates AFTER calculating, bending the estimate to fit the answer already found
errorPatterns.nextMove: Discuss why the estimate must come FIRST to be a check; revisit a case where their exact answer was wrong but they had already 'confirmed' it. Not scored.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child produces an 'estimate' that conveniently matches their exact answer, or only estimates once prompted after the fact

errorPatterns.pattern: Checks by repeating the identical operation rather than using the inverse
errorPatterns.nextMove: Discuss why adding the answer back is an independent check while redoing the same subtraction is not; link to the fact family. Reteach the inverse relationship if it's shaky.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked how to check a subtraction, the child just subtracts again — reproducing any original error

responseLevels.gap: Treats estimation as guessing or insists on exact recomputation; would check by repeating the same operation.
responseLevels.full: Estimates before calculating, uses the estimate to flag unreasonable answers, checks with the inverse, and articulates why rounding bounds the answer and why the inverse re-derives it independently.
responseLevels.partial: Can round to make an estimate but doesn't reliably use it to judge reasonableness, or knows the inverse check as a rule without seeing why it is independent.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Treat this as a discussion, not a marked task — you want the child's reasoning. Say: 'A friend adds 412 + 389 and gets 121; another gets 801. Without working out the exact sum, how could you tell which answer must be wrong?' Then: 'When someone finishes a subtraction like 623 − 178, how could they check it's right WITHOUT just doing the same subtraction again?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The probe separates a child who sees estimation as a tool for judging reasonableness — and the inverse as an independent check — from one who believes you can only know by exact recomputation, or who would 'check' by repeating the same sum. It is surfaced for discussion, not scored right/wrong; what matters is the quality of the epistemic reasoning.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 6-7 (Y2), CONCEPTUAL. Understand and APPLY the commutative property of addition: addends can be added in any order (3+8 = 8+3), and recognise that subtraction is NOT commutative (5−3 ≠ 3−5). A central property node (0.16) — it halves the facts to learn and licenses 'put the bigger number first' to count on.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y2): 'show that addition of 2 numbers can be done in any order (commutative) and subtraction of 1 number from another cannot'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.OA.3 'apply properties of operations as strategies to add and subtract… (Commutative property of addition)'.
• Operational details — Show commutativity structurally, not as a rule to memorise: the SAME set of objects seen two ways (a rod of 3 and a rod of 8 make the same length however ordered; a part-whole with parts swapped gives the same whole). Then exploit it strategically — to add 3+8, start from 8 and count on 3. Deliberately CONTRAST subtraction (take 3 from 5 vs 5 from 3) to show order matters there, preventing over-generalisation.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 6): show 3+8 and 8+3 give the same total with objects. Tier B (age 6-7): use commutativity to count on from the larger addend. Tier C (age 7): explain why addition is commutative but subtraction is not, with an example.
bestPractices: Demonstrate commutativity with a model that is literally unchanged by reordering — the same two rods/bars, the same part-whole with parts swapped — so it's seen as structural, not a memorised rule.
Immediately put it to work: 'start with the bigger number and count on', showing the property makes calculation easier.
Explicitly contrast subtraction (5−3 vs 3−5) so children learn the property is specific to addition and don't over-generalise 'you can swap them'.
Use it to reduce fact load — knowing 3+8 gives 8+3 — linking to fluency work.
Have children justify with a drawing or rearrangement rather than just asserting the rule.
keyRepresentations: Two number rods/bars combined, then physically swapped (same total length)
Part-part-whole model with the two parts swapped
A rotated array/ten-frame showing the same quantity two ways
Empty number line: 8 then +3 vs 3 then +8 landing on the same point
Contrast pair for subtraction (5−3 and 3−5) showing different results
commonMisconceptions: Over-generalising to subtraction (thinking 5−3 = 3−5) — the key error this topic must pre-empt.
Treating a+b and b+a as different facts to learn separately.
Believing the answer changes with order because the counting process feels different.
Applying 'swap them' to word problems where order encodes meaning (start/change).
Not using commutativity strategically (counting on from the smaller number, doing more work).

learn.summary: For ages 6-7, teach the commutative property of addition structurally: the same two amounts combine to the same whole whichever order they are taken (3+8 = 8+3), then exploit this to count on from the larger addend. Deliberately contrast subtraction (5−3 ≠ 3−5) so children do not over-generalise 'you can swap them'. The core insight is invariance (the addition total holds under reordering) versus change (the subtraction result shifts), and children should justify why, not just recite a rule.

activities.title: Swap bench: watch the addition total hold
feedback: If the child expects the total to change after swapping: rebuild both orders on the SAME set of objects so there is visibly one unchanging quantity combined two ways.
If the child says 5−3 and 3−5 are the same: show that 3 cannot have 5 removed (you run out), while 5−3 = 2 can be done — so order is load-bearing for take-away.
Reinforce by asking them to predict the swapped total before revealing it, then confirm it matches.
activities.rationale: A model that is literally unchanged by reordering (same rods, same part-whole) lets children see commutativity as structural rather than a memorised rule, and contrasting subtraction in the same model targets the main over-generalisation error.
sourceClaims: Y2 pupils show that addition of two numbers can be done in any order (commutative) and subtraction cannot.
Commutativity is best shown structurally (same quantity rearranged) and contrasted with non-commutative subtraction to prevent over-generalisation.
learnerActions: Combine two bars or rods — one of 3 and one of 8 — into a single total bar, and note the total (11).
Swap the two parts so 8 comes first and 3 second, and check whether the total bar's length changes.
On a number line, trace 8 then count on 3, and separately 3 then count on 8, and mark where each lands.
Say aloud what stayed the same and what moved: the parts traded places but the whole did not change.
Switch to subtraction: build 5 then remove 3, then try 3 then remove 5, and describe what happens when you try to take 5 from 3.
activities.intendedInsight: Reordering the two addends rearranges the parts but leaves the whole unchanged, so a+b = b+a; subtraction starts from one amount and removes the other, so swapping changes what you begin with and the result changes.

activities.title: Count on from the bigger number
feedback: If the child recounts from scratch instead of reusing the known fact: build both orders on the same counters to show it is one unchanging total, then practise stating the swapped fact immediately.
If the child counts on from the smaller number: compare how many steps each order takes to make the efficiency visible.
activities.rationale: Putting the property to work shows it reduces fact load and makes calculation easier, linking commutativity to fluency rather than leaving it as an abstract statement.
sourceClaims: 1.OA.3: apply properties of operations as strategies, including the commutative property of addition.
learnerActions: Given 3+8, decide which number to start from so there is less counting on to do, and explain your choice.
Count on from the larger addend to reach the total, then check against counting on from the smaller to confirm they agree.
Try 2+9: say which order you would count on from and why.
State the matching fact instantly: if you know 8+3, say 3+8 without recounting.
activities.intendedInsight: Because order does not change an addition total, you can always start from the larger number and count on the smaller one, which takes fewer steps (unless the two numbers are equal, as in 6+6) — commutativity is a calculation-saving strategy, and knowing one fact gives you its partner.

activities.title: Convince me: why addition swaps but subtraction doesn't
feedback: If the child claims 8−5 = 5−8: have them physically attempt to take 8 from a pile of 5 — it cannot be done — and name addition as the only one of the two that is commutative.
If the justification is 'because that's the rule': ask for a drawing or counter arrangement that shows the whole staying the same.
activities.rationale: The objective includes justifying why addition commutes but subtraction does not; prompting the child to explain and to test the claim on subtraction develops that reasoning directly through the structural contrast.
sourceClaims: Commutativity is best shown structurally (same quantity rearranged) and contrasted with non-commutative subtraction to prevent over-generalisation.
learnerActions: Argue why 3+8 must equal 8+3, using a drawing or a rearrangement of objects rather than just asserting the rule.
Test whether the same swap works for take-away: predict, then model 8−5 and 5−8 with counters and report what happens.
Consider 6+6: does order matter here, and what does that tell you about the rule?
State in your own words which operation can be reordered and why the other cannot.
activities.intendedInsight: Addition combines the same two amounts whichever order you take them, so the whole is unchanged; subtraction removes one amount from another, so swapping changes the starting amount and the result. Justifying this builds reasoning beyond recall.

activities.title: True/false and matching checks
feedback: If a subtraction pair is marked true: return to counters to show the results differ (5−3 = 2, but with 3 counters you run out and cannot take 5 away).
If the child cannot pick the efficient order: compare the number of count-on steps for each option.
activities.rationale: True/false, matching and strategy-choice items assess the property and the non-commutativity of subtraction. These recognition items check understanding but do not on their own elicit the child rearranging quantities or justifying; pair them with the swap and justification activities.
learnerActions: Decide whether statements are true or false: is 3+8 = 8+3? is 5−3 = 3−5?
Match each addition to its swapped partner that gives the same total.
Choose which order is easier to count on from for a given sum, and say why.
activities.intendedInsight: Addition statements hold when the order is swapped; subtraction statements do not. Recognising this consolidates the distinction and the strategic use of counting on from the larger number.

constraints: Show commutativity structurally — the same quantity rearranged — not as a rule to memorise.
Always include the subtraction contrast (e.g. 5−3 vs 3−5); omitting it risks children over-generalising 'you can swap them'.
Watch for word-problem contexts where order encodes meaning (start/change); 'swap them' should not be applied there.

Recognition-only items (true/false, matching, multiple choice) assess understanding but do not by themselves elicit the child independently rearranging quantities or justifying; use them alongside construction and explanation tasks.

A static side-by-side of 3+8 and 8+3 with the same objects can anchor the property, but it does not let the child perform the swap and watch the total hold; treat it as a scaffold toward hands-on or responsive work.
When demonstrating 5−8 or 3−5 with young children, frame it as 'you run out / cannot take that many away' rather than introducing negative numbers as a target concept.
When contrasting a subtraction pair, keep the two numbers consistent across the action and its feedback (e.g. 5−3 vs 3−5), so the 'you run out' example matches the pair the child is working with.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original labelled a live invariance-vs-change contrast as 'impossible statically' and said 3D 'adds nothing'; these are catalog-fit claims, not established necessity. They have been softened to scoped affordances (a static image cannot be manipulated but can still anchor the property).

Of the three cited sources, two are marked unverified in the source row (CCSS-M 1.OA.3 and the NCETM mastery claim); only the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified. Treat citation strength accordingly.

The assessment's probe '5 − 8' and 'take 5 cubes and try to remove 8' edges toward negative numbers; for ages 6-7 this is best handled as 'cannot be done / goes below what you have' rather than teaching negatives, which has been reflected in the constraints.

Independent re-audit confirmed Activity 1's subtraction feedback now matches its stated 5−3/3−5 pair ('3 cannot have 5 removed'), Activity 3 consistently uses the 8−5/5−8 pair, and all arithmetic (3+8=8+3=11, 2+9, 5−3=2, 8−5=3) is correct; no remaining internal contradictions or unsupported categorical modality claims were found.

assess.poeTask: Predict whether 5 − 8 gives the same answer as 8 − 5. Say your prediction and WHY first. Then take 8 cubes and remove 5, and take 5 cubes and try to remove 8. What happened, and what does it tell you about doing subtraction 'in any order'?
probeDeeper: Why does swapping the two numbers not change the total in an addition?
You said 8 − 5 isn't the same as 5 − 8 — show me with counters why not.
What about 6 + 6 — does order matter there? What does that tell you about the rule?
For 2 + 9, which order would you choose to count on from, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: 5 + 8 = 13 (the same, because order doesn't change an addition). But 8 − 5 and 5 − 8 are NOT the same: 8 − 5 = 3, while 5 − 8 cannot be done with these counters / goes below zero. Reason: addition combines the same two amounts whichever order you take them; subtraction starts from one amount and removes the other, so swapping changes what you begin with.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'You can do any sum in any order' — over-applies commutativity to subtraction, claiming 5 − 8 = 8 − 5 = 3.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model 8−5 and 5−8 with counters — you cannot take 8 from a pile of 5; order matters. Name addition as the only one of the two that is commutative.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — 8 − 5 and 5 − 8 both make 3.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: asserts subtraction gives the same answer whichever way round.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'I'd better count it again' — does not trust that swapping preserves the total, so recomputes 5 + 8 from one instead of using the known fact.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show both orders built on the SAME set of counters or the same bar; the total is one unchanging quantity. Practise stating the swapped fact instantly.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Counts all / counts on from scratch rather than stating 13 immediately.

responseLevels.gap: Recomputes both additions and/or thinks order changes an addition total, or claims subtraction is commutative.
responseLevels.full: States the addition total is unchanged because the same amounts are combined, uses commutativity to count on from the larger addend, AND correctly denies that subtraction is commutative, justifying with counters.
responseLevels.partial: Knows addition works in any order and uses it to count on from the larger, but over-generalises to subtraction OR cannot explain why the total is unchanged.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I know that 8 + 5 = 13. So what is 5 + 8? And does the same trick work for taking away — do 8 − 5 and 5 − 8 give the same answer? Tell me why.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child running a shallow 'any order works' rule gives the addition right AND wrongly says 8−5 = 5−8; a child who understands commutativity as 'the same quantities combined' restricts it to addition and rejects it for subtraction. The addition half is easy for everyone — the subtraction contrast is what separates real understanding from an over-applied slogan.

pedagogy.summary: This Y6 topic consolidates three configurations of angle facts at their sharpest: angles at a point (sum 360°), angles on a straight line (sum 180°), and — the new element — vertically opposite angles (EQUAL). The pedagogical crux is getting children to hold TWO relationships apart on the same intersecting-lines diagram: the OPPOSITE pair is equal, while each ADJACENT pair (on a straight line) is supplementary (sums to 180°). Confusing which pair does which is the characteristic error. The NCETM's recommended route is a dynamic one — two hinged sticks crossing at a point — so children SEE that as one angle grows its vertically opposite partner grows with it and stays equal, while the neighbour shrinks to keep the straight line at 180°. The signature task is 'given one angle, what else do you know?', reasoning out and JUSTIFYING every other angle from the two rules.
bestPractices: Surface both relationships side by side on one crossing-lines diagram: 'opposite = equal' AND 'adjacent (on a straight line) = supplementary', so children see they are different claims, not the same one (NCETM).

Use a hinged two-sticks / dynamic-geometry model: as one angle opens, its vertically opposite partner opens equally and the adjacent angle closes — the equality is seen to be invariant, not memorised.
Teach with 'given one angle, find and justify the others': mark one angle (e.g. 43°) at an intersection and have the child deduce and NAME the rule for each remaining angle.
Insist on reasoned language — 'this angle is 130° BECAUSE vertically opposite angles are equal' / '…because angles on a straight line sum to 180°' — not shape mnemonics.
Vary orientation: present tilted intersections (neither line horizontal) so 'vertically opposite' is understood as sharing the vertex, not as up-and-down.
Derive vertically-opposite-equal from the straight-line rule (both angles are 180° minus the shared neighbour) rather than adding it as a separate fact to memorise.
keyRepresentations: Two straight lines crossing at a point, forming two pairs of equal opposite angles and two straight lines of supplementary angles
Hinged two-sticks / dynamic model where opposite angles stay equal as the crossing angle changes
'Given one angle, find the rest' diagram (e.g. 43° marked, three unknowns)
Angles-at-a-point (360°) and angles-on-a-line (180°) diagrams as the two 'wholes'
commonMisconceptions: Confuses the two relationships — applies the straight-line 180° rule to the opposite pair, giving the vertically opposite angle as 180° minus the known angle instead of equal to it.
Over-generalises 'opposite angles are equal' to conclude all four angles at the intersection are equal, ignoring the supplementary straight-line pairs.
Attaches 'vertically opposite' to up–down orientation, so fails to recognise the opposite pair when the lines are tilted, or mislabels which angles are opposite.
Carries over the wrong whole — uses 180° for angles at a point (or 360° on a straight line).

learn.summary: Year 6 geometry consolidating three angle configurations: angles at a point (sum 360°), angles on a straight line (sum 180°), and the new element — vertically opposite angles (equal). The pedagogical crux is holding TWO relationships apart on one intersecting-lines diagram: the opposite pair is EQUAL, while each adjacent pair (on a straight line) is SUPPLEMENTARY (sums to 180°). The signature task is 'given one angle, find and justify every other angle', naming the rule used each time. Deriving 'opposite = equal' from the straight-line rule (both angles equal 180° minus the shared neighbour) is preferred to memorising it as a separate fact. Orientation should be varied — tilted intersections — so 'vertically opposite' is understood as two angles opposite each other across the shared vertex (sharing no arm), not as up-and-down.

activities.title: Crossing-lines reasoner: watch the opposite pair stay equal
feedback: If a learner expected the angle opposite 130° to be '180 − 130 = 50°', highlight that this value belongs to the ADJACENT angle (on the straight line); the OPPOSITE angle tracks at 130°. Show both on the diagram at once.
If a learner thinks all four angles are equal, draw attention to one straight line and its two angles summing to 180°: a = a and b = b, but a ≠ b unless the lines are perpendicular.

If a learner loses the opposite pair once the figure is tilted, clarify that 'vertically opposite' means opposite each other across the shared vertex (vertex, not up-and-down), with no arm in common, and rotate the same intersection through several orientations while tracking the pair.
activities.rationale: NCETM recommends a hinged two-sticks / dynamic model so children SEE that as one angle increases its vertically opposite partner increases equally while the neighbour closes to hold the straight line at 180°; manipulating the crossing angle makes the invariance observable rather than asserted. OPTIONAL interactive features that make this concrete: draggable crossing lines, all four angles labelled with live-updating values, the opposite pair highlighted as it stays equal, and each straight line showing its two angles summing to 180°.
sourceClaims: Vertically opposite angles are equal, learned at Upper Key Stage 2 ('recognise angles where they meet at a point, are on a straight line, or are vertically opposite, and find missing angles'); students must distinguish pairs of EQUAL angles (vertically opposite) from pairs of SUPPLEMENTARY angles (adjacent, summing to 180°); a hinged two-sticks model shows that as one angle increases so does its opposite and that they must be equal; the key task is 'given one angle, find and justify the others'.
learnerActions: Work with two straight lines crossing at a point, with all four angles labelled.

Rotate one line and observe how all four angle values change together: each pair of vertically opposite angles grows and shrinks TOGETHER and stays equal, while each adjacent angle changes so that the two angles on each straight line always sum to 180°.
Set the crossing angle to several values and each time read off the opposite pair, confirming it matches the given angle exactly (not 180° minus it).

Deliberately predict what the angle opposite a 130° angle will be; set the crossing angle to 130° and check the opposite angle reads exactly 130° rather than 50°, then rotate and check the opposite angle keeps matching the changing angle.

Repeat with the whole figure tilted so neither line is horizontal or vertical, confirming the opposite pair is still identified as the two angles opposite each other across the vertex, sharing no arm.
activities.intendedInsight: As an intersection turns, vertically opposite angles stay equal while each adjacent pair stays supplementary — these are two different claims about the same diagram, and 'vertically opposite' means opposite each other across the shared vertex (sharing no arm), not pointing up-and-down.

activities.title: Given one angle, find and justify the rest
feedback: If a learner gives the angle opposite 130° as 50° or justifies it with 'angles on a straight line', the rules have been swapped: the opposite pair is equal; only the adjacent pair is supplementary.
If a learner subtracts from 180° at a point, re-anchor the whole: a full turn around a point is 360°. Check: 360 − (150 + 90) = 120°, not 180 − (150 + 90).
If values are given without justification, ask 'which rule tells you that?' before accepting the answer — a correct number reasoned from the rule is the goal, not a lucky guess.
activities.rationale: NCETM's signature task 'given one angle, find and justify the others' forces deployment of BOTH relationships and makes any confusion immediately visible. Requiring the named rule for each angle distinguishes reasoning from guessing. Common Core notes angle measure is additive: unknown angles at a point and on a straight line are found by adding/subtracting known angles. Tilting the figure prevents up-and-down intuition standing in for reasoning.
sourceClaims: Vertically opposite angles are equal, learned at Upper Key Stage 2 ('recognise angles where they meet at a point, are on a straight line, or are vertically opposite, and find missing angles'); students must distinguish pairs of EQUAL angles (vertically opposite) from pairs of SUPPLEMENTARY angles (adjacent, summing to 180°); a hinged two-sticks model shows that as one angle increases so does its opposite and that they must be equal; the key task is 'given one angle, find and justify the others'.
Angle measure is additive; unknown angles at a point (360°) and on a straight line (180°) are found by adding/subtracting the known angles (4.MD.7).
learnerActions: On a tilted intersection with one angle marked (e.g. 43°), work out each of the other three angles.

For EACH angle, state both the value AND the rule that justifies it — e.g. 'this angle is 43° BECAUSE vertically opposite angles are equal' or 'this angle is 137° BECAUSE angles on a straight line sum to 180°'.
Repeat with a different given angle (e.g. 130°, giving an opposite angle of 130° and adjacent angles of 50° each).
Switch to an angles-at-a-point diagram: given two angles (e.g. 150° and 90°) find the unknown as 360 − (150 + 90) = 120°, naming the 360° whole.
Write down every equation you can for an intersection diagram, surfacing both the equal pairs and the two 180° straight lines.
activities.intendedInsight: Every unknown angle at an intersection or point can be deduced and JUSTIFIED from a named rule, and the correct 'whole' must be chosen — 360° at a point, 180° on a straight line.

activities.title: Sort angle pairs: equal or supplementary
feedback: A choice of '180 − known' for a vertically opposite angle reveals the straight-line rule wrongly applied to the opposite pair; mark it and show the opposite pair is equal.
If the derivation is unclear, walk through it: angle A and its opposite each sit with the same neighbour B on a straight line, so A = 180 − B and the opposite = 180 − B, hence they are equal.
Errors on tilted items signal orientation-dependence; return to rotating a single intersection and tracking the pair.
activities.rationale: Classification and fill-in practice with a deliberate '180 − known' distractor targets the characteristic error directly and checks the two relationships are held apart. This supports and assesses the reasoning but, on its own, presents fixed diagrams the learner cannot manipulate, so pair it with a dynamic model to let the equality be observed changing. Deriving the equality rather than memorising it is an NCETM best practice.
sourceClaims: Vertically opposite angles are equal, learned at Upper Key Stage 2 ('recognise angles where they meet at a point, are on a straight line, or are vertically opposite, and find missing angles'); students must distinguish pairs of EQUAL angles (vertically opposite) from pairs of SUPPLEMENTARY angles (adjacent, summing to 180°); a hinged two-sticks model shows that as one angle increases so does its opposite and that they must be equal; the key task is 'given one angle, find and justify the others'.
learnerActions: Look at a crossing-lines diagram with the four angles labelled and sort each pair of angles into 'vertically opposite — equal' or 'adjacent (straight line) — supplementary'.
Answer which rule applies to a specifically named pair, choosing between 'equal' and 'sums to 180°'.
Fill in the value of each unknown angle, resisting the tempting '180 − known' value when the angle is actually the opposite (equal) one.
Try a tilted-intersection item where orientation cannot be used to guess, and a point-diagram item that uses the 360° whole.
Explain WHY vertically opposite angles are equal: both equal 180° minus their shared straight-line neighbour, so they equal each other.
activities.intendedInsight: Classifying each pair by its relationship — and deriving 'opposite = equal' from the straight-line rule — cements that the two claims are distinct and reasoned, not interchangeable.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal angle relationships (vocabulary scaffold)
feedback: Confirm correct naming; where a learner swaps the rules, re-show the straight-line pair and the opposite pair side by side.
Encourage stating the rule before revealing, so the reveal confirms reasoning rather than supplying it.
activities.rationale: A static reveal can introduce the vocabulary and the paired structure and can be used during teaching, but it shows fixed values and cannot let the learner watch the opposite pair stay equal as the angle changes, so the invariance is told rather than observed. Use it to seed language, then move to a manipulable model and to reasoning tasks.
sourceClaims: Vertically opposite angles are equal, learned at Upper Key Stage 2 ('recognise angles where they meet at a point, are on a straight line, or are vertically opposite, and find missing angles'); students must distinguish pairs of EQUAL angles (vertically opposite) from pairs of SUPPLEMENTARY angles (adjacent, summing to 180°); a hinged two-sticks model shows that as one angle increases so does its opposite and that they must be equal; the key task is 'given one angle, find and justify the others'.
learnerActions: On a static crossing-lines diagram, tap an angle to reveal its vertically opposite partner (equal) and its two straight-line (adjacent) partners (each supplementary to it).
Use a 'given 130°, what are the other three?' reveal: predict each value and its rule, then lift the flap to check (opposite 130°, adjacent 50° each).
Name each revealed pair aloud with its rule before moving on.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeds the vocabulary — 'vertically opposite' vs 'adjacent/straight-line' — and the paired structure of an intersection.

constraints: Learners must JUSTIFY each angle with its named rule, not just state values; a correct number without reasoning does not demonstrate understanding.
Both relationships must appear on the SAME intersecting-lines diagram so children see they are different claims: opposite = equal, adjacent = supplementary.
Vary orientation with tilted intersections so 'vertically opposite' is understood as two angles opposite each other across the shared vertex (sharing no arm), not up-and-down.
Keep the two 'wholes' distinct: 360° at a point, 180° on a straight line.
Prefer deriving 'vertically opposite angles are equal' from the straight-line rule over memorising it as a separate fact.
The static tap-to-reveal image is a vocabulary scaffold only: it shows fixed values and cannot display the equality holding as the angle changes.

Fill-in and sorting practice can score reasoning and target the characteristic error, but on their own present non-manipulable diagrams; pair them with a dynamic model so the invariance can be observed.

Vertically opposite angles are always equal; an adjacent angle equals the given one only in the special perpendicular (90°) case, where all four angles become 90° — do not let learners generalise all four angles to be equal otherwise.
OPTIONAL interactive features (draggable lines, live angle readouts, highlighting, tilt) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory requirements.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row claimed a 3D environment 'adds no conceptual value' and that a character/dialogue 'cannot' teach the distinction. These are categorical catalog-fit opinions, not established pedagogical laws, and have been dropped rather than propagated; a conversation could still support reasoning talk, and a 2D dynamic model is proposed on its stated affordance (manipulable, live-updating) without claiming other media are incapable.

The legacy recommendation's strong framing ('it must be manipulated to be felt', opposite pair 'locked equal') was softened: manipulation makes the invariance observable but is one effective route, not the only possible one.

Self-audit arithmetic checks all passed: angle opposite 130° = 130°; adjacent = 180 − 130 = 50°; at a point 360 − (150 + 90) = 120°; opposite 43° = 43°, adjacent = 137°. The error value '50°' for the opposite angle is retained only as a labelled misconception/distractor, never as a correct answer.

Confirmed the special-case caveat: the two adjacent angles equal the given one only when the lines are perpendicular (all four become 90°); the diagnostic counterexample about 90° crossings was preserved in substance within constraints and feedback.

The DfE curriculum claim was removed from activity 1's sourceClaims because it is a general topic/necessity requirement and does not support that activity's specific dynamic-model teaching principle; it remains part of the source record but is not cited as supporting a teaching principle in any activity.

Activity 4's NCETM sourceClaim is retained because the activity's learning target is distinguishing the equal pair from the supplementary pair, which the claim directly supports; the static-medium limitation is stated as an affordance observation, not as a source-backed efficacy claim.

probeDeeper: 'You said this angle is 130° — which rule tells you that, and which rule tells you the one next to it?' — checks the two relationships are held apart, not blurred.

Counterexample: 'If I told you these lines crossed at exactly 90°, would the opposite angle still equal the given one? Would the neighbours?' — probes that equal-opposite always holds while supplementary-opposite is only the perpendicular special case.
'I've turned the whole diagram on its side. Which angles are vertically opposite now?' — tests that opposite-ness survives rotation (not orientation-bound).
'Write down every equation you can for this diagram' — surfaces whether the child sees both the equal pairs and the 180° straight lines (NCETM 'what else do you know?').
assess.correctAnswer: At the intersection: the angle vertically opposite the 130° is 130° (vertically opposite angles are equal); the two adjacent angles are each 50° (angles on a straight line sum to 180°, 180−130). At the point: unknown = 360 − (150+90) = 120°. Justifies each with the correct named rule and is not misled by the tilt.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses the two relationships — applies the straight-line rule to the opposite pair, giving the vertically opposite angle as 180 − 130 = 50° instead of 130°.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Put both relationships on the same diagram with the hinged model: show the opposite pair staying EQUAL as it turns while each straight line holds at 180°; name which pair is which explicitly.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: States the angle opposite 130° as 50°, or justifies it with 'angles on a straight line' when the two angles are actually the opposite pair; may get the genuinely adjacent angle right, showing the rules are swapped.

errorPatterns.pattern: Over-generalises 'opposite angles are equal' — declares all four angles at the intersection equal (all 130°), ignoring the supplementary straight-line pairs.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw attention to each straight line and its two angles summing to 180°; show that a=a and b=b but a≠b unless the lines are perpendicular.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels every angle 130°; no angle is given as 50°; cannot say why the neighbours differ.

errorPatterns.pattern: Ties 'vertically opposite' to up–down orientation — on the tilted diagram fails to identify the opposite pair, or insists the term needs a vertical line.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Clarify 'vertical' means sharing the vertex, not up–down; rotate the same intersection through several orientations so the opposite pair is tracked as the figure turns.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cannot pick out the vertically opposite pair once the figure is tilted, or points to an adjacent pair as 'opposite'; comments about the lines not being upright.

errorPatterns.pattern: Carries over the wrong whole at a point — subtracts the known angles from 180° instead of 360°.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor the whole to the configuration — a full point is a whole turn 360° — before computing; no reteaching of vertically-opposite needed.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the point diagram gives 180 − (150+90) or an answer 180° short of 120°; the intersection work may be correct.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot find the other angles reliably: guesses, uses no named rule, or cannot identify the opposite pair; wrong whole at a point.
responseLevels.full: Finds all angles at an intersection using BOTH relationships correctly, justifies each with the named rule, is unfazed by tilt, keeps the point (360°) and line (180°) wholes distinct, and can explain WHY vertically opposite angles are equal (via the shared straight-line neighbour).
responseLevels.partial: Finds the vertically opposite angle equal in a simple upright cross and can state 'they add to 180°' for a straight line, but blurs the two on a tilted diagram (opposite comes out as 180−given, or all four equal), or gives values without justifying them — lists angles without relating the equal and supplementary structures.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Draw two straight lines crossing at a point, TILTED so neither line is horizontal or vertical, and mark just one of the four angles as 130°. Say: 'Find the other three angles, and tell me how you know each one.' Then show a second diagram — angles round a point marked 150°, 90° and an unknown — and ask for the unknown. Watch which rule they use for each angle and whether tilt throws them; do not prompt.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: One given angle forces the child to deploy BOTH relationships — equal for the opposite, supplementary for the adjacent — so confusing them is immediately visible (the opposite comes out as 50°, or all four as 130°). The deliberate tilt separates a child who understands 'vertically opposite = shares the vertex' from one who relies on up–down orientation. The second diagram checks the point (360°) rule is not swapped with 180°. Requiring the justification distinguishes a correct answer reasoned from the rule from a lucky guess.
