pedagogy.summary: Solving a linear equation means finding the value of the unknown that makes the two sides genuinely equal, by doing the SAME operation to both sides until the unknown is isolated. The relational meaning of the equals sign is the foundation: each written line must be a true equality, not a running commentary strung together with '='. The persistent errors — treating subtraction as commutative, refusing negative solutions, mishandling the unknown on both sides, and operating on one side only — are addressed with a balance model, inverse operations, and a substitution check.
bestPractices: Teach 'do the same to both sides' with a balance model so operations that keep the scale level are felt as legal and one-sided moves as illegal.
Insist on ONE valid equality per line — forbid run-on chains like 5−x=6=x=−1; each line must itself be true.
Isolate the unknown with inverse operations; for the unknown on both sides, gather it on one side by subtracting the smaller term from both.
Always check by substituting the solution back into the ORIGINAL equation.
Handle negatives explicitly (number line / zero-pairs) rather than assuming the answer must be positive; discuss whether an equation has one, none, or infinitely many solutions.
keyRepresentations: Balance scale (unknown-boxes and unit-weights; same action on both pans)
Algebra tiles with zero-pairs for negatives and unknown-on-both-sides
Inverse-operation / function-machine unwinding
Number line for negative solutions
Substitution-back check
commonMisconceptions: Treats subtraction as commutative: 5−x=6 solved as x−5=6 giving x=11.
Considers positive numbers only, so rejects or never reaches a negative solution.
Run-on / operational equals sign: writes 5−x=6=x=−1 or 3x−5=2x=x=5, using '=' to mean 'and then'.
Mishandles the unknown on both sides (8x−6=2x): stops at 'unlike terms' or subtracts incorrectly.
Performs an operation on one side only, unbalancing the equation.
Thinks every equation has exactly one solution (misses none/infinitely-many).

learn.summary: Solving a linear equation means finding the value of the unknown that makes both sides genuinely equal, by doing the SAME operation to both sides until the unknown is isolated. The relational meaning of '=' is the foundation: each written line must itself be a true equality, not a running commentary strung together with '='. Target the persistent errors — treating subtraction as commutative, refusing negative solutions, mishandling the unknown on both sides, and operating on one side only — with a balance model, inverse operations, explicit handling of negatives, and a substitution check back into the original equation.

activities.title: Balance-scale solver: keep both pans level
feedback: If a one-sided action is attempted: the scale tips because the two sides are no longer equal; redo the same action on both pans.

When isolating 8x − 6 = 2x: after removing 2 x-boxes from each side you have 6x − 6 = 0; adding 6 to both sides gives 6x = 6; dividing both sides by 6 gives x = 1. Substitute back: 8(1) − 6 = 2 and 2(1) = 2 — equal, so x = 1 checks.
For 5 − x = 6: using zero-pairs gives −x = 1, so x = −1. Substitute back: 5 − (−1) = 6 — correct; note 5 − x is NOT the same as x − 5.
activities.rationale: 'Do the same to both sides' is a physical intuition made legal-feeling by a balance the learner must keep level; illegal one-sided moves visibly tip it, so the rule is enforced by the model. Dragging actions onto both pans, live tipping, and zero-pair anti-weights are offered as concrete ways to make the balancing mechanism visible; they are examples, not the only possible setup, and are proposed rather than validated as superior to other media.
sourceClaims: Trials show students solving linear equations assume subtraction is commutative (5−x=6 → x=11), consider positive numbers only, misuse the equals sign in run-on chains (5−x=6=x=−1; 3x−5=2x=x=5), and mishandle equations with the unknown on both sides (8x−6=2x); many also assume every equation has exactly one solution.
Children frequently read the equals sign operationally ('work out the answer') rather than relationally (the two sides are equal), which underlies run-on chains and difficulty balancing equations.
learnerActions: Represent an equation as two pans: unknown-boxes (x) and unit-weights, using 'anti-weights' (zero-pairs) for any negative amount. Set up 8x − 6 = 2x with the −6 shown as six anti-weights on that pan.

Choose an action (add or remove the same number of units, using zero-pairs where a pan has none to remove; remove an x-box; halve everything) and apply it to BOTH pans at once; watch the scale stay level.
Try a one-sided action on purpose and observe that the scale tips — that move is not allowed because it breaks the equality.

Solve 8x − 6 = 2x: remove 2 x-boxes from each pan to reach 6x − 6 = 0, then add 6 units to each pan (cancelling the six anti-weights) to reach 6x = 6, then divide both pans into 6 equal groups (÷6) to reach x = 1.

Use an anti-x-box for −x, plus unit zero-pairs, to model 5 − x = 6: remove 5 units from both pans to reach −x = 1, then swap every item on both pans for its opposite (multiply both sides by −1) to reach x = −1, so the negative solution is something you build and see rather than distrust.
Write down each balanced state as its own line — one true equality per line.
activities.intendedInsight: The only way to keep the scale level while stripping it down to a single x is to mirror every move on both sides — that mirroring IS the solving method, and a negative result is a legitimate, visible outcome.

activities.title: One true equality per line: fix the run-on equals sign
feedback: In 5 − x = 6 = x = −1, the middle '6 = x' is false (6 does not equal −1); the valid working is 5 − x = 6 → −x = 1 → x = −1, one true equality per line.

For 3x − 5 = 2x: subtract 2x from both sides to get x − 5 = 0, then add 5 to both sides to get x = 5. Check: 3(5) − 5 = 10 and 2(5) = 10 — equal, so x = 5. (Note the first item here, 5 − x = 6, has solution x = −1; the two tasks are different equations.)
activities.rationale: The operational (left-to-right 'compute') reading of '=' underlies run-on chains; reading written maths aloud and reformatting into vertical true equalities confronts that reading directly.
sourceClaims: Children frequently read the equals sign operationally ('work out the answer') rather than relationally (the two sides are equal), which underlies run-on chains and difficulty balancing equations.

Trials show students solving linear equations assume subtraction is commutative (5−x=6 → x=11), consider positive numbers only, misuse the equals sign in run-on chains (5−x=6=x=−1; 3x−5=2x=x=5), and mishandle equations with the unknown on both sides (8x−6=2x); many also assume every equation has exactly one solution.
learnerActions: Read aloud, left to right, the chain 5 − x = 6 = x = −1. Decide whether each '=' states a genuine equality (does 6 really equal x?).
Rewrite the working as a vertical chain where every single line is itself true: 5 − x = 6, then −x = 1, then x = −1.
Do the same for 3x − 5 = 2x: rewrite the run-on 3x − 5 = 2x = x = 5 as separate true lines, subtracting 2x from both sides first (3x − 5 = 2x → x − 5 = 0 → x = 5), and check by substitution.
Spot the invalid line: given a worked solution containing a run-on chain, identify which '=' is false and correct it.
activities.intendedInsight: '=' means the two sides have equal value, not 'and then'. Every line of correct working must be a standalone true statement.

activities.title: Solve, then check by substitution; classify how many solutions
feedback: 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6 expands to 2x + 6 = 2x + 6, true for every x, so infinitely many solutions — an identity, not a single answer.
If substitution does not make both sides equal, the solution is wrong; retrace which line first stopped being a true equality.
activities.rationale: Substitution into the original equation makes correctness self-verifiable and pushes past guess-and-check; the identity 2(x+3)=2x+6 is a concrete counterexample to 'every equation has one solution'.
sourceClaims: Trials show students solving linear equations assume subtraction is commutative (5−x=6 → x=11), consider positive numbers only, misuse the equals sign in run-on chains (5−x=6=x=−1; 3x−5=2x=x=5), and mishandle equations with the unknown on both sides (8x−6=2x); many also assume every equation has exactly one solution.
KS3 pupils should use algebraic methods to solve linear equations in one variable, including all forms that require rearrangement.
learnerActions: Solve a set of equations by inverse operations, writing one true equality per line: start with 5 − x = 6 and 8x − 6 = 2x, then extend to equations with brackets and fractional/negative coefficients.
For each solution, substitute it back into the ORIGINAL equation and confirm both sides are equal.
Solve 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6 and decide what happens: after expanding the bracket, both sides are identical (2x + 6 = 2x + 6), so every value of x works — infinitely many solutions.
Construct or examine an equation that simplifies to a false statement (e.g. a contradiction) and recognise it has no solution.
Sort equations into 'one solution', 'no solution', 'infinitely many solutions'.
activities.intendedInsight: A solved equation must survive a substitution check in the original; and not every equation has exactly one solution — some have none and some have infinitely many.

activities.title: Sequenced steps and worked-solution annotation (supporting practice)
feedback: 3x + 5 = 20: subtract 5 from both sides (3x = 15), then divide both sides by 3 (x = 5); check 3(5) + 5 = 20. ✓
If a line in the annotated solution alters only one side, it is invalid — the equality no longer holds; the matching move must act on both sides.
A static worked solution can display one correct balanced chain, but it does not itself let the learner perform the balancing; pair it with the balance-scale activity where the construction happens.
activities.rationale: Sequencing and fill-in-the-line tasks make the stepwise structure explicit and can surface run-on-equals and one-sided errors through forced choices; annotation of a fixed solution can display a model chain and support recognition/consolidation, but recognition alone does not elicit the learner's own production of the balancing moves.
sourceClaims: Trials show students solving linear equations assume subtraction is commutative (5−x=6 → x=11), consider positive numbers only, misuse the equals sign in run-on chains (5−x=6=x=−1; 3x−5=2x=x=5), and mishandle equations with the unknown on both sides (8x−6=2x); many also assume every equation has exactly one solution.
learnerActions: Order the correct solving steps for 3x + 5 = 20 from a scrambled set, stating what is done to both sides at each step.
Fill in each missing line of the working for 8x − 6 = 2x, keeping one true equality per line.
For a step in progress, state what operation should be applied to both sides next.
Examine an annotated worked solution and, line by line, name the inverse operation applied to both sides; then flag any invalid line (e.g. a run-on chain like 5 − x = 6 = x = −1).
activities.intendedInsight: Solving is a reproducible sequence of 'same operation to both sides' moves, and being able to name each inverse operation and reject invalid lines consolidates the procedure.

constraints: Each written line must be a single true equality; forbid run-on chains like 5 − x = 6 = x = −1 or 3x − 5 = 2x = x = 5 where the '=' means 'and then'.
Every operation must be applied to BOTH sides; operating on one side only unbalances the equation and makes the line false.
Handle negatives explicitly (number line or zero-pairs) rather than assuming the answer must be positive; 5 − x is not the same as x − 5.
On a balance model, represent any negative amount (e.g. the −6 in 8x − 6) with anti-weights (zero-pairs) so the pans and the written equality stay consistent.
For the unknown on both sides, gather it on one side by subtracting the same term from both sides (e.g. subtract 2x from 8x − 6 = 2x to reach 6x − 6 = 0).
Always check by substituting the solution back into the ORIGINAL equation.
Discuss that an equation may have one solution, no solution, or infinitely many (e.g. the identity 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6).

A fixed/annotated worked solution and ordering/fill-in tasks support recognition and consolidation but do not elicit the learner's own balancing; they complement, rather than replace, hands-on solving where the learner performs each move.
Prerequisite support for negative-number reasoning and collecting like terms may be needed before equations with negative/fractional coefficients or the unknown on both sides.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labels the balance-scale approach as uniquely able to 'force' discovery and claims 3D 'adds nothing' and that a static image 'cannot' fix the misconceptions. These are catalog-style comparative claims not established by the cited sources; they have been softened to a scoped proposal (balance model as a vivid way to make the rule visible) and the static worked solution retained as a consolidation/recognition support rather than dismissed.
The Kieran (1981) source is marked verified:false in the row; treat its support for the relational-equals principle as unconfirmed here.

Independent self-audit of worked examples: 5 − x = 6 → x = −1 (check 5 − (−1) = 6); 8x − 6 = 2x → x = 1 (check 8 − 6 = 2 = 2); 3x − 5 = 2x → x = 5 (check 10 = 10); 3x + 5 = 20 → x = 5 (check 20 = 20); 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6 is an identity. The incorrect misconception outputs (x = 11 for 5 − x = 6; the run-on chains) are presented only as errors to confront, never as valid answers.

Balance-scale walkthrough is coherent: after removing 2 x-boxes the state is 6x − 6 = 0, the −6 is modelled with anti-weights so adding 6 units to both pans cancels them to 6x = 6, then ÷6 gives x = 1. Activity 0 feedback was made explicit about the ÷6 step to match the learnerActions and the 'show every line' emphasis.

The diagnostic items 5 − x = 6 and 8x − 6 = 2x are reused across activities as teaching items; they are kept as distinct equations with distinct solutions (−1 and 1) to avoid confusion when both appear in one task.

probeDeeper: Check your answer to (a) by putting it back into 5 − x = 6 — does it work?
In (b), how do you know x = 1 is the ONLY solution and not just A solution? (pushes past guess-and-check)
You wrote 5−x=6=x=−1 — read that out loud left to right. Is 6 really equal to x? (confronts the run-on equals sign)
Here is 2(x+3) = 2x + 6 — solve it. What happens, and what does that tell you about how many solutions it has? (counterexample: an identity / infinitely many solutions)

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats subtraction as commutative / rejects negatives — solves 5−x=6 as if it were x−5=6 to get x=11, or insists 'you can't take x from 5 to make 6' and stops.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Substitute x=11 to show 5−11=−6≠6; rewrite as −x=1 and use a number line to reach x=−1; establish that 5−x is not x−5.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes x=11, or abandons the problem as impossible; does not consider a negative solution.

errorPatterns.pattern: Run-on / operational equals sign — writes 5−x=6=x=−1 or 3x−5=2x=x=5, using '=' to mean 'and then' rather than 'is equal to'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: One equation per line; read the written maths aloud left-to-right — 'does 6 really equal x?'; rewrite as a vertical chain of true equalities.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A single strung-together line whose equalities are not actually true when read left to right.

errorPatterns.pattern: Mishandles the unknown on both sides — for 8x−6=2x either stops at 'these aren't like terms' or subtracts wrongly (e.g. treats 8x−6 as 2x).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the balance model to remove 2x from each side, reaching 6x−6=0; then isolate x; check by substitution.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Does not subtract 2x from both sides; leaves the unknown on both sides or mis-collects.

errorPatterns.pattern: Operates on one side only — changes one side without doing the same to the other, unbalancing the equation.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Balance-scale model — every operation must act on both pans or the scale tips; redo the step on both sides.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A line where one side has been altered (a term added/removed) but the other has not, yet an '=' is kept.

responseLevels.gap: Treats subtraction or sides as swappable (x=11), operates on one side only, or strings steps together with '=' incorrectly; no valid balancing and answers fail a substitution check.
responseLevels.full: Solves equations with the unknown on both sides, negative/fractional coefficients and brackets by doing the same to both sides, writes one valid equality per line, checks by substituting into the original, and can classify an equation as having one, none, or infinitely many solutions.
responseLevels.partial: Solves one- and two-step equations with positive whole-number solutions by inverse operations, but breaks down with negatives, fractional coefficients, brackets, or the unknown on both sides, and may not check.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Hand the child this card and say 'solve these, showing every line of your working': (a) 5 − x = 6 and (b) 8x − 6 = 2x. Say nothing about method. Watch how they deal with the subtraction and the negative in (a), and how they gather the unknown from both sides in (b), and whether each line is a genuine equality.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The two items expose different faults on paper without a single question being asked: 5−x=6 catches treating subtraction as commutative (x=11) and refusing negatives; 8x−6=2x catches failure to gather the unknown from both sides and the run-on equals-sign chain. A child who is secure keeps the scale balanced, reaches x=−1 and x=1, and writes one true equality per line.

sources.claim: KS3 pupils should use algebraic methods to solve linear equations in one variable, including all forms that require rearrangement.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (KS3 Algebra)

sources.claim: Trials show students solving linear equations assume subtraction is commutative (5−x=6 → x=11), consider positive numbers only, misuse the equals sign in run-on chains (5−x=6=x=−1; 3x−5=2x=x=5), and mishandle equations with the unknown on both sides (8x−6=2x); many also assume every equation has exactly one solution.
sources.source: Mathematics Assessment Project — 'Solving Linear Equations in One Variable' Classroom Challenge (Common Issues table, teacher guide)

sources.claim: Children frequently read the equals sign operationally ('work out the answer') rather than relationally (the two sides are equal), which underlies run-on chains and difficulty balancing equations.
sources.source: Kieran, C. (1981). Concepts associated with the equality symbol. Educational Studies in Mathematics, 12(3).

pedagogy.summary: Composing 3-D shapes — stacking and combining solids to build new structures and composite shapes — develops through a well-charted progression from unsystematic stacking, through trial-and-error assembly, to composing WITH ANTICIPATION ('I know the cone goes on top'). It is best taught with plentiful block-building using real solids, where the teacher notices and gently nudges children toward the next level — asking them to predict which shape will fit before placing it and to describe their creation by its component solids. Matched building challenges pitched one level ahead move children forward more effectively than jumping straight to the target.
bestPractices: Give rich, open block-building with a range of solids (cubes, prisms, cylinders, cones) and let children build and knock down freely at first.
Nudge toward anticipation: 'Can you see which shape will fit on top before you place it?' — shifting from trial and error to planning.
Pitch challenges one level beyond the child's current building (e.g. from stacking identical blocks to combining a cone on a cylinder), scaffolding then fading support.
Ask the child to describe the composite by its parts — name each component solid and where it sits.
Attend to which faces sit flat: choosing a flat-faced solid for the base keeps a structure stable.
keyRepresentations: Real 3-D blocks and construction manipulatives
Target-picture cards of composites (cone-on-cylinder rocket, cube tower, house)
The stack ('on') relationship; flat-faced base vs rolling curved base
Component-labelled composite diagrams
commonMisconceptions: Adds blocks unsystematically and only recognises what it 'looks like' after building — no advance plan (a normal early trajectory level, not a fault).
Builds a composite but describes it only as one whole ('a rocket') and cannot name the component solids or their positions.
Places solids without regard to which faces are flat, so a cone or sphere used as a base makes the structure topple.

learn.summary: Children aged 6–7 learn to compose 3-D shapes by stacking and combining real solids (cubes, prisms, cylinders, cones, spheres) into composite structures. The target skill is a progression: from unsystematic stacking, through trial-and-error assembly, to composing WITH ANTICIPATION — knowing in advance which shape will fit ('the cone goes on top') and naming a build by its component solids and their positions. Hands-on block-building with challenges pitched one level ahead, plus prompts to predict and describe, carries children forward; because this is a procedural, construction-based goal, physical block-building is the core medium. An on-screen 3-D sandbox is an optional supplementary model that preserves stacking, balance and depth, while flat drag-and-combine and matching tasks are useful scaffolds for naming parts but do not exercise balance or anticipation.

activities.title: Build a rocket with real solids
feedback: If the child places shapes at random and names the result only afterwards, do not mark this wrong — it is an expected early level. Offer a challenge one step ahead and prompt 'can you see which shape will fit before you place it?'
If the child names only the whole ('a rocket') but not the parts, take the composite apart and name each solid together, then rebuild it, naming each shape as it goes on.

If the tower topples, look together at which faces rest on the table or on the shape below: a sphere rolls because it has no flat face, a cone balanced on its point has no flat face down, and a piece placed off-centre can tip over. So choose a flat-faced solid (a cube, prism, or cylinder on a flat face) for the base, keep each piece centred, and don't stack anything on a cone's point, rather than blaming the blocks.
Reinforce correct anticipation: when the child reaches for the cone before placing it, confirm the plan aloud ('yes — the cone fits on top of the cylinder').
activities.rationale: Composing is an action: building, balancing and anticipating are exercised by actual construction with solids, not by recognising a finished picture. The documented trajectory runs from trial-and-error, post-hoc recognition to composing with anticipation and advance planning, and the curriculum asks children to compose and model shapes by building from components.
sourceClaims: Composing 3-D shapes develops through levels — Stacker and Same-Shape Stacker (using the 'on' relationship), Piece Assembler and Picture Maker (building components, arches and enclosures by unsystematic trial and error), then Shape Composer (composing with anticipation, understanding what 3-D shape a combination will produce and building systematically).

Shape composition progresses from trial-and-error, post-hoc recognition (Piece Assembler, Picture Maker) to composing with anticipation and advance planning (Shape Composer); teaching contiguous trajectory levels, scaffolded one level ahead, produced greater learning than jumping to the target level (effect size .55).
Kindergarten geometry asks children to compose simple shapes to form larger shapes and to model shapes by building from components.
learnerActions: Offer a set of real 3-D blocks: cubes, a cylinder, a cone, some prisms, and a sphere.
Ask the child to build a rocket by combining shapes so that it stands up.
Before each placement, prompt: 'Which shape will fit on top before you place it? Where will it go and why does it fit?'
After building, ask the child to point to and name each shape used and say where it sits (e.g. 'a cylinder at the bottom, a cone on top').

Try using the sphere as the base (or balancing the cone on its point) and let the child notice that it rolls or will not support more shapes, then choose a flat-faced solid — a cube, prism, or cylinder resting on a flat face — for the base.
activities.intendedInsight: A composite is made of named component solids combined on purpose; resting flat faces down keeps a structure stable, and you can plan which shape fits before placing it rather than only recognising the result afterwards.

activities.title: Challenges pitched one level ahead
feedback: If the challenge is too hard, step back one level and rebuild success before advancing again.
Praise the planning talk ('I'll put the cone on top next'), not just the finished structure.
activities.rationale: Teaching contiguous trajectory levels, scaffolded one level ahead, produced greater learning than jumping to the target level in the cited study.
sourceClaims: Shape composition progresses from trial-and-error, post-hoc recognition (Piece Assembler, Picture Maker) to composing with anticipation and advance planning (Shape Composer); teaching contiguous trajectory levels, scaffolded one level ahead, produced greater learning than jumping to the target level (effect size .55).
learnerActions: Watch how the child currently builds to judge their level (free stacking, trial-and-error assembly, or anticipating).
Set a building challenge just one step beyond that level — for example, from stacking identical cubes to combining a cone on a cylinder, or from trial-and-error assembly to predicting the next piece.
Scaffold with prompts and modelling, then gradually fade support as the child succeeds.
Repeat the same build and ask the child to say each shape as they add it.
activities.intendedInsight: Children advance most when the next task is just ahead of their current building, with support that fades, rather than jumping straight to the final target.

activities.title: On-screen 3-D building sandbox (optional)
feedback: If a build topples because of a rolling base, let the child retry with a flat-faced base and connect the failure to the face that rolled.
Use the tap-to-name feature to help a child who sees only the whole begin to decompose it into component solids.
activities.rationale: An interactive 3-D build space preserves the stacking, balance and depth that define 3-D composition, which flat 2-D drag-and-combine loses. It is offered as a supplementary medium option alongside physical blocks, not as a replacement for hands-on construction, and the cited sources do not establish that either medium is superior.
learnerActions: Drag 3-D solids into a build space and snap a cone onto a cylinder to make a rocket.
Try placing a sphere as a base; if the sandbox simulates gravity, watch whether it rolls and the tower falls, and talk about which faces must sit flat.
Before placing a piece, respond to the prompt 'which shape will fit on top?'
Tap the finished build to hear its component solids named in order ('cylinder… cone').
activities.intendedInsight: A 3-D model lets a child stack, combine and test balance, plan placements and have parts named — exercising the composing skill, including why a solid with no flat face, such as a sphere, makes a poor base.

activities.title: Match composites to their parts (naming activity)
feedback: If the child names only the whole, point to each region and name the solid, then ask them to repeat which part is the cylinder and which is the cone.
Treat this as a recognition and vocabulary scaffold; follow it with actual building so the child plans and balances, not just recognises.
activities.rationale: Matching and tap-to-name references can build and check part-naming vocabulary, but they support and check recognition rather than the act of composing with anticipation or managing balance; no cited source establishes a matching task as necessary or sufficient for the composing skill.
learnerActions: Show a picture or model of a composite (e.g. a cone-on-cylinder rocket, a cube tower, a house).
Ask the child to choose which component solids make it up and where each one sits.
Optionally use a reference image where tapping a part names it (rocket = cone + cylinder).
activities.intendedInsight: A composite can be decomposed into named component solids, each in a particular position — reinforcing part-naming vocabulary.

constraints: The core objective is composing with anticipation and describing a build by its component solids and their positions — this is a procedural curriculum goal that requires actual construction, with physical block-building as the core medium, not only recognising a finished shape.
Treat unsystematic stacking and post-hoc recognition as an expected early developmental level, not an error to drill or mark wrong; advance with one-step-ahead challenges.
Matching tasks and tap-to-name reference images support/check part-naming vocabulary (recognition) but do not themselves elicit independent construction, balancing, or advance planning.
Flat 2-D drag-and-combine can name parts but cannot convey which faces sit flat or how a tower balances; use it only as a naming scaffold.

Balance depends partly on resting flat faces down: a sphere (no flat face) rolls; a cone stands steadily base-down, but it topples if balanced on its point, rolls if laid on its side, and cannot hold a block on its apex; a cube, prism, or cylinder resting on a flat face is stable on its own, although a tower can still topple if pieces are placed off-centre or it gets too tall and narrow. Use this to explain why a flat-faced base is a good choice, not as a claim about any specific product.
A fixed labelled picture can still teach part-naming as a reference, but cannot be manipulated to practise stacking or anticipation.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The cited effect size (.55) and the trajectory-level descriptions are copied from the original source claims and were not independently re-verified here.

The original marked an on-screen 3-D sandbox as 'ideal' and dialogue/2-D as poor; these catalog fit rankings have been removed. Comparative-necessity framing ('dialogue cannot substitute', 'a static picture cannot teach') has been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements. The cited sources establish the developmental trajectory and one-level-ahead scaffolding, not the superiority of any particular medium.

Physical blocks and an on-screen model offer different experiences (real tactile balance vs. resettable digital trials); physical construction is the curriculum-required core medium and neither is asserted as universally necessary over the other for every learner.

The original row stated a cone used as a base topples; this was clarified because a cone can sit stably on its flat circular face. The instability is specific to a sphere (no flat face) or a cone balanced on its point / used to support further stacking on its apex.

probeDeeper: Before you place that shape — can you tell me where it will go and why it fits?
Point to each shape you used and name it — which is the cylinder, which is the cone?
Why does the tower fall when the cone is at the bottom? Which shapes make a good base?
Can you build the same rocket again, telling me each shape as you add it?
assess.correctAnswer: Selects and stacks solids with anticipation to make the intended composite (e.g. a cylinder body with a cone on top), keeps it stable by resting flat faces down, and describes the result by naming its component solids and their positions ('a cylinder at the bottom, a cone on top').

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds blocks unsystematically and recognises what the structure 'looks like' only after building — no advance plan for the composite
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill or mark this 'wrong' — it is an expected early level; offer building challenges one step ahead and prompt 'can you see which shape will fit before you place it?'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Places shapes at random and names the result post hoc; cannot say in advance which shape will fit

errorPatterns.pattern: Builds a composite but describes it only as one whole ('a rocket') and cannot name the component solids or their positions
errorPatterns.nextMove: Take the composite apart and name each solid, then rebuild it naming each shape as it goes on
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names the whole structure but not the cylinder/cone parts

errorPatterns.pattern: Places solids without regard to which faces are flat, so the structure will not balance — a cone or sphere used as a base makes it topple
errorPatterns.nextMove: Notice together which faces are flat and rest on the table, and choose a flat-faced solid for the base
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The tower falls; the child blames the blocks rather than the choice of base

responseLevels.gap: Stacks blocks unsystematically and names only the whole ('a tower'); cannot say which solids make it up.
responseLevels.full: Selects and combines solids with anticipation to make a planned composite, keeps it stable by resting flat faces down, and describes the result by its component solids and their positions.
responseLevels.partial: Builds the intended composite, often by trial and error, and names some parts, but does not choose shapes with anticipation or explain why a shape fits or balances.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are some 3-D blocks — cubes, a cylinder, a cone, some prisms. Build me a rocket by putting shapes together so it stands up. As you build, and when you finish, tell me which shapes you used and where each one is.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the build separates the child who composes with anticipation ('I know the cone goes on top', reaching for it before placing) from the trial-and-error assembler who stacks unsystematically and recognises the result only afterwards. Asking the child to name the parts exposes whether they can decompose the composite into its component solids rather than seeing it as one undifferentiated 'rocket'.

sources.claim: Composing 3-D shapes develops through levels — Stacker and Same-Shape Stacker (using the 'on' relationship), Piece Assembler and Picture Maker (building components, arches and enclosures by unsystematic trial and error), then Shape Composer (composing with anticipation, understanding what 3-D shape a combination will produce and building systematically).

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 9-10. Recognise that in a multi-digit whole number, a digit in one place is worth TEN TIMES what the same digit is worth in the place to its right (and one-tenth of the place to its left): the 3 in 3,000 is ten times the 3 in 300; 700 ÷ 70 = 10. This names the multiplicative ×10 structure that has been implicit since 'ten ones make a ten'.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 5): place value work where pupils recognise the value of each digit and the relationships between places (×10 between adjacent columns).
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.NBT.1 'a digit in one place represents ten times what it represents in the place to its right'; 5.NBT.1 extends to 1/10 to the left.
• Operational details — Make explicit the multiplicative relationship between adjacent columns using a Gattegno/place-value chart: sliding a digit one column left multiplies its value by 10; one column right divides by 10. Contrast with the ADDITIVE view (partitioning) so children hold both: 3,452 is 3000+400+50+2 AND each place is ×10 the next. Use division sentences (700÷70=10) to expose the relationship.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9, emerging): states the 3 in 3,000 is worth more than in 300 and by how much with support. Tier B (age 9-10, secure): explains any digit is ×10 the place to its right and computes 700÷70. Tier C (age 10, extending): quantifies 'how many times greater' across non-adjacent places (5 in 50,000 vs 5 in 5,000) and links to ×/÷ by powers of 10.
bestPractices: Use a Gattegno / place-value chart: sliding a digit left ×10s its value, right ÷10s it — make the multiplicative move physical.
Hold the additive (partition) and multiplicative (×10 between places) views together so place value is understood both ways.
Expose the relationship with division/multiplication sentences (700 ÷ 70 = 10; 30 = 3 × 10).
Compare the same digit across places ('how many times greater is the 5 in 50,000 than in 5,000?').
Bridge to multiplying/dividing by 10/100/1000 so the pattern has calculation payoff.
keyRepresentations: Gattegno place-value chart (rows scale ×10 down each column)
Place-value chart with a digit sliding between columns
Base-ten pieces showing ten-of-one-unit = one-of-next
Multiplication/division sentences (×10, ÷10) between places
Arrow-card / expanded form as the additive counterpart
commonMisconceptions: Seeing place value only additively and missing the ×10 relationship between places.
Thinking the 3 in 3,000 is '10 more' than in 300 rather than 10 times.
Confusing 'ten times' with 'add a zero' as a meaningless trick (fails for decimals later).
Miscounting the factor across non-adjacent places (×10 vs ×100).
Not connecting 700÷70=10 to the adjacent-place relationship.

learn.summary: For ages 9-10: pupils recognise that in a multi-digit whole number a digit in one place is worth ten times what the same digit is worth in the place to its right (and one-tenth of the same digit in the place to its left). The 3 in 3,000 is ten times the 3 in 300; 700 ÷ 70 = 10. The aim is to name the multiplicative ×10 structure between adjacent places that has been implicit since 'ten ones make a ten', and to hold it alongside the additive (partition) view. A central scaffold is a place-value / Gattegno chart where moving a digit one column left multiplies its value by 10 and one column right divides it by 10; a static or paper chart with counters can serve the same purpose.

activities.title: Slide a digit across the place-value chart
feedback: If a learner says the move 'adds a zero', agree the written numeral gains a zero (for whole numbers) but ask WHY: push for 'because its value became ten times bigger' so the idea still works for decimals later, where 'add a zero' breaks down.
If a learner says 3,000 is '10 more' than 300, build 300 with place-value counters and stack it ten times to reach 3,000, showing it is ten lots of 300, i.e. ten TIMES, not ten more.

Confirm correct answers by having the learner read both numbers aloud with place names (three hundred vs three thousand) so the VALUE, not just the digit, is heard — this also counters 'they're the same, both are 3'.
activities.rationale: Making the ×10/÷10 move physical on a chart turns an abstract multiplicative fact into an observable action and directly contrasts with the 'add a zero' trick. An interactive chart that recomputes the value live as the digit moves (e.g. a '×10' tag flashing on the leftward move) may make the relationship vivid; a static annotated chart or a paper chart with counters can serve the same purpose with the learner stating the change.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils recognise the value of each digit and the ×10 relationships between adjacent places in numbers to 1,000,000.
The multiplicative ×10 relationship between places should be taught explicitly (Gattegno chart) to avoid the 'add a zero' misconception that breaks with decimals.
learnerActions: Set up a place-value chart with columns for ones, tens, hundreds, thousands (and more).
Place a single digit — say a 3 — in the hundreds column so it is worth 300.

Move that same 3 one column to the LEFT and state its new value (3,000). Say what happened to the value and by how much: it became ten TIMES as much, not 'ten more'. (For whole numbers the written numeral also gains a zero, but that is a by-product — the reason is the ×10 in value.)
Move the 3 back to the RIGHT (÷10): from 3,000, one column right returns it to 300, and a further column right makes it 30.
Write the matching sentence each time, e.g. 300 × 10 = 3,000 and 3,000 ÷ 10 = 300.
activities.intendedInsight: Shifting a digit one place left multiplies its value by 10 and one place right divides it by 10; place value is multiplicative between adjacent columns, not merely 'adding a zero'.

activities.title: How many times greater? Counting the place-shifts
feedback: If a learner answers 'ten times' for a two-shift gap (50,000 vs 500), have them slide the digit place by place and count: one shift ×10, a second shift ×10 again, so ×100 in total.

If a learner gives a subtraction answer ('45,000 more' for 50,000 vs 5,000, or '49,500 more' for 50,000 vs 500), re-voice the question as scaling: 'how many of the smaller value fit into the larger?' and build with counters.
Praise answers that name both the factor and the reason (number of shifts), not just a number.
activities.rationale: Comparing a digit across adjacent and non-adjacent places exposes the common over-application of 'ten times' to any gap, and ties the factor to counting place-shifts rather than to a memorised rule. The adjacent ×10 relationship is the defining structure of base-ten place value; the two-shift ×100 case is its direct consequence.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils recognise the value of each digit and the ×10 relationships between adjacent places in numbers to 1,000,000.
A digit in one place represents ten times what it represents in the place to its right (4.NBT.1); extended to 1/10 to the left (5.NBT.1).
learnerActions: Compare the same digit in two different places, e.g. the 5 in 50,000 and the 5 in 5,000.
Slide one placement of the 5 towards the other, counting the number of column hops.
State the factor: one hop = ×10, so the 5 in 50,000 is ten times the 5 in 5,000.
Repeat for a non-adjacent pair, e.g. the 5 in 50,000 compared with the 5 in 500: count the hops (two), so the factor is ×10×10 = ×100.
Say in words how many times greater, and justify by the number of place-shifts.
activities.intendedInsight: The factor between two placements of a digit equals ten raised to the number of column shifts: one shift is ×10, two shifts is ×100. Non-adjacent places are not automatically 'ten times'.

activities.title: Division and multiplication sentences as the place-value step
feedback: If a learner computes 700 ÷ 70 as something other than 10, have them see 700 as ten 70s on the chart (70 shifted one place left) before recomputing.
If a learner gets 10 but cannot explain it, ask them to point to where 70 and 700 sit and say how many columns apart they are.
Give full credit only when the sentence is linked to the place-shift, not just the correct number.
activities.rationale: Using ÷ and × sentences gives the ×10 structure calculation payoff and prevents it from being an isolated verbal fact; linking the quotient to adjacent columns anchors the abstract result in place value.
sourceClaims: The multiplicative ×10 relationship between places should be taught explicitly (Gattegno chart) to avoid the 'add a zero' misconception that breaks with decimals.
learnerActions: Complete 700 ÷ 70 = ___ and explain the answer using place names, not just the computed digits.
Explain how 700 ÷ 70 = 10 connects to 70 and 700 sitting in adjacent place-value columns (the 7 in 700 is one place to the left of the 7 in 70, so 700 is ten times as much as 70).
Write a few matched pairs showing both directions, e.g. 30 = 3 × 10 and 3 = 30 ÷ 10.
Point to or highlight the two adjacent columns involved for each sentence so the quotient of 10 is seen as a single left/right place step.
activities.intendedInsight: Division and multiplication sentences such as 700 ÷ 70 = 10 express the adjacent-place relationship itself: moving one place is ×10 or ÷10.

activities.title: Ten times or ten more? Correcting the claim
feedback: If a learner cannot say why 'ten more' fails, compute 300 + 10 = 310 and compare with 3,000, showing 'ten more' gives the wrong number.
Reinforce that the multiplicative view is what lets the ÷10 direction keep going into tenths and hundredths.
If the learner self-corrects confidently, extend by asking them to state the one-tenth (÷10) relationship: this place is one-tenth of the same digit in the place to its left.
activities.rationale: Explicitly confronting the additive-vs-multiplicative confusion, rather than only demonstrating the correct move, gives learners a chance to articulate and repair the misconception. A short Socratic exchange in which a character insists on 'ten more' and the learner corrects to 'ten times' is one way to surface this; it is a proposed scaffold, not the only effective medium.
sourceClaims: The multiplicative ×10 relationship between places should be taught explicitly (Gattegno chart) to avoid the 'add a zero' misconception that breaks with decimals.
learnerActions: Consider a claim that 'the 3 in 3,000 is ten MORE than the 3 in 300' and decide whether it is right.
Explain why it is wrong and restate it correctly as 'ten TIMES'.
Support the correction with evidence: 300 × 10 = 3,000, or ten stacks of 300 reaching 3,000, or the single left-shift on the chart.
Preview the right-hand direction: a dimmed column to the right of the ones is where tenths will later live (the ÷10 direction continues past the ones).
activities.intendedInsight: 'Ten times' (multiplicative) and 'ten more' (additive) are different; place value is multiplicative, which is why the pattern extends consistently into decimals.

constraints: Hold the additive (partition) view and the multiplicative (×10 between places) view together: 3,452 is 3,000+400+50+2 AND each place is ten times the next. Do not drop the partition view.

Avoid teaching 'add a zero' as the rule; name the underlying ×10 relationship so the idea still works when extended to decimals (÷10 into tenths). For whole numbers the written zero is a by-product, not the explanation.
A static or paper place-value chart is a valid reference and teaching tool; an interactive sliding chart may make the live recompute more vivid but is not the only way to teach this relationship.

Recognition/fill-in-the-blank items (e.g. '700 ÷ 70 = __', 'which is ten times 400?') are useful for consolidation and assessment but do not by themselves require the learner to construct and explain the place-shift reasoning; pair them with tasks that ask for the factor AND its justification.
When comparing non-adjacent places, require the number of place-shifts to be counted (one shift ×10, two shifts ×100); do not let any gap be treated as a single ×10.
Distinguish the digit's face value (3 in both 300 and 3,000) from its place value (300 vs 3,000) whenever learners say the numbers are 'the same'.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified, and the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source citations for CCSS-M (4.NBT.1 / 5.NBT.1) and the NCETM Primary Mastery claim are marked verified:false in the source row; the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified:true. Treat the unverified claims accordingly.

Arithmetic check: 300 × 10 = 3,000; 700 ÷ 70 = 10; 300 + 10 = 310 (≠ 3,000, correctly showing 'ten more' ≠ 'ten times'); 5 in 50,000 vs 5 in 5,000 = one shift = ×10 (ratio 10); 5 in 50,000 vs 5 in 500 = two shifts = ×100 (ratio 100). The additive-difference '2,700 bigger' (3,000 − 300) appears only as an error pattern to correct, never as a valid answer.

The source Tier C example '5 in 50,000 vs 5 in 5,000' is labelled a 'non-adjacent' comparison but is in fact adjacent (one shift, ×10); the activities use the correct factors and reserve the two-shift ×100 case for 50,000 vs 500.

The non-adjacent over-application error (answering 'ten times' for a two-shift gap) is a critical learner error; it is addressed directly by requiring the learner to count place-shifts, not merely flagged.
Source claims support the adjacent per-place ×10 convention; the two-shift ×100 composition in activity 2 is a mathematical derivation of that principle, not an independently cited claim.

Independent re-audit found the content mathematically sound and internally coherent across summary, insights, actions, feedback and constraints; no unsupported categorical modality claims remain and medium-efficacy wording is appropriately qualified.

probeDeeper: Now the 5 in 50,000 and the 5 in 5,000 — how many times bigger? Why?
And the 5 in 50,000 compared with the 5 in 500 — is it still ten times? (two shifts)
Complete 700 ÷ 70 = ___ and explain it using places.
assess.correctAnswer: Ten times bigger. Each place to the left is worth ten times the place to its right, and 3,000 is one place to the left of 300, so its 3 is worth ten times as much.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares the two values by subtracting instead of by a scale factor: '3,000 is 2,700 more than 300'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-voice the question as scaling: '300 fits into 3,000 how many times?' Build both with place-value counters and show 300 stacked ten times to reach 3,000.
errorPatterns.distractor: It is 2,700 bigger.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives an additive difference when asked 'how many times'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Attends to the face value of the digit, not its place: 'they're the same — both are 3'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast value vs digit: the digit is 3 in both, but its VALUE is 300 vs 3,000. Read each aloud with place names.
errorPatterns.distractor: They're the same — both are 3.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says there is no difference because the digit is 3 in both.

errorPatterns.pattern: Over-applies 'ten times' to non-adjacent places, treating any gap as a single ×10
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the place-shifts explicitly: one shift = ×10, two shifts = ×10×10 = ×100. Have them slide the digit place by place.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the follow-up (5 in 50,000 vs 5 in 500) the child still answers 'ten times' rather than 'a hundred times'.

responseLevels.gap: Gives an additive difference or says the digits are 'the same', with no scaling idea.
responseLevels.full: States each left place is ×10, and composes shifts multiplicatively (two places = ×100), justifying with place-value reasoning and inverse (÷10).
responseLevels.partial: Says 'ten times' for the adjacent pair but treats it as a rote 'one more zero' rule and calls non-adjacent pairs ten times too.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Write 300 and 3,000 side by side. Point to the 3 in each. Ask: 'The value of this 3 compared with that 3 — how many times bigger is one than the other? How do you know?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A multiplicative place-value thinker says 'ten times' and justifies by the single left-shift; an additive thinker gives the difference ('2,700 more'); a face-value thinker says 'they're the same, both are 3'. The reason tier, plus the non-adjacent follow-ups, separates a rote 'count the extra zero' rule from genuine ×10-per-place reasoning.

sources.claim: Year 5 pupils recognise the value of each digit and the ×10 relationships between adjacent places in numbers to 1,000,000.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (Year 5 Number & place value)

sources.claim: A digit in one place represents ten times what it represents in the place to its right (4.NBT.1); extended to 1/10 to the left (5.NBT.1).
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Number & Operations in Base Ten, Grades 4-5

sources.claim: The multiplicative ×10 relationship between places should be taught explicitly (Gattegno chart) to avoid the 'add a zero' misconception that breaks with decimals.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 10–11: solve problems that require answers to be ROUNDED to a specified degree of accuracy — rounding a computed (often decimal) result appropriately for the question or context.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y6): pupils 'solve problems which require answers to be rounded to specified degrees of accuracy' and 'determine, in the context of a problem, an appropriate degree of accuracy'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): builds on 5.NBT.4 (round decimals to any place) applied within 4.OA.3-style problem solving; SMP MP6 (attend to precision) frames choosing accuracy.
• Operational details — two intertwined skills: (i) rounding a result to a stated place (round 3.6875 to 1dp → 3.7), and (ii) deciding the SENSIBLE degree of accuracy from context, including cases where mathematical rounding must be overridden — money to the nearest penny, but 'how many containers hold the juice?' means rounding UP regardless of the digit (3.2 containers → 4). The child computes, then interprets: round conventionally, round up for 'enough', round down for 'how many complete', keep exact for money.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): compute a division and round to a specified decimal place. Tier B (10–11): choose the appropriate accuracy for a measurement/money context and round accordingly. Tier C (11): solve a problem where the unrounded decimal must be interpreted against context (whole containers needed → round up even though the digit says round down).
bestPractices: Distinguish ROUNDING RULES (nearest, by the following digit) from CONTEXTUAL rounding (round up for 'enough', down for 'complete whole units') — the classic buses/containers problems where the maths rule is deliberately overridden.
Round only at the END: teach children to keep full precision through a multi-step calculation and round the final answer, to avoid accumulated rounding error.
Use money and measures as the natural home: 'to the nearest penny' (2dp), 'to the nearest 10th of a second', so degree of accuracy is a real, purposeful decision.
Pair every rounded answer with the question 'does this level of accuracy make sense here?' — connecting to estimation/appropriate-accuracy (mt_ilPrU0cbtT) and to what the answer will be used for.
Rehearse the three context moves explicitly with sorting tasks: which problems round up, which round down, which round to nearest — so children choose the move by meaning, not habit.
keyRepresentations: Number line with the answer marked between the two candidate rounded values and the midpoint, to justify nearest-value rounding.
Context decision card: the problem, the raw answer, and a choice of round up / down / nearest with the reason.
Place-value view highlighting the digit being rounded and the deciding digit to its right.
Real-world icons (coins to the penny, containers that must be whole) anchoring why context overrides the plain rule.
commonMisconceptions: Applying the nearest-value rule when context demands rounding up ('need 3.2 buses' → answering 3 instead of 4) or down ('how many whole boxes fill' → rounding up wrongly).
Rounding at intermediate steps and accumulating error into the final answer.
Rounding to the wrong place, or using the wrong deciding digit (looking two places along).
Giving impossible precision for the context (money to 3dp, a count of people as a decimal).
Truncating (chopping digits) instead of rounding, e.g. 3.68 to 1dp given as 3.6.

learn.summary: For ages 10–11: solving problems whose answers must be rounded to a specified degree of accuracy, AND deciding the sensible degree of accuracy from context. Two intertwined skills: (i) rounding a computed result to a stated place using the deciding digit (e.g. 3.6875 to 1 d.p. → 3.7), and (ii) judging from the situation when the plain nearest-value rule must be overridden — round UP for 'how many are needed/enough' (3.2 containers → 4), round DOWN for 'how many complete whole units', keep to the penny for money, keep whole for counts of people. Keep full precision through multi-step work and round only at the end.

activities.title: Round it right: scenarios where the rounding move has consequences
feedback: If a child rounds to the nearest whole (5 buses), ask what happens to the extra 5 people; a 'how many are needed to fit everyone' question rounds UP whenever the division leaves any remainder, however small the decimal part.
If a child rounds a 'how many complete units' problem up, ask whether a partial unit actually counts as a completed one — if not, round DOWN.
When the child correctly rounds up to 6 even though the decimal (.33) is below .5, name the reasoning: 'you rounded by the meaning of the problem, not by the deciding digit.'
For 47 ÷ 6 = 7.833..., confirm the deciding digit (the second decimal, 3, which is below 5) sends 7.83 down to 7.8 at one decimal place.
activities.rationale: Choosing and seeing the consequence of a rounding move is intended to make contextual rounding concrete, which is the central judgement in this problem-solving objective rather than rule recitation.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils solve problems which require answers to be rounded to specified degrees of accuracy and determine, in the context of a problem, an appropriate degree of accuracy.
Context can require rounding up ('enough') or down ('complete units') irrespective of the standard nearest-value rule, and answers should be rounded only at the end to avoid accumulated error.
learnerActions: Compute a problem that yields a raw decimal, e.g. 80 people needing 15-seat buses: 80 ÷ 15 = 5.33 (to 2 d.p.).
Choose a rounding move — round to the nearest whole, round down, or round up — and, where relevant, to which place.
Play out or describe the result of your choice in the situation: rounding to the nearest whole (5 buses) seats only 75 and leaves 5 people stranded at the kerb; rounding up to 6 buses seats everyone.
State in words why context (needing to carry everyone), not the deciding digit, forces rounding up here: the deciding digit (the 3 in 5.33) would round down to 5, yet the situation needs 6.
Repeat with a 'round down' context, e.g. 'How many complete 50 cm lengths can be cut from 3.4 m?' 340 ÷ 50 = 6.8 → 6 complete lengths, not 7, even though 6.8 is nearer to 7.
Repeat with a 'nearest' context where the plain rule does apply, e.g. 'round 47 ÷ 6 to one decimal place' → 7.8.
activities.intendedInsight: The context — what the answer is used for — decides whether you round up, down, or to the nearest, and this can override the mechanical nearest-value rule.

activities.title: Number-line rounder for the pure mechanic
feedback: If a child gives 3.68 to 1 d.p. as 3.6, point out they chopped rather than rounded: 3.68 is past the midpoint 3.65, so it rounds up to 3.7.
If a child looks two places along for the deciding digit, refocus them on the single digit immediately to the right of the rounding place.
For a borderline value with 5 in the deciding place, state the convention used (5 or more rounds up) and rehearse a few such cases.
activities.rationale: A visual number-line placement with the deciding digit highlighted supports the standard rounding mechanic and directly confronts truncation and wrong-place errors.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils solve problems which require answers to be rounded to specified degrees of accuracy and determine, in the context of a problem, an appropriate degree of accuracy.
learnerActions: Mark the raw answer on a number line between the two candidate rounded values, with the midpoint shown.
Identify the digit being rounded and the deciding digit immediately to its right.
Decide which candidate the value is nearer to and round to it.
Deliberately contrast rounding with truncating: show that 3.68 to 1 d.p. is 3.7, NOT 3.6 (chopping).
activities.intendedInsight: Nearest-value rounding is justified by position on the number line and the single deciding digit; truncating (chopping digits) is a different, incorrect move.

activities.title: Money and measures: choosing a sensible degree of accuracy
feedback: If a child gives money to 3 d.p., ask what 0.001 of a pound would be in coins — there is no such coin, so round to the penny.
If a child reports a count of people as a decimal, ask how you could have part of a person; counts stay whole.
Praise reasoning that ties the chosen accuracy to how the answer is used.
activities.rationale: Money and measures give authentic reasons for choosing accuracy, making 'degree of accuracy' a real decision.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils solve problems which require answers to be rounded to specified degrees of accuracy and determine, in the context of a problem, an appropriate degree of accuracy.
Pupils round decimals to any place and attend to precision, applying rounding within problem solving.
learnerActions: For a money result, round to the nearest penny (2 d.p.) and explain why 3 d.p. is not sensible for pounds and pence.
For a measurement context, round to the stated accuracy, e.g. nearest tenth of a second.
For a count of people, give a whole number and explain why a decimal count is impossible.
For each context, answer the question: 'Does this level of accuracy make sense here, and what will the answer be used for?'
activities.intendedInsight: The appropriate degree of accuracy is a purposeful decision set by the context and the use of the answer, not an arbitrary number of decimal places.

activities.title: Sort the problems: up, down, or nearest
feedback: If a child sorts by surface words rather than meaning, ask what the answer is being counted for.
Check that each sorting decision is matched by a stated reason, not just a category guess.
activities.rationale: Explicit sorting with reasons rehearses the three context moves and separates meaning-driven choice from reflex; on its own a sort checks classification rather than eliciting the full compute-then-interpret performance.
sourceClaims: Context can require rounding up ('enough') or down ('complete units') irrespective of the standard nearest-value rule, and answers should be rounded only at the end to avoid accumulated error.
learnerActions: Read a set of word problems and sort each into 'round up', 'round down', or 'round to nearest'.
For each, write the reason in words (e.g. 'need enough to fit everyone' → up; 'how many complete' → down; 'to the nearest tenth' → nearest).
Then solve two or three and carry out the move you sorted it into.
activities.intendedInsight: Children should choose the rounding move by the meaning of the problem, not by habit.

activities.title: Round at the end, not in the middle
feedback: If the two answers differ, ask the child to locate where the early rounding introduced the discrepancy.
Reinforce that the specified accuracy applies to the final answer, not to the working.
activities.rationale: Working the calculation both ways is intended to let the learner see accumulated error for themselves, which may motivate the 'round last' habit more concretely than simply being told it.
sourceClaims: Context can require rounding up ('enough') or down ('complete units') irrespective of the standard nearest-value rule, and answers should be rounded only at the end to avoid accumulated error.
learnerActions: Work a multi-step calculation twice: once rounding each intermediate value early, once keeping full precision and rounding only the final answer.
Compare the two final answers and describe whether and how early rounding changed the result (choose numbers where it does, so the effect is visible).
State the rule: keep precision through the steps, round last.
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding at intermediate steps can accumulate error; rounding only the final answer protects accuracy.

activities.title: Justify-the-accuracy discussion
feedback: If the child cannot explain why 5.2 coaches rounds up to 6, revisit that 0.2 of a coach still carries 10 people who need seats (0.2 × 50 = 10).
If the child says the answer never changes with re-wording, contrast 'coaches needed' (round up to 6) with 'nearest whole number' (5.2 → round to 5).
activities.rationale: Spoken Socratic reasoning targets the judgement aspect of choosing accuracy and surfaces whether the choice is understood or habitual; a discussion can prompt justification but does not by itself confirm the child can compute and round a fresh problem.
learnerActions: Given a real situation posed aloud, say whether you would round up, down, or to the nearest, and why, BEFORE the outcome is revealed.
Answer probing questions: 'Why round UP to 6 coaches even though 5.2 is nearer 5?'; 'If the question asked for the nearest whole number instead of coaches needed, would your answer change?'
Defend your chosen degree of accuracy in words.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to justify the accuracy decision in context — and recognising that re-wording the question can change the correct move — shows command of the objective.

constraints: A sorting/categorisation or multiple-choice format can rehearse and check which rounding move fits, but on its own it does not require the learner to carry out the full compute-then-interpret problem or explain the reasoning — pair it with worked problems and justification.
A static number-line reference supports the rounding mechanic but does not let learners play out contextual consequences; use it alongside scenario and discussion work.
Treat animated scenario outcomes as one way to make consequences visible; the same insight can come from drawing, acting out, or discussing what happens to the extra people/units.
Distinguish arithmetic slips from rounding misconceptions: if the rounding logic is right but the division is wrong, have the child recompute and re-round rather than reteaching rounding.

Choose scenario numbers so the intended teaching point is genuine: to show context overriding the plain rule, a 'round up' context needs a fractional part below .5 (e.g. 5.33 → 6 needed), and a 'round down' context needs a fractional part of .5 or more (e.g. 6.8 → 6 complete lengths); otherwise the rule and the context agree and no override is demonstrated.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of worked examples: 80 ÷ 15 = 5.333..., so nearest whole = 5 by the rule but 6 buses are needed — a clean rule-vs-context contrast now used in Activity 1. 47 ÷ 6 = 7.833... → 7.8 to 1 d.p. (correct). 260 ÷ 50 = 5.2 → 6 coaches (correct). 320 ÷ 50 = 6.4 → 6 complete lengths (correct). 3.6875 → 3.7 and 3.68 → 3.7 (not 3.6) (correct). The ORIGINAL row used 74 ÷ 15 = 4.93 for the override lesson, but 4.93 rounds up to 5 by the plain rule anyway, so it does not separate rule from context; the original 'close to 5 for a different reason' phrasing is muddled and was replaced.
The CCSS (5.NBT.4) and NCETM source claims are marked unverified in the original row; do not treat the mapping or the in-context rounding guidance as independently confirmed.
'Round half up' is stated as the convention; some curricula/contexts use round-half-to-even. Confirm the convention against the intended standard before teaching borderline (deciding-digit 5) cases.
Efficacy framing: activity rationales were softened to intended/may wording because these are unvalidated proposals; no empirical effectiveness or human review has been established.

probeDeeper: Why do you round UP to 6 coaches even though 5.2 is nearer 5?
To round 47 ÷ 6 to one decimal place, which digit decides whether you round up or down?
When is it right to round to the nearest, and when must you round up no matter what?
If the question asked for the nearest whole number instead of coaches needed, would your answer change?
assess.correctAnswer: 47 ÷ 6 = 7.83..., to 1 d.p. = 7.8. Coaches: 260 ÷ 50 = 5.2, but you need 6 coaches (the 0.2 of a coach still carries people, so round UP). The teacher watches for correct rounding-rule application AND context-driven rounding that overrides the rule when whole units are required.

errorPatterns.pattern: applies 'round to nearest' mechanically in the coaches context — 5.2 rounds to 5, stranding people
errorPatterns.nextMove: ask what happens to the extra 10 people; a real 'how many needed' context always rounds UP to fit everyone, regardless of the decimal.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer of 5 coaches; child rounds down because 5.2 is nearer 5

errorPatterns.pattern: rounds to the wrong place, or rounds the intermediate value too early distorting the result
errorPatterns.nextMove: round only the FINAL answer to the specified place; identify the digit that decides the rounding.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer given to the wrong decimal place, or rounded mid-calculation causing error

errorPatterns.pattern: uses the round-half-up rule inconsistently — unsure what to do with a 5 in the deciding place
errorPatterns.nextMove: state the convention (deciding digit 5 or more rounds up) and rehearse a few borderline cases.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child hesitates or rounds 7.85-type values inconsistently

errorPatterns.pattern: rounds correctly, arithmetic slip in the division
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach rounding; have the child recompute the division and re-round.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: right rounding logic, wrong quotient

responseLevels.gap: rounds mechanically to nearest even in a 'how many needed' context (stranding people), or rounds to the wrong place.
responseLevels.full: rounds the final answer to a specified accuracy correctly AND rounds up/down as the context demands, explaining why the context governs the choice.
responseLevels.partial: applies the rounding rule correctly when asked for a decimal place but doesn't let context override it (or vice versa).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child problems where the rounding decision matters and watch how they round the RESULT: 'Work out 47 ÷ 6 and give the answer to one decimal place'; and a context one — '260 people travel in coaches holding 50 each. How many coaches are needed?' Watch whether they round by the rule when asked, but round UP for whole coaches regardless of the decimal.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The two items pull in opposite directions: one wants the rounding rule (7.83→7.8), the other wants rounding UP against the rule (5.2→6 coaches). A child who always applies 'round to nearest' answers 5 coaches and strands 10 people. Watching both reveals whether they let context govern accuracy — the objective's core.
