pedagogy.summary: Children extend coordinate work to the full plane: plotting and reading points such as (−3,4) and (2,−5) across all four quadrants, naming which quadrant a point lies in, and describing positions where either or both coordinates are negative. The new demand is not the (across, up) convention itself — that carries over from the first quadrant — but reading a SIGNED scale on each axis: a negative x means left of the origin, a negative y means below it, and the numbers run symmetrically outward from 0 in both directions. Success rests on secure directed-number sense fused to the ordered-pair rule.
bestPractices: Anchor both axes as signed number lines meeting at the origin: rehearse pointing and chanting positive and negative values on a counting stick held horizontally (x) and vertically (y), forwards and backwards, so left/below map to negatives (NCETM).
Emphasise the symmetry about 0 — the numbers mirror outward from the origin — so children read −3 as three to the LEFT, not three to the right.
Keep the reading rule explicit and mnemonic — 'along the corridor and up (or down) the stairs', 'x is a-cross', 'x before y' — to hold off the perennial y-before-x reversal (NCETM).
Always plot the first coordinate along x from the origin THEN the second along y, treating each sign as a direction, not a decoration on the digit.
Name the four quadrants by the sign pattern of their points (+,+), (−,+), (−,−), (+,−) so 'which quadrant?' becomes a reading of the two signs, and connect this to reflections in the axes.
Use problems that force reasoning across quadrants (find the fourth vertex of a square given (3,0), (0,3), (−3,0)) rather than isolated plotting, so signs must be coordinated.
keyRepresentations: Four-quadrant coordinate grid with the origin and both signed axes labelled
Counting stick / number line held horizontally and vertically to model signed movement along each axis
Thermometer or below-ground scale as a familiar signed vertical axis
Sign-pattern labels for the four quadrants: (+,+), (−,+), (−,−), (+,−)
commonMisconceptions: Moving the wrong way for a negative coordinate — counting right for −3 or up for −5 — through weak grasp of order on a signed scale.
Putting the y-coordinate before the x-coordinate, placing the point in the wrong quadrant.
Mis-ordering negatives (treating −5 as further out than −3 because 5>3), so points on a negative axis are misplaced.
Counting from '1' at the origin instead of '0', landing one square off.

learn.summary: Children extend coordinate work to all four quadrants: plotting and reading points such as (−3,4) and (2,−5), naming which quadrant a point lies in, and reasoning about positions where either or both coordinates are negative. The new demand is reading a SIGNED scale on each axis — a negative x means left of the origin, a negative y means below it, with numbers running symmetrically outward from 0 — fused to the ordered-pair (across, then up/down) rule. Live plotting with immediate feedback lets wrong-direction and reversed placements surface and be corrected; discrete practice items and labelled grids can check and clarify but elicit less of the felt signed movement.

activities.title: Plot it as a signed journey from the origin
feedback: If (−3,4) lands in the top-right (first) quadrant, the x-move went the wrong way: count the negative as LEFT from 0 and re-plot.
If the point lands as if it were (4,−3), the pair was reversed — move along x first ('along the corridor, then up or down the stairs').
Linked feedback that lights each axis's signed count as the marker travels makes the two moves and the landing quadrant visible together.
Reflecting (−3,4) in the x-axis gives (−3,−4) — the y-sign flips and the point drops to the third quadrant; check which single sign changed.
activities.rationale: Plotting on a signed grid is direct manipulation: the child performs two signed movements and can see a wrong direction or a reversed pair immediately, which is where signed-coordinate errors surface. Reading the quadrant from the sign pattern and linking sign flips to reflection connects the skill to geometry the child already knows.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils should describe positions on the full coordinate grid (all four quadrants), including with negative numbers.

Recommended teaching includes mnemonics ('along the corridor and up the stairs', 'x is a-cross', 'x before y'), chanting positive and negative numbers on a counting stick held both horizontally and vertically for the two axes, and referring to the symmetry of the numbers about 0.
learnerActions: On a four-quadrant grid with a labelled origin and signed axes, plot (−3,4): move LEFT 3 along the x-axis from the origin, then UP 4 along the y-axis, treating each sign as a direction.
Name the quadrant from its sign pattern: (−,+) is the second (top-left) quadrant.
Plot (2,−5) (two right, five down) and (−4,−1) (four left, one down), naming each quadrant from its two signs.

If a live tool is available, place the marker yourself and watch it replay the two signed moves; if you counted right for the −3 and landed in the (+,+) quadrant, notice the mismatch and re-plot reading the minus as 'left'.
Where offered, use a reflect-in-axis toggle to flip (−3,4)↔(3,4)↔(3,−4) and watch a single sign change hop the point across an axis.
activities.intendedInsight: A minus sign is a DIRECTION (left of, or below, the origin), not decoration on the digit; the quadrant is read directly from the pair of signs, and flipping one sign reflects the point across an axis.

activities.title: Anchor each axis as a signed number line
feedback: If the child taps the origin while saying 'one', re-establish the origin as 0 and count moves from there; otherwise every point lands one square off.
If −5 is placed nearer the origin than −3 because 5>3, count steps out from 0 on the line: −5 is five steps out, −3 is three.
A counting stick or washing-line chanted in both directions makes the symmetry about 0 audible and visible.
activities.rationale: Secure directed-number sense underpins signed plotting; ordering negatives is genuinely hard because children treat magnitude as value, and number-line / thermometer / depth models address this by foregrounding position on the scale.
sourceClaims: Children find ordering negative integers difficult — numbers less than zero represent 'the non-existent' and the idea that 0 is greater than −1 is hard; the underlying error is treating the magnitude/digit as the value rather than the position on the scale, best addressed with number-line, washing-line, thermometer and swimming-pool (depth) models.

Recommended teaching includes mnemonics ('along the corridor and up the stairs', 'x is a-cross', 'x before y'), chanting positive and negative numbers on a counting stick held both horizontally and vertically for the two axes, and referring to the symmetry of the numbers about 0.
learnerActions: Treat the x-axis as a horizontal number line and the y-axis as a vertical one, both meeting at 0 at the origin.
Point and chant positive and negative values along a counting stick held horizontally, then vertically, forwards and backwards, so left and below map to negatives.
Use a thermometer or below-ground/depth scale as a familiar signed vertical axis.
Count the MOVES from the origin (which is 0), not the lines including it, so you do not land one square off.
Say aloud why −3 goes three to the LEFT: the numbers mirror symmetrically outward from 0.
activities.intendedInsight: Each axis is a signed number line symmetric about 0; reading position (not the bare digit) on that scale is what fixes direction and ordering.

activities.title: Reason across quadrants and name the quadrant from the signs
feedback: If a quadrant is named by memorised position rather than sign pattern, re-read the two signs: (−,−) is the third (bottom-left) quadrant.
If the child says (−3,0) is further from the origin than (−5,0), count steps from 0 along the negative axis.
For the square, use the symmetry about the origin: the vertex opposite (0,3) completes it, so the fourth vertex is (0,−3).
activities.rationale: Problems that force coordination of signs across quadrants, and distinguishing distance-from-0 from the digit, reveal whether the child reads signs as direction and can transfer to unplotted points rather than reaching a square by rote.
sourceClaims: For the Year 6 objective 'read and plot coordinates in all four quadrants', two named misconceptions are putting the y-coordinate before the x-coordinate, and misplaced positions due to a lack of understanding of the order of negative numbers on a scale.
Year 6 pupils should describe positions on the full coordinate grid (all four quadrants), including with negative numbers.
learnerActions: Without plotting, state which quadrant (−2,−7) lies in and explain how you can tell from the two signs.
Find the fourth vertex of a square given three vertices such as (3,0), (0,3), (−3,0), coordinating the signs rather than plotting in isolation.
Compare (−5,0) and (−3,0): decide which is further from the origin and justify it by position on the negative scale (five to the left versus three).
Label each quadrant by its sign pattern: (+,+), (−,+), (−,−), (+,−), and connect this to reflections in the axes.
Respond to a counterexample: 'A friend plotted (−3,4) in the top-right — what would you say?' (a negative x must go left).
activities.intendedInsight: For a point with two non-zero coordinates, quadrant membership is a reading of the two signs; a point with a zero coordinate, such as (3,0), (0,3) or (−5,0), lies on an axis and is in no quadrant. Coordinating signs across quadrants and comparing negatives by distance from the origin transfers the skill beyond single plots.

activities.title: Check and diagnose with targeted items
feedback: Picking the sign-flipped option signals a sign was read as decoration; return to reading the minus as direction.
Picking the reversed-pair option signals y-before-x; re-anchor 'x before y'.
activities.rationale: Well-designed items assess cleanly and the pattern of wrong options chosen can pinpoint the misconception, but recognition and single-step plotting elicit less independent, felt signed movement than live plotting, so they complement rather than replace it.
sourceClaims: For the Year 6 objective 'read and plot coordinates in all four quadrants', two named misconceptions are putting the y-coordinate before the x-coordinate, and misplaced positions due to a lack of understanding of the order of negative numbers on a scale.
learnerActions: Tap/draw to plot (−3,4); choose which quadrant (2,−5) is in; fill in the coordinates of a plotted point; put −5, −3, 0, 2 in order along an axis.

For multiple-choice quadrant questions, the wrong options should encode real errors — the reversed point, the same point with one sign flipped, and the point mis-ordered on the negative scale — so a wrong answer shows which misconception is present.
activities.intendedInsight: Discrete items confirm the skill and diagnose which specific error (reversal, sign-as-decoration, or mis-ordered negatives) is present.

constraints: The (across, then up/down) ordering convention carries over from the first quadrant; the genuinely new demand is reading the SIGNED scale on each axis, so secure directed-number sense is a prerequisite.
Recognition-only practice items confirm and diagnose but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of the two signed movements; pair them with actual plotting where possible.

A static labelled four-quadrant grid can reveal a point's signed path and each quadrant's sign pattern on tap, which clarifies layout, but it does not let the child plot and self-check, which is where signed errors surface — treat it as a scaffold.
Keep to the 2D plane for this objective; introducing a third axis brings octants and z-values beyond this topic and would obscure the signed 2D reading.
Reflect-in-axis toggles, axis-lighting counts, and live replay are optional feedback examples that make the mechanism concrete; they are not mandatory.
Always count MOVES from the origin (0), not the grid lines including it, to avoid the one-square-off error.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The square example (vertices (3,0), (0,3), (−3,0)) has fourth vertex (0,−3) if the intended figure is a square centred on the origin (verified: right angle at (0,3), diagonal length 6); confirm the intended shape before use, as other three-point arrangements could complete different quadrilaterals.
One cited claim (National Curriculum, all-four-quadrants with negatives) is marked verified:false in the source row; treat its evidential weight accordingly.

The original source framed the live-plotting tool as uniquely building fluency and a conversation/3D as unable to teach this; softened to scoped affordances/limits without asserting comparative efficacy, which the exact sources do not establish.

probeDeeper: Point at (2,−5): 'How did you know to go down rather than up for the −5?' (listen for the sign read as direction, not a rule recited).
'Which quadrant would (−2, −7) be in, without plotting it? How can you tell?' (tests reading the quadrant from the two signs alone).
Counterexample: 'A friend plotted (−3,4) up here in the top-right. What would you say to them?' (elicits that a negative x must go left, exposing the sign-as-decoration error).
'If you reflect (−3,4) in the x-axis, what are the new coordinates and which quadrant is it in now?' (links sign change to reflection across an axis).
assess.correctAnswer: The child moves along x first then y, treating each sign as a direction — (−3,4) three left and four up (second quadrant), (2,−5) two right and five down (fourth quadrant), (−4,−1) four left and one down (third quadrant) — labels each pair as (across, up), names the quadrant from the sign pattern, and reasons that (−5,0) is further from the origin than (−3,0) because −5 is further along the negative scale (five to the left versus three).

errorPatterns.pattern: Moves the wrong way for a negative coordinate — counts right for −3 or up for −5 — treating the minus as decoration rather than a direction
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rehearse the axis as a signed number line with a counting stick — negatives go left/down from 0, symmetric about the origin; re-plot reading the sign as the direction.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: (−3,4) lands in the first quadrant instead of the second; the child counts away from 0 in the positive direction regardless of sign.

errorPatterns.pattern: Puts the y-coordinate before the x-coordinate, so the point lands in the wrong place
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor 'along the corridor, then up/down the stairs', 'x before y'; check one point together, moving x first.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: (−3,4) plotted as if (4,−3) — wrong quadrant — though the child clearly used both numbers; often surfaces as a swapped quadrant.

errorPatterns.pattern: Mis-orders negatives, treating −5 as nearer the origin than −3 (or vice versa) because 5>3 — magnitude read as value
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a number line / thermometer through 0: count steps from the origin, showing −5 is five steps out and −3 is three; contrast distance-from-0 with the digit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says (−3,0) is further from the origin than (−5,0), or spaces negative points as if −5 sits between 0 and −3.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts from '1' at the origin rather than '0', landing one square short or long
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish the origin as 0; count the MOVES from the origin, not the lines including it; re-plot one point together.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Every plotted point is consistently one square off along an axis; the child taps the origin as they say 'one'.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot reliably place signed points — ignores signs or reverses the pair, so points land in the wrong quadrants — and cannot compare negatives on a scale (thinks −3 is further out than −5).
responseLevels.full: Plots points in all four quadrants by reading each sign as a direction (x then y), labels them (across, up), names each quadrant from its sign pattern, orders negatives correctly by distance from the origin, and transfers — e.g. states a point's quadrant without plotting and predicts the effect of reflecting it in an axis.
responseLevels.partial: Plots first-quadrant and single-negative points but falters when both coordinates are negative or when asked to justify — e.g. reaches the right square by rule yet cannot explain WHY −3 goes left, or names quadrants by memorised position rather than by sign pattern, and mis-orders negatives on the scale. Executes the steps but cannot connect sign to direction or transfer to an unplotted point.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put a four-quadrant grid with a labelled origin and signed axes in front of the child. Say: 'Plot these three points and label each with its coordinates: (−3, 4), (2, −5), and (−4, −1). For each one, tell me which quadrant it is in. Then look at (−5, 0) and (−3, 0) — which is further from the origin, and how do you know?' Set the task and WATCH how each point is reached from the origin; do not explain the axes.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Points with mixed signs give a DIFFERENT landing quadrant for a child who reads signs as directions than for one who ignores the sign, reverses the pair, or mis-orders negatives — each error sends the point to a distinct, visible wrong place. Watching the origin-to-point movement (which axis first, which direction) reveals the reasoning directly, and the (−5,0) vs (−3,0) question isolates negative-scale ordering from the plotting itself.

sources.claim: For the Year 6 objective 'read and plot coordinates in all four quadrants', two named misconceptions are putting the y-coordinate before the x-coordinate, and misplaced positions due to a lack of understanding of the order of negative numbers on a scale.
sources.source: NCETM 'Misconceptions with the Key Objectives'

sources.claim: Recommended teaching includes mnemonics ('along the corridor and up the stairs', 'x is a-cross', 'x before y'), chanting positive and negative numbers on a counting stick held both horizontally and vertically for the two axes, and referring to the symmetry of the numbers about 0.
sources.source: NCETM 'Misconceptions with the Key Objectives'

sources.claim: Children find ordering negative integers difficult — numbers less than zero represent 'the non-existent' and the idea that 0 is greater than −1 is hard; the underlying error is treating the magnitude/digit as the value rather than the position on the scale, best addressed with number-line, washing-line, thermometer and swimming-pool (depth) models.
sources.source: NCETM 'Misconceptions with the Key Objectives' (Year 5 ordering objective)

sources.claim: Year 6 pupils should describe positions on the full coordinate grid (all four quadrants), including with negative numbers.
sources.source: UK National Curriculum, Mathematics KS2 (Year 6 geometry: position and direction)

pedagogy.summary: Classifying figures by their line properties is the procedural core of van Hiele level 2: instead of sorting shapes by overall look, the child TESTS each figure for a property — are these two sides parallel? do these two meet at a right angle? is there a 90° angle in this triangle? — and sorts on the result. The skill is applying a reliable CHECK (sliding or extending a ruler, using a set-square or the corner of a page) rather than eyeballing. Two obstacles dominate: confusing the words parallel and perpendicular, and treating a non-defining feature — line length, or horizontal/vertical orientation — as if it decided the classification, because textbook examples almost always show equal-length parallel lines in standard orientation.
bestPractices: Teach a physical CHECK for each relation: parallel = the gap stays constant / the lines never meet (slide a ruler between them or extend them); perpendicular / right angle = test with a set-square or the square corner of a card
Show parallel and perpendicular lines of DIFFERENT lengths, thicknesses and orientations, so pupils sort on the property rather than the appearance (NCETM)
Use 'nearly' examples — lines that are almost-but-not-parallel, a triangle with an almost-right angle — so a checking method is genuinely needed; obvious examples let pupils guess by eye
Ask pupils to DRAW a line parallel or perpendicular to a given one, and to draw a right triangle in a non-standard orientation — producing, not just spotting
Present right triangles rotated and in scalene form so 'right triangle' is defined by the 90° angle, not by a horizontal-and-vertical-legs prototype
keyRepresentations: Set-square or the square corner of a card as a right-angle checker; a ruler slid between two lines to test constant distance
Carroll and Venn sorting grids with criteria ('has parallel sides', 'has a right angle', regular/irregular)
A dynamic pair of lines whose length and orientation vary while the parallel/perpendicular relation is held or broken
Sets of triangles varied by orientation and side length — some right-angled, some not
commonMisconceptions: Confuses the vocabulary — mixes up 'parallel' and 'perpendicular'
Thinks parallel lines must be the same length (reinforced by always-equal-length textbook examples)
Only recognises parallel/perpendicular when the lines are horizontal or vertical; misses tilted pairs
Fails to recognise a right triangle when it is rotated or looks scalene (right-angle-legs prototype)

learn.summary: Help 9-10 year olds classify 2-D figures by TESTING line properties (parallel sides, perpendicular sides, right angles in triangles) rather than sorting by overall appearance. The core skill is applying a reliable physical check — sliding or extending a ruler to confirm a constant gap for parallel lines, and using a set-square or the square corner of a card to confirm a 90 degree angle — and then sorting on the result. A single figure may carry more than one property (a rectangle has parallel sides AND right angles), so each property is decided by its own independent check. Two obstacles dominate: confusing the words 'parallel' and 'perpendicular', and treating non-defining features (unequal line length, or horizontal/vertical orientation) as if they decided the classification, because typical textbook pictures show equal-length parallel lines in standard orientation.

activities.title: Sort the tray: test every figure before you bin it
feedback: If a learner rejects the tilted unequal-length pair, saying the lines are 'not the same length so not parallel', show two parallel lines of very different lengths and slide the ruler between them — parallel means the gap stays constant / the lines never meet, and length does not matter.

If a learner only accepts horizontal or vertical parallels or an upright right triangle, slowly rotate the same figure and let them watch the ruler gap stay constant or the set-square still fit — the property is preserved when you turn the figure.

If a learner accepts the slowly-converging pair as parallel by eye, have them measure the gap straight across at each end to see that it changes, and extend both lines in the direction they close up to show they would meet (if the meeting point is off the page, the changing gap is still the evidence), showing the eyeball guess was wrong.

If a learner is unsure where the rectangle belongs, have them run the two checks separately — slide the ruler for the constant gap and fit the set-square in a corner — and see that it passes both, so it is recorded as having parallel sides AND a right angle.

If a learner swaps the words, re-anchor each to its check: parallel lines run alongside and never meet (the ruler gap holds); perpendicular lines cross at a right angle (the set-square fits the corner). Have them name the relation while performing the check.
activities.rationale: Classifying by property is a doing-and-checking skill at the heart of this objective; building figures that defeat eyeballing (unequal-length tilted parallels, near-parallels, rotated right triangles) is intended to require a genuine check rather than a glance, which can help counter the equal-length and horizontal-orientation prototypes. Testing each property independently keeps multi-property figures like rectangles coherent.
sourceClaims: Year 5 objective 'Recognise parallel and perpendicular lines, and properties of rectangles'; misconceptions = pupils confuse the vocabulary 'parallel'/'perpendicular', and think parallel lines must be the same length (reinforced by equal-length examples); remedies = show lines of differing lengths/thicknesses and orientations, use 'nearly' examples that force a checking method, and ask pupils to DRAW a line parallel/perpendicular to a given one

Children reason from prototypes and impose non-defining/salient attributes (e.g. orientation, a horizontal base) as if defining, and reject non-prototypical or rotated examples of a shape category — the mechanism behind not recognising a rotated right triangle
learnerActions: Lay out a mixed tray of shapes and lines including a pair of parallel lines of clearly DIFFERENT lengths tilted off horizontal, a pair that looks parallel but slowly converges, a right-angled triangle rotated so neither leg is horizontal or vertical, a rectangle, and a non-right triangle.

For each pair of sides, test for parallel: slide a ruler along one side keeping it touching, and check whether the gap to the opposite side stays the same, measuring straight across (at right angles to the lines) at two or more places, including near both ends where the lines lie alongside each other, or extend both lines to see whether they would meet.
For each corner you suspect is a right angle, drop a set-square or the square corner of a card into the corner and check whether it fits exactly against both sides.

Record each figure by property, testing the two properties independently: does it have a pair of parallel sides? does it have a right angle / is it a right triangle? A figure may pass BOTH tests (a rectangle has parallel sides AND right angles), just one, or neither — note what each check shows rather than forcing it into a single exclusive box, and only decide after the check, not after a glance.

Say out loud, for at least three figures, which check you used and what it showed (for example: 'I slid the ruler and the gap never changed, so these sides are parallel even though one line is longer' or 'the rectangle passed both — parallel sides and a right-angle corner').
activities.intendedInsight: A property, not the look of a figure, decides the category: a tilted, unequal-length pair is just as parallel as a tidy horizontal pair, and a rotated triangle is still a right triangle if a corner tests at 90 degrees. Properties are independent, so a figure can have both (a rectangle), one, or neither. The question shifts from 'does it look like the book example?' to 'does it pass the test?'

activities.title: Draw it, don't just spot it
feedback: If the learner's 'parallel' line visibly converges on checking, point to where the gap changes and ask them to redraw keeping the ruler's reported gap constant.
If the 'perpendicular' line fails the set-square, show the gap between the card's square corner and the line and have them adjust until it fits.
If the learner only draws an upright right triangle, ask them to draw one more tilted so no side is straight across or straight up, then confirm the 90 degree corner is still present.
activities.rationale: Construction tasks require the learner to generate the property themselves and check their own work; because recognising ready-made examples does not by itself elicit production, a drawing task adds evidence that the learner can produce the property, and drawing in non-standard orientations directly targets the orientation prototype.
sourceClaims: Year 5 objective 'Recognise parallel and perpendicular lines, and properties of rectangles'; misconceptions = pupils confuse the vocabulary 'parallel'/'perpendicular', and think parallel lines must be the same length (reinforced by equal-length examples); remedies = show lines of differing lengths/thicknesses and orientations, use 'nearly' examples that force a checking method, and ask pupils to DRAW a line parallel/perpendicular to a given one
learnerActions: Given a line drawn at an angle (not horizontal or vertical), draw a second line parallel to it, then check your own drawing by sliding a ruler to confirm the gap is constant.
Given another angled line, draw a line perpendicular to it, then check with a set-square or square corner that the crossing is a right angle.
Draw a right triangle that stands on its point or sits at an angle, so that neither of the two shorter sides is horizontal or vertical; mark the right angle and verify it with the set-square.
Swap drawings with a partner and test each other's lines and triangle with the ruler and set-square, reporting whether each one passes.
activities.intendedInsight: Producing parallel and perpendicular lines, and a right triangle in a non-standard orientation, is evidence the learner holds the defining property rather than copying a familiar picture.

activities.title: Sorting grids for mixed properties
feedback: If a learner cannot place a rectangle in the 'both' cell, have them separately test a pair of sides for the constant gap and a corner for 90 degrees, then see both tests pass.
If placements are made by appearance, ask them to demonstrate the check for one figure in each cell before moving on.
activities.rationale: Carroll/Venn-style grids make the independence of the two properties explicit and reveal whether a learner can hold more than one criterion at once, which a single-bin sort does not require.
sourceClaims: Year 5 statutory content: pupils use the properties of rectangles and recognise/use parallel and perpendicular lines; classify shapes by their properties
learnerActions: Set up a two-way sorting grid: one axis 'has parallel sides / no parallel sides', the other 'has a right angle / no right angle'.
Place each figure from a mixed set into the correct cell, including shapes that belong in the cell with BOTH parallel sides and a right angle (such as a rectangle).
For each placement, state the check you used and keep the ruler and set-square to hand so you can re-test any figure a classmate questions.
activities.intendedInsight: Properties combine: a figure can have parallel sides, a right angle, both, or neither, and each property is decided by its own independent check.

activities.title: Quick reference card for the two words
feedback: If a learner relies on the card to decide a figure's classification, redirect them to run the check on the figure itself, since the card only reminds them what the words mean.
activities.rationale: A static reference may support vocabulary recall and self-correction, but because nothing on it recomputes for a specific figure, it should sit alongside — not replace — the hands-on checking that carries the concept.
sourceClaims: Year 5 objective 'Recognise parallel and perpendicular lines, and properties of rectangles'; misconceptions = pupils confuse the vocabulary 'parallel'/'perpendicular', and think parallel lines must be the same length (reinforced by equal-length examples); remedies = show lines of differing lengths/thicknesses and orientations, use 'nearly' examples that force a checking method, and ask pupils to DRAW a line parallel/perpendicular to a given one
learnerActions: Keep a small reference card where pointing to a pair of sides shows 'parallel: always the same distance apart, never meet' and pointing to a corner shows the 90 degree square for 'perpendicular / right angle'.
Use the card to settle vocabulary disputes during the sorting and drawing tasks, then return to the physical check to confirm the actual figure.
activities.intendedInsight: A quick visual anchor helps keep 'parallel' and 'perpendicular' straight, but naming is not the same as verifying — the figure in front of you still has to pass the ruler or set-square test.

constraints: The classification skill is a doing-and-checking action: learners must physically test figures (slide/extend a ruler, apply a set-square or square card corner), not only name or recognise properties.

Include figures that defeat eyeballing — a tilted pair of parallel lines of unequal length, a slowly-converging near-parallel pair, and a right triangle rotated off the horizontal-and-vertical-legs position — because obvious upright examples let learners guess by appearance.

Treat the two properties as independent and test each on its own: a figure such as a rectangle can have both parallel sides and right angles, so do not force figures into a single exclusive bin — record each property separately or use a two-way grid.

Tasks that only ask learners to select or drag pre-made figures into categories test the classification outcome but do not require the learner to perform the ruler/set-square check, which is the actual skill; pair any such recognition task with hands-on checking or construction.
A reference poster or card supports vocabulary but does not let the learner verify an individual figure; treat it as a summary aid after hands-on work, not as the main activity.
Spoken discussion can rehearse the vocabulary and reasoning but does not itself perform the manual test; use talk to accompany checking rather than replace it.
This objective concerns parallel and perpendicular relations within flat 2-D figures; parallel/perpendicular in three dimensions is a later, distinct idea and is not required here.

The ruler, set-square and square card corner are physical approximations with real thickness; use them as practical checking tools, and keep the focus on the relation they reveal (constant gap, 90 degree corner) rather than on the tool itself.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One cited source (National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study) was marked verified:false in the source row; treat its statutory-content claim accordingly.

The original framing asserted that dialogue 'cannot deliver' the manual test and that a third spatial dimension 'adds nothing'; these have been softened to scoped statements about affordances and scope (2-D vs later 3-D), since the sources do not establish comparative efficacy or necessity.

Editor correction: Activity 1 originally used three mutually-exclusive bins while including a rectangle, which has both parallel sides and right angles; the sort was reframed to test each property independently so multi-property figures remain coherent and consistent with the two-way grid in Activity 3.

Efficacy wording in the Activity 1 and Activity 2 rationales was scoped to intended/observable limits (requiring a check; production not elicited by recognition alone) rather than asserting demonstrated effectiveness, since no activity has been tested.

Self-audit found no arithmetic or geometric errors in the retained content; the geometric content (parallel = constant distance/never meet; right angle = 90 degrees tested by set-square; property preserved under rotation) is sound.

probeDeeper: How did you CHECK that these two lines are parallel — what did you do to be sure they never meet?
These two lines are different lengths — can they still be parallel? How do you know?
I'll turn this right triangle so it stands on its point — is it still a right triangle? Show me how you can tell.
Here are two lines that look parallel but slowly get closer together — how would you find out for certain?
assess.correctAnswer: The child uses a physical check — slides or extends lines to confirm two sides stay the same distance apart (parallel), and applies the set-square/paper corner to confirm a 90° angle — and sorts on the result: places the tilted, unequal-length pair with the parallels, rejects the slowly-converging pair, and identifies the rotated triangle as a right triangle regardless of its orientation.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses the vocabulary — swaps 'parallel' and 'perpendicular', e.g. calls a right-angle corner 'parallel' or a pair of parallel sides 'perpendicular'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor each word to its check and image: parallel lines run alongside and never meet (slide the ruler, the gap holds); perpendicular lines cross at a right angle (set-square clicks). Rehearse naming while checking.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Applies the parallel label to lines meeting at 90° or vice-versa; uses the two words interchangeably while sorting

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks parallel lines must be the SAME LENGTH — rejects a genuinely parallel pair because the two lines are unequal in length
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show parallel lines of very different lengths and thicknesses; define parallel by constant distance / never meeting, tested by sliding a ruler or extending them — length is irrelevant (NCETM).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Excludes the tilted, unequal-length pair from the parallel set, giving a length reason ('they're not the same length, so they can't be parallel')

errorPatterns.pattern: Orientation-bound — only accepts parallel/perpendicular when the lines are horizontal or vertical, and does not recognise a right triangle once it is rotated off a horizontal-and-vertical-legs position
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rotate the same figures slowly so the child sees the property is preserved under turning, and test the right angle with the set-square in any orientation (prototype/imposed-attribute: orientation wrongly treated as defining).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Sorts the tilted parallel pair and the rotated right triangle as 'not parallel' / 'not a right triangle'; only the upright examples are accepted

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges by eye without testing — calls an almost-90° angle 'a right angle' or the slowly-converging pair 'parallel' because they look right
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist on the check with the 'nearly' examples where eyeballing fails — obvious examples do not need a method, near ones do (NCETM).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Accepts the near-right angle or the converging pair without sliding/extending or applying the set-square

responseLevels.gap: Sorts by overall appearance or the equal-length/horizontal prototype; rejects the tilted unequal-length parallels and the rotated right triangle; uses 'parallel' and 'perpendicular' interchangeably; does not apply a check.
responseLevels.full: Tests each figure with a reliable method (constant distance / extend for parallel; set-square for right angles) and sorts on the property regardless of length or orientation — correctly placing the tilted unequal-length parallels, rejecting the converging pair, and identifying the rotated right triangle; explains the check and transfers to a new mixed set.
responseLevels.partial: Applies a check to the obvious, upright examples and classifies them correctly, but reverts to appearance on the tilted/unequal or rotated items, or is unsure which word is which — can list the properties but does not reliably test every figure.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put out a mixed set of shapes and lines. Include: (i) a pair of parallel lines of clearly DIFFERENT lengths, tilted off horizontal; (ii) a pair that looks parallel but slowly converges; (iii) a right-angled triangle rotated so neither leg is horizontal or vertical; and (iv) a rectangle and a non-right triangle. Give the child a set-square or the square corner of a card and say: 'Sort these — which have parallel sides, and which have a right angle or are right triangles — and show me how you check each one.' Say nothing about method; watch what they DO.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The items are built so that eyeballing fails and only a check succeeds. A child who sorts by property uses the tools and gets the tilted unequal-length pair and the rotated right triangle right; a child ruled by the equal-length/horizontal prototype rejects the tilted unequal pair ('they're different lengths / not straight across') and misses the rotated right triangle; a child who confuses the words applies the wrong test to the wrong figure. Watching the checking action — not asking 'what does parallel mean?' — reveals which.

pedagogy.summary: At 8-9, picture and bar graphs become SCALED: one square (or symbol) represents several units — 2, 5 or 10 — so reading and drawing now depend on the scale/key, on reading intermediate values (a half-symbol, a bar top between gridlines), and on solving one- and two-step comparison, sum and difference problems. This is the NC Year 3-4 step from single-unit to scaled representations. The core new demand is that height/length no longer equals count directly — it must be read THROUGH the scale. Teaching should make the scale explicit and chosen for the data, model reading intermediate values, and rehearse two-step problems as two separate reads-then-combine.
bestPractices: Read the scale/key first, every time ('each square stands for 5'), before reading any value
Choose a sensible even scale for the data when constructing (so the largest value fits and marks are equal), and connect it to multiplication/counting in that step
Model reading intermediate values — half a symbol is half the key; a bar top halfway between 10 and 15 is 12 or 13 depending on the scale
Break two-step problems into explicit steps: read each value, then decide and do the combine (sum or difference)
keyRepresentations: Scaled bar graph on squared paper (each square = 2/5/10)
Scaled pictogram with a stated key and part-symbols
Frequency table as the source, with the scale chosen from the largest value
Two bars aligned for a difference, or stacked for a sum
commonMisconceptions: Ignores the scale and reads each square/symbol as one unit (or just counts symbols)
Cannot read an intermediate value — rounds a mid-interval bar to a gridline or ignores a part-symbol
Collapses a two-step problem to one step (reads a value but doesn't combine, or does the wrong operation)
Constructs a scaled axis with unequal intervals, so positions no longer map to values

learn.summary: For ages 8-9, picture and bar graphs become SCALED: one square or symbol stands for several units (2, 5 or 10). The core new demand is that a bar's height or a row's length no longer equals the count directly — it must be read THROUGH the scale/key. Learners should read the key first every time, read intermediate values (a half-symbol = half the key; a bar top read by counting the sub-intervals between gridlines), choose a sensible scale (such as 2, 5 or 10) with equally spaced intervals when constructing, and solve one- and two-step comparison, sum and difference problems as explicit 'read each value, then combine' steps. This is the NC Year 3-4 step from single-unit to scaled representations.

activities.title: Flip the scale: watch the same bars change value
feedback: If a learner reads each square as one unit, have them read the key aloud first and re-read each value by multiplying by the scale (e.g. 3 squares at 'each square = 5' is 3 × 5 = 15).
If an axis is drawn with unequal intervals, point out that positions no longer map to values; redraw with equal spacing and connect each step to counting on by the scale.
When the scale flip is understood, prompt: 'you chose each square = 5 — why is that a good scale for this data?' to confirm the choice is owned, not copied.
activities.rationale: Making the scale selectable or re-labelled turns 'reading through the scale' into a felt action: the same bars mean different amounts as the key changes, which targets the misconception of reading each square as one unit. Choosing a scale connects the representation to multiplication/counting.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils interpret and present data using scaled bar charts, pictograms and tables and solve one- and two-step 'how many more/fewer' problems; non-statutory guidance specifies simple scales (2, 5, 10 units) with increasing accuracy
learnerActions: Draw bars for a small data set on squared paper where 'each square = 1'.
Then change the key to 'each square = 5' and re-read every bar: say what each bar now means (e.g. a 4-square bar is now 20, not 4).
State out loud: 'The height on its own doesn't tell me the value — I only know the value once I read it through the scale.'
Optional with an interactive scaled-graph builder: use a scale selector (each square = 2/5/10) that re-labels the axis live, so the same drawn bars instantly re-map to new values.
Choose a sensible scale (e.g. 2, 5 or 10) for a given data set so the largest value fits, mark the axis in equally spaced intervals, and explain why that scale works.
activities.intendedInsight: A bar's or symbol's size maps to a value only via the scale; changing the scale re-maps every value, and a sensible scale (e.g. 2, 5 or 10) makes the largest value fit with equal intervals.

activities.title: Reading values between the marks
feedback: If a half-symbol is read as a whole symbol, show that half a symbol equals half the key's value and re-read the row (e.g. half of a key of 10 is 5).

If a mid-interval bar is rounded to a gridline, have the learner count the sub-intervals of the scale between the two gridlines to find the in-between value, and state the exact value (including a half, e.g. 12½, when the bar lands at a midpoint).
activities.rationale: Intermediate reading is a distinct skill from reading marked points; isolating half-symbols and sub-interval bars targets the specific error of rounding to a gridline or ignoring a part-symbol. Using an even key keeps the learner-facing values exact rather than rounding a 2½.
sourceClaims: A pictograph uses a symbol to represent several items in a category (many-to-one), distinct from a picture graph's one-symbol-per-individual — the basis of reading a scaled key correctly
learnerActions: Read a scaled pictogram with a stated key (e.g. one symbol = 10 children) that includes half-symbols, and give the value of a row ending in a half-symbol: a half-symbol is half the key (with a key of 10 that is 5). Note that with a key of 5 a half-symbol is 2½, which is why pictograms are usually built with an even key so half-symbols land on whole numbers.

Read a scaled bar whose top reaches a specific sub-interval mark between two gridlines — e.g. a bar reaching the 13 mark between the 10 and 15 lines — and state its value by counting the scale's sub-intervals. Separately, note that a bar sitting exactly at the midpoint of 10 and 15 reads as 12½, not a whole number.
Optional with draggable part-symbols or a draggable bar top: hit an exact intermediate value and check it against the key by counting sub-intervals.
activities.intendedInsight: Part-symbols and bar tops between gridlines carry real values: a half-symbol is half the key, and you read between gridlines by counting the scale's sub-intervals rather than rounding to the nearest line.

activities.title: Two-step problems as two reads then combine
feedback: If a learner gives a single value for 'total of the top two', scaffold the two steps explicitly: read value one, read value two, then combine.
If a learner subtracts when a sum is needed (or vice versa), ask what the question is asking for — a total (add) or a difference (subtract) — before computing.
For 'how many more', watch for giving the larger value instead of the difference; prompt for the gap between the two readings.
activities.rationale: Separating the read step from the combine step directly addresses collapsing two-step problems to one step and choosing the wrong operation, the common performance errors at this stage.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils interpret and present data using scaled bar charts, pictograms and tables and solve one- and two-step 'how many more/fewer' problems; non-statutory guidance specifies simple scales (2, 5, 10 units) with increasing accuracy
learnerActions: From a scaled graph, answer a 'how many more' comparison (e.g. how many more chose football than tennis?) by reading each value through the key and finding the difference.
Solve a two-step problem such as 'how many altogether for the top two choices?' by first reading each of the two values separately, then deciding whether to add or subtract, then doing it.
Say the two steps aloud before answering: 'First I read these two values; then I [add/subtract] them.'
Optional with a question panel that shades each bar as it is read before combining, so the two reads are visible as two distinct actions rather than one glance.
activities.intendedInsight: The two-step data problems here are two reads followed by one combine (sum or difference); naming both steps helps prevent collapsing it to a single glance or using the wrong operation.

activities.title: Construct a scaled graph from a frequency table
feedback: If the chosen scale makes the largest value overflow the grid or produces awkward marks, prompt choosing a larger scale (e.g. moving from 2 to 5 or 10) so the biggest value fits.
If intervals are uneven, re-space them equally so each step up the axis adds the same amount.
Confirm ownership by having the learner read their own graph back through its scale and compare to the table.
activities.rationale: Producing a graph (not just reading one) exposes whether the scale idea is genuinely owned; choosing the scale and spacing intervals equally is where unequal-axis errors surface.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils interpret and present data using scaled bar charts, pictograms and tables and solve one- and two-step 'how many more/fewer' problems; non-statutory guidance specifies simple scales (2, 5, 10 units) with increasing accuracy
learnerActions: Take a frequency table (e.g. swimming 20, cycling 15) and choose a sensible scale that fits the largest value with equal intervals (e.g. each square = 5, giving 4 squares and 3 squares).
Draw the bars from the baseline with equal width, each reaching the correct scaled position.
Alternatively draw a scaled pictogram with a stated key, using a part-symbol where the value is not a whole multiple of the key.
Check: does each drawn bar/row read back to the original data value when read through the chosen scale?
activities.intendedInsight: Constructing a scaled graph requires choosing a workable scale from the data, keeping intervals equal and bars from the baseline, so that positions map back to the intended values.

constraints: Always read the key/scale first, before reading any value ('each square stands for 5').

Learners should both READ and CONSTRUCT scaled graphs; recognition-only or tap-to-reveal items that show a key and values can check reading but do not themselves elicit the independent scale choice or multi-step solving that construction and open problems require.
A static scaled graph with a tappable key can serve as a reference, but it cannot let the learner change the scale or solve multi-step problems; use it as a scaffold, not the main task.
Multiple-choice two-step items should include a 'one-step' wrong option (just the top value) so collapsing to one step is detectable; such items check reading/solving but do not require construction.
Half-symbols and bar tops between gridlines must be included so intermediate reading is practised, not avoided.

When a half-symbol or mid-interval value is used with learners, choose a key/scale that yields an exact value (e.g. an even key so a half-symbol is a whole number), or state the half value explicitly (2½, 12½) rather than rounding to a nearby whole number.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original 'conversation' and '3D' entries were marked poor fit with claims that dialogue 'supplies none' and '3D adds nothing'. These are not established as universal laws; discussion can support naming the two steps and choosing a scale, so talk prompts are retained within activities. The narrow objective point — flat scaled graphs do not require a 3D model, and learners need the graph itself to act on — is preserved as a scaffolding limit, not a universal claim about media.

With a key of 5, a half-symbol is exactly 2½; the original's '2 or 3' is a rounding choice, not a clean value. Learner-facing examples now use an even key (10) so a half-symbol reads as a whole number, and the 2½ case is stated explicitly rather than rounded.

A bar 'halfway between 10 and 15' is exactly 12½; the original '12 or 13' is only correct if the bar actually reaches the 12 or 13 sub-interval mark. The learner example now uses a single determinate sub-interval value, and the specific grid's sub-intervals should be checked before asserting a single whole value.
Mid-interval values such as 12½ do not occur for whole-count data; such examples illustrate the reading arithmetic rather than realistic discrete counts.

The source claims support the curriculum content (scaled charts with 2/5/10 scales; many-to-one pictograph keys) but do not establish that the proposed interactive scale-selector or any specific medium is necessary or more effective than another; efficacy is treated as intended, not demonstrated.

probeDeeper: Ask 'what does one symbol/square stand for here — how did you use that?' to check the scale is applied, not ignored
Counterexample tuned to this topic: 'this bar reaches halfway between 10 and 15 — what value is that?' to test intermediate reading
Ask 'for the total of the top two, what two things do you have to do?' to surface the two-step structure
Ask 'you chose each square = 5 — why is that a good scale for this data?' to probe sensible scale choice when constructing
assess.correctAnswer: Interpreting: reads values THROUGH the key (symbols ×5, half-symbol = 2 or 3), and gives the difference for 'how many more'. Translating: draws bars for 20 and 15 using an even scale that fits (e.g. each square = 5), equal width from the baseline.

errorPatterns.pattern: Ignores the scale/key and reads each symbol or square as one unit
errorPatterns.nextMove: Read the key aloud first; overlay the count each symbol carries; re-read via multiplication by the scale
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child reads 3 football symbols as 3 rather than 15

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot read an intermediate value — rounds a mid-interval bar to a gridline or ignores a part-symbol
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show half a symbol = half the key; count the sub-intervals of the scale to read between gridlines
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child reads a half-symbol as a whole, or a bar halfway between 10 and 15 as 10 or 15

errorPatterns.pattern: Collapses a two-step problem to one step — reads the values but doesn't combine, or applies the wrong operation
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the two steps explicitly: read each value, then decide sum or difference and do it
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives a single value for 'total of the top two', or subtracts when a sum is needed

responseLevels.gap: Ignores the scale (reads as units), can't read part-values, and solves only single steps or draws uneven axes
responseLevels.full: Reads scaled and intermediate values via the key, solves two-step sum/difference problems, and constructs a scaled bar graph choosing a sensible even scale
responseLevels.partial: Reads scaled values at marked points and solves one-step problems, but misses intermediate values or the second step, or needs the scale chosen for them

assess.diagnosticPrompt: First: here is a scaled pictogram of favourite sports where one symbol stands for 5 children (and half-symbols appear) — how many chose football, and how many MORE chose football than tennis? Then: here is the data for two more sports (swimming 20, cycling 15) — draw them as bars on this grid, choosing a sensible scale.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with scaled-graph fluency reads via the key/scale, handles part-symbols, computes differences, and chooses a workable even scale when drawing; a child without it counts symbols as ones, ignores half-symbols, gives the larger value for 'how many more', or draws an uneven axis. The construct step exposes whether the scale idea is owned.

pedagogy.summary: This topic is the APPLICATION layer: pupils meet real contexts and must decide which unit-fraction division is happening and set it up — partition ('3 people share 1/2 lb → how much each?', 1/2 ÷ 3 = 1/6) versus measurement ('how many 1/3-cup servings in 2 cups?', 2 ÷ 1/3 = 6). The hard part is not the computation but reading the STRUCTURE: which quantity is being split, which is the dividend, and whether the answer should grow or shrink. Teach it by modelling each story on a bar/number line before writing the equation, always sanity-checking the answer against 'more or fewer than I started with?', and by having pupils invent stories for a bare expression so the structure runs both ways.
bestPractices: Model the story before the symbols: draw the sharing or the fitting on a bar/number line, then write the matching ÷ equation — IES found personalising/real contexts improves fraction-division performance
Explicitly sort the two structures — 'sharing an amount out' (partition, gets smaller) vs 'how many portions fit' (measurement, gets bigger) — and name which each word problem is
Gate every answer with estimation: 'should there be more or fewer than 2 servings?' catches a quotient pointing the wrong way
Have pupils create a story to MATCH a given expression (e.g. 4 ÷ 1/5), forcing them to own the structure, not just crank a rule
Verify with the inverse operation (6 × 1/3 = 2) so the word-problem answer is checked, not trusted
keyRepresentations: Bar model of the amount being shared (partition) or filled with portions (measurement)
Number line for 'how many 1/3s fit in 2'
Story ↔ equation ↔ picture triple laid side by side
Inverse check written under the answer
commonMisconceptions: Picks the wrong operation — multiplies, or divides in the wrong order (2 ÷ 1/3 done as 1/3 ÷ 2)
Reverses dividend and divisor — computes 3 ÷ 1/2 = 6 for '3 share 1/2 lb' instead of 1/2 ÷ 3
Expects the quotient to be smaller in a measurement problem, so distrusts '6 servings' being more than 2
Sets up the numbers but cannot tell which quantity is being split, so the model does not match the story

learn.summary: Pupils (ages 10-11) apply unit-fraction division to real contexts, deciding which structure a story has — partition ('3 people share 1/2 lb → how much each?', 1/2 ÷ 3 = 1/6) versus measurement ('how many 1/3-cup servings in 2 cups?', 2 ÷ 1/3 = 6). The core difficulty is reading the STRUCTURE — which quantity is split, which is the dividend, and whether the answer should grow or shrink — not the arithmetic. Guidance centres on modelling each story on a bar/number line before writing the equation, sanity-checking the answer against 'more or fewer than I started with?', and having pupils invent stories for bare expressions so they run the structure both ways.

activities.title: Build the model, then write the equation
feedback: If you built a sharing model for a 'how many fit' story, look: the picture cannot be made to match the words — reread which quantity is the whole and which is the portion.
When six 1/3-cup scoops fill the 2-cup bar, that is 2 ÷ 1/3 = 6 — count the portions in the picture to confirm.
Before trusting the number, ask 'should there be more or fewer than 2 servings?' A quotient pointing the wrong way signals a setup error.
activities.rationale: Modelling the situation before the symbols, with a visual model that matches the story, is the heart of this skill; both measurement and partition interpretations need pictures tied to the context.
sourceClaims: Presenting fraction-division problems in real/personalised contexts improves students' ability to solve them; the measurement ('how many fit') and partition ('share out') interpretations both need visual models that match the situation
Solve real-world problems involving division of unit fractions by whole numbers and whole numbers by unit fractions using visual fraction models and equations, and create story contexts
learnerActions: Read a word problem, e.g. 'How many 1/3-cup servings of raisins are in 2 cups?'
Decide whether the story is sharing an amount out among groups (partition) or finding how many portions fit inside an amount (measurement).
Choose and build the matching model on a bar or number line: either share one bar among N people, or fill a 2-cup bar with 1/3-cup portions and count them.
Write the matching division equation (2 ÷ 1/3 = 6) once the picture matches the words.
Lay the story, the picture, and the equation side by side so the three represent the same situation.

If a digital modeller is available, dragging the story onto a bar so the equation and answer recompute live lets pupils see a mismatched picture when they pick the wrong structure — this is one helpful interaction, not a required one.
activities.intendedInsight: The story tells you which division it is: sharing an amount out among more than one group gives each less than the whole, while asking how many sub-one-unit portions fit inside an amount gives more than you started with — and the picture either matches the words or it visibly does not.

activities.title: Sort the two structures, name the dividend, then compute
feedback: If you wrote 3 ÷ 1/2 for the chocolate story, ask: what is actually being cut up and given out? The half pound — so model that amount split into 3 before writing the equation.
If you reached for 2 × 1/3, check whether the story asks you to combine amounts or to find how many portions fit — these are different operations.
A quick estimate ('more or fewer than I started with?') catches a quotient pointing the wrong way.
activities.rationale: Explicitly separating partition from measurement, naming each, and then requiring a matching model is intended to confront the wrong-operation and reversal misconceptions, rather than letting pupils crank a rule.
sourceClaims: Presenting fraction-division problems in real/personalised contexts improves students' ability to solve them; the measurement ('how many fit') and partition ('share out') interpretations both need visual models that match the situation
learnerActions: Take several word problems and classify each as 'sharing an amount out' (partition: shared among more than one group, each share is smaller than the amount) or 'how many portions fit' (measurement: when the portion is smaller than one unit, as in these problems, the count is larger than the amount).
Name, for each, which quantity is being split and which is the dividend.
For the sharing problem '3 friends share 1/2 lb of chocolate equally', identify that the half pound is what is cut up, so it is 1/2 ÷ 3, not 3 ÷ 1/2.
After classifying and naming, build the matching bar model and only then write and solve the equation.
activities.intendedInsight: Naming the structure and the dividend first helps prevent reversing dividend and divisor and reaching for multiplication out of habit; classifying is a start, but the setup is not complete until the model and equation match the words.

activities.title: Confront 'the answer must get smaller'
feedback: If you distrusted '6 servings' because 6 is more than 2, count the scoops in the filled bar — six 1/3-cups really do fit in 2 cups.

With 3-cup servings there would be two-thirds of one serving (2 ÷ 3 = 2/3), i.e. fewer than one whole 3-cup serving fits in 2 cups; with 1/3-cup servings there are many — the portion size decides the direction.
activities.rationale: The belief that a quotient must be smaller than the dividend interferes with measurement-division problems and is best confronted with visual counting and estimation.
sourceClaims: The misconception that a quotient must be smaller than the dividend interferes with solving measurement-division word problems and must be confronted with visual counting and estimation
learnerActions: Predict, before computing, whether 'how many 1/3-cup servings in 2 cups' should be more or fewer than 2.
Fit 1/3-cup portions into 2 cups on a bar or number line (or with real measuring cups) and count them: there are 6.
State in words why counting portions smaller than one unit inside a larger amount gives a count bigger than the amount.
Contrast: if servings were 3-cup servings instead of 1/3-cup, would there be more or fewer in 2 cups, and why?
activities.intendedInsight: A quotient can be larger than the dividend: when you count how many portions smaller than one unit fit inside an amount, the count exceeds the amount.

activities.title: Invent a story for a bare expression, then check it
feedback: If your story for 4 ÷ 1/5 is actually a sharing story or a 'four fifths' multiplication story, it does not match the division — revise it to 'how many 1/5-sized portions fit in 4'.
Solve your own story back: if it does not give 20, the story does not match 4 ÷ 1/5.
Writing the inverse (6 × 1/3 = 2) under your answer checks it rather than trusting it.
activities.rationale: Creating story contexts for a given expression forces ownership of the structure, and verifying with the inverse makes the answer checked rather than assumed. Being able to invent a correct story goes beyond merely recognising one among options.
sourceClaims: Solve real-world problems involving division of unit fractions by whole numbers and whole numbers by unit fractions using visual fraction models and equations, and create story contexts
learnerActions: Write your own word problem that 4 ÷ 1/5 would solve, e.g. 'How many 1/5-metre ribbons can I cut from a 4-metre roll?' (= 20).
Identify which structure your story uses (here, measurement — how many 1/5-sized portions fit in 4).
Solve your own story to confirm it really gives 20 and really matches division, not multiplication.
Check a given answer with the inverse operation, writing e.g. 6 × 1/3 = 2 under the answer to confirm 2 ÷ 1/3 = 6.
activities.intendedInsight: Running the structure backwards — building a valid story from the symbols and verifying by the inverse — shows the structure is owned, not merely recognised.

activities.title: Talk through the direction with a context character
feedback: If your prediction and your computed answer disagree, revisit which quantity is the whole — one of them is set up wrong.
Explaining why each share shrinks (sharing) or why the count grows (fitting) shows you have read the structure, not just the numbers.
activities.rationale: A role-play dialogue set in a real context can probe 'more or fewer?' reasoning and story invention; it supplements, rather than replaces, the visual modelling where pupils build and test a setup.
sourceClaims: Presenting fraction-division problems in real/personalised contexts improves students' ability to solve them; the measurement ('how many fit') and partition ('share out') interpretations both need visual models that match the situation
learnerActions: Take a kitchen or shop scenario where a character (cook, shopkeeper) poses a sharing problem and a portioning problem.
Before computing, predict aloud whether each answer will be more or fewer than the starting amount, and justify.
Explain to the character which quantity is being split and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the predicted direction and the dividend in a concrete context reinforces structure-reading and the 'more or fewer?' sanity check.

constraints: Matching stories to expressions and multiple-choice 'which calculation solves this?' check the choice only; classifying stories into 'sharing' vs 'how many fit' usefully targets the core difficulty (reading the structure, a source-endorsed move) but on its own does not elicit building the matching model and writing the equation. Pair classification with pupil-built models and pupil-written equations rather than treat selection alone as the whole learning.
Story invention must be produced by the pupil (constructing/writing a context), not selected from options, to reveal whether the measurement structure is owned.

A static worked pair of stories with reveal-the-setup flaps can illustrate the two structures but does not let a pupil attempt and test their own setup on a new story; treat it as a scaffold or reference.
When counting portions physically (measuring cups, cut ribbons), these are concrete approximations of the bar/number-line model; keep the link to the written equation explicit.

Contexts here are quantity and length sharing, which model naturally on a bar or number line; three-dimensional representations are not needed for these particular contexts (this is a scope note, not a claim that 3D could never help elsewhere).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the arithmetic: 1/2 ÷ 3 = 1/6; 2 ÷ 1/3 = 6; 4 ÷ 1/5 = 20; 2 ÷ 3 = 2/3 (two-thirds of one 3-cup serving); inverse check 6 × 1/3 = 2 — all consistent across the source. The common reversal error 3 ÷ 1/2 (= 6) is flagged only as an error, never offered as a valid answer or option.

The Common Core 5.NF.7c source is marked verified:false in the row; it is cited only for the standard's description of using visual models and creating story contexts, not as evidence of comparative efficacy.

No source establishes that any one artefact format is uniquely able to teach this; claims about a format being superior, or that 3D 'adds nothing conceptual', are presented as scope-limited design notes rather than established pedagogical law, and the conversation/dialogue format's efficacy is not source-established.

probeDeeper: In (b), is your answer bigger or smaller than 2 — does that make sense for 'how many servings'?
In (a), which number is being shared out — the half pound or the 3 people? How do you know?
If the servings were 3-cup servings instead of 1/3-cup, would there be more or fewer of them in 2 cups — why?
Check your answer to (b) with a multiplication.
assess.correctAnswer: (a) 1/2 ÷ 3 = 1/6 lb each. (b) 2 ÷ 1/3 = 6 servings. Story for 4 ÷ 1/5: any 'how many 1/5-sized portions fit in 4' context, e.g. 'how many 1/5-metre ribbons can I cut from a 4-metre roll?' (= 20).

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses dividend and divisor in the sharing problem: '3 people, half a pound' → 3 ÷ 1/2 = 6, instead of 1/2 ÷ 3 = 1/6
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'what is actually being cut up and given out?' — the half pound — and model that amount split into 3 on a bar before writing the equation; reteach the partition meaning
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Working shows 3 ÷ 1/2 (or answer 6 lb each); the quantity being shared is not identified as the dividend

errorPatterns.pattern: Expects the measurement answer to be smaller than the amount: distrusts or won't produce '6 servings' because 6 is more than 2 cups
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fit 1/3-cup portions into the 2 cups and count them physically; name that counting small portions gives many, so the answer exceeds the amount; reteach the how-many-fit meaning
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In (b), answers a value below 2 (e.g. 2/3), or hesitates/changes 6 because 'it can't be more than 2'

errorPatterns.pattern: Chooses the wrong operation — multiplies, or cannot decide — because the story's structure (sharing vs fitting) is not read; the numbers are combined by habit
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort several stories into 'sharing out' vs 'how many fit' before computing any; require a bar model that matches the words; check the invented story by solving it back
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 2 × 1/3 or 1/2 × 3; or the invented story for 4 ÷ 1/5 does not match division (e.g. a 'four fifths' multiplication story)

responseLevels.gap: Picks the wrong operation or reverses the order on one or both problems, cannot set up a matching model, and cannot invent a valid story for 4 ÷ 1/5.
responseLevels.full: Sets up and solves both with the correct operation and order, justifies each answer's direction (1/6 smaller, 6 bigger) against the context, verifies with the inverse, and invents a valid measurement story for 4 ÷ 1/5; transfers cleanly to an unfamiliar context.
responseLevels.partial: Solves the familiar sharing problem correctly but muddles the measurement one (or vice versa), or gets both numerically yet cannot judge whether the answers should grow or shrink, and writes a story that only loosely matches 4 ÷ 1/5 — lists numbers without owning the structure.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Solve these two, showing your working: (a) 3 friends share half a pound of chocolate equally — how much does each get? (b) How many 1/3-cup servings of raisins are in 2 cups? Then make up your own word problem that 4 ÷ 1/5 would solve.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the SETUP separates real understanding from rule-chasing. The two problems pull in opposite directions — (a) shares an amount so the answer shrinks below 1/2; (b) counts portions so the answer grows above 2 — so a child who blindly applies one procedure gets one right and one absurd. The order of dividend and divisor in (a) exposes reversal (3 ÷ 1/2 = 6 instead of 1/6). And inventing a story for 4 ÷ 1/5 exposes whether the measurement structure is owned or only recognised — a child who writes a sharing story, or a multiplication story, reveals the gap.
