pedagogy.summary: Building 3-D shapes from nets is a procedural skill that consolidates the 2-D↔3-D relationship. It is best taught by having children construct a net (measure, draw, cut, fold, tape), predict which solid it makes, and verify by folding — then check that every face, edge and vertex of the built solid matches the target. Anchoring on a base face and adding faces as composites reduces trial-and-error, and diagnosing why a faulty net won't close (gaps or overlaps) turns errors into structural learning.
bestPractices: Construct-then-fold-to-verify; have the child predict the solid before folding rather than assembling by trial and error.
Start from a base face and add faces in composites; include tabs for assembly so the model closes cleanly.
Check the count: the built solid's faces, edges and vertices should match the target (a triangular prism has 5 faces, 9 edges, 6 vertices).
Compare several valid nets for the same solid and diagnose why a non-closing net fails — is it the face-set or the arrangement?
keyRepresentations: Card or Polydron nets folded into solids
A tabbed net template that folds and tapes shut
The triangular-prism net: two congruent triangles plus three rectangles forming a band
Base-face-plus-composite layout (band of rectangles, then the two ends)
commonMisconceptions: Falls back on the familiar cube 'cross' net and cannot generate a net for a different solid.
Chooses the wrong face-set (e.g. all rectangles, or two triangles and two rectangles for a prism).
Arranges the correct faces so the net cannot close; blames ragged cutting rather than the layout.

learn.summary: Building 3-D shapes from nets is a procedural skill that consolidates the 2-D to 3-D relationship. Children construct a net (measure, draw, cut, fold, tape), predict which solid it makes, then fold to verify and check that every face, edge and vertex of the built solid matches the target. Anchoring on a base face and adding faces as composites (e.g. a band of rectangles plus two triangular ends) reduces trial-and-error, and diagnosing why a faulty net won't close — gaps or overlaps — turns errors into structural learning. The worked example throughout is the triangular prism: two congruent triangles plus three rectangles, with 5 faces, 9 edges and 6 vertices.

activities.title: Construct and fold the net of a triangular prism
feedback: Before folding, ask: which rectangle is the base, and how will each face meet its neighbours when folded? A band of three rectangles with a triangle on each end is one reliable layout to start from. Other valid layouts exist, such as one with a rectangle attached to a triangle, so test the fold rather than rejecting a net only because it has no band.

If a triangle is left flapping, or a gap remains even though the pieces were cut accurately, check two things. First, the layout: will each face meet its neighbour when folded? If not, try redrawing from the band-plus-ends composite. Second, the measurements: each triangle side should equal the width of the rectangle it joins, and all rectangles should have the same length. If the net itself is correct but only the cutting or taping is ragged, provide a pre-scored, tabbed template so the check tests the layout reasoning rather than scissor control.

When counting, prompt: how many corners does each triangular end have? So how many vertices altogether? How many edges are on each triangular end, and how many edges join the two ends? Check the totals against 5 faces, 9 edges, 6 vertices.
If the child reproduces a familiar cube 'cross' net, unfold a real triangular prism to reveal its actual net and contrast the two.
activities.rationale: The procedure ends in a genuinely 3-D solid, so folding the net up and rotating the sealed shape to count faces, edges and vertices is the target skill. Successful builders anchor imaged folding to a base face and known composites; diagnosing why a net won't close moves children from judging by appearance to reasoning about structure.
sourceClaims: Successful builders use imaged folding anchored to a base face and known composites (a 'line of four' wraps the cube's sides); the weakest reproduce a memorised prototype net; teacher questioning that maps net shapes/sides/points to faces/edges/vertices moves children from appearance to structure.
learnerActions: Using card, a ruler and scissors, draw the net of a triangular prism: two congruent triangles and three rectangles of equal length, each rectangle as wide as the triangle side it joins.
Before cutting, predict and say which shape will be the bottom (base) and which two shapes will cap the ends.
Cut out the net, fold along the edges and tape it shut.
Point to the finished solid and count its faces, edges and vertices (target: 5 faces, 9 edges, 6 vertices).
activities.intendedInsight: A valid net is more than the right set of faces — the faces must be arranged so they fold into a closed solid, and the structure of that solid (faces, edges, vertices) can be read off the built 3-D shape rather than the flat drawing.

activities.title: Drag-to-build a net and predict the fold
feedback: On folding, flag gaps, overlaps and any face left flapping so the child can see exactly where the layout fails.
Immediate close/fail feedback on the fold doubles as a check of the construction procedure.
A flat on-screen view slightly under-sells the real 3-D fold, so confirm the count on a rotatable solid or a physical model.
activities.rationale: A drag-to-build editor with a fold animation and immediate close/fail feedback exercises the construction procedure and lets children test many layouts quickly. It is offered as a supplement to physical construction, not a replacement; a flat screen view represents, rather than replaces, the 3-D fold. Efficacy relative to physical building is not established by the cited sources.
sourceClaims: Successful builders use imaged folding anchored to a base face and known composites (a 'line of four' wraps the cube's sides); the weakest reproduce a memorised prototype net; teacher questioning that maps net shapes/sides/points to faces/edges/vertices moves children from appearance to structure.
learnerActions: Drag two triangles and three rectangles onto a grid to lay out a candidate net.
State which solid you predict it will make and which faces will be the base and the ends.
Fold the layout and watch how the rectangles and triangles move. Check whether every face meets its neighbour so the ends are capped and the prism closes.

If a face is left flapping or a gap or overlap appears, rearrange the faces so they meet correctly, for example by re-anchoring on a band of three rectangles with a triangle on each end, then fold again.
Rotate the sealed solid and tap round it to tally faces, edges and vertices.
activities.intendedInsight: A layout that 'looks fine' flat may still fail to close. Checking how each face will meet its neighbours when folded is what shows whether the prism seals. A band of three rectangles with triangular ends is one dependable layout, but not the only valid one.

activities.title: Compare and diagnose nets for the same solid
feedback: If the child counts wrong faces (e.g. four rectangles, or two triangles and two rectangles), hand them the target prism and match each of its faces to a net shape before deciding; count faces first.

For an arrangement failure, have the child trace which edges will meet when folded and find where faces overlap or leave a gap. Rearranging into a band of three rectangles between the two triangular ends is one reliable fix, though not the only valid net.
A sorting task like this can check and build classification of nets, but it does not itself elicit independent construction of a net from scratch; use it alongside, not instead of, building.
activities.rationale: Comparing valid nets and diagnosing why a non-closing net fails separates face-set errors from arrangement errors and builds the structural scheme. Coordinating spatial visualisation with property-based reasoning is what lets children see past the 'look' of the flat drawing.
sourceClaims: Spatial visualisation and property-based reasoning must be coordinated by domain knowledge to overcome the 'look' of a 2-D representation, which is why some children build by appearance rather than structure.
learnerActions: Given several candidate nets for a triangular prism, sort them into those that will fold shut and those that will not.

For each failing net, say whether the problem is the face-set (wrong shapes, wrong number or mismatched sizes) or the arrangement (correct faces placed so that, when folded, some overlap or leave a gap).
Find two different valid nets for the same prism and explain why both work.
Reason about a near-miss: if a net has three triangles and two rectangles, could it fold into this prism, or into any closed solid at all? Explain using the faces a triangular prism needs.
activities.intendedInsight: Nets fail for two distinct reasons — the wrong set of faces, or a correct set arranged so it cannot close — and the same solid can have more than one valid net.

constraints: A static exploded or net diagram (even one tagged face-to-face, or where tapping a net face shows where it lands on the solid) is a useful planning reference but does not enact the fold-and-check procedure; use it to support planning, not as the build itself.
Matching or sequencing tasks that pair solids to nets and counts check recognition of nets and counts but do not elicit independent construction of a net; use them as a post-check.
Discussion can prompt a prediction for the child to justify, but talking does not itself elicit the physical construction and folding that is the target skill.
When cutting, folding or taping leaves ragged gaps, the fold-check becomes inconclusive — provide a pre-scored, tabbed template so the check tests the reasoning rather than scissor control.
A flat 2-D interactive represents the 3-D fold and may under-sell it; confirm face/edge/vertex counts on a rotatable or physical solid.
Include assembly tabs so the model closes cleanly.

Building simple 3-D shapes, including making nets, is part of the Key Stage 2 (Year 6) national curriculum for England. Physical construction with card, ruler and scissors is the core experience in this guidance; digital editors are a supplementary option, not a replacement.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the triangular prism: 2 triangular faces + 3 rectangular faces = 5 faces; 3 edges on each triangular end (6) + 3 connecting edges = 9 edges; 3 vertices on each triangular end = 6 vertices. These match the source values (5 faces, 9 edges, 6 vertices).

The near-miss prompt (three triangles and two rectangles) is retained as a reasoning probe: that face-set does not form a triangular prism, so the expected answer is 'no'. Kept as a diagnostic question, not as a construction instruction.

The legacy row ranked a 3-D interactive as 'ideal' and a conversation as 'poor'. Comparative efficacy/necessity is not established by the cited sources, so artefacts are presented as options with stated affordances and limits rather than universal claims.

The National Curriculum claim was removed from Activity 1's sourceClaims because that activity's rationale concerns a teaching principle (imaged folding/structure) rather than the curriculum objective itself; the curriculum requirement is retained as a constraint and in the audit.

probeDeeper: Before you fold — which shape will be the bottom, and which two will be the ends?
Your model has a gap here. Is the net wrong, or the way it is arranged? Show me.
How many edges meet at that top corner? So how many vertices altogether?
If I gave you a net with three triangles and two rectangles, what solid would that build — could it be this prism?
assess.correctAnswer: Draws a net of two congruent triangles and three rectangles positioned so the rectangles form a band that wraps between the triangular ends; folds it to a closed prism with no gaps or overlaps; and, pointing to the built solid, counts 5 faces, 9 edges and 6 vertices — self-correcting the layout if a first attempt won't close.

errorPatterns.pattern: Chooses the wrong faces for the solid — e.g. draws four rectangles, or two triangles and two rectangles, for a triangular prism
errorPatterns.nextMove: Hand the child the target prism and match each of its faces to a net shape before drawing; count faces first
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The net has too few or too many faces, or the wrong shapes, and won't wrap between the two triangular ends

errorPatterns.pattern: Places the correct faces in an arrangement that cannot fold shut — the three rectangles don't form a continuous band, so the ends never meet
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor a base rectangle, fold the band of three rectangles first, then attach the two triangular ends; re-draw from that composite
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Folding leaves a gap or overlap; the child blames the cutting rather than the layout

errorPatterns.pattern: Falls back on the familiar cube 'cross' net and cannot generate a net for a different solid
errorPatterns.nextMove: Unfold a real triangular prism to reveal its actual net and contrast it with the cube net
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Attempts a cross of six shapes regardless of the target prism

errorPatterns.pattern: Has the right net but cutting, folding or taping leaves gaps, so the fold-check is inconclusive
errorPatterns.nextMove: Provide a pre-scored, tabbed template so the check tests the reasoning, not scissor control
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The net is correct on paper but the model is ragged and the child is unsure whether it 'worked'

responseLevels.gap: Cannot produce a net that closes into the target solid; reproduces a memorised cube net or an unfoldable arrangement.
responseLevels.full: Constructs a valid net by choosing the right faces and arranging them as a band-plus-ends composite, folds to a closed solid, self-corrects a faulty layout, and reads faces, edges and vertices off the 3-D structure.
responseLevels.partial: Builds the solid when given a correct net or after trial and error and counts faces, but cannot construct a valid net from scratch or explain why an arrangement fails — parts without structure.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is card, a ruler, and scissors. Construct the net of a triangular prism, then fold and tape it to check it makes the solid. When it is built, tell me how many faces, edges and vertices it has by pointing to them.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the child build separates those holding a structural scheme (base band plus two ends, faces in the right composite) from those assembling by trial and error or reproducing a memorised cube net. A wrong face-set or a net that won't close is visible immediately, and the face/edge/vertex count exposes whether the child reads the 3-D structure rather than the flat drawing.

sources.claim: Successful builders use imaged folding anchored to a base face and known composites (a 'line of four' wraps the cube's sides); the weakest reproduce a memorised prototype net; teacher questioning that maps net shapes/sides/points to faces/edges/vertices moves children from appearance to structure.
sources.source: Knight & Wright (2014), 'Will this Net Work?', MERGA proceedings (ERIC ED572616)

sources.claim: Recognising, describing and building simple 3-D shapes, including making nets, is a Key Stage 2 geometry objective in the English National Curriculum.
sources.source: National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (gov.uk)

sources.claim: Spatial visualisation and property-based reasoning must be coordinated by domain knowledge to overcome the 'look' of a 2-D representation, which is why some children build by appearance rather than structure.
sources.source: Fujita, Kondo, Kumakura, Kunimune & Jones (2020), Mathematics Education Research Journal 32(2)

pedagogy.summary: At 7-8, children learn (still with teacher support) to break a multi-step problem into sub-problems, choose and sequence strategies, and check answers for reasonableness using estimation and inverse operations. This is where the keyword strategy becomes actively harmful: research on released test items shows that tying a word to an operation succeeds on fewer than half of single-step problems and under 10% of multi-step problems, so a habit that seemed to 'work' earlier now fails badly. The parallel risk is the compulsion to calculate — producing an answer with no estimate benchmark and no check. Effective teaching builds the estimate-first-then-verify routine, teaches self-monitoring via modelled self-questioning (strong evidence), and uses visual representations to expose the sequence of steps (strong evidence), while normalising strategy-switching when the first approach stalls.
bestPractices: Estimate first to set a reasonableness benchmark, then compute, then check by an inverse operation or a different method — revise if they disagree
Teach problem structure (schema), not keywords: the keyword strategy collapses on multi-step problems (match rate <10%)
Model self-questioning aloud and provide a prompt list for monitoring progress across the sub-steps (WWC Rec 2, strong evidence)
Represent the problem with a bar/strip diagram so the sub-problems and their order are visible (WWC Rec 3, strong evidence)
Break the problem into named sub-problems and solve each, keeping the whole plan in view
Normalise strategy-switching: if the first approach stalls, deliberately try a different representation or method rather than abandoning
keyRepresentations: Bar / strip diagram decomposing a multi-step problem into sub-parts
Number line for sequencing multi-step jumps
Estimation / rounding to a benchmark before computing
Inverse-operation check (work backwards to the start)
A monitoring prompt list across the sub-steps: plan → do a step → check → next
commonMisconceptions: Keyword strategy on multi-step problems — tying a word to an operation and applying operations in the wrong order
Computing an answer with no estimate and no check, accepting answers that are wildly off (compulsion to calculate)
Believing that if the first method doesn't work, you're simply stuck (no strategy-switching)
Doing the sub-steps but not connecting them — losing track of what has been found and what remains

learn.summary: For ages 7-8 (with teacher support): make sense of multi-step problems within 1000 by breaking them into ordered sub-problems, choosing and sequencing strategies, estimating a reasonableness benchmark first, and checking with an inverse operation or a different method — revising when the two disagree. The central aim is to replace the keyword habit (tying a word to an operation), which research on released items reports succeeds on under 50% of single-step and under 10% of multi-step problems, with attention to problem structure, and to counter the compulsion to calculate (answering with no estimate and no check). Self-questioning aloud and visual representations (e.g. bar/strip diagrams and number lines for sequencing jumps) are the two levers cited with strong evidence in the WWC grades 4-8 guide; strategy-switching when the first approach stalls should be normalised.

activities.title: Estimate-first multi-step solver with inverse check
feedback: If a child seizes on 'left' and subtracts 50 from 320 immediately, never forming the 4×50 sub-step: have them retell and represent the problem as ordered sub-problems on a strip diagram, and discuss why the cue word misleads here

When a keyword-driven wrong-order calculation lands far from the estimate and working backwards through the story (adding back all 200 pencils sold, e.g. 270 + 200 = 470, not 320) fails to return the starting number, point out the two mismatches and invite re-sequencing the steps
If the answer is 'more left than it started with' and the child is untroubled: require an estimate before computing and an inverse/alternative check after — do not reteach the arithmetic itself

If the child stalls and stops, model 'change course if necessary': show a second way to represent the same problem — for instance switching from a strip/bar diagram to a number line of the multi-step jumps — and name switching as a normal part of solving
activities.rationale: Operationalises the two strong-evidence WWC levers (visual representation of the problem structure and monitoring) and the plan-monitor-check-revise practice described in SMP1, while directly targeting the keyword habit the keyword-investigation reports as failing on multi-step problems. Optional interactive affordances (sequenceable sub-problem cards on a bar-model canvas, an estimate slider, an inverse-check panel that works backwards, a reasonableness gauge, and a 'try another way' button) are illustrations of how to make these signals visible, not required mechanisms; the same can be done on paper with a drawn strip diagram or number line and a written-out backwards check.
sourceClaims: Tying a keyword to an operation leads to a correct solution less than 50% of the time on single-step routine problems and under 10% on multi-step problems (0% for the comparison schema) — keywords are an ineffective strategy educators should avoid in favour of schema instruction.

Modelling a self-questioning process to help students monitor and reflect (Rec 2) and teaching students to build and use visual representations of the problem (Rec 3) each have strong evidence for improving problem solving in grades 4-8.
Proficient solvers plan a solution pathway, monitor and evaluate progress and change course if necessary, and check answers using a different method while asking 'Does this make sense?'.
learnerActions: Take a two-step problem, e.g. 'A shop had 320 pencils. It sold 4 boxes of 50. How many pencils are left?' and arrange it as two connected sub-problem cards in the order you will solve them (first 4×50 = 200 sold, then 320 − 200), adding more cards only if a longer problem needs them
Before computing, state 'about how big' the answer should be — set an estimate benchmark (e.g. 'about 300 sold... no, 200, so a bit over 100 left')
Solve each sub-step in order, keeping the whole plan visible

After you have an answer, work backwards through the story (inverse) to see whether you return to the starting number: put back the pencils that were sold, 120 + 4×50 = 120 + 200 = 320. Undo the actions in the problem, not just your own calculation, because undoing a wrong calculation (e.g. 320 − 50 = 270, then 270 + 50 = 320) would still get you back to 320
Compare your answer against your own estimate: if it is wildly off, treat that as a signal to recheck both the answer and the estimate
If an approach stalls, deliberately re-represent the problem a different way — for example switch between a strip/bar diagram and a number line that sequences the jumps — rather than stopping
activities.intendedInsight: Decomposition is something you physically arrange and sequence, not a rule triggered by a cue word; the estimate and a backwards check that undoes the problem's actions (not merely the child's own calculation) are two separate signals that can catch a wrong-order or wrong-operation answer.

activities.title: Think-aloud study partner for self-monitoring
feedback: Prompt for a plan and an estimate first; withhold steps
When the child states a result, ask 'how could you be sure?' and prompt an inverse or alternative check
If the child treats a stall as failure, ask 'what's another way we could show this?' — for instance a number line instead of a strip diagram — to model switching representations
activities.rationale: Rehearses the modelled self-questioning routine cited with strong evidence, and pressing for justification of sequence and check surfaces decomposition versus keyword-triggered ordering. Spoken, responsive dialogue is well suited to rehearsing self-monitoring aloud, and does not substitute for the child actually doing the arithmetic.
sourceClaims: Modelling a self-questioning process to help students monitor and reflect (Rec 2) and teaching students to build and use visual representations of the problem (Rec 3) each have strong evidence for improving problem solving in grades 4-8.
Proficient solvers plan a solution pathway, monitor and evaluate progress and change course if necessary, and check answers using a different method while asking 'Does this make sense?'.
learnerActions: Work with a partner (or in-role coach) who never hands over the steps but asks you to state a plan and an estimate before computing
Use a monitoring prompt list to pace yourself through the sub-steps: plan → do a step → check → next
Answer monitoring questions aloud: 'What have you found so far? What's still unknown? How could you check that?'
Justify the order you chose for the sub-steps and explain your reasonableness check in your own words
When you are stuck, respond to the prompt to represent the problem a different way — for example a number line for the sequence of jumps — instead of being given the answer
activities.intendedInsight: Self-questioning across sub-steps is a repeatable routine for monitoring progress and catching errors, and being able to explain the sequence and the check shows understanding of the structure.

activities.title: Worked-example reference with revealed self-questions
feedback: Point to the self-question tied to each sub-step so the child connects each move to a reason
Follow up by having the child perform the sequencing and check unaided on a new problem
activities.rationale: A revealed worked example can display the decomposition and the check and acts as a scaffold or reference. On its own it does not have the child sequence the steps or perform the reasonableness check, so it must be paired with independent practice; this is a limitation of the format for this objective, not evidence that a fixed example cannot teach.
sourceClaims: Modelling a self-questioning process to help students monitor and reflect (Rec 2) and teaching students to build and use visual representations of the problem (Rec 3) each have strong evidence for improving problem solving in grades 4-8.
learnerActions: Study a worked multi-step problem where each sub-step can be revealed one at a time
For each revealed sub-step, read the self-question the solver asked and see why the estimate rules certain answers out
After studying, re-solve a fresh but similar problem yourself, sequencing the steps and doing your own check
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing the decomposition and the reasonableness reasoning laid out gives a model of what good monitoring looks like before you do it independently.

activities.title: Reasonableness and wrong-order spotting items
feedback: If a child picks an impossible answer, ask them to estimate first and compare against each option
For the runner item, if the child just multiplies, discuss what the situation implies about the real answer (more than 10× the 100 m time, not exactly it)
activities.rationale: Targeted estimation/reasonableness items can probe whether a child reasons about reasonableness and can detect wrong-order calculations. A scored linear format tends to reward fast computing and does not elicit the child's own decomposition or self-monitoring, so it should supplement, not replace, construction tasks.
sourceClaims: The compulsion to calculate leads students to compute without reasoning about reasonableness; realistic/'problematic' items (e.g. the runner and plank problems) show the vast majority of students compute regardless of whether the answer makes sense.
learnerActions: Given a problem and several candidate answers, decide 'which of these answers is impossible, and why?' using estimation
Examine two worked solutions and 'spot the wrong-order calculation' — identify where operations were applied in the wrong sequence

Reason about a realistic item: 'A runner's best time for 100 m is 20 seconds. How long for 1 km?' — explain why it will be more than 10× the 100 m time (tiring over the longer distance), rather than multiplying blindly
activities.intendedInsight: Estimation and attention to the real situation let you reject answers that cannot make sense, even before checking the full computation.

constraints: Teach problem structure (schema), not keywords: cue words like 'left' can trigger the wrong operation or wrong order on multi-step problems.
Always require an estimate benchmark before computing and a check (an inverse that undoes the problem's actions, or a different method) after — revise if they disagree.
Normalise strategy-switching: a stalled first approach is a cue to re-represent the problem (e.g. swap a strip diagram for a number line), not evidence of failure.
Worked, reveal-only examples are scaffolds or references: they show the decomposition and check but do not have the child sequence steps or perform the check — pair them with independent practice.
Scored linear items can assess estimation and wrong-order spotting but do not elicit independent decomposition or self-monitoring and tend to reward fast computing; do not use as the primary task.

Interactive affordances (sequenceable cards, estimate slider, backward-working inverse panel, reasonableness gauge, 'try another way' button) are optional illustrations; the learning can be done on paper with drawn diagrams and written checks.

This multi-step arithmetic content is not spatial, so a 3-D environment adds set-up cost without a clear benefit here — a judgement for this specific content, not a general claim that 3-D media add nothing elsewhere.
At this age children develop the habit with teacher support; independent strategy evaluation comes later, so expect to scaffold the plan-estimate-check routine.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Worked the diagnostic arithmetic independently: 4×50 = 200 sold; 320 − 200 = 120 left; inverse check 120 + 200 = 320. These are consistent across the source and retained as the target reasoning.

The original 'ideal/strong/possible/poor' artefact rankings and the claim that a 3-D environment 'adds cost without benefit' were catalog fit judgements; the non-spatial observation is retained as a content-specific constraint rather than asserted as a universal pedagogical law.

The under-10% multi-step (and under-50% single-step) keyword success figures and the strong-evidence WWC claims are carried from legacy sources marked verified; no independent re-verification was performed in this rewrite.
The legacy 'actively harmful' framing of the keyword strategy is presented here as a low-yield risk, since the cited sources establish low match rates rather than demonstrated harm.

probeDeeper: 'How did you break this into parts — which part did you do first, and why that order?' (surfaces decomposition vs keyword-triggered ordering)
'About how big should the answer be? What tells you a wrong answer is wrong?' (estimate as benchmark)
'Check it a different way — can you work backwards to the 320?' (inverse verification)

Counterexample: 'A runner's best time for 100 m is 20 seconds. How long for 1 km?' — does the child reason about the real situation (it will be more than 10× because of tiring), or just multiply blindly?
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for a child who decomposes it (first 4×50 = 200 sold, then 320 − 200), estimates ('about 300 sold... no, 200, so a bit over 100 left'), gets 120, and checks by a different method or inverse (120 + 200 = 320). The decomposition, the estimate benchmark, and a genuine check are the targets.

errorPatterns.pattern: Keyword strategy on a multi-step problem — tying a word to an operation and applying operations in the wrong order or using an irrelevant one.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Teach structure over words: have the child retell and represent the problem as ordered sub-problems on a strip diagram; discuss why the cue word misleads here.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child seizes on a word ('left' → subtract) and subtracts 50 from 320 immediately, never forming the 4×50 sub-step; keyword-operation matching is known to succeed under 10% of the time on multi-step problems.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compulsion to calculate: produces an answer with no estimate and no check, accepting results that are clearly unreasonable.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the routine the child already half-knows: require an estimate benchmark before computing and an inverse/alternative check after; do not reteach the arithmetic.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives an answer (e.g. 'more left than it started with') and is untroubled; offers no estimate and does not check by inverse when asked what they could do to be sure.

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes that if the first method doesn't work, you're stuck — does not switch strategy or representation.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model 'change course if necessary' — show two ways to represent the same problem and name switching as a normal part of solving; prompt 'what's another way we could show this?'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When the first approach stalls the child stops rather than trying a different representation; treats a stall as failure, not as a cue to change course.

responseLevels.gap: Picks an operation from a word, runs steps in the wrong order or uses the wrong numbers, offers no estimate, and accepts an unreasonable answer.
responseLevels.full: Breaks the problem into ordered sub-problems, sets an estimate benchmark, solves, and verifies with an inverse or alternative method — revising when they disagree — switches representation when stuck, and transfers the estimate-then-check routine to a new multi-step problem unprompted.
responseLevels.partial: Can decompose the problem and, when prompted, estimate or check — but performs the sub-steps as a disconnected sequence: does not spontaneously use the estimate or an inverse check to catch an error, and stalls rather than switching strategy.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give a two-step problem within 1000, e.g. 'A shop had 320 pencils. It sold 4 boxes of 50. How many pencils are left?' Before any answer ask: 'How would you break this into parts? About how big should the answer be? Once you have it, how could you check it a different way?' Then discuss what they did — you are surfacing how they plan, estimate and check, not marking the number.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child breaking the problem down reasons about the sub-structure and can state roughly how big the answer must be, then verifies. A child on the keyword habit ties a word to an operation and often runs the steps in the wrong order (e.g. 320 − 50, then ×4) with no estimate to catch it; a compulsion-to-calculate child computes something and accepts it however unreasonable. The estimate and the independent check are where correct and incorrect reasoning diverge — hard to fake either.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 10–11 — use negative numbers in context (temperature, finance, sea level) and calculate intervals across zero.
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y6 'use negative numbers in context, and calculate intervals across zero.'
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): 6.NS.C.5 and 6.NS.C.7 — understand positive and negative numbers in real-world contexts and find distances between them (US formally introduces negatives in Grade 6).
• Operational details: Ground negatives in directed real contexts (temperature above/below 0, credit/debt, above/below sea level). Compute an interval across zero as a DISTANCE on the number line — count/measure from the lower value up through 0 to the higher, or add the two magnitudes on opposite sides of zero (−5 to 3 = 5 + 3 = 8). Keep this as counting/measuring intervals; DEFER formal signed arithmetic rules.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): 'Temperature rises from −2°C to 3°C — how many degrees?' Tier B: 'Difference between a balance of −£120 and £350?' Tier C: 'Order −7, −3, 0, 2, 5 and give the interval from −7 to 5.'
bestPractices: Anchor every negative in a directed context (temperature, sea level, bank balance) so the sign means a direction, not a smaller ordinary number
Compute intervals across zero as a distance on the number line — count/measure through zero, or add the two sides' magnitudes
Use a VERTICAL number line (thermometer) for temperature/sea level so 'colder/lower' maps to physically down
Keep the focus on ordering and intervals; defer signed +/−/× arithmetic rules to KS3
Contrast 'the difference between −5 and 3' (interval = 8) with the values themselves, so distance is not confused with a single number's value
keyRepresentations: Vertical number line / thermometer spanning below and above zero
Horizontal number line with zero as the crossing point and interval arcs
Real-context strips: temperature scale, sea-level cross-section, bank balance line
Interval arcs decomposed at zero (−5→0 is 5, 0→3 is 3, total 8)

Adding the numbers instead of finding a distance (−5 to 3 answered as −2)

learn.summary: For ages 10–11: use negative numbers in directed real-world contexts (temperature, bank balance, sea level) and calculate intervals across zero as a distance on the number line. The key insight is that an across-zero interval decomposes at zero into two magnitudes that ADD (e.g. −2 to 3 = 2 + 3 = 5), and that ordering depends on direction, not digit size (−5 sits below −3 even though 5 > 3). Signed +/−/× arithmetic rules are deferred to later study.

activities.title: Dragging across zero on a vertical number line (thermometer)
feedback: If the learner answers −2 for 'from −5 to 3' (i.e. adds the signed numbers), show the two arcs meeting at zero: 5 (below) + 3 (above) = 8; the gap is a distance, never negative.
If the learner subtracts magnitudes (e.g. 3 to −5 answered as 2), prompt: 'and how far below zero do you still have to travel?' then mark both parts on the line: 3→0 is 3, 0→−5 is 5, total 8.
If the learner says −5 is greater than −3 because 5 > 3, point to the scale: the mark for −5 is physically lower/colder, so −5 is the smaller value.

If the learner reads a fall as a rise because the digit grows (e.g. treats −2 to −8 as getting warmer), use the vertical scale: −8 sits lower/colder than −2, so this is a fall of 6 degrees (both marks are below zero, so no crossing: 8 − 2 = 6), not a rise.

If the learner gives 9 for −5 to 3 (usually from counting the marks −5, −4, …, 3 instead of the gaps between them, or from counting zero as an extra step), explain that an interval is measured in steps, not marks: zero is a point you pass through, not a step. Count the steps below zero (5) and the steps above zero (3) and add them to get 8.
When both arcs are correctly summed, confirm: 'You crossed zero once and added both sides — that is why it isn't just the difference of the digits.'
activities.rationale: Grounding each negative in a directed context makes the sign mean a direction rather than a smaller ordinary number, and letting the learner traverse and measure an arbitrary interval makes the 'split at zero and add' structure felt directly. A vertical scale maps 'colder/lower' to physically down. Dragging with a live running interval is an optional mechanism that makes the decomposition concrete, but a well-marked static number line that the learner annotates by hand can serve the same purpose.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils use negative numbers in context and calculate intervals across zero.
6.NS.C.5/C.7: understand positive and negative numbers in real-world contexts and find distances between them.
learnerActions: Set a start value (e.g. −2°C) and an end value (e.g. 3°C) on a vertical number line scaled like a thermometer.
Drag a marker from the start up through zero to the end, watching the interval light up as two arcs meeting at zero: '2 below → 0' and '0 → 3'.
Read the running interval as it decomposes: 2 + 3 = 5, rather than a single subtraction.
Switch the context (temperature → sea-level cross-section → bank balance, e.g. −£120 below zero and £350 above) while the same number line stays, and repeat the drag.
Compare the positions of −5 and −3 on the scale and state which is lower and why.
activities.intendedInsight: An interval that spans zero is the sum of the two distances on each side of zero; direction (not the size of the digit) sets the order of negative numbers, so −5 lies below −3.

activities.title: Explain-the-error dialogue: 'convince me on the line'
feedback: If the learner accepts the 2-degree claim, ask them to count aloud from 3 down to −5 on the line and notice they pass through zero: 3→0 is 3, then 0→−5 is 5, total 8.

If the learner correctly rejects it, ask them to generalise: 'When does the simple digit difference give the right answer, and when does it fail?' (It gives the right answer when both values are on the same side of zero, and it fails whenever the interval spans zero.)
activities.rationale: A dialogue can surface the '−5 > −3' and 'subtract magnitudes' errors and demand reasoning in words; pairing it with the number line keeps the inherently spatial measurement visible. This is a complement to, not a replacement for, hands-on interval work.
learnerActions: Consider a claim such as: 'The temperature fell from 3°C to −5°C, so it dropped 2 degrees.'
Decide whether it is right or wrong, and use a number line to justify your answer.
State where zero is in the journey and how far you travel on each side of it.
Explain in words why the answer is not simply 5 − 3 = 2.
activities.intendedInsight: Verbalising why the zero crossing must be counted exposes the 'subtract the magnitudes' error and reinforces that the interval is the sum of both sides.

activities.title: Ordering and interval consolidation
feedback: For the −£120 to £350 difference, if the learner gives £230 (subtracting magnitudes) or −£470 (signing the distance), restate that a difference is a positive distance: 120 + 350 = £470.
For ordering, if −5 is placed above −3, return to the scale and the directed meaning of the sign.
Confirm a correct interval by having the learner show the two parts that sum to it.
activities.rationale: Ordering, value-setting and multiple-choice question formats cleanly check ordering and across-zero interval skills once the underlying intuition is built, acting as a consolidator rather than the first teaching step.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils use negative numbers in context and calculate intervals across zero.
learnerActions: Order a set such as −7, −3, 0, 2, 5 from lowest to highest and place them on a number line.
Find the interval from −7 to 5 by splitting at zero: 7 (below) + 5 (above) = 12.
Set a temperature after a stated fall (e.g. start 3°C, fall 8 degrees → −5°C) by marking it on the line.
Find the difference between a balance of −£120 and £350 and check it against the 'add both sides' method: 120 + 350 = 470.
activities.intendedInsight: Ordering negatives and computing across-zero intervals become reliable once the number-line intuition is applied consistently across contexts.

constraints: Keep the focus on ordering and measuring/counting intervals; defer formal signed +/−/× arithmetic rules to later (KS3) study.
Anchor every negative in a directed context (temperature, sea level, bank balance) so the sign denotes direction, not a smaller ordinary number.

A labelled thermometer with tap-to-reveal readings illustrates the scale but does not let the learner traverse and measure an arbitrary interval across zero; treat it as an illustrative scaffold, not the core interval task.
A multiple-choice or value-setting check consolidates and assesses the skill but does not by itself build the across-zero intuition; introduce the hands-on or annotated number-line work first.
Report intervals as positive distances; contrast 'the difference between −5 and 3' (interval = 8) with the individual values so distance is not confused with a single number's value.
Distinguish the ideal number line (direction and position) from any physical thermometer prop used to represent it.

Zero is neither positive nor negative; treat it as the single crossing point where an across-zero interval splits: count the steps (unit gaps) from the start to zero and from zero to the end, so zero is a boundary point, not an extra step.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original claim that '3D adds nothing' for one-dimensional interval work was removed as an unsupported universal; the directed number line is adequately represented in one dimension, which is a design observation, not a proof that other media cannot teach it.

Self-audit of worked values: −2 to 3 = 5 (2+3); −5 to 3 = 8 (5+3); 3 to −5 drop = 8 (3+5); −7 to 5 = 12 (7+5); −£120 to £350 = £470 (120+350); −2 to −8 = 6 (no zero crossing, 8−2). All check out. The −£470/−£230 error pair in the original check note corresponds to the signed-answer and subtract-magnitudes errors and is retained only as error feedback, not as a valid answer.

The original reteach-link and fit-ranking metadata were not carried into learner-facing content; only their pedagogical substance (split-at-zero reteach, one-side-only under-count) was preserved as feedback.

Two source misconceptions — 'zero is negative/positive' and 'there is no number between −1 and 1' — were not built into standalone activity feedback; the zero-neutral point is now stated as a constraint, but the density-of-numbers point could be added as a further prompt. Flagged as a residual preservation gap, not a learner-facing error.

probeDeeper: Count from 3 down to −5 on a number line — how many steps, and where is zero?
How far is −7 from 5? Split the distance at zero.
Why isn't the drop just 5 − 3 = 2?
assess.correctAnswer: 8 degrees; £470; 12 — found by adding the distance on each side of zero (or counting across it).

errorPatterns.pattern: Subtracts the magnitudes as if both were positive: 3 to −5 gives a drop of 2; −£120 to £350 gives £230
errorPatterns.nextMove: Split the journey at zero: 3→0 is 3, 0→−5 is 5, total 8. Draw it on a number line.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The interval ignores the crossing of zero; answers are too small.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts only one side of zero — stops at zero or forgets the negative part
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach negatives — prompt 'and how far below zero?' so both parts are added; mark both on the line.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer equals just the positive portion (e.g. 3, or the 5, not 8).

responseLevels.gap: Subtracts magnitudes and misses the zero crossing entirely.
responseLevels.full: Calculates intervals across zero by adding the distances on each side, in temperature, finance and pure-number contexts.
responseLevels.partial: Handles intervals on one side of zero but under-counts when the interval spans zero.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set the problems and watch the working: 'The temperature falls from 3°C to −5°C — what is the drop? A bank balance goes from −£120 to £350 — what is the difference? What is the interval from −7 to 5?' Watch how they handle the zero crossing.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Each interval straddles zero, so a child who subtracts magnitudes (5 − 3, 350 − 120) gets the wrong gap; a child who splits at zero and adds the two parts gets it right. Watching whether they account for the part below zero is the discriminator.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 11–12 — understand the absolute value of a rational number as its distance from zero on the number line; interpret it as magnitude in context; distinguish absolute-value comparisons from ordering statements.
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics, KS3): supports work on negatives and number-line reasoning; absolute value as magnitude underpins later work (bounds, error, modulus).
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): 6.NS.C.7c — 'understand the absolute value of a rational number as its distance from 0 on the number line; interpret absolute value as magnitude for a positive or negative quantity in a real-world situation' and 7d distinguish comparisons of absolute value from statements about order.
• Operational details: Define |x| as DISTANCE from zero (always ≥0), so |−5| = |5| = 5. Keep the distinction sharp between magnitude (how far) and order (which is greater): −7 < −3 but |−7| > |−3|. Ground in context — a debt of −£30 is a bigger amount than −£5 even though it is 'less'. Read |·| aloud as 'distance from zero'.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 11): 'What is |−8|?' Tier B: 'Which is greater: −9 or −2? Which has the greater absolute value?' Tier C: 'A balance of −£40 vs −£15 — which is the larger debt, and which is the smaller number? Explain.'
bestPractices: Define absolute value strictly as distance from zero on the number line, so it is never negative and |−5| = |5|
Hold magnitude and order apart explicitly with paired statements (−7 < −3 but |−7| > |−3|)
Anchor in contexts where magnitude matters (size of a debt, depth below sea level) versus signed order
Read |x| aloud as 'the distance of x from zero' rather than 'make it positive' (a rule that hides the meaning)
Use symmetric points about zero to show two different numbers share one absolute value
keyRepresentations: Number line with a distance arc from 0 to the point (length = |x|)
Mirror/fold about zero showing −a and a mapping to the same distance
Context strips (debt size, depth) where magnitude is the salient quantity
Paired statement cards contrasting order (<, >) with absolute value (|·|)
commonMisconceptions: Believing |x| just 'removes the minus sign' as a symbol trick rather than measuring distance (fails for expressions like |x−3|)
Thinking the number with the greater absolute value is automatically the greater number (−9 > −2)
Assuming absolute value can be negative
Conflating 'larger debt/depth' (magnitude) with 'larger number' (order)
Treating |−5| and −5 as interchangeable

learn.summary: For learners aged 11–12: build absolute value as distance from zero on the number line (always ≥0, so |−5| = |5| = 5), interpret it as magnitude in real contexts (size of a debt, depth below sea level), and keep it sharply separate from ordering (−7 < −3 but |−7| > |−3|). Read |x| aloud as 'the distance of x from zero', not 'make it positive'. A manipulable number line is the core activity; an annotated static line, a consolidation set of short items, and a context dialogue are supporting approaches with distinct purposes.

activities.title: Measure distance from zero on a draggable number line
feedback: If the learner expects |x| to carry a minus sign on the left of zero, point to the arc: it is a length, so it reads the same magnitude on both sides.
When the arc for −9 is longer than for −2, ask them to say aloud which number is greater (−2) and which is further from zero (−9) — two different answers.
At the crossing point, highlight that |x| touches 0 exactly at zero, then grows again in either direction.
activities.rationale: Absolute value is defined as distance from zero on the number line; making that distance visible and live as the point moves ties the symbol to its meaning and separates magnitude from order. The dragging/mirror/dual-read-out details are illustrative affordances, not required technology, and are a research-informed proposal rather than a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: 6.NS.C.7c/7d: understand absolute value as distance from 0, interpret it as magnitude in context, and distinguish absolute-value comparisons from order statements.
KS3 number work develops reasoning with negative numbers and magnitude on the number line, underpinning absolute value / modulus.
learnerActions: Drag a point along a number line and watch a glowing arc from 0 to the point report its length as |x|, which is positive on either side of zero and is 0 only when the point is at zero.
Park the point at −5, then flip on a mirror toggle so the reflection at +5 lays down an identical arc — observe |−5| = |5| = 5.

Read a twin read-out that shows the signed value beside its absolute value; move the point to −9 then to −2 and notice the arc for −9 is LONGER even though −9 sits further LEFT (is the smaller number).
Drag the point across zero and watch the |x| read-out shrink to 0 and climb again — distance tracks how far from zero, never which side.
activities.intendedInsight: Absolute value is a distance (a length) from zero: it is never negative, two symmetric points share one absolute value, and 'further from zero' is a different question from 'greater number'.

activities.title: Annotated number line with distance arcs (static anchor)
feedback: If a learner reads the longer arc as 'the bigger number', separate the two questions: length of arc = magnitude; position left/right = order.
Confirm both arcs for −5 and 5 are the same length before moving on.
activities.rationale: A static annotated line anchors the distance meaning and the two-numbers-one-magnitude idea; it supports the same objective as the draggable version without live dragging and works on paper. It lacks the live across-zero movement, so add tracing tasks if used alone.
sourceClaims: 6.NS.C.7c/7d: understand absolute value as distance from 0, interpret it as magnitude in context, and distinguish absolute-value comparisons from order statements.
learnerActions: On a number line, mark −5 and 5 and draw the arc from 0 to each, confirming both measure 5 units.
Reveal a callout that contrasts the order statement (−5 < 5) with the magnitude statement (|−5| = |5|).
For a second pair such as −9 and −2, draw both arcs and state separately which number is greater (−2) and which has the greater absolute value (−9).
activities.intendedInsight: Even without live movement, measuring arcs from zero establishes 'distance from zero' and the idea that two different numbers can share one absolute value.

activities.title: Consolidation: evaluate and discriminate
feedback: If a learner answers the same way to '−9 > −2' and '|−9| > |−2|', reread each using the number line: position for order, distance from zero for absolute value.
If an absolute value is given as negative, restate |x| as a length that cannot be negative.
activities.rationale: Evaluation and magnitude-vs-order discrimination are cleanly checkable in short structured items, making this a useful consolidator after the distance meaning is established. Recognition and selected-response items chiefly check and reinforce classification; they do not by themselves elicit independent reasoning or construction, which the number-line work is intended to develop.
sourceClaims: 6.NS.C.7c/7d: understand absolute value as distance from 0, interpret it as magnitude in context, and distinguish absolute-value comparisons from order statements.
learnerActions: Evaluate absolute values, e.g. 'What is |−8|?' (= 8).
Match signed values to their absolute values.
Judge paired true/false statements such as '−9 > −2' (false) versus '|−9| > |−2|' (true), and explain each by the number line.
activities.intendedInsight: Once the distance meaning is built, learners can reliably compute absolute values and tell absolute-value comparisons apart from ordering comparisons.

activities.title: Context talk: larger debt vs larger number
feedback: If the learner equates 'bigger debt' with 'bigger number', place −40 and −15 on a line: −40 sits further left, so it is the smaller number though the larger debt.
Encourage the learner to state the two questions separately before answering.
activities.rationale: Grounding magnitude in debt/depth/temperature contexts targets the common conflation of magnitude with order and gives learners language for the distinction. Dialogue here addresses the contextual magnitude-vs-order question and works alongside the spatial number-line model; its advantage over other media is not established by the sources.
sourceClaims: 6.NS.C.7c/7d: understand absolute value as distance from 0, interpret it as magnitude in context, and distinguish absolute-value comparisons from order statements.
learnerActions: Discuss a scenario: 'You owe £40, I owe £15 — whose debt is bigger, and whose balance is the greater number?'
Explain that −40 is the larger debt (greater magnitude) yet the smaller/lower balance (−40 < −15).
Try a second context (−8°C vs −3°C, or a diver at −8 m vs −3 m): name who is deeper/colder/further from zero and whose value is the greater number.
activities.intendedInsight: In real contexts, magnitude (how far from zero) and order (which value is greater) answer different questions, and conflating them produces errors like '−40 is the greater number'.

constraints: Define |x| strictly as distance from zero on the number line (always ≥0); avoid teaching it as 'remove the minus sign', which hides the meaning and fails for expressions like |x−3|.
Always pair order and magnitude explicitly (e.g. −7 < −3 but |−7| > |−3|) so learners do not assume greater absolute value means greater number.
Distinguish |−5| from −5: they are not interchangeable.
Recognition/matching/true-false items consolidate and check classification but do not elicit independent construction; use them after the number-line meaning is built, not as the primary teaching.
The static annotated line is a scaffold that lacks live movement across zero; if used alone, add tasks where learners trace the distance changing on both sides of zero.
A 3D representation was judged to add little because absolute value is a one-dimensional distance; this is a design judgement for this topic, not a general claim that 3D adds nothing to learning.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Both cited standards sources are marked verified:false in the source row; treat the citations as unconfirmed.
The original rated a quiz and a 3D interactive by catalog 'fit'; those ranking labels were removed and the quiz and dialogue retained as supporting approaches with distinct pedagogical purposes.
Arithmetic and logic checked: |−8| = 8; −3 > −8 while |−8| > |−3|; −40 < −15 while |−40| > |−15|; −5 < 5 with |−5| = |5| — all consistent across every action, feedback item and note.

probeDeeper: On a number line, which is further from zero, −8 or −3?
Can an absolute value ever be negative? Why not?
A diver at −8 m and one at −3 m: who is deeper, who is further from the surface, and whose depth is the 'bigger' number?
assess.correctAnswer: −3 is the greater number (it is closer to zero / further right on the number line). But −8 has the greater absolute value, because |−8| = 8 and |−3| = 3 — absolute value is distance from zero, ignoring direction.

errorPatterns.pattern: Orders negatives by magnitude: '−8 is greater than −3 because 8 > 3'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Place both on a number line: −3 sits to the right of −8, so −3 is greater. Reason from position, not digit size.
errorPatterns.distractor: −8 is the greater number.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child ranks −8 above −3 when asked which is the greater number.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks absolute value keeps the sign: |−8| = −8
errorPatterns.nextMove: Define absolute value as distance from zero — a length, never negative. Read |−8| off the number line as 8 units.
errorPatterns.distractor: The absolute value of −8 is −8.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives a negative absolute value.

errorPatterns.pattern: Assumes greater absolute value means greater number (treats the two comparisons as identical)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a context (−8°C vs −3°C): −8 is colder/lower yet 'further from zero'. Name the two different questions explicitly.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives the same answer to both questions.

responseLevels.gap: Orders negatives by magnitude or gives a negative absolute value; treats the two comparisons as the same.
responseLevels.full: Distinguishes ordering (−3 > −8) from absolute value (|−8| > |−3|), defines |x| as distance from zero, and applies both correctly in context.
responseLevels.partial: Computes absolute values correctly but still conflates 'greater absolute value' with 'greater number' in context.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask: 'Which is the greater number, −8 or −3? And which has the greater absolute value? How do you know?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Asking for BOTH the ordering and the absolute value in one prompt forces the child to separate 'which is bigger' from 'which is further from zero'. A child conflating them gives the same answer twice; a child who understands gives opposite answers and can justify each by the number line.
