pedagogy.summary: Solving problems with up to three decimal places extends place value to thousandths and demands careful alignment. Adding and subtracting means lining up the decimal points and equalising lengths (1.5 = 1.500), treating each column as ones, tenths, hundredths and thousandths, and carrying or borrowing across columns exactly as with whole numbers. Tasks like 'find two numbers to 3 d.p. that make 1' exercise complements to a whole (0.375 + 0.625). Estimation guards against place-value slips.
bestPractices: Align the decimal points and pad ragged lengths with zeros (1.500 − 0.375) so every place value lines up
Read numbers by place value all the way to thousandths
Carry and borrow across decimal columns just as with whole numbers
Use complement-to-1 reasoning (subtract from 1.000) for 'add to make 1' tasks and check by adding
Estimate first (1.5 − 0.375 ≈ 1.5 − 0.4 ≈ 1.1) to catch magnitude errors
keyRepresentations: Place-value columns to thousandths, aligned on the point
Number line zoomed to thousandths
Bar / complement model for 'make 1'
Measuring contexts (litres, metres) for the quantities
commonMisconceptions: Right-justifies ragged decimals instead of aligning the point (1.234 + 0.567 + 2.199)
Treats the decimal tail as a separate whole number ('longer is larger')
Forgets to pad and borrow across the point (1.5 − 0.375)
Complement-to-1 errors: completes each column to 10 independently (0.375 + 0.725) or ignores the required 3 d.p. (0.4 + 0.6)

learn.summary: Solving problems with numbers to three decimal places extends place value to thousandths and depends on careful alignment. Adding and subtracting means lining up the decimal points, equalising lengths by padding with zeros (1.5 = 1.500), reading each column as ones, tenths, hundredths and thousandths, and carrying or borrowing across columns exactly as with whole numbers. 'Find two numbers to 3 d.p. that make 1' exercises complements to a whole (0.375 + 0.625 = 1.000). Estimating first guards against place-value slips.

activities.title: Column workbench: aligning and padding to thousandths
feedback: If columns are lined up by their last digits instead of the point, the sum comes out the wrong size (far from 4): re-align so tenths sit under tenths and thousandths under thousandths, padding shorter numbers with zeros.
If 1.5 is left as two digits, there is nothing to subtract the thousandths from: rewrite it as 1.500 first, then borrow across the hundredths and tenths to reach 1.125 l.
If the estimate (about 1.1) and the written answer disagree in size, a place-value slip has happened — recheck the alignment and borrowing.
activities.rationale: Place-value alignment to thousandths and borrowing across the point is the core procedural skill, and ragged-length numbers are where whole-number thinking (right-justifying, 'longer is larger') shows up; making the padding and the column structure visible turns alignment into a deliberate, checkable step. An interactive medium that snaps digits into labelled columns, shows faint ghost zeros when padding 1.500, and animates the borrow rippling left may make this mechanism concrete; these are optional illustrative supports, not required mechanisms. A static aligned-columns reference with tap-to-reveal place values can model a single worked calculation but does not enforce alignment on new problems, so it suits review rather than independent practice.
sourceClaims: Decimal size and calculation depend on place value, and errors arise from whole-number thinking (treating the decimal tail as a separate whole number, 'longer is larger'); ragged-length decimals are essential for revealing these errors, whereas tidy same-length items let faulty rules pass.
learnerActions: Set out the subtraction 1.5 − 0.375 in place-value columns (ones, tenths, hundredths, thousandths) aligned on the decimal point — the measuring context is a 1.5-litre bottle from which 0.375 l is poured out, finding how much is left.
Rewrite 1.5 as 1.500 by writing zeros in the empty hundredths and thousandths columns before subtracting.
Carry out the subtraction, borrowing just as with whole numbers (from the tenths through the hundredths to the thousandths), to reach 1.125 l remaining.
Add the three ragged measurements 1.2 m + 0.567 m + 2.233 m by first aligning on the point and padding every number to the same length (1.2 = 1.200), then summing each column to get 4.000 m.
Estimate first (1.5 − 0.375 ≈ 1.5 − 0.4 ≈ 1.1) and check the answer's size against the estimate.
activities.intendedInsight: 1.5 and 1.500 are the same number, but writing the padding zeros makes the hundredths and thousandths columns available so the digits line up and the borrow can ripple from the tenths through the hundredths to the thousandths.

activities.title: Make 1: complements to a whole at three decimal places
feedback: If a pair like 0.375 + 0.735 is chosen, each column was completed to 10 separately (that pair totals 1.110, not 1): instead subtract the whole number 1.000 − 0.375 to get 0.625, then add to check the total is exactly 1.000.

If the total comes to 0.999 or similar, each column (including the thousandths) was probably completed to 9, giving 0.624 instead of 0.625. Only the thousandths should make 10, with the tenths and hundredths making 9 because of the carries, so that the total is one whole, written 1.000.
If a pair is not written to three decimal places, rewrite it to 3 d.p. and confirm it still totals 1.000.
activities.rationale: Complement-to-1 tasks rehearse decomposing a whole and expose the common error of completing each column to ten. Checking by adding back links the complement to addition and reinforces that the parts must reconstitute exactly one whole. A bar/length model where the two parts must fill one whole may make 'completing the whole' felt as a length; it is an optional illustrative support, not a required medium.
learnerActions: Given 0.375, find the second number to 3 d.p. that makes exactly 1.000, by subtracting from 1.000 (1.000 − 0.375 = 0.625).
Check the pair by adding the two numbers back together and confirming they total exactly 1.000.
Explain why 0.4 + 0.6, though it equals 1, does not meet the 'three decimal places' requirement, and give a valid 3-d.p. pair (such as 0.001 + 0.999).
Optionally model the complement as two lengths placed end to end along a bar representing one whole, where only the correct pair closes the gap with no gap or overlap and a running total shows 1.000.
activities.intendedInsight: A complement to 1 is found by subtracting from the whole written as 1.000, not by completing each column to 10 independently; the two parts together must make exactly one whole.

constraints: Use ragged-length decimals (different numbers of decimal places) in practice, not only tidy same-length items: equal-length items can let faulty right-justify or 'longer is larger' rules pass undetected.

A static aligned-columns picture or tap-to-reveal reference can illustrate one calculation but does not enforce alignment on new problems; reserve it for modelling or review and require learners to lay out and compute fresh problems themselves.

Multiple-choice or fill-in checks can diagnose misalignment and complement errors but assess recognition of a final value; independent construction requires learners to set out the columns, pad, and carry/borrow themselves.
Insist complements be written to the required three decimal places (reject 0.4 + 0.6 for a 3-d.p. task even though it sums to 1).

When writing distractors for 1.5 − 0.375, the correct answer is 1.125; plausible error-based distractors include 1.275 (subtracting the smaller digit from the larger in each column instead of borrowing) and 1.225 (borrowing without reducing the tenths digit from 5 to 4). Include 1.125 once as the correct option, and make sure no distractor equals it.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources have not been re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 1.234 + 0.567 + 2.199 = 4.000; 1.500 − 0.375 = 1.125; 1.000 − 0.375 = 0.625; 0.375 + 0.625 = 1.000 and 0.001 + 0.999 = 1.000 — all verified correct. The original row's complement-error example (0.375 + 0.725 = 1.100) is intentionally used only as an error to diagnose, never as a correct answer.

The source claim supports using ragged-length decimals to reveal place-value errors; it does not establish comparative efficacy of any particular medium (interactive columns vs. picture vs. quiz). Medium recommendations are framed as affordances/limits, not necessity.

The legacy claim that depth/3D 'adds nothing' and that in-role dialogue cannot carry the insight were catalog fit judgements, not established facts; softened or omitted rather than asserted as universal laws.

The litre/bottle measuring context for 1.5 − 0.375 and the metre context for the three-measurement sum are retained to preserve the row's concrete measuring representations; the 'number line to thousandths' representation from the pedagogy field was not expanded into an activity.

probeDeeper: Before adding, roughly what should 1.234 + 0.567 + 2.199 be near — more or less than 4? Why?
Why write 1.5 as 1.500 before subtracting 0.375?
Do 0.4 and 0.6 have three decimal places? Give me a pair written to 3 d.p. that makes exactly 1.
How can you check that your two numbers really add to exactly 1?

errorPatterns.pattern: Right-justifies ragged decimals instead of aligning the point — lines up 1.234, 0.567, 2.199 by their last digits
errorPatterns.nextMove: Align on the decimal point and pad shorter numbers with zeros so tenths sit under tenths, thousandths under thousandths.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Columns don't match place value; the sum is the wrong size (not near 4)

errorPatterns.pattern: Fails to pad and borrow across the point — tackles 1.5 − 0.375 without rewriting 1.500, botching the borrow
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rewrite 1.5 as 1.500, then subtract with borrowing across the hundredths and tenths just as in whole-number subtraction.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer like 1.175 or 1.235; leaves 1.5 as two digits and cannot subtract thousandths from nothing

errorPatterns.pattern: Complement-to-1 error — completes each column to 10 independently (0.375 + 0.725) or ignores the 3-d.p. requirement (0.4 + 0.6)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Find the complement by subtracting from 1.000 (1.000 − 0.375 = 0.625) and check by adding; stress the whole is 1.000, not 0.999 or ten in each column.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The chosen pair does not total exactly 1.000, or is not to three decimal places

responseLevels.gap: Right-justifies ragged decimals; cannot borrow across the point; gives complements that don't total 1.
responseLevels.full: Aligns on the point and pads ragged lengths, adds and subtracts to 3 d.p. with correct borrowing (4.000; 1.125), finds a valid 3-d.p. complement to 1, and estimates to check; transfers to a new problem.
responseLevels.partial: Adds/subtracts equal-length decimals correctly but misaligns ragged ones or forgets to pad, or finds a 'make 1' pair only when it is tidy (0.5 + 0.5) rather than to 3 d.p.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'Show me your method for each. First, add 1.234 m + 0.567 m + 2.199 m. Second, a 1.5-litre bottle has 0.375 litres poured out — how much is left? Third, find two numbers, each with three decimal places, that add up to exactly 1.' Watch how they line the numbers up and handle the borrow.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The ragged sum (three different lengths) exposes right-justify misalignment; 1.5 − 0.375 forces padding to 1.500 and a borrow across the point; 'make 1' to 3 d.p. exposes complement errors (many write 0.375 + 0.725, completing each column to 10). A child who aligns on the point, pads with zeros and borrows correctly gets 4.000, 1.125 and a valid complement; a misaligner or column-completer does not.

sources.claim: Decimal size and calculation depend on place value, and errors arise from whole-number thinking (treating the decimal tail as a separate whole number, 'longer is larger'); ragged-length decimals are essential for revealing these errors, whereas tidy same-length items let faulty rules pass.
sources.source: SMART / Steinle & Stacey, 'Comparing Decimal Numbers' (Specific Mathematics Assessments that Reveal Thinking, University of Melbourne)

pedagogy.summary: This topic formalises 2-D shape description with two properties: the number of sides, and line symmetry (in Year 2, specifically a vertical line). The conceptual heart is symmetry — and the single idea children must build is that a line of symmetry is a FOLD line where the two halves land exactly on top of each other (mirror images that coincide), NOT merely a line that splits the shape into two same-sized pieces. It is best taught by folding paper cut-outs and using mirrors, so 'the halves match' is something the child physically verifies rather than judges by eye, and by combining side-count and symmetry to describe and tell shapes apart.
bestPractices: Teach a line of symmetry as a FOLD: cut out the shape and fold along the candidate line; it is a line of symmetry only if the two halves land exactly on top of each other.
Use mirrors (and mirror-drawing) so children see one half as the reflection of the other — reinforcing 'mirror image', not just 'same size'.
Deliberately test a non-example that has two congruent halves but is NOT symmetric (the diagonal of a non-square rectangle) so children learn congruence is not enough.
Count sides by touching and marking each one; then combine properties ('4 sides AND 2 lines of symmetry') to distinguish shapes such as a square from a non-square rectangle.
Present shapes in varied orientations so a vertical line of symmetry is recognised as a property of the shape, not of the page.
keyRepresentations: Paper/card shape cut-outs for folding along a candidate line
A small mirror (or Mira) placed on the line to check the reflection
Pegboard/dot-paper symmetric-pattern completion (draw the missing mirror half)
Side-by-side square vs non-square rectangle for comparing side-count and number of symmetry lines
commonMisconceptions: Thinks any line drawn down the middle of a shape is a line of symmetry, without checking the halves coincide.
Thinks any line that cuts a shape into two equal/congruent parts is a line of symmetry — e.g. accepts the diagonal of a rectangle because it makes two identical triangles.
Judges 'the halves are the same' by eye/size rather than by folding or mirroring to see if they actually land on each other.
Confuses the vertical line of symmetry with 'any line through the centre' and does not realise a shape can have several (or no) lines of symmetry.

learn.summary: Year 2 learners describe 2-D shapes by number of sides and by line symmetry (specifically a vertical line). The conceptual crux is that a line of symmetry is a FOLD line where the two halves land exactly on top of each other (mirror images that coincide) — NOT merely a line that splits a shape into two same-sized pieces. The decisive non-example is the diagonal of a non-square rectangle: it makes two congruent triangles yet does not coincide on folding. Physical folding of paper cut-outs and mirrors let children verify matching rather than judging by eye; side-count combines with symmetry to tell shapes apart.

activities.title: Fold test: does each half land on the other?
feedback: When the vertical midline fold makes the halves land exactly on each other with no overhang, that IS a line of symmetry.

When you fold the rectangle along its diagonal, a corner pokes out past the edge — the halves do not land on each other, so the diagonal is NOT a line of symmetry even though both triangles are the same size.
If you accepted the diagonal 'because it makes two equal triangles', re-fold and look for the overhanging corner: equal size is not the same as the halves matching.
A square's folds work down the middle, across the middle, AND along both diagonals — fold to find all four.

The paper cut-out has a very slight thickness but stands in for the ideal flat (zero-thickness) mathematical shape. An optional on-screen fold/reflection tool models the same reflection without the thickness — for example recolouring the outline green when the swung half coincides and red when a corner overhangs.
activities.rationale: Folding cut-outs makes 'the halves match' something the child physically verifies rather than judges by eye, and the rectangle diagonal is the targeted non-example that separates congruence from coincidence. The shape used must be a non-square rectangle, since a square's diagonal IS a line of symmetry.
sourceClaims: A line of symmetry is a fold line where the two halves are mirror images that coincide (match exactly); a line dividing a figure into two CONGRUENT parts is not necessarily a line of symmetry — the diagonal of a non-square rectangle makes two congruent triangles but folding gives a non-matching (kite) result, so congruence is not sufficient.

Common Year 2 misconception: children may think that any line drawn down the middle of a shape is a line of symmetry; remedy is to fold cut-outs so the two halves match (one half a reflection of the other) and to use mirrors.
learnerActions: Cut out a paper/card rectangle (a non-square one).
Fold it along the vertical line down the middle: check whether the two halves land exactly on top of each other.
Now fold the same rectangle corner-to-corner along the diagonal and watch what happens to the corners.
Say out loud for each fold whether it is a line of symmetry and why.
Repeat the fold test on other cut-out shapes (square, triangle), hunting for every fold where the halves coincide.
activities.intendedInsight: A line of symmetry is a fold where the two halves land exactly on top of each other (coincide), not just a line that makes two pieces the same size. The diagonal of a non-square rectangle makes two congruent triangles but a corner overhangs when folded — so congruence is not enough.

activities.title: Mirror check and completing the mirror half
feedback: If the half in front of the mirror plus its reflection looks exactly like the whole shape (with a see-through Mira, if the reflection lines up with the real half behind it), the line is a line of symmetry.
If the reflection does not match the shape's outline, that line is not a line of symmetry even if the two parts are the same size.
When you complete the mirror half on dot-paper, each point should sit the same distance from the line as its partner.
Optionally, a draggable on-screen mirror can sweep across a shape to find every line of symmetry — for a non-square rectangle it finds two, while a square has four.
activities.rationale: Mirrors reinforce 'mirror image' rather than merely 'same size', offering a second concrete test that complements folding.
sourceClaims: Common Year 2 misconception: children may think that any line drawn down the middle of a shape is a line of symmetry; remedy is to fold cut-outs so the two halves match (one half a reflection of the other) and to use mirrors.
learnerActions: Place a small mirror (or Mira) upright along a candidate line on a shape and look at the reflection.
Check whether the reflection in the mirror continues the shape exactly — if it does, the line is a line of symmetry.
On dot-paper or a pegboard, draw/build half of a pattern, then draw or build the missing mirror half so the whole is symmetric.
Describe one half as the reflection of the other, not just 'the same size'.
activities.intendedInsight: One half of a symmetric shape is the mirror image (reflection) of the other; reflecting, like folding, tests whether the halves actually coincide.

activities.title: Count sides and combine with symmetry to tell shapes apart
feedback: Marking each side as you count stops you from double-counting or missing one.
A square has four lines of symmetry; a non-square rectangle has two — so number of symmetry lines, not just side-count, distinguishes them.
If a shape is turned on the page, fold or mirror-test again — a true line of symmetry travels with the shape.
activities.rationale: Combining side-count with symmetry supports the describe-and-distinguish objective, and varied orientations prevent symmetry being tied to the prototypical upright image.
sourceClaims: Early-years/KS1 practice: attend to shape properties (number of sides/corners) and present shapes in varied orientations, sizes and materials rather than a single prototypical image.
learnerActions: Count the sides of a given 2-D shape by touching and marking each side as you count.
Count the lines of symmetry of the same shape by folding or mirroring.
Place a square beside a non-square rectangle and compare both properties: '4 sides AND how many lines of symmetry?'
State how the square differs from the rectangle using BOTH the number of sides and the number of lines of symmetry.

Try the same shapes turned to different angles and fold or mirror-test again to confirm they still have the same lines of symmetry. The lines turn with the shape, so a line that was vertical may now be slanted or horizontal.
activities.intendedInsight: Shapes are described and distinguished by combining properties — a square and a non-square rectangle both have 4 sides, but a square has four lines of symmetry and this rectangle has two. Symmetry is a property of the shape, not of how it sits on the page.

activities.title: Predict-then-fold diagnostic conversation
feedback: Predicting 'yes, they'll match' and then seeing the corner overhang is the moment 'two equal halves' turns into 'the halves must land on each other'.
If you can explain WHY the diagonal fails — the halves don't coincide — you are reasoning by folding/reflecting, not by equal size.

Note the square is different: its diagonal fold DOES make the halves coincide, so a square's diagonal is a line of symmetry while this rectangle's is not — the test is always whether the halves land on each other.
activities.rationale: A predict-observe-explain exchange is an assessment-aligned diagnostic that exposes the load-bearing congruence-vs-coincidence misconception; it uses the non-square rectangle so the non-example holds.
sourceClaims: A line of symmetry is a fold line where the two halves are mirror images that coincide (match exactly); a line dividing a figure into two CONGRUENT parts is not necessarily a line of symmetry — the diagonal of a non-square rectangle makes two congruent triangles but folding gives a non-matching (kite) result, so congruence is not sufficient.
learnerActions: Before folding, predict: 'If we fold this non-square rectangle exactly along its diagonal, corner to corner, will the two halves land exactly on top of each other?' Say yes or no first.
Fold along the diagonal and compare what happened to your prediction.
Explain in your own words why two halves being the same size is not enough for a line of symmetry.
Show, by folding, which lines of a square are lines of symmetry and which lines of the rectangle are not.
activities.intendedInsight: Committing to a prediction before folding surfaces whether you are reasoning about matching halves or about equal-sized pieces; the overhang resolves it.

constraints: Line symmetry of a 2-D shape is planar; keep the work flat (folding, mirrors, dot-paper) — adding depth/3-D is not needed for this concept and can distract from the flat fold.

Watching pre-drawn lines of symmetry or tap-to-reveal mirror highlights can show correct examples, but a watch-only display does not let the child test their OWN candidate line or resolve the diagonal misconception through their own folding; treat such displays as a scaffold and still have the child perform a fold or mirror test.

Multiple-choice ('which line is a line of symmetry?') and draw-the-line tasks can check the skill but do not themselves perform the fold, so they do not let the child feel whether the halves coincide; use them to assess, not as the primary teaching of the crux.

Paper/card cut-outs have slight thickness; treat them as a good physical approximation of the ideal flat (zero-thickness) shape. If an on-screen fold/reflection tool is used, note it models the same zero-thickness reflection.

Recognition-only responses (picking a line from options) do not require the learner to construct or verify the fold themselves; include folding, mirroring, or completing a mirror half for independent construction.
The diagnostic non-example must be a NON-SQUARE rectangle: a square's diagonal IS a line of symmetry, so using a square would break the congruence-vs-coincidence contrast.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source states folding a non-square rectangle along its diagonal yields a 'non-matching (kite) result' with a corner overhanging — geometrically correct for a non-square rectangle. For a SQUARE the diagonal IS a line of symmetry, so the diagnostic shape must be explicitly a non-square rectangle, as the original specifies.

The original claimed the on-screen fold tool 'directly targets the crux' and that a static image 'can only be watched, not resolved'; these are catalog fit judgements, not established efficacy claims, and have been softened to scaffold/affordance framing.

On-screen green-coincide/red-overhang recolouring and the draggable mirror are offered as optional display aids; their teaching efficacy versus physical folding/mirrors is not established by the cited sources.
Lines-of-symmetry counts (square: 4, non-square rectangle: 2) are stated as factual and are correct by standard geometry; no empirical re-verification was performed.

assess.poeTask: Hold up a cut-out non-square rectangle. 'Predict: if we fold this rectangle exactly along its diagonal, corner to corner, will the two halves land exactly on top of each other? Say yes or no before we fold.' A child who equates congruence with symmetry predicts YES (two identical triangles). Folding reveals NO — a corner overhangs and the shape becomes a kite-like flap. The prediction, and their reaction to the overhang, is the diagnostic: it exposes whether they are reasoning about matching halves or about equal-sized pieces.
probeDeeper: Fold this cut-out rectangle along the middle line. Do the two halves land exactly on top of each other? Now try the diagonal — what happens?
This shape splits into two halves the same size, but they don't match when folded. Is it symmetrical? Why not?
Does a square have more lines of symmetry than this rectangle? Show me each one by folding.
Use both the number of sides AND the number of lines of symmetry to tell me how a square is different from this rectangle.
assess.correctAnswer: The vertical line down the middle IS a line of symmetry — folding along it, the two halves land exactly on top of each other. The diagonal is NOT — folding along it, the two triangular halves do not coincide (a corner overhangs). The check is to fold (or use a mirror) and see whether the halves land on each other, not merely whether they are the same size.

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes any line that divides a shape into two equal/congruent parts is a line of symmetry — accepts the rectangle's diagonal 'because it makes two triangles the same'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Cut out the rectangle and fold along the diagonal — the halves do not land on each other, a corner overhangs; contrast with folding along the vertical midline where they coincide exactly. Establish: a line of symmetry is a fold where the halves MATCH, not just where the pieces are the same size.
errorPatterns.distractor: The diagonal is a line of symmetry because it splits the rectangle into two equal triangles.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names the diagonal as a line of symmetry and justifies it by the two equal triangles, not by folding.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks any line drawn down the middle of a shape is a line of symmetry, without checking that the halves coincide.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make the fold-test / mirror-test the habitual check: if the halves don't land on each other it isn't a line of symmetry, wherever the line is drawn.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Accepts a central line automatically ('it goes through the middle') without folding or mirroring to verify.

responseLevels.gap: Accepts any central or halving line as a line of symmetry (including the rectangle's diagonal) and checks only whether the two parts look the same size.
responseLevels.full: Uses the fold/reflection test — the halves must land exactly on each other — to accept the vertical midline and reject the diagonal, explains why two congruent halves are not enough, and combines side-count and symmetry to distinguish shapes (SOLO relational, with transfer).
responseLevels.partial: Correctly identifies the vertical line of symmetry by folding and counts sides, but treats these as separate facts — cannot yet reject the diagonal by reasoning that the halves must coincide, or does not transfer the fold-test to a new shape (SOLO multistructural).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show the child a non-square rectangle with two lines drawn on it: one straight down the middle (vertical) and one from corner to corner (the diagonal). Ask: 'Which of these lines are lines of symmetry for the rectangle? How would you check?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The rectangle's diagonal DOES cut it into two congruent triangles, so a child who believes 'any line making two equal parts is a line of symmetry' will accept it. It can only be rejected by fold/mirror reasoning — realising the halves must coincide. That makes it very hard to answer correctly for the wrong reason: the second tier ('how would you check') exposes whether the child reasons by folding/reflecting or by judging equal size.

sources.claim: A line of symmetry is a fold line where the two halves are mirror images that coincide (match exactly); a line dividing a figure into two CONGRUENT parts is not necessarily a line of symmetry — the diagonal of a non-square rectangle makes two congruent triangles but folding gives a non-matching (kite) result, so congruence is not sufficient.

pedagogy.summary: A terminating decimal IS a fraction with a power-of-ten denominator: 0.375 = 375/1000, which simplifies to 3/8. Converting a fraction to a decimal is division (3 ÷ 8 = 0.375) or, equivalently, scaling the denominator up to 10, 100, 1000… Whether a fraction terminates is decided entirely by the prime factors of its denominator in lowest terms: only 2 and 5 (the prime factors of ten) give a terminating decimal; any other prime factor (3, 7, 11…) produces a recurring decimal. Fractions, decimals and percentages are three notations for one value.
bestPractices: Read a decimal by its LAST place value to get the denominator (0.375 = 375 thousandths), then simplify to lowest terms
Teach fraction→decimal two ways — as division (numerator ÷ denominator) AND as scaling the denominator to a power of ten (3/8 = 375/1000 via ×125)
Make the '2s and 5s only' test explicit by contrasting terminators (1/8, 1/20, 1/40) with recurrers (1/3, 1/6, 1/7) and factorising each denominator
Treat FDP as three views of one number on a triple number line so conversion is re-notation, not new arithmetic
Show a recurring decimal actually recurring (1/3 = 0.333…) so children do not truncate it and call it exact
keyRepresentations: Place-value columns (tenths, hundredths, thousandths)
Prime-factor trees of denominators
Short division for fraction→decimal
FDP triple number line / equivalence cards
Hundredths and thousandths grids
commonMisconceptions: Reads 0.375 as 375/100 (denominator doesn't match the last place value)
Inverts the division, computing 8 ÷ 3 instead of 3 ÷ 8
Believes every fraction terminates, or truncates a recurring decimal (1/3 = 0.3) and treats it as exact
Decides whether a decimal terminates from the numerator or 'how neat it looks' rather than the denominator's prime factors

learn.summary: Terminating decimals and fractions are two notations for one value, with percentages a third. A terminating decimal is read by its LAST place value to get a power-of-ten denominator (0.375 = 375/1000), then simplified (= 3/8). Converting a fraction to a decimal is division (3 ÷ 8 = 0.375) or, equivalently, scaling the denominator up to a power of ten (3/8 = 375/1000 via ×125). The deep idea: a fraction in lowest terms terminates exactly when its denominator's only prime factors are 2 and/or 5 (the primes of ten); any other prime factor (3, 7, 11…) makes it recur. Learners should both convert fluently in both directions AND predict termination from the denominator's prime factorisation, not by dividing and guessing.

activities.title: Scale to a power of ten — does it land?
feedback: If a learner says 1/6 stops: factorise 6 = 2×3. The factor 3 is not 2 or 5, so no power of ten is a multiple of 6 and the decimal recurs (0.1666…). Show it recurring rather than truncating to 0.17.

If they truncate a recurring decimal and call it exact (1/3 = 0.3): run the division further so the 3s keep coming; 0.333… is not equal to 0.3. (Year 6 learners meet rounding recurring decimals to three decimal places — rounding is an approximation, not the exact value.)

If they decide termination from the numerator or 'how neat it looks': remind them the numerator is irrelevant once the fraction is simplified — only the lowest-terms denominator's prime factors decide.
activities.rationale: Contrasting a fraction that scales onto a power of ten against one that never does, with prime-factor readouts shown together, is intended to make the 2-and-5 rule discoverable rather than merely asserted; sorting fractions and factorising each denominator is a documented route to the rule.
sourceClaims: A fraction IN LOWEST TERMS gives a terminating decimal if and only if its denominator's only prime factors are 2 and/or 5; the reason is base-10 (10 = 2x5), so the denominator terminates exactly when it divides a power of ten. Sorting fractions into terminating/recurring columns and writing each denominator as its prime factorisation makes the rule discoverable; the numerator is irrelevant and the fraction must be simplified first.

Year 6 pupils 'associate a fraction with division and calculate decimal fraction equivalents [0.375] for a simple fraction [3/8]'; for simple fractions with recurring decimal equivalents they learn about rounding to three decimal places - so recurring decimals are met and must not be treated as terminating.
learnerActions: Take 1/8 and try to turn it into tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths: find the multiplier (×125) that makes the denominator 1000, giving 125/1000 = 0.125; confirm it 'lands' exactly.
Now try 1/3 the same way: aim for 10, 100, 1000… and find that no power of ten works; carry out the division 1 ÷ 3 and watch the 3s continue (0.333…), a recurring decimal that never stops.
Write each denominator as a product of primes side by side: 8 = 2×2×2; 6 = 2×3; 3 = 3. Mark which denominators are built only from 2s and 5s.
State the rule you discover in your own words, then test it on 1/20, 1/40 (should terminate) and 1/6, 1/7 (should recur), factorising each denominator first.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction in lowest terms terminates exactly when its denominator is built only from the primes 2 and/or 5 — because those are the primes of ten, so the denominator can be scaled to a power of ten. Any other prime factor forces a recurring decimal.

activities.title: Read a decimal by its last place value
feedback: If a learner writes 0.375 = 375/100: the last digit (5) sits in the thousandths place, so the denominator is 1000, not 100. Re-read several decimals aloud by their final place value before writing the fraction.

If they invert the division and compute 8 ÷ 3 for 3/8 (getting 2.66…): re-establish that a/b means a ÷ b — numerator divided by denominator — grounded in sharing 3 wholes among 8 people, which gives less than one each (0.375).
activities.rationale: Anchoring the denominator to the last place value is intended to address the most common conversion error (reading onto the wrong power of ten), and practising division-as-conversion in the reverse direction aims to reinforce fraction-as-division, a documented sticking point.
sourceClaims: Converting a fraction to a decimal is the division numerator / denominator (fraction-as-division); understanding fractions as division underpins decimal equivalence and is a documented sticking point.

Year 6 pupils 'associate a fraction with division and calculate decimal fraction equivalents [0.375] for a simple fraction [3/8]'; for simple fractions with recurring decimal equivalents they learn about rounding to three decimal places - so recurring decimals are met and must not be treated as terminating.
learnerActions: Name the place value of the LAST digit of 0.375 (thousandths), so the starting denominator is 1000: write 0.375 = 375/1000.
Simplify stepwise to lowest terms: 375/1000 = 3/8 (divide both by 125). Check the simplified fraction against the original decimal.
Repeat with other decimals (0.2 = 2/10 = 1/5; 0.25 = 25/100 = 1/4; 0.35 = 35/100 = 7/20), each time naming the last place value first.
Reverse the direction: convert 3/8 to a decimal two ways — divide 3 ÷ 8, and scale 3/8 to 375/1000 — and confirm both give 0.375.
activities.intendedInsight: A terminating decimal IS a fraction with a power-of-ten denominator; reading the last place value gives that denominator, and simplifying gives lowest terms. Fraction→decimal is division (numerator ÷ denominator), equivalently scaling to a power of ten.

activities.title: Sort, match and fill the gaps (consolidation)
feedback: If a learner sorts by dividing and rounding: that only shows what happens to begin with, not whether it stops forever. Ask them to factorise the denominator in lowest terms and apply the 2-and-5 test instead.
If a chain step is wrong, point back to the place-value reading (last digit → denominator) and the simplification factor (×125 or ÷125).
activities.rationale: Matching, categorising and fill-in-and-explain tasks give repeated, checkable practice across both directions and foreground the structural (prime-factor) test over empirical division; the fill-in step asks the learner to produce values and explain each one, so this activity consolidates and partly requires articulation of the discovered rule, not its first teaching.
sourceClaims: A fraction IN LOWEST TERMS gives a terminating decimal if and only if its denominator's only prime factors are 2 and/or 5; the reason is base-10 (10 = 2x5), so the denominator terminates exactly when it divides a power of ten. Sorting fractions into terminating/recurring columns and writing each denominator as its prime factorisation makes the rule discoverable; the numerator is irrelevant and the fraction must be simplified first.
learnerActions: Match terminating decimals to their simplest fractions: 0.375 ↔ 3/8, 0.2 ↔ 1/5, 0.25 ↔ 1/4.
Sort a set of fractions into two columns, 'terminates' and 'recurs', by inspecting each denominator's prime factors (not by dividing): e.g. 7/40 and 1/20 terminate; 5/12 and 1/6 recur.
Fill in the chain 0.375 = __/1000 = __/8, then explain each step (last place value → denominator, then the ÷125 simplification).

Transfer to unfamiliar fractions: predict whether 9/25, 4/15 and 6/15 terminate, justify from the prime factors of each denominator in lowest terms (6/15 = 2/5), then check by converting (9/25 = 0.36; 4/15 = 0.2666…; 6/15 = 0.4).
activities.intendedInsight: Bidirectional conversion to simplest form becomes fluent, and the terminate/recur judgement is made from the denominator's prime factors rather than by trial division.

activities.title: Predict and justify: will it stop? (optional discussion)
feedback: Accept only reasons that cite the denominator's prime factors; 'it looks neat' or 'I tried dividing' is not a structural justification.
If the learner can convert but cannot say why 1/8 stops and 1/6 does not, return to factorising the two denominators side by side.
activities.rationale: A short predict-and-justify exchange is proposed to supplement procedural practice by targeting the 'why do some fractions never stop?' reasoning; it supplements rather than replaces conversion practice, since the objective is procedural fluency. Its effect on reasoning is untested here.
learnerActions: Before converting, predict aloud whether a given fraction (e.g. 1/6, 7/40, 5/12) terminates or recurs, and say WHY from the denominator.
Justify the prediction by naming the prime factors of the denominator and relating them to the primes of ten (2 and 5).
Have a partner or adult pose the question 'How could you know without doing the whole division?' and respond with a reasoned argument, then check by converting.
activities.intendedInsight: Verbalising the prediction and its reason is intended to reveal whether the learner reasons from structure (prime factors) or merely from procedures; articulating the reason aims to strengthen the conceptual link, though that effect is not established here.

constraints: Recurring decimals must be shown genuinely recurring (1/3 = 0.333…); do not truncate (0.3 or 0.33) and call it exact. Rounding a recurring decimal to a set number of places is an approximation introduced for Year 6, not the exact value.
The 2-and-5 rule applies only to the denominator IN LOWEST TERMS; simplify first and ignore the numerator when judging termination.

Matching is recognition-and-recall practice, a sort checks classification of denominators, and a fill-in chain asks the learner to produce values; on their own these task types do not require the learner to carry out a full conversion in both directions and articulate the reason, so pair them with at least one activity where the learner constructs and explains a full conversion and a termination prediction (as the fill-in-and-explain and predict-and-justify steps do).

A tap-to-reveal equivalence card (fraction → decimal → percentage with denominator prime factors) is a useful reference aid but cannot let a learner test the terminate/recur boundary themselves; use it alongside, not instead of, the scaling/conversion work.
Fraction-as-division must be the direction numerator ÷ denominator (3 ÷ 8), not denominator ÷ numerator.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and no claim of empirical testing is made.

Legacy design described two linked on-screen panels (scale-to-power-of-ten with a prime-factor readout, and place-value decimal-to-fraction simplifier) with a 'lights up/it fits' response. These interaction examples are preserved as optional ways to make the mechanism concrete; they are not mandatory. A fixed printed chart can still teach the conversions even though it cannot be manipulated.

The legacy source framed interactive scaling as the way the rule 'clicks' and rated dialogue/3D as weaker. Those comparative fit judgements are catalog preferences, not established efficacy; the alternatives are kept here as activities with stated purposes and limits rather than as a ranking.

Editorial change: efficacy-asserting wording in the activity rationales and in activity[3]'s intendedInsight ('removes the error', 'reinforces', 'strengthening the conceptual link') was softened to intended/aims wording, since the sources identify the misconceptions/sticking points but do not establish that these specific activities fix them.

Self-audit of arithmetic and logic: 0.375 = 375/1000 = 3/8 (÷125) is correct; 3/8 = 0.375 is correct; 1/8 = 0.125 via ×125 to 125/1000 is correct; 8 = 2³, 6 = 2×3, 3 = 3 are correct; 1/6 = 0.1666… recurs (3 is not 2 or 5) is correct; 7/40 terminates (40 = 2³×5) and 5/12 recurs (12 = 2²×3) are correct; 0.2=1/5, 0.25=1/4, 0.35=7/20 are correct; 8 ÷ 3 = 2.66… correctly identifies the inverted-division error. No arithmetic errors found in learner-facing content.

probeDeeper: What place value is the last digit of 0.375 in? So what denominator do you start with before simplifying?
For 3/8, which number do you divide by which — and why that way round?
Will 1/6 stop or go on forever? What is it about the 6 that tells you, without dividing all the way?
1/8 stops but 1/3 does not. What is different about the denominators when you break each into prime factors?
assess.correctAnswer: 0.375 = 375/1000 = 3/8 (dividing by 125); 3/8 = 0.375 (3 ÷ 8, or ×125 to make 375/1000). 1/6 does NOT stop — 6 = 2×3, and the factor 3 is not 2 or 5, so it recurs (0.1666…).

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the decimal onto the wrong power of ten: 0.375 = 375/100
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name the last digit's place (thousandths), so the denominator is 1000; then simplify. Re-read several decimals by their final place value.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denominator does not match the last digit's place value; the simplified fraction is wrong or won't simplify to 3/8

errorPatterns.pattern: Inverts the division for fraction→decimal: computes 8 ÷ 3 for 3/8
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-establish fraction-as-division: a/b means a ÷ b (numerator into denominator), grounded in sharing 3 wholes among 8.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Divides the larger number by the smaller, or gets 2.66… for 3/8

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges whether a fraction terminates from the numerator or how 'neat' it looks, or believes every fraction terminates — so claims 1/6 stops, or truncates it to 0.17 and calls it exact
errorPatterns.nextMove: Factorise the denominators side by side (8 = 2³ terminates; 6 = 2×3 recurs) and connect 2 and 5 to the primes of ten; show 1/6 genuinely recurring.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 1/6 stops; decides by trying to divide and rounding rather than by the denominator's prime factors; cannot explain WHY 1/8 stops but 1/6 does not

responseLevels.gap: Mis-reads the decimal's denominator or inverts the division; believes all fractions terminate; cannot connect terminating to the denominator.
responseLevels.full: Converts both directions fluently to simplest form AND predicts termination from the denominator's prime factorisation (only 2 and 5), explaining why (it can be scaled to a power of ten); transfers to a new fraction such as 7/40 (terminates) or 5/12 (recurs).
responseLevels.partial: Converts 0.375 ↔ 3/8 correctly by procedure, but decides termination empirically by dividing and rounding rather than from the denominator's prime factors, or states the 2-and-5 rule only after prompting.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'Convert 0.375 to a fraction in its simplest form, and convert 3/8 to a decimal. Then tell me — will 1/6 give a decimal that stops, or one that goes on forever? How could you know without doing the whole division?' Watch how they work and listen to the reason for 1/6.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Converting 0.375 both ways is routine and does not separate understanding from memorised steps. The 1/6 question is the hinge: a child who grasps the structure inspects the denominator's prime factors (only 2 and 5 terminate) and answers WITHOUT dividing; a child who has only procedures tries to divide and rounds, guesses, or asserts that all fractions stop. Reasoning correctly and reasoning wrongly give visibly different responses here.

pedagogy.summary: This is the representational core of transformations: reading a picture of an object and its image and saying precisely WHICH transformation maps one onto the other — and, conversely, producing the image from a described transformation. Each transformation has a defining set of marks a child must read and generate: a reflection needs a mirror line (and reverses sense); a translation needs a vector/displacement (and keeps orientation and sense); a rotation needs three things — a centre, an angle of turn, and a direction. Fluency means translating freely between the drawn image and its precise verbal description, checking congruence throughout.
bestPractices: Teach each transformation by its distinguishing evidence: reflection is the only one that reverses 'sense' (handedness); rotation changes orientation but keeps sense; translation keeps both. Have children CHECK sense to tell rotation from reflection.
Insist a rotation is described by all THREE pieces — centre of rotation, size of turn, and direction (clockwise/anticlockwise); a description missing any one is incomplete (NCETM KS3 6.3).

For reflection, draw the perpendicular lines joining each object vertex to its image and show the mirror line is their perpendicular bisector; avoid 'straight across/down' so the idea survives sloping mirror lines.
Move both ways: given an image, have the child NAME and fully describe the transformation; given a description, have the child PRODUCE the image — the two directions reinforce each other.
Use tracing paper for rotation — pin the centre, turn to the stated angle and direction — so the abstract description becomes a felt movement, and to verify congruence.

Include non-standard cases (a rotation that could be read clockwise or anticlockwise; a reflection in a sloping line) to force analysis rather than pattern-matching, and to surface the 'same-plane' and direction misconceptions.
keyRepresentations: Coordinate/squared grid showing object and image together
Mirror line with perpendicular 'joining lines' to corresponding vertices (reflection)
Centre-of-rotation marked, with an angle arc and a direction arrow (rotation)
Translation vector arrow (displacement) applied to every vertex
Tracing paper as the physical model for rotation and for congruence checks
commonMisconceptions: Calling a rotation a reflection (or vice versa) because sense/handedness is not checked.
Describing a rotation incompletely — giving the angle but omitting the centre and/or the direction.
When reflecting in a sloping mirror, keeping the image in the same horizontal/vertical plane instead of moving each point perpendicular to the mirror.
Reversing coordinates (up before across) when labelling where the image landed.

learn.summary: Learners read a picture of a shape and its image on a squared/coordinate grid and say precisely WHICH transformation maps one onto the other, then work the other way — producing the image from a stated transformation. The defining evidence differs per transformation: reflection reverses 'sense' (handedness) and is built with a mirror line that is the perpendicular bisector of segments joining object and image points; translation keeps orientation and sense and is described by a vector/displacement applied to every vertex; rotation keeps sense but changes orientation and must be described by three things — centre, size (angle) of turn, and direction (clockwise/anticlockwise). Fluency means translating freely between the drawn image and its precise verbal description while checking congruence throughout, including non-standard cases such as sloping mirror lines and ambiguous turn directions.

activities.title: Name it: reconstruct the transformation that produced the image
feedback: If you named a reflection: ask 'does the shape read the same way round, or the mirror way round?' Only reflection reverses sense — re-decide from that check.

If you gave only the angle: a rotation needs three things — centre, size, direction. Add each and test by reproducing the image (tracing paper pinned at the centre lets you turn to the stated angle and direction and verify congruence).
If the image lands in the wrong place: check whether the centre is correct; if it turns the wrong way, check the direction.
Mark a rotation description as incomplete until centre, angle AND direction are all present.
activities.rationale: Identifying and describing a transformation is strengthened by setting the very parameters that define it and watching the image obey — binding each verbal descriptor to its visible effect. Mixing a reflection among rotations deliberately draws attention to what a rotation is not.
sourceClaims: A rotation must be described by three pieces of information — a centre of rotation, a size of turn, and a direction — and direction ambiguity (clockwise vs anticlockwise) is a documented difficulty.

Reflection is the only transformation that changes 'sense'; rotation changes orientation but maintains sense, and translation maintains congruence and orientation — so sense distinguishes rotation from reflection. Examples deliberately mix a reflection among rotations to draw attention to what a rotation is not.
learnerActions: On a grid showing a shape and its image already placed (produced by a rotation), work out which single transformation maps the first onto the second and reproduce it by setting the parameters yourself.
First try a reflection: flip the shape and compare handedness to the target — notice the 'sense' no longer matches (the target reads the same way round), so it cannot be a reflection.
Switch to rotation: choose a centre of rotation, set the angle of turn, and choose the direction (clockwise/anticlockwise) until your image lands exactly on the target.

State the full description aloud or in writing, e.g. 'rotation, 90° clockwise, about (2,1)', and check what each part controls: turning the same amount about a different centre makes the shape land somewhere else, and for a 90° turn, going the opposite direction lands it in a different place. (For a 180° turn, clockwise and anticlockwise give the same image, but still state the direction to keep the description complete.)
Confirm the image is congruent to the original (e.g. by tracing or matching vertices).
activities.intendedInsight: Checking sense is what distinguishes a rotation from a reflection, and a rotation is only fully specified by centre, size AND direction together. The centre and the angle always affect where the image lands. The direction matters for 90° turns, but a 180° turn lands in the same place either way.

activities.title: Produce a reflection in a sloping mirror line
feedback: If the image sits level with the object rather than square across a sloping mirror: your joining lines are not perpendicular to the mirror. Draw the perpendicular from each vertex and step the equal distance beyond.
Avoid 'straight across' language so the idea survives sloping mirror lines.
If sense is not reversed, you have not reflected — check the handedness of the image against the original.
activities.rationale: A frequent error is keeping the image in the same horizontal/vertical plane instead of moving each point perpendicular to the mirror; building the perpendicular-equidistant structure explicitly and testing it on a sloping line generalises the method.
sourceClaims: A common reflection misconception is keeping the image in the same vertical/horizontal plane rather than moving each point perpendicular to the mirror line; the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of segments joining object and image points.
learnerActions: Given a shape and a mirror line (including sloping or offset lines, not just horizontal/vertical), draw the reflected image.
For each vertex, draw the perpendicular from the vertex to the mirror line and step an equal distance beyond it to place the image vertex.
Check that the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of each segment joining a vertex to its image, and that the sense (handedness) of the shape is reversed.
Describe what you did as 'a reflection in [this] mirror line' and confirm the image is congruent to the original.
Repeat with a sloping mirror to make sure your method does not rely on 'straight across/down'.
activities.intendedInsight: A reflection moves every point perpendicular to the mirror by an equal distance on the other side, so the mirror is the perpendicular bisector of each joining segment — this holds for sloping mirrors, not just level ones.

activities.title: Translate by a vector and label coordinates carefully
feedback: If a landed vertex is reported as (up, across): re-anchor with 'across the corridor, then up the stairs' and re-check one labelled vertex together.
If only some vertices moved the right amount, remember the same displacement applies to every vertex.
activities.rationale: Reversing the ordered pair is a recurring coordinate error; anchoring 'across then up' and checking a vertex guards against it while reinforcing that translation preserves orientation and congruence.
sourceClaims: Reversing the ordered pair (reading the second coordinate before the first) is a recurring coordinate error to guard against.

Reflection is the only transformation that changes 'sense'; rotation changes orientation but maintains sense, and translation maintains congruence and orientation — so sense distinguishes rotation from reflection. Examples deliberately mix a reflection among rotations to draw attention to what a rotation is not.
learnerActions: Translate a shape by a given displacement (e.g. 3 right and 2 up), applying the same movement to every vertex.
Describe the movement both as a vector and in left/right/up/down words.
Label the coordinates of the translated vertices, writing each as (across, up).
Check that orientation and sense are unchanged and that the image is congruent to the original.
activities.intendedInsight: A translation slides every point by the same displacement, preserving orientation, sense and size; coordinates are read across first, then up.

activities.title: Precision check: discrete items for describing transformations
feedback: Score a rotation description as correct only if centre, angle AND direction are all present.
For the rotation-vs-reflection item, point to sense: if handedness flipped it is a reflection, if sense is unchanged it is a rotation.
activities.rationale: Discrete items are useful for checking precision of description and for surfacing the rotation-vs-reflection confusion via a sense-reversed distractor; on their own they check recognition and stated description rather than independent construction of the image.
sourceClaims: A rotation must be described by three pieces of information — a centre of rotation, a size of turn, and a direction — and direction ambiguity (clockwise vs anticlockwise) is a documented difficulty.
learnerActions: Answer 'which transformation maps A to B?' where one distractor shows the same shape reflected (sense reversed) rather than rotated.
Match written descriptions to images.
Fill in the three parts of a rotation description (centre, size, direction) for a shown image.
Draw the path/image to produce a reflection in a given mirror line.
activities.intendedInsight: Describing a transformation precisely means using the correct defining marks — and a rotation description counts only when centre, angle and direction are all given.

activities.title: Annotated worked examples as a reference
feedback: Answer 'rotation or reflection?' by checking whether sense reversed, then confirm against the revealed marks.
Treat this as a reference: to build the skill, move on to naming an unlabelled image and producing images yourself.
activities.rationale: A fixed annotated example cannot be manipulated by the learner, but it can make the defining marks and the sense check explicit and serve as a reference alongside generative tasks.
sourceClaims: Reflection is the only transformation that changes 'sense'; rotation changes orientation but maintains sense, and translation maintains congruence and orientation — so sense distinguishes rotation from reflection. Examples deliberately mix a reflection among rotations to draw attention to what a rotation is not.
learnerActions: Study one worked example of each transformation with its defining marks revealed: the mirror line and perpendicular joining lines for reflection; the vector arrow for translation; the centre, angle arc and direction arrow for rotation.
For each, identify whether the sense is reversed and use that to decide 'rotation or reflection?'.
Use these as a reference while attempting your own naming and producing tasks.
activities.intendedInsight: Each transformation has a distinct set of marks to read; sense reversal is the tell for reflection.

constraints: A complete rotation description requires all three parts — centre, size of turn, and direction; treat any missing part as incomplete.
Avoid 'straight across/down' language for reflection so methods generalise to sloping and offset mirror lines; use perpendicular-and-equidistant instead.
Label image coordinates consistently as (across, up) to guard against reversing the ordered pair.
Include non-standard cases (a turn that could be read clockwise or anticlockwise; a reflection in a sloping line) to force analysis rather than pattern-matching.
Discrete/recognition items (multiple choice, matching) check precision of stated description but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of an image; pair them with producing tasks.
Tracing paper (pin the centre, turn to the stated angle and direction) is a useful physical model for rotation and for checking congruence; it is a supportive tool, not a required mechanism.

Interactive controls (mode buttons, draggable mirror line, pinnable centre with angle dial and CW/ACW toggle, live sense indicator and congruence overlay) are optional ways to make the descriptor-to-motion link concrete; the same learning can be done on paper.

These transformations are planar and are read from marks on a grid, so a third dimension is not needed to read a mirror line, vector or centre. A dialogue/persona format can discuss and prompt transformation work but does not itself present or manipulate the grid, so producing an image would still happen on the learner's own paper. These are scoping affordance notes, not claims that any medium is uniquely necessary, superior, or impossible.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source claims about sense/handedness, the three parts of a rotation, perpendicular-bisector reflection, and coordinate reversal are cited from NCETM materials as recorded in the source row; comparative efficacy of any specific activity format is not established by these citations.

Legacy 'fit' rankings asserting that a third dimension 'adds nothing' and that a conversation 'cannot' teach this were softened to scoped affordance notes; the source ratings do not establish universal necessity or impossibility.

The diagnostic and these activities assume a scalene/asymmetric shape so that sense and orientation changes are visible; ensure any chosen shape is asymmetric enough that reflection vs rotation genuinely differs, otherwise the sense check is not discriminating.
Note for 180° rotations specifically, clockwise and anticlockwise give the same image, so the 'direction turns it the wrong way' feedback applies to turns such as 90°, not to 180°.

probeDeeper: 'How can you be sure this is a rotation and not a reflection?' (listen for sense/handedness as the deciding evidence, not orientation alone).
'If I only told you the shape was rotated 90°, could you draw exactly where it lands? What else do you need?' (elicits centre and direction as required parameters).

Counterexample: 'Your friend says the second shape is a reflection. Show me the mirror line that would do it — does one exist?' (a rotated shape has no consistent mirror line; the search exposes the error).
'Is the image congruent to the original after your reflection? How would you check?' (tracing/matching; congruence is invariant under all three transformations).
assess.correctAnswer: For the shown image: 'a rotation' named with all three descriptors — centre (the marked point), size (90°/quarter turn) and direction (clockwise or anticlockwise, matching the picture) — justified by the shape keeping its sense while changing orientation. For the produced reflection: each vertex placed perpendicular to and equidistant from the mirror, sense reversed, described as a reflection in that mirror line, and the image confirmed congruent to the original.

errorPatterns.pattern: Calls the rotation a reflection (or vice versa) without checking sense
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'does the shape read the same way round or the mirror way round?' Establish that only reflection reverses sense; re-decide from that check.
errorPatterns.distractor: A reflection in a line through the marked point
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names 'reflection' for an image whose sense is unchanged, or 'rotation' for one whose handedness has flipped; cannot cite sense as the deciding evidence.

errorPatterns.pattern: Describes the rotation incompletely — gives the angle but omits the centre and/or the direction
errorPatterns.nextMove: State that a rotation needs three things — centre, size, direction; have the child add each and test by reproducing the image with tracing paper pinned at the centre.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 'it's turned 90°' or 'a quarter turn' with no centre named and no clockwise/anticlockwise; treats 'rotation' as fully specified by its angle.

errorPatterns.pattern: When producing a reflection in a sloping or offset mirror, keeps the image in the same horizontal/vertical plane instead of moving each point perpendicular to the mirror
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw the perpendicular from each vertex to the mirror and step the equal distance beyond; avoid 'straight across' language so it generalises to sloping mirrors.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The produced image sits level with the object rather than square across the mirror line; joining lines are not perpendicular to the mirror.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses coordinates (states the up-value before the across-value) when labelling the image
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor 'across the corridor, then up the stairs'; check one labelled vertex together.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reports a landed vertex as (up, across) though the point drawn is correct.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot reliably name the transformation — confuses rotation and reflection, or offers only a bare word with no defining marks — and cannot produce a correct reflection (image not perpendicular/equidistant, sense not reversed).
responseLevels.full: Names each transformation from its evidence (using sense to separate rotation from reflection), describes a rotation completely (centre, size, direction), produces a reflection with each vertex perpendicular and equidistant and sense reversed, labels image coordinates as (across, up), and confirms congruence — transferring correctly to non-standard mirror lines and centres.
responseLevels.partial: Reads and names each transformation and can produce a reflection in a vertical/horizontal mirror, but treats the descriptors as a checklist rather than a structure — e.g. identifies a rotation yet omits centre or direction, or produces a reflection correctly only in standard positions while failing a sloping mirror. Lists the parts of a transformation but cannot yet explain how they jointly fix the image or transfer to a non-standard case.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a squared grid with a scalene shape and its image, where the image is the shape turned a quarter-turn about a marked point (sense unchanged). Say: 'What single transformation maps the first shape onto the second? Describe it as fully as you can.' Then give a fresh copy of the original next to a mirror line and say: 'Now YOU produce the reflection of this shape in this mirror line, and describe what you did.' Read what they say about the shown transformation, then watch what they draw.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The reading move forces a choice between rotation and reflection that only checking SENSE resolves — a child who reasons from sense names it correctly, one who guesses from orientation alone may call it a reflection. Requiring a FULL description exposes whether the child knows a rotation needs centre, angle and direction, not just the word. The producing move then shows whether they can generate the perpendicular-equidistant structure themselves, so reading and producing are checked separately.
