pedagogy.summary: At 8-9, multi-step problem solving becomes independent enough that the child identifies the sub-steps themselves, chooses a strategy (e.g. drawing a diagram versus writing equations), and monitors progress across a problem that may involve four operations, fractions, or area/perimeter. The reasonableness check sharpens: a child should be able to say, before or after computing, that 3/5 of 20 must be more than half of 20. The persistent risks are the same two documented habits — the keyword strategy (which collapses on multi-step problems) and the compulsion to calculate (computing with no estimate or monitoring). Teaching leans on modelled self-questioning to monitor progress (strong evidence), student-built visual representations to expose sub-structure (strong evidence), and estimation as a reasonableness benchmark.
bestPractices: Have the child identify and name the sub-steps and state a plan before calculating
Teach strategy choice explicitly: when is a diagram better than an equation? Compare both on the same problem
Build the child's own bar/strip or area diagram to expose the sub-structure of the problem (WWC Rec 3, strong evidence)
Model self-questioning to monitor progress across sub-steps ('what have I found? what's left?') (WWC Rec 2, strong evidence)
Use estimation as a reasonableness benchmark (3/5 of 20 must exceed half of 20); check by an inverse or different method
Teach structure/schema, not keywords — keyword-to-operation matching fails on multi-step problems
keyRepresentations: Bar / strip diagram decomposing the sub-steps
Area model for area/perimeter and fraction-of-quantity problems
Number line and equations as alternative strategies to compare
Estimation / benchmarking (half, rounding) for reasonableness
Monitoring prompt list: plan → do a step → check → next
commonMisconceptions: Keyword strategy on multi-step problems — an operation chosen from a word, applied in the wrong order
Computing with no estimate or reasonableness check (compulsion to calculate) — e.g. a fraction-of-quantity answer larger than the whole passes unnoticed
Doing the sub-steps but not monitoring — losing track of what has been found versus what remains, or failing to combine sub-results
Defaulting to one strategy (always equations, or always drawing) regardless of which fits the problem

learn.summary: For 8-9 year olds working on multi-step problems (four operations, fractions, area/perimeter), the goal is independent problem solving: the child identifies and names the sub-steps, states a plan, chooses a strategy (diagram vs equation), monitors progress, and brackets the answer's size for reasonableness (e.g. 3/5 of 20 must be more than half of 20). Two documented risks persist: the keyword strategy (picking an operation from a word, which collapses on multi-step problems) and the compulsion to calculate (computing with no estimate or monitoring, so an impossible answer passes unnoticed). Teaching leans on modelled self-questioning to monitor progress, student-built visual representations to expose sub-structure, and estimation as a reasonableness benchmark.

activities.title: Build the sub-structure and bracket the answer
feedback: If a child finds 3/4 of 8 rather than 3/4 of the area, have them retell the problem and point to each sub-step on their own diagram so the order follows the structure.
If an answer comes out larger than the whole rectangle and the child is untroubled, ask 'can a part of the rectangle be bigger than the whole rectangle?' and return to the area model.
If the estimate and the computed answer clash, treat the clash as the signal to re-check a sub-step rather than to discard the estimate.
When comparing diagram vs equation, ask the child to say which exposed the sub-steps more clearly and why, rather than declaring one always better.
activities.rationale: Building one's own visual representation of problem structure and estimating for reasonableness target the two documented failure habits; an act-and-recompute workspace lets the child see sub-structure and catch impossible answers. Optional supports that make the mechanism concrete: sub-step cards to sequence on an area canvas the child builds, an estimate slider ('less than half / about half / more than half'), a reasonableness gauge that flags an answer exceeding the whole, a strategy toggle to view the same problem as diagram and as equations, and a running 'found / still to find' tracker. These are examples of how to make the levers visible, not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: The keyword strategy ties a word to an operation without understanding structure and fails on multi-step problems (match rate under 10%); schema/structure instruction is the evidence-based alternative.

Modelling a self-questioning routine to monitor and reflect (Rec 2) and teaching students to build their own visual representations of problem structure (Rec 3) each have strong evidence for improving multi-step problem solving.
The compulsion to calculate leads students to compute without checking reasonableness; teachers should focus on relationships and reasonableness rather than rushing to an answer.
learnerActions: Take a multi-step problem such as 'A rectangle is 8 cm by 5 cm. You colour 3/4 of it. What is the coloured area?'

Before calculating, name and sequence the sub-steps in order (first find the area, then find 3/4 of it) — arrange them as cards or a written plan so the order comes from the structure, not from a word
Build your own bar/strip or area diagram of the problem to expose its sub-structure
Before computing the fraction, state an estimate: is 3/4 of the rectangle less than half, about half, or more than half? Record it
Compute the sub-steps (area = 8×5 = 40; then 3/4 of 40 = 30)

Check the answer against your estimate and the whole: 30 is more than half of 40 and less than the whole 40, so it is sensible — if an answer comes out bigger than the whole rectangle, or below your 'more than half' estimate, return to the area diagram to find where a sub-step went wrong
Replay the same problem as equations and compare: which strategy made the structure clearer here, and why?
activities.intendedInsight: Multi-step answers should be bracketed for size before and after computing, and a self-built diagram makes the order of sub-steps and the reasonableness of the result visible; strategy choice is a felt comparison, not a fixed rule.

activities.title: Think-aloud coaching partner for monitoring
feedback: If the child treats an intermediate value as the final answer, use the 'what have you found / what's left?' prompt to surface the missing combination step.
If the child insists on one strategy regardless of fit, invite them to try the alternative on the same problem and compare which revealed the sub-steps.
The partner should prompt and nudge, not state the next step; the aim is for the child to internalise the self-questioning routine.
activities.rationale: Modelled self-questioning to monitor progress has strong evidence for multi-step problem solving; rehearsing it aloud with a non-supplying partner can build the monitoring the child otherwise skips. The coach prompts strategy justification and progress tracking.
sourceClaims: Modelling a self-questioning routine to monitor and reflect (Rec 2) and teaching students to build their own visual representations of problem structure (Rec 3) each have strong evidence for improving multi-step problem solving.
Proficient solvers plan a pathway, monitor and evaluate progress and change course if necessary, and check answers by a different method, continually asking 'Does this make sense?'.
learnerActions: Work a multi-step problem while a partner (teacher, peer, or in-role coach) asks self-questioning prompts without supplying the steps
Answer aloud: 'What are the sub-steps here, and which do you do first and why that order?'
Answer: 'Would a drawing or an equation help more here — why?'
Mid-solution, answer: 'What have you found so far? What's left to find?'
After computing, answer: 'Does that answer make sense? More or less than half? Bigger or smaller than the whole?'
When stalled, consider switching strategy when the partner nudges (e.g. try a diagram if the equation is not revealing the structure)
activities.intendedInsight: Running self-questions — plan, do a step, check, next — keep track of progress across sub-steps and turn strategy choice into a deliberate decision.

activities.title: Worked-example companion: reveal the decomposition
feedback: Point out when the revealed self-question is the move the child skipped on their own attempt.
Follow every worked example with an independent attempt — studying the decomposition is a scaffold, and recognising a worked step is not evidence the child can produce the decomposition unaided.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal worked example can display the decomposition and reasonableness check and model the self-questioning routine, but by itself the child does not identify sub-steps or monitor — so it is a stepping stone toward independent construction, not a substitute for it.
sourceClaims: Modelling a self-questioning routine to monitor and reflect (Rec 2) and teaching students to build their own visual representations of problem structure (Rec 3) each have strong evidence for improving multi-step problem solving.
learnerActions: Study a fully worked multi-step problem where each sub-step is initially hidden
Reveal each sub-step one at a time, and at each reveal read the monitoring self-question that accompanies it ('what have I found? what's left?')

At the fraction step, read the estimate that rules an answer in or out (e.g. for the 8 cm by 5 cm rectangle with area 40 cm²: '3/4 is more than half, so the coloured area must exceed 20 cm² but be less than 40 cm²')
After studying, attempt a fresh multi-step problem yourself, naming the sub-steps and the estimate without the reveal
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing how an expert decomposes a problem and checks reasonableness models the routine before the child performs it independently.

activities.title: Reasonableness and wrong-order checks
feedback: If a learner cannot say whether 3/4 of 20 should be more or less than 10, make benchmarking routine before returning to computation (3/4 of 20 = 15, which is more than half of 20).

For the tin problem, prompt reasoning about the total poured (3/4 × 4 = 3 litres) versus the 2-litre capacity, so the answer comes from the situation — starting from empty, it overflows (already on the third pour, since 3 × 3/4 = 2 1/4 litres).
activities.rationale: Targeted reasonableness and spot-the-wrong-order items can probe the benchmarking and structural-order habits at this age. Note the limit: a scored, fast-answer format rewards quick computing and cannot by itself assess whether a child independently identifies sub-steps or monitors progress, so keep these items as checks alongside, not as the main teaching.
sourceClaims: The compulsion to calculate leads students to compute without checking reasonableness; teachers should focus on relationships and reasonableness rather than rushing to an answer.
Proficient solvers plan a pathway, monitor and evaluate progress and change course if necessary, and check answers by a different method, continually asking 'Does this make sense?'.
learnerActions: Given a set of candidate answers, use benchmarks alone (without computing exactly) to pick the one(s) that are impossible — e.g. 'Which of these is impossible for 3/5 of 20?' including an option larger than 20 and an option less than half of 20
Explain why the impossible answer is impossible using a benchmark (more/less than half, bigger/smaller than the whole)
Look at a short worked solution where the sub-steps are done in the wrong order and identify where the order breaks the problem's structure
Try a situational problem: 'An empty tin holds 2 litres. You pour in 3/4 of a litre four times. Does it overflow?' — reason about the situation, not just the numbers
activities.intendedInsight: Reasonableness is about bracketing an answer's size and respecting the order the situation requires, not about computing fast.

constraints: Teach structure/schema, not keyword-to-operation matching: keyword matching fails on multi-step problems (reported match rate under 10%).
The child should identify and name the sub-steps and state a plan themselves before calculating — do not pre-decompose the problem for them.
Estimation should bracket the answer's size before or after computing (e.g. 'more than half of 40, less than 40'); do not supply the answer in place of a reasonableness check.

Worked-example and tap-to-reveal companions show decomposition and reasonableness but do not require the child to identify sub-steps or monitor; use them as scaffolds followed by an independent attempt.

Scored, fast-answer formats can probe reasonableness and wrong-order recognition but cannot assess sub-step identification or ongoing monitoring and tend to reward fast computing; keep them secondary.
When a strategy stalls, support switching rather than enforcing one strategy; strategy choice should be deliberate and problem-dependent.
If the underlying fraction-of-a-quantity skill is shaky, revisit that prerequisite skill rather than treating the error as only a monitoring lapse.

Treat the earlier framing that a spatial/3D medium 'adds nothing' because the content 'is not spatial' as a catalog preference, not an established fact; area and fraction problems do have spatial representations (diagrams, area models), so avoid asserting any medium is universally unsuitable.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved research row without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Self-audit of the worked example: area = 8×5 = 40; 3/4 of 40 = 30; 30 is between half (20) and the whole (40), so the stated reasoning is internally consistent and correct.
Self-audit of the tin counterexample: 3/4 litre poured four times = 3 litres, which exceeds a 2-litre tin, so it does overflow — the prompt is sound as a situational reasoning check.
The source claim that keyword matching has a 'match rate under 10%' is carried from the row's sources as stated; it has not been independently re-verified here.

The earlier artefact ranking placed a 3D/spatial medium as least suitable because the content was deemed 'not spatial'; this was softened to a scoped preference rather than a universal law, since area/fraction problems are commonly represented spatially.

The 'reasonableness gauge' and 'estimate slider' were originally presented as a preferred build; retained here as optional illustrative mechanisms, not mandatory, and their empirical effectiveness is untested.
The internal prerequisite identifier was removed from learner-facing text; the fraction-of-a-quantity prerequisite is referenced by name only.

probeDeeper: 'What are the sub-steps here — which do you do first, and why that order?' (surfaces decomposition vs keyword ordering)
'Should 3/4 of the rectangle be more or less than half? How do you know before computing?' (reasonableness bracket)
'Would a drawing or an equation help more here — why?' (deliberate strategy choice)
Counterexample: 'A tin holds 2 litres. You pour in 3/4 of a litre four times. Does it overflow?' — does the child reason about the situation, or just multiply the numbers?
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for a child who identifies the sub-steps (area = 8×5 = 40, then 3/4 of 40 = 30), reasons that 3/4 is more than half so the answer must exceed 20, gets 30, and confirms it is sensible (less than the whole 40, more than half). Sub-step identification, the estimate benchmark, and the reasonableness check are the targets.

errorPatterns.pattern: Keyword strategy on a multi-step problem — an operation chosen from a word and applied in the wrong order.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have the child retell the problem and build their own area/strip diagram so the order of sub-steps comes from the structure, not a word.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child fixes on a word and computes in an order the situation does not support (e.g. finds 3/4 of 8 rather than of the area), with no plan for the sub-steps; keyword matching fails on multi-step problems.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compulsion to calculate with no reasonableness bracket — accepts a fraction-of-quantity answer even when it is larger than the whole or below half when it should exceed it.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make benchmarking routine ('more or less than half?'); if the underlying fraction-of-amount skill is shaky, revisit it. Do not just supply the answer.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child produces an answer bigger than the whole rectangle, or cannot say whether 3/4 of 20 should be more or less than 10, and is untroubled.

errorPatterns.pattern: Does the sub-steps but does not monitor — loses track of what has been found versus what remains, or defaults to one strategy regardless of fit.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce a 'found / still to find' tracker and compare a diagram strategy against an equation strategy on the same problem so strategy choice becomes deliberate.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child computes an intermediate value and treats it as final, or insists on equations for a problem a diagram would make obvious, showing no running check of progress.

responseLevels.gap: Combines numbers or picks an operation from a word; no estimate; accepts an impossible answer (bigger than the whole) without noticing; sticks to one strategy regardless.
responseLevels.full: Names the sub-steps, brackets the answer's size before/after computing, monitors progress, chooses a fitting strategy with a reason, confirms reasonableness, and transfers the routine to a new multi-step problem unprompted.
responseLevels.partial: Identifies the sub-steps and, when prompted, estimates or picks a strategy — but runs the steps without monitoring: does not spontaneously bracket the answer for reasonableness or notice an impossible result unless asked.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give a multi-step problem involving a fraction of an area, e.g. 'A rectangle is 8 cm by 5 cm. You colour 3/4 of it. What is the coloured area?' Before any answer ask: 'How would you break this into parts? About how big should the coloured area be — more or less than half the rectangle? How would you check your answer makes sense?' Discuss the reasoning; do not mark the number.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who monitors and reasons about structure names the sub-steps and can bracket the answer ('more than half of 40, less than 40') before or after computing. A child on the keyword/compulsion habit combines the numbers (e.g. 8×5×3÷4 blindly, or a fraction answer bigger than the whole) with no estimate and does not notice an impossible result. The tell is the reasonableness bracket, not whether they can multiply.

sources.claim: The keyword strategy ties a word to an operation without understanding structure and fails on multi-step problems (match rate under 10%); schema/structure instruction is the evidence-based alternative.
sources.source: Powell, Namkung & Lin (2022), An Investigation of Using Keywords to Solve Word Problems, The Elementary School Journal 122(3) (ERIC full text ED628160)

sources.claim: Modelling a self-questioning routine to monitor and reflect (Rec 2) and teaching students to build their own visual representations of problem structure (Rec 3) each have strong evidence for improving multi-step problem solving.
sources.source: IES/WWC Educator's Practice Guide, Improving Mathematical Problem Solving in Grades 4 Through 8 (NCEE 2012-4055)

sources.claim: The compulsion to calculate leads students to compute without checking reasonableness; teachers should focus on relationships and reasonableness rather than rushing to an answer.
sources.source: Colorado Department of Education, Word Problems: Research and Practice Guide

sources.claim: Proficient solvers plan a pathway, monitor and evaluate progress and change course if necessary, and check answers by a different method, continually asking 'Does this make sense?'.
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Standard for Mathematical Practice 1

pedagogy.summary: Plotting and reading ordered pairs in the first quadrant is a procedure built on the coordinate-system convention (x before y, both measured from the origin). Best taught by first securing the convention as a rule of movement — 'along the corridor, then up the stairs' — then having children plot given pairs, read back plotted points, and crucially graph real data pairs (e.g. time vs distance) so a coordinate stops being an abstract dot and becomes a meaningful statement about a situation. The interpret-in-context step (evidence bullet 3) is what separates fluent plotting from mechanical dot-placement.
bestPractices: Rehearse the x-before-y convention as a fixed sequence of movements from the origin ('across, then up') before any data work, so the ordered pair is read as a route, not two loose numbers
Insist children count along the numbered lines/gridlines, not the squares between them, to pre-empt the off-by-one error
Move quickly from plotting bare pairs to graphing real data pairs (time vs distance, cost vs quantity) and asking 'what does this point tell us?' so coordinates carry meaning
Use grids whose axes are scaled in steps other than one (twos, fives) once the basic convention is secure, so children read the scale rather than assuming one-square-equals-one
Have children both plot (given the pair, mark the point) and read (given the point, state the pair) in the same session — the two directions expose different errors
keyRepresentations: First-quadrant coordinate grid with clearly numbered axes and a marked origin
'Corridor then stairs' / 'along then up' movement metaphor for the x-then-y order
Data table paired with its plotted graph (e.g. time in column 1, distance in column 2) so each row becomes a point
Journey/time-distance line built from plotted points, linking each dot to a moment in a story
commonMisconceptions: Reversing the coordinates — plotting (a,b) as if it were (b,a), going up before across
Counting the squares rather than the numbered gridlines, landing one place off
Assuming one square always equals one unit and ignoring an axis scaled in twos or fives
Treating a plotted point as just a dot, unable to say what its coordinates mean in the given scenario

learn.summary: Plotting and reading ordered pairs in the first quadrant is a procedure built on the coordinate convention: x before y, both counted from the origin along numbered gridlines. Secure the convention as a fixed rule of movement ('along the corridor, then up the stairs'), have children both plot given pairs and read plotted points back, then graph real data pairs (e.g. time vs distance) so each coordinate becomes a meaningful statement about a situation rather than a bare dot. Interpreting a point in context is part of the objective, not an add-on, and is what separates fluent plotting from mechanical dot-placement.

activities.title: Plot a journey: the snail's progress
feedback: If the point lands as a mirror image across the diagonal, the pair has been reversed — re-narrate 'along before up, x always first' and re-place it

If a point sits one place short or beyond, the child has probably miscounted, for example by counting the origin line as 1 or by counting squares rather than numbered lines — put a finger on the origin and count the numbered lines aloud, touching each number, noting the numbers label the lines not the spaces

If the child places the point correctly but says 'it's just the point', read the axes aloud together ('this way is minutes, this way is centimetres') and ask them to finish 'after ___ minutes the snail had gone ___'
activities.rationale: Graphing real data pairs and interpreting them in context is an explicit part of the fifth-grade standard; the ordered pair (x,y) gives horizontal then vertical distance from the origin.
sourceClaims: Fifth-grade coordinate work is to 'represent real world and mathematical problems by graphing points in the first quadrant' and 'interpret coordinate values of points in the context of the situation' — the interpret-in-context step is part of the standard, not an add-on
A coordinate is fixed by two perpendicular number lines meeting at an origin; the ordered pair (x,y) gives horizontal then vertical distance from the origin
learnerActions: On a numbered first-quadrant grid, plot the ordered pairs (1,2), (2,4), (3,6) for a snail logging its distance each minute, marking each point at the intersection of the numbered gridlines
Narrate the route aloud while plotting: 'along the corridor to 3, then up the stairs to 6'
After plotting (3,6), answer 'what does this point tell us?' by completing the sentence 'after 3 minutes the snail had gone 6 centimetres'
Join the plotted points to see the journey line emerge
activities.intendedInsight: A coordinate is not just a dot: it is a two-number route from the origin (x first, then y) and, on a data graph, a statement about a real situation.

activities.title: Read it back: from point to pair to meaning
feedback: If the child reads (5,8) as (8,5), the pair has been reversed — reinforce x first by counting along before up
If the child claims (7,4) and (4,7) are the same point, have both marked at once so the mismatch is visible and the order is forced to matter
activities.rationale: Plotting and reading in the same session exposes different errors; pupils commonly reverse coordinates, so explicitly contrasting (a,b) with (b,a) targets that misconception.
sourceClaims: Pupils commonly reverse coordinates (plotting y before x / 'up before across') and count squares rather than the numbered gridlines when reading and plotting points
learnerActions: On a new graph for a different journey — a car this time — read the marked point at (5,8), stating its coordinates by counting along then up from the origin
Say what the point means in the car's journey: 'after 5 minutes the car had gone 8 km'
Compare (7,4) and (4,7) by plotting both, confirming they are different points, so the order of the pair matters
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a plotted point reverses the plotting procedure and exposes different errors; order is not interchangeable because (a,b) and (b,a) are different points whenever a and b differ.

activities.title: Read the scale, don't count squares
feedback: If a point lands at the wrong height on the twos-scaled axis, the child has counted squares — point to the printed axis numbers and ask 'what number is this line?' before replacing the point
Practise on grids scaled in twos and fives, reading a value before plotting each time
activities.rationale: Introducing non-unit scales once the basic convention is secure pre-empts the assumption that one square equals one unit and makes children read the numbered axis.
learnerActions: Work on a grid whose vertical axis is numbered 0,2,4,6,8,10 in twos while the horizontal is in ones
Before plotting a value, read aloud the number printed on the target gridline ('what number is this line?')
Plot a point that 'looks like 4 squares up' but is actually at 8 on the twos-scaled axis, reading the printed number rather than counting squares
activities.intendedInsight: One square does not always equal one unit; the numbers printed on the axis determine position, so the scale must be read before plotting.

activities.title: Predict the next point
feedback: If the child can only place given dots but not predict, draw attention to how the distance changes with each extra minute in the table (it goes up by 2 each time)
If the child treats (0,0) as meaningless, prompt: at 0 minutes the snail has travelled 0 centimetres — the starting point of the journey
activities.rationale: Reading the data relationship and interpreting coordinate values in context, including the origin, extends plotting beyond mechanical dot-placement as required by the standard.
sourceClaims: Fifth-grade coordinate work is to 'represent real world and mathematical problems by graphing points in the first quadrant' and 'interpret coordinate values of points in the context of the situation' — the interpret-in-context step is part of the standard, not an add-on
learnerActions: Given the snail's plotted pattern (1,2), (2,4), (3,6), work out where the point for 4 minutes would go if the pattern continued, and plot it at (4,8)
Explain the relationship in the data table (distance = 2 x minutes) that lets you predict the un-plotted point
Interpret the origin (0,0) in context: what does it mean about the snail at time zero?
activities.intendedInsight: A graph of data pairs encodes a relationship, so points can be predicted, not just copied from a table; the origin itself carries meaning in context.

constraints: Count along the numbered gridlines, not the squares between them, to pre-empt the off-by-one error; make explicit that the numbers label the lines, not the spaces
Rehearse the x-before-y convention as a fixed sequence of movements from the origin ('across, then up') before any data work, so the ordered pair is read as a route rather than two loose numbers
Introduce non-unit axis scales (twos, fives) only once the basic convention is secure
Children should both plot (mark the point from a pair) and read (state the pair from a point) in the same session — the two directions expose different errors

Keep each activity's real-data scenario internally consistent (same object and same distance unit throughout a single activity) so a coordinate reliably maps to one situation; where the object changes between activities, frame the new journey explicitly

Recognition-only or recall tasks (e.g. selecting the right pair from options) assess the plot/read skill but do not elicit the independent construction of plotting a point or an open explanation of what a coordinate means; include tasks that require actually placing points and stating meaning in a child's own words

A tap-to-reveal static grid can introduce the convention (e.g. tap a point to reveal 'across 4, up 7') but does not let the child perform a placement or receive feedback on their own plotting; treat it as a pre-teach scaffold, not practice of the skill
The skill is planar (two axes in a flat plane); a third dimension is not part of this objective

Interactive grid examples (snapping a placed point to the gridline intersection, a growing journey line, a data-table row lighting up its point, live confirmation of a placement) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not required features
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source lists National Curriculum (England) Year 6 as verified:false; treat that claim as unconfirmed. The two Common Core 5.G claims and the NCETM misconceptions claim are marked verified in the source but have not been re-checked here.

Arithmetic and ordering are consistent: (1,2),(2,4),(3,6) follow distance = 2 x minutes, so a 4-minute point at (4,8) is a valid prediction and (0,0) is the snail's starting point; (5,8) reads as 5 along, 8 up.

The guidance uses two separate real-data scenarios across activities — a snail measured in metres (Activities 1, 3, 4) and a car measured in km (Activity 2). The split is inherited from the original (snail in the recommendation, car in the assessment) and is deliberate because (5,8) does not fit the snail's distance = 2 x minutes pattern (its 5-minute point is (5,10)). Activity 2 now frames the car as a different journey so the object change is explicit; a single learner path could instead be unified by substituting a read-back point consistent with the snail's pattern.

The original row framed conversation and 3D formats as having no value; this has been reframed in constraints as scope limits (the skill is planar; talk about coordinates differs from performing the procedure) rather than universal claims about those media.

probeDeeper: Point to the 2-minute point and ask 'how do you know this one is 4 km and not 2?' — pushing them to justify reading from the numbered scale
'If I plotted (7,4) instead of (4,7), would it be the same point? Show me both' — a counterexample that forces the order to matter
'What would the point for 4 minutes be, if the pattern carried on?' — checking they read the data relationship, not just place given dots
'This point is at (0,0) — what does that mean about the car?' — probing whether the origin carries meaning in context
assess.correctAnswer: For (a) they go 4 along then 7 up and mark the intersection. For (b) they plot (1,2),(2,4),(3,6) reading the twos-scale correctly, and say the 3-minute point means 'after 3 minutes the car had travelled 6 km'. For (c) they read (5,8) — 5 along, 8 up — and say it means 'after 5 minutes the car had gone 8 km'. Throughout they count numbered gridlines from the origin, x before y.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses the pair — goes up before across, plotting (4,7) where (7,4) belongs ('you go up 4 and along 7')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach the fixed order as a movement rule — 'along the corridor before up the stairs', x always first — and have them narrate the route aloud as they plot
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On (a) the marked point is the mirror-image across the diagonal; on (c) they read the point as (8,5) instead of (5,8)

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts the squares rather than the numbered gridlines, landing one place off ('one, two, three, four squares' starting inside the first square)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have them put a finger on the origin and count the numbered lines aloud, touching each number; make explicit that the numbers label the lines, not the spaces
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Plotted points sit consistently one unit short of or beyond the target on the ones-scaled axis

errorPatterns.pattern: Assumes one square equals one unit and ignores the twos scale, plotting 7 as seven squares up instead of reading the numbered axis
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point to the printed axis numbers and ask 'what number is this line?'; practise on grids with twos and fives scales, reading a value before plotting
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the twos-scaled vertical axis, the 6-km and 7-up points land at the wrong height because the child counted squares instead of reading the printed numbers

errorPatterns.pattern: Plots and reads correctly but cannot say what a coordinate means in the scenario — treats the point as a bare dot, not a statement about the car's journey
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold by reading the axes aloud together — 'this way is minutes, this way is km' — then ask them to finish the sentence 'after ___ minutes the car had gone ___'; do not reteach plotting, the procedure is intact
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On (b)/(c) they give the pair fluently but stall or say 'it's just the point' when asked what it shows about the car

responseLevels.gap: Cannot reliably plot a given pair — reverses coordinates or counts squares so points land in the wrong place, and cannot read a marked point back
responseLevels.full: Plots and reads pairs accurately including on a scaled axis, counting numbered gridlines from the origin, AND interprets each point as a statement about the situation ('after 3 minutes it had gone 6 km'), transferring to predict an un-plotted point
responseLevels.partial: Plots and reads pairs correctly on a ones-scaled grid but stumbles on the twos-scaled axis, or places every point accurately yet cannot say what a coordinate means for the car's journey — has the procedure but not the meaning

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put a first-quadrant grid in front of the child with the horizontal axis numbered 0–8 in ones and the VERTICAL axis numbered 0,2,4,6,8,10 in twos. Ask them to: (a) plot the point (4,7); then (b) here is a table of a car's journey — after 1 min it had gone 2 km, after 2 min 4 km, after 3 min 6 km — plot those three points, and tell me what the point for 3 minutes shows; then (c) I've marked a point here [mark (5,8)] — read me its coordinates and tell me what it means for the car. Watch how they move from the origin and how they read the vertical scale.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who holds the convention moves across-then-up and reads the numbered vertical scale; a child who has only half the idea reveals it precisely here — reversing produces a visibly different point, and the twos-scaled axis separates those who read the numbers from those who count squares. The 'what does it mean?' request cannot be answered by mechanical plotting, so it exposes the child who places dots correctly but cannot connect a coordinate to the situation.

sources.claim: Fifth-grade coordinate work is to 'represent real world and mathematical problems by graphing points in the first quadrant' and 'interpret coordinate values of points in the context of the situation' — the interpret-in-context step is part of the standard, not an add-on
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, 5.G.2

sources.claim: A coordinate is fixed by two perpendicular number lines meeting at an origin; the ordered pair (x,y) gives horizontal then vertical distance from the origin
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, 5.G.1

sources.claim: Pupils commonly reverse coordinates (plotting y before x / 'up before across') and count squares rather than the numbered gridlines when reading and plotting points
sources.source: NCETM, 'Misconceptions with the Key Objectives'

sources.claim: Upper-KS2 pupils should describe positions on the first quadrant of the coordinate plane and plot specified points
sources.source: National curriculum in England: mathematics programmes of study (Year 6)

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 10–11: multiply numbers with up to two decimal places by a whole number (e.g. 3.47 × 6), using place-value reasoning and a written method, understanding the answer's decimal places.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y6): 'multiply one-digit numbers with up to two decimal places by whole numbers'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 5.NBT.7 — multiply decimals to hundredths using concrete models/drawings and strategies based on place value; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning.
• Operational details — the powerful approach is 'multiply as whole numbers, then scale back by the powers of ten you removed': treat 3.47 as 347 hundredths, compute 347×6 = 2082, then ÷100 to get 20.82. Support with the area model (partition 3.47 into 3 + 0.4 + 0.07, multiply each by 6, recombine) and with estimation (3.47×6 ≈ 3.5×6 = 21) to place the point. Emphasise WHY the answer has the decimal places it does, not a 'count the decimal places' rule applied blindly.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): compute 3.2×5 and explain via place value why it is 16.0. Tier B (10–11): compute 4.56×7 with a written method and a matching estimate. Tier C (11): model 3.47×6 with an area diagram or expanded form and justify the placement of the decimal point.
bestPractices: Teach 'compute as whole numbers, then rescale by the powers of ten': 3.47 = 347 ÷ 100, so 3.47×6 = (347×6) ÷ 100 — connecting to the ×÷-by-powers-of-ten work (mt_wPgpMJ0-PA) and giving a reason for the decimal placement.
Always pair the calculation with an ESTIMATE (3.47×6 ≈ 21) so the decimal point is placed by sense, not by a mechanical digit-count that fails learners when trailing zeros vanish.

Use the area model / expanded form: partition the decimal into whole, tenths and hundredths, multiply each part by the whole number, and sum — making the distributive structure and each place's contribution visible.

Confront the 'line up the decimal points' import from addition: it does NOT apply to this multiplication — the answer's places come from the scaling, and children should predict then check with an estimate.
Address trailing zeros explicitly (3.2×5 = 16.0 = 16): the 'count decimal places' rule seems to give 16.0, and children must understand equivalence rather than think a place has been lost.
keyRepresentations: Area model / grid: rows for 3, 0.4, 0.07 (or expanded 3.47) × the whole number, each cell a partial product to be summed.
'Scale out, scale back' chain: 3.47 → ×100 → 347 → ×6 → 2082 → ÷100 → 20.82, linking to powers-of-ten shifting.
Place-value columns showing the partial products aligned by place (ones, tenths, hundredths).
Estimate bracket: 3.47×6 sitting between 3×6 = 18 and 4×6 = 24, anchoring the point at 20.82.
commonMisconceptions: Blindly 'counting decimal places' without understanding, then mishandling trailing zeros (3.2×5 → thinking 16.0 is wrong, or 1.60).
Importing 'line up the decimal points' from decimal addition into multiplication.
Multiplying only the whole-number part or only one place (3.47×6 done as 3×6 = 18).
Misplacing the decimal point (2.082 or 208.2) because the point was not reasoned via scaling or estimate.
Forgetting to rescale after computing the whole-number product (leaving 2082 instead of 20.82).

learn.summary: For ages 10–11: multiply numbers with up to two decimal places by a whole number (e.g. 3.47 × 6) by computing as whole numbers and rescaling by the powers of ten removed, supported by the area/expanded model and estimation to place the decimal point by reasoning rather than a rote 'count the decimal places' rule.

activities.title: Decimal area builder: partition, multiply, recombine
feedback: If the learner only computes 3 × 6 = 18 (or 4 × 7 = 28), point out that the tenths and hundredths parts still have to be multiplied and added in — ask what 0.4 × 6 and 0.07 × 6 contribute.
If the partial products are right but the sum is wrong, have them re-add aligning ones with ones, tenths with tenths, hundredths with hundredths.
Confirm 20.82 and 31.92 by checking each coloured partial product lines up in the correct place column.
activities.rationale: An area/expanded-form partition makes the distributive contribution of each place visible and directly counters the error of multiplying only the whole-number part. A live or hands-on build where partial products recombine can make the recombination concrete, though a static coloured grid can also anchor the same structure.
sourceClaims: Pupils multiply decimals to hundredths using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, relating the strategy to a written method and explaining the reasoning.
learnerActions: Break 3.47 into place-value parts: 3, 0.4 and 0.07.
Multiply each part by 6 and record the partial products: 3 × 6 = 18, 0.4 × 6 = 2.4, 0.07 × 6 = 0.42.
Add the partial products to recombine: 18 + 2.4 + 0.42 = 20.82.
Shade or colour each partial product by its place (ones, tenths, hundredths) so each place's contribution to the total is visible.
Repeat independently for 4.56 × 7: partition into 4, 0.5, 0.06; multiply each by 7 (28, 3.5, 0.42); sum to 31.92.
activities.intendedInsight: Every part of the decimal multiplies by the whole number, and the total is the sum of the partial products — the distributive structure, not just a digit the child forgot.

activities.title: Scale out, scale back
feedback: If the learner leaves the answer as 2082 or 3192, ask what scaling they still owe — they multiplied by 100 at the start and must divide by 100 to finish.
If they place the point as 2.082 or 208.2, walk back through the ÷100 step: 2082 ÷ 100 shifts two places to give 20.82.
Link this to earlier work on multiplying and dividing by powers of ten — the same place-value shift is happening here.
activities.rationale: Treating the decimal as a whole number and rescaling connects decimal multiplication to powers-of-ten reasoning and gives a justified basis for decimal placement. This supports learners who misapply or get confused by a 'count the places' rule, for example with trailing zeros (writing 160 as 16 first and then counting one place to get 1.6, or worrying that 16.0 = 16 has 'lost' a place).
sourceClaims: Estimating the product first, and reasoning via place-value scaling, places the decimal point more reliably than a mechanical 'count the decimal places' rule.
learnerActions: Scale 3.47 up by ×100 to the friendly whole number 347.
Multiply: 347 × 6 = 2082.
Scale back down by ÷100 to recover 20.82.
Explain in your own words why the ÷100 is needed: you removed a factor of 100 at the start, so you must put it back.
activities.intendedInsight: The decimal places in the answer come from the scaling you did (and undid), giving a reason for the decimal point's position rather than a memorised count.

activities.title: Estimate first, place the point by sense
feedback: If the learner gives 3.192 or 319.2, ask how big the answer should be: since 4.56 × 7 ≈ 32, only 31.92 fits.
If they cannot estimate, prompt them to round 4.56 to 4.5 (or to 5) and multiply that by 7.
Praise placing the point by comparing to the estimate rather than by counting digits alone.
activities.rationale: Pairing every calculation with an estimate makes decimal placement a reasoned act and provides a self-check. An out-of-range flag (e.g. an estimate bracket the answer must sit within) makes the magnitude check concrete.
sourceClaims: Estimating the product first, and reasoning via place-value scaling, places the decimal point more reliably than a mechanical 'count the decimal places' rule.
learnerActions: Before computing 4.56 × 7, estimate: 4.56 ≈ 4.5, so 4.56 × 7 ≈ 4.5 × 7 = 31.5, i.e. about 32 (bracket it between 4 × 7 = 28 and 5 × 7 = 35).
Compute the whole-number product and place the decimal point so the answer is close to your estimate (about 32), giving 31.92.
Test the wrong placements: check whether 3.192 or 319.2 is anywhere near 32 — they are not, so they must be wrong.
State out loud how your estimate told you where the point belongs.
activities.intendedInsight: An estimate of the product's size tells you where the decimal point must go, catching off-by-a-power-of-ten mistakes that a rote count would miss.

activities.title: Trailing zeros: why 3.2 × 5 = 16.0 = 16
feedback: If the learner worries a decimal place disappeared, show 16.0 and 16 mark the same point on a number line.
If they offer 1.60, ask whether 3.2 × 5 should be about 15 or about 1.6 — the estimate settles it.
Reinforce that equivalence (16.0 = 16), not a lost digit, explains the tidy whole-number answer.
activities.rationale: Trailing zeros are a known stumbling block when a mechanical count rule is applied; making the equivalence explicit and checking with an estimate defuses the 'I lost a decimal place' worry.
learnerActions: Compute 3.2 × 5: multiply 32 × 5 = 160, then rescale ÷10 to get 16.0.
Explain why 16.0 and 16 are the same number — the trailing zero after the decimal point adds no value.
Discuss why a blind 'count one decimal place in, so one decimal place out' seems to demand 16.0 but does not mean a place was 'lost'.
Contrast with the wrong answer 1.60: use an estimate (3.2 × 5 ≈ 15) to show 1.60 is far too small.
activities.intendedInsight: A result like 16.0 simplifies to 16 by equivalence; no place is lost, and an estimate confirms the true size.

activities.title: Don't line up decimal points as in addition
feedback: If the learner keeps the point aligned through the multiplication and muddles the digits, have them redo it ignoring the point, then replace it using the estimate.
Name the habit explicitly: 'point alignment belongs to adding and subtracting, not to this multiplication.'
Confirm the final placement against the estimate (≈32 for 4.56 × 7).
activities.rationale: Importing point-alignment from addition is a documented misconception; explicitly separating the two procedures and placing the point last prevents it.
learnerActions: Set out 4.56 × 7 by multiplying as if the number were whole (456 × 7), ignoring the point during the multiplication.
Place the decimal point only at the end, using the scaling or estimate.
Compare this with decimal addition, where points ARE aligned, and state why the two procedures differ.
Catch the muddle: try to 'keep the point aligned' through the multiplication and notice how the digits become confused.
activities.intendedInsight: Lining up decimal points is an addition habit; in this multiplication the point is placed at the end from the scaling, not kept aligned during the digit work.

constraints: This objective is multiplying a number with up to two decimal places by a whole number (e.g. 3.47 × 6, 4.56 × 7); it is not multiplying two decimals together.
Learners must be able to justify decimal placement via place-value scaling or estimation, not merely recite a 'count the decimal places' rule they cannot explain.
Address trailing zeros explicitly: 3.2 × 5 = 16.0 = 16; ensure learners understand the equivalence rather than fearing a lost place.

A pre-built, tap-to-reveal worked model can anchor the method but does not let learners vary the numbers or perform the recombination themselves; use it as a reference alongside tasks where learners build and compute.

Multiple-choice point-placement items (e.g. choosing between 208.2 / 20.82 / 2.082) and fill-the-blank partial products test the outcome and are useful for practice, but recognition-only responses do not by themselves elicit independent construction of the method or the reasoning behind placement.

For this planar place-value/area concept, a 2D area model is sufficient and a genuine third spatial dimension offers no clear additional affordance over it; 3D representation is not required here. This is a scoped observation about this topic, not a universal rule that 3D adds nothing in general.
Prerequisite: multiplying and dividing by powers of ten (the scale-out/scale-back move depends on it).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labels the US standard 5.NBT.7 claim and the NCETM claim as unverified (verified:false); only the DfE Year 6 claim is marked verified. Treat the estimation-reliability claim as guidance, not established comparative efficacy.

The pedagogy frames the whole-number-then-rescale method as 'the powerful approach'; this is a reasonable, standards-aligned strategy but is presented without comparative evidence of superiority over other valid written methods.

The original research ranked a 3D interactive as 'poor' with the categorical claim that 3D 'adds nothing'; this has been rewritten as a scoped, qualified limitation about this planar topic rather than a universal law.

probeDeeper: Roughly how big should 4.56 × 7 be? How does that help you place the decimal point?
Why does 3.2 × 5 come out as 16.0 and not 1.60?
Where did you put the decimal point in your answer, and how did you decide?
Show me with an area diagram how each part of 4.56 contributes to the answer.
assess.correctAnswer: 31.92. The teacher watches for the child multiplying as if whole (456 × 7 = 3192) then placing the decimal point so the answer has two decimal places / is about 4.5 × 7 ≈ 32 — using place-value or estimation reasoning, not just a memorised digit-count that they can't justify.

errorPatterns.pattern: misplaces the decimal point — gives 3.192 or 319.2 by mis-counting or guessing places
errorPatterns.nextMove: estimate first (4.56 ≈ 4.5, ×7 ≈ 32) so the point must land making ≈32; connect places-in × places-in.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer off by a power of ten; point placement not checked against magnitude

errorPatterns.pattern: lines up decimal points as if adding, or tries to align the point through the calculation
errorPatterns.nextMove: multiply ignoring the point (as whole numbers) then place it at the end using estimation/place value; point-alignment is an ADDITION habit, not a multiplication one.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child sets out the multiplication trying to keep the point aligned, muddling the digits

errorPatterns.pattern: treats 4.56 × 7 as 4 × 7 with the decimal part ignored or handled separately and wrongly
errorPatterns.nextMove: use an area/expanded model: 4×7 + 0.5×7 + 0.06×7 all contribute; every part multiplies by 7.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer near 28 (only the whole part multiplied) or decimal part mishandled

errorPatterns.pattern: correct method, carrying/arithmetic slip; caught by estimate
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach; have the child recompute the whole-number product and re-place the point.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: one digit wrong; estimate (≈32) flags a wildly off answer

responseLevels.gap: misplaces the point (off by powers of ten), aligns points as in addition, or multiplies only the whole part.
responseLevels.full: multiplies accurately, places the decimal point using place-value/estimation reasoning, and confirms the answer's magnitude is sensible.
responseLevels.partial: gets the digits right but places the point by an unjustified counting rule, or cannot estimate to check.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to compute 4.56 × 7 using a written method while you watch, and then to explain (or check) roughly how big the answer should be. Watch how they handle the decimal point in the product and whether they reason about place value rather than 'counting decimal places' as a rote rule.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Decimal multiplication fails at point placement: children put the point in the wrong place (3.192 or 319.2) or line up points as in addition. Watching the placement AND asking for a magnitude estimate reveals whether the child reasons about size (4.56×7 must be near 32) or applies a fragile counting rule.

pedagogy.summary: Year 6 (age 10–11) pupils solve MULTI-STEP real-world problems that require converting units and then calculating (or comparing) — e.g. scaling a recipe given in kilograms into grams across several batches, or comparing 2.5 l with 2450 ml. The new demand over pure conversion is SEQUENCING: decide when to convert, put quantities into a common unit before comparing or operating, and check the result is reasonable. It rests on secure decimal conversion (Y6) and on word-problem modelling; the classic failures are comparing raw numbers without converting, and dropping or reversing the conversion step inside a longer chain.
bestPractices: Insist on a COMMON unit before comparing or combining — convert 2.5 l to 2500 ml (or 2450 ml to 2.45 l) first; never compare '2450 vs 2.5'.
Model the problem structure (bar model / double number line) and plan the steps: which quantities to convert, in which direction, then which operation.
Keep the unit-size reasoning and digit-movement conversion from earlier years, and label units at every step so a stray 'g' vs 'kg' is caught.
Estimate first and sense-check the final answer's size and unit (2250 g is sensible for 3 batches; 2250 kg is not).
Vary contexts (mass, capacity, length, time, money) and step order (convert-then-operate vs operate-then-convert) so the method generalises.
keyRepresentations: Bar model / double number line for the multi-step structure
Common-unit number line for comparisons
Place-value chart for the embedded conversion step
Labelled step-by-step working (unit tracked at each line)
commonMisconceptions: Compares measurements without converting to a common unit ('2450 ml > 2.5 l because 2450 > 2.5').
Drops the conversion step or reverses its direction inside a multi-step chain (0.75 × 3 = 2.25 reported as '2.25 g').
Loses track across steps or never estimates, so an unreasonable answer (2250 kg of flour) passes unnoticed.
Treats a mixed/decimal measure as two separate whole numbers when operating.

learn.summary: Year 6 pupils (age 10–11) solve multi-step, real-world measurement problems that require unit conversion plus calculation or comparison — e.g. scaling a 0.75 kg recipe across 3 batches, or deciding whether 2.5 litres or 2450 ml is more. The new demand beyond pure conversion is SEQUENCING: deciding when and in which direction to convert, putting quantities into a common unit before comparing or operating, labelling units at every step, and sense-checking the final answer's size and unit against an estimate. Classic failures are comparing raw numbers without converting, dropping or reversing the conversion inside a longer chain, treating a decimal measure as two separate whole numbers, and accepting an unreasonable answer unchecked.

activities.title: Recipe scaler: convert, operate, and track the unit
feedback: If a learner writes '2.25 g', prompt: '2.25 what? You multiplied kilograms — is 2.25 g sensible for three batches of flour, or did the kg→g conversion get dropped?'
If the answer comes out as 2250 kg, prompt: 'Roughly how much flour did you expect for 3 batches? Does 2250 kg fit that estimate?'
If a learner converts the wrong way (e.g. 0.75 kg → 0.00075 g), ask them to reason about unit size: grams are smaller than kilograms, so the number of grams should be larger, not smaller.

If a learner treats 2.25 as the separate whole numbers '2' and '25', remind them a decimal measure is one quantity, not two: in 2.25 kg the '.25' means 0.25 kg, which is 250 g (NOT a separate '25'), so 2.25 kg = 2250 g — the digits after the point are not a second whole number.
Reinforce correct work: 'You labelled the unit on each line, so a stray g vs kg would have been caught — that is exactly the habit that guards multi-step answers.'
activities.rationale: Year 6 curricula require solving problems involving the calculation AND conversion of units of measure with decimal notation; embedding a ×/÷ by 10/100/1000 conversion inside a longer chain is where drop-a-step and direction errors appear, and estimating first gives a sense of a reasonable answer so errors are detected.
sourceClaims: Grade 5 pupils use unit conversions in solving multi-step, real-world problems (5.MD.A.1 explicitly names multi-step real-world problem solving).
Convert measures via ×/÷ by 10/100/1000 (digits move, point fixed); this conversion skill is what a multi-step problem embeds, and direction errors follow from not reasoning about unit size.
Pupils rarely estimate before calculating and so lack a sense of a reasonable answer, leaving multi-step errors undetected.
UK DfE Year 6 pupils solve problems involving the calculation and conversion of units of measure, using decimal notation up to three decimal places where appropriate.
learnerActions: Take the problem 'A recipe uses 0.75 kg of flour — how many grams are needed for 3 batches?' and FIRST write a rough estimate of the expected answer (about 2 to 2.5 kg, i.e. roughly 2000–2500 g).
Plan the steps on a bar model or double number line: decide which quantity needs converting and in which direction (0.75 kg → 750 g), then which operation (×3).
Execute either order — convert then operate (0.75 kg → 750 g, ×3 = 2250 g) or operate then convert (0.75 × 3 = 2.25 kg = 2250 g) — writing the unit on every line of working.
Compare the final answer to your up-front estimate: check both the size and the unit (2250 g is sensible for 3 batches; 2250 kg or '2.25 g' is not).

Repeat with a different context and step order (e.g. mass, capacity, length, time, money) so the method generalises, remembering that time conversions use 60 (minutes/seconds) or 24 (hours/days) rather than 10, 100 or 1000 (e.g. 1.5 hours = 90 minutes, not 150).
activities.intendedInsight: A multi-step measurement answer is only trustworthy when each quantity is converted correctly, the unit is carried through every step, and the final size and unit match a sensible up-front estimate.

activities.title: Which is more? Compare on a common-unit number line
feedback: If a learner decides 2450 ml > 2.5 l 'because 2450 > 2.5', ask: 'Are those in the same unit yet? Make them match first, then decide.'
After a correct conversion, confirm: 'Now both are in millilitres — 2500 vs 2450 — so the comparison is fair and 2.5 l is more.'
Challenge with a pair where the bigger number is the smaller amount, so that converting first becomes essential rather than optional.
activities.rationale: Children commonly treat measurements as separate whole numbers and compare on the digits without a common unit; competence with two-place amounts does not guarantee correct handling across units, so forcing a common unit before deciding targets the misconception directly.
sourceClaims: Children treat measurements as separate whole numbers and compare/operate on the digits without putting them in a common unit; competence with two-place amounts does not guarantee correct handling across units.
learnerActions: Take two measurements in different units — 2.5 litres and 2450 ml — and notice they cannot be judged directly because '2.5' and '2450' are not in the same unit.
Convert one to match the other (2.5 l → 2500 ml, or 2450 ml → 2.45 l), stating which unit you chose and why.
Place both converted values on a single common-unit number line and read off which is larger (2500 ml clearly overtakes 2450 ml).
State the comparison in words: 'you can only compare like with like,' then explain which original measurement was more.
Try further pairs across mass, capacity and length where the raw digits are misleading (e.g. the amount with the bigger bare number is actually smaller).
activities.intendedInsight: Two measurements cannot be compared or combined until they are expressed in the same unit; the bare digits can be misleading, so convert to a common unit first.

activities.title: Order the solution steps
feedback: If steps are ordered so the conversion is omitted, point to the resulting mis-unit answer and ask the learner to reinsert the missing conversion.
Praise an ordering that converts to a common unit before comparing or operating, noting this is the habit that keeps the unit correct through the chain.
activities.rationale: Solving multi-step real-world problems requires correct sequencing of conversion and operation steps; an ordering task is proposed as a way to make that structure explicit and to surface the drop-a-step error, and planning the structure (bar model / double number line) may reduce working-memory load so steps are monitored rather than lost. Such a task can both rehearse and reveal sequencing, not only grade it.
sourceClaims: Grade 5 pupils use unit conversions in solving multi-step, real-world problems (5.MD.A.1 explicitly names multi-step real-world problem solving).
learnerActions: For a multi-step problem (e.g. time, distance and unit conversion combined), lay out the solution stages as cards or lines and put them in the correct order BEFORE computing; note that any time conversion uses 60 or 24, not a power of 10.
Decide explicitly where the conversion belongs in the sequence and which direction it goes, then fill in each conversion and operation.
After solving, justify why that order works: say which quantity ends up larger or which operation must come next and why.
Mark where a 'drop-a-step' error would occur if the conversion were skipped, and show what wrong answer it would produce.
activities.intendedInsight: Multi-step problems succeed or fail on the ORDER and completeness of steps; naming where the conversion sits in the chain helps prevent dropping or reversing it.

constraints: Always require a COMMON unit before comparing or combining; never let a learner compare '2450 vs 2.5' as bare numbers.

Label the unit at every line of working so a stray 'g' vs 'kg' is caught, and keep the unit-size reasoning from earlier years; digit-movement (×/÷ 10, 100, 1000) only works for metric conversions and money (£ to p), not time, which uses 60 and 24.
Estimate first and sense-check the final answer's size AND unit before accepting it.
Vary contexts (mass, capacity, length, time, money) and both step orders (convert-then-operate and operate-then-convert) so the method generalises rather than being tied to one worked example.

Recognition-only or multiple-choice checks can confirm which is more after conversion but do not by themselves elicit the independent planning and step-tracking; pair them with constructed working where the learner writes and labels each step.

A static worked example can show the method but cannot give per-step feedback or let the learner commit a conversion and get it flagged; treat any fixed picture as a reference, not the main vehicle for practising sequencing.
Spatial/3D representation adds little for this particular task since the reasoning here is numeric and sequential; bar models and number lines carry the structure for these problems.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 0.75 kg = 750 g; 750 × 3 = 2250 g; equivalently 0.75 × 3 = 2.25 kg = 2250 g — consistent, so a rough estimate of about 2–2.5 kg brackets the answer. 2.5 l = 2500 ml > 2450 ml — correct. The deliberately wrong learner outputs ('2.25 g', 2250 kg, 0.00075 g) are flagged as errors in feedback, not presented as valid answers. Note 0.25 kg = 250 g (clarified in Activity 1 feedback to avoid reinforcing a '25 g' misread).

The source notes two citations (NCETM 'Misconceptions with the Key Objectives' and the DfE National Curriculum) carry verified:false in the original row; their supporting claims are retained but their verification status is unconfirmed here.

Original guidance framed a static image as unable to 'support sequencing' and a conversation as unable to 'drive multi-step calculation'; these were softened to scoped affordance/limit statements, since catalog fit ratings do not establish universal necessity.

Activity 3's claim that the ordering task is diagnostic of the drop-a-step error and reduces working-memory load is a design proposal; the retained CCSS source claim establishes the multi-step problem-solving context but does not itself verify that diagnostic/load benefit.

Editorial changes on review: Activity 1 feedback on reading a decimal as two whole numbers was clarified so the correction explicitly states 0.25 kg = 250 g (not 25 g); earlier edits had raised the Activity 1 estimate band to about 2–2.5 kg so it brackets 2250 g and removed the 'rarely estimate' claim from the ordering activity.

probeDeeper: 'Before comparing, are 2.5 litres and 2450 ml in the same unit? Make them match, then decide.'
'Your answer is 2.25 — 2.25 what? Is that grams or kilograms, and is that sensible for three batches?'
'Roughly how much flour did you expect for 3 batches? Does your exact answer fit that?'
'Show me the order of your steps — where did you convert, and why there?'
assess.correctAnswer: (1) 0.75 kg = 750 g, ×3 = 2250 g (or 0.75×3 = 2.25 kg = 2250 g). (2) 2.5 l = 2500 ml, which is more than 2450 ml. Converts to a common unit, sequences convert-and-operate correctly, and reports a sensible unit.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares without a common unit — decides 2450 ml is more than 2.5 l because 2450 > 2.5, treating the two measures as bare numbers.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Always convert to one unit first: put both on a common-unit number line (2500 ml vs 2450 ml) and compare then; rehearse 'you can only compare like with like'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A comparison made on the digits with the units ignored; no conversion performed before deciding.

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops or reverses the conversion step in a multi-step chain — computes 0.75 × 3 = 2.25 and reports '2.25 g' (no kg→g conversion), or converts the wrong way.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Plan the steps explicitly on a bar model and label the unit at every line; decide up front which quantities need converting and in which direction.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A final answer with the wrong unit or magnitude because the conversion was omitted or reversed mid-solution.

errorPatterns.pattern: No estimate / loses track across steps — accepts an unreasonable result (2250 kg of flour) because working memory was overloaded and nothing was sense-checked.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach: estimate before calculating and check the answer's size and unit against it; break the chain into recorded steps to reduce load.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: An out-of-range final answer left unchallenged; steps done but not monitored.

responseLevels.gap: Compares raw numbers, drops or reverses the conversion, and accepts unreasonable answers; no common unit, no estimate.
responseLevels.full: Converts to a common unit before comparing or combining, sequences multi-step conversion-and-operation correctly with sensible units, checks reasonableness against an estimate, and transfers across measures and contexts.
responseLevels.partial: Solves a single-step converted problem but loses a step in a multi-step chain, or compares only when the units already match; does not sense-check the result.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set two problems and watch the working: (1) 'A recipe uses 0.75 kg of flour. How many grams are needed for 3 batches?' (2) 'Which is more — 2.5 litres or 2450 ml? How do you know?' Watch whether they convert to a common unit before comparing, whether the conversion step survives the multi-step calculation, and whether they sense-check the size and unit of the answer.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A pupil who plans the steps converts to a common unit and keeps the unit correct through the chain (2250 g; 2500 ml > 2450 ml); a pupil who doesn't compares 2450 with 2.5 directly, or computes 0.75×3 and mislabels it '2.25 g', or reports an unreasonable 2250 kg. Converting-before and tracking-units diverge exactly on the comparison and on the embedded conversion step.
