pedagogy.summary: Formal columnar addition and subtraction to three digits is the compact, efficient written algorithm. It should be introduced only once children understand composing/decomposing concretely, and taught as a bridge FROM the expanded method (writing partial sums) TO the compact one, so each carried or exchanged digit still means a real ten or hundred. The skill has three parts: correct place-value alignment, the carry/exchange mechanic, and checking with estimation or the inverse.
bestPractices: Bridge expanded-to-compact: start with partitioned partial sums, then compress, so the compact carries keep their meaning (NCETM; DfE Appendix 1)
Insist on place-value alignment — use a column grid or squared paper so ones sit under ones
Keep base-ten/place-value counters available alongside the written method during the transition, especially for exchange
Teach subtraction exchange as decomposition ('take a ten, make ten ones'), not a memorised 'borrow', and rehearse across-zero cases
Always check: estimate first (round) and verify with the inverse (DfE Year 3)
keyRepresentations: Column grid / squared paper with H-T-O headings
Place-value counters alongside the algorithm
Expanded written method (partial sums) as the stepping stone
Base-ten blocks for the exchange step
Number line / estimation for the check
commonMisconceptions: Place-value misalignment: writing digits ragged so ones and tens are added together
Smaller-from-larger: subtracting the smaller digit from the larger in each column regardless of position (83−25→62 pattern, now at three digits)
Carry omitted or mis-placed: forgetting to add the carried ten/hundred to the next column
Borrow-across-zero errors when the adjacent column is 0 (502−276)

learn.summary: Teach formal columnar addition and subtraction to three digits as a compact written algorithm that keeps its place-value meaning. Introduce it only after children can compose/decompose concretely, and bridge from the expanded method (partial sums) to the compact one so each carried or exchanged digit still stands for a real ten or hundred. The skill has three parts: correct place-value alignment, the carry/exchange mechanic, and checking with estimation or the inverse. Pair written work with place-value counters during the transition, and rehearse the hard across-zero exchange explicitly.

activities.title: Carry and exchange with counters beside the columns
feedback: If digits are added across different columns, rebuild on a headed H-T-O grid so ones sit under ones; connect each column to its counter so alignment has a reason.
If the across-zero step stalls, model the cascade with counters slowly and narrate: one hundred becomes ten tens, then one ten becomes ten ones.
If a carry is dropped, have the child write the small carried digit and say what it is ('one ten') before adding the next column.
Confirm success when the estimate is close to the answer (about 500–550 for the addition, about 220 for the subtraction) and 226 + 276 returns 502.
activities.rationale: Linking the written carry/exchange to the quantity it represents keeps the compact algorithm meaningful; a live counter panel that moves as the child records the digit is one effective way to make the mechanism concrete, not the only way.
sourceClaims: Columnar methods are developed by bridging from an expanded written layout (partial sums) to the compact algorithm so that carried digits retain their place-value meaning.

Year 3 pupils are taught to 'add and subtract numbers with up to 3 digits, using formal written methods of columnar addition and subtraction; estimate the answer to a calculation and use inverse operations to check answers' (statutory).
learnerActions: Set out 347 + 185 in columns on squared paper or a headed H-T-O grid, ones under ones.

Add the ones: 7 + 5 = 12. Write the 2 in the ones column and the carried 1 above the tens; alongside, exchange ten of the 12 one-counters for a single ten-counter and place it in the tens column, so the written '1' and the real ten move together.
Add the tens: 4 + 8 + 1 = 13. Write 3, carry 1 hundred, and exchange ten of the 13 ten-counters for a single hundred-counter, placing it in the hundreds column.
Add the hundreds: 3 + 1 + 1 = 5, giving 532.

Now set out 502 − 276. To take 6 from 2 in the ones you need more ones, but the tens column is 0: first break one hundred into ten tens (502 becomes 400 + 90 + 12 after the cascade), then break a ten into ten ones.
Estimate first by rounding (≈ 350 + 200 = 550, or 300 + 200 = 500, for the addition; ≈ 500 − 280 = 220 for the subtraction) and check the subtraction by adding 226 + 276 back to 502.
activities.intendedInsight: A carried or exchanged digit is a real ten or hundred moving between columns, not a meaningless mark; across a zero you must decompose a hundred into tens before you can get a ten, then a ten into ones.

activities.title: Bridge from expanded partial sums to the compact column
feedback: If the compact and expanded answers disagree, line up each partial sum with its column to find the mislaid ten or hundred.
If the child cannot explain a carry, return to the partial sum (12 = 10 + 2) to show the ten being carried.
activities.rationale: Starting from partitioned partial sums and then compressing keeps the compact carries meaningful rather than memorised, following the expanded-to-compact bridge.
sourceClaims: Columnar methods are developed by bridging from an expanded written layout (partial sums) to the compact algorithm so that carried digits retain their place-value meaning.
learnerActions: Solve 347 + 185 first in the expanded written layout, writing each partial sum: 7 + 5 = 12, 40 + 80 = 120, 300 + 100 = 400.
Add the partial sums (12 + 120 + 400 = 532) and notice where the extra ten and the extra hundred come from.
Rewrite the same calculation in the compact column, carrying the 1 ten and 1 hundred, and check the answer matches 532.
Say aloud what each carried digit in the compact version stands for, pointing back to the partial sum it came from.
activities.intendedInsight: The compact algorithm is a shorthand for the expanded method; every carry corresponds to a partial sum crossing into the next place.

activities.title: Spot the error in a worked column
feedback: For misalignment, re-copy onto grid paper with place-value headings.
For smaller-from-larger, show that 2 ones cannot give 6, so a ten (via the hundred here) must be broken open first; check by adding the answer back.
For borrow-across-zero, rehearse several across-zero cases with counters and narration.
activities.rationale: Critiquing wrong worked examples targets the stable, documented bugs directly; practice builds accuracy but should sit alongside meaning-building work rather than replace it.
sourceClaims: Smaller-from-larger and borrow-from-zero are among the most common systematic, STABLE subtraction bugs: in Brown & Burton's data (1325 students) 'smaller-from-larger' (subtract the smaller digit from the larger regardless of position — the '437−284=253' pattern) was used by 54 students, and 'borrow-from-zero' (change the 0 to a 9 but fail to continue borrowing leftward) was the single most common bug at 107 occurrences; ~40% of students showed consistently buggy behaviour. Errors that look careless are the surface manifestation of a systematic wrong procedure.
learnerActions: Examine a worked example where the digits are set out ragged (for example the 5 of 185 placed under the 4 of 347) and identify what has gone wrong and why the answer is unreliable.
Examine a worked across-zero subtraction where a 9 or 0 has been written at the empty tens column without decomposing a hundred, and explain the correct cascade.
Rework each flawed example correctly on a headed grid and state what the fixed carry or exchange represents.
Complete a few mixed column calculations for fluency, estimating first and checking with the inverse.
activities.intendedInsight: Many errors that look careless are the surface of a systematic wrong procedure (misalignment, smaller-from-larger, borrow-across-zero); naming the bug helps avoid it.

activities.title: Explain your steps aloud
feedback: Accept explanations that name real quantities ('one ten', 'a hundred broken into ten tens'); redirect vague 'you just carry it' answers back to the counters.
If the inverse check fails, revisit the exchange step that produced the wrong ones or tens.
activities.rationale: Explaining each step surfaces reasoning and meaning; used as a supplement it exposes misconceptions but does not by itself supply the volume of aligned written practice the skill needs.
learnerActions: After solving a column calculation, answer: 'Point to the little 1 you carried — what does that 1 actually stand for?'
For 502 − 276, explain: 'There were no tens to take from — how did you get them?'
Justify the estimate: 'Round 347 + 185 — is your answer sensible?'
Verify: 'Add your subtraction answer to 276 — does it come back to 502?'
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating why a carry or exchange happens exposes whether the procedure is understood or merely copied.

constraints: Introduce the compact algorithm only after children can compose and decompose numbers concretely.
Keep base-ten blocks or place-value counters available alongside the written method during the transition, especially for exchange.
Teach subtraction exchange as decomposition ('take a ten, make ten ones'), not a memorised 'borrow', and rehearse across-zero cases.
Always estimate first by rounding and verify with the inverse operation; any close rounded estimate (not an inflated one) serves the sanity-check.
Insist on place-value alignment using a column grid or squared paper so ones sit under ones.
Error-spotting and repeated drill rehearse and check accuracy but do not on their own build the place-value understanding; pair them with meaning-focused work.
Explain-aloud discussion is a supplement for reasoning; it cannot replace sufficient aligned written practice.
A worked annotated example is useful reference but cannot catch a child's own alignment slips; have the child produce calculations too.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Independent re-review self-audit of arithmetic: 347 + 185 = 532 (ones 7+5=12 write 2 carry 1; tens 4+8+1=13 write 3 carry 1; hundreds 3+1+1=5). 502 − 276 = 226 (decompose to 400+90+12; 12−6=6, 90−70=20, 400−200=200). Expanded partial sums 12+120+400=532. Inverse check 226 + 276 = 502. All confirmed.

A prior candidate error had the addition estimate as ≈500+200=700, which mis-rounds 347 and is far from 532; the corrected activity uses ≈350+200=550 or ≈300+200=500, and the success feedback now accepts either (about 500–550). The ≈500−280=220 subtraction estimate is sound.
The NCETM/DfE Appendix 1 bridging claim is marked verified:false in the row; treat as unconfirmed.

The original row's catalog-fit judgements ('3D adds nothing', quiz 'rehearses rather than builds understanding') have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements and are not asserted as universal laws.

probeDeeper: Point to the little 1 you carried — what does that 1 actually stand for?
For 502 − 276 there were no tens to take from — how did you get them?
Estimate 347 + 185 by rounding — is your answer sensible?
Check 502 − 276 by adding your answer to 276 — does it come back to 502?
assess.correctAnswer: 532 and 226. 347+185: ones 7+5=12 (write 2, carry 1 ten), tens 4+8+1=13 (write 3, carry 1 hundred), hundreds 3+1+1=5 → 532. 502−276: exchange needed in ones but tens is 0, so decompose a hundred to tens then a ten to ones (502 as 400+90+12), 12−6=6, 90−70=20, 400−200=200 → 226.

errorPatterns.pattern: Place-value misalignment — writes the digits ragged so, say, the 5 of 185 lines up under the 4 of 347
errorPatterns.nextMove: Provide a column grid/headed H-T-O paper and rebuild; connect each column to its place-value counter so alignment has a reason, not just a rule.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Digits not aligned by place value on the page; unlike columns added together

errorPatterns.pattern: Smaller-from-larger — in 502−276 does 6−2 in the ones ('six take two is four') rather than exchanging
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to concrete decomposition; show 2 ones cannot give 6, so a ten (here, via the hundred) must be broken open first. Check by adding the answer back.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Ones column done as larger-minus-smaller with no exchange; often a suspiciously 'clean' subtraction

errorPatterns.pattern: Carry omitted or misplaced — in 347+185 forgets to add the carried ten/hundred to the next column
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach: have the child write the small carried digit explicitly and say what it is ('one ten') before adding the next column. This is a tracking lapse.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Column sums correct but the carried digit is dropped or added to the wrong column; answer off by 10 or 100

errorPatterns.pattern: Borrow-across-zero — in 502−276 tries to take a ten from the empty tens column, fabricating a digit instead of decomposing the hundred first
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model the cascade with counters: a hundred becomes ten tens, then a ten becomes ten ones. Rehearse several across-zero cases slowly with narration.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child stalls at the zero or writes 9/0 there without decomposing a hundred to feed it

responseLevels.gap: Misaligns digits, drops carries, does smaller-from-larger, or stalls at the zero; the algorithm produces unreliable answers.
responseLevels.full: Aligns correctly, carries and exchanges accurately including across a zero, explains what each carried/exchanged digit represents, and checks with estimation or the inverse.
responseLevels.partial: Executes the algorithm correctly on the straightforward addition but stumbles on the across-zero exchange, or gets answers without being able to say what a carried/exchanged digit means; check step omitted.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to set out and solve two calculations in columns on squared paper, then check each: 347 + 185, then 502 − 276. Watch how they align the digits, handle the carry, and manage the exchange across the zero.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 347+185 requires two carries; an omitted or misplaced carry, or ragged alignment, shows immediately. 502−276 forces exchange across a zero — the borrow-across-zero and smaller-from-larger bugs surface, and a child running the algorithm without understanding cannot resolve the empty column.

sources.claim: Year 3 pupils are taught to 'add and subtract numbers with up to 3 digits, using formal written methods of columnar addition and subtraction; estimate the answer to a calculation and use inverse operations to check answers' (statutory).
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (Year 3, Number — addition and subtraction)

sources.claim: Smaller-from-larger and borrow-from-zero are among the most common systematic, STABLE subtraction bugs: in Brown & Burton's data (1325 students) 'smaller-from-larger' (subtract the smaller digit from the larger regardless of position — the '437−284=253' pattern) was used by 54 students, and 'borrow-from-zero' (change the 0 to a 9 but fail to continue borrowing leftward) was the single most common bug at 107 occurrences; ~40% of students showed consistently buggy behaviour. Errors that look careless are the surface manifestation of a systematic wrong procedure.
sources.source: Brown & Burton, 'Diagnostic Models for Procedural Bugs in Basic Mathematical Skills', Cognitive Science 2(2), 1978 (full text: ERIC ED159036)

sources.claim: Columnar methods are developed by bridging from an expanded written layout (partial sums) to the compact algorithm so that carried digits retain their place-value meaning.
sources.source: NCETM Primary Mastery PD / DfE Mathematics Appendix 1

pedagogy.summary: This is the strategic, problem-solving capstone of early fractions: given a word problem, the child must recognise WHICH fraction idea it calls for (finding a fraction of a quantity, comparing/ordering, equivalence, or adding/subtracting), choose an appropriate method, carry it out, and judge whether the answer is reasonable. As a META topic the object of learning is not a single procedure but the disposition and habits of a strategic problem-solver — sense-making before calculating, monitoring progress, and checking plausibility. It is best developed through rich, varied, non-routine problems, worked examples that model strategy SELECTION (not just execution), and talk that makes children's reasoning and planning audible.
bestPractices: Teach strategy selection explicitly: present mixed problem sets where children must first decide 'is this a fraction-of, a compare, an equivalence, or an add/subtract problem?' before doing any arithmetic — the recognition step is the skill.

Use worked and partially-worked examples that model the PLANNING and monitoring, not just the answer (Polya / Schoenfeld): understand the problem, choose a strategy, carry it out, look back and check.
Insist on a plausibility / looking-back check every time ('a fraction of 20 can't be more than 20'; 'the larger share should have the answer we expect') to build self-monitoring.
Keep contexts and surface features varied so children generalise the underlying structure rather than pattern-matching key words ('altogether' → add is a trap).
Make reasoning audible: use talk moves (revoicing, 'why did you choose that?', 'does that answer make sense?') so strategic thinking is surfaced, discussed, and named rather than assumed.
Include problems with no single stated operation and multi-step problems, so children practise imposing structure themselves.
keyRepresentations: Bar / strip models to represent the quantities and relationships in a word problem before choosing an operation
A visible problem-solving frame (understand → plan → do → check) the child fills in
Double number line for fraction-of and comparison problems
Recording that separates the CHOICE of strategy from its execution (e.g. 'this is a fraction-of problem because...')
commonMisconceptions: Key-word matching: latches onto a surface word ('altogether', 'left') and applies the associated operation regardless of the problem's meaning
Applies the most recently taught procedure to every problem regardless of what it asks
Calculates without a plan and never checks whether the answer is plausible
Cannot start a problem unless the operation is explicitly stated ('but it doesn't tell me to divide')

learn.summary: Capstone for early fractions (ages 7-8): given a word problem, the child must recognise WHICH fraction idea it calls for (finding a fraction of a quantity, comparing/ordering, equivalence, or adding/subtracting), choose a method, carry it out, and judge whether the answer is reasonable. The object of learning is the disposition of a strategic problem-solver — sense-making before calculating, monitoring progress, and checking plausibility — developed through rich, varied, non-routine problems, worked examples that model strategy SELECTION (not just execution), and talk that makes reasoning audible. Recognition-before-calculation is the core skill; key-word matching ('altogether' → add) is the central trap to dismantle.

activities.title: Solve it WITH a mentor who never gives the method
feedback: When a child names an operation by quoting a surface word, don't just mark it wrong — offer a counter-problem where that word points the wrong way and let them discover the mismatch ('you said add because it says altogether — what if the problem is about finding 1/4 of the sweets? Would altogether still mean add?').
Revoice the child's plan back to them and push gently: 'are you sure this is an adding problem?'
If an answer is implausible, prompt the looking-back move rather than supplying the answer: 'could a fraction smaller than one whole, like 3/4, of 12 be more than 12?'
Keep problems mixed across the four fraction ideas so the child cannot pattern-match and must genuinely choose.
activities.rationale: Strategy selection and self-monitoring are dialogic, metacognitive skills that live in articulated reasoning, not a computed answer. A responsive partner can pose varied problems, probe the plan before the arithmetic, and prompt the plausibility check — the moves that build a strategic problem-solver. This is proposed as a strong fit for the metacognitive objective; a scripted or static resource cannot respond to a child's particular reasoning in the moment, though it may still teach other aspects. Efficacy of this specific activity is untested.
sourceClaims: Assisting students to MONITOR AND REFLECT on the problem-solving process is Recommendation 2, rated STRONG evidence (nine qualifying studies, positive effects on word-problem solving, persisting 4+ months); exposing students to MULTIPLE strategies so they select appropriately is Recommendation 4 (MODERATE); the guide warns 'too often students become wedded to just one approach and then flounder', and frames problem solving as reasoning about structure, not 'using key words'.
Mathematical problem solving depends on strategy selection, planning and looking-back/self-monitoring, not just execution; these metacognitive phases should be made explicit in instruction.
learnerActions: Work through a mixed bag of fraction word problems with a partner or in-role mentor (a teacher, another child, or a Socratic tutor character) who reads each problem aloud.
Before doing any arithmetic, say out loud what KIND of problem this is — find-a-fraction-of, compare/order, equivalence, or add/subtract — and HOW you can tell from the situation.
Talk through a plan (what will you do first, and why) before calculating.

When the mentor deliberately offers a tempting key word ('it says altogether, so we add?'), decide whether that word really fits the situation or whether the problem is actually about something else (e.g. finding 1/4 of a set).
After getting an answer, check it makes sense ('could 3/4 of 12 be more than 12?') every single time.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising what a problem is really asking — and checking whether an answer is plausible — is the skill, not the arithmetic. The habit becomes owned when the child hears themselves catch a key-word trap and reason from the situation's structure instead.

activities.title: Sort-then-model workspace: tag the problem, build a model, then answer
feedback: Target feedback at the CHOICE of type and the plausibility of the result, not only at final correctness.
If the type tag is wrong, prompt the child to re-read and describe what is happening before re-tagging.
A plausibility gate before submission ('is this answer bigger than it could possibly be?') makes looking-back routine.
activities.rationale: A sorting-and-modelling workspace can make the recognition step mandatory and let the child externalise the plan with immediate feedback. Dragging to build a bar model or a double number line and a 'does this make sense?' gate are concrete interaction examples that make the plan-then-do mechanism visible; they are offered as options, not required mechanics. This develops recognition and modelling but, being more structured, supports the open monitoring disposition less than live dialogue. Efficacy of this specific activity is untested.
sourceClaims: Assisting students to MONITOR AND REFLECT on the problem-solving process is Recommendation 2, rated STRONG evidence (nine qualifying studies, positive effects on word-problem solving, persisting 4+ months); exposing students to MULTIPLE strategies so they select appropriately is Recommendation 4 (MODERATE); the guide warns 'too often students become wedded to just one approach and then flounder', and frames problem solving as reasoning about structure, not 'using key words'.
learnerActions: For each word problem, first TAG it by type: fraction-of, compare, equivalence, or add/subtract.
Build a bar/strip model — or a double number line for fraction-of and comparison problems — of the situation to show the quantities and relationships BEFORE choosing an operation.
Use the model structure to decide what to do, then calculate.
Pass a 'does this make sense?' check before submitting your answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Externalising the plan-then-do structure — tag, model, then calculate — forces the recognition step and makes the situation's structure (not a key word) the basis for choosing an operation.

activities.title: Mixed problem set that discourages key-word matching
feedback: When a key-word-based option is chosen, return to the situation and ask what is actually happening before re-selecting.

Because a scored set checks the OUTCOME of strategy selection, follow up every item with a short 'how did you know?' so the monitoring and looking-back disposition is still exercised, not just measured.
Design some items so a tempting option matches a surface key word ('altogether' → add) or the most recently practised procedure, so pattern-matching is surfaced rather than rewarded.
activities.rationale: A scored set can efficiently test whether children pick the right strategy across varied problems, with tempting options encoding the two main misconceptions. On its own it assesses the outcome of strategy selection rather than building the monitoring disposition, which needs open reasoning — so it is best paired with discussion. Efficacy of this specific activity is untested.
sourceClaims: Assisting students to MONITOR AND REFLECT on the problem-solving process is Recommendation 2, rated STRONG evidence (nine qualifying studies, positive effects on word-problem solving, persisting 4+ months); exposing students to MULTIPLE strategies so they select appropriately is Recommendation 4 (MODERATE); the guide warns 'too often students become wedded to just one approach and then flounder', and frames problem solving as reasoning about structure, not 'using key words'.
learnerActions: Work a mixed set of varied fraction word problems, first categorising each by type.
For problems presented as multiple choice, pick the answer, then check whether your choice came from the situation's structure or from a surface word.
Where possible, write or say why the chosen type fits the situation, not just which answer you picked.
activities.intendedInsight: Across varied surface features, the underlying structure determines the method; options that reward key-word matching or last-procedure-applied reveal when a child is pattern-matching instead of reasoning.

activities.title: Model the planning, not just the answer (worked and partial examples)
feedback: Prompt for the 'look back and check' phase whenever a child stops at the answer.

When a child cannot begin because no operation is stated, do not supply the operation — ask them to draw what's happening with a bar model; the structure of the drawing can help them work out the operation.
Use talk moves — revoicing, 'why did you choose that?', 'does that answer make sense?' — to surface and name strategic thinking.
activities.rationale: Worked and partially-worked examples that model planning and monitoring (not just the answer) and a visible solving frame make the metacognitive phases explicit, which the sources describe as the aim of instruction. Multi-step and no-stated-operation problems require the child to impose structure, intended to build transfer. Efficacy of this specific activity is untested.
sourceClaims: Mathematical problem solving depends on strategy selection, planning and looking-back/self-monitoring, not just execution; these metacognitive phases should be made explicit in instruction.

Assisting students to MONITOR AND REFLECT on the problem-solving process is Recommendation 2, rated STRONG evidence (nine qualifying studies, positive effects on word-problem solving, persisting 4+ months); exposing students to MULTIPLE strategies so they select appropriately is Recommendation 4 (MODERATE); the guide warns 'too often students become wedded to just one approach and then flounder', and frames problem solving as reasoning about structure, not 'using key words'.
learnerActions: Study worked and partially-worked examples that show understand → plan → do → check, with the CHOICE of strategy made visible ('this is a fraction-of problem because...').
Fill in a visible problem-solving frame (understand → plan → do → check) for new problems, completing missing steps in partially-worked examples.
Include at least some problems with no stated operation and some multi-step problems, so you practise imposing structure yourself.
activities.intendedInsight: Expert problem-solving has explicit phases — planning and looking-back are as important as execution. Separating the choice of strategy from its execution makes the strategic step learnable rather than assumed.

constraints: This is a META objective: the goal is the disposition and habits of a strategic problem-solver (sense-making, monitoring, plausibility-checking), not mastery of a single procedure. Children must already be able to find a fraction of a set, compare/order fractions, work with equivalence, and add/subtract fractions; if a child cannot find a fraction of a set at all, revisit that prerequisite before this work.
Keep problems MIXED across the four fraction ideas and vary surface features; a single-type set lets children pattern-match and defeats the recognition objective.
Deliberately include key words that point the wrong way ('altogether' in a fraction-of problem) so key-word matching can be surfaced and challenged rather than rewarded.

Insist on a plausibility / looking-back check every time (for a proper fraction of a positive quantity the answer is smaller than the whole, e.g. 'a fraction less than one whole, such as 3/4, of 20 can't be more than 20').

Recognition-only or multiple-choice responses measure the OUTCOME of strategy selection but do not by themselves elicit the independent planning, justification, and self-monitoring that the objective targets; pair them with open 'how did you know?' reasoning.

Scaffolds such as a fixed solving frame or a sort-tag-model workspace structure the thinking but constrain openness; fade them so the child eventually imposes structure unprompted on novel, multi-step problems.
When a child cannot begin because no operation is stated, scaffold sense-making (draw the situation) rather than supplying the operation.

Static tap-to-reveal pictures and 3D manipulation were judged poor fits for THIS metacognitive objective because strategic problem-solving is generative and dialogic and has no spatial content to manipulate; this is a scope judgement for this objective, not a universal claim that such media cannot teach.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed PROPOSALS, not validated interventions, and no claim of empirical testing of these specific activities is made.

One cited source (Polya/Schoenfeld) is marked unverified in the original row; the IES/WWC Practice Guide claim is marked verified. Evidence strength has not been re-checked and should not be upgraded.

The original framed the dialogic tutor as 'ideal' and static-image/3D artefacts as 'poor'. These were catalog fit rankings; they have been softened to scoped suitability judgements with stated affordances/limits rather than universal pedagogical laws. A fixed worked example cannot be manipulated but can still teach; a multiple-choice format can be used during teaching, not only to assess.

Plausibility example '3/4 of 12 cannot be more than 12' verified: 3/4 of 12 = 9 < 12. The shorthand 'a fraction of 20 can't be more than 20' is strictly true for proper fractions (less than 1); this is appropriate for the age 7–8 examples but is not a universal statement about all fractions and should be stated with that scope.

The double number line representation (original keyRepresentation) was missing from all activities in an earlier candidate; it is present in the sort-then-model workspace for fraction-of and comparison problems, matching the preservation claim.

Activity 3 asks the child to check whether a chosen option came from structure or a surface word; this is metacognitive priming appropriate to a learning (not purely diagnostic) context and does not pre-label specific options for the child.

No arithmetic, force/motion, or geometric idealisation errors were identified in the source to correct; the main risk flagged was the key-word trap, which is handled deliberately. Independent re-audit found no new critical learner-facing errors.

probeDeeper: 'How did you know this was a comparing problem and not an adding one?' — pushes the recognition into an explicit justification.

'You said add because it says altogether — what if I told you the problem was about finding 1/4 of the sweets? Would altogether still mean add?' — a counterexample that tests whether key-word matching survives challenge.
'Once you have an answer, how would you check it's sensible?' — surfaces whether a monitoring/looking-back strategy exists.
'If you got stuck, what would you try?' — reveals whether the child has any strategic repertoire (draw it, try a simpler case) or only waits to be told.
assess.correctAnswer: There is no single right answer to score — the aim is to surface HOW the child decides what a problem is asking and how they judge an answer. A strong response recognises each problem's underlying structure (this is a find-a-fraction-of problem; this is a compare/order problem), states a sensible first step and why, and offers a plausibility check ('the answer should be smaller than the whole').

errorPatterns.pattern: Key-word matching: 'it says altogether so I add' / 'it says left so I take away' — follows a surface word instead of the problem's meaning
errorPatterns.nextMove: Surface it for discussion — offer a counter-problem where the key word points the wrong way and let the child discover the mismatch; build the habit of describing the situation before naming an operation. Do not simply mark it wrong.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child names the operation by quoting a word from the problem rather than describing the situation; picks 'add' for a fraction-of problem that happens to contain 'altogether'

errorPatterns.pattern: Applies the most recently taught procedure to every problem regardless of what it asks
errorPatterns.nextMove: Discuss what is DIFFERENT about the three problems; make the recognition step explicit ('these aren't all the same kind — how are they different?'). A disposition to build, not an error to reteach.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child treats all three varied problems as the same type (e.g. adds fractions in all of them) because that was the last thing practised

errorPatterns.pattern: No plausibility check: accepts an answer larger than the whole for a fraction-of problem, or a smaller fraction 'winning' a comparison, without noticing
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the looking-back move rather than reteaching the calculation: 'could a fraction of 12 be more than 12?' Make plausibility-checking a routine final step.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives an unreasonable answer and, when asked 'does that make sense?', has no way to judge — the checking habit is absent, not the arithmetic

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot begin unless the operation is stated: 'but it doesn't tell me what to do'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not supply the operation — scaffold sense-making of the situation with a bar model ('draw what's happening'); the structure will suggest the operation. If the child also cannot find a fraction of a set at all, revisit that prerequisite.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child stalls on a problem with no explicit operation word, waiting to be told to divide or add

responseLevels.gap: Chooses operations by key words or applies one procedure to everything; cannot say why a problem is a particular type; has no way to judge whether an answer is reasonable and stalls when no operation is stated.
responseLevels.full: Reads a novel or multi-step problem, justifies which fraction idea it needs from the situation's structure, plans and carries out an appropriate method, and routinely checks the answer is plausible — transferring the recognise-plan-do-check habit to unfamiliar contexts and resisting key-word traps.
responseLevels.partial: Can name the type and method for familiar, single-step problems and often gets them right, but selection is fragile — lists what to do without explaining why it fits the situation, is misled by surface wording, or omits the plausibility check unless prompted (the multistructural level: knows the pieces, doesn't coordinate recognise→plan→check).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I'm going to give you three different fraction problems, one at a time. Before you work any of them out, just tell me: what kind of problem is this, and what would you do first? Then we'll talk about how you'd know if your answer makes sense.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Asking the child to name the TYPE and first step BEFORE calculating separates strategic reasoners from key-word matchers and last-procedure appliers: a strategic child reads the situation and justifies the choice; a non-strategic child either grabs a surface word ('altogether means add'), applies whatever was taught most recently to all three, or freezes because no operation is stated. Because it is surfaced for discussion and not scored, it reveals the child's problem-solving disposition rather than their arithmetic.

pedagogy.summary: This topic is fluency with C = πd (= 2πr) and A = πr², and applying them to composite shapes with circular parts. Best taught by deriving both from the meaning of π rather than memorising two similar-looking formulae: π is the constant ratio of every circle's circumference to its diameter (a little over 3), so C = πd is almost a definition; and A = πr² comes from cutting the circle into thin wedges and rearranging them into a near-rectangle of length πr (half the circumference) and height r. The two persistent hazards are confusing radius with diameter, and swapping the circumference and area formulae — both eased by keeping the meaning of each in view (circumference is a length, area is a covering in square units).
bestPractices: Establish π as circumference ÷ diameter — measure round several circular objects and divide by the diameter to find it is always ≈ 3.14; this makes C = πd meaningful, not arbitrary
Derive A = πr² by cutting the circle into wedges and rearranging into a near-rectangle of length πr and height r (πr × r = πr²)
Drill the radius/diameter link (d = 2r) explicitly and check which the formula needs before substituting — circumference uses d (or 2r), area uses r²
Distinguish 'squaring' from 'doubling': r² means r × r, not 2r; area grows with the square of the radius, giving square units
For composite shapes, decompose into a rectangle plus a semicircle, find each part, then add — watching which lengths are the circle's radius
Keep dimensions and units in view: circumference is a length (cm), area is a covering (cm²)
keyRepresentations: A circle with radius, diameter and circumference labelled; the d = 2r link
π as the ratio of circumference to diameter (a string round a tin measured against the diameter, ≈ 3.14)
The circle cut into wedges rearranged into a near-rectangle of length πr and height r (derivation of πr²)
A composite shape decomposed into a rectangle plus a semicircle
Unit labels distinguishing length (cm) from area (cm²)
commonMisconceptions: Confusing radius and diameter — substituting the diameter where the radius is needed (or vice versa)
Swapping the circumference and area formulae (using πr² for circumference or 2πr for area)
Forgetting to square the radius, or squaring as 'doubling' (treating r² as 2r or as the diameter)
Giving an area in linear units, or a circumference in square units
On composite shapes, using the diameter as the radius of the semicircle, or dropping a straight edge from the perimeter

learn.summary: Pupils (ages ~12–14) build fluency with C = πd (= 2πr) and A = πr² and apply them to composite shapes with circular parts. The emphasis is on deriving both formulae from the meaning of π — the constant ratio of every circle's circumference to its diameter, a little over 3 — rather than memorising two similar-looking formulae. π is almost a definition of C = πd; A = πr² follows from cutting a circle into thin wedges and rearranging them into a near-rectangle of length πr (half the circumference) and height r. The two persistent hazards are confusing radius with diameter, and swapping the circumference and area formulae; both are eased by keeping each quantity's meaning and units in view (circumference is a length in cm, area is a covering in cm²).

activities.title: Discover π by unrolling the circumference
feedback: If your ratios differ wildly between circles, re-check your measurements — the string should wrap exactly once with no slack, and the diameter must pass through the centre and be measured where the string wraps; all circles should give roughly the same value close to 3.14, with small differences due to measurement error.
Prompt: 'Roughly how many diameters fit around the edge of a circle, and what do we call that number?'

If a learner thinks π changes with circle size, point to their own table of results showing roughly the same value (close to 3.14) for every circle, and explain that the small differences come from measurement error, not from π changing.
activities.rationale: Grounding π as a measured ratio addresses the vague-notion-of-π misconception and makes C = πd meaningful rather than memorised. An optional interactive 'roll the circle' animation — laying the circumference along a line marked in diameters — can make the ≈ 3.14 result vivid, but physical measurement of real objects achieves the same discovery.
sourceClaims: Learners confuse 'squaring' the radius with 'doubling' it (treating r² as equivalent to the diameter), reason about area as a sum of lengths rather than a product in square units, and hold vague notions of π rather than seeing it as the ratio of circumference to diameter
learnerActions: Take several circular objects (tins, lids, cups) of different sizes; wrap a string once around each and measure that length, then measure the diameter across each.

Divide each circumference by its diameter and record the result; notice the results are all close to the same value, a little over 3 (near π ≈ 3.14, allowing for small measurement errors), whatever the size of the circle.
Lay the measured circumference along a line marked off in lengths equal to that circle's own diameter, and see that it reaches to just past three diameters.
State in your own words: C = πd means the way round is 'a bit more than 3 diameters'.
activities.intendedInsight: π is the fixed ratio of any circle's circumference to its diameter (≈ 3.14), so C = πd is almost a definition, not an arbitrary formula to recall.

activities.title: Build the area formula by rearranging wedges
feedback: If a learner labels the length as the full circumference, remind them each long edge of the rearranged shape is made of only half the arcs, so the length is πr, not 2πr.
Prompt: 'Which of your two results is a length and which is an area? How can you tell from the units?'
If the height is mislabelled as the diameter, point back to the wedge: its straight side is the radius.
activities.rationale: Deriving πr² from decomposition addresses treating area as a sum of lengths rather than a product in square units, and helps keep area distinct from circumference. An optional drag-the-wedges tool that builds the πr × r rectangle can reinforce the same idea; paper cutting achieves it concretely. Note that a paper circle has slight thickness and models the ideal zero-thickness plane figure it represents — reason about the mathematical circle, not the card.
sourceClaims: Pupils must know d = 2r and be able to convert between radius and diameter; confusion among the variables C, d and r is a flagged hazard; A = πr² is derived by decomposing the circle into wedges rearranged into a rectangle of length πr (half the circumference) and height r

Learners confuse 'squaring' the radius with 'doubling' it (treating r² as equivalent to the diameter), reason about area as a sum of lengths rather than a product in square units, and hold vague notions of π rather than seeing it as the ratio of circumference to diameter
learnerActions: Cut a paper circle into a number of thin equal wedges (sectors) and fan them out, alternating points up and down, to form a shape close to a rectangle (parallelogram).
Identify the height of the near-rectangle as the radius r, and its length as half the way round the circle — half the circumference, which is πr.
Compute the area of the near-rectangle as length × height = πr × r = πr², and connect this to the circle's area.
Explain why cutting into more, thinner wedges makes the shape look more like a true rectangle.
activities.intendedInsight: A = πr² is a product of a length (πr) and a length (r) giving square units, derived from rearranging the circle — not a lookalike string to confuse with C = πd.

activities.title: Radius-or-diameter: check before you substitute
feedback: If a learner computes π × 10² = 100π for area in the diameter-given case, flag that they used the diameter as the radius — halve it first: r = 5, A = 25π ≈ 78.5 cm².
If a learner reports area as π × 2 × 5 or π × 10, they have doubled instead of squared — r² means r × r, the area of a little square of side r.
Prompt: 'You were given the diameter — why can't you put it straight into πr²?'
Prompt: 'If the radius doubled, what happens to the circumference, and what happens to the area?' (area ×4, not ×2).
activities.rationale: Making the radius/diameter check an explicit first step and distinguishing squaring from doubling target the two most flagged hazards. An optional radius/diameter toggle that recomputes C and A, and flags a squared-vs-doubled slip, can make the check vivid; the self-check questions work on paper too.
sourceClaims: Pupils must know d = 2r and be able to convert between radius and diameter; confusion among the variables C, d and r is a flagged hazard; A = πr² is derived by decomposing the circle into wedges rearranged into a rectangle of length πr (half the circumference) and height r

Learners confuse 'squaring' the radius with 'doubling' it (treating r² as equivalent to the diameter), reason about area as a sum of lengths rather than a product in square units, and hold vague notions of π rather than seeing it as the ratio of circumference to diameter
learnerActions: For each problem, first write 'What am I given — radius or diameter?' and 'What does this formula need?' before substituting.
Given a diameter of 10 cm, find the area: halve it to get r = 5 cm, then compute A = π × 5² = 25π ≈ 78.5 cm² (not π × 10²).
Given a radius of 5 cm, find both the circumference C = π × 10 = 10π ≈ 31.4 cm and the area A = π × 5² = 25π ≈ 78.5 cm².
Investigate: if the radius doubles, what happens to the circumference and to the area? Confirm circumference doubles (×2) but area quadruples (×4).
activities.intendedInsight: Circumference uses d (or 2r) and area uses r²; you must convert a given diameter to a radius before using πr², and squaring is r × r (not doubling), so area grows with the square of the radius.

activities.title: Composite shapes: rectangle plus semicircle
feedback: If a learner uses r = 4 for the semicircle, remind them 4 cm is the diameter across the short end; the radius is 2 cm.
If a learner leaves in a straight edge where the semicircle joins (or omits the arc), re-trace the boundary: the arc takes the place of that edge.
Prompt: 'Which of your answers is a length and which is an area? How can you tell from the units?'
Check: did you keep straight which number is the radius for each circular part?
activities.rationale: Decomposing and tracing the real boundary addresses using the diameter as the semicircle's radius and dropping/adding wrong edges in the perimeter. An optional composite-shape builder that shows each part's contribution can scaffold this; careful labelled sketching achieves the same decomposition.
sourceClaims: Pupils must know d = 2r and be able to convert between radius and diameter; confusion among the variables C, d and r is a flagged hazard; A = πr² is derived by decomposing the circle into wedges rearranged into a rectangle of length πr (half the circumference) and height r
Pupils commonly confuse area and perimeter, which for circles surfaces as swapping circumference (a length) with area (square units)
KS3 pupils should calculate the circumference and area of circles and solve problems involving the perimeters and areas of composite shapes that include circular parts
learnerActions: Take a composite shape — e.g. a rectangle 10 cm by 4 cm with a semicircle of diameter 4 cm on one short (4 cm) end — and sketch it, labelling every given length.
Find the semicircle's radius as half its diameter (here r = 2 cm), not the full width.
For the area, add the rectangle's area to half the circle's area: 10 × 4 + ½ × π × 2² = 40 + 2π ≈ 46.3 cm².
For the perimeter, trace the actual boundary: include the rectangle's exposed edges plus the semicircle arc (½ × π × diameter = ½ × π × 4 = 2π), with NO straight edge where the semicircle sits.
State the units: area in cm², perimeter in cm.
activities.intendedInsight: Composite shapes are decomposed into parts whose areas are added, while the perimeter follows the true outline — the arc replaces the covered straight edge, and the semicircle's radius is half its diameter.

activities.title: Formula-choice and unit checks (retrieval practice)
feedback: If the two answers are switched (circumference in cm², area in cm), you have swapped the formulae — anchor each to what it measures: circumference from πd is a length, area from πr² is a covering.
If a method is correct but the unit is wrong, re-check the unit against what was calculated — don't re-derive, just correct the label.
If a diameter distractor is chosen in πr², note the full width was used instead of the radius — halve the diameter to the radius first.
activities.rationale: Spaced retrieval with targeted distractors (diameter-in-πr², swapped formulae, wrong units) consolidates fluency and surfaces residual misconceptions, including the radius/diameter slip. Scored recognition and matching tasks assess and rehearse choices but do not by themselves require independent derivation or transfer to a novel composite figure — pair with the construction activities above.
sourceClaims: Pupils commonly confuse area and perimeter, which for circles surfaces as swapping circumference (a length) with area (square units)

Pupils must know d = 2r and be able to convert between radius and diameter; confusion among the variables C, d and r is a flagged hazard; A = πr² is derived by decomposing the circle into wedges rearranged into a rectangle of length πr (half the circumference) and height r
learnerActions: Match each circle to its correct circumference and area expressions, watching for distractors that use πr² for circumference or 2πr for area.
Answer a question whose tempting wrong choice uses the diameter in πr² — reject it by halving to the radius first.
For each completed calculation, label the result with its unit and justify: a distance round is cm, a covering is cm².
Given a diameter, first find the radius before applying πr².
activities.intendedInsight: Keeping the two formulae distinct and attaching correct units (cm for circumference, cm² for area) consolidates the derived understanding, while converting a given diameter to a radius before using πr² guards the most common slip.

constraints: Learners should be able to convert between radius and diameter (d = 2r) and to find the area of a rectangle before this topic; semicircle composite work also builds on perimeter/area of composite shapes.

Recognition and matching tasks (matching circles to formulae, multiple-choice with distractors) are useful for rehearsal and assessment but do not require independent derivation or application to a novel figure; they should supplement, not replace, the measurement, wedge-rearranging, and composite-construction activities.

A static labelled circle with tap-to-reveal can name radius, diameter and circumference and display both formulae, but cannot let a learner derive π, rearrange the wedges, or apply the formulae to a new shape — treat it as a reference scaffold, not the main learning activity.

Paper circles and string-and-tin measurements are physical approximations of ideal plane figures (paper and card have slight thickness); use them to approximate the mathematical circle and reason about the represented figure rather than the physical cutout.

Interactive features named here (roll-the-circle animation, drag-the-wedges tool, radius/diameter toggle, composite-shape builder, unit labels) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete — they are illustrative, not mandatory; the same insights are reachable with physical materials and sketching.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support teaching principles/misconceptions rather than proving any specific activity was tested or superior to another medium.

Worked values were independently checked: for a diameter of 10 cm, r = 5 cm, A = 25π ≈ 78.5 cm² and C = 10π ≈ 31.4 cm; using the diameter wrongly gives π × 10² = 100π ≈ 314 cm². For the composite shape (10×4 rectangle, semicircle of diameter 4 ⇒ r = 2): area = 40 + ½π·2² = 40 + 2π ≈ 46.3 cm²; the semicircle arc = ½·π·4 = 2π. These match the source's correctAnswer.

The KS3 national-curriculum source is marked verified:false in the row; it is cited only for the composite-shape objective in the composite activity, with the verified NCTM claim supporting the radius-is-half-diameter decomposition principle. No efficacy is claimed for it, and it is a topical/curriculum requirement rather than a teaching-principle claim.

The original source claimed a 3D artefact 'adds nothing' and that unscripted dialogue does not serve this skill; these were catalog fit judgements and have been softened — circle circumference and area are planar, so 3D is not required here, and calculation practice benefits from doing-and-checking, but no universal claim of necessity or exclusion is asserted.

The source stated a static tap-to-reveal image 'cannot' let the child derive or apply; retained only as a narrowly scoped affordance limitation (it is a reference scaffold), not as a universal law about static images.

probeDeeper: 'You were given the diameter — why can't you put it straight into πr²?' — forcing the radius/diameter distinction
'Which of your answers is a length and which is an area? How can you tell from the units?' — separating circumference from area
'If the radius doubled, what happens to the circumference, and what happens to the area?' — a counterexample exposing square-vs-linear growth (area ×4, not ×2)
'Roughly how many diameters fit around the edge of a circle, and what do we call that number?' — probing π as a ratio
assess.correctAnswer: (a) C = π×10 = 10π ≈ 31.4 cm; A = π×5² = 25π ≈ 78.5 cm². (b) radius = 5 cm, so A = π×5² = 25π ≈ 78.5 cm² (NOT π×10²). (c) perimeter = the rectangle's exposed edges plus the semicircle arc (½×π×4 = 2π), with no straight edge where the semicircle sits; area = 10×4 + ½×π×2² = 40 + 2π ≈ 46.3 cm². π is the ratio of any circle's circumference to its diameter, a little over 3. Circumference in cm, area in cm².

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses radius and diameter — substitutes the diameter where the radius is needed ('the size across is 10, so r² is 10²')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach d = 2r and make 'which do I have, which does the formula need?' an explicit first step; halve a diameter to the radius before substituting
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On (b) computes π×10² = 100π instead of π×5²; uses the full width in πr²

errorPatterns.pattern: Swaps the circumference and area formulae — uses πr² for circumference or 2πr (or πd) for area
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor each formula to what it measures — circumference is the distance round (a length, from πd), area is the covering (square units, from πr²); derive both so they are not two lookalike strings
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reports the circumference in square units or the area as a linear multiple of the radius; the two answers are switched

errorPatterns.pattern: Forgets to square the radius, or 'squares' by doubling — treats r² as 2r or as the diameter
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make squaring explicit as r × r (the area of a little square), distinct from doubling; show the area is a covering that grows with r², not the diameter
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On (a)/(b) computes π×2×5 or π×10 for the area instead of π×5²; equates r² with the diameter

errorPatterns.pattern: On the composite shape, uses the semicircle's DIAMETER as its radius, or includes/omits the wrong edges in the perimeter
errorPatterns.nextMove: Decompose explicitly: label each part, identify the semicircle's radius (half its diameter), and trace the actual boundary for the perimeter, arc replacing the covered edge
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On (c) uses r = 4 for the semicircle, or adds a straight edge where the arc replaces it (or omits the arc)

errorPatterns.pattern: Gives area in linear units or circumference in square units
errorPatterns.nextMove: Prompt 'a distance round is cm, a covering is cm²'; check the unit against what was calculated rather than reteaching
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Method correct but the unit is wrong — cm for an area or cm² for a circumference

responseLevels.gap: Cannot calculate reliably — uses the diameter in πr², swaps circumference and area, or doubles instead of squaring; units muddled
responseLevels.full: Calculates circumference and area correctly, converting diameter to radius as needed, keeps the two formulae distinct and can explain π as a ratio and A = πr² informally, handles composite shapes with circular parts, and uses correct linear/square units — transferring to a novel composite figure
responseLevels.partial: Uses the formulae correctly when handed the radius directly, but is caught by a diameter-given problem, cannot say why the formulae work or what π is, or mishandles the semicircle in a composite shape — has two formulae as strings, not a derived, distinguished pair

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a calculator and three tasks: (a) a circle with radius 5 cm — find its circumference and its area; (b) a circle given by its DIAMETER of 10 cm — find its area; (c) a composite shape: a rectangle 10 cm by 4 cm with a semicircle of diameter 4 cm on one short end — find the perimeter and the area. Also ask them to explain, roughly, what π has to do with a circle. Watch whether they use the radius (not the diameter) in πr², whether they keep circumference and area formulae apart, whether they square rather than double the radius, and whether they use square units for area.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands halves the diameter to a radius before using πr² and keeps the two formulae distinct; a child with the classic error uses the diameter in the area formula (π×10² = 314) or squares πr rather than r, giving a wildly different answer traceable to one mistake. The diameter-given circle (b) directly separates those who track radius vs diameter, and asking about π distinguishes derived understanding from formula-recall.

pedagogy.summary: Comparing and ordering fractions with different numerators AND denominators, using either a common denominator (rename both with equivalent fractions, then compare numerators) or benchmark reasoning (is each fraction less than, equal to, or more than 1/2 — or near 0 or 1?). Benchmarks are fast and build number sense; common denominators are general. Conclusions are justified with visual models. This is a known hard skill — on the 2004 NAEP, 50% of 8th-graders could not order three fractions from least to greatest.
bestPractices: Teach benchmark reasoning with 0, 1/2 and 1: decide which side of 1/2 each fraction sits on (5/8 > 1/2 because 5 is more than half of 8; 3/7 < 1/2) (IES Rec 3).
Teach the common-denominator method as renaming both fractions with equivalents, then comparing numerators.
Use minimally-labelled number lines (0, 1/2, 1) for landmark placement, and dual-labelled lines (one unit sequence above, another below) for different denominators (IES Rec 2).
Choose the strategy to fit the numbers — benchmarks when they straddle 1/2, common denominator when they are close.
Keep the same-numerator shortcut available (2/3 > 2/5).
Justify with a model and guard against whole-number bias.
keyRepresentations: Common denominator via equivalent-fraction renaming
Number line marked 0, 1/2, 1 (benchmark lane)
Dual-labelled number line for different denominators
Ratio table / times-tables for the common multiple
commonMisconceptions: Whole-number bias — ordering by numerator or denominator alone (3/8 vs 5/12 → '5 > 3 so 5/12 is bigger', or '12 > 8 so smaller') (IES)
Comparing without a common denominator (cross-adding, or comparing tops and bottoms separately)
Renaming only one fraction, or using a non-common multiple
Benchmark misapplied — e.g. judging 3/7 > 1/2

learn.summary: Learners compare and order fractions with different numerators and denominators using two complementary strategies: (1) renaming both fractions to a common denominator and comparing numerators, and (2) benchmark reasoning with 0, 1/2, and 1 (deciding which side of 1/2 each fraction sits on, or whether it is near 0 or 1). Benchmarks are quick and build number sense; common denominators are general-purpose. Conclusions are justified with visual models (partitioned bars, number lines). The core misconception to guard against is whole-number bias — ordering by numerator or denominator alone. This is a known hard skill: on the 2004 NAEP, 50% of 8th-graders could not order three fractions from least to greatest.

activities.title: Strategy workbench: common denominator OR benchmark
feedback: If a learner compares numerators and denominators separately or cross-adds, show that only a shared denominator licenses comparing the top numbers — re-partition both bars to the same grid and compare again.

If a learner renames only one fraction or uses a denominator that is not a common multiple of both, point out both fractions must reach the SAME denominator; verify each rename with the ×n/n equivalence.
If a learner misplaces a fraction relative to 1/2 (e.g. calls 3/7 more than 1/2), have them compare the numerator to half the denominator: half of 7 is 3.5, and 3 is less than 3.5, so 3/7 < 1/2.
Confirm correct reasoning by asking them to justify with the visual model, not just the final symbols.
activities.rationale: The IES/WWC guide recommends benchmarks 0, 1/2, 1 as reference points and number lines (minimally-labelled for landmarks; dual-labelled for different denominators) to support comparison, and names whole-number bias as the core misconception. Offering both renaming and benchmark strategies lets learners pick the efficient method and build general competence.
sourceClaims: Comparing/ordering fractions is a key indicator of understanding and is hard (2004 NAEP: 50% of 8th-graders could not order three fractions least-to-greatest); benchmarks 0, 1/2, 1 are recommended reference points, dual-labelled and minimally-labelled number lines support comparison of different denominators, and whole-number bias is the core misconception.
learnerActions: Take a pair such as 3/8 versus 5/12. Choose the common-denominator path: re-partition both bars (on paper or with a model) to the same fine grid — twenty-fourths — so 3/8 becomes 9/24 and 5/12 becomes 10/24, then compare the numerators 9 versus 10.

Take a pair such as 5/8 versus 3/7. Choose the benchmark path: place each on a number line marked 0, 1/2, 1. Decide which side of 1/2 each sits on (5/8 is more than 1/2 because 5 is more than half of 8; 3/7 is less than 1/2 because 3 is less than half of 7).
Switch into an ordering task: drag or write three or more fractions (e.g. 2/3, 3/5, 7/10) onto a line or into order, choosing whichever strategy fits the numbers.
State, for each comparison, which strategy you chose and why it suited those particular numbers.
activities.intendedInsight: Renaming two fractions to the same denominator makes them directly comparable (the comparison collapses to comparing numerators), and the 1/2 benchmark settles many comparisons at a glance without full computation. Choosing the strategy to fit the numbers is part of the skill.

activities.title: Dual-labelled and benchmark number lines
feedback: If a learner places a fraction on the wrong side of 1/2, return to comparing the numerator with half the denominator.
If a learner is unsure whether a fraction is near 0 or near 1, check how close the numerator is to 0 or to the denominator (e.g. 1/5 is near 0, 4/5 is near 1).
If a learner struggles to compare across the two denominators, align the two labelled sequences and read off which mark lies further right.
activities.rationale: IES/WWC recommends minimally-labelled number lines for landmark placement and dual-labelled lines for comparing different denominators. A reference line aids recall and placement; note it does not by itself carry out a full ordering or re-partition, so pair it with the active strategies above.
sourceClaims: Comparing/ordering fractions is a key indicator of understanding and is hard (2004 NAEP: 50% of 8th-graders could not order three fractions least-to-greatest); benchmarks 0, 1/2, 1 are recommended reference points, dual-labelled and minimally-labelled number lines support comparison of different denominators, and whole-number bias is the core misconception.
learnerActions: Use a number line marked only 0, 1/2, 1 and place common fractions where they belong relative to those landmarks; for each, say whether it is more than, equal to, or less than one half.
Decide whether 4/9 is more or less than a half by comparing 4 with half of 9 (4.5): 4 is less than 4.5, so 4/9 < 1/2 — no common denominator needed.
Order 1/5, 4/5, 5/9 using only benchmarks: 1/5 sits just above 0, 5/9 is just over 1/2 (5 is more than 4.5), and 4/5 is near 1, giving 1/5 < 5/9 < 4/5.
For two different denominators, use a dual-labelled line (one unit sequence of marks above the line, the other below) to see where each fraction falls and which is larger.
Explain how the landmarks 0, 1/2 and 1 let you decide a comparison without finding a common denominator.
activities.intendedInsight: A number line anchored to 0, 1/2 and 1 gives fractions a magnitude and a 'side of 1/2' (and a sense of nearness to 0 or 1), so many comparisons can be read off directly; dual labelling lets two different denominators be compared on one line.

activities.title: Check and consolidate ordering and benchmark decisions
feedback: If a learner orders by single digits ('7/10 is smallest because 10 is biggest'), rename all three to a common denominator or place them on a 0/½/1 line and compare magnitudes.
If a learner grinds a full common-denominator computation for 5/8 vs 3/7, prompt the quicker 1/2 benchmark.
Reward correct answers that also carry a model-based justification.
activities.rationale: Recognition and fill-in tasks efficiently check whether learners can apply each strategy and avoid whole-number bias, and surface whether a learner works in only one register (benchmark or common denominator). These checks confirm application but do not, on their own, elicit the independent construction that the workbench tasks require.
learnerActions: Order a set such as 2/3, 3/5, 7/10 from smallest to largest and show working (e.g. common denominator 30: 3/5 = 18/30, 2/3 = 20/30, 7/10 = 21/30, giving 3/5 < 2/3 < 7/10).
Answer a quick benchmark question: 'Is 5/8 more or less than 1/2?' and justify.
Rename both fractions of a pair to a shared common denominator before comparing, and check the order you get.
Sort a set of fractions into 'less than 1/2' and 'more than 1/2'.
Keep the same-numerator shortcut in play: with equal numerators, the larger denominator gives the smaller fraction (2/3 > 2/5).
Check that a different common denominator does not change the order (e.g. using 60 instead of 30 gives the same ordering).
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent comparison means ordering correctly, choosing an efficient strategy, and justifying with a model — not just getting a final symbol right. Any valid common denominator yields the same order.

constraints: Learners must reach fractions with DIFFERENT numerators and denominators; same-denominator or same-numerator pairs alone are stepping stones, not the full objective.
Both strategies should be available: benchmark reasoning when fractions straddle 1/2 or sit near 0 or 1, and common denominators when fractions are close together or benchmarks do not separate them.

A benchmark/reference number line with fractions pre-placed is a recall and placement scaffold; it does not re-partition fractions or carry out an ordering, so it must be combined with active renaming and ordering work.

Recognition-only responses (multiple choice, sorting, fill-in) check application but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of a full ordering with justification; include a task where the learner produces the ordering and its reasoning.
Always require justification with a visual model and explicitly guard against whole-number bias (ordering by numerator or denominator alone).
Verify each rename with the ×n/n equivalence and ensure both fractions reach the same common multiple.

Comparing a fixed numerator (as in same-numerator pairs) with a fixed denominator varies different quantities; there is no 'denominator rule that flips', so explain each comparison by magnitude rather than a sign-flip rule.

Live re-partitioning of bars to a shared grid and drag-to-order on a line are example interaction mechanisms that make the strategies concrete; they are illustrative, not required mechanisms — the same work can be done with drawn bars and written orderings.

Interpret this content for approximately ages 9–10; in the England curriculum Year 5 pupils compare and order fractions whose denominators are all multiples of the same number, and Year 6 extends this to comparing and ordering fractions more generally, including fractions greater than 1 (source marked unverified).
