pedagogy.summary: Year 2 sharpens the movement vocabulary: children add clockwise and anti-clockwise to whole, half, quarter and three-quarter turns, link a quarter turn to a right angle, and give and follow multi-step directions combining straight-line moves with turns. The words are to be used, not defined — the aim is fluent, correct use in routes and turn descriptions. Clockwise/anti-clockwise is a new convention layered onto the still-developing left/right, and the quarter-turn = right-angle link is the crucial bridge to the formal angle work that follows.
bestPractices: Introduce clockwise from a real clock's hands, then transfer it to the body and to turning objects, contrasting it explicitly with anti-clockwise each time.
Make the quarter-turn = right-angle link concrete: turn a quarter and mark the right angle between the start and finish arms (an angle is an amount of turn shown by two adjoining lines).
Combine moves and turns into routes to give and follow (barrier games, floor robots) so the vocabulary is productive.
Keep turns embodied and referenced to target facings before moving to described or drawn routes.
Continue supporting left/right on the body and expect residual errors as frame-dependence is still developing.
keyRepresentations: A clock face for clockwise and anti-clockwise
Body or floor-robot turns with start/finish facings, and the right-angle mark left by a quarter turn
Route maps and grids to describe and to follow with combined moves and turns
Two adjoining arms (the start and finish of a turn) showing the angle turned through
commonMisconceptions: Clockwise and anti-clockwise confused with each other or with left/right — a new convention on top of frame-dependent left/right
A quarter turn not connected to a right angle — the two treated as separate, unrelated facts
Turn amounts miscounted — a half or a quarter turn produced when a three-quarter turn is asked for
Egocentric direction-giving: routes given from the child's own viewpoint without accounting for the follower's facing

learn.summary: Year 2 children use (not merely define) movement vocabulary: clockwise and anti-clockwise added to whole, half, quarter and three-quarter turns; a quarter turn linked to a right angle; and multi-step directions combining straight-line moves with turns that another person can actually follow. Clockwise/anti-clockwise is a new convention layered on still-developing left/right, and the quarter-turn = right-angle link bridges to later formal angle work. Guidance keeps turns embodied and routes followable, with feedback on wrong direction or amount.

activities.title: Clockwise, anti-clockwise and the right angle a quarter turn leaves
feedback: If a child turns the wrong way on a clockwise/anti-clockwise instruction, return to a real clock's hand direction as the anchor and label both ways explicitly each time.
If a child makes the quarter turn but cannot name or denies the right angle, mark the right angle between the start and finish arms every single time until the link becomes automatic.
When a child miscounts the turn amount (e.g. a half or quarter turn when a three-quarter turn was asked), count the quarter turns aloud — one, two, three — marking each right angle as it is passed.
Confirm when two clockwise quarter turns are recognised as a half turn, reinforcing that quarters accumulate.
activities.rationale: The curriculum expects pupils to distinguish rotation as a turn and in terms of right angles for quarter, half and three-quarter turns, clockwise and anti-clockwise. An angle is an amount of turn shown by two adjoining lines, and the dynamic (turn) and static (corner) conceptions of a right angle must be brought together, which marking the arms of a quarter turn supports. A manipulable clock/dial with a stamped right angle makes the mechanism concrete; a fixed diagram can still illustrate the link but cannot be turned by the child.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils should use mathematical vocabulary to describe position, direction and movement, including movement in a straight line and distinguishing between rotation as a turn and in terms of right angles for quarter, half and three-quarter turns (clockwise and anti-clockwise).

An angle is an amount of turn represented by two adjoining lines (start and finish positions); children develop right angles as quarter turns by turning with one arm fixed while the other moves, linking turn to the right angle formed — the static (corner) and dynamic (turn) conceptions must come together.
learnerActions: Watch a real clock's hands and name the direction they travel as 'clockwise'; then turn your own body a quarter turn clockwise (towards your right, the way the hands would go on a clock lying face-up on the floor and seen from above) and say where you now face.
Make a quarter turn clockwise and mark or point out the corner (angle) between where you started facing and where you finish facing; name it as a right angle.
Make the same quarter turn anti-clockwise and describe how the finishing facing differs.

On a clock face or turn dial, spin an arrow with a 'clockwise, quarter turn' control so it moves 90° and leaves a right-angle mark between start and finish; use 'anti-clockwise' to send it back the other way.
Make two quarter turns clockwise in a row and decide whether that equals one half turn, counting each quarter aloud.
Make a three-quarter turn clockwise, counting the quarters, and point out that three right angles have been passed.
activities.intendedInsight: A quarter turn always leaves a right angle between the start and finish arms, and clockwise versus anti-clockwise decides which way you turn — turning fuzzy words into exact instructions.

activities.title: Give and follow a multi-step route that someone else can act on
feedback: If a child gives directions from their own viewpoint so 'turn left' is wrong for the follower, do NOT treat it as a failure: walk the route exactly as they said so they SEE the mismatch, then model taking the follower's view. De-centring matures with age.
When a robot hits a wall, name whether the direction or the amount of turn was wrong and let the child re-string the instruction.
Probe with 'turn that quarter anti-clockwise this time — where do you face now?' to check the direction convention under a new turn.
Ask 'when you say turn left, is that your left or mine?' to surface the follower's frame of reference.
activities.rationale: Giving and following directions that combine straight-line movement and turns makes the vocabulary productive rather than merely recognised. Left/right and route-taking are frame-dependent and late-developing; young children are egocentric and find it hard to imagine a route from another's viewpoint, so making the follower act it out literally is a developmental support, not a test to pass. Immediate feedback on wrong direction or amount (a wall, a mismatch walked out) ties the words to consequences.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils should use mathematical vocabulary to describe position, direction and movement, including movement in a straight line and distinguishing between rotation as a turn and in terms of right angles for quarter, half and three-quarter turns (clockwise and anti-clockwise).

Left and right are frame-dependent (relative to the direction the child faces) and late-developing; young children are egocentric and find it hard to de-center and imagine how a space or route looks from another point of view, which they master only as they get older.
learnerActions: Guide a partner (or a floor robot) from one point to another using a sequence such as 'forward 2, turn clockwise quarter, forward 3', combining straight-line moves with named turns.
Have the follower act out the route exactly as given, from the follower's own facing, and watch what happens.
On a grid, drive a programmable robot through a maze by stringing moves and turns; a wrong turn direction or wrong amount sends it into a wall, prompting a correction.
Play a barrier game: describe a route to someone who cannot see your map, using direction and turn words precisely enough for them to reproduce it.
When a route 'goes wrong', revise the instructions so the follower, not just you, can reach the target.
activities.intendedInsight: Direction and turn words are most useful when they form a sequence another person can follow from their own viewpoint — producing a followable route is the real goal.

activities.title: Check and sort turn and route language
feedback: If a selection is wrong, re-make the turn physically and compare the finishing facing.
For a mismatched quarter-turn/right-angle pairing, mark the angle between start and finish arms and compare.
Treat recognition choices as a check only; always follow with giving or following a live route so the child constructs instructions, not just identifies them.
activities.rationale: Selecting a facing, matching a quarter turn to a right angle, and sequencing a route give a reliable, quick check of the vocabulary. Such recognition tasks confirm what a child can identify but do not by themselves elicit the child's own construction of turns and routes, so they supplement rather than replace the embodied and productive activities above.
learnerActions: After a stated clockwise or anti-clockwise quarter turn, pick which direction you now face from given options.
Match a quarter turn to one right angle, a half turn to two right angles, and a three-quarter turn to three right angles.
Put a jumbled set of move-and-turn instructions into the order that reaches a target, then test the order by walking or driving it.
activities.intendedInsight: You can recognise correct turn facings and the quarter-turn/right-angle link quickly, then confirm sequences by acting them out.

constraints: The goal is fluent, correct USE of the words in routes and turn descriptions, not reciting definitions.
Keep turns embodied and referenced to target facings before moving to described or drawn routes.
Introduce clockwise from a real clock's hands, then transfer to the body and to turning objects, contrasting it explicitly with anti-clockwise each time.
Continue supporting left/right on the body and expect residual errors: frame-dependence is still developing at this age.
Egocentric direction-giving is developmentally expected, not a failure; surface it by having the follower act the route out literally rather than correcting abstractly.

Recognition/selection and matching tasks can check the vocabulary but do not by themselves elicit the child producing turns and followable routes, so the child must still construct turns and routes themselves.

A fixed picture or diagram can illustrate the quarter-turn/right-angle link but cannot be turned by the child; a manipulable dial or embodied turn supplies the dynamic experience. Neither claim is that a static image 'cannot teach' the idea.

Interactive controls (clockwise/anti-clockwise and quarter/half buttons, a stamped right-angle mark, a robot that hits a wall on a wrong move) are optional ways to make feedback concrete, not required mechanisms.
Rendering turns and routes in 3D is optional; the ideas are planar and do not require it.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: a quarter turn = one right angle (90°); two quarter turns = one half turn (180°) = two right angles; a three-quarter turn = three right angles. These were checked and are correct. The three-quarter-turn mis-count example (producing a half or quarter instead) is retained as an error pattern, not taught as correct.

The original source row rated open conversation as a 'poor' fit and framed a recognition/selection artefact as assessing 'without building the doing'; these are framed here as scope limits (recognition does not by itself elicit construction) rather than universal claims that dialogue or static media cannot teach.

Legacy comparative framing ('a static picture cannot deliver', '3D adds little') has been softened to stated affordances/limits without asserting new efficacy comparisons, since the exact sources do not establish necessity or comparative effectiveness.
Activity 3 sourceClaims set to [] because no cited source supports its recognition-versus-construction principle; the curriculum claim covers only the vocabulary topic, not that principle.

probeDeeper: Do that turn again but anti-clockwise this time — where do you face now?
You turned a quarter. Show me the corner you made between where you started and where you're facing — what kind of angle is that?
Make two quarter turns clockwise — is that the same as a half turn?
I'm going to actually follow your directions from where I'm standing — when you say 'turn left', is that your left or mine?
assess.correctAnswer: Turns the correct direction for clockwise, names the quarter turn as a right angle, and gives the route as a followable sequence using correct directional and turn vocabulary — adjusted so that the follower, not just the child, can act on it.

errorPatterns.pattern: Turns anti-clockwise when told clockwise (or treats the two as the same) — the new convention not yet stable ('clockwise... this way?')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to a real clock's hand direction as the anchor and label both ways explicitly each time.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Turns the wrong direction on a clockwise or anti-clockwise instruction

errorPatterns.pattern: Does not link a quarter turn to a right angle — treats 'quarter turn' and 'right angle' as unrelated
errorPatterns.nextMove: Mark the right angle between the start and finish arms of the quarter turn every single time until the link is automatic.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Makes a quarter turn but cannot name the angle turned through, or denies that it is a right angle

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscounts the turn amount — produces a half or a quarter turn when a three-quarter turn is asked for
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the quarter turns aloud (one, two, three), marking each right angle as it is passed.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The finish facing after the requested turn is wrong

errorPatterns.pattern: Gives directions from own viewpoint without adjusting for the follower's facing, so 'turn left' is wrong for the person following
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT treat as a failure — walk it exactly as they said so they SEE the mismatch, and model taking the follower's view; de-centring matures with age.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When you follow their route exactly from your own facing, the turns come out wrong

responseLevels.gap: Confuses clockwise and anti-clockwise, does not link a quarter turn to a right angle, and gives unfollowable or purely egocentric routes.
responseLevels.full: Uses clockwise / anti-clockwise and quarter / half / three-quarter turns correctly, names a quarter turn as a right angle, and gives and follows multi-step routes combining moves and turns that another person can act on, transferring to new routes (relational) — beginning to adjust for the follower's viewpoint.
responseLevels.partial: Uses quarter and half turns and follows single instructions, and can echo clockwise and right-angle language, but turns the wrong way on clockwise/anti-clockwise, does not spontaneously name the quarter turn as a right angle, or gives routes only from their own viewpoint (multistructural).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give a context and listen for USE: 'Face the window. Make a quarter turn clockwise — which way did you go, and what is the angle you turned through? ... Now guide me from the door to your chair, telling me every move and every turn.' Listen for correct use of clockwise / anti-clockwise, quarter / half / three-quarter, right angle, and a route someone could actually follow.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Combining clockwise with a turn amount, then requiring the right-angle naming and a followable route, separates a child who uses the vocabulary as precise instructions from one who parrots the words but turns the wrong way, omits the right-angle link, or gives an egocentric route. Producing a route the teacher can actually follow is the discriminator.

pedagogy.summary: This is the step up from knowing individual angle facts (angles at a point sum to 360°, on a straight line 180°, vertically opposite are equal) to CHAINING them across a single diagram to find several unknowns, and to setting up and solving an EQUATION for an unknown. Best taught by insisting that every step names the fact that licenses it (reasoning from geometrical structure, not from how the diagram looks), by keeping the 'whole' explicit (180° for a line, 360° at a point), and by holding apart the two relationships at a crossing — vertically opposite angles are EQUAL, adjacent angles are SUPPLEMENTARY. Diagrams are given not-to-scale so pupils must deduce rather than measure.
bestPractices: Require a named reason for every step ('angles on a straight line sum to 180°'), not 'Z-angle'/'F-angle' style mnemonics — reasoning from structure generalises, tricks don't
Name the WHOLE before calculating: a straight line is a half-turn (180°), a point a whole turn (360°); the unknown is the whole minus the known parts
Teach the crossing-lines diagram as two facts held apart — opposite angles equal, adjacent angles supplementary — one diagram, two relationships
Present diagrams NOT to scale so pupils cannot measure or eyeball; the marks and given values carry the facts
Progress to letting an unknown be a letter and writing an equation (e.g. 2x+10 = 130 for a vertically opposite pair), linking angle facts to algebra
Build multi-step problems where one found angle becomes the input to the next, and ask pupils to carry the value forward onto the diagram
keyRepresentations: Crossing-lines ('hinged sticks') diagram for vertically-opposite versus adjacent angles
The whole as a fixed total shared among parts — half-turn 180° on a line, whole-turn 360° at a point
Not-to-scale multi-angle diagrams that force deduction over measurement
An equation written from the diagram (known + unknown = whole; or an opposite pair set equal)
commonMisconceptions: Treating vertically opposite angles as supplementary (subtracting from 180 to find the opposite angle)
Over-generalising that all four angles at a crossing are equal
Using the wrong whole — 360° where 180° applies, or vice versa
Measuring or reading the not-to-scale diagram instead of deducing from facts

learn.summary: Pupils (age 11+) move from knowing isolated angle facts (angles at a point sum to 360°, angles on a straight line sum to 180°, vertically opposite angles are equal) to CHAINING those facts across a single not-to-scale diagram to find several unknowns, and to writing and solving an equation for an unknown angle. The core discipline: name the fact that licenses every step (reason from geometrical structure, not from how the diagram looks or from F/Z mnemonics), keep the 'whole' explicit (180° for a line, 360° at a point) for line/point calculations, and hold apart the two relationships at a crossing — vertically opposite angles are EQUAL (found by equality, not subtraction), adjacent angles are SUPPLEMENTARY.

activities.title: Chaining angle facts across a not-to-scale crossing
feedback: For (a): the angle vertically opposite 130° is 130° (vertically opposite angles equal — found by equality, not by subtracting); each adjacent angle is 50° (angles on a straight line sum to 180°, so 180−130). Check: 130 + 50 + 130 + 50 = 360° (angles at a point sum to 360°).
For (b): the split angle totals 130° (vertically opposite the 130°), so the remaining part is 130−40 = 90°.
For (c): 2x+10 = 130 (vertically opposite equal), so 2x = 120 and x = 60.
If you gave 50° for the angle vertically OPPOSITE 130°, you treated an opposite pair as supplementary — opposite angles are equal; it is the ADJACENT angle that is 180−130 = 50°.
If you used 360° for an angle on a straight line (or 180° at a point), you named the wrong whole — a straight line is 180°, a full point is 360°; sanity-check the answer against that total.
If you found the first angle but stalled, write it onto the diagram and use it as the given for the next step — the facts are sound, the chain just needs the value carried forward.
activities.rationale: The objective is multi-step deduction and justification, so the task must require an actual chain where each found angle becomes an input and a named reason is stated at every step; a not-to-scale figure means measuring is unreliable so pupils must deduce from facts, and part (c) links angle facts to setting up and solving an equation.
sourceClaims: Vertically opposite angles are EQUAL while adjacent angles are SUPPLEMENTARY, and pupils must hold the two apart; the hinged two-sticks model shows that as one angle increases so does its opposite (so they must be equal); teaching should ask pupils to find and JUSTIFY the other angles given one, using named rules rather than F/Z mnemonics
Pupils should apply the properties of angles at a point, angles on a straight line, and vertically opposite angles to find unknown angles in multi-step problems
Angle measure is additive: a whole angle decomposed into parts is the sum of the parts, and unknown angles are found by writing an equation with a symbol for the unknown
learnerActions: Work from a not-to-scale diagram: two straight lines crossing at a point, with one of the four angles marked 130°, and a third ray splitting the opposite angle into two parts, one marked 40°.

(a) Find the three unmarked angles at the crossing. For each, write the exact fact you used (e.g. 'vertically opposite angles are equal', 'angles on a straight line sum to 180°'). Then check that the four angles at the crossing total 360° (angles at a point sum to 360°).
(b) Find the remaining part of the split angle, carrying the already-found angle forward as a given.
(c) Two vertically opposite angles are labelled (2x+10)° and 130°; write an equation and solve it for x.

Before calculating, name which relationship applies: for an angle on a line or at a point, say the WHOLE (a straight line is a half-turn 180°, a point is a whole turn 360°) and take the unknown as the whole minus the known parts; but for a vertically opposite angle the unknown is simply EQUAL to its given partner, NOT whole-minus-parts.
Write each found angle onto the diagram so it becomes a visible given for the next step.
activities.intendedInsight: Unknown angles are deduced by combining named facts in a chain, where one result feeds the next; a vertically opposite angle is found by equality while line/point unknowns are found by subtracting from the whole, and the not-to-scale picture cannot be measured, so only the facts license the answer.

activities.title: Hinged sticks: why opposite is equal and adjacent is supplementary
feedback: If you expected all four angles to be equal, look at a wide, non-perpendicular crossing: two clearly larger angles and two clearly smaller, with each large–small pair summing to 180°.
If you subtracted the given from 180 to get the OPPOSITE angle, the hinge shows the opposite angle grows with the original — equal, not supplementary.
The opposite pair being equal and each adjacent pair summing to 180° are consistent: 130° + 50° = 180° on each side, and the two 130°s face each other.
activities.rationale: The dynamic hinge gives a direct counterexample to the dominant misconception (treating vertically opposite as supplementary) and to the over-generalisation that all four angles are equal, by letting pupils see opposite angles change together while adjacent angles trade off.
sourceClaims: Vertically opposite angles are EQUAL while adjacent angles are SUPPLEMENTARY, and pupils must hold the two apart; the hinged two-sticks model shows that as one angle increases so does its opposite (so they must be equal); teaching should ask pupils to find and JUSTIFY the other angles given one, using named rules rather than F/Z mnemonics
learnerActions: Model a crossing with two hinged sticks (or two rulers pinned at a point).

Open the crossing wider and watch the angle you are opening and the one directly opposite it: observe that they grow TOGETHER and appear to stay equal (the hinge illustrates this; the straight-line facts explain why they must be exactly equal).
At the same time watch an adjacent angle: as one opens the neighbour shrinks, and each adjacent pair still sums to 180°.
State in words why the two opposite angles must be equal, and why an opposite pair cannot both be found by 'take it from 180'.
Contrast with a clearly non-perpendicular crossing where the two sizes are obviously different, to check that NOT all four angles are equal — only opposite pairs are.
Optional screen version: drag one ray so the linked opposite angle updates equal in real time while the adjacent value updates to keep the pair summing to 180°.
activities.intendedInsight: At a crossing there are two distinct relationships held apart: vertically opposite angles are equal, adjacent angles are supplementary — they cannot both be 'subtract from 180'.

activities.title: Introducing the vocabulary on a labelled crossing
feedback: Opposite pairs: equal. Adjacent pairs along either straight line: sum to 180°.
A tap-reveal confirms the name of a relationship but does not set or check a solved problem; once the vocabulary is secure, move to the chaining task to practise applying it.
activities.rationale: A static or tap-to-reveal diagram efficiently introduces the naming of relationships; it is a vocabulary scaffold and does not itself require solving or chaining, so it should precede, not replace, the multi-step task.
sourceClaims: Vertically opposite angles are EQUAL while adjacent angles are SUPPLEMENTARY, and pupils must hold the two apart; the hinged two-sticks model shows that as one angle increases so does its opposite (so they must be equal); teaching should ask pupils to find and JUSTIFY the other angles given one, using named rules rather than F/Z mnemonics
learnerActions: On a static crossing-lines diagram, identify the vertically opposite pair and state the relationship: equal.
Identify an adjacent pair and state the relationship: sum to 180°.
Where available as a reveal, tap an opposite pair to confirm 'equal' and an adjacent pair to confirm 'sum to 180°'.
Name each of the four angles and say which relationship each neighbour has to it.
activities.intendedInsight: The vocabulary — vertically opposite (equal) versus adjacent (supplementary) — is attached to the right pairs on a crossing before any multi-step problem is attempted.

activities.title: Quick checks: spot the supplementary-for-opposite trap and match steps to reasons
feedback: For the opposite angle, the correct option equals the given angle; the 180−x option is the supplementary (adjacent) value and is the common error.
A step is only justified when paired with the named fact that licenses it; 'Z-angle'/'F-angle' labels do not count as reasons.
activities.rationale: Short recognition and matching items efficiently probe the key misconception and reason-naming, but they assess isolated facts; they do not require a learner to build and carry a genuine multi-step chain, so they supplement rather than replace the chaining task.
sourceClaims: Vertically opposite angles are EQUAL while adjacent angles are SUPPLEMENTARY, and pupils must hold the two apart; the hinged two-sticks model shows that as one angle increases so does its opposite (so they must be equal); teaching should ask pupils to find and JUSTIFY the other angles given one, using named rules rather than F/Z mnemonics
learnerActions: Fill in a missing angle given one angle at a crossing or on a straight line.
Answer a multiple-choice item for the angle vertically opposite a given one, where one option is the supplementary value (180−x) — choose the equal value and reject the trap.
Match each found angle in a worked solution to the exact fact that justifies it.
Set a slider or chosen value for one angle and state the resulting opposite and adjacent angles.
activities.intendedInsight: These recognition and matching items are intended to rehearse the equal-versus-supplementary distinction and the habit of naming a reason; they check isolated facts rather than demonstrate a mastered multi-step chain.

constraints: Diagrams must be presented NOT to scale so pupils cannot reliably measure or eyeball; the marks and given values carry the facts, and a reminder that the picture is not to scale is appropriate.
Every step must be justified with a named angle fact (e.g. 'angles on a straight line sum to 180°'), not with F/Z/Z-angle mnemonics — reasoning from structure generalises.

Name the WHOLE before calculating line/point unknowns (180° on a line, 360° at a point) and sanity-check against it; but do NOT apply whole-minus-parts to a vertically opposite angle — it is found by equality.
Hold the two crossing relationships apart explicitly: vertically opposite = equal, adjacent = supplementary; do not let pupils apply 'subtract from 180' to an opposite pair.
Tap-to-reveal / static diagrams introduce vocabulary only; they cannot set a problem or check a chained deduction and must not be the sole activity for the multi-step skill.

Recognition and multiple-choice items assess isolated facts and the key trap; they do not elicit an independent multi-step chain with a stated reason at each step, which requires the construction task.

Live-recolouring, dragging rays and sliders are optional ways to make the equal/supplementary relationships visible; they are illustrative, not mandatory, and a physical hinged-stick model achieves the same demonstration.

The additive and equation-based steps rely on correct arithmetic: 180−130=50, 130−40=90, and 2x+10=130 ⇒ 2x=120 ⇒ x=60; check these when authoring items and do not offer wrong partial values as valid alternatives.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support the stated teaching principles, not the specific tasks.

One cited source (National curriculum in England mathematics KS3) is marked verified:false in the row and is cited in Activity 1 as an exact copy supporting the multi-step application principle; treat its claim as unconfirmed pending a fresh check and do not read it as verified evidence.

Fixed an over-generalisation: the original 'the unknown is the whole minus the known parts' was being applied to EVERY unknown; this is only valid for line/point angles, so the guidance now scopes subtraction to those cases and states that a vertically opposite angle is found by equality, preventing reinforcement of the subtract-from-180 misconception.

The original claims that a static image 'cannot' teach the skill and that a third dimension or a persona/conversation 'adds nothing' reflect catalog fit judgements, not established comparative efficacy; these have been softened to scoped affordances/limits (e.g. static diagrams are a vocabulary scaffold). No universal necessity of the interactive format is asserted.

Arithmetic independently checked and correct: opposite of 130° is 130°; adjacent 180−130=50°; split remainder 130−40=90°; 2x+10=130 gives x=60. No dubious alternative values were carried into learner items.

probeDeeper: Point to the angle opposite 130° and ask 'how do you KNOW it's 130 and not 50?' — forcing the equal-versus-supplementary distinction into a reason
'If I opened the crossing wider, what happens to this angle and to the one next to it?' — a dynamic counterexample separating opposite from adjacent
'The diagram isn't drawn to scale — why can you still be sure of your answer?' — pressing that the facts, not the picture, license the deduction
'You found this angle was 90° — where does that value come from, and what can you now work out with it?' — checking they can carry a result forward
assess.correctAnswer: For (a): the angle vertically opposite 130° is 130° (vertically opposite equal); the two adjacent angles are 50° each (angles on a straight line sum to 180°). For (b): the split angle totals 130° (vertically opposite the 130°), so the remaining part is 130−40 = 90°. For (c): 2x+10 = 130 (vertically opposite equal), so 2x = 120, x = 60. Each step is justified by a named angle fact, not by measuring.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats vertically opposite angles as supplementary — subtracts from 180 to find the opposite angle ('they're next to each other so they add to 180')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach the crossing as two relationships held apart — opposite EQUAL, adjacent supplementary — with the hinged-sticks model: as one angle opens, its opposite opens equally
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On (a)/(c) gives 50° (or 180−value) for the angle vertically OPPOSITE the given one, instead of the equal value

errorPatterns.pattern: Over-generalises that all four angles at a crossing are equal ('they're all made by the same two lines, so they're the same')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast with a clearly non-perpendicular crossing where the two sizes are obviously different; establish that only opposite pairs are equal, adjacent pairs sum to 180°
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reports all four angles as 130° (or all equal), ignoring the supplementary adjacent pair

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses the wrong whole — treats a straight line as 360° or a point as 180° when setting up the calculation
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name the whole aloud before calculating — half-turn 180° on a line, whole-turn 360° at a point — and sanity-check the answer against it
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Subtracts from the wrong total (e.g. 360−130 for an angle on a straight line), giving an out-of-range or impossible answer

errorPatterns.pattern: Finds the first angle correctly but cannot chain — doesn't carry a found value into the next step, or makes an arithmetic slip mid-chain
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold by writing each found angle onto the diagram before the next step so it becomes a visible given; do not reteach the facts — the reasoning is sound, the chain just needs support
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gets the first unknown right then stalls on (b), or the individual facts are right but the final chained value is wrong through a slip

responseLevels.gap: Cannot apply the facts reliably — treats vertically opposite as supplementary, uses the wrong whole, or measures the not-to-scale diagram; single angles come out wrong
responseLevels.full: Chains multiple facts to find several angles, naming the reason at each step, carries found values forward, and sets up and solves an equation for an unknown — transferring to a new configuration and justifying from structure not appearance
responseLevels.partial: Finds single angles using one fact each and can state the facts, but cannot chain them across the diagram, mis-handles the equation, or reverts to measuring — has the facts as isolated statements, not as tools that combine

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a NOT-TO-SCALE diagram: two straight lines crossing at a point, with one of the four angles marked 130°, plus a third ray splitting the angle opposite into two parts, one of which is marked 40°. Set them to: (a) find the three unmarked angles at the crossing and, for each, say the fact they used; (b) find the remaining part of the split angle; then (c) here two vertically opposite angles are labelled (2x+10)° and 130° — write and solve an equation for x. Watch whether they treat the opposite angle as equal or as 180 minus, whether they name a reason at each step, and whether they carry found angles forward rather than measuring the picture.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who holds the facts gives 130° for the opposite angle and 50° for the adjacent, naming each; a child with the common error gives 50° for the OPPOSITE angle (treating it as supplementary) — a visibly different answer. The not-to-scale figure means a child who measures lands wrong, and the multi-step chain and the equation reveal whether the facts are merely recognised or can be applied and carried forward.

sources.claim: Angle measure is additive: a whole angle decomposed into parts is the sum of the parts, and unknown angles are found by writing an equation with a symbol for the unknown
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, 4.MD.C.7

sources.claim: Pupils should apply the properties of angles at a point, angles on a straight line, and vertically opposite angles to find unknown angles in multi-step problems

pedagogy.summary: Multiplying a fraction by a whole number, understood as repeated addition of a unit fraction: a/b is a multiple of 1/b, so 5 × 1/4 is five quarters (5/4) and n × a/b = (n×a)/b. The whole number multiplies the COUNT of unit parts while the denominator — the size of the part — stays fixed. This is the first fraction multiplication and the bridge from 'a/b as a sum of 1/b' to the general product; taught on a model, 4 × 3/8 is simply four lots of three-eighths = twelve eighths.
bestPractices: Build from repeated addition: 4 × 3/8 = 3/8 + 3/8 + 3/8 + 3/8, so the numerators accumulate and the eighth stays the unit.
State the rule as scaling the count only: n × a/b = (n×a)/b, with the denominator unchanged because the unit doesn't change.
Use number lines and bars where n jumps of a/b land past one whole, then re-group into a mixed number (5 × 1/4 = 5/4 = 1 1/4).
For a mixed number × whole, multiply EVERY part (2 1/3 × 3 = three 2s and three thirds = 6 + 3/3 = 7), ideally via the improper form 7/3 × 3.
Contrast with addition of fractions so children don't blur the two procedures.
keyRepresentations: Number line with repeated equal jumps of the unit/non-unit fraction
Fraction bars showing n copies of a/b combined
Repeated-addition equation aligned with the (n×a)/b rule
Improper↔mixed conversion of the product (6/5 = 1 1/5)
commonMisconceptions: Multiplies the denominator too: 4 × 3/8 = 12/32, applying the whole number to both parts instead of just the count of unit fractions.
Incompletely distributes over a mixed number: 2 1/3 × 3 = 6 1/3, multiplying the whole but forgetting the fraction part.
Confuses the operation with addition (adds 4 + 3/8) or cannot see 5 × 1/4 as five quarters.

learn.summary: Multiplying a fraction by a whole number as repeated addition of a unit fraction: a/b is a multiple of 1/b, so 5 × 1/4 is five quarters (5/4), and n × a/b = (n×a)/b. The whole number scales the COUNT of unit parts while the denominator — the size of each part — stays fixed. For a mixed number × whole, every part is multiplied (2 1/3 × 3 = three 2s and three thirds = 6 + 3/3 = 7; equivalently 7/3 × 3 = 21/3 = 7). This is the bridge from 'a/b as a sum of 1/b' to the general product.

activities.title: Jump-counter number line for n × a/b
feedback: If a learner expects the denominator to change, point to the fixed jump size: the eighth is the step, so four hops of three-eighths are still measured in eighths — only how many eighths grows.
If four 3/8 hops are read as landing before one whole, recount the hops aloud (3/8, 6/8, 9/8, 12/8) and mark where 8/8 = one whole falls so the past-one total is seen.
In mixed-number mode, if only the whole part is tripled, point to the three separate thirds in the three bars: three thirds make a whole, so 2 1/3 × 3 is 7, not 6 1/3.
Prompt: 'Should four lots of 3/8 be bigger or smaller than one 3/8?' to check the answer grew.
activities.rationale: An interactive number line/bar where the learner controls the number of jumps but the jump size is locked makes the count-scales-not-the-unit idea watchable, enacting repeated addition that underlies the rule. A mixed-number mode showing copies of the whole bar makes complete distribution visible. Efficacy over other media is not established; this is a proposed design on its stated affordance.
sourceClaims: Non-unit fractions are composed of unit fractions (3/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4); this repeated-addition composition is the conceptual basis for multiplying a fraction by a whole number, and understanding why procedures work reduces forgetting/confusing them.
Pupils should understand a/b as a multiple of 1/b and multiply a fraction (and mixed number) by a whole number, e.g. n × a/b, supported by visual models.
learnerActions: Set the jump size to 3/8 and dial the number of jumps to 4; watch four identical hops march along the line and land on 12/8.
Re-group the landing point into a mixed number: 12/8 = 1 4/8 (= 1 1/2).

Keep the jump size fixed and change only how many jumps there are for n × 1/4 with n = 3, 5, 8, each time reading off the total count of quarters and converting past-one results to mixed or whole numbers (e.g. 5 × 1/4 = 5/4 = 1 1/4; 8 × 1/4 = 8/4 = 2).
Switch to a mixed-number mode: lay three whole 2 1/3 bars end to end so every part is tripled, and read that three 2s and three thirds make 6 + 3/3 = 7.
Say aloud what changed and what stayed the same after each build: the unit (the eighth, the third) never changed, only how many of them there were.
activities.intendedInsight: Because the unit part stays the same size, multiplying by a whole number only multiplies the COUNT of parts: n × a/b = (n×a)/b, with the denominator unchanged. A mixed number × whole requires multiplying every part.

activities.title: Build from repeated addition before stating the rule
feedback: If a learner adds the whole number to the fraction (4 + 3/8), re-read the expression as 'four lots of three-eighths' and lay out the four copies to be summed.
When converting 12/8, ask how many eighths make one whole (8) so the mixed number 1 4/8 is reasoned, not guessed.
activities.rationale: Explicitly connecting the repeated-addition form to the (n×a)/b rule, and contrasting with the additive error, targets the common error of confusing the two operations and grounds the procedure in why it works.
sourceClaims: Non-unit fractions are composed of unit fractions (3/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4); this repeated-addition composition is the conceptual basis for multiplying a fraction by a whole number, and understanding why procedures work reduces forgetting/confusing them.
learnerActions: Write 4 × 3/8 as 3/8 + 3/8 + 3/8 + 3/8 and add the numerators while keeping the eighth as the unit, reaching 12/8.
Contrast this with the additive slip of adding the whole number to the fraction (e.g. 4 + 3/8) and explain in words how multiplication differs from addition, so the operations are not blurred.
Convert the improper product to a mixed number (12/8 = 1 1/2; 6/5 = 1 1/5) and back, naming how many whole ones and what is left over.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplication of a unit or non-unit fraction by a whole number is accumulation of equal parts; the numerators accumulate and the denominator is the unchanging unit. This is distinct from adding a whole number to a fraction.

activities.title: Targeted practice that baits the multiply-denominator error
feedback: For the 12/32 option: compute 12/32 and notice it equals 3/8 — the answer did not grow, so it cannot be four lots of 3/8.
For a 6 1/3 answer to 2 1/3 × 3: ask explicitly 'what is three lots of one-third?' (3/3 = 1 whole), then replace the single 1/3 with that whole: 6 + 1 = 7.
activities.rationale: Scorable items with a pre-identified distractor surface the two documented misconceptions and ask for justification, so the response reveals whether the unit is held fixed and every part scaled. Fixed items elicit recognition/computation and can check these errors but do not by themselves require the learner to construct the model or justify aloud.
learnerActions: Complete fill-in equations such as '4 × 3/8 = _/8 = 1 _/8', writing the missing count and the mixed number.
Choose the correct value of 4 × 3/8 from options that include 12/32 (denominator wrongly multiplied), then justify why 12/32 cannot be right.
Order n × 1/4 for n = 3, 5, 8 from smallest to largest and, where it exceeds one, state each as a mixed number or whole number (5/4 = 1 1/4; 8/4 = 2).
Work 2 1/3 × 3, showing both the part-by-part method and the improper-fraction method (7/3 × 3 = 21/3 = 7).
activities.intendedInsight: Fraction × whole and mixed × whole can be computed reliably by scaling the count and keeping the unit fixed; the multiply-denominator slip gives an answer equal to the original fraction, which therefore cannot be four lots of it — a whole-number multiple greater than one must be larger than the original.

constraints: A static worked example (e.g. tapping 5/4 to reveal five quarter-pieces) can anchor the idea but does not let the learner build and vary the jumps; use it as a reference, not the main construction activity.

Multiple-choice and fill-in items elicit recognition and computation and can bait the denominator error, but do not by themselves require independent construction of the repeated-addition model or spoken justification; pair them with build-and-explain work.
Keep the unit (denominator) genuinely fixed in any model so the learner changes only the count; the pedagogical point is lost if the part size appears to change.
For mixed numbers, ensure the model or working shows EVERY part multiplied; only tripling the whole part reproduces the incomplete-distribution error.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One listed source (CCSS-M 4.NF.4 / DfE) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its citation as unconfirmed.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 4 × 3/8 = 12/8 = 1 4/8 = 1 1/2 ✓; 5 × 1/4 = 5/4 = 1 1/4 ✓; 2 1/3 × 3 = 7 (6 + 3/3), and 7/3 × 3 = 21/3 = 7 ✓; 3 × 2/5 = 6/5 = 1 1/5 ✓; 6/5 = 1 1/5 ✓. The distractor 12/32 reduces to 3/8 ✓ — retained only as an incorrect option to be refuted, never as a valid answer.

Note on multiples: 3/8 is trivially the 1× multiple of itself; activity[2] insight now says the slip answer cannot be FOUR lots of the original (must be larger), avoiding the false claim that a fraction cannot be a multiple of itself.

The 3D and conversation artefact ratings in the source asserted these media add nothing / cannot teach this; such comparative-necessity claims are not established by catalog ratings and have been dropped rather than restated as universal laws. A number-line/bar model was retained on its stated affordance (locked unit with variable count), not as the only possible medium.

probeDeeper: Show me 5 × 1/4 as a repeated addition — how many quarters is that altogether?
A friend says 4 × 3/8 = 12/32. Work out what 12/32 is — is it bigger than 3/8? Should four lots of 3/8 be bigger or smaller than 3/8?
In 2 1/3 × 3, did you multiply BOTH the 2 and the 1/3 by 3? What is three lots of one-third?
Your answer 12/8 — how many whole ones is that, and what's left over?

errorPatterns.pattern: Multiplies the denominator as well as the numerator: '4 times 3 is 12, 4 times 8 is 32, so 12/32' — applies the whole number to both parts.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to repeated addition on a number line: 4 × 3/8 is four hops of three-eighths; the eighth (the unit) never changes, only how many. Contrast 12/32 = 3/8 — the answer didn't grow, so it can't be four lots.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 12/32 (or reduces it back to 3/8); the denominator changes when it shouldn't.

errorPatterns.pattern: Incompletely distributes over the mixed number: '2 1/3 times 3 is 6 1/3' — multiplies the whole part but leaves the fraction part unmultiplied.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show three whole 2 1/3 bars: three 2s AND three thirds; or convert to 7/3 first and multiply. Emphasise every part is copied three times.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer keeps the original fraction part (6 1/3) instead of tripling it; only the 2 was multiplied.

responseLevels.gap: Multiplies the denominator too (12/32) or treats the problem additively; cannot see 5 × 1/4 as five quarters.
responseLevels.full: Computes n × a/b = (n×a)/b keeping the denominator fixed, multiplies every part of a mixed number, converts to a mixed-number answer, and justifies via repeated addition; transfers to a new case.
responseLevels.partial: Gets fraction × whole by the rule (12/8) but falters on mixed numbers (incomplete distribution) or can't connect the rule to repeated addition of unit fractions.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these out, showing how you get each: 4 × 3/8, and 2 1/3 × 3. Write each answer as a mixed number where it helps.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who sees a/b as a multiple of the unit fraction multiplies only the count: 4 × 3/8 = twelve eighths, denominator fixed. Multiplying the denominator too (12/32) reveals the whole number is being wrongly applied to the size of the part. The mixed-number case exposes incomplete distribution — multiplying the whole but not the fraction part (6 1/3). Watching the working, not just the answer, shows whether the unit is held fixed and every part is scaled.

sources.claim: Non-unit fractions are composed of unit fractions (3/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4); this repeated-addition composition is the conceptual basis for multiplying a fraction by a whole number, and understanding why procedures work reduces forgetting/confusing them.
sources.source: IES/WWC Practice Guide, Developing Effective Fractions Instruction for K–8 (Siegler et al., 2010), Recs 1 & 3

sources.claim: Pupils should understand a/b as a multiple of 1/b and multiply a fraction (and mixed number) by a whole number, e.g. n × a/b, supported by visual models.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 6-7 (Y2). Understand that the two digits of a two-digit number represent amounts of TENS and ONES: in 47, the 4 means 4 tens (40) and the 7 means 7 ones. This is the central node of early place value — the tens/ones column idea that every later place-value column extends.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y2): 'recognise the place value of each digit in a two-digit number (tens, ones)'; 'identify, represent and estimate numbers using different representations, including the number line'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.NBT.2 'understand that the two digits of a two-digit number represent amounts of tens and ones' with 1.NBT.2a/b/c; consolidated in 2.NBT.1.
• Operational details — Build every two-digit number CONCRETELY first (bundled tens + loose ones), then match to the written numeral and to expanded form (47 = 40 + 7). Insist the child reads the tens digit as a QUANTITY OF TENS, not the face value ('four tens', not 'four'). Contrast standard partition (47 = 40 + 7) with non-standard partition (47 = 30 + 17) once secure, because flexible partitioning underpins later column addition/subtraction.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 6): with base-ten blocks present, build 47 and say '4 tens and 7 ones'. Tier B (age 6-7): given 47 with no blocks, state the value of each digit (40 and 7) and write 47 = 40 + 7. Tier C (age 7): identify the tens/ones digit in any two-digit number and give a non-standard partition (47 = 30 + 17).
bestPractices: Follow the CPA sequence: bundle ten loose ones into a labelled 'ten' (concrete), draw it as a ten-rod/line (pictorial), then link to the numeral 47 and expanded form 40+7 (abstract) — never leave the digit floating free of a quantity.
Use a place-value chart with only two columns (tens | ones) and physically place bundled tens in the tens column and loose ones in the ones column so the position IS the meaning.
Read the digits by value out loud — '4 tens' and '7 ones' — and resist 'four, seven'; language that names the unit prevents the digits-are-just-two-separate-numbers error.
Introduce non-standard partitioning (47 = 30 + 17) deliberately once standard partitioning is secure, so children see the tens/ones split as flexible, not a single fixed answer.
Use 'the same number, many ways' tasks: show 47 as blocks, as 40+7, as a point on a 0-100 line, and as a bead string of 4 tens + 7 — same quantity, different representation.
keyRepresentations: Base-ten blocks (tens rods + unit cubes) — the canonical proportional model where a ten is physically ten ones
Two-column tens|ones place-value chart with bundled tens and loose ones placed in position
Expanded-form / part-whole (cherry) diagram: 47 splits into 40 and 7
Bead strings and ten-frames grouped into complete tens plus extras
Arrow/place-value cards (40 and 7) that physically overlap to build 47, making expanded form tangible
commonMisconceptions: Reading the tens digit as its face value — treating the 4 in 47 as 'four' rather than 'forty/four tens'.
Concatenation error: thinking 47 is '4 and 7' side by side (so 4+7=11 or two separate numbers) rather than 40+7.
Digit-reversal / transposition — writing or building 74 for 47 because spoken language and column order are conflated (a hangover from the teen-number naming trap).
Believing a number can only be partitioned one way (47 = 40 + 7 only), missing 47 = 30 + 17, which blocks later regrouping in subtraction.
Losing the unit when there are zero ones — thinking a decade like 40 has 'no place value in the ones' rather than 4 tens and 0 ones.

learn.summary: For ages 6-7 (Y2 / US Grade 1-2), build the understanding that the two digits of a two-digit number stand for a quantity of tens and a quantity of ones: in 47, the 4 means 4 tens (40) and the 7 means 7 ones. Centre the learning on concrete grouping — bundling ten loose ones into one ten — then link that quantity to the written numeral, to expanded form (47 = 40 + 7), and to flexible (non-standard) partitioning (47 = 30 + 17). Read digits by value ('four tens', 'seven ones'), never as bare faces.

activities.title: Bundling: ten ones become one ten
feedback: If the child says 'the 4 means four', have them count the single cubes inside the four bundles: there are forty, so the 4 is worth 4 tens = 40.

If the child places tens in the ones column (or vice versa), name the columns again — tens on the left, ones on the right — and compare 47 with 74 built side by side so the positions are visibly different quantities.
When partitioning as 30 + 17, confirm by re-counting the whole pile: if it is still 47, the split is valid; the quantity is conserved even though the grouping changed.
If the child thinks a decade like 40 has 'nothing' in the ones, show 40 as four tens and zero loose ones — the ones place is still there, holding none.
activities.rationale: Place value is a quantity re-seen as grouped units. Acting out the bundling (ten ones fusing into one ten) makes unitising something the child does rather than a label they repeat, which is the standard concrete-first (CPA) route and is intended to target the face-value and concatenation errors.
sourceClaims: 1.NBT.2 states the two digits of a two-digit number represent amounts of tens and ones, with 10 as a bundle of ten ones.
Explicit CPA (concrete-pictorial-abstract) sequencing and standard/non-standard partitioning are recommended for building place-value understanding.
learnerActions: Set out a two-column mat labelled 'tens' on the left and 'ones' on the right.
Drop loose cubes one at a time into the ones column; each time you reach ten loose cubes, bundle those ten into a single labelled 'ten' (a rod) and move it to the tens column.
Build 47 by placing four bundled tens in the tens column and seven loose ones in the ones column.
Say aloud 'four tens and seven ones', then write the numeral 47 and the expanded form 47 = 40 + 7.
Break one of the four tens back into ten loose ones and re-count: show the pile is still 47 but now reads as 30 + 17.
activities.intendedInsight: The '4' in 47 is not 'four' — it is four whole bundles of ten (40). Position gives the digit its value, and the same quantity can be split in more than one way without changing how much there is.

activities.title: Many ways to show the same number
feedback: If the child marks 47 near the wrong end of the line, count up in tens (10, 20, 30, 40) then on by ones to locate it.
For 44, if the child says both 4s mean the same, point to the place of each: the left 4 sits in the tens column (40), the right 4 in the ones column (4).
If the child drops the ones place for 40, have them state it as '4 tens and 0 ones' to keep the place visible.
If the arrow cards are read as '4' and '7', separate then re-overlap them so the '40' card is seen whole underneath the '7'.
activities.rationale: Linking multiple representations of one quantity is intended to build the flexible, connected understanding named in the Y2 standard, including representing numbers on a number line, and guards against treating each representation as a separate fact.
sourceClaims: Y2 pupils should recognise the place value of each digit in a two-digit number (tens, ones) and identify/represent/estimate numbers using different representations including the number line.
learnerActions: Take one number, e.g. 47, and represent it several ways: as bundled tens + loose ones, as expanded form 40 + 7, as a part-whole (cherry) diagram with 47 at the top splitting into 40 and 7, as a point marked at 47 on a 0-100 number line, as a bead string of 4 tens plus 7 beads, and by overlapping arrow/place-value cards (a '40' card with a '7' card sliding over it to read 47).
Check that every representation is the same quantity by counting back to 47 each time.
Repeat with a decade number such as 40 and with a number containing a repeated digit such as 44, explaining why the two 4s in 44 are worth different amounts (40 and 4).
activities.intendedInsight: A number is a single quantity that can be shown in many different ways; the tens/ones meaning stays the same across blocks, numerals, expanded form, the part-whole diagram, arrow cards, and the number line.

activities.title: Convince me the 4 means forty
feedback: Accept any justification that ties the digit to its place and counts the underlying ones (four tens = forty).
If the child only restates 'it's forty because it is', ask them to point to and count the actual tens to ground the claim.
Treat this as a short follow-up after concrete building, not a substitute for it — the child's reasoning can then be tied to bundles they have actually handled.
activities.rationale: A brief reasoning prompt may surface whether the child attaches the digit to its place or is reciting; it is proposed to work best as consolidation after hands-on grouping rather than as the first encounter, since the concept is grounded in manipulating quantities. Discussion alone can elicit an explanation but does not itself provide the physical grouping.
learnerActions: Respond to the challenge: 'Convince me the 4 in 47 is worth forty, not four.'
Justify using a model you built — e.g. 'because the 4 is four bundles, and each bundle is ten, so that is forty.'
Extend to a prove-it task: 'Show that the two 4s in 44 are worth different amounts.'
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to explain and defend why a digit's value comes from its place cements the idea beyond stating the rule.

activities.title: Check and sort by place value
feedback: For a swap error, rebuild 47 and 74 side by side so the different tens counts are visible.
For 4 + 7 = 11, show that the digits are not added together; the 4 counts tens and the 7 counts ones, giving 40 + 7 = 47.
For 47 = 30 + ___, confirm the missing part is 17 by regrouping one ten into ten ones.
For 47 = ___ + 7, confirm the missing part is 40 (four tens).
activities.rationale: Targeted checks that include the two headline distractors (transposition, 74, and adding the digits at face value, 11) can confirm the idea is held and probe the specific misconceptions. A check or sort can classify and verify a child's answers but does not itself elicit the physical grouping, so pair it with the building activity.
learnerActions: Complete expanded-form blanks, e.g. 47 = ___ + 7 and 47 = 30 + ___.
Choose which picture shows 4 tens and 7 ones, and match written numerals to their block pictures.
Sort or state, for a given two-digit number, which digit is the tens digit and which is the ones digit, and the value of each.
Consider tempting wrong answers — e.g. 74 (digits swapped) and 11 (adding 4 + 7) — and explain why each is wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure recall that each digit's value is fixed by its place, and conscious rejection of the swap error (74) and the digit-adding/face-value error (11, from adding 4 + 7).

constraints: Always build a two-digit number concretely first (bundled tens + loose ones), then connect it to the numeral and expanded form; never leave a digit floating free of a quantity.
Read digits by unit aloud — 'four tens', 'seven ones' — not 'four, seven'; naming the unit prevents the digits-as-two-separate-numbers error.
Introduce non-standard partitioning (47 = 30 + 17) only once standard partitioning (47 = 40 + 7) is secure.
A fixed labelled picture of 47-with-blocks is a useful reference anchor but shows one number only and does not let the child perform the bundling; use it alongside, not instead of, hands-on grouping.
Recognition and fill-in-the-blank checks can confirm the idea is held and classify answers but do not on their own build the unitising insight; use them for consolidation and diagnosis.

The reasoning/convince-me prompt is proposed as a short follow-up after concrete work; grouping quantities may help young children reach this insight more reliably than discussion alone, but this comparison is not established by the provided sources.

A dynamic model where ten cubes snap into one rod (and a rod breaks back into ten) is one way to make bundling visible; physical bundles, bead strings, ten-frames, part-whole (cherry) diagrams, and overlapping arrow/place-value cards are equally valid concrete and pictorial routes.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Of the cited sources, the row marks the DfE National Curriculum claim as verified and the CCSS-M (1.NBT.2) and NCETM claims as unverified; confidence levels were not upgraded here.

The original labelled the topic the 'central node' of place value and asserted that a 3D rendering 'adds nothing' and that an interactive drag model makes insight 'felt, not told'. These are catalog-fit opinions, not established efficacy claims; they have been softened to scoped, proposed wording. Whether a dynamic auto-bundling model outperforms physical bundling for this age is not established by the sources provided.
The original flagged 'tens-and-ones is an inherently planar concept' to justify dropping 3D; retained only as a design preference, not a universal law.

Arrow/place-value cards (40 and 7 overlapping to build 47) and the part-whole (cherry) diagram, both present in the original key representations, had been dropped from or thinned in the candidate and are restored in the 'Many ways' activity and the concrete-routes constraint.

The assessment/check activity previously carried 1.NBT.2 as a sourceClaim; since its rationale states an assessment-design principle rather than the sourced content, the sourceClaims were set to [] (the tens/ones content remains sourced in the building activity).

probeDeeper: Build 47 with tens and ones — how many tens did you use?
Is the 4 worth more or less than the 7? Why?
If I swap the digits to 74, what changed and by how much?
assess.correctAnswer: The 4 is worth 4 tens (40); the 7 is worth 7 ones. Because in a two-digit number the left digit counts tens and the right digit counts ones.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the digit at face value: 'the 4 means four'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build 47 with 4 tens rods and 7 ones; count the ones inside the rods (40). Say 'the 4 is in the tens place, so it's 4 tens = 40'.
errorPatterns.distractor: The 4 means four.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says the 4 stands for four ones/things rather than four tens.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses which digit is tens and which is ones (reads right-to-left)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name the columns explicitly (tens on the left, ones on the right); build and compare 47 vs 74 to fix the positions.
errorPatterns.distractor: The 4 means four ones and the 7 means seven tens.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child calls the 7 the tens or says 47 is 'seven tens and four ones'.

responseLevels.gap: Reads both digits at face value or reverses tens and ones.
responseLevels.full: States the 4 is 4 tens (40) and the 7 is 7 ones, and can build/partition the number by place.
responseLevels.partial: Identifies the tens digit but is shaky on its value (says '4' not '40').

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Write 47. Point to the 4, then the 7. Ask: 'What is the 4 worth, and what is the 7 worth? How do you know?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with tens-and-ones place value says the 4 is worth 40; a face-value thinker says the 4 'means four'. The reason tier reveals whether they attach the digit to its place (tens) or read both digits as bare counts.

sources.claim: Y2 pupils should recognise the place value of each digit in a two-digit number (tens, ones) and identify/represent/estimate numbers using different representations including the number line.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (Key Stage 1, Year 2 Number & place value)

sources.claim: 1.NBT.2 states the two digits of a two-digit number represent amounts of tens and ones, with 10 as a bundle of ten ones.
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Number & Operations in Base Ten (Grade 1)

sources.claim: Explicit CPA (concrete-pictorial-abstract) sequencing and standard/non-standard partitioning are recommended for building place-value understanding.
sources.source: NCETM Primary Mastery Professional Development — Place Value materials

pedagogy.summary: Adding up to four two-digit numbers is where the properties of operations become a practical tool: because addition is commutative and associative, children may reorder and regroup the addends to make the work easier — hunting for pairs that make a multiple of ten, then partitioning the rest into tens and ones. The efficiency insight (look before you leap) matters as much as accuracy; the composing of several tens at once is the new demand over two-addend work.
bestPractices: Teach 'look for pairs that make ten (or a multiple of ten)' before adding — reorder using commutativity/associativity (extends adding three one-digit numbers)
Partition all addends into tens and ones, sum the tens, sum the ones, then recombine — composing as many tens/hundreds as needed
Encourage jottings to keep track when combining many ones, to prevent accumulation slips
Discuss which grouping was smartest and why, so the properties are used deliberately not accidentally
Use manipulatives/ten-frames so 'making a ten' from a pair is seen, then move to numbers
keyRepresentations: Ten-frames / bead strings (spotting pairs that make ten)
Draggable number cards (reorder addends to pair)
Part-whole / column jottings (tens together, ones together)
Number line (cumulative jumps)
Base-ten blocks (composing several tens)
commonMisconceptions: Adding strictly left-to-right and missing pairs that make ten (not using commutativity to simplify)
Losing track when combining many ones, or forgetting to compose more than one ten (ones sum to 23, only one ten carried)
Believing the addends must be added in the given order (no reordering allowed)
Miscounting during a long running total

learn.summary: Children add up to four two-digit numbers by using the commutative and associative properties as a practical tool: reorder and regroup addends to find pairs that make a multiple of ten, then partition the rest into tens and ones, sum each, and recombine. The 'look before you leap' efficiency insight matters alongside accuracy, and composing several tens at once is the new demand over two-addend work. The strongest version lets the child physically reorder addends and see pairs combine into round numbers; recognition tasks and static ringed examples are useful rehearsal and reference, but because they do not themselves require the child to reorder addends they check the strategy more than they elicit the independent habit of looking for pairs first.

activities.title: Snap the pairs that make a tidy number
feedback: If the child adds left-to-right without scanning, don't reteach addition: ask 'before you start, can you see any two that make a tidy number?' and let them re-experience the shortcut.
When two cards combine into a round number (e.g. 15 and 25 becoming 40), name it: 'those two made exactly 40, so now you only have round numbers left.'

If the child insists the numbers must stay in the written order, demonstrate with counters that the total is the same in any order, and connect it to adding three one-digit numbers where pairing to ten was allowed.

OPTIONAL: on a screen version, cards whose sum is a multiple of ten can snap into a labelled '40' or '20' block, remaining tens and ones can auto-partition and recombine to show the composed tens, and a side-by-side 'left-to-right vs paired' race can make the efficiency gain visible. These are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete, not required features.
activities.rationale: Physically reordering and watching pairs fuse into round numbers rewards spotting the number bond and makes the commutative/associative strategy deliberate rather than accidental. Reordering to check and simplify is the curriculum route by which these properties are established at this stage.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils add three one-digit numbers and, building on this, add numbers including combining several addends; adding numbers in a different order is used to check and establishes commutativity and associativity.
Choosing an efficient order of addition (identifying two addends that make ten) uses the associative and commutative laws; children need not use the formal terms at this stage.
learnerActions: Take four addends to add, e.g. 15, 8, 25, and 12, arranged as cards that can be physically moved (paper cards, counters on a tray, or draggable on-screen tiles).
Before adding anything, scan the four numbers and decide which two, placed together, would make a multiple of ten.
Pair 15 with 25 to make 40, and 8 with 12 to make 20, then add the two round numbers: 40 + 20 = 60.
Repeat with 24, 17, 6, 13 (24+6=30 and 17+13=30, giving 60) and say aloud which pair you spotted first and why.
Try one example by adding strictly left-to-right, then again by pairing first, and compare how much easier the paired route felt.
activities.intendedInsight: Because addition can be done in any order and grouping, reordering to make pairs that total a multiple of ten turns a fearsome four-number sum into an easy sum of round numbers. The properties of operations are a lever, not an abstraction.

activities.title: Partition into tens and ones, and compose the tens carefully
feedback: If the answer is off by exactly ten, the child likely composed one ten from the ones and dropped a second: have them pool all the ones again and count how many full tens they can make.
Encourage jottings to track the running total of ones so slips don't accumulate.
If the tens are right but the total drifts, slow the recombination step and check how many tens came out of the ones.
activities.rationale: Composing several tens at once is the genuinely new demand of four-addend work; pooling all ones before exchanging and making the exchange visible with base-ten targets the specific 'dropped a composed ten' error.
learnerActions: Take all four addends and split each into its tens and its ones: for 15, 8, 25, 12 the tens are 10, 0, 20, 10 (the single-digit 8 has no tens) and the ones are 5, 8, 5, 2.
Add all the tens together (10 + 0 + 20 + 10 = 40), then pool ALL the ones together before exchanging.

From the pooled ones, exchange every full ten you can: here 5 + 8 + 5 + 2 = 20, which makes two tens and no leftover ones; if the ones had totalled 23 you would make two tens (not one) and keep 3 ones.
Recombine the composed tens with the tens you already had (40 + 20 = 60) and check it matches the paired-up method.
Use base-ten blocks or ten-frames so that making more than one ten from the ones is something you can see, not just carry in your head.
activities.intendedInsight: When many ones are combined they can compose more than one ten. Pooling all the ones and exchanging every full ten before recombining is a reliable way to make sure no composed ten is lost. If a composed ten is dropped, the answer comes out ten too small, or more than ten too small if several tens are dropped.

activities.title: Explain and defend the smartest grouping
feedback: If the child can solve but can't explain, ask them to point to the pair that made a round number and say the new, simpler sum it created.
Accept informal language; the formal terms 'commutative' and 'associative' are not required at this stage.
If the child spots pairs only when prompted, praise the find and ask them to scan unprompted on the next sum to build the habit.
activities.rationale: Articulating the strategy distinguishes a child using the properties deliberately from one who adds accurately but never looks for simplifying pairs; reasoning about reordering is how the curriculum establishes commutativity and associativity.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils add three one-digit numbers and, building on this, add numbers including combining several addends; adding numbers in a different order is used to check and establishes commutativity and associativity.
Choosing an efficient order of addition (identifying two addends that make ten) uses the associative and commutative laws; children need not use the formal terms at this stage.
learnerActions: After solving a four-addend sum, say which two numbers you added first and why that order made the work easier.
Answer 'you added them in a different order than they're written — does that change the answer, and how do you know?'
Given 19 + 4 + 1 + 6, decide which you would add first and justify it (19 + 1 makes 20, then + 4 + 6 reaches 30).
Pick a sum where no neat pair exists and explain what you do then (partition into tens and ones).
activities.intendedInsight: Explaining the chosen grouping makes the properties a conscious, reusable strategy and shows that reordering never changes the total.

constraints: Prerequisite: pairing numbers to make ten (as in adding three one-digit numbers) and exchanging ten ones for a ten; revisit these if a child insists order is fixed or loses a composed ten.

Recognition-style tasks (matching pairs that make ten, choosing the smartest first step, filling blanks in running totals) rehearse and check the strategy and can catch left-to-right grinding, but because they do not require the child to reorder the addends themselves they do not on their own elicit the independent habit of looking for pairs first; pair them with tasks where the child reorders the addends.
A static worked example with the pairs ringed is useful reference but does not let the child try reordering; use it alongside, not instead of, hands-on regrouping.
Manipulatives (ten-frames, bead strings, base-ten blocks) should make 'making a ten' and composing several tens visible before moving to numbers alone.
Keep sums engineered so tidy pairs exist when teaching the strategy, but also include a sum with no neat pair so the child learns the fallback of partitioning into tens and ones.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched and the listed source claims retain their original verification status (one marked verified, one not). Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The original 'worked correct answer' example lists ones such as 5+8+5+2=20 for the first sum (composing two tens), consistent with the 'ones can exceed ten' point; retained as-is.

The original row asserted '3D adds nothing' and 'talk cannot supply the manipulation-and-feedback practice the strategy needs'. These comparative/necessity claims are not established by the sources and have been softened: spoken discussion is used productively in the explain/defend activity, and the hands-on reordering is proposed on its affordances (physical regrouping and feedback) rather than as the only possible medium.

Comparative efficacy wording in the summary was tightened to the observable limit that recognition/static tasks do not require the child to reorder; no claim of tested superiority of any medium is made.

probeDeeper: Before adding, did any two of these numbers jump out as making a tidy total? Which?
You added them in a different order than they're written — does that change the answer? How do you know?
Your ones added up to more than ten — how many tens did you make from them?
If I gave you 19 + 4 + 1 + 6, which would you add first, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: 60 and 60. Efficiently: 15+25=40 and 8+12=20 → 60; 24+6=30 and 17+13=30 → 60. Alternatively partition all into tens and ones (tens 10+20+... , ones summed and composed). Both reach 60; the strategy question is whether pairs are spotted.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds strictly left-to-right, never scanning for pairs that make ten — '15 and 8 is 23, and 25 is 48…'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach addition; prompt 'before you start, can you see any two that make a tidy number?' and let them re-experience the shortcut. Build the looking-first habit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child works in given order with no pause to look for bonds; the skill of pairing is available but not deployed

errorPatterns.pattern: Loses a composed ten when combining many ones — ones total 23 but only one ten is carried, or the running total drifts
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have the child pool ALL the ones first and exchange as many tens as possible before recombining; use base-ten so multiple composed tens are visible.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The tens are right but the answer is off by ten; the child composed one ten from the ones and dropped the second

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes the numbers must be added in the order written — resists reordering
errorPatterns.nextMove: Demonstrate with counters that the total is the same in any order; connect to adding three one-digit numbers where pairing to ten was allowed.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When invited to reorder, the child says you can't, or that it would change the answer

responseLevels.gap: Adds left-to-right, drops composed tens, or insists order is fixed; answers unreliable and slow.
responseLevels.full: Scans for pairs making multiples of ten, reorders confidently using the properties, composes multiple tens correctly, and explains why the chosen grouping was efficient.
responseLevels.partial: Adds accurately by partitioning but doesn't yet look for pairs to simplify, or spots pairs only when prompted.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set two calculations and watch how the child tackles each, thinking aloud: 15 + 8 + 25 + 12, then 24 + 17 + 6 + 13. Notice whether they look for pairs that make a multiple of ten before adding, and how they combine the ones.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Both sums are engineered so pairs make tidy multiples of ten. A child who uses commutativity spots the pairs and finishes quickly and accurately; a child who grinds left-to-right is slower and far more likely to slip when the running total's ones exceed ten.
