Base-ten blocks and the drawn number line are physical representations with slight thickness; they stand for the abstract numerical values being compared, not the values themselves.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source noted CCSS alignment as 1.NBT.3 (Grade 1) while targeting UK Y2 (ages 6-7); the standards citations are from different jurisdictions/grades and were preserved as written, not independently reconfirmed.

The source's error-pattern note '34 vs 38: choosing by 4 vs 8 alone is fine here, but 52 vs 48 wrongly judged by 2 vs 8' is accurate: when tens are equal the ones decide, but when tens differ the ones must not. Activities make this distinction explicit (crossed-decade pairs) so learners do not over-generalise 'compare the first/last digit'.

The original claimed a static picture 'can only show one fixed pair', that 3D 'adds no comparative information', and that the judgement is 'better trained by manipulating symbols than by talking'; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the sources, so they were softened to scoped statements about what fixed images, drill tasks and dialogue do and do not do here.

The UK NC claim and CCSS 1.NBT.3 establish the topic/standard; the UK NC claim was not attached to any activity's sourceClaims because it supports the curriculum requirement (preserved in summary/constraints) rather than a specific pedagogical principle in a rationale.

Two of three cited sources were marked verified:false in the source row; their claims were retained only where they directly support a stated teaching principle, and claims that only establish the topic/standard were not used to justify specific pedagogical moves.

probeDeeper: Which digit did you look at first — tens or ones? Why the tens?
34 and 43 use the same two digits — how can one be bigger?
Put a symbol between 60 and 60 — which one, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: 34 < 43; order 19, 27, 51, 72; and they compare the tens digit first, ones only to break a tie.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares by a single digit's size regardless of place: thinks 19 > 51 because 9 > 1
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build both with tens and ones; establish that tens are worth more, so compare tens first. Re-order with the models in view.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Ordering puts numbers with a big ones digit too high; 34/43 judged by the shared digits.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses the < / > symbol — opens it toward the smaller number
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor the symbol: the open (wide) side faces the larger number, the point faces the smaller. Read the whole statement aloud to check.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reasoning is right ('43 is bigger') but the symbol written points the wrong way.

responseLevels.gap: Orders by a single digit ignoring place, or the symbol is reversed with no place reasoning.
responseLevels.full: Compares and orders two-digit numbers by tens-then-ones, writes >, <, = correctly, and justifies by place value.
responseLevels.partial: Compares correctly for clearly different numbers but stumbles on same-digit pairs, or reasons right yet writes the symbol backwards.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Watch them compare and order. 'Put the right symbol between 34 and 43. Now order these smallest to largest: 27, 72, 19, 51. Tell me how you decided.' The 34/43 pair (same digits) is the key — watch whether they weigh the tens first.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 34 vs 43 uses identical digits so a child comparing digit-by-digit without place weighting cannot fake it; ordering a mixed set reveals whether tens govern the comparison. The '<'/'>' choice also exposes pure symbol reversal separately from the reasoning.

pedagogy.summary: At Year 3 children learn to see lines by ORIENTATION and RELATIONSHIP rather than as mere marks: horizontal (flat, like the horizon), vertical (upright), parallel (two lines that stay the same distance apart and never meet, however far extended) and perpendicular (two lines that cross at a right angle). The idea rests on the right-angle concept (perpendicular = a right angle between the lines) and on positional language. The characteristic errors treat a non-defining feature as defining — that parallel lines must be equal in length, or must be horizontal/vertical — and confuse the two relationship words with each other, because early examples nearly always show equal-length horizontal/vertical pairs.
bestPractices: Anchor the orientation words to images: horizontal = flat like the horizon or a table top; vertical = straight up like a wall or a standing person
Define parallel by the relationship — always the same distance apart, never meeting even if extended — and TEST by extending the lines or sliding a ruler, not by length or direction
Define perpendicular as meeting at a right angle and check with the corner of a card or a known right angle (links to the right-angle prerequisite)
Show parallel and perpendicular pairs in many orientations and unequal lengths, and in real contexts (railway tracks, window frames, the letter H) so the relationship, not the look, is learned
Separate the two relationship words explicitly and rehearse naming while pointing: these run alongside = parallel; these make a right angle = perpendicular
keyRepresentations: Real-world referents: horizon/table (horizontal), wall/lamppost (vertical), railway tracks (parallel), window corner / plus-sign (perpendicular)
The corner of a card or a set-square as a right-angle checker for perpendicular
A ruler slid between two lines, or the lines extended, to test 'always the same distance / never meet'
Letters and shapes marked up — an H has parallel verticals and a perpendicular cross-bar; a rectangle's sides
commonMisconceptions: Confuses 'horizontal' and 'vertical' (which word is which)
Thinks parallel lines must be the same length
Thinks lines only count as parallel/perpendicular when they are horizontal or vertical; misses tilted pairs
Confuses 'parallel' and 'perpendicular'

learn.summary: Year 3 learners classify lines by orientation and relationship, not by their look: horizontal (flat like the horizon or a tabletop), vertical (upright like a wall or standing person), parallel (always the same distance apart, never meeting however far extended) and perpendicular (meeting or crossing at a right angle). The core work is replacing appearance-based judgements (that parallel must be equal length, or that only horizontal/vertical pairs count) and separating the two relationship words. The practical test for parallel is extending the lines and checking that the gap between them stays the same; a drawing can only be extended so far, so 'not meeting on the page' supports, but does not by itself prove, 'never meeting'. The practical test for perpendicular is checking the angle where the lines meet against a known right angle, in any orientation.

activities.title: Extend and rotate: what parallel really means
feedback: If a learner says a tilted, unequal pair 'isn't parallel because the lines are different lengths', show parallel pairs of very different lengths and re-test by extending: length is irrelevant, only constant distance / never meeting matters.

If a learner rejects a tilted pair because it is 'slanted/wonky', rotate a pair they already accept as parallel off horizontal so they see the relationship is preserved, then use tilted real examples.
When the extended lines cross, point back to the prediction and connect the outcome: converging means not parallel, however small the lean.
When the right-angle checker reads a tilted cross as perpendicular, name it: these meet at a right angle, so they are perpendicular even though the whole cross is tilted.
activities.rationale: Extending and rotating live lines makes the defining relationship (never meet / same distance apart) observable rather than inferred from appearance, directly targeting the equal-length and orientation-bound errors reinforced by typical equal-length horizontal/vertical examples. An extend-to-edge control, draggable/rotatable lines, an any-orientation right-angle detector, and a labelled gallery of real photos are concrete ways to make the mechanism visible; they are optional illustrations, not required tools — paper, a ruler and a card corner achieve the same tests.
sourceClaims: Pupils confuse the vocabulary 'parallel'/'perpendicular', and think parallel lines must be the same length (reinforced by equal-length examples); remedies = show lines of differing lengths/orientations and use a checking method

Children reason from prototypes and impose non-defining/salient attributes (e.g. standard orientation) as if defining, rejecting non-standard examples — the mechanism behind rejecting a tilted parallel pair
learnerActions: Start with two lines on screen or drawn on paper that look 'wonky' and are different lengths; predict aloud whether they will ever cross if extended, and say why before testing.

Extend both lines all the way to the edges (press an EXTEND button, or continue the lines with a ruler across a large sheet), observe whether they meet, and measure the gap between them at several places to see whether it stays the same.

Drag or draw a second pair that looks nearly parallel but leans enough to converge within the page or screen; extend them and watch them cross. Note that a very tiny lean might only cross beyond the edge, and the narrowing gap still shows the lines are not parallel.
Rotate a known parallel pair off horizontal and confirm the relationship is kept when tilted.

Use a right-angle checker (the corner of a card, a set-square, or a detector that glows green) on a perpendicular crossing pair tilted to 45 degrees to confirm a right angle is still a right angle whichever way the corner faces.
Label real photos or scenes — railway tracks, ladder rungs, window frames, the letter H — as parallel or perpendicular, including tilted and unequal examples.
activities.intendedInsight: Parallel means staying the same distance apart and never meeting however far extended — not being flat and not being equal in length; and a right angle stays a right angle at any orientation.

activities.title: Anchor and separate the four words
feedback: If a learner calls a right-angle pair 'parallel', re-anchor: parallel lines run alongside and never meet; perpendicular lines meet at a right angle — check the corner with a card.
If a learner points to a vertical line when asked for a horizontal one, re-anchor horizontal to the flat horizon/tabletop and vertical to an upright wall or standing person, then re-ask.
activities.rationale: Early examples almost always show equal-length horizontal/vertical pairs, so the words are learned by association and get swapped; explicit naming-while-pointing and real referents (horizon, wall, tracks, window corner, letter H) separate orientation from relationship. This activity rehearses vocabulary; it supports but does not replace the extend/never-meet work.
sourceClaims: Pupils confuse the vocabulary 'parallel'/'perpendicular', and think parallel lines must be the same length (reinforced by equal-length examples); remedies = show lines of differing lengths/orientations and use a checking method
learnerActions: Point to a horizontal line in the room and a vertical one, naming each and saying a memory hook (horizontal = flat like the horizon; vertical = upright like a wall).
For each pair of lines shown, point and say which relationship it is: 'these run alongside and never meet = parallel'; 'these make a right angle = perpendicular'.
Mark up letters and shapes: find the parallel verticals and the perpendicular cross-bar in an H; mark a rectangle's parallel sides and perpendicular corners.
Deliberately practise cases that are easy to mix up — a right-angle crossing (perpendicular, not parallel) and a vertical line asked for when a horizontal one is shown.
activities.intendedInsight: The four terms name distinct ideas: horizontal/vertical are orientations, parallel/perpendicular are relationships between two lines; naming while pointing keeps them apart.

activities.title: Predict, observe, explain and a sorting check
feedback: Treat the reason the learner gives before testing as diagnostic: a length reason ('one's longer, so not parallel') or a tilt reason ('too slanted') signals an appearance-based rule — respond with extended unequal and rotated examples.
Reinforce the full justification: 'parallel because they stay the same distance apart and would never meet however far extended; their tilt and lengths don't matter.'
activities.rationale: Predicting and justifying before observing exposes whether the learner is applying a length or orientation rule rather than the defining relationship; sorting and matching assess recognition cleanly but test the outcome rather than building the never-meet intuition, so they work best after the manipulation activity. Choosing tilted and rotated items prevents appearance-based guessing from succeeding.
sourceClaims: Pupils confuse the vocabulary 'parallel'/'perpendicular', and think parallel lines must be the same length (reinforced by equal-length examples); remedies = show lines of differing lengths/orientations and use a checking method

Children reason from prototypes and impose non-defining/salient attributes (e.g. standard orientation) as if defining, rejecting non-standard examples — the mechanism behind rejecting a tilted parallel pair
learnerActions: Given two genuinely parallel lines drawn tilted and of different lengths, predict whether they will ever cross if extended across the room, and give a reason before extending.
Extend them and compare the result to the prediction; explain any surprise.
Sort a set of line-pairs into parallel / perpendicular / neither, including tilted parallel pairs and rotated right-angle crosses chosen so appearance-based answers fail.
Match each word (horizontal, vertical, parallel, perpendicular) to a picture, including non-standard orientations.
activities.intendedInsight: A correct answer must rest on the relationship (same distance / never meet; meet at a right angle), not on tilt or length; the reason a learner gives before testing reveals which rule they are using.

constraints: Perpendicular depends on the right-angle concept; learners need to recognise or check a right angle (card corner / set-square) first.

Recognition-only formats (sorting, matching, multiple choice) assess the outcome and do not elicit the independent prediction-and-justification that reveals a learner's underlying rule; use them alongside, not instead of, extend/predict tasks. This is a narrow affordance point, not a claim that sorts cannot support classification.

A static reference scene (tap tracks -> 'parallel'; tap a window corner -> 'perpendicular') is a useful poster but cannot be extended or re-tested, so it cannot run the never-meet check; use it as a reference after the interactive work.
Always include tilted and unequal-length examples; equal-length horizontal/vertical pairs alone reinforce the very misconceptions being targeted.

Interactive controls (extend button, drag/rotate, right-angle detector, photo gallery) are illustrative examples of making the test concrete, not mandatory tools; paper, ruler and card corner serve equally.

At this level these are planar page relations and extending to three dimensions is unnecessary here. A flat on-screen or paper diagram represents ideal lines, which have no thickness; the drawn marks are thin, finite approximations, and the 'extend forever / never meet' test reasons about the idealised lines.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The statutory Year 3 content claim is flagged verified:false in the row and supports only the topic/curriculum scope, not a specific teaching principle; it is retained here as context and was not used as an activity sourceClaim. The two misconception/prototype claims are flagged verified:true; verification status was not re-checked here. The NCETM claim directly covers parallel/perpendicular vocabulary confusion; its use for the horizontal/vertical swap component is by extension.

The legacy 'poor fit' claims that dialogue 'cannot deliver the seeing' and that a third dimension 'adds nothing' were softened to narrowly scoped affordance statements; catalog fit ratings do not establish universal necessity or that one medium cannot teach the concept.

Drawn lines on paper or screen have thickness and finite length, which are approximations of ideal lines; distinguish the idealised line (no thickness, extends without end) from the visible mark, including in child-facing talk about 'extending forever'. Screen edges are finite, so pair on-screen extension with ruler/paper extension to convey 'never meet, however far extended'.

assess.poeTask: Show two genuinely parallel lines drawn tilted and of different lengths. Ask the child to PREDICT — 'if we keep extending both lines further and further, will they ever cross?' — and to say WHY before you do it. Then extend both lines to the edges of the page and OBSERVE that they never meet. Ask the child to EXPLAIN the result if they predicted the lines would cross. The reason given before extending is the diagnostic part: a child judging by length or tilt often predicts the lines will meet.
probeDeeper: If we made these two lines much longer, stretching them right across the room, would they ever cross? How do you know?
Point to a horizontal line in the room, and a vertical one. Which is which, and how do you remember?
Here are two lines that make a right angle where they cross — are those parallel or perpendicular?
These two lines lean the same way but one is short and one is long — can they still be parallel?
assess.correctAnswer: Yes — they are parallel. They stay exactly the same distance apart all the way along and would never meet, however far you extended them. Their tilt and their different lengths don't matter; parallel is about staying the same distance apart and never meeting.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks parallel lines must be the SAME LENGTH — says the tilted unequal pair is not parallel because the lines differ in length
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show parallel pairs of very different lengths; define parallel by constant distance / never meeting, tested by extending — length is irrelevant (NCETM).
errorPatterns.distractor: No — the two lines are different lengths
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'no' and, on the reason tier, gives a length reason ('one's longer, so they can't be parallel')

errorPatterns.pattern: Orientation-bound — thinks lines are only parallel/perpendicular when horizontal or vertical, so a tilted parallel pair 'isn't parallel'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rotate a known parallel pair off horizontal so the child sees the relationship is preserved; use tilted real examples (prototype/imposed-attribute: orientation wrongly treated as defining).
errorPatterns.distractor: No — they are slanted, not straight across or straight up
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'no' because the lines are 'slanted/wonky', or accepts only flat/upright pairs

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses the relationship or orientation words — swaps 'parallel'/'perpendicular', or 'horizontal'/'vertical'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor each word: parallel = run alongside, never meet; perpendicular = meet at a right angle; horizontal = flat like the horizon, vertical = upright. Rehearse naming while pointing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls a right-angle pair 'parallel', or points to a vertical line when asked for a horizontal one

responseLevels.gap: Judges parallel/perpendicular by length or by horizontal/vertical orientation; says the tilted unequal pair isn't parallel; swaps the relationship terms or the horizontal/vertical labels.
responseLevels.full: Says the tilted unequal pair is parallel and justifies by 'same distance apart / never meet, even if extended'; identifies horizontal and vertical lines and perpendicular (right-angle) pairs in any orientation and in real contexts, using the terms correctly.
responseLevels.partial: Identifies parallel/perpendicular and horizontal/vertical in standard (flat/upright, equal-length) cases and can state a definition, but reverts to appearance on tilted or unequal-length pairs, or occasionally mixes the two relationship words.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show the child two lines that are genuinely parallel but drawn TILTED (diagonal) and of clearly DIFFERENT lengths. Ask: 'Are these two lines parallel?' Then, whatever they say: 'How do you know?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The pair is tilted and unequal in length precisely so that a child judging by orientation or length says 'no'. A child holding the relationship (same distance / never meet) says yes and justifies by imagining the lines extended; a child running the same-length or horizontal-only rule says no, exposing the non-defining feature on the reason tier.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–10y; interpret a multiplication equation as a COMPARISON (35 = 5×7 means 35 is 5 times as many as 7), and translate verbal multiplicative-comparison statements into equations.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y4–Y5 scaling problems ('n times as tall/heavy/many') and multiplicative reasoning underpinning ratio.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.OA.1 — 'interpret a multiplication equation as a comparison, e.g. 35 = 5×7 as a statement that 35 is 5 times as many as 7 and 7 times as many as 5. Represent verbal statements of multiplicative comparisons as multiplication equations.'
• Operational details — this is a NEW meaning of multiplication beyond equal groups: a relationship between two quantities where one is 'n times' the other. The load-bearing distinction is multiplicative ('5 times as many') vs additive ('5 more') — children habitually confuse them. Teach with the comparison bar model: a short bar (the referent) and a bar n times as long (the compared quantity); the scale factor is the multiplier. Note 35=5×7 supports TWO comparisons (35 is 5 times 7 AND 7 times 5). This is the conceptual seed of ratio, rate and proportion.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): translate '4 times as many' to ×4 and draw the two bars. Tier B (age 9–10): write an equation for a verbal multiplicative-comparison statement. Tier C (age 10): distinguish multiplicative from additive comparison and explain both comparisons a single equation encodes.
bestPractices: Use the comparison bar model — referent bar vs a bar n times as long — so 'times as many' is seen as a scaling relationship, not an equal-groups count.
Directly contrast multiplicative ('5 times as many') with additive ('5 more') using the same numbers, since children conflate them.
Show that one equation (35=5×7) encodes two comparisons, building flexibility.
Move both ways — verbal→equation and equation→verbal — to secure the translation.
Frame it as the gateway to ratio/rate so the multiplicative relationship is seen as foundational.
keyRepresentations: Comparison bar model (referent bar and the n-times bar)
Double number line — the scaling relationship between two quantities
Scale-factor arrow (×n) between the two quantities
Equation linking the comparison (blue = 3 × red)
commonMisconceptions: Confusing multiplicative comparison ('3 times as many') with additive ('3 more').
Treating multiplicative comparison as equal groups and losing the relational meaning.
Getting the direction wrong (which quantity is the referent / which is n times the other).
Not seeing that 35=5×7 expresses both '5 times 7' and '7 times 5'.
Adding when the language says 'times as many' (or vice versa).

learn.summary: For ages 9–10: interpret a multiplication equation as a COMPARISON (35 = 5×7 means 35 is 5 times as many as 7, and also 7 times as many as 5) and translate verbal 'n times as many' statements into equations. The load-bearing distinction is multiplicative ('5 times as many') versus additive ('5 more') — children habitually confuse these. Activities centre on the comparison bar model (a referent bar and a bar n times as long), explicit multiplicative-vs-additive contrast using the same numbers, two-way verbal↔equation translation, and the insight that a single equation encodes two multiplicative comparisons. This is the conceptual seed of ratio, rate and proportion.

activities.title: Scaling bars: times as many vs more than
feedback: If the additive and multiplicative bars come out the same, re-count: 5 copies of 7 (end-to-end) is very different from 7 with 5 added on. Compare the two blue bars directly.
If the equation direction is reversed, name the referent first: red is 'one unit', blue is n of those units, so blue = n × red.
When you re-read the bars, check both statements describe the same picture: if 35 is 5 times 7, then 7 is one of the 5 equal parts of 35.
activities.rationale: Building and comparing bars makes the multiplicative-vs-additive difference concrete using the same numbers, which is exactly the confusion to resolve; re-reading one picture two ways builds relational flexibility. An optional live version (a ×n dial that recolours/rescales the blue bar while the equation updates, with a toggle overlaying an additive 'ghost' bar) can make the contrast dynamic, but stacking physical or drawn copies achieves the same insight.
sourceClaims: Comparison bar models support multiplicative comparison; multiplicative and additive comparison must be explicitly contrasted.
4.OA.1 requires interpreting a multiplication equation as a comparison and representing verbal multiplicative comparisons as equations.
Y4–Y5 pupils solve scaling ('n times as many') problems, developing the multiplicative reasoning that underpins ratio.
learnerActions: Start with a short referent bar labelled red (e.g. red = 7). Build a second bar, blue, that is 'n times as long' by stacking n copies of the red bar end to end; for ×5 this makes blue = 35.

Alongside the multiplicative bar, build an ADDITIVE comparison bar: red plus a fixed amount (red + 5 = 12). Place the two blue results side by side so '5 times as many' (35) visibly towers over '5 more' (12).
Write the equation that matches the multiplicative bars: blue = n × red (e.g. blue = 5 × red, so blue = 35).

Re-read the SAME pair of bars (7 and 35) two ways: the multiplicative-comparison statement '35 is 5 times as many as 7', and its reciprocal '7 is one-fifth of 35 / 7 is one of the five equal copies that make 35'. State both out loud. (The matching equation 35 = 5 × 7 also carries two multiplicative comparisons — '35 is 5 times as many as 7' and '35 is 7 times as many as 5' — which you will write out in the sort-and-translate activity.)
Take verbal cards such as 'Sarah has 3 times as many stickers as Tom, who has 8' and build the correct bars, then write the equation (3 × 8 = 24).
activities.intendedInsight: 'n times as many' is a scaling relationship — n copies of the referent — not n added on; and the same pair of bars can be read two ways: the multiplicative comparison '35 is 5 times as many as 7' and its reciprocal '7 is one-fifth of 35'.

activities.title: Tower comparison: how many copies fit?
feedback: If the answer is 8 ('4 taller' / 'add 4'): that is the additive reading. Physically stack four whole red towers to see four copies — '4 more' only adds 4 cubes, which is a much shorter tower.

If red and blue get swapped (computing 4 ÷ 16 or treating blue as the unit): name red as the single unit and show blue is 4 of those units (16 ÷ 4 = 4); a double number line with red at 1 and blue at 4 helps.
If 16 is computed but explained only as '4 times 4' with no meaning: ask 'how many red towers would you need to match blue?' to surface the copies-of relationship already implicit in the answer.
activities.rationale: A referent/compared pair with a clean right answer (16, not 8) targets the signature additive error directly; asking for the meaning, not just the number, reveals copies-of versus more-than reasoning.
sourceClaims: Comparison bar models support multiplicative comparison; multiplicative and additive comparison must be explicitly contrasted.
learnerActions: The red tower is 4 cubes tall; the blue tower is 4 TIMES as tall. Build blue by stacking four separate red towers end to end, then count: 4 × 4 = 16 cubes.
Explain in words what '4 times as tall' means: blue is four copies of red's height.
Now build a '4 MORE than red' tower (4 + 4 = 8) beside it and describe how it differs from the '4 times' tower.
Given both towers (red = 4, blue = 16), work out how many times as tall blue is, and say how you know (how many red towers fit into blue).
Try a variant: if red were 5 cubes and blue is 4 times as tall, how tall is blue? (20)
activities.intendedInsight: 'Times as tall' compares by how many COPIES of the referent fit, not by how many more; the multiplier tells you how many copies.

activities.title: Sort and translate: multiplicative or additive?
feedback: A statement that uses 'times as many' but is matched to a '+' equation is the core confusion — reread it as copies: '5 times as many' means 5 copies, so multiply.
When writing the two statements for one equation, swap which factor is the referent: 5×7 reads as both '5 copies of 7' (35 is 5 times 7) and '7 copies of 5' (35 is 7 times 5).
activities.rationale: Checking translation and the multiplicative/additive distinction with targeted contrasting items (×5 versus +5 on the same numbers) verifies whether the relational meaning is secure. A sort/match task can check recognition and translation, but it does not itself elicit the scaling feel, so pair it with the bar-building work above.
sourceClaims: 4.OA.1 requires interpreting a multiplication equation as a comparison and representing verbal multiplicative comparisons as equations.
Comparison bar models support multiplicative comparison; multiplicative and additive comparison must be explicitly contrasted.
learnerActions: Sort word-problem statements into two piles: 'times as many' (multiplicative) and 'more than' (additive). Example multiplicative: 'Sam has 5 times as many as Jo.' Example additive: 'Sam has 5 more than Jo.'
Match each verbal statement to its equation, e.g. 'Sam has 5 times as many' → ×5 (not +5).
Translate both ways: given an equation like 6 × 4 = 24, write a 'times as many' sentence; given a sentence, write the equation.
For 35 = 5 × 7, write both multiplicative comparisons it supports: '35 is 5 times as many as 7' and '35 is 7 times as many as 5'.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Times as many' describes a multiplicative relationship (larger = n × smaller) and 'more than' describes an additive relationship (larger = smaller + n); the operation you actually carry out depends on which quantity is unknown (e.g. finding the smaller quantity from 'Sam has 3 times as many as Jo, and Sam has 24' means dividing). Translation must run reliably in both directions, and one equation can encode two multiplicative comparisons.

activities.title: Talk it through: times, or just more?
feedback: If reasoning drifts to adding, redirect to copies: how many copies of the smaller quantity make the larger one?
Accept an answer only when it names the relationship (copies-of / groups), not just a number.
activities.rationale: A Socratic dialogue may build the distinction and translation habit through explanation (efficacy untested); the scaling relationship itself is most vivid in built or drawn bars, so use discussion to accompany, not replace, the modelling.
sourceClaims: Comparison bar models support multiplicative comparison; multiplicative and additive comparison must be explicitly contrasted.
learnerActions: With a character comparing two collections, answer the recurring question: 'Does "times as many" mean add, or multiply? How do you know?'
Justify each answer by describing the bars or copies you would draw, e.g. '3 times as many is 3 copies, so multiply'.
When the character offers an additive answer to a 'times as many' problem, explain why that is wrong and give the correct multiplicative reading.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating why 'times as many' is multiplicative, and defending it against an additive suggestion, strengthens the distinction and the translation habit.

constraints: Tier A (age 9): translate '4 times as many' to ×4 and draw the two bars. Tier B (age 9–10): write an equation for a verbal multiplicative-comparison statement. Tier C (age 10): distinguish multiplicative from additive comparison and explain both comparisons a single equation encodes.

This is a NEW meaning of multiplication beyond equal groups: a relationship between two quantities where one is 'n times' the other. Keep the relational meaning central; do not let it collapse back into plain equal-groups counting.
Always contrast multiplicative and additive comparisons using the SAME numbers so the difference is visible, since children conflate them.

Move translation both ways (verbal→equation and equation→verbal); the standard requires both interpreting equations as comparisons and representing verbal statements as equations, so do not drill only one direction.
Sorting/matching tasks can check recognition and translation; they do not themselves build the scaling intuition, so pair them with bar-building or tower-building activities.

Paper or cube bars have slight real thickness and are approximations of the idealised bar diagram, and an on-screen scalable bar is also a model; what carries the comparison is the bar LENGTH, not the material. Both media are fine; neither is uniquely necessary.
A dynamic scaling dial, live recolouring, or an additive 'ghost' bar are optional aids that may make the contrast vivid; static drawn or stacked bars can achieve the same insight.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic check (all correct as used): red=7, ×5 → 35 while 7+5=12; 4 cubes × 4 = 16 while 4+4=8; 3×8=24; red=5, ×4 → 20; 6×4=24. The original source's additive 'ghost' example for red=7 used '12' in one place and '7+3=10' in another; the ×5 case gives 7+5=12. Learner text uses 12 consistently for the +5 additive comparison; the stray '7+3=10' appears to be a leftover ×3 example and was not carried forward.
Two source claims (CCSS-M 4.OA.1 and NCETM guidance) were marked verified:false in the original; their cited principles are retained but their verification status is unconfirmed here.

The bar re-reading '7 is one-fifth of 35' introduces division/fraction language and is the reciprocal of the bar's multiplicative comparison, not one of the standard's two 'n times as many' comparisons (those — '35 is 5 times 7' and '35 is 7 times 5' — are written in the sort-and-translate activity, where both factors appear). It is included as scoped enrichment and may be simplified to '7 is one of the five equal copies' for Tier A/B learners.

Independent re-audit confirms: no learner question offers an additive reading as a valid/correct option; the additive value (8, or +5 → 12) appears only as a contrasted wrong reading that is explicitly corrected; the two distinct insights (reciprocal reading of bars vs two multiplicative comparisons of the equation) are kept in separate activities and do not contradict each other.

probeDeeper: You said 16. What does '4 times as tall' tell you about how many red towers fit into blue?
If blue were '4 MORE than red' instead, how tall would it be? How is that different from '4 times'?
The red tower is 4 and blue is 16. How many times as tall is blue — and how do you know?
What if red had been 5 cubes and blue was 4 times as tall — how tall is blue?
assess.correctAnswer: 16 cubes. A child reasoning correctly interprets '4 times as tall' multiplicatively: the blue tower is four copies of the red tower's height, 4 × 4 = 16 — not 4 more than red. The explanation names that 'times as many' compares by how many COPIES/groups, not by how many more.

errorPatterns.pattern: reads 'N times as many/tall' additively — interprets '4 times as tall as 4' as '4 more', giving 8
errorPatterns.nextMove: build it: stack four separate red towers end to end to SEE four copies; contrast with '4 more' by adding just 4 cubes, so 'times as many' and 'more than' become physically different.
errorPatterns.distractor: 8 cubes (4 times as tall means 4 taller, so 4 + 4)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child answers 8 and explains 'it's 4 taller' or 'add 4'

errorPatterns.pattern: confuses which quantity is the referent — makes red the multiple of blue, or divides when they should multiply
errorPatterns.nextMove: name the '1 unit' explicitly (red = one unit of height) and show blue is 4 of those units; use a double-number-line with red at 1 and blue at 4.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child sets up 4 ÷ 4 or treats blue as the unit being copied

errorPatterns.pattern: gets 16 by rote multiplication but cannot say it means 'four copies of red' — no comparative meaning attached
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach multiplication; ask 'how many red towers would you need to match blue?' to surface the comparison already implicit in their answer.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child computes 4×4 correctly yet, asked what '4 times as tall' means, restates the calculation rather than the copies-of relationship

responseLevels.gap: answers 8 (additive) or divides; interprets 'times as many' as 'more than'.
responseLevels.full: gives 16, explains '4 times as tall' as four copies of the red unit, distinguishes it from '4 more', and can find the multiplier when given both quantities.
responseLevels.partial: computes 16 correctly but explains it only as a calculation, not as 'four copies of red' — cannot cleanly contrast multiplicative with additive comparison when probed.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: The red tower is 4 cubes tall. The blue tower is 4 TIMES as tall as the red one. How tall is the blue tower — and explain what '4 times as tall' means about how the two towers compare.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The signature error is reading multiplicative comparison as additive ('4 times as tall' → 4 + 4 = 8, 'four taller'). Asking for the meaning, not just the number, forces the child to reveal whether they see copies-of vs more-than. A child who answers 16 but explains it as 'add 4 four times to 4' also reveals a shaky grasp on probing.

sources.claim: Y4–Y5 pupils solve scaling ('n times as many') problems, developing the multiplicative reasoning that underpins ratio.

pedagogy.summary: This LANGUAGE topic is the vocabulary of data handling — data, tally, frequency, survey, pictogram, bar chart, axis/axes, scale, label, category, discrete vs continuous, line graph, pie chart — learned by USING the words while collecting, organising and presenting data, not by reciting definitions. The two load-bearing distinctions are frequency (the COUNT) versus tally (the marks) versus category (the group), and discrete (counted, whole-number) versus continuous (measured, any value in between). Teaching should introduce each term at the moment it is needed in a real data activity and lean on contrast pairs, because the meaning of 'continuous' lives in its difference from 'discrete'.
bestPractices: Introduce each term in the act of doing — 'we'll TALLY as we count, and the total is the FREQUENCY' — rather than as a word list
Teach the tricky terms as contrast pairs (discrete vs continuous; tally vs frequency; label vs scale) so meaning sits in the difference
Have children LABEL real charts they build (title, axis labels, scale) and say the terms aloud as they place them
Sort real variables into discrete (number of pets, goals scored) vs continuous (height, time, temperature) with a 'could it be in between?' test
keyRepresentations: A chart the child annotates: title, both axis labels, an even scale, category names
Contrast-pair cards (discrete/continuous; tally/frequency)
A sorting mat for variables: counted vs measured
Tally chart feeding a frequency table (marks → count)
commonMisconceptions: Confuses discrete and continuous — e.g. thinks height is discrete because it's written as a whole number, or that 'continuous' just means 'a lot of data'
Uses 'frequency' for the category name, or conflates the tally marks with the frequency total
Muddles 'label' and 'scale' — calls the category names the scale, or numbers an axis in uneven steps yet still calls it a scale
Calls every display a 'bar chart' or 'graph', not matching the term to the representation

learn.summary: This is a LANGUAGE topic: the vocabulary of data handling — data, tally, tally chart, frequency, frequency table, survey, pictogram, bar chart, axis/axes, scale, label, category, discrete data, continuous data, line graph, pie chart. The words are learned by USING them while collecting, organising and presenting real data, not by reciting definitions. Two load-bearing distinctions carry the topic: frequency (the COUNT) versus tally (the marks) versus category (the group); and discrete (separate values, usually counted, often whole numbers) versus continuous (measured, can take values in between). Introduce each term at the moment it is needed in a real data activity, and lean on contrast pairs, because the meaning of 'continuous' lives in its contrast with 'discrete'.

activities.title: Label the chart and sort the data
feedback: If 'scale' is placed on the category names: the scale is the row of equal number steps up the axis; the labels say what each axis shows. Move it to the number steps.
If height is tagged 'discrete' because it was written as a whole number: ask 'could someone be 125-and-a-half cm?' — yes, so height is continuous; the written figure is just rounded.
If 'frequency' is placed on a category name: the category is the group; the frequency is the count you end with (shown by how tall each bar is). Separate the two roles.
When a tag lands on the part it truly names, confirm it and ask the child to read the term aloud with what it does.
activities.rationale: Vocabulary used in context is best taught by having the child label real charts and sort real variables with immediate feedback — active use rather than passive recognition. An optional interaction that only accepts a tag on the part it truly names (so 'scale' will not stick to the category row) and an 'in-between?' prompt on the sorter make the distinctions concrete; these are illustrative mechanisms, not required ones.
sourceClaims: The statistics programme requires pupils to interpret and construct pictograms, tally charts, block diagrams, tables, bar charts and (later) line and pie charts, and to interpret discrete and continuous data — fixing the vocabulary pupils must use in context

A picture graph uses one symbol per individual whereas a pictograph uses a symbol for several; displays represent the distribution of a categorical or discrete quantitative variable — grounding the terms category, frequency and display type in use
learnerActions: Finish a half-built bar chart by placing the right term onto each part: the title, each axis label, the scale (the equal number steps up the side), the category names along the bottom, and the frequency (the count shown by the height of each bar on the value axis).
Say each term aloud as you place it — 'this is the scale', 'these are the category names', 'this axis shows the frequency' — so you are wielding the word, not just matching it.
Sort real variables into 'discrete (counted)' or 'continuous (measured)': e.g. 'number of pets', 'goals scored' versus 'how tall', 'time taken', 'temperature'.
For each variable, apply the test: 'Could there be a value in between?' — someone can be 125-and-a-half cm tall (continuous) but cannot have two-and-a-half pets (discrete).
activities.intendedInsight: Data vocabulary is mastered by using it correctly in a real chart and a real sorting task — height is continuous because a value can fall in between, even when it is written as a whole number.

activities.title: Tally to frequency: marks become a count
feedback: If the child calls the marks 'the frequency': the marks are the tally; the frequency is the number you get when you total them.
If the child labels the category column 'frequency': the category names the group; the frequency column holds the counts.
Confirm correct use by asking the child to restate 'tally marks -> total -> frequency' in their own words.
activities.rationale: Separating the roles in a real recording task directly targets the common conflation of tally, frequency and category, teaching the terms through the action of recording data.
sourceClaims: The statistics programme requires pupils to interpret and construct pictograms, tally charts, block diagrams, tables, bar charts and (later) line and pie charts, and to interpret discrete and continuous data — fixing the vocabulary pupils must use in context
learnerActions: Run a quick survey (e.g. favourite fruit) and record responses by making tally marks in a tally chart as each one comes in.

When counting is done, total each row and write the frequency in a frequency table — pointing out that the tally is the marks and the frequency is the final count. Then show the same frequencies as a pictogram, with a key that says what one picture stands for, and say 'this is a pictogram' while you build it.
As you work, answer: 'Which part is the tally and which is the frequency?' and 'Which part is the category?'
activities.intendedInsight: Tally (the marks), frequency (the count) and category (the group) are three different roles; the tally feeds the frequency, they are not the same thing.

activities.title: Contrast-pair glossary (scaffold)
feedback: Prompt the child to generate their own example for each side of a pair (one discrete, one continuous) rather than only reading the given one.
If they only read definitions back, return them to the label-and-sort activity to use the term on a real chart or variable.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal, contrast-pair glossary suits vocabulary by showing discrete beside continuous and tally beside frequency with examples. It is a support for recall and contrast; on its own it is recognition-only and does not require the child to construct correct use, so it should feed into, not replace, the label-and-sort activity.
learnerActions: View 'discrete' and 'continuous' side by side, each with a canonical example and the 'could there be a value in between?' test.
View 'tally' beside 'frequency', and 'label' beside 'scale', comparing what each one does.
Tap or point to parts of a chart to reveal their names, then try to name the next part before revealing it.
activities.intendedInsight: Tricky terms are easier to hold when seen as contrast pairs, because the meaning sits in the difference between the two words.

constraints: Teach each term at the point it is needed inside a real data activity, not as an up-front word list.
Recognition and tap-to-reveal glossary tasks support recall but do not, by themselves, elicit independent construction; pair them with building and labelling a chart and sorting real variables.
The contrast-pair glossary is a scaffold: it displays comparisons but does not require the child to use the term, so confirm mastery through active labelling and sorting with feedback.

Matching, categorisation and fill-the-blank items can check correct use (e.g. a discrete/continuous sort with a 'whole-number-written' trap, a tally-versus-frequency match), but keep them as checks alongside the hands-on build rather than the main teaching.

A real survey/chart with actual categories, an even scale and variables to sort is the core for this LANGUAGE objective; picture-only or definition-reciting versions are weaker for eliciting correct use because the vocabulary is learned by wielding it.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row claimed 'Data vocabulary is not spatial; 3D adds nothing' and that open conversation is a poor fit. These are catalog-fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws: a conversation can support vocabulary use if anchored to a real chart/variable, and 3D is simply not needed here rather than proven worthless. Softened accordingly; spoken discussion while building a chart is useful.
The 'tool only accepts a tag on the part it truly names' behaviour is presented as an optional illustrative interaction, not a mandatory mechanism.

The first activity's 'frequency' tag (referenced in feedback) is present in the learner actions and described as the bar chart's value-axis count, matching the original design; verified coherent on this independent pass.

Diagnostic/assessment content (diagnosticPrompt, probeDeeper, errorPatterns) remains in the assessment fields; only its teaching-relevant substance was mirrored into feedback and no assessment field was altered.
The ASA GAISE source distinguishes 'picture graph' from 'pictograph'; the topic uses 'pictogram'. Kept the claim verbatim as source grounding, not as a child-facing definition.

probeDeeper: Counterexample tuned to this topic: 'could someone be 125-and-a-half centimetres tall? could someone have two-and-a-half pets?' to test the discrete/continuous boundary by use
Ask 'as you fill this in, which part is the tally and which is the frequency?' to check the terms are distinguished in action
Ask 'why do the numbers up the side need equal steps — what do we call that part?' to surface 'scale' used correctly
Ask 'is this a bar chart, a pictogram or a line graph — and how can you tell?' to check terms match representations
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for correct USE in context: naming the title, axis labels, an even scale and the categories; using 'frequency' for the counts and 'tally' for the marks; and identifying number of pets as discrete (counted, whole) and height as continuous (measured, can fall between values), justified by the 'in-between' test.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses discrete and continuous — calls height discrete because it's recorded as a whole number, or thinks 'continuous' just means 'lots of data'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Apply the 'could there be a value in between?' test — someone can be 125.5 cm but not have 2.5 pets; contrast the pair explicitly
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child tags height 'discrete' citing the written figure, or can't apply the counted-vs-measured distinction

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses 'frequency' for the category name, or treats the tally marks and the frequency total as the same thing
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the roles in the activity: category = the group, tally = the marks you make, frequency = the count you end with
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child labels the category column 'frequency', or calls the marks the frequency

errorPatterns.pattern: Muddles 'label' and 'scale' — calls the category names the scale, or numbers an axis in uneven steps yet still calls it a scale
errorPatterns.nextMove: Define by use in the chart: the scale is the equal number steps up the axis; the labels say what each axis shows
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child places the 'scale' tag on the labels, or draws unequal number steps

responseLevels.gap: Misuses core terms in context — mislabels chart parts and cannot tell discrete from continuous
responseLevels.full: Uses the full data vocabulary accurately in the activity — labels title/axes/scale/categories, distinguishes tally and frequency, and justifies discrete vs continuous with the in-between test
responseLevels.partial: Uses the everyday terms (bar chart, tally, category) correctly while building, but muddles frequency vs tally or discrete vs continuous

assess.diagnosticPrompt: We counted how many pets each child has, and we also measured how tall everyone is. Set up a bar chart for the pet data and talk me through it as you go — and for each of the two things we collected, tell me whether it's discrete or continuous. (Listen for the terms USED correctly in the activity, not for definitions.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Using the words correctly WHILE building and describing the chart reveals real command; a child who has only memorised definitions mislabels the scale, calls the counts 'categories', or tags height 'discrete' because it's written as a whole number. Requiring use-in-action, not a definition, is what discriminates.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 11–13 — round numbers and measures to an appropriate degree of accuracy, including to a specified number of decimal places or significant figures.
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics, KS3): 'round numbers and measures to an appropriate degree of accuracy (e.g. to a number of decimal places or significant figures).'
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): builds on 5.NBT.A.4 (round decimals to any place); significant figures are not a named CCSS strand but appear in science/measurement and high-school modelling (N.Q). Emphasis in US is on appropriate precision.
• Operational details: Extend nearness-based rounding to (a) a stated number of decimal places and (b) significant figures. The key new idea is IDENTIFYING significant figures — the first significant figure is the first non-zero digit; leading zeros are not significant; trailing/placeholder zeros hold magnitude. Round using the digit AFTER the last significant/required place (midpoint rule), then restore place value with zeros (2 sig figs of 34,700 → 35,000). Choose accuracy to suit context.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 11): 'Round 3.4567 to 2 dp.' Tier B: 'Round 0.004982 to 2 significant figures.' Tier C: 'Round 34,750 to 2 sig figs and explain why the answer needs its zeros.'
bestPractices: Teach significant-figure identification first: the first sig fig is the first non-zero digit; leading zeros never count; placeholder zeros preserve magnitude
Keep rounding as a nearness/midpoint decision, then RESTORE place value with the right zeros (35,000, not 35)
Contrast dp and sig figs on the same number so pupils see they can differ (0.004982 to 2 dp = 0.00 vs to 2 sf = 0.0050)
Attend to the round-up cascade and trailing zeros that record precision (2.988 to 2 dp → 2.99; 1.998 to 2 dp → 2.00)
Link accuracy to context — choose dp/sf appropriate to the measurement's precision
keyRepresentations: Place-value chart marking the rounding place and the deciding next digit
Number line with the two candidate rounded values and the midpoint
Significant-figure highlighter (first non-zero digit onward)
Side-by-side dp-vs-sf comparison of the same number
commonMisconceptions: Counting leading zeros as significant (0.0049 seen as 4 sig figs)
Dropping the placeholder zeros after rounding to sig figs (35,000 written as 35)
Confusing decimal places with significant figures
Truncating instead of rounding, or double-rounding through intermediate digits
Losing the trailing zero that records the rounded precision (2.90 written as 2.9 when 2 dp is required)

learn.summary: For ages 11–13: round numbers and measures to a stated number of decimal places or significant figures, and choose an accuracy appropriate to context. The central new skill is identifying significant figures (first sig fig = first non-zero digit; leading zeros never count; placeholder/trailing zeros do real work holding magnitude and recording precision), then making a single nearness/midpoint rounding decision and restoring place value with zeros (34,750 to 2 sf → 35,000, not 35).

activities.title: Highlight the significant figures, round once, rebuild the size
feedback: If a learner writes 34,750 to 2 sf as 35, ask them to say the value aloud — 35 is thirty-five, not thirty-five thousand; the thousands zeros are load-bearing placeholders.
If leading zeros are counted (treating 0.004982 as having significant leading zeros), re-establish that counting begins at the first non-zero digit (the 4); leading zeros only hold place.

If a learner rounds digit-by-digit (e.g. 3.1449 to 2 dp: 3.1449 → 3.145 → 3.15), show that only the digit immediately after the required place matters (here the 4), so the decision is made once and gives 3.14; chain rounding made the answer drift to 3.15.
If the trailing zero is lost (0.0050 written as 0.005, or 2.90 to 2 dp written as 2.9), point out the final zero records the rounded precision and is required.
activities.rationale: The curriculum goal here is identifying significant figures and restoring place value, which is the step learners find new and error-prone. Making the highlighting, the single deciding digit, and the zero-restoration visible is intended to target the conflation between dp and sf and the 'drop the zeros' error. A live sig-fig highlighter, a number-line midpoint marker, and a dp/sf toggle on the same number are optional interaction examples that may make the mechanism concrete; they are not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils round numbers and measures to an appropriate degree of accuracy, including a specified number of decimal places or significant figures.
learnerActions: Take a number such as 34,750 and decide to round it to 2 significant figures.
Mark the counted significant digits (the 3 and the 4), confirming you start at the first non-zero digit.

Identify the single deciding digit immediately after the last required place (the 7) and place the number on a number line between its two candidate rounded values (34,000 and 35,000) and their midpoint (34,500); decide the round-up in one step.
Reassemble the answer as 35,000, writing in the placeholder zeros that keep the number in the thousands — do NOT stop at 35.

Now take 0.004982 and round to 2 significant figures: cross out the leading zeros as 'not significant', count the 4 and 9, apply the deciding digit (8) so 49 rounds up to 50, and write 0.0050 — keeping the front zeros for magnitude and the trailing zero for precision.
Repeat 0.004982 rounded to 2 decimal places (= 0.00) and place both answers side by side to see that dp and sf give genuinely different results.
activities.intendedInsight: Significant figures are counted from the first non-zero digit; zeros can be placeholders that hold a number's size or trailing zeros that record precision, so they cannot simply be dropped. Rounding is one nearness decision based on the next digit, after which place value must be restored.

activities.title: Contrast decimal places with significant figures on one number
feedback: If both methods give the same answer, check where the first significant figure is. With the same count (e.g. 2 dp and 2 sf), the answers agree when the first non-zero digit is in the tenths place (e.g. 0.364 → 0.36 both ways). They differ for numbers with leading zeros after the decimal point (0.004982) or with digits before the decimal point (3.14159, 47,320).
If a learner says the rules are 'the same', show 0.004982: 2 dp = 0.00 but 2 sf = 0.0050.
activities.rationale: Contrasting dp and sf on the same number is intended to address the named dp-vs-sf confusion. Presenting the comparison explicitly may help learners see that the two instructions are not interchangeable.
learnerActions: Pick a single number (e.g. 0.004982) and round it both to 2 decimal places and to 2 significant figures.
Record the two answers side by side (0.00 vs 0.0050) and write a sentence explaining why they differ.
Do the same for a large number such as 47,320: to 2 sf it is 47,000 (zeros needed), and note how that differs from a decimal-place instruction.
State in your own words when leading zeros are ignored and when zeros must be kept.
activities.intendedInsight: Decimal places and significant figures are different rules: dp counts from the decimal point, while sf counts from the first non-zero digit. The difference is most striking with leading zeros and with large numbers that need placeholder zeros, but they also differ for ordinary numbers (3.14159 is 3.14 to 2 dp and 3.1 to 2 sf). The same number can give very different rounded values under each.

activities.title: Choose and justify an appropriate degree of accuracy
feedback: If the justification ignores magnitude, prompt: does your rounded answer still describe roughly the same quantity as the original?
If a learner cannot name the deciding digit, revisit that only the digit immediately after the required place determines the round.
activities.rationale: The standards emphasise choosing accuracy appropriate to context (US N.Q; UK 'appropriate degree of accuracy'). Requiring spoken or written justification is intended to build reasoning beyond procedural execution. A short mentor-style challenge can surface the 'drop the zeros' and 'leading zeros count' errors during teaching; this is one useful format, not the only way to teach the procedure.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils round numbers and measures to an appropriate degree of accuracy, including a specified number of decimal places or significant figures.
Rounding to accuracy builds on 5.NBT.A.4 (round decimals to any place); appropriate precision is emphasised in high-school modelling (N.Q).
learnerActions: Given a context such as measuring a room's length, decide whether rounding to 2 decimal places or 2 significant figures is more appropriate, and explain why.
Explain to a partner (or in writing) why 47,320 to 2 sf needs its zeros on the end but 47 to 2 sf would not.
Respond to a challenge like: 'You rounded 34,750 to 2 significant figures and wrote 35 — convince me that is the right size.'
Justify which single digit decided each of your roundings and why the remaining digits did not matter.
activities.intendedInsight: Accuracy should suit the precision of the measurement or context, and learners should be able to justify both the rounded value's size and the choice of dp vs sf.

activities.title: Consolidation: quick-check rounding problems
feedback: For 0.004621 to 2 sf, confirm the answer is 0.0046 (the 4 and 6 are the sig figs); 0.00 would come from confusing sf with 2 dp.
For 47,320 to 2 sf, confirm 47,000; an answer of 47 has lost its magnitude.
For 1.998 to 2 dp, note the cascade carries to 2.00 and the trailing zeros must be written.
For 0.004982 to 2 sf, confirm 0.0050; the 0.00 option reflects the dp-vs-sf confusion.
activities.rationale: Short closed-response items can consolidate and check outcomes efficiently, including with a deliberate distractor exposing the dp/sf confusion. Such items check outcomes rather than build the identification skill, so they suit practice after the construction activities rather than instead of them.
learnerActions: Round 3.14159 to 2 decimal places (answer 3.14).
Round 0.004621 to 2 significant figures (answer 0.0046).
Round 47,320 to 2 significant figures (answer 47,000).
Round 0.004982 to 2 significant figures, choosing from answers that include the dp-confusion value 0.00 so you can check you avoid it (the correct value is 0.0050).
Round 2.988 to 2 dp (→ 2.99, a simple round-up) and 1.998 to 2 dp (→ 2.00, where the round-up carries through several places and the trailing zeros must be written).
activities.intendedInsight: After building the identification skill, learners can reliably apply dp and sf rounding, including the round-up cascade and placeholder/trailing zeros, in short targeted items.

constraints: Teach significant-figure identification before rounding to sf: the first sig fig is the first non-zero digit, leading zeros never count, and placeholder/trailing zeros hold magnitude and record precision.
Treat rounding as a single nearness/midpoint decision using only the digit immediately after the required place; avoid digit-by-digit chain rounding, which can make the answer drift.
Always restore place value with zeros after rounding large numbers to sf (35,000 not 35; 47,000 not 47) and keep trailing zeros that record precision (2.90, 0.0050).
Contrast dp and sf on the same number so learners see the rules diverge, especially on leading zeros and large magnitudes.
Closed-response/quick-check items check outcomes and do not, on their own, build significant-figure identification; use them to consolidate after construction work, not instead of it.
A single static worked example illustrates one case but cannot cover arbitrary numbers or let a learner test the dp-vs-sf divergence interactively; use it as a reference, not the whole task.

The legacy row's claim that '3D adds nothing' to this one-dimensional symbolic task was removed as an unsupported universal; 3D was simply not adopted as a format here, without asserting it can never help.

probeDeeper: Which single digit decided each rounding, and why did the rest not matter?
Why is 0.0046 to 2sf, not 0.00 — which zeros count and which don't?
Why does 47,320 to 2sf need the zeros on the end but 47 to 2sf wouldn't?
For measuring a room, would you round the length to 2 decimal places or 2 sig figs — why?

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts leading zeros as significant figures — rounds 0.004621 to 2sf as 0.00 or 0.0046 treated as 4 sf.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish that significant figures start at the first non-zero digit (the 4), so the 4 and 6 are the two sig figs; leading zeros only hold place.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Significant-figure count starts at the decimal point or at the first zero, not the first non-zero digit.

errorPatterns.pattern: Chain / digit-by-digit rounding — rounds 3.14159 stepwise (→3.1416→3.142→3.14) or rounds each digit in turn.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Round in one step: look only at the digit immediately after the required place (the 1 in the thousandths) and decide once.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Multiple intermediate roundings appear; the final answer sometimes drifts (e.g. 3.15).

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops digits without placeholder zeros for large numbers — rounds 47,320 to 2sf as 47 instead of 47,000.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Keep the two significant digits (4 and 7) but preserve place with zeros so the value stays in the ten-thousands; check the size is still reasonable.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rounded large number loses its magnitude (answer is 47, not 47,000).

responseLevels.gap: Confuses sig figs with decimal places, counts leading zeros, or drops magnitude on large numbers.
responseLevels.full: Rounds accurately to a specified number of decimal places and significant figures, handles leading/trailing zeros, and chooses an appropriate degree of accuracy for a context with justification.
responseLevels.partial: Rounds to decimal places correctly but is unreliable on significant figures with leading or trailing zeros.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Round these, showing your steps. (1) 3.14159 to 2 decimal places. (2) 0.004621 to 2 significant figures. (3) 47,320 to 2 significant figures.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watch which digit the child treats as significant and how they handle the deciding digit. Decimal-place rounding and significant-figure rounding pull apart on leading zeros (task 2) and on large numbers needing placeholder zeros (task 3); a child conflating the two rules, counting leading zeros as significant, or chain-rounding will produce revealing errors.

sources.claim: KS3 pupils round numbers and measures to an appropriate degree of accuracy, including a specified number of decimal places or significant figures.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (KS3)

sources.claim: Rounding to accuracy builds on 5.NBT.A.4 (round decimals to any place); appropriate precision is emphasised in high-school modelling (N.Q).
