pedagogy.summary: Ordering likelihoods asks children to compare several events and rank them least-to-most likely, including situations where outcomes are unequal (a bag with more of one colour, a spinner with uneven sections). Same-total comparisons are solvable by simple 'more/less' reasoning; the deeper demand — comparing across different totals — requires proportional reasoning, which the research shows develops slowly. Teaching should secure confident additive comparison and begin nudging children from absolute counts toward the proportion of favourable outcomes.
bestPractices: Build from same-total comparisons (which bag/section gives red the best chance when totals match) before introducing different totals
Make the proportional jump visible with a two-bag comparison where the bag with MORE red counters actually has a LOWER chance of red (e.g. 3 red of 4 vs 6 red of 12)
Have children physically order event cards along a least→most-likely line and defend each move
Press for reasons in terms of 'how many out of the whole' rather than 'how many reds', to shift attention from absolute number to proportion
Confront the 'it's random so you can't tell' response by sampling repeatedly and tallying, so order shows up in the long run
keyRepresentations: Least-to-most-likely ordering line
Two (or more) bags of counters compared side by side, part-whole visible
Spinners with sections of different sizes
Fraction/area strips linking proportion of red to chance of red
commonMisconceptions: Comparing by absolute count of favourable outcomes ('Bag B has 6 reds, Bag A only 3, so B is better') instead of proportion
The 'difference' strategy — comparing by the gap between the two colours (reds minus blues) rather than the fraction of the whole
Equiprobability bias — 'it's random, so every bag/colour is equally likely and you can't rank them'
Ranking by personal desire or by which outcome happened last, rather than by composition

learn.summary: Children aged 9–10 rank several chance events from least to most likely, including unequal outcomes (a bag with more of one colour, a spinner with uneven sections). Same-total comparisons yield to simple more/less reasoning; comparing across different totals demands proportional reasoning, which research shows develops slowly. Teaching should secure confident additive comparison, then nudge attention from absolute counts toward the proportion of favourable outcomes. The signature task sets up a case where the bag with MORE red counters has a LOWER chance of red (3 red of 4 vs 6 red of 12), and uses repeated sampling to let a count-based guess be publicly corrected by a long-run tally.

activities.title: Rank two bags, then test by sampling
feedback: If the child ranks Bag B higher because 'six reds beats three', run the sampling: over many draws Bag A will usually pull red more often (about three in every four draws against about one in two), and if a short run happens to mislead, pool more draws. Then point to all the counters in each bag, blues included, and ask 'out of ALL the counters, how much of each bag is red?' and shade three-quarters of A beside one-half of B.

If the child says 'it's random, you can't tell which is better', sample many draws from each bag and tally; the long-run difference is visible even though each single draw is unpredictable — this separates 'random' from 'equally likely'.

When the child re-ranks Bag A to the top and justifies with the share of the whole, confirm that this share is what the growing tally gets close to: over many draws the fraction of reds moves towards the share, but it rarely matches it exactly.

On the 60-red/40-blue extension, if the child now favours Bag B because the numbers are big, compare shares directly: three-fifths is still less than three-quarters, so bigger raw counts do not by themselves make a better chance.
activities.rationale: Comparing across different totals requires proportional reasoning, and children frequently fall back on raw frequency; making the count-based ordering publicly wrong and then visible as a share targets that shift. Repeated sampling addresses the belief that a random situation cannot be ranked. An editable-bag-plus-sampler arrangement is one concrete way to let a wrong ranking be tested; a physical version with real bags, replacing each counter before the next draw, and tally marks works the same way.
sourceClaims: Comparing likelihoods across situations with different totals requires proportional reasoning; children frequently fall back on additive strategies — giving the raw frequency, or the 'difference' between the two colours (Falk & Wilkening) — rather than the proportion of the whole, and success on genuinely proportional comparison develops slowly.

The equiprobability bias — assuming outcomes are all equally likely / that a random situation cannot be ranked — is documented in children as young as 10 (Pratt) as a first response to chance situations.
learnerActions: Look at Bag A (3 red, 1 blue) and Bag B (6 red, 6 blue), both fully visible, and rank which gives the better chance of pulling red before any draws.
State a reason for the ranking out loud.

Draw many times from each bag (e.g. 50 draws each), noting each drawn counter's colour and returning it to the bag before the next draw so the proportion stays fixed, and tally how often red comes up, comparing the two tallies.
Revise the ranking if the tally contradicts the first guess, and say why — in terms of how big a share of each bag is red, not how many reds.
Look at a shaded red-fraction strip beside each tally (three-quarters of A, one-half of B) and connect the share to the observed long-run frequency.

As an extension, suppose Bag B instead held 60 red and 40 blue: check whether these bigger numbers change the ranking (60 of 100 is three-fifths, higher than one-half but still below Bag A's three-quarters, so Bag A is still the better bet).
activities.intendedInsight: A better chance of red depends on the proportion of red in the whole bag (three-quarters beats one-half), not on the raw number of red counters — so a bag with more reds can still be the worse bet.

activities.title: Order four or more events on a least→most-likely line
feedback: If the child orders by raw count of reds, swap in a card with more reds but a smaller share and ask them to predict and then check by sampling.
If the child ranks by personal preference or by which outcome happened last, redirect to the composition: 'how many out of the whole is red here?'
Press for 'how many out of the whole' rather than 'how many reds' on every placement.
activities.rationale: Physically ordering and defending each move makes the ranking an explicit, revisable claim rather than a one-off guess, and building from same-total to different-total comparisons sequences the additive before the proportional demand. Socratic challenge ('what if I doubled the blues?') surfaces the reasoning; the proportional point may land more firmly when the child can also manipulate and sample, so pair argument with testing where possible.
sourceClaims: Comparing likelihoods across situations with different totals requires proportional reasoning; children frequently fall back on additive strategies — giving the raw frequency, or the 'difference' between the two colours (Falk & Wilkening) — rather than the proportion of the whole, and success on genuinely proportional comparison develops slowly.
Likelihood is described with a graded word-scale and 'even chance' applies only when outcomes genuinely match in number, motivating comparison of bags/spinners by composition.
learnerActions: Physically place four or more event cards along a 'least likely → most likely' rail (e.g. different bags or spinners with varying red fractions).
Defend each placement, and each time a card is moved, say why it should sit higher or lower.
Respond to a challenge such as 'why is that one higher? what if I doubled the blues?' by giving a reason in terms of the share of the whole, not just the number of reds.
Start with cards that share the same total (so simple more/less reasoning works) before mixing in cards with different totals.
activities.intendedInsight: Events can be placed in a consistent order of likelihood by comparing the proportion of favourable outcomes; same-total cases need only more/less, but different-total cases need the share of the whole.

activities.title: Spinner prediction: does section size matter?
feedback: If the child predicts roughly equal because 'it could land on either', spin and tally: red near 15 vs blue near 5 confronts the prediction and forces attention to section size.
Use the follow-up 'could the less-likely colour still come up next spin?' to separate 'more likely in the long run' from 'certain on a single trial'.
Reserve 'even chance' for cases where the outcomes genuinely match in number, so the child does not over-apply it to unequal spinners.
activities.rationale: Predict-then-test on an unequal spinner directly targets equiprobability bias by letting a prediction of 'about the same' be contradicted by the tally, while the single-trial follow-up guards against treating 'more likely' as 'certain'. The graded likelihood word-scale and the restriction of 'even chance' to matched outcomes motivate comparing by composition.
sourceClaims: The equiprobability bias — assuming outcomes are all equally likely / that a random situation cannot be ranked — is documented in children as young as 10 (Pratt) as a first response to chance situations.
Likelihood is described with a graded word-scale and 'even chance' applies only when outcomes genuinely match in number, motivating comparison of bags/spinners by composition.
learnerActions: Look at a spinner where red fills three-quarters and blue one-quarter, alongside a fair coin.
Before spinning, predict: over 20 spins, will red and blue come up about the same number of times, or will one come up much more — and state a reason.
Spin 20 times and tally red versus blue (expect red near 15, blue near 5).
Compare the tally to the prediction and explain what the size of each section did to the outcome.
Consider follow-ups: could the less-likely colour still come up on the very next spin? What does 'more likely' actually mean here?
activities.intendedInsight: When outcomes are not equally sized, 'it could land on either' does not make them equally likely — the size (proportion) of each section governs the long-run frequency, and a more-likely outcome can still fail on a single trial.

activities.title: The 'difference' trap: 20 red vs 18 blue
feedback: If the child says the two bags are equally good because each has 2 more reds than blues, show that 3 of 4 is three-quarters while 20 of 38 is barely above one-half: equal gaps, very different chances — this forces the comparison onto the fraction of the whole.
If the child still leans on the gap, convert each bag to 'how many out of the whole is red' and compare those shares directly.
Confirm success when the child abandons the gap and ranks by the share of red in each bag.
activities.rationale: The 'difference' strategy is a documented additive fallback; pairing two bags with an identical gap but very different proportions exposes it without relying on the child already trusting the proportional rule. This is a targeted correction to use once absolute-count errors are being addressed.
sourceClaims: Comparing likelihoods across situations with different totals requires proportional reasoning; children frequently fall back on additive strategies — giving the raw frequency, or the 'difference' between the two colours (Falk & Wilkening) — rather than the proportion of the whole, and success on genuinely proportional comparison develops slowly.
learnerActions: Compare a bag of 20 red and 18 blue with a clearly lopsided bag of 3 red and 1 blue, and decide which gives the better chance of red. Notice that BOTH bags have the same gap: 2 more reds than blues.
Explain the reasoning, noticing whether it rests on the gap between the colours (reds minus blues) or on the share of the whole.
Work out what share of each bag is red (close to one-half for 20 of 38, three-quarters for 3 of 4) and use that to place both in order.
Check the conclusion by sampling (with each counter returned before the next draw) if a count-based or difference-based answer is given.
activities.intendedInsight: Comparing by the gap between the two colours (reds minus blues) can mislead: 20 red and 18 blue and 3 red and 1 blue both have a gap of 2, yet 20 of 38 is almost an even chance while 3 of 4 is three-quarters — so the fraction of the whole, not the surplus of reds, decides likelihood.

constraints: Build from same-total comparisons (which bag/section gives red the best chance when totals match) before introducing different totals.

A pre-ordered likelihood line with tap-to-reveal reasons ('X out of Y, so …') is a useful worked reference, but as a fixed display it does not itself let the child test a wrong ranking or carry out the proportional correction; use it to model good ordering, not as the sole activity.

Multiple-choice or drag-to-order response formats can carry the key discriminator (e.g. 3-of-4 vs 6-of-12 with distractors 'B, it has more reds' and 'the same, it's random') and can be used during teaching as well as for checking; recognition-format responses alone do not require the child to construct and defend a ranking, so pair them with spoken or written justification.

Repeated sampling is central to confronting the 'it's random, you can't tell' response: a single draw is unpredictable, but tallying many draws reveals the long-run order. Sample with replacement (return each counter) so the stated proportions stay fixed across many draws.
Always press for reasons in terms of 'how many out of the whole' rather than 'how many reds'.
Reserve 'even chance' for situations where the outcomes genuinely match in number.
When observing spinners or bags, inspect the actual drawn/spun outcomes and tallies; a short run may vary from the expected proportion, so pool more draws if a run happens to mislead.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labelled ranking likelihoods a non-spatial task where '3D adds no leverage'; this catalog-fit judgement is not an established pedagogical law and has been dropped rather than asserted. No universal claim about any medium is made here.

The suggestion that manipulation/sampling makes the proportional insight land more firmly than argument alone is a comparative-efficacy framing not established by the cited literature; it is stated with 'may' as a design suggestion only.

The sampling activities assume drawing with replacement; with only 4 and 12 counters, the child must return each drawn counter before the next draw for many-draw tallies to reflect the fixed proportion.

Sampling 50 or 20 draws yields outcomes near the expected proportions (e.g. red near 15 of 20 for a three-quarter spinner) but will vary run to run; frame these as approximate long-run tendencies, and if a short run happens to mislead, pool more draws or combine results across the group.

The worked numbers are internally consistent: 3 of 4 = three-quarters > 6 of 12 = one-half, so Bag A is correctly the better chance of red; 20 of 38 for the 20-red/18-blue bag is just above one-half, consistent with 'nearly even'; and 60 of 100 = three-fifths is below three-quarters, so Bag A stays ahead in the extension.
The 'difference' trap pairs two bags with an identical gap of 2 (20/18 and 3/1) so that a reds-minus-blues strategist is genuinely misled, matching the original diagnostic intent.

assess.poeTask: Show a spinner divided so that red fills three-quarters and blue one-quarter, alongside a fair coin. Ask: 'Over 20 spins, will red and blue come up about the same number of times, or will one come up much more — and why?' Have the child state a prediction AND a reason before spinning. A child who thinks 'it could land on either, so about the same' predicts roughly equal; spinning 20 times and tallying (red near 15, blue near 5) confronts that prediction and forces attention to the size of each section.
probeDeeper: What if I now told you Bag B had 60 red and 40 blue — would that change your answer? Why?
Cover up the blue counters. Just from the reds, can you tell which bag is better? What else do you need to know?
Suppose a third bag had 20 red and 18 blue — where would it go in the order, and why?
You said one is 'more likely'. Could the less-likely bag still give a red on the very next pull? So what does 'more likely' actually mean here?
assess.correctAnswer: Bag A. Even though Bag B contains more red counters (6 versus 3), three of the four counters in Bag A are red — three-quarters — while only six of the twelve in Bag B are red — one half. Bag A has the higher proportion of red, so a better chance.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares by absolute count of favourable outcomes — 'Bag B, it has more red counters (6 beats 3)'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Direct attention to the whole: cover the blues and ask 'out of ALL the counters, how much of each bag is red?'; shade three-quarters of A and one-half of B side by side
errorPatterns.distractor: Bag B, because it has more red counters — 6 reds, and Bag A only has 3.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks Bag B and reasons from the raw number of reds, ignoring how many counters there are altogether

errorPatterns.pattern: Equiprobability bias — 'it's the same, pulling a counter is random so you can't say which bag is better'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sample many draws from each bag and tally; the long-run difference is visible even though each single draw is unpredictable, separating 'random' from 'equally likely'
errorPatterns.distractor: It's the same — pulling a counter is random, so you can't say which bag is better.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says both bags are equally good and appeals to randomness/luck rather than composition

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Difference' strategy — compares by the gap between the colours (reds minus blues) rather than the proportion of the whole
errorPatterns.nextMove: Offer the 20-red/18-blue counterexample: a difference of 2 but almost an even chance; force the comparison onto the fraction of the whole, not the gap
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reason cites the surplus of reds over blues ('A has 2 more reds than blues; B has none more'); gives the wrong answer when shown a bag like 20 red / 18 blue (gap of 2 but nearly even)

responseLevels.gap: Cannot rank beyond guessing or says 'it's random, you can't tell'; ordering ignores composition entirely
responseLevels.full: Ranks by the proportion of favourable outcomes, picks Bag A and justifies with three-quarters vs one-half, and keeps the ranking correct when totals are changed; recognises a more-likely event can still fail on a single trial
responseLevels.partial: Ranks correctly when totals are equal or by counting favourable outcomes, but picks the larger-count bag when proportion and count diverge, or reasons from the red-minus-blue difference — lists the numbers without converting to a share of the whole

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show two bags of counters, both visible. Bag A: 3 red and 1 blue. Bag B: 6 red and 6 blue. Ask: 'Which bag gives you a better chance of pulling out a red — and why?' Take their answer, then ask them to explain their reason fully (Tier 2).
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A proportional reasoner picks Bag A and justifies with the fraction of red in each bag; a child using absolute counts picks Bag B because it has more red counters; an equiprobability-biased child says 'the same, it's random'. The Tier-2 reason exposes which, and only the proportional reason survives when the totals are then changed.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 11–12 — order positive and negative integers, decimals and fractions on a number line; use =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥ to compare values, including negatives and mixed representations.
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics, KS3): 'order positive and negative integers, decimals and fractions; use the symbols =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥.'
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): 6.NS.C.7 — understand ordering and absolute value of rational numbers; write, interpret and explain statements of order (e.g. −3 > −7).
• Operational details: Order by POSITION on the number line (left = less), which handles negatives and mixed forms uniformly. Convert mixed representations to a common form (decimal or common denominator) or place each on the line before applying symbols. Introduce ≠, ≤, ≥ alongside <, >, = and distinguish strict from inclusive. Interpret order statements in context ('−3 > −7 means −3°C is warmer').
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 11): 'True or false: −5 < −2.' Tier B: 'Order 0.75, 3/4, −0.8, 7/10.' Tier C: 'Write a single statement using ≤ that is true for all of 2, 2.0, 4/2.'
bestPractices: Order by position on the number line (leftmost is least) so negatives and mixed forms are handled by one rule, not sign-specific tricks
Convert mixed representations to a common form (decimal or common denominator) before comparing, and verify by placing on the line
Introduce ≠, ≤, ≥ explicitly alongside <, >, = and contrast strict (<) with inclusive (≤)
Read comparison statements aloud in context ('−3 is greater than −7 because it is warmer / further right')
Bait the 'bigger digit = bigger value' error deliberately with negatives (−5 vs −2) and unequal-length decimals
keyRepresentations: Number line as the arbiter of order (left → right = least → greatest)
Common-form conversion (3/4 → 0.75) to compare across representations
Symbol cards =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥ placed between two values
Sorting track / ordering slots that snap items into line positions
commonMisconceptions: Ordering negatives by magnitude (−5 placed as greater than −2)
Comparing fractions and decimals by surface features instead of converting to a common form
Confusing < and > direction (the 'alligator eats the bigger' heuristic misapplied)
Treating ≤/≥ as identical to </> and missing the equality case
Assuming a longer decimal or larger denominator is automatically larger/smaller

learn.summary: For ages 11–12: order positive and negative integers, decimals and fractions on a single number line (leftmost = least), and use =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥ to compare values, including negatives and mixed representations. The core principle is that POSITION on the line — not sign, digit count, or denominator size — is the single rule that orders every kind of number, and that equal values (e.g. 0.75 and 3/4) sit at the same point, so neither < nor > holds between them; = is the precise relation, and ≤ and ≥ are also true. The primary activity is a hands-on positional sort of mixed-form cards with a common-form conversion check; supporting activities consolidate symbol conventions, interrogate wrong orderings, and read statements in context.

activities.title: Drop mixed-form numbers onto one number line and choose the symbol between neighbours
feedback: If negatives are ordered by magnitude (e.g. −1.5 written as less than −2, or −2 placed to the right of −1.5): anchor on position — further left = smaller; −2 is left of −1.5, so −2 < −1.5. Reason from where it sits, not from digit size.
If 0.75 and 3/4 are placed at different points or not joined by '=': convert one form to the other (3 ÷ 4 = 0.75) and land both on the same point, then compare.
If ≤ is used where = or < is meant, or the inequality opens toward the smaller value: read the statement aloud in words — the open side faces the larger value, and ≤ means 'less than OR equal'.

If a longer decimal or larger denominator is assumed automatically larger: place both on the line to test — e.g. 0.8 vs 0.75, where the shorter decimal 0.8 is the larger value, so more digits does not mean larger. (For negatives the extra wrinkle is that −0.8 < −0.75.)
activities.rationale: Ordering mixed forms is decided by position, so letting the learner perform the sort, convert to a common form to check, and attach symbols between neighbours makes the one positional rule visible and surfaces the equal-values-coincide case. Dragging, the decimal-conversion toggle, and stacking of coincident cards are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete; they are not required mechanisms, and their comparative effectiveness over other media is not established by the cited sources.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils order positive and negative integers, decimals and fractions and use the symbols =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥.
learnerActions: Take a set of mixed cards — 0.75, 3/4, −0.8, −0.75, 7/10, −2, −1.5, 1/2 — and place each at its correct position on a shared number line.
Use a 'show as decimal' conversion (e.g. 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75) to check cross-form values before placing them.
Notice that 0.75 and 3/4 land on the IDENTICAL point and coincide there.
Between each adjacent pair of placed cards, select a symbol from =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥ and justify the choice.
Confirm that between the two coincident cards the strict symbols < and > (and ≠) are false; = is the most precise choice, and the inclusive ≤ and ≥ are also true because they allow equality.
Deliberately test the surprise case: see that −0.8 sits LEFT of −0.75, so −0.8 is smaller, even though 0.8 > 0.75 for positives — defeating the 'bigger magnitude wins' instinct for negatives.
activities.intendedInsight: Position on the number line (left = less) is a single rule that orders integers, decimals, fractions, positives and negatives uniformly; equal values coincide, so < and > cannot hold between them, while = (and the inclusive ≤, ≥) are true.

activities.title: Consolidate the symbol conventions with true/false and ordering checks
feedback: For '−5 < −2': it is TRUE because −5 is further left on the line than −2.
If ≤ and < are treated as identical: recall ≤ also holds when the two values are equal, so a statement using ≤ can be true for equal values like 2, 2.0 and 4/2 (all equal to 2).
If a sequence mis-ranks negatives or equal forms: re-place the items on a line to check before fixing the symbols.
activities.rationale: Recognition and selection items are a useful consolidation companion for the symbol conventions, best used after the positional meaning is established. These items check and reinforce convention use; they do not by themselves elicit independent construction of an ordering.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils order positive and negative integers, decimals and fractions and use the symbols =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥.
learnerActions: Judge true/false statements such as '−5 < −2' and explain the reasoning from position.
Match order statements to the correct symbol from =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥.
Order a mixed-form set smallest to largest as a sequence.
Write a single statement using ≤ that is true for all of 2, 2.0, 4/2.
activities.intendedInsight: Order statements and symbol conventions (including strict vs inclusive) can be applied fluently once positional ordering is understood.

activities.title: Interrogate and repair a wrong ordering in discussion or context
feedback: If the learner cannot say why −5 belongs left of −2: tie '−5 < −2' to temperature — −5°C is colder, so smaller, and sits further left.

If strict and inclusive are confused: have them state in words whether equality is possible for the pair; < needs the values to be different, while ≤ is true both when the first is smaller and when they are equal, so ≤ is the natural choice when equality could hold.
activities.rationale: Dialogue can interrogate a wrong ordering and surface reasoning, and reading statements in context ('warmer / further right') supports interpretation of order statements such as −3 > −7. This complements, rather than replaces, performing the positional sort.
sourceClaims: 6.NS.C.7: understand ordering of rational numbers and write/interpret statements of order such as −3 > −7.
learnerActions: Examine a given ordering that mis-ranks negatives (e.g. −5 placed to the right of −2) and explain why it is wrong, referring to position.
Read comparison statements aloud in context, e.g. '−3 > −7 means −3°C is warmer / further right than −7°C'.
Decide when ≤ would be used instead of < between two values, and say why.
State an inference about relative size from a placement, e.g. which of −2 and −1.5 is smaller and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating WHY an ordering is right or wrong — in words and in real contexts like temperature — reinforces positional reasoning and distinguishes strict from inclusive comparison.

constraints: Order by POSITION on the number line (leftmost is least) so negatives and mixed forms are handled by one rule rather than sign-specific tricks.
Convert mixed representations to a common form (decimal or common denominator) before comparing, and verify by placing on the line.
Introduce ≠, ≤, ≥ explicitly alongside <, >, = and contrast strict (<) with inclusive (≤), making the equality case explicit.

Deliberately bait the 'bigger digit = bigger value' error two ways: with negatives (−5 vs −2, where the larger-magnitude number is smaller; and −0.8 vs −0.75, where −0.8 < −0.75) and with unequal-length positive decimals (0.8 vs 0.75, where the shorter decimal is larger) so the misconception is confronted directly rather than accidentally confirmed.
Recognition/selection items (true/false, matching) check convention use but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of an ordering; use the hands-on positional sort for that.

A static labelled line with forms placed and symbols shown can illustrate a completed ordering but does not let the learner perform the sort or select symbols with feedback; it is a worked-example scaffold, not the full task.

Position-order for this objective is represented along a single line (one dimension), so a third spatial dimension is not needed here; this is a scoped observation about representing order, not a general claim that 3D 'adds nothing'.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Both cited sources carry verified:false in the row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Math check: −0.8 < −0.75 (−0.8 is further from zero on the negative side, hence further left); −2 < −1.5; 0.75 = 3/4; 1/2 = 0.5; 7/10 = 0.7. Full order of the 8-card activity set: −2 < −1.5 < −0.8 < −0.75 < 1/2 < 7/10 < 3/4 = 0.75. The smaller 5-item diagnostic answer −2 < −1.5 < 1/2 < 3/4 = 0.75 is consistent for its own set.

Original-row inconsistency: the recommendation names −0.75 as the surprise neighbour but never lists it among the cards (0.75, 3/4, −0.8, 7/10, −2). This was corrected by including both −0.8 and −0.75 so the intended comparison is actually available; the original wording is retained only as an uncertainty note.
The 'alligator eats the bigger' heuristic is listed as a common misconception in the source; it is reframed here as reading the open side as facing the larger value, rather than taught as a mnemonic.

Efficacy/necessity of the hands-on track relative to the consolidation checks, static image or dialogue is not established by the standards documents, which support the objective rather than any medium's superiority.

probeDeeper: Is 0.75 the same as 3/4? Convert one to check, then place both.
On the line, which is further left, −2 or −1.5 — and so which is smaller?
Put the correct symbol between −1.5 and −2, and say why.
When would you use ≤ instead of < between two of these?

errorPatterns.pattern: Orders negatives by magnitude: places −2 to the right of −1.5 or writes −1.5 < −2
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor on the number line: further left = smaller. −2 is left of −1.5, so −2 < −1.5. Reason from position.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the line −2 sits nearer zero than −1.5, or the inequality between them is reversed.

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot compare across representations: treats 0.75 and 3/4 as different sizes, or ranks 0.75 > 3/4
errorPatterns.nextMove: Convert one form to the other (3 ÷ 4 = 0.75) and land both on the same point; then compare.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 0.75 and 3/4 are placed at different points, or = is not chosen between them.

errorPatterns.pattern: Misuses the strict vs inclusive symbols, or reverses < / >
errorPatterns.nextMove: Read each statement aloud as words; the open side faces the larger value, and ≤ means 'less than OR equal'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Uses ≤ where = or < is meant, or opens the inequality toward the smaller value.

responseLevels.gap: Orders negatives by magnitude or cannot equate 0.75 and 3/4; symbols used loosely.
responseLevels.full: Places integers, decimals and fractions (positive and negative) on one line, equates equivalent forms, and uses =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥ correctly.
responseLevels.partial: Orders within one representation (or the positives) but slips on cross-form equality or negative ordering.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give a mixed set: −2, 0.75, 3/4, −1.5, 1/2. Say: 'Place these on a number line and order them smallest to largest. Then put the right symbol between 0.75 and 3/4, and between −1.5 and −2.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The set mixes representations (fraction vs decimal for the same value) and negatives, so it cannot be ordered by surface features. Placing them on ONE line and choosing = vs <,> reveals whether the child translates between forms and reasons about negative position rather than digit size.

pedagogy.summary: Factorising by common factors is the inverse of expanding: rewrite a sum as a product by pulling out the highest common factor (HCF) of every term, leaving a bracket that itself has no common factor. 6x+9 = 3(2x+3). It is best taught alongside expanding, using the reverse area model (arrange the terms into a rectangle; the common side is the factor, and the WIDEST rectangle uses the HCF) and always checking by expanding the answer back. The signature errors are taking a common factor that is not the HIGHEST (incomplete factorisation) and dropping or mis-dividing a term.
bestPractices: Teach it as the reverse of expanding — do an expansion, then run it backwards — and always CHECK by expanding the factorised form.
Find the HCF of the coefficients (and any common variable) first; stress 'fully' means no common factor is left inside the bracket.
Use the reverse area/array model: the terms tile a rectangle whose common side is the factor; the HCF gives the neatest single rectangle.
Divide EVERY term by the factor — 6x÷3 and 9÷3 — and write each result inside the bracket; a dropped term is the classic slip.
Extend to a common variable factor, e.g. x²+3x = x(x+3), so 'common factor' includes letters, not just numbers.
keyRepresentations: Reverse area/array model (terms arranged into a rectangle; common side = factor)
HCF via prime factors or factor lists of the coefficients
Expand-back check (product → sum)
Side-by-side expand/factorise pair showing the inverse relationship
commonMisconceptions: Takes a common factor that is not the HIGHEST: 12x+8 → 2(6x+4) instead of 4(3x+2) — 'factorised' but not fully.
Drops or fails to divide a term: 6x+9 → 3(2x) or 3(2x+9) (the 9 not divided).
Only spots numeric factors and misses a common variable: x²+3x left unfactorised or written 3(x²)... .
Does not check by expanding, so an incorrect factorisation goes unnoticed.
Confuses factorising (→ product) with simplifying/collecting (→ fewer terms).

learn.summary: Factorising by common factors is the inverse of expanding: rewrite a sum as a product by pulling out the highest common factor (HCF) of every term, leaving a bracket with no remaining common factor, e.g. 6x+9 = 3(2x+3). Teach it alongside expanding, use a reverse area/array model (arrange the terms into a rectangle whose common side is the factor; the HCF gives the single rectangle with the LARGEST common side — the most compact block, not the long thin strip a smaller factor leaves), and always check by expanding the answer back. Signature errors are taking a factor that is not the highest (incomplete factorisation) and dropping or mis-dividing a term. Extend 'common factor' to a shared letter, e.g. x²+3x = x(x+3).

activities.title: Build the rectangle with the largest common side: the reverse area model
feedback: If you pulled out 2 from 12x+8: look inside the bracket — 6x and 4 are both still even, so a factor of 2 can still be shared. Ask 'is there still a number that divides everything in the bracket?' and pull it out too, or find the HCF of 12 and 8 first (it is 4).
If you wrote 3(2x) for 6x+9, a term has gone missing: every original term must appear as factor × bracket-entry. 9 must be divided too — 9÷3 = 3 — giving 3(2x+3).
If you wrote 3(2x+9), the 9 was not divided: divide each term by 3, then expand back to test — 3(2x+3) = 6x+9, but 3(2x+9) = 6x+27.
To check any answer, multiply it out: if it does not give the expression you started with, a term was dropped or mis-divided.
For x²+3x, a number alone is not the common factor — every term also contains an x, so x(x+3) is the fully factorised form.
activities.rationale: Arranging terms into a rectangle is intended to make 'find the HCF' concrete as 'make the rectangle with the largest common side that leaves nothing to share', and pairing it with an expand-back step is intended to build the inverse relationship with expanding and the self-check habit. Area representations are documented as linking the two directions.
sourceClaims: Factorising is best taught explicitly as the inverse of expanding/the distributive law ('factor × factor = product', 3(a+b)=3a+3b; pose the reverse question 'if the product is 3a+3b, what are the factors?'), and the distributive law's 'every term inside the brackets is multiplied by the term outside' principle is what prevents dropping/mis-dividing a term when working the inverse (factorising) direction; the objective is to factorise expressions where there is a common factor (e.g. 3a+12b).
Factorising is the inverse of expanding a single bracket; the correct expansions the expand-back check relies on (e.g. 2(n+3)=2n+6) are documented, and area representations link the two directions.
learnerActions: Take the tiles for 12x + 8 (twelve x-tiles and eight unit tiles) and try to arrange them into one solid rectangle.

First try a common side of 2: notice the result is a long 2-by-(6x+4) strip. Check whether each row could be split again into equal parts — it can, because 6x and 4 both still divide by 2, so the strip can be regrouped into a taller rectangle. That means 2 is a common factor but not the highest, so 2(6x+4) is not fully factorised.
Now try a common side of 4: the tiles form a compact 4-by-(3x+2) block with nothing left to share, giving 12x + 8 = 4(3x + 2).
Divide EVERY original term by the factor you pulled out (12x÷4 = 3x and 8÷4 = 2) and write each result inside the bracket.
Use an 'expand back' action to re-spread the rectangle into 12x + 8 and confirm the product equals what you started with.
Repeat with a shared letter: arrange x² + 3x and find that the common side is x, giving x(x + 3).
activities.intendedInsight: The highest common factor is 'the biggest common side that leaves nothing left to share', so fully factorised means no common factor remains inside the bracket; factorising and expanding are inverse moves.

activities.title: Factorise then expand-back: the routine check
feedback: 2(6x+4) is a correct factorisation but NOT fully factorised: 6x and 4 both still divide by 2, so the HCF (4) was not used. Fully factorised is 4(3x+2).
If expanding back does not return the original, look for a term that was dropped from the bracket or a term that was not divided by the factor.
Finding the HCF first (here 4 for 12x+8, 3 for 6x+9) lets you factorise fully in one step instead of stopping early.
Factorising undoes expanding: expanding turns a product into a sum; factorising turns a sum back into a product.
activities.rationale: Judging 'fully vs not fully' and verifying by expanding back are intended to target the two signature errors (incomplete factorisation and dropped/mis-divided terms). Partial factorisation is a documented student response.
sourceClaims: Partial / not-fully factorisation — removing only one available common factor and stopping (on 9x²+6x, taking out only the 3 or only the x rather than the full 3x) — is a documented, recognised student response, explicitly built into the mark scheme as a one-mark partial factorisation.
Factorising is the inverse of expanding a single bracket; the correct expansions the expand-back check relies on (e.g. 2(n+3)=2n+6) are documented, and area representations link the two directions.
learnerActions: Given 6x + 9, find the HCF of 6 and 9 using prime factors or factor lists, then write 6x+9 = 3(2x+3), dividing each term by 3.
Immediately expand your product back out and confirm it returns the original expression.
Decide whether a given bracket is fully factorised: is 2(6x+4) fully factorised? Explain how you can tell.
Explain in your own words what factorising is 'undoing'.
activities.intendedInsight: A factorisation is only complete when the bracket shares no further common factor, and expanding back is the way to catch dropped or mis-divided terms.

activities.title: Annotated worked example: where each number comes from
feedback: Check that each original term (6x and 9) is accounted for inside the bracket: 6x÷3 = 2x and 9÷3 = 3. If one is missing, the factorisation is wrong, because expanding it back will not give the original expression.
This worked example is fixed and cannot be re-arranged, so follow it up by factorising a fresh expression yourself and expanding it back.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal annotated example is intended to make the origin of each part explicit and to support learners before they search for the HCF independently; it shows the parts but does not let the learner search for the HCF by building, so it works as a scaffold rather than the main task.
sourceClaims: Factorising is best taught explicitly as the inverse of expanding/the distributive law ('factor × factor = product', 3(a+b)=3a+3b; pose the reverse question 'if the product is 3a+3b, what are the factors?'), and the distributive law's 'every term inside the brackets is multiplied by the term outside' principle is what prevents dropping/mis-dividing a term when working the inverse (factorising) direction; the objective is to factorise expressions where there is a common factor (e.g. 3a+12b).
learnerActions: Study the worked line 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3) and reveal, one piece at a time, where the 3, the 2x and the 3 inside the bracket each come from (3 is the HCF; 2x = 6x÷3; 3 = 9÷3).
Trace each original term to its matching entry inside the bracket, confirming no term was dropped.
activities.intendedInsight: Every term in the sum maps to factor × a term in the bracket, which is why no term may be dropped or left undivided.

constraints: 'Fully factorised' means no common factor (number or letter) remains inside the bracket; stopping at a smaller common factor is incomplete.
Every original term must be divided by the factor and appear inside the bracket; a dropped or undivided term is the classic slip.
Always verify by expanding the product back to the original sum before accepting an answer.
The annotated worked example is a fixed scaffold: it displays the parts but cannot let the learner search for the HCF by building, so pair it with learner-constructed factorisations.
The array/rectangle model is planar; representing it in three dimensions can misleadingly suggest volume, so keep it two-dimensional.
Selecting the fully factorised option or answering yes/no about completeness checks recognition; require learners to produce the factorisation and expand it back to evidence independent construction.
Distinguish factorising (produces a product) from simplifying/collecting like terms (produces fewer terms).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit arithmetic check (all confirmed): HCF(12,8)=4, 12x÷4=3x, 8÷4=2, so 12x+8=4(3x+2); the smaller-factor trap 2(6x+4) is a genuine but incomplete factorisation. HCF(6,9)=3, 6x÷3=2x, 9÷3=3, so 6x+9=3(2x+3). x²+3x=x(x+3). 3(2x+9) wrongly expands to 6x+27, confirming it as an error. All consistent with source fields.

The source frames the reverse area model and the quiz as the strongest fits; these are catalog preferences, not evidence of comparative efficacy or necessity, and have been presented as options with stated affordances/limits rather than universal laws.

The original pedagogy summary's 'widest rectangle' phrasing is ambiguous because a smaller factor actually leaves a longer strip; it has been reworded to 'largest common side / most compact block' so the summary matches the activity descriptions and the intended insight.

Removed the KS3 curriculum claim from the reverse area-model activity's sourceClaims because it supports the topic/objective generally rather than that activity's specific rationale; retained the claims that directly support the inverse-of-expanding and area-representation principles.

probeDeeper: Is 2(6x+4) fully factorised? How can you tell? (counterexample — the incomplete factorisation; the tell is a factor still shared inside the bracket)
Expand your answer back out — do you get 12x+8?
How is factorising related to expanding — what is it 'undoing'?
Now try x² + 3x — is there a common factor that isn't a number?

errorPatterns.pattern: Takes a common factor that is not the highest — 12x+8 → 2(6x+4) — stopping before it is fully factorised.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'is there still a number that divides everything inside the bracket?'; find the HCF of the coefficients first (prime factors), then factorise in one step.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The bracket still contains terms with a common factor (6x+4 both divide by 2); the pulled-out number is smaller than the HCF.

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops or fails to divide a term — 6x+9 → 3(2x) losing the 9, or 3(2x+9) with the 9 not divided.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach via the inverse: EVERY original term must be the factor times its bracket entry; divide each term and check by expanding the answer back to 6x+9.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A term is missing from the bracket, or a term inside was not divided by the factor; expanding back does not give the original.

errorPatterns.pattern: Gives a factorisation but never checks, so an error stands — does not expand the product back to test it.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the expand-back habit (don't reteach factorising): 'multiply your answer out — do you get what you started with?' Make the check a routine final step.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Presents an answer that does not expand to 12x+8 with no attempt to verify; the method is known but the check is skipped.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot find a common factor, or factors only one term / drops a term; the result does not expand back to the original.
responseLevels.full: Extracts the HCF so the bracket has no remaining common factor, divides every term correctly, verifies by expanding back, articulates factorising as the inverse of expanding, and transfers to a common variable factor (x²+3x = x(x+3)).
responseLevels.partial: Extracts A common factor and forms a correct bracket, but not the HIGHEST (leaves a shared factor inside), or omits the expand-back check — factorises but not fully or not reliably.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child this card and say 'factorise this fully, showing your working': 12x + 8. Say nothing about method. Watch whether they pull out the HIGHEST common factor (4) or a smaller one (2), and whether every term inside the bracket is correct.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 12x+8 has HCF 4 but is ALSO divisible by 2, so a child with partial mastery produces 2(6x+4) — genuinely a factorisation, but not full, because the bracket still shares a factor of 2. Watching which factor they pull out separates full from partial mastery, and asking them to expand back exposes any dropped or mis-divided term.
