pedagogy.summary: Children read and write time to the EXACT minute. The efficient procedure is NOT counting single minutes from the 12 but finding the last 5-minute interval the minute hand has passed and counting on the extra minutes (e.g. 23 past = 4x5 = 20, then +3). 'To' times add a further step: converting minutes-past into minutes-to the next hour (44 past 3 = 16 to 4, a number bond to 60). Reading the hour hand precisely also matters — near the top of the hour it sits almost on the next numeral, but the hour is the number it has LAST PASSED.
bestPractices: Teach 'find the 5-minute interval before the hand, then count on' rather than counting every minute from 12
Use a number line / number bond to 60 to convert minutes past to minutes to
Check the hour hand carefully: at 7:43 the hour hand is nearly on 8 but the hour is still 7
Match analogue and digital to the exact minute, both directions
Rehearse the multi-step 'minutes to' reading, where errors cluster
keyRepresentations: Analogue clock with a minute scale (tick marks)
Counting on from the last multiple of five
Number line for past-to-to conversion; part-whole bond to 60
Paired analogue and digital displays
commonMisconceptions: Counts individual minutes from 12 to the hand instead of counting on from the nearest 5 below (slow and error-prone)
Multi-step 'minutes to' reading breaks down (miscounts the bond to 60)
Reads the hour as the numeral the hour hand is nearest, so 7:43 becomes '8:43' (hour hand almost on 8)
Reads a digital time literally rather than converting it (says 'seven forty-three' but can't render it on analogue or as a 'to' time)

learn.summary: Children read and write time to the exact minute on analogue and digital clocks. The efficient method is not counting single minutes from the 12 but finding the last 5-minute interval the minute hand has passed and counting on (e.g. 23 past = 4×5 = 20, then +3). 'To' times add a conversion step: turning minutes-past into minutes-to the next hour using a number bond to 60 (44 past 3 = 16 to 4). The hour hand also needs care: late in the hour it moves close to the next numeral, but the hour is the number it has LAST passed (at 7:43 the hour hand is about three-quarters of the way to 8, but the hour is still 7; at 9:57 it is almost on 10, but the hour is still 9).

activities.title: Count on from the last five on a moveable clock
feedback: If the child counts every minute from the 12, prompt: 'Which five has the hand just passed?' then count on only the extra minutes from there.

If the child reads 7:43 as 8:43, say: 'The hour is the number the hour hand has LAST passed — it is still before the 8, so the hour is 7.' Slowly sweep the hour hand across the whole hour so they see it travel from just-past-7 to the 8.
For 9:57, if the child says 10, point out the hand has not yet reached the 10, so the hour is still 9 — read last-passed, not nearest.
Confirm a correct reading by restating the method: 'You found 40, then counted on 3 — that's 43, and the hour hand is still past 7, so 7:43.'
activities.rationale: Guidance documenting this error reports children count individual minutes to the hand instead of finding the 5-minute interval before and counting on, and recommends the 4×5=20 then +3 method. A moveable clock lets the child rehearse the count-on procedure and watch the hour hand travel; a static annotated clock can still show one worked example but does not let the child try the count themselves.
sourceClaims: White Rose Y3 Time (Step 3, Tell the time to the minute) documents that children may count individual minutes until they reach the minute hand instead of finding the 5-minute interval before and counting on, and that 'minutes to the hour' has several steps where errors cluster; the recommended method is 4x5=20 then +3, with a number line and part-whole bond to 60 for past-to conversion.

The hour hand is significantly harder for children to read than the minute hand, and children tend to read hour and minute separately; near the top of the hour the hour hand's position (just before the next numeral) is a documented source of error.
learnerActions: On a clock with moveable hands and a minute scale (tick marks), set the minute hand to a target such as 43 minutes.
Find the last 5-minute mark the hand has passed (40) by counting the fives: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40.
Count on the extra single minutes from there: 41, 42, 43 — do not count all 43 ticks one at a time from the 12.
Check the hour hand: notice it has moved about three-quarters of the way toward the next numeral, and say the hour as the number it has LAST passed.
Try another near-the-hour example: set 9:57 — the hour hand is almost on 10, but the hour is still 9 because that is the number it has last passed.
Read the whole time aloud (e.g. 'forty-three minutes past seven' / 'seven forty-three').
activities.intendedInsight: The quick, reliable way to read exact minutes is to land on the nearest 5-minute mark below the hand and count on the remaining minutes, and to read the hour as the numeral the hour hand has last passed.

activities.title: Convert 'past' to 'minutes to' with a bond to 60
feedback: If the child gives a wrong 'to' time such as '23 to 8' for 7:43, bring back the number line: 'How many more from 43 to reach 60?' (17), so it is 17 to 8.
If the child cannot convert at all, rehearse just the bond to 60 first (e.g. 43 + ? = 60) before returning to the clock; do not re-teach whole-clock reading.
Watch that the stated hour is the NEXT hour (8, not 7) when giving a 'to' time.
activities.rationale: The multi-step 'minutes to' reading is where errors cluster, and a number line / part-whole bond to 60 is the recommended scaffold for the past-to-to conversion. Isolating the conversion step from the reading step targets the specific breakdown.
sourceClaims: White Rose Y3 Time (Step 3, Tell the time to the minute) documents that children may count individual minutes until they reach the minute hand instead of finding the 5-minute interval before and counting on, and that 'minutes to the hour' has several steps where errors cluster; the recommended method is 4x5=20 then +3, with a number line and part-whole bond to 60 for past-to conversion.
learnerActions: Start from an exact 'past' reading such as 43 minutes past 7.
On a number line from 0 to 60 (or a part-whole bond), find how far it is from 43 up to 60: 43 + 17 = 60.
State the 'to' time: 43 past 7 is 17 minutes to 8.
Repeat with other examples, e.g. 44 past 3 = 16 to 4; 57 past 9 = 3 to 10.
Say both forms of the same time aloud to connect them.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a 'to' time is one extra step on top of reading the 'past' time: use a number bond to 60 to find the gap to the next hour, and remember the hour named is the NEXT hour.

activities.title: Match and write analogue and digital to the exact minute, both directions
feedback: If a digital reading is copied literally but cannot be set on analogue (reads 'seven forty-three' but cannot place the hands or give the 'to' form), practise placing the minute hand at the counted-on position and sweeping the hour hand to just-past the hour.
For the hour-hand check: the answer is 7 because the hand has not yet reached 8 — read last-passed, not nearest.
For the fill-in: 44 + 16 = 60, so 44 past 3 = 16 to 4.
activities.rationale: Matching analogue to digital to the exact minute, the hour-hand question, and past-to conversion are the curriculum reading/writing/converting targets. Writing and hand-setting require the child to produce a time, not just recognise one; a recognition-only check would not show whether the child can construct the reading independently.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils should 'estimate and read time with increasing accuracy to the nearest minute'; Year 4 pupils 'read, write and convert time between analogue and digital 12- and 24-hour clocks', so reading to the nearest minute is the age-8+ consolidation of this strand.
learnerActions: Read an analogue clock set to 7:43 and write it as a digital time.
Given a digital time such as 11:06, set the hands: minute hand just past the 1 (at the 6-minute tick), hour hand just past the 11.
Match several analogue faces to their digital equivalents to the exact minute.
For each, say the hour it has last passed and the minutes found by counting on.
Answer targeted checks, e.g. 'The hour hand is almost on 8 — what is the hour?' and 'Fill in: 44 minutes past 3 = ___ minutes to 4.'
activities.intendedInsight: Exact-minute times can be translated faithfully between analogue and digital in both directions, keeping the count-on method and the last-passed hour.

constraints: A static labelled clock can display one worked time but does not let the child rehearse the count-on procedure or watch the hour hand travel; use it as a worked example, not as the main practice.
Prompted oral readings (a character asking 'what time is it?') can elicit answers but do not reveal HOW the child finds the minutes; pair them with tasks where the method is visible.
Recognition/matching tasks assess and reinforce but do not by themselves require the child to construct a reading or set the hands; include writing and hand-setting for production.

Optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete: lighting the 5-minute marks in groups up to the last interval in one colour, then single count-on minutes in another colour; a toggle that rolls the reading round a 0–60 number line to show the 'to' form; an hour hand that creeps toward the next numeral so the child must read last-passed. These are illustrative, not required.
When scaffolding a child who counts single minutes, do not reteach clock reading from scratch — prompt them to the nearest five and count on.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the arithmetic and logic: 4×5=20 then +3 = 23 (correct); 43+17=60 so 7:43 is 17 to 8 (correct); 44+16=60 so 44 past 3 = 16 to 4 (correct); 57+3=60 so 57 past 9 = 3 to 10 (correct); for 11:06 the minute hand sits at the 6-minute tick just past the 1 (correct); for 9:57 the hour hand is nearly on 10 but the hour is still 9 (correct).
The '23 to 8' value is a documented learner ERROR, not a correct answer, and is used only as a feedback example to correct — never offered as a valid option.

The hour-hand rule ('the hour is the number the hour hand has last passed') is the key conceptual correction and is taught directly in activity 1 so the 'nearest numeral' error is fixed, not merely flagged. Independent re-check confirms the 9:57 example is present in activity 1 actions and feedback.
The source's catalog claim that '3D adds nothing' has been omitted as a comparison not established as a pedagogical fact; nothing here depends on it.

Independent review found no critical learner-facing errors; the arithmetic, hour-hand logic, and both-direction conversions are coherent from first action through final feedback. Remaining uncertainty is confined to unre-verified source evidence.

probeDeeper: 'Show me how you found 43 minutes — did you count every minute, or start from a five?'
'The hour hand is almost touching the 8 — so is the hour 7 or 8? How do you know?'
'You read 7:43 — can you say that as minutes TO the next hour?'
'Set the clock to 9:57 — where does the hour hand go, and what is the hour?' (hour hand almost on 10, still 9)
assess.correctAnswer: Finds the last 5-minute mark (40) and counts on 3 to reach 43; reads the hour as 7 (the number the hour hand has last passed); writes 7:43; sets 11:06 with the minute hand just past the 1 and the hour hand just past the 11.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts individual minutes from the 12 up to the hand instead of counting on from the last multiple of five
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, do not reteach reading from scratch: prompt 'which five has the hand just passed?' then count on the extra minutes; rehearse with a clock whose fives are marked.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Taps round the dial one minute at a time; slow, and miscounts on larger minute values

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the hour as the numeral the hour hand is nearest, so 7:43 becomes 8:43
errorPatterns.nextMove: Emphasise 'the hour is the number the hour hand has LAST PASSED'; use a moveable clock to watch the hour hand travel between two numbers across the hour.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives the hour as 8 when the hour hand sits just before the 8

errorPatterns.pattern: The multi-step 'minutes to' reading breaks down — miscounts the number bond to 60
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold with a number line / part-whole bond to 60 (43 + 17 = 60); rehearse the extra conversion step, don't re-teach whole-clock reading.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reads 7:43 as the wrong 'to' time (e.g. '23 to 8'), or can't convert past to to at all

responseLevels.gap: Counts single minutes from the 12 and/or reads the hour by nearest numeral; can't convert to 'to' times.
responseLevels.full: Reads and writes any exact-minute time both directions (analogue to digital), counting on from the nearest five, reads the hour as last-passed even near the top of the hour, and converts past to to fluently.
responseLevels.partial: Reads exact minutes for 'past' times by counting on, but slips on the hour when the hour hand is near the next numeral, or on the multi-step 'minutes to' conversion.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set exact-minute reading and writing tasks and WATCH the method: (1) Analogue clock set to 7:43 with the hour hand nearly on 8: 'Read this time to me — tell me the hour and the minutes — and show me how you work out the minutes.' (2) 'Now write it as a digital time.' (3) Give a digital 11:06: 'Set these hands on the clock.' Watch whether they count on from the last five (40, then 41-42-43) or count single minutes from the 12, and whether they keep the hour at 7 (not 8).
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching HOW the minutes are found (count-on from the nearest five vs one-by-one from the 12) separates the efficient procedure from a fragile one; the hour-hand-nearly-on-8 setup catches the child who reads the hour by nearest numeral rather than last-passed.

sources.claim: Year 3 pupils should 'estimate and read time with increasing accuracy to the nearest minute'; Year 4 pupils 'read, write and convert time between analogue and digital 12- and 24-hour clocks', so reading to the nearest minute is the age-8+ consolidation of this strand.
sources.source: National Curriculum in England: Mathematics, Year 3 and Year 4 Measurement (statutory), gov.uk

sources.claim: White Rose Y3 Time (Step 3, Tell the time to the minute) documents that children may count individual minutes until they reach the minute hand instead of finding the 5-minute interval before and counting on, and that 'minutes to the hour' has several steps where errors cluster; the recommended method is 4x5=20 then +3, with a number line and part-whole bond to 60 for past-to conversion.
sources.source: White Rose Education, Year 3 Summer Block 3: Time (scheme of learning), Step 3

sources.claim: The hour hand is significantly harder for children to read than the minute hand, and children tend to read hour and minute separately; near the top of the hour the hour hand's position (just before the next numeral) is a documented source of error.
sources.source: Earnest, Gonzales & Plant (2018), 'Time as a measure: elementary students positioning the hands of an analog clock', Journal of Numerical Cognition 4(1)

pedagogy.summary: Recognising that the faces of a 3-D shape are themselves 2-D shapes (a circle on a cylinder, triangles on a pyramid) is the bridge that connects the flat and solid worlds. It is best taught by taking solids apart — unfolding or 'popping up' a solid so its faces lie flat as recognisable 2-D shapes, tracing or paint-stamping a face to print its 2-D shape, and handling solids to feel which surfaces are flat faces and which are curved. The key idea to build is that a solid is BUILT FROM 2-D faces, and that a face keeps its 2-D shape whether drawn on paper or sitting on the solid.
bestPractices: Unfold or 'pop up' a solid from flat paper so children see the faces are 2-D shapes and can touch and count them (Mohamed & Kandeel 2023).
Trace round, or dip-and-stamp, a face to print its 2-D shape — the print of a tin's end is a circle.
Name the face by its 2-D shape (circle, triangle, square) distinct from the solid's name (cylinder, pyramid, cube).
Contrast flat faces (rest flat on the table) with curved surfaces (roll), so a cylinder's curved side is not mistaken for a flat face.
Link explicitly: a cube is made of six squares; a cylinder has two circular faces — every 3-D shape is made up of 2-D shapes.
keyRepresentations: Pop-up / unfoldable solids whose faces flatten into 2-D shapes
Paint-stamp or trace-around prints of each face
A cube shown as six squares; a pyramid as triangles plus a square base; a cylinder as two circles plus a curved surface
Face-count charts (faces, edges, vertices)
commonMisconceptions: Names a face by the whole solid's name — calls the flat round end of a cylinder 'a cylinder' rather than 'a circle'.
Cannot separate face from solid because the solid itself is mis-named — a cube called 'a square' has no distinct square faces to find (Mohamed & Kandeel 2023).
Sees the solid as one undifferentiated whole and does not decompose it into faces (van Hiele visual level).

learn.summary: Children aged 6–7 learn that the flat faces of a 3-D solid are themselves 2-D shapes — a circle on a cylinder, triangles on a pyramid. A solid with only flat faces, such as a cube or pyramid, is built FROM those flat faces; some solids, such as a cylinder, also have a curved surface, which is not a flat face. The core teaching moves are taking solids apart (unfolding or popping up a solid so faces lie flat), tracing or paint-stamping a face to print its 2-D shape, and handling solids to feel which surfaces are flat faces and which are curved. A face keeps its 2-D shape whether drawn on paper or sitting on the solid; the whole tin is a cylinder, but each flat end is a circle.

activities.title: Take a solid apart into its flat faces
feedback: If a child names a face by the solid's name (calls a cylinder's end 'a cylinder'), trace round or stamp that face onto paper — the print is a circle; the face is the 2-D shape, the whole tin is the 3-D cylinder.
If a child calls a cube 'a square', pop up or unfold the six square faces so they see the solid is made OF squares, then help them re-name the solid.
If a child treats the solid as one undifferentiated whole, unfold it so each face lies flat and gets named, then rebuild it face by face.

Note for the teacher: a paper or card face has slight thickness and stands in for the ideal flat (zero-thickness) 2-D shape of the solid's face; ask the child what mathematical shape the flattened face represents, treating the paper as a stand-in rather than the mathematical shape itself.
activities.rationale: Physically constructing and taking apart solids lets children hold, cut, fold and touch the faces, supporting them to distinguish and name component shapes; instruction is needed to move from seeing a shape as one whole to describing and composing its parts.
sourceClaims: Building solids from flat paper (pop-up) so children hold, cut, fold and touch the faces, sides and vertices improved their ability to distinguish and name the shapes; children preferred 2-D shape names for solids until they physically constructed them, and the circle/sphere pair was the most secure.

At the van Hiele visual level shapes are viewed as a whole rather than by distinguishing their parts; instruction is needed to move children to describing shapes by their component parts and properties.
learnerActions: Handle a real solid (a tin/cylinder, a cube, a square-based pyramid) and run a finger over its surfaces.
Unfold or 'pop up' a solid made from flat paper/card so its faces lie flat, then touch and count the separated faces.

Name each flattened face by its 2-D shape (circle, triangle, square) and rebuild the solid face by face. If a paper cylinder is unrolled, its curved side flattens into a rectangle, but on the cylinder that part is the curved surface, not a flat face.
State the link aloud: 'a cube is made of six squares', 'a cylinder has two circular faces and a curved surface'.
activities.intendedInsight: A solid's flat faces are 2-D shapes; a solid with only flat faces (such as a cube or pyramid) is built from them, while a cylinder also has a curved surface. A face keeps its 2-D shape whether it is drawn on paper or sitting on the solid.

activities.title: Print the face: trace and paint-stamp
feedback: When the stamped circle appears beside the tin, confirm: 'the flat end is a circle; the whole tin is the cylinder'.
If a child tries to stamp the curved side, notice it cannot print a single flat shape — only flat faces rest flat and print cleanly.
Note for the teacher: the printed mark (and the paper it is on) has slight thickness; it represents the ideal flat 2-D shape of the solid's face, which is the shape the child names.
activities.rationale: Printing or tracing a face gives a child a 2-D artefact tied to the solid, which may reinforce that a face retains its 2-D shape off the solid as well as on it. This is a proposed activity; the cited study examined pop-up construction rather than stamping, so its efficacy here is unverified.
learnerActions: Dip the flat end of a tin in paint (or ink pad) and stamp it on paper; name the shape that appears.
Trace round a flat face of a cube or the square base of a pyramid and name the printed 2-D shape.
Set the printed 2-D shape beside the solid and say which face of the solid it came from.
activities.intendedInsight: The print of a solid's flat face is a plain 2-D shape (a tin's end prints a circle), making concrete that the face is itself a 2-D shape.

activities.title: Flat faces versus curved surfaces
feedback: If a child calls the cylinder's curved side a face, have them try to make it rest flat — it rolls, so it is a curved surface, not a flat face.
Confirm the cylinder has exactly two flat circular faces plus one curved surface.
activities.rationale: Explicitly contrasting flat faces with curved surfaces prevents miscounting the curved side of a cylinder as a flat face and sharpens the idea of a face as a flat 2-D shape. A sort can check how a child classifies surfaces but does not by itself elicit handling or an explanation, so it is paired with the resting-flat test.
learnerActions: Try to rest each surface of a cylinder flat on the table: the two ends sit flat, the curved side rolls.
Sort surfaces into 'flat faces' (rest flat) and 'curved surfaces' (roll).
Count and name the flat faces on a cube, a square-based pyramid, and the cylinder; note the cylinder's side is curved, not a flat face.
activities.intendedInsight: A flat face rests flat and has a 2-D shape; a curved surface rolls and is not a flat face — so a cylinder's curved side should not be counted as a flat face.

activities.title: Decompose every face (screen peel or physical net)
feedback: When a peeled or unfolded face matches the drawn 2-D shape, confirm they are the same shape shown in different places.
If a child forgets hidden faces, rotate the solid (or use the full net) to reveal them and count all faces before reassembling.
activities.rationale: Rotating a solid and separating each face addresses faces on all sides, including hidden ones, extending the decomposition idea beyond the faces a child can see at rest. A rotatable screen model is one optional way to show hidden faces; a physical unfoldable net works too — neither is uniquely required.
sourceClaims: At the van Hiele visual level shapes are viewed as a whole rather than by distinguishing their parts; instruction is needed to move children to describing shapes by their component parts and properties.
learnerActions: Rotate a solid, or its on-screen model, so faces on every side — including hidden ones — come into view.
On a screen model, peel each face off as a plain 2-D shape; with a physical solid, use an unfoldable net or pop-up so each face lies flat. Set each face beside a drawn version to compare.
Reassemble the solid from its faces and state how many of each 2-D shape it is made from.
activities.intendedInsight: Every flat face of a solid — not just the visible ones — is a 2-D shape, and a solid with only flat faces can be composed and decomposed from those flat shapes; a solid with a curved surface, such as a cylinder, also needs that curved part.

activities.title: Predict-then-stamp check
feedback: If a child predicts 'a cylinder' for the end's print, let the stamp reveal a circle, then discuss why the face is a circle while the whole tin is a cylinder.
A matching task confirms the outcome but not the take-apart reasoning — pair it with asking the child to explain how the solid is built from those faces.
activities.rationale: A predict-justify-observe routine makes the child's reasoning explicit before the stamp confirms or challenges it, which is more diagnostic than a match-only check.
learnerActions: Before stamping, predict and justify what shape the flat end of the tin will print.
Stamp it and compare the result with the prediction.
Match which 2-D shapes make up a given solid (e.g. two circles plus a curved surface for a cylinder) and explain the match.
activities.intendedInsight: Stating a prediction and reason in advance surfaces whether a child sees the face as a 2-D shape or conflates it with the whole solid.

constraints: Use real 3-D solids and named flat faces; ensure the solid itself is correctly named, because a child who calls a cube 'a square' has no distinct square faces to find.
Use a cube-shaped object when naming a cube, and a square-based pyramid when describing triangular faces plus a square base, so the named example matches the shape.

Paper or card cutouts, printed marks, and pop-up nets have slight thickness and approximate ideal zero-thickness mathematical faces; a flattened paper face represents the 2-D shape of the solid's face. Ask children what mathematical shape it represents, not whether the paper can be picked up, and state this approximation within the activity.
A screen model where a face peels off is an idealised representation; label it as a model and pair it with handling real solids so children also feel flat versus curved surfaces.
Matching 2-D shapes to solids checks the outcome only; it does not by itself show the child understands decomposition — combine it with constructing, unfolding, or explaining.

A fixed labelled image where tapping a face reveals its 2-D shape can serve as a reference, but it does not let the child physically separate and count faces; use it as a scaffold, not the main activity.

A sort or recognition/matching task may teach or check classification but does not itself elicit the child's own explanation of how a solid is built from faces; include tasks where the child names, counts, and reassembles.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The printing/tracing activity has no sourceClaims attached because the cited pop-up study examined building solids from flat paper, not stamping or tracing; its efficacy here is unverified.

The Common Core claim frames the overall objective (analysing 2-D/3-D shapes, describing parts, composing shapes) rather than directly evidencing any single activity's teaching move; it is retained as curriculum framing, not as efficacy evidence, and so is not attached to specific activities.

The original 'conversation' entry asserted that 'talk cannot carry the visual decomposition of a solid into faces'. This is a catalog comparison, not an established law; softened to: spoken explanation is useful to elicit a child's reasoning but is best paired with handling or constructing solids, since the decomposition is primarily visual and tactile.

The original claimed a rotatable 3-D model is 'ideal' and uniquely shows hidden faces ('the spatial crux'). The affordance (revealing faces on all sides) is retained, but comparative necessity over physical unfoldable solids is not established by the sources; both are offered.
The source efficacy claim (pop-up construction improved naming) comes from one kindergarten study; this micro-topic targets ages 6–7, so transfer is plausible but not directly verified.

assess.poeTask: Give the child a solid cylinder (a tin) and a stamp pad or paint. BEFORE stamping, ask them to predict and justify what shape the flat end will print. A child who thinks the tin 'is a cylinder' may predict 'a cylinder'; a child who sees the face predicts 'a circle'. Stamp it: a circle appears. The pre-stated reason is the diagnostic part — the print forces the idea that the solid's face is a 2-D circle.
probeDeeper: If I dip this flat face in paint and stamp it on the paper, what shape appears?
You called the whole tin a cylinder — but what shape is just this flat end?
How many flat faces can you find on the cube, and what shape is each one?
Is the curved side of the tin a flat face too? Can it rest flat on the table like the ends?
assess.correctAnswer: Identifies the flat round ends of the cylinder as circles and the faces of the pyramid as triangles (with a square base); explains that a face is the flat surface of the solid and is itself a 2-D shape, so the solid is built from 2-D faces — the whole tin is the 3-D cylinder, but each flat end is a circle.

errorPatterns.pattern: Names a face by the whole solid's name — calls the flat round end of a cylinder 'a cylinder' rather than 'a circle'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace round or stamp the face onto paper — the print is a circle; the face is a 2-D shape, the whole tin is the 3-D cylinder
errorPatterns.distractor: It is a cylinder (naming the face with the solid's name)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked the shape of the flat face, gives the solid's name

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot separate a face from the solid because the solid itself is mis-named — a cube called 'a square' has no distinct square faces to point to
errorPatterns.nextMove: Pop up or unfold the six square faces of a cube so the child sees the solid is made of squares and re-names the solid correctly
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls the cube 'a square' and cannot pick out its separate square faces

errorPatterns.pattern: Sees the solid as one undifferentiated whole and does not decompose it into faces at all
errorPatterns.nextMove: Unfold the solid so each face lies flat and is named; rebuild it face by face
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats the solid as a single object and cannot point out its separate faces

responseLevels.gap: Sees the solid as one whole and names its faces with the solid's name (a face of the cylinder is 'a cylinder').
responseLevels.full: Identifies each flat face by its 2-D shape and explains the solid is built from 2-D faces (a cylinder has two circular faces; a pyramid has triangular faces and a square base), distinguishing flat faces from curved surfaces.
responseLevels.partial: Points to faces and names familiar ones (the square faces of a cube) but inconsistently — misses faces on less familiar solids or denies a face is 'really' a 2-D shape.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Run your finger over this tin (a cylinder). Point to a flat face on it — what 2-D shape is that face? Now look at this pyramid: what shape are its faces? Tell me how a face can be a 2-D shape when it is part of a solid.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands names the face by its 2-D shape (a circle) as distinct from the solid (a cylinder); a child who conflates them answers with the solid's name ('it's a cylinder') or denies the flat part is 'really' a circle because it is on a solid. The reason tier — how a face can be a 2-D shape — separates those who see the solid as built from flat shapes from those who see it as one whole object.

sources.claim: Building solids from flat paper (pop-up) so children hold, cut, fold and touch the faces, sides and vertices improved their ability to distinguish and name the shapes; children preferred 2-D shape names for solids until they physically constructed them, and the circle/sphere pair was the most secure.
sources.source: Mohamed & Kandeel (2023), 'Playful Learning: Teaching the Properties of Geometric Shapes through Pop-up Mechanisms for Kindergarten', IJEMST 11(1) (ERIC EJ1357339)

sources.claim: At the van Hiele visual level shapes are viewed as a whole rather than by distinguishing their parts; instruction is needed to move children to describing shapes by their component parts and properties.
sources.source: Way (2011), 'The Development of Spatial and Geometric Thinking: The Importance of Instruction', NRICH, University of Cambridge

sources.claim: Kindergarten geometry asks children to analyse and compare 2-D and 3-D shapes and describe their parts using informal language, and to compose simple shapes to form larger shapes — framing the link between 2-D shapes and the solids built from them.
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, K.G.B.4 and K.G.B.6

pedagogy.summary: A translation is a slide: every point of a shape moves the same distance left/right and the same distance up/down, and nothing else changes (size, shape and orientation stay the same). This topic makes that concrete on a coordinate grid — describing the move from one position to another ('3 units right'), carrying out a two-part translation ('4 right and 2 up') and stating the new coordinates, and PREDICTING an image without plotting. The key procedural insight is that a horizontal move changes only the x-coordinate and a vertical move only the y-coordinate: right adds to x, up adds to y. Built on first-quadrant coordinates, it is the child's first taste of transformations, and its errors mirror coordinate errors — reversal (swapping the right and up amounts) and changing the wrong coordinate.
bestPractices: Separate the two components explicitly: a rightward move changes only x (add to the first number), an upward move only y (add to the second) — do the horizontal and vertical parts one at a time.
Describe moves precisely and consistently: 'units right/left and up/down', matching the along-then-up order of coordinates.
Have children PREDICT the new coordinates by adjusting x and y before plotting, then check by plotting — so the rule is used, not just the picture.
Stress translation invariance: the shape does not turn, flip, or resize — every vertex shifts by the same amounts; check two vertices moved identically.
Count moves against numbered lines from the start point, not squares, to avoid off-by-one slips.
Contrast a horizontal-only move (y unchanged) with a two-part move, so children see when a coordinate should and shouldn't change.
keyRepresentations: Coordinate grid showing a start point and its translated image with the slide arrow
Component decomposition: horizontal move (Δx) then vertical move (Δy)
Rule form: (x, y) → (x + right, y + up)
A shape and its translated copy, same size and orientation, every vertex shifted equally
Number-line counting of the move along each axis from the start position
commonMisconceptions: Reversal — swapping the right and up amounts (applying the horizontal shift to y and the vertical to x).
Changing the wrong coordinate — altering y for a move described as 'right', or changing both coordinates for a single-direction move.
Getting the direction sign wrong — moving left when 'right' is stated, or subtracting instead of adding.
Counting squares rather than numbered lines, giving an off-by-one image position.
Confusing the description of the MOVE with the destination coordinates (stating where it ends when asked how it moved, or vice versa).

learn.summary: Translation is a slide: every point of a shape moves the same amount left/right and up/down, with size, shape and orientation unchanged. On a first-quadrant coordinate grid, learners describe a move from one position to another ('3 units right'), carry out a two-part translation ('4 right and 2 up') and state new coordinates, and predict an image before plotting. The core procedural insight: a horizontal move changes only the x-coordinate (right adds to x), a vertical move only the y-coordinate (up adds to y). The main errors mirror coordinate errors — reversing the right/up amounts, changing the wrong coordinate, direction/sign slips, off-by-one line counting, and confusing the description of the move with the destination coordinates.

activities.title: Predict-then-slide on a coordinate grid
feedback: If the prediction swaps the amounts (e.g. gives (4,7) for '4 right, 2 up' from (2,3)), do the parts one at a time: right changes only the first number, up only the second — tie this back to the along-then-up order of coordinates.
If a 'right' move changed the up-number, show on the grid that a purely horizontal slide leaves the height (y) unchanged; label which number each direction affects before moving.
If the image lands one line off, recount the move as jumps from the start point: the start line is 0, and the first jump lands on the next line. Do not count the starting line as 1.
For opposite directions ('2 left, 1 down' from (5,4)), confirm left subtracts from x and down subtracts from y, landing at (3,3).
activities.rationale: Setting a move, predicting coordinates, then watching the slide turns the coordinate rule into something tested against the motion, exposing reversal and wrong-coordinate errors immediately. Live-updating coordinates, a colour-coded ('coded') grid that makes a rightward move visibly change only x, and the uniform vertex shift make the component structure (Δx separate from Δy) and translation invariance concrete. These coordinate readouts, colour-coding and the predict-then-reveal loop are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism visible, not required technology.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should describe movements between positions as translations of a given unit to the left/right and up/down.
Points are located by ordered pairs from the origin along the x- and y-axes in the first quadrant, so a horizontal move changes the x-coordinate and a vertical move the y-coordinate (5.G.1, 5.G.2).

A common documented coordinate misconception is reversing x and y (putting the y-coordinate before the x), and off-by-one errors from counting squares rather than the numbered grid lines — errors that carry into describing moves as changes in coordinates.
learnerActions: Set a translation such as '4 right and 2 up' on a first-quadrant grid containing a shape.
Before anything moves, predict and state (or type) the new coordinates of one named vertex — e.g. from (2,3) you should get (6,5).
Trigger the slide and watch every vertex glide by the same 4-across, 2-up while a coordinate readout ticks from the old to the new values.
Run a horizontal-only move (e.g. '3 right') and confirm the up-number (y) stays fixed while only the across-number changes.
Check two different vertices moved by identical amounts, confirming the shape did not turn, flip or resize.
Count the move in unit jumps from the start point, without counting the starting line itself as 'one'.
activities.intendedInsight: A horizontal move changes only x and a vertical move only y; the whole shape shifts uniformly without changing size or orientation, and predicting from the (x+right, y+up) rule can be checked against the actual slide.

activities.title: Describe the move between two positions
feedback: If the move is answered with '(5,3)' instead of '3 right', ask explicitly 'how did it move?' versus 'where is it now?' and have the learner give both for the same slide.
If direction is reversed (saying 'left' for a rightward shift), compare the two numbered positions and read which way along the axis the point travelled.
activities.rationale: Requiring a worded description catches children who confuse the move with the destination, a documented pattern, and reversing the move builds the idea that translations are undoable by the opposite shift. A scorable version (multiple-choice naming the move between two points, with reversed-component and 'up' distractors) can be used during teaching or for assessment, though a selection response does not elicit independent construction of the description.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should describe movements between positions as translations of a given unit to the left/right and up/down.
learnerActions: Look at two marked positions on the grid, e.g. a start at (2,3) and an image at (5,3).
State the move in words — '3 units right' — using units and direction, not the destination coordinates.
For the same slide, separately answer 'where is it now?' with the end coordinates, so the two questions are practised side by side.
Describe the reverse move that returns the image to the start (e.g. (5,3) back to (2,3) is '3 units left'), surfacing reversibility.
activities.intendedInsight: Describing a move ('how did it move?' — units and direction) is a different answer from naming the destination ('where is it now?' — coordinates); learners must hold both apart.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal before-and-after picture (scaffold)
feedback: Point out that only the across-number changed for a horizontal slide, and that both corners moved by the same amount.
Prompt the learner to say the move in words before lifting the flap, then compare.
activities.rationale: A fixed picture can present and label a completed slide, but it cannot let the learner set, carry out or predict a move, so the procedure is not exercised — use it as an introduction or revision aid, not the main practice.
learnerActions: Study a fixed picture showing a shape in its start position and its translated image with a slide arrow.
Tap the start and the image to reveal how the x- and y-coordinates changed between them.
Use a 'where does it land after 3 right?' flap to check a predicted position against the revealed answer.
activities.intendedInsight: A worked before-and-after slide shows how each coordinate changed and reinforces that the shape keeps its size and orientation.

constraints: Built on first-quadrant coordinate knowledge; learners should already read ordered pairs along-then-up before describing moves as coordinate changes.

Recognition/selection responses (multiple-choice, tap-to-reveal) can be used while teaching and for scoring, but they do not require the learner to independently construct a predicted coordinate or a worded description — keep genuine prediction and production in the sequence.

The tap-to-reveal picture is a scaffold: because the slide is fixed, the learner cannot set, carry out or predict their own move; progress to an interactive or hand-plotted grid so the rule is used, not just read.

Count moves as unit jumps from the start point: do not count the starting line as 'one'; the first jump lands on the next line. (When points sit on grid intersections, counting square widths crossed gives the same count.) This avoids off-by-one images.
Keep directions and signs explicit: right/up add, left/down subtract; state them when working opposite directions.
Translations here are planar left/right/up/down slides; a 3D setting adds complexity irrelevant to this objective rather than being inherently unteachable in other media.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic/geometry: '4 right, 2 up' from (2,3) gives (6,5); (3,1) after '2 right, 3 up' gives (5,4); '2 left, 1 down' from (5,4) gives (3,3); (2,3)→(5,3) is '3 right' and reverses as '3 left'. The worked examples are internally consistent across summary, actions and feedback.

The original listed a reversal distractor producing '(4,7) or (6,5)' for '4 right, 2 up' from (2,3) — but (6,5) is the correct answer, so it cannot also be the swapped-components distractor; the genuinely swapped result is (4,7). All learner-facing text uses (4,7) as the reversal example and (6,5) only as the correct target.

Legacy source claims were marked verified in the row but have not been re-checked here; comparative-efficacy or necessity framing from the original ('can't show the slide', 'cannot let the child predict') has been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements.

probeDeeper: 'When the counter moved 3 to the right, why did only the first number change?' — listen for horizontal = x, height unchanged.
Counterexample: 'If I slide the whole shape 4 right and 2 up, does it get bigger or turn at all? How do you know?' — tests translation invariance.
'Predict the landing spot after 2 left and 1 down from (5,4)' — checks the rule works for the opposite directions (subtracting).
'Describe the move that takes (5,3) back to (2,3)' — surfaces reversibility and separates move-description from position.
assess.correctAnswer: (1) '3 units to the right' (only x changes, 2→5). (2) the corner moves from (2,3) to (6,5) — x + 4, y + 2 — and the whole shape slides by the same amount, same size and orientation. (3) (5,4) — predicts by adding 2 to x and 3 to y without needing to plot.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reversal — swaps the horizontal and vertical amounts, applying '4 right' to the y-coordinate and '2 up' to the x.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do the parts one at a time — right changes only x (first number), up only y (second) — tying the order back to along-then-up coordinates.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: After '4 right, 2 up' gives (4,7) or (6,5) with the components swapped; the image is in the wrong place along both axes.

errorPatterns.pattern: Changes the wrong coordinate — for a move described as 'right' alters the up-number, or changes both coordinates for a single-direction move.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show on the grid that a purely horizontal slide leaves the height (y) unchanged; label which number each direction affects before moving.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Moving (2,3) to the right yields a change in the second number, or both numbers change when only a horizontal move was asked.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts squares not numbered lines — the image lands one line off, or the start of the count is misplaced.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the move on the numbered lines from the start position; no reteaching of translation needed — the count slipped.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: New coordinates are off by one; the child counts cells crossed rather than reading line labels from the start point.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses the move with the destination — when asked to DESCRIBE the move, states the end coordinates instead (or vice versa).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish the two questions explicitly — 'how did it move?' (units and direction) versus 'where is it now?' (coordinates); practise stating both for the same slide.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers (1) with '(5,3)' rather than '3 right'; or when asked for the new position gives the shift amounts.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot describe or carry out a translation reliably: changes the wrong coordinate, reverses components, or the shape does not slide uniformly; predictions are guesses.
responseLevels.full: Describes moves precisely, carries out horizontal-and-vertical translations by adjusting x and y correctly, states the new coordinates, predicts an image without plotting, and knows the shape's size and orientation are unchanged — the (x+right, y+up) structure is applied, not just enacted.
responseLevels.partial: Describes and carries out a single-direction move (e.g. 3 right) correctly, but a two-part translation trips reversal or a wrong-coordinate change, or the child can only find the image by plotting rather than predicting from the rule — knows the pieces but doesn't combine them.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: On a first-quadrant grid, mark a point at (2,3). Say: (1) 'Move a counter from (2,3) to (5,3) — describe that move in words.' (2) 'Now translate this shape 4 units right and 2 units up; plot it and write the new coordinates of this corner.' (3) 'A point is at (3,1). Without plotting, tell me where it lands after moving 2 right and 3 up.' Watch how they handle each — do not prompt the rule.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The single-direction move (1) exposes children who change both coordinates or the wrong one; the two-part move (2) exposes reversal of the right/up amounts and non-uniform sliding; the predict item (3) separates children who can only move by counting on the grid from those who apply the (x+right, y+up) rule. Requiring a worded description in (1) also catches confusing the move with the destination.

sources.claim: Year 4 pupils should describe movements between positions as translations of a given unit to the left/right and up/down.
sources.source: UK Department for Education, Mathematics programmes of study: Key Stages 1 and 2 (Year 4 geometry — position and direction)

sources.claim: Points are located by ordered pairs from the origin along the x- and y-axes in the first quadrant, so a horizontal move changes the x-coordinate and a vertical move the y-coordinate (5.G.1, 5.G.2).
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 5 Geometry

sources.claim: A common documented coordinate misconception is reversing x and y (putting the y-coordinate before the x), and off-by-one errors from counting squares rather than the numbered grid lines — errors that carry into describing moves as changes in coordinates.
sources.source: NCETM, Misconceptions with the Key Objectives (Position, Direction, Movement and Angle)

pedagogy.summary: Adding and subtracting two two-digit numbers is introduced through concrete and pictorial regrouping before any formal column method. The central idea is composing a ten when the ones exceed nine (34+27) and decomposing a ten when there are too few ones to subtract (63−28). Base-ten blocks make the exchange physical; number lines and partitioning jottings connect it to recording. This is where 'carrying' and 'borrowing' are given meaning as exchange rather than taught as digit tricks.
bestPractices: Establish the exchange principle with base-ten blocks: ten ones can be fairly swapped for one ten, and one ten for ten ones (NRICH: exchange/unitising)
Partition both numbers into tens and ones, combine like with like, then compose/decompose a ten as needed (NCETM Spine 1.15/1.16)
Use a number line for subtraction as finding a difference (count up 28→63) as an alternative to take-away
Move concrete → pictorial → jotting for the SAME calculation so the recording mirrors the action
Ask the child to explain their strategy and why 34+27 is not 511 — the recombination is where meaning is tested
keyRepresentations: Base-ten blocks with a place-value mat (compose/decompose a ten)
Number line (jumps for adding; count-up for difference)
Part-whole / partitioning jottings (30+20 and 4+7)
Bar model (comparison and missing-part subtraction)
Hundred square
commonMisconceptions: Failing to compose the ten: adding tens (50) and ones (11) and writing them side by side (511) or keeping 51
Smaller-from-larger subtraction: 63−28 done as 8−3 in the ones, answer 45
Counting every unit and losing the ten-structure (not treating a ten-rod as one ten)
Misaligning tens and ones when recording without a place-value mat

learn.summary: Ages 6–7 add and subtract two two-digit numbers (e.g. 34+27, 63−28) by giving meaning to 'carrying' and 'borrowing' as fair exchange: ten ones can be swapped for one ten and vice versa. Learners partition into tens and ones, combine like with like, then compose a ten when the ones exceed nine, or decompose a ten when there are too few ones to subtract. Concrete base-ten work and pictorial jottings for the SAME calculation let the recording mirror the physical action, so regrouping is felt as a swap rather than rehearsed as a digit trick.

activities.title: Exchange on a place-value mat: compose and decompose a ten
feedback: If the child writes 511 or keeps 51: have them physically swap ten of the eleven ones for one ten-rod on the mat, then re-read the result; name it — 'ten ones is the same as one ten'.
If the child does the ones of 63−28 as 8−3 and answers 45: show on the mat that 3 ones cannot give 8, so a ten must be broken open first (63 = 50+13); check by adding 45+28, which gives 73, not 63.

If the child breaks rods apart to recount everything in ones: do not stop them handling the blocks or drill exchange in isolation — treating a rod as one 'ten' is a maturing shift; each time they exchange, read both ways aloud together, 'that's ten ones AND one ten', so unitising develops.

Probe: 'You made eleven ones — can you swap some for a ten? Show me.' 'For 63−28 you needed more ones — where did the extra ones come from?' 'Would 34+25 still need an exchange? Why not?' (For 34+25 the ones are 4+5=9, below ten, so no exchange is needed.)
activities.rationale: The concept being taught is exchange, so the learner should perform the regroup, not just watch it. Partitioning into tens and ones and composing/decomposing a ten is the standard mastery progression, and pairing the concrete action with a matching jotting makes the recording mirror the exchange. Reading a ten-rod as both 'ten ones' and 'one ten' builds unitising.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils add and subtract two two-digit numbers using concrete objects, pictorial representations and mentally, and recording in columns supports place value and prepares for formal written methods.
Two two-digit numbers are added by partitioning one or both into tens and ones; subtraction partitions the subtrahend into tens and ones, decomposing a ten where the ones are insufficient.

Exchange — fairly swapping ten ones for one ten (and vice versa) — and unitising a ten as a single entity are the ideas underpinning regrouping; such resources can be used diagnostically to assess whether place value is genuinely understood.
learnerActions: Set out 34 + 27 on a place-value mat using base-ten blocks (or draggable on-screen tens and ones).

Pile the ones together to find there are eleven; because that is ten or more, perform a 'make a ten' action that swaps ten loose ones for one ten-rod moved into the tens column, leaving one loose one, then read the answer as 61 (not 511, not 51).
Set out 63 − 28; find there are not enough ones to give eight, so take a ten-rod and break it into ten loose ones, so 63 is now 50 and 13.
Hand over eight ones (13−8=5) and subtract the tens (50−20=30) to reach 35.
Record each physical step as a matching jotting: 30+20=50, 4+7=11, exchange → 61; and 63 = 50+13, 13−8=5, 50−20=30 → 35.
Say aloud why 34+27 cannot be 511 ('ten ones is the same as one ten, so the extra ten joins the tens').
activities.intendedInsight: Composing a ten (addition) and decomposing a ten (subtraction) are the same exchange run in opposite directions; 'carrying' and 'borrowing' are fair swaps between ones and tens, not separate digit tricks.

activities.title: Subtraction as finding a difference on a number line
feedback: If jumps don't land cleanly, suggest jumping first to the next multiple of ten (28 → 30) before the big jump.

If the count-up answer differs from the take-away answer, check both: revisit the ones step on the mat for a missed exchange, and re-add the jumps on the number line, since either method may hold the slip.
Ask: 'Which method did you find easier for 63 − 28, counting up or taking away? Why?'
activities.rationale: A number line presents subtraction as finding a difference (count up 28→63) as an alternative to take-away, giving a complementary model and a self-check; a bar model and hundred square are further optional representations. This is offered as an alternative representation, not a replacement for the exchange work. A number line is a pictorial method, but no cited source directly validates the count-up-as-difference principle, so no source claim is attached.
learnerActions: Place 28 and 63 on a number line.
Count up from 28 to 63 in convenient jumps (e.g. 28 → 30 is 2, 30 → 60 is 30, 60 → 63 is 3).
Total the jumps (2 + 30 + 3 = 35) and state 63 − 28 = 35.
Compare this count-up answer with the take-away/exchange answer from the mat and confirm they agree.
Optionally model the same subtraction with a bar model (whole 63, known part 28, missing part found as the difference) or on a hundred square, as further representations of the same difference.
activities.intendedInsight: Subtraction can be read as the difference between two numbers found by counting up, which offers a second route to the same answer and a self-check against the smaller-from-larger error.

activities.title: Annotated worked example and targeted consolidation
feedback: For a chosen '511'/'51': return to the eleven-ones-make-a-ten step and have the learner state where the extra ten goes.
For a chosen '45': have the learner break a ten in 63 to make 50+13 and redo the ones step, then check by adding.
Encourage the learner to narrate the exchange aloud each time, since the explanation is where understanding is tested.
activities.rationale: A staged annotated example can show the partition and exchange as a reference, and a set of two-digit ± two-digit items consolidates and catches the 511 and smaller-from-larger errors — but reference and recognition rehearse rather than build the exchange insight, so they follow the hands-on exchange rather than replace it. Recognising a correct answer does not by itself elicit independent production of the exchange. Asking the child to explain why 34+27 is not 511 is where the recombination meaning is tested.
sourceClaims: The 'smaller-from-larger' subtraction error is a classic systematic buggy algorithm.
Two two-digit numbers are added by partitioning one or both into tens and ones; subtraction partitions the subtrahend into tens and ones, decomposing a ten where the ones are insufficient.
learnerActions: Study a worked example of 34+27 and 63−28 where the partition and exchange step are revealed one stage at a time (e.g. reveal 4+7 becoming 'one ten and one'; reveal the tens as 30+20+10).
Explain in your own words what happened at the exchange step before moving on.
Then work a short set of two-digit ± two-digit items, including 34+27 and the decomposition of 63 into 50+13, choosing or writing the answer and giving the exchange reasoning.
When a '511', '51' or '45' answer appears, say why it is wrong rather than only marking the correct one.
activities.intendedInsight: A clearly staged worked example makes the partition and exchange visible for reference, and a focused problem set surfaces whether the compose-a-ten and smaller-from-larger errors have really been overcome.

constraints: Build the skill from repeated hands-on exchange with base-ten blocks and a place-value mat before any formal column method; introduce 'carrying'/'borrowing' only as names for the exchange already performed.
Move concrete → pictorial → jotting for the SAME calculation so the recording mirrors the action; do not jump straight to abstract digit manipulation.
A static annotated worked example or tap-to-reveal reference can show the steps but does not let the child perform the regroup; use it as reference alongside, not instead of, hands-on exchange.

A set of items that includes the common wrong answers 511/51 and 45 can consolidate and expose errors, but recognition-only responses do not by themselves elicit independent construction of the exchange; pair with the learner performing and recording the swap.
When describing whether an exchange is needed (e.g. 34+25 vs 34+27), check the ones sum directly — exchange is needed only when the ones reach ten or more (4+5=9 needs none; 4+7=11 does).
Treat a ten-rod being recounted as ten separate ones as a developmental stage in unitising, not an error to drill away; keep reading it both ways aloud.

The place-value mat is essentially planar (tens and ones, place value), so these activities do not propose a third dimension or spoken-only delivery as the main medium for the exchange insight; this is a design preference, not evidence that 3D or dialogue cannot teach it, and talk is still used so the child can explain their strategy.

A bar model (comparison and missing-part subtraction) and a hundred square remain available as further optional representations and should not be presented as replacements for the base-ten exchange work.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched and the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two cited sources are marked unverified in the source row (NCETM Spine 1.15/1.16 partitioning claim; Brown & Burton 1978 / VanLehn 'Mind Bugs' 1990 on the smaller-from-larger buggy algorithm); treat their support as provisional.

Arithmetic self-check: 34+27 → 30+20=50, 4+7=11, 50+11=61 (not 511, not 51). 63−28 → 63=50+13, 13−8=5, 50−20=30, so 35; number-line count-up 28→30→60→63 gives 2+30+3=35. The smaller-from-larger error 8−3=5 yields the incorrect 45, and 45+28=73≠63. These confirm the answers used; 511/51/45 appear ONLY as named incorrect responses to diagnose, never as valid answers.

The legacy source framed digit-based side-by-side work as something hands-on exchange 'cannot fake' and spoken discussion as unable to substitute for exchange; these comparative-necessity claims are softened here to scoped affordances/limits rather than asserted as established efficacy.

No source directly supports subtraction read as a difference found by counting up on a number line; it is a pictorial method and a self-check, so the number-line activity carries no source claim rather than citing the broad DfE pictorial/mental claim as if it validated the count-up principle.

The source misconception 'misaligning tens and ones when recording without a place-value mat' is addressed implicitly by consistent use of the place-value mat and matched jottings across the first activity.

probeDeeper: You made eleven ones — can you swap some of those for a ten? Show me what you do.
For 63 − 28 you needed more ones than you had — where did the extra ones come from?
Explain to me why 34 + 27 isn't five hundred and eleven.
What if it were 34 + 25 instead of 34 + 27 — would you still need to exchange? Why not?
assess.correctAnswer: 61 and 35. For 34+27: 30+20=50 and 4+7=11, exchange ten ones for a ten → 61. For 63−28: too few ones, exchange a ten for ten ones (63 as 50+13), 13−8=5 and 50−20=30 → 35.

errorPatterns.pattern: Doesn't compose the ten — 'thirty and twenty is fifty, four and seven is eleven, so five hundred and eleven' (or keeps 51)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have the child physically swap ten of the eleven ones for one ten-rod on the mat, then read the result. Name it: ten ones is the same as one ten.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child records 50 and 11 but never exchanges the eleven ones for a ten; writes 511 or 51

errorPatterns.pattern: Smaller-from-larger in subtraction — '63 take 28: eight take three is five', answering 45
errorPatterns.nextMove: On the mat, show 63 cannot give 8 ones from only 3, so a ten must be broken open first (63 = 50+13). Check by adding 45+28.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The ones column of 63−28 is done as 8−3 with no decomposition; answer 45

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts every cube in ones and loses the ten-structure — treats a ten-rod as ten separate things to recount rather than one ten
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT stop them handling the blocks or drill exchange in isolation — treating a rod as one 'ten' is a maturing shift. Keep pairing the two readings aloud ('that's ten ones AND one ten') each time they exchange, so unitising develops.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child breaks rods apart to count all in ones, or recounts the whole set, rather than operating with rods as tens

responseLevels.gap: Gives 511/51 for the addition or 45 for the subtraction; tens and ones are handled separately with no exchange.
responseLevels.full: Composes and decomposes a ten correctly for both calculations, records the exchange in a jotting, and explains why (e.g. 'ten ones is the same as one ten').
responseLevels.partial: Exchanges correctly with the blocks in front of them but cannot yet carry it into a recording or do it mentally, or manages the addition compose but not the subtraction decompose.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child base-ten blocks and paper and set two calculations to work with the blocks and record: 34 + 27, then 63 − 28. Watch what they do at the ones in each case.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 34+27 requires composing a ten from eleven ones; a child who answers 511 or 51 has added the parts but not exchanged. 63−28 requires decomposing a ten; the smaller-from-larger child answers 45. Doing both correctly shows exchange is understood in both directions, which side-by-side digit work cannot fake.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 7–8 (UK Y2–Y3, US Grade 2). Partitioning a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares and counting to find the total — the array formalised into a grid, and the direct precursor to area.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2–Y3 array and repeated-addition work; underpins Y4 area by counting squares.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.G.2 'partition a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares and count to find the total number of them'; feeds 3.MD.7 (area) and 3.OA (array multiplication).
• Operational details: fill a rectangle completely with equal (same-size) squares in aligned rows and columns, then find the total by rows × columns rather than counting one-by-one — making the array/area structure explicit. Squares must tile with no gaps or overlaps.
• Checkpoint: partition and count by structure. Tier A (7): partition a rectangle into equal squares and count them. Tier B (7–8): find the total using number of rows and number in each row (rows × columns). Tier C (8): explain that the squares must be equal-size with no gaps/overlaps, and connect the grid to a multiplication fact.
bestPractices: Insist the squares are the SAME size and tile the rectangle with no gaps or overlaps — the equal-unit requirement is what makes the count structural (and it underpins area later).
Move children from counting every square one-by-one to using rows × columns, making the array structure of the grid explicit.
Explicitly connect the partitioned rectangle to the array and to a multiplication fact (4 rows of 6 squares = 4×6 = 24) so this is seen as the same structure, not a new one.
Foreshadow area: the count of unit squares that fills the rectangle IS its area — building the bridge to the area topics without yet formalising units.
Use aligned gridlines so rows and columns are unambiguous, avoiding ragged partitions.
keyRepresentations: Rectangle partitioned into a grid of equal unit squares
Rows × columns structure (the array within the grid)
Link to a multiplication fact for the total
Precursor to the area-by-counting-squares model
commonMisconceptions: Partitioning into unequal squares/pieces (not same-size units).
Leaving gaps or overlapping squares when tiling.
Counting every square one-by-one instead of using rows × columns.
Confusing the number of rows with the number of squares in a row.
Not connecting the grid count to a multiplication fact (treating it as pure counting).

learn.summary: For ages 7–8 (UK Y2–Y3, US Grade 2): partition a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares, then find the total using rows × columns rather than counting one by one. The equal-unit tiling (no gaps or overlaps) makes the count structural, formalises the array, and builds the bridge to area-by-counting-squares (CCSS 2.G.2 feeding 3.MD.7 and 3.OA; UK Y2–Y3 array work underpinning Y4 area). The central insight is that a tiled rectangle IS an array and its total comes from its structure.

activities.title: Build and read a tiled rectangle grid
feedback: If squares come out different sizes or ragged, first mark ticks the same distance apart along both the length and the width, then rule straight lines through matching ticks so the squares are equal and aligned.

If a learner counts one-by-one, do not insist on the shortcut — model the structural count for the grid they built (e.g. for 4 rows of 6: 'each row has 6; four rows: 6, 12, 18, 24'); the structural count is adopted with exposure.
If rows and columns are muddled (e.g. a 3-row grid called '4 rows of 3'), point along a row and down a column, labelling each dimension before writing the array.
activities.rationale: Varying the grid and contrasting one-by-one counting against rows × columns is intended to let the child discover that structure beats counting; dragging/toggling makes the array concrete as a tiled rectangle. The count toggle and gap/overlap flagging are illustrative interaction examples that make the mechanism visible, not required features.
sourceClaims: 2.G.2 partition a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares and count to find the total number of them.
Array and repeated-addition work in Y2–Y3 underpins area by counting squares in Y4; the tiled rectangle is the bridge from array multiplication to area.
learnerActions: Set the number of rows and the number of columns for a rectangle, and watch it fill with same-size squares that snap to a grid; if a partition leaves gaps or overlaps, notice it flagged and correct it so the squares are equal and aligned.
First count the squares one-by-one (slowly), then switch to a rows × columns view and watch the same rectangle resolve to its total instantly — e.g. 4 rows of 6 squares becoming 4×6 = 24.
Write the multiplication fact that matches the grid you built, and say how many squares are in each row and how many rows there are.
Add one more column (or one more row) and predict the new total before revealing it.
activities.intendedInsight: A rectangle tiled with equal squares is a rectangular array; its total comes from rows × columns, not from counting each square, and this square-count is what area will later measure.

activities.title: Partition on paper and count by structure (performance task)
feedback: Prompt with: 'How many squares in each row? How many rows? What multiplication matches your grid? If you added one more column, how many squares then?'
A strong response is a tidy 3-by-4 grid of 12 equal squares, counted as 4 + 4 + 4 or 4, 8, 12 (or 3 × 4) rather than one-by-one, with the grid related to a rectangular array.

Uneven squares, columns that don't align across rows, or one-by-one counting reveal a weak grasp of the array structure — reteach by marking equal ticks first and labelling each dimension; one-by-one counting alone is a developmental stage, not an error to penalise.
activities.rationale: A hands-on partition-and-count task on an actual rectangle elicits independent construction of the grid and surfaces the specific error patterns (ragged/unequal squares, muddled rows/columns, one-by-one counting) that distinguish structural understanding from mere line-drawing.
sourceClaims: 2.G.2 partition a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares and count to find the total number of them.
learnerActions: On a given rectangle whose width is 4/3 of its height (e.g. 8 cm wide by 6 cm tall), mark ticks the same distance apart (e.g. every 2 cm) along a long side and a short side, then rule lines through them to divide it into 3 rows and 4 columns of equal-sized squares.
Find the total number of squares and say aloud how you counted — one by one, by repeated addition (4 + 4 + 4), by skip-counting (4, 8, 12), or as 3 × 4.
State which multiplication fact matches your grid.
activities.intendedInsight: Creating equal, aligned squares and then using the row/column structure to count — rather than drawing any lines and tallying singly — is what shows a secure grasp of the array that underlies area.

activities.title: Check the equal-unit requirement and the array link
feedback: If a ragged or overlapping partition is chosen, show that it no longer forms a grid of same-size squares: overlaps get counted twice, gaps get missed, and unequal pieces mean the total is no longer a count of equal units, so rows × columns does not give a fair measure of the rectangle.
If the product is miscalculated, re-count one row, then skip-count by that amount for each row to confirm the total.
activities.rationale: A recognition/matching check reinforces the equal-unit requirement and the grid-to-multiplication link. This format checks whether the structure is recognised; it does not by itself elicit the child constructing a partition, so it is a companion to the construction tasks, not a replacement.
learnerActions: Choose the correctly-tiled rectangle from options that include a ragged or overlapping partition, and say why the equal-size, gap-free one is correct.
Give the total for a shown grid by completing rows × columns = ?.
Match a shown grid to its matching multiplication fact.
activities.intendedInsight: Equal-size squares that tile with no gaps or overlaps are what make the count structural; the grid's total is the product of its rows and columns.

constraints: Squares must be the same size and tile the rectangle with no gaps or overlaps — this equal-unit requirement is what makes the count structural and underpins area.

Do not force the rows × columns shortcut; the structural count is adopted with exposure. A child who partitions correctly but still counts one-by-one has a developmental gap, not an error to penalise.

A static labelled grid (tap-to-reveal rows, columns, total) is a useful reference but cannot let the child vary the grid or contrast counting versus structure, so use it alongside, not instead of, construction tasks.
Recognition/matching items check that the structure is understood but do not elicit independent construction of a partition; pair them with a hands-on partition task.
Keep this planar: volume and 3D packing are a separate later topic and are not part of this objective.

A paper/card rectangle has slight real thickness; treat it as an approximation of the ideal flat figure when discussing the squares as area units, and talk about the mathematical shape represented, not the physical sheet.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The two cited sources are curriculum-standard statements (CCSS 2.G.2 verified:false in the row; UK NC verified:true). They support the learning objective and the array-to-area bridge but do not establish comparative efficacy of any particular activity format.
Arithmetic check of examples: 4 rows of 6 = 24 ✓; 3 × 4 = 12, 4 + 4 + 4 = 12, skip-count 4, 8, 12 ✓; 4 rows of 6 skip-counted 6, 12, 18, 24 ✓. No erroneous distractors were introduced.

Activity 1's one-by-one feedback example is aligned to the activity's 4×6 worked example to avoid a mixed-grid inconsistency; Activity 2 deliberately uses the original 3×4 diagnostic grid, which is internally consistent within that scenario.
Efficacy/discovery wording in rationales is phrased as intended/proposed, since the row's 'moment of insight' design claim is not empirically validated by the cited standards.

The original row claimed dialogue 'adds no unique value' and 3D 'adds no gain'; these categorical modality claims were rescoped to observable limits (planar topic; recognition does not elicit construction) rather than universal laws.

probeDeeper: How did you count the squares — one by one or a quicker way?
How many squares in each row? How many rows?
What multiplication matches your grid?
If you added one more column, how many squares then?
assess.correctAnswer: A tidy 3-by-4 grid of 12 equal squares, counted efficiently as 4 + 4 + 4 or 4, 8, 12 (or 3 × 4) rather than one-by-one — relating the rows-and-columns to a rectangular array.

errorPatterns.pattern: unequal or misaligned partition — rows and columns don't line up, making squares of different sizes or a ragged grid
errorPatterns.nextMove: mark equal ticks along both sides first, then rule lines through them so the squares come out equal and aligned
errorPatterns.revealedBy: uneven squares; columns not aligned across rows

errorPatterns.pattern: counts the squares one by one — tallies all 12 individually instead of using the rows/columns
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT insist on the shortcut — model 'each row has 4, three rows: 4, 8, 12'; the structural count is adopted with exposure
errorPatterns.revealedBy: one-by-one counting with no skip-count or repeated addition

errorPatterns.pattern: muddles rows and columns — relates the grid to the wrong array (e.g. calls a 3-row grid '4 rows of 3')
errorPatterns.nextMove: point along a row and down a column, labelling each dimension before writing the array
errorPatterns.revealedBy: the array label doesn't match the grid drawn

responseLevels.gap: Cannot partition into equal aligned squares; the grid is ragged or the squares differ in size.
responseLevels.full: Partitions a rectangle into equal, aligned rows and columns, counts efficiently by rows/skip-counting, and relates the grid to a rectangular array.
responseLevels.partial: Partitions into a correct grid but counts one-by-one, or muddles rows and columns when naming the array.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a rectangle. Divide it into 3 rows and 4 columns of equal-sized squares, then find the total number of squares — and tell me how you counted them. (Watch whether the squares are equal-sized and gap-free, whether rows and columns align, and whether they count by ones or by rows.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Partitioning tests whether the child creates EQUAL, aligned squares (not just any lines) and then uses the row/column structure to count. Uneven partitions, misaligned columns, or one-by-one counting reveal a weak grasp of the array structure that underlies area.

sources.claim: Array and repeated-addition work in Y2–Y3 underpins area by counting squares in Y4; the tiled rectangle is the bridge from array multiplication to area.
