pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 5-7 (Y1/early Y2). Solve one-step WORD PROBLEMS involving addition and subtraction to 20, INCLUDING missing-number problems (7 = ? − 9). Extends within-10 modelling to a larger range and, importantly, to problems where the unknown is not the result.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1): 'solve one-step problems that involve addition and subtraction… and missing number problems such as 7 = ? − 9'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.OA.1 'use addition and subtraction within 20 to solve word problems… with unknowns in all positions'; 1.OA.8 determine the unknown in an equation.
• Operational details — Continue modelling the SITUATION (act out / draw / bar model) rather than keyword-matching, now with numbers to 20 and with the unknown in the start, change or result position. Missing-number problems are the key new demand: the child must represent an unknown and reason to it, often using the inverse or a known bond. Bar/part-whole models become powerful here for making the unknown visible.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 5): solve result-unknown add/subtract problems to 20 by modelling. Tier B (age 6): solve change-unknown problems and simple missing-number equations with support. Tier C (age 6-7): solve start-unknown and missing-number problems (7 = ? − 9), explaining the model and using the inverse to find the unknown.
bestPractices: Keep teaching modelling of the situation (act-out, drawing, bar/part-whole) over keyword strategies, extending to numbers to 20.
Introduce the unknown in all positions (result, change, start) and use part-whole/bar models to make the unknown visible so children can reason to it.
Connect missing-number problems to the inverse relationship and to known bonds (7 = ? − 9 → ? = 16 via 7 + 9).
Have children write the equation that matches the situation, placing the unknown where it belongs (not always after =).
Progress difficulty by problem structure, not just larger numbers, and discuss why a chosen model fits the story.
keyRepresentations: Bar/tape model showing known parts and an unknown
Part-part-whole model with the unknown in any slot
Objects/drawings acted on to match the story
Empty number line for counting on to find a difference/unknown
Equations with a box/letter for the unknown in varied positions
commonMisconceptions: Keyword-matching (fails on missing-number and compare problems).
Assuming the unknown is always the result, so start- and change-unknown problems stump them.
Rejecting missing-number forms because = is read as 'answer here'.
Combining the two given numbers regardless of the structure (e.g. adding in a start-unknown problem that needs subtraction).
Not using the inverse/known bond to find the unknown, instead guessing.

learn.summary: For ages 5-7 (Y1/early Y2): solve one-step word problems involving addition and subtraction to 20, including missing-number problems such as 7 = ? − 9. The core objective is modelling the situation (acting out, drawing, bar/part-whole models) rather than keyword-matching, and crucially handling problems where the unknown sits in the start, change or result position — not only the answer slot. Bar/part-whole models make the unknown visible so children can reason to it using the inverse or a known bond.

activities.title: Story-to-bar-model builder
feedback: Check the structure of the model, not just the final number: does the bar place the known parts and the unknown where the story puts them?

If the pieces dragged in don't match the story — for example a given whole treated as a part, or both numbers entered as parts when one of them is actually the whole — ask them to re-read it event by event: 'What was there to begin with? What happened? What is left?'
For 7 = ? − 9, prompt: 'We start with a mystery number, take away 9, and 7 are left — so the mystery number is 9 and 7 put together, 16.'

Praise correctly reasoning to an unknown via the inverse or a known bond, and show how the model did the work: adding the parts to find a missing whole, or taking a known part from the whole to find a missing part.
activities.rationale: The skill is modelling situations with the unknown in varied positions; a build-your-own bar/part-whole model lets the child place the unknown and manipulate it so the inverse is made visible, with varied problem structures generated across a session. An interactive model can rotate the unknown position and give feedback on the structure of the model, which a fixed worked example cannot do, though a fixed example can still illustrate the method. Proposed design; efficacy not independently verified.
sourceClaims: Y1 pupils solve one-step addition and subtraction problems and missing-number problems such as 7 = ? − 9, using concrete objects and pictorial representations.
1.OA.1: use addition and subtraction within 20 to solve word problems with unknowns in all positions; 1.OA.8 determine the unknown in an equation.
Bar/part-whole modelling makes the unknown visible and supports reasoning (including via the inverse) across all unknown positions; keyword strategies fail on missing-number problems.
learnerActions: Listen to or read a one-step problem with numbers to 20, e.g. 'I had some sweets, ate 9, and 7 are left.'
Drag the quantities you know into a bar or part-whole frame — for this story, split a whole into a '9 eaten' part and a '7 left' part.
Mark where the unknown sits in the model (here the WHOLE — the number you started with — is the mystery).
Act on the model to find the unknown — combine the two parts to fill the whole (7 + 9 = 16), or count on along a number line.
Repeat with problems that rotate the unknown through result, change and start positions, and with pure missing-number equations like 7 = ? − 9.
Write the equation that matches your model, placing the unknown where it belongs (not always after the = sign).
activities.intendedInsight: A problem where the unknown is the START or the CHANGE, not the answer, is not impossible: the bar model shows exactly where the mystery sits. If the unknown is the whole, combining the known parts finds it. If the unknown is a part, taking the known part away from the whole (or counting on from it) finds it. Children learn to model any structure rather than hope a keyword tells them what to do.

activities.title: Hands-on modelling with counters, drawings and paper bars
feedback: If the model and story disagree, re-read the story one event at a time and adjust the counters/bar.
Reinforce that 'took away / left' does not automatically mean subtract — the structure of the story decides the operation.
Celebrate explanations that justify the operation from the situation, not from a single word.
activities.rationale: Concrete acting-out and drawing underpin the pictorial bar model and give young children a tangible way to represent an unknown before abstract equations. This supports the standards' call for concrete objects and pictorial representations.
sourceClaims: Y1 pupils solve one-step addition and subtraction problems and missing-number problems such as 7 = ? − 9, using concrete objects and pictorial representations.
Bar/part-whole modelling makes the unknown visible and supports reasoning (including via the inverse) across all unknown positions; keyword strategies fail on missing-number problems.
learnerActions: Act out or draw the story with physical counters before choosing any operation.
Lay out a paper tape/bar strip and partition it into known parts and an unknown part to match the story.
Use an empty number line to count on and find a difference or an unknown.
Say aloud what you know, what you are trying to find, and why the operation you chose fits the story.
activities.intendedInsight: Modelling the situation with concrete materials — rather than matching keywords — reveals the correct operation even when the unknown is not the result.

activities.title: Coaching dialogue: 'What do we know, what are we finding?'
feedback: When a child applies an operation to the two given numbers automatically, without checking the story (e.g. trying 7 − 9 or 9 − 7 for 7 = ? − 9), redirect to the story structure with a question rather than giving the answer.
Follow the child's approach and ask for justification; adapt prompts to whether they are stuck on parsing '=' or on choosing the operation.
activities.rationale: Missing-number and start-unknown problems demand reasoning to an unknown; a Socratic dialogue may develop that reasoning by adapting to the child's approach. Dialogue complements, and does not replace, hands-on and pictorial modelling. This medium's efficacy is a proposal, not verified.
learnerActions: Respond to a coach who asks you to name what is known and what is unknown in a problem.
Justify which operation you will use and where the unknown sits, especially for start-unknown and missing-number problems.
Talk through 7 = ? − 9: identify that you need a starting number which, after removing 9, leaves 7.
activities.intendedInsight: Reasoning aloud about knowns and the unknown can develop the modelling and inverse reasoning needed for harder problem structures.

activities.title: Worked bar-model example with revealable steps
feedback: Prompt the learner to predict each next step before revealing it.
Ask them to point to where the unknown sits before the final number is shown.
activities.rationale: A static worked example anchors the pictorial modelling method and can be revisited; it cannot generate varied structures or let the child model their own problem, so it works best as a scaffold before or alongside the interactive builder.
sourceClaims: Y1 pupils solve one-step addition and subtraction problems and missing-number problems such as 7 = ? − 9, using concrete objects and pictorial representations.
learnerActions: Study one worked problem shown with a bar model.
Reveal the solution steps one at a time and relate each step to the story.
Restate how the parts and whole map onto what the story gave and what it asked.
activities.intendedInsight: A clearly worked bar model anchors the method and shows how the unknown is found from the known quantities: combining the parts when the whole is unknown, or taking a known part from the whole when a part is unknown.

activities.title: Missing-number and word-problem practice set
feedback: If a child answers 7 = ▢ − 9 as 7 − 9 or refuses, return to the bar model: whole ▢, parts 9 and 7, so ▢ = 16.

If a child subtracts on a take-away start-unknown problem (e.g. 'I had some, ate 9, 7 are left'), have them act it out to see that the start was larger than what remained. (On an add-on start-unknown problem such as 'I had some, got 5 more, now I have 12', subtracting 12 − 5 is correct.)
activities.rationale: Varied-position items probe the target directly and surface misconceptions, but practice/fill-in tasks present problems to solve and may not by themselves build the modelling process, so they belong after modelling work rather than before it.
sourceClaims: 1.OA.1: use addition and subtraction within 20 to solve word problems with unknowns in all positions; 1.OA.8 determine the unknown in an equation.
learnerActions: Fill in equations with the unknown in different positions, e.g. 7 = ▢ − 9, ▢ + 5 = 12, 12 − ▢ = 8.
Answer word problems with picture support where the unknown is the result, change or start.
Mark which problems were 'find the start' problems rather than 'find what's left'.
activities.intendedInsight: Problems with the unknown in varied positions require the same modelling reasoning; recognising the structure matters more than the keyword.

constraints: Keep teaching modelling of the situation (act-out, drawing, bar/part-whole) over keyword strategies, extending the number range to 20.
Introduce the unknown in all positions (result, change, start) and use part-whole/bar models to make the unknown visible.
Connect missing-number problems to the inverse relationship and known bonds (7 = ? − 9 → ? = 16 via 7 + 9).
Have children place the unknown where it belongs in the equation, not always after the = sign.
Progress difficulty by problem STRUCTURE, not just larger numbers, and discuss why a chosen model fits the story.
Practice/fill-in items probe the target and surface misconceptions but do not by themselves build the modelling process; use them after hands-on and pictorial modelling.
A worked example is a scaffold: it anchors the method but cannot generate varied structures or let the child model their own problem.
Do not teach keyword-to-operation rules ('away/left' → subtract); these fail on start-unknown, change-unknown and missing-number problems.
Reading '=' as 'the answer goes here' causes children to reject missing-number forms; treat '=' relationally.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the diagnostic arithmetic: (1) 12 − 4 = 8 ✓; (2) start-unknown 'some cars, 5 drive away, 7 left' → start = 5 + 7 = 12 ✓; (3) 7 = ▢ − 9 → ▢ = 7 + 9 = 16 ✓. Added practice items also check out: ▢ + 5 = 12 → ▢ = 7; 12 − ▢ = 8 → ▢ = 4. These are used consistently in the activity feedback.

The source row lists two of three sources as verified:false (CCSS-M and the NCETM/IES bar-model claim). Comparative/efficacy framing from these should be treated as unverified; the rewrite scopes the 'interactive vs static', 'worked example' and 'dialogue' claims to stated affordances/limits rather than universal necessity or medium superiority.
The dialogue activity carries no sourceClaims because no listed source supports the efficacy of a Socratic dialogue medium; its benefit is stated as a proposal only.

The original rationale stated 'a static picture can't' generate varied structures and that a quiz 'presents problems rather than teaching'. These are retained only as qualified affordance/limit statements; a fixed example can still teach the method and practice items can still probe the target.
Independent re-audit confirms no learner-facing arithmetic, structural or contradiction errors; feedback remains coherent with the stated sweets example (whole = 16 from parts 9 and 7) throughout.

probeDeeper: In the cars problem, did the number of cars at the start get bigger or smaller after some drove away?
For 7 = ▢ − 9, what number do we start with so that taking 9 leaves 7?
How could counters or a bar help you see the cars problem?
Which of these was a 'find the start' problem, not a 'find what's left' problem?

errorPatterns.pattern: Keyword strategy — picks the operation from a word ('away/left' → subtract) regardless of structure, so start-unknown '5 drive away, 7 left' is computed as 7 − 5 or 5 − 7.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model the situation with counters or a bar model before choosing an operation; do not teach keyword-to-operation rules.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child subtracts on the start-unknown problem (answers 2) instead of adding.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the missing-number equation left-to-right as 'compute the two numbers' — 7 = ▢ − 9 answered as 7 − 9 (or 'can't do it', or 2).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Treat = relationally with a part-whole / bar model (whole ▢, parts 9 and 7, so ▢ = 9 + 7).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives −2, 2, or refuses, treating ▢ as 'the answer of a sum'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Correct set-up but a counting / arithmetic slip within 20.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the calculation; the modelling and operation choice are sound, so do not reteach them.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Right operation and structure, answer off by one or two.

responseLevels.gap: Applies a keyword/default operation; cannot handle start-unknown or missing-number equations.
responseLevels.full: Models and solves varied structures within 20 — result-unknown, start-unknown, and missing-number equations — choosing the operation from the situation.
responseLevels.partial: Solves result-unknown problems reliably but defaults to subtracting on start-unknown, or cannot parse 7 = ▢ − 9.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Solve these — you can use counters. (1) I have 12 sweets and eat 4 — how many are left? (2) There were some cars; 5 drive away and 7 are left — how many were there at the start? (3) Fill the box: 7 = ▢ − 9.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The three problems are deliberately different STRUCTURES (result-unknown is easy; start-unknown and the missing-minuend equation are hard — CGI/Carpenter). A keyword solver does 12 − 4 fine but subtracts on 'drive away' for the start-unknown and cannot handle 7 = ▢ − 9. Watch whether the child models the situation or grabs numbers plus a keyword.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 7-8. Read and write numbers to 1000 in three registers — numerals (342), number names ('three hundred and forty-two') and expanded form (300 + 40 + 2) — and move fluently between them. This is the LANGUAGE/notation face of three-digit place value.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 3): 'read and write numbers up to 1000 in numerals and in words'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.NBT.3 'read and write numbers to 1000 using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form'.
• Operational details — Teach the three registers as mutually-translatable views anchored to a build. Attend hard to the spoken-to-written mapping ('and', the hundreds word, internal zeros): 'three hundred and six' → 306, not 3006 or 36. Practise both directions (read a numeral aloud; write a spoken number). Expanded form is the bridge that exposes each digit's value.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 7, emerging): reads/writes three-digit numerals with no internal zero. Tier B (age 7-8, secure): translates among numeral, words and expanded form including one internal zero. Tier C (age 8, extending): writes tricky spoken numbers (306, 340) correctly and explains the expanded form's link to place value.
bestPractices: Treat numeral / words / expanded form as three views of one number and translate in all directions, always tied to a build.
Target the spoken→written danger zone: the hundreds word, the connective 'and', and internal zeros (306, 640).
Use expanded form (300+40+2) as the explicit bridge from words to place value.
Dictate numbers for children to write (and vice versa) so both encode and decode directions are fluent.
Sequence from no-zero → one internal zero → trailing zero to isolate the hard cases.
keyRepresentations: The three registers side by side: numeral | words | expanded form
Place-value chart / arrow cards linking words to columns
Base-ten build under each register as the anchor
Number-word cards (hundred, and, -ty, teen) for constructing names
0-1000 number line for locating the number named
commonMisconceptions: Writing what you hear literally: 'three hundred and six' → 3006 or 30006.
Dropping or misplacing internal zeros (340 written as 34; 306 as 36).
Mis-ordering words vs digits, or omitting the hundreds word.
Confusing teen and -ty words within the tens part (forty vs fourteen).
Treating expanded form as separate numbers (300, 40, 2) rather than a partition of one number.

learn.summary: Ages 7-8: read and write numbers to 1000 across three registers — numerals (342), number names ('three hundred and forty-two') and expanded form (300 + 40 + 2) — and translate fluently in both directions. The hardest cases are the spoken→written mapping and internal/placeholder zeros (306, 340, 305). Expanded form acts as an explicit bridge from number names to place value. Core activities give learners genuine two-way production (encode and decode) anchored to a base-ten build; a static reference wall and light oral reading are preserved as scaffolds with stated limits.

activities.title: Three-pane number translator (build, type, name)
feedback: If the words-to-numeral entry comes out too long (e.g. 30042 for 'three hundred and forty-two'), build 342 with base-ten blocks and place each part into a hundreds/tens/ones frame so parts land in columns rather than being appended.
For a placeholder-zero number, show 3 hundreds, 0 tens, 5 ones: the 0 holds the tens place so the 3 stays in hundreds; contrast 35, 305 and 350 directly.
Optionally, a 'dictation' mode can speak a trap number (306, 340) for the child to write, flagging a wrong or missing internal zero against the empty column in the build.
activities.rationale: Translating among the three registers is production in both directions, which a two-way build+type+name tool exercises directly while the base-ten model anchors meaning. Expanded form is used as the bridge from number names to place value, and the live base-ten column makes the placeholder-zero rule visible.
sourceClaims: Read and write numbers to 1000 using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form (2.NBT.3).
Expanded form bridges number names and place value; internal-zero numbers (e.g. 306) are the key error source in reading/writing.
Year 3 pupils should 'read and write numbers up to 1000 in numerals and in words'.
learnerActions: Work with three linked views of one number side by side: a numeral display, a word-tile builder, and an expanded-form strip, with a base-ten build (flats/rods/cubes) shown beneath.

Change any one view and watch the others and the blocks rebuild: assemble the word-tiles 'three hundred and forty-two' and confirm 342 appears alongside 300 + 40 + 2 and three flats, four rods, two cubes.
Translate deliberately in BOTH directions: read a shown numeral and build its words; and start from spoken/word form and write the numeral.
Sequence difficulty: start with no-zero numbers (342), then one internal zero (306), then a trailing zero (340).
activities.intendedInsight: Numeral, words and expanded form are three views of ONE number; expanded form reveals each digit's place value, and the empty column shows why a placeholder zero must be written (306, not 36 or 3006).

activities.title: Two-way translation practice (write it, name it, expand it)
feedback: If expanded form of 637 is written as 600 + 3 + 7, read each digit with its place ('3 tens = 30') and check the parts add back to 637.
If 305 is read or written as 'thirty-five'/35 or 3005, re-show 3 hundreds, 0 tens, 5 ones and contrast 35, 305, 350.
Check teen vs -ty words in the tens part (forty vs fourteen) when a name is miswritten.
activities.rationale: Reading and writing to 1000 is a two-way production and checking skill; targeted practice in both directions, including the internal-zero danger zone, builds and verifies fluency. This format both teaches by practice and can check the same skills.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils should 'read and write numbers up to 1000 in numerals and in words'.
Read and write numbers to 1000 using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form (2.NBT.3).
Expanded form bridges number names and place value; internal-zero numbers (e.g. 306) are the key error source in reading/writing.
learnerActions: Write a spoken or word-form number as a numeral (e.g. write 'six hundred and forty' as 640).
Write a given numeral in words (e.g. write 306 as 'three hundred and six').
Complete expanded form from a numeral (e.g. 485 = 400 + __ + 5) and the reverse.
Match numeral ↔ words ↔ expanded form for a set of numbers, deliberately including internal-zero and trailing-zero cases (305, 340).
Decide the correct written form among plausible errors for internal-zero numbers.
activities.intendedInsight: Both encode (spoken/words → numeral) and decode (numeral → words) directions become reliable, especially for the zero traps and the tens digit's place value.

activities.title: Reference wall: one number in three registers
feedback: Point back to the anchor when a learner omits the hundreds word or mis-orders words and digits: match each spoken chunk to its column.
Use the 306 flap to re-explain the placeholder whenever an internal zero is dropped.
activities.rationale: A fixed, aligned reference consolidates the correspondence between registers and names the placeholder-zero rule. As a reference scaffold it does not by itself elicit the two-way writing/reading production, so it is paired with the translation activities.
sourceClaims: Expanded form bridges number names and place value; internal-zero numbers (e.g. 306) are the key error source in reading/writing.
learnerActions: Study a fixed anchor card showing 342 as numeral, words and expanded form at once, with a base-ten build.
Tap the words to highlight the matching digits and expanded parts (where an interactive display is available).
Open a 306 'card flap' that explains why the 0 is written in the tens place.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing all three registers of the same number aligned, with the placeholder zero explained, gives a stable mental model to refer back to.

activities.title: Read-it-back oral warm-up
feedback: If 'three hundred and six' is misheard as a longer number, slow the chunks (three hundred / and / six) and match each to a column.
Prompt for the hundreds word when it is dropped.
activities.rationale: Reading numbers aloud is genuinely oral, so spoken practice has a real place as a warm-up. It is light practice only: reliably capturing a child's WRITTEN numeral needs an input surface, so follow oral work with writing.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils should 'read and write numbers up to 1000 in numerals and in words'.
learnerActions: Listen to a spoken three-digit number and read a number back aloud.
Say aloud the number shown on a card, attending to the connective 'and' and the hundreds word.
activities.intendedInsight: Hearing and saying numbers aloud rehearses the spoken register and the 'and' connective, supporting the spoken→written mapping.

constraints: Always tie the three registers to a base-ten build so translation stays anchored to meaning rather than word order.
Deliberately sequence no-zero → one internal zero → trailing zero (342 → 306 → 340) to isolate the hard cases.
Expanded form must partition ONE number into place values (300 + 40 + 2), not be treated as three separate numbers; the tens digit must be expanded by place value (30, not 3).
A fixed reference image consolidates the correspondence but does not by itself elicit two-way reading/writing production; use it alongside, not instead of, tasks where the child writes and reads.
Oral read-it-back is light practice; it does not reliably capture a child's written numeral, so pair it with a writing task.

This is a notation/language task with no spatial dimension; a 3D spatial build is not expected to add a relevant affordance here, so it is not prioritised (this is a scoping judgement, not a claim that 3D cannot teach).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Source metadata marks only the DfE Year 3 claim as verified; the CCSS 2.NBT.3 and NCETM claims are recorded as unverified in the row and should not be treated as confirmed.

The legacy entry stated the spoken→written and internal-zero traps are 'self-correcting' and that a fixed image 'can't' exercise two-way production; these have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements rather than universal claims, as internal fit ratings do not establish necessity or comparative efficacy.
The legacy poor-fit note on 3D was reworded from a categorical 'adds nothing' verdict to a scoped prioritisation judgement.

The 0-1000 number line listed among the pedagogy key representations ('locating the number named') was not built into any activity; it is secondary for a notation task but remains available as an optional locating aid if desired.

Self-audit of arithmetic/examples: 300+40+2=342 OK; 600+30+7=637 OK (face-value error 600+3+7 correctly flagged); 400+80+5=485 so the blank in 485=400+__+5 is 80 OK; 'six hundred and forty'=640 OK; 305='three hundred and five' with 0 tens, 300+5 OK. No arithmetic errors found.
The '30042 for three hundred and forty-two' and '3005 for 305' strings are misconception examples to diagnose and correct in feedback, never correct forms to teach.

probeDeeper: Write 305 — what job is the 0 doing?
Your friend wrote 30042 for three hundred and forty-two — what went wrong?
Write 637 as hundreds + tens + ones and add the parts back up.
assess.correctAnswer: Reads 342 correctly; writes 342; 637 = 600 + 30 + 7; 305 = 'three hundred and five' and 300 + 5 (with 0 tens).

errorPatterns.pattern: Concatenates the spoken chunks into digits: writes 30042 (or 300402) for 'three hundred and forty-two'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build 342 with base-ten blocks and write it into a hundreds/tens/ones frame so each part lands in one column, not appended.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Words-to-numeral yields a too-long number that literally spells out 'three hundred' + 'forty' + 'two'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Mishandles the placeholder zero: reads/writes 305 as 'thirty-five'/35, or writes it 3005, dropping or misplacing the empty tens
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show 3 hundreds, 0 tens, 5 ones; the 0 holds the tens place so the 3 stays in hundreds. Contrast 35, 305, 350.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The 305 item loses the zero or inserts extra digits.

errorPatterns.pattern: Expanded form uses face value not place value: writes 600 + 3 + 7 for 637
errorPatterns.nextMove: Read each digit with its place ('3 tens = 30') and check the parts add back to 637.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The tens digit is expanded as 3 rather than 30.

responseLevels.gap: Concatenates words into numerals or loses the placeholder zero; expanded form uses face values.
responseLevels.full: Reads and writes three-digit numbers as numerals, words, and expanded form, including placeholder zeros, giving each digit its place value.
responseLevels.partial: Handles numbers without a zero but slips on 305-type numbers or on expanded form of the tens digit.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Watch the child read and write. 'Read 342 aloud. Now write “three hundred and forty-two” as a numeral. Write 637 in expanded form. Now write 305 in words, and in expanded form.' The 305 item is the key — watch the zero.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Producing all three forms exposes the two classic errors: concatenating the spoken parts (writing 30042 for three hundred and forty-two) and mishandling the placeholder zero in 305. Expanded form separately checks whether the middle digit is given its PLACE value (30) or face value (3).

sources.claim: Read and write numbers to 1000 using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form (2.NBT.3).

pedagogy.summary: The conceptual glue beneath fraction operations: understanding addition and subtraction as JOINING and SEPARATING like parts, and being able to DECOMPOSE a fraction into a sum of same-denominator parts in more than one way (3/8 = 1/8+1/8+1/8 and also 1/8+2/8; 2 1/8 = 1+1+1/8). It moves a child from 'apply the numerator rule' to 'a fraction is a flexible collection of unit parts I can split and recombine however I like'. This flexibility is what makes later work — mixed-number arithmetic, common denominators, regrouping in subtraction — make sense rather than being separate tricks.
bestPractices: Frame + and − explicitly as joining and separating the SAME unit parts, keeping the denominator (the unit) fixed throughout.
Demand MORE THAN ONE decomposition of the same fraction so flexibility, not a single memorised split, is the goal (5/6 = 1/6+4/6 = 2/6+3/6 = ...).
Connect decomposition to the whole: 2 1/8 is two whole sets of eighths plus one eighth (16/8 + 1/8 = 17/8), so mixed numbers are seen as one quantity of like parts.
Justify each decomposition on a visual model (bar/number line) where the total length is invariant — different sums, same measure.
Use decomposition to explain, not just compute: e.g. why 5/6 − 2/6 separates two sixths from five.
keyRepresentations: Fraction bar that can be sliced into groups in multiple ways, total length fixed
Number line showing a fraction reached by different combinations of unit-fraction jumps
Part-part-whole / bar model linking a fraction to its decompositions
Mixed-number bar showing whole sets of the unit plus the extra part (2 1/8 = 8/8+8/8+1/8)
commonMisconceptions: Alters denominators when decomposing (a reverse add-across): writes 5/6 = 2/3 + 3/3 because 2+3=5 and 3+3=6, so the parts don't actually total 5/6.
Believes a fraction has only one 'correct' break-up (3/8 must be 1/8+1/8+1/8) and cannot produce a different valid decomposition.
Treats a mixed number's whole and fraction parts as disconnected numbers, unable to express 2 1/8 as a single count of eighths (17/8).

learn.summary: Children aged 9–10 learn to see fraction addition and subtraction as JOINING and SEPARATING the same unit parts, with the denominator (the unit) held fixed throughout. The central skill is decomposing a fraction into a sum of same-denominator parts in MORE THAN ONE way (5/6 = 1/6+4/6 = 2/6+3/6 = 1/6+1/6+3/6), and expressing a mixed number as a single count of like parts (2 1/8 = 8/8+8/8+1/8 = 17/8). The aim is to shift from 'apply the numerator rule' to 'a fraction is a flexible collection of unit parts I can split and recombine', which later makes mixed-number arithmetic, common denominators, and regrouping in subtraction coherent rather than separate tricks.

activities.title: Slice one bar many ways
feedback: When several different sums all align with the same bar length, point out explicitly: different sums, same measure — that is what makes 5/6 flexible.

If a learner relabels a piece's denominator wrongly (e.g. calls a two-sixths piece '2/3'), rebuild that piece from sixth-sized units on the bar and recount: it is 2/6. A two-sixths piece does equal 1/3, but this task asks for same-denominator sums, so record every part in sixths.
If a learner can give only one break-up, prompt: 'Find a genuinely different way, then another' until two or more distinct valid sums appear.
Optional live interaction, where available: let cuts on the bar auto-write the matching sum and refuse any attempt to relabel a piece's denominator, so the reverse add-across cannot be recorded.
activities.rationale: Decomposition is literally slicing one fixed quantity into groups in different ways. A model whose total length is invariant lets a child generate many decompositions, see they all measure the same, and keeps attention on the unit. Understanding why procedures work by composing/decomposing into like units is what prevents treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers.
sourceClaims: Fraction computation errors stem from not treating the fraction as a single number and operating on numerators and denominators as separate whole numbers; understanding why procedures work (composition/decomposition into like units) prevents this.
Decomposing a non-unit fraction into unit fractions and multiple same-denominator sums, via dual naming, builds the flexible joining/separating that underpins mixed-number arithmetic.
learnerActions: Start with a bar whose total length represents 5/6 of a whole, marked off into five equal sixths (each one-sixth of the whole) against a fixed ruler so its length cannot change.
Group the sixths one way (e.g. 1 and 4) and write the matching sum of sixths underneath: 5/6 = 1/6 + 4/6.
Regroup the SAME bar differently (2 and 3; then 1, 1 and 3) and write each new sum: 2/6 + 3/6, 1/6 + 1/6 + 3/6.
Line up all the sums you have written against the single unchanged bar and say aloud: 'all of these are 5/6'.
Repeat the whole process with a fresh fraction you have not seen (e.g. 7/8) to produce at least two distinct decompositions.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction is not one fixed break-up: any grouping of its unit parts that uses the same denominator and the same total count measures the same quantity. Addition joins those parts and subtraction separates them, while the unit stays fixed.

activities.title: Mixed number as one count of like parts
feedback: If a learner writes 2 1/8 as 2/8 + 1/8, show each whole bar as 8/8 on the model and recount: two wholes are 16/8, so 16/8 + 1/8 = 17/8.
If the '2' is ignored, ask first 'How many eighths are in one whole? in two wholes?' before writing the conversion.
Reinforce by reversing it: start from 17/8 and build back the two whole eighths-bars plus one eighth.
activities.rationale: Treating a mixed number's whole and fraction as disconnected numbers blocks mixed-number arithmetic. Building the wholes out of the same unit on a model makes the conversion a count, not a memorised rule.
sourceClaims: Decomposing a non-unit fraction into unit fractions and multiple same-denominator sums, via dual naming, builds the flexible joining/separating that underpins mixed-number arithmetic.
learnerActions: Lay out 2 1/8 as two whole bars, each cut into eight eighths, plus one extra eighth.
Count the eighths in each whole bar (8/8 and 8/8), then join the extra eighth.
Write the quantity as a single count of eighths: 8/8 + 8/8 + 1/8 = 17/8, confirming the 2 wholes contribute 16/8, not 2/8.
State in words why the whole and the fraction are one quantity: 2 1/8 is seventeen eighths altogether.
activities.intendedInsight: A mixed number's whole part and fraction part are the same kind of unit part; the wholes can be recounted as eighths so the whole quantity is a single count of like parts (17/8).

activities.title: Check and sort candidate decompositions
feedback: For a learner who accepts 2/3+3/3: compute 2/3+3/3 (= 5/3, more than a whole) and compare to 5/6 — it is clearly not equal, and the pieces are not sixths.
Correct answer reference: 5/6 = any two distinct sums of sixths totalling 5/6 (e.g. 1/6+4/6 and 2/6+3/6); 2 1/8 = 8/8+8/8+1/8 = 17/8; the denominator stays fixed throughout.
Recognising a correct option is a check on reasoning; it does not by itself show the learner can build one, so always pair it with the learner producing their own second decomposition.
activities.rationale: Distinguishing valid from invalid decompositions surfaces the reverse-add-across misconception, and requiring the learner to add the parts and compare keeps the focus on the fraction as a single quantity. The add-across error is a documented, common mistake among primary pupils.
sourceClaims: The add-across (adding numerators and denominators) error is a common, documented mistake among primary pupils, evidencing that fractions are being treated as pairs of whole numbers rather than single quantities.

Fraction computation errors stem from not treating the fraction as a single number and operating on numerators and denominators as separate whole numbers; understanding why procedures work (composition/decomposition into like units) prevents this.
learnerActions: Given several candidate sums for 5/6, decide which equal 5/6 and which do not — e.g. 1/6+4/6, 2/6+3/6, and the trap 2/3+3/3.
For each candidate, add the parts and compare the total to 5/6 to justify the decision, not just guess.
Explain why 2/3 + 3/3 fails: adding them gives 5/3 (more than a whole), not 5/6, and the parts are not measured in sixths.
Fill in a second valid decomposition of a given fraction, and match each mixed number to its improper form (e.g. 2 1/8 ↔ 17/8).
activities.intendedInsight: A valid same-denominator decomposition must keep the denominator fixed AND have parts that actually total the original fraction; the reverse add-across (2/3+3/3 because 2+3=5 and 3+3=6) produces parts that do not sum to 5/6.

activities.title: Explain, don't just compute, subtraction as separating
feedback: If a learner changes the denominator during subtraction, re-anchor on the unit: both numbers are sixths, so the answer is counted in sixths.
Ask the learner to verify by re-joining the result to the amount removed and checking they return to 5/6.
activities.rationale: Using decomposition to explain rather than only compute builds the conceptual glue that makes regrouping in subtraction sensible later. Holding the unit fixed prevents treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers.
sourceClaims: Fraction computation errors stem from not treating the fraction as a single number and operating on numerators and denominators as separate whole numbers; understanding why procedures work (composition/decomposition into like units) prevents this.
learnerActions: Show 5/6 − 2/6 on a bar or number line by separating two sixths from five sixths and reading the remaining three sixths.
Say in words what subtraction did: it separated two of the same unit parts, leaving 3/6; the denominator (sixths) did not change.
Connect it to joining: 3/6 + 2/6 rebuilds the original 5/6, so joining and separating are opposite moves on the same unit parts.
activities.intendedInsight: Subtraction separates like unit parts just as addition joins them; the denominator names the unit and stays fixed, so only the count of parts changes.

constraints: Keep the denominator (the unit) fixed throughout every join, separate, and decomposition; this is the non-negotiable idea that blocks the reverse add-across.
Always demand MORE THAN ONE decomposition of the same fraction; a single memorised split does not demonstrate flexibility.

The reverse add-across (5/6 = 2/3 + 3/3) is a genuine error, not an acceptable alternative answer: its parts sum to 5/3, not 5/6, and are not measured in sixths. Never present it as valid; use it only as a checked-and-rejected trap.
2 wholes of eighths are 16/8, not 2/8; ensure the whole part is recounted in the shared unit before converting (2 1/8 = 16/8 + 1/8 = 17/8).

Selecting or recognising a correct decomposition is a check on reasoning and does not by itself show independent construction; pair recognition tasks with the learner producing their own decompositions.
Static worked examples can show a couple of decompositions for reference but cannot let the child generate new groupings, which is the actual skill; treat them as support, not the main activity.
Justify each decomposition against a model where the total measure is invariant (fixed-length bar or number line), so different sums are seen to share one measure.

Narrow medium affordances (not universal laws): discussion alone can support explaining a decomposition but does not itself let a child perform the slicing and grouping; and because this content is planar part-whole reasoning, a 3D/spatial model adds no dimension the task needs. Neither observation means any medium 'cannot teach' — explaining aloud is retained as part of several activities.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

One cited source (NCETM Primary Mastery / Spine 3 Fractions, supporting the dual-naming/decomposition principle used in Activities 1 and 2) was marked verified:false in the source row; treat that claim as unconfirmed even though its exact text is copied where used.

Self-audit: confirmed 2 1/8 = 16/8 + 1/8 = 17/8 (two wholes contribute 16/8, not 2/8). Confirmed 2/3 + 3/3 = 5/3 ≠ 5/6, so it is correctly treated as an invalid decomposition rather than an alternative answer. Confirmed example decompositions of 5/6 (1/6+4/6, 2/6+3/6, 1/6+1/6+3/6) and of 7/8 each total the named fraction.

The original material's 'denominator relabelling is refused' is retained only as an optional interaction affordance, not as a claim that one medium is uniquely able to teach this. The source's categorical dismissals of 3D and conversation were reworded into narrow affordances rather than carried as universal pedagogical laws.

probeDeeper: You wrote 5/6 = 1/6 + 4/6 — can you find a different way? And another after that?
A friend says 5/6 = 2/3 + 3/3. Add 2/3 and 3/3 and check — does it come to 5/6?
How many eighths are in the two whole ones of 2 1/8? So how many eighths altogether?
If addition is joining parts, what is subtraction doing — show 5/6 − 2/6 as separating.
assess.correctAnswer: 5/6 = e.g. 1/6 + 4/6 AND 2/6 + 3/6 (any two distinct sums of sixths totalling 5/6). 2 1/8 = 1 + 1 + 1/8 = 8/8 + 8/8 + 1/8 = 17/8. Denominator stays sixths/eighths throughout.

errorPatterns.pattern: Alters the denominators when decomposing: '5/6 is 2/3 + 3/3 because 2 and 3 make 5, and 3 and 3 make 6' — a reverse add-across, so the parts don't total 5/6.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to unit-fraction building blocks: 5/6 is five one-sixths, so every piece of it must be measured in sixths; rebuild the sum from sixth-pieces on a bar and check the total length.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Offers a 'decomposition' whose pieces don't share the denominator 6 (2/3+3/3, 1/2+2/4); checking the sum gives the wrong total.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats a mixed number's whole and fraction as unrelated: writes 2 1/8 as '2/8 + 1/8' or can't count the wholes in eighths, so never reaches 17/8.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the two whole bars each as 8/8 on the model, then join the extra 1/8: 8/8 + 8/8 + 1/8 = 17/8; count the whole-groups of eight before writing the numeric conversion.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cannot express 2 1/8 as a single count of eighths; the '2' is ignored or mis-scaled (2/8 instead of 16/8).

responseLevels.gap: Alters denominators when decomposing (reverse add-across); can give at most one break-up; treats a mixed number's whole and fraction as unrelated numbers.
responseLevels.full: Gives two distinct sixth-decompositions of 5/6 keeping the denominator fixed, expresses 2 1/8 as a sum crossing the whole (1+1+1/8, or 17/8), and explains + and − as flexible joining/separating of like parts; transfers to a new fraction.
responseLevels.partial: Produces valid same-denominator decompositions and one way for 5/6, but struggles to find a genuinely different SECOND way, or can't link 2 1/8 to its total in eighths — can join but not yet flexibly, or can't cross the whole.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show me TWO different ways to break 5/6 into a sum of sixths. Then take 2 1/8 and write it as a sum that includes its whole parts — show it however helps you (a picture, a number line, or numbers).
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Asking for TWO decompositions forces flexible joining rather than one memorised split, and exposes the child who can only give a single break-up. A child who alters denominators (5/6 = 2/3 + 3/3) reveals the reverse add-across — valid sixths must keep the denominator 6. The 2 1/8 task reveals whether the whole and the fraction are seen as one quantity of eighths (17/8) or two disconnected numbers. Watching the moves shows whether the unit is held fixed while the counts are recombined.

pedagogy.summary: At 7-8, children draw picture graphs (one symbol = one unit) and bar graphs (labelled axes, single-unit scale) with up to four categories, and use a bar graph to solve put-together, take-apart and compare problems (CCSS 2.MD.10). This is the translation between organised counts and a scaled visual, and back again to answer questions — crucially, comparison questions ('how many more votes did cats get than dogs?') that require a difference. Teaching should build the graph from the child's own data, insist on equal-width bars rising from a common baseline read against the scale, and connect reading a value to the count it represents.
bestPractices: Build the graph from data the children collected, mapping each unit to one square/symbol so height means count
Insist on the grammar of a bar graph: equal-width bars, common baseline, evenly spaced, axes labelled, single-unit scale
Read values by tracking the bar top across to the scale, and model comparison as the difference between two bars
Pose put-together (combine two categories), take-apart and compare ('how many more') problems on the finished graph
keyRepresentations: Bar graph with single-unit scale on squared paper
Picture graph with one symbol per unit, aligned in rows
Two bars aligned to show the difference for 'how many more'
Frequency table as the source the graph is drawn from
commonMisconceptions: Answers 'how many more' with the taller bar's value instead of the difference between the bars
Reads a bar's value off by one (counts gridlines instead of the value the top reaches, or bars not starting at zero)
Draws bars of unequal width, floating off the baseline, or unevenly spaced, so height no longer means count
Draws picture-graph symbols of different sizes or unaligned, so rows can't be compared by length

learn.summary: For ages 7-8, learners draw picture graphs (one symbol = one unit) and bar graphs (labelled axes, single-unit scale) with up to four categories, then use the finished graph to solve put-together, take-apart and compare ('how many more') problems. The core skill is translating both ways: from organised counts to a scaled visual, and from the visual back to a count that answers a question. Teaching builds the graph from the children's own data, insists on equal-width bars rising from a common baseline read against the scale, and models 'how many more' as the difference (the gap) between two bars rather than the taller bar's value.

activities.title: Build a bar graph from our data on gridded paper
feedback: If a bar doesn't start at zero or floats off the baseline, point out that height can only mean count when every bar starts at the same line; redraw from the baseline.

If a learner reads a value off by one, have them track the bar top straight across to the scale number and check whether they counted gridlines (including the baseline) instead of the value the top reaches.
If bars differ in width, ask what the extra width is supposed to represent; re-establish that only height carries the count, so widths must match.
activities.rationale: Constructing the graph from the learner's own counts, mapping one unit to one square, makes 'height = count' concrete and exposes whether the grammar of a bar graph (equal width, common baseline, labelled single-unit scale) is understood. An optional gridded builder where bars snap to equal width on a baseline can reduce drawing friction, but drawing by hand also surfaces form errors for feedback.
sourceClaims: Pupils draw a picture graph and a bar graph (single-unit scale) for up to four categories and solve put-together, take-apart and compare problems using a bar graph (e.g. 'how many more')

At Level A students represent the distribution of a categorical variable with bar graphs and read them to answer questions about their group; awareness that changing the vertical scale distorts perception begins here
learnerActions: Collect or use a given data set with up to four categories (e.g. favourite pets: cats 9, dogs 6, fish 4, birds 2)
On squared/gridded paper or a gridded canvas, draw one bar per category, shading one square per unit so each bar's height equals its count
Keep every bar the same width, rising from a common baseline (zero line), evenly spaced, and label both axes with a single-unit scale
Read a chosen bar's value back by tracking its top straight across to the scale number, and check it matches the original count
activities.intendedInsight: Height means count: a bar's top read against the scale gives the number of items in that category. This only works if every bar starts from the shared zero baseline. Equal widths keep the bars fair to compare by eye, so that only height carries the count.

activities.title: 'How many more' as the gap between two bars
feedback: If a learner answers 'how many more' with the taller bar's value (e.g. 9), align the two bars and count only the squares the taller one sticks up by; name that gap as 'how many more', then re-ask.
If they ask 'how did you get how many more?', check they computed a difference rather than simply reading a height.
For a put-together question, confirm they read both bar values and added them rather than reading one.
For a take-apart question, confirm they read the known part against the scale and took it away from the given total (e.g. 15 − 9 = 6), then checked the result against the other bar.
activities.rationale: The most common error is reporting the taller bar's value for a difference question. Physically aligning the bars and counting the gap gives a visual meaning to subtraction and distinguishes 'how many more' from a single reading. An optional interaction that glides the two bars together and shades the extra squares makes the difference visible, but the subtraction must still be stated.
sourceClaims: Pupils draw a picture graph and a bar graph (single-unit scale) for up to four categories and solve put-together, take-apart and compare problems using a bar graph (e.g. 'how many more')
learnerActions: On a finished bar graph, pick two categories and state a comparison question, e.g. 'how many more children chose cats than dogs?'
Line the two bars up side by side and count the squares by which the taller bar sticks up above the shorter one
Write the answer as a subtraction, e.g. cats 9 − dogs 6 = 3, and say in words that 3 is 'how many more'

Repeat with a put-together question ('how many chose cats and dogs together?') and a take-apart question ('15 children chose cats or dogs; use the cats bar to find how many of them did NOT choose cats, then check with the dogs bar') to practise combining and separating counts
activities.intendedInsight: A comparison answer is the difference between two bars (the gap at the top), not the height of the taller bar; put-together and take-apart questions use the same read-the-scale skill with addition or subtraction.

activities.title: Picture graph with uniform, aligned symbols
feedback: If symbols vary in size or rows aren't aligned, ask whether a longer-but-fewer row could look bigger; redraw with equal, aligned symbols.
If a learner gives the longer row's total for 'how many more', line the rows up and count only the extra symbols; name that as the difference, then re-ask.
If a learner miscounts, have them count one symbol per unit and check the total against the data table.
activities.rationale: Picture graphs reinforce one-unit-one-mark and make the need for uniformity and alignment felt, paralleling the equal-width requirement for bars. Keeping 'how many more' as the difference generalises that idea from bars to rows across two representations.
sourceClaims: Pupils draw a picture graph and a bar graph (single-unit scale) for up to four categories and solve put-together, take-apart and compare problems using a bar graph (e.g. 'how many more')
learnerActions: Represent the same data as a picture graph, placing exactly one equal-sized symbol per unit in each category's row
Align symbols in rows so the length of a row can be compared at a glance

Read a category's count by counting its symbols, and answer a 'how many more' question by lining up the two rows and counting only the EXTRA symbols in the longer row (the difference, not the longer row's total)
Discuss what goes wrong if symbols are different sizes or not lined up
activities.intendedInsight: Symbols must be uniform and aligned so that a row's length faithfully represents its count; 'how many more' is still the difference between the two counts, read as the extra symbols in the longer row.

activities.title: Check questions: read, compare, and construct
feedback: If the taller-bar answer is chosen, revisit aligning the bars and counting the gap.
If a constructed bar doesn't start at zero, note that a shifted baseline changes the apparent value even when the count is unchanged.
Short-answer or spoken explanation is preferable where possible, since it reveals whether a difference was computed rather than a height read.
activities.rationale: A recognition-only item can check interpretation but does not by itself show independent construction; pairing a comparison item with a construction step exposes whether 'height means count' is truly understood. A wrong answer equal to the taller bar's value targets the specific misconception.
sourceClaims: At Level A students represent the distribution of a categorical variable with bar graphs and read them to answer questions about their group; awareness that changing the vertical scale distorts perception begins here
learnerActions: Answer a 'how many more' multiple-choice or short-answer item where one tempting wrong answer is the taller bar's raw value
Set bar heights (by drawing or dragging a slider) to match given counts, keeping equal width and a zero baseline
Explain in one sentence how you found a difference, so the reasoning (subtraction vs. height) is visible
Answer a scale-awareness prompt: 'if the dogs bar started halfway up, would it still tell us 6? why not?'
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency means reading values against the scale, computing comparisons as differences, and constructing well-formed bars — all three, not just recognising a correct graph.

constraints: Use the child's own collected data where possible so each unit maps to one square/symbol and height visibly means count.
Insist on the grammar of a bar graph: equal-width bars, common baseline (zero), even spacing, labelled axes, single-unit scale.

A static labelled bar graph or tap-to-reveal annotation is a reference/scaffold only: it can name the parts but does not let the learner construct a graph or compute a comparison, so it cannot by itself evidence the construction skill.
A multiple-choice or recognition item can assess interpretation but does not elicit independent construction; include an actual drawing/placing step to assess 'translating'.

A snap-to-equal-width builder lowers drawing friction but can mask form errors; also observe free-hand or manual construction to check the learner can produce equal-width bars from a baseline unaided.
Optional interactions (sliding bars together, shading the difference, dragging bar heights) are illustrative aids, not required mechanisms; the learner must still state the subtraction or count.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source claim string is attributed to a gov.uk (England National Curriculum) URL but labelled as Common Core 2.MD.B.10 aligned with England NC Year 3; this cross-labelling was preserved as-is and not independently re-verified.

The legacy row asserts '3D adds nothing' and that dialogue 'offers nothing to construct'; these were softened — a conversation can support reasoning about a graph, and 3D is simply unnecessary for single-unit flat graphs rather than proven to add nothing. No comparative-efficacy claim is made.

Neither source directly supports the equal-width/common-baseline 'grammar' requirement as such; it is retained from the pedagogy best-practices as a conventional teaching point, not as a source-verified claim.
Worked example cats 9 − dogs 6 = 3 was checked and is correct; fish 4 and birds 2 bars were checked as consistent with the stated data.

probeDeeper: Ask 'how did you get how many MORE?' to check a difference was computed, not a height read
Counterexample tuned to this topic: 'if I drew the dogs bar starting halfway up, would it still tell us 6? why not?' to probe the baseline
Ask 'how many chose cats AND dogs together?' to test put-together reading
Ask 'why must the bars be the same width?' to surface why height alone must carry the count
assess.correctAnswer: Interpreting: reads both bars against the scale and gives the DIFFERENCE (e.g. cats 9 − dogs 6 = 3), explaining the comparison. Translating: draws a fish bar to 4 and a birds bar to 2, equal width, rising from the baseline, correctly against the scale.

errorPatterns.pattern: Answers 'how many more' with the taller bar's value instead of the difference between the two bars
errorPatterns.nextMove: Align the two bars and count the squares the taller one sticks up by; name 'how many more' as that gap, then re-ask
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives the cats value (9) rather than 9 − 6 = 3

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads a bar's value off by one — counts gridlines rather than the value the top reaches, or reads a bar not starting at zero
errorPatterns.nextMove: Track the bar top straight across to the scale number; check bars start at zero — a reading lapse to steady
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child's read value is consistently one out, or they count lines including the baseline

errorPatterns.pattern: Draws bars of unequal width, floating off the baseline, or unevenly spaced, so height no longer represents count
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-establish the grammar: equal-width bars from a common baseline, one square per unit; connect back to one unit = one item
errorPatterns.revealedBy: New bars don't start at the baseline, differ in width, or the picture-graph symbols vary in size

responseLevels.gap: Misreads the scale, gives the taller value for 'how many more', and draws malformed bars
responseLevels.full: Reads bars against the scale, computes 'how many more' as a difference, and constructs equal-width bars from the baseline to the right heights — moving fluently between graph and data
responseLevels.partial: Reads values and draws bars correctly with support, but the comparison is done by value not difference, or bar form needs reminding

assess.diagnosticPrompt: First: here is a bar graph of our class's favourite pets — how many MORE children chose cats than dogs, and how do you know? Then: here is the data for fish (4) and birds (2) — add those two bars to the graph correctly.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with representational fluency reads bar heights against the scale, computes the difference for 'how many more', AND constructs new bars to the right heights with correct form; a child without it reports the taller bar's value, misreads the scale by one, or draws bars off the baseline / unequal width. The construct step exposes whether height-means-count is truly understood.

sources.claim: Pupils draw a picture graph and a bar graph (single-unit scale) for up to four categories and solve put-together, take-apart and compare problems using a bar graph (e.g. 'how many more')
