pedagogy.summary: Substitution is a procedure: replace each letter with its given value — keeping the operations the notation encodes — then evaluate using the correct order of operations. It is best taught by making the hidden multiplication and the protective brackets EXPLICIT: rewrite 3a as 3×a and always drop the substituted value inside brackets, e.g. 3×(5)² or (−2)², so that powers, signs and order of operations are handled correctly. Practise across a deliberate range of values — positive, zero, negative and fractional — because each exposes a different error.
bestPractices: Rewrite implicit operations before substituting: 3a becomes 3×a, a² becomes a×a — this pre-empts concatenation ('34') and the '×2' misreading of squaring.
Always substitute the value inside brackets, especially for negatives: (−2)² not −2², so two negatives making a positive is visible.
Contrast a² and 2a on the same value (a=5 gives 25 vs 10) so the child feels the difference.
Substitute a spread of values including 0 and negatives, and use a function machine or spreadsheet/table to generate many results and reveal patterns.
After substituting, treat the result as an ordinary arithmetic expression and apply order of operations (powers, then ×÷, then +−), boxing each term first.
keyRepresentations: Function machine / 'substitution machine' (value in, result out)
Area square for a² (a by a) contrasted with a bar of length 2a
Bracket-inserting template: 3×(  )² − 2×(  )
Table/spreadsheet of values for one expression
Number line for negative substituted values
commonMisconceptions: Concatenation: substitutes to make digits, e.g. 3a with a=4 read as '34' instead of 3×4=12.
Reads a² as a×2, e.g. a² with a=5 evaluated as 10 rather than 25.
Ignores order of operations after substituting, e.g. 2+3a with a=4 done left-to-right as (2+3)×4=20 instead of 14.
Drops brackets on a negative value, e.g. (−2)² evaluated as −4 instead of 4 (−x² vs (−x)² confusion).
Assumes a=0 makes every term vanish, forgetting constants.

learn.summary: Substitution is a procedure: replace each letter with its given value, keep the operations the notation encodes, then evaluate using the correct order of operations. Make the hidden multiplication and the protective brackets explicit — rewrite 3a as 3×a and place every substituted value inside brackets, e.g. 3×(5)² or (−2)² — so powers, signs and order of operations are handled correctly. Practise across a deliberate spread of values (positive, zero, negative and fractional), and transfer the same discipline to an unfamiliar formula, because each value and each new formula exposes a different error.

activities.title: Rebuild-the-expression substitution with a sliding value
feedback: If a value and coefficient are written side by side as digits (e.g. 3a with a=4 read as '34'), re-establish that 3a means 3×a by expanding 3a as a+a+a for a small value, then rewrite with explicit × signs before substituting.
If a² with a=5 is evaluated as 10, contrast a² and 2a at a=5 (25 vs 10): rewrite a² as a×a explicitly, and compare a 5-by-5 area square with a bar of length 10.
If a negative gives (−2)² = −4 or the bracket is dropped as −2², write (−2)×(−2) in full, link to two negatives making a positive, and contrast −2² with (−2)² side by side.
If operations are taken left-to-right (e.g. 2+3a with a=4 done as (2+3)×4=20 instead of 14), the substitution itself was fine — box each term first, then resolve powers, then ×÷, then +−.
activities.rationale: Substitution is a procedure built by repeated doing with feedback across a range of values; making the implicit multiplication and the protective brackets explicit pre-empts the concatenation, squaring-as-doubling, sign and order-of-operations errors that are documented when pupils interpret and evaluate algebraic notation.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should substitute numerical values into formulae and expressions, including scientific formulae, and use conventional algebraic notation (3y, a² etc.).

Students misread algebraic notation — e.g. treating 3a as concatenation rather than 3×a — and apply operations left-to-right rather than by order of operations when interpreting/evaluating expressions.
Students assume −(x²) is the same as (−x)², e.g. classifying x²+4=0 as true at x=−2 — the documented negative-square/sign error that shows up when substituting negative values.
Reading a² as doubling and letter-as-object interpretations are persistent, documented difficulties among 11–16 year-olds that resurface during substitution.
learnerActions: Take the expression 3a² − 2a and first rewrite the implicit operations explicitly: 3×a×a − 2×a, or 3×(a)² − 2×(a).
Choose a value for a and drop it inside the brackets so the expression becomes 3×( )² − 2×( ), e.g. 3×(5)² − 2×(5).
Evaluate in order: resolve the power first, then the multiplications, then the subtraction. For a=5: 3×25 − 10 = 75 − 10 = 65.
Repeat the same expression for a sequence of values — try a = 3, then a = 0, then a = −2, then a = 1/2 — writing out every step each time.
For each value, note alongside what the two parts (a² and 2a) came to separately, and watch how a² stays non-negative while 2a goes negative as a crosses zero.
activities.intendedInsight: Substitution means replacing the letter with its value while preserving the encoded operations; brackets protect negatives so (−2)² = +4, and a² (=a×a) behaves differently from 2a (=2×a).

activities.title: Contrast a² against 2a on the same value
feedback: If the learner still reads the exponent as a doubling coefficient, return to a×a written in full and the area-square picture before trying another value.
If they claim a² and 2a are always different, prompt them to test a=0 and a=2, where the two happen to coincide, so the generalisation is tested rather than assumed.
activities.rationale: Directly contrasting a² and 2a on shared values targets the persistent 'square as doubling' misinterpretation; an area model makes the a×a meaning concrete.
sourceClaims: Reading a² as doubling and letter-as-object interpretations are persistent, documented difficulties among 11–16 year-olds that resurface during substitution.
learnerActions: Pick a value, e.g. a=5, and evaluate a² and 2a separately: a² = 5×5 = 25, 2a = 2×5 = 10.
Draw a 5-by-5 square for a² next to a bar of length 10 for 2a, and compare their sizes.
Repeat for a=0 (both give 0) and for a=3, recording how the two results diverge.
State in your own words why a² and 2a are generally not the same, and identify when they do coincide.
activities.intendedInsight: a² means a×a, not a×2; the exponent is not a coefficient, so the two expressions generally give very different values (coinciding only at a=0 and a=2).

activities.title: Negative and fractional values that expose the rules
feedback: If (−2)² comes out as −4, rewrite it as (−2)×(−2) and connect to two negatives multiplying to a positive; contrast −2² with (−2)² explicitly.
For −a², if the sign flips between a=3 and a=−3, point out that the square is taken first and is always non-negative, so the leading minus gives −9 in both cases.
If a=0 makes the learner zero out a constant term, point back to the constant and ask what it equals when nothing is multiplied by a.
activities.rationale: Negative, zero and fractional values each trigger a distinct documented error; deliberately sampling them while insisting on brackets and order of operations surfaces and corrects the sign and over-generalisation mistakes.
sourceClaims: Students assume −(x²) is the same as (−x)², e.g. classifying x²+4=0 as true at x=−2 — the documented negative-square/sign error that shows up when substituting negative values.
learnerActions: Evaluate 3a² − 2a at a = −2, substituting inside brackets: 3×(−2)² − 2×(−2) = 3×4 + 4 = 12 + 4 = 16.

Evaluate −a² at a = 3 and at a = −3, substituting inside brackets (−(3)² and −(−3)²), and check that BOTH give −9; then evaluate (−a)² at the same values, (−3)² and (3)², which both give +9 — confirming −a² differs from (−a)².
Evaluate the expression at a = 1/2, keeping the fraction inside the bracket for the square and ordering the operations correctly.
Try a = 0 and check each term explicitly, including any constant, instead of assuming everything vanishes.
Optionally use a number line to place each negative substituted value and keep track of its sign before applying the power.
activities.intendedInsight: Brackets around a substituted value preserve its sign under powers, so (−2)² = 4; −a² and (−a)² are different; and special values like 0 and fractions must still be evaluated term by term with correct order of operations.

activities.title: Check and talk-through across error-triggering values
feedback: Build comparison options from documented errors — e.g. 34 (concatenation), 10 (square read as doubling) — and ask the learner to identify and correct each.
If the correct final value is reached but a step is skipped, ask for the intermediate power and product values to check the reasoning, not just the answer.

If the method breaks down on the unfamiliar formula (e.g. v = u + a×t evaluated left-to-right as (3+2)×4 = 20 instead of 11), re-apply the box-each-term rule — multiplication before addition — to the substituted formula, showing the substitution itself was fine.
activities.rationale: Checking performance across the error-triggering values and extending to an unfamiliar formula confirms fluency and transfer; using documented wrong answers as discussion points turns common errors into teaching moments. A completion/selection check confirms the procedure but, on its own, elicits less independent step-by-step construction than open working, so pair it with talk-through.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should substitute numerical values into formulae and expressions, including scientific formulae, and use conventional algebraic notation (3y, a² etc.).

Students misread algebraic notation — e.g. treating 3a as concatenation rather than 3×a — and apply operations left-to-right rather than by order of operations when interpreting/evaluating expressions.
Reading a² as doubling and letter-as-object interpretations are persistent, documented difficulties among 11–16 year-olds that resurface during substitution.
learnerActions: Given 3a² − 2a, complete the partially-worked line 3×(5)² − 2×(5) = __, showing the power step, the multiplication step and the subtraction step.
For a second expression such as 3a − 1, find its value when a = 4 and explain each step.

Transfer the same procedure to an unfamiliar formula with given values — e.g. find v in v = u + a×t when u = 3, a = 2, t = 4, giving v = 3 + 2×4 = 3 + 8 = 11 — to confirm the discipline carries beyond the practised expression.
Explain why a wrong value such as 34 (for 3a with a=4) or 10 (for a² with a=5) is incorrect, naming the mistake.
When finished, point to the step where the power was worked out and talk through just that step to show the order-of-operations reasoning.
activities.intendedInsight: Evaluating at given values, transferring the method to an unfamiliar formula, and explaining why common wrong answers are wrong consolidates the correct procedure and reveals whether order of operations and notation are genuinely understood.

constraints: Choose an expression that contains BOTH a square and a coefficient, e.g. 3a² − 2a, so the a² vs 2a distinction and the sign rules both come into play.
Always substitute the value inside brackets, especially for negatives — (−2)² not −2² — so the sign is protected.
After substituting, treat the result as an ordinary arithmetic expression and apply order of operations (powers, then ×÷, then +−), boxing each term first.

Deliberately sample positive, zero, negative and fractional values; each exposes a different error, and the negative case is decisive because it requires keeping the bracket AND knowing two negatives multiply to a positive.
Include transfer to at least one unfamiliar formula (the curriculum scope covers scientific formulae) so the procedure is shown to generalise beyond the practised expression.

A completion or selection check (fill-in-the-blank, set-the-value, or pick-the-answer with distractors like 34 and 10) confirms the procedure but does not by itself elicit independent step-by-step construction; pair it with open working and talk-through.
A tap-to-reveal worked example can show one substitution's steps as a scaffold, but the learner still needs to perform the procedure across several values to build fluency.

Live manipulation (sliding a value through positive, zero and negative while the expression auto-rebuilds and brackets snap around the value) is an optional way to make the a² vs 2a difference and the (−2)²=+4 behaviour visible; it is one helpful presentation, not a required mechanism, and the same learning can be reached with written working, a number line for negatives, or a table/spreadsheet of values.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One listed source (Hodgen, Küchemann, Brown & Coe 2009) is marked unverified in the row; treat its 'reading a² as doubling' claim with corresponding caution.

Self-audit of arithmetic: a=5 gives 3×25 − 10 = 65; a=−2 gives 3×4 + 4 = 16; −a² at a=3 and a=−3 both give −9; a²=2a only at a=0 and a=2; transfer example v = u + a×t with u=3,a=2,t=4 gives 3 + 8 = 11. All checked and retained.

The original catalog fit-rankings claiming dialogue 'cannot efficiently' teach the procedure, that a static image 'cannot let the child DO the procedure', and that a third dimension 'adds nothing' were comparative-efficacy assertions, not established evidence; they have been removed or softened to scope-limited statements about affordances.

The gap description (notation misread so no correct value is produced) and the distinction between substitution errors and order-of-operations errors are preserved as feedback branches; an order-of-operations error after substitution does not require reteaching substitution.

Source-claim attachments were tightened: the MAP concatenation/order claim was kept only where the relevant errors are actually addressed; the generic KS3 claim was attached to the core substitution activity and the transfer-to-formula step, not to the a²-vs-2a or the negative/fractional-value activities whose principles it does not directly support.

A transfer step to an unfamiliar formula was added to the check activity to honour the objective's 'including scientific formulae' scope and the assessment's 'full' transfer criterion, which the earlier candidate had dropped; this addition is a proposal, not an empirically validated task.

probeDeeper: Now find it for a = 0 — watch whether they still evaluate each term or assume '0 makes everything 0' and forget the constant behaviour. (counterexample: a special value that tempts over-generalisation)
Change it to −a² and do a = 3 and a = −3 — watch whether BOTH give −9 (correct) or whether the sign flips between them. (counterexample separating −a² from (−a)²)
Give a = 1/2 and watch whether they can substitute a fraction into the square and still order the operations.
After they finish, point to the step where they worked out the power and say 'talk me through just that step' — surfaces their order-of-operations reasoning without having pre-cued it.

errorPatterns.pattern: Concatenation — substitutes to form digits rather than multiply, e.g. treats 3a as '34' when a=4, or writes the coefficient beside the value.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to notation: 3a means 3×a. Re-establish by expanding 3a as a+a+a for a small value, then rewrite the expression with explicit × signs before substituting.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes the coefficient and the substituted value side by side as a multi-digit number instead of multiplying (e.g. 3a² with a=5 becomes 3 then 25 written as '325' or similar).

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads a² as a×2, e.g. a² with a=5 evaluated as 10 rather than 25.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast a² and 2a with a=5 (25 vs 10) using an area square (5 by 5) beside a bar of length 10; rewrite a² as a×a explicitly before substituting.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Computes 5×2=10 (or 3×10) where the square is required; treats the exponent as a coefficient.

errorPatterns.pattern: Ignores order of operations after substituting — works left-to-right, e.g. does the subtraction or the multiplication before the power.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT reteach substitution — the substitution was fine. Reteach order of operations on the resulting numerical expression: box each term first, resolve powers, then ×÷, then ±.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Squares last, or evaluates 2+3a as (2+3)×4; the written steps show operations taken in reading order rather than powers→×÷→+−.

errorPatterns.pattern: Mishandles a negative value — (−2)² evaluated as −4, or the bracket is dropped giving −2² = −4 (−x² vs (−x)² confusion).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist on substituting inside brackets always; write (−2)×(−2) in full and connect to two-negatives-make-a-positive; contrast −2² with (−2)² explicitly.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For a=−2 writes (−2)²=−4, or drops the bracket entirely; the a=−2 answer comes out negative or otherwise wrong while a=5 was right.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot begin, or the substitution is meaningless because notation is misread — concatenates (34 for 3a with a=4) or reads the square as doubling, so no correct value is produced.
responseLevels.full: Substitutes positive AND negative values, handles powers and multi-operation expressions with correct order of operations, protects negatives with brackets so (−2)²=4, and transfers the same discipline to an unfamiliar formula.
responseLevels.partial: Substitutes correctly for a positive whole number with straightforward operations (gets the a=5 case right), but breaks down on the a=−2 case, on the power, or on order of operations — handles the routine value but not the ones that expose a rule.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Hand the child this card and say 'work these out, thinking aloud, and show every step': Find the value of 3a² − 2a when a = 5, and then when a = −2. Say NOTHING about method — watch the order they compute, how they handle the square, and how they deal with the negative.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Because the teacher WATCHES rather than asks, each error surfaces as a different visible line of working: a child who concatenates writes 35 for 3a²; one who reads the square as ×2 writes 3×10; one who ignores order of operations squares last or subtracts first; one who mishandles the negative writes (−2)²=−4 or drops the bracket. The a=−2 case is decisive — it cannot be got right by a child who does not both keep the bracket and know two negatives multiply to a positive.

pedagogy.summary: This is the procedural fluency of moving both ways between decimal notation and tenths/hundredths fractions: read 0.62 as 62/100, write 3/10 as 0.3, read 0.07 as 7/100, and locate them on a number line. It rests on the place-value meaning that the first place after the point is tenths and the second is hundredths, so the number of decimal places is governed by the denominator (10 → one place, 100 → two places) and a placeholder zero is required when the numerator has fewer digits than the denominator has zeros (7/100 = 0.07). The skill is assessed by WATCHING the child convert both directions, especially on the placeholder cases that a digit-copying rule gets wrong.
bestPractices: Practise BOTH directions from the start (decimal→fraction and fraction→decimal) using a place-value chart so the child reads the denominator off the final place.
Foreground the placeholder: pair 3/10 = 0.3 with 7/100 = 0.07 and 3/100 = 0.03 so the child learns that hundredths always occupy two places and a zero holds an empty tenths place.
Link every conversion to a picture — a hundredths grid and a number-line location — so the symbolic answer is checked against a quantity, catching reversals like 0.62 → 6/2.
Use ragged and single-digit-numerator cases deliberately (0.4, 0.07, 9/100) because these are where the placeholder rule bites and hollow digit-copying fails.
Have the child read the decimal aloud in place-value language ('sixty-two hundredths') before writing the fraction, so the denominator is heard.
keyRepresentations: Place-value chart (tenths | hundredths) beside the fraction
10×10 hundredths grid shaded to match the decimal and the fraction
Number line for locating 0.3, 0.4, 0.62
Contrasting sets {3/10, 3/100} and {0.7, 0.07} to drill the placeholder
Bidirectional conversion cards (decimal on one side, fraction on the other)
commonMisconceptions: Dropping the placeholder zero: writing 9/100 as 0.9, or reading 0.07 as 7/10.
Adding an unneeded zero: writing 3/10 as 0.03 by over-applying 'hundredths = two places'.
Using one denominator for every decimal: writing 0.4 as 4/100 regardless of the number of places.
Reversing digits or reading position wrong: 0.62 → 6/2 or 26/100.
Placing decimals on the number line by whole-number reasoning rather than by tenths/hundredths.

learn.summary: Learners move fluently in BOTH directions between decimal notation and tenths/hundredths fractions: read 0.62 as 62/100, write 3/10 as 0.3, read 0.07 as 7/100, and locate these on a 0–1 number line. The skill rests on place-value meaning — the first place after the point is tenths, the second is hundredths — so the denominator is read from the final place (10 → one place, 100 → two places), and a placeholder zero is needed when the numerator has fewer digits than the denominator has zeros (7/100 = 0.07). Learning and checking should deliberately use placeholder and single-digit-numerator cases, because a digit-copying rule produces correct answers on easy items but fails exactly there.

activities.title: Two-way converter checked against a grid and a number line
feedback: If a learner writes 0.9 for 9/100, point to the grid: ninety squares versus nine. The nine belongs in the hundredths (second) place, so a zero holds the empty tenths place — contrast 9/10 = 0.9 with 9/100 = 0.09.
If a learner writes 0.4 as 4/100, read the final place aloud: 0.4 ends in the tenths place, so it is 4/10 (or equivalently 40/100). Shade 4 columns versus 4 single squares to contrast.

If a learner over-applies 'hundredths means two places' and writes 3/10 as 0.03, contrast 3/10 = 0.3 (one place) with 3/100 = 0.03 (two places): a placeholder is needed only when the denominator has more zeros than the numerator has digits.
If a learner reverses digits (0.62 → 26/100) or loses the place value (0.62 → 6/2), use the place-value chart to name each digit's place before writing the fraction.
activities.rationale: Bidirectional conversion is a doing-skill, so the learner should produce many items with immediate quantity-based feedback rather than only reading a worked rule. Linking symbol, grid and number line lets placeholder errors show as mismatched pictures, turning a rote rule into a self-correcting action. Deliberately including placeholder and ragged cases targets exactly where digit-copying fails. Live grid shading and the number-line marker are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete; a paper hundredths grid and a drawn number line serve the same purpose.
sourceClaims: Errors in decimal notation stem largely from false analogies with whole numbers and incomplete place-value understanding; because faulty digit-based rules can produce correct answers on easy items, instruction and assessment must use cases (single-digit numerators, ragged decimals) that expose the placeholder and place-value meaning.
learnerActions: Enter a decimal (e.g. 0.62) and write the matching fraction; confirm against a 10×10 hundredths grid that shades 62 squares and a number-line marker that lands just past halfway.
Enter a fraction (e.g. 3/10) and write the matching decimal (0.3); confirm by shading 3 of the ten columns and placing the point on the line.
Do the hard placeholder case: for 9/100, if you write 0.9 the grid floods with ninety squares — far more than nine — so the mismatch is obvious; correct it to 0.09 so exactly nine squares glow.
Run rapid two-way rounds (decimal→fraction and fraction→decimal) across a deliberate set of placeholder and ragged cases: 0.07, 9/100, 0.4, 3/100.
Read each decimal aloud in place-value language ('sixty-two hundredths', 'seven hundredths') before writing the fraction, so the denominator is heard.
activities.intendedInsight: The placeholder zero is not a rule to memorise but something you can see: for 9/100 the zero keeps the nine out of the tenths place. The denominator is determined by the final decimal place, and every symbolic answer can be checked against a shaded quantity and a position on the line.

activities.title: Contrast sets that drill the placeholder
feedback: If a learner treats 3/10 and 3/100 as the same, compare the two shaded grids directly — the quantities are visibly different.
If a learner uses one denominator for every decimal, have them name the final place of each decimal aloud before choosing the denominator.
activities.rationale: Deliberately pairing ragged and single-digit-numerator cases targets exactly where digit-copying fails, as the decimal-research-based source recommends. Contrasting cards (decimal one side, fraction the other) support self-checking without requiring any particular device.
sourceClaims: Errors in decimal notation stem largely from false analogies with whole numbers and incomplete place-value understanding; because faulty digit-based rules can produce correct answers on easy items, instruction and assessment must use cases (single-digit numerators, ragged decimals) that expose the placeholder and place-value meaning.
learnerActions: Work matched pairs side by side: {3/10, 3/100} and {0.7, 0.07}, writing each as both a fraction and a decimal.
For each pair, shade a hundredths grid for both members so the size difference is visible (3 columns vs 3 squares; 70 squares vs 7 squares).
State in words why one needs a placeholder zero and the other does not.
Sort a mixed set of cards (decimal on one side, fraction on the other) and self-check by flipping, giving special attention to 0.4, 0.07 and 9/100.
activities.intendedInsight: Tenths and hundredths of the same digit look similar in writing but differ ten-fold in size; the number of decimal places and the presence of a placeholder zero both follow from which place the final digit occupies.

activities.title: Annotated place-value chart as a reference (scaffold)
feedback: After reading, ask the learner to convert a fresh placeholder case unaided (e.g. 0.07 → 7/100) and explain each step in place-value terms.
activities.rationale: A static annotated chart can present the rule and worked examples as a reference, which supports learners who need the method spelled out. It is a scaffold: on its own it does not provide the repeated production-with-feedback that builds conversion fluency, so it should lead back into active conversion.
learnerActions: Study a place-value chart (tenths | hundredths) beside a couple of worked conversions, e.g. 0.62 = 62/100 and 9/100 = 0.09.
Read a short explanation of why the placeholder zero appears in 0.09 but not in 0.3.
Return to the converter or contrast-set tasks and reproduce the method on new values without looking.
activities.intendedInsight: A worked reference makes the place–denominator link and the placeholder rule explicit, but fluency comes from doing many items, not from reading examples.

constraints: Practise both directions (decimal→fraction and fraction→decimal) from the start; a learner may be fluent one way but not the other.
Deliberately include placeholder and single-digit-numerator cases (0.07, 9/100, 0.4, 3/100): easy items can be answered correctly by digit-copying and so do not reveal understanding.
Correct answers: 0.62 = 62/100; 0.07 = 7/100; 0.4 = 4/10 (equivalently 40/100); 3/10 = 0.3; 9/100 = 0.09; 0.03 = 3/100; 0.4 sits at four tenths, just below halfway on a 0–1 line.
Check every conversion against a quantity (shaded grid) and a position (number line) to catch place-value errors such as 0.62 → 6/2 (dropping the place value) or 0.62 → 26/100 (reversing digits).
The annotated chart is a reference scaffold, not a substitute for repeated production with feedback.
Fixed worked examples can still teach the method; they simply cannot be manipulated, so pair them with learner-generated items.

A scored check can be used during teaching to surface errors, but on its own it measures the skill more than it builds it; use its placeholder distractors (e.g. 0.9 for 9/100, 7/10 for 0.07) diagnostically.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source national-curriculum claim is marked verified:false in the original row and supports the topic/statutory requirement rather than any activity's teaching principle; it was therefore not retained as an activity sourceClaim. It remains relevant as age-appropriate curriculum context (Year 4, ages 9–10): pupils should recognise and write decimal notation for fractions with denominators 10 or 100.

The original artefact ratings asserted that 3D 'adds no conceptual value', that a character/dialogue format 'adds nothing', and that assessment-format steps 'do not build' the skill. These are catalog-preference judgements, not established pedagogical laws; they have been softened to scoped statements about affordances or omitted as universal claims.
No arithmetic or place-value error was found in the source conversions; all stated conversions (0.62=62/100, 0.07=7/100, 0.4=4/10, 3/10=0.3, 9/100=0.09, 3/100=0.03) are correct and retained.

probeDeeper: You wrote 0.07 = 7/100. What would 0.7 be instead — and how do the two differ in size?
How did you decide 0.4 is 4/10 and not 4/100? What tells you the denominator?
Where does 0.4 sit relative to a half on this line — and how do you know without measuring?
A friend writes 3/10 as 0.03. Is that right? If not, what is 0.03 as a fraction?

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops the placeholder zero — reads 0.07 as 7/10, or writes 9/100 as 0.9 — mapping the digit straight after the point.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the place-value chart / grid: the 9 belongs in the hundredths (second) place, so a zero holds the tenths place; contrast 9/10 = 0.9 with 9/100 = 0.09. Reteach that place fixes the denominator.

errorPatterns.pattern: Forces one denominator on every decimal — writes 0.4 as 4/100 (or 40/1000), ignoring the number of places.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Read the final place aloud: 0.4 ends in the tenths place, so 4/10; shade 4 columns vs 4 squares to contrast. Reteach reading the denominator from the last place.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 0.4 → 4/100; treats every decimal as hundredths regardless of length.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds an unneeded zero — over-applies 'hundredths means two places' and writes 3/10 as 0.03.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast 3/10 = 0.3 (one place) with 3/100 = 0.03 (two places) on the chart; the placeholder is needed only when the denominator has more zeros than the numerator has digits. Reteach the place–denominator link.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 3/10 → 0.03; inserts a placeholder where none is needed.

responseLevels.gap: Converts by copying digits regardless of place (0.07 → 7/10, 0.4 → 4/100), reverses digits, or places 0.4 by whole-number reasoning. No reliable link to place value.
responseLevels.full: Converts both directions accurately including placeholder cases (0.07 = 7/100, 9/100 = 0.09), chooses the denominator from the final place (0.4 = 4/10), locates 0.4 correctly on the line, and explains each step in place-value terms; transfers to new values.
responseLevels.partial: Converts tenths and most hundredths correctly but slips on placeholder cases (0.07, 9/100) or on choosing the denominator (0.4), or converts fluently one way but not the other; can execute without explaining the place–denominator link.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Write these decimals as fractions: 0.62, 0.07, 0.4. Now write these as decimals: 3/10, 9/100. Last, mark 0.4 on this number line from 0 to 1. Show me how you work each one out.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the work separates place-value understanding from digit-copying. The 0.07 and 9/100 items are placeholder discriminators — a hollow rule yields 7/10 and 0.9. The 0.4 item checks whether the child forces every decimal to hundredths (4/100) or reads the place. Doing both directions and locating on the line exposes reversals and whole-number placement that a one-way written check would miss.

pedagogy.summary: Children learn to draw 2-D shapes accurately, to make 3-D shapes from modelling materials (e.g. straws for edges and connectors for vertices), and to recognise a 3-D shape when it is rotated or seen from a different angle. Two procedural strands matter: constructing a solid correctly requires coordinating its edge/vertex/face structure (a cube needs 12 equal edges, 8 vertices, 6 square faces), and orientation recognition requires naming a shape by properties that stay the same under rotation. The central obstacle is orientation dependence — children anchored to a canonical view judge a rotated or point-down solid to be 'a different shape'. Best taught by handling and rotating real solids, and by building frames while counting edges and vertices.
bestPractices: Build 3-D frames from straws (edges) and connectors (vertices), counting how many of each are needed first (a cube: 12 edges, 8 vertices) and checking equal straw lengths so faces are square.
Let children physically rotate a solid — point-up, on its side, point-down, viewed from above — and re-name it each time, so the name is seen to be invariant to orientation.
Name solids by their properties (a pyramid has triangular faces meeting at an apex) rather than by a single remembered picture, so rotation doesn't change the name.
Draw 2-D shapes on dotted paper/geoboards, marking each side as it is drawn to keep the count and closure accurate.
Connect nets and faces to the built solid, so each face is seen as a 2-D shape within the 3-D model.
keyRepresentations: Straws-and-connectors (or clay balls and sticks) for building edge/vertex frames
A real solid to grab and rotate through many orientations
Dotted paper / geoboard for accurate 2-D drawing
Nets that fold into the solid, linking 2-D faces to the 3-D shape
commonMisconceptions: Does not recognise a solid (or 2-D shape) in an unfamiliar orientation — calls a rotated or point-down pyramid 'a different shape' or 'not a pyramid'.
Builds the wrong frame — incorrect number of edges/vertices, or unequal edges so the faces are not square (a wonky frame or a cuboid when a cube was asked for).
Draws 2-D shapes inaccurately — non-closed, curved-sided, or with the wrong number of sides.
Treats a shape's name as tied to its usual position, so turning it seems to change what it is.

learn.summary: Children (age 7-8) learn to draw 2-D shapes accurately, build 3-D solids from modelling materials, and recognise a 3-D shape as the same shape when it is rotated or seen from a new angle. Two procedural strands matter: constructing a solid correctly requires coordinating its edge/vertex/face structure (a cube has 12 equal edges, 8 vertices, 6 square faces), and orientation recognition requires naming a shape by properties that stay the same under rotation. The central obstacle is orientation dependence: a child anchored to a canonical view judges a rotated or point-down solid to be 'a different shape'. The curriculum calls for making 3-D shapes from modelling materials, so hands-on building, rotating real solids, and careful drawing on dotted paper/geoboards are the core activities; on-screen builders and spinners are useful complements, and recognition tasks can check outcomes but do not by themselves elicit construction.

activities.title: Build a cube frame from straws and connectors
feedback: If the frame has the wrong number of straws or connectors, re-establish the target first (12 edges, 8 vertices) and rebuild, counting each piece as it is added.

If the faces are not square, check that all straws are equal length and that the corners are right angles; unequal straws give a cuboid or an irregular frame rather than a cube, and even equal straws can lean into diamond-shaped faces unless the frame is squared up.
Compare the built frame side by side with a real cube-shaped solid to spot missing or extra edges.
activities.rationale: Properties of 3-D shapes are faces (flat 2-D surfaces), edges (straight lines where two faces meet) and vertices (corners where edges meet); handling real solids and marking each feature supports accurate counting and grounds the structure a child must coordinate when building a cube.
sourceClaims: Properties of 3-D shapes are the faces (flat 2-D surfaces), edges (straight lines where two faces meet) and vertices (corners where two or more edges meet); handling real solids and marking each feature supports accurate counting — grounds the edge/vertex/face structure a child must coordinate when building a cube.
learnerActions: Before building, predict and count how many edges (straws) and vertices (connectors) a cube needs, and state the target: 12 edges, 8 vertices, 6 square faces.
Build the cube frame, snapping straws (edges) onto connectors (balls of clay or plastic joints for vertices).

Check that every straw is the same length and that the corners are square (right angles, not leaning), because equal straws alone can still give a squashed frame with diamond-shaped faces; then compare the finished frame against a real cube-shaped solid.
Point to and count the edges, vertices and faces on the completed frame to confirm the structure.
Try building a cuboid with edges of different lengths as a contrast and describe how it differs from the cube (not all edges equal, so some faces are rectangles that are not squares).
activities.intendedInsight: A cube is defined by its structure — 12 equal edges, 8 vertices and 6 square faces — and building it requires coordinating that structure rather than approximating a box shape.

activities.title: Rotate a solid and keep naming it
feedback: If the child renames a point-down or sideways shape, hand them the same object and let them rotate it continuously so they see it never changed into something else.
Redirect naming to invariant properties (triangular faces meeting at an apex) rather than to a remembered picture of its usual position.
The point-down pyramid is often a hard case — linger there and ask the child to name the faces they can see and feel.
activities.rationale: Young children often treat orientation as a defining feature and may reject a rotated shape as not matching their prototype; rotated or non-standard triangles are commonly among the harder 2-D cases, and similar orientation dependence can affect 3-D solids such as a point-down pyramid. The suggested remedy is to present and handle shapes in varied orientations and to name by properties.
sourceClaims: A common misconception is that children may not recognise a 2-D shape when it is presented in a different orientation; the remedy is to let children handle and rotate cut-outs to explore how a shape looks in different orientations, and to touch the sides and vertices as they count.

Young children treat orientation as a defining feature (e.g. rejecting a rotated shape), an 'imposed attribute' matching the prototype; a rotated isosceles triangle is the hardest case, with even a prototypical triangle missed by ~15% once rotated. Remedy: present shapes in varied orientations.
learnerActions: Hold a real pyramid (or cube) and physically turn it: point-up, on its side, point-down, and viewed from directly above.
At each orientation, say what the shape is and how you know, naming it by its properties (e.g. 'a pyramid has triangular faces meeting at an apex').
State explicitly whether the name changed when the shape turned, and explain why it should not.
Repeat with a cuboid laid on different faces, confirming it is the same solid each time.
activities.intendedInsight: A shape's name comes from properties that do not change when it is rotated or viewed from a new angle; turning a solid does not make it a different shape.

activities.title: Draw 2-D shapes accurately on dotted paper or a geoboard
feedback: If the figure is not closed, return to the starting dot and count sides until the path closes.
If a side is curved, redraw it as a straight segment between two dots.
If there are too few or too many sides, re-count aloud while re-drawing, marking each side as it is placed.
activities.rationale: Marking each side as it is drawn and using dotted paper/geoboards supports accurate counting and closure; varying size while keeping the name reinforces that the name derives from invariant properties, not appearance. This strand follows the pedagogy's stated best practice; no cited source directly establishes its efficacy.
learnerActions: Draw named 2-D shapes (triangle, rectangle, pentagon, hexagon) on dotted paper or a geoboard.
Count and mark each side as it is drawn, keeping track so the figure closes with the right number of straight sides.
After drawing, re-count the sides and check the shape is closed and has straight (not curved) edges.
Draw the same shape again at a different size and confirm it keeps its name (a bigger hexagon is still a hexagon).
activities.intendedInsight: An accurate 2-D shape is a closed figure with the correct number of straight sides; its name depends on properties such as closure, side count and, for shapes like rectangles, right angles, not on size.

activities.title: Link nets and faces to the built solid
feedback: If the child cannot see a face as a 2-D shape, lay the net flat and trace one face, then fold it back into place on the solid.
Count the faces on both net and solid to confirm they match.
Note that a folded card net is a thin physical approximation of the ideal solid, which has zero-thickness faces — it stands in for the mathematical shape it represents.
activities.rationale: Connecting nets and faces to the built solid lets each face be seen as a 2-D shape within the 3-D model, reinforcing the face/edge/vertex structure. This activity extends the pedagogy's stated best practice; no source directly establishes its efficacy.
learnerActions: Fold a net into a solid, then identify each face as a 2-D shape within the 3-D model.
For a built cube frame, point out where each square face sits between four edges.
Match the faces on the net to the faces on the solid, naming the 2-D shape of each (square, triangle).
activities.intendedInsight: Each face of a solid is a 2-D shape, so 2-D and 3-D shape knowledge connect: a cube's faces are squares, a pyramid's faces include triangles.

activities.title: On-screen builder and spinner (complementary digital practice)
feedback: If the digital frame will not close, use the tally to find which count is short and add or correct that feature.
After watching the point-down pyramid keep its name on screen, re-do the same rotation with a real wooden pyramid to confirm it feels the same.

A recognition choice (e.g. 'which picture is the same pyramid rotated?') can check whether orientation is understood, but follow it with an actual build or rotation task, since choosing does not show the child can construct or turn a solid themselves.
activities.rationale: Both hard parts are spatial — coordinating edge/vertex/face structure while building and seeing a shape as the same under rotation — and interactive builders with a live tally plus a grab-and-spin solid can make these visible. A flat projection only approximates free 3-D construction and rotation, so physical materials remain central; comparative efficacy is not established by the sources.
learnerActions: Using a construction tool, snap virtual edges onto vertices to build a cube; watch a live tally of edges, vertices and faces update as you work.
Notice that a lopsided attempt with unequal edges does not resolve into a correct cube until the structure matches 12 edges, 8 vertices and six square faces.
Grab and spin an on-screen pyramid through point-up, on-its-side, point-down and top-down views, reading a label that continues to name it 'a pyramid' in every orientation.
Where possible, pair each on-screen task with the matching physical build or real solid so the hands confirm the screen.
activities.intendedInsight: A live edge/vertex/face tally and free rotation make the structure and its invariance under rotation visible; the digital model complements, and does not replace, handling real solids.

constraints: The curriculum requires making 3-D shapes from modelling materials, so children should build frames and turn real solids, not only watch or tap.

Recognition tasks (multiple-choice 'which is the same shape rotated?', or picking a drawn path) can check outcomes but do not let a child build a frame or freely rotate a solid, so they must not replace construction and manipulation.

On-screen builders and spinners are useful complements but approximate true 3-D construction and free rotation in a flat projection; pair them with real straws, clay/connectors and a wooden solid where possible.

Paper and card cut-outs and straw frames have real thickness; treat them as physical approximations of the ideal mathematical solid (whose faces have zero thickness), and treat any zero-thickness screen model as a model of the solid it represents.

Name shapes by invariant properties (for 2-D: closure, number of straight sides and, where relevant, angles such as a rectangle's right angles; for 3-D: faces/edges/vertices and how they meet), not by a single remembered picture or usual position.
The point-down pyramid is often a particularly demanding orientation case for recognition and deserves extra attention.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The dotted-paper/geoboard drawing activity and the nets activity derive from the pedagogy's stated best practices; no cited source directly establishes their efficacy, so both carry sourceClaims [].

In 'Rotate a solid and keep naming it', the Oak claim cited is about 2-D shapes in different orientations; it is applied here to 3-D solids by analogy. The orientation-invariance principle transfers and is independently supported by the EJMSTE finding, but no cited source tests this specifically for 3-D solids at this age.

The cited ~15% miss rate for a rotated prototypical triangle and the 'rotated isosceles triangle is hardest' finding come from a single study (Yeşil Dağlı & Halat, 2016) and are reported as claimed, not independently re-verified here.

The original recommendation leaned heavily on a specific 3D interactive and asserted a flat medium 'cannot' teach these spatial skills; that comparative/necessity claim is not established by the sources and has been softened to a complement with stated affordances and limits.

The original marked a static tap-to-reveal image and an in-role conversation as poor fits because they do not support active production; this is retained as the narrow observable point that recognition-only or role-play formats do not themselves elicit independent construction, without claiming they teach nothing.

The source claim about faces as 'flat 2-D surfaces' is strictly true for polyhedra like cubes and pyramids but not for curved solids; the activities here concern polyhedra, so the claim is applied appropriately.

probeDeeper: Turn the pyramid so it points downwards. Is it still a pyramid? How do you know?
Your cube frame — how many straws (edges) did you use? How many corners? Should a cube have that many?
Draw the same shape again but a different size. Is it still a hexagon?
I'll lay the cuboid down on a different face — is it a different shape now?
assess.correctAnswer: (1) A closed, six-sided, straight-edged figure. (2) A cube built from 12 equal straws (edges) and 8 connectors (vertices), giving 6 square faces. (3) Identifies it as the same pyramid in every orientation — a shape's name does not change when it is rotated or viewed from a different angle.

errorPatterns.pattern: Fails to recognise a solid (or 2-D shape) in an unfamiliar orientation — says a rotated or point-down pyramid is 'a different shape' or 'not a pyramid'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Let them handle and physically rotate the solid so they see it is the same object throughout; name it by properties (triangular faces meeting at an apex) that do not change with orientation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When the pyramid is turned point-down or laid on its side, the child renames it or says it is no longer a pyramid.

errorPatterns.pattern: Builds the wrong frame — incorrect number of edges/vertices, or unequal edges so the faces are not square (a wonky frame or a cuboid when a cube was asked for).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish the target structure first — a cube needs 12 edges and 8 vertices — and check equal straw lengths for square faces, comparing the frame against a real cube.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The built frame has the wrong number of straws/connectors, or unequal straws so the faces are not square.

errorPatterns.pattern: Draws 2-D shapes inaccurately — non-closed, curved-sided, or the wrong number of sides.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold: draw on dotted paper/a geoboard, counting and marking each side as it is drawn so the figure closes with the right number of straight sides.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The drawn hexagon is not closed, has a curved side, or has the wrong number of sides.

responseLevels.gap: Renames a shape when it is rotated or reoriented, builds a frame with the wrong edge/vertex structure, or draws non-closed/inaccurate figures.
responseLevels.full: Draws 2-D shapes accurately, constructs a cube/cuboid with the correct edges, vertices and faces, and recognises a solid as the same shape in ANY orientation — naming it by properties invariant to rotation and size (SOLO relational, with transfer).
responseLevels.partial: Draws and builds correctly for familiar, canonical presentations and names a shape in its usual orientation, but falters when a solid is rotated to an unfamiliar view or when asked to reproduce an irregular/different-size version (SOLO multistructural).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set three tasks and watch: (1) 'Draw a hexagon as accurately as you can.' (2) 'Build a cube using these straws and connectors.' (3) Show a pyramid, then rotate it — lay it on its side, stand it point-down, show it from directly above — asking each time: 'Is this still the same shape? What is it?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The construction is a direct performance of edge/vertex/face structure: a child who holds the properties builds 12 edges and 8 vertices, while one who does not makes the wrong frame. The rotation task is the classic orientation probe — a child who names by properties keeps the name under rotation, while one anchored to a canonical view says the shape 'became different' when point-down. Watching the building and turning (not asking about them) shows which.

Remedy: present shapes in varied orientations.

pedagogy.summary: Fraction notation (a/b) is a compact language: the denominator names how many equal parts one whole is split into, the numerator counts how many of those parts we have — and the two together name a SINGLE number, not two separate whole numbers. Teach the vocabulary in use, always anchored to a model (bar/circle/number line), and stretch the language to name unit (1/b), proper (a<b), improper (a≥b) and mixed numbers so children meet the full grammar early rather than believing 'you can't have 5/4'.
bestPractices: Introduce numerator/denominator as JOBS ('how many equal parts in the whole' vs 'how many we took') tied to a shaded model, not as memorised top/bottom labels
Say the fraction as a quantity ('three-quarters') and read the symbol together, so 3/4 is heard as one number, never 'three, four'
Deliberately include improper and mixed forms (5/4, 1 1/4) so children learn the notation can name amounts greater than one
Contrast unit and non-unit fractions (1/4 vs 3/4) and classify examples so the words attach to structure
Link symbol, spoken words and diagram three ways (write it, say it, shade it) and back again
keyRepresentations: Bar/area model with the symbol written alongside and each number labelled to its job
Number line locating the fraction as a single point (a fraction is a number)
Fraction wall showing unit vs non-unit and proper vs improper
Word-symbol-picture triple card (three-quarters / 3/4 / shaded bar)
commonMisconceptions: Reads 3/4 as two separate whole numbers ('three, four') rather than one quantity
Writes the fraction upside down — swaps numerator and denominator
Believes an improper fraction like 5/4 or 4/3 'isn't a real number / can't exist'
Mixes the vocabulary — calls the bottom number the numerator
Thinks 2/4 and 1/2 must be different amounts because the numbers differ

learn.summary: Fraction notation a/b is a compact language naming a SINGLE number: the denominator says how many equal parts one whole is split into, and the numerator counts how many of those parts we have. Teach the vocabulary in use, always anchored to a model (bar, circle, number line), and deliberately stretch the language to name unit (1/b), proper (a<b), improper (a>=b) and mixed numbers so children meet the full grammar early rather than believing 'you can't have 5/4'. A proposed emphasis is on GENERATING notation (shade N of M equal parts and watch the symbol form) so the symbol is tied to an amount, rather than only memorising top/bottom labels.

activities.title: Build the fraction, build the name
feedback: If a learner reads 5/4 as impossible, have them collect five quarter-pieces one at a time and watch the pile pass one whole and land at 1 1/4; then place that point on a number line beyond 1 so it is visibly one number.

If a learner writes the symbol upside down (for example 8/3 for 'three of eight slices'), have them re-shade and write bottom-first: 'How many equal parts in the whole? That is the bottom. How many did we take? That is the top.'
If a learner says 2/4 and 1/2 must differ because the numbers differ, return to the overlay: same shaded length, two names.
If a learner is unsure whether a unit fraction like 1/4 is unit or proper, confirm it is both a proper fraction and specifically a unit fraction, so it goes in the unit tray.
Optional: let the symbol N/M write itself above the bar as the dial and shade controls change, and let a voice name each number to its job, so the link between action and symbol is immediate.
activities.rationale: Writing, saying and shading the notation together, and seeing the symbol respond to the amount, may consolidate the vocabulary and the parts-of-one-whole meaning. Deliberately including improper and mixed forms targets the documented belief that an improper fraction is not a number, and the overlay targets treating numerator and denominator as separate numbers.
sourceClaims: A facet of poor fraction understanding is focusing on numerators and denominators as separate numbers rather than a single number; and many students believe an improper fraction such as four-thirds is not a number.
Year 2/3 pupils name and write fractions, recognise unit and non-unit fractions and fractions greater than one; fraction vocabulary is a national-curriculum expectation.
learnerActions: Cut a bar into M equal parts (for example set it to 4) and shade N of them (for example 3), then write the symbol that matches: the parts taken on top, the equal parts in one whole on the bottom.
As you shade, say the fraction as one spoken quantity ('three-quarters'), not 'three, four'.
Label each number to its job: the numerator is 'the 3 parts we took' and the denominator is 'the 4 equal parts in one whole'.

Now push the numerator past the denominator (shade 5 parts when the whole holds 4): the shading overflows into a second whole. Record that this is called an improper fraction (5/4) and write its mixed twin beside it (1 1/4).

Sort every fraction you build into four trays: unit (numerator 1 and denominator more than 1, like 1/4), proper-but-not-unit (numerator more than 1 but less than the denominator, like 3/4), improper (numerator as big as or bigger than the denominator, like 5/4 or 4/4; 1/1 also goes here because it equals one whole), and mixed (like 1 1/4). A unit fraction like 1/4 is a special kind of proper fraction, so sort each card into its most specific tray.

Shade 2/4 of a bar, then slide that shaded length to overlay 1/2 of a bar of the same length (the same whole): notice the symbols differ but the shaded length is identical, so they name the same amount.
activities.intendedInsight: Fraction notation names one number. The bottom number tells how many equal parts one whole is cut into; the top counts how many we have. Pushing the numerator past the denominator shows 5/4 is a real number greater than one (equal to 1 1/4), and overlaying 2/4 on 1/2 shows different symbols can name the same quantity.

activities.title: Label the fraction's jobs
feedback: If a learner mixes the vocabulary (calls the bottom number the numerator), reconnect each number to its job on the shaded model before naming it.
If a learner reads the symbol as two separate numbers, read symbol to word to shaded amount as one quantity several times ('three-quarters').
activities.rationale: A clear labelled reference reinforces naming and the parts-of-one-whole meaning. This is a naming and reading scaffold; on its own it does not let a child build improper or mixed forms or manipulate equivalence, so pair it with the builder.
sourceClaims: Year 2/3 pupils name and write fractions, recognise unit and non-unit fractions and fractions greater than one; fraction vocabulary is a national-curriculum expectation.
learnerActions: Look at 3/4 beside its shaded bar. Point to the numerator and say what it does ('the parts we took'); point to the denominator and say what it does ('the equal parts in one whole').
Point to the whole bar and explain it is the one whole that was cut up.
Answer the prompt 'What if the top number were bigger than the bottom?' and predict what the picture and the name would become.
Link the three forms both directions: write the symbol, say the words, shade the picture, and go back again.
activities.intendedInsight: Each part of the written symbol has a fixed job tied to the model, and the symbol, spoken words and diagram are three views of the same single quantity.

activities.title: Classify and match for fluency
feedback: Correct classification requires a reason: ask 'How do you know this is improper?' and expect 'the top is as big as or bigger than the bottom, so it is one whole or more.'

If matching or filling in is correct but the learner still cannot read 5/4 as one quantity greater than one, return to the builder and number line, because recognition and fluency practice alone does not by itself elicit construction of the single-number idea.
activities.rationale: Classification and matching assess fluency with the four fraction types and the vocabulary. They check recall and recognition; a sort or match can check that the vocabulary attaches to structure but does not by itself elicit the building and explaining that construct the single-number understanding, so use them after the building work.
sourceClaims: Year 2/3 pupils name and write fractions, recognise unit and non-unit fractions and fractions greater than one; fraction vocabulary is a national-curriculum expectation.
learnerActions: Sort a set of fraction cards into unit, proper, improper and mixed, giving one example of each; remember a unit fraction (numerator 1, denominator more than 1, like 1/4) is a special kind of proper fraction, so place it in the unit tray and keep the proper tray for proper fractions whose numerator is greater than 1 (a card such as 1/1 equals one whole and goes in the improper tray).
Match spoken words to written symbols (for example 'three-quarters' to 3/4).
Fill in the missing number: a shaded picture shows ?/? parts; write both the numerator and the denominator.
Explain in your own words why 2/4 and 1/2 are equivalent.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure classification and word-symbol matching show the vocabulary has attached to structure, not just to top/bottom positions.

constraints: Always anchor the vocabulary to a model (bar, circle or number line); do not teach numerator/denominator as memorised top/bottom labels.
Deliberately include improper and mixed forms (5/4, 1 1/4) so children learn the notation can name amounts greater than one; do not leave them believing 'you can't have 5/4'.
Say fractions as single spoken quantities ('three-quarters') so the symbol is heard as one number, never 'three, four'.

When sorting into unit / proper / improper / mixed, make clear that a unit fraction is a special proper fraction (sort it as unit) so the categories are not treated as if a fraction like 1/4 belonged in two trays.

The labelled-reference activity supports naming and reading only; it cannot let a child build improper/mixed forms or manipulate equivalence, so it is a scaffold, not a replacement for generating notation.

Classification, matching and fill-in tasks check fluency and recognition; a sort or match does not itself elicit independent construction of the single-number idea, so follow them with building and explaining.

A spoken quiz or dialogue can check naming, but it does not by itself elicit the writing and shading that produce the notation; pair any dialogue with building rather than treating talk as a substitute.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and no comparative efficacy of the builder over the reference or fluency tasks is claimed.

The legacy row dismissed a third dimension with a banked 'flat concept rendered in 3D isn't 3D' rule. That is a catalog-style universal claim not established by the cited sources; it has been dropped. Fraction notation is planar symbol-and-model work, so a 3D rendering has no clear affordance here, but no universal impossibility is asserted.

Self-audit of worked values: a bar cut into 4 equal parts with 5 parts shaded gives 5/4 = 1 1/4 (one whole and one quarter) - correct. 2/4 and 1/2 name the same length - correct. 3 of 8 equal slices is 3/8, and the upside-down error 8/3 is flagged as the error to fix, never presented as acceptable.

The diagnostic reasoning that the bottom number being bigger than the top tells us the fraction is less than one whole is sound for positive fractions and is retained as reasoning behind classification. Note this compares a fixed structure (top vs bottom within one symbol) and does not involve any denominator rule 'flipping'.

The original four-way sort treated 'unit' and 'proper' as separate trays, but every unit fraction (numerator 1) is also a proper fraction. The activities now state that a unit fraction is a special proper fraction and is sorted into the unit tray, removing the double-placement ambiguity.
Original probeDeeper content (e.g. eating all 8 slices gives 8/8 = 1) is a useful extension not fully expanded into an activity here; it can be added when the builder reaches a full whole.

probeDeeper: You wrote 3/8. If you had eaten all 8 slices, what fraction is that, and what number does it equal?
Someone writes 4/3 and says 'that's impossible — you can't split 4 things into 3'. What would you tell them?
Why does the bottom number being bigger than the top tell us the fraction is less than one whole?
Is 2/4 a different amount from 1/2, or the same? How do the numbers show it?
assess.correctAnswer: Writes 3/8; says the bottom number 8 (denominator) is the number of equal slices the whole pizza was cut into and the top number 3 (numerator) is how many of those slices were eaten. Reads 5/4 as 'five-quarters' (five-fourths), explains it means five parts each a quarter, which is more than one whole (one whole and one more quarter, 1 1/4), and yes it is allowed — an improper fraction is still a single number.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the symbol as two separate whole numbers — '3/8' becomes 'three, eight' rather than one quantity, three-eighths
errorPatterns.nextMove: Locate the fraction as one point on a number line and say it as one word ('three-eighths'); repeatedly read symbol→word→shaded amount as a single quantity
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the numbers aloud separately, or compares fractions by looking at numerator and denominator independently, never naming a single amount

errorPatterns.pattern: Writes the fraction upside down — puts the number of parts taken on the bottom (numerator and denominator swapped)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reconnect each number to its job on a shaded model ('how many equal parts in the whole? that's the bottom'); write the symbol WHILE shading, bottom-first
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 8/3 for 'three of eight slices', or shades correctly but records the symbol reversed

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes an improper fraction isn't a real number — '5/4 isn't allowed, you can't have five quarters / four thirds'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build 5/4 by collecting five quarter-pieces; show it passes one whole and equals 1 1/4; place it on a number line beyond 1 so it is visibly a single number
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Refuses to read 5/4, calls it a mistake, or tries to 'fix' it to 4/5

responseLevels.gap: Reads 3/8 as 'three, eight' and cannot say which number is the numerator/denominator or swaps them; says 5/4 'isn't allowed'.
responseLevels.full: Uses the vocabulary fluently in context, writes 3/8 with each number justified as parts-of-one-whole, reads and interprets 5/4 as one number greater than one (1 1/4), and classifies unit/proper/improper/mixed correctly.
responseLevels.partial: Names numerator and denominator and writes 3/8 correctly in the pizza context, but treats the two numbers as separate counts — cannot read 5/4 as a single quantity greater than one, and cannot reliably classify unit/proper/improper/mixed.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a pizza cut into 8 equal slices, and you eat 3 of them. Write that as a fraction, and as you write it tell me what each number in it stands for. Then I have written 5/4 on the board for a recipe — read it aloud for me and tell me what it means, and whether writing a fraction like that is allowed.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has only memorised 'top and bottom' can still parrot the labels, but two moves separate real notation understanding from label-recall: reading 5/4 as a single quantity greater than one (vs 'you can't do that') exposes the belief that improper fractions aren't numbers, and justifying 3 and 8 as parts-of-one-whole (vs reading '3/8' as 'three, eight') exposes the separate-whole-numbers facet.
