pedagogy.summary: Interpreting multiplication as SCALING (resizing) rather than only repeated addition: the size of a product relative to a factor depends on whether the OTHER factor is greater than, equal to, or less than 1. Multiplying by 5/3 enlarges, by 1 leaves unchanged, by 2/5 shrinks. This directly confronts the deep-rooted 'multiplication always makes bigger' belief and lets children judge a product's size WITHOUT computing (3/4 × 7 is less than 7 because we take three-quarters of it). It also unifies with equivalence: multiplying by n/n = 1 rescales the name without changing the value.
bestPractices: Teach prediction before calculation: ask whether a product will be bigger or smaller than a factor and WHY, using the size of the multiplier relative to 1.
Directly name and refute 'multiplication makes bigger' — show a <1 multiplier shrinks (3/4 of 7 < 7) and a >1 multiplier grows (5/3 of 7 > 7).
Use a stretch/shrink model (number line, elastic, photo enlargement) so 'scale by' is felt as resizing.
Connect × n/n = ×1 to fraction equivalence: rescaling by a name for 1 keeps the value.
Anchor with benchmarks 0, 1, and the multiplier: compare the multiplier to 1 to decide the direction of change.
keyRepresentations: Number line / elastic band stretched (×>1) or compressed (×<1) relative to the original length
Photo or shape enlargement/reduction by a scale factor
Double number line pairing a quantity with its scaled image
× n/n = ×1 shown as re-partitioning without changing length (equivalence link)
commonMisconceptions: 'Multiplication always makes the number bigger' (and division always smaller) — predicts 3/4 × 7 > 7 (Fischbein's primitive intuitive model; named explicitly in the IES guide).
Over-corrects to 'any fraction makes it smaller' — predicts 5/3 × 7 < 7 because the multiplier is written as a fraction, ignoring that 5/3 > 1.
Thinks multiplying by n/n changes the value (because 'you multiplied'), not recognising n/n = 1.

learn.summary: Interpret multiplication as scaling (resizing): for a positive quantity, the size of the product relative to that quantity depends on whether the OTHER factor (a positive multiplier) is greater than, equal to, or less than 1. Multiplying 7 by 5/3 enlarges it, by 1 (e.g. 4/4) leaves it unchanged, by 2/5 or 3/4 shrinks it. This confronts the 'multiplication always makes bigger' belief and lets learners judge a product's size WITHOUT computing (3/4 × 7 is part of 7, so less than 7). It also unifies with equivalence: multiplying by n/n = 1 (n not zero) rescales the name without changing the value. Emphasise predicting direction before calculating and comparing the multiplier to 1 — not whether it is written as a fraction.

activities.title: Stretch-and-shrink bar: predict before you scale
feedback: If a learner predicted 'longer' for 3/4 and the bar shrank, reframe as 'three-quarters OF 7' — a part of 7 is less than 7.
When the bar holds at 4/4, point out 4/4 is one whole, so ×4/4 is ×1: the value is unchanged, only re-partitioned.
If a learner expected 5/3 to shrink because 'it's a fraction', have them compare 5/3 to 1: it is more than one whole, so it stretches past 7.
Ask the learner to point to where on the dial the bar switches between shrinking and growing, and name that number (1).
activities.rationale: Scaling is resizing; a model that varies the multiplier across 1 makes the >1/<1 threshold visible and supports predict-first reasoning rather than computation. An interactive dial is one proposed way to make the pivot concrete; a stretched or compressed number line, an elastic band, a double number line pairing a quantity with its scaled image, or a 7 cm photo enlarged/reduced can serve the same purpose. The re-partitioning at 4/4 links scaling to equivalence. These are research-informed proposals, not validated against outcomes.
sourceClaims: Interpret multiplication as scaling (resizing): compare the size of a product to one factor by the size of the other, and explain that multiplying by a fraction >1 enlarges, =1 leaves unchanged, <1 reduces; relate multiplying a/b by n/n to equivalence.

The misconception that multiplying two numbers must result in a larger number is a common, named misconception that interferes with learning; estimation and reasoning about magnitude (e.g. 1/2 × 1/2 asks for half of a half, so the product is smaller than either factor) are the remedy.
learnerActions: Look at a 7-unit bar placed beside a faint marker of the original length 7.
Before anything moves, predict out loud or in writing whether scaling by a chosen multiplier will make the bar longer, shorter, or the same, and say WHY.
Set the multiplier to 3/4 and watch the bar contract to sit short of 7 (3/4 × 7 = 5.25).
Set the multiplier to 5/3 and watch the bar stretch past 7 (5/3 × 7 ≈ 11.67).
Set the multiplier to 4/4 and watch the bar hold exactly at 7, re-partitioned to show it is still the same length.
Sweep the multiplier dial slowly across 1 and notice the exact point where the bar flips from shrinking to growing.
State the rule: multiplying a positive quantity makes it bigger only when the multiplier is more than 1.
activities.intendedInsight: For a positive quantity scaled by a positive multiplier, the product is larger than, equal to, or smaller than the quantity exactly according to whether the multiplier is greater than, equal to, or less than 1 — the number 1 is the pivot, not whether the multiplier is written as a fraction.

activities.title: Predict and sort multipliers by direction
feedback: If a learner picks 'greater, because multiplying always makes bigger', ask when multiplying actually makes a number bigger, steering to the multiplier>1 condition.
If 5/3 is sorted into 'makes smaller', ask them to compare 5/3 with one whole before deciding.
Reward reasons that cite the multiplier's size relative to 1, not reasons that cite 'it's a fraction' or a remembered answer.
activities.rationale: Prediction-and-sort items can surface both the 'always bigger' and the 'any fraction shrinks' errors and give scorable practice on the size-relative-to-1 principle. A sort can check and exercise the direction classification, but on its own it asks for selection rather than independent construction of a reason; pair it with the prediction-and-explanation work.
sourceClaims: Interpret multiplication as scaling (resizing): compare the size of a product to one factor by the size of the other, and explain that multiplying by a fraction >1 enlarges, =1 leaves unchanged, <1 reduces; relate multiplying a/b by n/n to equivalence.
learnerActions: For each of 3/4 × 7, 5/3 × 7, 2/5 × 7, and 4/4 × 7, predict without calculating whether the product is greater than, less than, or equal to 7, and give a reason.
Sort a set of multipliers into three groups: 'makes bigger', 'leaves the same', 'makes smaller'.
For a prompt such as 'is 3/4 × 7 greater, less than, or equal to 7?', choose and justify an answer, and explain why 'greater, because multiplying makes bigger' is not correct.
Estimate the rough size of a product on a scale before revealing the exact value.
activities.intendedInsight: Deciding a product's direction is a comparison of the multiplier to 1, which can be done reliably before any arithmetic.

activities.title: Find the counterexample to 'multiplying always makes bigger'
feedback: Accept a counterexample only if the learner explains why that multiplier shrinks (it is less than 1 / a part of the quantity).
If the corrected rule says 'fractions make it smaller', challenge with 5/3 × 7 and ask them to refine the rule to 'less than 1'.
activities.rationale: Scaling is argument-rich, and critiquing a stated claim lets the learner surface and challenge the misconception by constructing a counterexample and a precise rule. A spoken or written exchange with a character who makes the wrong claim is one proposed way to prompt this; it complements, rather than replaces, seeing the resize on a model.
sourceClaims: 'Multiplication makes bigger, division makes smaller' is a primitive intuitive model children over-generalise from whole-number experience and must be overcome for rational-number operations.

The misconception that multiplying two numbers must result in a larger number is a common, named misconception that interferes with learning; estimation and reasoning about magnitude (e.g. 1/2 × 1/2 asks for half of a half, so the product is smaller than either factor) are the remedy.
learnerActions: Consider the claim 'multiplying a number always makes it bigger.'
Find a specific case that shows the claim is false and explain why it fails (e.g. 3/4 × 7 is three-quarters OF 7, so less than 7).
Then state the corrected, precise rule: multiplying a positive quantity makes it bigger only when the multiplier is greater than 1; by 1 it stays the same; by less than 1 it gets smaller.
Explain why 5/3 × 7 does make 7 bigger, so the rule is about size relative to 1, not about being a fraction.
activities.intendedInsight: Refuting the over-generalised belief requires producing a counterexample and restating the condition precisely, which strengthens understanding of why the threshold is 1.

activities.title: Multiplying by n/n keeps the value
feedback: If a learner says 7 × 4/4 is bigger or smaller 'because you multiplied', point out that 4/4 = 1 and that ×1 leaves the quantity unchanged.
Have the learner show the bar holding its length while the partition changes, linking equal length to equal value.
activities.rationale: Treating n/n as 1 ties the scaling view directly to equivalence and addresses the specific belief that any multiplication must change the value. Showing length held constant while re-partitioning makes 'same value, different name' concrete.
sourceClaims: Interpret multiplication as scaling (resizing): compare the size of a product to one factor by the size of the other, and explain that multiplying by a fraction >1 enlarges, =1 leaves unchanged, <1 reduces; relate multiplying a/b by n/n to equivalence.
learnerActions: Predict what 7 × 4/4 equals and whether it is bigger, smaller, or the same as 7.
Show on a bar or number line that 4/4 is one whole, so the length holds while being re-partitioned into quarters.
Connect this to fraction equivalence: multiplying a/b by n/n (n a whole number greater than 1) gives a different name for the same value.
Explain why 3/4 × 2/2 names the same value as 3/4.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying by n/n is multiplying by 1: it rescales the name (re-partitions) without changing the value, which is exactly what underlies equivalent fractions.

constraints: Target age roughly 10–11 (Year 5 / Grade 5); conceptual objective, not a computation drill.

Insist on prediction and reasoning BEFORE any calculation — the reason is the diagnostic part. A learner can guess 'less than 7' without understanding; require 'because 3/4 is less than 1, so it's part of 7'.
Always pair a multiplier >1 (e.g. 5/3) with one <1 (e.g. 2/5 or 3/4) so learners must track size relative to 1 rather than applying a blanket 'fractions shrink' rule.
Sorting and multiple-choice items assess direction and can bait errors, but they ask for selection; include tasks where the learner constructs a reason, a counterexample, or a corrected rule.
A static before/after image can show one enlargement and one reduction but does not let the learner vary the multiplier across 1; treat it as a reference scaffold, not the main concept-building task.
Keep concrete numbers correct: 3/4 × 7 = 5.25 (short of 7), 5/3 × 7 ≈ 11.67 (past 7), 2/5 × 7 = 2.8 (short of 7), 4/4 × 7 = 7.

A zero-thickness on-screen bar or elastic is an idealised model of magnitude/length; physical strips, elastic bands, or photos are approximations with their own properties (slight thickness, stretch limits) — use either to make resizing felt, without claiming one is required or superior.
Compare fractions here as numbers/multipliers against 1; do not teach any 'denominator rule flips' idea — the direction of change comes from the multiplier's size relative to 1.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Of the three cited sources, only the IES/WWC practice guide is marked verified in the source row; the CCSS-M 5.NF.5 statement and the Fischbein/Greer claim are marked unverified. Treat the scaling framing and the 'primitive intuitive model' description as resting on unverified citations.

The original labelled a 3D treatment 'poor' because resizing is one-dimensional. That is a catalog fit judgement, not an established pedagogical law; the ranking is dropped, with the neutral observation that extra depth is simply not needed for a length/magnitude resize here.
Self-audit of arithmetic: 3/4 × 7 = 5.25, 5/3 × 7 ≈ 11.666…, 2/5 × 7 = 2.8, 4/4 × 7 = 7 — all consistent with the direction claims used in the activities.
The source distractor 'any fraction makes it smaller' is deliberately retained as an error to challenge (via 5/3 > 1), never offered as a correct rule.
The 'bigger only when the multiplier is more than 1' rule is stated for positive quantities, matching the Grade 5 scope of this objective.

assess.poeTask: Before any calculation, show a 7-unit strip (or a photo 7 cm wide). Ask the child to PREDICT what happens to its length when we scale it by 3/4 — longer, shorter, or the same — and to say WHY before anything moves. Then scale it (fold/measure, or reveal 3/4 × 7 = 5.25) and compare. A child holding 'multiplication makes bigger' predicts longer; the strip visibly shrinks to three-quarters of its length. The reason stated before scaling is the diagnostic part — a correct child says 'shorter, because we're taking three-quarters OF it'.
probeDeeper: What does '3/4 of 7' mean — is a part of 7 more or less than 7?
Why is 5/3 × 7 different from 3/4 × 7? What's special about 5/3?
What does multiplying by 4/4 do to a number, and why?
When IS it true that multiplying makes a number bigger? Give me the rule.
assess.correctAnswer: 3/4 × 7 is LESS than 7 (three-quarters OF 7 is part of it, and 3/4 < 1). 5/3 × 7 is BIGGER than 7 (5/3 > 1); 2/5 × 7 is SMALLER than 7 (2/5 < 1). The product's size depends on whether the multiplier is greater or less than 1.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Multiplying always makes the number bigger, so 3/4 × 7 is more than 7' — the primitive multiplication-as-enlargement intuition.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reframe as 'three-quarters OF 7' and show on a stretch model that a <1 multiplier shrinks; ask when multiplying DOES make bigger to surface the multiplier>1 condition.
errorPatterns.distractor: Greater than 7, because multiplying always makes a number bigger
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts 3/4 × 7 > 7, and predicts every multiplier grows the number; reason cites 'times makes bigger'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Over-corrects: 'multiplying by a fraction makes it smaller, so 5/3 × 7 is less than 7' — treats any fraction multiplier as shrinking, ignoring that 5/3 > 1.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare 5/3 to 1 (it's more than one whole): scaling by more than one grows the quantity; show 5/3 of 7 stretching past 7 on the model. Distinguish 'a fraction' from 'less than 1'.
errorPatterns.distractor: Smaller, because multiplying by a fraction always makes it smaller
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts 5/3 × 7 < 7; reason is 'it's a fraction'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks multiplying by n/n changes the value because 'you multiplied', not seeing n/n = 1.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Link to equivalence: 4/4 is one whole, so ×4/4 is ×1 — the value is unchanged, only re-partitioned; show the length holding on the model.
errorPatterns.distractor: It changes the value, because you multiplied by something
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 7 × 4/4 (or 3/4 × 2/2) is bigger/smaller than the original rather than equal.

responseLevels.gap: Applies 'multiplication always makes bigger' (predicts 3/4 × 7 > 7) or over-corrects to 'any fraction shrinks it'; no reference to the multiplier's size relative to 1.
responseLevels.full: Predicts without computing that 3/4 × 7 < 7, 5/3 × 7 > 7, 2/5 × 7 < 7, explaining the product's size depends on whether the multiplier is greater or less than 1, and connects × n/n = ×1 to equivalence; transfers to a new multiplier.
responseLevels.partial: Predicts the <1 case correctly but reasons from a memorised 'fractions make it smaller' rule or from having computed, and can't reliably handle the >1 multiplier (5/3) or explain ×n/n = ×1 — lists effects without the unifying 'compare the multiplier to 1' principle.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Without working it out: is 3/4 × 7 greater than 7, less than 7, or equal to 7 — and WHY? Then tell me, again without calculating: does multiplying 7 by 5/3 make it bigger or smaller, and does multiplying 7 by 2/5 make it bigger or smaller?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The reason tier is the whole game: a child can guess 'less than 7' but only correct scaling reasoning gives 'because 3/4 is less than 1, so it's part of 7'. Pairing a >1 multiplier (5/3) with a <1 multiplier (2/5) forces the child to track the multiplier's size relative to 1 — something neither 'multiplication makes bigger' (predicts all three grow) nor 'any fraction shrinks it' (predicts 5/3 shrinks) can do. Requiring prediction WITHOUT computing stops a child back-reasoning from an arithmetic answer.

pedagogy.summary: At KS3 the probability scale is formalised: every probability is a measure from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain), expressible as fraction, decimal or percentage, and read fluently in both directions between a described event and a numeric position. The distinctive KS3 demand is separating equally-likely situations (where P = favourable/total can be calculated) from biased ones (a loaded spinner, a drawing pin) where the scale still applies but the value cannot be got by symmetry — and refusing the equiprobability shortcut of 'n outcomes so 1/n each'.
bestPractices: Treat probability explicitly as a MEASURE on a bounded line, with 0, 1/2 and 1 as fixed landmarks and events justified by position
Contrast fair devices (calculable by favourable/total) with biased ones (a drawing pin, a bent coin) where the value must be estimated, not calculated — the scale holds either way
Confront the equiprobability shortcut directly: 'three colours' does not mean 1/3 each unless the sections are genuinely equal
Keep fraction/decimal/percentage fluency live — the same probability written three ways is one point on the line
Re-anchor the bounds: no probability is below 0 or above 1, unlike quantities in general
keyRepresentations: 0-to-1 measure line with impossible / even chance / certain landmarks
Fraction = decimal = percentage triple labels on the line
Fair vs biased devices (equal spinner vs loaded spinner vs drawing pin)
Everyday-event cards placed and justified on the scale
commonMisconceptions: Equiprobability bias — assuming n possible outcomes means each has probability 1/n even when they are not equally likely (biased spinner)
Believing a probability can exceed 1 or be stated as a raw count of outcomes
Comparing probabilities written in different notations by their surface digits without converting
Assuming every probability can be CALCULATED from symmetry, with no notion that some must be estimated from data

learn.summary: KS3 learners formalise probability as a measure on a bounded 0-to-1 line: 0 = impossible, 1/2 = even chance, 1 = certain, with the same point expressible as fraction, decimal or percentage and read fluently in both directions (event → position, position → event). The distinctive demand is separating fair/equally-likely devices (where P = favourable/total can be calculated by symmetry) from biased ones (loaded spinner, bent coin, drawing pin) where symmetry no longer gives the value — it is either stated/given or, where neither symmetry nor a stated value is available, estimated from repeated data — and refusing the equiprobability shortcut 'n outcomes, so 1/n each' unless the sections/outcomes are genuinely equal. Learners also re-anchor the bounds: no probability is below 0 or above 1, and a probability is never a raw count of outcomes.

activities.title: Placing probabilities on the 0-to-1 measure line
feedback: If a learner compares 1/4 and 0.3 by surface digits, have them convert both to decimals (1/4 = 0.25) or to positions on the line; 0.25 sits below 0.3.
If a marker is pushed past the certain end, re-anchor: nothing is more likely than certain, so probability tops out at 1 — unlike a general fraction of a quantity, a probability cannot exceed 1.
If a probability is stated as a whole-number count of outcomes, point back to the line: a probability is a position between 0 and 1, not a tally.
activities.rationale: Treating probability explicitly as a measure on a bounded line, with 0, 1/2 and 1 as fixed landmarks and triple fraction/decimal/percentage labelling, keeps notation fluency live and makes the 0–1 bounds concrete. An optional draggable marker with a live tri-notation readout, blocked past 0 and 1, makes the mechanism vivid but is not required — a static labelled scale with tap-to-reveal triple notations works as a reference.
sourceClaims: Probability is a measure on a 0-to-1 scale expressed as fraction, decimal or percentage, with 'even chance' at 1/2; and having two (or n) outcomes does not make them equally likely — a 1-red/5-blue device has probabilities 1/6 and 5/6, not equal.
learnerActions: Work with a 0-to-1 line marked with the fixed landmarks 0 (impossible), 1/2 (even chance) and 1 (certain).
Place a probability of 0.7 and a probability of 1/4 at their correct positions, and read off the same point shown three ways as a fraction, a decimal and a percentage.
For each placement, state which landmark the event sits near and justify its position ('0.7 is above even chance, so toward the certain end').
Place a set of everyday-event cards on the scale and justify each position in words.
Test the bounds: try to place a marker beyond the certain end or below the impossible end and state why no probability can go there.
activities.intendedInsight: A probability is one point on a bounded measure line; the same value can be written as a fraction, decimal or percentage, and nothing can lie below 0 or above 1.

activities.title: Fair vs biased: when symmetry works and when it doesn't
feedback: If a learner assigns 1/3 to every colour on the biased spinner, point back to the stated 70% and the unequal sections: equal probabilities require equal sections, which this spinner does not have.

If a learner says the drawing-pin probability is 1/2 ('two ways to land'), note that the pin is not symmetric — two outcomes do not make them equally likely, and no value is stated, so it must be read off where repeated data settle.
Reinforce: P(not red) = 1 − P(red); the complement is found by subtracting from the certain bound, not by counting colours.
activities.rationale: Contrasting a calculable fair device (equal spinner, fair die) with a biased one directly confronts the equiprobability bias, and extending to a drawing pin shows a case with no symmetry and no stated value, so the probability can only be estimated. An optional sampler that runs repeated trials and lets markers approach their positions on the line makes a data-driven estimate concrete; it is a way to show the mechanism, not a mandatory tool. Note: with a finite number of trials an estimated position scatters around the true value rather than landing exactly on it.
sourceClaims: Probability is a measure on a 0-to-1 scale expressed as fraction, decimal or percentage, with 'even chance' at 1/2; and having two (or n) outcomes does not make them equally likely — a 1-red/5-blue device has probabilities 1/6 and 5/6, not equal.

The equiprobability bias — assuming all outcomes of a situation are equally likely — is a documented misconception, and children often judge fairness arbitrarily rather than from the structure of the device (Watson & Moritz).
learnerActions: Start with a fair 3-section spinner (equal sections) and calculate each colour's probability as favourable/total — here the three colours genuinely sit at equal thirds; similarly a fair six-sided die gives each number a probability of 1/6 by symmetry.
Switch to a biased spinner that is STATED to be designed so red comes up 70% of the time, with the red section much larger. Predict where the three colours sit on the line BEFORE checking.

Use the stated 70% to place red, and run or observe repeated spins to see that the three colours do not come out at equal thirds — red's observed proportion tends to sit near 0.7, above even chance and toward the certain end, while blue and yellow together share roughly the remaining 0.3 (they may be close to each other, since their split is not given); a finite run only approximates each value rather than landing on it exactly.

Place P(red) = 0.7 above even chance, toward the certain end, and work out P(not red) = P(blue or yellow) = 0.3 by subtracting from 1, placing it below even chance (blue and yellow share that 0.3, and the split between them is not given).
State in words why 'three colours' did not guarantee '1/3 each' — only equal sections would.
Then consider a plain drawing pin, whose point-up probability is neither given by symmetry nor stated: decide that it can only be estimated from data, and explain why there is no symmetry to use.
activities.intendedInsight: Equal probabilities require equal sections/outcomes. For a biased device symmetry no longer gives the value: if the bias is stated you use the given value (red = 0.7); where neither symmetry nor a stated value is available (a drawing pin), the probability can only be estimated from repeated data. The scale applies in every case.

activities.title: Predict-observe-explain with a real drawing pin
feedback: If the learner predicted 1/2, compare the prediction with the recorded tallies and ask what feature of the pin breaks the symmetry argument; even if the tallies happen to be near half, two possible outcomes did not justify assuming 1/2.
Stress that an estimate from 40–50 drops is approximate: more trials give a more stable position, but it will still scatter around the true value.
Connect back: this is the same point as the biased spinner — the number of possible outcomes does not fix their probabilities.
activities.rationale: A predict-observe-explain task with a physical pin surfaces the equiprobability bias through the learner's own stated reasoning and shows that some probabilities are only knowable from data. The equiprobability bias is a documented misconception, so provoking and then confronting it is appropriate; the physical pin is a concrete way to run the trials, not evidence that touch is required to learn the idea.
sourceClaims: The equiprobability bias — assuming all outcomes of a situation are equally likely — is a documented misconception, and children often judge fairness arbitrarily rather than from the structure of the device (Watson & Moritz).
learnerActions: Before any testing, predict the probability that a dropped drawing pin lands point-up, and write down the number AND the reasoning.
Drop the pin 40–50 times, recording point-up and point-down tallies.

Compare the observed proportion to the prediction and note whether point-up and point-down came out roughly equal or clearly different; whatever the tallies show, explain why the pin's lack of symmetry means a value of 1/2 cannot simply be assumed.
Mark the estimated point-up probability on the 0-to-1 line at the position the data settle toward.
Explain what the stated-beforehand prediction revealed about the equiprobability assumption, and why this probability had to be estimated rather than calculated.
activities.intendedInsight: Stating a prediction and reason before testing exposes the 'two ways to land, so even chance' assumption; because the pin is asymmetric and no value is stated, its probability must be estimated from experiment rather than assumed to be a half, and the recorded data give that estimate.

activities.title: Ordering and converting mixed-notation probabilities
feedback: If the set is ordered by visible digits, require conversion to decimals first; the surface digits mislead (1/4 looks like '4' but is 0.25).
For a 'probability = 6' or 'probability > 1' choice, re-anchor on the certain bound: a probability tops out at 1.
For the '1/3 each' claim, accept only answers that tie the equal split to equal sections, and reject it for a biased spinner.
activities.rationale: Short placement, ordering and judgement tasks drill conversion fluency, the bounds, and the equiprobability trap. These response formats can be used during teaching for practice as well as for checking; recognition or ordering items alone do not elicit the learner's own reasoning, so pair them with the explain-why prompts.
sourceClaims: Probability is a measure on a 0-to-1 scale expressed as fraction, decimal or percentage, with 'even chance' at 1/2; and having two (or n) outcomes does not make them equally likely — a 1-red/5-blue device has probabilities 1/6 and 5/6, not equal.
learnerActions: Order a mixed set such as 40%, 1/4 and 0.3 from least to most likely by first converting all to a common form.
Convert each probability to a decimal (or a position on the line) and check: 1/4 = 0.25, which sits below 0.3, which sits below 40% = 0.4.
Decide whether each of several statements is possible — e.g. 'a probability of 6' or 'a probability bigger than 1' — and justify using the bounds.
Judge a fair-vs-biased claim: 'there are three colours, so each has probability 1/3' — decide whether it is right and explain when it would and would not hold.
activities.intendedInsight: Probabilities written in different notations must be converted to a common form before comparison; values cannot exceed 1 or be raw counts; '1/n each' holds only for genuinely equal sections/outcomes.

activities.title: Socratic challenges to the bounds and the 1/n shortcut
feedback: Prompt for the structural reason (section size, bounds), not just a yes/no answer.
If the learner stalls, direct them to place the value on the line and read off whether it is possible.
activities.rationale: Socratic questioning can surface the bounds and equiprobability errors and push learners to justify their answers. It complements, rather than replaces, placement work: dialogue elicits reasoning while a line or device shows the placement more directly.
learnerActions: Respond to a prompt such as 'Could a probability be 2?' and justify the answer using the 0–1 bounds.
Respond to 'Why isn't each colour 1/3 on this biased spinner?' and explain what would have to be true for 1/3 each to hold.
Explain how you would find P(not red) from P(red), and where it sits relative to even chance.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating why values cannot exceed 1 and why '1/n each' needs equal sections consolidates the two central KS3 ideas in the learner's own words.

constraints: Equal probabilities (P = favourable/total, or '1/n each') are only valid for genuinely equal sections/outcomes; do not apply symmetry to biased devices.

For asymmetric or biased devices where no value is stated (loaded spinner of unknown bias, bent coin, drawing pin) the probability cannot be got by symmetry and must be estimated from repeated data; where a bias value is stated/given (e.g. red = 70%), use the stated value directly. Any estimate from a finite number of trials is approximate and scatters around the true value.
No probability is below 0 or above 1, and a probability is never a raw count of outcomes — unlike a general fraction of a quantity, it cannot exceed 1.
Compare probabilities by converting to a common notation (or to line positions); do not compare by surface digits.

A draggable marker, live tri-notation readout, bias/fair switch and repeated-trial sampler are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete; a static labelled scale with tap-to-reveal notations is a valid reference but cannot flag a mis-placement on its own.
Recognition/ordering items can be used while teaching, but used alone they do not elicit the learner's own construction and reasoning; pair them with explain-why prompts.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row claimed 3D 'adds nothing' to a one-dimensional measure scale; this universal dismissal has been dropped. The point retained is only that a 0-to-1 scale is one-dimensional, so a 3D representation offers no obvious extra affordance here — not that it could never teach.

Precision: the worked biased spinner is STATED to be designed at 70% red, so red = 0.7 is used from the stated value, not discovered by sampling; estimation-from-data is reserved for the drawing pin (no symmetry and no stated value). An earlier draft blurred these by saying every biased value 'must be estimated'.
Preservation: the objective-evidence example 'a fair six-sided die gives each number 1/6' is retained as a calculable fair-device example alongside the fair spinner.

Precision: P(red)=0.7 is described as above even chance, toward the certain end (not 'hugging'/'at' the certain end); 0.7 is on the certain side but not adjacent to 1. Data-run wording changed from 'settle' to 'approach/approximate' to reflect finite-sample scatter.

Self-audit of arithmetic/logic: P(red) = 0.7 and P(not red) = 1 − 0.7 = 0.3 (below even chance) are consistent; 1/4 = 0.25 < 0.3 < 0.4 (40%) for the ordering example checks out; a fair die gives 1/6 per face. The drawing-pin '1/2 prediction' is the misconception to confront, not an instruction.

An estimate from 40–50 trials is approximate and scatters; the source rows implied the markers 'settle' on the true value, which could overstate how exactly a finite sample lands — caveated throughout.

assess.poeTask: Hand the child an ordinary drawing pin and ask: 'If I drop this pin, what is the probability it lands point-up? Predict the number and explain your reasoning before we test it.' Many predict 1/2 ('two ways it can land, so even chance'). Then drop the pin 40–50 times and record: point-up and point-down do NOT come out equal (the pin is not symmetric). The prediction-and-reason stated beforehand exposes the equiprobability assumption, and the data shows the probability had to be estimated, not assumed to be a half.
probeDeeper: Where exactly does P(not red) sit on the line, and how did you get it from P(red)?
Could this spinner's red probability ever be written as a number bigger than 1? Why not?
If I gave you a plain drawing pin, could you CALCULATE the probability it lands point-up, or would you have to find it another way?
Is 1/4 bigger or smaller than 0.3? How can you be certain?
assess.correctAnswer: P(red) = 0.7, placed near the certain end; P(not red) = P(blue or yellow) = 0.3, below even chance; blue and yellow share the 0.3 between them. The classmate is wrong: 1/3 each would only hold if the three sections were equal, but this spinner is biased toward red — the number of colours does not fix the probabilities.

errorPatterns.pattern: Equiprobability bias — assumes n outcomes means 1/n each even for a biased device ('three colours, so 1/3 each')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point back to the stated 70% and the unequal sections; equal probabilities require equal sections/outcomes, which this spinner does not have
errorPatterns.distractor: Each colour has probability 1/3, because there are three colours.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Assigns every colour 1/3 despite being told red is 70%

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes a probability can exceed 1 or be given as a raw count
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor the bounds — nothing is more likely than certain, so probability tops out at 1; unlike a general fraction of a quantity, a probability cannot exceed 1
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Places a marker beyond the certain end, or states a probability above 1 / as a whole number of outcomes

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares probabilities written in different notations by their surface digits
errorPatterns.nextMove: Convert all to decimals (or scale positions) before comparing; 1/4 = 0.25 sits below 0.3
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Orders 70%, 1/4 and 0.3 by the visible numbers rather than converting to a common form

responseLevels.gap: Treats every outcome as equally likely regardless of bias, or places marks outside 0–1; cannot convert between notations
responseLevels.full: Places biased probabilities correctly as a measure on 0–1, finds P(not red) by subtracting from 1, rejects '1/n each' for unequal sections, converts freely between notations, and recognises some probabilities must be estimated from data rather than calculated
responseLevels.partial: Places fair-device probabilities and knows the endpoints, but applies 1/n-each to a biased device, is unsure a probability cannot exceed 1, or compares mixed notations by raw digits

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a biased spinner with red, blue and yellow sections, and state that it is designed so red comes up 70% of the time. Ask the child to place P(red), P(blue or yellow), and describe P(not red) on a 0-to-1 scale. Then a classmate says 'there are three colours, so each has probability 1/3'. Ask: is that right, and why? Take the answer, then ask for the full reasoning (Tier 2).
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who treats probability as a measure places 0.7 and 0.3 correctly and rejects '1/3 each' because the spinner is biased; an equiprobability-biased child assigns 1/3 to every colour; others may drift a marker past 1 or compare notations by raw digits. The Tier-2 reason — attending to section size and the 0–1 bounds — is the separator.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 10–11: perform MENTAL calculations, including mixed operations and large numbers, using strategies such as partitioning, compensation and derived facts (flexible, fact-based mental methods).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y6): 'perform mental calculations, including with mixed operations and large numbers' and 'use their knowledge of the order of operations'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): the mental-strategy expectation is distributed — 3.OA.5 properties as strategies, 4.NBT.5/6 place-value & properties strategies, 5.NBT.6, and MP7 (structure) / MP8 (regularity) underpin flexible mental methods.
• Operational details — the child chooses an efficient mental route: partitioning (45×8 = 40×8 + 5×8 = 360), compensation (99×6 = 100×6 − 6), derived facts (knowing 6×4 to get 6.5×4), doubling/halving, and factorising. Mixed-operation strings (250×3 + 500) require applying order of operations mentally. The emphasis is on SELECTING and EXPLAINING a strategy, and on flexibility rather than one prescribed method.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): mentally compute 45×8 by partitioning and state the partition used. Tier B (10–11): derive 6.5×4 from a known fact, explaining the derivation. Tier C (11): solve a mixed-operation mental calculation like 250×3 + 500 and justify the strategy and order.
bestPractices: Teach a REPERTOIRE of strategies (partition, compensate, double/halve, derive, factorise) and, crucially, WHEN each is efficient — the goal is flexible choice, not one algorithm done in the head.
Make strategy TALK routine: children explain and compare methods ('I did 40×8 then 5×8; you doubled 45 three times') so efficiency and structure become explicit and shareable.
Use derived-fact chains from a known core fact — from 6×4 reach 60×4, 6.5×4, 12×4 — to show mental maths is about leveraging what you already know, reducing memory load.
Ground partitioning and compensation in place value and the distributive/associative laws so mental methods are understood, not tricks; connect to the area-model and properties work already secured.
Fold in order of operations for mixed strings (250×3 + 500) so children apply BODMAS mentally, and always encourage an estimate to sanity-check the mental result.
keyRepresentations: Partitioning diagrams / bar splits: 45 shown as 40 + 5, each part multiplied then recombined (distributive law made visible).
Empty number line for compensation and doubling/halving jumps (99×6 as 100×6 then back 6).
Derived-fact 'spider' or web from a core fact to its relatives (6×4 → 60×4, 6.5×4, 3×4).
Jottings scaffold — minimal written support for intermediate results in a multi-step mental calculation (not a full written method).
commonMisconceptions: Attempting the formal WRITTEN algorithm in the head (carrying columns mentally) instead of using an efficient mental strategy — error-prone and slow.
Partitioning errors: multiplying only one part (45×8 → 40×8 = 320 and forgetting 5×8) — dropping a partial product.
Compensation without adjusting back (99×6 = 100×6 but forgetting to subtract 6).
Ignoring order of operations in mixed mental strings (doing 250×3+500 left-to-right differently).
Believing there is one 'right' mental method, so failing to pick the most efficient route for the particular numbers.

learn.summary: For ages 10–11, develop flexible mental calculation for multiplication, large numbers and mixed-operation strings. Learners build a repertoire of strategies — partitioning, compensation, doubling/halving, derived facts, factorising — and learn to SELECT and EXPLAIN the most efficient route for the particular numbers, applying order of operations mentally and sanity-checking with estimation. The central objective is flexible, structure-seeking judgement and strategy talk, not running a written column algorithm in the head.

activities.title: Mental maths strategy workspace: split, compensate, derive
feedback: If a partial product is dropped (e.g. answering 320 for 45×8, forgetting 5×8), prompt: say each partial product aloud and add them; jot the parts down if working memory overloads.
If compensation is left unadjusted (99×6 = 600), ask: what did you change about 99, and what must you do to put that back? (Subtract 6 to reach 594.)

If the written column method is attempted mentally and a carry is lost (answer off by tens), suggest partitioning or doubling (45×8 = 45×4×2 = 180×2 = 360) as a carrying-free mental route; reserve columns for paper.
If order of operations is ignored in a mixed string (e.g. computing 250×(3+500)), clarify: multiply before add here — do 250×3 first, then add 500.
If the strategy is sound but a sub-total is miscomputed, do not reteach the strategy: have the learner re-state and recompute the slipped part, then check by estimation.
activities.rationale: Effective mental calculation depends on a repertoire of strategies and efficient choice grounded in place value and properties of operations, rather than mentally running the written algorithm. Making decomposition explicit lets the classic dropped-partial-product error become visible and correctable.
sourceClaims: Pupils use place-value understanding and properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide; flexible mental strategies rest on structure and repeated reasoning.
Effective mental calculation depends on a repertoire of strategies (partitioning, compensation, derived facts) and choosing efficiently, not on mentally running the written algorithm.
learnerActions: Given 45 × 8, partition 45 into 40 and 5, multiply each part by 8 (40×8 = 320, 5×8 = 40), then recombine the partial products to reach 360.
Use compensation on 99 × 6: compute 100 × 6 = 600, then subtract the adjustment 6 to get 594 — stating both the rounding move and the adjust-back step.
Grow a derived-fact chain from a known core fact: from 6 × 4 reach 60 × 4, 6.5 × 4 and 12 × 4, saying how each relative is obtained.
Solve a mixed-operation string such as 250 × 3 + 500: multiply first (250 × 3 = 750), then add 500 to get 1250, stating the order used.
For at least one calculation, try two different strategies (e.g. partitioning vs doubling 45 three times) and judge which was more efficient for those numbers.
Before finalising, give a rough estimate (45 × 8 lies between 40 × 8 = 320 and 50 × 8 = 400, so around 360) and check the answer fits.
activities.intendedInsight: Mental calculation is about decomposing numbers flexibly using place value and the distributive/associative laws, leveraging known facts to reduce memory load, and choosing the route that suits the particular numbers — not visualising a column method.

activities.title: Explain and compare: strategy talk
feedback: Reward reasoning about WHY a route is efficient for these numbers, not just fast answers.
If the learner believes there is one 'right' mental method, present a case where a different strategy is clearly quicker (e.g. 99×6 by compensation vs partitioning) to prompt flexible selection.
When comparing, ask the learner to state the condition that makes each strategy efficient (numbers near a round number favour compensation; even factors favour doubling/halving).
activities.rationale: Strategy talk and comparison help develop flexible mental calculation; explaining and judging which route is more efficient rehearses the efficient-choice reasoning the objective targets. A responsive questioner may prompt this articulation during teaching, though its instructional effect here is proposed rather than independently validated.
sourceClaims: Effective mental calculation depends on a repertoire of strategies (partitioning, compensation, derived facts) and choosing efficiently, not on mentally running the written algorithm.
learnerActions: After solving a calculation mentally, explain aloud how it was worked out ('I did 40×8 then 5×8 and added them').
Compare your method with a different method for the same calculation (e.g. 'you doubled 45 three times') and decide which is more efficient and why.
Respond to prompts such as: 'How did you break up 45 × 8 to make it easier?', 'Could doubling help instead?', and 'In 250 × 3 + 500, which do you do first and why?'
Judge whether a proposed shortcut is valid and efficient for the given numbers, not just whether it reaches an answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating and comparing methods makes efficiency and mathematical structure explicit and shareable, and builds the metacognition behind flexible choice — the real target beyond speed.

activities.title: Strategy reference and fluency practice
feedback: For a missing-partial item, if the blank is filled wrongly, return to the partition and recompute each part separately.
For strategy-matching, if an inefficient strategy is chosen, ask the learner to try both and time or count the steps to feel the difference.
Recognition-only matching confirms identification but does not by itself build the decomposition move; follow with an active calculation the learner performs from scratch.
activities.rationale: Reference material and matching/completion items support fluency and strategy identification; however such formats confirm or check rather than elicit the independent decomposition and recombination that is the core skill, so they should accompany active construction. No cited source directly establishes this affordance distinction.
learnerActions: Consult a worked reference showing partition, compensate and derive each worked once, with a note of when each is most useful, then apply the matching strategy to new calculations.
Complete fill-in-the-missing-partial items (e.g. 40×8 + __ = 360) to confirm all parts are tracked.
Match each calculation to its most efficient strategy and justify the match.
Practise derived-fact chains for fluency, timing optional, always stating the known fact the answer was derived from.
activities.intendedInsight: A reference of worked strategies plus targeted practice consolidates fluency and strategy-identification, provided the learner is actively producing or completing calculations rather than only recognising answers.

constraints: The objective is flexible mental strategy and explanation, not merely obtaining the correct answer; assessment should watch for a deliberate, tracked strategy across steps.

Recognition-only formats (multiple choice, matching) confirm strategy identification and fluency but do not elicit the independent decomposition and recombination that is the core skill; pair them with learner-constructed calculations.
A static strategy poster or worked reference is a useful aid but does not substitute for active practice of mental strategies; use it alongside the learner doing calculations.

Draggable partition tiles, compensation sliders and derived-fact webs are optional ways to externalise the mental move and make a dropped partial visible; they are illustrative, not required mechanisms, and the ultimate aim is for the learner to perform the move in their head.
Jottings are a legitimate minimal scaffold for intermediate results when working memory overloads; they should not become a full written column method, which is a different (paper) competence.
Ground partitioning and compensation in place value and the distributive/associative laws so methods are understood rather than applied as tricks.
Always include an estimate to sanity-check the mental result.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three cited sources (CCSS-M 4.NBT and NCETM) were marked verified:false in the source row; treat the mental-strategy repertoire and efficiency claims as reasonable guidance that has not been independently re-checked here.

Arithmetic self-check of the examples: 40×8 = 320 and 5×8 = 40 sum to 360; 45×4×2 = 180×2 = 360; 99×6 via 100×6 = 600 then −6 = 594 (the source gave the method without stating 594, added for completeness); 250×3 = 750 then +500 = 1250. No arithmetic errors found in the source examples.

The original 'parentTitle' was 'Ratio (age 10+)' while the content is mental multiplication/mixed operations — this appears to be a mislabel in the source metadata and does not affect the learning content; the original row field was not altered.

The source asserted that 3D 'adds nothing' and that a static picture 'can't' provide active practice; these have been softened to scoped affordance/objective-limit statements, since comparative necessity is not established by the sources.

Activity 1 (reference and fluency) sourceClaims were set to [] because no sources[].claim directly supports the reference/practice-format affordance principle. The Y6 claim was also removed from activity 0's sourceClaims because it supports the topic rather than that activity's repertoire/decomposition teaching principle.

probeDeeper: How did you break up 45 × 8 to make it easier?
Is there another mental route to 45 × 8 — could doubling help?
In 250 × 3 + 500, which do you do first and why?
Roughly, about how big should 45 × 8 be? Does your answer fit?
assess.correctAnswer: 360 (e.g. 40×8 + 5×8 = 320 + 40; or 45×8 = 45×4×2 = 180×2). 1250 (250×3 = 750, + 500 = 1250). The teacher watches for a deliberate mental strategy — partitioning, doubling, or compensation — held together across steps, not a mentally-visualised column algorithm.

errorPatterns.pattern: partitions but forgets to combine all parts — does 40×8 = 320 and forgets 5×8, answering 320
errorPatterns.nextMove: rehearse holding two parts: say each partial product aloud and add; jot the parts if working memory overloads.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer missing a partial product; child loses track of the second piece

errorPatterns.pattern: attempts the column algorithm mentally and loses carries
errorPatterns.nextMove: teach partitioning/compensation as the mental route (45×8 = 45×4×2), which avoids carrying; reserve columns for paper.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child visualises columns, drops a carry, gives an answer off by tens

errorPatterns.pattern: ignores order of operations in the mixed calculation — does 250×(3+500) or adds before multiplying
errorPatterns.nextMove: clarify multiply before add here; compute 250×3 first, then add 500.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer far too large; child combined 3 and 500 first

errorPatterns.pattern: correct strategy, arithmetic slip in a partial step
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach; have the child re-state and recompute the slipped part, then check by estimation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: right method described, wrong sub-total

responseLevels.gap: has no mental strategy, tries columns in the head and loses carries, or mis-orders the mixed calculation.
responseLevels.full: selects an efficient mental strategy (partition, compensate, derive), tracks the parts, respects operation order in the mixed calculation, and sanity-checks by estimation.
responseLevels.partial: partitions or doubles for the multiplication but drops a part, or needs support to sequence the mixed-operation calculation.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to do these in their head, saying their strategy aloud: 45 × 8, then 250 × 3 + 500. Watch whether they partition, compensate, or use derived facts — and whether they keep track of the parts mentally rather than reaching for a written method.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The objective is FLEXIBLE mental strategy, not just getting the answer. Watching whether the child partitions/compensates and tracks partial results reveals strategic fluency; a child who tries to 'do the written method in their head' typically loses the carries and stalls — exposing the absence of genuine mental strategies.

sources.claim: Y6 pupils perform mental calculations, including with mixed operations and large numbers.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (Year 6)

sources.claim: Pupils use place-value understanding and properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide; flexible mental strategies rest on structure and repeated reasoning.
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, 4.NBT.5/6 (with 3.OA.5, MP7/MP8)

sources.claim: Effective mental calculation depends on a repertoire of strategies (partitioning, compensation, derived facts) and choosing efficiently, not on mentally running the written algorithm.

pedagogy.summary: Nets make the 2-D↔3-D relationship visible and are the standard route to spatial visualisation in upper primary. The concept is best taught by folding and unfolding physical models and, crucially, by having children PREDICT whether an arrangement will fold before checking it. Structural reasoning is built by anchoring on a base face, tracking composites of faces (a 'line of four' wraps the sides of a cube), and mapping net features to solid features (shape→face, side→edge, point→vertex) so children move from judging by overall appearance to reasoning from properties.
bestPractices: Predict-then-fold: the child commits to a prediction ('will this fold into a cube?') and justifies it before physically folding to verify (Knight & Wright 2014).
Anchor a base face and fold the others up around it — this reduces the number and complexity of mental transformations and the load on working memory.
Build and track composites: a line of four squares wraps to form the sides of a cube; the remaining two cap top and bottom.
Use teacher questioning to map specific net features to solid features (shape→face, side→edge, point→vertex), shifting attention from holistic perception to structure.
Show many valid nets for the same solid (a cube has eleven) and contrast valid with invalid arrangements to break the single-prototype belief.
keyRepresentations: Physical fold-up nets (card, Polydron) folded and unfolded from the solid
The eleven cube nets chart; the T/cross prototype set beside non-standard nets
Base-face plus a 'line of four squares' composite
Face-to-face mapping diagram linking each net shape to a solid face
commonMisconceptions: Only the familiar T/cross net makes a cube (prototype-as-only-net; Mariotti 1989) — other valid nets are rejected and near-prototypes trusted.
Any arrangement with the right number of faces folds up — attends to face count, not arrangement.
Cannot predict the fold direction of an L-shape, so mis-assigns which faces meet — a face is thought 'stuck in the corner' or two squares that should be opposite are left adjacent.

learn.summary: Teach nets as the visible 2-D↔3-D relationship by having children PREDICT whether a flat arrangement of squares will fold into a cube, then fold to check. Build structural reasoning by anchoring on a base face, tracking composites (a 'line of four squares' wraps the cube's sides while the remaining two cap top and bottom, in nets that contain such a line), and mapping net features to solid features (each shape→a face; each fold line→an edge, while pairs of outer sides join to make the remaining edges; several corner points of the net meet at each vertex). The central goal is to move children from judging by whether a net 'looks like the usual one' to reasoning from structure — accepting unfamiliar valid nets (a cube has eleven), rejecting arrangements whose layout cannot close, and producing a genuinely new valid net.

activities.title: Predict then fold: does this arrangement close into a cube?
feedback: If the child rejects the staircase, fold it physically so they see it closes, then unfold several different valid nets from the same cube so they see there are many, not one (eleven in all).

If the child accepts the 2-by-3 block ('six squares, so it makes a cube'), fold it so they see squares land on the same face while other faces are left uncovered; mark a base face and track where each square lands.
Praise justification by imagined folding ('these two wrap round to opposite sides') over justification by resemblance ('it looks like the usual net').
activities.rationale: Committing to a prediction before verifying surfaces the child's reasoning and makes the folding the moment that confirms or overturns it. Contrasting a valid non-prototype net with an invalid six-square block directly targets the prototype-as-only-net and face-count misconceptions.
sourceClaims: Successful net-reasoners use imaged folding anchored to a base face and known composites (a 'line of four squares' wraps the cube's sides); the least successful rely on recognising the prototypical net rather than reasoning about structure, and inferences are rare without teacher support that maps net features to solid features. Potari & Spiliotopoulou categorised primary students' attention from holistic appearance to full geometric structure.
Mariotti (1989) found 10–13 year olds consistently found the prototypical T-shaped net by unfolding a cube but often believed it the ONLY possible net, neglecting symmetry to judge other nets.
learnerActions: Look at a flat arrangement of six squares and, before folding, commit to a prediction: 'will this fold into a closed cube?' and say WHY.

Fold the arrangement (physical card/Polydron cut-outs, or by folding a paper net) to check the prediction — treating the card as a stand-in for the ideal flat net and asking about the cube it would form, not about the card as an object.
Start with the familiar cross/T net, then meet an unfamiliar 'staircase' zig-zag (2-2-2) net and predict it before folding.
Fold the staircase and observe that it ALSO closes into a cube, with every face covered once and no face left open (allowing for slight gaps from card thickness).
Try a 2-by-3 block of six squares: predict, fold, and watch squares overlap onto the same face while other cube faces are left uncovered.
activities.intendedInsight: Whether a net closes into a cube is decided by the ARRANGEMENT of the squares, not merely by having six of them. Unfamiliar nets can be valid and prototype-looking blocks can fail.

activities.title: Anchor a base and track where every square lands
feedback: If the child names adjacent squares when asked which become opposite, re-anchor the base and narrate each square's destination as it folds; if the net contains a 'line of four', fold it to wrap the sides and place the last two as top and bottom.
If a face seems 'stuck in the corner', slow the fold and track that single square from flat to its final position.
Reinforce naming each square's destination out loud as it folds.
activities.rationale: Anchoring and composite-/destination-tracking are the strategies that distinguish successful from unsuccessful net-reasoners and lower working-memory load; L-shape fold-direction errors are a known difficulty that this activity directly rehearses.
sourceClaims: Successful net-reasoners use imaged folding anchored to a base face and known composites (a 'line of four squares' wraps the cube's sides); the least successful rely on recognising the prototypical net rather than reasoning about structure, and inferences are rare without teacher support that maps net features to solid features. Potari & Spiliotopoulou categorised primary students' attention from holistic appearance to full geometric structure.
learnerActions: Choose one square as the base face and fold the others up around it.

Where the net contains one (as in the cross/1-4-1 layout), identify the 'line of four squares' that wraps to form the sides, then place the remaining two as top and bottom; for other valid layouts such as the 2-2-2 staircase, track each individual square's destination from the base instead.
For an L-shape or line arrangement, predict the fold direction and name which two squares end up on OPPOSITE faces before folding.
After folding, point to the two squares that face each other across the cube and explain how you know they never touch.
activities.intendedInsight: Anchoring on a base face and tracking where each square lands (using composites like a line of four when the net has one) lets you predict which faces meet and which become opposite, reducing the amount you have to hold in your head at once.

activities.title: Make it fail, then make a new one
feedback: If the child can only reproduce the familiar net, show several unfolded valid nets from one cube to establish there are many.
Check the drawn net by folding it (physically or mentally, square by square) rather than by how it looks.

When mapping features, confirm explicitly that each shape→a face, each fold line or pair of joining outer sides→an edge, and that several net corners meet at each vertex (the cube has 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices).
activities.rationale: Requiring generation of a new valid net and face-to-feature mapping moves the child from holistic appearance to full geometric structure, and coordinates spatial visualisation with property-based reasoning.
sourceClaims: Property-based (spatial) reasoning and spatial visualisation must be coordinated by domain-specific knowledge to overcome the 'look' of a 2-D diagram; neither alone suffices, and the difficulty persists across grades 4–9.

Successful net-reasoners use imaged folding anchored to a base face and known composites (a 'line of four squares' wraps the cube's sides); the least successful rely on recognising the prototypical net rather than reasoning about structure, and inferences are rare without teacher support that maps net features to solid features. Potari & Spiliotopoulou categorised primary students' attention from holistic appearance to full geometric structure.
learnerActions: Starting from a valid net, slide ONE square to a new spot and predict whether it still folds into a cube; fold to check and describe what goes wrong when it fails.
Turn a valid net into a DIFFERENT valid net by moving just one square.
Draw a genuinely different arrangement of six squares that also folds into a cube (e.g. a 1-4-1 or 2-2-2 layout) and map each square to the cube face it becomes.

Map net features to solid features: each square→a face; each shared side (fold line)→an edge, and each pair of outer sides that join when folded→one more edge; several corner points of the net come together at each vertex (count them: 12 edges and 8 vertices on the cube).
activities.intendedInsight: Producing a new valid net and explaining why a moved square breaks or preserves the fold shows structural understanding that cannot be faked by matching the prototype.

activities.title: Extend the reasoning to other solids
feedback: If faces/edges/vertices don't match after building, return to the net and re-track the mis-folded face.
For the square-based pyramid, check that the four triangular faces fold up to meet at a single apex above the square base.
Encourage justifying rejections by what goes wrong in the fold, not by appearance.
activities.rationale: The curriculum covers nets of cubes, cuboids, prisms and pyramids; transferring the structural strategy across solids is the intended breadth and demonstrates the reasoning is not tied to one prototype.
sourceClaims: Nets of cubes, cuboids and other 3-D shapes are part of upper Key Stage 2 geometry in the English National Curriculum.
learnerActions: Draw and fold (mentally or physically) the net of a cuboid and a triangular prism, checking which faces connect.
Build a 3-D shape from its net and verify that all faces, edges, and vertices match.
Sketch a net of a square-based pyramid from a description or a 3-D model, transferring the base-and-fold reasoning from the cube.
Given several nets for one target solid, identify which fold correctly and explain why the others won't.
activities.intendedInsight: The same strategy — anchor a base, track how faces wrap, check faces/edges/vertices — applies beyond the cube to cuboids, prisms and pyramids.

constraints: Suitable for ages roughly 8–11 (upper Key Stage 2 geometry).
The predict-then-fold step is load-bearing: a prediction must be committed to and justified BEFORE folding, not after. Omitting the prediction reduces the task to observation.

Physical card/Polydron cut-outs have slight thickness and can be held, but they stand in for ideal flat (zero-thickness) faces; frame questions around the mathematical net and the cube it would fold into, not around whether the physical card can be picked up.

The 'line of four squares' composite applies to nets that contain such a line (e.g. the cross/1-4-1); it is not present in every valid net (e.g. the 2-2-2 staircase), where the general strategy is to track each square's destination from the base.

A static labelled net (each square tagged to the cube face it becomes, optionally with lift-the-flap or tap-to-highlight mappings) is a useful reference and reinforces face-to-face mapping, but it cannot be folded, so on its own it cannot provide the predict-then-fold experience.

A flat 2-D fold animation (drag squares, press fold, with overlap/missing-face flags) supports prediction and immediate close/fail feedback, but a flat animation can under-represent the spatial depth of the fold; pair it with physical folding or a rotatable model where possible.

A rotatable 3-D fold (watch faces swing up around a base, rotate the closing solid, see which squares become opposite) and hands-on physical card/Polydron both make the spatial fold concrete; they offer different experiences and either can carry the core mental action. Supporting non-standard nets on screen or in card lets 'only the T-net works' be disproved directly.

A 'which of these fold into a cube?' selection question is a useful CHECK after folding work; include a valid non-prototype net and an invalid six-square block as options. Recognition-only selection does not by itself elicit the folding reasoning or the production of a new net — pair it with asking the child to name opposite faces or draw a new valid net.
Spoken explanation of a prediction is a valuable prompt but is not a substitute for the spatial folding itself.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The claim that 'a cube has eleven distinct nets' is a well-known mathematical fact used in the source; it is stated as context, not re-derived here.

Legacy entries asserted 'dialogue cannot carry the spatial folding' and framed the 3-D interactive as uniquely 'ideal'; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the cited sources, so they have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements in constraints. Physical folding, flat animation, and rotatable 3-D are presented as different means to the same mental action rather than a strict ranking.

The legacy row described the 2-by-3 block fold as 'two squares overlap, two faces missing'; the qualitative point (squares overlapping onto a face while other faces are uncovered) is sound, but the exact counts are a simplification and have been phrased qualitatively for learners.

The 'line of four squares' composite has been scoped to nets that contain it, to avoid conflicting with the 2-2-2 staircase example used elsewhere, which folds correctly without a straight line of four.

The source claims are drawn from the original row and support the general teaching principles (imaged folding, prototype misconception, coordination of spatial and property reasoning, curriculum placement); they do not demonstrate that any specific activity format above was empirically tested.

probeDeeper: Point to the two squares that end up facing each other on opposite sides of the cube — how do you know they don't touch?
If I slide this square from here to there, does it still fold into a cube? Why?
A cube has eleven different nets — can you turn your net into another valid one by moving just one square?
Here is an arrangement of six squares that does NOT fold into a cube — what goes wrong when we fold it?
assess.correctAnswer: Accepts the cross and the staircase as valid and rejects the 2-by-3 block; justifies by imagined folding anchored to a base face — tracking which squares wrap to the sides and which two become top and bottom / opposite faces, not by resemblance to a 'usual' net — and draws a fourth genuinely different valid net (e.g. a 1-4-1 or 2-2-2 arrangement) mapping its squares to cube faces.

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes only the familiar cross/T net makes a cube ('that's how a cube is always made'), so rejects valid non-standard nets and trusts anything resembling the prototype
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fold the rejected staircase physically to show it closes, then unfold several different valid nets from the same cube so the child sees 'there are eleven, not one'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rejects the valid staircase net and accepts near-prototype look-alikes, justifying by resemblance rather than folding

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges by the number of faces, not their arrangement — 'it has six squares so it must fold into a cube'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fold the block so the child sees two squares overlap and two faces missing; mark a base face and track where each square lands
errorPatterns.distractor: The 2-by-3 block of six squares — 'six squares, so it makes a cube'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Accepts the 2-by-3 rectangular block of six squares

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot predict the fold direction of an L-shape or line, so mis-assigns which faces meet — thinks a face is 'stuck in the corner' or that two squares that should be opposite end up adjacent
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor a base and fold the 'line of four' to wrap the sides, then place the last two as top and bottom, narrating each square's destination
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked which faces become opposite, names adjacent squares, or loses track of a face while folding the staircase

responseLevels.gap: Judges nets by whether they look like the usual cube net; accepts or rejects on appearance and cannot say which faces meet.
responseLevels.full: Anticipates the fold by anchoring a base and tracking composites, identifies opposite faces, explains why an invalid arrangement fails, and generates a genuinely different valid net — transferring the reasoning to the square-based pyramid.
responseLevels.partial: Correctly folds the familiar nets and names faces one at a time, but cannot coordinate a composite (e.g. predict the L-shape's fold) or reliably produce a new valid net — listing the squares without tracking how they act on each other.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are three flat arrangements of six squares: the usual cross-shaped net, a 2-by-3 block of six squares, and a 'staircase' zig-zag net. For each one, tell me whether it will fold into a closed cube and how you know — point to which square becomes the top and which two faces end up opposite each other. Then draw me a different arrangement of six squares that also folds into a cube.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child reasoning structurally accepts the unfamiliar staircase and rejects the six-square block because folding makes two faces overlap and leaves two missing; a child reasoning by appearance does the opposite — trusting the block because 'six squares equals a cube' and rejecting the staircase because it doesn't look like the usual net. Requiring them to name opposite faces and to PRODUCE a new valid net cannot be faked by prototype-matching.
