pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 11–12: recognise and USE relationships between operations, especially INVERSE operations (+/−, ×/÷, squaring/square-rooting), to check answers and simplify calculations — the formal foundation for solving and rearranging equations.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, KS3): 'recognise and use relationships between operations, including inverse operations' and use inverse operations/estimation to check calculations.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): builds on the inverse relationship of ×÷ (3.OA.6, unknown-factor division) and of +−, extended toward 6.EE.5–7 (solving one-step equations by inverse) and squaring/rooting (8.EE.2).
• Operational details — make explicit that each operation is UNDONE by its inverse: add↔subtract, multiply↔divide, square↔square-root. Use this two ways: (i) CHECK a result (compute 156÷12 = 13, verify 13×12 = 156), and (ii) SOLVE for an unknown by applying the inverse to isolate it (□ + 7 = 20 → □ = 20 − 7). Emphasise 'doing the same to both sides' and the balance/equation model. This is the bridge to linear equations (dependent mt_QhFEDyIwSO) and rearranging formulae (mt_3qrCtdoVAU).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 11): use ×÷ as inverses to check a calculation. Tier B (11–12): solve a one-step unknown by applying the inverse and justify it. Tier C (12): recognise squaring and square-rooting as inverses and use inverse operations to check a multi-step result.
bestPractices: Make CHECKING routine: after any calculation, undo it with the inverse (13×12 to check 156÷12) — embedding inverse relationships as a self-verification habit, connecting to estimation-checking.

Use the BALANCE / equation model — whatever you do to one side you do to the other — so applying an inverse is seen as keeping equality, not a trick; build from fact families and bar models already secured.

Teach inverse operations in ORDER-OF-OPERATIONS reverse when unpicking multi-step expressions (undo +/− outer layer, then ×÷), foreshadowing equation rearrangement — the prerequisite BODMAS understanding (mt_jHgRQ4hR0g) is exactly why the undo order matters.
Include squaring↔square-rooting as an inverse pair, noting the ± subtlety (√ of a square recovers the magnitude), to broaden 'inverse' beyond the four basic operations.
Use empty-box and function-machine tasks (input→×3→+2→output; run backwards to find the input) so inverse becomes 'run the machine in reverse'.
keyRepresentations: Function machine run forwards and BACKWARDS, each step replaced by its inverse in reverse order.
Balance-scale / equation model showing the same inverse applied to both sides to isolate the unknown.
Fact-family triangle (a, b, a×b) linking a multiplication to its two divisions — inverse made concrete.
Inverse-pair chart: + ↔ −, × ↔ ÷, square ↔ √.
commonMisconceptions: Undoing operations in the WRONG order (undoing the × before the + in a two-step machine) — not reversing the order of operations.
Applying the inverse to only one side of an equation, breaking the balance.
Confusing inverse (undo) with commutative/associative relationships, or thinking subtraction 'undoes' multiplication.
Believing squaring and square-rooting are perfect inverses without the ± / non-negative subtlety.
Treating 'inverse' as merely reversing the numbers (12÷156 to check 156÷12) rather than applying the inverse operation.

learn.summary: For ages 11–12, teach inverse operations (add↔subtract, multiply↔divide by a non-zero number, square↔square-root for non-negative numbers) as a way to UNDO calculations — both to check results and to solve for an unknown by isolating it. Core principles: undoing a multi-step process reverses both the operations AND their order (last done, first undone); and 'do the same to both sides' keeps an equation balanced. This is the concrete foundation for solving and rearranging equations. Build the do/undo intuition through function-machine and balance-scale work, then consolidate and probe reasoning.

activities.title: Function machine: run it forwards, then run it backwards
feedback: If a learner reverses the operations but keeps the forward order, have them compare the two attempts numerically: only 'undo +2, then ÷3' returns the start value. Rehearse with a second two-step example.
If they only swap the numbers (e.g. 12÷156 to 'check' 156÷12), point out that an inverse changes the OPERATION, not just the order of the numbers.
Reinforce with a fact-family triangle (a, b, a×b) so the undo is concrete: one multiplication and its two divisions live in the same triangle.
activities.rationale: Running a function machine forwards and then backwards makes 'undo in reverse order' a felt consequence rather than a stated rule, directly confronting the common error of reversing operations without reversing their order.
sourceClaims: The balance/equation model and function machines run in reverse make inverse operations and 'do the same to both sides' explicit, bridging to solving and rearranging equations.
learnerActions: Build a two-step machine, e.g. '×3 then +2'. Drop in an input (say 5) and record the output (17).
Now recover the original input WITHOUT being told it: work out which operation to undo first and which second. (Undo +2 first → 15, then ÷3 → 5.)
Deliberately try undoing in the forward order instead (÷3 first, then −2) and check whether you get back the start number. Notice it does NOT return 5 — this shows why the order must reverse.
State the rule in your own words: to undo a chain, reverse both the operations and their order (last done is first undone).

If a live model is available, flip the machine into REVERSE mode so each step is automatically swapped for its inverse and reordered, and compare it with a manual attempt that undoes the steps in the forward order; that wrong-order attempt visibly fails to return the starting value.
activities.intendedInsight: Each operation is undone by its inverse, and to undo a sequence you must reverse BOTH the operations and their order.

activities.title: Balance scale: solving one-step unknowns by keeping both sides equal
feedback: If a learner changes only one side, use the tilting balance (or draw the scale tipping) to show equality is broken; redo applying the inverse to both sides.
If they pick the wrong inverse (e.g. add 7 to solve □ + 7 = 20), ask what operation currently acts on □ and what undoes it.
Connect to fact families and bar models already secured so the move feels familiar.
activities.rationale: The balance model represents applying an inverse as maintaining equality, addressing the misconception of operating on only one side and building the bridge to formal equation solving.
sourceClaims: Division is defined as an unknown-factor problem (the inverse of multiplication), and one-step equations are solved by applying inverse operations while maintaining equality.
The balance/equation model and function machines run in reverse make inverse operations and 'do the same to both sides' explicit, bridging to solving and rearranging equations.
learnerActions: Look at a balance representing □ + 7 = 20. Decide which inverse isolates the unknown (subtract 7).
Apply that inverse to BOTH sides and read off □ = 20 − 7 = 13.
Try applying the inverse to only one side and predict what happens to the balance — it tilts, because the two sides are no longer equal.
Repeat with a multiplication case, e.g. 3·□ = 21 (divide both sides by 3 → □ = 7).
Explain why 'do the same to both sides' keeps the statement true.
activities.intendedInsight: Applying an inverse isolates the unknown, and doing it to both sides preserves equality — it is not a trick but a consequence of keeping the balance level.

activities.title: Checking a calculation by undoing it
feedback: If a learner checks by redoing the same operation, show that the same error (especially a method error) is likely to reappear; the inverse (×) tests the result more independently.

If they invert incorrectly — for example repeating the same division, or multiplying an unrelated/wrong pair such as 156 × 12 instead of computing the correct 13 × 12 — build the fact-family triangle for the three numbers so the correct check is visible. (Note: dividing the dividend by the quotient, 156 ÷ 13 = 12, is actually a valid alternative check, so do not treat it as an error.)
For squaring/rooting, note the ± / non-negative subtlety so learners do not treat them as perfectly symmetric inverses.
activities.rationale: Embedding inverse-checking as a self-verification routine consolidates the relationship and connects to estimation-checking, while addressing the error of 'checking' by repeating the same operation.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils recognise and use relationships between operations including inverse operations, and use inverse operations and estimation to check calculations.
learnerActions: Compute a division such as 156 ÷ 12 = 13.
Check it by applying the inverse: 13 × 12. Confirm it returns exactly 156.

Discuss why re-dividing (156 ÷ 12 again) is a weaker check: repeating the same operation tends to repeat the same mistake (especially a mistake in method), whereas the inverse is a more independent check.
Try a square/root pair: check √49 = 7 by squaring (7² = 49). Note the subtlety that √ of a square recovers the non-negative magnitude.
Make checking a habit: after any calculation, undo it with its inverse.
activities.intendedInsight: Inverse operations provide an independent verification of a result; redoing the same operation does not.

activities.title: Talk it through: how would you check that, and which inverse isolates it?
feedback: If the learner only says 'do the division again', prompt: what operation would UNDO the division? Steer toward multiplication and have them explain why it is independent.
If they reverse a two-step calculation but keep the order, rehearse 'last done, first undone' with the ×3-then-+4 example.
Listen for the reason, not just the right calculation: a strong response names multiplication and division as inverses that undo each other.
activities.rationale: A relational idea like inverse operations is well probed by questioning that elicits the learner's reasoning about undoing, including reversing the order of steps, surfacing whether a learner checks by inverse or merely by repeating; questioning may elicit this reasoning but does not by itself guarantee it.
learnerActions: A child worked out 138 ÷ 6 = 23. Without redoing the division, say what single calculation would CHECK whether 23 is right, and explain why that check works.
Answer and justify: multiply 23 × 6; if it returns 138 the answer is right, because multiplication undoes division.
Respond to the probe: 'Someone checked 138 ÷ 6 by dividing again and got 23 — does that prove it is right?' Explain why repeating the same operation is not an independent check.
Tackle a two-step undo: 'If I did ×3 then +4 to a number, how would you get back to the start?' (Undo +4 first, then ÷3.)
Consider squaring/rooting: how would you check √49 = 7?
activities.intendedInsight: Verbalising the inverse relationship — naming the OPPOSITE operation and why undoing works — distinguishes genuine understanding from merely re-running a procedure.

activities.title: Consolidation: match, sequence and solve
feedback: Matching and sequencing confirm recall but do not by themselves build the do/undo intuition — pair them with at least one 'explain why' prompt so reasoning is exercised, not only recognition.
If undo order is sequenced wrongly, send the learner back to a function machine to test the sequence numerically.
activities.rationale: Recognition and fill-in tasks are efficient for consolidation once the do/undo intuition is built; they test rather than construct it, so they follow the hands-on and dialogic activities.
learnerActions: Match each operation to its inverse: + ↔ −, × ↔ ÷ (by a non-zero number), square ↔ √ (for non-negative numbers).
Given a two-step machine, put the undo steps in the correct reverse order.
Fill in the solving step for one-step unknowns, e.g. □ + 7 = 20 → □ = 20 − 7.
Explain, for at least one item, WHY the chosen inverse is correct, not just which it is.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent recall of inverse pairs and correct reverse-order undoing supports later equation work.

constraints: Matching, sequencing and fill-in-the-blank tasks assess recall and recognition; they do not by themselves elicit the independent construction of a check or the felt experience of reversing order, so they are best used to consolidate rather than introduce the idea.

A static labelled diagram of a function machine or balance can serve as a reference, but it cannot let the learner run the chain backwards or see the balance tilt when only one side is changed; those consequences are what make the rule stick.
Treat squaring and square-rooting as inverses WITH the non-negative/± subtlety: √ of a square returns the magnitude. Do not present them as perfectly symmetric inverses.
To undo a multi-step calculation, reverse both the operations AND their order; reversing operations while keeping the forward order is a common and specific error to confront directly.
An inverse changes the operation, not merely the order of the numbers (12 ÷ 156 is not the inverse check of 156 ÷ 12).

A valid inverse check of 156 ÷ 12 = 13 can be either 13 × 12 = 156 or 156 ÷ 13 = 12; both independently recover a known quantity. The genuine error is repeating the same division or multiplying an unrelated pair.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 5→×3→15→+2→17, and undoing 17→−2→15→÷3→5 is correct; undoing in forward order (17÷3≈5.67, then −2) does not return 5, confirming order must reverse. 156 ÷ 12 = 13 and 13 × 12 = 156 check out. 138 ÷ 6 = 23 and 23 × 6 = 138 are correct. 3·□ = 21 → □ = 7 is correct. √49 = 7 and 7² = 49 are correct.

The original assessment probe asks 'Why does multiplying 23 by 6 check the division' — correct, since 23 × 6 = 138. A source distractor listed '138 × 6' (=828) as a wrong check, which is genuinely wrong and is retained only as an error pattern, never as a valid check.

The original assessment error pattern lists 'divides 138 by 23' (and an analogous '156 ÷ 13') as a wrong inverse. This is a questionable original example: dividing the dividend by the quotient recovers the divisor and is in fact a valid independent check. The corrected feedback uses genuinely wrong moves (repeating the same division, or multiplying an unrelated/wrong pair) instead, and this is noted in the activity feedback itself, not only here.

Activity 4 (dialogic probing) carries no sourceClaim: the available claims support function-machine/balance representations, not the efficacy of Socratic questioning, so [] is used. Efficacy of the questioning approach is proposed, not established.

The balance model is a representation of equality maintenance; it is offered as an effective scaffold, not as the only possible way to teach inverse operations. Comparative efficacy/necessity is not established by the available sources.

probeDeeper: Why does multiplying 23 by 6 check the division, instead of dividing again?
Squaring and square-rooting — are those inverses too? How would you check √49 = 7?
If I did '×3 then +4' to a number, how would you undo it to get back to the start?
Someone checked 138÷6 by dividing again and got 23 again — does that prove it's right? Why not?
assess.correctAnswer: Multiply 23 × 6 and see if you get 138 (you do, so it's correct). It works because multiplication and division are inverse operations — multiplying the quotient by the divisor undoes the division and must return the original number. A child reasoning well names the inverse relationship, not just 'do it again'.

errorPatterns.pattern: checks by repeating the SAME operation (divides 138÷6 again) rather than using the inverse
errorPatterns.nextMove: show that redoing repeats any mistake; the inverse (×) is an independent check because it undoes the division. Use a fact-family triangle to make the undo visible.
errorPatterns.distractor: Divide 138 by 6 again to see if you get 23 the second time
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child says 'do the division again'; cannot offer multiplication as the check

errorPatterns.pattern: picks the wrong inverse or inverts incorrectly — e.g. divides 138 by 23, or multiplies 138×6
errorPatterns.nextMove: build the fact family for 138, 6, 23; the check multiplies the two SMALLER results to recover the original.
errorPatterns.distractor: Work out 138 × 6 to check
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child multiplies the wrong pair or divides again by the quotient

errorPatterns.pattern: over-generalises 'inverse undoes' but mishandles order in multi-step or non-commutative cases (thinks subtraction/division order doesn't matter when undoing)
errorPatterns.nextMove: stress that to undo a sequence you reverse BOTH the operations AND their order (last done, first undone); rehearse with a two-step example.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: when asked to undo a two-step calculation, child reverses the operations but not their order

responseLevels.gap: checks by repeating the same operation, or applies the wrong inverse; no notion of undoing.
responseLevels.full: selects the inverse operation to check independently, explains that inverses undo each other, and correctly reverses both operations and order in multi-step cases (incl. squaring/rooting).
responseLevels.partial: uses the correct inverse for a single-step check but cannot articulate why undoing works, or mishandles order when undoing a two-step calculation.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A child worked out 138 ÷ 6 = 23. Without redoing the division, how could you CHECK whether 23 is right? Tell me what calculation you'd do and why that check works.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who merely knows procedures suggests re-dividing (repeating the same operation, which repeats the same error). A child who holds the inverse relationship reaches for the OPPOSITE operation to check, and can say why undoing works. The reason-tier distinguishes 'check by redoing' from 'check by inverse'.

sources.claim: KS3 pupils recognise and use relationships between operations including inverse operations, and use inverse operations and estimation to check calculations.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (Key Stage 3)

sources.claim: Division is defined as an unknown-factor problem (the inverse of multiplication), and one-step equations are solved by applying inverse operations while maintaining equality.
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, 3.OA.6 and 6.EE.5–7 (with 8.EE.2 for square/root inverses)

sources.claim: The balance/equation model and function machines run in reverse make inverse operations and 'do the same to both sides' explicit, bridging to solving and rearranging equations.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 12–14 — use approximation through rounding to estimate answers and calculate possible resulting errors; express error intervals using inequality notation a < x ≤ b; understand upper and lower bounds of rounded values.
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics, KS3): 'use approximation through rounding to estimate answers and calculate possible resulting errors expressed using inequality notation a < x ≤ b.'
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): relates to 7.EE.B.3 (estimate to check reasonableness) and high-school N.Q.A (accuracy, error, appropriate quantities); explicit bound-interval notation is more prominent in UK than US.
• Operational details: A rounded value stands for a RANGE: a measurement given to the nearest unit lies within half a unit either side (a length 'to the nearest cm' of 12 cm means 11.5 ≤ x < 12.5). Find lower and upper bounds as rounded-value ± half the rounding unit, and write the interval with the correct inclusive/exclusive symbols (lower bound included, upper bound excluded by convention). Use rounding to estimate calculation results and judge reasonableness.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 12): 'A mass is 5 kg to the nearest kg — give the smallest it could be.' Tier B: 'Write the error interval for a length of 24 cm measured to the nearest cm.' Tier C: 'Estimate 61.2 × 3.9 by rounding, then state whether your estimate is over or under and why.'
bestPractices: Treat a rounded value as representing a half-unit-wide interval, not a single exact number
Compute lower/upper bounds as value ± half the rounding unit, and use the a ≤ x < b convention (lower included, upper excluded)
Distinguish strict from inclusive symbols carefully at each bound
Use estimation (round each value) to check calculations and judge whether the estimate over- or under-shoots
Ground bounds in measurement contexts (the true length lies within the interval implied by the instrument's precision)
keyRepresentations: Number line with the rounded value central and the half-unit interval bracketed (open/closed ends)
Bound-bracket diagram: lower bound ●──rounded value──○ upper bound
Half-unit strip showing ±0.5 of the rounding unit
Estimation strips pairing rounded factors with exact values and over/under flags
commonMisconceptions: Treating a rounded measurement as exact (12 cm means exactly 12)
Using ± a whole unit rather than half a unit for the bounds
Getting the inclusive/exclusive symbols the wrong way round at the bounds
Assuming the upper bound is the rounded value itself (12.5 rounded to 12 but writing x ≤ 12)
Forgetting to halve the LAST place unit (nearest 10 → ±5, nearest 0.1 → ±0.05)

learn.summary: For ages 12–14: treat a rounded value as an interval on the number line that is one rounding unit wide (half a unit on each side), compute lower and upper bounds as value ± half the rounding unit, and write error intervals with the correct inclusive/exclusive convention for round-half-up (lower bound included, upper bound excluded, e.g. 11.5 ≤ x < 12.5). Also use rounding to estimate calculation results and judge whether an estimate over- or under-shoots, comparing with the exact value when the rounding directions conflict. The central insight is that a single rounded number stands for a RANGE, and the upper end is excluded because at exactly halfway it would round up to the next value.

activities.title: Bounds explorer on a number line
feedback: If the interval is sized ±1 (e.g. 11 to 13): the interval only reaches HALFWAY to each neighbour, so it is ±0.5 — 11.5 up to 12.5. Mark the midpoints between 12 and its neighbours.
If both ends are drawn closed: ask what 12.5 rounds to — it rounds up to 13, so 12.5 is excluded (open). The lower bound 11.5 rounds up to 12, so it IS included (closed).
If the ±5 / ±0.05 cases are missed: halve the LAST place unit — nearest 10 gives ±5, nearest 0.1 gives ±0.05.
activities.rationale: Bound intervals are spatial regions around a value; a manipulable number line with open/closed ends and a draggable true-value marker is intended to make both the half-unit width and the exclusion of the top end concrete, and dragging the marker to the top end to see it round up is intended to help with the misconception that the upper bound is included. This is a research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention.
learnerActions: Enter a rounded value and its rounding unit (e.g. 12 to the nearest cm).
Mark on a number line a closed point at the lower bound (11.5) and an open point at the upper bound (12.5), labelling the interval 11.5 ≤ x < 12.5.
Place a 'true measurement' marker anywhere inside the bracket and check it stays within the half-unit each side.
Drag the true marker to the open upper end and reason about what happens: 12.5 would round up to 13, so it is excluded from this interval.
Change the rounding unit to 'nearest 10' and redraw the bracket at ±5; try 'nearest 0.1' and redraw at ±0.05.
activities.intendedInsight: A single rounded number really stands for an interval one rounding unit wide, with half a unit on EACH side; the upper bound is the excluded (open) end of the bracket because exactly halfway rounds up to the next value.

activities.title: Writing and checking error intervals
feedback: Correct interval for 24 cm to nearest cm: 23.5 ≤ x < 24.5.
If both ends are inclusive (23.5 ≤ x ≤ 24.5): 24.5 rounds to 25, not 24, so it is excluded — use <. The lower end 23.5 rounds up to 24, so it is included — use ≤.
Smallest mass for 5 kg to nearest kg: 4.5 kg (included). There is no single largest value: the mass can be any value less than 5.5 kg, and 5.5 kg is the upper bound but is excluded.
If the top is written as ≤ the rounded value (x ≤ 24): the upper bound is 24.5, not 24 — the rounded value sits in the MIDDLE of the interval.
activities.rationale: Once the interval idea is built, stating bounds and writing intervals can be practised with short fill-in and multiple-choice style prompts, intended to consolidate the mixed ≤ / < convention. This format may consolidate and check, but does not by itself build the spatial interval idea, and recognising a correct interval is not the same as producing one.
learnerActions: Write the error interval for a length of 24 cm measured to the nearest cm, using inequality notation.
State the lower and upper bounds separately and choose the correct symbol at each end.
Answer: for a mass given as 5 kg to the nearest kg, what is the smallest it could be?
Explain why the top bound uses < and not ≤ by saying what that top value would round to.
activities.intendedInsight: Bounds are value ± half the rounding unit, and the two ends use different symbols: the lower bound is included (it rounds up into the value) and the upper bound is excluded (it would round up to the next value).

activities.title: Estimate by rounding and judge over/under
feedback: Sensible estimate for 61.2 × 3.9: round to 60 × 4 = 240. Here 61.2 was rounded down and 3.9 up, so the over/under direction is not obvious from rounding alone — compare with the exact value (238.68): the estimate 240 is slightly over.
Sensible estimate for 412 × 5.8: round each to one significant figure, 400 × 6 = 2400. Note 5.8 rounds UP to 6, not down to 5. (Exact is 2389.6, so this estimate is slightly over.)
If the 'estimate' is barely simpler than the exact calculation (e.g. keeping 412 as 412): round to one significant figure so the mental arithmetic is easy.
If 5.8 is rounded down to 5: 5.8 is closer to 6, so it rounds up.
activities.rationale: Estimation through rounding is a distinct procedural skill that supports checking reasonableness; pairing rounded factors with the exact result and flagging over/under is intended to make the effect of each rounding visible.
sourceClaims: 7.EE.B.3 and high-school N.Q.A: estimate to assess reasonableness and reason about accuracy and error in measured quantities.
KS3 pupils use approximation through rounding to estimate answers and calculate possible errors expressed using inequality notation a < x ≤ b.
learnerActions: Estimate 61.2 × 3.9 by rounding each factor sensibly, then check against the exact value to say whether your estimate is over or under the true answer, noting which factor was rounded up and which down.
Estimate 412 × 5.8 by rounding each factor to one significant figure, and state what you rounded each number to.
Compare your estimate with the exact value to find the direction of the error, and explain why the rounding alone could not tell you the direction when one factor was rounded up and the other down.
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding each value to a convenient figure gives a quick reasonableness check; when both positive factors round the same way the over/under direction of the product is clear, but when they round in opposite directions you must compare with the exact value to see the actual direction.

constraints: The half-unit applies to the LAST place of the rounding unit: nearest unit → ±0.5, nearest 10 → ±5, nearest 0.1 → ±0.05.
Use the convention lower bound included (≤) and upper bound excluded (<); keep the strict/inclusive symbols distinct at each end.

A static labelled bracket diagram (e.g. 11.5 ●─ 12 ──○ 12.5 with the convention annotated) can illustrate one case, but on its own does not let the learner test the top-end exclusion or vary the rounding unit — use it as an illustration, not the main investigation.

Fill-in / multiple-choice prompts can consolidate and check stating bounds and intervals, but do not by themselves build the spatial interval concept; recognising a correct interval is not the same as producing one.

A mentor question such as 'the sign says 12 cm to the nearest cm — what is the smallest and largest it could truly be?' can productively challenge the belief that 12 is exact, as a complement to manipulating the interval.

Estimation requires actually rounding to a convenient figure (ideally one significant figure) and comparing with the exact value; when the two factors round in opposite directions, do not assert a single over/under direction from the rounding alone — compare with the exact value.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched and both listed sources carry verified:false. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and efficacy wording in the rationales has been qualified accordingly.

Activities[0] and [1] have sourceClaims set to [] because no source claim directly supports their design/format rationales (interactive-makes-concrete; fill-in consolidation). The KS3 notation claim supports the curriculum topic only, which is already carried by the objective and constraints.

The original assessment text states the correct answer interval as '23.5 ≤ x < 24.5' while the topic/standard wording cites 'a < x ≤ b'. For a value rounded to the nearest unit under round-half-up, the lower bound rounds up into the value (included, ≤) and the upper bound would round up to the next value (excluded, <), giving 23.5 ≤ x < 24.5. The activities use this correct convention; the quoted standard's 'a < x ≤ b' ordering is reproduced only as the cited claim and may reflect a general notational illustration — flagged for reviewer attention.

The original probe 'Why is the upper bound 24.5 and not 24.49?' is sound: 24.5 is the boundary because every value up to but not including 24.5 rounds to 24; it is retained in spirit within the interval feedback.

For 61.2 × 3.9 the original asks whether the estimate is over or under; because one factor rounds down and the other up, the direction is not determinable from rounding alone — the activity directs comparing with the exact value (238.68), which shows the estimate 240 is slightly over.

probeDeeper: Why is the upper bound 24.5 and not 24.49?
Does 24.5 round to 24 or 25? So which inequality sign belongs at the top?
What did you round 412 and 5.8 to, and why those values?
assess.correctAnswer: 23.5 ≤ x < 24.5 (lower bound 23.5, upper bound 24.5); and about 400 × 6 = 2400.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the rounded value as exact, or sizes the interval by ±1 (23 to 25) instead of ±0.5
errorPatterns.nextMove: The interval reaches halfway to each neighbour: 23.5 up to 24.5. Mark the midpoints on a number line either side of 24.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: No interval is given, or bounds are 23 and 25.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses the wrong inequality at the top — 23.5 ≤ x ≤ 24.5 (including 24.5)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask what 24.5 rounds to (25, not 24), so 24.5 is excluded: 23.5 ≤ x < 24.5. The lower bound 23.5 rounds up to 24, so it IS included.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Both ends are inclusive.

errorPatterns.pattern: Rounds factors to over-precise or unhelpful values when estimating (e.g. keeps 412 as 412, or rounds 5.8 to 5)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Round each to one significant figure (400 and 6) for a quick check; note 5.8 rounds to 6.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The 'estimate' is barely simpler than the exact calculation, or 5.8 is rounded down.

responseLevels.gap: Treats the rounded value as exact or sizes the interval as ±1; estimates with no useful rounding.
responseLevels.full: States bounds as 23.5 ≤ x < 24.5 with correct signs and estimates by rounding each value sensibly.
responseLevels.partial: Gives a half-unit interval but muddles the ≤ / < convention, or rounds inconsistently when estimating.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set the task and watch the working: 'A length is measured as 24 cm to the nearest centimetre. Write its error interval using inequalities. Then estimate 412 × 5.8 by rounding, and say what you rounded each number to.' Watch the bounds and the inequality signs.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The rounded measurement forces the half-unit interval and the mixed ≤ / < convention (24.5 would round up, so it's excluded); the estimate checks sensible rounding of each factor. Watching reveals whether the child treats 24 as exact, mis-sizes the interval, or misuses the inequality signs.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 8-9. Count backwards through zero into negative numbers (5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0, −1, −2…), understand that negatives are less than zero, place them on a number line, and read them in context (temperature). The number line EXTENDS left past zero — the first genuinely new territory beyond the counting numbers.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 4): 'count backwards through zero to include negative numbers'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): formal integers are Grade 6 (6.NS.5-6), but temperature/number-line intuition is built earlier; treat this as pre-integer number-line reasoning.
• Operational details — Build negatives on a horizontal or (temperature-style) vertical number line, counting continuously down through zero so the sequence's symmetry about 0 is felt. Anchor to a real context — the thermometer is ideal — so 'below zero' has meaning. Stress that −2 is less than −1 (further from zero going left = smaller), which contradicts children's 'bigger digit = bigger' intuition. Avoid formal negative arithmetic here; focus on ordering, counting, and reading in context.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8, emerging): counts back through zero to −5 with a number line. Tier B (age 8-9, secure): places negatives on a line and reads temperatures below zero. Tier C (age 9, extending): orders negatives correctly (−5 < −2) and explains why, using the line.
bestPractices: Count continuously DOWN through zero on a number line so the symmetry about 0 is experienced, not stated.
Anchor to the thermometer / temperature context — the most intuitive real model of below-zero.
Explicitly confront the 'bigger digit = bigger' clash: −5 is LESS than −2 because it is further left/colder.
Use a vertical number line (thermometer) as well as horizontal so direction-of-decrease is felt two ways.
Keep to counting/ordering/reading in context; defer negative arithmetic (adding/subtracting integers) to later.
keyRepresentations: Horizontal number line extended left of zero
Vertical thermometer / temperature scale (below zero)
Number track counting down through zero
Real contexts: temperature, sea level, later bank balance/floors
Symmetry-about-zero image (mirror at 0)
commonMisconceptions: Thinking −5 > −2 because 5 > 2 (ignoring direction/order).
Believing zero is the smallest number, so negatives 'can't exist' or are 'just zero'.
Reading −3 as 'three' and losing the sign's meaning.
Miscounting across zero (skipping 0, or 1, 0, 1 back up).
Treating the minus as subtraction rather than a position/label below zero.

learn.summary: For ages 8-9: counting backwards through zero into negative numbers, placing negatives on a number line, and reading them in context (temperature). The core insight is that the number line extends left past zero, and that −5 is LESS than −2 because it lies further from zero on the negative side — directly confronting the 'bigger digit = bigger' intuition. Work stays with counting, ordering, and reading in context; formal negative arithmetic is deferred. The primary vehicle is a number-line/thermometer activity the child drives, with reference images and conversational context as supports.

activities.title: Count down through zero on a thermometer line
feedback: If the child reverses upward at zero (0 then 1 again), extend the line/thermometer visibly below zero and re-count −1, −2, −3 so the continuation is seen; do not accept 'nothing is below zero'.
If the child says numbers stop at zero, anchor in a real below-zero context (temperature, floors below ground) so numbers less than zero are legitimate.
If the child reads −3 as 'three', pause and have them say 'negative three / three below zero' so the minus is read as a position/label below zero, not as a subtraction to carry out.
activities.rationale: Counting continuously down through zero lets the unbroken continuation past zero be experienced rather than merely stated, and the thermometer gives 'below zero' a concrete meaning. A horizontal line offers a second felt direction of decrease. A live, learner-driven scale (dragging the marker so the reading updates past zero) can make the continuation vivid, though a reference image or spoken counting can also support this.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'count backwards through zero to include negative numbers'.
The temperature/thermometer context and continuous counting through zero address the persistent −5>−2 ordering misconception.
learnerActions: Start at a reading (e.g. 3°C) on a vertical thermometer (or a horizontal number line) and count the marker down continuously: 3, 2, 1, 0, −1, −2, −3, watching it pass zero in one unbroken descent rather than stopping or bouncing.
Narrate each step aloud, including the names of the negatives as the marker crosses zero.
Repeat the descent on a horizontal number line, moving steadily left through zero, to feel that the decrease keeps going in the same direction past zero (toggle between the two if available).
Then count back UP through zero from a negative start (e.g. −4, −3, −2, −1, 0, 1) to check the sequence works both ways.
activities.intendedInsight: Below-zero numbers are a genuine continuation of the counting sequence, not a separate set; the line extends left/below zero, and counting down keeps going in the same direction past zero. Only the number names repeat as mirror images (1 and −1, 2 and −2), and each step down still gives a smaller number.

activities.title: Order negatives: colder is lower is smaller
feedback: If the child ranks −5 as larger because 5 > 2, walk both onto a horizontal number line: −5 sits further left, and further left means smaller, so −5 < −2 even though 5 > 2.
Reinforce with the thermometer image: a lower reading is colder, and colder is a smaller temperature.
If the child names 0 as the smallest possible number, use a below-zero context so numbers less than zero are accepted as comparable.
activities.rationale: The −5 vs −2 comparison is the central misconception, so it deserves dedicated ordering practice with an explanation, not just the correct label. Tying 'smaller' to position (further left / further below zero / colder) gives the child a stable rule that survives the digit-size clash. A drag-to-order interaction where −5 correctly lands below −2 with 'colder = lower = smaller' feedback can make the mechanism concrete; ordering on paper with stated reasons works too.
sourceClaims: The temperature/thermometer context and continuous counting through zero address the persistent −5>−2 ordering misconception.
learnerActions: Given numbers such as −5, −2, 0, 3, place each on the scale and arrange them smallest to largest.
Specifically compare −2 and −5: place both and decide which is smaller, stating a reason.
Explain in words why −5 is smaller than −2 even though 5 is bigger than 2 — e.g. 'it is further below zero / further left / colder'.
Answer context questions: Is −10°C warmer or colder than −2°C? Which is bigger, −1 or 0?
activities.intendedInsight: On the negative side, further from zero (further left / lower / colder) means SMALLER, so −5 < −2, reversing the digit-size intuition.

activities.title: Predict-then-check: drop below zero
feedback: A child expecting numbers to stop predicts 0 or 'it can't go lower'; show the continuation below zero and re-count through zero to −2.
A child who predicts −2 and justifies by continuing past zero (…1, 0, −1, −2) has the target understanding; ask them to explain the crossing point.
Follow-up probes: What comes after −3 if I keep counting back? If I started at −4 and counted up through zero, what would I say?
activities.rationale: A predict-then-check task surfaces the 'numbers stop at zero' and magnitude-ordering misconceptions through the child's stated reason before the answer is revealed, making the diagnostic value come from the justification rather than the final label.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'count backwards through zero to include negative numbers'.
learnerActions: Set a thermometer to 3°C. Before moving anything, predict the reading after it drops 5 degrees, and say WHY.
Commit to the prediction and reason out loud (the reasoning is the important part).
Then slide/count the marker down 5 steps through zero to check against the prediction.
Discuss any mismatch: where did the count cross zero, and what came after?
activities.intendedInsight: Counting down past zero from 3 by 5 reaches −2 (3 − 5 = −2); numbers do not stop at zero, and predicting forces the child to apply the continuation rather than read it off.

activities.title: Negatives in the real world (context talk)
feedback: If the child treats −20 as warmer than −5 because 20 > 5, return to the thermometer: −20 is lower, so colder and smaller.
Keep the focus on ordering and reading; do not drift into adding/subtracting negatives.
activities.rationale: Context motivates and reinforces, and reading real sub-zero values gives extra ordering practice; the ordering rule itself is secured on the line, so context work supports and applies the idea rather than being the only route to it.
learnerActions: Discuss or read about places and situations with below-zero values: last night's temperatures, a polar region at −20°C vs −5°C, sea level, floors below ground.
Decide which of two sub-zero values is colder/lower and justify using the line idea.
Match a few real readings (e.g. fridge, freezer, a frosty morning) to positions on a thermometer scale.
activities.intendedInsight: Negative numbers describe real quantities below a chosen zero, giving the abstract line a meaningful anchor and extra ordering practice.

constraints: Keep to counting, ordering, and reading negatives in context; defer formal negative arithmetic (adding/subtracting integers) to later.
Explicitly confront the 'bigger digit = bigger' clash: −5 is less than −2 because it is further left / lower / colder.

A static thermometer or number-line poster is a useful reference and can support counting, but cannot itself be dragged or stepped; pair it with active ordering/counting on a line rather than relying on it alone.
Conversation/context framing (e.g. a polar scientist) can motivate and give extra ordering practice, but should not be the sole route to the ordering concept.
US note: formal integers are Grade 6 (CCSS-M 6.NS.5-6); for this age treat the work as pre-integer number-line and temperature intuition.
When counting across zero, guard against skipping 0 or bouncing (1, 0, 1); ensure zero is named as a step and the sequence continues below it.
reviewNotes: Independent editorial review performed on the saved teaching research; sources were not re-fetched and no fresh source verification, human review, or empirical effectiveness testing occurred. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of three cited sources (CCSS-M Grade 6; NCETM guidance) were marked verified:false in the source row; the DfE Year 4 claim was marked verified:true. Evidence strength is unchanged and not independently confirmed here.

The CCSS-M Grade 6 claim is retained only as standards-placement context (US constraint); it is correctly not used as a sourceClaim for the context activity, because it does not establish that activity's teaching principle (context supports while ordering is secured on the line).

The original noted 3D 'adds nothing'. That is a catalog-fit judgement, not an established pedagogical law; a 3D treatment is simply not needed because the concept is essentially one-dimensional (a line/scale). Softened accordingly.
Arithmetic check: starting at 3°C and dropping 5 degrees gives −2°C (3 − 5 = −2); matches the source and the predict-then-check activity.
Ordering checks: −5 < −2 is correct (further from zero on the negative side is smaller); −10°C and −20°C are colder/smaller than −2°C and −5°C respectively.

The 'minus read as subtraction' misconception from the source is covered only indirectly via the sign-meaning feedback in the first activity; it could warrant a more explicit treatment if expanded later.

assess.poeTask: Set a model thermometer to 3°C. Before moving anything, ask the child to predict the reading after it drops 5 degrees and to say why. A child who thinks numbers stop at zero predicts 0 (or 'it can't go lower'); a child who understands negatives predicts −2. Then slide the marker down through zero to check — the pre-observation reason is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: If I keep counting back, what comes after −3?
On a thermometer, is −10°C warmer or colder than −2°C — why?
Which is bigger, −1 or 0? How can you tell?
What if I started at −4 and counted UP through zero — what would I say?
assess.correctAnswer: After 0 comes −1, −2, −3 … −5 is smaller than −2 because it is further below zero (further left on the number line).

errorPatterns.pattern: Orders negatives by magnitude — '−5 is bigger than −2 because 5 is bigger than 2'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Walk both on a horizontal number line; show −5 sits further left, and 'smaller' means further left, so −5 < −2 even though 5 > 2.
errorPatterns.distractor: −2 is smaller, because 2 is less than 5.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child ranks −5 as the larger / −2 as the smaller, reasoning from the digits.

errorPatterns.pattern: Numbers stop at (or bounce off) zero — after 0 the child says 1 again, treating zero as the floor.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Extend the number line and a thermometer below zero so the sequence −1, −2, −3 is seen as a real continuation; do not accept 'nothing is below zero'.
errorPatterns.distractor: After 0 you go back up to 1.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Counting back reaches 0 and then reverses upward, or child says 'you can't go past zero'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Zero-as-smallest — believes 0 is the least possible number, so there is no answer 'below' it.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a context that clearly goes below zero (temperature, floors below ground) to establish numbers less than zero as legitimate.
errorPatterns.distractor: Zero — it's the smallest, nothing is less.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child names 0 as the smallest number when asked, or refuses to compare negatives.

responseLevels.gap: Stops or bounces at zero, or orders negatives purely by digit size.
responseLevels.full: Continues the sequence past zero and orders negatives by position on the number line, justifying that further-left / further-below-zero means smaller, and applies it in context (temperature).
responseLevels.partial: Counts back through zero correctly but reverts to magnitude reasoning when comparing two negatives (−5 vs −2).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Count back from 3, out loud: 3, 2, 1, 0 ... what comes next? And which is smaller, −2 or −5? How do you know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands the number line continues past zero into negatives and knows −5 is smaller because it is further from zero the other way. A child treating negatives as ordinary numbers picks −2 as smaller (2<5), and a child who thinks numbers stop at zero bounces back to 1. The justification, not the label, reveals which.

sources.claim: Year 4 pupils should 'count backwards through zero to include negative numbers'.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (Year 4 Number & place value)

sources.claim: Understanding integers and their ordering on the number line (negatives as positions less than zero) is formalised in Grade 6 (6.NS.5-6), with earlier temperature intuition.
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, The Number System, Grade 6

sources.claim: The temperature/thermometer context and continuous counting through zero address the persistent −5>−2 ordering misconception.
sources.source: NCETM Primary Mastery PD: Number / negative numbers guidance

pedagogy.summary: This is the shared LANGUAGE of the fraction–decimal–percentage world: the terms decimal, decimal point, tenths/hundredths/thousandths, per cent and the % symbol, convert, terminating decimal — and, crucially, the understanding that a fraction, a decimal and a percentage are THREE NOTATIONS FOR ONE VALUE (1/2 = 0.5 = 50%). Fluency here is not reciting definitions but USING the words correctly in context: reading 0.09 as 'nine hundredths' (not 'point oh nine'), reading 50% as 'fifty out of a hundred', and moving between the three forms as names for the same amount. The place-value reading of decimals and the 'out of 100' meaning of per cent are the load-bearing habits; sloppy digit-string reading ('point oh nine') is where meaning leaks away.
bestPractices: Teach the three forms together as one value using a single quantity shown four ways — a shaded hundred square, the fraction (with denominator 100), the decimal, and a position on a 0%–100% number line — so 1/2, 0.5 and 50% are visibly the same.
Insist on place-value reading of decimals: 0.09 is 'nine hundredths', 0.7 is 'seven tenths', never 'point oh nine' or 'point seven', so the digits keep their meaning.
Model correct percentage language: per cent means 'out of / for every hundred'; 100% is the whole; write 'X% of N', never the bare 'X% = value'.
Use real contexts (sales '50% off', a half-full jug, test scores out of 100) and ask children to state the same fact as a fraction, a decimal and a percentage.
Introduce 'terminating decimal' and 'convert' as working vocabulary in the act of converting, so the words are attached to actions rather than defined in isolation.
keyRepresentations: Four-way display: shaded hundred square + fraction (n/100) + decimal + point on a 0%–100% number line
0–1 / 0%–100% double number line linking the three forms
Place-value chart for reading decimals aloud (ones | tenths | hundredths | thousandths)
Real-context cards (50% off, jug 0.5 full, 3/4 of a pizza) matched across notations
Matching sets of fraction–decimal–percentage cards for one value
commonMisconceptions: Reading decimals as digit strings ('point oh nine', 'point seven') instead of place-value names ('nine hundredths', 'seven tenths').
Treating fraction, decimal and percentage as different, unrelated things rather than three names for one value.
Misusing percentage notation — writing '10% = 42' instead of '10% of 420 = 42'.
Reading the percentage number as the whole ('50% means 50') rather than as parts per hundred.
Confusing per cent (out of 100) with a plain count.

learn.summary: Teaches the shared language of fractions, decimals and percentages: that 1/2, 0.5 and 50% are three notations for ONE value, and that the words (tenths/hundredths/thousandths, per cent, % symbol, convert, terminating decimal) must be USED correctly in context, not just recited. The load-bearing habits are place-value reading of decimals (0.09 can be read 'nine hundredths'; the digit reading 'zero point zero nine' is also conventional, but the place-value name shows what it means) and the 'out of 100' meaning of per cent (writing '9% of £420 = £37.80', never '9% = £37.80', while equivalences such as '9% = 0.09' remain correct). The flagship activity ties one shaded quantity to its fraction, decimal, percentage and number-line position so all forms move together; alternatives (matching/diagnostic practice, explaining to a younger child, a labelled reference display) exercise and check the same vocabulary with different affordances.

activities.title: One quantity, three names — fill and watch them move together
feedback: If a learner reads 0.09 only as 'point oh nine', accept it as a valid digit reading, then point to the nine in the hundredths column and the 9/100 fraction and ask them to give the place-value name 'nine hundredths' too.
If a learner treats the forms as unrelated, highlight that one fill action moved all three labels and the number-line marker at once — one point, three names.
If a learner writes '9% = £37.80', recast as '9% OF £420 = £37.80' and show that 9% means 9 parts per hundred of the base £420, so 9% on its own is not £37.80.
activities.rationale: Manipulating a single quantity and watching the fraction, decimal, percentage and number-line marker update together couples the vocabulary to the relationship between representations, which is what using the terms in context requires. The live 'read it' voicing targets the digit-string misconception at the moment it would otherwise occur. This is a research-informed design proposal, not a tested intervention; a static or recorded display can also teach these links, though it cannot be re-driven from the learner's own action.
sourceClaims: Instruction should build the understanding that per cent means 'number of parts per hundred' and that percentages have fraction and decimal equivalents (three forms of one value); a documented notation error is writing 9% as 0.9 (remedied by reading 0.09 as 'nine hundredths' and 0.9 as 'nine tenths'), and pupils must write 'X% of N' rather than the bare 'X% = value'. Four parallel representations are recommended: the written percentage, a fraction with denominator 100, shading on a hundred square, and a position on a 0%–100% number line.
A percentage represents part of a quantity (an operator on a base), not a plain number; failing to keep this in view underlies base-neglect errors.
learnerActions: Fill a hundred square (or slide a bar) to show a chosen amount, e.g. drag to fill fifty squares.
Read the linked panel as it updates in lockstep: 50/100, 0.5, 50%, with a marker halfway along a 0%–100% number line.
Say the decimal aloud in place-value language ('five tenths, one half, fifty per cent'); use a 'read it' option to hear the correct reading.
Fill nine squares and confirm the panel reads 9/100, 0.09, 9% and voices the place-value name 'nine hundredths' alongside the digit reading 'zero point zero nine'.
Switch to context skins (a '9% off' price tag, a jug 0.5 full) and state the same fact as a fraction, a decimal and a percentage.
When finding part of an amount, practise saying and writing 'X% of N' (e.g. '9% of £420 = £37.80') rather than '9% = £37.80'; equivalences such as '9% = 0.09 = 9/100' are still correct.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction, a decimal and a percentage are not three separate topics but one quantity wearing three names; the correct place-value reading and the 'per cent = out of 100' meaning are visible in the same moment the learner acts.

activities.title: Match, read and complete — diagnostic usage practice
feedback: If 'nine tenths' or 'nine' is chosen for 0.09, state the place-value name 'nine hundredths' and point back to the hundredths place.
If equivalent forms are grouped wrongly, show the shared value on a hundred square or number line so the three cards name one point.
For '__% of 420 = 42', confirm 10% (since 1% of 420 = 4.20, so 10% of 420 = 42) and stress the phrase '10% OF 420'.
activities.rationale: Matching, reading-choice and fill-in tasks score correct usage and, with distractors drawn from the digit-string and base-neglect misconceptions, surface specific errors. They assess and rehearse usage rather than building the linked-representation habit, so they complement rather than replace the manipulable display.
sourceClaims: Instruction should build the understanding that per cent means 'number of parts per hundred' and that percentages have fraction and decimal equivalents (three forms of one value); a documented notation error is writing 9% as 0.9 (remedied by reading 0.09 as 'nine hundredths' and 0.9 as 'nine tenths'), and pupils must write 'X% of N' rather than the bare 'X% = value'. Four parallel representations are recommended: the written percentage, a fraction with denominator 100, shading on a hundred square, and a position on a 0%–100% number line.
A percentage represents part of a quantity (an operator on a base), not a plain number; failing to keep this in view underlies base-neglect errors.
learnerActions: Match cards so that each value's three forms are grouped, e.g. 1/2 ↔ 0.5 ↔ 50%.
Choose the correct place-value reading of a decimal, e.g. 'What is the place-value name for 0.09?' with 'nine tenths' or 'nine' offered as tempting wrong answers.
Complete 'X% of N' statements, e.g. fill the blank in '__% of 420 = 42'.
Sort a mixed set of cards by the single value each one names.
activities.intendedInsight: Correct use of the vocabulary is checkable: the right place-value reading, the right grouping of equivalent forms, and the correct 'X% of N' phrasing distinguish understanding from digit-string reading and base-neglect.

activities.title: Explain it to a younger child
feedback: If the learner says 'per cent means the number', prompt: 'out of how many?' to recover 'out of 100'.
If they claim 1/2 and 50% are different, ask them to shade half a hundred square and count the shaded squares as a percentage.
If they ignore the base when comparing 9% off and 50% off, ask '9% of what? 50% of what?' to surface that the amount depends on each item's price.
activities.rationale: Explaining a real sale or a half-full jug exercises genuine production of the vocabulary in context and can expose base-neglect. Spoken explanation does not display the forms updating together, so it supports practice alongside, not instead of, a representation that moves in lockstep.
sourceClaims: A percentage represents part of a quantity (an operator on a base), not a plain number; failing to keep this in view underlies base-neglect errors.
learnerActions: Explain a shop's '9% off' sign or a half-full jug to a younger character who asks 'what does per cent mean?' and 'is that the same as a half?'
Say a single quantity three ways (fraction, decimal, percentage) and read each aloud correctly.
Answer whether '9% off' could ever take off more money than '50% off', and say what it depends on (the base amount).
activities.intendedInsight: Being pressed to explain forces the learner to produce and justify the three forms and the 'parts per hundred of a base' meaning in their own words.

activities.title: Four-way reference display
feedback: When a reading is unsure, tap to hear the place-value name and compare it with the shaded square.
Use the 'per cent = out of 100' flap whenever a learner starts treating the percentage number as the whole.
activities.rationale: A fixed labelled display with tap-to-hear readings is a useful reference and models the four recommended representations. Because it shows one value at a time rather than being re-driven by the learner across many values, pair it with activities where the learner changes the quantity themselves.
sourceClaims: Instruction should build the understanding that per cent means 'number of parts per hundred' and that percentages have fraction and decimal equivalents (three forms of one value); a documented notation error is writing 9% as 0.9 (remedied by reading 0.09 as 'nine hundredths' and 0.9 as 'nine tenths'), and pupils must write 'X% of N' rather than the bare 'X% = value'. Four parallel representations are recommended: the written percentage, a fraction with denominator 100, shading on a hundred square, and a position on a 0%–100% number line.
learnerActions: Study one value shown four ways at once: shaded hundred square, fraction with denominator 100, decimal, and a point on a 0%–100% number line.
Tap each form to hear its correct reading (e.g. 'nine hundredths').
Open the flap on 'per cent = out of 100' to check the meaning.
activities.intendedInsight: Having the four parallel representations of one value side by side, each with its correct reading, gives a stable reference for the shared-value idea and place-value language.

constraints: Insist that learners can give the place-value reading of decimals: 0.09 is 'nine hundredths', 0.7 is 'seven tenths'. Digit readings such as 'zero point zero nine' or 'point seven' are conventional and not wrong, but they do not show place value, so always ask for the place-value name as well.

When finding a percentage of an amount, always write 'X% of N' (e.g. '9% of £420 = £37.80'), never '9% = £37.80', including in worked feedback; per cent means parts per hundred of a base, and 100% is the whole. Equivalences between forms, such as '9% = 0.09 = 9/100' or '50% = 0.5 = 1/2', are correct and should be encouraged.
Treat the three forms as names for one value, not as separate topics; show them together on a shaded hundred square and/or a 0%–100% number line.
Introduce 'terminating decimal' and 'convert' as working vocabulary during the act of converting, attached to actions rather than defined in isolation.
Matching, multiple-choice and sorting tasks check correct usage but do not by themselves build the linked-representation habit; use them alongside an activity where the learner drives the change.
A fixed reference display shows one value at a time and cannot be re-driven by the learner; pair it with manipulable work across many values.
The target is USE in context, not reciting definitions; judge success by how a learner reads, writes and moves between forms with real quantities.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

One listed source (DfE National Curriculum, Years 4–6) carries verified:false in the row; treat its claim as unconfirmed, and it was removed from activity 1's sourceClaims as a general statutory-requirement assertion rather than direct support for that activity's design principle.
Self-audit: 1% of 420 = 4.20, so 9% of 420 = 37.80 and 10% of 420 = 42; these figures from the source row are arithmetically consistent and were used as given.

The original row asserted '3D adds no meaning' and that 'dialogue cannot show the forms moving together' as near-absolute claims; these have been softened to affordance-based statements (a conversation produces spoken usage but no synchronised display), since catalog fit ratings do not establish comparative necessity or medium superiority.

The source's own example '9% off could be more than 50% off depending on the base' holds only across different base prices; the activity frames it explicitly as depending on the amount each percentage is taken of.
Fixed earlier: activity 2 feedback had modelled the forbidden bare notation '10% = 42'; it now reads '10% of 420 = 42', consistent with the 'X% of N' rule stated everywhere else.

probeDeeper: Read these aloud for me: 0.7, 0.07, 0.75. Now which fraction is each one?
If I say a bottle is 0.25 full and you say it's a quarter full, are we disagreeing? Why not?
Is it ever right to write '50% = 10'? When — and how should it be written properly?
The coat is '9% off'. Could 9% off ever be MORE money than 50% off? On what would that depend?
assess.correctAnswer: Half full = 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%, read as 'one half', 'five tenths / nought point five', 'fifty per cent'. 9% means nine out of every hundred (of the price); as a decimal 0.09; the money off is 9% OF £420, i.e. £37.80 (children may reason 1% of 420 = 4.20, so 9% = 37.80). The key usage: '9% of £420', never '9% = £37.80'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads decimals as digit strings — '0.09 is point oh nine', '0.5 is point five' — with no place-value meaning.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model place-value reading ('nine hundredths', 'five tenths') and tie each to the hundred square / place-value chart; have the child re-read in those terms. Reteach in place (no prerequisite gap named).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reads decimals digit-by-digit; cannot say which fraction 0.09 or 0.5 is.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats fraction, decimal and percentage as different, unrelated things — does not accept 1/2, 0.5 and 50% as the same value.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show all three on one shaded hundred square / number line so they name one point; practise stating a single quantity three ways. Reteach in place.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives one form but cannot supply the others for the same amount, or denies they are equal.

errorPatterns.pattern: Misuses percentage notation — says '9% = £37.80' or '9% means 9', dropping the base.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist on 'X% OF N' phrasing; per cent is parts per hundred OF a quantity; contrast '9%' with '9% of £420'. Reteach in place.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes/says the percentage as a bare value without 'of the whole'; treats the % number as an absolute.

responseLevels.gap: Reads decimals as digit strings, treats the three forms as unrelated, and uses percentage as a bare number ('9% = 9'). Vocabulary is disconnected from meaning.
responseLevels.full: Reads decimals in place-value language, uses 'per cent'/'%' correctly as parts per hundred of a base ('9% of £420'), and treats fraction, decimal and percentage as three names for one value, converting between them in real contexts; transfers to unfamiliar quantities.
responseLevels.partial: Reads and writes each form and knows some equivalences (1/2 = 0.5 = 50%), but still reads a decimal as 'point five' rather than in place value, or cannot move fluently among all three forms in context.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A jug is half full. Give me three different ways to say how full it is — as a fraction, as a decimal, and as a percentage — and read each one aloud the proper way. Then: a shop sign says '9% off a £420 coat'. Say what 9% means here, write it as a decimal, and tell me how much money comes off.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Listening for USE, not definitions: a child with the language reads 0.5 and 0.09 in place-value terms, treats 1/2, 0.5, 50% as one value, and says '9% OF £420'. A child without it reads 'point oh nine', treats the three forms as separate, or says '9% = 37.80' / '9% means 9'. The half-full context forces the three-forms-one-value link; the sale context forces correct per-cent-of-a-base usage.

Four parallel representations are recommended: the written percentage, a fraction with denominator 100, shading on a hundred square, and a position on a 0%–100% number line.
