pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 8–9y; identify arithmetic patterns (in the addition/multiplication table) and EXPLAIN them using properties of operations — not just spot them.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y4–Y5 'recognise and use … patterns'; explaining patterns using properties supports reasoning across number.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.OA.9 — 'identify arithmetic patterns (including patterns in the addition table or multiplication table), and explain them using properties of operations. For example, observe that 4 times a number is always even, and explain why 4 times a number can be decomposed into two equal addends.'
• Operational details — the load-bearing verb is EXPLAIN. Children notice patterns (5s end in 0/5; the 9s digits sum to 9; even×anything is even; the multiplication table is symmetric across the diagonal) and then justify them using structure/properties: symmetry = commutativity; every-other-even in a row = the distributive/doubling structure; 5s pattern = 5=half of 10. This moves maths from 'noticing' to 'reasoning why', the heart of early mathematical argument. Use the multiplication square and colour/highlighting to surface patterns, then press for a structural explanation, not just a restatement.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8): spot a pattern (all 5s end in 0 or 5; the 2s are all even). Tier B (age 8–9): explain a pattern using structure ('4×n is always even because it's double 2n'). Tier C (age 9): explain the table's diagonal symmetry using commutativity and predict/extend a pattern.
bestPractices: Demand explanation, not just noticing — always ask 'why does that happen?' and accept a structural/property-based reason, not a restatement of the pattern.
Use the multiplication square with colour-coding to make patterns visible (shade multiples, the diagonal of squares, the symmetric pairs).
Link each pattern to its property: table symmetry → commutativity; 4×n even → doubling/distributive; 5s → half of 10s.
Encourage prediction — 'if the pattern holds, what comes next?' — then verify, building conjecture-and-check habits.
Connect number patterns to the addition table too, and to later shape/number sequence work.
keyRepresentations: Multiplication square with colour-coded multiples and the symmetry diagonal
Highlighted rows/columns showing within-table patterns (evens, 9s)
Array/doubling diagrams to justify 'even' and step patterns
Hundred square for multiples patterns
commonMisconceptions: Describing a pattern but 'explaining' it by restating it rather than giving a structural reason.
Over-generalising a pattern beyond where it holds without checking.
Missing that the multiplication table is symmetric (not linking it to commutativity).
Thinking a pattern is coincidence rather than a consequence of properties.
Confusing multiples patterns with place-value digit patterns without understanding the cause.

learn.summary: For 8–9 year olds: identify arithmetic patterns in the addition/multiplication tables AND explain them using the structure of operations — moving from 'noticing' to 'reasoning why'. The load-bearing verb is EXPLAIN: a child should justify a pattern using a structural reason (the table is symmetric because of commutativity, a×b = b×a; 4×n is even because it is double 2n; multiples of 5 end in 0 or 5 because 5 is half of 10 / each +5 step moves the ones digit between 5 and 0), not merely restate the observation. A colour-coded multiplication square that the learner can shade, fold across the diagonal and decompose makes the structure visible and interrogable; a Socratic 'why?' partner pushes explanation past description.

activities.title: Shade, fold and decompose the multiplication square
feedback: If the child only restates ('because it's the 5 times table'), press on the +5 step: show the ones digit going 5, 0, 5, 0 as you add five each time — that alternation is the reason.

If the child thinks a pattern might break for large multiples, reason from the repeating +5 step, which never changes, so the ones-digit cycle continues; test a large case such as 5×70 (=350) to reassure.

When the child folds the whole table onto itself and sees every cell meet its mirror, name the reason: the symmetry happens because of commutativity (a×b = b×a) — swapping the order of the two factors never changes the product, so each cell equals its mirror cell.
activities.rationale: Manipulating structure on the same surface where the pattern appears lets conjecture and justification happen together, supporting the standard's demand to explain patterns using properties of operations. A live interactive grid is one effective medium; a printed square the child shades and physically folds, an array/doubling diagram drawn by hand, or a hundred square with multiples of 5 highlighted serve the same purpose for surfacing and explaining multiples patterns.
sourceClaims: 3.OA.9 requires identifying arithmetic patterns and explaining them using properties of operations (e.g. 4×n is always even, decomposable into two equal addends).
The multiplication square's diagonal symmetry embodies commutativity; explaining (not just noticing) patterns builds early mathematical reasoning.
Y4–Y5 pupils recognise and use number patterns; explaining patterns via structure supports mathematical reasoning.
learnerActions: Shade a chosen times-table on a multiplication square (e.g. shade every multiple of 5) and describe what you notice about the digits — for 5s, every product ends in 0 or 5.
Fold or reflect the grid across its main diagonal so a cell like 7×8 lands exactly on 8×7; observe that every cell matches its mirror.
State WHY the table is symmetric: because 7×8 and 8×7 are the same product (commutativity).
Pick a 4×n cell and split it into two equal addends (2n + 2n) to show why 4×n is always even.
Use a 'predict the next' prompt: extend a shaded pattern one or two steps, say what you expect, then check against the grid.
activities.intendedInsight: A noticed pattern can be explained from the structure of the operation itself — the table's symmetry is a consequence (and a picture) of commutativity, and 'always even' follows from decomposing into equal addends — so maths patterns are consequences of properties, not coincidences.

activities.title: Be the pattern detective: tell me WHY
feedback: If the child justifies 'even + even = even' with only a couple of examples, distinguish spotting from proving: show that an even number can be made entirely of pairs (groups of two), so putting two evens together still gives only pairs, with none left over.
If the child restates rather than explains, reply 'you told me WHAT — now tell me WHY it must be so' and prompt for the operation's structure.
Accept the answer when the reason uses structure, not when it repeats the observation.
activities.rationale: Because the objective is EXPLAIN, a Socratic dialogue that repeatedly asks 'why?' and refuses restatement targets the reasoning gap of restating rather than justifying. Spoken or written back-and-forth can serve this; dialogue alone lacks a manipulable representation, so it pairs well with a visual grid the child can point to.
sourceClaims: The multiplication square's diagonal symmetry embodies commutativity; explaining (not just noticing) patterns builds early mathematical reasoning.
3.OA.9 requires identifying arithmetic patterns and explaining them using properties of operations (e.g. 4×n is always even, decomposable into two equal addends).
learnerActions: State a pattern you have spotted (e.g. 'multiples of 5 end in 0 or 5', 'the sum of two even numbers is always even').

When a 'mathematician' partner accepts only a structural reason, give the WHY: for 5s, each step adds 5 and two fives make a ten, so the ones digit lands back on 0; for even+even, each even is made of groups of two, so combining them still gives groups of two.
Explain the table's diagonal symmetry using commutativity, and predict whether a pattern will still hold for a large case (e.g. 5×100) and justify without computing it all.
activities.intendedInsight: An explanation names a cause grounded in properties; a few examples suggest a pattern, but a structural reason shows it must always hold.

activities.title: Match the pattern to its reason (check your explanation)
feedback: If a restatement distractor is chosen, highlight that it repeats the observation without giving a cause, then point to the decomposition that supplies the reason.
For a wrong 'next in sequence', return to the repeating step (e.g. +5) and re-derive the next entry.
activities.rationale: A recognition/matching task can specifically contrast explanation versus restatement and confirm prediction, which is useful for checking. Selecting an explanation verifies that a child recognises structural reasoning but does not itself elicit the child's own constructed justification; use it alongside tasks where the child states the reason in their own words.
sourceClaims: 3.OA.9 requires identifying arithmetic patterns and explaining them using properties of operations (e.g. 4×n is always even, decomposable into two equal addends).
learnerActions: Given a pattern, choose the correct explanation from options that include a tempting restatement distractor — e.g. 'Why is 4×n always even?' with a restatement ('because it's in the 4 times table') versus the doubling explanation ('because 4×n is 2n + 2n, two equal groups').
Predict the next entry in a shaded pattern on the table and check it.

Decide whether a stated related pattern (e.g. 'odd + odd is always even') is true and identify the structural reason or counter-reason — odd + odd is indeed always even, because each odd is a group of twos plus one, and the two extra ones pair up.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to select or reject explanations — not just spot patterns — checks whether reasoning is structural rather than a restatement.

constraints: Always demand a structural/property-based reason, not a restatement — ask 'why does that happen?' and accept only a cause (symmetry → commutativity; 4×n even → doubling/distributive; 5s → half of 10).

Multiple-choice or matching tasks verify whether a child can recognise a correct explanation; they do not elicit the child's own independently constructed reasoning, so pair them with tasks that require stating the reason.

A static DIGITAL tap-to-reveal multiplication square anchors and showcases patterns well but does not let the child fold or decompose cells on the same surface; supply physical folding of a paper square, hand-drawing, or an interactive fold/split tool so the child builds the explanation rather than only reading it. (A printed paper square, unlike a fixed digital image, can itself be folded along the diagonal.)
Paper/card cutouts of the square have real thickness and can be folded physically; a screen 'fold' is an idealised model of the same reflection — both represent the diagonal symmetry.
Guard against over-generalising a pattern beyond where it holds without checking, and against treating a pattern as coincidence rather than a consequence of properties.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source marks the CCSS-M 3.OA.9 claim and the NCETM claim as verified:false, and the DfE claim as verified:true; evidence strength is carried over unchanged and not independently confirmed here.

The original rated a third-dimension (3D) representation as adding no explanatory power for 2D-table patterns. This is a catalog fit judgement, not an established pedagogical law; it has been omitted rather than asserted as universal. A 2D representation is proposed on the observable affordance that these patterns are naturally arranged in a table.

Self-audit of examples: 4×n = 2n + 2n (two equal addends) is correct; multiples of 5 cycling the ones digit 0/5 via the +5 step is correct (e.g. 5×70 = 350, 5×100 = 500); table symmetry from commutativity (a×b = b×a) is correct; even+even via groups of two and odd+odd = even are correct. No arithmetic errors found in the migrated examples.

probeDeeper: Why does adding 5 each time make the last digit go 5, 0, 5, 0?
Will 5 × 100 still end in 0 or 5? How can you be sure without working it all out?
Why is the sum of two even numbers always even — can you explain, not just check?
How could commutativity explain why the multiplication table is symmetric?
assess.correctAnswer: Every multiple of 5 ends in 0 or 5. A child reasoning well explains WHY: adding 5 each time flips the ones digit between 0 and 5 (5→10 ones-digit 0, +5→15 ones-digit 5…), or because 5 is half of 10 so two fives make a full ten. The explanation, grounded in the structure, is the target — not just noticing the pattern.

errorPatterns.pattern: notices the pattern but explains it only by restating ('because it's the 5 times table') — no structural reason
errorPatterns.nextMove: prompt attention to the +5 step: show the ones digit going 5,0,5,0 as you add five each time; that alternation is the reason.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: when asked why, child repeats the observation rather than giving a cause

errorPatterns.pattern: believes the pattern is a coincidence that might break for large multiples
errorPatterns.nextMove: reason from the repeating +5 step, which never changes, so the ones-digit cycle continues forever; test a large case to reassure.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child is unsure whether 5×70 or 5×123 still ends in 0/5

errorPatterns.pattern: over-generalises 'even + even = even' or other table patterns without checking the property behind them
errorPatterns.nextMove: distinguish spotting from proving: a few examples suggest a pattern; a reason using properties (an even is two groups, so two evens combine into groups of two) explains it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child asserts a related pattern (e.g. sum of two evens) as true but justifies by a couple of examples, not structure

responseLevels.gap: cannot spot the pattern, or 'explains' only by restating the observation.
responseLevels.full: identifies the pattern AND explains it using the structure (repeated +5 flips the ones digit; properties of operations), generalising to large cases and to related table patterns.
responseLevels.partial: notices the pattern reliably and believes it always holds but justifies only by examples, without a structural reason.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Look at the 5 times table: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30... What do you notice about the last digit of every answer? Now tell me WHY that pattern happens — why must every multiple of 5 end in 0 or 5?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Noticing the pattern is easy; the objective is EXPLAINING it using the structure of the operation. The reason tier separates a child who describes ('they end in 0 or 5') from one who explains ('because each step adds 5, and 5+5 makes a ten so it lands back on 0'). Empirical-only noticing is the partial level.

sources.claim: Y4–Y5 pupils recognise and use number patterns; explaining patterns via structure supports mathematical reasoning.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (KS1–2), Years 4–5 Number

sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 3, Operations & Algebraic Thinking (3.OA.D.9)

pedagogy.summary: Money and measure problems weave fractions and decimals together in context: finding a fraction of an amount (¼ of £3.20 = 80p), subtracting decimal measures (2.5 − 0.75 = 1.75 m), and moving between fractions, decimals and units (3/10 of 1 kg = 300 g = 0.3 kg). Success rests on reading a decimal by its place value rather than as two whole numbers, keeping units consistent, and choosing whether a fraction-of or a decimal calculation is easiest.
bestPractices: Read money by place value: £3.20 is 3 pounds and 2 tenths of a pound = 20p, NOT '3 pounds 2 pence'
Equalise decimal lengths and align the point before subtracting (2.50 − 0.75)
Connect a fraction of an amount to division: ¼ of £3.20 = £3.20 ÷ 4 = 80p
Convert between units deliberately and both ways (0.3 kg = 300 g; 300 g = 0.3 kg)
Estimate first to sense-check the size of the answer
keyRepresentations: Bar model partitioned for a fraction of an amount
Place-value columns aligned on the decimal point
Number line / ruler for the rope-length problem
kg↔g (or £↔p) double number line for unit conversion
Coins and notes for money
commonMisconceptions: Reads money as two whole numbers: '£3.20 = 3 pounds 2 pence', '£3.5 = 3 pounds 5 pence'
Misaligns decimals of unequal length when subtracting (2.5 − 0.75)
Miscomputes a fraction of an amount (¼ of £3.20 ≠ 80p)
Unit slips: 0.3 kg read as 30 g or 3000 g, or gives grams but not the decimal of a kg

learn.summary: Children solve money and measure problems that weave fractions and decimals together: finding a fraction of an amount (¼ of £3.20 = 80p), subtracting decimal measures of unequal length (2.5 − 0.75 = 1.75 m), and moving between fractions, decimals and units (3/10 of 1 kg = 300 g = 0.3 kg). Success rests on reading each decimal digit by its place value rather than as two separate whole numbers, keeping units consistent, aligning on the decimal point before subtracting, and connecting 'a fraction of' to division.

activities.title: Split the £3.20 bar: a quarter as division
feedback: If a part reads 8p or 12.8p, check: do the four equal parts add back to £3.20? 80p × 4 = £3.20, so each quarter is 80p.
The 12.8p trap treats £3.20 as the bare number 3.2 and multiplies (3.2 × 4 = 12.8) instead of dividing; 'a quarter OF' makes the amount smaller, so you divide.
If 'a quarter' was treated as 25 of something, connect ¼ to one of four equal parts of this specific amount.
activities.rationale: A partitioned bar model makes the fraction-of-an-amount concrete and links it directly to division, targeting the common error of computing ¼ of £3.20 by an unclear operation. A live splittable bar lets the child act and see each equal part, but a drawn-and-divided paper bar serves the same purpose.
learnerActions: Take a bar representing £3.20 and split it into four equal parts.
Read what one part is worth and label it (80p / £0.80).
Write the matching calculation: ¼ of £3.20 = £3.20 ÷ 4 = 80p.
Check by adding or multiplying back: 80p × 4 = £3.20.
State in your own words why 'a quarter of' means dividing by 4.
activities.intendedInsight: Finding a fraction of an amount is a division: a quarter of £3.20 is £3.20 shared into 4 equal parts, which is 80p.

activities.title: Cut the rope: align the point before subtracting
feedback: If your answer is not 1.75 m, or does not match your ruler estimate, check whether 2.5 and 0.75 were lined up by their last digits instead of by the decimal point, and whether the exchange (borrowing) was done correctly.
Rewriting 2.5 as 2.50 does not change its value — it just makes the hundredths column visible for 0.75.
Compare your answer to the ruler: cutting a bit less than 1 m off 2.5 m should leave a bit more than 1.5 m and less than 2 m, so 1.75 m is sensible.
activities.rationale: The unequal lengths of 2.5 and 0.75 directly expose the misalignment error (right-justifying ragged decimals). A ruler or number line gives an independent size-check. Showing the aligned column subtraction makes the place-value structure explicit.
sourceClaims: Decimal errors in money and measurement contexts stem from whole-number thinking — reading the digits after the point as a separate whole number (the 'longer-is-larger' / whole-number-bias family) — rather than reasoning about each digit's place value; secure work requires place-value reasoning, not memorised digit rules.

KS2 money/measure problems require reading £3.20 as 3 pounds 20 pence (the tenths digit = 20p) and aligning decimal points when calculating; unit conversion (1 kg = 1000 g) links fractions, decimals and measures.
learnerActions: Start with a 2.5 m rope marked on a ruler or number line.
Cut off 0.75 m and predict the remaining length before calculating.
Rewrite 2.5 as 2.50 so both numbers have the same number of decimal places.
Stack 2.50 above 0.75 with the decimal points lined up vertically, then subtract with borrowing.
Read the remaining length (1.75 m) and check it against your prediction on the ruler.
activities.intendedInsight: Decimals with different numbers of decimal places must be aligned on the decimal point before subtracting, because columns must match in place value; writing 2.5 as 2.50 is a helpful way to make the empty hundredths column visible.

activities.title: One mass, two notations: 3/10 of 1 kg
feedback: If 0.3 kg is converted to 30 g or 3000 g, recount the powers of ten: 3/10 of 1000 g is 300 g.
If only the grams (or only the decimal) were given, remember the question asks for both forms of the same mass.
A slider or double number line that lights up 300 g and 0.3 kg together shows they mark the same point.
activities.rationale: Converting both ways and expressing a single mass in two notations targets the unit-slip error and the half-answered question. The double number line keeps 1 kg = 1000 g visible as the anchor.
sourceClaims: KS2 money/measure problems require reading £3.20 as 3 pounds 20 pence (the tenths digit = 20p) and aligning decimal points when calculating; unit conversion (1 kg = 1000 g) links fractions, decimals and measures.
learnerActions: Anchor the fact 1 kg = 1000 g, e.g. on a double number line (kg on one side, g on the other).
Express the same mass as a decimal of a kilogram: 300 g = 0.3 kg.
Convert back the other way too: 0.3 kg = 300 g.
Explain why 300 g and 0.3 kg are two notations for the same amount.
activities.intendedInsight: A quantity can be written as a fraction, as grams, or as a decimal of a kilogram, and converting fluently in both directions depends on anchoring 1 kg = 1000 g.

activities.title: Read the money by place value
feedback: If £3.20 is read as '3 pounds 2 pence', place coins: 2 tenths of a pound is two 10p coins = 20p.
If 2.5 m is read as '2 m and 5 cm', note that 5 tenths of a metre is 50 cm, since 1 m = 100 cm.
On the trap case, £3.5 is £3.50, because the 5 sits in the tenths place.
activities.rationale: This activity confronts the whole-number-bias misconception head-on by making the tenths digit concrete with coins and a ruler. The trap case is a diagnostic discrimination that is immediately resolved in favour of the place-value reading. Coins and a ruler are optional supports that make the tenth tangible; the reasoning is about place value, not the manipulative itself.
sourceClaims: Decimal errors in money and measurement contexts stem from whole-number thinking — reading the digits after the point as a separate whole number (the 'longer-is-larger' / whole-number-bias family) — rather than reasoning about each digit's place value; secure work requires place-value reasoning, not memorised digit rules.

KS2 money/measure problems require reading £3.20 as 3 pounds 20 pence (the tenths digit = 20p) and aligning decimal points when calculating; unit conversion (1 kg = 1000 g) links fractions, decimals and measures.
learnerActions: Look at £3.20 and say what each digit is worth: 3 pounds, 2 tenths of a pound, and 0 hundredths of a pound.
State what the 2 is worth in pence (20p, not 2p) and justify it.
Discuss the trap case: does £3.5 mean 3 pounds 5 pence or 3 pounds 50 pence? Explain which is correct and why.
Model an amount with coins and notes to confirm the tenths of a pound are 10p coins.
Repeat for a length: in 2.5 m, the 5 is 5 tenths of a metre = 50 cm, not 5 cm.
activities.intendedInsight: The digit after the decimal point is tenths of the unit, so the 2 in £3.20 is 20p and the 5 in £3.5 is 50p — not a separate whole number of the smaller unit.

activities.title: Quick checks on money, measure and conversion
feedback: 80p is correct because £3.20 ÷ 4 = 80p; the 12.8p trap comes from treating £3.20 as the bare number 3.2 and multiplying (3.2 × 4 = 12.8) instead of dividing, and the 8p trap from dividing (3.2 ÷ 4 = 0.8) and misreading 0.8 of a pound as 8p rather than 80p.
For 2.50 − 0.75, align the points and exchange 1 one for 10 tenths: the answer is 1.75. A different result usually means the numbers were not lined up by the decimal point or the exchange went wrong.
0.3 kg = 300 g because 1 kg = 1000 g; 30 g or 3000 g uses the wrong power of ten.
activities.rationale: A short recognition/fill check consolidates the procedures and surfaces named error patterns. Recognition and fill-in-the-blank confirm answers but do not by themselves show independent construction of the method, so pairing them with a written step keeps the reasoning visible.
learnerActions: Answer: what is ¼ of £3.20? (Correct: 80p / £0.80. The traps 8p and 12.8p are wrong.)
Fill the blank: 2.50 − 0.75 = ___ m. (Correct: 1.75 m.)
Match 0.3 kg to its equivalent in grams (300 g).
For each, briefly write the step you used so the method is visible, not just the answer.
activities.intendedInsight: These calculations are cleanly checkable, and the wrong options correspond to specific errors (money-as-two-numbers, misalignment, unit slips) worth recognising and avoiding.

constraints: A static labelled shopping or measuring scene with tap-to-reveal can consolidate known facts and act as a reference, but it does not let the child perform the calculation, so it is a scaffold rather than the main activity.

Multiple-choice and fill-in-the-blank items confirm correct answers and catch specific errors, but recognition-only responses do not elicit independent construction of the method; ask the child to show steps.

Coins, notes, rulers, bar models and double number lines are optional supports that make tenths and conversions tangible; the target reasoning is place value and division, which can also be shown on paper.
Always require the child to show method (how they align the subtraction, how they divide for the fraction), not just the final number, because the method reveals the misconception.
Encourage estimating first to sense-check the size of each answer.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched this session. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

One listed source (DfE national curriculum) is marked verified:false / not fetched this session in the original row; its claim is retained only where it directly supports a principle (reading £3.20 as 20p, point alignment, unit conversion), and its evidentiary strength is unconfirmed.

Independent self-audit of arithmetic: ¼ of £3.20 = £3.20 ÷ 4 = 80p (80p × 4 = £3.20 ✓); the 12.8p trap = 3.2 × 4 (bare-number multiply) and the 8p trap = 3.2 ÷ 4 = 0.8 misread as 8p; 2.50 − 0.75 = 1.75 m ✓; 3/10 of 1 kg = 300 g = 0.3 kg ✓; £3.5 = £3.50 (tenths place) ✓. The 8p/12.8p attributions are consistent across activities 1 and 5.

The DfE source claim was removed from the fraction-of-an-amount activity, where it supported only the money topic and not the division principle; it remains where it directly supports reading £3.20 as 20p, point alignment, or unit conversion.

The £3.20-as-20p and £3.5-as-£3.50 prompts deliberately present the misconception as a discrimination to be explained, mirroring the original assessment's probing; each is immediately resolved in favour of the place-value reading in the feedback, so the wrong reading is never left standing as valid.

The original artefact-fit notes claimed depth 'adds nothing' for 3D and that in-role dialogue cannot deliver the insight; these are catalog preferences, not established facts, and have been dropped rather than asserted as universal laws.
The original suggestion to let the child mis-key '£3.20 = 302p' so a coin view corrects it is retained in spirit as an optional error-surfacing interaction, not as a required mechanism.

probeDeeper: In £3.20, what is the 2 worth — 2 pence or 20 pence? How do you know?
Why did you (or should you) write 2.5 as 2.50 before taking away 0.75?
How could you check that 80p really is a quarter of £3.20?
3/10 of 1 kg is 300 g — how do you write that as a decimal part of a kilogram, and why?

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads a money or measure decimal as two whole numbers — '£3.20 is 3 pounds 2 pence', or 2.5 m is '2 m and 5 cm'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild place value: the 2 in £3.20 is 2 tenths of a pound = 20p; 0.5 m is 5 tenths of a metre = 50 cm. Use coins/ruler to make the tenth concrete.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats the digit after the point as ones of the smaller unit regardless of place; ¼ of £3.20 comes out as pennies of '3.2', or 2.5 m handled as 2 m 5 cm

errorPatterns.pattern: Misaligns decimals of unequal length when subtracting — lines up 2.5 and 0.75 by their last digits instead of the point
errorPatterns.nextMove: Equalise lengths (2.50) and align on the decimal point, then subtract with borrowing exactly as for whole numbers.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Does not rewrite 2.5 as 2.50; subtracts columns that don't match place value; answer like 1.85 or 2.25

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscomputes the fraction of an amount — ¼ of £3.20 by an unclear operation, not £3.20 ÷ 4
errorPatterns.nextMove: Connect 'a quarter of' to dividing by 4 on the bar model; check 80p × 4 = £3.20.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: ¼ of £3.20 ≠ 80p; multiplies by 4, or takes 'a quarter' as 25 of something

errorPatterns.pattern: Unit-conversion slip — 0.3 kg given as 30 g or 3000 g, or grams found but not expressed as a decimal of a kg
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor 1 kg = 1000 g on a double number line; 3/10 of 1000 g = 300 g, and 300 g of 1000 is 0.3 kg.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Wrong power of ten in the kg→g conversion, or only half the question answered

responseLevels.gap: Reads money/measure decimals as two whole numbers and misaligns ragged subtractions; cannot reliably find a fraction of an amount or convert units.
responseLevels.full: Computes all three correctly with place-value reasoning — 80p as £3.20÷4, 1.75 m by aligned subtraction, 300 g = 0.3 kg both ways — estimates to check, and transfers to a new money/measure problem.
responseLevels.partial: Handles one or two parts correctly (e.g. ¼ of £3.20) but slips on the ragged subtraction or the unit conversion, or answers only part of the kilogram question.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'Work these out and show your steps. First, what is 1/4 of £3.20? Second, a rope is 2.5 metres long and you cut off 0.75 metres — how much is left? Third, find 3/10 of 1 kilogram, and give the answer both in grams and as a decimal of a kilogram.' Watch the method — especially how they line up 2.5 and 0.75.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The rope (2.5 − 0.75, unequal lengths) exposes decimal misalignment; the money reveals whether the child reads the 2 in £3.20 as 2 tenths of a pound (20p) or as 2 pence; the kilogram question checks unit fluency in both directions. A child who reads decimals as two whole numbers or right-justifies the subtraction gets the rope or the money wrong; a child reasoning by place value gets 80p, 1.75 m and 300 g / 0.3 kg.

sources.claim: Decimal errors in money and measurement contexts stem from whole-number thinking — reading the digits after the point as a separate whole number (the 'longer-is-larger' / whole-number-bias family) — rather than reasoning about each digit's place value; secure work requires place-value reasoning, not memorised digit rules.

pedagogy.summary: A linear function y = mx + c produces a straight-line graph, where m (the gradient) is the constant rate of change — the line's steepness and direction — and c is the starting value, the y-intercept. It is best taught by generating (x, y) pairs from the equation and plotting them so the straight line is DISCOVERED from a constant rate, then varying m and c independently so each parameter is bound to its visual effect. Rate contexts such as distance-time (where gradient = speed) give the numbers meaning, and the graph-as-picture and slope-height misconceptions must be confronted directly.
bestPractices: Build the line from a table of values first, so 'constant rate produces a straight line' is discovered rather than asserted.
Vary m and c independently and watch the effect: a larger m steepens the line, a negative m flips its direction, and changing c slides the whole line up or down through its intercept.
Use rate contexts (distance-time, cost-per-item) so the gradient means something real — speed, price per unit — not a bare number.
Confront graph-as-picture explicitly: a distance-time graph is a record of a relationship, not a picture of the route; a rising line is not a hill.
Contrast linear with non-linear (plot y = x^2 beside y = 2x + 1) so 'straight line' becomes a property to test, not an assumption.
keyRepresentations: Table of values → plotted points → straight line
y = mx + c with m (gradient) and c (y-intercept) annotated on the line
Distance-time graph where the gradient of the line is the speed
A family of lines pivoting (as m changes) and sliding (as c changes)
commonMisconceptions: Graph-as-picture / iconic: reads the shape of the line as a literal picture of the situation (the line goes up, so the person went up a hill).
Slope-height confusion: judges the line that is HIGHER on the graph as faster/greater, rather than the STEEPER one.
Gradient/intercept swap: reads c as the slope or m as where the line crosses the axis.
Believes every equation gives a straight line, and is surprised that y = x^2 curves.

learn.summary: A linear function y = mx + c produces a straight-line graph, where m (the gradient) is the constant rate of change — the line's steepness and direction — and c is the starting value (the y-intercept). The concept is best built by generating (x, y) pairs from the equation and plotting them so the straight line is DISCOVERED from a constant rate, then varying m and c independently so each parameter is bound to its visual effect. Rate contexts such as distance-time (gradient = speed) give the numbers meaning, and the graph-as-picture and slope-height misconceptions must be confronted directly. For ages 12-14 (KS3).

activities.title: Build the line from a table of values
feedback: If the points don't line up, check your arithmetic: each y should change by the same amount (here +2) for each step of +1 in x.
Point out that y when x = 0 is 1 — this is exactly the c value and the point where the line crosses the y-axis.
activities.rationale: Deriving the line from a value table lets 'constant rate produces a straight line' be discovered rather than asserted, and exposes the intercept concretely as the value at x = 0.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should 'recognise, sketch and produce graphs of linear and quadratic functions of one variable' and 'calculate and interpret gradients and intercepts of graphs of such linear equations numerically, graphically and algebraically'.
learnerActions: Take the equation y = 2x + 1 and complete a table of values for x = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2 (giving y = -3, -1, 1, 3, 5).
Plot each (x, y) pair on axes and join them.
Observe that equal steps in x give equal steps in y, and that the points fall exactly on a straight line.
State in your own words why a constant rate of change produces a straight line.
activities.intendedInsight: A straight line is a consequence of a constant rate of change, not an assumption — 'straight' is something you can test from the numbers.

activities.title: Vary m and c independently
feedback: When a learner predicts where the line will cross the axis for a given c, confirm it lands exactly at (0, c).
If a learner thinks a negative m just makes a 'smaller' uphill line, show two points and compute the change: y decreases as x increases, so the line falls.
Emphasise that changing c never changes the steepness, and that changing m never moves the y-axis crossing (it stays at (0, c)) — this separation is the key reading.
activities.rationale: Binding each parameter to its own visual role (pivot for m, slide for c) is the central conceptual payload and directly counters the gradient/intercept swap. Live sliders with a recomputing line and a synced value table can make this relationship felt; predicting the intercept before it appears tests understanding.
learnerActions: Keep c fixed and change m: try m = 1, then m = 3, then m = -2, replotting or predicting each line.

Describe what happens as positive m gets larger (the line steepens) and as m goes negative (the line flips from climbing to falling, pivoting about the same intercept); steepness depends on the size of m ignoring its sign, so m = -2 is steeper than m = 1.
Now keep m fixed and change c: try c = 0, then c = 2, then c = -3.
Describe what happens (the whole line slides up or down and crosses the y-axis exactly at c), and predict the crossing point before plotting.
activities.intendedInsight: m controls steepness AND direction (sign), while c slides the whole line to its y-intercept — each parameter is bound to a distinct visual effect.

activities.title: Distance-time race: steepness is speed, not height
feedback: If a learner picks Maggie because her line is higher at 4 seconds, take two points on each line and compute distance-per-second together, then show Emma's steeper line draws level at 5 seconds and pulls ahead afterward — steepness, not height, is speed.

If a learner talks about hills, going uphill, or the shape of a 'track', ask: 'If someone walked in a circle around their home, what would a distance-time graph look like?' Contrast a picture of the route with a record of distance over time.
If a learner names the head-start number (the 10) as the speed, change c only (steepness untouched) and then m only (line pivots), and re-read the equation to re-attach 'speed' to the gradient.
activities.rationale: A distance-time context gives gradient real meaning (speed) and directly confronts the slope-height and graph-as-picture misconceptions in one experience, especially when two lines cross so the higher-but-slower line is visible. Choosing a comparison time before the crossing (here t = 4, where the higher-at-4-seconds runner is the slower one) forces the discrimination, and the meeting point at t = 5 makes the catch-up concrete.
sourceClaims: Students confuse 'higher on the graph' with 'faster', assuming a runner is fastest because at 5 seconds her line is above another's, and make y-intercept and slope-direction errors when producing a linear graph (e.g. drawing a positive slope where negative is needed, or an incorrect intercept such as f=30); some assume two matched graphs must share the same vertical intercept.

Students interpret distance-time graphs as pictures of the situation ('as the graph goes up and down, Tom's path is going up and down'; a straight line means a straight path; a negative slope means a detour) — the graph-as-picture / iconic misconception — and misread slope direction as speeding up/slowing down; the hill-shaped graph is a deliberate distractor (Card 2 matched to interpretation E).
learnerActions: Plot two runners' distance over time on the same axes, e.g. Emma d = 6t and Maggie d = 4t + 10.
Before computing, predict who is faster and write your reason.
At 4 seconds, note that Maggie's line is higher (26 m versus Emma's 24 m), but Emma's line is steeper.
Take two points on each line and compute distance-per-second (Emma gains 6 per second; Maggie gains 4 per second).
Identify where/whether the lines cross — here they meet at 5 seconds (both at 30 m), after which Emma pulls ahead — and say what that crossing means in the race.
In the equations, identify which number is the speed (the coefficient of t, the gradient) and which is the head start (the constant, the intercept).
activities.intendedInsight: Speed is the gradient (steepness), not the height of the line; a runner can start ahead (large c) yet be slower (small m). Emma is faster because her line is steeper, covering more distance each second, even though Maggie's line sits higher at 4 seconds — until the lines meet at 5 seconds, after which Emma pulls ahead.

activities.title: Predict-then-test: does every equation give a straight line?
feedback: If a learner predicts 'straight' because 'it's an equation with x in it, like the straight ones', the emerging parabola confronts this directly — revisit the value table and show the changing step size.
Point out the symmetry of the parabola about x = 0 and that the differences between successive y-values are themselves changing, unlike the constant difference in a linear table.
activities.rationale: A prediction stated before observing is diagnostic of the all-equations-are-linear misconception, and contrasting a curve with a line beside it makes 'straight' a testable property. Contrasting the differing step sizes grounds the distinction numerically (the constant-difference test holds for equally spaced x-values, as used in the suggested tables).
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should 'recognise, sketch and produce graphs of linear and quadratic functions of one variable' and 'calculate and interpret gradients and intercepts of graphs of such linear equations numerically, graphically and algebraically'.
learnerActions: Before plotting, predict: will y = x^2 give a straight line or a curve? Write your answer AND your reason first.
Build a table of values for x = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2 (giving y = 4, 1, 0, 1, 4), plot the points, and join them.
Plot y = 2x + 1 on the same axes for comparison.
Compare how y changes: for y = 2x + 1 the step is constant (+2 each time); for y = x^2 the steps differ (-3, -1, +1, +3), so the graph curves.
State what makes an equation produce a straight line versus a curve.
activities.intendedInsight: Not every equation is linear; a straight line requires a constant rate of change. 'Straight' is a property that depends on the equation, discovered by testing, not assumed.

activities.title: Check and consolidate: match, judge, and sort
feedback: Include a 'which line is faster/steeper' item where the correct line is NOT the one highest on the graph at the compared time, so the slope-height misconception is actively tested.
For any item answered via height rather than steepness, return to taking two points and computing the change per step.
activities.rationale: Matching, comparison, and categorisation are efficient checks of the concept; a 'higher but slower' item surfaces the slope-height misconception. These checks confirm the parameter-to-feature link rather than building it, so they work best after the dynamic exploration.
sourceClaims: Students confuse 'higher on the graph' with 'faster', assuming a runner is fastest because at 5 seconds her line is above another's, and make y-intercept and slope-direction errors when producing a linear graph (e.g. drawing a positive slope where negative is needed, or an incorrect intercept such as f=30); some assume two matched graphs must share the same vertical intercept.
learnerActions: Match each equation to its graph.
Given two straight-line graphs, decide which is steeper (and in a distance-time context, which is faster), explicitly reasoning from steepness rather than height.
Sort a set of equations into 'produces a straight line' and 'produces a curve'.
For an equation like d = 6t + 10, state which number is the gradient (speed) and which is the intercept (head start).
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidates reading gradient and intercept from both equation and graph, and distinguishing linear from non-linear, while resisting the slope-height distractor.

constraints: Matching, multiple-choice comparison, and categorisation confirm understanding but do not themselves build the dynamic link between a parameter and its visual feature; use them after exploration, not instead of it.

A static annotated y = mx + c diagram (tap m to highlight steepness, tap c to highlight the crossing point) can summarise the gradient and intercept on one line but cannot itself show the pivot-and-slide; it works as a recap card after dynamic work, not as the first teacher of the relationship.

The slope-height and graph-as-picture misconceptions must be confronted with a case where the higher line (at the compared time) is the slower one; a single rising line can reinforce rather than break 'higher = faster'.

When using Emma d = 6t and Maggie d = 4t + 10, compare at a time before the lines cross (they meet at t = 5, both 30 m); t = 4 gives Maggie higher (26) but Emma steeper and faster, with Emma pulling ahead after t = 5.

Interactive sliders, a live-redrawing line, and a synced value table are optional ways to make the equation-to-graph relationship concrete; the same insight can be reached by hand-plotting several lines and comparing them.
Require learners to state reasons, not just answers, when judging which runner is faster — the reason is what distinguishes gradient reasoning from slope-height reasoning.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original material claimed 3D rendering 'adds nothing' and that open dialogue is not a natural vehicle; these categorical modality claims have been removed. A 3D view is not the natural representation for a two-variable linear relationship, and a coaching conversation can still probe reasoning ('how do you know Emma is faster?') — such prompts are retained inside activity feedback — without claiming dialogue cannot teach the concept.

Arithmetic checked: y = 2x + 1 over x = -2..2 gives -3,-1,1,3,5 (constant +2); y = x^2 gives 4,1,0,1,4 with non-constant differences -3,-1,+1,+3. Emma d = 6t vs Maggie d = 4t + 10 are EQUAL at t = 5 (both 30 m) and cross there, so the original row's claim that 'Maggie's line is higher at 5 seconds' is false for these numbers. The race activity's comparison has been corrected to t = 4 (Maggie 26, Emma 24), with the lines meeting at t = 5 and Emma pulling ahead afterward; the steeper = faster teaching point is preserved.

At exactly t = 5 neither runner is ahead (both 30 m); Emma leads only for t > 5, so learner-facing text describes t = 5 as the meeting/catch-up point and 'pulls ahead afterward' rather than an overtake exactly at 5 seconds.
The constant-difference argument distinguishes linear from quadratic only for equally spaced x-values; this condition is built into the suggested tables.

assess.poeTask: Before plotting anything, ask the child: 'Will y = x^2 give a straight line or a curved one? Write down your answer AND your reason first.' Then have them build a table of values for x = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, plot the points, and join them. The reason stated before observing is the diagnostic part: children who predict 'straight' because 'it is an equation with x in it, like the straight ones' reveal the all-equations-are-linear misconception, and the emerging parabola confronts it directly.
probeDeeper: At the very start (0 seconds) Maggie's line begins higher than Emma's. Does starting further ahead mean running faster? Why or why not?
Suppose Emma's race is d = 6t and Maggie's is d = 4t + 10. Which number tells you the speed, and which tells you the head start?
If the two lines crossed at some point, what would that moment mean in the race?
Would a runner who is gradually slowing down give a straight line or a curved one — and why?
assess.correctAnswer: Emma is running faster, because speed is shown by the steepness (gradient) of the line, not by how high it is: a steeper line covers more distance in each second. Maggie's line being higher at 5 seconds only means she was further ahead at that moment, not that she is faster.

errorPatterns.pattern: Slope-height confusion: 'Maggie is faster because her line is higher up the graph at 5 seconds' — reads vertical position as speed rather than steepness
errorPatterns.nextMove: Take two points on each line and compute distance-per-second together; show that the steeper line overtakes, so steepness (not height) is speed.
errorPatterns.distractor: Maggie — at 5 seconds her line is higher up the graph, so she must be the faster runner.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Chooses Maggie and justifies by how high her line sits, not by how steep it is.

errorPatterns.pattern: Graph-as-picture / iconic: reads the line as a literal picture of the route (a rising line means the runner went uphill; a steeper line means a steeper hill)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask the classic MAP prompt: 'If someone walked in a circle around their home, what would the graph look like?' Contrast a picture of the route with a record of distance over time.
errorPatterns.distractor: The steeper line just means that runner's track went up a steeper hill.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Talks about hills, going up, or the shape of the track rather than distance-over-time; may pick the 'steeper hill' reading.

errorPatterns.pattern: Gradient/intercept swap: when reading an equation like d = 6t + 10, names c (the 10) as the speed or m (the 6) as the starting distance
errorPatterns.nextMove: Bind each parameter with the slider — change c only and the steepness is untouched; change m only and the line pivots — then re-read the equation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Surfaces on the follow-up equation probe, not the runners graph: the child attaches 'speed' to the wrong number.

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes all equations give straight lines: expects y = x^2 to be straight and is surprised by the curve
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build a table for y = x^2 alongside y = 2x + 1 and plot both; the curvature is discovered, and 'straight' becomes a property that depends on the equation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Surfaces on the POE / follow-up, not the runners graph: predicts 'straight' for y = x^2 because 'it's an equation like the others'.

responseLevels.gap: Picks the higher line as faster, or reads the graph as a literal picture of the route; makes no link between steepness and speed.
responseLevels.full: Identifies Emma as faster because gradient = speed, distinguishes head-start (intercept) from speed (gradient), maps both onto the equation, and predicts a curve for a non-constant rate — relating the parameters and transferring to a new case.
responseLevels.partial: Says the steeper line is faster, and can point to gradient and intercept when prompted, but cannot yet explain how m and c act together or map them onto the equation form (d = 6t vs d = 4t + 10) — lists the features without relating them.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are two straight-line graphs showing two runners' distance from the start over time, drawn on the same axes. At 5 seconds, Maggie's line is higher than Emma's line, but Emma's line is steeper. Who is running faster — and how do you know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands gradient-as-rate chooses Emma and justifies by steepness; a child holding the slope-height misconception chooses Maggie precisely BECAUSE her line is higher. The two reasoning paths give opposite first-tier answers, and the required reason (tier two) reveals whether 'faster' is being read from steepness or from height — a child cannot easily land the right answer for the wrong reason here.

pedagogy.summary: Perimeter is the total distance around the boundary of a 2-D shape, found by measuring every side and adding the lengths (or, for a regular shape, multiplying one side by the number of sides). The concept to secure is that perimeter is a length — the once-around distance — and is distinct from area (the surface covered inside).
bestPractices: Define perimeter physically as walking all the way around the edge and back to the start.
Measure and label every side, then add — for a rectangle, remind pupils the two unmarked sides equal their opposites.
For regular shapes, connect equal sides to multiplication (side length × number of sides).
Deliberately contrast perimeter (distance around) with area (surface covered) on the same shape so the two are not confused.
Keep the length unit in the answer (cm, m).
keyRepresentations: A shape with each side measured and labelled, summed around the boundary
A finger/marker tracing the whole boundary back to the start
A regular polygon: one side labelled, perimeter = side × number of sides
A rectangle with only two adjacent sides given, the opposite two to be filled in
commonMisconceptions: Adds only the two given sides of a rectangle, forgetting the opposite two.
Confuses perimeter with area — counts the squares inside instead of the distance around.
For a regular shape, measures one side but doesn't account for all the equal sides.
Gives the perimeter as a bare number without a length unit.

learn.summary: Perimeter is the total distance once around the boundary of a 2-D shape — found by measuring every side and adding the lengths, or for a regular shape multiplying one side by the number of sides. The core idea to secure is that perimeter is a length (the once-around distance) and is distinct from area (the surface covered inside). Target age 7–8.

activities.title: Walk the boundary and build the total
feedback: If a child adds only the two given sides of a rectangle, have them first label the two opposite sides (which equal their partners), then add all four; trace the full boundary to check nothing is missed.

If a child reports the number of squares inside or an area figure, contrast the two measures on the same shape — trace the boundary for perimeter, shade the interior for area — and name which the question asks for.
If a child gives only one side of a regular polygon, establish that it has n equal sides so perimeter = side × n, and check the number of sides.
If the total is correct but the unit is missing, treat the answer as incomplete and build the habit of writing cm/m; the adding itself is sound.
activities.rationale: Tracing the boundary makes 'distance around' concrete; hiding two rectangle sides forces the learner to supply the equal opposite sides, directly targeting the most common error; a regular-shape step links equal sides to multiplication. An optional interactive version — dragging a marker so each side lights and its length clicks into a running total that will not advance past a hidden side until the opposite side is supplied, plus an area/perimeter shading toggle and a regular-polygon side×n mode — makes the once-around mechanism visible, but the same learning works with paper shapes, a ruler and labelled drawings.
sourceClaims: The perimeter of a polygon is the sum of the lengths of its sides. For rectangles and parallelograms often only two adjacent side lengths are given, and the common error is to add just those two numbers; having students first label the lengths of the other two sides is a helpful reminder. For regular polygons the perimeter is the product of one side length and the number of sides.
learnerActions: Trace a finger or marker all the way around the edge of a shape, starting and finishing at the same corner, so 'perimeter' is felt as walking once around and back to the start.
On a rectangle that shows only two adjacent side lengths, work out the two hidden opposite sides (opposite sides are equal), label them, then add all four sides.
Keep a running total as you cover each side, and only count the perimeter as complete when the whole boundary has been traced back to the start.
On a regular pentagon with one side labelled, find the perimeter as side length × 5 (or by adding five equal sides) and explain why the shortcut works.
Measure every side of a small irregular shape with a ruler and add the lengths.
Write each answer with its length unit (cm or m).
activities.intendedInsight: Perimeter is the complete once-around distance: you must account for every side (including hidden equal ones), it is a length with a unit, and for a regular shape equal sides let you multiply instead of adding one by one.

activities.title: Perimeter is not area
feedback: If the learner counts interior squares when asked for perimeter, point back to the boundary trace: perimeter follows only the edge.
If they are unsure which is asked, have them underline the word 'around' or 'covered/inside' in the question and match it to the correct action.
activities.rationale: Distinguishing area from perimeter is a distinction that must be maintained; deliberately performing both on the same shape makes the contrast explicit and discriminating.
sourceClaims: With strong, distinct concepts of perimeter and area, students differentiate the two measures; abstraction underscores the importance of distinguishing area from perimeter, a distinction that must be maintained across grades.
learnerActions: On one straight-sided shape drawn along the lines of a square grid, first trace the boundary and add the side lengths to find the perimeter, then shade the interior and count the unit squares to find the area (in square units).
State in your own words which measure is a distance around the edge and which is the surface covered inside.
Given a question, decide whether it is asking for perimeter or area before you start, and say how you know.
activities.intendedInsight: Perimeter (distance around the edge, a length) and area (surface covered inside) are different measures on the very same shape and must not be swapped.

activities.title: Spot-the-error and mixed practice
feedback: For the spot-the-error item, confirm the fix is to add all four sides after supplying the equal opposite pair.
For the area distractor, confirm the learner traced the boundary rather than counting interior squares.
Flag any missing unit as an incomplete answer.
activities.rationale: Discriminating items — a two-sides-given rectangle, a side×n regular polygon, a spot-the-error on adding only two sides, and a perimeter-vs-area distractor — target the documented errors. These check and reinforce the procedure; use them alongside, not instead of, hands-on measuring and summing.
sourceClaims: The perimeter of a polygon is the sum of the lengths of its sides. For rectangles and parallelograms often only two adjacent side lengths are given, and the common error is to add just those two numbers; having students first label the lengths of the other two sides is a helpful reminder. For regular polygons the perimeter is the product of one side length and the number of sides.
learnerActions: Solve fill-the-blank items: a rectangle with only two adjacent sides given (supply the opposite two, then total), and a regular polygon with one side labelled (use side × number of sides).
Judge a worked example where another child added only the two given rectangle sides — say what went wrong and give the correct perimeter.
Answer a mixed item where one option is the area of the shape, choosing and justifying the correct perimeter.
Check every answer carries its length unit.
activities.intendedInsight: Applying perimeter across rectangle (hidden sides), regular-polygon (side×n), and perimeter-vs-area cases, and critiquing a wrong method, consolidates accurate, unit-bearing reasoning.

constraints: Keep the length unit (cm, m) in every perimeter answer; a bare number is incomplete. Area answers use square units (e.g. square centimetres or 'squares'), not length units.

A static labelled shape with the boundary highlighted can illustrate 'distance around', but it does not let the learner rehearse measuring and summing all sides — use it as a reference, not as the main practice.
Recognition-only or multiple-choice items check and reinforce the procedure but do not by themselves elicit independent measuring and summing; pair them with hands-on construction.
When using a regular-shape shortcut, first establish how many equal sides the shape has, so side × n is justified rather than guessed.
For a rectangle with only two adjacent sides given, require the learner to supply the opposite two sides before totalling; do not let them stop at the two given numbers.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated 3D and conversation artefacts as 'poor' with claims that '3D adds nothing' and perimeter 'is not a dialogue'. These are catalog preferences, not established pedagogical laws, and have not been carried forward as universal claims; discussion (e.g. explaining where the boundary starts and ends) can usefully support this topic even if measure-and-add is the core performance.

One cited source (UK National Curriculum, Year 3 measures perimeter) is marked verified:false in the row; it is treated as unconfirmed and is not used as a sourceClaim because it supports only the topic/curriculum requirement, not a specific teaching principle.
The regular-polygon step depends on the prerequisite that the shape has n equal sides; ensure learners can identify a regular polygon before applying side×n.

probeDeeper: Show me with your finger — where does the perimeter start and where does it finish?
This rectangle only shows two side lengths — how long are the other two, and how do you know?
Is the perimeter the distance around the edge, or the space covered inside? Which did you find?
For this regular pentagon, do you need to measure all five sides, or is there a quicker way?
assess.correctAnswer: The child finds the total distance around each shape: for the rectangle, uses all four sides (supplying the two unlabelled opposite sides); for the regular pentagon, multiplies the side by 5 (or adds five equal sides); measures every side of the irregular shape and sums them; and states each perimeter with a length unit.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds only the two given sides of a rectangle, forgetting the opposite two.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have the child label the lengths of the other two sides first (opposite sides equal), then add all four; trace the full boundary to check.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For a rectangle with only length and width shown, gives length + width as the perimeter.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses perimeter with area: counts the squares inside the shape instead of the distance around it.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast the two on one shape — trace the boundary for perimeter, shade the interior for area; name which measure the question asks for.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reports the number of interior squares, or an area figure, when asked for perimeter.

errorPatterns.pattern: For a regular shape, doesn't account for all the equal sides — measures/uses one side but doesn't multiply by the number of sides.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish the shape has n equal sides, so perimeter = side × n; check the number of sides of the shape.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives the single side length, or a partial sum, for the regular polygon's perimeter.

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops the length unit: gives the perimeter as a bare number.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Treat a perimeter without a unit as incomplete; build the habit of writing cm/m; the summing is sound.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct total, no unit; supplies it only when asked.

responseLevels.gap: Adds only two sides of the rectangle, or reports an area, or uses a single side of the regular shape.
responseLevels.full: Finds the total distance around each shape — supplying unlabelled equal sides, using side×n for regular shapes — keeps it distinct from area, and states the perimeter with its length unit.
responseLevels.partial: Finds the perimeter of a fully-labelled shape by adding sides, but is caught when opposite sides must be inferred or when a regular shape invites side×n — or omits the unit.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give a rectangle (with only two adjacent sides labelled), a regular pentagon (one side labelled), and a small irregular shape, with a ruler. Say: 'Find the perimeter of each.' Watch whether they measure/account for every side, whether they add all sides (not just the two given), whether they confuse it with the area, and whether they keep the unit.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands perimeter accounts for every side and gives a once-around length; a child who does not adds only the two given rectangle sides, counts the squares inside (area), or uses just one side of the regular shape — each visible in the working.

For regular polygons the perimeter is the product of one side length and the number of sides.

sources.claim: With strong, distinct concepts of perimeter and area, students differentiate the two measures; abstraction underscores the importance of distinguishing area from perimeter, a distinction that must be maintained across grades.
