pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 8–9y; fluently multiply and divide within 100, using strategies — especially the ×÷ relationship and derived facts — not just rote recall.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y3–Y4 recall and USE ×÷ facts, and 'use place value, known and derived facts to multiply and divide mentally' — fluency includes derivation and application.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.OA.7 — 'Fluently multiply and divide within 100, using strategies such as the relationship between multiplication and division (e.g. knowing that 8 × 5 = 40, one knows 40 ÷ 5 = 8) … By the end of Grade 3, know from memory all products of two one-digit numbers.'
• Operational details — fluency = efficiency + accuracy + flexibility. Beyond recall, children deploy strategies: derive an unknown from a known (9×7 = 10×7−7 = 63; 6×8 = 5×8+8), use commutativity to reduce load, and use the inverse to get ÷ from ×. The distinguishing skill from bare table-recall is CHOOSING an efficient strategy and using facts within calculations and problems. Retrieval should be mixed, spaced, and applied, with derivation strategies made explicit and discussed.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8): answer any 2/5/10 and 3/4/8 × or ÷ fact quickly. Tier B (age 8–9): answer any fact within 100 in ~3s and state its ÷ partner. Tier C (age 9): derive a not-yet-memorised fact from a known one and explain the strategy (e.g. 7×6 via 7×5+7).
bestPractices: Make derived-fact strategies explicit and named — near-tens (9s from 10s), doubling (4s from 2s, 8s from 4s), partitioning (6×8 = 5×8 + 8) — and have children compare strategies.
Interleave × and ÷ so the inverse relationship is exercised as a retrieval strategy, not just taught as a fact.
Use short, frequent, mixed, spaced retrieval and apply facts inside larger calculations and word problems so fluency transfers.
Keep timing low-stakes to protect against maths anxiety while still building speed; emphasise a correct efficient method over raw speed alone.
Diagnose which specific facts/strategies are missing and target them, rather than re-drilling everything.
keyRepresentations: Derivation chains and 'fact from a fact' diagrams (10×7−7 → 9×7; double 2→4→8)
Array/area model — justifies the partitioning strategy (6×8 = 5×8 + 1×8)
Fact-family triangle — the inverse as a fluency strategy
Multiplication square — to locate a known neighbour to derive from
commonMisconceptions: Equating fluency with speed alone, leading to guessing under time pressure instead of using a reliable strategy.
Being able to recite a table in order but unable to answer a fact out of sequence or its ÷ partner.
Not using the inverse, so division facts lag behind multiplication.
Failing to derive — stuck facts stay stuck because the child has no strategy to rebuild them.
Not transferring facts into multi-step calculations (knows 7×8 in isolation but not inside a written method).

learn.summary: For ages 8–9, build fluent multiplication and division within 100 as strategic fluency (efficiency, accuracy, and flexibility) rather than bare recall. The core skills are: deriving an unknown fact from a known one (9×7 = 10×7−7 = 63; 6×8 = 5×8+8 = 48), using the multiplication–division inverse to get division facts from multiplication (knowing 7×8=56 gives 56÷8=7), using commutativity to reduce load, and choosing an efficient strategy and applying facts inside larger calculations and word problems. Make derived-fact strategies explicit and named, interleave × and ÷, and use short, spaced, mixed retrieval, keeping timing low-stakes.

activities.title: Derive-it: rebuild hard facts from known ones
feedback: If you revert to skip-counting on a tricky fact, prompt: 'What easy fact is nearby?' Then rehearse the near-fact move (×9 via ×10 then subtract; ×6 via ×5 then add) until it is reached for first.
For a division answered by trial or counting, prompt 'what times 6 makes 54?' and link it to the matching multiplication fact family (6×9=54, so 54÷6=9).

If answers are correct but slow and effortful, treat this as developmental: do not equate slow with wrong or pile on timed pressure. Reinforce the secure strategy and use spaced retrieval over time; protect confidence.
activities.rationale: Fluency comprises efficiency, accuracy and flexibility; derived-fact strategies and the inverse are central to fluency and should be made explicit and practised until reached for first, with × and ÷ interleaved so the inverse is exercised as a retrieval strategy. An adaptive practice format may detect a stall and offer a fact-matched scaffold (an array shedding one column; an array split into 5×8+8; a one-tap flip to the solving multiplication), making strategy use a repeated felt experience. These interaction examples are illustrative of the mechanism, not required, and such adaptive benefit is proposed rather than established.
sourceClaims: Fluency comprises efficiency, accuracy and flexibility; derived-fact strategies and the inverse should be taught explicitly, with spaced interleaved retrieval.
Y3–Y4 pupils recall and use ×÷ facts and use place value, known and derived facts to calculate mentally.
3.OA.7 requires fluently multiplying and dividing within 100 using strategies such as the multiplication–division relationship.
learnerActions: Face a mixed stream of × and ÷ questions within 100.
When you stall on a fact, use a named derivation strategy rather than counting up: for 9×7, start from 10×7=70 and subtract one group of 7 to get 63; for 6×8, split into 5×8+8 = 48.
Take a round of 'derive-it' challenge facts chosen so they are best cracked by transforming a fact you already know (rather than counting up), and state the known fact you started from.
For division questions, flip to the multiplication fact family (e.g. for 54÷6 ask 'what times 6 makes 54?' → 9).
Say or write which strategy you used after each hard fact.
activities.intendedInsight: Once a few anchor facts are secure (such as ×2, ×5 and ×10), unknown facts within 100 can be reached from facts you already own, so fluency is a connected web of strategies rather than a wall of isolated things to memorise.

activities.title: Mixed ×÷ fluency check (spaced retrieval)
feedback: If you can recite a table in order but stumble on a fact out of sequence or its division partner, practise facts in random order and always pair each × fact with its ÷ partner.
Target the specific facts and strategies you marked as 'worked out' rather than re-drilling everything.
activities.rationale: A fixed, non-adaptive fact check is an authentic fluency measure and good for spaced checking; it measures fluency more than it teaches the strategies that create it, so pair it with explicit strategy work rather than treating it as the only route to fluency. Short, frequent, mixed, spaced retrieval helps fluency transfer.
sourceClaims: Fluency comprises efficiency, accuracy and flexibility; derived-fact strategies and the inverse should be taught explicitly, with spaced interleaved retrieval.
learnerActions: Answer a rapid mixed set of × and ÷ questions within 100, aiming for roughly three seconds each but keeping timing low-stakes.
Tackle a few deliberately paired items, e.g. 10×7 immediately followed by 9×7, so you can notice the derivation link.
After the set, mark which facts you 'just knew' and which you worked out, and revisit the worked-out ones in later spaced sessions.
activities.intendedInsight: Mixed, spaced retrieval measures and consolidates fluency across all facts, including the inverse division partners, not just a table recited in order.

activities.title: Multiplication square with derivation and fact-family overlays
feedback: If you rely on reading the grid rather than recalling, follow each look-up by attempting the fact unaided so the reference becomes a bridge, not a crutch.
Prompt comparison: 'Which nearby fact did you derive from, and could another neighbour work too?'
activities.rationale: A tappable square with derivation overlays and fact-family reveals is a strong strategy reference; because it shows strategies rather than drilling their fluent use, it supports but does not replace retrieval practice. Array/area and fact-family representations justify the partitioning strategy and the inverse.
learnerActions: Use a multiplication square as a reference and locate a known neighbour to a fact you are unsure of.
For a hard fact such as 9×7, trace how it is built from a neighbouring easy fact (10×7 then subtract 7 → 63).
Reveal the fact family for any cell to see its division partners (e.g. 7×8=56, 8×7=56, 56÷7=8, 56÷8=7).
After consulting it, close the reference and try to reproduce the derivation and the division partner from memory.
activities.intendedInsight: Many hard facts sit next to or near easier ones on the grid, and each product belongs to a fact family linking multiplication and division.

activities.title: Coach talk: choosing a strategy (metacognition)
feedback: Praise a clear, correct method over raw speed alone; a good strategy choice is the goal at this stage.
If no strategy is offered, model one near-fact move and have the learner apply it to a sibling fact.
activities.rationale: A short Socratic exchange may teach strategy selection and metacognition; however, conversational pacing yields relatively few rapid retrievals per session, so on its own it is not suited to building the quick, efficient retrieval that fluency also calls for (fluency being efficiency, accuracy and flexibility) — it supports but does not substitute for timed, spaced practice.
learnerActions: When a fact is tricky, answer the prompt 'What do you already know that's close?' before attempting it.
Name the strategy you will use (near-ten, doubling 2→4→8, partitioning, or inverse flip) and explain why it fits this fact.
Compare two possible strategies for the same fact and say which is more efficient here.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent calculators consciously select an efficient strategy rather than defaulting to counting; naming the choice strengthens flexibility.

constraints: Keep timing low-stakes to protect against maths anxiety while still building speed; emphasise a correct efficient method over raw speed alone, and do not equate slow-but-correct with wrong.
A fixed, non-adaptive fact check chiefly measures fluency; pair it with explicit strategy teaching rather than using it as the only route to fluency.
A reference grid or overlay shows strategies but does not drill fluent retrieval; always follow look-ups with unaided practice.

Conversation can build strategy selection and metacognition, but its slower pacing limits rapid repeated retrieval, so on its own it is not suited to building the quick retrieval that supports the efficiency side of fluency (which is efficiency, accuracy and flexibility, not speed alone).
Interleave × and ÷ so the inverse is practised as a retrieval strategy; division facts lag when only multiplication is drilled.
Apply facts inside multi-step calculations and word problems so fluency transfers beyond isolated recall.
Interaction examples (array peeling a column, splitting into 5×8+8, one-tap division flip) are illustrative of the learning mechanism and optional, not mandatory mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source row marks the CCSS-M 3.OA.7 claim and the NCETM/IES fluency claim as verified:false; only the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified:true. Treat citations accordingly and do not upgrade their confidence.
The original '3 seconds' / 'few seconds' targets are retained as loose, low-stakes guidance consistent with the row's anxiety caution; they are age-norm heuristics, not strict thresholds.
The non-preferred 3D entry was dropped because its only content was a universal-inferiority claim ('3D adds nothing'); no qualified affordance remained to preserve.

Editor note: fluency wording was corrected so rapid retrieval is tied to the efficiency component of fluency rather than being described as what 'defines' fluency, consistent with the row's warning against equating fluency with speed alone; and catalog artefact-type vocabulary (e.g. 'quiz') was replaced with plain descriptions such as 'fixed, non-adaptive fact check'.

probeDeeper: Show me how 10 × 7 helps with 9 × 7.
What multiplication fact gives you 54 ÷ 6?
Which facts do you just know, and which do you work out?
Derive 6 × 8 from a fact you know.
assess.correctAnswer: 42, 9, 72; 9 × 7 = 10 × 7 − 7 = 70 − 7 = 63; 49 ÷ 7 = 7 because 7 × 7 = 49. Facts answered within a few seconds, with derivation and the inverse relationship used deliberately.

errorPatterns.pattern: no derived-fact strategy — when a fact isn't instantly known, counts up rather than deriving from a near fact (9 × 7 via 10 × 7 − 7)
errorPatterns.nextMove: explicitly teach near-fact strategies (×9 via ×10 then subtract; ×6 via ×5 then add) and rehearse them until they are reached for first
errorPatterns.revealedBy: reverts to skip-counting and can't produce a derivation when asked

errorPatterns.pattern: division not linked to multiplication — solves 54 ÷ 6 by trial or counting, not by recalling 6 × 9
errorPatterns.nextMove: use fact-family triangles and prompt 'what times 6 makes 54?'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: cannot state the × fact behind a ÷

errorPatterns.pattern: accurate but not yet fluent — gets everything right but well over a few seconds, still reconstructing
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT equate slow with wrong or pile on timed pressure — fluency follows from secure strategies plus spaced retrieval; protect confidence
errorPatterns.revealedBy: correct but slow and effortful answers

responseLevels.gap: Cannot answer within 100 reliably; no link between × and ÷.
responseLevels.full: Answers × and ÷ within 100 in a few seconds, deploys derived-fact strategies (e.g. 9 × 7 = 10 × 7 − 7), and uses the inverse relationship for division facts.
responseLevels.partial: Recalls facts but slowly, reconstructing by counting rather than deriving from near facts; division lags.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I'll time you loosely — aim for about three seconds each. 6 × 7? 54 ÷ 6? 8 × 9? Now show me a clever way (not counting): work out 9 × 7 using 10 × 7. And 49 ÷ 7 — what multiplication tells you the answer? (Watch speed, use of derived-fact strategies, and the multiplication–division link.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: This topic is about strategic fluency, not bare recall — the derive-9×7 and 'what × gives 49 ÷ 7' tasks reveal whether the child owns near-fact strategies and the inverse relationship, or falls back on rote recall and laborious counting when a fact isn't instant.

pedagogy.summary: Ordering and continuing patterns and sequences develops from duplicating and extending by visual matching to abstracting the UNIT OF REPEAT and identifying the smallest repeating unit — and only these last two mark genuine understanding rather than surface matching (Rittle-Johnson et al. 2013). Teaching should move children beyond 'what comes next' to seeing a pattern as made of repeating units: naming and circling the unit, recreating a pattern with different materials (abstraction, which cannot be done by visual matching), and asking for the smallest arrangement that keeps the pattern.
bestPractices: Shift the focus from 'what comes next' to structure: name and circle the unit of repeat, not just append the next item.
Use abstraction tasks — recreate the same kind of pattern with different materials or colours — which force attention to structure because visual matching won't work.
Ask for the smallest unit ('what is the smallest tower that still keeps the pattern?') to assess unit identification, the hardest and most telling skill.
Include units beyond simple AB (ABB, AAB, ABC), because children over-rely on alternation; watch for them reverting to AB.
Model 'same, same, different' language and 'start over' framing to make the repeating unit explicit.
keyRepresentations: Colour/shape cube or bead strings
The unit of repeat circled or boxed
ABB / AAB units contrasted with AB
'Same, same, different' labelling of the unit
Number sequences and skip-counting as patterns
commonMisconceptions: Extends a pattern by visually matching and appending the last item, without grasping that there is a repeating unit.
Reverts to a simple AB pattern when the model unit is longer (makes ABAB for an ABB model).
Produces a partially correct pattern — one full unit plus extra items that break the unit.

learn.summary: Patterns and sequences teaching should move children beyond 'what comes next' to seeing a pattern as made of a repeating UNIT. The telling skills are abstracting a pattern onto new materials and identifying the smallest repeating unit — both of which, according to Rittle-Johnson et al. (2013), cannot be done by visual matching alone and so reveal genuine structural understanding rather than surface copying. Build, extend, abstract, and isolate the unit, using units beyond simple AB (ABB, AAB, ABC) because children over-rely on alternation.

activities.title: Build, extend, and name the unit of repeat
feedback: If the child only appends the last item without a sense of the unit, label the model with 'same' and 'different' and box the repeating chunk, then rebuild from that unit before extending.
If they produce one full unit then stray cubes that break it, treat this as emerging knowledge, not simply wrong: ask 'where does the pattern start again?' and practise shorter units first.
Prompt: 'Point to the part of the pattern that repeats — where does it start again?'
activities.rationale: Economopoulos (quoted in Rittle-Johnson et al.) argues children must move from seeing a pattern as a sequence of 'what comes next' to analysing its structure as repeating units in order to generalise and predict. Naming and circling the unit makes that structure explicit.
sourceClaims: To generalise and predict, children must move from looking at a pattern as a sequence of 'what comes next' to analysing its structure — seeing that it is made of repeating units (Economopoulos, 1998, quoted in the study).
learnerActions: Continue a given model pattern, e.g. red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue — carry it on further with cubes, beads, or drawn shapes.
Circle or box the part that repeats and say where the pattern 'starts over'.

Name which items are the SAME and which is DIFFERENT: for red, blue, blue the two blues are the same and the red is the different cube that starts the chunk (spoken in order: different, same, same). The plain 'same, same, different' chant maps most cleanly to a two-same-then-different unit such as AAB.
activities.intendedInsight: A repeating pattern is built from a unit that repeats; the pattern is the unit, not just the next item you could add.

activities.title: Abstract the same KIND of pattern onto new materials
feedback: If the child reverts to green-yellow-green-yellow (AB) for an ABB model, lay the new pattern under the model and check unit-for-unit; count how many yellows come before the next green.
If they merely copy surface colours or cannot reproduce the structure on new materials, return to boxing the unit in the model and rebuild from that chunk.
Prompt: 'Is your green-and-yellow pattern the SAME KIND as the red-and-blue one? How can you check?'
activities.rationale: Rittle-Johnson et al. report that abstracting a pattern onto new materials is a harder skill than extending, cannot be done by visual matching, and clearly demonstrates understanding; children commonly revert to AB for longer units, so non-AB models (ABB, AAB) are important.
sourceClaims: Children can often duplicate and extend repeating patterns by visual matching without knowing there is a pattern unit that repeats; abstracting a pattern onto new materials and identifying the smallest unit of repeat are harder skills that cannot be done by visual matching and are the ones that clearly demonstrate understanding. Common errors include reverting to a simple AB pattern for a longer unit and producing one full unit plus extraneous items; longer units are harder to preserve.
learnerActions: Given a red-blue-blue model, use a different set (e.g. green and yellow cubes) to make 'the same KIND of pattern' — green, yellow, yellow, repeated.
Lay the new pattern directly under the model and check unit-for-unit: count how many yellows come before the next green.
Explain why your new pattern is the same kind even though the colours are different.
activities.intendedInsight: Making the 'same kind' of pattern means reproducing the STRUCTURE (one cube, then two matching cubes, then start over), not the colours — abstraction that colour matching alone cannot accomplish.

activities.title: Shrink to the smallest tower that keeps the pattern
feedback: If the child offers a longer stretch than one unit, ask them to take away cubes one whole unit at a time until only one copy of the unit is left (taking away more would break it). Then check that it still has the full arrangement: for red-blue-blue, the red that starts it and then the two matching blues; for AAB, two matching cubes then a different one; for ABC, three different cubes.
Prompt: 'If I take some cubes away, is it still the same pattern? Why?' and 'What is the smallest tower you could build that still has this pattern?'
Watch for reverting to AB on longer units; if it happens, return to the unit-for-unit check from the abstraction task.
activities.rationale: Rittle-Johnson et al. identify smallest-unit identification as the hardest and most telling patterning skill, not achievable by visual matching. Including units beyond AB counters children's over-reliance on alternation.
sourceClaims: Children can often duplicate and extend repeating patterns by visual matching without knowing there is a pattern unit that repeats; abstracting a pattern onto new materials and identifying the smallest unit of repeat are harder skills that cannot be done by visual matching and are the ones that clearly demonstrate understanding. Common errors include reverting to a simple AB pattern for a longer unit and producing one full unit plus extraneous items; longer units are harder to preserve.
learnerActions: From a repeating pattern, build the smallest tower that still has the same pattern (for red-blue-blue, the three-cube unit red, blue, blue).
Decide whether removing cubes keeps or breaks the pattern, and explain why.
Try the same with AAB and ABC units, not just AB.
activities.intendedInsight: The smallest arrangement that preserves the pattern IS the unit of repeat; isolating it is the clearest sign of understanding structure.

activities.title: Describe the rule and connect to number sequences
feedback: If the rule given is only 'the next one is blue', press for the whole unit and where it restarts.
If a self-made 'longer' pattern collapses to AB, prompt the unit-for-unit check before they hand it over.
Encourage children to say which items are the same and which are different (for an ABC unit, all three are different), and to use 'start over' language, to make the unit clear.
activities.rationale: The micro-topic requires describing rules and creating patterns. Using 'same/different' and 'start over' language makes the repeating unit clear. Number sequences and skip-counting can be linked as rule-based patterns, but their rule is a repeated step (e.g. add 2), not a repeating unit of items, and this difference should be pointed out.
sourceClaims: To generalise and predict, children must move from looking at a pattern as a sequence of 'what comes next' to analysing its structure — seeing that it is made of repeating units (Economopoulos, 1998, quoted in the study).
learnerActions: Say aloud the rule for a given sequence of objects ('it goes red, then two blues, then starts over').

Look at number sequences and skip-counting as patterns too, but notice the difference: in skip-counting (2, 4, 6, 8, …) the numbers keep growing and do not repeat, but the step does (add 2 each time). Some parts can repeat like a unit, e.g. the last digits when counting in 5s (5, 10, 15, 20 → 5, 0, 5, 0).
Create your own pattern with a chosen unit (ABB, AAB, or ABC) and challenge someone else to find the smallest unit.
activities.intendedInsight: Saying the rule out loud and making your own patterns help children move from 'what comes next' to thinking about the repeating unit. Number sequences such as skip-counting are a different kind of pattern: the numbers grow, and what repeats is the rule or step (e.g. +2), not a unit of items.

constraints: A static pattern with the unit highlighted (e.g. tap to box the unit and reveal which items are same/different) is a useful reference, but a fixed display on its own does not let the child extend, abstract, or isolate the unit; pair it with building/doing tasks.

Sequence and fill-in-the-blank response formats can check 'what comes next' and 'circle the unit', but risk rewarding visual matching; always add an abstraction (new-materials) task and a smallest-unit task to go beyond appending.
Extending a pattern can be achieved by visual matching without understanding; use the abstraction and smallest-unit tasks to distinguish surface copying from structural understanding.
Use units beyond AB (ABB, AAB, ABC) because children over-rely on alternation and may revert to AB on longer units.
A partially correct pattern (one full unit plus stray items) is a transitional, emerging state — do not treat it as simply wrong.

The 'same, same, different' chant describes a two-same-then-different unit (AAB); for the ABB example (red, blue, blue) name the two blues as the same and the red as the different start rather than chanting the phrase in order over it.

Optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete: swapping to a new colour set for the abstraction task, a 'shrink to the smallest tower' control, laying the new pattern under the model for unit-for-unit comparison, and flagging reversions to AB. These are suggestions, not required mechanisms.

Hands-on construction is central for building and abstracting patterns; conversation can support prompting an explanation of the rule alongside that construction, without being treated as a substitute for it.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated 3D as adding nothing and conversation/static image as poor. These have been softened: patterning structure is not inherently spatial, and a fixed display or dialogue can still support reference and explanation respectively. No comparative efficacy or necessity claim is asserted beyond the specific source claim that extending can be done by visual matching while abstraction and smallest-unit identification cannot.
The claim that abstraction and smallest-unit tasks 'cannot be done by visual matching' is attributed to Rittle-Johnson et al. (2013) and retained as sourced, not generalised beyond it.

The original row applied 'same, same, different' to its red-blue-blue (ABB) example, which read in order is different-same-same. The learner-facing text now names which items are same and which is different instead of chanting the phrase over ABB, so the label and example no longer disagree; the phrase is noted as fitting an AAB unit.
Example pattern (red, blue, blue = ABB; green, yellow, yellow abstraction; three-cube smallest unit) checked for internal consistency and found coherent.

probeDeeper: Point to the part of the pattern that repeats — where does it start again?
Is your green-and-yellow pattern the SAME KIND as the red-and-blue one? How can you check?
What is the smallest tower you could build that still has this pattern?
If I take some cubes away, is it still the same pattern? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: Extends the pattern preserving the red-blue-blue unit; abstracts the ABB structure into green-yellow-yellow (neither reverting to an AB alternation nor merely copying the colours); and offers the three-cube unit (green, yellow, yellow) as the smallest tower that keeps the pattern.

errorPatterns.pattern: Extends by visually matching and appending the last item, without grasping there is a repeating unit
errorPatterns.nextMove: Label the model 'same, same, different' and box the repeating chunk; rebuild from that unit before extending
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Continues the given pattern acceptably but on the new-materials task cannot reproduce the structure

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverts to a simple AB pattern when the model unit is longer than two
errorPatterns.nextMove: Lay the new pattern under the model and check unit-for-unit — count how many yellows come before the next green
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Makes green-yellow-green-yellow (AB) for a red-blue-blue (ABB) model

errorPatterns.pattern: Produces a partially correct pattern — one full unit followed by extra items that break the unit
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT treat as simply wrong — it shows emerging knowledge; ask 'where does the pattern start again?' and practise shorter units first
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Builds one red-blue-blue unit then adds stray cubes that don't continue it (a transitional state)

responseLevels.gap: Appends items by matching the last one; on new materials reverts to AB or copies colours — no sense of a unit.
responseLevels.full: Extends, abstracts to new materials, and identifies the smallest unit of repeat for multi-element units, explaining the pattern as a repeating unit rather than 'what comes next'.
responseLevels.partial: Extends and often abstracts familiar AB patterns, but breaks down on longer units (ABB/AAB) — reverting to AB or adding extra items — and cannot isolate the smallest unit.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a pattern made with coloured cubes: red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue. First, carry it on for me. Now, using these different cubes (green and yellow), make the same KIND of pattern. Last, show me the smallest tower you could make that still keeps the same pattern.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Extending alone can be done by visual matching; the abstraction task (new materials) and the 'smallest unit' task cannot. A child who only appends by look reverts to AB or copies surface colours; a child who holds the unit reproduces the ABB structure and isolates the three-cube unit. The three tasks together separate visual matching from structural understanding.

Common errors include reverting to a simple AB pattern for a longer unit and producing one full unit plus extraneous items; longer units are harder to preserve.

pedagogy.summary: This topic is about APPLYING addition and subtraction to real problems — including two-step problems, money, and measures — and choosing between a mental method and a written one. The mathematical challenge is less about calculating and more about modelling: reading the situation, deciding what operation each step needs, and picking an efficient method. Bar models and part-whole diagrams are the key tools for representing the structure before computing.
bestPractices: Teach the child to represent the situation first (bar model / part-whole) before choosing numbers or method — structure before calculation
For two-step problems, make the intermediate result explicit ('how much after spending, before finding?')
Discuss method choice: some problems are quicker mentally (35p−12p), some warrant a jotting/written method — build the judgement
Attend to units and context in measures/money (cm, p) so answers are labelled and sensible
Use the DfE problem vocabulary (total, difference, more/less, change) so the operation is drawn from the situation, not from keywords
keyRepresentations: Bar model (comparison, part-whole, two-step)
Part-whole diagram
Number line (count-on for change/difference)
Coins / ruler as concrete context for money and measures
Jottings vs mental — an anchor chart of when to use each
commonMisconceptions: Keyword strategy: picking the operation from words ('left'→subtract, 'altogether'→add) rather than the situation — breaks on multi-step and compare problems
Doing only the first step of a two-step problem and stopping
Losing or misusing the intermediate result
Ignoring units, or mixing units in measures/money problems
Defaulting to a written method when a mental one is far quicker (or vice versa)

learn.summary: Year 2 children learn to apply addition and subtraction to real problems — two-step problems, money, and measures — and to choose between a mental and a written method. The core challenge is modelling: reading the situation, deciding what each step needs, and tracking an intermediate result, rather than picking an operation from keywords. Bar models and part-whole diagrams represent the structure before any computing.

activities.title: Build the story as a bar model (money two-step)
feedback: If the child answers 23p for the money problem, point to the third part of the story: 'then found 5p' — ask 'is 23p the final answer, or is there another step?' and have them add the last bar.
If the answer has no unit or mixes cm and p, ask 'how many WHAT?' and require a labelled answer, keeping coins or a ruler in view.
If they reach for an operation before drawing, ask them to show who has what as a bar first, before choosing to add or subtract.
activities.rationale: Representing the relationships between quantities with a strip/bar diagram, rather than attending to surface features, supports genuine problem solving; making the intermediate result explicit directly addresses the common error of doing only the first step.
sourceClaims: Genuine problem solving is reasoning about a problem's structure, 'not the execution of memorized rules or shortcuts, such as using key words'; teaching students to represent the relationships between quantities with visual representations (strip/bar diagrams), rather than attending to surface features, improves problem solving (Recommendation 3, STRONG evidence).
learnerActions: Take the problem 'I had 35p, spent 12p, then found 5p — how much now?' and draw a bar to represent the starting 35p.
Cut 12p off the bar for the spending, and label the segment that is left — write 35−12=23 and mark 23p as the intermediate result.
Add a 5p bar for 'then found 5p' and compute the final total: 23+5=28p. Label the answer with its unit.
Repeat with a lengths story, e.g. 'a ribbon is 45cm, I cut off 18cm — how long is left?', drawing and labelling the bar and giving the answer in cm (45−18=27cm).
activities.intendedInsight: Drawing the situation turns a confusing word problem into visible parts; seeing the middle number (23p) appear is what stops a child from stopping after step one, and labelling keeps the units correct.

activities.title: Compare problems that defeat keyword guessing
feedback: If the child chooses an operation from a cue word, have them draw both people's bars first: in the first problem Tom's bar is longer, so we add; in the contrasting problem Sam's bar is shorter, so we subtract.
Ask 'could more than ever mean subtract?' to surface that keywords are unreliable and the drawn structure is the guide.
activities.rationale: Some compare and start-unknown structures are where keyword strategies often fail. Children solve them more reliably by modelling the situation. Setting the Sam/Tom problem, where 'more than' does mean add, beside a problem where 'more' needs subtraction makes the keyword strategy visibly break down.
sourceClaims: Word-problem difficulty follows the problem's semantic structure: result-unknown (join/separate) problems are easier than compare and start-unknown structures, on which keyword strategies systematically fail; children solve most reliably by modelling the situation.

Genuine problem solving is reasoning about a problem's structure, 'not the execution of memorized rules or shortcuts, such as using key words'; teaching students to represent the relationships between quantities with visual representations (strip/bar diagrams), rather than attending to surface features, improves problem solving (Recommendation 3, STRONG evidence).
learnerActions: Solve 'Sam has 24 stickers. Tom has 8 more than Sam. How many does Tom have?' by drawing Sam's bar and building Tom's bar as Sam's amount plus 8 more.
State the operation you used (24+8=32) and explain why 'more than' here means add, even though 'more than' can sometimes cue the wrong choice.

Try a contrasting compare problem where the cue word misleads, e.g. 'Tom has 32 stickers. He has 8 more than Sam. How many does Sam have?' Draw both bars and notice that, even though it says 'more', Sam's bar is shorter, so you subtract (32−8=24). Modelling, not the cue word, tells you whether to add or subtract.
activities.intendedInsight: The operation comes from the situation, not from a trigger word; a bar model makes compare problems (where keywords can mislead) solvable by showing the structure.

activities.title: Mental or written? Choosing an efficient method
feedback: If the child always writes everything out, ask whether 35p−12p really needed paper, and invite a mental attempt.
If a larger problem goes wrong in the head, suggest a jotting or a number-line count-on and compare which felt more reliable.
activities.rationale: The curriculum expects pupils to use both mental and written methods; building the judgement of when each is efficient is part of the objective rather than defaulting to one.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils solve problems with addition and subtraction using concrete objects, pictorial representations and mental and written methods, including problems involving numbers, quantities and measures.
learnerActions: For each problem decide: can I do this quickly in my head, or should I jot it down? Then solve it.
Compare 35p−12p (quick mentally) with a larger measures problem such as 45cm−18cm that may be easier with a jotting or bridging step.
Build a short anchor chart of 'when I use mental' versus 'when I jot/write', and justify one of your choices aloud.
activities.intendedInsight: Method choice is a judgement about efficiency, not a rule; small, friendly numbers often suit mental work while larger or multi-digit ones may warrant a written method.

activities.title: Talk through the structure before solving
feedback: If the child jumps to an answer, pause and ask them to re-tell the story in their own words and count the steps.
Keep the discussion on eliciting structure and steps — avoid simply supplying the answer so the child still does the modelling.
activities.rationale: Spoken elicitation of 'what we know / what we need' keeps attention on the problem's structure rather than on cue words, but talk alone does not provide the manipulable diagram or practice volume, so it is paired with actually building and computing the model rather than offered as a substitute.
sourceClaims: Genuine problem solving is reasoning about a problem's structure, 'not the execution of memorized rules or shortcuts, such as using key words'; teaching students to represent the relationships between quantities with visual representations (strip/bar diagrams), rather than attending to surface features, improves problem solving (Recommendation 3, STRONG evidence).
learnerActions: With a partner or adult, answer three questions about a new story: what is happening, what do we know, and what do we need to find?
Say how many steps the problem has before computing anything, and name the intermediate quantity for a two-step problem.
Only then draw the bar model and solve, checking your spoken plan against your diagram.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the structure first guards against grabbing an operation prematurely and against stopping halfway through a two-step problem.

constraints: Represent the situation first (bar model or part-whole) before choosing numbers or method — structure before calculation.
For two-step problems, make the intermediate result explicit ('how much after spending, before finding?') so the child does not stop after step one.
Attend to units and context in money and measures (p, cm) so answers are labelled and sensible.
Use problem vocabulary (total, difference, more/less, change) so the operation is drawn from the situation, not from keywords.

Checking an operation choice with a multiple-choice or matching question can diagnose keyword or method-choice errors, but recognising the right operation does not by itself show the child can construct and track a model; pair any such check with building and solving.
A static worked bar model with tap-to-reveal labels is a useful reference for structure but does not let the child model a new problem, so it is a scaffold, not the main task.
Spoken discussion can elicit structure well but does not provide the manipulable diagram or practice volume on its own.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Self-audit of arithmetic: 35−12=23 and 23+5=28p (correct); 45−18=27cm (correct); compare problem 24+8=32 (correct). The source correctAnswer values are consistent.

One legacy entry asserted that for this topic '3D adds nothing'. This comparative/necessity claim is not established by the cited sources and has been dropped rather than restated as a universal law; the narrower point that the mathematics here is not inherently spatial is retained only as the reason the proposed activities use bars, coins, rulers and discussion.

The Cognitively Guided Instruction / problem-type hierarchy source is marked verified:false in the row; its claim about compare and start-unknown difficulty is retained in activity 2 but should be treated as unverified pending review.

The National Curriculum claim is scoped to activity 3, whose rationale invokes using both mental and written methods; it was not carried into activity 1, whose rationale concerns bar-model representation and the intermediate result and is supported by the WWC strip/bar claim alone.

Activity 4 is a spoken/dialogue scaffold. Its WWC sourceClaim is cited only for the medium-agnostic 'reason about structure, not shortcuts' principle; the sources do not establish dialogue as a necessary or superior medium, so the activity avoids any such categorical claim and pairs talk with building and computing the diagram.

probeDeeper: Show me your problem as a bar model — which part are we trying to find?
For the sticker problem, why did you add when it says 'more than'? Could 'more than' ever mean subtract?
You got 23p — is that the final answer, or is there another step?
Was this one quicker in your head or written down? How did you decide?
assess.correctAnswer: (1) 28p — two steps: 35−12=23, then 23+5=28. (2) 27cm — 45−18 (mental bridging or jotting). (3) 32 — a compare problem needing addition (24+8) despite 'more than' sometimes cueing the wrong choice for keyword users.

errorPatterns.pattern: Keyword strategy — picks the operation from a word rather than the situation ('more than' or 'left' triggers a fixed operation)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist on a bar model first: represent who has what before choosing an operation. Use compare problems where the keyword misleads, so the strategy visibly fails.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In the compare problem the child subtracts because of a cue word, or reaches for an operation without modelling the story

errorPatterns.pattern: Stops after the first step — answers the two-step money problem with 23p
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach: have the child underline both actions in the story and use a bar model that shows the intermediate result is not the final answer. This is a tracking lapse.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child computes 35−12 and gives 23p, ignoring the 'then found 5p'

errorPatterns.pattern: Ignores or mixes units — gives an unlabelled number, or muddles cm/p
errorPatterns.nextMove: Prompt 'how many WHAT?' and require a labelled answer; keep the concrete context (ruler, coins) in view.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The answer has no unit, or the units are inconsistent with the problem

responseLevels.gap: Chooses operations by keyword, stops after one step, or gives unlabelled/mismatched answers; cannot represent the situation.
responseLevels.full: Models each situation (bar/part-whole), carries out both steps tracking the intermediate result, chooses an efficient method and justifies it, and gives labelled, sensible answers.
responseLevels.partial: Solves single-step and straightforward problems and can model with support, but stumbles on the compare problem or the second step, or doesn't yet choose method deliberately.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set three problems and watch the child solve each, choosing their own method and jotting if they wish: (1) 'I had 35p, spent 12p, then found 5p — how much now?' (2) 'A ribbon is 45cm; I cut off 18cm — how long is left?' (3) 'Sam has 24 stickers. Tom has 8 more than Sam. How many does Tom have?' Notice how they decide the operation and whether they finish two-step problems.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Problem (1) exposes whether the child carries out BOTH steps and tracks the intermediate 23p. Problem (3) is a compare problem where a keyword solver may be pulled by 'more than'; a child reading the situation adds. Problem (2) checks method choice and unit-labelling. Together they separate a situation-modeller from a keyword-matcher who stops early.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 11–12: extend the order of operations to include POWERS, ROOTS and RECIPROCALS — use conventional priority notation (BIDMAS/BODMAS) to evaluate complex numerical expressions, and understand a number times its reciprocal is 1.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, KS3): 'use conventional notation for priority of operations, including brackets, powers, roots and reciprocals'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 6.EE.1 (write and evaluate numerical expressions involving whole-number exponents); the precedence of exponents within order of operations is formalised in Grade 6.
• Operational details — insert the Indices/Orders tier between Brackets and ×÷: Brackets → Indices (powers & roots) → ×÷ (L→R) → +− (L→R). Evaluate expressions like 3 + 2³ × 4 or √(9+16). Introduce the reciprocal (1/n) as the multiplicative inverse — n × 1/n = 1 — and note division by n equals multiplication by its reciprocal. Reinforce that the whole convention is an agreed anti-ambiguity notation, extended, not a new rule set.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 11): evaluate an expression with one power correctly (3 + 2³×4 = 35). Tier B (11–12): evaluate an expression mixing brackets, a root/power and all four operations. Tier C (12): explain why order of operations avoids ambiguity, and use a reciprocal (n × 1/n = 1; ÷n = ×1/n).
bestPractices: Slot the new INDICES tier explicitly into the already-secured Y6 hierarchy (prerequisite mt_jHgRQ4hR0g): powers and roots sit just below brackets and above ×÷ — present it as an extension of a known ladder, not a fresh acronym.
Keep reinforcing that ×÷ share a tier and +− share a tier (swept L→R); the BIDMAS acronym still misleads on D-before-M and A-before-S, so rehearse counterexamples with powers added.
Teach the reciprocal via the defining property n × 1/n = 1 and connect ÷n = ×1/n — seeding fraction division and later algebra; use it to show why reciprocals are 'undo by multiply'.
Confront power-specific traps directly: 2³ means 2×2×2 = 8 (not 2×3 = 6), and −3² vs (−3)² differ because the power binds tighter than the negative sign unless bracketed.
Motivate with genuine ambiguity: show a calculator or two people disagreeing on 3 + 2³ × 4, then resolve with the extended hierarchy, so the convention is felt as necessary.
keyRepresentations: Extended hierarchy ladder with the new Indices step inserted between Brackets and ×÷.
Colour-tiered annotation of an expression (brackets, then powers/roots, then ×÷, then +−) before evaluation.
Reciprocal pairing: n and 1/n shown multiplying to 1 (e.g. on a number line or as a product returning to unity).
Step-by-step rewrite chain collapsing one tier per line (3 + 2³×4 → 3 + 8×4 → 3 + 32 → 35).
commonMisconceptions: Evaluating powers as multiplication: 2³ = 6 instead of 8.
Applying the acronym literally — doing division before multiplication or addition before subtraction because I/D/A appear first.
Mishandling sign vs power: −3² taken as (−3)² = 9 rather than −(3²) = −9.
Thinking the reciprocal of n is −n (confusing multiplicative inverse with additive inverse) rather than 1/n.
Treating roots as outside the hierarchy, or evaluating under a root before resolving the bracket-like grouping the root implies (√(9+16) ≠ √9 + √16).

learn.summary: For ages 11–12: extend the order of operations to include an Indices tier (powers and roots) sitting between brackets and ×÷, and introduce the reciprocal as the multiplicative inverse (n × 1/n = 1, with ÷n = ×1/n). Learners evaluate complex expressions tier by tier, confront power-specific traps (2³ ≠ 2×3; −3² vs (−3)²; a root sign implies grouping), and grasp that the whole convention is an agreed anti-ambiguity notation, not an arbitrary rule. Activities range from a live expression-resolving tool (primary proposal) through anchor charts, consolidation questions, and Socratic justification.

activities.title: Resolve the expression one tier at a time
feedback: If a learner gives 2³ = 6, write 2×2×2 and count the factors: the exponent says how many copies of the base are multiplied together, not what to multiply the base by.
If a learner evaluates √9 + √16 = 7, point to the grouping the root sign implies: resolve 9+16 = 25 first, then √25 = 5.

If a learner adds before multiplying (power resolved to 2³ = 8, then 3 + 8 = 11, ×4 = 44), replay both orders side by side so the diverging answers (44 vs 35) show why multiplication is resolved before addition; separately, if a learner misreads the power itself (e.g. 2³ read as 2×3 = 6), handle that as the power-meaning error above.

Optional live supports that make the mechanism concrete: a tier-highlighter that shades each band as it is resolved; a step-by-step rewrite chain collapsing one tier per line; a tool that refuses the mis-ordered path and plays out both answers for comparison. These are illustrative, not required.
activities.rationale: Order of operations with an added tier is structural and sequential; resolving an expression step by step, including a deliberate wrong-order comparison, targets the common error of treating the acronym as a literal sequence and of mishandling powers and roots. KS3 names powers and roots within priority notation and Grade 6 formalises the precedence of exponents.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils use conventional notation for the priority of operations, including brackets, powers, roots and reciprocals.
Grade 6 pupils write and evaluate numerical expressions involving whole-number exponents, formalising the precedence of exponents within the order of operations.
learnerActions: Work with a live expression such as 3 + 2³ × 4 and decide which operation to resolve next, following the hierarchy Brackets → Indices (powers & roots) → ×÷ (left to right) → +− (left to right).
Resolve the power first: 2³ = 8 (write out 2×2×2 to confirm it is not 2×3 = 6), then ×4 = 32, then +3 = 35.
Deliberately try the wrong order — doing the addition before the multiplication: 3 + 2³ = 11, then × 4 = 44 — and compare 44 with the correct 35 so the two answers are seen to diverge.
Annotate an expression by shading each tier a different colour (brackets, then powers/roots, then ×÷, then +−) before collapsing it one tier per line: 3 + 2³×4 → 3 + 8×4 → 3 + 32 → 35.
Evaluate √(9+16): resolve the grouping under the root first (9+16 = 25) then take √25 = 5, and check that this is not √9 + √16 = 3+4 = 7.
activities.intendedInsight: Indices (powers and roots) rank just below brackets and above ×÷; evaluating in the agreed order produces one unambiguous value, and a root implies grouping of what sits under it.

activities.title: The sign-versus-power boundary: −3² vs (−3)²
feedback: If a learner says −3² = 9, show that the exponent attaches to the 3 only: −3² reads as the negative of 3², i.e. −(9) = −9.
If a learner treats (−3)² as −9, point out the bracket groups the minus with the 3 so both factors are negative, giving +9.
An optional toggle that drops a bracket in and shows the answer flip 9 ↔ −9 makes the boundary vivid; a fixed worked pair of both cases also teaches it.
activities.rationale: The −3² vs (−3)² confusion is a named misconception; making the bracket's effect explicit addresses it directly without claiming a single medium is required.
learnerActions: Evaluate −3² by noting the power binds tighter than the negative sign: −3² = −(3²) = −9.
Evaluate (−3)² where the bracket groups the negative with the base: (−3)² = (−3)×(−3) = 9.
Add or remove a bracket around a negative number and predict how the value flips between −9 and 9 before confirming.
activities.intendedInsight: Without brackets, a power applies only to the number immediately beneath it, not to a preceding minus sign; bracketing changes what the exponent acts on.

activities.title: Reciprocals as multiplicative inverse
feedback: If a learner says the reciprocal of n is −n, check the defining property: n × (−n) is not 1, but n × 1/n = 1.
If a learner cannot link reciprocals to division, show ÷n and ×1/n acting on the same number and compare the results.

An optional reciprocal station where a number is dragged onto its ×1/n partner and the product settles to 1, with a ÷n swapped for ×1/n to see them land identically, makes the inverse relationship observable; a number line showing n and 1/n multiplying to unity works similarly.
activities.rationale: Teaching the reciprocal via its defining property seeds fraction division and later algebra and counters the additive-vs-multiplicative inverse confusion. KS3 priority notation explicitly includes reciprocals.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils use conventional notation for the priority of operations, including brackets, powers, roots and reciprocals.
learnerActions: State the reciprocal of a non-zero number n as 1/n and multiply n × 1/n, confirming the product is exactly 1 (e.g. 5 × 1/5 = 1); note that 0 has no reciprocal.
Compare dividing by n with multiplying by 1/n on the same number, checking the two operations give the same result (÷n = ×1/n).
Distinguish the reciprocal (multiplicative inverse, 1/n) from the negative (additive inverse, −n): the reciprocal of 5 is 1/5, not −5.
Match each number to its reciprocal (e.g. 4 ↔ 1/4, 2/3 ↔ 3/2).
activities.intendedInsight: Any non-zero number times its reciprocal is 1, so the reciprocal is what you multiply by to 'undo' multiplication, and dividing by a non-zero number is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal (0 has no reciprocal).

activities.title: Why do we need an agreed order? (justify the convention)
feedback: If a learner says 'that's just the rule', show the same expression producing two answers under two orders and ask which one others should read it as.
Accept any explanation that captures the idea that shared notation must yield one value to be useful for communicating calculations.
activities.rationale: The conceptual heart of this topic is ambiguity-removal; a discussion or Socratic prompt supports justification, which procedural practice alone may leave implicit. This is complementary to the hands-on evaluation, not a substitute for it.
learnerActions: Take a single expression such as 3 + 2³ × 4 and compute it under two different orders, recording the two different values (e.g. 35 vs 44).
Explain in your own words why mathematicians need one agreed order: so the same written expression communicates a single unambiguous value.
Respond to a prompt that offers two conflicting values and justify which order and result is correct and why.
activities.intendedInsight: The order of operations exists to remove ambiguity so notation communicates one value, not because any single order is inherently 'more correct'.

activities.title: Consolidation check
feedback: For 3 + 2³ × 4, flag 44 as the 'added before multiplying' error (power resolved to 8, then 3 + 8 = 11, ×4 = 44) and any value using 2³ = 6; confirm 35 with the tier order.
For √(9+16) + 2×5, check the learner resolved the grouping under the root (25 → 5) before combining with 2×5 = 10, giving 15.
activities.rationale: Short checks consolidate and surface residual errors (adding first, exponent-as-multiplier, sign/power). Recognition and matching test outcomes rather than building the structural insight, so use them after the construction activities.
learnerActions: Evaluate 3 + 2³ × 4 and justify why 35 is correct (not 44 from adding before multiplying, and not using 2³ = 6).
Decide whether −3² equals −9 or 9 and explain the bracket rule.
Resolve √(9+16) + 2×5 in correct priority.
Match numbers to their reciprocals and state what each pair multiplies to.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can evaluate expressions with the new tier correctly and articulate the reciprocal relationship under assessment conditions.

constraints: Present the Indices tier as an extension of the already-secured brackets→×÷→+− hierarchy, not a brand-new acronym.

Keep reinforcing that ×÷ share one tier and +− share one tier, both swept left to right; BIDMAS/BODMAS still misleads on division-before-multiplication and addition-before-subtraction even with indices added — rehearse counterexamples.
A root sign implies grouping of what sits beneath it: resolve under the root before taking the root (√(9+16) = √25 = 5, not √9 + √16 = 7).

Recognition/matching and multiple-choice checks assess outcomes but do not by themselves build the structural, step-by-step insight; pair them with activities where learners resolve expressions and witness the reciprocal returning to 1.

Optional interactive supports (tier-highlighter, wrong-path comparison, drag-to-reciprocal station) make mechanisms concrete but are illustrative examples, not required mechanisms; the same ideas can be taught on paper or with worked pairs.
A fixed worked example cannot be manipulated live but can still teach the −3² vs (−3)² and reciprocal relationships.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and no empirical effectiveness is claimed.

The 44 value is the intended wrong-order result for 3 + 2³ × 4, reached by resolving the power first (2³=8) and then adding before multiplying (3+8=11, ×4=44). It demonstrates that multiplication precedes addition, and is used only as a flagged error, never as a correct option.

Audit of the original assessment: the diagnostic prompt 'Evaluate 2 + 3 × 4²' has correctAnswer 50 (4²=16, 3×16=48, 2+48=50) — arithmetically correct, and the probeDeeper question 'Why did you work out 4² before multiplying by 3?' is consistent with it.

The assessment distractor '2 + (3×4)² = 146' is arithmetically correct ((12)²=144, +2=146) and is a valid wrong-order distractor; used conceptually in consolidation without presenting it as a correct answer.
The source claim that BIDMAS/BODMAS misleads on D-before-M and A-before-S is NCETM-attributed guidance (verified:false in the row); preserved in constraints but not cited as established efficacy.
The parentTitle 'Ratio (age 11+)' appears inconsistent with the order-of-operations/reciprocals content; flagged as a possible source mislabel, not resolved here.

probeDeeper: Why did you work out 4² before multiplying by 3?
What would this expression equal if we just went left to right — and why is that not allowed?
Why do mathematicians need an agreed order at all?
What is the reciprocal of 5, and what do you get when you multiply 5 by it?
assess.correctAnswer: 50 (indices first: 4² = 16; then multiply: 3 × 16 = 48; then add: 2 + 48 = 50). The reason tier: without an agreed order the same expression would give different answers for different people, so the notation would be ambiguous and useless for communicating calculations.

errorPatterns.pattern: handles indices in the wrong place — multiplies 3×4 before squaring, or squares the product (3×4)²
errorPatterns.nextMove: place indices just after brackets in the priority; 4² binds tighter than the multiplication — evaluate the power before combining.
errorPatterns.distractor: 2 + (3×4)² = 146 (multiplied 3 by 4 first, then squared)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer such as 2 + 12² or (3×4)²-based value; power not evaluated first

errorPatterns.pattern: reads the exponent as a multiplier — 4² as 4×2 = 8
errorPatterns.nextMove: 4² means 4×4; distinguish the exponent (how many factors) from a multiplier.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: uses 8 for 4², giving 2 + 24 = 26

errorPatterns.pattern: sees order-of-operations as an arbitrary rule with no purpose — cannot say why agreement matters
errorPatterns.nextMove: show the SAME expression giving two different answers under two orders; the convention exists so notation communicates one unambiguous value.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: on the reason tier the child says 'that's just the rule' with no notion of ambiguity

errorPatterns.pattern: does not connect reciprocals to division — unsure that a × (1/a) = 1
errorPatterns.nextMove: define the reciprocal as the number you multiply by to get 1; ×(1/a) undoes ×a, linking to inverse operations.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: when asked, cannot state that a number times its reciprocal is 1

responseLevels.gap: mis-orders indices or reads the exponent as a multiplier; sees the convention as purposeless.
responseLevels.full: evaluates brackets/indices/operations in correct priority, justifies the convention as removing ambiguity, and understands reciprocals as multiplicative inverses giving 1.
responseLevels.partial: evaluates the expression correctly but explains the order only as 'the rule', without the ambiguity rationale; shaky on reciprocals.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Evaluate 2 + 3 × 4². Then tell me: why must everyone agree on an order for working this out — what would go wrong if they didn't?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Adding indices to the mix is where children who 'know BODMAS' as a word but not as a priority reveal gaps — they may do the multiplication before the power, or add first. The reason tier tests whether they grasp that order-of-operations exists to remove AMBIGUITY, the conceptual heart, not just a mnemonic.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 5–6: read and write NUMERALS 0–100 — extending secure 0–20 numeral reading/writing across the full two-digit range, leaning on the regular tens-and-ones pattern of the written system.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1): 'count, read and write numbers to 100 in numerals'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.NBT.1 'count to 120 ... read and write numerals'; the numeral system to 100 is embedded here and in K.CC.3.
• Operational details — once 0–20 numerals and rote counting to 100 are secure, reading/writing to 100 is mostly about the REGULAR two-digit pattern: the left digit says the tens, the right digit the ones, and decade words map to the tens digit. The persistent trouble spots are the teens/twenties boundary and the said-first-heard-first mismatch (writing 'forty-two' as 24). This is procedural fluency, not yet full place-value reasoning (that is the two-digit-composition topic).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 5): read two-digit numerals up to 100 on sight. Tier B (5–6): write any number 0–100 as a numeral from dictation. Tier C (6): read and write across a decade boundary (e.g. 79–80) and place/find numerals on a 0–100 grid without error.
bestPractices: Lean on the REGULAR pattern of two-digit numerals with a 100-square / Gattegno chart: the tens digit changes down the columns, the ones digit across the rows, making 0–100 a system rather than 100 things to memorise.

Directly rehearse the hear-it/write-it order for two-digit numbers where speech and writing agree in English above twenty (forty-TWO → 4 then 2) but the teens don't (thirteen) — contrast the two explicitly.
Practise decade boundaries (29→30, 79→80) which is where reading/writing and rote counting most often break down.
Keep numerals connected to quantity/position via a bead string or 0–100 number line so a two-digit numeral means 'this far along', not just two digits.
Give balanced read AND write practice (say-it → write it; show it → read it; point on the grid) to avoid one-way fluency.
keyRepresentations: 100-square and Gattegno tens-and-ones chart exposing the regular two-digit pattern.
0–100 bead string / number line linking each numeral to a position/quantity.
Place-value / arrow (Dienes) cards building 42 as 40 and 2 to reinforce which digit is which.
Decade-boundary number tracks (25–35, 75–85) for the tricky crossings.
commonMisconceptions: Transposing spoken two-digit numbers (writing 'forty-two' as 24) — confusing the ones-first teens with the tens-first pattern of the rest.
Decade-boundary errors when counting/writing (after 29 saying/writing 'twenty-ten', or 39→50).
Reading a two-digit numeral as two separate digits ('four, two' for 42) rather than as forty-two.
Miswriting the 'ty' decades (writing 70 as 17, confusing seventy/seventeen).
Omitting or misplacing 0 in decade numbers (writing 40 as 4, or 'forty' as 400).

learn.summary: For children aged 5–6 extending secure 0–20 numeral reading/writing to the full 0–100 range. The goal is procedural fluency in reading and writing two-digit numerals by exploiting the regular pattern (left digit = tens, right digit = ones), targeting the persistent trouble spots: the spoken-order transposition (writing 'forty-two' as 24), decade-boundary crossings (29→30, 79→80), and keeping the 0 in decade numbers. This is numeral fluency, not yet full place-value reasoning.

activities.title: Hear-it, build-it, place-it on a hundred square
feedback: If a learner writes 24 for 'forty-two', place both 24 and 42 on the grid and show how far apart they sit — the transposed numeral is visibly in the wrong region.

If a learner drops the zero when writing a decade number (writing 40 as 4, or 'forty' as 400), point out that the 0 holds the ones place so forty needs both digits and no extra ones; contrast 4 and 40 on the number line to show they are different sizes.
When a number is placed on the grid, an optional response is to light up the cell so a correct answer settles into the right column/row and a wrong one shows the mismatch in position.
For decade-boundary slips (saying 'twenty-ten' after 29, or 39→50), slow down and count along a bead string or number line so 29→30 is felt as one step forward.
Reinforce by linking the numeral to quantity/position on a bead string or number line so the written symbol stays tied to 'how far along'.
activities.rationale: Letting children act on the regular two-digit system — composing from tens and ones, writing from dictation, and seeing position feedback — is intended to build the pattern actively and to target the transposition, zero-omission and decade-boundary errors. Linking numerals to position/quantity keeps the symbol meaningful. Efficacy is proposed, not established.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils count, read and write numbers to 100 in numerals.
A 100-square / Gattegno chart exposes the regular tens-and-ones structure of two-digit numerals; decade boundaries and spoken-order transposition are the key difficulties.
learnerActions: Listen to a spoken two-digit number (e.g. 'sixty-eight') and write or point to its numeral.
Place the numeral in its position on a 100-square (state whether it is a 1–100 or a 0–99 layout), then check whether it lands where that number belongs.
Build a number from tens-and-ones cards: compose 42 by taking the '40' card and placing the '2' over its zero, so the tens and ones are explicitly separated.
Work across decade boundaries: continue 28, 29, __ and 78, 79, __ , writing each numeral (30 and 80).
Do both directions: say-it → write it; show it → read it aloud; point-to-it on the grid.
activities.intendedInsight: 0–100 is one regular system, not a hundred separate facts: moving down a column the tens digit goes up while the ones digit stays the same, and moving along a row the ones digit changes. On a 0–99 square each row shares one tens digit. On a 1–100 square the decade number (10, 20, … 100) ends each row, so it is the one cell in its row with a different tens digit. Either way, each numeral means 'this far along', not just two loose digits.

activities.title: Minimal-pair contrast: -teen versus -ty
feedback: If a learner writes 14 for 'forty', swaps 13/30, or confuses seventeen/seventy (writing 70 as 17), slow the word ending and contrast the pair with base-ten sticks (4 tens versus one ten and 4); firm the decade sequence by rote count.

If dictated teens come out reversed (41 for 'fourteen') while other numbers are fine, treat it as a normal transcription stage: keep modelling teens with a tens/ones frame and let exposure resolve it, rather than marking it wrong repeatedly.
activities.rationale: Minimal pairs isolate the genuine error types — auditory -teen/-ty confusion and teen transposition — so practice targets where fluency breaks rather than re-drilling secure numbers.
sourceClaims: A 100-square / Gattegno chart exposes the regular tens-and-ones structure of two-digit numerals; decade boundaries and spoken-order transposition are the key difficulties.
learnerActions: Read aloud the auditory -teen/-ty pairs: 13 and 30, 14 and 40, 17 and 70 (seventeen/seventy); then the separate reading-order/transposition pair 17 and 71 (seventeen/seventy-one).
Take dictation of 'forty' then 'fourteen'; write each and compare.
Explain or show how 40 and 14 differ, e.g. with base-ten sticks: forty is 4 tens; fourteen is one ten and 4.
Say the endings clearly: contrast the spoken ones-first teens (thir-TEEN) with the spoken tens-first rest (FORTY-two), while noting both are written tens-first (13 and 42).
activities.intendedInsight: The teens 13–19 are SAID with the ones idea first (a special '-teen' word), and eleven and twelve are irregular words. All of them, like every two-digit number, are WRITTEN tens-first (11, 12, 13, 14). Numbers from 20 up are both said and written tens-first. Seeing that teens are spoken in a different order from how they are written helps keep the two patterns apart and supports moving past writing 41 for fourteen as place value develops.

activities.title: Fluency check: read, write, place, order
feedback: A correct answer confirms fluency; a wrong one points back to the build/contrast activities — e.g. a transposition sends the learner to the tens-and-ones card build, a -teen/-ty slip to the minimal-pair contrast, a dropped zero back to placing 4 versus 40.
When a dictated 'forty-two' is written as 24, show the gap between 24 and 42 on the line rather than just marking it wrong.
activities.rationale: Two-digit numeral reading/writing is highly checkable in multiple formats; a check can consolidate and surface which specific trouble spot remains. It tests fluency rather than building the pattern insight, so it follows the active work; it does not by itself teach the pattern.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils count, read and write numbers to 100 in numerals.
learnerActions: Write the numeral for a spoken number (e.g. 'forty-two' → 42).
Read a shown numeral aloud (e.g. 68 as 'sixty-eight', not 'six, eight').
Place a numeral on a 0–100 line (e.g. position 68).
Order a short sequence across a decade boundary, e.g. fill the gaps around 29→30.
Write the number that is one more than 19 (20); write 'sixty-two' then 'twenty-six' and check they differ.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading and writing to 100 should be reliable in both directions and across decade crossings, with minimal pairs kept distinct and the zero kept in decade numbers.

constraints: Secure 0–20 numeral reading/writing and rote counting to 100 are prerequisites before extending to 100.

This is procedural numeral fluency, not full place-value reasoning (two-digit composition/decomposition is a separate topic); keep representations tied to quantity/position but do not assume full place-value understanding.
Writing teen numbers in spoken order (41 for 'fourteen') is a normal developmental transcription stage that matures with place value; do not drill it as a careless error or mark it wrong repeatedly.

A static tappable 100-square is a useful reference and can present a numeral and its word, but it cannot by itself rehearse the productive skills of writing from dictation or free reading; use it as a scaffold alongside writing/speaking practice.
Recognition-only (multiple-choice) responses confirm reading but do not elicit independent numeral writing; include actual writing-from-dictation for the production half of the skill.
Decade numbers keep the 0 as a ones-place holder (40, not 4 or 400); treat zero omission/misplacement as its own error alongside transposition and -teen/-ty confusion.

Teens are written tens-first (13, 14) just like all two-digit numerals; only the SPOKEN order of teens differs, so teach the spoken/written order distinction rather than implying teens are written ones-first.

Position-lighting, grid cells, card-dragging and spoken prompts are optional ways to make feedback concrete, not required mechanisms; the same work can be done on paper, with a bead string, or with spoken dictation.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources have not been re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three sources (CCSS-M 1.NBT.1 and the NCETM 100-square guidance) are marked verified:false in the source row; the claims that the 100-square exposes the regular structure and that transposition/decade boundaries are the key difficulties are cited but not independently verified here.

Corrected a factual error in the -teen/-ty activity's intended insight: the candidate stated teens are 'said and written with the ones idea first'. Teens are only SPOKEN ones-first; they are written tens-first (13, 14) like every other two-digit numeral, which is precisely why writing 41 for fourteen is a mismatch error.

The legacy entries asserted 'a static picture cannot rehearse' the skill and '3D adds nothing' for flat symbols; these have been softened to narrowly scoped affordance/limit statements rather than universal claims, and the 3D dismissal was dropped as unsupported boilerplate.
The original commonMisconception on omitting/misplacing the 0 in decade numbers (40 as 4, 'forty' as 400) is reinstated in activity feedback and constraints.

The source's diagnostic prompt says to watch rather than question the child; this observation framing is retained descriptively, but comparative-efficacy claims about watching versus questioning are not asserted as established.

probeDeeper: Write the number that is one more than 19.
Read this: 40. Now this: 14. Say how you can tell them apart.
Write 'sixty-two', then 'twenty-six' — check they're different.
assess.correctAnswer: Reads all four correctly and writes 40, 14, 62, 26 — distinguishing 13 from 30 and not transposing 62/26.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses the -teen and -ty sounds: writes 14 for 'forty' or reads 30 as 'thirteen'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Slow the ending, contrast the pair with base-ten sticks (forty = 4 tens; fourteen = ten and 4). Firm the decade sequence in rote count.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Dictation of 'forty' yields 14, or reading 13/30 aloud swaps them.

errorPatterns.pattern: Writes teen numbers in spoken order: 41 for 'fourteen' (hears 'four' first)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill it as a careless error or mark it wrong repeatedly — it is a normal transcription stage that resolves as place value matures. Keep modelling teens with a tens/ones frame and let exposure do the work.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Dictated teens come out reversed (41, 61) while decades and other two-digit numbers are fine.

responseLevels.gap: Confuses teen/decade pairs or cannot write two-digit numerals from dictation.
responseLevels.full: Reads and writes all numerals 0–100 accurately from dictation and by sight, reliably distinguishing minimal pairs.
responseLevels.partial: Reads and writes most numerals 0–100 but slips on -teen/-ty minimal pairs or occasionally transposes teens.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Watch the child read and write. First: 'Read these aloud: 13, 30, 17, 71.' Then dictate for them to write: 'forty … fourteen … sixty-two … twenty-six.' Watch the minimal pairs (13/30, 14/40, 62/26) rather than asking them about the numbers.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The contrasting minimal pairs isolate the two real errors: -teen/-ty auditory confusion (40 vs 14) and teen transposition (writing 41 for fourteen). A child who has the numeral system handles both directions; watching, not questioning, catches the slip in the act.
