pedagogy.summary: Partitioning continuous shapes (circles, rectangles) into two and four EQUAL parts, naming them halves and quarters, and describing the whole as 'two halves' or 'four quarters'. The emphasis is on equal parts and on the part-whole relationship: the equal parts together reconstitute the whole. Children meet that a shape can be partitioned validly in more than one way, provided the parts are equal.
bestPractices: Partition by folding and cutting so equality is physical; verify by overlaying parts
Show more than one correct way to halve/quarter the same shape (e.g. a rectangle split vertically or horizontally) so 'halves' is not tied to one cut
Always recompose: 'two halves make the whole', 'four quarters make the whole'
Count the resulting PARTS (regions), not the cuts
Name as you go and have children label their partitions
keyRepresentations: Circles partitioned into 2 and 4 equal sectors
Rectangles partitioned into 2 and 4 equal parts (different orientations)
Overlay/rotation to check parts are equal
Parts reassembling into the whole shape
commonMisconceptions: Accepting unequal parts as halves/quarters because the number of pieces is right
Thinking a shape can only be partitioned one 'correct' way (rejecting valid alternative cuts)
Confusing the number of CUTS with the number of PARTS
Not seeing the whole as composed of its equal parts (cannot say two halves/four quarters make the whole)

learn.summary: Children partition continuous shapes (circles, rectangles) into two and four EQUAL parts, name them halves and quarters, and describe the whole as 'two halves' or 'four quarters'. The core ideas are equality of parts (equal in size, not necessarily the same shape), the part-whole relationship (equal parts recompose the whole), and that a shape can be partitioned validly in more than one way as long as the parts are equal.

activities.title: Cut it, check it, rebuild it
feedback: If parts don't match when overlaid, even after rotating or flipping them, they are not the same shape and size. For the strip, grid and straight-cut halves in this activity, that means they are not equal, so they are not halves/quarters even if the number of pieces looks right. (Pieces with equal area but different shapes, like the diagonal triangles below, need a different check.)
When a horizontal, vertical, or single-diagonal cut each produce two equal parts, each is a valid way to make halves: there is no single 'right' cut, only the equal-parts rule.

A rectangle can be quartered in more than one way too (four equal strips, or a 2x2 grid). Drawing BOTH diagonals also gives four triangles that each have one quarter of the AREA, but in a non-square rectangle they are different shapes and will not match when overlaid, so use strips or a 2x2 grid when you want quarters you can check by overlaying. Remember that equal parts must be the same SIZE, not necessarily the same shape.
After rebuilding, prompt: 'Two halves make what? Four quarters make what?' to rehearse the whole as composed of its equal parts.
Count the regions you ended up with, not the lines you drew: one cut through a shape makes two parts.
Real paper has slight thickness and cuts are never perfectly clean, so overlaying is a practical equality check; the cutouts stand for idealised flat shapes with zero thickness.
activities.rationale: Partitioning is a physical cutting/folding action; folding and overlaying makes equality concrete, showing several valid cuts confronts the 'only one correct way' misconception, and recomposing rehearses the part-whole relationship. Early fraction work centres on partitioning single objects into equal parts, naming them, and reconstituting the whole.
sourceClaims: Early fraction work partitions single objects into equal parts and names them (halves, quarters); equal parts and reconstituting the whole are central
Year 2 pupils recognise, name, and write fractions and can partition shapes; equal shares of identical wholes are emphasised
learnerActions: Take a paper circle and a paper rectangle and fold or draw a line to make two parts.
Overlay or rotate the two parts on top of each other to check they match exactly (equal).

On fresh copies of the same rectangle, make two halves a DIFFERENT way (e.g. vertically, then horizontally, then a single diagonal through opposite corners) and check equality again. For the diagonal, cut along it and turn one triangle half a turn to lay it on the other, because folding a non-square rectangle along its diagonal will not make the halves line up.
Now partition a circle and a rectangle into four equal parts (e.g. the rectangle as four equal strips or a 2x2 grid) and check all four match.
Slide or stick the parts back together to rebuild the whole, saying aloud 'two halves make the whole' and 'four quarters make the whole'.
Label each partition with 'halves' or 'quarters' and count the PARTS (regions), not the cuts.
activities.intendedInsight: Halves are two equal parts and quarters are four equal parts; the equal parts together rebuild the whole, and the same shape can be halved or quartered in more than one correct way provided the parts are equal in size.

activities.title: Halves, quarters, or neither?
feedback: A shape with two parts is only 'halves' if the two parts are equal: two unequal parts belong in 'neither'.
A rectangle cut by a single diagonal, or a circle halved by a slanted line through its centre, is still valid halves because the parts are equal.
Watch for judging by appearance of a usual cut: check equality directly by comparing part sizes.
A sorting task can check and teach how you classify partitions, but it does not itself give the experience of producing a partition; pair it with the cutting/folding activity.
activities.rationale: Categorising and matching partitions to names lets children apply the equal-parts rule and surfaces both the 'count the pieces' and 'only one correct cut' misconceptions through deliberate distractors. This is recognition practice that complements, rather than replaces, hands-on partitioning.
sourceClaims: Early fraction work partitions single objects into equal parts and names them (halves, quarters); equal parts and reconstituting the whole are central
learnerActions: Sort a set of partitioned shapes into three groups: 'halves', 'quarters', and 'neither'.
Include a shape split into two UNEQUAL parts (right number of pieces, wrong equality) to place in 'neither'.
Include a non-standard but valid cut (e.g. a diagonally-halved rectangle or a circle halved by a slanted line through its centre) to place in 'halves'.
For each decision, explain how you know, e.g. 'the parts are equal' or 'the parts are not the same size'.
activities.intendedInsight: Deciding whether a partition shows halves or quarters depends on whether the parts are equal in size, not on the number of pieces or on a familiar orientation.

activities.title: Diagnostic: unequal pieces with the right count
feedback: Neither shape is correctly cut: in each, the parts are not equal. Halves are two equal parts (for example, a straight line through the centre of a circle or rectangle); quarters are four equal parts.
Put back together, the four parts still make the whole rectangle, but because they are not equal they are not quarters; four equal quarters would also rebuild the whole rectangle.
A circle can be halved by any line through its centre, so there is more than one correct way.
If a child says 'yes, there are two parts so they are halves', overlay or rotate the parts to test equality and contrast an equal with an unequal partition of identical shapes.
activities.rationale: Both shapes have the right number of pieces but unequal sizes, so a piece-counting child says yes while a child requiring equal parts says no; the follow-up probes whether they see the parts recompose the whole and accept more than one valid partition.
sourceClaims: Early fraction work partitions single objects into equal parts and names them (halves, quarters); equal parts and reconstituting the whole are central
learnerActions: Look at a circle divided by an off-centre line into two clearly unequal parts, and a rectangle divided into four parts where three are small and one is large.
Answer: 'Is the circle cut into two halves? Is the rectangle cut into four quarters? How do you know?'
Then answer: 'If you put the parts of the rectangle back together, what do they make? Is there more than one way to cut the circle into two halves?'
activities.intendedInsight: Having the right NUMBER of pieces is not enough; halves and quarters must be EQUAL parts, which together recompose the whole, and there can be more than one valid partition.

constraints: Emphasise EQUAL parts throughout; a partition with the correct number of pieces but unequal sizes is not halves/quarters. Equal means equal in size, not necessarily the same shape.

Show more than one correct way to halve the same shape (e.g. a rectangle split vertically, horizontally, or by a single diagonal through opposite corners) and more than one way to quarter it (e.g. four equal strips or a 2x2 grid). Both diagonals of a rectangle also make four triangles of equal AREA (each one quarter), but for a non-square rectangle these triangles are not congruent, so they cannot be confirmed by overlaying - prefer strips or a 2x2 grid when children verify quarters by overlay.
Always recompose the whole: 'two halves make the whole', 'four quarters make the whole'.
Count the resulting PARTS (regions), not the cuts.
A sorting/matching task checks and can teach recognition and classification; it does not by itself give children the experience of producing partitions, so pair it with hands-on cutting/folding.
A poster or display of partitioned shapes is a useful reference but does not let a child partition and test equality themselves; treat it as a scaffold, not the main activity.
Paper cutouts have slight thickness and imperfect cuts; use overlaying as a practical equality check and treat the paper as an approximation of the idealised flat (zero-thickness) shape.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source noted '3D adds nothing' for these planar shapes; dropped as a universal claim. These shapes are plane figures so a solid model is not needed here, but that is a scope point, not evidence that 3D can never help.

An interactive version could shade equal parts green and unequal parts red, accept several valid halving cuts, and provide a 'rebuild' button that slides parts back and labels 'two halves'/'four quarters'. These are optional feedback mechanisms that make the equality check and recomposition concrete; they are not required.

The source labelled a conversation format 'poor' because this is a hands-on skill; spoken discussion while cutting (naming parts, explaining equality) remains valuable and is retained within the activities, so the format is not treated as useless.
Description mixes 'quarters' and 'fourths'; both name four equal parts and are used interchangeably here.

Corrected an earlier geometry error: both diagonals of a rectangle produce four triangles of EQUAL AREA (each a quarter), not unequal parts; for a non-square rectangle they are not congruent and so cannot be verified by overlay. A single diagonal is presented as a halving method because its two triangles are congruent and overlay-checkable. This reinforces that equal fractional parts must be equal in size, not identical in shape.

probeDeeper: Put the four pieces back together - what do you get?
Is there more than one way to cut this square into two halves? Show me another.
How is this different from just cutting it into any two pieces?
If I cut the rectangle into four equal parts, what is each part called, and what do all four make?
assess.correctAnswer: No to both - the parts are not equal. Halves are two equal parts (a line through the middle); quarters are four equal parts. Put back together, the four equal quarters make the whole rectangle, and a circle can be halved by any line through its centre (more than one way).

errorPatterns.pattern: The right number of pieces means the fraction - accepts unequal parts as halves/quarters
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay/rotate the parts to test equality; contrast an equal and an unequal partition of identical shapes.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes - there are two parts, so they are halves
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the unequal circle shows halves, or the unequal rectangle shows quarters

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot describe the whole as composed of its equal parts (two halves / four quarters make the whole)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Physically reassemble the parts into the whole; rehearse 'four quarters make one whole'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cannot answer what the parts make when reassembled

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks a shape can be partitioned only one 'correct' way (rejects a valid alternative cut)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show several equal partitions of the same shape side by side; the rule is equal parts, not a fixed cut.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says a horizontally- or diagonally-halved rectangle is 'wrong' because it isn't the usual vertical cut

responseLevels.gap: Accepts unequal parts as halves/quarters; counts pieces only.
responseLevels.full: Partitions circles and rectangles into equal halves and quarters, recognises different equal partitions are all valid, and describes the whole as composed of its equal parts.
responseLevels.partial: Identifies equal halves/quarters in the standard orientation but rejects valid alternative cuts, or cannot describe the whole as two halves / four quarters.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a circle divided by an off-centre line into two clearly unequal parts, and a rectangle divided into four parts where three are small and one is large. Ask: 'Is the circle cut into two halves? Is the rectangle cut into four quarters? How do you know?' Then ask: 'If you put the parts of the rectangle back together, what do they make - and is there more than one way to cut the circle into two halves?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Both shapes have the RIGHT NUMBER of pieces but UNEQUAL sizes, so a child who counts pieces says yes while a child who requires equal parts says no. Tier 2 exposes whether they see the parts recompose the whole and accept more than one valid partition.

pedagogy.summary: Expressing one quantity as a fraction of another means writing 'a as a fraction of b' = a/b, where the quantity AFTER 'of' is the denominator (the whole) and the other is the numerator (the part). Two ideas make it conceptual rather than mechanical: (1) both quantities must be in the SAME UNIT before you form the fraction (45 minutes as a fraction of 2 hours is 45/120 = 3/8, not 45/2), and (2) the result can be MORE THAN ONE when the first quantity is bigger than the second (3 hours as a fraction of 2 hours = 3/2), which contradicts the young child's belief that a fraction is always less than a whole. Mastery is forming, simplifying, and INTERPRETING such a fraction in context.
bestPractices: Foreground the phrase structure: 'a as a fraction of b' → the thing after 'of' is the denominator. Rehearse identifying which quantity is the whole before writing anything.
Always convert to a common unit first; make 'same units?' a required checkpoint (45 min and 2 h → 45 min and 120 min).
Deliberately include cases where the answer exceeds 1 (e.g. 150 cm as a fraction of 1 m) so pupils accept improper-fraction results and interpret them as 'more than the whole'.
Simplify and then interpret in words — '3/8 of the two hours' — so the fraction is tied back to the situation, not left as a bare number.
Connect to ratio and percentage: a/b is the same comparison expressed as a fraction, and ×100 gives the percentage — building the ratio–fraction–percentage web.
keyRepresentations: Bar / double number line with both quantities in a common unit (45 out of 120 minutes shaded)
The sentence frame 'a as a fraction of b = a/b' with 'of' → denominator
Fraction-of-a-quantity strip that can exceed one whole (improper result)
Equivalent-fraction simplification chain (45/120 → 3/8)
commonMisconceptions: Writing the raw numbers without converting to a common unit (45/2 for 45 minutes as a fraction of 2 hours).
Putting the quantities the wrong way round — ignoring that the quantity after 'of' is the denominator.
Believing a fraction must be less than 1, so being unable to accept or interpret a result greater than 1 (3 hours as a fraction of 2 hours = 3/2).
Forgetting to simplify, or simplifying incorrectly, leaving the comparison obscured.

learn.summary: Learners express one quantity as a fraction of another: 'a as a fraction of b' = a/b, where the quantity after 'of' is the denominator (the whole). Mastery requires (1) converting both quantities to the SAME unit before forming the fraction (45 minutes as a fraction of 2 hours is 45/120 = 3/8, not 45/2), (2) accepting results greater than one whole when the first quantity is bigger (3 hours as a fraction of 2 hours = 3/2), and (3) simplifying and interpreting the fraction back in context.

activities.title: The fraction-of bench: convert units, then form the fraction
feedback: If a learner writes 45/2, ask: 'Are minutes and hours the same unit?' Convert 2 hours to 120 minutes on the bar, then re-form 45/120 = 3/8.

If a learner writes 120/45 or 8/3, rehearse the sentence frame: 'a as a fraction of b' means b (after 'of') is the whole/denominator; test it on 1 hour as a fraction of 2 hours, which must be 1/2, not 2.

If a learner refuses 3/2, flips it to 2/3, or says 'that can't be a fraction', return to the overflowing bar: 3 hours shaded past the 2-hour whole is 3/2 = 1½ wholes — an improper fraction meaning more than the whole amount.
If a learner stops at 45/120, prompt them to simplify and then say the answer in context ('3/8 of the two hours').
activities.rationale: Seeing both quantities on a common-unit bar grounds the part–whole comparison; a strip that overflows one whole makes an improper result visible rather than abstract, which targets the belief that a fraction must be less than 1. An optional unit toggle that withholds the fraction until units match makes the 'convert first' step explicit at the moment the error would occur. Laying both quantities on a shared scale is a concrete way to reason multiplicatively about part relative to whole.
sourceClaims: KS2/KS3 pupils should express one quantity as a fraction of another and solve problems involving relative sizes of two quantities, including where units must be made common and results simplified.
Comparing two quantities as a fraction is part of the ratio–fraction–proportion web; reasoning multiplicatively about part relative to whole underpins it.
learnerActions: Start with two quantities in different units, e.g. 45 minutes and 2 hours, and say in words which quantity is the whole (the one after 'of' — here 2 hours).
Before writing any fraction, convert both to a common unit: split the 2-hour bar into 120 minute-segments and highlight the 45.
Form the fraction from the shaded bar: 45 out of 120, then simplify the equivalent-fraction chain 45/120 → 9/24 → 3/8.

In a second round, take 3 hours as a fraction of 2 hours: shade 3 hours against a 2-hour whole bar so the shading runs past the end of one whole and spills into a second bar; read the fraction as 3/2.
State what 3/2 means here in words: '3 hours is one and a half times the two hours' / 'more than the whole'.
Check yourself with an obvious case: 1 hour as a fraction of 2 hours should be 1/2 — confirm your method gives it.
activities.intendedInsight: Both quantities must be in the same unit before forming a fraction, the quantity after 'of' is the denominator, and the comparison fraction can exceed one whole when the first quantity is larger.

activities.title: Form, simplify and interpret — including improper results
feedback: For 45/2: this did not convert hours to minutes; 2 h = 120 min, so the fraction is 45/120 = 3/8.
For 150/1: 1 m = 100 cm, so 150 cm as a fraction of 1 m is 150/100 = 3/2, not 150/1.
For 2/3 on the 150 cm item: the quantity after 'of' (1 m = 100 cm) is the whole/denominator, so 150 goes on top — the answer 3/2 is greater than 1.
Connect a/b to percentage: ×100 turns 3/8 into 37.5% and 3/2 into 150%, linking the fraction, ratio and percentage.
activities.rationale: Short constructed and selection items let learners rehearse forming, simplifying and interpreting the fraction and confront targeted distractors (no conversion, wrong way round, improper result). Recognition/selection confirms the rule but does not by itself require the learner to build the common-unit bar, so it complements rather than replaces the hands-on forming activity.
sourceClaims: KS2/KS3 pupils should express one quantity as a fraction of another and solve problems involving relative sizes of two quantities, including where units must be made common and results simplified.
learnerActions: Fill in the blank: '45 min as a fraction of 2 h = ___', giving the simplified fraction (3/8) and rejecting the un-converted 45/2.
Identify which quantity is the denominator in a given 'a as a fraction of b' statement and justify why.
Tackle an item whose answer exceeds 1: write 150 cm as a fraction of 1 m in simplest form (= 3/2), avoiding 2/3 (wrong way round) and 150/1 (no conversion).
After each answer, write one sentence interpreting the fraction in the original context.
activities.intendedInsight: Forming, simplifying and interpreting the fraction — including when it is greater than 1 — is a single connected skill, with the not-converting and wrong-way-round errors as the key pitfalls.

activities.title: Annotated reference bar: 'of → denominator' and 'convert units first'
feedback: If a learner still mixes up the order, point back to the tapped 'of → denominator' annotation and re-test on 1 hour as a fraction of 2 hours = 1/2.
If a learner forgets conversion, re-reveal the 2 h = 120 min step on the bar.
activities.rationale: A fixed annotated bar consolidates the rule and serves as a reference card. As a static scaffold it cannot make the learner perform the conversion or watch a fraction overflow one whole, so it supports but does not substitute for the interactive forming activity.
learnerActions: Study a bar showing 45 of 120 minutes shaded; tap the word 'of' to reveal that it marks the whole/denominator.
Tap the bar to reveal the common-unit conversion (2 h = 120 min) that had to happen first.
Use this card as a quick check before forming any 'fraction-of' answer.
activities.intendedInsight: The phrase 'a as a fraction of b' always puts the quantity after 'of' as the denominator, and units must be made common before the fraction is formed.

constraints: Always require a 'same units?' checkpoint before any fraction is written; converting to a common unit must precede forming the fraction.
Deliberately include cases where the answer exceeds 1 (e.g. 3 hours as a fraction of 2 hours = 3/2, 150 cm as a fraction of 1 m = 3/2) so learners accept and interpret improper results.
Simplify and then interpret the fraction in words tied to the situation ('3/8 of the two hours'); do not leave it as a bare number.
Selection/recognition items confirm the rule and surface distractors but do not elicit independent construction of the common-unit comparison; pair them with hands-on forming.
The static annotated bar is a reference scaffold: it cannot make the learner perform the conversion or dynamically witness a fraction exceeding one whole.
Connect to ratio and percentage (a/b as the same comparison; ×100 for percentage) to build the ratio–fraction–percentage web.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original 'persona dialogue' and '3D' entries were rated poor-fit; those were catalog-fit judgements for this one-dimensional comparison, not established pedagogical laws, so they are omitted rather than asserted as universal claims about the media.

The claim that only the overflowing-bar visual can dismantle the 'fractions are always <1' misconception is a catalog preference; it is presented here as a well-motivated proposal, not proven necessity.

Independent editor arithmetic/coherence check: 45/120 = 9/24 = 3/8; 150/100 = 3/2; 1 h/2 h = 1/2; 120/45 = 8/3; 3/8 = 37.5% and 3/2 = 150% all verify. 45/2 and 120/45 (=8/3) are framed only as errors, never as valid answers, and no denominator-'flip' claim is made (the unit-fraction comparison here fixes the numerator and varies the whole, so no 'flipping rule' is implied).

probeDeeper: Are 45 and 2 measured in the same unit? What do you have to do before you can compare them?
Which is the WHOLE here — the 45 minutes or the 2 hours? How does the wording tell you which goes on the bottom?
Now write 3 hours as a fraction of 2 hours. Can the answer be bigger than 1? What does 3/2 mean here? (counterexample forcing an improper result.)
Check yourself: 1 hour as a fraction of 2 hours — what should that be? Does your method give that?
assess.correctAnswer: 3/8. Because 2 hours = 120 minutes, 45 minutes as a fraction of 2 hours is 45/120, which simplifies to 3/8. (Both quantities must be in the same unit — minutes — before forming the fraction.)

errorPatterns.pattern: Does not convert to a common unit — writes 45/2 straight from the numbers as they appear
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'are minutes and hours the same unit?' Convert 2 hours to 120 minutes on a bar, then re-form 45/120. Make 'same units first' a fixed checkpoint.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer is 45/2 or 22.5, and the explanation is 'the 45 goes over the 2' with no mention of minutes vs hours

errorPatterns.pattern: Puts the quantities the wrong way round — ignores that the amount after 'of' is the denominator
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rehearse the sentence frame: 'a as a fraction of b' → b (after 'of') is the whole/denominator. Check with an obvious case: 1 hour as a fraction of 2 hours must be 1/2, not 2.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 120/45 (or 8/3), treating the first-mentioned or larger quantity as the whole

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes a fraction must be less than 1, so cannot accept or interpret a result greater than one whole
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the overflowing bar: 3 hours shaded past the 2-hour whole gives 3/2 = 1½ wholes. Name it an improper fraction and interpret it as 'more than the whole amount'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a case like 3 hours as a fraction of 2 hours, refuses 3/2, flips it to 2/3, or says 'that can't be a fraction'

responseLevels.gap: Writes 45/2 (or flips to 120/45) without converting units or identifying the whole; treats it as a bare number-placing exercise.
responseLevels.full: Converts 2 h to 120 min, forms 45/120 with the correct quantity as denominator, simplifies to 3/8, interprets it in context, AND accepts and interprets an improper result such as 3/2 for 3 hours as a fraction of 2 hours.
responseLevels.partial: Converts to a common unit and forms 45/120 but stops without simplifying, or simplifies yet cannot handle a result greater than 1, or cannot say which quantity is the whole and why.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Write 45 minutes as a fraction of 2 hours, as simply as you can. Then explain how you got it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands must first notice the units differ and convert 2 hours to 120 minutes; the answer 3/8 can ONLY be reached that way. A child who just writes the numbers gives 45/2 (or 22.5) and their reason reveals they never converted. The reason-tier separates 'I made the units the same first' from 'I put 45 over 2', so the two children give different answers and different explanations.

pedagogy.summary: At 9-10 precision covers number vocabulary (prime, factor, multiple), polygon regularity, units including cm², m³ and degrees, and index/percentage notation. Two confusions are load-bearing: factor versus multiple (a factor divides INTO a number; a multiple is built by multiplying it), and reading index notation — 5² is 'five squared' (5×5 = 25), not 'five times two'. Precision also means matching the unit's dimension to the quantity (cm² for area, cm³ for volume) and marking an estimate as approximate ('approximately 60 cm³') rather than presenting it as exact. Teaching rephrases vague language into structural terms (EEF).
bestPractices: Distinguish factor and multiple with arrays and factor pairs — a factor fits into the number, a multiple is a step in its times-table — and rephrase pupils' loose usage into the precise term (EEF)
Teach 5² as a square of side 5 (5×5) and read it 'five squared', contrasting it directly with 5×2 to break the index-as-multiplier error (CCSS: state the meaning of symbols)
Match the unit to the dimension: area counts squares (cm²), volume fills cubes (cm³); make the little index meaningful
Mark estimates as approximate, expressing answers to a precision appropriate for the context (CCSS)
Use non-examples and counterexamples to test a definition (is 1 prime? is 6 a factor of 12?) (EEF)
keyRepresentations: Arrays / factor pairs for factor vs multiple
A square of dots for n² and a cube for n³
Unit-square (cm²) and unit-cube (cm³) diagrams
Regular vs irregular polygons side by side
Notation cards linking symbol, word and value (5² = 'five squared' = 25)
commonMisconceptions: Confuses factor and multiple, using them interchangeably or in the wrong direction ('6 is a multiple of 12')
Reads index notation as multiplication by the index — 5² as 5×2 = 10
Uses cm for an area or volume, or writes cm² where cm³ is needed
Presents an estimate as an exact value, omitting 'approximately'

learn.summary: Builds precise mathematical vocabulary and notation for 9-10 year olds: distinguishing factor from multiple, reading index notation (5² = 'five squared' = 5×5 = 25, not 5×2), matching units to dimension (cm² for area, cm³ for volume), and marking estimates as approximate. Core approach: let children test definitions with arrays and dot-squares, rephrase loose language into structural terms, and justify each convention. Two load-bearing confusions are targeted: factor vs multiple (a factor divides INTO a number; a multiple is built FROM it by multiplying) and the index-as-multiplier misread.

activities.title: Testing factor vs multiple with arrays
feedback: If a learner says '6 is a multiple of 12', ask them to build 6 by counting up in 12s; when that fails, ask whether 6 fits into a 12-array. The array shows factor; the times-table step shows multiple.
If they state the relationship backwards or cannot say which term applies, rephrase their loose usage into the precise term and re-test with the arrays before moving on.

Reinforce by testing the definition with both examples and non-examples: is 6 a factor of 12 (yes)? is 5 a factor of 12 (no — 12 ÷ 5 leaves a remainder)? is 1 prime (no — a prime has exactly two different factors, and 1 has only one)? Let them test rather than recall.
activities.rationale: Arrays and factor pairs make the divides-into vs built-from distinction concrete and testable; rephrasing vague usage into structural terms and probing definitions with non-examples/counterexamples follows EEF guidance on vocabulary and misconceptions.
sourceClaims: Teachers should rephrase pupils' vague, non-mathematical language into language reflecting mathematical structure, and address misconceptions by exploring their partial truth and using counterexamples and non-examples
learnerActions: Take the statement '6 is a multiple of 12' and test it: try to build 6 by stepping up in 12s (12, 24, 36...) — it never lands on 6.
Now test whether 6 fits INTO a 12-array (arrange 12 as two rows of 6, or six columns of 2) — it does, evenly.
State the corrected sentence: '6 is a FACTOR of 12' (equivalently, '12 is a multiple of 6'), and say why.
Repeat with a second pair: is 24 a factor or a multiple of 12? Build it by stepping up in 12s (12, 24) to show it is a multiple.
Write the definition in your own words: a factor fits into a number exactly, with no remainder; a multiple is a step in that number's times-table.
activities.intendedInsight: A factor divides evenly INTO a number, while a multiple is built FROM it by multiplying — so direction matters and the terms are not interchangeable.

activities.title: Drawing 5² to break the index-as-multiplier error
feedback: If a learner reads 5² as 'five times two' or '10', have them draw the 5×5 square and count the dots, then place the 5×2 strip of 10 next to it to see the gap.
Insist on the spoken form 'five squared' and ask them to state what the symbol means, linking symbol, word and value (5² = 'five squared' = 25).
If they transfer the error to 5³, build it as a cube (5×5×5 = 125) so 'cubed' is visible.
activities.rationale: Representing n² as a square of dots directly contrasts the correct value with the 5×2 misread, and stating the meaning of the symbol aloud supports precise notation use (CCSS MP6).
sourceClaims: Proficient students use clear definitions and vocabulary, state the meaning of symbols, specify units, and express answers to a degree of precision appropriate to the context (including marking estimates)
learnerActions: Draw 5² as a square of dots, 5 across and 5 down, and count them: 25.
Right beside it, draw 5×2 as a strip of 10 dots.
Say each aloud: '5 squared is 5×5 = 25' and '5 times 2 is 10' — notice they are different.
Explain in words why 5² means a square of side 5, not 'five times two'.
Extend: sketch what 5³ would mean (a cube, 5×5×5 = 125) and read it 'five cubed'.
activities.intendedInsight: The small raised index counts how many copies of the base are multiplied together — two for a square (5²=5×5=25), three for a cube (5³=5×5×5=125) — so the index is not a multiplier, and 5² is 25, not 10.

activities.title: Matching units to dimension and marking estimates
feedback: If a learner writes cm for an area or volume, have them count the squares or cubes and ask which index records what they counted.
If they give an estimated volume as an exact figure, ask how a reader would know it was an estimate; prompt the 'approximately' tag.
Connect back to notation: the little number on cm² is the same squaring idea as the index on 5² — cm² is cm×cm, so it records a dimension.
activities.rationale: Using unit-square and unit-cube models grounds the dimension-matching convention, and expressing answers to a precision appropriate to context (including marking estimates) is an explicit precision practice (CCSS MP6).
sourceClaims: Proficient students use clear definitions and vocabulary, state the meaning of symbols, specify units, and express answers to a degree of precision appropriate to the context (including marking estimates)
learnerActions: Cover a flat shape with 1 cm by 1 cm unit squares and write its area with cm² — the little ² records that you counted square centimetres.
Fill a box with 1 cm unit cubes and write its volume with cm³ — the ³ records that you filled cubic centimetres.
Given an estimated volume of about 60 cm³, write it as 'approximately 60 cm³' rather than '60 cm³', and say why the word matters.
Spot and fix errors: correct '48' (an area measured in square centimetres) to '48 cm²', and correct an estimate written as an exact figure by adding 'approximately'.
Explain what the index on the unit tells you about the dimension being measured.
activities.intendedInsight: The unit's index matches the dimension measured — area counts squares (cm²), volume fills cubes (cm³) — and an estimate must be flagged 'approximately' so it is not read as exact.

activities.title: Spot-the-error diagnostic dialogue
feedback: Listen for the correction of '6 is a multiple of 12' to '6 is a FACTOR of 12' (or '12 is a multiple of 6') WITH the reason that a factor divides into a number while a multiple is what you get by multiplying it.
Listen for 5² read as 'five squared' = 5×5 = 25, not 5×2; if the learner accepts the wrong statements, reteach using the array and dot-square activities.
An in-role mathematician who insists on the right term and challenges a misread can surface the vocabulary through dialogue, prompting the child to correct and justify rather than simply be told.
activities.rationale: A dialogue that rephrases loose language into structural terms and challenges a misread can elicit the learner's own reasoning about definitions; recognition-only sort/label items do not themselves elicit that explanation or the independent production of the corrected term. Surfaced for discussion, not scored.
sourceClaims: Teachers should rephrase pupils' vague, non-mathematical language into language reflecting mathematical structure, and address misconceptions by exploring their partial truth and using counterexamples and non-examples
learnerActions: Read two statements written by another child: '6 is a multiple of 12' and '5² is five times two, which is 10'.
Decide whether each is right or wrong.
Fix each one and explain the difference that makes the original wrong.
Respond when a partner (or teacher in role) pushes back — 'did you mean factor or multiple?', 'read that power aloud' — and justify your correction.
Answer the follow-ups: Is 24 a factor or a multiple of 12? Why is a volume in cm³ and an area in cm²?
activities.intendedInsight: Both wrong statements look plausible; precision means catching the definite reason each is wrong — the factor/multiple direction and the meaning of the squared symbol — and justifying the fix.

constraints: Sort/label and 'read the notation' screener items can efficiently flag factor/multiple and index errors, but recognition-only responses do not elicit the child's reasoning about the definitions or independent construction of the corrected term — pair any screener with a task requiring the learner to explain or produce.
A static reference card of terms and notation can support recall, but does not let the child test a definition or produce notation; treat it as a reference scaffold, not the main activity.

A unit-cube model is useful for grounding 'cubed' and cm³, which is genuinely spatial; factor/multiple and most of this band are not spatial, so a 3D model is a companion for the volume-notation strand only, not a general requirement.
Drawn dot-squares and unit-square/cube diagrams are concrete approximations; distinguish the counted squares/cubes from the quantity (area/volume) they represent.
Estimate-tagging ('approximately') depends on the task being genuinely an estimate — do not apply it to exact measured or computed values.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy '60 cm³' figure is used ONLY as an estimate that must be tagged 'approximately', consistent with the diagnostic prompt; it is never presented as an exact computed volume, so no arithmetic error is propagated.
Arithmetic checked: 5² = 25 and 5×2 = 10; 5³ = 125; 24 is a multiple of 12 and 6 is a factor of 12; 5 is not a factor of 12.

The 'is 1 prime?' (not prime, by convention) and '1 is a factor of every number' (true) probes are definition conventions implied by the source non-examples guidance; use them carefully and only as optional definition checks.

The wider strands named in the source pedagogy/description (primes, polygon regularity, angle types, m³, degrees, percentages) were outside the original learn recommendation and are not built out here; they could be added later.
The source reteachPrerequisiteId and other internal catalog IDs are internal references and were omitted from learner-facing guidance.

probeDeeper: Is 6 a factor or a multiple of 12? And is 24 a factor or a multiple of 12?
Read 5² aloud — what does it mean, and how is it different from 5 × 2?
You wrote the volume as 60 cm³ but you estimated it — how should you show it's an estimate?
Why is a volume in cm³ and an area in cm² — what does the little number tell you?
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for correcting '6 is a multiple of 12' to '6 is a FACTOR of 12' (or '12 is a multiple of 6'), with the reason that a factor divides into a number while a multiple is what you get by multiplying it; and reading 5² as 'five squared' = 5×5 = 25, not 5×2. Surfaced for discussion, not scored.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses factor and multiple — uses them interchangeably or in the wrong direction ('6 is a multiple of 12')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use arrays and factor pairs — a factor fits into the number, a multiple is a step in its times-table — and rephrase loose usage into the precise term. Reteach in place.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: States the relationship backwards or cannot say which term applies

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads index notation as multiplication by the index — 5² as 5×2 = 10
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show 5² as a 5×5 square (25) beside 5×2 (10); read it 'five squared'. Reteach square and cube notation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says '5 squared is 10' or 'five times two'

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses the wrong-dimension unit or presents an estimate as exact — cm for an area/volume, or '60 cm³' for an estimate with no 'approximately'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Match unit to dimension (cm² counts squares, cm³ fills cubes) and tag estimates 'approximately'. Reteach in place.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes cm for area/volume, or gives an estimated volume as an exact figure

responseLevels.gap: Swaps factor and multiple, reads 5² as 5×2, and uses cm for area/volume or states estimates as exact.
responseLevels.full: Unprompted, distinguishes factor and multiple with a reason, reads and writes index notation correctly, uses cm²/cm³ appropriately and flags estimates as approximate, and can justify each convention.
responseLevels.partial: When prompted, gives the right factor/multiple direction and reads 5² correctly, but not reliably, and may still drop the index on units.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A child wrote '6 is a multiple of 12', and read '5²' as 'five times two, which is 10'. Are these right? Fix them, and explain the difference that makes each one wrong.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Both statements look plausible and are wrong for a definite reason. A precise child fixes the factor/multiple direction and the squared meaning and can state the definitions; a loose child accepts them. Neither error is caught by arithmetic fluency — only attention to the vocabulary and notation separates the children.

pedagogy.summary: Complementary events formalises two linked KS3 ideas: the probabilities of a complete set of mutually exclusive outcomes sum to 1, and the complement rule P(not A) = 1 − P(A). The crux distinctive to this level is the word MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE — adding probabilities (and the sum-to-1 argument) only works when outcomes cannot occur together. The classic failure is adding the probabilities of overlapping events (e.g. 'even' and 'prime' on a die, which share the number 2) and getting a nonsensical total.
bestPractices: Define mutually exclusive precisely (cannot happen at the same time) and test each situation for overlap before adding
Teach P(not A) = 1 − P(A) as the efficient route, contrasted with counting every unfavourable outcome
Use a complete outcome table / unit bar so 'exhaustive and mutually exclusive' is visible as segments filling the whole with no overlap
Expose the overlapping trap deliberately: ask for P(even or prime) on a die and show why 1/2 + 1/2 is wrong
Practise spotting invalid distributions whose probabilities don't sum to 1
keyRepresentations: Unit bar partitioned into non-overlapping outcome segments
Complete probability distribution table totalling 1
Two-circle diagram showing overlap vs no overlap (mutually exclusive or not)
P(not A) as the whole minus the A-segment
commonMisconceptions: Adding probabilities of events that are NOT mutually exclusive (overlapping events like even/prime) as though they were
Computing P(not A) by something other than 1 − P(A), or thinking P(not A) = P(A)
Assuming any list of events sums to 1 even when it is not exhaustive
Adding fractions without a common denominator when combining or complementing

learn.summary: Teach complementary events as two linked ideas: the probabilities of a complete set of mutually exclusive outcomes sum to 1, and P(not A) = 1 − P(A). The distinctive crux is the condition MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE — adding probabilities only works when outcomes cannot occur together. Make the overlap trap explicit: even/prime on a die share the number 2, so adding 1/2 + 1/2 reaches exactly 1 and falsely suggests 'certain', when the true probability is only 5/6. Practise finding complements efficiently and rejecting distributions that do not total 1.

activities.title: Unit bar: complement and the overlap trap
feedback: If a learner says P(even or prime) = 1, ask them to list every face that is even or prime and mark any counted twice — the shared 2 reveals the overlap; counting distinct favourable outcomes gives 5/6.
If a learner computes P(not 6) by listing and miscounting, point to the whole bar minus the 6-segment: 1 − 1/6 = 5/6.
Reinforce that 'even or prime' leaves out only the number 1, so the sum of 1 is misleading: the event is very likely but not certain, with true probability 5/6.
activities.rationale: A partitioned unit bar makes 'exhaustive and mutually exclusive' visible: segments filling the whole with no overlap. An overlay of overlapping events makes the double-counting of the shared 2 concrete, directly confronting the classic failure of adding non-mutually-exclusive events — insidious here because the sum lands on exactly 1 and looks valid. Live shading/overlap toggling is offered as an optional way to make the mechanism visible, not a required technology.
sourceClaims: For mutually exclusive events P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B), but this fails for events that can occur together — e.g. rolling a 3 and a prime, or an even and a prime, share outcomes, so they are not mutually exclusive and cannot simply be added.
When events are exhaustive and mutually exclusive their probabilities total 1, so a complementary or missing probability is found by subtracting from 1 (e.g. 1 − 0.85 = 0.15).
learnerActions: Use a bar representing probability 1, divided into the six equally likely outcomes of a fair die (each 1/6).

Choose an event, e.g. 'rolling a 6'. Shade that segment, then see that P(not 6) is the whole bar minus that one segment: 1 − 1/6 = 5/6. Confirm this matches the five remaining faces without counting them one by one.
Switch to overlap mode and select BOTH 'even' (2, 4, 6) and 'prime' (2, 3, 5). Shade each region on the bar.

Add P(even) = 1/2 and P(prime) = 1/2 to get 1, then compare with the bar: the arithmetic sum of the two lengths reaches the whole bar (suggesting 'certain'), yet the actual shaded union only covers five of the six segments (5/6). The extra 1/6 is the number 2, which sits in both regions and has been counted twice.
List the distinct outcomes that are even OR prime: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 — five faces — so P(even or prime) = 5/6. Note that 1 is neither, so the event is NOT certain.
activities.intendedInsight: Non-overlapping segments of a complete outcome set fill the bar to exactly 1, and P(not A) is simply the rest. Adding probabilities only works when the events share no outcome; overlapping events double-count the shared outcome, so the sum overstates the true probability — here it reaches exactly 1 while the true value is only 5/6.

activities.title: Predict, roll, explain: is 'even or prime' certain?
feedback: If the prediction was 'certain', link any rolled 1 back to the claim. If no 1 came up, point out that 1 is still a possible face that is neither even nor prime: one outcome is left out, so the event cannot be certain.
Draw out that the shared outcome 2 made 1/2 + 1/2 reach 1 instead of the true 5/6; the honest count of distinct outcomes is 5/6.

Ask the probing questions: Which numbers are even OR prime, and did any appear in both sets? What is P(not even) and how did you get it? If a distribution's total came out above 1, what does that immediately tell you?
activities.rationale: A predict–test–explain cycle with a real die can create a surprise if a 1 appears and the 'certain' prediction fails, which motivates the overlap check. Whatever the rolls show, listing the possible faces confirms that 1 is excluded. Spoken prediction and explanation make the reasoning audible and responsive.
sourceClaims: For mutually exclusive events P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B), but this fails for events that can occur together — e.g. rolling a 3 and a prime, or an even and a prime, share outcomes, so they are not mutually exclusive and cannot simply be added.
learnerActions: Before rolling: 'On a fair die, is rolling a number that is even OR prime certain? Predict yes or no, give a probability, and explain your reasoning.'
Record the prediction (a learner who adds 1/2 + 1/2 will predict 'certain, probability 1').

Roll the die several times. A 1 is likely to appear but is not guaranteed in a small number of rolls (each roll has a 1/6 chance). If a 1 appears, note that it is neither even nor prime, which contradicts a 'certain' prediction. If no 1 appears, check the faces anyway: 1 is a possible outcome that is neither even nor prime, so the event still cannot be certain. Not rolling a 1 does not show the event is certain.
Revisit the reasoning: list the even-or-prime outcomes, find the double-counted 2, and correct the probability to 5/6.
Discuss: when is it safe to add two probabilities, and when is it not?
activities.intendedInsight: An outcome (1) that is neither even nor prime disproves the 'certain' claim and exposes that adding overlapping probabilities over-counts the shared outcome. Checking for a shared outcome BEFORE adding is the deciding skill.

activities.title: Sort and check: mutually exclusive or overlapping, and valid distributions
feedback: If a learner forces a non-exhaustive list to total 1, ask whether every possible outcome is included; if outcomes are missing the given probabilities need not total 1.
If a learner adds fractions without a common denominator, pause to rewrite them over a shared denominator first.
When a distribution's total exceeds 1 or falls short, treat that as an immediate signal that it cannot be a valid complete distribution.
activities.rationale: Classifying and complement-filling exercises each sub-skill — overlap detection, the complement rule, and validity of distributions — including the common error of assuming any list sums to 1. These tasks check and build fluency; they confirm classification and procedure but do not by themselves elicit an extended spoken justification.
sourceClaims: When events are exhaustive and mutually exclusive their probabilities total 1, so a complementary or missing probability is found by subtracting from 1 (e.g. 1 − 0.85 = 0.15).
learnerActions: Sort pairs of events into 'mutually exclusive' (cannot both happen) or 'overlapping' (share at least one outcome). Include die examples such as {even}/{prime} (overlap at 2), {1,2,3}/{4,5,6} (no overlap), {multiple of 3}/{even} (overlap at 6).
For each overlapping pair, list the shared outcome(s) explicitly.
Fill in complements directly: P(not 6) = 1 − 1/6 = 5/6; P(not even) = 1 − 1/2 = 1/2.
Examine several probability distributions and decide which are invalid because the probabilities do not sum to 1, or because the list is not exhaustive. Explain each decision.
Verify that the probabilities listed for a given spinner sum to 1, and find any missing probability by subtracting from 1.
activities.intendedInsight: Testing for overlap is a prerequisite to adding; sum-to-1 only applies to a complete (exhaustive) set of mutually exclusive outcomes; complements are found by subtracting from 1.

constraints: Define mutually exclusive precisely (cannot happen at the same time) and test each situation for overlap before adding any probabilities.
Teach P(not A) = 1 − P(A) as the efficient route, contrasted with counting every unfavourable outcome, but ensure learners can justify why it works (the whole minus the A part).
Sum-to-1 reasoning requires the outcome set to be BOTH exhaustive and mutually exclusive; do not apply it to partial or overlapping lists.

Make clear that adding overlapping events (whose shared outcomes have nonzero probability) overstates the true probability. The incorrect sum need not exceed 1: the even/prime sum lands on exactly 1 and still misleads.
Watch for fraction errors: combining or complementing probabilities needs a common denominator.

Classification and fill-in tasks can confirm sub-skills but do not by themselves require a learner to construct a full spoken or written justification; pair them with the predict–explain activity so independent reasoning is elicited.

A fixed diagram or single overlaid example can illustrate overlap but does not let a learner test new cases themselves; use adjustable or multiple examples when the goal is for learners to discover the condition.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original 'recommendation' wording said the bar 'visibly overflows past 1' when adding 1/2 + 1/2. This is imprecise: 1/2 + 1/2 = 1 exactly, filling the bar but not exceeding it. The migrated guidance emphasises that the sum reaches exactly 1 (and so looks 'certain') while the true union probability is only 5/6, the 1/6 gap being the double-counted 2.

Self-audit confirmed: on a fair die, even = {2,4,6} and prime = {2,3,5} share only 2; their union is {2,3,4,5,6} = 5 outcomes, so P = 5/6 and 1 is the sole excluded outcome — the 'certain' claim is correctly refuted. P(not 6)=5/6 and P(not even)=1/2 are correct; {multiple of 3}={3,6} overlaps {even}={2,4,6} at 6.

A 3D treatment was judged a poor fit in the source because complement/overlap are 1D/2D partition ideas; this is a design preference, not a proven limitation, so it is not asserted as a universal law here.

assess.poeTask: Ask: 'On a fair die, is rolling a number that is even OR prime certain? Predict yes or no, give a probability, and explain — before we roll.' A child who adds 1/2 + 1/2 predicts 'certain (probability 1)'. Then roll the die repeatedly; sooner or later it lands on 1, which is neither even nor prime — violating the 'certain' prediction. This forces the explanation: 2 was double-counted, the events overlap, and the true probability is 5/6.
probeDeeper: Which numbers on the die are even OR prime? Did any of them get counted in both sets?
What is P(not even) on the die, and how did you get it?
When is it safe to add two probabilities together, and when is it not?
If the classmate's total came out as more than 1, what would that tell you immediately?
assess.correctAnswer: The classmate is wrong — it is not certain. 'Even' (2, 4, 6) and 'prime' (2, 3, 5) both include 2, so they are NOT mutually exclusive and cannot simply be added. Listing the outcomes that are even or prime gives 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 — five of the six — so P(even or prime) = 5/6. Only 1 is neither, so it is very likely but not certain.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds probabilities of events that are not mutually exclusive as though they were
errorPatterns.nextMove: List the actual outcomes for 'even or prime' and mark any counted twice; the shared 2 means the events overlap, so P(A)+P(B) over-counts — count the distinct favourable outcomes instead
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — P(even) + P(prime) = 1/2 + 1/2 = 1, so it is certain.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives P(even or prime) = 1/2 + 1/2 = 1 and calls it certain, without noticing 2 is in both sets

errorPatterns.pattern: Computes P(not A) by something other than 1 − P(A), or thinks P(not A) = P(A)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the complement: P(not 6) = 1 − 1/6 = 5/6; 'not 6' is every other outcome, found by taking P(6) from the whole 1
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a follow-up 'P(not 6)?' gives 1/6 (mirroring P(6)) or tries to list and mis-count the other faces

errorPatterns.pattern: Assumes any list of events must sum to 1 even when it is not exhaustive
errorPatterns.nextMove: Check the list is exhaustive AND mutually exclusive before applying sum-to-1; if outcomes are missing the given probabilities need not total 1
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats a partial list of outcomes as if it covered everything and forces it to total 1

responseLevels.gap: Adds probabilities regardless of overlap and accepts totals of 1 or more without question; cannot find a complement except by faulty listing
responseLevels.full: Tests events for mutual exclusivity before adding, finds P(even or prime) = 5/6 by counting distinct outcomes, uses the complement rule fluently, and rejects distributions that cannot be valid
responseLevels.partial: Applies P(not A) = 1 − P(A) for a single simple event and knows outcomes 'should' total 1, but adds overlapping events without spotting the shared outcome, or forces a non-exhaustive list to sum to 1

assess.diagnosticPrompt: On a fair six-sided die, a classmate calculates P(even or prime) = P(even) + P(prime) = 1/2 + 1/2 = 1, and concludes that rolling 'even or prime' is certain. Ask the child: is the classmate right? What is P(even or prime) really, and why? Take the answer, then ask for the full reasoning (Tier 2).
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands mutually exclusive spots the shared 2, refuses to add blindly, and gets 5/6; a child who adds any probabilities gets 1 and wrongly says 'certain'. The Tier-2 reason — checking for overlap before adding — is the separator, and the leftover outcome (1) exposes that the sum-to-1 claim was false.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 11–12: use the vocabulary and concepts of primes, factors, multiples, common factors/multiples, HCF and LCM, and PRIME FACTORISATION with index notation and the unique-factorisation property (every integer has exactly one prime-factor decomposition).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, KS3): 'use the concepts and vocabulary of prime numbers, factors (divisors), multiples, common factors, common multiples, highest common factor, lowest common multiple, prime factorisation, including using product notation and the unique factorisation property'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 6.NS.4 (GCF and LCM, distributive use of GCF); prime factorisation and index notation formalise Grade 4 factor/multiple work (4.OA.4).
• Operational details — build a number's prime factorisation with a factor tree, record it in index form (360 = 2³ × 3² × 5), and USE factorisations to find HCF (product of shared prime powers, the lowest index of each) and LCM (highest index of each prime present). The unique-factorisation property is the conceptual anchor: however you build the tree, the prime 'fingerprint' is the same. Venn-diagram-of-primes is the canonical HCF/LCM organiser.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 11): express a number as a product of primes in index form via a factor tree. Tier B (11–12): find HCF and LCM of two numbers from their prime factorisations. Tier C (12): explain, via unique factorisation, why every integer has exactly one set of prime factors and why HCF×LCM = product of the two numbers.
bestPractices: Anchor on the UNIQUE FACTORISATION property by having children build the SAME number with different first splits (360 = 4×90 or 8×45) and confirm the prime fingerprint is identical — the tree branches differ, the primes don't.

Teach HCF and LCM THROUGH prime factorisation rather than as separate list-and-compare tricks: a Venn diagram of the two numbers' prime factors gives HCF (intersection product) and LCM (whole-diagram product) at a glance.
Insist on index notation as compact, meaningful shorthand (2³ not 2×2×2) and connect it to the powers/indices work (dependent mt_hCVPYlF-7Y).

Ground HCF/LCM in problems that MOTIVATE them — HCF for simplifying/sharing into equal groups, LCM for repeating-event and fraction-denominator problems — so the concepts have purpose, not just procedure.
Reinforce that 1 is neither prime nor composite and that primes are the multiplicative 'atoms', linking back to the Y5-6 primes and factor-pairs work (prerequisite mt_FHIAv6dfhU).
keyRepresentations: Factor tree branching a number down to its prime leaves, then collected into index form.
Venn diagram of two numbers' prime factors: intersection → HCF, union (whole diagram) → LCM.
Index-notation product (360 = 2³ × 3² × 5) as the number's unique 'prime fingerprint'.
Prime-factor tiles/counters that can be regrouped to show different trees yield the same multiset of primes.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking a number can have different prime factorisations depending on how the tree is drawn (missing the uniqueness property).
Treating 1 as prime, or including 1 in a factorisation.
Confusing HCF with LCM (taking the largest common multiple or smallest common factor), or muddling which is 'highest' vs 'lowest'.
Taking the highest index for HCF / lowest for LCM (rule reversed).
Stopping a factor tree at composite leaves (e.g. leaving 4 or 6 unfactored) so the factorisation isn't fully prime.

learn.summary: For ages 11–12: build a number's prime factorisation with a factor tree, record it in index form (e.g. 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5), and use prime factorisations to find HCF (lowest power of each shared prime) and LCM (highest power of each prime present). The conceptual anchor is the unique-factorisation property — however the tree is built, the multiset of primes is identical. A Venn diagram of two numbers' prime factors organises HCF (intersection product) and LCM (whole-diagram product). Includes production, reference/anchor, consolidation, and Socratic-discussion activities, with scaffold limits noted.

activities.title: Prime factory: build the tree, discover uniqueness
feedback: If two differently built trees give different prime sets, either a leaf was left composite or a split was miscalculated (the two factors do not multiply back to the number above them) — check every split by multiplying and check that every leaf is prime, then compare again.
If a leaf like 4, 6, or 9 remains, the factorisation is not finished: 4 = 2×2, 6 = 2×3, 9 = 3×3. Split until only primes remain.
Remember that 1 is neither prime nor composite and never belongs in the factorisation.
activities.rationale: Prime factorisation is an active decomposition; building the same number two ways and seeing the identical prime set is intended to let uniqueness be discovered rather than asserted. Index notation is taught as meaningful shorthand (2³ not 2×2×2). Supported by the KS3 requirement to use product notation and the unique factorisation property; the specific method is a research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils use the concepts and vocabulary of prime numbers, factors, multiples, common factors/multiples, HCF, LCM, and prime factorisation including product notation and the unique factorisation property.
learnerActions: Take a number such as 360 and repeatedly split it into a factor pair (e.g. 4 × 90), then keep splitting each branch until every leaf is a prime.
Collect the prime leaves and write them in index form: 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5.
Now build 360 a second time starting from a different first split (e.g. 8 × 45 instead of 4 × 90). Record the prime leaves again.
Lay the two sets of prime leaves side by side and check: the trees branched differently, but the collected primes are identical (2³ × 3² × 5 both times).
Check each tree for composite leaves left unsplit (e.g. a 4 or a 9 that should become 2×2 or 3×3) and finish splitting them.
activities.intendedInsight: Every whole number greater than 1 has exactly one prime 'fingerprint': the order and shape of the splits do not change which primes (and how many of each) you end up with. Composite leaves must be fully broken down before the factorisation is complete.

activities.title: Venn organiser for HCF and LCM
feedback: If a learner gives 72 for the HCF, they took the highest power of each prime — that is the LCM. A common factor must divide BOTH numbers, so it can only use the powers BOTH have, i.e. the lowest; correct the HCF to 2² × 3 = 12.

If a learner multiplies together every prime that appears in either number, remind them a common factor must divide BOTH, so a prime appearing in only one number cannot be part of it. Note that 24 and 36 actually share both their primes (2 and 3), so no unshared prime arises here — this error is clearest with a pair like 24 and 25, where 5 belongs only to 25 and cannot divide 24. The related slip for 24 and 36 is taking too many copies of a shared prime: use 2² (not 2³) in the HCF, because 36 has only two 2s.
If the overlap is empty (coprime numbers), the HCF is 1, not zero and not undefined.

Optional interactive version: dragging shared prime tiles into the overlap can recompute the HCF and LCM live, so changing which primes are shared updates both results. This is an illustration of the mechanism, not a required mechanism.
activities.rationale: Teaching HCF and LCM through prime factorisation and a Venn organiser connects the procedure to its meaning, instead of list-and-compare tricks, and directly targets the common HCF/LCM reversal. The Venn-to-HCF/LCM relationship is supported by the NCETM guidance; the CCSS claim supports that finding HCF/LCM of two numbers is a standard target.
sourceClaims: A Venn diagram of two numbers' prime factors yields HCF (intersection) and LCM (union), making the relationship between factorisation and HCF/LCM explicit.
Grade 6 pupils find the greatest common factor and least common multiple of two numbers and use the distributive property with the GCF.
learnerActions: Write the prime factorisations of two numbers, e.g. 24 = 2³ × 3 and 36 = 2² × 3².
Place each number's prime factors (as individual copies) in a two-circle Venn diagram, putting the factor copies both numbers share in the overlap and the leftover copies in the outer regions.
Read the HCF as the product of the overlap (the shared primes, each taken at the lowest power both numbers have): 2² × 3 = 12.
Read the LCM as the product of the whole diagram (each prime at its highest power): 2³ × 3² = 72.
Check the relationship HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers: 12 × 72 = 864 = 24 × 36.
Try a coprime pair such as 24 and 25 (24 = 2³ × 3, 25 = 5²): the overlap is empty, so HCF = 1 and LCM = 600.
activities.intendedInsight: A common factor can only be built from primes BOTH numbers have, taken at the lowest shared power — that is the HCF. The LCM must contain enough of every prime to be a multiple of both, so each prime appears at its highest power. The Venn regions are intended to make lowest-for-HCF / highest-for-LCM visible rather than a rule to memorise.

activities.title: Reference anchor: reveal the index form and the Venn result
feedback: Use any mismatch between prediction and reveal to pinpoint whether the slip is in factorising, in index notation, or in choosing powers for HCF vs LCM.
activities.rationale: A fixed worked example is a useful anchor/reference for the format and the region logic. Its limit (noted in constraints): a fixed tree cannot itself be re-split, so it does not by itself demonstrate uniqueness — pair it with the build activity.
sourceClaims: A Venn diagram of two numbers' prime factors yields HCF (intersection) and LCM (union), making the relationship between factorisation and HCF/LCM explicit.
learnerActions: Study a completed factor tree for a number; before revealing, predict each leaf's prime value and the full index form.
Reveal the index form (e.g. 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5) and compare with your prediction.
Study a two-number Venn of prime factors; predict the HCF (overlap) and LCM (whole diagram) before revealing them.
Reveal the HCF and LCM and check your reasoning about which powers went where.
activities.intendedInsight: A worked tree plus Venn serves as a clear reference for the layout of index form and the intersection/union logic of HCF and LCM.

activities.title: Consolidation checks
feedback: For 360 = 2^□ × 3^□ × 5 the indices are 3 and 2 (2³ × 3² × 5); check by multiplying: 8 × 9 × 5 = 360.
Watch for an HCF/LCM swap: the smaller result (12) is the HCF of 24 and 36, the larger (72) is the LCM.
If 1 is placed with the primes, recall it is neither prime nor composite.
activities.rationale: Short checks consolidate results and can surface the HCF/LCM swap, but they test outcomes rather than build the decomposition or the uniqueness insight — best used after the build and Venn work. A sort checks classification but does not itself elicit construction of a factorisation.
learnerActions: Complete the missing indices: 360 = 2^□ × 3^□ × 5.
Find the HCF and LCM of 24 and 36 and state which is which.
Sort a set of numbers into prime vs composite (remembering 1 is neither).
Match each number to its correct prime factorisation.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent recall of index form and correct HCF/LCM selection, with the prime/composite distinction secure.

activities.title: Socratic challenge: why is factorisation unique and why 1 isn't prime
feedback: If the learner says a different tree could give different primes, prompt them to actually build it both ways and compare the leaves.

If they can compute 12 but cannot say why the method works, connect it: because each number is ONE product of primes, their common divisors are exactly the products of shared primes, each used no more times than it appears in both numbers (including 1, using none) — so the HCF uses each shared prime at the lowest common power.
activities.rationale: A Socratic probe suits the conceptual core (uniqueness, why 1 isn't prime); dialogue can prompt justification but recognition of a correct statement does not by itself guarantee the learner can produce the reasoning. Best paired with the build-and-compare activity, since manipulation is what makes uniqueness concrete.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils use the concepts and vocabulary of prime numbers, factors, multiples, common factors/multiples, HCF, LCM, and prime factorisation including product notation and the unique factorisation property.
learnerActions: Respond to the question: 'Could 360 have a different set of prime factors if we split it a different way?' — justify your answer.
Explain why 1 is not counted as a prime, and what would go wrong with uniqueness if we allowed it.
Explain in your own words why taking shared primes at the lowest power gives the HCF, referring to what a common factor must divide.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the reasoning — common divisors are built only from shared primes, and every number is exactly one product of primes — is intended to cement the conceptual objective, not just the recipe.

constraints: 1 is neither prime nor composite and never appears in a prime factorisation; primes are the multiplicative 'atoms'.
A factor tree is only finished when every leaf is prime — composite leaves (4, 6, 9, …) must be split further.
HCF takes the LOWEST power of each shared prime; LCM takes the HIGHEST power of each prime present. These are different selections and are easy to reverse — guard against the swap explicitly.

A common factor is built only from primes BOTH numbers share; a prime appearing in just one number cannot be part of it. Where two numbers share all their primes (e.g. 24 and 36), the only error to guard is taking too high a power, not an unshared prime.
HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers holds for a pair; use it as a check, not as a definition.

Reveal-on-tap worked trees/Venns are reference anchors: they show the format and region logic but cannot be re-split or re-grouped, so they do not by themselves demonstrate uniqueness — pair them with learner-built trees.
Consolidation checks test results (recognition/recall) and do not elicit independent construction of the decomposition or the uniqueness reasoning.

Index notation should be connected to prior powers/indices work, and HCF/LCM grounded in motivating problems (sharing into equal groups for HCF; repeating events and fraction denominators for LCM) so the concepts have purpose.

Optional live/drag interactions (dragging shared prime tiles into a Venn overlap, auto-collecting leaves into index form) are helpful illustrations of the mechanism, not required mechanisms, and their effectiveness relative to static anchors is not established.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified, and all activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Source claims carry verified:false in the original row; treat the DfE KS3, CCSS 6.NS.4 and NCETM Venn-guidance citations as unconfirmed.

The KS3 source claim attached to the build and Socratic activities supports the curriculum content/convention (unique factorisation and product notation are taught), not the efficacy of the particular method; method efficacy remains an untested proposal.

Correction applied this pass: the unshared-prime feedback for 24 and 36 previously claimed their 'extra' factors of 2 and 3 'cannot divide the other number', which is false (2 divides 36, 3 divides 24). 24 and 36 share both primes, so the unshared-prime error is now illustrated with 24 and 25, and the 24/36 slip is described accurately as excess copies of a shared prime.
Self-audit arithmetic checks: 24 = 2³×3, 36 = 2²×3²; HCF = 2²×3 = 12, LCM = 2³×3² = 72; 12×72 = 864 = 24×36. Coprime example: 24 & 25 give HCF 1, LCM 600. 360 = 2³×3²×5 = 8×9×5 = 360. All consistent.
The original's catalogue framing that '3D adds nothing' for these abstract ideas was a product fit judgement; it is omitted rather than restated as a universal pedagogical claim.

The 'different tree, same primes' uniqueness claim is mathematically sound (fundamental theorem of arithmetic) and is retained as a demonstrable activity; its instructional efficacy as implemented remains an untested proposal.
The classic error of taking highest powers for the HCF (giving 72) appears only as a misconception to correct to 12, never as a valid option in a learner task.

probeDeeper: Why do you take the LOWEST power of each shared prime for the HCF, but the highest for the LCM?
Why can a common factor of 24 and 36 only be built from primes they both have?
Every number has exactly one prime factorisation — why does that matter for this method?
What if it had been 24 and 25 — what's their HCF, and what does the prime factorisation tell you?
assess.correctAnswer: 24 = 2³ × 3, 36 = 2² × 3²; the HCF takes the lowest power of each shared prime: 2² × 3 = 12. A child reasoning well explains that any common divisor can only be built from primes both numbers share, and taking the most of each shared prime that BOTH have gives the largest such divisor — resting on unique factorisation.

errorPatterns.pattern: confuses HCF and LCM — takes the HIGHEST power of each prime (2³×3² = 72) for the HCF
errorPatterns.nextMove: reason about meaning: a COMMON factor must divide BOTH, so it can use only the powers BOTH have (the lowest); highest powers give the smallest common MULTIPLE instead.
errorPatterns.distractor: The HCF of 24 and 36 is 72
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer of 72 for the HCF; child uses highest powers

errorPatterns.pattern: multiplies ALL primes appearing in either number, ignoring which are shared
errorPatterns.nextMove: highlight only primes present in BOTH factorisations contribute to a common factor; cross out unshared primes.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child includes a prime that only one number has

errorPatterns.pattern: gets 12 by listing factors but cannot justify the prime-factor method — no link to unique factorisation
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach the calculation; connect it to uniqueness — every number is ONE product of primes, so common divisors are exactly the shared-prime products.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: correct answer, but 'why does taking shared primes work?' draws a blank

errorPatterns.pattern: prime factorisation itself incomplete — stops before fully breaking to primes (e.g. leaves 4 or 9)
errorPatterns.nextMove: keep splitting until every leaf is prime; 4 = 2×2, 9 = 3×3.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: factor tree left with composite leaves

responseLevels.gap: confuses HCF with LCM (takes highest powers), includes unshared primes, or cannot factorise to primes.
responseLevels.full: factorises to primes, takes the lowest power of each shared prime for HCF (highest for LCM), and justifies the method via common divisors being built only from shared primes and unique factorisation.
responseLevels.partial: computes the HCF correctly via prime factors but cannot explain why shared-primes-at-lowest-power works, or is shaky on the HCF/LCM distinction.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Find the highest common factor (HCF) of 24 and 36 using prime factorisation. Show your prime factors, then explain WHY taking the shared prime factors gives the HCF — why must that be the biggest number dividing both?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Students can get 12 by listing factors without understanding WHY the prime-factor method works. The reason tier tests whether they connect HCF to shared prime factors and the uniqueness of factorisation — the conceptual objective — rather than executing a memorised recipe. The classic error (taking highest powers, giving the LCM) also surfaces.
