pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 10–11y; fluently multiply multi-digit whole numbers up to 4-digit × 2-digit using formal long multiplication, explaining each partial product.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y6 'multiply multi-digit numbers up to 4 digits by a two-digit whole number using the formal written method of long multiplication'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 5.NBT.5 — 'fluently multiply multi-digit whole numbers using the standard algorithm'.
• Operational details — by Y6 the area-model scaffolding is largely internalised; the goal is FLUENT, accurate execution of 4-digit × 2-digit (2463×37) and the ability to EXPLAIN each partial product and the placeholder shift. The two partial-product rows are ×ones and ×tens; errors are now overwhelmingly procedural — lost placeholder zero, carry mistakes across many columns, misaligned addition. Fluency practice should pair speed/accuracy with a retained conceptual check (relate to the area model / estimate) so slips are caught. Estimate first (2463×37 ≈ 2500×40 = 100000).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): 3-digit × 2-digit accurately with correct placeholder. Tier B (age 10–11): 4-digit × 2-digit (2463×37) fluently and checked against an estimate. Tier C (age 11): explain each partial product's place value and diagnose a planted error in a worked long multiplication.
bestPractices: Prioritise fluent, accurate execution while retaining the area-model rationale for the two rows and the placeholder zero, so errors remain self-diagnosable.
Estimate first (round both factors) and check the final answer against it to catch place-value slips.
Target the common procedural errors explicitly — missing placeholder zero, multi-column carries, misaligned partial-product addition — through error-spotting practice.
Require explanation of each partial product's place value, not just a correct answer, to keep procedure and meaning linked.
Check via the inverse or estimation and build accuracy under increasing digit-length.
keyRepresentations: Compact long-multiplication layout with the placeholder zero
Area/grid model (as an internalised check, revisited on error)
Estimation (rounding both factors) to bound the product
Partial-product annotation (×ones row, ×tens row) for explanation
commonMisconceptions: Omitting the placeholder zero on the ×tens partial product.
Carry errors accumulating across many columns in large calculations.
Misaligning the partial products when adding them.
Multiplying by only one digit of the two-digit multiplier.
Executing fluently but with no conceptual check, so a wrong-magnitude answer slips through.

learn.summary: For 10–11 year-olds: fluently multiply multi-digit whole numbers (up to 4-digit × 2-digit, e.g. 2463×37) using formal long multiplication, explaining each partial product and the placeholder zero. By this stage the area-model scaffold is largely internalised; the aim is accurate, confident execution paired with a retained conceptual check (estimate and area model) so place-value slips are caught. Target the common procedural errors directly — missing placeholder zero, multi-column carry mistakes, misaligned addition, or multiplying by only one digit of the two-digit factor — and require learners to say what each row represents.

activities.title: Step-by-step long multiplication with an estimate check
feedback: If the ×tens row comes out about ten times too small, you probably dropped the placeholder zero — remember that row is 2463 groups of thirty, so it must start in the tens column; the zero holds the ones place.

If one digit of a partial product is wrong, slow down the carries: write each carry above the correct column and re-check it. Your estimate (~100000) only catches errors that change the size of the final answer; a single wrong digit can still give a plausible-looking total, so re-check each multiplication and carry directly.
If you multiplied by only one digit of 37, remember 37 = 30 + 7, so you need one row for ×7 and one for ×30.
If the answer is correct but you cannot say what each row means, link back to the area model: 2463 splits into (2463×30) and (2463×7), and the two parts recombine when you add.
activities.rationale: Y6/Grade 5 standards require fluent, accurate use of the standard algorithm; pairing step-by-step execution with an estimate and area-model check keeps procedure and meaning linked so procedural slips remain self-diagnosable.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils multiply multi-digit numbers up to 4 digits by a two-digit number using formal long multiplication.
5.NBT.5 requires fluently multiplying multi-digit whole numbers using the standard algorithm.
Fluency should retain a conceptual check (area model/estimation) so procedural errors like the missing placeholder zero remain self-diagnosable.
learnerActions: Before calculating, estimate 2463×37 by rounding both factors: 2500×40 = 100000, and write this down as the expected ballpark.
Work 2463×37 by long multiplication, writing the ×ones row (2463×7 = 17241) and the ×tens row underneath.
When starting the ×tens row, write the placeholder zero in the ones column first, then multiply by 3 tens to get 73890.
Add the two rows: 17241 + 73890 = 91131, keeping the columns aligned.
Compare the final answer with your estimate of ~100000 — 91131 is in the right ballpark, so the magnitude is plausible.
At each step, check that any carry is jotted above the correct column and added into the next multiplication.
activities.intendedInsight: Each partial-product row multiplies the whole of 2463 by a part of 37 (by 7 ones, then by 30), and the rows are added to recombine the parts. The placeholder zero is there because the second row is really ×30, not ×3. The estimate bounds the answer's size, so a lost zero shows up as a clearly wrong magnitude. A carry slip usually changes only one or two digits and can still look plausible, so it has to be caught by checking the working itself.

activities.title: Spot-the-error and fill-the-gap in a worked long multiplication
feedback: Missing placeholder zero: the ×tens row is ten times too small; it must begin in the tens column.
Misaligned addition: re-align each row by place value (ones under ones, tens under tens) before summing.
Carry error: check each carried digit is above and added into the correct next column.
For a fill-in-the-blank partial product, compute it directly and confirm it is consistent with the neighbouring digits and the carries recorded.

For the estimate, round each factor to one significant figure and multiply: 5000×30 = 150000. The exact product 4762×28 = 133336 sits below this estimate — because rounding both factors up gives an over-estimate, the true answer should fall under it.
activities.rationale: Error-spotting, gap-filling, and estimate selection consolidate and assess the specific procedural slips that dominate at this stage. This is assessment/consolidation of fixed examples rather than feedback on a learner's own live working.
sourceClaims: Fluency should retain a conceptual check (area model/estimation) so procedural errors like the missing placeholder zero remain self-diagnosable.
learnerActions: Examine worked examples of 4-digit × 2-digit long multiplication that contain a single planted mistake.
Identify the error type: a missing placeholder zero, a misaligned partial-product addition, a dropped or misplaced carry, or multiplying by only one digit.
Complete a fill-in-the-blank worked example where one partial product (or one digit of a partial product) is left empty, computing the missing value and checking it against the rest of the working.
Estimate the correct answer by rounding both factors, and use it to judge whether the worked total is plausible before pinpointing the error.
Rewrite the step correctly and recompute the final total.
Choose the best estimate for a calculation such as 4762×28 from a short list of magnitudes, justifying the rounding used (≈5000×30 = 150000).
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to diagnose a planted error or complete a missing step shows you understand each step's role — especially why the ×tens row is shifted by a placeholder zero and why rows must be aligned before adding. Estimation is a fast first filter for implausible answers.

activities.title: Annotate each partial product with its place value
feedback: If the explanation of the zero is 'that's just the rule', push further: the second row multiplies by 3 tens, so its smallest place is tens — the zero holds the empty ones place.
If the rows are not matched to area regions, draw the split 37 = 30 + 7 and show each part covering the full width 2463.
activities.rationale: A static annotated worked example is a strong reference for the explanation demand, keeping the compact algorithm linked to the area-model conceptual check; it cannot, however, give feedback on the learner's own fluent execution, so use it alongside live practice.
sourceClaims: Fluency should retain a conceptual check (area model/estimation) so procedural errors like the missing placeholder zero remain self-diagnosable.
learnerActions: Take a completed long multiplication of 2463×37 and label the first row '×7 (ones)' and the second row '×30 (tens)'.
Explain in writing or aloud why there is a zero at the end of the second row.
Match each partial-product row to the corresponding region of an area/grid model: the rectangle 2463×30 and the rectangle 2463×7.
State why the two rows are added together to get the total.
activities.intendedInsight: Each row corresponds to multiplying the whole number by a part of the multiplier; the placeholder zero marks that the second part is tens. Connecting the compact algorithm to the area model keeps the procedure meaningful.

constraints: Learners must actually perform the multiplication and explain each row; recognition-only or multiple-choice formats can assess or consolidate classification of errors but do not themselves elicit independent construction of the algorithm.

Annotated worked examples, gap-fill, and spot-the-error tasks use fixed examples: they build reference understanding and diagnosis but do not give feedback on a learner's own live working — pair them with learner-generated calculations.
Estimation bounds magnitude but does not confirm exact correctness; use it as a first filter, then verify the full computation.

Tier the digit length: 3-digit × 2-digit with correct placeholder first, then 4-digit × 2-digit fluently and checked against an estimate, then explain each partial product's place value and diagnose a planted error.
Any 'show why' area-model link should be available on demand when a step goes wrong, not forced on every step, so fluent learners are not slowed.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Independent re-audit of arithmetic: 2463×7 = 17241; 2463×30 = 73890; 17241 + 73890 = 91131, matching the assessment's stated values. 4762×28 = 133336. No arithmetic errors found.

Estimate check: 2500×40 = 100000 (both factors rounded up) and 91131 sits plausibly below it; 5000×30 = 150000 is likewise an upper over-estimate for 4762×28 (actual 133336, about 11% under). Feedback wording was corrected to state the actual value and the direction of the bound.
Source status unchanged: CCSS 5.NBT.5 and the NCETM guidance were marked unverified in the original and are retained only as curriculum-requirement / conceptual-check attributions, not upgraded.

The original material asserted '3D adds no value' and that dialogue 'can't' support a multi-digit algorithm; these catalog-fit judgements are not treated as universal pedagogical laws and have been omitted rather than restated as facts.

probeDeeper: What does the second row of your working (73,890) represent?
Why do you add the two rows together at the end?
Estimate 2,463 × 37 roughly — is 91,131 in the right ballpark?
Where did the placeholder zero come from, and what would happen without it?
assess.correctAnswer: 2,463 × 37 = 91,131 (2463×7 = 17,241; 2463×30 = 73,890; sum 91,131). The teacher watches for a fluent, error-free execution: correct partial products, the placeholder zero on the ×30 row, accurate carrying across four digits, and correct addition — plus the child explaining the first row is ×7 and the second is ×30.

errorPatterns.pattern: omits or misplaces the placeholder zero on the tens-digit row
errorPatterns.nextMove: reinforce that the second row multiplies by 3 TENS, so it must start in the tens column — write the zero to hold the ones place; connect to 'thirty groups'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: second partial product ten times too small; total wildly off

errorPatterns.pattern: carrying errors compound across the four digits — a carry dropped or added into the wrong column
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach the method; slow the carries, jotting each above the correct column, and check against the estimate.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: one digit of a partial product wrong; estimate (2500×40 = 100,000) flags it

errorPatterns.pattern: executes correctly but cannot explain what each row represents or why they are summed — pure rote
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach steps; link to the area model — the number splits into 30 and 7, each multiplies the whole 2463, and the parts recombine.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: right answer, but 'why add the two rows?' draws a blank

responseLevels.gap: makes placeholder/carrying errors that derail the calculation; cannot explain the partial products.
responseLevels.full: computes 4-digit × 2-digit fluently and accurately, explains each partial product and the summation, and checks against an estimate.
responseLevels.partial: reaches the correct answer but only slowly or with a self-corrected slip, or executes fluently yet cannot say what the rows mean.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to compute 2,463 × 37 by long multiplication while you watch, then to point at each partial product row and tell you what it represents and why the two rows are added. Watch fluency, the placeholder zero, carrying across four digits, and the final column addition.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: At this stage the objective is FLUENCY without procedural errors plus understanding what each partial product means. Watching a four-by-two-digit case surfaces both accuracy (placeholder, carries) and comprehension (can the child say the second row is 2463 groups of thirty?) — a rote executor computes but cannot explain the rows.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 5–7 (CONCEPTUAL): understand that the teen numbers 11–19 are 'a ten and some ones' — the FIRST appearance of place value, and a very central node (0.41). This is where quantity stops being a pile of ones and gains structure.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1): identify/represent numbers using objects and pictorial representations; non-statutory guidance has pupils understand teen numbers as ten and ones (partitioning), leading into Y2 two-digit place value.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.NBT.2b 'the numbers 11 to 19 are composed of a ten and one, two, three ... nine ones' (and K.NBT.1 'compose/decompose 11–19 into ten ones and some further ones').
• Operational details — the child composes a teen number as one group of ten plus extra ones (14 = 10 + 4) and decomposes it back, using ten-frames, bead strings and Dienes so 'ten' becomes a single UNIT. The hard part is the naming mismatch: the words hide the structure ('eleven'/'twelve' opaque; 'thir-teen' says ones first) while the numeral 1_ shows the ten. This concept underpins ALL later place value (a ten is one unit made of ten).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 5): compose 14 as a ten and 4 ones with objects. Tier B (5–6): decompose 17 into 10 + 7 and record the equation. Tier C (6–7): explain that 13 is 'one ten and three ones' and connect the numeral 13 to that structure.
bestPractices: Make the TEN a single unit the child can see and handle — a filled ten-frame, a ten-bead bar, a Dienes ten-rod — so a teen is 'one ten and some ones', not fourteen separate ones; this is the seed of all place value.
Use the SECOND ten-frame / part-full frame so 14 is a full ten-frame plus a frame with 4 — the '10 and 4' structure is literally visible, and record it as 10 + 4.
Confront the language trap explicitly: the words for teens hide the ten (eleven, twelve) or say the ones first (thir-teen); anchor the meaning to the ten-and-ones model rather than the word order.
Emphasise the numeral shows the structure the words don't — the '1' in 14 is one TEN — to pre-empt reading it as 'one and four'.
Move fluently between compose (make 16 from a ten and 6) and decompose (break 16 into 10 + 6), recording equations both ways to build flexible part-whole understanding.
keyRepresentations: Double ten-frame: one full (the ten) + one partly filled (the ones) showing 10 + n.
Ten-bead bar / bead string with the first ten a distinct colour, then extra beads.
Dienes ten-rod + unit cubes composing a teen number.
Part-whole model / equation (14 = 10 + 4) linking the structure to symbols.
Numeral with the tens digit and ones digit colour-linked to the ten-group and the extra ones.
commonMisconceptions: Seeing a teen number as a heap of individual ones, with no 'ten' unit (no place-value structure yet).
Reading the numeral literally as two ones ('one, four' for 14) rather than 'one ten and four'.
Teen word transposition (thirteen → 31) from the ones-first naming.
Thinking 'eleven' and 'twelve' are unrelated to ten because the words give no clue.
Miscounting the ten (treating the ten-rod as one object = 1, so 14 becomes 5) — unitising confusion.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, build the understanding that teen numbers (11–19) are 'a ten and some ones' — the first appearance of place value. The central move is unitising: bundling ten single ones into one TEN unit the child can see and handle, then recognising the extras. Learners should compose teens (14 = 10 + 4) and decompose them (16 → 10 + 6), record equations both ways, and connect the written numeral to the grouped quantity so the '1' in 14 reads as one TEN. Confront the language trap directly: 'eleven'/'twelve' hide the ten, and 'thir-teen' says the ones first, while the numeral 1_ shows the ten first.

activities.title: Make a ten and the leftovers
feedback: If the child leaves ten ungrouped and calls 14 'fourteen ones', pause them at the tenth counter: 'Watch — these ten become ONE ten. Now how many are left over?' Then read it as 'a ten and four'.
If the child treats the full ten-frame as a single object counting '1' (so 14 looks like 5), slide back to ten single counters, count them to ten, then bundle: 'This one bar is worth ten, not one.'
When correct, ask them to prove it: 'Unbundle the ten back into ten ones and count the whole lot — do you still get fourteen?'
activities.rationale: Bundling ten ones into a single 'ten' unit, shown with ten-frames and base-ten materials, is the foundational move of place value, and the teens are where it first appears. Physically grouping makes the structure felt and lets the child self-correct.
sourceClaims: Bundling ten ones into a single 'ten' unit (unitising), shown with ten-frames and base-ten materials, is the foundational move of place value and the teens are where it first appears despite opaque number-word naming.
Kindergarten/Grade 1 pupils understand that the numbers 11 to 19 are composed of a ten and one to nine further ones, composing and decomposing them into ten ones and some further ones.
learnerActions: Count out loose counters for a teen number such as 14.
Fill a ten-frame by placing counters one at a time until the frame holds ten.
Once ten are grouped, treat the full frame (or a ten-bead bar / Dienes ten-rod) as ONE 'ten' unit; put the remaining counters in a second frame.
Say the result aloud: 'one ten and four ones'.
Repeat with 13, 16, 17, 19, each time grouping exactly ten and naming the leftovers.
activities.intendedInsight: A teen number is not a heap of single ones — ten of them bundle into one 'ten' unit, and the rest are the extra ones. This bundling (unitising) is the seed of all place value.

activities.title: Compose and decompose, both ways
feedback: If composing and decomposing are treated as unrelated, demonstrate the reverse immediately after the forward build with the same materials so the child sees it is one structure read two ways.
If the equation is written but not matched to the materials, point to each part: 'Where is the 10 in your counters? Where is the 4?'
activities.rationale: Moving fluently between composing and decomposing, recording equations both ways, builds flexible part–whole understanding rather than a one-directional procedure.
sourceClaims: Kindergarten/Grade 1 pupils understand that the numbers 11 to 19 are composed of a ten and one to nine further ones, composing and decomposing them into ten ones and some further ones.
Year 1/2 pupils identify and represent numbers using objects and partition numbers, understanding teen and two-digit numbers as tens and ones (early place value).
learnerActions: Compose: 'Build 16 from a ten and some ones' — make one ten, add 6 extras, then write 16 = 10 + 6.
Decompose: start with 18 shown as a ten and extras; break the ten back into ten single ones and write 18 = 10 + 8.
Do several in each direction, recording the equation each time (13 = 10 + 3, 17 = 10 + 7).
Explain in words: 'Thirteen is one ten and three ones.'
activities.intendedInsight: Teen numbers can be put together from a ten and some ones and taken apart again; the equation 14 = 10 + 4 captures this part–whole structure flexibly in both directions.

activities.title: The numeral shows what the word hides
feedback: If the child reads the 1 at face value ('one and four'), return to the bundled counters: 'The 1 stands for the ten you grouped — show me that ten.'
If the child writes thirteen as 31, show 13 as a ten-unit and three ones side by side with the numeral, and compare directly with 31 (three tens and one): 'How is 13 different from 31?'
Confirm success by asking them to explain to someone else why the 1 in 14 is worth ten.
activities.rationale: Teen number words hide or reorder the ten relative to the numeral, which is a known source of error; linking the numeral's digits to the ten-group and the extras explicitly pre-empts face-value reading and transposition.
sourceClaims: Bundling ten ones into a single 'ten' unit (unitising), shown with ten-frames and base-ten materials, is the foundational move of place value and the teens are where it first appears despite opaque number-word naming.
learnerActions: Lay the grouped quantity (a ten unit + extras) beside the written numeral, e.g. 14.
Point to the '1' and say what it stands for: 'This is the one TEN I bundled, not one.'
Point to the '4' and tie it to the leftover ones.
Say the number word 'fourteen' and notice it says 'four' first even though the numeral writes the ten first; then say 'thir-teen' and notice the same ones-first naming.
Say 'eleven' and 'twelve' and note the words give no clue about the ten — only the model and numeral reveal it.
activities.intendedInsight: The written numeral 1_ shows the ten-first structure, while teen words either hide the ten (eleven, twelve) or say the ones first (thir-teen). Anchoring meaning to the ten-and-ones model guards against reading 14 as 'one and four' and against writing thirteen as 31.

activities.title: Explain and check with a diagnostic prompt
feedback: Full understanding: the child makes ONE ten, reads the leftovers, and connects this to the written numeral.
Partial: the child makes a ten with support but doesn't yet describe the teen as 'a ten and some ones' independently — give more compose/decompose practice and fade the prompting.
Gap: the child treats 14 as fourteen separate ones with no ten inside, or reads the 1 as one unit — return to the bundling activity before re-attempting.
activities.rationale: Asking the child to show it and then explain why discriminates a child who sees the ten as a unit from one who still treats the teen as unstructured ones or reads the 1 at face value.
learnerActions: Put out 14 counters (or another teen quantity) and answer: 'How is 14 made up out of tens and ones? Show me with the counters and tell me how you know.'
Make one group of ten, read the leftover four, and state '14 = 10 + 4'.
Answer probes: 'Make a group of ten — how many are left over?', 'How is 14 different from 41?', 'Show 17 as a ten and some ones and write it as 10 + 7.'
activities.intendedInsight: Independently describing a teen number as one ten and some ones, and linking it to the numeral, is the sign the ten is now seen as a unit within the number.

constraints: Make the TEN something the child can see and handle as a single unit — a filled ten-frame, a ten-bead bar, or a Dienes ten-rod — so a teen is 'one ten and some ones' rather than many separate ones.

Fill-in-the-blank, matching teen numerals to ten-and-ones pictures, and multiple-choice ('which shows one ten and three ones?') can check whether the structure is understood, but recognition responses do not elicit the physical bundling that builds the unitising insight; use them to verify, not to teach it.

A fixed labelled double-ten-frame image (tap to reveal 'one ten', 'and four ones', and link digits to groups) is a useful anchor, but because it is not manipulable it cannot provide the act of bundling ten ones into a ten; pair it with hands-on grouping.

A dialogue or character prompt can ask the child to explain how many tens and ones are in a teen number (e.g. fifteen) and probe the naming trap, which may elicit or check an explanation of the structure; on its own it does not provide the physical bundling/handling, so pair it with hands-on grouping.
Watch for unitising confusion: a child may count the ten-rod as '1' and get 14 → 5. Re-ground by unbundling to ten single ones and recounting.

Optional interactive supports can make the mechanism concrete: dragging loose ones so the tenth one closes a frame into a single 'ten' bar, extras spilling into a second frame, the numeral assembling with its '1' visibly tied to the ten-bar and '4' to the extras, a decompose mode that bursts the ten-bar back into ten ones while recording 14 = 10 + 4, and a 'name vs structure' panel that plays 'thirteen' beside 10 + 3. These are helpful examples, not required mechanisms.

assess.correctAnswer: 14 is one ten and four ones. Group ten counters into a ten; four are left over, so 14 = 10 + 4.

errorPatterns.distractor: It's just 14 ones — there's no ten in it.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the 1 in 14 at face value: 'the 1 means one, so it's one and four'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Match the numeral to the grouped counters: the 1 stands for the ten you bundled, the 4 for the leftovers.
errorPatterns.distractor: The 1 means one, so 14 is one and four.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child treats the written 1 as one unit rather than one ten.

responseLevels.gap: Treats the teen number as unstructured ones, or reads the 1 as one unit.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 9-10 (META). Solve number and practical problems involving reading, writing, ordering, comparing and rounding whole numbers to 1,000,000 — e.g. 'largest six-digit number whose digits sum to 15', round a stadium capacity for a headline, order five city populations and find a range. Applying the whole Year-5 place-value toolkit flexibly and in context.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 5): 'solve number problems and practical problems that involve all of the above [place value to 1,000,000]'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.NBT / 4.OA multi-step problem-solving with multi-digit numbers, rounding for reasonableness.
• Operational details — Pose rich, multi-step and real-context problems (populations, distances, money, digit-constraint puzzles) that reward choosing among reading, comparing, ordering, rounding and place-value reasoning. Model with number lines, bar models, place-value charts; require justification and appropriate accuracy. Include 'construct a number' puzzles that exercise place value creatively.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9, emerging): solves a one-step large-number problem with a model. Tier B (age 9-10, secure): solves multi-step problems in context, choosing and explaining the strategy. Tier C (age 10, extending): tackles digit-constraint/optimisation puzzles and selects appropriate accuracy.
bestPractices: Pose rich, real-context, multi-step problems (populations, distances, budgets) plus digit-constraint puzzles.
Provide the full toolkit (number line, bar model, chart) and require the child to choose and justify a strategy.
Use rounding to estimate and check reasonableness; choose appropriate accuracy for the context.
Include 'build the largest/smallest number with these constraints' tasks to exercise place value creatively.
Externalise reasoning (think-aloud then child-explains) so strategy choice becomes deliberate.
keyRepresentations: Number line (compare/round/estimate)
Bar model for multi-step structure
Place-value chart / counters
Real data sets (populations, distances)
Digit-tile constraint puzzles
commonMisconceptions: Applying a memorised procedure without checking it fits.
Rounding at the wrong stage / to unhelpful accuracy.
Ordering/comparing errors with multi-zero or mixed-length numbers.
Not sense-checking against an estimate.
In digit-constraint puzzles, ignoring the place-value impact of digit position.

learn.summary: For ages 9-10: solve multi-step number and practical problems involving reading, writing, ordering, comparing and rounding whole numbers up to 1,000,000. Learners apply the full place-value toolkit flexibly in context (populations, stadium capacities, distances, budgets) and tackle digit-constraint puzzles such as building the largest number with a given digit sum. The central insight is that place value drives strategy: to maximise a number you load the biggest digits into the highest-value places first. Rounding, ordering and estimation are chosen deliberately to fit each problem and checked for reasonableness.

activities.title: Build the largest number: a digit-constraint puzzle
feedback: If a learner spreads the sum evenly or fills low places (e.g. 333,330, which sums to 15, or 111,138, which also sums to 15), the number is not maximised: compare it against 960,000 column by column. A 9 in the hundred-thousands place beats any arrangement with a smaller leading digit, so the leading place dominates.
If the digits no longer sum to 15, recount the chosen digits before judging size — any counterexample used here must itself sum to 15.
Prompt: 'Why put the 9 in the hundred-thousands place and not in the ones?' to surface that the leftmost place carries the most value.
activities.rationale: A constructive, manipulable puzzle lets children test arrangements, see the value update, and work toward the place-value principle rather than guess. Arranging movable digit-tiles into a chart and comparing candidates can make the strategy explicit; this is a proposed design, not a claim that only this format can teach it.
sourceClaims: Digit-constraint/optimisation puzzles and strategy-selection deepen place-value problem solving.
learnerActions: Take the task: 'Make the LARGEST six-digit number whose digits add up to 15.'
Arrange digit choices into a six-column place-value chart (hundred-thousands down to ones) and write the value they build.
Compare two of their own candidate numbers place by place, starting from the highest place, and decide which is larger and why.
State the rule they discovered in their own words: to make a number as large as possible, put the biggest digits in the highest-value places first.
Verify the digits still sum to 15 after arranging them (9 + 6 = 15, then zeros gives 960,000).
activities.intendedInsight: Magnitude is controlled by the highest-value places, so maximising a number means front-loading the biggest digits into the leftmost columns while respecting the digit-sum constraint.

activities.title: Round in context for a headline
feedback: If a learner rounds 67,450 up to 68,000, they may be rounding in steps (the 5 tens lift 67,450 to 67,500, then that rounds up to 68,000) or treating the tens digit 5 as the decider: isolate the decider. For nearest thousand, look at the hundreds digit — 4 is less than 5, so round down.
Use the number line: 67,450 sits left of the midpoint 67,500, so it is nearer 67,000.
Prompt: 'Is 67,450 nearer 67,000 or 68,000? How do you know?'
activities.rationale: Rounding errors in context often come from attending to the wrong digit or to the full tail. Naming the deciding digit and anchoring on a number line targets this directly.
sourceClaims: Solve multi-step problems with multi-digit numbers and use rounding to assess reasonableness (4.NBT / 4.OA.3).
learnerActions: Take a real-context item: 'A stadium holds 67,450 people — round it to the nearest thousand for a news headline.'
Identify the deciding digit for 'nearest thousand' (the hundreds digit) before rounding.
Place 67,450 on a number line between 67,000 and 68,000 and judge which it is nearer.
Give the rounded answer (67,000) and justify it from the deciding digit (the hundreds digit, 4), not by rounding in steps from the tens digit (67,450 → 67,500 → 68,000).
Explain in a sentence why 450 keeps the thousands the same (rounds DOWN to 67,000).
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding to a named place depends on the single deciding digit immediately to the right of that place; here the hundreds digit is 4, which is below 5, so the thousands stay the same.

activities.title: Order populations and find the range
feedback: If a learner orders by the first visible digit (e.g. treating 90,000; 9,000; 900,000 as equal or mis-ordering them because each starts with 9), line the numbers up right-aligned in columns and compare starting from the highest place.
Prompt: 'Order 90,000; 9,000; 900,000 — what do you compare first?' to make column alignment the deciding move.
After finding the range, compare the exact difference to a rounded estimate to catch slips.
activities.rationale: Multi-zero and mixed-length numbers are a classic source of comparison errors; explicit column alignment and highest-place-first comparison address the misconception.
learnerActions: Take five city populations (mixed-length numbers, some with internal zeros) and right-align them by place-value column.
Compare from the highest place downward to order them from smallest to largest.
Order the trio 90,000; 9,000; 900,000 as a focused check, saying which place you compare first.
Find the range by subtracting the smallest from the largest and sense-check the answer against a rounded estimate.
activities.intendedInsight: Correct ordering comes from aligning place-value columns and comparing from the highest place down. For whole numbers, more digits means a larger number, but when numbers have the same number of digits you must compare place by place, not just look at the first visible digit.

activities.title: Choose and justify the strategy (think-aloud)
feedback: If a learner applies a memorised procedure without checking it fits the question, ask them to name the tool and why before computing.
If an answer is wildly off a rounded estimate, treat the mismatch as a signal to recheck rather than to accept the computation.
Naming the strategy after solving (e.g. 'I rounded to estimate, then compared from the highest place') can reinforce transfer.
activities.rationale: This is a META problem-solving topic: externalising reasoning (think-aloud, then child-explains) and estimation-checking support flexible strategy selection. A spoken dialogue and a worked anchor example are useful supplements for eliciting reasoning, not the sole route.
sourceClaims: Digit-constraint/optimisation puzzles and strategy-selection deepen place-value problem solving.
Solve multi-step problems with multi-digit numbers and use rounding to assess reasonableness (4.NBT / 4.OA.3).
learnerActions: For each problem, first answer 'which tool fits?' — number line, bar model, place-value chart, or digit arrangement — before solving.
Hear or read a worked example thought aloud, then re-solve a similar problem explaining each decision.
Estimate first by rounding, then compute the exact answer, and check the exact answer against the estimate.
Discuss with a partner or respond to prompts such as 'how did you decide?' to make the strategy deliberate.
activities.intendedInsight: In multi-step problems the hard part is choosing which place-value tool to use and checking reasonableness; making the choice explicit and estimating first turns strategy into a deliberate repertoire.

constraints: Multi-step and context problems can be assessed with fixed-response items (best-estimate choices, largest-number choices, estimate-then-check sliders, fill-in-the-blank), but recognition-only items do not themselves elicit the independent construction that the digit-building puzzle requires; use a construction task for the maximising strategy.
A worked, tapped-through example (e.g. a solved population-range problem) is a reference anchor, not varied practice; pair it with problems the learner solves themselves.

A live-updating value display and movable digit-tiles are optional supports that make the place-value mechanism concrete; they are helpful illustrations, not mandatory mechanisms, and the same insight can be reached on paper with a drawn chart.
For this abstract/contextual numeric reasoning there is little spatial payoff, so 3D manipulation adds little here; prefer number lines, bar models and place-value charts.
Any 'spread evenly / fills low places' counterexample used with the digit-sum-15 task must itself sum to 15 (e.g. 333,330 or 111,138); do not use 333,300, which sums to 12.

Tier expectations: emerging learners solve a one-step large-number problem with a model; secure learners solve multi-step context problems choosing and explaining a strategy; extending learners tackle digit-constraint/optimisation puzzles and select appropriate accuracy.

The ordering 9,000 < 90,000 < 900,000 is confirmed. These match the source's stated correct answers.

The original framing that the construction puzzle 'cannot be solved by trial alone' is softened: trial-and-error can reach the answer, but the puzzle is designed to make the place-value strategy the efficient, reasoned route.

probeDeeper: Why put the 9 in the hundred-thousands place and not in the ones?
Is 67,450 nearer 67,000 or 68,000? How do you know?

assess.correctAnswer: 960,000 (load the biggest digits into the highest places: 9 + 6 = 15, then zeros); and 67,000 (450 is below 500, so round down).

errorPatterns.pattern: Doesn't prioritise place value for magnitude — spreads the digit-sum evenly or fills low places, so the number isn't the largest (e.g. 333,300 or 111,138)

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares/orders large numbers by first digit or digit-count alone, misaligning place values

responseLevels.gap: Cannot systematically maximise value or rounds the wrong way in context; orders by the wrong feature.

responseLevels.partial: Handles single steps (rounds, or orders) but stumbles when a problem combines maximising, rounding, and comparing.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set the problem and watch the reasoning: 'Make the largest six-digit number whose digits add up to 15.' Then a context item: 'A stadium holds 67,450 people — round it to the nearest thousand for a news headline.' Watch how they place digits to maximise value and which way they round in context.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The 'largest number' task cannot be solved by trial alone — it reveals whether the child knows value is maximised by loading the most-significant places first. The stadium item checks rounding to a named place IN CONTEXT, where children often round the visible hundreds up regardless of the thousand rule.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 10–11 — solve number and practical problems involving reading, writing, ordering, comparing, rounding and negative numbers up to 10,000,000 (a synthesising META-topic).
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y6 'solve number and practical problems that involve all of the above' — i.e. the applied capstone over the Y6 place-value objectives (to 10,000,000, rounding, negatives).
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): draws on 4.NBT.A (read/write/compare/round multi-digit), 5.NBT.A (place value, rounding) and 6.NS.C (negatives in context) applied to problem contexts.
• Operational details: Pose realistic multi-step problems — populations, distances, temperatures, sea depths, attendances — that require choosing WHICH place-value skill to deploy (round for a headline, compare/order to rank, use negatives for depths). Emphasise sense-making: estimate first by rounding, then check the exact answer is reasonable, and interpret the result back in context (a rounded headline vs an exact count).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): 'Population 8,274,500 — round to the nearest million for a headline.' Tier B: 'Order three ocean-trench depths given as negatives.' Tier C: 'Estimate total attendance at three events by rounding each to the nearest 100,000 and judge if your estimate is over or under.'
bestPractices: Use authentic large-number contexts (populations, distances, depths, attendances) so pupils choose the appropriate place-value tool rather than being told which
Teach estimate-first: round to get a ballpark, then compute/compare exactly and check reasonableness against the estimate
Require interpretation back in context — when is a rounded headline appropriate, when is the exact figure needed
Blend the sub-skills within a single problem (round AND order AND read negatives) to build flexible selection
Model judging whether a rounded estimate is an over- or under-estimate, connecting rounding direction to context
keyRepresentations: Number line / magnitude bars for ordering and rounding seven-digit values
Period-grouped place-value chart for reading and writing the numbers in play
Vertical number line for negative contexts (depths, temperatures)
Estimation strips pairing rounded values with the exact figures
commonMisconceptions: Applying a rounding rule mechanically without checking the answer makes sense in context
Ordering by digit count or face value rather than aligned place value for seven-digit numbers
Mishandling negatives in context (ranking −900 m as shallower than −300 m)
Rounding to the wrong place for the purpose (nearest 10 when a million is asked for a headline)
Losing placeholder zeros when reading/writing the large numbers within a problem

learn.summary: Applied capstone for place value to 10,000,000: learners choose and combine place-value tools — rounding to a stated place, ordering/comparing seven-digit and negative numbers, and reading/writing with placeholder zeros — within realistic multi-step problems (populations, distances, temperatures, sea depths, attendances). Core habit: estimate first by rounding, compute/compare exactly, then interpret the result back in context and judge whether an estimate is over or under.

activities.title: Large-number problem workspace: pick the right tool
feedback: If a learner rounds 8,274,500 to 9,000,000 'because the rest is big', have them underline the millions digit and box only the single digit to its right (2); state 'only that one digit decides' and locate the number on a line between 8,000,000 and 9,000,000.

If a learner ranks -7,921 m as deepest because '7 thousand is the smallest number', use a vertical number line with 0 at sea level to show that -9,052 m, the most negative reading, sits furthest below zero, so it is deepest and least in value.

If rounded parts come out the wrong order of magnitude (e.g. reading 214,600 as 21,460), rebuild the period structure (ones, thousands, millions) on a place-value grid and read each number aloud by period before rounding.

To decide whether an estimate is over or under, check each addend: did it round up or down, and by how much? Add up the up-adjustments and the down-adjustments and compare them — the estimate is over when the ups outweigh the downs and under when the downs outweigh the ups. Note that rounding can go in mixed directions: for 214,600 + 388,050 + 96,700 to the nearest 100,000, 214,600 rounds down while 388,050 and 96,700 round up, and here the ups slightly outweigh the down, giving a small over-estimate (700,000 vs exact 699,350).
activities.rationale: The objective is choosing and combining place-value skills in context, so an open workspace where learners select a tool, see the consequence and self-check against an estimate is proposed to target that selection skill directly. An optional interactive version can offer a magnitude number line, a rounding bracket that snaps to a chosen place, comparison/ordering slots, a negative-scale toggle, and an over/under flag on the estimate — these make the mechanism concrete but are not required; the same work can be done on paper with a drawn number line and place-value grid.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils solve number and practical problems involving reading, writing, ordering, comparing, rounding and negative numbers up to 10,000,000.
Applied place-value problem solving draws on read/write/compare/round of multi-digit numbers (4.NBT.A, 5.NBT.A) and negatives in context (6.NS.C).
learnerActions: Load a scenario with mixed demands, e.g. three ocean trenches at -8,376 m, -9,052 m and -7,921 m plus a country's population of 8,274,500 needed for a news headline.

For the headline, round 8,274,500 to the nearest million and state the result (8,000,000); name the single digit that decided the rounding (the hundred-thousands digit, 2) and explain why the digits after it do not change the decision.

Order the three trench depths from deepest to shallowest, placing each on a vertical number line with 0 at sea level, and justify ordering by position (more negative = lower = deeper), not by comparing the digits while ignoring the minus sign.

Estimate a combined attendance for three events by rounding each to the nearest 100,000, then compute the exact total and state whether your rounded estimate came out over or under, explaining how you can tell.
Say back in context which figure each situation needs: a rounded headline for the population, exact negatives for ranking the trenches.
activities.intendedInsight: The same set of numbers can demand different place-value tools — rounding for a headline, exact negatives for a ranking — and estimating first tells you whether the exact answer is believable.

activities.title: Fluency check on the component skills
feedback: For ordering: the correct deepest-to-shallowest order for -4,000, -10,900, -7,200 is -10,900, -7,200, -4,000, because more negative is lower (further below sea level).
For the estimate: rounding to the nearest 100,000 gives 200,000 + 400,000 + 100,000 = about 700,000; then check the exact total (699,350) is close to it.
For rounding to the nearest million: the deciding digit is the hundred-thousands digit (2), so 8,274,500 rounds down to 8,000,000, not up to 9,000,000.
activities.rationale: The component skills are cleanly assessable, so short targeted items are a useful companion for checking applied fluency. These items check recognition and execution of each skill; on their own they do not elicit the open multi-step tool-selection that the workspace activity targets.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils solve number and practical problems involving reading, writing, ordering, comparing, rounding and negative numbers up to 10,000,000.
learnerActions: Round 8,274,500 to the nearest million and choose the correct result.
Order three negative trench depths (e.g. -4,000 m, -10,900 m, -7,200 m) from deepest to shallowest.
Estimate a total attendance (e.g. 214,600 + 388,050 + 96,700) by rounding each to the nearest 100,000.
activities.intendedInsight: Each component place-value skill — rounding to a stated place, ordering negatives by position, estimating by rounding addends — can be executed accurately on its own.

activities.title: Framing contexts before computing
feedback: If a learner rounds a figure to the wrong place for the purpose (e.g. nearest 10 for a headline about millions), ask what level of precision a reader needs and point them to the relevant period.

If they would round depths used for a ranking, remind them that ranking needs the exact ordering, so the comparison should use exact values: rounding (even consistently to the same place) can make different depths equal, e.g. -8,376 m and -8,420 m both round to -8,000 m to the nearest thousand, so the order is lost.
activities.rationale: Framing and discussion build the sense-making and interpretation the topic emphasises; a dialogue can coach problem framing, while the compute-and-check work is best carried out in the workspace, so this activity should lead into, not replace, the workspace task.
learnerActions: Study a labelled population/depth chart or world map and tap or point to regions to reveal exact figures.
For each figure, state what you would round it to for a fair headline, and which figures you would keep exact for ranking.
Take on a journalist's brief: turn a set of exact figures into fair rounded headlines, then explain why the rounded version is appropriate for a headline but not for a precise ranking.
activities.intendedInsight: Deciding which place-value tool a situation calls for — and whether a rounded headline or an exact figure is appropriate — is itself part of the problem.

constraints: Use authentic large-number contexts (populations, distances, depths, attendances) so learners choose the appropriate place-value tool rather than being told which.

Teach estimate-first: round for a ballpark, then compute/compare exactly and check reasonableness against the estimate; require interpreting the result back in context (when a rounded headline suffices vs when the exact figure is needed).
Blend sub-skills within a single problem (round AND order AND read negatives) to build flexible selection.
Recognition/short-answer items check component fluency but do not on their own elicit the open multi-step tool selection; use them as a companion, not a substitute.

A static chart cannot host the compute-and-check work, and a dialogue is better suited to coaching problem framing than to carrying the full multi-step working; treat these as scaffolds leading into the problem-solving rather than substitutes.

Any interactive features (snapping rounding bracket, draggable number line, negative-scale toggle, over/under flag) are optional ways to make the mechanism visible; the same learning can occur on paper with a drawn number line and place-value grid.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of worked numbers: 8,274,500 rounds to 8,000,000 (deciding hundred-thousands digit 2 -> round down) — correct. Ordering -4,000, -10,900, -7,200 deepest-to-shallowest = -10,900, -7,200, -4,000 — correct. Estimate 214,600+388,050+96,700 rounded to nearest 100,000 = 200,000+400,000+100,000 = 700,000; exact = 699,350, so the estimate is a slight over-estimate (by 650) — consistent; up-adjustments (11,950 + 3,300 = 15,250) exceed the down-adjustment (14,600) by 650.

The over/under feedback in Activity 1 handles the mixed-rounding case correctly: learners weigh total up-adjustments against total down-adjustments rather than assuming all addends round the same way.

The second CCSS source is marked verified:false in the row; the standards mapping (4.NBT.A/5.NBT.A/6.NS.C) is retained as sourced but its verification status is unconfirmed, and no claim of medium effectiveness rests on it.
The probe 'Why is -10,900 m deeper than -4,000 m when 10,900 is the bigger number?' is pedagogically sound and is reflected via the number-line position argument in the ordering feedback.

probeDeeper: For the rounding, which single digit made the decision, and why did the rest not matter?
Why is -10,900 m deeper than -4,000 m when 10,900 is the bigger number?
Would your estimate be too high or too low compared with the exact total — how can you tell?
What if the reading had been 8,724,500 — would it still round to 8,000,000?

errorPatterns.pattern: Rounds using the wrong place — looks at a later digit or rounds 8,274,500 up to 9,000,000 because 'the rest is big', instead of reading the hundred-thousands digit (2).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Underline the millions digit and box the single digit to its right; state the rule 'only that one digit decides'. Model on a number line between 8,000,000 and 9,000,000.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rounds to 9,000,000, or hesitates over which digit decides; cannot name the deciding digit.

errorPatterns.pattern: Orders the negative depths by magnitude, treating -4,000 as deepest because '4 thousand is the smallest number'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront on a vertical number line with 0 at sea level; show -10,900 sits furthest below zero, so it is deepest and least in value.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child ranks -4,000 as deepest / -10,900 as shallowest, ignoring that more-negative is lower.

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscounts the periods in the seven-digit numbers — misplaces commas or reads 214,600 as 21,460 / 2,146,000, so the estimate is off by a factor of ten.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild the period structure (ones, thousands, millions) with a place-value grid; read each number aloud by period before rounding.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rounded parts are the wrong order of magnitude; total estimate is 70,000 or 7,000,000.

responseLevels.gap: Rounds on the wrong digit, orders negatives by magnitude, or produces an estimate of the wrong order of magnitude.
responseLevels.full: Executes all three fluently — names the deciding digit when rounding, orders negatives by number-line position, rounds each addend before summing, and can say whether the estimate is over or under.
responseLevels.partial: Completes one or two tasks correctly (often the rounding) but cannot reliably order the negatives or justify the estimate's direction.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Three tasks laid out on paper. (1) Round 8,274,500 to the nearest million. (2) Three ocean-trench readings are -4,000 m, -10,900 m and -7,200 m; order them from deepest to shallowest. (3) Estimate 214,600 + 388,050 + 96,700 by rounding each first.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watch the working, not the answers. Correct rounding requires looking at the digit to the RIGHT of the millions place (2 → round down) — a child who rounds on the wrong digit or rounds up 'because there's lots after it' is exposed. The negatives task separates children who order by magnitude (calling -4,000 deepest) from those who order by position on the number line. The estimate reveals whether they round before adding or add then round.

sources.claim: Y6 pupils solve number and practical problems involving reading, writing, ordering, comparing, rounding and negative numbers up to 10,000,000.

sources.claim: Applied place-value problem solving draws on read/write/compare/round of multi-digit numbers (4.NBT.A, 5.NBT.A) and negatives in context (6.NS.C).

pedagogy.summary: Partitioning shapes into 2, 3 or 4 equal parts is where children learn that a fraction demands EQUAL parts — equal in AMOUNT (area), not necessarily equal in shape or appearance. The two load-bearing ideas: any-number-of-pieces is not enough (unequal pieces are not halves/thirds/quarters), and two shares that look completely different can still be equal if they cover the same amount. Teach by cutting the same shape more than one way, and by comparing equal-area-but-different-shape pieces, so children judge shares by amount, not by look.
bestPractices: Partition the SAME shape several different ways into the same fraction (a rectangle into quarters by vertical cuts, a 2×2 grid, two diagonals) so no single picture becomes 'the' way
Deliberately show equal-AREA but different-SHAPE pieces and have children verify equality by rearranging/overlaying or counting unit squares
Contrast a correct partition with an unequal one that has the right NUMBER of pieces, forcing the equal-parts criterion open
Move beyond halving to thirds (a circle into three) where children cannot rely on repeated halving
Check equality physically — cut and re-lay pieces, or tile them onto a grid — rather than trusting appearance
keyRepresentations: Rectangle partitioned several ways into the same fraction (multiple valid cuts)
Circle partitioned into thirds (120° shares)
Equal-area different-shape pieces that rearrange onto one another
Faint unit-square grid under a shape for checking equal area
commonMisconceptions: Equal shares must look the same / be congruent — rejects equal-area different-shape pieces as 'not fair'
Any N pieces count as Nths regardless of size (ignores the equal-parts requirement)
A shape can only be partitioned into a fraction one 'proper' way
Judges share size by one dimension (length) rather than area
Thinks halving repeatedly is the only way to make parts, so thirds feel impossible

learn.summary: Children learn that a fraction requires EQUAL parts — equal in AMOUNT (area), not necessarily equal in shape or appearance. Two load-bearing ideas: having the right NUMBER of pieces is not enough (unequal pieces are not halves/thirds/quarters), and two shares that look completely different can still be equal if they cover the same amount. Teach by partitioning the same shape several ways and by comparing equal-area-but-different-shape pieces, so children judge shares by amount, not by look. Thirds (and a circle into three) force children off repeated halving.

activities.title: Cut it, re-lay it: equal amount beats equal look
feedback: If the learner says 'the long one is more/less' by looking: have them cut and re-lay the strip onto the fat piece, so they see equal amount despite different shape.
If the learner calls any four pieces 'quarters' regardless of size: set a correct equal partition beside an unequal four-piece one and recompose/rearrange to show only equal amounts count.
If the learner insists only one 'proper' way makes quarters: show several equal-area-checked quarterings side by side and ask them to invent a new valid one.
When a second and third distinct partition each check out as equal, name this explicitly: many partitions give the same fraction.

For thirds, prompt: how do you know all three are equal? Because the three 120-degree sectors are congruent, you can overlay one onto another; otherwise compare the area each covers rather than judging by appearance.

A faint on-screen grid that tints pieces green only when every piece covers the same area is one optional way to make the equal-area check concrete; counting whole squares works only where piece edges follow the grid, and cutting and rearranging is needed to prove equality of differently shaped pieces whose edges cross grid squares.
activities.rationale: Equal-partitioning is a documented roadblock; instruction should establish that parts be equal in amount rather than accept any partition. Partitioning shapes into equal parts in different ways is a stated Year 2 expectation. Physically rearranging or tiling equal-area different-shape pieces, and producing several valid partitions, is intended to target the 'must look the same', 'any N pieces', and 'one right way' misconceptions.
sourceClaims: Equal-partitioning is a documented roadblock: children must treat the parts as equal (equal amount), and instruction should establish this rather than accept any partition; the guide addresses accepting approximate drawings only if treated as equal.
Year 2 pupils recognise, find, name and write fractions of shapes and quantities and recognise equivalence, including partitioning shapes into equal parts in different ways.
learnerActions: Partition a square into four parts where the pieces look different — e.g. one long thin strip plus some oddly-shaped bits — but each covers the same amount.
Before checking, predict: is the long thin piece the same amount of the square as a fat corner piece? Say why.

Check equality physically: cut the long strip and lay it over the fat piece to see it rearranges exactly onto it. For pieces whose edges follow a faint underlying grid you can also count the unit squares each covers; for diagonal or irregular pieces use cutting and rearrangement rather than counting, since squares get split.
Decide whether all four pieces are quarters and give the reason (each is the same AMOUNT, one of four equal parts).

Now quarter the SAME shape in a completely different way (e.g. three equally spaced vertical cuts giving four equal strips, then a 2x2 grid, then two diagonals) and argue each piece is still a quarter.

Partition a circle into three equal parts (120-degree slices) and explain how you could check the three parts really are equal (overlay one onto another — they are congruent — or compare the area each covers).
activities.intendedInsight: A quarter means each part is the same amount (area) of the whole, one of four equal parts — the pieces may look different as long as each covers the same amount; and the same shape can be partitioned into the same fraction in many valid ways.

activities.title: Sort the partitions: quarters or not?
feedback: If an equal-area different-shape case is sorted into 'does not': ask how the amounts compare, and suggest rearranging/recomposing the pieces (cut and re-lay), or counting grid-aligned squares, to check before deciding — simply laying differently shaped pieces on top of each other will not make them coincide.
If an unequal four-piece case is sorted into 'shows quarters': point to the four-piece-but-unequal trap — four pieces is not enough, they must each be the same amount.
Praise reasons that mention 'same amount / same area / same number of squares' over reasons that mention how pieces look.
activities.rationale: Categorising partitions as equal vs unequal tests the equal-parts and different-shape criteria cleanly. This is a recognition/classification task: it may check and sharpen the criterion, but it does not by itself let the child construct a partition or physically prove equality, so pair it with hands-on cutting and rearranging rather than using it alone.
sourceClaims: Equal-partitioning is a documented roadblock: children must treat the parts as equal (equal amount), and instruction should establish this rather than accept any partition; the guide addresses accepting approximate drawings only if treated as equal.
learnerActions: Sort a set of partitioned shapes into 'shows quarters' and 'does not show quarters'.
Include cases that are equal-area but different-shape (these ARE quarters) and cases with four pieces of unequal size (these are NOT quarters).
For each 'does not' card, say what is wrong (pieces are not the same amount).
For each tricky 'is' card where pieces look different, say how you could prove they are equal (cut and rearrange/recompose, or count squares where edges follow the grid).
activities.intendedInsight: Whether a partition shows quarters depends on equal amount, not on the number of pieces or on whether the pieces look alike.

activities.title: Which is the bigger share: a third or a quarter?
feedback: If the learner thinks 'four parts means bigger because there are more': have them overlay a third onto a quarter of an identical shape, both cut the same way (e.g. strips in the same direction), to see the third covers the quarter and sticks out, so it is larger.
Tie the result back to the equal-amount idea: thirds are only thirds if all three cover the same amount, and of the same whole each must therefore be larger than one of four equal parts.

Keep the comparison to identical wholes — this is about which portion of the same shape is larger. (As abstract numbers, fractions remain comparable without a shared whole, but that is not this activity's focus.)
activities.rationale: Comparing a third with a quarter of the same whole is intended to address judging share size by appearance or by piece-count, and reinforces that thirds cannot be reached by repeated halving. Partitioning into equal parts and naming thirds/fourths is within the stated age expectations; the size-ordering of unit fractions is a research-informed extension beyond what the cited sources state directly.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils recognise, find, name and write fractions of shapes and quantities and recognise equivalence, including partitioning shapes into equal parts in different ways.
learnerActions: Take two identical shapes; partition one into three equal parts and the other into four equal parts.
Predict which single piece is bigger: one of three equal parts, or one of four equal parts, of the same shape.

Check by overlaying one piece on the other when both wholes are cut the same way (e.g. both into strips the same direction, or both into slices from the centre of a circle) so the larger covers the smaller and sticks out; otherwise compare the area each covers.
State the reasoning: cutting the same whole into more equal parts makes each part smaller.
activities.intendedInsight: For the same whole, one of three equal parts is bigger than one of four equal parts — cutting the same whole into more equal parts makes each part smaller.

constraints: Equal shares must be equal in AMOUNT (area); they need not be congruent or look the same.
Having the right NUMBER of pieces is not sufficient — unequal pieces are not halves/thirds/quarters.
Move beyond halving to thirds so children cannot rely on repeated halving; a circle into three (120-degree shares) is a good non-halving case.

Compare share sizes (e.g. a third vs a quarter) only for identical wholes; this scopes the comparison to represented portions. As numbers, fractions remain comparable without a shared whole, but that is not this activity's focus.

Counting unit squares is a valid equal-area check only where piece edges follow the grid; for diagonal or irregular pieces use cutting and rearrangement, since grid squares get split. Overlay alone proves equality only for congruent pieces; for equal-area pieces of different shape, cut and recompose (or count unit squares if their edges follow the grid).

Sorting/categorisation tasks are recognition: they may check and sharpen the equal-parts criterion but do not let a child physically prove equality by rearranging, so use them alongside hands-on cutting and overlaying, not instead of it.
Physical paper/card cutouts have slight thickness and model the ideal flat figure being partitioned; the lesson is about the 2D area partition they represent, for which thickness is irrelevant.

An on-screen faint unit grid that tints pieces green when areas match is one optional way to make the equal-area check concrete, not a required mechanism — cutting and rearranging pieces works too, and is needed for differently shaped pieces whose edges do not follow the grid.
Static galleries of correct/incorrect partitions can serve as a reference but do not let the child test equality by rearranging pieces; pair them with a hands-on check.
A third spatial dimension is not needed for partitioning 2D shapes; keep the work planar unless there is a specific reason otherwise.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row framed a conversation-only approach as 'poor' and claimed talk 'can't replace' cutting/rearranging, and that a static image or 3D 'cannot' teach the equal-area judgement. These are catalog-fit opinions, not established necessity claims; they are softened here to scoped, observable affordances/limits. Discussion and static references can support this learning, even if hands-on manipulation is particularly well suited to proving equal area.
The 'green only when areas are equal' grid and draggable re-tiling pieces are preserved as an optional illustrative example, not a mandatory mechanism, and whether it was ever tested is unknown.

Geometry self-audit: three equal vertical cuts give four equal strips; a 2x2 grid gives four equal quarters; the two diagonals of a rectangle give four triangles each of area (width x height)/4, i.e. equal-area quarters (congruent only when the shape is a square); three 120-degree slices give equal thirds of a circle. No numerical errors found in the source to correct.

Activity 3's unit-fraction size ordering (a third > a quarter of the same whole) is mathematically correct but not directly stated by either cited source; the attached DfE claim supports only the partitioning-and-naming context in the rationale, so the ordering is flagged as an unvalidated extension.
Terminology note: the base shape is kept as a single 'square/shape' through Activity 1 to avoid the inherited square/rectangle switch; any rectangle works equally for the quartering demonstrations.

assess.poeTask: Show a square quartered into four equal-AREA but different-shaped pieces — one long thin strip, one fat corner piece. Ask the child to predict whether the long thin piece and the fat piece are the SAME amount of the square, and to say why before checking. A child judging by shape predicts 'the long one is more' (or 'less'). Then rearrange — cut the strip and lay it over the fat piece, or count the unit squares under each — to reveal they match. The pre-observation reason (shape-based) is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: Cut this rectangle into four equal parts a completely different way from your first. How do you know the new pieces are still quarters?
Here is a circle. Cut it into three equal parts. How could you check the three parts really are equal?
If one piece is tall-and-thin and another is short-and-wide but they cover the same amount, are they equal shares? Why?
Which is a bigger share: one of three equal parts, or one of four equal parts, of the same shape? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: Amir is wrong — they ARE quarters, because a quarter means each part is the same AMOUNT (area) of the whole, one of four equal parts; the pieces can look different as long as each covers the same amount. For the rectangle, shows two valid quarterings (e.g. three equal vertical cuts, and a 2×2 grid, or two diagonals) and can argue each piece is a quarter.

errorPatterns.pattern: Equal shares must look the same — rejects equal-area but different-shape pieces as not being quarters
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rearrange/overlay the different-shaped pieces so they tile onto one another; count unit squares under each; establish equal AMOUNT as the test
errorPatterns.distractor: They're not quarters — the pieces are different shapes, so they can't be equal.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 'not quarters, the pieces are different shapes', judging by appearance rather than amount

errorPatterns.pattern: Equal-parts ignored — any four pieces are called quarters regardless of their sizes
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast an equal partition with an unequal one that also has four pieces; check by recomposing; only equal amounts count
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes, quarters — there are four pieces.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls an unequally-cut four-piece square 'quarters' because there are four pieces

errorPatterns.pattern: One-right-way — believes a shape can only be partitioned into a fraction a single 'proper' way
errorPatterns.nextMove: Demonstrate several valid quarterings side by side, each grid-checked for equal area; have the child invent a new one
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Produces only one quartering and insists other valid cuts 'aren't real quarters'

responseLevels.gap: Judges equal shares by shape (rejects equal-area different-shape pieces) or calls any four pieces quarters regardless of size.
responseLevels.full: Judges shares by equal AMOUNT not shape, produces two or more different valid partitions (including a circle into thirds), justifies equality by area/recomposition, and rejects an unequal cut with a reason.
responseLevels.partial: Agrees equal parts must be the same size and can quarter a rectangle one standard way, but cannot yet accept different-shaped equal-area pieces as equal, produce a second distinct partition, or reliably make thirds.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a paper square cut into four parts. The parts look different from each other — one is a long strip, the others are smaller shapes — but they all cover the same amount of the square. Amir says these can't be quarters, because the pieces are different shapes. Is Amir right? Say why or why not. Then show me two DIFFERENT ways to cut this rectangle into four equal parts.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who believes equal parts must be congruent judges by shape and says 'not quarters — different shapes'; correct reasoning attends to equal AREA, not look. Producing a SECOND distinct partition further separates 'one right way' thinking from a genuine grasp that many partitions give the same fraction.
