pedagogy.summary: Mentally adding or subtracting hundreds to a three-digit number is the simplest of the three: within 1000 only the hundreds digit changes, and the tens and ones stay fixed. Children reuse a single-digit fact (3+2 hundreds) at the scale of hundreds. It is the cleanest demonstration of place-value invariance — the local part left untouched — and is taught with a place-value chart and hundred-scaled number line. (Bridging a thousand is a later topic, so within-1000 cases do not bridge.)
bestPractices: Anchor the tens and ones; operate only on the hundreds — 345+200 keeps '_45' and works 3+2 hundreds
Reuse the known single-digit fact at the scale of hundreds (3 hundreds + 2 hundreds = 5 hundreds)
Use a place-value chart to show only the hundreds row changing
Contrast with the ones/tens topics so the child generalises 'the added amount changes its own column'
Ask the child to state which digits stay the same and why (DfE evidence)
keyRepresentations: Place-value / Gattegno chart (only the hundreds row moves)
Number line marked in hundreds
Base-ten hundred-flats (add/remove flats)
Partitioning jotting (345 = 300 + 45)
Place-value counters on a H-T-O grid
commonMisconceptions: Changing the wrong digit (adding the hundreds amount to the tens or ones)
Miscounting the hundreds (762 − 400 given as 462 vs correct 362 — a single-digit subtraction slip at the hundreds scale)
Disturbing the tens/ones when they should be untouched
Overreaching to bridge a thousand when the numbers don't require it

learn.summary: Year 3 learners mentally add and subtract hundreds to/from a three-digit number with answers below 1000, where only the hundreds digit changes and the tens and ones stay fixed. The core insight is place-value invariance: a known single-digit fact (3+2 hundreds) is reused at the scale of hundreds while the other columns are left untouched. Work with a place-value chart, a number line marked in hundreds, base-ten hundred-flats, partitioning jottings (345 = 300 + 45), and place-value counters on an H-T-O grid; contrast with +tens/+ones (using examples that need no regrouping) so children generalise that an added amount lands in its own column when that column does not go past 9. With answers below 1000 these cases never bridge a thousand.

activities.title: Freeze the tens and ones: only the hundreds move
feedback: If the learner alters the 45 in 345+200, re-anchor on the chart: 200 is two hundreds, so it joins the hundreds. Cover or grey out the tens and ones to show they cannot change, then re-read 545.
If the learner disturbs the tens/ones in subtraction, physically hold or cover the '62' of 762 and only operate on the hundreds.

If the answer to 762−400 comes out as 462, this is most likely a single-digit fact slip (the learner found 4 hundreds instead of 7−4=3 hundreds): rehearse 7−4 on its own, then reapply at the hundreds scale to get 362. The tens and ones were kept, so place value does not need reteaching.
Prompt: 'Is 762−400 bigger or smaller than 762? Should it be?' to catch direction-of-operation errors.
activities.rationale: The objective is place-value invariance, so the activity makes the stable columns visible and asks the learner to predict and name what stays fixed before checking. A manipulable or clearly staged chart lets the learner act on the hundreds while the tens and ones remain visibly still; a static reveal can show the same contrast but does not let the learner operate the pieces.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils add and subtract mentally a three-digit number and hundreds.
Place-value understanding lets a known single-digit fact be reused at the scale of hundreds, with the other columns left invariant (unitising).
learnerActions: Show 345 on a place-value chart (hundreds, tens, ones). Add 200 and watch only the hundreds change from 3 to 5, giving 545 — say aloud that the '45' tail is unchanged.
Now do 762 − 400 on the same chart: the hundreds drop from 7 to 3 while the '62' stays put, giving 362.
Before revealing each answer, point to the tens and ones and state that they will not change, then check after.
Repeat with 518 + 300, predicting the answer (818) and naming which digits stay the same.
Articulate the rule in your own words: the amount you add or take away is a number of hundreds, so it lands only in the hundreds column.
activities.intendedInsight: When the answer stays below 1000, adding or subtracting hundreds changes only the hundreds digit; the tens and ones are invariant because the added amount belongs to the hundreds column.

activities.title: Same place-value idea, one column along
feedback: If the learner moves the change to the wrong column, restate where each amount belongs (200 = hundreds, 20 = tens) and re-anchor on the chart.

If the learner thinks a different column should change when switching between +hundreds and +tens, clarify that adding tens and adding hundreds are simply different amounts, each landing in its own column — there is no rule reversing, just a different column changing.
activities.rationale: Contrasting +hundreds with +tens/+ones helps the learner generalise beyond a single case and prevents the 'change any digit' error. Juxtaposition makes the invariance principle explicit across columns.
sourceClaims: Place-value understanding lets a known single-digit fact be reused at the scale of hundreds, with the other columns left invariant (unitising).
learnerActions: Place a +hundreds example (345 + 200) beside a +tens example (345 + 20) and work both.
For each, say which single column changes and read off the two different answers (545 vs 365).
State the shared principle: when the column does not go past 9 (no regrouping), the added amount changes only its own column and leaves the others alone.
Try a mixed set, e.g. 345+200, 345+20, 345+2, naming the changing digit each time before answering.
activities.intendedInsight: The place-value rule generalises: whether you add hundreds, tens, or ones, the added amount changes only its own column as long as that column does not go past 9 (no regrouping), as in 345+200, 345+20 and 345+2.

activities.title: Explain what stays the same
feedback: Full understanding: answers quickly in the head, keeps tens and ones untouched, and explains that only the hundreds change because the added amount is a number of hundreds.

Partial: reaches answers with the chart or number line but is unsure which digits stay fixed, or makes single-digit hundreds slips — revisit the invariance naming step and rehearse the hundreds facts.
Gap: changes the tens/ones or lands the hundreds in the wrong column and cannot say what stays the same — return to the chart activity with the tens and ones covered.
activities.rationale: Articulating which digits stay fixed surfaces whether the learner understands invariance or is guessing, and separates a conceptual gap from a mere single-digit fact slip. Reasoning-focused discussion complements, rather than replaces, the hands-on chart work.
learnerActions: Work 345 + 200, 762 − 400, and 518 + 300 mentally, thinking aloud.
After each, answer: which digits changed and which stayed exactly the same, and why?
Answer the probes: How is 762−400 like 7−4, and what is different? If it were 345+20 instead of 345+200, which digit would change?
Explain in a sentence why the tens and ones do not change.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to state that only the hundreds digit changes — and why — demonstrates genuine place-value understanding rather than a memorised procedure.

activities.title: Quick checks for the two common slips
feedback: A 462 answer signals a 7−4 fact slip at the hundreds scale: rehearse the single-digit fact and reapply to reach 362.
An answer where the tens/ones changed signals a wrong-column error: re-anchor on the chart and name the column the added amount belongs to.
activities.rationale: Rapid, mixed items are efficient for rehearsal and for catching the two predicted error patterns, and asking for a brief justification adds a little reasoning; even so, they do not by themselves demand the sustained construction and explanation of the chart activities, so they follow rather than replace them.
learnerActions: Answer rapid items such as 762 − 400, choosing between 362 and a tempting 462, and justify the correct choice.
Work items that mix +hundreds with +tens (e.g. 345+200 next to 345+20) and state which column moved before answering.
For any item where the tens or ones changed, go back and re-anchor on the chart.
activities.intendedInsight: Fast, mixed practice rehearses the skill and exposes wrong-digit and single-digit miscount slips.

constraints: Keep all answers below 1000 so they never bridge a thousand; bridging a thousand is a later topic and should not be introduced here.

Recognition/multiple-choice items check fluency and catch slips but do not by themselves require the learner to construct or sustain the reasoning — use them after, not instead of, the chart and explanation activities.
A static reveal can show which digit changes but does not let the learner operate the pieces; prefer a manipulable chart when the goal is for the learner to act on the hundreds.
Distinguish a single-digit hundreds-fact slip (762−400→462) from a place-value gap: the first is a fact rehearsal, not a reason to reteach place value.
Base-ten hundred-flats and place-value counters are physical approximations of the abstract place-value structure; use them as representations, not as the concept itself.
The 462 answer is an error to be diagnosed (correct is 362); never present it as a valid option.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Checked arithmetic: 345+200=545, 762−400=362, 518+300=818, 345+20=365 — all correct. The 462 answer is explicitly an error pattern (should be 362) and is only used as a labelled distractor/slip to diagnose, never presented as valid.
The '3→5' phrasing for the hundreds in 345+200 corresponds to 3 hundreds + 2 hundreds = 5 hundreds, which is correct.

An irrelevant fraction 'denominator flips' framing that had been inserted into the +hundreds vs +tens activity has been kept out; this topic has no denominators and that framing would confuse learners.

Partitioning jottings (345 = 300 + 45) and place-value counters were restored to the summary so the full set of original representations is represented; they can be used interchangeably with the chart.

Non-preferred alternatives (static reveal, spoken reasoning discussion, rapid recognition items) were retained as distinct activities with their stated pedagogical purposes rather than collapsed into the preferred chart approach.

Activities 3 and 4 have sourceClaims set to [] because no original source claim directly supports their specific pedagogical principles (articulation surfacing understanding; rapid items catching slips) beyond the general topic.

probeDeeper: For 345 + 200, which digits stayed exactly the same? Why don't they change?
How is 762 − 400 like 7 − 4? What's different?
If it were 345 + 20 instead of 345 + 200, which digit would change then?
Is your answer to 762 − 400 bigger or smaller than 762? Should it be?
assess.correctAnswer: 545, 362, 818. In each, only the hundreds digit changes: 3+2=5 hundreds (545); 7−4=3 hundreds (362); 5+3=8 hundreds (818). The tens and ones stay fixed throughout.

errorPatterns.pattern: Changes the wrong digit — adds the hundreds amount to the tens or ones ('345 + 200' altering the 45)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor with the chart: 200 is two hundreds, joining the hundreds; grey out the 45 to show it cannot change.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The tens or ones change; the hundreds addition lands in the wrong column

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscounts the hundreds — '762 − 400 is 462' (a single-digit subtraction slip at the hundreds scale)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach place value: rehearse the single-digit hundreds fact (7−4=3) then reapply. This is a fact slip, not a place-value gap.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The tens and ones are correct but the hundreds digit is off by one; underlying 7−4 done as 7−3 or similar

responseLevels.gap: Changes the tens/ones, or lands the hundreds in the wrong column; cannot say what stays the same.
responseLevels.full: Answers all three instantly in his head, keeps the tens and ones untouched, and explains that only the hundreds digit changes because the added amount is a number of hundreds.
responseLevels.partial: Gets answers with the chart or number line but is unsure which digits stay fixed, or makes single-digit hundreds slips.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to do these mentally, thinking aloud: 345 + 200, then 762 − 400, then 518 + 300. After each, ask which digits changed and which stayed the same.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Because within 1000 these never bridge a thousand, a fluent child answers almost instantly and can state that the tens and ones are untouched. A child without place-value invariance changes the wrong digit or disturbs the tens/ones; a single-digit slip at the hundreds scale (762−400→462) reveals shaky hundreds facts.

sources.claim: Year 3 pupils add and subtract mentally a three-digit number and hundreds.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (Year 3)

sources.claim: Place-value understanding lets a known single-digit fact be reused at the scale of hundreds, with the other columns left invariant (unitising).
sources.source: NRICH place-value articles (unitising, position)

pedagogy.summary: Naming the parts of a circle (radius, diameter, circumference) and knowing the diameter is twice the radius is taught best by grounding each term in its DEFINING PROPERTY — the radius runs from the centre to the edge, the diameter is a line through the centre from edge to edge, the circumference is the distance all the way round — rather than by rote labels. Drawing and measuring many circles of different sizes and tabulating radius against diameter lets pupils discover the invariant d = 2r for themselves, and practising the conversion in BOTH directions guards against the pervasive radius/diameter swap.
bestPractices: Anchor each term in its defining property: a radius touches the centre; a diameter passes through the centre; the circumference is the perimeter (distance around).
Draw and measure several circles of different sizes and tabulate radius vs diameter, so pupils see d = 2r holds at every scale.
Practise conversion in both directions — diameter from radius AND radius from diameter — and monitor for confusion between the two (NCTM).
Label parts on circles in varied positions and surface the longest-chord property (the diameter is the longest line across).
Provide a vocabulary word bank (radius, diameter, circumference) and require pupils to use the terms when they reason.
keyRepresentations: A labelled circle: centre, radius, diameter, circumference
Radius vs diameter vs an off-centre chord, contrasted
A radius/diameter table across several circle sizes
String wrapped round a circle to show the circumference as a length
commonMisconceptions: Swaps radius and diameter, or substitutes a diameter where a radius is needed — the 'half/twice' error (NCTM).
Treats any line across the circle as a diameter, or draws a radius/diameter that does not reach or pass through the centre.
Applies the conversion in the wrong direction (doubles when it should halve), or thinks the radius equals the diameter.

learn.summary: Pupils (age 10–11) learn to name and identify the radius, diameter and circumference of a circle by their DEFINING PROPERTIES — the radius runs from the centre to the edge, the diameter is a straight line from edge to edge through the centre (the longest line across), and the circumference is the distance all the way around — and to apply d = 2r in both directions. The core work is drawing and measuring many circles, tabulating radius against diameter so the invariant d = 2r is discovered rather than told, and practising conversion both ways to guard against the pervasive radius/diameter swap. Several complementary media (dynamic manipulation, paper-and-string measurement, a labelled reference, and a short conversion check) each support a different part of this objective.

activities.title: Measure many circles and discover d = 2r
feedback: If a pupil's pairs don't come out close to double, check that the diameter was drawn through the centre and that both were measured along a straight line — an off-centre line is shorter and will break the pattern.
Prompt: 'Does your doubling pattern still hold for your biggest circle and your smallest circle?' to surface that the relationship is scale-independent.
If a pupil writes the names interchangeably, ask them to point to where each line starts and ends relative to the centre.
activities.rationale: Grounding each term in its defining property and tabulating radius against diameter across sizes lets pupils see d = 2r hold at every scale, which the curriculum expects pupils to know and the geometry research links to moving beyond naming toward defining properties.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils should be taught to illustrate and name parts of circles, including radius, diameter and circumference, and know that the diameter is twice the radius; the non-statutory guidance expresses this as d = 2 × r.

Pupils often reason about shapes at the van Hiele visual level — by overall appearance and prototype rather than defining properties — and misconceptions are strikingly stable across ages; teaching should present shapes in varied positions with counterexamples and insist that knowing a shape's name is not enough without knowing and naming its defining properties.
learnerActions: Draw several circles of clearly different sizes (small, medium, large).
For each circle, mark the centre, draw a radius from the centre to the edge and a diameter from edge to edge through the centre.
Measure the radius and the diameter of each circle and record them in a two-column table (radius | diameter).
Look across the table and describe the pattern you notice between the radius and the diameter.
State the relationship in your own words and as d = 2 × r.
activities.intendedInsight: Across every size of circle, the diameter is exactly twice the radius. Pupils' own measurements will come out close to double, allowing for small measuring errors, so they can see the pattern holding for themselves rather than memorising a rule.

activities.title: Which line is longest? Predict then measure
feedback: Many pupils pick a long-looking slanted line; after measuring, point out that the through-centre line always wins, which is why the diameter is defined by the centre, not by looking long.
If a pupil labels an off-centre chord a diameter, have them check whether it passes through the marked centre.
Fold a paper circle in half (and again) to locate the centre, then confirm which drawn lines actually pass through it.
activities.rationale: Predicting before measuring makes the reasoning visible and the counterexample (an off-centre chord) directly tests the through-centre defining property rather than surface appearance, countering prototype-based reasoning.
sourceClaims: Pupils often reason about shapes at the van Hiele visual level — by overall appearance and prototype rather than defining properties — and misconceptions are strikingly stable across ages; teaching should present shapes in varied positions with counterexamples and insist that knowing a shape's name is not enough without knowing and naming its defining properties.
learnerActions: On a circle with the centre marked, draw several straight lines from edge to edge — some passing through the centre and some not.
Before measuring, PREDICT which line is the longest and write down why you think so.
Measure each line and compare with your prediction.
Decide which lines pass through the centre (diameters) and which do not (other chords), and explain the difference using the word 'centre'.
activities.intendedInsight: The longest straight line across a circle is always the one through the centre — the diameter — so a line that misses the centre is a shorter chord, not a diameter. The pre-stated reason is what reveals a pupil's thinking.

activities.title: Convert both ways and reason aloud
feedback: Worked check: a radius of 4.5 cm gives a diameter of 9 cm because the diameter is twice the radius (2 × 4.5). A diameter of 10 cm gives a radius of 5 cm because the radius is half the diameter.
If a pupil gives 2.25 cm as the diameter of a 4.5 cm radius, they halved instead of doubling — return to the measured table showing the diameter is always the larger, doubled value.
Require the pupil to name which quantity is which before computing, so a radius isn't treated as a diameter.
activities.rationale: Practising conversion in both directions and requiring reasoning with correct vocabulary targets the flagged radius/diameter confusion and supports fluent, justified use of the terms.
sourceClaims: Teachers should make sure pupils identify the radius and the diameter, realise that d = 2r, be able to calculate radius from diameter and diameter from radius, and should monitor for misconceptions; difficulty using the variables C, d and r is a flagged misconception, and a word bank of circumference/diameter/radius supports the vocabulary.
learnerActions: Given a radius (e.g. 4.5 cm), work out the diameter and state how you did it.
Given a diameter (e.g. 10 cm), work out the radius and state how you did it.
For each, say in words whether you doubled or halved and why.
Use a vocabulary word bank (radius, diameter, circumference) and use the correct term in each explanation.
activities.intendedInsight: Converting diameter-from-radius and radius-from-diameter are different directions of the same relationship; knowing which to double and which to halve, with a reason, prevents the half/twice swap.

activities.title: Feel the circumference as a length
feedback: If a pupil calls a straight line across the circle 'the circumference', have them trace the edge with a finger: the circumference is the whole way round.
Compare the straightened string length with the diameter drawn straight across to reinforce that they measure different things.
activities.rationale: A tactile wrap-and-straighten activity is intended to make the circumference concrete as a go-around length, addressing the confusion between circumference and a straight measurement across. Proposed as a hands-on scaffold; its effectiveness is not established by the cited sources.
learnerActions: Wrap a length of string once around the edge of a circle, mark where it meets, then straighten it against a ruler to measure the distance around.
Run a finger all the way around the edge and say in your own words what the circumference is.
Contrast this with a straight line drawn across the circle and explain why the circumference is not a straight line.
activities.intendedInsight: The circumference is the distance all the way around the edge — a curved length — not a straight line across the circle.

activities.title: Dynamic circle: watch d = 2r hold as the circle resizes (optional screen scaffold)
feedback: Live readout feedback: as the pupil stretches the circle, the diameter reading stays at twice the radius (the last digit may differ slightly if the display rounds), so the relationship can be observed across scales.
When a dragged line misses the centre and is refused the 'diameter' label, prompt: 'What do you need to change so it becomes a diameter?'
Pair this with the paper-and-ruler measuring so the relationship is grounded in real measurement, not only an on-screen readout.
activities.rationale: A dynamic, draggable model lets the invariant be experienced across many sizes in quick succession and can enforce the through-centre property via snapping/labelling; a static labelled reference states d = 2r but cannot show it varying. Offered as a complement to, not a replacement for, hands-on measuring; its efficacy relative to other media is not established here.
sourceClaims: Pupils often reason about shapes at the van Hiele visual level — by overall appearance and prototype rather than defining properties — and misconceptions are strikingly stable across ages; teaching should present shapes in varied positions with counterexamples and insist that knowing a shape's name is not enough without knowing and naming its defining properties.
learnerActions: Drag a point to make the circle bigger and smaller and watch a live readout of the radius and the diameter.
Notice whether the diameter readout always shows twice the radius as the size changes.

Drag the endpoint of a line inside the circle; observe that it is labelled 'diameter — the longest line across' only when it passes through the centre, and is refused the label when it misses the centre.
Say what stays the same (d = 2r) and what must be true for a line to be a diameter (it passes through the centre).
activities.intendedInsight: The 2× relationship is invariant across every size, and only a through-centre line earns the name 'diameter' — both the invariant and the defining property made visible together.

activities.title: Labelled circle reference (supporting scaffold)
feedback: Reveal-on-tap can confirm each term's defining property as a reference, but d = 2r is stated here, not discovered — use it alongside the measuring activity.
Varying the position of the labelled parts guards against pupils only recognising a standard horizontal diameter.
If a pupil can label a standard diagram but slips on a slanted or off-centre line, return to the defining-property test (does it pass through the centre?).
activities.rationale: A clear labelled reference with varied positions supports the vocabulary and surfaces the longest-chord property; presenting shapes in varied positions counters prototype-based recognition. This is a reference scaffold and cannot by itself build the measured discovery of the invariant.
sourceClaims: Teachers should make sure pupils identify the radius and the diameter, realise that d = 2r, be able to calculate radius from diameter and diameter from radius, and should monitor for misconceptions; difficulty using the variables C, d and r is a flagged misconception, and a word bank of circumference/diameter/radius supports the vocabulary.

Pupils often reason about shapes at the van Hiele visual level — by overall appearance and prototype rather than defining properties — and misconceptions are strikingly stable across ages; teaching should present shapes in varied positions with counterexamples and insist that knowing a shape's name is not enough without knowing and naming its defining properties.
learnerActions: Study a labelled circle showing centre, radius, diameter and circumference.
Reveal or read each term's defining property: radius = centre to edge; diameter = edge to edge through the centre (the longest line across); circumference = the distance all the way round.
Label parts yourself on circles drawn in varied positions and orientations, including ones where the diameter is slanted.
Match each term to its definition.
activities.intendedInsight: Each circle part is identified by its defining property and position relative to the centre, not by a fixed picture orientation.

constraints: A static labelled diagram or reveal-on-tap reference states d = 2r but does not let pupils see it vary across sizes; pair it with hands-on drawing and measuring so the invariant is genuinely discovered.

A label/match/slider conversion check can verify vocabulary and the d = 2r computation but does not by itself build the defining-property understanding; use it as a check after the measuring and reasoning activities.
Recognition-only responses (matching terms to a standard diagram) do not elicit independent construction; require pupils to draw, measure, convert both ways, and justify.
Present diameters and radii in varied positions (including slanted and non-standard) so pupils do not over-rely on a horizontal prototype.
Always insist pupils state WHY (which line passes through the centre, whether they doubled or halved); the reason is what distinguishes understanding from a lucky guess.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labelled a 3-D environment as 'adding nothing' for a planar concept. This comparative/necessity claim is not established by the cited sources; it has been dropped rather than asserted. A planar concept is naturally well-served by 2-D media, but no universal 'adds nothing' claim is made here.

The source stated conversation is 'poor' for this concept. This is not a general pedagogical law; spoken justification is used throughout (predict-and-explain, reason-aloud conversion) as part of teaching, not only assessment. The medium-ranking boilerplate was removed.
The 'diameter is the longest line across (longest chord)' property is stated correctly for a circle and is used as a measurable, verifiable prediction task.

Self-audit of the worked conversions: radius 4.5 cm → diameter 9 cm (2 × 4.5) is correct; the distractor 2.25 cm correctly models halving instead of doubling; diameter 10 cm → radius 5 cm is correct. No arithmetic errors found.

The circumference string activity and the circumference-vs-straight-line confusion it targets come from the pedagogy/assessment material, not from the cited sources; its sourceClaims were set to [] and the rationale hedged accordingly, as no source establishes the method's effectiveness.
All sourceClaims were re-checked to be verbatim copies of the three original sources[].claim strings; this addresses the prior validation failure caused by a non-matching claim string.

assess.poeTask: Draw several straight lines from edge to edge across a circle, some through the marked centre and some not, and ask the pupil to PREDICT which line is longest before measuring — and to say why. Many pick a long-looking slanted chord. Then measure: the longest is always the line through the centre — the diameter. The pre-stated reason is the diagnostic part; the result forces the defining property that a diameter must pass through the centre and is the longest chord.
probeDeeper: If I make the circle twice as big, is the diameter still twice the radius? Why?
This line goes across the circle but not through the centre — is it a diameter? Why not?
A circle's diameter is 10 cm — what is its radius, and how did you work it out?
Which straight line across a circle is the longest, and where must it pass?
assess.correctAnswer: The diameter is 9 cm, because the diameter is twice the radius (2 × 4.5). The centre-to-edge line is the radius and the edge-to-edge line through the centre is the diameter; a radius goes from the centre to the edge and a diameter passes through the centre, so the third line is neither (it is a chord) because it does not pass through the centre.

errorPatterns.pattern: Swaps radius and diameter or applies the relationship the wrong way — the 'half/twice' error (halves when it should double)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw and measure circles and tabulate radius against diameter to see the diameter is always double the radius; practise both conversion directions
errorPatterns.distractor: 2.25 cm (halved the radius instead of doubling it)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives the diameter as 2.25 cm, or labels the centre-to-edge line as the diameter

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats any line across the circle as a diameter, or a line to the edge as a radius, ignoring the centre — the defining property
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fold a paper circle to find the centre; only a line through the centre is a diameter (and it is the longest line across), and a radius must start at the centre
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks the off-centre chord as the diameter, or draws a 'radius' that does not reach the centre

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses the circumference with a straight measurement — calls a diameter or a line across 'the circumference'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Run a finger all the way round the edge — the circumference is the distance around, not a straight line across
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels a straight line as the circumference

responseLevels.gap: Uses the terms interchangeably or halves/doubles in the wrong direction; treats any line across the circle as a diameter.
responseLevels.full: States and applies d = 2r in both directions with a reason, identifies parts by their defining properties (radius from the centre, diameter through the centre, circumference around), rejects an off-centre chord as a diameter, and knows the relationship holds at any size.
responseLevels.partial: Converts one way (e.g. radius to diameter) and labels a standard diagram, but slips on the reverse conversion or on a non-standard/off-centre line — knows the names without the defining property.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A circle has a radius of 4.5 cm. What is its diameter, and how do you know? Then look at this diagram of a circle with its centre marked and three straight lines drawn on it: one from the centre to the edge, one from edge to edge passing through the centre, and one from edge to edge that does NOT pass through the centre. Which line is the radius, which is the diameter, and how can you tell?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The reason tier separates a pupil who applies d = 2r with understanding from one who guesses or halves. The diagram forces the defining-property test: a pupil who thinks any line across the circle is a diameter picks the off-centre chord, whereas a pupil who knows the property rejects it because it misses the centre. Together the tiers catch both the half/twice swap and the through-centre confusion.

pedagogy.summary: 'Equally likely' means every outcome has exactly the same chance. The concept underpins the whole equally-likely model of probability (and the favourable-over-total formula that follows), so children must be able to decide whether a situation is fair — a coin, a balanced die, a spinner with equal sections — or not — a bag with more of one colour, a spinner with uneven sections. The crux is attending to the SIZE/number of each outcome region, not the number of different outcomes, and separating 'equally likely' from 'random'.
bestPractices: Contrast a spinner with equal sections against one with the same colours but unequal sections, so children see that equal chance depends on section size, not on how many colours there are
Use identical-face devices (coin, balanced die) to define equal likelihood by symmetry — the faces are interchangeable
Directly challenge 'two outcomes means 50-50' with a 1-red / 5-blue cube: two outcomes, but chances of 1/6 and 5/6
Distinguish 'equally likely' from 'random': an uneven spinner is still random, but its outcomes are not equally likely — sample repeatedly to show the unequal long-run pattern
Have children both identify and CREATE fair and unfair devices, explaining what makes each fair or not
keyRepresentations: Spinners: equal sections vs unequal sections (area = chance)
Fair coin and balanced die (identical, interchangeable faces)
Bags with equal vs unequal numbers of each colour
Area/region model in which equal chance corresponds to equal area
commonMisconceptions: Assuming that because there are two (or three) possible outcomes, they must be equally likely — counting the number of outcome types rather than their sizes
Equiprobability bias — believing any chance situation gives all outcomes an equal chance because the result is 'random/luck'
Judging a die or coin's fairness by how it is thrown or how well it is made, rather than by its identical faces (Watson & Moritz)
Confusing 'fair' as equal-chance with 'fair' as 'I have a good chance of winning'

learn.summary: Children learn that 'equally likely' means every outcome has exactly the same chance, decided by the SIZE/number of each outcome region rather than by how many different outcomes there are. They distinguish fair devices (balanced coin, balanced die, equal-section spinner) from unfair ones (bags with more of one colour, uneven spinners), confront the 'two outcomes means 50-50' trap, and separate 'equally likely' from 'random'.

activities.title: Build a fair three-colour spinner and test it by sampling
feedback: If a child eyeballs the wedges and one ends up bigger, point to the uneven tally: over many spins the biggest wedge tends to win most (though a small sample may not show this) — ask which section is larger and what that does to its chance.
When the three wedges are matched in size, highlight that the tally now evens out to roughly a third each (over many spins; small samples will vary).

For the 1-red / 5-blue case with six equal parts, if a child expected 50-50 'because there are two colours', show the tally landing near 1-in-6 for red: two outcomes, but very unequal chances (1/6 and 5/6).
Reinforce: equal chance is about equal size / number of equal ways, not the count of different colours.
activities.rationale: Because fairness is decided by region size, letting a child manipulate section size and then observe the long-run tally makes the deciding feature explicit and lets them test a wrong judgement empirically, which a fixed picture cannot support. The 1-red/5-blue case (six equal parts) directly challenges the 'two outcomes means 50-50' misconception.
sourceClaims: Having two outcomes does not make them equally likely: a cube with one red and five blue faces has two outcomes but probabilities 1/6 and 5/6 — equal chance requires the outcomes to be genuinely equal in number/size.
learnerActions: Try to divide a spinner into three colours (red, blue, green) so that each colour is equally likely to be landed on.
Spin the spinner many times (e.g. 100 times) and keep a tally of how often each colour comes up.

If one colour comes up clearly more often over many spins, examine the spinner: is one wedge bigger than the others? (Small differences in the tally can happen by chance even on a fair spinner.) Adjust the boundaries until the three wedges are the same size, checking the sizes directly, then spin and tally again.
State in your own words what makes the three colours equally likely — the equal AREA of each section, not the fact that there are three colours.
Then build the opposite: a cube with 1 red face and 5 blue faces (six equal faces), or a spinner split into six equal sections with 1 red and 5 blue; predict and then tally the long-run result.
Compare your prediction with the tally and explain why two colours did NOT give a 50-50 result.
activities.intendedInsight: Equal chance depends on each outcome region being the same size (or the same number of equal ways), not on how many different outcomes there are; sampling many times reveals equal-area regions producing roughly equal frequencies and unequal regions producing a lopsided tally.

activities.title: Sort and decide: fair or not fair?
feedback: If a child says the uneven three-colour spinner is fair 'because it has three colours', have them compare red against blue and green together: red covers as much as the other two combined, so it cannot have the same chance.
If a child says 'it's random, so every colour has an equal chance', note that an uneven spinner is still random yet lands on red far more often — random does not mean equally likely.
Praise reasoning that explicitly refers to equal size or equal counts rather than the number of colours.
activities.rationale: A categorisation task with carefully chosen contrasting cases surfaces whether the child reasons from region size/count or from the number of outcome types. This is a recognition task: a sort may check classification but does not itself elicit the child building a device or explaining it unprompted, so pair it with the construction activity.
sourceClaims: Having two outcomes does not make them equally likely: a cube with one red and five blue faces has two outcomes but probabilities 1/6 and 5/6 — equal chance requires the outcomes to be genuinely equal in number/size.
learnerActions: Look at a set of chance devices — spinners with equal and unequal sections, a balanced coin, a balanced die, bags with equal and unequal numbers of each colour.
Sort each device into 'equally likely outcomes' or 'not equally likely'.
For a spinner that has three colours but with red filling half and blue and green each a quarter, decide whether the three colours are equally likely and explain why or why not.
For each device, give the reason that decided your answer — equal section size or equal counts, not the number of different colours.
Answer the trap question: 'A cube has one red face and five blue faces — there are two colours, so does that make red and blue equally likely?' Explain why not.
activities.intendedInsight: Deciding fair vs not-fair is a categorisation grounded in comparing the size or number of each outcome; the sharpest traps are the three-colour uneven spinner ('three colours so equal') and the two-outcome cube ('two outcomes so 50-50').

activities.title: Argue down the carnival host (equally likely vs random)
feedback: If the child accepts 'three colours so fair', prompt them to compare the sizes of the sections.
If the child conflates random with equally likely, ask: 'If we spun it 100 times, would the colours come up about the same? Why not?'
Confirm when the child names 'make the three sections the same size' as the fix.
activities.rationale: Arguing against an asserted-but-false claim can make the size-vs-count and random-vs-equal distinctions explicit through the child's own reasoning. A sampling demonstration can make the equal-area insight even more convincing, so combine with tallying where possible.
sourceClaims: The equiprobability bias — assuming all outcomes of a random situation are equally likely — is a documented misconception; and Watson & Moritz found the large majority of children judged a die's equiprobability arbitrarily or attributed it to how well the die is made or how it is thrown rather than to its identical faces.
learnerActions: Listen to a carnival host who insists a spinner with a big red section is 'totally fair — three colours, three chances'.
Explain to the host why having three colours does not make the colours equally likely.
Point out that red's section is bigger than the others, so red is more likely.

Address the host's fallback claim that 'it's random, so you can't say one colour is more likely' — explain that the spin is random but the colours are still NOT equally likely because the sections differ in size.
Say what the host would have to change to make the spinner genuinely fair (three equal-sized sections).
activities.intendedInsight: Children can separate two ideas: an outcome being random (unpredictable on a single spin) versus outcomes being equally likely (same chance each). An uneven spinner is random but not equally likely.

activities.title: Why is a balanced die fair? (structure vs execution)
feedback: If a child attributes fairness to how hard the die is thrown, separate structure from execution: a balanced die has six identical faces and even weight, so no face is favoured; how hard you throw does not change which faces exist. If a child mentions how the die is made, agree that this matters: a die must be evenly made (not weighted) for its identical faces to give equal chances.
Reinforce that identical/interchangeable faces on an evenly weighted (balanced) die are what make the outcomes equally likely by symmetry.
activities.rationale: Watson & Moritz found many children judge a die's equiprobability by how it is thrown or made rather than by its identical faces; directly contrasting structure with execution targets this documented error. The tap-to-reveal comparison can present the definition but cannot let the child test a wrong judgement by sampling, so it works as a scaffold alongside the construction activity. A physical die, if used, can support the identical-faces insight without implying any medium is required.
sourceClaims: The equiprobability bias — assuming all outcomes of a random situation are equally likely — is a documented misconception; and Watson & Moritz found the large majority of children judged a die's equiprobability arbitrarily or attributed it to how well the die is made or how it is thrown rather than to its identical faces.
learnerActions: Examine a balanced die and a fair coin: count the faces and check that the faces are identical/interchangeable.
Explain why each face of a balanced die is equally likely — because the six faces are identical in shape and size and the die is evenly weighted, so no face is favoured.
Answer the question: 'Is a die fair because of how hard you throw it, or because of something about the die itself?' Explain your reasoning.
Reveal and compare each section of a fair and an unfair spinner (its size and its chance), noting 'equal sections → equal chance'.
activities.intendedInsight: Fairness comes from the structure of the device (identical faces, equal-sized sections, and even weighting so that no face or section is favoured), not from how hard it is thrown.

constraints: Target the crux: equal chance is decided by the SIZE/number of each outcome region, not by how many different outcomes there are.
Explicitly separate 'equally likely' from 'random': an uneven spinner is still random but its outcomes are not equally likely.
Also distinguish the two senses of 'fair': equal-chance versus 'I have a good chance of winning'.

Sorting/categorisation is a recognition task: it may check classification but does not itself elicit the child independently building a fair device and explaining it; pair it with a construction task.
A static tap-to-reveal comparison can present the definition but cannot let the child test a wrong judgement by sampling; treat it as a scaffold, not the main mechanism.

Sampling (spinning many times and tallying) is what reveals that equal-area regions give roughly equal frequencies and imbalance gives a lopsided tally; keep this as the empirical check, noting small samples vary.

Optional interaction examples (dragging spinner-section boundaries, adding/removing counters in a bag, a 'spin many times' tally, highlighting equal vs unequal area) make the mechanism concrete but are not mandatory.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources have not been re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated a real 3D die as adding 'no conceptual leverage a 2D model lacks'. This comparative-efficacy claim is not established by the cited sources; a physical die can still support the structure-vs-execution insight (identical faces). Retained here as the structure-vs-execution activity without asserting any medium is unnecessary or superior.

The source assessment uses roughly 20 spins for Spinner Y (red half, blue/green quarters) and expects red near 10, blue and green near 5 each. These are expected-value approximations; small samples vary, so a single run may not match — frame tallies as 'about' these values and, where possible, use larger samples to make the long-run pattern reliable.
The 1-red/5-blue trap relies on six EQUAL parts/faces to give probabilities 1/6 and 5/6; a cube supplies this naturally, and any spinner version must use six equal sections.
Legacy confidence was 'high'; this rewrite does not independently upgrade or verify that rating.

assess.poeTask: Show Spinner Y (red half, blue quarter, green quarter). Ask: 'If I spin this 20 times, will the three colours come up about the same number of times, or not — and why?' Have the child predict AND give a reason before spinning. A child holding 'three colours, so about equal' predicts roughly equal thirds; spinning 20 times and tallying (red near 10, blue and green near 5 each) confronts the prediction and forces attention onto the differing section sizes.
probeDeeper: What would you have to change about Spinner Y to make its colours equally likely?
A cube has one red face and five blue faces. There are two colours — does that make red and blue equally likely? Why not?
If I spin the uneven spinner is the result still random? Is 'random' the same as 'equally likely'?
Is a balanced die equally likely because of how you throw it, or because of something about the die itself?
assess.correctAnswer: Spinner X. Its three sections are the same size, so red, blue and green each have an equal chance. On Spinner Y the red section is bigger — half the spinner — so red is more likely than blue or green. Both spinners have three colours, but equal chance depends on the sections being the same SIZE, which only X has.

errorPatterns.pattern: Number of outcome types implies equal likelihood — 'both spinners are fair because each has three colours'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay the sections: red on Y covers as much as blue and green together, so it cannot have the same chance; ask what would make Y fair (three equal sections)
errorPatterns.distractor: Both spinners — each one has three colours, so each colour has an equal chance.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks 'both' and reasons from the count of colours, ignoring that Y's red section is larger

errorPatterns.pattern: Equiprobability bias — 'both, it's random so every colour has an equal chance'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Spin Y many times and tally; red lands far more often even though each spin is random — separating 'random' from 'equally likely'
errorPatterns.distractor: Both — spinning is random, so you can't say one colour is more likely than another.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says both spinners give equal chances and appeals to randomness/luck rather than section size

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges fairness by the physical act or the make of the device rather than its structure (Watson & Moritz)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate structure from execution: a balanced die has six identical faces, so no face is favoured; how hard you throw does not change which faces exist
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked why a fair die's faces are equally likely, cites how it is thrown or how well it is made rather than the six identical faces

responseLevels.gap: Decides fairness by the number of colours or by 'it's random', with no reference to section size or equal counts; calls the uneven spinner fair
responseLevels.full: Correctly identifies fair vs unfair by equal SIZE (or equal counts) of outcomes, picks Spinner X and justifies by equal area, dismisses the 'three colours so equal' and 'it's random so equal' claims, and can construct a fair device and say why it is fair
responseLevels.partial: Recognises equal-section spinners and balanced coins/dice as fair, but slips on the two/three-outcome trap or attributes fairness to throwing/making the device; can identify clear cases but not justify by equal size across all cases

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show two spinners. Spinner X has three equal sections — red, blue, green. Spinner Y has the same three colours but red fills half the spinner and blue and green each fill a quarter. Ask: 'On which spinner are the three colours equally likely — and why?' Take the answer, then ask them to explain the reason fully (Tier 2).
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands equal likelihood attends to section size and picks X, justifying by equal area; a child counting outcome types says 'both, each has 3 colours'; an equiprobability-biased child says 'both, it's random'. The Tier-2 reason — size versus number-of-colours versus luck — is the separator.

sources.claim: Having two outcomes does not make them equally likely: a cube with one red and five blue faces has two outcomes but probabilities 1/6 and 5/6 — equal chance requires the outcomes to be genuinely equal in number/size.
sources.source: Third Space Learning — Describing Probability

sources.claim: The equiprobability bias — assuming all outcomes of a random situation are equally likely — is a documented misconception; and Watson & Moritz found the large majority of children judged a die's equiprobability arbitrarily or attributed it to how well the die is made or how it is thrown rather than to its identical faces.
sources.source: Bryant & Nunes, Children's Understanding of Probability: A Literature Review (Nuffield Foundation, 2012)

pedagogy.summary: At KS3 (ages 11-13) children move from calculating a single mean to DESCRIBING and COMPARING whole distributions: computing mean, median, mode and range, choosing which average best represents a data set, and reasoning about how an outlier affects each measure. Two ideas carry the teaching, and both are about judgement rather than calculation. First, the three averages are not interchangeable: the mean is influenced by every value (so a single outlier drags it), while the median is robust and stays representative when the data is skewed — so the CHOICE of average must fit the shape of the data. Second, an average alone does not describe a distribution: comparing two data sets requires a measure of CENTRE and a measure of SPREAD (range) together, because two sets with the same mean can differ wildly in variability. The characteristic errors are reporting the mean regardless of skew, treating the outlier as affecting all averages equally (or deleting it unthinkingly), and comparing sets on the mean alone while ignoring spread.
bestPractices: Compute all three averages on the SAME data set (especially a skewed one or one with an outlier) so children see them diverge and can discuss which best represents a typical value
Make the outlier's differential effect explicit: recompute mean and median with and without the outlier — the mean chases it, the median barely moves — so 'robust' has a concrete meaning
Teach that describing a distribution needs CENTRE and SPREAD together; compare two data sets on an average AND the range, and show two sets with equal means but different spreads
Tie the choice of average to the data's shape: median for skewed data or data with an outlier, mode for categorical / most-common questions, mean for roughly symmetric numerical data
Insist the range is a single number (highest minus lowest), a measure of spread — not the two extreme values
Draw conclusions in context ('Class A did better on average but was less consistent') so measures are used to argue, not just calculated
keyRepresentations: A data set shown on a number line with mean and median both marked, and an outlier that can be added/removed to see each measure respond
Side-by-side dot plots of two data sets with the same mean but different spreads (centre vs spread made visible)
A skewed distribution where mean, median and mode fall in visibly different places
The range shown as a labelled distance from lowest to highest value
commonMisconceptions: Reporting the mean as 'the average' regardless of skew or outliers, when the median would better represent a typical value
Thinking an outlier affects the mean and median equally, or deleting an outlier without justification, rather than seeing the mean is dragged while the median is robust
Comparing two data sets on their averages alone and ignoring the spread (a frequent error is to ignore variability entirely)
Giving the range as the two extreme values rather than their difference; or situating the mean at the centre of the range even when the data is skewed

learn.summary: KS3 learners (ages 11-13) move from calculating a single mean to describing and comparing whole distributions of one variable: computing mean, median, mode and range, judging which average best represents a data set given its shape, and reasoning about how an outlier affects each measure differently. Two judgements carry the topic: (1) the three averages are not interchangeable — the mean is pulled by every value (so an outlier drags it) while the median is robust, so the choice of average must fit the data's shape; and (2) an average alone does not describe a distribution — comparing two sets needs a measure of centre AND a measure of spread (range) together, because two sets with the same mean can differ widely in variability.

activities.title: Watch the averages diverge: move a value far out
feedback: If the learner says the median moved as much as the mean, have them recount the ordered values: the middle position stays near the cluster, whereas the sum rises by how far the value was moved, so the mean shifts by that amount divided by the number of values — a change the median does not share.

If the learner deletes the far-out value without justification, ask what real reason (e.g. a recording error versus a genuine value) would justify removing it, and show what each average does when it is kept.
If the learner reports the pulled-up mean as 'the typical score', point to the cluster and ask whether that mean sits among most of the data.
activities.rationale: Computing all three averages on a clustered set and recomputing them after one value is moved far out lets learners see the measures diverge, giving 'the mean is pulled by outliers, the median is robust' a concrete meaning rather than being a slogan. Moving an existing point (rather than adding one) keeps the count fixed so the median's stability is clearly attributable to order statistics.
sourceClaims: The mean is influenced by every value, so a single extreme value shifts it, whereas exploratory methods based on order statistics (such as the median) are robust and not very sensitive to outliers; a frequent error is to situate the mean at the centre of the range even when the distribution is skewed, where the median or mode would be a better representative
learnerActions: Start with a small set of values on a stated scale (for example reaction times in whole seconds, or scores out of 40) clustered around 4-5, and compute the mean, median, mode and range by hand.
Record all four measures, then take ONE of those values and move it far out to a value the scale allows (for example 30), keeping the number of data points the same.
Recompute the mean and median with the far-out value, and compare each to its value before.
State in words which measure moved a lot and which barely moved, and explain why the mean was dragged while the median held.

If a draggable dot plot with mean, median, mode and range read out live is available, drag one point far from the cluster and watch the mean line chase it while the median stays put or moves at most to a neighbouring value in the cluster (for example, if the dragged point crosses from below the middle to above it) — this makes the differential effect visible in real time.
activities.intendedInsight: The mean is influenced by every value, so a single extreme value shifts it a lot; the median, based on order/position, is robust and barely moves. 'Robust' becomes concrete when you see the two measures respond differently to the same far-out value.

activities.title: Same mean, different spread: why centre is not enough
feedback: If the learner concludes the sets are 'the same' from equal means, show the two ranges side by side and ask which class has students scoring far from the average.
If the learner lists the two extreme values instead of the range, ask for the single distance between them (highest − lowest).
If the learner reports only the range and forgets the centre, point out that spread without a centre also fails to describe the data.
activities.rationale: Describing and comparing distributions needs centre and spread together; comparing on an average alone is a frequent error, so building the comparison from both measures targets that gap directly.
sourceClaims: A frequent error is to ignore the spread of data; the intuitive notion of variability concerns how much values differ from each other, and different words (variation, dispersion, spread) are open to different interpretations — so describing data needs an explicit measure of spread

KS3 pupils describe, interpret and compare observed distributions of a single variable through appropriate measures of central tendency (mean, mode, median) and spread (range), including consideration of outliers
learnerActions: Take two data sets (for example two classes' test scores) that have the same mean but clearly different spreads.
Compute the mean and the range (highest minus lowest, a single number) for each set.
Decide whether 'same mean' means the classes performed identically, and justify the answer using the ranges.
Write a conclusion in context that mentions BOTH centre and spread, e.g. 'Both classes scored about the same on average, but Class A was far more consistent.'
If side-by-side dot plots with adjustable spreads at a fixed mean are available, line the two plots up and compare how wide each is while the mean stays equal.
activities.intendedInsight: An average alone does not describe a distribution. Two sets with equal means can differ widely in variability, so a fair comparison reports a measure of centre AND a measure of spread.

activities.title: Which average would you report, and why?
feedback: If the learner defaults to the mean on a skewed set, ask whether that mean sits among most of the values or is pulled toward the tail.
If the learner assumes the mean is always central, have them locate the mean and the bulk of the data on the skewed set and compare.
If the learner picks the mode where values are all distinct numerical measurements, ask whether 'most common' is meaningful here.
activities.rationale: Tying the choice of average to the data's shape confronts the fragmented notions of 'average' and the characteristic error of reporting the mean regardless of skew.
sourceClaims: Students' notions of 'average' fragment into most-frequent-value/mode, reasonable value, midpoint and algorithmic relationship — each true in some circumstances but not others — so which average is appropriate depends on the data

The mean is influenced by every value, so a single extreme value shifts it, whereas exploratory methods based on order statistics (such as the median) are robust and not very sensitive to outliers; a frequent error is to situate the mean at the centre of the range even when the distribution is skewed, where the median or mode would be a better representative
learnerActions: Given a skewed data set (or one with an outlier), compute mean, median and mode and note where each falls.
Choose which average best represents a typical value and write a one-sentence justification tied to the data's shape.
For a most-common / categorical question, decide whether the mode is the right choice and say why.
Check a tempting claim such as 'the mean always sits in the middle of the range' against your skewed data and explain whether it holds.
activities.intendedInsight: The appropriate average depends on the data: the median represents a typical value better for skewed data or data with an outlier; the mode suits most-common / categorical questions; the mean suits roughly symmetric numerical data. Learners' informal notions of 'average' (most frequent, reasonable value, midpoint, algorithm) are each true only in some circumstances.

activities.title: Compute-and-justify checks
feedback: If a comparison answer mentions only averages, prompt: 'What about how spread out each set is?'
If the range is given as two values, require the single difference.
If the learner says the mean and median change equally when the outlier is removed, have them actually recompute both.
activities.rationale: Short scorable items using data sets where the averages genuinely diverge give a check that can catch report-the-mean-regardless and ignore-the-spread errors. Such items verify both procedure and judgement but do not by themselves build the underlying reasoning, which the manipulation and comparison activities develop.
learnerActions: Compute mean, median, mode and range for a given set, stating the range as one number (highest − lowest).
For a skewed set, pick which average best represents it and give the reason.
For two sets, write a conclusion that cites BOTH an average AND the range, so a centre-only comparison is marked incomplete.
For an outlier item, state which of the mean or median changes more when the outlier is removed, and by roughly how much.

Optional: a usable worked set is sleep hours 7, 8, 8, 7, 9, 8, 2 (mean 7, median 8, mode 8, range 7), where the outlier 2 pulls the mean DOWN below the cluster — note this direction is opposite to an upward-pulling outlier, and the median stays representative.
activities.intendedInsight: Correct computation plus correct judgement (choice of average, differential outlier effect, centre-and-spread comparison) are both required; getting the arithmetic right is not the same as reasoning about the distribution.

constraints: Use data sets where the three averages genuinely diverge (skewed data or a clear outlier); on near-symmetric data the point about choosing the right average is invisible.
State the measurement context/scale for any example so the outlier is a plausible value on that scale (not off-scale), and match the direction of pull (up or down) to the data.
State the range as a single number (highest − lowest), a measure of spread, not the pair of extreme values.
Always draw conclusions in context (e.g. 'better on average but less consistent') so measures are used to argue, not merely calculated.

A fixed annotated distribution can mark where mean, median and mode fall and label the range as a distance, and is useful as a reference or worked example; because its data cannot be moved, pair it with an activity where learners change the data and watch the measures respond.

Scorable compute-and-justify items can assess both procedure and judgement and can be used during teaching, but recognition/selection responses do not by themselves elicit the independent reasoning that choosing an average and comparing distributions require; include construction and explanation.

An in-role 'data analyst' who argues a naive claim ('same mean, so the classes are identical') for the learner to challenge can surface and sharpen reasoning; use it as a follow-on once learners have manipulated or computed the measures, since dialogue alone does not show the measures changing.
Removing an outlier must be justified by a reason (e.g. a recording error), not done reflexively to tidy the data.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original claimed a live manipulable tool achieves what 'calculation alone cannot', that a static image 'cannot' teach the core idea, and that a third spatial dimension 'adds nothing'. These comparative-necessity claims are not established by the cited sources and have been softened to affordances/limits (manipulation makes the differential effect visible; a fixed image serves as reference; single-variable data is one-dimensional so an extra spatial axis is not needed here).

The outlier direction differs between the upward illustration (moving a value to 30) and the original diagnostic (sleep value 2 pulling the mean DOWN). Both are valid; facilitators should ensure the chosen direction matches the data so learners see the correct direction of pull. The concrete sleep dataset (7, 8, 8, 7, 9, 8, 2; mean 7, median 8, mode 8, range 7) from the original diagnostic is retained as an optional worked example.

Activity 1 was adjusted to MOVE an existing value far out (count fixed) rather than ADD a value, so the median's robustness is clearly due to order statistics and not to a change in the number of data points. Feedback was corrected so the mean's sensitivity is stated accurately: the sum changes by the displacement and the mean by that displacement divided by the number of values, not by the 'full size' of the value.
Source claims were retained only where they directly support an activity's teaching principle; the fourth activity cites none because no source establishes efficacy of scorable items.
Legacy confidence was 'high'; this has not been independently re-validated here.

probeDeeper: 'The mean is about 7 but one person slept only 2 hours — which number better describes a typical night, and why?' — pushes the skew/outlier → median reasoning into words
'What happens to the mean and to the median if I remove the 2? Which changes more?' — tests the differential effect directly
Counterexample: 'Both classes have a mean of 60 — does that mean they did equally well? What else would you check?' — forces spread into the comparison
'When would the MODE be the best average to report?' — probes appropriateness of measure on a fresh case
assess.correctAnswer: A correct performance: computes mean, median, mode and range correctly (range = highest − lowest, one number); recognises the 2 as an outlier that drags the MEAN down while the MEDIAN stays representative, and reports the median as the typical value with that reason; and when comparing the two classes uses BOTH an average AND the range/spread ('similar on average but Class A is more consistent'), not the average alone. Seeing the outlier's differential effect and comparing on centre AND spread are the marks of mastery.

errorPatterns.pattern: Outlier treated as affecting all averages equally, or reported mean regardless of the outlier — not seeing the mean is dragged while the median is robust
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach on the mean prerequisite: recompute mean and median with and without the outlier so the child sees the mean chase it while the median holds; the mean is influenced by every value, the median is not
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On tasks (1)-(2) the child reports the mean as the typical value despite the 2 pulling it below the cluster, or claims the median is affected as much as the mean, or deletes the 2 without justification

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares two data sets on the average alone, ignoring the spread — concludes two sets with similar means are 'the same'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront in place: show two sets with equal means but very different ranges and ask 'are these really the same?'; describing a distribution needs centre AND spread
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (3) the child bases the conclusion only on the means and does not mention the range/spread, missing that one class is far more variable

errorPatterns.pattern: Chooses the wrong average for the data's shape — uses the mean for skewed data (or thinks the mean always sits in the middle of the range) rather than the more representative median/mode
errorPatterns.nextMove: Tie the choice to the shape: for skewed data or data with an outlier the median represents a typical value better; for most-common/categorical questions the mode; reteach the meaning of the measures via the vocabulary prerequisite
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (2) the child defaults to the mean without considering that the skew/outlier makes the median more representative, or expects the mean to be central regardless of shape

errorPatterns.pattern: Range as the extremes, not their difference: gives the range as the two end values rather than the single number highest − lowest
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish the range as one number — a distance/spread from lowest to highest — by marking both ends and computing the difference; reteach the term via the vocabulary prerequisite
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (1) the child states the range as '2 to 9' (or names lowest and highest) instead of 7

responseLevels.gap: Computes the measures unreliably or gives the range as two numbers; reports the mean regardless of an outlier; compares two sets on the mean alone
responseLevels.full: Computes all four measures, recognises and explains the outlier's differential pull on mean versus median, chooses the appropriate average for the data's shape, and compares two distributions on BOTH centre and spread — transferring the reasoning to a fresh pair of data sets
responseLevels.partial: Correctly computes mean, median, mode and range, but treats the mean as the average to report regardless of skew/outliers, or compares distributions using centre only — has the procedures without the judgement about which measure fits or that spread matters

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a small data set with a clear outlier — e.g. hours of sleep: 7, 8, 8, 7, 9, 8, 2 — and a second pair of data sets for comparison (two classes' test scores with similar means but different spreads). Set these tasks and WATCH how they work: (1) 'Find the mean, median, mode and range of the sleep data.' (2) 'Which average best describes a typical night's sleep here? Use it.' (3) 'Compare these two classes and tell me what you can conclude.' (Set the task and WATCH — do not hint that the 2 is an outlier, nor that comparing needs spread as well as an average.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Task (2) forces the choice of average: a child who reports the mean regardless reveals they don't grasp that an outlier makes it unrepresentative, while a child who has the idea switches to the median and says why. Task (3) is built with similar means but different spreads, so a child comparing on the mean alone concludes 'the same' whereas a child who understands distributions cites the spread. The two separate calculation from the judgement the topic is about.

sources.claim: The mean is influenced by every value, so a single extreme value shifts it, whereas exploratory methods based on order statistics (such as the median) are robust and not very sensitive to outliers; a frequent error is to situate the mean at the centre of the range even when the distribution is skewed, where the median or mode would be a better representative

sources.claim: A frequent error is to ignore the spread of data; the intuitive notion of variability concerns how much values differ from each other, and different words (variation, dispersion, spread) are open to different interpretations — so describing data needs an explicit measure of spread
sources.source: Batanero et al. (1994), citing Campbell and Loosen et al.

sources.claim: Students' notions of 'average' fragment into most-frequent-value/mode, reasonable value, midpoint and algorithmic relationship — each true in some circumstances but not others — so which average is appropriate depends on the data
