pedagogy.summary: By Y4, children move from naming shapes by look (van Hiele level 1) to reasoning about defining properties (level 2), and start the class-inclusion idea (level 3): a square is a special rectangle (and a special rhombus) because it has every property a rectangle needs plus the extra property of four equal sides. The obstacle is prototype/partition thinking — a child sorts each shape into exactly one box and rejects a square as a rectangle because it doesn't look like the 'long' rectangle they picture. Teaching works by shifting the question from 'what does it look like?' to 'what tests must it pass?', so category membership is decided by properties, not appearance.
bestPractices: Define categories by an explicit checklist of properties (rectangle = 4 right angles, opposite sides equal and parallel) and let children TEST a shape against the checklist rather than judge by eye
Use nested/overlapping Venn or set diagrams so a shape can visibly sit in two categories at once — this attacks the partition assumption that each shape belongs to exactly one box
Deliberately include non-prototypical examples: a square, a rectangle tilted 45°, a very-nearly-square rectangle, so 'rectangle' is not welded to the long-oblong prototype
Contrast examples with non-examples: ask children to draw a quadrilateral that is NOT a rectangle, rhombus, or square, forcing them to reason about which properties are absent
Insist on justification in the child's own words ('it is a rectangle because...') — knowing the shared properties is the point, not the yes/no answer
keyRepresentations: Property checklist / definition card for each category (right-angle marks, equal-side tick marks, parallel arrows)
Nested Venn diagram: quadrilaterals ⊃ rectangles ⊃ squares, with rhombuses overlapping so square sits in the intersection
A 'stretchy' square that can be pulled into an oblong rectangle or squashed to a rhombus, showing square as the special case where both hold
Set-square and ruler to physically verify right angles and equal sides
commonMisconceptions: A square is not a rectangle — they are two different, separate kinds of shape (exclusive/partition thinking)
A rectangle must have two long sides and two short sides, so a square cannot be one (oblong prototype; the unequal-sides attribute is wrongly treated as defining)
A shape can only belong to one category, so it cannot be a rectangle AND a square at the same time
A square turned 45° is a 'diamond', not a square (orientation bound to the prototype)

learn.summary: Help Year 4 children (age 8–9) move from naming quadrilaterals by appearance to deciding category membership by property tests, and begin class-inclusion reasoning: a square is a special rectangle (and a special rhombus) because it passes every rectangle test (four right angles, opposite sides equal and parallel) plus has the extra property of four equal sides. The core obstacle is partition/prototype thinking — a child files each shape in exactly one box and rejects a square as a rectangle because it doesn't match the 'long oblong' they picture. Teaching shifts the question from 'what does it look like?' to 'what tests must it pass?'

activities.title: Sort and stretch: does the shape pass the rectangle tests?
feedback: When a learner says a square is 'too square' to be a rectangle, walk the rectangle checklist together item by item; if it passes every test, the square belongs in the 'rectangle' ring without leaving 'square'.

If a learner thinks a rectangle must have two long and two short sides, show a run of rectangles from very long to nearly square to square, confirming each passes the same tests — length is not a defining property.

If a learner accepts the shared properties yet still won't let one shape be in two categories, offer everyday inclusion analogies (a spaniel is a dog AND an animal at once) and more nested-set practice rather than drilling the yes/no fact.
Reinforce justification: the point is naming the shared properties ('four right angles, opposite sides equal and parallel'), not the bare yes/no answer.
activities.rationale: A live, manipulable surface lets children test a shape against a visible checklist and watch labels attach or drop as properties change — making 'membership by property, not appearance' concrete. A stretch tool that keeps the 'rectangle' label while dropping the 'square' badge, and nested rings that show one shape in two boxes at once, directly address partition and oblong-prototype thinking. Optional interaction examples (draggable handles, a checklist that ticks green as each test passes, snapping to the deepest qualifying region) make the mechanism tangible but are not mandatory.
sourceClaims: Attributes belonging to a category also belong to all its subcategories (all rectangles have four right angles, so a square, being a rectangle, does too); classify two-dimensional figures in a hierarchy based on properties
A square is a subclass of rectangle; young children must learn class inclusion and often resist that a square can also be a rectangle
Children reject non-prototypical examples and impose non-defining attributes (e.g. a square is not accepted as a rectangle because a rectangle is expected to have unequal adjacent sides)
'A square is a special type of rectangle... all squares are rectangles, but not all rectangles are squares'; guiding questions 'Is a square a special rectangle? Is a rhombus a special kite?'

learnerActions: Take a plain quadrilateral and adjust its corners until all four angles are right angles (check with a set-square); confirm whether opposite sides are equal and parallel.
Run the rectangle checklist item by item — '4 right angles? ✓ opposite sides equal and parallel? ✓' — and place the shape inside the 'rectangle' ring of a nested diagram when it passes all tests.

Now, starting from a rectangle with all four sides equal (a square), pull one pair of opposite sides longer while keeping all four right angles, so the shape stays a rectangle but is no longer a square; then shorten them, still keeping the right angles, until all four sides are equal again and watch it move into the innermost 'square' region nested inside 'rectangle', which is nested inside 'quadrilateral'.
Say out loud, in your own words, why the SAME shape can sit in two boxes at once ('it is a rectangle because... and also a square because...').
Repeat with a rhombus checklist to see the square also sits inside 'rhombus' where the rings overlap.
activities.intendedInsight: Category membership is decided by which property tests a shape passes, not by how it looks; a square passes every rectangle test, so a square is a special rectangle (and a special rhombus) — and one shape can belong to two nested categories at once.

activities.title: Predict, test, explain with a real square
feedback: A correct answer is 'yes — a square is a rectangle: it has four right angles and opposite sides equal and parallel, plus its four sides happen to be equal, so it is a special rectangle.'
If a learner judges by appearance ('it's too square-looking') and cannot state the defining properties, build the checklist together and test item by item.
For 'a square turned 45° is a diamond', confirm turning a shape does not change which property tests it passes, so it is still a square and still a rectangle.

When asked to draw a square that is NOT a rectangle, the learner should discover this is impossible: every square passes all the rectangle tests, so no such shape exists — whereas a rectangle that is not a square CAN be drawn. Noticing this one-way asymmetry is the sign of real property-based understanding.
Treat 'it can be a square OR a rectangle but not both' as a maturing class-inclusion stage, not a false fact; give more nested-set experience rather than correction drills.
activities.rationale: A predict–test–explain routine with a physical square, set-square and ruler makes the diagnostic reasoning visible and lets children verify right angles and equal sides themselves. Asking for the reason, not just the answer, discriminates property-based reasoning from a lucky 'yes' backed only by 'both have four sides'.
sourceClaims: A square is a subclass of rectangle; young children must learn class inclusion and often resist that a square can also be a rectangle
Children reject non-prototypical examples and impose non-defining attributes (e.g. a square is not accepted as a rectangle because a rectangle is expected to have unequal adjacent sides)
'A square is a special type of rectangle... all squares are rectangles, but not all rectangles are squares'; guiding questions 'Is a square a special rectangle? Is a rhombus a special kite?'
learnerActions: Before testing, predict whether a square 'counts as' a rectangle and say WHY.
Check the square against a rectangle checklist using a set-square and ruler: four right angles? opposite sides equal and parallel?
If the result differs from your prediction, explain what changed your mind.

Answer probing questions: Does it matter how long the sides are? Is a square turned to look like a diamond still a square and still a rectangle? Can you draw a rectangle that is NOT a square? Can you draw a square that is NOT a rectangle?
Decide whether a square is also a special rhombus, and justify.
activities.intendedInsight: Stating a reason before testing exposes prototype thinking; reconciling a 'no, too square' prediction with the square passing every rectangle test is where the concept takes hold. The asymmetry — you can draw a rectangle that is not a square, but not a square that is not a rectangle — is the tell of genuine understanding.

activities.title: Draw the exceptions and defend the claim
feedback: Accept a non-example only when the learner shows a defining property is missing for each category it must be excluded from. Some missing properties exclude only some categories: 'no right angles → not a rectangle or square' still leaves rhombus open, so also check 'the four sides are not all equal → not a rhombus or square'. One missing property can exclude all three: rectangles, rhombuses and squares all have both pairs of opposite sides parallel, so a shape without two pairs of parallel sides (e.g. a kite or trapezium) is none of them.
Accept the inclusion claim only when the learner cites the defining properties the square passes, not just that 'it looks like one' or 'both have four sides'.
If a learner cannot produce a non-prototypical rectangle, offer tilted and nearly-square examples and have them verify each against the checklist.
activities.rationale: Contrasting examples with non-examples forces attention to defining versus non-defining attributes, and justification in the child's own words is the learning target. An in-role classifier who presses 'but it doesn't look like a rectangle — why does it still count?' surfaces and names the reasoning; dialogue here supports the property inspection rather than replacing it.

Attributes belonging to a category also belong to all its subcategories (all rectangles have four right angles, so a square, being a rectangle, does too); classify two-dimensional figures in a hierarchy based on properties
learnerActions: Draw a quadrilateral that is NOT a rectangle, rhombus, or square, and say which defining property it is missing for EACH of those three categories.
Draw a rectangle that is not a square.
Explain to a sceptical 'shape detective' why a square still counts as a rectangle even though it doesn't look like a long oblong, citing the defining properties it passes.
Sort a mixed set of quadrilaterals (including a square, a 45°-tilted rectangle, and a nearly-square rectangle) into a nested/overlapping Venn, justifying each placement by properties.
activities.intendedInsight: Reasoning about which properties are ABSENT (for non-examples) and which are PRESENT (for inclusion) consolidates definition-based classification and loosens the oblong prototype.

constraints: Target concept is property-based classification and class inclusion, not shape naming; always require justification by defining properties, not a bare yes/no.

A scored sort/multiple-choice can assess whether a child accepts the inclusion (e.g. 'Is a square a rectangle?' with distractor 'No, they are different shapes') but does not by itself let the child feel a square pass the tests; use it to check, not to build, the insight.

A static tap-to-reveal Venn or hierarchy is a useful summary/reference showing where a square sits, but because nothing recomputes the child cannot TEST a shape's membership; best used after hands-on testing rather than as the primary route.

Distinguish an ideal zero-thickness plane figure from physical card/cutouts, which have slight thickness and can be held and turned; treat cutouts as approximations of the represented flat shape and ask about the mathematical shape represented, not whether the physical card can be picked up. Quadrilateral classification is a planar, 2D property idea, so a third spatial dimension is not needed here (a limit of relevance, not evidence that any one medium is superior).
Treat the one-box (class-inclusion) stage as developmental: give more nested-set and everyday-inclusion experience rather than drilling the fact.
Set-square/ruler verification and recolouring/ticking checklists are optional supports to make the mechanism concrete; they are not required mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One source (National Curriculum Year 4 Geometry) is marked verified:false in the row; treat that claim with corresponding caution.

The row frames the topic as Year 4 (age 8–9) while citing Common Core 5.G.3/5.G.4 (Grade 5) for hierarchy/subcategory attributes; this grade-band mismatch is a migration ambiguity, though the inclusion content is consistent with the stated evidence targets.

The original 'poor fit / 3D adds nothing' and 'static image can only reference, cannot teach' framings were softened to scoped affordance/limit statements; catalog fit rankings and product/tool-type labels were removed. No claim of one medium's superiority is intended.
The 'diamond' probe is retained as a counterexample: turning a shape does not change which property tests it passes, so a tilted square remains both a square and a rectangle.

The 'draw a square that is not a rectangle' probe is deliberately impossible; feedback now states this explicitly so the task is used to reveal the one-way asymmetry, not left as an answerable request.

assess.poeTask: Hold up a square and ask the child to PREDICT whether it will 'count as' a rectangle — and to say WHY before testing. Then together OBSERVE: check the square against a rectangle checklist using a set-square and ruler — four right angles? opposite sides equal and parallel? It passes every test. Ask the child to EXPLAIN why the result differs from a prediction of 'no'. The stated reason before testing is the diagnostic part; a child who predicted 'no, it's too square' must now reconcile that with the square passing every rectangle test.
probeDeeper: 'You said a rectangle has four right angles and opposite sides equal — does it matter how long the sides are?' (pushes them to see length is not a defining property)
'Here is the square turned to look like a diamond — is it still a square? Is it still a rectangle?' (counterexample against orientation binding)
'Can you draw a rectangle that is NOT a square? Now can you draw a square that is NOT a rectangle?' (the second is impossible — the asymmetry is the tell of real understanding)
'A square has four equal sides and four right angles — is it also a special rhombus? Why?' (transfer to the second inclusion)
assess.correctAnswer: Yes — a square is a rectangle. A rectangle needs four right angles and opposite sides that are equal and parallel; a square has all of those, plus its four sides happen to be equal too, so it is a special kind of rectangle.

errorPatterns.pattern: Exclusive/partition thinking: 'a square is not a rectangle — they're two different shapes' (each shape belongs in exactly one box)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build a rectangle property checklist together and test the square against it item by item; use a nested Venn so the child sees the square can sit inside 'rectangle' without leaving 'square'. Reteach in place — this is the target concept.
errorPatterns.distractor: No — a square and a rectangle are different kinds of shape
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'no' and, on the reason tier, treats square and rectangle as separate named categories rather than comparing properties

errorPatterns.pattern: Oblong prototype: 'a rectangle has two long sides and two short sides, so a square can't be one' (the unequal-sides look is wrongly treated as a defining property)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate defining properties (right angles, opposite sides equal/parallel) from typical appearance; show a range of rectangles from very long to nearly square to square so the prototype loosens. Revisit shape-property work.
errorPatterns.distractor: No — a rectangle must have two long sides and two short sides
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the reason tier gives a definition of rectangle that requires it to be longer than it is wide

errorPatterns.pattern: One-box assumption: accepts that a square and a rectangle share properties yet still won't let one shape belong to two categories at once
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill the yes/no fact. Give more nested-set experience (Venn diagrams, 'all squares are inside the rectangle ring') and everyday inclusion analogies (a spaniel is a dog and an animal at once) so the inclusion logic matures; it self-corrects with exposure.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says something like 'it can be a square OR a rectangle but not both' — a class-inclusion (part–whole) reasoning stage rather than a false fact

responseLevels.gap: Says a square is not a rectangle, or judges purely by appearance ('it's too square-looking'); cannot state the properties that define a rectangle.
responseLevels.full: Says yes and argues that the square passes every defining test of a rectangle (four right angles, opposite sides equal and parallel) and is therefore a special rectangle; extends the same reasoning to 'special rhombus', and can draw a quadrilateral that belongs to none of the subcategories.
responseLevels.partial: Says yes and can list shared features ('both have four sides / four corners') but does not use the defining properties to justify inclusion, and cannot transfer to 'square is a special rhombus' or explain why a rectangle need not be a square.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show the child a square (and, alongside, an oblong rectangle). Ask: 'Is this square also a rectangle?' — then, whatever they answer: 'How do you know? What makes something a rectangle?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child reasoning from defining properties says yes and can name the rectangle tests the square passes. A child reasoning from appearance/prototype says no because the square doesn't look like the 'long' rectangle. The reason tier is decisive: a lucky 'yes' backed only by 'they both have four sides' is not mastery, and a confident 'no, a rectangle has to be longer than it is wide' exposes the prototype directly. Correct reasoning and prototype reasoning give genuinely different answers to 'what makes something a rectangle?'

pedagogy.summary: Missing-number problems (245 + ? = 380) push children beyond 'compute the answer' to reasoning about the STRUCTURE of an equation: what is unknown, and how the inverse relationship or a count-on finds it. The equals sign must be read relationally ('is the same as'), not as 'the answer comes next'. Children choose a method from the numbers — count-on to find a missing addend, inverse to undo, or a written method — and increasingly combine steps with three-digit numbers.
bestPractices: Establish the equals sign as 'is the same as / balances', using balance and bar-model images, so a missing addend isn't read as 'add the two numbers shown'
Teach missing addend as either count-on (245 up to 380) or inverse (380 − 245); missing minuend/subtrahend via the inverse
Represent with a bar model so the unknown's position (part vs whole) dictates the operation
Choose method by the numbers — near numbers invite counting up, others a written method
Check by substituting the found number back into the original equation
keyRepresentations: Bar model / part-whole (unknown part vs unknown whole)
Balance scale image (both sides equal)
Number line (count-on to find a difference)
Equation with a box for the unknown
Base-ten / columns for the calculation
commonMisconceptions: Operator view of '=': for 245 + ? = 380 computing 245 + 380 ('the answer goes after the equals')
Not using the inverse — guessing/trial instead of 380 − 245 or counting on
Position confusion: treating ? − 120 = 250 as 250 − 120
Choosing subtraction/addition by habit rather than by where the unknown sits

learn.summary: Missing-number problems (e.g. 245 + □ = 380) move children from 'compute the answer' to reasoning about an equation's structure: what is unknown, where it sits, and how an inverse operation or a count-on finds it. The equals sign is read relationally ('is the same as / balances'), not as 'the answer comes next'. Children choose a method from the numbers — count-on for a missing addend, inverse to undo, or a written method — check by substituting back, and increasingly combine steps with three-digit numbers.

activities.title: Balance the equation: find the missing number
feedback: If a child puts 380 (or 245 + 380) in the box, point to the overloaded side: 'Both sides must match — is this side the same as 380 now?' Let them see it is far too big.

For □ − 120 = 250, if the child computes 250 − 120, use a part-whole bar: the box is the WHOLE, and we know a part (120) and what is left (250), so we add: 250 + 120 = 370. Ask: must the starting number be bigger or smaller than 250?
For 500 − □ = 340, show that the box is a part being taken away: 500 − 340 = 160, or count up 340 → 500.
If a child guesses or stalls, model two routes for a missing addend — count on from 245 to 380, and subtract 380 − 245 — and connect them as a fact family (245 + 135 = 380 ⇔ 380 − 245 = 135).
Praise correct substitution checks: 'You put 135 back and both sides came to 380 — that proves it.'
activities.rationale: A manipulable balance or bar model makes the unknown's position visible and lets the child test values, so the 'answer comes next' misreading may be confronted in action rather than only asserted. A relational view of '=' is reported to need explicit teaching over time, supported by non-standard equations and pan-balance/seesaw images.
sourceClaims: Children commonly hold an operational ('do something / put the answer next') rather than relational ('is the same value as') view of '='; Falkner, Levi & Carpenter (1999) found only 5% of grade 1-2 students answered 7 to 8 + 4 = □ + 5, most answering 12 (left side only) or 17 (sum of all numbers). A relational understanding must be explicitly taught over time, aided by non-standard equations and a pan-balance/seesaw.
Year 3 pupils solve problems, including missing-number problems, using number facts, place value and more complex addition and subtraction, and use inverse operations to check.
learnerActions: Work with a balance or bar model showing 245 and an empty box on one side and 380 on the other, with the beam tilted.
Try putting 380 in the box and observe that the side becomes far too heavy (245 + 380 = 625) — much more than 380.
Adjust the box until the two sides match, finding 135, and say in words why 135 balances it.
Use a number-line route for the same problem: start at 245 and count on to 380, noticing the jump is 135.
Repeat with the unknown in other positions, e.g. □ − 120 = 250 (answer 370) and 500 − □ = 340 (answer 160), deciding each time whether the missing quantity is a part or the whole.
Check every answer by substituting it back into the original equation (does 245 + 135 really equal 380?).
activities.intendedInsight: The equals sign means the two sides are the same value; the position of the unknown (part vs whole) decides whether you add or subtract, and you can verify an answer by putting it back.

activities.title: True-or-false equations and choosing a strategy
feedback: If a child marks '245 + 380 = 380' as true, revisit the balance idea: the left side comes to 625, so the two sides are not the same value.
When near numbers appear, prompt 'these are close — would counting up be quicker?'; for far-apart numbers, a written subtraction may be easier.
Reinforce that method choice should follow the unknown's position and the numbers, not habit.
activities.rationale: True/false sorting and method-selection items can target the operator view of equals and prompt flexible strategy choice. These checking-style tasks confirm and diagnose reasoning but do not themselves require the child to construct a method, so they are best paired with the constructive balance/bar work.
sourceClaims: Children commonly hold an operational ('do something / put the answer next') rather than relational ('is the same value as') view of '='; Falkner, Levi & Carpenter (1999) found only 5% of grade 1-2 students answered 7 to 8 + 4 = □ + 5, most answering 12 (left side only) or 17 (sum of all numbers). A relational understanding must be explicitly taught over time, aided by non-standard equations and a pan-balance/seesaw.
learnerActions: Sort equations as true or false — e.g. '245 + 135 = 380' (true) and '245 + 380 = 380' (false, since 245 + 380 = 625) — to challenge the 'answer-next' habit.
For each of several missing-number problems with the box in different positions, say whether you would count on or use the inverse, and explain what about the numbers made you choose.
Solve and then justify: in 245 + □ = 380 the box is a part; in □ − 120 = 250 the box is the whole.
Check each solution by substitution before moving on.
activities.intendedInsight: Equations assert that both sides are equal and can be judged true or false; the choice between counting on and using the inverse depends on where the unknown sits and on how near the numbers are.

activities.title: Static balance/bar model as a reference
feedback: Prompt the child to name which quantity is missing and whether it is a part or the whole before deciding to add or subtract.
If the two revealed totals differ, ask what would make them match.
activities.rationale: A fixed diagram cannot be adjusted to test candidate values, but it serves as a useful reference for the part/whole structure and for what 'balances' means. Use it alongside, not instead of, tasks where the child tests values.
learnerActions: Study a labelled balance or part-whole bar diagram that shows which quantity is a part and which is the whole.
Tap or point to each side to reveal its total and whether the two sides match.
Use the diagram as a reference while solving problems, naming part and whole before choosing an operation.
activities.intendedInsight: A clear diagram of what balances and of part-vs-whole gives a stable mental image to reason from when identifying the unknown.

constraints: Establish '=' as 'is the same as / balances' before missing-addend work, so the box is not read as 'add the two numbers shown'.
Vary the unknown's position across all addend, minuend, subtrahend, result and whole placements; a diet of result-position problems lets position confusion go undetected.
Always require a substitution check against the original equation.

True/false and multiple-choice items primarily confirm and diagnose reasoning; they do not by themselves require the child to construct a strategy, so pair them with tasks where the child finds and justifies the missing number.
A static diagram is a reference only: it cannot let the child test candidate values, so it supports but does not replace manipulable or written solving.
Connect count-on and inverse as fact families so children can move between them rather than relying on one by habit.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were not re-fetched or re-verified, and the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row judged a conversation 'poor' because 'talk cannot supply the balancing/positioning practice' and that a third dimension 'adds nothing'. These are catalog-format judgements, not established pedagogical laws; spoken explanation and justification can support this learning, so they were softened/omitted rather than asserted as universal limits.
Efficacy of the live-balance format over other media is not established by the sources; activity 1's rationale now uses 'may be confronted' rather than claiming the misreading is defeated.

Worked values verified against the original: 245 + 135 = 380; 380 − 245 = 135; for □ − 120 = 250 the whole is 250 + 120 = 370; for 500 − □ = 340 the part is 500 − 340 = 160; and 245 + 380 = 625 (the deliberate 'too big' demonstration). All consistent with the source's stated answers 135, 370, 160.

probeDeeper: Point to what's unknown in 245 + □ = 380 — is it a part or the whole? So do you add or subtract?
Substitute your answer back in — does 245 + 135 really equal 380?
For □ − 120 = 250, should the missing number be bigger or smaller than 250? Why?
Which of these did you count on for, and which did you subtract — what about the numbers made you choose?

errorPatterns.pattern: Operator view of '=' — 'the answer comes after the equals', so 245 + □ = 380 is done as 245 + 380 = 625
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a balance/bar model to re-establish '=' as 'the same as'; both sides must match. Sort true/false equations to break the 'answer next' habit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child adds the two visible numbers regardless of the box's position; answer far exceeds 380

errorPatterns.pattern: Doesn't use the inverse — guesses or trials numbers instead of 380−245 or counting on
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model finding a missing addend by counting on and by subtracting; connect to fact families (245+135=380 ⇔ 380−245=135).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child tries random values or stalls, showing no inverse/count-on strategy

errorPatterns.pattern: Position confusion — treats □ − 120 = 250 as 250 − 120 (=130) because the box is where an answer usually is
errorPatterns.nextMove: Represent with a part-whole bar: here the box is the WHOLE, and we know a part (120) and the result (250), so we add. Sanity-check that the start must be bigger than what's left.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child subtracts when the unknown is the whole/minuend; answer smaller than 250 rather than larger

responseLevels.gap: Adds the two visible numbers (operator view), or subtracts regardless of the box's position; no inverse/count-on strategy.
responseLevels.full: Reads '=' relationally, reasons from the unknown's position (part vs whole) to choose count-on or inverse, solves the box in any position, and checks by substituting back.
responseLevels.partial: Solves missing-addend problems (box in the result position) but is thrown when the unknown is the minuend/whole, or finds answers without checking by substitution.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set three missing-number problems and watch how the child finds each, letting them choose a method: 245 + □ = 380, then □ − 120 = 250, then 500 − □ = 340. Notice whether they use the inverse or count on, and whether the position of the box changes what they do.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 245+□=380 exposes the operator view of '=' (a child adds 245+380). □−120=250 exposes position confusion (a child does 250−120 instead of 250+120). 500−□=340 checks flexible inverse/count-on. A child who reads '=' relationally and reasons from the unknown's position gets all three; a left-to-right computer fails predictably.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 6–7: count to 120 starting at ANY number below 120, and read/write numerals to 120 — pushing counting and numeral fluency just past the 100 boundary into early three-digit territory.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1–Y2): 'count to and across 100, forwards and backwards, beginning with 0 or 1, or from any given number' (Y1); the to-120 extension mirrors the US Grade 1 expectation.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.NBT.1 'count to 120, starting at any number less than 120; read and write numerals and represent a number of objects with a written numeral'.
• Operational details — two things matter: (i) counting on from any starting number (not always from 1), which shows counting is a movable sequence, and (ii) crossing 100 — reading/writing 100–120 (one hundred and eight = 108), where the hundreds place appears and children must not write 'one hundred and eight' as 1008. Rests on secure numerals to 100 and rote counting.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 6): count from 47 to 120 without error. Tier B (6–7): read the numeral 108 correctly. Tier C (7): write the numeral for 'one hundred and fifteen' (115), not 10015 or 1015.
bestPractices: Practise counting on FROM ANY number (start at 47, at 96, at 112) so children internalise that the count sequence can be entered anywhere — not a fixed chant from 1.
Give special attention to the 99→100 and 109→110 crossings and the 100–120 numerals, where the new hundreds place trips reading/writing.
Confront the write-what-you-hear trap for three-digit words: 'one hundred and eight' → 108, NOT 1008; use place-value/arrow cards (100 + 8) to show the zero tens placeholder.
Extend the 100-square to a 120-grid so the pattern continues visibly past 100 and children see 101–120 as 'one hundred and ...'.
Balance count / read / write and forwards/backwards across the boundary to build robust fluency.
keyRepresentations: 120-grid (extended 100-square) showing the pattern continuing past 100.
Bead string / number line to 120 for counting on from any point and crossing 100.
Place-value / arrow cards composing 108 as 100 + 8 (zero-tens placeholder visible).
Number track segments across the 99→100 and 109→110 crossings.
commonMisconceptions: Writing three-digit words literally: 'one hundred and eight' → 1008, or 'one hundred and fifteen' → 10015/1015 (missing the zero-tens placeholder or concatenating).
Stalling or resetting at 100 (saying 'one hundred, two hundred' or restarting at 1) when counting on.
Only being able to count from 1, not from an arbitrary start number.
Boundary slips: 99→'nine hundred' or 109→200-type errors.
Reading 108 as 'ten eight' or 'one-oh-eight' without the hundred meaning.

learn.summary: For ages 6–7: count to 120 starting from ANY number below 120, and read/write numerals to 120. Two skills carry the load: (i) counting on from an arbitrary start (not always from 1), so children feel the count as a movable sequence they can enter anywhere; and (ii) crossing 100 — reading and writing 100–120, where the hundreds place appears and children must learn that 'one hundred and eight' is 108, not 1008. Give special attention to the 99→100 and 109→110 crossings and to the write-what-you-hear trap. The primary approach is an interactive 120-grid twinned with a number line; a static grid and short written/spoken checks are useful supporting tools with their own limits.

activities.title: Count on from any number across 100 (interactive grid and line)
feedback: If the count breaks at 99→100 or 109→110, don't reteach the whole sequence — rehearse just that boundary on a short track around it: 99, 100, 101 and 108, 109, 110.
If the child restarts at 1 or stalls at 100, nudge exactly at the boundary and model continuing: 'ninety-nine, one hundred, one hundred and one'.
If the child says 'nine hundred' after 99 or jumps to 200, point back to the grid so the next cell is visibly 100, then 101.
activities.rationale: Counting on from any number and crossing 100 are the known difficulty points for this age; rehearsing the exact boundary where errors cluster, with the sequence advancing visibly, is intended to build robust fluency. An interactive grid/line lets the child count, see the sequence advance, and get feedback at the boundary; a highlight-as-you-go display and a count-back mode make the mechanism concrete without being required.
sourceClaims: Grade 1 pupils count to 120 starting at any number less than 120, and read and write numerals in this range.
Year 1 pupils count to and across 100, forwards and backwards, beginning with 0 or 1 or from any given number.
Counting on from any number (not just from 1) and crossing the 100 boundary are known difficulty points; three-digit number words invite literal 'one hundred and eight = 1008' writing errors.
learnerActions: Pick any starting number — for example 47, 96, or 112 — and count on out loud, one number at a time, as each number is highlighted in turn on a 120-grid and a matching number line.

Deliberately practise starts that sit just before a boundary (start at 96 and count 97, 98, 99, 100, 101; start at 108 and count 109, 110, 111) so the century and decade rollovers get extra rehearsal.
Count backwards too (for example from 112 down past 100) to show the sequence runs both ways across the boundary.
While counting, keep the single running count going — avoid resetting to 1 or jumping to 'two hundred' after 100.
activities.intendedInsight: The count is a movable window you can enter at any number, not a fixed chant that must start at 1; it continues smoothly past 100, where 101–120 are 'one hundred and ...'.

activities.title: Build the numeral from the spoken words with place-value cards
feedback: If the child writes 1008 for 108 or 10015 for one hundred and fifteen, build the number with a hundred, tens and ones and write it into a hundreds/tens/ones frame; the 0 in 108 marks the empty tens.
If the child reads 108 as 'ten eight' or 'one-oh-eight' without the hundred meaning, point to the hundred card and reread 'one hundred and eight'.
When a written numeral like 1008 is 'too long', compare it to the 120-grid to show it would land far off the board.
activities.rationale: The literal 'write what you hear' error is a specific, documented misconception for three-digit words; making the zero-tens placeholder visible through arrow/place-value cards is intended to directly address how the numeral is composed. Rejecting 1008 by showing it lands off a 120-grid is an optional feedback device that makes the error visible, not a required mechanism.
sourceClaims: Counting on from any number (not just from 1) and crossing the 100 boundary are known difficulty points; three-digit number words invite literal 'one hundred and eight = 1008' writing errors.
Grade 1 pupils count to 120 starting at any number less than 120, and read and write numerals in this range.
learnerActions: Hear or read a number word such as 'one hundred and eight' and build it with place-value / arrow cards: pull the '100' card, note there are zero tens, then the '8' card, so the cards overlay to read 108.
Say what job the 0 is doing in 108 — it holds the empty tens place.
Do the same for 'one hundred and fifteen' → compose 100, then 1 ten, then 5, reading 115.
Confront the trap directly: write the words out literally (1008, 10015) and compare that number to where it would sit relative to the 120-grid — far off the board — to see why it can't be right.
activities.intendedInsight: Three-digit numerals are built by place value, not by stringing the spoken words together; the zero in 108 is a tens placeholder, and concatenating words gives numbers far too large.

activities.title: Fluency and trap checks: sequence, read, and write across 100
feedback: If a written answer is 1015 or 10015 for one hundred and fifteen, revisit the place-value build: 100, then 1 ten, then 5 → 115.
If a sequence answer breaks at 99→100, rehearse just that short run on a number line.
Confirm correct responses by rereading the numeral with its hundred meaning (108 = 'one hundred and eight').
activities.rationale: Short checks over sequence-filling, reading and words-to-numeral writing surface both the rollover stall and the concatenation error. These response formats are useful for checking fluency; note that choosing or completing an answer checks recognition and recall more than it elicits sustained independent counting, so pair it with the counting activity.
sourceClaims: Grade 1 pupils count to 120 starting at any number less than 120, and read and write numerals in this range.
Year 1 pupils count to and across 100, forwards and backwards, beginning with 0 or 1 or from any given number.
learnerActions: Fill the missing numbers in a run that crosses the boundary, e.g. 97, 98, __, __, 101.
Read a given numeral aloud, e.g. 108, as 'one hundred and eight'.
Write the numeral for a spoken/written number word, e.g. 'one hundred and fifteen' → 115.
Use a slider or marker to land on target numbers up to 120.
activities.intendedInsight: These checks show whether a learner can complete sequences across 100, read numerals 100–120 with their hundred meaning, and write them by place value rather than concatenating words; sustained counting across 100 is confirmed through the spoken counting activity.

activities.title: 120-grid as a reference map
feedback: If a child is unsure what follows 99 or 109, locate it on the grid and read the next cell.
Reinforce that the two rows above 100 repeat the pattern of the first two rows: 101–110 matches 1–10, and 111–120 matches 11–20, with 'one hundred and ...' in front.
activities.rationale: A static 120-grid is a valuable reference that makes the continuing pattern visible, which supports the extension past 100. On its own a fixed grid does not rehearse the productive skills of counting on and writing numerals, so use it alongside counting and composing activities rather than as the main vehicle.
learnerActions: Explore a 120-grid, tapping cells to hear and see each numeral, with 101–120 displayed as 'one hundred and ...'.
Trace the pattern down each column and across each row to see how the sequence continues past 100 just as it did below it.
Point to where 99, 100, 109 and 110 sit and name them.
activities.intendedInsight: The counting pattern continues unbroken past 100, and 101–120 keep the same ones/tens pattern with 'one hundred and ...' in front.

constraints: Rests on secure numerals to 100 and secure rote counting; if counting across 100 fails, check these prerequisites first.
Give deliberate extra practice at the 99→100 and 109→110 crossings and across 100–120, where reading/writing most often breaks.
A static 120-grid is a reference scaffold: it shows the pattern but does not itself let a child rehearse counting on or writing numerals, which are productive skills.
Choosing or completing answers checks recognition and recall; it does not by itself demonstrate sustained independent counting, so include spoken/written counting over a run that crosses 100.
Keep a single running count across the boundary — watch for resetting to 1, stalling at 100, or jumping to 'two hundred'.
Balance count / read / write and forwards/backwards across the boundary.
Checkpoints: count from 47 to 120 without error (age 6); read 108 correctly (6–7); write 115 for 'one hundred and fifteen', not 10015 or 1015 (age 7).

Arithmetic/representation check: 108 = one hundred + zero tens + eight and 115 = one hundred + one ten + five are correct; the error targets 1008, 1015 and 10015 are correctly flagged as concatenation mistakes.

The static-grid reference activity's sourceClaims were set to [] because the available claims support the counting-across-100 topic rather than the specific principle that a static grid is a useful-but-limited reference.

probeDeeper: What comes right after 99? And right after 109?
Write 108 — what job is the 0 doing?
Read this: 120.
assess.correctAnswer: Counts 97, 98, 99, 100, 101 … 110, 111 … without stalling; reads 108 as 'one hundred and eight'; writes 115.

errorPatterns.pattern: Stalls or resets at the century/decade rollover: after 99 goes back to a lower number, or after 109 is unsure what follows
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the whole count — rehearse just the boundary on a 100–120 track/number line: 99, 100, 101 and 108, 109, 110.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The count breaks at 99→100 or 109→110.

errorPatterns.pattern: Concatenates the spoken words into digits: writes 1008 for 108 or 10015 for one hundred and fifteen
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build the number with a hundred, tens and ones and write it into a H/T/O frame; the 0 in 108 holds the empty tens.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Words-to-numeral produces a too-long number spelling out 'one hundred' + 'eight/fifteen'.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot count across 100 or writes concatenated numerals (1008, 10015).
responseLevels.full: Counts fluently from any start past 120 and reads/writes numerals to 120 including placeholder zeros.
responseLevels.partial: Counts and writes within the range but stalls at a rollover or drops/adds a placeholder digit.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Watch counting and writing across 100. 'Count on from 97 up past 110 for me. Read this: 108. Now write “one hundred and fifteen” as a numeral.' Watch the century rollover and the placeholder zero in 108.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Crossing 99→100 and 109→110 is where the sequence breaks down; 108 and 115 both test whether the child builds the numeral by place value or concatenates the spoken words (1008, 10015). Watching the count in real time catches the stall.

pedagogy.summary: Children move from 'which is longer?' to 'how much longer?' — measuring both objects in the same standard unit and subtracting the smaller from the larger to give the difference expressed with its unit ('7 cm longer'). This is the additive-comparison (difference-unknown) structure applied to measured lengths, and it is best made visible as the overhang between two bars aligned at a common baseline.
bestPractices: Measure both objects in the same unit first, then find the difference by subtracting the smaller from the larger.
Demand the amount, not just the direction: the answer is '7 cm taller', not 'the shelf is taller'.
Make the difference visible — align the two lengths at a common baseline (bar model / number line) so the overhang IS the difference.
Use comparison ('difference unknown') word problems and represent them with tape/bar diagrams and an equation with the unknown.
Keep both measures in one unit before subtracting; expose the error of subtracting across different units.
keyRepresentations: Two bars aligned at a common baseline with the overhang marked as the difference
A number line showing both lengths from 0 and the gap between their endpoints
A tape/bar 'comparison' diagram with the difference as the missing part
An equation with a symbol for the unknown difference (32 + ? = 45)
commonMisconceptions: Gives only the comparison ('the shelf is taller') without quantifying by how much.
Subtracts the wrong way or mis-subtracts, or compares by lining objects up with mismatched endpoints.
Compares the bare numbers when the two measures are in different units (shelf in m, desk in cm).
Treats the difference as the sum, or adds when the problem asks how much longer.

learn.summary: Children move from 'which is longer?' to 'how much longer?' — measuring both objects in the same standard unit and subtracting the smaller from the larger to state the difference WITH its unit ('7 cm taller'). This is the additive-comparison (difference-unknown) structure applied to measured lengths, made visible as the overhang between two lengths aligned at a common baseline.

activities.title: How much taller? Measure, align, and find the overhang
feedback: If the learner answers only 'the bookshelf is taller' with no number, point to the overhang above the shorter object's top and ask 'how much is this extra bit?' so the difference becomes a quantity.
If the learner subtracts larger-from-smaller or lines objects up with unequal starting points, re-align both at a common baseline/zero and read the gap; then subtract smaller from larger.
Confirm a full answer states the difference with its unit and can be shown as the overhang on the bar model or number line.
activities.rationale: Aligning both lengths at a common baseline turns the abstract 'difference' into a visible, measurable overhang, matching the difference-unknown comparison structure; measuring and expressing with a unit (2.MD.4) and representing with tape/number-line diagrams and an unknown-symbol equation (2.MD.5–6) are the grade-level targets.
sourceClaims: Second graders learn to measure two objects and subtract the smaller measurement from the larger to find how much longer one object is than the other, expressing the difference in a standard length unit (2.MD.4); they can add two lengths to obtain the whole and subtract to find the difference.

Length addition/subtraction problems (2.MD.5) are represented with drawings of rulers, tape or number-bond diagrams, and equations with a symbol for the unknown; a number line diagram is a measurement model in which consecutive whole numbers are one unit apart, so children reason about distances between positions.
Year 3 pupils measure, compare, add and subtract lengths and solve 'how much longer/taller' comparison problems, expressing the difference in standard units.
learnerActions: Place two objects of clearly different height/length (e.g. a desk and a bookshelf) so both stand on the SAME baseline, with a ruler, metre stick or tape measured from zero at that baseline.
Measure both in the same unit (e.g. desk 118 cm, shelf 125 cm) and write each measurement with its unit.
Identify the strip of the longer object that sticks up above the top of the shorter one — this overhang is the answer to 'how much taller?'
Find the difference by subtracting the smaller measurement from the larger (125 − 118) and state the answer with its unit: 'the bookshelf is 7 cm taller.'

In a word-problem round, both measures are given (for example, stated in the problem's words in the same unit rather than read from the ruler), and the DIFFERENCE is the unknown: draw a comparison bar/tape diagram with two bars from a common baseline, mark the difference as the missing part, then write an equation with a symbol for the unknown difference (e.g. 32 + ? = 45, or 45 − 32 = ?) and solve it.
activities.intendedInsight: The difference is a real, measurable piece of length — the overhang between two lengths aligned at a common baseline — not just the fact that one object 'wins'. The answer must be an amount with a unit.

activities.title: Same unit first: the mixed-unit trap
feedback: If the learner writes '1 − 80' or keeps mismatched units, prompt: 'What is 1 m in centimetres?' then redo the subtraction in one unit (100 cm − 80 cm = 20 cm).
Reinforce attending to the unit while measuring and whenever the two measures look different in size.
activities.rationale: A deliberate mixed-unit item exposes and corrects bare-number subtraction, a documented error; it reinforces that a difference is only meaningful in a shared unit.
sourceClaims: Second graders learn to measure two objects and subtract the smaller measurement from the larger to find how much longer one object is than the other, expressing the difference in a standard length unit (2.MD.4); they can add two lengths to obtain the whole and subtract to find the difference.
learnerActions: Take a pair of objects measured in different units (e.g. a shelf labelled 1 m and a desk labelled 80 cm).
Before subtracting, re-express both in one common unit (e.g. 1 m = 100 cm).
Then subtract smaller from larger in that common unit and state the difference with its unit (100 cm − 80 cm = 20 cm taller).
Say aloud why '1 − 80' is wrong: the numbers are in different units and cannot be subtracted as bare numbers.
activities.intendedInsight: You can only subtract lengths once they are expressed in the same unit; comparing bare numbers across different units gives a meaningless answer.

activities.title: Check questions: comparison word problems and 'by how much?'
feedback: Catch the 'names the taller one but not the amount' error by requiring a numeric answer with a unit.
If a mixed-unit item is answered by bare-number subtraction, re-express to one unit and re-solve.
activities.rationale: Response-format items can check whether the amount-with-unit and common-unit requirements are met and can surface the comparison-only and bare-number errors; such items check performance rather than build the bar-model reasoning, so pair them with the construction activities.
sourceClaims: Second graders learn to measure two objects and subtract the smaller measurement from the larger to find how much longer one object is than the other, expressing the difference in a standard length unit (2.MD.4); they can add two lengths to obtain the whole and subtract to find the difference.
learnerActions: Answer 'how much longer/taller?' items where you enter the amount (fill-in or slider), not just which object is longer.
Work at least one item that gives the two measures in different units, so you must convert to a common unit before subtracting.
For a comparison word problem, pick the correct equation with the unknown difference and justify it with a bar diagram.
activities.intendedInsight: A correct answer to a comparison problem is an amount with a unit, obtained by subtracting in a common unit — not a choice of 'which one'.

constraints: The answer must state an AMOUNT with its unit ('7 cm taller'), not just a direction ('the shelf is taller').
Both measures must be in the same unit before subtracting; subtract the smaller from the larger so the difference is positive.

To read a difference directly as a visible gap, the objects must be aligned at a common baseline/zero, because mismatched starting points produce a wrong gap. When each object is measured separately from the ruler's zero, the two measurements can be subtracted without physically lining the objects up.
A static bar-model diagram can illustrate the overhang idea but does not let the learner measure and compute across new cases; use it as a reference scaffold alongside hands-on measuring.

Recognition/selection items (choosing which is longer, or multiple choice) can check understanding but do not by themselves elicit independent measuring, subtracting and expressing — include at least one task where the learner constructs the measurement and difference.

Interactive examples (dragging objects to a shared baseline, live-shaded overhang that updates as lengths change, auto-labelled difference) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not required mechanisms.

The legacy entry rated a 3D format 'poor' ('3D adds no insight') and a conversation format 'poor' ('not a dialogue'); these are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws, and have been dropped rather than asserted as universal truths. The mixed-unit example '1 m vs 80 cm' is used to expose the bare-number error; the correct worked value is 100 cm − 80 cm = 20 cm. The erroneous '1 − 80' appears only as something to catch, never as a valid answer in learner-facing text.

Activity 1's word-problem step was clarified so that one measure is supplied in words (not deleted) and the DIFFERENCE is the single unknown, removing an ambiguity about which quantity the bar diagram's missing part represents.

probeDeeper: You said the bookshelf is taller — by how much? Show me how you'd find that.
Where on the ruler is the 'extra bit' that makes the shelf taller than the desk?
This one is 1 m and that one is 80 cm — how much taller? Can you subtract 80 from 1?
If the desk were actually the taller one, how would your calculation change?
assess.correctAnswer: The child measures both objects in the same unit, subtracts the smaller from the larger, and states the difference WITH its unit ('the bookshelf is 7 cm taller'); for the mixed-unit pair, converts or re-expresses to a common unit before subtracting rather than comparing the bare numbers.

errorPatterns.pattern: Comparison, not difference: reports which is longer/taller but not by how much.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reframe with a bar model — align both at a baseline and point to the overhang; ask 'how much is the extra bit?' so the difference becomes a measurable quantity.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'the bookshelf is taller' or 'that one', with no number, when asked how much taller.

errorPatterns.pattern: Subtracts the wrong way or mis-subtracts / mismatched endpoints: subtracts larger-from-smaller, miscomputes, or lines the objects up with unequal starting points before comparing.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold subtracting smaller from larger and aligning both at a common baseline/zero before reading the gap; the measuring skill itself is intact.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives a nonsensical or negative-feeling difference, or eyeballs a difference from objects not aligned at the same baseline.

errorPatterns.pattern: Bare-number subtraction across different units: subtracts the numbers when the two measures are in different units (e.g. shelf 1 m, desk 80 cm -> '1 - 80').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-express both in one unit before subtracting; return to attending to the unit when measuring and choosing units.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Subtracts across the mixed-unit pair without converting; keeps the numbers, drops the unit mismatch.

responseLevels.gap: Names which is longer but gives no amount, or subtracts the wrong way / across mismatched units.
responseLevels.full: Measures both in a common unit, subtracts smaller from larger, expresses the difference with its unit, converts a mixed-unit pair to a common unit first, and can show the difference as the overhang on a bar/number line.
responseLevels.partial: Finds and expresses the difference with a unit when both measures share a unit, but is caught by a mixed-unit pair or needs prompting to quantify rather than just compare.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set out two objects of clearly different height/length (e.g. a desk and a bookshelf) with a metre stick or tape, and pose it as a question: 'How much taller is the bookshelf than the desk?' Then give a second pair whose measures come in different units (one labelled in metres, one in centimetres). Watch whether they measure both, subtract correctly, express the difference with a unit, and whether they attend to the units.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who grasps the difference-unknown structure gives an amount with a unit; a child who does not answers only 'the shelf is taller' (comparison, no quantity), subtracts the wrong way, or subtracts across mismatched units — each visible in what they measure and write.
