pedagogy.summary: This is the procedural core of ratio notation: writing a relationship as a:b, simplifying it to its simplest form by dividing both parts by their highest common factor, and converting between a ratio and the fractions of the whole it implies (3:2 means 3/5 and 2/5). The work rests directly on factors/HCF and on the part-to-part vs part-to-whole distinction. Teaching should keep the notation tied to meaning — a:b is 'for every a there are b' — so that simplifying is understood as keeping the same relationship with smaller numbers (an equivalent ratio), and so that the leap to fractions correctly uses the WHOLE (a+b) as the denominator, not the other part.
bestPractices: Tie a:b to 'for every a there are b' and keep order fixed to the wording (boys:girls must be written boys-first) to prevent order reversal.

Teach simplifying as dividing BOTH parts by a common factor, and 'simplest form' as dividing by the highest common factor — explicitly check nothing divides both parts again (12:8 ÷4 = 3:2, and 3,2 share no factor).
Make equivalent ratios explicit: 12:8, 6:4, 3:2 all describe the same relationship — use a ratio table or scaled bars to show they are the same 'for every'.
Draw the part-to-whole conversion from a bar: 3:2 has 5 equal blocks, so 3/5 are the first part and 2/5 the second — the denominator is the total number of parts.
Handle decimal/fraction ratios by scaling up to whole numbers first (0.5:2 → 1:4; 1/2:1/3 → 3:2 via a common multiplier) before simplifying.
Contrast the ratio 3:2 with the fraction 3/2 aloud so children do not read a:b as a/b.
keyRepresentations: a:b notation anchored to 'for every a there are b'
Ratio table showing equivalent ratios (12:8 = 6:4 = 3:2)
Bar model of a+b equal blocks for the part-to-whole conversion (3:2 → 3/5, 2/5)
HCF/common-factor working shown beside the ratio (÷4)
Scaling-up step for decimal/fraction ratios (×2, ×10) to reach whole numbers
commonMisconceptions: Stops before simplest form — divides by a common factor but not the HCF (12:8 → 6:4 and leaves it)
Reverses the order relative to the wording (writes girls:boys)
Converts a:b to fractions using the other part as the denominator (3:2 → 3/2) instead of the whole (3/5)
Simplifies by subtracting a constant from both parts (12:8 → 4:0 or 11:7) rather than dividing — an additive slip

learn.summary: Teach ratio notation as meaning before manipulation: a:b means 'for every a there are b', with order fixed to the wording (boys:girls written boys-first). Simplify by dividing BOTH parts by a common factor, reaching simplest form only when no common factor other than 1 remains (equivalently, once the parts have been divided by their highest common factor). Convert to fractions of the whole using the TOTAL of the parts as the denominator (3:2 means 3/5 and 2/5, not 3/2). Handle decimal or fraction ratios by first scaling up to whole numbers. The core insight is that simplifying keeps the SAME relationship with smaller numbers (an equivalent ratio).

activities.title: Ratio simplifying bench with a shape-stays-the-same check
feedback: If a child stops at 6:4, the 'can this go smaller?' indicator stays red — prompt: 'Is there a number that divides BOTH again?' Both parts still share a factor of 2, so divide again to reach 3:2.
If a child reads 3:2 as 3/2, point to the snapped whole: count ALL the parts (3+2=5); the denominator is the total five blocks, so boys are 3/5.
If the scaled bars change shape after an operation, that operation did not preserve the relationship — check whether both parts were divided by the SAME factor (subtracting a constant does not work).
activities.rationale: Simplifying and converting are manipulations that this activity has learners perform directly — dividing both parts, seeing the relationship preserved, and reading off the part-to-whole fractions — with immediate feedback aimed at the 'not fully simplified' and 'wrong denominator' errors. The scaled bars and the green/red checker are intended to make the preserved relationship and the simplest-form end-state visible.
sourceClaims: A ratio a:b is a part-to-part comparison ('for every a there are b'); the part-to-whole fraction uses the total of the parts, which children conflate with the part-to-part relationship.

Using ratio notation including reduction to simplest form, and understanding that a multiplicative relationship can be expressed as a ratio or a fraction related to the arithmetic of fractions, is the required KS3 content (introduced informally at Year 6 with a:b notation).
learnerActions: Enter a ratio such as 12:8 and simplify it by repeatedly choosing a number to divide BOTH parts by (e.g. ÷4 straight to 3:2, or ÷2 to 6:4 then ÷2 again).
Watch two scaled bars drawn beside the numbers: as 12:8 becomes 6:4 becomes 3:2, the bars keep the same shape/proportion, showing the relationship is preserved.

Use a 'can this go smaller?' indicator that stays red while a common factor greater than 1 still divides both parts and turns green only when none does, so 'simplest form' becomes a testable end-state.
Then snap the 3 and 2 blocks together into one whole of 5 and read off the part-to-whole fractions 3/5 and 2/5 from the total number of blocks.
For a decimal or fraction ratio (0.5:2, or 1/2:1/3), first apply a scale-up step (×2, ×10, or a common multiplier) to reach whole numbers (0.5:2 → 1:4; 1/2:1/3 → 3:2), then simplify.
activities.intendedInsight: Simplifying a ratio keeps the same 'for every' relationship with smaller numbers; simplest form means no common factor remains; and converting to a fraction uses the whole (a+b) as the denominator.

activities.title: Scored practice set with targeted ratio errors
feedback: If 3/2 is chosen for the fraction of the whole, explain it compares the two parts, not part to whole; the denominator must be the total of the parts (5), so boys are 3/5.
If 2/5 is chosen for the fraction of the whole, note that 2/5 is the second part's share; the first part is 3 of the 5 equal parts in total, giving 3/5.
If 6:4 is left as the simplify answer, note both parts still divide by 2, so it is not yet simplest form.
If a match is wrong, check that both parts of the matched ratio divide down to the same pair of numbers (3 and 2).
activities.rationale: Writing, simplifying and converting ratios is well suited to a scored set with fill-in and matching items and incorrect options aimed at the exact misconceptions. This checks recognition and fluency after the meaning is established but does not itself elicit the full self-directed simplifying procedure, so it complements rather than replaces the manipulation activity.
learnerActions: Fill in the blanks to simplify: 12:8 = ☐:☐ (expecting 3:2 in simplest form).
Match several ratios (12:8, 6:4, 9:6) to their shared simplest form 3:2.

Choose what fraction of the whole the first part of 3:2 represents, from options including 3/5 (correct), 3/2 (the part-to-part comparison read as a fraction) and 2/5 (the other part's share of the whole).
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent writing, simplifying and converting of ratios, with the common errors made explicit through the wrong-answer options offered.

activities.title: Verbal coaching of the simplest-form check
feedback: If the child declares a ratio finished too early, ask again whether a single number divides both parts.
If the child subtracts, show that 12:8 → 4:0 removes one quantity entirely and no longer describes the same situation.
activities.rationale: Spoken coaching can rehearse the HCF check and the divide-not-subtract principle; because a symbolic-procedural skill needs repeated independent practice for fluency, this is intended to support the manipulation and practice activities rather than stand alone. The relative efficacy of coaching versus doing is a design judgement, not an established result.
learnerActions: Work through one ratio aloud with a prompt such as 'Can both numbers be divided again?' at each step until no common factor remains.
State why 4:0 (from subtracting) cannot be a valid simplification: it would mean 'no girls', which changes the relationship.
activities.intendedInsight: Simplest form is reached only when no factor divides both parts, and simplifying must preserve the 'for every' relationship (divide, do not subtract).

activities.title: Worked simplify-and-convert reference
feedback: Point back to the ÷4 step when a learner forgets that both parts share that factor.
Point back to the 5-part bar when a learner is unsure where the denominator 5 comes from.
activities.rationale: A fixed worked example shows one complete simplify-and-convert chain and serves as a reference; because it cannot be manipulated across many ratios it does not by itself build fluency, so it is intended for use alongside active practice.
learnerActions: Reveal, on a fixed example, that 12:8 divides by 4 to give 3:2.
Reveal on the bar for 3:2 that there are 5 equal parts, so the fractions of the whole are 3/5 and 2/5.
activities.intendedInsight: A single clear chain from a ratio to its simplest form and then to fractions of the whole, available as a reference model.

constraints: Keep order fixed to the wording: boys:girls must be written boys-first, to prevent order reversal.

Simplest form is reached once both parts have been divided by their highest common factor, either in one step or in several smaller steps; always check that no number other than 1 divides both parts again (e.g. 12:8 ÷4 = 3:2, and 3 and 2 share no common factor other than 1). Stopping at 6:4 is not simplest form.
The part-to-whole fraction uses the TOTAL of the parts as the denominator (3:2 → 3/5 and 2/5), never the other part (not 3/2).
Decimal or fraction ratios must first be scaled up to whole numbers (0.5:2 → 1:4; 1/2:1/3 → 3:2 via a common multiplier) before simplifying.
Contrast the ratio 3:2 with the fraction 3/2 aloud so a:b is not misread as a/b.
Simplifying must preserve the relationship by dividing, not subtracting: 12:8 → 4:0 or 11:7 is an additive error that changes the 'for every'.

The scored practice set checks recognition and fluency but does not elicit the full independent simplifying procedure; it complements active manipulation rather than replacing it. In a fraction-of-the-whole item, keep the incorrect options genuinely distinct in value (e.g. 3/2, the part-to-part reading, versus 2/5, the other part's share of the whole), not numerically equal forms of the same error.
The fixed worked example is a reference only; it cannot be manipulated across many cases and so does not build fluency by itself.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh retrieval or re-verification of the cited sources; activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Source citations support the general principles (part-to-part vs part-to-whole; KS3/Year 6 curriculum placement) but do not establish the efficacy of any specific activity described here.

Comparative-efficacy framings (a symbolic skill 'better drilled by doing than by talking', or that a 3D treatment 'adds nothing') reflect design preference, not established comparative efficacy; retained only as narrowly scoped design notes, not universal laws.

On the original diagnostic counterexample '10:15 boys to girls': the original '5:7.5' is arithmetically correct (10÷2=5, 15÷2=7.5). The point is that halving does NOT reach an integer simplest form because 15 is odd; only dividing by the HCF (5) gives 2:3. Treated as a reasoning note, kept out of learner-facing text.

probeDeeper: 'Is 6:4 the same relationship as 3:2? How do you know?' — checks equivalent-ratio understanding behind simplifying.
'You wrote 3/5 are boys — where does the 5 come from?' — forces the whole-as-denominator to be justified.
Counterexample: 'A different class has ratio 10:15 boys to girls — simplify that' — a child with the HCF idea gives 2:3; a child who only halves gives 5:7.5 or stalls on the odd numbers.
'Could you write this ratio with even smaller whole numbers than your answer?' — tests whether they can confirm simplest form.
assess.correctAnswer: Ratio 12:8, simplified to 3:2 (dividing both by the HCF 4). Boys are 3 out of the 5 equal parts, so 3/5 of the class.

errorPatterns.pattern: Stops before simplest form: divides by a common factor but not the HCF (12:8 → 6:4 and leaves it), thinking it is simplified
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'is there a number that divides BOTH again?' and rebuild the highest-common-factor idea; check simplest form by confirming no common factor remains.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child writes 6:4 (or 12:8 ÷2) and moves on; both parts still share a factor of 2

errorPatterns.pattern: Converts the ratio to a fraction using the other part as the denominator: gives boys as 3/2 (out of the girls) instead of 3/5 (of the whole)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the bar: count ALL the parts in the whole class (3+2 = 5) to set the denominator; distinguish part-to-part (ratio) from part-to-whole (fraction).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child writes 3/2, or uses 2 or the un-simplified 8 as the denominator, not the total number of parts (5)

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses the order: writes 8:12 / 2:3 for boys-to-girls, not matching the wording
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach ratio — scaffold careful mapping: underline the order in the question ('boys : girls') and write the parts in that order. A lapse, not a gap.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The ratio is correct in value but the parts are the wrong way round relative to 'boys to girls'

errorPatterns.pattern: Simplifies by subtracting rather than dividing (12:8 → 4:0, or takes a constant off both parts)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that 4:0 means 'no girls', which is false — simplifying must keep the same 'for every'. Rebuild simplifying as dividing both parts by the same factor.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child subtracts from both parts; the resulting 'ratio' no longer preserves the relationship

responseLevels.gap: Cannot write the ratio in the right order or simplify it; subtracts instead of divides, or gives a fraction with the wrong denominator and cannot correct it.
responseLevels.full: Writes the ratio in the correct order, simplifies to simplest form by the HCF, confirms no common factor remains, and converts correctly to fractions of the whole (a/(a+b)), transferring to new and awkward (decimal/fraction) ratios.
responseLevels.partial: Writes and partially simplifies the ratio (e.g. reaches 6:4) and can convert to a fraction for the practised case, but does not reliably reach simplest form or mishandles the part-to-whole denominator, or the method is fragile when numbers are awkward (odd, decimal).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In a class there are 12 boys and 8 girls. Write the ratio of boys to girls, then simplify it as far as it will go. After that, tell me what fraction of the whole class are boys. Do it however you like — I'll watch, you don't need to explain the rule.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the work reveals the two hinge points: whether the child simplifies to the HIGHEST common factor (3:2) or stops early (6:4), and whether the fraction uses the WHOLE as the denominator (3/5) or the other part (3/2). A child with the procedure divides both parts by 4 and reads 3/5 off the five parts; a child without it leaves a shared factor, reverses the order, or gives 3/2 — each visible in the written work without being asked about it.

sources.claim: Using ratio notation including reduction to simplest form, and understanding that a multiplicative relationship can be expressed as a ratio or a fraction related to the arithmetic of fractions, is the required KS3 content (introduced informally at Year 6 with a:b notation).
sources.source: National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (KS3 ratio, proportion and rates of change; Year 6)

sources.claim: A ratio a:b is a part-to-part comparison ('for every a there are b'); the part-to-whole fraction uses the total of the parts, which children conflate with the part-to-part relationship.
sources.source: NRICH (University of Cambridge) — 'Ratio or Proportion?' article

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 8–9y; determine the unknown whole number in a × or ÷ equation relating three numbers (8×?=48, ?×6=42, ?÷5=9).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y3–Y4 'solve missing number problems' involving ×÷ using known facts and the inverse.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.OA.4 — 'determine the unknown whole number in a multiplication or division equation relating three whole numbers, e.g. 8 × ? = 48, 5 = ? ÷ 3, 6 × 6 = ?'.
• Operational details — this applies division-as-unknown-factor and the ×÷ inverse to solve for a missing value in ANY position (missing factor, missing product, missing dividend/divisor/quotient). The key strategy is rewriting via the fact family: 8×?=48 → 48÷8=?; ?÷5=9 → ?=9×5. Children must attend to WHERE the unknown sits, because the rescue operation differs (a missing dividend is found by multiplying, a missing factor by dividing). This also nurtures the relational (not operational) view of '=' as balance, seeding algebra. Use the bar model and fact-family triangle; cover one number and decide how to find it.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8): find a missing factor with a known fact (7×?=63). Tier B (age 8–9): find the unknown in any position, including ?÷5=9 (missing dividend). Tier C (age 9): explain the strategy for each position and check by substituting back.
bestPractices: Use the fact-family triangle: cover any one of the three numbers and decide whether to × or ÷ to find it — making the unknown's position drive the method.
Rewrite the equation using the inverse (8×?=48 → ?=48÷8; ?÷5=9 → ?=9×5) and verbalise why.
Stress the relational meaning of '=' as balance, not 'the answer comes next', to prevent left-to-right misreading and seed algebra.
Include unknowns in every position (factor, product, dividend, divisor, quotient), not just missing products.
Always check by substituting the found value back into the original equation.
keyRepresentations: Fact-family triangle — cover-a-number to choose the operation
Bar model — whole/part structure showing which quantity is missing
Balance/scale image — the relational equals sign
Inverse-rewrite chains (8×?=48 → 48÷8=?)
commonMisconceptions: Applying the same operation regardless of the unknown's position (e.g. always dividing), so a missing dividend is wrong.
Reading '=' operationally ('do something to get the answer') rather than as balance, mishandling 5 = ?÷3.
Treating division as commutative when rewriting (?÷5=9 → ?=5÷9).
Guess-and-check without using the inverse, which is slow and error-prone.
Not checking the answer back in the original equation.

learn.summary: For 8–9 year-olds: find the unknown whole number in a multiplication or division equation relating three numbers, with the unknown in ANY position (missing factor 8×?=48 or ?×6=42, missing product 6×7=?, missing dividend ?÷5=9, missing divisor 48÷?=6, missing quotient 42÷6=?). The central idea is that the operation you use to 'rescue' the unknown depends on WHERE the gap sits: a missing factor is found by dividing, a missing dividend by multiplying. Build this on the fact-family/inverse relationship and a relational (balance) reading of '=', and always check by substituting the found value back into the original equation.

activities.title: Cover-and-solve with a fact-family triangle
feedback: If a learner always divides regardless of position, point to the covered corner on the triangle: when the TOP (product/dividend) is hidden, the two bottom numbers are multiplied to find it.
When a learner correctly flips the operation as the gap moves, name it: 'You chose the operation from where the gap was — that's the whole strategy.'
If a learner treats ?÷5=9 as 5÷9 or 9÷5, show that division is not commutative here: ?÷5=9 rearranges to ?=9×5=45, and checking 45÷5=9 confirms it.
activities.rationale: Making the unknown's position drive the method, and seeing one trio solve several equations, is intended to build the position-dependent strategy rather than a single memorised move. The fact-family/inverse structure supports missing-number reasoning.
sourceClaims: The fact-family/inverse strategy and a relational (balance) meaning of '=' support missing-number work and seed algebra.
Y3–Y4 pupils solve missing-number problems involving ×÷ using known facts and the inverse.
3.OA.4 requires determining the unknown in a × or ÷ equation relating three whole numbers, in any position.
learnerActions: Work with one trio of linked numbers, e.g. 6, 7 and 42 arranged on a fact-family triangle (42 at the top as the product; 6 and 7 at the bottom as the factors).
Cover one of the three numbers and decide: to find THIS number, do I multiply or divide? State your choice aloud before revealing.
Now cover a DIFFERENT number of the same trio and decide again. Notice when the operation flips: cover 42 (acting as product or dividend) → multiply 6×7; cover a factor like 7 → divide 42÷6.
Write the matching equation for each covered case: 6×?=42, ?×6=42, 42÷?=6, and ?÷6=7. Confirm the single trio solves them all.
Say in your own words: 'What I do — times or divide — is decided by WHERE the gap is, not by the numbers.'
If a bar model or balance view is available, use it to see which quantity (whole or part) is missing and recolour/update it as you solve.
activities.intendedInsight: The operation needed to find an unknown is determined by its position in the equation (missing factor → divide; missing dividend/product → multiply), and one fact family generates every related missing-number equation.

activities.title: Rewrite with the inverse, then check by substituting back
feedback: If a learner subtracts or adds the two visible numbers (e.g. treats 7×?=63 as 63−7=56), restate it as 'seven times WHAT is 63?' and reach for the times-table fact or 63÷7.
If a learner reaches the right method but makes a fact slip, don't reteach the strategy — have them check by substituting back, which surfaces the arithmetic error.
Praise substituting-back as the habit that catches mistakes: 'Putting it back in and seeing it balance is how you know you're right.'
activities.rationale: Explicit inverse-rewriting and a balance meaning of '=' are intended to help counter left-to-right misreading and reduce the division-commutativity error, and the substitute-back habit is intended to seed algebraic checking.
sourceClaims: The fact-family/inverse strategy and a relational (balance) meaning of '=' support missing-number work and seed algebra.
Y3–Y4 pupils solve missing-number problems involving ×÷ using known facts and the inverse.
learnerActions: Take a missing-number equation and rewrite it using the inverse operation, saying why: 8×?=48 becomes ?=48÷8; ?÷5=9 becomes ?=9×5.
Solve the rewritten equation using a known fact rather than guessing.
Substitute your answer back into the ORIGINAL equation and check both sides are equal, e.g. for ?=45: 45÷5=9 ✓.
Try the relational reading of '=' with a reversed equation like 5=?÷3: read '=' as 'both sides balance', find ?=15, and check 5=15÷3.
Compare rewriting-with-the-inverse to trial-and-error on 7×?=63: find it directly with 63÷7=9 and notice the inverse avoids repeated guessing.
activities.intendedInsight: Rewriting an equation with the inverse operation gives the unknown directly, and substituting back verifies it; '=' means both sides balance, not 'the answer comes next'.

activities.title: Mixed-position practice and spot-the-error
feedback: If a learner divides when a missing dividend needs multiplying (producing e.g. 1.8 from 9÷5), return to the fact-family triangle: with 5 and 9 at the bottom, the missing dividend sits at the top and is found by multiplying, 9×5=45.
For the reversed equation 5=?÷3, if the learner stalls, remind them '=' balances both sides; ?÷3 must equal 5, so ?=15.
Reinforce the discriminating point: a single fixed move (always divide, or always multiply the two shown numbers) will fail at least one item — the position tells you which operation.
activities.rationale: Deliberately varying the unknown's position and including error-analysis targets the most common misconceptions and is intended to check that the strategy generalises rather than being tied to one format.
sourceClaims: 3.OA.4 requires determining the unknown in a × or ÷ equation relating three whole numbers, in any position.
Y3–Y4 pupils solve missing-number problems involving ×÷ using known facts and the inverse.
learnerActions: Solve a set with the unknown in every position: 8×?=48 (missing factor), ?×6=42 (missing factor), ?÷5=9 (missing dividend), 48÷?=6 (missing divisor), 42÷6=? (missing quotient), 6×7=? (missing product), 5=?÷3 (reversed).
For each, first say which operation you need and WHY, then solve.
Spot-the-error: review a worked solution where ?÷5=9 was 'solved' as ?=5÷9, explain what went wrong, and give the correct value with a check.
Answer: 'Which operation finds a missing dividend — multiply or divide?' and justify with an example.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency comes from correctly choosing the operation by position across all cases, and from recognising common wrong moves (fixed operation, treating division as commutative).

activities.title: Talk it through: 'what's missing, times or divide?'
feedback: If explanations default to 'I just divided', press for the position reason: 'Which number was hidden, and why does that mean divide?'
Encourage checking each stated fact-family member against the trio so none is missed or malformed.
activities.rationale: A Socratic exchange can rehearse the reasoning and the relational view, complementing hands-on work; it is a useful rehearsal of justification rather than a substitute for manipulating cases. Spoken justification does not by itself guarantee the strategy transfers to independent written work.
sourceClaims: The fact-family/inverse strategy and a relational (balance) meaning of '=' support missing-number work and seed algebra.
learnerActions: With a partner or adult, play a 'mystery number' game: one person hides a value in an equation, the other must say how they'll find it (which operation and why) before computing.
Explain the strategy for each position in words: why a missing factor is found by dividing and a missing dividend by multiplying.
Write out the full fact family for a trio you are given, e.g. 7, 9 and 63: 7×9=63, 9×7=63, 63÷7=9, 63÷9=7.
activities.intendedInsight: Verbalising the choice of operation and generating the full fact family externalises the reasoning and is intended to help consolidate relational understanding.

constraints: Include unknowns in EVERY position (factor, product, dividend, divisor, quotient), not just missing products.
Always require checking by substituting the found value back into the original equation.
Emphasise the relational meaning of '=' (both sides balance), not 'the answer comes next', to prevent misreading reversed equations like 5=?÷3.
Division is not commutative: ?÷5=9 rearranges to ?=9×5, never 5÷9 or 9÷5. Correct this error directly rather than leaving it uncorrected.

A fill-in-the-blank or multiple-choice format is well suited to assessing across positions but, being fixed, tests the strategy more than it elicits the position-dependent reasoning; pair it with manipulable or verbalised work for teaching.
A static tap-to-reveal fact-family triangle is a clean strategy anchor but does not let the learner try many cases with feedback; use it alongside active practice.

Optional supports such as a bar model, a balance view, live recolouring of the missing quantity, or a hidden-card triangle make the mechanism concrete; they are helpful examples, not required mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and efficacy wording has been qualified accordingly.
Self-audit arithmetic check: 8×6=48, 7×9=63, 63÷7=9, 9×5=45 and 45÷5=9, 6×7=42, 48÷6=8, 15÷3=5 all verified correct as used.
The legacy claim that '3D adds cost without insight' for this topic has been removed as an unsupported universal; the comparative efficacy of representations is not established by the cited sources.
Two of three sources are marked verified:false in the original row (CCSS-M 3.OA.4 and NCETM guidance); the standards content is widely known but was not re-checked here.

The error pattern 'child divides when missing dividend needs multiplication, giving 1.8' (9÷5=1.8) is retained ONLY as a diagnostic signal; the activity corrects it to ?=9×5=45 and never presents 1.8 as an acceptable answer.

The 'Talk it through' activity cites the fact-family/relational source for the content being rehearsed; that source does not establish that a conversational format is effective or necessary, so the medium's benefit is stated only as a narrow affordance.

probeDeeper: How did you find what goes in the box for 7 × □ = 63?
For □ ÷ 5 = 9, why do you multiply rather than divide?
How can you check your box value is right by putting it back in?
Write the fact family that goes with 7, 9 and 63.
assess.correctAnswer: 9 (7×9 = 63, or 63÷7); 45 (because □÷5 = 9 means □ = 9×5). The teacher watches for the child using the inverse operation / related fact — recognising the first as a missing-factor and the second as a missing-dividend recovered by multiplying.

errorPatterns.pattern: operates on the two visible numbers with the operation shown — for □ ÷ 5 = 9 computes 9 ÷ 5 or 5 ÷ 9 rather than 9 × 5
errorPatterns.nextMove: use the fact-family triangle: with 5 and 9 at the corners the missing dividend is at the top, found by multiplying; the ÷ sentence rearranges to ×.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child divides when the missing dividend needs multiplication, giving 1.8 or similar

errorPatterns.pattern: adds/subtracts to fill the box — treats 7 × □ = 63 as 63 − 7 = 56
errorPatterns.nextMove: restate as 'seven times WHAT is 63' and reach for the times-table fact or 63÷7.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child subtracts or adds the two numbers

errorPatterns.pattern: relies on slow trial-and-error, plugging numbers in, with no use of known facts or inverse
errorPatterns.nextMove: show the inverse gives the answer directly (63÷7 = 9); trial-and-error is unnecessary once the relationship is seen.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child tries 7×5, 7×6… until it works, rather than dividing

errorPatterns.pattern: correct method, fact/arithmetic slip
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach; have the child check by substituting the answer back into the equation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: right approach, wrong number

responseLevels.gap: adds/subtracts to fill boxes, or divides when the missing dividend needs multiplication; no inverse reasoning.
responseLevels.full: uses the inverse relationship / related fact to find the unknown in any position, explains the strategy, and checks by substituting back.
responseLevels.partial: solves the missing-factor case via a known fact but mishandles the missing-dividend case, or leans on trial-and-error.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to find the missing number in each while you watch their method: 7 × □ = 63, then □ ÷ 5 = 9. Encourage them to say how they worked it out. Watch whether they use a related multiplication/division fact and the inverse relationship, or resort to trial-and-error.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The two boxes sit in different positions (missing factor vs missing dividend), and children who apply one fixed move (always divide, or always multiply the two visible numbers) fail one. Watching the method reveals whether they reason from the inverse relationship or guess-and-check.

pedagogy.summary: Similarity is the relationship where one shape is an enlargement of another: corresponding ANGLES are equal and corresponding SIDES are in a constant ratio — the scale factor. The single load-bearing obstacle is that children reason ADDITIVELY (add a constant to each side) where the concept is MULTIPLICATIVE (multiply each side by the scale factor). A rectangle grown from 3×5 to 8×10 by 'adding 5 to each side' looks bigger but is NOT similar, because 8÷3≠10÷5. Teaching must make this multiplicative structure felt — through enlargement from a centre with ray lines (every distance from the centre is multiplied by the scale factor while angles stay fixed) and through exposing the additive error directly.
bestPractices: Confront the additive misconception head-on: present a shape 'enlarged' by adding the same amount to each side and have children test whether corresponding side ratios match — the diagonal of the original, extended, misses the corner of the fake enlargement

Enlarge from a centre of enlargement using ray lines: draw rays from the centre through each vertex, and multiply each vertex's distance from the centre by the scale factor — makes visible that enlargement scales distances, not adds to them
Build a corresponding-sides ratio table so children check the scale factor on EVERY pair of corresponding sides, not just one
Keep angles explicit throughout: measure or mark corresponding angles before and after enlargement to establish they are invariant while sides scale
Connect to ratio and to the multiplier: scale factor is the constant ratio between corresponding sides, linking similarity to y=mx proportional reasoning
keyRepresentations: Centre of enlargement with ray lines through vertices (distances × scale factor)
Corresponding-sides ratio table (each pair reduced to the same scale factor)
Two overlaid shapes with corresponding angles marked equal and sides labelled with their ratio
Diagonal test: extending the diagonal of the original passes through the corner of a true enlargement but misses a fake (additive) one
commonMisconceptions: Additive reasoning: treats 'add the same amount to each side' as an enlargement (3×5 → 8×10 by +5), when similarity requires multiplying each side by a constant
Believes angles get bigger when a shape is enlarged (scales the angles along with the sides)
Uses a different multiplier for different sides, or checks the scale factor on only one pair of corresponding sides and assumes the rest match
Enlarges the shape but does not scale each vertex's distance from the centre of enlargement, so the image is the wrong size or position

learn.summary: Similarity means one shape is an enlargement of another: corresponding angles stay equal and corresponding sides share a single constant ratio (the scale factor). The central obstacle is additive reasoning — treating 'add the same amount to each side' as an enlargement. A 3×5 rectangle grown to 8×10 by adding 5 looks bigger but is not similar, because 8÷3≈2.67 while 10÷5=2. Learners need to see the structure as multiplicative: enlargement from a centre multiplies every vertex's distance from the centre by the scale factor while leaving angles fixed, and a genuinely similar rectangle (e.g. 6×10, each side ×2) must be contrasted with the additive fake.

activities.title: Grow it by adding, then test whether it stays the same shape
feedback: If a learner says the 8×10 is similar because '+5 was added to each side', have them divide both pairs of corresponding sides: 8÷3 ≈ 2.67 is not equal to 10÷5 = 2, so there is no single scale factor — adding equal amounts does not in general keep a shape similar (it only works when the sides being compared are equal, as in a square)
If they check only one pair (e.g. 10÷5 = 2) and conclude similar, ask them to test the other pair (8÷3) too; a single matching pair is not enough

Where a tool can recompute live, let a slider add a constant c to each side while the ratio table and extended-diagonal overlay update, so the ratios visibly diverge as the rectangle distorts — this is one way to make the failure felt rather than told; a hand-computed table achieves the same reasoning
Reinforce the contrast: 6×10 is similar because both sides are ×2; 8×10 is not, because the two ratios differ
activities.rationale: Confronting the additive misconception directly — with learner-computed corresponding-side ratios and the diagonal test — targets the single load-bearing obstacle, and contrasting a true multiple (6×10) with the additive fake (8×10) prevents 'right answer for the wrong reason'.
sourceClaims: Students attend to the additive difference a−b between corresponding sides rather than the multiplicative ratio a:b when judging similarity; the 'add five to each side' construction (Example 5) looks like an enlargement but is not similar, and drawing a diagonal reveals the shapes are not similar; scale factor is the constant multiplier linking corresponding sides, connecting to y=mx.

Enlargement multiplies each side length by the scale factor (you multiply, not add); corresponding angles are identical while corresponding sides are in proportion, which is what makes shapes similar; the scale factor is found by dividing a new side by the corresponding original side; enlarging from a centre uses ray lines that scale each vertex's distance from the centre.
learnerActions: Start with a 3 cm by 5 cm rectangle and predict, in writing, whether making it '8 by 10 by adding 5 to each side' keeps it the same shape just bigger — say yes or no and WHY before checking
Divide each pair of corresponding sides and build a ratio table: 8÷3 ≈ 2.67 beside 10÷5 = 2

Place the 3×5 rectangle on the 8×10 rectangle at a shared corner, with the 3 cm side along the 8 cm side and the 5 cm side along the 10 cm side. Extend the diagonal of the 3×5 that starts at the shared corner and observe whether it passes through the opposite corner of the 8×10 rectangle (it misses it)

Now compare the 3×5 against a 6×10 rectangle: check both ratios (6÷3=2 and 10÷5=2). Then, with the 3 cm side along the 6 cm side at a shared corner, extend the diagonal from that shared corner to see it pass through the opposite corner of the 6×10
State which rectangle is similar to the original and justify using a single shared scale factor
activities.intendedInsight: Adding a constant to each side does not in general preserve shape (the only exception is when the sides being compared are equal, as in a square); similarity requires every pair of corresponding sides to reduce to the SAME multiplier. The 8×10 fails the ratio test; the 6×10 (×2) passes.

activities.title: Enlarge from a centre with ray lines
feedback: If the image is the wrong size or in the wrong place, check that every vertex's distance from the centre was multiplied by the scale factor, not just some vertices
If a learner expects angles to grow, have them measure corresponding angles before and after: only distances scale, angles stay fixed

Where a tool allows it, a draggable scale-factor control that fires ray lines, multiplies each vertex distance live, keeps angle readouts constant, and snaps the ratio table to one shared number can make the multiplicative structure visible as it changes — but a hand-drawn ray diagram achieves the same reasoning
Connect the result to proportional reasoning: the scale factor is the constant ratio between corresponding sides, like the multiplier m in y = mx
activities.rationale: Enlarging from a centre with ray lines makes visible that enlargement multiplies distances rather than adding to them, and keeping angles explicit establishes their invariance — both named best practices for this concept.
sourceClaims: Enlargement multiplies each side length by the scale factor (you multiply, not add); corresponding angles are identical while corresponding sides are in proportion, which is what makes shapes similar; the scale factor is found by dividing a new side by the corresponding original side; enlarging from a centre uses ray lines that scale each vertex's distance from the centre.
KS3 pupils should interpret and use scale factors and understand similar figures as enlargements with corresponding sides in a fixed ratio and equal corresponding angles.
learnerActions: Mark a centre of enlargement and draw rays from it through each vertex of the 3×5 rectangle
Choose a scale factor and multiply EACH vertex's distance from the centre by that factor to place the image vertices
Measure or mark the corresponding angles before and after enlarging, confirming they are unchanged
Fill a ratio table for every pair of corresponding sides, confirming they all reduce to the same scale factor
activities.intendedInsight: Enlargement scales distances from a centre by a constant multiplier and preserves angles; the one shared ratio IS the scale factor, which is why the image is similar to the original.

activities.title: Decide similar or not, and find the scale factor
feedback: A judgement/sorting task can check and reinforce the multiplicative test, but on its own it does not let a learner feel distances scaling from a centre; pair it with hands-on enlargement for that
If a learner picks 'yes — you added 5 to each side', treat it as the additive error and return to dividing corresponding sides
When finding a scale factor, remind learners to verify it on every pair of corresponding sides, not just the first
activities.rationale: Discrimination tasks with the additive answer as an explicit distractor assess the multiplicative check cleanly and surface the target misconception; they complement, rather than replace, the constructive enlargement work.
sourceClaims: Enlargement multiplies each side length by the scale factor (you multiply, not add); corresponding angles are identical while corresponding sides are in proportion, which is what makes shapes similar; the scale factor is found by dividing a new side by the corresponding original side; enlarging from a centre uses ray lines that scale each vertex's distance from the centre.
learnerActions: Judge whether 3×5 is similar to 8×10 or to 6×10, giving a reason — and reject 'yes, you added 5 to each side' as a justification
Find a scale factor by dividing a new side length by its corresponding original side
Match corresponding sides between two similar shapes and sort several shape-pairs into 'similar' and 'not similar'
For a stated enlargement by scale factor 3 applied to a triangle, say what happens to its angles (unchanged) and its sides (×3)
activities.intendedInsight: The multiplicative test — all corresponding-side ratios equal, angles unchanged — can be applied consistently to classify and quantify similarity.

activities.title: Summary reference: angles equal, sides in one ratio
feedback: Use this as a reference card AFTER constructing and testing enlargements; because it does not recompute, it confirms rather than discovers the multiplicative structure
If a learner is unsure why the additive 8×10 fails, send them back to the ratio table and diagonal test rather than relying on the summary alone
activities.rationale: A static, tap-to-reveal reference can label corresponding angles as equal and sides with their ratio and annotate a ray-line diagram — useful for consolidation, though it cannot let the learner vary the scale factor and watch the structure respond.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils should interpret and use scale factors and understand similar figures as enlargements with corresponding sides in a fixed ratio and equal corresponding angles.
learnerActions: Reveal, on two overlaid shapes, the corresponding angles marked equal and the corresponding sides labelled with their shared scale factor
Reveal that angles are unchanged under enlargement while each side is multiplied by the scale factor
Re-read a labelled ray-line diagram showing distances from the centre multiplied by the scale factor
activities.intendedInsight: Similarity consolidated as a single statement: corresponding angles equal, corresponding sides in one constant ratio, produced by enlargement from a centre.

constraints: Target the additive misconception explicitly: learners must compute corresponding-side ratios themselves and see the additive construction fail, not merely be told the rule.
Require the scale factor to be verified on EVERY pair of corresponding sides; one matching pair does not establish similarity.
Keep a genuinely similar contrast case available (e.g. 6×10, each side ×2) alongside the additive fake (8×10) so a correct 'not similar' verdict cannot come from a lucky guess.

A judgement/classification task assesses and reinforces the multiplicative test but does not by itself give the experience of distances scaling from a centre; pair it with hands-on or live enlargement.
A static reference card confirms the structure but cannot recompute as the scale factor changes; use it after construction, not instead of it.

Spoken or in-role framing can pose the additive trap, but whatever the medium the learner must themselves perform and see the corresponding-side computation; hearing a stated ratio is recognition, which does not by itself elicit that production.
Scaling solids (volume scale factor = SF³) is a later extension beyond this topic's 2D objective and should not be mixed in here.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Independent re-audit confirmed the key arithmetic: 8÷3 ≈ 2.67 and 10÷5 = 2 are unequal, so 3×5 to 8×10 is correctly NOT similar; 6÷3 = 2 and 10÷5 = 2, so 3×5 to 6×10 IS similar (×2). These are consistent across summary, activities and feedback, and the diagonal test (shared-corner alignment) agrees with the ratio test.
The original 'angles get bigger when enlarged' is a stated misconception, correctly handled by measuring invariant angles; retained as an error to confront, never as a learner instruction.

The source row's claim that '3D adds nothing to the core insight' is a catalog-style comparative judgement; softened here to note only that solid scaling is an out-of-scope later extension, without asserting universal necessity or superiority of any medium.

Modality statements about conversation and static reference cards are kept as narrow observable affordances (a sort/summary can check or confirm the test but does not itself elicit the learner's computation or let the scale factor vary), not as categorical claims that any medium cannot teach.
The National Curriculum source is flagged verified:false in the row; cited only as a curriculum-scope reference, with no claim of empirical efficacy.

Activity 4's cited NC claim supports the mathematical facts being summarised but not the design judgement that a static card 'confirms rather than discovers'; that limitation is an unsourced pedagogical note.

assess.poeTask: Show the 3-by-5 rectangle and say: 'I am going to make a bigger rectangle by adding 5 to each side, giving 8 by 10. PREDICT: will the new rectangle be a SIMILAR shape — the same shape, just bigger? Write down yes or no and WHY before we check.' The stated reason is the diagnostic part. Then OBSERVE: extend the diagonal of the small rectangle — it misses the corner of the 8×10 — and compute 8÷3 against 10÷5. The additive prediction ('yes, similar') is violated: the ratios differ and the diagonal does not line up. EXPLAIN: adding a constant does not preserve the shape; only multiplying every side by the same scale factor does.
probeDeeper: Counterexample: 'What about a 6 by 10 rectangle — is THAT one similar to the 3 by 5? How do you know?' (both ratios = 2, so yes — tests whether the child applies the multiplicative test consistently.)
'You checked one pair of sides. Do the OTHER corresponding sides give the same scale factor? Show me.'
'If I enlarge a triangle by scale factor 3, what happens to its angles? Why?' (should say angles unchanged, only sides ×3.)
'Extend the diagonal of the 3 by 5 rectangle. For a true enlargement it passes through the far corner — does it pass through the corner of the 8 by 10? What does that tell you?'
assess.correctAnswer: No, it is not similar. The corresponding sides are not in the same ratio: 8÷3 ≈ 2.67 but 10÷5 = 2, so there is no single scale factor. (A similar rectangle would be, e.g., 6 by 10 — each side multiplied by 2. The 8×10 was made by ADDING 5 to each side, which does not preserve the shape.)

errorPatterns.pattern: Additive reasoning about enlargement: 'yes, it's similar — you add 5 to each side, so it's just bigger'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront directly: have the child divide each pair of corresponding sides (8÷3 vs 10÷5) and extend the original's diagonal to see it miss the new corner; then contrast with 6×10 where both ratios are 2. Reteach scale-factor-as-multiplier.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — you add 5 to each side, so the new one is just the first rectangle made bigger
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says yes; justifies by the equal amount added to each side rather than a common multiplier; does not divide corresponding sides

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes angles enlarge too: 'it's similar but the corners are bigger now because the whole shape got bigger'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Measure corresponding angles before and after a true enlargement to show they are unchanged; establish that only distances scale, angles are invariant.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes, it's similar, and its angles are bigger too because everything got bigger
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats angle size as scaling with the sides; may say the shapes are 'similar but with bigger angles', which is self-contradictory

errorPatterns.pattern: Checks only one pair of corresponding sides (or uses a different multiplier per side) and assumes the rest match
errorPatterns.nextMove: Require the scale factor to be verified on EVERY pair of corresponding sides via a ratio table; a single matching pair is not sufficient. Reteach ratio-as-constant-relationship.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Divides just one pair — e.g. 10÷5=2 — and concludes similar without testing 8÷3; or accepts different multipliers on different sides

responseLevels.gap: Says the 8×10 is similar and justifies additively (added the same amount to each side), or judges by 'it looks like a bigger rectangle'; does not compare side ratios.
responseLevels.full: Divides corresponding sides, finds 8÷3≠10÷5 so no common scale factor and declares not similar; contrasts with 6×10 (SF 2) which is; explains angles stay equal while sides scale by a constant multiplier; transfers the multiplicative test to a new pair unprompted.
responseLevels.partial: Knows similarity needs corresponding sides 'in proportion' and can find a scale factor when handed one matching pair, but lists the parts (equal angles, sides in ratio) without reliably testing every pair — e.g. checks 10÷5 only, or cannot yet explain WHY the additive 8×10 fails.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a rectangle that is 3 cm by 5 cm. I make a new rectangle that is 8 cm by 10 cm. Is the new rectangle a similar shape to the first one — the same shape, just a different size? Tell me yes or no, and then tell me how you decided.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child reasoning multiplicatively divides corresponding sides, finds 2.67≠2, and says not similar. A child reasoning additively sees +5 applied to both sides and says 'yes, similar' — the two lines of reasoning give OPPOSITE answers. The numbers are chosen so the additive answer (8×10) is a plausible 'enlargement' yet fails the ratio test, and a genuinely similar option (6×10) exists to contrast. Getting it right for the wrong reason is hard: 'yes' can only come from the additive error.

pedagogy.summary: Children measure area by covering a figure with unit squares and counting them — in square centimetres, square metres, square inches or square feet — including irregular and L-shaped figures, and compare two shapes by their counts. The counting must be of the squares that COVER the interior with no gaps or overlaps (not the boundary), done systematically so every square is counted once, with the answer stated in square units.
bestPractices: Cover the whole interior with unit squares, no gaps or overlaps, and count the covering squares — not the squares around the edge.
Count systematically (row by row, or decompose an L-shape into rectangles) so no square is missed or double-counted.
Use real square-unit tiles (square-centimetre tiles on a book cover) before squared-paper diagrams.
Compare areas of two shapes directly by their counts.
Always state the area in square units (square cm, square m).
Keep to whole unit squares at this stage; treat part-squares informally rather than with a formula.
keyRepresentations: Square-centimetre tiles covering a book cover
L-shaped and irregular figures on squared paper
A shape decomposed into rectangles for systematic counting
A count recorded with its square unit (e.g. '18 square cm')
commonMisconceptions: Counts the squares around the boundary (perimeter) instead of the squares covering the interior.
Leaves gaps or overlaps, or counts unsystematically so squares are missed or double-counted (especially on L-shapes).
Counts every partly-covered square at the edge as a whole square, overestimating.
Gives the count as a bare number without the square unit.

learn.summary: Children measure area by covering a figure's interior with unit squares — no gaps or overlaps — and counting the covering squares systematically, stating the answer in square units (square cm, square m, square in, square ft). Work includes irregular and L-shaped figures (decomposed into rectangles), comparing two shapes by their counts, and telling the area (every covering square, including the squares along the inner edge) apart from the length of the boundary (unit lengths around the outline, i.e. perimeter) and from a count of only the border squares. Concrete tiles on a real surface precede squared-paper diagrams. Keep to whole unit squares at this stage, treating edge part-squares informally.

activities.title: Tile and count an L-shaped garden
feedback: If a child counts only the squares along the border, point out that the border squares are part of the covering but the squares further in must be counted too; shade the whole interior, border squares included, and recount every covering square. If they count unit lengths around the outline instead, explain that this is the distance around (perimeter), not the area.
If tiles leave gaps or overlap, or recounting gives a different total, cover fully with no gaps/overlaps and count row by row or by decomposing into rectangles, marking each square as it is counted.
If they lose track in the L's notch, decompose the L into two rectangles and count each separately, then add.
If they give '18' with no unit, treat the answer as incomplete and build the habit of naming the square unit — the counting itself is sound.
activities.rationale: Covering a region with no gaps or overlaps and counting the whole unit squares, including decomposing rectilinear (L-shaped) figures into rectangles, is the Grade-3 area practice described in the source progressions. Making the systematic covering the act the child performs targets the gap/overlap and edge-counting difficulties directly.
sourceClaims: Area is measured by counting unit squares — square cm, square m, square in, square ft and improvised units (3.MD.6) — covering the region with a two-dimensional unit and parts of the unit without gaps or overlaps; instruction often begins by comparing which of several rectangles covers the most area, and discussions must clearly distinguish area from length. Grade-3 area instruction focuses on covering with whole unit squares.

When iterating units children may leave gaps or overlaps, treating measuring as placing units along a path rather than covering a region with no gaps; L-shaped (rectilinear) figures are decomposed into rectangles, and coordinating the covering requires spatial structuring that develops with many array activities.
learnerActions: Cover an L-shaped figure's whole interior with unit squares so there are no gaps and no overlaps, including the awkward squares inside the notch of the L.
Count the covering squares systematically — row by row, or by splitting the L into two rectangles and counting each — marking each square as you count it so none is missed or double-counted.
State the result in square units, e.g. '18 square cm' or in square metres, not just a bare number.
Repeat with a plain rectangle and then compare two shapes side by side, deciding which covers more by comparing their counts.
activities.intendedInsight: Area is the count of unit squares that cover the inside of a shape — notches and all — and is about the surface inside, not the fence or distance running around the edge.

activities.title: Tile a real surface before squared paper
feedback: If tiles overlap or leave bare patches, rearrange so they tile the surface completely and evenly before counting.
If the paper-diagram count differs from the count of physical tiles, line the two up and check that each paper square stands for exactly one tile.
activities.rationale: The progressions describe starting from covering with a two-dimensional unit; using real square-unit tiles on a concrete surface before abstract squared-paper diagrams is intended to ground the covering idea, though the cited sources do not establish the ordering's comparative efficacy.
sourceClaims: Area is measured by counting unit squares — square cm, square m, square in, square ft and improvised units (3.MD.6) — covering the region with a two-dimensional unit and parts of the unit without gaps or overlaps; instruction often begins by comparing which of several rectangles covers the most area, and discussions must clearly distinguish area from length. Grade-3 area instruction focuses on covering with whole unit squares.
learnerActions: Lay square-centimetre tiles across a small real surface such as a book cover, filling it with no gaps or overlaps; if strips narrower than a tile are left at the edges, note them informally as part-squares rather than counting them as whole tiles.
Count the tiles and say the area in square centimetres.
Then move to a squared-paper diagram of the same shape drawn at the same size (one paper square for each tile) and count the covering squares there.
activities.intendedInsight: Measuring area means physically covering a surface with equal square units and counting them; the squared-paper diagram is a picture of that same covering.

activities.title: Compare and check with quick counting questions
feedback: If a child picks the answer that comes from counting only the border squares, show that the inside squares were left out: the area includes every covering square, the border squares and the ones further in.
For part-squares at an edge, discuss them informally — do not count every touched square as a whole one, and do not apply a formula at this stage.
activities.rationale: Checking understanding with comparison and count items, including an edge-counting distractor, surfaces the boundary-counting difficulty; such questions verify understanding rather than build the systematic covering, so pair them with hands-on tiling. The part-square figure is used for discussion, not a scored count, because whole-square counting is the Grade-3 focus.
sourceClaims: Area is measured by counting unit squares — square cm, square m, square in, square ft and improvised units (3.MD.6) — covering the region with a two-dimensional unit and parts of the unit without gaps or overlaps; instruction often begins by comparing which of several rectangles covers the most area, and discussions must clearly distinguish area from length. Grade-3 area instruction focuses on covering with whole unit squares.
learnerActions: Given two shapes on squared paper, decide which covers more area by counting each one's squares.

Answer a short set of count-the-squares questions using whole-square figures — a plain rectangle and an L-shape, each with a definite count — then separately look at one shape with part-squares at the edge and discuss (rather than score) how to handle the part-squares informally.

Watch for a tempting wrong answer that comes from counting only the border squares (or the unit lengths around the outline) instead of all the squares covering the inside, and explain why it is wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: Comparing areas means comparing counts of all the covering squares, edge squares included; counting only the border squares does not give the area, and the distance around the outline (perimeter) is a different thing from the area inside.

activities.title: Read a finished counted figure
feedback: Use this reference to contrast with a child's own counting — ask them to point to any square they counted that the reference did not, and discuss.
activities.rationale: A static filled figure with the count shown illustrates the target result and can prompt discussion, but it cannot rehearse the systematic gap-free counting itself, so it serves as a worked reference rather than the main practice.
learnerActions: Study a figure already filled with unit squares and its revealed count, e.g. '18 square cm'.
Retrace which squares were counted and confirm every square inside the outline, including those along the edge, is counted exactly once, and nothing outside the outline is counted.
Say back how the count and unit were obtained.
activities.intendedInsight: A completed, correctly counted figure models what a finished area measurement looks like: every interior square counted once, with the square unit named.

constraints: Count every square that covers the inside of the outline, with no gaps or overlaps — including the squares along the edge, which are part of the area. Do not count only the border squares, and do not count squares outside the outline. The distance around the outline (perimeter, measured in unit lengths) is a different kind of quantity from an area count.
Count systematically (row by row, or by decomposing an L-shape into rectangles) so each square is counted exactly once.
Always state the area in square units (square cm, square m, etc.); a bare number is an incomplete answer.

Keep to whole unit squares at this stage; treat edge part-squares informally (e.g. pairing two halves) and do NOT drill a part-square formula yet — part-square figures are for discussion, not scored counts.
Real tiles and squared-paper diagrams each support learning differently — tiles ground the physical covering, diagrams abstract it; neither is claimed as universally necessary.
A revealed static figure is a reference/scaffold: it shows the result but does not let the child practise the covering and counting, so it should not replace hands-on tiling.
A count-the-squares check verifies understanding and can catch edge-counting, but does not by itself build the systematic covering skill.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original row framed the boundary-counting misconception as a total that 'matches the perimeter'. A count of boundary squares is not generally equal to the perimeter (a length); learner-facing text uses an inside-vs-around distinction without asserting a numeric match. This original imprecision was not re-verified against sources.

The source row rated a 3D scene 'poor' (risk of conflating area with volume) and a conversation 'poor'; these are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws, and have been dropped rather than asserted as universal claims. A spoken discussion of what was counted remains valuable (see the probe questions).

Interactive affordances from the source (tiles greying out when counted to prevent double-counting, uncovered cells flashing, a running square-unit tally, side-by-side compare mode) are preserved as optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not as mandatory requirements.

The source claim supports covering with a two-dimensional unit but does not directly establish the concrete-tiles-before-diagram ordering's efficacy; that ordering is retained as curriculum best practice with hedged wording.

'18 square cm' is used only as an illustrative label, not a computed answer to verify; boundary vs interior counting, no-gaps/no-overlaps covering, L-shape decomposition, and informal handling of part-squares (as discussion rather than scored counts) are internally consistent.

probeDeeper: Show me which squares you counted — the ones inside the shape, or the ones around the edge?
This L-shape — how did you make sure you counted every square once and none twice?
There are some half-squares at the edge here — what did you do with those?
You said 18 — 18 what? What is the unit for area?
assess.correctAnswer: The child covers each interior with unit squares (no gaps or overlaps) and counts them systematically — decomposing the L-shape so every square is counted once — gives the count in square units (e.g. '18 square cm'), handles edge part-squares sensibly rather than as whole units, and compares two shapes by their counts.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts the boundary, not the interior: counts squares around the edge (perimeter) rather than the squares covering the surface.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to what area means — the surface covered; shade the interior and count only covering squares, contrasting with the distance around.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Points to and counts the squares along the border; the total matches the perimeter, not the area.

errorPatterns.pattern: Gaps/overlaps or unsystematic counting: covers with gaps or overlaps, or counts without a system so squares are missed or double-counted, especially on the L-shape.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Cover fully with no gaps/overlaps and count row by row or by decomposing into rectangles, marking each square as counted.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Tiles don't fully cover or overlap; recounting gives a different total; loses track in the L's notch.

errorPatterns.pattern: Part-squares counted as whole: counts each partly-covered edge square as a full square, overestimating the area.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill a part-square formula at this stage — Grade-3 area focuses on whole unit squares; use whole-square shapes and treat part-squares informally (pair two halves) until later.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Every touched square counted as one; total inflated on the irregular figure.

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops the square unit: gives the count as a bare number ('18') without 'square cm'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Treat an area answer without a square unit as incomplete; build the habit of naming the unit; the counting is sound.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct count, no unit; supplies it only when asked.

responseLevels.gap: Counts the boundary/perimeter, leaves gaps or overlaps, or gives a bare number with no square unit.
responseLevels.full: Systematically counts every covering unit square once (decomposing the L-shape), handles part-squares sensibly, compares areas by their counts, and states the area in square units.
responseLevels.partial: Counts the covering squares correctly for a plain rectangle but loses systematicity on the L-shape (double-counts or misses) or mishandles part-squares — succeeds in the clean case but not the irregular one.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give a few figures on squared paper — a plain rectangle, an L-shape, and one with part-squares at the edge — plus a book cover and square-centimetre tiles. Say: 'Find the area of each by counting.' Watch whether they count the covering squares or the boundary, whether they cover with no gaps/overlaps and count systematically, what they do with part-squares, and whether they state the unit.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands area counts the interior covering squares once each and names the square unit; a child who does not counts the boundary, leaves gaps/overlaps, double-counts on the L-shape, treats part-squares as whole, or drops the unit — each visible in the counting.

sources.claim: Area is measured by counting unit squares — square cm, square m, square in, square ft and improvised units (3.MD.6) — covering the region with a two-dimensional unit and parts of the unit without gaps or overlaps; instruction often begins by comparing which of several rectangles covers the most area, and discussions must clearly distinguish area from length. Grade-3 area instruction focuses on covering with whole unit squares.
