pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–10y; know and use the vocabulary of prime, prime factor and composite numbers; establish whether a number up to 100 is prime; recall primes up to 19.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5 'know and use the vocabulary of prime numbers, prime factors and composite numbers'; 'establish whether a number up to 100 is prime and recall prime numbers up to 19'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.OA.4 — 'determine whether a given whole number in the range 1–100 is prime or composite.'
• Operational details — the definition is exact-and-fragile: a prime has EXACTLY two factors (1 and itself); composite has more than two; and 1 is NEITHER (only one factor) — a point pupils routinely get wrong. Build primeness ON factor-finding: a prime is a number whose only rectangle is 1×n (one factor pair). To test primality efficiently, check divisibility only by primes up to the square root (test 97: not ÷2,3,5,7 → prime). Divisibility rules (2,3,5,10) accelerate this. Recall of primes to 19 (2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19) should be memorised. Seeds prime factorisation, HCF/LCM.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): state the definition and list primes to 19. Tier B (age 9–10): determine whether a number like 51 is prime and justify (51=3×17 → composite). Tier C (age 10): explain why 1 is not prime and use square-root-bounded checking to test a number like 97.
bestPractices: Define prime as EXACTLY two factors and build it on factor-finding — a prime is a number with only the 1×n rectangle — so the definition is grounded, not memorised.
Address the '1 is prime' misconception head-on: 1 has only one factor, so it is neither prime nor composite.
Teach efficient primality testing — check divisibility by primes up to the square root — supported by divisibility rules for 2, 3, 5.
Use the Sieve of Eratosthenes on a hundred square to reveal the primes and why multiples are composite.
Require justification ('51 = 3×17 so it's composite'), not just a prime/composite label; memorise primes to 19.
keyRepresentations: Rectangle/array — a prime makes only the 1×n rectangle (one factor pair)
Sieve of Eratosthenes on a hundred square — crossing out multiples leaves the primes
Factor list / factor rainbow — counting factors to classify
Divisibility-rule checks up to the square root
commonMisconceptions: Believing 1 is prime (it has only one factor — it is neither).
Thinking all odd numbers are prime (9, 15, 21, 51 are composite) or that 2 isn't prime because it's even.
Classifying by 'feel' without checking factors/divisibility.
Checking divisibility inefficiently (testing all numbers, not just primes to the square root).
Confusing 'prime factor' with 'factor' — not every factor is prime.

learn.summary: For 9–10 year-olds learning prime, prime factor and composite numbers: establish whether a number up to 100 is prime and recall the primes to 19. Primeness is grounded on factor-finding — a prime is a number whose only rectangle is 1×n (exactly two factors: 1 and itself); composite has more than two; 1 is neither because it has only one factor. Learners build this through rectangle-building, the Sieve of Eratosthenes, efficient square-root-bounded divisibility testing, and justified classification (e.g. 51 = 3×17 → composite), with checkable recall and reasoning to confirm the definition they actually hold.

activities.title: Rectangle-building: when is only 1×n possible?
feedback: If a learner calls 51 prime, prompt: try arranging the counters into 3 equal rows — do they fill? (3×17 = 51, so it is composite.)
If a learner says 1 is prime, point to the single 1×1 square: that is only one factor, and a prime needs exactly two, so 1 is neither.

When 97 forms only the 1×97 line after testing the primes up to its square root, confirm: since any larger factor would pair with a smaller one already tested, no other rectangle is possible, so its only factors are 1 and 97 and it is prime.
activities.rationale: Building primeness on factor-finding with a concrete rectangle/array model grounds the definition rather than leaving it memorised, and lets learners see directly why 1 is neither.
sourceClaims: Prime should be defined as exactly two factors (1 is neither); the Sieve of Eratosthenes and square-root-bounded divisibility testing support efficient classification.
learnerActions: Take a number and try to arrange that many counters (or squares on grid paper) into complete rectangles with more than one row and more than one column (a single line, 1×n, does not count as another rectangle).
For 51, find that a 3×17 rectangle can be built, so 51 has factors other than 1 and itself — it is composite.

For 97, try rows of 2, 3, 5 and 7 — the primes up to its square root (just under 10), since any larger factor would pair with a smaller one already tested — and find that only a single 1×97 line forms, so 97 is prime.
Try the number 1: it forms only a single 1×1 square — one factor — so it fits neither the prime nor the composite group.
Record each verdict with its factor pair as justification (e.g. '51 = 3×17, composite'; '97, only 1×97, prime').
activities.intendedInsight: A prime number can only be made into the 1×n rectangle (exactly two factors); a composite makes at least one other rectangle; and 1 is neither prime nor composite because it has only a single factor.

activities.title: Sieve of Eratosthenes on a hundred square
feedback: If a learner expects to keep crossing out past 7 to find the primes under 100, note that once multiples of primes up to √100 = 10 are removed (2, 3, 5, 7), the survivors other than 1 are already prime.
If a learner crosses out 2 itself, remind them to circle (keep) the first number and cross out only its later multiples.
activities.rationale: The sieve reveals why multiples are composite and leaves the primes visible, connecting classification to divisibility structure.
sourceClaims: Prime should be defined as exactly two factors (1 is neither); the Sieve of Eratosthenes and square-root-bounded divisibility testing support efficient classification.
learnerActions: On a 1–100 grid, first cross out 1 (it is neither prime nor composite), then circle 2 and cross out every later multiple of 2.
Move to the next uncrossed number (3) and cross out its multiples; repeat for 5, then 7.

Notice that the numbers still standing (circled or uncrossed) are exactly the primes, and that every number crossed out as a multiple is a multiple of a smaller prime, so it is composite (1 was crossed out separately because it is neither).
Highlight the primes up to 19 (2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19) for memorisation.
activities.intendedInsight: Composite numbers are exactly the multiples that get crossed out; once 1 is set aside as neither, the survivors are the primes. This also makes the primes to 19 visible for recall.

activities.title: Efficient primality testing to the square root
feedback: If a learner keeps testing divisors above the square root, explain that any factor larger than √n would pair with one smaller than √n, which would already have been found.
If a learner tests every number rather than just primes, note that a composite divisor (e.g. 4) is already covered by its prime factor (2).
activities.rationale: Square-root-bounded checking with divisibility rules gives an efficient, reasoned method for establishing primality rather than exhaustive trial.
sourceClaims: Prime should be defined as exactly two factors (1 is neither); the Sieve of Eratosthenes and square-root-bounded divisibility testing support efficient classification.
learnerActions: To test whether a whole number greater than 1 is prime, divide only by the primes 2, 3, 5, 7… up to its square root (1 is neither prime nor composite, so it is not tested this way).
Use divisibility shortcuts: even → ÷2; digit sum divisible by 3 → ÷3; ends in 0 or 5 → ÷5.
Test 97: not even, digit sum 16 (not divisible by 3), does not end in 0/5, not divisible by 7 — and since the next prime 11 has 11×11 = 121 > 97, there is no need to test further, so 97 is prime.
Test 51: digit sum 5+1 = 6, divisible by 3, so 51 = 3×17 → composite.
activities.intendedInsight: For a whole number greater than 1, you only need to check divisibility by primes up to the square root; if none divide the number, it is prime. Divisibility rules make this fast.

activities.title: Classify and justify, including the tricky cases
feedback: If a learner calls 51 prime because it is odd and unfamiliar, prompt them to check the digit sum (6) → divisible by 3 → 51 = 3×17, composite.
If a learner says 2 is not prime because it is even, point out it has exactly two factors (1 and 2), which is the definition — evenness is irrelevant.
If a learner calls 9 prime, prompt 9 = 3×3, so it has a third factor (3) beyond 1 and 9, making it composite.
If a learner confuses 'prime factor' with 'factor', note that 51's factors are 1, 3, 17, 51, but its prime factors are only 3 and 17.
activities.rationale: Direct, justified classification confronts the most common misconceptions (1 is prime, odd=prime, 2 isn't prime) and distinguishes factor from prime factor.
sourceClaims: Y5 pupils know and use the vocabulary of prime numbers, prime factors and composite numbers; establish whether a number up to 100 is prime; recall primes up to 19.
4.OA.4 requires determining whether a whole number 1–100 is prime or composite.
learnerActions: Sort numbers into three groups: prime, composite, and neither — placing 1 in 'neither'.
Decide whether 51 is prime or composite and justify using a factor pair (51 = 3×17 → composite).
Explain why 2 is prime (exactly two factors) even though it is even, and why 9, 15, 21 and 51 are composite even though they are odd.
List all primes up to 19 from memory and state for each why it is prime.
activities.intendedInsight: Classification requires checking factors, not 'feel': parity does not decide primeness, 1 is neither, and every classification needs a factor justification.

activities.title: Prove it: Socratic justification challenge
feedback: If the learner says they must test all numbers up to 96, guide them to the square-root bound and to testing only primes.
If the learner struggles to say why 1 is neither, return them to the rectangle/factor count: one factor only.
Accept a correct verdict only when it comes with a factor-based justification, not just a label.
activities.rationale: A discussion/justification task surfaces the actual definition a learner holds and builds efficient-testing reasoning; it complements the concrete rectangle and sieve work.
learnerActions: Respond to the question 'How could you prove 97 is prime without checking every number below it?' by describing which divisors you need to test and why.
Explain in your own words why 1 is neither prime nor composite.
Argue whether a classmate who called 51 prime is right, and show the check that settles it.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to articulate and defend the reasoning — which divisors to test, why 1 is neither, how to catch a false positive like 51 — shows the definition is genuinely held.

constraints: A pre-made, tap-to-reveal hundred square and definition card are useful as a reference and primes-to-19 memory aid, but do not let the learner test arbitrary numbers or run the sieve themselves; use them alongside, not instead of, hands-on building.

Multiple-choice or categorisation tasks (prime / composite / neither, 'is 51 prime?') verify recognition and recall but do not by themselves build the rectangle/sieve intuition; pair recognition with construction and justification.
Always require a factor justification ('51 = 3×17 so composite'), not just a prime/composite label.
Distinguish 'factor' from 'prime factor': not every factor is prime.
The definition is exact and fragile — a prime has exactly two distinct factors (1 and itself); 1 has only one factor and is neither; 2 is prime despite being even.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Independent re-review self-audit of arithmetic/logic: 51 = 3×17 (digit sum 6, divisible by 3) — correct. 97 is prime (not divisible by 2,3,5,7; next prime 11, 11²=121>97; √97≈9.85) — correct. 97 digit sum = 16, not divisible by 3 — correct. √100=10, so sieving multiples of primes up to 10 (2,3,5,7) suffices for numbers to 100 — correct. 9 = 3×3 has three factors; 51 has factors 1,3,17,51 with prime factors 3,17 — correct. All checked and consistent.

The legacy source characterised a static hundred square as unable to let a child test arbitrary numbers, and characterised 3D as adding 'no insight'; these catalog-fit judgements are reframed as affordance/limit notes rather than universal claims, since the sources do not establish comparative efficacy, necessity, or medium superiority.

The US standard claim (4.OA.4) and the NCETM guidance claim are marked verified:false in the source row; they are retained only because they align with established curriculum conventions and the core definition, and their evidentiary weight should be treated as unconfirmed.

probeDeeper: What exactly makes a number prime — how many factors must it have?
How could you test 51 for a factor other than 1 and 51?
Is 2 a prime number? Is 9? What does that say about 'odd means prime'?
List the prime numbers up to 19 — how do you know each one is prime?
assess.correctAnswer: 51 is composite, not prime, because it has factors other than 1 and itself: 51 = 3 × 17. A child reasoning correctly defines prime as having EXACTLY two factors (1 and itself) and shows 51 fails because 3 divides it.

errorPatterns.pattern: judges primeness by 'odd and not a number I recognise' — calls 51 prime because it's odd and not in the obvious tables
errorPatterns.nextMove: test 51 ÷ 3 = 17 (digit sum 6 flags divisibility by 3); primeness is about factors, not familiarity.
errorPatterns.distractor: 51 is prime because it is odd and not in the times tables I know
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child declares 51 prime citing oddness/unfamiliarity, without testing divisibility by 3

errorPatterns.pattern: thinks a prime has exactly ONE factor, or that primes are 'numbers you can't make by timesing' without pinning the two-factor definition
errorPatterns.nextMove: state precisely: exactly TWO distinct factors, 1 and itself; 1 has only one factor so is not prime.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: definition given is vague or off (‘only divisible by itself’, forgetting 1; or ‘one factor’)

errorPatterns.pattern: believes all odd numbers are prime / all primes are odd (so misses that 2 is prime, 9 and 51 are not)
errorPatterns.nextMove: counterexamples: 2 is an even prime; 9 = 3×3 is odd but composite; parity is irrelevant.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child links prime to odd; would call 9 or 15 prime and 2 composite

responseLevels.gap: declares 51 prime on the strength of oddness/unfamiliarity, or cannot define prime correctly.
responseLevels.full: defines prime as exactly two factors, tests 51 and finds 3×17 so classifies it composite, handles 1 and 2 correctly, and recalls primes to 19.
responseLevels.partial: defines prime as two factors but doesn't systematically test 51 (misses the ÷3), or is shaky on 1 and 2 as special cases.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Is 51 a prime number or a composite number? Decide, and then explain how you know — what makes a number prime, and what did you check for 51?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 51 looks prime (odd, not obviously in a small table) and is a classic false-positive. A child who checks divisibility properly (digit sum 5+1 = 6, divisible by 3) catches it; one who judges by 'odd and unfamiliar = prime' declares it prime. The reason tier exposes the definition they actually hold.

pedagogy.summary: This is embodied direction and rotation: children physically move (forward, backward, turn left/right) and demonstrate whole, half and quarter turns with their bodies, then describe routes with directional words. It is a doing skill — a turn is felt as an amount of rotation about a fixed spot, distinct from travelling a distance — and it seeds the dynamic angle-as-turn conception developed later. The main hurdles are confusing turning with moving, under- or over-rotating when there is no target to turn to, and left/right, which is frame-dependent and late-developing.
bestPractices: Turn the WHOLE body on the spot first, marking the start and finish facing, so a turn is felt as rotation rather than travel.
Use fixed reference facings — face the door, now the window — so a 'quarter turn' lands on a checkable target rather than a random amount.
Sequence whole → half → quarter turns, linking a half turn to 'facing the opposite way' and a whole turn to 'facing the same way again'.
Play route and floor-robot games ('give me directions to the door') so children both FOLLOW and GIVE directional instructions.
Anchor left and right on the body (right-hand sticker) before using them in directions, and expect residual errors.
keyRepresentations: The child's own body turning on a spot, with start and finish facings marked by footprints
A programmable floor robot or a marked floor grid for building and walking routes
Quarter / half / three-quarter turn language tied to fixed landmarks to face
A simple route to follow and then to describe
commonMisconceptions: Confusing a turn (rotation on the spot) with moving forward — 'turning' by walking in a curve or stepping sideways
Under- or over-rotating: a 'quarter turn' that is a random amount because it is not referenced to a target facing
Left/right reversed, especially relative to the direction of travel or a facing partner (frame-dependence)
Treating half or quarter of a turn as unrelated to half or quarter of anything else — no sense of a fractional turn amount

learn.summary: Young children (around ages 5–6) learn direction and turning as a doing skill: physically moving forward/backward and turning their whole body through whole, half, quarter and three-quarter turns, then both following and giving route directions. The core insight is that a turn is an amount of rotation about a fixed spot — felt in the body — distinct from travelling a distance. Main hurdles are confusing turning with moving, under-/over-rotating when there is no target to turn toward, and left/right (which is frame-dependent and matures later). Embodied whole-body movement is the primary teaching medium; a programmable floor-robot or route game is proposed as a companion that can show the result of a turn immediately (a wrong turn visibly misses the goal), though its relative teaching value over embodied movement is not established.

activities.title: Turn your whole body on the spot
feedback: If the child travels across the floor or steps sideways instead of pivoting, mark the spot with a hoop or footprints and require both feet to stay put while turning to face a named target.

If the finish facing is a random amount (not toward the named target), give fixed facings to turn TO — door then window — so a quarter turn lands on a checkable target rather than reteaching the whole idea; the concept may well be held, with only the execution lacking a reference point.
When two quarter turns leave them facing the opposite way, name it: 'two quarter turns make a half turn.'
activities.rationale: Turning the whole body on the spot with marked start/finish facings makes rotation felt as rotation rather than travel, and referencing each turn to a fixed landmark gives the turn amount a checkable target. This dynamic turn experience seeds the later angle-as-turn conception.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils should describe position, direction and movement, including whole, half, quarter and three-quarter turns.

An angle is an amount of turn represented by two adjoining lines (a start position and the position after the turn); children develop this dynamically by turning — stretching out arms and turning while one arm stays in place — and the dynamic turn conception appears early, with children talking about whole and half turns from Year 1.
learnerActions: Stand on a marked spot (hoop or footprints) with both feet staying put throughout the turn.
Mark your start facing (e.g. 'I'm facing the door'), then make a quarter turn to your right and name your new facing ('now the window').

Go back to your start facing (the door). Make a half turn and check you are facing the opposite way from the start; go back to the start facing, make a whole turn and check you are facing the same way as the start.

Go back to your start facing, then make a three-quarter turn to your right and check where you now face (three quarter-turns to the right from the start, the same facing as one quarter turn to the left).
Make two quarter turns in a row in the same direction (both to the right) and compare: is that the same as one half turn?
activities.intendedInsight: A turn is an amount of rotation about a fixed point, felt in the body — not travelling. A quarter turn lands you on a new facing (about 90° from the start), a half turn faces you the opposite way, a three-quarter turn is three quarter-turns on, and a whole turn returns you to the same facing.

activities.title: Give and follow a route
feedback: If the route is only 'go forward' steps with the turns left out, walk their exact words back to them so they SEE the path miss the bookshelf (or hit a wall), then have them re-give it including the turns.

If they turn the wrong way, reinforce body left/right (e.g. a sticker on the right hand) and keep up exposure; do not drill it as a failure — frame-dependent left/right matures later, especially after they have turned to a new facing or face a partner.
activities.rationale: Both following and producing directions develops directional language as a usable tool; producing a route reveals gaps that imitation hides. Anchoring left/right on the body before using it in directions respects that left/right is frame-dependent and late-developing.
sourceClaims: Left and right are notoriously difficult and frame-dependent (relative to the direction the child faces) and not mastered until early elementary school; children engage in locating and directional activities (hopscotch, board games moving forward and backward) that build directional understanding.
learnerActions: Follow a spoken route given by an adult or partner: 'go forward two, turn left a quarter, go forward one.'
Then GIVE directions yourself: describe how to walk from here to the bookshelf as a sequence of moves and turns.
Have your listener walk your exact words — if they miss the bookshelf or hit a wall, find the missing or wrong move or turn and re-give the route.
Try describing the route for walking backward from the bookshelf to the start.
activities.intendedInsight: A followable route is a coordinated sequence of moves AND turns with correct directional words — leaving out the turns breaks the path. Giving a route (not just following one) shows the directional words have become a productive tool.

activities.title: Program a robot along a floor grid (companion)
feedback: When the robot misses the goal, point to the arrow's facing after the turn and ask which turn was the wrong amount or direction.
If a quarter turn does not land 90° on, let the child re-enter the command and re-run it so the correction is immediate and visible.
activities.rationale: A programmable route game is proposed as a companion that may give immediate visual feedback on turn direction and amount and capture route-building; it cannot reproduce the proprioceptive feedback of the child's own felt rotation, so it is best paired with, not a replacement for, the child doing the same turns with their own body. No source directly establishes its relative efficacy.
learnerActions: On a floor grid or maze, string commands for a character/robot: 'forward 2', 'turn left a quarter', 'forward 1'.
Aim the robot at a goal; if a turn is the wrong direction or amount, the robot faces the wrong way and misses or runs into a wall.
Watch the start and finish facings shown as an arrow, and adjust so a quarter turn visibly lands the arrow 90° on.
Compare turning-then-walking with walking-then-turning and notice the different results.
activities.intendedInsight: A 'quarter turn' only makes sense as landing on a new facing toward the next target, and the order of turning and walking matters: turn-then-walk is different from walk-then-turn.

constraints: This is a bodily performance skill: assess and teach by watching the child move and listening to the route, not by asking them to explain the procedure.

The child's own felt rotation about a fixed spot is where the idea lives; a screen or floor-robot game does not reproduce proprioceptive turning feedback and should be a companion to embodied movement, not a substitute.

Sequencing a route or picking the picture after a quarter turn can check the idea but does not itself elicit the physical rotation or route production — recognition-only tasks do not demonstrate the doing.

Left/right is frame-dependent and late-developing; expect residual reversal errors, especially after a change of facing or when facing a partner. Reinforce body-anchored left/right and keep exposure rather than drilling errors as failures.
A static picture cannot be turned, so it cannot by itself practise the rotation; use it only as a prompt alongside movement.
When a turn amount drifts, scaffold with a fixed target to turn TO rather than reteaching the concept — the under-/over-rotation is an execution gap, not necessarily a conceptual one.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The companion robot activity's sourceClaims were set to [] because no source in the row supports the medium's efficacy; the curriculum and left/right claims are topical only and do not establish that the floor-robot teaches or assesses better than embodied movement.

Activity 2's sourceClaims were reduced to the left/right frame-dependence claim, which directly supports anchoring body left/right and directional activities; the curriculum turns claim was removed there as merely topical to route-giving.

The source framed a static image, 3D avatar, and open dialogue as poorly or marginally suited and asserted that '3D adds nothing' and that a dialogue 'cannot deliver or assess' the skill. These are catalog-fit judgements, not established necessity claims; retained here only as the narrow objective limit that recognition/explanation tasks do not build or demonstrate the physical performance.

The original claim that 'no screen artefact reproduces the proprioceptive feedback of turning your own body' is a reasonable affordance point and is preserved as a scope limit, not as proof that only embodied activity can teach the concept.
The comparison between two quarter turns and a half turn, and between turn-then-walk vs walk-then-turn, is geometrically sound for planar turns and retained as stated.

probeDeeper: Do that quarter turn again but the other way — where do you face now?
Make two quarter turns — where are you facing? Is that the same as a half turn?
Give me the directions again, but for walking backwards from the bookshelf to here.
You turned to your right — if you were facing me, would 'your right' point the same way as 'my right'?
assess.correctAnswer: Rotates on the spot without walking; a quarter turn lands them facing 90° from the start (toward the next target) and a half turn faces them the opposite way; and their route directions are a followable sequence of moves and turns with correct directional words.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Mark the spot with a hoop or footprints and require both feet to stay put, turning to face a named target.

responseLevels.gap: Walks or steps instead of pivoting, turn amounts are random, and left/right is frequently reversed; route directions cannot be followed.
responseLevels.full: Rotates a referenced quarter / half / three-quarter turn on the spot, links two quarter turns to a half turn, and both gives and follows a route as a coordinated sequence of moves and turns with correct directional words, transferring to a new start and goal (relational).
responseLevels.partial: Pivots on the spot and demonstrates a quarter or half turn to a named facing, and follows directional instructions, but turn amounts drift without a target, left/right reverses when the facing changes, or self-given routes omit the turns (multistructural — parts done, not coordinated into a reliable route).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set the task and watch: 'Stand on this spot facing the door. Make a quarter turn to your right. ... Now make a half turn. ... Now give me directions to walk from here to the bookshelf.' Watch the body rotation and listen to the route — do not ask them to explain the procedure.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching separates a child who ROTATES on the spot by a referenced amount from one who walks, steps sideways, or turns a random amount; and asking them to GIVE a route (not just follow one) shows whether the directional words are a productive tool. A child can follow 'turn right' by imitation but reveal the gap the moment they must produce a route.

pedagogy.summary: An equation with two unknowns (a + b = 12, or 2x + y = 20) does NOT have a single answer — it has many solution pairs. The child generates such pairs and, within the stated constraints (whole numbers, positive, a range), lists them SYSTEMATICALLY so none is missed and none repeated. Fixing one unknown and stepping it through its possible values in order, computing the partner each time, makes the search exhaustive and reveals the pattern. It is a Year 6 precursor to simultaneous equations, where a SECOND equation pins the pair down to one.
bestPractices: Establish first that there are MANY pairs, not one — contrast a + b = 12 with a one-variable equation like a + 7 = 12
Fix one unknown and step it through its permitted values in order (a = 1 → b = 11, a = 2 → b = 10, …), computing the partner each time so the list is complete and ordered
Record pairs in a two-column table so completeness is visible and answer 'how do you know you've found them all?'
Attend to the stated constraints (positive, whole, within a range) — they bound how many pairs exist
For 2x + y = 20, substitute the chosen x and compute y = 20 − 2x, respecting the coefficient
Link to 'what two numbers can add up to' puzzles and to plotting the pairs as points on a line
keyRepresentations: Ordered two-column table of (a, b) pairs
A 'fix one unknown and step it' systematic list
Bar / part-whole model for a + b = 12
The pairs as points on a straight line (bridge to graphs and simultaneous equations)
commonMisconceptions: Treats it like a single-answer equation — finds ONE pair and stops, as if a and b are unique fixed unknowns
Searches unsystematically, so pairs are missed or duplicated and completeness cannot be judged
Ignores the constraints — includes 0, negatives, or non-whole values when only positive whole numbers are allowed
For 2x + y = 20 mishandles the coefficient, treating it as x + y (offering pairs like (3, 17))
Cannot say whether the list of pairs is complete

learn.summary: Year 6 learners discover that an equation with two unknowns (e.g. a + b = 12, or 2x + y = 20) has MANY solution pairs, not one. They generate these pairs systematically by fixing one unknown and stepping it through its permitted values in order, computing the partner each time, so no pair is missed or repeated. Stated constraints (such as whole numbers, positive, or within a range) decide which pairs are valid; when values must be whole numbers within limits, the number of pairs is finite and can be counted. This is a precursor to simultaneous equations, where a second equation can usually pin the pair down to one answer.

activities.title: Build the pair-finder: sweep one unknown and watch the pairs appear
feedback: If the learner gives one pair as 'the answer' and stops: ask 'Is there another pair that works? And another?' Then fix a and step it through its values to reveal them all.
If the search is random with gaps or repeats: have them step one unknown through its values in order and record in a table — 'I know I have them all because I worked systematically.'
If they cannot say whether the list is complete: point to the ordered column of a-values and ask which values of a have not yet been tried.

Full solution for a + b = 12 (whole, > 0): (1,11), (2,10), (3,9), (4,8), (5,7), (6,6), (7,5), (8,4), (9,3), (10,2), (11,1) — 11 pairs, complete because every value of a from 1 to 11 has been tried in order.
activities.rationale: The Year 6 objective is to find pairs satisfying a two-unknown equation, framed as generating MULTIPLE pairs. Working randomly first hides which cases are missing; ordering and systematising exposes gaps and answers 'how do you know you've found them all?'. Fixing one unknown and stepping it makes the search exhaustive and reveals the linear pattern.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils should 'find pairs of numbers that satisfy an equation with 2 unknowns'; the non-statutory guidance includes number puzzles such as 'what 2 numbers can add up to', framing the task as generating multiple pairs.

When children are asked to find all possibilities they first work randomly and cannot see which cases are missing; sorting and ordering their attempts exposes the gaps, and having a system is what ensures no options are left out ('how do you know you've found them all?' — 'I worked systematically').
learnerActions: Before starting, compare a + b = 12 with a + 7 = 12: how many answers does each have? Notice that the one-variable equation has a single answer but the two-unknown equation has many.
Start with a + b = 12 (whole numbers, greater than 0). Set a = 1 and work out b; record (1, 11). Set a = 2 and work out b; record (2, 10). Continue in order: a = 3 → b = 9, a = 4 → b = 8, and so on.
Record each pair in an ordered two-column table (a | b) so completeness is visible.
After listing, answer: 'How many pairs are there? How do you know you have found them ALL?' State the justification: 'I tried every value of a from 1 to 11 in order.'

Optional interactive version: drag a slider for a that moves in whole-number steps from 1 to 11 and watch b recompute live so a + b = 12 always holds; each pair drops into the ordered table AND lights a point on a grid. Sweeping the slider fills the table in order while the separate points line up along a straight line — showing at once that there are many solutions and that stepping a through every permitted value catches them all.
activities.intendedInsight: An equation with two unknowns has a whole family of solution pairs; stepping one unknown through its permitted values in order generates every pair and lets you prove the list is complete.

activities.title: Let the constraints bound the count
feedback: If pairs like (0, 12), (13, −1), or decimals appear despite a 'whole, greater than 0' condition: reread the constraint together; it fixes which values of a are permitted and therefore how many pairs there are.
If allowing 0 or any whole number changes the count, ask the learner to re-list in order under the new rule and recount.
activities.rationale: Ignoring constraints produces invalid pairs and an incorrect count. Attending to the stated conditions makes the search both correct and finite, and shows why the number of pairs is what it is.
learnerActions: Reread the stated condition (whole numbers, positive, within a range) and decide which values of a are allowed before listing.
For a + b = 12 with 'whole, greater than 0', check: is (0, 12) allowed? Is (13, −1) allowed? Are decimals allowed? Explain why each is excluded by the condition.
Try a different constraint, e.g. 'a and b are whole numbers from 0 to 10 inclusive', and work out how the list of valid pairs changes and how many remain (a can now only be 2 to 10, so 9 pairs).

Optional interactive version: a constraints toggle ('whole numbers only', 'positive only', 'between 0 and 10') greys out the pairs that break the rule, so the learner SEES how the constraint bounds how many pairs exist.
activities.intendedInsight: The constraints bound which values of the stepped unknown are allowed, and therefore exactly how many valid pairs exist.

activities.title: Respect the coefficient: 2x + y = 20
feedback: If the learner offers (3, 17) for 2x + y = 20: have them substitute the numbers — 2×3 + 17 = 23 ≠ 20. The pair satisfies x + y = 20, not 2x + y = 20.
Prompt: substitute the chosen x and compute y = 20 − 2x explicitly rather than guessing a partner that sums to 20.
activities.rationale: Mishandling the coefficient (treating 2x + y as x + y) is a common error. Substituting and computing y = 20 − 2x each time makes the coefficient's role concrete and transfers the systematic method to a new two-unknown equation.
learnerActions: For 2x + y = 20, choose a value for x, then compute y = 20 − 2x explicitly — the 2 doubles x BEFORE y is added.
Find three valid pairs, e.g. x = 1 → y = 18 giving (1,18); x = 2 → y = 16 giving (2,16); x = 3 → y = 14 giving (3,14).
Check a tempting wrong pair: does (3, 17) satisfy 2x + y = 20? Substitute: 2×3 + 17 = 23, not 20. Note that (3, 17) fits x + y = 20, a different equation.
Explain in your own words how 2x + y = 20 differs from x + y = 20.
Optional interactive version: a 2x + y = 20 preset shows y recomputing as 20 − 2x as x changes, making the coefficient's effect visible.
activities.intendedInsight: A coefficient changes the partner computation: for 2x + y = 20 the partner is y = 20 − 2x, which is not the same as x + y = 20.

constraints: Establish FIRST that there are many pairs, not one — contrast a + b = 12 with a one-variable equation like a + 7 = 12.
The ordered two-column table (or a 'fix one unknown and step it' list) is essential for judging completeness; recording pairs out of order defeats the purpose.

Recognition-only or fill-in-the-blank items (complete-the-pair, categorise valid vs invalid, 'how many pairs?') can check the skill but do NOT by themselves build the systematic, exhaustive search; the learner must generate and order the pairs independently.

A static completed table beside the line of points can display the full solution set, but it does the discovery for the learner — they do not generate the pairs or test completeness themselves. Treat it as a reveal/illustration, not as the generating activity.
Plotting the pairs as points on a straight line is a bridge to graphs and simultaneous equations; keep it linked to the ordered table so the pattern connects back to the stepping method.

Interactive slider/toggle/point-lighting features named above are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete; the underlying learning (stepping one unknown in order, computing the partner, justifying completeness) can also be done with pencil, paper, and a hand-drawn table.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: a + b = 12 (whole, >0) yields exactly 11 pairs (a from 1 to 11) — verified. For 2x + y = 20, y = 20 − 2x: (1,18), (2,16), (3,14) all satisfy 2x + y = 20 — verified. (3,17) gives 2×3+17 = 23 ≠ 20 and satisfies x + y = 20 instead — the distractor is correctly characterised.

The legacy row's claim that 3D and in-role dialogue formats 'add nothing' / 'cannot build' the skill was not established by the cited sources and has been removed rather than asserted as a universal law; the point retained is the narrowly scoped one that recognition-only responses do not elicit independent systematic generation.

The source claims cited in Activity 1 support the general teaching principle (generate multiple pairs; work systematically to prove completeness). No cited source directly supports the constraint-bounding principle (Activity 2) or the coefficient-handling principle (Activity 3), so those carry empty sourceClaims and remain qualified proposals.
The bar/part-whole model from the original keyRepresentations is not instantiated in these activities; it is left as an optional representation, apt for a + b = 12 but less natural for 2x + y = 20.

probeDeeper: You found one pair. Is there another that works? How many are there altogether — and how can you be sure you haven't missed any?
Why is a + b = 12 different from a + 7 = 12 — how many answers does each have?
For 2x + y = 20, does (3, 17) work? Check it by putting the numbers in.
If a and b were allowed to be any whole numbers including 0, how would your list change?
assess.correctAnswer: a + b = 12 (whole, > 0): (1,11), (2,10), (3,9), (4,8), (5,7), (6,6), (7,5), (8,4), (9,3), (10,2), (11,1) — 11 pairs, found by stepping a from 1 to 11; complete because every value of a has been tried in order. For 2x + y = 20: any three pairs with y = 20 − 2x, e.g. (1,18), (2,16), (3,14).

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats it like a single-answer equation — finds ONE pair and stops, as if a and b are unique unknowns to be solved for
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show it is a whole family of solutions — 'is there another pair? and another?'; fix a and step it through its values to reveal them all
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Offers one pair as 'the answer' and is surprised that others also work

errorPatterns.pattern: Searches unsystematically — jumps around, so pairs are missed or duplicated and completeness cannot be judged
errorPatterns.nextMove: Step one unknown through its values in order and record in a table; 'I know I have them all because I worked systematically'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Random order with gaps or repeats; cannot answer 'have you found them all?'

errorPatterns.pattern: Ignores the constraints — includes 0, negatives, or non-whole values when only positive whole numbers are allowed
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reread the constraint; it fixes which values of a are allowed and therefore how many pairs there are
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Lists pairs such as (0, 12) or (13, −1) or decimals despite the 'whole, greater than 0' condition

errorPatterns.pattern: Mishandles the coefficient in 2x + y = 20, treating it as x + y = 20
errorPatterns.nextMove: Substitute the chosen x and compute y = 20 − 2x explicitly; the 2 doubles x before y is added
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Offers (3, 17) for 2x + y = 20 (which satisfies x + y = 20, not 2x + y = 20)

responseLevels.gap: Finds one pair or none; no system; cannot say how many pairs there are or whether the list is complete; for 2x + y ignores the coefficient.
responseLevels.full: Generates all valid pairs by stepping one unknown through its permitted values in order, records them in a table, justifies completeness ('every value of a from 1 to 11'), respects the constraints, and handles 2x + y = 20 by computing y = 20 − 2x — transferring the systematic method to a new two-unknown equation.
responseLevels.partial: Finds several pairs and knows there is more than one, but searches unsystematically (misses or repeats), cannot justify completeness, or slips on the constraints or the coefficient — has some pairs but not the ordered, exhaustive method.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is an equation: a + b = 12, where a and b are whole numbers greater than 0. Find ALL the pairs of numbers that work, and show me how you know you have every one. Then find three different pairs that satisfy 2x + y = 20.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands generates MANY ordered pairs and justifies completeness by 'I went through every value of a in order'; a child treating it as a single-answer equation gives one pair and stops, or searches randomly and cannot tell whether the list is complete. For 2x + y = 20, respecting the coefficient (y = 20 − 2x, e.g. (3, 14)) versus offering pairs that only fit x + y = 20 (like (3, 17)) separates coefficient understanding.
