pedagogy.summary: This is the conceptual heart of the strand: understanding that a ratio expresses a MULTIPLICATIVE relationship between two quantities — one is always a constant number of times the other — and that this same relationship can be written as a ratio (a:b), as a fraction (a/b), and as a linear function (y = (a/b)x) whose graph is a straight line through the origin. The learning goal is to see these as one idea in three costumes, and above all to distinguish a multiplicative relationship (constant ratio) from an additive one (constant difference). Teaching should surface the invariant — what stays the same as the quantities grow — using ratio tables, double number lines and graphs, and should repeatedly contrast 'so many times as' against 'so much more than'.
bestPractices: Foreground the invariant: as both quantities scale, the DIFFERENCE changes but the MULTIPLE stays constant — make 'how many times' the thing children look for.
Move fluently between the three representations on one example: ratio 1:3, fraction 1/3 (or 3 times), and y = 3x graphed as a line through the origin — name them as the same relationship.
Use a ratio table and read it both ways: down the columns (scaling, the multiplier) and across (the constant a:b relationship / the y = kx rule).
Directly contrast multiplicative and additive tables side by side (one where y = 3x, one where y = x + 4) and ask which is a ratio relationship and why.
Connect the straight-line-through-the-origin graph to proportionality: doubling x doubles y only when the line passes through (0,0).
Ground the abstraction in a perceptible constant-ratio context (paint shade, concentration, speed) so 'same relationship' is something the child can see or taste, not just assert.
keyRepresentations: Ratio table with the constant multiplier visible down the columns and the a:b relationship across
Double number line aligned at 0 (equal ratios line up)
Straight-line graph through the origin (y = kx) with gradient = the ratio
The triple 1:3 = 1/3-relationship = y = 3x shown together
Paired multiplicative vs additive tables for contrast (y = 3x vs y = x + 4)
commonMisconceptions: Reads a relationship additively — fixes on the difference between a pair of values ('y is 4 more than x') instead of the constant multiple
Sees the constant multiplier for whole-number rows but cannot express it as a ratio, fraction, or y = kx
Confuses the part-to-part ratio a:b with the fraction a/b of the whole
Thinks any straight-line graph shows proportionality, not noticing it must pass through the origin

learn.summary: Learners come to see a ratio as a MULTIPLICATIVE relationship — one quantity is always a constant number of times the other — and to recognise this same relationship in three forms: a ratio a:b, a fraction a/b (x is a/b of y), and a linear function y=kx whose constant multiple k is the gradient and whose graph is a straight line through the origin. For the worked ratio 1:3 (x:y), x is 1/3 of y and y=3x, where the gradient 3 is y÷x. The central work is distinguishing a multiplicative relationship (constant ratio/multiple) from an additive one (constant difference). Vary the quantities, surface what stays the same (the multiple), and read the invariant across ratio tables, double number lines, graphs and a perceptible context such as paint shade. Keep part-to-part ratio a:b (x is 1/3 OF y) distinct from part-to-whole fraction (x out of the total x+y).

activities.title: One ratio, three costumes — and what breaks under 'add 4'
feedback: If a learner says the bigger batch is darker because there is 'more red', have them test y÷x on each row: it is always 3, so the proportion of red is unchanged — only the total amount grew.

If a learner fixes on a single pair's difference (e.g. '2 to 6 is +4'), have them test +4 on the next rows: 9 would have to be 7 and 12 would have to be 8, so +4 fails — the difference is not constant.
When the additive toggle is on, point to the line lifting off (0,0) and the shifting shade as the visible signs that the relationship is no longer a constant ratio.
Confirm that '×3', '1:3', 'x is 1/3 of y' and 'y=3x' are all names for the same relationship, and that the straight line passes through the origin because when x=0, y=0.
activities.rationale: The defining feature of this concept is an invariant that is felt by varying the quantities and watching what stays the same; linking a table, a graph and a perceptible mixture lets the constant multiple, the fraction and the gradient move together under scaling and break together under an additive rule. Linked panels with live recolouring and a rule toggle are offered as one concrete way to make the mechanism visible, not as the only means; this is a proposed design, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: At KS3 pupils 'understand that a multiplicative relationship between two quantities can be expressed as a ratio or a fraction' and 'relate the language of ratios and the associated calculations to the arithmetic of fractions and to linear functions'.

NCETM names as a central misconception that 'students often assume that relationships are additive... in situations where the actual relationship is multiplicative', considering the difference a−b rather than the ratio a:b (e.g. assuming a ratio 2:5 means one share is always £3 more than the other). It presents the one structure x×k=y expressible as ratio, fraction and the linear function y=mx (a straight line through the origin), and distinguishes scalar from functional multipliers using ratio tables and double number lines (which must both start at aligned zeros).
learnerActions: Work with the ratio 1:3 (e.g. red:yellow paint) and extend a ratio table: 1:3, 2:6, 3:9, 4:12, scaling both quantities together.
For each new row, plot the point (x,y) on a coordinate graph and note that the points fall on a straight line passing through the origin (0,0).
Observe a perceptible constant-ratio context alongside: in an idealised, thoroughly mixed model, a paint swatch mixed in that ratio keeps the same orange shade as the batch grows.
Name the same relationship in three forms on this one example: ratio 1:3, fraction/multiple (y is 3 times x; x is 1/3 of y), and linear function y=3x with gradient 3 (the gradient equals y÷x).

Switch the rule from multiplicative (y=3x) to additive (y=x+4) and watch what changes: the graph's line no longer passes through the origin, the plotted points leave the straight proportional line, and the swatch shade shifts row by row.
State in your own words which quantity stays constant in each case — the MULTIPLE stays fixed for a ratio relationship, while the DIFFERENCE stays fixed for an additive one.
activities.intendedInsight: A ratio is a single multiplicative idea wearing three costumes (ratio a:b, fraction a/b, straight line y=kx through the origin); its signature is a constant multiple, not a constant difference. When the quantities scale, the difference changes but the multiple — and the colour, the ratio and the gradient — stay the same. An additive rule breaks the line-through-origin and changes the shade, which is what separates it from a ratio.

activities.title: Read the ratio table both ways
feedback: If a learner extends row by row to reach x=10, prompt them to use the ×3 multiplier directly: 10×3=30.
If a learner writes the fraction using the total as denominator (e.g. 2/8 for x:y=2:6), separate the readings: the ratio compares x to y (x is 1/3 of y); part-to-whole would compare x to x+y=8.
Confirm a double number line only shows equal ratios when both lines start at aligned zeros.
activities.rationale: Reading a ratio table down (scalar) and across (functional), with an aligned double number line, is the representation NCETM uses to distinguish scalar from functional multipliers; keeping part-to-part separate from part-to-whole addresses a documented confusion. These are proposed uses of standard representations, not tested interventions.
sourceClaims: NCETM names as a central misconception that 'students often assume that relationships are additive... in situations where the actual relationship is multiplicative', considering the difference a−b rather than the ratio a:b (e.g. assuming a ratio 2:5 means one share is always £3 more than the other). It presents the one structure x×k=y expressible as ratio, fraction and the linear function y=mx (a straight line through the origin), and distinguishes scalar from functional multipliers using ratio tables and double number lines (which must both start at aligned zeros).
learnerActions: Take a ratio table and read DOWN the columns to find the scalar multiplier (how each row scales from the previous).
Read ACROSS the rows to find the constant functional relationship a:b / the y=kx rule between the two quantities.
Use a double number line aligned at 0 so that equal ratios line up, and check that both lines start at aligned zeros.
Given x=10 for a 1:3 relationship, work out y directly using the multiplier (×3) rather than extending the table row by row.

Distinguish 'x is 1/3 OF y' (part-to-part, the correct multiplicative reading) from 'x is a fraction of the whole x+y' (part-to-whole); for example, with 2 red : 5 blue beads, red is 2/5 of the blue count (part-to-part) but 2 out of 7 total beads (part-to-whole), anchoring each reading to its own picture.
activities.intendedInsight: A ratio table encodes both a scalar multiplier (down columns) and a functional multiplier (across, the y=kx rule); the multiple can be used directly to predict any value. A double number line aligned at zero shows equal ratios lining up. Part-to-part and part-to-whole are different comparisons.

activities.title: Sort and match: is it a ratio relationship?
feedback: For the x=2,y=5 / x=4,y=7 table, if a learner calls it a ratio, have them compute 5÷2=2.5 and 7÷4=1.75: the multiple is not constant, so it is additive (+3), not a ratio.
If a learner picks any straight line as proportional, ask where it crosses the y-axis: only a line through (0,0) represents y=kx.
When a learner matches 1:3 to y=3x, ask them to confirm the gradient of the line equals the multiple (3).
activities.rationale: Distinguishing multiplicative from additive tables and translating between forms can be checked with sorting, matching and prediction tasks using additive distractors. A sort can check classification and translation but does not itself require the learner to construct the invariant by varying quantities, so pair it with the manipulation activity above.
sourceClaims: At KS3 pupils 'understand that a multiplicative relationship between two quantities can be expressed as a ratio or a fraction' and 'relate the language of ratios and the associated calculations to the arithmetic of fractions and to linear functions'.
learnerActions: Sort several tables of values into 'ratio relationship' vs 'not a ratio relationship', justifying each by whether y÷x is constant.
Match equivalent forms: connect 1:3 with y=3x and with a straight line through the origin.
Predict y for a new x in a given table, with an additive answer offered as a tempting but wrong option, and explain why the additive choice fails.
Given two graphs, identify which shows proportionality and explain that it must pass through the origin.
Test a tricky table — x=2,y=5 and x=4,y=7 — and decide whether it is a ratio relationship (it is additive: +3 each time, but 5÷2 ≠ 7÷4, so no constant multiple).
activities.intendedInsight: Sorting and matching across forms, with deliberate additive distractors, can check whether a learner can translate among ratio, fraction and linear form and can reject an additive table as not proportional. A straight-line graph only shows proportionality when it passes through the origin.

activities.title: Justify it: times or more than?
feedback: If the learner reasons 'more red so darker' or 'different amounts so different', treat this as additive/absolute-amount reasoning and have them predict then check against y÷x.
Accept a full explanation only when it names the constant multiple AND notes that the difference is not constant.
Use the predict-observe-explain paint task so the reason stated before mixing is the diagnostic part.
activities.rationale: A Socratic challenge with a scaled counter-case targets the additive-vs-multiplicative distinction directly. Verbal justification can complement seeing the invariant across linked representations; use it alongside the manipulation activity rather than in place of it.
sourceClaims: NCETM names as a central misconception that 'students often assume that relationships are additive... in situations where the actual relationship is multiplicative', considering the difference a−b rather than the ratio a:b (e.g. assuming a ratio 2:5 means one share is always £3 more than the other). It presents the one structure x×k=y expressible as ratio, fraction and the linear function y=mx (a straight line through the origin), and distinguishes scalar from functional multipliers using ratio tables and double number lines (which must both start at aligned zeros).
learnerActions: Face a mentor who presents tables and asks for each: 'is it times, or more than? How do you know?'
Defend your classification by pointing to the constant multiple and showing that the difference changes down the table.
Respond to a scaled counter-case when you give an additive answer — e.g. 'you said +4; check the next row, does +4 still work?'
Explain, before mixing any paint, whether a 2:6 batch will be darker, lighter or the same shade as a 1:3 batch, and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Being pressed to justify whether a relationship is multiplicative or additive, and to meet a scaled counter-case, brings the reasoning into the open and can check whether the learner gives the right answer for the right reason.

constraints: Target age 12–14 (KS3); this is a conceptual objective about ratio notation and multiplicative relationships.
Ground the abstraction in at least one perceptible constant-ratio context (paint shade, concentration, speed) so 'same relationship' can be seen, not merely asserted.

The invariant is best surfaced by varying values and watching what stays fixed; a static annotated triple (table, ratio, graph) can summarise and reference the connections but does not itself let the learner vary quantities, so use it as a summary rather than the sole discovery activity.

Sorting, matching and prediction tasks can check and consolidate translation between forms but are recognition-level; they do not by themselves require independent construction of the invariant, so pair them with activities where the learner scales the quantities and states the relationship.

Express the linear form as y=kx where k (the gradient) is the constant multiple y÷x; for ratio 1:3 that is y=3x. Do not write the gradient as a/b (which for 1:3 would give the incorrect 1/3); a/b=1/3 is the separate fraction reading 'x is 1/3 of y'.
Keep part-to-part ratio a:b ('x is 1/3 OF y') distinct from part-to-whole fraction (x out of total x+y); do not let learners write the fraction with the total as denominator.
Double number lines must start at aligned zeros for equal ratios to line up; a ratio table does not need a 0:0 row, though including one can show the link to the origin on the graph.
A straight-line graph shows proportionality only when it passes through the origin; a line not through (0,0) represents y=kx+c, not a ratio relationship.

Live recolouring, a rule toggle (y=3x vs y=x+4), draggable/extendable table rows and linked plotting are offered as optional ways to make the mechanism concrete; they are examples of interaction, not required mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original row expressed the linear function both as 'y=(a/b)x' and as the triple '1:3 = y=3x'. These are inconsistent: for the ratio a:b = 1:3 (x:y), the gradient is y÷x = b/a = 3, so y=3x, whereas y=(a/b)x gives the incorrect y=(1/3)x. The guidance has been corrected to state y=kx with gradient = y÷x; the original formula is recorded as an error, not offered to learners.

The legacy row rated a 3D artefact 'poor' with the claim '3D adds nothing'. This comparative/necessity claim is not established by the cited sources and has been dropped; the relationship is primarily numeric/graphical, a reasonable scoping note, but no universal medium superiority is implied.
The legacy framing that the linked-panel tool is uniquely able to teach the concept has been softened: linked panels are one concrete way to expose the invariant, not the only way.

Arithmetic self-audit: for the counter-case table x=2,y=5 and x=4,y=7 the differences are +3 (5−2 and 7−4); the ratios 5÷2=2.5 and 7÷4=1.75 are unequal, confirming it is additive, not a ratio. For the 1:3 relationship, rows 2:6, 3:9, 4:12 give y÷x=3 throughout with differences 4,6,8 (not constant), confirming multiplicative. x=10 gives y=30. For the bead example 2 red : 5 blue, the total is 7, so part-to-whole red is 2/7, distinct from the part-to-part reading 2/5.

The original assess 'additive' distractor 'y is always 4 more than x' refers to the first pair 2→6 (difference 4); it is retained only as a diagnostic distractor to be challenged, never taught as correct.
The original part-to-whole distractor 'x is 2 out of the whole 8, so the relationship is 2/8' is retained only as a misconception to separate and correct, not as a valid reading.
Whether any of these proposed activities improve learning is untested; sources support the curriculum content and the additive misconception, not the specific interventions.

assess.poeTask: Show the child a jar of orange paint made from 1 spoon red and 3 spoons yellow, and a second, bigger batch you will make from 2 spoons red and 6 spoons yellow. PREDICT before mixing: will the bigger batch be a darker orange, a lighter orange, or exactly the same shade — and WHY? (A child reasoning 'more red, so darker' or 'different amounts, so different' is reasoning additively/by absolute amount; the reason stated before mixing is the diagnostic part.) OBSERVE: mix both — the shades match exactly. EXPLAIN: because 2:6 is the same ratio as 1:3 (both parts multiplied by 2), the multiplicative relationship — and so the colour — is unchanged; adding different amounts to each part is what would change the shade.
probeDeeper: 'Write this relationship as a ratio x:y, and as y = ? × x' — checks the translation among ratio, fraction and linear form.

Counterexample: 'Another table has x = 2, y = 5 and x = 4, y = 7. Is THAT a ratio relationship? How do you know?' — this one is additive (+3, but 5÷2 ≠ 7÷4); a child with the concept identifies it as 'add', NOT a constant ratio.
'If x = 10, what is y — and how do you know without extending the table row by row?' — tests whether the multiplier is used directly.
'If we plotted these points, what would the graph look like, and why does it go through (0,0)?' — links proportionality to the line through the origin.
assess.correctAnswer: y is always the same number of TIMES x — y is 3 times x (y = 3x). You can tell because the AMOUNT bigger changes (6 is 4 more than 2, 9 is 6 more, 15 is 10 more) so it is not a constant 'more than', but y ÷ x is always 3, a constant multiple — this is the multiplicative relationship, the ratio x:y = 1:3.

errorPatterns.pattern: Additive: fixes on the difference in the first pair ('y is 4 more than x, because 2 and 6') and treats the relationship as constant addition
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have the child test '+4' on every row (9 would need to be 7; 15 would need to be 9) — the difference is not constant. Then find y÷x for each row (all 3) to surface the constant multiple. Documented additive-strategy interference.
errorPatterns.distractor: y is always 4 more than x
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives '+4' (or another single-row difference) and does not check it against the other rows, where it fails

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses the part-to-part ratio with a part-to-whole fraction: reads x:y = 2:6 and says 'so x is 2/6... 1/3 of the whole' misapplying the fraction
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the two readings: the ratio compares x to y (x is 1/3 of y); part-to-whole would compare x to x+y. Anchor each to its own picture.
errorPatterns.distractor: x is 2 out of the whole 8, so the relationship is 2/8
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child mixes up 'x is 1/3 OF y' (correct multiplicative reading) with 'x is 1/3 of the whole' (part-to-whole), or writes the fraction with the total 8 as denominator

errorPatterns.pattern: Sees the ×3 for the whole-number rows but cannot express the relationship as a ratio, a fraction, or y = 3x
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach the concept — scaffold the notation link: 'times 3' = ratio 1:3 = y = 3x; connect to the straight-line-through-origin graph. The idea is present; the representations need joining.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says 'times 3' correctly but cannot write it as 1:3 or y = 3x when asked

responseLevels.gap: Reads the relationship additively (a constant 'more than') and cannot see that the difference changes; treats one pair's difference as the rule.
responseLevels.full: States that y is a constant number of times x, justifies it by the changing difference vs constant multiple, expresses the relationship as 1:3, 1/3 and y = 3x, links it to a straight line through the origin, and correctly rejects an additive table as not a ratio relationship.
responseLevels.partial: Identifies the constant multiple (×3) for the given rows but cannot yet express it as a ratio/fraction/linear function, or slips between part-to-part and part-to-whole, or does not connect it to the line through the origin — knows the pieces without coordinating them.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a table of matching values. When x = 2, y = 6; when x = 3, y = 9; when x = 5, y = 15. I want two things. First: is y always the same AMOUNT bigger than x, or always the same number of TIMES x? Second, and most important: how can you tell from the table which one it is?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Asking for the REASON (tier two), not just the classification, is what separates genuine multiplicative understanding from a guess. A child reasoning multiplicatively points to the constant multiple (3) and notes the difference is NOT constant; a child reasoning additively latches onto one pair's difference (2 to 6 is +4) and cannot see that the +4 fails on the next row. Because the 'amount bigger' visibly changes down the table while the multiple stays fixed, a correct answer is hard to give for the wrong reason and a wrong answer is hard to give for the right reason.

sources.claim: At KS3 pupils 'understand that a multiplicative relationship between two quantities can be expressed as a ratio or a fraction' and 'relate the language of ratios and the associated calculations to the arithmetic of fractions and to linear functions'.
sources.source: DfE, National curriculum in England: mathematics programmes of study (KS3 ratio, proportion and rates of change) (Crown copyright)

sources.claim: NCETM names as a central misconception that 'students often assume that relationships are additive... in situations where the actual relationship is multiplicative', considering the difference a−b rather than the ratio a:b (e.g. assuming a ratio 2:5 means one share is always £3 more than the other). It presents the one structure x×k=y expressible as ratio, fraction and the linear function y=mx (a straight line through the origin), and distinguishes scalar from functional multipliers using ratio tables and double number lines (which must both start at aligned zeros).
sources.source: NCETM KS3 Mastery PD, 3.1 Understanding multiplicative relationships (Crown Copyright)

pedagogy.summary: At 6-8, sorting matures into ORGANISING and RECORDING data: given a question, sort items into 2-3 categories, count each, and capture the result as a simple table or list of category-names-with-counts, then order the categories. The shift from the 5-6 skill is that the count is now written down as a record that can be read back to answer the question — the beginning of GAISE's data sense (data are information about a context). Teaching should start from a genuine question ('which packed-lunch fruit is most popular?'), collect and tally, transfer to a table, and always return to the question so the table is a tool, not a decoration.
bestPractices: Begin with a statistical question worth asking, so the organised data has a purpose to answer
Model the tally-then-table pipeline: sort/tally the raw data, then write each category name beside its count in a table or list
Keep category totals reconciling with the whole set ('7 + 5 + 4 = 16, and we had 16 cards') to build a self-check habit
Read the table back to answer the question and to order the categories most-to-fewest
keyRepresentations: Simple frequency table / list (category name + count)
Tally chart feeding the table
Sorted objects or cards arranged in rows as the concrete source
Ordered list of categories from most to fewest
commonMisconceptions: Records counts that don't line up with their categories (rows misaligned in the table)
Organises the data but cannot read it back to answer the original question (table treated as decoration)
Miscounts categories or the totals don't reconcile with the full set
Forces every item into the given categories (or invents overlaps) when some items fit none

learn.summary: For ages 6-8, sorting matures into organising AND recording categorical data: starting from a genuine statistical question, children sort items into 2-3 categories, count each, write each category name beside its count in a simple table or list, and order the categories by quantity. The new skill beyond the 5-6 level is that the count becomes a written record that can be read back to answer the question — the table is a tool, not a decoration. Teaching should begin from a real question (e.g. 'which packed-lunch fruit is most popular?'), collect and tally, transfer to a table with totals that reconcile against the whole set, and always return to the question.

activities.title: Survey organiser: from response cards to a table that answers the question
feedback: If row counts don't add up to the number of cards, a card may have been lost or double-counted — recount by moving each card aside as it is tallied, and check the parts sum to the whole
If asked 'which does the class like best?' and the child re-counts cards instead of reading the table, model reading it: 'the biggest number is beside…' and return to the question
If a card fits none of the given categories, don't force it into a pile — allow an 'other' category if genuinely needed
Point to each pile and its matching table row together as the number is written, so counts and labels stay correctly paired
activities.rationale: Organising categorical data is a procedural build-it task: sorting raw cards and watching a table populate makes the tally-then-table pipeline concrete and gives immediate feedback. Ordering the rows makes the answer surface, reinforcing that data are collected to answer a question about a context.
sourceClaims: At Level A students represent the distribution of a categorical variable using tables and picture/bar graphs and develop 'data sense' — that data are information collected to answer a statistical investigative question about a context
Year 2 pupils interpret and construct simple tables and sort categories by quantity, asking and answering questions about totalling and comparing categorical data
learnerActions: Start from a real question the class cares about, e.g. 'which of these three snacks is most popular?' or 'which of these three fruits does our class like best?'
Take a shuffled stack of class response cards and sort each card into one of 2-3 categories, building a tally as you go
Write each category name beside its count in a simple table or list
Check that the row counts add up to the number of cards you started with (e.g. '7 + 5 + 4 = 16, and we had 16 cards')
Order the categories from most to fewest so the category with the biggest count rises to the top (if two categories have the same biggest count, say that they are tied rather than naming one winner)
Read the table back aloud to state which category answers the question

Test the table as a live record: if two more children chose one fruit, update that count, check that the new total is 2 more than before (e.g. 18 instead of 16), and see whether the ordered answer changes
activities.intendedInsight: An organised table is a tool that ANSWERS a question, not just a store of numbers: once ordered, the record visibly shows the most popular category, the totals should reconcile with the whole set, and updating a count updates the answer.

activities.title: Interactive reconcile-and-order check (optional self-check mechanism)
feedback: A reconcile flag when totals don't match the card count makes a lost or double-counted response visible — treat it as a prompt to recount, not a failure
When 'order' is pressed the rows re-rank most-to-fewest so the most popular category rises to the top, showing the answer emerging from the data itself
activities.rationale: Optional interactive mechanisms (drag-to-sort, a tally that builds, a count cell that checks against the raw data, an 'order' control) make the recording-and-reconciling of a constructed table concrete and give feedback as each count is entered. These are illustrative affordances, not required tools — the same pipeline of constructing a table and sorting categories by quantity works with physical cards and a paper table.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils interpret and construct simple tables and sort categories by quantity, asking and answering questions about totalling and comparing categorical data
learnerActions: Drag each response card to a category pile and watch a tally build
Type each count into a table's cells
Notice when the row counts are flagged for not reconciling with the number of cards, and fix the lost or double-counted response
Press an 'order' control and watch the rows rank themselves most-to-fewest, lifting the winning category to the top
Answer a final question — which category answers our question?
activities.intendedInsight: A live record stays trustworthy only when its parts reconcile with the whole; ordering the rows turns the record into a visible answer.

activities.title: Read a completed table to say what it means (annotation scaffold)
feedback: If the child reads a count without naming its category, re-pair the label and number together
This reference-only reading supports interpretation but does not itself practise organising raw data — pair it with a hands-on sort so the child also builds the table
activities.rationale: A labelled, static table can teach interpretation (what each row means, which is largest) as a reference scaffold. It is a complement to, not a replacement for, the build-it task, because it does not let the child organise raw data into a table.
sourceClaims: At Level A students represent the distribution of a categorical variable using tables and picture/bar graphs and develop 'data sense' — that data are information collected to answer a statistical investigative question about a context
learnerActions: Look at a completed, labelled frequency table of category names and counts
Point to each row and say what it means ('this row says 5 children chose banana')
Say which row has the biggest count and what question that answers
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a table back — pairing each label with its count and identifying the largest — is a necessary step toward using data to answer a question.

constraints: Begin from a genuine statistical question so the organised data has a purpose to answer; always return to the question so the table is a tool, not a decoration
Model the full tally-then-table pipeline: sort/tally raw data, then write each category name beside its count
Build a reconcile habit: category totals should sum back to the whole set, and this self-check should be modelled explicitly
Limit to 2-3 categories with counts within young children's secure cardinality

Allow an 'other' category for items that fit none of the given categories, rather than forcing or double-placing them; keep the total number of categories, including 'other', within the 2-3 category limit (e.g. two named categories plus 'other')
The reading/annotation scaffold assesses and supports interpretation but does not elicit independent construction of a table from raw data; pair it with hands-on organising
Interactive reconcile/order controls are illustrative affordances; the same learning can occur with physical cards and a paper table — do not treat the digital tool as mandatory
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source row asserts '3D adds no value' and that conversation 'offers nothing to sort or tabulate'; these are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws. They are omitted as universal claims — spoken discussion can still support framing the question and reading a table back, even if it is not the primary medium for the recording procedure.
An earlier candidate feedback line claimed 'live recolouring' of rows; this was not in the source and has been removed, leaving only the supported re-ranking behaviour.

The KS1 source claim is retained on the interactive activity only because that activity genuinely rehearses constructing a table and sorting categories by quantity; it is not evidence that the interactive medium outperforms paper, which remains an untested affordance.
The original assessment's gap/partial/full response tiers are not reproduced verbatim but are reflected in the feedback's distinction between supported and independent performance.
Prerequisite reteach links from the source (secure cardinality; clean non-overlapping sorting) are noted here as teaching dependencies but are not learner-facing citations.
The arithmetic example '7 + 5 + 4 = 16' checks out and is retained as a reconcile illustration.

probeDeeper: Ask 'do your table numbers add up to how many cards we started with?' to check the reconcile habit
Ask 'which fruit does the class like best — how does your table show that?' to see if the record is used to answer the question
Counterexample tuned to this topic: slip in a card for a fruit that isn't one of the three and watch whether they force it or handle it as 'other'
Ask 'if two more people chose apple, what changes in your table — and does the answer change?' to test that the table is a live record
assess.correctAnswer: A correct performance: sorts all cards into the three fruit categories, counts each, writes each fruit name beside its correct count in a table (totals reconciling with the number of cards), orders the categories, and states which fruit answers the question.

errorPatterns.pattern: Records counts that don't line up with their categories — the table's numbers and labels are mismatched
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the transfer — point to each pile and its row together as the number is written; a recording slip, so steady the pipeline rather than reteach sorting
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The count written for a fruit doesn't match the pile the child actually made for it

errorPatterns.pattern: Organises the data but cannot read it back to answer the original question (table as decoration)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model reading a table to answer a question ('the biggest number is beside…'); keep returning to the question so the table becomes a tool
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked 'so which fruit does the class like best?' the child re-counts cards or shrugs instead of reading the table

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscounts a category or the totals don't reconcile with the full set (insecure cardinality)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild cardinality — move each card aside as counted and check the parts sum to the whole
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Row counts don't sum to the number of cards, and a recount gives a different figure

errorPatterns.pattern: Forces cards that fit no category into a group, or double-places ambiguous ones, because the categorisation isn't kept clean
errorPatterns.nextMove: Revisit clean, non-overlapping sorting from the earlier skill; allow an 'other' category if genuinely needed
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A 'neither' card is jammed into a pile, or an item appears counted twice

responseLevels.gap: Sorts unreliably, mis-pairs or miscounts in the table, and cannot answer the question from it
responseLevels.full: Independently sorts, records reconciling counts correctly paired to categories, orders them, and reads the table back to answer the question
responseLevels.partial: Produces a table with correct counts when supported, but totals may not reconcile or the child re-counts rather than reading the table to answer

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Our question is: which of these three fruits does our class like best? Here are everyone's choice cards. Organise them so we can answer the question, and show me the counts in a table. (Set the task and WATCH how they organise and record.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Observing the organising-and-recording shows what a verbal answer hides. A child with the skill produces a table whose counts are correctly paired and reconcile, and reads it back to answer the question; a child without it mis-pairs counts, loses cards, or organises the data yet cannot use it to answer 'which best'.

sources.claim: At Level A students represent the distribution of a categorical variable using tables and picture/bar graphs and develop 'data sense' — that data are information collected to answer a statistical investigative question about a context
sources.source: ASA GAISE II (PreK-12) framework, Level A (statistical problem-solving process and analysis)

sources.claim: Year 2 pupils interpret and construct simple tables and sort categories by quantity, asking and answering questions about totalling and comparing categorical data
sources.source: National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study — Statistics (KS1)

pedagogy.summary: At 10-11 modelling reaches its primary-school capstone: ratio, scale, volume and proportional reasoning, and — decisively — deciding whether an answer should be rounded and to what accuracy. This is where the interpret-back becomes a judgement, not just a re-labelling: the classic case is the bus problem (328 people, 40-seat buses → 8.2 → you must order 9 whole buses), where the mathematically 'exact' answer is the wrong answer to the real question. The teaching goal is a child who chooses a fit-for-purpose tool (bar, double number line, ratio table, labelled diagram + formula), computes, and then asks 'what does this decimal mean here — do I round, which way, and to what precision?' before trusting it.
bestPractices: Foreground the rounding-in-context judgement: after the calculation, ask 'does this answer need rounding, which way, and to what accuracy — and why does the SITUATION decide, not the maths?'

Use authentic 'order the buses / fill the boxes' framings where rounding the wrong way fails visibly — research shows far more children reason correctly when the context is real than when the division is bare (DeFranco & Curcio)
Teach tool CHOICE for proportional problems: double number line and ratio table for ratio/rate, labelled diagram + formula for volume, scale factor for similar shapes
Keep units alive through volume work (cm³ vs cm² vs cm) and interpret the final quantity as a real capacity a container could hold
Demand a reasonableness pass on every model: estimate first, then check the computed answer sits near the estimate and makes sense in the situation
keyRepresentations: Double number line and ratio table for ratio/rate and proportion
Bar model for part-whole ratio and comparison
Labelled 3D diagram with volume formula (V = l×w×h / B×h)
Scale factor / scaled drawing for similar shapes
commonMisconceptions: Reports the bare quotient (8.2 buses) and never rounds to the whole buses the situation demands, or rounds the wrong way (down) leaving people stranded
Rounds by rote to the nearest whole/decimal place regardless of what the context needs (money to 2 dp, buses always UP, lengths to sensible precision)
Reasons additively about ratio/scale (adds the same amount to both quantities) instead of multiplicatively
Blurs volume with area or length, or reports cm³ answers in the wrong unit
Chooses a tool by habit (single bar) that hides the two covarying quantities in a rate/ratio problem

learn.summary: For 10-11 year olds, this is the capstone of mathematical modelling: choosing a fit-for-purpose tool (bar model, double number line, ratio table, labelled 3D diagram + volume formula, scale factor), computing, and then making the decisive judgement — does this answer need rounding, which way, and to what accuracy, and does the SITUATION rather than a rote rule decide? The anchor case is the bus problem (328 people, 40-seat coaches → 8.2 → you must book 9), where the 'exact' decimal is the wrong real answer. Core activities put the child in authentic decisions where naive rounding visibly fails, kept alongside spatial volume work and a dialogue variant that presses for a committed, justified answer.

activities.title: Order the coaches: when 8.2 is the wrong answer
feedback: If a learner reports '8.2 coaches' untroubled, ask: 'Can the organiser book two-tenths of a coach? What can they actually order?' Route the quotient back to a bookable whole.

If a learner rounds down to 8 citing '.2 rounds down', ask them to work out 8 × 40 and compare with 328 — surface the 8 people with no seat, then establish that here the context forces rounding UP however small the remainder.
For the 320-people case, affirm that an exact quotient (8) needs no rounding judgement, so the child can see the decision is driven by the leftover, not by habit.
When a learner commits to 9 and justifies it by the stranded people, affirm that they have modelled, not just computed.
For the crates variant, if a learner rounds up by habit, ask what a partly-filled crate means for a FULL-crate count, so they see the direction flips with the situation.
activities.rationale: Research cited for this topic reports children reason correctly about rounding far more often when a bare division is reframed as an authentic ordering task, so staging a real decision with a visible consequence targets the modelling judgement rather than the easy arithmetic.
sourceClaims: Modelling requires interpreting mathematical results in context and reflecting on whether they make sense; the situation, not the bare computation, determines the acceptable answer

In DeFranco & Curcio's bus problem (328 people, 40-seat buses), few children rounded to whole buses when the division was bare, but most reasoned correctly when the task was framed as authentically ordering the buses — context restores sense-making and drives rounding
learnerActions: Take the real job: 328 people need to travel to a match; each coach seats 40. Build a ratio table or double number line, or divide, and land on 8.2.
Make the rounding decision explicitly: do I round? which way? to what accuracy? and WHY — state the reason before trusting the number.
Check the consequence of rounding down: 8 coaches × 40 = 320 seats, leaving 8 people with no seat. Commit to 9 coaches and justify it by those stranded people.
Explain in your own words why the SITUATION (a coach is indivisible, nobody can be left behind) decides the direction, not the nearest-whole rule.
Try the exact-division contrast: if only 320 people travelled, 320 ÷ 40 = 8 exactly, so no rounding decision arises — notice the dilemma only appears when the division leaves a remainder.

Try a variant that rounds the OTHER way: 'how many FULL crates can we pack from 328 apples, 40 to a crate?' — here you round down to 8 full crates (8 apples left over). Explain why the direction differs.
activities.intendedInsight: A computed decimal must be interpreted back against the real question; whether and which way to round is a judgement the context makes, not a rule applied on autopilot. The same arithmetic rounds up for coaches and down for full crates, and when the division is exact (320 ÷ 40 = 8) there is no rounding decision at all.

activities.title: Choosing the right tool for a proportional problem
feedback: If a learner adds a constant to both quantities on a scale variant, show two rows of a ratio table and ask what you multiply the first row by to reach the second — reassert the multiplicative relationship.
If a learner reaches for a single bar that can't show the rate, ask where the second quantity lives on their diagram, and rebuild with a double number line or ratio table.
Affirm tool choices the learner can justify by the structure of the situation rather than by habit.
activities.rationale: Guidance cited here holds that bar models and part-whole/comparison diagrams expose proportional structure so children set up and solve rather than manipulate numbers by rule, which motivates explicit, structure-matched tool choice.
sourceClaims: Bar models and part-whole/comparison diagrams expose ratio and proportional structure so children can set up and solve rather than manipulate numbers by rule
learnerActions: Before computing, pick a tool that matches the structure: double number line or ratio table for ratio/rate, bar model for part-whole ratio and comparison, scale factor for similar shapes.
Set up a ratio/scale problem and keep BOTH covarying quantities visible — e.g. on a double number line label litres against cost, or recipe quantities against servings.
Scale multiplicatively, not additively: check that if one quantity is multiplied by a factor, the other is multiplied by the same factor, rather than adding the same amount to both.
Explain why a single bar that shows only one quantity would hide the rate, and choose a tool that doesn't.
activities.intendedInsight: Proportional situations covary multiplicatively; choosing a representation that keeps both quantities in view prevents the common additive error and sets up a correct model before any rounding question arises.

activities.title: Volume as capacity: pack it, compute it, then decide the accuracy
feedback: If a learner reports a cm³ answer in cm or cm², ask whether they measured length, surface, or space filled, and relabel.
If a learner over- or under-states precision, ask what decision the number is for — a tank that must not overflow vs a rough estimate call for different accuracy.
When a learner rounds full-crate counts down and justifies it by the leftover not filling a crate, affirm the context-driven direction.
activities.rationale: Modelling guidance cited here treats interpreting the result in context as essential, and volume is a genuinely spatial quantity at this band; packing cubes makes capacity concrete so the precision/rounding decision is meaningful. Comparative claims that a physical model teaches this better than a diagram are not established by the cited sources.
sourceClaims: Modelling requires interpreting mathematical results in context and reflecting on whether they make sense; the situation, not the bare computation, determines the acceptable answer
learnerActions: Pack a box or tank with unit cubes to feel volume as capacity, then connect this to the formula V = l×w×h (or V = base area × height).
Compute the volume of a labelled container and keep units alive: distinguish cm (length), cm² (area) and cm³ (volume), and report the answer in the right unit.
Answer a real decision that forces rounding the correct way, e.g. 'how many full crates fit inside?' (round down) or 'will this tank overflow if we pour in X litres?'.

For a measurement like a tank holding 12.7 litres, decide to what accuracy you should state it and say who or what in the situation decides that precision (note: 12.7 is an illustrative figure, not computed from given dimensions).
activities.intendedInsight: Volume is a real capacity, not just a formula output; units must be tracked (cm³ ≠ cm² ≠ cm), and the required precision and rounding direction depend on the physical situation (not overflowing, counting only full containers).

activities.title: Defend your answer to the client (spoken variant)
feedback: If a learner says 'always round up', ask for the full-crates case and let them find that it rounds down, so the rule is replaced by situation-reading.
If a learner offers 8.2 to the client, have the client ask what that means to book, pushing interpretation into whole units.
Affirm answers where the learner names the real consequence (people stranded, a crate left part-empty) as the reason for the direction.
activities.rationale: A client who needs a real decision is a natural foil for the interpret-in-context judgement, consistent with cited modelling guidance that the situation determines the acceptable answer; this is a research-informed proposal, not a tested intervention.
sourceClaims: Modelling requires interpreting mathematical results in context and reflecting on whether they make sense; the situation, not the bare computation, determines the acceptable answer
learnerActions: Role-play with an event organiser or engineer who presses for a real decision: 'The maths said 8.2 — do I book 8 or 9? What happens to the other people?'
Commit to a whole, bookable answer and defend the direction of rounding out loud by naming the consequence.
Handle a sprung variant that tests transfer, e.g. 330 people with 44-seat coaches (330 ÷ 44 = 7.5 → 8 coaches), or a round-down full-boxes case, and justify the new decision.
Respond to the challenge 'you always round up in word problems — true?' with a counter-example where rounding up would be wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to commit to and justify a context-appropriate rounded answer in dialogue — and to say when 'always round up' fails — shows the judgement is situation-driven, not a memorised rule.

activities.title: Sub-skill checks feeding the real task
feedback: If a learner is fluent on sub-skills but stalls on the modelling decision, direct them to the ordering/crates/tank tasks where the computed number must be interpreted.
Note that a correct bare quotient (e.g. 8.2) can be 'right' as arithmetic yet wrong as the real answer.
activities.rationale: A check of an isolated computation assesses the component skill but does not by itself elicit or observe the situated rounding judgement, so such checks are positioned as feeders to the full modelling task rather than as the capstone itself. The cited principle that the situation (not the bare computation) determines the acceptable answer underpins treating computation as only the start.
sourceClaims: Modelling requires interpreting mathematical results in context and reflecting on whether they make sense; the situation, not the bare computation, determines the acceptable answer
learnerActions: Practise isolated sub-skills on short items: compute a volume from a labelled diagram, simplify a ratio, or complete a row of a ratio table.
Immediately feed each checked sub-skill back into a full modelling task that requires the rounding-in-context decision, rather than stopping at the computed number.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency with the component operations supports, but does not replace, the modelling judgement; a correct computation is only the start of answering the real question.

constraints: The learning objective is the situated judgement of whether/which-way/how-precisely to round, plus choosing a structure-matched tool — not just producing a correct quotient.

A check of an isolated computation (compute a volume, simplify a ratio) assesses the component skill but does not elicit the independent rounding-in-context decision; use such checks only as sub-skill feeders into a full modelling task. A bare '8.2' can score as correct arithmetic while being the wrong real-world answer.

A static labelled diagram can illustrate a finished model or serve as a reference for what each tool represents, but does not itself host the computation, tool-choice or rounding judgement that is being taught.
Keep units explicit through volume work (cm vs cm² vs cm³) and interpret the final quantity as a real capacity.
Always include a reasonableness pass: estimate first, then check the computed answer sits near the estimate and makes sense in the situation.

Include at least one round-up case (coaches), one round-down case (full crates), and ideally an exact-division case (no rounding needed) so the direction is read from the situation, not fixed as a rule; avoid teaching 'always round up in word problems'.
Physical cube-packing and on-screen models offer different experiences of volume; do not claim one is universally necessary or that a diagram cannot convey capacity.
When the proportional set-up or the interpret-into-context step is missing, a flagged earlier prerequisite topic should be revisited; confirm the correct prerequisite linkage before relying on it.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The bus/coach numbers were audited: 328 ÷ 40 = 8.2; 8 coaches seat 320, leaving 8 people without a seat, so rounding up to 9 is correct. The 330 people / 44-seat variant gives 330 ÷ 44 = 7.5 → 8 coaches; the full-crates case (328 apples, 40 per crate) gives 8 full crates with 8 left over (round down); the restored 320-people case gives 320 ÷ 40 = 8 exactly (no rounding). These are consistent as stated.

The source row's diagnostic '12.7 litres' tank figure is used illustratively for a precision discussion; no specific tank dimensions are given, so it is treated as an example precision decision rather than a computed result.

Original source framing included strong comparative/necessity claims (e.g. a quiz 'cannot compel' the judgement, a static diagram 'cannot host' the practice, 3D conveys capacity more viscerally than 2D). These have been softened to scoped affordances/limits because the cited sources establish the value of context-rich modelling but not comparative efficacy between media.

Cited evidence (CCSS MP4, Colorado/DeFranco & Curcio, NCETM Bar Model) supports the teaching principles about context-driven interpretation and structure-exposing diagrams; it does not establish that the specific proposed activities were tested.

probeDeeper: If it had been 320 people instead of 328, how many coaches — and does the .0 vs .2 change how you round?
Now: 'how many FULL crates can we pack from 328 apples, 40 to a crate?' — do you round the same way? Why is it different from the coaches?
A tank calculation gives 12.7 litres — to what accuracy would you give that answer, and who decides?
Someone says 'you always round up in word problems' — is that true? Give me a case where it's wrong.
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child recognising that 8.2 coaches is not a bookable quantity, that you must round UP to 9 (8 coaches leaves 8 people with no seat), and that the SITUATION, not a rounding rule, decides the direction. A child who accepts '8.2', or who rounds to 8 'because .2 rounds down', has computed correctly but not modelled — they haven't interpreted the result against the real question.

errorPatterns.pattern: Accepts the bare decimal as the answer — '8.2 coaches' — without recognising a coach is indivisible and the result must be interpreted into whole bookable units
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make the situation concrete: 'can you book two-tenths of a coach?' Route the quotient back through 'what can the organiser actually order?' until interpret-into-context is automatic. This is the DeFranco/Curcio bus finding — reasserting the situation restores sense.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child reports 8.2 (or 8.2 coaches) untroubled, treating the exact quotient as the final answer to a real-world question

errorPatterns.pattern: Rounds by rote against the context — '8.2 rounds to 8' — applying the nearest-whole rule and leaving 8 people with no seat
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast the rule with the need: check the consequence (8×40 = 320 < 328). Establish that the CONTEXT sets the direction — here you must round UP however small the remainder. Practise paired cases (buses round up, full-boxes round down).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child rounds down citing the .2 < .5 rule, showing the rounding procedure has overridden the situation

errorPatterns.pattern: Reasons additively / uses a habitual tool that hides the covarying quantities, so the proportional set-up itself is wrong before rounding even arises
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild with a double number line or ratio table that keeps both quantities visible and scales multiplicatively; check the tool fits the structure before computing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a ratio/scale variant the child adds a constant to both quantities or picks a single bar that can't show the rate, giving a set-up that doesn't match the situation

responseLevels.gap: Accepts '8.2 coaches', or rounds to 8 by the nearest-whole rule, and cannot say why the situation might override the rule; no consequence-checking.
responseLevels.full: Unprompted, rejects 8.2 as unbookable, rounds UP to 9 justified by the 8 people otherwise stranded, articulates that the CONTEXT sets whether and which way to round and to what accuracy, and transfers correctly to a round-down (full crates) and a precision (tank litres) variant.
responseLevels.partial: When prompted, rounds to 9 and can compute, and lists that you 'round up here', but treats it as a remembered rule rather than a situation-driven judgement, and does not spontaneously check the consequence or transfer the direction to a round-down case.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: 328 people need to travel to a match. Each coach holds 40 people. A pupil divides and gets 8.2, and writes '8.2 coaches'. Is that the answer the organiser needs? Talk me through what you'd actually tell them to book, and why.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The arithmetic is correct and easy, so computation is not the tell. The discriminator is whether the child interprets the quotient against the situation and rounds for the context — and critically the direction is AGAINST the standard 'round 8.2 to 8' rule, so a child running rounding on autopilot gives the wrong real answer while a child modelling gives 9 and can justify it by the people left behind.

sources.claim: Modelling requires interpreting mathematical results in context and reflecting on whether they make sense; the situation, not the bare computation, determines the acceptable answer
sources.source: CCSS Standards for Mathematical Practice — MP4 Model with mathematics

sources.claim: In DeFranco & Curcio's bus problem (328 people, 40-seat buses), few children rounded to whole buses when the division was bare, but most reasoned correctly when the task was framed as authentically ordering the buses — context restores sense-making and drives rounding
sources.source: Colorado Dept of Education — Word Problems Guide (citing DeFranco & Curcio 1997)

sources.claim: Bar models and part-whole/comparison diagrams expose ratio and proportional structure so children can set up and solve rather than manipulate numbers by rule
sources.source: NCETM — The Bar Model

pedagogy.summary: Solving one- and two-step word problems within 100 with unknowns in all positions is fundamentally about MODELLING the situation, not about the arithmetic. Children must read what is happening (joining, separating, comparing), identify the unknown's position (result, change, or start), represent it — ideally with a bar model and an equation using a symbol for the unknown — and only then compute. The research-critical point is that keyword strategies fail, and problem difficulty is governed by semantic structure: start-unknown and compare problems are far harder than result-unknown.
bestPractices: Model before calculating: draw a bar model / part-whole and write an equation with a symbol for the unknown, then solve
Explicitly teach all problem structures — join/separate with result, change, or start unknown, and compare (how many more/fewer) — not just result-unknown
Do NOT teach keyword shortcuts ('more'→add); they break on compare and start-unknown problems
For two-step problems, name and hold the intermediate result before the second step
Use the DfE additive vocabulary (total, difference, more/less, change) tied to the situation, and connect comparison to 'difference'
keyRepresentations: Bar model (part-whole, comparison, two-step)
Part-whole diagram
Equation with a symbol/box for the unknown (e.g. 28 = □ − 15)
Number line (count-on for difference/change)
Cubes/counters to act out the situation
commonMisconceptions: Keyword strategy: choosing the operation from a cue word rather than the situation (fails on compare/start-unknown)
Start-unknown problems solved as if result-unknown (doing the stated operation forwards instead of its inverse)
Doing only the first step of a two-step problem
Compare problems: subtracting the wrong way or not seeing 'difference' as subtraction
Writing the equation to mirror word order rather than structure

learn.summary: Children aged 7–8 solve one- and two-step word problems within 100 with the unknown in any position (result, change, or start) and including comparison. The core skill is MODELLING the situation — reading whether it is joining, separating, or comparing; locating where the unknown sits; representing it with a bar model and an equation using a symbol for the unknown — and only then computing. Keyword shortcuts ('more'→add) are explicitly discredited because they break on compare and start-unknown problems, which are the hardest structures.

activities.title: Build the bar model, then write the equation (start-unknown focus)
feedback: If the learner subtracts (28 − 15) on the start-unknown story: ask 'which part are we trying to find — is it a part or the whole?' With a part-whole bar, the start is the whole; we know the two parts (15 who got off and 28 who remain), so we add them back to find the start (15 + 28 = 43). Act it out in reverse with counters.
If the learner's equation box sits where the answer 'usually' goes: ask 'does your box go where the answer usually goes, or somewhere else?' — reposition it to match the structure of the story.

If, on a two-step story, the learner stops after the first step: point to the labelled intermediate bar and ask 'is this the final answer, or is there more to do?' This may be a tracking lapse rather than a conceptual gap — underline both actions.
activities.rationale: Representing a problem's underlying structure with a strip/bar diagram before writing an equation, and attending to structure rather than surface story features, is supported as a problem-solving practice. Start-unknown is among the hardest structures and is precisely where keyword strategies fail, so it is a strong discriminating context for building genuine modelling and for writing an equation with a symbol for the unknown.
sourceClaims: Problem solving 'is not the execution of memorized rules or shortcuts, such as using key words'; teaching students to represent a problem's underlying STRUCTURE with visual/schematic representations (strip diagrams — i.e. bar models) BEFORE writing an equation makes them more effective problem solvers, and teachers should attend to structure rather than surface story features. This recommendation carries a STRONG evidence rating (six studies).

Year 2 pupils solve problems with addition and subtraction involving numbers, quantities and measures, and use a symbol for an unknown in missing-number problems (e.g. 7 = □ − 9); comparison uses the language of difference.

Problem difficulty follows semantic structure: result-unknown is easiest, while start-unknown (change/start unknown) and compare structures are substantially harder; keyword strategies break down on precisely these structures.
learnerActions: Read a start-unknown story such as: 'Some children were on the bus. 15 got off. Now there are 28. How many were there at the start?'
Build a bar model: place the known parts (15 and 28) and leave the start as a labelled empty segment — decide whether the unknown is a part or the whole
Recognise that here the START is the whole, so the empty bar is found by adding the known parts 15 and 28
Write a matching equation using a symbol for the unknown, e.g. 28 + 15 = □ (equivalently □ − 15 = 28), so the picture and equation agree
Compute and check the equation and diagram tell the same story
For a two-step story, build a labelled intermediate bar and name that middle amount before doing the second step
activities.intendedInsight: The structure of the situation — not a cue word — determines the operation. 'Got off' suggests subtraction to a keyword solver, but when the start is the unknown whole and the two parts are known, you add. Seeing the diagram contradict the cue word is the moment modelling beats keyword-hunting.

activities.title: Model across all structures with a drag-to-build bar tool
feedback: If a comparison problem is subtracted the wrong way or the learner cannot start: show a comparison bar with the two quantities aligned; the overhang IS the difference. When the difference is unknown, find it by subtracting the smaller from the larger, or by counting on along a number line from the smaller to the larger. When the difference is known and one quantity is unknown, use the bar to decide whether to add or subtract.
If the written equation mirrors word order rather than structure: rebuild the bar first and let the equation follow the diagram.

OPTIONAL interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete (not mandatory): dragging segments to size them, a labelled empty segment for the unknown, and the tool live-writing the matching equation as the bar changes. A labelled intermediate bar can be revealed for two-step stories.
activities.rationale: Explicitly teaching all problem structures (not just result-unknown) and connecting comparison to 'difference' follows the semantic-structure hierarchy and the curriculum's use of a symbol for the unknown. A drag-to-build diagram supports construction and practice volume, which a static reference cannot.
sourceClaims: Problem difficulty follows semantic structure: result-unknown is easiest, while start-unknown (change/start unknown) and compare structures are substantially harder; keyword strategies break down on precisely these structures.

Year 2 pupils solve problems with addition and subtraction involving numbers, quantities and measures, and use a symbol for an unknown in missing-number problems (e.g. 7 = □ − 9); comparison uses the language of difference.

Problem solving 'is not the execution of memorized rules or shortcuts, such as using key words'; teaching students to represent a problem's underlying STRUCTURE with visual/schematic representations (strip diagrams — i.e. bar models) BEFORE writing an equation makes them more effective problem solvers, and teachers should attend to structure rather than surface story features. This recommendation carries a STRONG evidence rating (six studies).
learnerActions: Work through stories spanning every structure: join and separate with the result, change, OR start unknown, and compare (how many more/fewer)
For each, drag bars to represent the known quantities and leave the unknown as a labelled empty segment
Let the tool write the matching equation with a symbol as you build, so you check that the equation mirrors the STRUCTURE, not the word order

Tackle deliberately chosen compare problems where a cue word would mislead — e.g. 'Sam has 34 stickers. That is 12 fewer than Ana. How many does Ana have?' The word 'fewer' tempts subtraction, but the comparison bar shows Ana's amount is the longer bar, so the answer is found by adding (34 + 12 = 46), decided by the structure and NOT by the word 'fewer'
For comparison stories, set the two quantities side by side so the extra length IS the difference
For a difference or change, you can also use a number line: count on from the smaller quantity up to the larger to find how many more/fewer
Use the DfE additive vocabulary — total, difference, more/less, change — tied to what is happening in the situation
activities.intendedInsight: Problems that look similar in words can have very different structures, and the position of the unknown changes which operation is needed. A manipulable bar (and a number line for difference) lets the learner construct and compare structures rather than match surface cues.

activities.title: Check understanding: match stories to equations and name the intermediate result
feedback: If the keyword-trap option is chosen: return to a bar model of the story and ask which quantity is unknown and whether it is a part or whole.
If only the intermediate result is given on a two-step item: prompt 'is that the final answer, or is there more to do?'
activities.rationale: Selection and matching tasks across all structures efficiently surface keyword-strategy and start-unknown errors. This format checks and reinforces recognition and justification rather than eliciting independent construction of a fresh model, so it complements — does not replace — the build activities above.
sourceClaims: Problem difficulty follows semantic structure: result-unknown is easiest, while start-unknown (change/start unknown) and compare structures are substantially harder; keyword strategies break down on precisely these structures.
learnerActions: Match stories to equations where the unknown sits in different positions (result, change, start)
On a compare story, choose among equations that include a keyword-trap option (a tempting equation that matches a cue word but not the structure), and justify the choice by the structure
On a two-step fill-in-the-blank, state the intermediate result explicitly before giving the final answer
Explain in words why each chosen operation fits the situation
activities.intendedInsight: When a learner can both pick the correct equation for each structure and say WHY — especially explaining why the keyword-trap option is wrong — that spoken/written justification shows structure, not a cue word, is driving the choice.

activities.title: Talk through the situation: what's happening, what do we know, what are we finding?
feedback: Elicit the structure and both steps from the learner; do NOT hand over the operation — ask questions that lead them to decide it from the situation.
Follow talk with an actual diagram and equation so modelling is completed, not left verbal.
activities.rationale: Discussion that foregrounds structure supports the modelling goal, but on its own lacks the manipulable diagram and practice volume; pair it with building and solving.
sourceClaims: Problem solving 'is not the execution of memorized rules or shortcuts, such as using key words'; teaching students to represent a problem's underlying STRUCTURE with visual/schematic representations (strip diagrams — i.e. bar models) BEFORE writing an equation makes them more effective problem solvers, and teachers should attend to structure rather than surface story features. This recommendation carries a STRONG evidence rating (six studies).
learnerActions: Before computing, say what is happening in the story (joining, separating, comparing)
State what is known and what is being found, and where the unknown sits
For two-step stories, name both steps and the intermediate amount out loud
Then represent with a bar/equation and solve
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the situation first helps separate structure from surface wording and prevents jumping straight to an operation.

constraints: Do NOT teach keyword shortcuts ('more'→add, 'eaten'→subtract, 'fewer'→subtract); they break on compare and start-unknown problems. Use problems where a cue word misleads to discredit the shortcut.
Model before calculating: draw a bar/part-whole and write an equation with a symbol for the unknown, then solve.
Teach all problem structures — join/separate with result, change, or start unknown, and compare — not just result-unknown.
For two-step problems, name and hold the intermediate result before the second step.
Use DfE additive vocabulary (total, difference, more/less, change) tied to the situation; connect comparison to 'difference'.
A static worked bar model is useful as a reference for structure but cannot let the child model a fresh problem; treat it as a scaffold, not the goal.
Matching/selection tasks check and reinforce recognition and justification; they do not elicit independent construction of a model, so use them alongside build-and-solve activities.
Interaction examples (dragging, live equation writing, labelled intermediate bars) are illustrative of the learning mechanism, not required features.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified this session. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Self-audit of arithmetic in the source diagnostic problems: (1) 34+18=52, then 52−9=43 ✓; (2) compare 52−38=14 ✓; (3) start-unknown 28+15=43 ✓. All checked and consistent.

The semantic-structure difficulty hierarchy (result-unknown easiest; start-unknown and compare hardest) is attributed to Cognitively Guided Instruction / Carpenter & Moser and is marked unverified (not fetched this session). The bar-model/structure-before-equation practice is cited with a STRONG rating; the start-unknown example here is a proposal informed by it, not a separately tested intervention.
The source states the equivalence '28 + 15 = □ (or □ − 15 = 28)'. These are mathematically equivalent (28+15=43 and 43−15=28); both are retained as valid ways to express the start-unknown structure.
Restored the original keyRepresentation 'number line (count-on for difference/change)', which an earlier candidate had dropped; it is offered as an option, not a required method.
Reworded the compare example so subtraction is justified by the comparison bar/structure, explicitly not by the word 'fewer', to avoid accidentally reinstating a keyword rule.

probeDeeper: Show me this story as a bar model — which part are we trying to find, and is it a part or the whole?
For the apples problem, why did you add when it says 'eaten'? Could a 'taking away' story ever need adding?
You got 52 for Maya — is that the final answer, or is there more to do?
Write an equation with a box for the unknown — does your box go where the answer usually goes, or somewhere else?
assess.correctAnswer: (1) 43 — two steps: 34+18=52, then 52−9=43. (2) 14 — compare: 52−38. (3) 43 — start-unknown: 28+15 (the inverse of the stated 'eaten').

errorPatterns.pattern: Keyword strategy — picks the operation from a cue word rather than the situation ('eaten'/'fewer'→subtract)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Require a bar model first so the structure, not the word, drives the operation; use start-unknown and compare problems where the keyword misleads to discredit the shortcut.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In the start-unknown problem the child does 28−15; in the compare problem they wait for a keyword that never comes

errorPatterns.pattern: Start-unknown solved as result-unknown — performs the stated operation forwards instead of its inverse
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model with a part-whole bar: the START is the whole here, and we know a part and the result, so we add back. Act it out in reverse with counters.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For problem (3) the child subtracts the change from the current amount rather than recognising the start is the whole

errorPatterns.pattern: Stops after the first step of a two-step problem — answers (1) with 52
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach: underline both actions and use a bar model where the intermediate result is visibly not the final answer. This is a tracking lapse.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The child computes 34+18 and gives 52, ignoring 'then lost 9'

errorPatterns.pattern: Compare problem subtracted the wrong way, or 'difference' not seen as subtraction
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a comparison bar model showing the two quantities side by side; the extra length IS the difference, found by subtraction.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For (2) the child adds, or subtracts the larger from... gives a nonsensical value, or cannot start

responseLevels.gap: Chooses operations by keyword, treats start-unknown as result-unknown, or stops after one step; cannot represent the structure.
responseLevels.full: Models every structure with a bar/equation (unknown in any position), carries out both steps tracking the intermediate result, handles compare and start-unknown, and explains why each operation fits the situation.
responseLevels.partial: Solves result-unknown and straightforward two-step problems and can model with support, but stumbles on compare or start-unknown, or mirrors word order in the equation.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set three problems and watch the child solve each, encouraging a drawing or equation: (1) 'Maya had 34 marbles, won 18, then lost 9 — how many now?' (2) 'Tom has 52 stickers. Anna has 38. How many fewer does Anna have?' (3) 'Some apples were in a bowl. 15 were eaten. Now there are 28. How many at the start?' Watch how they decide operations and whether they finish two-step problems.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Problem (1) tests whether both steps are carried out and the intermediate 52 is tracked. Problem (2) is a compare problem — a keyword solver hunting for 'take away' has no cue and may stall or add. Problem (3) is start-unknown — the hardest structure — where a keyword solver subtracts (28−15) because 'eaten' says take away, but the situation requires addition. Together they separate a structure-modeller from a keyword-matcher.
