pedagogy.summary: Estimating angles is the sense-making partner of protractor measuring: the child judges an angle's size in degrees WITHOUT a tool, by comparing it against internalised benchmark angles (30°, 45°, 60°, 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°). The pedagogical goal is a stable mental image of a right angle and a half/three-quarter turn, so that any angle can be placed relative to them ('a bit more than a right angle, so roughly 100°'). This extends the acute/obtuse vocabulary to REFLEX angles (between 180° and 360°), which children meet here for the first time and which the semicircular protractor cannot directly read. Estimation is what makes measuring self-correcting: a child who expects 'about 130°' will not accept a protractor read of 50°.
bestPractices: Anchor a small set of benchmark angles as physical/mental images first — the right angle (corner, quarter turn), the straight angle (180°), 45° as half a right angle, 270° as three right angles — then estimate everything by comparison to the nearest benchmark.
Always estimate BEFORE measuring, then measure to check; treat a big estimate-vs-measure gap as a signal to recheck placement, not to discard the estimate.
Introduce reflex angles explicitly as 'more than a straight line, less than a full turn' and estimate them as 360° minus the smaller angle, since a semicircular protractor reads only to 180°.
Order/compare several angles by eye before any measuring, so relative judgement (which is bigger) is trained alongside absolute estimation (how many degrees).
Use bodily and everyday referents — clock hands, opening doors, ramps, turns — to build the benchmark images.
keyRepresentations: Benchmark angles as mental anchors: 45°, 90° (right angle), 180° (straight), 270°, 360°
The right angle as the master reference ('a bit more / a bit less than a corner')
Reflex angle as 360° minus its companion angle (turn imagery)
Clock hands / opening door as dynamic referents for angle size
commonMisconceptions: Judges size by ray length rather than opening, so estimates a wide-but-short angle as smaller than a narrow-but-long one (arm-length carryover).
Has no reflex concept — sees a 270° reflex angle and reads/estimates the smaller 90° companion instead.
Anchors only to 90° and 180°, so estimates cluster at right angles and straight lines with poor resolution in between (e.g. calls everything obtuse '120°').
Treats 'estimate' as 'measure without care' and expects an exact answer rather than a reasoned approximate range.

learn.summary: Teach angle estimation as the sense-making partner of protractor measuring: the child judges an angle's size in degrees WITHOUT a tool by comparing it to internalised benchmarks (45°, 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°). The goal is a stable mental image of a right angle, a straight angle and a three-quarter turn, so any angle can be placed relative to them ('a bit more than a right angle, so roughly 100°'). This extends acute/obtuse vocabulary to REFLEX angles (between 180° and 360°), met here for the first time and not directly readable on a semicircular protractor. Estimation makes measuring self-correcting: a child who expects 'about 130°' will not accept a protractor read of 50°.

activities.title: Predict-then-reveal angle estimation trainer
feedback: Reward closeness within a tolerance band rather than exactness, so an estimate stays a reasoned range, not a failed exact answer.

When a child guesses '90-ish' for a clearly reflex angle, reveal the turn swinging past the straight line and show its true size as 360° minus the companion angle (for example about 270° when the companion is about 90°), so reflex stops being invisible.

When a child under-estimates wide-but-short-armed angles, let the error score flag the pattern, then overlay the two angles vertex-to-vertex so their openings compare directly regardless of arm length, and extend the short arms and re-order to show the size is unchanged.
Treat a big estimate-vs-measure gap as a signal to recheck both the protractor reading (placement and scale) and the estimate, not simply to discard the estimate.
activities.rationale: Estimation is a perceptual-numerical skill proposed to be built by repeated visual trials with feedback: a predict-then-reveal loop over many varied angles commits the child to an estimate, then feeds back the error, intended to calibrate the benchmark sense. Varying ray length independently of opening directly targets the documented arm-length misconception; including reflex angles forces the '360 minus companion' reasoning that a semicircular protractor cannot read directly.
sourceClaims: Angle size is measured with reference to a circle whose whole is 360°; benchmark fractions of a turn (right angle = 90°, straight = 180°) anchor degree understanding, and an n-one-degree-angle turn measures n degrees (4.MD.5).

The Progressions treat angle classification and benchmark degrees (acute/right/obtuse and turn fractions) as the basis for reasoning about angle size before and alongside protractor measurement, and note children judge angle size by arm length rather than opening.
Judging angle size by the length of the arms rather than the amount of opening is a persistent, documented misconception.
learnerActions: Look at an angle shown in a random orientation and, BEFORE any measuring, commit an estimate of its size in degrees (set a slider or type a number).
In ordering rounds, drag four angles into order from smallest to largest by eye before anything is measured.
Reveal the true measure and your error; when offered, fade in a faint benchmark 'ghost' (right-angle corner, or 180° straight line) over the angle to see how your estimate compared.
Meet angles whose ray (arm) lengths are varied at random so a wide angle sometimes has short arms — estimate by the opening, not the line length.
Meet reflex angles that swing past the straight line, and estimate them as 360° minus the smaller companion angle.
activities.intendedInsight: Any angle can be placed relative to a small set of benchmarks, and reflex angles (between 180° and 360°) are real angles estimated as 360° minus their companion — not the smaller angle on the other side.

activities.title: Scored estimation and classification practice
feedback: Score the slider estimate against a tolerance band so a near miss counts as success.
Flag an arm-length error when ordering tracks ray length rather than opening, and prompt direct comparison of the openings.
If the child mis-classifies the reflex angle as acute or right, show that it opens past the straight line.
activities.rationale: Estimation maps cleanly onto scored response formats (slider estimate, ordering, classification choice), giving varied practice and checking. A response-format task may give less rapid many-trial feedback than a live predict-reveal loop, so it is proposed as a complement rather than a replacement. Including a short-ray wide-angle item targets the arm-length misconception.
sourceClaims: Judging angle size by the length of the arms rather than the amount of opening is a persistent, documented misconception.

The Progressions treat angle classification and benchmark degrees (acute/right/obtuse and turn fractions) as the basis for reasoning about angle size before and alongside protractor measurement, and note children judge angle size by arm length rather than opening.
learnerActions: Use a slider to estimate a shown angle's degrees, aiming to land within a tolerance band.
Order four angles smallest-to-largest by eye as an ordering task before any measure is shown.
Classify shown angles as acute, right, obtuse, straight or reflex, and pick out the reflex angle in a diagram.
Tackle at least one deliberately short-armed, wide-opening item designed to catch the arm-length habit.
activities.intendedInsight: Relative judgement (which is bigger), absolute estimation (how many degrees) and classification (acute/obtuse/reflex) are distinct skills that can each be practised and checked.

activities.title: Benchmark-angle gallery with everyday referents
feedback: Confirm the benchmark image and name when revealed, and connect it to its everyday referent.
When the child decides 'more or less than a right angle', show the angle against the corner image to confirm.
activities.rationale: A static or tap-to-reveal gallery can seed estimation by anchoring the benchmark set as stable mental images with everyday referents. It is a scaffold: it may establish the anchors but does not itself run the estimate-check loop that calibrates estimation, so it is intended to precede, not replace, repeated estimation practice.
sourceClaims: Angle size is measured with reference to a circle whose whole is 360°; benchmark fractions of a turn (right angle = 90°, straight = 180°) anchor degree understanding, and an n-one-degree-angle turn measures n degrees (4.MD.5).
learnerActions: Tap or reveal each benchmark in turn — 45° (half a right angle), 90° (right angle/corner/quarter turn), 180° (straight), 270° (three right angles), 360° (full turn) — and link it to a reference image.
Connect each benchmark to a bodily or everyday referent: clock hands, an opening door, a ramp, a turn.
Use a lift-the-flap or 'more or less than a right angle?' layer to decide, for a shown angle, whether it is above or below the corner benchmark.
activities.intendedInsight: A small set of benchmark angles, anchored as physical and mental images, is the master reference set against which every other angle is judged ('a bit more / a bit less than a corner').

activities.title: Add intermediate anchors to sharpen resolution
feedback: If estimates snap only to 90° or 180°, point out the gap and introduce an intermediate anchor the angle sits near.
Accept a reasoned range stated against two anchors rather than demanding one exact number.
activities.rationale: When benchmark resolution is too coarse, estimates cluster at right angles and straight lines; this is a sparse-anchor-deployment issue, not a concept failure, so the fix is to bring in and practise intermediate anchors rather than reteach the concept of angle.
sourceClaims: The Progressions treat angle classification and benchmark degrees (acute/right/obtuse and turn fractions) as the basis for reasoning about angle size before and alongside protractor measurement, and note children judge angle size by arm length rather than opening.
learnerActions: For a learner whose estimates snap only to 90° and 180°, bring in the half-right-angle (45°) and 'a right angle plus a third of a right angle' (120°) as working anchors alongside the secure 90° and 180° images.
Estimate angles that deliberately sit BETWEEN benchmarks, such as 60°, 110° or 130°, naming the two anchors each one falls between.
Justify at least one estimate aloud with benchmark language ('a bit more than a right angle, so roughly 100°').
activities.intendedInsight: Anchoring only to 90° and 180° makes estimates cluster there with poor resolution in between; deploying intermediate anchors gives the mental ruler finer gradations.

constraints: Always estimate BEFORE measuring, then measure to check; a large estimate-vs-measure gap signals that both should be rechecked (protractor placement and which scale was read, and the estimate itself), not that the estimate was worthless.
Reward closeness within a tolerance band, not exactness: an estimate is a reasoned approximate range, not a failed exact answer. An estimate of 120° when the protractor reads 128° is a good estimate.
A semicircular protractor reads only to 180°, so reflex angles must be reasoned as 360° minus the smaller companion angle; do not treat the smaller companion as the answer.

The benchmark gallery is a scaffold that anchors reference images; it may seed estimation but does not build the skill on its own, which requires repeated estimate-then-check trials. It is a useful precursor, not a universal requirement.

Classification and ordering response items check relative and absolute angle sense but, used alone, may give less rapid many-trial feedback than a live predict-reveal loop; combine formats rather than claiming any one medium is required.
Vary ray length independently of opening deliberately: wide-but-short-armed angles are the key trap for the arm-length misconception and should be included on purpose.

45° is part of the target benchmark set; the resolution-sharpening activity only re-deploys it for learners who have anchored to 90°/180° alone, and does not imply 45° is an optional extra for everyone.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The ±15° tolerance band and the specific benchmark set (45°, 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°) come from the legacy assessment and pedagogy fields; they are reasonable for ages 9–10 but are design choices, not values established by the cited sources.

The original pedagogy summary additionally lists 30° and 60° as benchmark angles, which its own keyRepresentations omits. This rewrite follows keyRepresentations: 30° is not carried through, and 60° appears only as an intermediate anchor in the resolution-sharpening activity. The inconsistency is inherited from the source and is not resolved by the cited references.

Legacy catalog rationales claiming a 3D environment 'adds spatial overhead without improving' estimation, that a character 'cannot show hundreds of angles', and that a static image 'cannot run the estimate-check loop' were medium-comparison statements; they have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements, not asserted as universal pedagogical laws. A fixed image can still teach the benchmark set.

The sources support benchmark-degree reasoning and the arm-length misconception; they do not establish the comparative efficacy of any specific interactive medium or the stated tolerance band. Efficacy-flavoured comparisons are stated with proposed/may wording only.

probeDeeper: Point to the short-armed wide angle and a long-armed narrow one: 'You said this one is smaller — what if I made its lines just as long as the other's? Would it still be smaller?' (counterexample: arm length is irrelevant.)
'How did you decide this one was about 130° — what did you compare it to?' — listen for a benchmark (right angle) rather than a guess.
'This reflex angle — how could you use the smaller angle next to it to work out its size?' (probes 360°-minus-companion reasoning.)
'Your estimate was 120° and the protractor says 128° — is your estimate wrong?' — checks the child understands an estimate is a reasoned range, not a failed exact answer.
assess.correctAnswer: Orders the four correctly by opening (not by arm length), estimates each within roughly ±15° of its true size, classifies the ~270° one as reflex (over a straight line, under a full turn) rather than reading its 90° companion, and uses benchmark language ('a bit more than a right angle') to justify at least one estimate.

errorPatterns.pattern: Orders by arm length not opening — puts the short-armed wide angle earlier (smaller) than a long-armed narrow one.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay the two angles vertex-to-vertex so the openings compare directly regardless of arm length; extend the short arms and re-order to show the size is unchanged.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The ordering tracks ray length rather than degrees; the child may point to the longer lines as the reason it's 'bigger'.

errorPatterns.pattern: No reflex concept — estimates the ~270° reflex angle as its ~90° companion, or as 'about 90°', reading the wrong side of the opening.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the turn dynamically past the straight line; estimate reflex as 360° minus the companion; explicitly name 'reflex: more than 180°, less than 360°'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls the reflex angle acute/right or gives a sub-180° number; treats the reflex mark as if it were the smaller angle.

errorPatterns.pattern: Benchmark resolution too coarse — snaps every estimate to 90° or 180°, so a 130° angle is called '90' or '180' with nothing in between.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Add the half-right-angle (45°) and 'a bit past a right angle' (~120°) as extra anchors; practise estimating angles that sit between benchmarks. No reteaching of concept — the anchor set is just sparse.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Estimates cluster only at right angles and straight lines; no use of 45°/60°/120° as intermediate anchors.

responseLevels.gap: Estimates bear little relation to actual size and ordering follows arm length or orientation; no benchmark reasoning and no reflex concept (reads reflex as its companion).
responseLevels.full: Orders all four by opening regardless of arm length, estimates each within about ±15° using benchmark comparisons including intermediate anchors, correctly identifies and estimates the reflex angle via 360°-minus-companion, and treats the estimate as a reasoned range confirmed (not replaced) by measuring.
responseLevels.partial: Estimates acute and obtuse angles reasonably against 90°/180° and orders standard angles correctly, but is caught by at least one of: the short-arm wide angle (orders by length), the reflex angle (no over-180° concept), or coarse resolution (snaps to 90/180). Can name benchmarks but not deploy intermediate ones.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Lay out four angles the child can see but not measure — include one clearly acute (~40°), one obtuse (~130°), one drawn with short arms but a wide opening, and one reflex (~270°), with ray lengths deliberately uneven. Say: 'Without measuring, put these in order from smallest to largest, and tell me roughly how many degrees each one is.' Then let them measure to check. Watch the ordering and the estimates — do not coach.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The uneven ray lengths separate opening-based judgement from arm-length judgement; the short-arm wide angle is the trap. The reflex angle separates a child who has extended their concept past 180° from one who collapses it back to the acute companion. Ordering plus numeric estimate together expose both relative and absolute angle sense in one two-minute task.

sources.claim: Angle size is measured with reference to a circle whose whole is 360°; benchmark fractions of a turn (right angle = 90°, straight = 180°) anchor degree understanding, and an n-one-degree-angle turn measures n degrees (4.MD.5).
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grade 4 Measurement & Data

pedagogy.summary: Extending the standard columnar algorithm to whole numbers with more than four digits. The procedure is identical to four-digit work — align by place value, compose on carrying, decompose on borrowing — but scale raises the stakes: subtraction from large round numbers (500,000 - 234,178) forces an exchange that ripples across many zeros, and adding three or more five-digit numbers produces carries greater than one. Estimation-first and inverse checking remain essential because a single misaligned digit is now worth thousands.
bestPractices: Reinforce that nothing new is happening — same exchange rule, just more columns — to prevent 'big numbers are different' anxiety
Estimate by rounding before computing so a place-value slip in the thousands/ten-thousands is caught
Deliberately include a subtraction from a round number with several zeros (the extended borrow-across-zero)
When adding three or more numbers, make the >1 carry explicit ('13 ones = 3, carry 1 ten... but this column totals 24, carry 2')
Use place-value headers / squared paper so five- and six-digit numbers stay aligned
keyRepresentations: Place-value columns with headers to hundred-thousands
Base-ten / place-value counters for the exchange rationale
Empty number line for the estimate and for counting-up subtraction
Part-whole bar for multi-addend structure
commonMisconceptions: Extended borrow-across-zero fails — cannot cascade an exchange through several zeros (500,000 - 234,178)
Smaller-from-larger bug persists at larger scale
Misaligns digits when numbers have different lengths
When a column totals 20+ (three addends), carries only 1 instead of 2
Checks by redoing rather than estimating or using the inverse

learn.summary: Extend the standard columnar algorithm to whole numbers with more than four digits. The procedure is identical to four-digit work (align by place value, compose when carrying, decompose when borrowing), but larger scale raises the stakes: subtracting from a large round number such as 500,000 − 234,178 forces an exchange that cascades across several zeros, and adding three or more five-digit numbers can produce carries greater than one. Estimation-first and inverse checking matter more because a single misaligned digit is now worth thousands.

activities.title: Borrowing across a row of zeros (500,000 − 234,178)
feedback: If the child stalls at the zeros or does not carry the exchange through every column (e.g. 265,832, where the tens was left as 10 instead of 9, or 275,822, where the ten-thousands was left as 10 instead of 9), model with place-value counters: exchange one hundred-thousand and walk it down column by column so each 0 becomes 9 with a ten passed on until the ones hold 10.
If a smaller digit is subtracted from a larger one regardless of position, do a concrete exchange on the failing column and reassert that you cannot take more than is there without borrowing.
If the child checks only by redoing the same subtraction, scaffold the estimate (round both numbers) and the inverse addition, or a counting-up number line, instead of reteaching the algorithm.
activities.rationale: Borrow-from-zero is a well-documented systematic subtraction bug that intensifies when a minuend has several adjacent zeros, so a deliberate round-number case targets the most-failed large-number hazard. A live place-value/counters model can animate the exchange as the child performs it; physical counters, squared paper, or a counting-up number line serve the same rationale without requiring a specific tool.
sourceClaims: Borrow-from-zero is the single most common systematic subtraction bug (Brown & Burton, 1325 students, 107 occurrences): the student changes a 0 to 9 but fails to continue borrowing leftward. When a minuend has several adjacent zeros (e.g. 500,000) the exchange must cascade through them, and this zero-borrow bug intensifies; smaller-from-larger (54 students) persists at scale. These are stable procedural bugs — ~40% of students showed consistently buggy behaviour — not carelessness.
Composing/decomposing (exchange) is the conceptual basis of the columnar algorithm regardless of digit count; DfE Appendix 1 sets out the formal written methods.

Year 5 pupils are taught to 'add and subtract whole numbers with more than 4 digits, including using formal written methods (columnar addition and subtraction)' and to 'use rounding to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, levels of accuracy' (statutory).
learnerActions: Set out 500,000 − 234,178 in columns aligned by place value, from the ones on the right.
Before computing, estimate by rounding (about 500,000 − 234,000 = 266,000) and note the expected size of the answer.

At the ones there is nothing to take 8 from, and every column to the left is 0; work the exchange by taking one hundred-thousand and walking it down column by column so each 0 becomes 9 as a ten is passed along, until the ones finally hold 10.
Complete the subtraction to get 265,822.
Check with the inverse: 265,822 + 234,178 should return 500,000, and compare to your estimate (~266,000).
Optionally model the same subtraction as counting up on an empty number line — jump from 234,178 up to 500,000 and total the jumps — as an independent alternative that should also give 265,822.
Optionally repeat with an easier round-number case such as 500,000 − 234,000 and discuss why that borrow is simpler.
activities.intendedInsight: A single exchange can cascade through a row of zeros — each zero becomes a 9 as the ten is passed along, and the ones finally hold 10 — so a wall of zeros is not a dead end.

activities.title: Adding three numbers of up to five digits: when the carry is more than one
feedback: If the child carries only 1 from a column totalling 20 or more (e.g. 9 + 8 + 7 = 24), total the column aloud, separate it into 4 ones and 2 tens, and make the size of the carry explicit.

If a three-number sum is too small by exactly one (or more) in the column just above a heavy column (e.g. 10 too small when the ones totalled 24 but only 1 was carried), this may point to an undersized carry. Recount that column and check how many tens it holds.
If numbers of different lengths are misaligned so place values don't line up, use squared paper or place-value headers anchored from the ones on the right.
activities.rationale: A child drilled only on two-addend sums tends to assume a carry is always 1; a three-addend column that totals into the twenties surfaces and corrects that assumption. The original diagnostic problem does not actually create such a column, so a correctly chosen example is used for the larger carry while the given problem still serves alignment and repeated-carry practice. A part-whole bar can make the multi-addend structure explicit. A fill-in-the-blank format on carried digits plus a rounded estimate can assess this at scale but cannot verify handwritten alignment, so paper setup should also be observed.
sourceClaims: Composing/decomposing (exchange) is the conceptual basis of the columnar algorithm regardless of digit count; DfE Appendix 1 sets out the formal written methods.

Year 5 pupils are taught to 'add and subtract whole numbers with more than 4 digits, including using formal written methods (columnar addition and subtraction)' and to 'use rounding to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, levels of accuracy' (statutory).
learnerActions: Set out 12,340 + 8,706 + 15,058 in a single column layout, aligning by place value from the ones on the right (numbers of different lengths must still line up); optionally show the three addends as parts of a part-whole bar whose whole is the total.
Add the ones column aloud and name the full total (0 + 6 + 8 = 14): write 4, carry 1.

Work through the rest of this sum: note that every carry here is only 1 (column totals including carries: tens 10, hundreds 11, thousands 16; the ten-thousands totals 3 with no carry), finishing at 36,104. This is good practice at keeping three different-length addends aligned and tracking repeated carries.

Now tackle a case that genuinely produces a larger carry, e.g. 36,489 + 27,858 + 15,937: the ones column totals 9 + 8 + 7 = 24, so write 4 and carry 2 (not 1); completing it gives 80,284, with several columns (ones, hundreds and thousands) carrying 2.
Compute 34,567 + 28,945 = 63,512 as a clean two-addend check that the basic algorithm is intact.
Estimate by rounding before computing so a place-value slip in the thousands or ten-thousands is caught.
activities.intendedInsight: When a column of three or more addends totals 20 or more, the carry can be 2 (or more), not automatically 1. (Not every three-addend sum reaches that — 12,340 + 8,706 + 15,058 only ever carries 1 — so a case whose column actually totals into the twenties is needed to surface the larger carry.)

activities.title: Worked-example reference and estimate-then-check routine
feedback: If the child's answer is far from the estimate, that gap is the signal to recheck alignment and exchanges (and quickly confirm the rounding in the estimate itself). Do not simply change the estimate to match the answer.
A revealed worked example is reference only; the child should then set out and solve a fresh case themselves on paper.
Praise specifically when the child catches their own error via estimate or inverse, reinforcing why that beats redoing the sum.
activities.rationale: Rounding-to-check is a statutory expectation and a reliable guard against single-digit place-value slips at scale; the inverse operation is independent of the original method, so it catches errors a re-run would reproduce. A revealed worked example is a useful static reference but exercises recognition rather than independent construction, so it must be paired with the child doing the work.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils are taught to 'add and subtract whole numbers with more than 4 digits, including using formal written methods (columnar addition and subtraction)' and to 'use rounding to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, levels of accuracy' (statutory).
learnerActions: Study a tap-to-reveal or step-by-step worked example of the across-many-zeros borrow, revealing each 0-becomes-9 exchange in turn to see the cascade clearly.
For every large calculation, first write a rounded estimate, then compute, then compare the answer to the estimate.
Check subtractions with the inverse addition (or a counting-up number line) and additions with an estimate rather than by redoing the same calculation.

Answer prompts: roughly how big should 500,000 − 234,178 be before working it out? Why did all those zeros turn into 9s? Would 500,000 − 234,000 be easier to borrow, and why? Why carry 2 and not 1 when a three-addend column totals into the twenties?
activities.intendedInsight: Estimating first and checking by the inverse catch place-value slips that are now worth thousands; redoing the same method just reproduces the same error.

constraints: This is a doing-on-paper procedural skill: the child must actually set out and compute the algorithm, not only recognise or describe correct steps.
Reinforce that nothing new is happening — same exchange rule, just more columns — to prevent 'big numbers are different' anxiety.

Deliberately include at least one subtraction from a round number with several zeros (the extended borrow-across-zero) and at least one three-or-more-addend sum whose column genuinely totals 20 or more (so a carry of 2 actually occurs).
Use place-value headers or squared paper so five- and six-digit numbers of different lengths stay aligned from the ones on the right.
A fill-in-the-blank or slider-based quiz can check carried/borrowed digits and estimates but cannot verify handwritten alignment, so observe paper setup directly.
A tap-to-reveal worked example is a static scaffold exercising recognition; it supports but does not replace independent construction on paper.

Base-ten counters, an empty number line, and on-screen place-value models offer different experiences of the exchange; any can make the cascade or the structure concrete, and none is strictly required.
Checking must use estimation or the inverse operation (or an independent counting-up method), not a re-run of the same calculation.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

ORIGINAL ERROR CORRECTED: the row's assess.correctAnswer/diagnostic states the three-addend sum 12,340 + 8,706 + 15,058 'carries 2 where a column totals 20+', but no column of this sum reaches 20 even with incoming carries (column totals 14, 10, 11, 16, 3) — it carries only 1 throughout. To actually demonstrate a carry of 2, an agent-proposed example 36,489 + 27,858 + 15,937 = 80,284 is used (ones 9+8+7=24, write 4 carry 2; self-audit: 36,489+27,858=64,347, 64,347+15,937=80,284; columns carrying 2 are ones, hundreds and thousands). This replacement example is an unvalidated agent proposal and was not independently verified.

Representations restored: the original row's empty number line (estimate / counting-up subtraction) and part-whole bar (multi-addend structure) were only implicit in the earlier draft and are now offered as explicit optional representations.

The original catalog rationale claimed a conversation 'cannot exercise' a written algorithm and that a third dimension 'adds nothing'. These are fit judgements, not pedagogical laws; softened to narrow affordances/limits (dialogue supports but does not substitute for doing it on paper; the task is planar, so a 3D model offers no clear added value here).
One source (NRICH place-value material; DfE Appendix 1) is marked verified:false / not fetched this session; treat its claim as unconfirmed.

probeDeeper: Roughly how big should the answer to 500,000 - 234,178 be, before you work it out?
Why did all those zeros turn into 9s when you subtracted?
What if it had been 500,000 - 234,000 - would the borrowing be any easier?
When you added the three numbers, why did you carry 2 and not 1 from the ones column?
assess.correctAnswer: 34,567 + 28,945 = 63,512 (composes through the columns). 500,000 - 234,178 = 265,822, cascading one exchange through the zeros. The three-addend sum = 36,104, carrying 2 where a column totals 20+. Estimate for the subtraction approx 500,000 - 234,000 = 266,000, close to 265,822; inverse 265,822 + 234,178 = 500,000.

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot cascade an exchange through several zeros in 500,000 - 234,178 - stalls, or borrows only one column and leaves the rest as 0/9 wrongly
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model with place-value counters: exchange one hundred-thousand and walk it down column by column so each 0 becomes 9 with a ten passed on.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Wrong middle digits (e.g. 265,882, 275,822) or the child freezes at the wall of zeros

errorPatterns.pattern: Subtracts the smaller digit from the larger regardless of position (smaller-from-larger bug) at five-digit scale
errorPatterns.nextMove: Concrete exchange on the failing column; reassert you cannot take more than is there without borrowing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Columns 'flipped' wherever the top digit is smaller

errorPatterns.pattern: When the three-addend column totals 20 or more, carries only 1 instead of 2
errorPatterns.nextMove: Total the column aloud (13 + 8 + 6 = 24), separate into 4 ones and 2 tens; make the size of the carry explicit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The three-number sum is out by a multiple of ten in the next column up

errorPatterns.pattern: Misaligns digits when the numbers differ in length, so place values do not line up
errorPatterns.nextMove: Squared paper / place-value headers, anchored from the ones on the right.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Column setup on paper

errorPatterns.pattern: Checks by redoing the same subtraction rather than estimating or using the inverse
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the estimate (round both) and the inverse addition; do not reteach the algorithm.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The check reproduces the original method

responseLevels.gap: Misaligns, or breaks down at the row of zeros; carries only 1 from a 20+ column; no sense of the answer's size.
responseLevels.full: Solves all three including the zero-cascade subtraction and the double carry, aligns correctly, AND verifies with an estimate and the inverse; transfers to a similar round-number subtraction.
responseLevels.partial: Handles the clean addition and can describe the steps, but fails the across-many-zeros exchange or the >1 carry, or checks only by redoing and never estimates.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child three to set out and solve on paper, watching alignment and exchange: 34,567 + 28,945; 500,000 - 234,178; and add these three in one column: 12,340 + 8,706 + 15,058. Then ask them to check the subtraction by estimating and by the inverse.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 500,000 - 234,178 forces an exchange through five zeros - the extended borrow-across-zero, the most-failed large-number case. The three-addend column forces a carry greater than one, which a child drilled only on two-addend sums mishandles. The clean addition confirms the basic algorithm is intact, so failures localise to the scale-specific hazards.

pedagogy.summary: Generating sequences at KS3 extends the KS2 term-to-term idea to a second, more powerful engine: the position-to-term (nth-term) rule, which gives any term directly from its position. The concept is best taught by contrasting the two rules on the same sequence — term-to-term chains from the previous term, position-to-term substitutes the position number into a formula such as 3n−2 — and by classifying sequences as arithmetic (constant difference), geometric (constant ratio) or neither by explicitly testing the differences and the ratios.
bestPractices: Generate the same sequence two ways (term-to-term and position-to-term) so pupils see they describe the same numbers, and that position-to-term reaches the 50th term without listing the first 49.
Require pupils to generate a position-to-term rule by substituting n = 1, 2, 3, … , not by treating the formula as a term-to-term instruction.
Classify by writing the successive differences AND the successive ratios underneath: a constant difference means arithmetic, a constant ratio means geometric, neither means 'other'.
Explicitly contrast 'multiples of 3' (3n) with 'increases by 3' (e.g. 3n−2) so pupils see a sequence that increases by 3 need not contain multiples of 3.
Use a varied diet — increasing, decreasing, decimal, geometric and 'neither' — to prevent an only-increasing over-generalisation.
keyRepresentations: Position-to-term table (positions n=1,2,3,4 above; terms below)
Dual display: term-to-term arrows vs position-to-term substitution
Differences row and ratios row written under a sequence
Graph of terms against position (constant difference = constant steepness)
commonMisconceptions: Treating a position-to-term rule as a term-to-term instruction (reading 3n−2 as 'start at 3, subtract 2'), so the first term is wrong.
Classifying by 'it goes up' alone, failing to distinguish arithmetic from geometric or to spot a non-constant difference (1, 4, 9, 16).
Confusing 'multiples of 3' with 'increases by 3'.
Assuming a later term can be reached by multiplying an earlier one (10th term = 2 × 5th term).

learn.summary: KS3 pupils extend the KS2 term-to-term idea to the position-to-term (nth-term) rule, which gives any term directly from its position. The core moves: generate the SAME sequence two ways (chaining from the previous term vs substituting n=1,2,3,… into a formula like 3n−2); and classify sequences as arithmetic (constant difference), geometric (constant ratio) or other by explicitly writing the successive differences AND successive ratios. Key pitfalls to address: reading 3n−2 as a term-to-term instruction ('start at 3, subtract 2'), classifying by 'it goes up' alone, and confusing 'multiples of 3' with 'increases by 3'.

activities.title: Dual-engine generator: the same sequence built two ways
feedback: If a position rule is being applied term-to-term, flag the first-term mismatch: write n=1 explicitly and substitute into 3n−2 to show the first term should be 1 (3×1−2=1), not 3.
When the learner jumps to the 50th term, contrast the instant position-to-term result with the slow term-to-term chain to make the efficiency concrete.
When the coefficient is dragged, show the inter-term step updating live so 'coefficient = common difference' is visible rather than asserted.
activities.rationale: Generating the same sequence two ways and contrasting the cost of reaching a distant term targets the statutory 'generate terms from either a term-to-term or a position-to-term rule' and is intended to address the misconception of reading a position rule as a term-to-term instruction. A position→term table and live coefficient linking are intended to make the mechanism concrete. This is a research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory Algebra: 'generate terms of a sequence from either a term-to-term or a position-to-term rule'; 'recognise arithmetic sequences and find the nth term'; 'recognise geometric sequences and appreciate other sequences that arise'.

The nth term is new learning at KS3; a sequence can be generated by a term-to-term OR a position-to-term rule and pupils should progress from one to the other. Pupils confuse 'multiples of three' with 'numbers which increase by three' (Example 6), and must be taught to attend to the position of a term rather than the term-to-term rule (Example 7b/7c — 'Liam' claims −5, 0, 5, 10, 15 is '5n' because it increases by 5). An arithmetic sequence adds/subtracts a constant amount; the coefficient of n equals the common difference.
learnerActions: Build a sequence term-to-term: set a start value and an operation (e.g. start at 1, add 3) and generate the chain one step at a time.
Build the same sequence position-to-term: type a rule such as 3n−2 and substitute n=1,2,3,4,5 to light up each term under its position.
Switch a sequence between the two modes and confirm the numbers are identical.
Press 'jump to the 50th term': in position-to-term mode the answer for 3n−2 appears at once; in term-to-term mode the machine visibly grinds through the 49 predecessors first.
Drag the coefficient of n in 3n−2 and watch the inter-term step change to match, so the coefficient is seen to equal the common difference.
activities.intendedInsight: A term-to-term rule chains from the previous term; a position-to-term rule substitutes the position number into a formula and so reaches any term (e.g. the 50th) directly without listing the earlier ones. In a linear rule such as 3n−2 (of the form an + b), the coefficient of n equals the common difference.

activities.title: Classify by writing differences AND ratios
feedback: If a learner calls 1, 4, 9, 16 arithmetic, point to its differences 3, 5, 7 — not constant — and to its non-constant ratios, so it is 'other'.
Reveal the differences and ratios rows on demand so the row that stays constant names the type.
If the learner checks only differences, prompt them to also write the ratios before deciding geometric vs other.
When the learner builds their own sequence, ask them to show which row stays constant so the type they claim is evidenced.
activities.rationale: Requiring both a differences row and a ratios row operationalises classification and is intended to counter the 'classify by direction' misconception and the failure to separate arithmetic from geometric. The 1, 4, 9, 16 example makes a changing difference visible on the differences row, and asking for a constructed example practises the production skill named in the assessment.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory Algebra: 'generate terms of a sequence from either a term-to-term or a position-to-term rule'; 'recognise arithmetic sequences and find the nth term'; 'recognise geometric sequences and appreciate other sequences that arise'.
learnerActions: For each sequence, write the row of successive differences and the row of successive ratios underneath it.
Sort sequences into arithmetic (constant difference), geometric (constant ratio) or other (neither constant).
Work the worked set: 5, 8, 11, 14 (arithmetic, difference +3); 2, 6, 18, 54 (geometric, ratio ×3); 1, 4, 9, 16 (other — differences 3, 5, 7 not constant, ratios not constant).
State explicitly which row you checked to make each decision, so classification is a test rather than a guess.

Construct your own sequence of a requested type (for example a geometric sequence that starts at 5, with a ratio other than 1) and verify it with the differences and ratios rows. Note that a constant sequence such as 5, 5, 5 has both a constant difference (0) and a constant ratio (1), so it is both arithmetic and geometric.
activities.intendedInsight: A sequence is arithmetic when the successive differences are constant and geometric when the successive ratios are constant; 'it goes up' is not enough, because 1, 4, 9, 16 increases but has a changing difference. The same differences/ratios test can be used to build and check a sequence of a requested type.

activities.title: 'Multiples of 3' versus 'increases by 3'
feedback: If the learner expects 3n−2 to produce multiples of 3, line up 3n and 3n−2 so both increase by 3 but only one hits the multiples.
If they are surprised 1, 4, 7, 10 contains no multiples of 3, confirm the common difference is still +3.
activities.rationale: Side-by-side generation of 3n and 3n−2 targets the specific documented confusion between 'multiples of three' and 'numbers which increase by three'.
sourceClaims: The nth term is new learning at KS3; a sequence can be generated by a term-to-term OR a position-to-term rule and pupils should progress from one to the other. Pupils confuse 'multiples of three' with 'numbers which increase by three' (Example 6), and must be taught to attend to the position of a term rather than the term-to-term rule (Example 7b/7c — 'Liam' claims −5, 0, 5, 10, 15 is '5n' because it increases by 5). An arithmetic sequence adds/subtracts a constant amount; the coefficient of n equals the common difference.
learnerActions: Generate 3n (3, 6, 9, 12, …) and 3n−2 (1, 4, 7, 10, …) side by side.
Check each sequence against the 3-times table and record which terms are multiples of 3.
Explain why 1, 4, 7, 10 increases by 3 yet contains no multiples of 3.
activities.intendedInsight: A sequence that increases by 3 need not be the multiples-of-3 sequence; the constant difference (+3) and membership of the 3-times table are different properties.

activities.title: Which rule reaches the 50th term faster, and why? (discussion)
feedback: If a learner claims the 10th term is twice the 5th, have them generate both terms of, say, 3n−2 and compare: 3×5−2=13 and 3×10−2=28, which is not 2×13=26.
Surface the efficiency argument by comparing the work needed for each method to reach term 50.
activities.rationale: A Socratic efficiency discussion can surface why the nth-term rule matters and is intended to address the misconception that later terms are simple multiples of earlier ones. This is a complement to the generator, which demonstrates the efficiency directly.
learnerActions: Discuss with a partner (or a questioning prompt): to find the 50th term of 3n−2, which rule gets you there faster — term-to-term or position-to-term — and why?
Articulate that substitution reaches any term directly while chaining requires all earlier terms.

Challenge the claim '10th term = 2 × 5th term' and test it against an actual arithmetic sequence with a nonzero constant term, such as 3n−2. Then notice that it does happen to hold for 3n, so one example that works does not prove the general claim.
activities.intendedInsight: The position-to-term rule is powerful because it gives any term directly; you cannot in general reach a later term by multiplying an earlier one (doubling the 5th term does not in general give the 10th: it fails for 3n−2, although it happens to work for rules with no constant term, such as 3n).

activities.title: Practice set: generate, fill and match
feedback: Mark substitution errors by checking against n=1,2,3; a wrong first term may flag a term-to-term misreading (e.g. giving 3 as the first term of 3n−2), but it could also be a simple arithmetic slip.
For sorting errors, prompt the learner back to the differences/ratios rows.
activities.rationale: Categorisation, fill-in and matching map cleanly onto the required procedures and give retrieval practice. This set scores answers and supports fluency, but on its own it does not build the two-engines insight, which the generator and discussion are intended to build.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory Algebra: 'generate terms of a sequence from either a term-to-term or a position-to-term rule'; 'recognise arithmetic sequences and find the nth term'; 'recognise geometric sequences and appreciate other sequences that arise'.
learnerActions: Generate the first five terms of a position-to-term rule such as 3n−2 by substitution (fill in the blanks).
Sort a mixed set of sequences into arithmetic / geometric / other.
Match each nth-term rule to the sequence it produces.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency in substituting positions into a rule and in categorising sequences by the correct test.

constraints: Use a varied diet — increasing, decreasing, decimal, geometric and 'neither' sequences — to prevent an only-increasing over-generalisation.
Require pupils to generate a position-to-term rule by substituting n=1,2,3,… , not by treating the formula as a term-to-term instruction.
The practice/quiz set gives retrieval practice and scoring but does not by itself build the position-vs-term-to-term insight; pair it with generation and discussion.
A static side-by-side reference of the two rule types is a useful worked example but cannot recompute for a learner's own rule; treat it as a reference scaffold, not the main generative task.
Interaction examples (mode switching, jump-to-50th button, coefficient dragging, live differences/ratios rows) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched and 'verified':true is legacy. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and efficacy is untested.

Self-audit (arithmetic/logic checks): 3n−2 for n=1..5 gives 1,4,7,10,13 — consistent across the row. 2,6,18,54 has ratio ×3 — correct. 1,4,9,16 has differences 3,5,7 (non-constant) and non-constant ratios — correctly classified as 'other'. The claim '10th term = 2 × 5th term' is a listed misconception; it is used only as something to challenge/disprove (for 3n−2: 5th=13, 10th=28, and 2×13=26≠28) and never as a valid rule.

Residual untested-efficacy wording in activities[4].rationale ('which the generator and discussion provide') and activities[3].rationale ('addresses the misconception') was softened to 'intended to build'/'intended to address' for consistency with the proposal (not validated) framing.

The source line 'a 3D rendering adds nothing' was treated as a catalog preference, not a universal law; the 3D alternative was omitted (sequence generation is non-spatial, so 3D is not required here) rather than propagated as a pedagogical rule.
The original 'scoring answers does not build the two-engines insight' was scoped to 'supports fluency but not, on its own, the insight' rather than an absolute 'a quiz only assesses' claim.

A construct-a-sequence-of-requested-type action was added to the classification activity to preserve the assessed production skill (responseLevels.full / probeDeeper); recognition and generation alone do not elicit this production.

Activity 2 cites only the statutory recognise-claim; the NCETM 'arithmetic adds/subtracts a constant amount; coefficient of n equals the common difference' claim also supports its differences test, but was not copied there to avoid importing unrelated content. Reviewers may add it if a tighter citation is wanted.
The pedagogy keyRepresentation 'graph of terms against position (constant difference = constant steepness)' was not carried into an activity and could optionally be added.

probeDeeper: For 3n − 2, what is the 10th term — and did you have to write out all ten to get it?
Your sequence 5, 8, 11, 14 — is it arithmetic or geometric, and what exactly did you check to decide?
1, 4, 9, 16 goes up by more each time. Does 'it goes up' make it arithmetic? What is different about it compared with 5, 8, 11, 14?
Give me a geometric sequence that starts with 5 — how did you build it?
assess.correctAnswer: 3n−2 gives 1, 4, 7, 10, 13 (substituting n = 1,2,3,4,5). 5, 8, 11, 14 is arithmetic (constant difference +3); 2, 6, 18, 54 is geometric (constant ratio ×3); 1, 4, 9, 16 is neither (differences 3, 5, 7 — not constant; ratios not constant). The child decides by checking the successive differences and the successive ratios.

errorPatterns.pattern: Applies the position rule as a term-to-term instruction — reads 3n−2 as 'start at 3, subtract 2' and writes 3, 1, −1, … instead of substituting n.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Write n = 1, 2, 3 explicitly and substitute each into 3n−2 under its position; use a position→term table so the formula is read as 'multiply the position by 3, then subtract 2'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The first term is not 1; the terms do not match a substitution check for n = 1, 2, 3.

errorPatterns.pattern: Classifies by 'it goes up' alone — calls 1, 4, 9, 16 arithmetic because it increases, or cannot tell geometric from arithmetic.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have the child write the differences row and the ratios row under each sequence; the row that stays constant names the type, and if neither is constant it is 'other'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Sorts by direction rather than by a constant difference vs a constant ratio; misses that 1, 4, 9, 16 has a changing difference (3, 5, 7).

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses 'multiples of 3' with 'increases by 3' — expects 3n−2 to produce multiples of 3, or expects any '+3' sequence to be the 3-times table.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Generate 3n (3, 6, 9, …) and 3n−2 (1, 4, 7, …) side by side; both increase by 3 but only one is the multiples sequence.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Checks terms against the 3-times table, or is surprised that 1, 4, 7, 10 increases by 3 yet contains no multiples of 3.

responseLevels.gap: Generates 3n−2 wrongly (applies it term-to-term or gets the first term wrong) and sorts sequences by 'goes up/down' without checking a difference or a ratio.
responseLevels.full: Generates by substitution, classifies all three by explicitly testing constant difference against constant ratio, articulates the position-to-term versus term-to-term distinction, and can construct a new sequence of a requested type.
responseLevels.partial: Substitutes correctly to generate the five terms and identifies arithmetic by a constant difference, but cannot reliably distinguish geometric (checks difference only, not ratio) or mislabels 1, 4, 9, 16 — has the parts but not the unifying difference-vs-ratio test.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Generate the first five terms of the sequence whose rule is 3n − 2. Then look at these three sequences — 5, 8, 11, 14, …; 2, 6, 18, 54, …; 1, 4, 9, 16, … — and sort each as arithmetic, geometric or neither, showing me how you decide.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Substituting the position numbers into 3n−2 (rather than treating it as a term-to-term instruction) reveals position-to-term fluency; classifying by testing BOTH constant difference and constant ratio (rather than 'it goes up') reveals the arithmetic/geometric structure. A child who conflates the two rule types produces the wrong first term, and a child who classifies by direction alone mis-sorts 1, 4, 9, 16 — so watching what they generate and sort discriminates without asking them to describe the method.

pedagogy.summary: Tenths are the first structured step into fractions born from dividing ONE whole into ten equal parts — the bridge from fractions to decimal place value. The load-bearing ideas: ten equal tenths recompose exactly one whole (10/10 = 1), each tenth is small (it takes ten to rebuild the whole), and 3/10 is the same as 3÷10 (three wholes shared among ten). Teach with strips, tens-frames-as-lengths and number lines so counting in tenths lands cleanly at one whole rather than becoming 'ten'.
bestPractices: Count up and down in tenths on a number line and a strip, stopping deliberately at 10/10 = one whole to break the 'ten-tenths is ten' bias
Insist on ten EQUAL parts of one whole (not any ten pieces) using a partitioned strip
Connect 3/10 to 3÷10 by sharing three whole strips across ten places
Compare a tenth with a half (5/10 = 1/2) so children feel a tenth is far smaller than a half
Keep the whole visible and constant so a tenth of a bigger whole is seen to be a bigger piece with the same name
keyRepresentations: Whole strip partitioned into ten equal tenths (recomposes to one whole)
0-to-1 number line marked in tenths
Sharing model: three wholes shared among ten to show 3/10 = 3÷10
Overlay of tenths against a half (5/10 = 1/2)
commonMisconceptions: Whole-number bias — reads ten-tenths as 'ten', or thinks a tenth is big 'because 10 is a big number'
Larger denominator = larger part (a tenth 'bigger than a half because 10 > 2')
Accepts any ten pieces as tenths, ignoring that the parts must be equal
Sees no connection between 3/10 and 3÷10 ('3 ÷ 10 can't be done, 3 is smaller than 10')
Thinks a tenth of a large whole and a tenth of a small whole are the same size

learn.summary: Tenths build on earlier work with fractions such as halves and quarters: dividing ONE whole into ten equal parts, and the bridge toward decimal place value. The load-bearing ideas are that ten equal tenths recompose exactly one whole (10/10 = 1), that each tenth is small because it takes ten of them to rebuild the whole, and that 3/10 is the same as 3÷10 (three wholes shared among ten). Partitioned strips, length-based number lines, and sharing models let counting in tenths land cleanly at one whole rather than drifting into 'ten'.

activities.title: Collect the tenths back into one whole
feedback: If the learner says ten-tenths is 'ten', physically recompose the ten tenths against the original whole: the row is the same length as one whole, not longer.
If the learner says a tenth is bigger than a half 'because 10 is more than 2', overlay five tenths onto one half so they see it takes five tenths just to make one half.
Reinforce that the denominator names how many equal parts make ONE whole, so with the same whole more parts means each part is smaller.
activities.rationale: A counting-and-recomposing sequence that deliberately stops at 10/10 = one whole is intended to address whole-number bias (reading fractions by their digits) and to build the magnitude sense Year 3 pupils are expected to develop when counting up and down in tenths; its effectiveness here is proposed rather than tested.
sourceClaims: Students commonly show whole-number bias, viewing fractions with larger denominators as larger (e.g. 1/8 > 1/3), and must be helped to see fractions as single numbers with magnitude; equal-partitioning (parts must be equal) is a documented roadblock.
Year 3 pupils count up and down in tenths, recognise that tenths arise from dividing an object into ten equal parts, and connect tenths to dividing one-digit numbers or quantities by 10.
learnerActions: Start with a single whole bar or strip and partition it into ten equal segments.
Collect the segments one at a time while counting aloud: one-tenth, two-tenths, three-tenths … up to ten-tenths.
At the tenth count, reassemble the ten segments end-to-end against the original whole and check that they match exactly, labelling the result '10/10 = 1 whole'.
Lay a piece covering exactly five tenths over one half of the whole and confirm that 5/10 = 1/2, so a single tenth is plainly far smaller than a half.
activities.intendedInsight: Ten equal tenths put back together remake exactly one whole, so 10/10 = 1 (not 'ten'), and each tenth is small because it takes ten of them to rebuild the whole — far smaller than a half.

activities.title: Share three wholes among ten to see 3/10 = 3÷10
feedback: If the learner says '3 ÷ 10 can't be done because 3 is smaller than 10', carry out the sharing concretely so they watch each place receive three tenths.
Name the completed share out loud: 'three shared among ten gives three tenths each, so 3 ÷ 10 = 3/10.'
If they write 10/3, re-link the notation: three of the ten equal pieces of one whole is 3/10.
activities.rationale: Connecting the fraction notation to an equal-sharing division is intended to address the misconception that 3/10 and 3÷10 are unrelated and matches the Year 3 expectation to connect tenths with dividing quantities by 10.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils count up and down in tenths, recognise that tenths arise from dividing an object into ten equal parts, and connect tenths to dividing one-digit numbers or quantities by 10.
learnerActions: Set out three identical whole bars and ten plates (or ten places) to share them among.
Partition each whole into tenths and deal the tenths out equally, one at a time, until each of the ten places has received the same amount.
State how much each place received (three tenths) and write the sharing as 3 ÷ 10 = 3/10.
Discuss why this works even though 3 is smaller than 10: you share the three wholes into smaller pieces rather than giving whole bars each.
activities.intendedInsight: A fraction such as 3/10 is the result of sharing three wholes equally among ten, so 3/10 = 3÷10; dividing by a number larger than the dividend is possible and gives a fraction less than one.

activities.title: Equal parts only, and the same whole
feedback: If the learner accepts unequal pieces as tenths, contrast the equal and unequal splits and ask which one is made of ten pieces that are all the same size.
If the learner thinks a tenth is always the same absolute size, place the two different-sized wholes side by side so the two tenths can be compared directly.
Emphasise that the name 'tenth' tells you the number of equal parts in its whole, not a fixed length.
activities.rationale: Equal-partitioning is a documented roadblock, and the relative nature of a fraction (the piece that is a tenth of a bigger whole is bigger when both wholes are visible) is a known source of confusion; contrasting cases and keeping the whole visible make the condition explicit.
sourceClaims: Students commonly show whole-number bias, viewing fractions with larger denominators as larger (e.g. 1/8 > 1/3), and must be helped to see fractions as single numbers with magnitude; equal-partitioning (parts must be equal) is a documented roadblock.
learnerActions: Compare a whole split into ten EQUAL pieces with a whole split into ten UNEQUAL pieces.
Decide which one shows tenths and explain why (the ten parts must be the same size).
Check by trying to recompose each set back into the whole and noticing which one tiles the whole with matching equal pieces.

Then compare a tenth of a small whole bar with a tenth of a larger whole bar, keeping both wholes visible, and describe how the two tenths differ in physical size even though both are called 'a tenth'.
activities.intendedInsight: Only ten EQUAL parts of one whole count as tenths; and because a tenth is defined relative to its whole, the physical piece that is a tenth of a larger whole is larger than a tenth of a smaller whole when both wholes are shown, though both pieces share the name 'a tenth' and name the same fraction of their own whole.

activities.title: Place and name tenths on a number line
feedback: If a learner places 5/10 anywhere other than halfway, relate the point to the half-overlay from the first activity.
If they answer 'ten' for 10/10, point to where the tenth tenth lands — exactly at 1, the end of the whole.
Encourage reading each mark as a quantity, not just as a count of ticks.
activities.rationale: Positioning tenths on a line as single numbers with magnitude reinforces the magnitude understanding that counters whole-number bias; placing and naming on a line checks and consolidates this understanding rather than building the recompose-to-one-whole insight, and recognising a correct position does not by itself confirm the learner can produce the reasoning, so use it after the hands-on work.
sourceClaims: Students commonly show whole-number bias, viewing fractions with larger denominators as larger (e.g. 1/8 > 1/3), and must be helped to see fractions as single numbers with magnitude; equal-partitioning (parts must be equal) is a documented roadblock.
learnerActions: Use a 0-to-1 number line marked in tenths.
Count up and down the line in tenths, naming each mark.
Place given tenths (for example 3/10) at the correct point and identify which point equals one half (5/10).
Fill in missing values such as 'ten-tenths = __' and justify with the recomposition idea rather than by counting ticks.
activities.intendedInsight: Tenths are single numbers with a fixed position and magnitude between 0 and 1, with 10/10 sitting exactly at one and 5/10 exactly at one half.

constraints: Keep the whole visible throughout, and keep it the same size except when deliberately comparing tenths of different-sized wholes, so that a tenth is always understood relative to its own whole.
Insist on ten EQUAL parts of one whole; any ten pieces are not tenths unless they are the same size.
Deliberately pause counting at 10/10 and reassemble to one whole, rather than letting the count slide into 'ten'.

Placing, naming, matching, and fill-in tasks (e.g. on a number line) check and consolidate understanding but do not by themselves build the recompose-to-one-whole insight; use them after the hands-on partitioning and sharing work.

A static labelled tenths strip can show the facts (this is 3/10; these ten make one whole; 5/10 = one half) but cannot itself enact the moment ten tenths fuse back into one whole; pair it with a recomposition the learner performs.

Partitioning and recomposing a visible whole provides the concrete experience of ten tenths reforming one whole; spoken discussion can support the reasoning about why a tenth is small but does not itself supply that partitioning and recomposition, so include the hands-on work rather than relying on discussion to provide it.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and their efficacy is untested.

Self-audit of the magnitude claims: 10/10 = 1, 5/10 = 1/2, and 3÷10 = 3/10 are correct; a tenth is correctly described as far smaller than a half (five tenths make one half). No arithmetic errors found.
The original assessment correctly reads the denominator as the number of equal parts in one whole; this was preserved, and no conceptual corrections to the source were required.

As a number, one-tenth is always the same fraction; the 'bigger/smaller piece' point concerns the physical portion of a particular whole and holds only when both wholes are shown together, so it is retained with the explicit 'keep both wholes visible' condition.
The original's stronger comparative wording about dialogue adding little and 3D being decorative was softened to scoped affordances; comparative efficacy of media is untested and not asserted.

assess.poeTask: Show the child a whole strip. Ask: 'If I cut this into ten equal pieces and then lay all ten back end-to-end in a row, will the row be shorter than, the same length as, or LONGER than the whole strip? Predict, and say why.' A whole-number-biased child predicts 'longer, because now there are ten of them.' Then lay the ten tenths against the original whole — they match exactly. The pre-observation reason ('ten pieces so more') is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: How many tenths make one whole? And how many tenths is one half?
I have a bigger bar, also cut into ten equal pieces. Is one piece of that bar also called a tenth? Is it the same size as a tenth of the small bar?
Which is more, 3 tenths or 3 halves? Why?
Why do we write 3/10 and not 10/3 for three of the ten pieces?
assess.correctAnswer: Ten-tenths equals 1 (one whole), because ten equal tenths put back together make the whole bar again. Each tenth is much smaller than a half, because it takes ten tenths to make a whole but only two halves — so a tenth is far smaller (five tenths make one half).

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number bias — ten-tenths read as 'ten', and a tenth judged bigger than a half 'because 10 is more than 2'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Recompose ten tenths into one whole in front of the child; overlay five tenths on one half; reteach the denominator as parts-of-one-whole
errorPatterns.distractor: Ten-tenths is 10, because I counted ten pieces.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'ten' for 10/10, or says a single tenth is bigger than a half

errorPatterns.pattern: Equal-parts ignored — thinks 'tenths' just means ten pieces, regardless of whether they are the same size
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast an equal ten-split with an unequal one; only equal parts can be called tenths; check by recomposing to one whole
errorPatterns.distractor: Any bar broken into ten pieces shows tenths, even if the pieces are different sizes.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Accepts a bar broken into ten UNEQUAL pieces as showing tenths

errorPatterns.pattern: Fraction disconnected from division — does not see 3/10 as 3÷10 ('you can't do 3 ÷ 10, three is smaller than ten')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Share three whole strips across ten places so each place gets 3/10; name the share as 3÷10 = 3/10
errorPatterns.distractor: 3 ÷ 10 can't be done, because 3 is smaller than 10.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 3÷10 is impossible or 0, and treats 3/10 as unrelated to sharing three wholes among ten

responseLevels.gap: Says ten-tenths equals ten; judges a tenth bigger than a half because 10 > 2; accepts unequal pieces as tenths.
responseLevels.full: States ten-tenths = 1 and justifies by recomposition, orders a tenth as far smaller than a half by the ten-vs-two-parts argument, connects 3/10 with 3÷10, and transfers (a tenth of a different-sized whole is correspondingly bigger or smaller).
responseLevels.partial: Counts in tenths and states 10/10 makes one whole and that tenths are ten equal parts, but lists these facts without connecting them — cannot explain a tenth is small BECAUSE ten rebuild the whole, cannot link 3/10 to 3÷10, and stumbles on a tenth of a different-sized whole.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A chocolate bar is one whole. It is snapped into ten equal pieces. I eat the pieces one at a time and count: one-tenth, two-tenths, three-tenths… When I have eaten all of them, I have eaten ten-tenths. What number does ten-tenths equal, and why? And is each single piece bigger or smaller than a half — how do you know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A whole-number-biased child says ten-tenths is 'ten' (treating 10/10 as the count) and/or says a tenth is big 'because 10 is a big number'. Correct reasoning requires reading the denominator as the number of equal parts in ONE whole, so 10/10 rebuilds one and each part is small — the reason (tier 2) exposes the bias even when a rehearsed child guesses 'one'.
