pedagogy.summary: A percentage is a proportion expressed as parts per hundred: 40% means 40 out of every 100, so it is naturally 40/100 and 0.40, and 100% is the whole while 50% is half of it. The decisive idea — and the one children most often miss — is that a percentage is an OPERATOR ON A BASE, not a plain number: 50% is not 'fifty', it is half of whatever the whole is, so 50% of 20 is 10 while 50% of 200 is 100. Because a percentage is inherently 'out of 100', its size relative to the whole is fixed but its actual amount depends entirely on the base. Teach it on the hundred square (40 of 100 shaded) tied to the fraction n/100, the decimal, and a 0%–100% number line, and confront base-neglect head-on.
bestPractices: Anchor 'per cent = parts per hundred' on a 10×10 hundred square: shade 40 squares to show 40%, and read off 40/100 and 0.40 from the same picture.

Foreground the base from the outset: a percentage is a proportion OF a whole, so always ask '% of what?'; show that 50% of a small set and 50% of a large set are the same proportion but different amounts.
Link the three forms explicitly — 40% = 40/100 = 0.40 — and simplify where natural (40/100 = 2/5) so percentage sits inside the fraction–decimal web.
Establish landmarks: 100% = the whole, 50% = a half, 25% = a quarter, 10% = a tenth, 1% = a hundredth; and seed that percentages can exceed 100%.
Confront base-neglect with deliberate comparisons (10% of 500 = 50 versus 90% of 60 = 48) so children see a smaller percentage of a bigger base can be the larger amount.
keyRepresentations: 10×10 hundred square shaded to the percentage
Four-way link: percentage + fraction n/100 + decimal + 0%–100% number line
Bar model of a whole partitioned to show a percentage of it
Landmark strip (0%, 10%, 25%, 50%, 100%) against fractions/decimals
Two different-sized wholes each showing '50%' to expose the role of the base
commonMisconceptions: Base-neglect: treating a percentage as a fixed number independent of the whole ('50% is always 50 / a lot').
Reading a percentage as a fraction with the number as denominator ('24% means 1/24', '40% means 1/40').
Percentage–decimal placeholder error: writing 9% as 0.9 instead of 0.09.
Believing 100% is the maximum — that you cannot have more than 100%.
Thinking a bigger percentage always means a bigger amount, regardless of the base.

learn.summary: A percentage is a proportion expressed as parts per hundred: 40% means 40 out of every 100, so it equals 40/100 and 0.40, with 100% as the whole and 50% as half of it. The decisive idea — and the one children most often miss — is that when we find a percentage OF an amount, the percentage acts on a base rather than standing for a fixed amount: 50% is not 'fifty' (it equals 50/100 = 0.5), it is half of whatever the whole is, so 50% of 20 is 10 while 50% of 200 is 100. Teach percentage on the hundred square (40 of 100 shaded) tied to the fraction n/100, the decimal, and a 0%–100% number line, establish landmarks (100%, 50%, 25%, 10%, 1%) and that percentages can exceed 100%, keep asking '% of what?', and confront base-neglect directly through deliberate comparisons.

activities.title: Same percentage, different whole: resize the base
feedback: If a learner says 50% is 'always 50' or 'always a lot', show 50% of 20 and 50% of 200 side by side: the square is half-shaded in both, but one amount is 10 and the other is 100 — same proportion, different amount.
Confirm the three forms read from one picture: 40 shaded of 100 is 40/100 and 0.40; where natural, 40/100 simplifies to 2/5.
If they treat the square as fixed, point out the square always shows 'out of 100' (the proportion) while the amount tracks the size of the whole.
activities.rationale: Letting the base vary while the percentage is held constant makes base-dependence something the learner observes directly, rather than being told; linking shading, fraction, decimal and number line welds percentage into the fraction–decimal web. A live, controllable base is one concrete way to make this visible; a fixed picture cannot be varied, though it can still illustrate 'parts per hundred'.
sourceClaims: A percentage represents part of a quantity and functions as an operator on a base, not a plain number; base-neglect — not attending to the whole from which the percentage is taken — is a robust, documented misconception (e.g. treating 32% of one amount as identical to 32% of another). The essential teaching principle is to establish which whole the percentage is calculated from.

'Per cent' means number of parts per hundred and a percentage can be an operator on a quantity; percentages have fraction and decimal equivalents; proportion is independent of the size of the number, so 10% of 500 (=50) can exceed 90% of 60 (=48); a documented error is writing 9% as 0.9; percentages can exceed 100%.

Pupils should understand the per cent symbol and that per cent relates to 'number of parts per hundred', and write percentages as a fraction with denominator 100 and as a decimal (Year 5 statutory content).
learnerActions: Set a percentage (e.g. 50%) and shade that proportion of a 10×10 hundred square.
With the whole set to 20, read off the actual amount (50% of 20 = 10); then change the whole to 200 and read the new amount (50% of 200 = 100).
Describe what stays the same (the proportion / the shaded half of the square) and what changes (the actual amount) as the base changes.
Alongside the shading, write the percentage as a fraction n/100 and as a decimal, and locate it on a 0%–100% number line.
activities.intendedInsight: A percentage fixes the PROPORTION of a whole, not a fixed number; the actual amount depends entirely on the base, so you must always ask '% of what?'.

activities.title: Bigger percentage, smaller amount: compare across different bases
feedback: 10% of 500 = 50; 80% of 60 = 48, so 10% of 500 is the larger amount even though 10% < 80%.
If a learner assumes the bigger percentage must win, point back to the base: 10% of a large whole can beat 80% of a small whole.
A twin-panel or two-bar display of the two amounts makes the 50-versus-48 comparison visible side by side.
activities.rationale: A deliberately contrasting pair where the smaller percentage yields the larger amount directly challenges the belief that 'bigger percentage = bigger amount'. The numbers (50 vs 48) are chosen so the gap is small and surprising.
sourceClaims: 'Per cent' means number of parts per hundred and a percentage can be an operator on a quantity; percentages have fraction and decimal equivalents; proportion is independent of the size of the number, so 10% of 500 (=50) can exceed 90% of 60 (=48); a documented error is writing 9% as 0.9; percentages can exceed 100%.
learnerActions: Work out 10% of 500 and 80% of 60, showing each amount.
State which is the larger AMOUNT and explain how you know without guessing.
Reflect on why the 'smaller' percentage (10%) gave the bigger amount (50 beats 48).
activities.intendedInsight: A bigger percentage does not guarantee a bigger amount, because the amount also depends on the size of the base being taken.

activities.title: Writing and checking the three forms
feedback: 9% = 9/100 = 0.09, not 0.9: nine hundredths needs a zero in the tenths place; similarly 5% = 0.05. Read 0.09 aloud as 'nine hundredths' to check.
40% means 40 out of 100 = 40/100, NOT 1/40: per cent is parts per HUNDRED, so 100 is the denominator. The '24% means one twenty-fourth' error has the same cause.
Check the landmarks against the hundred square: 25% is a quarter (25 of 100 = 1/4 = 0.25), 10% is a tenth (10 of 100 = 1/10 = 0.1), 1% is a hundredth (1 of 100 = 1/100 = 0.01).
100% is not a maximum: 150% means one and a half wholes (150 parts per hundred).
activities.rationale: These conversions are cleanly checkable and the common errors (1/n denominator, missing decimal placeholder, '100% is the maximum') are diagnostic. Landmark percentages give familiar anchors across the three forms. Single-digit cases are included deliberately because 40% → 0.40 can hide the placeholder error that 5% → 0.5 exposes.
sourceClaims: In national Key Stage 2 test analysis, percentages caused particular difficulty; a common error in finding 24% of 525 was to calculate 24% as one twenty-fourth — evidence of connecting percentages to fractions but not understanding what a percentage is or how it acts on a quantity.

'Per cent' means number of parts per hundred and a percentage can be an operator on a quantity; percentages have fraction and decimal equivalents; proportion is independent of the size of the number, so 10% of 500 (=50) can exceed 90% of 60 (=48); a documented error is writing 9% as 0.9; percentages can exceed 100%.

Pupils should understand the per cent symbol and that per cent relates to 'number of parts per hundred', and write percentages as a fraction with denominator 100 and as a decimal (Year 5 statutory content).
learnerActions: Complete links such as 40% = __/100 = 0.__ and 35% = 35/100 = 0.35.
Shade 40 of 100 squares to match 40%, and simplify 40/100 to 2/5 where asked.

Place landmark percentages on a 0%–100% strip and match them to their fraction and decimal: 100% = the whole = 1, 50% = a half = 0.5, 25% = a quarter = 0.25, 10% = a tenth = 0.1, 1% = a hundredth = 0.01.
Convert single-digit percentages carefully: write 9% as a decimal and as a fraction, and 5% as a decimal.
Decide whether a percentage can exceed 100% and say what 150% would mean.
activities.intendedInsight: Percentage, fraction (over 100) and decimal are three names for the same proportion; 'per cent' means parts per hundred, key landmarks (100%, 50%, 25%, 10%, 1%) link to familiar fractions and decimals, 100% is the whole, and percentages can exceed 100%.

activities.title: Predict, count, reconcile: '50% is always 50?'
feedback: A base-neglecter predicts 'same, both 50%'; the count (5 vs 50) contradicts this — same proportion, different amount because the wholes differ.
Jo is wrong: 50% means half of whatever the whole is (fifty parts per hundred), so 50% of 20 is 10 and 50% of 200 is 100.
For the sale claim, 50% off £40 saves £20 while 50% off £1000 saves £500 — the saving tracks the price, so the £50 claim fails.
If a learner cannot say '50% of what?', return to two different-sized wholes and reteach that a percentage is always OF a whole.
activities.rationale: A predict-then-check task with a stated reason makes the misconception observable and gives a moment of contradiction to resolve. A character's wrong claim can surface the misconception for discussion; the resolution is strengthened by actually computing and comparing the amounts.
sourceClaims: A percentage represents part of a quantity and functions as an operator on a base, not a plain number; base-neglect — not attending to the whole from which the percentage is taken — is a robust, documented misconception (e.g. treating 32% of one amount as identical to 32% of another). The essential teaching principle is to establish which whole the percentage is calculated from.
learnerActions: PREDICT first: Ann eats 50% of a plate of 10 grapes; Ben eats 50% of a plate of 100 grapes. Since both ate 50%, do they eat the same NUMBER of grapes? Give your reason before working it out.
Then count: Ann eats 5, Ben eats 50.
Reconcile the result with your prediction — same proportion, different amount.
Respond to the claim 'Jo says 50% is always 50': is Jo right, and what does 50% really mean?
Discuss or argue the case 'a 50%-off sale always saves £50' and explain why the saving depends on the original price.
activities.intendedInsight: Stating a reason before calculating exposes base-neglect; reconciling prediction with the count cements that 50% is a proportion of a base, not a fixed number.

constraints: Always tie the percentage to a named whole: ask '% of what?' every time an amount is computed, so the base stays visible.

A fixed/static hundred square annotated with 40% = 40/100 = 0.40 is a useful reference and can illustrate 'parts per hundred', but it cannot itself vary the base; base-dependence is best experienced by changing the whole or by comparing two different-sized wholes.

Recognition-only responses (e.g. choosing 'Jo is right/wrong') check understanding but do not by themselves require the learner to construct and justify the amount; include tasks where the learner computes and explains.
Include single-digit percentages (5%, 9%) as well as 40% so the decimal placeholder error cannot hide behind cases like 40% → 0.40.
Simplify fractions (40/100 = 2/5) only where it is natural and does not obscure the 'out of 100' meaning that defines percentage.

Establish landmark percentages (100%, 50%, 25%, 10%, 1%) alongside their fraction and decimal equivalents, and seed deliberately that percentages can exceed 100% so '100% is the maximum' does not take hold.

Any base-comparison example used with learners must be arithmetically correct and must actually demonstrate the intended point (e.g. 10% of 500 = 50 truly exceeds 80% of 60 = 48); do not reuse the source row's '90% of 60 = 48' figure, which is wrong (90% of 60 = 54).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the four cited sources were flagged in the source row as verified:false (the KS2 'Misconceptions with the Key Objectives' analysis and the DfE National Curriculum programmes of study); treat the claims drawn from them — including the 24%-as-one-twenty-fourth error pattern and the Year 5 statutory conversion requirement — as unconfirmed.

The source row and the NCETM sourceClaim state the base-comparison as '90% of 60 (=48)', but 90% of 60 = 54, not 48. With the correct value (54) the smaller percentage would NOT exceed it (50 < 54), defeating the intended point. Learner-facing content has therefore been corrected to 80% of 60 = 48 so that 10% of 500 = 50 genuinely beats the larger-percentage amount while 10% < 80%. The verbatim source quote retaining '90%...(=48)' is kept only as the cited claim and must not be used as the computed example.

The original row rated 3D as 'poor' with 'adds no conceptual value' and framed a fixed image/dialogue as unable to 'deliver' the insight. These comparative/necessity claims are not established by the cited sources and have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements; the live-base, twin-panel, two-bar, and tap-to-reveal elements are retained as optional concrete mechanisms, not mandatory ones.

assess.poeTask: Ask the child to PREDICT before working: 'Ann eats 50% of a plate of 10 grapes; Ben eats 50% of a plate of 100 grapes. Since both ate 50%, do they eat the same NUMBER of grapes? Why?' The stated reason is the diagnostic part — a base-neglecter predicts 'same, both 50%'. Then count: Ann eats 5, Ben eats 50. Have the child reconcile this with their prediction (same proportion, different amount).
probeDeeper: Is 50% of this small square the same AMOUNT as 50% of that big square? Is it the same PROPORTION? Why?
Can you have more than 100% of something? What would 150% mean?
You wrote 40% = 40/100. Can you write that fraction more simply?
Which is more: 10% of 500, or 90% of 60? How do you know without guessing?
assess.correctAnswer: Shade 40 of the 100 squares; 40% = 40/100 (= 2/5) = 0.40. Jo is wrong: 50% means half of whatever the whole is (fifty parts per hundred), so 50% of 20 is 10 and 50% of 200 is 100 — the amount depends on the base. 100% is the whole; 50% is half of it.

errorPatterns.pattern: Base-neglect: treats a percentage as a fixed number — 'Jo's right, 50% is 50 / 50% is just a lot' — ignoring the whole it is taken from.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show 50% of two different-sized wholes (20 and 200) on hundred squares so the amounts differ though the proportion is the same; establish '% is always OF a whole'. Reteach the meaning of per cent.
errorPatterns.distractor: Jo is right — 50% is 50.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Agrees with Jo, or gives a single amount for 50% regardless of the base; cannot say '50% of what?'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the percentage as a fraction with the number as denominator — '40% means 1/40' (the classic '24% = one twenty-fourth').
errorPatterns.nextMove: On the hundred square, 40% is 40 of 100 squares = 40/100; per cent is parts per HUNDRED, so 100 is the denominator. Reteach 'out of 100'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 40% as 1/40 instead of 40/100; connects percentage to fractions but with the wrong denominator.

errorPatterns.pattern: Percentage–decimal placeholder error: writes a single-digit percentage such as 9% as 0.9 instead of 0.09.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Read 0.09 as 'nine hundredths'; 9% = 9/100 sits in the hundredths place, needing a zero in tenths. Reteach decimal notation for hundredths.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On single-digit percentages, drops the placeholder (9% → 0.9); 40% → 0.40 may look fine but 5% → 0.5.

responseLevels.gap: Treats a percentage as a fixed number (agrees '50% is always 50') or as 1/n; cannot shade the grid to match or write the fraction/decimal.
responseLevels.full: Explains a percentage as parts per hundred of a base, so 50% depends on the whole (10 of 20, 100 of 200); shades 40 of 100, writes 40/100 = 0.40 = 2/5; knows 100% is the whole and >100% is possible; judges base-dependent comparisons and transfers to new cases.
responseLevels.partial: Writes 40% = 40/100 = 0.40 and knows 100% is the whole and 50% is half, but still treats the amount as fixed regardless of the base, or converts without articulating that a percentage is parts per hundred OF a whole.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Shade 40% of this 10×10 grid, and write 40% as a fraction and as a decimal. Then tell me: Jo says '50% is always 50'. Is Jo right? Explain what 50% really means.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The grid + fraction + decimal checks the 'parts per hundred' meaning; the Jo question is the hinge — a child who understands percentage as a proportion of a base rejects '50% is always 50' and ties the amount to the whole, while a base-neglecter agrees or treats 50% as a fixed number. Reasoning correctly and incorrectly give opposite verdicts on Jo, which is hard to fake.

pedagogy.summary: At 6-7 tool choice moves from purely concrete objects to REPRESENTATIONS — number line, hundred square, ruler, part-whole model — and the strategic act becomes matching the representation to the problem's PURPOSE and to the size of the numbers. A jump-counting addition suits a number line; a place-value addition suits a hundred square; a length problem needs a ruler. As numbers grow past ten, counting single cubes in ones becomes slow and error-prone, so a key lesson is trading the concrete tool for a representation that carries the tens. Press children to explain why one representation beats another for a given problem.
bestPractices: Sort problems by 'what are we trying to find?' and match the tool to that purpose (measure → ruler; jump-add → number line) before choosing numbers (EEF: clear rationale)
Show number lines explicitly — EEF finds them a particularly effective representation across KS2/3 — modelling jumps of ten rather than counting marks in ones
Compare two representations for the same problem and discuss 'which helped more and why', which EEF finds develops conceptual understanding
Make the inefficiency of counting big numbers in ones felt, so children choose a representation for efficiency, not just because it is allowed
Keep naming each tool's limitation (a number line doesn't measure a real object; cubes are unwieldy past twenty) so choice stays a fit judgement
keyRepresentations: Number line (jump in tens and ones)
Hundred square (place-value moves — down a row = +10)
Ruler / measuring tools
Part-whole model
Cubes / base-ten (for smaller numbers)
commonMisconceptions: Persists with counting single cubes in ones for two-digit numbers (34+28), which is slow and error-prone (EEF: over-reliance on concrete)
Mismatches the tool to the problem's purpose — e.g. reaches for a number line for a 'how long is it?' measuring task instead of a ruler
Draws a number line but counts every mark in ones anyway, using it as a ritual rather than to jump in tens (EEF: answer, not structure)
Thinks a representation is 'babyish' or 'proper' rather than fit-for-purpose, so choice is about status not the problem

learn.summary: For 6-7 year-olds, strategic tool choice shifts from concrete objects to REPRESENTATIONS (number line, hundred square, ruler, part-whole model), and the skill becomes matching the representation to the problem's PURPOSE and to the size of the numbers. As numbers grow past ten, counting single cubes in ones becomes slow and error-prone, so a key lesson is trading the concrete tool for a representation that carries the tens. The central proposed activity gives a child the same chooser facing two problems — a two-digit addition (34+28) where a number line's tens-and-ones jumps are genuinely quicker than counting a cube pile, and a measuring task where a ruler (or a metre stick for a large object), not a number line, fits — then invites them to justify why each tool fits its problem. Alternatives (a convince-a-partner dialogue, a primer comparison board) are intended to serve different pedagogical purposes.

activities.title: Pick the tool, work the problem, justify the fit
feedback: If the child builds 34+28 from single cubes and miscounts, or insists cubes are the way even for big numbers: contrast directly with a +20-then-+8 number-line jump, showing how the representation holds the tens so the ones needn't be counted. Revisit place-value adding strategies.

If the child grabs a number line for the measuring task: sort the two problems by 'what are we trying to find?' and match each tool's purpose; name what a ruler or metre stick does that a number line cannot here.

If the child reaches for a short ruler to measure the door: ask which measuring tool matches the size of the object, prompting the metre stick, so size as well as purpose drives the choice. Revisit measuring with length units.

If the child draws a number line but counts every mark in ones: model the +10 jump and ask 'can you get there in fewer jumps?', linking the tool to place-value structure rather than to the ritual of having drawn it.
Praise specifically when the child names both the efficiency gain (fewer jumps, no miscounting) and a case where the rejected tool would still win.
activities.rationale: A 2D surface with a tool palette lets the child actually pick, use, and feel the efficiency difference between a slow cube pile and a two-jump number line, then justify the choice. The same-child, two-problems contrast is intended to make the strategy concrete rather than a stated rule, though this specific activity is a research-informed proposal, not a separately validated intervention. Number lines modelling jumps of ten, and comparing two representations of the same idea, are highlighted in the EEF guidance.
sourceClaims: Manipulatives and representations must be used purposefully with a clear rationale and to reveal structure not just get an answer; number lines are a particularly effective representation, and comparing different representations of an idea develops conceptual understanding
Proficient students make sound decisions about when a tool is helpful, recognising the insight it gives and its limitations
learnerActions: Solve 34 + 28 using a palette of tools: cubes/base-ten, a number line, a hundred square, a ruler.
If you reach for single cubes, build and count 62 in ones — notice it is slow and easy to miscount. (Base-ten rods group the tens, so they avoid most of this counting.)
On the number line, jump 34 → +20 → 54 → +8 → 62 in two jumps.
On the hundred square (numbered with 1 at the top), add the 20 by moving two rows down to 54, then add 8 by moving forward eight squares (crossing into the next row) to reach 62.
After solving, answer: 'Why did that tool help?' and 'When would cubes actually be the better choice?'

Then tackle a measuring task: 'How long is the ribbon?' (a ruler fits, the number line does not) and 'How tall is the door?' (a metre stick fits better than a short ruler). Explain why the tool follows the problem's purpose AND the size of the object.
activities.intendedInsight: The right tool follows the PURPOSE of the problem and the size of the numbers or object, not habit: a representation that carries the tens (number line, hundred square) spares you counting ones, while a length problem needs a measuring tool matched to the object's size. Cubes remain a good fit for small numbers — this is a fit judgement, not a ranking of tools as 'babyish' or 'proper'.

activities.title: Convince a partner who defaults to cubes
feedback: If the child only says the number line is 'quicker' but cannot name when cubes would be better, prompt: 'Give me a problem where cubes really would be the BEST choice.'
If the child dismisses cubes outright as 'babyish', redirect to fit: cubes are fine, even best, for small numbers — the issue is efficiency with large numbers.
Affirm when the child both defends the efficient tool and identifies a genuine case for cubes.
activities.rationale: A dialogue partner who must be convinced can surface the fit-and-efficiency reasoning aloud and expose whether the child's reason is fit-based or status-based. This is intended as a complementary purpose to the hands-on palette: it targets articulation and justification rather than doing. It is a proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Proficient students make sound decisions about when a tool is helpful, recognising the insight it gives and its limitations
learnerActions: Work with a partner (or in-role character) who always reaches for cubes, even for 34 + 28.
Argue why a number line or hundred square is more efficient for big numbers — point to jumping the tens and avoiding miscounts.
Concede honestly where cubes still win: give a problem (e.g. a small total like 3 + 4) where cubes really would be the best choice.
Answer a probe such as 'What can a hundred square show you that a number line doesn't when you add 28?'
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to explain why one representation beats another for a given problem — and when the rejected tool would in fact be right — is what separates a real fit judgement from a blanket ranking of tools.

activities.title: Primer: what each tool is for
feedback: If the child treats the board as the whole lesson, move them promptly to actually working a problem with a chosen tool — naming purposes is only a warm-up and does not by itself show they can choose and use a tool when solving.
activities.rationale: A static annotated comparison can prime awareness of each tool's purpose and lets the child compare representations, but on its own it does not let the child act, feel the inefficiency, or justify a choice; keep it as a brief primer before the hands-on activity.
sourceClaims: Manipulatives and representations must be used purposefully with a clear rationale and to reveal structure not just get an answer; number lines are a particularly effective representation, and comparing different representations of an idea develops conceptual understanding
learnerActions: Explore a comparison board for number line vs hundred square vs ruler, revealing 'best for…' and 'not for…' notes for each.
Before the main task, predict which tool you would reach for in an addition and in a measuring problem.
activities.intendedInsight: Each representation has a purpose and a limitation — a number line jumps along a count but does not measure a real object; cubes become unwieldy past twenty — so a warm-up can prime 'what each is for'.

constraints: Choose numbers large enough that counting in ones is genuinely inefficient (e.g. 34+28), so the efficiency case for a tens-carrying representation is real rather than asserted.

Frame tool choice as a fit judgement tied to the problem's purpose and number/object size — not as some tools being 'babyish' or 'proper'. Always include a case where the rejected tool (cubes for small numbers) is the better fit.
A comparison/primer board naming 'what each tool is for' is a warm-up: it does not elicit the child working a problem or justifying efficiency, so do not treat it as the main activity.

A single matching/recognition item can ask 'which tool?' but cannot observe the child using the tool or justifying fit and efficiency; recognition-only responses do not elicit independent construction of a strategy.
Keep naming each tool's limitation (a number line doesn't measure a real object; cubes are unwieldy past twenty) so the choice stays a fit judgement.

Include at least one measuring task, and vary the object's size (e.g. ribbon vs door) so the child experiences matching a measuring tool — ruler vs metre stick — to the object, and that a number line does not fit a length problem.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and efficacy wording has been kept qualified accordingly.

The legacy row claimed '3D adds no purchase on tool-fit here' and that a quiz 'cannot observe the child... the WHY is invisible'. These are catalog-fit opinions, not established findings. Retained only the narrowly objective point that recognition-only items do not elicit independent construction; dropped the universal dismissals.

The legacy 'possible'/'poor' fit rankings and product-format vocabulary were removed; the underlying distinct pedagogical purposes (dialogue for justification, primer for priming) were preserved as separate activities.

Arithmetic check: 34 + 28 = 62, and 34 → +20 → 54 → +8 → 62 is correct; on the hundred square +20 is two rows down to 54 and +8 moves forward eight squares (crossing a row boundary) to 62. No arithmetic errors found.
The part-whole model is listed among the topic's tools but is not exercised in any activity, matching the original recommended task; it could optionally be added to the palette.

probeDeeper: Can you give me a problem where cubes really would be the BEST choice?
Show me the fewest jumps you can do on the number line for 34 + 28 — why fewer jumps?
If the problem was 'how tall is the door', which would you pick — number line, ruler, or metre stick — and why?
What can a hundred square show you that a number line doesn't, when you add 28?
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child recognising that counting single cubes for numbers this big is slow and error-prone (a limitation), that the number line lets you jump in tens and ones (efficiency and structure), AND that cubes are fine for small numbers — a fit judgement, not 'cubes are babyish'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Persists with counting single cubes in ones for two-digit numbers — slow, error-prone — rather than a representation that carries the tens
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast directly with a +20-then-+8 number-line jump; show how the representation holds the tens so ones needn't be counted. Reteach place-value adding strategies.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Builds 34+28 from single cubes and miscounts, or insists cubes are the way even for big numbers

errorPatterns.pattern: Mismatches the tool to the problem's purpose — grabs a number line for a 'how long is it?' measuring task instead of a ruler
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort problems by 'what are we trying to find?' then match the tool's purpose; name what a ruler does that a number line cannot here. Reteach measuring with length units.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Chooses the wrong class of tool for what the problem asks to find

errorPatterns.pattern: Draws a number line but counts every mark in ones anyway, using it as a ritual rather than to jump in tens
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model the +10 jump and ask 'can you get there in fewer jumps?'; link the tool to place-value structure, not just to having drawn it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Number line present but every step is a single mark, no tens jumps

responseLevels.gap: Reaches for one tool by habit (usually cubes) or mismatches the tool to the problem's purpose, with no efficiency or fit reasoning.
responseLevels.full: Unprompted, matches the tool to the problem's purpose and the size of the numbers, justifies by efficiency and structure (jump the tens), names when the rejected tool would in fact be the right choice, and picks a ruler for a measuring task.
responseLevels.partial: Chooses a reasonable representation and, when prompted, says the number line is 'quicker', but cannot say when cubes would be better or slips back into counting marks in ones.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: To work out 34 + 28, one child got out 62 cubes and counted them one by one; another used a number line and jumped +20 then +8. Which was the better tool for these numbers, and why? And when WOULD cubes be the better choice?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 34+28 is big enough that counting cubes in ones is genuinely inefficient, so a strategic chooser points to efficiency and place-value jumps; a non-strategic child either counts everything or dismisses cubes outright with no fit reason. The 'when would cubes be better?' turn separates a real fit judgement from a blanket ranking of tools.

sources.claim: Proficient students make sound decisions about when a tool is helpful, recognising the insight it gives and its limitations
sources.source: CCSS Standards for Mathematical Practice — MP5 Use appropriate tools strategically

sources.claim: Manipulatives and representations must be used purposefully with a clear rationale and to reveal structure not just get an answer; number lines are a particularly effective representation, and comparing different representations of an idea develops conceptual understanding
sources.source: EEF — Improving Mathematics in Key Stages 2 and 3 (Recommendation 2)

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–10y; solve problems involving scaling by simple fractions and simple rates (recipe for 4→6 people; 3 kg costs £12 → 5 kg; scale a shape by 1/2).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5–Y6 'solve problems involving … scaling by simple fractions and problems involving simple rates'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): connects to 4.OA.2 (multiplicative comparison) and 6.RP.1–3 (ratios and unit rates) — this topic is the bridge from whole-number scaling to proportional reasoning.
• Operational details — two related structures: SCALING by a fraction (multiply a quantity by a fraction >1 or <1: enlarge/reduce; e.g. ×6/4 for the recipe, ×1/2 for the shape) and RATES (a per-unit relationship: £12 per 3 kg → £4 per kg → ×5). The powerful general strategy is the UNITARY METHOD — find the value of one unit, then scale — supported by the double number line and ratio table. Children must see scaling as multiplicative (a fraction/rate multiplier), not additive. This is the conceptual launchpad for ratio and proportion (a separate domain) and must stay grounded in known multiplicative-comparison ideas.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): scale a quantity by a simple whole factor and by 1/2 with a double number line. Tier B (age 9–10): solve a rate problem via the unitary method (3 kg=£12 → 1 kg=£4 → 5 kg=£20) and a fraction-scaling recipe problem. Tier C (age 10): choose unitary vs scale-factor efficiently and justify with a ratio table / double number line.
bestPractices: Teach the unitary method — find one unit then scale — as the reliable general strategy, supported by a double number line and ratio table.
Represent rates on a double number line (kg vs £) so the proportional (multiplicative) relationship is visible and both quantities scale together.
Treat scaling as multiplicative (× a fraction/rate), explicitly contrasting with additive change, to prevent the classic 'add the difference' error.
Use both directions — scale up and scale down (×1/2) — and connect fraction-of-quantity skills to scaling.
Ground problems in authentic contexts (recipes, prices, maps/shapes) and check reasonableness.
keyRepresentations: Double number line (two quantities scaling together) — core rate/scaling tool
Ratio table — unit value and scaled values
Bar model — fraction scaling of a quantity
Scale-factor arrow (×6/4, ×1/2) linking original to scaled
commonMisconceptions: Scaling additively — adding the difference in people/kg instead of multiplying by the ratio (recipe for 6 = recipe for 4 + 2 portions of everything, done wrongly).
Not finding the unit value, so unable to scale to a new amount.
Inverting the rate (£12 per 3 kg treated as £3 per kg).
Confusing scaling up with down, or mis-applying ×1/2.
Treating rate problems as unrelated to multiplicative comparison / fractions.

learn.summary: For 9–10 year olds: solve problems involving scaling by simple fractions and simple rates (e.g. a recipe for 4→6 people; 3 kg costs £12 → cost of 5 kg; scale a shape by 1/2). The through-line is the UNITARY METHOD — find the value of one unit, then scale — supported by a double number line, ratio table and bar model. Learners should experience scaling as multiplicative (× a fraction or rate), explicitly contrasted with the common additive 'add the difference' error, across authentic contexts (recipes, prices, maps/shapes). Activities range from a manipulable double-number-line scaler that builds the proportional feel, through a Socratic unit-rate dialogue, a worked annotated exemplar, to checkable practice with targeted distractors.

activities.title: Double-number-line scaler: find one unit, then scale
feedback: When the child finds 1 kg = £4 and reaches £20 for 5 kg, affirm the unitary route: 'you found the cost of one, then multiplied by five'.

If the additive-trap attempt is tried, point out that adding the same number to both quantities (£12 + 2 = £14 for 5 kg) knocks the two lines out of alignment and gives a wrong amount. The rate holds only when each quantity changes by matching amounts (2 kg with £8), which is the same as scaling by the unit rate.
In recipe mode, if a learner adds 200 g for the '2 extra people', show that per-person is 50 g, so 6 people need 300 g, not 400 g.
activities.rationale: Direct manipulation of two locked quantities makes the multiplicative nature of scaling tangible and exposes the unitary method; sliding one quantity and watching the other move proportionally helps learners feel why adding the same amount to both quantities breaks the relationship. The additive-trap comparison is one optional device for making the contrast visible, not a claim that only manipulation can teach this.
sourceClaims: The unitary method, double number line and ratio table support scaling/rate problems; scaling must be treated as multiplicative, not additive.
learnerActions: On two parallel lines locked by a rate (e.g. kilograms against cost in pounds, £), slide to mark 3 kg opposite £12.
Use a 'find 1 unit' action to collapse the lines to 1 kg = £4, then slide on to 5 kg and read off £20.
Switch to a recipe mode: scale ingredients by ×6/4 (e.g. 200 g flour for 4 people → how much for 6?) shown on a bar model.
Switch to a shape mode: halve every dimension (×1/2) and read the new measurements.

Try the 'additive trap' toggle: add the same number to both lines (3 kg + 2 = 5 kg, so £12 + 2 = £14), then compare with the locked-rate result of £20. Notice that adding matching amounts instead (2 kg and its value, £8) keeps the lines aligned and gives £20.
activities.intendedInsight: Scaling and rates are proportional, multiplicative relationships: finding the value of one unit unlocks any target amount, and adding the same difference to both quantities does not preserve the relationship.

activities.title: Unit-rate dialogue: 'what does one cost?'
feedback: If the learner gives the unit value and scales correctly, name the strategy: 'you used the unitary method'.
If the learner answers the additive-objection probe by defending adding 200 g, redirect to per-person value (50 g) and ask them to total for 6.
For the 4→10 stretch, confirm that per-person value scales to any target, unlike hunting for a whole-number factor.
activities.rationale: A Socratic dialogue builds the unitary habit and can pose rich, varied contexts and challenge the additive misconception verbally. It cannot render a manipulable double number line, so it complements rather than replaces the interactive scaler.
sourceClaims: The unitary method, double number line and ratio table support scaling/rate problems; scaling must be treated as multiplicative, not additive.
learnerActions: Respond to a market-trader or chef character posing rate and recipe problems: 'If 3 kg costs £12, what does ONE kilogram cost? So what about five?'
State the unit value aloud or in writing, then state how you scale it to the target amount.
Answer the probe 'Someone said 6 people is 2 more than 4, so add 200 g more — what's wrong with that?' and explain the flaw.
Tackle a stretch case ('a recipe for 4, but you need it for 10') and say whether the unit-value method still works.
activities.intendedInsight: Routing every proportional problem through 'the value of one, then times the target' is a reliable general habit that works even when the scale factor is not a whole number.

activities.title: Worked exemplar: annotated double number line and ratio table
feedback: After revealing each step, restate the move: 'divide by 3 to get one, then multiply by 5'.
Prompt the learner to apply the same two-step reveal to their own new problem rather than only reading the exemplar.
activities.rationale: A worked, tap-to-reveal exemplar is a useful reference for the structure of the method, but a fixed image cannot provide new problems to solve, so it should be paired with independent problem-solving.
sourceClaims: The unitary method, double number line and ratio table support scaling/rate problems; scaling must be treated as multiplicative, not additive.
learnerActions: Study an annotated double number line (kg vs £) and a ratio table with a unit-value column.
Reveal the unitary steps one at a time: 3 kg = £12 → 1 kg = £4 → 5 kg = £20.
Read the ratio table to see the unit column (1 person = 50 g) and how scaled values follow from it.
Use the exemplar as a reference, then solve a new, different rate/scaling problem yourself.
activities.intendedInsight: The unit value is the key column of a ratio table / anchor point of a double number line; scaled values are multiples of it.

activities.title: Checkable practice with additive-error distractors
feedback: For a chosen additive distractor, explain that it adds an amount that does not match the change (e.g. adding 200 g, the amount for 4 people, for only 2 extra people, or adding 2 to the quantity) rather than scaling; show the per-unit route: 50 g per person, so 2 more people need 100 g, giving 300 g.

If division is inverted (e.g. 4 ÷ 200 or 3 kg treated as £3 per kg), prompt labelling units (g per person, £ per kg) to orient the division and check the unit value is reasonable (50 g per person, not 0.02).
activities.rationale: Rate and scaling answers are checkable, so targeted distractors can verify the method and surface the additive and inversion misconceptions. This format is better suited to checking and diagnosing than to first building the proportional feel, so it works best after the interactive and dialogue activities.
learnerActions: Fill in the unitary steps: 3 kg = £12 → 1 kg = □ → 5 kg = □.
Choose the correct recipe-for-6 amount from options that include an additive distractor (e.g. 400 g from 'add 200 g for 2 more people' vs the correct 300 g).
Select the correct multiplier for a scaling problem (e.g. ×6/4 = ×1.5, ×1/2).
Use a slider to set the scaled quantity and check it against the unit value.
activities.intendedInsight: Correct proportional answers come from multiplying the unit value or applying the right fractional multiplier; additive answers are identifiable errors.

constraints: Scaling must be taught as multiplicative (× a fraction or rate), explicitly contrasted with additive 'add the difference' change.
Use both directions — scale up and scale down (×1/2) — and connect fraction-of-quantity skills to scaling.
Include at least one non-integer scale factor (e.g. 4→6, factor 6/4) so learners cannot rely on whole-number multiples; the unit-value route always works.
Ground problems in authentic contexts (recipes, prices, maps/shapes) and check reasonableness of the unit value (e.g. 50 g per person, not 0.02).
This topic is the launchpad for formal ratio and proportion (a separate domain); keep it grounded in known multiplicative-comparison and fraction ideas rather than introducing formal ratio notation.

The worked exemplar and quiz are scaffolds/checks: a fixed image and recognition items cannot by themselves elicit independent solving of new problems, so pair them with activities where the learner constructs the solution.

The 'additive trap' toggle and live sliders are optional devices for making the mechanism concrete; they are illustrative, not mandatory, and manipulation is not asserted to be the only way to learn this.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Self-audit of arithmetic: 200÷4 = 50 g per person, ×6 = 300 g (scale factor 6/4 = 1.5, 200×1.5 = 300) — correct; £12÷3 = £4 per kg, ×5 = £20 — correct. These match the source's correctAnswer.

The source lists an error pattern '200÷4 = 40' as an example of a performance slip; the correct value is 50. It is presented in the source as a learner error, not as a taught fact, so it is not reproduced as correct in any activity.

Two of three cited sources are marked verified:false in the row (CCSS bridge claim and NCETM guidance); the DfE claim is verified:true. No new verification is asserted here. The CCSS bridging claim was not used as a sourceClaim since no activity's rationale depends on it directly.

The DfE curriculum claim is a topic-level claim and was not attached to activities whose rationales turn on the multiplicative/unitary principle (activity 1) or answer-checkability (activity 4); the NCETM claim, which states the teaching principle, is used instead.
The source's artefact-fit note that '3D adds no proportional insight' is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law, and has been omitted rather than asserted as universal.

Activity 4's rationale was softened from a categorical 'verifies rather than builds' to a relative affordance (better suited to checking than to first building the feel) to avoid an unsupported 'quiz only assesses' claim.

probeDeeper: How much flour would ONE person need? How did that help you get to 6?
Someone said '6 people is 2 more than 4, so add 200 g more'. What's wrong with that?
If 3 kg costs £12, what does 1 kg cost — and how do you know?
What if the recipe were for 4 people and you needed it for 10 — would your method still work?
assess.correctAnswer: Flour: 300 g (200 ÷ 4 = 50 g per person, × 6 = 300; or scale factor 6/4 = 1.5, 200 × 1.5). Cost: £20 (£12 ÷ 3 = £4 per kg, × 5 = £20). The teacher watches for a multiplicative route — unit rate or scale factor — not additive 'add 2 more people so add 200 g'.

errorPatterns.pattern: uses additive reasoning instead of multiplicative — '6 is 2 more than 4, so add 200 g' giving 400 g, or 'add £12 again'
errorPatterns.nextMove: set up a ratio table (people | flour) and fill the unit column (1 person = 50 g) so scaling becomes 'per one, then times'; contrast with the wrong additive jump side by side.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child changes the quantity by the DIFFERENCE between the two situations rather than by a ratio

errorPatterns.pattern: finds the unit rate but then multiplies by the wrong quantity, or inverts the division (4 ÷ 200)
errorPatterns.nextMove: label units on every number (g per person) so the division is oriented correctly; check the unit rate is 'reasonable' (50 g per person, not 0.02).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child divides the wrong way (people by grams) or scales by the original count not the target

errorPatterns.pattern: can only scale by whole-number factors — stalls when 6/4 is not a whole multiple of 4
errorPatterns.nextMove: route through the unit value (per one person) which always works, rather than hunting for a whole-number scale factor.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child solves 3→6 (×2) confidently but freezes on 4→6

errorPatterns.pattern: sets up the proportion correctly but slips in the arithmetic (200÷4 = 40)
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach proportion; have the child check the unit rate against the original (50 × 4 = 200?).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: correct method, wrong division/multiplication result

responseLevels.gap: scales additively (adds the difference) or inverts the rate; answer bears no multiplicative relationship to the given values.
responseLevels.full: routes reliably through unit rate or scale factor for both integer and non-integer cases, orients the division by units, and rejects additive scaling with a reason.
responseLevels.partial: solves whole-number-multiple cases (3→6) by scaling but stalls on non-integer factors (4→6), or finds a unit rate inconsistently.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child rate/scaling problems to solve, watching their method: 'A recipe for 4 people needs 200 g of flour — how much for 6 people?' and 'If 3 kg costs £12, how much does 5 kg cost?' Watch whether they find a unit value or a scale factor, or whether they just add on a difference.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The signature error in proportional reasoning is additive: '4→6 people is +2, so +2 of something'. Watching the method (unit rate vs adding a constant) reveals whether the child reasons multiplicatively. The non-integer scale factor (6/4) also catches children who can only scale by whole numbers.

sources.claim: Y5–Y6 pupils solve problems involving scaling by simple fractions and simple rates.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study (KS1–2), Years 5–6 Number — multiplication and division / ratio and proportion

sources.claim: Scaling and rate problems bridge multiplicative comparison (4.OA.2) to ratios and unit rates (6.RP.1–3).
sources.source: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Grades 4 & 6 (4.OA.A.2, 6.RP.A)

sources.claim: The unitary method, double number line and ratio table support scaling/rate problems; scaling must be treated as multiplicative, not additive.
sources.source: NCETM ratio, proportion and multiplicative reasoning guidance

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 6–7 (UK Y2, US Grade 3). Reading, writing and interpreting the ×, ÷ and = symbols in multiplication and division number sentences — the notation that records the concepts (LANGUAGE topic).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2 'calculate mathematical statements for multiplication and division within the multiplication tables and write them using the multiplication (×), division (÷) and equals (=) signs'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.OA.1/3.OA.2 interpret products and quotients; the equals sign as relational is emphasised across CCSS-M (e.g. 3.OA.4 finding the unknown that makes an equation true).
• Operational details: bind each symbol to a meaning and a representation — × = 'groups of' / an array, ÷ = sharing or grouping, = 'is the same value as' (NOT 'the answer comes next'). The relational meaning of = is the load-bearing idea: children must accept 12 = 3×4 and 3×4 = 2×6 as valid. Translate freely between story, picture and symbol sentence.
• Checkpoint: read, write and balance. Tier A (6): write × and = to match an array (3×4=12). Tier B (6–7): write a division sentence for a sharing story and read it aloud correctly. Tier C (7): judge whether sentences like 12 = 3×4 and 10 = 2×5 are true, showing = means 'same value'.
bestPractices: Attach every symbol to its meaning and a representation: × read as 'groups of' shown by an array, ÷ read as 'shared into / grouped into' shown by counters, = spoken as 'is the same value as'.

Directly confront the equals-sign misconception: use a balance model and present sentences with the answer on the LEFT (12 = 3×4) and equalities with no operation on the right (3×4 = 2×6) so = cannot be misread as 'write the answer here'.
Have children translate in all directions — story → array → symbol sentence and back — so the notation is a record of meaning, not a detached ritual.
Read sentences aloud precisely, attending to order for division (12÷3 is 'twelve divided by three', not 'three into twelve' muddled), since ÷ is not commutative.
Contrast × with + explicitly (3×4 is not 3+4) to prevent symbol confusion.
keyRepresentations: Number sentences mapping symbols to arrays/groups
Balance / pan-scale model for the equals sign (relational meaning)
Story ↔ array ↔ symbol translation triples
Symbol reference (×, ÷, = with spoken names and meanings)
commonMisconceptions: Reading = as 'the answer is / write the result here' (operational) rather than 'is the same value as' (relational) — the single most damaging notation error, blocking later algebra.
Rejecting true sentences like 12 = 3×4 or 3×4 = 2×6 because 'the sum isn't on the right'.
Confusing × with + (treating 3×4 as 3+4).
Writing division in the wrong order (since ÷ is not commutative, 12÷3 and 3÷12 are different).
Reading a symbol sentence with no attached meaning — manipulating symbols without knowing what they represent.

learn.summary: For ages 6–7 (UK Year 2, roughly US Grade 1), teach children to read, write and interpret the ×, ÷ and = symbols in multiplication and division number sentences. Bind each symbol to a meaning and a representation: × as 'groups of' shown by an array, ÷ as 'shared/grouped into' shown by counters, and = as 'is the same value as' shown by a level balance. The load-bearing idea is the relational meaning of =: children must accept 12 = 3×4 and 3×4 = 2×6 as valid, so = is never misread as 'write the answer here'. Children should translate freely between story, picture and symbol sentence and read sentences aloud precisely, respecting that ÷ is not commutative.

activities.title: Build-and-balance: linking pictures, symbol sentences and equal value
feedback: If a child writes 3 + 4 for an array of 3 rows of 4, show the repeated equal groups and contrast: 3 × 4 is three groups of four (12), while 3 + 4 is just 3 and 4 together (7).

If a child swaps × and ÷ (reading 3 × 4 as 'three divided by four', or choosing ÷ for the array), anchor each symbol to its action: × builds equal groups into a total, while ÷ breaks a whole up into equal parts; pair each symbol with its picture repeatedly.
If a child can read 3 × 4 = 12 aloud but cannot produce a sentence for a picture, scaffold with 'how many rows? how many in each? so what times what?' to move from picture to words to symbols.

When a child is uneasy that 12 = 3×4 'is backwards', place 12 identical cubes on one pan and 3 groups of 4 of the same cubes on the other (or use a screen balance) and let them see the beam sit level — same value, either way round.
If a child balances 3×4 against 2×6, invite them to count each side (12 and 12) and state that equal value is why = links them.

When 3×4 is set against 3+4 (built from identical cubes) and the beam tips, ask the child to say which side is heavier and by how much (12 cubes against 7, so 5 more), reinforcing that = requires genuine sameness.
activities.rationale: Attaching every symbol to both a spoken meaning and a representation, and using a balance so = is felt as sameness, targets a well-documented and damaging notation error (reading = as 'write the answer'), which the cited sources describe as a barrier to later algebra. A live balance and auto-forming picture make the sameness and the symbol–meaning bond concrete; a linked build-and-record surface and a pan-balance are two optional interaction examples that make the mechanism vivid without being the only way to teach it.
sourceClaims: Y2: calculate mathematical statements for multiplication and division within the tables and write them using the ×, ÷ and = signs.
The equals sign must be taught as relational ('same value as') not operational ('write the answer'); the operational misconception is a well-documented barrier to later algebra.
learnerActions: Make an array (for example 3 rows of 4 counters) and write the multiplication sentence that matches it: 3 × 4 = 12.
Share a set of counters into equal groups (for example 12 counters shared into 3 groups of 4) and write the matching division sentence: 12 ÷ 3 = 4.
Go the other direction too: given a sentence like 2 × 5 = 10, build the array or grouping picture that matches it.

Place expressions on each side of a two-pan balance and check whether it sits level: show 12 as 12 identical cubes on the LEFT pan and 3 × 4 as 3 groups of 4 of the same cubes on the right (or use a screen balance), and check that the beam sits level.
Using the same identical cubes, try 3 × 4 against 2 × 6 (it should balance) and 3 × 4 against 3 + 4 (it should tip), and say in words why each result makes sense.
Say each symbol aloud as you work: × as 'times / groups of', ÷ as 'divided by', = as 'is the same value as'.
activities.intendedInsight: Each symbol records a meaning and a picture, and = means 'the two sides have the same value' — not 'the answer comes next'. A true equation can be written with the product on the left (12 = 3×4) or with an expression on each side (3×4 = 2×6).

activities.title: Symbol reference you build and talk about
feedback: If a child names a symbol but not its meaning, ask them to show the matching picture too, so name, meaning and picture always travel together.
Caption the = picture with 'same value as' and revisit it whenever a child defaults to 'the answer'.
activities.rationale: A concise symbol reference supports a notation topic and keeps spoken names bound to meanings and pictures. On its own it supports recall and self-checking but does not exercise the relational balance or translation, so it works best alongside the build-and-balance activity rather than replacing it.
learnerActions: For each of ×, ÷ and =, record its spoken name, its meaning, and a small picture: × = 'groups of' with an array; ÷ = 'shared into / grouped into' with counters; = 'is the same value as' with a level balance.
Point to each symbol and say its name and meaning aloud before using it in a sentence.
Use the reference to check yourself while writing a sentence for a new picture.
activities.intendedInsight: Notation is a record of meaning: knowing the name, meaning and picture for each symbol lets you read and write sentences deliberately rather than by rote.

activities.title: Read, write and judge sentences aloud
feedback: If a child reads 12 ÷ 3 as 'three into twelve' muddled with order, slow down and separate: the first number is the whole being divided.
If a child rejects 12 = 3 × 4 as 'not allowed', return to the balance idea: both sides have value 12, so = fits.
For a false equation such as 10 = 2 × 4, have the child compute each side (10 and 8) and state that unequal values mean = does not hold.
activities.rationale: True/false judgements on reversed and operation-free equalities are especially diagnostic of the relational-equals idea, and reading aloud with correct order exposes ÷ order errors. Judging truth and producing sentences goes beyond recognition toward independent reading and writing.
sourceClaims: The equals sign must be taught as relational ('same value as') not operational ('write the answer'); the operational misconception is a well-documented barrier to later algebra.
3.OA.1/3.OA.2 interpret products and quotients; CCSS-M emphasises the equals sign as relational (the unknown that makes an equation true, 3.OA.4).
learnerActions: Read 3 × 4 = 12 aloud as 'three times four equals twelve' and 12 ÷ 3 = 4 as 'twelve divided by three equals four'.
Write a division sentence for a sharing story and read it back correctly, keeping the order right: 12 ÷ 3, not 3 ÷ 12.
Judge whether sentences are true: is 12 = 3 × 4 true? is 10 = 2 × 5 true? is 3 × 4 = 2 × 6 true? Explain each answer using 'same value'.
Fill in a missing symbol in a sentence (for example 3 __ 4 = 12) and justify the choice.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading order matters for ÷ because it is not commutative, and deciding whether an equation is true tests whether = is understood as 'same value'.

activities.title: Convince the doubter
feedback: Prompt the child to back up their justification with a count of each side (both are 12) or a balance check rather than just asserting it.
If the child cannot explain, return to building the two sides and comparing their values.
activities.rationale: Having to justify a true equation against a mistaken claim gives mild Socratic value and surfaces the child's reasoning. This is a supplement to, not a substitute for, the hands-on balance work where the sameness is directly experienced.
sourceClaims: The equals sign must be taught as relational ('same value as') not operational ('write the answer'); the operational misconception is a well-documented barrier to later algebra.
learnerActions: Respond to a character who insists '3 × 4 = 2 × 6 can't be right' and explain, using value or a balance, why it is correct.
Respond to a character who reads = as 'the answer goes next' and show them 12 = 3 × 4 to correct the idea.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to justify why an unusual-looking equation is true cements the relational meaning of = more firmly than just accepting it.

constraints: The relational meaning of = ('is the same value as') is the load-bearing idea; never let = be presented or read as 'the answer comes next'. Deliberately include equations with the product on the left (12 = 3×4) and with an expression on each side (3×4 = 2×6).
Keep division order explicit: ÷ is not commutative, so 12 ÷ 3 and 3 ÷ 12 are different; the first number is the whole being divided.
Explicitly contrast × with + (3 × 4 is three groups of four = 12, not 3 + 4 = 7) to prevent symbol confusion.
A symbol-reference display supports recall and self-checking but does not exercise the balance or translation; use it alongside the build-and-balance work, not instead of it.
True/false and fill-in-symbol items check reading and judging, but children must also PRODUCE a sentence for a picture; recognition-only tasks do not show independent construction.

A flat/planar treatment suits this abstract notation; no claim is made that any one medium is required — paper, counters and a screen model can each serve. A physical pan balance and a screen balance offer different experiences of the same sameness idea.

Interaction examples such as auto-forming pictures, typing a sentence to build a picture, dragging expressions onto pans, and a live tipping beam are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory features.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three cited sources are marked unverified in the source row (the CCSS-M Grade 3 claim and the NCETM/relational-equals claim). The relational-equals teaching principle is widely discussed in mathematics education (e.g. Carpenter, Franke & Levi), but comparative efficacy or necessity of any specific activity or medium is not established by these sources.

The original research asserted '3D adds no value', framed the balance tool as uniquely able to fix the relational-equals misconception, and called the operational-equals error 'the single most damaging notation error'; these comparative/necessity/superlative claims are not established by the cited sources and have been softened to scoped proposals and the source-supported 'barrier to later algebra'.
Restored two source error-pattern responses that an earlier draft had dropped: the ×/÷ swap reteach and the 'can read but not generate' scaffold are in the build-and-balance feedback.

Self-audit of arithmetic in examples: 3 × 4 = 12, 2 × 6 = 12, 2 × 5 = 10, 12 ÷ 3 = 4 all check out; 3 + 4 = 7 (distinct from 3 × 4). The false example 10 = 2 × 4 used in feedback evaluates to 8 ≠ 10, correctly illustrating a false equation.

probeDeeper: Which picture goes with a ÷ sentence? Why?
Read this: 12 = 3 × 4 — is that allowed?
Say a 'times' sentence for 2 rows of 5.
What does the = sign tell you?
assess.correctAnswer: For the array: 'three times four equals twelve' (3 × 4 = 12). For the sharing: 'twelve divided by three equals four' (12 ÷ 3 = 4). Reads × as 'times/multiplied by', ÷ as 'divided by', and = as 'equals / is the same as'.

errorPatterns.pattern: swaps × and ÷ — reads or writes one where the other is meant; the two symbols aren't distinguished
errorPatterns.nextMove: anchor each symbol to its action — × builds equal groups into a total, ÷ breaks the whole up — pairing symbol with picture repeatedly
errorPatterns.revealedBy: reads 3 × 4 as 'three divided by four', or picks ÷ for the array

errorPatterns.pattern: reads = only as 'makes the answer' — uneasy with sentences like 12 = 3 × 4 that aren't written answer-on-the-right
errorPatterns.nextMove: read = as 'is the same as / balances' and show true equations written both ways round
errorPatterns.revealedBy: rejects or mis-reads an equation not in 'sum = answer' form

errorPatterns.pattern: can read but not generate — reads 3 × 4 = 12 aloud but can't produce a sentence to match the picture
errorPatterns.nextMove: scaffold 'how many rows? how many in each? so…' to move from picture to words to symbols
errorPatterns.revealedBy: fluent reading, but stuck when asked to say/write a sentence for the array or sharing picture

responseLevels.gap: Swaps × and ÷, or reads = only as 'the answer is'; cannot match a symbol sentence to a picture.
responseLevels.full: Reads ×, ÷, = accurately, generates a correct number sentence for both a grouping and a sharing picture, and treats = as 'is the same as'.
responseLevels.partial: Reads the standard sentences correctly but hesitates to generate one for a picture, or is unsettled by equations not written answer-on-the-right.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Look at this array (3 rows of 4) and this picture of 12 sweets shared into 3 groups of 4. Say out loud a number sentence that goes with each picture, using the words 'times', 'divided by', and 'equals'. Then read these back to me: 3 × 4 = 12 and 12 ÷ 3 = 4.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Because the child must PRODUCE a sentence for a picture and READ symbols aloud, the task shows whether the symbols carry meaning. A child who has it maps × to the grouping picture and ÷ to the sharing picture and reads both fluently. A child without it swaps × and ÷, reads = only as 'makes the answer', or can read the symbols but cannot generate a sentence for the picture.

sources.claim: Y2: calculate mathematical statements for multiplication and division within the tables and write them using the ×, ÷ and = signs.
