pedagogy.summary: At age 12-14 pupils learn the classical ruler-and-compass constructions — perpendicular bisector of a segment, perpendicular to a line from/at a point, and angle bisector — using ONLY compasses and a straight edge, with no measuring of lengths or angles. The essential shift is from DRAWING (find a midpoint with a ruler, judge a right angle by eye or protractor) to CONSTRUCTING (produce the result from geometric properties). The unifying property is the rhombus: equal-radius arcs from two points create four equal lengths, so the figure is a rhombus, whose diagonals perpendicularly bisect each other and bisect their angles. Taught this way, every construction is a deduction, and the commonest error — changing the compass radius between the two endpoints — is instantly diagnosable: unequal radii give a KITE (diagonals perpendicular but NOT bisecting), so the line is perpendicular but misses the midpoint. Because compasses are usually new at KS3, motor coordination is a real, separable hurdle; developing the concept first with dynamic geometry lets pupils reason about 'perfect' circles before wrestling the physical tool.
bestPractices: Teach the draw-vs-construct distinction explicitly: a construction uses geometric properties (equidistance), not measurement; require pupils to leave their construction arcs as evidence of method
Anchor every construction in the rhombus/isosceles-triangle property (equal radii → rhombus → diagonals perpendicularly bisect and bisect the angle), so steps are deductions, not a memorised routine
Make the equal-radius rule meaningful via the kite counter-case: unequal arcs build a kite whose diagonals are perpendicular but do not bisect, so the midpoint is missed
Ensure the compass opening exceeds half the segment so the arcs intersect above and below; discuss why a smaller radius fails and a huge one is just wasteful

Present non-standard (diagonal, rotated) segments and angles, not only horizontal/vertical prototypes, and give time to build compass dexterity — ideally after establishing the idea with dynamic geometry
keyRepresentations: Two equal-radius circles/arcs from the segment ends and the rhombus they define
The rhombus-around-a-diagonal image (segment as one diagonal; the construction produces the other)
Kite counter-example (unequal radii) showing perpendicular-but-not-bisecting diagonals
Isosceles triangle whose altitude bisects the base at right angles and bisects the apex angle
Dynamic-geometry compass/straightedge for concept-before-dexterity
commonMisconceptions: Changing the compass radius between the two endpoints, constructing a kite instead of a rhombus, so the line is perpendicular but does not pass through the midpoint
Drawing rather than constructing — using a ruler to find the midpoint and a protractor/eye for the right angle — and leaving no construction marks
Opening the compasses to less than half the segment, so the arcs never intersect
Memorising the steps as an isolated routine with no link to the properties of circles and rhombuses
Treating the construction as valid only for horizontal/vertical segments (prototype-orientation bias)

learn.summary: Pupils aged 12–14 construct a perpendicular bisector, a perpendicular to a line from a point off it or at a point on it, and an angle bisector using compasses and an unmarked straight edge. Explain the equal-distance and congruent-triangle properties, leaving arcs visible rather than finding positions by measurement. Equal-radius circles centred at segment endpoints yield a perpendicular bisector; unequal radii can still give a perpendicular common chord, but it misses the segment midpoint. Optional dynamic geometry can separate reasoning from tool dexterity; physical compass practice remains part of the proposed tasks. Verification by measurement may check accuracy afterwards, but it does not justify the construction.

activities.title: Construct the perpendicular bisector with compasses and straight edge
feedback: If the line does not cross PQ at its midpoint, check whether the two sets of arcs have equal radii: unequal radii make a KITE (the line is perpendicular to PQ but does not bisect it), equal radii make a rhombus (the line is perpendicular to PQ AND bisects it).

If equal-radius arcs do not cross at two points, check the opening: below half PQ they do not meet; at exactly half they touch only at the midpoint. Use an opening greater than half PQ and allow enough space on the page.

If there are no arcs on the page and the midpoint was found with a ruler or the angle judged by eye, that is drawing, not constructing: redo it so every point of the line is equidistant from P and Q, shown by equal arcs.
Keeping the compass width unchanged between P and Q is the whole point — it is what forces the rhombus.
activities.rationale: Constructing is a doing-and-reasoning skill: pupils must physically execute equal-radius arcs and justify them from the rhombus/equidistance property. A finished static picture cannot be manipulated and does not require the pupil to perform the arcs or articulate the reasoning, so it serves at most as a labelled reference for the rhombus property. Leaving arcs visible makes the method inspectable and distinguishes construction from measurement.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory: pupils 'use the standard ruler and compass constructions (perpendicular bisector of a line segment, constructing a perpendicular to a given line from/at a given point, bisecting a given angle); recognise and use the perpendicular distance from a point to a line as the shortest distance to the line'.

A construction uses geometric properties, not measurement; changing the compass radius between endpoints builds a KITE not a rhombus, and a kite's diagonals are perpendicular but do not bisect, so no perpendicular bisector results (the 'Tinashe' example); the radius must exceed half the segment for the arcs to intersect; constructions should be linked to circle/rhombus properties rather than memorised, presented in non-standard orientations, and compass dexterity is a new KS3 hurdle (aim within ±2 mm/±2°).
learnerActions: Take a line segment PQ drawn diagonally (not horizontal or vertical), a pair of compasses and a straight edge — no ruler measuring and no protractor.
Open the compasses to MORE than half of PQ; discuss why an opening of half or less means the arcs only touch or never meet, and why an enormous opening just wastes space.
Place the compass point on P and sweep an arc above and below the segment; WITHOUT changing the radius, place the point on Q and sweep again so the arcs cross at two points.
Rule the straight line through the two crossing points, leaving all construction arcs visible as evidence of method.
Explain why the line passes through the midpoint at 90°: the four equal radii form a rhombus, whose diagonals perpendicularly bisect each other.
Repeat on segments at several different orientations, not only horizontal/vertical ones.
activities.intendedInsight: Every point on the perpendicular bisector is equidistant from P and Q. Equal-radius arcs locate two such points, and the straight line through them is the perpendicular bisector; visible arcs make the method inspectable, though arcs alone do not prove they were placed correctly.

activities.title: Bisect an angle using the same equal-arc idea
feedback: If the line does not appear to split the angle equally, check that the two inner arcs were drawn with the same radius from each arm-crossing point.

Leave your arcs visible — they show you constructed the bisector from equal lengths rather than measuring halves with a protractor. (The congruent halves follow from the equal arcs, so no measuring is needed to justify it.)
activities.rationale: Equal lengths and congruent triangles provide the justification for the angle bisector. After constructing, measuring both angles can be an optional check of drawing accuracy; it is not the construction method or a proof. This is a proposed property-based activity, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory: pupils 'use the standard ruler and compass constructions (perpendicular bisector of a line segment, constructing a perpendicular to a given line from/at a given point, bisecting a given angle); recognise and use the perpendicular distance from a point to a line as the shortest distance to the line'.

A construction uses geometric properties, not measurement; changing the compass radius between endpoints builds a KITE not a rhombus, and a kite's diagonals are perpendicular but do not bisect, so no perpendicular bisector results (the 'Tinashe' example); the radius must exceed half the segment for the arcs to intersect; constructions should be linked to circle/rhombus properties rather than memorised, presented in non-standard orientations, and compass dexterity is a new KS3 hurdle (aim within ±2 mm/±2°).
learnerActions: Take a marked angle (try one at a non-standard orientation), compasses and a straight edge.
Place the compass point at the vertex and sweep an arc that crosses both arms of the angle at two points.
WITHOUT changing the radius, place the point on each of those two crossing points in turn and sweep equal arcs that meet inside the angle.
Rule the line from the vertex through that meeting point, leaving the arcs visible.
Explain how this reuses the equal-radius property: equal lengths from the vertex and equal arcs from the arm-crossings force the two halves to be congruent, so the line bisects the angle.
activities.intendedInsight: The same equidistance principle that bisects a segment also bisects an angle — one property, reused, rather than a second memorised routine.

activities.title: See the rhombus break into a kite with a dynamic compass (concept-before-dexterity scaffold)
feedback: When the figure flips to KITE, note exactly where the line crosses PQ relative to the midpoint — that gap is why unequal radii fail.
If you can state why the rhombus's crossing line bisects PQ but the kite's does not, you are reasoning from the property; move on to building the same construction by hand.
activities.rationale: A dynamic-geometry tool can separate the concept (equidistance locus, rhombus-vs-kite) from manual dexterity, and may let pupils reason about ideal 'perfect' circles before coping with the practical difficulties of real compasses, which some pupils may still find hard to control. The live slider and label flip are intended to make the failure mode concrete. This is a proposed scaffold: it does not develop the manual construction skill, which must be practised separately on paper, and its effectiveness over other media is untested.
sourceClaims: A construction uses geometric properties, not measurement; changing the compass radius between endpoints builds a KITE not a rhombus, and a kite's diagonals are perpendicular but do not bisect, so no perpendicular bisector results (the 'Tinashe' example); the radius must exceed half the segment for the arcs to intersect; constructions should be linked to circle/rhombus properties rather than memorised, presented in non-standard orientations, and compass dexterity is a new KS3 hurdle (aim within ±2 mm/±2°).
learnerActions: Use an on-screen compass whose radius locks once set: plant it on P and sweep an arc, then on Q and sweep an equal arc so the two equal circles cross at two points.
Rule the line through the crossings and observe the highlighted locus showing every point on it is equidistant from P and Q.

Now drag a slider that shrinks the second circle's radius (keeping it large enough that the two circles still cross); watch the crossing points drift, the line slide sideways while staying perpendicular to PQ, and the label flip from RHOMBUS to KITE — the line visibly misses the midpoint.
Articulate in your own words why 'keep the compass fixed' is a consequence of the rhombus property, not an arbitrary rule.
Transfer to real compasses and paper once the concept is secure.
activities.intendedInsight: When two circles cross, their common chord is perpendicular to the line through their centres. With equal radii, that chord also bisects PQ; with unequal radii it does not. Keep both circles crossing during the comparison, and explain the equal-radius rule rather than memorising it.

activities.title: Diagnose: construction or drawing? Which radius? Which shape failed?
feedback: For the 8 cm segment, any opening at or below 4 cm leaves arcs that cannot cross on both sides (at exactly 4 cm they only touch at the midpoint); the opening must exceed half the length.
The diagram with no arcs cannot be shown to be a construction — without equal arcs there is no evidence the equidistance property was used.
Unequal arcs give a kite: perpendicular, yes, but the line through the crossings does not bisect PQ (only PQ bisects it), so the line misses the midpoint.
activities.rationale: Questions of this kind assess the reasoning behind the construction and surface the specific misconceptions (radius too small, kite error, drawing vs constructing). They complement but cannot replace the performance task, since recognising a correct diagram is not the same as producing one.
sourceClaims: A construction uses geometric properties, not measurement; changing the compass radius between endpoints builds a KITE not a rhombus, and a kite's diagonals are perpendicular but do not bisect, so no perpendicular bisector results (the 'Tinashe' example); the radius must exceed half the segment for the arcs to intersect; constructions should be linked to circle/rhombus properties rather than memorised, presented in non-standard orientations, and compass dexterity is a new KS3 hurdle (aim within ±2 mm/±2°).
learnerActions: For an 8 cm segment, choose which compass opening will work for the perpendicular bisector (more than 4 cm) and say why openings of 4 cm or less fail.

Compare a diagram with visible equal-radius construction arcs with a bare line. Explain which supplies evidence of the method and which does not; a bare line alone does not reveal whether someone constructed it and erased the arcs or drew it by measurement.

Given a diagram where the line is perpendicular to PQ but misses the midpoint, name the shape that was built (a kite) and explain why the line through the arc crossings does not bisect PQ, even though PQ bisects that line.

Answer: Why must the compass stay the same width from both P and Q, and what shape are you really making? How does the same equal-arc idea bisect an angle? Why would a ruler-and-protractor method not count as a construction?
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to diagnose the radius condition, the kite failure, and construction-vs-drawing demonstrates understanding of the underlying properties — though recognising a correct diagram does not substitute for executing the construction by hand.

activities.title: Construct a perpendicular from a point off a line
feedback: If the circle centred at A only touches l or misses it, increase the radius until it meets l twice. A single touch does not provide distinct B and C for this construction.
If an arc crossing coincides with A, use the other crossing, or adjust the common radius so D is distinct from A; two distinct points are needed to draw AD.
If the perpendicular does not pass through A, return to the given point and the equidistance argument. A perpendicular somewhere else on the line does not meet this task.
activities.rationale: This editorially added construction covers the explicit curriculum objective missing from the saved activities. It reuses the perpendicular-bisector equidistance reasoning; the specific procedure is a proposed task rather than an empirically tested design.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory: pupils 'use the standard ruler and compass constructions (perpendicular bisector of a line segment, constructing a perpendicular to a given line from/at a given point, bisecting a given angle); recognise and use the perpendicular distance from a point to a line as the shortest distance to the line'.
learnerActions: Draw a line l and a point A not on it. With centre A, choose a compass radius large enough for a circle to cross l at two distinct points B and C; extend l with the straight edge if needed.
Using equal radii from B and C, each greater than half BC, draw crossing arcs to locate a point D off l and distinct from A. Draw the straight line through A and D, keeping the arcs visible.
Explain why AB = AC and DB = DC place both A and D on the perpendicular bisector of BC. Since B and C lie on l, AD is perpendicular to l. Mark the foot H where AD meets l.
Explain that AH is the shortest distance from A to l. Repeat with a rotated line and A on the other side.
activities.intendedInsight: A point equidistant from B and C lies on their perpendicular bisector. Finding a second distinct equidistant point locates a perpendicular through the given off-line point without measuring a right angle.

activities.title: Construct a perpendicular at a point on a line
feedback: If B and C are not equally far from A, redraw them using the same circle centred at A; estimating their positions by eye does not establish that A is the midpoint.
If the arcs from B and C fail to cross away from l, increase their common radius beyond half BC.
A measured 90° angle can be an accuracy check, but explain the equal distances to justify why the construction works.
activities.rationale: This editorial addition covers the at-a-point case of the named objective and connects it to the already taught perpendicular bisector. It does not claim measured educational effectiveness.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory: pupils 'use the standard ruler and compass constructions (perpendicular bisector of a line segment, constructing a perpendicular to a given line from/at a given point, bisecting a given angle); recognise and use the perpendicular distance from a point to a line as the shortest distance to the line'.
learnerActions: Draw a line l with a given point A on it. Draw a circle centred at A to mark B and C on l, on opposite sides of A, so AB = AC.
Without changing the compass opening between B and C, draw equal-radius arcs from them, using a radius greater than half BC, to meet at D off l.
Rule AD and leave the arcs visible. Explain that A is the midpoint of BC and both A and D are equidistant from B and C, so AD is the perpendicular bisector of BC and is perpendicular to l at A.

Try a sloping line and then explain how this task differs from constructing a perpendicular through a point off the line. After the construction, a protractor can check practical accuracy without replacing the property-based justification.
activities.intendedInsight: The given point on the line can be made the midpoint of a constructed segment BC, so its perpendicular bisector passes through that point.

constraints: Use compasses and an unmarked straight edge to locate the required points and lines from geometric properties, rather than by measuring. A ruler or protractor may check practical accuracy afterwards; such checks do not prove or replace the construction.
Require pupils to leave their construction arcs visible as evidence that the equidistance/rhombus property, not measurement, produced the result.
Keep the compass width unchanged between the two endpoints, and open it to more than half the segment so the arcs intersect above and below.
Present segments and angles at non-standard (diagonal, rotated) orientations, not only horizontal/vertical prototypes.

A dynamic-geometry compass is a concept-building scaffold: it may help pupils reason about equidistance and the rhombus-vs-kite distinction but does not develop the manual dexterity, which must be practised with real compasses afterwards.
Recognition/multiple-choice items assess the reasoning only; they do not evidence the pupil actually executing the construction, which is the performance target.

Treat tolerances such as ±2 mm / ±2° as accuracy targets for the manual skill, distinguishing a dexterity lapse (correct method, slipped arcs) from a conceptual error (unequal radii, measuring instead of constructing).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated a static picture and 3D as 'poor' and asserted '3D adds nothing' and that a static picture 'cannot build' the reasoning. These universal comparative claims are replaced here with narrow affordances (a fixed image cannot be manipulated and does not elicit the pupil executing arcs; recognition items do not elicit independent construction). These constructions are planar, so a 3D medium is simply not needed for the 2D locus reasoning; a labelled reference image can still support recall of the rhombus property.

Geometry self-audit: the rhombus/kite reasoning is internally consistent — equal radii from both endpoints give four equal sides (a rhombus) whose diagonals perpendicularly bisect; unequal radii give a kite (axis of symmetry PQ) with perpendicular diagonals, where PQ bisects the constructed line but the constructed line does NOT bisect PQ, so it misses the segment's midpoint. No arithmetic or force/motion content to correct. The 8 cm example (opening must exceed 4 cm, and exactly 4 cm only touches at the midpoint) is correct.

Paper diagrams are flat representations of ideal plane constructions; no solid-shape idealisation issue arises here, but treat drawn arcs as physical approximations of ideal circles when discussing tolerance.

The saved activities omitted perpendiculars from or at a given point even though the objective names them. Two conservative editorial activities now cover these cases using the perpendicular-bisector equidistance property. Original pedagogy and assessment remain unchanged.

The original evidence suggests measuring the two angle halves. This is compatible with a post-construction accuracy check; the construction itself and its justification use equal lengths and congruent triangles, not measurement.

Useful factual-audit repairs retain the common-chord perpendicular direction, correct the kite diagonal scope, and keep circles intersecting in the slider activity. Source claims remain verbatim even where their compressed kite wording needs the qualification given in the activities. No fresh source verification was performed.

probeDeeper: Why must the compass stay open to the same width from both P and Q — what shape are you really making?
If someone changed the compass width and got a line perpendicular to PQ that isn't the bisector, what shape did they make, and why doesn't it bisect?
Could you do this with a ruler and protractor instead? Why would that not count as a construction?
How does the same equal-arc idea let you bisect an ANGLE?
assess.correctAnswer: Opens the compasses to more than half PQ and, WITHOUT changing the radius, draws equal arcs from P and from Q that intersect above and below, then rules the line through the two intersections — leaving the arcs visible; the line passes through the midpoint at 90° (within about ±2 mm / ±2°). For the angle, draws an arc from the vertex crossing both arms, then equal arcs from those two points, and rules the vertex-to-intersection line. Relies on the equal-radius (rhombus) property, not measurement.

errorPatterns.pattern: Changes the compass radius between the two endpoints, constructing a kite instead of a rhombus — so the line is perpendicular to PQ but does not pass through the midpoint (does not bisect)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reground on the rhombus property — four equal radii make a rhombus whose diagonals bisect; a kite's diagonals are perpendicular but do not bisect — and insist the compass width is unchanged between endpoints
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The arcs from P and from Q have visibly different radii, and the resulting line does not cross PQ at its midpoint

errorPatterns.pattern: Draws rather than constructs — uses a ruler to find the midpoint and a protractor or eye for the right angle — and leaves no construction arcs
errorPatterns.nextMove: Teach the draw-vs-construct distinction: a construction produces the result from geometric properties (equidistance), not measurement; require visible construction marks
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Measures PQ to mark its midpoint, judges 90° by eye/protractor, and the page shows a bare line with no arcs

errorPatterns.pattern: Opens the compasses to less than half the segment, so the arcs from P and Q never intersect
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish that the radius must exceed half the segment for the arcs to intersect on both sides; connect to the equidistant-locus reason
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The arcs fail to meet above and/or below the segment, leaving no crossing points to rule through

errorPatterns.pattern: Compass dexterity lapse — the method is right but the arcs slip or are placed imprecisely, so the construction falls outside tolerance
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach: give practice time with the equipment (this is usually new at KS3) and consider establishing the concept first with dynamic geometry
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Equal radii and visible arcs, but the point/needle slipped and the result is off by more than ±2 mm / ±2°

responseLevels.gap: Cannot produce the construction from properties — measures the midpoint, judges the angle by eye, or changes the radius so it fails — with no sense of why it should work.
responseLevels.full: Constructs the perpendicular bisector and angle bisector from the equidistance/rhombus property — radius equal and more than half, arcs left visible, at any orientation — and explains why equal radii force a rhombus whose diagonals perpendicularly bisect.
responseLevels.partial: Executes the memorised steps and often gets a correct-looking bisector, but cannot explain why the equal radii are needed or link it to the rhombus/equidistance property — slips to a kite or to measuring when the orientation is unfamiliar.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a pair of compasses, a straight edge, and a line segment PQ drawn diagonally (not horizontal), plus a marked angle. Say: 'Construct the perpendicular bisector of PQ using only the compasses and straight edge — no ruler measuring and no protractor. Then construct the bisector of this angle.' Watch whether they keep the compass radius equal from both endpoints, open it to more than half PQ, leave their construction arcs, and work from properties rather than measuring.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The finished construction is the evidence: equal-radius arcs and a line through the midpoint show the child used the rhombus/equidistance property; unequal arcs (a kite whose line misses the midpoint), or a ruler-found midpoint with an eyeballed right angle and no arcs, show drawing rather than constructing. A correct property-based construction cannot be produced by measuring.

pedagogy.summary: Calculating simple probability is the procedural skill of applying P(event) = favourable outcomes / total outcomes to equally-likely situations and giving the answer as a fraction in simplest form. The work is fluent, accurate execution across contexts (dice, bags, spinners): counting the favourable outcomes, counting the TOTAL (which includes the favourable ones), forming the fraction, checking the outcomes are equally likely, and simplifying.
bestPractices: Rehearse the same three-step routine across varied contexts — count favourable, count total, write and simplify — so it transfers beyond dice
Make explicit that the total is the WHOLE set of outcomes (favourable included), heading off the part-part error
Require a check that outcomes are equally likely BEFORE applying the formula
Connect 'more favourable outcomes → larger probability' by varying a bag's composition and watching the fraction grow
Always express in simplest form and confirm the simplified fraction names the same point on the 0-to-1 scale
keyRepresentations: P(event) = favourable/total written under the situation
Bags, dice, spinners with countable equally-likely outcomes
Simplified-fraction equivalence (2/8 = 1/4) on the 0-to-1 scale
Part-whole diagram of the outcome set
commonMisconceptions: Writing favourable-to-unfavourable (part-part) instead of favourable-over-total — e.g. 3/7 rather than 3/10 for 3 blue among 10
Applying the formula to situations whose outcomes are not equally likely (an uneven spinner, a weighted die)
Failing to simplify, or simplifying incorrectly
Miscounting the total — forgetting to include the favourable outcomes in the denominator

learn.summary: Learners build fluency with P(event) = favourable outcomes / total outcomes for equally-likely situations, giving answers as fractions in simplest form. The core routine is: check the outcomes are equally likely, count favourable outcomes, count the TOTAL (which includes the favourable ones), form the fraction, and simplify. Practice should span varied contexts (dice, bags, spinners) and target the part-part error (favourable-to-unfavourable) and the misapplication of the formula to unequal outcomes.

activities.title: Varied probability ladder with simplest form
feedback: If a learner writes 3/7 for the bag, recount the whole set aloud including the favourable outcomes: everything that could be drawn is 10, so 10 goes on the bottom, giving 3/10.

If a learner applies the formula to an uneven spinner, prompt the equally-likely check first: when sections are different sizes the colour counts are not counts of equally-likely outcomes, so the simple formula does not apply.

If a learner leaves 2/8 unsimplified or reduces it wrongly, scaffold the simplifying step and confirm 1/4 sits at the same point on the 0-to-1 scale \u2014 simplifying does not change the actual chance.
If a learner combines numbers arbitrarily with no favourable-over-total structure, return to counting favourable, then total, then writing the fraction.
activities.rationale: The objective is fluent, accurate execution of favourable/total across contexts with simplest-form answers. Varied contexts support transfer beyond dice, and items built from the exact errors (part-part, unsimplified, formula on an uneven spinner) make the common mistakes surface and get corrected.
sourceClaims: The probability of an equally-likely event is favourable outcomes over total outcomes, written and simplified as a fraction; e.g. P(blue) for 3 blue among a total of counters is favourable/total.

Children tend to use additive/part-part comparisons and give the raw frequencies of outcomes rather than the part-whole proportion, so favourable-over-total must be taught explicitly against the part-part error.
learnerActions: Work a short series of problems, each a probability to be formed and then simplified: (a) a bag of 3 blue and 7 red marbles \u2014 find P(blue); (b) a fair six-sided die \u2014 find P(rolling a 4); (c) a spinner with 8 equal sections, 2 of them gold \u2014 find P(gold).
For each item, first confirm the outcomes are equally likely, then count the favourable outcomes, then count the WHOLE set of possible outcomes (including the favourable ones) for the denominator.
Write each probability as a fraction and simplify where possible (e.g. 2/8 \u2192 1/4).
On the bag item, if you write 3/7, stop and recount: the denominator is all 10 marbles, including the 3 blue ones, so the answer is 3/10.
Encounter at least one unequal-outcome situation (e.g. an uneven spinner with different-sized sections) and decide whether the simple formula applies before using it.
activities.intendedInsight: The denominator is the whole set of equally-likely outcomes, favourable included \u2014 so P(blue) among 3 blue and 7 red is 3/10, not 3/7. The simple favourable/total formula only applies when outcomes are equally likely, and simplifying (2/8 = 1/4) names the same point on the 0-to-1 scale.

activities.title: Editable bag: watch the fraction form and simplify
feedback: If a learner expects only the numerator to matter, vary the non-favourable counts and show that the denominator (whole set) and the scale marker both respond \u2014 e.g. adding red marbles enlarges the total, so P(blue) falls (as long as the bag has at least one blue; with no blue it stays 0).
Confirm that the simplified fraction lands on the same point of the 0-to-1 line as the unsimplified one \u2014 the chance is unchanged.
activities.rationale: A live model that forms favourable/total as the child edits the bag, shows simplification, and marks the scale can reinforce WHY the denominator is the whole set and how composition drives the value. This may support conceptual understanding alongside the procedural fluency. The interactive updating (live fraction, scale marker) is an optional illustrative mechanism, not required equipment.
sourceClaims: The probability of an equally-likely event is favourable outcomes over total outcomes, written and simplified as a fraction; e.g. P(blue) for 3 blue among a total of counters is favourable/total.
learnerActions: Edit the composition of a bag (e.g. add or remove blue and red counters) and read the probability fraction as it forms.
Identify the WHOLE set as the denominator each time the bag changes, confirming favourable counters are part of that total.
Watch the simplified form of the fraction and a marker on a 0-to-1 line move as the composition changes.
Predict: 'If I add 5 more red marbles, which number in the fraction changes, and does P(blue) go up or down?' then check against the live display.
activities.intendedInsight: More favourable outcomes relative to the whole set raise the probability; the denominator is always the whole outcome set. Seeing the fraction and its position on the scale update as the bag changes connects composition to the value of the probability.

activities.title: Worked example and Socratic 'out of how many?' check
feedback: If a learner gives odds (part-part, e.g. 3 to 7), re-pose 'and out of how many altogether?' until they name 10 as the whole set.
Confirm the worked fraction is in simplest form before moving on.
activities.rationale: A worked example plus targeted questioning models the routine and can surface the part-part misconception through explanation. This may build understanding but, on its own, does not supply the repeated varied practice that fluency needs \u2014 pair it with the practice ladder.
sourceClaims: Children tend to use additive/part-part comparisons and give the raw frequencies of outcomes rather than the part-whole proportion, so favourable-over-total must be taught explicitly against the part-part error.
learnerActions: Study a worked die or bag example: identify the favourable outcomes, then the whole set, then reveal the simplified fraction.
When asked 'and out of how many altogether?', state the full count of possible outcomes, not just the non-favourable ones.
Explain in your own words why the total includes the favourable outcomes.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the total as the whole set (favourable included) catches the part-part slip before it becomes a habit and makes the structure of the formula explicit.

constraints: Require an equally-likely check BEFORE applying favourable/total; the simple formula does not apply to uneven spinners, weighted dice, or other unequal-outcome situations.
Make explicit that the total is the WHOLE set of outcomes, with favourable outcomes included \u2014 this heads off the part-part (favourable-to-unfavourable) error.
Always express answers in simplest form and confirm the simplified fraction names the same point on the 0-to-1 scale.
A worked example with tap-to-reveal counts models the routine but cannot by itself provide the repeated, varied practice fluency requires; use it as an introduction alongside practice.

A single final answer does not reveal whether the learner counted the whole set, checked equal-likelihood, or simplified; favour formats that require constructing and simplifying the fraction across varied contexts.
The editable-bag live fraction, simplification display, and 0-to-1 scale marker are optional illustrative supports, not mandatory mechanisms or specific products.

Self-audit of worked values: P(blue) with 3 blue of 10 total = 3/10; P(4) on a fair six-sided die = 1/6; P(gold) with 2 of 8 equal sections = 2/8 = 1/4. These are internally consistent across the source fields.
The part-part value 3/7 (3 blue to 7 red) is intentionally retained only as an error to be corrected, never presented as a valid answer.

Source claims support the favourable/total principle and the need to teach against the part-part error; they do not establish comparative efficacy of any particular activity format (quiz vs interactive vs dialogue). Any 'only a quiz drills this' or '3D adds nothing' framing has been reduced to scoped statements about observable affordances.

The legacy pedagogy summary listed the equally-likely check after forming the fraction, while its best-practice guidance placed the check before applying the formula; the corrected routine places the check first, consistent with the stated best practice.

probeDeeper: In 3/10, where does the 10 come from — is blue part of it?
You wrote P(gold) = 2/8. Can you write that more simply? Does simplifying change the actual chance?
If I added 5 more red marbles, which number in your fraction changes, and does P(blue) go up or down?
Would this formula still work if the spinner's sections were different sizes? Why or why not?
assess.correctAnswer: A correct performance: (a) P(blue) = 3/10 — three favourable out of ten counters altogether, blue included in the total; (b) P(4) = 1/6; (c) P(gold) = 2/8 = 1/4 simplified. The child forms favourable/TOTAL each time, puts the whole set in the denominator, and simplifies where possible.

errorPatterns.pattern: Writes favourable-to-unfavourable (part-part) instead of favourable-over-total — e.g. 3/7 for 3 blue among 10
errorPatterns.nextMove: Recount the whole set aloud including the favourable outcomes; the total is everything that could be drawn, so 10 not 7 goes on the bottom
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The denominator is the count of the OTHER outcomes rather than the whole set

errorPatterns.pattern: Applies favourable/total to a situation whose outcomes are not equally likely
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist on the equally-likely check first; if sections are unequal the colour counts are not counts of equally likely outcomes and the simple formula does not apply
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Uses the formula straight onto an uneven spinner or weighted device without checking the sections/outcomes are equal

errorPatterns.pattern: Fails to simplify, or simplifies incorrectly
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the simplifying step and confirm the simplified fraction sits at the same point on the scale; this is an execution lapse, not a conceptual gap

responseLevels.gap: Cannot form the fraction or combines numbers arbitrarily; no favourable-over-total structure
responseLevels.full: Computes favourable/total across all three contexts with the whole set in the denominator, checks the outcomes are equally likely, and gives each answer in simplest form
responseLevels.partial: Forms favourable/total for the easy die case but writes part-part for the bag, forgets or botches simplifying, or applies the formula without checking equal-likelihood

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child three problems on cards with paper: (a) a bag of 3 blue and 7 red marbles — find P(blue); (b) a fair six-sided die — find P(rolling a 4); (c) a spinner with 8 equal sections, 2 of them gold — find P(gold). Say: 'Work out each probability and write it as a fraction in its simplest form.' (Set the task and WATCH — watch whether they count the TOTAL correctly, whether they check the outcomes are equally likely, and whether they simplify.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching reveals whether the denominator is the whole set (3/10) or the leftovers (3/7), whether they check equal-likelihood before applying the formula, and whether they simplify — none of which a single final answer would expose.

pedagogy.summary: Children learn to recognise and DRAW shapes that satisfy a specified attribute (e.g. exactly five sides, a given number of angles) and to identify triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons and hexagons within a mixed set. The procedural work is building or selecting to a property — a pentagon is any closed figure with five straight sides — rather than reproducing a memorised prototype. The central obstacle is the prototype effect: children draw and accept only the regular, symmetrical, 'textbook' version and miss irregular or rotated members of the class. Best taught by generating many varied and irregular examples, defining each class by its attribute, and hunting for ALL members (including non-prototypical ones) in mixed sets.
bestPractices: Define each shape class by its attribute (a hexagon is ANY closed shape with 6 straight sides / 6 vertices) and check drawn shapes against it.
Demand and celebrate IRREGULAR and rotated examples — 'draw a different pentagon that doesn't look like that one' — to break the single-prototype image.
Give mixed 'find them all' sets that include irregular, tilted and near-miss shapes so identifying a class means applying the attribute, not matching a picture.
Model counting and marking each side/vertex once when drawing or checking, so the side-count is accurate.
Use dotted paper, geoboards or a peg grid to support accurate drawing of straight-sided closed figures.
keyRepresentations: Geoboard / pegboard and dotted paper for constructing polygons to a target side-count
Mixed shape sets containing regular, irregular, tilted and near-miss examples plus non-examples
Side/vertex tally marks made while counting
Side-by-side regular vs irregular pentagon/hexagon to show both satisfy the attribute
commonMisconceptions: Draws or accepts only the prototypical regular, symmetrical, horizontal-base example and misses irregular or rotated members of a class.
Miscounts sides or vertices when drawing or identifying (draws six sides when asked for five; loses track counting an irregular shape).
Draws a non-closed figure or one with curved sides, not attending to 'closed' and 'straight-sided'.
Judges class membership by the name/look ('that's not a quadrilateral, it's a diamond') rather than by counting the sides.

learn.summary: Children learn to draw and identify polygons by their defining attribute — a pentagon is ANY closed figure with five straight sides whose sides do not cross each other, not one memorised 'textbook' shape. The core obstacle is the prototype effect: learners draw and accept only the regular, symmetrical, horizontal-base version and miss irregular, tilted or rotated members of a class. Guidance centres on generating many varied and irregular examples, defining each class by its attribute (side/vertex count, closed, straight-sided, sides not crossing), and hunting for ALL members in mixed sets that include non-prototypical and near-miss shapes. Accurate side/vertex counting is scaffolded by marking each once.

activities.title: Build a polygon to a target side-count
feedback: If the shape has the wrong number of sides, recount together, marking each side exactly once from a clear start point; dotted paper or pegs keep sides straight.
If only a regular/symmetrical version is produced, prompt: 'Make one that is squished, tilted, or spiky but still has five straight sides' and affirm that it counts just as much.
If the figure has a gap or a curved/bulging edge, check it against the attributes aloud: is it closed? is every side straight?
Celebrate an irregular valid solution explicitly so the learner sees it is as correct as the neat one.
activities.rationale: Constructing to an attribute is an active production task that confronts the prototype effect directly; demanding varied and irregular examples is intended to break the single-image definition. Counting sides, checking closure (whether by the learner, an adult, or an optional live side-counter) and visibly accepting ANY valid (including irregular) shape are intended to make the defining attribute the thing being rewarded.
sourceClaims: A polygon is a 2-D shape made of three or more straight sides that meet at vertices; children are taught to identify and sort polygons by number of sides/vertices, using varied examples (all sides/vertices the same, some the same, all different). A common misconception is inaccurate counting of sides/vertices from losing track of the start point; remedy is to mark each side/vertex once as it is counted.

The instructional goal is to analyse shapes by defining properties (e.g. a triangle has three straight sides and is closed), invariant to size, orientation and colour, rather than by holistic appearance.
learnerActions: Given an instruction such as 'build a shape with exactly five straight sides', construct the figure on dotted paper, a geoboard, or a peg/rubber-band grid.
Count and mark each side (and vertex) once as it is drawn, so the total is checked rather than guessed.
Ensure the figure CLOSES and that every side is straight before declaring it finished.
When one valid shape is made, draw 'a different pentagon that does NOT look like the first one' — a long, spiky, or irregular one.
Compare a regular and an irregular example of the same class side by side and state why both satisfy the attribute.
activities.intendedInsight: A polygon class is defined by its attribute (number of straight sides meeting at vertices, closed figure with sides that do not cross), invariant to size, orientation and regularity — not by matching a single remembered prototype.

activities.title: Find them all in a mixed set
feedback: If an irregular or tilted member is skipped, draw attention to it and recount its sides together; attending to the awkward four-sided shape is intended to loosen the prototype grip as the learner sees the squished one also counts.
If a shape is included or excluded by its name/look alone (e.g. 'that's a diamond, not a quadrilateral'), redirect to counting the four straight sides.
If counting on an irregular shape loses track, model starting at one vertex and marking each side once around the figure.
activities.rationale: A 'find them all' set that deliberately contains non-prototypical and near-miss shapes is designed to require attribute-based classification and to surface the prototype misconception; it is hard to fake because the regular example alone is insufficient to complete the task.
sourceClaims: Young children over-rely on a prototypical exemplar: 93-96% identify a prototypical (equilateral, horizontal-base) triangle but far fewer accept atypical types (only ~30.5% identified all three of scalene/right/isosceles) or rotated versions; a non-formal attribute matching the prototype (e.g. horizontal base) is treated as defining ('imposed attribute'). Remedy: typical + atypical examples and non-examples.

The instructional goal is to analyse shapes by defining properties (e.g. a triangle has three straight sides and is closed), invariant to size, orientation and colour, rather than by holistic appearance.
learnerActions: From a mixed set that includes regular, irregular, tilted, rotated and near-miss shapes plus non-examples, mark EVERY member of a named class (e.g. 'circle all the quadrilaterals').
For each shape marked or skipped, justify by counting sides/vertices and checking closed + straight-sided, not by its name or look.
Deliberately inspect the awkward shapes — a long thin tilted four-sided shape, a dented pentagon — and decide membership by the attribute.
Explain why a square is a quadrilateral, and why a 'diamond' is also a quadrilateral regardless of its orientation.
activities.intendedInsight: Identifying a class means applying its attribute to every candidate, including irregular and rotated ones, rather than recognising a familiar picture.

activities.title: Name, draw and justify by attribute
feedback: If the count is wrong, recount marking each side/vertex once; dotted paper keeps the sides straight.
If both drawings look the same, ask for a genuinely different-looking version with the same number of sides.
Accept and praise any closed, straight-sided figure with the correct count regardless of regularity.
activities.rationale: Requiring a spoken/written justification by attribute, plus a deliberately varied second example, checks that the class is defined by count rather than appearance.
sourceClaims: The instructional goal is to analyse shapes by defining properties (e.g. a triangle has three straight sides and is closed), invariant to size, orientation and colour, rather than by holistic appearance.

A polygon is a 2-D shape made of three or more straight sides that meet at vertices; children are taught to identify and sort polygons by number of sides/vertices, using varied examples (all sides/vertices the same, some the same, all different). A common misconception is inaccurate counting of sides/vertices from losing track of the start point; remedy is to mark each side/vertex once as it is counted.
learnerActions: Draw a named polygon (e.g. a hexagon) and explain how you know it is one by counting its six straight sides and six vertices/angles.
Produce a second example of the same name that looks clearly different from the first.
State the defining attributes in your own words ('a hexagon is any closed shape with six straight sides that do not cross each other').
activities.intendedInsight: Justifying class membership by the attribute count — and producing a non-prototypical second example — demonstrates the definition is understood, not just a remembered shape.

constraints: Tasks must require active drawing/construction and selection, not tap-to-reveal recognition: a static labelled picture can show examples but does not itself let the learner build or choose, and active production and selection are where the prototype misconception can surface.
Mixed 'find them all' sets must include irregular, tilted, rotated and near-miss shapes plus non-examples; a set of only regular shapes cannot discriminate attribute-use from picture-matching.

Any 'draw a pentagon' response format should be paired with a side-count check (counting/marking by the learner or an adult), since free drawing alone does not reliably verify the exact number of straight sides.

A fixed single-answer format under-rewards the many-different-valid-answers goal; whatever format is used, multiple distinct correct shapes (including irregular ones) must be treated as equally valid.

A live side-counter, closure check, and visible acceptance of any valid shape (e.g. a highlight on a correct irregular pentagon, a pulse on a missed tilted quadrilateral) are helpful ways to make the mechanism concrete, but are optional illustrations, not required technology.

The topic is primarily 2-D polygon drawing and identification; the single 'cubes' reference does not require a 3-D spatial environment. If cube identification is added, ask about the mathematical solid REPRESENTED on a thin card (which itself has slight thickness and can be held), not whether the physical card can be picked up.
Scaffolds (dotted paper, geoboards, peg grids) support accurate straight sides and counting but should not become the only medium; plain drawing and physical shape sorting are also valid.

Is THIS a quadrilateral? [show a long, thin, tilted, irregular four-sided shape] How do you know?

assess.correctAnswer: (1) Draws any closed figure with exactly five straight sides — need not be a regular pentagon. (2) Circles every four-sided shape, including irregular and rotated ones, and no others. (3) Draws a six-sided closed figure and justifies by counting six sides (and six vertices/angles). The attribute is satisfied by the count, not by matching a prototype.

errorPatterns.pattern: Draws or accepts only the prototype — a regular, symmetrical, horizontal-base example — and misses irregular or rotated members of the class.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Define the class by its attribute (a quadrilateral is ANY closed shape with four straight sides), then present many varied and irregular examples with non-examples to sort, and ask for a 'different one that doesn't look like that'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In the quadrilateral hunt, skips irregular or tilted four-sided shapes; when asked to draw, produces only the textbook-regular version.

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscounts sides or vertices when drawing or identifying — draws six sides when asked for five, or loses track counting an irregular shape.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold: model numbering/marking each side as it is drawn or counted so each is counted exactly once; use dotted paper for accurate straight sides.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The drawn shape has the wrong number of sides; a recount gives a different total.

errorPatterns.pattern: Draws a non-closed figure or one with curved sides, not attending to 'closed' and 'straight-sided'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: State and check the defining attributes — closed, straight sides — against each drawn shape, using the 'is it / is it not a polygon' test.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The drawn polygon has a gap or a bulging/curved side.

responseLevels.gap: Draws or selects only the prototypical regular example, draws the wrong number of sides, or draws non-closed/curved figures — attends to the picture, not the attribute.
responseLevels.full: Draws any closed figure with the exact specified number of straight sides in varied/irregular forms, identifies ALL members of a class including irregular and rotated ones while excluding non-members, and justifies by the defining attribute (SOLO relational, with transfer).
responseLevels.partial: Draws a correct example and identifies prototypical members, but misses irregular or rotated instances (circles the square but not an irregular quadrilateral) or occasionally miscounts sides (SOLO multistructural).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set three short tasks and watch how the child works: (1) 'Draw me a shape with exactly five straight sides.' (2) Hand them a mixed set of shapes (including irregular and tilted ones): 'Circle all the quadrilaterals.' (3) 'Draw a hexagon, and show me how you know it is a hexagon.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the child draw and select reveals whether they build to the specified attribute or reach for a memorised prototype. The quadrilateral hunt deliberately includes irregular and tilted four-sided shapes: a child who circles only the square/rectangle is matching a picture, while one who circles the awkward ones is applying 'four straight sides'. This is hard to fake because the mixed set contains non-prototypical members.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Add three one-digit numbers, using strategies including looking for a pair that makes 10 (e.g. 5 + 7 + 3 → 7 + 3 = 10, then 5 + 10 = 15). Ages 6–7, procedural application of associativity/commutativity plus bonds to 10.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2 'add numbers using concrete objects, pictorial representations, and mentally, including... three one-digit numbers'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.OA.2 fluency and 1.OA.3 strategy use; 'add three whole numbers whose sum is less than or equal to 20' with make-ten grouping as the exemplar strategy.
• Operational details: the point is strategic grouping — scan the three addends for a bond to 10 (or a double), add that pair first, then add the third. Depends on quick recall of bonds to 10 and the freedom (commutative/associative) to reorder. Teach scanning explicitly rather than defaulting to left-to-right.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (age 6) — adds three one-digit numbers correctly by any method. Tier B (age 7) — for 5 + 7 + 3 chooses 7 + 3 first because it makes ten. Tier C (age 7+) — reliably scans any three addends for the most useful pair (ten or double) and explains the choice.
bestPractices: Teach an explicit 'scan for a pair that makes ten (or a double)' habit before adding.
Rehearse bonds to 10 to fluency so the make-ten pair is spotted instantly.
Use rearrangeable counters/tiles so children physically move the useful pair together.
Contrast a make-ten route with a left-to-right route on the same triple to show the efficiency gain.
Keep sums within 20 initially so the third addition crosses ten at most once.
keyRepresentations: Three movable number tiles that can be reordered
Ten-frame that fills to ten from the chosen pair, then takes the third
Empty number line with a jump to ten then on
Bar/part-whole with three parts
Bonds-to-10 pairs chart as a scanning aid
commonMisconceptions: Always adding left-to-right and never scanning for a make-ten pair.
Not recognising a pair that makes ten because bonds to 10 aren't fluent.
Losing or double-counting the third addend after making ten.
Thinking the numbers must be added in the written order.
Miscounting when crossing ten while adding the third number by ones.

learn.summary: Teaches ages 6–7 to add three one-digit numbers efficiently by scanning for a pair that makes ten (or a double), adding that pair first, then adding on the third number — e.g. 5 + 7 + 3 → 7 + 3 = 10, then 5 + 10 = 15. The objective is the strategic habit of scanning and reordering (supported by commutativity/associativity and fluent bonds to 10), not merely getting a correct total. Includes a hands-on manipulative core, fluency/strategy-choice practice, a narration conversation, and a worked anchor, with each scaffold's role made explicit. Interactive and efficacy details are proposed, not validated.

activities.title: Drag a pair to make ten on the ten-frame
feedback: When a chosen pair makes exactly ten, the two tiles fuse into a '10' and the frame fills (e.g. with a glow/click) — immediate confirmation that these two tiles make exactly ten, the pair the make-ten strategy looks for.

When the triple contains a make-ten pair but the chosen pair does not make ten (it goes past ten, e.g. 5 + 7 = 12, or falls short), the frame does not land cleanly on ten, showing why that pairing is less tidy here. The total can still be found, just by a longer route. For triples built around a double (e.g. 6 + 6 + 3, which has no make-ten pair), the double is the useful pair even though it does not fill the frame to exactly ten, so do not mark it as less tidy.
A live-updating running total tile lets the child check the sum as each tile is added.
If the third addend is lost or double-counted, prompt: set the third tile aside and bring it in last, then recount.
activities.rationale: The target is a strategic move — scan, pair, regroup — so physically reordering tiles and seeing a pair snap to ten is intended to train the scanning habit and to make the regrouping concrete through handling. Live recolouring/overflow feedback is intended to show whether a chosen pair makes ten. These interactive details are illustrative of the mechanism, proposed and not validated or required implementations.
sourceClaims: Y2 pupils add three one-digit numbers using concrete, pictorial and mental methods.
Applying properties of operations as strategies (1.OA.3) includes grouping addends to make ten; 2.OA.2 targets fluency of such sums within 20.
Looking for pairs that make ten is a key mental-calculation strategy taught in early KS1.
learnerActions: Start with three movable number tiles above a ten-frame, e.g. 5, 7 and 3.
Scan the three tiles and decide which two you would add first: a pair that makes exactly ten, or, if there is no such pair, a double.
Drag two tiles together; if they make ten the frame fills completely and leaves a simpler 'ten and a bit' (here 5 + 10).
Deliberately try a less useful pairing first (e.g. 5 + 7 = 12) and notice the frame does not land on a clean ten, then find the better pair — it still gives a correct total, just by a slower route.
Repeat with triples that reward a make-ten pair, and with at least one triple that rewards a double instead.
Add the remaining third tile on last and read the running total.
activities.intendedInsight: Spotting the pair that makes ten (or a double) first turns an awkward three-number sum into an easier one: a make-ten pair leaves 'ten and a bit', and a double gives a known fact to add on to. The written order is not fixed, you are free to reorder, and any ordering still gives the same total.

activities.title: Which pair makes it easiest? — fluency and strategy choice
feedback: Confirm the efficient pair (e.g. 7 + 3) and point out that it is not the first two numbers written.
If the child selects the first two numbers by default, ask 'can you see two that make ten?' and rehearse the relevant bond.
Keep any timing light and supportive so it builds automaticity rather than anxiety.
activities.rationale: Practice with strategy-choice and quick retrieval is intended to build the automaticity that makes scanning easier. Recognition/selection items check whether the child chooses the efficient pair; they complement, but do not by themselves elicit, the hands-on reordering where the child freely moves the tiles and feels the ten form.
sourceClaims: Applying properties of operations as strategies (1.OA.3) includes grouping addends to make ten; 2.OA.2 targets fluency of such sums within 20.
Looking for pairs that make ten is a key mental-calculation strategy taught in early KS1.
learnerActions: Given a triple such as 5 + 7 + 3, choose which two numbers you would add first and say why.
Complete fill-in-the-blank totals for a set of triples, each containing a make-ten pair that is not the first two written.
Do a short, light timed set of spotting make-ten pairs to build quick recall of bonds to 10.
For each item, state the pair chosen and the leftover number before giving the total.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent recall of bonds to 10 lets you spot the useful pair quickly; deliberately choosing a make-ten pair can make the addition quicker and less error-prone than always adding left-to-right.

activities.title: Narrate the pair you chose
feedback: If the child narrates adding the first two written numbers every time, highlight the ten pair and rehearse the scan-first habit — the skill, not the concept, is what's missing.
If the child insists numbers must be added in written order, demonstrate that reordering keeps the total the same (any two may be added first).
When a pair makes ten but the third number is lost or doubled, bring the third number in last and recount.
activities.rationale: Narration can reveal the underlying strategy and prompt reflection on order and choice, though a conversation alone does not have the child physically handle and reorder the addends. Best used alongside doing and watching the procedure rather than as a substitute for hands-on practice.
learnerActions: A tutor poses triples such as 5 + 7 + 3, 8 + 2 + 6 and 4 + 9 + 1.
For each, work out the total and say which two numbers you added first and why that choice helps.
Answer follow-ups: 'Is there a pair here that makes exactly ten?', 'Would you get the same total in a different order?', 'For 4 + 9 + 1, which pair makes ten and which number is left to add on?'
activities.intendedInsight: Explaining the chosen pair makes the scanning strategy explicit and surfaces whether the child is truly scanning or just adding in written order.

activities.title: Worked anchor: see the make-ten pair highlighted
feedback: Point to the highlighted pair and the resulting 'ten and a bit' to anchor the method.
Note that this is an example to study: it shows the method but does not give feedback on the child's own attempts, so follow it with hands-on practice.
activities.rationale: A fixed worked example cannot be manipulated and gives no feedback on the learner's own pairings, but it can provide a useful reference model of the two-step strategy. Treat it as a scaffold that precedes, not replaces, active practice.
learnerActions: Study a worked triple, e.g. 5 + 7 + 3, with the 7 + 3 pair highlighted as it makes ten.
Follow the two steps: pair to ten (7 + 3 = 10), then add the third (5 + 10 = 15).
Describe in your own words how the pair was chosen before moving to practice items.
activities.intendedInsight: A clear model of the scan-pair-add sequence gives a reference point for the strategy before independent practice.

constraints: Keep sums within 20 initially so adding the third number crosses ten at most once.
Depends on quick recall of bonds to 10; rehearse these to fluency so the make-ten pair is spotted readily.
Offer triples where the make-ten pair is NOT the first two numbers written, so the task genuinely requires scanning and reordering.
Include some triples that reward a double rather than a ten, so the habit generalises to 'useful pair', not only 'exactly ten'.

Recognition/selection items (choosing which pair is easiest) check strategy choice but do not by themselves elicit the child freely reordering and feeling the ten form; pair them with hands-on or spoken production.
The worked example is a reference anchor only: it provides no feedback on the child's attempts.
Watch for losing or double-counting the third addend after making ten; bring it in last and recount rather than reteaching the whole strategy.
A correct total alone is not evidence of the strategy — ask which two were added first to distinguish scanning from left-to-right adding.
A less useful pairing (e.g. 5 + 7 first) still reaches the correct total; frame it as slower/less tidy, not as wrong.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and the interactive/efficacy details are untested.
Self-audit of arithmetic: 5+7+3=15, 8+2+6=16, 4+9+1=14 (matches the source answer key); make-ten pairs are 7+3, 8+2, 9+1 respectively — all consistent.
The claim that the make-ten route is 'faster and less error-prone' than left-to-right is taken from the row's discriminate note, not from independent empirical validation; it is kept qualified.

The source claim that '3D adds nothing' to adding three small numbers was removed as an unsupported categorical universal; the kept point is only that this task is planar/non-spatial, so a 3D model offers no particular affordance here.
One source (CCSS-M 1.OA.3/2.OA.2) and the NCETM guidance are marked verified:false in the row; treat their claims as unconfirmed.
The source describes timed/speeded retrieval; kept but framed as light and supportive to avoid implying speed pressure is required.
Pedagogy listed further representations (empty number line, bar/part-whole, bonds-to-10 chart) not developed into activities here; they remain legitimate scaffolds if elaborated.

probeDeeper: Which two did you add first, and why did you choose those?
Is there a pair here that makes exactly ten?
Would you get the same total if you added them in a different order?
For 4 + 9 + 1, which pair makes ten — and which number is left to add on?
assess.correctAnswer: 15, 16, 14. Watch for the child spotting and adding the make-ten pair first (7+3, then 8+2, then 9+1) and adding the remaining number on — rather than ploughing left-to-right.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds strictly left-to-right, never scanning for a make-ten pair (5 + 7 = 12, then + 3).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Prompt 'can you see two that make ten?'; highlight bonds to 10 and rehearse the scan-first habit — the skill, not the concept, is missing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Narrates adding the first two written numbers every time; ignores the ten pair.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'You have to add them in the order they're written' — refuses to reorder to pair the ten.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Remind that any two may be added first (associative/commutative); demonstrate reordering keeps the total.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Resists adding 7 + 3 first because 5 comes first on the page.

errorPatterns.pattern: Makes ten with a pair but then loses or double-counts the third addend.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Physically set the third tile aside and bring it in last; check the count. Don't reteach the strategy.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reaches ten then forgets to add the leftover number, or adds it twice.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot reliably total three one-digit numbers, or loses an addend when combining.
responseLevels.full: Scans the three addends, pairs the one that makes ten (or a double) first, adds the third on, and totals accurately and efficiently — explaining the choice.
responseLevels.partial: Totals correctly but always left-to-right, not spotting or using the make-ten pair.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these out, and each time tell me which two numbers you added first: 5 + 7 + 3; 8 + 2 + 6; 4 + 9 + 1.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Each triple contains an obvious make-ten pair that is NOT the first two numbers written. A child using the target strategy reorders to pair the ten; a child adding left-to-right can still get the totals but reveals no scanning, and is slower and more error-prone. Asking 'which two first?' exposes the strategy directly, so it discriminates even when totals are correct.
